## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the stochastic-integral interfaces
below. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ and finite integers $d,m\ge1$. Work on
a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$ (the usual conditions).

Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] adapted to this filtration, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let
$X_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, satisfy
$E|X_0|^2<\infty$, and be independent of the future Brownian increments.
Explicitly, $X_0$ is independent of the sigma-algebra
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.

Continuity of a process means continuity on one measurable event of
probability one. We use an everywhere-continuous adapted representative: if
the chosen process is continuous only on such an event $A$, replace it off $A$
by its initial value. Since $A^c$ is a null set and the filtration is complete,
$A^c\in\mathcal F_0$; the replacement preserves adaptedness and changes the
SDE identity only on a null event, hence preserves it up to
indistinguishability.

The drift and diffusion coefficients are jointly Borel maps
$$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad \sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}.$$
For nonnegative finite constants $L,K$, assume for every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ that
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|).$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and
$\|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^m|A^{ik}|^2$ is the Frobenius norm.

For an adapted continuous candidate $X:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$,
the vector Itô equation
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(s,X_s)\,ds+\left(\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}(s,X_s)\,dW_s^k\right)_{i=1}^d,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
uses a pathwise Lebesgue integral for the drift and, in each coordinate, the
localized Itô integral from
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], clause 2. Require
$\int_0^T|b(s,X_s)|ds<\infty$ and
$\int_0^T\|\sigma(s,X_s)\|_F^2ds<\infty$ almost surely; these are the local
coefficient-integrability conditions in that definition. When a coordinate
integrand has finite expected energy, its integral is the square-integrable
Itô integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]];
the Picard estimates below establish that stronger condition for every input
in $\mathcal H_T$. Equality of processes means
equality for every $t$ on one measurable event of probability one, that is,
indistinguishability
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. A **strong
solution on $[0,T]$** is an adapted continuous process satisfying this
integral equation indistinguishably. No moment bound is included in the
definition; the existence theorem proves its $L^2$ path-sup bound.
The usual-filtration, continuity, and finite-coordinate conventions agree
with the multidimensional class of continuous Brownian Itô processes
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. This definition makes no ellipticity,
transition-density, forward-equation, or time-reversal assertion.

Brownian motion here means the finite-horizon version of the cited definition:
$W_0=0$ almost surely, with continuous paths and the stated increments on
$[0,T]$. All cited stochastic-calculus interfaces are used on this interval.
Their constructions require no extension of $W$ beyond $T$: elementary
integrals use only increments between partition points in $[0,T]$, and their
$L^2$ limits and continuous versions are constructed on that same interval.
For a predictable scalar integrand $H$ with finite pathwise energy, localize
at $\rho_n=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:\int_0^t H_s^2ds\ge n\}\wedge T$.
Here $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$.
The stopped integrands have expected energy at most $n$; their continuous
integrals agree up to the smaller stop by the finite-energy stopping identity.
On the full event of finite energy, $\rho_n=T$ for all sufficiently large
$n$, so these integrals paste uniquely on the whole closed interval $[0,T]$,
exactly as in the localized construction of
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. At $T=0$ every integral is zero.

## Sources

Van Handel's Chapter 5.1 specifies the integral-equation interpretation and
finite-horizon filtered setup. Van der Vaart's Section 7.1 treats strong
solutions on a given filtered space and indistinguishability. The local
definition fixes the vector/matrix coordinate convention and the exact
coefficient and initial-value assumptions used by the following proofs.

## Statement

Assume the data and hypotheses of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, finite
dimensions $d,m\ge1$, Lipschitz constant $L$, and linear-growth constant
$K$. There is a strong solution $X$ on the given filtered probability space.
It is unique up to indistinguishability among strong solutions with the same
initial value and Brownian driver, and it satisfies
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^2\le(1+3E|X_0|^2)e^{C_TT},\qquad C_T:=6K^2T+24mK^2.$$
The bound is independent of any later numerical mesh.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the complete usual filtered Brownian space, $T\ge0$, finite
$d,m\ge1$, jointly Borel coefficients with the stated uniform global
Lipschitz and linear-growth constants, an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable
$X_0\in L^2$ independent of future Brownian increments, and the Axiom of
Choice as required by the Itô-integral interfaces.

[F1] The Picard map $\Phi$ is well-defined on adapted continuous inputs with
finite $L^2$ path supremum; it has the path-sup difference estimate with
$C_d=2TL^2+8mL^2$, the growth estimate with
$C_T=6K^2T+24mK^2$, and the first-iterate bound
$(4K^2T^2+16mK^2T)(1+E|X_0|^2)$. [[lem-lipschitz-sde-map-is-well-defined]]

[F2] A strong solution is an adapted continuous process on the given space
with the locally defined finite-coordinate Itô integral equation satisfied
indistinguishably. The complete filtration contains all null sets at time zero.
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]]

[F3] The declared Itô-integral and martingale interfaces use the Axiom of
Choice; the Picard recursion, integer bounds, and stopping conventions below
make no further selections. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F4] Cauchy–Schwarz bounds expectations by second moments; monotone
convergence passes to expectations of nonnegative partial sums, and Fatou
passes the finite-tail $L^2$ bounds to their pointwise limit.
[[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] [[thm-fatou-lemma]]

[F5] For a continuous path, its supremum on $[0,T]$ equals the supremum over
rational times in $[0,T]$ and the endpoint $T$. [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]

[F6] Every adapted continuous solution of the same SDE with the stated
initial-value and coefficient hypotheses has finite $E\sup_{t\le T}|Y_t|^2$.
[[lem-lipschitz-sde-local-solution-has-finite-path-moment]]

[F7] Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges. Hence, on each path
where the Picard iterates are uniformly Cauchy, their finitely many coordinate
sequences have real limits; these limits form the pointwise $\mathbb R^d$
limit, and the uniform Cauchy bound passes to that limit.
[[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]]

## Proof

1.1 If $T=0$, set $X_0$ as the sole value of the process; both integrals vanish, the path-sup bound follows from $(1+3E|X_0|^2)\ge E|X_0|^2$, and any two solutions with that initial value agree. For $T>0$, let $\Phi$ be the map of [F1], set $X^0_t=X_0$, and recursively set $X^{n+1}=\Phi(X^n)$. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 Put $a_n(t)=E\sup_{u\le t}|X^n_u-X^{n-1}_u|^2$ for $n\ge1$. By [F1], $a_1(T)\le A_T:= (4K^2T^2+16mK^2T)(1+E|X_0|^2)$ and $a_{n+1}(t)\le C_d\int_0^t a_n(s)ds$. Induction on $n$ gives $a_n(t)\le A_TC_d^{n-1}t^{n-1}/(n-1)!$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The majorant series $\sum_{n\ge1}\sqrt{A_TC_d^{n-1}T^{n-1}/(n-1)!}$ converges. If $A_T=0$, it is identically zero; if $C_dT=0$, every term after the first is zero; otherwise the ratio of consecutive terms is $\sqrt{C_dT/n}\to0$. By [F4], $E\sup|X^n-X^{n-1}|\le\sqrt{a_n(T)}$ and monotone convergence gives $E\sum_n\sup|X^n-X^{n-1}|=\sum_nE\sup|X^n-X^{n-1}|<\infty$; hence that nonnegative series is finite almost surely. On this event, for every $t$ the vector sequence $(X^n_t)_n$ is Cauchy, since $\sup_{u\le T}|X^m_u-X^n_u|\le\sum_{j=n+1}^m\sup_{u\le T}|X^j_u-X^{j-1}_u|$; [F7] gives the coordinate limits and therefore a vector limit $X_t$. Letting $m\to\infty$ in the same inequality bounds $\sup_{t\le T}|X^n_t-X_t|$ by the tail of the summable series, which tends to zero. Thus the convergence is almost surely uniform. For finite tails the $L^2$ triangle inequality follows by expanding the square and applying Cauchy–Schwarz, so $\|X^m-X^n\|_{L^2(\sup)}\le\sum_{j=n+1}^m\sqrt{a_j(T)}$. Fatou's lemma [F4] then gives $E\sup_{t\le T}|X^n_t-X_t|^2\le(\sum_{j=n+1}^{\infty}\sqrt{a_j(T)})^2\to0$. [F4, F7, step 2.1, algebra, construct]

4.1 Let $A$ be the measurable probability-one event on which that series of path suprema is finite; measurability follows because each supremum is a supremum over the countable dense set in [F5]. Uniform convergence makes $X$ continuous on $A$; completeness gives $A^c\in\mathcal F_0$, so set $X_t=X_0$ on $A^c$. For each fixed $t$, the limit on $A$ of the $\mathcal F_t$-measurable $X^n_t$, together with the $\mathcal F_0$-measurable value on $A^c$, is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable. Thus $X$ is adapted and continuous, and its $L^2$ path-sup convergence places it in the class of [F2]. [F2, F5, step 3.1, given]

5.1 For every $n$, $X^{n+1}=\Phi(X^n)$. The difference estimate of [F1] gives $E\sup_{u\le T}|\Phi(X^n)_u-\Phi(X)_u|^2\le C_dT E\sup_{u\le T}|X^n_u-X_u|^2\to0$. Since $X^{n+1}\to X$ in the same norm by step 3.1, uniqueness of an $L^2$ limit implies $\Phi(X)=X$ indistinguishably. Hence $X$ satisfies the SDE. [F1, F2, step 3.1, step 4.1]

6.1 Write $f(t)=E\sup_{u\le t}|X_u|^2$. The growth estimate of [F1] and $X=\Phi(X)$ imply $f(t)\le3E|X_0|^2+C_T\int_0^t(1+f(s))ds$. Put $g=1+f$ and $H(t)=1+3E|X_0|^2+C_T\int_0^tg(s)ds$. Then $g\le H$, $H(0)=1+3E|X_0|^2$, and $H'(t)=C_Tg(t)\le C_TH(t)$ almost everywhere. Consequently $(e^{-C_Tt}H(t))'\le0$ almost everywhere, so $f(T)\le g(T)\le(1+3E|X_0|^2)e^{C_TT}$. [F1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 If $Y$ is any other strong solution with the same data, then $Y=\Phi(Y)$ by [F2] and $Y\in\mathcal H_T$ by [F6]. The difference estimate in [F1] gives $q(t):=E\sup_{u\le t}|X_u-Y_u|^2\le C_d\int_0^tq(s)ds$. With $Q(t)=C_d\int_0^tq(s)ds$, one has $Q(0)=0$ and $Q'\le C_dQ$ almost everywhere, hence $Q=q=0$. Thus $\sup_{t\le T}|X_t-Y_t|=0$ almost surely, which is indistinguishability. AC is exactly the inherited assumption [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, F6, step 5.1] ∎

## Remarks

The proof uses no ellipticity or nondegeneracy of $\sigma$. The result gives
strong existence, uniqueness, and moment control only; it implies no
transition-density regularity, forward Kolmogorov uniqueness, or reversal
theorem.

## Sources

Van Handel, Chapter 5.1, Theorems 5.1.3 and 5.1.5 with proofs, and van der
Vaart, Section 7.1, Theorem 7.8 with proof, independently develop Picard
iteration and Gronwall uniqueness. The proof here supplies the vector
coordinate estimates, complete path-space limit argument, and exact
finite-horizon supremum bound under the displayed hypotheses.

## Definition

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Independent random elements $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$.

[L1] Independence of random elements is equivalent to factorization on measurable rectangles. ([[thm-rectangle-criterion-for-independent-random-elements]])

[L2] The law of a random element is a probability measure. ([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]])

[L3] For sigma-finite factors, the product measure is the unique measure on the product sigma-algebra having the rectangle formula. ([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]])

[L4] The finite product sigma-algebra is generated recursively by measurable rectangles. ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]])

[L5] Measures agreeing on a generating pi-system with an increasing finite-measure exhaustion from that pi-system are equal ([[thm-measure-uniqueness-on-a-sigma-finite-pi-system]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 First prove that all-coordinate rectangles generate the recursively defined finite product sigma-algebra. This is immediate for one factor. Suppose it holds for $k$ factors, write $T_k=\prod_{i<k}S_i$ and $\mathcal A_k=\bigotimes_{i<k}\Sigma_i$, and let $\mathcal H$ be the sigma-algebra generated by the $(k+1)$-coordinate rectangles. These rectangles belong to $\mathcal A_k\otimes\Sigma_k$, so $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal A_k\otimes\Sigma_k$. Fix $B\in\Sigma_k$. The class $\mathcal C_B=\{A\in\mathcal A_k:A\times B\in\mathcal H\}$ contains $T_k$, since $T_k\times B$ is an all-coordinate rectangle. It is closed under complements relative to $T_k$, because $(T_k\setminus A)\times B=(T_k\times B)\setminus(A\times B)$, and under countable unions because product with $B$ commutes with them. Hence it is a sigma-algebra containing all $k$-coordinate rectangles. The induction hypothesis gives $\mathcal C_B=\mathcal A_k$. As this holds for every $B$, every binary rectangle $A\times B$ generating $\mathcal A_k\otimes\Sigma_k$ lies in $\mathcal H$, proving equality and completing the finite induction. [given, L4]

2.1 Let $\mathcal D:=\{E\subseteq\prod_{i<n}S_i:X^{-1}(E)\in\mathcal F\}$. Preimages preserve complements and countable unions, so $\mathcal D$ is a sigma-algebra. If $R=\prod_{i<n}B_i$ is a measurable rectangle, then $X^{-1}(R)=\bigcap_{i<n}X_i^{-1}(B_i)\in\mathcal F$. By step 1.1, the product sigma-algebra is generated by these all-coordinate rectangles, so $X$ is measurable for $\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i$. [given, L4, step 1.1]

3.1 For every measurable rectangle $R=\prod_{i<n}B_i$, [L1] gives $$\mathbb P_X(R)=\mathbb P(X_0\in B_0,\dots,X_{n-1}\in B_{n-1})=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb P(X_i\in B_i)=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}(B_i).$$ [L1, L2, step 2.1]

3.2 By step 2.1, the law $\mathbb P_X$ is defined, and [L2] makes it a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra. [step 2.1, L2]

4.1 For every $n\ge1$, put $\nu_1:=\mathbb P_{X_0}$ and, for $1\le m<n$, define recursively $\nu_{m+1}:=\nu_m\otimes\mathbb P_{X_m}$. For $n=1$, step 3.1 already identifies $\mathbb P_X$ with $\nu_1$. For $n\ge2$, repeated use of the rectangle formula in [L3] shows that $\nu_n\left(\prod_{i<n}B_i\right)=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}(B_i)$ for every measurable rectangle. Therefore $\mathbb P_X$ and $\nu_n$ agree on all measurable rectangles. [step 3.1, step 3.2, L3, algebra]

5.1 All-coordinate rectangles are closed under intersections, because intersections are taken coordinatewise; they contain the whole product and generate its sigma-algebra by step 1.1. By step 4.1, $\mathbb P_X$ and $\nu_n$ agree on this pi-system. Both have total mass one: [L2] gives this for the joint law, and the rectangle formula [L3] gives it at every stage of the product-law recursion. The constant exhaustion by the whole product therefore satisfies the finite-measure hypothesis of [L5], which gives $$\mathbb P_X=\nu_n=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$ This is the claimed product joint law. [L2, L3, L5, step 1.1, step 3.2, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Positive integers $m,n$ and the identification $\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n$.

[L1] The Borel sigma-algebra on a topological space is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]])

[L2] Continuous maps pull Borel sets back to Borel sets. ([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]])

[A1] The coordinate projections $\pi_1 : \mathbb R^{m+n} \to \mathbb R^m$ and $\pi_2 : \mathbb R^{m+n} \to \mathbb R^n$ are continuous.

[L3] Rational open boxes form a countable basis of the Euclidean product topology: every point of an open set lies in a rational box contained in that set ([[thm-rational-points-and-boxes-in-rn]], [[thm-rational-box-generators-of-the-borel-sigma-algebra-on-rn]]). These results use rational density and only finitely many coordinate choices, not an axiom of countable or arbitrary choice.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $A \subseteq \mathbb R^m$ and $B \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ are Borel, then $$A \times B = \pi_1^{-1}(A) \cap \pi_2^{-1}(B),$$ so [L2] makes $A \times B$ Borel in $\mathbb R^{m+n}$. Therefore every measurable rectangle for $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)$ belongs to $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n})$, and hence $$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) \subseteq \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$ [A1, L2]

2.1 Let $O$ be open in $\mathbb R^{m+n}$ and let $\mathcal R_O$ be the family of all rational open boxes contained in $O$. By [L3], every $x\in O$ lies in a member of $\mathcal R_O$, so $O=\bigcup\mathcal R_O$; the reverse containment follows from its definition, including when $O$ is empty. This is a subfamily of one fixed countable basis, hence is at most countable; no choice of a box for each point is made. Each box $\prod_{j=1}^{m+n}(a_j,b_j)$ splits into the open rectangle $U\times V$, with $U=\prod_{j=1}^m(a_j,b_j)$ and $V=\prod_{j=m+1}^{m+n}(a_j,b_j)$. Both factors are Borel, so each box belongs to the product sigma-algebra. Closure under countable unions puts $O$ there as well. Since [L1] says the open sets generate the Euclidean Borel sigma-algebra, this proves the reverse inclusion. Combining with step 1.1 proves the equality, without any choice assumption. [L1, L3, step 1.1] ∎

## Definition

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

## Statement

Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[thm-exponential-definition-equivalence]]: The following descriptions give the same function $\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$: the power series $\sum x^n/n!$; the product limit $\lim_n(1+x/n)^n$; the normalized solution of $y'=y,\ y(0)=1$; the normalized continuous multiplicative function; and the compact-uniform limit of the Picard iterates.

[F2] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$, $$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$ In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

[F3] [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]]: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in the sense of def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn.

[F4] [[thm-of-square-roots]]: Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (def-complete-ordered-field). Then every $a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$; we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

[F5] [[thm-substitution]]: Let $c < d$ be reals and let $\varphi : [c,d] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every point of $[c,d]$ as a function on $[c,d]$ (def-derivative), with $\varphi'$ integrable on $[c,d]$ (def-darboux-integral). Let $J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements (def-interval) with $\varphi[\,[c,d]\,] \subseteq J$, and let $f : J \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $J$ (def-continuity-real).

Then $(f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi'$ is integrable on $[c,d]$ and

$$\int_{\varphi(c)}^{\varphi(d)} f \;=\; \int_c^d (f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi' ,$$

the left-hand integral being the oriented one of def-oriented-integral.

**Neither injectivity nor monotonicity of $\varphi$ is assumed**, and that is exactly why the left-hand side is written with oriented limits: $\varphi(d)$ may lie below $\varphi(c)$, and $\varphi$ may return to the same value many times. The proof runs through a primitive of $f$ and the chain rule, and no inverse function is ever formed.

**Continuity of $f$ is a hypothesis and cannot be weakened to integrability.** With $f$ merely integrable the composite $f \circ \varphi$ need not be integrable at all, so the right-hand side need not exist; that is the false statement that weakens it on the companion page.

[F6] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ (def-continuity-real). Then $f$ is bounded (def-bounded-set) and Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$ (def-darboux-integral).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that $(b-a)/N$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for $\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one $\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

[F7] [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]]: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral: $$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere, and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

[F8] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]: Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x$. Then $$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

[F9] [[thm-gaussian-integral]]: $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

[F10] [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]: The nonnegative integral is monotone, and for every positive real scalar $c$, $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. The zero-scalar case is separate: the integral of the zero function is $0$.

[F11] Under Countable Choice, every Borel subset of $\mathbb R$ is Lebesgue measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). Thus a Borel real-valued function is Lebesgue measurable, since its inverse images of Borel sets are Lebesgue measurable.

## Proof

**Given:** The objects, hypotheses and definitions in the statement. Its conclusions are to be established below.

1.1 F1 gives positivity of the exponential, and F2 gives continuity. Thus $\phi$ is positive and continuous. AC restricts to a choice function on every countable nonempty family, giving CC; F3 therefore applies to $\phi$. F4 makes its positive denominator well defined. [F1, F2, F3, F4]

2.1 For integer $n\ge1$, F5 with $\varphi(x)=x/\sqrt2$ and continuous f(t)=exp(-t^2) gives $\int_{-n}^n e^{-x^2/2}\,dx=\sqrt2\int_{-n/\sqrt2}^{n/\sqrt2}e^{-t^2}\,dt$. The derivative is the constant 1/sqrt2, hence integrable. Both integrands are continuous on the compact intervals, so F6 gives bounded Riemann integrability. F7 identifies the left side with its Lebesgue integral, under the CC in step 1.1. [F5, F6, F7, step 1.1]

3.1 Put $g_n(x)=e^{-x^2/2}\mathbf1_{[-n,n]}(x)$. Each $g_n$ is Borel measurable: for $a<0$, $\{x:g_n(x)>a\}=\mathbb R$, while for $a\ge0$ it is $[-n,n]\cap\{x:e^{-x^2/2}>a\}$, a Borel set because the exponential expression is continuous by step 1.1. By F11 and the CC established in step 1.1, each Borel $g_n$ is also Lebesgue measurable. Thus the nonnegative Lebesgue measurable functions $g_n$ increase pointwise to $e^{-x^2/2}$. By F8, its Lebesgue integral is the limit of the compact integrals in step 2.1. F9 identifies the right-hand improper limit as $\sqrt2\sqrt\pi=\sqrt{2\pi}$; the equality follows because both sides are positive with square $2\pi$, by square-root uniqueness. Applying F10 with the positive scalar $1/\sqrt{2\pi}$ gives $\int\phi\,d\lambda_1=1$. [F8, F9, F10, F11, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, open sets $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $T : U \to V$, and a nonnegative Lebesgue measurable function $f : V \to [0,\infty]$.

[L1] The formula already holds for continuous compactly supported integrands. ([[lem-c-one-change-of-variables-for-continuous-compactly-supported-integrands]])

[L2] Monotone convergence passes increasing limits through the integral. ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]])

[L3] Every nonnegative measurable function admits increasing simple approximations. ([[thm-nonnegative-measurable-functions-admit-increasing-simple-approximations]])

[L4] Assuming countable choice, Lebesgue measurable sets are Borel up to null sets, and $T$ preserves both null sets and Lebesgue measurability. ([[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]], [[lem-c-one-diffeomorphisms-map-lebesgue-null-sets-to-null-sets]], [[lem-c-one-diffeomorphisms-map-lebesgue-measurable-sets-to-lebesgue-measurable-sets]])

[L5] Two measures on $V$ agreeing on a generating pi-system with a common increasing finite-mass exhaustion from that system agree on all Borel sets ([[thm-measure-uniqueness-on-a-sigma-finite-pi-system]]).

[L6] The nonnegative integral is additive ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 On Borel subsets $E$ of $V$ define $$\nu(E):=\int_U\mathbf1_E(T(x))|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x).$$ This is a measure: the nonnegative Jacobian weight is measurable, inverse images under $T$ take disjoint countable unions to disjoint countable unions, [L6] gives finite additivity, and [L2] passes the increasing finite sums through the integral. [L2, L6, given]

2.1 Let $W=V\cap R$ for a bounded open rectangle $R$ with rational endpoints. Write $d(y,W^c)$ for Euclidean distance to the complement and $\|y\|_\infty$ for the maximum coordinate modulus. The functions $$\varphi_j(y)=\min\{1,\max(0,jd(y,W^c)-1)\}\min\{1,\max(0,j+1-\|y\|_\infty)\}$$ are continuous, nonnegative and increase pointwise to $\mathbf1_W$. Each support is contained in the compact set $\{d(y,W^c)\ge1/j,\ \|y\|_\infty\le j+1\}\subset W$, so $\varphi_j|_V$ has compact support in $V$. Applying [L1] to each $\varphi_j$ and [L2] to the two monotone limits gives $\nu(W)=\lambda_n(W)$. The empty $W$ is immediate. [L1, L2, step 1.1]

3.1 The family $\mathcal P=\{\varnothing\}\cup\{V\cap R:R\text{ is a bounded open rectangle with rational endpoints}\}$ is nonempty and closed under binary intersections: an intersection is empty or again of the displayed rectangle form. It generates the Borel sigma-algebra of $V$, since rational open rectangles form a Euclidean base. Both measures give $\varnothing$ mass zero, and step 2.1 proves agreement on every other member. The increasing members $P_j=V\cap(-j,j)^n$ cover $V$ and satisfy $\lambda_n(P_j)<\infty$; step 2.1 gives $\nu(P_j)=\lambda_n(P_j)$. Hence [L5] makes $\nu(E)=\lambda_n(E)$ for every Borel $E\subseteq V$. This proves the set formula without assuming that an infinite-measure equality class is closed under decreasing intersections. [L5, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j \mathbf 1_{E_j}$ be a nonnegative simple Lebesgue measurable function. By [L4], replace each $E_j$ by a Borel set differing from it only by a null set. The set formula from step 3.1 and null-set invariance in [L4] then give the change-of-variables formula for $s$. [L2, L4, step 3.1]

5.1 Choose simple functions $s_k \uparrow f$ by [L3]. Step 4.1 applies to each $s_k$, and [L2] lets $k \to \infty$ on both sides. This yields the formula for $f$. [L2, L3, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $d\ge1$, $T>0$, a finite $R\ge0$, and a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in $\overline B(0,R)$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, let $X_0$ be measurable at time zero with law $\mu$ and independent of future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ for every $s<t$, and let $X$ be the unique strong solution of $X_t=X_0+\int_0^t g(r)\,dW_r$. For $a>0$ define $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ set

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),$$

and set $\mu_0=\mu$. Let $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ denote the real infinitely differentiable functions with compact support. For every $t>0$, $p_t$ is positive and infinitely differentiable in $x$. On each interval $[\epsilon,T]$ with $0<\epsilon<T$, it is continuously differentiable in time and satisfies

$$\partial_t p_t(x)=\frac{g(t)^2}{2}\Delta_xp_t(x),\qquad \Delta_x=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}^2.$$

A family $(\nu_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ of Borel probability measures is narrowly continuous when $t\mapsto\int f\,d\nu_t$ is continuous for every bounded continuous real function $f$. It is a weak forward solution with initial law $\mu$ when it is narrowly continuous, $\nu_0=\mu$, and, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and every real-valued function $\psi:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first time derivative and continuous spatial derivatives through order two, whose spatial support lies in one compact set for all $s$, it satisfies

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(t,x)\,\nu_t(dx)-\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(0,x)\,\mu(dx)=\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^d}\left(\partial_s\psi(s,x)+\frac{g(s)^2}{2}\Delta_x\psi(s,x)\right)\nu_s(dx)\,ds.$$

Then $(\mu_t)_{0\le t\le T}$, where $\mu_t(dx)=p_t(x)\,dx$ for $t>0$ and $\mu_0=\mu$, is the unique narrowly continuous weak forward solution with initial law $\mu$. No density for $\mu$ at $t=0$ is asserted.

## Statement references

[Hunter, *Notes on Partial Differential Equations*, Chapter 5, §§5.1.1–5.1.2](https://math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/pde_notes.pdf)

[Särkkä and Solin, *Applied Stochastic Differential Equations*, Chapter 5, §§5.1–5.2](https://users.aalto.fi/~asolin/sde-book/sde-book.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the compactly supported initial probability measure, the scalar noise coefficient, and the density and transition formulas from the preceding definition.

[A1] The full Axiom of Choice is assumed by the inherited Brownian and Itô interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For $t>0$, $p_t$ is the positive normalized density of the strong solution's law, and the initial law is $\mu$. [[def-gaussian-smoothed-data-law-and-transition-density]]

[F2] The SDE data include a complete usual filtered probability space, adapted Brownian motion with increments independent of the past, and an initial value independent of future increments. [[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]]

[F3] Under these Lipschitz and linear-growth hypotheses there is a unique strong solution with continuous paths. [[thm-global-strong-well-posedness-for-lipschitz-ito-sdes]]

[F4] Dominated convergence passes almost-everywhere limits through an integral under one integrable majorant. [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[F5] Fubini interchanges absolutely integrable iterated Lebesgue integrals on sigma-finite product spaces. [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

[F6] Narrow continuity and weak convergence of Borel probability measures are tested by bounded continuous real functions. [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]

[F7] Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with the same characteristic function are equal under AC. [[thm-uniqueness-of-a-law-from-its-characteristic-function]]

[F8] Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ are determined by the laws of all one-dimensional linear projections under AC. [[thm-cramer-wold-device]]

[F9] The law of a random element is the probability of its measurable inverse images. [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]

[F10] A centered normal law with covariance $aI_d$ has characteristic function $\theta\mapsto\exp(-a|\theta|^2/2)$. [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multivariate-normal-law]]

## Proof

**Given:** The statement's hypotheses and definitions.

1.1 For $a>0$, direct differentiation gives $\partial_a\phi_a(z)=\tfrac12\Delta_z\phi_a(z)$. Every finite spatial derivative of $\phi_a(z)$ is a polynomial in $z$ and $a^{-1}$ times $\phi_a(z)$. Fix $\epsilon>0$ and compact sets $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $J\subset[\epsilon,T]$. Since $a=v(t)$ is bounded above and away from zero on $J$, and $z$ lies in the compact support of $\mu$, each such derivative is uniformly bounded for $x\in K$, $t\in J$, and $z\in\operatorname{supp}\mu$. Difference quotients are bounded by the same type of constant on a slightly larger compact set, by the one-variable fundamental theorem of calculus. Dominated convergence [F4] therefore permits differentiation under the finite measure $\mu$ to every spatial order and once in time. The chain rule and $v'(t)=g(t)^2$ give $\partial_t p_t(x)=\int \frac{g(t)^2}{2}\Delta_x\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz)=\frac{g(t)^2}{2}\Delta_xp_t(x).$ Positivity follows from the positive kernel and the nonzero probability measure. [F1, F4, given]

1.2 The SDE setup in [F2] and well-posedness theorem [F3] give a common continuous-path event. For bounded continuous $f$, $X_t\to X_s$ almost surely as $t\to s$ on that event, and [F4] applied to the bounded variables $f(X_t)$ gives $\mathbb E f(X_t)\to\mathbb E f(X_s)$. By [F9], these expectations are $\int f\,d\mu_t$; also $\mu_0=\mu$. [F2, F3, F4, F6, F9, given]

1.3 Fix $t\in(0,T]$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$. For $0\le s<t$ set $h(s,x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(x+z)\phi_{v(t)-v(s)}(z)\,dz,\qquad h(t,x)=f(x).$ For $a=v(t)-v(s)>0$, write $P_af(x)=\int f(x+z)\phi_a(z)\,dz$. Differentiating the explicit Gaussian and integrating by parts twice, with boundary terms zero because $f$ is compactly supported, gives $\partial_aP_af=\tfrac12P_a\Delta f$. Thus $\partial_sh+\tfrac12g(s)^2\Delta_xh=0$ for $s<t$. Spatial derivatives may be moved onto $f$, so $h$, $\nabla h$, and $\Delta h$ are bounded by the corresponding sup norms of $f$, $\nabla f$, and $\Delta f$. For any such derivative $q$ and $\eta>0$, $\sup_x|P_aq(x)-q(x)|\le\|\nabla q\|_\infty\eta+2\|q\|_\infty\int_{|z|>\eta}\phi_a(z)\,dz.$ The tail equals $\int_{|u|>\eta/\sqrt a}\phi_1(u)\,du$ and tends to zero as $a\downarrow0$ because $\phi_1$ is integrable. Letting first $a\downarrow0$ and then $\eta\downarrow0$ proves uniform convergence of $P_aq$ to $q$, including $q=\Delta f$; hence the backward equation and bounds extend continuously to $s=t$. [F1, F4, given]

2.1 At $t=0$ the weak identity has equal endpoint terms and a zero right-hand integral. For $t>0$, fix an admissible test $\psi$ and $0<\delta<t$. On the common compact spatial support, $p_s$ and $\partial_s p_s$ are continuous and bounded for $s\in[\delta,t]$ by step 1.1. Differentiation under the space integral is therefore justified by [F4]. Using step 1.1 and integrating by parts twice in each coordinate, with no boundary terms because $\psi$ has compact spatial support, gives $\frac{d}{ds}\int\psi(s,x)p_s(x)\,dx=\int\left(\partial_s\psi(s,x)+\frac{g(s)^2}{2}\Delta_x\psi(s,x)\right)p_s(x)\,dx.$ Integrating from $\delta$ to $t$ gives the weak identity with lower endpoint $\int\psi(\delta,x)\,\mu_\delta(dx)$. Its difference from $\int\psi(0,x)\,\mu(dx)$ tends to zero: the term $\sup_x|\psi(\delta,x)-\psi(0,x)|$ tends to zero by the bounded continuous time derivative on the common compact support, and $\int\psi(0,\cdot)\,d\mu_\delta\to\int\psi(0,\cdot)\,d\mu$ by step 1.2. The omitted right-hand integral over $[0,\delta]$ tends to zero because each $\mu_s$ has mass one and the derivatives of $\psi$ and $g$ are bounded on the common compact support. Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ proves the weak identity, so $\mu_t$ is a weak forward solution. [F1, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, given]

3.1 Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi_L$ equal to one on $|x|\le L$ and zero on $|x|\ge2L$, with $|\nabla\chi_L|\le C/L$ and $|\Delta\chi_L|\le C/L^2$. For completeness, take $\chi_L(x)=\eta(|x|^2/L^2)$, where $\rho(u)=0$ for $u\le0$, $\rho(u)=e^{-1/u}$ for $u>0$, and $\eta(u)=\rho(4-u)/(\rho(4-u)+\rho(u-1))$. The function $\psi_L(s,x)=\chi_L(x)h(s,x)$ is an admissible compactly supported test in the weak equation. By step 1.3, $\partial_s\psi_L+\frac{g(s)^2}{2}\Delta\psi_L=\frac{g(s)^2}{2}\left(2\nabla\chi_L\cdot\nabla h+h\Delta\chi_L\right),$ whose absolute value is at most $C_t(L^{-1}\|\nabla f\|_\infty+L^{-2}\|f\|_\infty)$. Since each $\nu_s$ is a probability, the time-integrated error tends to zero as $L\to\infty$. For all sufficiently large $L$, $\chi_L=1$ on the support of $f$ and on the support of $\mu$. Letting $L\to\infty$ in the weak identity therefore gives $\int f\,d\nu_t=\int h(0,x)\,\mu(dx).$ The same cutoff argument applied to the weak solution $\mu_t$ from step 2.1 gives $\int f\,d\mu_t=\int h(0,x)\,\mu(dx)$. Thus $\nu_t$ and $\mu_t$ agree on every compactly supported smooth real function. [step 2.1, step 1.3, given]

4.1 For any fixed $t>0$, any $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, and integer $n\ge1$, apply step 3.1 to $\chi_n(x)\cos(\theta\cdot x)$ and $\chi_n(x)\sin(\theta\cdot x)$ and combine the resulting identities into one complex identity. Let $n\to\infty$. The left side converges to the characteristic function of $\nu_t$ by dominated convergence [F4]. For each fixed $x$, the backward averages on the right converge by [F4] and [F10] to $e^{i\theta\cdot x}e^{-v(t)|\theta|^2/2}$; they are bounded by one, so another application of [F4] gives the limit $e^{-v(t)|\theta|^2/2}\int e^{i\theta\cdot x}\,\mu(dx)$. By [F1], $\mu_t$ is the convolution of $\mu$ with the centered Gaussian of covariance $v(t)I_d$; Fubini [F5] and [F10] show that its characteristic function is exactly this product. Hence the vector characteristic functions of $\nu_t$ and $\mu_t$ agree for every $\theta$. For each $u\in\mathbb R^d$, take $\theta=ru$ for arbitrary $r\in\mathbb R$; scalar uniqueness [F7] gives equality of the laws of $u\cdot x$ under the two measures, and [F8] then gives $\nu_t=\mu_t$. This holds for every $t>0$; at $t=0$ both laws equal $\mu$ by the initial condition, proving uniqueness. AC is used only through the inherited Brownian/Itô interfaces and the cited Fourier-uniqueness results. [A1, F1, F4, F5, F7, F8, F10, step 3.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An arbitrary measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$; measurable complex-valued functions $f,f_n$ with $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for one nonnegative measurable function $g$ of finite integral.

[L1] Reverse Fatou's lemma holds under an integrable majorant ([[cor-reverse-fatou-lemma-under-an-integrable-majorant]]).

[L2] The integral is linear on $L^1(\mu)$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

[L3] The integral triangle inequality holds on $L^1(\mu)$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]).

[L4] Real and complex integrability are defined in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]].

[L5] The nonnegative integral is additive, and a nonnegative integral over a null set vanishes ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]).

[L6] A nonnegative measurable function with finite integral is finite almost everywhere ([[cor-finite-nonnegative-integral-implies-finite-almost-everywhere]]).

[L7] The nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $N_0$ be a measurable null set outside which $f_n(x)\to f(x)$ and $|f_n(x)|\le g(x)$ for every $n$, and let $N_\infty:=\{g=\infty\}$. By [L6], the set $N_\infty$ is null. Put $N:=N_0\cup N_\infty$, $E:=X\setminus N$, $$\widetilde g:=g\chi_E,\qquad h_n:=|f_n-f|\chi_E.$$ Then $h_n\to0$ pointwise, $0\le h_n\le2\widetilde g$, and $\widetilde g$ is nonnegative, measurable, and finite everywhere. Also $$|f|\le|f|\chi_N+\widetilde g.$$ By [L5] and [L7], $$\int|f|\,d\mu\le\int|f|\chi_N\,d\mu+\int\widetilde g\,d\mu =0+\int\widetilde g\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu<+\infty,$$ so $f\in L^1(\mu)$ by [L4]. The same null-set and domination argument gives $\int|f_n|\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu<\infty$ for each $n$, so every $f_n$ also belongs to $L^1(\mu)$. [L4, L5, L6, L7, given]

2.1 The functions $h_n$ are nonnegative, converge pointwise to $0$, and are dominated by the finite everywhere majorant $2\widetilde g$. Applying [L1] therefore gives $$\limsup_n\int h_n\,d\mu\le\int0\,d\mu=0.$$ Hence $\int h_n\,d\mu\to0$. [step 1.1, L1]

3.1 Because $|f_n-f|\chi_N$ is supported on the null set $N$, [L5] gives $$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu=\int h_n\,d\mu+\int|f_n-f|\chi_N\,d\mu=\int h_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow0.$$ Therefore, by [L2] and [L3], $$\left|\int f_n\,d\mu-\int f\,d\mu\right| =\left|\int(f_n-f)\,d\mu\right| \le\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu,$$ and the right-hand side tends to $0$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L2, L3, L5] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Sigma-finite measure spaces $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$, and a function $f \in L^1(\mu \times \nu)$.

[L1] Tonelli's theorem holds for nonnegative measurable functions on $X \times Y$. ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])

[L2] A complex-valued function belongs to $L^1$ exactly when its absolute value has finite integral. ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]])

[L3] The Lebesgue integral is linear on $L^1$. ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]])

[L4] The triangle inequality gives $$\left|\int g\,d\eta\right| \le \int |g|\,d\eta$$ for every integrable function $g$. ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L2], the function $|f|$ is nonnegative measurable, and [L1] gives $$\int_X \left(\int_Y |f_x|\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_{X \times Y} |f|\,d(\mu \times \nu) < \infty.$$ Therefore $\int_Y |f_x|\,d\nu < \infty$ for $\mu$-almost every $x$, so $f_x \in L^1(\nu)$ for $\mu$-almost every $x$. The same argument with the variables reversed gives $f^y \in L^1(\mu)$ for $\nu$-almost every $y$ and shows that the section integrals of $|f|$ are integrable. [L1, L2]

2.1 For almost every $x$ from step 1.1, [L4] gives $$\left|\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right| \le \int_Y |f_x|\,d\nu.$$ Define the section integral to be $0$ on the exceptional null set where $f_x\notin L^1(\nu)$. The right-hand side is integrable over $X$ by step 1.1, so this extended section-integral function is integrable. The same convention and conclusion hold for $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$. [step 1.1, L4]

3.1 Write $f=u-v+i(p-q)$, where $u,v,p,q \ge 0$ are the positive and negative parts of the real and imaginary parts of $f$. Each of $u,v,p,q$ is integrable because $|u|,|v|,|p|,|q| \le |f|$. Applying [L1] to these four nonnegative functions and recombining with [L3] yields the stated equality of the three integrals. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L1, L3] ∎

## Definition

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

## Statement

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses and conventions in the statement.

[F1] For a Borel probability law $\mu$, the characteristic function is $\varphi_\mu(t)=\int e^{itx}\,d\mu(x)$ ([[def-characteristic-function-of-a-real-random-variable]]). The finite-measure Fourier convention is $\widehat\mu(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi ix\xi}\,d\mu(x)$ ([[thm-fourier-transform-of-a-finite-complex-measure]]). These bounded integrands are integrable; the latter theorem's countable-choice premise is covered by the stated AC.

[F2] Under AC finite complex Borel measures with equal transforms are equal. [[cor-uniqueness-of-finite-borel-measures-from-their-fourier-transforms]].

[F3] AC supplies the choices in the Fourier uniqueness proof. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F4] Reflection conjugates a characteristic function. [[lem-basic-properties-of-characteristic-functions]].

[F5] The reflected law has characteristic function phi(-t). [[lem-characteristic-functions-under-affine-maps-and-independent-sums]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $\mu,\nu$ be the two laws. Each positive probability law, regarded as a complex measure, has total variation one: every measurable partition has sum of absolute masses equal to its total mass. Thus [F1] applies in dimension one under the stated AC. For every real $\xi$ and $x$, $e^{i(-2\pi\xi)x}=e^{-2\pi ix\xi}$, so the defining bounded integrands are identical. Integrating this pointwise identity against either law gives $\widehat\mu(\xi)=\varphi_\mu(-2\pi\xi)$ and $\widehat\nu(\xi)=\varphi_\nu(-2\pi\xi)$. Since the characteristic functions agree at every real argument, $\widehat\mu(\xi)=\widehat\nu(\xi)$ for every $\xi$. This also verifies the finite-variation hypotheses of Fourier uniqueness. [F1, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Apply F2 in dimension one to obtain $\mu=\nu$. AC is inherited from that proof: it supplies the Hahn/Jordan and Radon–Nikodym selections used in Gaussian smoothing and covers its regularity argument. No inversion result from this page is used. [step 1.1, F2, F3]

3.1 For the final equivalence, F5 with $a=-1,b=0$ and F4 give $\varphi_{-X}(t)=\varphi_X(-t)=\overline{\varphi_X(t)}$. If $\varphi_X$ is real-valued, the two characteristic functions agree and step 2.1 proves symmetry of the law. Conversely, symmetry means the two laws, hence their defining integrals, agree; the displayed identity then forces $\varphi_X(t)=\overline{\varphi_X(t)}$, so every value is real. [step 2.1, F4, F5] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer and $p_\theta(x)=\theta\cdot x$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ are determined by all the laws $(p_\theta)_*\mu$. Moreover, if $(p_\theta)_*\mu_n\Rightarrow(p_\theta)_*\mu$ for every $\theta$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$, then $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If dimension zero is admitted, interpret $\mathbb R^0$ as the singleton empty tuple; both conclusions then hold as well.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses and conventions in the statement.

[F1] Characteristic functions are expectations of the complex exponential. [[def-characteristic-function-of-a-real-random-variable]].

[F2] AC gives uniqueness of finite-variation Borel measures in every positive finite dimension. [[cor-uniqueness-of-finite-borel-measures-from-their-fourier-transforms]].

[F3] The Fourier convention in dimension d is exp(-2 pi i x dot xi). [[thm-fourier-transform-of-a-finite-complex-measure]].

[F4] A continuous map carries weak convergence to weak convergence. [[thm-continuous-mapping-theorem]].

[F5] Under AC a weakly convergent sequence on a Polish space is tight. [[cor-weakly-convergent-sequences-are-tight]].

[F6] Under AC tight sequences on Polish spaces have weakly convergent subsequences. [[thm-prokhorov-tightness-theorem-on-polish-spaces]].

[F7] Weak convergence is tested by bounded continuous real functions. [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]].

[F8] AC covers Prokhorov and the finite-dimensional Fourier uniqueness proof. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F9] A finite union has measure at most the sum of its measures. [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]].

[F10] Euclidean spaces in positive finite dimension are complete. [[thm-euclidean-space-complete]].

[F11] Separable completely metrizable spaces are Polish. [[def-polish-space]].

[F12] The rationals are countable. [[thm-rationals-countable]].

[F13] Rationals approximate every real coordinate. [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]].

[F14] Finite products of countable sets remain countable by iteration. [[thm-product-of-countable]].

[F15] Closed boxes are compact; compact real sets are bounded. [[thm-heine-borel-rn]].

[F16] One-dimensional weak convergence yields pointwise convergence of characteristic functions. [[thm-levy-continuity-theorem-forward-direction]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Write $\Phi_\rho(\theta)=\int e^{i\theta\cdot x}\,\rho(dx)$. The map $p_\theta$ is continuous: $|p_\theta(x)-p_\theta(y)|\le(\sum_{j=1}^d|\theta_j|)\|x-y\|_2$. Hence its pushforward is a Borel probability, and $\Phi_\rho(\theta)=\varphi_{(p_\theta)_*\rho}(1)$. In particular $\widehat\rho(\xi)=\Phi_\rho(-2\pi\xi)$. Positive probability measures have total variation one, since the absolute masses of any measurable partition sum to one. Thus if all projection laws of $\rho$ and $\tau$ agree, their finite-dimensional Fourier transforms agree at every $\xi$; the finite-measure uniqueness theorem gives $\rho=\tau$. The zero projection has the law of the constant zero and introduces no exception. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Euclidean space is complete. The set $\mathbb Q^d$ is countable by induction using the product theorem, and dense: approximate each of the finitely many coordinates of $x$ within $\eta/(2d)$ by a rational to get a vector within Euclidean distance $\eta$. Thus $\mathbb R^d$, and in particular $\mathbb R$, is Polish. For each coordinate vector $e_j$, the assumed convergence and the tightness corollary give a compact real set with uniform complement mass below $\varepsilon/(2d)$ for all projected laws. Enlarge each such bounded compact set to $[-R_j,R_j]$. For the compact box $K=\prod_{j=1}^d[-R_j,R_j]$, finite subadditivity yields $$\mu_n(K^c)\le\sum_{j=1}^d\mu_n\{|x_j|>R_j\}<\varepsilon/2<\varepsilon.$$ This proves tightness of the original laws, not just of their projections. [F5, F9, F10, F11, F12, F13, F14, F15]

2.1 Prokhorov gives a weakly convergent further subsequence from every subsequence; write one such limit as $\nu$. For fixed $\theta$, continuous mapping gives convergence of its projected laws to $(p_\theta)_*\nu$, whereas the hypothesis gives convergence to $(p_\theta)_*\mu$. Apply the one-dimensional forward theorem to these two convergences at frequency one: the same numerical sequence has limits $\Phi_\nu(\theta)$ and $\Phi_\mu(\theta)$, so they are equal. This is true for every $\theta$. The Fourier identity and uniqueness argument of step 1.1 give $\nu=\mu$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F4, F6, F16]

3.1 If convergence failed for a bounded continuous real test $f$, some positive error threshold would be exceeded at infinitely many indices. List those indices increasingly using the least next one. Step 2.1 supplies a further weakly convergent subsequence with limit $\mu$, contradicting that fixed error bound. Hence all such tests converge, which is $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. AC is inherited from tightness/Prokhorov and finite-dimensional Fourier uniqueness, including its countable-choice transform and smoothing prerequisites; only finitely many coordinate choices are made locally. For $d=1$ the argument is unchanged. For $d=0$ the space is one point with zero metric and its only probability is unit mass there, so equality and convergence are immediate without a maximum over an empty coordinate set. Point masses in positive dimension are also covered. [step 2.1, F7, F8] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in $\overline B(0,R)$ for some finite $R\ge0$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable and satisfy $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$; set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, let $X_0$ be measurable at time zero with law $\mu$ and independent of future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard adapted $d$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increment $W_t-W_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X$ be the unique strong solution of $X_t=X_0+\int_0^t g(r)\,dW_r$, and write $\mu_t=\operatorname{Law}(X_t)$. For Borel probability laws $\alpha,\beta$ with finite second moments, write $W_2(\alpha,\beta)$ for the square root of the infimum of $\int|x-y|^2\,d\pi(x,y)$ over Borel probability couplings $\pi$ of $\alpha$ and $\beta$. For every $0<\epsilon\le T$,

$$\mathbb E|X_\epsilon-X_0|^2=d\,v(\epsilon),\qquad W_2(\mu_\epsilon,\mu)\le\sqrt{d\,v(\epsilon)}.$$

As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, $X_\epsilon\to X_0$ in probability and $\mu_\epsilon$ converges weakly to $\mu$, meaning that $\int f\,d\mu_\epsilon\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function $f$ on $\mathbb R^d$. This estimate controls endpoint truncation only: it gives no bound for learned-score error or numerical-discretization error, and asserts no density or score regularity at $\epsilon=0$.

## Statement references

[Lawler, *Stochastic Calculus: An Introduction with Applications*, Sections 3.2.2–3.2.3](https://www.math.uchicago.edu/~lawler/finbook.pdf)

[Hunter, *Notes on Partial Differential Equations*, Chapter 5, §§5.1.1–5.1.2](https://math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/pde_notes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The probability space, Brownian motion, initial random vector, coefficient, and strong solution in the statement.

[A1] The full Axiom of Choice is assumed by the inherited Brownian and Itô interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The deterministic Itô increment $\int_s^t g(r)\,dW_r$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N_d(0,(v(t)-v(s))I_d)$. [[lem-deterministic-ito-integral-has-gaussian-independent-increments]]

[F2] The strong-solution equation identifies $X_t-X_0$ with the corresponding Itô integral. [[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]]

[F3] Under the stated globally Lipschitz and linear-growth SDE hypotheses there is a unique strong solution with continuous paths. [[thm-global-strong-well-posedness-for-lipschitz-ito-sdes]]

[F4] The positive-time law $\mu_t$ has the stated Gaussian-mixture density, and $\mu_0=\mu$. [[def-gaussian-smoothed-data-law-and-transition-density]]

[F5] The law of a random element is its probability pushforward. [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]

[F6] Weak convergence of Borel probability laws is tested by bounded continuous real functions. [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]

[F7] For laws with finite second moments, $W_2$ is the infimum of quadratic costs over their Borel couplings. [[def-wasserstein-two-space-and-couplings]]

[F8] The Borel sigma-algebra on a finite-dimensional Euclidean product is the product of its Borel sigma-algebras. [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]]

## Proof

**Given:** The statement's hypotheses and notation.

1.1 The coefficients $b(t,x)=0$ and $\sigma(t,x)=g(t)I_d$ are jointly Borel, globally Lipschitz in $x$ with constant zero, and satisfy $|b|+\|\sigma\|_F=\sqrt d\,g(t)\le\sqrt d\,g_{\max}$. The initial support gives $\mathbb E|X_0|^2\le R^2$, and the complete usual filtered space, adapted Brownian increments, and independence of $X_0$ are exactly [F2]. Thus [F3] supplies the unique continuous strong solution. By [F2], $X_\epsilon-X_0=\int_0^\epsilon g(r)\,dW_r$. The characteristic-function identity in [F1] identifies this vector with $N_d(0,v(\epsilon)I_d)$, whose coordinate variances sum to $d\,v(\epsilon)$. Thus $\mathbb E|X_\epsilon-X_0|^2=d\,v(\epsilon)$. Also $v(\epsilon)\le g_{\max}^2\epsilon\to0$. For every $a>0$, $|X_\epsilon-X_0|^2\ge a^2\mathbf1_{\{|X_\epsilon-X_0|>a\}}$; taking expectations gives $P(|X_\epsilon-X_0|>a)\le d\,v(\epsilon)/a^2\to0$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The support condition gives $\mathbb E|X_0|^2\le R^2$, and step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E|X_\epsilon|^2\le2R^2+2d\,v(T)<\infty$. Hence both laws lie in the quadratic Wasserstein space. The measurable pair $(X_\epsilon,X_0)$ has a Borel law on $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d$ by [F8]; by [F5] its marginals are $\mu_\epsilon$ and $\mu$, and [F4] identifies $\mu_\epsilon$ as the smoothed law from the definition. Thus it is a coupling. Its cost is $\mathbb E|X_\epsilon-X_0|^2=d\,v(\epsilon)$. Taking the infimum in [F7] proves $W_2(\mu_\epsilon,\mu)\le\sqrt{d\,v(\epsilon)}$. [F4, F5, F7, F8, step 1.1, given]

3.1 Fix bounded continuous $f$ and let $K=\overline B(0,R+1)$. Its restriction to compact $K$ is uniformly continuous; define $\omega_K(\delta)=\sup\{|f(x)-f(y)|:x,y\in K,\ |x-y|\le\delta\}$, which tends to zero as $\delta\downarrow0$. For $0<\delta<1$, on the event $|X_\epsilon-X_0|\le\delta$, both vectors belong to $K$, so their $f$-values differ by at most $\omega_K(\delta)$. On the complementary event the difference is at most $2\|f\|_\infty$. Step 1.1 and Markov's inequality therefore give $\left|\int f\,d\mu_\epsilon-\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\omega_K(\delta)+2\|f\|_\infty\frac{d\,v(\epsilon)}{\delta^2}.$ For fixed $\delta$ the second term tends to zero as $\epsilon\downarrow0$; then letting $\delta\downarrow0$ proves convergence for every such $f$. This is weak convergence by [F6]. The estimates establish only the endpoint statements in the theorem. [F5, F6, step 1.1, given] ∎

## Definition

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathbb R^d$ have its Euclidean norm and Borel sigma-algebra. Define $\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ to be the Borel probability measures $\mu$ with $\int |x|^2\,d\mu(x)<\infty$. A coupling of $\mu,\nu\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ is a Borel probability measure $\pi$ on $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d$ whose first and second coordinate marginals are $\mu$ and $\nu$; write $\Gamma(\mu,\nu)$ for the set of couplings. Define
$$W_2(\mu,\nu)=\left(\inf_{\pi\in\Gamma(\mu,\nu)}\int_{\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d}|x-y|^2\,d\pi(x,y)\right)^{1/2}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $d\ge1$ and $\mu,\nu\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$.

[F1] The product of two probability measures exists, is a probability, and has the two given marginals. [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]

[F2] For a nonnegative function on a product probability space, Tonelli identifies its integral with either iterated integral; $|x-y|^2\le2|x|^2+2|y|^2$. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]

## Proof
1.1 The product law $\mu\otimes\nu$ is a Borel probability on $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d$ with marginals $\mu,\nu$ by [F1], so it belongs to $\Gamma(\mu,\nu)$. Thus the coupling set in the definition is nonempty. [given, F1]

2.1 By the inequality in [F2] and the finite second moments of $\mu,\nu$, Tonelli gives $\int|x-y|^2d(\mu\otimes\nu)\le2\int|x|^2d\mu+2\int|y|^2d\nu<\infty.$ All coupling costs are nonnegative, so their infimum is finite and nonnegative; its square root in the displayed definition is therefore a finite real number. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

For $a>0$, define the product Gaussian density $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. The operator norm below is induced by the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^d$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the hypotheses of the compactly supported Gaussian smoothing setup: $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure supported in $\overline B(0,R)$ for finite $R\ge0$, $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ is continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$, and $p_t(x)=\int\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz)$ for $t>0$. Fix $0<\epsilon<T$. For $t\in[\epsilon,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R^d$, define the probability measure

$$\nu_{t,x}(dz)=\frac{\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)}{p_t(x)}\,\mu(dz),\qquad m_{t,x}=\int z\,\nu_{t,x}(dz),$$

and the matrix

$$C_{t,x}=\int (z-m_{t,x})(z-m_{t,x})^{\mathsf T}\,\nu_{t,x}(dz).$$

The density $p_t$ is positive and smooth, and its score $s_t(x):=\nabla_x\log p_t(x)$ satisfies

$$s_t(x)=-\frac{x-m_{t,x}}{v(t)},\qquad D_xs_t(x)=-\frac{I_d}{v(t)}+\frac{C_{t,x}}{v(t)^2}.$$

For all $t\in[\epsilon,T]$ and $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,

$$\|D_xs_t(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\frac1{v(\epsilon)}+\frac{R^2}{v(\epsilon)^2},\qquad |s_t(x)|\le\frac{|x|+R}{v(\epsilon)},$$

so $s_t$ is globally Lipschitz in $x$, uniformly over this truncated time interval, with Lipschitz constant at most $1/v(\epsilon)+R^2/v(\epsilon)^2$. No such bound is asserted uniformly as $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compactly supported probability law, positive scalar time-dependent noise variance, explicit Gaussian convolution, and truncated interval in the statement.

[A1] The full Axiom of Choice is assumed by the inherited Itô and probability interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For every $t>0$, $p_t$ is a positive normalized density and is the Gaussian convolution of $\mu$ with covariance $v(t)I_d$. [[def-gaussian-smoothed-data-law-and-transition-density]]

[F2] On every interval bounded away from zero, $p_t$ is smooth in space and continuously differentiable in time; the spatial derivatives are obtained by differentiating the Gaussian kernel under the compactly supported measure. [[thm-gaussian-smoothing-density-and-forward-equation]]

[F3] Dominated convergence permits differentiation under an integral when the difference quotients converge pointwise and share an integrable majorant. [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[F4] The support of $\mu$ lies in $\overline B(0,R)$, so every measure absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$ is also supported there; all coordinate products in the displayed covariance integral are bounded and integrable. [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]

## Proof

**Given:** The statement's hypotheses and notation.

1.1 For fixed $t>0$, positivity in [F1] makes the quotient defining $\nu_{t,x}$ meaningful. Its density relative to $\mu$ is measurable and nonnegative, and its integral equals $p_t(x)/p_t(x)=1$, so it is a probability measure. By [F4], it is supported in $\overline B(0,R)$ and has finite first and second moments. The regularity conclusion [F2] applies on $[\epsilon,T]$. On each compact set of $x$ values, every spatial derivative of $\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)$ is bounded uniformly for $z\in\overline B(0,R)$ because $v(t)>0$ is fixed and the Gaussian derivatives are polynomials times a Gaussian. The finite measure $\mu$ supplies an integrable constant majorant. Difference quotients have the same kind of bound on a slightly larger compact set by the fundamental theorem of calculus, so [F3] justifies differentiating the convolution and its bounded-moment numerators under the integral. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given]

2.1 For each coordinate $i$, differentiation of $p_t$ gives $\partial_i p_t(x)=\int -\frac{x_i-z_i}{v(t)}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz)=-\frac{x_i-m_{t,x,i}}{v(t)}p_t(x).$ Dividing by the positive $p_t(x)$ proves $\nabla\log p_t(x)=-(x-m_{t,x})/v(t)$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Differentiate $m_{t,x,j}=p_t(x)^{-1}\int z_j\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz)$ in coordinate $i$. Differentiating the score identity from step 2.1 therefore gives $D_xs_t=-I_d/v(t)+C_{t,x}/v(t)^2$. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

5.1 For any $x,y$, the fundamental theorem of calculus along the segment $y+r(x-y)$ gives $s_t(x)-s_t(y)=\int_0^1D_xs_t(y+r(x-y))(x-y)\,dr$. Taking norms and using step 4.1 proves the global Lipschitz bound uniformly for $t\in[\epsilon,T]$. Since $g\ge g_{\min}>0$, $v(\epsilon)\downarrow0$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$; the bound therefore supplies no uniform-in-$\epsilon$ constant. [step 4.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Example

For $z\in\mathbb R^d$, $\delta_z$ denotes the probability concentrated at $z$. Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $a,b\in\mathbb R^d$, $\alpha\in[0,1]$, and $\mu=\alpha\delta_a+(1-\alpha)\delta_b$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$, and define $\phi_c(z)=(2\pi c)^{-d/2}\exp(-|z|^2/(2c))$ for $c>0$. For every $t>0$, the smoothed law has density

$$p_t(x)=\alpha\phi_{v(t)}(x-a)+(1-\alpha)\phi_{v(t)}(x-b).$$

At time zero its law remains $\mu$. If $a=b$, or if $\alpha$ is $0$ or $1$, the displayed density reduces to the single Gaussian centered at the atom carrying all mass.

## Proof

**Given:** The example's parameters and the Gaussian smoothing density in [F1].

1.1 Substitute $\mu=\alpha\delta_a+(1-\alpha)\delta_b$ in the defining integral. By the defining property of point masses, integration of any nonnegative Borel function $h$ gives $\int h(z)\,\mu(dz)=\alpha h(a)+(1-\alpha)h(b)$. Taking $h(z)=\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)$ yields the displayed formula, using $\phi_c(z)=\phi_c(-z)$. The initial law is $\mu$ by [F1]. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 If $a=b$, the two weights sum to one and both Gaussian terms have the same center. If $\alpha=1$, only the first term remains; if $\alpha=0$, only the second remains. In each case the stated single Gaussian is normalized and positive by [F1]. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $\lambda_1$ be one-dimensional Lebesgue measure and define $\mu(A)=\lambda_1(\{u\in[0,1]:(u,0)\in A\})$ for every Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^2$. The box measure formula gives $\lambda_1([0,1])=1$, so $\mu$ is a Borel probability supported on $L=[0,1]\times\{0\}$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$ and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. For every $t>0$, the Gaussian convolution of $\mu$ has the density

$$p_t(x_1,x_2)=\frac1{2\pi v(t)}\int_0^1\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x_1-u)^2+x_2^2}{2v(t)}\right)du.$$

The initial law $\mu$ is singular with respect to two-dimensional Lebesgue measure, meaning it assigns mass one to a Borel set of planar Lebesgue measure zero, while $p_t$ is strictly positive and infinitely differentiable in $(x_1,x_2)$ for each $t>0$.

## Example references

[Hunter, *Notes on Partial Differential Equations*, Chapter 5, §§5.1.1–5.1.2](https://math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/pde_notes.pdf)

[Särkkä and Solin, *Applied Stochastic Differential Equations*, Chapter 5, §§5.1–5.2](https://users.aalto.fi/~asolin/sde-book/sde-book.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A uniform random variable on $[0,1]$, the embedded line-supported law, and the compactly supported scalar-noise Gaussian smoothing setup.

[A1] The full Axiom of Choice is inherited from the Gaussian smoothing and probability interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] Countable Choice is assumed by the box-measure theorem used below; the item's SDE and smoothing interfaces also carry the stronger Full AC assumption. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] For any compactly supported probability law in $\mathbb R^2$, the positive-time law has the explicit Gaussian-convolution density and is strictly positive. [[def-gaussian-smoothed-data-law-and-transition-density]]

[F2] The convolution density is infinitely differentiable in space for each positive time. [[thm-gaussian-smoothing-density-and-forward-equation]]

[F3] The Lebesgue measure of an axis-aligned rectangle in $\mathbb R^2$ is the product of its side lengths. [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]

[F4] The law of a measurable map is its pushforward probability measure. [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]

## Proof

**Given:** The example's random vector and the Gaussian smoothing setup.

1.1 The map $u\mapsto(u,0)$ is continuous and hence Borel measurable; [F4] makes the formula in the statement its pushforward measure, and [A2, F3] give its total mass $\lambda_1([0,1])=1$. It assigns mass one to the Borel segment $L$. For each integer $n\ge1$, the segment lies in the rectangle $[0,1]\times[-1/n,1/n]$, whose Lebesgue area is $2/n$ by [F3]. Therefore its outer measure is at most $2/n$ for every $n$, hence its Lebesgue measure is zero. Since $\mu(L)=1$ and Lebesgue measure of $L$ is zero, $\mu$ is singular with respect to two-dimensional Lebesgue measure. [A2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 Applying the convolution formula [F1] to $\mu$ gives $p_t(x)=\int_0^1\phi_{v(t)}(x-(u,0))\,du$. In dimension two, $\phi_{v(t)}(x-(u,0))=(2\pi v(t))^{-1}\exp(-((x_1-u)^2+x_2^2)/(2v(t)))$, which is the displayed expression. The integrand is strictly positive for every $u$, so its integral over a unit interval is strictly positive; [F2] gives infinite spatial differentiability for every $t>0$. Thus the initial singularity does not prevent positive-time smoothing. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, given] ∎

## Definition

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

## Remarks

- **The two formulations are equivalent, and the passage between them uses no
  choice.** Given an at most countable family $\mathcal{F}$ of nonempty sets,
  either $\mathcal{F} = \varnothing$, where the empty function is a choice
  function, or a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathcal{F}$ exists
  ([[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]]); applying the indexed form to
  $X_n := s(n)$ gives $f$ with $f(n) \in s(n)$, and
  $g(S) := f(\min\{\, n : s(n) = S \,\})$ is a choice function for $\mathcal{F}$,
  the minimum being canonical by [[thm-well-ordering-principle]]. Conversely a
  choice function $g$ on the at most countable family $\{\, X_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$
  gives $f(n) := g(X_n)$.

- **AC implies countable choice.** The Axiom of Choice
  ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) applies to the family of values of any sequence of
  nonempty sets; composing the resulting choice function with the sequence
  gives the function required above.

- **Dependent choices and independent choices have different input data.**
  Countable choice selects from a family fixed in advance. Dependent choice
  instead asks for a sequence following an entire relation, where the available
  successors depend on the preceding term. The later
  [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]] proves
  $\mathrm{AC}\Rightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Rightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ in ZF.
  This remark makes no assertion about reversing either implication.

- **A locally proved failure comparison appears later.**
  [[cor-relative-consistency-of-feferman-levy-choice-failures-over-zf]] proves
  the external implication from consistency of ZF to consistency of
  $\mathrm{ZF}+\neg\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, together with the stated
  Feferman–Levy properties. Hence, if ZF is consistent, it cannot prove
  countable choice: a ZF proof would also hold in that consistent extension.
  This is a conditional consistency comparison, not an assertion that
  countable choice fails in the present development.

- **Being an axiom, $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ carries no well-definedness obligation**,
  which is why this item has no `justified_by`. Its role in this library is
  bookkeeping: [[thm-countable-union-of-countable]] assumes it and flags the
  exact step that spends it. No necessity claim is inferred from that proof.

- Every result *proved* on this page other than
  [[thm-countable-union-of-countable]] is a theorem of ZF alone. In particular
  [[lem-subset-of-countable]], [[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]],
  [[thm-schroder-bernstein]], [[thm-rationals-countable]], [[thm-cantor-powerset]]
  and [[thm-r-uncountable]] are choice free, and each says so.
