## Statement

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $n \ge 1$, the Axiom of Countable Choice, reals $a_i \le b_i$ for $i<n$, and the sets $R^\circ$, $\overline{R}$ displayed in the Statement.

[L1] Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra, $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure on it, every set of Lebesgue outer measure zero is Lebesgue measurable of measure zero, and $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

[L2] Assuming countable choice, every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]).

[L3] Assuming countable choice, $\lambda_n^*$ is an outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]), so it is monotone and countably subadditive ([[def-outer-measure]], [[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]).

[L4] For a nonempty box $\operatorname{vol}(B) := \prod_{i<n}(b_i - a_i)$ when every $a_i$ and every $b_i$ is real, and a box is nonempty exactly when $a_i < b_i$ for every $i < n$ ([[def-half-open-box]]).

[F1] $[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\}$ and $\operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j)$ ([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]).

[F2] A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function $\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty]$ with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$ that is countably additive on pairwise disjoint sequences ([[def-measure]]).

[F3] For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a natural number $k \ge 1$ with $1/k < \varepsilon$ ([[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]]).

[F4] $\prod_{k<n}(a_kb_k) = (\prod_{k<n}a_k)(\prod_{k<n}b_k)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k<n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, with $\prod_{k<n}a_k>0$ when every $a_k>0$; and finite products are defined by the recursion $\Pi_0 = 1$, $\Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], claim 6; [[def-finite-sum]]).

[F5] A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$; a subset $F$ is **closed** if its complement is open ([[def-metric-topology]]).

[F6] The forms $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are **half-open**, and an interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, **closed** when both are included ([[def-interval]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 $R^{\circ}$ is open and $\overline{R}$ is closed in $(\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)$, by the same coordinatewise estimate in each case, so both are Borel and hence Lebesgue measurable. [L2, F1, F5, F6]

1.2 A closed rectangle with a degenerate side is Lebesgue null: let $u_i \le v_i$ be reals with $u_{i_0} = v_{i_0} = c$ for some $i_0 < n$, and let $\eta$ be a positive real; the half-open box with parameter pairs $(u_i-1, v_i]$ for $i \ne i_0$ and $(c-\eta, c]$ in coordinate $i_0$ is nonempty, contains $[u,v]$, and has volume $\eta\,C$ where $C := \prod_{i<n}w_i > 0$ with $w_{i_0} := 1$ and $w_i := v_i-u_i+1$ otherwise, so monotonicity of the outer measure gives $\lambda_n^*([u,v]) \le \eta C$ for every positive real $\eta$ and hence $\lambda_n^*([u,v]) = 0$. [L1, L3, L4, F1, F3, F4]

2.1 The difference $\overline{R} \setminus R^{\circ}$ is contained in the union of the $2n$ closed rectangles obtained from $[a,b]$ by replacing the $i$-th side by the degenerate side $[a_i,a_i]$ or by $[b_i,b_i]$, each of which is Lebesgue null by step 1.2, so countable subadditivity of the outer measure, applied to that finite list padded with empty sets, gives $\lambda_n^*(\overline{R}\setminus R^{\circ}) = 0$; every subset of $\overline{R}\setminus R^{\circ}$ is therefore Lebesgue measurable of measure $0$. [step 1.2, L1, L3]

2.2 Suppose instead $a_{i_0} = b_{i_0}$ for some $i_0<n$. Then $R^{\circ} = \varnothing$, the rectangle $\overline{R}$ is Lebesgue null by step 1.2, every $R$ between them is a subset of it and so is measurable of measure $0$, and the product $\prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i)$ has the factor $0$ and is therefore $0$ as well. [step 1.2, L1, F4]

3.1 Suppose first that $a_i < b_i$ for every $i<n$. Then $B(a,b)$ is a nonempty half-open box with $R^{\circ} \subseteq B(a,b) \subseteq \overline{R}$ and $\lambda_n(B(a,b)) = \operatorname{vol}(B(a,b)) = \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i)$. For $R$ with $R^{\circ}\subseteq R\subseteq\overline{R}$, both $R \setminus B(a,b)$ and $B(a,b)\setminus R$ are contained in $\overline{R}\setminus R^{\circ}$, hence are measurable of measure $0$ by step 2.1, so $R = \big(B(a,b)\setminus(B(a,b)\setminus R)\big)\cup\big(R\setminus B(a,b)\big)$ is measurable, and additivity on the two disjoint decompositions $R = (R\cap B(a,b)) \sqcup (R\setminus B(a,b))$ and $B(a,b) = (R\cap B(a,b)) \sqcup (B(a,b)\setminus R)$ gives $\lambda_n(R) = \lambda_n(R\cap B(a,b)) = \lambda_n(B(a,b))$. [step 2.1, L1, L4, F2]

4.1 Steps 3.1 and 2.2 exhaust the two cases and give the displayed value in each, and step 1.1 supplies the Borel and measurability clauses for $R^{\circ}$ and $\overline{R}$. [step 1.1, step 2.2, step 3.1] ∎

## Example

For $a\in\mathbb R^d$, $\delta_a$ denotes the probability measure concentrated at $a$. For $q>0$, write $\phi_q(z)=(2\pi q)^{-d/2}\exp(-|z|^2/(2q))$.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a horizon $T>0$, $0<\epsilon<T$, $a\in\mathbb R^d$, and $c>0$. Take $\mu=\delta_a$ and constant scalar noise $g(t)=c$, so $v(\epsilon)=c^2\epsilon$. Let $\mu_\epsilon$ be the Gaussian-smoothed law with density $\phi_{c^2\epsilon}(x-a)$. For Borel probability laws with finite second moments, define $W_2$ as the square root of the infimum of the quadratic cost over all Borel couplings. Then

$$W_2(\mu_\epsilon,\delta_a)=\sqrt{d}\,c\sqrt{\epsilon}.$$

The coupling bound from the endpoint theorem is therefore an equality in this case.

## Example references

[Lawler, *Stochastic Calculus: An Introduction with Applications*, Sections 3.2.2–3.2.3](https://www.math.uchicago.edu/~lawler/finbook.pdf)

[Hunter, *Notes on Partial Differential Equations*, Chapter 5, §5.1.1](https://math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/pde_notes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The point-mass initial law, constant positive noise, and quadratic Wasserstein distance.

[A1] The full Axiom of Choice is inherited from the smoothing and coupling interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For constant $g=c$, the positive-time smoothed law of $\delta_a$ has Gaussian density $\phi_{c^2\epsilon}(x-a)$. [[def-gaussian-smoothed-data-law-and-transition-density]]

[F2] The endpoint coupling estimate is $W_2(\mu_\epsilon,\mu)\le\sqrt{d\,v(\epsilon)}$. [[thm-gaussian-smoothing-endpoint-weak-limit]]

[F3] $W_2^2$ is the infimum of quadratic costs among Borel couplings, and its arguments must have finite second moments. [[def-wasserstein-two-space-and-couplings]]

[F4] A random element's law is its probability pushforward, and the Euclidean product Borel sigma-algebra is the product sigma-algebra. [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]]

## Proof

**Given:** The example's parameters and the coupling definition in [F3].

1.1 The density in [F1] is the product of $d$ one-dimensional normal densities translated by $a$. Each coordinate has mean $a_j$ and variance $c^2\epsilon$, so its second moment about $a$ is $d c^2\epsilon$; both laws therefore have finite second moments. [A1, F1, F3, given]

2.1 If $\pi$ is any coupling of $\delta_a$ and $\mu_\epsilon$, its first marginal assigns mass one to $\{a\}$, hence $\pi(\{a\}\times\mathbb R^d)=1$. Its quadratic cost is therefore $\int|x-y|^2\,\pi(dx,dy)=\int|a-y|^2\,\mu_\epsilon(dy)=d c^2\epsilon.$ There is at least one coupling: the continuous map $y\mapsto(a,y)$ pushes $\mu_\epsilon$ forward to a Borel probability on $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d$ with marginals $\delta_a$ and $\mu_\epsilon$ by [F4]. Thus the infimum over all couplings equals this common cost. Taking the square root gives the stated equality. The endpoint bound [F2] has the same value because $v(\epsilon)=c^2\epsilon$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, given] ∎

## Example

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and $a\in\mathbb R^d$; take $\mu=\delta_a$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. Then $p_t(x)=\phi_{v(t)}(x-a)$ and

The exact global Lipschitz constant of $s_t$ is $1/v(t)$. For every $0<\epsilon<T$, its best uniform Lipschitz constant on $[\epsilon,T]$ is $1/v(\epsilon)$, which diverges as $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

## Example references

[Tang, Touzi, Zhang, and Zhou, *Tweedie's Formulae and Diffusion Generative Models Beyond Gaussian*, Section 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.19391)

[Särkkä and Solin, *Applied Stochastic Differential Equations*, Chapter 5, §§5.1–5.2](https://users.aalto.fi/~asolin/sde-book/sde-book.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The point-mass initial law, Gaussian convolution, and score convention from the example.

[A1] The full Axiom of Choice is inherited from the smoothing and score interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The Gaussian-smoothed density of a compact initial law is the mixture $p_t(x)=\int\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz)$. [[def-gaussian-smoothed-data-law-and-transition-density]]

[F2] The score and posterior mean satisfy $s_t(x)=-(x-m_{t,x})/v(t)$ and its derivative is $-I_d/v(t)+C_{t,x}/v(t)^2$. [[thm-gaussian-mixture-score-and-global-lipschitz-bound]]

## Proof

**Given:** The example's point mass and the score identities in [F2].

1.1 Substituting $\mu=\delta_a$ into [F1] gives $p_t(x)=\phi_{v(t)}(x-a)$. The posterior measure $\nu_{t,x}$ is then $\delta_a$, so its mean is $a$ and its covariance matrix is zero. [A1, F1, F2, given]

2.1 Applying [F2] yields $s_t(x)=-(x-a)/v(t)$ and $D_xs_t=-I_d/v(t)$. For any $x\ne y$, $|s_t(x)-s_t(y)|=|x-y|/v(t)$, so the global Lipschitz constant is exactly $1/v(t)$. On $[\epsilon,T]$, $v$ is increasing, making the largest such constant $1/v(\epsilon)$. Since $v(\epsilon)\le g_{\max}^2\epsilon\to0$ and $v(\epsilon)>0$, this bound tends to infinity. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Definition

A **supervised prediction problem** consists of nonempty measurable spaces $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ of instances, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ of labels, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ of prediction actions; the product measurable space $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$; a probability measure $P$ on that product; a nonempty class $\mathcal F$ of measurable predictors $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$; and a loss $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ that is measurable with respect to $\Sigma_A\otimes\Sigma_Y$. The law $P$ need not be supported on a deterministic labeling function, and this definition imposes no assumption that sample observations be independent or share a common law.

## Definition references

[[def-measurable-space]]: a measurable space is a set with a specified sigma-algebra.

[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]: a function is measurable when preimages of measurable sets are measurable.

[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: the product sigma-algebra is generated by measurable rectangles.

[[def-probability-measure]]: a probability measure has total mass one.

[[def-loss-function-and-risk]]: a loss is nonnegative and measurable in the action variable; risk is an extended nonnegative integral.

## Remarks

The joint law $P$ can be used at a fixed member of a statistical experiment. If it is selected from a parametric family, this prediction definition makes no parameter-recovery claim, and the family of laws need not distinguish parameter labels.

## Remarks references

[[def-statistical-experiment]]: an experiment is a measurable sample space with a parameter-indexed family of probability measures.

[[def-parametric-statistical-model]]: the parameter-to-law map need not be injective.

      url: "https://www.dropbox.com/s/38p0j6ds5q9c8oe/10290.pdf?dl=1"

## Definition

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

[[def-supervised-learning-problem]]: fixes the measurable spaces, joint law, predictor class and loss.

[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]: the expectation of a nonnegative measurable function is its extended integral.

      url: "https://www.dropbox.com/s/38p0j6ds5q9c8oe/10290.pdf?dl=1"

## Definition

Fix a sample $S$ and a nonempty class $\mathcal F$ of predictors. Its **empirical minimum** is $\widehat R_S^*(\mathcal F):=\inf_{f\in\mathcal F}\widehat R_S(f)\in[0,+\infty]$. An **exact empirical risk minimizer** is a predictor $f\in\mathcal F$ with $\widehat R_S(f)=\widehat R_S^*(\mathcal F)$. If the infimum is finite but is not attained, no exact minimizer exists. If the infimum is $+\infty$, nonemptiness implies that every member has infinite empirical risk and is an exact minimizer.

For finite $\eta\ge0$, a predictor $f\in\mathcal F$ is an **$\eta$-approximate empirical risk minimizer** if either the empirical minimum is $+\infty$ and $f$ is an exact minimizer, or the empirical minimum is finite and $f$ has finite empirical risk at most $\widehat R_S^*(\mathcal F)+\eta$. The membership requirement $f\in\mathcal F$ applies in both branches. Thus the definition never forms $+\infty+\eta$. When $\eta=0$ and the finite infimum is not attained, no such predictor exists.

For a fixed sample size $m$, a **measurable prediction rule** with class $\mathcal F$ is a jointly measurable evaluation map from the sample space $((\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y)^m, (\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)^{\otimes m})$ and a new instance in $\mathsf X$ to $\mathsf A$, whose slice at each sample belongs to $\mathcal F$. It is an exact or approximate ERM rule when every slice satisfies the corresponding samplewise definition above. This definition asserts no existence of a measurable selector for an arbitrary class.

## Statement

In a supervised prediction problem, for every measurable predictor $f$, the function $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(f(x),y)$ is measurable, so its population risk is a defined extended nonnegative integral. For every sample size $m\ge1$, the empirical risk $S\mapsto\widehat R_S(f)$ is an extended nonnegative measurable function on the finite product sample space.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A supervised prediction problem, a measurable predictor $f\in\mathcal F$, and a positive integer $m$. The sample domain is $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y)^m$ with its recursively formed product sigma-algebra.

[F1] Predictors are measurable, and the loss is measurable on the action-label product. [[def-supervised-learning-problem]]

[F2] The product sigma-algebra is generated by measurable rectangles and finite products are formed recursively. [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]

[F3] Population risk is the nonnegative integral of $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(f(x),y)$, and empirical risk is its finite sample average. [[def-population-and-empirical-risk]]

[F4] Finite sums of measurable extended-real functions are measurable when pointwise defined; real scalar multiples of real-valued measurable functions, functions $f\mathbf1_E$ for nonnegative measurable extended-real $f$ and measurable $E$, countable infima, and increasing pointwise limits of measurable extended-real functions are measurable. [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]

[F5] A map is measurable when preimages of measurable sets are measurable; preimages under a composition are taken successively. [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]

[F6] An extended-real-valued function is measurable when all of its strict-superlevel preimages are measurable. [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]

## Proof

1.1 Define $\Phi_f(x,y)=(f(x),y)$. For each measurable rectangle $U\times V$ in $\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y$, its preimage is $f^{-1}(U)\times V$, which belongs to $\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y$ by measurability of $f$. Since the rectangles generate the target product sigma-algebra by [F2], $\Phi_f$ is measurable by [F5]. Therefore $\ell_f:=\ell\circ\Phi_f$ is measurable by successive preimages in [F5] and nonnegative; [F3] defines $R_P(f)=\int\ell_f\,dP$. [F1, F2, F3, F5]

2.1 For each coordinate $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, the sample projection $\pi_i: (\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y)^m\to\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$ is measurable by the finite product construction in [F2]. Hence $S\mapsto\ell_f(\pi_i(S))$ is measurable by [F5]. The finite sum $s(S):=\sum_{i=1}^m\ell_f(\pi_i(S))$ is a defined nonnegative extended-real function and is measurable by [F4]. Since $m>0$, for every real $a$ we have $\{S:s(S)/m>a\}=\{S:s(S)>ma\}$, including when $s(S)=+\infty$. Thus $s/m$ is measurable by the strict-superlevel criterion [F6], and [F3] gives measurability of $S\mapsto\widehat R_S(f)$. [given, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and functions or sets as in the relevant clause.

[L1] A function $h:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is measurable exactly when $\{h>a\}\in\mathcal A$ for every real $a$ ([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]).

[L2] A sigma-algebra contains $X$ and $\varnothing$ and is closed under complements and countable unions; countable intersections follow by taking complements ([[def-sigma-algebra]]).

[L3] The rationals are countable and dense in the reals ([[thm-rationals-countable]], [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For any extended-real-valued $h$, the identities $\{h<a\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q,\ q<a}(X\setminus\{h>q\})$ and $\{h>a\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q,\ q>a}(X\setminus\{h<q\})$ follow from rational density, including when $h(x)$ is infinite. Thus [L2] and [L3] show that measurability of all strict sublevels is equivalent to measurability of all strict superlevels. [L1, L2, L3]

1.2 Put $h=f\chi_E$ as defined in clause 4. For $a<0$, $\{h>a\}=X$, since $h\ge0$. For $a\ge0$, $\{h>a\}=E\cap\{f>a\}$. Both sets are measurable, including at $a=0$, so clause 4 follows. [given, L1, L2]

1.3 For a pointwise-defined sum, $\{f+g>a\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}(\{f>q\}\cap\{g>a-q\})$. Indeed, if both summands are finite and their sum exceeds $a$, choose a rational strictly between $a-g(x)$ and $f(x)$. If one summand is $+\infty$, the other is not $-\infty$, and a rational meeting the two inequalities still exists; if a summand is $-\infty$, the defined sum cannot exceed $a$. The reverse inclusion follows by adding the inequalities. The union is countable and measurable, proving clause 1. [L1, L2, L3, given]

2.1 For $c>0$, $\{cf>a\}=\{f>a/c\}$; for $c<0$, $\{cf>a\}=\{f<a/c\}$. If $c=0$, each superlevel is either $X$ or $\varnothing$. Step 1.1 and [L1] therefore prove clause 2. [L1, L2, step 1.1]

2.2 Put $u=\inf_n f_n$ and $v=\sup_n f_n$. The defining order properties of infimum and supremum give $\{u<a\}=\bigcup_n\{f_n<a\}$ and $\{v>a\}=\bigcup_n\{f_n>a\}$, including infinite values. By step 1.1 and [L2] these sets are measurable, so $u$ and $v$ are measurable by [L1]. If $f_n\uparrow f$, then $f=v$ pointwise. This proves clause 5. [given, L1, L2, step 1.1]

3.1 The function $-f$ is measurable by step 2.1. For any real-valued measurable $h$, the superlevel of $\max(h,0)$ is $X$ when $a<0$ and $\{h>a\}$ when $a\ge0$. Apply this to $h=f$ and $h=-f$ to obtain measurable $f^+$ and $f^-$. They are finite-valued, so step 1.3 makes $|f|=f^++f^-$ measurable, proving clause 3. [L1, L2, step 1.3, step 2.1]

4.1 Clauses 1–5 follow respectively from steps 1.3, 2.1, 3.1, 1.2, and 2.2. [step 1.3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, step 2.2] ∎

## Definition

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ be standard Borel spaces, let $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be a measurable action space, and let $P$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$. Write $P_X$ and $P_Y$ for its coordinate marginals. There are regular conditional probability kernels $Q(y,dx)$ for $X$ given $Y$ and $K(x,dy)$ for $Y$ given $X$, with
$$P(C\times D)=\int_D Q(y,C)\,P_Y(dy)=\int_C K(x,D)\,P_X(dx)\qquad(C\in\Sigma_X,\ D\in\Sigma_Y).$$
Let $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable with respect to $\Sigma_A\otimes\Sigma_Y$ and define $q(x,a):=\int_{\mathsf Y}\ell(a,y)K(x,dy)$. If a measurable predictor $f^*:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ has a measurable set $E\in\Sigma_X$ with $P_X(E)=1$ such that $q(x,f^*(x))\le q(x,a)$ for every $x\in E$ and every $a\in\mathsf A$, then
$$R_P(f^*)\le R_P(g)$$
for every measurable predictor $g:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$. All risks may be $+\infty$.

## Statement references

[[def-standard-borel-space]]: a standard Borel space is measurably isomorphic to a Polish space.

[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]: a regular conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the conditional-event integral identities.

[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: product sigma-algebras are generated by measurable rectangles.

[[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC asserts that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; standard Borel instance and label spaces; a joint probability law $P$; a measurable action space; a nonnegative product-measurable loss; and a measurable predictor $f^*$ that minimizes conditional risk on one measurable $P_X$-full-measure set.

[A1] Assume the Axiom of Choice. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A standard Borel space is measurably isomorphic to a Polish space. [[def-standard-borel-space]]

[F2] Under AC, a joint law on a product of standard Borel spaces admits a probability kernel in either coordinate direction with the rectangle disintegration identity. [[thm-disintegration-of-a-joint-law-on-standard-borel-spaces]]

[F3] The disintegration identity also holds for every nonnegative product-measurable integrand, including value infinity. [[thm-disintegration-of-a-joint-law-on-standard-borel-spaces]]

[F4] Under AC and standard Borel parameter/data hypotheses, a measurable rule attaining posterior minimum almost everywhere minimizes prior-integrated risk among all randomized rules. [[thm-bayes-rule-minimizes-prior-risk]]

[F5] Population risk is the extended nonnegative integral of the loss under the joint law. [[def-population-and-empirical-risk]]

[F6] A regular conditional distribution is a probability kernel whose evaluations satisfy the conditional-event integral identity. [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]

[F7] Integrating a nonnegative product-measurable function against a probability kernel gives a measurable extended-valued function. [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]

[F8] Product sigma-algebras are generated by measurable rectangles, so the coordinate swap between finite products is measurable. [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]

[F9] A map is measurable when preimages of measurable sets are measurable; this criterion is preserved by composition. [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]

## Proof

1.1 The spaces satisfy the standard-Borel hypothesis [F1]. Apply [F2] to $P$ and to its coordinate swap. This gives $Q(y,dx)$ and $K(x,dy)$ with the two displayed disintegrations; [F6] identifies them as regular conditional distributions. With prior $\pi=P_Y$ and sampling kernel $Q$, the joint prior-data law is $P$ and the posterior is $K$. The loss $L(y,a):=\ell(a,y)$ is jointly measurable because the coordinate swap on product spaces has rectangle preimages that are rectangles by [F8], and composition preserves measurability by [F9]. The lifted kernel $\widetilde K((x,a),D):=K(x,D)$ is a probability kernel, since its evaluations are measurable by projection from $x$; [F7] therefore makes $q(x,a)$ measurable. [A1, F1, F2, F6, F7, F8, F9]

2.1 For any measurable $g:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$, the point-mass rule $\delta_g(x,B):=\mathbf1_B(g(x))$ is a probability kernel, since each section is a Dirac probability measure and each evaluation is measurable by [F9]. The function $(y,x)\mapsto\ell(g(x),y)$ is product-measurable by the rectangle-preimage criterion [F8, F9]. Its prior-integrated risk is $\int_{\mathsf Y}\int_{\mathsf X}\ell(g(x),y)Q(y,dx)P_Y(dy)=R_P(g)$ by [F3, F5], with the same identity for $f^*$. Under [F4], use parameter $y$, prior $P_Y$, data $x$, model kernel $Q$, posterior $K$, action space $\mathsf A$, loss $L$, and rule $f^*$. Its posterior risk is $q$, so the common full-measure minimizing premise applies; the theorem gives prior risk of $f^*$ no larger than that of $\delta_g$. Thus $R_P(f^*)\le R_P(g)$. Since $g$ was arbitrary, the claim follows. [A1, F3, F4, F5, F8, F9, given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses and conventions in the statement.

[F1] Under AC the first coordinate has an everywhere RCD given the second-coordinate sigma-algebra; the same repaired construction supplies a countable determining algebra on E. [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]].

[F2] Such a kernel factors through Y under AC. [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]].

[F3] Two RCDs of the same standard-Borel variable agree as measures almost surely. [[lem-simultaneous-ae-uniqueness-of-regular-conditional-distributions]].

[F4] The repaired local integral interface supplies nonnegative additivity, monotone convergence, and bounded decreasing convergence. [[lem-simultaneous-rational-conditional-distribution-function-versions]].

[F5] A lambda-system containing rectangles contains the product sigma-algebra. [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]].

[F6] Prescribed nonnegative simple approximants increase pointwise to every nonnegative measurable test. [[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]].

[F7] Pointwise limits of measurable functions are measurable. [[thm-sequential-suprema-infima-limsup-liminf-and-pointwise-limits-are-measurable]].

[F8] AC supplies RCD existence, bin-lift factorization and the countable determining algebra. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 On $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T,\lambda)$ use the coordinate maps X and Y. Both targets are nonempty because the product carries a probability. By [F1], X has an RCD L given $\sigma(Y)$; by [F2] it factors as $K(Y,\cdot)$ for a probability kernel K. The RCD identity gives $\lambda(A\times B)=\int\mathbf1_B(Y)K(Y,A)\,d\lambda$. We prove the needed marginal substitution locally. For $g=\mathbf1_C$, $$\int g(Y)\,d\lambda=\lambda(Y^{-1}C)=\beta(C)=\int g\,d\beta.$$ Finite additivity from [F4] gives this for nonnegative simple g; apply [F6] and the local monotone convergence [F4] to get it for every nonnegative measurable g. Taking $g(y)=\mathbf1_B(y)K(y,A)$ yields the rectangle formula. [F1, F2, F4, F6, F8]

2.1 We also prove kernel-integral measurability locally. Let $\mathcal M$ be the product-measurable sets C for which every section $C_y$ belongs to $\mathcal S$ and $y\mapsto K(y,C_y)$ is measurable. It contains rectangles: each section is A or empty and its evaluation is $\mathbf1_B(y)K(y,A)$. It contains the whole product. Under complements, $(C^c)_y=(C_y)^c$ is measurable and its evaluation is $1-K(y,C_y)$. Under pairwise disjoint countable unions, the sections are measurable disjoint unions, while sectionwise countable additivity gives the evaluation as a pointwise limit of measurable partial sums, measurable by [F7]. Thus [F5] gives both properties for every product event. Let $\mathcal D$ be the product events satisfying the iterated indicator identity. It contains rectangles by step 1.1 and the whole product by normalization. Complements subtract from the finite total one. For disjoint $C_j\in\mathcal D$, sectionwise countable additivity and monotone convergence from [F4], first under $K(y,\cdot)$ and then under $\beta$, prove the union identity. Hence [F5] gives every product event. [step 1.1, F4, F5, F7]

3.1 Finite nonnegative combinations of step 2.1 give both measurability and the iterated formula for nonnegative simple f. For arbitrary nonnegative f, use the prescribed $s_n\uparrow f$ of [F6]. Apply the locally proved monotone convergence [F4] under $\lambda$, in every probability section K, and then under $\beta$. By [F7] the inner limit is measurable. These passages give the displayed formula, including value infinity, with no subtraction. [step 2.1, F4, F6, F7]

4.1 If K and J both satisfy the rectangle formula, their compositions with Y are RCDs of X given $\sigma(Y)$: the collection $\{Y^{-1}(B):B\in\mathcal T\}$ is already a sigma-algebra. By [F3], they agree as measures outside one $\lambda$-null set. Fix the countable determining algebra $\mathcal A$ supplied by [F1] and set $D=\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal A}\{y:K(y,A)\ne J(y,A)\}$. This set is measurable. Its preimage under Y lies in the exceptional set from [F3], so $\beta(D)=\lambda(Y^{-1}D)=0$. Off D the probabilities agree on $\mathcal A$, hence on every event by its locally proved determining property. If the joint law comes from actual X,Y, the rectangle calculation gives the same conditional-law assertion. [step 1.1, F1, F3, F8] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a probability
kernel from a standard-Borel parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to a
standard-Borel data space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, where standard Borel means
measurably isomorphic to a Polish space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]). Let $\pi$ be a prior,
and let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be jointly measurable for a
measurable action space $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$. Let $J$ be the joint prior-data
law of [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]], let $M$ be its data
marginal, and let $\Pi_x(d\theta)$ be a regular posterior distribution of
$\theta$ given $x$ (the disintegration is supplied by
[[thm-disintegration-of-a-joint-law-on-standard-borel-spaces]]).
Define posterior risk
$$q(x,a)=\int_\Theta L(\theta,a)\,\Pi_x(d\theta).$$
Suppose a measurable deterministic rule $d^*:\mathcal X\to\mathsf D$
attains the posterior minimum for $M$-almost every $x$; that is,
$q(x,d^*(x))\leq q(x,a)$ for every $a\in\mathsf D$ on one measurable
$M$-full-measure set. Then $d^*$ minimizes prior-integrated risk among all randomized decision
rules $\delta$:
$$r_\pi(d^*)\leq r_\pi(\delta).$$
No conclusion is asserted when a measurable posterior minimizer does not
exist. All risks may be $+\infty$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The kernels, prior, joint loss, posterior, and measurable minimizing rule in the statement.

[A1] Assume AC, as required by standard-Borel disintegration ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] The model is a probability kernel from parameters to data ([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]).

[F2] A randomized decision rule is a probability kernel and its risk is the iterated nonnegative loss integral ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]], [[def-loss-function-and-risk]]).

[F3] A prior and model kernel define a joint probability whose integral of each nonnegative product-measurable function is the iterated kernel integral ([[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]).

[F4] On standard-Borel spaces, the joint law disintegrates through its data marginal into a regular posterior, and the integral identity holds for every nonnegative product-measurable function ([[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], [[thm-disintegration-of-a-joint-law-on-standard-borel-spaces]]).

[F5] Integrals of nonnegative product-measurable functions against kernels are measurable ([[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]).

[F6] Tonelli's theorem equates iterated integrals of nonnegative measurable functions on product probability spaces ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F7] The nonnegative integral over a measurable null set is zero ([[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]).

[F8] The nonnegative integral is monotone ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[F9] The nonnegative integral is additive on finite sums ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

[F10] A function between measurable spaces is measurable when preimages of measurable sets are measurable ([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

[F11] Prior-integrated risk is $r_\pi(\delta)=\int_\Theta R(\theta,\delta)\,\pi(d\theta)$ ([[def-bayes-and-minimax-risk]]).

[F12] Product sigma-algebras are generated by measurable rectangles, so coordinate projections and measurable pairing maps into finite products are measurable ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix a randomized rule $\delta$ and put $h_\delta(\theta,x)=\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)$. The lifted kernel $((\theta,x),B)\mapsto\delta(x,B)$ is a probability kernel because the coordinate projection $(\theta,x)\mapsto x$ is measurable by [F12]. The lifted integrand $(\theta,x,a)\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is product-measurable because the pairing map $((\theta,x),a)\mapsto(\theta,a)$ is measurable by [F12]. By [F5], $h_\delta$ is product-measurable. The risk definition [F2], prior-risk definition [F11], and joint-law identity [F3] therefore give $r_\pi(\delta)=\int h_\delta\,dJ$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F11, F12]

2.1 Apply the posterior disintegration identity [F4] to $h_\delta\geq0$. If $M$ is the second marginal of $J$, then $r_\pi(\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_\Theta h_\delta(\theta,x)\,\Pi_x(d\theta)\right)M(dx)$. Every integral is an extended nonnegative integral, so no integrability beyond the stated measurability is needed. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Lift $\Pi$ to the kernel $((x,a),B)\mapsto\Pi_x(B)$ from $\mathcal X\times\mathsf D$ to $\Theta$. The pairing map $((x,a),\theta)\mapsto(\theta,a)$ is measurable by [F12], so [F5] makes $q(x,a)$ product-measurable. For each fixed $x$, [F6] applied to the product probability $\Pi_x\times\delta(x,\cdot)$ and $L(\theta,a)$ gives $\int_\Theta h_\delta(\theta,x)\,\Pi_x(d\theta)=\int_{\mathsf D}q(x,a)\,\delta(x,da)$. The right side is measurable in $x$ by [F5]. Thus step 2.1 yields $r_\pi(\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\int_{\mathsf D}q(x,a)\,\delta(x,da)\,M(dx)$. [F2, F5, F6, F12, step 2.1]

4.1 The point-mass kernel $\delta^*(x,B)=1_B(d^*(x))$ is measurable because $d^*$ is measurable by [F10]; applying step 3.1 gives $r_\pi(d^*)=\int g\,dM$ for $g(x)=q(x,d^*(x))$. The pairing map $x\mapsto(x,d^*(x))$ is measurable by [F10, F12], so $g$ is measurable. Put $h(x)=\int q(x,a)\,\delta(x,da)$, which is measurable by [F5]. On the measurable full-measure set $E$ from the statement, $g1_E\leq h1_E$, so [F8] gives $\int g1_E\,dM\leq\int h1_E\,dM$. The complementary integrals vanish by [F7]; additivity [F9] gives $\int g\,dM\leq\int h\,dM=r_\pi(\delta)$ by step 3.1. The rule $\delta$ was arbitrary. [given, F2, F5, F7, F8, F9, F10, F12, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\Tau)$ be a measurable random element and $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra. A **regular conditional distribution of X given $\mathcal G$** is a probability kernel $K:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\to(T,\Tau)$ satisfying
$$\int_H K(\omega,A)\,P(d\omega)=P(H\cap\{X\in A\})\qquad(H\in\mathcal G,\ A\in\Tau).$$

“Probability kernel” has the pointwise meaning of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: every $K(\omega,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, and every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable. Its evaluations lie in $[0,1]$ and are integrable. Thus the testing identity says exactly that $K(\cdot,A)$ is a conditional-expectation version of $1_{\{X\in A\}}$ in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. Conversely, a probability kernel with these version identities satisfies the displayed definition.

The kernel requirement holds at every sample point. Separate eventwise choices of conditional-expectation versions do not imply it and do not by themselves provide one exceptional set valid for all A. When A is empty the testing identity is zero on both sides, and when A=T it is P(H) on both sides. This defines a property of a supplied kernel and makes no existence or AC assertion.

## Statement

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses and conventions in the statement.

[F1] Kernel evaluations are measurable and every section is a measure. [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]].

[F2] A lambda-system containing a pi-system contains its generated sigma-algebra. [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]].

[F3] Nonnegative measurable functions have explicit increasing simple approximations. [[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]].

[F4] Monotone convergence applies to each section measure. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]].

[F5] Measurable functions are closed under defined sums, real scalars, nonnegative restriction and increasing limits. [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]].

[F6] Every section of a product-measurable function is measurable. [[thm-sections-of-product-measurable-functions-are-measurable]].

[F7] Measurable rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra. [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 First suppose K finite and write $m(s)=K(s,T)<\infty$. For a product-measurable set E, its section $E_s$ is measurable, by applying the section theorem to its indicator. Let $\mathcal D$ consist of those E for which $s\mapsto K(s,E_s)$ is measurable. It contains every rectangle $A\times B$, whose evaluation is $1_A(s)K(s,B)$, and it contains $S\times T$. If E belongs to this class, then $(E^c)_s=T\setminus E_s$ and $K(s,(E^c)_s)=m(s)-K(s,E_s)$; both terms are finite measurable real functions, so the difference is measurable. If E_j are disjoint class members, their sections are disjoint and $K(s,(\bigcup_j E_j)_s)=\sum_jK(s,(E_j)_s)$ is an increasing limit of measurable finite sums. Thus this class is a lambda-system. Rectangles form a pi-system, so Dynkin's theorem gives every product-measurable E in the class. The measurable-closure proposition can be used on S equipped with its zero measure; its conclusions concern only Sigma and do not require a preexisting source probability. [F1, F2, F5, F6, F7]

2.1 For a nonnegative simple product-measurable function $g=\sum_{j=1}^r a_j1_{E_j}$ with disjoint E_j and finite nonnegative coefficients, its section integral is $\sum_j a_jK(s,(E_j)_s)$ and is measurable by step 1.1. Choose the prescribed increasing simple approximation $g_n\uparrow f$ on the product. For every s the section theorem and monotone convergence give $I_f(s)=\lim_n I_{g_n}(s)$, so the increasing-limit closure proves measurability. No uniform bound in s was used; only the individual finite masses entered the complement calculation. [step 1.1, F3, F4, F5, F6]

3.1 Now let $(T_n)$ be the specified common exhaustion. Define $K_n(s,A)=K(s,A\cap T_n)$. For each s this is the restriction of a measure, its evaluations are measurable by the kernel hypothesis, and $K_n(s,T)=K(s,T_n)<\infty$. Apply step 2.1 to K_n. Sectionwise integration against the restriction equals integration of $f(s,\cdot)1_{T_n}$ against K(s,·): this holds for indicators by definition, for simple functions by finite sums, and for nonnegative functions by monotone convergence. Since $T_n\uparrow T$, $I_f(s)=\lim_n\int f(s,t)K_n(s,dt)$; another increasing-limit argument proves the result. If T is empty all these integrals are zero; if S is empty the assertion is vacuous. [step 2.1, F1, F3, F4, F5]

4.1 For real f its positive and negative parts and absolute value are product-measurable. The proved result makes $I_{f^+},I_{f^-},I_{|f|}$ measurable. Therefore $D=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{I_{|f|}<n\}$ is measurable. On D both part integrals are finite since each is at most $I_{|f|}$. Define $J_+(s)=I_{f^+}(s)$ on D and zero otherwise, and define J_- similarly. Nonnegative measurable restriction makes both J_± measurable; they are finite everywhere. Their real difference is the requested signed integral on D and zero elsewhere. This never subtracts two infinities. For a zero kernel all integrals vanish and D=S, even if f is unbounded; for f=0 the same holds for every permitted kernel. All approximations and the exhaustion are specified; no AC is used. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F5] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ be a nonempty measurable space, let $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ be a nonempty standard Borel space, and let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$. Put $P_X(C)=P(C\times\mathsf Y)$. There exists an everywhere probability kernel $K:(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)\to(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ such that

$$P(C\times A)=\int_C K(x,A)\,P_X(dx)\qquad(C\in\Sigma_X,\ A\in\Sigma_Y).$$

No standard-Borel, countable-generation, or completeness hypothesis is imposed on the instance space.

## Statement references

[[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[[def-standard-borel-space]]

[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]

[[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]]

[Kallenberg, *Foundations of Modern Probability*, 2nd ed., Theorem 6.3](https://djvu.online/file/t4FlvxuKFFZGW)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the nonempty measurable instance space, the nonempty standard Borel label space, and the joint law $P$ in the Statement.

[A1] AC is assumed for the regular-conditional-distribution existence supplier. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Under AC, a measurable random element with standard-Borel target has a regular conditional distribution given any sub-sigma-algebra; all sections are probability measures everywhere, with no completeness or countable-generation assumption on the conditioning sigma-algebra. [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]]

[F2] A regular conditional distribution $L$ of $Y$ given $\mathcal G$ is a probability kernel from $(\Omega,\mathcal G)$ whose evaluations satisfy $\int_B L(\omega,A)P(d\omega)=P(B\cap\{Y\in A\})$ for every $B\in\mathcal G$ and $A\in\Sigma_Y$. In particular every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable everywhere and every section is a probability measure. [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]

[F3] Product sigma-algebras are generated by measurable rectangles; coordinate projections are measurable. A map is measurable when preimages of all target measurable sets are measurable, and this criterion is preserved by composition. [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]], [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]

[F4] Between two unequal real numbers there is a rational number. [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]]

[F5] If a random element $X$ has law $P_X$ and $g$ is nonnegative real-valued measurable, then $\int g(X(\omega))P(d\omega)=\int g(x)P_X(dx)$. [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]

[F6] Restricting a nonnegative measurable function to a measurable set and setting it to zero elsewhere preserves measurability. [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]

## Proof

1.1 Work on $\Omega=\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$ with sigma-algebra $\mathcal F=\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y$ and probability $P$. Let $X(x,y)=x$ and $Y(x,y)=y$. These projections are measurable by [F3], and $X$ has law $P_X$. The family $\mathcal G:=\{X^{-1}(C):C\in\Sigma_X\}$ is a sigma-algebra, since inverse images preserve the full set, complements and countable unions; it is contained in $\mathcal F$ and is exactly $\sigma(X)$. Apply [F1] to the label coordinate $Y$ given this exact, uncompleted $\mathcal G$, obtaining a kernel $L$ as in [F2]. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 Fix one $y_0\in\mathsf Y$ and define $s:\mathsf X\to\Omega$ by $s(x)=(x,y_0)$. As a map into $(\Omega,\mathcal G)$ it is measurable: for every $C\in\Sigma_X$, $s^{-1}(X^{-1}(C))=C$, and step 1.1 describes every set of $\mathcal G$ in this form. Also $X(s(x))=x$ for every $x$. [given, F3, step 1.1, choose, construct]

3.1 Every $\mathcal G$-measurable real function $v$ is constant on each $X$-fiber. Indeed, if $X(\omega)=X(\omega')$ but $v(\omega)<v(\omega')$, choose a rational $r$ strictly between these values by [F4]. The measurable set $\{v\le r\}$ equals $X^{-1}(C)$ for some $C\in\Sigma_X$ by step 1.1, and so cannot contain exactly one of $\omega,\omega'$, a contradiction. Reversing the two points rules out the other inequality. Applying this to $v(\omega)=L(\omega,A)\in[0,1]$ separately for each $A\in\Sigma_Y$ gives $L(\omega,A)=L(s(X(\omega)),A)$ for every $\omega$ and every $A$. These are pointwise identities, with no event-dependent null sets. [F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, cases]

4.1 Define $K(x,A):=L(s(x),A)$. Every $K(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure by [F2]. For fixed $A$, the evaluation is the composition of the $\mathcal G$-measurable evaluation of $L$ with the measurable map $s$ from step 2.1, so it is $\Sigma_X$-measurable by [F3]. Thus $K$ is an everywhere probability kernel, and step 3.1 gives $K(X(\omega),A)=L(\omega,A)$ for every $\omega,A$. [F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Fix $C\in\Sigma_X$ and $A\in\Sigma_Y$. The real function $g(x)=\mathbf1_C(x)K(x,A)$ is measurable, nonnegative and bounded by one by [F6] and step 4.1. Apply [F5] and then [F2] to obtain $\int_C K(x,A)P_X(dx)=\int_{X^{-1}(C)}K(X(\omega),A)P(d\omega)=\int_{X^{-1}(C)}L(\omega,A)P(d\omega)=P(X^{-1}(C)\cap Y^{-1}(A))=P(C\times A)$. Since $C,A$ were arbitrary, this proves the Statement on the original arbitrary measurable instance space. [F2, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable random element with standard-Borel target, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be any sub-sigma-algebra. There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. Every section is a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points, and no countable-generation or completeness assumption on $\mathcal G$ is required.

For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses and conventions in the statement.

[F1] An everywhere probability kernel is a regular conditional distribution precisely when all conditioning-event identities hold. [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]].

[F2] A real random variable has an everywhere probability kernel with every Borel conditional identity, using the locally repaired integral interface. [[lem-rational-conditional-distribution-functions-produce-real-regular-kernels]], [[lem-simultaneous-rational-conditional-distribution-function-versions]].

[F3] A standard-Borel presentation is a measurable isomorphism with a Polish space; bounded remetrisation preserves its topology. [[def-standard-borel-space]], [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]].

[F4] Finite-coordinate cylinders generate the cube topology, and the relevant geometric series converge. [[def-product-topology]], [[thm-geometric-series]], [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]].

[F5] Under DC, a completely metrizable subspace of a metric space is $G_\delta$. [[thm-completely-metrizable-subspaces-of-metric-spaces-are-g-delta]].

[F6] The Hilbert cube has an explicit bimeasurable coding onto a Borel subset of $[0,1]$. [[lem-hilbert-cube-has-a-bimeasurable-real-coding]].

[F7] Rational cuts generate the real Borel sigma-algebra, rationals are countable and separate reals, and pi-lambda proves finite-measure determination. [[thm-seven-generators-of-the-borel-sigma-algebra-on-r]], [[thm-rationals-countable]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]], [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]].

[F8] Under countable choice, a countable union of finite sets is countable. [[thm-countable-union-of-countable]], [[def-countable-choice]].

[F9] AC supplies the metric and dense-set witnesses, their enumeration, DC, countable choice, and the choices in the real-kernel construction. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The probability space is nonempty, so the existence of $X$ makes $E$ nonempty. By [F3] fix a Borel isomorphism $h:E\to P$, where $P$ has a complete compatible metric $\rho$ and a countable dense set. Use [F9] to enumerate that set as $(p_n)$ and put $d=\min(1,\rho)$. A $d$-Cauchy sequence is eventually at $d$-distance below one, hence is $\rho$-Cauchy; its $\rho$-limit is also its $d$-limit. Thus $d$ is complete and compatible. Define $$e(x)=(d(x,p_n))_{n\ge0}\in Q=[0,1]^{\mathbb N}.$$ Each coordinate is one-Lipschitz. If $x\ne y$, choose $p_n$ with $d(x,p_n)<d(x,y)/3$; the reverse triangle inequality makes the $n$th distances different, so $e$ is injective. It is continuous by the initial description of the product topology. Its inverse on $e[P]$ is continuous: for $\varepsilon<1$, choose $p_n$ with $d(x,p_n)<\varepsilon/4$; if $z=e(y)$ and $|z_n-e(x)_n|<\varepsilon/2$, then $d(x,y)<\varepsilon$. Hence $e$ is a homeomorphism onto its image, with the inverse-continuity estimate explicit. [F3, F4, F7, F9]

2.1 On $Q$ set $D(u,v)=\sum_{n\ge0}2^{-(n+1)}|u_n-v_n|$. The geometric tail bound makes this finite; termwise separation and the triangle inequality make it a metric. A $D$-ball controls every prescribed finite set of coordinates because $|u_n-v_n|\le2^{n+1}D(u,v)$. Conversely, after choosing $N$ with $\sum_{n\ge N}2^{-(n+1)}<\varepsilon/2$, sufficiently small restrictions on the first $N$ coordinates force $D<\varepsilon$. Thus $D$ induces the product topology. A $D$-Cauchy sequence is Cauchy in every coordinate, whose limit lies in $[0,1]$ by completeness of the reals; a finite-head plus geometric-tail estimate proves convergence in $D$. Therefore $D$ is complete. The image $Y=e[P]$ is completely metrizable by transport of $d$. AC supplies DC by choosing a successor for every admissible finite history and iterating, so [F5] makes $Y$ a $G_\delta$, hence Borel, subset of $(Q,D)$. [step 1.1, F4, F5, F9]

3.1 Let $a:Q\to C\subseteq[0,1]$ be [F6]. Since $a^{-1}$ is measurable and $Y$ is Borel, $B=a[Y]=(a^{-1})^{-1}[Y]$ is Borel in $C$ and hence in $[0,1]$. Restricting $a$ and its inverse shows that $c=a\circ e\circ h:E\to B$ is bimeasurable. For $q\in\mathbb Q$, set $H_q=c^{-1}[B\cap(-\infty,q]]$. Let $\mathcal A_n$ be the finite Boolean algebra generated by the first $n$ rational cuts in a fixed enumeration and $\mathcal A=\bigcup_n\mathcal A_n$. By [F8] and [F9], $\mathcal A$ is countable; it is an algebra and generates $\mathcal S$ by [F7] and bimeasurability. Rational separation and injectivity of $c$ show that it separates points. If finite measures $\mu,\nu$ agree on $\mathcal A$, their equality class is a lambda-system: complements subtract from their common finite total and disjoint unions use countable additivity. It contains the pi-system $\mathcal A$, so [F7] gives equality on $\mathcal S$. This proves the two auxiliary conclusions without using either affected published standard-Borel interface. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F6, F7, F8, F9]

4.1 Fix $e_0\in E$ and put $Z=c\circ X$. By [F2] it has an everywhere real conditional probability kernel $\nu$. The evaluation $b(\omega)=\nu(\omega,B)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and $0\le b\le1$. Since $Z\in B$, its conditional identity gives $\int b\,dP=1$. The repaired finite-additivity interface in [F2] gives $\int(1-b)=0$; for each integer $k\ge1$, on $N_k=\{1-b\ge1/k\}$ monotonicity gives $P(N_k)/k\le0$. Thus $N=\{b\ne1\}=\bigcup_{k\ge1}N_k$ is measurable and null. Define $$K(\omega,A)=\begin{cases}\nu(\omega,c[A]),&\omega\notin N,\\ \mathbf1_A(e_0),&\omega\in N.\end{cases}$$ Bimeasurability makes $c[A]$ Borel in the real line, so every evaluation is measurable. Off $N$, injectivity and $\nu(\omega,B)=1$ give a probability on $E$; on $N$ the filler is Dirac. The two evaluations differ only on a measurable null set, and the local null-integral clause in [F2] gives $$\int_HK(\omega,A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{c(X)\in c[A]\})=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$ By [F1], $K$ is the required everywhere regular conditional distribution. [step 3.1, F1, F2, F9] ∎

## Definition

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

## Statement

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ of $\mathbb{Q}$ into $\mathbb{R}$, its image $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$, and the complement $X = \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$.

[L1] $\overline{A}$ is the set of points every neighbourhood of which meets $A$; $A$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$ when $\overline{A} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[thm-closure-characterisations-r]], [[def-limit-point-r]]).

[L2] $N_\varepsilon(x) = (x - \varepsilon, x + \varepsilon)$ for real $\varepsilon > 0$, and $x - \varepsilon < x + \varepsilon$ ([[def-neighbourhood-r]], [[def-interval]]).

[L3] $U$ is open when every $x \in U$ admits $\varepsilon > 0$ with $N_\varepsilon(x) \subseteq U$ ([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]).

[L4] Strictly between any two reals lies an element of $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$, and $q \mapsto \hat q$ is injective ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]).

[L5] $\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-rationals-countable]]); an injection is a bijection onto its image, and $\approx$ is symmetric and transitive ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]], [[def-equinumerous]]).

[L6] Every subset of an at most countable set is at most countable, and uncountable means not at most countable ([[lem-subset-of-countable]], [[def-countable]]).

[L7] For $a < b$ the interval $(a,b)$ is uncountable ([[cor-interval-uncountable]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense: let $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $\varepsilon > 0$ be real; by [L2] one has $x - \varepsilon < x + \varepsilon$, so [L4] supplies $\hat q$ with $x - \varepsilon < \hat q < x + \varepsilon$, that is $\hat q \in N_\varepsilon(x) \cap \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$. Every real is therefore an adherent point of $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ and claim 1 follows from [L1]. [L1, L2, L4]

1.2 $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is at most countable: the embedding is an injection of $\mathbb{Q}$ with image $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$, hence a bijection onto it, so $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}} \approx \mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$. [L4, L5]

1.3 For all reals $a < b$ the interval $(a,b)$ is uncountable. [L7]

2.1 For all reals $a < b$ the interval $(a,b)$ contains an irrational: if it did not, then $(a,b) \subseteq \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$, so $(a,b)$ would be a subset of an at most countable set by step 1.2 and hence at most countable by [L6], contradicting step 1.3. So some $z \in (a,b)$ lies in $X$. [step 1.2, step 1.3, L6]

2.2 Every nonempty open $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is uncountable: fix $x \in U$ and, by [L3], a real $\varepsilon > 0$ with $N_\varepsilon(x) \subseteq U$; by [L2] the set $N_\varepsilon(x)$ is the interval $(x - \varepsilon, x + \varepsilon)$ with $x - \varepsilon < x + \varepsilon$, hence uncountable by step 1.3. Were $U$ at most countable, its subset $N_\varepsilon(x)$ would be at most countable by [L6], which it is not; so $U$ is uncountable, which is claim 3. [step 1.3, L2, L3, L6, choose]

3.1 $X$ is dense: let $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $\varepsilon > 0$ be real; applying step 2.1 with $a = x - \varepsilon$ and $b = x + \varepsilon$ gives $z \in (x - \varepsilon, x + \varepsilon) \cap X$, which is $N_\varepsilon(x) \cap X$ by [L2]. Every real is therefore an adherent point of $X$, so $\overline{X} = \mathbb{R}$ by [L1], which is claim 2. [step 2.1, L1, L2]

4.1 Claims 1, 2 and 3 are steps 1.1, 3.1 and 2.2, so both $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ and its complement are dense in $\mathbb{R}$ and every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable. [step 1.1, step 2.2, step 3.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **Two dense sets can be disjoint.** $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ and $X$ partition $\mathbb{R}$ and both are dense, so density says nothing about size: one of them is countable and the other is not ([[cor-irrationals-uncountable]]). What density does say is that neither has interior: a set whose complement is dense has empty interior, which is the computation carried out for $\mathbb{Q}$ in [[ex-closure-interior-boundary-of-q]].

- **Claim 3 is a statement about open sets, not about intervals.** It follows from the uncountability of intervals ([[cor-interval-uncountable]]) only because openness supplies an interval inside the set at each of its points. A nonempty set with empty interior can perfectly well be countable, as $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ shows.

- **An explicit irrational is not produced here.** Step 2.1 is a counting argument and exhibits nothing. The library does exhibit one separately, $\sqrt 2$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]], [[fs-sqrt2-rational]]), and an explicit irrational in a given interval $(a,b)$ can be built from it as $q_1 + (q_2 - q_1)/\sqrt 2$ for suitable rationals $q_1 < q_2$ in the interval; that route is longer and is not the one taken above.

## Statement

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A random element $X$, its law $\mathbb P_X$, and a measurable map $g$ as in the Statement.

[L1] The law $\mathbb P_X$ is a probability measure on $(S,\Sigma)$ ([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]).

[L2] Measurable outer maps preserve measurability under composition ([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]).

[L3] Every nonnegative measurable function is the increasing limit of nonnegative simple functions, monotone convergence holds, and the nonnegative integral agrees with the simple integral on simple functions ([[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]], [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]], [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]]).

[L4] Expectation is integration against $\mathbb P$, and real or complex integrability uses the positive-negative and real-imaginary decompositions ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]).

[L5] Measurable functions are closed under the elementary operations used by the integral, and the Lebesgue integral is linear on $L^1$ ([[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L2], the composite $g\circ X$ is measurable. If $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{B_j}$ is a nonnegative simple function on $S$ with the $B_j$ pairwise disjoint, then $s\circ X=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{X^{-1}(B_j)}$ is a nonnegative simple function on $\Omega$. Using [L1], [L3], and [L4], $$\mathbb E[s(X)]=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\,\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B_j))=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\,\mathbb P_X(B_j)=\int_S s\,d\mathbb P_X.$$ [L1, L2, L3, L4]

2.1 Assume now that $g\ge0$. By [L3], choose nonnegative simple functions $s_n\uparrow g$ on $S$. Then $s_n\circ X\uparrow g\circ X$ by step 1.1, so monotone convergence on both spaces and step 1.1 give $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E[s_n(X)]=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_S s_n\,d\mathbb P_X=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$ [step 1.1, L3, L4]

3.1 Assume $g(X)$ is integrable. Then $\mathbb E[|g(X)|]<\infty$, so step 2.1 applied to $|g|$ gives $$\int_S |g|\,d\mathbb P_X=\mathbb E[|g(X)|]<\infty.$$ Hence $g$ is $\mathbb P_X$-integrable. For real-valued $g$, [L4] and [L5] give $g=g^+-g^-$ with both parts nonnegative, so step 2.1 and linearity yield $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\mathbb E[g^+(X)]-\mathbb E[g^-(X)]=\int_S g^+\,d\mathbb P_X-\int_S g^-\,d\mathbb P_X=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$ [step 2.1, L4, L5]

4.1 If $g$ is complex-valued, write $g=u+iv$ with real measurable parts $u,v$. The inequality $|u|,|v|\le|g|$ and step 3.1 show that $u(X)$ and $v(X)$ are integrable, so the real-valued case applied to $u$ and $v$, followed by complex-linearity from [L5], gives $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\mathbb E[u(X)]+i\mathbb E[v(X)]=\int_S u\,d\mathbb P_X+i\int_S v\,d\mathbb P_X=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$ [step 3.1, L4, L5]

5.1 Step 2.1 proves the nonnegative case, while steps 3.1 and 4.1 prove the integrable real and complex cases. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $\mathcal M$ be the class of all measurable predictors from $\mathsf X$ to $\mathsf A$. The **class Bayes risk** is $R_P^*(\mathcal F):=\inf_{f\in\mathcal F}R_P(f)$, and the **unrestricted Bayes risk** is $R_P^*:=\inf_{g\in\mathcal M}R_P(g)$. A class Bayes predictor is a member of $\mathcal F$ attaining the first infimum; an unrestricted Bayes predictor, also called a Bayes predictor, is a member of $\mathcal M$ attaining the second. No attainment is asserted. If an infimum is $+\infty$, every member of its nonempty class has infinite risk and attains that extended infimum, but no finite excess risk results.

For $f\in\mathcal F$ with both terms finite, its **class excess risk** is $R_P(f)-R_P^*(\mathcal F)$. For a measurable predictor $g\in\mathcal M$ with both terms finite, its **unrestricted excess risk** is $R_P(g)-R_P^*$. These differences are left undefined if either risk is infinite.

Write $P_X(C):=P(C\times\mathsf Y)$ for the instance marginal. If a regular conditional label law $K(x,dy)$ given $x$ is supplied, its **conditional risk** is $q(x,a):=\int_{\mathsf Y}\ell(a,y)K(x,dy)$. This function is measurable when the loss is product-measurable. A **conditional Bayes rule** is a measurable predictor that attains $\inf_{a\in\mathsf A}q(x,a)$ on one measurable set of full $P_X$-measure. Such a kernel exists under AC whenever the label space is standard Borel, even if the instance space is an arbitrary measurable space; if the label space is an arbitrary measurable space, no conditional law or measurable minimizer is asserted. When both instance and label spaces are standard Borel and AC holds, the conditional Bayes theorem shows that any such rule is an unrestricted Bayes predictor.

[[def-population-and-empirical-risk]]: defines $R_P(f)$ as the extended nonnegative population risk.

[[def-standard-borel-space]]: a standard Borel space is measurably isomorphic to a Polish space.

[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]: a regular conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the conditional-event integral identities.

[[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC asserts that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

[[lem-standard-borel-label-kernel-over-arbitrary-instance-space]]: under AC, a joint law with standard Borel label space admits an everywhere label-given-instance probability kernel even for an arbitrary measurable instance space.

[[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]: integration of a nonnegative product-measurable function against a probability kernel is measurable.

[[thm-conditional-bayes-rule-minimizes-population-risk]]: under standard-Borel and AC hypotheses, a measurable conditional minimizer is globally risk-minimizing.

[Kallenberg, *Foundations of Modern Probability*, 2nd ed., Theorem 6.3](https://djvu.online/file/t4FlvxuKFFZGW): a Borel target admits a conditional-distribution kernel from any measurable conditioning space.

## Definition

Given a sample $S$ of length $m\ge1$, an ordered finite nonempty list of measurable predictors $(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$, and a finite tolerance $\eta\ge0$, compute $r_j:=\widehat R_S(f_j)$ for each $j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$. If every $r_j=+\infty$, return index $1$. Otherwise set $r_*:=\min_{1\le j\le n}r_j$ and return the least index $j$ for which $r_j<+\infty$ and $r_j\le r_*+\eta$. The output index denotes the selected predictor from the supplied list. When $\eta=0$, the output is a first exact minimizer, including the all-infinite case. The algorithm evaluates only a finite number of empirical risks and makes no population-risk guarantee.

## Definition

Fix a positive sample size $m$, a nonempty predictor class $\mathcal F$, and a finite tolerance $\eta\ge0$. The input includes a supplied jointly measurable evaluation map $A_\eta: (\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y)^m\times\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ such that every sample slice $A_\eta(S,\cdot)$ belongs to $\mathcal F$. For each sample $S$, require that the slice is an exact empirical risk minimizer if $\widehat R_S^*(\mathcal F)=+\infty$, and otherwise has finite empirical risk at most $\widehat R_S^*(\mathcal F)+\eta$. The procedure returns the predictor $A_\eta(S,\cdot)$ on input $S$. Its selector is an explicit input; this procedure asserts no existence or construction of such a selector for an arbitrary class. In particular, $\eta=0$ requires attainment whenever the empirical minimum is finite.

## Statement

For a sample of positive length, a finite ordered nonempty list of measurable predictors, and finite tolerance $\eta\ge0$, let $J(S)$ be the index returned by the finite-list empirical-risk algorithm. Then $J$ is measurable into the finite index set with its discrete sigma-algebra, the evaluation map $(S,x)\mapsto f_{J(S)}(x)$ is jointly measurable, and the returned predictor is an $\eta$-approximate empirical risk minimizer as defined in the algorithm's input conditions. When $\eta=0$, it is an exact minimizer.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A supervised prediction problem, sample size $m\ge1$, an ordered list $(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$ of measurable predictors with $n\ge1$, and finite tolerance $\eta\ge0$.

[F1] The algorithm returns index $1$ when every list risk is infinite; otherwise it returns the first finite-risk index within $\eta$ of the finite list minimum. [[alg-finite-list-empirical-risk-minimizer]]

[F2] For each fixed predictor, the empirical-risk map on the sample space is extended-real measurable. [[lem-population-and-empirical-risk-are-measurable]]

[F3] A finite-list exact or approximate ERM is defined by its empirical risk relative to the list infimum, with a separate all-infinite case. [[def-empirical-risk-minimizer]]

[F4] Finite sums of measurable extended-real functions are measurable when pointwise defined; real scalar multiples of real-valued measurable functions, functions $f\mathbf1_E$ for nonnegative measurable extended-real $f$ and measurable $E$, countable infima, and increasing pointwise limits of measurable extended-real functions are measurable. [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]

[F5] The finite sample-and-instance product sigma-algebra contains measurable rectangles and is closed under finite unions and differences. [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]

[F6] An extended-real function is measurable when preimages of Borel sets, including the finite-value ray, are measurable. [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]

[F7] A map between measurable spaces is measurable exactly when preimages of measurable sets are measurable. [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]

## Proof

1.1 For $j=1,\ldots,n$, put $r_j(S)=\widehat R_S(f_j)$ and $r_*(S)=\min_j r_j(S)$. By [F2] each $r_j$ is measurable. The finite minimum is the infimum of the measurable sequence $r_1,\ldots,r_n,r_n,r_n,\ldots$, so [F4] makes $r_*$ measurable. Thus $E:=\{S:r_*(S)<+\infty\}$ is measurable by [F6]. [F2, F4, F6]

2.1 Define finite nonnegative measurable functions $u_j:=r_j\mathbf1_{\{r_j<+\infty\}}$ and $u_*:=r_*\mathbf1_E$. Their measurability follows from [F4], including the convention $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$. The sets $\{r_j<+\infty\}$ and $E$ are measurable by [F6]. On $E$, $u_*=r_*$ and each finite $r_j$ equals $u_j$, so $C_j:=E\cap\{r_j<+\infty\}\cap\{u_j-u_*\le\eta\}$ is measurable by [F4, F6]. At every $S\in E$ a finite minimizing index lies in some $C_j$. [F1, F4, F6, step 1.1]

3.1 The algorithm's selected-index events are $\{J=1\}=E^c\cup C_1$ and, for $j>1$, $\{J=j\}=C_j\setminus\bigcup_{k<j}C_k$. They are measurable by step 2.1, so $J$ is measurable into the finite discrete index set by [F7]. For each measurable $B\subseteq\mathsf A$, the evaluation preimage is $\bigcup_{j=1}^n(\{J=j\}\times f_j^{-1}(B))$, a finite union of measurable rectangles by [F5]; hence $(S,x)\mapsto f_{J(S)}(x)$ is jointly measurable by [F7]. [F1, F5, F7, step 2.1]

4.1 On $E^c$ all list risks are $+\infty$, so the returned first predictor is an exact minimizer by [F3]. On $E$, at least one finite minimizer exists in the finite list, belongs to some $C_j$, and the first selected $C_j$ has finite risk at most $r_*+\eta$ by its definition. If $\eta=0$, this inequality forces the selected risk to equal $r_*$. Thus the output has the asserted ERM property in both branches. [F1, F3, given, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Example

Let $\mathsf X=\{u,v\}$ with its discrete sigma-algebra, let $\mathsf Y=\{0,2,4,6\}$ with its discrete sigma-algebra, let the action space be $\mathsf A=\mathbb R$ with its Borel sigma-algebra, and let $\mathcal F$ be all functions from $\mathsf X$ to $\mathbb R$. Define $X(x,y)=x$ and $Y(x,y)=y$ on $\Omega=\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$. Give the joint law by
$$P(u,0)=\tfrac18,\quad P(u,2)=\tfrac14,\quad P(u,4)=\tfrac18,\quad P(v,2)=\tfrac14,\quad P(v,6)=\tfrac14,$$
with all other atoms having probability zero, and set $P_X(x):=\sum_yP(x,y)$. Use squared loss $\ell(a,y)=(a-y)^2$. For $x\in\{u,v\}$ define the conditional mean $m(x):=\sum_y yP(x,y)/P_X(x)$. Then $m(u)=2$ and $m(v)=4$, and the predictor $f^*(x)=m(x)$ uniquely minimizes population squared risk over $\mathcal F$, with risk $3$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite spaces, joint law, real-valued predictor class and squared loss stated in the example.

[F1] Population risk is the expectation of the nonnegative loss under the joint law. [[def-population-and-empirical-risk]]

[F2] On a positive-probability event in a finite probability space, conditional expectation is the normalized finite weighted sum. [[lem-finite-event-conditional-expectation-formula]]

[F3] Expectation splits over a finite positive-probability partition as the probability-weighted sum of the conditional expectations. [[lem-finite-event-conditional-expectation-formula]]

1.1 The displayed atom weights sum to one and $P_X(u)=P_X(v)=1/2$. Applying [F2] to the two events $\{X=u\}$ and $\{X=v\}$ gives conditional means $m(u)=2$, $m(v)=4$, and conditional second moments $E[Y^2\mid X=u]=6$, $E[Y^2\mid X=v]=20$. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 For any predictor $g$, expansion on each event gives $E[(g(u)-Y)^2\mid X=u]=(g(u)-2)^2+2$ and $E[(g(v)-Y)^2\mid X=v]=(g(v)-4)^2+4$. The partition identity in [F3] and [F1] therefore give $R_P(g)=\tfrac12((g(u)-2)^2+2)+\tfrac12((g(v)-4)^2+4)\ge3$, with equality exactly when $g(u)=2$ and $g(v)=4$. [F1, F3, given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

    - title: "Charles M. Grinstead and J. Laurie Snell, Introduction to Probability, 2nd ed., Chapter 6 §6.1, Definition 6.2 and Theorem 6.5"
      url: "https://chance.dartmouth.edu/teaching_aids/books_articles/probability_book/Chapter6.pdf"
