## Statement

Let $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m$ be independent random variables with values in $\{-1,+1\}$, let $c_1,\ldots,c_m\in\mathbb R$, and put $V=\sum_{i=1}^m c_i^2$ and $S=\sum_{i=1}^m c_i(\xi_i-\mathbb E\xi_i)$. For every $t>0$, if $V>0$ then
$$\mathbb P(S\ge t)\le e^{-t^2/(2V)},\qquad \mathbb P(S\le-t)\le e^{-t^2/(2V)},\qquad \mathbb P(|S|\ge t)\le2e^{-t^2/(2V)}.$$
If $V=0$, then $S=0$ almost surely and all three tail probabilities are zero. The empty sum $m=0$ is included with $V=S=0$.

## Statement references

[Schmidt et al., Appendix F.2, Lemma 29 and Theorem 31 proof, PDF pp. 33–37](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.11285v2).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite independent family of sign-valued random variables, real coefficients, and $t>0$.

[A1] No choice axiom is used; every construction and product is finite.

[F1] Independence means independence of the sigma-algebras generated by the random variables. [[def-independent-random-elements]].

[F2] Expectations are Lebesgue integrals against the probability law. [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].

[F3] For a nonnegative random variable $U$ and $a>0$, $\mathbb P(U\ge a)\le\mathbb E[U]/a$. [[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]].

[F4] The natural logarithm differentiates as $1/x$, and $\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y)$. [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]], [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]], [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]].

[F5] A finite union of events has probability at most the sum of its event probabilities. [[thm-finite-union-bound]].

[F6] For independent real random variables and nonnegative Borel functions, the expectation of their finite product factors, including extended-valued expectations. [[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]].

## Proof

1.1 For one sign variable $\xi$ with $p=\mathbb P(\xi=+1)$ and $\mu=\mathbb E\xi=2p-1$, put $\psi(s)=\log\mathbb E e^{s(\xi-\mu)}$. The two-point formula gives $\psi(s)=\log(pe^s+(1-p)e^{-s})-s\mu$, so $\psi(0)=\psi'(0)=0$ and $\psi''(s)=\frac{4p(1-p)}{(pe^s+(1-p)e^{-s})^2}\le1$. The inequality follows from $4ab\le(a+b)^2$ with $a=pe^s$ and $b=(1-p)e^{-s}$. Integrating the second-derivative bound twice from $0$ to $s$, in either direction, gives $\psi(s)\le s^2/2$ for every real $s$; if $p=0$ or $p=1$, $\psi$ is identically zero and the same bound holds. [given, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 Apply step 1.1 to each $\xi_i$ with $s=\lambda c_i$. The functions $x\mapsto e^{\lambda c_i(x-\mathbb E\xi_i)}$ are nonnegative Borel functions, so [F6] factors their expectations; [F4] combines the exponentials. Thus $\mathbb E e^{\lambda S}=\prod_{i=1}^m\mathbb E e^{\lambda c_i(\xi_i-\mathbb E\xi_i)}\le \exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda^2}{2}\sum_{i=1}^m c_i^2\right)=e^{\lambda^2V/2}$ for every real $\lambda$. [step 1.1, F4, F6, algebra, F1]

3.1 Suppose $V>0$ and choose $\lambda=t/V>0$. Markov's inequality [F3] applied to $e^{\lambda S}$ and the MGF bound in step 2.1 give $\mathbb P(S\ge t)\le e^{-\lambda t+\lambda^2V/2}=e^{-t^2/(2V)}$. Applying the same argument to $-S$ gives $\mathbb P(S\le-t)\le e^{-t^2/(2V)}$. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F5], $\mathbb P(|S|\ge t)\le\mathbb P(S\ge t)+\mathbb P(S\le-t)$, which gives the stated two-sided bound from step 3.1. If $V=0$, every $c_i=0$, so $S=0$ almost surely; the empty-sum case is the same. [F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## References

[[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]]: the MGF bound is converted to a tail by Markov's inequality.

[[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]]: factors the expectations of the nonnegative exponential functions of the independent signs.

[[thm-finite-union-bound]]: combines the two one-sided tails.

## Statement

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The exponential power series.

[L1] A real power series may be differentiated termwise inside its radius ([[thm-termwise-differentiation-of-a-real-power-series]]), and its sum is smooth there ([[cor-power-series-sums-are-smooth-with-coefficient-formula]]).

[L2] The radius is infinite, $(n+1)!=(n+1)n!$, and the canonical embedding preserves products and sends positive naturals to nonzero reals ([[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]], [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], [[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Termwise differentiation gives $(\exp)'(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}\iota(n)x^{n-1}/\iota(n!)$.  [L1, L2]

2.1 Reindex $n=j+1$ and cancel $\iota(j+1)$ using the factorial recurrence. The series becomes $\sum_{j\ge0}x^j/\iota(j!)=\exp(x)$.  [step 1.1, L2, algebra]

3.1 Smoothness follows from [L1] and the infinite radius; iterating step 2.1 gives every higher derivative.  [step 2.1, L1, L2] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, $0<\tau\le1/4$, and let $n\ge0$ be an integer with $n\le\tau^{-2}$. Draw $\Theta$ uniformly from $\{-1,+1\}^d$ and, conditionally on $\Theta$, draw $n$ independent observations $S=((X_i,Y_i))_{i=1}^n$ from the binary-feature Bernoulli model with parameters $\Theta,\tau$. For each coordinate $j$, define the posterior log odds $L_j(S):=\log\bigl(\mathbb P(\Theta_j=+1\mid S)/\mathbb P(\Theta_j=-1\mid S)\bigr)$; these probabilities are positive for every sample because $\tau<1/2$. Then for every $j$ and every sample $S$,
$$L_j(S)=\log\!\left(\frac{1+2\tau}{1-2\tau}\right)\sum_{i=1}^nY_iX_{ij}.$$Moreover, the coordinates of $\Theta$ are conditionally independent given $S$. For every $0<\delta<1$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over the joint prior-sample experiment,$$\max_{1\le j\le d}|L_j(S)|\le15\tau\sqrt{2n\log\!\left(\frac{2d}{\delta}\right)}.$$

## Statement references

[Schmidt et al., Appendix F.2, Lemma 29 and Theorem 31 proof, PDF pp. 34–37](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.11285v2).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

[F1] Under fixed $\Theta=\theta$, the signs $Y_iX_{ij}\theta_j$ are independent over $i$ and each equals $+1$ with probability $1/2+\tau$ and $-1$ with probability $1/2-\tau$. [[def-binary-feature-bernoulli-model]].

[F2] The natural logarithm converts finite products to sums and satisfies $\log b-\log a=\int_a^b dx/x$ for $0<a\le b$. [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]], [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]].

[F3] For independent sign variables and coefficients $c_i$, the centered sum has tails $\mathbb P(|\sum_i c_i(\xi_i-\mathbb E\xi_i)|\ge t)\le2e^{-t^2/(2\sum_i c_i^2)}$. [[lem-finite-independent-sign-sum-tail]].

[F4] A union of finitely many events has probability at most the sum of their probabilities. [[thm-finite-union-bound]].

## Proof

1.1 Fix a sample $S=((x_i,y_i))_{i=1}^n$. The prior mass of each $\theta$ is $2^{-d}$, and the likelihood factors over coordinates because the model's conditional coordinate probabilities do. Write $L_j(t)=\prod_i[(1/2+\tau)\mathbf1_{\{y_ix_{ij}=t\}}+(1/2-\tau)\mathbf1_{\{y_ix_{ij}=-t\}}]$ for $t\in\{-1,+1\}$. The posterior mass at $\theta$ is proportional to $\prod_jL_j(\theta_j)$, and its normalizing sum is $\prod_j(L_j(+1)+L_j(-1))$; hence it factors as a product of coordinate posterior masses, proving conditional independence. The $j$th marginal odds are $L_j(+1)/L_j(-1)=((1/2+\tau)/(1/2-\tau))^{\sum_i y_ix_{ij}}$. Bayes' finite formula and [F2] give the displayed log identity. Positivity of both coordinate probabilities makes each posterior denominator nonzero. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Put $a_\tau=\log((1+2\tau)/(1-2\tau))$. With $x=2\tau\le1/2$, [F2] gives $a_\tau=2\int_0^x(1-u^2)^{-1}\,du$. For $0\le u\le1/2$, $(1-u^2)^{-1}=1+u^2/(1-u^2)\le1+4u^2/3$, so $a_\tau\le2x+8x^3/9=4\tau+64\tau^3/9\le40\tau/9<5\tau$. [F2, algebra]

1.3 Assume $n>0$, fix $\theta$ and $j$, and put $\xi_i=\theta_jY_iX_{ij}$. By [F1], these are independent signs with mean $2\tau$. Let $t=\sqrt{2n\log(2d/\delta)}$. [F3] with all coefficients equal to one gives conditional failure probability at most $2e^{-t^2/(2n)}=\delta/d$ for $|\sum_i(\xi_i-2\tau)|>t$. Since $|\sum_iY_iX_{ij}|=|\sum_i\xi_i|$, this proves $\mathbb P(|\sum_iY_iX_{ij}|>2\tau n+t\mid\Theta=\theta)\le\delta/d$. By [F4] and averaging over the finite prior, with probability at least $1-\delta$ every coordinate obeys $|\sum_iY_iX_{ij}|\le2\tau n+t$. [given, F1, F3, F4]

2.1 Since $n\le\tau^{-2}$, $\tau n\le\sqrt n$. Also $2d/\delta\ge2$ and $\log2=\int_1^2 dx/x>1/2$, so $t\ge\sqrt n$. On the event from step 1.3, step 1.1 and step 1.2 now yield $|L_j(S)|\le5\tau(2\tau n+t)\le15\tau t$ for every $j$, which is the asserted bound. If $n=0$, the posterior equals the uniform prior, so every $L_j=0$ and the claimed bound holds with equality. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, F2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For $w\in\mathbb R^d$, let $f_w(x)=+1$ when $\langle w,x\rangle\ge0$ and $f_w(x)=-1$ otherwise. In the following lower-bound branch, let $d\ge1$, $0<\tau\le1/4$, $0<\gamma<1/2$, and $0\le\epsilon<3\tau$. Draw $\Theta$ uniformly from $\{-1,+1\}^d$ and, conditional on $\Theta$, draw $n\ge0$ independent training observations $S$ from the binary-feature Bernoulli model with parameters $\Theta,\tau$. Let $g_n$ be any function from the finite sample space to $\mathbb R^d$, set $w=g_n(S)$, and use $f_w$. If
$$n\le\frac{\epsilon^2\gamma^2}{5000\tau^4\log(4d/\gamma)},$$
then the expected robust risk for the closed threat $\Delta_\epsilon(x)=\{x+\delta:\|\delta\|_\infty\le\epsilon\}$ of $f_w$, averaged over $\Theta,S$, and a fresh test pair from $P_{\Theta,\tau}$, is at least $1/2-\gamma$.

In the separate thresholded upper-bound branch, let $d\ge1$, $0<\tau\le1/2$, $0<\beta<1$, and let $\theta\in\{-1,+1\}^d$ satisfy $\tau\ge(\log(1/\beta)/(2d))^{1/4}$. Draw one training pair $(X_0,Y_0)$ from $P_{\theta,\tau}$, set $W=Y_0X_0$, and define $T:\mathbb R^d\to\{-1,+1\}^d$ by $T(x)_j=+1$ when $x_j\ge0$ and $T(x)_j=-1$ otherwise. Then for every $0\le\epsilon<1$, with training-sample probability at least $1-e^{-\tau^2d/2}$, the robust risk for the closed threat $\Delta_\epsilon(x)=\{x+\delta:\|\delta\|_\infty\le\epsilon\}$ of $f_W\circ T$ under $P_{\theta,\tau}$ is at most $\beta$.

## Statement references

[Schmidt et al., Theorem 10, Corollary 28 and Theorem 31, main text and Appendix B, PDF pp. 7, 31–37](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.11285v2).

[Kolter–Madry, Chapter 2, linear classification and $\ell_\infty$ geometry](https://adversarial-ml-tutorial.org/linear_models/).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement; each branch is proved with its own parameter and probability quantifiers.

[F1] In the Bernoulli model, conditional on $\Theta=\theta$, the signs $Y_iX_{ij}\theta_j$ are independent over observations and coordinates and have mean $2\tau$. [[def-binary-feature-bernoulli-model]], [[def-independent-random-elements]].

[F2] For the uniform hypercube prior, conditional on a sample $S$ the parameter coordinates are independent and their log odds are $L_j(S)=\log((1+2\tau)/(1-2\tau))\sum_iY_iX_{ij}$. If $n\le\tau^{-2}$, then with probability at least $1-\delta$, all $|L_j(S)|\le15\tau\sqrt{2n\log(2d/\delta)}$. [[lem-bernoulli-coordinate-posterior-odds-bound]].

[F3] A finite independent sign sum with coefficients $c_j$ satisfies $\mathbb P(\sum_jc_j(\xi_j-\mathbb E\xi_j)\le-t)\le e^{-t^2/(2\sum_jc_j^2)}$ for $t>0$. [[lem-finite-independent-sign-sum-tail]].

[F4] If $A\ge0$ and $b>0$, then $\mathbb P(A>b)\le\mathbb E[A]/b$. [[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]].

[F5] The natural logarithm is increasing and $\log(x/y)=\log x-\log y$; $\log b-\log a=\int_a^b du/u$ for $0<a\le b$. [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]], [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]].

[F6] $e^x=\sum_{k\ge0}x^k/k!$ for real $x$. [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]].

[F7] Finite integrable sums have expectation equal to the sum of expectations. [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]].

[F8] Under the closed $\ell_\infty$ threat, robust zero-one loss is one exactly when some admissible perturbation changes the label. [[def-adversarial-threat-set-and-robust-risk]].

[F9] The coordinate threshold rule has $T(x)_j=+1$ for $x_j\ge0$ and $-1$ for $x_j<0$. [[alg-coordinate-threshold-preprocessing]].

## Proof

1.1 For the lower-bound branch put $\Lambda=\log(4d/\gamma)$. Since $4d/\gamma>8$ and $\log8=3\log2>3/2>1$ by [F5], the sample-size hypothesis and $\epsilon<3\tau$, $\gamma<1/2$ imply $n<9/(20000\tau^2)<\tau^{-2}$. Apply [F2] with $\delta=\gamma/2$. With probability at least $1-\gamma/2$ over $(\Theta,S)$, every posterior log odds obeys $|L_j(S)|\le B:=15\tau\sqrt{2n\Lambda}$. Moreover $B\le(3/10)\epsilon\gamma/\tau<9/20<1$. [given, F2, F5, algebra]

1.2 For the thresholded upper branch, fix $\theta$ and a training pair $(X_0,Y_0)$. The signs $R_j=Y_0X_{0j}\theta_j$ are independent with mean $2\tau$ by [F1]. Apply [F3] with coefficients all one and $t=\tau d$ to obtain $\mathbb P(\langle W,\theta\rangle\le\tau d)\le e^{-\tau^2d/2}$. Outside this event, $u=W/\sqrt d$ is unit and $\langle u,\theta\rangle>\tau\sqrt d$. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 Write $m_j(S)=\mathbb E[\Theta_j\mid S]$. If $r_j=e^{L_j(S)}$ is the posterior odds, then $m_j=(r_j-1)/(r_j+1)$ by the inverse relation in [F5], so on the event in step 1.1, $|m_j|\le(e^B-1)/2$. For $0\le x\le1$, [F6] and $x^k\le x$ give $e^x-1\le x\sum_{k\ge1}1/k!=(e-1)x<2x$: indeed induction using $k+1\ge2$ gives $k!\ge2^{k-1}$ for $k\ge1$, strictly for some $k$, so $e<1+1+\sum_{k\ge2}2^{-(k-1)}=3$. Therefore $|m_j|\le B$. Set $a:=2\tau B=30\tau^2\sqrt{2n\Lambda}$. The sample-size condition yields $a\le(3/5)\epsilon\gamma<9\tau/10\le9/40<1$ and $a/\gamma\le3\epsilon/5<\epsilon$ when $\epsilon>0$. [step 1.1, F2, F5, F6, algebra]

2.2 Fix a sample $S$ in the event of step 1.1 and its learned vector $w$. Conditional on $S$, the posterior coordinates $\Theta_j$ are independent by [F2]. For a fresh pair put $Q_j=YX_j$. Conditional on $\Theta_j=t$, $Q_j=t$ with probability $1/2+\tau$ and $Q_j=-t$ with probability $1/2-\tau$, independently across coordinates and independently of the value of $Y$. Averaging over the product posterior shows that the $Q_j$ are independent of one another and of $Y$, with $\mathbb E[Q_j\mid S]=2\tau m_j(S)$. [given, F1, F2]

2.3 For a fresh pair, the signs $R_j=YX_j\theta_j$ are independent with mean $2\tau$. The signed margin of $f_W$ is $Y\langle u,X\rangle=\sum_j u_j\theta_jR_j$, whose mean is $2\tau\langle u,\theta\rangle$ and whose centered coefficient square-sum is $\sum_j(u_j\theta_j)^2=1$. If $f_W(X)\ne Y$, then this signed margin is at most zero under the stated tie rule. By [F3], its probability is at most $\exp(-2\tau^2\langle u,\theta\rangle^2)\le e^{-2\tau^4d}\le\beta$, where the last inequality is the assumed lower bound on $\tau$. [step 1.2, F1, F3, F5, algebra]

3.1 For each $j$ with $w_j\ne0$, the sign $V_j:=\operatorname{sgn}(w_j)Q_j$ has mean at most $a$ and is supported on $\{-1,+1\}$. Couple independent signs $E_j$ of mean $a$ using independent uniform variables so that $V_j\le E_j$ coordinatewise: if $p_j=\mathbb P(V_j=+1\mid S)\le(1+a)/2$, use the same uniform variable to set $V_j=+1$ below $p_j$ and $E_j=+1$ below $(1+a)/2$. Coordinates with $w_j=0$ contribute zero. Thus the margin $M:=\sum_jw_jQ_j$ is stochastically at most $\widetilde M:=\sum_j|w_j|E_j$. [step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Represent each $E_j=A_j+B_j$, where $A_j$ is Bernoulli with mean $a$, $B_j=0$ if $A_j=1$, and conditional on $A_j=0$, $B_j$ is a uniform sign. Then $\mathbb E\sum_j|w_j|A_j=a\|w\|_1$. If $w\ne0$ and $a>0$, [F4] gives $\mathbb P(\sum_j|w_j|A_j>a\|w\|_1/\gamma)\le\gamma$. Conditional on the vector $(A_j)$, the sum $\sum_j|w_j|B_j$ is symmetric about zero, so it is nonpositive with probability at least $1/2$. Hence $\mathbb P(\widetilde M\le a\|w\|_1/\gamma)\ge(1-\gamma)/2$, and step 3.1 gives the same lower bound for $\mathbb P(M\le a\|w\|_1/\gamma\mid S)$. The same conclusion holds if $a=0$ by taking $A_j=0$ surely. If $w=0$, the constant classifier has robust error $1/2$ under the balanced labels. [step 3.1, F4, F7]

5.1 Suppose $\epsilon>0$ and $w\ne0$. On the event in step 4.1, step 2.1 gives $M\le(a/\gamma)\|w\|_1<\epsilon\|w\|_1$. For the fresh label $Y$, choose $\delta_j=-\epsilon Y$ if $w_j>0$, choose $\delta_j=+\epsilon Y$ if $w_j<0$, and choose $\delta_j=0$ if $w_j=0$. By [F8], $\|\delta\|_\infty\le\epsilon$ and $Y\langle w,X+\delta\rangle=M-\epsilon\|w\|_1<0$, so this perturbation misclassifies. Thus on every good training sample the posterior-averaged robust risk is at least $(1-\gamma)/2$. If $\epsilon=0$, the sample-size hypothesis forces $n=0$; after averaging the uniform prior, $X$ is uniform on the hypercube independently of $Y$, so every classifier has natural and robust error $1/2$. [step 2.1, step 4.1, F1, F8]

6.1 The good training-sample event has probability at least $1-\gamma/2$ by step 1.1. The expected robust risk is therefore at least $(1-\gamma/2)(1-\gamma)/2\ge1/2-\gamma$, since the difference is $\gamma/4+\gamma^2/4\ge0$. The zero-weight and $\epsilon=0$ cases in step 5.1 satisfy the same final bound. [step 1.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 If $x\in\{-1,+1\}^d$ and $\|\delta\|_\infty\le\epsilon<1$, then $x_j+\delta_j>0$ when $x_j=+1$ and $x_j+\delta_j<0$ when $x_j=-1$. By [F9], $T(x+\delta)=x$ coordinatewise. Thus every allowed adversarial perturbation leaves $f_W(T(x+\delta))=f_W(x)$, so its robust error equals the natural error bounded in step 2.3. The failure probability is at most $e^{-\tau^2d/2}$ by step 1.2. [step 1.2, step 2.3, F9, algebra] ∎

[[lem-finite-independent-sign-sum-tail]]: supplies the choice-free sign concentration used in both Bernoulli branches.

[[alg-coordinate-threshold-preprocessing]]: supplies the coordinatewise sign threshold with zero mapped to $+1$.

## Example

Let $d\ge1$, $\theta\in\{-1,+1\}^d$, $0<\tau\le1/2$, $0\le\epsilon<1$, and let $(X,Y)\sim P_{\theta,\tau}$ be the binary-feature Bernoulli model. Let $T(x)_j=+1$ for $x_j\ge0$ and $T(x)_j=-1$ for $x_j<0$. For every classifier $g:\{-1,+1\}^d\to\{-1,+1\}$, the classifier $g\circ T$ has exactly the same $\ell_\infty$ robust risk at radius $\epsilon$ as $g$ has natural risk:
$$R^{\mathrm{rob}}_{P_{\theta,\tau},\Delta_\epsilon}(g\circ T)=\mathbb P(g(X)\ne Y).$$
For $w\in\mathbb R^d$, define $f_w(x)=+1$ when $\langle w,x\rangle\ge0$ and $f_w(x)=-1$ otherwise. In particular, if $0<\beta<1$ and $\tau\ge(\log(1/\beta)/(2d))^{1/4}$, then the one-sample classifier $f_{Y_0X_0}\circ T$ has robust risk at most $\beta$ with training-sample probability at least $1-e^{-\tau^2d/2}$.

## Example references

[Schmidt et al., Theorem 10 and Corollary 28, main text and Appendix B.1, PDF pp. 7, 31–32](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.11285v2).

[Kolter–Madry, Chapter 2, thresholding and linear models](https://adversarial-ml-tutorial.org/linear_models/).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Example.

[F1] The Bernoulli model is supported on $\{-1,+1\}^d\times\{-1,+1\}$. [[def-binary-feature-bernoulli-model]].

[F2] $T$ maps a nonnegative coordinate to $+1$ and a negative coordinate to $-1$. [[alg-coordinate-threshold-preprocessing]].

[F3] Robust zero-one loss is one exactly when some admissible perturbation changes the label; robust risk is the expectation of this loss. [[def-adversarial-threat-set-and-robust-risk]].

[F4] Under the stated $\tau,\beta$ condition, the one-sample thresholded Bernoulli classifier has robust risk at most $\beta$ with the stated training-sample probability. [[thm-architecture-dependent-robustness-binary-feature-model]].

## Proof

1.1 Fix $x\in\{-1,+1\}^d$ and any $\delta$ with $\|\delta\|_\infty\le\epsilon<1$. If $x_j=+1$, then $x_j+\delta_j\ge1-\epsilon>0$, so [F2] gives $T(x+\delta)_j=+1=x_j$. If $x_j=-1$, then $x_j+\delta_j\le-1+\epsilon<0$, so $T(x+\delta)_j=-1=x_j$. Hence $T(x+\delta)=x$ for every admissible perturbation. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 For each support point $(x,y)$, every allowed perturbation therefore makes $g(T(x+\delta))=g(x)$. The robust zero-one loss of $g\circ T$ equals $\mathbf1\{g(x)\ne y\}$ pointwise. Taking expectation under $P_{\theta,\tau}$ proves the displayed equality. [step 1.1, F3]

3.1 Under the final $\tau,\beta$ condition, [F4] gives the one-sample risk bound for $f_{Y_0X_0}\circ T$ with the stated probability. The pointwise identity in step 2.1 explains why every radius $\epsilon<1$ has the same risk. [step 2.1, F4] ∎

## References

[[def-binary-feature-bernoulli-model]]: the support is exactly the sign hypercube with a binary label.

[[thm-architecture-dependent-robustness-binary-feature-model]]: supplies the one-sample high-probability error guarantee.

## Definition

Let $\Sigma$ and $\mathcal B$ be nonempty finite sets of feature types and score bins. For each group $t\in\{1,2\}$, let $N_t>0$ be its total mass and let $a_{t\sigma}\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}a_{t\sigma}=1$. Let $p_\sigma\in[0,1]$ be the probability of the positive binary outcome $Y=1$ for feature type $\sigma$, with the same $p_\sigma$ in both groups. A randomized risk assignment consists of scores $v_b\in[0,1]$ for $b\in\mathcal B$ and a single matrix $X_{\sigma b}\ge0$ with $\sum_{b\in\mathcal B}X_{\sigma b}=1$ for each $\sigma$; conditional on feature type $\sigma$, the assignment chooses bin $b$ with probability $X_{\sigma b}$, independently of group and outcome. Thus, for a group-$t$ individual chosen according to its feature distribution, $\Pr_t(\Sigma=\sigma,Y=1,B=b)=a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}$ and $\Pr_t(\Sigma=\sigma,Y=0,B=b)=a_{t\sigma}(1-p_\sigma)X_{\sigma b}$, and the assigned score is $S=v_B$. The expected positive mass is $\mu_t=N_t\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma$, and the group base rate is $\rho_t=\mu_t/N_t$.

The assignment is **calibrated within group $t$** if for every $b\in\mathcal B$,
$$
\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}=v_b\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}a_{t\sigma}X_{\sigma b}.
$$
This cross-multiplied condition also covers bins with zero assigned mass. The instance permits perfect prediction when $p_\sigma\in\{0,1\}$ for every feature type with $a_{1\sigma}+a_{2\sigma}>0$; a score assignment is perfectly predictive when $S=Y$ almost surely in each group.

## Definition references

[[def-probability-calibration]]: within each group, full reliability of the binary forecast $(1-S,S)$ gives the calibration identity for each distinct score value. This is the per-bin identity above when every score value occurs in only one bin; if distinct bins share a score, full reliability gives only the aggregate identity across those bins.

[Kleinberg, Mullainathan, and Raghavan, complete 23-page paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1609.05807v2): §§1.1–1.2 define the finite feature-type, group, randomized-bin model and calibration within each group.

[Applied Statistics: From Data to Decisions, full chapter](https://stanford-mse-125.github.io/book/lec20-fairness.html): the section “The impossibility: you cannot satisfy them all” treats calibration within groups for real-valued scores and distinguishes the score theorem from its binary-classifier companion.

## Definition

Let $\Sigma$ and $\mathcal B$ be nonempty finite sets, and let $t\in\{1,2\}$ index two groups. In group $t$, feature type $\sigma$ has proportion $a_{t\sigma}\ge0$, where $\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}=1$, and total mass $N_t>0$. The positive binary outcome $Y=1$ has probability $p_\sigma\in[0,1]$ for feature type $\sigma$, with the same $p_\sigma$ in both groups. A common randomized assignment sends feature type $\sigma$ to bin $b\in\mathcal B$ with probability $X_{\sigma b}\ge0$, where $\sum_bX_{\sigma b}=1$, independently of group and outcome; bin $b$ has score $v_b\in[0,1]$. Set $\rho_t=\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma$ and $\mu_t=N_t\rho_t$. Assume $0<\mu_t<N_t$ for each group, so both outcome classes have positive mass. Define the mean score among positive outcomes and among negative outcomes in group $t$ by
$$
\alpha_t=\frac{\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}\sum_{b\in\mathcal B}a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}v_b}{\rho_t},\qquad \beta_t=\frac{\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}\sum_{b\in\mathcal B}a_{t\sigma}(1-p_\sigma)X_{\sigma b}v_b}{1-\rho_t},
$$
where the finite group law is $\Pr_t(\Sigma=\sigma,Y=1,B=b)=a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}$ and $\Pr_t(\Sigma=\sigma,Y=0,B=b)=a_{t\sigma}(1-p_\sigma)X_{\sigma b}$. The assignment is **balanced for positive outcomes** if $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$, and **balanced for negative outcomes** if $\beta_1=\beta_2$. These are class-conditioned mean-score criteria; they do not assert equal mean scores over whole groups or equal thresholded error rates.

## Definition references

[Kleinberg, Mullainathan, and Raghavan, complete 23-page paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1609.05807v2): §1.1 defines balance for the negative and positive classes as equality of the corresponding groupwise mean assigned scores.

[Applied Statistics: From Data to Decisions, full chapter](https://stanford-mse-125.github.io/book/lec20-fairness.html): the section “The impossibility: you cannot satisfy them all” states both score-balance criteria and distinguishes them from the binary-classifier theorem.

## Statement

Fix a group $t\in\{1,2\}$ with a finite joint law $\Pr_t$ for a binary outcome $Y\in\{0,1\}$ and a score $S$ taking finitely many values in $[0,1]$, and assume $\Pr_t(Y=1)>0$ and $\Pr_t(Y=0)>0$. For each threshold $u\in[0,1]$, define the true-positive rate $\operatorname{TPR}_t(u)=\Pr_t(S\ge u\mid Y=1)$ and the false-positive rate $\operatorname{FPR}_t(u)=\Pr_t(S\ge u\mid Y=0)$. These are finite step functions and
$$
\mathbb E_t[S\mid Y=1]=\int_0^1\operatorname{TPR}_t(u)\,du,\qquad \mathbb E_t[S\mid Y=0]=\int_0^1\operatorname{FPR}_t(u)\,du.
$$
The integrals are ordinary Riemann integrals of the finite step functions.

## Statement references

[[def-group-risk-score-and-calibration]]: provides the finite group-conditional law and the finite $[0,1]$-valued score used in this statement.

[Kleinberg, Mullainathan, and Raghavan, complete 23-page paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1609.05807v2): §§1.1–2 define groupwise positive/negative score means and use these class-conditioned score distributions in Theorem 1.1.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A group $t\in\{1,2\}$ in the finite-bin risk-score model. Write its distinct score values as $s_1,\ldots,s_m$; conditional on $Y=1$ let their probabilities be $w_j^+$, and conditional on $Y=0$ let them be $w_j^-$. Prove that each class-conditional mean score is the area under its corresponding threshold rate.

[F1] [[def-group-risk-score-and-calibration]]: the feature, outcome, bin, and score variables have a finite joint law in each group, and each score value lies in $[0,1]$.

## Proof

1.1 For each $j$, the threshold indicator is $\mathbf1_{[0,s_j]}(u)$. Hence $\operatorname{TPR}_t(u)=\sum_{j=1}^m w_j^+\mathbf1_{[0,s_j]}(u)$. Integrating this finite sum term by term gives $\int_0^1\operatorname{TPR}_t(u)\,du=\sum_{j=1}^m w_j^+s_j=\mathbb E_t[S\mid Y=1]$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The same indicator calculation gives $\operatorname{FPR}_t(u)=\sum_{j=1}^m w_j^-\mathbf1_{[0,s_j]}(u)$ and $\int_0^1\operatorname{FPR}_t(u)\,du=\sum_{j=1}^m w_j^-s_j=\mathbb E_t[S\mid Y=0]$. [given, F1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The identity uses only finite support; no interchange theorem or choice principle is needed.

## Statement

Let $\Sigma$ and $\mathcal B$ be nonempty finite sets. In group $t\in\{1,2\}$, feature type $\sigma\in\Sigma$ has proportion $a_{t\sigma}\ge0$, where $\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}=1$, and total mass $N_t>0$. The positive binary outcome $Y=1$ has probability $p_\sigma\in[0,1]$ for feature type $\sigma$, with $p_\sigma$ the same in both groups. A common randomized assignment chooses bin $b\in\mathcal B$ from feature type $\sigma$ with probability $X_{\sigma b}\ge0$, where $\sum_bX_{\sigma b}=1$; this choice is independent of group and outcome. Bin $b$ has score $v_b\in[0,1]$, and $S=v_B$. Define $\rho_t=\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma$ and $\mu_t=N_t\rho_t$. Assume $0<\mu_t<N_t$ for both groups. Define the positive- and negative-outcome mean scores by
$$
\alpha_t=\frac{\sum_{\sigma,b}a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}v_b}{\rho_t},\qquad \beta_t=\frac{\sum_{\sigma,b}a_{t\sigma}(1-p_\sigma)X_{\sigma b}v_b}{1-\rho_t}.
$$
Suppose $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$ and $\beta_1=\beta_2$, and the assignment is calibrated within each group, meaning
$$
\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}=v_b\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}X_{\sigma b}
$$
for every group $t$ and bin $b$, and suppose the mean score among positive outcomes is equal across groups and the mean score among negative outcomes is equal across groups. Then either $\rho_1=\rho_2$ or $S=Y$ almost surely under each group law. In the latter case, every feature type with positive mass in either group has $p_\sigma\in\{0,1\}$, so the instance permits perfect prediction.

## Statement references

[Kleinberg, Mullainathan, and Raghavan, complete 23-page paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1609.05807v2): Theorem 1.1 and the complete proof in §2 establish the equal-base-rate or perfect-prediction alternatives under these three named score criteria.

[Applied Statistics: From Data to Decisions, full chapter](https://stanford-mse-125.github.io/book/lec20-fairness.html): the section “The impossibility: you cannot satisfy them all” states the real-valued score theorem and distinguishes it from the separate binary-classifier theorem.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite two-group risk-score model in the statement, groupwise calibration, and balance of the positive-class and negative-class mean scores. Prove equal base rates or perfect prediction.

[F1] [[def-group-risk-score-and-calibration]]: the group law is finite, and the same row-stochastic feature-to-bin assignment is used independently of group and outcome, with scores in $[0,1]$.

[F2] [[def-group-risk-score-and-calibration]]: for every group and bin, calibration gives $\Pr_t(Y=1,B=b)=v_b\Pr_t(B=b)$.

[F3] [[def-positive-and-negative-score-balance]]: the class-conditioned means are $\alpha_t=\mathbb E_t[S\mid Y=1]$ and $\beta_t=\mathbb E_t[S\mid Y=0]$; balance means $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$ and $\beta_1=\beta_2$.

[F4] [[lem-score-means-as-threshold-rate-areas]]: in each group, $\alpha_t=\int_0^1\operatorname{TPR}_t(u)\,du$ and $\beta_t=\int_0^1\operatorname{FPR}_t(u)\,du$.

## Proof

1.1 Set $\alpha=\alpha_1=\alpha_2$ and $\beta=\beta_1=\beta_2$ by [F3]; since $S\in[0,1]$, both common means lie in $[0,1]$. By [F4], these means are the respective areas under the groups' true-positive-rate and false-positive-rate threshold functions. Summing the calibration identity [F2] over all bins gives $\mathbb E_t[S]=\Pr_t(Y=1)=\rho_t$ for each $t$. Partitioning this finite expectation by $Y$ gives $\rho_t=\rho_t\alpha+(1-\rho_t)\beta$, hence $\rho_t(1-\alpha)=(1-\rho_t)\beta$. [given, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 If $\alpha<1$, then $1-\alpha>0$ and $1-\rho_t>0$, so the last identity yields $\rho_t/(1-\rho_t)=\beta/(1-\alpha)$ for both groups. Therefore $\rho_1/(1-\rho_1)=\rho_2/(1-\rho_2)$; cross-multiplication gives $\rho_1=\rho_2$. If instead $\alpha=1$, the identity and $1-\rho_t>0$ give $\beta=0$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 In the branch $\alpha=1$ and $\beta=0$, each group has positive and negative mass by hypothesis. The score has finite support in $[0,1]$, so a conditional mean of one on $Y=1$ is possible only when every positive-mass score value is $1$; a conditional mean of zero on $Y=0$ is possible only when every positive-mass score value is $0$. Thus $S=Y$ almost surely in both groups. If a feature type $\sigma$ with positive mass had $0<p_\sigma<1$, both outcomes would have positive mass at $\sigma$. The same assignment row $X_{\sigma b}$ is used for both outcomes [F1], so their conditional score laws would agree, contradicting concentration at scores $1$ and $0$, respectively. Hence every occupied feature type has $p_\sigma\in\{0,1\}$, which permits perfect prediction. [given, F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The proof is choice-free: it uses finite sums, finite conditional means, and algebra only. The theorem concerns the named calibration and class-conditioned score means; it does not assert a theorem about demographic parity, equalized odds, causal fairness, or all fairness criteria. The approximate result in KMR Theorem 1.2 is not asserted here; it requires its own exact approximation definitions and function $f(\varepsilon)$.

## Definition

Let $n,p\ge1$, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ be a fixed design matrix, let $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $\beta\in\mathbb R^p$. The empirical squared loss is

$$\ell_n(\beta)=\frac{1}{2n}\|y-X\beta\|_2^2.$$

Ordinary least squares minimizes $\ell_n(\beta)$ over $\mathbb R^p$. For $\lambda>0$, the ridge (Tikhonov) objective is

$$J^{\mathrm{ridge}}_\lambda(\beta)=\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_2^2.$$

For $\lambda>0$, the lasso objective in the empirical-loss convention is

$$J^{\mathrm{lasso}}_\lambda(\beta)=\ell_n(\beta)+\lambda\|\beta\|_1,\qquad \|\beta\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^p|\beta_j|.$$

This lasso has the same minimizers as $n^{-1}\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+2\lambda\|\beta\|_1$, the fixed-design convention with penalty parameter $\tau=\lambda$.

For a partition $G_1,\ldots,G_m$ of $\{1,\ldots,p\}$, fixed weights $w_g>0$, and $\lambda\ge0$, the group-lasso objective is

$$J^{\mathrm{group}}_{\lambda}(\beta)=\ell_n(\beta)+\lambda\sum_{g=1}^m w_g\|\beta_{G_g}\|_2.$$

For a fixed matrix $D\in\mathbb R^{q\times p}$ and $\lambda_1,\lambda_2\ge0$, a fused-lasso objective is

$$J^{\mathrm{fused}}_{\lambda_1,\lambda_2}(\beta)=\ell_n(\beta)+\lambda_1\|\beta\|_1+\lambda_2\|D\beta\|_1.$$

These group and fused formulas define objectives only; no existence, uniqueness, or algorithm guarantee is asserted for them here. The formulas use the displayed feature scales, so rescaling a column changes the penalty unless its coefficient and penalty weight are adjusted. If an intercept is included, write $X=[\mathbf 1\;X_0]$ and $\beta=(\beta_0,\gamma)$, define the loss by $\|y-\beta_0\mathbf1-X_0\gamma\|_2^2/(2n)$, partition only the coordinates of $\gamma$, and use a fused matrix of the form $D=[0\;D_0]$. Each penalty then acts only on $\gamma$ and the intercept coordinate $\beta_0$ is unpenalized.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $d_k,n_k\ge1$ be integer sequences with $d_k/n_k\to0$. For each $k$, let $G_k\in\mathbb R^{n_k\times d_k}$ have mutually independent $N(0,1)$ entries. Then

$$\left\|\frac{G_k^{\mathsf T}G_k}{n_k}-I_{d_k}\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}\xrightarrow[k\to\infty]{\mathbb P}0.$$

## Statement references

[Wainwright, Appendix K, Gaussian matrix spectral-norm concentration](https://arindam.cs.illinois.edu/courses/s14cs598/paper/spt1.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, integer sequences $d_k,n_k\ge1$ with $d_k/n_k\to0$, and matrices $G_k$ with independent standard-normal entries.

[A1] The finite-dimensional Gaussian construction assumes AC and gives standard-normal linear projections with the stated covariance ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]).

[F1] A standard normal has density $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ ([[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]).

[F2] For a nonnegative random variable $U$ and $a>0$, $\mathbb P(U\ge a)\le\mathbb E[U]/a$ ([[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]]).

[F3] For a real symmetric matrix $H$, $\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}|x^{\mathsf T}Hx|$ ([[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]).

[F4] The Euclidean inner product satisfies $|x^{\mathsf T}y|\le\|x\|_2\|y\|_2$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]]).

## Proof

1.1 Fix $k$, abbreviate $d=d_k$, $n=n_k$, and take a fixed unit $v\in\mathbb R^d$. The row products $Z_i=(G_kv)_i$ are independent $N(0,1)$ by [A1]. From [F1], $\mathbb E e^{tZ_i^2}=(1-2t)^{-1/2}$ for $t<1/2$; applying [F2] at $t=\delta/(2(1+\delta))$ gives $\mathbb P(n^{-1}\sum_iZ_i^2\ge1+\delta)\le e^{-n[\delta-\log(1+\delta)]/2}\le e^{-n\delta^2/8}$ for $0<\delta\le1$, since $\delta-\log(1+\delta)=\int_0^\delta t/(1+t)\,dt\ge\delta^2/4$. For $0<\delta<1$, applying [F2] at $u=\delta/(2(1-\delta))$ gives $\mathbb P(n^{-1}\sum_iZ_i^2\le1-\delta)\le e^{-n[-\delta-\log(1-\delta)]/2}\le e^{-n\delta^2/4}$, since $-\delta-\log(1-\delta)=\int_0^\delta t/(1-t)\,dt\ge\delta^2/2$; at $\delta=1$ this event requires all $Z_i=0$ and has probability zero. Thus $\mathbb P(|v^{\mathsf T}(G_k^{\mathsf T}G_k/n-I_d)v|>\delta)\le2e^{-n\delta^2/8}$. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Fix $0<\varepsilon<1$ and greedily add unit vectors at distance greater than $1/4$ from those already chosen whenever possible. The open balls of radius $1/8$ around a finite separated set are disjoint and lie in the radius-$9/8$ ball, so volume comparison gives $|\mathcal N|(1/8)^d\le(9/8)^d$; hence the process terminates within $9^d$ choices and its maximal set is a $1/4$-net. Applying step 1.1 with $\delta=\varepsilon/2$ and taking a union bound yields $\mathbb P(\max_{v\in\mathcal N}|v^{\mathsf T}(G_k^{\mathsf T}G_k/n-I_d)v|>\varepsilon/2)\le2\exp(d\log9-n\varepsilon^2/32)\to0$ because $d/n\to0$. [step 1.1, choose, algebra]

3.1 For any symmetric $H$, [F3] gives $\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}|x^{\mathsf T}Hx|$. For each unit $x$, choose $v\in\mathcal N$ with $\|x-v\|_2\le1/4$. By [F4] and the operator-norm definition, $$|x^{\mathsf T}Hx-v^{\mathsf T}Hv|=|(x-v)^{\mathsf T}Hx+v^{\mathsf T}H(x-v)|\le2(1/4)\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}.$$ Hence $\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2\max_{v\in\mathcal N}|v^{\mathsf T}Hv|$. On the complementary event in step 2.1, take $H=G_k^{\mathsf T}G_k/n-I_d$ to obtain $\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon$. Since this holds for every $0<\varepsilon<1$, larger tolerances follow by monotonicity, and the claimed convergence in probability follows. [F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite-dimensional real inner product space $V$ and a self-adjoint endomorphism $T:V\to V$.

[L1] Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal ([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]).

[L2] A real normal endomorphism admits an orthonormal block decomposition by $1\times1$ real blocks and $2\times2$ blocks $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}$ ([[thm-real-normal-endomorphism-classification]]).

[L3] In an orthonormal basis, self-adjointness means symmetry of the matrix ([[prop-self-adjoint-and-normal-matrix-criteria-in-orthonormal-bases]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1] and [L2], there is an orthonormal basis in which the matrix of $T$ is block diagonal with $1\times1$ real blocks and $2\times2$ blocks $B=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}$. [L1, L2]

2.1 Because $T$ is self-adjoint, [L3] says that the same matrix is symmetric. A block $B$ above is symmetric exactly when $b=0$, so every $2\times2$ block is the diagonal block $aI_2=\operatorname{diag}(a,a)$. Therefore the whole matrix is diagonal. [L3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 A diagonal matrix acts on each basis vector by scalar multiplication, so the orthonormal basis from step 2.1 is an orthonormal eigenbasis of $T$. [step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $r_k,n_k$ be positive integers with $n_k\to\infty$ and $r_k/n_k\to1$. For each $k$, let $Z_{k,1},\ldots,Z_{k,r_k}$ be independent $N(0,1)$ random variables and set $D_k=\sum_{j=1}^{r_k}Z_{k,j}^2$. Then $D_k/n_k\to1$ in probability.

## Statement references

[Wainwright, Appendix K, chi-square concentration](https://arindam.cs.illinois.edu/courses/s14cs598/paper/spt1.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, integer sequences $r_k,n_k$ with $n_k\to\infty$ and $r_k/n_k\to1$, and independent standard-normal variables $Z_{k,j}$.

[F1] A standard normal has density $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ ([[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]).

[F2] For a nonnegative random variable $U$ and $a>0$, $\mathbb P(U\ge a)\le\mathbb E[U]/a$ ([[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]]).

[A1] AC supplies the finite independent normal coordinates used in the statement ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

## Proof

1.1 Integration by parts against [F1], using $\phi'(x)=-x\phi(x)$ and the vanishing Gaussian boundary terms, gives $\mathbb E Z_{k,j}^2=1$ and $\mathbb E Z_{k,j}^4=3$, hence $\operatorname{Var}(Z_{k,j}^2)=2$. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 Independence and step 1.1 give $\mathbb E D_k=r_k$ and $\mathbb E(D_k-r_k)^2=2r_k$. Fix $\eta>0$; eventually $|r_k/n_k-1|<\eta/2$, so $|D_k/n_k-1|>\eta$ implies $|D_k-r_k|>\eta n_k/2$. Applying [F2] to $(D_k-r_k)^2$ gives $\mathbb P(|D_k/n_k-1|>\eta)\le8r_k/(\eta^2n_k^2)\to0$, since $r_k/n_k\to1$ and $n_k\to\infty$. This is convergence in probability. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

The cited appendix supplies the Gaussian matrix concentration context. The displayed ratio conclusion is proved here directly from the standard-normal second and fourth moments.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $m\ge2$, and let $X,Y\in\mathbb R^m$ be independent, centered Gaussian vectors with finite covariance matrices. If

$$\mathbb E[(X_i-X_j)^2]\ge\mathbb E[(Y_i-Y_j)^2]\qquad(i,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}),$$

then $\mathbb E[\max_iX_i]\ge\mathbb E[\max_iY_i]$.

## Statement references

[Wainwright 2006, Appendix B, Lemma 10](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0605740)

[Wainwright 2009, §VI](https://arindam.cs.illinois.edu/courses/s14cs598/paper/spt1.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and independent centered Gaussian vectors $X,Y\in\mathbb R^m$ satisfying the displayed increment-variance inequalities.

[A1] Under AC, a centered Gaussian vector with covariance $C\succeq0$ has the law of $C^{1/2}Z$ for a vector $Z$ of independent standard normals ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]).

[F1] A standard normal coordinate has density $\phi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$, with $\phi'(x)=-x\phi(x)$ ([[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]).

[F2] A product of sigma-finite measure spaces has a product measure with the rectangle formula ([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).

[F3] Dominated convergence permits passage to limits when the integrands have an integrable common majorant ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

## Proof

1.1 For $a>0$ define $\Phi_a(x)=a^{-1}\log\sum_{i=1}^m e^{ax_i}$ and $p_i(x)=e^{ax_i}/\sum_j e^{ax_j}$. Direct differentiation gives $\partial_i\Phi_a=p_i$ and $\partial_{ij}\Phi_a=a(p_i\mathbf1_{i=j}-p_ip_j)$, while $\max_i x_i\le\Phi_a(x)\le\max_i x_i+\log(m)/a$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Let $C_X,C_Y$ be the covariance matrices. On the product probability space [F2], represent $X=A\xi$, $Y=B\eta$ by independent standard-normal coordinate vectors using AC and the Gaussian realization [A1]. Put $Z_t=\sqrt tX+\sqrt{1-t}Y$ and $F_a(t)=\mathbb E\Phi_a(Z_t)$. For $0<t<1$, differentiate under the expectation; on every closed subinterval of $(0,1)$ the derivative is bounded by a constant times $\|\xi\|_2+\|\eta\|_2$, which is integrable, so [F3] applies. One-dimensional integration by parts against [F1], with the bounded first and second derivatives from step 1.1, gives
$$F_a'(t)=\frac12\sum_{i,j}(C_X-C_Y)_{ij}\,\mathbb E[\partial_{ij}\Phi_a(Z_t)].$$
The boundary terms vanish because $\phi(x)$ decays to zero and $\partial_i\Phi_a$ is bounded. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Substituting the Hessian from step 1.1 into step 2.1 and using $\sum_i p_i=1$ rewrites the derivative as $$F_a'(t)=\frac a4\mathbb E\left[\sum_{i,j}p_i(Z_t)p_j(Z_t)\left(\mathbb E[(X_i-X_j)^2]-\mathbb E[(Y_i-Y_j)^2]\right)\right]\ge0.$$ Therefore $F_a(1)\ge F_a(0)$ by integration over $t\in(0,1)$ and continuity at the endpoints, which follows from the same integrable bound. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 The uniform approximation in step 1.1 gives $|\mathbb E\Phi_a(X)-\mathbb E\max_iX_i|\le\log(m)/a$ and the analogous bound for $Y$. Letting $a\to\infty$ in step 3.1 proves the asserted comparison. [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. There is an integer $m_0$ such that for every $m\ge m_0$ and independent standard-normal random variables $G_1,\ldots,G_m$,
$$\mathbb E\max_{1\le i\le m}G_i\ge\frac14\sqrt{\log m}.$$

## Statement references

[Rigollet and Hütter, §1.4, maximal inequalities](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.19244v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and independent standard-normal random variables $G_1,\ldots,G_m$.

[F1] A standard normal has density $\phi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$, which is decreasing for $x\ge0$ ([[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]).

[A1] AC supplies the finite independent Gaussian family ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

## Proof

1.1 Put $t_m=\tfrac12\sqrt{\log m}$ and $q_m=\mathbb P(G_1\ge t_m)$. Since $\phi$ decreases on $[0,\infty)$, $q_m\ge\phi(t_m+1/(t_m+1))/(t_m+1)\ge e^{-t_m^2/2-t_m-1/2}/(\sqrt{2\pi}(t_m+1))$; the last inequality follows from $t_m/(t_m+1)\le t_m$ and $1/(2(t_m+1)^2)\le1/2$. Hence $m q_m\to\infty$. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 Let $M_m=\max_iG_i$. Independence gives $\mathbb P(M_m<t_m)=(1-q_m)^m\le e^{-m q_m}\to0$ and $\mathbb E[G_1\mathbf1_{\{M_m<t_m\}}]=\mathbb E[G_1\mathbf1_{\{G_1<t_m\}}](1-q_m)^{m-1}\ge-(1-q_m)^{m-1}/\sqrt{2\pi}$. Splitting at $M_m=t_m$ yields $\mathbb E M_m\ge t_m(1-(1-q_m)^m)-(1-q_m)^{m-1}/\sqrt{2\pi}\ge t_m/2=\frac14\sqrt{\log m}$ for all sufficiently large $m$. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

The cited notes give maximal-inequality context. The stated lower bound is derived here from a direct Gaussian-tail lower estimate and independence.

## Statement refuted

For every real symmetric positive-definite covariance matrix $\Sigma$ with unit diagonal, every coordinate set $S$ for which both $S$ and $S^c$ are nonempty and $\Sigma_{SS}$ is invertible, and constants $C_{\min}>0$, $D_{\max}<\infty$, $C_{\max}<\infty$, and $0<\epsilon\le1$ satisfying
$$\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{SS})\ge C_{\min},\qquad \lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\le C_{\max},\qquad \|(\Sigma_{SS})^{-1}\|_\infty\le D_{\max},\qquad \|\Sigma_{S^cS}(\Sigma_{SS})^{-1}\|_\infty\le1-\epsilon,$$
the Schur conditional covariance
$$\Sigma_{S^c\mid S}:=\Sigma_{S^cS^c}-\Sigma_{S^cS}(\Sigma_{SS})^{-1}\Sigma_{SS^c}$$
satisfies $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{S^c\mid S})\ge1/C_{\max}$. Here $\|M\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|M_{ij}|$.

## Statement references

[Wainwright 2006, Appendix D.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0605740)

[Wainwright 2009, §IV.A, equations (28)–(30)](https://arindam.cs.illinois.edu/courses/s14cs598/paper/spt1.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The matrix inequality stated above is proposed for all positive-definite unit-diagonal $\Sigma$ and admissible $S,C_{\max}$.

[A1] For a block matrix with invertible leading block, the expression $\Sigma_{S^cS^c}-\Sigma_{S^cS}(\Sigma_{SS})^{-1}\Sigma_{SS^c}$ is the Schur complement; here it is defined by the displayed formula.

## Counterexample

1.1 Fix any integer $s\ge1$, set $p=2s$, $S=\{1,\ldots,s\}$, and take $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}I_s&\frac34I_s\\[2pt]\frac34I_s&I_s\end{pmatrix}$ with $C_{\min}=1$, $C_{\max}=7/4$, $D_{\max}=1$, and $\epsilon=1/4$. The vectors $(u,u)$ and $(u,-u)$ have eigenvalues $7/4$ and $1/4$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^s$, and these subspaces span $\mathbb R^{2s}$; hence $\Sigma$ is positive definite with unit diagonal and maximum eigenvalue $C_{\max}$. Also $\Sigma_{SS}=I_s$, so its minimum eigenvalue is $C_{\min}$ and its inverse infinity norm is $D_{\max}$, while $\|\Sigma_{S^cS}\Sigma_{SS}^{-1}\|_\infty=3/4=1-\epsilon$. Thus all stated covariance hypotheses hold. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Substitution in [A1] gives $\Sigma_{S^c\mid S}=I_s-(3I_s/4)I_s^{-1}(3I_s/4)=7I_s/16$, so $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{S^c\mid S})=7/16<4/7=1/C_{\max}$ since $49<64$. Direct block multiplication gives $\Sigma^{-1}=(16/7)\begin{pmatrix}I_s&-3I_s/4\\[2pt]-3I_s/4&I_s\end{pmatrix}$, whose lower-right block is $16I_s/7$, the inverse of the conditional covariance rather than the conditional covariance itself. Thus the proposed bound is false. [A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

For this block family, the lower-right block of $\Sigma^{-1}$ is $16I_s/7$, the inverse of $\Sigma_{S^c\mid S}$, not $\Sigma_{S^c\mid S}$ itself.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Wainwright's planned lower-threshold claim is the following: along a sequence of real Gaussian linear models with $S=\{j:\beta_j^*\ne0\}$, $s=|S|$, $N=p-s$, $s,n-s,N\to\infty$, and independent observations
$$y_i=x_i^{\mathsf T}\beta^*+w_i,\qquad x_i\sim N_p(0,\Sigma),\quad w_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2),$$
where $X$ has rows $x_i^{\mathsf T}$, $y=(y_i)$, design and noise are independent, there is no separate intercept, and $\Sigma$ has unit diagonal. Suppose constants $C_{\min}>0$, $C_{\max}<\infty$, $D_{\max}<\infty$, and $0<\epsilon\le1$ satisfy
$$\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{SS})\ge C_{\min},\qquad \lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\le C_{\max},\qquad \|(\Sigma_{SS})^{-1}\|_\infty\le D_{\max},\qquad \|\Sigma_{S^cS}(\Sigma_{SS})^{-1}\|_\infty\le1-\epsilon,$$
with $\|M\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|M_{ij}|$. Define
$$\theta_\ell=\frac{\bigl(\sqrt{C_{\max}}-\sqrt{C_{\max}-1/C_{\max}}\bigr)^2}{C_{\max}(2-\epsilon)^2}.$$
For every fixed $\nu>0$ and every positive non-increasing sequence $\lambda_n$, if $n<2(\theta_\ell-\nu)s\log N+s+1$, then the probability that there exists an optimizer with $\operatorname{sgn}(\widehat\beta)=\operatorname{sgn}(\beta^*)$ for $\|y-X\beta\|_2^2/(2n)+\lambda_n\|\beta\|_1$ tends to zero.

## Statement references

[Wainwright 2006, Theorem 1(a)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0605740)

[Wainwright 2009, §IV.A, revised lower-threshold interface](https://arindam.cs.illinois.edu/courses/s14cs598/paper/spt1.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Gaussian model, covariance hypotheses, exact loss normalization, success event, and claimed lower implication in the Statement.

[F1] For an iid standard-Gaussian matrix of dimension $d=o(n)$, its Gram matrix divided by $n$ converges in operator norm to identity ([[lem-gaussian-sample-covariance-operator-concentration]]).

[F2] A sum of $q$ independent squared standard normals divided by $n$ converges in probability to one if $q/n\to1$ and $n\to\infty$ ([[lem-chi-square-degree-ratio]]).

[F3] Under AC, a centered Gaussian vector with covariance $C\succeq0$ can be realized as $C^{1/2}G$ for a vector of independent standard normals ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]]).

[F4] A nondegenerate multivariate normal has its usual Gaussian density; in particular the density with identity covariance factors into independent standard-normal densities ([[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]], [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]).

[F5] A standard normal has density $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ ([[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]). Completing the square gives $\mathbb E e^{tU}=e^{v t^2/2}$ for $U\sim N(0,v)$; applying Markov to $e^{tU}$ with $t=1/v$, and likewise to $e^{-tU}$, yields $\mathbb P(|U|\ge1)\le2e^{-1/(2v)}$ when $v>0$ ([[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]]). For $v=0$ the probability is zero.

[F6] The Lasso objective is $F(\beta)=\|y-X\beta\|_2^2/(2n)+\lambda\|\beta\|_1$ ([[def-linear-regression-objectives]]).

[A1] AC is assumed for the finite Gaussian constructions and suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

## Refutation

1.1 Fix $\delta=\epsilon=10^{-6}$, $c=(1-\epsilon)/2$, $a=1/1000$, and $\nu=1/100000$. For integers $N\ge2$ tending to infinity set $$s=N^3,\qquad p=s+N,\qquad n=s+\lceil a s\log N\rceil,\qquad S=\{1,\ldots,s\},\qquad \lambda_n=1.$$ In each observation let the first $2N$ active coordinates consist of independent pairs $(U_j,V_j)$, $1\le j\le N$, each with covariance $$B=\begin{pmatrix}1&-(1-\delta)\\-(1-\delta)&1\end{pmatrix},$$ and let the other $s-2N$ active coordinates be independent standard normals, independent of these pairs. Take independent standard normals $Z_j$, independent also of all active variables, and define the inactive coordinates by $$T_j=c(U_j-V_j)+\sqrt r Z_j,\qquad r=1-(1-\epsilon)^2(1-\delta/2).$$ Take independent observations and independent standard-normal noise $w_i$; set $\beta_i^*=n$ on $S$ and zero off $S$. These finite Gaussian constructions define the model in the Statement, with $\sigma^2=1$ and no intercept. [A1, F3, F4, given, construct]

2.1 The eigenvalues of $B$ are $\delta$ and $2-\delta$, and each row of $B^{-1}$ has absolute sum $1/\delta$. Thus $C_{\min}=\delta$ and $D_{\max}=1/\delta$ work. Each inactive coordinate regresses on its pair with coefficients $(c,-c)$, so $\|\Sigma_{S^cS}\Sigma_{SS}^{-1}\|_\infty=2c=1-\epsilon$. Its variance is one by the definition of $r$, and $0<r<2\epsilon+\delta/2<3\cdot10^{-6}$. The full covariance, after reordering, is a direct sum of positive-definite three-dimensional covariance blocks and singleton identity blocks: each triple is an invertible linear image of $(U_j,V_j,Z_j)$ because $r>0$. Every triple has trace three, so every eigenvalue is at most three. Consequently $C_{\max}=3$ bounds the maximum eigenvalue of the full covariance, and all its diagonal entries are one. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For these constants, $$\sqrt3-\sqrt{8/3}=\frac{1/3}{\sqrt3+\sqrt{8/3}}>\frac1{12},\qquad 3(2-\epsilon)^2<12,$$ so the precise claimed constant satisfies $\theta_\ell>1/1728$ and $2(\theta_\ell-\nu)>2(1/1728-1/100000)>a$. Since $\lceil a s\log N\rceil\le a s\log N+1$, the claimed failure inequality $n<2(\theta_\ell-\nu)s\log N+s+1$ holds. Also $s,n-s,N\to\infty$ and $s/n\to0$. The constant penalty is positive and non-increasing. The lower claim puts no restriction on $\rho_n=n$. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Write $X_S=Z\Sigma_{SS}^{1/2}$, with $Z$ an $n\times s$ iid standard-Gaussian matrix, and put $G=X_S^{\mathsf T}X_S$ and $A=G/n$. By [F1] and $s/n\to0$, with probability tending to one the minimum eigenvalue of $A$ is at least $\delta/2$ and $\|A^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2/\delta$. On this event define $$\widehat\beta_S=n\mathbf1+\eta-A^{-1}\mathbf1,\qquad \eta=A^{-1}X_S^{\mathsf T}w/n,\qquad \widehat\beta_{S^c}=0.$$ The shrinkage term satisfies $\|A^{-1}\mathbf1\|_\infty\le2\sqrt{s}/\delta=o(n)$. Conditional on $X_S$, $\eta$ is centered Gaussian with covariance $A^{-1}/n$, so [F5] and a finite union bound give $$\mathbb P(\|\eta\|_\infty\ge1\mid X_S)\le2s e^{-n\delta/4}\longrightarrow0$$ uniformly on the spectral event. Thus every active candidate coordinate is positive with probability tending to one. [F1, F3, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

4.2 Put $b=\mathbf1_s$ and $T=b^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_{SS}^{-1}b=s-2N+2N/\delta$, so $T/s\to1$. To compute $Q=b^{\mathsf T}G^{-1}b$, put $v=\Sigma_{SS}^{-1/2}b$ and choose a fixed orthogonal matrix with first column $v/\|v\|_2$. Orthogonal invariance and [F4] make the rotated columns of $Z$, written $[h,H]$, mutually independent standard-Gaussian columns. They have full column rank almost surely: condition successively on earlier columns; for each fixed proper column subspace, projection onto any fixed nonzero normal vector has a continuous normal law, so a new standard-Gaussian column belongs to that subspace with probability zero. For full-rank $H$ put $$P_H=H(H^{\mathsf T}H)^{-1}H^{\mathsf T},\qquad D=h^{\mathsf T}(I-P_H)h.$$ Block elimination in the Gram matrix of $[h,H]$ gives exactly $Q=T/D$. For each fixed full-rank $H$, the projector $I-P_H$ has rank $n-s+1$, so orthogonal invariance gives the conditional law $D\sim\chi^2_{n-s+1}$. This conditional law is the same for every such $H$; the projector is a measurable function of $H$, and no random basis is selected. Since $(n-s+1)/n\to1$, [F2] gives $D/n\to1$ in probability, and therefore $Q/(s/n)\to1$ in probability. [A1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra, choose]

5.1 Let $P=X_SG^{-1}X_S^{\mathsf T}$. The candidate residual is $$u=y-X_S\widehat\beta_S=(I-P)w+nX_SG^{-1}b,\qquad X_S^{\mathsf T}u/n=b.$$ Its two displayed summands are orthogonal. For inactive column $j$, the construction gives $X_j=X_S a_j+\sqrt r z_j$, where $a_j$ has entries $(c,-c)$ on its pair and zero elsewhere, and the $z_j$ are mutually independent standard-Gaussian vectors independent of $X_S,w$. Because $a_j^{\mathsf T}b=0$, the dual variables $$V_j=X_j^{\mathsf T}u/n=\sqrt r z_j^{\mathsf T}u/n$$ are, conditional on $X_S,w$, independent centered normals of common variance $$rM,\qquad M=\|u\|_2^2/n^2=Q+\|(I-P)w\|_2^2/n^2.$$ By [F2], $\|w\|_2^2/n\to1$ in probability. Since the second term is at most $\|w\|_2^2/n^2$, step 4.2 and $s\to\infty$ show $\mathbb P(M\le4s/n)\to1$. This event depends only on $X_S,w$ and is independent of all inactive residual vectors. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 On the event $M\le4s/n$, since $n\ge a s\log N$ and $r<3\cdot10^{-6}$, $$rM\le\frac{4r}{a\log N}<\frac{3}{250\log N}.$$ Applying [F5] and a finite union bound conditionally on $X_S,w$ yields the uniform bound $$\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{1\le j\le N}|V_j|\ge1\,\middle|\,X_S,w\right)\le2N\exp\!\left(-\frac1{2rM}\right)\le2N^{1-125/3}\longrightarrow0.$$ Removing the conditioning and adding the probability of $M>4s/n$ proves $\max_j|V_j|<1$ with probability tending to one. Intersecting with the event in step 4.1 preserves probability tending to one and gives both active sign correctness and inactive dual feasibility. [F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 On this intersection put $z=X^{\mathsf T}u/n$. It equals one on $S$ and satisfies $|z_j|<1$ off $S$. Since the candidate is positive on $S$ and zero off $S$, the scalar inequality $|\widehat\beta_i+h_i|-|\widehat\beta_i|\ge z_i h_i$ holds for every coordinate and every real $h_i$. Its existence has probability tending to one, whereas step 3.1 meets the exact hypotheses that predict probability tending to zero. This refutes the stated lower implication. [F6, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

This refutes the conclusion itself, independently of the erroneous inverse-block identity in the 2006 Appendix D.6. The construction uses $s/(p-s)\to\infty$, which the stated source and planned hypotheses permit; it does not refute a theorem with an additional dimensional restriction. The 2009 journal article's equation (27) defines $\rho_\ell(C)=\frac12\min_{i\ne j}(C_{ii}+C_{jj}-2C_{ij})$, a minimum pairwise increment-variance parameter, not a least eigenvalue. Its revised threshold interface is distinct and is not substituted for the claim refuted here.

## Statement

Let $n,p\ge1$, $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$, and $y\in\mathbb R^n$. The ordinary least-squares minimizers of $\|y-X\beta\|_2^2$ are exactly the solutions of $X^{\mathsf T}X\beta=X^{\mathsf T}y$; if $\beta_0$ is one such solution, the full minimizer set is $\beta_0+\ker X$. It is a singleton if and only if the columns of $X$ are linearly independent. For every $\lambda>0$, the ridge objective $\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_2^2$ has the unique minimizer
$$\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{ridge}}=(X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I_p)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}y.$$

## Statement references

[The Elements of Statistical Learning, Chapter 3 §§3.2 and 3.4](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1--Wo5Hcl2y_v3DL-tGgcJHRPdtjiVYjS)

[Rigollet and Hütter, §2.2, unconstrained least squares](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.19244v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite real design matrix $X$, a response vector $y$, and, for the ridge claim, a real $\lambda>0$.

[F1] Finite-dimensional least-squares minimizers exist, satisfy the normal equations, and form $\beta_0+\ker X$ ([[thm-least-squares-solutions-and-normal-equation]]).

[F2] A finite real matrix has a singular value decomposition with orthonormal left and right bases ([[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]).

[F3] The ridge objective is $\|X\beta-y\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_2^2$ for $\lambda>0$ ([[def-tikhonov-regularised-least-squares]]).

[F4] That objective is strictly convex and has unique minimizer $(X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I_p)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}y$ ([[thm-tikhonov-regularised-least-squares-has-a-unique-minimiser]]).

[F5] The empirical squared-loss convention for OLS and the ridge objective is fixed in [[def-linear-regression-objectives]].

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] to the linear map $\beta\mapsto X\beta$ between finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces. It gives existence, the equation $X^{\mathsf T}(X\beta-y)=0$, and the full set $\beta_0+\ker X$. [F1, F5]

2.1 The translate $\beta_0+\ker X$ has exactly one element if and only if $\ker X=\{0\}$. By definition this is equivalent to linear independence of the columns, proving the OLS uniqueness assertion. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F2], there is an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb R^p$ in which $X^{\mathsf T}X$ is diagonal with entries $\sigma_1^2,\ldots,\sigma_r^2,0,\ldots,0$. Thus $X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I_p$ has positive diagonal entries $\sigma_j^2+\lambda$ and $\lambda$, so the inverse exists. The objective in [F3] is exactly the ridge objective in [F5], and [F4] gives its unique minimizer in the displayed formula. [F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces and let $b\in W$. A vector $x\in V$ minimises $\lVert Tx-b\rVert$ if and only if

$$T^*(Tx-b)=0,$$

equivalently $T^*Tx=T^*b$. Minimisers exist, and if $x_0$ is one minimiser, then the full set of minimisers is $x_0+\ker T$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite-dimensional map $T:V\to W$ and $b\in W$.

[L1] Orthogonal projection onto a finite-dimensional subspace is its unique nearest point ([[thm-orthogonal-projection-is-the-unique-nearest-point]]).

[L2] The adjoint is defined by $\langle Tv,w\rangle=\langle v,T^*w\rangle$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]).

[L3] The identity $\ker T^*=(\operatorname{im}T)^\perp$ holds in finite dimension ([[thm-adjoint-kernel-and-range-orthogonality]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The subspace $\operatorname{im}T$ has the unique nearest point $P_{\operatorname{im}T}b$ to $b$ by [L1]. Choose $x_0$ with $Tx_0=P_{\operatorname{im}T}b$. Thus a minimiser exists. [L1, choose]

2.1 A vector $x$ is a minimiser exactly when $Tx=P_{\operatorname{im}T}b$, which by orthogonal projection is exactly when $b-Tx\in(\operatorname{im}T)^\perp$. By [L3], this is exactly $T^*(b-Tx)=0$. [step 1.1, L1, L3]

3.1 Linearity turns the last equation into $T^*Tx=T^*b$, equivalently $T^*(Tx-b)=0$. [step 2.1, L2, algebra]

4.1 If $x$ and $x_0$ are minimisers, uniqueness of the nearest image point gives $Tx=Tx_0$, so $x-x_0\in\ker T$. Conversely, adding any element of $\ker T$ leaves the image and residual unchanged. Hence the minimisers are exactly $x_0+\ker T$. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces.

[L1] The singular values of $T$ are the eigenvalues of the non-negative operator $|T|=\sqrt{T^*T}$ ([[def-singular-values-of-an-endomorphism]], [[prop-singular-values-are-well-defined]]).

[L2] A non-negative operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis with nonnegative eigenvalues ([[thm-non-negative-operator-characterisations]]).

[L3] Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis ([[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]]).

[L4] A subspace of a finite-dimensional inner-product space and its orthogonal complement form an internal direct sum ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1] and [L2], the non-negative operator $|T|$ on $V$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ with $|T|e_j=s_je_j$ and $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0=s_{r+1}=\cdots=s_n$. Because $|T|^2=T^*T$, one has $\langle T^*Te_j,e_j\rangle=s_j^2$ and therefore $\lVert Te_j\rVert=s_j$. [L1, L2, algebra]

2.1 For each $j\le r$, define $f_j:=s_j^{-1}Te_j$. Then $\lVert f_j\rVert=1$, and for $i\ne j$ one has $\langle f_i,f_j\rangle=(s_is_j)^{-1}\langle T^*Te_i,e_j\rangle=(s_is_j)^{-1}s_i^2\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=0$. For $j>r$, step 1.1 gives $\lVert Te_j\rVert=s_j=0$, so $Te_j=0$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Put $F=\operatorname{span}(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$, allowing $F=0$ when $r=0$. By [L4], $W=F\oplus F^\perp$. Choose an orthonormal basis of $F^\perp$ by [L3] and append it to $(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$. The combined list is orthonormal because the two subspaces are orthogonal, and it spans $W$ by the direct-sum decomposition. It is therefore an orthonormal basis $(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$ of $W$. If $W=0$, both lists are empty; if $r=0$, the complement basis alone is the required basis. If $v=\sum_{j=1}^n \langle v,e_j\rangle e_j$, then step 2.1 gives $Tv=\sum_{j=1}^n \langle v,e_j\rangle Te_j=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$, and when $r=0$ this is the empty sum $0$. [L3, L4, step 2.1, choose, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, let $b\in\mathbb F^m$, and let
$\lambda\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\lambda>0$. The **Tikhonov regularised
least-squares objective** is the map

$$ J_\lambda(x):=\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2 \qquad(x\in\mathbb F^n), $$

where $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm induced by the standard inner product
([[def-inner-product-norm]]).

The parameter $\lambda$ is part of the problem data. The second term penalises
large norms of $x$, so the regularised problem is not the same optimisation
problem as the unregularised least-squares problem.

## Statement

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, let $b\in\mathbb F^m$, and let
$\lambda\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\lambda>0$. Then
the Tikhonov objective

$$J_\lambda(x)=\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2$$

is strictly convex and has the unique minimiser

$$x_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*b.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, a vector $b\in\mathbb F^m$, and a real parameter $\lambda>0$, where $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

[L1] The regularised objective is $J_\lambda(x)=\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2$ ([[def-tikhonov-regularised-least-squares]]).

[L2] $A$ admits a singular value decomposition $A=U\Sigma V^*$ ([[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L2], write $A=U\Sigma V^*$ and set $x=Vy$ and $\widehat b:=U^*b$. Since $U$ and $V$ are unitary, $$ J_\lambda(Vy)=\|\Sigma y-\widehat b\|_2^2+\lambda\|y\|_2^2. $$ [L1, L2, algebra]

2.1 If $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_r$ are the nonzero singular values, then step 1.1 becomes $$ J_\lambda(Vy)=\sum_{i=1}^r |\sigma_i y_i-\widehat b_i|^2 +\sum_{i=r+1}^m |\widehat b_i|^2 +\lambda\sum_{i=1}^n |y_i|^2. $$ Each variable $y_i$ appears in a one-variable quadratic with positive coefficient $\sigma_i^2+\lambda$ or $\lambda$, so the objective is strictly convex. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Minimising coordinatewise gives $$ y_i=\frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_i^2+\lambda}\widehat b_i \quad(1\le i\le r), \qquad y_i=0 \quad(r<i\le n). $$ Equivalently, $$ y=(\Sigma^*\Sigma+\lambda I)^{-1}\Sigma^*\widehat b. $$ [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Returning to $x=Vy$ and using $A^*A=V\Sigma^*\Sigma V^*$, one gets $$ x_\lambda =V(\Sigma^*\Sigma+\lambda I)^{-1}\Sigma^*U^*b =(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*b. $$ [L2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Step 2.1 proves strict convexity and step 4.1 gives the unique minimiser. [step 2.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $n,p\ge1$, $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ satisfy $X^{\mathsf T}X=I_p$, and let $y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $\lambda>0$. The objective
$$\frac{1}{2n}\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_1$$
has the unique minimizer $\widehat\beta_j=S_{n\lambda}((X^{\mathsf T}y)_j)$, where $S_a(t)=\operatorname{sgn}(t)(|t|-a)_+$, $(u)_+=\max\{u,0\}$, and $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$. Thus the threshold is $n\lambda$ under this loss normalization.

## Statement references

[The Elements of Statistical Learning, §3.4.1 and §18.4](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1--Wo5Hcl2y_v3DL-tGgcJHRPdtjiVYjS)

[Rigollet and Hütter, §§2.3–2.4, soft thresholding and the Lasso objective](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.19244v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $n,p\ge1$, $X^{\mathsf T}X=I_p$, $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and $\lambda>0$.

[F1] The fixed-design empirical squared loss is $\|y-X\beta\|_2^2/(2n)$ and the Lasso penalty is $\lambda\|\beta\|_1$ ([[def-linear-regression-objectives]]).

## Proof

1.1 Put $z=X^{\mathsf T}y$. Expanding the squared norm and using $X^{\mathsf T}X=I_p$ gives $\frac{1}{2n}\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_1=\frac{\|y\|_2^2-\|z\|_2^2}{2n}+\sum_{j=1}^p\left(\frac{(\beta_j-z_j)^2}{2n}+\lambda|\beta_j|\right)$. The first term is constant in $\beta$, so the minimization separates into scalar strictly convex objectives. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For a scalar $z$, the derivative of $(t-z)^2/(2n)+\lambda|t|$ on $t>0$ is $(t-z)/n+\lambda$, and on $t<0$ it is $(t-z)/n-\lambda$. The positive stationary point is $t=z-n\lambda$ exactly when $z>n\lambda$; the negative stationary point is $t=z+n\lambda$ exactly when $z<-n\lambda$. When $|z|\le n\lambda$, the one-sided derivatives at zero satisfy $(-z/n-\lambda)\le0\le(-z/n+\lambda)$, so zero minimizes. Strict convexity makes each minimizer unique, and these cases are precisely $S_{n\lambda}(z)$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Applying step 2.1 to every coordinate yields the stated vector formula and uniqueness. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$, $y\in\mathbb R^n$, $\lambda>0$, and let $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}$ be nonempty. Assume the active design $X_S$ has full column rank. If an optimizer $\widehat\beta$ of $\|y-X\beta\|_2^2/(2n)+\lambda\|\beta\|_1$ has support exactly $S$ and sign vector $b=\operatorname{sgn}(\widehat\beta_S)\in\{-1,1\}^{|S|}$, then
$$\widehat\beta_S=(X_S^{\mathsf T}X_S/n)^{-1}(X_S^{\mathsf T}y/n-\lambda b).$$
This is a necessary active-coordinate condition only; it does not assert that the candidate satisfies any inactive-coordinate condition.

## Statement references

[Wainwright 2006, §2.3, primal-dual witness construction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0605740)

[Rigollet and Hütter, Definition 2.12](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.19244v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite fixed-design Lasso problem, a nonempty active set $S$, an optimizer supported on $S$ with nonzero active coordinates, and full column rank of $X_S$.

[F1] The objective uses loss $\|y-X\beta\|_2^2/(2n)$ and penalty $\lambda\|\beta\|_1$ ([[def-linear-regression-objectives]]).

## Proof

1.1 Fix an active coordinate $j$. For $|h|<|\widehat\beta_j|$, changing that coefficient by $h$ preserves its sign $b_j$, so the restricted objective is differentiable in $h$ and has a local minimum at $h=0$. Its positive difference quotients are nonnegative and its negative difference quotients are nonpositive; since the derivative exists, it is zero. Differentiating the squared loss and the fixed-sign penalty in each active coordinate gives $X_S^{\mathsf T}(X_S\widehat\beta_S-y)/n+\lambda b=0$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Full column rank makes $X_S^{\mathsf T}X_S/n$ invertible. Rearranging step 1.1 and multiplying by this inverse gives the displayed formula. The argument uses only active stationarity and makes no assertion about inactive coordinates. [step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎
