## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
normed space. The published metric completion of the norm metric on $X$ admits
a unique vector-space structure and norm whose induced metric is the
published completion metric and such that the constant sequence embedding
$i:X\to \widehat X$ is a dense linear isometry. With this structure,
$\widehat X$ is a Banach space.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice; a normed space $X$, its published metric completion $\widehat X$ by Cauchy classes, and the constant-sequence embedding $i:X\to\widehat X$.

[A1] Countable Choice has the meaning fixed in [[def-countable-choice]].

[L1] Under Countable Choice, the published metric completion exists, is complete, and $i[X]$ is dense in it ([[thm-metric-completion-exists]]).

[L2] Termwise addition, scalar multiplication, and the limiting norm on Cauchy classes are well defined ([[lem-completion-operations-are-well-defined]]).

[L3] A Banach space is a normed space complete for its norm metric, and a completion of a normed space is a Banach space with dense linear isometry from the original space ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]).

[L4] Addition and scalar multiplication are continuous in every normed space ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L2], the Cauchy classes carry termwise addition and scalar multiplication, and each class has a well-defined norm $\|[x_n]\|:=\lim_n\|x_n\|$. [L2]

2.1 On constant sequences these operations agree with those of $X$, and $\|i(x)\|=\|x\|$ by definition, so $i$ is a linear isometry. [step 1.1, L2]

2.2 For classes $[x_n]$ and $[y_n]$, the distance of the published metric completion is $\lim_n\|x_n-y_n\|$, while the new difference class is $[x_n-y_n]$; therefore the completion metric is exactly the metric induced by the norm from step 1.1. [step 1.1, L1, L2]

3.1 By [A1], the underlying metric space is complete by [L1], so step 2.2 makes $\widehat X$ complete for its new norm metric. Thus $\widehat X$ is Banach and $(\widehat X,i)$ is a completion of $X$ in the sense of [L3]. [step 2.1, step 2.2, A1, L1, L3]

3.2 Suppose a second Banach-space structure on the same underlying set induces the published completion metric and also makes $i$ a dense linear isometry. Its addition and scalar multiplication are continuous by [L4], and they agree with the operations of step 1.1 on the dense subset $i[X]\times i[X]$ and on $\mathbb K\times i[X]$; therefore they agree everywhere. [step 2.1, L4]

4.1 The norm is then forced as well, because in any compatible normed structure $\|u\|$ equals the metric distance from $u$ to $0$. So the compatible Banach-space structure is unique. [step 2.2, step 3.2] ∎

## Definition

Let $X$ be a normed space. A **completion of $X$** is a pair
$\bigl(\widehat X,\iota\bigr)$ such that

- $\widehat X$ is a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]);
- $\iota:X\to \widehat X$ is a linear isometry
  ([[def-linear-isometry-and-isometric-isomorphism]]);
- $\iota[X]$ is dense in $\widehat X$
  ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

Equivalently, a completion of a normed space is a completion of its norm metric
([[def-metric-completion]]) together with compatible linear structure on the
complete space.

## Remarks

- The embedding is part of the data, exactly as for metric completions.
- Uniqueness means uniqueness up to a linear isometric isomorphism commuting
  with the dense embeddings.

      url: "https://live.ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-102-introduction-to-functional-analysis-spring-2021/8fb8d5c170f1613151aca71de21027bc_MIT18_102s21_full_lec.pdf"

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a real or complex inner-product space and let $(\widehat X,\kappa)$ be its norm completion ([[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]). Then $\widehat X$ carries a unique inner product that extends the given one along $\kappa$ and whose induced length is the completion norm; with it $\widehat X$ is a Hilbert space, and the extension is unique among inner products that extend the given pairing and induce the completion norm.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] The completion $(\widehat X,\kappa)$ is a Banach space, $\kappa:X\to\widehat X$ is a dense linear isometry, and $\widehat X$ carries the unique compatible vector-space structure of the published metric completion ([[thm-metric-completion-carries-a-unique-banach-space-structure]], [[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]).

[A2] The induced length of an inner-product space is a norm ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]). Conversely, a norm on a real or complex vector space is induced by an inner product if and only if it satisfies the parallelogram law. That inner product is unique and is recovered by the real or first-linear complex polarisation formula ([[thm-jordan-von-neumann-polarization]]).

[A3] Cauchy–Schwarz holds in every inner-product space; the resulting two-variable difference estimate proves joint continuity ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[lem-inner-product-is-jointly-continuous]]).

[A4] Vector addition and scalar multiplication are continuous, and $\bigl|\|u\|-\|v\|\bigr|\le\|u-v\|$ ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]], [[lem-reverse-triangle-inequality-in-a-normed-space]]).

[A5] Countable Choice selects a point from every member of a countable family of nonempty sets, and $1/(n+1)\to0$ ([[def-countable-choice]], [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]]).

[A6] Every real or complex inner-product norm satisfies the parallelogram law ([[thm-parallelogram-law]]).

[A7] A Hilbert space is an inner-product space complete for its induced-norm metric ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** Countable Choice, an inner-product space $X$ with norm $\|\cdot\|$, and its norm completion $(\widehat X,\kappa)$ with completion norm also written $\|\cdot\|$.

1.1 Let $\xi,\eta\in\widehat X$. For every $n$, density makes the sets $\{x\in X:\|\kappa x-\xi\|<1/(n+1)\}$ and $\{y\in X:\|\kappa y-\eta\|<1/(n+1)\}$ nonempty. Countable Choice selects $x_n,y_n$ from these sets. Thus $\kappa(x_n)\to\xi$ and $\kappa(y_n)\to\eta$, the selected sequences are Cauchy, and continuity of the vector operations gives $\kappa(x_n\pm y_n)=\kappa(x_n)\pm\kappa(y_n)\to\xi\pm\eta$. [A1, A4, A5]

2.1 The parallelogram identities $\|x_n+y_n\|^2+\|x_n-y_n\|^2=2\|x_n\|^2+2\|y_n\|^2$ hold in $X$ by [A6]; passing to the limit using continuity of the norm and of sums, and the isometry $\|\kappa z\|=\|z\|$, gives $\|\xi+\eta\|^2+\|\xi-\eta\|^2=2\|\xi\|^2+2\|\eta\|^2$, so the completion norm satisfies the parallelogram law. [step 1.1, A1, A4, A6]

3.1 The Jordan–von Neumann theorem applied to the Banach space $\widehat X$ therefore produces an inner product $B$ on $\widehat X$ whose induced length is exactly the completion norm and which is the unique such inner product. [step 2.1, A2, A7]

4.1 $B$ extends the original pairing: for $x,y\in X$, the polarisation formula of [A2] together with $\kappa(x\pm y)=\kappa x\pm\kappa y$ and the isometry property gives $B(\kappa x,\kappa y)=\tfrac14(\|\kappa(x+y)\|^2-\|\kappa(x-y)\|^2)=\tfrac14(\|x+y\|^2-\|x-y\|^2)=\langle x,y\rangle$ in the real case, and the four-term complex formula likewise in the complex case. [step 3.1, A1, A2]

5.1 Uniqueness: if $B'$ is any inner product on $\widehat X$ that extends the pairing along $\kappa$ and induces the completion norm, then for $\xi,\eta$ and approximating sequences as in step 1.1 the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for both forms gives $|B'(\xi,\eta)-B'(\kappa x_n,\kappa y_n)|\le\|\xi-\kappa x_n\|\,\|\eta\|+\|\kappa x_n\|\,\|\eta-\kappa y_n\|$ and the same bound for $B$, so both pairings are the limits of the common values $\langle x_n,y_n\rangle$ and $B'=B$. [step 1.1, step 4.1, A1, A3]

6.1 Hence $\widehat X$ carries the inner product $B$ extending the original one with the completion norm as induced length, so it is complete and therefore a Hilbert space by [A7]. Countable Choice is used in the published completion interface and explicitly in step 1.1 to select the two approximating sequences; no further choice enters the limit arguments. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, A1, A5, A7] ∎

## Statement

Let $k$ be a real positive semidefinite kernel on a set $X$, let $n\ge1$, and let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$. There are vectors $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in\mathbb R^n$ such that $k(x_i,x_j)=z_i^Tz_j$ for every $1\le i,j\le n$. The vectors may be zero and need not be linearly independent.

## Statement references

[Sheldon Axler, *Linear Algebra Done Right*, 4th ed., §7B, Theorem 7.29](https://linear.axler.net/LADR4e.pdf)

[Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, §12.3.1](https://gitlab.com/primishra/Books/-/raw/main/ESLII_print12.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real positive semidefinite kernel $k$, an integer $n\ge1$, and points $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$.

[A1] The Gram matrix $K=(k(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^n$ is real symmetric and satisfies $c^TKc\ge0$ for every $c\in\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-positive-semidefinite-kernels-and-reproducing-kernel-hilbert-spaces]]).

[F1] Every self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis ([[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]).

## Proof




1.1 Regard $K$ as an endomorphism of $\mathbb R^n$ with its usual dot product. By [A1], $K$ is symmetric, hence self-adjoint. By [F1], there are an orthonormal eigenbasis $q_1,\ldots,q_n$ and real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$ with $Kq_\ell=\lambda_\ell q_\ell$. [given, A1, F1, construct]


2.1 Since $\|q_\ell\|_2=1$, [A1] gives $\lambda_\ell=q_\ell^TKq_\ell\ge0$ for each $\ell$. Thus each $\sqrt{\lambda_\ell}$ is a real number, including when $\lambda_\ell=0$. [step 1.1, A1]


3.1 For $1\le i\le n$, define $z_i=(\sqrt{\lambda_1}(q_1)_i,\ldots,\sqrt{\lambda_n}(q_n)_i)\in\mathbb R^n$. The spectral decomposition $K=\sum_{\ell=1}^n\lambda_\ell q_\ell q_\ell^T$ then gives $z_i^Tz_j=\sum_{\ell=1}^n\lambda_\ell(q_\ell)_i(q_\ell)_j=K_{ij}=k(x_i,x_j)$ for all $i,j$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathcal H$ be a real reproducing kernel Hilbert space with kernel $k$, let $n\ge0$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ be sample points, let $L:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be finite-valued, and let $\Omega:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be nondecreasing. Define $J(f):=L(f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_n))+\Omega(\|f\|_{\mathcal H})$. If $J$ has a minimizer, then it has a minimizer in $\operatorname{span}\{k(\cdot,x_i):1\le i\le n\}$; equivalently, at least one minimizer has the finite expansion $f(\cdot)=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i k(\cdot,x_i)$. This is an existence-conditional statement and asserts no minimizer exists when none is separately guaranteed.

## Statement references

[Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, §5.8](https://gitlab.com/primishra/Books/-/raw/main/ESLII_print12.pdf)

[Rasmussen and Williams, *Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning*, §6.2](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW6.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real RKHS $\mathcal H$ with kernel $k$, finitely many sample points, a finite-valued loss $L$, a nondecreasing penalty $\Omega$, and a minimizer $f$ of $J$.

[F1] For each $x$, the section $k_x=k(\cdot,x)$ lies in the RKHS and $\langle h,k_x\rangle=h(x)$ ([[def-positive-semidefinite-kernels-and-reproducing-kernel-hilbert-spaces]]).

[F2] Every finite-dimensional subspace of a real inner-product space admits a unique orthogonal projection, the residual is orthogonal to the subspace, and the projection does not increase norm ([[lem-finite-dimensional-projection-in-a-real-inner-product-space]]).

## Proof




1.1 Let $M:=\operatorname{span}\{k_{x_i}:1\le i\le n\}$. It is finite-dimensional. Apply [F2] to $f$ and $M$, and write $f=p+h$ with $p\in M$ and $h\perp M$. [given, F2, construct]


2.1 For every $i$, [F1] gives $h(x_i)=\langle h,k_{x_i}\rangle=0$, so $p(x_i)=f(x_i)$. Hence the loss terms in $J(p)$ and $J(f)$ agree. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]


3.1 The norm-contraction clause of [F2] gives $\|p\|_{\mathcal H}\le\|f\|_{\mathcal H}$. Monotonicity of $\Omega$ therefore gives $J(p)\le J(f)$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2]


4.1 Since $f$ is a minimizer, $J(f)\le J(p)$. Thus $J(p)=J(f)$ and $p$ is also a minimizer; by its definition $p$ is a finite linear combination of the sample kernel sections. [given, step 3.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $X$ be a set, let $\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, and let $\phi:X\to\mathcal H$ be a feature map. Define its kernel by $k(x,z):=\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. For a finite labeled sample $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ with $n\ge1$, $x_i\in X$, and $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, the **soft-margin support-vector machine** with cost $C>0$ is

$$\min_{w\in\mathcal H,\ b\in\mathbb R,\ \xi\in\mathbb R^n}\ \frac12\|w\|_{\mathcal H}^2+C\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_i$$

subject to

$$y_i\bigl(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b\bigr)\ge1-\xi_i,\qquad \xi_i\ge0\quad(1\le i\le n).$$

The bias $b$ is unpenalized. The associated real score is $s_{w,b}(x):=\langle w,\phi(x)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b$. If a binary label is required, use the deterministic rule $+1$ when $s_{w,b}(x)\ge0$ and $-1$ otherwise. The score is not defined as a probability, and this optimization includes no probability-calibration map.

The **hard-margin** problem removes the slack variables and minimizes $\frac12\|w\|_{\mathcal H}^2$ subject to $y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b)\ge1$ for every $i$. In this library, “margin-separable sample” means exactly that this hard-margin feasible set is nonempty; no hard-margin conclusion is asserted for a sample that fails this condition.

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $C>0$, and let $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ be a finite labeled sample with $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$ in a real Hilbert feature space $\mathcal H$, with feature map $\phi$. The soft-margin SVM primal has a finite attained minimum. At least one minimizing tuple has its weight vector in $M:=\operatorname{span}\{\phi(x_i):1\le i\le n\}$. This conclusion includes samples with only one label and does not assert uniqueness of the bias or slack variables.

## Statement references

[Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, §12.2.1](https://gitlab.com/primishra/Books/-/raw/main/ESLII_print12.pdf)

[Rasmussen and Williams, *Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning*, §6.4.1](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW6.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The sample, a real Hilbert feature space, its feature map, and $C>0$.

[A1] The soft-margin primal minimizes $\frac12\|w\|^2+C\sum_i\xi_i$ over $w,b,\xi$ subject to $y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle+b)\ge1-\xi_i$ and $\xi_i\ge0$ ([[def-hard-and-soft-margin-support-vector-machines]]).

[F1] Projection onto a finite-dimensional subspace preserves inner products with that subspace and does not increase norm ([[lem-finite-dimensional-projection-in-a-real-inner-product-space]]).

[F2] $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|\|v\|$ in a real inner-product space ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]]).

[F3] Every finite-dimensional real inner-product space has an orthonormal basis ([[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]]).

[F4] A nonempty closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, is compact, and every continuous real-valued function on it attains a minimum ([[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]).

## Proof




1.1 The tuple $w=0$, $b=0$, and $\xi_i=1$ is feasible and has objective $Cn$. Every feasible objective is nonnegative, so the primal infimum lies in $[0,Cn]$. [given, A1, construct, algebra]


1.2 Let $M=\operatorname{span}\{\phi(x_i):1\le i\le n\}$. For any feasible tuple, project $w$ onto $M$ using [F1]. The residual is orthogonal to every $\phi(x_i)$, so all sample scores and constraints are unchanged, while the norm does not increase. Thus minimizing over $M\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ has the same infimum as minimizing over the full feature space. [given, F1, A1]


2.1 If all labels are $+1$, then $w=0$, $b=1$, and $\xi=0$ is feasible with objective $0$, which is globally minimal by step 1.1. If all labels are $-1$, then $w=0$, $b=-1$, and $\xi=0$ gives the same conclusion. [step 1.1, A1, construct]


3.1 Suppose both labels occur. Set $R=\max_i\|\phi(x_i)\|$ and let $S$ be the subset of $M\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ consisting of feasible tuples with objective at most $Cn$. By step 1.1, $S$ is nonempty. It is closed because the constraints are continuous affine inequalities and the objective is continuous; continuity of each score follows from [F2]. Every tuple in $S$ satisfies $\|w\|\le\sqrt{2Cn}$ and $0\le\xi_i\le n$. Choose indices $i_+$ and $i_-$ with labels $+1$ and $-1$. Their constraints and [F2] give $b\ge1-n-\sqrt{2Cn}R$ and $b\le n-1+\sqrt{2Cn}R$, so $b$ is bounded. By [F3], an orthonormal basis identifies the finite-dimensional product space with $\mathbb R^d$ for some $d\ge1$; hence $S$ is a nonempty closed bounded subset of that Euclidean space. By [F4], the continuous objective attains a minimum on $S$. Any feasible tuple outside $S$ has objective greater than $Cn$, whereas $S$ contains a feasible tuple of objective $Cn$; therefore this minimum is also the global primal minimum. By step 1.2 it is a full-space minimizer with $w\in M$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, A1, F2, F3, F4, choose, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite-dimensional inner product space $V$.

[L1] A finite-dimensional vector space has a finite basis, with the empty list serving when $V=0$ ([[def-linear-basis]]).

[L2] Gram–Schmidt converts every finite independent list into an orthonormal list with the same span ([[thm-gram-schmidt-orthonormalisation]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Choose a finite basis $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ of $V$ using [L1]. [L1, choose]

2.1 Apply [L2]. The resulting orthonormal list has the same span as the basis, namely $V$, and therefore is an orthonormal basis. This also covers $r=0$. [step 1.1, L2] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty subset $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n\ge1$, carrying the Euclidean subspace topology.

[L1] In Euclidean space, a subset is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[L2] A pseudocompact Euclidean subset is bounded and is closed ([[lem-pseudocompact-euclidean-subset-is-bounded]], [[lem-pseudocompact-euclidean-subset-is-closed]]).

[L3] A continuous real-valued map on a nonempty compact topological space attains a maximum and a minimum ([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]], claim 2).

[L4] Pseudocompactness means that every continuous real-valued function has bounded image ([[def-pseudocompact-space]]).

[L5] Compactness for the Euclidean metric and for its metric topology is the same condition ([[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Conditions 1 and 2 are equivalent by [L1] and [L5]. [L1, L5]

1.2 Condition 3 implies condition 2 by [L2]. [L2]

1.3 Suppose condition 1 holds. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ then attains a maximum and a minimum by [L3], so condition 4 holds. [L3]

1.4 Suppose condition 4 holds. For every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$, its maximum and minimum bound $f[A]$, so $A$ is pseudocompact and condition 3 holds. [L4]

2.1 The implications $1\Leftrightarrow2$, $3\Rightarrow2\Rightarrow1$, and $1\Rightarrow4\Rightarrow3$ prove all four conditions equivalent. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, $C>0$, let $\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, and let $\phi:X\to\mathcal H$ be a feature map with kernel $k(x,z)=\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. For any finite sample $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ with $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, the soft-margin SVM primal attains its minimum. Its Lagrangian dual is

$$\max_{\alpha\in\mathbb R^n}\ \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_jk(x_i,x_j)$$

subject to $0\le\alpha_i\le C$ for every $i$ and $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0$. The dual maximum is attained and equals the primal minimum. For every primal minimizer there are dual multipliers $\alpha_i$ and $\mu_i$ such that

$$w=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i y_i\phi(x_i),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i y_i=0,\qquad C-\alpha_i-\mu_i=0,$$

$$\alpha_i\bigl(1-\xi_i-y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle+b)\bigr)=0,\qquad \mu_i\xi_i=0,$$

with $\alpha_i\ge0$ and $\mu_i\ge0$. Conversely, any primal-feasible tuple and nonnegative multipliers satisfying these stationarity and complementarity equations are globally optimal. An index with $\alpha_i>0$ is a support vector; if $0<\alpha_i<C$, then $\xi_i=0$ and its signed margin equals $1$. The single dual equality row is independent because $(y_1,\ldots,y_n)\ne0$.

## Statement references

[Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, §§12.2.1 and 12.3.1–12.3.3](https://gitlab.com/primishra/Books/-/raw/main/ESLII_print12.pdf)

[Rasmussen and Williams, *Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning*, §6.4.1](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW6.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite labeled sample in a real Hilbert feature space, the induced kernel, and $C>0$.

[F1] The soft-margin primal has an attained minimum ([[lem-soft-margin-svm-primal-attainment]]).

[F2] Projection onto a finite-dimensional subspace preserves the residual orthogonality and does not increase norm ([[lem-finite-dimensional-projection-in-a-real-inner-product-space]]).

[F3] Orthogonal vectors satisfy the Pythagorean identity ([[prop-pythagorean-parallelogram-and-polarisation-identities]]).

[F4] For a finite sample, the kernel Gram matrix has vectors $z_i\in\mathbb R^n$ with $K_{ij}=z_i^Tz_j$ ([[lem-positive-semidefinite-gram-matrix-has-euclidean-feature-factorization]]).

[F5] A finite-dimensional convex program uses proper closed convex objective and constraint functions, a full-row-rank equality matrix, and the inequality convention $g_i\le0$ with nonnegative Lagrange multipliers ([[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]]).

[F6] For a finite-dimensional convex program with independent equality rows, relative-interior Slater, and a finite attained primal value, the dual optimum is attained, the values agree, and inequality complementarity holds ([[thm-slater-strong-duality-and-dual-attainment]]).

[F7] The inequality-program convention uses $g_i\le0$ and Lagrangian $f+\lambda^Tg$ with $\lambda\ge0$ ([[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]).

[F8] In a differentiable convex program on an open convex domain, every feasible tuple satisfying KKT conditions is a global minimizer ([[thm-convex-kkt-sufficiency-and-normal-cone-certificate]]).

## Proof




1.1 Let $(w_*,b_*,\xi_*)$ be any primal minimizer, which exists by [F1], and let $M=\operatorname{span}\{\phi(x_i):1\le i\le n\}$. Project $w_*$ onto $M$ using [F2]; its residual is orthogonal to every $\phi(x_i)$, so the projection preserves all margins and slacks. If the residual were nonzero, [F3] would give a strictly smaller squared norm and hence a strictly smaller objective, contradicting minimality because the regularization coefficient is $1/2>0$. Thus every primal minimizer has $w_*\in M$. [given, F1, F2, F3, construct]


2.1 Identify $M$ with a Euclidean space using an orthonormal basis. In the finite-dimensional variable space $M\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$, the objective is a proper continuous convex function and the $2n$ inequality constraints are continuous affine functions with the sign convention [F7]. No inequality is removed by the domain-preserving convention in [F5]: all functions have full domain, and sending the corresponding $\xi_i\to-\infty$ makes either constraint function positive. There are no primal equality rows, so the full-row-rank condition in [F5] holds vacuously. [step 1.1, F5, F7, algebra]


3.1 The point $w=0$, $b=0$, $\xi_i=2$ has strict slack in every constraint: $1-\xi_i-y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle+b)=-1<0$ and $-\xi_i=-2<0$. The objective and all constraint domains are the whole finite-dimensional variable space, so this point lies in their relative interiors. Together with the finite attained primal value from [F1], this verifies every hypothesis of [F6]. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, F6, construct]


3.2 Write the margin constraints as $g_i^{(m)}:=1-\xi_i-y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle+b)\le0$ and the nonnegative-slack constraints as $g_i^{(s)}:=-\xi_i\le0$. Give them multipliers $\alpha_i\ge0$ and $\mu_i\ge0$, respectively. The Lagrangian is $L=\frac12\|w\|^2+C\sum_i\xi_i+\sum_i\alpha_i g_i^{(m)}+\sum_i\mu_i g_i^{(s)}$. [step 2.1, F5, F7, construct]


4.1 Put $v:=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\phi(x_i)$. The terms of $L$ depending on $w$ are $\frac12\|w\|^2-\langle w,v\rangle=\frac12\|w-v\|^2-\frac12\|v\|^2$, so their infimum is $-\frac12\|v\|^2$. The infimum over the unrestricted bias $b$ is finite exactly when $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0$, and the infimum over each unrestricted $\xi_i$ is finite exactly when $C-\alpha_i-\mu_i=0$. Thus the dual-feasible conditions are $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0$ and $0\le\alpha_i\le C$. [step 3.2, algebra]


4.2 Apply [F6] using the verified hypotheses in [step 3.1]. It gives an attained dual optimum $(\alpha,\mu)$ with the same value as the primal optimum and complementarity for both families $g_i^{(m)}$ and $g_i^{(s)}$. At any fixed primal minimizer, these equal values and complementarity make $L$ attain its unconstrained infimum; its derivatives in $w$, $b$, and each $\xi_i$ therefore vanish. [step 3.1, step 3.2, F6, algebra]


5.1 For any finite list $u_1,\ldots,u_m\in X$ and $c_1,\ldots,c_m\in\mathbb R$, symmetry and bilinearity of the real inner product give $\sum_{r,s}c_rc_sk(u_r,u_s)=\langle\sum_r c_r\phi(u_r),\sum_s c_s\phi(u_s)\rangle=\|\sum_r c_r\phi(u_r)\|^2\ge0$. Thus the feature-induced kernel $k$ is real positive semidefinite, so its sample Gram matrix satisfies the hypothesis of [F4]. Since $k(x_i,x_j)=\langle\phi(x_i),\phi(x_j)\rangle$, $\|v\|^2=\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_jk(x_i,x_j)$. By [F4], the matrix $(y_iy_jk(x_i,x_j))_{i,j}$ is the Gram matrix of $y_i z_i$, so its quadratic form is nonnegative. Hence the displayed dual objective is concave. Its equality row has coefficient vector $y\ne0$, because $n\ge1$ and each $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, so that row is independent. [step 4.1, F4, algebra]


5.2 Differentiating the Lagrangian of [step 3.2] gives $w=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\phi(x_i)$, $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0$, and $C-\alpha_i-\mu_i=0$. The last equation and $\mu_i\ge0$ give $\alpha_i\le C$; together with $\alpha_i\ge0$ these are the dual box constraints. The complementarity equations supplied by [F6] are $\alpha_i g_i^{(m)}=0$ and $\mu_i g_i^{(s)}=0$, which are exactly the two equations in the Statement. [step 4.2, step 3.2, F6, algebra]


6.1 The finite-dimensional primal has differentiable convex objective and affine convex constraints on the open convex variable space identified in [step 2.1]. Thus [F8] certifies that any feasible tuple satisfying the stationarity and complementarity equations is a global primal minimizer. If $0<\alpha_i<C$, then $\mu_i=C-\alpha_i>0$, so $\mu_i\xi_i=0$ forces $\xi_i=0$; then $\alpha_i g_i^{(m)}=0$ forces the signed margin to equal $1$. Finally, for any input $x$, stationarity gives the score $s(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i k(x_i,x)+b$. [step 5.2, step 2.1, F8, algebra] ∎

## Definition

A subset is convex when it contains the segment joining each pair of its
points ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). A function
$F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is proper if it never equals
$-\infty$ and is finite at at least one point. Its domain is
$\operatorname{dom}F=\{x:F(x)<+\infty\}$. Its epigraph is
$\operatorname{epi}F=\{(x,t):F(x)\le t\}$. It is closed convex when its
epigraph is a closed convex set. For a nonempty convex set $S$,
$\operatorname{aff}S$ is its smallest containing affine subspace and
$\operatorname{ri}S$ is its interior relative to $\operatorname{aff}S$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $m,p\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed, let
$f_0,g_1,\ldots,g_m$ be proper closed convex functions on $\mathbb R^n$,
let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$ have full row rank, and let
$b\in\mathbb R^p$. Full row rank means that the rows are linearly
independent, vacuously when $p=0$. The common domain is
$D=\operatorname{dom}f_0\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}g_i$. The primal
problem is to minimize $f_0(x)$ over $x\in D$ satisfying $Ax=b$ and
$g_i(x)\le0$. An inequality is removable if, with
$D_{-i}=\operatorname{dom}f_0\cap\bigcap_{j\ne i}\operatorname{dom}g_j$,
$D_{-i}\subseteq\operatorname{dom}g_i$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $x\in D_{-i}$.
Then $D=D_{-i}$, so removing that function and its inequality leaves the
feasible set unchanged. While a removable inequality exists, delete the one
with smallest original index, recomputing $D_{-i}$ using the currently retained
family after each deletion. Stop when none is removable, then relabel the
remaining inequalities consecutively in their original order and let $m$
denote their number. An inequality that is nonpositive only on $D$
but whose function domain restricts $D$ is not removable. Unless stated
otherwise, the inequalities below are the remaining ones after only these
domain-preserving deletions. The primal value is
$$
p^*=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in D,\ Ax=b,\ g_i(x)\le0\text{ for all }i\}.
$$

For $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$ and $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, the extended
Lagrangian is
$$
L(x,\lambda,\nu)=\begin{cases}f_0(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)+\nu^T(Ax-b),&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D.\end{cases}
$$
The dual function and dual value are
$$
q(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}L(x,\lambda,\nu),\qquad d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0,\ \nu\in\mathbb R^p}q(\lambda,\nu).
$$
The dual supremum is attained when some admissible $(\lambda,\nu)$ has
$q(\lambda,\nu)=d^*$; the optimal duality gap is $p^*-d^*$ when both values
are finite.

Slater's condition means that there is
$x_s\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_0)\cap
\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g_i)$ with $Ax_s=b$ and
$g_i(x_s)<0$ for every remaining inequality. Relative interior is used in
the affine hull of each domain, so the domain need not have ambient interior.

## Remarks

The equality rows are assumed independent after consistent redundant rows are
removed. The theorem on this page assumes a finite attained primal value;
Slater's strict inequalities alone do not assert primal attainment.
The deletion convention depends on the indexed representation; Slater's
condition is tested on the resulting family, not asserted to be invariant
under other deletion orders or equivalent constraint representations.

## Statement

Consider the finite-dimensional convex program of
[[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]]. Assume its equality
matrix has independent rows, Slater's condition holds, and the finite primal
value $p^*\in\mathbb R$ is attained at $x_*$. Then there are
$\lambda_*\ge0$ and $\nu_*$ such that
$$q(\lambda_*,\nu_*)=d^*=p^*.$$
Moreover, every inequality multiplier satisfies
$\lambda_{*,i}g_i(x_*)=0$. The Slater and attainment hypotheses do not assert
that a primal minimizer is unique.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Proper closed convex data $f_0,g_i$, independent affine
equalities $Ax=b$, a Slater point, and an attained finite primal value.

[F1] The common domain, primal and dual values, relative-interior Slater
condition, and Lagrangian are defined in
[[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]].

[F2] Every dual feasible pair satisfies $q(\lambda,\nu)\le p^*$
([[thm-lagrangian-weak-duality]]).

[F3] A proper convex value function finite at a relative-interior domain
point has a supporting affine lower bound there
([[thm-convex-value-function-support-at-relative-interior-domain-points]]).

[F4] A finite convex function on an open convex set in finite dimensions is
continuous there ([[thm-convex-functions-on-open-convex-sets-are-locally-lipschitz]]).

## Proof

1.1 For perturbations $u\in\mathbb R^m$ and $v\in\mathbb R^p$, define $ P(u,v)=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in D,\ g_i(x)\le u_i\ (1\le i\le m),\ Ax-b=v\}. $ This value function is convex. Indeed, for two perturbations with finite values, choose feasible points with objective within $\epsilon$ of their respective infima. A convex combination of those points lies in $D$, its inequalities and equality residual are bounded by the same convex combination of perturbations, and convexity of $f_0$ bounds its objective. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves the convex inequality. If one perturbation value is $-\infty$, arbitrarily low feasible objective values and the same convex-combination argument give value $-\infty$ at each strict convex combination with another feasible perturbation. [given, F1, construct]

1.2 Let $S=\operatorname{aff}D$ and $Y=A(S)-b$. Since the Slater point $x_s$ lies in every relative-interior domain, $x_s$ has a relative neighborhood in $S$ contained in $D$. Each $g_i$ is finite and convex on its domain and continuous near $x_s$ in its affine hull by [F4]; after intersecting finitely many neighborhoods, there are a relative neighborhood $U_s\subseteq D$ of $x_s$ and $\eta>0$ with $g_i(y)<-\eta$ on $U_s$ for every $i$ (take any $\eta>0$ if $m=0$). The affine map $y\mapsto Ay-b$ from $S$ onto $Y$ has a linear right inverse on its direction space: choose preimages of a finite basis of $Y$. Consequently, its image of $U_s$ contains a relative neighborhood $W$ of $0$ in $Y$. For every $v\in W$, choose the corresponding $y\in U_s$; for every $u\in\prod_i(-\eta,\infty)$, that $y$ satisfies $g_i(y)<u_i$ and $Ay-b=v$. Thus $P(u,v)<+\infty$ on a relative neighborhood of $0$ in $Z=\mathbb R^m\times Y$. [given, F1, F4, construct]

2.1 The value $P(0,0)=p^*$ is finite. The convexity from step 1.1 and the neighborhood from step 1.2 imply that $P$ never equals $-\infty$: if $P(z)=-\infty$ for some perturbation $z$, choose a small $\theta>0$ so $-\theta z/(1-\theta)$ lies in that neighborhood. Convexity would give $P(0)\le\theta P(z)+(1-\theta)P(-\theta z/(1-\theta))=-\infty$, contrary to finiteness. Hence $P$ is proper and $0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}P)$ relative to $Z$. By [F3] there is a linear functional $\ell(u,v)=a^Tu+c(v)$ on $Z$ such that $P(u,v)\ge p^*+a^Tu+c(v)$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Relaxing one inequality right-hand side cannot increase the infimum, so $P(te_i,0)\le P(0,0)=p^*$ for small $t>0$. The support inequality in step 2.1 gives $P(te_i,0)\ge p^*+t a_i$, hence $a_i\le0$. Define $\lambda_*=-a\ge0$ and extend $c$ from the finite-dimensional subspace $Y$ to a linear functional on $\mathbb R^p$ by extending a basis; write the negative of this extension as $\nu_*^T$. For any $x\in D$, the perturbation $(g(x),Ax-b)$ is feasible using $x$ itself, so $ f_0(x)\ge P(g(x),Ax-b)\ge p^*+a^Tg(x)+c(Ax-b). $ Thus $L(x,\lambda_*,\nu_*)\ge p^*$ for all $x$, and $q(\lambda_*,\nu_*)\ge p^*$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra, construct]

4.1 At the primal minimizer, weak duality [F2] and feasibility give $ p^*\le q(\lambda_*,\nu_*)\le L(x_*,\lambda_*,\nu_*)= p^*+\sum_i\lambda_{*,i}g_i(x_*)\le p^*. $ Every inequality is therefore equality. Since every summand $\lambda_{*,i}g_i(x_*)$ is nonpositive, their sum being zero forces each one to be zero. Thus $q(\lambda_*,\nu_*)=p^*=d^*$, the dual supremum is attained, and complementarity holds. [F1, F2, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The $C^2$ inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$
The critical cone for a KKT tuple is
$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

## Remarks

This page uses $g_i\le0$ and nonnegative inequality multipliers throughout.
The equality-only Lagrange multiplier rule does not supply any inequality
multiplier assertion.

    - title: Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, second edition
      url: https://www.ime.unicamp.br/~pulino/MT404/TextosOnline/NocedalJ.pdf
      locator: Chapter 12, Section 12.4, printed pp. 348–350, convex programs and global optimality.
---

## Statement

Let $m\ge0$ be an integer. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex,
and suppose the objective $f:U\to\mathbb R$ and inequalities
$g_i:U\to\mathbb R$ $(1\le i\le m)$ are differentiable and convex.
Let the equalities be $Ax=b$ and define the feasible set
$C=\{x\in U:Ax=b,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. If a feasible tuple
$(x_*,\nu,\lambda)$ satisfies the KKT conditions with $\lambda\ge0$, then
$x_*$ is a global minimizer over the feasible set $C$. Moreover,
$-\nabla f(x_*)\in N_C(x_*)$, where the normal cone has the convention of
[[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The convex program, feasible KKT tuple, and normal-cone
definition.

[F1] For differentiable convex $\varphi$ on an open convex set,
$\varphi(y)\ge\varphi(x)+\nabla\varphi(x)^T(y-x)$
([[thm-differentiable-convex-functions-and-gradient-inequality]]).

[F2] The normal cone is
$N_C(x)=\{v:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\}$
([[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]]).

## Proof

1.1 Fix any feasible $y$ and put $d=y-x_*$. Then $Ad=0$. KKT stationarity gives $\nabla f(x_*)^Td=-\sum_i\lambda_i\nabla g_i(x_*)^Td$. If $\lambda_i=0$ its term is zero. If $\lambda_i>0$, complementarity gives $g_i(x_*)=0$, and [F1] applied to $g_i$ gives $\nabla g_i(x_*)^Td\le g_i(y)\le0$. Hence $\nabla f(x_*)^Td\ge0$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Applying [F1] to $f$ yields $f(y)\ge f(x_*)+\nabla f(x_*)^Td\ge f(x_*)$. Since $y$ was arbitrary, $x_*$ is globally minimizing. Step 1.1 also gives $\langle-\nabla f(x_*),y-x_*\rangle\le0$ for every feasible $y$, which is exactly $-\nabla f(x_*)\in N_C(x_*)$ by [F2]. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Example

For $p\ge1$ and $\sigma>0$, the Gaussian radial kernel on $\mathbb R^p$ is $k_\sigma(x,z)=\exp(-\|x-z\|_2^2/(2\sigma^2))$. It is a real positive semidefinite kernel, including on finite samples with repeated points or a singular Gram matrix.

## Example references

[Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, §5.8.2](https://gitlab.com/primishra/Books/-/raw/main/ESLII_print12.pdf)

[Rasmussen and Williams, *Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning*, §6.2.1](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW6.pdf)

[[def-positive-semidefinite-kernels-and-reproducing-kernel-hilbert-spaces]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $p\ge1$, $\sigma>0$, a finite sample $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb R^p$ with $m\ge1$, and real coefficients $c_1,\ldots,c_m$.

[F1] Positive semidefiniteness means symmetry and nonnegative finite Gram quadratic forms ([[def-positive-semidefinite-kernels-and-reproducing-kernel-hilbert-spaces]]).

## Verification

1.1 For each sample point put $a_i=c_i\exp(-\|x_i\|_2^2/(2\sigma^2))$. The identity $\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2=\|x_i\|_2^2+\|x_j\|_2^2-2x_i^Tx_j$ gives $\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jk_\sigma(x_i,x_j)=\sum_{i,j}a_i a_j\exp(x_i^Tx_j/\sigma^2)$. [given, algebra]

1.2 For each fixed pair $i,j$, the exponential series has the absolutely convergent multi-index expansion $\exp(x_i^Tx_j/\sigma^2)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^p}(x_i^\alpha x_j^\alpha)/(\sigma^{2|\alpha|}\alpha!)$, since the corresponding series of absolute values is $\prod_{r=1}^p\exp(|x_{ir}x_{jr}|/\sigma^2)<\infty$. The sample sums are finite, so they can be interchanged with this absolutely convergent series. [given, algebra]

2.1 Substitution into [step 1.1] yields $\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jk_\sigma(x_i,x_j)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^p}\frac{1}{\sigma^{2|\alpha|}\alpha!}(\sum_i a_ix_i^\alpha)^2\ge0$. Symmetry of $k_\sigma$ is immediate from $\|x-z\|_2=\|z-x\|_2$, so [F1] proves positive semidefiniteness; zero eigenvalues or repeated points do not affect the sum-of-squares argument. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Take $X=\mathbb R$, $\mathcal H=\mathbb R$, $\phi(x)=x$, and $k(x,z)=xz$. For $C>0$ and the ordered sample $(-1,-1),(1,+1),(1,-1)$, the soft-margin SVM has the optimum $w=0$, $b=-1$, $\xi=(0,2,0)$ with objective $2C$; dual multipliers are $\alpha=(0,C,C)$ and $\mu=(C,0,0)$. Its score is $-1$ at $x=1$, where the sample has one positive and one negative label. Applying the separately specified logistic map $\sigma(t)=(1+e^{-t})^{-1}$ to that score gives $1/(1+e)$, not the empirical positive-label frequency $1/2$. These are finite-sample quantities; the SVM score is not a probability supplied by the SVM optimization.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The feature map, the ordered sample, $C>0$, and the soft-margin definition.

[F1] The soft-margin constraints and objective are those in the hard- and soft-margin SVM definition ([[def-hard-and-soft-margin-support-vector-machines]]).

[F2] The SVM KKT equations include $w=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\phi(x_i)$, $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0$, $C-\alpha_i-\mu_i=0$, and complementarity for both inequality families ([[thm-soft-margin-svm-dual-and-kkt-conditions]]).

[F3] The feature map $\phi(x)=x$ realizes the positive semidefinite linear kernel $k(x,z)=xz$ ([[ex-linear-and-polynomial-kernels]]).

## Verification




1.1 The feature map in [F3] realizes the stated linear kernel. At $w=0$, $b=-1$, the scores at all three observations equal $-1$. Their signed margins are respectively $1,-1,1$, so $\xi=(0,2,0)$ satisfies every soft-margin constraint, with objective $2C$. [given, F1, F3, construct, algebra]


2.1 For any feasible tuple, let $t=w+b$, the score at $x=1$. The two observations at $x=1$ require $\xi_2\ge\max(0,1-t)$ and $\xi_3\ge\max(0,1+t)$. If $-1\le t\le1$ these lower bounds sum to $2$; if $t>1$, the second is $1+t>2$; and if $t<-1$, the first is $1-t>2$. Thus $\xi_2+\xi_3\ge2$ for every feasible tuple, and its objective is at least $C(\xi_2+\xi_3)\ge2C$. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]


3.1 The candidate in [step 1.1] is therefore globally optimal. For $\alpha=(0,C,C)$ and $\mu=(C,0,0)$, $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\phi(x_i)=C-C=0=w$, $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=C-C=0$, and $C-\alpha_i-\mu_i=0$ for all three indices. Each margin constraint is active, so $\alpha_i g_i^{(m)}=0$; also $\mu_i\xi_i=0$ for each $i$. These are the KKT conditions in [F2]. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, F2, algebra]


4.1 The dual objective is $\sum_i\alpha_i-\frac12\|\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\phi(x_i)\|^2=2C$, equal to the primal value. The score at $x=1$ is $-1$, while the empirical positive-label frequency among the two observations at $x=1$ is $1/2$. The logistic transform of the score is $(1+e)^{-1}\ne1/2$; the SVM optimization does not assert that this transformed value is a probability. [step 1.1, step 3.1, F2, algebra] ∎

      url: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2006/01/Bishop-Pattern-Recognition-and-Machine-Learning-2006.pdf
---

## Definition

Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, let $m:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$, and let
$k:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and positive
semidefinite, meaning that for every finite ordered list $t_1,\ldots,t_r$
in $\mathcal X$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^r$,
$$\sum_{i,j=1}^r a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)\ge0.$$
For finite ordered lists $A=(a_i)_{i=1}^r$ and $B=(b_j)_{j=1}^s$ in
$\mathcal X$, define
$$K_{AB}=(k(a_i,b_j))_{i,j};$$
repeated indices are allowed.

Given a real Gaussian process $f=(f_t)_{t\in\mathcal X}$ with mean
$m(t)=\mathbb E[f_t]$ and covariance
$k(s,t)=\mathbb E[(f_s-m(s))(f_t-m(t))]$, and a nonempty finite training list
$X=(x_i)_{i=1}^n$ in $\mathcal X$, define $f_X=(f_{x_i})_{i=1}^n$ and
$m_X=(m(x_i))_{i=1}^n$. For a centered Gaussian noise vector
$\varepsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ with symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance
$R$ that is independent of $f$, define the observation vector
$Y=f_X+\varepsilon$ and the matrix
$A_X=K_{XX}+R$.

For a nonempty finite test list $X_*=(x_j^*)_{j=1}^p$ in $\mathcal X$,
define the latent test
vector $f_*=f_{X_*}$. If a centered Gaussian vector
$\eta_*\sim N_p(0,R_*)$ with symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance
$R_*$ is independent of the pair $(f,\varepsilon)$, define the noisy test
vector $Y_*=f_*+\eta_*$.

## Definition references

[[def-gaussian-process|A Gaussian process has multivariate-normal finite evaluation vectors, including singular laws and repeated indices.]]

[[def-multivariate-normal-law|Finite Gaussian laws allow positive-semidefinite, possibly singular covariance matrices.]]

[[def-independent-random-elements|Independence means independence of the sigma-algebras generated by the random elements.]]

[Rasmussen and Williams, GPML, Chapter 2 §2.2, printed pp. 13–18](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW2.pdf)

[Bishop, PRML, §6.4.2, printed pp. 306–310](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2006/01/Bishop-Pattern-Recognition-and-Machine-Learning-2006.pdf)

## Model diagram

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth]
  \node[draw,rounded corners] (prior) at (0,0) {$f\sim\mathrm{GP}(m,k)$};
  \node[draw] (train) at (-2,-1.5) {$f_X$};
  \node[draw] (test) at (3,-1.5) {$f_*$};
  \node[draw] (noise) at (-2,-3) {$\varepsilon$};
  \node[draw,rounded corners] (obs) at (0,-3) {$Y=f_X+\varepsilon$};
  \node[draw] (testnoise) at (3,-3) {$\eta_*$};
  \node[draw,rounded corners] (testobs) at (5,-3) {$Y_*=f_*+\eta_*$};
  \draw[->] (prior) -- (train);
  \draw[->] (prior) -- (test);
  \draw[->] (train) -- (obs);
  \draw[->] (noise) -- (obs);
  \draw[->] (test) -- (testobs);
  \draw[->] (testnoise) -- (testobs);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

The single prior node represents one process, so $f_X$ and $f_*$ may be
correlated. Arrows into $Y$ and $Y_*$ denote vector addition. The training
noise $\varepsilon$ is independent of $f$, and the test noise $\eta_*$ is
independent of the pair $(f,\varepsilon)$; the diagram records no posterior
independence claim.

title: Projection onto a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner-product space
status: draft

sources:

      url: https://www.math.brown.edu/streil/papers/LADW/HTML_2026_04-30/Ch5.html
---

## Statement

Let $H$ be a real inner-product space and $V\subseteq H$ a finite-dimensional
subspace. For each $f\in H$ there is a unique $p\in V$ such that $f-p$ is
orthogonal to $V$, meaning $\langle f-p,v\rangle=0$ for every $v\in V$.
For every $v\in V$,
$$\|f-v\|^2=\|f-p\|^2+\|p-v\|^2.$$
In particular, $\|f\|^2=\|p\|^2+\|f-p\|^2$.

## Statement references

[[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases|Every finite-dimensional inner-product space has an orthonormal basis, with the empty basis in dimension zero.]]

[Treil, Linear Algebra Done Wrong, Chapter 5 §5.3.2](https://www.math.brown.edu/streil/papers/LADW/HTML_2026_04-30/Ch5.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real inner-product space $H$, a finite-dimensional subspace $V\subseteq H$, and $f\in H$.

[F1] Every finite-dimensional real inner-product space has an orthonormal basis; the basis is empty when the dimension is zero. [[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_r$ of $V$ by [F1], allowing $r=0$, and set $p=\sum_{j=1}^r\langle f,e_j\rangle e_j$. For each $\ell$, orthonormality gives $\langle f-p,e_\ell\rangle=\langle f,e_\ell\rangle-\sum_{j=1}^r\langle f,e_j\rangle\langle e_j,e_\ell\rangle=0$; since the basis spans $V$, $f-p$ is orthogonal to $V$. [F1, given, choose, construct, algebra]

2.1 For any $v\in V$, $p-v\in V$ and $f-p$ is orthogonal to $V$. Expanding the squared norm of $f-v=(f-p)+(p-v)$ therefore gives $\|f-v\|^2=\|f-p\|^2+\|p-v\|^2$. If $q\in V$ also has $f-q$ orthogonal to $V$, then $p-q=(f-q)-(f-p)$ lies in $V^\perp$ and in $V$, hence $\|p-q\|^2=0$ and $p=q$. Taking $v=0$ gives the stated norm identity. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

In the finite observation model, let $K=K_{XX}$ and let $R$ be symmetric and
positive semidefinite. Then $A=K+R$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
Its ordinary inverse exists if and only if $A$ is positive definite,
equivalently if and only if all singular values of $A$ are positive. Thus the
standard inverse formulas are defined exactly under $A\succ0$; no ordinary
inverse formula applies when $A$ is singular.

## Statement references

[[def-gaussian-process-regression-observation-model|The finite Gram and observed matrices are K_XX and A_X=K_XX+R, with positive-semidefinite kernel and noise covariances.]]

[Rasmussen and Williams, GPML, Chapter 4 §4.1, printed pp. 79–80](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW4.pdf)

[Bishop, PRML, §6.4.2, printed pp. 306–309](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2006/01/Bishop-Pattern-Recognition-and-Machine-Learning-2006.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite observation matrix $K=K_{XX}$ from a symmetric positive-semidefinite kernel and a symmetric positive-semidefinite noise covariance $R$.

[F1] Every finite Gram matrix of the kernel is positive semidefinite, and the observed matrix is $A=K_{XX}+R$. [[def-gaussian-process-regression-observation-model]]

[F2] A finite-dimensional nonnegative operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis with nonnegative eigenvalues. [[thm-non-negative-operator-characterisations]]

[F3] The singular values of an endomorphism are the eigenvalues of $|A|=\sqrt{A^*A}$. [[def-singular-values-of-an-endomorphism]]

[F4] A nonnegative finite-dimensional operator has a unique nonnegative square root. [[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]]

[F5] A finite-dimensional linear map has a singular-value decomposition with exactly its positive singular values in the nonzero diagonal block. [[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]

## Proof

**Given:** The matrices $K$ and $R$ in the Statement.

1.1 For every $z\in\mathbb R^n$, $z^TAz=z^TKz+z^TRz\ge0$ by [F1], and $A$ is symmetric. Hence $A$ is a nonnegative endomorphism of the finite-dimensional real inner-product space $\mathbb R^n$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ of $A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_j\ge0$. In this basis, $A$ is invertible exactly when no $\lambda_j$ is zero, while $z^TAz=\sum_j\lambda_j c_j^2$ for $z=\sum_j c_je_j$ is positive for every nonzero $z$ exactly when all $\lambda_j>0$. Thus $A$ is invertible if and only if it is positive definite. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 In the same basis, $A^*A=A^2$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_j^2$. By [F4], its unique nonnegative square root has eigenvalues $\lambda_j$, so [F3] says the singular values of $A$ are precisely these $\lambda_j$. By [F5], the SVD has full rank exactly when all $n$ singular values are positive, which is exactly the invertibility condition in step 2.1. [F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$ and a linear endomorphism $T:V\to V$.

[L1] A self-adjoint operator on a finite-dimensional real inner product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis ([[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]).

[L2] A normal operator on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis ([[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]).

[L3] Every nonnegative real number has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Assume $T$ is non-negative. Then $T$ is self-adjoint by [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. If $V$ is real, [L1] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis; if $V$ is complex, the identity $T=T^*$ yields $TT^*=T^*T$, so [L2] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis. For any eigenvector $v\ne0$ with $Tv=\lambda v$, the equality $\langle Tv,v\rangle=\lambda\lVert v\rVert^2$ and non-negativity give $\lambda\ge0$, and self-adjointness makes $\lambda$ real. Thus claim 1 implies claim 2. [L1, L2, algebra]

1.2 Assume claim 3. If the diagonal entries are $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\ge0$, then [L3] gives square roots $\sqrt{\lambda_j}\ge0$; the diagonal operator $S$ with diagonal entries $\sqrt{\lambda_j}$ satisfies $S^*S=T$. Thus claim 3 implies claim 4. [L3, algebra]

1.3 Assume claim 2, so $T$ is self-adjoint. If $V$ is real, [L1] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis. If $V$ is complex, $T=T^*$ implies $TT^*=T^*T$, so [L2] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis. In either case the matrix of $T$ in this basis is diagonal, and its diagonal entries are nonnegative real numbers by claim 2. Thus claim 2 implies claim 3. [L1, L2, algebra]

2.1 Assume claim 4, so $T=S^*S$. Then for every $v\in V$ one has $\langle Tv,v\rangle=\langle S^*Sv,v\rangle=\langle Sv,Sv\rangle\ge0$, and for all $u,v$ one has $\langle Tu,v\rangle=\langle Su,Sv\rangle=\langle u,Tv\rangle$. Hence $T$ is self-adjoint and non-negative. Thus claim 4 implies claim 1. [algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. Because

$$\langle T^*Tv,v\rangle=\langle Tv,Tv\rangle\ge0$$

for every $v\in V$, and because $(T^*T)^*=T^*T$ by [[prop-adjoint-algebra]],
the operator $T^*T$ is non-negative. Let

$$|T|:=\sqrt{T^*T},$$

the unique non-negative square root from
[[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]]. The **singular values**
of $T$ are the eigenvalues of $|T|$, listed with multiplicity in weakly
decreasing order.

In particular, this definition applies to endomorphisms by taking $W=V$.

## Statement

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$ and a non-negative endomorphism $T:V\to V$.

[L1] A non-negative operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis with nonnegative eigenvalues ([[thm-non-negative-operator-characterisations]]).

[L2] Every nonnegative real number has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], there is an orthonormal basis $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and numbers $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\ge0$ such that $Te_j=\lambda_j e_j$. By [L2], each $\lambda_j$ has a nonnegative square root. Define $R$ by $Re_j=\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,e_j$. Then $R^2e_j=\lambda_j e_j=Te_j$ for every $j$, so $R^2=T$; the same basis shows that $R$ is self-adjoint with nonnegative eigenvalues, hence non-negative by [L1]. [L1, L2, algebra]

2.1 Let $Q$ be another non-negative square root of $T$. Because $Q^2=T$, each eigenspace $E_\lambda(T)$ is $Q$-invariant. On $E_\lambda(T)$ one has $Q^2=\lambda I$, and [L1] applied to the non-negative operator $Q|_{E_\lambda(T)}$ shows that all its eigenvalues are nonnegative; by [L2], the only nonnegative number whose square is $\lambda$ is $\sqrt{\lambda}$, so $Q=\sqrt{\lambda}\,I$ on $E_\lambda(T)$. Thus $Q$ acts on every basis vector $e_j$ exactly as $R$ does, and therefore $Q=R$. [L1, L2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, let $f=(f_t)_{t\in\mathcal X}$ be a
real Gaussian process with mean $m$ and symmetric positive-semidefinite
covariance kernel $k$, and let $X=(x_i)_{i=1}^n\in\mathcal X^n$ with $n\ge1$.
For independent observation noise $\varepsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ with symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariance $R$, set $Y=f_X+\varepsilon$,
$m_X=(m(x_i))$, $K_{XX}=(k(x_i,x_j))$, and $A_X=K_{XX}+R$. Suppose
$A_X$ is positive definite. Define the log marginal likelihood at
$y\in\mathbb R^n$ as the logarithm of the Lebesgue density of $Y$ at $y$
under this prior-predictive model. Then $Y\sim N_n(m_X,A_X)$ and
$$\log p(y\mid X,m,k,R)=-\frac12(y-m_X)^TA_X^{-1}(y-m_X)-\frac12\log\det(A_X)-\frac n2\log(2\pi).$$
This formula is asserted only for the nonsingular observed-covariance case
$A_X\succ0$.

## Statement references

[Rasmussen and Williams, GPML, Chapter 2 §§2.2–2.3, equations (2.28)–(2.30), printed pp. 18–20](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW2.pdf)

[Bishop, PRML, §6.4.2, equations (6.61)–(6.62), printed pp. 306–307](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2006/01/Bishop-Pattern-Recognition-and-Machine-Learning-2006.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the finite Gaussian-process observation model, a nonempty evaluation list $X$, independent noise $\varepsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ with $R\succeq0$, and $A_X=K_{XX}+R\succ0$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice states that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The finite observation model defines $Y=f_X+\varepsilon$, $m_X$, $K_{XX}$, and $A_X=K_{XX}+R$, with $\varepsilon$ independent of $f$. [[def-gaussian-process-regression-observation-model]]

[F2] A Gaussian process has multivariate-normal finite evaluation vectors, including singular covariance matrices. [[def-gaussian-process]]

[F3] Under AC, a multivariate-normal law is characterized by its normal scalar projections and allows symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F4] A finite stack of independent Gaussian vectors is jointly multivariate normal with block-diagonal covariance. [[lem-finite-independent-gaussian-vectors-form-joint-multivariate-normal]]

[F5] Under AC, $N_n(a,\Sigma)$ with $\Sigma\succ0$ has Lebesgue density $(2\pi)^{-n/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\bigl(-\frac12(x-a)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-a)\bigr)$. [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 By [F1] and [F2], $f_X\sim N_n(m_X,K_{XX})$. The independent noise has law $N_n(0,R)$, so [F4] makes $U=(f_X,\varepsilon)$ jointly Gaussian with mean $(m_X,0)$ and block-diagonal covariance $\operatorname{diag}(K_{XX},R)$. For any $a\in\mathbb R^n$, $a^TY=(a^T,a^T)U$ is a normal scalar projection by [F3]; its mean is $a^Tm_X$ and its variance is $a^T(K_{XX}+R)a$. Thus the projection definition [F3] gives $Y\sim N_n(m_X,A_X)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F5] to the law from step 1.1, using the hypothesis $A_X\succ0$. Its density at $y$ is $(2\pi)^{-n/2}\det(A_X)^{-1/2}\exp\!\bigl(-\frac12(y-m_X)^TA_X^{-1}(y-m_X)\bigr)$. This is positive, so taking its logarithm and expanding products gives the displayed formula. [A1, F5, given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real stochastic process
$X=(X_t)_{t\in I}$ [[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]
is a **Gaussian process** if, for every integer $n\ge 1$, every time list
$t_1,\ldots,t_n\in I$, and every $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R$, the random
variable
$$
\sum_{j=1}^n a_jX_{t_j}
$$
has a normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ for some $m\in\mathbb R$ and
$\sigma\ge0$. Variance zero is allowed, so constant linear combinations are
included.

Equivalently, for every such time list the evaluation vector
$(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})$ has a possibly singular multivariate normal law in
the sense of [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. Indeed, that definition says
exactly that every scalar projection of the vector is normal. This also covers
repeated times, zero coefficients, and singular covariance matrices; no
distinct-time convention is needed for this definition.

Choice is declared because the library's scalar and multivariate normal-law
interfaces construct their probability laws and independent standard-normal
realizations under AC. The equivalence itself is only an unpacking of the
finite-dimensional projection definition and makes no further selection.

## Source notes

Sousi, Section 6.1, defines a Gaussian process through normal finite linear
combinations. Yoshida, Section 6.1 (printed p. 173), uses the equivalent
finite-dimensional multivariate-normal formulation. The present definition
retains singular laws explicitly, as required by the library's normal-law
interface.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume AC and mutually independent Borel random vectors
$Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$ for a finite nonempty index set.

[A1] AC is the explicit axiom used by the multivariate-normal existence,
scalar characteristic-function uniqueness, and Cramer–Wold suppliers below.
([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[F1] Independence of random elements means independence of their generated
sigma-algebras. ([[def-independent-random-elements]])

[F2] A finite mutually independent family of random elements has product
joint law. ([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]])

[F3] Under AC, $N_d(a,\Sigma)$ exists for every finite $d\ge1$ and symmetric
positive-semidefinite $\Sigma$, and every scalar projection has its specified
normal law. ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]])

[F4] Under AC, the characteristic function of $N_d(a,\Sigma)$ is
$\exp(iu\cdot a-u^T\Sigma u/2)$, including singular $\Sigma$.
([[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multivariate-normal-law]])

[F5] Characteristic functions of finite sums of mutually independent real
random variables multiply. ([[lem-characteristic-functions-under-affine-maps-and-independent-sums]])

[F6] Under AC, equal characteristic functions determine equal Borel
probability laws on $\mathbb R$. ([[thm-uniqueness-of-a-law-from-its-characteristic-function]])

[F7] Under AC, all one-dimensional projection laws determine a Borel
probability law on finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
([[thm-cramer-wold-device]])

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 By [F2], the finite tuple $Z$ is a Borel random vector with product joint law. For any $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_m)$, each scalar map $z_j\mapsto u_j\cdot z_j$ is Borel, so preimages of Borel sets lie in $\sigma(Z_j)$. Independence [F1] therefore makes the scalars $u_j\cdot Z_j$ mutually independent. By [A1, F3], each is normal with mean $u_j\cdot a_j$ and variance $u_j^T\Sigma_j u_j$. [A1, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 For any $s\in\mathbb R$, [F5] and [F4] give $\varphi_{u\cdot Z}(s)=\prod_{j=1}^m\exp\!\left(is\,u_j\cdot a_j-\tfrac12s^2u_j^T\Sigma_j u_j\right)=\exp\!\left(is\,u\cdot a-\tfrac12s^2u^T\Sigma u\right)$. The last expression is the characteristic function of $N_1(u\cdot a,u^T\Sigma u)$ by [F4] in dimension one. Scalar uniqueness [F6] gives $u\cdot Z\sim N_1(u\cdot a,u^T\Sigma u)$, including the zero-variance point-mass case. [F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The block matrix $\Sigma$ is positive semidefinite because $u^T\Sigma u=\sum_j u_j^T\Sigma_j u_j\ge0$. By [A1, F3], the law $N_D(a,\Sigma)$ exists and its projection laws are the normal laws found in step 2.1. Cramer–Wold [F7] therefore identifies the law of $Z$ with $N_D(a,\Sigma)$. This also covers singular blocks and uses no inverse. [A1, F3, F7, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, $m:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$, and
$k:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ a symmetric kernel whose every
finite Gram quadratic form on points of $\mathcal X$ is nonnegative. Let
$f=(f_t)_{t\in\mathcal X}$ be the canonical Gaussian process with
$m(t)=\mathbb E[f_t]$ and
$k(s,t)=\mathbb E[(f_s-m(s))(f_t-m(t))]$. For finite ordered lists
$A=(a_i)_{i=1}^r$ and $B=(b_j)_{j=1}^s$ in $\mathcal X$, set
$K_{AB}=(k(a_i,b_j))$; repetitions are allowed. Take
$X=(x_i)_{i=1}^n\in\mathcal X^n$ and
$X_*=(x_j^*)_{j=1}^p\in\mathcal X^p$ with $n,p\ge1$, and write
$m_X=(m(x_i))$, $m_*=(m(x_j^*))$, $f_X=(f_{x_i})$, and
$f_*=(f_{x_j^*})$. Let $\varepsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ be independent of $f$,
where $R$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and set $Y=f_X+\varepsilon$ and
$A_X=K_{XX}+R$. Suppose $A_X$ is positive definite. Then for every
$y\in\mathbb R^n$ the conditional law of $f_*$ given $Y=y$ has mean
$$m_*+K_{*X}A_X^{-1}(y-m_X)$$
and covariance
$$K_{**}-K_{*X}A_X^{-1}K_{X*}.$$
This covariance is positive semidefinite and may be singular. If
$\eta_*\sim N_p(0,R_*)$ is independent of the pair $(f,\varepsilon)$, where
$R_*$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, then the conditional law of
$f_*+\eta_*$ has the same mean and covariance with $R_*$ added. The displayed
kernel is defined for every $y$, although regular conditional versions are
determined only $P_Y$-almost surely.

## Statement references

[Rasmussen and Williams, GPML, Chapter 2 §2.2, equations (2.18)–(2.24), printed pp. 15–18](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW2.pdf)

[Bishop, PRML, §6.4.2, equations (6.61)–(6.68), printed pp. 306–309](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2006/01/Bishop-Pattern-Recognition-and-Machine-Learning-2006.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; a set $\mathcal X$, mean $m$, symmetric positive-semidefinite kernel $k$; finite ordered lists $X$ and $X_*$ of positive lengths; observation noise $\varepsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ independent of the process with $R\succeq0$; optional test noise $\eta_*\sim N_p(0,R_*)$ independent of the pair $(f,\varepsilon)$ with $R_*\succeq0$; and $A_X=K_{XX}+R\succ0$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice states that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Under AC, a mean function and symmetric positive-semidefinite kernel on an arbitrary index set determine a unique canonical process on the cylinder sigma-algebra with the stated finite Gaussian marginals; the construction supplies no sample-path continuity. [[thm-gaussian-process-exists-from-mean-and-positive-semidefinite-covariance-kernel]]

[F2] A real Gaussian process has multivariate-normal finite evaluation vectors, including repeated indices and singular covariance matrices. [[def-gaussian-process]]

[F3] For finite lists, independent Gaussian observation noise with PSD covariance and positive-definite observed covariance gives the stated all-$y$ conditional Gaussian kernel; its predictive covariance may be singular, and Gaussian test noise independent of the pair $(f,\varepsilon)$ adds its covariance. [[thm-finite-gaussian-process-posterior-and-predictive-laws]]

[F4] In this model, $A_X=K_{XX}+R$ is invertible exactly when it is positive definite. [[lem-gp-regression-observed-covariance-invertibility]]

## Proof

**Given:** The assumptions in the Statement.

1.1 By [A1] and [F1], the specified mean and kernel give the canonical cylinder-space Gaussian process. By [F2], its finite evaluations on $X$ and $X_*$ are jointly multivariate normal, including when either list has repetitions or a covariance block is singular. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 In the notation of the finite model, the observed block in [F3] is $C=K_{XX}+R=A_X$. By the hypothesis and [F4], $C\succ0$, so every inverse required by [F3] exists. Under the optional noisy-prediction hypothesis, $\eta_*$ is independent of the pair $(f,\varepsilon)$, exactly the joint-independence premise for [F3]'s Gaussian stack. Applying [F3] with these lists, means, noise covariance, and observed block gives the displayed conditional mean and covariance; its statement also gives positive semidefiniteness, possible singularity, the all-$y$ version, and the test-noise covariance addition. ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a set, let $m:T\to\mathbb R$, and let
$k:T\times T\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning that
for every finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_n\in T$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\sum_{i,j=1}^n a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)\ge0.$$
There is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the cylinder sigma-algebra
$\mathcal C_T$ of $\mathbb R^T$ whose marginal on each finite-coordinate space
$\mathbb R^F$, for $F\subseteq T$ finite, is the Gaussian law with mean
$(m(t))_{t\in F}$ and covariance matrix $(k(s,t))_{s,t\in F}$. The coordinate
process $X_t(x)=x(t)$ is Gaussian, has mean function $m$, and has covariance
kernel $k$. This construction gives only the cylinder-space process; it
asserts no sample-path continuity, joint measurability in $(t,x)$, or tight
Banach-valued law.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a set $T$, a real-valued mean function $m$, and a symmetric
positive-semidefinite kernel $k$ as stated.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice states that every family of nonempty sets has a
choice function. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Every finite-dimensional symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix has a
unique positive-semidefinite square root. [[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]]

[F2] Under AC, a finite mean vector and symmetric positive-semidefinite
covariance matrix define a possibly singular multivariate normal law; its
scalar projections have the corresponding normal laws. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F3] Under AC, the characteristic function of $N_n(a,\Sigma)$ is
$u\mapsto\exp(iu^Ta-\tfrac12u^T\Sigma u)$, and it uniquely determines the
law, including when $\Sigma$ is singular.
[[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F4] A family of finite-coordinate probability laws is consistent when each
larger law pushes forward under restriction to the smaller law.
[[def-consistent-family-of-finite-dimensional-distributions]]

[F5] The real line with its Borel sigma-algebra is standard Borel.
[[lem-real-line-is-standard-borel]]

[F6] Under AC, a consistent family on arbitrary standard-Borel coordinates
has a unique extension to the cylinder sigma-algebra.
[[thm-kolmogorov-extension-for-standard-borel-coordinate-spaces]]

[F7] On the cylinder sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^T$, every coordinate map is
measurable. [[def-coordinate-maps-and-cylinder-sigma-algebra]]

[F8] A stochastic process is a family of random elements on one probability
space; it is Gaussian when every finite linear combination of its coordinates
is normally distributed. [[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]
[[def-gaussian-process]]

## Proof

**Given:** AC, $T$, $m$, and $k$ as in the Statement.

1.1 For each nonempty finite $F\subseteq T$, use AC to choose an enumeration $e_F:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to F$. Set $a_i=m(e_F(i))$ and $\Sigma_{ij}=k(e_F(i),e_F(j))$. Positive semidefiniteness of $k$ makes $\Sigma$ positive semidefinite; [F1] supplies its positive square root and [F2] gives the possibly singular law $N_n(a,\Sigma)$. Push this law to $\mathbb R^F$ by relabelling coordinate $i$ as $e_F(i)$. A different enumeration changes both the mean and covariance by the same permutation; [F3] shows that the relabelled law is unchanged. For $F=\varnothing$, take the unique law on the singleton empty product. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, choose, construct]

2.1 If $F\subseteq G$ are finite, the characteristic function of the restriction pushforward of the $G$-law at $u\in\mathbb R^F$ is $ \exp\!\left(i\sum_{t\in F}u_t m(t)-\frac12\sum_{s,t\in F}u_su_t k(s,t)\right). $ This is also the characteristic function of the $F$-law. By [F3] the two pushforward laws agree, so the family constructed in step 1.1 is consistent in the sense of [F4]. The empty marginal is the singleton law. [F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Each coordinate space $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is standard Borel by [F5]. The consistent family from step 2.1 therefore satisfies [F6], which gives a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_T$ with exactly these finite-coordinate marginals. [A1, F5, F6, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Define $X_t(x)=x(t)$ on $(\mathbb R^T,\mathcal C_T,\mu)$. By [F7] these coordinates are measurable, and step 3.1 gives each finite evaluation vector the stated multivariate normal law. Every finite linear combination is a scalar projection of such a vector, hence is normal by [F2]. Thus [F8] makes $X$ a Gaussian process. Its one- and two-coordinate laws give mean $m$ and covariance $k$, including zero-variance coordinates and singular finite covariance matrices. [F2, F6, F7, F8, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The extension in step 3.1 is unique on $\mathcal C_T$. It supplies no topology or probability law on a path-continuous or Banach-valued function space, so no such regularity or tightness conclusion is included. [F6, step 3.1] ∎

## Source notes

van der Vaart–van Zanten define an arbitrary-index Gaussian process through
its finite-dimensional Gaussian laws and covariance function. Rasmussen–Williams
give the mean/covariance and marginalization convention for Gaussian processes.
The finite-coordinate consistency and cylinder extension are proved here from
the cited local suppliers; neither source is used to infer path regularity.
