## Statement

Assume AC and let $f=(f_t)_{t\in T}$ be a real Gaussian process with mean
$m$ and covariance kernel $k$; when $m$ and $k$ are specified as a prior,
the canonical cylinder-space process exists by
[[thm-gaussian-process-exists-from-mean-and-positive-semidefinite-covariance-kernel]].
Let $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in T^n$ and $X_*=(x_1^*,\ldots,x_p^*)\in T^p$,
where $n,p\ge1$ and repeated indices are allowed. Write
$f_X=(f_{x_i})_{i=1}^n$, $f_{X_*}=(f_{x_j^*})_{j=1}^p$,
$m_X=(m(x_i))_{i=1}^n$, and $m_*=(m(x_j^*))_{j=1}^p$. For finite lists
$A=(a_i)$ and $B=(b_j)$, define
$K_{AB}=(k(a_i,b_j))_{i,j}$.

Let $\epsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ be independent of the process, where $R$ is
symmetric positive semidefinite, and set $Y=f_X+\epsilon$. Assume the
observed covariance $C=K_{XX}+R$ is positive definite. Then a version of the
conditional law of $f_{X_*}$ given $Y=y$ is, for every $y\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$N_p\!\left(m_*+K_{*X}C^{-1}(y-m_X),\;K_{**}-K_{*X}C^{-1}K_{X*}\right).$$
The displayed conditional covariance is positive semidefinite and may be
singular; $K_{XX}$ and $K_{**}$ may also be singular. If a prediction-noise
vector $\eta_*\sim N_p(0,R_*)$ jointly independent of the process and
$\epsilon$ is added to $f_{X_*}$, with $R_*$ symmetric positive semidefinite,
the conditional mean is unchanged and
$R_*$ is added to the conditional covariance. The displayed kernel is a
version defined at every $y$; conditional-law versions are determined only
$P_Y$-almost surely.

For computation, the occurrences of $C^{-1}v$ mean solving $Cu=v$. Since
$C$ is positive definite, its Cholesky factorization and forward/back
substitution evaluate these solves without forming $C^{-1}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the Gaussian process and finite lists in the Statement; an
independent Gaussian observation-noise vector with covariance $R\succeq0$;
$C=K_{XX}+R\succ0$; and, for the noisy-prediction clause, an independent
Gaussian vector with covariance $R_*\succeq0$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is part of the finite Gaussian-law and conditional
normal interfaces used below. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A Gaussian process has multivariate-normal finite evaluation vectors,
including repeated indices and singular covariances. [[def-gaussian-process]]

[F2] Independence of random elements means independence of their generated
sigma-algebras. [[def-independent-random-elements]]

[F3] A finite independent stack of possibly singular Gaussian vectors is
jointly multivariate normal. [[lem-finite-independent-gaussian-vectors-form-joint-multivariate-normal]]

[F4] A multivariate normal law is characterized by its normal scalar
projections, and singular positive-semidefinite covariance is allowed.
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F5] For a jointly Gaussian pair with observed covariance $B\succ0$, the
conditional law has mean $a+CB^{-1}(y-b)$ and covariance
$A-CB^{-1}C^T$, which is positive semidefinite and may be singular.
[[thm-multivariate-normal-conditional-law]]

[F6] A real symmetric positive-definite matrix has a unique Cholesky
factorization $C=LL^T$ with $L$ lower triangular and positive diagonal.
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]

[F7] Forward and backward substitution are the recursive procedures for
triangular systems with nonzero diagonal.
[[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]]

[F8] Forward and backward substitution return the unique solutions of their
triangular systems. [[thm-forward-and-back-substitution-are-correct-unique-and-quadratic-cost]]

## Proof

**Given:** The assumptions in the Statement.

1.1 By [F1], the concatenated finite evaluation vector $U=(f_{X_*},f_X)$ is multivariate normal with mean $(m_*,m_X)$ and covariance $ \begin{pmatrix}K_{**}&K_{*X}\\K_{X*}&K_{XX}\end{pmatrix}. $ This remains valid when either list has repetitions. [A1, F1, given]

2.1 The vector $\epsilon$ is multivariate normal with mean zero and covariance $R$. Each coordinate of $U$ is a measurable function of the process coordinates, so $\sigma(U)\subseteq\sigma(f)$. By [F2] and the independence hypothesis, $\sigma(\epsilon)$ is independent of $\sigma(f)$ and hence of $\sigma(U)$. Applying [F3] to $U$ and $\epsilon$ shows that $Z=(f_{X_*},f_X,\epsilon)$ is jointly multivariate normal with block-diagonal covariance between $U$ and $\epsilon$. [A1, F2, F3, given, step 1.1]

3.1 Apply the linear map $(u,v,e)\mapsto(u,v+e)$ to $Z$. Every scalar projection of the result is a scalar projection of $Z$, hence is normal by [F4]; its mean is $(m_*,m_X)$. The Gaussian vectors have finite second moments, so independence and $E\epsilon=0$ give $\operatorname{Cov}(f_{X_*},\epsilon)=0$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(Y)=K_{XX}+R=C$. By step 1.1, $\operatorname{Cov}(f_{X_*},f_X)=K_{*X}$, so $(f_{X_*},Y)$ is jointly Gaussian with covariance $ \begin{pmatrix}K_{**}&K_{*X}\\K_{X*}&C\end{pmatrix}. $ [F2, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Apply [F5] with $A=K_{**}$, cross-covariance $K_{*X}$, and observed covariance $B=C\succ0$. The result is a probability-kernel version for every $y$, with the displayed mean and Schur-complement covariance; [F5] also proves this covariance is positive semidefinite even if singular. [A1, F5, given, step 3.1]

4.2 If $\eta_*$ is present, it is jointly independent of the process and $\epsilon$ by hypothesis. By [F3], the stack $(f_{X_*},f_X,\epsilon,\eta_*)$ is jointly Gaussian. The linear map $(u,v,e,h)\mapsto(u+h,v+e)$ has mean $(m_*,m_X)$, cross-covariance $K_{*X}$, observed covariance $C$, and prediction covariance $K_{**}+R_*$. Applying [F5] to this pair gives the stated noisy-prediction law. [A1, F3, F4, F5, given, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 By [F6], write $C=LL^T$. For any right-hand side $b$, solve $Lz=b$ by forward substitution and $L^Tu=z$ by backward substitution; [F8] gives both unique solutions. Then $Cu=L(L^Tu)=Lz=b$, so $u=C^{-1}b$. Applying this to $b=y-m_X$ and, column by column, to $K_{X*}$ evaluates both formula terms without forming the inverse. [F6, F7, F8, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

Only the observed covariance $C$ is inverted, and its positive-definiteness is
an explicit hypothesis. The result makes no pseudoinverse claim when $C$ is
singular. The conditional formula specifies a valid all-$y$ version, while
another regular conditional version may differ on a $P_Y$-null set.

## Source notes

Rasmussen–Williams derive the finite Gaussian-regression mean and covariance
for zero-mean priors and independent homoscedastic noise, and describe the
multiple-test-vector case. The local proof extends the calculation to nonzero
means, general positive-semidefinite noise covariance, singular prior and
predictive blocks, and the exact positive-definite observed-block hypothesis.
The conditional-normal supplier provides the complete probability-kernel
argument.

## Remark

A real Gaussian process is a family whose finite evaluation vectors are
multivariate normal. Let $T$ be a set and let $f=(f_t)_{t\in T}$ be a real
Gaussian process with mean $m(t)=\mathbb E f_t$ and symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariance kernel
$k(s,t)=\mathbb E[(f_s-m(s))(f_t-m(t))]$; positive semidefinite means every
finite Gram quadratic form is nonnegative. For $n\ge1$ and a finite training
list $X=(x_i)_{i=1}^n$ in $T$, set $f_X=(f_{x_i})$, $K_{XX}=(k(x_i,x_j))$,
and let $\varepsilon$ be centered Gaussian observation noise independent of
$f$, with symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance $R$. Set
$Y=f_X+\varepsilon$ and $A_X=K_{XX}+R\succ0$. Write the dense Cholesky
factorization as
$A_X=LL^T$, where $L$ is lower triangular with positive diagonal. In the
scalar-operation model, where each addition, subtraction, multiplication,
division, or square root counts as one operation, factorization costs
$n^3/3+O(n^2)$ operations. For a test input $x_*\in T$, define
$k_{x_*X}=(k(x_*,x_i))_{i=1}^n$ and $k_{Xx_*}=k_{x_*X}^T$. After factorization,
the latent predictive variance
$k(x_*,x_*)-k_{x_*X}A_X^{-1}k_{Xx_*}$ requires $O(n^2)$ operations, where
$O(n^2)$ denotes an asymptotic operation count as $n$ grows. These are
arithmetic counts, not accuracy guarantees. For an invertible real $n\times n$
matrix $A$, define its spectral condition number by
$\kappa_2(A)=\lVert A\rVert_2\lVert A^{-1}\rVert_2$, where
$\lVert A\rVert_2=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_2=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_2$ for
$x\in\mathbb R^n$. For $0<\epsilon<1$,
$A_\epsilon=\operatorname{diag}(1,\epsilon)$ has condition number
$1/\epsilon$, while $E=\operatorname{diag}(0,-\epsilon)$ has relative
spectral-norm size $\lVert E\rVert_2/\lVert A_\epsilon\rVert_2=\epsilon$
even though $A_\epsilon+E$ is singular.

The negative log marginal likelihood need not be convex in a covariance
hyperparameter. On the one-point set $T=\{t\}$, take the centered Gaussian
prior $f_t\sim N(0,\theta)$ with $\theta\ge0$, covariance kernel
$k_\theta(t,t)=\theta$, and independent observation noise
$\varepsilon\sim N(0,1)$. For observation $Y=f_t+\varepsilon$ at $y=0$, the
observed covariance is $A_\theta=1+\theta>0$ and the negative log marginal
likelihood is
$$L(\theta)=\tfrac12\log(1+\theta)+\tfrac12\log(2\pi).$$
For every $\theta>0$, its second derivative is
$L''(\theta)=-1/(2(1+\theta)^2)<0$, so $L$ is not convex on its parameter
domain.

The finite Gaussian-process regression posterior formula uses Gaussian
observation noise. Write
$\phi(z)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/2}$ for the standard normal density and
$\Phi(z)=\int_{-\infty}^z\phi(t)\,dt$ for its cumulative distribution
function. With one latent value $z\sim N(0,1)$ and one positive label, the
logistic likelihood $P(y=1\mid z)=\sigma(z)=(1+e^{-z})^{-1}$ or probit
likelihood $P(y=1\mid z)=\Phi(z)$ gives a non-Gaussian posterior: the
posterior log density has nonzero third derivative at $z=\log 3$ for logistic
and $z=0$ for probit. Both likelihoods lie in $(0,1)$, so multiplying by the
standard normal density gives a finite, positive normalizing integral. Finally,
a Gaussian process
specifies finite-dimensional laws but need not have continuous paths. A
continuous modification means a process on the same probability space that
agrees almost surely at each fixed input and has almost surely continuous
sample paths. Under AC, on $T=[0,1]$ the equality kernel $k(s,t)=1$ when $s=t$
and $0$ otherwise has no continuous modification.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and models in the Remark.

1.1 Cholesky factorization costs $n^3/3+O(n^2)$ by [F5]. For one test point, the posterior variance formula requires solving $A_Xu=k_{X*}$ and forming $k_{**}-k_{*X}u$. Factoring $A_X=L L^T$ reduces this to two triangular solves, each with $O(n^2)$ cost by [F5], followed by an $O(n)$ inner product. Therefore the variance calculation after factorization is $O(n^2)$. [F5, F6, given, algebra]

1.2 The spectral norm of $A_\epsilon=\operatorname{diag}(1,\epsilon)$ is $1$, its smallest singular value is $\epsilon$, and therefore its spectral condition number is $1/\epsilon$. The perturbation $E=\operatorname{diag}(0,-\epsilon)$ has norm $\epsilon$, so $\lVert E\rVert_2/\lVert A_\epsilon\rVert_2=\epsilon$, while $A_\epsilon+E=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ is singular. Thus operation counts alone do not control sensitivity to finite-precision perturbations near singularity. [given, algebra]

1.3 The scalar kernel $k_\theta(t,t)=\theta$ is positive semidefinite for $\theta\ge0$, and the observed covariance is $A_\theta=1+\theta>0$. Apply [F1] with $m=0$ and $y=0$ to get $L(\theta)=\tfrac12\log(1+\theta)+\tfrac12\log(2\pi)$. Differentiating twice gives $L''(\theta)=-1/(2(1+\theta)^2)<0$ for every $\theta>0$, so this negative log marginal likelihood is not convex on its parameter domain. [F1, given, algebra]

1.4 Write $\sigma(z)=(1+e^{-z})^{-1}$; then $0<\sigma(z)<1$ for all $z$, so $\int_{\mathbb R}\phi(z)\sigma(z)\,dz$ is finite and positive. The logistic posterior is therefore a positive density whose log, up to an additive constant, is $q(z)=-z^2/2-\log(1+e^{-z})$. Differentiation gives $q'''(z)=-\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))(1-2\sigma(z))$. At $z=\log 3$ this equals $3/32\ne0$. A positive density on all of $\mathbb R$ cannot be a degenerate Gaussian; every nondegenerate univariate Gaussian log density is quadratic and has third derivative zero, so this posterior is not Gaussian. [given, algebra]

1.5 Since $0<\Phi(z)<1$ for all $z$, the probit posterior normalizer $\int_{\mathbb R}\phi(z)\Phi(z)\,dz$ is finite and positive. Its positive log density, up to an additive constant, is $q(z)=-z^2/2+\log\Phi(z)$. Put $h=\phi/\Phi$ and $c=h(0)=\sqrt{2/\pi}$. Since $(\log\Phi)'=h$ and $h'=-zh-h^2$, differentiation yields $(\log\Phi)'''(0)=h''(0)=-c+2c^3=c(4/\pi-1)\ne0$; the last inequality uses $\pi<4$. A positive density on all of $\mathbb R$ cannot be a degenerate Gaussian; every nondegenerate univariate Gaussian log density is quadratic and has third derivative zero, so this posterior is not Gaussian. [given, algebra]

1.6 Let $D=\{t_i:1\le i\le r\}$ for any finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_r\in[0,1]$. The equality kernel has Gram form $\sum_{t\in D}(\sum_{i:t_i=t}a_i)^2\ge0$. Therefore it is positive semidefinite, and by [A1, F2] it defines a cylinder-space Gaussian process with standard normal coordinates and covariance $1_{s=t}$. [A1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For any finite list of distinct inputs in $[0,1]$, [F3] gives a centered Gaussian vector with covariance identity. By [F4] its characteristic function is $\exp(-\tfrac12\sum_i u_i^2)$, which factors into the univariate standard-normal characteristic functions; uniqueness therefore gives independent standard-normal coordinates. [F3, F4, step 1.6, algebra]

3.1 Let $q_j=1/(j+2)$. If a continuous modification $G$ existed, the equalities $G_{q_j}=f_{q_j}$ for all $j$ and $G_0=f_0$ would hold simultaneously almost surely, since there are countably many coordinates. Let $E_0=\{|f_0|<1\}$, which has positive probability, and $E_j=\{|f_{q_j}|>2\}$, each of probability $p>0$ by [F2]. The finite-coordinate independence from step 2.1 gives $\Pr(E_0\cap\bigcap_{j=N}^M E_j^c)=\Pr(E_0)(1-p)^{M-N+1}$. By [F7], letting $M\to\infty$ gives $\Pr(E_0\cap\bigcap_{j=N}^\infty E_j^c)=0$ for each $N$; the countable union over $N$ then shows $E_0$ and infinitely many $E_j$ occur together with probability $\Pr(E_0)>0$. On that event $|G_0|<1$ while $|G_{q_j}|>2$ infinitely often, contradicting continuity at $0$. No continuous modification exists. [F2, F7, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 The scope distinction in [F6] concerns a Gaussian observation likelihood; the explicit logistic and probit posterior calculations in steps 1.4 and 1.5 have nonzero third derivatives and are not Gaussian. Thus the exact finite Gaussian regression formula does not give an exact Gaussian posterior for those classification models. [F6, step 1.4, step 1.5] ∎

## Statement

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ be Hermitian positive definite and let
$A=LL^*$ be its Cholesky factorisation with positive diagonal.

1. For every right-hand side $b\in\mathbb C^n$, the system $Ax=b$ is solved by
   first solving $Ly=b$ and then solving $L^*x=y$.
2. The two triangular solves cost $2n^2+O(n)$ scalar operations altogether, and
   the dense Cholesky factorisation costs
   $$\frac{1}{3}n^3+O(n^2)$$
   scalar operations, compared with
   $$\frac{2}{3}n^3+O(n^2)$$
   for dense LU factorisation without exploiting symmetry.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A Hermitian positive-definite matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, its Cholesky factor $A=LL^*$, and a right-hand side $b\in\mathbb C^n$.

[L1] Forward and backward substitution correctly and uniquely solve triangular systems in $O(n^2)$ scalar operations ([[thm-forward-and-back-substitution-are-correct-unique-and-quadratic-cost]]).

[L2] Hermitian positive-definite matrices admit a unique Cholesky factorisation with positive diagonal ([[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]).

[L3] Cholesky factorisation means $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and positive diagonal ([[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** factor the solve through two triangular systems and count the work column by column.

1.1 By [L2] and [L3], the equation $Ax=b$ is $LL^*x=b$. Solve $Ly=b$ by forward substitution and then $L^*x=y$ by backward substitution. Stepwise uniqueness in [L1] makes both solves unique, and substituting $y=L^*x$ back into the first equation gives $Ax=b$. [L1, L2, L3, algebra]

1.2 The solve cost is the sum of two triangular solves, so [L1] gives $$2\left(n+\frac{n(n-1)}{2}+\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\right)=2n^2+O(n)$$ scalar operations, or $n^2+O(n)$ multiply-add pairs. [L1, algebra]

2.1 In the dense factorisation, column $k$ computes one square root, $n-1-k$ divisions in the column below the pivot, and updates the trailing symmetric submatrix of size $n-1-k$ by a rank-one outer product. That update touches $\frac{(n-1-k)(n-k)}{2}$ stored entries, and each one costs one multiplication and one subtraction, so the update work is $$(n-1-k)(n-k).$$ Summing with $m=n-1-k$ gives $$\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}m(m+1)=\frac{1}{3}n(n-1)(n+1)=\frac{1}{3}n^3+O(n^2),$$ which dominates the cost. LU performs the same style of update on the full trailing matrix, giving $$2\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}m^2=\frac{1}{3}n(n-1)(2n-1)=\frac{2}{3}n^3+O(n^2)$$ scalar operations. Thus Cholesky uses about half the factorisation work. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Step 1.1 proves the solve statement, while steps 1.2 and 2.1 give the operation counts. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Measurable sets $E_0\supseteq E_1\supseteq\cdots$, an index $n_0$ with $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$, and $E=\bigcap_nE_n$.

[L1] For increasing measurable $A_n$, $\mu(\bigcup_nA_n)=\sup_n\mu(A_n)$ ([[thm-continuity-from-below-for-measures]]).

[L2] If $A\subseteq B$ and $\mu(A)<+\infty$, then $\mu(B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B\setminus A)$, with real subtraction valid when $\mu(B)<+\infty$ ([[prop-measure-of-a-set-difference]]).

[L3] Every subset of $\overline{\mathbb R}$ has an infimum there ([[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $k\in\mathbb N$ put $H_k:=E_{n_0}\setminus E_{n_0+k}$. Then $(H_k)$ increases and $\bigcup_kH_k=E_{n_0}\setminus E$. [given]

1.2 Every $E_{n_0+k}$ and $E$ has finite measure by inclusion in $E_{n_0}$, and [L2] gives $\mu(H_k)=\mu(E_{n_0})-\mu(E_{n_0+k})$ and $\mu(E_{n_0}\setminus E)=\mu(E_{n_0})-\mu(E)$. [given, L2]

2.1 Apply continuity from below to $(H_k)$ and substitute step 1.2: taking the supremum of the left differences is the same as subtracting the infimum of the decreasing finite values, so cancellation of the finite number $\mu(E_{n_0})$ yields $\mu(E)=\inf_k\mu(E_{n_0+k})$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L1, L3, algebra]

3.1 A decreasing sequence has the same infimum as any of its tails, so step 2.1 gives $\mu(E)=\inf_n\mu(E_n)$; this includes $E=\varnothing$, $\mu(E)=0$, and a sequence that is constant from $n_0$ onward. [step 2.1, L3] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $T$ be a set, let $k:T\times T\to\mathbb R$ be a symmetric
kernel whose every finite Gram quadratic form is nonnegative, and let
$m:T\to\mathbb R$. Let $H$ be a real
Hilbert space of functions on $T$ such that, for every $x\in T$, the section
$k_x:T\to\mathbb R$, $k_x(t)=k(t,x)$, belongs to $H$ and satisfies
$h(x)=\langle h,k_x\rangle_H$ for every $h\in H$. Assume $m\in H$. For a
nonempty finite ordered list $X=(x_i)_{i=1}^n$ (repetitions allowed), let
$K=K_{XX}=(k(x_i,x_j))$, $m_X=(m(x_i))$, and take $y\in\mathbb R^n$ and
$\sigma>0$. On the affine space $m+H$, define
$$J(g)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-g(x_i))^2+\sigma^2\lVert g-m\rVert_H^2.$$
Then $J$ has a unique minimizer
$$g_*=m+\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i k_{x_i},\qquad \alpha=(K+\sigma^2 I_n)^{-1}(y-m_X).$$
Its evaluation vector is
$$ (g_*(x_i))_{i=1}^n=m_X+K(K+\sigma^2I_n)^{-1}(y-m_X). $$
Under AC, the mean and kernel determine a canonical cylinder-space
Gaussian-process prior. If it is observed at $X$ with independent
$N_n(0,\sigma^2I_n)$ noise, this vector is the conditional mean of the latent
evaluation vector given the observation $Y=y$. The Hilbert-space existence
and reproducing-section properties are hypotheses here; the theorem makes no
general kernel-to-Hilbert-space existence claim.

## Statement references

[Rasmussen and Williams, GPML, Chapter 6 §§6.1–6.4, printed pp. 129–150](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW6.pdf)

[Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, ESL, 2nd ed., §5.8, printed pp. 167–173](https://esl.hohoweiya.xyz/book/The%20Elements%20of%20Statistical%20Learning.pdf)

[Treil, Linear Algebra Done Wrong, Chapter 5 §§5.3.2, 5.4.1](https://www.math.brown.edu/streil/papers/LADW/HTML_2026_04-30/Ch5.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the kernel, real Hilbert space, reproducing-section identities, mean function $m\in H$, finite list $X$, response $y$, and scalar $\sigma>0$ in the Statement; and the Gaussian-process observation model for the final comparison.

[A1] AC is the axiom used by the Gaussian-process and finite conditional-normal interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The observation model defines $K_{XX}$, $m_X$, and $Y=f_X+\varepsilon$; an independent Gaussian noise vector with covariance $R$ is added to the latent evaluations. [[def-gaussian-process-regression-observation-model]]

[F2] Every finite-dimensional subspace of a real inner-product space has an orthonormal basis, and projection onto it gives a unique orthogonal decomposition with the Pythagorean identity. [[lem-finite-span-orthogonal-projection-in-inner-product-space]]

[F3] A finite-dimensional positive-semidefinite operator has a positive-semidefinite square root whose square is the operator. [[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]]

[F4] For a linear map $C$ between finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, $\beta$ minimizes $\lVert C\beta-b\rVert$ exactly when $C^*(C\beta-b)=0$. [[thm-least-squares-solutions-and-normal-equation]]

[F5] Under AC, the finite Gaussian-process posterior at test list $X_*$ has mean $m_*+K_{*X}(K_{XX}+R)^{-1}(y-m_X)$ when the observed covariance is positive definite. [[cor-gp-regression-posterior-predictive-law]]

[F6] In the finite observation model, $K_{XX}+R$ is positive definite exactly when its ordinary inverse formulas are defined. [[lem-gp-regression-observed-covariance-invertibility]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Define the linear evaluation map $S:H\to\mathbb R^n$ by $(Sh)_i=h(x_i)$. It is bounded because $\lVert Sh\rVert_2^2=\sum_i|\langle h,k_{x_i}\rangle_H|^2\le\lVert h\rVert_H^2\sum_i\lVert k_{x_i}\rVert_H^2$. The reproducing identities then give its adjoint $S^*\beta=\sum_i\beta_i k_{x_i}$, since $\langle Sh,\beta\rangle=\sum_i\beta_i\langle h,k_{x_i}\rangle_H=\langle h,S^*\beta\rangle_H$. Consequently $SS^*=K$ and $V=\operatorname{ran}(S^*)=\operatorname{span}\{k_{x_i}:1\le i\le n\}$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For every $c\in\mathbb R^n$, $c^T(K+\sigma^2I_n)c=c^TKc+\sigma^2\lVert c\rVert^2\ge\sigma^2\lVert c\rVert^2$, because $K$ is a Gram matrix of the positive-semidefinite kernel. Hence $A=K+\sigma^2I_n$ is positive definite and, by [F6], its ordinary inverse exists. Put $r=y-m_X$, $\alpha=A^{-1}r$, and $h_0=S^*\alpha$. [F1, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 Write $g=m+h$, so $J(m+h)=\lVert r-Sh\rVert^2+\sigma^2\lVert h\rVert_H^2$. By [F2], each $h$ decomposes uniquely as $p+q$ with $p\in V$ and $q\perp V$. Then $Sq=0$ by the reproducing identities, and $\lVert p+q\rVert_H^2=\lVert p\rVert_H^2+\lVert q\rVert_H^2$. Thus $J(m+p+q)=J(m+p)+\sigma^2\lVert q\rVert_H^2$, so minimization reduces to $V$. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

2.2 Let $B=K^{1/2}$ be supplied by [F3], and define $C:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\oplus\mathbb R^n$ by $C\beta=(K\beta,\sigma B\beta)$. For $h=S^*\beta$, its objective is $\lVert C\beta-(r,0)\rVert^2$, because $Sh=K\beta$ and $\lVert S^*\beta\rVert_H^2=\beta^TK\beta=\lVert B\beta\rVert^2$. The normal equation is $C^*C\beta=C^*(r,0)$, that is $(K^2+\sigma^2K)\beta=Kr$. Our $\alpha$ satisfies it because $(K^2+\sigma^2K)\alpha=K(K+\sigma^2I_n)\alpha=Kr$. Therefore [F4] makes $h_0$ a minimizer on $V$. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.3 For any $d\in H$, $Sh_0-r=K\alpha-r=-\sigma^2\alpha$ and $S^*(Sh_0-r)=-\sigma^2h_0$. Expanding both squared norms and using the adjoint identity gives $J(m+h_0+d)-J(m+h_0)=\lVert Sd\rVert^2+\sigma^2\lVert d\rVert_H^2$. This is nonnegative and is zero only for $d=0$, so the minimizer is unique on all of $H$, not just on $V$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The minimizing function is $g_*=m+h_0=m+\sum_i\alpha_i k_{x_i}$, and $S h_0=K\alpha$, giving the displayed evaluation vector. For Gaussian observations with $R=\sigma^2I_n$, [F5] at test list $X_*=X$ gives the same conditional-mean vector; $A=K+R\succ0$ by step 1.2, so its inverse hypothesis holds. [A1, F1, F5, step 1.2, step 2.2] ∎

## Example

Assume AC and take $T=\{a,b\}$ with distinct points, mean $m=0$, and
equality kernel $k(s,t)=1$ if $s=t$ and $0$ otherwise. Use the canonical
cylinder-space Gaussian-process prior with this mean and kernel. For
$X=(a,b)$, set $K_{XX}=(k(x_i,x_j))=I_2$ and observe with centered Gaussian
noise $\varepsilon\sim N_2(0,I_2)$ independent of $f$, so
$A_X=K_{XX}+I_2=2I_2$, with data $y=(2,-1)^T$. Predict at
$X_*=X$. The latent posterior mean is $(1,-\tfrac12)^T$ and its covariance is
$\tfrac12 I_2$. If a centered Gaussian test-noise vector
$\eta_*\sim N_2(0,R_*)$ with $R_*=I_2$ is independent of the pair
$(f,\varepsilon)$, then the noisy predictive mean is unchanged and its
covariance is $\tfrac32 I_2$.

## Example references

[Rasmussen and Williams, GPML, Chapter 2 §2.2, printed pp. 13–18](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW2.pdf)

[Bishop, PRML, §6.4.2, printed pp. 306–309](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2006/01/Bishop-Pattern-Recognition-and-Machine-Learning-2006.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the two-point set, equality kernel, zero mean, ordered training and test lists, centered Gaussian training noise $\varepsilon\sim N_2(0,I_2)$ independent of $f$, optional test noise $\eta_*\sim N_2(0,I_2)$ independent of $(f,\varepsilon)$, and observation $y$ as stated.

[A1] AC is the axiom used by the canonical GP construction and finite conditioning interface. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F0] Under AC, a symmetric positive-semidefinite kernel and mean define a canonical Gaussian process with the specified finite Gaussian laws. [[thm-gaussian-process-exists-from-mean-and-positive-semidefinite-covariance-kernel]]

[F1] The observation model permits finite ordered lists and defines $K_{AB}$, $m_X$, $Y=f_X+\varepsilon$, and test noise independent of the pair $(f,\varepsilon)$. [[def-gaussian-process-regression-observation-model]]

[F2] For $A_X\succ0$, the posterior latent mean and covariance are $m_*+K_{*X}A_X^{-1}(y-m_X)$ and $K_{**}-K_{*X}A_X^{-1}K_{X*}$; test noise independent of the pair $(f,\varepsilon)$ adds its covariance. [[cor-gp-regression-posterior-predictive-law]]

[F3] For PSD Gram and noise matrices, the observed covariance is invertible exactly when it is positive definite. [[lem-gp-regression-observed-covariance-invertibility]]

## Verification

**Given:** The finite model in the Example.

1.1 For any finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_r\in T$ and scalars $c_i$, the equality-kernel Gram form is $\sum_{t\in T}(\sum_{i:t_i=t}c_i)^2\ge0$. Thus the kernel is positive semidefinite, and [A1, F0] supplies the stated canonical prior. At $X=(a,b)$, $K=I_2$, so $A_X=K+R=2I_2\succ0$ and the inverse required in [F2] exists by [F3]. [A1, F0, F1, F2, F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Since $m_X=0$ and $K_{*X}=K_{XX}=I_2$, [F2] gives posterior mean $(2I_2)^{-1}y=\tfrac12(2,-1)^T=(1,-\tfrac12)^T$. It gives posterior covariance $I_2-I_2(2I_2)^{-1}I_2=\tfrac12I_2$. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By the Example's hypothesis, $\eta_*$ is independent of the pair $(f,\varepsilon)$, so [F2]'s test-noise clause applies: the conditional mean is unchanged and $I_2$ is added to the covariance, yielding $\tfrac12I_2+I_2=\tfrac32I_2$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume AC. Let $T=\{a,b\}$ with distinct points, $\phi(a)=1$,
$\phi(b)=2$, $m=0$, and $k(s,t)=\phi(s)\phi(t)$. Use the canonical
cylinder-space Gaussian-process prior with this mean and kernel. For
$X=X_*=(a,b)$, set $v=(1,2)^T$, $K_{XX}=K_{**}=vv^T$, and $R=I_2$, so
$A_X=K_{XX}+R=I_2+vv^T\succ0$. With data $y=(1,0)^T$, the latent posterior
mean is $v/6$ and the latent posterior covariance is $K_{XX}/6$, which is
singular.

## Example references

[Rasmussen and Williams, GPML, Chapter 2 §2.2, printed pp. 13–18](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW2.pdf)

[Bishop, PRML, §6.4.2, printed pp. 306–309](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2006/01/Bishop-Pattern-Recognition-and-Machine-Learning-2006.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the two-point set, feature values $\phi(a)=1,\phi(b)=2$, kernel $k(s,t)=\phi(s)\phi(t)$, zero mean, ordered lists $X=X_*=(a,b)$, noise covariance $R=I_2$, and $y=(1,0)^T$.

[A1] AC is the axiom used by the canonical GP construction and finite conditioning interface. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F0] Under AC, a symmetric positive-semidefinite kernel and mean define a canonical Gaussian process with the specified finite Gaussian laws. [[thm-gaussian-process-exists-from-mean-and-positive-semidefinite-covariance-kernel]]

[F1] The finite observation model defines Gram matrices, the observation vector, and noise covariance. [[def-gaussian-process-regression-observation-model]]

[F2] For positive-definite observed covariance, the posterior latent mean and covariance are $m_*+K_{*X}A_X^{-1}(y-m_X)$ and $K_{**}-K_{*X}A_X^{-1}K_{X*}$. [[cor-gp-regression-posterior-predictive-law]]

[F3] The observed matrix of PSD Gram and noise matrices is invertible exactly on the positive-definite branch. [[lem-gp-regression-observed-covariance-invertibility]]

## Verification

**Given:** The finite model in the Example.

1.1 For any finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_r\in T$ and real $c_i$, the Gram form for $k(s,t)=\phi(s)\phi(t)$ is $(\sum_i c_i\phi(t_i))^2\ge0$. Thus [A1, F0] supplies the canonical prior. At $X=(a,b)$ this gives $K=vv^T=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$. Therefore $A_X=I_2+vv^T$ satisfies $c^TA_Xc=\lVert c\rVert^2+(v^Tc)^2>0$ for every nonzero $c$; [F3] confirms the inverse branch applies. [A1, F0, F1, F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The identity $(I_2+vv^T)v=(1+v^Tv)v=6v$ gives $A_X^{-1}v=v/6$, and hence $A_X^{-1}y=A_X^{-1}(1,0)^T=(5/6,-1/3)^T$. Since $K=v v^T$, $K A_X^{-1}y=v(v^TA_X^{-1}y)=v/6$. Formula [F2] therefore gives the stated posterior mean. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Also $K A_X^{-1}K=v(v^TA_X^{-1}v)v^T=(5/6)vv^T$, because $v^TA_X^{-1}v=5/6$. Thus the posterior covariance is $K-(5/6)K=K/6$. The nonzero vector $(2,-1)^T$ is annihilated by $K/6$, while $K/6\ne0$, so this covariance is singular. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix a finite labeled sample $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ with $n\ge1$, $x_i\in\mathbb R^p$ and $p\ge1$. In regression, $y_i\in\mathbb R$. In classification, the labels lie in a fixed ordered finite set $\mathcal C=\{c_1<\cdots<c_K\}$ with $K\ge1$. A finite empirical axis-aligned binary decision tree has root sample-index set $I_{\mathrm{root}}=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Each internal node $v$ stores a coordinate $j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$ and threshold $t\in\mathbb R$; its left and right child sample sets are $I_v^L=\{i\in I_v:x_{ij}\le t\}$ and $I_v^R=\{i\in I_v:x_{ij}>t\}$, and both are required to be nonempty. A leaf is a terminal node. The leaf sample sets partition $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and each node's feature region is the intersection of its path inequalities. Every input feature vector follows the unique path determined by the stored comparisons.

For a regression leaf with sample set $I$, put $N_I=|I|$, $\bar y_I=N_I^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}y_i$, and $Q_I=N_I^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}(y_i-\bar y_I)^2$; its prediction is $\bar y_I$ and its total squared-error loss is $N_IQ_I$. For a classification leaf, put $p_{Ik}=N_I^{-1}|\{i\in I:y_i=c_k\}|$ and predict the class $c_k$ with largest $p_{Ik}$, choosing the least index in a tie. Its optional impurities are misclassification $Q_I^{\mathrm{mis}}=1-\max_k p_{Ik}$, Gini $Q_I^{\mathrm{Gini}}=1-\sum_{k=1}^Kp_{Ik}^2$, and entropy $Q_I^{\mathrm{ent}}=-\sum_{k=1}^Kp_{Ik}\log p_{Ik}$, where $\log$ is the natural logarithm and $0\log0=0$. A chosen classification criterion determines $Q_I$ and the corresponding total leaf impurity is $N_IQ_I$.

## Statement

Let $I$ be a nonempty finite set of sample indices and let $y_i\in\mathbb R$ for every $i\in I$. Put $N=|I|$ and $\bar y_I=N^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}y_i$. Among all constants $c\in\mathbb R$, the unique minimizer of $\sum_{i\in I}(y_i-c)^2$ is $c=\bar y_I$, and the minimum value is $\sum_{i\in I}(y_i-\bar y_I)^2$.

## Statement references

[Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, §9.2.2, equations (9.10)–(9.14), printed p. 307](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1--Wo5Hcl2y_v3DL-tGgcJHRPdtjiVYjS)

[MIT OpenCourseWare, 15.097, Lecture 8: Decision trees, slide 15](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/15-097-prediction-machine-learning-and-statistics-spring-2012/f5678de0e329ce097fc6ec6182ebaea2_MIT15_097S12_lec08.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty finite sample-index set $I$ and real responses $(y_i)_{i\in I}$.

[F1] [[def-empirical-decision-tree]]: A regression leaf with sample set $I$ has $N_I=|I|\ge1$, mean $\bar y_I=N_I^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}y_i$, and squared-error impurity $Q_I=N_I^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}(y_i-\bar y_I)^2$.

[F2] [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]: For every $n$, the standard coordinate dot product on $\mathbb R^n$ is an inner product; in particular, identifying $\mathbb R$ with $\mathbb R^1$ supplies the standard inner products on both $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb R^N$.

[F3] [[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]: An adjoint satisfies $\langle T a,v\rangle=\langle a,T^*v\rangle$ for every $a$ and $v$.

[F4] [[thm-least-squares-solutions-and-normal-equation]]: For a linear map between finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, $T^*(Tc-b)=0$ characterizes minimizers of $\lVert Tc-b\rVert$; minimizers exist.

## Proof

1.1 Enumerate $I$ in increasing sample-index order as $i_1,\ldots,i_N$ and define $T(c)=(c,\ldots,c)$ and $b=(y_{i_1},\ldots,y_{i_N})$. For all scalars $a,c,d\in\mathbb R$, $T(ac+d)=aT(c)+T(d)$ coordinatewise, so $T$ is linear. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Identify $\mathbb R$ with $\mathbb R^1$. By [F2] for $n=1$ and $n=N$, the standard coordinate inner products make $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb R^N$ finite-dimensional inner-product spaces. Hence $\lVert Tc-b\rVert^2=\sum_{i\in I}(y_i-c)^2$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Define $S:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R$ by $S(v_1,\ldots,v_N)=\sum_{k=1}^Nv_k$. This map is linear, and for every $c\in\mathbb R$ and $v\in\mathbb R^N$, $\langle T(c),v\rangle_{\mathbb R^N}=c\sum_{k=1}^Nv_k=\langle c,S(v)\rangle_{\mathbb R}$. Thus $S$ is an adjoint of $T$ by [F3]. If another map also satisfied this identity, its value at each $v$ would differ from $S(v)$ by a scalar pairing to zero with every $c\in\mathbb R$, hence would equal $S(v)$ by positive definiteness. Therefore $T^*=S$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra, construct]

4.1 Now [F4] applies to the linear map $T$ between these finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, with its adjoint established in step 3.1. The normal equation $T^*(Tc-b)=0$ is $Nc-\sum_{i\in I}y_i=0$, whose unique solution is $c=\bar y_I$ because $N\ge1$. By [F4], this solution is the unique minimizer. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra, F1]

5.1 Expanding around $\bar y_I$ gives $\sum_{i\in I}(y_i-c)^2=\sum_{i\in I}(y_i-\bar y_I)^2+N(c-\bar y_I)^2$, since $\sum_{i\in I}(y_i-\bar y_I)=0$. Therefore the minimum value is $\sum_{i\in I}(y_i-\bar y_I)^2$. [given, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $n$ and the two displayed coordinate pairings.

[L1] Finite products in a commutative monoid have an empty value and may be read additively as finite sums ([[def-monoid-finite-product]]).

[L2] Complex conjugation preserves sums and products, and $z\overline z=|z|^2\ge0$, with equality exactly when $z=0$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

[L3] The standard unit vectors form an ordered basis of $F^n$, including $n=0$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]).

[L4] An inner product is linear in the first argument, conjugate symmetric, positive on the diagonal, and definite ([[def-inner-product-space]]).

[L5] The reals form a totally ordered field, so addition preserves order; the square of a nonzero real number is positive ([[thm-reals-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-square-positive]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Distributivity of the finite sums in [L1] gives linearity in the first variable. In the complex case [L2] gives conjugate-linearity in the second and conjugate symmetry; in the real case conjugation is the identity. [L1, L2, algebra]

1.2 For a finite list of nonnegative real numbers $a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1}$, put $S_0=0$ and $S_{j+1}=S_j+a_j$ as in [L1]. By [L5], if $S_j\ge0$ and $a_j\ge0$, then $S_{j+1}\ge S_j$ and $S_{j+1}\ge a_j$. Hence $S_{j+1}=0$ holds exactly when both $S_j=0$ and $a_j=0$. Starting with the empty sum, induction proves $S_n\ge0$ and $S_n=0$ exactly when every $a_k=0$. On the diagonal, take $a_k=x_k^2$ in the real formula and $a_k=|z_k|^2$ in the complex formula. By [L5], $x_k^2$ is nonnegative and equals zero exactly when $x_k=0$; [L2] gives the corresponding assertion for $|z_k|^2$. Thus both diagonal pairings are real and nonnegative, and each vanishes exactly when all coordinates vanish, which by [L3] means the vector is zero. [L1, L2, L3, L5, induction, algebra]

2.1 Hence all the axioms in [L4] hold. When $n=0$, the sum is empty and equals $0$, while the zero vector is the only vector, so definiteness is valid. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L1, L3, L4] ∎

## Definition

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

## Definition

Let $T_0$ be a fixed finite binary tree grown on the sample from an empirical decision tree. A subtree $T\subseteq T_0$ is obtained by collapsing zero or more internal nodes and all their descendants to leaves. For each leaf $m$ of $T$, let $N_m$ be its sample count and let $Q_m(T)$ be its regression squared-error impurity or its chosen classification impurity, computed as in the empirical decision-tree definition. Define the total training impurity $R(T)=\sum_{m\in\mathrm{leaves}(T)}N_mQ_m(T)$, the terminal-node count $|T|$, and for $\alpha\ge0$ the cost-complexity criterion $C_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha|T|$.

For a current nonterminal node $t$, let $I_t$ be its sample set and let $T_t$ be its current descendant subtree. Let $R(t)=N_tQ_t$ be the training impurity if $t$ is collapsed to a leaf, using the same response or class rule as for a leaf; let $R(T_t)$ be the sum of the impurities of the current descendant leaves. Define the weakest-link quotient $g(t)=[R(t)-R(T_t)]/(|T_t|-1)$. The denominator is the number of leaves removed by collapsing $t$. This definition makes no claim that a weakest-link sequence globally minimizes $C_\alpha$ for every $\alpha$ or that validation selection guarantees test-risk performance.

## Definition references

[[def-empirical-decision-tree|Regression and classification leaf impurities and sample counts]]

[Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, §9.2.2–9.2.3, printed pp. 308–310](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1--Wo5Hcl2y_v3DL-tGgcJHRPdtjiVYjS)

## Remark

Choosing $\alpha$ by validation or cross-validation is a data-selection procedure; by itself, that choice does not guarantee test-risk performance.

## Definition

The inputs are observations $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ with $n\ge1$ and $x_i\in\mathbb R^p$ for an integer $p\ge1$, a response mode (regression with $y_i\in\mathbb R$ or classification with labels in a fixed finite ordered class set), a fixed classification impurity criterion when in classification mode, and a finite integer maximum depth $d_{\max}\ge0$. The root has sample set $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and depth $0$. At a current leaf with nonempty sample set $I$ and depth $d<d_{\max}$, perform the following procedure.

1. For each coordinate $j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$, sort the distinct observed values in that coordinate as $u_1<\cdots<u_r$. For each $k=1,\ldots,r-1$, form the candidate threshold $t=(u_k+u_{k+1})/2$ and its child sets $I_L=\{i\in I:x_{ij}\le t\}$ and $I_R=\{i\in I:x_{ij}>t\}$. These are the finite candidates at the node; if no coordinate has at least two distinct values, the candidate set is empty.

2. For each candidate, compute its child score. In regression the score is $\sum_{i\in I_L}(y_i-\bar y_{I_L})^2+\sum_{i\in I_R}(y_i-\bar y_{I_R})^2$. In classification it is $|I_L|Q_{I_L}+|I_R|Q_{I_R}$ for the fixed chosen impurity criterion. Select the candidate with the smallest score; when scores tie, select the least pair $(j,k)$ by comparing coordinate first and cut index second.

3. Store the selected coordinate and threshold at the current node, create its left and right children, and apply this procedure to the left child and then the right child at depth $d+1$. If $d=d_{\max}$ or the candidate set is empty, leave the current node as a leaf.

The output is the finite tree whose leaves use the regression means or classification majority labels from the empirical decision-tree definition. No strictly positive loss reduction is required for a split below the depth cap, and the returned tree is not asserted to be globally optimal among all trees.

## Definition

The input is a fixed finite empirical decision tree $T_0$. Start with the current tree $T=T_0$ and output sequence $(T_0)$. At each iteration, if $T$ consists of its root leaf, stop and return the sequence. Otherwise, for every current nonterminal node $t$, compute $g(t)=[R(t)-R(T_t)]/(|T_t|-1)$ using the current subtree quantities from the cost-complexity definition. Select a node minimizing $g(t)$; if several tie, select the node whose root-to-node address is least in lexicographic order with $L<R$. Collapse the current descendant subtree at that node to a leaf, using the empirical tree's leaf prediction rule on its sample set, and append the resulting subtree to the output sequence. Repeat on that new current tree.

The sequence contains the initial tree and each successive collapse through the root leaf. This procedure makes no claim that its subtrees globally minimize the cost-complexity criterion for every penalty or that a validation choice of penalty guarantees test-risk performance.

## Statement

Fix a finite labeled sample, response mode, classification impurity criterion when needed, and finite maximum depth as in greedy CART growth. At any node where the procedure splits, its selected coordinate and midpoint threshold minimize the declared child-weighted empirical loss among all nonempty coordinate-threshold partitions of that node's sample, with the specified lexicographic tie rule. The procedure produces a finite tree of depth at most the maximum depth, with nonempty children at every split. This is a nodewise candidate-optimality result only; it gives no global tree-optimality claim.

## Statement references

[Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, §9.2.2–9.2.3, printed pp. 307–310](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1--Wo5Hcl2y_v3DL-tGgcJHRPdtjiVYjS)

[MIT OpenCourseWare, 15.097, Lecture 8: Decision trees, slides 14–15](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/15-097-prediction-machine-learning-and-statistics-spring-2012/f5678de0e329ce097fc6ec6182ebaea2_MIT15_097S12_lec08.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite labeled sample with $n\ge1$, a regression or classification mode, the fixed classification impurity criterion when applicable, and a finite integer maximum depth $d_{\max}\ge0$.

[F1] [[def-empirical-decision-tree]]: Each split compares the nonempty child sample sets formed by one coordinate threshold; regression leaf loss is the sum of squared deviations from its sample mean, and classification leaf loss is sample count times the selected impurity.

[F2] [[thm-node-mean-minimizes-squared-error]]: On a nonempty regression leaf, the unique constant minimizing the sum of squared errors is the sample mean.

[F3] [[alg-cart-greedy-split]]: At each eligible node, the algorithm forms midpoint thresholds between adjacent distinct observed coordinate values and selects the least child score, resolving score ties by coordinate and cut-index order.

## Proof

1.1 At a node with finite nonempty sample set $I$, each coordinate has finitely many distinct observed values. Arrange them in increasing order $u_1<\cdots<u_r$. For every $k<r$, the midpoint between $u_k$ and $u_{k+1}$ gives two nonempty children. Conversely, any real threshold with two nonempty children has a unique gap $u_k\le s<u_{k+1}$ and induces the same partition as that midpoint. Thus the algorithm's candidate list is finite and contains every nonempty partition produced by one coordinate threshold. [F1, F3, construct]

2.1 For each candidate the child score is a finite real sum. If the candidate list is nonempty, repeatedly comparing its finite list of scores produces a minimum, and the coordinate/cut-index order selects a unique first minimizer among ties. By [F2], the regression child means attain the least squared error on each child; by [F1], the classification score is the declared weighted impurity. The chosen candidate therefore minimizes the declared child loss over all such partitions. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, choose]

3.1 Every recursive call increases depth by one, and calls at depth $d_{\max}$ stop. Each split creates two disjoint nonempty sample sets from its parent, so every terminal leaf contains at least one of the $n$ sample indices. Each split increases the number of leaves by one; hence there are at most $n-1$ splits. The recursion terminates with depth at most $d_{\max}$ and all created children nonempty. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $T_0$ be a finite empirical binary tree with $L_0\ge1$ terminal nodes and nonempty sample set at every leaf. The weakest-link pruning procedure that repeatedly collapses a current nonterminal node minimizing $g(t)$ terminates at the root leaf after at most $L_0-1$ collapses. This is a termination statement only; it does not assert global cost-complexity optimality.

## Statement references

[Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, §9.2.2, printed p. 308](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1--Wo5Hcl2y_v3DL-tGgcJHRPdtjiVYjS)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite empirical binary tree $T_0$ whose internal nodes each have two nonempty child sample sets.

[F1] [[def-empirical-decision-tree]]: Every internal node splits its sample set into two nonempty child sets, and the terminal sample sets partition the original sample.

[F2] [[def-cost-complexity-pruning]]: For a current nonterminal node $t$, $g(t)=[R(t)-R(T_t)]/(|T_t|-1)$, where $T_t$ is its current descendant subtree.

[F3] [[alg-weakest-link-pruning]]: At each iteration the algorithm chooses a current nonterminal node minimizing $g(t)$, collapses its descendant subtree to a leaf, and stops when the current tree is the root leaf.

## Proof

1.1 If the current tree has more than one leaf, its root is nonterminal. Every nonterminal node $t$ has two finite child subtrees. Starting at either child and following descendants must reach a leaf because the tree is finite, so $|T_t|\ge2$ and every denominator in [F2] is positive. The tree has finitely many nonterminal nodes, and every loss in [F2] is a finite real number because the sample and chosen impurity formulas are finite. Hence the candidate quotients form a finite nonempty set of real numbers, which has a minimum by repeated pairwise comparison. [given, F1, F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], the algorithm selects a minimizing candidate, using its fixed tie rule. If that node has $k=|T_t|\ge2$ descendant leaves, collapsing it replaces those $k$ leaves by one, reducing the current leaf count by $k-1\ge1$. The resulting tree is still a finite subtree of $T_0$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, choose]

3.1 Starting from $L_0$ leaves, each collapse strictly decreases the positive integer leaf count, so there are at most $L_0-1$ collapses. If more than one leaf remains, the root is nonterminal and is among the available candidates by step 1.1; therefore the algorithm cannot stop early. A nonterminal root has at least two descendant leaves by step 1.1, so a tree with one leaf is the root leaf. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The four regression observations and the greedy growth procedure with maximum depth $1$.

[F1] [[def-empirical-decision-tree]]: A nonempty regression leaf predicts its sample mean and has residual sum of squares $\sum_{i\in I}(y_i-\bar y_I)^2$.

[F2] [[alg-cart-greedy-split]]: Candidate thresholds lie between adjacent distinct coordinate values, and the procedure chooses the candidate minimizing the child score.

[F3] [[thm-cart-greedy-split-is-best-listed-split-and-terminates]]: Every nonempty coordinate-threshold partition occurs among the midpoint candidates, and the chosen split minimizes the child loss on that finite list.

1.1 The four distinct coordinate values are $0<1<2<3$, so the midpoint candidates are exactly $0.5$, $1.5$, and $2.5$. At $0.5$, the right child has responses $0,1,1$, mean $2/3$, and residual sum $2/3$. At $1.5$, both children have constant responses, so the score is $0$. At $2.5$, the left child has responses $0,0,1$, mean $1/3$, and residual sum $2/3$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The middle threshold is therefore the unique minimum-scoring candidate. By [F3], it is the best listed split and the procedure chooses it. Its two leaves have means $0$ and $1$, as displayed. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The root split has depth $1=d_{\max}$, so the procedure stops there and returns the stated two-leaf tree. The diagram merely records the split and leaf predictions; the previously computed scores and the depth cap establish the output independently of the diagram. [F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix training data $D=((x_i,y_i))_{i=1}^n$ with $n\ge1$, features $x_i\in\mathbb R^p$ with $p\ge1$, and one response mode: regression with $y_i\in\mathbb R$, or classification with labels in a fixed ordered finite set $\mathcal C=\{c_1<\cdots<c_J\}$, $J\ge1$. Choose a finite depth cap $d_{\max}\ge0$, a tree count $B\ge1$, and a feature count $m\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$. Choosing $m=p$ disables feature randomization.

For every tree index $b\in\{1,\ldots,B\}$, draw $n$ independent uniform indices $I_{b1},\ldots,I_{bn}$ from $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and put $N_{bi}=|\{r:I_{br}=i\}|$. For every possible binary node address $\nu$ of depth less than $d_{\max}$, draw a subset $M_{b,\nu}$ uniformly from the $m$-element subsets of $\{1,\ldots,p\}$. All bootstrap-index and feature-subset draws are mutually independent across trees, index positions, and node addresses. Write $\Theta_b=(N_{b1},\ldots,N_{bn},(M_{b,\nu})_\nu)$; thus the $\Theta_b$ are independent with a common law conditional on the fixed data and chosen settings.

At a node with bootstrap position set $I$, define $\bar y_I=|I|^{-1}\sum_{r\in I}y_{I_{br}}$ in regression. In classification define $q_{Ik}=|I|^{-1}|\{r\in I:y_{I_{br}}=c_k\}|$ and choose one fixed impurity, either misclassification $1-\max_kq_{Ik}$, Gini $1-\sum_kq_{Ik}^2$, or entropy $-\sum_kq_{Ik}\log q_{Ik}$, with $0\log0=0$.

For tree $b$, write the resampled rows as $D_b^*=((x_{I_{br}},y_{I_{br}}))_{r=1}^n$, so bootstrap positions remain distinct even when they contain the same original row. Build $T_b$ from $D_b^*$, starting at the root with position set $I=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. At a node of depth $d<d_{\max}$, form the candidate midpoint thresholds between consecutive distinct observed values using the coordinates in that node's set $M_{b,\nu}$. A candidate at coordinate $j$ and threshold $t$ partitions the current bootstrap positions into $I_L=\{r\in I:x_{I_{br},j}\le t\}$ and $I_R=\{r\in I:x_{I_{br},j}>t\}$; only candidates with both children nonempty are used. Score each candidate by $\sum_{r\in I_L}(y_{I_{br}}-\bar y_{I_L})^2+\sum_{r\in I_R}(y_{I_{br}}-\bar y_{I_R})^2$ in regression or by $|I_L|Q_{I_L}+|I_R|Q_{I_R}$ in classification, where $Q$ is the chosen impurity. Select a candidate of least score, breaking ties by coordinate index and then cut index, and recurse on its two children. If $d=d_{\max}$ or there is no candidate, make the node a leaf. When $m=p$, this is the greedy CART growth procedure on the bootstrap sample; when $m<p$, the same procedure restricts each node's candidate coordinates to its sampled subset. Each regression leaf predicts its sample mean; each classification leaf predicts its most frequent class, choosing the least class index in a tie. Define $h(x,\Theta_b)$ by following the unique tree path for $x$.

For regression, the finite-forest prediction is $B^{-1}\sum_{b=1}^B h(x,\Theta_b)$. For classification, it is the class receiving the largest number of votes, with the least class index breaking ties. For a training observation $i$, let $O_i=\{b:N_{bi}=0\}$. Its out-of-bag prediction is formed using only trees indexed by $O_i$, with the same regression average or classification vote rule; if $O_i=\varnothing$, no out-of-bag prediction is returned. An out-of-bag prediction is a diagnostic computed from this finite forest, not an exact identity for its full-forest prediction or risk.

The data flow is shown below. The arrows mean that the same fixed $D$ and the independent randomization vector determine each tree, and the stated aggregation combines the resulting predictions; the diagram records the procedure and is not a proof of a performance claim.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth]
  \node[draw,rounded corners] (data) at (0,0) {fixed data $D$};
  \node[draw,rounded corners] (random) at (0,-1.2) {IID $\Theta_b$};
  \node[draw,rounded corners] (tree) at (3,-0.6) {$T_b(x)=h(x,\Theta_b)$};
  \node[draw,rounded corners] (aggregate) at (6,-0.6) {vote or average over $b=1,\ldots,B$};
  \draw[->] (data) -- (tree);
  \draw[->] (random) -- (tree);
  \draw[->] (tree) -- (aggregate);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Statement

Fix a finite training dataset and a classifier $h(x,\theta)$ taking values in an ordered finite class set $\mathcal C=\{c_1<\cdots<c_J\}$ with $J\ge2$. Let $\Theta_1,\Theta_2,\ldots$ be IID random elements of a measurable space $(\mathsf T,\mathcal T)$ with common law $Q$. Regard the sequence as a random element of $(\mathsf T^{\mathbb N},\mathcal T^{\otimes\mathbb N})$ and assume it is independent of a test pair $(X,Y)$ with law $P$ on $\mathcal X\times\mathcal C$. Assume $h$ is jointly measurable in $(x,\theta)$. For $j\in\{1,\ldots,J\}$ define $p_j(x)=Q\{\theta:h(x,\theta)=c_j\}$, and let

$$
m(x,y)=p_{k}(x)-\max_{j\ne k}p_j(x),\qquad y=c_k.
$$

For each $B\ge1$, let $G_B(x)$ be the class with the largest number of votes among $h(x,\Theta_1),\ldots,h(x,\Theta_B)$, choosing the least class index in a tie. Define the finite-forest conditional risk by

$$
PE_B(\Theta_{1:B})=\int_{\mathcal X\times\mathcal C}\mathbf1\{G_B(x)\ne y\}\,dP(x,y).
$$

If $P\{(x,y):m(x,y)=0\}=0$, then, almost surely with respect to the IID tree-randomization sequence,

$$
PE_B(\Theta_{1:B})\longrightarrow P\{(x,y):m(x,y)<0\}.
$$

## Statement references

[Breiman, “Random Forests,” Theorem 1.2 and Appendix I, printed pp. 7 and 29–30](https://mfm.uchicago.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Breiman-Random-Forests.pdf)

[Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, §15.2, printed pp. 587–593; used for the forest construction, not as a proof of this risk limit](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1--Wo5Hcl2y_v3DL-tGgcJHRPdtjiVYjS)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The fixed training data, measurable classifier and IID tree-randomization sequence, independent test pair, finite ordered class set, and zero-margin hypothesis in the Statement.

[F1] [[alg-bagged-random-forest]]: Classification uses the class with the largest number of tree votes and the least class index for a tie.

[F2] [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]: IID means mutual independence together with identical laws; it includes no moment assumption.

[F3] [[lem-measurable-functions-preserve-independence]]: Applying the same measurable map to each member of an independent family preserves independence.

[F4] [[thm-kolmogorov-iid-l1-strong-law]]: For IID real random variables with finite first absolute moment, their sample averages converge almost surely to their common mean.

[F5] [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]: The joint law of a finite independent family of random elements is the product of their marginal laws.

[F6] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: For an integrable function on a product of sigma-finite measure spaces, either order of iterated integration gives the product integral.

[F7] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: Almost-everywhere convergence under a common integrable majorant implies convergence of the integrals.

[F8] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]: Expectation on a probability space is integration against its probability measure.

## Proof

1.1 Fix a test pair $(x,y)$ outside the zero-margin set. For each class $c_j$, the variables $\mathbf1\{h(x,\Theta_b)=c_j\}$ are identically distributed because they use the same measurable map on randomizations with common law, independent by [F3], and integrable because they are bounded by $1$. Applying [F4] to each of the finitely many classes shows that every vote proportion converges almost surely to $p_j(x)$. [given, F2, F3, F4]

2.1 On a sequence where those proportions converge, if $m(x,y)>0$, the true class has a strictly larger limiting vote proportion than each wrong class, so the finite forest eventually predicts $y$. If $m(x,y)<0$, a wrong class attaining the finite maximum in the definition of $m$ has a strictly larger limiting proportion than $y$, so the finite forest eventually predicts a wrong class. Thus the finite-forest error indicator converges almost surely in the randomizations to $\mathbf1\{m(x,y)<0\}$ for $P$-almost every test pair. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The functions $p_j(x)$ are measurable by [F6] applied to the bounded jointly measurable indicators $\mathbf1\{h(x,\theta)=c_j\}$. Hence the error indicators and the limiting margin indicator are jointly measurable and bounded. Independence of the sequence-valued randomization and test pair lets [F5] give their product joint law. Applying [F6] to the indicator of the nonconvergence set and using step 2.1 shows that for almost every randomization sequence the error indicators converge for $P$-almost every test pair. [given, F5, F6, step 2.1]

4.1 For each such sequence, the error indicators are dominated by the integrable constant $1$ on the probability space $(\mathcal X\times\mathcal C,P)$. By [F7] their integrals converge to the integral of $\mathbf1\{m<0\}$, which by [F8] is $P\{m<0\}$. These integrals are exactly $PE_B(\Theta_{1:B})$, proving the claimed limit. [F7, F8, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

Assume $h$ is jointly measurable on the product of the test-feature space and the randomization space. Let $Z=(X,Y)$ have test law $P$. $$
m(x,y)=p_k(x)-p_{\hat j(x,y)}(x),\qquad s=\mathbb E_P[m(Z)].
$$

Assume $s>0$. For a tree randomization $\theta$, define the raw margin $r_\theta(x,y)=\mathbf1\{h(x,\theta)=y\}-\mathbf1\{h(x,\theta)=c_{\hat j(x,y)}\}$ and $sd(\theta)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_P(r_\theta(Z))}$. Put $d=\mathbb E_Q[sd(\Theta)]$. If $d=0$, then $P\{m(Z)<0\}=0$. If $d>0$, define

$$
\rho=\frac{\mathbb E_{Q\times Q}[\operatorname{Cov}_P(r_\Theta(Z),r_{\Theta'}(Z))]}{d^2}.
$$

Then $\rho\ge0$ and

$$
P\{m(Z)<0\}\le \rho\frac{1-s^2}{s^2}.
$$

The covariance formula for $\rho$ is Breiman's weighted mean raw-margin correlation written without undefined zero-standard-deviation correlation terms.

## Statement references

[Breiman, “Random Forests,” Definitions 2.1–2.2 and Theorem 2.3, printed pp. 8–9](https://mfm.uchicago.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Breiman-Random-Forests.pdf)

[Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, §15.4, printed pp. 597–602; used for the variance/correlation context, not as a proof of this bound](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1--Wo5Hcl2y_v3DL-tGgcJHRPdtjiVYjS)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The fixed data, classifier jointly measurable on the product of the test-feature and randomization spaces, finite ordered class set, independent randomizations and test pair, and positive-strength condition in the Statement.

[F1] [[alg-bagged-random-forest]]: The tree law is fixed conditional on the training data, and each tree takes one class value at an input.

[F2] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]: Expectation on a probability space is integration against its probability measure.

[F3] [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]: For square-integrable real random variables, variance is the mean squared centered value and covariance is the mean product of centered values.

[F4] [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]: The joint law of a finite independent family of random elements is the product of their marginal laws.

[F5] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: For an integrable function on a product of sigma-finite measure spaces, either order of iterated integration gives the product integral.

[F6] [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]: If $U,V\in L^2(Q)$, then $\mathbb E_Q|UV|\le(\mathbb E_QU^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E_QV^2)^{1/2}$.

[F7] [[cor-chebyshev-inequality-for-random-variables]]: For square-integrable $W$ and $a>0$, $P(|W-\mathbb E W|\ge a)\le\operatorname{Var}(W)/a^2$.

## Proof

1.1 For each fixed $z=(x,y)$, the definition of $\hat j$ gives $\mathbb E_Q[r_\Theta(z)]=p_k(x)-p_{\hat j(x,y)}(x)=m(z)$. Also $|r_\theta(z)|\le1$, so all displayed means and covariances are finite. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The bounded jointly measurable class indicators and [F5] make $p_j$ and the finite maximizer $\hat j$ measurable. By [F4] the pair $(\Theta,\Theta',Z)$ has product law, and [F5] permits exchanging the integrals of these bounded functions. Thus $\mathbb E_{Q\times Q}[\operatorname{Cov}_P(r_\Theta,r_{\Theta'})]=\mathbb E_P[m(Z)^2]-s^2=\operatorname{Var}_P(m(Z))$. Indeed, the product of the two conditional raw-margin means is $m(z)^2$, while the product of their $P$-means integrates to $(\mathbb E_Pm)^2=s^2$. If both standard deviations are positive, covariance equals correlation times their product; if either is zero, both the covariance and the weighted correlation term are zero. Thus the covariance expression for $\rho$ is exactly Breiman's weighted mean raw-margin correlation. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $d>0$. From step 2.1, $\rho=\operatorname{Var}_P(m)/d^2\ge0$. Since $r_\theta^2\le1$, $\mathbb E_Q[sd(\Theta)^2]=\mathbb E_{Q\times P}[r_\Theta^2]-\mathbb E_Q[(\mathbb E_Pr_\Theta)^2]\le1-s^2$. The final inequality uses $\mathbb E_Q[(\mathbb E_Pr_\Theta)^2]\ge(\mathbb E_Q\mathbb E_Pr_\Theta)^2=s^2$, by [F6] with one factor equal to $1$; [F5] and step 1.1 give $\mathbb E_Q\mathbb E_Pr_\Theta=s$. The same inequality gives $d^2\le\mathbb E_Q[sd(\Theta)^2]$. Therefore $\operatorname{Var}_P(m)=\rho d^2\le\rho(1-s^2)$. [F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Since $s>0$, the event $\{m(Z)<0\}$ is contained in $\{|m(Z)-s|\ge s\}$. Applying [F7] and then step 3.1 gives $P\{m(Z)<0\}\le\operatorname{Var}_P(m(Z))/s^2\le\rho(1-s^2)/s^2$. [F7, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If $d=0$, then $sd\ge0$ and $\mathbb E_Qsd=0$. For each $n\ge1$, $Q\{sd\ge1/n\}=0$, since otherwise $\mathbb E_Qsd>0$; taking the countable union gives $sd=0$ $Q$-almost everywhere. For each such $\theta$, $\mathbb E_P(r_\theta-\mathbb E_Pr_\theta)^2=0$, so the same nonnegative-integral argument makes $r_\theta(Z)=\mathbb E_Pr_\theta$ $P$-almost surely. By [F5], $m(Z)=\mathbb E_Qr_\Theta(Z)$ is therefore the constant $\mathbb E_Pm(Z)=s>0$ for $P$-almost every $Z$. Hence $P\{m(Z)<0\}=0$, as claimed in this case. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Real random variables $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$.

[L1] Holder's inequality on a probability space specializes to $$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\|X\|_2\|Y\|_2$$ ([[cor-holder-inequality-for-random-variables]]).

[L2] The $L^2$ Cauchy-Schwarz equality criterion is already proved for general measure spaces ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Step [L1] at $p=q=2$ gives $$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\|X\|_2\|Y\|_2=\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$ [L1]

2.1 The equality clause is exactly the probability-measure specialization of [L2]. [step 1.1, L2] ∎

## Statement

If $X$ is a square-integrable real random variable and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A square-integrable real random variable $X$ and a real number $a>0$.

[L1] Variance is the expectation of the squared centered variable ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]).

[L2] Markov's inequality applies to every nonnegative random variable ([[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The random variable $Y:=(X-\mathbb E[X])^2$ is nonnegative, and $$\{Y\ge a^2\}=\{|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a\}.$$ [given, algebra]

2.1 Applying [L2] to $Y$ and using [L1] gives $$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a)=\mathbb P(Y\ge a^2)\le\frac{\mathbb E[Y]}{a^2}=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.$$ [step 1.1, L1, L2] ∎

## Statement

Fix a finite training dataset and a jointly measurable real-valued tree predictor $h(x,\theta)$. Let $Z=(X,Y)$ have test law $P$. Let $\Theta,\Theta'$ be independent randomizations with common law $Q$, assume the pair $(\Theta,\Theta')$ is independent of $Z$, and assume $\mathbb E_PY^2<\infty$ and $h(X,\Theta)\in L^2(P\times Q)$. For every allowed tree randomization $\theta$, assume $h(X,\theta)\in L^2(P)$ and $\mathbb E_PY=\mathbb E_Ph(X,\theta)$. Put $e_\theta(Z)=Y-h(X,\theta)$ and $sd(\theta)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_P(e_\theta(Z))}$. Define

$$PE^*(\mathrm{forest})=\mathbb E_P\left(Y-\mathbb E_Qh(X,\Theta)\right)^2$$

$$PE^*(\mathrm{tree})=\mathbb E_Q\mathbb E_P e_\Theta(Z)^2$$

$$d=\mathbb E_Q[sd(\Theta)]$$

If $d=0$, then both risks are zero. If $d>0$, define

$$
\rho=\frac{\mathbb E_{Q\times Q}[\operatorname{Cov}_P(e_\Theta(Z),e_{\Theta'}(Z))]}{d^2}.
$$

Then $\rho\ge0$ and

$$
PE^*(\mathrm{forest})\le\rho\,PE^*(\mathrm{tree}).
$$

The covariance formula for $\rho$ is Breiman's weighted mean residual correlation written without undefined zero-standard-deviation correlation terms.

## Statement references

[Breiman, “Random Forests,” Theorem 11.2, printed pp. 25–26](https://mfm.uchicago.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Breiman-Random-Forests.pdf)

[Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, §§15.1 and 15.4.1–15.4.3, printed pp. 587, 597–602; used for the regression forest and variance/correlation context, not as a proof of this bound](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1--Wo5Hcl2y_v3DL-tGgcJHRPdtjiVYjS)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The fixed data, jointly measurable square-integrable predictor, unbiasedness condition for every allowed tree randomization, and independent randomizations and test pair in the Statement.

[F1] [[alg-bagged-random-forest]]: For regression, each tree predicts its leaf sample mean and the forest prediction is the average of its tree predictions.

[F2] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]: Expectation on a probability space is integration against its probability measure.

[F3] [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]: For square-integrable real random variables, variance is the mean squared centered value and covariance is the mean product of centered values.

[F4] [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]: The joint law of a finite independent family of random elements is the product of their marginal laws.

[F5] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: For an integrable function on a product of sigma-finite measure spaces, either order of iterated integration gives the product integral.

[F6] [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]: If $U,V\in L^2(Q)$, then $\mathbb E_Q|UV|\le(\mathbb E_QU^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E_QV^2)^{1/2}$.

## Proof

1.1 For every allowed $\theta$, the mean condition gives $\mathbb E_Pe_\theta(Z)=0$. Hence [F3] gives $\operatorname{Cov}_P(e_\theta,e_{\theta'})=\mathbb E_P[e_\theta e_{\theta'}]$. If both residual standard deviations are positive, define their correlation as this covariance divided by their product; if either is zero, the covariance is zero. Thus the covariance expression for $\rho$ agrees with Breiman's weighted mean residual correlation, including zero-standard-deviation pairs. The products are integrable by [F6] and square-integrability. Also $\mathbb E_{P\times Q}e_\Theta^2<\infty$, since $(a-b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2$ and both $Y$ and $h(X,\Theta)$ are square-integrable. [given, F2, F3, F6, algebra]

2.1 By [F4] the pair $(\Theta,\Theta',Z)$ has product law. For $P$-almost every $z$, [F6] gives $(\mathbb E_Q|e_\Theta(z)|)^2\le\mathbb E_Qe_\Theta(z)^2$; integrating and using step 1.1 shows $e_\theta(z)e_{\theta'}(z)$ is integrable on $P\times Q\times Q$. Thus [F5] permits the following integrations. The $Q$-average is the infinite-forest prediction obtained from the same regression tree predictions that the algorithm averages at finite $B$ [F1]. Also $\mathbb E_Qe_\Theta(Z)=Y-\mathbb E_Qh(X,\Theta)$ for $P$-almost every $Z$. Consequently $PE^*(\mathrm{forest})=\mathbb E_P[(\mathbb E_Qe_\Theta(Z))^2]=\mathbb E_{Q\times Q}[\mathbb E_P(e_\Theta(Z)e_{\Theta'}(Z))]=\mathbb E_{Q\times Q}[\operatorname{Cov}_P(e_\Theta(Z),e_{\Theta'}(Z))]$. Thus when $d>0$, $PE^*(\mathrm{forest})=\rho d^2$ and $\rho\ge0$. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The zero-mean condition and [F3] give $PE^*(\mathrm{tree})=\mathbb E_Q[sd(\Theta)^2]$. By [F6] with one factor equal to $1$, $d^2=(\mathbb E_Qsd(\Theta))^2\le\mathbb E_Q[sd(\Theta)^2]$. For $d>0$, combining with step 2.1 and $\rho\ge0$ yields $PE^*(\mathrm{forest})\le\rho\,PE^*(\mathrm{tree})$. [F2, F3, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $d=0$, then the nonnegative function $sd$ vanishes $Q$-almost everywhere: each set $\{sd\ge1/n\}$ has measure zero since otherwise $\mathbb E_Qsd>0$. For $Q$-almost every $\theta$, the mean-zero residual has variance zero, so the same argument applied to $(e_\theta-\mathbb E_Pe_\theta)^2$ gives $e_\theta=0$ $P$-almost surely. Fubini then gives $e_\Theta(Z)=0$ for $P\times Q$-almost every $(Z,\Theta)$; both displayed risks are zero. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.1] ∎

## Example

Take the classification sample $D=((0,0),(1,1))$ with ordered labels $0<1$, grow depth-zero trees, and use $B=2$ bootstrap trees. A tree is out of bag for observation $1$ exactly when its bootstrap count for training index $1$ is zero. On the event that the first bootstrap count vector is $(2,0)$ and the second is $(0,2)$, the full forest receives one vote for each class and predicts $0$ by the least-index tie rule. The out-of-bag set for observation $1$ is then $\{2\}$, so its out-of-bag prediction is $1$. This event has probability $1/16$, and it exhibits a finite-forest out-of-bag prediction that differs from the full finite-forest prediction.

## Example references

[[alg-bagged-random-forest|Bootstrap counts, class ties, and out-of-bag predictions]]

[[def-empirical-decision-tree|Classification leaf predictions]]

[Breiman, “Random Forests,” §3.1 and Appendix II, printed pp. 11 and 31–32](https://mfm.uchicago.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Breiman-Random-Forests.pdf)

[Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, §15.3.1, printed pp. 592–593](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1--Wo5Hcl2y_v3DL-tGgcJHRPdtjiVYjS)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Two independent size-$2$ bootstrap samples drawn uniformly with replacement from the two-observation training sample, with depth cap zero and the class tie rule in the Example.

[F1] [[alg-bagged-random-forest]]: The out-of-bag set for observation $i$ consists exactly of tree indices $b$ with $N_{bi}=0$, and no prediction is returned when this set is empty.

[F2] [[def-empirical-decision-tree]]: A classification leaf predicts the most frequent class, choosing the least class index in a tie.

[F3] [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]: The joint law of a finite independent family of random elements is the product of their marginal laws.

## Verification

1.1 Each tree draws two independent uniform indices from $\{1,2\}$. The probability of counts $(2,0)$ for tree $1$ is $1/4$, and the probability of counts $(0,2)$ for tree $2$ is $1/4$. Independence of the two trees gives probability $(1/4)(1/4)=1/16$ for the stated event. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 With depth cap zero, each tree is a single leaf. Its bootstrap sample contains only label $0$ for counts $(2,0)$ and only label $1$ for counts $(0,2)$, so [F2] gives predictions $0$ and $1$, respectively. [given, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 The full forest has one vote for each class, so its least-index tie rule returns $0$. For observation $1$, the first tree has $N_{11}=2$ and is excluded from the out-of-bag set, while the second has $N_{21}=0$ and is the only included tree; its prediction is $1$. The two predictions differ on the positive-probability event from step 1.1. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y=X$, with $P(X=0,Y=0)=3/4$ and $P(X=1,Y=1)=1/4$. Conditional on fixed training data, let each randomized tree independently be the constant class-$0$ stump with probability $3/4$ and the constant class-$1$ stump with probability $1/4$. For a randomization $\theta$, write $p_c(x)=Q\{h(x,\theta)=c\}$; for $y\in\{0,1\}$ define $m(x,y)=p_y(x)-p_{1-y}(x)$, $s=\mathbb E[m(X,Y)]$, and $PE^*=P\{m(X,Y)<0\}$. For each tree set $r_\theta(x,y)=\mathbf1\{h(x,\theta)=y\}-\mathbf1\{h(x,\theta)=1-y\}$ and $sd(\theta)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_{X,Y}(r_\theta(X,Y))}$. For independent randomizations $\Theta,\Theta'$ let $d=\mathbb E_Qsd(\Theta)$ and $\rho=\mathbb E_{Q\times Q}[\operatorname{Cov}_{X,Y}(r_\Theta,r_{\Theta'})]/d^2$. Then the limiting margins at the two test pairs are $m(0,0)=1/2$ and $m(1,1)=-1/2$, so $s=1/4$ and $PE^*=1/4$. Each tree's raw-margin standard deviation is $\sqrt{3/4}$, the covariance numerator defining $\rho$ is $3/16$, and $\rho=1/4$. The strength-correlation bound has right-hand side $15/4$ in this example.

## Example references

[[thm-random-forest-strength-correlation-bound|Strength, raw margins, and the correlation bound]]

[Breiman, “Random Forests,” Definitions 2.1–2.2 and Theorem 2.3, printed pp. 8–9](https://mfm.uchicago.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Breiman-Random-Forests.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The test law and independent two-stump randomization law in the Example.

[F1] [[alg-bagged-random-forest]]: A regression or classification forest aggregates trees with a fixed class order, and a classification tree casts one class vote.

[F2] [[thm-random-forest-strength-correlation-bound]]: The strength is $s=\mathbb E_Pm$, tree standard deviations are $sd(\theta)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_P(r_\theta)}$, and for $d>0$ the correlation parameter is the expected independent-pair covariance divided by $d^2$.

[F3] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]: Expectation on a probability space is integration against its probability measure.

[F4] [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]: Variance and covariance are expectations of the corresponding centered products.

[F5] [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]: The joint law of a finite independent family of random elements is the product of their marginal laws.

## Verification

1.1 By the tree-vote convention [F1], at $Z=(0,0)$ the correct class receives probability $3/4$ and the wrong class $1/4$, giving margin $1/2$. At $Z=(1,1)$, the correct class receives probability $1/4$ and the wrong class $3/4$, giving margin $-1/2$. Therefore $s=(3/4)(1/2)+(1/4)(-1/2)=1/4$ and $PE^*=1/4$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 For tree type $A$, the raw margin is $+1$ at $(0,0)$ and $-1$ at $(1,1)$; its mean is $1/2$ and its second moment is $1$, so its variance is $3/4$. Type $B$ reverses the two signs, giving mean $-1/2$ and the same variance $3/4$. Thus $sd(A)=sd(B)=\sqrt{3/4}$ and $d^2=3/4$. [F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 The independent pair has probabilities $P(A,A)=9/16$, $P(B,B)=1/16$, and total mixed probability $6/16$. The covariance over $Z$ is $3/4$ for equal types and $-3/4$ for mixed types, so its expectation is $[(9+1-6)/16](3/4)=3/16$. By [F2] and [F5], $\rho=(3/16)/(3/4)=1/4$. [F2, F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Substitution gives $\rho(1-s^2)/s^2=(1/4)(15/16)/(1/16)=15/4$, and the example's error $1/4$ satisfies the bound. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
