## Definition

Fix a finite training sample $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^N$ with $N\ge1$, $x_i\in\mathcal X$, and $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, a finite round limit $M\ge0$, and a weak-learning routine which at each requested round returns a classifier $h_m:\mathcal X\to\{-1,+1\}$ for the current observation weights. Initialize $w_i^{(1)}=1/N$ and $F_0(x)=0$. At round $m$, compute the weighted error $e_m=\sum_{i=1}^N w_i^{(m)}\mathbf 1\{h_m(x_i)\ne y_i\}$. If $e_m=0$, halt and return $h_m$ itself as a perfect classifier with zero training error; do not form an infinite coefficient. If $e_m\ge1/2$, halt and report that the weak-learning condition failed. For $0<e_m<1/2$, set

$$a_m=\frac12\log\frac{1-e_m}{e_m},\qquad Z_m=2\sqrt{e_m(1-e_m)},$$

update $w_i^{(m+1)}=w_i^{(m)}\exp(-a_my_ih_m(x_i))/Z_m$, and set $F_m(x)=F_{m-1}(x)+a_mh_m(x)$. After $M$ completed weak rounds, return the classifier $\widehat y_M(x)=\operatorname{sign}_+(F_M(x))$, where $\operatorname{sign}_+(u)=+1$ for $u\ge0$ and $-1$ for $u<0$. Thus ties are assigned to $+1$. The coefficient convention is the half-log convention; multiplying every coefficient by the same positive factor does not change the sign classifier. The definition makes no claim about test error or generalization.

## Definition

Let $N\ge1$, let $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^N$ be a finite sample with $x_i\in\mathcal X$ and $y_i\in\mathcal Y$, let $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ be a score function, and let $\ell:\mathcal Y\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be finite-valued. Assume that for each $i$, the one-variable function $t\mapsto\ell(y_i,t)$ is differentiable at $z_i=f(x_i)$. For a score vector $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_N)$, define the empirical score loss $\Phi(z)=\sum_{i=1}^N\ell(y_i,z_i)$. The pseudo-residual at observation $i$ for $f$ is

$$r_i(f)=-\left.\frac{d}{dt}\ell(y_i,t)\right|_{t=f(x_i)}.$$

The sample-score gradient, when its coordinate partial derivatives exist, is the vector $\nabla\Phi(z)=(\partial_{z_1}\Phi(z),\ldots,\partial_{z_N}\Phi(z))$. The sample pseudo-residual vector is $(r_1(f),\ldots,r_N(f))$; the word “pseudo” distinguishes these score derivatives from derivatives with respect to parameters of a restricted model.

## Definition references

[Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani, and Jerome Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, 2nd ed., §10.10.3, printed p. 361](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1--Wo5Hcl2y_v3DL-tGgcJHRPdtjiVYjS)

[Alexey Natekin and Alois Knoll, “Gradient boosting machines, a tutorial,” §2.4](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neurorobotics/articles/10.3389/fnbot.2013.00021/full)

## Statement

Let $N\ge1$, let $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^N$ be a finite sample, let $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open with $z_i=f(x_i)\in U$ for every $i$. Suppose each scalar loss $t\mapsto\ell(y_i,t)$ is defined on $U$ and differentiable at $z_i$. Write $\partial_2\ell(y_i,z_i)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\ell(y_i,t)\right|_{t=z_i}$ and define $\Phi:U^N\to\mathbb R$ by $\Phi(w)=\sum_{i=1}^N\ell(y_i,w_i)$. Then $\Phi$ is totally differentiable at $z$, its derivative in a score increment $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_N)$ is

$$D\Phi(z)v=\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_2\ell(y_i,z_i)v_i,$$

and its Euclidean gradient is $\nabla\Phi(z)=(\partial_2\ell(y_i,z_i))_{i=1}^N$. Therefore the pseudo-residual vector associated with $f$ on this sample is exactly $-\nabla\Phi(z)$ in sample-score space.

## Statement references

[Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani, and Jerome Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, 2nd ed., §§10.10.1–10.10.3, equations (10.35)–(10.37), printed pp. 358–361](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1--Wo5Hcl2y_v3DL-tGgcJHRPdtjiVYjS)

[Alexey Natekin and Alois Knoll, “Gradient boosting machines, a tutorial,” §§2.3–2.4](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neurorobotics/articles/10.3389/fnbot.2013.00021/full)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Sample scores $z_i=f(x_i)$ in an open scalar domain $U$ and scalar losses differentiable at those scores.

[F1] [[def-negative-gradient-pseudo-residual]]: The empirical score loss is $\Phi(z)=\sum_i\ell(y_i,z_i)$, and the pseudo-residual is $r_i=-\partial_2\ell(y_i,z_i)$.

[F2] [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]: Total differentiability at a point means a linear first-order approximation whose remainder divided by the increment norm tends to zero.

[F3] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: If $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and $g$ at $f(a)$, then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable and $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$.

[F4] [[thm-algebra-of-total-derivatives]]: Finite sums of totally differentiable maps are totally differentiable and their derivatives add.

[F5] [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]: A coordinate partial derivative is the directional derivative along the corresponding standard basis direction.

[F6] [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]: When a total derivative exists, its value on each coordinate direction is the corresponding partial derivative.

[F7] [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]: For a scalar-valued function, the Euclidean gradient is the vector of coordinate partial derivatives in standard coordinate order.

## Proof

1.1 For each $i$, let $\pi_i(z)=z_i$ and $g_i(t)=\ell(y_i,t)$. The coordinate projection has derivative $D\pi_i(z)v=v_i$ because its linear approximation has zero remainder. Differentiability of $g_i$ at $z_i$ gives $g_i(z_i+u)=g_i(z_i)+\partial_2\ell(y_i,z_i)u+o(|u|)$, so $Dg_i(z_i)u=\partial_2\ell(y_i,z_i)u$. [given, F2, construct]

2.1 By the chain rule, $\psi_i=g_i\circ\pi_i$ is totally differentiable and $D\psi_i(z)v=\partial_2\ell(y_i,z_i)v_i$. [F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Since $\Phi=\sum_{i=1}^N\psi_i$, the finite-sum rule gives $D\Phi(z)v=\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_2\ell(y_i,z_i)v_i$. [F4, step 2.1, induction]

4.1 Evaluating step 3.1 on the coordinate direction that changes only $z_i$ gives the $i$-th partial derivative $\partial_{z_i}\Phi(z)=\partial_2\ell(y_i,z_i)$ by [F5] and [F6]. The gradient convention [F7] and pseudo-residual definition [F1] now give $\nabla\Phi(z)=(\partial_2\ell(y_i,z_i))_{i=1}^N$ and $(r_i)_{i=1}^N=-\nabla\Phi(z)$. [F1, F5, F6, F7, step 3.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open in the metric induced by its Euclidean norm, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ for which

$$\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2\le\varepsilon\|h\|_2\qquad\text{whenever }a+h\in U\text{ and }\|h\|_2<\delta.$$

The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with the displayed remainder estimate for every $\varepsilon>0$. At $h=0$ the remainder is zero because $L0=0$.

For $m\ge1$, openness of $U$ provides admissible nonzero increments arbitrarily near zero, and dividing the estimate by $\|h\|_2>0$ gives the usual notation

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. Conversely this punctured normwise limit gives the estimate above (using a smaller positive tolerance if necessary). Thus the positive-dimensional definition is unchanged. This is the multivariate normwise remainder condition; no limit at an isolated point is asserted.

When $m=0$, the Euclidean zero space consists only of $0$, so $a=0$ and $U=\{0\}$; its Euclidean norm and induced metric exist by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]. The unique linear map $L:\mathbb R^0\to\mathbb R^n$ sends $0$ to $0$, and its remainder is identically zero. It is therefore the total derivative by the displayed estimate, with any $\delta>0$. When $n=0$, the unique map $f$ and the unique linear map into $\mathbb R^0$ likewise have zero remainder, in every source dimension.

## Statement

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The total first-order expansions of $f$ at $a$ and $g$ at $f(a)$.

[L1] The total-derivative definition supplies the normwise remainder estimate for every $\varepsilon>0$; in positive source dimension this is equivalently the normalized remainder tending to zero as $h$ tends to zero ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]).

[L2] Total differentiability gives a local $O(\|h\|_2)$ increment bound and therefore continuity ([[thm-total-differentiability-gives-a-local-linear-bound-and-continuity]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If the source dimension is zero or $p=0$, the derivative of the composite and the displayed composite of derivatives are the unique zero linear map, and the remainder estimate is identically zero. If the intermediate dimension $n=0$, then $f$ is constant with value $0$, $Df(a)=0$, and $g\circ f$ is constant with zero derivative; again both sides agree. For the remaining proof all three dimensions are positive. [given, L1, L2, algebra]

1.2 Write $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r_f(h)$ and $g(f(a)+k)=g(f(a))+Dg(f(a))k+r_g(k)$, with both normalized remainders tending to zero. [L1, L2]

2.1 By [L2], $k=f(a+h)-f(a)=O(\|h\|_2)$; boundedness of $Dg(f(a))$ and the two remainder limits show both $Dg(f(a))r_f(h)$ and $r_g(k)$ are $o(\|h\|_2)$, including the case $k=0$. [step 1.2, L2, algebra]

3.1 Substitution into the two expansions leaves $g(f(a+h))-g(f(a))-Dg(f(a))Df(a)h=o(\|h\|_2)$, and the composite of linear maps is linear. [step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

If $f,g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ are totally differentiable at $a$ and $c\in\mathbb R$, then $f+g$ and $cf$ are totally differentiable at $a$, with

$$D(f+g)(a)=Df(a)+Dg(a),\qquad D(cf)(a)=cDf(a).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Total first-order expansions for $f$ and $g$ at $a$.

[L1] The total-derivative definition supplies the normwise remainder estimate for every $\varepsilon>0$; in positive source dimension this is equivalently the normalized remainder tending to zero as $h$ tends to zero ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]).

[L2] A norm satisfies the triangle inequality and $\|cw\|=|c|\,\|w\|$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If the source dimension is zero, each derivative is the unique map from the zero space and the remainder condition holds on its sole increment. If $n=0$, both functions and all candidate derivatives take only the zero value. In either case the displayed sum and scalar-multiple identities hold for these unique zero linear maps. For the remainder assume that both source and target dimensions are positive. [given, L1, L2, algebra]

1.2 Add the two expansions and multiply the first by $c$ to obtain remainders $r_f+r_g$ for $f+g$ and $cr_f$ for $cf$, with the displayed candidate linear maps. [L1, L2]

2.1 By [L2], $\|r_f(h)+r_g(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2$ is bounded by the sum of two quantities tending to zero, and $\|cr_f(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2=|c|\,\|r_f(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2$ tends to zero (also when $c=0$). [step 1.2, L2, algebra]

3.1 Sums and scalar multiples of linear maps are linear, so step 2.1 verifies the definition with exactly the two stated derivatives. [step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. For $n\ge1$, these are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

For $n=0$, use the zero-space case directly, without invoking that supplier's positive-codomain standing hypothesis. The space $\mathbb R^0$ has only its zero vector and carries the zero Euclidean norm and its induced metric ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5, [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). Whenever the line map is defined near $0$, every difference quotient for real $t\ne0$ is this zero vector; define $D_vf(a)=0$. This is the unique possible derivative value, and its normwise difference-quotient error is exactly zero for all such $t$, so the real parameter still approaches an actual limit point. Every existing coordinate direction therefore has $\partial_jf(a)=0$; these zero-valued partial maps are continuous in the induced norm metrics. If the source dimension is zero, there are no partial indices and the sole direction is $v=0$; its constant line map is defined near $0$.

## Statement

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a$, then $D_vf(a)$ exists for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$ and equals $Df(a)v$. In particular $\partial_jf(a)=Df(a)e_j$, and the matrix of $Df(a)$ is $Jf(a)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A total derivative $Df(a)$ and a direction $v\in\mathbb R^m$.

[L1] The total-derivative definition supplies the normwise remainder estimate for every $\varepsilon>0$; in positive source dimension this is equivalently the normalized remainder tending to zero as $h$ tends to zero ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]).

[L2] The directional derivative is the derivative of $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ at zero, and partial derivatives use standard-basis directions ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $n=0$, the line map has only the zero value, so its directional derivative is the zero vector by the zero-target case of [L2], and this is $Df(a)v$. Every column identity then has zero rows. The case of a zero-dimensional source has only $v=0$ and no partial directions; it is covered by the zero-direction argument below. For the remaining nonzero-direction argument assume $n\ge1$. [given, L1, L2, algebra]

1.2 If $v=0$, then $(f(a+tv)-f(a))/t=0=Df(a)0$ for every $t\ne0$, so [L2] gives $D_0f(a)=Df(a)0$. For the remaining case assume $v\ne0$. For sufficiently small $t\ne0$, openness of $U$ gives $a+tv\in U$ and $tv\ne0$. Write $f(a+tv)-f(a)=tDf(a)v+r(tv)$, where $\|r(tv)\|_2/\|tv\|_2\to0$ by [L1]. [L1, L2, algebra]

2.1 Dividing by $t$ gives $(f(a+tv)-f(a))/t=Df(a)v+r(tv)/t$, and $\|r(tv)/t\|_2=\|v\|_2\,\|r(tv)\|_2/\|tv\|_2\to0$; hence [L2] yields $D_vf(a)=Df(a)v$. [step 1.2, L2, algebra]

3.1 Taking $v=e_j$ identifies the $j$th column of the matrix of $Df(a)$ with the vector of $j$th partial derivatives, which is precisely the Jacobian. [step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

## Definition

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

## Statement

Let $M\ge0$ be a finite sequence of completed rounds of finite-sample AdaBoost.M1, with weighted errors $0<e_m<1/2$, scores $F_M(x)=\sum_{m=1}^M a_mh_m(x)$, and $Z_m=2\sqrt{e_m(1-e_m)}$. Then

$$\sum_{i=1}^N e^{-y_iF_M(x_i)}=N\prod_{m=1}^M Z_m$$

and

$$\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf 1\{y_iF_M(x_i)\le0\}\le\prod_{m=1}^M Z_m.$$

The empty product for $M=0$ is $1$. Under the algorithm's $+1$ tie rule, the empirical classification error is also at most this product. This is a finite training-margin bound only and makes no test-generalization claim.

## Statement references

[Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani, and Jerome Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, 2nd ed., §10.4, equations (10.8)–(10.15), printed pp. 343–344](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1--Wo5Hcl2y_v3DL-tGgcJHRPdtjiVYjS)

[Robert E. Schapire, “The Boosting Approach to Machine Learning: An Overview,” §3, equations (2)–(6), PDF pp. 4–5](https://people.csail.mit.edu/dsontag/courses/ml12/notes/schapire_boosting_tutorial.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A fixed finite binary-labeled sample and a finite sequence of completed rounds with $0<e_m<1/2$.

[F1] [[alg-adaboost-m1]]: The initialization is $w_i^{(1)}=1/N$ and $F_0=0$.

[F2] [[alg-adaboost-m1]]: The weighted error is $e_m=\sum_{i=1}^N w_i^{(m)}\mathbf 1\{h_m(x_i)\ne y_i\}$.

[F3] [[alg-adaboost-m1]]: For $0<e_m<1/2$, $a_m=\frac12\log\frac{1-e_m}{e_m}$ and $Z_m=2\sqrt{e_m(1-e_m)}$.

[F4] [[alg-adaboost-m1]]: The update is $w_i^{(m+1)}=w_i^{(m)}\exp(-a_my_ih_m(x_i))/Z_m$ and $F_m(x)=F_{m-1}(x)+a_mh_m(x)$.

[F5] [[alg-adaboost-m1]]: The classifier uses $\operatorname{sign}_+(u)=+1$ for $u\ge0$ and $-1$ for $u<0$, so ties are assigned to $+1$.

## Proof

1.1 The initial weights sum to $1$ by [F1]. Inductively assume the weights at round $m$ sum to $1$; by [F2], the total weights on correct and incorrect examples are $1-e_m$ and $e_m$. For a temporary coefficient $a\ge0$, the exponential reweighting sum is $q_m(a)=(1-e_m)e^{-a}+e_me^a$. Its second derivative is positive, and $q_m'(a)=e_me^a-(1-e_m)e^{-a}$ vanishes uniquely at $a=\frac12\log((1-e_m)/e_m)>0$, which equals the algorithm's coefficient by [F3]. Substitution gives $q_m(a_m)=2\sqrt{e_m(1-e_m)}=Z_m$. By [F4], the next weights divide the reweighted terms by this exact sum, so they also sum to $1$. Induction proves normalization at every round and the stated minimization formula. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra, induction]

2.1 Put $S_m=\sum_i e^{-y_iF_m(x_i)}$. By [F1], $S_0=N$ and $w_i^{(1)}=e^{-y_iF_0(x_i)}/S_0$. If $w_i^{(m)}=e^{-y_iF_{m-1}(x_i)}/S_{m-1}$, then [F4] gives $w_i^{(m+1)}=e^{-y_iF_m(x_i)}/(S_{m-1}Z_m)$. Step 1.1 establishes that the weights normalize, so the update denominator is the sum of the reweighted terms and $S_m=S_{m-1}Z_m$. Induction yields $S_M=N\prod_{m=1}^M Z_m$. [F1, F4, step 1.1, induction, algebra]

3.1 If $y_iF_M(x_i)\le0$, then $e^{-y_iF_M(x_i)}\ge1$; if the margin is positive, its indicator is zero. Hence each nonpositive-margin indicator is at most its exponential term, and summing and applying step 2.1 proves the stated bound. By [F5], a misclassified positive-label example has negative margin and a misclassified negative-label example has nonpositive margin, so training error is no larger than the bounded nonpositive-margin fraction. [F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix a finite regression sample $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^N$ with $N\ge1$, $x_i\in\mathbb R^p$ for a finite $p\ge1$, and $y_i\in\mathcal Y$. Let $\ell:\mathcal Y\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be a finite-valued per-observation loss, differentiable in its second argument at every score used. Choose a finite round count $M\ge0$ and finite integer tree-depth cap $d_{\max}\ge0$. The algorithm is admissible only when the following required minima are attained: an initial constant minimizer and, at every round, a line minimizer in each terminal leaf. For any admitted run, choose any one such minimizer at each finite stage.

Initialize $f_0(x)=c_0$ with
$$c_0\in\arg\min_{c\in\mathbb R}\sum_{i=1}^N\ell(y_i,c).$$
For each round $m=1,\ldots,M$, perform the following steps.

1. For each observation compute the negative score derivative
$$r_{im}=-\partial_2\ell\bigl(y_i,f_{m-1}(x_i)\bigr).$$

2. Run finite-depth CART regression-tree growth, using squared error and depth cap $d_{\max}$, on the responses $r_{im}$ at features $x_i$. Let its nonempty terminal feature regions be $R_{1m},\ldots,R_{J_m m}$; their training-index sets partition $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. This tree fit approximates the unrestricted negative score gradient. Its fitted leaf means are used to determine the regression-tree fit and regions, but are not the boosting update offsets.

3. For each leaf region choose an attained exact line minimizer
$$\gamma_{jm}\in\arg\min_{\gamma\in\mathbb R}\sum_{i:x_i\in R_{jm}}\ell\bigl(y_i,f_{m-1}(x_i)+\gamma\bigr).$$
In particular, zero is an admissible comparison offset.

4. Update
$$f_m(x)=f_{m-1}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{J_m}\gamma_{jm}\mathbf 1\{x\in R_{jm}\}.$$

The output is $f_M$. Because the run has finitely many rounds and finitely many leaves, choosing one attained minimizer at each stage requires no axiom of choice. The defined variant uses the full training sample and exact leafwise line minimization; shrinkage and subsampling are separate variants. This definition asserts no convergence or generalization result.

## Statement

For any finite run of the defined gradient tree boosting algorithm for which the initial constant and every leaf line minimizer are attained, let $L_m=\sum_{i=1}^N\ell(y_i,f_m(x_i))$. At every completed round $m$, $L_m\le L_{m-1}$, and hence $L_M\le L_0$. This is a finite-step empirical-loss statement only; it asserts no convergence or generalization result.

## Statement references

[Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani, and Jerome Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, 2nd ed., §10.10.3, Algorithm 10.3, printed p. 361](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1--Wo5Hcl2y_v3DL-tGgcJHRPdtjiVYjS)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** One completed finite boosting round, the finite training sample, and the attained leafwise minimizers.

[F1] [[alg-gradient-boosting]]: The tree's terminal regions determine the update, and each $\gamma_{jm}$ attains the minimum of the corresponding leaf loss over all real offsets.

[F2] [[def-empirical-decision-tree]]: A finite tree has nonempty terminal sample sets that partition the training indices, and each training observation follows its unique leaf path.

[F3] [[thm-cart-greedy-split-is-best-listed-split-and-terminates]]: With finite depth, the CART procedure returns a finite tree with nonempty children at every split.

## Proof

1.1 Fix a completed round $m$. By [F2] and [F3], its leaf index sets $I_{jm}=\{i:x_i\in R_{jm}\}$ are finitely many nonempty sets whose disjoint union is $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. [given, F2, F3]

2.1 For every leaf $j$, its attained minimizer $\gamma_{jm}$ has loss no greater than the admissible offset $0$, so $\sum_{i\in I_{jm}}\ell\bigl(y_i,f_{m-1}(x_i)+\gamma_{jm}\bigr)\le\sum_{i\in I_{jm}}\ell\bigl(y_i,f_{m-1}(x_i)\bigr)$. [F1, step 1.1, given]

3.1 By the update rule, each training score $f_m(x_i)$ uses the offset for its unique leaf. Summing the inequalities in step 2.1 over the partition in step 1.1 gives $L_m=\sum_j\sum_{i\in I_{jm}}\ell\bigl(y_i,f_{m-1}(x_i)+\gamma_{jm}\bigr)\le\sum_j\sum_{i\in I_{jm}}\ell\bigl(y_i,f_{m-1}(x_i)\bigr)=L_{m-1}$. Applying this to each of the finitely many rounds yields $L_M\le L_0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Take $x_1=0$, $x_2=1$, labels $y_1=+1$, $y_2=-1$, squared loss $\ell(y,z)=\frac12(z-y)^2$, initial scores $f_0(x_1)=f_0(x_2)=0$, and maximum tree depth $0$. The pseudo-residual vector is $(1,-1)$, but its one-leaf least-squares tree fit predicts $0$ on both observations. Let $\Phi(z_1,z_2)=\frac12(z_1-1)^2+\frac12(z_2+1)^2$. A vector $u$ is a strict descent direction at $0$ when the derivative of $t\mapsto\Phi(tu)$ at $t=0$ is negative. The fitted vector $u=(0,0)$ has derivative $0$, although the unrestricted score gradient is $(-1,+1)\ne0$. The exact leaf loss minimizer is also $0$, so the empirical loss stays at $1$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two-observation sample, squared loss, zero initial scores, and depth cap $0$ stated in the Example.

[F1] [[def-negative-gradient-pseudo-residual]]: The pseudo-residual at observation $i$ is the negative second-argument derivative of its loss at the current score.

[F2] [[lem-pseudo-residuals-are-negative-score-gradient]]: The pseudo-residual vector is the negative Euclidean gradient of the empirical score loss.

[F3] [[def-empirical-decision-tree]]: The root sample set contains the training indices, and a regression tree's terminal leaf sets partition those indices.

[F4] [[alg-cart-greedy-split]]: At a node whose depth equals the maximum depth, the procedure leaves the node unsplit; regression leaf predictions are sample means.

[F5] [[alg-gradient-boosting]]: Each leaf update uses an attained exact minimizer of the empirical loss over its real offset.

[F6] [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]: The directional derivative in direction $u$ is the derivative of the line map $t\mapsto\Phi(0+tu)$ at $t=0$.

## Verification

## Definition

Let $n,p$ be positive integers, let $1\le K\le n$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$ be observed vectors, and let $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_K\in\mathbb R^p$ be centers. A labeling is a vector $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in\{1,\ldots,K\}^n$, and its $k$th cluster is $C_k(z):=\{i:z_i=k\}$. For $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_p)\in\mathbb R^p$, set $\|v\|_2^2:=\sum_{j=1}^p v_j^2$. The K-means objective is

$$J(z,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_K):=\sum_{i=1}^n\|x_i-\mu_{z_i}\|_2^2=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k(z)}\|x_i-\mu_k\|_2^2.$$

An empty cluster contributes zero to the sum.

## Definition

Assume AC. Let $p\ge1$, $\mu\in\mathbb R^p$, and let $\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric positive definite, meaning $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$. Define the component function

$$\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma):=(2\pi)^{-p/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^p.$$

The component law is $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$, the $p$-dimensional normal law with mean $\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$. The separate local normalization result proves that $\phi_p$ is its Lebesgue density.

A finite $K$-component Gaussian mixture has an integer $K\ge1$, weights $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_K>0$ with $\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k=1$, means $\mu_k\in\mathbb R^p$, and symmetric positive-definite covariance matrices $\Sigma_k\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$. Its density is

$$f_\theta(x):=\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k\phi_p(x;\mu_k,\Sigma_k),$$

where $\theta=((\pi_k,\mu_k,\Sigma_k))_{k=1}^K$. For a positive integer $n$ and an ordered sample $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ modeled as conditionally independent observations from this mixture, define the likelihood $L(\theta;x_{1:n}):=\prod_{i=1}^n f_\theta(x_i)$ and log likelihood $\ell(\theta;x_{1:n}):=\sum_{i=1}^n\log f_\theta(x_i)$. The responsibility weight of component $k$ for observation $x_i$ is

$$\gamma_{ik}(\theta):=\frac{\pi_k\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_j\phi_p(x_i;\mu_j,\Sigma_j)}.$$

## Definition references

[[def-multivariate-normal-law]] — $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$ is the probability law whose scalar projections along $u\in\mathbb R^p$ are normal with mean $u^{\mathsf T}\mu$ and variance $u^{\mathsf T}\Sigma u$; AC supplies its stated construction.

[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] — covariance is the expectation of the product of centered coordinates.

[[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]] — $\det\Sigma$ is the determinant of the square matrix $\Sigma$.

[[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]] — $\Sigma^{-1}$ denotes the two-sided inverse, which exists for positive-definite $\Sigma$.

[[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] — real symmetric matrices admit orthonormal eigenbases; positive definiteness makes all eigenvalues positive.

[[thm-finite-gaussian-component-density-normalized]] — the displayed component function is normalized and is the Lebesgue density of $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$.

## Statement

Let $p\ge1$ and let $A_0,A_1\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric positive-definite matrices. For $0<t<1$ and $A_0\ne A_1$,

$$\log\det((1-t)A_0+tA_1)>(1-t)\log\det A_0+t\log\det A_1.$$

If $A_0=A_1$, equality holds. Thus $A\mapsto\log\det A$ is strictly concave on the positive-definite cone.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Symmetric positive-definite matrices $A_0,A_1\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ with $p\ge1$.

[F1] [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]: a real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F2] [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]: the determinant is the finite signed Leibniz sum; in particular $\det I=1$.

[F3] [[thm-determinant-differential-and-jacobis-formula]]: for invertible $A$, $D\det(A)[H]=\det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}H)$.

[F4] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: for $x>0$, $\log'(x)=1/x$.

[F5] [[thm-derivative-of-matrix-inversion]]: on the invertible locus, $D\operatorname{inv}(A)[H]=-A^{-1}HA^{-1}$.

[F6] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: derivatives of differentiable compositions are the compositions of the derivatives.

[F7] [[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]: $\operatorname{tr}(M)$ is the finite sum of diagonal entries of $M$.

[F8] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: if a real function is continuous on a closed interval and differentiable on its interior, its secant slope equals its derivative at some interior point.

## Proof
1.1 Put $H:=A_1-A_0$ and $A_s:=A_0+sH$ for $0\le s\le1$. For every nonzero $v$, $v^{\mathsf T}A_sv=(1-s)v^{\mathsf T}A_0v+s v^{\mathsf T}A_1v>0$, so each $A_s$ is symmetric positive definite. By [F1], all eigenvalues of $A_s$ are positive; hence $\det A_s>0$ and $g(s):=\log\det A_s$ is real and continuous on $[0,1]$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 On $0<s<1$, Jacobi's formula [F3], the scalar derivative [F4], and the chain rule [F6] give $g'(s)=\operatorname{tr}(A_s^{-1}H)$. [F3, F4, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Differentiate the expression in step 2.1 along the same affine path. The inverse derivative [F5] and linearity of the finite trace [F7] give $g''(s)=-\operatorname{tr}(A_s^{-1}H A_s^{-1}H)$. [F5, F6, F7, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F1], form the symmetric positive-definite inverse square root $A_s^{-1/2}$, and set $B:=A_s^{-1/2}HA_s^{-1/2}$. Since $H$ is symmetric, $B$ is symmetric; if $A_0\ne A_1$, then $H\ne0$ and invertibility of $A_s^{-1/2}$ gives $B\ne0$. Expanding the finite trace sum and interchanging its indices gives $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\operatorname{tr}(YX)$; applying this identity yields $\operatorname{tr}(A_s^{-1}HA_s^{-1}H)=\operatorname{tr}(B^2)=\sum_{i,j}B_{ij}^2>0$. Thus $g''(s)<0$ for every $0<s<1$. For any $0<a<b<1$, $g'$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$ because $g$ is twice differentiable on $(0,1)$. By [F8] applied to $g'$, there is $c\in(a,b)$ with $g'(b)-g'(a)=g''(c)(b-a)<0$. Hence $g'$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,1)$. [F1, F7, F8, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For $0<t<1$, step 1.1 shows that $g$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ and differentiable on $(0,1)$, so [F8] applies on both $[0,t]$ and $[t,1]$. Their secant slopes are $g'(a)$ and $g'(b)$ for some $a\in(0,t)$ and $b\in(t,1)$. Step 4.1 makes $g'$ strictly decreasing, so the first slope is strictly larger than the second; rearranging yields $g(t)>(1-t)g(0)+tg(1)$. If $A_0=A_1$, the path is constant and equality holds. [given, F8, step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

## Statement

Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix and let $H$ be a direction matrix. Then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)H).$$

If $A$ is invertible, then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}H).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Matrices $A,H\in M_n(\mathbb F)$, where $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and the real Fréchet derivative with the Frobenius norm. In the complex case the target is $\mathbb C$ viewed as a two-dimensional real normed space with modulus.

[A1] Matrix spaces include $n=0$. For that case only, use the local conventions $\det(\varnothing)=1$ and $\operatorname{adj}(\varnothing)=\varnothing$. The empty matrix has Frobenius norm and trace zero and is its own inverse. For $n\ge1$, determinant and adjugate have the published meanings below. [[def-matrix-space]], [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]], [[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]], [[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]

[L1] For $n\ge1$, determinant is the signed Leibniz sum of the $n!$ products $\prod_{j<n}a_{\sigma(j),j}$. [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]

[L2] That determinant is multilinear in its columns over every commutative ring. [[thm-leibniz-determinant-is-alternating-multilinear-and-normalized]]

[L3] The cofactor is $C_{ij}(A)=(-1)^{i+j}\det(A^{(i,j)})$ and $\operatorname{adj}(A)_{ji}=C_{ij}(A)$. When $n=1$, the deleted minor has determinant $1$. [[def-matrix-minors-cofactors-and-adjugate]]

[L4] Laplace expansion along column $j$ is $\det(B)=\sum_{i<n}b_{ij}C_{ij}(B)$. [[thm-laplace-cofactor-expansion]]

[L5] For every positive-sized square matrix, $A\operatorname{adj}(A)=\det(A)I_n$. [[thm-adjugate-identity-over-a-commutative-ring]]

[L6] Matrix multiplication is the entrywise finite-sum product, is associative and unital, and obeys the scalar laws. Over a field this agrees with the ring-matrix interface; invertibility means $A^{-1}A=AA^{-1}=I_n$. [[def-ring-matrix-product-identity-and-transpose]], [[thm-ring-matrix-arithmetic-laws]], [[prop-field-and-ring-matrix-interfaces-agree]], [[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]

[L7] Scalar modulus is multiplicative and satisfies the triangle inequality, including for real scalars. [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]

[L8] The Frobenius norm is $\|H\|_F=(\sum_{i,j}|h_{ij}|^2)^{1/2}$. The real Fréchet criterion is the normwise first-order remainder estimate; in a positive-dimensional source this is equivalently that the remainder after a bounded real-linear map, divided by $\|H\|_F$, tends to zero as $H\to0$, $H\ne0$. [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]], [[def-real-frechet-derivative-on-real-and-complex-matrix-spaces]]

[L9] Trace is the sum of the diagonal entries. [[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** expand all column perturbations and bound the terms of degree at least two uniformly in the direction.

1.1 For $n=0$, the domain is the zero vector space and the determinant is the constant $1$ by [A1]. Its derivative is the unique linear map from that space, namely zero; its Fréchet remainder vanishes identically. The adjugate product has trace zero, as does $A^{-1}H$, so both asserted formulas hold. Henceforth let $n\ge1$. [A1, L8, L9, given]

1.2 Write $A_j,H_j$ for the columns. For $S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, let $B_S$ have column $H_j$ if $j\in S$ and $A_j$ otherwise. By [L2], $$\det(A+H)=\sum_S\det(B_S)=\det(A)+L_A(H)+R_A(H),$$ where $L_A(H)=\sum_{j<n}\det(B_{\{j\}})$ and $R_A(H)=\sum_{|S|\ge2}\det(B_S)$. Expanding $B_{\{j\}}$ along column $j$ with [L4], its deleted-column minors are those of $A$, so $$L_A(H)=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{i<n}h_{ij}C_{ij}(A)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)H)$$ by [L3], [L6] and [L9]. This map is $\mathbb F$-linear and in particular real-linear. Each $|h_{ij}|\le\|H\|_F$ by [L8], so [L7] gives $|L_A(H)|\le(\sum_{i,j}|C_{ij}(A)|)\|H\|_F$; thus it is bounded. [L2, L3, L4, L6, L7, L8, L9, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Put $h=\|H\|_F$ and $M=\max(1,\|A\|_F)$. Every entry of $A$ has modulus at most $M$, and every entry of $H$ has modulus at most $h$. A Leibniz monomial of $B_S$ contains exactly $k=|S|$ entries from $H$ and $n-k$ from $A$, so [L1] and [L7] imply $$|\det(B_S)|\le n! M^{n-k}h^k.$$ For $0<h\le1$ and $k\ge2$, this is at most $n!M^n h^2$. There are at most $2^n$ subsets $S$, hence $$|R_A(H)|\le n!2^n M^n\|H\|_F^2.$$ When $n=1$, the remainder sum is empty and the same bound holds with remainder zero. Dividing by $\|H\|_F$ makes the bound tend to zero independently of the direction of $H$. The bounded real-linear map from step 1.2 therefore satisfies the full Fréchet criterion [L8], over both real and complex matrices, including every singular $A$. Consequently $D\det(A)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)H)$. [L1, L7, L8, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 If $A$ is invertible and $n\ge1$, multiply [L5] on the left by $A^{-1}$. By [L6], $$\operatorname{adj}(A)=\det(A)A^{-1}.$$ Substitute this into step 2.1 and take the scalar outside the finite diagonal sum [L9] to obtain $$D\det(A)[H]=\det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}H).$$ Step 1.1 already proves the same formula at the invertible empty matrix. No inverse is used in the general adjugate formula, so its singular-matrix scope is retained. [L5, L6, L9, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $A$ be invertible. Then the inversion map is real Fr\'echet differentiable
at $A$, and for every direction $H$,

$$D\operatorname{inv}(A)[H]=-A^{-1}HA^{-1}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An invertible matrix $A$ and a perturbation direction $H$.

[L1] Matrix differentials satisfy the product rule $d(AB)=dA\,B+A\,dB$ ([[prop-matrix-differentials-obey-sum-product-and-adjoint-rules]]).

[L2] Matrix real Fr\'echet differentiability is the normwise remainder estimate, including a zero-entry source ([[def-real-frechet-derivative-on-real-and-complex-matrix-spaces]]). The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean entry norm ([[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]).

[L3] The operator norm on finite-dimensional real or complex inner-product spaces bounds $\|Xv\|_2$ by $\|X\|_2\|v\|_2$ by rescaling a nonzero $v$ ([[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]). It is submultiplicative ([[cor-operator-norm-submultiplicative-and-t-star-t-identity]]). Singular-value formulas give $\|X\|_2\le\|X\|_F$ and unitary invariance of both norms ([[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]]); a singular value decomposition exists over both fields ([[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]).

[L4] For positive-sized real or complex matrices, determinant has the real Fr\'echet derivative $D\det(A)[K]=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)K)$ ([[thm-determinant-differential-and-jacobis-formula]]). Trace is the finite diagonal sum ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]). A positive-sized square matrix over a commutative ring is invertible exactly when its determinant is a unit ([[cor-square-matrix-invertible-iff-determinant-is-a-unit]]); in a field the units are exactly the nonzero elements ([[lem-field-is-a-commutative-ring]]). The ring and field matrix/inverse interfaces agree exactly ([[prop-field-and-ring-matrix-interfaces-agree]]). Scalar modulus is multiplicative and satisfies the triangle inequality ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $A$ has size zero, the unique empty matrix is its own inverse. Inversion is a map on the zero matrix space and its normwise remainder is identically zero; its unique real-linear derivative and $-A^{-1}HA^{-1}$ are both the empty zero matrix. Hence the full conclusion holds in that case. For the remainder let the size be $n\ge1$. [given, L2, algebra]

1.2 The norm estimates needed below hold over either field. Zero-domain cases have zero norm directly; in the following unit-vector argument the domain is nonzero. For compatible $X,Y$, applying [L3] to each column of $Y$ and summing squares gives $\|XY\|_F\le\|X\|_2\|Y\|_F$. For the right-hand estimate write $Y=U\Sigma V^*$ using [L3]. Unitary Frobenius invariance gives $\|XY\|_F=\|(XU)\Sigma\|_F$; multiplying columns by the singular values, each at most $\|Y\|_2$, gives $\|XY\|_F\le\|XU\|_F\|Y\|_2=\|X\|_F\|Y\|_2$. Thus also $\|XY\|_F\le\|X\|_F\|Y\|_F$. The operator triangle inequality follows by applying the vector triangle inequality at each unit vector and taking the maximum. [L2, L3, algebra]

1.3 Invertibility gives $\det A\ne0$ by [L4]. That supplier also supplies determinant's bounded first-order expansion. Explicitly, $|\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)K)|\le C_A\|K\|_F$, where $C_A:=\sum_{i,j}|\operatorname{adj}(A)_{ij}|$, by the finite trace formula, scalar triangle inequality and $|K_{ij}|\le\|K\|_F$. Hence $|\det(A+K)-\det A|\to0$ as $\|K\|_F\to0$ by the normwise remainder estimate. Choose $\delta>0$ so that this difference is less than $|\det A|/2$ when $\|K\|_F<\delta$. Then $\det(A+K)\ne0$, and [L4] makes $A+K$ invertible. The inverse domain is therefore open, over both real and complex matrices. For such $K$, the inverse identities give $(A+K)^{-1}-A^{-1}=-A^{-1}K(A+K)^{-1}$ and consequently $(A+K)^{-1}-A^{-1}+A^{-1}KA^{-1}=A^{-1}KA^{-1}K(A+K)^{-1}$. [given, L2, L4, algebra]

2.1 Put $a:=\|A^{-1}\|_2$ and shrink $\delta$ so that $a\|K\|_F\le1/2$ whenever $\|K\|_F<\delta$. Taking operator norms in the first inverse identity, using [L3] and step 1.2, gives $\|(A+K)^{-1}\|_2\le a+a\|K\|_F\|(A+K)^{-1}\|_2$, hence $\|(A+K)^{-1}\|_2\le2a$. For the second identity write its remainder as $A^{-1}(KA^{-1})(K(A+K)^{-1})$. Step 1.2 bounds its Frobenius norm by $a(\|K\|_F a)(\|K\|_F\,2a)=2a^3\|K\|_F^2$. The candidate $K\mapsto-A^{-1}KA^{-1}$ is real-linear and has Frobenius bound $a^2\|K\|_F$, again by step 1.2. The remainder estimate is therefore $o(\|K\|_F)$ and proves the full real Fr\'echet derivative by [L2]. [L2, L3, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Differentiating the identity $A\,A^{-1}=I$ and using the product rule [L1] gives $H\,A^{-1}+A\,D\operatorname{inv}(A)[H]=0$. Left-multiplying by $A^{-1}$ recovers $D\operatorname{inv}(A)[H]=-A^{-1}HA^{-1}$, which is the formula claimed in the statement; step 1.1 handles the empty matrix as well. [L1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

## Statement

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Reals $a < b$ and a function $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$.

[L1] Cauchy's mean value theorem ([[thm-cauchy-mean-value]]): for $f, g$ continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ there is $c \in (a,b)$ with $\bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)g'(c) = \bigl(g(b)-g(a)\bigr)f'(c)$.

[L2] The identity $x \mapsto x$ is continuous at every point of any $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ ([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], claim 5).

[L3] The identity $g$ on $[a,b]$ is differentiable at every $c \in [a,b]$ with $g'(c) = 1$: with $a < b$ the set $[a,b]$ is order-convex with at least two elements, so every one of its points is a limit point of it ([[def-derivative]], [[def-interval]]); and the difference quotient of $g$ at $c$ is $(x - c)/(x - c) = 1$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ with $x \ne c$, a constant function, whose limit at $c$ is $1$ ([[def-function-limit]], [[def-derivative]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Define $g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ by $g(x) := x$. [construct]

2.1 $g$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ by [L2]; it is differentiable at every $c \in (a,b)$ with $g'(c) = 1$ by [L3]; and $g(b) - g(a) = b - a$. [step 1.1, L2, L3]

3.1 By step 2.1 the pair $f, g$ satisfies every hypothesis of [L1], so there is $c \in (a,b)$ with $\bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)g'(c) = \bigl(g(b)-g(a)\bigr)f'(c)$. Substituting $g'(c) = 1$ and $g(b)-g(a) = b-a$ gives $f(b) - f(a) = f'(c)(b-a)$. [step 2.1, L1] ∎

## Remarks

- **The geometric reading, and what it is not.** The conclusion says that some tangent line is parallel to the chord from $(a, f(a))$ to $(b, f(b))$. It does not say which one, it does not say there is only one, and it says nothing at all about $f$ between the endpoints beyond the hypotheses. Every use of the theorem on this page is a use of the equation, never of the picture.

- **Why this is a corollary and not the primitive statement.** [[thm-cauchy-mean-value]] is proved from [[thm-rolle]] with one auxiliary function, and this statement is that theorem at $g(x) = x$; deriving it the other way round, from this statement to Cauchy's, is also possible but needs an auxiliary function of its own, so nothing is saved. What matters is that both rest on Rolle, and Rolle on the extreme value theorem.

- **The two hypotheses are on different sets on purpose.** Continuity is asked for on the closed interval and differentiability only on the open one, so nothing at all is required of the difference quotients at $a$ and at $b$. Weakening the continuity in step with the differentiability, so that both are asked for on $(a,b)$ only, destroys the theorem, which is exactly what [[cex-mean-value-theorem-fails-without-continuity-at-the-endpoints]] shows on the companion page.

## Statement

Let $n,p,K$ be positive integers, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_K\in\mathbb R^p$, and fix positive weights $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_K$ with $\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k=1$. Put $d_{ik}:=\|x_i-\mu_k\|_2^2$, $d_i^*:=\min_{1\le k\le K}d_{ik}$, and $M_i:=\{k:d_{ik}=d_i^*\}$. For every $\sigma>0$, define the normalized soft-assignment weights

$$\rho_{ik}^{(\sigma)}:=\frac{\pi_k\exp(-d_{ik}/(2\sigma^2))}{\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_j\exp(-d_{ij}/(2\sigma^2))}$$

and the finite-data objective

$$\Psi_\sigma:=-2\sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n\log\left(\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k\exp(-d_{ik}/(2\sigma^2))\right).$$

As $\sigma\downarrow0$, for each $i$ and $k$,

$$\rho_{ik}^{(\sigma)}\longrightarrow\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\pi_k}{\sum_{j\in M_i}\pi_j},&k\in M_i,\\[6pt]0,&k\notin M_i,\end{cases}$$

and

$$\Psi_\sigma\longrightarrow\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^*=\min_{z\in\{1,\ldots,K\}^n}\sum_{i=1}^n d_{i,z_i}.$$

Thus a unique nearest center receives limiting weight one, while tied nearest centers divide limiting weight in proportion to their fixed mixture weights. This is a fixed-parameter finite-data limit and asserts no convergence of EM iterates.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Finite positive integers $n,p,K$, fixed vectors $x_i,\mu_k\in\mathbb R^p$, and fixed positive weights $\pi_k$ summing to one.

[A1] All indices range over finite sets and all data, centers, and weights are fixed; no probability-space assumption or choice axiom is used.

[F1] [[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]]: $\exp(u)\to0$ as $u\to-\infty$.

## Proof
1.1 Fix $i$ and write $R_i(\sigma):=\sum_{k\in M_i}\pi_k+\sum_{k\notin M_i}\pi_k\exp(-(d_{ik}-d_i^*)/(2\sigma^2))$. Every difference in the second sum is strictly positive, so each exponential there tends to zero by [F1], since its exponent tends to $-\infty$ as $\sigma\downarrow0$; the sum is finite. Hence $R_i(\sigma)\to\sum_{k\in M_i}\pi_k>0$. [given, A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 Factoring $\exp(-d_i^*/(2\sigma^2))$ from the denominator of $\rho_{ik}^{(\sigma)}$ gives $\rho_{ik}^{(\sigma)}=\pi_k\exp(-(d_{ik}-d_i^*)/(2\sigma^2))/R_i(\sigma)$. If $k\in M_i$, its exponential is one and the limit is $\pi_k/\sum_{j\in M_i}\pi_j$; if $k\notin M_i$, its positive distance gap makes the numerator tend to zero while the denominator tends to a positive number. This proves the stated responsibility limits. [given, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The same factorization gives $-2\sigma^2\log\sum_k\pi_k e^{-d_{ik}/(2\sigma^2)}=d_i^*-2\sigma^2\log R_i(\sigma)$. The nearest terms give $R_i(\sigma)\ge\sum_{k\in M_i}\pi_k>0$, while $d_{ik}-d_i^*\ge0$ and $\sum_k\pi_k=1$ give $R_i(\sigma)\le1$. Thus $\log R_i(\sigma)$ stays between two finite constants, so the second term tends to zero. Summing over the finite set of observations gives $\Psi_\sigma\to\sum_i d_i^*$. [given, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For each labeling $z\in\{1,\ldots,K\}^n$, $d_{i,z_i}\ge d_i^*$ for every $i$, so $\sum_i d_{i,z_i}\ge\sum_i d_i^*$. Define $z_i:=\min M_i$, which exists because $M_i$ is a nonempty finite subset of $\{1,\ldots,K\}$. This labeling attains equality, proving the displayed minimum without any choice principle. [given, A1, step 2.2, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

$$\exp(x)\to+\infty\quad(x\to+\infty),\qquad \exp(x)\to0\quad(x\to-\infty),$$
and the range of $\exp$ is contained in $(0,\infty)$ and is unbounded above with infimum $0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The exponential series.

[L1] For $x\ge0$, every exponential-series term is nonnegative, so its sum dominates every partial sum and in particular $\exp(x)\ge1+x$ ([[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]]).

[L2] $\exp(-x)=1/\exp(x)>0$ ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]).

[L3] Finite and infinite limits of functions at infinity have the quantified definitions in [[def-limits-at-infinity]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Given a real $M$, every $x>\max\{0,M-1\}$ satisfies $\exp(x)\ge1+x>M$. Hence $\exp(x)\to+\infty$.  [L1, L3]

1.2 Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $X>0$ with $1+X>1/\varepsilon$. If $x<-X$, then $-x>X$, so [L1] gives $\exp(-x)\ge1-x>1+X>1/\varepsilon$; [L2] yields $0<\exp(x)<\varepsilon$.  [L1, L2, choose]

2.1 The range assertions follow from positivity and the two limit conclusions.  [step 1.1, step 1.2, L2] ∎

## Definition

**Input.** Let $n,p$ be positive integers, let $1\le K\le n$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$, and supply initial centers $\mu_1^{(0)},\ldots,\mu_K^{(0)}\in\mathbb R^p$.

**Initialization.** Assign each $x_i$ to a nearest initial center, choosing the smallest center index in a tie. Denote these labels by $z_i^{(0)}$.

**Iteration.** For $t=0,1,2,\ldots$:

1. With the current centers fixed, assign each $x_i$ to a nearest center. If its current label $z_i^{(t)}$ is among the nearest-center indices, retain $z_i^{(t)}$; otherwise choose the smallest nearest-center index. Call the resulting labels $z_i^{(t+1)}$.
2. For each nonempty cluster $C_k^{(t+1)}:=\{i:z_i^{(t+1)}=k\}$, set
   $$\mu_k^{(t+1)}:=\frac{1}{|C_k^{(t+1)}|}\sum_{i\in C_k^{(t+1)}}x_i.$$
   If $C_k^{(t+1)}$ is empty, set $\mu_k^{(t+1)}:=\mu_k^{(t)}$.
3. If both $z^{(t+1)}=z^{(t)}$ and $\mu^{(t+1)}=\mu^{(t)}$, return these labels and centers. Otherwise continue with the updated labels and centers.

The procedure makes no global-minimization claim. Its termination under these tie rules is proved separately.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $p\ge1$, let $\mu\in\mathbb R^p$, and let $\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric positive definite. Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_p$ be independent standard normal random variables, let $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_p)^{\mathsf T}$, and set $X=\mu+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$, where $\Sigma^{1/2}$ is the symmetric positive-definite square root. Then the law of $X$ has Lebesgue density

$$\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma)=(2\pi)^{-p/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^p.$$

In particular, $\phi_p$ is nonnegative and $\int_{\mathbb R^p}\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma)\,dx=1$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume AC, $p\ge1$, a mean $\mu\in\mathbb R^p$, and a real symmetric positive-definite covariance matrix $\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Here AC supplies the independent normal coordinates in the multivariate-normal construction and countable choice for the two cited Lebesgue change-of-variables results.

[F1] [[def-finite-gaussian-mixture]]: for SPD $\Sigma$, $\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma)$ is the displayed nonnegative formula using $\det\Sigma$ and $\Sigma^{-1}$.

[F2] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: $N(0,1)$ has Lebesgue density $\phi_1(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$ with total mass one.

[F3] [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: under AC, $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$ can be realized as $\mu+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates.

[F4] [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]: a finite family of independent random elements has joint law equal to the product of its marginal laws.

[F5] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: nonnegative measurable functions on sigma-finite product spaces have measurable sections and equal iterated and product integrals.

[F6] [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]]: under countable choice, product Lebesgue measure on finite-dimensional Euclidean factors agrees with Euclidean Lebesgue measure on Borel sets.

[F7] [[thm-measure-uniqueness-on-a-sigma-finite-pi-system]]: two measures agreeing on a generating pi-system and on an increasing finite-measure exhaustion from that system agree on the generated sigma-algebra.

[F8] [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]: a real symmetric endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F9] [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]: assuming countable choice, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $T:U\to V$ between open subsets of $\mathbb R^p$ satisfies $\int_V f(y)\,dy=\int_U f(T(x))|\det DT(x)|\,dx$ for every nonnegative Lebesgue-measurable $f$.

[F10] [[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]]: assuming countable choice, an invertible linear map with matrix $A$ scales Lebesgue measure by $|\det A|$.

[F11] [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]], [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]], [[thm-determinant-of-transpose]], and [[thm-determinant-of-a-triangular-matrix]]: determinant is the Leibniz sum, is multiplicative and transpose-invariant, and equals the product of diagonal entries for triangular matrices; $\det I=1$.

[F12] [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]]: AC implies countable choice, so the countable-choice hypotheses of [F6], [F9], and [F10] hold.

## Proof
1.1 By [F8], write $\Sigma=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p)U^{\mathsf T}$ with $U^{\mathsf T}U=I$. For a unit eigenvector $u_j$, $\lambda_j=u_j^{\mathsf T}\Sigma u_j>0$. Define $A:=U\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{\lambda_1},\ldots,\sqrt{\lambda_p})U^{\mathsf T}$. Its eigenvalues are the positive numbers $\sqrt{\lambda_j}$, so it is symmetric positive definite and invertible; in this basis, both $A^2$ and $\Sigma$ have diagonal entries $\lambda_j$, and both $A^{-2}$ and $\Sigma^{-1}$ have diagonal entries $1/\lambda_j$. By determinant multiplicativity and transpose invariance, $(\det U)^2=\det(U^{\mathsf T}U)=\det I=1$. Applying multiplicativity to the displayed diagonalizations and the triangular determinant formula to the diagonal matrices gives $\det\Sigma=(\det U)^2\prod_j\lambda_j=\prod_j\lambda_j$ and $\det A=(\det U)^2\prod_j\sqrt{\lambda_j}=\prod_j\sqrt{\lambda_j}=\sqrt{\det\Sigma}>0$. [given, F8, F11, construct, algebra]

1.2 By [F2] and [F4], the joint law of $Z$ is the product of its standard-normal marginals. Define $g(y):=\prod_{j=1}^p\phi_1(y_j)=(2\pi)^{-p/2}e^{-\|y\|_2^2/2}$. Tonelli [F5] and the product-measure identity [F6] give $\int_{\mathbb R^p}g\,d\lambda_p=\prod_{j=1}^p\int_{\mathbb R}\phi_1\,d\lambda_1=1$ and, for every Borel rectangle $R=\prod_{j=1}^p B_j$, $\int_R g\,d\lambda_p=\prod_{j=1}^p\int_{B_j}\phi_1\,d\lambda_1$. Thus $g\,d\lambda_p$ and the product law of $Z$ are probability measures agreeing on rectangles. The rational half-open rectangles form a generating pi-system; $(-N,N]^p$ is an increasing exhaustion from it, and the common rectangle values make their measures equal and finite on every such box. Hence [F7] identifies the measures. AC supplies countable choice for the product-Lebesgue identity [F6]. [A1, F2, F4, F5, F6, F7, F12, algebra]

2.1 Let $T(y)=\mu+Ay$. By step 1.1, $A$ is invertible, so $T$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^p$ with $|\det DT|=\det A$. The linear measure-scaling result [F10] confirms this is the Lebesgue volume factor. The displayed function $\phi_p$ is continuous and positive, so $f(x)=\mathbf1_E(x)\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma)$ is nonnegative Borel for every Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^p$. AC supplies the countable-choice assumption of [F9] by [F12]. Apply [F9] to $f$ and the change of variables by $T$ to obtain $\int_E\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma)\,dx=\int_{T^{-1}(E)}\phi_p(T(y);\mu,\Sigma)\det A\,dy.$ For $x=T(y)$, $x-\mu=Ay$ and $A^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}A=A A^{-2}A=I$. Thus the exponent in [F1] becomes $-\|y\|_2^2/2$, while $(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\det A=1$ by step 1.1. Hence $\phi_p(T(y);\mu,\Sigma)\det A=g(y)$. The last integral equals $\int_{T^{-1}(E)}g(y)\,dy=\mathbb P(X\in E)$ by step 1.2 and the definition of $X$. Thus $\phi_p$ is the Lebesgue density of $X$. [A1, F1, F9, F10, F12, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By [F3], $X$ has law $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$. Step 2.1 identifies that law on every Borel set with integration against $\phi_p$; taking $E=\mathbb R^p$ gives $\int_{\mathbb R^p}\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma)\,dx=\mathbb P(X\in\mathbb R^p)=1$. Nonnegativity follows directly from [F1] and $\det\Sigma>0$ in step 1.1. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, positive integers $m,n$, and the identification $\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n$.

[L1] The Borel sigma-algebra on $\mathbb R^{m+n}$ is $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)$. ([[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]])

[L2] The product measure on sigma-finite spaces exists and satisfies the rectangle formula. ([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]])

[L3] Assuming countable choice, Lebesgue measure of a box is the product of its side lengths. ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]])

[L5] Two measures that agree on a sigma-finite generating pi-system agree on the generated sigma-algebra. ([[thm-measure-uniqueness-on-a-sigma-finite-pi-system]])

[A1] Rational half-open boxes, together with the empty set, form a generating pi-system for $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n})$. The increasing boxes $Q_N=(-N,N]^{m+n}$ exhaust the space and have finite measure for both measures in the Statement.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $d=m,n$, the cubes $(-N,N]^d$ exhaust $\mathbb R^d$ and have finite measure by [L3], so the sigma-finite product theorem [L2] applies. Let $Q=\prod_{i<m+n}(a_i,b_i]$ be a rational half-open box. Split it as $Q=A \times B$ with $A \subseteq \mathbb R^m$ and $B \subseteq \mathbb R^n$. Then the rectangle formula of [L2] and [L3] give $$ (\lambda_m \times \lambda_n)(Q) = \lambda_m(A)\lambda_n(B) = \prod_{i<m+n}(b_i-a_i) = \lambda_{m+n}(Q). $$ [L2, L3]

2.1 Each $Q_N$ from [A1] has finite $\lambda_{m+n}$-measure by [L3], and finite product measure by [L2] and [L3]; step 1.1 shows these values agree. The same step gives agreement on the whole generating pi-system, while [L1] identifies its generated sigma-algebra with $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n})$. Therefore [L5] implies $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n=\lambda_{m+n}$ on every Borel set. [A1, L1, L2, L3, L5, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Measures $\mu,\nu$, a generating pi-system $\mathcal P$, and an increasing finite-measure exhaustion $(P_n)$ as in the Statement.

[L1] Finite measures agreeing on a generating pi-system and on the whole space are equal ([[lem-finite-measure-uniqueness-on-a-pi-system]]).

[L2] Measures are continuous from below ([[thm-continuity-from-below-for-measures]]).

[L3] A pi-system is closed under binary intersections ([[def-pi-system]]).

[L4] For a measurable $P_n$, the set function $A\mapsto\mu(A\cap P_n)$ is a measure on the original sigma-algebra ([[prop-restriction-is-a-measure]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $n$ and define $\mu_n(A):=\mu(A\cap P_n)$ and $\nu_n(A):=\nu(A\cap P_n)$ on $\mathcal A$. By [L4] these are measures, and their total masses are the common finite value $\mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)$. [given, L4]

1.2 If $Q\in\mathcal P$, then $Q\cap P_n\in\mathcal P$ by [L3], so $\mu_n(Q)=\mu(Q\cap P_n)=\nu(Q\cap P_n)=\nu_n(Q)$. [given, L3]

2.1 The finite uniqueness lemma applied to steps 1.1 and 1.2 gives $\mu(A\cap P_n)=\nu(A\cap P_n)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and every $n$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L1]

3.1 For fixed $A$, the sets $A\cap P_n$ increase to $A$; continuity from below and step 2.1 give $\mu(A)=\sup_n\mu(A\cap P_n)=\sup_n\nu(A\cap P_n)=\nu(A)$. Thus the measures agree everywhere. [step 2.1, L2] ∎

## Statement

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $n \ge 1$, the Axiom of Countable Choice, a linear map $T$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with matrix $A$, and a set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

[L1] An invertible linear map carries Borel sets to Borel sets, and there is a strictly positive real $c(T) = \lambda_n\big(T[(0,1]^n]\big)$ with $\lambda_n(T[E]) = c(T)\lambda_n(E)$ for every Borel $E$, with $c(S\circ T) = c(S)c(T)$ and $c(\mathrm{id})=1$ ([[thm-invertible-linear-images-scale-lebesgue-measure-by-a-constant]]).

[L2] $\lambda_n\big(D_p(c)[(0,1]^n]\big) = |c| = |\det D_p(c)|$ and $\lambda_n\big(E_{pq}[(0,1]^n]\big) = 1 = |\det E_{pq}|$ ([[lem-coordinate-scalings-and-permutations-scale-the-unit-cube-by-the-absolute-determinant]]).

[L3] For $n \ge 2$ a shear satisfies $\lambda_n\big(T_{ij}(t)[(0,1]^n]\big) = 1 = |\det T_{ij}(t)|$ ([[lem-shear-images-of-the-unit-cube-have-lebesgue-measure-one]]).

[L4] Every proper linear subspace $W \subsetneq \mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(W) = 0$ ([[thm-affine-hyperplanes-and-proper-subspaces-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]]).

[L5] A Lipschitz self-map of $\mathbb{R}^n$ carries a set of Lebesgue outer measure zero to a Lebesgue measurable set of measure zero ([[lem-lipschitz-images-of-lebesgue-null-sets-are-lebesgue-null]], [[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]).

[L6] $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E = H\cup W$ for an $F_\sigma$ set $H$ and a set $W$ with $\lambda_n^*(W)=0$ ([[thm-littlewood-characterisations-of-lebesgue-measurability]], condition 4; [[def-g-delta-and-f-sigma-in-a-topological-space]]).

[L7] Assuming countable choice, $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure on $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]) and every Borel set is Lebesgue measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]], [[def-measure]]).

[F1] Every invertible matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ is a finite product of elementary matrices, the identity being the empty product ([[thm-invertible-matrices-factor-into-elementary-matrices]]), and every elementary matrix is invertible ([[cor-elementary-matrices-are-invertible]], [[def-elementary-matrix]]).

[F2] For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring, $\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)$ ([[thm-determinant-multiplicative]], [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]], [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), and a triangular matrix has determinant the product of its diagonal entries ([[thm-determinant-of-a-triangular-matrix]]).

[F3] For every $n\ge1$ and every real matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$, $A$ is invertible if and only if $\det(A)\ne0$ ([[thm-real-square-matrix-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]).

[F4] For every linear $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ there is a unique matrix $A$ with $(Lh)_i=\sum_{j<m}a_{ij}h_j$, and there is $K\ge0$ with $\|Lh\|_2\le K\|h\|_2$ for every $h$ ([[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]], [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

[F5] For a linear map $T:V\to W$, $\operatorname{im}T:=\{T(v):v\in V\}$ ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]), and it is a linear subspace ([[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]]).

[F6] Every product with one factor $0$ and the other $\pm\infty$ is left undefined in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]).

[F7] Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$; if $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-induction-principle]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Suppose $\det A = 0$. Then $\operatorname{im}T$ is a proper linear subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$: were $T$ surjective, each standard vector $e_i$ would be $T(v_i)$ for some $v_i$, finitely many instantiations, and the matrix $B$ with $b_{ji} := (v_i)_j$ would satisfy $(AB)_{ki} = \sum_j a_{kj}(v_i)_j = (Tv_i)_k = (e_i)_k$, so $AB = I_n$ and $\det A\,\det B = \det I_n = 1$, contradicting $\det A = 0$. [F2, F3, F4, F5]

1.2 $T$ is Lipschitz, since $\lVert Tx - Ty\rVert_2 = \lVert T(x-y)\rVert_2 \le K\lVert x-y\rVert_2$ for a real $K \ge 0$. [F4]

1.3 Every elementary matrix $M$ of $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ satisfies $c(M) = |\det M|$: at $n=1$ the only elementary matrices are the scalings $D_0(c)$, and for $n \ge 2$ the three types are the scalings, the transpositions and the shears, whose unit-cube images have the measures $|c|$, $1$ and $1$, matching $|\det|$ in each case. [L1, L2, L3, F1]

2.1 Suppose $\det A \ne 0$, so $A$ is invertible and factors as a finite product $M_1\cdots M_r$ of elementary matrices, each invertible. Multiplicativity of $c$ and of the determinant then give $c(T) = \prod_{s}c(M_s) = \prod_s|\det M_s| = |\det A|$ by induction on $r$, the empty product giving $c(\mathrm{id}) = 1 = |\det I_n|$. [step 1.1, step 1.3, L1, F1, F2, F3, F7]

2.2 For $\det A = 0$, step 1.1 makes $\operatorname{im}T$ a proper linear subspace, hence Lebesgue null; every $T[E]$ is a subset of it, so completeness makes $T[E]$ Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$, which is claim 2; stating it as a product would require the undefined $0\cdot(+\infty)$ when $\lambda_n(E)=+\infty$. [step 1.1, L4, L7, F6]

 3.1 For $\det A \ne 0$ and $E$ Lebesgue measurable, write $E = H\cup W$ with $H$ an $F_\sigma$ set, hence Borel, and $\lambda_n^*(W) = 0$; then $T[E] = T[H]\cup T[W]$, where $T[H]$ is Borel and $T[W]$ is Lebesgue measurable of measure $0$ by step 1.2 and the Lipschitz lemma, so $T[E]$ is measurable. Since $H \subseteq E$ and $E\setminus H \subseteq W$, and $T[H]\subseteq T[E]$ with $T[E]\setminus T[H] \subseteq T[W]$, both pairs differ by null sets, so $\lambda_n(E) = \lambda_n(H)$ and $\lambda_n(T[E]) = \lambda_n(T[H]) = c(T)\lambda_n(H) = |\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$, which is claim 1; claim 2 is step 2.2. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, L1, L5, L6, L7] ∎

## Statement

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A fixed matrix $A\in M_n(R)$ and a variable matrix $B\in M_n(R)$.

[L1] Determinant is the unique normalized alternating column-multilinear matrix function ([[thm-determinant-is-the-unique-normalized-alternating-multilinear-function]]).

[L2] Every alternating column-multilinear $F$ satisfies $F(B)=F(I_n)\det(B)$ ([[lem-rigidity-of-alternating-multilinear-matrix-functions]]).

[L3] Matrix multiplication is associative, distributive and unital ([[thm-ring-matrix-arithmetic-laws]]).

[L4] Determinant is defined for every square matrix over the commutative ring ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Define $F(B):=\det(AB)$. Each column of $AB$ is $A$ times the corresponding column of $B$, so distributivity makes $F$ column-multilinear; equal columns of $B$ give equal columns of $AB$, so $F$ is alternating. [L1, L2, L3, L4]

2.1 Since $AI_n=A$, one has $F(I_n)=\det(A)$. [step 1.1, L3, L4]

3.1 Apply [L2] to $F$: $\det(AB)=F(B)=F(I_n)\det(B)=\det(A)\det(B)$. Neither matrix was assumed invertible. [step 2.1, L2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every $n\ge1$, every commutative ring $R$, and every $A\in M_n(R)$,
$$\det(A^{\mathsf T})=\det(A).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A square matrix $A=(a_{ij})$ over a commutative ring.

[L1] Determinant is the Leibniz sum over permutations ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

[L2] Transpose satisfies $(A^{\mathsf T})_{ij}=a_{ji}$ ([[def-ring-matrix-product-identity-and-transpose]]).

[L3] Sign is a homomorphism into $\{1,-1\}$, so $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma^{-1})=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ ([[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]).

[L4] A finite sum may be reindexed by a bijection ([[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Substituting [L2] into [L1] gives $\det(A^{\mathsf T})=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{i,\sigma(i)}$. [L1, L2]

2.1 Reindex the sum by $\tau=\sigma^{-1}$ and the product by $j=\sigma(i)$. Commutativity and [L3] turn the expression into $\sum_{\tau\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)\prod_{j<n}a_{\tau(j),j}=\det(A)$. [step 1.1, L3, L4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A triangular $n\times n$ matrix $A$ over a commutative ring.

[L1] Upper triangular means $a_{ij}=0$ for $i>j$, while lower triangular means $a_{ij}=0$ for $i<j$ ([[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]).

[L2] Determinant is the sum of the signed products $\prod_i a_{\sigma(i),i}$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

[L3] The identity permutation has sign $1$ ([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For an upper triangular matrix, a nonzero Leibniz term requires $\sigma(i)\le i$ for every $i$. A permutation with these inequalities is the identity: starting at $i=0$ and proceeding upward, bijectivity forces $\sigma(i)=i$. Thus every nonidentity term contains a zero entry. [L1, L2, L3]

2.1 The identity term has sign $1$ and equals $\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}$, so it is the whole determinant. [step 1.1, L2, L3]

3.1 For a lower triangular matrix the same argument uses $\sigma(i)\ge i$ and proceeds downward, again forcing the identity. The argument includes $n=1$ and makes no cancellation assumption, so zero divisors and the zero ring cause no exception. [step 2.1, L1, L2] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] AC supplies a choice function on a set of nonempty sets. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F2] Countable choice is selection from an omega-indexed nonempty family. [[def-countable-choice]].

[F3] DC requires a serial path starting at a prescribed point. [[def-dependent-choice]].

[F4] A given self-map and initial point have a uniquely specified natural-number iterate sequence. [[thm-recursion]].

## Proof

**Given:** Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

1.1 For an omega-indexed family $(A_n)$ of nonempty sets, its image $\mathcal S=\{A_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ is a set of nonempty sets. By [F1] choose $c$ with $c(A)\in A$ for every $A\in\mathcal S$. Then $b(n)=c(A_n)$ is a function and $b(n)\in A_n$, which is [F2]. Repeated sets use the same selected value and cause no ambiguity. For an empty index family the empty function already suffices; singleton fibers force their unique value. [F1, F2]

1.2 For the stated serial R, every fiber $R[x]=\{y\in X:xRy\}$ is nonempty. AC applied to the set of all these fibers gives c with $c(R[x])\in R[x]$. Define the self-map $s(x)=c(R[x])$ on X. No recursively changing choice is being assumed: s is now one fixed function chosen from a fixed set of nonempty fibers. It satisfies $xRs(x)$ for every x. [F1, F3]

2.1 Apply [F4] to X, the prescribed a and s to obtain $x_0=a$ and $x_{n+1}=s(x_n)$ for every natural n. The defining property of s gives $x_nRx_{n+1}$, precisely [F3]. If X has one element and R is serial, this is its constant sequence. Empty X is excluded by the prescribed a. The uses of AC are exactly the two fixed-family selections in steps 1.1 and 1.2; recursion itself requires no further choice. This proves the two implications from AC, not either converse. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F3, F4] ∎

## Statement

Let $n,p$ be positive integers, let $1\le K\le n$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$, and supply any initial centers in $(\mathbb R^p)^K$. The tie-sensitive Lloyd algorithm defined on this page terminates after finitely many iterations. At each fixed-center assignment, the K-means objective does not increase, and it strictly decreases if any label changes. At each center update, the objective does not increase, and it strictly decreases if a nonempty-cluster center changes. At termination each label is a nearest-center label under the stated retention rule, and every nonempty-cluster center is its sample mean; no global-minimum conclusion is made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite data and initial centers in the Statement, the K-means objective $J$, and the specified Lloyd iteration.

[F1] [[def-k-means-objective]]: $J(z,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_K)=\sum_{i=1}^n\|x_i-\mu_{z_i}\|_2^2$; an empty cluster contributes zero.

[F2] [[alg-lloyd-k-means]]: an assignment retains its current label when that label is among the nearest centers, otherwise it chooses the smallest nearest-center index; every nonempty cluster center is replaced by its sample mean and an empty-cluster center is unchanged.

[F3] [[thm-least-squares-solutions-and-normal-equation]]: for a linear map $T$ between finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, $x$ minimizes $\|Tx-b\|$ exactly when $T^*(Tx-b)=0$; minimizers exist and form one minimizer plus $\ker T$.

## Proof
1.1 Fix the current centers. For each observation, the old label is one of the available centers, so choosing a nearest center cannot increase its squared distance. If the label changes, its new distance is strictly smaller: an equal-distance tie would retain the old label by [F2]. Summing the pointwise inequalities gives nonincrease of $J$, strict when any label changes. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Fix a nonempty cluster $C$ and set $T(u)=(u)_{i\in C}$ from $\mathbb R^p$ to $(\mathbb R^p)^C$, with product inner product, and $b=(x_i)_{i\in C}$. For $u,v\in\mathbb R^p$, $\langle Tu,Tv\rangle=|C|\langle u,v\rangle$, so $T^*T=|C|I$; also $\langle Tu,b\rangle=\langle u,\sum_{i\in C}x_i\rangle$, so $T^*b=\sum_{i\in C}x_i$. Minimizing $\|Tu-b\|$ is equivalent to minimizing its square, since squaring is increasing on nonnegative reals. Thus [F3] gives the unique minimizer $\bar x_C=|C|^{-1}\sum_{i\in C}x_i$; uniqueness follows because $T$ is injective for nonempty $C$. Replacing a center by this mean cannot increase the cluster contribution and strictly decreases it if the old center differed. Empty clusters contribute zero and retain their centers. [given, F1, F3, construct, algebra]

2.1 A nonterminal iteration changes either the labels or at least one nonempty center. By steps 1.1 and 1.2, its full assignment-and-center update therefore strictly decreases $J$. After every center update, the nonempty centers are the means for that labeling, so the resulting objective value is determined by the labeling alone; empty centers do not affect it. A labeling cannot recur after a nonterminal update, because its objective value would then repeat despite strict decrease. There are only $K^n$ labelings, so only finitely many nonterminal iterations are possible and the algorithm terminates. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 At termination the labels and centers are unchanged by the next iteration. The assignment rule therefore certifies that each label is nearest under the retention convention, while the center update certifies that every nonempty-cluster center is its sample mean. This is the stated coordinatewise fixed point. [F2, step 2.1] ∎

## Definition

**Inputs.** Assume AC. Supply positive integers $n,p,K$, observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$ whose affine span is $\mathbb R^p$ (equivalently, no nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$ has $v^{\mathsf T}x_i$ constant over all $i$), an initial finite Gaussian mixture parameter $\theta_0=((\pi_k^{(0)},\mu_k^{(0)},\Sigma_k^{(0)}))_{k=1}^K$ in the domain of the finite-mixture definition, and a positive integer $T$.

**Procedure.** For $t=0,1,\ldots,T-1$, compute the responsibilities

$$\gamma_{ik}^{(t)}:=\frac{\pi_k^{(t)}\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k^{(t)},\Sigma_k^{(t)})}{\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_j^{(t)}\phi_p(x_i;\mu_j^{(t)},\Sigma_j^{(t)})},\qquad N_k^{(t)}:=\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_{ik}^{(t)}.$$

Then make the exact updates

$$\pi_k^{(t+1)}:=\frac{N_k^{(t)}}{n},\qquad \mu_k^{(t+1)}:=\frac{1}{N_k^{(t)}}\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_{ik}^{(t)}x_i,$$

$$\Sigma_k^{(t+1)}:=\frac{1}{N_k^{(t)}}\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_{ik}^{(t)}(x_i-\mu_k^{(t+1)})(x_i-\mu_k^{(t+1)})^{\mathsf T}.$$

**Output.** Return the finite parameter sequence $(\theta_0,\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_T)$. Every E-step uses the current parameter and every M-step uses that E-step's responsibilities. The affine-span hypothesis is imposed for the unrestricted positive-definite covariance update; constrained covariance domains require their own M-step. This definition makes no claim about convergence of parameters or a global maximum.
