## Statement

Assume AC. Let $n,p,K$ be positive integers, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$ have affine span $\mathbb R^p$ (equivalently, no nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$ makes $v^{\mathsf T}x_i$ constant over all $i$), and let $\theta=((\pi_k,\mu_k,\Sigma_k))_{k=1}^K$ be a finite Gaussian-mixture parameter with every $\pi_k>0$ and every $\Sigma_k$ symmetric positive definite. Define

$$\gamma_{ik}=\frac{\pi_k\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_j\phi_p(x_i;\mu_j,\Sigma_j)},\qquad N_k=\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_{ik},\qquad \bar x_k=\frac1{N_k}\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_{ik}x_i,$$

and

$$S_k=\frac1{N_k}\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_{ik}(x_i-\bar x_k)(x_i-\bar x_k)^{\mathsf T}.$$

For a candidate parameter $\vartheta=((\rho_k,m_k,V_k))_{k=1}^K$ in the same domain, let

$$Q(\vartheta\mid\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K\gamma_{ik}\log\!\left(\rho_k\phi_p(x_i;m_k,V_k)\right).$$

Then every $N_k$ is positive, $\sum_kN_k=n$, every $S_k$ is positive definite, and the unique global maximizer of $Q(\vartheta\mid\theta)$ over all positive mixture weights summing to one, means in $\mathbb R^p$, and symmetric positive-definite covariances is

$$\rho_k^*=N_k/n,\qquad m_k^*=\bar x_k,\qquad V_k^*=S_k.$$

In particular, the displayed E-step responsibilities and M-step update formulas are well-defined and attain this maximum.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume AC, positive integers $n,p,K$, observations whose affine span is $\mathbb R^p$, and a current finite Gaussian-mixture parameter with positive weights and symmetric positive-definite covariances.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is assumed by the KL definition and its nonnegativity theorem; this is the only choice use in the proof.

[F1] [[def-finite-gaussian-mixture]]: mixture weights are strictly positive and sum to one, covariances are symmetric positive definite, and the component formula $\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma)$ is used for finite observations.

[F2] [[thm-finite-gaussian-component-density-normalized]]: for these parameters, each Gaussian component formula is finite, strictly positive, and normalized; its logarithm is finite at every finite observation.

[F3] [[def-probability-measure]]: a probability measure has total mass one.

[F4] [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]: for probability measures $P\ll R$, the directional divergence is $D(P\|R)=\int\log(dP/dR)\,dP$; on a finite set with positive atom masses $a_k,r_k$, this is $\sum_k a_k\log(a_k/r_k)$.

[F5] [[thm-kullback-leibler-is-nonnegative]]: under AC, $D(P\|R)\ge0$, with equality exactly when $P=R$, for probability measures with the first absolutely continuous with respect to the second.

[F6] [[lem-log-determinant-strictly-concave-on-positive-definite-matrices]]: $A\mapsto\log\det A$ is strictly concave on the symmetric positive-definite cone.

[F7] [[thm-determinant-differential-and-jacobis-formula]]: for invertible $A$, $D\det(A)[H]=\det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}H)$.

[F8] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: for $u>0$, $(\log u)'=1/u$.

[F9] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the derivative of a differentiable composition is given by the chain rule.

[F10] [[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]: $\operatorname{tr}(M)$ is the sum of the diagonal entries; finite coordinate expansion gives $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ whenever the products are defined.

[F11] [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]] and [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]: $\det I=1$ and $\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)$, so for invertible $V$, $\det(V^{-1})=1/\det(V)$.

[F12] [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]: a real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis; in particular its eigenvalues are positive when it is positive definite, and its inverse is positive definite.

[F13] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\log$ is inverse to $\exp$, and for positive $u,v$, $\log(uv)=\log u+\log v$ and $\log(1/u)=-\log u$; hence for $a>0$, $\log(a^{-1/2})=-\tfrac12\log a$.

## Proof
1.1 By [F1] and [F2], every numerator and denominator in $\gamma_{ik}$ is finite and strictly positive. Hence $\gamma_{ik}>0$. Summing the responsibility formula over $k$ gives $\sum_k\gamma_{ik}=1$, so $N_k>0$ and $\sum_kN_k=n$. Thus all displayed weighted means and scatters are defined. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 For each nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$, $v^{\mathsf T}S_kv=N_k^{-1}\sum_i\gamma_{ik}(v^{\mathsf T}(x_i-\bar x_k))^2$. If it were zero, positivity of each $\gamma_{ik}$ would force $v^{\mathsf T}x_i=v^{\mathsf T}\bar x_k$ for every $i$. That would put all observations in the proper affine hyperplane $\{x:v^{\mathsf T}x=v^{\mathsf T}\bar x_k\}$, contradicting their full affine span. Since $S_k$ is visibly symmetric, it is positive definite. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Expanding the component density in [F1,F2] in the definition of $Q$ gives $Q(\vartheta\mid\theta)=\sum_kN_k\log\rho_k-\frac{np}{2}\log(2\pi)-\frac12\sum_k\left(N_k\log\det V_k+\sum_i\gamma_{ik}(x_i-m_k)^{\mathsf T}V_k^{-1}(x_i-m_k)\right).$ Here [F13] supplies $\log(\exp u)=u$ and the product and reciprocal laws. For each positive $a$, $\log(a^{-1/2})=-\frac12\log a$ follows by applying those laws to $(a^{-1/2})^2=1/a$; applying the product law $p$ times gives $\log((2\pi)^{-p/2})=-\frac p2\log(2\pi)$. All logarithms are finite: weights are positive, and [F2] gives finite positive component densities for each positive-definite covariance, so their determinants are positive. [F1, F2, F13, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Define $\alpha_k=N_k/n$, and for each subset $B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,K\}$ set $P(B):=\sum_{k\in B}\alpha_k$ and $R(B):=\sum_{k\in B}\rho_k$. Finite sums make these set functions additive on disjoint subsets; a disjoint sequence has at most $K$ nonempty members, so they are countably additive. Step 1.1 and the candidate weight constraint give total mass one, hence [F3] makes $P,R$ probability measures. Each $\rho_k>0$, so $P\ll R$. For every subset $B$, $\sum_{k\in B}(\alpha_k/\rho_k)\rho_k=P(B)$, hence $dP/dR(k)=\alpha_k/\rho_k$. The KL definition [F4] therefore gives $D(P\|R)=\sum_k\alpha_k\log(\alpha_k/\rho_k)\ge0$ by [A1,F5]. The weight-dependent part of $Q$ at $\alpha$ minus that at $\rho$ is $\sum_kN_k\log(\alpha_k/\rho_k)=nD(P\|R)\ge0$, with equality only when $P=R$, hence $\rho_k=\alpha_k$ for every $k$ by [F5]. [A1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra]

3.2 For fixed candidate covariance $V_k$, write $d_i=x_i-\bar x_k$ and $e=\bar x_k-m_k$. Since $\sum_i\gamma_{ik}d_i=0$, expanding the quadratic form gives $\sum_i\gamma_{ik}(x_i-m_k)^{\mathsf T}V_k^{-1}(x_i-m_k)=\sum_i\gamma_{ik}d_i^{\mathsf T}V_k^{-1}d_i+N_ke^{\mathsf T}V_k^{-1}e.$ The last term is nonnegative and is zero exactly when $m_k=\bar x_k$, because $V_k^{-1}$ is positive definite by [F12]. It occurs with a negative coefficient in $Q$ by step 2.2, so the unique maximizing mean is $\bar x_k$. [F1, F12, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra]

3.3 At this mean, coordinate expansion of the finite trace gives $\sum_i\gamma_{ik}d_i^{\mathsf T}V_k^{-1}d_i=N_k\operatorname{tr}(V_k^{-1}S_k)$. Therefore the covariance-dependent part of $Q$ is $-\frac{N_k}{2}(\log\det V_k+\operatorname{tr}(V_k^{-1}S_k))$ by step 2.2. Set $A=V_k^{-1}$; determinant identity [F11], the logarithm reciprocal law [F13], and the finite trace identity [F10] rewrite this as $\frac{N_k}{2}(\log\det A-\operatorname{tr}(AS_k))$. The candidate $A_*=S_k^{-1}$ is symmetric positive definite by step 2.1 and [F12]. Conversely, every symmetric positive-definite $A$ has positive-definite inverse, so this reparameterization ranges over the full covariance domain. [F10, F11, F12, F13, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

3.4 Fix any other positive-definite $A$ and put $H=A-A_*$, $A_t=A_*+tH$, and $h(t)=\log\det A_t-\operatorname{tr}(A_tS_k)$. Each $A_t$ is positive definite by convexity of the cone. By [F6], $h$ is strictly concave when $H\ne0$. Jacobi's formula [F7], the scalar logarithm derivative [F8], and the chain rule [F9] give $h'(0)=\operatorname{tr}(A_*^{-1}H)-\operatorname{tr}(HS_k)=0$, since $A_*^{-1}=S_k$ and [F10] permits cyclic rearrangement of the finite trace. If $h(1)\ge h(0)$, strict concavity gives $h(s)>h(0)$ for each $0<s<1$. For $0<u<s$, concavity gives $(h(u)-h(0))/u\ge(h(s)-h(0))/s>0$. Letting $u\downarrow0$ contradicts $h'(0)=0$. Hence $h(1)<h(0)$ for every $A\ne A_*$, so $V_k=S_k$ is the unique maximizing covariance. [F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The expression for $Q$ is a sum over components of a weight term, a mean-dependent quadratic term, and a covariance-dependent term, with no cross-component parameter terms. Steps 3.1, 3.2, and 3.4 show each is uniquely maximized by the displayed parameters; step 2.1 ensures each maximizing covariance remains in the permitted positive-definite domain. The product choice is therefore an admissible attained global maximizer, and equality forces every component parameter to equal the displayed update formulas. Thus the displayed E-step responsibilities and M-step formulas are well-defined and attain the claimed maximum, without using a procedure-level property. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 3.4, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

## Statement

Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

## Facts & Assumptions


**Given:** AC and probability measures $P,Q$; for the normalized-density
clause, a sigma-finite measure space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, finite-valued
measurable $\gamma,q\ge0$, $0<Z=\int\gamma\,d\mu<\infty$, $\pi=\gamma/Z$,
$\int q\,d\mu=1$, $q=0$ almost everywhere on $\{\gamma=0\}$, and the
stated absolute-integrability condition.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC supplies the Radon–Nikodym representative used by the published KL definition. The marginalization and density computations below use no further choice.

[F1] [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]: if $P\not\ll Q$, then
$D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$ and $r=dP/dQ$, then
$D(P\|Q)=\int\log r\,dP=\int r\log r\,dQ$, with $0\log0=0$ and a finite
negative part; the definition sets the logarithm to zero on $\{r=0\}$.

[F2] [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]]:
for finite positive $P\ll Q$, a measurable density $r=dP/dQ$ satisfies
$P(E)=\int_Er\,dQ$ for every measurable $E$.

[F3] [[thm-jensens-integral-inequality]]: on a probability space, if $r$ and
$\varphi(r)$ are integrable and $\varphi$ is convex, then
$\varphi(\int r)\le\int\varphi(r)$.

[F4] [[def-integral-logarithm]] and
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]]: for $t>0$,
$\log t=\int_1^tdu/u$ and this integral logarithm is the natural logarithm.

[F5] [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]]: for $t>0$,
$(\log t)'=1/t$.

[F6] [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\log(1/t)=-\log t$ for $t>0$.

[F7] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: $(t\log t)'=\log t+1$ for $t>0$.

[F8] [[cor-second-derivative-characterises-convexity]]: a twice
differentiable function on an open interval with nonnegative second
derivative is convex there.

[F9] [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]: pointwise bounds on integrable
functions on a nondegenerate interval pass to their Riemann integrals.

[F10] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: a continuous real-valued function
on a compact interval is Riemann integrable.

[F11] [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]]: for an integrable function and
oriented endpoints in its interval of integrability,
$\int_u^v h+\int_v^w h=\int_u^w h$.

[F12] [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]]: a
nonnegative measurable function has integral zero exactly when it vanishes
almost everywhere.

[F13] [[def-measure-space]] and
[[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]: a measure space is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure; sigma-finiteness means there is a countable
measurable cover by sets of finite measure.

[F14] [[def-probability-measure]]: a probability measure has total mass one.

[F15] [[def-measure-with-density]]: for a nonnegative measurable density $f$,
the associated measure is $(f\,d\mu)(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu$.

[F16] [[thm-integration-against-a-density]]: for nonnegative measurable $g,f$,
$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu$.

[F17] [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]: multiplying a
nonnegative measurable function by a positive finite scalar multiplies its
integral by that scalar.

[F18] [[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]]: the extended-real
Borel sigma-algebra is generated by rays $(a,+\infty]$ and contains Borel
intervals in $[0,+\infty]$.

[F19] [[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]]:
an extended-real function is Borel measurable if all strict upper threshold
preimages are Borel.

[F20] [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]:
composition of a measurable map with a Borel measurable outer map is
measurable.

[F21] [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]:
pointwise products of extended-real measurable functions are measurable under
its stated zero-times-infinity convention.

[F22] [[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]: for a measurable
real-valued function $h$, $h=h^+-h^-$ and $|h|=h^++h^-.$

[F23] [[lem-of-abs-value]]: $-|a|\le a\le|a|$ and $|-a|=|a|$ for real $a$. Adding the bounds for $a$ and $b$ gives $-(|a|+|b|)\le a+b\le|a|+|b|$, hence $|a+b|\le|a|+|b|$.

[F24] [[lem-integral-elementary-bounds]]: for a continuous constant function
$c$ on $[a,b]$, $\int_a^b c=c(b-a)$.

[F25] [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]: $L^1(Q)$ is a
vector space and the integral is linear on it.

## Proof

1.1 If $P\not\ll Q$, [F1] gives $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$ but $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$, nonnegativity is immediate. It remains to consider $P\ll Q$ with finite divergence; let $r=dP/dQ$. [F1, given]

1.2 Put $\varphi(0)=0$ and $\varphi(t)=t\log t$ for $t>0$. By [F5] and [F7], $\varphi''(t)=1/t>0$ for $t>0$, so [F8] makes $\varphi$ convex on $(0,\infty)$. Its continuity at zero is part of [F1]; taking limits in the convexity inequality as a positive endpoint tends to zero extends convexity to $[0,\infty)$. [F1, F5, F7, F8, algebra]

1.3 Define $g(t):=t\log t-t+1$ for $t>0$ and $g(0):=1$. For $s>1$, set $c=(1+s)/2$. By [F11], $\log s=\int_1^cdu/u+\int_c^sdu/u$. On $[1,c]$, $1/u\le1$, while on $[c,s]$, $1/u\le1/c<1$; [F9] and [F24] give $\log s<s-1$. For $0<s<1$, set $c=(1+s)/2$. By [F11], $\log s=-\int_s^1du/u=-\left(\int_s^cdu/u+\int_c^1du/u\right)$. On $[s,c]$, $1/u\ge1/c>1$, and on $[c,1]$, $1/u\ge1$; [F9] and [F24] give $\log s<s-1$. The integrands and comparison constants are integrable on these compact intervals by [F10]. Equality holds at $s=1$. Applying this inequality to $s=1/t$ and using [F6] gives $t\log t\ge t-1$, strictly unless $t=1$. Hence $g\ge0$ and its only zero is $1$. [F4, F6, F9, F10, F11, F24, algebra]

1.4 For the normalized-density clause on the measure space [F13], put $P:=q\,\mu$ and $Q:=\pi\,\mu$. By [F17], $\int\pi\,d\mu=Z^{-1}\int\gamma\,d\mu=1$; hence [F15] and [F14] make $P$ and $Q$ probability measures. [F13, F14, F15, F17, given, algebra]

1.5 If $Q(E)=0$, [F15] gives $\int_E\pi\,d\mu=0$, hence $\int_E\gamma\,d\mu=0$ because $Z$ is finite and positive, using [F17]. By [F12], $\gamma=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $E$. The support hypothesis on $q$ then gives $P(E)=0$, so $P\ll Q$. Define $\rho:[0,\infty]\to[0,\infty]$ by $\rho(t)=1/t$ for finite $t>0$ and $\rho(0)=\rho(+\infty)=0$. For $a<0$, $\{\rho>a\}=[0,\infty]$; for $a=0$ it is $(0,\infty)$; and for $a>0$ it is $(0,1/a)$. These are Borel by [F18], so [F19] makes $\rho$ Borel. By [F20]–[F21], $r:=q\,\rho(\pi)$ is measurable and equals $q/\pi$ on $\{\pi>0\}$ and zero on $\{\pi=0\}$. For every measurable $E$, [F16] gives $$\int_E r\,dQ=\int_Er\pi\,d\mu=\int_Eq\,d\mu=P(E),$$ because $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{\pi=0\}$. Thus $r=dP/dQ$. [F12, F15, F16, F17, F18, F19, F20, F21, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F2] with $E$ equal to the whole space, $\int r\,dQ=P(\Omega)=1$. The negative part of $r\log r$ is finite by [F1], so finiteness of $D(P\|Q)$ also makes its positive part finite. Thus $r$ and $r\log r$ are integrable with respect to the probability measure $Q$. The Radon–Nikodym representative here is the one whose selection is covered by [A1]. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1]

2.2 On the $P$-full-measure subset of $\{q>0\}$ where $\gamma>0$, we have $\pi=\gamma/Z>0$ and $\ell:=\log r=\log q-\log\gamma+\log Z$. Where $q=0$, the KL logarithm $\ell$ is defined to be zero. By [F23], $q|\ell|\le q|\log q|+q|\log\gamma|+q|\log Z|$ almost everywhere. The right-hand side has finite integral by the hypotheses and $\int q=1$; hence [F16] gives $\int|\ell|\,dP=\int q|\ell|\,d\mu<\infty$. By [F1], [F16], and [F22], applying [F16] to the positive and negative parts of $\ell$ gives $$D(P\|Q)=\int\log r\,dP =\int q(\log q-\log\gamma+\log Z)\,d\mu.$$ Using $\int q\,d\mu=1$ and rearranging proves the identity. [A1, F1, F16, F22, F23, given, step 1.5, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F3] on $(\Omega,\mathcal A,Q)$ to $r$ and $\varphi$. Steps 2.1 and 1.2 check its integrability and convexity hypotheses, and $\int r\,dQ=1$ by step 2.1. Therefore $$0=\varphi(1)=\varphi\!\left(\int r\,dQ\right) \le\int\varphi(r)\,dQ=D(P\|Q).$$ [F1, F3, step 2.1, step 1.2]

3.2 The representative $r$ is finite-valued and measurable by [F1], and $\varphi(r)$ is measurable there; the arithmetic measurability result [F21] therefore makes $g(r)=\varphi(r)-r+1$ measurable. It is nonnegative by step 1.3. By step 2.1, $r,\varphi(r)\in L^1(Q)$, and $1\in L^1(Q)$ because $Q$ is a probability measure. Linearity [F25] now gives $g(r)\in L^1(Q)$ and $$\int g(r)\,dQ=\int\varphi(r)\,dQ-\int r\,dQ+\int1\,dQ=D(P\|Q)-1+1=D(P\|Q).$$ Thus if $D(P\|Q)=0$, [F12] applies to the measurable nonnegative integrand and gives $g(r)=0$ $Q$-almost everywhere. By step 1.3, $r=1$ $Q$-almost everywhere, and the Radon–Nikodym identity [F2] gives $P(E)=Q(E)$ for every measurable $E$. Conversely, if $P=Q$ then $r=1$ almost everywhere and [F1] gives $D(P\|Q)=0$. [A1, F1, F2, F12, F21, F25, step 2.1, step 1.3, algebra]

4.1 Step 2.2 identifies the normalized-density divergence as finite, and step 3.1 proves it is nonnegative. Therefore $\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu\le\log Z$, as claimed. [step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $n,p,K$ be positive integers, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$ have affine span $\mathbb R^p$ (equivalently, no nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$ makes $v^{\mathsf T}x_i$ constant over all $i$), and start from a finite Gaussian-mixture parameter $\theta_0=((\pi_k^{(0)},\mu_k^{(0)},\Sigma_k^{(0)}))_{k=1}^K$ with positive weights summing to one and symmetric positive-definite covariances. For $t=0,\ldots,T-1$, where $T\ge1$, set

$$\gamma_{ik}^{(t)}:=\frac{\pi_k^{(t)}\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k^{(t)},\Sigma_k^{(t)})}{\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_j^{(t)}\phi_p(x_i;\mu_j^{(t)},\Sigma_j^{(t)})},\qquad N_k^{(t)}:=\sum_i\gamma_{ik}^{(t)},$$

and update

$$\pi_k^{(t+1)}:=N_k^{(t)}/n,\qquad \mu_k^{(t+1)}:=\frac{\sum_i\gamma_{ik}^{(t)}x_i}{N_k^{(t)}},\qquad \Sigma_k^{(t+1)}:=\frac{\sum_i\gamma_{ik}^{(t)}(x_i-\mu_k^{(t+1)})(x_i-\mu_k^{(t+1)})^{\mathsf T}}{N_k^{(t)}}.$$

For each $t$, define

$$\ell(\theta_t;x_{1:n}):=\sum_{i=1}^n\log\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k^{(t)}\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k^{(t)},\Sigma_k^{(t)})\right).$$

Every update is well-defined, every $\theta_t$ remains in the stated mixture domain, and

$$\ell(\theta_{t+1};x_{1:n})\ge\ell(\theta_t;x_{1:n})\qquad(0\le t<T).$$

No strict increase, parameter convergence, or global maximum conclusion is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume AC; take positive integers $n,p,K$, a full-affine-span sample $x_{1:n}$, an initial finite Gaussian-mixture parameter, and a finite number $T$ of exact EM updates.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is assumed by the finite-Gaussian density construction and by the published KL/EM interface. The density construction also uses countable choice, which AC supplies through [F10]. No stronger choice principle is used.

[F1] [[def-finite-gaussian-mixture]]: a finite mixture has positive weights summing to one, SPD component covariances, component density $\phi_p$, observation density $f_\theta(y)=\sum_k\pi_k\phi_p(y;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)$, and iid-sample log likelihood $\sum_i\log f_\theta(x_i)$.

[F2] [[thm-finite-gaussian-component-density-normalized]]: for every positive-definite component covariance, $\phi_p$ is finite, strictly positive at each finite observation, and integrates to one with respect to $p$-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

[F3] [[def-latent-variable-joint-and-observed-data-factorization]]: a latent-variable model supplies one jointly measurable nonnegative density on parameter, observation, and latent spaces, normalized on every parameter fibre; the observed marginal is its latent integral and the posterior is defined on positive finite marginal fibres.

[F4] [[thm-observed-density-is-latent-marginal-under-tonelli]]: under [F3], the observed marginal is a density, and the normalized latent fibre is a probability density wherever its marginal is positive and finite.

[F5] [[alg-expectation-maximization]]: exact mode selects an attained maximizer of the expected complete-data log density over an admissible candidate set containing the current parameter; admissible candidates satisfy positive finite observed marginal, directional support, finite KL, and absolute log integrability.

[F6] [[thm-em-observed-log-likelihood-is-nondecreasing]]: for a normalized jointly measurable complete-data density and current/candidate parameters satisfying those conditions, the observed log-likelihood difference equals the Q difference plus the directional KL divergence; an admissible Q-ascent update therefore cannot decrease observed log likelihood.

[F7] [[thm-gaussian-mixture-exact-m-step-maximizes-q]]: under the stated full-affine-span hypothesis, the finite Gaussian responsibilities have positive effective counts, their weighted covariance matrices are SPD, and the displayed updates are an attained global maximizer of the finite expected complete-data log density over the full mixture domain.

[F8] [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]: for $P\ll R$, $D(P\|R)$ is the integral of the log Radon–Nikodym derivative with respect to $P$; on a finite space with positive masses it is a finite sum.

[F9] [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]] and [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]: finite-dimensional Lebesgue measure and counting measure on the finite label set are sigma-finite, and their product reference measure exists with the rectangle formula.

[F10] [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]]: AC implies countable choice, as required for the product-Lebesgue identity and the local component-density normalization proof.

[F11] [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]]: under countable choice, finite products of Euclidean Lebesgue measures agree with Lebesgue measure on the corresponding Euclidean product space.

[F12] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: a nonnegative product-measurable function on sigma-finite factors has measurable section integrals, and its product integral equals either iterated integral.

[F13] [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: finite product sigma-algebras are generated by measurable rectangles.

[F14] [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]]: a continuous function on a finite-dimensional Euclidean space is Borel measurable; the relative version on a Borel parameter domain follows by taking relative Borel preimages.

[F15] [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]], [[thm-determinant-differential-and-jacobis-formula]], and [[thm-derivative-of-matrix-inversion]]: real symmetric matrices diagonalize orthogonally; determinant and matrix inverse are continuous on their respective finite-dimensional domains (the cited differentiability statements imply continuity).

[F16] [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]]: for finite-dimensional Euclidean factors, the product Borel sigma-algebra is the Euclidean Borel sigma-algebra.

[F17] [[def-measure-with-density]] and [[def-probability-measure]]: a nonnegative density $q$ relative to counting measure defines the measure $q\,\#$, and when its finite sum is one this is a probability measure.

[F18] [[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]: the nonnegative integral is additive for finite sums of nonnegative measurable functions.

[F19] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]]: for finite real lists $(a_r)$ and $(b_r)$, $|\sum_r a_rb_r|\le(\sum_r a_r^2)^{1/2}(\sum_r b_r^2)^{1/2}$.

## Proof
1.1 Let $\Theta_K$ be the set of mixture parameters in [F1], let $Y=(\mathbb R^p)^n$ with product Lebesgue measure $\nu=\lambda_p^{\otimes n}$, and let $Z=\{1,\ldots,K\}^n$ with counting measure $\#(B):=|B|$ for $B\subseteq Z$. The parameter domain is Borel: the positive-weight simplex is relatively open in its affine hyperplane, and the SPD cone is open as follows. For a symmetric positive-definite matrix $A$, the spectral theorem [F15] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis. Every eigenvalue $\lambda$ has a unit eigenvector $u$ with $\lambda=u^{\mathsf T}Au>0$, so the least eigenvalue $\lambda_{\min}(A)$ is positive. For a symmetric perturbation $E$, define $\|E\|_F:=(\sum_{i,j}e_{ij}^2)^{1/2}$. Applying [F19] to the finite lists $(e_{ij})$ and $(v_iv_j)$ gives $|v^{\mathsf T}Ev|\le\|E\|_F(\sum_{i,j}v_i^2v_j^2)^{1/2}=\|E\|_F\|v\|_2^2$. Therefore, whenever $\|E\|_F<\lambda_{\min}(A)$, $$v^{\mathsf T}(A+E)v\ge(\lambda_{\min}(A)-\|E\|_F)\|v\|_2^2>0$$ for every nonzero $v$, so $A+E$ is positive definite. This supplies a relative open neighborhood of each $A$ in the symmetric-matrix subspace. For each fixed $z\in Z$, the formula below is continuous in $(\eta,y)\in\Theta_K\times Y$: determinants and inverses are continuous on the SPD cone by [F15], and the remaining operations are sums, products, and exponentials. A continuous map on this Borel subspace has Borel preimages relative to it; those relative Borel sets are ambient Borel. The product-Borel identification for Euclidean factors [F16] and finite discreteness of $Z$ then make the function jointly measurable for the required product sigma-algebra. [A1, F1, F10, F13, F14, F15, F16, F19, algebra]

2.1 Define the complete-data density, relative to $\nu$ times counting measure on $Z$, by $p(\eta,y,z):=\prod_{i=1}^n\pi_{z_i}\phi_p(y_i;\mu_{z_i},\Sigma_{z_i}).$ Repeated use of [F9] constructs the finite product measures, including $\nu\otimes\#$, and preserves sigma-finiteness. AC supplies the countable-choice premise of [F11] by [F10]; repeated use of [F11] then identifies $\nu=\lambda_p^{\otimes n}$ with Euclidean Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^{pn}$. For each component, [F1,F2] and finite-sum additivity [F18] give $\int f_\eta(y_i)\,\lambda_p(dy_i)=\sum_k\pi_k=1$. Distributing the finite sum over labels gives $\sum_{z\in Z}p(\eta,y,z)=\prod_i f_\eta(y_i)$. Repeated Tonelli integration [F12] therefore gives $\sum_{z\in Z}\int_Yp(\eta,y,z)\,\nu(dy)=\int_Y\prod_i f_\eta(y_i)\,\nu(dy)=\prod_i\int_{\mathbb R^p}f_\eta(y_i)\,\lambda_p(dy_i)=1.$ Thus $p$ is normalized on each parameter fibre as required by [F3]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F9, F10, F11, F12, F18, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For a fixed observed sample $x_{1:n}$, summing the complete density over the finite label set yields $m_\eta(x_{1:n})=\sum_{z\in Z}p(\eta,x_{1:n},z)=\prod_i\sum_k\pi_k\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)=\prod_i f_\eta(x_i).$ Every factor is finite and strictly positive by [F1,F2], so this marginal is positive and finite. Its logarithm is exactly the likelihood $\ell(\eta;x_{1:n})$ in the statement. By [F4], every normalized posterior $q_\eta^{x_{1:n}}(z)=p(\eta,x_{1:n},z)/m_\eta(x_{1:n})$ is a probability mass function. More explicitly it is $q_\eta^{x_{1:n}}(z)=\prod_i\gamma_{i,z_i}(\eta),$ and every one of its finitely many masses is positive. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 At any current parameter $\theta$ and its exact update $\theta'$, both posterior measures obtained from the probability masses in step 3.1 by [F17] are strictly positive on the same finite label set. Hence $q_\theta^{x_{1:n}}\ll q_{\theta'}^{x_{1:n}}$, and the directional KL divergence is a sum of finitely many finite terms by [F8], so it is finite. For each $z$, $p(\theta,x_{1:n},z)$ and $p(\theta',x_{1:n},z)$ are strictly positive and finite; their logarithms are finite. The posterior expectations of the absolute log densities are finite sums and therefore finite. Thus every admissibility condition in [F5,F6] holds for this current/candidate pair. [F5, F6, F8, F17, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 The posterior in step 3.1 factors over observations. Taking the finite expectation of the complete log density gives $\sum_{z\in Z}q_\theta^{x_{1:n}}(z)\log p(\vartheta,x_{1:n},z)=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K\gamma_{ik}(\theta)\log\!\left(\rho_k\phi_p(x_i;m_k,V_k)\right)=Q(\vartheta\mid\theta),$ where $Q$ is the function in [F7]. Indeed, expand $\log p$ as the sum over $i$, sum first over $z_i=k$, and use $\sum_{j\ne i}\sum_{z_j}\gamma_{j,z_j}(\theta)=1$ for each other coordinate. This is a finite-sum identity, and all terms are finite by step 3.1. [F1, F7, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The local exact M-step result [F7] says $\theta'$ globally maximizes this same Q over the full mixture domain. Step 4.1 verifies that both $\theta$ and $\theta'$ are admissible, so the two-point candidate set $\{\theta,\theta'\}$ is admissible and contains the current parameter; the global maximizer $\theta'$ is therefore an attained maximizer over this set as required by the exact mode of [F5]. Consequently $Q(\theta'\mid\theta)\ge Q(\theta\mid\theta)$. Applying the identity and nonnegativity conclusion of [F6], with the verified conditions from step 4.1, yields $\ell(\theta';x_{1:n})-\ell(\theta;x_{1:n})=Q(\theta'\mid\theta)-Q(\theta\mid\theta)+D(q_\theta^{x_{1:n}}\|q_{\theta'}^{x_{1:n}})\ge0.$ Thus one exact update does not decrease observed log likelihood. [F5, F6, F7, step 4.1, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 Initially $\theta_0$ is in the mixture domain by hypothesis. If $\theta_t$ is in that domain, step 3.1 supplies positive finite marginals and positive responsibilities, and [F7] supplies the next positive weights and SPD covariances; hence $\theta_{t+1}$ is again in the domain. Induction gives valid parameters through $T$, and step 5.1 applies at each $t<T$, proving every displayed likelihood inequality. This proves the claim without asserting strict increase or convergence. [given, F1, F7, step 3.1, step 5.1, induction] ∎

## Definition

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, and
$(\mathsf Z,\mathcal C)$ be measurable spaces (sets equipped with
sigma-algebras; [[def-measurable-space]]). Let $\nu$ and $\mu$ be sigma-finite
reference measures on the observation and latent spaces; each has a countable
measurable cover by sets of finite measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). The finite product
sigma-algebra is generated by measurable rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The product
reference measure $\nu\otimes\mu$ is the one supplied by
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]].

A **jointly measurable latent-variable density** is a specified function
$$p:\Theta\times\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z\longrightarrow[0,\infty]$$
measurable for $\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal C$ and normalized
on every parameter fibre:
$$\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\, (\nu\otimes\mu)(d(x,z))=1\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Here $x$ is the observed coordinate and $z$ the latent coordinate. The
observed marginal density is
$$m(\theta,x):=\int_{\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz).$$
The valid-fibre set is
$V:=\{(\theta,x):0<m(\theta,x)<\infty\}$. Only on $V$ define the normalized
latent-fibre density
$$q(z\mid\theta,x):=\frac{p(\theta,x,z)}{m(\theta,x)}.$$
This definition requires a single jointly measurable density as an input.
[[def-likelihood-density]] supplies neither a sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ nor
joint parameter measurability from separately specified likelihood sections;
the joint measurability above is an additional hypothesis. Because $p$ is
already supplied as one joint function, this definition uses no choice axiom.
It does not assert that AC can turn separately specified pointwise likelihood
versions into a jointly measurable version. No quotient or pointwise
conditional density is asserted on a zero or infinite marginal fibre.

## Statement

Assume the hypotheses of
[[def-latent-variable-joint-and-observed-data-factorization]]. Then
$m(\theta,x)=\int p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz)$ is jointly measurable in
$(\theta,x)$. For each fixed $\theta$, it is an observed-data probability
density: it is $\mathcal A$-measurable and
$$\int_{\mathsf X}m(\theta,x)\,\nu(dx)=1.$$
Consequently $m(\theta,x)<\infty$ for $\nu$-almost every $x$. On every valid
fibre $0<m(\theta,x)<\infty$, $q(z\mid\theta,x)=p(\theta,x,z)/m(\theta,x)$ is
a measurable $\mu$-density of total mass one. Finally, if $h:\Theta\times\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z\to\mathbb C$ is product
measurable and
$\int |h(\theta,x,z)|p(\theta,x,z)\,d(\nu\otimes\mu)<\infty$ for a fixed
$\theta$, Fubini permits exchanging the latent and observed integrals of
$hp$. No exchange is claimed without this absolute integrability.

## Facts & Assumptions


**Given:** The parameter and data spaces, sigma-finite measures $\nu,\mu$,
jointly measurable normalized $p$, and, for the last clause, a product
measurable complex-valued $h$ with $\int |h|p<\infty$.

[F1] [[def-latent-variable-joint-and-observed-data-factorization]]: $p$ is
jointly measurable, each fixed-$\theta$ joint density integrates to one,
$m(\theta,x)=\int p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz)$, and $q=p/m$ is defined only when
$0<m<\infty$.

[F2] [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: a uniformly sigma-finite
kernel comes with a specified exhaustion $(Z_n)$ for which each kernel mass
on $Z_n$ is finite.

[F3] [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]: integrating a
nonnegative product-measurable function against a finite or uniformly
sigma-finite kernel gives a measurable function of the parameter.

[F4] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: for
nonnegative product-measurable $p$, its section integrals are measurable and
the iterated and product integrals agree.

[F5] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: for an
$L^1(\nu\otimes\mu)$ function, almost every section is integrable and the
iterated integrals equal the product integral.

[F6] [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]: pointwise
order and multiplication by a positive finite scalar pass to nonnegative
integrals.

[F7] [[thm-of-archimedean]]: the positive integers are unbounded in $\mathbb R$.

[F8] [[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]]: the extended-real
Borel structure contains $[0,\infty]$ and its Borel subsets.

[F9] [[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]]:
an extended-real function is measurable if all strict upper threshold preimages
are measurable.

[F10] [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]:
composition of a measurable map with a Borel measurable outer map is measurable.

[F11] [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]:
products of extended-real measurable functions are measurable under its stated
zero-times-infinity convention.

[F12] [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: the
finite product sigma-algebra is generated by measurable rectangles.

[F13] [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]: sigma-finiteness
provides a countable measurable exhaustion by sets of finite measure.

## Proof

1.1 Fix $\theta$ and let $\mathcal D_\theta$ be the collection of subsets $E\subseteq\Theta\times\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z$ whose section $E_\theta:=\{(x,z):(\theta,x,z)\in E\}$ belongs to $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal C$. Sections commute with complements and countable unions, so $\mathcal D_\theta$ is a sigma-algebra. It contains each measurable rectangle $T_0\times A_0\times C_0$, whose section is $A_0\times C_0$ if $\theta\in T_0$ and empty otherwise. By [F12], every product-measurable set has a measurable section. Applying this to preimages of Borel sets shows that $p_\theta(x,z):=p(\theta,x,z)$ is product-measurable. For complex $h$, first compose with the continuous Borel coordinate maps $\operatorname{Re},\operatorname{Im}:\mathbb C\to\mathbb R$; the same section argument makes both $\operatorname{Re}h_\theta$ and $\operatorname{Im}h_\theta$ measurable, hence $h_\theta$ is complex-measurable. [F10, F12, given]

1.2 By [F13], choose a measurable exhaustion $Z_n\uparrow\mathsf Z$ with $\mu(Z_n)<\infty$. On $S:=\Theta\times\mathsf X$, the constant assignment $K(s,B):=\mu(B)$ is a measure kernel: each section is $\mu$ and each evaluation map is constant. The same exhaustion makes it uniformly sigma-finite by [F2]. [F2, F13, given, choose]

2.1 For fixed $\theta$, step 1.1 makes $p_\theta$ product-measurable, so Tonelli [F4] gives $$\int_{\mathsf X}m(\theta,x)\,\nu(dx)=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z}p_\theta(x,z)\,d(\nu\otimes\mu)=1$$ by [F1]. Thus $m(\theta,\cdot)$ is a probability density. Also $E_\theta:=\{(x,z):p_\theta(x,z)=\infty\}$ is measurable. For every positive integer $n$, $n\mathbf1_{E_\theta}\le p_\theta$, so [F6] gives $n(\nu\otimes\mu)(E_\theta)\le1$. Since this holds for every $n$, [F7] implies $(\nu\otimes\mu)(E_\theta)=0$. [F1, F4, F6, F7, given, step 1.1]

2.2 The function $p$ is nonnegative and product-measurable by [F1]. Under the finite-product identification $S\times\mathsf Z=(\Theta\times\mathsf X)\times\mathsf Z$ from [F12], apply [F3] to the constant kernel $K$ from step 1.2. It follows that $s\mapsto\int p(s,z)\,\mu(dz)=m(s)$ is measurable on $S$. [F1, F3, F12, step 1.2]

3.1 For fixed $\theta$, write $u_\theta=\operatorname{Re}h_\theta$ and $v_\theta=\operatorname{Im}h_\theta$. Define the finite-valued measurable function $\widetilde p_\theta:=p_\theta\mathbf1_{\{p_\theta<\infty\}}$ and then $$H_\theta:=u_\theta\widetilde p_\theta+i v_\theta\widetilde p_\theta.$$ By [F11] this is complex-valued product-measurable; it is defined to be zero on the null set where $p_\theta=\infty$. It agrees with $h_\theta p_\theta$ off that null set, and the assumed absolute integrability gives $\int|H_\theta|\,d(\nu\otimes\mu)<\infty$. Fubini [F5] applies to this $L^1$ representative and gives $$\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z}H_\theta\,d(\nu\otimes\mu)=\int_{\mathsf X}\left(\int_{\mathsf Z}H_\theta(x,z)\,\mu(dz)\right)\nu(dx)=\int_{\mathsf Z}\left(\int_{\mathsf X}H_\theta(x,z)\,\nu(dx)\right)\mu(dz),$$ with its zero assignment on exceptional null sections. Since $H_\theta=hp$ almost everywhere on the fixed-$\theta$ product space, these are the asserted exchanges for $hp$. [F5, F11, given, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.2 Let $E:=\{x:m(\theta,x)=\infty\}$, measurable by step 2.2. For each positive integer $n$, $n\mathbf1_E\le m(\theta,\cdot)$, so [F6] and step 2.1 give $n\nu(E)\le1$. Since this holds for every $n$, [F7] forces $\nu(E)=0$. If $0<m(\theta,x)<\infty$, division by that scalar and the definition of $m$ give $\int q(z\mid\theta,x)\,\mu(dz)=m(\theta,x)/m(\theta,x)=1$. The valid-fibre set $V=m^{-1}((0,\infty))$ is measurable by step 2.2 and [F8]. For measurability, define $\rho:[0,\infty]\to[0,\infty]$ by $\rho(t)=1/t$ for finite $t>0$ and $\rho(0)=\rho(+\infty)=0$. For $a<0$, $\{\rho>a\}=[0,\infty]$; for $a=0$ it is $(0,\infty)$; and for $a>0$ it is $(0,1/a)$. These sets are Borel by [F8], so [F9] makes $\rho$ Borel. By [F10], $\rho\circ m$ is measurable on $\Theta\times\mathsf X$. Pulling it back along the measurable coordinate projection from the finite product space, which is measurable by [F12], gives a product-measurable function; multiplying by $p$ preserves measurability by [F11]. This product restricts to $q=p/m$ on $V\times\mathsf Z$, so $q$ is measurable on the valid-fibre set. [F1, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, step 2.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Steps 2.2, 2.1, 3.2, and 3.1 prove the marginal measurability, normalization, valid-fibre density, and integrable-exchange clauses. [step 2.2, step 2.1, step 3.2, step 3.1] ∎

## Definition

**Inputs.** Supply a measurable parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, sigma-finite measure spaces $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\nu)$ and $(\mathsf Z,\mathcal C,\mu)$, and a jointly measurable complete-data density $p(\theta,x,z)$ relative to $\nu\otimes\mu$ that integrates to one on each parameter fiber, as in [[def-latent-variable-joint-and-observed-data-factorization]]. This joint measurability is supplied explicitly and is not inferred from separate likelihood-density versions ([[def-likelihood-density]]). Also supply fixed observed data $x$, an initial value $\theta_0$, a mode `exact` or `generalized`, and a candidate selector that returns either a candidate or `unavailable` in finite time at each call. Require $0<m_{\theta_0}(x)<\infty$ and
$$\int q_{\theta_0}^x(z)\,|\log p(\theta_0,x,z)|\,\mu(dz)<\infty.$$

Write
$$m_\theta(x):=\int_{\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz),\qquad q_\theta^x(z):=\frac{p(\theta,x,z)}{m_\theta(x)}$$
only when $0<m_\theta(x)<\infty$. By [[thm-observed-density-is-latent-marginal-under-tonelli]], $m_\theta$ is the observed-data density and $q_\theta^x$ is a probability density on every such fiber. The observed log likelihood is $\ell_x(\theta):=\log m_\theta(x)$ on those fibers.

At each valid iterate $\theta_t$, set $q_t:=q_{\theta_t}^x$ and define
$$Q(\theta\mid\theta_t):=\int_{\mathsf Z}\log p(\theta,x,z)\,q_t(z)\,\mu(dz)$$
only for candidates where this integral is finite. Use $\log0=-\infty$ and set $q_t|\log p|=0$ wherever $q_t=0$. The Q integral itself is choice-free. To test finite KL when $q_t\mu\ll q_\theta^x\mu$, assume AC as required by [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]; when absolute continuity fails, $D=+\infty$ by that definition without AC. An **admissible candidate** $\theta$ also satisfies $0<m_\theta(x)<\infty$, $q_t\mu\ll q_\theta^x\mu$, and
$$D(q_t\mu\|q_\theta^x\mu)<\infty,$$
where the direction of $D$ is that of [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. Require $\int q_t|\log p(\theta,x,\cdot)|\,d\mu<\infty$ for each candidate and $\int q_t|\log p(\theta_t,x,\cdot)|\,d\mu<\infty$ for the current iterate.

**Output.** Emit the iterate sequence beginning with $\theta_0$. If a stopping condition occurs after $T$ successful updates, return the finite list $(\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_T)$ and a status recording the first unavailable condition or selector result; do not append a failed candidate. If no stopping condition occurs, the emitted sequence is infinite and there is no finite stopping status.

**Procedure.** For $t=0,1,2,\ldots$, check that $0<m_{\theta_t}(x)<\infty$; if not, return the current list with status `stopped: invalid current marginal`. Form $q_t$ and $Q(\cdot\mid\theta_t)$ on admissible candidates. If $Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t)$ is not finite, return with status `stopped: current Q is not finite`. Call the supplied selector. In **exact mode**, its candidate set must consist of admissible candidates and contain $\theta_t$; it returns an attained maximizer of $Q$ on that set, or `unavailable` if no attained maximum is available. In **generalized mode**, it returns any admissible $\theta_{t+1}$ with $Q(\theta_{t+1}\mid\theta_t)\ge Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t)$, or `unavailable` if no such update is supplied. If the selector returns `unavailable`, return with status `stopped: no required update supplied`; otherwise append its candidate and continue. The procedure asserts no convergence or global-optimality property and makes no assertion for a candidate that loses current latent support.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $p(\theta,x,z)$ be a jointly measurable normalized complete-data density as in [[def-latent-variable-joint-and-observed-data-factorization]], and fix observed data $x$. Put $m_\theta(x)=\int p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz)$. Let $\theta_t$ and $\theta$ satisfy $0<m_{\theta_t}(x),m_\theta(x)<\infty$. Define $q_t(z)=p(\theta_t,x,z)/m_{\theta_t}(x)$ and $q_\theta^x(z)=p(\theta,x,z)/m_\theta(x)$. Assume
$$q_t\mu\ll q_\theta^x\mu,\qquad \int q_t(z)\bigl(|\log p(\theta_t,x,z)|+|\log p(\theta,x,z)|\bigr)\,\mu(dz)<\infty,$$
and $D(q_t\mu\|q_\theta^x\mu)<\infty$. Use $\log0=-\infty$ and set $q_t|\log p|=0$ wherever $q_t=0$. Then, with $Q(\theta\mid\theta_t)=\int q_t(z)\log p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz)$,
$$\ell_x(\theta)-\ell_x(\theta_t) =Q(\theta\mid\theta_t)-Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t) +D(q_t\mu\|q_\theta^x\mu).$$
Consequently, any admissible update with $Q(\theta\mid\theta_t)\ge Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t)$ does not decrease $\ell_x$. An exact M-step has this property when its maximum is attained over an admissible candidate set containing $\theta_t$. No equality-of-parameter conclusion is asserted when the KL divergence is zero.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume AC, the supplied measurable spaces and density, a fixed observation $x$, current and candidate parameters with positive finite observed marginals, the stated absolute integrability and support conditions, and finite directional KL divergence.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is assumed by the finite-valued Radon–Nikodym representative in the KL definition, the nonnegativity theorem, and uniqueness of Radon–Nikodym densities.

[F1] [[def-latent-variable-joint-and-observed-data-factorization]]: $p$ is one jointly measurable nonnegative function normalized on every parameter fiber; $m_\theta(x)=\int p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz)$ and $q_\theta^x=p/m_\theta(x)$ is defined only on a positive finite fiber.

[F2] [[thm-observed-density-is-latent-marginal-under-tonelli]]: $q_t$ and $q_\theta^x$ are probability densities on the positive finite fibers in the statement.

[F3] [[def-measure-with-density]]: $q\,\mu$ is the measure $A\mapsto\int_Aq\,d\mu$.

[F4] [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]: under AC and $P\ll Q$, the divergence is $\int\log r\,dP$ for a finite-valued Radon–Nikodym representative $r=dP/dQ$.

[F5] [[thm-integration-against-a-density]]: for nonnegative measurable $f,g$, $\int g\,d(f\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu$.

[F6] [[thm-kullback-leibler-is-nonnegative]]: under AC and the stated directional convention, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$.

[F7] [[alg-expectation-maximization]]: generalized mode requires nondecreasing $Q$, and exact mode selects an attained maximizer over an admissible set containing the current iterate.

[F8] [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]: pointwise order and multiplication by a positive finite scalar pass to nonnegative integrals.

[F9] [[thm-of-archimedean]]: the positive integers are unbounded in $\mathbb R$.

[F10] [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]: a nonnegative measurable function integrates to zero over a measurable null set.

[F11] [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]]: under AC, a finite absolutely continuous measure has a density unique up to almost-everywhere equality when the positive reference measure is sigma-finite.

## Proof

1.1 By [F2] and [F3], $P:=q_t\mu$ and $Q:=q_\theta^x\mu$ are probability measures. For $u=q_t$ and $u=q_\theta^x$, $n\mathbf1_{\{u=\infty\}}\le u$ and $\int u\,d\mu=1$, so [F8] gives $n\mu\{u=\infty\}\le1$ for every positive integer $n$; [F9] forces both infinite-value sets to be $\mu$-null. Let $N$ be their union. By [F10], $P(N)=Q(N)=0$. Also $P\{q_\theta^x=0\}=0$, since $Q\{q_\theta^x=0\}=0$ and $P\ll Q$. Finally $P\{q_t=0\}=0$ by the definition of $P$. Thus $q_t$ and $q_\theta^x$ are finite and strictly positive on a $P$-full set. [given, F2, F3, F8, F9, F10]

2.1 By [A1] and [F4], choose a finite-valued Radon–Nikodym derivative $r=dP/dQ$. Define $\widetilde r=rq_\theta^x$ off $N$ and $\widetilde r=0$ on $N$, and define $\widetilde q_t=q_t$ off $N$ and $\widetilde q_t=0$ on $N$. These are finite-valued measurable functions. For every measurable $A$, [F5] and [F10] give $$\int_A\widetilde r\,d\mu=\int_A rq_\theta^x\,d\mu=\int_A r\,dQ=P(A)=\int_Aq_t\,d\mu=\int_A\widetilde q_t\,d\mu.$$ Since $\mu$ is sigma-finite and $P$ is finite, a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for $P$. Uniqueness [F11] therefore gives $\widetilde r=\widetilde q_t$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. On the $P$-full set from step 1.1, $r=q_t/q_\theta^x$ and $$\log r=\log p(\theta_t,x,z)-\log m_{\theta_t}(x)-\log p(\theta,x,z)+\log m_\theta(x).$$ The stated absolute-integrability conditions make these log terms integrable. Integrating this equality with respect to $P=q_t\mu$ and using [F4] yields $$D(P\|Q)=Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t)-Q(\theta\mid\theta_t)+\ell_x(\theta)-\ell_x(\theta_t),$$ which rearranges to the claimed identity. [given, A1, F1, F2, F4, F5, F10, F11, algebra]

3.1 By [F6], the KL term in the identity is nonnegative, so the observed log-likelihood difference is at least the Q difference. A generalized admissible update has nonnegative Q difference by [F7]. An attained exact maximizer over a set containing $\theta_t$ has the same property. Hence either update does not decrease the observed log likelihood. [given, F6, F7, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, natural numbers $n,m\ge1$, and a continuous function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$.

[L1] A continuous map has Borel preimages of Borel sets. ([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $B \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ be Borel. By [L1], the preimage $f^{-1}(B)$ is a Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$. [L1]

## Statement

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then

$$\Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}\Big),$$

and, in root form ([[thm-of-square-roots]]),

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}} \; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}}.$$

Equality holds in the first display if and only if the two lists are
proportional, in the symmetric sense that there is a pair
$(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every
$k < n$.

**No root is used in the proof of the squared form.** That form is an identity
plus a sign argument in the ordered field, and the root form is only a
restatement of it through the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); the root enters nowhere but the last step, where
that restatement is made and [[thm-of-square-roots]] is what supplies the
square-root symbol. This matters here, because it makes the squared
inequality independent of the existence theorem for roots.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural $n$ and reals $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$, $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$. Write $A := \sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}$, $B := \sum_{k<n} a_k b_k$ and $C := \sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}$.

[L1] Laws of finite sums ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[def-finite-sum]]): additivity, scaling, monotonicity, and the fact that a sum of nonnegative terms is nonnegative and vanishes only if every term vanishes.

[L2] Squares ([[lem-of-square-positive]], [[def-integer-power]]): $x^{2} \ge 0$ for every $x$, and $x^{2} = 0$ only for $x = 0$; and a product with a zero factor vanishes, $0 \cdot x = 0$ ([[lem-of-zero-mult]]).

[L3] Square roots ([[thm-of-square-roots]]): every $c \ge 0$ has a unique $\sqrt{c} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{c})^{2} = c$.

[L4] Monotonicity of squaring ([[lem-of-square-monotone]]): for $x, y \ge 0$, $x \le y \iff x^{2} \le y^{2}$; and $|x|^{2} = x^{2}$ with $|x| \ge 0$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]], [[def-abs-value]]).

[L5] Order arithmetic in an ordered field: adding inequalities ([[lem-of-add-order]]) and scaling an inequality by a positive element ([[lem-of-sign-rules]], claim 4) are both stated there for the STRICT order alone, so the nonstrict uses below are those statements together with the case of equality, settled by trichotomy ([[def-ordered-field]]); the inverse of a positive element is positive ([[lem-of-inverse-positive]], claim 1); and a nonzero factor cancels, since $\lambda x = 0$ with $\lambda \ne 0$ gives $x = \lambda^{-1}(\lambda x) = \lambda^{-1} \cdot 0 = 0$, a product with a zero factor ([[lem-of-zero-mult]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For every $t \in \mathbb{R}$ each term $(a_k t + b_k)^{2}$ is nonnegative, so the sum is nonnegative, and expanding with additivity and scaling gives $0 \le \sum_{k<n}(a_k t + b_k)^{2} = A t^{2} + 2 B t + C$. [L1, L2]

1.2 In particular $A \ge 0$ and $C \ge 0$, being sums of squares. [L1, L2]

1.3 Proportionality forces equality: assume $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for all $k < n$ with $(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$; if $\mu \ne 0$ then $b_k = c a_k$ with $c = \lambda/\mu$, so $B = cA$ and $C = c^{2}A$ by scaling, whence $B^{2} = c^{2}A^{2} = A\big(c^{2}A\big) = AC$; and if $\mu = 0$ then $\lambda \ne 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for all $k$, so $A = B = 0$ and both sides vanish. [L1, L5]

2.1 Suppose first $A = 0$: then every term of $\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}$ vanishes, so $a_k = 0$ for all $k < n$, hence $B = \sum_{k<n} 0 \cdot b_k = 0$ and both sides of the squared inequality are $0$, so it holds with equality; and the pair $(\lambda, \mu) = (1, 0)$ satisfies $\lambda a_k = 0 = \mu b_k$. [step 1.2, L1, L2]

2.2 Suppose instead $A > 0$ and substitute $t = -B/A$ into step 1.1: $0 \le A\frac{B^{2}}{A^{2}} - 2\frac{B^{2}}{A} + C = C - \frac{B^{2}}{A}$, so $\frac{B^{2}}{A} \le C$, and multiplying by $A > 0$ gives $B^{2} \le AC$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L5]

3.1 The squared inequality therefore holds in both cases, which exhaust the possibilities since $A \ge 0$. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 1.2]

3.2 Equality forces proportionality: in the case $A = 0$ this was step 2.1; in the case $A > 0$, if $B^{2} = AC$ then putting $t_0 = -B/A$ in step 1.1 gives $\sum_{k<n}(a_k t_0 + b_k)^{2} = A t_0^{2} + 2Bt_0 + C = C - \frac{B^{2}}{A} = 0$, so every term vanishes and $b_k = -t_0 a_k$ for all $k$, and the pair $(\lambda, \mu) = (-t_0, 1) \ne (0,0)$ works. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, L1, L2, L5]

4.1 The root form: by step 3.1, $|B|^{2} = B^{2} \le AC = \big(\sqrt{A}\,\sqrt{C}\big)^{2}$, and both $|B|$ and $\sqrt{A}\sqrt{C}$ are nonnegative, so monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives gives $|B| \le \sqrt{A}\,\sqrt{C}$; note also that $\sqrt{A}\sqrt{C}$ is the nonnegative square root of $AC$, by uniqueness. [step 3.1, step 1.2, L3, L4] ∎

## Example

For the data $x_1=0,x_2=1,x_3=2,x_4=3$ in $\mathbb R$ and $K=2$, use nearest-center initialization with smallest-index initialization ties, retain the current label on later ties, replace each nonempty center by its assigned-data mean, and leave empty centers unchanged. For clusters $C_1,C_2$ and centers $c_1,c_2$, define the cost by $J=\sum_{k=1}^2\sum_{x_i\in C_k}(x_i-c_k)^2$. Initial centers $(0,11/10)$ yield the fixed clusters $\{0\}$ and $\{1,2,3\}$ with centers $(0,2)$ and cost $2$. Initial centers $(3,19/10)$ yield the fixed clusters $\{3\}$ and $\{0,1,2\}$ with centers $(3,1)$ and cost $2$. Initial centers $(1/2,5/2)$ yield the fixed clusters $\{0,1\}$ and $\{2,3\}$ with centers $(1/2,5/2)$ and cost $1$. In the first two runs, the boundary observation is tied between the two updated centers and stays in its current cluster by the retention rule; each output is a fixed point, while the third has lower cost.

## Example references

[[alg-lloyd-k-means]] — initialization, tie retention, empty-center handling, and the stop condition requiring unchanged labels and centers.

[[def-k-means-objective]] — the squared Euclidean within-cluster objective used for the reported values.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Data $0,1,2,3\in\mathbb R$, two clusters, and the Lloyd rules in the Example.

[F1] [[def-k-means-objective]]: for labels $c_i\in\{1,2\}$ and centers $\mu_1,\mu_2$, the objective is $J=\sum_{i=1}^4(x_i-\mu_{c_i})^2$.

[F2] [[alg-lloyd-k-means]]: initialization selects a nearest center with smallest-index ties; later assignments retain the current label on a tie and otherwise select a nearest center; each nonempty center is replaced by its assigned-data mean; the algorithm stops when both labels and centers are unchanged.

## Proof
1.1 From initial centers $(0,11/10)$, the nearest labels are $(1,2,2,2)$: the respective comparisons are $0<121/100$, $1>1/100$, $4>81/100$, and $9>361/100$. The mean update gives centers $0$ and $(1+2+3)/3=2$. [given, F2, algebra]

1.2 From initial centers $(3,19/10)$, nearest labels are $(2,2,2,1)$: observations $0,1,2$ are strictly nearer $19/10$, while $3$ equals the first center. Their means become $3$ for cluster $1$ and $(0+1+2)/3=1$ for cluster $2$. [F2, algebra]

1.3 From initial centers $(1/2,5/2)$, nearest labels are $(1,1,2,2)$. The means of these clusters are again $1/2$ and $5/2$, so labels and centers are unchanged and the procedure stops. The objective is $4(1/2)^2=1$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 With centers $(0,2)$, observations $0,2,3$ keep labels $1,2,2$ by strict nearest comparisons; observation $1$ is at distance $1$ from each center and retains its current label $2$. The labels remain $(1,2,2,2)$, so their means remain $(0,2)$ and the procedure stops. The objective is $(0-0)^2+(1-2)^2+(2-2)^2+(3-2)^2=2$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 With centers $(3,1)$, observations $0,1,3$ keep labels $2,2,1$ by strict nearest comparisons; observation $2$ is tied at distance $1$ and retains label $2$. The labels stay $(2,2,2,1)$, their means remain $(3,1)$, and the procedure stops. The objective is $(0-1)^2+(1-1)^2+(2-1)^2+(3-3)^2=2$. [F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The three explicitly computed terminal states have objective values $2,2,1$, respectively, so they are distinct fixed points and the third has strictly lower objective than the first two. In the first and second runs, changing the tied boundary point to the other cluster would change the fixed partition; under the stated rule it remains with its current label. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume AC. Take one observation $x=0\in\mathbb R$, two Gaussian components with means $\mu_1=-1$ and $\mu_2=1$, common variance $\sigma^2>0$, and mixture weights $\pi_1=1/3$ and $\pi_2=2/3$. Their component density is $\phi_1(x;\mu,\sigma^2)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\exp(-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2))$, and the responsibility of component $k$ is $\gamma_k=\pi_k\phi_1(0;\mu_k,\sigma^2)/\sum_{j=1}^2\pi_j\phi_1(0;\mu_j,\sigma^2)$. The two squared distances from the observation to the component means are both $1$. For every $\sigma>0$, the responsibility vector is exactly $(1/3,2/3)$; therefore as $\sigma\downarrow0$ it remains fractional rather than converging to $(1,0)$ or $(0,1)$.

## Example references

[[def-finite-gaussian-mixture]] — the positive-weight Gaussian component formula and responsibility definition.

[[thm-equal-spherical-mixture-low-variance-kmeans-limit]] — tied nearest centers receive limiting responsibilities proportional to their fixed mixture weights.

[[thm-finite-gaussian-component-density-normalized]] — each component formula is a normalized Gaussian density.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume AC; take one observation at $0$, means $-1$ and $1$, common variance $\sigma^2>0$, and positive weights $1/3,2/3$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is the stated assumption of the finite-Gaussian definition and the local component-density normalization theorem.

[F1] [[def-finite-gaussian-mixture]]: in one dimension, $\phi_1(x;\mu,\sigma^2)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\exp(-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2))$, and the responsibility is the weighted component density divided by their sum.

[F2] [[thm-finite-gaussian-component-density-normalized]]: for positive variance, this component formula is finite and strictly positive and integrates to one.

[F3] [[thm-equal-spherical-mixture-low-variance-kmeans-limit]]: at a tied nearest-center set, fixed positive weights yield limiting responsibilities equal to those weights renormalized over the tied set.

## Proof
1.1 Substitution in [F1] gives $\phi_1(0;-1,\sigma^2)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}e^{-1/(2\sigma^2)}=\phi_1(0;1,\sigma^2)=:c_\sigma.$ By [F2], $c_\sigma$ is finite and positive under [A1]. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The responsibility denominator is $c_\sigma(1/3+2/3)=c_\sigma$. Dividing the two weighted component values by that denominator gives $\gamma_1=(1/3)c_\sigma/c_\sigma=1/3$ and $\gamma_2=(2/3)c_\sigma/c_\sigma=2/3$ for every $\sigma>0$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since the vector is constant for all positive $\sigma$, its limit as $\sigma\downarrow0$ is $(1/3,2/3)$, which is not one-hot. Both centers are nearest to $0$, so [F3] gives the same tied-center limit, proportional to the fixed weights. [F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume AC. For the observations $x_1=0,x_2=1\in\mathbb R$, use two Gaussian components of weights $1/2,1/2$, both with mean $0$, with variances $\varepsilon^2$ and $1$ for $\varepsilon>0$. Write $\phi_1(x;0,s^2)=(2\pi s^2)^{-1/2}\exp(-x^2/(2s^2))$, $f_\varepsilon(x)=\tfrac12\phi_1(x;0,\varepsilon^2)+\tfrac12\phi_1(x;0,1)$, and $L_\varepsilon=f_\varepsilon(0)f_\varepsilon(1)$. Every parameter in this family has positive weights and positive-definite one-dimensional covariances. The likelihood $L_\varepsilon$ is unbounded above as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$; hence its log likelihood is unbounded above as well.

## Example references

[[def-finite-gaussian-mixture]] — the finite-mixture likelihood and Gaussian density formula.

[[thm-finite-gaussian-component-density-normalized]] — the component functions are normalized probability densities for every $\varepsilon>0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume AC; take observations $0,1$, two components with weights $1/2,1/2$, common mean $0$, and variances $\varepsilon^2$ and $1$ with $\varepsilon>0$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is the stated assumption of the finite-Gaussian definition and the local component-density normalization theorem.

[F1] [[def-finite-gaussian-mixture]]: the one-dimensional component density is $\phi_1(x;\mu,s^2)=(2\pi s^2)^{-1/2}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2s^2)}$ and the sample likelihood is the product of the mixture densities at the observations.

[F2] [[thm-finite-gaussian-component-density-normalized]]: for each $s^2>0$, the displayed component function is a normalized Gaussian density and is finite and positive at every real observation.

[F3] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\log$ is the increasing inverse of $\exp$, so $\log(\exp R)=R$ for every real $R$.

## Proof
1.1 Let $f_\varepsilon$ be the mixture density. From [F1], $f_\varepsilon(0)=\tfrac12\phi_1(0;0,\varepsilon^2)+\tfrac12\phi_1(0;0,1)\ge\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\pi}\,\varepsilon}.$ Also $f_\varepsilon(1)=\tfrac12\phi_1(1;0,\varepsilon^2)+\tfrac12\phi_1(1;0,1)\ge\frac{e^{-1/2}}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}>0.$ These bounds hold for every $\varepsilon>0$, for which both variances are positive; [F2] supplies the stated density interpretation under [A1]. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The sample likelihood $L_\varepsilon=f_\varepsilon(0)f_\varepsilon(1)$ therefore satisfies $L_\varepsilon\ge\frac{e^{-1/2}}{8\pi\varepsilon}.$ Given any real $R$, choose $0<\varepsilon<e^{-1/2}/(8\pi e^R)$; then step 1.1 gives $L_\varepsilon>e^R$. By [F3], $\log L_\varepsilon>\log(e^R)=R$. Thus both the likelihood and its log are unbounded above. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $n\ge1$, $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let $W=(w_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfy $w_{ij}=w_{ji}\ge0$ and $w_{ii}=0$. Define $d_i=\sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij}$, $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)$, and $L=D-W$. The support graph has vertex set $V$ and edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $w_{ij}>0$; isolated vertices are singleton connected components. Put $V_+=\{i\in V:d_i>0\}$, let $D_+$ and $L_+$ be the principal submatrices indexed by $V_+$, and, only when $V_+\ne\varnothing$, define $L_{\mathrm{sym},+}=D_+^{-1/2}L_+D_+^{-1/2}$ on $\mathbb R^{V_+}$.

## Statement

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric, let $\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_n$ be its real eigenvalues repeated with multiplicity, and define $\operatorname{tr}(B)=\sum_i B_{ii}$ for square $B$. For $1\le k\le n$, $$\min_{Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times k},\ Q^TQ=I_k}\operatorname{tr}(Q^TAQ)=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i.$$ The minimum is attained by taking the columns of $Q$ to be orthonormal eigenvectors for the $k$ smallest eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity; when an eigenvalue at the cutoff is repeated, the minimizer need not be unique.

## Statement references

[Ulrike von Luxburg, A Tutorial on Spectral Clustering, Statistics and Computing 17(4), 2007](https://cs.brown.edu/courses/csci1820/spring-2022/resources/vonLuxburg_2007.pdf)

[Jean Gallier, Notes on Elementary Spectral Graph Theory: Applications to Graph Clustering Using Normalized Cuts, 2013](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1311.2492)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real symmetric matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and an integer $1\le k\le n$.

[F1] [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]: a self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F2] [[cor-rayleigh-quotient-extreme-eigenvalue-characterisation]]: for a self-adjoint endomorphism with eigenvalues ordered decreasingly, the minimum nonzero-vector Rayleigh quotient is the smallest eigenvalue.

## Proof

1.1 If $k=1$, every feasible $Q$ is a unit column $q$, so $\operatorname{tr}(Q^TAQ)=q^TAq=R_A(q)$. By [F2], its minimum is the smallest eigenvalue, which is $\lambda_1$ in the increasing order of the Statement. [given, F2, algebra]

1.2 Suppose $k\ge2$. By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $u_1,\ldots,u_n$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_n$, and let $U$ be the matrix with these columns. For any feasible $Q$, put $C=U^TQ$; then $C^TC=I_k$ and $Q^TAQ=C^T\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)C$. Writing $c_{ij}$ for the entries of $C$ and $p_i=\sum_{j=1}^k c_{ij}^2$, direct expansion of the diagonal sum gives $\operatorname{tr}(Q^TAQ)=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i p_i$. [given, F1, algebra, choose]

2.1 The matrix $P=CC^T$ is symmetric and idempotent because $C^TC=I_k$. Hence it is the orthogonal projection onto the column space of $C$, and $p_i=e_i^TPe_i=\|Pe_i\|_2^2$ lies in $[0,1]$. Also $\sum_i p_i=\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}^2=\sum_j(C^TC)_{jj}=k$. [given, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Using $\sum_i p_i=k$, subtract the bottom-$k$ eigenvalue sum to obtain $$\sum_i\lambda_i p_i-\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=\sum_{i=1}^k(\lambda_k-\lambda_i)(1-p_i)+\sum_{i=k+1}^n(\lambda_i-\lambda_k)p_i\ge0.$$ Every term on the right is nonnegative. Taking $Q=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$ gives equality, so the stated minimum is attained. This proves the claim for $k\ge2$ as well as the $k=1$ case of step 1.1. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra, construct] ∎

## Statement

If $T$ is self-adjoint on a nonzero finite-dimensional real inner product space and its
eigenvalues are ordered as

$$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n,$$

then

$$\lambda_1=\max_{v\ne0} R_T(v)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \lambda_n=\min_{v\ne0} R_T(v).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A self-adjoint endomorphism $T$ on a nonzero finite-dimensional real inner product space.

[L1] Courant-Fischer gives $\lambda_k=\min_{\dim W=n-k+1}\max_{0\ne v\in W}R_T(v)=\max_{\dim U=k}\min_{0\ne v\in U}R_T(v)$ ([[thm-courant-fischer-min-max-principle]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Taking $k=1$ in [L1] gives $\lambda_1=\max_{\dim U=1}\min_{0\ne v\in U}R_T(v)=\max_{v\ne0}R_T(v)$, because every one-dimensional subspace consists of the nonzero scalar multiples of any one of its nonzero vectors. [L1]

2.1 Taking $k=n$ in [L1] gives $\lambda_n=\min_{\dim W=1}\max_{0\ne v\in W}R_T(v)=\min_{v\ne0}R_T(v)$ for the same reason. [L1] ∎

## Statement

Let $m\ge1$, let $E$ be a subspace of $\mathbb R^m$ with its standard inner product, and let $P_E$ be the orthogonal projection onto $E$. Let $e_1,\ldots,e_m$ be the standard coordinate vectors. Start a list with an optional unit vector $q_0\in E$. For each $i=1,\ldots,m$ in order, set $v_i=P_Ee_i$, subtract from $v_i$ its orthogonal projections onto the vectors already in the list, discard the residual if it is zero, and otherwise append the residual divided by its Euclidean norm. The resulting list is an orthonormal basis of $E$, beginning with $q_0$ when it is supplied.

## Statement references

[Ulrike von Luxburg, A Tutorial on Spectral Clustering, Statistics and Computing 17(4), 2007](https://cs.brown.edu/courses/csci1820/spring-2022/resources/vonLuxburg_2007.pdf)

[Jean Gallier, Notes on Elementary Spectral Graph Theory: Applications to Graph Clustering Using Normalized Cuts, 2013](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1311.2492)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A subspace $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ with the standard inner product, its orthogonal projection $P_E$, the standard coordinate vectors $e_1,\ldots,e_m$, and an optional unit vector $q_0\in E$.

[F1] [[def-orthogonal-projection]]: every vector has a unique decomposition as a component in $E$ plus a component in $E^\perp$, and $P_Ev$ is the $E$-component.

## Proof

1.1 Write $x=\sum_{i=1}^m x_i e_i$. The unique decompositions of two vectors add, and scalar multiples of a decomposition remain decompositions, so uniqueness makes $P_E$ linear. If $x\in E$, its decomposition is $x+0$, hence $P_Ex=x$. Therefore $x=P_Ex=\sum_i x_iP_Ee_i$, and the projected coordinate vectors span $E$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Start with $q_0$ if supplied, then process $v_i=P_Ee_i$ in order. Each residual $r_i=v_i-\sum_j\langle v_i,b_j\rangle b_j$ lies in $E$ and is orthogonal to every previously accepted orthonormal vector $b_j$. If $r_i=0$, then $v_i$ is already in their span; if $r_i\ne0$, appending $r_i/\|r_i\|_2$ preserves orthonormality and the span of all processed vectors. By induction, after the finite scan the accepted list is orthonormal and spans the initial vector together with all $P_Ee_i$. Step 1.1 shows this span is $E$, and the initial unit vector is first when present. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra, construct] ∎

## Definition

Let $n\ge1$, $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let $W=(w_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric, entrywise nonnegative, and zero-diagonal. Define $d_i=\sum_jw_{ij}$, $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)$, $L=D-W$, and $V_+=\{i:d_i>0\}$. For $A\subseteq V$, put $A^c=V\setminus A$, $\operatorname{cut}(A,A^c)=\sum_{i\in A,j\in A^c}w_{ij}$, and $\operatorname{vol}(A)=\sum_{i\in A}d_i$. For a partition $\mathcal A=(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$ of $V$ into pairwise disjoint nonempty sets, define $$\operatorname{RatioCut}(\mathcal A)=\sum_{r=1}^k\frac{\operatorname{cut}(A_r,A_r^c)}{|A_r|}.$$ For a partition of $V_+$ into pairwise disjoint nonempty sets, each of positive volume, define $$\operatorname{Ncut}(\mathcal A)=\sum_{r=1}^k\frac{\operatorname{cut}(A_r,A_r^c)}{\operatorname{vol}(A_r)}.$$ For these partitions, the RatioCut indicator column is $h_r=\mathbf1_{A_r}/\sqrt{|A_r|}$, and the Ncut indicator column is $h_r=\mathbf1_{A_r}/\sqrt{\operatorname{vol}(A_r)}$, extended by zero on isolated vertices.

## Statement

Let $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $n\ge1$, let $W$ be symmetric, nonnegative, and zero-diagonal, let $D=\operatorname{diag}(\sum_jw_{ij})$, let $L=D-W$, and let the support graph have edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $w_{ij}>0$. For every $f\in\mathbb R^n$, $$f^TLf=\frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2.$$ Consequently $L$ is positive semidefinite and $$\ker L=\{f\in\mathbb R^n:f\text{ is constant on each connected component of the support graph}\},$$ including isolated singleton components.

## Statement references

[Ulrike von Luxburg, A Tutorial on Spectral Clustering, Statistics and Computing 17(4), 2007](https://cs.brown.edu/courses/csci1820/spring-2022/resources/vonLuxburg_2007.pdf)

[Jean Gallier, Notes on Elementary Spectral Graph Theory: Applications to Graph Clustering Using Normalized Cuts, 2013](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1311.2492)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite symmetric nonnegative zero-diagonal weight matrix $W$, its degree matrix $D$, Laplacian $L=D-W$, support graph, and an arbitrary vector $f\in\mathbb R^n$.

[F1] [[def-finite-weighted-graph-laplacian]]: $d_i=\sum_jw_{ij}$, $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_i)$, $L=D-W$, and the support graph has edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $w_{ij}>0$.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], $f^TLf=\sum_i d_i f_i^2-\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}f_if_j$. Replacing $d_i$ by $\sum_jw_{ij}$, using $w_{ij}=w_{ji}$ to identify the two square sums, and collecting terms gives $f^TLf=\frac12\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}(f_i^2-2f_if_j+f_j^2)=\frac12\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The displayed sum is nonnegative for every $f$, and $L$ is symmetric because both $D$ and $W$ are symmetric. Therefore $L$ is positive semidefinite. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 If $Lf=0$, then $f^TLf=0$. By step 1.1 this is a finite sum of nonnegative terms, so every term with $w_{ij}>0$ vanishes and $f_i=f_j$ on every support edge. Equality propagates along each finite path, hence $f$ is constant on every connected component, including an isolated singleton. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Conversely, suppose $f$ is constant on each support component. For each vertex $i$, every $j$ with $w_{ij}>0$ lies in the same component, so $f_i=f_j$. Hence $(Lf)_i=d_if_i-\sum_jw_{ij}f_j=\sum_jw_{ij}(f_i-f_j)=0$ for every $i$, and $Lf=0$. The two inclusions give the stated kernel equality. [given, F1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

Let $W,D,L,V,V_+$ be as in the finite weighted graph definition. For a square matrix $B$, set $\operatorname{tr}(B)=\sum_i B_{ii}$. If $A_1,\ldots,A_k$ partition $V$, define $H_R\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ by $(H_R)_{ir}=|A_r|^{-1/2}$ for $i\in A_r$ and $0$ otherwise. Then $H_R^TH_R=I_k$ and $\operatorname{RatioCut}(A_1,\ldots,A_k)=\operatorname{tr}(H_R^TLH_R)$. If $A_1,\ldots,A_k$ partition $V_+$, define $H_N\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ by $(H_N)_{ir}=\operatorname{vol}(A_r)^{-1/2}$ for $i\in A_r$ and $0$ otherwise. Then $H_N^TDH_N=I_k$ and $\operatorname{Ncut}(A_1,\ldots,A_k)=\operatorname{tr}(H_N^TLH_N)$.
