## Statement

Let $d\ge1$ and let $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be real symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning $v^TMv\ge0$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^d$. Define $q_M(x,x')=(x-x')^TM(x-x')$ and $d_M(x,x')=\sqrt{q_M(x,x')}$. Then there is a real matrix $L\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ with $M=L^TL$ and, for all $x,x'\in\mathbb R^d$, $d_M(x,x')=\|Lx-Lx'\|_2$. Consequently $d_M$ is nonnegative, symmetric, zero on the diagonal, and satisfies the triangle inequality, without asserting separation of distinct points.

## Statement references

[[def-mahalanobis-pseudometric|Definition of q_M and d_M]]

[[prop-operator-positivity-agrees-with-form-positivity-over-the-reals|Positive semidefinite forms and nonnegative operators over the reals]]

[[thm-non-negative-operator-characterisations|Factorization of nonnegative operators]]

[[def-euclidean-inner-product|Euclidean inner product and norm]]

[[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm|Triangle inequality for the Euclidean norm]]

[[thm-of-square-roots|Nonnegative square-root uniqueness]]

[Weinberger and Saul, §2.1, printed pp. 209–210](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume10/weinberger09a/weinberger09a.pdf)

[Bellet, Habrard, and Sebban, Mahalanobis distance and interpretation, printed pp. 10–11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1306.6709)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $d\ge1$, a real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$, and $x,x'\in\mathbb R^d$.

[F1] For a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, a symmetric bilinear form is positive semidefinite exactly when its associated self-adjoint operator is nonnegative ([[prop-operator-positivity-agrees-with-form-positivity-over-the-reals]]).

[F2] Every nonnegative endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space has the form $S^*S$ for a linear endomorphism $S$ ([[thm-non-negative-operator-characterisations]]).

[F3] The Euclidean inner product is $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^{d}u_jv_j$ and its induced norm satisfies $\|u\|_2^2=\langle u,u\rangle$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F4] The Euclidean norm is nonnegative, symmetric under sign change, vanishes only at zero, and satisfies the triangle inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

[F5] Every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

## Proof

1.1 Regard $M$ as the matrix of an endomorphism $T_M:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$, $T_Mv=Mv$. The associated symmetric bilinear form is $(u,v)\mapsto u^TMv$, so its positive-semidefinite hypothesis and [F1] imply that $T_M$ is nonnegative. [given, F1]

2.1 By [F2], there is an endomorphism $S$ with $T_M=S^*S$. Let $L$ be its real matrix in the standard basis; the Euclidean adjoint has matrix $L^T$, hence $M=L^TL$. [step 1.1, F2, algebra]

3.1 For $h=x-x'$, steps 2.1 and [F3] give $q_M(x,x')=h^TMh=h^TL^TLh=\langle Lh,Lh\rangle=\|Lh\|_2^2$. Both $d_M(x,x')$ and $\|Lh\|_2$ are nonnegative and their squares agree, so [F5] gives $d_M(x,x')=\|Lx-Lx'\|_2$. [step 2.1, F3, F5, algebra]

4.1 Nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the corresponding properties of the Euclidean norm in [F4]. For any $x,y,z\in\mathbb R^d$, $d_M(x,z)=\|Lx-Lz\|_2\le\|Lx-Ly\|_2+\|Ly-Lz\|_2=d_M(x,y)+d_M(y,z)$ by the triangle inequality in [F4]. The pseudometric axioms follow. [step 3.1, F4] ∎

## Statement

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb S^d$ be a closed convex set of real symmetric matrices in the Frobenius metric, let $F:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex, let $\operatorname{svec}:\mathbb S^d\to\mathbb R^m$ be the symmetric vectorization isometry, and define $C'=\operatorname{svec}(C)$ and $f:C'\to\mathbb R$ by $f(z)=F(\operatorname{svec}^{-1}(z))$. Then $C'$ is closed and convex and $f$ is convex. If $G$ is a Frobenius subgradient of $F$ at $M\in C$, meaning $F(N)\ge F(M)+\langle G,N-M\rangle_F$ for every $N\in C$, then $\operatorname{svec}(G)$ is a Euclidean subgradient of $f$ at $\operatorname{svec}(M)$.

## Statement references

[[lem-symmetric-matrix-frobenius-isometry|Symmetric vectorization preserves inner products and distances]]

[[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential|Subgradient inequality on a convex domain]]

[[def-euclidean-inner-product|Euclidean inner product in coordinates]]

[[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets|Convex functions]]

[[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space|Convex sets]]

[[def-metric-topology|Closed sets and open complements in a metric topology]]

[[def-metric-ball|Metric balls]]

[Bubeck, §3.1, printed pp. 262–266](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1405.4980)

[Bertsekas, MIT 6.253 Lecture 15, printed pp. 200–205](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-253-convex-analysis-and-optimization-spring-2012/6c63c6219c60378bc27d5b4a9167f1bc_MIT6_253S12_lec_comp.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A closed convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb S^d$, a convex function $F:C\to\mathbb R$, a point $M\in C$, and a Frobenius subgradient $G$ at $M$.

[F1] The map $\operatorname{svec}$ is a linear bijection and preserves inner products and distances ([[lem-symmetric-matrix-frobenius-isometry]]).

[F2] A function is convex when it satisfies the convex-combination inequality, and a set is convex when it contains every convex combination of its points ([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]], [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]).

[F3] A set is closed when its complement is open, and an open set contains a positive-radius ball around each of its points ([[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metric-ball]]).

[F4] A subgradient supplies a global supporting affine lower bound on the convex function ([[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]]).

## Proof

1.1 If $z_0,z_1\in C'$, choose $M_0,M_1\in C$ with $z_i=\operatorname{svec}(M_i)$. For $t\in[0,1]$, linearity gives $tz_0+(1-t)z_1=\operatorname{svec}(tM_0+(1-t)M_1)$, and the matrix on the right is in $C$ by [F2]. Thus $C'$ is convex. [given, F1, F2, construct]

1.2 Let $z\notin C'$ and set $M=\operatorname{svec}^{-1}(z)\notin C$. Since $C$ is closed, [F3] gives $r>0$ such that $B_F(M,r)\subseteq\mathbb S^d\setminus C$, where $B_F(M,r)=\{A\in\mathbb S^d:\|A-M\|_F<r\}$. For any $w\in B_2(z,r)$, isometry [F1] gives $\operatorname{svec}^{-1}(w)\in B_F(M,r)$, hence $w\notin C'$. Therefore $B_2(z,r)\subseteq\mathbb R^m\setminus C'$, so the complement of $C'$ is open and $C'$ is closed. [given, F1, F3]

1.3 For $z_0,z_1\in C'$ with preimages $M_0,M_1$, linearity yields $\operatorname{svec}^{-1}(tz_0+(1-t)z_1)=tM_0+(1-t)M_1$. Applying convexity of $F$ from [given] proves $f(tz_0+(1-t)z_1)\le t f(z_0)+(1-t)f(z_1)$, so $f$ is convex. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Let $z=\operatorname{svec}(M)$ and take any $w\in C'$, with preimage $N\in C$. The assumed subgradient inequality gives $f(w)=F(N)\ge F(M)+\langle G,N-M\rangle_F$. By inner-product preservation [F1], this equals $f(z)+\langle\operatorname{svec}(G),w-z\rangle_2$; hence $\operatorname{svec}(G)$ is a Euclidean subgradient by [F4]. [given, F1, F4] ∎

## Definition

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be convex ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). The function $f:C\to\mathbb R$ is convex when $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for all $x,y\in C$ and $t\in[0,1]$. The parameter interval is the closed interval of [[def-interval]].

It is strictly convex when the inequality is strict for distinct $x,y$ and $0<t<1$. No strict inequality is required at $t=0$ or $t=1$, where the two sides coincide. The empty set and a singleton support convex functions, and strict convexity on either is vacuous.

## Definition

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

## Definition

Let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex on a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]), and let $a\in C$. A vector $v$ is a subgradient of $f$ at $a$ when $f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle$ for every $y$ in the domain.

The **subdifferential** is the set

$$\partial f(a):=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle\text{ for every }y\in C\},$$

with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The definition permits $\partial f(a)$ to be empty or to contain more than one vector.

## Statement

Let $d,n,C$ be positive integers, let $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^{n}$ be a finite sample with $x_i\in\mathbb R^d$ and $y_i\in\{1,\ldots,C\}$, let each fixed target set satisfy $N_i\subseteq\{j\ne i:y_j=y_i\}$, and let $\mu\in[0,1]$. For symmetric $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ write $q_M(x,x')=(x-x')^TM(x-x')$ and define

$$F_\mu(M)=(1-\mu)\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\in N_i}q_M(x_i,x_j)+\mu\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\in N_i}\sum_{\substack{1\le l\le n\\y_l\ne y_i}}[1+q_M(x_i,x_j)-q_M(x_i,x_l)]_+,$$

where $[z]_+=\max\{z,0\}$. Then $F_\mu$ is convex on the real vector space of symmetric matrices. The feasible set $\mathbb S_+^d=\{M=M^T:v^TMv\ge0\text{ for all }v\in\mathbb R^d\}$ is convex, so minimizing $F_\mu$ over $\mathbb S_+^d$ is a convex optimization problem.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite sample, fixed target sets, and parameter $\mu\in[0,1]$ in the Statement.

[F1] For fixed $a,b\in\mathbb R^d$, $q_M(a,b)=\operatorname{tr}(M(a-b)(a-b)^T)$, so it is affine-linear in the entries of $M$ ([[def-lmnn-fixed-target-objective]], [[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]).

[F2] A real-valued function on a convex set is convex when its value at every convex combination is at most the same convex combination of its values ([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]).

[F3] A subset of a real vector space is convex when it contains every convex combination of any two of its points ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]).

## Proof

1.1 For each fixed pair $(i,j)$, let $C_{ij}=(x_i-x_j)(x_i-x_j)^T$. By [F1], $q_M(x_i,x_j)=\operatorname{tr}(MC_{ij})$ is linear in $M$, so every pull term is affine-linear. Each margin expression $h_{ijl}(M)=1+\operatorname{tr}(M(C_{ij}-C_{il}))$ is also affine-linear. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For any affine-linear $h$ and $0\le t\le1$, $h(tM+(1-t)N)=t h(M)+(1-t)h(N)$. The number $t[h(M)]_++(1-t)[h(N)]_+$ is at least $0$ and at least $t h(M)+(1-t)h(N)$, hence it is at least their maximum $[h(tM+(1-t)N)]_+$. Thus each hinge term is convex by [F2]. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Finite sums of affine-linear functions and convex hinge functions are convex, and the coefficients $1-\mu$ and $\mu$ are nonnegative because $\mu\in[0,1]$. Applying the convexity inequality term by term proves $F_\mu$ is convex on all symmetric matrices, including the endpoint cases $\mu=0$ and $\mu=1$. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, algebra]

4.1 If $M,N\in\mathbb S_+^d$ and $0\le t\le1$, then $tM+(1-t)N$ is symmetric and for every $v$, $v^T(tM+(1-t)N)v=t\,v^TMv+(1-t)\,v^TNv\ge0$. Hence $\mathbb S_+^d$ is convex by [F3]. Restricting the already convex function $F_\mu$ to this convex feasible set yields a convex optimization problem. [F3, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Fix the finite labeled sample, fixed target sets, and $\mu\in[0,1]$ of the LMNN objective. For each $j\in N_i$ and each impostor index $l$ with $y_l\ne y_i$, set $C_{ij}=(x_i-x_j)(x_i-x_j)^T$, $D_{ijl}=C_{ij}-C_{il}$, and $h_{ijl}(M)=1+\langle M,D_{ijl}\rangle_F$, where $\langle A,B\rangle_F=\sum_{r,s}A_{rs}B_{rs}$. Define $\gamma_{ijl}(M)=1$ if $h_{ijl}(M)>0$ and $\gamma_{ijl}(M)=0$ if $h_{ijl}(M)\le0$. Put

$$G(M)=(1-\mu)\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}C_{ij}+\mu\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}\sum_{l:y_l\ne y_i}\gamma_{ijl}(M)D_{ijl}.$$

For the convex objective $F_\mu$ on $\mathbb S_+^d$, a Frobenius subgradient at $M$ means a symmetric matrix $G$ such that $F_\mu(N)\ge F_\mu(M)+\langle G,N-M\rangle_F$ for every $N\in\mathbb S_+^d$. Then $G(M)$ is a subgradient at every $M\in\mathbb S_+^d$. Moreover, uniformly in $M$,

$$\|G(M)\|_F\le B_{\rm data}:=(1-\mu)\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2+\mu\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}\sum_{l:y_l\ne y_i}\bigl(\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2+\|x_i-x_l\|_2^2\bigr).$$

At an exact hinge kink $h_{ijl}(M)=0$, the selected subgradient coefficient is $0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite sample, fixed target sets and weight $\mu$ in the Statement, and $M\in\mathbb S_+^d$.

[F1] The objective is the finite weighted sum of linear pull terms and positive-part hinge terms with affine arguments ([[def-lmnn-fixed-target-objective]]).

[F2] The objective is convex on $\mathbb S_+^d$ ([[thm-lmnn-fixed-target-objective-is-convex]]).

[F3] A subgradient is a vector whose inner product gives a global supporting affine lower bound on the convex function ([[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]]).

[F4] The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean entry norm and satisfies the triangle inequality ([[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]).

## Proof

1.1 For $a_{ij}=x_i-x_j$, the entrywise inner product satisfies $\langle M,C_{ij}\rangle_F=\sum_{r,s}M_{rs}(a_{ij})_r(a_{ij})_s=a_{ij}^TMa_{ij}=q_M(x_i,x_j)$. Thus each hinge has the form $\phi(M)=\max\{0,1+\langle M,D_{ijl}\rangle_F\}$, with affine argument $h_{ijl}(M)$. [F1, algebra]

1.2 For any $a\in\mathbb R^d$, $\|aa^T\|_F^2=\sum_{r,s}(a_ra_s)^2=(\sum_r a_r^2)^2$, so $\|C_{ij}\|_F=\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2$. By [F4], $\|D_{ijl}\|_F\le\|C_{ij}\|_F+\|C_{il}\|_F=\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2+\|x_i-x_l\|_2^2$. [F4, algebra]

2.1 If $h_{ijl}(M)>0$, then $\phi(M)=h_{ijl}(M)$ and $\phi(N)\ge h_{ijl}(N)=\phi(M)+\langle D_{ijl},N-M\rangle_F$ for every $N$. If $h_{ijl}(M)\le0$, then $\phi(M)=0$ and $\phi(N)\ge0=\phi(M)+\langle0,N-M\rangle_F$ for every $N$. Hence $\gamma_{ijl}(M)D_{ijl}$ is a subgradient of this hinge, including the selected zero coefficient at equality. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Each $C_{ij}$ and $D_{ijl}$ is symmetric, so their weighted sum $G(M)$ is symmetric. Each pull term is linear with Frobenius subgradient $C_{ij}$. Adding its supporting equality to the hinge supporting inequalities in step 2.1, weighted by the nonnegative coefficients $1-\mu$ and $\mu$, proves $F_\mu(N)\ge F_\mu(M)+\langle G(M),N-M\rangle_F$ for every $N\in\mathbb S_+^d$. Thus $G(M)$ is a subgradient by [F3]. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, F3, algebra]

4.1 Since each $\gamma_{ijl}(M)\in\{0,1\}$, the triangle inequality and step 1.2 give $\|G(M)\|_F\le(1-\mu)\sum_{i,j\in N_i}\|C_{ij}\|_F+\mu\sum_{i,j\in N_i,l:y_l\ne y_i}\|D_{ijl}\|_F\le B_{\rm data}$. The bound is finite because the sample and all index sets are finite, and it is independent of $M$. [step 1.2, given, F4, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Use the finite sample, fixed target sets, weight $\mu\in[0,1]$, and objective $F_\mu$ defined by the LMNN objective item. The inputs are an integer budget $T\ge1$, an initial matrix $M_0\in\mathbb S_+^d$, and positive step sizes $\eta_0,\ldots,\eta_{T-1}$. Let $m=d(d+1)/2$ and use $\operatorname{svec}:\mathbb S^d\to\mathbb R^m$, the linear isometry that lists the diagonal entries followed by the $\sqrt2$-scaled upper-triangle entries in lexicographic order. Set $C'=\operatorname{svec}(\mathbb S_+^d)$ and $f(z)=F_\mu(\operatorname{svec}^{-1}(z))$; this is a nonempty closed convex domain and $f$ is convex.

Initialize $z_0=\operatorname{svec}(M_0)$. At each $t=0,\ldots,T-1$, put $M_t=\operatorname{svec}^{-1}(z_t)$ and compute the Frobenius subgradient

$$G_t=(1-\mu)\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}C_{ij}+\mu\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}\sum_{l:y_l\ne y_i}\gamma_{ijl}(M_t)(C_{ij}-C_{il}),$$

where $C_{ij}=(x_i-x_j)(x_i-x_j)^T$, $h_{ijl}(M)=1+\langle M,C_{ij}-C_{il}\rangle_F$, $\gamma_{ijl}(M)=1$ when $h_{ijl}(M)>0$, and $\gamma_{ijl}(M)=0$ when $h_{ijl}(M)\le0$. Supply the successful oracle response $(f(z_t),\operatorname{svec}(G_t))$ to the finite-budget projected-subgradient method on $C'$ with step size $\eta_t$. It updates $z_{t+1}=P_{C'}(z_t-\eta_t\operatorname{svec}(G_t))$, where $P_{C'}$ is the unique nearest point in the Euclidean norm. Equivalently, form $A_t=M_t-\eta_tG_t$, choose an orthogonal eigendecomposition $A_t=U_t\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{t,1},\ldots,\lambda_{t,d})U_t^T$, and set

$$M_{t+1}=U_t\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\max\{\lambda_{t,1},0\},\ldots,\max\{\lambda_{t,d},0\}\bigr)U_t^T.$$

All $T$ oracle calls succeed; the generic method reports budget-exhausted after $T$ updates. The requested final iterate is $M_T$; its status, completed update count, weighted average, and least-index best observed iterate are also defined by the generic method. The explicit spectral-clipping implementation is choice-free. The equivalent abstract Hilbert-projection interface assumes Countable Choice, as in the general closest-point theorem; that axiom branch is retained separately for the conditional analysis. This finite procedure makes no unconditional convergence, optimality, empirical-error, or generalization claim.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $d,n,C$ be positive integers, let $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^{n}$ be a finite sample with $x_i\in\mathbb R^d$ and $y_i\in\{1,\ldots,C\}$, let fixed target sets satisfy $N_i\subseteq\{j\ne i:y_j=y_i\}$, and let $\mu\in[0,1]$. For symmetric $M$ put $q_M(x,x')=(x-x')^TM(x-x')$ and

$$F_\mu(M)=(1-\mu)\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}q_M(x_i,x_j)+\mu\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}\sum_{l:y_l\ne y_i}[1+q_M(x_i,x_j)-q_M(x_i,x_l)]_+,$$

where $[z]_+=\max\{z,0\}$, and minimize over $\mathbb S_+^d=\{M=M^T:v^TMv\ge0\text{ for every }v\in\mathbb R^d\}$. Let $T\ge1$ be an integer, choose $M_0\in\mathbb S_+^d$ and step sizes $\eta_0,\ldots,\eta_{T-1}>0$, and suppose a global minimizer $M^*\in\mathbb S_+^d$ of $F_\mu$ exists. For each $t<T$, put $C_{ij}=(x_i-x_j)(x_i-x_j)^T$, $h_{ijl}(M)=1+\langle M,C_{ij}-C_{il}\rangle_F$, and $\gamma_{ijl}(M)=1$ if $h_{ijl}(M)>0$ and $0$ if $h_{ijl}(M)\le0$. Form

$$G_t=(1-\mu)\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}C_{ij}+\mu\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}\sum_{l:y_l\ne y_i}\gamma_{ijl}(M_t)(C_{ij}-C_{il}),\qquad M_t-\eta_tG_t=U_t\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{t,1},\ldots,\lambda_{t,d})U_t^T,$$

where $U_t$ is orthogonal, and define

$$M_{t+1}=U_t\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\max\{\lambda_{t,1},0\},\ldots,\max\{\lambda_{t,d},0\}\bigr)U_t^T.$$

Set

$$A_T=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\eta_t,\qquad \overline M_T=\frac{1}{A_T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\eta_tM_t,$$

let $M_{\rm best}$ be the least-index minimizer of $F_\mu(M_t)$ over $0\le t<T$, and define

$$B_{\rm data}=(1-\mu)\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2+\mu\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}\sum_{l:y_l\ne y_i}\bigl(\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2+\|x_i-x_l\|_2^2\bigr),\qquad R=\|M_0-M^*\|_F,$$

where $\|z\|_2=(\sum_{r=1}^d z_r^2)^{1/2}$ and $\|\cdot\|_F$ is the entry-sum Frobenius norm.

Then $A_T>0$, $M_{\rm best},\overline M_T\in\mathbb S_+^d$, and

$$\max\{F_\mu(M_{\rm best})-F_\mu(M^*),\,F_\mu(\overline M_T)-F_\mu(M^*)\}\le\frac{R^2+B_{\rm data}^2\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\eta_t^2}{2A_T}.$$

This conditional bound applies to the best observed iterate and weighted average; it does not assert the same bound for the final iterate $M_T$ or any test-error improvement.

[F1] The finite target objective is convex on $\mathbb S_+^d$, and this cone is convex ([[thm-lmnn-fixed-target-objective-is-convex]]).

[F4] Euclidean space $\mathbb R^m$ is complete and hence a real Hilbert space under its Euclidean inner product ([[thm-euclidean-space-complete]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F5] Under Countable Choice, every point of a real Hilbert space has a unique nearest point in each nonempty closed convex set ([[thm-projection-onto-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]]).

[F6] The local subgradient formula returns valid subgradients and satisfies $\|G(M_t)\|_F\le B_{\rm data}$ for every iterate ([[lem-lmnn-explicit-subgradient-and-data-bound]]).

[F7] The finite-budget projected-subgradient method updates $z_{t+1}=P_{C'}(z_t-\eta_tg_t)$ and records its finite status, final iterate, weighted average, and least-index best observed point ([[alg-projected-subgradient-method]]).

[F8] For a convex objective on a nonempty closed convex Euclidean domain, a finite projected-subgradient run with valid bounded subgradients, an attained minimizer, and an initial-distance bound satisfies the stated best-observed and weighted-average gap estimate ([[thm-projected-subgradient-best-and-average-bound]]).

[F9] The explicit eigenvalue-clipping update is the unique Frobenius projection onto $\mathbb S_+^d$ ([[thm-frobenius-projection-onto-psd-cone-is-spectral-clipping]]).

## Proof

1.1 Put $m=d(d+1)/2$ and $C'=\operatorname{svec}(\mathbb S_+^d)$. The cone contains $0$; [F1] makes it convex, [F2] makes it closed in Frobenius distance, and [F3] transfers both properties to $C'$. By [F4], $\mathbb R^m$ is a real Hilbert space; under [A1], [F5] gives a unique Euclidean projection onto $C'$, which is the projection used in [F7]. The explicit matrix update is that projection because [F9] identifies the unique Frobenius-nearest PSD matrix. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F7, F9, given]

1.2 For every $t<T$, the displayed data formula in [F6] computes $G(M_t)$ and its bound. The coordinate transport [F3] makes $\operatorname{svec}(G(M_t))$ a Euclidean subgradient of $f=F_\mu\circ\operatorname{svec}^{-1}$ with norm $\|\operatorname{svec}(G(M_t))\|_2=\|G(M_t)\|_F\le B_{\rm data}$. Thus all $T$ oracle calls in [F7] are valid. [F3, F6, F7, given]

1.3 The point $M^*$ maps to a global minimizer $z^*=\operatorname{svec}(M^*)$ of $f$ on $C'$, the initial point satisfies $\|z_0-z^*\|_2=R$, and the positive step sizes give $A_T>0$. Apply [F8] to the generic run with $N=T$, subgradient bound $B_{\rm data}$, and distance bound $R$. It yields the asserted upper bound for the least-index best observed objective gap and the weighted-average objective gap in Euclidean coordinates. [F3, F7, F8, given, algebra]

2.1 By linearity of $\operatorname{svec}^{-1}$, the Euclidean weighted average maps to $\overline M_T$ as defined in the Statement. Each iterate lies in $\mathbb S_+^d$, so convexity [F1] puts $\overline M_T$ there; bijectivity also preserves the finite-list minimum, so the Euclidean bound from step 1.3 is exactly the displayed matrix bound. [step 1.3, F1, F3, algebra] ∎
## Remarks

The explicit eigenvalue-clipping implementation and its finite local projection formula are choice-free. The proof above separately records the stronger abstract Hilbert-projection route required by the current interface; that branch uses only $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, not the full Axiom of Choice. The hypothesis that $M^*$ exists is essential to this stated application and is not derived from convexity alone.

## Statement

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural $n \ge 1$; $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$ with $d_2(x,y) = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^2}$; a real $\varepsilon > 0$.

[A1] Cauchy criterion in $\mathbb{R}$: every Cauchy sequence of reals converges to a real ([[thm-cauchy-criterion-via-lub]], [[def-real-limit]]).

[L1] The usual metric of $\mathbb{R}$ is $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]).

[L2] Convergence in a metric space: $x_k \to p$ in $(X,d)$ means $d(x_k,p) \to 0$ in $\mathbb{R}$; Cauchyness means $d(x_m,x_n) < \varepsilon$ for $m,n$ beyond an index ([[def-metric-convergence]], [[def-cauchy-in-metric]], [[def-metric-space]]).

[L3] $d_2$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}^n$ for $n \ge 1$, its defining sum is a finite sum, and the sum of squares is nonnegative with a unique nonnegative square root ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-finite-sum]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]).

[L4] Finite sums of nonnegative terms dominate each term and are monotone, and $\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], claims 2 and 4).

[L5] For $a, b \ge 0$: $a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2$ and $a < b \iff a^2 < b^2$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); and $|t|^2 = t^2$ for every real $t$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]).

[L6] A nonempty finite set of naturals has a maximum, and every nonempty set of naturals has a least element ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]], [[thm-well-ordering-principle]]).

[L7] $n \ge 1$ gives $0 < 1/n \le 1$ and $0 < \varepsilon/(2n)$ ([[lem-of-inverse-positive]]).

[L8] Limits of real sequences are unique, which is what licenses writing $\lim_k x_k$ for a sequence already known to converge ([[lem-limit-unique]]).

[L9] Between any two distinct reals lies an embedded rational, in particular below any positive real lies a positive rational ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1] a sequence $(x_k)$ of reals is Cauchy in $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ exactly when $|x_m - x_n| < \varepsilon$ for all $m,n$ beyond an index and every rational $\varepsilon > 0$, which is verbatim the Cauchy condition of [[def-real-limit]]; and $x_k \to p$ in $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ exactly when $|x_k - p| \to 0$, which is verbatim convergence to $p$ there. [L1, L2]

1.2 Let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $j < n$. The terms $(x_k - y_k)^2$ are nonnegative, so $(x_j - y_j)^2 \le \sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^2 = d_2(x,y)^2$; both $|x_j - y_j|$ and $d_2(x,y)$ are nonnegative and $|x_j-y_j|^2 = (x_j-y_j)^2$, so $|x_j - y_j| \le d_2(x,y)$. [L3, L4, L5]

1.3 Let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ satisfy $|x_j - y_j| < \varepsilon/(2n)$ for every $j < n$. Then $(x_j-y_j)^2 \le (\varepsilon/(2n))^2$ for every $j < n$, so $d_2(x,y)^2 \le n \cdot \varepsilon^2/(4n^2) = \varepsilon^2/(4n) \le \varepsilon^2/4 < \varepsilon^2$, and therefore $d_2(x,y) < \varepsilon$. [L3, L4, L5, L7]

2.1 Claim 1: let $(x_k)$ be a Cauchy sequence in $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$. By step 1.1 it is a Cauchy sequence of reals, so by [A1] it converges to some $x \in \mathbb{R}$, and by step 1.1 again $x_k \to x$ in $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$. Hence every Cauchy sequence in $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ converges in it. [step 1.1, A1, L2]

2.2 Now let $(x^{(k)})$ be a Cauchy sequence in $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ and fix $j < n$. By step 1.2, $|x^{(m)}_j - x^{(l)}_j| \le d_2(x^{(m)}, x^{(l)})$ for all $m, l$, so the real sequence $(x^{(k)}_j)_{k}$ is Cauchy, and by [A1] it converges; its limit is unique, so the notation $y_j := \lim_{k} x^{(k)}_j$ denotes a single real. [step 1.2, A1, L2, L8]

3.1 The assignment $j \mapsto y_j$ is a function $n \to \mathbb{R}$, hence an element $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$; no choice is used, because $y_j$ is the unique limit of the $j$-th coordinate sequence. [step 2.2, L3, construct]

3.2 By [L7] and rational density [L9], fix a rational $q>0$ with $\hat q<\varepsilon/(2n)$. For each $j<n$, convergence of its coordinate sequence in step 2.2, as defined in [A1], gives a natural threshold beyond which $|x^{(k)}_j-y_j|<\hat q<\varepsilon/(2n)$. Thus the set of naturals $M$ such that $|x^{(k)}_j-y_j|<\varepsilon/(2n)$ for all $k\ge M$ is nonempty. Let $K_j$ be its least member by [L6], and put $K:=\max\{K_j:j<n\}$, a maximum of a nonempty finite set of naturals since $n\ge1$. [step 2.2, A1, L6, L7, L9, choose]

4.1 For every $k \ge K$ and every $j < n$ we have $k \ge K_j$, hence $|x^{(k)}_j - y_j| < \varepsilon/(2n)$, and therefore $d_2(x^{(k)}, y) < \varepsilon$ by step 1.3. [step 1.3, step 3.1, step 3.2]

5.1 Since $\varepsilon > 0$ was an arbitrary real, $x^{(k)} \to y$ in $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ with $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$; so every Cauchy sequence in $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ converges in it, which with step 2.1 gives claims 1 and 2. [step 2.1, step 4.1, L2] ∎

## Remarks

- **The proof is the Cauchy criterion plus two inequalities.** Step 1.2 says a coordinate difference is at most the Euclidean distance, which turns a Cauchy sequence of points into $n$ Cauchy sequences of reals; step 1.3 says that coordinates uniformly below $\varepsilon/(2n)$ force the Euclidean distance below $\varepsilon$, which turns $n$ convergent coordinate sequences back into one convergent sequence of points. Nothing else about $\mathbb{R}^n$ is used, and in particular the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality is not needed here.
- **The same two inequalities hold for $d_1$ and $d_\infty$**, with the same proof of completeness. For $d_1(x,y) = \sum_{k<n}|x_k-y_k|$: each term is at most the sum ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), so $|x_j-y_j| \le d_1(x,y)$; and $|x_j-y_j| < \varepsilon/(2n)$ for all $j < n$ gives $d_1(x,y) \le n\varepsilon/(2n) = \varepsilon/2 < \varepsilon$. For $d_\infty(x,y) = \max\{|x_k-y_k| : k<n\}$: the maximum dominates each entry and is one of them ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]]), so $|x_j-y_j| \le d_\infty(x,y)$, and entries all below $\varepsilon/2$ make the maximum at most $\varepsilon/2$. Substituting either pair of inequalities for steps 1.2 and 1.3 leaves the rest of the proof unchanged, so $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_1)$ and $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_\infty)$ are complete as well. Nothing later on this page uses that.
- **No choice is spent.** The limit point $y$ is assembled coordinatewise in step 3.1 from limits that are unique, and the finitely many indices $K_j$ of step 3.2 are made canonical by taking the least one. This matters because completeness proofs elsewhere on this page do spend $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and the contrast is worth keeping visible.
- **Where the least-upper-bound property is.** Entirely inside [[thm-cauchy-criterion-via-lub]]. This theorem is a transfer result: it moves completeness from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$ and adds no new content about the reals.

## Definition

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $C\subseteq H$ be nonempty, closed and convex, and let $x\in H$. Then there is exactly one point $p\in C$ with $\|x-p\|=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|$, that is, a unique nearest point of $C$ to $x$.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] A Hilbert space is an inner-product space complete for its induced norm: every Cauchy sequence converges to a point of the space ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

[A2] Every nonempty real set bounded below has an infimum, characterised by points arbitrarily close from above ([[thm-infimum-property]], [[lem-inf-epsilon]]).

[A3] Countable Choice selects a point from each set of a countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[A4] A minimizing sequence in a nonempty convex set is Cauchy ([[lem-minimizing-sequence-in-a-closed-convex-set-is-cauchy]]).

[A5] $C$ is convex and $d\le\|x-c\|$ for every $c\in C$ ([[def-relative-normed-convexity-and-separation]], [[def-infimum]]). A closed set equals its closure, and a point lies in the closure whenever every ball about it meets the set ([[thm-metric-closure-characterisation]]); limits in a metric space are unique ([[lem-metric-limits-unique]]).

[A6] Norm distance is continuous: $\bigl|\|u\|-\|v\|\bigr|\le\|u-v\|$ ([[lem-reverse-triangle-inequality-in-a-normed-space]]).

[A7] Convergence of a sequence of reals to $L$ means that for every $\varepsilon>0$ the terms are eventually within $\varepsilon$ of $L$, and for every $\varepsilon>0$ some $1/n$ is below $\varepsilon$ ([[def-real-limit]], [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]]).

[A8] Every inner-product norm satisfies the parallelogram law ([[thm-parallelogram-law]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** Countable Choice, a real or complex Hilbert space $H$, a nonempty closed convex set $C\subseteq H$ and a vector $x\in H$.

1.1 The set $D=\{\|x-c\|:c\in C\}$ is nonempty and bounded below by $0$, so $d=\inf D$ exists and for every $n$ some $c\in C$ has $\|x-c\|<d+1/(n+1)$ by the epsilon characterisation of the infimum. [A2]

2.1 Countable Choice selects for every $n$ a point $c_n\in C$ with $\|x-c_n\|<d+1/(n+1)$, the sets being nonempty by step 1.1. [step 1.1, A3]

3.1 Then $0\le\|x-c_n\|-d<1/(n+1)$ for every $n$, so $\|x-c_n\|\to d$ by the Archimedean reciprocal bound; hence $(c_n)$ is Cauchy by the minimizing-sequence lemma, completeness of $H$ gives a limit $p\in H$, and closedness of $C$ places $p$ in $C$. [step 2.1, A1, A4, A5, A7]

4.1 Moreover $\|x-p\|=d$: norm continuity along the limit gives $\bigl|\|x-p\|-\|x-c_n\|\bigr|\le\|p-c_n\|\to0$, and a limit of the sequence $\|x-c_n\|$ is unique. [step 3.1, A5, A6]

5.1 If $p,q\in C$ both satisfy $\|x-p\|=\|x-q\|=d$, then the midpoint $\tfrac12(p+q)$ lies in $C$ by convexity, so $\|x-\tfrac12(p+q)\|\ge d$, and the parallelogram law gives $\|p-q\|^2=2\|x-p\|^2+2\|x-q\|^2-4\|x-\tfrac12(p+q)\|^2\le4d^2-4d^2=0$, whence $p=q$: the nearest point is unique. [step 4.1, A5, A8, algebra] ∎

## Definition
Finite sums of vectors in $\mathbb R^n$ use the additive finite-list sum of [[def-linear-combination-and-span]]; sums of real coefficients use [[def-finite-sum]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex. The finite-budget projected subgradient procedure takes $x_0\in C$, an integer budget $N\ge1$, and positive stepsizes $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{N-1}$. At iteration $k$, an oracle returns either failure or a pair $(f(x_k),g_k)$ with $g_k\in\partial f(x_k)$, where subgradient has the meaning in [[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]]. On a valid response set
$$x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k),$$
where $P_C(u)$ is the unique nearest point in $C$ to $u$. On an oracle failure at iteration $k$, return status **oracle-failure**, the feasible current iterate, the completed update count, and the least-index best among values observed so far if any (otherwise report none); a full-horizon average is not returned. If all $N$ calls succeed, return status **budget-exhausted**, the final iterate, the weighted average $\bar x_N=(\sum_{k<N}\alpha_kx_k)/(\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k)$, and a least-index minimizer of observed values among $x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1}$. Report status and completed update count. This finite procedure makes no convergence claim.

## Statement

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex, and run [[alg-projected-subgradient-method]] for $N\ge1$ steps with positive $\alpha_k$. Assume all $N$ oracle calls return valid pairs. Suppose a global minimizer $x^*\in C$ exists and the oracle vectors obey $\|g_k\|_2\le G$; let $R\ge\|x_0-x^*\|_2$. Set $A_N=\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k>0$ and $\bar x_N=A_N^{-1}\sum_{k<N}\alpha_kx_k$. Then
$$\max\left\{\min_{0\le k<N}\bigl(f(x_k)-f(x^*)\bigr),\ f(\bar x_N)-f(x^*)\right\}\le\frac{R^2+G^2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2}{2A_N}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite algorithm [[alg-projected-subgradient-method]], its one-step estimate [[lem-projected-subgradient-one-step-estimate]], convexity [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]], and finite Jensen [[thm-finite-jensen-inequality-in-euclidean-space]].

[F1] For each $k$, $\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|_2^2\le\|x_k-x^*\|_2^2-2\alpha_k(f(x_k)-f(x^*))+\alpha_k^2\|g_k\|_2^2$ ([[lem-projected-subgradient-one-step-estimate]]).

[F2] For a convex function and nonnegative weights summing to one, its value at the weighted average is at most the weighted average of its values ([[thm-finite-jensen-inequality-in-euclidean-space]]).

2.1 By [F3] the iterates lie in $C$, and by [F4] the normalized positive weights sum to one. Apply [F2] to get $f(\bar x_N)-f(x^*)\le A_N^{-1}\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k(f(x_k)-f(x^*))$. ## Definition

Assume AC. Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple undirected graph, with $E$ a set of unordered two-element subsets of $V$. A clique is a nonempty subset $C\subseteq V$ whose distinct vertices are adjacent. Let $(X_i)_{i\in V}$ be random elements on a common probability space, and for $U\subseteq V$ put $\mathcal F_U=\sigma(X_i:i\in U)$, with $\mathcal F_\emptyset=\{\emptyset,\Omega\}$. A path is a finite sequence of distinct vertices with adjacent consecutive vertices; $C$ separates $A$ from $B$ if every path from $A$ to $B$ meets $C$. The pairwise Markov property is $\mathcal F_{\{i\}}\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal F_{\{j\}}\mid\mathcal F_{V\setminus\{i,j\}}$ whenever $i\ne j$ and $\{i,j\}\notin E$. The global Markov property is $\mathcal F_A\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal F_B\mid\mathcal F_C$ whenever $A,B,C\subseteq V$ are pairwise disjoint and $C$ separates $A$ from $B$. If each $X_i$ takes values in a finite nonempty state space $\mathcal X_i$, a finite-state clique-factorized mass function on $G$ is $p(x)=Z^{-1}\prod_{C\in\mathcal C}\psi_C(x_C)$, where $\mathcal C$ is a finite collection of nonempty cliques, $\psi_C:\prod_{i\in C}\mathcal X_i\to(0,\infty)$, and $Z=\sum_{x\in\prod_{i\in V}\mathcal X_i}\prod_{C\in\mathcal C}\psi_C(x_C)$. The product state space and sum are finite, and every potential is positive and finite, so $0<Z<\infty$ and $p$ is a probability mass function. No equivalence between the clique-factorized class and either Markov property is asserted here.

## Definition references

[The Elements of Statistical Learning, §17.2](https://course.ccs.neu.edu/ds4420sp20/readings/ESLII.pdf)

[Evans, Graphical Models, §§4.1–4.3](https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~evans/gms/lecturenotes.pdf)

## Definition

For $N,p\ge1$ and data $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^p$, put $\bar x=N^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^N x_r$ and $S=N^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^N(x_r-\bar x)(x_r-\bar x)^T$. For any symmetric positive-semidefinite $S$ and any $\Theta\in\mathbb S_{++}^p$, set $\ell_S(\Theta)=\log\det\Theta-\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)$, where $\mathbb S_{++}^p$ is the cone of symmetric positive-definite $p\times p$ matrices. Define $\|\Theta\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^p\sum_{j=1}^p|\Theta_{ij}|$, including diagonal entries, and for $\lambda>0$ define $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)=\ell_S(\Theta)-\lambda\|\Theta\|_1$. The off-diagonal-only convention $F^{\mathrm{off}}_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)=\ell_S(\Theta)-\lambda\sum_{i\ne j}|\Theta_{ij}|$ is a separate objective.

      locator: "§§2–3, printed pp. 3–6"
---

## Definition

Assume AC. Let $m,n\ge1$, visible states $v\in\{0,1\}^m$, hidden states $h\in\{0,1\}^n$, biases $a\in\mathbb R^m$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, and weights $W\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$; a finite bipartite graph is specified by requiring $W_{ij}=0$ at every absent visible-hidden edge. Define $E(v,h)=-a^Tv-b^Th-v^TWh$, $Z=\sum_{v,h}\exp(-E(v,h))$, and $p(v,h)=Z^{-1}\exp(-E(v,h))$; $Z$ is finite and positive. Set $p(v)=\sum_h p(v,h)$, and let $V,H$ be the coordinate variables under $p$. For a finite mass function $q$, write $\mathbb E_q[g]=\sum_xq(x)g(x)$. With $\sigma(t)=(1+\exp(-t))^{-1}$, and $\operatorname{Bernoulli}(u;r)$ the mass on $\{0,1\}$ with probability $r$ at $1$, the layer conditionals factorize as
$$p(h\mid v)=\prod_{j=1}^n\operatorname{Bernoulli}\!\left(h_j;\sigma\!\left(b_j+(W^Tv)_j\right)\right),\qquad p(v\mid h)=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname{Bernoulli}\!\left(v_i;\sigma\!\left(a_i+(Wh)_i\right)\right),$$
so each layer is conditionally independent given the other. For one observed $v$, the exact gradients are
$$\frac{\partial\log p(v)}{\partial W_{ij}}=v_i\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v)}[h_j]-\mathbb E_p[V_iH_j],\qquad \frac{\partial\log p(v)}{\partial a_i}=v_i-\mathbb E_p[V_i],\qquad \frac{\partial\log p(v)}{\partial b_j}=\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v)}[h_j]-\mathbb E_p[H_j].$$
These are ambient derivatives in all parameters, evaluated at the specified $W$; when a graph fixes absent-edge weights to zero, retain only allowed-edge derivatives as free parameters. Define $K(v,v')=\sum_h p(h\mid v)p(v'\mid h)$, a row-stochastic transition matrix. Starting from $q_0^v=\delta_v$, let $q_k^v=q_0^vK^k$ for a finite integer $k\ge1$. For one observed $v$, define the finite contrastive-divergence components by
$$\widehat g^{(k)}_{W_{ij}}(v)=v_i\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v)}[h_j]-\sum_{v'}q_k^v(v')v'_i\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v')}[h_j],\quad \widehat g^{(k)}_{a_i}(v)=v_i-\sum_{v'}q_k^v(v')v'_i,\quad \widehat g^{(k)}_{b_j}(v)=\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v)}[h_j]-\sum_{v'}q_k^v(v')\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v')}[h_j].$$
They replace the exact negative-phase expectations under $p(v')$ by expectations under the finite $k$-step law $q_k^v$ and conditional hidden law $p(h\mid v')$. This finite-chain statistic is an approximation; no equality to the exact likelihood gradient or chain-convergence claim is asserted.

## Definition references

[The Elements of Statistical Learning, §17.4.1 and §17.4.4](https://course.ccs.neu.edu/ds4420sp20/readings/ESLII.pdf)

[Hinton, A Practical Guide to Training Restricted Boltzmann Machines, §§2–3](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/absps/guideTR.pdf)

## Bipartite architecture diagram

In this instance the left vertices are visible units, the right vertices are hidden units, and each drawn line is an allowed visible-hidden interaction; its weight may be zero for a particular parameter choice. Omitted pairs have weight fixed to zero. The diagram only records the bipartite interaction pattern. The conditional laws and proofs below follow from the displayed finite-state energy formula.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={draw,circle,minimum size=8mm}]
  \node (v1) at (0,1) {$V_1$};
  \node (v2) at (0,0) {$V_2$};
  \node (h1) at (2,1) {$H_1$};
  \node (h2) at (2,0) {$H_2$};
  \draw (v1)--(h1);
  \draw (v1)--(h2);
  \draw (v2)--(h2);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite binary state spaces, parameters and energy in the Definition, with AC for the library's conditional-independence convention.

[F1] A random element is a measurable map on a probability space, so the visible and hidden coordinate maps are random elements of finite spaces. [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]].

[F2] Conditional independence given a sigma-algebra means factorization of conditional expectations for every pair of bounded measurable real functions. [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]].

[F3] Expectation of an integrable random variable is its Lebesgue integral; on a finite probability space it is the finite weighted sum used in the Definition. [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].

[A1] AC is the explicit hypothesis of the conditional-independence convention, and here means that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The state space $\{0,1\}^m\times\{0,1\}^n$ has $2^{m+n}$ elements. Every term $\exp(-E(v,h))$ is finite and positive, so their finite sum $Z$ is finite and positive; therefore $p$ is a probability mass function. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For fixed $v$, put $c_j=b_j+(W^Tv)_j$. Then $\exp(-E(v,h))=\exp(a^Tv)\prod_j\exp(h_jc_j)$, and summing over binary $h$ gives $\exp(a^Tv)\prod_j(1+\exp(c_j))$. Thus $p(h\mid v)$ is the product of Bernoulli masses with success probabilities $\exp(c_j)/(1+\exp(c_j))=\sigma(c_j)$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For fixed $h$, put $d_i=a_i+(Wh)_i$. Then $\exp(-E(v,h))=\exp(b^Th)\prod_i\exp(v_id_i)$, and summing over binary $v$ gives $\exp(b^Th)\prod_i(1+\exp(d_i))$. Hence $p(v\mid h)$ is the product of Bernoulli masses with success probabilities $\exp(d_i)/(1+\exp(d_i))=\sigma(d_i)$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 For fixed observed $v$, $p(v)=Z^{-1}\exp(a^Tv)\sum_h\exp(b^Th+v^TWh)$. Differentiating these finite sums gives $\partial_{W_{ij}}\log p(v)=v_i\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v)}[h_j]-\partial_{W_{ij}}\log Z$; the same calculation gives $\partial_{a_i}\log p(v)=v_i-\partial_{a_i}\log Z$ and $\partial_{b_j}\log p(v)=\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v)}[h_j]-\partial_{b_j}\log Z$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The product conditional mass functions in steps 2.1–2.2 make the conditional expectations of any bounded measurable functions of disjoint coordinates factor into the product of their conditional expectations. By [F1]–[F2], each layer is therefore conditionally independent given the other in the stated sigma-algebra sense. This use of the conditional-expectation convention is the only proof point needing [A1]. [F1, F2, A1, step 2.1, step 2.2]

3.2 Differentiating the finite partition sum yields $\partial_{W_{ij}}\log Z=\sum_{v',h'}v_i'h_j'p(v',h')=\mathbb E_p[V_iH_j]$, $\partial_{a_i}\log Z=\mathbb E_p[V_i]$, and $\partial_{b_j}\log Z=\mathbb E_p[H_j]$. Substitution in step 2.3 gives the exact gradients in the Definition. [F3, step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 For each visible state $v$, $\sum_{v'}K(v,v')=\sum_h p(h\mid v)\sum_{v'}p(v'\mid h)=\sum_hp(h\mid v)=1$. Thus K is a stochastic matrix and each $q_k^v$ is a well-defined finite probability distribution. Replacing the exact negative-phase marginal $p(v')$ in the gradient formulas by $q_k^v(v')$ gives the finite contrastive-divergence statistic defined in the Statement. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $p\ge2$ and let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ have multivariate normal law $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$ with real symmetric positive-definite covariance $\Sigma$; put $\Theta=\Sigma^{-1}$. For every pair of distinct indices $i,j$, $X_i$ and $X_j$ are conditionally independent given $\sigma(X_k:k\notin\{i,j\})$ if and only if $\Theta_{ij}=0$. Thus the graph whose edges are exactly the nonzero off-diagonal entries of $\Theta$ is the Gaussian pairwise conditional-dependence graph.

## Statement references

[The Elements of Statistical Learning, §17.3.1 and Exercise 17.3](https://course.ccs.neu.edu/ds4420sp20/readings/ESLII.pdf)

[Evans, Graphical Models, §5.1, Proposition 5.2](https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~evans/gms/lecturenotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $p\ge2$, a random vector $X$ with law $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$, and real symmetric positive-definite $\Sigma$.

[F1] A multivariate normal law has the scalar normal projections prescribed by its mean and covariance, including the covariance of every linear projection. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]].

[F2] When $\Sigma$ is positive definite, the law has density $(2\pi)^{-p/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu))$. [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]].

[F3] For a joint density with positive finite marginal sections, normalizing each section gives a regular conditional distribution of the first coordinate given the second. [[thm-conditional-density-formula]].

[F4] Conditional independence given a sigma-algebra is factorization of conditional expectations for every pair of bounded measurable real functions. [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]].

[F5] A scalar $N(m,s^2)$ law has characteristic function $\exp(itm-\tfrac12s^2t^2)$. [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-normal-law]].

[F6] On Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^{r+s}$, product Lebesgue measure agrees with Euclidean Lebesgue measure under countable choice. [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] [[def-countable-choice]].

[F7] AC implies countable choice. [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]].

[F8] The pairwise Markov property tests conditional independence exactly at nonedges of a finite simple undirected graph. [[def-undirected-graphical-model-and-markov-properties]].

[A1] AC is the explicit hypothesis of the conditional-independence convention, and here means that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

## Proof

1.1 Fix distinct $i,j$. By [A1], [F1] and [F2], the joint density of $X$ is the stated nondegenerate Gaussian density; here positive definiteness is an additional hypothesis beyond the singular-covariance multivariate-normal definition. [given, A1, F1, F2]

2.1 Reorder coordinates so $Y=(X_i,X_j)$ and $Z=(X_k)_{k\notin\{i,j\}}$. In the correspondingly permuted precision matrix write $\Theta=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^T&C\end{pmatrix}$, where $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$. For every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^2$, $u^TAu=(u,0)^T\Theta(u,0)>0$, so $A$ is positive definite and $\det A=ad-c^2>0$. If $p=2$, the $Z$ coordinate is a singleton and the following conditional-density calculation is the unconditional bivariate density. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $p>2$, [F7] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F6], so the joint Euclidean density in [F2] is also a density relative to $\lambda_2\otimes\lambda_{p-2}$. Put $u=y-\mu_Y$, $w=z-\mu_Z$, and $D=C-B^TA^{-1}B$. For nonzero $w$, $(-A^{-1}Bw,w)^T\Theta(-A^{-1}Bw,w)=w^TDw>0$, hence $D$ is positive definite. Completing the square gives $u^TAu+2u^TBw+w^TCw=(u+A^{-1}Bw)^TA(u+A^{-1}Bw)+w^TDw$. The section integral over $y$ is therefore positive and finite for every $z$: its $y$ factor is the normalized two-dimensional Gaussian density with precision $A$, multiplied by a finite positive constant. [step 2.1, F2, F6, F7, algebra]

4.1 For $p>2$, use the explicit filler probability concentrated at $(0,0)$ on $\mathbb R^2$ in [F3]; the positive finite marginal sections from step 3.1 show that the conditional law at every $z$ has density $\frac{\sqrt{\det A}}{2\pi}\exp(-\tfrac12(u+A^{-1}Bw)^TA(u+A^{-1}Bw))$. It is the bivariate normal law with mean $\mu_Y-A^{-1}B(z-\mu_Z)$ and covariance $A^{-1}$. For $p=2$, this is the unconditional law with covariance $\Theta^{-1}=A^{-1}$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F2, F3]

5.1 If $\Theta_{ij}=c=0$, then $A$ is diagonal and the conditional density in step 4.1 is a product of two univariate Gaussian densities for every $z$. Its conditional expectations therefore factor for all bounded measurable coordinate functions; [F4] gives $X_i\perp\!\!\!\perp X_j\mid\sigma(Z)$. [step 4.1, F4, algebra]

5.2 Conversely, suppose $X_i\perp\!\!\!\perp X_j\mid\sigma(Z)$. Apply [F4] to the four bounded pairs formed from $\cos(X_i),\sin(X_i)$ and $\cos(X_j),\sin(X_j)$ and combine the resulting identities. For almost every $z$, the conditional joint characteristic function at $(1,1)$ equals the product of its conditional marginal characteristic functions. By [F1], [F4] and [F5], the joint characteristic function from step 4.1 is $\exp(i(m_1(z)+m_2(z))-\tfrac12((A^{-1})_{11}+2(A^{-1})_{12}+(A^{-1})_{22}))$, whereas that product omits the middle covariance term. Equality implies $\exp(-(A^{-1})_{12})=1$, and since $(A^{-1})_{12}$ is real this forces $(A^{-1})_{12}=0$. [step 4.1, F1, F4, F5]

6.1 The inverse of $A$ is $(ad-c^2)^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}d&-c\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$. Since $\det A>0$, $(A^{-1})_{12}=0$ if and only if $c=0$, which is exactly $\Theta_{ij}=0$. Steps 5.1 and 5.2 prove the two implications; by [F8], these are exactly the nonedge and conditional-independence cases of the Gaussian pairwise Markov graph. [step 2.1, step 5.1, step 5.2, F8, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(E,\mathcal S,\mu)$ and $(T,\mathcal T,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces. Let a joint probability $\lambda$ on $E\times T$ have nonnegative product-measurable density $p:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$ relative to $\mu\times\nu$. A fixed probability $\rho$ on $(E,\mathcal S)$ is supplied. Put
$$m(y)=\int_E p(x,y)\,\mu(dx),\qquad D=\{y:0<m(y)<\infty\},$$
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ap(x,y)\,\mu(dx)}{m(y)},&y\in D,\\ \rho(A),&y\notin D.\end{cases}$$

Then K is an everywhere probability kernel from T to E. If $\beta$ is the second marginal of $\lambda$, then $\beta(D)=1$ and
$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy).$$

For any random elements X,Y with joint law $\lambda$, $K(Y,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$. These event identities require no AC. If interpreted with the library's conditional-expectation class existence convention, assume AC. Neither zero nor infinite marginal-density fibres are normalized by the displayed quotient.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses and conventions in the statement.

[F1] Probability-kernel sections must have mass one at every source point and measurable evaluations. [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]].

[F2] Nonnegative product-measurable functions on the stated sigma-finite spaces have measurable section integrals and equal iterated integrals. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]].

[F3] Each nonnegative measurable section density defines a measure. [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

[F4] All conditioning-event identities characterize a supplied RCD. [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]].

[F5] Bounded measurable functions of Y integrate against its marginal. [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]].

[F6] AC is only for the inherited conditional-class existence notation, not for the density construction with supplied rho. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F7] Integrating against a density measure equals integrating the product. [[thm-integration-against-a-density]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F2], m is measurable and $\int_T m\,d\nu=\int p\,d(\mu\times\nu)=\lambda(E\times T)=1$. For each measurable B, apply [F2] to $p\mathbf1_{E\times B}$ to obtain $\beta(B)=\int_Bm\,d\nu$. Put $Z=\{m=0\}$ and $I=\{m=\infty\}$. Then $\beta(Z)=0$. Also $n\nu(I)\le\int m\,d\nu=1$ for all $n\ge1$, so $\nu(I)=0$; the nonnegative integral over this measurable null set is zero, even though m is infinite there, giving $\beta(I)=0$. Therefore $D=T\setminus(Z\cup I)$ is measurable and has full marginal mass. No finite value of m at each point follows from total integrability. [F2]

2.1 For $A\in\mathcal S$, let $a_A(y)=\int_Ap(x,y)\,\mu(dx)$. Tonelli applied to $p\mathbf1_{A\times T}$ makes $a_A$ measurable. It satisfies $0\le a_A\le m$ everywhere. On D both are finite and the denominator is positive, so $a_A/m$ is a measurable real function there; reciprocal and multiplication are continuous on this finite positive domain. Pasting the constant $\rho(A)$ off D proves measurable evaluations of K. For each $y\in D$, [F2] ensures that $p(\cdot,y)$ is measurable and [F3] makes $A\mapsto a_A(y)$ a measure of mass m(y); dividing by this finite positive number gives a probability. Off D, K is the supplied probability $\rho$. This proves [F1], including the empty-event and whole-target evaluations. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3]

3.1 For measurable A,B, the contribution of $B\setminus D$ to the K-integral under $\beta$ is zero because $0\le K\le1$ and $\beta(D^c)=0$. On D the density conversion [F7] and $\beta=m\,d\nu$ give $$\int_BK(y,A)\,\beta(dy)=\int_{B\cap D}\frac{a_A(y)}{m(y)}m(y)\,\nu(dy)=\int_{B\cap D}a_A(y)\,\nu(dy).$$ On Z, $a_A=0$ since $a_A\le m$; on I its integral is zero because I is $\nu$-null. Thus the last integral is $\int_Ba_A\,d\nu$, which equals $\int_{A\times B}p\,d(\mu\times\nu)=\lambda(A\times B)$ by [F2]. All cancellation was restricted to finite positive m. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, F7]

4.1 If X,Y have joint law $\lambda$, [F5] applied to the bounded measurable function $\mathbf1_B(y)K(y,A)$ converts step 3.1 into $$\int_{\{Y\in B\}}K(Y,A)\,dP=P(X\in A,Y\in B).$$ The collection of inverse images $Y^{-1}(B)$ is already a sigma-algebra and is exactly $\sigma(Y)$. These are therefore all required conditioning events. Measurability and probability sections follow from step 2.1 under composition with Y, so [F4] proves the RCD assertion. The proof selected no points, versions or exhaustion: the sigma-finite measures, product density and filler probability are supplied. [F6] is required only when using the library conditional-class existence convention. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F4, F5, F6] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $N,p\ge1$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^p$ be independent observations with common law $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$, where $\Sigma$ is real symmetric positive definite; put $\Theta=\Sigma^{-1}$, $\bar x=N^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^N x_r$, and $S=N^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^N(x_r-\bar x)(x_r-\bar x)^T$. The log-likelihood maximized over $\mu$ is
$$-\frac{Np}{2}\log(2\pi)+\frac N2\bigl(\log\det\Theta-\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)\bigr).$$
Thus, after removing the additive constant and multiplying by $2/N$, the normalized Gaussian profile-likelihood score is $\log\det\Theta-\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)$.

## Statement references

[The Elements of Statistical Learning, §17.3.1](https://course.ccs.neu.edu/ds4420sp20/readings/ESLII.pdf)

[Evans, Graphical Models, §5.2](https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~evans/gms/lecturenotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, observations $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^p$, an iid model $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$ with $\Sigma$ positive definite, and $\Theta=\Sigma^{-1}$.

[F1] For the data, $\bar x=N^{-1}\sum_r x_r$ and $S=N^{-1}\sum_r(x_r-\bar x)(x_r-\bar x)^T$; the score is defined on symmetric positive-definite $\Theta$. [[def-graphical-lasso-objective]].

[F2] A positive-definite multivariate normal law has density $(2\pi)^{-p/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu))$. [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]].

[F3] The law $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$ is the multivariate normal law with the given mean and covariance. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]].

[F4] A probability kernel has probability-measure sections and measurable evaluations; a constant probability law on a singleton source is a probability kernel. [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]].

[F5] A finite product of dominated probability kernels has the product density relative to the product reference measure. [[lem-finite-products-of-dominated-kernels-have-product-density]].

[F6] Independent random elements have joint law equal to the finite product of their marginal laws. [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]].

[A1] AC is an explicit hypothesis of the cited multivariate-normal density supplier; here AC means every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

## Proof

1.1 Each independent observation with the common law in [F3] has the density in [F2]. On the one-point source $\{*\}$, the constant law $K_r(*,\cdot)=N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$ is a probability kernel: its sections are probability measures and each evaluation map is constant, hence measurable [F4]. The density $f_r(*,x)=f_{\mu,\Theta}(x)$ is continuous in $x$ and constant in $*$, hence jointly measurable; [F5] gives the product law density $\prod_{r=1}^N f_{\mu,\Theta}(x_r)$. By [F6], independence identifies this product law with the joint observation law. Its log-likelihood for fixed $\mu$ and $\Theta$ is $$L(\mu,\Theta)=-\frac{Np}{2}\log(2\pi)+\frac N2\log\det\Theta-\frac12\sum_{r=1}^N(x_r-\mu)^T\Theta(x_r-\mu).$$ [given, A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6]

2.1 Write $y_r=x_r-\bar x$, so $\sum_r y_r=0$ and $x_r-\mu=y_r+(\bar x-\mu)$. Expanding and summing removes the cross term: $$\sum_{r=1}^N(x_r-\mu)^T\Theta(x_r-\mu)=\sum_{r=1}^Ny_r^T\Theta y_r+N(\mu-\bar x)^T\Theta(\mu-\bar x).$$ [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Positive definiteness of $\Theta$ makes the last quadratic term nonnegative and equal to zero exactly at $\mu=\bar x$. Therefore $\bar x$ uniquely maximizes $L(\mu,\Theta)$ over $\mu$. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F1], $\sum_r y_ry_r^T=NS$. Cyclicity of the finite matrix trace gives $\sum_r y_r^T\Theta y_r=\sum_r\operatorname{tr}(\Theta y_ry_r^T)=N\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)$. Substituting this identity and $\mu=\bar x$ into step 1.1 yields the displayed profile log-likelihood and its normalization. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$ and let $(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. For each $j<n$, let
$K_j$ be a probability kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T_j,\Tau_j)$, let
$\nu_j$ be sigma-finite on $(T_j,\Tau_j)$, and let
$f_j:S\times T_j\to[0,\infty]$ be a specified
jointly measurable function such that
$$K_j(s,B)=\int_B f_j(s,t_j)\,\nu_j(dt_j)\qquad(B\in\Tau_j).$$
On the finite product spaces, let $K=\bigotimes_{j<n}K_j$ be the product
probability kernel, let $\nu=\bigotimes_{j<n}\nu_j$, and put
$$f(s,t)=\prod_{j<n}f_j(s,t_j),$$
using the extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=0$. Then $f$ is jointly
measurable and, for every $s\in S$, it is a density of $K(s,\cdot)$
with respect to $\nu$ on the entire product sigma-algebra.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A positive finite number of probability kernels $K_j$, sigma-finite measures $\nu_j$, and specified nonnegative jointly measurable densities $f_j$ as in the Statement.

[F1] Finite products of probability kernels exist, are probability kernels, and have the product rectangle formula. [[lem-finite-products-of-probability-kernels]]

[F2] Finite products of sigma-finite measures exist, are sigma-finite, and have the product rectangle formula. [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]

[F3] For a nonnegative product-measurable function, Tonelli gives measurable section integrals and identifies the product integral with either iterated integral. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

[F4] Integrating a nonnegative measurable function over measurable sets defines a measure. [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]

[F5] Measures agreeing on a generating pi-system are equal when that pi-system supplies an increasing finite-measure exhaustion. [[thm-measure-uniqueness-on-a-sigma-finite-pi-system]]

[F6] Extended nonnegative measurability is determined by strict superlevel sets; between any two distinct real numbers there is a rational. [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]], [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]]

[F7] The finite product sigma-algebra is generated by measurable rectangles, and its coordinate projections are measurable. [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** construct the product density and compare its induced measure with the product kernel on rectangles.

**Given:** The hypotheses and conventions in the Statement.

1.1 The product kernel $K$ is a probability kernel by [F1]. Construct the finite product measure recursively: the one-factor case is $\nu_0$, and each next product is sigma-finite by [F2] applied to the preceding sigma-finite product and the next $\nu_j$. By [F7], each coordinate pullback $(s,t)\mapsto f_j(s,t_j)$ is measurable on $S\times\prod_{j<n}T_j$. For two nonnegative extended-measurable functions $u,v$ and $a\ge0$, $$\{uv>a\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q,\ q>0}\{u>q\}\cap\{v>a/q\};$$ when $uv>a$, one can choose a positive rational $q$ with $a/v<q<u$, with the evident choice of any $0<q<u$ when $a=0$; this also covers infinite factors and excludes a zero factor under the stated $0\cdot\infty=0$ convention. For $a<0$ the superlevel set is the whole domain. Thus finite multiplication preserves measurability by [F6], and $f$ is jointly measurable. [F1, F2, F6, F7, given]

1.2 Fix $s$ and define $\lambda_s(A)=\int_A f(s,t)\,\nu(dt)$. By [F4], $\lambda_s$ is a measure. Repeated Tonelli [F3] and the probability-kernel density identities give $$\lambda_s\!\left(\prod_{j<n}T_j\right)=\int\prod_{j<n}f_j(s,t_j)\,d\nu=\prod_{j<n}\int f_j(s,t_j)\,\nu_j(dt_j)=\prod_{j<n}K_j(s,T_j)=1.$$ Hence $\lambda_s$ is a probability measure. [F3, F4, given]

2.1 For a measurable rectangle $R=\prod_{j<n}B_j$, repeated Tonelli and the density identities yield $$\lambda_s(R)=\prod_{j<n}\int_{B_j}f_j(s,t_j)\,\nu_j(dt_j)=\prod_{j<n}K_j(s,B_j)=K(s,R),$$ where the last equality is [F1]. Rectangles form a generating pi-system containing the whole product. Both measures are probabilities by step 1.2 and [F1], so the constant exhaustion by the whole product has common finite mass one. [F5] therefore gives $\lambda_s=K(s,\cdot)$ on the full product sigma-algebra. This holds for every $s$, proving the density assertion. [F1, F5, step 1.2] ∎

## Definition

Input an integer $p\ge2$, a real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix $S\in\mathbb S_+^p$, a real $\lambda>0$, and positive integers $R,K$. The output is either `failure` or a matrix $\Theta\in\mathbb S_{++}^p$. Let $I_p$ be the $p\times p$ identity, $t_+=\max(t,0)$, $\operatorname{sign}(t)=1$ for $t>0$, $0$ for $t=0$, and $-1$ for $t<0$, and $\mathsf{Soft}(t,\lambda)=\operatorname{sign}(t)(|t|-\lambda)_+$. Initialize $W=S+\lambda I_p$.

For each outer sweep $r=1,\ldots,R$, and within it for each original-coordinate index $j=1,\ldots,p$, use the temporary coordinate order $\pi_j=(1,\ldots,j-1,j+1,\ldots,p,j)$. Form the same reindexing of both matrices, $S^{(j)}_{ab}=S_{\pi_j(a),\pi_j(b)}$ and $W^{(j)}_{ab}=W_{\pi_j(a),\pi_j(b)}$, for $1\le a,b\le p$. Set $V=(W^{(j)}_{ab})_{a,b<p}$, $s=(S^{(j)}_{a,p})_{a<p}$, and $d=W^{(j)}_{pp}$. Initialize $\beta=0\in\mathbb R^{p-1}$. For each of $K$ inner sweeps, update coordinates $\ell=1,\ldots,p-1$ in increasing order: if $V_{\ell\ell}\le0$, return `failure`; otherwise set
$$\beta_\ell\leftarrow\frac{\mathsf{Soft}\!\left(s_\ell-\sum_{\substack{1\le k<p\\k\ne\ell}}V_{\ell k}\beta_k,\lambda\right)}{V_{\ell\ell}}.$$

After the inner sweeps, form $\widetilde W^{(j)}=\begin{pmatrix}V&V\beta\\(V\beta)^T&d\end{pmatrix}$. Restore original indexing by forming the candidate matrix $W^{\mathrm{cand}}$ with $W^{\mathrm{cand}}_{\pi_j(a),\pi_j(b)}=\widetilde W^{(j)}_{ab}$ for all $1\le a,b\le p$. Compute a symmetric eigendecomposition of $W^{\mathrm{cand}}$; if any eigenvalue is nonpositive, return `failure`. Otherwise set $W=W^{\mathrm{cand}}$ before proceeding to the next original-coordinate index $j$. After all $R$ sweeps, return $\Theta=W^{-1}$. This bounded truncation of the coupled block and lasso updates makes no convergence or optimizer claim.

## Definition references

[The Elements of Statistical Learning, §17.3.2](https://course.ccs.neu.edu/ds4420sp20/readings/ESLII.pdf)

[Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani, §§2–3](https://hastie.su.domains/Papers/graph.pdf)

## Statement

Let $p\ge2$ be an integer, $S\in\mathbb S_+^p$ be real symmetric positive semidefinite, $\lambda>0$, and $R,K$ be positive integers. Execute the finite-budget block and cyclic-coordinate graphical-lasso procedure with these inputs in exact real arithmetic, treating its finite-dimensional matrix operations as exact operations. The initialized matrix and every accepted matrix $W$ are symmetric positive definite. In every block reached before failure, its principal matrix $V$ is positive definite, every $V_{\ell\ell}>0$, and every coordinate update is well-defined and uniquely minimizes
$$Q_{V,s}(\beta)=\tfrac12\beta^TV\beta-s^T\beta+\lambda\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}|\beta_k|$$
with all other coordinates fixed. Each candidate matrix is finite and symmetric; it is accepted exactly when positive definite. The procedure terminates after at most $RpK(p-1)$ coordinate updates and $Rp$ candidate eigenvalue tests, returning either `failure` or a symmetric positive-definite matrix $\Theta=W^{-1}$. These assertions do not assert convergence of the iterates or global optimality for the sparse-precision objective.

## Statement references

[[alg-graphical-lasso-coordinate-descent]]

[[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The inputs and execution specified in the Statement.

[F1] The procedure initializes $W=S+\lambda I_p$, uses the same temporary permutation for $S$ and $W$, resets $\beta=0$ for each block, makes $K$ finite cyclic sweeps with the specified soft-threshold update, restores the original indexing, accepts a candidate only if all its eigenvalues are positive, and returns $W^{-1}$ after $R$ outer sweeps unless an explicit guard returns `failure`. [[alg-graphical-lasso-coordinate-descent]].

[F2] Every real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis, by applying the real spectral theorem to its self-adjoint endomorphism on Euclidean space. [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Initially $W$ is symmetric, and for every nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^p$, $x^TWx=x^TSx+\lambda\|x\|^2\ge\lambda\|x\|^2>0$. Thus initialization is positive definite. If the current $W$ is positive definite, reindexing both its rows and columns only reindexes this quadratic form. For a nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^{p-1}$, extending $z$ by a last zero in the temporary ordering gives $z^TVz>0$. Hence $V$ is positive definite and $V_{\ell\ell}=e_\ell^TVe_\ell>0$ at each coordinate. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Hold all coordinates except $\beta_\ell=t$ fixed, and write $v=V_{\ell\ell}>0$ and $r=s_\ell-\sum_{k\ne\ell}V_{\ell k}\beta_k$. Expanding the symmetric quadratic gives $Q_{V,s}(\beta)=q(t)+C$, where $q(t)=\tfrac12vt^2-rt+\lambda|t|$ and $C$ is independent of $t$. Put $a=(r-\lambda)/v$ if $r>\lambda$, $a=0$ if $|r|\le\lambda$, and $a=(r+\lambda)/v$ if $r<-\lambda$. In these three cases respectively put $u=1$, $u=r/\lambda$, and $u=-1$. Then $va-r+\lambda u=0$, $|u|\le1$, and $ua=|a|$, so $|t|-|a|-u(t-a)=|t|-ut\ge0$. Consequently $q(t)-q(a)=\tfrac12v(t-a)^2+\lambda(|t|-|a|-u(t-a))\ge\tfrac12v(t-a)^2$, and the lower bound is strictly positive whenever $t\ne a$. Thus $a=\mathsf{Soft}(r,\lambda)/v$ is the unique coordinate minimizer. All quantities are real and division is by a positive number, so finitely many such updates produce a finite real vector $\beta$; the nonpositive-diagonal guard cannot fire while the current $W$ is positive definite. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For such a block, $V\beta$ and $d$ are finite and the block candidate $\begin{pmatrix}V&V\beta\\(V\beta)^T&d\end{pmatrix}$ is symmetric. Restoring original indexing preserves symmetry. By [F2] any symmetric candidate $A$ has a representation $A=UDU^T$ with $U$ orthogonal and $D$ real diagonal. The identity $x^TAx=\sum_iD_{ii}(U^Tx)_i^2$ shows that $A$ is positive definite if all $D_{ii}>0$; conversely applying positive definiteness to $x=Ue_i$ shows that every $D_{ii}>0$. Thus the candidate guard accepts exactly the positive-definite candidates. Initialization, the within-block reasoning and this acceptance rule give induction over all reached blocks: every accepted $W$ is symmetric positive definite, and each later block again has the properties proved above until a candidate guard returns `failure`. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 There are at most $Rp$ blocks, each with $K(p-1)$ coordinate updates and one finite-dimensional eigenvalue test; early failure only decreases these counts. Every reached operation is well-defined by the preceding steps and the stipulated exact matrix operations, so execution terminates with failure or completes all blocks. In the latter case the final $W=UDU^T$ has positive diagonal eigenvalues by step 3.1. Hence $W^{-1}=UD^{-1}U^T$ exists, is symmetric and has $x^TW^{-1}x=\sum_iD_{ii}^{-1}(U^Tx)_i^2>0$ for every nonzero $x$. This proves every asserted property without a convergence or global-optimizer inference. [given, F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathbb S_+^p$ be the real symmetric positive-semidefinite $p\times p$ matrices and $\mathbb S_{++}^p$ the real symmetric positive-definite ones. For $p\ge1$, $S\in\mathbb S_+^p$ and $\lambda>0$, maximize
$$F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)=\log\det\Theta-\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)-\lambda\sum_{i=1}^p\sum_{j=1}^p|\Theta_{ij}|$$
over $\Theta\in\mathbb S_{++}^p$. The objective is strictly concave and attains a unique maximizer $\Theta^*$. A feasible $\Theta$ is this unique maximizer if and only if there is a symmetric matrix $\Gamma$ such that $\Theta^{-1}-S-\lambda\Gamma=0$, with $\Gamma_{ii}=1$, $\Gamma_{ij}=\operatorname{sign}(\Theta_{ij})$ when $\Theta_{ij}\ne0$, and $\Gamma_{ij}\in[-1,1]$ when $\Theta_{ij}=0$.

## Statement references

[The Elements of Statistical Learning, §17.3.2](https://course.ccs.neu.edu/ds4420sp20/readings/ESLII.pdf)

[Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani, §2](https://hastie.su.domains/Papers/graph.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $p\ge1$, $S\in\mathbb S_+^p$, $\lambda>0$, and the symmetric positive-definite domain and all-entry objective in the Statement.

[F1] The all-entry graphical-lasso functional is $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)=\log\det\Theta-\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)-\lambda\sum_{i,j}|\Theta_{ij}|$ on $\mathbb S_{++}^p$. [[def-graphical-lasso-objective]].

[F2] A finite-dimensional nonnegative self-adjoint operator has a factorization $S=R^*R$. [[thm-non-negative-operator-characterisations]].

[F3] A real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis. [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]].

[F4] For a twice continuously differentiable function on an open convex Euclidean domain, positive-semidefinite Hessian everywhere implies convexity. [[thm-hessian-characterises-convexity]].

[F5] Convexity on a convex set is the chord inequality; strict convexity requires strict inequality for distinct points and interior weights. [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]].

## Proof

1.1 By the all-entry objective definition [F1] and the nonnegative-operator factorization [F2], write $S=R^TR$. Thus $\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)=\operatorname{tr}(R\Theta R^T)\ge0$ for $\Theta\succ0$. Also $\|\Theta\|_1=\sum_{i,j}|\Theta_{ij}|\ge\sum_i\Theta_{ii}=\operatorname{tr}\Theta$, since positive-definite matrices have positive diagonal entries. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 The cone $\mathbb S_{++}^p$ is open and convex: positive quadratic forms remain positive under sufficiently small symmetric perturbations, and convex combinations of positive quadratic forms remain positive. For symmetric $H$, determinant expansion gives $\left.\frac{d}{dt}\log\det(\Theta+tH)\right|_{t=0}=\operatorname{tr}(\Theta^{-1}H)$. Differentiating $(\Theta+tH)(\Theta+tH)^{-1}=I$ gives $\left.\frac{d}{dt}(\Theta+tH)^{-1}\right|_{t=0}=-\Theta^{-1}H\Theta^{-1}$, so the second directional derivative is $-\operatorname{tr}(\Theta^{-1}H\Theta^{-1}H)$. [given, F3, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], the eigenvalues $t_1,\ldots,t_p$ of $\Theta\succ0$ are positive and $\log\det\Theta=\sum_k\log t_k$, $\operatorname{tr}\Theta=\sum_k t_k$. Hence $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)\le\sum_{k=1}^p h(t_k)$ for $h(t)=\log t-\lambda t$. The function $h$ is bounded above and tends to $-\infty$ as $t\downarrow0$ or $t\to\infty$. For any $c$, the upper level set $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)\ge c$ therefore forces each eigenvalue into a compact interval $[a_c,b_c]\subset(0,\infty)$: if $M=\sup_{t>0}h(t)$, then each $h(t_k)\ge c-(p-1)M$. These matrices form a closed bounded set of symmetric matrices contained in $\mathbb S_{++}^p$, hence a compact set. Taking $c=F_{S,\lambda}(I)$ gives a nonempty compact upper level set, and continuity of $F$ yields a maximizer. [step 1.1, F3, algebra]

2.2 Let $B=\Theta^{-1/2}H\Theta^{-1/2}$, using the positive square root from the orthonormal eigenbasis [F3]. Then $B$ is symmetric and $\operatorname{tr}(\Theta^{-1}H\Theta^{-1}H)=\operatorname{tr}(B^2)=\|B\|_F^2$, strictly positive when $H\ne0$. Thus the second derivative of $\log\det$ along every nonconstant segment is strictly negative, giving its strict chord inequality. The Hessian of $-\log\det$ is positive semidefinite by step 1.2, so [F4] gives convexity in the chord sense of [F5]. The trace term is linear and the entrywise $\ell^1$ norm is convex by the triangle inequality, so its negative is concave; adding these terms preserves the strict chord inequality. Hence $F_{S,\lambda}$ is strictly concave on its open convex domain. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

2.3 Put $G=\Theta^{-1}-S$. At a maximizer every feasible one-coordinate directional derivative is at most zero, and when the objective is differentiable in both directions its derivative is zero. Since $\Theta_{ii}>0$, the diagonal penalty is locally differentiable with slope $1$, so the diagonal equation is $G_{ii}-\lambda=0$ and $\Gamma_{ii}=1$. For $i<j$, a symmetric perturbation by $t(E_{ij}+E_{ji})$ has smooth derivative $2G_{ij}t$ and changes the penalty by $2\lambda(|\Theta_{ij}+t|-|\Theta_{ij}|)$. If $\Theta_{ij}\ne0$, testing both signs of small $t$ gives $G_{ij}=\lambda\operatorname{sign}(\Theta_{ij})$. If $\Theta_{ij}=0$, taking $t>0$ gives $G_{ij}\le\lambda$ and taking $t<0$ gives $G_{ij}\ge-\lambda$. Defining $\Gamma_{ij}=\Gamma_{ji}=G_{ij}/\lambda$ at zero and the sign otherwise yields the stated KKT equation for the all-entry penalty [F1]. [given, F1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Conversely, suppose $\Theta\succ0$ and a symmetric $\Gamma$ satisfies the stated entrywise conditions and $\Theta^{-1}-S-\lambda\Gamma=0$. Put $T=\Theta^{-1/2}\Theta'\Theta^{-1/2}$ for any $\Theta'\succ0$; its eigenvalues $t_r$ are positive. Since $\log t\le t-1$ for $t>0$ (the function $t-1-\log t$ has its minimum $0$ at $t=1$), $\log\det\Theta'-\log\det\Theta=\sum_r\log t_r\le\operatorname{tr}(T)-p=\operatorname{tr}(\Theta^{-1}(\Theta'-\Theta))$. For each scalar $x$ and each allowed subgradient $\gamma$ of $|x|$, $|y|\ge|x|+\gamma(y-x)$: if $x\ne0$, this follows from $|y|\ge\operatorname{sign}(x)y$, while for $x=0$ it follows from $|\gamma|\le1$. Summing gives $\|\Theta'\|_1\ge\|\Theta\|_1+\sum_{i,j}\Gamma_{ij}(\Theta'_{ij}-\Theta_{ij})$ for the all-entry objective [F1]. Combining these bounds with the linear trace term and the KKT equation yields $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta')-F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)\le\operatorname{tr}((\Theta^{-1}-S-\lambda\Gamma)(\Theta'-\Theta))=0$. Thus every such KKT point is a maximizer. The maximizer exists by step 2.1 and is unique by strict concavity from step 2.2, so the KKT condition is both necessary and sufficient for that unique optimum. [given, F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, algebra] ∎
