## Example

Assume AC. In a binary restricted Boltzmann machine with two visible units, one hidden unit, $a=(0,0)$, $b=0$ and $W_{11}=W_{21}=\log3$, the visible units are independent conditional on the hidden unit. Each conditional success probability is $1/2$ when $H=0$ and $3/4$ when $H=1$. Marginally, $P(V_1=1)=P(V_2=1)=7/10$ and $P(V_1=1,V_2=1)=1/2\ne49/100$, so $V_1$ and $V_2$ are dependent.

## Example references

[Hinton, A Practical Guide to Training Restricted Boltzmann Machines, §2](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/absps/guideTR.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The RBM parameters and binary state spaces in the Example.

[F1] The binary RBM conditionals are products of Bernoulli laws with success probabilities $\sigma(b_j+(W^Tv)_j)$ and $\sigma(a_i+(Wh)_i)$. [[def-restricted-boltzmann-machine]].

[F2] Conditional independence given a sigma-algebra is the bounded-function conditional-expectation factorization. [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]].

[A1] AC is the explicit hypothesis of the conditional-independence convention, and here means every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 With $a_i=0$, $b=0$ and $W_{i1}=\log3$, [F1] gives $P(V_i=1\mid H=h)=\sigma(h\log3)$, which is $1/2$ at $h=0$ and $3/4$ at $h=1$. The conditional visible mass factors as the product of these two Bernoulli masses, so [A1] and [F2] give conditional independence. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Summing the unnormalized joint mass over the two visible bits gives weight $(1+1)^2=4$ to $h=0$ and $(1+3)^2=16$ to $h=1$. Thus $Z=20$ and $P(H=0)=1/5$, $P(H=1)=4/5$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Averaging the conditional success probabilities from step 1.1 yields $P(V_i=1)=\tfrac15\cdot\tfrac12+\tfrac45\cdot\tfrac34=\tfrac7{10}$ for each i. Likewise, conditional independence gives $P(V_1=1,V_2=1)=\tfrac15\cdot\tfrac14+\tfrac45\cdot\tfrac9{16}=\tfrac12$, whereas the product of the marginals is $\tfrac{49}{100}$. Since these differ, the visible variables are marginally dependent. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Take observations $x_1=(1,1)^T$ and $x_2=(-1,-1)^T$, so their centered sample covariance is $S=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Under the all-entry penalty objective, every $\lambda\ge1$ gives the unique maximizer $\Theta=(1+\lambda)^{-1}I_2$ with $\Theta_{12}=0$, while for $0<\lambda<1$ every optimizer has $\Theta_{12}\ne0$. In particular, $\lambda=2$ yields a zero edge and $\lambda=\tfrac12$ yields a nonzero edge.

## Example references

[Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani, §2](https://hastie.su.domains/Papers/graph.pdf)

[The Elements of Statistical Learning, §17.3.2](https://course.ccs.neu.edu/ds4420sp20/readings/ESLII.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two observations and the all-entry graphical-lasso convention in the Example.

[F1] The centered sample covariance and objective use $\|\Theta\|_1=\sum_{i,j}|\Theta_{ij}|$, including diagonal entries. [[def-graphical-lasso-objective]].

[F2] For $S\succeq0$ and $\lambda>0$, the objective has a unique maximizer characterized by the symmetric entrywise KKT condition; at a zero off-diagonal entry the subgradient lies in $[-1,1]$. [[thm-graphical-lasso-convexity-and-kkt]].

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The sample mean is zero, and $S=\tfrac12(x_1x_1^T+x_2x_2^T)=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. This matrix is positive semidefinite because $u^TSu=(u_1+u_2)^2\ge0$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Let $\lambda\ge1$, $a=(1+\lambda)^{-1}$, $\Theta=aI_2$, and let $\Gamma$ have diagonal entries $1$ and off-diagonal entries $-1/\lambda$. Then $\Theta\succ0$, $\Gamma_{12}\in[-1,1]$, and $\Theta^{-1}-S-\lambda\Gamma=0$: the diagonal entries are $(1+\lambda)-1-\lambda=0$ and the off-diagonal entries are $0-1-\lambda(-1/\lambda)=0$. By [F2], this is the unique maximizer, with zero off-diagonal edge. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $0<\lambda<1$. If an optimizer had $\Theta_{12}=0$, its off-diagonal KKT equation from [F2] would require $-1-\lambda\Gamma_{12}=0$ for some $\Gamma_{12}\in[-1,1]$, hence $\Gamma_{12}=-1/\lambda<-1$, a contradiction. Existence in [F2] therefore forces every optimizer to have $\Theta_{12}\ne0$. Taking $\lambda=2$ and $\lambda=\tfrac12$ gives the stated two cases. [given, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $V$ be a finite set of observed vertices, let $G$ be a directed acyclic graph
on $V$, and let $(X_v)_{v\in V}$ be the endogenous variables of a finite
recursive structural causal model whose observed set is all of $V$ and whose
latent set is empty. The model is Markovian: its exogenous random elements are
mutually independent. Require that the full-joint law $P$ of $(X_v)_{v\in V}$
has a topological probability-kernel factorization: for a topological order
$v_1,\ldots,v_p$, its joint law is formed by composing probability kernels
$K_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)},dx_{v_r})$ that depend only on the parents
of $v_r$. Also require that $P$ is faithful to $G$, meaning its conditional
independences among vertex subvectors are exactly the d-separations in $G$.
Assume AC for these probability interfaces.

A **perfect conditional-independence oracle** for this regime accepts any
pairwise disjoint $A,B,S\subseteq V$ and returns “independent” exactly when
$\sigma(X_A)$ and $\sigma(X_B)$ are conditionally independent given
$\sigma(X_S)$. The **causally sufficient perfect-oracle regime** consists of
the finite observed DAG, its Markovian recursive model and full-joint law, the
faithfulness condition, and this exact oracle. No latent vertex is omitted
from the graph supplied to the oracle.

## Definition

Fix a finite vertex set $V$. For a DAG $G$ on $V$, its **skeleton** is the
undirected graph with edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $G$ contains $i\to j$ or
$j\to i$. An **unshielded triple** is a triple of distinct vertices $i,k,j$
with edges $i-k$ and $k-j$ in the skeleton and no edge between $i$ and $j$.
It is an **unshielded collider** (also called a v-structure) when its arrows are
$i\to k\leftarrow j$. Two DAGs on $V$ are **Markov equivalent** when they
induce the same d-separation relations: for every pairwise disjoint
$A,B,S\subseteq V$, $A$ and $B$ are d-separated by $S$ in one DAG exactly
when they are d-separated by $S$ in the other. The equivalence class of $G$ is
denoted $[G]$.

A **partially directed acyclic graph** (PDAG) on $V$ is a simple mixed graph
whose directed edges contain no directed cycle. A **consistent DAG extension**
of a PDAG preserves every directed edge, orients every undirected edge, is
acyclic, and creates no unshielded collider absent from the PDAG. For an
equivalence class with a common skeleton, its **completed pattern** directs an
edge exactly when that orientation occurs in every DAG of the class and leaves
the edge undirected when both orientations occur. A **completed partially
directed acyclic graph** (CPDAG) for $[G]$ is this unique completed pattern
when its consistent DAG extensions are exactly $[G]$. Thus its directed edges
are compelled, while each undirected edge occurs in both directions among its
consistent extensions.

## Statement

Let $G$ be a finite DAG on $V$. For distinct vertices $i,j\in V$, the pair
$\{i,j\}$ is an edge of the skeleton of $G$ if and only if there is no
$S\subseteq V\setminus\{i,j\}$ that d-separates $i$ and $j$ in $G$.

## Statement references

[Kalisch and Bühlmann, §2.1](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume8/kalisch07a/kalisch07a.pdf)

[Lauritzen, Lemma 2.57](https://web.math.ku.dk/~lauritzen/papers/gmnotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite DAG $G$ and distinct vertices $i,j\in V$.

[F1] In a finite DAG, a path is active given $S$ when each internal noncollider is outside $S$ and each collider has a descendant in $S$, with membership in $S$ counted as being its own descendant. [[def-d-separation-in-a-dag]]

## Proof

1.1 If $i$ and $j$ are adjacent, the one-edge path between them has no internal vertices, so it is active given every $S\subseteq V\setminus\{i,j\}$ by [F1]. Hence no such $S$ d-separates them. [given, F1]

1.2 Suppose $i$ and $j$ are nonadjacent. Acyclicity implies that at least one of $i,j$ is not a descendant of the other; after interchanging labels, assume $j$ is not a descendant of $i$. Since $i,j$ are nonadjacent, $j$ is a non-descendant non-parent of $i$. Put $S=\operatorname{pa}_G(i)$. Then $S$ excludes both endpoints. Consider any path $i=v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_r=j$. If its first arrow points into $i$, then $v_1\in S$ and the occurrence of $v_1$ is a noncollider, because the arrow $v_1\to i$ has its tail at $v_1$; the path is blocked. If the first arrow points out of $i$, follow arrows that point forward along the path until the first arrow that points backward. Such a reversal must occur because $j$ is not a descendant of $i$. At the reversal vertex $v_t$, both incident arrows point into $v_t$, so it is a collider and the initial segment is a directed path $i\to\cdots\to v_t$. If $v_t$ had a descendant $p\in S$, then $i\to\cdots\to v_t\to\cdots\to p\to i$ would be a directed cycle. Thus this collider has no descendant in $S$, and the path is blocked by [F1]. Every path is blocked, so $S$ d-separates $i$ and $j$. [given, F1, construct, choose]

2.1 The adjacent and nonadjacent cases prove both implications. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

A **finite directed acyclic graph** (DAG) is a finite vertex set $V$ with an
arrow set $E\subseteq V\times V$ and no directed cycle. A **path** from $u$ to
$v$ is a finite sequence of distinct vertices beginning at $u$ and ending at
$v$ in which each consecutive pair is joined by an arrow in either direction;
the arrows are not required to point along the sequence. An internal vertex of
a path is a **collider on that path** when the two arrows on the path both point
into it, and is a **noncollider** otherwise. A vertex $w$ is a **descendant** of
$v$ if there is a directed path from $v$ to $w$; for this definition
$\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ includes $v$ itself as well as its descendants.

For pairwise disjoint vertex sets $X,Y,C\subseteq V$, a path joining $X$ to
$Y$ is **active given $C$** when every internal noncollider is outside $C$ and
every internal collider has at least one member of $\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ in
$C$. The set $C$ **d-separates** $X$ and $Y$ in $G$ when no path joining $X$ to
$Y$ is active given $C$; write $X\perp_d Y\mid C$ in $G$. The empty set of
vertices is allowed for any of $X,Y,C$; in particular d-separation is vacuous
if either endpoint set is empty.

For $T\subseteq V$, $G_{\underline T}$ is obtained by deleting every arrow
whose tail lies in $T$, and $G_{\overline T}$ by deleting every arrow whose
head lies in $T$. These are graph operations only; they do not by themselves
specify a probability law under intervention.

## Statement

Let $G$ be a finite DAG and let $x\to y$ be a covered arrow, meaning
$\operatorname{pa}_G(y)=\operatorname{pa}_G(x)\cup\{x\}$. Replacing $x\to y$
by $y\to x$ gives a DAG $G'$ with exactly the same d-separation relations as
$G$.

## Statement references

[Lauritzen, Lemma 2.59](https://web.math.ku.dk/~lauritzen/papers/gmnotes.pdf)

[Meek, Appendix](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.4972)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite DAG $G$, a covered arrow $x\to y$, and $G'$ obtained by reversing that arrow.

[F1] D-separation is equivalent to undirected separation by $S$ in the moral graph induced on the ancestors of the endpoints and $S$. [[lem-d-separation-ancestral-moral-separation]]

[F2] The ancestral moral graph keeps the skeleton on the ancestral set and joins distinct parents of each common child in that set. [[def-ancestral-moral-graph-of-a-dag]]

## Proof

1.1 Put $P=\operatorname{pa}_G(x)$, so $\operatorname{pa}_G(y)=P\cup\{x\}$. If reversing the arrow created a directed cycle, that cycle would use the new arrow $y\to x$, and the remaining part would be a directed path $x\to\cdots\to z\to y$ in $G$ with $z\ne x$. Then $z\in P$, so $z\to x$ is also in $G$, making the directed cycle $x\to\cdots\to z\to x$ in $G$, a contradiction. Thus $G'$ is acyclic. [given, choose, construct]

1.2 The full moral graphs of $G$ and $G'$ coincide. Their skeletons coincide. The only changed parent sets are $\operatorname{pa}_G(x)=P$, $\operatorname{pa}_G(y)=P\cup\{x\}$ and $\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(x)=P\cup\{y\}$, $\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(y)=P$. Any pair newly married at $y$ in $G$ or at $x$ in $G'$ already belongs to the clique on $P\cup\{x,y\}$: pairs involving $x$ or $y$ are skeleton edges, and pairs in $P$ are married at both $x$ and $y$. All other parent sets are unchanged, so the moral edge sets are identical. [given, F2, algebra]

1.3 Fix pairwise disjoint query sets $A,B,S$ and put $T=A\cup B\cup S$. The ancestor sets of $T$ in $G$ and $G'$ differ, if at all, only by $x$ or $y$. Indeed, a directed path whose existence changes must use the reversed edge. A path in $G$ that uses $x\to y$ and starts at $v\ne x$ enters $x$ from some $p\in P$; in $G'$ replace $p\to x\to y$ by the unchanged arrow $p\to y$. Therefore only $x$ can cease to be an ancestor. Symmetrically, a path in $G'$ using $y\to x$ and starting at $v\ne y$ enters $y$ from $p\in P=\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(y)$; in $G$ replace $p\to y\to x$ by $p\to x$. Therefore only $y$ can become an ancestor. If $x$ is lost, $y$ belongs to both ancestor sets; if $y$ is gained, $x$ belongs to both. [given, construct]

2.1 If the ancestor sets are equal, step 1.2 shows the induced ancestral moral graphs are equal. Suppose instead that $x$ is an ancestor only in $G$. Then $x\notin T$ and $y$ is a common ancestor of $T$. In the moral graph induced on $\operatorname{An}_G(T)$, every neighbor of $x$ is in $P\cup\{y\}$: its parents lie in $P$; among its children only $y$ can be ancestral, since any other child has an unchanged arrow from $x$ and would make $x$ an ancestor in $G'$; and a marriage through a child other than $y$ would have the same consequence, while a marriage through $y$ uses another parent in $P$. The vertices in $P\cup\{y\}$ form a clique because they are parents of $y$ in $G$. Hence $x$ is simplicial in the ancestral moral graph. The case that $y$ is gained only in $G'$ is symmetric, with its neighbors contained in the clique $P\cup\{x\}$. [given, F2, step 1.2, step 1.3, construct]

3.1 Removing an unconditioned simplicial vertex does not change separation between $A$ and $B$ after deleting $S$: the vertex is not in $T$, and any path through it can be shortened by replacing its two incident edges with the edge joining its neighbors, which exists because the neighborhood is a clique. Conversely, every path in the smaller graph remains in the larger graph. Thus the two ancestral moral graphs separate $A$ and $B$ by $S$ in exactly the same cases. By [F1], $G$ and $G'$ have the same d-separation relations. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For disjoint $X,Y,C\subseteq V$, $C$ d-separates $X$ and $Y$ in $G$ if and
only if deleting $C$ from $\operatorname{mor}_G(X\cup Y\cup C)$ leaves no
undirected path from $X$ to $Y$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite DAG, disjoint vertex sets, and graph conventions above.

[F1] A path is active exactly when it has no conditioned noncollider and
every collider has a conditioned descendant, including itself.
[[def-d-separation-in-a-dag]]

[F2] The ancestral moral graph retains ancestors of $X\cup Y\cup C$, forgets
arrow directions, and joins distinct parents of a common child.
[[def-ancestral-moral-graph-of-a-dag]]

[F3] Every active finite route between distinct endpoints outside $C$ has an active path. [[lem-active-routes-in-a-finite-dag-have-active-paths]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** expand moral paths into routes, remove inactive collider occurrences by directed splices, then shorten active routes.

**Given:** The hypotheses in the statement.

1.1 Suppose an active path joins $X$ to $Y$. From any noncollider follow an outgoing path edge forward until reaching an endpoint or a collider. The reached endpoint is in $X\cup Y$, while a reached collider is an ancestor of $C$ by activity. Thus every path vertex is in $H=\operatorname{An}_G(X\cup Y\cup C)$. Replace each collider segment $u\to w\leftarrow v$ by its moral edge $u-v$; colliders cannot be consecutive along a path. The resulting walk avoids $C$, since all retained internal vertices were noncolliders and the endpoints are outside $C$. Loop deletion in this undirected graph yields a moral path avoiding $C$. [F1, F2, construct]

1.2 Conversely suppose a moral path avoiding $C$ joins $X$ to $Y$. Keep its skeleton edges, and expand each remaining moral edge $u-v$ using a common child $w\in H$ as $u\to w\leftarrow v$. This is a finite route; its inserted occurrences are colliders and all its other occurrences are outside $C$. Every collider is in $H$. Call a collider occurrence bad if its vertex is not an ancestor of $C$. Among routes joining $X$ to $Y$ with every vertex in $H$ and every noncollider outside $C$, minimize the number of bad collider occurrences; the expanded route makes the class nonempty. If $w$ is a bad occurrence, it is an ancestor of some $s\in X\cup Y$. A directed path from $w$ to $s$ avoids $C$, since otherwise $w$ would be an ancestor of $C$. If $s\in X$, replace the whole prefix up to this occurrence of $w$ by that directed path traversed backward; if $s\in Y$, replace the suffix by the path traversed forward. If $w=s$, simply terminate at that occurrence. Otherwise the retained incident arrow points into $w$ and the new incident arrow points out of $w$, making it an allowed noncollider. All new internal chain occurrences are noncolliders outside $C$, and other retained occurrences have their original incidences. Intersections of the chain with the retained segment cause repetitions only; no loops are deleted in this step, and activity is defined occurrence by occurrence. At least the selected bad occurrence disappears and no new bad occurrence is introduced, contradicting minimality. Thus the minimum route is active. Its endpoints are distinct because $X,Y$ are disjoint, and [F3] gives an active path with those endpoints. [F1, F2, F3, construct, choose]

2.1 An active path therefore exists if and only if there is a moral path avoiding $C$. Negating this equivalence proves the claim. If either endpoint set is empty, neither type of path exists and both separation statements hold. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

For $S\subseteq V$, its **ancestral set** is
$$\operatorname{An}_G(S):=\{v\in V:\text{there is a directed path from }v\text{ to some }s\in S\},$$
where paths of length zero are allowed, so $S\subseteq\operatorname{An}_G(S)$.
The induced directed subgraph on this set keeps exactly the arrows of $G$
whose two endpoints lie in $\operatorname{An}_G(S)$. Its **moral graph** is
the undirected simple graph obtained by replacing every arrow by an
undirected edge and joining every distinct pair of parents of a common child
by an undirected edge; loops and duplicate edges are discarded. This
undirected graph is the **ancestral moral graph** on $S$ and is denoted
$\operatorname{mor}_G(S)$.

      url: "https://web.math.ku.dk/~lauritzen/papers/gmnotes.pdf"
---

## Statement

An undirected graph is **chordal** when it has no induced cycle of length at
least four. A vertex is **simplicial** when all of its neighbors are pairwise
adjacent. A **perfect elimination order** is a total order in which the later
neighbors of each vertex form a clique. For every finite chordal undirected
graph $H$ and every edge $\{u,v\}$ of $H$, there are acyclic orientations of
all edges of $H$ with no unshielded collider $a\to w\leftarrow b$ with
$a,b$ nonadjacent, one having $u\to v$ and another having $v\to u$.

## Statement references

[Meek, Appendix](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.4972)

[Lauritzen, §2.6](https://web.math.ku.dk/~lauritzen/papers/gmnotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite chordal undirected graph $H$ and an edge $\{u,v\}$.

[A1] Chordality means that every induced cycle in $H$ has length at most three; all subgraphs used below are finite.

## Proof

1.1 We first show by induction on the number of vertices that a connected noncomplete chordal graph has two nonadjacent simplicial vertices. Choose nonadjacent vertices $a,b$ and an inclusion-minimal separator $S$ whose removal disconnects them. Let $C_a,C_b$ be the components of $H-S$ containing $a,b$. For every $s\in S$, minimality gives a path from $a$ to $b$ after restoring only $s$, so $s$ has a neighbor in each of $C_a,C_b$. If $x,y\in S$ were nonadjacent, shortest paths from $x$ to $y$ with internal vertices in $C_a$ and in $C_b$ would form an induced cycle of length at least four: each path is chordless by shortestness, there are no edges between the two components, and $x,y$ are nonadjacent. This contradicts chordality, so $S$ is a clique. The induced graphs on $C_a\cup S$ and $C_b\cup S$ are smaller connected chordal graphs. By induction, each is either complete, in which case any vertex in its nonempty component $C_a$ or $C_b$ is simplicial, or noncomplete, in which case it has two nonadjacent simplicial vertices and at least one lies outside the clique $S$. Such a vertex has no neighbors outside its component together with $S$, so it is simplicial in $H$. The chosen vertices from $C_a$ and $C_b$ are nonadjacent. Complete connected graphs have every vertex simplicial, and disconnected graphs have a simplicial vertex in each component. Therefore every nonempty finite chordal graph has a simplicial vertex. [given, A1, construct, choose]

2.1 Repeatedly remove a simplicial vertex. Each induced subgraph remains chordal, so step 1.1 supplies a simplicial vertex until the graph is empty. The removal order $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ is a perfect elimination order because the neighbors of $v_t$ that remain at its removal are pairwise adjacent. [A1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 For each $t$, let $K_t=\{v_t\}\cup N_t^+$, where $N_t^+$ is the set of neighbors of $v_t$ later in the elimination order. Each $K_t$ is a clique by step 2.1. If $N_t^+$ is nonempty, let $p(t)$ be its earliest vertex and join the clique node $K_t$ to $K_{p(t)}$. The index strictly increases along parent edges, so these edges form a forest. Since $N_t^+$ is a clique, every vertex of $N_t^+$ other than $p(t)$ is a later neighbor of $p(t)$; hence $K_t\cap K_{p(t)}=N_t^+$. If a vertex $x$ belongs to $K_t$ with $t<x$, then $x\in N_t^+$ and this membership propagates to the parent node, eventually to $K_x$. Thus the clique nodes containing any fixed vertex form a connected subtree. Every graph edge lies in some $K_t$ by taking its earlier endpoint. This is a clique forest with the running-intersection property. [step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Root one tree of this forest. Each vertex $x$ belongs to a connected subtree of clique nodes, so there is a unique root-nearest node $C_x$ containing it. Order the clique nodes in postorder, and list the vertices owned by each node $C_x$ in any order. For any neighbor $y$ of $x$, a clique node $D$ contains both. The nodes $C_x,C_y,D$ lie in the connected subtrees of cliques containing $x$ and $y$, so $C_x,C_y$ are comparable along the root-to-$D$ path. If $C_y$ is an ancestor of $C_x$, the running-intersection property gives $y\in C_x$; if it is a strict descendant of $C_x$, its block is earlier in postorder; and if it is $C_x$, both vertices are in the same clique block. Thus any neighbor $y$ later than $x$ belongs to the clique $C_x$. All later neighbors of $x$ therefore lie in the clique $C_x$, so this order is a perfect elimination order. [step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Direct every edge from its later endpoint in this order to its earlier endpoint. The orientation is acyclic because every arrow decreases the order. The parents of any vertex are among its later neighbors, which form a clique by step 4.1; hence there is no unshielded collider. [step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Since $\{u,v\}$ is an edge, some clique node $C$ contains both. Root its clique tree at $C$. Then $C$ is the root-nearest node containing each of $u,v$, so both are owned by its vertex block. List $v$ before $u$ in that block; step 5.1 directs $u\to v$. Reversing their order directs $v\to u$. The remaining vertices in the block may retain any order, and other trees may be rooted and ordered independently. Both resulting orientations are acyclic and collider-free by steps 4.1–5.1. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, choose] ∎

## Definition

Assume AC. Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ have a nondegenerate multivariate-normal
law with mean $\mu$ and positive-definite covariance matrix $\Sigma$. For
distinct indices $i,j$ and $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\setminus\{i,j\}$, define
the conditional covariance block
$$
K_{ij\mid S}=\Sigma_{\{i,j\},\{i,j\}}-\Sigma_{\{i,j\},S}\Sigma_{S,S}^{-1}\Sigma_{S,\{i,j\}},
$$
with $K_{ij\mid\varnothing}=\Sigma_{\{i,j\},\{i,j\}}$. Whenever the diagonal
entries of this block are positive, the **partial correlation** is
$$
\rho_{ij\mid S}=\frac{(K_{ij\mid S})_{12}}{\sqrt{(K_{ij\mid S})_{11}(K_{ij\mid S})_{22}}}.
$$
The nondegenerate Gaussian case makes the conditioning covariance block
invertible; the following theorem proves that $K_{ij\mid S}$ is positive
definite, so this definition applies to every such $i,j,S$.

## Statement

Let $i-k-j$ be an unshielded triple in a finite DAG and let
$S\subseteq V\setminus\{i,j\}$ d-separate $i$ and $j$. Then the triple is a
v-structure $i\to k\leftarrow j$ if and only if $k\notin S$.

## Statement references

[Kalisch and Bühlmann, §2.3](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume8/kalisch07a/kalisch07a.pdf)

[Meek, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.4972)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite DAG, an unshielded triple $i-k-j$, and a separating set $S$ for its endpoints.

[F1] A path is active given $S$ when its internal noncolliders are outside $S$ and each collider has a descendant in $S$. [[def-d-separation-in-a-dag]]

[F2] An unshielded triple and a v-structure have the meanings stated in the CPDAG interface. [[def-cpdag-markov-equivalence-class]]

## Proof

1.1 If $i\to k\leftarrow j$, then $k$ is a collider on the length-two path from $i$ to $j$. If $k\in S$, it is its own conditioned descendant, so this path is active by [F1], contradicting that $S$ separates the endpoints. Therefore $k\notin S$. [given, F1, F2]

1.2 If the unshielded triple is not a v-structure, then $k$ is a noncollider on its length-two path. If $k\notin S$, that path has no conditioned internal noncollider and no collider, so it is active by [F1], again contradicting separation. Hence a noncollider requires $k\in S$. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 The two implications prove the equivalence. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Two finite DAGs on the same vertex set are Markov equivalent, meaning that they
induce the same d-separation relations, if and only if they have the same
skeleton and the same unshielded colliders.

## Statement references

[Meek, Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.4972)

[Lauritzen, Theorem 2.62](https://web.math.ku.dk/~lauritzen/papers/gmnotes.pdf)

[Kalisch and Bühlmann, §2.1](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume8/kalisch07a/kalisch07a.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Finite DAGs $G_1,G_2$ on the same vertex set.

[F1] Markov equivalence means equality of the induced d-separation relations; skeleton and unshielded-collider conventions are fixed. [[def-cpdag-markov-equivalence-class]]

[F2] Two distinct vertices are nonadjacent exactly when some conditioning set d-separates them. [[lem-pc-skeleton-separation]]

[F3] Reversing a covered arrow in a finite DAG preserves acyclicity and every d-separation relation. [[lem-covered-edge-reversal-preserves-d-separation]]

## Proof

**Given:** $G_1,G_2$ have the hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 First assume that $G_1,G_2$ have the same skeleton and the same unshielded colliders. A finite DAG has a topological order: if every remaining vertex had an incoming arrow, following incoming arrows in the finite graph would repeat a vertex and create a directed cycle; remove a source and repeat. Fix such an order $\prec$ for $G_1$. If the DAGs differ, choose the $\prec$-earliest vertex $\beta$ with $\operatorname{pa}_{G_1}(\beta)\setminus\operatorname{pa}_{G_2}(\beta)\ne\varnothing$, and choose the $\prec$-latest $\alpha$ in that difference. Then $\alpha\to\beta$ occurs in $G_1$ and $\beta\to\alpha$ in $G_2$. [given, F1, construct, choose]

1.2 Conversely, assume $G_1,G_2$ are Markov equivalent. If their skeletons differed, [F2] would give a pair separated in one graph but not the other. Thus their skeletons agree. If an unshielded collider $i\to k\leftarrow j$ occurred in $G_1$ but not in $G_2$, then $i,j$ are nonadjacent in both. By [F2] choose $S$ that d-separates $i,j$ in $G_1$. The path $i\to k\leftarrow j$ shows that no descendant of $k$, including $k$, can lie in $S$, because otherwise that path would be active. In $G_2$, the same unshielded triple has a noncollider at $k$; since $k\notin S$, the two-edge path is active, so $S$ does not d-separate $i,j$ there. This contradicts Markov equivalence. Interchanging $G_1,G_2$ rules out a collider present only in $G_2$. [F1, F2, construct, choose]

2.1 Let $\gamma\ne\alpha$ be another parent of $\beta$ in $G_1$. If $\gamma$ were not a parent of $\alpha$, then either $\gamma$ and $\alpha$ would be nonadjacent, making $\alpha\to\beta\leftarrow\gamma$ an unshielded collider absent from $G_2$, or they would be adjacent with $\alpha\to\gamma$ in $G_1$. The first case contradicts equality of colliders; in the second case, $G_2$ cannot retain both $\alpha\to\gamma$ and $\gamma\to\beta$, because together with $\beta\to\alpha$ they form a directed cycle. If $\alpha\to\gamma$ is reversed in $G_2$, then $\gamma\prec\beta$ is an earlier vertex with a differing parent; if $\gamma\to\beta$ is reversed, then $\gamma$ is a later member than $\alpha$ of $\operatorname{pa}_{G_1}(\beta)\setminus\operatorname{pa}_{G_2}(\beta)$. Both contradict the choices in step 1.1. Hence every parent of $\beta$ other than $\alpha$ is a parent of $\alpha$. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 To prove $\operatorname{pa}_{G_1}(\alpha)\subseteq\operatorname{pa}_{G_1}(\beta)$, suppose instead that $\gamma\to\alpha$ in $G_1$ but $\gamma\notin\operatorname{pa}_{G_1}(\beta)$. Minimality of $\beta$ implies $\gamma\to\alpha$ is also present in $G_2$; otherwise the earlier vertex $\alpha$ would already have a differing parent. If $\gamma$ were not adjacent to $\beta$, then $G_2$ would contain the unshielded collider $\beta\to\alpha\leftarrow\gamma$, while $G_1$ has the noncollider chain $\gamma\to\alpha\to\beta$, contradicting equality of colliders. Thus $\gamma$ is adjacent to $\beta$. In $G_1$ it must be oriented $\gamma\to\beta$, since $\beta\to\gamma$ would make a directed cycle with $\gamma\to\alpha\to\beta$. This contradicts the assumption that $\gamma$ is not a parent of $\beta$. Therefore the inclusion holds. Together with step 2.1, $\operatorname{pa}_{G_1}(\beta)=\operatorname{pa}_{G_1}(\alpha)\cup\{\alpha\}$, so $\alpha\to\beta$ is covered. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, contradiction]

4.1 Reverse this covered arrow in $G_1$. By [F3] the result remains a DAG and is Markov equivalent to $G_1$. It has the same skeleton, and it has the same unshielded colliders: an edge in an unshielded collider cannot be covered, because the other parent of the collider would then also be a parent of the edge's tail and hence adjacent to it. Exactly one edge now agrees with $G_2$, so the finite number of edge-orientation disagreements decreases by one. If any disagreement remains, choose the earliest differing parent set again; the argument in steps 1.1–3.1 applies because the skeleton and collider set are unchanged. Thus finitely many covered reversals transform $G_1$ into $G_2$, and each reversal preserves d-separation. [F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 The two directions prove the equivalence. [step 4.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

**Input:** A finite vertex set $V$, a perfect conditional-independence oracle
for a law in the causally sufficient discovery regime, and a fixed total order
of $V$. For every adjacent pair and conditioning set $S$ tested below, the
oracle returns whether $X_i$ and $X_j$ are conditionally independent given
$X_S$.

**Output:** An undirected skeleton $C$, a separator record $\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)$
for each deleted edge, and a partially directed graph.

1. Initialize $C$ to the complete undirected graph on $V$ and set the level
$\ell=0$.

2. In the fixed lexicographic order of unordered vertex pairs, process each
pair $i-j$ that is still an edge of $C$. First test every $\ell$-element
subset of $\operatorname{Adj}_C(i)\setminus\{j\}$ in lexicographic order;
then test every $\ell$-element subset of
$\operatorname{Adj}_C(j)\setminus\{i\}$ in lexicographic order. On the first
oracle result of conditional independence given a tested set $S$, delete
$i-j$, record $\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)=\operatorname{Sep}(j,i)=S$, and do
not test that pair again. If no set separates the pair, leave it adjacent.
Adjacency sets are read from the current graph, including deletions already
made at level $\ell$.

3. If at least one remaining edge has an endpoint with at least $\ell+1$
neighbors other than the other endpoint, increment $\ell$ and repeat step 2.
Otherwise stop the skeleton search.

4. For each unshielded triple $i-k-j$ in $C$, replace $i-k-j$ by
$i\to k\leftarrow j$ exactly when $k\notin\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)$.

5. Repeatedly orient edges to closure under the following background-free rules,
using fixed lexicographic order on rule instances:

   - **R1:** If $i\to j-k$ and $i,k$ are nonadjacent, orient $j-k$ as $j\to k$.
   - **R2:** If $i-j$ is undirected and $i\to k\to j$, orient $i-j$ as $i\to j$.
   - **R3:** If $i-j$, $i-k$, and $i-\ell$ are undirected, $k\to j$,
     $\ell\to j$, and $k,\ell$ are nonadjacent, orient $i-j$ as $i\to j$.

Do not apply a background-knowledge rule.

## Definition

Let $x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(n)}\in\mathbb R^p$ be a sample, let $i\ne j$, and
let $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\setminus\{i,j\}$. Let $\mathbf x_k\in\mathbb
R^n$ be the sample column for coordinate $k$, and let $\Pi_S$ be the orthogonal
projection onto the span of the all-ones vector and $\{\mathbf x_s:s\in S\}$.
When the sample covariance matrix of coordinates $\{i,j\}\cup S$ is positive
definite, define the residual columns
$$R_{i\mid S}=(I-\Pi_S)\mathbf x_i,\qquad R_{j\mid S}=(I-\Pi_S)\mathbf x_j.$$
The **sample partial correlation** is
$$\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S}=\frac{R_{i\mid S}^{T}R_{j\mid S}}{\|R_{i\mid S}\|_2\,\|R_{j\mid S}\|_2}.$$
For $-1<r<1$, the **Fisher transform** is
$g(r)=\frac12\log\frac{1+r}{1-r}$, and the sample Fisher statistic is
$Z_{ij\mid S}=g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})$. For a test using multiplier
$\sqrt{n-|S|-3}$, require $n-|S|-3>0$ so that this factor is positive. Under independent samples
from a nondegenerate Gaussian law, the stated covariance block is positive
definite almost surely whenever $n-|S|-3>0$.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $X\sim N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$ be a nondegenerate multivariate-normal
vector, so $\Sigma$ is positive definite. For distinct $i,j$ and
$S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\setminus\{i,j\}$, the block
$K_{ij\mid S}$ in the definition of Gaussian partial correlation is positive
definite, and
$$ \rho_{ij\mid S}=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sigma(X_i)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(X_j)\mid\sigma(X_S). $$

## Statement references

[Kalisch and Bühlmann, Proposition 2](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume8/kalisch07a/kalisch07a.pdf)

[Lauritzen, §2.6](https://web.math.ku.dk/~lauritzen/papers/gmnotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a positive-definite Gaussian covariance matrix, and the indices $i,j,S$ in the Statement.

[F1] A finite vector is multivariate normal when every linear projection is a univariate normal with the corresponding projected mean and variance; its covariance is the stated matrix. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F2] A positive-definite multivariate-normal law has density proportional to $\exp(-\frac12(x-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu))$. [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]

[F3] Conditional independence is the conditional-product identity for every pair of bounded measurable real functions. [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]

[F4] Finite random vectors use the finite product sigma-algebra. [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]

[F5] Independence of random elements means independence of their generated sigma-algebras. [[def-independent-random-elements]]

[A1] AC is assumed, as required by [F1]–[F3]. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Partition $X=(Y,Z)$ with $Y=(X_i,X_j)$ and $Z=X_S$; if $S=\varnothing$, omit the $Z$ block. For nonempty $S$, $\Sigma_{S,S}$ is positive definite because every nonzero vector supported on $S$ has positive $\Sigma$-quadratic form, so it is invertible. Put $A=\Sigma_{Y,S}\Sigma_{S,S}^{-1}$ and $U=Y-\mu_Y-A(Z-\mu_Z)$. Then $\operatorname{Cov}(U,Z)=0$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(U)=K_{ij\mid S}$. For every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^2$, the quadratic form of $\Sigma$ at $(u,-\Sigma_{S,S}^{-1}\Sigma_{S,Y}u)$ equals $u^TK_{ij\mid S}u>0$. Thus $K_{ij\mid S}$ is positive definite; for empty $S$ this follows directly from the principal $2\times2$ covariance block. [given, F1, A1, construct]

2.1 The vector $(U,Z)$ is a linear image of $X$, hence is jointly Gaussian by [F1]. Its covariance is block diagonal with blocks $K_{ij\mid S}$ and $\Sigma_{S,S}$. By [F2], the joint density factors as the product of the two Gaussian densities, since the inverse and determinant of a block-diagonal covariance split by blocks. Integrating over measurable rectangles shows $U$ and $Z$ are independent by [F5]. It follows that, conditionally on $Z$, $Y$ is the translate $\mu_Y+A(Z-\mu_Z)+U$ and has conditional covariance $K_{ij\mid S}$. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $(K_{ij\mid S})_{12}=0$, the positive-definite bivariate Gaussian density of $U$ factors into its one-coordinate densities. Thus the coordinates of $U$ are independent. Since $U$ is independent of $Z$, the conditional law of $X_i,X_j$ given $Z$ is the product of its conditional marginals. Integrating bounded measurable functions against this product conditional law gives the identity in [F3], hence conditional independence. [F2, F3, F5, step 2.1]

3.2 Conversely assume the conditional independence in the Statement. Apply [F3] to the sine and cosine functions of each coordinate and combine the four real identities to obtain factorization of the conditional characteristic function at $(1,1)$. By step 2.1, the joint conditional characteristic function is the product of the marginal factors times $\exp(-(K_{ij\mid S})_{12})$. All other factors are nonzero; therefore $\exp(-(K_{ij\mid S})_{12})=1$. The covariance entry is real, so $(K_{ij\mid S})_{12}=0$. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The diagonal entries of $K_{ij\mid S}$ are positive by step 1.1. Its off-diagonal entry is zero exactly when the normalized entry $\rho_{ij\mid S}$ is zero, proving both implications. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Fix $0\le M<1$. There are constants $c_M>0$ and $C_M<\infty$ such that the
following holds. Let $X^{(1)},\ldots,X^{(n)}$ be independent observations from
a nondegenerate Gaussian law, and let $i,j,S$ be as in the definitions of
population and sample partial correlation. Suppose
$|\rho_{ij\mid S}|\le M$ and $n-|S|-3>0$. Then, for $0<t\le1$,
$$ \mathbb P\!\left(\left|g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})-g(\rho_{ij\mid S})\right|>t\right) \le C_M\exp\!\left(-c_M(n-|S|-1)t^2\right), $$
where $g(r)=\tfrac12\log((1+r)/(1-r))$. The constants do not depend on
$i,j,S,n$ or the Gaussian mean and covariance beyond the bound $M$.

## Statement references

[Kalisch and Bühlmann, Appendix A.2.3](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume8/kalisch07a/kalisch07a.pdf)

[Lauritzen, §2.6](https://web.math.ku.dk/~lauritzen/papers/gmnotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nondegenerate Gaussian law, independent observations, a pair $i,j$, a conditioning set $S$, the bound $|\rho_{ij\mid S}|\le M<1$, and $n-|S|-3>0$.

[F1] The population partial correlation is the normalized off-diagonal entry of the Gaussian conditional covariance block. [[def-gaussian-partial-correlation]]

[F2] Under a nondegenerate Gaussian law, the sample partial correlation is the correlation of the two residual columns after projection off the intercept and conditioning columns; the Fisher transform is $g(r)=\operatorname{atanh}(r)$. [[def-sample-partial-correlation]]

[F3] The Gaussian block-regression residual has covariance $K_{ij\mid S}$, is independent of $X_S$, and this block is positive definite. [[thm-gaussian-zero-partial-correlation-is-conditional-independence]]

[F4] A nondegenerate Gaussian vector has its usual Lebesgue density, so every proper linear subspace has probability zero. [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]

[A1] The Gaussian law is nondegenerate, so the finite design-rank and residual-rank statements below hold almost surely. [[def-gaussian-partial-correlation]]

[A2] AC is assumed by the supplied Gaussian probability interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

1.1 By [F3], each observation's pair $(X_i,X_j)$ is a linear function of $X_S$ plus a Gaussian residual independent of $X_S$ with covariance $K_{ij\mid S}$. Across observations these residual pairs are independent. The $S$ coordinates have a nondegenerate Gaussian density because their covariance is a positive-definite principal submatrix. If $|S|=0$, the intercept design has rank one. If $s=|S|>0$, successive independent sample points in $\mathbb R^s$ are affinely independent until there are $s+1$: after $r\le s$ affinely independent points, their affine span has dimension $r-1<s$, and the next point has a density, so lies in that span with probability zero by [F4]. Thus the intercept and $S$ design has rank $s+1$ almost surely. Conditional on that design, an orthonormal basis of its orthogonal complement has dimension $m=n-|S|-1$. In that basis the projected residual pairs are $m$ independent copies of this Gaussian residual; standardizing the two coordinates does not change their sample correlation. Thus the sample partial correlation has the same distribution as $R_m=\frac{\sum_{r=1}^m U_rV_r}{(\sum_{r=1}^mU_r^2)^{1/2}(\sum_{r=1}^mV_r^2)^{1/2}},\qquad m=n-|S|-1,$ for $m$ independent copies $(U_r,V_r)$ of the standardized pair, whose correlation is $\rho=\rho_{ij\mid S}$ by [F1]. The hypothesis gives $m\ge3$. Their covariance block is positive definite by [F3], so the first residual sample column is nonzero almost surely, and conditional on that column the second has a density in $\mathbb R^m$. Its probability of lying in the first column's one-dimensional span is zero by [F4], since $m\ge2$. Therefore $R_m\in(-1,1)$ almost surely and the Fisher transform is defined. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, A1, A2, algebra]

2.1 Represent $U_r=X_r$ and $V_r=\rho X_r+\sqrt{1-\rho^2}E_r$ with independent standard normal vectors $X,E\in\mathbb R^m$. Put $A=\|X\|$, $Z=\langle E,X/A\rangle$, and $W=\|E-ZX/A\|$. Rotational invariance of the standard Gaussian density implies that $A^2\sim\chi_m^2$, $Z\sim N(0,1)$, and $W^2\sim\chi^2_{m-1}$ are independent. Direct substitution gives $R_m=\frac{q}{\sqrt{q^2+W^2}},\qquad q=\frac{\rho A}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}+Z,$ and hence $g(R_m)=\operatorname{arsinh}(q/W)$. Rotational invariance follows directly from the standard Gaussian density, and it makes $A,Z,W$ independent. Also $\operatorname{arsinh}(\rho/\sqrt{1-\rho^2})=g(\rho)$. [step 1.1, F4, construct, algebra]

3.1 Let $B=M/\sqrt{1-M^2}$ and $L=4B+2$. On the event $|A/\sqrt m-1|\le\delta,\quad |W/\sqrt m-1|\le\delta,\quad |Z|/\sqrt m\le\delta,$ where $0<\delta\le1/2$, one has $\left|\frac qW-\frac{\rho}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\right| \le \frac{(2B+1)\delta}{1-\delta}\le L\delta.$ Since $|\operatorname{arsinh}'(x)|=1/\sqrt{1+x^2}\le1$, step 2.1 yields $|g(R_m)-g(\rho)|\le L\delta$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For $Q\sim\chi_k^2$, its moment generating function, obtained by multiplying the $k$ one-dimensional Gaussian integrals, is $\mathbb E e^{sQ}=(1-2s)^{-k/2}$ for $s<1/2$. For $\delta>0$, Markov's inequality optimized at $s=\delta/[2(1+\delta)]$ gives $\mathbb P(Q/k\ge1+\delta)\le e^{-k(\delta-\log(1+\delta))/2}$. For $0<\delta<1$, the negative choice $s=-\delta/[2(1-\delta)]$ gives $\mathbb P(Q/k\le1-\delta)\le e^{-k(-\delta-\log(1-\delta))/2}$. Put $\delta_+=2u+u^2\le3$ and $\delta_-=2u-u^2\ge u$. The inequalities $\delta-\log(1+\delta)=\int_0^\delta x/(1+x)\,dx\ge\delta^2/8$ for $0\le\delta\le3$ and $-\delta-\log(1-\delta)\ge\delta^2/2$ imply $\mathbb P\bigl(|\sqrt{Q/k}-1|>u\bigr)\le2e^{-ku^2/8}\qquad(0<u<1).$ Applying this to $A^2$ and $W^2$, and using $|\sqrt{(m-1)/m}-1|\le1/m\le\delta/2$, shows that $|W/\sqrt m-1|>\delta$ implies $|W/\sqrt{m-1}-1|>\delta/2$. Thus for $2/m\le\delta\le1/2$, $\mathbb P\bigl(|A/\sqrt m-1|>\delta\text{ or }|W/\sqrt m-1|>\delta\bigr) \le4e^{-m\delta^2/64}.$ The standard normal moment generating function $\mathbb Ee^{sZ}=e^{s^2/2}$, with Markov's inequality optimized at $s=\delta\sqrt m$, gives $\mathbb P(|Z|/\sqrt m>\delta)\le2e^{-m\delta^2/2}$. For $0<\delta<2/m$, the trivial bound $1\le6e^{-m\delta^2/64}$ applies. Thus the complement of the event in step 3.1 has probability at most $6e^{-m\delta^2/64}$ for every $0<\delta\le1/2$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F4, algebra]

5.1 Set $\delta=t/L$. Since $L\ge2$ and $0<t\le1$, step 3.1 applies and its complement contains the event in the Statement. Step 4.1 therefore bounds that event by $6\exp(-mt^2/(64L^2))$. Taking $C_M=6$ and $c_M=(64L^2)^{-1}$ proves the claim. [given, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $G$ be a finite DAG. Start with its skeleton, orient exactly the edges in
its unshielded colliders, and leave all other edges undirected. Repeatedly apply
the background-free rules R1–R3 from the PC algorithm until no rule applies.
The resulting partially directed graph is the CPDAG for the Markov-equivalence
class of $G$.

## Statement references

[Meek, §§2.1–2.3 and Appendix](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.4972)

[Lauritzen, §2.6](https://web.math.ku.dk/~lauritzen/papers/gmnotes.pdf)

[Kalisch and Bühlmann, §2.3](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume8/kalisch07a/kalisch07a.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite DAG $G$ and the initialized pattern and R1–R3 rules stated above.

[F1] A PDAG, consistent DAG extension, Markov equivalence, and CPDAG have the definitions in the supplied interface. [[def-cpdag-markov-equivalence-class]]

[F2] R1, R2, and R3 are exactly the three background-free orientation rules stated in the PC algorithm. [[alg-pc-causal-discovery]]

[F3] Two finite DAGs are Markov equivalent exactly when they have the same skeleton and the same unshielded colliders. [[thm-dag-markov-equivalence-skeleton-vstructures]]

[F4] In every finite chordal undirected graph, each edge can be oriented either way as part of an acyclic orientation having no unshielded collider. [[lem-chordal-components-admit-both-orientations]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Every consistent extension of a current pattern must respect each R1–R3 conclusion. For R1, the opposite orientation would create the new unshielded collider $i\to j\leftarrow k$ with $i,k$ nonadjacent. For R2, the opposite orientation would close the directed path $i\to k\to j$ into a directed cycle. For R3, if $j\to i$, acyclicity forces $k\to i$ and $\ell\to i$ (the alternatives $i\to k$ or $i\to\ell$ each close a directed cycle through $j$); these arrows create the new unshielded collider $k\to i\leftarrow\ell$, since $k,\ell$ are nonadjacent. Each contradiction is forbidden for a consistent extension. Thus all rule orientations are compelled, and the original DAG $G$ remains a consistent extension at every stage. [given, F1, F2, cases, contradiction]

1.2 Every finite DAG has a topological order. In any nonempty induced subgraph, if every vertex had an incoming arrow, repeatedly following incoming arrows would revisit a vertex and create a directed cycle. Thus a source exists; remove one source and repeat on the remaining finite DAG. Listing the removed vertices in order gives a topological order, because an arrow's tail must be removed before its head. This argument uses only finite choices. [given, construct]

1.3 The R1–R3 closure reaches a final pattern after finitely many applications. Each scan checks finitely many rule instances on the finite vertex set; every nonterminal scan directs at least one previously undirected edge, and there are at most $\binom{|V|}{2}$ such edges. Therefore after finitely many scans a full scan applies no rule, so the final closed pattern $P$ used below exists. [F2, construct]

2.1 Write $P$ for the final closed pattern. We claim that whenever $a\to b$ and $b-c$ is undirected in $P$, the edge $a-c$ is directed $a\to c$. If $a,c$ were nonadjacent, R1 would orient $b-c$ as $b\to c$, contradicting closure. If $c\to a$, then $c\to a\to b$ and R2 would orient $c-b$ as $c\to b$, also contradicting closure. It remains to rule out $a-c$ undirected. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.3, cases, contradiction]

3.1 Suppose such an undirected $a-c$ exists, and choose a counterexample for which the arrow $a\to b$ was first oriented as early as possible in the finite sequence of rule applications. If $a\to b$ was initially oriented as part of a collider $a\to b\leftarrow d$, then $a,d$ are nonadjacent. Since $d\to b-c$ cannot satisfy R1, $d$ is adjacent to $c$. If $c\to d$, R2 on $c-b$ applies along $c\to d\to b$. If $d\to c$, R1 on $d\to c-a$ gives $c\to a$, and R2 on $c-b$ then applies along $c\to a\to b$. If $d-c$ is undirected, R3 on $c-b$ applies with its other two vertices $a,d$. Each case contradicts that $P$ is closed. [F2, step 2.1, cases, contradiction]

3.2 Iterating the claim in step 2.1 along an undirected path shows that a directed edge cannot have both endpoints in the same connected component of undirected edges: such a path from its head back to its tail would propagate $a\to b$ to a nonexistent loop $a\to a$. If an undirected component had an induced cycle of length at least four, take its latest vertex in a topological order of the consistent extension $G$ from step 1.2. Both cycle edges point into that vertex; their other endpoints are nonadjacent, since the cycle has no undirected chord and no directed edge can join vertices in the same component. This is an unshielded collider absent from $P$, contrary to consistency of $G$. Hence every undirected component is chordal. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, contradiction]

4.1 If $a\to b$ was added by R1 from $d\to a$ with $d,b$ nonadjacent, then either R1 on $d\to a-c$ directly gives $a\to c$, or $d$ is adjacent to $c$. If $c\to d$, R2 on $c-a$ along $c\to d\to a$ gives $c\to a$, and R2 on $c-b$ along $c\to a\to b$ then applies. If $d\to c$, R1 on $d\to c-b$ gives $c\to b$. If $d-c$ is undirected, the earlier arrow $d\to a$ together with $a-c$ is a counterexample of smaller orientation time, contrary to the choice in step 3.1. Thus this rule case is impossible. [F2, step 3.1, cases, contradiction]

4.2 If $a\to b$ was added by R2 from $a\to d\to b$, then $d$ must be adjacent to $c$, since otherwise R1 on $d\to b-c$ orients $b-c$. If $d\to c$, R2 on $a-c$ along $a\to d\to c$ gives $a\to c$. If $c\to d$, R2 on $c-b$ along $c\to d\to b$ gives $c\to b$. If $d-c$ is undirected, the earlier arrow $a\to d$ and $d-c$ form a counterexample of smaller orientation time. All alternatives contradict closure or minimality. [F2, step 3.1, cases, contradiction]

4.3 If $a\to b$ was added by R3, there are nonadjacent $d,e$ with $d\to b$, $e\to b$, and undirected $a-d$, $a-e$. Each of $d,e$ is adjacent to $c$, since otherwise R1 on $d\to b-c$ or $e\to b-c$ applies. If $c\to d$ or $c\to e$, R2 on $c-b$ applies along that arrow followed by $d\to b$ or $e\to b$. Otherwise each of $d-c,e-c$ is either undirected or points into $c$. If both point into $c$, R3 on $a-c$ gives $a\to c$. If exactly one points into $c$, say $d\to c$ while $e-c$ is undirected, R1 on $d\to c-e$ gives $c\to e$, and R2 on $c-b$ follows from $c\to e\to b$. If both are undirected, R3 on $c-b$ gives $c\to b$. Every case contradicts the alleged counterexample or closure, proving the claim. [F2, step 3.1, cases, contradiction]

4.4 Contract each undirected component to one vertex and retain the directed edges between components. There are no loops by step 3.2. For a supposed simple cycle of components $C_1\to C_2\to\cdots\to C_r\to C_1$, with $r\ge2$, choose an arrow $x_t\to y_{t+1}$ for each quotient edge, with cyclic indices. In component $C_t$, the vertices $y_t$ and $x_t$ are joined by an undirected path. The claim in step 2.1 propagates the incoming arrow $x_{t-1}\to y_t$ along that path to $x_{t-1}\to x_t$. These arrows give $x_1\to x_2\to\cdots\to x_r\to x_1$, contradicting that $G$ consistently extends $P$. Therefore the quotient is a finite DAG. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.2, contradiction, construct]

5.1 Fix any undirected edge $u-v$ and choose in its component one of the two orientations supplied by [F4] with the desired direction; orient every other nontrivial undirected component by any such acyclic collider-free orientation. Keep all directed edges of $P$. The combined graph is acyclic: a directed cycle contained in one component is excluded by its chosen orientation, while a cycle passing between components would project to a directed cycle in the quotient of step 4.4. [F1, F4, step 3.2, step 4.4, construct]

6.1 The combined DAG creates no unshielded collider absent from $P$. Two internal parents of a vertex cannot form one by the collider-free component orientation. If $x\to v$ is an external directed parent and $w\to v$ is an internal parent, then $v-w$ was undirected in $P$; step 2.1 forces $x\to w$ in $P$, so $x,w$ are adjacent and the collider is shielded. Two external directed parents already give a collider present in $P$ whenever they are nonadjacent. Thus the construction is a consistent extension, and the chosen edge $u-v$ has the requested orientation. [F1, step 2.1, step 5.1, cases]

7.1 By step 1.1 every consistent extension preserves every arrow of $P$, and by steps 5.1–6.1 each undirected edge occurs in consistent extensions with either orientation. The initial pattern has exactly the unshielded colliders of $G$, and $G$ remains its consistent extension, so every directed unshielded collider in $P$ is also one in $G$; thus $P$ and $G$ have the same skeleton and unshielded colliders. By [F3], every consistent extension is Markov equivalent to $G$. Conversely, any DAG Markov equivalent to $G$ has the same skeleton and colliders by [F3], hence extends the initial pattern; applying the soundness argument in step 1.1 successively shows that it preserves every arrow added by R1–R3 and therefore extends $P$. Thus the consistent extensions of $P$ are exactly $[G]$, and $P$ is its CPDAG. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and the causally sufficient perfect-oracle discovery regime for a
finite observed DAG $G$ and its full-joint law. The population PC algorithm
with any fixed vertex order terminates and returns exactly the skeleton of $G$,
records a d-separating set for every deleted pair, orients exactly the
unshielded colliders of $G$, and returns the CPDAG for the Markov-equivalence
class of $G$.

## Statement references

[Kalisch and Bühlmann, §§2.2.1 and 2.3](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume8/kalisch07a/kalisch07a.pdf)

[Meek, §§2.1–2.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.4972)

[Lauritzen, §2.6](https://web.math.ku.dk/~lauritzen/papers/gmnotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a finite observed DAG and law in the discovery regime, and a fixed-order perfect conditional-independence oracle.

[F1] The discovery regime supplies a finite observed DAG, full-joint parent-kernel factorization, faithfulness, and the exact conditional-independence oracle; AC is assumed. [[def-causal-discovery-oracle-regime]]

[F2] Under AC, a finite topological probability-kernel factorization implies the global Markov property: d-separation implies conditional independence. [[thm-dag-factorization-implies-d-separation-conditional-independence]]

[F3] Faithfulness gives the converse: conditional independence implies d-separation. [[def-faithfulness-of-a-dag-model]]

[F4] A pair is adjacent in a finite DAG exactly when no conditioning set d-separates it; a nonedge has a separating set among the parents of one endpoint. [[lem-pc-skeleton-separation]]

[F5] A separating set for an unshielded triple's endpoints omits the middle vertex exactly when that triple is a collider. [[lem-pc-separating-set-collider]]

[F6] The population PC algorithm searches levels in order, stores the first separating set, then orients unshielded colliders and closes under R1–R3. [[alg-pc-causal-discovery]]

[F7] The initialized collider pattern closed under R1–R3 is the CPDAG of the DAG's Markov-equivalence class. [[lem-meek-rules-complete-for-cpdag]]

[A1] AC is required by the supplied probability interfaces in [F1] and [F2]; no graph-theoretic step uses it. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 By [F2], every d-separation in $G$ is a conditional independence in its law. By [F3], every conditional independence is a d-separation. Since the oracle is exact by [F1], it answers “independent” exactly for d-separated pairs and sets. [given, F1, F2, F3, A1]

1.2 The skeleton search terminates. If $|V|\le1$, it has no pairs to test and stops at level $0$. Otherwise, at each level it processes finitely many pairs and finitely many subsets. An endpoint has at most $|V|-2$ neighbors other than the other endpoint, so at level $\ell=|V|-2$ no remaining edge can meet the condition requiring at least $\ell+1$ such neighbors; the level therefore cannot be incremented past this finite bound. The orientation phase scans finitely many rule instances on the finite vertex set. Every successful application directs one previously undirected edge, which is never undirected again, so there are at most $\binom{|V|}{2}$ successful applications before a scan finds none. Both phases, and hence the algorithm, terminate. [F6, construct]

2.1 Every true skeleton edge $i-j$ remains in the search graph: its one-edge path is active given every allowed conditioning set, so by [F1] and [F2] no oracle test deletes it. For a nonedge $i-j$, [F4] gives a separating set $S=\operatorname{pa}(i)$ or $\operatorname{pa}(j)$ that excludes the endpoints. Every vertex in that parent set remains adjacent to the chosen endpoint because all true edges remain. At any level $\ell<|S|$ while $i-j$ remains, that endpoint has at least $|S|\ge\ell+1$ other neighbors. The stopping condition therefore cannot stop before level $|S|$, and at that level the algorithm tests $S$ and deletes $i-j$. Thus the returned skeleton is exactly the skeleton of $G$. [F1, F2, F4, F6, step 1.1, cases]

3.1 Every set recorded when an edge is deleted was accepted by the exact oracle. By step 1.1 it d-separates the deleted endpoints. Since the skeleton from step 2.1 is exact, each unshielded triple is an unshielded triple of $G$; [F5] shows the algorithm orients its middle vertex as a collider exactly when it is a collider in $G$. [F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 The algorithm then applies R1–R3 to closure. Its pattern has the exact skeleton and exactly the unshielded colliders of $G$ by steps 2.1–3.1. Applying [F7] gives the CPDAG of $G$. By step 1.2 the finite procedure terminates, so this is the algorithm's output. [F6, F7, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(X_v)_{v\in V}$ be random elements in measurable spaces
whose joint law is generated, in a topological order of the finite DAG $G$,
by probability kernels $K_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},dx_v)$. For pairwise
disjoint $A,B,C\subseteq V$, if $C$ d-separates $A$ and $B$ in $G$, then
$$\sigma(X_A)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(X_B)\mid\sigma(X_C).$$
This is the global Markov implication. Its converse is the separate
faithfulness condition in [[def-faithfulness-of-a-dag-model]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite DAG-kernel factorization, measurable vertex spaces, and AC.

[F1] D-separation is equivalent to separation by $C$ in the ancestral moral
graph on $A\cup B\cup C$.
[[lem-d-separation-ancestral-moral-separation]]

[F2] In the moral graph each family $\{v\}\cup\operatorname{pa}(v)$ is a
clique, because every pair of parents of $v$ is joined by a moral edge.
[[def-ancestral-moral-graph-of-a-dag]]

[F3] A probability-kernel extension depending only on one side and the separator preserves conditional independence; conditioning on the extended variable also preserves independence of the two original sides. [[lem-conditional-independence-under-kernel-extension-and-conditioning]]

[F4] Supplied probability kernels have normalized finite associative composition. [[def-composition-of-probability-kernels]], [[lem-kernel-composition-is-well-defined-and-associative]]

[F5] Conditional independence is the bounded-function conditional-product identity. [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]], [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]

[F6] Finite measures agreeing on a generating rectangle pi-system agree on the product sigma-algebra. [[thm-measure-uniqueness-on-a-sigma-finite-pi-system]], [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** retain the ancestor kernels and prove moral-separator independence by induction deleting a sink, including conditioned sinks.

**Given:** The hypotheses in the statement.

1.1 Put $H=\operatorname{An}_G(A\cup B\cup C)$. Marginalize vertices outside $H$ in reverse topological order: at removal each has no surviving child, so integration of its kernel gives one. The marginal on $H$ is consequently generated by the original kernels at vertices of $H$, with their original parent sets. Reverse-order integration is elimination of final conditional kernels using [F4], not an interchange of arbitrary dependent integrations. [given, F4, construct]

1.2 We prove a stronger finite-graph assertion: if a DAG's full moral graph has a partition of all vertices into $L,R,D$ with no edge from $L$ to $R$, its kernel law satisfies $X_L\perp\!\!\!\perp X_R\mid\sigma(X_D)$. Induct on the number of vertices. For no vertices the variables are constants and the conditional-product identity is immediate. Choose a sink $v$ (the last vertex in a topological order). Marginalizing $v$ retains all other kernels and leaves the DAG with $v$ deleted; its moral graph is a subgraph of the former moral graph, so the remaining partition obeys the induction hypothesis. The original joint law is this marginal extended by $K_v(X_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},dx_v)$: no other kernel depends on $x_v$, as $v$ is a sink. This identity follows first on rectangles from the iterated composition, and then on their generated sigma-algebra by finite-measure uniqueness. [given, F2, F4, F5, F6, construct]

2.1 If $v\in L$, all its parents are in $(L\setminus\{v\})\cup D$, since a parent in $R$ would give a forbidden skeleton edge. Apply the first conclusion of [F3] to the induction hypothesis with left vector $X_{L\setminus\{v\}}$, right vector $X_R$ and separator $X_D$, extending the left vector by $X_v$. This proves the assertion. If $v\in R$, symmetry gives the same result. If $v\in D$, its parents outside $D\setminus\{v\}$ lie wholly in $L$ or wholly in $R$: two parents on opposite sides would be married by a forbidden moral edge. Choose that side (either side when there are no such parents). The induction hypothesis gives independence of $X_L,X_R$ given $X_{D\setminus\{v\}}$, and the second conclusion of [F3], applied to $K_v$, gives independence given $(X_{D\setminus\{v\}},X_v)=X_D$. Thus even a conditioned vertex's kernel is retained as a kernel extension before conditioning. This completes all cases of the induction. [F2, F3, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 By [F1], the moral graph on $H$ with $C$ deleted has no component meeting both $A$ and $B$. Let $L$ be the union of components meeting $A$, and $R=H\setminus(L\cup C)$. Then $B\subseteq R$, $A\subseteq L$, and no moral edge joins $L$ to $R$. Steps 1.2 and 2.1 applied to the marginal law of step 1.1 give independence of $X_L,X_R$ given $X_C$. Restrict its bounded-function identity to functions of $X_A,X_B$ to obtain the claim. Empty endpoint sets yield constant functions and satisfy the same identity. No density, positivity, faithfulness, or regular conditional distribution on an arbitrary measurable space is used. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct] ∎

## Definition

Assume AC, and let a joint law $P$ on the measurable vertex variables of a
finite DAG $G$ be given. The law is **faithful to $G$** if, for every triple
of pairwise disjoint vertex sets $A,B,C$, the conditional independence
$$\sigma(X_A)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(X_B)\mid\sigma(X_C)$$
implies that $C$ d-separates $A$ and $B$ in $G$. This is the converse of the
global Markov implication; faithfulness is a separate assumption on the
specified law, not a consequence of DAG factorization. No claim about Markov
equivalence, skeletons, or unshielded colliders is included. Here $X_A$ is
the finite random vector $(X_v)_{v\in A}$ with the finite-product
sigma-algebra; for $A=\varnothing$ it is the unique random element of the
empty-product singleton.

## Statement

Assume AC. For each $n$, let $p_n\ge2$ observed variables form a finite
causally sufficient Markovian recursive structural causal model over a DAG
$G_n$. Assume the full-joint law is nondegenerate Gaussian, has a finite
topological parent-kernel factorization, and is faithful to $G_n$. Let
$X^{(1)},\ldots,X^{(n)}$ be independent observations from that law. Let
$q_n$ be an integer with $0\le q_n\le p_n-1$ that bounds the maximum degree of the skeleton of $G_n$.
Suppose, for constants $a\ge0$, $0<b\le1$, $0<d<b/2$, and $M<1$,
$$ p_n=O(n^a),\qquad q_n=O(n^{1-b}),\qquad c_n^{-1}=O(n^d),\qquad 0<c_n\le M, $$
and every population partial correlation with $|S|\le q_n$ satisfies
$|\rho_{ij\mid S}|\le M$, while each nonzero such partial correlation has
$|\rho_{ij\mid S}|\ge c_n$. For sufficiently large $n$ with
$n-q_n-3>0$, and for each tested pair and conditioning set, define the
two-sided Fisher statistic
$$T_{ij\mid S}=\sqrt{n-|S|-3}\,\left|g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})\right|, \qquad g(r)=\tfrac12\log\frac{1+r}{1-r}.$$
Declare conditional independence exactly when
$$T_{ij\mid S}\le\frac{\sqrt n\,c_n}{2},$$
and for larger conditioning sets assign the test answer “dependent.” If a
tested sample covariance block is not positive definite, also assign
“dependent”; this affects only a probability-zero event for sufficiently large
$n$. Run the
PC skeleton and orientation steps in any fixed vertex order using
conditioning sets of size at most $q_n$, with $q_n$ as the maximum level cap:
after each level, stop if the ordinary degree stopping condition holds or the
current level equals $q_n$, then orient unshielded colliders and close under
R1–R3. Then for all sufficiently large $n$ the output equals the
CPDAG of $G_n$ with probability at least
$$1-\exp\bigl(-C n^{1-2d}\bigr)$$
for some constant $C>0$ independent of $n$. This is a theoretical threshold:
it depends on the unknown lower bound $c_n$.

## Statement references

[Kalisch and Bühlmann, Theorems 1–2 and Appendix A.2.3](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume8/kalisch07a/kalisch07a.pdf)

[Lauritzen, §2.6](https://web.math.ku.dk/~lauritzen/papers/gmnotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the Gaussian and DAG sequence, independent observations, the degree and partial-correlation bounds, and the thresholded PC procedure in the Statement.

[F1] The sample partial correlation is the residual correlation after projecting off the intercept and conditioning columns; the Fisher transform is $g(r)=\tfrac12\log((1+r)/(1-r))$. [[def-sample-partial-correlation]]

[F2] Gaussian partial correlation is the normalized off-diagonal entry of the conditional covariance block. [[def-gaussian-partial-correlation]]

[F3] For a nondegenerate Gaussian law, zero partial correlation is equivalent to conditional independence. [[thm-gaussian-zero-partial-correlation-is-conditional-independence]]

[F4] Uniformly over tested pairs and sets with $|S|\le q_n$, the Fisher-transform error has tail at most $C_M\exp(-c_M(n-|S|-1)t^2)$ for $0<t\le1$. [[lem-pc-fisher-transform-uniform-concentration]]

[F5] The population PC algorithm terminates and recovers the CPDAG when its oracle gives exact conditional-independence answers. [[thm-pc-oracle-correctness]]

[F6] The population PC algorithm tests current-adjacency subsets in level order, then orients colliders and closes under R1–R3. [[alg-pc-causal-discovery]]

[F7] The parent-kernel factorization implies d-separation conditional independence, and faithfulness gives the reverse implication. [[thm-dag-factorization-implies-d-separation-conditional-independence]] [[def-faithfulness-of-a-dag-model]]

[F8] Every nonadjacent pair in a finite DAG has a separating set among the parents of one endpoint. [[lem-pc-skeleton-separation]]

[F9] The finite observed Markovian SCM, full-joint factorization, and faithfulness conditions are those of the discovery regime. [[def-causal-discovery-oracle-regime]]

[A1] AC is required by the Gaussian conditional-independence and recursive-model probability interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Since $q_n=O(n^{1-b})$ with $b>0$, eventually $n-q_n-3>0$, so [F1] makes every sample statistic in the capped search defined almost surely. The sample procedure terminates for every answer sequence: it processes at most $q_n+1$ finite levels, each with finitely many pair-and-subset tests, and its finite R1–R3 closure directs at most $\binom{p_n}{2}$ edges. Since $c_n\le M<1$, take $t=c_n/4\le1$ in [F4]. For every tested triple $(i,j,S)$, the probability that $|g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})-g(\rho_{ij\mid S})|>c_n/4$ is at most $C_M\exp(-c_M(n-|S|-1)c_n^2/16)$. For large $n$, $q_n/n\to0$ and $n-q_n-1\ge n/2$, so each such probability is at most $C_M\exp(-c'_M n c_n^2)$ for a constant $c'_M>0$. [given, F1, F4, F6, A1, construct, algebra]

2.1 There are at most $N_n=\binom{p_n}{2}\sum_{\ell=0}^{q_n}\binom{p_n-2}{\ell} \le p_n^2(q_n+1)p_n^{q_n}\le p_n^{q_n+3}$ distinct pair-and-set tests, since $q_n\le p_n-1$ and $q_n+1\le p_n$. A union bound, which requires no independence between tests, shows that the event $E_n$ on which every test of size at most $q_n$ has Fisher-transform error at most $c_n/4$ has failure probability at most $C_M\exp\!\left((q_n+3)\log p_n-c'_M n c_n^2\right).$ The assumptions imply $n c_n^2\ge C_0 n^{1-2d}$ eventually and $(q_n+3)\log p_n=O(n^{1-b}\log n)=o(n^{1-2d})$, because $2d<b$. Thus, after reducing the positive constant in the exponent, $\mathbb P(E_n^c)\le\exp(-C n^{1-2d})$ for all sufficiently large $n$. [given, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 On $E_n$, if $\rho_{ij\mid S}=0$, then [F1] gives $|g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})|\le c_n/4$. By [F3], this is the population conditional-independence case. Hence $T_{ij\mid S}\le\sqrt n c_n/4<\sqrt n c_n/2$, so the test declares independence. If $\rho_{ij\mid S}\ne0$, then [F2] and the lower-bound hypothesis give $|\rho_{ij\mid S}|\ge c_n$, and $|g(\rho_{ij\mid S})|\ge|\rho_{ij\mid S}|$ because $|\operatorname{atanh}(r)|\ge|r|$ for $|r|<1$. Therefore $|g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})|\ge3c_n/4$. Since $(n-|S|-3)/n\ge(n-q_n-3)/n\to1$, for all sufficiently large $n$ we have $\sqrt{(n-|S|-3)/n}>2/3$, so $T_{ij\mid S}>\sqrt n c_n/2$ and the test declares dependence. By [F3] these are exactly the dependent cases. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 On $E_n$ the capped sample PC search makes the same decisions as the uncapped perfect-oracle procedure through level $q_n$. True edges are never removed, because their one-edge paths prevent d-separation and [F7] makes every such test dependent. For each nonedge, [F8] supplies a separating parent set of size at most the true maximum degree $q_n$; its parent edges remain, so the algorithm tests and removes that nonedge no later than level $q_n$. Thus by completion of that level the sample search and the perfect-oracle run have the exact skeleton and the same separating records. The oracle run cannot need another level: on an exact skeleton of maximum degree at most $q_n$, no remaining edge can have an endpoint with the $q_n+1$ other neighbors required to advance after level $q_n$. If either run stops earlier by its ordinary degree condition, their identical decisions make both stop; otherwise both stop after level $q_n$, the sample run by its cap. Their collider and R1–R3 orientations therefore agree, and [F5] identifies the oracle run's output, hence the sample output, as the CPDAG of $G_n$. [F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, step 3.1, cases]

5.1 The only failure event is contained in $E_n^c$, whose probability has the bound from step 2.1. Step 4.1 identifies the output on $E_n$ as the CPDAG. This proves the stated consistency bound. The threshold uses $c_n$, so the theorem does not provide a data-driven choice of that parameter. [given, F5, step 2.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Example

Let all exogenous variables below be mutually independent standard normals.
The chain model is $X=U_X$, $Y=X+U_Y$, $Z=Y+U_Z$, with graph
$X\to Y\to Z$. The collider model is $X=U_X$, $Z=U_Z$, $Y=X+Z+U_Y$, with
graph $X\to Y\leftarrow Z$. For a perfect conditional-independence oracle,
PC retains an undirected chain in the first model and orients both arrows into
$Y$ in the second: the chain's unique endpoint separator contains $Y$, whereas
the collider's endpoint separator is empty.

\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth, node distance=19mm]
