```tikz
  \draw[->] (x1) -- (y1); \draw[->] (y1) -- (z1);
  \node at (1.7,-0.55) {chain};
  \node at (0,-1.5) (x2) {$X$}; \node at (1.7,-1.5) (y2) {$Y$}; \node at (3.4,-1.5) (z2) {$Z$};
  \draw[->] (x2) -- (y2); \draw[<-] (y2) -- (z2);
  \node at (1.7,-2.05) {collider};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

The diagrams use vertices for variables and arrows for structural parenthood;
they illustrate the two DAGs but are not used in the verification.

## Example references

[Kalisch and Bühlmann, §2.3](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume8/kalisch07a/kalisch07a.pdf)

[Meek, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.4972)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Independent $N(0,1)$ exogenous variables and the two recursive Gaussian models in the Example.

[F1] Finite independent sums and affine shifts have the stated characteristic-function formulas. [[def-independent-random-elements]] [[lem-characteristic-functions-under-affine-maps-and-independent-sums]]

[F2] The standard normal has density $\phi$, scalar normal laws have characteristic function $\exp(i\mu t-\sigma^2t^2/2)$, and equal scalar characteristic functions determine equal laws. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-normal-law]] [[thm-uniqueness-of-a-law-from-its-characteristic-function]]

[F3] A finite vector is multivariate normal when every scalar linear projection has its corresponding normal law. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F4] For a nondegenerate Gaussian vector, zero conditional covariance between two coordinates is equivalent to conditional independence given the conditioning coordinates. [[thm-gaussian-zero-partial-correlation-is-conditional-independence]]

[F5] PC deletes a pair at the first conditioning level with a separating set, records that set, orients an unshielded triple as a collider exactly when the middle vertex is absent from its recorded set, then applies R1–R3. [[alg-pc-causal-discovery]]

[F6] The middle vertex of an unshielded triple lies outside a valid separating set exactly when the triple is a collider. [[lem-pc-separating-set-collider]]

[F7] A Gaussian law is faithful to a DAG when its conditional independences agree exactly with that DAG's d-separations. [[def-causal-discovery-oracle-regime]]

[F8] A recursive SCM is Markovian when its exogenous variables are mutually independent; its displayed structural functions define the endogenous variables along the graph. [[def-recursive-structural-causal-model-and-dag]]

[F9] Under the causally sufficient perfect-oracle regime, population PC terminates and returns the DAG's CPDAG. [[thm-pc-oracle-correctness]]

[F10] D-separation requires every path between the queried vertex sets to be blocked by the conditioning set. [[def-d-separation-in-a-dag]]

[A1] AC is assumed by the supplied Gaussian probability interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct covariance calculation and the population PC search.

1.1 Let $W_1,\ldots,W_m$ be a finite independent family of scalar normal variables with means $\mu_r$ and variances $\sigma_r^2$. For any real coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_m,b$, [F1]–[F2] give the characteristic function of $b+\sum_r a_rW_r$ as $\exp\!\left(it(b+\sum_r a_r\mu_r)-\frac{t^2}{2}\sum_r a_r^2\sigma_r^2\right)$; scalar uniqueness identifies this as the normal law with that mean and variance. Every scalar projection of a finite affine image of $W=(W_1,\ldots,W_m)$ is such a sum, so [F3] proves that every such image is multivariate normal, including when a projection has variance zero. [F1, F2, F3, A1, construct]

1.2 The chain model's density is $\phi(x)\phi(y-x)\phi(z-y)$, where $\phi$ is the standard-normal density. Its factors are exactly the parent probability kernels $K_X(dx)=N(0,1)(dx)$, $K_Y(x,dy)=N(x,1)(dy)$, and $K_Z(y,dz)=N(y,1)(dz)$, so the full-joint law factorizes in the topological order $X,Y,Z$. All three vertices are observed and [F8] gives the Markovian SCM condition. Its moments are $\operatorname{Var}(X)=1$, $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2$, $\operatorname{Var}(Z)=3$, and distinct covariances $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1$, $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)=2$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)=1$. The vector is multivariate normal by step 1.1, and its covariance matrix is positive definite because $(X,Y,Z)$ is an invertible triangular linear transform of $(U_X,U_Y,U_Z)$. The conditional covariance formula gives $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z\mid Y)=1-\frac{1\cdot2}{2}=0,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y\mid Z)=1-\frac{1\cdot2}{3}=\frac13,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z\mid X)=2-\frac{1\cdot1}{1}=1.$ Together with the nonzero marginal covariances, [F4] shows that the only conditional independence between distinct variables is $X\perp Z\mid Y$. By [F10], the only d-separated vertex pair is also $X,Z$ given $Y$: the adjacent pairs have an active one-edge path, and the $X$–$Z$ path is blocked only by conditioning on $Y$. Any conditional independence between vertex sets would imply the corresponding coordinate independences, so the set-level independence and d-separation models also agree. This verifies faithfulness in [F7]. [given, F1, F2, F4, F7, F8, F10, A1, algebra]

1.3 The collider model's density is $\phi(x)\phi(z)\phi(y-x-z)$. Its factors are exactly the parent probability kernels $K_X(dx)=N(0,1)(dx)$, $K_Z(dz)=N(0,1)(dz)$, and $K_Y(x,z,dy)=N(x+z,1)(dy)$, so the full-joint law factorizes in the topological order $X,Z,Y$. All vertices are observed and [F8] gives the Markovian SCM condition. Its variances are $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\operatorname{Var}(Z)=1$, $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=3$, its covariances are $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Cov}(Z,Y)=1$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)=0$. The vector is multivariate normal by step 1.1, and this covariance matrix is positive definite by the invertible triangular map from the exogenous variables. By [F10], this is exactly the collider DAG's d-separation list: the collider path is blocked unconditioned and opened by conditioning on $Y$, while each adjacent pair has an active one-edge path. Any set conditional independence would imply coordinate independences, so [F7] holds at the set level as well. [given, F1, F2, F4, F7, F8, F10, A1, algebra]

2.1 Thus PC does not delete any pair at level $0$. The sole unshielded triple has its middle vertex in the separator, so [F5] or [F6] leaves both edges undirected. No Meek rule applies without a directed edge, and the output is the undirected chain CPDAG. The run terminates under [F9], since step 1.2 verifies the chain model's discovery-regime hypotheses. [F5, F6, F9, step 1.2, cases]

3.1 PC deletes $X-Z$ at level $0$ and records the empty separator. It retains $X-Y$ and $Y-Z$ by their nonzero marginal covariances. Since $Y$ is absent from the separator, [F5] orients $X\to Y\leftarrow Z$; the output is the collider CPDAG. The run terminates under [F9], since step 1.3 verifies the collider model's discovery-regime hypotheses. These calculations verify both claimed outputs without relying on the diagrams. [F4, F5, F9, step 1.3, cases] ∎

## Definition

Fix a finite DAG $G=(V,E)$ and a specified topological ordering
$v_1,\ldots,v_n$ (every arrow points from an earlier to a later vertex).
Partition $V=O\sqcup H$ into **observed** vertices $O$ and **latent** vertices
$H$. For each $v\in V$, specify a measurable state space $(S_v,\mathcal
S_v)$, a measurable exogenous space $(E_v,\mathcal E_v)$, a jointly
measurable structural function
$$f_v:\prod_{u\in\operatorname{pa}(v)}S_u\times E_v\to S_v,$$
and an exogenous random element $U_v$ with values in $E_v$. Here
$\operatorname{pa}(v)=\{u:(u,v)\in E\}$; the empty product is a singleton.
The model is **Markovian** when the finite family $(U_v)_{v\in V}$ is mutually
independent. No parametric form or distributional truth is asserted. Correlated
disturbances may be represented by adding their common causes as latent
vertices, after which the exogenous family in the expanded model is required
to be mutually independent.

Recursion in the topological order defines the endogenous random elements
uniquely by $X_v=f_v(X_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},U_v)$. The full-joint law is the
law of $(X_v)_{v\in V}$; the observed law is its marginal law on $O$. An
observed-only DAG factorization is asserted only when $H=\varnothing$ or when
an additional stated latent-variable condition proves it.

For $I\subseteq V$ and a value $a=(a_v)_{v\in I}\in\prod_{v\in I}S_v$,
**$do(X_I=a)$** means replace only the equations indexed by $I$ by the
constants $X_v=a_v$, leaving every other structural function and every
exogenous law unchanged. Recursion then defines counterfactual values
$X_w^a$ for every vertex $w$; the interventional law is their joint law. The
response map $(a,\omega)\mapsto X_w^a(\omega)$ is jointly measurable, by
induction through the finite topological order and joint measurability of each
$f_v$. This permits evaluation at a random treatment value, such as
$X_w^{M^a}$. When $I=\{A\}$, write $X_w^a$ for the response under
$do(A=a)$. If the factual treatment is $A$, then on $\{A=a\}$ recursion
gives $X_w=X_w^a$ for every vertex $w$.

## Example

Let $L,U_X,U_Y$ be independent standard normals and set
$X=L+U_X$, $Y=L+U_Y$, with latent common-cause graph $L\to X$ and $L\to Y$;
only $X,Y$ are observed. Their joint law is the same as that of the observed
direct-edge model $X=V_X$, $Y=\tfrac12X+\varepsilon$, where
$V_X\sim N(0,2)$ and $\varepsilon\sim N(0,\tfrac32)$ are independent. A
perfect observational PC oracle therefore returns the undirected edge $X-Y$.
This identifies an association but cannot distinguish the hidden common cause
from a direct causal edge, and the latent model violates the observed-only
causal-sufficiency requirement.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth, node distance=16mm]
  \node[draw,dashed,rounded corners,inner sep=2pt] at (0,0) (l) {$L$};
  \node at (1.6,0) (x) {$X$}; \node at (1.6,-1.3) (y) {$Y$};
  \draw[->] (l) -- (x); \draw[->] (l) -- (y);
  \node at (0,0.6) {latent model};
  \node at (4,0) (x2) {$X$}; \node at (5.6,0) (y2) {$Y$};
  \draw[->] (x2) -- (y2);
  \node at (4.8,0.6) {observed direct-edge model};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

Arrows represent structural causes, the dashed box marks the unobserved vertex,
and the second graph is a different model with the same observed law. The
diagram is explanatory; equality of laws and the PC output are verified below.

## Example references

[Kalisch and Bühlmann, §2.1](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume8/kalisch07a/kalisch07a.pdf)

[Meek, §1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.4972)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Independent Gaussian exogenous variables in the latent model and independent variables $V_X,\varepsilon$ in the direct-edge model.

[F1] A recursive structural causal model may distinguish observed and latent vertices; its Markovian case uses mutually independent exogenous variables. [[def-recursive-structural-causal-model-and-dag]]

[F2] The causally sufficient discovery regime requires every graph vertex to be observed and the full-joint law to have a parent-kernel factorization, so an omitted latent vertex is outside that regime. [[def-causal-discovery-oracle-regime]]

[F3] Independent scalar normal inputs have product characteristic functions, and finite affine sums use the scalar normal characteristic formula and scalar uniqueness. [[def-independent-random-elements]] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] [[lem-characteristic-functions-under-affine-maps-and-independent-sums]] [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-normal-law]] [[thm-uniqueness-of-a-law-from-its-characteristic-function]]

[F4] A finite vector is multivariate normal when every scalar linear projection has its corresponding normal law. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F5] A multivariate normal law has characteristic function $\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)$, and this function uniquely determines its vector law. [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F6] DAGs with the same skeleton and no unshielded colliders are Markov equivalent. [[thm-dag-markov-equivalence-skeleton-vstructures]]

[F7] With two vertices, a CPDAG leaves the only edge undirected when both orientations occur among equivalent DAGs. [[def-cpdag-markov-equivalence-class]]

[F8] PC retains an edge unless a tested conditioning set establishes independence; with two vertices it has no unshielded triples or Meek-rule configurations. [[alg-pc-causal-discovery]]

[F9] Under the causally sufficient perfect-oracle regime, population PC terminates and returns the DAG's CPDAG. [[thm-pc-oracle-correctness]]

[A1] AC is assumed by the Gaussian-law probability interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Verification

**Proof technique:** covariance comparison and direct inspection of the two-vertex PC search.

1.1 Let $W_1,\ldots,W_m$ be a finite independent family of scalar normal variables with means $\mu_r$ and variances $\sigma_r^2$. For real coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_m,b$, [F3] gives the characteristic function of $b+\sum_r a_rW_r$ as $\exp\!\left(it(b+\sum_r a_r\mu_r)-\frac{t^2}{2}\sum_r a_r^2\sigma_r^2\right)$; scalar uniqueness identifies this as the normal law with that mean and variance. Every scalar projection of a finite affine image of $W=(W_1,\ldots,W_m)$ is such a sum, so [F4] proves that every such image is multivariate normal, including when a projection has variance zero. [F3, F4, A1, construct]

1.2 In the latent model, $\mathbb E(X,Y)=(0,0)$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1$, by independence of $L,U_X,U_Y$. In the direct-edge model, $\mathbb E(X,Y)=(0,0)$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=2$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\tfrac12\operatorname{Var}(X)=1$, and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\tfrac14(2)+\tfrac32=2$. Both vectors are Gaussian by step 1.1 and have the same positive-definite covariance matrix $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, whose leading principal minors are $2$ and $3$. By [F5], both vector characteristic functions equal $\exp(-t^T\Sigma t/2)$ for every $t\in\mathbb R^2$; the uniqueness clause of [F5] gives equality of the full observed laws. [given, F5, step 1.1, A1, algebra]

2.1 The latent model is a finite recursive Markovian SCM with observed set $\{X,Y\}$ and omitted latent vertex $L$, so it does not satisfy [F2]. The direct-edge model has observed set $\{X,Y\}$ and independent exogenous variables; its full-joint law factors as $N(0,2)(dx)N(x/2,3/2)(dy)$, the root probability kernel for $X$ followed by the probability kernel for $Y$ given its parent $X$. In its two-vertex graph $X\to Y$, the only pair of nonempty disjoint endpoint sets is $\{X\},\{Y\}$, which is not d-separated because of the direct path; step 1.2 gives $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1$, so they are not independent. Thus this law is faithful to the direct-edge DAG, and the direct-edge model satisfies the observed-only Markovian factorization and faithfulness conditions in the discovery regime. Since the observed laws agree by step 1.2, no procedure using only that law can distinguish the two causal explanations. [F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The common observed law has $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1\ne0$, so $X,Y$ are dependent and the perfect oracle does not delete their only edge. With only two vertices there is no unshielded triple and none of R1–R3 applies; by [F9] the regime-compliant run terminates, and its computed output is $X-Y$. Reversing the single edge in the direct-edge DAG keeps the same skeleton and no unshielded collider, so [F6] proves the reverse DAG is equivalent; [F7] therefore gives the same undirected CPDAG. The PC output reports adjacency but cannot recover the latent-versus-direct causal distinction. [F6, F7, F8, F9, step 1.2, step 2.1, A1, algebra] ∎

## Example

On vertices $A,B,C$, the DAGs $A\to B$, $A\to C$, $B\to C$ and
$C\to B$, $C\to A$, $B\to A$ have the same complete skeleton and no
unshielded colliders. They are Markov equivalent. Suppose the first DAG has a
full-joint law from an observed-only Markovian recursive model with a
topological parent-kernel factorization, faithful to that DAG, and a perfect
conditional-independence oracle for that law. Each edge points in opposite
directions in the two DAGs, so their CPDAG is the fully undirected triangle;
perfect-oracle PC retains all three edges and returns that pattern.

```tikz
  \node at (0,-3.1) (a3) {$A$}; \node at (1.5,-3.1) (b3) {$B$}; \node at (0,-4.4) (c3) {$C$};
  \draw[-] (a3) -- (b3); \draw[-] (a3) -- (c3); \draw[-] (b3) -- (c3);
  \node at (0.75,0.55) {first DAG};
```

segments denote undirected edges. The pictures illustrate the edge orientations;
the verification uses the path and equivalence definitions directly.

## Example references

[Meek, Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.4972)

[Lauritzen, Theorem 2.62](https://web.math.ku.dk/~lauritzen/papers/gmnotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two finite DAGs, the first DAG's observed-only Markovian recursive model and full-joint parent-kernel factorization, its faithful law, and its perfect conditional-independence oracle.

[F1] A direct one-edge path has no internal vertices and is active under every conditioning set disjoint from its endpoints. [[def-d-separation-in-a-dag]]

[F2] DAGs are Markov equivalent exactly when their skeletons and unshielded colliders agree. [[thm-dag-markov-equivalence-skeleton-vstructures]]

[F3] A CPDAG directs exactly the edges with one orientation throughout the class and leaves an edge undirected when both directions occur. [[def-cpdag-markov-equivalence-class]]

[F4] PC deletes a pair only after a conditional-independence answer, then orients unshielded colliders and closes under R1–R3. [[alg-pc-causal-discovery]]

[F5] The background-free R1–R3 closure of the collider pattern is the CPDAG. [[lem-meek-rules-complete-for-cpdag]]

[F6] The causally sufficient discovery regime supplies the observed-only Markovian parent-kernel model, faithfulness to the first DAG, and the exact oracle; hence oracle independences agree with its d-separations. [[def-causal-discovery-oracle-regime]]

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct graph comparison and the perfect-oracle algorithm.

1.1 Each graph has all three possible edges, so there is no triple with nonadjacent endpoints and in particular no unshielded collider. Their skeletons and unshielded colliders agree; [F2] proves Markov equivalence. Every distinct pair has a direct active path under every allowed conditioning set by [F1], so neither DAG has a d-separation between distinct vertices. Faithfulness in [F6] makes the oracle dependent on every pair and set. [given, F1, F2, F6, algebra]

1.2 In the two DAGs, the orientations of $A-B$, $A-C$, and $B-C$ are respectively $A\to B$ versus $B\to A$, $A\to C$ versus $C\to A$, and $B\to C$ versus $C\to B$. Thus each edge is oriented both ways in the equivalence class, and [F3] makes every edge undirected in the CPDAG. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The perfect oracle never reports independence for any pair by step 1.1, so the algorithm deletes no edge. With three vertices, after the level-$0$ tests the complete triangle permits level $1$; at level $1$ each pair has only one possible conditioning vertex at each endpoint, and the oracle again returns dependence by step 1.1. The stopping condition then fails because an endpoint has at most one neighbor other than the other endpoint, fewer than the required two. Thus the skeleton search terminates. There is no unshielded triple to orient, and none of R1–R3 can fire because each requires at least one directed edge; the finite orientation scan therefore terminates as well. PC returns the undirected triangle, which [F5] identifies with the CPDAG found in step 1.2. The diagram is only a rendering of these verified adjacencies and orientations. [F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, cases] ∎

## Definition

Fix a nonempty finite directed acyclic graph $G=(V,E)$ with a specified
topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$; every arrow points from an earlier to a
later vertex. For $j\in V$, let
$\operatorname{pa}(j)=\{i\in V:(i,j)\in E\}$ be its parent set, and let
$\operatorname{nd}(j)$ be the vertices other than $j$ that are not descendants
of $j$. A **continuous additive-noise model** on $G$ consists of real random
variables $X_j,N_j$ on a common probability space and continuous Borel
functions $f_j:\mathbb R^{\operatorname{pa}(j)}\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$$
recursively in the topological order. The finite family of noises is mutually
independent, and each $N_j$ has a strictly positive Lebesgue density $q_j$.
All vertices of $G$ are observed; no latent vertices are omitted from the
model. The **observational law** is the law of the vector
$X=(X_j)_{j\in V}$.

The model is **causally minimal** when every parent input is essential: for
each edge $i\to j$, there are values of the other parent coordinates and two
distinct real values of the $i$-coordinate at which $f_j$ takes different
values. A root has no parent-coordinate minimality condition.

## Statement

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$. If a real number
$a$ satisfies $\mu(A+a)=\mu(A)$ for every Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R$,
then $a=0$.

## Statement references

[[def-probability-measure|A probability measure has total mass one and is countably additive]]

[[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn|Translation of a subset of the real line]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$ and an $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $\mu(A+a)=\mu(A)$ for every Borel set $A$.

[F1] A probability measure is countably additive and has total mass one. [[def-probability-measure]]

[F2] $A+a=\{x+a:x\in A\}$ is the translate of $A$. [[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]

[F3] The real line is a complete ordered field, hence its positive reals satisfy the Archimedean property. [[def-complete-ordered-real-field]], [[thm-of-archimedean]]

## Proof
**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Suppose $a\ne0$ and put $\ell=|a|>0$. Invariance under translation by $a$ implies invariance under translation by $\ell$: when $a=-\ell$, apply the given identity to $A+\ell$. The half-open intervals $I_k=[k\ell,(k+1)\ell)$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, partition $\mathbb R$ and are translates of $I_0$, so they all have the same measure $c=\mu(I_0)$. [given, F2, construct]

2.1 If $c>0$, choose a natural $n>1/c$ by [F3]. The first $n$ intervals are disjoint, so finite additivity gives $1\ge\mu(\bigcup_{k=0}^{n-1}I_k)=nc>1$, a contradiction. Hence $c=0$. [step 1.1, F1, F3, contradiction]

3.1 Countable additivity over the partition $(I_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z}$ now gives $1=\mu(\mathbb R)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\mu(I_k)=0$, again a contradiction. Therefore $a=0$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Definition

Let $n\ge 1$, let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and let $a\in\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). The **translate** of $E$ by $a$ is

$$E+a:=\{x+a:x\in E\}.$$

Translation by $a$ is the bijection $\tau_a(x)=x+a$, whose inverse is $\tau_{-a}$. In particular, $\varnothing+a=\varnothing$.

## Statement

Every complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A complete ordered field $F$; write $A = \{\, n \cdot 1_F : n \ge 1 \,\}$ for the set of its canonical naturals.

[L1] Least-upper-bound property: every nonempty $S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound $\sup S \in F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

[L2] Each canonical natural satisfies $n \cdot 1_F > 0$, one has $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$, and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$ ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).

[L3] $0 < 1_F$ ([[cor-of-one-positive]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** contradiction.

1.1 Suppose, for contradiction, that $F$ is not Archimedean: there is some $x \in F$ with $n \cdot 1_F \le x$ for all $n \ge 1$, that is, $x$ is an upper bound of $A$. [assume-contra]

2.1 The set $A$ is nonempty, since $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F \in A$, and it is bounded above by $x$. [step 1.1, L2]

3.1 By the least-upper-bound property, $A$ has a least upper bound $s = \sup A \in F$. [step 2.1, L1]

4.1 Since $1_F > 0$, we have $s - 1_F < s$; as $s$ is the least upper bound, $s - 1_F$ is not an upper bound of $A$. [step 3.1, L3]

5.1 Hence there is some $m \ge 1$ with $m \cdot 1_F > s - 1_F$. [step 4.1]

6.1 Adding $1_F$ to both sides, $(m+1) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + 1_F > s$. [step 5.1, L2]

7.1 But $(m+1) \cdot 1_F \in A$, so $(m+1) \cdot 1_F \le s$ because $s$ is an upper bound of $A$, contradicting 6.1. [step 6.1, step 3.1, L2]

8.1 The assumption is therefore untenable, so $F$ is Archimedean. [step 7.1, discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Statement

Let $C$ be a finite-dimensional real random vector, let $(Y,C)$ have a
strictly positive $C^3$ joint density $p(y,c)$, and let
$m:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be $C^3$. If $R=Y-m(C)$ is independent of $C$, then there are
strictly positive $C^3$ Lebesgue density versions $q_R$ and $p_C$ such that
$$p(y,c)=q_R(y-m(c))p_C(c)$$
for every $(y,c)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$.

## Statement references

[[def-independent-random-elements|Independence of the residual and predictors]]

[[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law|The independent joint law is the product of its marginals]]

[[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant|Sectionwise translations preserve Lebesgue measure]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The random vector, density, function and independence assumption in the Statement.

[F1] Translation preserves Lebesgue measure and Lebesgue measurability. [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]

[F2] Independent random elements have product joint law. [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]

[F3] Nonnegative product-measurable functions can be integrated by iterated sections in any finite coordinate order. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

## Proof
**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 The coordinate change $(y,c)\mapsto(r,c)=(y-m(c),c)$ is a translation in each fixed $c$-section. By [F1] and iterated integration [F3], the law of $(R,C)$ has density $h(r,c)=p(r+m(c),c)$. Since $p$ and $m$ are $C^3$ and $p>0$, $h$ is a strictly positive $C^3$ function. [given, F1, F3, construct]

2.1 Independence and [F2] make the law with density $h(r,c)$ from step 1.1 the product of the marginal laws of $R$ and $C$. Tonelli [F3] gives marginal density versions, and therefore $h(r,c)=q_R(r)p_C(c)$ almost everywhere. Choose $c_0$ for which $0<p_C(c_0)<\infty$ and this equality holds for almost every $r$. Then $q_R(r)=h(r,c_0)/p_C(c_0)$ almost everywhere, so this formula supplies a strictly positive $C^3$ version of $q_R$. [step 1.1, given, F2, F3, construct]

3.1 By Fubini choose $r_0$ with $q_R(r_0)>0$ such that $h(r_0,c)=q_R(r_0)p_C(c)$ for almost every $c$. Set $p_C^*(c)=h(r_0,c)/q_R(r_0)$. This is a strictly positive $C^3$ function and equals $p_C$ almost everywhere. Thus $h(r,c)=q_R(r)p_C^*(c)$ almost everywhere; both sides are continuous, so the equality holds everywhere. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, F3, algebra]

4.1 Substituting $r=y-m(c)$ into step 3.1 yields $p(y,c)=q_R(y-m(c))p_C^*(c)$ for every $(y,c)$. Renaming $p_C^*$ as $p_C$ proves the Statement. [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
## References

[Peters et al., JMLR (2014), Appendix A.15, proof of Theorem 34](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume15/peters14a/peters14a.pdf)

## Statement

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $n \ge 1$, a vector $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and a subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

[L1] $\lambda_n^*(E) := \inf\{\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu_0(A_k) : A_k \in \mathcal{E}_n$ for every $k$ and $E \subseteq \bigcup_k A_k\}$ ([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]], [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]).

[L2] $B(a,b) := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i \le b_i \ \text{ for every } i < n \,\}$; a box is nonempty exactly when $a_i<b_i$ for every $i<n$; and for a nonempty box with real parameters $\operatorname{vol}(B) := \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i)$, the value being $+\infty$ when a parameter is infinite ([[def-half-open-box]]).

[L3] A subset $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is an **elementary set** when there are a natural number $m$ and a list $B_0, \dots, B_{m-1}$ of half-open boxes with $E=\bigcup_{j<m}B_j$ ([[def-elementary-set-in-rn]]), and every elementary set is the union of a finite list of pairwise disjoint half-open boxes ([[lem-elementary-sets-are-finite-disjoint-unions-of-half-open-boxes]]).

[L4] For every $n\ge1$, elementary volume $\mu_0$ on $\mathcal{E}_n$ has value at $A$ the sum of the volumes of the members of any presentation of $A$ by a finite list of pairwise disjoint half-open boxes ([[thm-elementary-volume-is-well-defined]]).

[L5] A set $E$ is **Lebesgue measurable** when $\lambda_n^*(A) = \lambda_n^*(A\cap E)+\lambda_n^*(A\setminus E)$ for every $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, and $\lambda_n$ is the restriction of $\lambda_n^*$ to the family of these ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]], [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]]).

[F1] The **translate** of $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ by $a$ is $E+a:=\{x+a:x\in E\}$; translation by $a$ is the bijection $\tau_a(x)=x+a$, whose inverse is $\tau_{-a}$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]).

[F2] Addition of a real to an extended real is defined in every case, with $a+b := +\infty$ when $a=+\infty$ and $b \ne -\infty$, and $a+b := -\infty$ when $a=-\infty$ and $b \ne +\infty$ ([[def-extended-reals]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For a parameter pair $(a,b)$ one has $B(a,b)+h = B(a+h,b+h)$, where $a+h$ is the parameter $i \mapsto a_i+h_i$: a point $y$ lies in the left side exactly when $y-h$ satisfies $a_i<y_i-h_i\le b_i$, that is $a_i+h_i<y_i\le b_i+h_i$. The translated box is empty exactly when the original is, and has the same volume, because $(b_i+h_i)-(a_i+h_i)=b_i-a_i$ when both are real and an infinite parameter stays infinite. [L2, F1, F2]

2.1 Consequently, if $A = \bigcup_{j<q}B_j$ is a presentation of an elementary set by pairwise disjoint half-open boxes, then $A+h = \bigcup_{j<q}(B_j+h)$ is such a presentation of $A+h$, so $A+h$ is elementary and $\mu_0(A+h)=\mu_0(A)$. [step 1.1, L3, L4]

3.1 A sequence $(A_k)$ of elementary sets covers $E$ if and only if the sequence $(A_k+h)$ covers $E+h$, and the two covering costs are equal by step 2.1; the correspondence is a bijection between the two families of covers, with inverse given by translating by $-h$, so the two infima agree and $\lambda_n^*(E+h)=\lambda_n^*(E)$. [step 2.1, L1, F1]

4.1 For test sets, $A\cap(E+h) = \big((A-h)\cap E\big)+h$ and $A\setminus(E+h) = \big((A-h)\setminus E\big)+h$, so by step 3.1 the Carathéodory identity for $E+h$ tested against $A$ is exactly the identity for $E$ tested against $A-h$; as $A$ ranges over all subsets so does $A-h$, and therefore $E+h$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E$ is, with $\lambda_n(E+h)=\lambda_n^*(E+h)=\lambda_n^*(E)=\lambda_n(E)$ in that case. [step 3.1, L5, F1] ∎

## Definition

Fix a finite nonempty ordered vertex set $V$ and a population law of a real
vector $X=(X_j)_{j\in V}$ generated by an additive-noise model. A **population
regression rule** $\mathcal R$ assigns to each target $j\in V$ and predictor
set $C\subseteq V\setminus\{j\}$ a Borel function
$m_{j,C}:\mathbb R^C\to\mathbb R$. A **perfect independence oracle** returns
“independent” exactly when the tested random variable and random vector are
independent under this population law. For a given ANM, $\mathcal R$ is
**population-consistent on that model** if for every $j$ and every
$C$ with $\operatorname{pa}(j)\subseteq C\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)$,
there is a constant $c_{j,C}\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$m_{j,C}(X_C)=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+c_{j,C}\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
This consistency condition concerns only the population regression target and
does not assert a finite-sample guarantee. The procedure itself is defined for
any supplied regression rule and oracle.

RESIT takes $X$, $\mathcal R$, and the perfect independence oracle and
performs the following steps, using a fixed total order on $V$ for every tie
and loop order.

1. Set the remaining set $S:=V$ and an empty sink list. While $S\ne\varnothing$,
   for each $j\in S$ form
   $$R_j:=X_j-m_{j,S\setminus\{j\}}(X_{S\setminus\{j\}}).$$
   Retain the vertices for which the oracle declares
   $R_j$ independent of $X_{S\setminus\{j\}}$. If there is no such vertex,
   return `failure`. Otherwise choose the least retained vertex $k$, record
   the provisional parent set $\widehat{\operatorname{pa}}(k):=S\setminus\{k\}$,
   append $k$ to the sink list, and remove $k$ from $S$.
2. Reverse the sink list to obtain an order $\pi$. In that order, for each
   vertex $j$ and each candidate $\ell$ in its provisional parent set, in the
   fixed order, let
   $C:=\widehat{\operatorname{pa}}(j)\setminus\{\ell\}$ and form
   $$R_{j,\ell}:=X_j-m_{j,C}(X_C).$$
   If the oracle declares $R_{j,\ell}$ independent of the vector of all
   vertices preceding $j$ in $\pi$, delete $\ell$ from
   $\widehat{\operatorname{pa}}(j)$; otherwise retain it.
3. Return the DAG with arrow $i\to j$ exactly when
   $i\in\widehat{\operatorname{pa}}(j)$ after pruning.

      url: "https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/12/gsm-126-tao5-measure-book.pdf"

## Statement

Let a finite additive-noise model have topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$,
equations $X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$, and strictly positive
Lebesgue densities $q_j$ for its mutually independent noises. Write
$\lambda^{\otimes p}$ for the finite product of one-dimensional Lebesgue
measure. Then the observational law of $X=(X_j)_{j\in V}$ has the strictly
positive density
$$p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
with respect to $\lambda^{\otimes p}$.

## Statement references

[[def-additive-noise-model|Finite continuous additive-noise models]]

[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique|Finite product reference measure and its rectangle formula]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite causally sufficient additive-noise model with a specified topological order and positive noise densities.

[F1] In topological order each variable is a measurable function of its parents plus its own noise; the noises are mutually independent and each density $q_j$ is normalized and strictly positive. [[def-additive-noise-model]]

[F2] The joint law of a finite independent family of random elements is the finite product of its marginal laws. [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]

[F3] For a nonnegative measurable density $g$, the measure with density $g$ relative to $\mu$ is $A\mapsto\int_A g\,d\mu$. [[def-measure-with-density]]

[F4] For sigma-finite factors, the product measure exists, has the rectangle product formula, and is unique among measures with that formula. [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]

[F5] Nonnegative product-measurable functions can be integrated by iterated sections in any finite coordinate order. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

[F6] Translation by a fixed real number preserves one-dimensional Lebesgue measure. [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]

[F7] Finite sums and pointwise products of measurable real-valued functions are measurable. [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]

[F8] Composition of measurable maps is measurable. [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]

## Proof
**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 For each $j$, let $Q_j=q_j\,d\lambda$; [F1, F3] makes $Q_j$ a probability measure. The function $g(n)=\prod_{r=1}^p q_{v_r}(n_{v_r})$ is product-measurable by [F7] and [F8]. Repeated Tonelli [F5] gives $\int g\,d\lambda^{\otimes p}=\prod_j\int q_j\,d\lambda=1$ and, on every measurable rectangle, $\int_{\prod B_j}g\,d\lambda^{\otimes p}=\prod_j Q_j(B_j)$. Thus $g\,d\lambda^{\otimes p}$ and $\bigotimes_j Q_j$ have the same rectangle formula; uniqueness [F4] identifies them. By [F2], this product measure is the joint law of the noise vector. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F7, F8]

1.2 Recursion in the stated topological order defines a Borel map $T:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^p$ from the noise vector to $X$: each new coordinate is a Borel function of earlier coordinates and its own noise. The inverse is triangular, $n_j=x_j-f_j(x_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})$, so the law of $X$ is the pushforward of the noise-vector law under $T$. [given, F1, F8, construct]

2.1 Starting with the product noise density from step 1.1, process the coordinates in topological order. At stage $r$, with earlier endogenous coordinates fixed, the next coordinate is $x_{v_r}=n_{v_r}+f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})$, a translation by a fixed real number. By [F6], this translation preserves Lebesgue measure and changes its density factor to $q_{v_r}(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)}))$. The shift depends only on earlier coordinates, so this is a sectionwise change in one coordinate; [F5] justifies each iterated integration for every nonnegative Borel test function. Induction over $r=1,\ldots,p$ gives the displayed product density for the pushforward law. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F5, F6, F7, F8, construct]

3.1 Every factor in the displayed density is strictly positive at its real argument by [F1], and a finite product of positive real numbers is positive. This proves strict positivity of the joint density. [given, step 2.1, F1, algebra] ∎
## References

[Peters et al., JMLR (2014), equation (6) and §3](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume15/peters14a/peters14a.pdf)

[Tao, An Introduction to Measure Theory, Theorem 1.7.18](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/12/gsm-126-tao5-measure-book.pdf)

    - title: "Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 2.1.10"
      url: "https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf"

## Statement

In a finite additive-noise model on a DAG $G$, for every vertex $j$ and every
set $S\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)$ of nondescendants, the noise $N_j$ is
independent of the random vector $X_S=(X_k)_{k\in S}$.

## Statement references

[[def-additive-noise-model|Finite recursive additive-noise models and nondescendants]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite recursive ANM with mutually independent exogenous noises.

[F1] Each endogenous variable is obtained recursively in a topological order as a Borel function of its parents and its own noise. [[def-additive-noise-model]]

[F2] The joint law of a finite independent family is the product of its marginal laws. [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]

[F3] Measurable functions of independent random elements remain independent. [[lem-measurable-functions-preserve-independence]]

## Proof
**Given:** The finite DAG, its topological structural equations, and mutually independent noises.

1.1 For each $k\in S$, define $A_k$ to be $k$ together with all vertices having a directed path to $k$, and put $A=\bigcup_{k\in S}A_k$. In topological order, a root variable is a measurable function of its own noise; if this representation has been obtained for each parent of $k$, substituting those representations into $X_k=f_k(X_{\operatorname{pa}(k)})+N_k$ shows that $X_k$ is a measurable function of $(N_i)_{i\in A_k}$. Finite induction therefore makes $X_S$ a measurable function of $(N_i)_{i\in A}$. Since $S$ contains only nondescendants of $j$, no directed path goes from $j$ to a vertex of $S$, so $j\notin A$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 The finite noise product law [F2] implies that $N_j$ is independent of the vector $(N_i)_{i\in A}$ because the two coordinate blocks are disjoint. Applying [F3] to the measurable map from that vector to $X_S$ from step 1.1 shows $N_j\perp X_S$. If $S=\varnothing$, $X_S$ is the constant empty tuple and the same independence statement holds. [F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

[Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 2.1.10](https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/PTE/PTE5_011119.pdf)

## Definition

For a smooth bivariate additive-noise model $Y=f(X)+N$, let $f$ be three
times continuously differentiable, and let $X$ and $N$ have strictly positive
three-times continuously differentiable densities $p_X$ and $p_N$. Put
$\xi(x)=\log p_X(x)$ and $\nu(z)=\log p_N(z)$. The triple $(f,p_X,p_N)$
satisfies **Condition 19** when there are $x,y\in\mathbb R$ with
$\nu''(y-f(x))f'(x)\ne0$ at which
$$\xi'''(x)\ne \xi''(x)\left(-\frac{\nu'''(y-f(x))f'(x)}{\nu''(y-f(x))}+\frac{f''(x)}{f'(x)}\right) -2\nu''(y-f(x))f''(x)f'(x) +\nu'(y-f(x))f'''(x) +\frac{\nu'(y-f(x))\nu'''(y-f(x))f''(x)f'(x)}{\nu''(y-f(x))} -\frac{\nu'(y-f(x))(f''(x))^2}{f'(x)}.$$
Here every derivative of $\nu$ is evaluated at $y-f(x)$ and every derivative
of $f$ at $x$. The nonzero-domain condition makes both denominators in this
formula well defined.

A finite additive-noise model is a **restricted additive-noise model** when
every structural function $f_j$ is $C^3$ and every noise has a strictly
positive $C^3$ Lebesgue density, and when for every vertex $j$, every parent
$i\in\operatorname{pa}(j)$, and every set
$S$ satisfying
$$\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}\subseteq S\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)\setminus\{i\},$$
there is a value $s$ with $0<p_S(s)<\infty$ such that the
conditional law of $X_i$ given $X_S=s$, together with the structural slice
$u\mapsto f_j(s_{\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}},u)$ and the noise $N_j$,
is a smooth bivariate additive-noise model satisfying Condition 19. The
conditional density is the ratio
$p_{X_i,X_S}(u,s)/p_S(s)$ for the finite positive-density version supplied
by the joint-density formula. The structural slice and conditional input
density have the smoothness and strict positivity required in the preceding
Condition 19 definition. If the model has no edges, the restricted condition
is vacuous.

## Statement

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite DAG, and let $X$ follow a recursive additive-noise
model on $G$ in a fixed topological order, with continuous Borel structural
functions $f_v:\mathbb R^{\operatorname{pa}(v)}\to\mathbb R$ and equations
$$X_v=f_v(X_{\operatorname{pa}(v)})+N_v,$$
mutually independent noises with strictly positive Lebesgue densities $q_v$,
and joint density
$$p_X(x)=\prod_{v\in V}q_v\!\left(x_v-f_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)})\right).$$
For $T\subseteq V$, let
$$p_T(x_T)=\int_{\mathbb R^{V\setminus T}}p_X(x)\,dx_{V\setminus T}$$
be the marginal density relative to finite product Lebesgue measure. Let
$A,B,C\subseteq V$ be pairwise disjoint with $A$ and $B$ nonempty. If $C$
d-separates $A$ and $B$ (every path from $A$ to $B$ has an internal
noncollider in $C$ or an internal collider with no descendant in $C$), then
$$p_{A\cup B\cup C}(x_A,x_B,x_C)p_C(x_C)=p_{A\cup C}(x_A,x_C)p_{B\cup C}(x_B,x_C)$$
for Lebesgue-almost every $(x_A,x_B,x_C)$. This identity is the
conditional-density factorization expressing conditional independence.

## Statement references

[[def-additive-noise-model|Finite recursive additive-noise equations and positive noise densities]]

[[def-d-separation-in-a-dag|Active paths and d-separation in a finite DAG]]

[[lem-anm-joint-density|Positive product density of a finite additive-noise model]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite ANM and pairwise disjoint sets in the Statement, with $C$ d-separating $A$ and $B$.

[F1] The ANM joint density is the product of the shifted noise densities displayed in the Statement. [[lem-anm-joint-density]]

[F2] Each $q_v$ is a normalized Lebesgue density, and translating its argument by a fixed real amount preserves its total mass because Lebesgue measure is translation invariant. [[def-additive-noise-model]] [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]

[F3] Nonnegative product-measurable functions can be integrated in successive coordinate sections, and the resulting parameter integrals are measurable. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

[F4] D-separation is equivalent to disconnection after deleting the conditioning set from the ancestral moral graph of the two endpoint sets and that conditioning set. [[lem-d-separation-ancestral-moral-separation]]

[F5] The ancestral moral graph retains all ancestors of its queried vertex set, forgets arrow directions, and joins each vertex to its parents and every distinct pair of parents of a common child. [[def-ancestral-moral-graph-of-a-dag]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Put $H=\operatorname{An}_G(A\cup B\cup C)$. No vertex outside $H$ is a parent of a vertex in $H$, since that would make it an ancestor of $A\cup B\cup C$. Integrate the product density [F1] over $V\setminus H$ in reverse topological order. At each elimination, all child factors have already been integrated and no child lies in $H$, so the only remaining factor involving the current coordinate $x_v$ is $q_v(x_v-f_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)}))$. Its section integral is one by [F2]. Tonelli [F3] justifies each section integral; consequently the marginal density on $H$ is $\prod_{v\in H}q_v(x_v-f_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)}))$. [given, F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 By [F4], deleting $C$ from the moral graph on $H$ leaves no path from $A$ to $B$. Partition its connected components into $L$, the union of components meeting $A$, and $R$, the union of the remaining components. Then $A\subseteq L$, $B\subseteq R$, and there is no moral edge between $L$ and $R$. For each $v\in H$, the factor indexed by $v$ in step 1.1 depends only on $\{v\}\cup\operatorname{pa}(v)\subseteq H$; this set is a clique in that moral graph by [F5]. Hence no such factor involves both an $L$-coordinate and an $R$-coordinate. Assign factors involving an $L$-coordinate to $U$, and assign all other factors to $W$. Their finite products give a factorization of the density on $H$ as $U(x_L,x_C)W(x_R,x_C)$. [given, F4, F5, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Integrate the factorization in step 2.1 over the hidden coordinates $L\setminus A$ and $R\setminus B$. Since the factors separate and are nonnegative, Tonelli [F3] yields measurable functions $u(x_A,x_C)$ and $w(x_B,x_C)$ such that $p_{A\cup B\cup C}(x_A,x_B,x_C)=u(x_A,x_C)w(x_B,x_C)$ almost everywhere. Each function is strictly positive because it integrates a strictly positive factor over its hidden coordinates; if that coordinate set is empty, it is the original strictly positive factor. [step 2.1, F1, F3, construct]

4.1 Define $\alpha(x_C)=\int u(x_A,x_C)\,dx_A$ and $\beta(x_C)=\int w(x_B,x_C)\,dx_B$. Tonelli makes these measurable and gives $p_{A\cup C}=u\beta$ and $p_{B\cup C}=w\alpha$ almost everywhere. Also $p_C(x_C)=\int u(x_A,x_C)w(x_B,x_C)\,dx_A dx_B$ for almost every $x_C$. The marginal $p_C$ is positive, since it integrates the everywhere-positive density over any unit box in the remaining coordinates, and it is finite almost everywhere since $\int p_C=1$. For almost every such $x_C$, strict positivity of $u,w$ gives $\alpha,\beta>0$. If, for example, $\alpha=\infty$, then $\beta>0$ supplies a set of $b$-values of positive measure where $w(b,x_C)>1/n$ for some $n$, so Tonelli makes $\int u(a,x_C)w(b,x_C)\,da\,db=\infty$; the same argument applies if $\beta=\infty$. Hence both integrals are finite almost everywhere, Tonelli factors the last integral as $p_C=\alpha\beta$, and multiplying the finite marginal identities gives the claimed conditional-density factorization. [given, step 3.1, F1, F3, algebra] ∎

[Peters et al., JMLR (2014), §1.1 and Appendix A.12](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume15/peters14a/peters14a.pdf)

## Statement

Let $X$ follow a finite additive-noise model with a strictly positive joint
density and continuous structural functions that are causally minimal in each
parent coordinate. For positive joint densities, write
$Y\perp_d A\mid Z$ when the conditional-density factorization
$$p_{Y,A,Z}(y,a,z)p_Z(z)=p_{Y,Z}(y,z)p_{A,Z}(a,z)$$
holds almost everywhere. For every edge $i\to j$ and every set $S$ such that
$$\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}\subseteq S\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)\setminus\{i\},$$
the density conditional-independence factorization
$X_j\perp_d X_i\mid X_S$ fails.

## Statement references

[[def-additive-noise-model|Causal minimality and finite additive-noise equations]]

[[lem-anm-joint-density|Positive joint density and conditional-density versions]]

[[lem-anm-noise-independent-of-nondescendants|Noise independence from nondescendants]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite ANM with positive joint density, continuous parent-coordinate functions, and causal minimality.

[F1] Every parent input is essential: for each edge $i\to j$, $f_j$ is nonconstant in the $i$-coordinate for some setting of the other parents; noises are independent and have positive densities. [[def-additive-noise-model]]

[F2] The joint density is the positive product $p_X(x)=\prod_k q_k(x_k-f_k(x_{\operatorname{pa}(k)}))$. Marginal densities are obtained by integrating this formula, and a conditional density at a positive finite marginal-density value is the corresponding ratio. [[lem-anm-joint-density]]

[F3] For every vertex $j$, $N_j$ is independent of any vector of nondescendants. [[lem-anm-noise-independent-of-nondescendants]]

## Proof
**Given:** Fix an edge $i\to j$ and a set $S$ in the range in the Statement. Put $P=\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}$ and $Q=S\setminus P$.

1.1 Every variable in $\{i\}\cup P\cup Q$ is a nondescendant of $j$. By [F3], $N_j$ is independent of the vector $(X_i,X_P,X_Q)$. Conditional on $(X_i=x,X_P=p,X_Q=q)$, the structural equation therefore gives the density $p_{X_j\mid X_i,X_P,X_Q}(y\mid x,p,q)=q_j(y-f_j(p,x))$ for almost every $(x,p,q,y)$. This density does not depend on $q$, so the joint conditional density of $(X_j,X_Q)$ given $(X_i,X_P)$ factors; hence $X_j\perp_d X_Q\mid(X_i,X_P)$. [given, F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Suppose, for contradiction, that $X_j\perp_d X_i\mid X_P$. Since $N_j$ is independent of the parent vector $(X_i,X_P)$, its conditional density is $q_j(y-f_j(p,x))$. The assumed factorization says this density is independent of $x$ for almost every $p$ and almost every $x$. The conditional density of $X_i$ given $X_P=p$ is positive for almost every $x$ at almost every $p$ with $0<p_P(p)<\infty$, because the full joint density is strictly positive. Therefore, for almost every such $p$, for almost every pair $x,x'$, the two translates $q_j(y-f_j(p,x))$ and $q_j(y-f_j(p,x'))$ agree for almost every $y$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 A positive integrable density cannot have a nonzero period: if $q_j(y-a)=q_j(y-b)$ almost everywhere with $a\ne b$, then $q_j$ repeats on every translate of an interval of length $|a-b|$; that interval has positive integral, so the integral over the disjoint translates is infinite, contradicting $\int q_j=1$. Thus step 1.2 forces $f_j(p,x)=f_j(p,x')$ for almost every pair $x,x'$ and almost every $p$. Continuity of $f_j$ extends this constancy to every setting of the other parent coordinates: any two unequal values would persist on open neighborhoods of positive Lebesgue measure. This contradicts [F1], so $X_j\not\perp_d X_i\mid X_P$. [step 1.2, F1, F2, algebra]

3.1 If $Q$ is empty, $S=P$ and step 2.1 is the required conclusion. Otherwise, suppose $X_j\perp_d X_i\mid X_{P,Q}$. By the conditional-density equality in step 1.1 and this supposition, for almost every $(p,y)$ one has $p_{X_j\mid X_i=x,X_P=p}(y)=p_{X_j\mid X_P=p,X_Q=q}(y)$ for almost every pair $(x,q)$. The left side depends only on $x$ and the right side only on $q$; by Fubini, each is therefore almost everywhere constant in its varying coordinate. Hence $X_j\perp_d X_i\mid X_P$, contradicting step 2.1. Thus the factorization given $X_S$ fails. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, algebra] ∎
## References

[Peters et al., JMLR (2014), Appendix A.10, Proposition 17 and Lemma 38](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume15/peters14a/peters14a.pdf)

[Peters, Janzing, and Schölkopf, Elements of Causal Inference, §4.1.4](https://web.math.ku.dk/~peters/jonas_files/ElementsOfCausalInference.pdf)

## Statement

Let a finite causally sufficient additive-noise model have graph $G$, and let
$y\to z$ be an edge such that there is no directed path from $z$ to any other
child of $y$. Write $D=\operatorname{de}_G(z)$ for the strict descendants of
$z$ and $S=V\setminus(D\cup\{y,z\})$. If $p$ is the positive joint density,
there are positive measurable functions $A(y,s,z)$ and $B(d,s,z)$ such that
$p(d,y,s,z)=A(y,s,z)B(d,s,z)$, where $A$ does not depend on $d$ and $B$ does
not depend on $y$. Use marginal density versions obtained by iterated
integration. Then
$$p_{X_D,X_y,X_S,X_z}(d,y,s,z)\,p_{X_S,X_z}(s,z)=p_{X_D,X_S,X_z}(d,s,z)\,p_{X_y,X_S,X_z}(y,s,z)$$
for almost every $(d,y,s,z)$. This is the density conditional-independence
factorization of $X_D$ and $X_y$ given $(X_S,X_z)$. Moreover, for every $s$
with $0<p_{X_S}(s)<\infty$, the conditional law of $(X_D,X_y)$ given
$X_S=s$ satisfies the density conditional-independence factorization given
$X_z$.

## Statement references

[[def-additive-noise-model|Finite recursive additive-noise equations and mutual noise independence]]

[[def-d-separation-in-a-dag|Children, descendants and directed paths in a finite DAG]]

[[lem-anm-joint-density|The positive product formula for the full joint density]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite causally sufficient additive-noise model, an edge $y\to z$ satisfying the youngest-child condition in the Statement, and its positive joint density.

[F1] In a topological order, $X_v=f_v(X_{\operatorname{pa}(v)})+N_v$ recursively, and the noises are mutually independent. [[def-additive-noise-model]]

[F2] The joint density is $p(x)=\prod_{v\in V}q_v(x_v-f_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)}))$, with each factor depending only on that vertex and its parents. [[lem-anm-joint-density]]

[F3] Nonnegative product-measurable functions can be integrated in any finite coordinate order by iterated sections. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

## Proof
**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 If $y$ were a parent of any $d\in D$, then $d$ would be another child of $y$ and also a descendant of $z$, contrary to the hypothesis. Thus no vertex in $D$ has $y$ as a parent. Every parent of a vertex in $D$ therefore lies in $D\cup\{z\}\cup S$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 No vertex in $D$ can be a parent of a vertex outside $D$: that would make the latter a descendant of $z$. Hence each density factor in [F2] for a vertex outside $D$ depends only on $(y,s,z)$, while each factor for a vertex in $D$ depends only on $(d,s,z)$. Regrouping the finite product gives $p(d,y,s,z)=A(y,s,z)B(d,s,z)$ for nonnegative measurable functions $A,B$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F3], the marginal densities obtained from the full product are $p_{X_S,X_z}(s,z)=\left(\int A(y,s,z)\,dy\right)\left(\int B(d,s,z)\,dd\right),$ $p_{X_y,X_S,X_z}(y,s,z)=A(y,s,z)\int B(d,s,z)\,dd,\qquad p_{X_D,X_S,X_z}(d,s,z)=B(d,s,z)\int A(y,s,z)\,dy.$ These identities hold almost everywhere where the marginal densities are finite; Tonelli also permits infinite values on exceptional null sets. Multiplying the last two identities and comparing with the first proves the factorization in the Statement almost everywhere. For any fixed $s$ with $0<p_{X_S}(s)<\infty$, put $a_s(z)=\int A(y,s,z)\,dy$ and $b_s(z)=\int B(d,s,z)\,dd$. Tonelli gives $p_{X_S}(s)=\int a_s(z)b_s(z)\,dz<\infty$, so for almost every $z$ under that conditional law both $a_s(z)$ and $b_s(z)$ are finite and positive. The conditional densities of $X_y$ and $X_D$ given $(X_S=s,X_z=z)$ are respectively $A(y,s,z)/a_s(z)$ and $B(d,s,z)/b_s(z)$; their product is the joint conditional density. This proves the stated conditional-independence factorization at each such $s$. [step 2.1, F3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let two finite causally sufficient additive-noise models on distinct DAGs
with the same vertex set have the same observational law, a strictly positive
joint density, and causal minimality in each model. If their DAGs are $G$ and $G'$, then there
are vertices $y,l$ and a set $S$ such that $y\to l$ in $G$, $l\to y$ in $G'$, and
$$\operatorname{pa}_G(l)\setminus\{y\}\subseteq S\subseteq \operatorname{nd}_G(l)\setminus\{y\},\qquad \operatorname{pa}_{G'}(y)\setminus\{l\}\subseteq S\subseteq \operatorname{nd}_{G'}(y)\setminus\{l\}.$$

## Statement references

[[def-additive-noise-model|Finite causally sufficient ANM models and causal minimality]]

[[def-d-separation-in-a-dag|Parents, children, descendants, and nondescendants in a finite DAG]]

[[lem-anm-joint-density|Positive product density of a finite additive-noise model]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Two different finite causally sufficient ANM DAGs with a common strictly positive observational density, and causal minimality in both.

[F1] Each noise density is normalized and positive, and each model has the positive product density of its shifted noise densities. [[def-additive-noise-model]] [[lem-anm-joint-density]]

[F2] Each ANM noise is independent of every finite vector of its nondescendants. [[lem-anm-noise-independent-of-nondescendants]]

[F3] In a positive-density causally minimal ANM, every edge $i\to j$ remains conditionally dependent for every $S$ with $\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}\subseteq S\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)\setminus\{i\}$. The conditional-independence convention is the marginal-density factorization from that supplier. [[lem-anm-parent-dependence-persists-under-conditioning]]

[F4] A path is active given a conditioning set exactly when each noncollider is outside the set and each collider has a descendant in it. [[def-d-separation-in-a-dag]]

[F5] Every active finite route between distinct endpoints outside a conditioning set contains an active path with the same endpoints. [[lem-active-routes-in-a-finite-dag-have-active-paths]]

[F6] If a set d-separates two vertex sets in a finite ANM with positive product density, their marginal densities satisfy the conditional-independence factorization almost everywhere. [[lem-anm-density-factorization-implies-dsep-conditional-independence]]

[F7] A fixed real translation preserves the integral of a nonnegative Lebesgue-measurable function. [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Repeatedly delete a vertex that is a sink in both graphs and has the same parent set in both. At each deletion, its equation contributes a single shifted noise-density factor, which integrates to one by [F7]; no remaining equation uses the deleted vertex, so the remaining law still has the positive ANM product density and all remaining edges remain causally minimal. The process cannot delete every vertex, since then the graphs would be equal. It stops only when no common sink with equal parent sets remains; therefore choose a remaining sink $l$ of $G$, which either has a different parent set in $G'$ or has a child in $G'$. [given, F1, F7, construct, contradiction]

2.1 Partition the incident vertices by $Z=\operatorname{pa}_G(l)\cap\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(l)$, $Y=\operatorname{pa}_G(l)\cap\operatorname{ch}_{G'}(l)$, $W=\operatorname{pa}_G(l)\setminus(Z\cup Y)$, $D=\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(l)\setminus\operatorname{pa}_G(l)$, and $E=\operatorname{ch}_{G'}(l)\setminus\operatorname{pa}_G(l)$. These sets are pairwise disjoint, $\operatorname{pa}_G(l)=Z\cup Y\cup W$, $\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(l)=Z\cup D$, and $\operatorname{ch}_{G'}(l)=Y\cup E$. Put $T=Y\cup W$. [step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Suppose $T=\varnothing$ and $D\ne\varnothing$, and choose $d\in D$. Since $l$ is a sink in $G$, all vertices in $D\cup Z$ are nondescendants of $l$. By [F2], $N_l$ is independent of $(X_D,X_Z)$; the equation $X_l=f_l(X_Z)+N_l$ therefore makes the conditional density of $X_l$ given $(X_D,X_Z)$ independent of $X_D$. Its density factorization gives $X_l\perp_d X_D\mid X_Z$. Weak union follows directly by writing this factorization for the split $D=\{d\}\cup(D\setminus\{d\})$ and dividing by the positive marginal density: $X_l\perp_d X_d\mid X_{Z\cup(D\setminus\{d\})}$. This conditioning set contains all other parents of $l$ in $G'$ and contains no descendant of $l$ there, contradicting [F3] for $d\to l$ in $G'$. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra, contradiction]

3.2 Suppose $T=D=\varnothing$ and $E\ne\varnothing$. Choose $e\in E$ and put $R=\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(e)\setminus\{l\}$. Since $l$ is a sink in $G$, every vertex of $\{e\}\cup Z\cup R$ is a nondescendant of $l$. By [F2], $N_l$ is independent of $(X_e,X_R,X_Z)$; hence the conditional density of $X_l$ given these variables depends only on $X_Z$. Splitting off $X_e$ and dividing by the positive marginal density gives $X_l\perp_d X_e\mid X_{Z\cup R}$. In $G'$, $l\to e$, the set $Z\cup R$ contains all other parents of $e$, and each $z\in Z$ is an ancestor of $e$ along $z\to l\to e$, so this set contains no descendant of $e$. This contradicts [F3] for $l\to e$. If also $E=\varnothing$, then $l$ is a common sink with the same parent set and would have been deleted in step 1.1. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra, contradiction]

4.1 It remains that $T\ne\varnothing$. Choose $t\in T$ with no directed path in $G'$ from $t$ to any other member of $T$; such a vertex exists because the induced graph on finite $T$ is acyclic. We show that $t\notin W$. For contradiction suppose $t=w\in W$, and form $\widetilde G'$ by adding arrows $y'\to w$ for all $y'\in Y$ and $w'\to w$ for all $w'\in W\setminus\{w\}$. The graph is still acyclic: a new arrow could create a cycle only if $w$ already reached its tail, contrary to the choice of $w$. Also $l$ and $w$ are nonadjacent in $\widetilde G'$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, F4, construct, choose]

5.1 In $\widetilde G'$, choose a d-separating set $S_0$ for the nonadjacent vertices $l,w$. If $l$ is an ancestor of $w$, take $S_0=\operatorname{pa}_{\widetilde G'}(w)$: every path into $w$ ends through a conditioned parent, which is a noncollider on that path. If $l$ is not an ancestor of $w$, take $S_0=\operatorname{pa}_{\widetilde G'}(l)$. A path from $l$ to the nondescendant nonparent $w$ that starts with an arrow into $l$ is blocked at that conditioned parent; if it starts with an arrow out of $l$, its first edge traversed backward creates a collider descended from $l$, and that collider cannot have a descendant in a parent of $l$ without a directed cycle. Thus this parent set also d-separates $l,w$. [F4, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Put $W_0=W\setminus\{w\}$ and $S=S_0\cup Y\cup Z\cup W_0$. Each $y'\in Y$ belongs to $S_0$, since $l\to y'\to w$ is a path with noncollider $y'$. Suppose a path $\pi$ from $l$ to $w$ is active given $S$. Its noncolliders lie outside $S_0$, and every collider with a descendant in $S_0$ is active given $S_0$. Since $S_0$ d-separates the endpoints, at least one collider on $\pi$ is not an ancestor of $S_0$; its descendant in $S$ must lie in $Z$ or $W_0$. Label every such collider by one such type, $Z$ or $W_0$. A labeled $Z$-collider $v$ has a directed path to some $z\in Z$, followed by $z\to l$; traversing this chain backward connects $l$ to $v$. The chain avoids $S_0$, since otherwise $v$ would be an ancestor of $S_0$. A labeled $W_0$-collider $u$ has a directed path to some $w'\in W_0$, followed by the added arrow $w'\to w$; this chain also avoids $S_0$. If only $Z$ labels occur, use the one nearest $w$, replace the prefix of $\pi$ by its backward chain from $l$, and retain the suffix. If only $W_0$ labels occur, use the one nearest $l$, retain the prefix, and replace the suffix by its forward chain to $w$. If both labels occur, take consecutive labeled colliders of different types; connect $l$ to the $Z$-collider by its backward chain, retain the segment between the two colliders in either direction, and connect the $W_0$-collider to $w$ by its forward chain. The resulting finite route has no conditioned noncollider: original noncolliders avoid $S_0$, connector interiors avoid $S_0$, and each selected collider becomes a noncollider at its junction. Every remaining collider has a descendant in $S_0$, because there is no differently labeled collider between the selected ones, and in the one-label cases the retained side contains no other newly opened collider. This is an active route given $S_0$, so [F5] gives an active path, contradicting the choice of $S_0$. Thus $S$ d-separates $l,w$ in $\widetilde G'$, and also in its subgraph $G'$. [F4, F5, step 5.1, construct, contradiction]

7.1 By [F6], $X_l\perp_d X_w\mid X_S$ in $G'$. In $G$, $w\to l$, and $S$ contains all other parents of $l$ and only nondescendants of the sink $l$. This contradicts [F3]. Therefore the selected maximal member $t$ cannot lie in $W$; it lies in $Y$. [F3, F6, step 2.1, step 6.1, contradiction]

8.1 Let the selected $y=t\in Y$, and set $Q=\operatorname{pa}_G(l)\setminus\{y\}$, $R=\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(y)\setminus\{l\}$, and $S=Q\cup R$. In $G$, $l$ is a sink, so every member of $S$ is a nondescendant of $l$, and $Q\subseteq S$. In $G'$, every member of $R$ is a parent of $y$. A vertex $z\in Z$ cannot be a descendant of $y$, since $z\to l\to y$ and a path $y\to\cdots\to z$ would create a directed cycle. Every vertex of $Y\setminus\{y\}\cup W$ is another member of $T$, so none is a descendant of $y$ by the choice of $t$. Hence $S$ is contained in the nondescendants of $y$ in $G'$ and contains all parents of $y$ other than $l$. The edges are $y\to l$ in $G$ and $l\to y$ in $G'$, so the vertices and $S$ satisfy the Statement. [step 2.1, step 4.1, step 7.1, construct] ∎

## References

[Peters et al., JMLR (2014), Proposition 29(i) and Appendix A.12](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume15/peters14a/peters14a.pdf)

[Peters et al., JMLR (2014), Appendix A.10, Lemma 38](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume15/peters14a/peters14a.pdf)

## Statement

In a finite DAG, a **route** is a finite sequence of vertices with consecutive vertices adjacent by an arrow in either direction; repeated vertices are allowed. Collider and noncollider status is assigned to each internal occurrence using its two incident route arrows. A route is **active given $C$** if each noncollider occurrence is outside $C$ and each collider occurrence is an ancestor of $C$, including membership in $C$. If an active route joins vertices $x,y\notin C$ with $x\ne y$, then an active distinct-vertex path joins $x$ and $y$ given $C$.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The active-path criterion and finite acyclic graph conventions are those of [[def-d-separation-in-a-dag]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** shorten repeated-vertex loops and check the only possible newly blocked junction.

**Given:** An active route from $x$ to $y$ and the hypotheses in the statement.

1.1 Among active routes with these endpoints choose one of minimum length. If a repeated vertex occurs at an endpoint, discard the initial segment through the later occurrence of $x$, or the terminal segment from the earlier occurrence of $y$. Endpoints are outside $C$, and all retained internal occurrences have their old incidences, so the shortened route is active. Consequently any repetition in a minimum route consists of two internal occurrences of a vertex $v$. Delete the segment between two such occurrences and identify them. Only the two incidences at the joined occurrence of $v$ change. If $v\in C$, its old occurrences were both colliders, so the joined occurrence is still a collider. If $v\notin C$ and the joined occurrence is a noncollider, it is allowed; if it is a collider and $v$ is an ancestor of $C$, it is also allowed. [given, F1, choose, construct]

2.1 The sole remaining possibility is that the join makes $v$ a collider although $v$ is not an ancestor of $C$. Both original occurrences were then noncolliders. The retained edge before the first occurrence points into $v$, so its deleted departure edge must point out of $v$; likewise the deleted arrival edge at the second occurrence points out of $v$, since its retained departure edge points into $v$. Traverse the deleted segment starting with its arrow out of $v$. There must be a first place where its arrows cease to point forward: the final arrow points backward, and an entirely forward return to $v$ would also contradict acyclicity. At that first change is a collider $w$, reached from $v$ by a directed segment. A directed segment in a DAG has no repetitions. Activity of the original route makes $w$ an ancestor of $C$, hence $v$ an ancestor of $C$, a contradiction. Thus every loop deletion above is active and strictly shorter, contradicting minimality. The minimum route is therefore a path. [F1, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Source notes

Pearl's d-separation criterion supplies the occurrence-wise activity conditions. The loop-junction argument above is supplied locally; the source's statement of the moralization test is not used in place of this proof.

## Statement

Let $X,N$ be independent real random variables, let $Y=f(X)+N$, and suppose
$f\in C^3(\mathbb R)$ is nonconstant while $X$ and $N$ have strictly positive
$C^3$ Lebesgue densities. If the triple of $f$ and these two densities
satisfies Condition 19, then there is no reverse additive-noise representation
$X=g(Y)+M$ with $M$ independent of $Y$ and $g\in C^3(\mathbb R)$. No density
regularity for $M$ is assumed; the proof derives a strictly positive $C^3$
density version from the forward joint density and reverse independence. Hence
the direction $X\to Y$ is identified from the observational law among these
smooth bivariate additive-noise models.

## Statement references

[[def-additive-noise-model|Bivariate additive-noise equations and causal minimality]]

[[def-restricted-additive-noise-model|Condition 19 and its nonzero domain]]

[[lem-anm-joint-density|Positive bivariate joint density]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $Y=f(X)+N$, independent $X,N$, strictly positive $C^3$ densities, nonconstant $f\in C^3$, and Condition 19.

[F1] A bivariate additive-noise model has $Y=f(X)+N$ with $N$ independent of $X$; causal minimality here is $f$ nonconstant. [[def-additive-noise-model]]

[F2] The forward joint density is $p(x,y)=p_X(x)p_N(y-f(x))$, and is strictly positive. [[lem-anm-joint-density]]

[F3] Condition 19 is failure of the displayed third-order differential equation at some $(x,y)$ where $\nu''(y-f(x))f'(x)\ne0$. [[def-restricted-additive-noise-model]]

[F4] Nonnegative product-measurable functions can be integrated by iterated sections, and the marginal density is finite almost everywhere when its integral is finite. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

[F5] Translation preserves Lebesgue measure and measurability, so sectionwise translation sends a density $h(x)$ to the translated density $h(x+a)$. [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]

[F6] A probability measure invariant under a nonzero translation cannot exist. [[lem-probability-measure-has-no-nonzero-period]]

## Proof
**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Put $\xi=\log p_X$, $\nu=\log p_N$, and $\pi(x,y)=\log p(x,y)$. By [F2], $\pi(x,y)=\xi(x)+\nu(y-f(x))$ is a $C^3$ function. The chain rule gives $\pi_{xy}=-\nu''(y-f(x))f'(x),\qquad \pi_{xx}=\nu''(y-f(x))(f'(x))^2-\nu'(y-f(x))f''(x)+\xi''(x).$ Thus both derivatives are defined, and $\pi_{xy}\ne0$ exactly on the Condition 19 domain. [given, F2, construct]

2.1 Suppose a reverse representation as in the Statement exists. By [F4] and [F2], $p_Y(y)=\int_{\mathbb R}p(x,y)\,dx$ is positive and finite for almost every $y$. The sectionwise translation $m=x-g(y)$ gives the joint density $p_{M,Y}(m,y)=p(m+g(y),y)$ by [F5]; independence makes it equal to $p_M(m)p_Y(y)$ almost everywhere. Choose $y_0$ for which $0<p_Y(y_0)<\infty$ and this factorization holds for almost every $m$. Then $p_M(m)=\frac{p(m+g(y_0),y_0)}{p_Y(y_0)}\quad\text{for almost every }m.$ The right side is a strictly positive $C^3$ function of $m$, so choose it as the density version of $M$ and put $\widetilde\nu=\log p_M$. Consequently the forward and reverse density formulas agree almost everywhere: $p(x,y)=p_Y(y)p_M(x-g(y)).$ For almost every $y$ with $0<p_Y(y)<\infty$, the two sides as functions of $x$ are continuous and agree almost everywhere, hence agree for every $x$. Taking logarithmic $x$-derivatives gives $\pi_x(x,y)=\widetilde\nu'(x-g(y))$ for almost every $(x,y)$. Both sides are continuous on $\mathbb R^2$, so this identity holds everywhere. Differentiating in $x$ and $y$ gives $\pi_{xx}=\widetilde\nu''(x-g(y))$ and $\pi_{xy}=-\widetilde\nu''(x-g(y))g'(y)$. Wherever $\pi_{xy}\ne0$, it follows that $\frac{\pi_{xx}}{\pi_{xy}}=-\frac1{g'(y)},$ which is independent of $x$; hence $\partial_x(\pi_{xx}/\pi_{xy})=0$. [given, F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 From the forward expressions in step 1.1, on the same nonzero domain, $\frac{\pi_{xx}}{\pi_{xy}} =-f'(x)+\frac{\nu'(y-f(x))}{\nu''(y-f(x))}\frac{f''(x)}{f'(x)} -\frac{\xi''(x)}{\nu''(y-f(x))f'(x)}.$ Differentiating this expression in $x$, using $\partial_x\nu'=-f'\nu''$ and $\partial_x\nu''=-f'\nu'''$, and setting the derivative to zero gives $\xi'''(x)= \xi''(x)\left(-\frac{\nu'''(y-f(x))f'(x)}{\nu''(y-f(x))}+\frac{f''(x)}{f'(x)}\right) -2\nu''(y-f(x))f''(x)f'(x) +\nu'(y-f(x))f'''(x) +\frac{\nu'(y-f(x))\nu'''(y-f(x))f''(x)f'(x)}{\nu''(y-f(x))} -\frac{\nu'(y-f(x))(f''(x))^2}{f'(x)}.$ The quotient rule is legitimate because both denominator factors are nonzero on this domain. [given, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Step 3.1 forces Condition 19's differential equation at every point where $\nu''(y-f(x))f'(x)\ne0$, contrary to [F3]. Therefore no reverse representation in the stated class exists. [F3, step 3.1]

5.1 The law cannot be independent: if $X$ and $Y$ were independent, positivity of $p_X$ and the forward density formula [F2] would make $p_N(y-f(x))$ equal $p_Y(y)$ for almost every $(x,y)$. By Fubini, for almost every pair $x,x'$, the translates $p_N(y-f(x))$ and $p_N(y-f(x'))$ agree for almost every $y$. Their probability laws are translates of the law of $N$; [F6] forces $f(x)=f(x')$ for almost every pair. Continuity of $f$ makes it constant everywhere, contradicting the hypothesis. Thus the empty graph is excluded as well, and the only smooth bivariate ANM direction in the class is $X\to Y$. [given, F1, F2, F6, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let a finite nonempty causally sufficient additive-noise model on a
DAG $G$ have a strictly positive joint density, be a restricted additive-noise
model, and be causally minimal. Then its observational law determines $G$
among all causally minimal restricted additive-noise models on the same
vertices.

For the population RESIT procedure, let $m_{j,C}:\mathbb R^C\to\mathbb R$ be
a supplied Borel regression rule and use an exact independence oracle and a
fixed total order for all ties and loops. Assume the rule is population
consistent on the model: whenever
$\operatorname{pa}(j)\subseteq C\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)$, there is a
constant $c_{j,C}$ such that
$$m_{j,C}(X_C)=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+c_{j,C}\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
Assume in addition that every Phase 1 regression function $m_{j,C}$ is $C^3$
on its full predictor space. Then RESIT terminates without failure and returns
the DAG $G$. This is a population statement and makes no finite-sample claim.
