## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$ be standard Borel spaces, let $\lambda$ be a probability measure on $E$, and let $M$ and $R$ be probability kernels from $E$ to $F$. Suppose $M(x,\cdot)\ll R(x,\cdot)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $x$. Then there is an $(\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F)$-measurable function $r:E\times F\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for $\lambda$-almost every $x$ and every $B\in\mathcal F$,
$$M(x,B)=\int_B r(x,y)\,R(x,dy).$$
The exceptional set in $x$ is a single null set, independent of $B$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, standard Borel spaces $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$, a probability measure $\lambda$ on $E$, probability kernels $M,R:E\rightsquigarrow F$, and $M(x,\cdot)\ll R(x,\cdot)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $x$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC supplies a choice function for every family of nonempty sets.

[F1] [[def-standard-borel-space]]: A standard Borel space is measurably isomorphic to a Polish space.

[F2] [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: Each kernel section is a measure, each set evaluation is measurable in the source variable, and a probability kernel has mass one in every section.

[F3] [[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]]: An initial probability and a sequence of probability kernels determine a unique path law whose finite-prefix laws are the ordered iterated kernel integrals.

[F4] [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]: For a probability kernel $K$ and a nonnegative product-measurable $f$, the map $x\mapsto\int f(x,y)K(x,dy)$ is measurable.

[F5] [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]]: A nonnegative measurable function with integral zero vanishes almost everywhere.

[F6] [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]]: Under AC, a finite measure absolutely continuous with respect to a probability measure has a measurable $L^1$ Radon–Nikodym density, unique almost everywhere.

[F7] [[cor-standard-borel-spaces-have-countable-generating-and-measure-determining-algebras]]: Under AC, a standard Borel space has a countable algebra that determines finite measures.

[F8] [[thm-integration-against-a-radon-nikodym-derivative]]: A Radon–Nikodym representative $h=dP/dQ$ satisfies $P(A)=\int_Ah\,dQ$ for every measurable $A$.

[F9] [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]: Composing a measurable function with a Borel function preserves measurability.

[F10] [[thm-sections-of-product-measurable-functions-are-measurable]]: For each fixed $x$, the section $y\mapsto h(x,y)$ of a product-measurable function is measurable.

[F11] [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]: If $g$ is nonnegative measurable on a measure space $(F,\mathcal F,\mu)$, then $B\mapsto\int_Bg\,d\mu$ is a measure.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Apply [F3] to $\lambda$ and each one-step kernel to obtain joint laws $P(dx,dy)=\lambda(dx)M(x,dy)$ and $Q(dx,dy)=\lambda(dx)R(x,dy)$. For any product-measurable $A$, the section integrals are measurable by [F4]. If $Q(A)=0$, then $R(x,A_x)=0$ for $\lambda$-almost every $x$ by [F5]; intersecting with the conull kernel-domination set gives $M(x,A_x)=0$ there, hence $P(A)=0$. Thus $P\ll Q$. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, given]

2.1 By [F6], choose a product-measurable density $h=dP/dQ$. On $N=\{h<0\}$, positivity of $P$ gives $0\le P(N)=\int_Nh\,dQ=-\int_Nh^-\,dQ$, so [F5] makes $h^-=0$ $Q$-almost everywhere on $N$. The Borel positive-part map preserves measurability by [F9], so replacing $h$ by $h^+=\max(h,0)$ leaves the density unchanged $Q$-almost everywhere and makes it nonnegative. [A1, F5, F6, F9, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 Let $\mathcal C$ be a countable measure-determining algebra on $F$ from [F7], containing $F$. For each $B\in\mathcal C$ and $D\in\mathcal E$, the rectangle laws and density identity [F8] give $\int_D M(x,B)\lambda(dx)=P(D\times B)=\int_D(\int_Bh(x,y)R(x,dy))\lambda(dx)$. Both integrands are measurable by [F2] and [F4] and integrable because their integrals over $E$ are at most one. Uniqueness of Radon–Nikodym densities in [F6] makes them equal $\lambda$-almost everywhere for each fixed $B$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, F7, F8, step 2.1]

4.1 Intersect the conull sets from step 3.1 over the countable algebra $\mathcal C$. For each $x$ in the intersection, the section $h(x,\cdot)$ is measurable by [F10], so [F11] makes $B\mapsto\int_Bh(x,y)R(x,dy)$ a measure. The kernel section $M(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure by [F2]. These two measures agree on $\mathcal C$ and have total mass one because $F\in\mathcal C$ and step 3.1 includes $B=F$. The measure-determining property [F7] makes them equal on every $B\in\mathcal F$, with the same exceptional null set for all $B$. Taking $r=h$ proves the assertion. [A1, F2, F7, F10, F11, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Every standard-Borel space $(E,\mathcal S)$ has a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures: if finite measures $\mu,\nu$ agree on $\mathcal A$, then $\mu=\nu$. In particular it determines probability measures.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and a standard-Borel space $(E,\mathcal S)$; in the determination assertion, two finite measures agreeing on the constructed algebra.

[F1] There is a bimeasurable bijection $f:E\to B$ with $B\subseteq[0,1]$ Borel. ([[thm-standard-borel-spaces-admit-bimeasurable-real-codings]])

[F2] The rational cuts can be enumerated. ([[thm-rationals-countable]])

[F3] Rational right rays generate real Borel sets; their complementary closed left rays do also. ([[thm-seven-generators-of-the-borel-sigma-algebra-on-r]])

[F4] Under countable choice a countable union of finite sets is countable. ([[thm-countable-union-of-countable]])

[F5] Countable choice selects from each nonempty set in a sequence. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F6] AC supplies that countable choice by restriction of a choice function. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[F7] A lambda-system containing a pi-system contains its generated sigma-algebra. ([[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]])

[F8] Rational cuts separate two distinct real numbers. ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $f$ from [F1]. Enumerate the pullbacks $H_q=f^{-1}[B\cap(-\infty,q]]$ using [F2]. Let $\mathcal A_n$ be the Boolean algebra on the first $n$ pullbacks, with $\mathcal A_0=\{\varnothing,E\}$. Its atoms are the at most $2^n$ intersections obtained by taking each generator or its complement; every member is a union of atoms. Thus each $\mathcal A_n$ is finite, and $\mathcal A=\bigcup_n\mathcal A_n$ is an algebra: any two elements lie in a common $\mathcal A_n$. [F1, F2]

2.1 AC implies [F5], so [F4] makes $\mathcal A$ countable. This is the exact countable-choice use for enumerating the finite algebras. The trace of the generators of [F3] generates $\mathcal B(B)$, so bimeasurability of $f$ gives $\sigma(\mathcal A)=\mathcal S$. If $x\ne y$, injectivity gives different codes; [F8] provides a rational between them, and its pullback contains exactly the lower-coded point. [step 1.1, F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, F8]

3.1 For finite $\mu,\nu$ agreeing on $\mathcal A$, their total masses agree because $E\in\mathcal A$. The equality class $\mathcal D=\{A\in\mathcal S:\mu(A)=\nu(A)\}$ contains $E$, is closed under complements by subtracting from the common finite total, and under countable disjoint unions by countable additivity. It is a lambda-system containing the pi-system $\mathcal A$. By [F7], $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal D$. This also covers zero total mass and $E=\varnothing$; finiteness prevents subtraction of infinite totals. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F7] ∎

## Source notes

Durrett Theorem 2.1.22 (printed pp.53–54) motivates real coding. The finite-algebra construction and finite-total lambda-system argument are derived here from the exact local countability and pi-lambda statements; arbitrary infinite measures are outside the claim.

## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces, and let
$$f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$$
be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
$x \in X$, and $f^y : X \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable
for every $y \in Y$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Measurable spaces $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$, and a product-measurable function $f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$.

[L1] A function into $\overline{\mathbb R}$ is measurable once the preimages of a generating family for $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ are measurable. ([[thm-generating-family-criterion-for-measurable-functions]])

[L2] Sections of product-measurable sets are measurable. ([[thm-sections-of-product-measurable-sets-are-measurable]])

[A1] For every Borel set $U \subseteq \overline{\mathbb R}$, $$f_x^{-1}(U) = (f^{-1}(U))_x,\qquad (f^y)^{-1}(U) = (f^{-1}(U))^y.$$

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $x \in X$ and let $\mathcal G$ be a generating family for $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$. For each $U \in \mathcal G$, the set $f^{-1}(U)$ is product-measurable, so [L2] and [A1] give $f_x^{-1}(U) = (f^{-1}(U))_x \in \mathcal B$. By [L1], $f_x$ is therefore $\mathcal B$-measurable. [L1, A1, L2]

2.1 Fix $y \in Y$. The same argument gives $(f^y)^{-1}(U) = (f^{-1}(U))^y \in \mathcal A$ for every generator $U \in \mathcal G$, so [L1] implies that $f^y$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable. Thus every horizontal and vertical section of $f$ is measurable. [step 1.1, A1, L1, L2] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathcal D$ be the finite-support count functions on a nonempty record universe, with neighbors formed by adding or removing one record occurrence. Let $k\ge1$ and let $\mathcal Y_1,\ldots,\mathcal Y_k$ be measurable output spaces. For each round $i$, let $K_i(D,h,\cdot)$ be a probability kernel on $\mathcal Y_i$ for every database $D\in\mathcal D$ and prior transcript $h\in\mathcal Y_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal Y_{i-1}$. Suppose that for every neighboring pair $D\sim D'$, every prior transcript $h$, and every measurable event $A\subseteq\mathcal Y_i$,
$$
K_i(D,h,A)\le e^{\varepsilon_i}K_i(D',h,A)+\delta_i,
$$
where $\varepsilon_i\ge0$ and $\delta_i\ge0$. If $\sum_{i=1}^k\delta_i\le1$, then the full transcript is $(\sum_{i=1}^k\varepsilon_i,\sum_{i=1}^k\delta_i)$-differentially private on the finite product sigma-algebra.

## Statement references

[[def-differential-privacy-and-adjacency|Differential privacy for every ordered neighboring pair]]

[Dwork and Roth, *The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy*, §3.5, printed pp. 41–50.](https://privacytools.seas.harvard.edu/resource/thealgorithmicfoundationsofdifferentialprivacypdf)

[Vadhan, *The Complexity of Differential Privacy*, §2.2, PDF pp. 14–16.](https://salil.seas.harvard.edu/sites/g/files/omnuum4266/files/salil/files/manuscript_2017.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite sequence of history-dependent probability kernels, common neighboring-database relation, and the conditional event inequalities in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-differential-privacy-and-adjacency|Differential privacy]] is the event inequality for every ordered neighboring pair; its database source has the power-set sigma-algebra, so all event-evaluation functions of the database are measurable.

[F2] [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel|Probability kernels]] have measurable event evaluations and probability-measure sections.

[F3] [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras|Finite product sigma-algebra]] is generated by measurable rectangles.

[F4] [[thm-sections-of-product-measurable-functions-are-measurable|Sections]] of product-measurable sets are measurable.

[F5] [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel|Kernel integration measurability]]: integrating a nonnegative product-measurable function against a probability kernel gives a measurable function of the history.

[F6] [[lem-dp-test-function-extension|Bounded-function extension]]: a prefix event inequality extends to every measurable function with values in $[0,1]$ with the same additive error.

[F7] [[def-composition-of-probability-kernels|Kernel composition]] uses iterated integration.

[F8] [[lem-kernel-composition-is-well-defined-and-associative|Composed probability kernels]] remain probability kernels and their event values are the iterated integrals.

[F9] [[thm-exponential-addition-formula|The exponential addition formula]] gives $\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y)$ for all real $x,y$.

## Proof

1.1 Put $H_0=\{*\}$ and $H_i=\mathcal Y_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal Y_i$. For fixed $D$ and $i$, define $T_i^D(h,B)=\int_{\mathcal Y_i}\mathbf1_B(h,y)K_i(D,h,dy)$ for measurable $B\subseteq H_i$. By [F4], $B_h$ is measurable; taking sections preserves the whole space, complements, and countable disjoint unions, so $B\mapsto T_i^D(h,B)=K_i(D,h,B_h)$ is a probability measure by [F2]. By [F5], $h\mapsto T_i^D(h,B)$ is measurable, so $T_i^D$ is a probability kernel. Starting with the point mass on $H_0$, compose these kernels using [F7]–[F8] to obtain transcript laws $\mu_i^D$ with $\mu_i^D(B)=\int_{H_{i-1}}K_i(D,h,B_h)\mu_{i-1}^D(dh)$. Every transcript-event evaluation is measurable in the database because its sigma-algebra is the power set by [F1]. No choice is used in these finite compositions. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F7, F8, given, construct]

2.1 Write $E_i=\sum_{j\le i}\varepsilon_j$ and $D_i=\sum_{j\le i}\delta_j$, with $E_0=D_0=0$. We prove by induction that $\mu_i^D(B)\le e^{E_i}\mu_i^{D'}(B)+D_i$ for every measurable $B\subseteq H_i$; it is equality at the one-point prefix $i=0$. Suppose it holds at $i-1$, fix an event $B\subseteq H_i$, and put $p(h)=K_i(D,h,B_h)$ and $q(h)=K_i(D',h,B_h)$. By [F2], [F4], and [F5], these are measurable and lie in $[0,1]$. The round-$i$ event inequality and $p\le1$ imply $p(h)\le\min\{1,e^{\varepsilon_i}q(h)\}+\delta_i$, because $\min\{1,x+\delta_i\}\le\min\{1,x\}+\delta_i$ for $x\ge0$. Let $g(h)=\min\{1,e^{\varepsilon_i}q(h)\}$; it is measurable and $[0,1]$-valued. Integrating first against $\mu_{i-1}^D$, applying [F6] to the induction hypothesis, then using $g\le e^{\varepsilon_i}q$ and [F9] with $E_i=E_{i-1}+\varepsilon_i$, gives $\mu_i^D(B)\le e^{E_{i-1}}e^{\varepsilon_i}\int q\,d\mu_{i-1}^{D'}+D_{i-1}+\delta_i=e^{E_i}\mu_i^{D'}(B)+D_i$. The same argument with $D,D'$ interchanged proves the reverse ordered inequality. At $i=k$, [F1] gives the asserted differential-privacy guarantee. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, F7, F9, step 1.1, algebra, induction] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal D$ be the finite-support count functions on a nonempty record universe, with neighbors formed by adding or removing one record occurrence. Let $k\ge1$, let each round output space and each finite transcript-prefix space be a measurable space measurably isomorphic to a Polish space, and let $K_i(D,h,\cdot)$ be the probability kernel for round $i$ conditional on prior transcript $h$. Suppose that for every $D\sim D'$, every $i$, every $h$, and every measurable round-$i$ event $A$,
$$
K_i(D,h,A)\le e^\varepsilon K_i(D',h,A)+\delta,
$$
where $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $0\le\delta\le1$. If $0<\delta'<1$ and $k\delta+\delta'\le1$, then the finite-product full transcript is $(\varepsilon',k\delta+\delta')$-differentially private, where
$$
\varepsilon'=\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}\,\varepsilon+k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon-1).
$$

## Statement references

[[def-differential-privacy-and-adjacency|The ordered event inequalities defining differential privacy]]

[Dwork and Roth, *The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy*, Theorem 3.20 and its complete proof, §3.5.1, printed pp. 45–50.](https://privacytools.seas.harvard.edu/resource/thealgorithmicfoundationsofdifferentialprivacypdf)

[Vadhan, *The Complexity of Differential Privacy*, Theorem 2.5 and proof sketch, §2.2, PDF pp. 14–16.](https://salil.seas.harvard.edu/sites/g/files/omnuum4266/files/salil/files/manuscript_2017.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $k\ge1$ adaptive rounds with $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-private conditional kernels for every history, standard-Borel output and finite-prefix spaces, and $0<\delta'<1$ with $k\delta+\delta'\le1$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice|Axiom of Choice]] is assumed by the RN, path-law, conditional-KL, and Azuma suppliers.

[F1] [[def-differential-privacy-and-adjacency|Differential privacy]] is the event inequality in both directions for every ordered neighboring pair; the database source has the power-set sigma-algebra, so transcript-event evaluations are measurable in the database.

[F2] [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel|Finite products of standard-Borel spaces]] remain standard Borel.

[F3] [[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain|Ionescu–Tulcea path law]]: under AC, an initial probability and a sequence of history-dependent probability kernels give a probability law whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals.

[F4] [[lem-jointly-measurable-radon-nikodym-derivatives-for-probability-kernels|Joint RN derivatives]]: dominated probability kernels on standard-Borel source and target spaces have a jointly measurable density representing every event on one common conull set.

[F5] [[lem-dp-pure-privacy-loss-kl-bound|Pure-DP KL bound]]: if two probability laws satisfy both pure $\varepsilon$ event inequalities, then $D(P\|Q)\le b$, where $b=\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon-1)$; the same holds with $P,Q$ reversed.

[F6] [[lem-dp-approximate-kernel-purification|Kernel purification]]: under AC, an $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ pair of kernels has a pure-$\varepsilon$ replacement within integrated total variation $\delta$ under any supplied history probability.

[F7] [[def-conditional-kl-for-probability-kernels|Conditional KL]] is the integral of the fiberwise KL divergence; [[thm-conditional-kl-is-measurable]] makes its integrand measurable.

[F8] [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra|Conditional expectation]] is characterized by measurability and equality of integrals over every event in the conditioning sigma-algebra.

[F9] [[thm-azuma-hoeffding-inequality|Azuma–Hoeffding]]: if martingale differences have history-measurable interval bounds of length $c_i$, then the upper tail at $t>0$ is at most $\exp(-2t^2/\sum_i c_i^2)$.

[F10] [[lem-dp-test-function-extension|Bounded-function extension]] applied in both directions converts an event bound with $\varepsilon=0$ and additive error $s$ into $|\int g\,dP-\int g\,dQ|\le s$ for every measurable $0\le g\le1$.

[F11] [[thm-integration-against-a-radon-nikodym-derivative|RN integration identity]] recovers integration against a measure by multiplying by its density.

[F12] [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel|Kernel integration measurability]] and [[thm-sections-of-product-measurable-functions-are-measurable]] make the history-section probabilities and their integrals measurable.

[F13] [[def-natural-logarithm|Natural logarithm]] is the inverse of the positive real exponential and is defined on the positive likelihood ratios used below.

[F14] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable|Expectation]] is integration against the path probability law; bounded privacy-loss variables are integrable.

[F15] [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws|The logarithm product law]] gives $\ln(xy)=\ln x+\ln y$ for positive $x,y$.

## Proof

1.1 Fix neighboring databases $D,D'$. By [F2], every finite history space is standard Borel. To apply the infinite-sequence form of [F3], append after round $k$ a singleton output space and its unique probability kernel at every later round. The first $k$ coordinates of the resulting path law have exactly the desired finite transcript law; do this for $D$ and $D'$ to obtain $P$ and $Q$. Event evaluations of these laws are measurable in the database by [F1]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, choose, construct]

1.2 We first prove the one-sided estimate from $P$ to $Q$. Set $P_0^*=Q_0$ equal to the point mass on the empty history. Recursively, after constructing the modified $D$-transcript prefix law $P_{i-1}^*$, apply [F6] to the round-$i$ pair $K_i(D,h,\cdot),K_i(D',h,\cdot)$ with base history law $\lambda_i=P_{i-1}^*$. This gives a probability kernel $K_i^*$ that is pure $\varepsilon$ relative to $K_i(D',h,\cdot)$ in both event directions for $\lambda_i$-almost every $h$, with $\int\operatorname{TV}(K_i(D,h,\cdot),K_i^*(h,\cdot))P_{i-1}^*(dh)\le\delta$. Composing the finite modified sequence by [F3] gives a law $P^*$ and its prefix laws $P_i^*$. [A1, F3, F6, given, construct]

2.1 The prefix laws $P_i^*$ and $Q_i$ are mutually absolutely continuous for each $i$. They agree at the empty history. If they are equivalent at $i-1$, then for a product-measurable event $B$ with $Q_i(B)=0$, the iterated integral formula [F3] gives $K_i(D',h,B_h)=0$ for $Q_{i-1}$-almost every $h$, hence for $P_{i-1}^*$-almost every $h$. The pure reverse inequality from step 1.2 gives $K_i^*(h,B_h)=0$, so $P_i^*(B)=0$. Reversing the two kernels proves the converse; induction gives prefix equivalence. [F1, F3, step 1.2, given, induction]

3.1 For each $i$, apply [F4] with base measure $P_{i-1}^*$ to obtain a jointly measurable density $r_i(h,y)$ of $K_i^*(h,\cdot)$ with respect to $K_i(D',h,\cdot)$ on one common conull history set. The pure event inequalities imply $e^{-\varepsilon}\le r_i\le e^\varepsilon$ almost surely there: if either bound failed on a positive-measure fiber set, some level set separated from that bound by $1/n$ would contradict one event inequality. Clip $r_i$ everywhere to $[e^{-\varepsilon},e^\varepsilon]$; Borel composition preserves measurability, the density is unchanged on the conull set, and $X_i(h,y)=\ln r_i(h,y)$ is jointly measurable with $|X_i|\le\varepsilon$. [F1, F4, F13, step 1.2, step 2.1, given, construct]

4.1 We prove the density formula by induction on prefix length. At the first round, [F4] gives $dP_1^*/dQ_1=r_1$. Suppose $R_{i-1}=\prod_{j<i}r_j$ is the density on the first $i-1$ outputs. For a measurable event $A$ on the first $i$ outputs, [F3] gives $P_i^*(A)=\int P_{i-1}^*(dh)\int\mathbf1_A(h,y)K_i^*(h,dy)$. For almost every $h$, [F4] replaces the inner integral by $\int\mathbf1_A(h,y)r_i(h,y)K_i(D',h,dy)$. Applying [F11] to the outer prefix integral with density $R_{i-1}$ yields $P_i^*(A)=\int Q_{i-1}(dh)R_{i-1}(h)\int\mathbf1_A(h,y)r_i(h,y)K_i(D',h,dy)=\int_A R_{i-1}(h)r_i(h,y)Q_i(dh,dy)$. This proves the induction and hence $dP^*/dQ=R=\prod_{i=1}^k r_i(H_{i-1},Y_i)$. Since every factor is positive and bounded, [F15] gives $\ln R=\sum_{i=1}^kX_i(H_{i-1},Y_i)$ almost surely under both laws. [F3, F4, F11, F13, F15, step 3.1, induction]

4.2 Put $m_i(h)=\int X_i(h,y)K_i^*(h,dy)$. By the density formula and KL definition, $m_i(h)=D(K_i^*(h,\cdot)\|K_i(D',h,\cdot))\le b$ for $P_{i-1}^*$-almost every $h$, using [F5]. It is measurable by [F7] and [F12]. For every measurable prefix event $C$, the iterated-prefix identity [F3] gives $\int_{\{H_{i-1}\in C\}}X_i\,dP^*=\int_Cm_i(h)P_{i-1}^*(dh)$. Thus [F8] identifies $m_i(H_{i-1})$ as the conditional expectation of $X_i$ given the previous transcript. By [F14], the variables are integrable, so $M_j=\sum_{i\le j}(X_i-m_i(H_{i-1}))$ is a martingale. Each increment lies in the history-measurable interval $[-\varepsilon-m_i,\varepsilon-m_i]$, of length $2\varepsilon$. [F3, F5, F7, F8, F12, F14, step 3.1, given, construct]

5.1 If $\varepsilon=0$, every $X_i=0$, so $P^*=Q$ and the pure transcript has zero privacy loss. If $\varepsilon>0$, apply [F9] to step 4.2 with $c_i=2\varepsilon$ and $t=\varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}$. It gives $P^*(M_k\ge t)\le\delta'$. Since $\sum_i m_i\le kb$ almost surely, the privacy loss exceeds $\varepsilon'=kb+t$ with probability at most $\delta'$. For any event $A$, split it into $A\cap\{\ln R\le\varepsilon'\}$ and $A\cap\{\ln R>\varepsilon'\}$; the density formula in step 4.1 bounds the first probability by $e^{\varepsilon'}Q(A)$ and the second by $\delta'$. Thus $P^*(A)\le e^{\varepsilon'}Q(A)+\delta'$. Applying the same argument under $Q$ with the roles reversed gives $Q(A)\le e^{\varepsilon'}P^*(A)+\delta'$, because the conditional kernels are pure in both directions and [F5] bounds both KL orientations. [F5, F9, step 4.1, step 4.2, given, algebra]

6.1 We compare $P$ and $P^*$ in total variation. For $i=0,\ldots,k$, let $H_i$ be the transcript law that uses the modified $D$ kernels for rounds $1,\ldots,i$ and the original $D$ kernels for rounds $i+1,\ldots,k$. Consecutive laws share the modified prefix through round $i-1$, whose law is $P_{i-1}^*$, and differ only in the round-$i$ kernel; after that round they use the same continuation kernels. For any final event, integrating that common continuation gives a measurable conditional probability $g(h,y)$ in $[0,1]$ by [F12]. The two-sided test-function bound [F10] and the integrated TV bound in step 1.2 yield $\operatorname{TV}(H_{i-1},H_i)\le\delta$. The triangle inequality gives $\operatorname{TV}(P,P^*)\le k\delta$, hence $P(A)\le P^*(A)+k\delta$. Combining with step 5.1 proves $P(A)\le e^{\varepsilon'}Q(A)+k\delta+\delta'$. [F3, F6, F10, F12, step 1.2, step 5.1, given, algebra]

7.1 Repeat steps 1.2–6.1 with $D'$ as the modified side and $D$ as the reference side. This gives $Q(A)\le e^{\varepsilon'}P(A)+k\delta+\delta'$. The ordered pair and event were arbitrary, so [F1] proves the stated differential-privacy guarantee. The condition $k\delta+\delta'\le1$ keeps the additive parameter in its declared nontrivial range; no step weakens the claimed epsilon. [F1, step 1.2, step 5.1, step 6.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $n$ and standard-Borel spaces $(E_j,\mathcal E_j)$ for $j<n$, with their finite product sigma-algebra.

[F1] A standard-Borel space admits a bijection to a Polish space transporting exactly its measurable sets to Borel sets. A Polish space is separable and has some compatible complete metric; separability means that some at-most-countable subset meets every nonempty open set ([[def-standard-borel-space]], [[def-polish-space]], [[def-separable-space]]).

[F2] Selecting data for a natural-number-indexed finite family of nonempty sets is a theorem of ZF and requires no choice axiom ([[lem-finite-choice]]).

[F3] Metrics are nonnegative and satisfy separation, symmetry and the triangle inequality; their open balls induce the metric topology, and completeness means that every Cauchy sequence has a limit in the space ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]], [[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metric-topology]], [[def-complete-metric-space]]).

[F4] Finite powers of at-most-countable sets and products of two such sets are at most countable. A nonempty at-most-countable set admits a surjective enumeration. The rationals are countable and dense in the reals ([[lem-finite-powers-of-countable-sets-are-countable]], [[thm-product-of-countable]], [[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]], [[thm-rationals-countable]], [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]]).

[F5] Finite product-open rectangles form a basis of the product topology, the coordinate projections have open preimages of open sets, and the empty product is a singleton ([[def-product-topology]], [[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]).

[F6] The Borel sigma-algebra is generated by open sets; sigma-algebras are closed under complements and countable unions. Finite product sigma-algebras are recursively generated by measurable rectangles, with the full singleton sigma-algebra for the empty product ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-sigma-algebra]], [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). Induction on natural numbers is valid ([[thm-induction-principle]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** finite complete product metrics, a countable rectangle basis, and transport of the generated sigma-algebras.

**Given:** The finite indexed family $(E_j,\mathcal E_j)_{j<n}$ in the Statement. No choice axiom is assumed.

1.1 If $n=0$, the product is the singleton with its full two-element sigma-algebra by [F5,F6]; the unique metric on a singleton is complete and its singleton set is dense, so it is Polish and standard Borel. If a factor is empty, the product is empty and its sigma-algebra is $\{\varnothing\}$; the empty metric is complete and the empty set is dense in the empty topology, so the empty space is Polish and standard Borel. These settle both boundary cases. [F1, F3, F5, F6, given]

1.2 For any finite family of sigma-algebras, their recursive product is the sigma-algebra generated by all full measurable rectangles $\prod_{j<n}A_j$. This follows by induction from [F6]. The zero and one cases follow directly from the definitions. At the successor stage, let $\mathcal T$ be generated by the full $(n+1)$-rectangles. For any measurable last-coordinate set $B$, the class of $A$ in the preceding product space for which $A\times B\in\mathcal T$ is a sigma-algebra: it contains the whole space since the whole-space rectangle times $B$ is a full rectangle, complements subtract from that rectangle, and countable unions commute with the product by $B$. It contains every preceding full rectangle, so the inductive hypothesis gives every preceding product-measurable $A$. Thus all recursive generating rectangles belong to $\mathcal T$. Conversely every full rectangle is a recursive generating rectangle because its preceding rectangle is measurable. This proves equality at the successor and hence at every finite stage. [F6, algebra]

2.1 Assume $n\ge1$ and all factors nonempty. For each $j<n$, [F1] provides a Polish presentation $h_j:E_j\to P_j$; use only finite choice [F2] to select these finitely many presentations, compatible complete metrics $d_j$, nonempty countable dense subsets $D_j$, and surjective enumerations of the $D_j$ from [F4]. The product map $h(x)_j=h_j(x_j)$ is a bijection from $\prod_{j<n}E_j$ onto $P=\prod_{j<n}P_j$, with inverse obtained by the finitely many $h_j^{-1}$. The product is nonempty by finite choice. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Put $\delta_j(x,y)=\min\{1,d_j(x,y)\}$. This is a metric: symmetry and separation are inherited, and for nonnegative $a,b$, $\min(1,a+b)\le\min(1,a)+\min(1,b)$ proves the triangle inequality from that of $d_j$. Balls of radius less than $1$ are unchanged, so its topology agrees with that of $d_j$. A $\delta_j$-Cauchy sequence is $d_j$-Cauchy by testing every tolerance less than $1$; its $d_j$-limit is also its $\delta_j$-limit. Hence $\delta_j$ is complete. Define $D(x,y)=\sum_{j<n}\delta_j(x_j,y_j)$ on $P$. Finite sums of the metric inequalities prove that $D$ is a metric. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The metric $D$ induces the product topology. For every $x$ and $\varepsilon>0$, the product of coordinate $\delta_j$-balls of radius $\varepsilon/n$ lies in $B_D(x,\varepsilon)$ by the finite sum inequality. Conversely, given a basic product-open neighbourhood $\prod_{j<n}U_j$ of $x$, choose positive coordinate radii $r_j$ with $B_{\delta_j}(x_j,r_j)\subseteq U_j$; a single positive radius smaller than every $r_j$ makes its $D$-ball lie in that rectangle. These are only finite selections. Both neighbourhood comparisons establish equality of the two topologies. [F2, F3, F5, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If $(x^{(k)})_k$ is $D$-Cauchy, each coordinate sequence is $\delta_j$-Cauchy since $\delta_j(x_j^{(k)},x_j^{(l)})\le D(x^{(k)},x^{(l)})$. Its unique limit $x_j$ exists by step 3.1. The finite tuple $x=(x_j)_{j<n}$ lies in $P$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, each coordinate error is eventually less than $\varepsilon/n$, and the maximum of the finitely many thresholds makes $D(x^{(k)},x)<\varepsilon$. Thus $D$ is complete. [F3, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

5.2 In each factor, the balls for $\delta_j$ centred in $D_j$ with positive rational radii form a countable basis. Indeed, for $x\in U$ choose $\varepsilon>0$ with $B_{\delta_j}(x,\varepsilon)\subseteq U$; choose $a\in D_j$ with $\delta_j(x,a)<\varepsilon/4$ and a rational $r$ between $\delta_j(x,a)$ and $\varepsilon-\delta_j(x,a)$. Then $x\in B_{\delta_j}(a,r)\subseteq U$ by the triangle inequality. Centres and radii have countable enumerations, so [F4] enumerates this basis. Finite products of the basis members form a countable product basis: a tuple of their natural indices is in $\mathbb N^n$, and every basic neighbourhood contains one of these boxes. Every product-open set is therefore the union of the members of this fixed countable rectangle basis contained in it; no point-indexed selection is made. [F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The product of the chosen dense sets is countable: the coordinate enumerations give a surjection from $\mathbb N^n$ onto $\prod_{j<n}D_j$, and the domain is at most countable by [F4]. It is dense in $P$, because a nonempty basic rectangle meets each $D_j$, and finite choice selects a point in the product of those intersections. Hence $P$ is separable and, by the topology and completeness proved above, Polish. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

6.2 Write $\mathcal S=\bigotimes_{j<n}\mathcal B(P_j)$. Every basic rectangle from step 5.2 belongs to $\mathcal S$, so every open subset of $P$ belongs to $\mathcal S$ as a countable union. Minimality of the Borel sigma-algebra gives $\mathcal B(P)\subseteq\mathcal S$. For the reverse inclusion, fix $j<n$ and let $\mathcal C_j=\{A\subseteq P_j:\pi_j^{-1}(A)\in\mathcal B(P)\}$. Preimages preserve complements and countable unions, so this is a sigma-algebra, and it contains every open $A$ by the projection property in [F5]. Hence it contains $\mathcal B(P_j)$ by [F6]. Every Borel rectangle is the finite intersection of these Borel cylinders, and is therefore Borel in $P$. Step 1.2 now gives $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(P)$, proving both inclusions. [F5, F6, step 5.2, step 1.2, algebra]

7.1 The bijection $h$ of step 2.1 carries each full measurable rectangle in $\prod E_j$ to a full Borel rectangle in $P$, and conversely, by the exact measurable-isomorphism property of every $h_j$ in [F1]. Since images and inverse images under a bijection preserve complements and countable unions, step 1.2 identifies the transported finite product sigma-algebra with $\bigotimes_{j<n}\mathcal B(P_j)$; step 6.2 identifies this with $\mathcal B(P)$. The Polish space $P$ and this bijection are thus a Polish presentation of the given product. Together with step 1.1 this proves the unchanged Statement, without AC or Countable Choice. [F1, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 6.1, step 1.2, step 6.2] ∎

## Remarks

The only selections are over the given natural-number-indexed finite family: presentations, metrics, dense sets and enumerations, and finitely many points or radii. Finite choice is proved in ZF. No infinite family of presentations or enumerations is selected, and no countable union of unspecified countable sets is used. The countable product basis is explicitly indexed by a fixed finite power of the naturals. The original source citation records the known Statement; the complete local proof above supplies the metric, countability, sigma-algebra and transport details. These local repair checks are not a new publication audit.

## Statement

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Choice, the measurable spaces, initial probability, and history-dependent probability kernels in the statement.

[F1] Integration of a nonnegative jointly measurable function against a finite kernel is measurable in the source variable. ([[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]])

[F2] A consistent family of finite-dimensional laws on a nonempty product gives a well-defined finitely additive cylinder law. ([[lem-cylinder-premeasure-from-consistent-finite-dimensional-laws-is-well-defined]])

[F3] A premeasure is countably additive for every disjoint algebra sequence whose union remains in the algebra. ([[def-premeasure-on-an-algebra]])

[F4] Under countable choice, the Caratheodory construction extends a premeasure to its generated sigma-algebra. ([[thm-caratheodory-extension-theorem]])

[F5] Dominated convergence passes pointwise bounded limits under an integral. ([[thm-dominated-convergence]])

[F6] Probability measures agreeing on a generating pi-system agree everywhere. ([[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]])

[F7] A homogeneous Markov chain is defined by the conditional one-step kernel identity. ([[def-time-homogeneous-markov-chain-with-transition-kernel]])

[F8] Monotone convergence passes increasing nonnegative limits through each integral. ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]])

## Proof

1.1 Construct prefix probabilities recursively. Given $\mu_n$ on [F1] $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$, define $$ \mu_{n+1}(A)=\int K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A_{(x_0,\ldots,x_n)})\,d\mu_n. $$ The integrand is measurable by [F1]. For disjoint $A_j$, sectionwise countable additivity and [F8] move the increasing partial sums through the outer integral; the empty set has mass $0$ and the whole product has mass $1$. Thus $\mu_{n+1}$ is a probability measure. Since $K_n(x,E_{n+1})=1$, its marginal on the first $n+1$ coordinates is $\mu_n$. Induction gives consistent prefix laws and hence consistent laws for arbitrary finite coordinate sets by marginalization. [F1, F8]

2.1 The spaces are nonempty along a compatible history: $\mu_0(E_0)=1$, and a [F2, step 1.1] probability section of each $K_n$ has nonempty target. Choice supplies one compatible infinite coordinate sequence. Together with the prefix construction in step 1.1, this shows the product is nonempty and [F2] defines a finitely additive probability $P_0$ on the cylinder algebra $\mathcal A$. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Starting from the cylinder law in step 2.1, we prove continuity at the empty set, the missing premeasure condition. Let [F1, F5, step 2.1] $C_j\downarrow\varnothing$ be cylinders and suppose instead that $P_0(C_j)\downarrow a>0$. Represent $C_j$ using the first $r_j+1$ coordinates, enlarging so that $r_j$ increases. For a prefix $x^{(k)}=(x_0,\ldots,x_k)$ and $j$ with $r_j\ge k$, let $p_j^{(k)}(x^{(k)})$ be the probability, under the remaining kernels through time $r_j$, that the completed prefix lies in $C_j$. These functions are measurable by repeated [F1], lie in $[0,1]$, and decrease in $j$. Put $m_k=\lim_jp_j^{(k)}$. Dominated convergence [F5] gives the recursion $$ m_k(x^{(k)})=\int m_{k+1}(x^{(k)},y)K_k(x^{(k)},dy), $$ while another use of [F5] gives $a=\int m_0(x_0)\mu_0(dx_0)$. [F1, F5, step 2.1]

4.1 Since $a>0$, some $x_0$ has $m_0(x_0)>0$. Whenever [step 3.1] $m_k(x^{(k)})>0$, the recursion in step 3.1 implies that some $x_{k+1}$ has $m_{k+1}(x^{(k)},x_{k+1})>0$. Choice selects these coordinates recursively. For fixed $j$, once the selected prefix reaches $r_j$, monotonicity gives $$ 0<m_{r_j}(x^{(r_j)})\le p_j^{(r_j)}(x^{(r_j)})=1_{C_j}(x^{(r_j)}). $$ Thus the selected infinite point belongs to every $C_j$, contradicting their empty intersection. Therefore $P_0(C_j)\downarrow0$. This is the exact nonempty-choice use in the proof; no compactness or tail measure is assumed. [step 3.1]

5.1 If disjoint cylinders $A_j$ have cylinder union $A$, then [F3, F4, step 4.1] $R_N=A\setminus\bigcup_{j<N}A_j$ is a decreasing cylinder sequence with empty intersection. Finite additivity and step 4.1 give $$P_0(A)=\sum_{j<N}P_0(A_j)+P_0(R_N)\longrightarrow\sum_jP_0(A_j).$$ Hence, by [F3], $P_0$ is a finite premeasure. Since Choice implies countable choice, [F4] extends it to a probability $P$ on the product sigma-algebra. [F3, F4, step 4.1]

6.1 If $P'$ is another extension, it agrees with $P$ on every cylinder by the [F6, step 5.1] prescribed finite laws. Cylinders form a pi-system containing the whole product and generate the product sigma-algebra, so [F6] gives $P'=P$. This also handles zero cylinder events and the total-mass-one cylinder. [F6, step 5.1]

7.1 Under the probability $P$ constructed and identified in step 6.1, in the homogeneous last-coordinate specialization, let [F7, step 1.1, step 6.1] $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)$. The recursive prefix law in step 1.1 says for every $B\in\mathcal F_n$ and $A\in\mathcal E$ that $$ \mathbb E_P[1_B1_{\{X_{n+1}\in A\}}] =\mathbb E_P[1_BK(X_n,A)]. $$ The right-hand random variable is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable, so it is the conditional probability. Hence [F7] says that the coordinates form the homogeneous Markov chain and they have initial law $\mu_0$. [F7, step 1.1, step 6.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $(Z,\mathcal Z)$ and $(E,\mathcal E)$ be standard-Borel spaces, let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $Z$, and let $K,L:Z\rightsquigarrow E$ be supplied probability kernels. Define their **conditional KL divergence with base $\mu$** by
$$D_\mu(K\|L):=\int_Z D(K(z,\cdot)\|L(z,\cdot))\,\mu(dz)\in[0,+\infty].$$
The integrand is measurable by [[thm-conditional-kl-is-measurable]], so this is a well-defined nonnegative extended integral. No absolute-continuity assumption is imposed on individual fibers; a singular fiber has divergence $+\infty$. Changing supplied kernel versions on a $\mu$-null set does not change the integral.

## Statement

Let K,L be probability kernels from a measurable space $(Z,\mathcal Z)$ into a standard-Borel space $(E,\mathcal E)$. Then $z\mapsto D(K(z,\cdot)\|L(z,\cdot))$ is $\mathcal Z$-measurable, with $+\infty$ allowed. Consequently the integral used to define conditional KL is well-defined.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the kernels K,L, and the standard-Borel target $(E,\mathcal E)$.

[A1] AC supplies the countable generating algebra for standard-Borel E and the Radon–Nikodym density in measurable-space KL. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A standard-Borel space has a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ generating its sigma-algebra and determining finite measures. [[cor-standard-borel-spaces-have-countable-generating-and-measure-determining-algebras]]

[F2] For a probability kernel, integration of a nonnegative product-measurable function is measurable in the base variable; signed integrals are measurable when the positive and negative parts are finite. [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]

[F3] For probability laws P,Q, KL equals the supremum of $\int g\,dP-\ln\int e^g\,dQ$ over bounded measurable real g. [[thm-general-kl-variational-and-partition-formulas]]

## Proof

**Given:** AC and probability kernels K,L into E.

1.1 Let $\rho=P+Q$ for arbitrary probability measures P,Q on E. [given, choose]
For the algebra $\mathcal A$ in [F1], the class of measurable $B$ approximable in $\rho$-measure by members of $\mathcal A$ is a sigma-algebra: complements preserve symmetric-difference measure, finite unions preserve approximation, and a countable union is approximated by first truncating the union using finiteness of $\rho$ and then approximating that finite union. It contains $\mathcal A$, so it is all of $\mathcal E$. Hence any bounded measurable real function can be approximated in $L^1(\rho)$ by bounded simple functions from a countable family $\mathcal G$ of rational-valued simple functions on $\mathcal A$. On a fixed bound $M$, the functional $\Phi_{P,Q}(g)=\int g\,dP-\ln\int e^g\,dQ$ is continuous under $L^1(\rho)$ approximation, because $e^t$ is Lipschitz on $[-M,M]$ and $\int e^g\,dQ\ge e^{-M}$. Thus [F3] gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\left(\int g\,dP-\ln\int e^g\,dQ\right).$$
The family $\mathcal G$ is countable and does not depend on P,Q. [A1, F1, F3, given, construct]

2.1 For fixed $g\in\mathcal G$, the functions $z\mapsto\int g(x)K(z,dx)$ and $z\mapsto\int e^{g(x)}L(z,dx)$ are measurable by [F2], applying it to positive and negative parts for the first function. If $|g|\le M$, then $\int e^g\,dL(z)\ge e^{-M}>0$, so its logarithm is measurable. Therefore each candidate $\Phi_z(g)$ is measurable. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Apply the identity in step 1.1 to $P=K(z,\cdot)$ and $Q=L(z,\cdot)$ for each fixed z. Then $D(K(z,\cdot)\|L(z,\cdot))=\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\Phi_z(g)$, a countable supremum of measurable functions by step 2.1. This proves measurability and makes its nonnegative integral against any supplied base probability well-defined. [A1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(M_k,\mathcal F_k)_{k=0}^n$ be a martingale. Suppose finite $\mathcal F_{k-1}$-measurable $A_k,B_k$ and deterministic $c_k\ge0$ satisfy
$$A_k\le M_k-M_{k-1}\le B_k,\qquad B_k-A_k\le c_k$$
almost surely. Then for every $t>0$,
$$\mathbb P(M_n-M_0\ge t)\le \exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{k=1}^n c_k^2}\right),$$
and the analogous lower-tail bound holds, with the zero-denominator expression interpreted as $0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses, objects, and conventions in the Statement.

[F1] [[lem-conditional-hoeffding-bound-for-bounded-martingale-differences]] controls each conditional exponential moment.

[F2] [[thm-tower-property-of-conditional-expectation]] iterates those controls through the filtration.

[F3] [[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]] supplies the exponential Markov bound.

[F4] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited from the conditional-expectation and martingale interfaces.

[F5] [[thm-taking-out-what-is-known]] permits the bounded $\mathcal F_{k-1}$-measurable accumulated exponential to be taken outside conditional expectation.

## Proof

1.1 Let $D_k=M_k-M_{k-1}$ and $V=\sum_{k=1}^n c_k^2$. For $\lambda>0$, F1, F2, and F5 give $$\begin{aligned} \mathbb Ee^{\lambda\sum_{k=1}^nD_k} &=\mathbb E\!\left[e^{\lambda\sum_{k<n}D_k} \mathbb E(e^{\lambda D_n}\mid\mathcal F_{n-1})\right]\\ &\le e^{\lambda^2c_n^2/8}\mathbb Ee^{\lambda\sum_{k<n}D_k} \le e^{\lambda^2V/8}. \end{aligned}$$ The final inequality follows by finite induction, with the empty sum at time $0$. [F1, F2, F5]

2.1 Markov applied to $e^{\lambda(M_n-M_0)}$ yields $$\mathbb P(M_n-M_0\ge t)\le \exp(-\lambda t+\lambda^2V/8).$$ If $V>0$, the quadratic is minimized at $\lambda=4t/V$, giving $\exp(-2t^2/V)$. [F3, step 1.1]

3.1 If $V=0$, every $c_k=0$. F1's hypotheses then force every $D_k=0$ almost surely, so the event is empty for $t>0$, agreeing with the stated convention. Apply step 1.1, step 2.1 to $-M$, whose endpoints are $-B_k,-A_k$, to obtain the lower-tail bound. AC has exactly the inherited role in F4. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $H,Y$ be arbitrary measurable spaces, let $\lambda$ be a probability measure on $H$, and let $K,L$ be probability kernels from $H$ to $Y$. Suppose $\varepsilon\ge0$, $0\le\delta\le1$, and, for every $h$ and every measurable $A\subseteq Y$,
$$K(h,A)\le e^\varepsilon L(h,A)+\delta,\qquad L(h,A)\le e^\varepsilon K(h,A)+\delta.$$
Define probability measures on the product sigma-algebra by
$$R(B)=\int_H K(h,B_h)\lambda(dh),\qquad S(B)=\int_H L(h,B_h)\lambda(dh).$$
There is a probability measure $T$ on $H\times Y$ whose $H$ marginal is $\lambda$, such that, as inequalities of measures,
$$e^{-\varepsilon}S\le T\le e^\varepsilon S,\qquad \operatorname{TV}(R,T)\le\delta.$$
Here $\operatorname{TV}(U,V)=\sup_B|U(B)-V(B)|$. No countability or topological condition is imposed on either measurable space.

## Statement references

[Dwork and Roth, Lemma 3.17 and the approximate-privacy reduction in Theorem 3.20.](https://privacytools.seas.harvard.edu/resource/thealgorithmicfoundationsofdifferentialprivacypdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, arbitrary measurable $H,Y$, probability $\lambda$, probability kernels $K,L$, and the pointwise two-directional event bounds in the Statement.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice|AC]] is assumed for [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality|ordinary Radon–Nikodym derivatives]] of finite measures; the whole space is a common finite exhaustion.

[F1] [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel|Probability kernels]], [[thm-sections-of-product-measurable-functions-are-measurable|measurable sections]], and [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel|kernel integration measurability]] apply on the arbitrary [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras|product sigma-algebra]].

[F2] [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure|A nonnegative density defines a measure]]. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral|Monotone convergence]] extends identities for indicator integrals first to simple functions and then to nonnegative measurable functions.

[F3] [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability|Borel composition]] preserves measurability of the finite scalar clipping and correction formulas below.

[F4] At $u=0$, [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]] gives $\exp(0)=1/\exp(0)>0$, hence $\exp(0)=1$. Then [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]] gives $a=\exp(\varepsilon)\ge1$ for $\varepsilon\ge0$, and the reciprocal identity gives $1/a=\exp(-\varepsilon)>0$.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], the integrands defining $R,S$ are measurable. Countable additivity follows by applying monotone convergence to disjoint sections, and total mass is one. The same argument gives $\mu=(R+S)/2=\lambda\otimes M$, where $M=(K+L)/2$ is the explicit mixture probability kernel and the notation $\lambda\otimes M$ denotes the displayed iterated integral. Both $R,S$ have marginal $\lambda$. By [A1], choose a density of $R$ relative to $\mu$. The inequality $0\le R\le2\mu$ forces this density into $[0,2]$ almost everywhere: a positive-measure level set violating a bound would contradict that measure inequality. Clip it into $[0,2]$ and call the result $p$; put $q=2-p$. Thus $p,q$ are finite nonnegative product-measurable densities of $R,S$ relative to $\mu$. The indicator identities extend to nonnegative integrands by [F2]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, choose, construct]

2.1 Write $a=\exp(\varepsilon)\ge1$ by [F4]. Let $E=\{p>aq\}$ and $F=\{p<q/a\}$, both product-measurable. For every measurable history event $C$, apply the assumed event inequality to $E_h$ for $h\in C$, and integrate. The density identities give $\int_{C\times Y}(p-aq)_+\,d\mu=R(E\cap(C\times Y))-aS(E\cap(C\times Y))\le\delta\lambda(C)$. Similarly $\int_{C\times Y}(q/a-p)_+\,d\mu\le(\delta/a)\lambda(C)$. Define $\alpha(h)=\int(p-aq)_+(h,y)M(h,dy)$ and $\beta(h)=\int(q/a-p)_+(h,y)M(h,dy)$. These are finite measurable functions. Localization over all $C$ implies $\alpha\le\delta$ and $\beta\le\delta/a$ almost everywhere, since a violating positive-measure level set could be used for $C$. Likewise, the common history marginals imply $\int p(h,y)M(h,dy)=\int q(h,y)M(h,dy)=1$ for $\lambda$-almost every $h$, by equality of their integrals over every $C$. Let $G$ be the measurable conull set where all four scalar conditions hold. Only the two specified joint level sets and scalar marginal identities have been used; no simultaneous fiberwise density representation is asserted. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, given, construct]

3.1 Put $c=\min\{\max\{p,q/a\},aq\}$ and $m(h)=\int c(h,y)M(h,dy)$. On $G$, $m=1-\alpha+\beta$ and $q/a\le c\le aq$. If $m<1$, set $w=c+\frac{1-m}{a-m}(aq-c)$; if $m>1$, set $w=c-\frac{m-1}{m-1/a}(c-q/a)$; if $m=1$, set $w=c$. Every used denominator is strictly positive and its fraction lies in $[0,1]$. These formulas give $q/a\le w\le aq$ and $\int w(h,y)M(h,dy)=1$ on $G$. Off $G$, set $w=q$. All formulas are measurable by [F1] and [F3]; each division is confined to its stated measurable branch. In particular, when $a=1$, $c=q$ and $m=1$ on $G$, so no zero denominator is used. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Define $T(B)=\int_B w\,d\mu$. By [F2] this is a measure. The conditional normalization on $G$ and the fact that $G^c$ is $\lambda$-null imply $T(C\times Y)=\lambda(C)$, so $T$ is a probability measure with the required marginal. Integrating $q/a\le w\le aq$ gives $S/a\le T\le aS$. On $G$, clipping changes $p$ by conditional absolute integral $\alpha+\beta$, and the correction changes $c$ in one direction by conditional absolute integral $|1-m|=|\alpha-\beta|$. Consequently $\int|p-w|\,d\mu\le2\int\max\{\alpha,\beta\}\,d\lambda\le2\delta$. Because $p,w$ have equal total integral, the positive and negative parts of $p-w$ have the same integral; every event integral lies between these two extrema, attained by its sign sets. Thus $\operatorname{TV}(R,T)=\frac12\int|p-w|\,d\mu\le\delta$. This proves all claims, including $\delta=0$ and $\varepsilon=0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

The source gives the clipping/redistribution idea and the advanced-composition reduction for discrete distributions. The proof here supplies the joint-measure construction on arbitrary measurable spaces. Its conclusion concerns measures with a fixed marginal and does not claim a measurable family of fiberwise Radon–Nikodym derivatives or a disintegration of $T$.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal D$ be a set equipped with its power-set sigma-algebra and a symmetric adjacency relation $\sim$; this includes finite-support record-count databases with neighbors differing by one added or removed occurrence. Let $k\ge1$, let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_k$ be arbitrary measurable output spaces, and let round $i$ be a probability kernel $K_i(D,h,\cdot)$ on $Y_i$, measurable in the previous transcript $h\in H_{i-1}=\prod_{j<i}Y_j$ for each database $D$. Suppose that for every ordered neighboring pair $D\sim D'$, every $i$, every $h$, and every measurable $A\subseteq Y_i$,
$$K_i(D,h,A)\le e^\varepsilon K_i(D',h,A)+\delta,$$
where $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $0\le\delta\le1$. If $0<\delta'<1$ and $k\delta+\delta'\le1$, then the full transcript, on the finite product sigma-algebra, is $(\varepsilon',k\delta+\delta')$-differentially private, where
$$\varepsilon'=\varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}+k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon-1).$$

## Statement references

**Given:** AC, the finite adaptive sequence on arbitrary measurable output spaces, the two ordered conditional privacy inequalities at every history, and the stated parameters.

[F3] [[lem-dp-joint-measure-purification|Joint-measure purification]] produces, for any supplied history probability $\lambda$, a probability $T$ with that marginal, $e^{-\varepsilon}(\lambda\otimes L)\le T\le e^\varepsilon(\lambda\otimes L)$, and $\operatorname{TV}(T,\lambda\otimes K)\le\delta$ under the two pointwise event inequalities.

[F4] [[thm-integration-against-a-radon-nikodym-derivative|RN integration]] identifies integrals against density measures; its indicator and simple identities extend to nonnegative functions by [F2], and then to integrable signed functions by positive and negative parts. [F5] [[lem-dp-test-function-extension|The bounded-test-function extension]] implies $|\int g\,dU-\int g\,dV|\le s$ for measurable $0\le g\le1$ whenever $\operatorname{TV}(U,V)\le s$.

[F6] [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra|Conditional expectation]] is characterized by equality of integrals over all conditioning events.

[F7] [[thm-azuma-hoeffding-inequality|Azuma–Hoeffding]] bounds the upper tail of a martingale with increment interval lengths $c_i$ by $\exp(-2t^2/\sum_i c_i^2)$.

[F8] [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability|Borel composition]] preserves scalar measurability. [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws|Logarithm laws]] and [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral|the integral formula $\log x=\int_1^x dt/t$]] apply to positive likelihood ratios. In particular $\log x\le x-1$ for $x>0$: integrate $1/t\le1$ from $1$ to $x$ when $x\ge1$, and integrate $1/t\ge1$ from $x$ to $1$ with a minus sign when $x\le1$.

[F9] At $u=0$, [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]] gives $\exp(0)=1/\exp(0)>0$, hence $\exp(0)=1$. Then [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]] gives $a=\exp(\varepsilon)\ge1$ for $\varepsilon\ge0$, and the reciprocal identity gives $a^{-1}=\exp(-\varepsilon)>0$.

Its history marginal is $\lambda$. Starting at the point mass on $H_0$, finite recursion constructs the original prefix laws $P_i=P_{i-1}\otimes K_i$ and $Q_i=Q_{i-1}\otimes L_i$. Integrals of product-measurable nonnegative functions have the corresponding iterated-integral formula, first for indicators and then by [F2]. No countable-generation hypothesis enters this construction. [F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 Set $T_0=P_0=Q_0$. Given $T_{i-1}$, form $R_i=T_{i-1}\otimes K_i$ and $S_i=T_{i-1}\otimes L_i$. The hypotheses hold at every history, hence also under the modified history law. These are measures only; no conditional kernel for $T_i$ is required. Finite iteration yields consistent prefix marginals of the final probability $T_k$. Moreover [F5], applied to $h\mapsto K_i(h,B_h)\in[0,1]$, gives $\operatorname{TV}(P_i,R_i)\le\operatorname{TV}(P_{i-1},T_{i-1})$. Thus the triangle inequality and induction give $\operatorname{TV}(P_i,T_i)\le i\delta$. [A1, F2, F3, F5, F9, step 1.1, construct, induction]

3.1 By [A1] choose a product-measurable density $r_i=dT_i/dS_i$. The measure bounds in step 2.1 force $a^{-1}\le r_i\le a$ almost everywhere, since otherwise a level set separated from one bound contradicts that bound after integration. Clip the representative into this positive interval everywhere. Write $Z_i=\prod_{j\le i}r_j$ as a function on $H_i$, with $Z_0=1$. We prove $dT_i/dQ_i=Z_i$ by induction. If $dT_{i-1}/dQ_{i-1}=Z_{i-1}$, then for any nonnegative measurable $g$ on $H_i$, [F2] and [F4] give $\int g\,dT_i=\int gr_i\,dS_i=\int T_{i-1}(dh)\int g(h,y)r_i(h,y)L_i(h,dy)=\int Q_{i-1}(dh)Z_{i-1}(h)\int g(h,y)r_i(h,y)L_i(h,dy)=\int gZ_{i-1}r_i\,dQ_i$. The base is the common point mass. Hence $Z_i$ is the asserted density and is everywhere positive and finite. In particular $\log Z_k=\sum_i X_i$ for the measurable prefix variables $X_i=\log r_i$, each in $[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$. [A1, F2, F4, F8, F9, step 1.1, step 2.1, choose, induction]

4.1 Define measurable functions on $H_{i-1}$ by $u_i(h)=\int r_i(h,y)L_i(h,dy)$ and $m_i(h)=\int r_i(h,y)\log r_i(h,y)L_i(h,dy)$. They are finite by the bounds in step 3.1. Because $T_i$ and $S_i$ have the same history marginal $T_{i-1}$, their density identity on $C\times Y_i$ gives $\int_Cu_i\,dT_{i-1}=T_{i-1}(C)$ for every $C$, so $u_i=1$ almost everywhere under $T_{i-1}$. On this conull set, $\log r_i\le r_i-1$ gives $\int\log r_i\,dL_i\le0$. Therefore $m_i\le\int(r_i-1)\log r_i\,dL_i\le\varepsilon\int|r_i-1|\,dL_i$. For every $a^{-1}\le r\le a$, $|r-1|\le(a-1)\min\{r,1\}$, by separately checking $r\ge1$ and $r\le1$. Thus $m_i\le\varepsilon(a-1)=:b$ almost everywhere. This scalar conditional calculation supplies the entropy bound without a fiberwise RN identity. [F2, F4, F8, F9, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Work on $(H_k,T_k)$ with the filtration $\mathcal F_i$ generated by the first $i$ coordinates. For any measurable history event $C$, consistency of marginals, the density identity for $T_i$ relative to $S_i$, and the iterated-integral formula give $\int_{\{H_{i-1}\in C\}}X_i\,dT_k=\int_Cm_i(h)T_{i-1}(dh)$. Hence $m_i(H_{i-1})$ is a version of $\mathbb E_{T_k}[X_i\mid\mathcal F_{i-1}]$ by [F6]. It is bounded, as are the $X_i$, so $M_j=\sum_{i\le j}(X_i-m_i(H_{i-1}))$ is an integrable martingale. Its $i$th increment lies in the $\mathcal F_{i-1}$-measurable interval $[-\varepsilon-m_i,\varepsilon-m_i]$, whose length is $2\varepsilon$. [F2, F4, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 If $\varepsilon=0$, all $r_i=1$, so $T_k=Q_k$ and the desired one-sided bound follows from step 2.1 with error $k\delta$. If $\varepsilon>0$, put $t=\varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}>0$. Applying [F7] with interval lengths $2\varepsilon$ gives $T_k(M_k\ge t)\le\exp(-t^2/(2k\varepsilon^2))=\delta'$. Step 4.1 bounds $\sum_i m_i\le kb$, so $T_k(\log Z_k>kb+t)\le\delta'$. Set $\varepsilon'=kb+t$. For every transcript event $B$, split at $\log Z_k\le\varepsilon'$ and use the density from step 3.1 to obtain $T_k(B)\le e^{\varepsilon'}Q_k(B)+\delta'$. Then step 2.1 gives $P_k(B)\le e^{\varepsilon'}Q_k(B)+k\delta+\delta'$. [F4, F7, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 The preceding construction applies to every ordered neighboring pair. In particular repeat it with $D,D'$ interchanged, constructing a new modified measure on that side, to get $Q_k(B)\le e^{\varepsilon'}P_k(B)+k\delta+\delta'$. This proves differential privacy by [F1]. The proof includes $k=1$, $\delta=0$, and equality $k\delta+\delta'=1$; $0<\delta'<1$ makes the logarithm finite and positive. All database event evaluations are measurable by the power-set database convention in [F1]. No modified law, density, or exceptional set needs to be selected measurably in the database pair: the event inequality has been proved for each pair separately. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 6.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Let databases be finite-support record-count functions, with neighbors differing by one added or removed record occurrence. For $k\ge1$, let round $i$ be a probability kernel $K_i(D,h,\cdot)$ from the $i$th arbitrary measurable output space, conditional on every prior transcript $h$. Suppose that for every ordered neighboring pair $D\sim D'$, every $h$, and every measurable round-$i$ event $A$,
$$
K_i(D,h,A)\le e^{\varepsilon_i}K_i(D',h,A)+\delta_i,
$$
where $\varepsilon_i\ge0$ and $\delta_i\ge0$. If $\sum_i\delta_i\le1$, the full transcript on the finite product sigma-algebra is $(\sum_i\varepsilon_i,\sum_i\delta_i)$-differentially private. Also, assuming AC, if every conditional round has the same parameters $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ with $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $0\le\delta\le1$, then for any $0<\delta'<1$ with $k\delta+\delta'\le1$, advanced composition on arbitrary measurable output spaces gives parameters $(\varepsilon',k\delta+\delta')$, where
$$
\varepsilon'=\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}\,\varepsilon+k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon-1).
$$

**Given:** The finite adaptive kernels and conditional event inequalities on arbitrary measurable output spaces in the Statement; AC for the advanced clause.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice|AC]] is assumed for the ordinary Radon–Nikodym and concentration suppliers used only by the advanced clause.

[F1] [[def-differential-privacy-and-adjacency|Differential privacy]] is the event inequality for every ordered neighboring pair.

[F2] [[thm-basic-adaptive-composition|Basic adaptive composition]] applies to arbitrary measurable output spaces and heterogeneous parameters, with additive sums of epsilon and delta.

[F3] [[thm-advanced-adaptive-composition-arbitrary-measurable-outputs|Advanced adaptive composition]] proves the exact displayed epsilon and additive error on arbitrary measurable output spaces under AC, using joint-measure purification and ordinary prefix-law densities.

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F2] to the stated round kernels and their parameters. Its every-history hypotheses and arbitrary measurable output scope agree with the Statement, and the condition on the sum of the additive errors places the resulting parameter in the declared range. This gives the basic clause without choice. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 For the common-parameter clause assume [A1] and apply [F3] to the same kernels with common parameters $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ and the stated $\delta'$. Its hypotheses are exactly the every-history event inequalities and parameter conditions here. Its full-transcript event inequality has epsilon $\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}\,\varepsilon+k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon-1)$ and additive error $k\delta+\delta'$, which gives the advanced clause by [F1]. [A1, F1, F3, given] ∎

## Remark

The definition on this page is central, record-level privacy for add/remove adjacency. It does not by itself define client-level or local privacy, and keeping data on a device or applying secure aggregation does not establish the event inequalities in this definition. Differential privacy limits the effect of one record on a release; it does not prevent conclusions about an attribute that is strongly correlated with other records or public information.

## Example

Let $U$ be a nonempty record universe and let databases be finite-support count functions $D:U\to\mathbb N_0$, with neighbors formed by adding or removing one occurrence. Let $P:U\to\{0,1\}$ be a predicate satisfied by at least one possible record, and let $f(D)$ count the occurrences satisfying $P$. Then the global add/remove $L^1$ sensitivity of $f$ is $1$. For $\varepsilon>0$, releasing $f(D)+Z$ with $Z\sim\operatorname{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)$ is $(\varepsilon,0)$-differentially private.

1.1 If $D'$ is obtained from $D$ by adding one occurrence of $u$, then $f(D')-f(D)=P(u)\in\{0,1\}$; removing one occurrence gives the negative of this change. ## Example

Let $U$ be a nonempty record universe, let $\mathcal D$ be its finite-support count databases with add/remove-one-occurrence adjacency, let $R=\{a,b\}$, and let $\varepsilon>0$. The constant utility $u(D,a)=1$, $u(D,b)=0$ has $\Delta_u=0$, so it is inadmissible for the positive-sensitivity exponential mechanism. Fix a possible record $u_*\in U$ and define $s(D)=1$ exactly when $D(u_*)>0$. Instead set $u(D,a)=1$ and $u(D,b)=1-s(D)$. Then $\Delta_u=1$, the mechanism is $(\varepsilon,0)$-differentially private, and it selects $a$ with probability
$$
\frac{e^{\varepsilon/2}}{e^{\varepsilon/2}+e^{\varepsilon(1-s(D))/2}}.
$$

[F3] [[alg-exponential-mechanism|Exponential-mechanism weights]] are $\exp(\varepsilon u(D,r)/(2\Delta_u))$, normalized by their finite positive sum, and require $\Delta_u>0$.

1.1 For the first utility, every score is independent of $D$, so every adjacent-pair difference is zero and $\Delta_u=0$ by [F2]. This fails the positive-sensitivity hypothesis in [F3], so the algorithm is not defined for that utility. [F2, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 For the second utility, adding or removing a record other than $u_*$ leaves $s(D)$ unchanged; adding or removing $u_*$ changes it by at most one. [Dwork and Roth, *The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy*, §§2.3 and 3.3, printed pp. 23–25 and 33–37.](https://privacytools.seas.harvard.edu/resource/thealgorithmicfoundationsofdifferentialprivacypdf)

[Vadhan, *The Complexity of Differential Privacy*, §§1.5 and 2.1, PDF pp. 7–8 and 13.](https://salil.seas.harvard.edu/sites/g/files/omnuum4266/files/salil/files/manuscript_2017.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A predicate $P$ satisfied by some record $u_0$, $\varepsilon>0$, and threshold $c\in\mathbb R$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice]] is inherited from the Laplace probability law; no stronger choice principle is used.

[F1] [[def-differential-privacy-and-adjacency|Neighboring databases]] differ by adding or removing one occurrence.

[F2] [[def-global-l1-sensitivity|Sensitivity]] is the attained maximum over neighboring query differences.

[F3] [[thm-laplace-mechanism-privacy|Laplace privacy theorem]] gives $(\varepsilon,0)$-DP for a scalar query of sensitivity one and $\varepsilon>0$.

[F4] [[def-borel-sigma-algebra|The Borel sigma-algebra]] contains closed and open intervals, including $[c,+\infty)$ and $(-\infty,c)$.

[F5] [[thm-dp-postprocessing|Postprocessing theorem]] preserves the same differential-privacy parameters under any data-independent probability kernel.

## Verification

1.1 Adding or removing a record $u$ changes $f(D)$ by $P(u)\in\{0,1\}$ in absolute value. Every neighboring difference is at most one, and the empty database versus the singleton database containing $u_0$ attains one. Thus $\Delta_1f=1$ by [F1] and [F2], and [A1, F3] gives the corresponding Laplace law, so the noisy count has noise scale $1/\varepsilon$ and is $(\varepsilon,0)$-DP. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Define $\phi(x)=\mathbf1_{\{x\ge c\}}$. Its preimages of $\{1\}$ and $\{0\}$ are $[c,+\infty)$ and $(-\infty,c)$, respectively, so [F4] makes $\phi$ Borel measurable. The deterministic kernel $L(x,B)=\mathbf1_B(\phi(x))$ on $\{0,1\}$ is a probability kernel and is independent of the database. Applying [F5] to the noisy-count release proves that the threshold output retains the same $(\varepsilon,0)$ guarantee. [F4, F5, step 1.1, given, construct] ∎

## Example

Model a database as a finite-support count function $D:U\to\mathbb N_0$, where $U$ is the record universe, and call two databases neighbors when one is obtained from the other by adding or removing one record occurrence. Suppose one client contributes 100 identified record occurrences to a database. Removing or adding any one of those occurrences is one neighboring step, while changing the database by the client’s entire 100-record contribution is not one neighboring step. A client-level guarantee therefore requires a client-level adjacency relation that treats that full contribution as one change and a proof using that relation.

## Example references

[[def-differential-privacy-and-adjacency|The add/remove-one-occurrence database relation]]

[[rem-differential-privacy-scope-and-limitations|Record-level privacy is distinct from client-level privacy]]

[Dwork and Roth, *The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy*, §§2.1 and 2.3, printed pp. 11–25.](https://privacytools.seas.harvard.edu/resource/thealgorithmicfoundationsofdifferentialprivacypdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite-support count database $D_0$ and 100 identified record occurrences contributed by one client.

[F1] [[def-differential-privacy-and-adjacency|Database]] is a finite-support record-count function, and two databases are neighbors exactly when one is obtained from the other by adding or removing one record occurrence.

[F2] [[rem-differential-privacy-scope-and-limitations|Scope distinction]]: the page definition is central record-level add/remove privacy and does not itself define client-level privacy.

## Verification

1.1 List the client’s 100 occurrences as $u_1,\ldots,u_{100}$, with repetitions allowed. For $j=0,\ldots,100$, let $D_j=D_0+\sum_{\ell=1}^{j}\mathbf1_{\{u_\ell\}}$. Then $D_{j-1}$ and $D_j$ differ by adding one occurrence, so [F1] makes each consecutive pair neighbors. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 The count-function difference between $D_0$ and $D_{100}$ has total absolute count $\sum_{u\in U}|D_{100}(u)-D_0(u)|=100$, counting repeated contributions with multiplicity. A single add/remove neighbor pair has this total equal to $1$ by [F1]. Hence the full contribution is not a record-level neighboring step. Treating it as one step changes the adjacency relation, and [F2] says that any claimed client-level guarantee needs that relation and a proof under it. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $k,T$ be positive integers, let $\eta>0$, and let $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$. A loss vector at round $t$ is $\ell_t=(\ell_t(1),\ldots,\ell_t(k))\in[0,1]^k$. Initialize $w_{1,j}=1$ for each $j\in[k]$. At round $t=1,\ldots,T$, choose action $a_t=j$ with probability
$$p_{t,j}=\frac{w_{t,j}}{\sum_{r=1}^k w_{t,r}}, \qquad w_{t,j}=\exp\!\left(-\eta\sum_{s<t}\ell_s(j)\right).$$
The empty sum at $t=1$ is zero. After drawing $a_t$, observe the entire vector $\ell_t$ and update $w_{t+1,j}=w_{t,j}\exp(-\eta\ell_t(j))$. Return the full transcript $(a_1,\ldots,a_T)$. Each action draw is fresh conditional on the loss history and previous actions. The finite history spaces carry their power-set sigma-algebras.

## Definition references

[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e|The real exponential function]]

[[def-probability-measure|Probability measures on finite action spaces]]

[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel|Probability kernels for the conditional action laws]]

Cynthia Dwork and Aaron Roth, *The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy*, Algorithm 15, printed pp. 223–224, and Algorithm 16, printed pp. 224–225: [full text](https://privacytools.seas.harvard.edu/resource/thealgorithmicfoundationsofdifferentialprivacypdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Positive integers $k,T$, an update parameter $\eta>0$, and full-information loss vectors in $[0,1]^k$.

[F1] The real exponential is finite at every real input and is strictly positive there. [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]

[F2] A measurable space is a set equipped with a sigma-algebra; a power-set sigma-algebra makes every subset measurable. [[def-measurable-space]]

[F3] A probability measure has total mass one. [[def-probability-measure]]

[F4] A probability kernel has probability-measure sections and measurable event evaluations. [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]

## Verification

**Given:** The hypotheses and procedure in the Definition.

1.1 For each $t$ and $j$, the sum $\sum_{s<t}\ell_s(j)$ is a finite real number. By [F1], every weight $w_{t,j}$ is finite and strictly positive. Since $[k]$ is finite and nonempty, $Z_t:=\sum_{r=1}^k w_{t,r}$ is finite and strictly positive, so every $p_{t,j}$ is defined and nonnegative. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 The finite sum of the action probabilities is $\sum_{j=1}^k p_{t,j}=Z_t/Z_t=1$. For each fixed loss input, every history-to-event map is a function on a finite history space with its power-set sigma-algebra; for each fixed history, the action law is the probability measure assigning mass $p_{t,j}$ to $j$. Thus the conditional action laws meet both conditions of [F4]. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

This is the full-information finite-action procedure. Its regret and privacy claims are proved separately; this definition alone makes no regret or privacy assertion.

## Definition

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma_X)$ be a nonempty measurable space, let the binary label set $\{0,1\}$ carry its power-set sigma-algebra, and let $\mathcal C$ be a finite nonempty class of measurable maps $h:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}$. Fix an integer $n\ge1$ and a parameter $\varepsilon>0$. On an ordered labeled sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ with $m\ge n$, or on its underlying finite multiset, define
$$\widehat L_S(h)=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf 1\{h(x_i)\ne y_i\},\qquad w_S(h)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\varepsilon n}{2}\widehat L_S(h)\right).$$
Output $h\in\mathcal C$ with probability $w_S(h)/\sum_{g\in\mathcal C}w_S(g)$. This formula is invariant under permutations of the sample. For the statistical input, the ordered sample space has its finite product sigma-algebra. For the private-database input, the same formula is defined on finite-support record-count functions of size at least $n$, with the power-set sigma-algebra; privacy is proved separately.

## Definition references

[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras|Finite product sigma-algebras for samples]]

[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e|The real exponential function]]

[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel|Probability kernels for randomized selection]]

Cynthia Dwork and Aaron Roth, *The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy*, Definition 3.4 and Chapter 11 §11.1: [full text](https://privacytools.seas.harvard.edu/resource/thealgorithmicfoundationsofdifferentialprivacypdf).

Salil Vadhan, *The Complexity of Differential Privacy*, Proposition 4.2: [full text](https://salil.seas.harvard.edu/sites/g/files/omnuum4266/files/salil/files/manuscript_2017.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The measurable binary class, $n\ge1$, $\varepsilon>0$, and a finite sample or multiset with at least $n$ records.

[F1] A measurable space is a set with a sigma-algebra; measurable rectangles generate the finite product sigma-algebra. [[def-measurable-space]], [[def-measurable-rectangle]], [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]

[F2] The real exponential is finite and strictly positive on every real input. [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]

[F3] The exponential is continuous, continuous real maps have Borel preimages, and composition with a Borel measurable outer map preserves measurability. [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]

[F4] Finite sums, scalar multiples, and products of measurable real functions are measurable. [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]

[F5] A real function is measurable exactly when its strict threshold sets are measurable. [[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]]

[F6] A probability measure has total mass one; a probability kernel has probability-measure sections and measurable event evaluations. [[def-probability-measure]], [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]

## Verification

**Given:** The hypotheses and procedure in the Definition.

1.1 For each $h\in\mathcal C$, its mismatch set is $(h^{-1}\{0\}\times\{1\})\cup(h^{-1}\{1\}\times\{0\})$, a finite union of measurable rectangles by [F1]. Thus each sample loss indicator and the finite average $\widehat L_S(h)$ are measurable in the ordered sample. By [F2]–[F4], the weight $w_S(h)$ is finite, positive, and measurable in $S$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

2.1 Since $\mathcal C$ is finite and nonempty, $Z_S:=\sum_{g\in\mathcal C}w_S(g)$ is finite, measurable, and strictly positive. For $a\le0$, $\{S:1/Z_S>a\}$ is the whole sample space; for $a>0$, it is $\{S:Z_S<1/a\}$, which is measurable by [F5]. Hence $1/Z_S$, and then each $w_S(h)/Z_S$, is measurable by [F4]. These probabilities sum to one, so every output section is a probability measure. For any event $A\subseteq\mathcal C$, its probability is a finite sum of the measurable output probabilities; the power-set private-database domain also makes each event evaluation measurable. Thus [F6] gives the probability-kernel conditions. [F2, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

The scale $1/n$ is used as a sensitivity upper bound. The private theorem proves its add/remove validity on the restricted size-at-least-$n$ domain and derives privacy and utility directly; no exact attained-maximum convention is assumed here.

## Definition

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. A subset of
$X \times Y$ is a **measurable rectangle** if it has the form $A \times B$ with
$A \in \mathcal A$ and $B \in \mathcal B$.

The ambient sigma-algebras matter: the same set may be a measurable rectangle
for one pair $(\mathcal A,\mathcal B)$ and not for another.
