## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $w\in\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $E\subseteq\mathbb R$ have Lebesgue outer measure zero. Then

$$\{x\in\mathbb R^d:w\cdot x+b\in E\}$$

is Lebesgue measurable and has $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Consequently, if two Lebesgue measurable real functions on $\mathbb R$ agree outside a null set, their compositions with the same nonconstant affine form $x\mapsto w\cdot x+b$ agree almost everywhere on $\mathbb R^d$.

## Statement references

[Tao, An Introduction to Measure Theory, product measures and linear changes of variables](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/12/gsm-126-tao5-measure-book.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $d\ge1$, a nonzero vector $w$, a real $b$, and a null set $E\subseteq\mathbb R$.

[F1] Under Countable Choice, every null subset of $\mathbb R$ is contained in a Borel null set: outer regularity supplies open covers of arbitrarily small measure, and their countable intersection is Borel; Borel sets are Lebesgue measurable and completeness makes the resulting outer-null set measurable and null ([[thm-lebesgue-outer-regularity-for-arbitrary-subsets]], [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

[F2] The product of two sigma-finite measures satisfies Tonelli's theorem for nonnegative measurable functions ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F3] Product Lebesgue measure agrees with Euclidean Lebesgue measure on Borel subsets of a Euclidean product ([[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]]).

[F4] Invertible linear maps scale Lebesgue measure by the absolute determinant; in particular an orthogonal map preserves it ([[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]]).

[F5] Translation and nonzero scalar dilation preserve Lebesgue nullity ([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]], [[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]]).

[F6] Lebesgue measure is complete under Countable Choice, so every subset of a measurable null set is measurable and null ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

[F7] Under Countable Choice every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^d$ is Lebesgue measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]).

[A1] Countable Choice means every sequence of nonempty sets has a function choosing one element from each ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

1.1 Put $u=w/\lVert w\rVert_2$. For $d\ge2$, start with $u$ and inspect the standard basis vectors in their finite order; for each $e_i$, subtract its orthogonal projection onto the span of the vectors already retained, and append and normalize the residual exactly when it is nonzero. Since the standard basis spans $\mathbb R^d$, this finite Gram–Schmidt procedure produces an orthonormal basis whose first vector is $u$. Let $Q$ be the associated orthogonal coordinate map. If $d=1$, take $Qx=ux$. In either case the first coordinate of $Qx$ is $u\cdot x$, and [F4] says $Q$ preserves Lebesgue measure. [given, F4, construct]

2.1 Fix an integer $R\ge1$. Since $Q$ is a finite matrix, choose $C_R<\infty$ greater than $R$ times the largest sum of absolute entries in any row; then $Q([-R,R]^d)\subseteq[-C_R,C_R]^d$. Set $E_R=((E-b)/\lVert w\rVert_2)\cap[-C_R,C_R]$. By [F5], $E_R$ is null. By [F1], choose a Borel null set $B_R\supseteq E_R$. If $d=1$, the image under $Q$ of the set in the Statement intersected with $[-R,R]$ is contained in $B_R$. If $d\ge2$, that image is contained in $B_R\times[-C_R,C_R]^{d-1}$. [step 1.1, F1, F5, A1, choose]

3.1 If $d=1$, the bounded pullback image is contained in the Borel null set $B_R$, and the inverse orthogonal map preserves nullity by [F4]. If $d\ge2$, the Borel set $B_R\times[-C_R,C_R]^{d-1}$ is Lebesgue measurable by [F7]; Tonelli [F2] gives it product measure zero because its one-dimensional section factor $B_R$ has measure zero, and [F3] identifies that product measure with $\lambda_d$. Applying the inverse orthogonal map preserves nullity by [F4]. In either case the ridge pullback inside $[-R,R]^d$ is contained in a Borel null set. [step 2.1, F2, F3, F4, F7, A1]

4.1 The full pullback is the countable union of its intersections with $[-R,R]^d$, $R\ge1$. Each intersection is a subset of the Borel null set from step 3.1, hence is measurable and null by [F6]; countable additivity makes the union measurable and null. If two functions differ only on $E$, their compositions differ only on this pullback, proving the consequence. [step 3.1, F6, A1] ∎

## Statement

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). For **every** subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$,
measurable or not,

$$\lambda_n^*(E) \;=\; \inf\,\{\, \lambda_n(U) \;:\; U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \text{ open and } E \subseteq U \,\},$$

the infimum being taken in $[0,+\infty]$ over a family that is nonempty because
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is open.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $n \ge 1$, the Axiom of Countable Choice, and a subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

[L1] $\lambda_n^*(E) := \inf\{\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu_0(A_k) : A_k \in \mathcal{E}_n$ for every $k$ and $E \subseteq \bigcup_k A_k\}$ ([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]], [[def-elementary-set-in-rn]]).

[L2] Assuming countable choice, $\lambda_n^*$ is an outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$, hence monotone and countably subadditive, and $\lambda_n^*(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for every elementary set $A$ ([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]], [[def-outer-measure]]).

[L3] Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure on it ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

[L4] Assuming countable choice, every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable; in particular every open set is ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]).

[L5] $A^{+\delta}$ is an elementary set determined by $A$ and $\delta$ alone, it contains $A$, and every point of $A$ is an interior point of $A^{+\delta}$; and for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there is $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $\mu_0\big(A^{+1/(m+1)}\big) \le \mu_0(A) + \varepsilon$ ([[lem-elementary-sets-admit-compact-inner-and-open-outer-approximations]], claims 1 and 2).

[L6] Elementary volume is finitely additive on pairwise disjoint elementary sets, monotone, and finitely subadditive ([[prop-elementary-volume-is-finitely-additive-and-monotone]], [[thm-elementary-volume-is-well-defined]]).

[F1] The interior $\operatorname{int}(A)$ is open, and an arbitrary union of open sets is open ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]], [[def-metric-topology]], [[thm-metric-open-set-algebra]], claim 2).

[F2] The **nonnegative extended sum** of a sequence in $[0,+\infty]$ is $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k:=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}s_n$, the supremum of its nondecreasing partial sums ([[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]).

[F3] Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]).

[F4] If $|r| < 1$ then $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} = 1/(1-r)$; in particular $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$ ([[thm-geometric-series]]).

[F5] For sequences of reals, $\sum_{k<n}(a_k+b_k) = \sum_{k<n}a_k+\sum_{k<n}b_k$, and if $a_k \le b_k$ whenever $0\le k<n$ then $\sum_{k<n}a_k \le \sum_{k<n}b_k$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], claims 1 and 4; [[def-finite-sum]]).

[F6] The **Axiom of Countable Choice** says that for every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Every open $U$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(U)=\lambda_n^*(U)$, so monotonicity of the outer measure gives $\lambda_n^*(E) \le \lambda_n(U)$ for every open $U \supseteq E$, and therefore $\lambda_n^*(E)$ is a lower bound of the family whose infimum is displayed; that family is nonempty since $\mathbb{R}^n$ is open. [L2, L3, L4, F1]

1.2 Suppose $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$ and let $\varepsilon$ be a positive real; by the definition of $\lambda_n^*$ as an infimum there is a sequence $(A_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ of elementary sets with $E \subseteq \bigcup_k A_k$ and $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu_0(A_k) \le \lambda_n^*(E)+\varepsilon$. [L1]

2.1 For each $k$ let $m_k$ be the least natural number with $\mu_0\big(A_k^{+1/(m_k+1)}\big) \le \mu_0(A_k)+\varepsilon 2^{-k}$, which exists because that set of naturals is nonempty and $\mathbb{N}$ is well ordered, and put $U_k := \operatorname{int}\big(A_k^{+1/(m_k+1)}\big)$; each $U_k$ is open and contains $A_k$, so $U := \bigcup_{k}U_k$ is open and contains $E$. [step 1.2, L5, F1, F3]

3.1 Countable subadditivity, monotonicity and the agreement of $\lambda_n^*$ with $\mu_0$ on elementary sets give $\lambda_n(U) \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lambda_n^*(U_k) \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu_0\big(A_k^{+1/(m_k+1)}\big)$; every partial sum of the last series is at most $\sum_{k<N}\mu_0(A_k)+\varepsilon\sum_{k<N}2^{-k} \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu_0(A_k)+2\varepsilon$, so the series itself, being the supremum of its partial sums, is at most $\lambda_n^*(E)+3\varepsilon$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, L2, L5, L6, F2, F4, F5]

4.1 So when $\lambda_n^*(E)<+\infty$ the infimum is at most $\lambda_n^*(E)+3\varepsilon$ for every positive real $\varepsilon$ and hence at most $\lambda_n^*(E)$; when $\lambda_n^*(E)=+\infty$ the infimum is at most $+\infty$ for the same reason of triviality; with step 1.1 the infimum equals $\lambda_n^*(E)$ in both cases. [step 1.1, step 3.1, F6] ∎

## Statement

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $n \ge 1$ and the Axiom of Countable Choice.

[L1] Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

[L2] $\sigma(\mathcal{H}_n) = \sigma(\mathcal{E}_n) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, where $\mathcal{H}_n$ is the family of half-open boxes and $\mathcal{E}_n$ the family of elementary sets ([[lem-half-open-boxes-generate-the-borel-sigma-algebra-on-rn]]).

[L3] At $m = 1$ every half-open box is elementary ([[def-elementary-set-in-rn]]).

[F1] $\sigma_X(\mathcal E)$ is the unique smallest sigma-algebra on $X$ containing $\mathcal E$ ([[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]], [[def-generated-sigma-algebra]]).

[F2] The **Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]); a **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets closed under countable unions ([[def-sigma-algebra]]).

[F3] The **Axiom of Countable Choice** says that for every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Under countable choice $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ containing every elementary set, hence containing the family $\mathcal{H}_n$ of half-open boxes. [L1, L3, F2, F3]

2.1 Since $\sigma(\mathcal{H}_n)$ is the smallest sigma-algebra containing $\mathcal{H}_n$, step 1.1 gives $\sigma(\mathcal{H}_n) \subseteq \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and $\sigma(\mathcal{H}_n)=\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)$; open sets, closed sets and countable intersections of open sets are Borel. [step 1.1, L2, F1, F2] ∎

## Statement

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $n \ge 1$, the Axiom of Countable Choice, Lebesgue outer measure $\lambda_n^*$, and the family $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ of sets Carathéodory measurable for it.

[L1] A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is **Lebesgue measurable** when it is Carathéodory measurable for $\lambda_n^*$, the family of these is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and $\lambda_n := \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)}$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]).

[L2] Assuming countable choice, $\lambda_n^*$ is an outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and $\lambda_n^*(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every elementary set $A$ ([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]).

[L3] $\lambda_n^*$ is the outer set function induced by the premeasure $\mu_0$ on the algebra $\mathcal{E}_n$ of elementary sets ([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]).

[L4] Elementary volume $\mu_0$ is a sigma-finite premeasure on $\mathcal{E}_n$ ([[thm-box-volume-is-a-premeasure-on-the-elementary-algebra]]); its value on a half-open box is the box volume ([[thm-elementary-volume-is-well-defined]], [[def-half-open-box]]), and $\mathbb R^n$ is elementary with infinite elementary volume ([[def-elementary-set-in-rn]]).

[F1] For an outer measure $\mu^*$ on $X$, the Carathéodory measurable subsets form a sigma-algebra, and the restriction of the outer measure to it is a complete measure ([[thm-caratheodory-outer-measure-theorem]]).

[F2] Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every member of the source algebra is Carathéodory measurable for the induced outer measure ([[lem-source-algebra-is-caratheodory-measurable]]).

[F3] Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $\mu_0$ is a premeasure on an algebra $\mathcal A_0$ of subsets of $X$ and $\mu^*$ is its induced outer set function, then $\mathcal A_0\subseteq\mathcal M_{\mu^*}$ and $\mu^*|_{\mathcal A_0}=\mu_0$ ([[thm-caratheodory-extension-theorem]]).

[F4] Every set of outer measure zero, and every subset of it, is Carathéodory measurable and has outer measure zero ([[prop-outer-null-sets-are-caratheodory-measurable]]).

[F5] A measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ is **complete** if every subset of every measurable $\mu$-null set is measurable ([[def-complete-measure-space]]); and a **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function $\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty]$ with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$ that is countably additive on pairwise disjoint sequences ([[def-measure]]).

[F6] The **Axiom of Countable Choice** says that for every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Under countable choice $\lambda_n^*$ is an outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$, so [F1] applies to it: its Carathéodory measurable sets, which are by definition the members of $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, form a sigma-algebra, and the restriction $\lambda_n$ of $\lambda_n^*$ to it is a complete measure. [L1, L2, F1, F5, F6]

1.2 Since $\lambda_n^*$ is the outer set function induced by the premeasure $\mu_0$ on $\mathcal{E}_n$, the extension theorem and the source-algebra lemma give $\mathcal{E}_n \subseteq \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $\lambda_n^*(A)=\mu_0(A)$ there; a half-open box and $\varnothing$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$ are elementary, so $\lambda_n(B)=\operatorname{vol}(B)$, $\lambda_n(\varnothing)=0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n)=+\infty$. [L1, L3, L4, F2, F3, F6]

1.3 A set $S$ with $\lambda_n^*(S)=0$ is Carathéodory measurable for $\lambda_n^*$, hence Lebesgue measurable, and its measure is its outer measure, namely $0$. [L1, F4]

2.1 Claim 1 and the completeness half of claim 2 are step 1.1, the null-set half of claim 2 is step 1.3, and claim 3 is step 1.2. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

## Statement

Let $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$. Let $D_I$ be the real-valued smooth functions $\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ that vanish outside $I$, with seminorms

$$p_M(\varphi)=\max_{0\le j\le M}\sup_{x\in I}|\varphi^{(j)}(x)|,\qquad M\in\mathbb N_0,$$

and metric

$$d(\varphi,\psi)=\sum_{M=0}^{\infty}2^{-M-1}\min(1,p_M(\varphi-\psi)).$$

Then $D_I$ is separable in this metric.

## Statement references

[Dyatlov, Lecture Notes for 18.155, fixed-support test-function spaces](https://math.mit.edu/~dyatlov/18.155/155-notes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nondegenerate compact interval $I=[a,b]$.

[F1] The fixed-support test-function space has the derivative seminorms and metric displayed in the Statement ([[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]).

[F2] The function $\theta(t)=q(t)/(q(t)+q(1-t))$, where $q(t)=e^{-1/t}$ for $t>0$ and $q(t)=0$ for $t\le0$, is smooth, equals zero on $t\le0$, and equals one on $t\ge1$; its flatness at the endpoints follows from the explicit construction ([[lem-schwartz-cutoffs-from-the-standard-smooth-step]], proof step 2.1).

[F3] Every continuous real function on $I$ is uniformly approximated by real polynomials ([[cor-weierstrass-approximation-on-a-closed-interval]]).

[F4] Taylor's formula with a Lagrange remainder bounds a smooth function whose first $N$ endpoint derivatives vanish by a constant times the $N$th power of the distance to that endpoint ([[lem-taylor-lagrange-remainder-from-mean-value]]).

[F5] For a continuously differentiable real function on an interval, the integral of its derivative equals the endpoint difference ([[lem-fundamental-theorem-and-integration-by-parts]]).

[F6] For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is an integer $n\ge1$ with $1/n<\varepsilon$ ([[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]]).

[F7] A continuous real function on a compact interval is bounded ([[lem-extreme-value-theorem-from-compactness]]); the chain and product rules hold ([[lem-derivative-algebra-and-chain-rules]]).

[F8] The natural numbers are unbounded in $\mathbb R$, so integers $n$ above the fixed cutoff can tend to infinity ([[thm-of-archimedean]]).

## Proof

1.1 For each integer $n>2/(b-a)$ define $\chi_n(x)=\theta(n(x-a))\theta(n(b-x))$; such integers exist by [F6], and can tend to infinity by [F8]. By [F2], $\chi_n$ is smooth, vanishes off $I$, and equals one on $[a+1/n,b-1/n]$. Every derivative of $\theta$ is continuous and vanishes outside $[0,1]$ in positive order, so [F7] bounds it on $[0,1]$; repeated chain and product rules [F7] bound $\chi_n^{(j)}$ by a constant times $n^j$. For every $\varphi\in D_I$, all derivatives of its zero extension vanish at $a$ and $b$. Fix $M$. Taylor's formula [F4] gives, for every $N\ge1$ and each $0\le r\le M$, bounds $|\varphi^{(r)}(x)|\le C_{r,N}|x-a|^N$ near $a$ and $|\varphi^{(r)}(x)|\le C'_{r,N}|b-x|^N$ near $b$. Applying the product rule on the two boundary strips, and taking $N>M$, shows $p_M(\varphi-\chi_n\varphi)\to0$. [given, F1, F2, F4, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

1.2 Fix $n$ and $M$. By [F3], choose a real polynomial $p$ uniformly approximating $\varphi^{(M)}$ on $I$, and integrate it $M$ times while matching the values $\varphi^{(j)}(a)$ for $0\le j<M$ to obtain a polynomial $q_0$. Put $e=\varphi-q_0$. Then $e^{(M)}=\varphi^{(M)}-p$ and $e^{(j)}(a)=0$ for $j<M$. Repeated application of [F5], inducting downward from $j=M-1$, gives $$\sup_I|e^{(j)}|\le (b-a)^{M-j}\sup_I|e^{(M)}|\qquad(0\le j<M);$$ for $j=M$ the error is just $\sup_I|e^{(M)}|$. Thus sufficiently accurate approximation at order $M$ makes every derivative through order $M$ uniformly close. Approximating the finitely many coefficients of $q_0$ by rational numbers gives $q\in\mathbb Q[x]$ with the same approximation to any prescribed tolerance. Since the finitely many derivatives of $\chi_n$ are bounded on $I$, the product rule makes $p_M(\chi_n(q-\varphi))$ arbitrarily small. Thus $\chi_nq\in D_I$ approximates $\chi_n\varphi$ in $p_M$. [F2, F3, F5, algebra, choose]

2.1 The set $\{\chi_nq:n\in\mathbb N,\ n>2/(b-a),\ q\in\mathbb Q[x]\}$ is countable. Given a metric neighborhood of $\varphi\in D_I$, the summable metric weights reduce it to finitely many seminorms, bounded by $p_M$ for the largest index. Choose $n$ in step 1.1 so that $p_M(\varphi-\chi_n\varphi)$ is less than half the target tolerance, then choose $q$ in step 1.2 so that $p_M(\chi_n\varphi-\chi_nq)$ is less than the other half. The triangle inequality places $\chi_nq$ in the neighborhood. Hence this countable set is dense. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, choose] ∎

## Definition

For an integer $n\ge1$, a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, and an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, put $\mathcal D_K=\{\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq K\}$, using [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. For integers $m\ge0$ set

$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in K}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|,\qquad d(\varphi,\psi)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty2^{-m-1}\min(1,p_m(\varphi-\psi)).$$

The topology is generated by the seminorms $p_m$: neighborhoods at zero contain finite intersections of $p_m<\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$. Derivatives are continuous on $K$, so these suprema are finite; for $K=\varnothing$ all suprema are defined as zero and $\mathcal D_K=\{0\}$. For nonempty $K$, $p_0$ separates functions because all functions vanish off $K$. These are increasing seminorms and the displayed series converges since its terms are at most $2^{-m-1}$.

The term **fixed-support Fréchet space** refers to this topology and metric. Their agreement and completeness are established by the registered justifier [[lem-fixed-support-test-function-spaces-are-complete]], rather than included as unproved consequences of the name. If $K$ has empty interior, every test supported in $K$ is zero: a nonzero continuous value would have a neighborhood of nonzero values inside $K$.

## Statement

For $n\ge1$, there exists $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $|x|\le1$, and $\chi=0$ on $|x|\ge2$. For $R>0$, $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ satisfies $\partial^\beta\chi_R(x)=R^{-|\beta|}(\partial^\beta\chi)(x/R)$. The construction requires no choice.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $n\ge1$ and multi-indices as in [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]].

[F1] Exponentials dominate fixed powers at positive infinity ([[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]]).

[F2] The total chain rule holds ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[F3] Closed bounded subsets of Euclidean space are compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[F4] The exponential is smooth with derivative equal to itself ([[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]), and $e^u>0$, $e^{-u}=1/e^u$ for every real $u$ ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]).

[F5] The scalar sum, product and quotient rules hold; in particular $(1/g)'=-g'/g^2$ wherever $g\ne0$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F6] Sums and products of continuous scalar functions are continuous, as are quotients on the domain of a nonvanishing denominator ([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Define $a(t)=e^{-1/t}$ for $t>0$ and $a(t)=0$ for $t\le0$. On $t>0$, put $s=1/t$. The quotient rule [F5] applied to $1/t$ gives $s'=-1/t^2=-s^2$, while [F2] and [F4] give $(e^{-s})'=-e^{-s}$ as a function of $s$. Thus the product and chain rules give $$\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(P_k(s)e^{-s}\bigr)=\bigl(P_k'(s)-P_k(s)\bigr)e^{-s}(-s^2)=s^2\bigl(P_k(s)-P_k'(s)\bigr)e^{-s}.$$ Starting at $P_0=1$, this proves $a^{(k)}(t)=P_k(s)e^{-s}$ with the polynomial recurrence $P_{k+1}(s)=s^2(P_k(s)-P_k'(s))$. By [F1], both $P_k(s)e^{-s}$ and $sP_k(s)e^{-s}$ tend to zero as $s\to\infty$. Extending each derivative by zero to $t\le0$ is therefore continuous; its difference quotient at zero also tends to zero. Induction proves $a\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with every derivative zero at zero. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, algebra, induction]

2.1 Set $\sigma(t)=a(t)/(a(t)+a(1-t))$. For $t\le0$, the second summand in the denominator is positive; for $t\ge1$, the first is positive; for $0<t<1$, both are positive. Write $g(t)=a(t)+a(1-t)$, which is smooth by step 1.1 and the sum and chain rules. Since $g>0$, [F6] makes $q=1/g$ continuous, and [F5] gives $q'=-g'q^2$. For every $k\ge0$, finite iteration of the product rule [F5] and continuity of products [F6] shows that products of $C^k$ functions are $C^k$. If $q\in C^k$, the displayed derivative is therefore $C^k$ because $g'$ is smooth; hence $q\in C^{k+1}$. Starting with $C^0$, induction proves $q\in C^\infty$ and then $\sigma=aq\in C^\infty$. Thus $0\le\sigma\le1$,  and $\sigma=0$ on $t\le0$, $\sigma=1$ on $t\ge1$. Define $\chi(x)=\sigma((4-|x|^2)/3)$. Repeated [F2] proves smoothness, and the two constant regions give the claimed unit and zero regions, including their boundaries. Its closed support lies in the closed radius-two ball and is compact by [F3]. [step 1.1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, induction]

3.1 Differentiating $\chi(x/R)$ once in coordinate $j$ gives $R^{-1}(\partial_j\chi)(x/R)$. Iterating this identity in the prescribed multi-index order gives the asserted factor, including $\beta=0$. No selection was made in any construction. [step 2.1, F2, given] ∎

## Statement

For $a\le b$, every continuous real function on $[a,b]$ is a uniform limit of polynomials.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** $f\in C([a,b],\mathbb R)$ and $\varepsilon>0$.

[L1] Polynomials are uniformly dense on $[0,1]$ ([[cor-weierstrass-approximation-on-the-unit-interval]]).

**Proof technique:** direct.

## Statement

Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the closed interval between $c$ and $x$, and define
$P_n(t)=\sum_{j=0}^n f^{(j)}(c)(t-c)^j/j!$. If $x\ne c$, there is a point
$\xi$ strictly between $c$ and $x$ such that
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}(x-c)^{n+1}.
$$
For $x=c$, the remainder is zero.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $n\ge0$, points $c,x$ in an open interval on which $f$ is
$C^{n+1}$ as defined in
[[def-continuity-and-derivative-on-real-interval]], the power rule in
[[lem-derivative-algebra-and-chain-rules]], and the closed-interval mean value
theorem [[lem-mean-value-theorem-on-closed-interval]].

[L1] [[lem-mean-value-theorem-on-closed-interval]]: a continuous function on
$[u,v]$ differentiable on $(u,v)$ has a point $w\in(u,v)$ with
$g(v)-g(u)=g'(w)(v-u)$.

[L2] [[lem-derivative-algebra-and-chain-rules]]: the chain rule holds and
$t^m$ has derivative $mt^{m-1}$ for each integer $m\ge1$, hence
$(t-c)^m$ has derivative $m(t-c)^{m-1}$.

## Proof

1.1 Fix $x\ne c$ and set $A=(f(x)-P_n(x))/(x-c)^{n+1}$ and $g(t)=f(t)-P_n(t)-A(t-c)^{n+1}$ on the interval between $c$ and $x$. Then $g(c)=g(x)=0$ and $g^{(j)}(c)=0$ for each $1\le j\le n$, because the Taylor polynomial matches those derivatives at $c$ by [L2] and the last term has a zero of order $n+1$. [given, L2, construct, algebra]

2.1 By [L1] applied to $g$ on the interval with endpoints $c,x$, there is a point $z_1$ strictly between them with $g'(z_1)=0$. If $n\ge1$, also $g'(c)=0$, so [L1] applied to $g'$ between $c$ and $z_1$ gives $z_2$ between them with $g''(z_2)=0$. Inductively, for each $j\le n$ the zeros $g^{(j)}(c)=0$ and $g^{(j)}(z_j)=0$ give a point $z_{j+1}$ between them with $g^{(j+1)}(z_{j+1})=0$. The last point is the required $\xi$; when $n=0$, take $\xi=z_1$. [step 1.1, L1, induction]

3.1 Since $P_n^{(n+1)}=0$ and the $(n+1)$st derivative of $A(t-c)^{n+1}$ is $A(n+1)!$, the equation $g^{(n+1)}(\xi)=0$ gives $A=f^{(n+1)}(\xi)/(n+1)!$ by [L2]. Substituting the definition of $A$ proves the formula. At $x=c$, $P_n(c)=f(c)$ directly. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $a,b$ lie in an open interval $J$, and let $f$ be continuously
differentiable on $J$. Then
$$
\int_a^b f'(t)\,dt=f(b)-f(a).
$$
If $f,g$ are continuously differentiable on $J$, then
$$\int_a^b f(t)g'(t)\,dt =f(b)g(b)-f(a)g(a)-\int_a^b f'(t)g(t)\,dt.$$
Both identities hold for oriented endpoints.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The difference-quotient definition of derivative, the local
oriented integral of continuous functions, linearity of that integral, the
product rule, and the closed-interval mean value theorem.

[F1] [[def-continuity-and-derivative-on-real-interval]]: continuous
differentiability on an open interval includes existence and continuity of
the derivative.

[L1] [[lem-continuous-functions-riemann-integrable]]: for continuous $h$,
$H(x)=\int_a^x h(t)\,dt$ is defined and $H'(x)=h(x)$; the integral is
additive and oriented.

[L2] [[lem-riemann-integral-linearity]]: the integral of a sum is the sum of
the integrals.

[L3] [[lem-derivative-algebra-and-chain-rules]]: differentiability implies
continuity and $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$.

[L4] [[lem-mean-value-theorem-on-closed-interval]]: a continuous function on
$[a,b]$ differentiable on $(a,b)$ satisfies the mean value theorem.

## Proof

1.1 Assume first $a<b$ and let $H(x)=\int_a^x f'(t)\,dt$. By [L1], $H'(x)=f'(x)$ on an open interval containing $[a,b]$, and $H(a)=0$. By [L3], $H$ is continuous there. Thus $q=f-H$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $q'=0$. Applying [L4] gives $q(b)-q(a)=0$, so $f(b)-H(b)=f(a)$. Rearranging proves the first identity. [given, F1, L1, L3, L4, construct, algebra]

1.2 For $a=b$ the first identity is $0=0$; reversing endpoints proves it for $a>b$. [L1, algebra]

2.1 Assume $a<b$. By [L3], $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$. These terms are continuous: for continuous $u,v$, $$|u(t)v(t)-u(t_0)v(t_0)| \le |u(t)|\,|v(t)-v(t_0)|+|v(t_0)|\,|u(t)-u(t_0)|,$$ and continuity of $u$ bounds $|u(t)|$ near $t_0$. Thus $fg$ is continuously differentiable. Apply step 1.1 to $fg$ and then [L2]: $$f(b)g(b)-f(a)g(a)=\int_a^b(f'g+fg') =\int_a^b f'g+\int_a^b fg'.$$ Rearranging gives the second identity. For $a=b$ both sides are zero, and for $a>b$ reverse endpoints using [L1]. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L1, L2, L3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and $a\le b$, then $f$ is bounded and
attains both a maximum and a minimum on $[a,b]$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A Dedekind-complete ordered field, $a\le b$, and continuity as in
[[def-continuity-and-derivative-on-real-interval]].

[L1] [[lem-closed-interval-compactness-from-completeness]]: every relative open
cover of a nondegenerate closed interval has a finite subcover.

[L2] [[lem-archimedean-property-from-completeness]]: the natural numbers are
unbounded above.

[L3] [[def-continuity-and-derivative-on-real-interval]]: continuity is the
relative epsilon-delta condition on $[a,b]$.

[A1] [[def-complete-ordered-real-field]]: every nonempty bounded-above subset
of the field has a least upper bound.

[L4] [[lem-real-and-complex-modulus-rules]]: real absolute value satisfies
$|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$.

## Proof

1.1 If $a=b$, the singleton range consists only of $f(a)$, so the conclusion holds. Suppose $a<b$. For each natural $n\ge1$, put $U_n=\{x\in[a,b]: |f(x)|<n\}$. These sets cover $[a,b]$ by [L2]. Each is relatively open: at any $x\in U_n$, the margin $n-|f(x)|>0$ and [L3] gives a neighborhood where $|f(t)-f(x)|$ is smaller than that margin; [L4] then gives $|f(t)|<n$. By [L1] a finite subcollection covers; taking its largest index shows $|f|$ is bounded. Consequently $M=\sup f([a,b])$ exists by [A1]. [given, L1, L2, L3, L4, A1, construct]

2.1 If $M$ is not attained, for every $n\ge1$ define $V_n=\{x\in[a,b]: f(x)<M-1/n\}$. For each $x$, $M-f(x)>0$; by [L2] choose $n$ with $1/n<M-f(x)$, so the $V_n$ cover. Each $V_n$ is relatively open by [L3] and the positive margin $M-1/n-f(x)$. A finite subcover and its largest index $N$ imply $f(x)<M-1/N$ for all $x$, making $M-1/N$ an upper bound for $f([a,b])$. This contradicts that $M$ is the least upper bound. Thus the maximum is attained. [step 1.1, L2, L3, A1, choose]

3.1 The function $-f$ is continuous because $|(-f(t))-(-f(x))|=|f(t)-f(x)|$. Applying steps 1.1 and 2.1 to $-f$, its attained maximum is the attained minimum of $f$. [step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Differentiability by the difference-quotient definition in
[[def-continuity-and-derivative-on-real-interval]] and the real modulus rules
[[lem-real-and-complex-modulus-rules]].

[F1] [[def-continuity-and-derivative-on-real-interval]]: $f'(c)$ is the
finite limit of $(f(c+h)-f(c))/h$ as $h\to0$, $h\ne0$.

[L1] [[lem-real-and-complex-modulus-rules]]: $|xy|=|x||y|$ for real $x,y$.

## Proof

1.1 If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, write $f(c+h)-f(c)=h q(h)$, where $q(h)\to f'(c)$. Then $q$ is bounded for sufficiently small $h$, so $|f(c+h)-f(c)|\le|h||q(h)|\to0$. Thus $f$ is continuous at $c$. [F1, L1, algebra]

2.1 The sum difference quotient is the sum of the two difference quotients, so it tends to $f'(c)+g'(c)$. For the product, use $$\frac{f(c+h)g(c+h)-f(c)g(c)}h =f(c+h)\frac{g(c+h)-g(c)}h+g(c)\frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}h.$$ By step 1.1, $f(c+h)\to f(c)$; taking limits gives the product rule. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 By step 1.1, $g$ is continuous at $c$. Since $g(c)\ne0$, $g(c+h)\ne0$ for sufficiently small $h$. Algebra gives $$\frac{f(c+h)/g(c+h)-f(c)/g(c)}h =\frac{g(c)(f(c+h)-f(c))/h-f(c)(g(c+h)-g(c))/h} {g(c+h)g(c)}.$$ The denominator tends to $g(c)^2\ne0$ and the numerator tends to $g(c)f'(c)-f(c)g'(c)$, proving the quotient rule. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 Put $y=f(c)$ and $\Delta(h)=f(c+h)-y$. Step 1.1 gives $\Delta(h)\to0$, and [F1] gives $\Delta(h)/h\to f'(c)$. Differentiability of $g$ at $y$ means $g(y+u)-g(y)=g'(y)u+u\epsilon(u)$ for $u\ne0$, where $\epsilon(u)\to0$; set $\epsilon(0)=0$. Then $$\frac{g(f(c+h))-g(f(c))}h =g'(y)\frac{\Delta(h)}h+\epsilon(\Delta(h))\frac{\Delta(h)}h.$$ The first term tends to $g'(y)f'(c)$; the second tends to zero because $\epsilon(\Delta(h))\to0$ and $\Delta(h)/h$ is bounded. This proves the chain rule, including increments with $\Delta(h)=0$. [F1, step 1.1, L1, algebra]

3.1 The case $m=1$ is the derivative of the identity function, whose quotient is exactly $1$. Suppose $(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$. Since $x^{m+1}=x\cdot x^m$, the product rule in step 2.1 gives $(x^{m+1})'=x^m+x(mx^{m-1})=(m+1)x^m$. Induction proves the power rule for all $m\ge1$. [step 2.1, algebra, induction] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $T$ be a distribution on the connected open set $\mathbb R$. Test functions are complex-valued and distributions are complex-linear; here, **real distribution** means that $\langle T,\psi\rangle\in\mathbb R$ for every real-valued test function $\psi$. If $T$ is a real distribution and its $(n+1)$st distributional derivative is zero, then there is a real algebraic polynomial $p$ of degree at most $n$ whose regular distribution equals $T$.

## Statement references

[Dyatlov, Lecture Notes for 18.155, distributions with vanishing derivative](https://math.mit.edu/~dyatlov/18.155/155-notes.pdf)

[Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I, Chapter 2](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-642-61497-2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $n\in\mathbb N_0$, and a real distribution $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R)$ with $D^{n+1}T=0$.

[F1] A distribution on a connected open set whose first derivative vanishes is a constant regular distribution, under Countable Choice ([[thm-a-distribution-with-zero-derivatives-on-a-connected-open-set-is-constant]]).

[F2] The distributional derivative acts by signed differentiation of test functions; derivatives preserve realness because derivatives of real-valued tests are real-valued ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

[F3] A smooth regular distribution differentiates to the regular distribution of its classical derivative, under Countable Choice ([[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]).

[F4] The formal derivative of $x^n/n!$ is $x^{n-1}/(n-1)!$ for $n\ge1$, and its $n$th derivative is $1$ ([[def-formal-derivative-of-a-polynomial]]).

[A1] Countable Choice means every sequence of nonempty sets has a function choosing one element from each ([[def-countable-choice]]); it is assumed by the supplied regular-distribution derivative theorem.

[F5] A compact subset of an open set admits a nonnegative smooth cutoff equal to one near it; for $\{0\}\subset\mathbb R$ this gives a real test function with positive finite integral (positivity follows from the positive measure of an interval), which can be normalized to have integral one ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

## Proof

1.1 Base case $n=0$: the hypothesis is $DT=0$, so [F1] gives a constant regular distribution with some value $c\in\mathbb C$. Choose a real test function $\eta$ with integral one by [F5]. Since $c=\langle T,\eta\rangle$ and $T$ is real, $c\in\mathbb R$. Thus $T$ is represented by a real polynomial of degree at most zero. [given, F1, F5, A1, base]

1.2 Inductive step: let $n\ge1$ and assume the result for $n-1$. The distribution $S=D^nT$ satisfies $DS=D^{n+1}T=0$ and is real by [F2]. By [F1], $S$ is the constant distribution with some value $c\in\mathbb C$. Choose a real test function $\eta$ with integral one by [F5]. Since $c=\langle S,\eta\rangle$ and $S$ is real, $c\in\mathbb R$. [given, F1, F2, F5, A1, IH]

2.1 The smooth polynomial $q(x)=c x^n/n!$ has $D^nq=c$ as a regular distribution by [F3] and [F4]. Thus $U=T-q$ satisfies $D^nU=0$. The induction hypothesis applied with index $n-1$ gives a polynomial $r$ of degree at most $n-1$ whose regular distribution is $U$. [step 1.2, F3, F4, A1, IH]

3.1 The polynomial $p=q+r$ has degree at most $n$ and its regular distribution is $T$, since regular distributions and distributional derivatives are linear. This completes the induction. [step 2.1, algebra, discharge-induction] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue regular-distribution convention. If $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is nonempty, open and connected and $\partial_j u=0$ for every $1\le j\le n$, then there is a unique $c\in\mathbb C$ such that $u(\psi)=c\int\psi$ for every test. Conversely every constant regular distribution has zero first derivatives. On a disconnected open set constants may differ on different connected components.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] Smooth local convolutions satisfy $\partial_j(u*\rho_\varepsilon)=(\partial_j u)*\rho_\varepsilon$ ([[thm-convolution-with-a-test-function-is-smooth]]).

[F2] Unit-mass mollifications converge locally in distribution pairings under Countable Choice ([[thm-mollifier-approximation-in-distributions]]).

[F3] A compact ball admits a nonnegative smooth compact cutoff, so a nonzero such bump inside any open ball can be normalized by its positive finite integral ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]).

[F4] The mean-value inequality for $\mathbb C=\mathbb R^2$ implies that a smooth function with zero gradient is constant on a ball ([[thm-mean-value-inequality]]).

[F5] Distributions equal on an open cover are equal globally ([[thm-distributions-form-a-sheaf]]).

[F6] Classical derivatives of smooth regular distributions agree with distribution derivatives under Countable Choice ([[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]). We assume [[def-countable-choice]] for F2 and this regular interpretation.

## Proof

**Given:** the vanishing first derivatives and the stated choice assumption.

1.1 Take any open ball $B$ with compact closure in $\Omega$. For all sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, F1 gives a smooth mollification on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ with every first derivative zero. Along the segment between any two points of $B$, the chain rule gives derivative zero; F4 with bound zero makes their values equal. Denote this value by $c_\varepsilon$. [given, F1, F2, F4]

2.1 Choose $\eta\in\mathcal D(B)$ with $\int\eta=1$ using F3. Then F2 gives $c_\varepsilon=\int (u*\rho_\varepsilon)\eta\to u(\eta)=c_B$. For every $\psi\in\mathcal D(B)$, F2 therefore gives $u(\psi)=\lim c_\varepsilon\int\psi=c_B\int\psi$. A unit-integral test also shows uniqueness of this constant on $B$. [step 1.1, F2, F3]

3.1 If two such balls overlap, their intersection contains an open ball and hence a unit-integral test by F3. Evaluation on that test proves that their constants agree. Consequently there is a well-defined locally constant function $c(x)$ on $\Omega$, whose value is the unique constant of any sufficiently small ball about $x$. For a fixed $x_0$, the set $\{x:c(x)=c(x_0)\}$ and its complement are open. It is nonempty, so connectedness forces the complement empty. F5 applied to the ball cover yields $u=c(x_0)$ as a regular distribution. A unit-integral test anywhere proves uniqueness. [step 2.1, given, F3, F5]

4.1 F6 proves the converse, since the classical first derivatives of a constant vanish. In any open subset of Euclidean space each connected component is open: a ball about a point is connected and belongs to its component. Applying the preceding argument in each component gives independent constants. Conversely such a componentwise constant function is locally constant, hence smooth, and F6 gives zero derivatives. On the empty domain the sole distribution is zero but its representing constant is not unique; this explains the nonempty hypothesis. Countable Choice is inherited only from the integral mollification and regular-derivative clauses, not from the overlap argument. $\square$ [step 3.1, F6]

## Definition

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

## Statement

Distributional derivatives satisfy $\partial^\alpha\partial^\beta u=\partial^{\alpha+\beta}u$ and are continuous linear maps on $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ for both the weak and strong distribution topologies. These claims hold in ZF. Assuming Countable Choice for the cited Riemann-to-Lebesgue comparison, if $f\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ and $|\alpha|\le k$, then $\partial^\alpha u_f=u_{\partial^\alpha f}$. In particular distributional differentiation extends classical smooth differentiation.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] Derivatives are signed transposes of test derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

[F2] Weak seminorms test one function, and strong seminorms test bounded sets ([[def-weak-and-strong-topologies-on-distributions]]).

[F3] Test differentiation is continuous and preserves compact supports with $p_m(\partial^\alpha\varphi)\le p_{m+|\alpha|}(\varphi)$ ([[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]).

[F4] Smooth mixed partials commute ([[thm-symmetry-of-higher-mixed-partials]]).

[F5] Regular functionals pair by the bilinear Lebesgue integral ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]).

[F6] Compact sets admit smooth compact cutoffs equal to one near them ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]).

[F7] One-dimensional integration by parts holds when the factors and their derivatives are continuous on a closed interval ([[thm-integration-by-parts]]).

[F8] For Riemann-integrable functions on boxes with integrable sections, iterated and multiple Riemann integrals agree ([[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]]).

[F9] Under Countable Choice, a bounded Borel Riemann-integrable real function on a nondegenerate box has the same Lebesgue integral ([[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]]).

[F10] Countable Choice, needed only for the classical-compatibility clause below, is [[def-countable-choice]].

## Proof

**Given:** a distribution $u$ and multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$.

1.1 Evaluating consecutive derivatives on a test gives $(-1)^{|\alpha|+|\beta|}u(\partial^\beta\partial^\alpha\varphi)$. By F4 this is $(-1)^{|\alpha+\beta|}u(\partial^{\alpha+\beta}\varphi)$, which is $\partial^{\alpha+\beta}u(\varphi)$ by F1. Linearity follows from the same formula. [given, F1, F4]

2.1 For a single test $\varphi$, the weak seminorm of $\partial^\alpha u$ equals $|u(\partial^\alpha\varphi)|$, a weak seminorm of $u$. For a bounded test set $B$, the set $\partial^\alpha B$ is bounded: any zero-neighborhood has a zero-neighborhood inverse image under the continuous linear test derivative of F3, and absorption of $B$ by that inverse image gives absorption of its image. Hence $p_B(\partial^\alpha u)=p_{\partial^\alpha B}(u)$, a strong seminorm. These equalities prove continuity in both topologies, including for nets, without choice. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3]

3.1 Now assume F10 and $f\in C^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)$, and fix a test $\varphi$. Use F6 to choose $\chi=1$ near $\operatorname{supp}\varphi$ with compact support in $\Omega$. Extend $g=\chi f$ by zero to $\mathbb R^n$; it is $C^1$ because it vanishes near the complement of $\Omega$. Choose a nondegenerate box containing the supports of $g$ and $\varphi$ in its interior. On each coordinate segment F7 gives $\int g\partial_i\varphi=-\int(\partial_i g)\varphi$, because $\varphi$ is zero at both endpoints. For complex functions expand into real and imaginary parts and apply the real identity to the four products. All integrands and sections are continuous on compact boxes and are Riemann integrable: uniform continuity makes their oscillation Darboux sums arbitrarily small on sufficiently fine uniform grids. For $n>1$, F8 integrates the one-coordinate identity over the remaining coordinates; for $n=1$ this is already the required identity. F9 componentwise converts the two multiple Riemann integrals to Lebesgue integrals. Near the test support $g=f$ and $\partial_i g=\partial_i f$, so the resulting equality is $-\int_\Omega f\partial_i\varphi=\int_\Omega(\partial_i f)\varphi$. [step 2.1, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10]

4.1 Continuous functions and their continuous derivatives are locally integrable by compact boundedness, and their regular functionals are continuous since their absolute pairings are bounded by $\int_K|f|\,p_0$ on each fixed support (or directly by the global $Q_0$ seminorm on that stage). F5 and step 3.1 therefore give $\partial_i u_f=u_{\partial_i f}$. Iterating this identity through at most $k$ derivatives for $f\in C^k$, and using step 1.1, proves the classical-compatibility formula. Degree zero is the identity. Zero functions and the empty domain give zero distributions. The additional axiom enters only through the integral comparison in the classical argument; the algebra and dual continuity remain choice-free. $\square$ [step 3.1, step 1.1, F1, F5]

## Definition

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $f=\sum_{i\ge0}a_i x^i\in R[x]$. Its **formal derivative** is

$$ f':=\sum_{i\ge1} i a_i x^{i-1}. $$

Here $i a_i$ means the sum of $i$ copies of $a_i$ in the additive group of $R$. Equivalently, the coefficient of $x^n$ in $f'$ is $(n+1)a_{n+1}$. The sequence defining $f'$ has finite support because the coefficient sequence of $f$ does ([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]). This is an algebraic operation and does not use a limit.

## Statement

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The explicit smooth cutoff $b$ equals one on the closed unit ball, vanishes outside the radius-two ball, and satisfies $0\le b\le1$; translated dilates have the stated derivative scaling ([[lem-schwartz-cutoffs-from-the-standard-smooth-step]]).

[F2] Smoothness and multi-index notation are as in [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], applied componentwise.

## Proof

**Given:** the compact set and open set of the first assertion; an open cover $\mathcal U$ of $\Omega$ for the second.

1.1 For each point of $K$, there is a rational center $q$ and positive rational $r$ such that the point belongs to $B(q,r)$ and $\overline B(q,2r)\subseteq\Omega$. These inner balls cover $K$, so a finite list suffices by compactness. Put $b_j(x)=b((x-q_j)/r_j)$ and $\chi=1-\prod_j(1-b_j)$. Then $\chi$ is smooth, lies in $[0,1]$, equals one on the union of the inner balls, and has support in the finite union of the compact outer balls inside $\Omega$. For $K=\varnothing$ take the empty product and $\chi=0$. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 For nonempty $\Omega$, set $K_j=\{x:|x|\le j,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega)\ge1/j\}$ for $j\ge1$, interpreting distance to the empty set as infinity; set $K_0=K_{-1}=\varnothing$. These are compact subsets of $\Omega$, $K_j\subseteq\operatorname{int}K_{j+1}$, and their interiors cover $\Omega$. Closedness follows from continuity of distance (its absolute difference is at most the distance of the two points), and boundedness gives compactness. The shell $H_j=K_j\setminus\operatorname{int}K_{j-1}$ is compact and lies in the open set $G_j=\operatorname{int}K_{j+1}\setminus K_{j-2}$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix an enumeration of rational center/radius pairs and a coding of finite lists by natural numbers. For each $j$, consider pairs with $\overline B(q,2r)\subseteq G_j$ and with this closed ball contained in some $U\in\mathcal U$. Their inner balls cover $H_j$: at any shell point openness of $G_j$ and of one cover member gives a sufficiently small ball, then a rational center and radius. Compactness gives a finite subcover. Select the least code of a finite list that covers $H_j$, taking the empty list for an empty shell. This is a specified function of $j$, not Countable Choice. [step 2.1, given]

4.1 Form the corresponding translated dilates $b_{j,k}$ of F1. Their supports lie in $G_j$, and each support lies in some cover member. This family is locally finite: a point has a neighborhood inside some $K_N$, and supports with $j\ge N+2$ miss $K_N$, while only finitely many balls occur at each of the finitely many earlier stages. Every point belongs to some shell, so $s=\sum_{j,k}b_{j,k}$ is everywhere positive. The sum is locally finite and smooth; hence $\eta_{j,k}=b_{j,k}/s$ are smooth, nonnegative, have compact support in the same outer balls, and sum to one. The double index is countable. For empty $\Omega$ use the empty family. These constructions choose no cover labels and no arbitrary sequence of witnesses. $\square$ [step 3.1, F1, F2]

    - title: "Kurt Hornik, Approximation Capabilities of Multilayer Feedforward Networks, §2"
      url: "https://web.njit.edu/~usman/courses/cs675_fall18/hornik-nn-1991.pdf"

## Statement

Let $\mu$ be a finite regular Borel measure on $\mathbb R^d$ concentrated on a compact set $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Form the real $L^p(\mu)$ space using the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Then restrictions to $K$ of real-valued compactly supported continuous functions on $\mathbb R^d$ are dense in $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$.

## Statement references

[Leshno et al., proof of Theorem 1, Lp approximation step](https://archive.nyu.edu/bitstream/2451/14329/1/IS-92-13.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite regular Borel measure $\mu$ concentrated on compact $K$, an exponent $1\le p<\infty$, a real-valued Borel class $[f]\in L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$, and $\varepsilon>0$.

[F1] $L^p(\mu)$ consists of measurable functions with finite $\left(\int|f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p}$, with functions identified when equal $\mu$-almost everywhere ([[def-calligraphic-l-p-on-a-measure-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

[F2] A measure is a nonnegative countably additive set function on a sigma-algebra, and regularity here means Borel sets can be approximated from inside by compact sets and outside by open sets with arbitrarily small measure excess ([[def-measure]]); regularity is the hypothesis on $\mu$.

[F3] If $F$ is compact and $O$ is open with $F\subset O$, there is a smooth compactly supported cutoff $\psi$ with $0\le\psi\le1$, $\psi=1$ near $F$, and $\operatorname{supp}\psi\subset O$ ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]).

[F4] Dominated convergence applies to $|f-f_M|^p\le|f|^p$ and $f_M\to f$ almost everywhere ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[F5] For $1\le p<\infty$, the quotient $L^p(\mu)$ has a norm whose triangle inequality is Minkowski's inequality ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

## Proof

1.1 Choose a measurable representative $f$ of $[f]$. Truncate it to $f_M=\max(-M,\min(f,M))$. Since $|f-f_M|^p\le |f|^p$ and $f_M\to f$ pointwise wherever $f$ is finite, [F4] makes $\|f-f_M\|_{L^p(\mu)}<\varepsilon/2$ for some large $M$. Partition $[-M,M]$ into finitely many intervals of length at most $\delta$ and replace each value of $f_M$ by a fixed endpoint of its interval. If $\mu(K)>0$, choose $\delta$ with $\delta\mu(K)^{1/p}<\varepsilon/2$; if $\mu(K)=0$, any $\delta>0$ suffices. The resulting finite-valued Borel simple function $s$ satisfies $|s-f_M|\le\delta$ pointwise, so $\|s-f_M\|_{L^p(\mu)}\le\delta\,\mu(K)^{1/p}$. By [F5] and the triangle inequality, $\|s-f\|_{L^p(\mu)}<\varepsilon$. Since $\mu$ is concentrated on $K$, replace $s$ by $\mathbf1_Ks$: this finite Borel simple function represents the same class and admits a representation with every set $E_j\subseteq K$. Thus such supported simple functions are dense in $L^p(\mu)$. [given, F1, F4, F5, choose]

2.1 Write such a simple function as $s=\sum_{j=1}^N c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$ with Borel $E_j\subseteq K$. For any $\eta>0$, regularity [F2] gives compact $F_j\subseteq E_j$ and open $O_j\supseteq E_j$ with $\mu(O_j\setminus F_j)<\eta$. By [F3] choose $\psi_j\in C_c^\infty(O_j)$ with $0\le\psi_j\le1$ and $\psi_j=1$ on $F_j$. Outside $O_j\setminus F_j$ the functions $\psi_j$ and $\mathbf1_{E_j}$ agree; everywhere their difference has magnitude at most one. Therefore $\|\psi_j-\mathbf1_{E_j}\|_{L^p(\mu)}^p\le\mu(O_j\setminus F_j)<\eta$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, choose]

3.1 The triangle inequality [F5] gives $\left\|\sum_{j=1}^N c_j\psi_j-s\right\|_{L^p(\mu)}\le\sum_{j=1}^N|c_j|\eta^{1/p}$. Choose $\eta$ small enough that this is below $\varepsilon/2$, and choose $s$ from step 1.1 within $\varepsilon/2$ of $f$. Then the compactly supported continuous function $\sum_jc_j\psi_j$ is within $\varepsilon$ of $f$ in $L^p(\mu)$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F5, choose] ∎

## Definition

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p$ be a real number with
$0<p<\infty$. Write $\mathcal M(X,\mu)$ for the measurable functions
$f:X\to\mathbb R$. For $f\in\mathcal M(X,\mu)$ define the extended-valued
$p$-functional

$$\|f\|_p:=\begin{cases}\left(\int |f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int |f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int |f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty.\end{cases}$$

The finite power uses [[def-real-power]], while the second clause avoids
applying real powers to the extended value $+\infty$. The integral is the
nonnegative Lebesgue integral of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

The class

$$\mathcal L^p(\mu):=\{f\in\mathcal M(X,\mu): \|f\|_p<\infty\}$$

is the measurable-function space used on this page before passing to
almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

For $1\le p<\infty$, the pointwise operations make $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ a real
vector space by
[[thm-calligraphic-l-p-and-l-infinity-are-vector-spaces-for-p-at-least-one]].

## Definition

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

## Definition

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For every integer $d\ge1$, if

$$P(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d}c_\alpha x_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots x_d^{\alpha_d},$$

is a nonzero real polynomial with finitely many nonzero coefficients, then its zero set $\{x\in\mathbb R^d:P(x)=0\}$ is Lebesgue measurable and has $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero.

## Statement references

[Leshno et al., proof of Theorem 1, polynomial-activation obstruction](https://archive.nyu.edu/bitstream/2451/14329/1/IS-92-13.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $d\ge1$, and a nonzero real polynomial $P$ in $d$ variables.

[F1] A nonzero univariate real polynomial has only finitely many distinct real roots ([[thm-nonzero-real-polynomial-has-at-most-degree-many-distinct-roots]]).

[F2] Tonelli's theorem computes the measure of a Borel set by integrating the measures of its coordinate sections ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F3] Product Lebesgue measure agrees with Euclidean Lebesgue measure on Borel sets ([[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]]).

[F4] Countable subsets of Euclidean space are Lebesgue null under Countable Choice, and Lebesgue measure is countably subadditive ([[prop-countable-subsets-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]], [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]).

[F5] Under Countable Choice every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^d$ is Lebesgue measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]).

[A1] Countable Choice means every sequence of nonempty sets has a function choosing one element from each ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

1.1 Base case $d=1$: [F1] makes the zero set finite, hence countable and null by [F4]. [given, F1, F4, A1, base]

1.2 Inductive step: let $d\ge2$ and assume the claim in dimension $d-1$. Write $P(x',t)=\sum_{j=0}^m Q_j(x')t^j$, where $x'\in\mathbb R^{d-1}$ and the highest coefficient $Q_m$ is a nonzero polynomial. By the induction hypothesis, $Z=\{x':Q_m(x')=0\}$ is null. For every $x'\notin Z$, the section $t\mapsto P(x',t)$ is a nonzero univariate polynomial, so its zero set is finite by [F1] and null by [F4]. [given, F1, F4, A1, IH]

2.1 Fix $R\ge1$. The set $\{(x',t)\in[-R,R]^d:P(x',t)=0\}$ is Borel because $P$ is continuous. Its section has measure at most $2R$ when $x'\in Z$ and measure zero otherwise. Tonelli [F2] shows that its product measure is zero, since $Z$ is null; [F3] identifies this with its Euclidean Lebesgue measure. [step 1.2, F2, F3, F5, A1]

3.1 The full zero set is the countable union of these Borel null intersections over integers $R\ge1$. Countable subadditivity [F4] makes it measurable and null. The base case and induction step prove the assertion for every $d\ge1$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, F4, F5, A1, discharge-induction] ∎

## Statement

A nonzero real polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct real roots. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]], [[lem-real-polynomial-factor-at-a-root]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonzero real polynomial of degree $n$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** induction.

1.1 At degree $0$ the polynomial is a nonzero constant and has no root. [base]

1.2 Assume the claim at degree $n$. [ih]

1.3 If a degree-$n+1$ polynomial has no root, its root count is already zero. Otherwise choose a root $a$ and write its actual coefficient list as $(c_0,\ldots,c_{n+1})$, with $c_{n+1}\ne0$. Use the explicit quotient construction in [[lem-real-polynomial-factor-at-a-root]]: its coefficient at $X^d$ is $\sum_{k=d+1}^{n+1}c_k a^{k-1-d}$ for $0\le d\le n$. The coefficient at $X^n$ is $c_{n+1}\ne0$, and there are no higher terms, so this particular formal quotient $q$ has degree exactly $n$. For any other root $b\ne a$, $0=p(b)=(b-a)q(b)$ and division by the nonzero real $b-a$ gives $q(b)=0$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 In the root case, the induction hypothesis in step 1.2 applied to the degree-$n$ quotient from step 1.3 gives at most $n$ distinct roots other than $a$, hence at most $n+1$ roots in all. The no-root case already satisfies the same bound. Induction proves the assertion at every degree. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, discharge-induction] ∎

## Statement

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Every at most countable subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-countable]]) is Lebesgue measurable with

$$\lambda_n(E) \;=\; 0,$$

so $E$ is a $\lambda_n$-null set ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).
In particular every singleton is null, and on the real line the set
$\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ of rational reals ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]) satisfies
$\lambda_1(\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}) = 0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $n \ge 1$, the Axiom of Countable Choice, and an at most countable set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

[L1] Every set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(R) = \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i)$, and this gives measure $0$ to all of them whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[L2] Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure on it ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

[F1] $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite ([[def-countable]]); a nonempty $A$ is at most countable if and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$ ([[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]]).

[F2] For a measure $\mu$ and measurable $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$, $\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k)$ ([[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]).

[F3] $\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$: the rationals are countably infinite ([[thm-rationals-countable]]), and $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ denotes the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$ under the canonical order-preserving field embedding ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]).

[F4] A measurable set $N\in\mathcal A$ is **$\mu$-null** if $\mu(N)=0$ ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]); a sigma-algebra is closed under countable unions ([[def-sigma-algebra]]).

[F5] $[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\}$ ([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 A singleton $\{x\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is the closed rectangle $[x,x]$, whose sides all satisfy $a_i = b_i = x_i$, so it is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(\{x\}) = 0$. [L1, F5]

1.2 The empty set is Lebesgue measurable with measure $0$. [L2, F4]

2.1 Let $E$ be nonempty and at most countable and fix a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to E$; then $E = \bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\{s(k)\}$ is a countable union of measurable sets, hence measurable, and countable subadditivity gives $\lambda_n(E) \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lambda_n(\{s(k)\}) = 0$. [step 1.1, L2, F1, F2, F4]

3.1 Steps 1.2 and 2.1 cover both cases, and $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a countably infinite subset of $\mathbb{R}$, so $\lambda_1(\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}) = 0$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, F3] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measure $\mu$ and a sequence $(E_k)$ of measurable sets.

[L1] A measure is countably additive on pairwise disjoint measurable sequences ([[def-measure]]).

[L2] If $A\subseteq B$ are measurable, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$ ([[prop-measure-monotonicity]]).

[L3] A nonnegative extended series is the supremum of its finite partial sums, beginning with the empty sum $0$ ([[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]).

[L4] Every nonempty subset of $\mathbb N$ has a least element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Define $F_k:=E_k\setminus\bigcup_{j<k}E_j$. Then every $F_k$ is measurable, the $F_k$ are pairwise disjoint, and $F_k\subseteq E_k$. [given]

1.2 The unions of the two sequences agree: if $x\in\bigcup_kE_k$, then the nonempty set $\{k:x\in E_k\}$ has a least member $r$, and the definition gives $x\in F_r$; the reverse inclusion follows from $F_k\subseteq E_k$. [given, L4]

2.1 Countable additivity, monotonicity, and the definition of a nonnegative series give $\mu(\bigcup_kE_k)=\sum_k\mu(F_k)\le\sum_k\mu(E_k)$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L1, L2, L3]

3.1 For $m\in\mathbb N$, apply step 2.1 to the sequence $E_0,\ldots,E_{m-1},\varnothing,\varnothing,\ldots$; its union and sum are the displayed finite union and finite sum, and when $m=0$ they are both empty and equal to $0$. [step 2.1, L1, L3] ∎

## Definition

Let $d\ge1$ and let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be an activation function. For a finite width $m\in\mathbb N_0$, output weights $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R$, input weights $w_1,\ldots,w_m\in\mathbb R^d$, hidden biases $b_1,\ldots,b_m\in\mathbb R$, and output bias $c\in\mathbb R$, the scalar single-hidden-layer realization is

$$N(x)=c+\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_j\sigma(w_j\cdot x+b_j),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

The family $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ consists of all such functions as $m$ and the real parameters vary; $m=0$ is allowed and gives constant functions. This is the scalar-output, one-hidden-layer specialization of a layered multilayer perceptron with linear output.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ and, for every real smooth test function $\varphi$ supported in $[-1,1]$, define

$$g_\varphi(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}\sigma(x-t)\varphi(t)\,dt. $$

If every $g_\varphi$ is a real polynomial, then there is one integer $N\in\mathbb N_0$ such that every $g_\varphi$ has degree at most $N$.

## Statement references

[Leshno et al., proof of Theorem 1, Baire-category common-degree step](https://archive.nyu.edu/bitstream/2451/14329/1/IS-92-13.pdf)

[Dyatlov, Lecture Notes for 18.155, fixed-support test-function spaces](https://math.mit.edu/~dyatlov/18.155/155-notes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ such that every displayed convolution is a polynomial.

[F1] Each $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ is measurable and essentially bounded on compact intervals, hence locally integrable; its regular distribution is defined by integration and embeds into distributions under Countable Choice ([[def-activation-class-locally-essentially-bounded-ae-continuous]], [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

[F2] The complex fixed-support test-function space is complete; its real-valued subspace $X$ is closed because uniform limits of real-valued functions are real, and is therefore complete with the induced metric ([[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], [[lem-fixed-support-test-function-spaces-are-complete]]).

[F3] This fixed-support test-function space is separable ([[lem-fixed-support-test-function-space-is-separable]]).

[F4] A separable complete metric space is Baire in ZF ([[thm-separable-complete-metric-baire-in-zf]]).

[F5] Convolution of a distribution with a test function is smooth, differentiates by moving derivatives to the test function, and agrees with the displayed integral for the regular distribution of $\sigma$ ([[thm-convolution-with-a-test-function-is-smooth]], [[def-convolution-of-a-distribution-with-a-test-function]], [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]).

[F6] A differentiable real function with zero derivative on an interval is constant there, by the mean-value theorem ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

[A1] Countable Choice means every sequence of nonempty sets has a function choosing one element from each ([[def-countable-choice]]); it is assumed for the Lebesgue-integral realization of $\sigma$.

## Proof

1.1 Let $X=D_{[-1,1]}$ with its fixed-support Fréchet topology. For each $n\in\mathbb N_0$, set $E_n=\{\varphi\in X:g_\varphi^{(n+1)}(x)=0\text{ for every }x\in\mathbb R\}$. Linearity of convolution makes $E_n$ a linear subspace. For fixed $x$, its defining functional is continuous: on the compact interval $x-[-1,1]$, local essential boundedness of $\sigma$ gives a finite bound $M_x$, and $|g_{\varphi}^{(n+1)}(x)-g_{\psi}^{(n+1)}(x)|\le 2M_xp_{n+1}(\varphi-\psi)$. Thus $E_n$, an intersection of kernels of continuous functionals, is closed. [given, F1, F5, A1, algebra]

1.2 If a smooth function $g$ has $(n+1)$st derivative zero, [F6] first makes $g^{(n)}$ constant; subtracting its corresponding multiple of $x^n/n!$ leaves an $n$th derivative equal to zero. Repeating this argument down to order zero shows $g$ is a polynomial of degree at most $n$. Conversely every such polynomial has $(n+1)$st derivative zero. Thus the hypothesis gives $X=\bigcup_{n=0}^\infty E_n$. [given, F6, induction, algebra]

2.1 By [F2]–[F4], the Baire theorem applies to $X$. Therefore some closed subspace $E_N$ has nonempty interior; otherwise the closed sets $E_n$ would all be nowhere dense and their countable union could not equal $X$. A linear subspace with nonempty interior contains a neighborhood of zero, and scaling any vector into that neighborhood shows it is the whole space. Hence $E_N=X$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

3.1 Membership $E_N=X$ says $g_\varphi^{(N+1)}=0$ for every test function supported in $[-1,1]$. Repeated application of [F6] then makes every $g_\varphi$ a polynomial of degree at most $N$, as claimed. [step 2.1, F6] ∎

## Definition

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The regular functional is well-defined modulo almost-everywhere equality and satisfies $|u_f(\varphi)|\le\int_K|f|\,p_0(\varphi)$ on $\mathcal D_K$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]).

[F2] Compactwise finite-order bounds characterize distributions ([[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]).

[F3] A unit-mass smooth bump has rescalings $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$ ([[def-mollifier-family-generated-by-a-unit-mass-smooth-bump]]); these form an $L^1$ approximate identity under Countable Choice ([[prop-mollifier-families-are-l-one-approximate-identities]]).

[F4] Under Countable Choice, convolution by such an approximate identity converges to each $g\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)$ in $L^1$ ([[thm-l-one-approximate-identities-converge-in-l-p]], with $p=1$).

[F5] Smooth nonnegative compact cutoffs equal to one near a compact set exist ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]).

[F6] Strong seminorms are uniform pairings over bounded test sets, which have common compact support and bounded derivative suprema ([[def-weak-and-strong-topologies-on-distributions]]).

[F7] Dominated convergence gives $L^1$ convergence for almost-everywhere convergent functions under one integrable majorant ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[F8] The assumed choice principle is [[def-countable-choice]].

## Proof

**Given:** Countable Choice and a locally integrable function $f$ on $\Omega$.

1.1 F1 and F2 show $u_f$ is a distribution, with compactwise order at most zero; linearity of the integral gives linearity in the equivalence class of $f$. For a bounded test set $B$, take its common compact $K$ and finite $M_B=\sup_{\varphi\in B}p_0(\varphi)$. Then $p_B(u_f)\le M_B\int_K|f|$. Thus each strong seminorm of the image is bounded by a constant times a defining local $L^1$ seminorm, proving continuity, including for nets. If $M_B=0$, the left side is zero. [given, F1, F2, F6]

2.1 Suppose $u_f=0$, and fix a closed ball $H$ compactly inside $\Omega$. Take $\chi$ from F5 equal to one near $H$ and compactly supported in $\Omega$, and extend $g=\chi f$ by zero to $\mathbb R^n$; it is in $L^1$ by local integrability. Also use F5 to obtain a nonnegative smooth compact bump equal to one on a ball, and divide it by its positive finite integral to obtain $\rho$ of mass one. Fix $R$ containing its support. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, every $x\in H$ has $x-\operatorname{supp}\rho_\varepsilon$ inside the neighborhood where $\chi=1$: the compact $H$ has positive distance from that neighborhood's closed complement. Consequently [step 1.1, given, F3, F5] $$g*\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\int_\Omega f(y)\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy=u_f(\rho_\varepsilon(x-\cdot))=0.$$ The integrals are absolutely finite because $g\in L^1$ and the kernel is bounded; the reflected kernel is a test compactly supported in $\Omega$. [step 1.1, given, F3, F5]

3.1 By F3, F4 and F8, $\|g*\rho_\varepsilon-g\|_1\to0$. Since $g=f$ on $H$ and step 2.1 makes the convolution zero there, $\int_H|f|\le\|g*\rho_\varepsilon-g\|_1\to0$. Hence $f=0$ almost everywhere on $H$. The closed rational balls compactly inside $\Omega$ are countable and their interiors cover $\Omega$; applying this conclusion to each and taking the countable union of the null sets $\{x\in H:f(x)\ne0\}$ gives $f=0$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$. No family of cutoffs was selected simultaneously. Apply the same argument to $f-h$ for injectivity of the map on equivalence classes. [step 2.1, F3, F4, F8]

4.1 As a useful convergence consequence, if $f_j\to f$ almost everywhere and for every compact $K$ there is an integrable majorant of all $|f_j|$ on $K$, F7 gives $\int_K|f_j-f|\to0$. Step 1.1 then gives strong convergence $u_{f_j}\to u_f$. On the empty domain there is only the zero class and zero distribution, so injection and continuity still hold. $\square$ [step 3.1, step 1.1, F7]
