## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $F_{1,1}$ be the unit ball of $W^{1,\infty}((0,1);\mathbb R)$ under the maximum norm of the function and its weak derivative, using the Lipschitz representative on $[0,1]$. There is an absolute constant $C$ such that for every $f\in F_{1,1}$ and $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, an architecture depending on $f$ computes a ReLU approximation with uniform error at most $\varepsilon$, depth $6$ counting input and output layers, and at most $C/[\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon)]$ weights, connections, and computation units.

## Statement references

[Yarotsky, Theorem 2 and complete proof: adaptive depth-six Lipschitz approximation](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1610.01145)

[Sullivan, §5.3: target-dependent approximation architecture](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/index.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, a function class element $f\in W^{1,\infty}((0,1);\mathbb R)$ with $\|f\|_{W^{1,\infty}}\le1$, and $0<\varepsilon<1/2$.

[F1] The $W^{1,\infty}$ norm is $\max(\|f\|_{L^\infty},\|Df\|_{L^\infty})$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]), and under the Axiom of Choice every such class on an open bounded convex domain has a Lipschitz representative with constant at most $\|Df\|_{L^\infty}$ ([[thm-w-one-infinity-functions-have-lipschitz-representatives]]).

[F2] The Axiom of Choice implies Countable Choice ([[lem-ac-supplies-countable-and-dependent-choice-for-banach-integration]]).

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F3] ReLU networks use hidden ReLU units and affine outputs, and depth counts input and output layers ([[def-relu-network]]).

## Proof

1.1 By [A1] and [F2], the Countable Choice convention in [F1] holds. Choose the Lipschitz representative on $(0,1)$ and extend it uniquely to $[0,1]$: values along any sequence approaching an endpoint are Cauchy and any two such limits agree by the Lipschitz bound. The continuous representative satisfies $|f|\le1$ everywhere, since any interior value with modulus greater than $1$ would by continuity violate the almost-everywhere bound on an interval of positive measure. Let $T\ge1$ be an integer and let $f_1$ linearly interpolate $f$ at $t/T$, $0\le t\le T$. Then $f_1$ is $1$-Lipschitz, and $f_2=f-f_1$ vanishes at every grid endpoint and is $2$-Lipschitz. Indeed, both summands are $1$-Lipschitz. [given, F1, F2, A1, construct]

2.1 Let $m\ge1$ and let $\Gamma$ be the set of piecewise-linear functions on the grid $r/m$, $0\le r\le m$, with endpoint values zero and successive increments in $\{-2/m,0,2/m\}$. Thus $|\Gamma|\le3^m$. For each coarse interval $I_t=[t/T,(t+1)/T)$, rescale $g_t(y)=Tf_2((t+y)/T)$. This function is $2$-Lipschitz and vanishes at both endpoints. Quantize each node value down to the nearest multiple of $2/m$; adjacent quantized values differ by one of the three allowed increments. At a fraction $\theta$ of a grid subinterval, a $2$-Lipschitz function differs from its endpoint chord by at most $4\theta(1-\theta)/m\le1/m$; quantizing both endpoint values changes that chord by at most $2/m$. Hence some $\gamma_t\in\Gamma$ satisfies $\sup_{x\in I_t}|f_2(x)-T^{-1}\gamma_t(Tx-t)|\le3/(Tm)$. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Define the discontinuous selector $\chi(z)=z$ for $0\le z<1$ and $0$ otherwise. For $x\in[0,1)$, exactly the index $t$ with $x\in I_t$ has $\chi(Tx-t)=Tx-t$; all other terms vanish. Therefore $$\widetilde f_2(x)=\frac1T\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\gamma\!\left(\sum_{t:\gamma_t=\gamma}\chi(Tx-t)\right)$$ equals the local interpolant $T^{-1}\gamma_t(Tx-t)$ and has error at most $3/(Tm)$. If $s_{\gamma,r}$ is the slope of $\gamma$ on $[r/m,(r+1)/m]$, then its zero value at $0$ gives $$\gamma(z)=s_{\gamma,0}\rho(z)+\sum_{r=1}^{m-1}(s_{\gamma,r}-s_{\gamma,r-1})\rho(z-r/m),\qquad 0\le z\le1,$$ by matching the initial slope and each slope jump. This uses $m$ ReLU hinges. The cache is a depth-five mixed-gate network with $O(T+m3^m)$ units and weights: $T$ selector units, at most $3^m$ grouped sums, $m3^m$ ReLU hinge units, and an affine output. For the coarse interpolant, set $s_t=T(f((t+1)/T)-f(t/T))$ for $0\le t<T$; then $$f_1(x)=f(0)+s_0\rho(x)+\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}(s_t-s_{t-1})\rho(x-t/T)$$ on $[0,1]$. This slope-jump identity has $T$ ReLU units and one affine output, so $f_1$ is a depth-three ReLU network of size $O(T)$. [step 2.1, F3, construct, algebra]

4.1 Replace each discontinuous selector by $$\chi_\delta(z)=\rho(z)-\delta^{-1}\rho(z-(1-\delta))+(\delta^{-1}-1)\rho(z-1).$$ This continuous piecewise-linear function agrees with $\chi$ on $[0,1-\delta]$, decreases linearly to zero on $[1-\delta,1]$, and is zero outside $[0,1]$. Let $\varphi_\delta$ be the piecewise-linear tent that is zero outside $[0,1-\delta]$, rises from $0$ to $1$ on $[0,\delta]$, equals $1$ on $[\delta,1-2\delta]$, and falls to $0$ on $[1-2\delta,1-\delta]$. Its four slope jumps give a representation by at most four ReLU hinges as in step 3.1. Put $\Phi_\delta(x)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\varphi_\delta(Tx-t)$; this comb is a ReLU spline with $O(T)$ units and weights. Replacing the $T$ selectors by three ReLU units each and adding the comb keeps the cache size $O(T+m3^m)$ independently of $\delta$. [step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Let $\widetilde f_{2,\delta}$ be the cache network using $\chi_\delta$, and set $$f_{2,\delta}(x)=\rho(\widetilde f_{2,\delta}(x)+2\Phi_\delta(x)-1)-\rho(2\Phi_\delta(x)-1).$$ At most one selector is nonzero at any $x$, its value lies in $[0,1]$, and each rescaled $\gamma_t$ vanishes at both endpoints and is $2$-Lipschitz; hence $|\widetilde f_{2,\delta}(x)|\le1$. On each plateau where $\Phi_\delta=1$, the selector is unchanged and the gate outputs the cache. Where $\Phi_\delta=0$, the two ReLU terms cancel. On the transition strips $y\in[0,\delta]$ or $y\in[1-2\delta,1-\delta]$ in a coarse coordinate $y=Tx-t$, $\chi_\delta(y)=\chi(y)$, so the cache equals the continuous piecewise-linear spline $\widetilde f_2$ from step 3.1. For $0\le p\le1$, the map $a\mapsto\rho(a+2p-1)-\rho(2p-1)$ is $1$-Lipschitz and vanishes at $a=0$, hence its output has modulus at most $|a|$. Every point where $0<\Phi_\delta<1$ is within $2\delta/T$ of a coarse endpoint; both $f_2$ and $\widetilde f_2$ vanish there and are $2$-Lipschitz, so on those strips $|f_2-f_{2,\delta}|\le8\delta/T$. Where $\Phi_\delta=0$, $f_{2,\delta}=0$ and $|f_2|\le4\delta/T$, which is also within this bound. On plateaus the quantization error is at most $3/(Tm)$ by step 2.1. Thus $$\|f_2-f_{2,\delta}\|_\infty\le 8\delta/T+3/(Tm).$$ The two final ReLU preactivations absorb the former affine cache output, followed by a shared affine output, so depth increases from five to six; complexity remains $O(T+m3^m)$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, F3, algebra]

6.1 Choose $m=\lceil\tfrac12\log_3(1/\varepsilon)\rceil$, $T=\lceil6/(m\varepsilon)\rceil$, and $0<\delta\le\min\{1/4,\varepsilon T/16\}$. Then both error terms in step 5.1 are at most $\varepsilon/2$, while $T+m3^m\le C/[\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon)]$: here $T=O(1/(\varepsilon m))$, $3^m=O(\varepsilon^{-1/2})$, and $m\varepsilon^{-1/2}=O(1/(\varepsilon m))$ because $\varepsilon^{1/2}(\log(1/\varepsilon))^2$ is bounded on $(0,1/2)$. The sum $f_1+f_{2,\delta}$ is the required ReLU approximation. [step 3.1, step 5.1, algebra, choose] ∎



## Proof notes

The source's printed intermediate estimate for the cache uses $2/m$. This proof uses the directly verified conservative $3/m$ bound and chooses $T$ with a corresponding larger constant; the asymptotic rate is unchanged.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every integer $m\ge0$ and every continuous map $h:S^m\to\mathbb R^m$, there exists $x\in S^m$ with $h(x)=h(-x)$. Here $S^m$ is the Euclidean unit sphere in $\mathbb R^{m+1}$.

## Statement references

[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]

[[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $m\ge0$, and continuous $h:S^m\to\mathbb R^m$.

[F1] With mod-two coefficients, $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^{\infty})=\mathbb F_2[a]$, $|a|=1$. The standard inclusion $i_k:\mathbb{RP}^k\to\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}$ induces an isomorphism in degrees at most $k$ ([[lem-mod-two-cohomology-ring-of-infinite-real-projective-space]]).

[F2] The space $\mathbb{RP}^k$, the quotient of $S^k$ identifying $x$ and $-x$, is a nonempty finite CW complex of dimension $k$ ([[lem-real-projective-space-cellular-homology-and-pinch-map]]). Its cohomology vanishes in degrees greater than $k$ ([[lem-cohomology-of-a-finite-cw-complex-vanishes-above-its-dimension]]).

[F3] Homotopic continuous maps induce equal cohomology maps ([[thm-homotopic-maps-induce-equal-maps-in-singular-cohomology]]). Pullback is a unital ring homomorphism and respects composition ([[prop-cup-product-is-natural-unital-and-associative]]).

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is assumed through the cohomology suppliers [F1]–[F2]; the explicit maps below require no further choice.

## Proof

1.1 We first rule out a continuous odd map $g:S^m\to S^{m-1}$ for $m\ge1$. Such a map descends to $b:\mathbb{RP}^m\to\mathbb{RP}^{m-1}$, $b([x])=[g(x)]$. This is continuous by the quotient topology, since the composite with the sphere quotient is continuous and $g(-x)=-g(x)$. [given, construct]

2.1 In the coordinate subspace $\mathbb R^{m+1}\oplus\mathbb R^m\subset\mathbb R^{\infty}$, define $$H([x],t)=[\cos(\pi t/2)x,\ \sin(\pi t/2)g(x)],\qquad 0\le t\le1.$$ Its representing vector has norm one. Replacing $x$ by $-x$ negates the whole vector, so the projective point is independent of representative. Continuity can be checked on each chart where a chosen coordinate of $x$ is nonzero: choose the unit representative with that coordinate positive, which varies continuously in the ratios of the remaining coordinates, and use the displayed formula. These charts cover projective space, proving joint continuity in $([x],t)$. Thus $H$ is a homotopy from $i_m$ to $j\circ b$, where $j([y])=[0,y]$ is the inclusion in the second block. The same formula with $y$ in the first $m$ coordinates and $y$ in the second block, namely $[\cos(\pi t/2)y,0,\sin(\pi t/2)y]$, is a homotopy from $i_{m-1}$ to $j$. Both homotopies lie in the finite projective subspace $\mathbb{RP}^{2m}$ of the infinite space and therefore are continuous there as well. [step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Put $a_k=i_k^*a$. By [F3] and step 2.1, $a_m=b^*a_{m-1}$, including $m=1$ when $a_0=0$. Consequently $$a_m^m=b^*(a_{m-1}^m)=0,$$ since $H^m(\mathbb{RP}^{m-1};\mathbb F_2)=0$ by [F2]. On the other hand, [F1] says $a^m\ne0$ and that $i_m^*$ is an isomorphism in degree $m$, so $a_m^m=i_m^*(a^m)\ne0$. These incompatible conclusions rule out every such odd map. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For $m\ge1$, if $h(x)-h(-x)$ never vanished, then $$g(x)=\frac{h(x)-h(-x)}{\|h(x)-h(-x)\|_2}$$ would be continuous, take values in $S^{m-1}$ and satisfy $g(-x)=-g(x)$. Step 3.1 rules this out, so an antipodal pair has equal images. When $m=0$, the codomain $\mathbb R^0$ consists of one point and the two points of $S^0$ have equal images directly. AC is inherited exactly as stated in [A1]. [given, A1, step 3.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Infinite real projective space has
$$H^*(\mathbb {RP}^{\infty};\mathbb F_2)\cong\mathbb F_2[a],\qquad |a|=1.$$

For every integer $n\geq0$, restriction along the standard skeletal inclusion
$i_n:\mathbb {RP}^n\hookrightarrow\mathbb {RP}^{\infty}$ is an isomorphism in
degrees at most $n$. For $n\geq1$ it sends $a$ to the unique nonzero
degree-one class on $\mathbb {RP}^n$; for $n=0$ it sends $a$ to zero.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The standard filtration $\mathbb {RP}^0\subset\mathbb {RP}^1\subset\cdots\subset\mathbb {RP}^{\infty}$ and coefficients $\mathbb F_2$.

[F1] [[lem-real-projective-space-cellular-homology-and-pinch-map]] constructs one cell in each dimension of each finite $\mathbb {RP}^m$ and computes cellular incidence numbers zero or two; over $\mathbb F_2$ every finite-stage cellular differential is zero.

[F2] [[thm-cellular-homology-computes-singular-homology]] applies to arbitrary, possibly infinite-dimensional CW complexes and is natural for cellular maps.

[F3] [[prop-cellular-maps-induce-cellular-chain-maps]] identifies the maps on cellular chains with the induced singular-homology maps.

[F4] Under AC, [[cor-cohomology-over-a-field-is-dual-to-homology-over-that-field]] identifies singular cohomology naturally with the full field dual of singular homology.

[F5] [[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair-in-singular-cohomology]] and [[thm-naturality-of-the-singular-cohomology-pair-sequence]] give exact pair sequences and their commuting restriction squares.

[F6] [[thm-homotopic-maps-induce-equal-maps-in-singular-cohomology]] applies to the explicit coordinate deformations below, and [[thm-excision-for-singular-cohomology]] removes a closed set lying inside the open relative subspace.

[F7] Under AC, [[lem-local-coordinate-cup-products-generate-top-relative-cohomology]] says that the two coordinate local generators in $\mathbb R^i\times\mathbb R^j$, for $i,j\geq1$, have nonzero top relative cup product.

[F8] [[prop-relative-cup-products-are-natural-and-compatible-with-connectors]] transports these relative products, while pullback is a unital ring homomorphism by [[prop-cup-product-is-natural-unital-and-associative]].

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is assumed exactly through [F4] and [F7].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** compute additive groups cellularly, prove the finite projective-space products by a local relative-cup calculation, and then detect the infinite powers on finite skeleta.

1.1 Mod-two singular homology is one-dimensional in every nonnegative degree, and $(i_n)_*$ is an isomorphism through degree $n$. Realize $\mathbb {RP}^{\infty}$ as the union of the projective spaces of lines in $\mathbb R^{m+1}$ under the coordinate inclusions. For each $j$, the lines whose last nonzero coordinate is the $j$th form an open $j$-cell: scale that coordinate to $1$ to identify it with $\mathbb R^j$. Its characteristic map is the quotient of the closed upper hemisphere in $S^j$, whose equator maps into $\mathbb {RP}^{j-1}$. Hence its closure is $\mathbb {RP}^j$, and these characteristic maps give the standard union its CW topology, one cell in every nonnegative degree. Restriction to the first $n+1$ coordinates is therefore the subcomplex consisting of the cells through dimension $n$. [given, F1, F2, F3]

These are the same upper-hemisphere characteristic maps used in [F1], so its incidence calculation gives every infinite cellular differential as zero or two. Modulo two all are zero, and cellular homology is one copy of $\mathbb F_2$ in every degree. The cellular chain map for $i_n$ is the identity on the common cells in degrees at most $n$, so it induces the identity there. Facts [F2]--[F3] transfer both assertions to singular homology.

2.1 The cohomology groups and restriction maps have the corresponding description. By [F4], $H^k(\mathbb {RP}^{\infty};\mathbb F_2)$ is the dual of the one-dimensional group in step 1.1, hence is $\mathbb F_2$ for every $k\geq0$. Naturality identifies $i_n^*$ with precomposition by $(i_n)_*$; since the latter is an isomorphism for $k\leq n$, so is the former. [F4, A1, step 1.1]

3.1 Set up complementary coordinate projective subspaces after fixing the additive generators. Fix $n\geq2$ and positive $r,s$ with $r+s=n$. Use homogeneous coordinates $x_0,\ldots,x_n$. Let $E\cong\mathbb {RP}^r$ use $x_0,\ldots,x_r$, let $F\cong\mathbb {RP}^s$ use $x_r,\ldots,x_n$, and put $p=E\cap F=[e_r]$, $V=\mathbb {RP}^n\setminus F$, and $W=\mathbb {RP}^n\setminus E$. Scaling $x_r,\ldots,x_n$ to zero retracts $V$ and $E\setminus\{p\}$ onto the same coordinate $\mathbb {RP}^{r-1}$; symmetrically $W$ and $F\setminus\{p\}$ retract onto $\mathbb {RP}^{s-1}$. Scaling only $x_r$ to zero retracts $\mathbb {RP}^n\setminus\{p\}$ onto a coordinate $\mathbb {RP}^{n-1}$. Each formula is well defined on projective classes, never sends a representative to zero on the stated domain, fixes its target, and depends continuously on the scaling parameter. [given, F6, step 2.1]

4.1 The following three relative-to-absolute maps are isomorphisms. $$H^r(\mathbb {RP}^n,V)\longrightarrow H^r(\mathbb {RP}^n),\qquad H^s(\mathbb {RP}^n,W)\longrightarrow H^s(\mathbb {RP}^n)$$ and $$H^n(\mathbb {RP}^n,\mathbb {RP}^n\setminus\{p\})\longrightarrow H^n(\mathbb {RP}^n)$$ For the first map, step 3.1 and [F6] identify the relevant groups of $V$ with those of $\mathbb {RP}^{r-1}$; step 1.1 and [F4] say that $H^{r-1}(\mathbb {RP}^n)\to H^{r-1}(V)$ is onto and $H^r(V)=0$. Exactness in [F5] gives the isomorphism. The second map is symmetric, and the last uses the punctured-space retraction in exactly the same two adjacent degrees. Naturality in [F5] and the restriction isomorphisms of step 2.1 further identify the first two relative groups with $H^r(E,E\setminus\{p\})$ and $H^s(F,F\setminus\{p\})$. [F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 The two complementary-degree generators have nonzero top product. In the affine chart $x_r\ne0$, ratios identify a neighborhood of $p$ with $\mathbb R^r\times\mathbb R^s$ and identify $E,F$ with its coordinate planes. ## Statement

For each integer $m\ge0$, $\mathbb{RP}^m=S^m/(x\sim-x)$ has a CW structure with one cell in each dimension $0,\ldots,m$. Orientations can be chosen so its integral cellular complex has $C_j=\mathbb Z$ in these degrees, $d_j=2$ for positive even $j$, and $d_j=0$ for odd $j$. Consequently its integral homology is $\mathbb Z$ in degree zero, $\mathbb Z/2$ in odd degrees $0<j<m$, $\mathbb Z$ in degree $j=m$ when $m$ is odd, and zero otherwise. For $m=0$ only the degree-zero copy occurs.

The quotient $q:\mathbb{RP}^2\to\mathbb{RP}^2/\mathbb{RP}^1\cong S^2$ induces an isomorphism $H_2(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb F_2)\to H_2(S^2;\mathbb F_2)$. Assuming AC, it therefore induces an isomorphism $q^*:H^2(S^2;\mathbb F_2)\to H^2(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb F_2)$, both groups being $\mathbb F_2$.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[thm-cellular-boundary-is-the-incidence-degree-matrix]] computes boundary coefficients by the attaching map followed by collapse to the previous cell sphere; oriented edges have endpoint difference. [[thm-cellular-homology-computes-singular-homology]] identifies cellular and singular homology, naturally for cellular maps.

[F2] [[prop-degree-of-identity-constant-reflection-and-antipodal-sphere-maps]] gives antipodal degree $(-1)^{r+1}$ on $S^r$, $r\ge1$. [[lem-local-sphere-orientations-and-finite-puncture-excision]] identifies local orientation generators as restrictions of global ones, and [[thm-global-sphere-degree-is-the-sum-of-local-degrees]] sums the contributions of a finite fibre.

[F3] [[prop-cellular-maps-induce-cellular-chain-maps]] defines the chain maps from the actual relative skeletal maps for any abelian coefficient group, compatible with singular homology.

[F4] Under [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[cor-cohomology-over-a-field-is-dual-to-homology-over-that-field]] identifies cohomology naturally with the full field dual of homology.

## Proof

**Given:** The finite integer $m\ge0$ and the quotient definition in the statement. AC is used only for the final application of [F4].

1.1 Regard $S^j$ as the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^{j+1}$ and let its last-coordinate upper hemisphere be $D^j$. In the antipodal quotient, each class outside the equatorial $S^{j-1}$ has a unique representative in its open upper hemisphere. The equator maps to $\mathbb{RP}^{j-1}$ by its antipodal quotient. Hence adjoining this closed hemisphere to $\mathbb{RP}^{j-1}$ attaches one $j$-disk by that equatorial quotient map. This is a homeomorphism of the attachment quotient with $\mathbb{RP}^j$: it is a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space. To check Hausdorffness here, two distinct antipodal orbits are finite disjoint subsets of the metric sphere, so sufficiently small disjoint neighborhoods of the two orbits may be chosen invariant under the antipodal map; their quotient images are disjoint open neighborhoods. Starting with $\mathbb{RP}^0=*$ and iterating these finite disk attachments gives the stated CW structure and the usual inclusions as skeleta. [given]

2.1 For $j\ge2$, the cellular incidence map is $f:S^{j-1}\to\mathbb{RP}^{j-1}/\mathbb{RP}^{j-2}\cong S^{j-1}$: quotient by antipodes and then collapse the lower skeleton. The preimage of the lower skeleton is the equatorial $S^{j-2}$. Off that equator, each of the two open hemispheres maps homeomorphically onto the open top cell in the target. Choose a point $y$ there, with preimages $x,-x$, and orient the characteristic $j$-disk so the local degree at $x$ is $+1$. Let $a$ be the antipodal map of the domain. Since $f a=f$, composition of the induced maps of local relative groups gives $\deg_x f=\deg_{-x}f\,\deg_x a$. The local degree of the homeomorphism $a$ equals its global degree: the global-to-local generator maps commute with $a$ and are isomorphisms by [F2]. Thus $\deg_x a=(-1)^j$ and $\deg_{-x}f=(-1)^j$. The finite-fibre formula yields $\deg f=1+(-1)^j$. With the preceding cell orientation fixed, the source cell can be oriented as above in each degree. By [F1], $d_j$ is therefore $2$ for even $j$ and zero for odd $j$. For $j=1$, both endpoints attach to the sole vertex, so $d_1=0$ directly, without a degree assertion for $S^0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 For $0<j<m$ even, $d_j=2$ is injective, so $H_j=0$. For $0<j<m$ odd, $d_j=0$ and $d_{j+1}=2$, so $H_j=\mathbb Z/2$. In top degree $m>0$, there is no incoming boundary: the kernel is $\mathbb Z$ for odd $m$ and zero for even $m$. In degree zero $d_1=0$ gives $H_0=\mathbb Z$. There are no chains above $m$ or below zero. [F1] transfers these cellular computations to integral singular homology. This also proves separately that $m=0$ is just the point case and $m=1$ has $H_0=H_1=\mathbb Z$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.2 With coefficients $\mathbb F_2$, each cellular group is $\mathbb F_2$ and every differential is zero. Indeed change of coefficients in the relative chain groups sends each oriented integral disk generator to the coefficient-one disk generator, and commutes with the defining connecting and quotient maps; hence the coefficients computed in step 2.1 reduce modulo two. These coefficient-one generators span each one-cell group, so this identifies its entire differential. For $\mathbb{RP}^2$ the resulting complex has one copy of $\mathbb F_2$ in degrees zero, one and two and zero differentials, in particular $H_2=\mathbb F_2$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Collapse $\mathbb{RP}^1$ in the disk attachment for $\mathbb{RP}^2$. This collapses the boundary of its characteristic $2$-disk and leaves its interior unchanged, so the quotient is $D^2/\partial D^2\cong S^2$ with one zero-cell and one two-cell. The map $q$ is cellular. Its map on degree-two cellular groups sends the characteristic disk generator to the same disk generator, since the composite characteristic disk map is the quotient $D^2\to D^2/\partial D^2$ used to define that target generator. Over $\mathbb F_2$ this is the identity, while the target degree-one group is zero. Both degree-two homology groups are their entire degree-two chain groups, so the cellular map induces an isomorphism. By [F3], this is the actual singular map $q_*$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 3.2]

5.1 Apply the natural field-duality isomorphism [F4] in degree two. Its naturality square identifies $q^*$ with precomposition by the isomorphism $q_*$ of step 4.1. Precomposition by an isomorphism has inverse precomposition by its inverse, so $q^*$ is an isomorphism as claimed. This uses singular cohomology throughout, with no assumption that a cellular cochain is a singular cochain. [F4, step 4.1]

6.1 The homology formula excludes negative degrees and handles the top degree separately, so it does not count the degree-zero group twice when $m=0$. For $m=2$ it gives $H_1=\mathbb Z/2$, $H_2=0$ integrally, while step 3.2 gives nonzero mod-two $H_2$; these are distinct coefficient assertions. Orienting the finitely many cells in a fixed $\mathbb{RP}^m$ makes only finite choices; the displayed local degrees are unchanged up to the controlled cell-orientation sign. The AC assumption in step 5.1 is inherited from field duality and is not used to prove the cellular boundary or integral homology calculation. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a nonempty finite CW complex of dimension $d$, and let
$R$ be a commutative ring. For every $n>d$ the singular cohomology vanishes:
$$H^n(X;R)=0.$$
More generally, for a CW pair $(X,A)$ with $X$ finite of dimension $d$ one has
$H^n(X,A;R)=0$ for every $n>d$.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed, exactly as inherited from the cellular-cochain comparison ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] For a CW pair and a local system the cellular cochain complex obtained from the skeletal filtration computes singular cohomology with local coefficients, naturally ([[thm-cellular-cochains-compute-cohomology-with-local-coefficients]]).

[F2] Taking the trivial local system with fiber $R$ recovers singular cohomology with coefficients in $R$ ([[def-singular-cohomology-with-coefficients]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** AC, a CW pair $(X,A)$ with $X$ finite of dimension $d$, and a commutative ring $R$.

1.1 By [F1] and [F2] the singular cohomology $H^*(X,A;R)$ is the cohomology of the cellular cochain complex $C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;R)$ built from the relative cells of the skeletal filtration. [F1, F2]

1.2 A finite CW complex of dimension $d$ has $X^n=X^{n-1}=X$ for $n>d$. The degree-$n$ cellular cochain group from the skeletal filtration of [F1] is the relative cohomology of the consecutive skeleta $(X^n\cup A,X^{n-1}\cup A)$, which is therefore the zero group. Thus $C^n_{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;R)=0$ for $n>d$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 A cochain complex whose groups vanish in all degrees above $d$ has cohomology zero above $d$, since a degree-$n$ cohomology class for $n>d$ is a class in a zero group; therefore $H^n(X,A;R)=0$ for $n>d$. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 In the absolute case $A=\varnothing$ this gives $H^n(X;R)=0$ for $n>d$, which is the first assertion. [step 2.1]

4.1 Boundary cases. For $d=0$ the complex is a finite discrete set, all cochains vanish in positive degrees and the statement reads $H^n(X;R)=0$ for $n\geq1$, which holds because $X$ is a disjoint union of points. For the empty complex both sides vanish in every degree (the empty CW complex has dimension $-\infty$ by convention, and the statement is vacuous). Negative degrees are outside the assertion. The ring $R$ may be the zero ring, in which case all groups vanish; no division or flatness is used. AC is used only through [A1] in the cellular comparison. [A1, F1, step 2.1] ∎

## Source notes

Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology* section 2.2 (printed pp. 139-141), records that cellular cohomology vanishes above the dimension because the cellular cochain complex is concentrated in degrees at most the dimension. The lemma is stated for arbitrary coefficient rings, since the argument only uses freeness of the cellular chain groups.

## Statement

If $f,g:X\to Y$ are homotopic continuous maps, then $f^*=g^*:H^n(Y;G)\to H^n(X;G)$ for every integer $n$ and every abelian coefficient group $G$.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[thm-singular-chain-homotopy-formula]] supplies a prism $P_j:C_j(X;\mathbb Z)\to C_{j+1}(Y;\mathbb Z)$ with $g_\#-f_\#=\partial P+P\partial$, using $P_{-1}=0$ in degree zero.

[F2] [[def-singular-cochain-complex-with-coefficients]] uses $\delta\varphi=\varphi\partial$ and zero negative cochains. [[def-singular-cohomology-with-coefficients]] takes cocycles modulo coboundaries.

[F3] [[prop-singular-cohomology-is-contravariantly-functorial]] gives the induced maps by cochain precomposition.

## Proof

**Given:** A homotopy from $f$ to $g$, its prism $P$ from [F1], and coefficients $G$.

1.1 For $n\ge1$ define $K^n:C^n(Y;G)\to C^{n-1}(X;G)$ by $K^n\varphi=\varphi P_{n-1}$, and set $K^n=0$ for $n\le0$. For $n\ge0$, the composite maps on a cochain satisfy $$\delta_X^{n-1}K^n\varphi+K^{n+1}\delta_Y^n\varphi=\varphi P_{n-1}\partial_{X,n}+\varphi\partial_{Y,n+1}P_n=\varphi(g_{\#,n}-f_{\#,n}).$$ When $n=0$ the first term is zero and the identity is exactly [F1]'s degree-zero formula. Thus $g^\sharp-f^\sharp=\delta K+K\delta$ with the stated positive sign. [F1, F2, F3]

2.1 If $\varphi$ is a cocycle, the last summand $K\delta\varphi$ vanishes; hence $g^\sharp\varphi-f^\sharp\varphi=\delta K\varphi$ is a coboundary. It follows on [F2] quotients that $g^*[\varphi]=f^*[\varphi]$. In degree zero this is equality of the actual cocycles, since $K^0=0$. In negative degrees both induced maps are the unique map of zero groups. [F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Step 2.1 proves equality in every degree. Empty source or target, zero coefficients, and a point cause no exception: where the maps exist, the same prism formula applies; zero cochains give zero maps. Constant homotopies need not have zero unnormalized prism, but step 1.1 still yields the correct equality. This proof composes explicitly given homomorphisms and uses no extension of homomorphisms, primitive selection or AC. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

For continuous $f:X\to Y$ and a commutative unital ring $R$, pullback on singular cohomology satisfies
$$f^*(a\smile b)=f^*a\smile f^*b,\qquad f^*(1)=1.$$
Cup product is associative already on cochains. Consequently $f^*:H^*(Y;R)\to H^*(X;R)$ is a unital graded-ring homomorphism. Homotopic maps give the same homomorphism.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[def-singular-cup-product-on-cochains]] is the front/back-face formula, bilinear over $R$.

[F2] [[def-singular-cohomology-ring]] supplies the quotient multiplication and the closed cochain assigning $1$ to every vertex as unit.

[F3] [[thm-homotopic-maps-induce-equal-maps-in-singular-cohomology]] proves equality of pullbacks in every degree for homotopic maps.

## Proof

**Given:** $f:X\to Y$ continuous, and homogeneous cochains $\varphi,\psi,\eta$ of degrees $p,q,r$. Write $f^\sharp\varphi(\sigma)=\varphi(f\sigma)$.

1.1 Face restriction commutes with postcomposition. On a $(p+q)$-simplex $\sigma$, evaluation of $f^\sharp(\varphi\smile\psi)$ is $\varphi(f\sigma[0,\ldots,p])\psi(f\sigma[p,\ldots,p+q])$, which is the evaluation of $f^\sharp\varphi\smile f^\sharp\psi$. Precomposition is linear and commutes with positive coboundary because each face does; it therefore induces the same multiplicative equality on cocycle classes. On a vertex $x$, $f^\sharp\mathbf1(x)=\mathbf1(f(x))=1$, giving the unit identity on classes. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 On a $(p+q+r)$-simplex $\sigma$, both $(\varphi\smile\psi)\smile\eta$ and $\varphi\smile(\psi\smile\eta)$ evaluate to $\varphi(\sigma[0,\ldots,p])\psi(\sigma[p,\ldots,p+q])\eta(\sigma[p+q,\ldots,p+q+r])$. Associativity in $R$ makes the results equal. Bilinearity extends this identity to finite sums of homogeneous cochains; descent gives associativity in the cohomology ring. Together with step 1.1 this proves the graded-ring homomorphism claim. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 If $f$ and $g$ are homotopic, [F3] gives equality on each homogeneous group. Every element of the graded direct sum has finite support, so the two ring homomorphisms are equal. Degree-zero factors in step 2.1 merely shorten blocks to vertices. The same formula covers degenerate simplices and points. Empty spaces and the zero ring give zero cochains and the stipulated zero-ring unit; any existing pullback still preserves this unit. All formulas are prescribed, so no AC is required. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $k,m,d\ge1$ be integers and let $p_1,\ldots,p_m$ be real polynomials in $k$ variables, each of total degree at most $d$ (including the zero polynomial). The number of strict sign vectors $(\operatorname{sgn}p_1(x),\ldots,\operatorname{sgn}p_m(x))\in\{-1,1\}^m$ attained at points where all polynomials are nonzero is at most $(2md+1)^k$. The number of binary vectors $(\mathbf1_{p_i(x)>0})_{i=1}^m$ is also at most $(2md+1)^k$, and the same bound holds with $\ge0$ in place of $>0$. The number of ternary sign vectors in $\{-1,0,1\}^m$ is at most $(4md+1)^k$. Each assertion remains valid when $x$ is restricted to any subset of $\mathbb R^k$.

## Statement references

[[def-monomials-multidegree-and-total-degree|Multivariate polynomials and total degree]]

[Telgarsky, Theorem 17.5: the sharper classical Warren bound](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/index.html#sec:gen:reluvc)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integers $k,m,d\ge1$ and real polynomials $p_i$ of total degree at most $d$.

[F1] Polynomials have finite monomial expansions and total degree as in [[def-monomials-multidegree-and-total-degree]].

[F2] A continuous function on a nonempty closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R^k$ attains its maximum ([[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]).

[F3] The gradient of a differentiable function vanishes at an interior local maximum ([[thm-fermat-for-euclidean-local-extrema]]).

## Proof

1.1 First establish an elementary zero-counting fact. If $D\ge1$ and $r_i(x)=x_i^D+s_i(x)$ with $\deg s_i<D$ for $1\le i\le k$, then these $k$ polynomials have at most $D^k$ distinct common real zeros. In the quotient vector space $V=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_k]/(r_1,\ldots,r_k)$, every monomial is a linear combination of the $D^k$ monomials $x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_k^{a_k}$ with $0\le a_i<D$. Indeed, if some exponent is at least $D$, replace its factor $x_i^D$ by $-s_i$ modulo the ideal. Every resulting monomial has strictly smaller total degree, so induction on total degree terminates and proves the spanning assertion. Thus $\dim V\le D^k$. [F1, algebra]

1.2 If no strict sign vector occurs, its bound is immediate. Otherwise choose one representative $a_\sigma$ for each attained strict vector $\sigma$. Only finitely many choices are involved, since there are at most $2^m$ vectors. Set $P=\prod_{i=1}^m p_i$ and $D=2md+1$. Then $P(a_\sigma)\ne0$. Choose a single $\delta>0$ so small that $H(a_\sigma)>0$ for every representative, where $H(x)=P(x)^2-\delta\sum_{i=1}^k x_i^{D+1}$. Such a choice exists: there are finitely many positive numbers $P(a_\sigma)^2$, and the other term has a fixed finite value at each representative. Since $D+1$ is even and greater than $2\deg P$, $H(x)\to-\infty$ as $\|x\|\to\infty$. Explicitly, $|P(x)|^2\le C(1+\|x\|^{2md})$ and $\sum_i x_i^{D+1}\ge k^{-(D+1)/2}\|x\|^{D+1}$. [given, F1, choose, construct, algebra]

2.1 For any finite list of distinct common zeros $z_1,\ldots,z_t$, evaluation defines a surjective linear map $V\to\mathbb R^t$. To see surjectivity, for every ordered pair $j\ne h$ choose a coordinate $i(j,h)$ in which $z_j$ and $z_h$ differ, and set $h_j(x)=\prod_{h\ne j}(x_{i(j,h)}-(z_h)_{i(j,h)})/((z_j)_{i(j,h)}-(z_h)_{i(j,h)})$. Then $h_j(z_h)$ is $1$ for $h=j$ and $0$ otherwise. Evaluation vanishes on the ideal because all its generators vanish at these zeros, so it is well defined on $V$ and the classes of $h_j$ map onto the standard coordinate vectors. The classes of $h_1,\ldots,h_t$ are linearly independent: applying evaluation to any relation gives the same relation among the standard coordinate vectors, so every coefficient is zero. A vector space spanned by $D^k$ vectors contains at most $D^k$ independent vectors. Explicitly, insert the independent vectors successively into the given spanning list: express the next one in the current spanning list, replace a listed vector with a nonzero coefficient outside the previously inserted independent vectors, and solve that expression for the replaced vector. The list still spans and has the same length. If there were no such outside coefficient, the new vector would lie in the span of the previously inserted ones, contradicting independence. Thus at most $D^k$ independent vectors can be inserted. This proves $t\le\dim V\le D^k$ using only finite linear algebra. If there were more than $D^k$ zeros, choosing a finite list of $D^k+1$ of them would contradict this inequality. This proves the zero-counting fact without a genericity or multiplicity assumption. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.2 For an attained strict vector $\sigma$, put $S_\sigma=\{x:\operatorname{sgn}p_i(x)=\sigma_i\text{ for all }i\}$. This is open. Its closure has a maximum of $H$: choose a closed ball containing $a_\sigma$ outside which $H<0$, and apply [F2] to its nonempty closed bounded intersection with $\overline{S_\sigma}$. The resulting maximum is positive, because $H(a_\sigma)>0$, and it is also the maximum over the full closure. Any point in $\overline{S_\sigma}\setminus S_\sigma$ has $p_i=0$ for some $i$ by continuity, so there $H=-\delta\sum_i x_i^{D+1}\le0$. Therefore the positive maximum is attained at a point $b_\sigma\in S_\sigma$, which is an interior local maximum of $H$. Distinct strict vectors give distinct such points. [F2, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 By [F3] every $b_\sigma$ is a common zero of the $k$ polynomials $\partial_i H=2P\partial_iP-\delta(D+1)x_i^D$. After division by the nonzero coefficient $-\delta(D+1)$, each has the form $x_i^D+s_i(x)$ with $\deg s_i\le2md-1<D$. The zero-counting fact therefore bounds their distinct common zeros, and hence the number of strict sign vectors, by $D^k=(2md+1)^k$. [F3, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 For binary vectors with $>0$, choose one representative per attained vector. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ smaller than every nonzero $|p_i|$ occurring at these finitely many representatives; if there are no such values, choose any positive $\varepsilon$. The strict signs of $p_i-\varepsilon$ at the representatives now encode their original binary vectors: positive values remain positive, and nonpositive values become negative. Applying the strict bound to the $m$ shifted polynomials gives the binary bound. For $\ge0$, use $p_i+\varepsilon$: nonnegative values become positive, and negative values remain negative. For ternary vectors choose representatives and $\varepsilon$ in the same way, and use the $2m$ polynomials $p_i-\varepsilon,p_i+\varepsilon$. Their strict sign pairs are $(-,-)$, $(-,+)$, and $(+,+)$ for the original negative, zero, and positive values, respectively, so distinct ternary vectors give distinct strict vectors. The strict bound with $2m$ polynomials gives $(4md+1)^k$. Restriction of the domain only removes vectors. [step 3.1, choose, construct, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The retained identifier connects to the missing polynomial sign-pattern supplier. The displayed estimate is an elementary coarse version, sufficient for the network bounds below; it does not assert Warren's sharp constant or the sharper division by $k$ in the base. The proof supplies the needed estimate locally and uses no unproved algebraic-geometric zero-counting theorem or choice axiom.

## Definition

Let $F$ be a field. Every polynomial in the iterated ring
$F[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ has a unique finite expansion

$$f=\sum_{\mathbf{t}}c_{\mathbf{t}}x^{\mathbf{t}},\qquad x^{\mathbf{t}}:=x_1^{t_1}\cdots x_n^{t_n},$$

over finitely many multi-indices $\mathbf{t}=(t_1,\dots,t_n)\in\mathbb{N}^n$.

For such an index, the scalar $c_{\mathbf{t}}$ is the **coefficient**
$[x^{\mathbf{t}}]f$ of the monomial $x^{\mathbf{t}}$.

The **degree in $x_i$** is the largest $t_i$ with $c_{\mathbf{t}}\ne0$, and the
**total degree** is the largest value of $t_1+\cdots+t_n$ with
$c_{\mathbf{t}}\ne0$. For the zero polynomial, every degree is left undefined.

Evaluation at a point $(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in F^n$ is the iterated substitution
supplied by the universal property of the polynomial ring.

## Remarks

- The page uses this expansion constantly. The Nullstellensatz and the grid
  reduction need both the separate variable degrees and the total degree, and
  neither is visible in the bare iterated-ring construction unless it is named
  here.

## Statement

If $f:U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable at an interior local maximum or minimum $a$, then $\nabla f(a)=0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A differentiable scalar field with a local extremum at $a$.

[L1] The one-variable Fermat theorem gives derivative zero at an interior differentiable local extremum ([[thm-fermat-interior-extremum]]).

[L2] The gradient consists of the coordinate partial derivatives ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Restrict $f$ to each coordinate line through $a$. The restriction has a local extremum at $0$, so [L1] makes its derivative zero. [L1, given]

2.1 These derivatives are the entries of $\nabla f(a)$ by [L2], so every entry vanishes. [step 1.1, L2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d,n\ge1$ be integers, $Q=[0,1]^d$, and let $F_{d,n}\subset C(Q;\mathbb R)$ consist of the continuous functions whose restrictions represent members of $W^{n,\infty}((0,1)^d)$ satisfying
$$\max_{|\alpha|\le n}\|D^\alpha f\|_{L^\infty((0,1)^d)}\le1.$$
There exists $c_{d,n}>0$ such that, for every integer $W\ge1$, every map $\eta:\mathbb R^W\to C(Q;\mathbb R)$, and every map $M:F_{d,n}\to\mathbb R^W$ continuous for the uniform norm on $F_{d,n}$,
$$\sup_{f\in F_{d,n}}\|f-\eta(M(f))\|_\infty\ge c_{d,n}(W+1)^{-n/d}.$$
No continuity or measurability assumption is imposed on $\eta$. In particular, if this supremum is at most $\varepsilon>0$, then $W\ge C_{d,n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}$ for some $C_{d,n}>0$ depending only on $d,n$.

## Statement references

[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]

[[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $d,n,W\ge1$, $F_{d,n}$, arbitrary $\eta$, and selection $M$ continuous for the uniform-norm topology as in the statement.

[F1] A function is in the indicated Sobolev ball exactly when its weak derivatives through order $n$, including the function itself, have $L^\infty$ norms at most one ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

[F2] Every continuous map $S^W\to\mathbb R^W$ takes the same value at some antipodal pair, under AC ([[thm-borsuk-ulam-general]]).

## Proof

1.1 Define $p(t)=(4t(1-t))^{n+1}$ for $0\le t\le1$ and $p(t)=0$ otherwise, and put $\psi(x)=\prod_{r=1}^d p(x_r)$. The one-sided derivatives of $p$ of orders $0,\ldots,n$ vanish at each endpoint because the polynomial has a zero of multiplicity $n+1$ there. Hence the zero extension is $C^n(\mathbb R)$, and $\psi\in C^n(\mathbb R^d)$ is supported in $[0,1]^d$, is one at its center, and lies between zero and one. Set $$B=\max_{|\alpha|\le n}\|D^\alpha\psi\|_\infty\ge1.$$ This is finite since the derivatives are continuous polynomials on the compact cube and zero outside it. Their classical derivatives are weak derivatives: integrate by parts successively in each coordinate against a compactly supported smooth test function; endpoint terms vanish because the derivatives below order $n$ match their zero extensions. This also verifies the weak derivative identity after every scaling and finite sum used below. [F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Set $N=W+1$ and $k=\lceil N^{1/d}\rceil$. Partition $Q$ into $k^d$ closed coordinate cubes of side $1/k$, and take the first $N$ in lexicographic order. Write $v_j$ for their lower vertices and put $$\phi_j(x)=B^{-1}k^{-n}\psi(k(x-v_j)),\qquad j=1,\ldots,N.$$ Distinct supports have disjoint interiors; all derivatives of orders at most $n$ vanish on their boundaries. Thus, for $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_N)\in[-1,1]^N$, the sum $T(u)=\sum_j u_j\phi_j$ satisfies $\|D^\alpha T(u)\|_\infty\le B^{-1}k^{|\alpha|-n}\|D^\alpha\psi\|_\infty\le1$. The weak derivative verification in step 1.1 proves $T(u)\in F_{d,n}$. Disjoint interiors, and evaluation at the centers, give the exact identity $$\|T(u)\|_\infty=B^{-1}k^{-n}\max_j|u_j|.$$ In particular $T$ is linear, odd and continuous into $C(Q)$ with its uniform norm. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For $z\in S^{N-1}=S^W$, put $R(z)=z/\|z\|_\infty$. Its denominator is nonzero, and $R$ is continuous and odd with $\|R(z)\|_\infty=1$. Therefore $z\mapsto M(T(R(z)))$ is continuous into $\mathbb R^W$. By [F2], some antipodal pair has equal images. Setting $f=T(R(z))$, we obtain $M(f)=M(-f)$ and $\|f\|_\infty=B^{-1}k^{-n}$. [F2, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Let $q=\eta(M(f))=\eta(M(-f))$. The triangle inequality yields $$2B^{-1}k^{-n}=\|f-(-f)\|_\infty\le\|f-q\|_\infty+\|-f-q\|_\infty.$$ At least one of the two errors is at least $B^{-1}k^{-n}$. Because $k\le2N^{1/d}$, this is at least $c_{d,n}N^{-n/d}$ with $c_{d,n}=2^{-n}B^{-1}>0$. This proves the asserted supremum bound without any regularity of $\eta$. [step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If every error is at most $\varepsilon$, step 4.1 gives $W+1\ge(c_{d,n}/\varepsilon)^{d/n}$. Since $W\ge1$ implies $W+1\le2W$, we obtain $W\ge\tfrac12 c_{d,n}^{d/n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}$. The construction works at $W=1$, $d=1$, $n=1$, on cubes touching the boundary and when $N=k^d$, with exactly the same vanishing-derivative argument. AC is inherited from [F2] and subsumes the countable choice in [F1]; choosing finitely many indexed cubes or derivatives introduces no new choice principle. [F1, F2, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Fix a scalar-output ReLU feedforward architecture on $[0,1]^d$, permitting skip edges, with $W\ge1$ scalar connection coefficients and unit biases, and depth at most $L$. Fix a real threshold $a$. For its realizations $f_\theta$, let $\mathcal H_a=\{\{x:f_\theta(x)>a\}:\theta\in\mathbb R^W\}$. There is an absolute constant $C$ such that $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal H_a)\le CW^2$ and $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal H_a)\le CW L\log(2W)$. In particular, for $W\ge2$ the bound $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal H_a)\le C L^2W\log W$ holds. The same assertions hold for $f_\theta(x)\ge a$. The parameter count includes every hidden and output bias, even when its chosen value is zero.

## Statement references

[[def-relu-network|ReLU network and complexity conventions]]

[[def-vc-class-of-sets-and-index|Shattering and VC dimension on an arbitrary domain]]

[Yarotsky, Theorem 4 proof: the two VC estimates used for approximation lower bounds](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1610.01145)

[Telgarsky, §17.3: the layer-partition argument](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/index.html#sec:gen:reluvc)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A fixed architecture with scalar output, $W$ counted coefficients and biases, depth at most $L$, and a fixed threshold $a$.

[F1] Each hidden unit applies $\max(0,z)$ to an affine combination of earlier values, and the output is affine; skip edges are permitted and each unit bias counts as a weight ([[def-relu-network]]).

[F2] For $M$ real polynomials of total degree at most $q$ in $w$ variables, the number of binary vectors of strict positivity, or of nonnegativity, is at most $(2Mq+1)^w$, also on an arbitrary subset of the parameter space ([[thm-warren-polynomial-sign-pattern-bound]]).

[F3] Shattering a finite set means realizing all its subsets; every subset of a shattered set is shattered ([[def-vc-class-of-sets-and-index]]).

## Proof

1.1 Remove all hidden units that have no path to the output. Also remove all hidden units having no input ancestor: for each fixed parameter assignment their values are constants in $x$, and their contributions to a remaining unit or the output can be added to its existing bias. Allowing these new biases to vary independently produces a fixed reduced architecture whose realization class contains the original class. No new coefficient slots are needed, because every surviving computation unit already has a bias; edges and removed units only disappear. If the output has no input ancestor, the original class consists of constant functions and has VC dimension at most $1$, which satisfies the conclusions. Otherwise the reduced graph has $w\le W$ counted slots, $U$ hidden units, and $U+1\le w$ because the output and every hidden unit have counted biases. Every remaining unit lies on an input-to-output path. Rank each hidden unit by the maximum number of computation units on an input-to-that-unit path, and give the output its analogous rank $K$. Then each edge increases rank, and $K\le L-1$ and $K\le U+1\le w$. Empty ranks can be omitted. It suffices to bound the reduced class. [F1, F3, construct]

2.1 Fix arbitrary sample points $x_1,\ldots,x_m$. For any prescribed binary mask $b\in\{0,1\}^U$, replace the ReLU at hidden unit $v$ by multiplication of its preactivation by $b_v$. Its preactivation and the final output are now polynomials in the $w$ parameters. By induction along the graph, a unit of rank $j$ has polynomial degree at most $j$: input values have degree zero, multiplication by an edge coefficient raises degree by one, addition of a bias has degree one, and multiplication by a fixed mask entry changes no degree. Thus every such polynomial has degree at most $K\le w$. On any actual parameter vector the convention $b_v=\mathbf1_{z_v>0}$ gives a unique mask, even when a preactivation is zero, and the masked polynomials then reproduce every actual unit value. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For each sample point and each of the $2^U$ masks, form the $U$ preactivation polynomials and the output polynomial minus $a$. There are $M=m(U+1)2^U$ polynomials, all of degree at most $w$. Their strict-positivity vector determines the actual output classification at every sample point: evaluate units in topological order, determining their actual mask by the relevant preactivation entry, then read the output entry for that mask. Hence the number of label vectors is at most $(2Mw+1)^w\le(3mw^2 2^w)^w$ by [F2]. If the classifier uses $\ge a$, take the hidden-unit mask $\mathbf1_{z_v\ge0}$ and use nonnegativity vectors throughout; at zero, multiplying by either mask value still gives the ReLU value, so the same count holds. [F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

3.2 For a second count, start with the single parameter-space cell $\mathbb R^w$. At stage $j$, refine every existing cell by the activation bits of all units of rank $j$ at all $m$ sample points; at the final stage refine by the output threshold bits. Within a cell, all earlier mask bits are fixed, so the relevant $mN_j$ preactivation polynomials, or output-minus-threshold polynomials, have degree at most $j\le K$ by step 2.1, where $N_j$ is the number of units at that rank, with $N_K=1$ for the output. By [F2] there are at most $(2mN_jK+1)^w\le(3mwK)^w$ refinements of each cell. This estimate holds on an arbitrary cell; no connectedness or openness is needed. After $K$ stages, the number of cells, hence the number of output label vectors, is at most $(3mwK)^{wK}$. The construction using $\ge0$ activation bits and nonnegativity output bits proves the identical bound for the other threshold convention. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Put $m_0=64w^2$. At this sample size the base-two logarithm of the last bound is $w(\log_2 3+\log_2m_0+2\log_2w+w)=w(w+\log_2 3+6+4\log_2w)\le13w^2<m_0$, using $\log_2w\le w$ for integers $w\ge1$. Thus no $m_0$-point set can be shattered, and [F3] rules out all larger shattered sets. Consequently $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal H_a)<64w^2\le64W^2$. [F3, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Write $A=wK$ and $B=\log_2(2w)\ge1$, and take the integer $m_1=\lceil64AB\rceil\le65AB$. Since $K\le w$, one has $\log_2 A\le2\log_2w$ and $\log_2B\le B$. The base-two logarithm of the label-count bound at $m=m_1$ is at most $A\log_2(195A^2B)\le A(8+4\log_2w+\log_2B)\le A(4+5B)\le9AB< m_1$. No set of $m_1$ points is shattered. Therefore $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal H_a)<m_1\le65wK\log_2(2w)\le65WL\log_2(2W)$. Conversion between logarithm bases changes only an absolute constant. For $W\ge2$, $\log(2W)\le2\log W$ and $L\ge1$, so this implies the requested $CL^2W\log W$ estimate. Together with step 4.1 and the constant-output case, this proves every assertion. [F3, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The stronger $CWL\log(2W)$ layer estimate is included because the same elementary proof gives it. The classical $CL^2W\log W$ estimate is used in Yarotsky's stated approximation lower bound and is preserved here. The use of $\log(2W)$ before imposing $W\ge2$ avoids the false zero bound at $W=1$. A variable final threshold can be absorbed into the already present output bias and does not require a new parameter slot.

## Definition

Let $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ be a family of subsets of an arbitrary set $X$. For a finite $T\subseteq X$, its trace is

$$\mathcal C|_T:=\{C\cap T:C\in\mathcal C\}.$$

The family $\mathcal C$ **shatters** $T$ when $\mathcal C|_T=\mathcal P(T)$. This extends the finite-ground-set trace convention of [[def-shattering-and-vc-dimension]]: any finite $T$ can be relabeled by $[|T|]$, and relabeling preserves all traces and their cardinalities.

For a nonempty class, its **VC dimension** $d(\mathcal C)$ is the greatest size of a finite shattered set if those sizes are bounded, is $0$ if no singleton is shattered, and is $+\infty$ if finite shattered sets have unbounded size. When the dimension is finite, its **VC index** is

$$V(\mathcal C):=d(\mathcal C)+1,$$

equivalently the least positive integer $V$ such that no $V$-point subset is shattered. The empty class is assigned $V=0$ by convention and is treated separately in the entropy theorem.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $F_{d,n}$ be the unit ball of $W^{n,\infty}((0,1)^d)$ for the maximum weak-derivative norm, identified with its continuous representatives on $[0,1]^d$. The following lower bounds have distinct hypotheses. (i) Let $W\ge1$, let $\eta:\mathbb R^W\to C([0,1]^d)$ be an approximation map, and suppose a parameter-selection map $M:F_{d,n}\to\mathbb R^W$, continuous for the uniform norm on $F_{d,n}$, satisfies $\|f-\eta(M(f))\|_\infty\le\varepsilon$ for every $f\in F_{d,n}$. Then $W\ge c\varepsilon^{-d/n}$. (ii) If one fixed ReLU architecture with $W$ weights approximates every $f\in F_{d,n}$ within $\varepsilon$, with no continuity assumption on weight selection, then $W\ge c\varepsilon^{-d/(2n)}$; if its depth is at most $c_1(\log(1/\varepsilon))^p$ for fixed $p\ge0$ and $c_1>0$, then $W\ge c_2\varepsilon^{-d/n}(\log(1/\varepsilon))^{-2p-1}$ for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. (iii) If $L\ge3$ is fixed and $f\in C^2([0,1]^d)$ is nonlinear, then every depth-$L$ ReLU network approximating $f$ uniformly within $\varepsilon$ has at least $c(f,L)\varepsilon^{-1/(2(L-2))}$ weights and computation units for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. All constants may depend only on the indicated fixed parameters.

## Statement references

[Yarotsky, Theorems 3, 4, and 6: approximation lower bounds](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1610.01145)

[DeVore, Howard, and Micchelli, Theorems 3.1 and 4.2: continuous nonlinear widths and Sobolev bump spaces](https://gwern.net/doc/cs/algorithm/1989-devore.pdf)

[Telgarsky lecture notes, §§5.3 and 17.3: lower-bound context and VC dimension](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/index.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, integers $d,n\ge1$, the class $F_{d,n}$, the parameter-selection hypotheses for clauses (i)–(ii), and the depth and smoothness hypotheses for clause (iii).

[F1] A scalar-input ReLU network with hidden widths $n_1,\ldots,n_H$ has at most $\prod_{\ell=1}^H(n_\ell+1)$ affine intervals ([[lem-univariate-relu-affine-interval-count]]).

[F2] Under AC, a uniform-norm continuous selector into $\mathbb R^W$ and arbitrary decoder on the stated Sobolev ball have worst-case error at least $c_{d,n}(W+1)^{-n/d}$ ([[thm-sobolev-continuous-nonlinear-width-lower-bound]]).

[F3] For a fixed scalar-output ReLU architecture with $W$ weights, including biases, and depth $L$, threshold classifiers have VC dimension at most $CW^2$ and at most $CL^2W\log(2W)$ ([[lem-relu-network-vc-dimension-bound]]).

## Proof

1.1 By [F2], the hypotheses of clause (i) imply $\varepsilon\ge c_{d,n}(W+1)^{-n/d}$. Since $W\ge1$, we have $W+1\le2W$, hence $W\ge\tfrac12 c_{d,n}^{d/n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}$. The decoder needs no continuity; exactly the selector topology in the statement is used. [given, F2, algebra]

1.2 For clause (ii), write $p(t)=(4t(1-t))^{n+1}$ on $[0,1]$, extended by zero, and $\psi(x)=\prod_{r=1}^d p(x_r)$. The polynomial has endpoint zeros of order $n+1$, so its zero extension is $C^n$. Put $B=\max_{|\alpha|\le n}\|D^\alpha\psi\|_\infty\ge1$. Partition the cube into $K^d$ cubes of side $1/K$, with lower vertices $v_j$, and define $\phi_j(x)=B^{-1}K^{-n}\psi(K(x-v_j))$. All derivatives through order $n$ vanish at support boundaries, so the weak derivatives of these finite sums are their classical derivatives, as follows by integration by parts with zero boundary terms. Disjoint support interiors imply that every $f_\sigma=\sum_{j=1}^{K^d}\sigma_j\phi_j$, $\sigma_j\in\{-1,1\}$, belongs to $F_{d,n}$, since $\|D^\alpha f_\sigma\|_\infty\le K^{|\alpha|-n}\le1$ for $|\alpha|\le n$. At the center $x_j$ of cube $j$, $f_\sigma(x_j)=\sigma_jB^{-1}K^{-n}$. [given, construct, algebra]

1.3 For clause (iii), nonlinearity of $f$ implies that its Hessian is nonzero at an interior point; otherwise all first derivatives are constant on the connected cube and $f$ is affine. A symmetric nonzero Hessian has a direction with nonzero second directional derivative. By continuity choose a short interior segment and parameterize it by $t\in[0,1]$, so $g(t)=f(a+tv)$ has either $g''\ge c_0>0$ throughout or $g''\le-c_0<0$ throughout. The approximating network restricts to a scalar-input network of at most the same depth and unit count. [given, choose, construct]

2.1 For sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, choose $K=\lfloor(1/(4B\varepsilon))^{1/n}\rfloor\ge\tfrac12(1/(4B\varepsilon))^{1/n}$. Then the center amplitude $B^{-1}K^{-n}$ is at least $4\varepsilon$. Every approximant to $f_\sigma$ within $\varepsilon$ has positive output at centers with $\sigma_j=1$ and negative output at centers with $\sigma_j=-1$. Thus the threshold classifiers from the one fixed architecture shatter these $K^d\ge c_{d,n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}$ centers. [step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 Combining step 2.1 with the first bound in [F3] gives $c_{d,n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}\le CW^2$, hence $W\ge c\varepsilon^{-d/(2n)}$. Shrinking the constant covers the remaining non-small accuracies, because any scalar-output architecture has $W\ge1$. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 If $L\le c_1(\log(1/\varepsilon))^p$, the second bound in [F3] gives $c_{d,n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}\le Cc_1^2W(\log(1/\varepsilon))^{2p}\log(2W)$. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, if $W\ge\varepsilon^{-d/n}$ the desired conclusion follows directly since $\log(1/\varepsilon)\ge1$. Otherwise $\log(2W)\le\log2+(d/n)\log(1/\varepsilon)\le C_{d,n}\log(1/\varepsilon)$, and rearrangement gives $W\ge c_2\varepsilon^{-d/n}(\log(1/\varepsilon))^{-2p-1}$. No assumption on continuity of the targetwise weight choices was made in either shattering argument. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Write $H=L-2$ and let $U$ be its hidden unit count. Discard units with no path to the output and absorb input-independent units into their downstream biases; this preserves the restricted function and does not increase the remaining hidden unit count. Partition the remaining hidden units by topological rank, where rank is the greatest number of hidden units on an input-to-that-unit path. Every rank is at most $H$, and every predecessor hidden unit has smaller rank. Let $n_\ell$ count rank $\ell$, setting $n_\ell=0$ for unused ranks; these are counts in a partition, not inserted computation layers. Maintain a common affine partition for the input and all earlier unit outputs, retaining those outputs when the next rank is processed. Every preactivation at that rank is affine on each existing interval, including all skip-edge terms, so its at most $n_\ell$ zeros split that interval into at most $n_\ell+1$ pieces. Thus the interval count in [F1] applies to this rank partition, and $\sum_\ell n_\ell\le U$. By AM–GM, the restricted network has at most $M\le\prod_{\ell=1}^{H}(n_\ell+1)\le(1+U/H)^H$ affine intervals. One has length $h\ge1/M$. On this interval the network output $r$ is affine. If $g''\ge c_0$, midpoint convexity applied to $g(t)-c_0t^2/2$ gives $g(a)+g(b)-2g((a+b)/2)\ge c_0h^2/4$; in the other case apply this to $-g$. The affine second difference of $r$ is zero; the three uniform errors bound the absolute second difference of $g$ by $4\varepsilon$. Thus $\varepsilon\ge c_0/(16M^2)$. Rearranging gives $U\ge c(f,L)\varepsilon^{-1/(2H)}$ for small $\varepsilon$. Each hidden unit has a counted bias parameter, so the number of weights is at least $U$, proving clause (iii). AC and its countable-choice consequence are inherited through the stated Sobolev representative and width suppliers; the finite sign and segment constructions require no additional choice. [F1, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For integers $m\ge0$ and $d\ge1$, the complement of any $m$ affine hyperplanes in $\mathbb R^d$ has at most $\sum_{j=0}^{d}\binom mj$ connected components, with $\binom mj=0$ for $j>m$. If the hyperplanes are in general position, meaning every $q\le d$ of them meet in codimension $q$ and no $d+1$ have a common point, the number of components is exactly this sum; such arrangements exist for every $m,d$. On a zero-dimensional affine image there is at most one full-dimensional activation cell.

## Statement references

[Serra et al., Lemma 5 and proof: hyperplane arrangement bound](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/serra18b/serra18b.pdf)

[Sullivan, §5.2: arrangement recurrence](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/index.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integers $m\ge0$, $d\ge0$, and an arrangement of $m$ affine hyperplanes in $\mathbb R^d$, where for $d=0$ the arrangement is interpreted as sign conditions on a single point.

## Proof

1.1 Let $R(m,d)$ be the largest possible number of complementary regions. With no hyperplanes or in dimension zero, $R(0,d)=R(m,0)=1$. Adding the last hyperplane $H$ splits only old regions that meet $H$; each old region is convex, so its intersection with $H$ contributes at most one region of the arrangement induced on $H\cong\mathbb R^{d-1}$. Hence $R(m,d)\le R(m-1,d)+R(m-1,d-1)$. [given, construct]

2.1 Induction on $m+d$ and Pascal's identity give $R(m,d)\le\sum_{j=0}^d\binom{m-1}{j}+\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\binom{m-1}{j}=\sum_{j=0}^{d}\binom mj$. If the arrangement is in general position, its restriction to $H$ is also in general position and has $m-1$ hyperplanes in dimension $d-1$; every one of its regions lies in one old region and cuts that region into two, so the recurrence is equality. Such arrangements exist: choose distinct $t_1,\ldots,t_m$ and use $H_i:\sum_{k=1}^d t_i^{k-1}x_k=t_i^d$. Any $q\le d$ normals are independent by the Vandermonde determinant, while no $d+1$ equations have a common solution because their augmented Vandermonde matrix is invertible. The same induction gives the claimed exact sum. [step 1.1, algebra, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $n_0,L,n_1,\ldots,n_L\ge1$ be integers, consider a layered ReLU network of input dimension $n_0$ and hidden widths $n_1,\ldots,n_L$, and let $r\in\mathbb N_0$. Set $R_{L+1}(r)=1$ and, for $1\le\ell\le L$, define $$R_\ell(r)=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(r,n_\ell)}\binom{n_\ell}{j}R_{\ell+1}\!\left(\min\{r,n_\ell-j\}\right).$$ After layers $\ell,\ldots,L$, any activation cell whose current affine image has dimension at most $r$ produces at most $R_\ell(r)$ activation cells.

## Statement references

[Serra et al., proof of Theorem 1 and Appendix C: rank-sensitive recursion](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/serra18b/serra18b-supp.pdf)

[Sullivan, §5.2: recursive arrangement count](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/index.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A layered ReLU network with widths $n_0,n_1,\ldots,n_L$, a layer index $\ell$, and an affine image of dimension at most $r$.

[F1] An arrangement of $n$ affine hyperplanes in dimension $r$ has at most $\sum_{j=0}^{\min(r,n)}\binom nj$ full-dimensional regions ([[lem-hyperplane-arrangement-region-count]]).

[F2] Each hidden unit applies $\rho(z)=\max\{0,z\}$ to its affine preactivation ([[def-relu-network]]).

## Proof

1.1 Restrict the $n_\ell$ preactivations to the current affine image. A restriction that is identically zero is forced inactive and does not cut the image; a nonzero constant restriction also has a fixed activation bit and does not cut it. The remaining zero sets are affine hyperplanes in a space of dimension at most $r$. By [F1], their complement has at most $S=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(r,n_\ell)}\binom{n_\ell}{j}$ full-dimensional chambers. Every full-dimensional activation-pattern cell has one of these chambers as its relative interior: nonzero preactivations are strictly signed there, while identically zero restrictions contribute the fixed inactive bit. Conversely, boundary points of nonconstant zero sets are assigned inactive and do not create additional full-dimensional patterns. For a fixed active subset $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n_\ell\}$, its constraints are affine strict or weak half-spaces on the current image, so their intersection is convex and gives at most one full-dimensional cell. By [F2], the layer output on that cell is the diagonal projection of the affine layer output that keeps coordinates in $A$ and sets the others to zero; its next affine image therefore has dimension at most $\min(r,|A|)$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Backward induction in the displayed recurrence shows that $R_{\ell+1}(s)$ is nondecreasing in $s$: increasing $s$ adds nonnegative terms and does not decrease any argument. Therefore, among at most $S$ distinct active subsets its sum is maximized by choosing the $S$ subsets of largest cardinality. Those can be taken to have sizes $n_\ell-j$ with multiplicities $\binom{n_\ell}{j}$ for $0\le j\le\min(r,n_\ell)$; their total number is exactly $S$. The associated next dimensions are at most $\min(r,n_\ell-j)$, giving the displayed recurrence. Induction backward from $R_{L+1}=1$ proves the claim. [step 1.1, induction, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n_0,L,n_1,\ldots,n_L\ge1$ be integers and consider a standard adjacent-layer ReLU network with input dimension $n_0$ and $L$ hidden layers of widths $n_1,\ldots,n_L$. Define $J$ to be the set of integer tuples $(j_1,\ldots,j_L)$ satisfying $$0\le j_\ell\le\min\{n_0,n_1-j_1,\ldots,n_{\ell-1}-j_{\ell-1},n_\ell\}\qquad(1\le\ell\le L),$$ where for $\ell=1$ the terms between $n_0$ and $n_\ell$ are absent. The number of full-dimensional activation-pattern regions is at most $$\sum_{(j_1,\ldots,j_L)\in J}\prod_{\ell=1}^L\binom{n_\ell}{j_\ell}.$$ For one hidden layer, the bound is attained by hyperplanes in general position.

## Statement references

[Serra et al., Theorem 1 and proof: exact ReLU region upper bound](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/serra18b/serra18b.pdf)

[Sullivan, §5.2: ReLU region upper bound](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/index.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The layer widths and region convention in the statement, and the recursion in [[lem-relu-rank-sensitive-region-recursion]].

[F1] Starting from an affine image of dimension $n_0$, the continuation count satisfies the recurrence defining $R_1(n_0)$ ([[lem-relu-rank-sensitive-region-recursion]]).

[F2] An arrangement of $n_1$ hyperplanes in general position in dimension $n_0$ has exactly $\sum_{j=0}^{\min(n_0,n_1)}\binom{n_1}{j}$ regions ([[lem-hyperplane-arrangement-region-count]]).

## Proof

1.1 Expand [F1]'s recurrence successively for $\ell=1,\ldots,L$. At layer $\ell$, the prior choices have reduced the available affine dimension to at most $\min(n_0,n_1-j_1,\ldots,n_{\ell-1}-j_{\ell-1})$, so the allowed next indices are exactly those in $J$. Each term contributes the factor $\binom{n_\ell}{j_\ell}$, and the terminal continuation is $1$. This gives the displayed sum. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 If $L=1$, the first layer is an arrangement of $n_1$ affine hyperplanes in the input space. By [F2], a general-position choice attains the sum, proving tightness for one hidden layer. [F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

For every integer $n\ge3$, there is a scalar-input standard adjacent-layer ReLU block with one hidden layer of width $n$ whose output is continuous and piecewise affine on $[0,1]$, has exactly $n$ interior breakpoints, and maps each of the resulting $n+1$ intervals bijectively onto $[0,1]$. Composing blocks of widths $n_1,\ldots,n_L\ge3$ yields $\prod_{\ell=1}^L(n_\ell+1)$ full-dimensional activation regions in one input dimension.

## Statement references

[Serra et al., Theorem 7 and Appendix D: exact one-dimensional fold construction](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/serra18b/serra18b.pdf)

[Sullivan, §5.2: composition of one-dimensional folds](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/index.html)

## Illustrative plot

The horizontal axis is the normalized input $x\in[0,1]$ and the vertical axis is the block output. The marked interior vertices are exactly the breakpoints $t_i=(2i-1)/7$; the graph shows each of the four subintervals mapping bijectively onto $[0,1]$. The proof verifies the hinge representation algebraically; this plot is illustrative.

  \node[left] at (0,1) {$1$};
\end{tikzpicture}

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The ReLU network convention in [[def-relu-network]] and an integer $n\ge3$.

[F1] A ReLU network may use affine skip connections and a final affine output, with depth counting input and output layers ([[def-relu-network]]).

## Proof

1.1 Set $t_0=0$, $t_{n+1}=1$, and $t_i=(2i-1)/(2n+1)$ for $1\le i\le n$. Put $y_i=0$ for even $i$ and $y_i=1$ for odd $i$, and define $s_i=(y_{i+1}-y_i)/(t_{i+1}-t_i)$ for $0\le i\le n$. The piecewise-affine interpolant through $(t_i,y_i)$ maps every interval bijectively onto $[0,1]$. Its first slope is $s_0=2n+1$, while $s_2=(2n+1)/2$ and $s_3=-(2n+1)/2$, so $s_3-s_2=-s_0$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Use hidden units $h_i(x)=\rho(x-t_i)$ for $i\ne3$ and $h_3(x)=\rho(t_3-x)$. Give unit $i$ output coefficient $a_i=s_i-s_{i-1}$, including $a_3=s_3-s_2=-s_0$, and set output bias $d=-a_3t_3$. Before $t_1$ only $h_3$ is active, so the output is $d+a_3(t_3-x)=s_0x$. At every $t_i$, the slope changes by $a_i$: for $i\ne3$ this is the right-facing ReLU slope jump, and for $i=3$ it is the left-facing ReLU slope jump. Thus the network output has the same initial value and slope jumps as the interpolant in step 1.1, so it equals that interpolant on $[0,1]$. This uses exactly $n$ hidden ReLU units and one affine output. [step 1.1, F1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Each fold block's output is affine in the current hidden layer, so it can be substituted into the affine preactivations of the next adjacent layer without adding an intervening layer. At each knot $t_i$, exactly the corresponding hidden unit changes activation, so the $n+1$ intervals have distinct activation patterns. Each existing interval is cut into $n_{\ell+1}+1$ subintervals, each mapped bijectively onto $[0,1]$; the new layer's patterns distinguish these subintervals, while earlier layer patterns distinguish their parent intervals. Induction over the blocks gives $\prod_{\ell=1}^L(n_\ell+1)$ intervals, each a distinct full-dimensional activation region. [step 2.1, induction] ∎

## Statement

For a standard adjacent-layer ReLU network with one input dimension and $L\ge1$ hidden layers of widths $n_1,\ldots,n_L\ge3$, the maximum number of full-dimensional activation regions is exactly $\prod_{\ell=1}^L(n_\ell+1)$. For integers $n_0,L\ge1$ and widths $n_1,\ldots,n_L\ge3n_0$, there exists a standard adjacent-layer ReLU network with at least $$\left(\prod_{\ell=1}^{L-1}\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n_\ell}{n_0}\right\rfloor+1\right)^{n_0}\right)\sum_{j=0}^{n_0}\binom{n_L}{j}$$ full-dimensional activation regions.

## Statement references

[Serra et al., Theorems 7–8 and Appendices D–E: exact 1D and multidimensional lower constructions](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/serra18b/serra18b.pdf)

[Sullivan, §5.2: repeated folds and activation-region counts](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/index.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The layer width conditions in the statement and the fold, region upper-bound, and hyperplane arrangement results below.

[F1] A width-$q$ ReLU block for $q\ge3$ maps each of its $q+1$ intervals bijectively onto $[0,1]$ ([[lem-relu-folding-block]]).

[F2] For input dimension $n_0$ and widths $n_1,\ldots,n_L$, the region count is at most the rank-sensitive sum in [[thm-relu-linear-region-upper-bound]].

[F3] $n$ hyperplanes in general position in dimension $d$ cut that space into $\sum_{j=0}^{d}\binom nj$ regions when $n\ge d$ ([[lem-hyperplane-arrangement-region-count]]).

## Proof

1.1 Compose the width-$n_\ell$ blocks from [F1]. Each existing interval is divided into $n_{\ell+1}+1$ intervals, each mapped onto $[0,1]$, so after all $L$ layers the number is $\prod_{\ell=1}^L(n_\ell+1)$. [given, F1, induction]

2.1 For $n_0=1$, each index $j_\ell$ in [F2]'s upper sum is $0$ or $1$: the previous factors leave $n_i-j_i\ge2$ for every $n_i\ge3$. Thus the sum factors as $\prod_{\ell=1}^L(1+n_\ell)$, so the count in step 1.1 is exact. For the multidimensional construction, in each of the first $L-1$ layers allocate $q_\ell=\lfloor n_\ell/n_0\rfloor\ge3$ units to each coordinate and implement an independent width-$q_\ell$ fold on that coordinate; set any remaining units constantly inactive. Each prior box is thereby subdivided into $(q_\ell+1)^{n_0}$ boxes, each mapped bijectively onto $[0,1]^{n_0}$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, construct, algebra]

3.1 Take an arrangement of $n_L$ hyperplanes in general position in $\mathbb R^{n_0}$. It has $S=\sum_{j=0}^{n_0}\binom{n_L}{j}$ chambers by [F3], and there are finitely many chambers. Choose one point $y_C$ in each chamber and set $A=\max_C\|y_C\|_\infty$. With $c=(1/2,\ldots,1/2)$ and $\lambda=1/(4(1+A))$, all points $c+\lambda y_C$ lie in the interior of $[0,1]^{n_0}$. ## Statement

Let $L\ge0$, let $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L|x-y|$, and let $N\ge1$ be an integer. The Bernstein polynomial $$B_Nf(x):=\sum_{j=0}^N f(j/N)\binom Njx^j(1-x)^{N-j}$$ satisfies $$\sup_{x\in[0,1]}|B_Nf(x)-f(x)|\le\frac{L}{2\sqrt N}.$$

## Statement references

[Lorentz, Chapter 1: Bernstein polynomials and binomial moments](https://archive.org/download/bernsteinpolynomi0000lore/bernsteinpolynomi0000lore.pdf)

[Sullivan, §5.1: Bernstein expectation representation](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/index.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real number $L\ge0$, an $L$-Lipschitz function $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$, an integer $N\ge1$, and $x\in[0,1]$.

## Proof

1.1 Take independent Bernoulli variables $X_1,\ldots,X_N$ with success probability $x$, and put $S=\sum_iX_i$. The binomial formula gives $B_Nf(x)=\mathbb E f(S/N)$, so the Lipschitz hypothesis yields $|B_Nf(x)-f(x)|\le L\mathbb E|S/N-x|$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Independence gives $\mathbb E S=\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb E X_i=Nx$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S)=\sum_{i=1}^N\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=Nx(1-x)$, because each Bernoulli variable has variance $x(1-x)$. Therefore Cauchy–Schwarz yields $\mathbb E|S/N-x|\le\sqrt{\mathbb E(S/N-x)^2}=\sqrt{x(1-x)/N}\le1/(2\sqrt N)$. The estimate holds for every $x$, proving the uniform bound. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎
