## Statement

Let integers $k,d,t,\alpha,\beta\ge1$ be given, put $q=k^3+4$, and define $f(x)=h^q(x_1)$ on $[0,1]^d$, where $h(z)=\rho(2\rho(z)-4\rho(z-1/2))$ and $\rho(z)=\max\{0,z\}$. A gate is $(t,\alpha,\beta)$-semi-algebraic if it is a finite sum of polynomial pieces of degree at most $\beta$ multiplied by conjunctions of the tests $p_i<0$ and $p_i\ge0$ for one common list of at most $t$ polynomials of degree at most $\alpha$. A computational layer counts gates and excludes input coordinates; the output gate is counted and may be ReLU. In this convention $f$ has $2q$ computational layers, $3q$ gates, and at most $d+4$ shared scalar parameter slots. In the affine-output ReLU convention one may instead append an identity affine output, adding one computation unit and one computational layer.

For an integer node budget $m\ge1$, define

$$B(k,m,t,\alpha,\beta)=\max_{1\le\ell\le\min(k,m)}2(2t\alpha m/\ell)^\ell\beta^{\ell(\ell+1)/2}.$$

Every network of these semi-algebraic gates with at most $k$ computational layers and $m$ gates satisfies

$$\|f-g\|_{L^1([0,1]^d)}\ge\max\{0,(2^q+1-2B(k,m,t,\alpha,\beta))/(16\cdot2^q)\}.$$

In particular its error is at least $1/64$ whenever $B(k,m,t,\alpha,\beta)\le2^{q-2}$. The original exponential budget $m\le2^{k/(t\alpha\beta)}$ is sufficient under the explicit parameter condition

$$(t\alpha\beta)2^{k/(t\alpha\beta)}\le2^k.$$

For each fixed gate class this condition holds for all sufficiently large $k$, and it holds for every $k\ge1$ for $(t,\alpha,\beta)=(1,1,1)$. Independently of that condition, every linear combination of at most $t$ affine-threshold decision trees, each with at most $2^{k^3/t}$ total nodes including leaves and constant leaf outputs, has error at least $1/64$ for every positive integer $t$. The gate-parameter condition cannot simply be dropped from the exponential-budget assertion.

## Statement references

[Telgarsky, Definition 2.1 and Sections 3.1–3.4](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v49/telgarsky16.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The parameters, gate definitions and complexity conventions in the statement. All root counts and interval partitions below disregard a finite set of endpoints, which has Lebesgue measure zero.

[F1] The $q$th tent iterate has $2^q$ equal affine intervals, with alternating slopes of magnitude $2^q$ and range $[0,1]$ on each ([[lem-relu-tent-iterate-depth]]).

[F2] An $L$-Lipschitz target has Bernstein error at most $L/(2\sqrt N)$ ([[lem-bernstein-polynomial-lipschitz-error]]).

## Proof

1.1 A computational block with two gates $\rho(z)$, $\rho(z-1/2)$ followed by the gate $\rho(2u-4v)$ computes $h$. Compose $q$ blocks, identifying repeated parameter slots. Only the coordinate-selection vector of length $d$ and the four scalar slots $0,-1/2,2,-4$ are needed: the first vector supplies coefficient $1$ for the selected coordinate and coefficient $0$ for the others, and its selected coefficient $1$ may also supply the fixed unit coefficient in subsequent blocks. There are $3q$ gates and $2q$ computational layers. Appending an affine identity produces the stated conversion. On the cube the output is the tent iterate in [F1]. [given, F1, construct]

1.2 Fix all coordinates except $x_1=z$, and consider any comparator with actual nonempty layer widths $m_1,\ldots,m_\ell$ and $\ell\le k$, $\sum_i m_i\le m$. Maintain one common partition of the line into open intervals on which all gates through layer $i$ are polynomials of degree at most $\beta^i$. Initially there is one interval and input coordinates are affine. In one previous interval, each of the at most $tm_i$ gate predicates at layer $i$ is a polynomial of degree at most $\alpha\beta^{i-1}$ after substitution, hence introduces at most that many roots unless identically zero, in which case its test is constant. Thus the new common partition has at most $1+tm_i\alpha\beta^{i-1}$ pieces per old piece. On each piece all indicators are constant, and the gate output is a polynomial of degree at most $\beta^i$. Skip edges cause no change: earlier outputs already have polynomial degree at most $\beta^{i-1}$ on this common partition. [given, construct, induction]

2.1 It follows that the threshold classifier $1[g(z)\ge1/2]$ is constant on at most $C=(1+\beta^\ell)\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}(1+tm_i\alpha\beta^{i-1})$ open intervals. Identically zero threshold polynomials contribute no roots. Since every factor's nonconstant term is at least one, $C\le2(2t\alpha)^\ell\beta^{\ell(\ell+1)/2}\prod_i m_i\le2(2t\alpha m/\ell)^\ell\beta^{\ell(\ell+1)/2}\le B$, where the penultimate inequality is AM–GM. The same partition argument applies for every fixed offset of the remaining coordinates. [step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Put $T=2^q$. By [F1], the target threshold classifier alternates on $N=T+1$ intervals in $[0,1]$. Its two end intervals have length $1/(2T)$ and each of the others length $1/T$. The integral of $|f-1/2|$ is $1/(8T)$ on each end interval and $1/(4T)$ on each other interval. A comparator classifier with at most $C$ intervals has at most $C-1$ internal boundaries. Discard target intervals containing such a boundary. At most $C-1$ intervals are discarded; in each of the at most $C$ remaining runs the alternating target labels disagree with the constant comparator on at least half the run length minus $1/2$. Hence at least $(N-2C)/2$ target intervals disagree throughout, whenever this quantity is positive. Their contribution gives $\int_0^1|f-g|\,dz\ge\max\{0,(N-2C)/(16T)\}$. Endpoint equalities have no effect on the integral. Integrating in the other coordinates gives the displayed bound and its $B\le T/4$ consequence. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Write $s=t\alpha\beta$. For $\ell=1$, the bound in step 2.1 is $4sm$. For $\ell\ge2$, use $(2/\ell)^\ell\le1$, $\ell(\ell+1)/2\le\ell^2$, and $\ell\le\ell^2$ to bound it by $2(sm)^{\ell^2}$. Therefore $B\le4(sm)^{k^2}$. If $m\le2^{k/s}$ and $s2^{k/s}\le2^k$, then $B\le2^{k^3+2}=T/4$. For $s=1$ the condition is equality; for fixed $s>1$ it is equivalent to $k\ge s\log_2(s)/(s-1)$, so it eventually holds. This proves the exponential-budget assertion with all its indicated parameter cases. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Remove any unary branches and branches whose two outcomes compute the same subtree function, replacing them by their sole or common continuation; these reductions preserve the represented function and never increase the node count. A decision tree is then full binary: every internal branch has exactly two children. If it has $I$ internal nodes and $J$ leaves, its edge count is both $2I$ and $I+J-1$, so $J=I+1$ and $r=2I+1$. Consequently a full binary decision tree with at most $r$ total nodes has at most $(r-1)/2$ internal branch nodes. On a fixed line each nonconstant affine test has at most one zero. A sum of at most $t$ such trees, with $r\le2^{A/t}$ and $A=k^3$, is constant away from at most $t(2^{A/t}-1)/2$ thresholds. Convexity of $u\mapsto2^u$ yields $t(2^{A/t}-1)\le2^A-1$ for $t\ge1$. Thus its threshold classifier has at most $(2^A+1)/2\le2^{A+2}=T/4$ intervals. Step 3.1 proves the tree assertion. Finally at $k=d=t=\alpha=1$, the target $h^5$ is $32$-Lipschitz; its degree-$2^{22}$ Bernstein polynomial has uniform error at most $32/(2\sqrt{2^{22}})=1/128$ by [F2]. This polynomial is one $(1,1,2^{22})$ gate, allowed by the node budget $2^{1/2^{22}}>1$, so the parameter restriction cannot be omitted. [step 3.1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every integer $k\ge1$ and dimension $d\ge1$, the stated Telgarsky bound asserts that there is a function $f(x)=h^{k^3+4}(x_1)$, where $h(z)=\rho(2\rho(z)-4\rho(z-1/2))$, computed by a ReLU network with $2k^3+8$ layers, $3k^3+12$ computation nodes, and $4+d$ distinct parameters, such that for every positive integer triple $t,\alpha,\beta$ its $L^1([0,1]^d)$ distance from every function in the following union is at least $1/64$: functions computed in at most $k$ computational layers by networks with at most $2^{k/(t\alpha\beta)}$ gate nodes whose gates are $(t,\alpha,\beta)$-semi-algebraic; and sums of at most $t$ affine-threshold decision trees, each with at most $2^{k^3/t}$ total nodes, including leaves. Here a $(t,\alpha,\beta)$-semi-algebraic gate is a map $g:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R$ expressible as a finite sum of polynomial pieces $p_j$ of degree at most $\beta$, each multiplied by indicators of conjunctions of signs of at most $t$ predicate polynomials $q_i$ of degree at most $\alpha$; an affine-threshold decision tree recursively branches on tests $\langle a,x\rangle-b\ge0$ and has constant real outputs at its leaves.

## Statement references

[Telgarsky, Theorem 1.1 and §3.4: depth-separation claim and proof](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v49/telgarsky16.pdf)

[Telgarsky lecture notes, §5.2: tent-map depth separation](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/index.html)

[Telgarsky lecture notes, §5.1: Bernstein expectation representation](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/index.html)

[Telgarsky lecture notes, §5.1: binomial approximation bound used in the refutation](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/index.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The claimed bound in the preceding statement.

[F1] The map $\tau(x)=2\rho(x)-4\rho(x-1/2)$ maps $[0,1]$ to itself and is $2$-Lipschitz ([[lem-relu-tent-iterate-depth]]).

[F2] Every $L$-Lipschitz function on $[0,1]$ has degree-$N$ Bernstein polynomial approximation error at most $L/(2\sqrt N)$ ([[lem-bernstein-polynomial-lipschitz-error]]).

## Refutation

1.1 Set $d=k=t=\alpha=1$, $\beta=N=2^{22}$. The gate $P_N(z)=B_N(h^5)(z)$ is a single $(1,1,N)$-semi-algebraic gate: use the constant predicate polynomial $q_1(z)=1$ with condition $q_1(z)\ge0$, and the one polynomial piece $p_1(z)=P_N(z)$, whose degree is at most $N$. The predicate condition holds for every $z$, and $q_1$ has degree $0\le\alpha$. The claimed node cap is $2^{1/N}<2$, so the integer node count of this network is at most one. Hence $P_N$ belongs to the first class in the claimed union. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 On $[0,1]$, the formula for $h$ reduces to $2x$ on $[0,1/2]$ and $2-2x$ on $[1/2,1]$, so it is the tent map in [F1], maps the interval into itself, and is $2$-Lipschitz. Thus $h^5$ is $32$-Lipschitz. Applying [F2] at $N=2^{22}$ gives $\|P_N-h^5\|_\infty\le32/(2\sqrt{2^{22}})=1/128$. Consequently $\int_0^1|P_N(x)-h^5(x)|\,dx\le1/128<1/64$, contradicting the claimed infimum lower bound. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Example

For $f(x)=x^2/2$ on $[0,1]$, which belongs to the unit ball of $W^{1,\infty}((0,1))$, the target-independent theorem supplies one architecture that works for the whole unit ball with size $O(\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\varepsilon))$, while the adaptive theorem supplies an architecture chosen for this $f$ with size $O(1/[\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon)])$ and depth $6$. 2.1 Apply [F2] and [F3] to this same target. Their size ratio is $[1/(\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon))]/[\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\varepsilon)]=(\log(1/\varepsilon))^{-2}$ up to constants, which tends to zero. This compares existence rates only and makes no claim about optimization or training. [step 1.1, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

Choose a one-hidden-layer ReLU network with input dimension $2$, hidden width $10$, and hidden preactivation hyperplanes in general position. ## Definition

Let $D,O\subseteq\mathbb Z^2$ be input and output index sets, let $C_{\rm in},C_{\rm out}$ be positive integers, and let $x:D\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}}$ assign a row vector of input channels to each input site. A boundary extension is a function $\widetilde x:\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}}$ whose restriction to $D$ is $x$; zero padding is the extension that is zero off $D$. Choose a finite receptive-field offset set $K\subseteq\mathbb Z^2$, a positive integer stride vector $s\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2$, an origin $a\in\mathbb Z^2$, one matrix $W_\delta\in\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}\times C_{\rm out}}$ for each $\delta\in K$, and an output bias row vector $b\in\mathbb R^{C_{\rm out}}$. The discrete convolutional layer is the map $y:O\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm out}}$ given by

$$
y(p)=b+\sum_{\delta\in K}\widetilde x(a+s\odot p+\delta)W_\delta\qquad(p\in O),
$$

where $s\odot p$ is coordinatewise multiplication. Thus each output uses only the input sites in its receptive field, mixes input channels by matrix multiplication, and uses the same weights and bias at every output site. With unit stride on the full lattice and no boundary truncation, this formula is a discrete cross-correlation; many machine-learning software packages call it convolution. Mathematical convolution instead reverses the kernel offsets. The choices of $O$, the extension $\widetilde x$, and the stride specify cropping, padding, and subsampling, and need not preserve a symmetry of the full lattice.

## Definition

Let $G$ be a group acting on the left on a set $S$, and let $V$ be a set of feature values. A feature map is a function $f:S\to V$. For $u\in G$, the induced transformation of feature maps is

$$
(L_u f)(x)=f(u^{-1}\cdot x)\qquad(x\in S).
$$

It is a left action on the set of feature maps: the group acts by reindexing sites and leaves the feature values unchanged. In particular, for maps $F:G\to V$ on the group itself with its left multiplication action, $(L_uF)(g)=F(u^{-1}g)$.

## Definition references

[[def-group-action|left action of a group on a set]]

[[def-function|functions and declared domains/codomains]]

[Cohen and Welling, “Group Equivariant Convolutional Networks,” §4.4, Eqs. (4)–(5)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1602.07576)

[Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville, *Deep Learning*, Chapter 9 §9.2](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/convnets.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A group $G$ acts on the left on a set $S$, and $f:S\to V$ is a feature map. Verify that the displayed transformations form a left action.

[F1] [[def-group-action]]: A left action satisfies $e\cdot x=x$ and $(gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$ for every $g,h\in G$ and $x\in S$.

[F2] [[def-group]]: A group operation is associative, has an identity, and every element has a two-sided inverse.

## Proof

1.1 For each $x\in S$, $(L_e f)(x)=f(e^{-1}\cdot x)=f(x)$ by the identity law in [F1], so $L_e f=f$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For $u,v\in G$, the element $v^{-1}u^{-1}$ is a two-sided inverse of $uv$, since $(uv)(v^{-1}u^{-1})=u(vv^{-1})u^{-1}=e$ and $(v^{-1}u^{-1})(uv)=v^{-1}(u^{-1}u)v=e$. Two two-sided inverses $a,b$ of an element $z$ coincide because $a=a(zb)=(az)b=b$; hence $(uv)^{-1}=v^{-1}u^{-1}$. Therefore, for each $x\in S$, $(L_u(L_v f))(x)=f(v^{-1}\cdot(u^{-1}\cdot x))=f((v^{-1}u^{-1})\cdot x)=f((uv)^{-1}\cdot x)=(L_{uv}f)(x)$ by [F1]. Thus $L_uL_v=L_{uv}$. [given, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$ and let $X$ be a set. A **left action** of
$G$ on $X$ is a function $G\times X\to X$, written $(g,x)\mapsto g\cdot x$,
such that

$$e\cdot x=x,\qquad (gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$$

for all $g,h\in G$ and $x\in X$. Then $X$ is a **$G$-set**. The action is
**transitive** when every $x,y\in X$ satisfy $g\cdot x=y$ for some $g\in G$.
It is **faithful** when $g\cdot x=x$ for every $x\in X$ implies $g=e$.

## Definition

A **group** is a monoid $(G,*,e)$ ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]) in which every
element is invertible ([[def-invertible-element]]). Written out, a group is a set
$G$ with a binary operation $*$ ([[def-binary-operation]]) and an element
$e \in G$ such that

- **(G1)** $(x * y) * z = x * (y * z)$ for all $x, y, z \in G$;
- **(G2)** $e * x = x = x * e$ for every $x \in G$;
- **(G3)** for every $x \in G$ there is $y \in G$ with $y * x = e = x * y$.

By [[lem-identity-unique]] the element $e$ of (G2) is unique, and by
[[lem-inverse-unique]] the element $y$ of (G3) is unique for each $x$ and is
determined by either one of the two equations alone. So the notations $e$ for the
identity and $x^{-1}$ for the inverse of $x$ are legitimate, and asserting
$y * x = e$ alone already says $y = x^{-1}$.

A group is **abelian**, or **commutative**, when its operation is commutative:
$x * y = y * x$ for all $x, y \in G$.

**Notation.** The operation is usually written multiplicatively, $xy$ for
$x * y$, with identity $e$ (or $1$) and inverse $x^{-1}$. For an abelian group it
is often written additively, $x + y$, with identity $0$ and inverse $-x$; the two
notations describe the same notion and nothing below depends on the choice. We
write $G$ for the group when the operation is understood.

## Remarks

- **Why (G3) may be stated one-sidedly in practice.** The axiom as written asks
  for a two-sided inverse. Because [[lem-inverse-unique]] is proved before this
  definition, and is proved in the sharp form "a left inverse and a right inverse
  of the same element coincide", verifying either equation for a candidate $y$
  suffices once the element is known to be invertible. Nothing on this page ever
  uses a one-sided inverse without that lemma standing behind it.

- **A group is a monoid, not merely like one.** Every statement proved for
  monoids applies verbatim to groups. In the other direction the invertible
  elements of a monoid form a group ([[lem-monoid-units-form-a-group]]), so
  groups arise inside every monoid.

- **The axioms are not independent of the notation, but the content is.** Read
  additively, (G1)–(G3) are exactly the additive axioms in the definition of a
  field ([[def-field]]), whose axiom (A) says in as many words that $(F,+)$ is an
  abelian group and whose axiom (M) says the same of
  $(F \setminus \{0\}, \cdot)$; so every field already carries two groups.

## Definition

Let $\rho=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ be the quarter-turn matrix and $\sigma=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ a reflection matrix. Let $C_4=\{\rho^j:j=0,1,2,3\}$ and $D_4=\{\rho^j,\rho^j\sigma:j=0,1,2,3\}$, with matrix multiplication. For $A=C_4$ or $D_4$, define $P_A=\mathbb Z^2\times A$ with multiplication

$$
(t,M)(s,N)=(t+Ms,MN).
$$

Each pair $(t,M)$ acts on lattice sites by $x\mapsto Mx+t$. The p4 lattice-symmetry group is $P_{C_4}$, generated by integer translations and quarter-turns. The p4m lattice-symmetry group is $P_{D_4}$, generated by integer translations, quarter-turns, and reflections. Their orientation subgroups have respectively four and eight elements, but both full groups are infinite because they contain every integer translation.

## Definition references

[[def-group|group axioms]]

[[def-group-action|left actions of groups on sets]]

[[def-function|functions and declared domains/codomains]]

[Cohen and Welling, “Group Equivariant Convolutional Networks,” §§4.1–4.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1602.07576)

[Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville, *Deep Learning*, Chapter 9 §§9.1–9.2](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/convnets.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The matrices $\rho,\sigma$, the sets $C_4,D_4$, and the pair multiplication displayed in the Definition. Prove that these are groups acting on $\mathbb Z^2$, and that the full groups are infinite.

[F1] [[def-group]]: A group operation is associative, has an identity, and every element has a two-sided inverse.

[F2] [[def-group-action]]: A left action satisfies $e\cdot x=x$ and $(gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$ for every $g,h\in G$ and $x$ in the acted-on set.

## Proof

1.1 The matrices satisfy $\rho^4=I$, $\sigma^2=I$, and $\sigma\rho\sigma=\rho^{-1}$. The rotation matrices are $I,\rho,-I,-\rho$, hence distinct; their products add exponents modulo $4$, and $(\rho^j)^{-1}=\rho^{-j}$. The four matrices $\sigma,\rho\sigma,-\sigma,-\rho\sigma$ are distinct, have determinant $-1$, and differ from the rotations, which have determinant $1$. Thus $C_4$ has four elements and $D_4$ has eight. Writing elements of $D_4$ as $\rho^j\sigma^\epsilon$ with $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}$, the relation $\sigma\rho^j=\rho^{-j}\sigma$ shows products stay in $D_4$, and $(\rho^j\sigma^\epsilon)^{-1}=\rho^{-(-1)^\epsilon j}\sigma^\epsilon$ also lies in $D_4$. Both matrix groups preserve $\mathbb Z^2$ because $\rho$ and $\sigma$ are signed permutation matrices. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For either matrix group $A$, the pair multiplication is closed on $\mathbb Z^2\times A$. It is associative because both parenthesizations of three factors $(t,M),(s,N),(r,Q)$ equal $(t+Ms+MN r,MNQ)$. Its identity is $(0,I)$. For every pair $(t,M)$, the pair $(-M^{-1}t,M^{-1})$ belongs to the same set by 1.1, and $(t,M)(-M^{-1}t,M^{-1})=(0,I)=(-M^{-1}t,M^{-1})(t,M)$. Thus $P_{C_4}$ and $P_{D_4}$ satisfy the group axioms in [F1]. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The identity pair acts identically because $(0,I)\cdot x=x$. The affine maps respect pair multiplication because $M(Nx+s)+t=MNx+Ms+t$, so $((t,M)(s,N))\cdot x=(t,M)\cdot((s,N)\cdot x)$ and [F2] holds. The translations $(t,I)$ are distinct as $t$ ranges over $\mathbb Z^2$, so each full group is infinite. [given, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let a group $G$ act on sets $X$ and $Y$ by left actions $T$ and $T'$, respectively. A layer is a function $\Phi:X\to Y$. It is $G$-equivariant when

$$
\Phi(T_gx)=T'_g\Phi(x)\qquad(g\in G,\ x\in X).

## Definition

Let $G$ be a discrete group acting on the lattice $\mathbb Z^2$ on the left. Let $C_{\rm in},C_{\rm out}$ be positive integers, and regard channel vectors as row vectors. For a feature map $f:G\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}}$ and a filter $\Psi:G\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}\times C_{\rm out}}$, the group-to-group cross-correlation is the map $C_\Psi f:G\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm out}}$ defined by

$$
(C_\Psi f)(g)=\sum_{h\in G} f(h)\Psi(g^{-1}h).
$$

For an image feature map $f:\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}}$ and a lattice filter $\Psi:\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}\times C_{\rm out}}$, the first-layer image-to-group cross-correlation is the map $E_\Psi f:G\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm out}}$ defined by

$$
(E_\Psi f)(g)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z^2} f(x)\Psi(g^{-1}\cdot x).
$$

Each displayed sum is required to have finite support or to converge absolutely in every output coordinate. The first operation takes group-indexed features and filters; the second takes lattice-indexed image features and filters and returns group-indexed features. These are cross-correlations, with the filter argument displayed as written; they need not be commutative, and no finiteness of $G$ is assumed.

## Definition

Let $G$ be a group and let $F:G\to\mathbb R^C$ be a feature map with $C$ channels. A pointwise nonlinearity determined by $\nu:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is $N_\nu F$, where $(N_\nu F)(g)_c=\nu(F(g)_c)$. For a nonempty finite set $U\subseteq G$, non-strided neighborhood max pooling is $P_UF$, where $(P_UF)(g)_c=\max_{u\in U}F(gu)_c$; the output is still indexed by $G$. For a subgroup $H\le G$, subgroup sampling is the restriction $R_HF=F|_H$, indexed by $H$.

The left-coset set is $G/H=\{gH:g\in G\}$, where $gH=\{gh:h\in H\}$. Its left $G$-action is $a\cdot(gH)=(ag)H$. For finite $H$, left-coset max pooling is the map $Q_HF:G/H\to\mathbb R^C$ given by $(Q_HF)(gH)_c=\max_{h\in H}F(gh)_c$. All maxima are taken separately in each channel. When $H=G$ is finite, $G/H$ has one element and $Q_HF$ is a group-invariant summary.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A group $G$, a finite subgroup $H\le G$, a nonempty finite $U\subseteq G$, and a feature map $F:G\to\mathbb R^C$. Verify that the coset action and pooling formulas are well-defined.

[F1] [[def-subgroup]]: A subgroup contains the identity and is closed under multiplication and inverses.

[F2] [[def-coset]]: The left coset represented by $g$ is $gH=\{gh:h\in H\}$.

[F3] [[def-group-action]]: A left action satisfies $e\cdot z=z$ and $(ab)\cdot z=a\cdot(b\cdot z)$ for each acted-on element $z$.

1.2 If $g'=gh_0$ with $h_0\in H$, then $h_0H=H$: closure gives $h_0H\subseteq H$, and for $k\in H$, $k=h_0(h_0^{-1}k)\in h_0H$ by [F1]. Hence $\{g'h:h\in H\}=\{gh:h\in H\}$, so the componentwise maximum defining $Q_HF(gH)$ is independent of the representative. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], $H$ contains the identity, so $H$ and the given set $U$ are nonempty and finite. ## Definition

Let $G$ be a group ([[def-group]]) with identity $e$. A subset $H \subseteq G$ is
a **subgroup** of $G$, written $H \le G$, when

- **(S1)** $e \in H$;
- **(S2)** $H$ is closed under the operation: $x, y \in H$ implies $xy \in H$
  ([[def-binary-operation]]);
- **(S3)** $H$ is closed under inverses: $x \in H$ implies $x^{-1} \in H$.

By (S2) the operation of $G$ restricts to a binary operation on $H$; it is
associative there because it is associative on $G$, the element $e$ of (S1) is a
two-sided identity for it ([[def-identity-element]]), and (S3) supplies for each
$x \in H$ a two-sided inverse lying in $H$ ([[def-invertible-element]]). So a
subgroup, with the restricted operation, is itself a group, and its identity and
its inverses are those of $G$.

Every group $G$ has the two **trivial subgroups** $\{e\}$ and $G$ itself; a
subgroup $H$ with $H \ne G$ is called **proper**.

## Remarks

- **The definition is stated so that no comparison of structures is needed.** A
  subgroup is a subset satisfying three closure conditions, and the group
  structure it carries is inherited rather than chosen. The converse reading, that
  a subset which happens to be a group under the restricted operation is a
  subgroup in the above sense, is a small theorem rather than a tautology,
  because a priori such a subset could carry a different identity; it is part of
  [[lem-subgroup-criterion]], and cancellation in $G$ is what rules that out.

- Conditions (S1)–(S3) are not independent as stated: if $H$ is nonempty and
  satisfies (S2) and (S3) then it satisfies (S1). The economical single test is
  [[lem-subgroup-criterion]].

- Intersections of subgroups are subgroups ([[lem-intersection-of-subgroups]]),
  which is what makes "the smallest subgroup containing a given subset"
  meaningful ([[def-generated-subgroup]]). Unions of subgroups are almost never
  subgroups.

## Definition

Let $G$ be a group and let $H\le G$ be a subgroup ([[def-group]],
[[def-subgroup]]). For $g\in G$, the **left coset** and **right coset** of $H$
represented by $g$ are

$$gH:=\{gh:h\in H\},\qquad Hg:=\{hg:h\in H\}.$$

The element $g$ is a **representative** of these cosets. The notation denotes
subsets of $G$; it does not assert that either subset is a subgroup.

## Remarks

- Because the identity $e$ belongs to $H$, every representative belongs to its
  two cosets: $g=ge=eg\in gH\cap Hg$.
- The identity cosets are $eH=H=He$. Left and right cosets can differ in a
  nonabelian group.

## Statement

Let $G$ be a discrete group acting on the left on the square lattice $\mathbb Z^2$, and let feature maps take values in finite-dimensional row-vector channel spaces. Assume every group or lattice sum below has finite support or converges absolutely in each output coordinate. For group-indexed features $f:G\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}}$ and a matrix-valued filter $\Psi:G\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}\times C_{\rm out}}$, group-to-group cross-correlation satisfies

$$
C_\Psi(L_u f)=L_u(C_\Psi f)\qquad(u\in G).
$$

For an image feature map $f:\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}}$ and a lattice filter $\Psi:\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}\times C_{\rm out}}$, the first-layer image-to-group cross-correlation also satisfies

$$
E_\Psi(L_u f)=L_u(E_\Psi f)\qquad(u\in G),
$$

where the input action is induced by the action on $\mathbb Z^2$ and the output action is the left action on maps on $G$. The bias-free sum in the ordinary full-lattice, unit-stride discrete layer with origin $a=0$ is the translation-group instance of this formula; any fixed origin shift and the layer's constant output bias preserve translation equivariance. Componentwise pointwise nonlinearities and finite-neighborhood max pooling without subsampling commute with the left action. Restricting a group feature map to a subgroup $H\le G$ preserves $H$-equivariance; for finite $H$, left-coset max pooling produces a $G$-equivariant feature map on $G/H$, and when $H=G$ is finite it is invariant. Finite compositions of equivariant layers remain equivariant.

The full p4 and p4m lattice symmetry groups are infinite because they contain all integer translations; no finiteness assumption on $G$ is made. On a finite grid, the theorem applies only when the domain, output sampling, and boundary convention respect the stated actions. Arbitrary cropping, padding, or stride need not do so. No continuous-rotation, universal-approximation, or empirical-superiority claim follows.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The group actions, feature maps, filters, finite-support or absolute-convergence conditions, and operators stated above. Prove the equivariance claims and the composition rule.

[F1] [[def-group-action]]: A left action satisfies $e\cdot x=x$ and $(gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$ for every $g,h$ and acted-on point $x$.

[F2] [[def-group]]: Group multiplication is associative and each element has a two-sided inverse.

[F3] [[def-group-action-on-feature-maps]]: The induced action is $(L_uf)(x)=f(u^{-1}\cdot x)$, and on group-indexed maps $(L_uF)(g)=F(u^{-1}g)$.

[F4] [[def-group-convolution]]: Group-to-group correlation is $(C_\Psi f)(g)=\sum_{h\in G}f(h)\Psi(g^{-1}h)$ when the sum is finite or absolutely convergent.

[F5] [[def-group-convolution]]: Image-to-group correlation is $(E_\Psi f)(g)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z^2}f(x)\Psi(g^{-1}\cdot x)$ when the sum is finite or absolutely convergent.

[F6] [[def-pointwise-nonlinearity-and-pooling-on-group-features]]: Pointwise maps act componentwise, $N_\nu F(g)_c=\nu(F(g)_c)$, and non-strided pooling is $(P_UF)(g)_c=\max_{v\in U}F(gv)_c$ for finite nonempty $U$. For a finite subgroup $H\le G$, left-coset pooling is $Q_HF:G/H\to\mathbb R^C$, where $G/H=\{gH:g\in G\}$ and $(Q_HF)(gH)_c=\max_{h\in H}F(gh)_c$; the induced left action on the index set is $a\cdot(gH)=(ag)H$.

[F7] [[def-equivariant-neural-layer]]: Equivariance between input and output actions is $\Phi(T_gx)=T'_g\Phi(x)$ for every $g$ and $x$.

[F8] [[def-discrete-convolutional-layer]]: The discrete layer uses a finite offset set $K$ and computes $y(p)=b+\sum_{\delta\in K}\widetilde x(a+s\odot p+\delta)W_\delta$ with the declared extension and stride.

[F9] [[def-p4-p4m-lattice-symmetry-groups]]: The full p4 and p4m groups contain every translation $(t,I)$ for $t\in\mathbb Z^2$ and are infinite.

[F10] [[def-equivariant-map-of-group-actions]]: An equivariant map between $G$-sets satisfies $f(g\cdot x)=g\cdot f(x)$ for every $g$ and $x$.

[F11] [[def-subgroup]]: A subgroup contains the identity and is closed under the group operation and inverses.

[F12] [[def-coset]]: The left coset of $H$ represented by $g$ is $gH=\{gh:h\in H\}$.

## Proof

1.1 For group-to-group correlation, $(C_\Psi(L_uf))(g)=\sum_{h\in G}f(u^{-1}h)\Psi(g^{-1}h)$. Reindex by the bijection $h=uk$ to obtain $\sum_{k\in G}f(k)\Psi(g^{-1}uk)$. The identity $(u^{-1}g)^{-1}=g^{-1}u$ follows because both products of $u^{-1}g$ and $g^{-1}u$ are $e$ by associativity and the two-sided inverse laws; two two-sided inverses $a,b$ of $z$ coincide since $a=a(zb)=(az)b=b$. Hence the sum is $\sum_{k\in G}f(k)\Psi((u^{-1}g)^{-1}k)=(C_\Psi f)(u^{-1}g)=(L_u(C_\Psi f))(g)$. The reindexing is valid for finite support or absolute convergence. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 For every channel $c$, $(N_\nu(L_uF))(g)_c=\nu(F(u^{-1}g)_c)=(L_u(N_\nu F))(g)_c$. Likewise, $(P_U(L_uF))(g)_c=\max_{v\in U}F(u^{-1}gv)_c=(P_UF)(u^{-1}g)_c=(L_u(P_UF))(g)_c$. Thus both operators commute with the left action. [given, F3, F6, algebra]

1.3 For $a\in H$ and $h\in H$, $(R_H(L_aF))(h)=F(a^{-1}h)=(L_a(R_HF))(h)$ because $a^{-1}h\in H$ by [F11]; this proves only $H$-equivariance after subgroup restriction. For finite $H$ and arbitrary $a\in G$, $(Q_H(L_aF))(gH)_c=\max_{h\in H}F(a^{-1}gh)_c=(Q_HF)((a^{-1}g)H)_c=(L_a^{G/H}(Q_HF))(gH)_c$, using the left-coset indexing in [F12] and the action stated in [F6]. If $H=G$ is finite then $G/H$ is a singleton, whose action is trivial, so the output is invariant. [given, F3, F6, F11, F12, algebra]

2.1 For the first-layer operation, $(E_\Psi(L_uf))(g)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z^2}f(u^{-1}\cdot x)\Psi(g^{-1}\cdot x)$. The map $x=u\cdot y$ is a bijection of $\mathbb Z^2$ with inverse $y=u^{-1}\cdot x$ by [F1], so reindexing gives $\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z^2}f(y)\Psi(g^{-1}\cdot(u\cdot y))=\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z^2}f(y)\Psi((g^{-1}u)\cdot y)=(E_\Psi f)(u^{-1}g)=(L_u(E_\Psi f))(g)$, using the inverse identity in 1.1. Absolute convergence or finite support justifies the reindexing. For $G=\mathbb Z^2$ acting by translations, $\Psi(\delta)=W_\delta$ with finite support, full-lattice input and output domains, unit stride, and origin $a=0$, setting $x=p+\delta$ identifies the sum in this formula with the cross-correlation term of the layer in [F8]. For any fixed origin $a$, that sum is instead $(E_\Psi f)(p+a)$, which remains translation-equivariant because translations of $\mathbb Z^2$ commute. The layer's output bias is constant across $p$, so the induced translation action fixes it; adding it preserves equivariance of the full layer. [given, F1, F2, F3, F5, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ are equivariant maps for compatible input, intermediate, and output actions, then $(\Psi\circ\Phi)(T_gx)=\Psi(T'_g\Phi(x))=T''_g(\Psi\circ\Phi)(x)$ by [F7] and [F10]; induction gives equivariance of any finite stack. The reindexings in steps 1.1 and 2.1 require actual group actions on the full index sets, while [F8] permits arbitrary finite-grid boundary and stride choices; therefore those choices are covered only when compatible with the actions. In particular [F9] shows no finite-group assumption was used for p4 or p4m. [given, F7, F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $X$ and $Y$ be $G$-sets ([[def-group-action]]). A function
$f:X\to Y$ ([[def-function]]) is **$G$-equivariant** when

$$f(g\cdot x)=g\cdot f(x)$$

for every $g\in G$ and $x\in X$. An **isomorphism of $G$-sets** is an
equivariant bijection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). Two actions are
**equivariantly isomorphic** when such a bijection exists between their
$G$-sets.

## Example

Let $f:\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb R$ have finite support, let $K\subseteq\mathbb Z^2$ be finite, and choose real weights $w_\delta$ for $\delta\in K$. The full-lattice layer $C_wf(p)=\sum_{\delta\in K}f(p+\delta)w_\delta$ commutes with every translation $L_tf(p)=f(p-t)$. A finite-grid boundary can fail: take $D=\{0,e_1\}$ with $e_1=(1,0)$, let $\tau$ swap the two sites and let $Tf=f\circ\tau^{-1}$, extend arrays by zero outside $D$, and define $C_0f(x)=\overline f(x-e_1)$ for $x\in D$. For $f(0)=1$ and $f(e_1)=0$, one obtains $T(C_0f)=(1,0)$ but $C_0(Tf)=(0,0)$, so this zero-padded layer is not equivariant for the swap action on the two-site grid.

## Example

Let $\rho=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ be the quarter-turn, $\sigma=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ a reflection, $e_1=(1,0)$, and $e_2=(0,1)$; define $\delta_a(x)=1$ when $x=a$ and $0$ otherwise. The ordinary planar cross-correlation $(f\star\psi)(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z^2}f(y)\psi(y-x)$ with $f=\delta_0$ and $\psi=\delta_{e_1}$ is not rotation-equivariant with a fixed filter: $L_\rho f=f$, but $f\star\psi=\delta_{-e_1}$ and $L_\rho(f\star\psi)=\delta_{-e_2}\ne\delta_{-e_1}=(L_\rho f)\star\psi$. In a p4 group layer, the feature map is indexed by pairs $(t,\rho^j)$, giving four orientation indices at each translation $t\in\mathbb Z^2$; in a p4m group layer it is indexed by $(t,\rho^j\sigma^\epsilon)$ for $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}$, giving eight. The full p4 and p4m groups remain infinite through their translations, and their group-correlation layers are equivariant for the full left action.

## Definition

Fix a set of labels $\Sigma$. A finite vertex-labeled simple undirected graph is a triple $G=(V,E,\ell)$ in which $V$ is a finite set of vertices, $E$ is a set of two-element subsets of $V$, and $\ell:V\to\Sigma$ assigns a label to each vertex. Its neighborhood at $v\in V$ is $N_G(v)=\{u\in V:\{u,v\}\in E\}$. Thus edges have no orientation, loops, or multiplicity. Graphs compared in one labeled-graph statement use the same label set $\Sigma$.

## Definition

Let $X$ be a set. A finite multiset on $X$ is a function $m:X\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite support $\operatorname{supp}(m)=\{x\in X:m(x)>0\}$. The multiplicity $m(x)$ is the number of occurrences of $x$, and the size is $|m|=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(m)}m(x)$. Two finite multisets are equal exactly when their multiplicity functions agree at every element of $X$. We write $\{\!\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\!\}$ for the multiset whose multiplicity at $x$ is the number of indices $i$ with $x_i=x$; $n=0$ denotes the empty multiset.

## Definition

Let $G=(V,E,\ell)$ and $H=(W,F,m)$ be finite vertex-labeled simple undirected graphs with labels in the same set $\Sigma$. A label-preserving graph isomorphism from $G$ to $H$ is a bijection $\varphi:V\to W$ such that $\ell(v)=m(\varphi(v))$ for every $v\in V$, and for all distinct $u,v\in V$, $\{u,v\}\in E$ if and only if $\{\varphi(u),\varphi(v)\}\in F$. The graphs are isomorphic when such a bijection exists, and nonisomorphic otherwise.

## Definition

Fix a finite vertex-labeled simple undirected graph $G=(V,E,\ell)$, a finite nonnegative depth $K$, feature sets $H_0,\ldots,H_K$, and an initial map $\eta:\Sigma\to H_0$. For each $k=1,\ldots,K$, choose a set $Z_k$, an aggregation function $A_k:\mathsf M_{\mathrm{fin}}(H_{k-1})\to Z_k$ on finite multisets, and an update function $U_k:H_{k-1}\times Z_k\to H_k$. Initialize $h_v^0=\eta(\ell(v))$ and recursively set

$$
a_v^k=A_k\!\left(\{\!\{h_u^{k-1}:u\in N_G(v)\}\!\}\right),\qquad h_v^k=U_k(h_v^{k-1},a_v^k).
$$

For a chosen output set $Y$, a graph readout is a function $R:\mathsf M_{\mathrm{fin}}(H_K)\to Y$; the graph output is $z_G=R(\{\!\{h_v^K:v\in V\}\!\})$. The same maps are used on every graph being compared. The model has no vertex-identity input and uses no graph-wide information before the readout. It distinguishes two graphs when their outputs differ.

## Definition

Let $G=(V,E,\ell)$ and $H=(W,F,m)$ be finite vertex-labeled simple undirected graphs with labels in a common set $\Sigma$. Define color sets recursively by $C_0=\Sigma$ and $C_{t+1}=C_t\times\mathsf M_{\mathrm{fin}}(C_t)$ for each integer $t\ge0$. Set $c_0^G(v)=\ell(v)$ and $c_0^H(w)=m(w)$; for $t\ge0$, update

$$ c_{t+1}^G(v)=\left(c_t^G(v),\{\!\{c_t^G(u):u\in N_G(v)\}\!\}\right),\qquad c_{t+1}^H(w)=\left(c_t^H(w),\{\!\{c_t^H(z):z\in N_H(w)\}\!\}\right). $$

The graph color multiset at round $t$ is $C_t(G)=\{\!\{c_t^G(v):v\in V\}\!\}$, and likewise for $H$. One-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman color refinement distinguishes $G$ and $H$ at round $t$ when $C_t(G)\ne C_t(H)$; it distinguishes the pair when this holds for some finite $t$. If no finite round distinguishes them, they are one-WL-indistinguishable. In the unlabeled case, take $\Sigma$ to be a singleton. The tuple update is the canonical collision-free color encoding.

## Statement

Let $\mathcal X$ be a countable set and let $M\in\mathbb N_0$. There is a map $\phi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb N_{>0}\subset\mathbb Q$ such that the sum $S\mapsto\sum_{x\in S}\phi(x)$ is injective on finite multisets $S$ of total multiplicity at most $M$. For every irrational $\varepsilon\in\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$, the map

$$
(c,S)\longmapsto(1+\varepsilon)\phi(c)+\sum_{x\in S}\phi(x)
$$

is injective on pairs with $c\in\mathcal X$ and $S$ a finite multiset of total multiplicity at most $M$. For $M=0$, the only allowed neighbor multiset is empty.

## Statement references

[Xu, Hu, Leskovec, and Jegelka, “How Powerful are Graph Neural Networks?”, Lemma 5 and Corollary 6](https://cs.stanford.edu/people/jure/pubs/gin-iclr19.pdf)

[Li and Leskovec, *Graph Representation Learning*, Chapter 5 §5.3.4, Lemma 5.1](https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/people/jure/pubs/gnnpower-springer22.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A countable set $\mathcal X$, a bound $M\in\mathbb N_0$, and an irrational real number $\varepsilon$. Prove both injectivity claims.

[A1] Countability means that an injection $\nu:\mathcal X\to\mathbb N_0$ is given.

[F1] [[def-multiset]]: A finite multiset on $\mathcal X$ is its finitely supported multiplicity function $m:\mathcal X\to\mathbb N_0$; its size is the sum of all multiplicities.

## Proof

1.1 Let $B=\max\{2,M+1\}$ and set $\phi(x)=B^{\nu(x)}$. If $M=0$, the only allowed multiset is empty, so its sum encoding is injective. If $M\ge1$ and two allowed multisets $S,T$ have equal sums, for each $j\in\mathbb N_0$ let $d_j$ be the multiplicity in $S$ minus the multiplicity in $T$ of the element with $\nu$-index $j$, and set $d_j=0$ when no element has that index. The sequence $(d_j)$ has finite support and $|d_j|\le M$. If some $d_j\ne0$, let $r$ be its largest such index. Equality of the sums gives $|d_r|B^r=|\sum_{j<r}d_jB^j|\le M(B^r-1)/(B-1)\le B^r-1$, contradicting $|d_r|B^r\ge B^r$. Hence all multiplicities agree and $S=T$. [given, A1, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Suppose $(1+\varepsilon)\phi(c)+\sum_{x\in S}\phi(x)=(1+\varepsilon)\phi(c')+\sum_{x\in T}\phi(x)$. Rearranging gives $A+\varepsilon D=0$, where $A=\phi(c)-\phi(c')+\sum_{x\in S}\phi(x)-\sum_{x\in T}\phi(x)$ and $D=\phi(c)-\phi(c')$ are integers. If $D\ne0$, then $\varepsilon=-A/D$ is rational, contrary to the hypothesis. Thus $D=0$; since $B\ge2$ has distinct powers and $\nu$ is injective, $\phi$ is injective and $c=c'$. The equality then reduces to equality of the neighbor sums; step 1.1 gives $S=T$. [given, A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix a finite depth $K\in\mathbb N_0$, positive integer dimensions $d_0,\ldots,d_K$, an initial embedding $\eta:\Sigma\to\mathbb R^{d_0}$, scalars $\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_K\in\mathbb R$, and maps $M_k:\mathbb R^{d_{k-1}}\to\mathbb R^{d_k}$ for $1\le k\le K$. Each $M_k$ is a multilayer perceptron, meaning a finite composition of affine maps between finite-dimensional real vector spaces and coordinatewise applications of a fixed scalar activation. On a finite vertex-labeled simple undirected graph $G$, initialize $h_v^0=\eta(\ell(v))$ and update

$$
h_v^k=M_k\!\left((1+\varepsilon_k)h_v^{k-1}+\sum_{u\in N_G(v)}h_u^{k-1}\right)\qquad(1\le k\le K).
$$

For a chosen output set $Y$, the graph readout is a map $R:\mathsf M_{\mathrm{fin}}(\mathbb R^{d_K})\to Y$ on the multiset of final vertex features. The neighbor sum counts each neighbor vertex once, so equal feature vectors at different neighbors contribute with their multiplicity. This definition imposes no injectivity condition on the perceptrons or the readout and makes no claim that a fixed finite architecture realizes an arbitrary injection.

## Statement

Let $G$ and $H$ be finite vertex-labeled simple undirected graphs with labels in a common set, and let $\varphi:G\to H$ be a label-preserving graph isomorphism. At every finite round $t$, corresponding vertices have equal one-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman colors: $c_t^G(v)=c_t^H(\varphi(v))$ for every $v\in V(G)$. Consequently their graph color multisets agree at every round, so the refinement does not distinguish isomorphic graphs.

## Statement references

[[def-graph-isomorphism|label-preserving graph isomorphisms]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite labeled graphs $G,H$ and label-preserving isomorphism $\varphi:G\to H$ in the Statement. Prove the color and histogram claims.

[F1] [[def-graph-isomorphism]]: $\varphi$ is a bijection preserving labels and adjacency in both directions.

[F2] [[def-one-dimensional-weisfeiler-lehman-test]]: The round-$t+1$ color is the ordered pair of the vertex's round-$t$ color and the multiset of round-$t$ colors of its neighbors.

[F3] [[def-multiset]]: Equality of finite multisets is equality of multiplicities at every element.

## Proof

1.1 By induction on $t$, $c_t^G(v)=c_t^H(\varphi(v))$ for every $v\in V(G)$. At $t=0$ this is label preservation from [F1]. If it holds at $t$, bijectivity and adjacency preservation in [F1] give a bijection $N_G(v)\to N_H(\varphi(v))$, and corresponding neighbors have equal round-$t$ colors by the induction hypothesis. Thus the neighbor-color multisets agree; the center colors agree as well, so the ordered-pair update [F2] gives equality at round $t+1$. [given, F1, F2, induction, algebra]

2.1 The same vertex bijection therefore sends every occurrence of each round-$t$ color in $G$ to an occurrence of that color in $H$, and its inverse gives the reverse correspondence. Hence the two graph color multisets have equal multiplicities for each color by [F3]. Their round-$t$ histograms agree for every finite $t$, so no round distinguishes them. [given, F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $G,H$ be finite vertex-labeled simple undirected graphs with labels in a common set, and let a depth-$K$ aggregation-based message-passing graph neural network use the same initial embedding, layer maps, and graph readout on both graphs. If one-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman color refinement has equal graph color multisets on $G$ and $H$ at every round $0,\ldots,K$, then the network gives the same graph output on $G$ and $H$. Equivalently, whenever this network distinguishes the pair, one-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman distinguishes the pair at some round at most $K$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two finite labeled graphs, their equal 1-WL color multisets through round $K$, and one shared depth-$K$ message-passing GNN as in the Statement. Prove its graph outputs agree.

[F1] [[def-message-passing-gnn]]: Each layer applies the same aggregation function to the multiset of neighbor states and then the same update function to the center state and aggregate.

[F2] [[def-one-dimensional-weisfeiler-lehman-test]]: Each next WL color is the ordered pair of the current color and the multiset of current neighbor colors; the graph color multiset records every vertex color with multiplicity.

[F3] [[def-multiset]]: A finite multiset is its multiplicity function, so applying a function to each occurrence preserves equality of multisets.

[F4] [[def-message-passing-gnn]]: The graph readout is a function of the multiset of final node states.

## Proof

1.1 By induction on $t=0,\ldots,K$, equal round-$t$ WL colors of vertices from either graph imply equal GNN states after $t$ layers. At $t=0$, the shared initial embedding gives this implication. If it holds at $t$ and two vertices have equal round-$(t+1)$ colors, [F2] says their center colors and neighbor-color multisets agree. By the induction hypothesis, equal neighbor colors have equal GNN states; applying this correspondence occurrence by occurrence gives equal neighbor-state multisets. The shared aggregation and update functions in [F1] therefore give equal next-layer states. Thus a well-defined map from each round-$t$ color occurring in either graph to its common GNN state exists. [given, F1, F2, induction, algebra]

2.1 At round $K$, the assumed equal WL color multisets become equal multisets of GNN states when each color is sent to its common state from step 1.1; multiplicities are preserved by [F3]. The shared graph readout in [F4] receives equal multisets, so the two graph outputs are equal. The contrapositive gives the stated distinguishing implication. [given, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $G,H$ be finite vertex-labeled simple undirected graphs with labels in a common set. Suppose one-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman distinguishes them at round $K$. Use a shared initial embedding that is injective on the labels occurring in the pair. Assume each message-passing layer's aggregation function is injective on the neighbor multisets encountered and its update function is injective on the center-state/aggregate pairs encountered. Assume also that the graph readout is injective on the final node-state multisets of the pair. Then a depth-$K$ aggregation-based message-passing graph neural network distinguishes $G$ and $H$.

For the GIN sum construction, if the active feature universe is countable and every neighbor multiset has size at most a fixed $\Delta\in\mathbb N_0$, the bounded-multiset lemma gives an injective scalar code for the GIN preactivation $(1+\varepsilon)h_v+\sum_{u\in N(v)}h_u$ for any irrational $\varepsilon$, when current feature values use that code. If each graph has at most a fixed $N\in\mathbb N_0$ vertices, the same lemma gives an injective sum encoding for the graph-level readout multiset. This is an existence statement for injective maps on the relevant code sets; it does not assert that every fixed finite MLP realizes an arbitrary such map. The post-MLP update and graph readout must still satisfy the injectivity hypotheses above.

**Given:** The graphs, finite round $K$, one shared message-passing network, and the injectivity hypotheses stated above. Prove that its depth-$K$ graph outputs differ, and justify the countable GIN sum-code clause.

[A1] The initial embedding is injective on the common labels occurring in $G$ and $H$.

[A2] At each round, the aggregation function is injective on the encountered neighbor multisets and the update function is injective on the encountered pairs of center state and aggregate.

[A3] The graph readout is injective on the two final multisets of node states.

[F1] [[def-one-dimensional-weisfeiler-lehman-test]]: A round-$(k+1)$ color is the ordered pair of a round-$k$ center color and the multiset of round-$k$ neighbor colors; the round-$k$ graph histogram is the multiset of all vertex colors.

[F2] [[def-message-passing-gnn]]: A shared layer aggregates the multiset of neighbor states and updates the center state.

[F3] [[lem-countable-bounded-multiset-sum-encoding]]: On a countable feature universe with multiset-size bound $M$, a sum code is injective on multisets, and for irrational $\varepsilon$ the code $(c,S)\mapsto(1+\varepsilon)\phi(c)+\sum_{x\in S}\phi(x)$ is injective on center/multiset pairs.

[F4] [[def-graph-isomorphism-network]]: The GIN preactivation is $(1+\varepsilon_k)h_v^{k-1}+\sum_{u\in N_G(v)}h_u^{k-1}$ before its layer MLP.

[F5] [[def-message-passing-gnn]]: The graph output is the readout of the final node-state multiset.

1.1 For each $k\le K$, we prove that there is an injective map $\psi_k$ from the WL colors occurring at round $k$ in either graph to their GNN states. For $k=0$, use the initial embedding and [A1]. 2.1 The WL histograms at round $K$ differ by hypothesis. Applying the injective map $\psi_K$ to each color occurrence preserves multiplicities and keeps these two multisets different. 3.1 If the active feature set is countable and neighbor multisets have size at most $\Delta$, apply [F3] with $M=\Delta$ to obtain the stated center/multiset preactivation code for any irrational $\varepsilon$. ## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, so the usual Lebesgue-measurable sets on $\mathbb R$ form a complete measure space with Lebesgue measure $\lambda$; restrict that measure to the interval $I$ when needed. Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with $t_0\in I$, and let $N,m,p\ge1$ be finite. A continuous-time linear state-space model consists of matrices $A\in\mathbb F^{N\times N}$, $B\in\mathbb F^{N\times m}$, $C\in\mathbb F^{p\times N}$, $D\in\mathbb F^{p\times m}$, an initial value $x_0\in\mathbb F^N$, and an input $u:I\to\mathbb F^m$ whose real and imaginary coordinates are Lebesgue measurable and integrable on every compact subinterval of $I$. A state trajectory is a function $x:I\to\mathbb F^N$ whose real and imaginary coordinates are absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of $I$ (with absolute continuity defined by the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ condition on finite families of disjoint subintervals), with $x(t_0)=x_0$ and $x'(t)=Ax(t)+Bu(t)$ outside a Lebesgue-null subset of $I$. Its output is $y(t)=Cx(t)+Du(t)$. The term $Du(t)$ is the direct input-to-output term and is separate from the state contribution $Cx(t)$.

## Definition

For a nonnegative integer $q$, let $M=2^q$, let $\omega=e^{-2\pi i/M}$ when $M>1$, and let $a=(a_0,\ldots,a_{M-1})\in\mathbb C^M$. The forward discrete Fourier transform (DFT) is the vector $\widehat a\in\mathbb C^M$ with $\widehat a_k=\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}a_j\omega^{jk}$. The radix-two procedure returns this vector by the following exact recursion. If $M=1$, return $(a_0)$. If $M>1$, recursively compute the length-$M/2$ DFTs $E$ and $O$ of $(a_0,a_2,\ldots,a_{M-2})$ and $(a_1,a_3,\ldots,a_{M-1})$, using the primitive root $\omega^2$. For $0\le k<M/2$, return $\widehat a_k=E_k+\omega^k O_k$ and $\widehat a_{k+M/2}=E_k-\omega^kO_k$. The inverse transform is obtained by running the same procedure with $\overline\omega$ and dividing every output by $M$.

## Definition references

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.00396"

## Statement

Let $D\in\mathbb C^{N\times N}$ be invertible, let $U,V\in\mathbb C^{N\times r}$, and set $W=I_r+V^*D^{-1}U$, where $^*$ denotes conjugate transpose. Then $D+UV^*$ is invertible if and only if $W$ is invertible. When these matrices are invertible,
$$
(D+UV^*)^{-1}=D^{-1}-D^{-1}U W^{-1}V^*D^{-1}.
$$

## Statement references

[Gu, Goel, and Ré, “Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces,” Appendix C.2–C.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.00396)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Finite integers $N,r\ge1$, matrices $D\in\mathbb C^{N\times N}$ and $U,V\in\mathbb C^{N\times r}$, with $D$ invertible, and $W:=I_r+V^*D^{-1}U$.

[A1] The inverse $D^{-1}$ exists, so all displayed matrix products are defined.

[A2] $W$ is an $r\times r$ matrix; a square linear map in finite dimension is invertible once its kernel is zero.

## Proof

1.1 Assume $W$ is invertible and define $X:=D^{-1}-D^{-1}UW^{-1}V^*D^{-1}$. Expansion gives $(D+UV^*)X=I+U(V^*D^{-1}-W^{-1}V^*D^{-1}-V^*D^{-1}UW^{-1}V^*D^{-1})=I$, because $(I_r+V^*D^{-1}U)W^{-1}V^*D^{-1}=WW^{-1}V^*D^{-1}=V^*D^{-1}$. [A1, algebra]

2.1 Expanding in the other order gives $X(D+UV^*)=I+D^{-1}U(V^*-W^{-1}V^*-W^{-1}V^*D^{-1}UV^*)=I$, because $W^{-1}(I_r+V^*D^{-1}U)V^*=W^{-1}WV^*=V^*$. Thus $X$ is the two-sided inverse of $D+UV^*$, proving this direction and the formula. [A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Conversely assume $D+UV^*$ is invertible and let $w\in\mathbb C^r$ satisfy $Ww=0$. Set $x=D^{-1}Uw$. Then $(D+UV^*)x=U(I_r+V^*D^{-1}U)w=UWw=0$, so invertibility gives $x=0$. Hence $Uw=Dx=0$, and therefore $Ww=w+V^*D^{-1}Uw=w$. Since $Ww=0$, we have $w=0$. Thus $W$ has zero kernel; by [A2] it is invertible. [A1, A2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix positive finite dimensions $d_x,d_h$, inputs $x_t\in\mathbb R^{d_x}$, hidden states $h_t\in\mathbb R^{d_h}$, cell states $c_t\in\mathbb R^{d_h}$, and initial values $h_0,c_0$. A standard long short-term memory (LSTM) cell without peephole connections or projection has shared matrices $W_i,W_f,W_o,W_c\in\mathbb R^{d_h\times d_x}$, $U_i,U_f,U_o,U_c\in\mathbb R^{d_h\times d_h}$, and biases $b_i,b_f,b_o,b_c\in\mathbb R^{d_h}$. Apply $\sigma(s)=(1+e^{-s})^{-1}$ and $\tanh(s)=(e^s-e^{-s})/(e^s+e^{-s})$ coordinatewise. At each time $t\ge1$, set

$$ i_t=\sigma(W_i x_t+U_i h_{t-1}+b_i),\qquad f_t=\sigma(W_f x_t+U_f h_{t-1}+b_f),\qquad o_t=\sigma(W_o x_t+U_o h_{t-1}+b_o), $$

$$ g_t=\tanh(W_c x_t+U_c h_{t-1}+b_c),\qquad c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot g_t,\qquad h_t=o_t\odot\tanh(c_t), $$

where $\odot$ is coordinatewise multiplication. The same matrices and biases are reused at every time step. The vectors $i_t,f_t,o_t$ are the input, forget, and output gates, and $g_t$ is the candidate state update.

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.00396"
---

## Definition

An $N$-state single-input, single-output complex linear state-space model has $B,C\in\mathbb C^N$, state equation $x'(t)=Ax(t)+Bu(t)$, and output $y(t)=C^*x(t)$; its direct term is set to zero in the S4 convolution convention. Here $X^*$ denotes conjugate transpose; a square complex matrix $H$ is normal when $H^*H=HH^*$; and a square matrix $V$ is unitary when $V^*V=VV^*=I$. A matrix is in diagonal-plus-low-rank (DPLR) form of rank $r$ if
$$
A=\Lambda-PQ^*,
$$
where $\Lambda\in\mathbb C^{N\times N}$ is diagonal and $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{N\times r}$. It is in normal-plus-low-rank (NPLR) form of rank $r$ if
$$
A=V\Lambda V^*-PQ^*,
$$
where $V\in\mathbb C^{N\times N}$ is unitary, $\Lambda$ is diagonal, and $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{N\times r}$. The unitary state change $\widetilde x=V^*x$ converts this NPLR representation to DPLR form and changes $B,C$ to $V^*B,V^*C$, respectively.

For a step size $\Delta>0$ such that $I-\Delta A/2$ is invertible, the bilinear recurrent matrices are
$$ \overline A=(I-\Delta A/2)^{-1}(I+\Delta A/2),\qquad \overline B=(I-\Delta A/2)^{-1}\Delta B,\qquad \overline C=C. $$
With initial state $x_{-1}=0$, the discrete recurrence is $x_t=\overline A x_{t-1}+\overline B u_t$, $y_t=\overline C^*x_t$. Its length-$L$ impulse kernel is the vector $K_L=(\overline C^*\overline A^j\overline B)_{j=0}^{L-1}$. For a nonzero direct term $D$, the output has the additional separate skip term $Du_t$.

For a filter evaluation of transform length $M\ge L$, the output vector for the length-$M$ truncated generating function is $\widetilde C_M=(I-\overline A^M)^*C$. A filter procedure may receive $\widetilde C_M$ as given data; an operation count for evaluating the filter from this transformed vector does not include the separate work of forming it from $C$.

kind: lemma
title: Roots-of-unity orthogonality and radix-two FFT cost
status: draft

sources:

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.00396"
    - title: "Pan, Fast Approximate Computations with Cauchy Matrices and Polynomials, §3.3"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/1506.02285"
---

## Statement

Let $M=2^q$ for an integer $q\ge0$, and let $\omega=e^{-2\pi i/M}$ (with $\omega=1$ when $M=1$). Define the forward DFT matrix $F\in\mathbb C^{M\times M}$ by $F_{kj}=\omega^{jk}$, where $^*$ denotes conjugate transpose. Then $F^*F=MI$, so the inverse DFT is $M^{-1}F^*$. The radix-two procedure defined on this page computes either transform exactly in $O(M\log(2+M))$ complex arithmetic operations and $O(M)$ space. Consequently, for every integer $n\ge1$, two polynomials of degree less than $n$ can be multiplied exactly in $O(n\log(2+n))$ complex arithmetic operations and $O(n)$ space by zero-padding to a radix-two transform length at least $2n-1$.

## Statement references

[Gu, Goel, and Ré, “Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces,” Appendix C.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.00396)

[Pan, “Fast Approximate Computations with Cauchy Matrices and Polynomials,” §3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1506.02285)

[[alg-radix-two-fft]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $q\ge0$, $M=2^q$, and the root $\omega=e^{-2\pi i/M}$.

[A1] For $M>1$, $\omega^M=1$ and $\omega^{M/2}=-1$; for $M=1$, the DFT is the identity on one coordinate.

[F1] [[alg-radix-two-fft]]: for $M>1$, split the even and odd input subsequences, recursively compute their length-$M/2$ DFTs using $\omega^2$, and combine as $E_k+\omega^kO_k$ and $E_k-\omega^kO_k$ for $0\le k<M/2$.

## Proof

1.1 For $0\le j,\ell<M$, the $(j,\ell)$ entry of $F^*F$ is $\sum_{k=0}^{M-1}\omega^{(\ell-j)k}$. If $j=\ell$, this sum is $M$. Otherwise $\omega^{\ell-j}\ne1$ and the finite geometric-sum identity gives $\sum_{k=0}^{M-1}\omega^{(\ell-j)k}=(1-\omega^{M(\ell-j)})/(1-\omega^{\ell-j})=0$. Thus $F^*F=MI$, which gives the asserted inverse. [A1, algebra]

2.1 Splitting the DFT sum into even and odd indices gives $E_k+\omega^kO_k$ for $0\le k<M/2$. For frequency $k+M/2$, the even factor is unchanged because $\omega^{jM}=1$, while the odd factor changes sign because $\omega^{M/2}=-1$. Therefore the outputs in [F1] are exactly the defining DFT sums. Induction on $q$, starting with $M=1$, proves exactness of the recursion. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 At length $M>1$, forming both half-length transforms and combining their $M$ outputs costs at most $cM$ arithmetic operations for an absolute constant $c$. Hence $T(M)\le2T(M/2)+cM$ and $T(1)=O(1)$; expanding this recurrence for $q=\log_2M$ levels gives $T(M)=O(M\log(2+M))$. The input, output, and one level of butterflies require $O(M)$ workspace; the inverse has the same cost plus coordinatewise scaling by $1/M$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $f,g$ have degree less than $n$, and choose $M'=2^{\lceil\log_2(2n-1)\rceil}$. Pad their coefficient lists to length $M'$, apply the forward DFT, multiply corresponding transformed coordinates, and apply the inverse DFT. For coefficient index $s$, the inverse-transform formula expands it as $\sum_{j,\ell} f_jg_\ell\,M'^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{M'-1}\omega^{(j+\ell-s)k}$; step 1.1 makes the inner sum one exactly when $j+\ell\equiv s\pmod {M'}$ and zero otherwise. Thus the result is cyclic convolution modulo $z^{M'}-1$. The ordinary product has degree at most $2n-2<M'$, so no coefficient wraps around and the result is the exact polynomial product. Since $2n-1\le M'<2(2n-1)$ when $n>1$ (and $M'=1$ when $n=1$), step 3.1 gives $O(n\log(2+n))$ operations and $O(n)$ space. [A1, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The proofs use only finite sums and arithmetic in $\mathbb C$; no choice principle is needed.

## Definition

Input an integer $M=2^q$ with $q\ge0$, a primitive $M$th root of unity $\omega$, a finite list of poles $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n\in\mathbb C$, and weights $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb C$. The required output is $y_k=\sum_{j=1}^n a_j/(\omega^k-\mu_j)$ for $0\le k<M$, provided no denominator is zero. If $n=0$, return the zero vector.

Here a primitive $M$th root means $\omega^M=1$ and $\omega^k\ne1$ for $1\le k<M$. For $n\ge1$, form a balanced binary tree on the pole indices, splitting each consecutive index interval into two intervals whose sizes differ by at most one. At a leaf containing index $j$, store polynomials $D_j(z)=z-\mu_j$ and $P_j(z)=a_j$. At an internal node with disjoint child index sets $I_1,I_2$, store
$$ D_I(z)=D_{I_1}(z)D_{I_2}(z),\qquad P_I(z)=P_{I_1}(z)D_{I_2}(z)+D_{I_1}(z)P_{I_2}(z). $$
At the root, fold the coefficients of each polynomial modulo $z^M-1$: the coefficient at degree $r$ is replaced by the sum of coefficients at degrees congruent to $r$ modulo $M$. Let $\omega_0=e^{-2\pi i/M}$, which equals $1$ when $M=1$. Apply the radix-two DFT procedure to each folded coefficient vector to evaluate $P_I$ and $D_I$ at $\omega_0^j$, $0\le j<M$. If $M>1$, find the unique odd integer $s\in\{1,3,\ldots,M-1\}$ with $\omega=\omega_0^s$ by generating and comparing the $M$ powers of $\omega_0$, then place the value at index $sk\bmod M$ at output index $k$; this is the supplied root order because $\omega^k=\omega_0^{sk}$. For $M=1$, the only root is $1$ and no reindexing is needed. This root search and reindexing use $O(M)$ operations. If some reindexed $D_I(\omega^k)=0$, return status `collision`; otherwise return $y_k=P_I(\omega^k)/D_I(\omega^k)$.

## Statement

Index rows and columns by $0,\ldots,N-1$. Define the real LegS coefficient matrix $G^S$ by $G^S_{nk}=-\sqrt{(2n+1)(2k+1)}$ when $n>k$, $G^S_{nn}=-(n+1)$, and $G^S_{nk}=0$ when $n<k$. In the LegS coefficient ODE for $t>0$ this matrix is multiplied by the time-dependent scalar $1/t$; the matrix assertion below does not make that ODE time-invariant. For $\theta>0$, define the LegT state generator by $G^T_{nk}=-(2n+1)(-1)^{n-k}/\theta$ when $n\ge k$ and $G^T_{nk}=-(2n+1)/\theta$ when $n<k$. Define the original HiPPO LagT state generator by $G^L_{nk}=-1$ when $n\ge k$ and $G^L_{nk}=0$ when $n<k$. Here $X^*$ is conjugate transpose, a complex matrix $H$ is normal when $H^*H=HH^*$, and a square matrix $V$ is unitary when $V^*V=VV^*=I$. For LegS and LagT use the identity similarity; for LegT use the invertible diagonal similarity $S_0=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{2n+1})_{n=0}^{N-1}\operatorname{diag}((-1)^n)_{n=0}^{N-1}$. Each transformed matrix is a difference $H-UV^*$ with $H$ normal and $\operatorname{rank}(UV^*)\le1$ for LegS and LagT and $\operatorname{rank}(UV^*)\le2$ for LegT. Consequently the equivalent finite-dimensional complex state-space matrix has a normal-plus-low-rank representation, and a unitary change of state coordinates gives diagonal-plus-low-rank form. Under any state change $x=S\widetilde x$, the input and output vectors change to $S^{-1}B$ and $S^*C$, respectively.

## Statement references

[Gu, Goel, and Ré, “Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces,” Theorem 1 and Appendix C.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.00396)

[Gu et al., “HiPPO: Recurrent Memory with Optimal Polynomial Projections,” §2.3 and Appendices D.1–D.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.07669)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite matrices in the Statement, the parameter $\theta>0$ for LegT, and finite-dimensional complex state coordinates.

[F1] [[def-s4-dplr-parameterization]]: a normal-plus-low-rank matrix has form $A=V\Lambda V^*-PQ^*$ with unitary $V$ and diagonal $\Lambda$; under the state change $\widetilde x=V^*x$, the input and output vectors become $V^*B$ and $V^*C$.

[F2] [[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]: every normal endomorphism of a finite-dimensional complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.

## Proof

1.1 Put $w_n=\sqrt{2n+1}$ and define the real skew-symmetric matrix $S$ by $S_{nk}=-w_nw_k/2$ for $n>k$, $S_{nk}=w_nw_k/2$ for $n<k$, and $S_{nn}=0$. The transpose is $-S$, so over $\mathbb C$ its conjugate transpose is also $-S$; hence $S$ is normal. With $v=w/\sqrt2$, entrywise comparison gives $G^S=(S-\tfrac12I)-vv^*$: below the diagonal the entries are $-w_nw_k$, above they cancel to zero, and on the diagonal they are $-\tfrac12-(2n+1)/2=-(n+1)$. Since a scalar shift of a normal matrix is normal and $vv^*$ has rank at most one, this is the required LegS decomposition. This assertion concerns the finite coefficient matrix only; the factor $1/t$ in the LegS ODE remains time-dependent. [F1, algebra]

1.2 Define $S$ with entries $-1/2$ below the diagonal, $+1/2$ above it, and zero on the diagonal. It is real skew-symmetric and therefore normal. For $e=(1,\ldots,1)^T$, entrywise comparison gives $G^L=(S-\tfrac12I)-\tfrac12ee^*$: below the diagonal the two terms sum to $-1$, above they sum to zero, and on the diagonal they sum to $-1$. Thus the original LagT generator is a normal matrix minus a rank-at-most-one matrix. [F1, algebra]

1.3 For LegT let $D=\operatorname{diag}(2n+1)_{n=0}^{N-1}$ and $E=\operatorname{diag}((-1)^n)_{n=0}^{N-1}$. Define $T_{nk}=1$ for $n\ge k$, and $T_{nk}=(-1)^{k-n}$ for $n<k$. Then direct entry evaluation gives $G^T=-DETE/\theta$: for $n\ge k$, $(-1)^n(-1)^k=(-1)^{n-k}$, while for $n<k$, $(-1)^n(-1)^{k-n}(-1)^k=1$. Write $T=S+R$, where $R_{nk}=1$ when $n$ and $k$ have the same parity and is zero otherwise. The matrix $R$ is the sum of the outer products of the even-index and odd-index indicator vectors, so its rank is at most two. For opposite parities, $S_{nk}=1$ below the diagonal and $S_{nk}=-1$ above it; for equal parities and on the diagonal, $S_{nk}=0$. Thus $S^T=-S$. The invertible diagonal matrix $S_0=D^{1/2}E$ gives $S_0^{-1}G^TS_0=-\theta^{-1}D^{1/2}SD^{1/2}-\theta^{-1}D^{1/2}RD^{1/2}$. The first term is real skew-symmetric and hence normal; the second has rank at most two. The diagonal similarity is essential: this proves the claim for an equivalent state-space matrix, not unitary similarity of the raw LegT matrix. [F1, algebra]

2.1 In each case write the resulting generator as $H-UV^*$ with $H$ normal: for LegS and LagT the factors are the displayed real vectors divided by $\sqrt2$, and for LegT use the even and odd indicator columns multiplied by $D^{1/2}/\sqrt\theta$ as both factors. By [F2], choose a unitary matrix $V_0$ with $V_0^*HV_0=\Lambda$ diagonal. Then $V_0^*(H-UV^*)V_0=\Lambda-(V_0^*U)(V_0^*V)^*$, preserving the low-rank bound. If the original coordinates were changed by $S_0$, the total state change is $x=S_0V_0z$; substitution into $x'=Gx+Bu$, $y=C^*x$ gives $z'=(V_0^*S_0^{-1}GS_0V_0)z+V_0^*S_0^{-1}Bu$ and output vector $V_0^*S_0^*C$. These are exactly the state-coordinate transformations required for an equivalent DPLR model. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite-dimensional complex inner product space $V$ and a linear endomorphism $T:V\to V$.

[L1] The field $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed ([[thm-the-complex-numbers-are-algebraically-closed]]).

[L2] If the characteristic polynomial splits, then some orthonormal basis makes the matrix upper triangular ([[thm-schur-triangularisation]]).

[L3] A normal upper-triangular complex matrix is diagonal ([[lem-normal-upper-triangular-matrix-is-diagonal]]).

[L4] In an orthonormal basis, a linear map is normal exactly when its matrix commutes with its conjugate transpose ([[prop-self-adjoint-and-normal-matrix-criteria-in-orthonormal-bases]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Assume $T$ is normal. By [L1], the characteristic polynomial of $T$ splits over $\mathbb C$, so [L2] gives an orthonormal basis in which the matrix of $T$ is upper triangular. Because $T$ is normal, [L4] makes that matrix normal, and then [L3] makes it diagonal. Hence the chosen orthonormal basis consists of eigenvectors of $T$. [L1, L2, L3, L4]

2.1 Conversely, assume $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of $T$, with $Te_j=\lambda_j e_j$. Then the matrix of $T$ in that basis is the diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$, and every diagonal matrix commutes with its conjugate transpose. By [L4], $T$ is normal. [L4, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $N,r\ge1$ and $A=\Lambda-PQ^*$ with $\Lambda\in\mathbb C^{N\times N}$ diagonal and $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{N\times r}$, where $^*$ denotes conjugate transpose; let $B,C\in\mathbb C^N$, let $\Delta>0$, and put $\alpha=\Delta/2$. The bilinear step is defined only when $G=I-\alpha A$ is invertible. Given an input sequence $(u_t)$ and state $x_{-1}$, its recurrent mode computes
$$ b_t=(I+\alpha A)x_{t-1}+\Delta Bu_t,\qquad Gx_t=b_t,\qquad y_t=C^*x_t. $$
For a zero initial state, the equivalent matrices and length-$L$ kernel are $\bar A=G^{-1}(I+\alpha A)$, $\bar B=G^{-1}\Delta B$, and $K_j=C^*\bar A^j\bar B$ for $0\le j<L$; a direct term $Du_t$, if present, is added separately.

For the filter mode, fix an integer $L\ge1$, let $M$ be the least power of two with $M\ge L$, let $\omega=e^{-2\pi i/M}$, and let $\widetilde C\in\mathbb C^N$ be supplied as the length-$M$ truncated-output parameter. When a conventional output vector $C$ is used, this parameter is $\widetilde C=(I-\bar A^M)^*C$. Define the $M$ root values $z_k=\omega^k$. The algorithm returns the first $L$ coefficients of the inverse radix-two transform of the values $H(z_k)$ below.

For $z_k=-1$, set $H(z_k)=(\Delta/2)\widetilde C^*B$. For each $z=z_k\ne-1$, put $s(z)=(2/\Delta)(1-z)/(1+z)$. If $s(z)-\lambda_j=0$ for some diagonal entry $\lambda_j$ of $\Lambda$, return status `resonant-diagonal`. If no diagonal resonance is present, write $R(z)=\operatorname{diag}((s(z)-\lambda_j)^{-1})$ and $W(z)=I_r+Q^*R(z)P$. If $W(z)$ is singular, return status `resonant-correction`. When this correction is invertible, the target root value is
$$ H(z)=\frac{2}{1+z}\left(\widetilde C^*R(z)B-\widetilde C^*R(z)P\,W(z)^{-1}Q^*R(z)B\right). $$
The preceding resolvent expression specifies the target root values. The filter evaluation computes them using $1+2r+r^2=(r+1)^2$ scalar Cauchy products as follows. Put $a=2/\Delta$, and for each $j$ with $\lambda_j\ne-a$ define $\mu_j=(a-\lambda_j)/(a+\lambda_j)$. For any pair of vectors $u,v\in\mathbb C^N$, compute on the root grid
$$ S_{uv}(z)=\frac{2}{1+z}u^*R(z)v =\frac{\Delta}{2}\sum_{j:\lambda_j=-a}\overline{u_j}v_j-2\sum_{j:\lambda_j\ne-a}\frac{\overline{u_j}v_j}{a+\lambda_j}\frac{1}{z-\mu_j} $$
by calling the roots-of-unity Cauchy procedure with poles $\mu_j$ and weights $-2\overline{u_j}v_j/(a+\lambda_j)$, then adding the displayed constant. A collision $\mu_j=z_k$ returns status `resonant-diagonal`. For $z=z_k\ne-1$, set
$$ W(z)=I_r+\frac{1+z}{2}S_{Q,P}(z),\qquad H(z)=S_{\widetilde C,B}(z)-\frac{1+z}{2}S_{\widetilde C,P}(z)W(z)^{-1}S_{Q,B}(z). $$
If $W(z)$ is singular, return status `resonant-correction`. The four families $S_{\widetilde C,B}$, $S_{\widetilde C,P}$, $S_{Q,B}$, and $S_{Q,P}$ contain $1$, $r$, $r$, and $r^2$ scalar products, respectively. The root $-1$ is handled directly and is never included in this Cauchy evaluation. Matrix products and inversions of the $r\times r$ corrections are performed separately at each root.

The recurrent solver may exploit the diagonal-plus-low-rank structure as follows. Write $d_j=1-\alpha\lambda_j$, let $J=\{j:d_j\ne0\}$ and $Z=\{j:d_j=0\}$. If $Z$ is empty, use the Woodbury inverse with $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_j)$ and correction $I_r+\alpha Q^*D^{-1}P$; if this correction is singular, return status `singular-bilinear-matrix`. If $s=|Z|>0$, then when $s\le r$ solve the bordered system
$$ \begin{bmatrix} I_r+\alpha Q_J^*D_J^{-1}P_J&-Q_Z^*\\ \alpha P_Z&0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}z\\x_Z\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}Q_J^*D_J^{-1}b_J\\b_Z\end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_J=D_J^{-1}(b_J-\alpha P_Jz), $$
where $D_J=\operatorname{diag}(d_j)_{j\in J}$; if $s>r$ or the bordered system is singular, return status `singular-bilinear-matrix`. Here $z=Q^*x$. This branch solves $Gx=b$ without assuming the diagonal base is invertible.

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, $M=2^q\ge1$, $\omega$ be a primitive $M$th root of unity, and let $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n\in\mathbb C$ and $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb C$ satisfy $\mu_j\ne\omega^k$ for every $j$ and $0\le k<M$. Then the Cauchy matrix-vector product $y_k=\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_j/(\omega^k-\mu_j)$, $0\le k<M$, is computed exactly by the balanced product-tree procedure using $O((n+M)\log^2(2+n+M))$ complex arithmetic operations and $O(n+M)$ space. Repeated poles are allowed.

## Statement references

[Pan, “Fast Approximate Computations with Cauchy Matrices and Polynomials,” §3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1506.02285)

[[alg-cauchy-matvec-at-roots-of-unity]]

[[lem-roots-of-unity-fft-complexity]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite data and noncollision hypothesis in the Statement.

[A1] For every $1\le j\le n$ and $0\le k<M$, $\omega^k-\mu_j\ne0$, so the target sums and all root-grid denominator evaluations are defined.

[F1] [[alg-cauchy-matvec-at-roots-of-unity]]: the product-tree leaves are $D_j(z)=z-\mu_j$, $P_j(z)=a_j$; internal nodes use $D_I=D_{I_1}D_{I_2}$ and $P_I=P_{I_1}D_{I_2}+D_{I_1}P_{I_2}$, then fold coefficients modulo $z^M-1$, evaluate on the standard radix-two root grid, reindex to the supplied primitive root, and divide the evaluated numerator by denominator.

[F2] [[lem-roots-of-unity-fft-complexity]]: polynomials of degree less than $s$ multiply exactly in $O(s\log(2+s))$ complex arithmetic operations and $O(s)$ space, and an $M$-point radix-two DFT costs $O(M\log(2+M))$ operations and $O(M)$ space.

## Proof

1.1 For a leaf containing index $j$, $P_j(z)/D_j(z)=a_j/(z-\mu_j)$ whenever $z\ne\mu_j$. If the identity $P_I/D_I=\sum_{j\in I}a_j/(z-\mu_j)$ holds for the two child sets, then the internal-node formulas in [F1] give $P_I/D_I=P_{I_1}/D_{I_1}+P_{I_2}/D_{I_2}$. Induction up the finite tree therefore gives $P_I(z)/D_I(z)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_j/(z-\mu_j)$ at the root wherever its denominator is nonzero. [A1, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 The balanced tree has height at most $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$. At a node whose index set has size $s$, its three polynomial products have operand degrees at most $s$; by [F2] they cost $O(s\log(2+s))$ operations. At a fixed height, the node index sets are disjoint and their sizes sum to at most $n$, so that height costs at most $O(n\log(2+n))$. Summing over the height gives $O(n\log^2(2+n))$ operations, including the coefficient additions. A depth-first evaluation stores at most one completed sibling subtree per level; their coefficient-array sizes form a geometric sum bounded by $O(n)$, so the product-tree workspace is $O(n)$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Write the root coefficients as $P_I(z)=\sum_j p_jz^j$ and $D_I(z)=\sum_j d_jz^j$. For each $0\le r<M$, fold them to $p'_r=\sum_{j\equiv r\pmod M}p_j$ and $d'_r=\sum_{j\equiv r\pmod M}d_j$. Since $\omega^{kM}=1$, evaluating the folded polynomials at $\omega^k$ gives exactly $P_I(\omega^k)$ and $D_I(\omega^k)$. The algorithm evaluates both folded arrays with two radix-two DFTs on the standard grid $\omega_0^j=e^{-2\pi i j/M}$; if $M>1$, the supplied primitive root is $\omega=\omega_0^s$ for a unique odd $s$, so reindexing the standard outputs at $sk\bmod M$ gives their values at $\omega^k$. For $M=1$ the grids coincide. By [F2] the two transforms cost $O(M\log(2+M))$ operations and $O(M)$ additional space; finding $s$ and reindexing cost $O(M)$ operations and space, within the same bounds. Folding costs $O(n)$ operations and $O(n+M)$ space. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The noncollision hypothesis makes $D_I(\omega^k)=\prod_j(\omega^k-\mu_j)\ne0$ for every $k$. Thus the divisions in [F1] are defined, and step 1.1 identifies each quotient with the required Cauchy sum. Adding the product-tree, folding, transform, and division costs gives $O((n+M)\log^2(2+n+M))$ operations and $O(n+M)$ space. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎
