## Statement

For PARITY, whose members are the bit strings with an even number of $1$s, no fixed finite-depth hard-attention sequence model with fixed parameters recognizes every sufficiently long input exactly. For 2DYCK, whose words are correctly balanced and properly nested strings over two bracket types, no such hard-attention model recognizes the language. In both cases the model appends an end marker before classification.

For all soft-attention conclusions below, fix the parameter matrices, depth, and number of heads independently of length; use scaled dot-product scores with fixed linear query/key/value maps, uniformly bounded token and positional embeddings combined by addition, globally Lipschitz positionwise maps, and a fixed globally Lipschitz logit readout followed by softmax. Under these one-symbol influence assumptions, the parity source process with fixed $p\in(0,1)$ has sharp unigram cross-entropy level
$$
H(u),\qquad u(\mathtt{eos})=p/2,\quad u(0)=u(1)=(2-p)/4.
$$
Every such predictor has limiting lower cross-entropy at least $H(u)$, and the constant predictor $u$ attains it.

For the 2DYCK PCFG with rules $S\to(S)S$ and $S\to[S]S$ each of probability $p/2$, and $S\to\epsilon$ of probability $1-p$, fix any $p\in(0,1)$. Read its left-to-right output as a finite or infinite bracket stream; sample a length-$k$ prefix conditional on at least $k$ bracket tokens having been emitted, and predict the ordinary next token, without conditioning on exact total length. Every fixed soft-attention predictor satisfying these one-symbol influence assumptions has
$$
\liminf_{k\to\infty}(\mathcal L_{p,k}-\mathcal L_{p,k}^*)\ge p^2(1-p)^2\log 2>0,
$$
where $\mathcal L_{p,k}$ is its expected next-token cross-entropy under this prefix law and $\mathcal L_{p,k}^*$ is the corresponding optimal conditional cross-entropy.

The PCFG is a probability law on finite words precisely when $p\le1/2$. For all $p\in(0,1)$ its finite output can instead be conditioned on eventual termination. For that finite-word probability law, sample prefixes conditional on reaching length $k$ and predict the next token without any additional length conditioning. The same positive-gap conclusion holds with $p$ replaced by $a=\min(p,1-p)$:
$$
\liminf_{k\to\infty}(\mathcal L^{\mathrm{fin}}_{p,k}-(\mathcal L^{\mathrm{fin}}_{p,k})^*)\ge a^2(1-a)^2\log 2>0.
$$
For $p\le1/2$ these two prefix laws agree. At $p=1/2$ finite words have infinite expected length, but the prefix bounds still hold. For $p>1/2$ the first law includes nonterminating streams and the second conditions them away; neither is an unconditioned probability distribution on finite words with the original parameter $p$. These are cross-entropy limits, not exact-classification impossibility theorems.

## Statement references

[Hahn, §§5–6: hard-attention language limits and soft-attention prediction bounds](https://aclanthology.org/2020.tacl-1.11.pdf)

[[lem-soft-attention-one-symbol-influence]]: the precise bounded dot-product model and globally Lipschitz readout followed by softmax.

[[lem-soft-2dyck-crossentropy-gap-paired-prefixes]]: the paired-prefix soft-attention gap.

[[lem-2dyck-pcfg-prefix-mass-positive]]: exact stream and finite-word prefix laws and a uniform equal-mass pairing.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The formal-language definitions and model conventions in the Statement.

[F1] Fixed-depth hard attention cannot recognize PARITY or 2DYCK with the stated end-marker convention ([[thm-hard-attention-languages]]).

[F2] For the stated parity source, every such soft predictor has limiting expected cross-entropy at least $H(u)$, and the constant predictor $u$ attains $H(u)$ ([[thm-soft-attention-parity-chance-limit]]).

[F3] Under a positive-mass disjoint equal-prefix pairing whose conditional closing targets are swapped, soft-attention next-token cross-entropy exceeds the conditional optimum by at least $P_0(1-p)\log 2$ in the limit ([[lem-soft-2dyck-crossentropy-gap-paired-prefixes]]).

[F4] The stream prefix law has disjoint equal-mass pairs of mass at least $p^2(1-p)$, obtained by flipping the outer opening in a final three-token opening-opening-closing pattern. Conditioning on finite output replaces the parameter by $a=\min(p,1-p)$ and gives the same pairing with that parameter ([[lem-2dyck-pcfg-prefix-mass-positive]]).

## Proof

1.1 The hard-attention assertions are exactly [F1], proved by the iterated restriction reduction for the fixed finite depth and finite alphabet, with the end marker fixed. [given, F1, construct]

1.2 The parity cross-entropy lower bound and its sharpness are exactly [F2]. The probability vector $u$ is the equal mixture of the even-parity target $(p,(1-p)/2,(1-p)/2)$ and odd-parity target $(0,1/2,1/2)$ in coordinate order $(\mathtt{eos},0,1)$. [given, F2, algebra]

1.3 Put $n=k+1$ and append the fixed readout end marker to each sampled length-$k$ prefix. By [F4], every prefix in the paired event ends with a closing bracket and has positive stack height; the flipped opening at position $k-2$ is nonfinal. The pair members have equal probability and ordinary next-token laws assigning $p/2$ to each opening and $1-p$ to opposite matching closing types. Hence all hypotheses of [F3] hold with $P_0=p^2(1-p)$. It gives excess cross-entropy at least $p^2(1-p)^2\log2$ in the lower limit. The appended readout marker is an input convention and does not assert that the sampled source prefix terminates there. [given, F3, F4, construct, algebra]

2.1 Under conditioning on eventual termination, [F4] identifies the entire prefix and target process with parameter $a=\min(p,1-p)$. Repeat step 1.3 with $a$ to prove the finite-word bound. The finite-word mass and extinction calculation in [F4] give the stated distinction between the two laws. At $p=1/2$, let $G_j$ be the nodes in generation $j$ of the derivation tree. A finite-generation induction gives $\mathbb E|G_j|=(2p)^j=1$ for every $j$. Hence the number $Z_N=\sum_{j=0}^{N}|G_j|$ of nodes through generation $N$ has expectation $N+1$. The total node count $Z$ is at least $Z_N$, so monotonicity of expectation gives $\mathbb E Z\ge N+1$ for every $N$ and therefore $\mathbb E Z=\infty$, without interchanging an expectation with an infinite sum. Finite derivations are full binary trees, and their word length is their node count minus one; thus the finite-word law has infinite expected length. Neither pairing proof uses finite expected length. [given, F4, step 1.3, algebra, induction] ∎

## Remarks

The explicit prefix-sampling law resolves the conditioning left implicit in Hahn's Theorem 6. Its finite-mean Markov-chain sketch is unnecessary: extending any surviving prefix by two openings and the matching inner close supplies positive paired mass directly. Exact-total-length conditioning is a different prediction problem; its next-token probabilities are not generally $p/2,p/2,1-p$. The fixed-length universality theorem concerns a separate regime with resources allowed to grow.

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$, $n\ge2$, $m\ge2$ be integers, set $\delta=1/m$ and $q=\delta^{-d}$, and assume $n\le q$. Define
$$G_\delta=\{0,\delta,\ldots,1-\delta\}^{d\times n},\qquad G_\delta^+=\{-\delta^{-nd},0,\delta,\ldots,1-\delta\}^{d\times n}.$$
Let $\widehat G_\delta$ consist of those $L\in G_\delta$ whose columns are pairwise distinct. For column-token matrices $Z\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}$, consider finite compositions of residual attention updates
$$Z\longmapsto Z+\sum_{h=1}^{2}o_h(v_h^{\mathsf T}Z)\, \operatorname{hmax}\!\left((k_h^{\mathsf T}Z)^{\mathsf T}(r_h^{\mathsf T}Z+b_h\mathbf1_n^{\mathsf T})\right)$$
and residual tokenwise updates
$$
Z\longmapsto Z+w\,\phi(v^{\mathsf T}Z+b\mathbf1_n^{\mathsf T}),
$$
where all displayed vectors and scalars are fixed across columns, $\operatorname{hmax}$ assigns equal weights to all maximizing entries in each column, and each scalar $\phi$ is piecewise affine on at most three intervals with at least one constant piece. If $A:\widehat G_\delta\to\mathbb R^{d\times n}$ satisfies $A(LP)=A(L)P$ for every column-permutation matrix $P$, then such a composition maps each $L\in\widehat G_\delta$ to $A(L)$ and each $L\in G_\delta^+\setminus\widehat G_\delta$ to $0$.

There is also a position-tagged version. For each $j=1,\ldots,n$, let
$$J_j=\{j-1,j-1+\delta,\ldots,j-\delta\}^d,\qquad G_{\delta,\mathrm{pos}}=J_1\times\cdots\times J_n,$$
where the $j$th factor specifies column $j$. For every function $A:G_{\delta,\mathrm{pos}}\to\mathbb R^{d\times n}$, with no permutation condition, a finite composition of the same updates maps each $L\in G_{\delta,\mathrm{pos}}$ to $A(L)$.

## Statement references

[Yun et al., Appendix B.4: scalar quantization by tokenwise layers](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.10077)

[Yun et al., Appendices B.5–B.6: contextual codes and finite tokenwise value lookup](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.10077)

[Yun et al., Appendix C.1–C.3: the position-tagged lookup construction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.10077)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The integer grids and finite tables in the Statement.

[F1] The Yun expressivity block has two heads of size one, shared query/key/value and output maps, a shared scalar query bias, residual attention, and a tokenwise ReLU feedforward sublayer of width four; it has no layer normalization ([[def-transformer-encoder-decoder-layer]]).

[F2] Every finite composition of the unmasked Yun attention and shared tokenwise maps is permutation equivariant ([[thm-transformer-permutation-equivariance-without-position]]).

[F3] Positional encodings are added columnwise to the token matrix before the position-aware stack ([[def-positional-encoding-and-causal-mask]]).

## Proof

For the unpositioned equivariance used below, let $P$ be any column-permutation matrix. In a shared Yun head, $v^{\mathsf T}ZP=(v^{\mathsf T}Z)P$ and the query and key projections transform the same way, so its score matrix satisfies $S(ZP)=P^{\mathsf T}S(Z)P$. Equal-weight hardmax acts columnwise and commutes with row and column permutations, giving $\operatorname{hmax}(S(ZP))=P^{\mathsf T}\operatorname{hmax}(S(Z))P$. Multiplication by the permuted value row then gives the permuted attention output, and residual addition preserves this identity. A shared tokenwise update also commutes with column permutations because $\mathbf1_n^{\mathsf T}P=\mathbf1_n^{\mathsf T}$ and its coordinatewise activation is applied identically in every column. Thus every modified Yun attention or tokenwise update, and every finite composition of them, is permutation equivariant. This is the unnormalized, hardmax version of the supplier calculation in [thm-transformer-permutation-equivariance-without-position].

1.1 Put $u=(1,\delta^{-1},\ldots,\delta^{-d+1})$. For a grid column $x=(a_1\delta,\ldots,a_d\delta)$, where $a_i\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$, its scalar code is $$\ell(x)=u^{\mathsf T}x,\qquad \ell(x)/\delta=a_1+a_2m+\cdots+a_dm^{d-1}.$$ Thus the valid column codes are distinct multiples of $\delta$ in $[0,B]$, where $B=\delta(q-1)$. If a column has a sentinel coordinate $-\delta^{-nd}$, the sum of all its other coordinate contributions is at most $\delta^{-d+1}-1$, so its code is at most $-\delta^{-nd}+\delta^{-d+1}-1<0$. [given, algebra]

1.2 For a scalar threshold $b$, the single-head update $$ \psi(Z;b)=e_1(u^{\mathsf T}Z)\operatorname{hmax}\!\left((u^{\mathsf T}Z)^{\mathsf T}(u^{\mathsf T}Z-b\mathbf1_n^{\mathsf T})\right) $$ is an allowed attention update contribution: its key and value projections are $u$, its query projection is $u$ with bias $-b$, and its output vector is $e_1$. In query column $j$, if $\ell_j>b$ it returns the largest current scalar code, and if $\ell_j<b$ it returns the smallest. If $\ell_j=b$, all query scores are zero and equal-weight hardmax returns the mean $\bar\ell=n^{-1}\sum_k\ell_k$. Thus, writing $\ell_{\max}=\max_k\ell_k$ and $\ell_{\min}=\min_k\ell_k$, the contribution $\psi(Z;b)-\psi(Z;b')$ for $b<b'$ is $\ell_{\max}-\ell_{\min}$ in the first coordinate when $b<\ell_j<b'$, $\bar\ell-\ell_{\min}$ when $\ell_j=b$, $\ell_{\max}-\bar\ell$ when $\ell_j=b'$, and zero when $\ell_j<b$ or $\ell_j>b'$. In particular, if no current code equals either threshold, it shifts exactly the columns strictly between them by $\ell_{\max}-\ell_{\min}$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Sweep the valid scalar codes $0,\delta,\ldots,B$ in increasing order, using the two-head update $\;Z\mapsto Z+q(\psi(Z;\ell-\delta/2)-\psi(Z;\ell+\delta/2))\;$ at code $\ell$. All initial codes, including sentinel codes, are multiples of $\delta$: every grid coordinate lies in $\delta\mathbb Z$ and every entry of $u$ is an integer. Since $q=m^d$ is an integer, each strict selective shift preserves this lattice; inductively no current code can equal any half-grid threshold $\ell\pm\delta/2$. This also applies to duplicate-column inputs and to the position-tagged lattice. For $L\in\widehat G_\delta$, order its distinct column codes as $\ell_1<\cdots<\ell_n$. The first sweep shifts only $\ell_1$ to $\widetilde\ell_1=\ell_1+q(\ell_n-\ell_1)>B$, since $\ell_n-\ell_1\ge\delta$ and $q\delta=B+\delta$. Each later sweep shifts the next unmodified code and gives $$ \widetilde\ell_j=\ell_j+q(\widetilde\ell_{j-1}-\ell_j)>\widetilde\ell_{j-1}\qquad(2\le j\le n). $$ Thus shifted columns leave all later threshold intervals, and the final scalar codes satisfy $0<\widetilde\ell_1<\cdots<\widetilde\ell_n$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 Write $g_j=\ell_{j+1}-\ell_j\ge\delta$. Unrolling the recurrence in step 2.1 gives $$ t:=\widetilde\ell_n=\ell_n+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(q^n-q^{n-j})g_j. $$ Consequently $$\delta q^{n-1}(q-1)\le t\le \delta q^n(q-1)-\delta(q-1)^2.$$ The lower bound follows from the $j=1$ term; the upper bound follows from $\ell_n\le B$ and $\sum_jg_j\le B$. The map $(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n)\mapsto t$ is injective: if two ordered tuples give the same $t$, put $a_j=(\ell_j-\ell'_j)/\delta\in\mathbb Z$, so $|a_j|\le q-1$. The difference equation is $$ a_n+q(a_{n-1}-a_n)+\cdots+q^{n-1}(a_1-a_2)+q^n(a_n-a_1)=0. $$ Reduction modulo $q$ first gives $a_n=0$; division by $q$ and repeated reduction modulo $q$ then gives $a_{n-1}=0,\ldots,a_1=0$. Hence distinct unordered column multisets have distinct $t$ values, separated by at least $\delta$. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Apply one final single-head update $Z\mapsto Z+K\psi(Z;0)$, with a positive integer $K$. For valid $L$, all $\widetilde\ell_j>0$, so it adds $Kt$ to every first coordinate and changes the scalar codes to $$ c_{L,j}=Kt+\widetilde\ell_j. $$ For different column multisets, their $t$ values differ by at least $\delta$, while $0<\widetilde\ell_j\le t$. Choose $K$ so that $K\delta>\max t$ over the finite valid grid. The intervals $[Kt,Kt+t]$ for different multisets are disjoint, and codes within one multiset are distinct by step 2.1. All resulting codes are multiples of $\delta$, hence distinct codes are at least $\delta$ apart. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F2, choose, algebra]

5.1 If $L$ has duplicate columns but no sentinel, its scalar codes have only $r<n$ distinct levels. The same sweep shifts these $r$ levels, and its largest value is at most $\delta q^r(q-1)-\delta(q-1)^2\le\delta q^{n-1}(q-1)-\delta(q-1)^2$, strictly below the lower bound for valid $t$ in step 3.1. A sentinel column has a negative code by step 1.1 and remains the minimum throughout the sweep. If all codes are negative, the final update in step 4.1 shifts every code further negative. If some codes are nonnegative, the first nonnegative code is shifted by at least $q(q^n-B)>\delta q^{n+1}$; the later positive codes are shifted by still larger amounts. This exceeds every valid $t$ in step 3.1. Thus, after the final update, each invalid scalar code has one of three forms: below every valid code, above every valid code, or negative. Since there are finitely many grid inputs and all codes are multiples of $\delta$, choose $K$ large enough that every invalid code lies at least $\delta$ outside the interval from the least to the greatest valid code. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra, choose]

6.1 The preceding construction gives a finite scalar code for each token of each valid context; these codes are all distinct, and column permutations carry each code and its token to the corresponding permuted token by [F2]. Let $\lambda_-$ and $\lambda_+$ be the least and greatest valid codes. Because the table $A$ and grid are finite, enlarge $K$ so that $|u^{\mathsf T}A(L)_{:,j}|<\lambda_- -\delta/3$ for every valid $L,j$. A three-piece constant activation that is zero on $[\lambda_- -\delta/3,\lambda_+ +\delta/3]$ and one outside this interval detects exactly the invalid codes. Subtracting a constant larger than the maximum absolute coordinate of every encoded grid state makes every invalid state strictly negative; coordinatewise clipping with $\phi(t)=\max(0,t)$ sends it to zero and leaves valid nonnegative codes unchanged. For each valid code $c_{L,j}$, a three-piece pulse equal to one on $[-\delta/3,\delta/3]$ and zero outside, applied to $u^{\mathsf T}Z-c_{L,j}$, selects exactly its token. Add the vector $A(L)_{:,j}-Z_{:,j}$ at that token. The updated token has scalar value $u^{\mathsf T}A(L)_{:,j}$ below every code, so later pulses cannot select it; the remaining tokens retain their codes until selected. Equivariance of $A$ makes each update correct for every permutation of $L$. This yields $A(L)$ on $\widehat G_\delta$ and zero on every other point of $G_\delta^+$. [step 4.1, step 5.1, F2, construct, choose, algebra]

7.1 For the position-tagged grid, the scalar code of column $j$ has the form $$ \ell_j=(j-1)S+r_j,\qquad S=\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\delta^{-k},\quad 0\le r_j\le B,\quad r_j\in\delta\mathbb Z. $$ Since $S-B\ge\delta$, codes in a matrix satisfy $\ell_1<\cdots<\ell_n$ and each individual code identifies its column vector. Sweep all possible position-tagged scalar codes in increasing order with the same selective shifts. The recurrence of step 2.1 holds, and different matrices give different ordered tuples $(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n)$. The divisibility argument in step 3.1 still applies because, for each fixed position, the offsets $(j-1)S$ cancel and the difference of two $r_j$ values has magnitude at most $B$. Thus the final maxima $t$ distinguish all position-tagged matrices, and the codes $Kt+\widetilde\ell_j$ distinguish every token in every matrix when $K\delta>\max t$. Choose $K$ still larger so these positive codes exceed all finitely many target values $|u^{\mathsf T}A(L)_{:,j}|+\delta/3$. The pulse layers of step 6.1 then implement the arbitrary table $A$; no permutation condition is needed because the position offsets distinguish columns. [given, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 6.1, F3, choose, algebra]

8.1 Each update used above is either a two-head attention update, a single-head attention update with the second head set to zero, or a tokenwise scalar piecewise-affine update; an unused attention or feedforward sublayer is made the identity by setting its output weights to zero. Therefore the finite constructions are compositions of the modified Yun blocks specified in the Statement, proving both lookup assertions. [step 1.2, step 6.1, step 7.1, F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Use the standard dense self-attention interaction with $n$ token rows, model width $d$, and $h$ heads whose total query/key/value width is $d$ (for example, $h$ heads of width $d/h$ when $h$ divides $d$). Counting scalar multiply-add operations in the direct matrix implementation, forming all query-key scores and applying the resulting dense weight matrix to all value rows costs $O(n^2d)$ per attention sublayer; row softmax adds $O(n^2)$. Every query position has a direct value path from every key position, so one unmasked self-attention sublayer gives path length one between any input token value and any output token. A fixed stack of $L$ such layers has a position-to-position path of at most $L$ attention edges, independent of $n$.

If each query, key, value, and output projection is a dense $d\times d$ linear map and the tokenwise feedforward width is $d_{\rm ff}$, those operations add $O(nd^2+ndd_{\rm ff})$ work per full Transformer layer. Thus the $O(n^2d)$ claim concerns the dense all-pairs attention interaction used in the source comparison; it does not assert that projections or the feedforward sublayer have that cost, and it makes no claim about sparse attention, linear attention, training work, memory traffic, or hardware speed.

## Statement references

[Vaswani et al., Table 1 and §4: self-attention interaction complexity, sequential operations, and maximum path length](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762)

[Dive into Deep Learning, §11.6.2: scaled-attention matrix multiplications and direct token connections](https://www.d2l.ai/chapter_attention-mechanisms-and-transformers/self-attention-and-positional-encoding.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Positive integers $n,d$, the dense multi-head self-attention dimensions in the Statement, and the direct matrix implementation.

[F1] The forward pass forms scaled query-key scores, applies row softmax, and multiplies the resulting attention weights by values ([[alg-transformer-forward-pass]]).

## Proof

1.1 For one head of width $d_h$, the score product has dimensions $(n\times d_h)(d_h\times n)$ and therefore uses $O(n^2d_h)$ scalar multiply-adds. The value product has dimensions $(n\times n)(n\times d_h)$ and also uses $O(n^2d_h)$ operations. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 For finite real scores, every softmax weight is strictly positive, so each output row uses the value row of every input position. This is one direct attention edge; composing $L$ layers yields at most one such edge per layer, hence at most $L$ attention edges independent of $n$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Summing over $h$ heads with total width $\sum_{a=1}^h d_h^{(a)}=d$ gives $O(n^2d)$ score and value work. Normalizing $n$ rows of $n$ scores costs $O(n^2)$, which is at most $O(n^2d)$ because $d\ge1$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 A dense projection of an $n\times d$ matrix by a $d\times d$ matrix costs $O(nd^2)$, and a two-map positionwise feedforward network of hidden width $d_{\rm ff}$ costs $O(ndd_{\rm ff})$. Adding these separate terms gives the full-layer operation count stated in the Statement. [given, F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, fix integers $d\ge1$ and $n\ge2$, and fix $1\le p<\infty$. For a matrix $Y\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}$, let $\|Y\|_p=(\sum_{r=1}^d\sum_{j=1}^n|Y_{rj}|^p)^{1/p}$, and for measurable maps on $\mathbb R^{d\times n}$ define
$$
d_p(f,g)=\left(\int_{\mathbb R^{dn}}\|f(X)-g(X)\|_p^p\,dX\right)^{1/p},
$$
using $dn$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Let $\mathcal T^{2,1,4}$ be the finite compositions of the two-head, head-size-one Yun blocks with tokenwise ReLU feedforward width four and no layer normalization. If $f:\mathbb R^{d\times n}\to\mathbb R^{d\times n}$ is continuous, has compact support, and satisfies $f(XP)=f(X)P$ for every $n\times n$ permutation matrix $P$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $g\in\mathcal T^{2,1,4}$ with $d_p(f,g)<\varepsilon$.

For every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^{d\times n}$ and every continuous $f:K\to\mathbb R^{d\times n}$, with no permutation condition, there are a trainable positional matrix $E\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}$ and $g\in\mathcal T^{2,1,4}$ such that
$$
\left(\int_K\|f(X)-g(X+E)\|_p^p\,dX\right)^{1/p}<\varepsilon.
$$

## Statement references

[Yun et al., Theorems 2–3: fixed-length permutation-equivariant and position-encoded approximation](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.10077)

[Kajitsuka and Sato, Proposition 1 and Appendix A.5: an independent, wider one-head universality construction](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/96ee35c170cb8720033b16259c305da9-Paper-Conference.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, fixed $d,n,p$, the target maps in the Statement, and $\varepsilon>0$.

[F1] Each block in $\mathcal T^{2,1,4}$ has two unmasked heads of size one, residual attention, a shared tokenwise ReLU feedforward sublayer of width four, and no layer normalization; a scalar query bias is allowed ([[def-transformer-encoder-decoder-layer]]).

[F2] The column-token Yun block and every unpositioned composition of it are permutation equivariant ([[thm-transformer-permutation-equivariance-without-position]]).

[F3] A two-head, head-size-one modified network with piecewise-affine scalar gates performs exact finite lookup on the distinct-column grid and on position-tagged grids; the first version returns zero on duplicate-column and sentinel grid points ([[lem-yun-transformer-grid-lookup]]).

[F4] A continuous map from a compact metric space to a metric space is uniformly continuous ([[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]).

[F5] Under Countable Choice, Lebesgue measure is a complete countably additive measure extending box volume, and compact subsets of Euclidean space are measurable ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]).

1.2 Now consider continuous $f$ on compact $K$ without symmetry. If $K$ has zero Lebesgue measure, the integral is zero for any network. Otherwise let $a,b$ be the minimum and maximum of its scalar entries; again $a<b$. Put $\alpha=(b-a)^{-1}$ and choose $$ E_{rj}=(b-a)(j-1)-a\qquad(1\le r\le d,\ 1\le j\le n). $$ The first residual width-four sublayers scale $X+E$ by $\alpha$, producing entries $(X_{rj}-a)/(b-a)+(j-1)$. For each feature row, apply the residual updates $t\mapsto t+\eta_\delta(t-k)$ in increasing order for $k=0,\delta,\ldots,n-\delta$. Thus the quantized matrices lie in $G_{\delta,\mathrm{pos}}$ from [F3], where position offsets make every column distinct. For each grid cell meeting $K$, choose a representative $X_L\in K$ and set $A(L)=f(X_L)$; set arbitrary values, for example zero, on cells disjoint from $K$. ## Example

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X=(x_1,x_2)\in[0,1]^{1\times2}$ and define the constant ordered-output map $f(X)=(0,1)$. A position-free unmasked self-attention stack followed by shared tokenwise maps must permute its two output entries when the two input tokens are exchanged, whereas a trainable positional matrix can distinguish the first and second token positions. On the compact square $[0,1]^2$, the position-encoded fixed-length theorem therefore approximates $f$ in integrated $L_p$ error for every $1\le p<\infty$.

## Example references

[Yun et al., Appendix A: permutation equivariance without positional encoding](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.10077)

[Yun et al., Theorem 3: trainable positional encodings on a compact domain](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.10077)

[[def-countable-choice]]: the inherited premise for the local integrated-Lebesgue approximation theorem.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the two-token input $X$, the coordinate-swap permutation $P$, the constant map $f$, and position-free or position-encoded Transformer stacks as in the Example.

[F1] The row-token theorem gives $R(PZ)=PR(Z)$. In the column-token convention used here, define $T(X)=R(X^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T}$; transposition gives $T(XP)=T(X)P$ for every unmasked position-free stack with shared tokenwise maps ([[thm-transformer-permutation-equivariance-without-position]]).

[F2] Assuming Countable Choice, for fixed $n\ge2$, $d\ge1$, and $1\le p<\infty$, a two-head, head-size-one Transformer with width-four ReLU feedforward layers, no layer normalization, and a trainable positional matrix approximates every continuous map on a compact domain in integrated $L_p$ error, for $1\le p<\infty$ ([[thm-fixed-width-transformer-lp-universality]]).

## Proof

1.1 Let $P$ swap the two columns. Since $f$ is constant, $f(XP)=(0,1)$, while $f(X)P=(1,0)$. Hence $f(XP)\ne f(X)P$, so $f$ is not permutation equivariant. By [F1], no position-free stack can equal $f$ on both $X$ and $XP$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The map $f$ is continuous on $K=[0,1]^{1\times2}$, which is compact, and $n=2,d=1$ meet the size hypotheses. Under the assumed Countable Choice, the position-encoded compact-domain branch of [F2] with any prescribed $\varepsilon>0$ gives a position-encoded stack whose integrated $L_p$ error from $f$ is less than $\varepsilon$. Thus positional tags remove the equivariance restriction for this fixed-length approximation problem. [given, F2] ∎

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and fix an integer maximum length $N\ge2$. For each individual integer length $2\le n\le N$, the fixed-length theorem concerns a compact-domain approximation problem and permits a Transformer chosen for that particular $n$ and error tolerance. The hard-attention language limit instead fixes one finite-depth model, with one set of parameter maps independent of length, and rules out exact recognition of PARITY and 2DYCK for all sufficiently long strings. For each fixed source parameter $p\in(0,1)$, the soft-attention parity result fixes one model satisfying the one-symbol influence hypotheses across lengths and bounds the limit inferior of its expected cross-entropy on the stated parity source from below by the sharp unigram chance entropy, attained by a constant predictor. ## Definition

Let $A$ and $U$ be real Banach spaces of functions on bounded domains $D$ and $D'$, with the input point evaluations used below defined. For every $n\ge1$, choose finite-dimensional normed spaces $E_n,F_n$, an exactly defined sampling map $S_n:A\to E_n$ (for example, $S_n(a)=(a(\xi_{n,1}),\ldots,a(\xi_{n,N_n}))$ at specified input points), a finite-dimensional map $\widetilde G_n:E_n\to F_n$, and an output reconstruction map $R_n:F_n\to U$. The reconstruction supplies a function with a defined value at every point of $D'$. The corresponding continuum-valued discrete map is
$$G_n(a):=R_n\bigl(\widetilde G_n(S_n(a))\bigr)\in U.$$
A family $(G_n)_{n\ge1}$ is a **discretization-invariant approximation** of an operator $G:A\to U$ if its sampling maps and output reconstructions are part of the family and it approximates this single continuum operator as the input discretization is refined. In the compact-uniform version, for every compact $K\subset A$,
$$\sup_{a\in K}\|G_n(a)-G(a)\|_U\longrightarrow0.$$
When $A$ consists of almost-everywhere equivalence classes, the sampling map must be explicitly defined on those classes or use a specified representative convention; point evaluation is not inferred from the equivalence class alone. This definition does not identify unrelated grid-specific maps as one operator family.

## Definition

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, let $\Gamma\subseteq\partial U$ be closed, let $L$ be a differential operator on $U$, and let $B$ be a boundary operator on $\Gamma$. Let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ and $g:\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ be target data. For a trial function $h$, define its residuals by $r_h(x)=L[h](x)-f(x)$ and $q_h(x)=B[h](x)-g(x)$. For $0<\alpha\le1$ and a function $v$ on a set $E$, define its Hölder seminorm by
$$[v]_{\alpha;E}=\sup_{x\ne y\in E}\frac{|v(x)-v(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
Only trial functions for which $L[h]$ on $U$ and $B[h]$ on $\Gamma$ are pointwise defined and finite are admitted. For the population loss, require $f,r_h$ to be measurable with respect to $(U,\mu_r)$ and $g,q_h$ to be measurable with respect to $(\Gamma,\mu_b)$. For positive fixed weights $\lambda_r,\lambda_b$ and probability measures $\mu_r$ on $U$, $\mu_b$ on $\Gamma$, the population loss is
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)=\lambda_r\int_U|r_h|^2\,d\mu_r+\lambda_b\int_\Gamma|q_h|^2\,d\mu_b.$$
These nonnegative population integrals take values in $[0,+\infty]$, so they may be infinite. The Hölder seminorms below may likewise be infinite.

For $d\ge2$, given positive integer counts $m_r,m_b$, residual collocation points $x_r^1,\ldots,x_r^{m_r}$, and boundary collocation points $x_b^1,\ldots,x_b^{m_b}$, the empirical loss is
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_{m}(h;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda_r}{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}|r_h(x_r^i)|^2+\frac{\lambda_b}{m_b}\sum_{j=1}^{m_b}|q_h(x_b^j)|^2.$$
For $d=1$, a bounded Lipschitz domain has finite boundary, so $\Gamma$ is finite. When every point of $\Gamma$ is available deterministically, define its exact full-boundary contribution by
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN},b}(h;\lambda_b)=\lambda_b\sum_{y\in\Gamma}\mu_b(\{y\})|q_h(y)|^2=\lambda_b\int_\Gamma|q_h|^2\,d\mu_b,$$
and, for a positive integer count $m_r$ and residual collocation points $x_r^1,\ldots,x_r^{m_r}$, set
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_{m}(h;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda_r}{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}|r_h(x_r^i)|^2+\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN},b}(h;\lambda_b).$$
For $d\ge2$, its Hölder-regularized version is
$$\operatorname{Loss}_{m}(h;\lambda,\lambda_m^R)=\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)+\lambda^R_{r,m}[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^{2}+\lambda^R_{b,m}[B[h]]_{\alpha;\Gamma}^{2}.$$
For $d=1$, the Hölder-regularized version is
$$\operatorname{Loss}_{m}(h;\lambda,\lambda_m^R)=\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)+\lambda^R_{r,m}[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^{2};$$
it uses the exact full-boundary contribution above, has no random boundary sample, and has no boundary seminorm penalty. Require the regularization coefficients appearing in either version to be nonnegative; a zero coefficient contributes zero even when its seminorm is infinite. For finite realized sample lists the empirical sums are finite; the regularized objective is allowed to take the value $+\infty$. These are population and empirical functionals; they do not specify an optimization algorithm or assert that training reaches a global minimizer.

## Definition

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open. For coefficients $a_{ij},b_i,c_i,d$ on $U$, define the positive divergence-form operator
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^d D_i(a_{ij}D_j u)+\sum_{i=1}^dD_i(b_i u)+\sum_{i=1}^d c_iD_i u+du.$$
When the coefficients are continuously differentiable where needed, its nondivergence expansion is
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^d a_{ij}D_iD_j u+\sum_{j=1}^d\widetilde b_jD_j u+\widetilde c\,u,$$
with
$$\widetilde b_j=\sum_{i=1}^dD_i a_{ij}+b_j+c_j,\qquad \widetilde c=\sum_{i=1}^dD_i b_i+d.$$
The **positive divergence convention** here means that the principal part is $+\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_j u)$. This sign is part of the definition.

## Definition references
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables|ck and multi index notation in several variables]]

[Shin et al., equation (3.6): elliptic divergence-form operator and expanded coefficients](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)


## Source indexing discrepancy

The source displays $\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_j u+b_i u)$ while its expanded coefficients and energy argument count $D_i(b_i u)$ only once. Read literally, that displayed sum instead gives $d\sum_iD_i(b_i u)$ and changes both the drift and potential. The active definition above separates the two sums explicitly and agrees with the stated expanded coefficients. The original printed expression is retained here as a source discrepancy, not used as an algebraic identity.

## Definition

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded, let $T>0$, and set $Q=U\times(0,T)$ and
$$\Gamma_T=(\bar U\times\{0\})\cup(\partial U\times[0,T]).$$
The final-time face $U\times\{T\}$ is excluded from $\Gamma_T$. For time-dependent coefficients define
$$L_t[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^dD_i(a_{ij}(x,t)D_j u)+\sum_{i=1}^dD_i(b_i(x,t)u)+\sum_{i=1}^d c_i(x,t)D_i u+d(x,t)u.$$
Where the coefficient derivatives exist, write its nondivergence expansion as
$$L_t[u]=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}D_iD_j u+\sum_i\widetilde b_iD_i u+\widetilde c\,u,$$
where $\widetilde b_i=\sum_jD_j a_{ji}+b_i+c_i$ and $\widetilde c=\sum_iD_i b_i+d$. For symmetric $a$, the drift also equals $\sum_jD_j a_{ij}+b_i+c_i$, the form used by the symmetric source consumers. The initial-boundary value problem uses the sign convention
$$-u_t+L_t[u]=f\quad\hbox{in }Q,\qquad u=\varphi\quad\hbox{on }\partial U\times[0,T],\qquad u=g\quad\hbox{on }\bar U\times\{0\},$$
with compatibility $g(x)=\varphi(x,0)$ on $\partial U$. Its residual for a trial function $h$ is $f+h_t-L_t[h]$, and its prescribed-data error is measured on $\Gamma_T$.

For the source notation $C_{2+\alpha}(Q)$, use the parabolic distance
$$d_p((x,t),(y,s))=(|x-y|^2+|t-s|)^{1/2}.$$
Let $B=U\times\{0\}$ and $S_\tau=\partial U\times[0,\tau]$. For $P=(x,\tau)\in Q$, set $\delta(P)=\inf_{R\in B\cup S_\tau}d_p(P,R)$ and $\delta_{P,Q}=\min\{\delta(P),\delta(Q)\}$. For an integer $m\ge0$, define
$$|v|_{m,\alpha}=\sup_{P\in Q}\delta(P)^m|v(P)|+\sup_{P\ne Q\in Q}\delta_{P,Q}^{m+\alpha}\frac{|v(P)-v(Q)|}{d_p(P,Q)^\alpha}.$$
The class $C_{2+\alpha}(Q)$ consists of functions for which
$$|u|_{0,\alpha}+\sum_i|D_i u|_{1,\alpha}+\sum_{i,j}|D_{ij}u|_{1,\alpha}+|u_t|_{2,\alpha}<\infty,$$
with the indicated derivatives continuous in $Q$. This fixes the source's weighted parabolic Hölder convention.

id: lem-pinn-random-samples-are-space-filling
kind: lemma
title: "Lower cell-mass bounds give a random fill-distance estimate"
status: draft
origin: pipeline

sources:
  references:
    - title: "Shin, Darbon, and Karniadakis, On the Convergence of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Linear Second-Order Elliptic and Parabolic Type PDEs"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806"
      locator: "Appendix B, Lemma B.2 and its proof"
---

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$, $s>0$, and let $X\subset\mathbb R^d$ carry a probability measure $\mu$. Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and $c>0$, and put $\varepsilon=(c\sqrt m)^{-1/s}$. Suppose there is a finite measurable partition $X_1,\ldots,X_K$ of $X$ at this particular scale such that each cell lies in a cube of side $\varepsilon$ and $\mu(X_j)\ge c\varepsilon^s$. Let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ be independent random points each with law $\mu$. Then with probability at least
$$1-\sqrt m\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt m}\right)^m$$
every point of $X$ lies within Euclidean distance $\sqrt d\,c^{-1/s}m^{-1/(2s)}$ of at least one sample point. For an interior space of dimension $d$, use $s=d$; for a boundary space of Hausdorff dimension $d-1>0$, use $s=d-1$ and its own cell-mass constant. If $d=1$ and every boundary point is available deterministically, the boundary fill distance is zero and no random boundary sample is needed.

## Statement references
[[def-probability-measure|probability measure]]

[[def-independent-random-elements|independent random elements]]

[Shin et al., Appendix B, Lemma B.2: probabilistic space-filling estimate](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

[Shin et al., Appendix B, proof of Lemma B.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite partition at the selected scale, its cell-mass lower bound, and $m$ independent samples with common law $\mu$.

[F1] A probability measure is finitely subadditive, so the probability of a finite union of missed-cell events is at most the sum of their probabilities ([[def-measure]], [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]).

[F2] Independent random elements with common law $\mu$ have product law on each finite tuple; hence the probability that all $m$ samples miss a cell of measure $p_j$ is $(1-p_j)^m$ ([[def-independent-random-elements]]).

[F3] Countable additivity, applied to the finite disjoint partition followed by empty sets, makes the cell measures sum to the measure of the whole space ([[def-measure]]).

## Proof

**Proof strategy:** coupon-collector union bound.

1.1 The cell measures sum to one by [F3], and each is at least $c\varepsilon^s=1/\sqrt m$. Therefore the number of cells is at most $\sqrt m$. [given, F3, algebra]

1.2 A fixed cell of mass $p_j\ge c\varepsilon^s=1/\sqrt m$ is missed by all $m$ independent samples with probability $(1-p_j)^m\le(1-1/\sqrt m)^m$ by [F2]. By [F1], the probability that at least one cell is missed is at most $\sqrt m(1-1/\sqrt m)^m$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 On the complementary event, every cell contains a sample. Since each cell lies in a cube of side $\varepsilon$, any point of the cell is within the cube's Euclidean diameter $\sqrt d\varepsilon$ of a sample in that same cell. Substituting $\varepsilon=(c\sqrt m)^{-1/s}$ gives the stated fill radius and probability. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

It suffices to assume the partitions exist for $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$ and then restrict to $m\ge\max\{1,c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-2s}\}$. Indeed, this is exactly the condition $(c\sqrt m)^{-1/s}\le\varepsilon_0$. For upper ball-mass bounds used at the fill radius, also require $\sqrt D(c\sqrt m)^{-1/s}\le\rho_0$ if their range is $0<\rho\le\rho_0$. The normalized Appendix B mass is $c\varepsilon^s=1/\sqrt m$, so its failure probability is $\sqrt m(1-1/\sqrt m)^m$, independently of $c$. If one deliberately chooses $0<c\le1$, this is no larger than $\sqrt m(1-c/\sqrt m)^m$, recovering the weaker later printed probability with those same chosen constants. Replacing a lower-mass constant by a smaller one is valid, but all radii, $C_m$, and regularization thresholds must then use the new constant. No such replacement is made implicitly.

## Statement

Let $X$ be a nonempty measurable space, let $d\ge1$, let $c>0$, and let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $X$. There is no family of finite measurable partitions $\mathcal P_\varepsilon$ of $X$, one for every $\varepsilon>0$, for which every cell $E\in\mathcal P_\varepsilon$ satisfies $\mu(E)\ge c\varepsilon^d$.

## Statement references

[Shin et al., Assumption 3.1, clause 3: the all-$\epsilon>0$ lower cell-mass condition](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A probability measure $\mu$ on nonempty $X$, an integer $d\ge1$, and a constant $c>0$.

[F1] A probability measure satisfies $\mu(X)=1$ ([[def-probability-measure]]).

[F2] If $E\subseteq X$ is measurable, then $\mu(E)\le\mu(X)$ ([[prop-measure-monotonicity]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** choose one scale at which the asserted lower bound exceeds total mass.

1.1 Choose $\varepsilon>c^{-1/d}$. Since $X$ is nonempty, any partition of $X$ has at least one cell $E$. The set $E$ is measurable and $E\subseteq X$, so [F1] and [F2] give $\mu(E)\le1$. [given, F1, F2, choose]

2.1 The asserted lower bound gives $\mu(E)\ge c\varepsilon^d>1$, contradicting step 1.1. Hence no such all-scale family of partitions exists. [given, step 1.1, algebra, contradiction] ∎

## Statement

There exists $b\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $0\le b\le1$, $b(x)=1$ for $|x|\le1$, and $b(x)=0$ for $|x|\ge2$, such that the profile $\chi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ defined by $\chi(r)=b(4r)$ is the restriction of a smooth function on $\mathbb R$, equals $1$ for $0\le r\le1/4$, and equals $0$ for $r\ge1/2$.

Here $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ denotes the infinitely differentiable, compactly supported real-valued functions.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A one-dimensional smooth cutoff with unit plateau radius $1$ and support radius $2$ as stated in [F1].

[F2] Composition of a smooth function with an affine map is smooth, by the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Choose $b$ supplied by [F1] and set $\chi(r)=b(4r)$ for $r\ge0$. [F1, choose]

2.1 The function $x\mapsto b(4x)$ is smooth by [F2], so its restriction is the stated smooth profile. If $0\le r\le1/4$, then $|4r|\le1$ and $b(4r)=1$; if $r\ge1/2$, then $|4r|\ge2$ and $b(4r)=0$. The bounds on $b$ are inherited by composition. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces, let $K\subseteq X$ be compact, and let $f,f_n:X\to Y$ be continuous for every integer $n\ge1$. Suppose that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N\ge1$ such that $d_Y(f_n(x),f(x))<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$ and all $x\in K$.
Then
$$W=f[K]\cup\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n[K]$$
is compact in $Y$. The empty-set case is included, and the proof uses no choice principle.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Metric spaces, a compact subset $K$, continuous maps, and uniform convergence on $K$ as stated.

[F1] Compactness means that every open cover has a finite subcover; this convention applies to compact subsets of metric spaces ([[def-metric-compactness]]).

[F2] A continuous map sends a compact subset of a metric space to a compact subset ([[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]).

[F3] In a metric space, open sets contain an open ball about each of their points, and open balls are open ([[def-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** open-cover argument with a uniform neighborhood of the limit image.

1.1 If $K=\emptyset$, then $W=\emptyset$ and it is compact. Otherwise let $\mathcal V$ be any open cover of $W$. By [F2], $f[K]$ is compact, so [F1] gives finitely many $V_1,\ldots,V_q\in\mathcal V$ covering $f[K]$. Set $O=\bigcup_{i=1}^qV_i$, an open set containing $f[K]$. [given, F1, F2, cases]

2.1 Form the family of all balls $B_Y(y,r)$ with $y\in f[K]$, $r>0$, and $B_Y(y,2r)\subseteq O$. This family covers $f[K]$ by openness and [F3], so [F1] gives a finite subcover with centers $y_1,\ldots,y_s$ and radii $r_1,\ldots,r_s$. Since $f[K]\ne\emptyset$, $s\ge1$; let $\delta=\min_i r_i>0$. If $z\in Y$ and $d_Y(z,y)<\delta$ for some $y\in f[K]$, choose $i$ with $d_Y(y,y_i)<r_i$; then $d_Y(z,y_i)<\delta+r_i\le2r_i$, so $z\in B_Y(y_i,2r_i)\subseteq O$. Thus every point within distance $\delta$ of some point of $f[K]$ lies in $O$. [step 1.1, F1, F3, algebra]

3.1 Uniform convergence supplies $N\ge1$ such that $d_Y(f_n(x),f(x))<\delta$ for every $x\in K$ and every $n\ge N$. Since $f(x)\in f[K]$, step 2.1 implies $f_n[K]\subseteq O$ for every $n\ge N$. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For each of the finitely many indices $1\le n<N$, [F2] makes $f_n[K]$ compact, so [F1] supplies a finite subfamily of $\mathcal V$ covering it. Together with $V_1,\ldots,V_q$ from step 1.1, these finitely many members cover $f[K]$, all $f_n[K]$ with $n\ge N$, and each remaining $f_n[K]$. Hence every open cover of $W$ has a finite subcover, so $W$ is compact by [F1]. The proof uses only finite subcovers and a finite minimum, not a choice axiom. [step 1.1, step 3.1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]].

- An **open cover** of $(X,d)$ is a family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$
  with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$, where
  $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily
  $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \emptyset$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,d)$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite subcover: for
  every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \emptyset$ and the empty subfamily
  covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the metric
  subspace $(A, d_A)$ is a compact metric space, $d_A$ being the restriction of
  $d$ to $A \times A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A,d_A)$ and its own open sets, not
about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do agree,
but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], and no item of this library may use the
ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading as the
definition is what makes "compact" a property of the metric space $(A,d_A)$
alone, so that a set compact in one ambient space is compact in every other one
containing it isometrically.

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. The
one-point space is compact too, and so is every space listed as
$\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$: given a cover, each $x_i$ lies in some member, and
finitely many members chosen in this way already cover.

**The finiteness convention, and how it is used both ways.** "Finite" above is
the listing form, matching the finite lists of
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. It agrees with the definition of
finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number ([[def-countable]]), and
both directions of the agreement are available and are used below:

- A nonempty finite set $F$ in the sense of [[def-countable]] satisfies
  $F \approx m$ for some $m \ge 1$, and a bijection $m \to F$ is exactly a
  listing $F = \{a_0, \dots, a_{m-1}\}$.
- Conversely a set listed as $A = \{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$, that is the image of a
  function $a$ with domain $\sigma(n)$, is finite in the sense of
  [[def-countable]]: the map sending $x \in A$ to the least $i \le n$ with
  $a_i = x$ is an injection of $A$ into $\sigma(n)$, so $A$ is equinumerous with
  a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ bounded above, and such a subset is finite
  ([[lem-subset-of-countable]]).

Neither direction uses a choice principle: the second selects nothing, taking a
least index instead.

## Remarks

**Why open covers rather than closed ones.** Nothing in the definition would
break if $\mathcal{U}$ were allowed to consist of arbitrary sets, but the
resulting notion would be uninteresting: every space is covered by its
singletons, and only a finite space would survive. Openness of the members is
what makes the condition a genuine restriction, and it is what
[[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] has to keep track of when the ambient space
changes.

**A warning about the word "cover".** A family may cover $A \subseteq X$ without
being a family of subsets of $A$: the members are open subsets of $X$ and their
union merely contains $A$. That is the ambient reading, and it is a different
statement from "$\mathcal{U}$ is an open cover of the metric space $(A,d_A)$",
whose members are open subsets of $A$. Which of the two is meant is written out
everywhere on this page.

## Statement

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Metric spaces $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ and a continuous $f : X \to Y$; images and preimages are written $f[\,\cdot\,]$ and $f^{-1}[\,\cdot\,]$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

[L1] A subset $A$ of a metric space is compact exactly when for every family $(V_i)_{i \in I}$ of open subsets of the ambient space with $A \subseteq \bigcup_{i \in I} V_i$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $i_0, \dots, i_n \in I$ with $A \subseteq V_{i_0} \cup \dots \cup V_{i_n}$, or else $A = \emptyset$; and a space is a compact subset of itself exactly when it is a compact metric space ([[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], [[def-metric-compactness]]).

[L2] $f$ is continuous exactly when $f^{-1}[V]$ is open in $X$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$ ([[thm-metric-continuity-characterisations]], [[def-metric-continuity]], [[def-metric-topology]]).

[L3] The restriction of $f$ to a metric subspace $(K,d_K)$ of $X$ is continuous as a map $(K,d_K) \to (Y,d_Y)$, since the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition at a point of $K$ is the condition for $f$ at that point read for the points of $K$ only, and $d_K$ is the restriction of $d_X$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]], [[def-metric-continuity]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Assume $(X,d_X)$ compact and let $(V_i)_{i \in I}$ be a family of open subsets of $Y$ with $f[X] \subseteq \bigcup_{i \in I} V_i$. [L1]

2.1 Each $f^{-1}[V_i]$ is open in $X$, and $X = \bigcup_{i \in I} f^{-1}[V_i]$, because every $x \in X$ has $f(x) \in f[X]$ and so $f(x) \in V_i$ for some $i$. [L2, step 1.1]

3.1 If $X = \emptyset$ then $f[X] = \emptyset$ and there is nothing to prove; otherwise compactness of $X$, read against the indexed family of step 2.1, gives $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $i_0, \dots, i_n \in I$ with $X = f^{-1}[V_{i_0}] \cup \dots \cup f^{-1}[V_{i_n}]$. [L1, step 2.1]

4.1 Every $y \in f[X]$ is $f(x)$ for some $x \in X$, and that $x$ lies in some $f^{-1}[V_{i_j}]$, so $y \in V_{i_j}$; hence $f[X] \subseteq V_{i_0} \cup \dots \cup V_{i_n}$ and $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$: claim 1. [L1, step 3.1]

5.1 For claim 2, let $K \subseteq X$ be a compact subset, so that $(K,d_K)$ is a compact metric space; the restriction of $f$ to $K$ is continuous, and its image is $f[K]$, so claim 1 applied to that restriction gives that $f[K]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. [L1, L3, step 4.1] ∎

## Remarks

**Compactness travels forwards, not backwards.** The preimage of a compact set under a continuous map need not be compact: a constant map from an unbounded space has a one-point image. What claim 1 uses is that preimages of *open* sets are open, which is the content of continuity, together with the fact that a finite subcover upstairs projects to a finite subcover downstairs.

**Consequences on this page.** Claim 1 with $Y = \mathbb{R}$ gives the extreme value theorem ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]), and claim 2 is what makes the inverse of a continuous bijection from a compact space continuous ([[thm-continuous-bijection-from-a-compact-space-has-continuous-inverse]]).

## Definition

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

## Remarks

- **(M3') is a genuine strengthening of (M3), not an independent axiom on top of
  it.** A function satisfying (M1), (M2) and (M3') automatically satisfies (M3):
  by [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] such a function is nonnegative, and for
  nonnegative reals $a, b$ one has $\max\{a,b\} \le a + b$, since the maximum is
  one of $a, b$ and the other summand is $\ge 0$. So "a metric satisfying (M3')"
  and "a function satisfying (M1), (M2), (M3')" describe the same objects, and
  the definition above may be read either way.

- **Why the biconditional form of (M1).** Splitting (M1) into "$d(x,x) = 0$" and
  "$d(x,y) = 0 \Rightarrow x = y$" gives the same notion; the split form is what
  makes the pseudometric weakening above a matter of deleting one clause. The
  naming fork between *pseudometric* and *semimetric*, which is live in the
  literature, is settled for this library in
  [[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]].

- **The metric is part of the data.** Two different metrics on the same set are
  two different metric spaces, even when they have the same open sets. That is
  why [[def-equivalent-metrics]] compares metrics at three separate strengths
  rather than one, and why a property can be invariant under one of them and not
  under another ([[fs-boundedness-is-a-topological-property]]).

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Each of the real spaces $L^p(D)$ for $1\le p<\infty$, $W^{m,p}(D)$ for $m\in\mathbb N$ and $1\le p<\infty$, and $C^m(\bar D)$ for $m\in\mathbb N_0$ has the approximation property: on every norm-compact subset, the identity can be approximated uniformly by bounded finite-rank linear maps. Here the $C^m$ norm is the maximum of the uniform norms of the derivatives through order $m$, extended continuously to $\bar D$. For any bounded Lipschitz domain $D'\subset\mathbb R^{d'}$, the corresponding real output spaces $L^{p_2}(D')$ for $1\le p_2<\infty$, $W^{m_2,p_2}(D')$ for $m_2\in\mathbb N$ and $1\le p_2<\infty$, and $C^{m_2}(\overline{D'})$ for $m_2\in\mathbb N_0$ also have the approximation property.

## Statement references

[[def-countable-choice]]

[[def-approximation-property-and-bounded-approximation-property]]

[Kovachki et al., Lemma 26](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume24/21-1524/21-1524.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, a bounded Lipschitz domain and one of the listed real function spaces.

[F1] For every listed space, every norm-compact set and every positive error, a bounded finite-rank map with that compact-uniform error exists, with range consisting of restrictions of compactly supported ambient smooth functions ([[lem-inward-mollification-and-finite-rank-approximation-on-lipschitz-domains]]).

[F2] AP for a Banach space means uniform approximation of the identity on each norm-compact subset by bounded finite-rank linear maps ([[def-approximation-property-and-bounded-approximation-property]]).

[F3] Under Countable Choice, the integer-order Sobolev formula is a norm and $W^{0,p}=L^p$, and real $L^p$ is complete ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]]).

[F4] Hölder bounds the integral pairing by the product of conjugate norms, including conjugate exponents $1$ and $\infty$ ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]).

[F5] For a continuously differentiable real curve on a compact interval, the integral of its derivative is its endpoint difference; a continuous integrand has its integral as a differentiable primitive ([[lem-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-banach-valued-continuous-curves]]).

**Choice use:** Countable Choice supplies the $L^p$ completeness and weak-derivative interfaces in [F3], the calculus interface [F5], and the inward-mollification lemma [F1]. The final passage to AP makes no additional selections from infinite families.

## Proof

1.1 The listed Sobolev spaces are Banach under the stated Countable Choice hypothesis. Indeed, let $(u_n)$ be Cauchy in $W^{m,p}(D)$. By [F3], for each of the finitely many $|\alpha|\le m$, $D^\alpha u_n$ converges in $L^p$ to a class $v_\alpha$; put $u=v_0$. For any $\phi\in C_c^\infty(D)$, its derivatives are bounded with compact support, hence belong to the conjugate $L^{p'}$ space, including $p'=\infty$ when $p=1$. By [F4], both integrals in $\int_Du_nD^\alpha\phi=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_DD^\alpha u_n\phi$ converge to the corresponding integrals of $u$ and $v_\alpha$. Thus $v_\alpha$ is the weak derivative $D^\alpha u$ by [F3], so $u\in W^{m,p}(D)$, and the finite norm sum gives $u_n\to u$ in that norm. This includes $m=0$, which gives $L^p(D)$. [F3, F4, given, construct]

1.2 The listed $C^m(\bar D)$ spaces are Banach as well. If $(u_n)$ is Cauchy in their norm, every derivative sequence has a uniform limit $g_\alpha$ on $\bar D$: pointwise real completeness gives the limit, and the uniform Cauchy estimate gives uniform convergence. Each $g_\alpha$ is continuous, since for a positive error one first approximates it uniformly by a fixed continuous $D^\alpha u_n$ and then applies continuity of that fixed function. Put $u=g_0$. For $|\alpha|<m$, an interior point $x$, and a coordinate direction $e_i$, take $h$ small enough that the segment $x+[0,h]e_i$ lies in $D$. By [F5], $D^\alpha u_n(x+he_i)-D^\alpha u_n(x)=\int_0^hD^{\alpha+e_i}u_n(x+se_i)\,ds$. Uniform convergence passes this identity to $g_\alpha(x+he_i)-g_\alpha(x)=\int_0^h g_{\alpha+e_i}(x+se_i)\,ds$, since the integral error is bounded by $|h|$ times the uniform error. By [F5], $\partial_i g_\alpha=g_{\alpha+e_i}$. Induction in $|\alpha|$ yields $D^\alpha u=g_\alpha$ in $D$ through order $m$, with the continuous extensions already supplied on $\bar D$. Thus $u\in C^m(\bar D)$ and $u_n\to u$ in norm. For $m=0$ only the uniform-limit continuity argument is needed. The displayed maximum is a norm because its order-zero term detects zero functions and the remaining norm axioms hold termwise. [F5, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Fix one listed space $X$, a norm-compact $K\subseteq X$, and $\varepsilon>0$. Its Banach-space status was established in the two preceding steps. Apply [F1], using $W^{0,p}=L^p$ in the Lebesgue case, to obtain a bounded finite-rank $F:X\to X$ with $\sup_{u\in K}\|Fu-u\|_X<\varepsilon$. These are exactly the quantified requirements of [F2], so every listed space has AP, including every $p=1$ case. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, given]

3.1 The argument in step 2.1 holds for every Euclidean dimension, every nonnegative integer regularity and every finite exponent in the stated ranges. Applying it with the output dimension and output regularity parameters proves the output-space clause. The proof establishes AP for $C^m(\bar D)$ without any basis assertion. [step 2.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz open set, with $d\ge1$, and let $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Let $X$ be either $W^{m,p}(D;\mathbb R)$ for $1\le p<\infty$, including $W^{0,p}(D)=L^p(D)$, or $C^m(\bar D;\mathbb R)$. In the latter space derivatives in $D$ extend continuously to $\bar D$, and the norm is $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{\bar D}|D^\alpha u|$. For every norm-compact $K\subseteq X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a bounded finite-rank linear map $F:X\to X$ such that $\sup_{u\in K}\|Fu-u\|_X<\varepsilon$ and whose range is contained in the restrictions to $D$ of functions in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, with their continuous boundary values in the $C^m$ case. In particular, such smooth restrictions are norm-dense in $X$.

Moreover, there are finitely many ambient smooth cutoffs $\psi_j$, vectors $v_j$, a unit-mass $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, and $t_0>0$ such that for $0<t<t_0$ the kernel $k_t(x,y)=\sum_j\psi_j(x)\rho_t(x+tv_j-y)$, with $\rho_t(z)=t^{-d}\rho(z/t)$, defines bounded linear smoothing maps $S_tu(x)=\int_Dk_t(x,y)u(y)\,dy$. They satisfy $\sup_{0<t<t_0}\|S_t\|_{X\to X}<\infty$ and $\sup_{u\in K}\|S_tu-u\|_X\to0$ for every norm-compact $K\subset X$. Each kernel is ambient smooth with fixed compact support in its first variable.

## Statement references

[[def-countable-choice]]

[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]

[Kovachki et al., Lemma 26](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume24/21-1524/21-1524.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $D,d,m,X,K,\varepsilon$ as in the statement. Lipschitz means that every boundary point has a rigid graph chart in which $D$ is the strict epigraph of a Lipschitz function.

[F1] The Sobolev norm is the finite $\ell^p$ sum of the $L^p$ norms of the weak derivatives through order $m$, and $W^{0,p}=L^p$; this is a well-defined norm under Countable Choice ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]]).

[F2] A finite open cover of a compact Euclidean set admits nonnegative ambient smooth functions compactly supported in the respective cover members and summing to one on a neighborhood of that set ([[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]]).

[F3] Interior mollification commutes with every weak derivative through order $m$ wherever the closed mollifier-support ball is compactly contained in the domain ([[lem-mollification-commutes-with-weak-derivatives-in-the-interior]]).

[F4] Under Countable Choice, translations are isometries in $L^p(\mathbb R^d)$ and are norm-continuous for $p<\infty$; convolution with a compact smooth kernel is smooth and differentiates by differentiating the kernel ([[lem-complex-translation-and-approximate-identity-interfaces]]).

[F5] Minkowski's integral inequality holds for all $1\le p<\infty$; its $p=1$ case is Tonelli's identity ([[thm-minkowski-integral-inequality]]).

[F6] Classical derivatives of a $C^m$ function are weak derivatives, and the weak Leibniz rule holds for a smooth multiplier with bounded derivatives ([[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]], [[lem-weak-leibniz-rule-with-a-smooth-factor]]).

[F7] Closed bounded Euclidean sets are compact, and continuous maps on compact metric spaces are uniformly continuous ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]).

[F8] Bounded measurable Euclidean sets have finite measure, and Hölder, including $p=1$, gives $\|u\|_{L^1(D)}\le |D|^{1-1/p}\|u\|_{L^p(D)}$ for nonempty open $D$ ([[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]).

[F9] Nested balls admit a nonnegative compactly supported smooth bump equal to one on the inner ball ([[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]).

**Choice use:** Countable Choice is used in the Sobolev, Lebesgue-measure, translation, convolution and weak-derivative interfaces [F1], [F3]–[F6], [F8]. The geometric cover and all later nets and cell selections are finite selections. No stronger choice axiom is used.

## Proof

1.1 If $D=\varnothing$, $X$ is the zero space; take $F=0$, the empty cutoff family, $k_t=0$, $S_t=0$ and $t_0=1$. If $K=\varnothing$ the compact approximation clause is vacuous and $F=0$ suffices; the smoothing construction below depends only on $D$ and $X$, and can be obtained by carrying it out with $K=\{0\}$. Henceforth both sets are nonempty. In particular $0<|D|<\infty$, because $D$ contains a ball and is bounded. Fix one boundary chart $Q$, with Lipschitz graph function $\varphi$ of constant $L$, and an ambient neighborhood $U$ of its boundary point with $\bar U\subset Q$ compact. In chart coordinates set $v=(L+2)e_d$. For $x\in\bar D\cap\bar U$, $|z|\le1$, and sufficiently small $t>0$, uniformly in $x,z$, the point $y=x+tv-tz$ stays in $Q$ because $t(|v|+1)<\operatorname{dist}(\bar U,Q^c)$. Moreover $y_d-\varphi(y')\ge x_d-\varphi(x')+t(L+2)-t|z_d|-Lt|z'|\ge t>0$. Thus $\overline B(x+tv,t)\Subset D$. Rotate $v$ back to the original coordinates. [given, F7, F8, construct, algebra]

2.1 The compact boundary admits finitely many such $U_j$, $1\le j\le J$, covering it. The compact remainder $\bar D\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^JU_j$ lies in $D$; cover it by finitely many balls with closures in $D$, and let $U_0$ be their union, omitting it if the remainder is empty. Then $\bar U_0\Subset D$, so $v_0=0$ has the same ball property for sufficiently small $t$. Apply [F2] to this finite open cover of $\bar D$, obtaining $\psi_j\in C_c^\infty(U_j)$ with $\sum_j\psi_j=1$ near $\bar D$. The minimum of the finitely many positive bounds on $t$ gives $t_0>0$ such that $\overline B(x+tv_j,t)\Subset D$ for every $x\in\bar D\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi_j$ and $0<t<t_0$. Taking the family of all admissible chart neighborhoods before extracting a finite subcover avoids selecting a chart independently at every boundary point. [F2, F7, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 By [F9] choose a nonnegative smooth bump compactly supported in $B_1(0)$ and positive on $\overline B_{1/2}(0)$, and divide it by its positive integral to obtain $\rho\in C_c^\infty(B_1(0))$ with $\int\rho=1$. Put $\rho_t(w)=t^{-d}\rho(w/t)$. Every $u\in X$ belongs continuously to $L^1(D)$: use [F8] for Sobolev spaces, and $\|u\|_1\le |D|\|u\|_{C^m}$ for $C^m$. For its zero extension $E_0u$ define $H_{j,t}u(x)=(\rho_t*E_0u)(x+tv_j)$ and $S_tu=\sum_j\psi_jH_{j,t}u$. By [F4] these are well-defined linear constructions independent of representatives and $S_tu\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$. [F4, F8, F9, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 First take $X=W^{m,p}(D)$. For every $|\gamma|\le m$ and $x\in\bar D\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi_j$, [F3] and step 2.1 give $$D^\gamma H_{j,t}u(x)=\int\rho(z)(E_0D^\gamma u)(x+t(v_j-z))\,dz.$$ The translated center has distance greater than $t$ from $D^c$: the entire closed ball of radius $t$ is a compact subset of $D$. The identity consequently holds on a neighborhood of each indicated $x$. Equivalently the defining weak-derivative identity can be tested against $y\mapsto\rho_t(x+tv_j-y)$, whose support is compact in $D$; its two derivative signs cancel. Only interior values are used, with no assertion that derivatives commute with zero extension across $\partial D$. [F1, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1]

4.2 For $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^d)$ define $T_{j,t}f(x)=\int\rho(z)f(x+t(v_j-z))\,dz$ and $\omega_f(r)=\sup_{|h|\le r}\|f(\cdot+h)-f\|_p$. Translation invariance and [F5] give $\|T_{j,t}f\|_p\le\|f\|_p$ and $$\|T_{j,t}f-f\|_p\le\omega_f((|v_j|+1)t).$$ By [F4], $\omega_f(r)\to0$ as $r\downarrow0$. The integral estimates also apply when $p=1$, where [F5] follows directly from Tonelli. [F4, F5, step 3.1, construct]

4.3 Fix $0<t<t_0$. Write $k_t(x,y)=\sum_j\psi_j(x)\rho_t(x+tv_j-y)$, so $S_tu(x)=\int_D k_t(x,y)u(y)\,dy$. Fix a closed box $Q$ containing $\bar D$. The finitely many $D_x^\alpha k_t$, $|\alpha|\le m$, are smooth and uniformly continuous on the compact set $\bar D\times Q$ by [F7]. For any $\eta>0$, partition $Q$ into finitely many measurable cells $Q_\ell$ of small enough diameter, assigning shared and outer faces consistently, and choose $y_\ell\in Q_\ell$. Their diameters can be chosen so that $|D_x^\alpha k_t(x,y)-D_x^\alpha k_t(x,y_\ell)|<\eta$ for $x\in\bar D$, $y\in Q_\ell$ and $|\alpha|\le m$. The point $y_\ell$ need not lie in $D$. [F7, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Set $f_\gamma=E_0D^\gamma u$. The finite Leibniz rule [F6], step 4.1 and $\sum_j\psi_j=1$ near $\bar D$ give, for $|\alpha|\le m$, the a.e. identity on $D$ $$D^\alpha(S_tu-u)=\sum_j\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\psi_j)\bigl(T_{j,t}f_{\alpha-\beta}-D^{\alpha-\beta}u\bigr).$$ Every derivative $D^\beta\psi_j$ vanishes off $\operatorname{supp}\psi_j$, so step 4.1 supplies exactly the identities used in this formula. All these fixed multiplier derivatives are bounded. Step 4.2 and the finite norm sum [F1] therefore imply $\|S_tu-u\|_{W^{m,p}}\to0$. The same Leibniz formula without subtracting $u$, and $\|T_{j,t}f_\gamma\|_p\le\|f_\gamma\|_p\le\|u\|_{W^{m,p}}$, give $\sup_{0<t<t_0}\|S_t\|_{X\to X}\le M_X<\infty$. For example take the $\ell^p$ norm over $\alpha$ of $\sum_{j,\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}\|D^\beta\psi_j\|_\infty$. This argument includes $m=0$ and $p=1$. [F1, F6, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 Now take $X=C^m(\bar D)$. By [F6] each bounded classical derivative is its weak derivative, so $u\in W^{m,1}(D)$ and step 4.1 applies. Each $D^\gamma u$ is uniformly continuous on $\bar D$ by [F7]. For $x\in\bar D\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi_j$, every sampled $y=x+t(v_j-z)$ lies in $D$ and $|y-x|\le(|v_j|+1)t$. Positivity and mass one of $\rho$ thus give $$\sup_{x\in\bar D\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi_j}|D^\gamma H_{j,t}u(x)-D^\gamma u(x)|\le\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\bar D\\|x-y|\le(|v_j|+1)t}}|D^\gamma u(y)-D^\gamma u(x)|\longrightarrow0.$$ The formula of step 5.1, first on $D$ and then by continuity on $\bar D$, gives $\|S_tu-u\|_{C^m}\to0$. Bounding each averaged derivative by $\|D^\gamma u\|_\infty$ and summing the same fixed multiplier constants gives $\sup_{0<t<t_0}\|S_t\|_{X\to X}\le M_X<\infty$ also in this case. [F6, F7, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Define $$F_{t,\eta}u(x)=\sum_\ell k_t(x,y_\ell)\int_{D\cap Q_\ell}u(y)\,dy.$$ Each coefficient is a bounded linear functional by step 3.1, and there are finitely many coefficients. Each range function $k_t(\cdot,y_\ell)$ belongs to $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, so the operator has finite rank with the required smooth range. Comparison with the integral for $S_t$ gives $$\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{\bar D}|D^\alpha(F_{t,\eta}-S_t)u|\le\eta\|u\|_{L^1(D)}.$$ For $X=C^m(\bar D)$, this yields $\|F_{t,\eta}-S_t\|_{X\to X}\le |D|\eta$. For $X=W^{m,p}(D)$ let $A_m$ be the finite number of multi-indices of order at most $m$. Taking the derivative $L^p$ norms and then applying [F8] gives $\|F_{t,\eta}-S_t\|_{X\to X}\le A_m^{1/p}|D|^{1/p}\eta |D|^{1-1/p}=A_m^{1/p}|D|\eta$. This includes $p=1$, and it shows each $F_{t,\eta}$ is bounded because $S_t$ is bounded. [F1, F8, step 3.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 4.3, construct, algebra]

7.2 By steps 5.1 and 6.1 the operators $S_t:X\to X$ converge pointwise to the identity and satisfy $\|S_t\|\le M_X$. Choose $\delta<\varepsilon/[4(M_X+1)]$. Compactness gives a finite $\delta$-net $u_1,\ldots,u_N$ in $K$. Pointwise convergence permits one $t\in(0,t_0)$ such that $\max_i\|S_tu_i-u_i\|<\varepsilon/4$. For any $u\in K$, choose one net point within $\delta$; then $\|S_tu-u\|\le(M_X+1)\delta+\max_i\|S_tu_i-u_i\|<\varepsilon/2$. Compactness also makes $R=\sup_{u\in K}\|u\|$ finite: a finite cover by unit balls bounds all these norms by one plus the largest center norm. [step 5.1, step 6.1, given, choose, algebra]

8.1 Choose $\eta>0$ small enough that the relevant bound in step 7.1 is below $\varepsilon/[2(R+1)]$. For $F=F_{t,\eta}$, $$\sup_{u\in K}\|Fu-u\|\le\|F-S_t\|R+\sup_{u\in K}\|S_tu-u\|<\varepsilon.$$ Its range is a finite span of ambient compactly supported smooth functions by step 7.1. Applying this conclusion to the singleton compact set $K=\{u\}$ proves smooth-restriction density for every $u\in X$. All net, partition and representative-point choices here are finite; Countable Choice enters only the analytical interfaces stated above. [step 7.1, step 7.2, choose, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $X$ be a Banach space. It has the **approximation property** (AP) if for
every norm-compact set $C\subseteq X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a
bounded finite-rank operator $T:X\to X$ such that

$$\sup_{x\in C}\|Tx-x\|<\varepsilon.$$

Here finite rank means that $T(X)$ is finite-dimensional.

For $\lambda\ge0$, $X$ has the **$\lambda$-bounded approximation property**
($\lambda$-BAP) if the same assertion holds with the additional operator-norm
bound $\|T\|\le\lambda$, where the norm is that of [[def-operator-norm]]. It
has the **bounded approximation property** (BAP) if it has $\lambda$-BAP for
some finite $\lambda$.

No sequence of approximating operators is required; this matters in
nonseparable spaces. Plainly $\lambda$-BAP implies AP.
