## Statement

Assume Countable Choice for the weak-derivative uniqueness interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$1\le p\le\infty$. For either real or complex scalars, the displayed
$W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ formula from
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] is independent of the representatives
of its Sobolev and derivative classes and defines a norm: it is finite,
absolutely homogeneous, subadditive, and zero exactly on the zero $L^p$ class.
This holds at $p=1$ and $p=\infty$, and when $k=0$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the only class is zero and the formula is zero.

## Sources

- Juha Kinnunen, *Sobolev Spaces*, Chapter 1 §1.2, Definition 1.8 and
  Remarks 1.9(1)–(3), printed pp. 4–6. Kinnunen uses the finite-$p$ sum and
  the sum of derivative norms for $p=\infty$, then notes that the maximum is
  an equivalent $p=\infty$ norm. The present definition uses that maximum.
- John K. Hunter, *Notes on Partial Differential Equations*, Chapter 3 §3.5,
  Definition 3.23, printed pp. 58–59. Hunter states the finite-$p$ formula,
  the $p=\infty$ maximum, and the almost-everywhere identification.
  These sources state the conventional formulas; the quotient and norm-axiom
  checks needed here are proved below.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, an open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and real or complex
$W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ classes.

[F1] The index set $\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}$
is finite and nonempty; $D^0u=u$; and the Sobolev formula is the finite-$p$
sum or the $p=\infty$ maximum over this set
([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

[F2] The weak-derivative property is invariant under almost-everywhere
changes to both its input and value classes ([[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]]).

[F3] Under Countable Choice, each locally integrable weak derivative is
unique as an almost-everywhere class
([[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]]).

[F4] Weak differentiation is complex-linear wherever the derivatives exist
([[lem-weak-derivative-linearity-locality-and-commutation]]).

[F5] The real $L^p$ quotient norm is well defined and gives a norm for every
$1\le p\le\infty$
([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

[F6] For complex $L^p$ classes, the quotient norm is well defined, homogeneous,
separating, and satisfies Minkowski for every $1\le p\le\infty$
([[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]]).

[F7] Real integral Minkowski holds on any measure space for $1\le p<\infty$;
in particular it applies to a finite set with counting measure
([[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]).

[F8] Countable Choice is the assertion that every natural-number-indexed
family of nonempty sets has a choice function
([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The set $\mathcal A_k$ is finite because each coordinate of every $\alpha$ lies in $\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and is nonempty because it contains $0$. By [F1], every derivative class in the formula has finite $L^p$ norm. If $k=0$, then $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$ and $D^0u=u$, so the expression is exactly $\|u\|_{L^p}$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, [F1] says the only class is zero and the expression is zero. [F1, given]

1.2 Under Countable Choice [F8], changing representatives of $u$ does not change the weak-derivative property or its value classes by [F2]. If two locally integrable values represent the weak derivative of the same input, [F3] makes them equal almost everywhere. Thus each $D^\alpha u$ is intrinsic as an $L^p$ class, and the real or complex quotient norm in [F5] or [F6] depends only on that class. Hence the formula is independent of all representative choices. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, F8, given]

1.3 For $u,v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ and scalars $a,b$ in the chosen field, [F4] gives $D^\alpha(au+bv)=aD^\alpha u+bD^\alpha v$ as weak-derivative classes for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$. The right side is an $L^p$ class by the vector-space properties in [F5] or [F6], so $au+bv\in W^{k,p}(\Omega)$. This covers $a=0$ or $b=0$ directly. Thus the usual operations make $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ a real or complex vector space. [F1, F4, F5, F6, given]

1.4 For a scalar $c$ and finite $p$, class homogeneity in [F5] or [F6] gives $\|cu\|_{W^{k,p}}^p=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k}\|cD^\alpha u\|_{L^p}^p=|c|^p\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k}\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p}^p=|c|^p\|u\|_{W^{k,p}}^p$; taking nonnegative $p$th roots proves absolute homogeneity. At $p=\infty$, the maximum formula and $\|cf\|_\infty=|c|\|f\|_\infty$ give the same conclusion. For $c=0$ both formulas give zero directly. [F1, F5, F6, given]

1.5 Suppose $1\le p<\infty$ and put $a_\alpha=\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p}$, $b_\alpha=\|D^\alpha v\|_{L^p}$. By [F4] and the componentwise $L^p$ triangle inequality in [F5] or [F6], $\|D^\alpha(u+v)\|_{L^p}\le a_\alpha+b_\alpha$ for each $\alpha$. Raising to $p$, summing, and taking the $p$th root bounds $\|u+v\|_{W^{k,p}}$ by $\left(\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k}(a_\alpha+b_\alpha)^p\right)^{1/p}$. Give the finite set $\mathcal A_k$ its counting measure; the real sequences $(a_\alpha)$ and $(b_\alpha)$ belong to this $L^p$ space, and their norms are the finite sums in [F1]. Applying [F7] yields $\left(\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k}(a_\alpha+b_\alpha)^p\right)^{1/p}\le\left(\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k}a_\alpha^p\right)^{1/p}+\left(\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k}b_\alpha^p\right)^{1/p}=\|u\|_{W^{k,p}}+\|v\|_{W^{k,p}}$. This proves subadditivity also at $p=1$. [F1, F4, F5, F6, F7, given]

1.6 At $p=\infty$, put $a_\alpha=\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty}$ and $b_\alpha=\|D^\alpha v\|_{L^\infty}$. By [F4] and [F5] or [F6], $\|D^\alpha(u+v)\|_{L^\infty}\le a_\alpha+b_\alpha\le\max_{\beta\in\mathcal A_k}a_\beta+\max_{\beta\in\mathcal A_k}b_\beta$. Taking the maximum over $\alpha$ and using [F1] gives $\|u+v\|_{W^{k,\infty}}\le\|u\|_{W^{k,\infty}}+\|v\|_{W^{k,\infty}}$. [F1, F4, F5, F6, given]

2.1 If the Sobolev expression is zero, then at finite $p$ each nonnegative summand is zero, and at $p=\infty$ every component norm is zero. Since $0\in\mathcal A_k$ and $D^0u=u$ by [F1], in either case $\|u\|_{L^p}=0$. The real or complex $L^p$ norm separates its quotient classes by [F5] or [F6], so $u$ is the zero class. Conversely, if $u=0$ as an $L^p$ class, zero is a weak derivative of zero at every order; uniqueness under [F8] and [F3] makes every $D^\alpha u$ the zero class, and [F1] gives $\|u\|_{W^{k,p}}=0$. Together with the homogeneity and triangle inequalities already proved, this establishes the norm and both directions of the zero equivalence for real and complex scalars and all endpoint exponents. [F1, F3, F5, F6, F8, given, step 1.4, step 1.5, step 1.6] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measure space, an exponent $1\le p\le\infty$, and countable choice, available under the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Its only use is to select a countable family of measurable representatives.

[L1] $L^p(\mu)$ is a normed space, so it has the norm metric ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], [[def-complete-metric-space]]).

[L2] Minkowski's inequality holds in $L^p$ ([[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]).

[L3] Monotone convergence and dominated convergence are available ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[L4] Pointwise limits of measurable functions are measurable ([[thm-sequential-suprema-infima-limsup-liminf-and-pointwise-limits-are-measurable]]).

[L5] Sums and absolute values of measurable functions are measurable ([[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]).

[L6] Countable unions of measurable null sets are measurable and null ([[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]).

[L7] Finite essential suprema are attained almost everywhere ([[prop-essential-supremum-is-attained-as-the-least-essential-bound]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** For $1 \le p < infinity$, choose a rapidly Cauchy subsequence by least indices, sum the successive differences with monotone convergence and Minkowski, and recover the limit by dominated convergence. For $p = infinity$, union the exceptional null sets and take the pointwise limit outside them.

1.1 Assume $1\le p<\infty$ and let $(u_n)$ be Cauchy in $L^p(\mu)$. Choose by least indices a strictly increasing sequence $(n_k)$ such that [L2, L3, L4, L5, given, choose] $$\|u_{n_{k+1}}-u_{n_k}\|_p<2^{-k}\qquad(k\ge0).$$ Use countable choice (the countable instance of AC) to choose measurable representatives $f_k$ of $u_{n_k}$, and put $h_k:=|f_{k+1}-f_k|$. Then each $h_k$ is measurable, belongs to $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, and satisfies $$\|h_k\|_p<2^{-k}.$$ If $g_m:=\sum_{k<m} h_k$, then $$\|g_m\|_p\le\sum_{k<m}\|h_k\|_p\le\sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{-k}<\infty,$$ so each $g_m$ lies in $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$. Monotone convergence then gives a measurable pointwise limit $g:=\sum_{k=0}^\infty h_k$ with $g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$. [given, L2, L3, L4, L5, choose]

1.2 Assume now $p=\infty$ and let $(u_n)$ be Cauchy in $L^\infty(\mu)$. Choose least indices $n_k$ with [L4, L6, L7, given, choose] $$\|u_{n_{k+1}}-u_{n_k}\|_\infty<2^{-k}.$$ Use countable choice (the countable instance of AC) to choose measurable representatives $f_k$ of $u_{n_k}$. By [L7], the explicitly defined measurable set $E_k:=\{x:|f_{k+1}(x)-f_k(x)|>2^{-k}\}$ is null, and $$|f_{k+1}-f_k|\le2^{-k}\qquad\text{on }X\setminus E_k.$$ With $E:=\bigcup_k E_k$, [L6] makes $E$ measurable and null, and for $x\in X\setminus E$ and $m>n$, $$|f_m(x)-f_n(x)|\le\sum_{k=n}^{m-1}2^{-k}.$$ So $(f_k(x))$ is Cauchy in $\mathbb R$, hence converges to some value $f(x)$. Set $f=0$ on $E$. The measurable functions equal to $f_k$ on $X\setminus E$ and zero on $E$ converge everywhere to $f$, so [L4] makes $f$ measurable. Indeed, their inverse images of Borel sets are obtained by intersecting those of $f_k$ with $X\setminus E$ and adjoining $E$ exactly when the Borel set contains zero. No completeness of the measure is assumed. [given, L4, L5, L6, L7, choose]

2.1 In the finite-$p$ case, $E:=\{g=\infty\}$ is measurable and null: for every $M>0$, $M^p\mu(E)\le\int g^p<\infty$, hence $\mu(E)=0$. On $X\setminus E$ the series $\sum_k |f_{k+1}-f_k|$ converges, so $f_k$ has a finite limit $f$. Set $f=0$ on $E$. Replacing each $f_k$ by zero on $E$ gives measurable functions converging everywhere to $f$, so [L4] gives measurability. Almost everywhere, $|f|\le |f_0|+g$, so [L2] gives $f\in\mathcal L^p$, and [step 1.1, L2, L3, L4] $$|f-f_k|\le\sum_{j\ge k} h_j\le g.$$ Dominated convergence in [L3] therefore gives $\|f-f_k\|_p\to0$. 3.1 Since $(u_n)$ is Cauchy, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $K$ with $\|u_n-u_m\|_p<\varepsilon/2$ whenever $m,n\ge K$. [step 2.1, L1, L2]

4.1 Step 2.1 proves the almost-everywhere convergent subsequence clause in the finite-$p$ case, and step 2.2 gives the same for $p=\infty$. Steps 3.1 and 2.2 prove completeness in every case, which by [L1] is exactly completeness of the norm metric. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, L1] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, conjugate exponents $p,q\in[1,\infty]$, and measurable real-valued functions $f,g$ in the spaces named in the relevant clause of the Statement.

[L1] Conjugate exponents are defined in [[def-conjugate-exponents]].

[L2] For $0<r<\infty$, membership in $\mathcal L^r(\mu)$ means $\int |h|^r\,d\mu<\infty$, while $L^\infty(\mu)$ means finite essential supremum ([[def-calligraphic-l-p-on-a-measure-space]], [[def-l-infinity-on-a-measure-space]]).

[L3] A nonnegative measurable function has integral $0$ exactly when it vanishes almost everywhere ([[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]]).

[L4] If $h\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then $|h|\le\|h\|_\infty$ almost everywhere ([[prop-essential-supremum-is-attained-as-the-least-essential-bound]]).

[L5] Young's inequality says $uv\le u^p/p+v^q/q$ for $u,v\ge0$ when $1<p,q<\infty$ are conjugate ([[thm-young-inequality-real-exponents]]).

[L6] The nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[L7] The nonnegative integral is additive ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

[L8] The integral of a nonnegative function over a null set is zero ([[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** For $1 < p < infinity$, normalize the nonzero norms and apply the published Young inequality pointwise before integrating. Treat the endpoint pairs $(1,\infty)$ and $(\infty,1)$ separately from the essential-bound definition.

1.1 Assume first $1<p,q<\infty$, and put $A:=\|f\|_p$ and $B:=\|g\|_q$. If $A=0$ or $B=0$, then the corresponding power integral is $0$, so [L3] makes the corresponding function vanish outside a measurable null set. By [L8], $\int|fg|\,d\mu=0$. Thus only the case $A,B>0$ remains. [L2, L3, L8, given]

1.2 For the endpoint pair $(p,q)=(1,\infty)$, let $M:=\|g\|_\infty$. By [L4] there is a measurable null set $N$ outside which $|fg|\le M|f|$. On $N$, [L8] gives zero integral for $|fg|\chi_N$ and $M|f|\chi_N$. Integrating the inequality on $X\setminus N$ with [L6] and [L7] therefore gives $\int|fg|\,d\mu\le M\int|f|\,d\mu=\|g\|_\infty\|f\|_1$. [L2, L4, L6, L7, L8, given]

2.1 In the remaining strict-exponent case, Young's inequality applied pointwise to $u=|f|/A$ and $v=|g|/B$ gives [step 1.1, L1, L2, L5, L6, L7, algebra] $$\frac{|f||g|}{AB}\le\frac{|f|^p}{pA^p}+\frac{|g|^q}{qB^q}.$$ Integrating and using additivity, monotonicity, homogeneity, and the definitions of $A$ and $B$ yields $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\frac{B}{pA^{p-1}}\int |f|^p\,d\mu+\frac{A}{qB^{q-1}}\int |g|^q\,d\mu=\frac{AB}{p}+\frac{AB}{q}=AB.$$ [step 1.1, L1, L2, L5, L6, L7, algebra]

2.2 The case $(p,q)=(\infty,1)$ is identical after exchanging $f$ and $g$. [step 1.2, given] $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$ [step 1.2, given]

3.1 Step 2.1 proves the strict-exponent case, and steps 1.2 and 2.2 prove the two endpoint cases. In every case the right-hand side is finite by [L2], so $fg$ is integrable. [step 2.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, L2] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; A Banach space $X$, real numbers $a<b$, a continuous $f:[a,b]\to X$, the primitive $G(t):=\int_a^tf(s)\,ds$ for $t\in[a,b]$, and a continuous $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ differentiable on $(a,b)$ whose derivative extends to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$.

[F1] Average convergence ([[lem-average-convergence-of-a-continuous-banach-valued-function]]): a continuous $f:[a,b]\to X$ is Bochner integrable, and for $t\in[a,b)$, $h>0$, $t+h\le b$, $\bigl\|\frac1h\int_t^{t+h}f-f(t)\bigr\|\le\sup_{[t,t+h]}\|f-f(t)\|\to0$, with the analogous backward limit for $t\in(a,b]$; the same one-sided limits hold for curves continuous at $t$ and Bochner integrable near $t$.

[F2] The Bochner integral is linear, so for $[c,d]\subseteq[a,b]$ the difference of primitives is $\int_c^df$ ([[lem-linearity-of-the-bochner-integral]], [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]).

[F4] Differentiability on $(a,b)$ means Fréchet differentiability at every point of the open interval ([[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces]]); at the endpoints only the relevant one-sided difference quotients are considered.

[F5] Mean value inequality ([[lem-mean-value-inequality-for-a-differentiable-banach-valued-curve]]): a curve continuous on an interval, differentiable inside with derivative bounded by $C$, changes by at most $C$ times the length; in particular a curve with vanishing interior derivative is constant.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct, computing the difference quotient of the primitive with the average-convergence lemma and then applying the mean value inequality to $\varphi$ minus its integral.

1.1 By [F1] the continuous $f$ is Bochner integrable on $[a,b]$, so $G(t)=\int_a^tf$ is defined for every $t\in[a,b]$; by [F2] $G(t+h)-G(t)=\int_t^{t+h}f$ for $[t,t+h]\subseteq[a,b]$. [F1, F2]

2.1 Difference quotients of $G$: for $t\in[a,b)$ and $h>0$ with $t+h\le b$, $\frac{G(t+h)-G(t)}{h}=\frac1h\int_t^{t+h}f\to f(t)$ by [F1]; similarly $\frac{G(t)-G(t-h)}{h}=\frac1h\int_{t-h}^tf\to f(t)$ for $t\in(a,b]$. Hence $G$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $G'=f$, and has the one-sided derivatives $f(t)$ at the endpoints. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 $G'=f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, and the existence of the one-sided derivative at $a$ and at $b$ makes $G$ continuous there from the appropriate side; at interior points $G$ is continuous by differentiability. [F4, step 2.1]

3.2 Since $\varphi'$ extends to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, denote the extension again by $\varphi'$ and put $\psi(t):=\varphi(t)-\int_a^t\varphi'(s)\,ds$ for $t\in[a,b]$. By [step 2.1] the primitive of $\varphi'$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative $\varphi'$, and $\psi$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$; by linearity of the derivative and of the integral, $\psi'=\varphi'-\varphi'=0$ on $(a,b)$, and $\psi(a)=\varphi(a)$. [F2, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 $\psi$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\psi'=0$ there; by [F5] (constant case) $\psi$ is constant on $[a,b]$, so $\psi(b)=\psi(a)=\varphi(a)$, that is $\varphi(b)-\int_a^b\varphi'=\varphi(a)$. [F5, step 3.2]

5.1 Therefore $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The same computation, applied to each compact subinterval $[a,b]\subseteq[0,\infty)$ after restricting a continuous curve on $[0,\infty)$, gives the stated identity in that setting. [step 2.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Definition

Inputs are a dimension $d\ge1$, the data and operators specified in the physics-informed residual loss definition, $0<\alpha\le1$, positive weights $\lambda_r,\lambda_b$, and an admissible trial function $h$. The procedure returns the scalar empirical objective value $J_m(h)$. It uses the realized sample points and target values as inputs; it does not generate random samples.

For $d\ge2$, also supply positive integer counts $m_r,m_b$, residual samples $x_r^1,\ldots,x_r^{m_r}\in U$ with their observed values $f(x_r^i)$, boundary samples $x_b^1,\ldots,x_b^{m_b}\in\Gamma$ with their observed values $g(x_b^j)$, constants $c_r,c_b,C_r,C_b>0$, and small-scale cutoffs $\ell_{0,i},\rho_{0,i}>0$. At the selected partition scales $0<\ell_i\le\ell_{0,i}$, require cells $U_j^{\ell_r}$ and $\Gamma_j^{\ell_b}$ with masses at least $c_r\ell_r^d$ and $c_b\ell_b^{d-1}$, each contained in a cube of side $\ell_i$. Require upper ball-mass bounds $\mu_r(\overline B_\rho(x)\cap U)\le C_r\rho^d$ and $\mu_b(\overline B_\rho(y)\cap\Gamma)\le C_b\rho^{d-1}$ for every center and for all $0<\rho\le\rho_{0,i}$. The admissible counts satisfy, for $i\in\{r,b\}$,
$$m_i\ge\max\{1,c_i^{-2}\ell_{0,i}^{-2s_i},c_i^{-2}d^{s_i}\rho_{0,i}^{-2s_i}\},$$
so the computed partition scales and fill radii lie in the specified ranges.

For $d=1$, supply a positive integer $m_r$, residual samples $x_r^1,\ldots,x_r^{m_r}\in U$ with observed values $f(x_r^i)$, constants $c_r,C_r>0$, and cutoffs $\ell_{0,r},\rho_{0,r}>0$. At the residual scale $\ell_r$ below, require a finite measurable partition with each cell contained in an interval of length $\ell_r$ and mass at least $c_r\ell_r$, and require upper ball-mass bounds $\mu_r(\overline B_\rho(x)\cap U)\le C_r\rho$ for every center $x\in U$ and all $0<\rho\le\rho_{0,r}$. The admissible count satisfies
$$m_r\ge\max\{1,c_r^{-2}\ell_{0,r}^{-2},c_r^{-2}\rho_{0,r}^{-2}\},$$
so $\ell_r=\delta_r$ is in the specified ranges. Supply the observed boundary values at every point of the finite set $\Gamma$ with their masses $\mu_b(\{y\})$. No random boundary sample or boundary sample count is used.

For $d\ge2$, set $s_r=d$, $s_b=d-1$, and, for $i\in\{r,b\}$, compute
$$\ell_i=(c_i\sqrt{m_i})^{-1/s_i},\qquad \delta_i=\sqrt d\,\ell_i,\qquad \kappa_i=C_i/c_i,$$
$$C_m=3\max_{i\in\{r,b\}}\{\kappa_i d^{s_i/2}m_i^{1/2}\},\qquad
\widehat\lambda^R_{i,m}=\frac{3\lambda_i\delta_i^{2\alpha}}{C_m}.$$
For $d=1$, compute
$$\ell_r=\delta_r=(c_r\sqrt{m_r})^{-1},\qquad \kappa_r=C_r/c_r,\qquad C_m=3\kappa_r m_r^{1/2},$$
$$\widehat\lambda^R_{r,m}=\frac{3\lambda_r\delta_r^{2\alpha}}{C_m}
=\frac{\lambda_r c_r^{-2\alpha}}{\kappa_r}m_r^{-\alpha-1/2},\qquad \widehat\lambda^R_{b,m}=0.$$
For $d\ge2$, use supplied regularization weights $\lambda^R_{i,m}$ satisfying $\lambda^R_{i,m}\ge\widehat\lambda^R_{i,m}$ componentwise; for a sequence of sample counts also require $\|\lambda_m^R\|_\infty=O(\|\widehat\lambda_m^R\|_\infty)$. For $d=1$, set $\lambda^R_{b,m}=0$ and choose $\lambda^R_{r,m}\ge\widehat\lambda^R_{r,m}$, with the corresponding one-coordinate max-norm order condition across a sequence of counts. If no residual weights are supplied, set them equal to their thresholds.

Finally evaluate and return $J_m(h)=\operatorname{Loss}_m(h;\lambda,\lambda_m^R)$ using the realized residual values, the realized boundary values when $d\ge2$, the exact weighted full-boundary contribution when $d=1$, and the residual seminorm penalty when $d=1$ or both seminorm penalties when $d\ge2$. The regularization thresholds are the source's exact thresholds and cannot be replaced by a generic positive penalty.

## Definition references
[[def-physics-informed-neural-network-loss|physics informed neural network loss]]

[Shin et al., equations (3.1)–(3.3): exact thresholds, scaling condition, and objective](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Remark

For $d\ge2$, the exact residual and boundary threshold coordinates are
$$\widehat\lambda^R_{r,m}=\frac{3\lambda_r(\sqrt d)^{2\alpha}c_r^{-2\alpha/d}m_r^{-\alpha/d}}{C_m},\qquad \widehat\lambda^R_{b,m}=\frac{3\lambda_b(\sqrt d)^{2\alpha}c_b^{-2\alpha/(d-1)}m_b^{-\alpha/(d-1)}}{C_m},$$
where $C_m=3\max\{(C_r/c_r)(\sqrt d)^d m_r^{1/2},(C_b/c_b)(\sqrt d)^{d-1}m_b^{1/2}\}$. For $d=1$, the residual threshold is $\widehat\lambda^R_{r,m}=(\lambda_r c_r^{-2\alpha}/\kappa_r)m_r^{-\alpha-1/2}$, with $\kappa_r=C_r/c_r$, and the boundary threshold is zero. The weight vector must satisfy the componentwise lower bound and max-norm order condition in the Algorithm.

The original all-$\varepsilon>0$ sampling quantifier has no probability-measure instances; it is preserved and refuted in the all-scale inconsistency lemma. The small-scale range above is the corrected active sampling convention. No lower-mass constant normalization is implicit in this algorithm.

## Definition

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $D'\subset\mathbb R^{d'}$ be bounded domains. Let $A$ and $U$ be real Banach spaces of scalar functions whose elements have continuous representatives on $\bar D$ and $\bar D'$, respectively, and suppose the inclusions into $C(\bar D)$ and $C(\bar D')$ are continuous. In the continuous-function setting, a **neural operator** is a composition of a pointwise lifting map, finitely many integral-kernel layers, and a pointwise projection map. A layer with channel dimensions $q_t,q_{t+1}\ge1$ has the form
$$v_{t+1}(x)=\sigma_t\!\left(W_tv_t(x)+\int_D\kappa_t(x,y)v_t(y)\,dy+b_t(x)\right),\qquad x\in\bar D,$$
where $v_t:\bar D\to\mathbb R^{q_t}$ is continuous, $W_t\in\mathbb R^{q_{t+1}\times q_t}$, $\kappa_t:\bar D\times\bar D\to\mathbb R^{q_{t+1}\times q_t}$ and $b_t:\bar D\to\mathbb R^{q_{t+1}}$ are continuous, and the scalar activation $\sigma_t$ is applied coordinatewise. The lifting and projection maps are finite feedforward networks applied pointwise, with their input and output channel dimensions chosen to make the composition well-defined. All integrals are Lebesgue integrals, which exist because the integrands are continuous on a compact set. For distinct input and output domains the final integral layer has kernel on $\bar D'\times\bar D$, integrates over $D$, and has zero local matrix term; subsequent projection acts on $\bar D'$. For any stronger specified output space, the selected composition is required actually to map into that space.

The **integral universality subclass** is defined separately on $L^1(D;\mathbb R^{q_0})$, including almost-everywhere equivalence classes. Fix continuous activations $\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3$ with $\sigma_1$ of at most linear growth, $N\ge2$, and channel dimensions $q_1,\ldots,q_N\ge1$. For $0\le t\le N-1$ let
$$S_t(v)(x)=\int_D\kappa_t(x,y)v(y)\,dy+b_t(x),\qquad x\in\bar D,$$
where $\kappa_t:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{q_{t+1}\times q_t}$ and $b_t:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{q_{t+1}}$ are finite MLPs with hidden activation $\sigma_2$ and affine output. Set $v_1=S_0(a)$, $v_2=S_1(v_1)$, and $v_{t+1}=S_t(\sigma_1(v_t))$ for $2\le t\le N-1$. An element of $\mathrm{NO}_N$ is
$$G(a)(x)=\int_D\kappa_N(x,y)v_N(y)\,dy,\qquad x\in\bar D',$$
where $\kappa_N:\mathbb R^{d'}\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{q_{\mathrm{out}}\times q_N}$ is a finite MLP with activation $\sigma_3$ and affine output. There are exactly $N-2$ intermediate $\sigma_1$ activations. Scalar input and output mean $q_0=q_{\mathrm{out}}=1$. The final integral is over $D$, with output variable in $D'$. This class has identity lifting and projection and zero local matrix terms. It specializes the architectural scheme with its first layer extended to $L^1$ classes; it does not require continuous input representatives.

The first integral is invariant under null changes and obeys $\|S_0(a)\|_\infty\le\|\kappa_0\|_\infty\|a\|_1+\|b_0\|_\infty$. Uniform continuity of its kernel on the compact product implies continuity of its output by the same $L^1$ estimate. All later fields are continuous and bounded, so their integrals and activations are defined; the output is continuous on $\bar D'$. Viewing it in a stronger Banach space $U$ requires the selected kernels actually to produce outputs in $U$. The universality theorem constructs such kernels; arbitrary continuous kernels alone do not guarantee this condition.

For equal input and output domains, the diagram records the composition order: a pointwise lift, integral-kernel layers on $D$, and a pointwise output projection. Each $\mathcal K_t$ box denotes the integral layer defined above; arrows denote function composition and do not assert a theorem.

## Definition

Fix an input dimension $q\ge1$ and an integer $m\ge0$. Let $\mathcal A_m^{(q)}$ be the class of continuous scalar activations $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ for which there is one depth $n\in\mathbb N$ such that, for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^q$, the scalar-output depth-$n$ multilayer perceptrons with activation $\sigma$ are dense in $C^m(K)$ in the $C^m$ norm. For vector outputs, stack scalar-output networks of that same depth. The source notation $\mathcal A_m$ suppresses the input dimension fixed by the finite-dimensional network under consideration. Let $\mathcal A_m^{L,(q)}$ be the subclass whose members are Borel measurable and have at most linear growth, meaning
$$\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}\frac{|\sigma(s)|}{1+|s|}<\infty.$$
For an integer $q\ge1$, define $\mathrm{BA}_q$ to consist of those $\sigma\in\mathcal A_0^{(q)}$ for which, for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^q$, every $\varepsilon>0$, and every $C\ge\operatorname{diam}_2(K)$, there is a finite multilayer perceptron $f:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^q$ with
$$|f(x)-x|_2\le\varepsilon\quad(x\in K),\qquad |f(x)|_2\le C\quad(x\in\mathbb R^q).$$
Here $\operatorname{diam}_2(K)=\sup_{x,y\in K}|x-y|_2$. The diameter-based global bound is part of this definition and is retained verbatim; its nonemptiness is checked separately.

kind: lemma
title: "Elliptic H1 error estimate from the source coefficient bound"
status: draft
origin: pipeline

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806"
      locator: "Assumption 3.3 and Appendix E, proof of Theorem 3.9"
---

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded Lipschitz. Let $A=(a_{ij})$ be a bounded measurable real symmetric matrix field, uniformly elliptic with eigenvalues at least $\lambda_0>0$, and let $b,c,d$ be bounded measurable real coefficient fields satisfying
$$\lambda_0^{-2}(\|b(x)\|^2+\|c(x)\|^2)+\lambda_0^{-1}|d(x)|\le v^2\qquad(x\in U).$$
For the divergence operator
$$L[e]=\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_j e)+\sum_iD_i(b_i e)+\sum_i c_iD_i e+de,$$
every real $e\in H^1_0(U)\cap C^2(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$ with $L[e]\in L^2(U)$ satisfies
$$\|e\|_{H^1(U)}^2\le C_E\bigl(\|L[e]\|_{L^2(U)}^2+\|e\|_{L^2(U)}^2\bigr),$$
where $C_E$ depends only on $\lambda_0$ and $v$. The zero-trace condition is required for the integration by parts.

## Statement references
[Shin et al., Appendix E: source elliptic H1 error estimate and coefficient bound](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

[Shin et al., Appendix E: energy estimate, with the lower-order coefficient absorption written out here](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The bounded Lipschitz domain, uniformly elliptic symmetric matrix, coefficient bound, zero-trace function, and divergence operator in the Statement.

[A1] Countable Choice is the explicit premise of the zero-boundary Sobolev closure convention ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

[F1] $H^1(U)=W^{1,2}(U)$ has norm squared $\|e\|_{L^2(U)}^2+\|\nabla e\|_{L^2(U)}^2$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

[F2] The divergence operator uses the positive-principal-part convention displayed in [[def-shin-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]].

[F3] $H^1_0(U)$ is the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(U)$, and the $H^1$ norm contains the $L^2$ norm and weak-gradient norm ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

## Proof

**Proof strategy:** integrate against the zero-trace error and absorb lower-order terms with Young's inequality.

1.1 By [F3], choose $\phi_n\in C_c^\infty(U)$ with $\phi_n\to e$ in $H^1(U)$. The distributional definition of each divergence term and the ordinary test-function integration by parts give $$\int_U\phi_nL[e]\,dx=-\int_U a_{ij}D_j eD_i\phi_n\,dx-\int_U b_i eD_i\phi_n\,dx+\int_U c_iD_i e\,\phi_n\,dx+\int_U d e\,\phi_n\,dx.$$ All coefficients are bounded and $e,\nabla e,L[e]\in L^2$, so each term is continuous under $H^1$ convergence. Taking $n\to\infty$ and using [F2] yields $$-\int_U eL[e]\,dx=\int_U a_{ij}D_j eD_i e\,dx+\int_U b_i eD_i e\,dx-\int_U c_i eD_i e\,dx-\int_U d e^2\,dx.$$ The principal term is at least $\lambda_0\|\nabla e\|_2^2$ by ellipticity. [given, A1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The coefficient bound gives $\|b\|^2+\|c\|^2\le\lambda_0^2v^2$ and $|d|\le\lambda_0v^2$. Hence the absolute value of the two first-order terms is at most $\sqrt2\lambda_0v\|e\|_2\|\nabla e\|_2$, and the zero-order term is at most $\lambda_0v^2\|e\|_2^2$. Young's inequality bounds the first-order contribution by $\frac{\lambda_0}{2}\|\nabla e\|_2^2+\lambda_0v^2\|e\|_2^2$. Therefore $$-\int_U eL[e]\,dx\ge\frac{\lambda_0}{2}\|\nabla e\|_2^2-2\lambda_0v^2\|e\|_2^2.$$ [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $L[e]\in L^2(U)$, Cauchy–Schwarz and step 2.1 imply $$\frac{\lambda_0}{2}\|\nabla e\|_2^2\le\|L[e]\|_2\|e\|_2+2\lambda_0v^2\|e\|_2^2\le\frac{1}{2\lambda_0}\|L[e]\|_2^2+\left(\frac{1}{2\lambda_0}+2\lambda_0v^2\right)\|e\|_2^2.$$ Thus $\|\nabla e\|_2^2\le\lambda_0^{-2}\|L[e]\|_2^2+(\lambda_0^{-2}+4v^2)\|e\|_2^2$. By [F1], adding $\|e\|_2^2$ gives the claimed $H^1$ estimate with $C_E=\max\{\lambda_0^{-2},1+\lambda_0^{-2}+4v^2\}$. [step 2.1, F1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

## Source notes

Kinnunen, Definition 1.23 and Remarks 1.24, printed pp. 21–22, defines
$W_0^{k,p}$ as the closure of the test functions and warns that this is not yet
a boundary-value statement. Laugesen, Definition 3.11, printed p. 59, uses the
same closure convention for $W_0^{k,p}$.

kind: lemma

status: draft

      locator: "Appendix D, Lemma D.2; source estimate (3.8)"

## Statement

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and let
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^d a_{ij}D_iD_j u+\sum_{j=1}^d\widetilde b_jD_j u+\widetilde c\,u$$
on $U$, where $a(x)$ is symmetric, $\xi^Ta(x)\xi\ge\lambda_0|\xi|^2$ for all $x\in U$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\lambda_0>0$, the coefficients are continuous and bounded, and $\widetilde c\le0$. There is a constant $C_L<\infty$, depending only on $U$, $\lambda_0$, and the coefficient bounds, such that every $w\in C^2(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$ with $L[w]\in C^0(U)$ satisfies
$$\|w\|_{C^0(U)}\le C_L\left(\|L[w]\|_{C^0(U)}+\|w\|_{C^0(\partial U)}\right).$$
In particular, for any two functions $u^*,h\in C^2(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$,
$$\|u^*-h\|_{C^0(U)}\le C_L\left(\|L[u^*]-L[h]\|_{C^0(U)}+\|u^*-h\|_{C^0(\partial U)}\right).$$

## Statement references
[Shin et al., Appendix D, Lemma D.2: residual and boundary stability estimate](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

[Shin et al., Appendix D, Lemma D.2: the stability interface that this barrier proof reconstructs](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The bounded domain, uniformly elliptic coefficient matrix, bounded lower-order coefficients with $\widetilde c\le0$, and $w\in C^2(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$.

[F1] The operator expands with the positive principal part and zero-order coefficient shown in [[def-shin-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]].

[F2] A continuous function on the compact set $\bar U$ attains its maximum; a $C^2$ function at an interior maximum has zero gradient and negative-semidefinite Hessian.

## Proof

**Proof strategy:** construct a strict positive barrier and apply the weak maximum principle by perturbation.

1.1 Since $U$ is bounded, choose real numbers $a_1<b_1$ with $a_1\le x_1\le b_1$ on $\bar U$. Let $B=\|\widetilde b_1\|_{C^0(U)}$ and $C_0=\|\widetilde c\|_{C^0(U)}$. Choose $\kappa>0$ large enough that $\kappa^2\lambda_0-\kappa B-C_0\ge1$. For $\psi(x)=e^{\kappa x_1}$, [F1] gives $$L[\psi](x)=e^{\kappa x_1}\bigl(\kappa^2a_{11}(x)+\kappa\widetilde b_1(x)+\widetilde c(x)\bigr)\ge e^{\kappa a_1}>0.$$ Choose $M>e^{\kappa b_1}$ and set $\Phi=M-\psi$. Then $\Phi>0$ on $\bar U$ and $L[\Phi]=M\widetilde c-L[\psi]\le-e^{\kappa a_1}$. [given, F1, algebra, choose]

2.1 Put $R=\|L[w]\|_{C^0(U)}$, $Q=\|w\|_{C^0(\partial U)}$, and $\eta=e^{\kappa a_1}$. For $z=w-Q-(R/\eta)\Phi$, the boundary values satisfy $z\le0$. In $U$, $$L[z]=L[w]-Q\widetilde c-(R/\eta)L[\Phi]\ge -R+R=0,$$ because $-Q\widetilde c\ge0$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $z(x_0)>0$ at some $x_0\in U$. Since $z\le0$ on $\partial U$ and $z$ is continuous on $\bar U$, its positive maximum is attained at an interior point. For sufficiently small $\delta>0$, $z+\delta\psi$ has an interior positive maximum as well: its value at $x_0$ is at least $z(x_0)>0$, while its boundary values are at most $\delta e^{\kappa b_1}<z(x_0)$. At that interior maximum [F2] and $\widetilde c\le0$ give $L[z+\delta\psi]\le0$, contradicting $L[z+\delta\psi]>0$. Hence $z\le0$ on $U$, and therefore $$w\le Q+(R/\eta)\|\Phi\|_{C^0(\bar U)}.$$ Applying the same argument to $-w$ yields the corresponding lower bound. Taking $C_L=\max\{1,\|\Phi\|_{C^0(\bar U)}/\eta\}$ proves the first estimate; applying it to $u^*-h$ proves the second. [step 2.1, F2, algebra] ∎

sources:

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/1709.08618v2.pdf"
      locator: "Chapter 11, evolution-space context; arbitrary bounded-open-set proof supplied locally"
---

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, $d\ge1$, and put $H=L^2(U;\mathbb R)$ and $V=H^1_0(U;\mathbb R)$, where the latter is the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(U)$. Then $V$ is a separable real Hilbert space, its inclusion into $H$ is continuous, injective and dense, and $(V,H,V^*)$ is a real evolution triple. The gradient norm and the full $H^1$ norm are equivalent on $V$. No regularity of $\partial U$ is required.

## Statement references

[Clason, Chapter 11: the Sobolev evolution-triple setting](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1709.08618v2.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, a bounded open $U\subset\mathbb R^d$, and the stated real spaces.

[A1] Countable Choice is carried by the $L^2$ completeness and density suppliers and by the countable selections below ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] $L^2(U)$ is a real Hilbert space; rational box-step functions are countable and dense in $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[thm-rational-box-step-functions-form-a-countable-dense-subset-of-l-p-of-rn]]).

[F2] Weak derivatives are defined by integration against compactly supported smooth tests; $H^1_0(U)$ is the $H^1$-closure of those smooth functions ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

[F3] On an open set bounded in one direction, $\|v\|_2\le C\|Dv\|_2$ for $v\in H^1_0(U)$ ([[thm-poincare-inequality-for-w-one-p-zero]]).

[F4] $C_c^\infty(U)$ is dense in $L^2(U)$ for every open $U$ ([[lem-smooth-compactly-supported-functions-are-dense-in-ltwo-of-an-open-set]]).

[F5] A continuous dense injective Hilbert inclusion $V\hookrightarrow H$ defines the canonical real evolution triple ([[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]]).

## Proof

1.1 If $U=\varnothing$, both spaces are zero and the conclusions hold. Otherwise choose finite $a<b$ with $U\subset\{a<x_1<b\}$. The zero extension of any $h\in H$ belongs to $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ with the same norm. Restricting the countable dense box-step family in [F1] to $U$ therefore gives a countable dense subset of $H$. The product $Z=H^{d+1}$ is a separable Hilbert space. [given, A1, F1, construct]

2.1 The map $J:H^1(U)\to Z$, $J(v)=(v,D_1v,\ldots,D_dv)$, is an isometry for the full Sobolev norm. Its range is closed: if $J(v_n)\to(v,g_1,\ldots,g_d)$ in $Z$, then for every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(U)$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\int vD_i\phi=\lim_n\int v_nD_i\phi=-\lim_n\int D_iv_n\phi=-\int g_i\phi$. Thus $g_i=D_iv$ weakly, so the limit is $J(v)$. A closed subspace of a Hilbert space is complete, hence $H^1(U)$ is Hilbert. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By the closure definition, $V$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(U)$ and is Hilbert. The Poincare inequality applies because $U$ is bounded in the first direction, and yields $\|Dv\|_2^2\le\|v\|_{H^1}^2\le(1+C^2)\|Dv\|_2^2$ on $V$. This proves norm equivalence and continuity of the inclusion $V\hookrightarrow H$. Injectivity holds because these spaces use the same almost-everywhere equivalence classes. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 A subspace $Y$ of a separable metric space $Z$ is separable under [A1]: if $(z_j)$ is dense in $Z$, the sets $Y\cap B(z_j,r)$ for positive rational $r$ form a countable base of $Y$; choose one point from every nonempty such set. Any relatively open neighborhood contains one of these sets, so the chosen points are dense. Apply this first to $J(H^1(U))\subset Z$ and then to $J(V)$; transport the dense subsets through the isometry $J$. Thus $V$ is separable. [A1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 By [F4], $C_c^\infty(U)$ is dense in $H$, and it is contained in $V$ by [F2]. Thus $V\hookrightarrow H$ is dense. The Hilbert, separability, continuity and injectivity conclusions already proved give the canonical evolution triple by [F5]. Every argument used an arbitrary bounded open $U$, so none requires a boundary chart or a polyhedral boundary. [F2, F4, F5, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

This reproduces the actual argument of the read published polyhedral Sobolev-evolution supplier on the larger bounded-open-set domain class. Its closed-graph, separability and compact-smooth-density arguments do not use polyhedral geometry. The bibliographic reference records the evolution-space context; no new reading of Clason's full text is claimed here.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] For $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ one has $\int|fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2<+\infty$, so $fg\in L^1(\mu)$; the integral is unchanged when a representative is replaced by an almost-everywhere equal one, and it is linear on $L^1$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

[A2] $L^2(\mu)$ is complete for $\|\cdot\|_2$, and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on the quotient, so the quotient metrics are the ones in which completeness is asserted ([[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]], [[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

[A3] For a nonnegative measurable $h$, $\int h\,d\mu=0$ if and only if $h=0$ almost everywhere; consequently $\langle f,f\rangle=0$ forces $f=0$ in $L^2(\mu)$ ([[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]]).

[A4] On complex $L^2$ the pairing $\int f\overline g$ is representative-independent, linear in the first variable, conjugate-linear in the second, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, satisfies $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$ and Cauchy–Schwarz, and complex $L^2$ is complete ([[lem-complex-lp-completeness-density-and-inner-product]]).

[A5] An inner product is linear in the first variable, conjugate symmetric and positive definite, and induces the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** Countable Choice and a measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$.

1.1 **Real case: the pairing.** For $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ the product $fg$ is integrable by [A1], so $\int fg\,d\mu$ is defined and depends only on the classes of $f$ and $g$ by [A1]; the assignment is bilinear by linearity of the integral on $L^1$ and symmetric because multiplication of real functions is commutative. [A1]

1.2 **Complex case.** The published complex interface [A4] states that on complex $L^2$ the pairing $\int f\overline g$ is representative-independent, linear in the first variable, conjugate-linear in the second, conjugate symmetric and positive definite with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$, and that complex $L^2$ is complete for $\|\cdot\|_2$; hence complex $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex Hilbert space for that pairing, with the established quotient norm. [A4, A5]

2.1 The real pairing is positive definite: $\langle f,f\rangle=\int f^2\,d\mu\ge0$ vanishes exactly when $f^2=0$ almost everywhere, that is exactly when $f$ represents the zero class, by [A3]; moreover $\langle f,f\rangle=\int f^2\,d\mu=\|f\|_2^2$ because the $L^2$ norm is the square root of $\int|f|^2$ and $f^2=|f|^2$ for real $f$. Hence the real pairing is an inner product inducing the quotient norm. [step 1.1, A2, A3, A5]

3.1 The real quotient is complete for that norm by [A2], so with this inner product real $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space. [step 2.1, A2, A5]

4.1 Steps 3.1 and 1.2 establish both claims for every measure space under Countable Choice, the norm in each case being the established quotient $L^2$ norm. [step 1.2, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, $1 \le p < \infty$ and $\varepsilon > 0$.

[L1] Box-step functions are dense in $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ ([[thm-box-step-functions-are-dense-in-l-p-of-rn]]).

[L2] Rational boxes form a countable basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[thm-rational-points-and-boxes-in-rn]]).

[L3] Every Euclidean box is Lebesgue measurable with its usual volume ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[L4] Countable sets are closed under finite products and countable unions, and subsets of countable sets are countable ([[def-countable]], [[thm-countable-union-of-countable]], [[thm-product-of-countable]], [[lem-subset-of-countable]]).

[L5] A space is separable exactly when it has a countable dense subset ([[def-separable-space]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $\mathcal{R}$ be the family of half-open boxes [L2, L4, given, algebra] $\prod_{i=1}^n (a_i,b_i]$ with rational endpoints. By [L2] there are countably many such boxes, and by [L4] the set $\mathcal S$ of all finite rational linear combinations of indicators $\mathbf{1}_R$ with $R \in \mathcal R$ is countable. [L2, L4, given, algebra]

2.1 By [L1], it is enough to approximate a single box indicator. So fix a [L1, L3, step 1.1, choose, algebra] $\delta>0$ and let $B = \prod_{i=1}^n (\alpha_i,\beta_i]$. Choose rationals $a_i < \alpha_i < \beta_i < b_i$ so close to the endpoints that, with $M:=1+\max_i\{|a_i|,|b_i|,|\alpha_i|,|\beta_i|\}$, $$ 2n(2M)^{n-1}\max_i\{(\alpha_i-a_i),(b_i-\beta_i)\}<\delta. $$ Then $B\triangle R$ is contained in the union of the $2n$ coordinate slabs where one coordinate lies in $(a_i,\alpha_i]$ or $(\beta_i,b_i]$ while the others stay in $[-M,M]$. By [L3], each slab has measure at most $(2M)^{n-1}\max_i\{(\alpha_i-a_i),(b_i-\beta_i)\}$, so $\lambda_n(B \triangle R) < \delta$ for the rational box $R := \prod_i (a_i,b_i]$. Hence $$ \|\mathbf{1}_B-\mathbf{1}_R\|_p = \lambda_n(B \triangle R)^{1/p} < \delta^{1/p}, $$ which can be made arbitrarily small; approximating finitely many coefficients by rationals then makes every box-step function arbitrarily close to an element of $\mathcal S$. [L1, L3, step 1.1, choose, algebra]

3.1 Therefore $\mathcal S$ is countable and dense. By [L5], [L5, step 1.1, step 2.1] $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is separable, with $\mathcal S$ as an explicit dense subset. [L5, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ bounded in the direction $e\in S^{n-1}$ between $a<b$; an exponent $1\le p<\infty$; a field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$; and a class $u\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

[F1] $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is the closure in $W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ of the compactly supported smooth functions $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and every such smooth function lies in $W^{1,p}$ with its classical derivatives as weak derivatives ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

[F2] Riemann vector-valued fundamental theorem: if $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^m$ is differentiable with integrable derivative, then $\int_a^bf'=f(b)-f(a)$ ([[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]]).

[F3] Holder's inequality for integrals ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]).

[F4] Tonelli's theorem on sigma-finite products, allowing iterated integrals of nonnegative measurable functions in either order ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F5] Linear set-measure scaling: an invertible linear map $T$ of $\mathbb R^n$ scales Lebesgue measure by $|\det T|$ ([[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]]). This set formula is distinct from the integrand substitution in [F9].

[F6] $W^{1,p}$ consists of $L^p$ classes with weak derivatives in $L^p$ and the norm is the $\ell^p$ norm of $u$ and its coordinate weak derivatives ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]); $L^p$ classes are almost-everywhere classes ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

[F7] Countable Choice, assumed for the measure and closure interfaces above ([[def-countable-choice]]).


[F8] A continuous real function on a compact nondegenerate interval is bounded and Riemann integrable; under Countable Choice its Riemann and Lebesgue integrals agree ([[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]], [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]]).

[F9] Under Countable Choice, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $T:U\to V$ between open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$ satisfies $\int_V f(y)\,dy=\int_U f(T(z))|\det DT(z)|\,dz$ for every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable $f$ ([[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]).

[F10] The Lebesgue integral of a complex integrable function is the integral of its real part plus $i$ times the integral of its imaginary part, and $|\int h|\le\int|h|$ for real or complex integrable $h$ ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The smooth case: pointwise bound. Let $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and extend it by zero to $\mathbb R^n$. Write $x=x_\perp+x_ne$ with $x_\perp\perp e$. For each fixed $x_\perp$, the profile $g(s):=\varphi(x_\perp+se)$ is smooth and supported in $(a,b)$, since $\Omega\subset\{a<y\cdot e<b\}$. If $x=x_\perp+x_ne\in\Omega$, then $a<x_n<b$ and $g(a)=0$. On $[a,x_n]$, each real component of $g'$ is continuous, so [F8] supplies its Riemann integrability and converts its Riemann integral to its Lebesgue integral. Thus [F2] applied componentwise and the complex integral convention in [F10] give $\varphi(x)=g(x_n)-g(a)=\int_a^{x_n}D\varphi(x_\perp+se)\cdot e\,ds$. The continuous derivative and its modulus are Lebesgue integrable on this compact interval by [F8]; [F10] and $|D\varphi\cdot e|\le|D\varphi|$ therefore give $|\varphi(x)|\le\int_a^{x_n}|D\varphi(x_\perp+se)|\,ds$. For $p=1$ the resulting integral bound is already the desired estimate; for $p>1$, Holder [F3] applied to the real nonnegative function $|D\varphi|$ and the constant $1$, followed by $x_n-a\le b-a$ and enlargement of the integration interval, yields $|\varphi(x)|^p\le(b-a)^{p-1}\int_a^b|D\varphi(x_\perp+se)|^p\,ds$. [F2, F3, F8, F10, given, algebra]

2.1 The smooth case: integration. If $n=1$, then $|\Omega|\le b-a$, so integrating step 1.1 gives $\int_\Omega|\varphi|^p\le(b-a)^p\int_a^b|D\varphi(se)|^p\,ds=(b-a)^p\int_\Omega|D\varphi|^p$ by [F9] for the global linear diffeomorphism $s\mapsto se$ of $\mathbb R$ (where $e=1$ or $e=-1$ and the absolute Jacobian is $1$), and the support of $D\varphi$ in $\Omega$. Now suppose $n\ge2$. Choose orthonormal coordinates with last vector $e$ and write $x=x_\perp+x_ne$; the corresponding orthogonal map $T:\mathbb R^{n-1}\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ is a global $C^1$ diffeomorphism with $|\det DT|=1$. By [F9], nonnegative integrands have the same integral after composing with $T$; this applies both to $\mathbf1_\Omega|\varphi|^p$ and to $|D\varphi|^p$, which are Borel measurable since the zero extension is smooth and $\Omega$ is open. For each $x_\perp$, the slice $S_{x_\perp}:=\{x_n:(x_\perp,x_n)\in\Omega\}$ is a measurable subset of $(a,b)$, so $|S_{x_\perp}|\le b-a$. Integrating step 1.1 over $\Omega$ and applying Tonelli [F4] gives $\int_\Omega|\varphi|^p\,dx\le(b-a)^{p-1}\int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}}\int_{S_{x_\perp}}\int_a^b|D\varphi(x_\perp+se)|^p\,ds\,dx_n\,dx_\perp\le(b-a)^p\int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}}\int_a^b|D\varphi(x_\perp+se)|^p\,ds\,dx_\perp$. The last integral equals $\int_{\mathbb R^n}|D\varphi|^p\,dx=\int_\Omega|D\varphi|^p$, since $\varphi$ and its gradient vanish outside $\Omega$ and $\Omega$ lies in the slab. Therefore $\|\varphi\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\le(b-a)^p\|D\varphi\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p$. [F4, F5, F9, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The general class. By [F1] there are $\varphi_k\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\varphi_k\to u$ in $W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$; by step 2.1, $\|\varphi_k\|_{L^p}\le(b-a)\|D\varphi_k\|_{L^p}$ for every $k$. Both sides are continuous in the $W^{1,p}$ norm: $\|\varphi_k\|_p\to\|u\|_p$ and $\|D\varphi_k\|_p\to\|Du\|_p$ by [F6]. Passing to the limit gives $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le(b-a)\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$, so the asserted inequality holds with $C(p)=1$. [F1, F6, F7, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

Kinnunen's Theorem 3.10 proves the estimate on bounded open sets by taking the primitive in one coordinate direction and applying Holder; the proof above runs the same argument along the unit vector $e$ of the hypothesis, uses the orthonormal coordinate decomposition for the integration, and then extends from $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ to $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ by the definition of the latter as a closure. The constant obtained is $1$, independent of $p$; the statement permits a $p$-dependent constant.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $n\ge1$; $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$; a class $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$; and a tolerance $\delta>0$.

[F1] $L^2$ classes and zero extension: $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a space of almost-everywhere classes with norm $\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}=(\int_\Omega|u|^2)^{1/2}$ and pairing $(u,v)_{L^2}=\int_\Omega u\overline v$; the zero extension $F=\mathbf 1_\Omega f$ of $f$, equal to $f$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ off $\Omega$, is a well-defined class in $L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with $\|F\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^n)}=\|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]).

[F2] A continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space attains its minimum ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]). Exhaustion tools: a closed and bounded subset of $\mathbb R^n$ is compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]), and for nonempty $A$ the function $x\mapsto\operatorname{dist}(x,A)$ is $1$-Lipschitz, hence continuous ([[lem-distance-to-set-is-lipschitz]]).

[F3] Mollifier existence: [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]] gives a smooth $0\le q\le1$ equal to $1$ on $\overline B_{1/4}(0)$ and supported in $B_{1/2}(0)$. Its support has finite measure by [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and its inner ball contains a positive-volume box by [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], so $0<\int q<\infty$. Thus $\rho=q/\int q$ is a real unit-mass smooth bump supported in $B_1(0)$; radiality is unnecessary.

[F4] Monotone and dominated convergence: a nondecreasing sequence of nonnegative measurable functions has integral limit equal to the integral of its pointwise limit, and a sequence dominated by one integrable function has integrals converging to the integral of its pointwise limit ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[F5] Global smoothing: if $G\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)$, Hölder on each finite-measure compact set makes $G$ locally integrable ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]). Its convolution with the real unit-mass bump of [F3] is smooth on all of $\mathbb R^n$ by [[thm-convolution-with-a-mollifier-is-smooth-and-differentiates-under-the-integral-sign]]. The rescaled family is that of [[def-mollifier-family-generated-by-a-unit-mass-smooth-bump]].

[F6] Approximate identity convergence: a mollifier family is an $L^1$ approximate identity ([[prop-mollifier-families-are-l-one-approximate-identities]]), and for every $1\le q<\infty$ and $g\in L^q(\mathbb R^n)$ one has $\|\rho_\varepsilon*g-g\|_{L^q}\to0$ as $\varepsilon\to0^+$ ([[thm-l-one-approximate-identities-converge-in-l-p]]).

[F7] Zero-boundary Sobolev space: every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ lies in $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ because its classical derivatives are weak derivatives ([[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]), and $H^1_0(\Omega)=W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)$ is by definition the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ in the $H^1$ norm ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

[F8] Inner product: on $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ the pairing of [F1] is an inner product inducing the $L^2$ norm ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]), and Cauchy--Schwarz gives $|(u,v)_{L^2}|\le\|u\|_{L^2}\|v\|_{L^2}$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $\Omega=\varnothing$, use $\varphi=0$. Otherwise, for $m=0,1,2,\ldots$, when $\Omega\ne\mathbb R^n$, set $K_m=\{x:|x|\le m+1,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega)\ge1/(m+1)\}$; when $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$, set $K_m=\overline B_{m+1}(0)$. By [F2] each $K_m$ is compact and contained in $\Omega$, the sets increase, and $\bigcup_mK_m=\Omega$: in the proper-open-set case every point has positive distance from the complement by openness. [F2, given]

2.1 Let $F:=\mathbf 1_\Omega f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ be the zero extension of [F1] and let $F_m:=\mathbf 1_{K_m}F$. Since $K_m\uparrow\Omega$, the sequence $|F-F_m|^2=|F|^2\mathbf 1_{\Omega\setminus K_m}$ decreases pointwise to $0$ and is bounded by the integrable function $|F|^2$; hence $\|F-F_m\|_{L^2}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^n}|F-F_m|^2\to0$ by dominated convergence, and $F_m\to F$ pointwise. Equivalently, the integrals $\int_{K_m}|F|^2$ increase to $\|F\|_{L^2}^2$ by monotone convergence, so the same limit follows. Choose $m$ with $\|F-F_m\|_{L^2}<\delta/2$. [F1, F4, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 Put $G=F_m$ for the $m$ selected in step 2.1, with a representative zero outside $K_m$. Then $\|F-G\|_2<\delta/2$. If $K_m=\varnothing$, $G=0$ and $\varphi=0$ already has error less than $\delta$; hence assume $K_m\ne\varnothing$. Consider every pair $(y,r)$ with $y\in K_m$, $0<r\le1$ and $B_r(y)\subseteq\Omega$. The balls $B_{r/2}(y)$ cover $K_m$, so compactness gives a finite nonempty subcover $B_{r_j/2}(y_j)$; put $\varepsilon_0=\min_j r_j/4>0$. If $y\in K_m$ and $|h|\le\varepsilon_0$, some covering ball gives $|y+h-y_j|<r_j/2+\varepsilon_0<r_j$, so $y+h\in\Omega$. Thus $K_m+\overline B_{\varepsilon_0}(0)\subseteq\Omega$. This sumset is compact: it is bounded, and for a point $x$ outside it the continuous function $y\mapsto|x-y|$ attains on $K_m$ a minimum greater than $\varepsilon_0$, so its complement is open. [F1, F2, step 2.1, choose, algebra]

4.1 Choose the unit-mass smooth bump $\rho$ constructed in [F3], and put $G_\varepsilon=G*\rho_\varepsilon$ for $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$. By [F5] this is smooth globally. If $x\notin K_m+\overline B_\varepsilon(0)$, every $y\in K_m$ has $\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)=0$, while $G(y)=0$ off $K_m$; hence the defining integral is zero. Its support therefore lies in the compact set $K_m+\overline B_\varepsilon(0)\subseteq\Omega$, so $G_\varepsilon|_\Omega\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$. [F3, F5, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 By [F6], $\|G_\varepsilon-G\|_2\to0$. Choose $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$ with this norm less than $\delta/2$ and set $\varphi=G_\varepsilon|_\Omega$. Since $F,G,G_\varepsilon$ vanish outside $\Omega$, $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}=\|G_\varepsilon-F\|_2\le\|G_\varepsilon-G\|_2+\|G-F\|_2<\delta$. [F1, F6, step 3.1, step 4.1, choose, algebra]

6.1 Density of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ in $L^2(\Omega)$ follows because $f$ and $\delta$ were arbitrary in step 5.1. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$: given $g\in L^2(\Omega)$ and $\eta>0$, step 5.1 supplies $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-g\|_{L^2}<\eta$, and $\varphi\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ by [F7]. Finally let $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfy $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. By density choose classes $v_k\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ with $\|v_k-h\|_{L^2}\to0$; then Cauchy--Schwarz [F8] gives $|(h,h)|=|(h,h-v_k)|\le\|h\|_{L^2}\|h-v_k\|_{L^2}\to0$, so $\|h\|_{L^2}^2=(h,h)=0$ and $h=0$. [F1, F7, F8, step 5.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $V$ and $H$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective,
continuous linear map with dense range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real linear
dual of $V$. Identify $H$ with its Hilbert dual by its inner product and embed
$H$ into $V^*$ by
$$h\longmapsto\bigl(v\longmapsto (h,i v)_H\bigr).$$
The resulting dense continuous embeddings are written
$$V\hookrightarrow H\cong H^*\hookrightarrow V^*$$
and $(V,H,V^*)$ is called an **evolution triple**. The pairing between $V^*$
and $V$ is denoted $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$.

For a Hilbert space $X$, $L^2(0,T;X)$ is the space of equivalence classes of
strongly measurable $X$-valued functions $w$ with
$$\int_0^T\|w(t)\|_X^2\,dt<\infty.$$
Strong measurability means being an almost-everywhere pointwise limit of
measurable simple functions. For $u\in L^2(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$,
say that $g$ is the **weak time derivative** of $u$ when
$$\int_0^T (i u(t),i v)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. The derivative is
unique up to equality almost everywhere. The **parabolic energy space** is
$$W(0,T;V):=\{u\in L^2(0,T;V):u'\in L^2(0,T;V^*)\},$$
with norm
$$\|u\|_{W(0,T;V)}:=\bigl(\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2+ \|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$
No endpoint values are part of this definition; they are assigned only after
a continuous $H$ trace representative has been proved. Separability is an
additional hypothesis when it is needed by a later result.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, $T>0$, $Q=U\times(0,T)$, and let
$$L_t[e]=\sum_{i,j=1}^dD_i(a_{ij}D_j e)+\sum_{i=1}^dD_i(b_i e)+\sum_i c_iD_i e+d e$$
with $a_{ij}=a_{ji}$, $a(x,t)\ge\lambda_0 I$ for some $\lambda_0>0$, and real measurable $a,b,c,d$ bounded with the spatial derivatives needed for the displayed divergence form. Let $V=H^1_0(U)$, $H=L^2(U)$, and let $e\in L^2(0,T;V)$ have weak derivative $e_t\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$ and satisfy $-e_t+L_t[e]=r\in L^2(U\times(0,T))$ weakly. Use its continuous $H$ representative for the initial datum $e(0)$ and endpoint norms. The source application has $e(0)=0$. Then there is $C_E<\infty$, depending only on $T$, $\lambda_0$, and the coefficient bounds, such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|e(t)\|_{L^2(U)}^2+\int_0^T\|\nabla e(t)\|_{L^2(U)}^2\,dt\le C_E\left(\|e(0)\|_{L^2(U)}^2+\|r\|_{L^2(Q)}^2\right).$$
The spatial zero trace is the stated $V$ membership almost everywhere in time. In particular, the estimate applies to locally classical continuous errors once their energy-space membership and weak equation have been established; no closed-cylinder derivatives are required.

## Statement references
[Shin et al., Appendix G: energy estimate for the parabolic error](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

[Hunter, §6.2: general variable-coefficient parabolic energy method](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/pde_notes.pdf)

[Shin et al., Appendix G: source energy argument reconstructed with explicit boundary flux and lower-order bounds](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The coefficient bounds, uniform ellipticity, zero spatial trace, initial $L^2$ trace, and the variational solution $e$ of the inhomogeneous error equation.

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed by the zero-boundary Sobolev closure convention used for each spatial slice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

[F1] On the real evolution triple the energy identity gives $\langle e_t,e\rangle=\tfrac12\frac{d}{dt}\|e(t)\|_{L^2(U)}^2$ almost everywhere, and the squared norm is absolutely continuous; it is proved by Bochner time mollification ([[lem-parabolic-energy-pairing-and-trace]], [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]]). The required triple on every bounded open set is supplied by [[lem-shin-bounded-open-set-hilbert-evolution-triple]].

[F2] The principal matrix satisfies $\int_U a_{ij}D_j eD_i e\,dx\ge\lambda_0\|\nabla e\|_{L^2(U)}^2$ by its pointwise ellipticity hypothesis.

[F3] The parabolic convention has initial and lateral boundary data on $\Gamma_T$ ([[def-shin-parabolic-operator-and-boundary]]).

[F4] $H^1_0(U)$ is the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(U)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

## Proof

**Proof strategy:** multiply by the error, integrate by parts, absorb lower-order terms, and apply Gronwall's inequality.

1.1 For almost every $t$, by [F4], approximate $e(\cdot,t)$ in $H^1(U)$ by compactly supported smooth functions. For each approximant the distributional definition of the divergence terms gives the spatial integration-by-parts identity; the coefficient bounds make every pairing continuous in $H^1$, so passing to the limit produces no boundary term because $e(\cdot,t)\in H^1_0(U)$. Pair the weak equation $-e_t+L_t[e]=r$ against $e$ in $V^*,V$ and use [F1] and [F2]. Moving the time derivative to the left gives $$\tfrac12 E'(t)+\lambda_0\|\nabla e(t)\|_2^2\le (\|b\|_\infty+\|c\|_\infty)\|e(t)\|_2\|\nabla e(t)\|_2+\|d\|_\infty E(t)+\|r(t)\|_2\|e(t)\|_2,$$ where $E(t)=\|e(t)\|_2^2$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 By Young's inequality, the first product on the right is at most $\frac{\lambda_0}{4}\|\nabla e\|_2^2+C_1E(t)$ and the last product is at most $\frac12\|r(t)\|_2^2+\frac12E(t)$, for a finite $C_1$ depending only on the coefficient bounds and $\lambda_0$. Hence for $C_2=C_1+\|d\|_\infty+\frac12$, $$E'(t)+\lambda_0\|\nabla e(t)\|_2^2\le 2C_2E(t)+\|r(t)\|_2^2.$$ [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Dropping the nonnegative gradient term in step 2.1 and multiplying by $e^{-2C_2t}$ gives $\frac{d}{dt}(e^{-2C_2t}E(t))\le e^{-2C_2t}\|r(t)\|_2^2$. Integrating from $0$ to any $s\le T$ yields $$\sup_{0\le s\le T}E(s)\le e^{2C_2T}\left(E(0)+\|r\|_{L^2(Q)}^2\right).$$ [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Integrating step 2.1 from $0$ to $T$ and using step 3.1 gives $$\lambda_0\int_0^T\|\nabla e(t)\|_2^2dt\le E(0)+2C_2T\sup_{0\le t\le T}E(t)+\|r\|_{L^2(Q)}^2.$$ Combining this with step 3.1 and dividing by $\lambda_0>0$ proves the stated estimate after increasing the constant. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be the real evolution triple of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]], and let
$u,v\in W(0,T;V)$. Each has a unique representative in $C([0,T];H)$, and
for all $0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2-\|u(s)\|_H^2 =2\int_s^t\langle u'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\,dr,$$
$$(u(t),v(t))_H-(u(s),v(s))_H =\int_s^t\bigl(\langle u'(r),v(r)\rangle_{V^*,V} +\langle v'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\bigr)\,dr.$$
Writing $c_i=\|i:V\to H\|$, the trace obeys
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_H^2 \le \frac{c_i^2}{T}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2 +2\|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real evolution triple, $T>0$, and $u,v\in W(0,T;V)$.

[F1] $W(0,T;V)$ consists of $u\in L^2(0,T;V)$ with weak derivative
$u'\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$; the embedding $V\to H$ is continuous
([[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]]).

[F2] Each such $u$ admits smooth $V$-valued approximants converging in
$L^2(V)$ whose time derivatives converge to $u'$ in $L^2(V^*)$
([[lem-parabolic-bochner-time-mollification]]).

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed by the time-mollification supplier
[[lem-parabolic-bochner-time-mollification]]
([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

1.1 For a smooth $V$-valued function $w$, the continuous inclusion into $H$ and the ordinary product rule give $\frac{d}{dt}\|w(t)\|_H^2=2(w'(t),w(t))_H =2\langle w'(t),w(t)\rangle_{V^*,V}$ by the canonical embedding [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]]. [F1, given]

2.1 For smooth $w$, choose $s$ with $\|w(s)\|_H^2\le T^{-1}\|w\|_{L^2(H)}^2$. Integrating step 1.1 from $s$ to any $t$ gives $\sup_t\|w(t)\|_H^2\le T^{-1}c_i^2\|w\|_{L^2(V)}^2 +2\|w'\|_{L^2(V^*)}\|w\|_{L^2(V)}.$ Apply this to differences of the approximants in [F2]; they are Cauchy in $C([0,T];H)$. Their uniform limit is continuous and agrees with $u$ almost everywhere by their $L^2(H)$ convergence. The same bound passes to the limit. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, choose]

2.2 For approximants $u_n$ from [F2], integrate step 1.1 between arbitrary $s,t$. Uniform $H$ convergence passes the two endpoint norms to those of the continuous representative. The integrands converge in $L^1$ because $\|\langle u_n',u_n\rangle-\langle u',u\rangle\|_{L^1} \le \|u_n'-u'\|_{L^2(V^*)}\|u_n\|_{L^2(V)} +\|u'\|_{L^2(V^*)}\|u_n-u\|_{L^2(V)},$ whose right-hand side tends to zero. This proves the energy identity for all $s,t$. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Apply the energy identity from step 2.2 to $u+v$ and $u-v$, subtract, and use the real polarization identity $\|u+v\|_H^2-\|u-v\|_H^2=4(u,v)_H$. Bilinearity gives the asserted integration-by-parts identity. [step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The trace estimate is the smooth bound in step 2.1 passed through the uniform approximation in [F2], with $\|u\|_{L^2(H)}\le c_i\|u\|_{L^2(V)}$. If two continuous representatives agree almost everywhere, their difference is continuous and zero on a dense subset of $[0,T]$, hence zero everywhere; the representative is unique. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded, $T>0$, and
$$P[w]=-w_t+\sum_{i,j=1}^d a_{ij}(x,t)D_iD_jw+\sum_{j=1}^d\widetilde b_j(x,t)D_jw+\widetilde c(x,t)w$$
on $Q=U\times(0,T)$. Suppose $a(x,t)$ is symmetric, $\xi^Ta(x,t)\xi\ge\lambda_0|\xi|^2$ with $\lambda_0>0$, $\widetilde b,\widetilde c$ are bounded and continuous, and $\widetilde c\le0$. There is $C_P<\infty$, depending only on $U,T,\lambda_0$ and the coefficient bounds, such that every $w\in C^{2,1}(Q)\cap C^0(\bar U\times[0,T])$ with $P[w]\in C^0(Q)$ satisfies
$$\|w\|_{C^0(Q)}\le C_P\left(\|P[w]\|_{C^0(Q)}+\|w\|_{C^0(\Gamma_T)}\right),$$
where $\Gamma_T=(\bar U\times\{0\})\cup(\partial U\times[0,T])$ excludes the final-time face.

## Statement references
[Shin et al., Appendix F, Lemma F.2: parabolic residual stability estimate](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

[Shin et al., Appendix F, proof of Lemma F.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The bounded cylinder, uniformly elliptic coefficient matrix, bounded drift and zero-order coefficients with $\widetilde c\le0$, and the regularity and data of $w$ in the Statement.

[F1] The parabolic operator has the sign convention $P=-\partial_t+L_t$ and its prescribed boundary is initial plus lateral data ([[def-shin-parabolic-operator-and-boundary]]).

[F2] On the final-time face the time derivative is the left derivative; at a final-time maximum it is nonnegative ([[def-parabolic-cylinder-and-parabolic-boundary]]).

## Proof

**Proof strategy:** use a spatial exponential barrier and the weak parabolic maximum principle.

1.1 Choose $a_1<b_1$ with $a_1\le x_1\le b_1$ on $\bar U$. Let $B=\|\widetilde b_1\|_\infty$, $C_0=\|\widetilde c\|_\infty$, and choose $\kappa>0$ so that $\kappa^2\lambda_0-\kappa B-C_0\ge1$. For $\psi(x,t)=e^{\kappa x_1}$, [F1] gives $P[\psi]=e^{\kappa x_1}(\kappa^2a_{11}+\kappa\widetilde b_1+\widetilde c)\ge\eta:=e^{\kappa a_1}>0$. Choose $M>e^{\kappa b_1}$ and put $\Phi=M-\psi$. Then $\Phi>0$ and $P[\Phi]=M\widetilde c-P[\psi]\le-\eta$. [given, F1, algebra, choose]

2.1 Let $R=\|P[w]\|_\infty$, $Q_0=\|w\|_{C^0(\Gamma_T)}$, and $z=w-Q_0-(R/\eta)\Phi$. On $\Gamma_T$, $z\le0$, and in $Q$, $$P[z]=P[w]-Q_0\widetilde c-(R/\eta)P[\Phi]\ge-R+R=0.$$ [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix any $0<\tau<T$ and work on $\bar U\times[0,\tau]$, where the time derivatives at spatial interior points at $t=\tau$ exist because $\tau<T$. Suppose $z>0$ somewhere on this stopped cylinder. Since $z\le0$ on $\Gamma_T$, a positive maximum occurs at a spatial interior point and at a time in $(0,\tau]$. For sufficiently small $\delta>0$, $z+\delta\psi$ still has a positive maximum away from $\Gamma_T$. At this maximum, the spatial gradient is zero and the spatial Hessian is negative semidefinite; the time derivative is zero for $t<\tau$ and nonnegative from the left if $t=\tau$. Thus [F2] and $\widetilde c\le0$ imply $P[z+\delta\psi]\le0$, while step 2.1 and step 1.1 give $P[z+\delta\psi]>0$. This contradiction shows $z\le0$ on every stopped cylinder; let $\tau\uparrow T$ and use continuity at the final face. Hence $w\le Q_0+(R/\eta)\|\Phi\|_\infty$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, contradiction]

4.1 Apply the same argument to $-w$, for which $P[-w]=-P[w]$ and the boundary norm is still $Q_0$. Combining the upper and lower bounds gives the asserted estimate with $C_P=\max\{1,\|\Phi\|_\infty/\eta\}$. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎
