## Definition

Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded open set with
closure $\overline\Omega$ and boundary $\partial\Omega$ in the sense of
[[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]], and let $T>0$. Write
$Q:=\Omega\times(0,T]$ for the **space-time cylinder** and
$$\overline Q:=\overline\Omega\times[0,T]\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$$
for its closure in the space-time variable; the **final-time face** is
$\Omega\times\{T\}$, while the **parabolic boundary** of $Q$ is
$$\partial_pQ:=(\overline\Omega\times\{0\})\cup(\partial\Omega\times[0,T]).$$
No point of the final-time face belongs to $\partial_pQ$: the intersections
$\bigl(\Omega\times\{T\}\bigr)\cap\bigl(\overline\Omega\times\{0\}\bigr)$ and
$\bigl(\Omega\times\{T\}\bigr)\cap\bigl(\partial\Omega\times[0,T]\bigr)$ are
empty because $T>0$ and $\Omega\cap\partial\Omega=\varnothing$.

A function $u$ on $\overline Q$ is of class $C^{2,1}(\overline Q)$ if it is
continuous there, is $C^2$ in $x$ and $C^1$ in $t$ on $Q$, and the functions
$u_t$ and $D_x^\alpha u$ for $|\alpha|\le2$ extend continuously to
$\overline Q$; the multi-index notation and the classes $C^k$ are those of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], and at $t=T$ the time
derivative means the left one-sided limit. The relevant operator is
$\partial_t-\Delta_x$, the heat operator of
[[def-heat-equation-heat-operator-and-cauchy-problem]], and the phrase
"$u_t-\Delta u\le0$ in $Q$" always refers to that cylinder, with the one-sided
interpretation of $u_t$ on the final-time face.

On this page a **classical heat solution** means a function with the stated $C^{2,1}$ regularity satisfying the equation pointwise; no second time derivative is required. Formulas that put time first use the canonical coordinate permutation $(x,t)\leftrightarrow(t,x)$; regularity and derivatives always refer to the named spatial and time variables. The analogous interior class has the same continuous derivatives without an up-to-boundary requirement.

Two elementary topological facts are part of the vocabulary. First,
$\overline Q$ is compact: $\Omega$ is bounded, so $\overline\Omega$ is closed and
bounded in $\mathbb R^n$, hence compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]); then
$\overline Q=\overline\Omega\times[0,T]$ is closed and bounded in
$\mathbb R^{n+1}$, hence compact by the same theorem
([[def-metric-compactness]]). Second, $\partial_pQ$ is closed in
$\mathbb R^{n+1}$, being the union of the two closed sets
$\overline\Omega\times\{0\}$ and $\partial\Omega\times[0,T]$; in particular it
is a closed subset of $\overline Q$
([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

## Remarks

- **The class $C^{2,1}(\overline Q)$ is a convention fixing where the one-sided
  time derivatives live.** The cylinder $Q=\Omega\times(0,T]$ is open in the
  spatial directions and half-open in time, and equation statements on $Q$ are
  read at points with $t<T$ in the usual two-sided sense and at $t=T$ with the
  left derivative. No global smoothness of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed; the
  maximum principles proved later on this page use only this vocabulary.

- **Top versus parabolic boundary.** The decomposition of $\overline Q$ into the
  parabolic boundary and the cylinder $Q$ is not a topological boundary
  decomposition: the final-time face is part of the topological boundary of $Q$
  but is deliberately excluded from $\partial_pQ$, which is exactly the set on
  which initial and lateral data are prescribed. A later counterexample on the
  companion page shows that this asymmetry is forced by the sign of the heat
  operator and cannot be removed.

## Statement

Let $X,U$ be real Banach spaces, and let continuous maps $H,H_n:X\to U$ satisfy $\sup_{a\in K}\|H_n(a)-H(a)\|_U\to0$ for every norm-compact $K\subset X$. Suppose continuous finite-dimensional sampling and reconstruction maps $S_n:X\to E_n$ and $J_n:E_n\to X$ are supplied and satisfy $\sup_{a\in K}\|J_nS_n(a)-a\|_X\to0$ on every such $K$. Then
$$G_n(a)=H_n(J_n(S_n(a)))$$
is a finite-sampling family in the displayed definition, with $F_n=E_n$, finite map the identity and output reconstruction $R_n=H_n\circ J_n:E_n\to U$, and $G_n\to H$ uniformly on every norm-compact input set in the actual $U$ norm.

For the supremum-norm continuous-input case these reconstruction hypotheses always hold with exactly the prescribed tags of arbitrary finite partitions of a nonempty bounded open $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ whose maximal cell diameters $h_n$ tend to zero. Namely let $X=C(\bar D;\mathbb R^q)$, let $S_n(a)=(a(\xi_{n,j}))_j$, and, when $h_n>0$, for $x\in\bar D$ put
$$w_{n,j}(x)=\max\{0,2h_n-|x-\xi_{n,j}|\},\qquad J_n(z)(x)=\frac{\sum_jw_{n,j}(x)z_j}{\sum_jw_{n,j}(x)}.$$
If $h_n=0$, the domain is the zero-dimensional singleton; define $J_n(z)$ to be the constant function with value $z_1$. This reconstructs every input exactly. In both branches $\|J_nS_n\|_{X\to X}\le1$, and the reconstruction error is bounded by the input modulus of continuity at $2h_n$, uniformly on every compact input family. In a stronger Banach input norm the first clause applies whenever the stated reconstructions converge in that norm; convergence in the supremum norm alone is not substituted for that condition.

A further case needs no input reconstruction. Suppose a raw finite architecture first uses its input only through the sampled pointwise lift in the integral-only field $v_{1,n}(x)=\sum_j\omega_{n,j}\kappa_n(x,\xi_{n,j})P(a(\xi_{n,j}))+b_n(x)$, and every later stage acts on this field and the fixed parameters without further access to the original input. Assume these stages are defined and continuous on the compatible Banach spaces in question. Then each raw map itself factors through the finite input sample vector. Its compact-uniform raw convergence therefore already gives a finite-sampling family in the actual output norm, regardless of whether a sample reconstruction into the input norm has been supplied. This includes the integral-only universality subclass, when its kernels and intermediate spaces satisfy the declared compatible norm hypotheses.

## Statement references

[[def-discretization-invariant-operator-family]]

[[lem-neural-operator-compact-union-under-uniform-convergence]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Banach spaces, continuous raw maps, finite-dimensional maps, and compact-uniform limits in the Statement. In the concrete branch the nonempty bounded open set and tagged partitions are given, with nonnegative maximal diameters tending to zero.

[F1] Uniformly convergent continuous images of a compact set have compact union, including the limit image ([[lem-neural-operator-compact-union-under-uniform-convergence]]).

[F2] Closed bounded Euclidean sets are compact, and a continuous map on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]).

[F3] Compact metric sets have finite nets in their own metric ([[thm-compact-implies-complete-and-totally-bounded]]).

[F4] A continuum-valued map factoring through the supplied finite sampling, finite map and output reconstruction has the required finite-dimensional type ([[def-discretization-invariant-operator-family]]).

## Proof

1.1 Fix compact $K\subset X$. If $K$ is empty the conclusion is vacuous. Otherwise put $A_n=J_nS_n$ and $L=K\cup\bigcup_{n\ge1}A_n(K)$. The maps $A_n$ are continuous and converge uniformly on $K$ to the identity. Thus [F1] makes $L$ compact in the actual $X$ norm. By hypothesis $\sup_{b\in L}\|H_n(b)-H(b)\|_U\to0$. [given, F1, construct]

1.2 In the concrete branch $0\le h_n<\infty$. If $h_n=0$, every cell is its singleton tag, so their finite union $D$ is finite. A nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^d$ with $d\ge1$ contains a ball and hence infinitely many points; therefore this case forces $d=0$ and $D=\bar D$ is the singleton of $\mathbb R^0$. All tags are that point, and $J_n(z)(x)=z_1$ is a bounded linear reconstruction of norm at most one, with $J_nS_n(a)=a$ and reconstruction error $0=\omega_a(0)$. Now suppose $h_n>0$. Every point of $D$ is within $h_n$ of some tag in its cell. The distance to the finite tag set is continuous, so the same inequality holds on $\bar D$. Consequently $\sum_jw_{n,j}(x)>0$ there. The normalized weights are continuous, nonnegative and sum to one. Thus $J_n$ is a bounded linear map from the finite sample space with its maximum norm into $C(\bar D;\mathbb R^q)$, of norm at most one. The sampling map is bounded with norm at most one. A positive weight implies $|x-\xi_{n,j}|<2h_n$, so $\|J_nS_n(a)-a\|_\infty\le\omega_a(2h_n)$, where $\omega_a(r)=\sup_{|x-y|\le r}|a(x)-a(y)|$. [given, F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 Continuity of $H$ controls uniform perturbations of the compact set $K$. Explicitly, for $\varepsilon>0$ collect every ball $B(x,r)$ with $x\in K$ and $r>0$ such that $\|H(z)-H(x)\|_U<\varepsilon/2$ for $\|z-x\|_X<3r$. These balls cover $K$; choose a finite subcover and take $\delta$ to be its smallest radius. If $a\in K$ and $\|b-a\|_X<\delta$, both points lie within $3r$ of one selected center, so $\|H(b)-H(a)\|_U<\varepsilon$. Hence $\sup_K\|H(A_n(a))-H(a)\|_U\to0$. Combining this with step 1.1 gives $\sup_K\|G_n-H\|_U\to0$. The maps $S_n$, identity on $E_n$, and $R_n=H_nJ_n$ provide exactly the factorization in [F4]; no access to the original input is used by $R_n$. [given, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For a compact $K\subset C(\bar D;\mathbb R^q)$ and $\eta>0$, [F3] gives a finite $\eta$-net $a_1,\ldots,a_s$. By [F2] their moduli tend to zero. For $a\in K$ within $\eta$ of $a_i$, $\omega_a(r)\le2\eta+\omega_{a_i}(r)$. Therefore $\sup_{a\in K}\omega_a(r)\to0$. Step 1.2 supplies the reconstruction hypotheses of steps 1.1–2.1 and proves the whole concrete branch. The general argument measured every reconstruction error in $X$ and every output error in $U$, so it also proves the first clause without any unproved norm upgrade. [F2, F3, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra]

4.1 For the last assertion set $E_n=F_n=(\mathbb R^{q_0})^{N_n}$ and let $S_n(a)$ be its prescribed sample vector. For $z\in E_n$, construct $v_{1,n}(z)(x)=\sum_j\omega_{n,j}\kappa_n(x,\xi_{n,j})P(z_j)+b_n(x)$ and apply the subsequent raw stages to this field; call the resulting output $R_n(z)$. The first field belongs to its designated auxiliary space because it is a finite sum of its kernel sections and bias with finite scalar/vector coefficients. Every subsequent field belongs to its designated space by the stated compatibility assumptions. The finite sum and continuity of the lift make the first field continuous in $z$, and continuity of the subsequent maps makes $R_n:E_n\to U$ continuous. Induction through those stages proves $H_n(a)=R_n(S_n(a))$ exactly. The identity finite map between $E_n$ and $F_n$ gives [F4], and the assumed compact-uniform raw limit proves its convergence in the actual $U$ norm. No off-grid original input is requested at any stage of this construction. [given, F4, construct, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

This statement is a local alteration and application of the compact-union mechanism in Kovachki et al., Appendix B, Lemma21, and its use for compact-uniform composition in the proof of Lemma22. The complete relevant source statements and printed proofs on PDF/printed pages74–77 of the cached JMLR full text were inspected in this provenance clarification. The source does not state the present finite-sampling bridge, the explicit normalized tag weights, or the integral-first factorization as these separate assertions; those adaptations are fully proved above. The source's printed closedness argument in Lemma21 assumes unjustified convergence of the selected integer indices. The locally proved open-cover compact-union supplier supplies the correct stated conclusion without relying on that step. The finite sampling/reconstruction interpretation is the explicit local definition of discretization invariance. No new retrieval, source-fetch stamp, whole-paper reread, or source attribution for the newly authored formulas is claimed.

## Statement

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]). Then $(X,d)$ is totally bounded
([[def-totally-bounded]]) and complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).

**Both implications are theorems of ZF.** Completeness is obtained here from the
finite intersection characterisation ([[thm-compact-iff-finite-intersection-property]])
applied to the closures of the tails of a Cauchy sequence, and not from the
extraction of a convergent subsequence, which would route the argument through
sequential compactness. What matters for the ledger is that the route taken below
selects nothing at all; the first remark below says why the other route was not
taken.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A compact metric space $(X,d)$.

[L1] Open balls are open ([[thm-metric-open-set-algebra]], [[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metric-topology]]).

[L2] $(X,d)$ is totally bounded exactly when for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a finite $F \subseteq X$ with $X = \bigcup_{y \in F} B(y,\varepsilon)$ ([[def-totally-bounded]]).

[L3] $X$ is a compact subset of itself, and for every family $(U_i)_{i \in I}$ of open subsets of $X$ with $X = \bigcup_{i \in I} U_i$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $i_0, \dots, i_n \in I$ with $X = U_{i_0} \cup \dots \cup U_{i_n}$, unless $X = \emptyset$ ([[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], [[def-metric-compactness]]).

[L4] $(X,d)$ is complete when every Cauchy sequence converges to a point of $X$; $(x_k)$ is Cauchy when for every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K$ with $d(x_m,x_l) < \varepsilon$ for all $m,l \ge K$; and $x_k \to p$ when for every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K$ with $d(x_k,p) < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$ ([[def-complete-metric-space]], [[def-cauchy-in-metric]], [[def-metric-convergence]]).

[L5] The closure $\overline{S}$ of $S \subseteq X$ is closed, contains $S$, and is contained in every closed superset of $S$; and $x \in \overline{S}$ exactly when $B(x,r) \cap S \ne \emptyset$ for every real $r > 0$ ([[thm-metric-closure-characterisation]], [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

[L6] $(X,d)$ is compact exactly when every family of closed subsets of $X$ with the finite intersection property has nonempty intersection, the empty finite list having intersection $X$ ([[thm-compact-iff-finite-intersection-property]], [[def-finite-intersection-property]]).

[L7] A metric satisfies the triangle inequality and is symmetric ([[def-metric-space]]).

[L8] A finite list $n_0, \dots, n_p$ of natural numbers has a greatest member. Indeed the reals $\iota(n_0+1), \dots, \iota(n_p+1)$, with $\iota$ the canonical natural of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-canonical-natural]]), form a nonempty finite set of reals and so have a maximum, which is one of them, say $\iota(n_j+1)$ ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]); the map $m \mapsto \iota(m)$ is strictly increasing on the naturals $\ge 1$ ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), so $n_j < n_i$ would force $\iota(n_j+1) < \iota(n_i+1)$, which the maximality forbids, and the order of $\mathbb{N}$ is linear ([[thm-nat-linear-order]]), whence $n_i \le n_j$ for every $i \le p$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be real; the family $(B(x,\varepsilon))_{x \in X}$ consists of open subsets of $X$ and has union $X$, since $x \in B(x,\varepsilon)$ for every $x$. [L1, L2]

2.1 If $X = \emptyset$ the empty set is a finite $\varepsilon$-net; otherwise the indexed characterisation gives $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $x_0, \dots, x_n \in X$ with $X = B(x_0,\varepsilon) \cup \dots \cup B(x_n,\varepsilon)$, so $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is a finite $\varepsilon$-net; as $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary, $(X,d)$ is totally bounded. [L2, L3, step 1.1]

3.1 Total boundedness being settled, take up completeness: let $(x_k)$ be a Cauchy sequence in $X$ and put $T_n := \overline{\{\, x_k : k \ge n \,\}}$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$, a definition by a rule and not by a selection. [L4, L5, step 2.1]

4.1 Each $T_n$ is closed and nonempty, containing $x_n$; and $T_m \subseteq T_n$ whenever $m \ge n$, since then $\{x_k : k \ge m\} \subseteq \{x_k : k \ge n\} \subseteq T_n$ and $T_m$ is the smallest closed superset of the first of these sets. [L5, step 3.1]

5.1 The family $\mathcal{A} := \{\, T_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ of closed sets has the finite intersection property: the empty list has intersection $X$, which contains $x_0$; and for a list $T_{n_0}, \dots, T_{n_p}$ take a greatest member $n_j$ of the list of indices, so that $T_{n_j} \subseteq T_{n_i}$ for every $i \le p$ and $x_{n_j}$ lies in every one of them. [L6, L8, step 4.1]

6.1 By the finite intersection characterisation of compactness there is a point $p \in \bigcap \mathcal{A}$, that is $p \in T_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$. [L6, step 5.1]

7.1 Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be rational and take $K \in \mathbb{N}$ with $d(x_m,x_l) < \varepsilon/2$ for all $m,l \ge K$; since $p \in T_K$, the ball $B(p,\varepsilon/2)$ meets $\{x_k : k \ge K\}$, so there is $j \ge K$ with $d(p,x_j) < \varepsilon/2$, and then $d(x_k,p) \le d(x_k,x_j) + d(x_j,p) < \varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon$ for every $k \ge K$. [L4, L5, L7, step 6.1]

8.1 Hence $x_k \to p$ with $p \in X$; every Cauchy sequence in $X$ converges, so $(X,d)$ is complete, and with step 2.1 the theorem is proved. [L4, step 2.1, step 7.1] ∎

## Remarks

**Why the textbook route is avoided.** The usual proof of completeness takes a Cauchy sequence, extracts a convergent subsequence and appeals to [[lem-metric-cauchy-with-convergent-subsequence]]. That is correct, but it goes through sequential compactness, and the reader tracking the ledger then has to check the cost of *that* implication before believing this one. The tail-closure argument above is shorter and manifestly selects nothing: the sets $T_n$ are given by a formula, the point $p$ is produced by one existential instantiation, and the index $j$ in step 7.1 by another.

**Neither converse holds.** A complete metric space need not be totally bounded and need not be compact ($\mathbb{R}$ is complete and unbounded), and a totally bounded space need not be compact ([[fs-totally-bounded-implies-compact]], [[cex-totally-bounded-not-compact]]). What is true is that, assuming the Axiom of Countable Choice, the two together are equivalent to compactness; the missing direction is [[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]], and that is exactly where the Axiom of Countable Choice is spent.

## Definition

The raw quadrature rule below takes the continuous input function, including any off-grid values used by a local term or pointwise lifting. It is not by itself asserted to factor through its stored input samples. A finite-sampling version is specified after the raw rule.

For the continuous-function architecture, given a finite partition of $D$ into measurable cells $E_1,\dots,E_N$, choose tags $\xi_j\in E_j$ and weights $\omega_j=|E_j|$. For input samples $v_0(\xi_j)$, replace each integral layer by
$$v_{t+1}^{(i)}=\sigma_t\!\left(W_tv_t^{(i)}+\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\kappa_t(\xi_i,\xi_j)v_t^{(j)}+b_t(\xi_i)\right),\qquad 1\le i\le N.$$
At an arbitrary output query $x\in\bar D'$, evaluate the same layer formula using $x$ in the first kernel argument and the stored input-cell values in the sum. Apply the pointwise lifting and projection networks with the same parameters at every discretization. A refinement changes the cells, tags, and weights, but not the continuum parameters $W_t,\kappa_t,b_t$ or the pointwise network parameters.

For a finite-sampling realization on continuous inputs, first reconstruct the input from its prescribed tags by the normalized nonnegative weights in the finite-sampling reconstruction bridge. Run the raw rule on this reconstructed function, including in the pointwise lifting and every local term. Its output is then a function of the finite input sample vector alone, with the same continuum parameters. The weights and reconstruction change with the partition; the learned parameters do not. The bridge proves compact-uniform convergence in the output supremum norm. For a stronger compatible Banach input/output formulation, supply reconstructions into the actual input Banach space that converge compact-uniformly in that input norm; the same bridge then preserves the raw rule's proved output Banach norm convergence. The explicit continuous-input weights alone do not assert this stronger reconstruction property.

## Definition references
[Kovachki et al., Appendix E: compatible finite-dimensional Riemann-sum maps](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.08481)

## Remark

At every refinement, each cell contributes its volume weight, all kernels and pointwise-network parameters are shared with the continuum operator, and the output can be evaluated at any query point. Changing only the mesh size without preserving these three conventions does not instantiate the discretization family defined above.

The integral universality subclass also admits $L^1$ input equivalence classes. Point samples of those classes are not canonical; this algorithm uses continuous representatives when applying sampling and makes no assertion of an intrinsic point-sampling rule on arbitrary $L^1$ classes. Norm convergence of the reconstructions requires the hypotheses of the discretization theorem for the chosen norm.

When the first input-dependent layer is integral-only, the raw rule already has a finite-sample reconstruction: its first output is a finite sum of kernel sections with coefficients given by the sampled lifting values. All later reconstructed fields depend only on those coefficients and fixed parameters. The finite-sampling bridge proves this exact factorization and transfers the full compatible-Banach raw convergence without an input-reconstruction premise. No such assertion is made for a raw local path retaining the original input.

The failure of exact finite sampling for an unchanged raw local path is illustrated in [[cex-raw-neural-operator-local-term-needs-input-reconstruction]]. This is a nonlogical reader example; the reconstruction and convergence claims above use the proved finite-sampling bridge.

## Statement refuted

For $d\ge2$, $0<\alpha\le1$, and positive constants in equation (3.1), the count condition $m_r=O(m_b^{d/(d-1)})$ alone does not imply that the two threshold coordinates have bounded max-to-min ratio. In particular, choosing $\lambda_m^R=\widehat\lambda_m^R$ satisfies the stated coordinatewise lower bound and norm upper bound, while that ratio can diverge.

## Statement references
[Shin et al., equations (3.1)–(3.2) and Appendix C: threshold and minimizer comparison](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

[Shin et al., Appendix C, equation (21): claimed regularizer-coordinate comparability](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The threshold definitions for $d\ge2$, positive fixed $\lambda_r,\lambda_b,c_r,c_b$, and the sample-count condition in the Statement.

[F1] The exact thresholds are
$$\widehat\lambda^R_{r,m}=\frac{3\lambda_r(\sqrt d)^{2\alpha}c_r^{-2\alpha/d}m_r^{-\alpha/d}}{C_m},\qquad \widehat\lambda^R_{b,m}=\frac{3\lambda_b(\sqrt d)^{2\alpha}c_b^{-2\alpha/(d-1)}m_b^{-\alpha/(d-1)}}{C_m},$$
where the same positive $C_m$ divides both coordinates ([[alg-empirical-pinn-objective]]).

## Proof

**Proof strategy:** explicit sample-count sequence.

1.1 Set $m_r=m_b=n$ for integers $n\ge1$. Since $d/(d-1)>1$, we have $n\le n^{d/(d-1)}$, so the required count condition holds. Choose $\lambda_m^R=\widehat\lambda_m^R$; then the coordinatewise lower-bound condition is equality and the max norm is exactly the prescribed comparison scale. [given, F1, algebra, choose]

2.1 Cancelling the common factor $C_m$ in [F1] gives $$\frac{\lambda^R_{r,m}}{\lambda^R_{b,m}}=\frac{\widehat\lambda^R_{r,m}}{\widehat\lambda^R_{b,m}}=\frac{\lambda_r c_r^{-2\alpha/d}}{\lambda_b c_b^{-2\alpha/(d-1)}}\,n^{\alpha/(d-1)-\alpha/d}=C\,n^{\alpha/(d(d-1))},$$ where $C>0$ is independent of $n$. The exponent is positive, so the ratio tends to infinity. Thus the two coordinates need not be comparable under the stated count condition. [step 1.1, F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

The following assertion is false under the library's bounded global Hölder norm: every bounded Lipschitz domain satisfying an exterior sphere condition at each boundary point, with a strictly elliptic operator having Hölder coefficients and nonpositive expanded zero-order coefficient, has for every Hölder forcing and continuous Dirichlet data a unique solution in $C^{2,\alpha}(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$.

## Statement references
[Shin et al., Theorem D.1: the exterior-sphere classical Dirichlet assertion](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

[Shin et al., Theorem D.1, PDF p.25: existence claim refuted here](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

[Hunter, §2.3: weak maximum principle used for uniqueness](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/pde_notes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $0<\alpha<1$ and the source's claimed $C^{2,\alpha}(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$ solution class.

[F1] The library's $C^{2,\alpha}(U)$ is the bounded global Hölder class; its norm includes the supremum of every second derivative over all of $U$ ([[def-holder-spaces-c-k-alpha-and-their-scaled-norms]]).

[F2] For $L=\Delta$, a bounded-domain function $w\in C^2(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$ with $\Delta w=0$ and $w|_{\partial U}=0$ vanishes identically ([[lem-shin-elliptic-residual-stability]]).

[F3] The locally proved radial profile $\chi$ is smooth, equals $1$ for $r\le1/4$, and equals $0$ for $r\ge1/2$ ([[lem-shin-radial-smooth-cutoff]]).

[F4] The Laplacian of a scalar $C^2$ function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^2$ is $w_{xx}+w_{yy}$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]).

[F5] The total chain rule applies to the smooth local polar-coordinate change on $r>0$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

## Counterexample

1.1 Let $U=\{(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta):0<r<1,\ 0<\theta<2\pi/3\}$. It is bounded and Lipschitz: its boundary consists of two line segments and a circular arc, meeting at finitely many corners of angles $2\pi/3$ and $\pi/2$. At a smooth boundary point, a sufficiently small ball tangent on the exterior side is disjoint from $U$; on the circular arc one can use a ball outside the unit disk. At a corner of interior angle $\beta<\pi$, choose a ball tangent at the corner with its center on the exterior angle bisector. Directions from the vertex to points in this ball lie within angle $\pi/2$ of the center direction, while the sector directions are at angular distance at least $\pi-\beta/2>\pi/2$; hence the ball is exterior. Therefore $U$ satisfies the exterior sphere condition everywhere. [given, cases]

1.2 Let $\chi$ be the profile supplied by [F3]. Set $$u(r,\theta)=\chi(r)r^{3/2}\sin(3\theta/2),\qquad L=\Delta,\qquad f=\Delta u,\qquad g=0.$$ Since $r>0$ on $U$, $u\in C^\infty(U)$. It extends continuously by zero at the vertex, vanishes on both straight sides because the sine factor vanishes, and vanishes on the circular arc because $\chi(1)=0$. To compute $\Delta w$ for any $C^2$ function in local polar coordinates, write $c=\cos\theta$ and $s=\sin\theta$. The chain rule [F5] gives $$w_{xx}=c^2w_{rr}+\frac{s^2}{r}w_r+\frac{s^2}{r^2}w_{\theta\theta}-\frac{2sc}{r}w_{r\theta}+\frac{2sc}{r^2}w_\theta,\quad w_{yy}=s^2w_{rr}+\frac{c^2}{r}w_r+\frac{c^2}{r^2}w_{\theta\theta}+\frac{2sc}{r}w_{r\theta}-\frac{2sc}{r^2}w_\theta.$$ By [F4], adding yields $\Delta w=w_{rr}+r^{-1}w_r+r^{-2}w_{\theta\theta}$. For $w=r^{3/2}\sin(3\theta/2)$, these derivatives are $w_r=\frac32r^{1/2}\sin(3\theta/2)$, $w_{rr}=\frac34r^{-1/2}\sin(3\theta/2)$, and $w_{\theta\theta}=-\frac94r^{3/2}\sin(3\theta/2)$, so the polar Laplacian is zero on $r<1/4$. On the annulus where $\chi$ varies, $r$ is bounded away from zero and all factors are smooth; outside $r<1/2$, $u=0$. Thus $f$ is smooth and supported in $1/4\le r\le1/2$. The domain $U$ is convex, so boundedness of $\nabla f$ gives a Lipschitz bound on $f$ along each segment in $U$; since $U$ is bounded and $0<\alpha<1$, this implies $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(U)$. [given, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 Along the ray $\theta=\pi/3$ and for $0<r<1/4$, $\partial_{rr}u=(3/4)r^{-1/2}$, which is unbounded as $r\downarrow0$. A bounded global $C^{2,\alpha}$ norm bounds every Cartesian second derivative and hence every unit-direction second derivative, so [F1] implies $u\notin C^{2,\alpha}(U)$. The coefficients of $L=\Delta$ are smooth, the ellipticity constant is $1$, and the expanded zero-order coefficient is $0\le0$. [step 1.2, F1, algebra]

3.1 The displayed $u$ is a classical solution in $C^2(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$ of $\Delta u=f$ with zero Dirichlet data. Any other solution in that class differs from $u$ by a zero-boundary harmonic function, which vanishes by [F2]. Hence it is the unique classical solution, and no solution in the asserted global $C^{2,\alpha}(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$ class exists. This refutes the assertion. [step 1.2, step 2.1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $k\ge0$ be an integer, let $0<\alpha<1$ and let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Fix an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and a function $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, where $C^k$ and the canonical-order derivatives $D^\beta u$ are those of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Put
$$[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}:=\sum_{|\beta|=k}\ \sup_{\substack{x,y\in\Omega\\ x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta u(x)-D^\beta u(y)|}{|x-y|^{\alpha}},\qquad \|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}\ \max_{|\beta|=j}|D^\beta u(x)|+[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega},$$
where the sums and maxima run over the finitely many multi-indices of the stated order. The quantity $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}$ is the **$k$-th order $\alpha$-Hölder seminorm** of $u$ and the quantity $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ the **$C^{k,\alpha}$ norm** of $u$; both are taken in $[0,+\infty]$, so the "norm" may be $+\infty$ and only the class below carries a genuine normed-space structure.

The **local Hölder class** $C^{k,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega'}<+\infty$ for every $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$. The **bounded class** $C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}<+\infty$. Thus $C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\subseteq C^{k,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and the inclusion may be strict: on $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$ the function $u(x)=\sin(|x|^2)$ lies in the local class (it is $C^1$, hence locally $\alpha$-Hölder on every compact set), while $[u]_{0,\alpha;\mathbb R^n}=+\infty$, because at the points $x_j=\sqrt{2\pi j}\,e_1$ and $y_j=x_j+(2\sqrt{2\pi j})^{-1}e_1$ the difference quotients are $\asymp(2\sqrt{2\pi j})^{\alpha}\to\infty$. On the bounded class the displayed formula is a norm, and the assignment $u\mapsto\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ is that norm.

**Scaled interior norm.** For a ball $B_R(x_0)\subseteq\Omega$ of radius $R>0$ and centre $x_0$, write $[v]_{0,\alpha;B}:=\sup\{|v(x)-v(y)|/|x-y|^{\alpha}:x,y\in B,\ x\ne y\}$ for the plain Hölder seminorm on a set $B$, and put
$$\|u\|^{*}_{k,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}R^{j}\max_{|\beta|=j}\ \sup_{B_R(x_0)}|D^\beta u|+R^{k+\alpha}\max_{|\beta|=k}[D^\beta u]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}.$$
On every ball, $C^{2,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$ therefore agrees with the finite-scaled-norm class of that dependency. This is the **scaled interior norm** of $u$ on the ball; for $k=2$ it is exactly the scaled quantity of [[def-local-holder-and-c-two-alpha-norms-on-euclidean-balls]], and it takes values in $[0,+\infty]$ as well. It is read off the open ball alone.

**Bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domains.** A **bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domain** in $\mathbb R^n$ is a bounded nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with the following local graph property: for every $x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood $W$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal $Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and a function $\varphi\in C^{k,\alpha}(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that $R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{y=(y',y_n)\in B\times\mathbb R:\ y_n<\varphi(y')\}.$$
This generalises the integer-order notion of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] to the Hölder scale, with the same one-sided graph convention; the regularity $\varphi\in C^{k,\alpha}(B)$ is the only strengthening, connectedness is not required, and no boundary seminorm is attached to the interior norms above. In dimension $n=1$ the corresponding sets are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals.

**The boundary-extension class.** Let $\Omega$ be bounded and let $u\in C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Say that $u$ lies in $C^{k,\alpha}(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when each derivative field $D^\beta u$ with $|\beta|\le k$ extends continuously to $\overline\Omega$. The extension of each field is then unique, since $\Omega$ is dense in $\overline\Omega$, and the sup and Hölder quantities formed with the extended fields and suprema over $\overline\Omega$ agree with those displayed above, formed over $\Omega$: a supremum over the dense subset $\Omega$ already computes the supremum of the extension, and for the seminorm the inequality $[\tilde v]_{0,\alpha;\overline\Omega}\le[v]_{0,\alpha;\Omega}$ follows by approximating a pair in $\overline\Omega$ by pairs in $\Omega$, so the two seminorms are equal. We equip $C^{k,\alpha}(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with this common norm. This is the Hölder-scale analogue of the interior-up-to-boundary convention for integer order $C^m(\overline\Omega)$ fixed in [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]].

## Remarks

- **Scaling.** If $R>0$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$ and $v(z):=u(x_0+Rz)$ on $B_1(0)$, then $D^\beta v(z)=R^{|\beta|}D^\beta u(x_0+Rz)$, and consequently $\|v\|^{*}_{k,\alpha;B_1(0)}=\|u\|^{*}_{k,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}$. The powers $R^{j}$ and $R^{k+\alpha}$ are exactly what makes this identity hold; the same computation with $k=2$ is the one recorded in [[def-local-holder-and-c-two-alpha-norms-on-euclidean-balls]].
- **Boundary extension.** For $k=0$, every element of $C_b^{0,\alpha}(\Omega)$ is uniformly continuous and extends uniquely to $\overline\Omega$: for any boundary point choose an interior sequence converging to it, use the Hölder bound to make its values Cauchy, and compare two sequences by the same bound. For $k\ge1$, boundedness of the lower-order fields need not give their boundary limits on an arbitrary open set. For example, let $\Omega=((0,1)\times(0,2))\cup((1,2)\times(0,2))$ and let $u$ equal $0$ on the first component and $1$ on the second. All positive-order derivatives vanish, so $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}=1$ for $k\ge1$, but $u$ has no limit at $(1,1)$. This set fails the one-sided boundary graph condition at the removed interface. The definitions assert no trace theorem, completeness or compactness.
- **Local versus bounded.** The local class tests compactly contained subsets; the bounded class additionally controls all derivative suprema and the global top-order seminorm. On arbitrary bounded open sets, lower-order suprema can also fail: on the disjoint intervals $I_j=(2^{-j},2^{-j}+2^{-j-2})$, the function equal to $j$ on $I_j$ is locally smooth with every positive-order derivative zero, but is unbounded. Thus boundedness of the domain alone does not identify the two classes.
- **Choice.** The definition itself uses no choice principle; later completeness, approximation and embedding statements on this page state their own Countable Choice hypotheses.

## Definition

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

## Remarks

- **The vector case is componentwise by convention, and the convention is stated because sources leave it implicit.** Nothing forces a single reading of $\Delta$ on a field; the componentwise one is the one that makes the curl-of-a-curl identity of [[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]] true as written, and it is the reading in force everywhere on this page.

- **Why $C^2$ and not $C^1$.** Forming $\nabla f$ consumes one degree of differentiability, so $\operatorname{div}\nabla f$ needs $\nabla f$ to be $C^1$; that is exactly $f$ being $C^2$. Nothing here interchanges two partial derivatives, so no appeal to a mixed-partials theorem is made in the definition itself, and $\Delta f$ is defined by the displayed sum in the fixed order $\partial_i\partial_i$.

- **The planar equation.** For $n=2$ the condition $\Delta f=0$ reads $\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf=0$. That is the equation written out in [[thm-c2-holomorphic-components-are-harmonic]] for the real and imaginary parts of a holomorphic function; a reader meeting the word "harmonic" in either place is meeting one notion.

## Statement

Let $0<\alpha<1$ and let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and satisfy an exterior sphere condition at every boundary point. Let $a_{ij}=a_{ji}\in C^{1,\alpha}(U)$ be uniformly elliptic with minimum eigenvalue at least $\lambda_0>0$, let $b_i\in C^{1,\alpha}(U)$ and $c_i,d\in C^\alpha(U)$, and define
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^dD_i(a_{ij}D_j u+b_i u)+\sum_{i=1}^d c_iD_i u+du.$$
Assume $\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}(x)|^2\le\Lambda$ and $\lambda_0^{-2}(\|b(x)\|^2+\|c(x)\|^2)+\lambda_0^{-1}|d(x)|\le v^2$ on $U$, and use the expanded coefficients $\widetilde b_j=\sum_iD_i a_{ij}+b_j+c_j$ and $\widetilde c=\sum_iD_i b_i+d\le0$. For every $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(U)$ and $g\in C^0(\partial U)$, the source assertion is that the Dirichlet problem $L[u]=f$ in $U$, $u=g$ on $\partial U$ has a unique solution $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$. For any $h\in C^0(U)$ with $L[h]\in C^{0,\alpha}(U)$ and $h\in C^{0,\alpha}(\partial U)$, the source further asserts
$$\|u-h\|_{C^0(U)}\le C\bigl(\|f-L[h]\|_{C^0(U)}+\|g-h\|_{C^0(\partial U)}\bigr),$$
where $C$ depends only on the domain and the displayed coefficient bounds. The global existence part of this assertion is false under the library's bounded global Hölder convention.

## Statement references

[Shin et al., Theorem D.1 and Lemma D.2, PDF p.26: source assertion retained here](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

[[cex-shin-elliptic-corner-regularity-on-exterior-sphere-domain]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The source assertion in the Statement, including its printed divergence indexing. The refutation uses $b=c=d=0$, so the indexing discrepancy does not affect it.

[A1] Assume for contradiction that the asserted global existence conclusion holds for every admissible datum.

[F1] The sector $U=\{0<r<1,0<\theta<2\pi/3\}$ is bounded Lipschitz and satisfies the exterior-sphere condition. With $L=\Delta$, $g=0$ and $u=\chi(r)r^{3/2}\sin(3\theta/2)$, its smooth forcing $f=\Delta u$ is globally Hölder, and $u$ is classical and continuous on the closure, but has unbounded second derivatives ([[cex-shin-elliptic-corner-regularity-on-exterior-sphere-domain]]).

[F2] The zero-boundary classical homogeneous Dirichlet problem is unique by comparison ([[lem-shin-elliptic-residual-stability]]).

[F3] The global bounded Hölder norm includes the supremum of every second derivative ([[def-holder-spaces-c-k-alpha-and-their-scaled-norms]]). The positive-principal convention is fixed by [[def-shin-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]].

## Refutation

1.1 Assume for contradiction the claimed global existence assertion [A1]. Use the sector and data from [F1]. The coefficient matrix is the identity and all lower coefficients vanish; uniform ellipticity holds with $\lambda_0=1$, the pointwise source bounds hold with $\Lambda=2$ and $v=0$, and the expanded zero-order coefficient is zero. Thus these data satisfy every hypothesis of the claimed existence assertion. [assume-contra, F1, F3]

1.2 Assumption [A1] gives a global bounded $C^{2,\alpha}(U)$ solution $u^*$ continuous on the closure. The explicit $u$ from [F1] is a second classical continuous Dirichlet solution. Their difference is zero-boundary harmonic, so [F2] implies $u^*=u$. [A1, F1, F2]

2.1 Along $\theta=\pi/3$ and $r<1/4$, $\partial_{rr}u=(3/4)r^{-1/2}$ is unbounded. A globally bounded Cartesian Hessian would bound this unit-direction second derivative. Therefore [F3] excludes $u$ from the asserted global class, contradicting step 1.2. The global existence claim is false; its failure does not refute the separately proved classical residual estimate. [step 1.2, F1, F3, discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Remarks

The printed source formula also repeats $b_i u$ inside the double divergence sum, although its stated expanded drift contains $b$ only once. This defect is retained visibly in the historical assertion above. The native Laplacian sector refutation is independent of that discrepancy. The repaired existence theorem uses the intended single $b$ divergence and preserves the correct local-interior and conditional smooth-boundary branches.

## Definition

Let $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized Lebesgue measure, represented by the unit cube $[0,1]^d$, and let $v\in C(\mathbb T^d;\mathbb R^q)$ be a periodic vector field. Let $K\ge0$ be a frequency cutoff, and let $R_k\in\mathbb C^{q'\times q}$ be trainable matrices for integer multi-indices $k$ with $\|k\|_\infty\le K$. Define the truncated Fourier integral layer by
$$\mathcal K_Rv(x)=\sum_{\|k\|_\infty\le K}e^{2\pi i k\cdot x}R_k\widehat v(k),\qquad \widehat v(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}e^{-2\pi i k\cdot y}v(y)\,dy.$$
For real-valued outputs require $R_{-k}=\overline{R_k}$ and $R_0$ real. A Fourier neural-operator layer is
$$v_{t+1}(x)=\sigma\bigl(W_tv_t(x)+\mathcal K_Rv_t(x)+b_t(x)\bigr),$$
where $W_t$ is a real pointwise channel map, $b_t$ is a real bias function, and $\sigma$ acts coordinatewise. This definition gives a Fourier-parameterized layer only. It does not assert that the architecture is universal in any specified function-space topology.

## Statement

For each $q\ge1$, the class $\mathrm{BA}_q$ in the displayed activation-class definition is empty.

## Statement references
[Kovachki et al., Definition 7: global bound indexed by $C\ge\operatorname{diam}_2(K)$](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.08481)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $q\ge1$ and the definition of $\mathrm{BA}_q$.

[F1] Membership in $\mathrm{BA}_q$ requires, for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^q$, every $\varepsilon>0$, and every $C\ge\operatorname{diam}_2(K)$, a network satisfying both the identity-approximation and global-bound inequalities ([[def-neural-operator-activation-classes]]).

## Proof

**Proof strategy:** direct.

1.1 Suppose $\sigma\in\mathrm{BA}_q$. Choose $x_0\in\mathbb R^q$ with $x_0\ne0$, set $K=\{x_0\}$, choose $C=0$, and choose $0<\varepsilon<|x_0|_2$. Since a singleton has diameter zero, these choices satisfy the quantifiers in [F1]. [given, F1, choose]

2.1 The required network would satisfy $|f(x)|_2\le0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^q$, hence $f(x_0)=0$. It would also satisfy $|f(x_0)-x_0|_2\le\varepsilon$, which becomes $|x_0|_2\le\varepsilon$, contrary to the choice of $\varepsilon$. Therefore no $\sigma$ belongs to $\mathrm{BA}_q$. [given, step 1.1, F1, contradiction] ∎

## Remark

The source's immediately adjacent assertion that ReLU belongs to this class cannot follow from the printed definition: the contradiction above applies to every activation. The global-output-bound branch of the source's Theorem 11 is therefore vacuous as printed. A change from diameter to a bound involving the location of $K$ would be a different definition and requires owner reconciliation.

## Statement

Let $d,d'\in\mathbb N$ with $d,d'\ge1$, let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, and Jordan measurable, let $D'\subset\mathbb R^{d'}$ be nonempty and bounded, let $\kappa\in C(\bar D'\times\bar D)$ be scalar-valued, and let $K\subset C(\bar D)$ be nonempty and compact in the supremum norm. Give products of metric spaces the max metric. Let $Q_n:C(\bar D)\to\mathbb R$ be bounded linear quadrature functionals with $\sup_n\|Q_n\|<\infty$ and $Q_n f\to\int_D f(y)\,dy$ for every $f\in C(\bar D)$. Then
$$\sup_{a\in K}\sup_{x\in\bar D'}\left|Q_n\bigl(\kappa(x,\cdot)a(\cdot)\bigr)-\int_D\kappa(x,y)a(y)\,dy\right|\longrightarrow0.$$
This conclusion is in the supremum norm on the output variable. It does not by itself establish convergence in an arbitrary Banach output norm $U$.

## Statement references
[Kovachki et al., Appendix E: compact-uniform approximation of the integral layers](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.08481)

[Kovachki et al., Appendix E: Riemann sums on compact families of integrands](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.08481)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact set $K$, the continuous kernel $\kappa$, and the quadrature functionals in the Statement.

[F1] A compact metric space is totally bounded, so for every $\delta>0$ it has a finite $\delta$-net ([[thm-compact-implies-complete-and-totally-bounded]], [[def-totally-bounded]]).

[F2] The hypotheses give pointwise convergence $Q_n f\to\int_D f$ on $C(\bar D)$ and a uniform bound on the operator norms of $Q_n$.

[F3] Heine–Borel makes $\bar D$ and $\bar D'$ compact. Finite products are compact in the product topology, which agrees with the topology of the max product metric because its balls are products of factor balls and such rectangles form a basis. The kernel is bounded and uniformly continuous on the compact metric product $\bar D'\times\bar D$, and each $a\in C(\bar D)$ is bounded on $\bar D$ ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], [[def-product-topology]], [[cor-compact-domain-maps-are-uniformly-continuous]], [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], [[def-continuous-real-functions-on-a-compact-metric-space]]).

[F4] The continuous image of a compact metric space is compact ([[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]).

## Proof

**Proof strategy:** direct finite-net argument.

1.1 Define $\Phi(x,a)=\kappa(x,\cdot)a(\cdot)$ on $\bar D'\times K$. For $(x,a),(x',a')$ in this product, $$\|\Phi(x',a')-\Phi(x,a)\|_\infty\le\|\kappa\|_\infty\|a'-a\|_\infty+\|a\|_\infty\sup_{y\in\bar D}|\kappa(x',y)-\kappa(x,y)|.$$ The constants are finite by [F3]. Given $\eta>0$, uniform continuity of $\kappa$ on $\bar D'\times\bar D$ gives a positive $\delta_1$ making the second term less than $\eta/2$ when $|x'-x|<\delta_1$; choosing $\delta_2>0$ with $\|\kappa\|_\infty\delta_2<\eta/2$ bounds the first term whenever $\|a'-a\|_\infty<\delta_2$ (if $\|\kappa\|_\infty=0$, that term is zero). Thus $\Phi$ is continuous for the max product metric. The domain is compact by [F3], so [F4] makes its image $S$ compact. [given, F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 Put $M=1+\sup_n\|Q_n\|+|D|>0$. For any $f,g\in C(\bar D)$, $$\left|Q_n(f)-\int_Df-Q_n(g)+\int_Dg\right|\le M\|f-g\|_\infty,$$ since $|\int_D(f-g)|\le |D|\|f-g\|_\infty$. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Put $M=1+\sup_n\|Q_n\|+|D|>0$. By [F1] and step 1.1, choose a finite $\varepsilon/(3M)$-net $f_1,\dots,f_J$ for $S$. For each $j$, [F2] gives an index $n_j$ such that $|Q_n(f_j)-\int_Df_j|<\varepsilon/3$ whenever $n\ge n_j$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, choose]

3.1 Let $n\ge\max_j n_j$ and $f\in S$. Choose $j$ with $\|f-f_j\|_\infty<\varepsilon/(3M)$. By [step 1.2] and the bound from [step 2.1], $$|Q_n(f)-\int_Df|\le M\|f-f_j\|_\infty+|Q_n(f_j)-\int_Df_j|+M\|f_j-f\|_\infty<\varepsilon.$$ Every $f\in S$ has this bound, so taking the supremum over $a\in K$ and $x\in\bar D'$ proves the assertion. [step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\varepsilon$ be a
real with $\varepsilon > 0$.

- A **finite $\varepsilon$-net** for $(X,d)$ is a finite subset $F \subseteq X$
  with
  $$X = \bigcup_{y \in F} B(y, \varepsilon) ,$$
  the balls being those of $(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). *Finite* is the
  listing form fixed in [[def-metric-compactness]]: $F = \emptyset$, or
  $F = \{y_0, \dots, y_m\}$ for some $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and points
  $y_0, \dots, y_m \in X$.
- $(X,d)$ is **totally bounded** when it has a finite $\varepsilon$-net for every
  real $\varepsilon > 0$.
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is **totally bounded** when the metric subspace
  $(A,d_A)$ is ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]); its nets are then finite
  subsets of $A$ and its balls are the balls $B_A(a,\varepsilon)$ of the
  subspace.

**The empty space is totally bounded**, the empty net serving for every
$\varepsilon$, since a union over no indices is empty. Every space listed as
$\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is totally bounded too, itself being an $\varepsilon$-net
for every $\varepsilon$.

**The centres are required to lie in the space.** Writing the condition with
centres in $X$ and balls of $X$ is what makes total boundedness a property of the
metric space $(X,d)$ alone, matching the treatment of compactness in
[[def-metric-compactness]]. For a subset $A$ this matters: the nets of $(A,d_A)$
consist of points of $A$, not of nearby points of the ambient space.

**Total boundedness is stronger than boundedness and is not the same thing.**
A totally bounded space is bounded in the sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] — that is claim 1 of
[[lem-totally-bounded-basic]] — and the converse fails, as
[[fs-bounded-implies-totally-bounded]] records. Boundedness asks for one ball
containing the space; total boundedness asks for finitely many balls of *every*
prescribed radius, and it is the second condition that controls how spread out
the space is at small scales.

## Remarks

**Why $\varepsilon$ ranges over the reals here.** Convergence and the Cauchy
condition are tested against rational $\varepsilon$ in this library
([[def-metric-convergence]], [[def-cauchy-in-metric]]), because that is how
[[def-real-limit]] is written; total boundedness is not a limit condition and is
stated for real $\varepsilon > 0$ directly. Nothing turns on the difference: a
net for a rational $\varepsilon' \le \varepsilon$ is a net for $\varepsilon$,
since $B(y,\varepsilon') \subseteq B(y,\varepsilon)$.

**A net is not unique and is not part of the data.** Total boundedness asserts
that nets exist; it names none. Producing one net for each $\varepsilon$
simultaneously, as a function of $\varepsilon$, is a further act of selection,
and where a proof needs that function it says so and pays for it — see
[[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]] and
[[lem-compact-metric-space-has-a-countable-dense-subset]], each of which spends
the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) exactly once and at
exactly that point.

## Statement

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]) and every family
$(X_k)_{k < n}$ of compact topological spaces ([[def-compact-space]],
[[def-topological-space]]), the product

$$\prod_{k < n} X_k$$

with the product topology ([[def-product-topology]]) is compact. In particular a
binary product $X \times Y$ of compact spaces is compact, and the empty product,
a one-point space, is compact.

**No choice principle is used beyond [[lem-finite-choice]]**, which is a theorem
of ZF. That is what separates the finite case from the arbitrary one, where the
Axiom of Choice is genuinely spent.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $n$, a family $(X_k)_{k < n}$ of compact topological spaces, and the product $P_n := \prod_{k<n} X_k$ with the product topology and projections $\pi_k$.

[A1] An element of $\prod_{k<n} X_k$ is a function $x$ with domain $n$ and $x(k) \in X_k$ for every $k < n$; the von Neumann natural satisfies $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$ with $n \notin n$; and the empty product is a one-point space ([[def-product-topology]], [[def-natural-numbers]]).

[L1] The projections of a product are continuous, and a map $h$ into a product is continuous exactly when every component $\pi_i \circ h$ is continuous ([[thm-product-universal-property]], claims 1 and 2).

[L2] A composite of continuous maps is continuous ([[lem-continuity-is-local-and-pastes]], claim 1).

[L3] The identity map of a space is continuous, and so is every constant map, the preimage of a set under a constant map being $\varnothing$ or the whole space ([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b); [[def-topological-space]]).

[L4] A continuous image of a compact space is a compact subset of the target ([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]], claim 1); a continuous bijection with continuous inverse is a homeomorphism ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]], [[lem-homeomorphism-criteria]]).

[L5] Tube lemma: if $K \subseteq X$ is compact, $N \subseteq X \times Z$ is open and $K \times \{z_0\} \subseteq N$, then $K \times W \subseteq N$ for some open $W \ni z_0$ ([[lem-tube-lemma-for-a-compact-factor]]).

[L6] $A$ is a compact subset of a space $Z$ exactly when every family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $Z$ with $A \subseteq \bigcup \mathcal{U}$ has finitely many members whose union contains $A$, or else $A = \varnothing$ ([[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], claim 1).

[L7] A function with domain a natural number all of whose values are nonempty sets has a choice function, and this is a theorem of ZF ([[lem-finite-choice]]).

[L8] A space is compact exactly when every open cover of it has a finite subcover; a one-point space and the empty space are compact ([[def-compact-space]]).

[L9] If $0 \in S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and $\sigma(m) \in S$ whenever $m \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-induction-principle]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** induction.

1.1 At $n = 0$ the index set is empty, so $\prod_{k<0} X_k$ is a one-point space by [A1] and is compact by [L8]; this is the case $n = 0$ of the statement. [A1, L8, base]

1.2 Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and assume, as the induction hypothesis, that $\prod_{k<m} Y_k$ is compact for every family $(Y_k)_{k<m}$ of compact spaces. [ih]

1.3 For the binary case let $X$ and $Z$ be compact, let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open cover of $X \times Z$, and for $z \in Z$ let $j_z : X \to X \times Z$ be $j_z(x) := (x,z)$; its components are the identity of $X$ and the constant map with value $z$, so it is continuous by [L1] and [L3], and $X \times \{z\} = j_z[X]$ is therefore a compact subset of $X \times Z$ by [L4]. [L1, L3, L4, construct]

1.4 Put $\mathcal{W} := \{\, W \subseteq Z : W \text{ is open and } X \times W \subseteq \bigcup \mathcal{V} \text{ for some finite } \mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U} \,\}$, a family cut out by a property of $W$ and not by any selection. [construct]

1.5 For the splitting, let $p \in \mathbb{N}$, let $(X_k)_{k < \sigma(p)}$ be a family of spaces, and define $r : \prod_{k<\sigma(p)} X_k \to \big(\prod_{k<p} X_k\big) \times X_p$ by $r(x) := (x \restriction p,\ x(p))$ and $s$ in the opposite direction by $s(y,a) := y \cup \{(p,a)\}$; by [A1] these are mutually inverse bijections, since $\sigma(p) = p \cup \{p\}$ and $p \notin p$. [A1, construct]

2.1 $Z \subseteq \bigcup \mathcal{W}$: given $z \in Z$, the set $X \times \{z\}$ is compact by step 1.3 and lies in $\bigcup \mathcal{U}$, so [L6] supplies a finite $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ with $X \times \{z\} \subseteq N := \bigcup \mathcal{V}$, an open set, the case $X = \varnothing$ being covered by $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$; since $X$ is compact, [L5] gives an open $W \ni z$ with $X \times W \subseteq N$, and that $W$ lies in $\mathcal{W}$. [L5, L6, step 1.3, step 1.4]

2.2 $r$ is continuous: by [L1] it suffices that its two components are, and they are $x \mapsto x \restriction p$ and $\pi_p$; the second is a projection, and the first is continuous by [L1] applied again, its own components being $\pi_k$ for $k < p$. [L1, step 1.5]

2.3 $s$ is continuous: by [L1] it suffices that $\pi_k \circ s$ is continuous for every $k < \sigma(p)$; for $k < p$ that map is the $k$-th projection of $\prod_{k<p} X_k$ composed with the first projection of the binary product, a composite of continuous maps, and for $k = p$ it is the second projection of the binary product. [L1, L2, step 1.5]

3.1 If $Z = \varnothing$ then $X \times Z = \varnothing$ is compact by [L8]; otherwise $\mathcal{W}$ is an open cover of the compact $Z$ by step 2.1, so [L8] gives $q \in \mathbb{N}$ and $W_0, \dots, W_q \in \mathcal{W}$ with $Z = W_0 \cup \dots \cup W_q$. [L8, step 2.1]

3.2 So $r$ is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse $s$, hence a homeomorphism, and $\prod_{k<\sigma(p)} X_k$ is homeomorphic to $\big(\prod_{k<p} X_k\big) \times X_p$. [L4, step 1.5, step 2.2, step 2.3]

4.1 For each $j \le q$ the set $T_j$ of finite subfamilies $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ with $X \times W_j \subseteq \bigcup \mathcal{V}$ is nonempty because $W_j \in \mathcal{W}$, and $j \mapsto T_j$ is a function with domain the natural number $\sigma(q)$, so [L7] supplies $\mathcal{V}_0, \dots, \mathcal{V}_q$; their union $\mathcal{V}$ is a finite subfamily of $\mathcal{U}$, a union of finitely many listable families being listed by concatenation, and $X \times Z = (X \times W_0) \cup \dots \cup (X \times W_q) \subseteq \bigcup \mathcal{V}$. So every open cover of $X \times Z$ has a finite subcover and $X \times Z$ is compact. [L7, L8, step 3.1]

5.1 Now let $(X_k)_{k < \sigma(m)}$ be a family of compact spaces. By step 1.2 the product $\prod_{k<m} X_k$ is compact, and $X_m$ is compact, so step 4.1 makes $\big(\prod_{k<m} X_k\big) \times X_m$ compact; by step 3.2 with $p := m$ the product $\prod_{k<\sigma(m)} X_k$ is homeomorphic to it, and a continuous image of a compact space is compact by [L4], so $\prod_{k<\sigma(m)} X_k$ is compact. [L4, step 1.2, step 3.2, step 4.1]

6.1 The set of $n \in \mathbb{N}$ for which the statement holds contains $0$ by step 1.1 and contains $\sigma(m)$ whenever it contains $m$ by step 5.1, so by [L9] it is all of $\mathbb{N}$; the binary case is $n = 2$ and the empty product is $n = 0$. [L9, step 1.1, discharge-induction: step 5.1] ∎

## Remarks

**Where the tube lemma does the work.** Compactness of $X$ alone thins a cover on one slice $X \times \{z\}$; what is needed is a cover of a whole band around that slice, and producing the band is exactly [[lem-tube-lemma-for-a-compact-factor]]. Compactness of $Z$ then thins the family of bands. Both factors are used, and in different ways.

**Why the bands are collected rather than chosen.** The family $\mathcal{W}$ of step 1.4 consists of *every* open $W$ admitting some finite subfamily of $\mathcal{U}$ over $X \times W$; it is defined by a formula. Writing $W_z$ for each $z \in Z$ instead would select a band for every point of $Z$ at once, which for an arbitrary $Z$ is the Axiom of Choice. The only selection made is over the finite index set $\sigma(q)$ at step 4.1.

**The hypothesis "finitely many" is not removable by this argument.** The induction runs on $\mathbb{N}$ and gives nothing about an infinite index set; [[thm-tychonoff]], later on this page, handles that case and pays the Axiom of Choice for it.

## Definition

**The product set.** Let $I$ be a set and let $X_i$ be a set for each $i \in I$.
The **product** is

$$\prod_{i \in I} X_i \;:=\; \Big\{\, x : x \text{ is a function with domain } I \text{ and } x(i) \in X_i \text{ for every } i \in I \,\Big\},$$

and we write $x_i := x(i)$, the $i$-th **coordinate** of $x$. Two elements of the
product are equal exactly when they agree at every index, functions being equal
when they have the same domain and the same values. For $j \in I$ the $j$-th
**projection** is

$$\pi_j : \prod_{i \in I} X_i \to X_j, \qquad \pi_j(x) := x_j .$$

**Notation for a finite product.** For $I = n$ a natural number, which is the set
$\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ of its predecessors, an element of $\prod_{k<n} X_k$ is a
function on $n$ and we write it $(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$. In particular $I = 2$
gives the **binary product**, written $X \times Y$ for $\prod_{i<2} X_i$ with
$X_0 = X$ and $X_1 = Y$, whose elements are written $(u,v)$ for the function
$0 \mapsto u$, $1 \mapsto v$. This is the only meaning the symbol $X \times Y$
carries on this page.

**Two facts about when the product is nonempty, stated because they are used and
because they cost something.** If some $X_{i_0}$ is empty then the product is
empty, since no function can take a value in $X_{i_0}$. Conversely, suppose every
$X_i$ is nonempty.

- For $I = n$ a natural number, the product is nonempty, and this is a theorem of
  ZF: [[lem-finite-choice]] applied to the function $i \mapsto X_i$ on $n$
  supplies a choice function $g$ for the family of values, and
  $x(i) := g(X_i)$ defines a member of $\prod_{k<n} X_k$.
- For an arbitrary $I$ the assertion "$\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \varnothing$
  whenever every $X_i$ is nonempty" **is** the Axiom of Choice: it is the
  formulation recorded in [[def-axiom-of-choice]], and the choice function of
  [[def-choice-function]] is exactly a point of the product of a family by
  itself. Every use of it below is flagged at the step that spends it.

**The box topology.** Now let each $X_i$ carry a topology $\mathcal{T}_i$
([[def-topological-space]]). Put

$$\mathcal{R} \;:=\; \Big\{\, \prod_{i \in I} U_i \;:\; U_i \in \mathcal{T}_i \text{ for every } i \in I \,\Big\},$$

the family of **boxes**. $\mathcal{R}$ is a basis for a topology
([[thm-basis-criterion]]): it contains $\prod_i X_i$, so it covers the product,
and it is closed under binary intersections, since

$$\Big(\prod_i U_i\Big) \cap \Big(\prod_i V_i\Big) = \prod_i (U_i \cap V_i)$$

and each $U_i \cap V_i$ is open by (T3). The topology it generates is the **box
topology** $\mathcal{T}^{\square}$, and $\mathcal{R}$ is a basis for it
([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]).

**The product topology.** The **product topology** $\mathcal{T}^{\Pi}$ on
$\prod_i X_i$ is the initial topology of the family of projections
$(\pi_i)_{i \in I}$ ([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]): the topology generated
by the subbasis

$$\mathcal{G} \;:=\; \{\, \pi_i^{-1}[U] : i \in I,\ U \in \mathcal{T}_i \,\}, \qquad \pi_i^{-1}[U] = \prod_{j \in I} W_j \ \text{ with } W_i = U \text{ and } W_j = X_j \text{ for } j \ne i .$$

By [[thm-basis-criterion]] the finite intersections of members of $\mathcal{G}$
form a basis for $\mathcal{T}^{\Pi}$, and those finite intersections are exactly
the boxes with all but finitely many factors unrestricted:

$$\mathcal{R}^{\Pi} \;=\; \Big\{\, \prod_{i \in I} U_i \;:\; U_i \in \mathcal{T}_i \text{ for every } i, \text{ and } U_i = X_i \text{ for all but finitely many } i \,\Big\}.$$

Indeed the intersection of $\pi_{i_1}^{-1}[U_1], \dots, \pi_{i_n}^{-1}[U_n]$ is
the box whose factor at $i$ is the intersection of those $U_m$ with $i_m = i$ and
is $X_i$ when no $i_m$ equals $i$; and the intersection of no members is the
whole product, the box with every factor $X_i$. Conversely a box with
$U_i = X_i$ off a finite set is such an intersection. Members of
$\mathcal{R}^{\Pi}$ are called **basic product-open** sets, and members of
$\mathcal{R}$ **boxes**. So $\mathcal{R}^{\Pi} \subseteq \mathcal{R}$, with
equality when $I$ is a natural number.

**The empty product.** For $I = \varnothing$ there is exactly one function with
domain $\varnothing$, the empty function, so $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} X_i$ is a
one-point set. A one-point set carries exactly one topology, namely
$\{\varnothing, \{\varnothing\}\}$, since a topology must contain the empty set
and the whole set and there is nothing else to contain
([[def-topological-space]]); so the box topology and the product topology agree
there, and both equal the discrete topology and the indiscrete topology
([[def-standard-topologies]]), which coincide on a one-point set. There are no
projections to speak of, and the initial topology of the empty family is indeed
the indiscrete one ([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]).

**Convention.** Unless the box topology is named explicitly, $\prod_i X_i$ always
carries the product topology in this library. That is not a matter of taste: the
product topology is the one with the characteristic property of the next item,
and the box topology has no such property.

## Remarks

- **Where the two topologies actually differ.** The box topology is finer than
  the product topology by construction, since $\mathcal{R}^{\Pi} \subseteq
  \mathcal{R}$. They agree whenever $I$ is finite; and, assuming the Axiom of Choice, for a
  family of **nonempty** spaces they differ for infinite $I$ as soon as infinitely
  many factors have a nonempty proper open subset. Nonemptiness is not decoration: if one factor is
  empty then the product is empty and carries exactly one topology, so the two
  agree however the other factors are chosen. Both statements are proved two items
  below, with that hypothesis, and the failure is recorded on this page as a false
  statement.

- **The product set is a set of functions, and that is not a technicality.** The
  factors are indexed by an arbitrary set, so there is no "list" to write down;
  writing $x = (x_i)_{i \in I}$ is notation for the function $x$. The finite case
  recovers the familiar tuple, and the identification of $\prod_{k<n}\mathbb{R}$
  with the $\mathbb{R}^n$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] is literal, that item defining
  $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$.

- **The projections carry no hypothesis.** They are defined for every product,
  including the empty one and products with an empty factor; what does need a
  hypothesis is their *surjectivity*, which is the point at which choice enters
  and which is stated separately in the next item.

## Statement

Every continuous map from a nonempty compact Hausdorff space to a uniform space is uniformly continuous.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A continuous map $f:X\to Y$ with $X$ nonempty compact Hausdorff and $Y$ uniform.

[L1] A compact Hausdorff space has one compatible uniformity ([[thm-compact-hausdorff-space-has-a-unique-compatible-uniformity]]).

[L2] Continuity means that every neighbourhood of $f(x)$ contains the image of some neighbourhood of $x$, while uniform continuity is the entourage condition ([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[def-uniformly-continuous-map]]).

[L3] Every entourage ball is a neighbourhood in the induced topology ([[thm-uniformity-induces-a-topology]]). Every open cover of a nonempty compact Hausdorff space is uniform ([[thm-compact-hausdorff-open-cover-uniformity]]), and every uniform cover has an entourage-ball cover refining it ([[lem-entourage-and-uniform-cover-dictionary]]); every target entourage has a symmetric square root ([[lem-symmetric-entourages-form-a-base]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $V$ be a target entourage and choose a symmetric $W$ with $W^{-1}\circ W=W^{\circ2}\subseteq V$. For each $x\in X$, let $O_x$ be the union of all open sets $O$ such that $x\in O$ and $f[O]\subseteq W[f(x)]$. Continuity makes this family nonempty, and its union is an open neighbourhood of $x$ satisfying $f[O_x]\subseteq W[f(x)]$. [L2, L3, construct]

2.1 The open cover $(O_x)_{x\in X}$ is uniform by [L3]. Hence there is a source entourage $E$ whose ball cover refines it: for each $a\in X$, some $O_x$ contains $E[a]$. [step 1.1, L1, L3]

3.1 If $(a,b)\in E$, then $a,b\in E[a]\subseteq O_x$ for some $x$. Thus $f(a),f(b)\in W[f(x)]$, so $(f(a),f(b))\in W^{-1}\circ W\subseteq V$. This is uniform continuity. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L2] ∎

## Statement

For $d\ge2$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^d$ be measurable, and let $\mu_r$ and $\mu_b$ be probability measures on them. For positive integers $m_r,m_b$, let the residual samples $x_1^r,\ldots,x_{m_r}^r$ and boundary samples $x_1^b,\ldots,x_{m_b}^b$ form $\varepsilon_r$- and $\varepsilon_b$-nets of $U$ and $\Gamma$ in Euclidean distance. Assume that for every center $x\in U$ and $y\in\Gamma$,
$$\mu_r(\overline B_{\varepsilon_r}(x)\cap U)\le C_r\varepsilon_r^d,\qquad \mu_b(\overline B_{\varepsilon_b}(y)\cap\Gamma)\le C_b\varepsilon_b^{d-1}.$$
Suppose $[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}$, $[B[h]]_{\alpha;\Gamma}$, $[f]_{\alpha;U}$, and $[g]_{\alpha;\Gamma}$ are finite, where $[v]_{\alpha;E}=\sup_{x\ne y\in E}|v(x)-v(y)|/|x-y|^\alpha$. Let $\lambda_r,\lambda_b>0$, and use the population and empirical weighted-square PINN losses
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)=\lambda_r\int_U|L[h]-f|^2\,d\mu_r+\lambda_b\int_\Gamma|B[h]-g|^2\,d\mu_b,$$
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda_r}{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}|L[h](x_i^r)-f(x_i^r)|^2+\frac{\lambda_b}{m_b}\sum_{j=1}^{m_b}|B[h](x_j^b)-g(x_j^b)|^2.$$
Define
$$C_m=3\max\{C_rm_r\varepsilon_r^d,\ C_bm_b\varepsilon_b^{d-1}\},\quad \lambda^R_{r,m}=\frac{3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}}{C_m},\quad \lambda^R_{b,m}=\frac{3\lambda_b\varepsilon_b^{2\alpha}}{C_m}.$$
Then
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)\le C_m\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)+C_m\left(\lambda^R_{r,m}[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^2+\lambda^R_{b,m}[B[h]]_{\alpha;\Gamma}^2\right)+3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}[f]_{\alpha;U}^2+3\lambda_b\varepsilon_b^{2\alpha}[g]_{\alpha;\Gamma}^2.$$

For $d=1$, assume $\mu_r$ is a probability measure on measurable $U\subset\mathbb R$, and $\Gamma$ is a nonempty finite measurable set with probability measure $\mu_b$. Every point of $\Gamma$ is available deterministically. For a positive integer $m_r$, let $x_1^r,\ldots,x_{m_r}^r$ form an $\varepsilon_r$-net of $U$, and assume $\mu_r(\overline B_{\varepsilon_r}(x)\cap U)\le C_r\varepsilon_r$ for every center $x\in U$. Suppose the same four Hölder seminorms are finite. Use the exact weighted boundary loss
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN},b}(h;\lambda_b)=\lambda_b\int_\Gamma|B[h]-g|^2\,d\mu_b=\lambda_b\sum_{y\in\Gamma}\mu_b(\{y\})|B[h](y)-g(y)|^2$$
and the empirical loss $\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda_r}{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}|L[h](x_i^r)-f(x_i^r)|^2+\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN},b}(h;\lambda_b)$. Set
$$C_m=3C_rm_r\varepsilon_r,\qquad \lambda^R_{r,m}=\frac{3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}}{C_m},\qquad \lambda^R_{b,m}=0.$$
Then
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)\le C_m\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)+C_m\lambda^R_{r,m}[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^2+3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}[f]_{\alpha;U}^2.$$
There is no random boundary term or boundary-data error term in this branch because the full boundary contribution is evaluated exactly.

## Statement references
[Shin et al., Appendix B, Lemmas B.1–B.2: deterministic fill-distance inequality](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

[Shin et al., Appendix B, proof of Lemma B.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The trial function, residual and boundary operators, sample sets, fill distances, measures, and positive loss weights in the Statement.

[F1] The population and empirical PINN losses use the weighted-square conventions in the local definition ([[def-physics-informed-neural-network-loss]]).

[F2] For $d\ge2$, the residual cells have mass at most $C_r\varepsilon_r^d$ and the boundary cells have mass at most $C_b\varepsilon_b^{d-1}$ by the upper ball-mass assumptions. For $d=1$, each residual cell has mass at most $C_r\varepsilon_r$ by the residual upper ball-mass assumption in the Statement.

[F3] The Hölder seminorm convention is $|v(x)-v(y)|\le[v]_{\alpha;E}|x-y|^\alpha$ ([[def-physics-informed-neural-network-loss]]).

[F4] In the one-dimensional branch, the exact full-boundary empirical contribution equals the population boundary integral, and a finite union of sample-centered $\varepsilon_r$-balls covers $U$ ([[def-physics-informed-neural-network-loss]], [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]).

## Proof

**Proof strategy:** integrate local collocation bounds over nearest-sample cells.

1.1 Order the finite residual sample set and assign each point of $U$ to a nearest residual sample, breaking ties by the least index. This produces a measurable finite Voronoi partition $V_1,\ldots,V_{m_r}$; each cell lies in the radius-$\varepsilon_r$ ball about its assigned sample. For $d\ge2$, also assign each point of $\Gamma$ to a nearest boundary sample to obtain cells $W_j$; for $d=1$, use every point of the finite boundary deterministically and make no boundary partition. [given, choose]

1.2 By [F2], $\mu_r(V_i)\le C_r\varepsilon_r^d$ in the $d\ge2$ branch and $\mu_r(V_i)\le C_r\varepsilon_r$ in the $d=1$ branch. If $x\in V_i$, the three-term square inequality and [F3] give $$|L[h](x)-f(x)|^2\le3|L[h](x_i^r)-f(x_i^r)|^2+3\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^2+3\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}[f]_{\alpha;U}^2.$$ For $d\ge2$, each boundary cell satisfies $\mu_b(W_j)\le C_b\varepsilon_b^{d-1}$, and its analogous local square bound holds. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Integrate the residual inequality over the cells. The collocation terms contribute at most $3C_rm_r\varepsilon_r^d\lambda_r m_r^{-1}\sum_i|L[h](x_i^r)-f(x_i^r)|^2$ for $d\ge2$, and $3C_rm_r\varepsilon_r\lambda_r m_r^{-1}\sum_i|L[h](x_i^r)-f(x_i^r)|^2$ for $d=1$. The seminorm and data terms contribute $3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}([L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^2+[f]_{\alpha;U}^2)$ because $\mu_r(U)=1$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, algebra]

2.2 For $d\ge2$, integrating the boundary inequality gives the estimate with $3C_bm_b\varepsilon_b^{d-1}$ multiplying the empirical boundary term and $3\lambda_b\varepsilon_b^{2\alpha}([B[h]]_{\alpha;\Gamma}^2+[g]_{\alpha;\Gamma}^2)$ for the remaining terms. For $d=1$, the weighted boundary term in the population loss is exactly $\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN},b}(h;\lambda_b)$ from [F4]. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F4, algebra]

3.1 For $d\ge2$, by the definition of $C_m$, the empirical residual and boundary coefficients in steps 2.1–2.2 are at most $C_m$. The seminorm coefficients equal $C_m\lambda^R_{r,m}$ and $C_m\lambda^R_{b,m}$ by definition, while the data terms already have their displayed coefficients. Adding the estimates yields the result. For $d=1$, the net and upper ball-mass bound imply $1=\mu_r(U)\le\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}\mu_r(\overline B_{\varepsilon_r}(x_i^r)\cap U)\le m_rC_r\varepsilon_r$, so $C_m\ge3$. Thus $C_m$ dominates the exact boundary term, the residual empirical coefficient from step 2.1 equals $C_m$, and $C_m\lambda^R_{r,m}=3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}$. Combining these bounds with the residual data term proves the one-dimensional inequality. [step 2.1, step 2.2, F4, algebra] ∎
