## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice; $n\ge2$; a bounded extension domain $\Omega$; $k\ge1$; $1\le p<\infty$; a class $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

[F1] Lower-order derivatives: for every multi-index $\beta$ with $|\beta|\le k$, $D^\beta u\in W^{k-|\beta|,p}(\Omega)$ and $\|D^\beta u\|_{W^{k-|\beta|,p}}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}}$ ([[lem-weak-partial-derivatives-lower-sobolev-order]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

[F2] For $1\le q<n$, the Sobolev conjugate $q^*=nq/(n-q)$ is finite and satisfies $1/q^*=1/q-1/n$; iterating this relation gives $p_k^*=np/(n-kp)$ when $kp<n$ ([[def-sobolev-conjugate-exponent]]).

[F3] The local Morrey estimate: for $n<q<\infty$, $w\in W^{1,q}$ has a continuous representative and $[w]_{C^{0,1-n/q}(B(a,r))}\le C(n,q)\|Dw\|_{L^q(B(a,2r))}$ when the doubled ball is compactly contained in its domain ([[thm-morrey-inequality-for-p-greater-than-n]], [[def-local-holder-and-c-two-alpha-norms-on-euclidean-balls]]).

[F4] Holder's inequality on a bounded measurable set $B$ compares $L^r(B)$ and $L^s(B)$ for $1\le r\le s<\infty$ ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]).

[F5] The extension operator and the whole-space results are used through the extension domain hypothesis ([[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]]); the Axiom of Choice is inherited from the suppliers.

[F6] Because $\Omega$ is bounded, $\overline\Omega$ is compact. Choose a ball $B$ containing $\overline\Omega$, a smooth cutoff $\eta\in C_c^\infty(B)$ equal to $1$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, and a bounded extension operator $E:W^{k,p}(\Omega)\to W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)$. Then $v:=\eta Eu$ is compactly supported in $B$, belongs to $W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)$, satisfies $v=u$ on $\Omega$, and $\|v\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; its weak derivatives restrict to those of $u$ on $\Omega$ ([[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]], [[lem-euclidean-bump-for-a-compact-set-inside-an-open-set]], [[lem-weak-leibniz-rule-with-a-smooth-factor]]).

[F7] The whole-space first-order inequality holds for $1<q<n$ ([[thm-gagliardo-nirenberg-sobolev-inequality]]). At $q=1$ it extends to $W^{1,1}$ from [[thm-gagliardo-nirenberg-sobolev-inequality-for-p-one]] using [[cor-compactly-supported-smooth-functions-are-dense-in-wkp-of-rn]]: apply the smooth estimate to differences; use [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]], [[thm-complex-lp-completeness-and-almost-everywhere-subsequences]] for the $L^{n/(n-1)}$ limit and successive almost-everywhere subsequences in that space and $L^1$ to identify it with the original class.

[F8] For $q>n$, apply the local Morrey estimate [F3] on a ball containing the compact support of $v$; it bounds the Holder seminorm of a representative by $C\|Dv\|_{L^q}$; its supremum on that ball is bounded by the average, at most $|B|^{-1/q}\|v\|_{L^q(B)}$, plus the oscillation bound. Hence it gives a $C^{0,1-n/q}$ representative with norm bounded by $C\|v\|_{W^{1,q}(\mathbb R^n)}$, in particular on $\overline\Omega$ ([[thm-morrey-inequality-for-p-greater-than-n]], [[def-local-holder-and-c-two-alpha-norms-on-euclidean-balls]]).

[F9] Continuous weak first derivatives are classical derivatives. On an inner ball, convolution of a continuous function converges uniformly on smaller compact balls, because $|(\rho_\varepsilon*f)(x)-f(x)|\le\sup_{|h|\le\varepsilon}|f(x-h)-f(x)|$ and continuity on the compact neighbourhood is uniform. The same applies to its continuous weak derivatives; [[lem-mollification-commutes-with-weak-derivatives-in-the-interior]] identifies their convolutions with derivatives of the smooth mollification. Pass to the limit in the coordinate segment identity from [[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]] to obtain $f(x+te_i)-f(x)=\int_0^t g_i(x+se_i)ds$. Differentiating this identity gives $\partial_i f=g_i$; repeat for higher orders. Weak representatives are unique ([[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]]).

## Proof

1.1 Whole-space iteration. Let $B$ be the fixed bounded support ball from [F6]. Suppose $1\le q_0<n$ and $w\in W^{\ell,q_0}(\mathbb R^n)$ is supported in $B$, with $\ell\ge1$, and put $1/q_1=1/q_0-1/n$, so $q_1=q_0^*$. For every $|\beta|\le\ell-1$, [F1] gives $D^\beta w\in W^{1,q_0}(\mathbb R^n)$ with norm bounded by $C\|w\|_{W^{\ell,q_0}}$. Applying the whole-space inequality [F7] to each derivative gives $D^\beta w\in L^{q_1}$; summing the finitely many norms shows $w\in W^{\ell-1,q_1}(\mathbb R^n)$ with controlled norm. Compact support is retained, and [F2] gives the invariant $\ell-n/q_0=(\ell-1)-n/q_1$. The $q_0=1$ case uses the p=1 inequality and its density passage in [F7]. [F1, F2, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

1.2 Assertion (3): global Holder representatives. Assume $kp>n$ and choose $m\ge0$, $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha\le k-\frac np$; for the endpoint equality, require $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ and $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$. Fix $\beta$ with $|\beta|\le m$ and put $\ell:=k-|\beta|$ and $t:=n/p$, so $\ell-t\ge\alpha$. By [F1] and [F6], $w:=D^\beta v$ is compactly supported in $W^{\ell,p}(\mathbb R^n)$ with norm at most $C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$. Starting from $(\ell,p)$, whenever the current exponent $q<n$ and current order $r\ge2$, apply [F7] to every derivative of $w$ of order at most $r-1$; this gives $w\in W^{r-1,q^*}$, where $1/q^*=1/q-1/n$, with controlled norm. The invariant $r-n/q=\ell-n/p\ge\alpha>0$ shows the process cannot stop with order $1$ and exponent below $n$. If it reaches $q>n$, write the remaining order as $r$. When $r=1$, take $q'=q$; Morrey gives exponent $1-n/q=\ell-n/p\ge\alpha$. When $r\ge2$, the first derivatives of $w$ lie in $W^{1,q}$; [F8] bounds them and $w$ on the fixed compact support, so $w\in W^{1,q'}(\mathbb R^n)$ for every finite $q'$, and choose $q'>n$ with $1-n/q'>\alpha$. If the iteration reaches $q=n$, then the invariant gives $r-n/q=r-1\ge\alpha>0$, hence $r\ge2$. Thus $w$ and its first derivatives are compactly supported in $W^{1,n}$; on their common bounded support, Holder puts them in $W^{1,s}$ for any $1<s<n$ sufficiently close to $n$, and [F7] then puts them in $L^{s^*}$ for $s^*=ns/(n-s)$, which can be chosen arbitrarily large. Hence again $w\in W^{1,q'}$ for some $q'>n$ with $1-n/q'>\alpha$. In every case $w\in W^{1,q'}$ for an exponent $q'>n$ with $1-n/q'\ge\alpha$, and its norm is bounded by $C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}}$. [F1, F3, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

2.1 Assertion (1). Assume $kp<n$ and take the compactly supported extension $v$ from [F6]. Iterating step 1.1 for $j=1,\dots,k-1$ gives $v\in W^{1,p_{k-1}}(\mathbb R^n)$ with $1/p_j=1/p-j/n$; all exponents are finite and $p_j<n$ because $(j+1)p<n$ for $j\le k-1$. One more application of [F7] gives $v\in L^{p_k^*}(\mathbb R^n)$, where $1/p_k^*=1/p-k/n$ by [F2]. For every $1\le q\le p_k^*$, Holder [F4] on the fixed support ball $B$ gives $\|v\|_{L^q(\mathbb R^n)}\le C(B,p,q)\|v\|_{L^{p_k^*}(\mathbb R^n)}$; the whole-space endpoint estimate and [F6] bound this by $C(n,k,p,q,\Omega)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$. Since $v=u$ on $\Omega$, restriction proves (1). [F2, F4, F6, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Assertion (2). Assume $kp=n$, and take $v$ from [F6]. Iterating step 1.1 through $k-1$ reductions gives $v\in W^{1,n}(\mathbb R^n)$ with support in $B$. If $1\le q\le n$, Holder [F4] on $B$ bounds $\|v\|_{L^q}$ by $C(B,q)\|v\|_{L^n}$. If $q>n$, set $s=nq/(n+q)$, so $1<s<n$ and $s^*=q$; compact support and Holder give $v\in W^{1,s}(\mathbb R^n)$ with $\|v\|_{W^{1,s}}\le C(B,s)\|v\|_{W^{1,n}}$, and [F7] gives $\|v\|_{L^q}\le C(n,s)\|v\|_{W^{1,s}}$. In both cases the norm is bounded by $C(n,k,q,\Omega)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ using [F6]; restriction to $\Omega$ proves (2), with no $L^\infty$ endpoint asserted. [F4, F6, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F3] and [F8] with this exponent $q'$ to $w$ on a ball containing $\overline\Omega$. This gives a representative $g_\beta\in C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|g_\beta\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$, uniformly over the finitely many $|\beta|\le m$. By [F9], whenever $|\beta|<m$, the classical derivatives of $g_\beta$ are the continuous representatives $g_{\beta+e_i}$, since these represent the weak derivatives of $D^\beta v$ and weak derivatives are unique. Therefore $g_0\in C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$, represents $u$, and its $C^{m,\alpha}$ norm is bounded by the sum of the finitely many bounds just obtained. This proves (3) for the strict range and also the stated fractional-endpoint case: there $\ell-t=\alpha$ for $|\beta|=m$, and the final Morrey exponent is exactly $\alpha$, which is allowed by [F8]. [F3, F8, F9, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

The higher-order embedding is the iteration of the first-order Sobolev inequalities motivated by Kinnunen (Theorem 3.23 and the local higher-order iteration of Remark 3.41) and Teschl (Theorem 9.22), followed by Morrey's estimate. The compactly supported whole-space extension reduces the boundary claim to one fixed ball containing the domain closure; it is essential here because the local Morrey statement alone only controls balls compactly contained in the open set. The finite iteration stops at a supercritical exponent, or at the critical exponent with at least two derivatives remaining, and supplies the global closure-wide Holder norm claimed above.

## Statement

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and the Axiom of Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]).** Let $K$ be a nonempty compact metric space and $\mathcal F\subseteq C(K,\mathbb R)$. Its closure in the supremum metric is compact if and only if $\mathcal F$ is equicontinuous and pointwise bounded.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, the Axiom of Dependent Choice, and a family $\mathcal F\subseteq C(K,\mathbb R)$.

[L1] Every open cover of the compact metric space $K$ has a finite subcover ([[def-metric-compactness]]).

[L2] $C(K,\mathbb R)$ is complete in the supremum metric ([[thm-c-k-complete-in-the-sup-metric]]).

[L3] A subspace of a complete metric space is complete exactly when it is closed; assuming Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, in a metric space compactness is equivalent to completeness together with total boundedness ([[thm-complete-subspace-iff-closed]], [[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]]).

[L4] Equicontinuity and pointwise boundedness are as defined in [[def-equicontinuity-and-boundedness-in-ck]].

[L5] A continuous function on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous ([[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $\mathcal F=\varnothing$, its closure is empty and compact, while both family properties hold vacuously. Hence assume $\mathcal F\ne\varnothing$. Suppose first that $\mathcal F$ is equicontinuous and pointwise bounded, and fix $\varepsilon>0$. Let $\mathcal U$ contain every ball $B(a,r)$ with $a\in K$, $r>0$, and $|f(x)-f(a)|<\varepsilon/3$ for all $f\in\mathcal F$ whenever $d(x,a)<2r$. Equicontinuity makes $\mathcal U$ an open cover without selecting a radius for every $a$. By [L1] take a finite subcover $B(a_i,r_i)$, $i=1,\ldots,N$. Pointwise boundedness supplies finite bounds $M_i$ for the values $|f(a_i)|$. Partition the bounded box $\prod_{i=1}^N[-M_i,M_i]$ into finitely many boxes of coordinate diameter less than $\varepsilon/3$, and choose one member of $\mathcal F$ from each box met by an evaluation vector $(f(a_i))_i$. For any $f\in\mathcal F$, a chosen $g$ in the same box satisfies $|f(a_i)-g(a_i)|<\varepsilon/3$ for all $i$; if $x\in B(a_i,r_i)$, the two equicontinuity bounds give $|f(x)-g(x)|<\varepsilon$. Thus these finitely many representatives form an $\varepsilon$-net. The closure is totally bounded as well, by using an $\varepsilon/2$-net for $\mathcal F$ and approximating each point of its closure by a member of $\mathcal F$. [L1, L4, algebra]

1.2 Conversely suppose the closure is compact. For $\varepsilon>0$, [L3] supplies a finite $\varepsilon/3$-net $g_1,\ldots,g_N$ in the closure. By [L5], a common positive radius makes every $g_i$ vary by less than $\varepsilon/3$. [L3, L5]

2.1 The closure of $\mathcal F$ is closed in the complete space of [L2], hence complete by [L3]. It is totally bounded by step 1.1, so [L3] makes it compact. [L2, L3, step 1.1]

2.2 For $f\in\mathcal F$, choose $g_i$ within $\varepsilon/3$ in supremum distance. The two uniform-distance bounds and step 1.2 give $|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $d(x,y)$ is below the common radius. [step 1.2, algebra]

2.3 The same finite net bounds $|f(a)|$ at each fixed $a\in K$, so $\mathcal F$ is pointwise bounded. [step 1.2, L4, algebra]

3.1 Step 2.1 proves the forward implication; steps 2.2 and 2.3 give equicontinuity and pointwise boundedness in the converse. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, L4] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open with an exterior tangent ball at every boundary point, and let $T>0$. Consider the intended divergence operator
$$L_tu=\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_ju)+\sum_iD_i(b_iu)+\sum_i c_iD_iu+du.$$
Assume $a=a^T\ge\lambda_0I$, $\lambda_0>0$, and $a,b,c,d$ bounded; the spatial derivatives of $a,b$ agree with distributional derivatives locally, and the expansion
$$\beta_j=\sum_iD_ia_{ij}+b_j+c_j,\qquad q=\sum_iD_ib_i+d$$
is locally valid with bounded $a,\beta,q$, locally parabolic $\alpha$-Hölder up to the final face, $0<\alpha<1$, and $q\le0$. Let $r$ be bounded and locally parabolic $\alpha$-Hölder up to that face. If $e$ is locally classical, bounded, continuous on the closed cylinder, zero on the initial and lateral faces, and satisfies $-e_t+L_te=r$, then
$$e\in L^2(0,T;H^1_0(U)),\qquad e_t\in L^2(0,T;H^{-1}(U)),\qquad e(0)=0\text{ in }L^2(U).$$
It is the unique zero-initial variational solution of that equation, and for a finite $C_E$ depending only on $T,\lambda_0$ and the divergence coefficient bounds,
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|e(t)\|_2^2+\int_0^T\|De(t)\|_2^2dt\le C_E\|r\|_{L^2(U\times(0,T))}^2.$$
Consequently a sequence of such errors with $\|e_m\|_\infty\to0$ and $\|r_m\|_\infty\to0$ converges strongly to zero in $L^2(0,T;H^1(U))$. No closed-cylinder derivative regularity is assumed.

## Statement references

[Shin et al., Appendices F–G: parabolic consistency and energy estimates](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The choice assumptions, domain, coefficients, distributionally compatible expansion, source and classical zero-data error in the Statement.

[A1] Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice are retained from the approximation, truncation and Sobolev suppliers ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] The bounded-open-set Sobolev triple is separable; $H^1_0(U)$ is the $H^1$-closure of compactly supported smooth functions ([[lem-shin-bounded-open-set-hilbert-evolution-triple]], [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

[F2] Smooth weak approximants on exhausting polyhedral domains have uniform compact-interior classical estimates and converge to the unique bounded classical solution with the prescribed continuous data; compatible divergence-coefficient convolutions are permitted ([[lem-shin-parabolic-classical-approximation-and-boundary-attainment]]).

[F3] Evolution-space solutions have continuous $L^2$ traces and satisfy the time energy-pairing identity ([[lem-parabolic-energy-pairing-and-trace]]).

[F4] A bounded sequence in a separable Hilbert space has a weakly convergent subsequence, and the corresponding Bochner spaces are separable Hilbert spaces ([[lem-parabolic-weak-compactness-separable-bochner-hilbert]]).

[F5] Every $L^1$ approximate identity converges strongly to the identity in finite $L^p$, in particular $p=2$; the kernel may be anisotropic provided its mass, uniformly bounded $L^1$ norm and shrinking-tail conditions hold ([[thm-l-one-approximate-identities-converge-in-l-p]]).

## Proof

1.1 Use the domains $U_n$ and divergence-compatible smooth convolution approximants from [F2], with zero initial and lateral data and source $r_n$. Their spatial mollifier support stays inside $U$ at every point of $U_n$; their temporal mollifier is supported at positive past lags, sampling $t-s$ with $s>0$. Thus $a_n$ retains ellipticity and its bound, $b_n,c_n,d_n$ retain their separate bounds, and the expanded $\beta_n,q_n$ are the convolutions of the bounded original expanded coefficients, retaining their bounds and $q_n\le0$. No endpoint limit of the original $b,c,d$ at $T$ is used. Each fixed smooth approximant may be extended locally past $T$ for its construction; compactness is used only at times below $T$. The resulting weak solutions $e_n$ are smooth in the interior, uniformly bounded, and have a locally classical subsequential limit with zero continuous initial/lateral data at every time below $T$ by [F2]. Classical comparison on cylinders ending below $T$ identifies the limit with $e$. [A1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 Test the weak equation $e_{n,t}-L_ne_n=-r_n$ with $e_n$. The divergence terms have no boundary contribution because $e_n\in H^1_0(U_n)$ in time-integrated sense. In particular the lower-order spatial form is $$\int_{U_n}a_nDe_n\cdot De_n+\int_{U_n}(b_n-c_n)\cdot De_n\,e_n-\int_{U_n}d_ne_n^2.$$ The cross term is $b_n-c_n$, since the $b$ term is integrated by parts and the $c$ term is not. Write $B=\|b\|_\infty+\|c\|_\infty$ and $D=\|d\|_\infty$. With $y_n=\|e_n\|_2^2$, [F3], ellipticity and Young's inequality give $$\frac12y_n'+\frac{\lambda_0}{2}\|De_n\|_2^2\le\left(\frac{B^2}{2\lambda_0}+D+\frac12\right)y_n+\frac12\|r_n\|_2^2.$$ The constants are uniform in $n$; derivatives of the smoothed coefficients do not occur. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Put $C_0=B^2/\lambda_0+2D+1$. The previous inequality gives $y_n'+\lambda_0\|De_n\|_2^2\le C_0y_n+\|r_n\|_2^2$. Multiply by $e^{-C_0t}$ and integrate, using $y_n(0)=0$. Then $\sup_ty_n\le e^{C_0T}\|r_n\|_{L^2}^2$. Integrating the same differential inequality without the factor bounds $\lambda_0\int\|De_n\|_2^2$ by $C_0T\sup y_n+\|r_n\|_{L^2}^2$. The boundedness of $r$ and the finite cylinder give a uniform right side. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Extend each $e_n$ by zero from $U_n$ to $U$. For almost every time this lies in $H^1_0(U)$: extend its compactly supported smooth $H^1(U_n)$ approximants by zero, which preserves their norms, and use the closure definition in [F1]. The bounds in step 3.1 therefore give a bounded sequence in $L^2(0,T;H^1_0(U))$. Apply [F4] and pass to a weakly convergent subsequence. The local uniform convergence from step 1.1 identifies this weak limit with $e$ almost everywhere, by testing on compact interior cylinders. Such cylinders exhaust $U\times(0,T)$; a locally zero $L^2$ function is zero almost everywhere on their union. Hence $e\in L^2(0,T;H^1_0(U))$. [A1, F1, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Fix a compact positive-time cylinder $K\Subset U\times(0,T)$ and a smooth spacetime cutoff $\chi$ equal to one near $K$. Extend each of $\chi b,\chi c,\chi d$ by zero to $\mathbb R^{d+1}$; these bounded compactly supported functions belong to $L^2$. The nonnegative product convolution kernels used in step 1.1 have mass one, $L^1$ norm one, and support shrinking to zero in both space and time (with positive past time lag). Thus they satisfy the approximate-identity conditions, although the spatial and temporal scales differ. Apply [F5] with $p=2$ to these extensions. For large $n$ their convolutions agree on $K$ with $b_n,c_n,d_n$, respectively, so $b_n\to b$, $c_n\to c$ and $d_n\to d$ strongly in $L^2(K)$, with their common uniform supremum bounds. Only $a_n,\beta_n,q_n,r_n$ are asserted to converge uniformly on such compact cylinders, by their local Hölder regularity. For a smooth test $\phi$ supported in $K$, the $a_nDe_n\cdot D\phi$ term passes by uniform coefficient convergence and weak $L^2$ gradient convergence. In the term $c_n\cdot De_n\,\phi$, the test vector $c_n\phi$ converges strongly in $L^2(K)$, so its pairing with the bounded weakly convergent gradients tends to $\int c\cdot De\,\phi$. In the $b_n e_n\cdot D\phi$ and $d_ne_n\phi$ terms, strong local coefficient convergence and local uniform convergence of $e_n$ imply strong $L^2$ convergence of the products. The source and time-test terms pass by local uniform convergence. These arguments prove the limiting weak identity on every compact positive-time cylinder without extra spatial $C^1$ assumptions on $b,c,d$. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 For a smooth spacetime test with compact spatial support in $U$ but not necessarily vanishing at initial time, first perform the passage above on $[\delta,T]$, taking its support strictly below $T$ when necessary. The common bounded coefficient and source norms, supremum bounds and energy bounds control the omitted interval $(0,\delta)$ uniformly: terms linear in gradients are at most a fixed constant times $\sqrt\delta\|De_n\|_{L^2}$ by Cauchy–Schwarz, and the zeroth-order, source and time-test terms are at most a constant times $\delta$. The same bounds hold for the limit by step 4.1. Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ therefore gives the identity with zero initial boundary term, inherited from the approximants. Density of spatial compact-smooth functions in $H^1_0(U)$ extends the positive-time identity to all variational tests, since the divergence coefficients are bounded and the limit has the membership established in step 4.1. It follows that $e_t=L_te-r\in L^2(0,T;H^{-1}(U))$. [F1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 By [F3], this evolution-space function has a continuous $L^2$ trace. Its integration-by-parts identity compared with the weak identity in step 6.1, for tests $\eta(t)\phi(x)$ with $\eta(0)\ne0$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(U)$, gives $(e(0),\phi)_{L^2}=0$. Density in $L^2(U)$ gives $e(0)=0$. Thus $e$ is a zero-initial variational solution as claimed. If two such weak solutions exist, their difference has zero source and zero initial value. The same test and integrating-factor argument as steps 2.1–3.1 on $U$ gives zero $L^2$ norm at every time, proving weak uniqueness. [F1, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 Apply [F3] to the now identified weak solution $e$, repeating step 2.1 on $U$ with its actual source $r$. The integrating-factor and integrated gradient arguments in step 3.1 yield the stated estimate with, for example, $C_E=e^{C_0T}+\lambda_0^{-1}(C_0Te^{C_0T}+1)$. The exact value is immaterial, but its dependence is only on the declared quantities, not on boundary derivatives of $e$. [F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 7.1, algebra]

9.1 For the final convergence assertion, $\|r_m\|_{L^2}^2\le T|U|\|r_m\|_\infty^2\to0$. The estimate in step 8.1 gives $\int\|De_m\|_2^2\to0$, and either that estimate or $\int\|e_m\|_2^2\le T|U|\|e_m\|_\infty^2$ gives the zeroth-order term. Their sum is the squared $L^2(0,T;H^1(U))$ norm. This proves strong convergence and completes the result. [step 8.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The expansion assumption is deliberately distributional as well as pointwise. Local $C^1$ spatial coefficients imply it. The source's word “differentiable” should not be used to conceal an unproved weak integration-by-parts identity for pathological pointwise derivatives. This helper imposes no extra boundary smoothness and no $C^{2,1}$ regularity on the closed cylinder.

The intended operator has a separately indexed $\sum_iD_i(b_iu)$ term. The source's printed $\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_ju+b_iu)$ repeats that term $d$ times and is incompatible with its own expanded drift and potential; it is not the operator used in this helper.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Every bounded sequence in a separable real Hilbert
space $X$ has a weakly convergent subsequence. If $V$ is a separable real
Hilbert space, then $L^2(0,T;V)$ and $L^2(0,T;V^*)$ are separable real Hilbert
spaces, their product is a separable Hilbert space, and the graph of the weak
time-derivative operator is closed there. Consequently $W(0,T;V)$ is a closed
Hilbert subspace of that product and every bounded sequence in $W(0,T;V)$ has
a weakly convergent subsequence.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A separable real Hilbert space $X$ and a sequence $(x_n)$ with $\sup_n\|x_n\|_X\le C<\infty$.

[F1] $L^2(0,T;X)$ consists of strongly measurable equivalence classes with the square-integral norm, and the weak time derivative is the scalar test identity stated for the parabolic energy space ([[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]]).

[F2] Riesz representation identifies the continuous dual of a real Hilbert space isometrically with that space; hence $V^*$ is separable when $V$ is separable ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]).

[F3] Rational box-step functions are countable and dense in scalar $L^2(\mathbb R)$ under Countable Choice; restricting them to $(0,T)$ gives a countable dense subset of $L^2(0,T)$ ([[thm-rational-box-step-functions-form-a-countable-dense-subset-of-l-p-of-rn]]).

[F4] Holder, Minkowski, monotone convergence and dominated convergence apply to the scalar integrals used below ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]], [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[F5] A countable union of measurable null sets is null ([[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]).

[F6] Measures of increasing sets converge to the measure of their union ([[thm-continuity-from-below-for-measures]]).

[F7] Every closed subspace of a Hilbert space and its orthogonal complement decompose the whole space ([[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]).

[F8] A Hilbert space is complete in its induced norm ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

[A1] Countable Choice supplies representatives for countably many $L^2$ classes and the assumptions of [F2], [F3] and [F7]; the coordinate extraction below is deterministic ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F9] Every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence ([[thm-bolzano-weierstrass]]).

## Proof
1.1 Apply Gram–Schmidt to a countable dense sequence in $X$, omitting zero remainders, to obtain a finite or countable orthonormal family $(e_j)$ with dense span. Use the following deterministic extraction for each bounded real sequence $(b_n)$ with $|b_n|\le C$. Start with $[-C,C]$; at each bisection retain the left closed half if it contains infinitely many terms, and otherwise the right closed half, which then contains infinitely many terms. From the $k$th retained interval select the least index larger than the preceding selected index whose term lies in that interval. The selected terms lie in nested intervals of diameters tending to zero, hence are Cauchy; [F9] gives a convergent subsequence, so the entire selected sequence converges. This rule determines the extracted indices uniquely, including when $C=0$, and can therefore be recursively applied to successive coordinates $(x_n,e_j)_X$ without dependent choice. For finitely many coordinates use the last extracted subsequence; for infinitely many take the diagonal of the nested subsequences, whose indices are strictly increasing and whose tail lies in every earlier subsequence. If the family is empty retain the original sequence. The resulting $(x_{n_k})$ has a limit $a_j=\lim_k(x_{n_k},e_j)_X$ for each coordinate present. [F9, given, construct]

1.2 Let $E$ be any separable real Hilbert space. The formula $(f,g)_{L^2(E)}=\int_0^T(f(t),g(t))_E\,dt$ is well-defined by pointwise Cauchy–Schwarz and Holder [F4], and its induced norm is the square-integral norm. To prove completeness, let $(f_n)$ be Cauchy. By [A1], choose a subsequence $(f_{n_k})$ with summable successive $L^2(E)$ distances and representatives for that countable subsequence. Put $h_k(t)=\|f_{n_{k+1}}(t)-f_{n_k}(t)\|_E$. Minkowski bounds partial-sum $L^2$ norms by the sums of the norms; monotone convergence [F4] gives $h=\sum_kh_k\in L^2(0,T)$. Its infinite-value set is null, since positive measure would force $\int h^2\ge N^2|\{h=\infty\}|$ for every $N$. Thus $f_{n_k}(t)$ converges in complete $E$ for a.e. $t$ to $f(t)$. The limit is strongly measurable: because $E$ is separable, distances to a countable dense set are measurable; first-dense-point approximants are countably valued, and finite truncations with summable exceptional-set measures converge a.e. by [F5]–[F6]. The pointwise tail estimate and Minkowski give $$\|f-f_{n_m}\|_{L^2(E)}\le\sum_{k\ge m}\|f_{n_{k+1}}-f_{n_k}\|_{L^2(E)}\to0.$$ The original Cauchy sequence then converges to $f$. This proves that $L^2(0,T;E)$ is Hilbert. [A1, F1, F4, F5, F6, given, choose]

1.3 Finite-valued simple functions are dense in $L^2(0,T;E)$: take the pointwise simple approximants from [F1], replace values by zero where their norm exceeds twice the target norm, and use dominated convergence [F4]; the squared error is at most nine times the target's squared norm. Approximate the finitely many values by a countable dense subset of $E$, and each scalar indicator by the countable dense family [F3]. Since $(0,T)$ has finite measure, these approximations produce a countable dense family of finite sums in $L^2(0,T;E)$. With [F2], this proves that both $L^2(0,T;V)$ and $L^2(0,T;V^*)$, and therefore their product, are separable Hilbert spaces. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given, construct]

2.1 For each $m$, orthogonality gives $\sum_{j=1}^m a_j^2=\lim_k\sum_{j=1}^m(x_{n_k},e_j)_X^2\le C^2$. Thus $(a_j)$ is square-summable, so its partial sums form a Cauchy sequence; completeness [F8] gives the Hilbert-series limit $x=\sum_j a_j e_j$ in $X$. [F8, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Inner products $(x_{n_k},y)_X$ converge to $(x,y)_X$ when $y$ lies in the finite span of the $e_j$, by coordinate convergence. For arbitrary $y\in X$, approximate it by such a finite-span vector $y_m$ using the dense span from step 1.1; the uniform bound gives $|(x_{n_k}-x,y-y_m)_X|\le(C+\|x\|_X)\|y-y_m\|_X$. First choose $m$ large, then $k$ large. Therefore $x_{n_k}\rightharpoonup x$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The derivative graph is closed in the product: if $(u_n,g_n)\to(u,g)$ strongly in both factors, continuous embedding $V\to H$ and Cauchy–Schwarz let every scalar test identity [F1] pass to the limit. Thus the graph is a closed Hilbert subspace. It is weakly closed: a weak limit is orthogonal to the graph's orthogonal complement, so [F7] gives $(S^\perp)^\perp=S$ for that closed subspace. Apply steps 1.1–3.1 to the separable product Hilbert space. Every bounded graph sequence has a weakly convergent subsequence by that argument, and its limit remains in the graph. This proves the asserted weak subsequential compactness in $W(0,T;V)$. [F1, F2, F7, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, an $L^1$ approximate identity, an exponent $1 \le p < \infty$, and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

[L1] Approximate identities are defined in [[def-l-one-approximate-identity-on-rn]].

[L2] Translation is continuous in finite $L^p$ ([[thm-translation-is-continuous-in-l-p-for-one-le-p-less-infinity]]).

[L3] Minkowski's integral inequality and Young's inequality are available ([[thm-minkowski-integral-inequality]], [[thm-young-convolution-inequality]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Because $\int K_\varepsilon = 1$, one may write [L1, L3, given, algebra] $$ f*K_\varepsilon - f = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} K_\varepsilon(y)\,(\tau_y f-f)\,dy. $$ Applying [L3] gives $$ \|f*K_\varepsilon-f\|_p \le \int |K_\varepsilon(y)|\,\|\tau_y f-f\|_p\,dy. $$ [L1, L3, given, algebra]

2.1 Let $\eta > 0$ be arbitrary. If $\|f\|_p=0$, then $f=0$ in $L^p$ and step [L1, L2, L3, step 1.1, choose, algebra] 1.1 gives $\|f*K_\varepsilon-f\|_p=0<\eta$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. Assume now $\|f\|_p>0$, and put $M := \sup_\varepsilon \|K_\varepsilon\|_1 < \infty$. By [L2], choose $\delta > 0$ so that $\|\tau_y f-f\|_p < \eta/(2M)$ whenever $|y|<\delta$. By [L1], choose $\varepsilon_0>0$ so that $$ \int_{|y|\ge\delta} |K_\varepsilon(y)|\,dy < \frac{\eta}{4\|f\|_p} \qquad (0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0). $$ For such $\varepsilon$, split the integral from step 1.1 into $|y|<\delta$ and $|y|\ge\delta$. The near part is at most $\eta/2$. For the far part, [L3] gives $\|\tau_y f-f\|_p \le 2\|f\|_p$, so $$ \int_{|y|\ge\delta} |K_\varepsilon(y)|\,\|\tau_y f-f\|_p\,dy \le 2\|f\|_p \int_{|y|\ge\delta} |K_\varepsilon(y)|\,dy < \eta/2. $$ Hence $\|f*K_\varepsilon-f\|_p<\eta$ whenever $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$. [L1, L2, L3, step 1.1, choose, algebra]

3.1 Because $\eta>0$ was arbitrary, $\|f*K_\varepsilon-f\|_p \to 0$ as [step 2.1] $\varepsilon \to 0^+$, proving the convergence in $L^p$. [step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded and open, $T>0$, $Q=U\times(0,T)$, and $0<\alpha<1$. Use the intended divergence operator
$$L_tu=\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_ju)+\sum_iD_i(b_iu)+\sum_i c_iD_iu+du,$$
and its spatially expanded coefficients
$$\widetilde b_j=\sum_iD_ia_{ij}+b_j+c_j,\qquad \widetilde c=\sum_iD_ib_i+d.$$
Assume $a,b$ have the pointwise spatial derivatives needed for the expanded coefficients, $a=a^T\ge\lambda_0I$ with $\lambda_0>0$, and every spatial boundary point has an exterior tangent ball. The classical equation is understood through these expanded nondivergence coefficients. Assume $a,\widetilde b,\widetilde c,f$ have finite source order-zero weighted parabolic Hölder norms and the additional source weighted bounds $|\delta\widetilde b|_\alpha,|\delta^2\widetilde c|_\alpha,|\delta^2f|_\alpha<\infty$. Here the order-zero convention is
$$|v|_{0,\alpha}=\sup_{P\in Q}|v(P)|+\sup_{P\ne R\in Q}\delta_{P,R}^{\alpha}\frac{|v(P)-v(R)|}{d_p(P,R)^\alpha},\qquad d_p(P,R)=(|x-y|^2+|t-s|)^{1/2},$$
with $\delta(P)=\min\{\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial U),\sqrt t\}$ and $\delta_{P,R}=\min\{\delta(P),\delta(R)\}$. Assume the initial datum $g$ and lateral datum $\varphi$ are Hölder continuous with compatible values $g(x)=\varphi(x,0)$ on $\partial U$. Retain the source barrier assumption that some $\theta>0$ satisfies $\theta^2a_{11}+\theta\widetilde b_1\ge1$ and its coefficient bounds
$$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^2\le\Lambda,\qquad \lambda_0^{-2}(|b|^2+|c|^2)+\lambda_0^{-1}|d|\le v^2.$$
Then the problem $-u_t+L_tu=f$, $u=g$ initially and $u=\varphi$ laterally has a unique solution
$$u^*\in C^{2+\alpha,1+\alpha/2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U\times(0,T])\cap C(\bar U\times[0,T]).$$
Write $\psi$ for the combined prescribed datum and $\Gamma_T=(\bar U\times\{0\})\cup(\partial U\times[0,T])$. If $\widetilde c\le0$, every $h\in C^{2,1}(Q)\cap C(\bar U\times[0,T])$ with finite residual norm satisfies
$$\|h-u^*\|_\infty\le\|h-\psi\|_{C(\Gamma_T)}+T\|f+h_t-L_th\|_\infty.$$
Consequently any sequence whose two right-hand errors tend to zero converges uniformly to $u^*$. If it exactly satisfies the initial and lateral conditions, its residuals are also locally parabolic Hölder, and the displayed divergence-to-nondivergence expansion agrees in distributions locally, it converges strongly in $L^2(0,T;H^1(U))$. In particular these deterministic implications apply on every probability-one event where a PINN residual-consistency theorem supplies the stated residual and prescribed-data limits.

## Statement references

[Shin et al., Assumption 3.4, Theorem 3.6 and Appendices F–G](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** All choices, domain, coefficient, Hölder, data, exterior-ball and retained source hypotheses in the Statement; the weak-expansion compatibility is additionally assumed for the energy clause.

[A1] Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice are retained from weak existence, Sobolev truncation, compactness and smooth-interior embedding ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] The parabolic operator uses $P=-\partial_t+L_t$ and prescribed initial plus lateral data, excluding the final-time face ([[def-shin-parabolic-operator-and-boundary]]).

[F2] Bounded locally parabolic Hölder nondivergence coefficients with elliptic principal part, nonpositive potential and exterior balls have a unique continuous-up-to-boundary interior classical solution; its proof includes weak approximation, interior regularity, boundary barriers and comparison ([[lem-shin-parabolic-classical-approximation-and-boundary-attainment]]).

[F3] A bounded zero-data locally classical error with bounded locally Hölder residual and the compatible bounded divergence representation is the unique zero-initial energy solution, with the stated $L^2_tH^1_x$ estimate ([[lem-shin-zero-data-parabolic-classical-energy-identification]]).

## Proof

1.1 The supremum term of $|\cdot|_{0,\alpha}$ gives boundedness of $a,\widetilde b,\widetilde c,f$. On every compact positive-time cylinder away from the spatial boundary, $\delta$ has a positive lower bound; hence its weighted seminorm gives an ordinary local parabolic Hölder bound there. Near a spatial interior point of the final face the same lower bound holds, since the final face is not part of the distance-defining boundary. Thus these coefficients and source have unique one-sided Hölder limits at $T$ and the regularity required in [F2]. The Frobenius bound on $a$ gives an upper eigenvalue bound in addition to uniform lower ellipticity. The two Hölder data sets define one continuous $\psi$ on the compact $\Gamma_T$ by the compatibility hypothesis. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Choose $k\ge\max\{0,\sup_Q\widetilde c\}$. Setting $u=e^{kt}w$ transforms the equation into $$-w_t+a:D^2w+\widetilde b\cdot Dw+(\widetilde c-k)w=e^{-kt}f,$$ with transformed datum $e^{-kt}\psi$. The potential is nonpositive and all other hypotheses of [F2] hold by step 1.1. Apply that supplier and multiply back by $e^{kt}$ to construct $u^*$ with the stated regularity and data. Applying its comparison uniqueness to differences after the same transformation gives uniqueness for the original equation. No assumption of closed-cylinder second derivatives is used. [A1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Assume now $\widetilde c\le0$, put $e=h-u^*$, $R=\|f+h_t-L_th\|_\infty$, and $E=\|h-\psi\|_{C(\Gamma_T)}$. The nonnegative barrier $W=E+tR$ satisfies $(\partial_t-L_t)W=R-\widetilde c(E+tR)\ge R$. The forward equation for $e$ has source $f+h_t-L_th$, of absolute value at most $R$. The comparison proved in [F2] applied to $e-W$ and $-e-W$ gives $|e|\le W$, and therefore the displayed stability bound. Its application on closed cylinders ending at $\tau<T$, followed by $\tau\uparrow T$, requires no unsupported derivative on the top face of the original open $Q$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 For any sequence with $E_m\to0$ and $R_m\to0$, step 3.1 gives $\|h_m-u^*\|_\infty\le E_m+TR_m\to0$. If these errors converge on a probability-one event, this same deterministic argument applies separately to every outcome in that event and proves almost-sure uniform convergence. It invokes no optimization property beyond the residual and boundary limits actually supplied. [step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Under the additional weak-expansion compatibility, if $h_m$ exactly satisfies the initial and lateral data, $e_m=h_m-u^*$ has zero prescribed data and $$-e_{m,t}+L_te_m=-\bigl(f+h_{m,t}-L_th_m\bigr).$$ Its residual is bounded and locally Hölder by the additional hypothesis; it is bounded and continuous on the closed cylinder. The coefficient bound controls $a,b,c,d$, and the compatible weak expansion is explicitly part of the contract, so all hypotheses of [F3] hold. It gives $e_m\in L^2_tH^1_0$, zero $L^2$ initial trace and the energy estimate; since the residual suprema tend to zero, its final convergence clause proves $e_m\to0$ in $L^2(0,T;H^1(U))$. This establishes the exact-data energy conclusion without asserting any closed-cylinder derivative regularity for $u^*$. [F3, step 2.1, step 4.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The order-zero weighted Hölder requirement makes the source word “Hölder” precise through its equation (2.7), including its supremum term. If instead the original statement intended merely local Hölder continuity with only the positive-order weighted bounds, this proof does not cover that larger class: the heat equation with source $\sin(x)/t$ on $(0,\pi)$ and zero initial data has no continuous zero-initial solution. Against a nonnegative compactly supported spatial test its equation would equate a time derivative of a bounded quantity plus a bounded quantity to a positive constant divided by $t$, contradicting integration near zero. The intended interpretation must be approved explicitly, not silently substituted.

The source assumes pointwise spatial differentiability. Distributional compatibility is needed only by the additional energy clause, not by classical existence or sup-norm stability. It is automatic for local spatial $C^1$ coefficients, but must be stated if that word is interpreted more broadly. The source's printed double sum places $b_iu$ inside the $i,j$ sum and repeats it $d$ times; this item uses the separately indexed divergence term matching its own displayed expanded coefficients.

The exact source trial-class convention weights $D_{ij}h$ by $\delta$ rather than $\delta^2$. It is retained as a source convention in the definition; neither existence nor this proof asserts that the solution has that stronger weighted norm. The stability conclusion applies to its classical trial members, and in fact to the larger classical class explicitly stated here.

The source barrier and divergence coefficient bounds are retained even where the existence construction does not need their full strength. The deterministic consistency clause is the PDE interface used by the separate regularized-PINN consumer; it is not a new sampling, global-minimizer, or optimizer theorem. The full Shin definitions, Assumption 3.4 and Appendix F were read. Its cited Friedman theorem was not represented as a local proof or as newly read full text.

## Statement

Let a finite neural operator have bounded domains, continuous kernels and biases, continuous pointwise activations, and continuous pointwise lifting and projection networks. For every integral use finite measurable partitions whose cells have tags, volume weights, and maximal diameter tending to zero. Its compatible quadratures converge in the output supremum norm uniformly on every compact input set in $C(\bar D)$, and hence on compact subsets of any Banach input space continuously included in $C(\bar D)$. Intermediate values in these realizations are evaluated by their defining functions at all required tags and output queries; changing meshes does not change the continuum parameters.

More generally, the same conclusion holds in the output Banach norm for the following compatible-space architecture. At each stage choose a Banach function space $X_t$ continuously included in $C(\bar D_t;\mathbb R^{q_t})$. For an integral layer from $X_t$ to an auxiliary Banach function space $Y_t$ of $\mathbb R^{q_{t+1}}$-valued functions on $\bar D_{t+1}$, require a continuous inclusion $Y_t\hookrightarrow C(\bar D_{t+1};\mathbb R^{q_{t+1}})$ and require that $y\mapsto\kappa_t(\cdot,y)$ be continuous from $\bar D_t$ into the space of linear maps $\mathbb R^{q_t}\to Y_t$, in operator norm. Every local linear term is a bounded map $X_t\to Y_t$, its bias belongs to $Y_t$, and its following activation is a continuous map $Y_t\to X_{t+1}$. Any separate lifting and projection maps are continuous between their specified Banach spaces. The same maps are used in the discrete and continuum constructions. No arbitrary output Banach norm follows from its continuous inclusion into the supremum norm alone.

The quadrature maps in these two assertions are the raw maps: their local paths may still evaluate the original continuous input at output queries. For the supremum-norm architecture, first reconstruct the input from the partition tags by the finite-sampling reconstruction bridge and apply the same raw quadrature maps to that reconstruction. This gives a genuine finite-sampling family with the same learned parameters, converging uniformly on every compact input set in the output supremum norm. In the general compatible-Banach architecture the identical finite-sampling conclusion follows whenever continuous finite-dimensional input reconstructions into its actual input space are supplied and converge compact-uniformly in that norm. The raw quadrature convergence in the full generality above remains valid without this extra reconstruction premise; it is not itself an assertion of finite-sample factorization of an unchanged local path. If the first input-dependent layer is integral-only and all later stages use only its reconstructed field and fixed parameters, the raw maps already factor through the finite sample vector, so their full compatible-Banach convergence gives a finite-sampling family without an input reconstruction.

## Statement references

[Kovachki et al., Theorem 8 and Appendix E](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.08481)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite composition and compatible tagged, volume-weighted partitions as in the Statement; all compact input sets use their specified norm topology.

[F1] The neural-operator layer and compatible quadrature conventions are [[def-neural-operator]] and [[alg-neural-operator-mesh-discretization]].

[F2] The scalar kernel quadrature estimate in the supremum norm is proved in [[lem-neural-operator-kernel-riemann-sums-uniform-on-compact-inputs]]. The direct modulus argument below also handles bounded measurable domains without an extra Jordan-boundary assumption.

[F3] Continuous raw maps converging compact-uniformly remain convergent after continuous finite-dimensional input reconstructions converging compact-uniformly in the actual input norm. Such reconstructions always exist for continuous inputs in the supremum norm, with the specified tags and normalized nonnegative weights. An integral-only first input stage already factors through its finite samples without an input reconstruction ([[lem-finite-sampling-reconstruction-bridge-for-neural-operator-quadratures]]).

## Proof

1.1 Write $I(v)=\int_D\kappa(\cdot,y)v(y)\,dy$ for one compatible Banach layer, and let $C$ be a compact subset of its input space $X$. Its image in $C(\bar D)$ is compact: pulling an open cover back through the continuous inclusion and using compactness proves this directly. Thus $R=\sup_{v\in C}\|v\|_\infty<\infty$. This family has a common modulus of continuity tending to zero. Indeed a finite $\eta$-net in the supremum norm and uniform continuity of its finitely many functions give $|v(y)-v(z)|\le2\eta+\max_j|v_j(y)-v_j(z)|$ for every $v\in C$. Uniform continuity of the finitely many functions follows by the compact-domain subsequence contradiction. Let $B=\sup_y\|\kappa(\cdot,y)\|_{\mathcal L(\mathbb R^q,Y)}$ and let $\omega_\kappa$ be its norm modulus. Compactness similarly proves $B<\infty$ and $\omega_\kappa(h)\to0$. Therefore the $Y$-valued integrands $\Phi_v(y)=\kappa(\cdot,y)v(y)$ have common modulus bounded by $R\omega_\kappa(h)+B\omega_C(h)$. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 A continuous $Y$-valued function $\Phi$ on $\bar D$ has an integral in $Y$: volume-weighted step sums on partitions of diameter $h$ form a Cauchy family, since comparing two sums on their common refinement bounds their difference by $|D|\omega_\Phi(h+h')$. Completeness of $Y$ gives a limit, independent of tags and partitions. Each coordinate of point evaluation on $Y$ is bounded by its specified continuous inclusion into $C(\bar D';\mathbb R^{q_{t+1}})$; explicitly, $|u_j(x)|\le c_Y\|u\|_Y$. Applying these bounded functionals to the convergent sums therefore identifies the limit with the pointwise integral in every coordinate. Comparing a fixed tagged sum to refinements and taking the limit gives $\|Q_n(v)-I(v)\|_Y\le |D|[R\omega_\kappa(h_n)+B\omega_C(h_n)]$ uniformly for $v\in C$. Also $\|Q_n(v)-Q_n(w)\|_Y\le |D|B\|v-w\|_\infty\le |D|Bc_X\|v-w\|_X$, where $c_X$ is the embedding bound. These estimates use only measurable disjoint cells, their volumes summing to $|D|$, and their diameter bound. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Suppose inductively that the discrete inputs $v_n(a)$ converge in $X$ to the continuum inputs $v(a)$ uniformly for $a$ in the original compact set $K$. The continuum map is continuous by the bound for $I$ from step 2.1 and continuity of all other maps, so $C=v(K)$ is compact. Comparing preactivations at $v_n(a)$ and $v(a)$, the quadrature Lipschitz bound and the bounded local-map norm give an upper bound $(|D|Bc_X+\|W\|)\|v_n(a)-v(a)\|_X+\|Q_n(v(a))-I(v(a))\|_Y$, which tends to zero uniformly in $a$. The continuum preactivations form a compact set $P\subset Y$. A continuous map $T:Y\to X'$ takes perturbations tending uniformly to zero around $P$ to uniformly vanishing output errors: for a prescribed $\varepsilon$, cover $P$ by finitely many balls $B(p_i,r_i)$ on each of which $\|T(z)-T(p_i)\|<\varepsilon/2$ for $\|z-p_i\|<3r_i$, and use a positive perturbation bound smaller than $\min_i r_i$. If $p\in B(p_i,r_i)$ and $\|z-p\|<\min_i r_i$, both images are within $\varepsilon/2$ of $T(p_i)$. Apply this to the activation. The same argument treats continuous lifting or projection maps. Starting with the identical input and proceeding through the finitely many stages proves uniform convergence in the final Banach norm. [step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

4.1 For the supremum-norm architecture take every relevant $X$ and $Y$ to be the continuous-function space with its supremum norm. Joint continuity of $\kappa(x,y)$ on the compact product implies continuity of $y\mapsto\kappa(\cdot,y)$ in that norm, by its uniform modulus on the product. Finite matrix local terms are bounded in that norm. For any fixed continuous scalar activation, its induced map on continuous functions is continuous in the supremum norm: near a function of norm $R$, all scalar arguments lie in $[-R-1,R+1]$, where the activation is uniformly continuous. Pointwise finite networks are finite compositions of these continuous maps. Thus all conditions in steps 1.1–2.1 hold, proving the first clause and then its continuously embedded input-space version. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, F2, algebra]

5.1 Each raw map is continuous between its specified spaces: finite quadrature sums use bounded point evaluations and bounded kernel maps, and all local, activation, lifting and projection maps are continuous by hypothesis. For continuous inputs, apply the explicit reconstructions in [F3]; steps 1.1–4.1 supply the raw compact-uniform convergence required there. The bridge gives finite-dimensional sampling and output reconstruction with the same continuum parameters and output supremum convergence. In the general Banach case use the supplied reconstructions converging in its actual input norm and apply the first clause of the same bridge; its compact-union argument preserves exactly the output norm proved in step 3.1. For an integral-only first layer, the last clause of [F3] constructs its finite-sample output reconstruction directly from the kernel-section sum and transfers the full raw Banach convergence without an input reconstruction. No exact factorization of a raw local identity path is inferred. [given, F3, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Remark

For example, kernels continuous in the output $C^r$ norm and norm-continuous local and nonlinear maps give convergence in $C^r$. The preceding arbitrary Banach formulation is useful beyond such examples. The stronger original assertion is retained verbatim in the proposal's archived preimage and is explicitly refuted by the separate one-neuron $C^1$ counterexample; neither an open-problem label nor an unqualified norm upgrade is warranted.

## Statement

Let $X\subset\mathbb R^D$ carry a probability measure $\mu$, let $s,c>0$, and fix an integer $m\ge1$. Put $\ell=(c\sqrt m)^{-1/s}$. Suppose a specified finite measurable partition $X_1,\ldots,X_K$ of $X$ has each cell contained in a cube of side $\ell$ and of mass at least $c\ell^s$. Let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ be independent points of law $\mu$, and put $\delta=\sqrt D\ell$. With probability at least $\max\{0,1-\sqrt m\exp(-\sqrt m/8)\}$ every cell contains at least $\sqrt m/2$ samples, counted with multiplicity. On this event, simultaneously for all real functions $v,g$ with finite $\alpha$-Hölder seminorms on $X$,
$$\|v-g\|_{\infty;X}^2\le6\sqrt m\left(\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m|v(Y_i)-g(Y_i)|^2\right)+3\delta^{2\alpha}([v]_{\alpha;X}^2+[g]_{\alpha;X}^2).$$
No independence between the functions and the samples is required.

## Statement references

[[def-independent-random-elements]]

[Shin et al., Appendix B: the underlying cell construction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The specified partition, iid samples, and functions in the Statement.

[F1] A probability measure assigns total mass one; independence gives product probabilities for finite sample tuples ([[def-probability-measure]], [[def-independent-random-elements]]).

[F2] The probability of a finite union of events is bounded by the sum of their probabilities ([[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]).

## Proof

1.1 Write $p_j=\mu(X_j)$ and $N_j=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1_{\{Y_i\in X_j\}}$. Since $p_j\ge c\ell^s=m^{-1/2}$ and $\sum_jp_j=1$, we have $K\le\sqrt m$. Independence gives $\mathbb E e^{-N_j/2}=(1-p_j+p_je^{-1/2})^m\le\exp(-mp_j(1-e^{-1/2}))$. For a nonnegative random variable $Z$, $a\mathbb P(Z>a)\le\mathbb E Z$, by integrating $Z\ge a\mathbf1_{Z>a}$. Apply this with $Z=e^{-N_j/2}$ and $a=e^{-mp_j/4}$ to get $\mathbb P(N_j<mp_j/2)\le\exp(mp_j/4-mp_j(1-e^{-1/2}))\le e^{-mp_j/8}$. Here $e^{1/2}\ge1+1/2+1/8=13/8>8/5$ implies $e^{-1/2}<5/8$, and $1-x\le e^{-x}$ follows by differentiating $e^{-x}-1+x$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The event $N_j<\sqrt m/2$ is contained in $N_j<mp_j/2$. By step 1.1 and [F2], its union over cells has probability at most $K e^{-\sqrt m/8}\le\sqrt m e^{-\sqrt m/8}$. This proves the probability assertion, with the trivial lower bound zero when necessary. [step 1.1, F2, algebra]

3.1 On the complementary event fix $x\in X_j$. Every sample $Y_i\in X_j$ is within $\delta$ of $x$. The three-term square inequality gives $|v(x)-g(x)|^2\le3|v(Y_i)-g(Y_i)|^2+3\delta^{2\alpha}([v]_{\alpha;X}^2+[g]_{\alpha;X}^2)$. Average over the $N_j\ge\sqrt m/2$ samples in this cell. Its first term is at most $(3/N_j)\sum_{i=1}^m|v(Y_i)-g(Y_i)|^2\le6\sqrt m\,m^{-1}\sum_i|v(Y_i)-g(Y_i)|^2$. Taking the supremum over $x$ proves the inequality. This is a deterministic inequality on the occupancy event, so it holds for sample-dependent trial functions as well. [step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $D\ge2$, $0<\alpha\le1$, and let the residual and boundary sets $U,\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^D$ carry probability measures $\mu_r,\mu_b$. Put $s_r=D$ and $s_b=D-1$. For $i=r,b$, fix $c_i,C_i,\ell_{0,i},\rho_{0,i}>0$ and a specified family of finite measurable partitions of the corresponding set at every $0<\ell\le\ell_{0,i}$. Each cell is contained in an ambient cube of side $\ell$ and has mass at least $c_i\ell^{s_i}$. Assume $\mu_i(\overline B_\rho(x))\le C_i\rho^{s_i}$ for centers in that set and $0<\rho\le\rho_{0,i}$. These are small-scale conditions. The usual Lipschitz-domain and positive-density hypotheses may be retained, but the explicit partition and ball bounds are the properties used below.

Take nested iid sample sequences of respective laws $\mu_r,\mu_b$ and counts $m_r,m_b\to\infty$. For sufficiently large counts put
$$\ell_i=(c_i\sqrt{m_i})^{-1/s_i},\qquad \delta_i=\sqrt D\ell_i,\qquad A_i=m_i^{-\alpha/s_i},$$
$$C_m=3\max_{i=r,b}\{(C_i/c_i)D^{s_i/2}\sqrt{m_i}\},\qquad \widehat\lambda^R_{i,m}=3\lambda_i\delta_i^{2\alpha}/C_m,$$
where $\lambda_r,\lambda_b>0$ are fixed. The count threshold is explicitly $m_i\ge\max\{1,c_i^{-2}\ell_{0,i}^{-2s_i},c_i^{-2}D^{s_i}\rho_{0,i}^{-2s_i}\}$; thus both partition and ball bounds apply. Choose weights $\lambda^R_{i,m}\ge\widehat\lambda^R_{i,m}$ and $\|\lambda_m^R\|_\infty=O(\|\widehat\lambda_m^R\|_\infty)$, with the same constants throughout the formulas.

Let $f,g$ have finite $\alpha$-Hölder seminorms on their respective sets. Let $H_m$ be trial classes for which $L[h]$ and $B[h]$ have finite such seminorms; in the PDE application retain $H_m\subset C^{k,\alpha}(U)\cap C^{0,\alpha}(\bar U)$. Suppose there are witnesses $u_m^*\in H_m$ with zero empirical PINN loss and $[L[u_m^*]]_{\alpha;U}^2+[B[u_m^*]]_{\alpha;\Gamma}^2\le M<\infty$, uniformly in $m$. Every global minimizer $h_m$ of the prescribed regularized empirical objective satisfies the following, uniformly for every such minimizer on the same sampling events.

On the hit-cell event, with probability at least $1-q(m_r)-q(m_b)$ (clipped at zero),
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h_m;\lambda)=O(A_r+A_b),\qquad q(n)=\sqrt n(1-1/\sqrt n)^n.$$
If the residual and boundary sample streams are independent, the lower bound improves to $(1-q(m_r))(1-q(m_b))$, exactly the Appendix B probability. If the chosen $c_r,c_b\le1$, this also implies the weaker later printed bound with $1-c_i/\sqrt{m_i}$ in place of $1-1/\sqrt{m_i}$. No normalization is implicit.

On the occupancy event, with probability at least $1-Q(m_r)-Q(m_b)$ (clipped at zero),
$$\|L[h_m]-f\|_{\infty;U}^2+\|B[h_m]-g\|_{\infty;\Gamma}^2=O(A_r+A_b),\qquad Q(n)=\sqrt n e^{-\sqrt n/8}.$$
For independent streams one may instead use $\max\{0,1-Q(m_r)\}\max\{0,1-Q(m_b)\}$. Almost surely the two uniform errors tend to zero along any count pairs tending to infinity. If $m_r=O(m_b^{D/(D-1)})$, both displayed right sides are $O(m_r^{-\alpha/D})$. No comparability of the regularization coordinates is required. Constants in these bounds depend on $M$, the fixed data, and the constant in the weight upper bound. If the witness bound is almost surely finite rather than deterministic, the eventual almost-sure assertions hold with that random finite constant. These are statements about global minimizers, not a training algorithm.

## Statement references

[[alg-empirical-pinn-objective]]

[[lem-pinn-cell-occupancy-controls-uniform-residual]]

[Shin et al., Theorems 3.1–3.2 and Appendices B–C](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The data, partitions, samples, exact thresholds, witnesses, and global minimizers in the Statement.

[F1] The objective is empirical weighted squared loss plus the two seminorm penalties ([[def-physics-informed-neural-network-loss]], [[alg-empirical-pinn-objective]]).

[F2] A hit in every cell gives the fill radii $\delta_i$ and failure bounds $q(m_i)$ ([[lem-pinn-random-samples-are-space-filling]]).

[F3] The deterministic population-loss bound uses $C_m$ and penalties $3\lambda_i\delta_i^{2\alpha}/C_m$ ([[lem-pinn-residual-loss-from-fill-distance]]).

[F4] The occupancy event and its deterministic uniform inequality have failure bound $Q(m_i)$ ([[lem-pinn-cell-occupancy-controls-uniform-residual]]).

[F5] Summable failure probabilities imply only finitely many failures almost surely ([[thm-first-borel-cantelli]]).

[F6] The original all-positive-scale lower mass assumption is impossible, and the original count condition does not imply threshold comparability ([[lem-shin-pinn-all-scale-cell-mass-assumption-inconsistent]], [[cex-pinn-regularization-thresholds-need-balanced-sample-counts]]).

## Proof

1.1 Write $J_m$ for the regularized objective at $h_m$ and $a_i=D^\alpha c_i^{-2\alpha/s_i}$, so $\delta_i^{2\alpha}=a_iA_i$. Minimality against $u_m^*$ and [F1] give $0\le J_m\le M\|\lambda_m^R\|_\infty\le K\max\{A_r,A_b\}/C_m$, for a fixed $K$. In particular, the $i$th empirical mean squared error is at most $J_m/\lambda_i$ and the squared operator seminorm is at most $J_m/\lambda^R_{i,m}$. No max-to-min ratio is used. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 On both hit-cell events, [F2] and [F3] give $\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h_m;\lambda)\le C_mJ_m+3\sum_i\lambda_i a_iA_i[\mathrm{data}_i]_{\alpha}^2=O(A_r+A_b)$ by step 1.1. The union bound gives the stated joint probability without an independence premise; independence of the streams gives the product. If $0<c_i\le1$, then $0\le1-1/\sqrt{m_i}\le1-c_i/\sqrt{m_i}$, which proves the stated normalized comparison of probabilities. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 On the two occupancy events apply [F4] with $(v,g)=(L[h_m],f)$ and $(B[h_m],g)$ respectively. For each $i$, step 1.1 yields $$\|\mathrm{error}_i\|_\infty^2\le\frac{6\sqrt{m_i}}{\lambda_i}J_m+3a_iA_i\frac{J_m}{\lambda^R_{i,m}}+3a_iA_i[\mathrm{data}_i]_{\alpha}^2\le\left(\frac{6\sqrt{m_i}}{\lambda_i}+\frac{C_m}{\lambda_i}\right)J_m+3a_iA_i[\mathrm{data}_i]_{\alpha}^2.$$ Here $\lambda^R_{i,m}\ge3\lambda_i a_iA_i/C_m$ gives the second inequality. Since $C_m\ge3(C_i/c_i)D^{s_i/2}\sqrt{m_i}$ for each component, step 1.1 makes the last expression $O(A_r+A_b)$. This proves the uniform bound and its event probability. It remains valid for all sample-dependent minimizers because [F4] is simultaneous for every function. [F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For every integer $n$, $Q(n)=\sqrt n e^{-\sqrt n/8}$. Grouping $k^2\le n<(k+1)^2$ bounds its sum by $\sum_{k\ge1}(2k+1)(k+1)e^{-k/8}<\infty$; convergence follows, for example, since the ratio of successive summands tends to $e^{-1/8}<1$. Apply [F5] separately to the occupancy failure events at every integer sample count in each fixed nested stream. Almost surely, beyond two finite count thresholds every occupancy event holds, so step 2.2 applies along every count pair tending to infinity, including arbitrarily slowly growing or repeated count pairs. Thus both uniform errors tend to zero. Finally $m_r\le C m_b^{D/(D-1)}$ implies $A_b\le C^{\alpha/D}A_r$, proving the rate specialization. The conclusion has been proved using the corrected small-scale events and without the invalid all-scale premise or weight-comparability inference recorded in [F6]. [F5, F6, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The original literal Assumption 3.1 quantifies its lower mass bound over every $\varepsilon>0$; [F6] refutes it. The corrected Statement explicitly restricts the range and does not claim the literal source hypotheses have instances. The original source uses the exact regularizers above and asserts uniform convergence, but Appendix C's bounded max-to-min inference is false by [F6]. The populated-cell proof above establishes that convergence with the same regularizers under the corrected nonvacuous sampling condition. Its occupancy probability is different from the Appendix B hit probability and is not attributed to the source. Appendix B's probability uses $1-1/\sqrt m$; the later printed $1-c/\sqrt m$ requires the explicitly stated normalization for this comparison. The complete pre-repair carrier, including its exact original statement, is preserved in the proposal's immutable before snapshot.

## Statement

Let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable sets in a measure space. If the nonnegative extended sum satisfies

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k)<+\infty,$$

then

$$\mu\left(\limsup_{k\to\infty}E_k\right)=0.$$

No independence hypothesis and no finiteness hypothesis on the whole space are required.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Measurable sets $(E_k)$ with $S:=\sum_k\mu(E_k)<+\infty$.

[L1] Measures are monotone ([[prop-measure-monotonicity]]) and countably subadditive ([[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]).

[L2] The set limsup is $\bigcap_N\bigcup_{k\ge N}E_k$ ([[def-set-limsup-and-liminf]]).

[L3] A nonnegative extended sum is the supremum of its partial sums ([[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]), while a convergent real series is the limit of its real partial sums ([[def-series]]).

[L4] A convergent real series and each of its tails converge, with total sum equal to the initial partial sum plus the tail sum ([[lem-series-tail-invariance]]).

[L5] Limits of real sequences respect addition and subtraction ([[thm-algebra-of-limits]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Since $S$ is finite, every $\mu(E_k)$ and every partial sum $s_n$ is real. The $s_n$ increase and have supremum $S$; given $\varepsilon>0$, the defining property of the supremum supplies $N$ with $S-\varepsilon<s_N\le S$, and then $S-\varepsilon<s_n\le S$ for every $n\ge N$. Thus the real series $\sum_k\mu(E_k)$ converges to $S$, and its tail sums $T_N:=\sum_{k\ge N}\mu(E_k)$ are real. [given, L3]

1.2 For every $N$, [L2] gives $\limsup_kE_k\subseteq\bigcup_{k\ge N}E_k$, so monotonicity and subadditivity give $\mu(\limsup_kE_k)\le T_N$. [given, L1, L2]

2.1 If $s_N=\sum_{k<N}\mu(E_k)$, then $T_N=S-s_N$ by tail invariance, and $s_N\to S$; hence $T_N\to0$ by the algebra of limits. [step 1.1, L4, L5]

3.1 The nonnegative number $\mu(\limsup_kE_k)$ is at most every $T_N$ by step 1.2, while step 2.1 makes those tails arbitrarily small; therefore it is $0$. [step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let all coefficients and data be real. Let $n\ge2$, and let $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and bounded with smooth boundary. Suppose $A,\beta,c,F,G$ are smooth on a neighborhood of $\bar V$, $A=A^T$, $\lambda I\le A\le\Lambda I$ for constants $0<\lambda\le\Lambda$, and $c\le0$. For $L=A:D^2+\beta\cdot D+c$, the Dirichlet problem $Lu=F$ in $V$, $u=G$ on $\partial V$ has exactly one solution $u\in C^\infty(\bar V)$. Here smoothness on the closure means that all interior derivatives extend continuously to the closure, equivalently that a smooth extension exists to every finite differentiability order.

## Statement references

[Hunter, Sections 4.9 and 4.11–4.12: Fredholm and Sobolev regularity framework](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/pde_notes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The dimension, smooth bounded domain, coefficient bounds, sign, forcing and lifting in the Statement. AC and CC are used through the Fredholm, extension, embedding and difference quotient suppliers.

[F1] Weak Fredholm theory for the negative-principal divergence operator gives existence for every $L^2$ forcing once its zero-boundary weak kernel is trivial ([[thm-fredholm-alternative-for-weak-elliptic-dirichlet-problems]], [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]]).

[F2] A zero-trace weak solution with Lipschitz principal coefficients and $L^2$ forcing lies in global $H^2$ on a bounded $C^2$ domain; its proof uses tangential flat-face $H^2$ estimates and recovery of the normal second derivative by division by $a^{nn}$ ([[thm-global-h-two-dirichlet-regularity]], [[lem-tangential-h-two-estimate-near-a-flat-dirichlet-boundary]], [[lem-normal-second-derivative-recovered-from-the-elliptic-equation]]).

[F3] Smooth-coefficient weak solutions have the higher integer Sobolev regularity locally in the interior ([[thm-interior-h-k-plus-two-elliptic-regularity]]).

[F4] Smooth bounded domains admit integer Sobolev extensions; sufficiently high Sobolev order gives continuous classical derivatives to any prescribed finite order. On these domains the zero trace agrees with zero classical boundary values ([[thm-extension-theorem-for-bounded-smooth-domains]], [[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]], [[lem-sobolev-trace-agrees-with-continuous-boundary-values]], [[thm-kernel-of-the-trace-is-w-one-p-zero]]).

[F5] For a positive-principal uniformly elliptic operator with nonpositive potential, a zero-boundary classical homogeneous solution is zero; the exponential perturbation proves comparison on every bounded open domain ([[lem-shin-elliptic-residual-stability]]).

[F6] The zero-trace space is the $H^1$ closure of compactly supported smooth functions; it is closed, tangential translations preserve the zero flat-face trace, and the weak product rules and tangential difference quotient limits used by [F2] hold ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]). The choices allowed here are AC and CC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

1.1 First establish the regularity fact needed to test the homogeneous kernel: a zero-trace weak solution with smooth coefficients and smooth forcing on a smooth bounded domain lies in $H^k(V)$ for every integer $k$. Write the negative operator as $$P=-L=-\partial_i(A_{ij}\partial_j)+(\partial_iA_{ij}-\beta_j)\partial_j-c.$$ Its principal coefficients are Lipschitz and uniformly elliptic, and its lower coefficients are bounded. Global $H^2$ regularity gives the base $u\in H^2(V)$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6]

1.2 Here is the full higher-order induction, rather than an appeal to boundary smoothness. Assume $u\in H^{m+1}(V)$ for some $m\ge1$. On an interior patch, the local higher-order Sobolev theorem gives $H^{m+2}$ on a smaller patch. On a boundary patch, use a smooth graph chart and nested smooth cutoffs as in the actual global $H^2$ proof. In the flattened coordinates the cutoff solution $v$ has compact lateral support in $\overline H$, belongs to $H^{m+1}(H)$, has zero trace, and satisfies $$Pv=-a^{ij}D_iD_jv+B^iD_iv+Cv=F_0.$$ The transformed coefficients are smooth with $a^{nn}\ge\lambda'>0$, and $F_0\in H^m$ on the patch after localization; the cutoff commutators have order at most one and thus belong to $H^m$ by the induction hypothesis. A further cutoff identically one on the desired smaller patch avoids all artificial lateral boundaries. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6]

1.3 For every tangential multi-index $\gamma$ of order $m$, put $w=D_{\mathrm{tan}}^\gamma v$. It belongs to $H^1$ and has zero trace on the flat face. The latter follows by tangential difference quotients: every quotient of a zero-trace $H^1$ function is zero trace, and the iterated quotients converge in $H^1$ when $v\in H^{m+1}$; the trace kernel is closed. Apply the product rule in distributions to obtain $$Pw=D_{\mathrm{tan}}^\gamma F_0+\sum_{0<\eta\le\gamma}\binom\gamma\eta(D_{\mathrm{tan}}^\eta a^{ij})D_iD_jD_{\mathrm{tan}}^{\gamma-\eta}v-\sum_{0<\eta\le\gamma}\binom\gamma\eta(D_{\mathrm{tan}}^\eta B^i)D_iD_{\mathrm{tan}}^{\gamma-\eta}v-\sum_{0<\eta\le\gamma}\binom\gamma\eta(D_{\mathrm{tan}}^\eta C)D_{\mathrm{tan}}^{\gamma-\eta}v.$$ Every term is $L^2$: the largest derivative of $v$ in a commutator has order $m+1$, since $|\eta|\ge1$. Multiplying $w$ by the further cutoff adds only $L^2$ commutators, since $w\in H^1$. Convert $P$ back to divergence form and apply precisely the flat-boundary tangential $H^2$ lemma plus normal recovery (and the interior $H^2$ input) used in the global $H^2$ proof. This gives $w\in H^2$ on the smaller half-patch. Therefore all derivatives of $v$ of total order $m+2$ with at most two normal differentiations are $L^2$ there. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6]

1.4 Recover the remaining order-$m+2$ derivatives by induction on their number $q\ge3$ of normal differentiations. In distributions differentiate the equation by $D_n^{q-2}D_{\mathrm{tan}}^\gamma$, where $|\gamma|=m+2-q$, and isolate the term $$-a^{nn}D_n^qD_{\mathrm{tan}}^\gamma v.$$ When all $m$ derivatives fall on $v$, every other principal term has at most $q-1$ normal differentiations and is already $L^2$ by this normal-count induction. If any derivative falls on a coefficient, the derivative of $v$ has order at most $m+1$, hence is $L^2$ by the original Sobolev induction. Differentiated lower-order terms also have order at most $m+1$, and the differentiated $F_0$ is $L^2$. The reciprocal $1/a^{nn}$ is smooth and bounded on the patch. Division proves that the missing distributional derivative is represented by an $L^2$ function. There is no circular assumption of its boundary integrability: the distribution identity itself supplies the derivative, exactly as in the normal-recovery lemma. This proves $H^{m+2}$ on every smaller boundary patch. A finite cover proves $u\in H^{m+2}(V)$, completing the induction. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6]

1.5 For any fixed $r$, choose $k$ with $k-n/2>r+1/2$. Smooth-domain extension and the higher-order Sobolev embedding give a $C^r(\bar V)$ representative. Representatives at different $r$ coincide, since continuous representatives equal almost everywhere must agree everywhere. Thus $u\in C^\infty(\bar V)$. Its zero trace equals its zero classical boundary value. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6]

2.1 Now apply the weak Fredholm theorem to $P$ on $H^1_0(V)$. Every element of the homogeneous kernel has the just-proved smoothness up to the boundary. The classical comparison principle for $L$ with $c\le0$ makes that kernel zero: apply it to $u$ and $-u$. The first Fredholm alternative therefore gives a unique weak solution for every smooth forcing. For the specified boundary value, apply it to $v=u-G$ with forcing $-F-PG\in C^\infty(\bar V)$. The regularity argument makes $v$ smooth to the boundary, and $u=v+G$ solves the required problem. Uniqueness follows from the same comparison principle. This proves the lemma without a boundary Schauder theorem or continuity-method premise. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6] ∎
