## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let all coefficients and data be real. Let $n\ge1$, $0<\alpha<1$, and let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, bounded and Lipschitz, with an exterior ball at every boundary point. Suppose $a_{ij}=a_{ji},b_i\in C^{1,\alpha}(U)$ and $c_i,d\in C^{0,\alpha}(U)$, with finite global norms, and $\lambda_0 I\le A=(a_{ij})\le\Lambda_0 I$ for constants $0<\lambda_0\le\Lambda_0$. Define
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_ju)+\sum_iD_i(b_i u)+\sum_i c_iD_iu+du,$$
$$\beta_j=\sum_iD_ia_{ij}+b_j+c_j,\qquad \gamma=\sum_iD_ib_i+d,$$
and assume $\gamma\le0$. Retain, when required by the source application, the bounds $\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^2\le\Lambda$ and $\lambda_0^{-2}(|b|^2+|c|^2)+\lambda_0^{-1}|d|\le v^2$.

For every $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(U)$ and $g\in C(\partial U)$ there is exactly one solution
$$u\in C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)\cap C(\bar U),\qquad Lu=f,\qquad u|_{\partial U}=g.$$
There is a finite constant $C_L$, depending on $U$, ellipticity and the sup bounds of the expanded coefficients $A,\beta,\gamma$, such that every $h\in C^2(U)\cap C(\bar U)$ with bounded residual satisfies
$$\|u-h\|_{\infty;U}\le C_L\bigl(\|f-Lh\|_{\infty;U}+\|g-h\|_{\infty;\partial U}\bigr).$$
If $g=0$, then $u\in H^1_0(U)$ and $\|u\|_{H^1(U)}\le C_E\|f\|_{\infty;U}$, where $C_E$ may additionally depend on $\|DA\|_\infty$. If $g$ is the restriction of an ambient $C^{2,\alpha}$ lifting $G$ near $\bar U$, then $u-G\in H^1_0(U)$. If in addition $U$ is $C^{2,\alpha}$ and $g$ has such a lifting $G$, the solution lies in $C^{2,\alpha}(\bar U)$ and satisfies
$$\|u\|_{2,\alpha;\bar U}\le C\bigl(\|f\|_{0,\alpha;U}+\|G\|_{2,\alpha;\bar U}\bigr).$$
The global branch follows by uniform estimates on smooth interior approximants and passage to the classical limit.

## Statement references

[Shin et al., Appendix D: exterior-sphere existence and stability formulation](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

[[lem-shin-smooth-dirichlet-approximants-from-sobolev-bootstrap]]

[[lem-shin-uniform-boundary-schauder-estimate-for-smooth-dirichlet-approximants]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The domain, coefficients, sign and finite norms, forcing and boundary datum in the Statement. Assume AC and CC; their uses are inherited by smooth weak solvability, Sobolev extension, measure theory and sequential compactness.

[F1] Smooth-domain, smooth-coefficient Dirichlet approximants exist by weak Fredholm theory and the locally proved boundary Sobolev bootstrap ([[lem-shin-smooth-dirichlet-approximants-from-sobolev-bootstrap]]).

[F2] Exponential barriers prove comparison and the residual estimate with the positive principal convention and nonpositive expanded potential ([[lem-shin-elliptic-residual-stability]], [[def-shin-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]]).

[F3] Interior Schauder estimates give uniform local $C^{2,\alpha}$ bounds from uniform coefficient Hölder bounds, the forcing norm and the solution supremum ([[thm-interior-schauder-estimate-for-uniformly-elliptic-equations]], [[def-holder-spaces-c-k-alpha-and-their-scaled-norms]]).

[F4] Mollification is smooth, commutes with the derivatives in use and preserves sup and Hölder bounds by integration; regular levels of smooth functions have smooth boundaries ([[thm-convolution-with-a-mollifier-is-smooth-and-differentiates-under-the-integral-sign]], [[thm-morse-sard-for-euclidean-maps]]).

[F5] A bounded continuous datum on the closed set $\partial U$ has a bounded continuous extension to the metric, hence normal, space $\mathbb R^n$ ([[thm-tietze-extension-theorem]]).

[F6] Pointwise bounded equicontinuous families on compact metric spaces have convergent subsequences; apply this to the function, gradient and Hessian jointly ([[cor-real-and-euclidean-vector-valued-ascoli-arzela]]).

[F7] Zero-trace spaces are closures of compactly supported smooth classes; extension by zero from $H^1_0(V)$ to $H^1_0(U)$ is therefore valid for $V\subset U$. On smooth domains the zero trace and classical zero boundary restriction agree ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[thm-kernel-of-the-trace-is-w-one-p-zero]], [[lem-sobolev-trace-agrees-with-continuous-boundary-values]]). Cauchy–Schwarz and Young inequalities control the energy products ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], [[thm-young-inequality-real-exponents]]).

[F8] Already smooth zero-boundary Dirichlet solutions on smooth domains with a common uniformly controlled $C^{2,\alpha}$ graph atlas obey a uniform global a priori Schauder bound from the supremum and forcing norm. Every bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain has relatively compact smooth approximating open sets with exactly those uniform atlas bounds, eventually containing every interior compact set ([[lem-shin-uniform-boundary-schauder-estimate-for-smooth-dirichlet-approximants]]). This estimate is used only on smooth approximants, not on the original solution before boundary regularity has been established.

[F9] The permitted choices are AC and CC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). The zero-boundary Sobolev space is Hilbert, Gram–Schmidt applies to every finite initial list after dependent vectors are discarded, and finite Bessel bounds control the coefficient sums ([[lem-w-one-two-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[thm-gram-schmidt-orthonormalisation]], [[thm-bessel-inequality-and-finite-parseval-identity]]). Every bounded linear functional on a Hilbert space is an inner product against a vector ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]). The proof below gives the weak subsequence argument directly in the separable closed span.

## Proof

1.1 Expand the intended divergence expression by the product rule to obtain $L=A:D^2+\beta\cdot D+\gamma$. On a bounded Lipschitz domain, two sufficiently close points in a fixed smaller graph patch can be joined inside a larger patch by a path of length at most a fixed multiple of their distance; bounded first derivatives therefore give a Lipschitz bound for $a,b$ there. A finite cover and the supremum bound for separated pairs give their global Hölder bounds. Thus the finite global coefficient assumptions give finite Hölder bounds for the expanded coefficients, $\gamma\le0$, and a finite bound for $DA$. Throughout the proof write $c=\gamma$, and use $\lambda=\lambda_0$, $\Lambda=\Lambda_0$. [given, F2, algebra]

1.2 If $n=1$, the bounded Lipschitz set is a finite union of open intervals: its compact boundary has a finite one-sided graph-chart cover, and in dimension one each such chart contains one boundary point. On each interval $(a,b)$ all coefficients and $f$ extend Hölder-continuously to $[a,b]$ and $A\ge\lambda$. Write $y=(u,u')$, so $y'=M(x)y+F(x)$, where $M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-c/A&-\beta/A\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $F=(0,f/A)$. For $Th(x)=\int_a^xM(t)h(t)\,dt$, iterated integration gives $\|T^kh\|_\infty\le \|h\|_\infty(\|M\|_\infty(b-a))^k/k!$. Therefore the uniformly convergent series $y=\sum_{k\ge0}T^k(y(a)+\int_a^{\cdot}F)$ solves the integral equation, hence the differential system; the factorial bound also proves uniqueness by iterating the homogeneous difference equation. Choose one particular solution with the prescribed left value and slope zero, and add $s$ times the homogeneous solution with initial value zero and slope one. That homogeneous solution cannot also vanish at $b$: otherwise [F2] would make it identically zero, contradicting its slope at $a$. Thus exactly one $s$ gives the prescribed right value. The equation makes $u''$ globally Hölder, so $u\in C^{2,\alpha}([a,b])$. Zero endpoint values imply $u\in H^1_0(a,b)$ directly: multiply by a cutoff vanishing within $\varepsilon$ of each endpoint, with derivative bounded by $C/\varepsilon$; since $|u|\le\|u'\|_\infty\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial(a,b))$, the cutoff error in $H^1$ tends to zero, and each compactly supported $H^1$ function is approximated by mollification. For zero data, integration against $u$ gives $\lambda\|u'\|_2^2\le\|f\|_2\|u\|_2+\|\beta-A'\|_\infty\|u'\|_2\|u\|_2+\|c\|_\infty\|u\|_2^2$; Young's inequality and [F2] then give the stated energy bound on these finitely many intervals. This proves all existence, energy, and global regularity conclusions in dimension one; [F2] gives stability. Henceforth take $n\ge2$. [given, F2, F4, F7, algebra]

1.3 Let $\delta(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus U)$ on all of $\mathbb R^n$; it is nonnegative, 1-Lipschitz, vanishes outside $U$, and has compact support because $U$ is bounded. Fix a nonnegative unit-mass smooth mollifier supported in the unit ball. Put $\varepsilon_j\downarrow0$ and $\delta_j=\rho_{\varepsilon_j}*\delta$. Then $$|\delta_j-\delta|\le\varepsilon_j.$$ Choose a regular value $t_j\in(2\varepsilon_j,3\varepsilon_j)$, using the local Euclidean Morse–Sard theorem, and set $V_j=\{\delta_j>t_j\}$. This is bounded with compact smooth boundary, satisfies $\bar V_j\subset U$ (indeed $\delta\ge t_j-\varepsilon_j>\varepsilon_j$ on its closure), and contains $\{\delta>4\varepsilon_j\}$. Every compact subset of $U$ is contained in $V_j$ for all sufficiently large $j$. Discard an initial empty $V_j$ if necessary. Nestedness is not required anywhere below. If there are several components, use the same argument componentwise; a compact smooth boundary has a finite graph cover and the proof supplies the same finite-cover regularity on their union. [given, F1, F4, F5]

1.4 Choose $s_j<\varepsilon_j/4$ tending to zero and mollify the original coefficients and forcing at scale $s_j$ on a neighborhood of $\bar V_j$: $$A_j=\rho_{s_j}*A,\quad\beta_j=\rho_{s_j}*\beta,\quad c_j=\rho_{s_j}*c,\quad f_j=\rho_{s_j}*f.$$ Only values inside $U$ are used there. Consequently $A_j=A_j^T$, $\lambda I\le A_j\le\Lambda I$, $c_j\le0$, and the sup bounds of $\beta_j,c_j,f_j,DA_j$ do not exceed the original corresponding bounds. On every fixed interior ball, their Hölder norms are uniformly bounded and they converge uniformly to the original coefficients/data; $DA_j\to DA$ uniformly locally as well. The Hölder bound follows directly by integrating $|F(x-z)-F(y-z)|\le[F]_\alpha|x-y|^\alpha$. Each coefficient is smooth near $\bar V_j$; its higher derivatives can grow with $j$, which does not matter. [given, F1, F4, F5]

1.5 Extend $g$ to a bounded continuous $G$ on $\mathbb R^n$ using Tietze and set $G_j=\rho_{s_j}*G$. Uniform convergence $G_j\to G$ holds on any fixed compact neighborhood of $\bar U$, by uniform continuity there. Also $\|G_j\|_\infty\le\|G\|_\infty$. The lemma gives a smooth classical $u_j$ on $\bar V_j$ satisfying $$L_ju_j=f_j\quad\hbox{in }V_j,\qquad u_j=G_j\quad\hbox{on }\partial V_j.$$ [given, F1, F4, F5]

1.6 Take a slab $a\le x_1\le b$ containing $\bar U$, put $B=\sup_j\|\beta_{j,1}\|_\infty$, $C_0=\sup_j\|c_j\|_\infty$, and choose $\kappa$ with $\lambda\kappa^2-B\kappa-C_0\ge1$. For $\psi=e^{\kappa x_1}$, $L_j\psi\ge e^{\kappa a}=:\eta>0$. Fix $M>e^{\kappa b}$ and put $\Phi=M-\psi>0$. Then $L_j\Phi\le-\eta$ for every $j$. [given, F2]

1.7 Let $Q=\|G\|_\infty$ and $R=\|f\|_\infty$. On $\partial V_j$, both $u_j-Q-(R/\eta)\Phi$ and $-u_j-Q-(R/\eta)\Phi$ are nonpositive. Their $L_j$ images are nonnegative, since $c_j\le0$, $|f_j|\le R$ and $L_j\Phi\le-\eta$. Comparison gives $$|u_j|\le Q+(R/\eta)\|\Phi\|_\infty=:M_0$$ on $V_j$. This constant depends only on the original domain/slab, uniform ellipticity and expanded coefficient sup bounds, $R,Q$. It is independent of $j$, of the smoothness of $\partial V_j$, and of all higher coefficient derivatives. [given, F2]

1.8 For every ball $B_{2r}(x)\Subset U$, it is contained in $V_j$ for large $j$. Apply the actual interior Schauder theorem to $u_j$ there. All coefficient $C^\alpha$ norms and ellipticity constants are uniformly controlled on that fixed ball, $\|u_j\|_\infty\le M_0$, and the $C^\alpha$ norm of $f_j$ is uniformly bounded. Hence $u_j$ is uniformly bounded in $C^{2,\alpha}(B_r(x))$. [given, F3, F6]

1.9 Cover $U$ by a countable family of such inner balls with rational centers/radii. Arzelà–Ascoli on each smaller closed ball and diagonal extraction give one subsequence for which $(u_j,Du_j,D^2u_j)$ converges uniformly on every compact subset of $U$. The fundamental theorem of calculus on coordinate segments identifies the limits with $(u,Du,D^2u)$; their compatibility on overlapping balls follows from uniform convergence. Passing each Hessian Hölder difference quotient to the limit proves $u\in C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Uniform local convergence of all coefficients/data and derivatives gives $Lu=f$ pointwise. The uniform bound gives $|u|\le M_0$. [given, F3, F6]

1.10 Fix $q\in\partial U$. Let $B_R(z)$ be an exterior ball tangent at $q$. Replace it by the smaller ball with center $z'=(z+q)/2$ and radius $r_0=R/2$. Its **closed** ball is contained in $B_R(z)\cup\{q\}$: for $x\ne q$ on the smaller closed ball, strict triangle inequality gives $|x-z|<R$. Thus $$|x-z'|\ge r_0\quad(x\in\bar U),\qquad |x-z'|=r_0\iff x=q.$$ This strict contact property is necessary; the original exterior ball could touch the boundary at several points. [given, F2]

1.11 Write $r=|x-z'|$, $e=(x-z')/r$, and let $R_1=\max_{\bar U}r$. Choose an integer $m>0$ so large that $$(m+2)\lambda-n\Lambda-R_1\sup_j\|\beta_j\|_\infty\ge1.$$ Define $W_0=r_0^{-m}-r^{-m}$. It is smooth near $\bar U$, nonnegative there, vanishes exactly at $q$, and a direct differentiation gives $$L_jW_0=m r^{-m-2}\bigl(\operatorname{tr}A_j-(m+2)e^TA_je+r\beta_j\cdot e\bigr)+c_jW_0\le-mr^{-m-2}\le-mR_1^{-m-2}.$$ After multiplying by $R_1^{m+2}/m$, obtain a single $W_q\ge0$ with $W_q(q)=0$, $W_q>0$ on $\bar U\setminus\{q\}$, and $L_jW_q\le-1$ for every $j$. [given, F2]

1.12 Fix $0<\epsilon<1$. Continuity of $G$ at $q$ gives a neighborhood $N$ of $q$ where $|G(x)-g(q)|<\epsilon/2$. Uniform approximation gives $|G_j-G|<\epsilon/2$ on $\bar U$ for all sufficiently large $j$. Thus $|G_j-g(q)|<\epsilon$ on $N\cap\bar U$. On the compact complementary set $\bar U\setminus N$, $W_q$ has a strictly positive minimum; choose $K$ so large that $$|G_j-g(q)|\le\epsilon+KW_q\quad\hbox{on all of }\bar U$$ for all sufficiently large $j$, and also $$K\ge R+C_0(|g(q)|+\epsilon).$$ Apply comparison on $V_j$ to $$z_j^+=u_j-g(q)-\epsilon-KW_q,\qquad z_j^-=-u_j+g(q)-\epsilon-KW_q.$$ They are nonpositive on $\partial V_j$, and $$L_jz_j^+=f_j-c_j(g(q)+\epsilon)-KL_jW_q\ge-R-C_0(|g(q)|+\epsilon)+K\ge0,$$ $$L_jz_j^-=-f_j+c_j(g(q)-\epsilon)-KL_jW_q\ge-R-C_0(|g(q)|+\epsilon)+K\ge0.$$ Therefore $$|u_j(x)-g(q)|\le\epsilon+KW_q(x)\quad(x\in V_j)$$ for all sufficiently large $j$. Passing to the interior limit gives the same bound for $u$ on $U$. Let $x\to q$ from inside $U$ and use $W_q(x)\to0$; then $\limsup_{x\to q}|u(x)-g(q)|\le\epsilon$. Since $\epsilon$ was arbitrary, $u(x)\to g(q)$. Set $u=g$ on $\partial U$. The resulting function is continuous at every boundary point and in the interior, hence belongs to $C(\bar U)$. [given, F2]

1.13 This proves existence. The exponential-barrier comparison from the residual-stability lemma applied to the difference of two solutions proves uniqueness. Its stated residual estimate applied to $u-h$ proves the stability branch without any regularity of $h$ stronger than $C^2(U)\cap C(\bar U)$ plus bounded residual. No boundary-correction existence needs to be assumed. [given, F2]

1.14 Now set $g=0$ and choose $G=G_j=0$ exactly. Let $u_j$ be the corresponding approximants above. For them, the positive equation expands equivalently to $$\operatorname{div}(A_jDu_j)+q_j\cdot Du_j+c_ju_j=f_j,\qquad q_j=\beta_j-\operatorname{div}A_j.$$ The bounds on $DA_j,\beta_j$ give $\sup_j\|q_j\|_\infty\le Q_1<\infty$. This is where the original $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity of $A$ is used; existence in the purely nondivergence formulation required only $C^\alpha$ principal coefficients after an appropriate different approximation argument. [given, F2, F7, F9]

1.15 Multiply by $u_j$, integrate over $V_j$, and use $u_j=0$ on its smooth boundary: $$\lambda\|Du_j\|_2^2\le\|f_j\|_2\|u_j\|_2+Q_1\|Du_j\|_2\|u_j\|_2+\|c_j\|_\infty\|u_j\|_2^2.$$ Young's inequality gives $$\|Du_j\|_2^2\le C\bigl(\|f_j\|_2^2+\|u_j\|_2^2\bigr).$$ The uniform supremum estimate with $Q=0$ yields $\|u_j\|_2\le |U|^{1/2}C\|f\|_\infty$, and $\|f_j\|_2\le|U|^{1/2}\|f\|_\infty$. Thus $$\sup_j\|u_j\|_{H^1(V_j)}\le C_U\|f\|_\infty.$$ Because $u_j$ is smooth to its smooth boundary and zero there, it lies in $H^1_0(V_j)$. Extend it by zero to $U$; approximation of each class by $C_c^\infty(V_j)\subset C_c^\infty(U)$ proves that this extension belongs to $H^1_0(U)$ and has the same $H^1$ norm. [given, F2, F7, F9]

1.16 For completeness, no unproved compactness premise is hidden here. In the Hilbert space $H^1_0(U)$, take the closed span of the countable sequence of extensions. Apply Gram–Schmidt to its listed vectors, discarding zeros, to obtain a finite or countable orthonormal basis of that span. Boundedness, diagonal extraction of the scalar coordinates, and Bessel's inequality give square-summable limiting coordinates and a vector in that closed span. Approximate each test vector by its finite basis sums; the common norm bound then proves convergence against every inner product test vector in that span. For any ambient Hilbert test vector $z$, finite Bessel bounds make the series of its coordinates in this basis converge in the closed span, and its residual is orthogonal to every basis vector and hence to the span; replacing $z$ by this series thus gives the same pairing; Riesz representation therefore proves weak convergence in the ambient Hilbert space, including convergence against the bounded $L^2$ pairings of functions and gradients. Its $L^2$ restriction to every compact interior ball agrees with $u$, since the chosen local-classical subsequence converges uniformly there. Thus the weak limit is the function $u$ almost everywhere on $U$. It follows that $$u\in H^1_0(U),\qquad\|u\|_{H^1(U)}\le C_U\|f\|_\infty.$$ Equivalently the weak limit in $H^1(U)$ remains in the closed linear subspace $H^1_0(U)$; the direct closed-span construction already takes place in that subspace. [given, F2, F7, F9]

1.17 Passing the original weak equations to the limit against any $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(U)$ is legitimate by local uniform convergence of coefficients/data and weak convergence of gradients. The divergence representation above shows that $u$ solves the variational equation; density extends it to all $H^1_0$ tests because $A,q,c,f$ are bounded. This establishes both the finite-energy membership and the correct weak interpretation, rather than inferring them from continuity and zero boundary values alone. [given, F2, F7, F9]

1.18 For a general $C^{2,\alpha}$ lifting $G$, apply this zero-boundary result to $v=u-G$ with forcing $f-LG\in C^{0,\alpha}(U)$. Uniqueness of the classical Dirichlet problem identifies that zero-boundary solution with $u-G$. [given, F2, F7, F9]

1.19 Suppose $n\ge2$, $U$ is $C^{2,\alpha}$ and the datum has the stated ambient lifting $G$. Use the smooth interior approximating domains $V_j$ from [F8], which have uniform $C^{2,\alpha}$ graph charts and eventually contain every compact subset of $U$. Write $d_j=\operatorname{dist}(\bar V_j,\mathbb R^n\setminus U)>0$. Repeat the already proved smooth-coefficient construction at scales $0<r_j<d_j/4$ tending to zero, so all coefficient, forcing and lifting convolution evaluations near $\bar V_j$ remain inside $U$. Uniform ellipticity, symmetry, the expanded-potential sign and all global $C^\alpha$ bounds are preserved. For the undifferentiated $a,b$ terms, their finite first-derivative bounds yield a global Lipschitz bound on this fixed smooth domain: in each graph patch, sufficiently close points are connected inside a slightly larger patch by a path of length at most $C|x-y|$; a finite cover handles close pairs and the supremum bound handles separated pairs. The prescribed highest-derivative Hölder norms then give the uniform expanded coefficient norms. The lifting mollifications have uniformly bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ norms and converge uniformly near the closure. [given, F1, F4, F8]

1.20 Let $u_j$ be the smooth Dirichlet solutions on $V_j$ with forcing $f_j$ and boundary lifting $G_j$. Their existence and smoothness up to the smooth boundary were proved by the Sobolev-bootstrap helper before using any boundary Schauder estimate. The exponential comparison gives a uniform supremum bound. Apply [F8] to the already smooth zero-boundary functions $w_j=u_j-G_j$, whose forcings $f_j-L_jG_j$ have uniformly bounded $C^\alpha$ norms. The domain geometry and coefficient controls are uniform, so $\sup_j\|u_j\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar V_j)}\le C(\|f\|_{0,\alpha;U}+\|G\|_{2,\alpha;\bar U})$. [given, F1, F2, F4, F8]

2.1 The existing interior compactness and exterior-ball boundary comparison arguments give a subsequence converging locally in $C^2(U)$ to the unique classical Dirichlet solution $u$. The displayed global derivative bounds pass to this local limit. For any fixed distinct $x,y\in U$, both points eventually lie in $V_j$, so their second-derivative Hölder quotient passes to the limit with the same common bound. Hence $D^2u$ is bounded and globally $\alpha$-Hölder on $U$, and extends continuously to the closure. The function and gradient extend continuously as well: bounded first and second derivatives give Lipschitz bounds along the controlled-length local interior paths in each graph patch, and separated pairs are bounded by the global suprema. These extensions are the continuous extensions of the interior derivatives. Consequently $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\bar U)$ with the stated data estimate, obtained entirely from smooth approximants without assuming the original solution's boundary Hölder norm. Together with the parent's one-dimensional argument and the prior local existence, uniqueness, stability and energy steps, all branches follow. [given, F2, F3, F6, F8] ∎

## Remarks

The source's globally bounded $C^{2,\alpha}(U)$ claim for merely continuous boundary data and an exterior-sphere domain is false; the separate false statement and its native sector counterexample preserve that assertion and its refutation. The correct unconditional class here is local $C^{2,\alpha}$ with continuity on the closure.

The printed expression $\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_ju+b_i u)$ repeats the $b$ term $n$ times. The intended single-divergence expression and the displayed expanded coefficients are used here. The simple residual barrier constant depends on the expanded drift and potential; no dependence solely on the source's pointwise $\lambda_0,\Lambda,v$ bounds is asserted.

The smooth-boundary global branch is proved using explicit Newtonian/Poisson half-ball estimates and freezing on smooth interior approximants. The solution's boundary regularity is obtained only after passing the resulting uniform estimates to the local classical limit. The published boundary Schauder carrier's externally quoted half-ball input is not consumed. No new external source-reading credit is claimed by this repair.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $0<\alpha<1$, $R>0$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on $B_R(x_0)$ with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, $[A]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\le K$, and $b,c\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$ with finite global Hölder seminorms. Let $u\in C^2(B_R(x_0))\cap L^\infty(B_R(x_0))$ satisfy $Lu=f$ pointwise with $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$. Then $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(B_{R/2}(x_0))$ and
$$\|u\|^{*}_{2,\alpha;B_{R/2}(x_0)}\le C\bigl(\|u\|_{\infty;B_R(x_0)}+R^2\|f\|_{\infty;B_R(x_0)}+R^{2+\alpha}[f]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\bigr),$$
where $C$ depends only on $n,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda$ and the finite dimensionless coefficient bounds $R^\alpha K+R\|b\|_\infty+R^{1+\alpha}[b]_{0,\alpha}+R^2\|c\|_\infty+R^{2+\alpha}[c]_{0,\alpha}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, $n\ge2$, $0<\alpha<1$, $R>0$, $x_0$, the operator $L$ with the stated bounds, $u\in C^2(B_R(x_0))\cap L^\infty$ and $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$ with $Lu=f$ pointwise.

[A1] The only choice assumption is Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, used through the measure, potential and estimate interfaces below. No full Axiom of Choice is used. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] The scaled norms are $\|w\|^{*}_{2,\alpha;B_\rho}=\sum_{j=0}^2\rho^j\max_{|\beta|=j}\sup_{B_\rho}|D^\beta w|+\rho^{2+\alpha}\max_{|\beta|=2}[D^\beta w]_{0,\alpha;B_\rho}$ and $\|g\|^{*}_{0,\alpha;B_\rho}=\sup_{B_\rho}|g|+\rho^\alpha[g]_{0,\alpha;B_\rho}$; the scaling identity $\|w\circ\sigma_\rho\|^{*}_{2,\alpha;B_1}=\|w\|^{*}_{2,\alpha;B_\rho}$ holds for $\sigma_\rho(z)=x_0+\rho z$. ([[def-local-holder-and-c-two-alpha-norms-on-euclidean-balls]], [[def-holder-spaces-c-k-alpha-and-their-scaled-norms]])

[F2] The interior Poisson (Laplace) estimate: for $n\ge2$, $0<\alpha<1$ and $v\in C^2(B_\tau)\cap L^\infty(B_\tau)$ with $-\Delta v=g\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_\tau)$ pointwise, one has $\|v\|^{*}_{2,\alpha;B_{\tau/2}}\le C_{n,\alpha}(\|v\|_{\infty;B_\tau}+\tau^2\|g\|_{\infty;B_\tau}+\tau^{2+\alpha}[g]_{0,\alpha;B_\tau})$. ([[thm-interior-estimate-for-poisson-equation-with-holder-data]])

[F3] Uniform small-ball freezing ([[lem-freezing-coefficients-and-schauder-error-estimate]]): for every $\epsilon>0$ there are $\eta_\epsilon\in(0,1]$ and $C_\epsilon$, depending only on the dimensionless coefficient bounds and ellipticity, such that the freezing bound holds for every $0<r\le R\eta_\epsilon$ on a ball centered at the frozen point. For a recentered patch with center $x\in B_{3R/4}(x_0)$, apply that lemma on the ambient ball $B_{R/8}(x)$, which lies in $B_{7R/8}(x_0)$ and has dimensionless coefficient bounds no larger than the original ones; hence the same normalized cutoff gives the bound for every $0<r\le R\eta_\epsilon/8$ on that patch.

[F4] Linear normalization and ellipsoid-to-ball geometry. If $A_0$ is symmetric positive definite with spectrum in $[\lambda,\Lambda]$, put $S=A_0^{1/2}$ and $v(y)=w(x+Sy)$. Then $A_0:D_x^2w(x+Sy)=\Delta_yv(y)$, $\|S\|\le\sqrt\Lambda$ and $\|S^{-1}\|\le1/\sqrt\lambda$ ([[def-uniformly-elliptic-nondivergence-operator]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]). For every $r>0$, $S(B_{r/\sqrt\Lambda})\subseteq B_r$ and $B_{\theta_{\rm geo}r}\subseteq S(B_{r/(2\sqrt\Lambda)})$ with $\theta_{\rm geo}:=\frac12\sqrt{\lambda/\Lambda}$. Consequently, for every $0<\theta\le\theta_{\rm geo}$, the Poisson estimate on $B_{r/\sqrt\Lambda}$ controls the original solution on $B_{\theta r}$, with norm-comparison constants depending only on $\lambda,\Lambda$.

[F5] Local $L^2$ Hessian bound for Newtonian potentials ([[lem-interior-w-two-p-regularity-for-the-laplacian]]): if $g\in L^2_c(\mathbb R^n)$ and $w=Ng$, then $w\in W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and its Hessian has the local estimate proved by Newtonian–Riesz representation. For $g$ supported in a ball $B_r$ with $\int g=0$, rescaling the fundamental solution and using the local Young bound for $N$ and $\nabla N$ gives, for every fixed $C_0>1$, $\|w\|_{L^2(B_{C_0r})}\le C r^2\|g\|_{L^2(B_r)}$; in dimension $2$ the logarithmic scaling term vanishes because $\int g=0$. Rescaling the local $W^{2,2}$ estimate on concentric balls then gives $\|D^2w\|_{L^2(B_r)}\le C\|g\|_{L^2(B_r)}$. The same conclusion for a frozen operator $A_0:D^2$ follows from [F4], with constants depending on $n,\lambda,\Lambda$. ([[lem-interior-w-two-p-regularity-for-the-laplacian]])

[F6] Harmonic excess decay. If $h$ is $A_0$-harmonic on $B_r(x)$, then for every sufficiently small $\theta=\theta(n,\lambda,\Lambda)\in(0,\theta_{\rm geo}]$,
$$\left(\frac{1}{|B_{\theta r}(x)|}\int_{B_{\theta r}(x)}|D^2h-(D^2h)_{B_{\theta r}(x)}|^2\right)^{1/2}\le C_0\theta\left(\frac{1}{|B_r(x)|}\int_{B_r(x)}|D^2h-(D^2h)_{B_r(x)}|^2\right)^{1/2}.$$
Indeed each component of $D^2h-(D^2h)_{B_r}$ is harmonic; transform by [F4], apply the interior derivative estimate for harmonic functions, and compare the contained and containing balls. Weakly harmonic components are smooth by [[cor-locally-integrable-weakly-harmonic-functions-are-smooth]], and the derivative bound is [[thm-interior-derivative-estimates-for-harmonic-functions]].

[F7] For $G\in L^1(B)$, write $(G)_B:=|B|^{-1}\int_BG$; this is the ball-average operator of [[def-ball-average-operator-on-r-n]]. In particular, $(G)_{B_r(x)}$ is constant in $x$ for each fixed ball and the volume ratio of concentric balls is $(r/s)^n$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Ellipsoid geometry for freezing. Fix $x\in B_{3R/4}(x_0)$, a radius $0<r\le R/8$ with $B_r(x)\subset B_{7R/8}(x_0)$, and set $A_0=A(x)$, $S=A_0^{1/2}$, and $\tau=r/\sqrt\Lambda$. For $v(y):=u(x+Sy)$, [F4] gives $\Delta v=(L_{x}u)\circ(x+S\cdot)$ on $B_\tau$, since $S(B_\tau)\subset B_r(x)$. Equivalently, $-\Delta v=-f\circ(x+S\cdot)+((L-L_x)u)\circ(x+S\cdot)$, so the estimate [F2] applies with this signed right-hand side. Fix any $0<\theta\le\theta_{\rm geo}$; the target ball $B_{\theta r}(x)$ lies in $x+S(B_{\tau/2})$. Thus [F2], restricted from this ellipsoid to the target ball, yields $\|u\|^*_{2,\alpha;B_{\theta r}(x)}\le C\Bigl(\|u\|_{\infty;B_r(x)}+r^2\|f\|_{\infty;B_r(x)}+r^{2+\alpha}[f]_{0,\alpha;B_r(x)}+r^2\|(L-L_x)u\|^*_{0,\alpha;B_r(x)}\Bigr),$ with $C=C(n,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda)$. This estimate is conditional on the Hessian having a finite Hölder seminorm on the patch. The independent bootstrap below establishes that condition before its later quantitative use; $C^2$ alone does not establish it. [F1, F2, F4, given, algebra]

1.2 A noncircular Campanato bootstrap. Put $H=D^2u$ and $Q:=1+\|u\|_{C^2(\overline{B_{7R/8}(x_0)})}+\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(B_{7R/8})}+\|b\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(B_R)}+\|c\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(B_R)}$. For $x\in B_{3R/4}(x_0)$ and $0<r\le R/8$, let $E_x(r):=\left(\frac{1}{|B_r(x)|}\int_{B_r(x)}|H-(H)_{B_r(x)}|^2\right)^{1/2},\qquad g_x:=f-b\cdot Du-cu-(A-A(x)):D^2u.$ Then $A(x):D^2u=g_x$ pointwise. The product oscillation estimate, $[A]_{0,\alpha}\le K$, and the boundedness of $Du,D^2u$ on $\overline{B_{7R/8}}$ give $\operatorname{osc}_2(g_x;B_r(x))\le C K r^\alpha\bigl(E_x(r)+|(H)_{B_r(x)}|\bigr)+C_Qr^\alpha\le C r^\alpha E_x(r)+C_Qr^\alpha,$ where $\operatorname{osc}_2(q;B):=(\frac{1}{|B|}\int_B|q-(q)_B|^2)^{1/2}$; $C_Q$ is finite and may depend on the preliminary bound $Q$. No Hölder regularity of $D^2u$ is used here. [F1, F7, given, algebra]

2.1 Constant-coefficient replacement and excess decay. Let $m_x=(g_x)_{B_r(x)}$. Extend $g_x-m_x$ by zero from $B_r(x)$, transform the frozen operator by [F4], and take $w_x$ to be the negative of its Newtonian potential, so $A(x):D^2w_x=g_x-m_x$ because $N$ is normalized by $-\Delta Ng=g$. The datum has mean zero, so [F5] gives $\|D^2w_x\|_{L^2(B_r(x))}\le C\|g_x-m_x\|_{L^2(B_r(x))}$. Choose a quadratic $q_x$ with $A(x):D^2q_x=m_x$ and put $h_x=u-w_x-q_x$. Then $h_x$ is weakly $A(x)$-harmonic on $B_r(x)$; its Hessian is smooth there by [F6], and $D^2q_x$ is constant. Apply [F6] to $h_x$, use $E_x(r)\le E_{h_x}(r)+C\operatorname{osc}_2(g_x;B_r)$ and the volume ratio between $B_r$ and $B_{\theta r}$ to obtain $E_x(\theta r)\le C_0\theta E_x(r)+C_1\theta^{-n/2}\operatorname{osc}_2(g_x;B_r)\le qE_x(r)+C_Qr^\alpha.$ Choose $\theta\le\theta_{\rm geo}$ so $C_0\theta<\frac14\theta^\alpha$, then choose a uniform $r_0\le R/8$ so $C_1\theta^{-n/2}CKr_0^\alpha<\frac14\theta^\alpha$; thus $q<\frac12\theta^\alpha$. Iterating over $r_j=\theta^jr_0$ and using $E_x(r_0)\le2\|H\|_{L^\infty(B_{7R/8})}$ gives $E_x(r_j)\le C_Qr_j^\alpha$. For intermediate radii, $E_x(s)\le(r_j/s)^{n/2}E_x(r_j)$ when $r_{j+1}<s\le r_j$, so the same bound holds for every $0<s\le r_0$, uniformly for $x\in B_{3R/4}$. [step 1.2, F4, F5, F6, F7, A1, algebra]

3.1 Campanato embedding on the nested-patch region. Since $H$ is continuous, the means $(H)_{B_s(x)}$ converge to $H(x)$ as $s\downarrow0$. Telescoping the dyadic means and using step 2.1 gives $|H(x)-(H)_{B_s(x)}|\le C_Qs^\alpha$ for every $x\in B_{3R/4}$ and $0<s\le r_0$. If $x,y\in B_{5R/8}$ and $d:=|x-y|<r_0/8$, then $B_{2d}(x)$ and $B_{2d}(y)$ are both contained in $B_{4d}(x)$; comparing each of their means with $(H)_{B_{4d}(x)}$ costs only the fixed volume ratio $|B_{4d}|/|B_{2d}|=2^n$ and is bounded by $C E_x(4d)$. Since $4d<r_0/2$, the Step 2.1 excess estimate applies at this radius, and the telescoping estimates for $x$ and $y$ give $|H(x)-H(y)|\le C_Qd^\alpha$. For $d\ge r_0/8$, the preliminary bound $2\|H\|_\infty\le C_Qd^\alpha$ applies. Therefore $D^2u\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_{5R/8})$, in particular on $B_{R/2}$, before the quantitative Schauder estimate is invoked. The preliminary constant $C_Q$ is used only to prove finiteness. [step 2.1, F7, given, algebra]

4.1 A local finite-norm estimate with corrected nested radii. Now that the norm is finite, apply [F3] in step 1.1 with arbitrary small error $\epsilon$ to the term $(L-L_x)u$ on any recentered patch of radius $r\le R\eta_\epsilon/8$. Use part (i) of the Hölder interpolation lemma to bound the first-derivative term in the local scaled norm by an arbitrarily small multiple of $r^2\|D^2u\|_\infty+r^{2+\alpha}[D^2u]_{0,\alpha}$ plus $C_\epsilon\|u\|_\infty$. Thus, for any prescribed $\eta>0$, the choices of the freezing and interpolation parameters give $\|u\|^*_{2,\alpha;B_{\vartheta r}(x)}\le C_\eta\bigl(\|u\|_{\infty;B_r(x)}+r^2\|f\|_{\infty;B_r(x)}+r^{2+\alpha}[f]_{0,\alpha;B_r(x)}\bigr)+\eta\bigl(r^2\|D^2u\|_{\infty;B_r(x)}+r^{2+\alpha}[D^2u]_{0,\alpha;B_r(x)}\bigr).$ The constant $C_\eta$ may depend on the dimensionless coefficient bounds, ellipticity, and the chosen normalized patch radius; the small factor $\eta$ multiplies only the top-order terms after interpolation. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, step 3.1]

5.1 Hole filling with interpolation of the separated-pair term. Write $H(s):=R^{2+\alpha}\max_{|\beta|=2}[D^\beta u]_{0,\alpha;B_s(x_0)}$, $M(s):=R^2\max_{|\beta|=2}\sup_{B_s(x_0)}|D^\beta u|$, and $S_R:=\|u\|_{\infty;B_R}+R^2\|f\|_{\infty;B_R}+R^{2+\alpha}[f]_{0,\alpha;B_R}$. Fix $\gamma\in(0,2^{-(2+\alpha)})$. For $R/2\le s<t\le5R/8$, put $r=(t-s)/2$, requiring $r\le R\eta_\epsilon/8$ as in step 4.1. Apply that estimate centered at every $x\in B_s(x_0)$, with one fixed target fraction $\vartheta>0$. If $x,y\in B_s$ and $|x-y|<\vartheta r/2$, the pair lies in the target ball centered at $x$, so dividing its local Hessian seminorm estimate by $r^{2+\alpha}$ bounds the corresponding quotient. For pairs with $|x-y|\ge\vartheta r/2$, use $|D^\beta u(x)-D^\beta u(y)|\le2\sup_{B_t}|D^\beta u|$. Thus, for $0<\eta\le1$, $$H(s)\le C_\eta(R/r)^{2+\alpha}S_R+C_0\eta H(t)+C_1(R/r)^\alpha M(t),$$ with $C_0,C_1$ fixed by $n,\alpha,\vartheta$; the last term includes both the local Hessian-sup error and the separated pairs. Part (ii) of the interpolation lemma on $B_t$, with $R/2\le t\le5R/8$, gives $M(t)\le\zeta H(t)+C(1+\zeta^{-2/\alpha})\|u\|_{\infty;B_t}$ for $0<\zeta\le1$: this quantitative dependence follows directly from its order-two difference estimate by choosing the normalized difference scale proportional to $\zeta^{1/\alpha}$. Choose $\eta$ with $C_0\eta\le\gamma/2$, then choose $\zeta=\min\{1,\gamma/(2C_1)\}(r/R)^\alpha$. The term containing $M(t)$ is at most $\gamma H(t)/2+C_\gamma(R/r)^{2+\alpha}S_R$. Consequently $$H(s)\le C_\gamma(R/r)^{2+\alpha}S_R+\gamma H(t).$$ After these choices, let $\delta_0=\min\{R/16,R\eta_\epsilon/4\}$, $\delta_j=\delta_0 2^{-j}$, $s_0=R/2$ and $s_{j+1}=s_j+\delta_j$. Then $r_j=\delta_j/2$ meets the local-radius restriction and $s_j\uparrow s_\infty\le5R/8$. Iteration has data series bounded by $C_\gamma(2R/\delta_0)^{2+\alpha}\sum_{j\ge0}(\gamma2^{2+\alpha})^jS_R$; its terminal term tends to zero because $H(s_j)\le H(5R/8)<\infty$ by step 3.1. Hence $H(R/2)\le CS_R$. Parts (ii) and (i) of the interpolation lemma, now at a fixed parameter on $B_{R/2}$, bound the scaled second- and first-derivative suprema by $C(H(R/2)+\|u\|_\infty)$. This proves the full scaled norm estimate, with constants depending only on the stated dimensionless bounds and not on the preliminary bootstrap constant $Q$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, F3, induction, algebra]

6.1 Conclusion. Step 3.1 establishes the claimed local regularity noncircularly, and step 5.1 proves the displayed quantitative estimate on the original half ball. The constant is uniform in $R$ when the stated dimensionless coefficient bounds are uniform. The strict range $0<\alpha<1$ enters through the Poisson estimate, the freezing lemma, and the Campanato iteration; no boundary condition is used. [step 3.1, step 5.1, given] ∎

## Remarks

- The two ingredients are exactly the constant-coefficient estimate for the frozen operator and the small-ball absorption of the coefficient oscillation; the lower-order coefficients are treated as data inside the freezing error.
- The dependence of the constant on $R$ enters only through the ratio $R/\rho$, where $\rho$ is determined by the dimensionless coefficient bounds; this is why those bounds are the natural parameters of the estimate.

## Statement

Let $m\ge0$, $n\ge1$, and $r\ge1$ be integers, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$
be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a $C^r$ map with

$$ r>\max\{m-n,0\}. $$

Then the critical value set of $f$ is a null subset of $\mathbb R^n$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $n\ge 1$ and a $C^r$ map $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ with $r>\max\{m-n,0\}$.

[F1] For every $C^1$ Euclidean map, the critical locus consists of points where the total derivative is not onto, and the critical-value set is its image, including for zero-dimensional source ([[def-c1-critical-locus-and-critical-value-set-in-euclidean-spaces]]). We write these sets as $\operatorname{Crit}(f)$ and $\operatorname{CV}(f)$.

[F2] Nullity is expressed by countable cube covers of arbitrarily small total volume ([[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]).

[L1] Compact null sections reassemble into a null set, and the nonflat and flat critical strata have null images under the hypotheses of the preceding lemmas ([[lem-sard-slicing-for-compact-null-sections]], [[lem-sard-on-the-nonflat-critical-strata]], [[lem-sard-on-the-infinitely-flat-critical-stratum]]).

[L2] A $C^1$ Euclidean map with invertible derivative has a local $C^1$ inverse $g$, with $Dg=(Df\circ g)^{-1}$ ([[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]). For a $C^r$ map this inverse is $C^r$: inductively, if $g$ is $C^k$ and $k<r$, then $Df\circ g$ is $C^k$, and matrix inversion is $C^k$ on invertible matrices by the adjugate-over-determinant formula; the displayed identity makes $Dg$ $C^k$, hence $g$ $C^{k+1}$.

## Proof
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Prove the assertion by induction on the source dimension $m$, keeping the differentiability order $r$ fixed. If $m=0$, then $U$ is at most a point, so $\operatorname{Crit}(f)$ and its image are finite, hence null in $\mathbb R^n$. Assume $m\ge1$ and the theorem proved for all smaller source dimensions and every positive target dimension satisfying the same differentiability inequality. Exhaust $U$ by the canonically enumerated rational closed cubes with closures inside $U$. We use the following choice-free countable-union observation throughout: every compact null subset of $\mathbb R^n$ has, for each positive rational budget, a **finite** rational-cube cover below that budget. Indeed, start with a countable cube cover of total volume below half the budget from [F2], enlarge its cubes slightly to rational open cubes while retaining the budget, and take a finite subcover by compactness. Enumerate all finite rational-cube families and use the first qualifying family for each compact set and budget. For a countable sequence of compact null sets, use budgets $\varepsilon2^{-i-1}$ and combine these canonical finite covers; [F2] makes their union null without making countably many arbitrary choices. Thus it suffices to prove $f(\operatorname{Crit}(f)\cap Q_\nu)$ null for each cube: these images are compact and their countable union is the critical value set of [F1]. [F1, F2, given, construct, cases]

2.1 Fix one cube $Q_\nu$ and put $$ C_0:=\operatorname{Crit}(f)\cap Q_\nu,\qquad C_j:=\{x\in Q_\nu:D^\alpha f(x)=0\text{ for every }1\le|\alpha|\le j\} \quad(j\ge 1). $$ These are the intersections of $Q_\nu$ with the corresponding closed strata in $U$. Then $$ C_0=(C_0\setminus C_1)\cup\bigcup_{j=1}^{r-1}(C_j\setminus C_{j+1})\cup C_r. $$ For each $1\le j<r$ and each $\ell\ge 1$, the set $$ K_{j,\ell}:=\{x\in C_j:\operatorname{dist}(x,C_{j+1})\ge 1/\ell\} $$ is compact and contained in $C_j\setminus C_{j+1}$ (take distance to the empty set as infinite). Because $$ C_j\setminus C_{j+1}=\bigcup_{\ell\ge 1}K_{j,\ell}, $$ the nonflat lemma in [L1] applies: its lower-dimensional Sard premise holds by the induction hypothesis at the unchanged order $r$, since $r>\max\{m-n,0\}$ implies $r>\max\{(m-1)-n,0\}$. Each $f(K_{j,\ell})$ is compact null, so the canonical-cover observation in step 1.1 makes $f(C_j\setminus C_{j+1})$ null. Also, $C_r$ is compact, and $r>\max\{m-n,0\}$ implies $rn\ge m$; the flat lemma in [L1] makes $f(C_r)$ null. [L1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 It remains to show that $f(C_0\setminus C_1)$ is null. If $n=1$, then a linear map $\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R$ is surjective exactly when it is nonzero, so $C_0=C_1$ and there is nothing to prove. Assume $n>1$, and fix $x\in C_0\setminus C_1$. Some first partial derivative of some component of $f$ is nonzero at $x$; after reordering coordinates and components, assume $$ \frac{\partial f^1}{\partial x^1}(x)\neq 0. $$ By [L2], after shrinking choose a neighbourhood $W_x$ of $x$ and a $C^r$ diffeomorphism $$ \Phi_x(y):=\bigl(f^1(y),y^2,\ldots,y^m\bigr) $$ from $W_x$ onto an open set $I_x\times\Omega_x\subseteq\mathbb R\times \mathbb R^{m-1}$. Write $$ f\circ\Phi_x^{-1}(t,u)=\bigl(t,\widetilde f_x(t,u)\bigr). $$ Each slice map $u\mapsto \widetilde f_x(t,u)$ is $C^r$, and because $$ r>\max\{m-n,0\}=\max\{(m-1)-(n-1),0\}, $$ the induction hypothesis applies to those maps. If $q=\Phi_x^{-1}(t,u)\in C_0\cap W_x$, then in these coordinates the differential of $f$ has block form $$ Df_q=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ *&D(\widetilde f_x)_t(u)\end{bmatrix}, $$ so $q$ is critical for $f$ exactly when $u$ is a critical point of the slice $u\mapsto\widetilde f_x(t,u)$. For every rational open cube $B$ whose closure lies in $W_x$, the compact set $f(C_0\cap\overline B)$ has sections contained in the slice critical value sets, hence null in $\mathbb R^{n-1}$ by induction. The slicing lemma in [L1] makes this compact image null in $\mathbb R^n$. Consider **all** rational cubes $B$ for which such an $x$ and chart exist; they form a countable family covering $C_0\setminus C_1$. Each has the compact-null conclusion just proved, independently of which witnessing chart exists. The canonical-cover observation in step 1.1 makes their image union $f(C_0\setminus C_1)$ null without selecting charts or covers countably. [L1, L2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Step 2.1 shows that $f(C_j\setminus C_{j+1})$ is null for every $1\le j<r$ and that $f(C_r)$ is null, while step 2.2 handles $f(C_0\setminus C_1)$. Hence $$ f(C_0)=f(\operatorname{Crit}(f)\cap Q_\nu) $$ is null. Applying step 1.1 shows that the whole critical value set of $f$ is null. [F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

**Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice** ([[def-dependent-choice]]). Let
$(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space.

1. If $X$ is normal ([[def-normal-and-t4-spaces]]), $A \subseteq X$ is closed
   ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]) and $a \le b$ are reals, then every
   continuous $f : A \to [a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) extends to a continuous
   $F : X \to [a,b]$ with $F|_A = f$.
2. Conversely, if for every closed $A \subseteq X$ and every reals $a \le b$
   every continuous $f : A \to [a,b]$ extends to a continuous $F : X \to [a,b]$
   with $F|_A = f$, then $X$ is normal. **This direction uses no choice
   principle.**

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A topological space $(X,\mathcal{T})$ and dependent choice; for clause 1, $X$ normal, $A \subseteq X$ closed, reals $a \le b$, and continuous $f : A \to [a,b]$; for clause 2, $X$ such that the extension property of clause 1 holds for every closed subspace and every $a \le b$.

[A1] $\mathrm{DC}$: for every nonempty set $P$, every relation $R$ entire on $P$, and every $a \in P$, there is a sequence $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ with $p_0=a$ and $p_k \mathbin{R} p_{k+1}$ for every $k$ ([[def-dependent-choice]]).

[A2] Normal: disjoint closed sets admit disjoint open supersets ([[def-normal-and-t4-spaces]]).

[L1] Urysohn's lemma, clause 1: assuming DC, if $X$ is normal and $P, Q \subseteq X$ are disjoint closed sets, there is a continuous $h : X \to [0,1]$ with $P \subseteq h^{-1}(\{0\})$, $Q \subseteq h^{-1}(\{1\})$ ([[thm-urysohn-lemma]]).

[L2] If $A$ is closed in $X$ and $C \subseteq A$ is closed in the subspace $A$, then $C$ is closed in $X$: by [[def-subspace-topology-top]] $C = F \cap A$ for some closed $F \subseteq X$, and an intersection of two closed sets of $X$ is closed ([[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]], [[def-topological-space]]).

[L3] Preimages of closed sets under a continuous map are closed ([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (c)); preimages of open sets are open (clause (b)).

[L4] The geometric series: $\sum_{n \ge 0} (2/3)^n = 1/(1-2/3) = 3$ ([[thm-geometric-series]]), so $\sum_{n\ge0} M_n/3 = r$ for $M_n := r(2/3)^n$ and any real $r$; and $(2/3)^n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ (the same theorem's proof, [[lem-geometric-sequence-null]]).

[L5] The $M$-test: continuous $(g_n)$ on $X$, nonnegative reals $(N_n)$ with $|g_n(x)|\le N_n$ for all $x,n$ and $\sum N_n$ convergent, give $\sum g_n(x)$ convergent for every $x$ and $\sum_n g_n$ continuous on $X$ ([[lem-a-uniformly-approximable-real-valued-map-is-continuous]], second clause).

[L6] Finite triangle inequality $|\sum_k u_k| \le \sum_k |u_k|$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]); a real sequence has at most one limit, and limits preserve non-strict order ([[lem-of-sequence-basics]]).

[L7] The order rays $(-\infty,\tfrac12)$ and $(\tfrac12,\infty)$ are open in the usual topology of $\mathbb R$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], clause 3), so their traces $[0,\tfrac12)$ and $(\tfrac12,1]$ are open in the subspace topology of $[0,1]$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]], [[def-interval]]). They are disjoint and contain $0$ and $1$, respectively.

[L8] $A$ and $B$ open in a subspace $S$, with $A \cup B = S$ and $A \cap B = \varnothing$: a function on $S$ constant on $A$ and constant on $B$ is continuous ([[lem-continuity-is-local-and-pastes]], clause 2).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** constructive.

1.1 Assume $X$ is normal, $A \subseteq X$ is closed, $a \le b$ are reals, and $f : A \to [a,b]$ is continuous. [assume-hyp]

1.2 Assume instead that $X$ is such that every continuous $g : C \to [p,q]$ on a closed $C \subseteq X$, $p \le q$ reals, extends continuously to $X \to [p,q]$. [assume-hyp]

2.1 Under step 1.1: if $a=b$ the constant map $F : X \to \{a\} \subseteq [a,b]$, $F \equiv a$, is continuous and $F|_A = f$, since $f : A \to \{a\}$ forces $f \equiv a$. Assume from here that $a<b$. [step 1.1, assume-hyp, construct]

2.2 Under step 1.2: let $C, E \subseteq X$ be disjoint closed sets; $C \cup E$ is closed, and $C, E$ are each open in the subspace $C \cup E$, being the complement there of the other, which is closed. Define $k : C \cup E \to \{0,1\} \subseteq [0,1]$ by $k \equiv 0$ on $C$ and $k \equiv 1$ on $E$; $k$ is constant, hence continuous, on each of $C$ and $E$, so $k$ is continuous on $C \cup E$ by [L8]. [step 1.2, L8, choose, construct]

3.1 Under steps 1.1 and 2.1: put $c := (a+b)/2$ and $r := (b-a)/2 > 0$, and define $f_0 : A \to \mathbb{R}$ by $f_0(x) := f(x)-c$; $f_0$ is continuous, being $f$ minus a constant, and $f_0[A] \subseteq [-r,r]$, since $f[A] \subseteq [a,b] = [c-r,c+r]$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra, construct]

3.2 Under step 1.2: by hypothesis applied to the closed set $C \cup E$ and $p:=0, q:=1$, fix a continuous $K : X \to [0,1]$ with $K|_{C\cup E} = k$. [step 1.2, step 2.2, choose]

4.1 Under step 1.1: for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ put $M_n := r(2/3)^n$. Call a pair $(f_n,g_n)$, with $f_n : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and $g_n : X \to \mathbb{R}$ continuous, **admissible at level $n$** when $|f_n(x)| \le M_n$ for $x \in A$; $|g_n(x)| \le M_n/3$ for $x \in X$; $g_n(x) = -M_n/3$ for $x \in A$ with $f_n(x) \le -M_n/3$; and $g_n(x) = M_n/3$ for $x \in A$ with $f_n(x) \ge M_n/3$. [step 3.1, construct]

4.2 Under step 1.2: by [L7], put $O_1 := K^{-1}(\,[0,\tfrac12)\,)$, $O_2 := K^{-1}(\,(\tfrac12,1]\,)$, open by [L3]. $C \subseteq O_1$, since $K \equiv 0 \in [0,\tfrac12)$ on $C$; $E \subseteq O_2$, since $K \equiv 1 \in (\tfrac12,1]$ on $E$; and $O_1 \cap O_2 = \varnothing$, the two target sets being disjoint. [step 3.2, L7, L3]

5.1 Under step 1.1: put $A_0^- := \{x \in A : f_0(x) \le -M_0/3\}$, $A_0^+ := \{x \in A : f_0(x) \ge M_0/3\}$; both closed in $A$ by [L3] and hence in $X$ by [L2], and disjoint since $-M_0/3 < M_0/3$. By [L1] fix continuous $h_0 : X \to [0,1]$ with $A_0^- \subseteq h_0^{-1}(\{0\})$ and $A_0^+ \subseteq h_0^{-1}(\{1\})$, and put $g_0 := (M_0/3)(2h_0-1)$, continuous. [step 3.1, step 4.1, L1, L2, L3, choose, construct]

5.2 Under step 1.1: let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $(f_n,g_n)$ be admissible at level $n$; define $f_{n+1} : A \to \mathbb{R}$ by $f_{n+1}(x) := f_n(x)-g_n(x)$, continuous. [step 4.1, construct]

5.3 Under step 1.2: since $C, E$ were an arbitrary disjoint closed pair, step 4.2 exhibits disjoint open supersets for every such pair, so $X$ is normal by [A2]; this is clause 2, and it uses [A1] nowhere. [step 4.2, A2]

6.1 Under step 1.1: $(f_0,g_0)$ is admissible at level $0$: $|f_0| \le M_0$ on $A$ by step 3.1; $|g_0(x)| = (M_0/3)|2h_0(x)-1| \le M_0/3$ for every $x$, since $h_0(x) \in [0,1]$; $g_0(x) = -M_0/3$ for $x \in A_0^-$, where $h_0(x)=0$; and $g_0(x)=M_0/3$ for $x \in A_0^+$, where $h_0(x)=1$. [step 5.1, algebra]

6.2 Under step 1.1, continuing under step 5.2: for $x \in A$ with $f_n(x) \le -M_n/3$: $g_n(x)=-M_n/3$ (admissibility), so $f_{n+1}(x) = f_n(x)+M_n/3 \in [-2M_n/3,\,0]$, using $-M_n \le f_n(x) \le -M_n/3$; for $x \in A$ with $f_n(x) \ge M_n/3$: $f_{n+1}(x) = f_n(x)-M_n/3 \in [0,\,2M_n/3]$; for $x \in A$ with $-M_n/3 < f_n(x) < M_n/3$: $|g_n(x)| \le M_n/3$ gives $f_{n+1}(x) \in (-2M_n/3,\,2M_n/3)$. In every case $|f_{n+1}(x)| \le 2M_n/3 = M_{n+1}$. [step 5.2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.3 Under step 1.1: put $A_{n+1}^- := \{x\in A: f_{n+1}(x)\le -M_{n+1}/3\}$, $A_{n+1}^+ := \{x\in A: f_{n+1}(x)\ge M_{n+1}/3\}$; closed in $X$ by [L2], [L3], and disjoint. By [L1] fix continuous $h_{n+1}:X\to[0,1]$ with $A_{n+1}^- \subseteq h_{n+1}^{-1}(\{0\})$, $A_{n+1}^+ \subseteq h_{n+1}^{-1}(\{1\})$, and put $g_{n+1} := (M_{n+1}/3)(2h_{n+1}-1)$. [step 5.2, step 4.1, L1, L2, L3, choose, construct]

7.1 Under step 1.1: $(f_{n+1},g_{n+1})$ is admissible at level $n+1$, by step 6.2 and the same computation as step 6.1 with $h_{n+1}, g_{n+1}, M_{n+1}$ in place of $h_0,g_0,M_0$. So every admissible pair at level $n$ has an admissible successor at level $n+1$. [step 6.2, step 6.3]

8.1 Under step 1.1: put $P := \{\, (n,f_n,g_n) : n \in \mathbb{N},\ (f_n,g_n) \text{ admissible at level } n \,\}$, and for $(n,f,g),(n',f',g') \in P$ say $(n,f,g) \mathbin{R} (n',f',g')$ when $n'=n+1$ and $f' = (f-g)|_A$ pointwise. $P$ is nonempty by step 6.1, and $R$ is entire on $P$ by steps 5.2, 6.2, 6.3 and 7.1 (the pair produced there has $f_{n+1} = (f_n-g_n)|_A$ exactly as step 5.2 defines it). By [A1] with $a := (0,f_0,g_0)$, fix a sequence $\big((n_k,F_k,G_k)\big)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ with $(n_0,F_0,G_0)=(0,f_0,g_0)$ and $(n_k,F_k,G_k) \mathbin{R} (n_{k+1},F_{k+1},G_{k+1})$ for every $k$; as $R$ forces $n'=n+1$, induction gives $n_k=k$, so $(F_k,G_k)$ is admissible at level $k$ for every $k$, with $F_{k+1} = (F_k-G_k)|_A$. [step 6.1, step 7.1, step 5.2, A1, construct]

9.1 Under step 1.1: by [L4], $\sum_n M_n/3 = r$, convergent; by [L5] applied to $(G_n)$ and $(M_n/3)$ (each $|G_n(x)| \le M_n/3$ for all $x$, by admissibility), for every $x \in X$ the series $\sum_n G_n(x)$ converges, and $F := \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} G_n$ is a continuous map $X \to \mathbb{R}$. [step 8.1, L4, L5, construct]

9.2 Under step 1.1: for $x \in A$ and $N \in \mathbb{N}$: by the telescoping of step 8.1, $\sum_{n<N} G_n(x) = F_0(x) - F_N(x) = f_0(x)-F_N(x)$, since $F_0=f_0$. [step 8.1, algebra]

10.1 Under step 1.1: for every $x \in X$ and $N \in \mathbb{N}$, $\big|\sum_{n<N} G_n(x)\big| \le \sum_{n<N}|G_n(x)| \le \sum_{n<N} M_n/3 \le r$, by [L6] and admissibility; letting $N \to \infty$, since $\sum_{n<N}G_n(x) \to F(x)$ (step 9.1) and order is preserved in the limit ([L6]), $|F(x)| \le r$. [step 9.1, L4, L6, algebra]

10.2 Under step 1.1: for $x \in A$: $|F_N(x)| \le M_N = r(2/3)^N \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$, by admissibility of $F_N$ (step 8.1) and [L4]; so by step 9.2, $\sum_{n<N} G_n(x) = f_0(x)-F_N(x) \to f_0(x)-0 = f_0(x)$. [step 9.2, step 8.1, L4]

11.1 Under step 1.1: for $x \in A$: $\sum_{n<N} G_n(x) \to F(x)$ by step 9.1 and $\to f_0(x)$ by step 10.2; since a real sequence has at most one limit ([L6]), $F(x) = f_0(x)$. [step 9.1, step 10.2, L6]

12.1 Under step 1.1: define $\hat F : X \to \mathbb{R}$ by $\hat F(x) := F(x)+c$, continuous; for $x \in X$, $\hat F(x) \in [c-r,c+r] = [a,b]$ by step 10.1; for $x \in A$, $\hat F(x) = F(x)+c = f_0(x)+c = f(x)$ by step 11.1 and the definition of $f_0$ in step 3.1. [step 10.1, step 11.1, step 3.1, algebra, construct]

13.1 Steps 2.1 and 12.1 show that, under the hypothesis of step 1.1, a continuous $F : X \to [a,b]$ with $F|_A=f$ exists — either the constant map of step 2.1 when $a=b$, or $\hat F$ of step 12.1 when $a<b$ — which is clause 1. [step 2.1, step 12.1]

14.1 Steps 13.1 and 5.3 establish clauses 1 and 2 respectively. [step 13.1, step 5.3, discharge-construct] ∎

## Remarks

- **The bound after $n$ stages is $M_n = r(2/3)^n$, with $M_0 = r$, not $r(2/3)^{n-1}$.** Indexing from $n=0$ is what makes step 6.1 the base case rather than a special first step, and it is why the geometric series of [L4] is summed from $n=0$.

- **Choice is spent once more here, genuinely as dependent choice and not in disguise.** Unlike the countable-choice step inside the previous item, the function $g_{n+1}$ chosen in step 6.3 depends on $f_{n+1}$, which is computed from $f_n$ and the *particular* $g_n$ retained in the state $(n,f_n,g_n) \in P$ of step 8.1 — not merely on the index $n$. So the relation $R$ genuinely cannot be replaced by one that ignores its first argument, and this is exactly the situation dependent choice, rather than countable choice alone, is for.

- **The target $[a,b]$ is handled by a shift, not a rescaling.** Working with $f_0 = f - c$ keeps every bound in the construction a plain multiple of $r$, and the final translation $\hat F = F + c$ is the only place $c$ reappears; no affine change of variable on $X$ or on $g_n$ is needed elsewhere.

## Statement

**Assume the Axiom of Choice.** Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq1$. For $Z=\mathbb R$ and for $Z=\mathbb R^n$ with its Euclidean metric:

1. A family $\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,Z)$ is compact in the uniform topology if and only if it is uniformly closed, equicontinuous, and pointwise bounded.
2. Every pointwise bounded equicontinuous sequence in $C(X,Z)$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence with limit in $C(X,Z)$.

For real-valued families, equicontinuity is uniform over the compact domain, and equicontinuity together with pointwise boundedness gives one bound for all values. The same one-bound conclusion holds for Euclidean-valued families.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Choice, a nonempty compact metric space $X$, and a natural number $n\geq1$.

[L1] For a proper metric target, a family is uniformly compact exactly when it is uniformly closed, equicontinuous, and pointwise bounded ([[cor-compact-subsets-of-cx-for-a-proper-metric-target]]).

[L2] A pointwise bounded equicontinuous sequence into a proper metric target has a uniformly convergent subsequence ([[cor-arzela-ascoli-subsequence-theorem-for-proper-metric-targets]]).

[L3] In $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb R^n$, closed and bounded subsets are compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[L4] Compact metric subsets are closed and bounded ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]).

[L5] For real-valued functions on a nonempty compact metric space, compactness of the supremum-metric closure is equivalent to equicontinuity and pointwise boundedness ([[thm-arzela-ascoli-for-real-ck]]).

[L6] A real-valued pointwise bounded equicontinuous sequence has a uniformly convergent subsequence ([[cor-equicontinuous-bounded-sequence-has-a-uniformly-convergent-subsequence]]).

[L7] A real-valued equicontinuous family on a nonempty compact metric domain is uniformly equicontinuous ([[lem-equicontinuity-on-a-compact-domain-is-uniform]]).

[L8] A real-valued equicontinuous pointwise bounded family on a nonempty compact metric domain is uniformly bounded ([[lem-equicontinuity-and-pointwise-boundedness-give-uniform-boundedness]]).

[L9] Every member of $C(X,\mathbb R)$ is bounded and the supremum metric $d_\infty(f,g)=\sup_{x\in X}|f(x)-g(x)|$ is defined there ([[thm-c-k-complete-in-the-sup-metric]]).

[L10] The uniform topology is induced by $\bar\rho(f,g)=\sup_{x\in X}\min\{|f(x)-g(x)|,1\}$ ([[def-topology-of-uniform-convergence]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L3], both $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb R^n$ are proper metric spaces: a closed bounded subset is compact. [L3]

1.2 By [L9] and [L10], $\bar\rho(f,g)=\min\{d_\infty(f,g),1\}$, so balls of radius below $1$ agree and the supremum-metric topology is the uniform topology. In the real case, compactness then implies uniform closedness by [L4], and [L5] gives equicontinuity and pointwise boundedness. Conversely, uniform closedness plus those two conditions makes the compact closure supplied by [L5] equal to the family. The subsequence conclusion is [L6], and the stated uniform equicontinuity and common value bound are exactly [L7] and [L8]. [L4, L5, L6, L7, L8, L9, L10]

1.3 For the Euclidean common bound, fix an equicontinuous, pointwise bounded family $\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,\mathbb R^n)$ and take the tolerance to be $1$. Equicontinuity of $\mathcal F$ gives, at every $x\in X$, a neighbourhood $U_x$ on which $\lVert f(y)-f(x)\rVert_2<1$ for all $f\in\mathcal F$; Choice, which the Given supplies, licenses the family $(U_x)_{x\in X}$. Compactness of $X$ gives a finite subcover $U_{x_1},\ldots,U_{x_m}$. [given]

2.1 Apply [L1] and [L2] to the proper target $\mathbb R^n$. This proves both numbered vector-valued assertions, including both directions of assertion 1. [L1, L2, step 1.1]

3.1 Pointwise boundedness of the family $\mathcal F$ fixed in step 1.3 gives, for each of the finitely many $i\le m$, a number $M_i$ with $\lVert f(x_i)\rVert_2\leq M_i$ for every $f\in\mathcal F$. For $y\in X$ take $i$ with $y\in U_{x_i}$; then $\lVert f(y)\rVert_2\le\lVert f(y)-f(x_i)\rVert_2+\lVert f(x_i)\rVert_2<1+M_i\leq1+\max_iM_i$. Thus one Euclidean bound serves all $f\in\mathcal F$ and all $y\in X$, and the converse from a common bound to pointwise boundedness is immediate. [step 1.3] ∎

## Statement

Let $p,q>1$ satisfy $1/p+1/q=1$. For $u,v\ge0$,
$$uv\le\frac{u^p}{p}+\frac{v^q}{q}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Conjugate real exponents $p,q>1$ and nonnegative reals $u,v$.

[L1] Weighted AM-GM applies to positive entries with nonnegative weights summing to one ([[thm-weighted-am-gm-real]]).

[L2] Positive-base real-power laws hold, and the zero-base convention is $0^r=0$ for $r>0$; positive-base real powers are positive ([[def-real-power]], [[thm-real-power-laws]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $u=0$ or $v=0$, the inequality is immediate from nonnegativity of the two terms on the right. [L2]

1.2 For $u,v>0$, apply [L1] to $u^p,v^q$ with weights $1/p,1/q$. [L1, given]

2.1 Its geometric side is $(u^p)^{1/p}(v^q)^{1/q}=uv$, and its arithmetic side is $u^p/p+v^q/q$. [step 1.2, L2]

3.1 Steps 1.1 and 2.1 cover all nonnegative $u,v$. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; an open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$; a field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$; the space $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with index set $\mathcal A_1=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le1\}=\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_n\}$ and the pairing $(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2}$.

[F1] Sobolev structure: each $D^\alpha u$ is a well-defined $L^2$ class and the $W^{1,2}$ norm is $\|u\|_{W^{1,2}}=\bigl(\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_1}\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^2}^2\bigr)^{1/2}$; $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ by notation ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]], [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

[F2] $L^2$ is a Hilbert space for the integral pairing: on real $L^2$ the pairing $\int fg$ and on complex $L^2$ the pairing $\int f\overline g$ are well-defined inner products with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$, complete for the quotient $L^2$ norm ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

[F3] An inner product is linear in the first argument, conjugate-symmetric, and positive definite; its induced length is a norm, and a Hilbert space is an inner-product space complete for that norm ([[def-inner-product-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]], [[def-hilbert-space]]).

[F4] H\"older: for $L^2$ classes $f,g$, $\bigl|\int f\overline g\bigr|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2$, with the real form $|\int fg|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2$ ([[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]], [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]).

[F5] $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a $\mathbb K$-vector space of test functions, and $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is its closure in $H^1$: explicitly, $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is a test function $\varphi$ with $\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{1,2}}<\delta$. A closure is closed and is the smallest closed superset ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[thm-metric-closure-characterisation]]).

[F6] A closed linear subspace of a Banach space, with the restricted norm, is a Banach space ([[lem-closed-subspace-of-a-banach-space-is-banach]]).



## Proof

1.1 The pairing is a well-defined inner product: each summand $(D^\alpha u,D^\alpha v)_{L^2}$ is the $L^2$ pairing of the well-defined classes $D^\alpha u$ and $D^\alpha v$, hence representative-independent; each is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second over $\mathbb K$, and conjugate-symmetric. A finite sum of maps with these properties again has them, so $(u,v)_{H^1}$ is well defined on classes, linear in $u$, conjugate-linear in $v$ and conjugate-symmetric. It is positive definite, since $(u,u)_{H^1}=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_1}\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^2}^2\ge0$ equals $0$ only when every $D^\alpha u=0$, in particular $u=D^0u=0$, while $u=0$ plainly gives $0$. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a linear subspace. It contains the zero class, as the zero test function shows. Let $u,v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb K$, and let $\delta>0$. Using the test-function approximation of [F5], choose test functions $\varphi,\psi$ with $\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{1,2}}<\delta/(2(|a|+|b|+1))$ and $\|v-\psi\|_{W^{1,2}}<\delta/(2(|a|+|b|+1))$; then $a\varphi+b\psi$ is again a test function, and $\|(au+bv)-(a\varphi+b\psi)\|_{W^{1,2}}\le|a|\,\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{1,2}}+|b|\,\|v-\psi\|_{W^{1,2}}<\delta$. So $au+bv\in H^1_0(\Omega)$; the space is a subspace and, being a closure, it is closed in $H^1(\Omega)$. [F5, algebra]

2.1 Its induced norm is the Sobolev norm: $(u,u)_{H^1}=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_1}\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^2}^2=\|u\|_{W^{1,2}}^2$, so the induced length is $\|u\|_{W^{1,2}}$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Completeness: let $(u_m)$ be a Cauchy sequence in $H^1$. For each $\alpha\in\mathcal A_1$ the inequality $\|D^\alpha u_m-D^\alpha u_l\|_{L^2}\le\|u_m-u_l\|_{W^{1,2}}$ shows that $(D^\alpha u_m)_m$ is Cauchy in $L^2$, so it has a limit class $f_\alpha$. Fix $i$ and a test function $\varphi$. The weak-derivative identity gives $\int_\Omega u_m\,D_i\varphi\,dx=-\int_\Omega D_iu_m\,\varphi\,dx$ for every $m$; H\"older's inequality makes both sides converge to $\int_\Omega f_0\,D_i\varphi\,dx$ and $-\int_\Omega f_i\,\varphi\,dx$, respectively, where $f_0$ is the limit of the classes $u_m=D^0u_m$. Hence $\int f_0D_i\varphi=-\int f_i\varphi$ for every test function $\varphi$, so $f_0\in W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $D_if_0=f_i$, and $\|u_m-f_0\|_{W^{1,2}}^2=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_1}\|D^\alpha u_m-f_\alpha\|_{L^2}^2\to0$. Thus every Cauchy sequence in $H^1$ converges in $H^1$: the space is complete in its Sobolev norm. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 Consequences for the pairing: by steps 1.1, 2.1 the pairing is an inner product inducing the Sobolev norm, and by step 3.1 the space is complete for that norm; therefore $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space over $\mathbb K$ for the pairing. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space: it is a closed linear subspace of the Hilbert space $H^1(\Omega)$, hence complete for the restricted norm by [F6] applied to the underlying Banach space, and the restriction of the inner product is an inner product whose induced norm is the restriction of the Sobolev norm. [F3, F5, F6, step 4.1, step 1.2]

6.1 The pairing $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is therefore an inner product on $H^1(\Omega)$ inducing the $W^{1,2}$ norm, making $H^1(\Omega)$ a Hilbert space, while $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace and a Hilbert space for the restricted pairing; the pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, as required. [step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

## Statement

If $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ is a finite orthonormal list and $v$ is any vector, then

$$\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2\le\lVert v\rVert^2.$$

Equality holds exactly when $v\in\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$. If the list is an orthonormal basis, then for all $v,w$,

$$v=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i,\qquad \langle v,w\rangle=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle\overline{\langle w,e_i\rangle},$$

and

$$\lVert v\rVert^2=\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2.$$

The empty-list case is included.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite orthonormal list $(e_i)_{i<r}$ and vectors $v,w$.

[L1] Orthonormality gives $\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$ ([[def-orthogonal-vectors-sets-and-orthonormal-bases]]).

[L2] Orthogonal vectors satisfy the Pythagorean identity ([[prop-pythagorean-parallelogram-and-polarisation-identities]]).

[L3] $\operatorname{span}(S)=L(S)$, the set of finite linear combinations $\sum_{i<n}\lambda_iv_i$ of elements of $S$ ([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]).

[L4] Finite sums include the empty sum, whose additive value is zero ([[def-monoid-finite-product]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Put $p=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i$. For each $j<r$, [L1] gives $\langle v-p,e_j\rangle=0$, so $v-p$ is orthogonal to $p$. [L1, algebra]

2.1 By [L2], $\lVert v\rVert^2=\lVert p\rVert^2+\lVert v-p\rVert^2$. A second use of orthonormality gives $\lVert p\rVert^2=\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2$, proving Bessel's inequality. [step 1.1, L1, L2]

3.1 Equality holds in step 2.1 exactly when $\lVert v-p\rVert=0$, hence exactly when $v=p$. By [L3], this is exactly $v$ belonging to the listed span. [step 2.1, L3]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] If $f$ is a bounded linear functional then $\|f\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|f(x)|$ and $|f(x)|\le\|f\|\,\|x\|$, and $f=0$ exactly when $\|f\|=0$ ([[def-operator-norm]], [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]).

[A2] Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|\,\|v\|$, and the pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second with $\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]).

[A3] The kernel of a bounded linear functional is either all of $H$ or a proper linear subspace, and the orthogonal complement of a subspace is closed under the decomposition $H=N\oplus N^\perp$ for closed $N$ ([[def-linear-subspace]], [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]).

[A4] For a subset $S$, $S^\perp=\{v:\langle v,s\rangle=0\ \forall s\in S\}$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

[A5] Countable Choice is the hypothesis under which the orthogonal decomposition, and hence this representation, is obtained ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** Countable Choice, a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ and a bounded linear functional $f$ on $H$.

1.1 If $f=0$, then $y=0$ represents $f$ because $\langle x,0\rangle=0$ for every $x$, and $\|f\|=0=\|y\|$; the same $f$ has no other representing vector, since a vector $y'$ representing $f$ satisfies $\langle y',y'\rangle=0$ and hence $y'=0$. [A1, A2]

1.2 If $f\ne0$, its kernel is a proper linear subspace of $H$: it is linear because $f(au+bv)=af(u)+bf(v)$, it is proper because $f$ takes a nonzero value, and it is closed because $x_n\to x$ and $f(x_n)=0$ give $|f(x)|\le|f(x)-f(x_n)|\le\|f\|\,\|x-x_n\|\to0$. [A1, A3]

2.1 Choose $z$ with $f(z)\ne0$ and put $u=z/f(z)$, so $f(u)=1$; decompose $u=m+n$ with $m\in\ker f$ and $n\in(\ker f)^\perp$, then $1=f(u)=f(m)+f(n)=f(n)$ shows $n\ne0$ and $f(n)=1$. [step 1.2, A3, A5]

3.1 For arbitrary $x$, the vector $v=x-f(x)u$ satisfies $f(v)=f(x)-f(x)\cdot1=0$, hence $\langle v,n\rangle=0$ and $\langle x,n\rangle=f(x)\langle u,n\rangle$; moreover $\langle u,n\rangle=\langle m+n,n\rangle=\langle m,n\rangle+\langle n,n\rangle=0+\|n\|^2$, so $f(x)=\langle x,n\rangle/\|n\|^2=\langle x,n/\|n\|^2\rangle$ with $y:=n/\|n\|^2$. [step 2.1, A2, A4, algebra]

4.1 Norm and uniqueness: Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|f(x)|=|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$, so $\|f\|\le\|y\|$, while $f(y)=\|y\|^2$ gives $\|f\|\ge\|y\|$; hence $\|f\|=\|y\|$, and this contains the case $f=0$. If also $f(x)=\langle x,y'\rangle$ for all $x$, then $\langle x,y-y'\rangle=0$ for all $x$, and the choice $x=y-y'$ gives $\|y-y'\|^2=0$, so $y=y'$. [step 3.1, A1, A2, algebra]

5.1 Conjugate linearity: if $f_i(x)=\langle x,y_i\rangle$ for $i=1,2$, then for all $x$ and scalars $a,b$ one has $(af_1+bf_2)(x)=a\langle x,y_1\rangle+b\langle x,y_2\rangle=\langle x,\overline a y_1+\overline b y_2\rangle$ by conjugate-linearity in the second argument; uniqueness of the representing vector therefore gives the representing vector $\overline a y_1+\overline b y_2$, so the map $f\mapsto y$ is conjugate-linear, and by step 4.1 it is isometric. [step 4.1, A2, algebra]

6.1 Steps 1.1, 3.1 and 4.1 produce the unique representing vector together with the norm identity for every bounded $f$, and step 5.1 records its conjugate-linear isometric dependence; Countable Choice is used exactly through the orthogonal decomposition of step 2.1. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, A5] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Use the corrected small-scale sampling, trial-class, exact-zero-witness, and exact regularization hypotheses of the regularized PINN theorem, with residual and boundary operators $L$ and boundary restriction. Let $d\ge2$ and let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded Lipschitz with an exterior sphere at every boundary point. For $0<\alpha<1$, let $a_{ij}=a_{ji}\in C^{1,\alpha}(U)$ have minimum eigenvalue at least $\lambda_0>0$, let $b_i\in C^{1,\alpha}(U)$ and $c_i,d\in C^{0,\alpha}(U)$, and put
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_j u)+\sum_iD_i(b_i u)+\sum_i c_iD_i u+du,$$
$$\widetilde b_j=\sum_iD_i a_{ij}+b_j+c_j,\qquad \widetilde c=\sum_iD_i b_i+d\le0.$$
All indicated Hölder norms are finite global norms. Retain the source coefficient bounds $\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^2\le\Lambda$ and $\lambda_0^{-2}(|b|^2+|c|^2)+\lambda_0^{-1}|d|\le v^2$. Let $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(U)$ and $g\in C^{0,\alpha}(\partial U)$. There is exactly one $u^*\in C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$ with $L[u^*]=f$ and $u^*=g$ on $\partial U$.

Every sequence of global regularized empirical minimizers $h_m$ converges to $u^*$ in $C^0(U)$ almost surely as both sample counts tend to infinity. If $m_r=O(m_b^{d/(d-1)})$, the occupancy-event squared uniform error is $O(m_r^{-\alpha/d})$, with the probability and constants of the regularized-loss theorem. If each minimizer satisfies the boundary data exactly, the errors belong to $H^1_0(U)$ and converge to zero in $H^1(U)$ almost surely. If in addition $U$ is $C^{2,\alpha}$ and $g$ has a $C^{2,\alpha}$ lifting, the usual global $C^{2,\alpha}(\bar U)$ branch applies with its stated coefficient/data hypotheses. No global Hölder regularity is claimed from the exterior-sphere condition alone, and no optimizer convergence is asserted.

## Statement references

[[thm-pinn-regularized-loss-consistency]]

[[thm-shin-elliptic-dirichlet-existence-and-residual-stability]]

[[lem-shin-elliptic-energy-estimate]]

[Shin et al., Theorems 3.3–3.4 and Appendices D–E](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated coefficient, sampling, witness, global-minimizer, and choice hypotheses.

[F1] The elliptic theorem gives unique local-Hölder classical existence with continuous boundary attainment, the smooth-boundary global branch under its extra hypotheses, and $H^1_0$ membership of every zero-boundary classical solution whose forcing is globally Hölder ([[thm-shin-elliptic-dirichlet-existence-and-residual-stability]]).

[F2] The populated-cell proof gives both residual errors tending uniformly to zero almost surely, without weight comparability, and its quantitative occupancy-event bounds ([[thm-pinn-regularized-loss-consistency]]).

[F3] The actual expanded coefficients satisfy the residual-stability estimate for any $C^2(U)\cap C(\bar U)$ error ([[def-shin-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]], [[lem-shin-elliptic-residual-stability]]).

[F4] The source coefficient bound and $H^1_0$ membership give the elliptic energy estimate ([[lem-shin-elliptic-energy-estimate]]).

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are inherited from the existence supplier; the zero-boundary closure/energy convention retains Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

1.1 The finite global $C^{1,\alpha}$ norms of $a,b$ make $\widetilde b,\widetilde c$ globally bounded and Hölder, with $\widetilde c\le0$. Thus [F1] yields the unique solution in the stated local class. Apply [F3] to $e_m=h_m-u^*$, whose boundary values are $h_m-g$ and whose forcing is $L[h_m]-f$. It gives $\|e_m\|_\infty\le C_L(\|L[h_m]-f\|_\infty+\|h_m-g\|_{\infty;\partial U})$. Both terms tend to zero almost surely by [F2]. Squaring this estimate transfers the occupancy-event rate and its event probability to the solution error. The constant may depend on the bounded expanded coefficients and thus their derivative bounds, not only $\Lambda,v$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 If the boundary data are exact, $e_m\in C^2(U)\cap C(\bar U)$ has zero boundary value and $L[e_m]=L[h_m]-f\in C^{0,\alpha}(U)$. The zero-boundary assertion in [F1] gives $e_m\in H^1_0(U)$; this is proved by zero extensions of the smooth approximants and weak convergence, not inferred from continuity alone. Since $|U|<\infty$, step 1.1 and [F2] imply $\|e_m\|_{L^2(U)}+\|L[e_m]\|_{L^2(U)}\to0$. Apply [F4] to obtain $\|e_m\|_{H^1(U)}\to0$. This statement is about the errors, and remains meaningful even if the individual nonzero-data solution is not in $H^1(U)$. [given, F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Under the extra smooth-boundary/data hypotheses, [F1] supplies the stated global regularity branch for this same unique solution. The native sector counterexample refutes extending that conclusion to every exterior-sphere Lipschitz domain. This completes all the stated convergence and regularity assertions. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The source's stronger global $C^{2,\alpha}(U)$ existence assertion for exterior-sphere domains is false for its own globally bounded Hölder convention; the native $2\pi/3$ cutoff-sector counterexample is retained. The exact original carrier is archived in the proposal. The active divergence formula counts $\operatorname{div}(bu)$ once, consistently with the expanded coefficients and energy calculation; the original repeated-index printed expression is recorded in the operator definition's source discrepancy. The minimizer conclusion uses the repaired populated-cell proof and the corrected small-scale sampling convention, with no hidden balance premise.
