## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded with an exterior ball at every spatial boundary point, $T>0$, and $Q=U\times(0,T)$. Use the full parabolic coefficient/data hypotheses of the variable-coefficient existence theorem: differentiability of $a_{ij},b_i$, symmetry and uniform ellipticity, the source weighted parabolic Hölder coefficient bounds, bounded locally parabolic Hölder expanded drift and potential, bounded locally parabolic Hölder forcing, compatible Hölder initial and lateral data, and one-sided local Hölder control at interior points of the final face. Use
$$L_t[u]=\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_j u)+\sum_iD_i(b_i u)+\sum_i c_iD_i u+du,$$
$$\widetilde b_i=\sum_jD_j a_{ij}+b_i+c_i,\qquad\widetilde c=\sum_iD_i b_i+d\le0.$$
Retain the source pointwise bounds with constants $\lambda_0,\Lambda,v$ and its auxiliary $\theta>0$ condition $\theta^2a_{11}+\theta\widetilde b_1\ge1$; the direct parabolic time barrier also works without that auxiliary condition. Boundedness is part of the source's order-zero Hölder norm, not a consequence of its weighted $\delta^2f$ bound alone.

Use the corrected small-scale sampling, data/trial-class, exact-zero-witness and exact regularization assumptions of the regularized PINN theorem in the ambient dimension $D=d+1$, with residual $-h_t+L_t[h]$, target $f$, and restriction to the initial-lateral boundary $\Gamma_T$ with target $\psi$ combining the compatible data. The Euclidean Hölder assumptions in this sampling interface are retained in addition to the parabolic PDE regularity assumptions. There is one classical solution $u^*\in C^{2,1}(Q)\cap C(\bar U\times[0,T])$, locally parabolic Hölder in its displayed derivatives, to $-u_t^*+L_t[u^*]=f$ and the prescribed data.

Every sequence of global empirical regularized minimizers converges to $u^*$ in $C^0(Q)$ almost surely as both counts tend to infinity. For $m_r=O(m_b^{(d+1)/d})$, the occupancy-event squared uniform solution error is $O(m_r^{-\alpha/(d+1)})$, with the probability and constants of the regularized-loss theorem at dimension $D=d+1$. If all minimizers satisfy both initial and lateral data exactly and the displayed divergence expansion agrees distributionally with the classical operator (in particular if $a,b$ are spatially $C^1$ locally), then their errors belong to $L^2(0,T;H^1_0(U))$ and tend to zero in $L^2(0,T;H^1(U))$ almost surely. The energy conclusion uses the actual bounded divergence coefficients and their source $v$ bound. No closed-cylinder $C^{2,1}$ regularity of $u^*$ or convergence of an optimizer is asserted.

## Statement references

[[thm-shin-parabolic-initial-boundary-existence-and-residual-stability]]

[[thm-pinn-regularized-loss-consistency]]

[[lem-shin-zero-data-parabolic-classical-energy-identification]]

[Shin et al., Theorems 3.6–3.7 and Appendices F–G](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The parabolic problem, full sampling and exact regularizer hypotheses, global minimizers and choice assumptions in the Statement.

[F1] The local variable-coefficient construction gives the unique classical solution with continuous initial/lateral/final boundary attainment and the residual stability estimate ([[thm-shin-parabolic-initial-boundary-existence-and-residual-stability]], [[lem-shin-parabolic-residual-stability]], [[def-shin-parabolic-operator-and-boundary]]).

[F2] The populated-cell theorem gives uniform convergence of the PDE and prescribed-data residuals almost surely, together with its count-dependent occupancy-event rate; weight comparability is not a premise ([[thm-pinn-regularized-loss-consistency]]).

[F3] A zero-data locally classical continuous error for the weak-compatible divergence operator has finite variational energy and zero $L^2$ initial trace ([[lem-shin-zero-data-parabolic-classical-energy-identification]]).

[F4] The variational zero-spatial-trace energy estimate applies in that class ([[lem-shin-parabolic-energy-estimate]]).

[A1] The existence and compactness suppliers carry AC and CC; the Sobolev energy-space convention carries CC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] under the full stated PDE hypotheses to obtain $u^*$. For $e_m=h_m-u^*$ the equation is $P[e_m]=-r_m$ with $r_m=f+(h_m)_t-L_t[h_m]$, and its boundary values are $h_m-\psi$. The residual stability estimate gives $\|e_m\|_{\infty;Q}\le C_P(\|r_m\|_{\infty;Q}+\|h_m-\psi\|_{\infty;\Gamma_T})$. By [F2] both terms tend to zero almost surely. Squaring this estimate transfers the occupied-cell error bound and its event probability to the solution error. With $D=d+1$, the count specialization in [F2] is exactly the one displayed here. [given, A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Under exact initial and lateral data the errors have zero classical prescribed values and bounded globally Hölder residuals. Under the explicit weak-compatible divergence hypothesis, [F3] identifies each with the zero-initial variational Dirichlet solution, so $e_m\in L^2(0,T;H^1_0(U))$ with the required time derivative in the dual space. There is no inference from continuous zero trace alone. Since $Q$ has finite volume, [F2] implies $\|r_m\|_{L^2(Q)}\to0$. Apply [F4] with $e_m(0)=0$ to get both $\sup_t\|e_m(t)\|_2\to0$ and $\|\nabla e_m\|_{L^2(Q)}\to0$. Their sum implies the asserted $L^2(0,T;H^1(U))$ convergence. [given, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The source's pointwise word “differentiable” is retained for its classical problem. Its integration-by-parts energy argument additionally uses the weak divergence identity; this requirement is explicit here, with local spatial $C^1$ as a sufficient interpretation. Merely continuous zero boundary data do not prove energy membership. The new energy-identification helper supplies that separate step once the divergence equation has its intended weak meaning. The source's unusual weighted $C_{2+\alpha}$ convention is preserved in the definition; this theorem does not claim that the limiting continuous-data solution has the printed weighted global trial norm.

## Statement

Let $G^\dagger:A\to U$ be continuous, $K\subset A$ compact, and $\varepsilon>0$. Suppose $\sigma_1\in\mathcal A_0^L$, $\sigma_2\in\mathcal A_0$, and $\sigma_3\in\mathcal A_{m_2}$ in every finite input dimension used below. Then some finite-layer neural operator $G$ in the specified integral architecture satisfies
$$\sup_{a\in K}\|G^\dagger(a)-G(a)\|_U<\varepsilon.$$

The printed additional source implication asserts that, if $U$ is Hilbert, $M>0$, $\|G^\dagger(a)\|_U\le M$ on all $A$, and $\sigma_1\in\mathrm{BA}$, then $\|G(a)\|_U\le4M$ on all $A$. This exact implication is vacuous because its diameter-bounded class is empty. A useful corrected implication replaces only that additional activation premise by the following explicitly different property: for every compact $S\subset\mathbb R^q$, every $C\ge\sup_{z\in S}|z|_2$ with the convention that the radius of the empty set is zero, and every $\eta>0$, there is a $\sigma_1$ MLP $b:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^q$ with $\sup_S|b(z)-z|_2<\eta$ and $\sup_{\mathbb R^q}|b(z)|_2\le C$. [Kovachki et al., Theorem 11, Definitions 5–7 and Appendices A, C, D, F](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.08481)

**Given:** The spaces, compact set, target, activation hypotheses and error in the Statement.

[F1] The activation hypotheses supply fixed-depth finite MLP density in the indicated finite-dimensional $C^m$ norms; stacking scalar networks of a common depth gives vector outputs. Their affine output layers allow linear combinations and constant functions ([[def-neural-operator-activation-classes]]).

[F2] The architecture uses affine integral maps on $D$, coordinatewise $\sigma_1$ between its intermediate affine maps, and a final kernel on $D'\times D$ integrated over $D$ ([[def-neural-operator]]).

1.1 If $K$ is empty choose the zero operator. Otherwise put $T=G^\dagger|_K$ and choose $0<\tau<\varepsilon/5$. Every listed input space injects continuously into $L^1(D)$: for finite $p$, $\|a\|_1\le |D|^{1-1/p}\|a\|_p\le |D|^{1-1/p}\|a\|_{W^{m,p}}$ when applicable, and for $C(\bar D)$ use $\|a\|_1\le|D|\|a\|_\infty$. Thus each smooth moment $a\mapsto\int_D\varphi a$ is continuous on $A$ and such moments separate distinct members of $K$, using [F4]; distinct continuous functions also differ on an interior set of positive measure. ## Statement

Let $X,Y$ be real Banach spaces with the approximation property, $T:X\to Y$ continuous, $K\subset X$ compact, and $\varepsilon>0$. There are integers $J,s\ge1$, bounded linear maps $E:X\to\mathbb R^J$ and $B:\mathbb R^s\to Y$, and continuous $h:\mathbb R^J\to\mathbb R^s$ such that $\sup_{x\in K}\|T(x)-Bh(E(x))\|_Y<\varepsilon$. In particular $E(x)=(\ell_j(x))_{j=1}^J$ for bounded linear functionals $\ell_j$, and $Bv=\sum_{i=1}^s v_i\beta_i$ for finitely many $\beta_i\in Y$.

## Statement references

[Kovachki et al., Lemma 22](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.08481)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Banach spaces with AP, the continuous map $T$, compact $K$, and error $\varepsilon>0$.

[F1] AP approximates the identity uniformly on any compact set by bounded finite-rank linear maps ([[def-approximation-property-and-bounded-approximation-property]]).

[F2] A chosen finite basis has bounded linear coordinate maps in both directions ([[thm-coordinate-map-for-a-finite-dimensional-normed-space]]).

## Proof

1.1 If $K$ is empty use zero maps. Otherwise consider all pairs $(x,\rho)$ with $x\in K$ and $\rho>0$ such that $\|T(z)-T(x)\|_Y<\varepsilon/4$ whenever $\|z-x\|_X<3\rho$. Continuity ensures that the balls $B(x,\rho)$ from this family cover $K$; take a finite subcover $B(x_i,\rho_i)$. Put $\delta=\min_i\rho_i>0$. For $x\in K$ and $z\in X$ with $\|z-x\|_X<\delta$, select $i$ with $\|x-x_i\|_X<\rho_i$; then both $x,z$ lie within $3\rho_i$ of $x_i$, so $\|T(z)-T(x)\|_Y<\varepsilon/2$. No compact neighborhood of $K$ is asserted or needed. [given, choose, construct, algebra]

2.1 Apply AP in $X$ to choose bounded finite-rank $P$ with $\sup_K\|Px-x\|_X<\delta$. By step 1.1, $\sup_K\|T(Px)-T(x)\|_Y<\varepsilon/2$. The set $T(P(K))$ is compact; apply AP in $Y$ to obtain bounded finite-rank $Q$ with $\sup_{x\in K}\|QT(Px)-T(Px)\|_Y<\varepsilon/2$. Thus $QT P$ approximates $T$ on $K$ within $\varepsilon$. This makes only two AP selections and does not require a sequence, an infinite union of compact sets, or a choice principle for sequences. [step 1.1, F1, choose, algebra]

3.1 Choose a finite basis $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_J$ of $P(X)$. Its coordinate functionals are bounded by [F2]; hence $Px=\sum_j\ell_j(x)\alpha_j$ with $\ell_j$ bounded on $X$, by composing those functionals with $P$. Write $Rz=\sum_jz_j\alpha_j$, $E(x)=(\ell_j(x))_j$. Choose a finite basis $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_s$ of $Q(Y)$, with bounded coordinate functionals $c_i$, and put $h_i(z)=c_i(QT(Rz))$ and $Bv=\sum_i v_i\beta_i$. Each $h_i$ is continuous on all $\mathbb R^J$, and $BhE=QTP$. For a zero-dimensional range use one zero basis vector and the zero coefficient map instead of an actual basis. These formulas prove the stated factorization and complete the proof. [step 2.1, F2, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K \in \{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and the complex case by [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. Let
$e:n\to X$ be an ordered basis ([[def-linear-basis]]), and write $e_j:=e(j)$.
Give $\mathbb K^n$ its coordinate $\ell^1$ norm

$$\|(a_0,\dots,a_{n-1})\|_1:=\sum_{j<n}|a_j|.$$

Define

$$T:\mathbb K^n\to X,\qquad T(a_0,\dots,a_{n-1})=\sum_{j<n} a_j e_j.$$

Then $T$ is a topological isomorphism of normed spaces in the sense of
[[def-topological-isomorphism-of-normed-spaces]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A normed space $X$ over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and an ordered basis $e:n\to X$.

[L1] An ordered basis is a finite list whose image is a basis ([[def-linear-basis]]), and [[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] identifies its span with exactly the vectors of the form $\sum_{j<n} a_j e_j$, with those coordinates unique.

[L2] A topological isomorphism of normed spaces is a bounded linear bijection whose inverse is bounded ([[def-topological-isomorphism-of-normed-spaces]]).

[L3] For $m\ge1$, every norm on $\mathbb R^m$ is equivalent to the Euclidean norm, and any two norms on $\mathbb R^m$ are equivalent ([[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]]).

[L4] The map $\Phi:\mathbb C\to\mathbb R^2$, $\Phi(a+bi)=(a,b)$, is a bijection with the stated coordinate arithmetic ([[thm-complex-numbers-are-the-real-coordinate-plane]]).

[L5] Complex norms have full complex absolute homogeneity ([[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]). Their realifications carry the same norm and metric ([[def-realification-of-a-complex-vector-space]], [[lem-complex-modulus-of-real-embedding-equals-real-absolute-value]], [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]). The coordinate $\ell^1$ function is a complex norm, including $n=0$ ([[lem-complex-coordinate-l1-is-a-norm]]).

[F1] Real absolute value is definite, multiplicative and subadditive ([[lem-of-abs-value]], [[lem-of-triangle-inequality]]).

[F2] Finite real sums distribute over addition and scaling and preserve inequalities ([[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], every $x\in X$ has exactly one coordinate list $a=(a_0,\dots,a_{n-1})\in\mathbb K^n$ with $x=\sum_{j<n} a_j e_j$. Therefore the displayed map $T$ is well defined, surjective, and injective. [L1]

1.2 $T$ is linear, because finite sums and scalar multiplication distribute over the coordinate formula: $T(\lambda a+b)=\sum_{j<n}(\lambda a_j+b_j)e_j=\lambda\sum_{j<n}a_je_j+\sum_{j<n}b_je_j =\lambda T(a)+T(b)$. [given, algebra]

2.1 In the complex case, [L5] makes both $P(a):=\|a\|_1$ and $N(a):=\|T(a)\|$ real norms on $(\mathbb C^n)_{\mathbb R}$: for $N$, separation uses injectivity in step 1.1, and homogeneity and the triangle inequality use step 1.2 and the norm on $X$. The coordinate map $\Psi(a)=(\operatorname{Re}a_0,\operatorname{Im}a_0,\ldots,\operatorname{Re}a_{n-1},\operatorname{Im}a_{n-1})$ is a real-linear bijection by [L4], so $P\circ\Psi^{-1}$ and $N\circ\Psi^{-1}$ are real norms on $\mathbb R^{2n}$. If $n\ge1$, the pairwise equivalence clause of [L3] gives a positive real $c$ such that $cP(a)\le N(a)$ for every $a$. Thus $\|T^{-1}x\|_1\le c^{-1}\|x\|$. If $n=0$, both spaces consist only of zero by [L1], and the inverse is bounded with bound zero. [L1, L3, L4, L5, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Put $C:=\sum_{j<n}\|e_j\|$, a finite real. Then $$\|T(a)\|=\left\|\sum_{j<n}a_je_j\right\|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_j|\,\|e_j\| \le C\sum_{j<n}|a_j|=C\|a\|_1,$$ so $T$ is bounded. [step 1.2, given, algebra]

2.3 In the real case $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$, the coordinate $P(a)=\sum_{j<n}|a_j|$ is a real norm: absolute-value definiteness, multiplicativity, and the triangle inequality give the three axioms by finite summation, including the empty list. The pullback $N(a):=\|T(a)\|$ is a norm on $\mathbb R^n$: definiteness uses step 1.1, and the triangle and homogeneity axioms come from the norm axioms on $X$ and the linearity of $T$. If $n=0$, then $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and the inverse of $T$ is the zero map, hence bounded. If $n\ge1$, [L3] gives $c>0$ with $c\|a\|_1\le N(a)=\|T(a)\|$ for every $a\in\mathbb R^n$, so $\|T^{-1}x\|_1\le c^{-1}\|x\|$ for every $x\in X$. Thus $T^{-1}$ is bounded in the real case. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L3, F1, F2, choose]

3.1 Steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3 verify the three clauses of [L2]. Therefore $T$ is a topological isomorphism of normed spaces. [L2, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3] ∎

## Remarks

- The proof uses the coordinate $\ell^1$ norm because it makes the boundedness of $T$ immediate. Any other standard coordinate norm would do, and on a fixed finite-dimensional coordinate space all of them are equivalent.
- The finite-dimensional language in the title is implemented here by the actual datum the page uses: a chosen ordered basis of finite length.

## Statement

Under the page measure convention, if a finite family of open sets $U_j\subset\mathbb R^n$ covers compact K, there are smooth nonnegative $\chi_j$ with compact support in $U_j$ such that $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ on a neighborhood of K. These are ambient smooth functions, also when K is only a $C^1$ hypersurface.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A compact Euclidean set K and a finite open cover of K, with the ambient smooth-step and bump conventions in the statement.

[F1] Nested balls admit smooth bumps with a strict compact support margin. ([[lem-scaled-euclidean-bumps-with-compact-support-and-gradient-bound]]).

[F2] Compact Euclidean sets admit finite subcovers. ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[F3] The standard step has values zero for inputs at most zero and one for inputs at least one. ([[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function]]).

## Proof

1.1 If K is empty take all chi_j zero. Otherwise consider all pairs of concentric balls with positive rational radii r<R whose closed outer ball lies in some U_j and whose inner ball meets K. Their inner balls cover K, because every point has a positive neighborhood inside a member of the given open cover. Compactness (F2) retains finitely many such inner balls covering K. F1 gives corresponding bumps b_l, equal to one on those inner balls and compactly supported in their assigned U_j. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 Put $s=\sum_l b_l$. Then s is smooth with compact support, and s at least one on K. Define $\theta=\sigma(4s-1)$. By F3 theta=1 wherever s at least one half, a neighborhood of K, and its support lies in the compact set where s at least one quarter. On s>0 put $f_l=\theta b_l/s$, and extend by zero on s=0. Because theta vanishes on s at most one quarter, this extension is smooth. Each f_l has compact support in the assigned U_j, is nonnegative, and their sum is theta. [step 1.1, F3, algebra]

3.1 For each j sum f_l over the finitely many bumps assigned to U_j, using zero if no bump is assigned. These sums are the required chi_j: their supports are finite unions of compact subsets of U_j, and their total is theta=1 near K. Since all constructions took place in the ambient Euclidean space, no differentiability of K was required. [step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

Hunter, §1.9.2 Theorem 1.31, printed pp. 12–13. A finite normalized-bump construction is supplied here.

## Statement

Assume countable choice, let $n\ge1$, and use Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$. Translation $\tau_hf(x)=f(x-h)$ is an isometry of complex $L^p$ for $1\le p\le\infty$ and depends norm-continuously on $h$ for $p<\infty$.

For complex $K\in L^1$ and $f\in L^p$, the convolution
$$(K*f)(x)=\int K(y)f(x-y)\,dy$$
exists absolutely a.e., defines a measurable class independent of representatives, and satisfies $\|K*f\|_p\le\|K\|_1\|f\|_p$.

If $K_\varepsilon\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ satisfy
$$\int K_\varepsilon=1,\qquad M:=\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\|K_\varepsilon\|_1<\infty,\qquad \int_{|y|\ge\delta}|K_\varepsilon(y)|\,dy\longrightarrow0\quad(\delta>0),$$
then $K_\varepsilon*f\to f$ in $L^p$ for $p<\infty$, and uniformly for $f\in C_0(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. For fixed $K\in L^1$, $K*f\in C_0$ when $f\in C_0$. These assertions allow complex and sign-changing kernels. In particular $K_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}K(x/\varepsilon)$ is such an approximate identity whenever $K\in L^1$ and $\int K=1$.

If $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R)$ has mass one, $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$, and $f$ is complex locally integrable, then $\rho_\varepsilon*f$ is smooth and
$$\partial^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*f)=(\partial^\alpha\rho_\varepsilon)*f.$$
A compactly supported input gives a compactly supported output. No general $L^\infty$ translation-continuity or approximate-identity convergence is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, Euclidean dimension $n\ge1$, and the kernels and inputs in the statement; limits of kernels are as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$.

[F1] Measurability, local integrability and smoothness have their componentwise meanings ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

[F2] Complex norms have component bounds, Hölder and the triangle inequality ([[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]]).

[F3] Under countable choice real translations are norm-continuous for finite p ([[thm-translation-is-continuous-in-l-p-for-one-le-p-less-infinity]]).

[F5] On sigma-finite spaces and for finite p, the norm of a nonnegative integral envelope is bounded by the integral of the section norms ([[thm-minkowski-integral-inequality]]).

[F21] On sigma-finite product spaces, Tonelli makes the integral of a jointly measurable nonnegative function over one variable measurable in the other ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F6] Under countable choice a completion-measurable real function has a base-measurable a.e.-equal representative ([[thm-completion-measurable-functions-have-base-measurable-representatives]]).

[F7] Borel representatives give jointly Borel convolution integrands ([[lem-borel-representatives-make-the-convolution-integrand-borel-measurable]]).

[F8] Translation preserves Lebesgue measurability and measure ([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]).

[F9] Under countable choice dilation by c scales measure by the factor |c|^n; reflection preserves measure ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-under-dilations-and-reflections]]).

[F10] A.e.-equal integrable functions have equal integrals ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]).

[F11] An integrable majorant permits passing a.e. limits through integrals ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[F12] A real smooth compactly supported mollifier differentiates by differentiating the kernel on locally integrable inputs ([[thm-convolution-with-a-mollifier-is-smooth-and-differentiates-under-the-integral-sign]]).

[F13] For Borel $L^1$ inputs, the convolution support lies in the closure of their support sum ([[thm-support-of-a-convolution-lies-in-the-closure-of-the-support-sumset]]).

[F14] Countable choice selects one element from each member of a natural-number-indexed family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F15] Complex integrals are linear ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

[F16] The modulus of a complex integral is bounded by the integral of the modulus ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]).

[F17] Closed bounded Euclidean sets are compact and compact sets are bounded ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[F18] Continuous functions on compact metric spaces are uniformly continuous ([[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]).

[F19] A continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space is bounded ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

[F20] Under countable choice Euclidean boxes have their volume as Lebesgue measure ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** Use real norm and measurability suppliers, then estimate the complex error by an absolute integral envelope.

1.1 Write $f=u+iv$. Translation invariance F8 gives $\int|f(x-h)|^p\,dx=\int|f(x)|^p\,dx$ for finite $p$: first substitute translated level sets for a nonnegative simple function, then take the supremum defining its nonnegative integral. For infinity the sets $\{|f(\cdot-h)|>a\}$ have the same measure as $\{|f|>a\}$, so the essential bounds coincide. Null disagreement sets also translate to null sets, so translations act on classes. For finite $p$, F3 and F2 give $\|\tau_hf-f\|_p\le\|\tau_hu-u\|_p+\|\tau_hv-v\|_p\to0$. The isometry gives continuity at every $h_0$ from $\|\tau_hf-\tau_{h_0}f\|_p=\|\tau_{h-h_0}f-f\|_p$. [F1, F2, F3, F8]

1.2 A complex $f\in C_0$ is bounded: its components are bounded on a sufficiently large closed ball by F17 and F19 and are small outside by definition. It is uniformly continuous: for a given $\eta>0$, take $R$ with $|f(x)|<\eta/2$ for $|x|>R$ and use F18 on the closed ball of radius $R+2$ to choose $0<\delta<1$ making differences below $\eta$ there. If $|x-z|<\delta$, either both points are in that ball or both have radius greater than $R$, in which case their values differ by less than $\eta$. This proves uniform continuity. Hence $K*f$ exists everywhere and $|(K*f)(x+z)-(K*f)(x)|\le\|K\|_1\sup_w|f(w+z)-f(w)|\to0$. As $|x|\to\infty$, $f(x-y)\to0$ for fixed $y$, dominated by the integrable function $\|f\|_\infty|K(y)|$; F11 gives $(K*f)(x)\to0$. Thus $K*f\in C_0$. [F1, F11, F16, F17, F18, F19]

1.3 For a fixed $K\in L^1$ of integral one, substitution $y=x/\varepsilon$ using F9 gives $\int K_\varepsilon=\int K=1$, $\|K_\varepsilon\|_1=\|K\|_1$, and $\int_{|x|\ge\delta}|K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx=\int_{|y|\ge\delta/\varepsilon}|K(y)|\,dy\to0$ by F11, dominated by $|K|$. Thus scaled integrable mass-one kernels satisfy all three conditions, whether or not they are nonnegative. [F9, F11, given]

1.4 For locally integrable $f=u+iv$, F1 gives locally integrable real components. Apply F12 to each with the real kernel $\rho_\varepsilon$. By F15 their recombination gives all ordered partial derivatives, equal to the integrals with the corresponding kernel derivatives. To check their continuity explicitly, fix $x_0$ and a closed unit ball of x-values about it. The y-supports of $\partial^\alpha\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)$ for those x-values lie in a fixed closed bounded ball $Q$, compact by F17. The derivative of the kernel is globally bounded, say by $C_\alpha$, by F19 on a ball containing its compact support. Thus the integrands are dominated by $C_\alpha|f|\mathbf1_Q$, integrable by local integrability. As $x\to x_0$ their pointwise limits are the integrands at $x_0$, so F11 gives continuity of every derivative integral. The change of variables between the two convolution orders follows from F8–F9. Hence the convolution is smooth with the stated formula. [F1, F8, F9, F11, F12, F15, F17, F19]

2.1 Under the given countable-choice hypothesis F14, F6 applied to each component supplies Borel representatives of $K,f$; any infinite component values in the base representative occur on a Borel null set and can be set to zero there. F7 makes $(x,y)\mapsto K(y)f(x-y)$ jointly Borel. Both Euclidean factors are sigma-finite, covered by the finite-measure boxes of F20. For $p<\infty$, apply F5 to $F(x,y)=K(y)f(x-y)$: step 1.1 gives $\|F(\cdot,y)\|_p=|K(y)|\|f\|_p$, so the envelope $A(x)=\int|F(x,y)|\,dy$ belongs to $L^p$ and $\|A\|_p\le\|K\|_1\|f\|_p$. For $p=\infty$, modify the Borel representative of $f$ on the Borel null set where $|f|>\|f\|_\infty$, setting it to zero. Then $A(x)\le\|f\|_\infty\|K\|_1$ for every $x$. By F21, $A$ and the positive and negative parts of the real and imaginary integrands have measurable section integrals. Where $A(x)<\infty$, their finite differences define a measurable complex integral with modulus at most $A(x)$ by F16; set it to zero on the measurable exceptional set. These bounds prove absolute a.e. existence, measurability and the sharp $L^p$ norm estimate independently of real Young. [F2, F5, F6, F7, F14, F16, F20, F21, step 1.1, given]

2.2 For $f\in C_0$, put $\omega_f(\delta)=\sup_{|y|<\delta,x}|f(x-y)-f(x)|$. Step 1.2 gives $\omega_f(\delta)\to0$. Taking pointwise absolute values in the normalized error integral and then the supremum gives $\|K_\varepsilon*f-f\|_{\mathrm{sup}}\le M\omega_f(\delta)+2\|f\|_{\mathrm{sup}}\int_{|y|\ge\delta}|K_\varepsilon(y)|\,dy$. First send $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, then $\delta\downarrow0$. This proves the uniform assertion by a direct supremum estimate. [F15, F16, step 1.2, given]

3.1 For any other measurable representatives let $N_K,N_f$ be their measurable null disagreement sets. For each fixed $x$, the integrands coincide outside $N_K\cup(x-N_f)$, a measurable null set by F8–F9. The same is true of their absolute values, so absolute integrability holds for either pair exactly when it holds for the other. At those points F10 gives equal integrals. Thus the measurable class in step 2.1 is representative-independent throughout $L^1$ times Lp, without restricting both inputs to $L^1$. [F8, F9, F10, step 2.1]

3.2 For finite $p$, normalization and F15 give $K_\varepsilon*f-f=\int K_\varepsilon(y)(f(\cdot-y)-f(\cdot))\,dy$ a.e. Its absolute value is bounded by the envelope with integrand $|K_\varepsilon(y)||f(x-y)-f(x)|$ by F16. This integrand is measurable by F7 applied to Borel representatives and ordinary products. Its section norm is $|K_\varepsilon(y)|\|\tau_yf-f\|_p$, measurable by step 1.1 and bounded by $2\|f\|_p|K_\varepsilon(y)|$, which is integrable. Euclidean Lebesgue measure is sigma-finite, since $[-j,j]^n$ for positive integers $j$ cover it and have finite measure $(2j)^n$ by F20. Therefore F5 applies and gives $\|K_\varepsilon*f-f\|_p\le\int|K_\varepsilon(y)|\|\tau_yf-f\|_p\,dy$. [F2, F5, F7, F15, F16, F20, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 For any $\eta>0$, step 1.1 gives $\delta>0$ with $\|\tau_yf-f\|_p<\eta$ whenever $|y|<\delta$. Splitting the last integral yields $\|K_\varepsilon*f-f\|_p\le M\eta+2\|f\|_p\int_{|y|\ge\delta}|K_\varepsilon(y)|\,dy$. The tail tends to zero, so the limit superior is at most $M\eta$. Let $\eta\downarrow0$ to obtain convergence. No separate normalization of the real and imaginary kernel parts has been used. [step 1.1, step 3.2, given]

5.1 If the locally integrable input has compact support $S$, then $\int|f|=\int_S|f|<\infty$. A Borel representative can be made zero outside the closed set $S$ while preserving its class by step 3.1. F13 gives output support inside $\overline{S+\operatorname{supp}\rho_\varepsilon}$. Both input supports are bounded, so this closed sum closure is bounded and hence compact by F17. The smooth output has closed support inside it, therefore compact support. Zero input or zero convolution yields the empty support; neither requires a nonempty support choice. All estimates above apply at p=1; the only general infinity assertion is the isometry and Young bound, with uniform approximation restricted to C0. [F13, F17, step 3.1, step 1.4] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\mu)$ and $(Y,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces, let
$1 \le p < \infty$, and let $F : X \times Y \to \mathbb{C}$ be measurable with

$$ \int_Y \|F(\cdot,y)\|_{L^p(X)}\,d\nu(y) < \infty. $$

Then the function
$$ H(x) := \int_Y |F(x,y)|\,d\nu(y) $$
belongs to $L^p(X)$ and

$$ \|H\|_{L^p(X)} \le \int_Y \|F(\cdot,y)\|_{L^p(X)}\,d\nu(y). $$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Sigma-finite measure spaces, an exponent $1 \le p < \infty$, and a measurable function $F$ satisfying the displayed integrability hypothesis.

[L1] For $1 < p < \infty$, the nonnegative duality formula is available ([[lem-elementary-duality-formula-for-nonnegative-l-p-functions]]).

[L2] Tonelli applies to nonnegative measurable functions on product spaces ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[L3] Holder's inequality is available ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]).

[L4] Monotone convergence is available for nonnegative measurable functions ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $p=1$, then Tonelli directly gives [L2, given, algebra] $$ \|H\|_{L^1(X)} = \int_X \int_Y |F(x,y)|\,d\nu(y)\,d\mu(x) = \int_Y \|F(\cdot,y)\|_{L^1(X)}\,d\nu(y). $$ [L2, given, algebra]

1.2 Assume $1 < p < \infty$ and let $q$ be conjugate to $p$. Put [L2, L3, given, algebra] $$ M := \int_Y \|F(\cdot,y)\|_{L^p(X)}\,d\nu(y). $$ For every nonnegative $g \in L^q(X)$ with $\|g\|_q \le 1$, $$ \int_X H(x)g(x)\,d\mu(x) = \int_Y \left(\int_X |F(x,y)|g(x)\,d\mu(x)\right)d\nu(y) $$ by [L2], and then [L3] yields $$ \int_X |F(x,y)|g(x)\,d\mu(x) \le \|F(\cdot,y)\|_p\|g\|_q \le \|F(\cdot,y)\|_p. $$ Hence $$ \int_X H g\,d\mu \le \int_Y \|F(\cdot,y)\|_p\,d\nu(y) = M. $$ [L2, L3, given, algebra]

1.3 Choose measurable sets $X_1 \subseteq X_2 \subseteq \cdots$ with [given, construct] $\mu(X_m)<\infty$ and $\bigcup_m X_m=X$, and define $$ H_m := \min(H,m)\,\mathbf{1}_{X_m}. $$ Then $0 \le H_m \uparrow H$ pointwise, and each $H_m$ lies in $L^p(X)$ because $H_m \le m\,\mathbf{1}_{X_m}$. [given, construct]

2.1 Applying [L1] to each nonnegative $H_m$ and using $0 \le H_m \le H$ with [L1, step 1.2, step 1.3] step 1.2 gives $$ \|H_m\|_p \le M $$ for every $m$. [L1, step 1.2, step 1.3]

3.1 By [L4], $$ \int_X H_m(x)^p\,d\mu(x) \uparrow \int_X H(x)^p\,d\mu(x). $$ Since $\int H_m^p\,d\mu=\|H_m\|_p^p \le M^p$ for every $m$, the limit is finite and satisfies $\|H\|_p^p \le M^p$. Hence $H \in L^p(X)$ and $$ \|H\|_p \le M = \int_Y \|F(\cdot,y)\|_{L^p(X)}\,d\nu(y). $$ Together with step 1.1, this proves the theorem for all $1 \le p < \infty$. [L4, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open,
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $u:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ have real
and imaginary parts of class $C^k$. For each multi-index
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ with $|\alpha|\le k$, the componentwise classical
derivative $\partial^\alpha u$ is locally integrable and is the weak
derivative $D^\alpha u$. By the uniqueness lemma, it represents the unique
locally integrable weak-derivative class. For $\alpha=0$, this says
$D^0u=u$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion is vacuous: there is only the zero
class and every displayed test identity is zero.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb C)$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and a multi-index $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le k$.

[F1] By the regular-distribution pairing and signed-transpose convention, the weak test identity is equivalent to $\partial^\alpha T_f=T_g$ as distributions ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]).

[F2] Under Countable Choice, classical derivatives of $C^k$ functions are compatible with distributional derivatives: [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]].

[F3] Under Countable Choice, a locally integrable weak derivative is unique almost everywhere ([[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Apply [F2] to $u$ and $\alpha$. The regular distributions of $u$ and $\partial^\alpha u$ are defined, so in particular both functions are locally integrable, and $$\partial^\alpha T_u=T_{\partial^\alpha u}.$$ The Countable Choice use is exactly the comparison of the compactly supported Riemann integrals with the corresponding Lebesgue integrals in [F2]. [F2, given]

2.1 By [F1], this distributional equality is equivalent to the weak test identity. Explicitly, evaluation on any $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ gives $$(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =\int_\Omega (\partial^\alpha u)\varphi\,dx.$$ Multiplying by $(-1)^{|\alpha|}$ gives the defining weak identity for $\partial^\alpha u$; the sign is its own inverse. Since the test was arbitrary, $\partial^\alpha u$ is a weak derivative. [F1, step 1.1, given]

3.1 The weak derivative class is unique by [F3], so the locally integrable class represented by $\partial^\alpha u$ is the class denoted $D^\alpha u$. When $\alpha=0$, the identity reduces to $u=u$. [F3, step 2.1, given] ∎

## Sources

- Juha Kinnunen, *Sobolev Spaces*, Chapter 1 §1.1, printed pp. 2–3: compact-support integration by parts has no boundary term, successive integrations give the multi-index identity, and Remarks 1.3(1) state that classical derivatives through order $k$ are weak derivatives.
- John K. Hunter, *Notes on Partial Differential Equations*, Chapter 3 §3.1, printed pp. 47–48, for the weak-derivative integration-by-parts convention.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, an open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, a smooth multiplier $\eta$, a locally integrable $u$, and a multi-index $\alpha$ for which the weak derivatives through $\alpha$ have locally integrable values.

[F1] The regular-distribution pairing is complex bilinear and depends only on the almost-everywhere class ([[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]]).

[F2] A weak derivative is characterized by the signed test identity, which is the distributional derivative identity for the corresponding regular distributions ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]).

[F3] Distributional Leibniz holds for a smooth complex multiplier and every multi-index, in the bilinear convention and without a choice assumption ([[thm-leibniz-rule-for-distributions]]).

[F4] Multiplication of distributions by smooth functions is defined by $\langle aT,\varphi\rangle=\langle T,a\varphi\rangle$, with no conjugation, and is associative ([[def-multiplication-of-a-distribution-by-a-smooth-function]]).

[F5] A locally integrable weak derivative, if it exists, is unique as an almost-everywhere class under Countable Choice ([[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]]).

[F6] The class $u\in W^{k,p}$ has an $L^p$ class for each weak derivative of order at most $k$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

[F7] Real $L^p$ elements are almost-everywhere classes ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

[F8] Complex $L^p$ elements are almost-everywhere classes and use pointwise complex products ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

[F9] Countable Choice asserts that every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]).

**Choice accounting:** Countable Choice is used only through [F5] to identify locally integrable derivative value classes, including at order zero; [F9] names this assumption. The test-identity transfers, distributional Leibniz identity, and finite algebraic expansion are choice-free. No full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** transfer the distributional product identity to regular distributions and identify its locally integrable value.

1.1 For every $\gamma\le\alpha$, the weak identity and [F2] give $$\partial^\gamma T_u=T_{v_\gamma}.$$ In particular, the derivative on the left is represented by a locally integrable function for each such $\gamma$. [F2, given]

1.2 Set $$w_\alpha=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)v_{\alpha-\beta}.$$ The sum is finite. On each compact subset of $\Omega$, every smooth $D^\beta\eta$ is bounded and every $v_{\alpha-\beta}$ is integrable, so $w_\alpha\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Changing any selected representative on a null set changes each product only on a null set; hence $w_\alpha$ defines a single almost-everywhere class. [F1, F7, F8, given]

2.1 Apply [F3] to $\eta$ and $T_u$, then substitute the identities of step 1.1. By [F4], the left side is the $\alpha$th distributional derivative of $T_{\eta u}$, while each term on the right is the regular distribution of the corresponding summand in $w_\alpha$. Thus $$\partial^\alpha T_{\eta u}=T_{w_\alpha}.$$ By the weak-derivative identity in [F2], $w_\alpha$ is a locally integrable weak $\alpha$-derivative of $\eta u$. By [F5] it is the unique value class, which proves the asserted local formula. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F9, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 Now suppose the global $W^{k,p}$ hypotheses hold. For each $|\alpha|\le k$, the local result applies because all weak derivatives $D^\gamma u$ with $\gamma\le\alpha$ are supplied by [F6]. For every $\beta\le\alpha$, the factor $D^\beta\eta$ is bounded, so $(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u$ is an $L^p$ class: for finite $p$ its modulus is bounded by $\|D^\beta\eta\|_\infty |D^{\alpha-\beta}u|$ almost everywhere, and for $p=\infty$ the same estimate bounds the essential supremum. The finite sum is therefore in $L^p$. Taking $\alpha=0$ also shows $\eta u\in L^p$; the local result for every $|\alpha|\le k$ now gives $\eta u\in W^{k,p}$ by its definition, and its weak derivative classes are exactly the displayed sums. [F6, F7, F8, step 2.1, given]

4.1 If $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, its support is compact in $\Omega$. Each derivative is continuous and vanishes off that compact support, so every derivative through order $k$ is bounded. Thus the preceding global argument applies. For $k=0$ the formula has only $\beta=0$ and says $D^0(\eta u)=\eta u$. When $\alpha=0$ the same order-zero identity holds in the local assertion. For the zero input class, zero is a weak derivative at every order by the defining test identity, and [F5] makes each supplied derivative class zero; if $\eta=0$, every summand is zero. On the empty domain every term is the zero class. [F2, F5, F9, step 3.1, given]

The argument treats real and complex values uniformly because all pairings and multiplier products are bilinear; no conjugation or additional choice principle enters. $\square$

## Statement

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $n \ge 1$, the Axiom of Countable Choice, and Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n$ on $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

[L1] Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra, $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure on it, and $\lambda_n(B)=\operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

[L2] Every set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(R) = \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[L3] Assuming countable choice, $\lambda_n^*$ is an outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$, hence monotone ([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]], [[def-outer-measure]]).

[L4] Assuming countable choice, every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]).

[L5] For a nonempty box $\operatorname{vol}(B) := \prod_{i<n}(b_i - a_i)$ when every $a_i$ and every $b_i$ is real, and $(u,v]^n := B(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})$ ([[def-half-open-box]], [[def-integer-power]]).

[F1] $\mu$ is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$ ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]).

[F2] $A$ is **bounded** if $A = \emptyset$ or there are $x_0 \in X$ and a real $r > 0$ with $A \subseteq B(x_0, r)$, where $B(x_0,r) := \{\, y : d(x_0,y) < r \,\}$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[def-metric-ball]]).

[F3] For every $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, $\lVert x\rVert_\infty \le \lVert x\rVert_2$, and $\lVert x-y\rVert_2 = d_2(x,y)$, $\lVert x-y\rVert_\infty = d_\infty(x,y)$, where $d_\infty(x,y) = \max\{|x_k-y_k| : k<n\}$ ([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]], claim 3; [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], claim 3; [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]; [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

[F4] A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is compact if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and bounded ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]], claim 2; [[def-metric-topology]]); and a compact subset of a metric space is closed and bounded ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]).

[F5] If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$ ([[prop-measure-monotonicity]]).

[F6] Every complete ordered field $F$ is Archimedean: for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Each cube $(-k,k]^n$ is a half-open box, hence Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big)=\prod_{i<n}\big(k-(-k)\big)=(2k)^n$, a real number; the cubes increase with $k$; and every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ lies in one of them, because the Archimedean property gives a natural $k \ge 1$ above each of the finitely many reals $|x_i|$, so their union is $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite. [L1, L2, L5, F1, F6]

1.2 Let $E$ be bounded and nonempty, say $E \subseteq B(x_0,r)$ with $r$ a positive real; every $y \in E$ satisfies $|y_i-(x_0)_i| \le d_2(x_0,y) < r$ in each coordinate, so $E$ is contained in the half-open box with parameter pairs $\big((x_0)_i-r,\ (x_0)_i+r\big]$, whose volume is $(2r)^n$; monotonicity of the outer measure therefore gives $\lambda_n^*(E) \le (2r)^n < +\infty$, and the empty set has outer measure $0$. [L1, L3, L5, F2, F3]

2.1 A bounded Lebesgue measurable set has $\lambda_n(E)=\lambda_n^*(E)<+\infty$ by step 1.2; and a compact $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is closed, hence Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and bounded, hence of finite measure. [step 1.2, L4, F4, F5]

3.1 Step 1.1 is claim 1 and steps 1.2 and 2.1 are claim 2. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Real numbers $0<r<R$.

[F1] The standard smooth step function $\sigma$ is smooth, takes values in $[0,1]$, vanishes on $(-\infty,0]$, and equals $1$ on $[1,\infty)$ ([[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function]]).

[L1] Coordinate differentiation uses the one-variable chain, sum and product rules ([[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]). Smoothness means that every iterated coordinate derivative exists and is continuous ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]).

[F2] The support is the closure of the nonzero locus ([[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Put $s=(r+R)/2$ and $d=s^2-r^2>0$, and define $u(x)=(s^2-\sum_{j=1}^n x_j^2)/d$ and $\rho(x)=\sigma(u(x))$. The coordinate derivatives of $u$ are $\partial_i u=-2x_i/d$, $\partial_j\partial_i u=-2\delta_{ij}/d$, and zero at every higher order, so $u$ is smooth. Here $\delta_{ij}$ is $1$ when $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. [L1, given, construct]

2.1 Every iterated coordinate derivative of $\rho$ is a finite sum of products of derivatives of $u$ and factors $\sigma^{(k)}(u)$: induction follows by applying the chain and product rules in [L1] to each factor. These factors are continuous by [F1] and step 1.1, so $\rho$ is smooth. [F1, L1, step 1.1]

2.2 If $\|x\|\le r$, then $u(x)\ge1$, so $\rho(x)=1$; if $\|x\|\ge s$, then $u(x)\le0$, so $\rho(x)=0$. Also $0\le\rho\le1$ by [F1]. [F1, step 1.1]

3.1 The nonzero locus lies in $B_s(0)$, whose closure is contained in the closed ball $\overline B_s(0)$. Thus [F2] gives $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\overline B_s(0)\subseteq B_R(0)$, since $s<R$. Together with steps 2.1 and 2.2 this proves the claim. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, and let $X=L^p(D)$, $X=W^{m,p}(D)$, or $X=C^m(\bar D)$, where $1\le p<\infty$ and $m\ge0$ wherever applicable. For every bounded linear functional $L:X\to\mathbb R$, every compact $K\subset X$, and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is $\kappa\in C_c^\infty(D)$ such that
$$\sup_{a\in K}\left|L(a)-\int_D\kappa(y)a(y)\,dy\right|<\varepsilon.$$

The input function in this integral is its zeroth derivative. The conclusion is compact-uniform, without an assertion of operator-norm density of these functionals.

## Statement references

[Kovachki et al., Appendix C, Lemmas 28–31; the present compact-set proof uses inward smoothing](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.08481)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $D,X,L,K,\varepsilon$ as in the Statement.

[F1] The inward smoothing construction supplies $S_ta(x)=\int_Dk_t(x,y)a(y)\,dy$, where $k_t$ is ambient smooth, has fixed compact support in $x$, and $S_ta\to a$ uniformly on each compact subset of $X$. Its explicit kernel is $k_t(x,y)=\sum_j\psi_j(x)\rho_t(x+tv_j-y)$ ([[lem-inward-mollification-and-finite-rank-approximation-on-lipschitz-domains]]).

[F2] All listed $X$ embed continuously into $L^1(D)$; this follows directly from Hölder's inequality on the bounded domain, or the sup norm in the continuous case. Countable Choice is used by the local smoothing supplier ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F3] The finite normalized-bump construction gives an ambient smooth cutoff equal to one near any compact subset of an open set, taking values between zero and one and compactly supported in that open set ([[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]]).

## Proof

1.1 Empty $K$ or $L=0$ is handled by $\kappa=0$. Otherwise [F1] permits choosing $t>0$ with $\sup_K\|S_ta-a\|_X<\varepsilon/(2\|L\|)$. For fixed $t$, the map $y\mapsto k_t(\cdot,y)|_D$ is ambient $C^\infty$ with values in $X$: every mixed $x$ and $y$ derivative is uniformly continuous on compact products, so the ordinary finite-dimensional Taylor remainders in $y$, uniformly for $x$ derivatives through order $m$, tend to zero in the $C^m$ norm and hence in the $X$ norm. Thus $\kappa_t(y)=L(k_t(\cdot,y)|_D)$ is ambient smooth, with $D_y^\alpha\kappa_t=L(D_y^\alpha k_t(\cdot,y)|_D)$. It is bounded on $\bar D$. [given, F1, F2, choose, construct]

1.2 Compactness of $K$ in $X$ implies its compactness in $L^1(D)$ by [F2]. Given $\theta>0$, take a finite $\theta/2$ net $a_1,\ldots,a_s$ in that $L^1$ image. By integrability and an exhaustion of $D$ by compact subsets, there is one compact $F\subset D$ with $\int_{D\setminus F}|a_i|<\theta/2$ for all $i$. Therefore $\sup_{a\in K}\int_{D\setminus F}|a|<\theta$. Choose a smooth cutoff $0\le\zeta\le1$, compactly supported in $D$, equal to one on $F$; use [F3] for the one-set open cover $\{D\}$ of $F$. Then $\sup_K\int_D(1-\zeta)|a|<\theta$. This uses a finite net and finitely many integrable tails, including at $p=1$; it requires no $L^\infty$ approximation of a dual coefficient. [F2, F3, choose, construct, algebra]

2.1 For each $a\in X$, one has $L(S_ta)=\int_D\kappa_t(y)a(y)\,dy$. To justify the identity without assuming a vector-integration theorem, partition a box containing $D$ into cells of diameter tending to zero and replace $k_t(\cdot,y)$ on each cell by $k_t(\cdot,y_l)$. Uniform continuity of every $x$ derivative through order $m$ makes the error in $X$ at most $c_X\eta\|a\|_1$, where $\eta\to0$ is the uniform kernel derivative error and $c_X$ converts a $C^m$ bound to an $X$ bound. Applying bounded $L$ to the finite sums is legitimate by linearity. Their scalar integral errors are at most $\|L\|c_X\eta\|a\|_1$ as well, so passing to the limit proves the identity. Consequently $\sup_K|L(a)-\int_D\kappa_ta|<\varepsilon/2$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, construct, algebra]

3.1 If $\|\kappa_t\|_{L^\infty(D)}=0$, choose $\kappa=0$. Otherwise use step 1.2 with $\theta=\varepsilon/(2\|\kappa_t\|_\infty)$ and set $\kappa=\zeta\kappa_t\in C_c^\infty(D)$. The cutoff error satisfies $\sup_K|\int_D(\kappa_t-\kappa)a|\le\|\kappa_t\|_\infty\sup_K\int_D(1-\zeta)|a|<\varepsilon/2$. Combining with step 2.1 proves the claim. [step 2.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra] ∎

## Example

For the scalar objective $J(\theta)=(\theta^2-1)^2$, the global minimum value is $0$ and is attained at $\theta=\pm1$, while $\theta=0$ is stationary with $J(0)=1$. Gradient descent $\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k-\eta J'(\theta_k)$ initialized at $\theta_0=0$ remains at $0$ for every step size $\eta>0$. Thus a theorem about global minimizers does not by itself imply that a gradient-based training procedure finds one.

## Example references
[Shin et al., Introduction: the analysis idealizes global minimizers and does not prove optimizer convergence](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

[Shin et al., Introduction: no general optimizer guarantee is asserted](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The polynomial objective and gradient-descent update in the Example.

[F1] $J'(\theta)=4\theta(\theta^2-1)$ by polynomial differentiation.

## Verification

**Proof strategy:** compare objective values and evaluate the update at zero.

1.1 Since $J(\theta)$ is a square, $J(\theta)\ge0$, with equality exactly when $\theta^2=1$. Also $J(0)=1$. Hence $0$ is not a global minimizer. [given, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], $J'(0)=0$. If $\theta_k=0$, the update gives $\theta_{k+1}=0-\eta J'(0)=0$; induction from $\theta_0=0$ yields $\theta_k=0$ for all $k$. The iterates therefore never reach either global minimizer. [given, F1, algebra, induction] ∎

## Example

On $U=(0,1)$ take the residual operator $L[h]=h'$, target $f=0$, boundary operator given by endpoint restriction, and boundary data $g=0$. For each integer $m\ge2$, set
$$h_m(x)=\frac{1-\cos(2\pi mx)}{2\pi m}.$$
At the residual collocation points $x_j=j/m$ for $1\le j<m$, the residual $L[h_m](x_j)$ is zero; the exact endpoint values are also zero. Nevertheless, for uniform population measure, the population residual loss is $\int_0^1|L[h_m](x)|^2dx=1/2$. This example concerns unregularized sparse collocation and does not claim that $h_m$ minimizes the regularized objective.

## Example references
[Shin et al., equations (2.4)–(2.6): empirical and population PINN losses](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01806)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The operator, data, collocation set, and trial functions in the Example.

[F1] The derivative of $h_m$ is $h_m'(x)=\sin(2\pi mx)$.

[F2] For every positive integer $m$, $\int_0^1\sin^2(2\pi mx)dx=1/2$, by $\sin^2 z=(1-\cos(2z))/2$ and direct integration.

## Verification

**Proof strategy:** evaluate the derivative at the grid points and integrate its square.

1.1 Differentiating the displayed formula gives [F1]. At $x_j=j/m$, $h_m'(x_j)=\sin(2\pi j)=0$. Also $h_m(0)=h_m(1)=0$ since $\cos(0)=\cos(2\pi m)=1$. Thus the empirical residual and exact boundary errors vanish. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The population residual loss is $\int_0^1|h_m'(x)|^2dx=1/2$ by [F2]. Therefore exact collocation fit at these sample points does not by itself force the population residual loss to be small. [step 1.1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Example

On the one-dimensional torus, let $v(x)=\sin(2\pi x)$ and use a Fourier cutoff $K\ge1$. If the spectral matrices satisfy $R_1=R_{-1}=1$ and all other retained matrices vanish, then the spectral part of the layer returns $v$ exactly. If the cutoff is $K=0$, its spectral part is zero because $\widehat v(0)=0$. These finite-mode computations illustrate the layer definition and make no approximation or universality claim for the full Fourier neural-operator architecture.

## Example references
[Kovachki et al., §5.3: finite Fourier-mode parameterization](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.08481)

[Kovachki et al., §5.3: Fourier-layer convention](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.08481)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $v(x)=\sin(2\pi x)$ on $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ and the Fourier coefficient convention in the Fourier neural-operator layer definition.

[F1] The Fourier coefficient of $e^{2\pi i kx}$ at index $j$ is $1$ if $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise, by integrating the exponential over one period.

## Verification

## Example

On the open domain $D=(0,1)$, use the continuous representatives $a\in C([0,1])$ and $G(a)\in C([0,1])$, and define $G(a)(x)=\int_0^1a(y)\,dy$ for every $x\in[0,1]$. Its midpoint-mesh realization with $n$ cells is the constant output $G_n(a)(x)=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n a((j-\frac12)/n)$. For a fixed continuous input $a$, these outputs converge uniformly in $x$ to $G(a)$. By contrast, the identity map $F_n:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ on a length-$n$ vector is defined on a different input and output space at each $n$; without an additional reconstruction rule it is not a single function-space operator that accepts arbitrary meshes and can be queried at arbitrary output points.

## Example references
[Kovachki et al., Definition 4, Theorem 8, and §1.2: continuum operators versus fixed-grid maps](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.08481)

[Kovachki et al., Appendix E: uniform Riemann-sum convergence for operator layers](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.08481)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A continuous function $a:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$, the integral operator $G$, and the midpoint quadrature rule in the Example.

[F1] A continuous function on the compact interval $[0,1]$ is uniformly continuous.

## Verification

**Proof strategy:** estimate each midpoint cell error by the modulus of continuity.

1.1 Let $I_j=[(j-1)/n,j/n]$ and define $\omega_a(\delta)=\sup\{|a(x)-a(y)|:x,y\in[0,1],\ |x-y|\le\delta\}$. For each $y\in I_j$, $|y-(j-\frac12)/n|\le1/(2n)$, so $$\left|\int_{I_j}a(y)\,dy-\frac1n a((j-\tfrac12)/n)\right|\le\frac1n\omega_a(1/(2n)).$$ Summing over $j$ gives $|G(a)(x)-G_n(a)(x)|\le\omega_a(1/(2n))$ for every $x$. [given, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], $\omega_a(\delta)\to0$ as $\delta\downarrow0$. The bound in step 1.1 is independent of $x$, so $G_n(a)\to G(a)$ in $C([0,1])$. The dimension of $F_n$ changes with $n$ and its definition returns only a length-$n$ vector, so no arbitrary-point output or common function-space domain follows from $F_n$ alone. [step 1.1, F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $D'\subset\mathbb R^{d'}$ be bounded domains. Let $A$ and $U$ be real Banach function spaces on $D$ and $D'$ that embed continuously into $C(\bar D)$ and $C(\bar D')$, respectively. Let $\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let $G:A\to U$ be any $N$-layer neural operator in the function-space class defined by the neural-operator construction. Then compatible finite-dimensional Riemann-sum realizations of $G$, using the same parameters at each refinement, converge to $G$ uniformly on every compact input set in the output-space norm $U$.

This is the exact originally authored stronger theorem statement, retained verbatim. Assume Countable Choice for the counterexample below. The assertion fails for input space $C([0,1])$, output space $C^1([0,1])$, and the singleton compact input set consisting of the constant function $1$, with a one-neuron final kernel in the specified integral subclass.

## Statement references

[Kovachki et al., Theorem 8 and Appendix E](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.08481)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $D=D'=(0,1)$, $A=C([0,1])$ with the supremum norm, and $U=C^1([0,1])$ with norm $\|u\|_U=\|u\|_\infty+\|u'\|_\infty$.

[F1] Smooth plateau cutoffs exist with prescribed nested compact supports by [[lem-schwartz-cutoffs-from-the-standard-smooth-step]]. In particular fix a smooth $\beta:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$, supported in $(-1,1)$, with $\beta(0)=1$.

[F2] A general integral-kernel neural operator and its volume-weighted tagged quadratures are defined in [[def-neural-operator]] and [[alg-neural-operator-mesh-discretization]].

[F3] Under Countable Choice, continuous nonpolynomial scalar activations give fixed-depth compact-uniform MLP density, by [[thm-single-hidden-layer-universal-approximation]]; the stated choice principle is [[def-countable-choice]].

## Counterexample

1.1 For integers $n\ge2$ put $t_n=3\cdot2^{-n-2}$, $w_n=2^{-4n-4}$, $H_n=2^{2n}$ and $\rho_n(s)=H_n\beta((s-t_n)/w_n)$. Their supports are disjoint subintervals of $(0,1)$: successive centers differ by $3\cdot2^{-n-3}$, which exceeds $w_n+w_{n+1}$, and each radius is smaller than its center. Define $\rho(s)=\sum_{n\ge2}\rho_n(s)$ for $s>0$, and $\rho(s)=0$ for $s\le0$. On each compact subinterval of $(0,\infty)$ only finitely many summands are nonzero. Moreover $m_n=\int\rho_n\le2H_nw_n=2^{-2n-3}$, so $B=\sum_{n\ge2}m_n<1$. Define $\sigma(s)=\int_0^s\rho(t)\,dt$ for $s\ge0$ and $\sigma(s)=0$ for $s<0$. The tail mass bound proves continuity at zero and uniform convergence of the primitives $\sigma_n(s)=\int_0^s\rho_n(t)\,dt$; thus $\sigma=\sum\sigma_n$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$, bounded by $B$, and smooth on $(0,\infty)$. It is a legitimate continuous activation. It is bounded and nonconstant, hence is not polynomial even almost everywhere: continuity would make an almost-everywhere polynomial identity hold everywhere, and a bounded polynomial is constant. Thus [F3] also places it in every finite-dimensional $\mathcal A_0$ class if that premise is imposed when defining the source integral subclass. ReLU belongs to $\mathcal A_0^L$ by the same supplier and its linear growth. [given, F1, F3, construct, algebra]

2.1 Set $\kappa(x,y)=\sigma(x+y)$ and $G(a)(x)=\int_0^1\sigma(x+y)a(y)\,dy$. The kernel is exactly a one-hidden-unit network on $(x,y)$ with weights $(1,1)$, activation $\sigma$, output weight $1$, and zero biases. The other activations can be the identity. Each $G_n^*(a)(x)=\int_0^1\sigma_n(x+y)a(y)\,dy$ is $C^1$, with derivative $\int_0^1\rho_n(x+y)a(y)\,dy$, and both its function norm and derivative norm are at most $m_n\|a\|_\infty$. Consequently both the function series and derivative series converge uniformly. To verify differentiation without an interchange assumption, the finite partial sums satisfy $S_N(x)-S_N(0)=\int_0^x S_N'(t)\,dt$; uniform convergence permits passage to the limit in this equality, and the fundamental theorem of calculus gives a continuous derivative. Hence $G:A\to U$ is bounded linear, with $\|G(a)\|_U\le2B\|a\|_\infty$. Both $A$ and $U$ embed continuously into $C([0,1])$. To instantiate the source integral subclass as well, take $S_0$ and $S_1$ to have constant kernel $1$ and zero bias, and use $\kappa(x,y)=\sigma(x+y)$ as the final kernel, choosing ReLU for the input and intermediate kernel networks and activations. No intermediate activation occurs at depth $N=2$. This yields $\widehat G(a)=(\int_0^1a)G(1)$, a bounded map $A\to U$. For $a=1$, both preceding integral layers and their quadratures are exactly the constant $1$, so its final continuum and quadrature outputs are precisely those analyzed below. Constant kernels are exact networks through their affine output biases. [step 1.1, F2, construct, algebra]

3.1 At refinement $n$ partition $(0,1)$ into $2^n$ dyadic cells of length $h_n=2^{-n}$. Choose the first tag to be $t_n\in(0,h_n)$ and choose the midpoint of every other cell. Let $Q_n(a)(x)=h_n\sum_{j=1}^{2^n}\sigma(x+\xi_{n,j})a(\xi_{n,j})$. These are compatible tagged Riemann sums, with mesh diameter tending to zero and the same continuum parameters at every refinement. Since every tag is positive, each summand is smooth in a neighborhood of $[0,1]$, so $Q_n(a)\in U$. For $a=1$, all derivative summands are nonnegative and $Q_n(1)'(0)\ge h_n\rho(t_n)=h_nH_n=2^n$. On the other hand, substitution in the continuum integral gives $G(1)(x)=\int_x^{x+1}\sigma(s)\,ds$ and $G(1)'(0)=\sigma(1)-\sigma(0)=B$. Thus $\|Q_n(1)-G(1)\|_U\ge2^n-B\to\infty$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, construct, algebra]

4.1 The set $K=\{1\}\subset A$ is compact. The continuous integrand $(x,y)\mapsto\sigma(x+y)$ on $[0,1]^2$ is uniformly continuous: otherwise pairs at distances tending to zero with a fixed positive function gap have convergent subsequences in the compact square and contradict continuity. Writing its modulus of continuity as $\omega$, the cellwise estimate gives $\|Q_n(1)-G(1)\|_\infty\le\omega(h_n)\to0$. Thus the genuine supremum-norm conclusion coexists with divergence in the admissible output norm, refuting the asserted inference. [step 3.1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Remark

The defect occurs in Appendix E's opening reduction from continuous embeddings to equality with $C(\bar D)$. Such an embedding bounds the supremum norm by the Banach norm; it supplies no reverse inequality. This counterexample also uses a network kernel, rather than only an arbitrary continuous kernel. It refutes the specified volume-weighted tagged quadratures in the asserted norm; it does not assert that no other finite-dimensional approximation to this bounded integral operator can exist.

## Definition

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

## Remarks

- **Why the Carathéodory criterion rather than the inner-outer criterion.**
  Lebesgue's original definition compares the outer measure of $E$ with that of
  its complement inside a large box, and it is available only for bounded $E$;
  the criterion above is stated for every subset at once and is what makes the
  published Carathéodory machinery apply verbatim. The two agree, and the
  equivalence with the approximation criteria is
  [[thm-littlewood-characterisations-of-lebesgue-measurability]].

- **The definition is relative to $\lambda_n^*$ and to nothing else.** Changing
  the outer measure changes the family; the family attached to a general outer
  measure is written $\mathcal{M}_{\mu^*}$ in
  [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]], and $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is the
  name reserved for the instance $\mu^* = \lambda_n^*$.

## Statement

Let $p,q\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $H\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, and let $T$ be a nonnegative integer. Suppose $h_0:\Theta\to H$, $\Phi_t:\Theta\times H\to H$ for $1\le t\le T$, and $\ell:\Theta\times H\to\mathbb R$ are continuously differentiable on open domains containing the trajectory at $\theta\in\Theta$. A continuously differentiable map is totally differentiable at each point and has a derivative matrix continuous on its domain. Define $h_0=h_0(\theta)$, $h_t=\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, and $J(\theta)=\ell(\theta,h_T)$. Write $A_t=D_\theta\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$ and $B_t=D_h\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, with each partial derivative holding the other argument fixed. Set $\lambda_T=(D_h\ell(\theta,h_T))^T$ and, in descending order, $\lambda_{t-1}=B_t^T\lambda_t$. Then the backpropagation algorithm returns $J(\theta)$ and

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta)=(D_\theta\ell(\theta,h_T))^T+\sum_{t=1}^{T}A_t^T\lambda_t+(Dh_0(\theta))^T\lambda_0,$$

where the sum is empty when $T=0$. The statement also applies when every primitive is evaluated on one fixed strict $C^1$ branch; it makes no assertion at a branch boundary.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite recurrence, its open domains, the parameter $\theta$, the fixed strict branch when maps are piecewise-$C^1$, and the scalar objective $J$.

[F1] [[def-finite-straight-line-computational-program]]: a finite topologically ordered program has a scalar output, and repeated parent slots are separate uses in its dependency graph.

[F2] [[alg-backpropagation-through-shared-parameter-recurrence]]: the forward pass computes $h_0,\ldots,h_T$; the reverse pass initializes the loss cotangent, adds each transition's parameter pullback to the same parameter accumulator, propagates the state cotangent backward, and finally pulls back through $h_0$.

[F3] [[thm-reverse-mode-computes-gradient]]: on a finite $C^1$ program and fixed strict branch, reverse mode returns the exact derivative transpose of its scalar output.

[F4] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: for totally differentiable finite-dimensional maps, the total derivative of a composition is the ordered composition of their total derivatives.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** identify the recurrence with its finite unrolling, then apply the chain rule backward.

1.1 Since $T$ is finite, the initial map, $T$ transition evaluations, and scalar loss form a finite program whose one parameter input $\theta$ is used at each transition and at the loss. Each map is $C^1$ on an open domain containing the trajectory, so repeated application of [F4] makes $J$ differentiable there; on a fixed strict branch the same conclusion holds branchwise. [F1, F4, given, construct]

2.1 The algorithm's primal pass evaluates this unrolled program. Its reverse pass seeds the loss, visits transitions in descending order, and sends each transition's parameter pullback to the same $\theta$ input while sending its state pullback to $h_{t-1}$; the initial-state pullback is then added at $\theta$. This is the reverse sweep on the finite graph in [F1], so [F3] gives the exact gradient of $J$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The terminal state's cotangent is $\lambda_T=(D_h\ell)^T$. At transition $t$, the chain rule gives the cotangent at $h_{t-1}$ as $B_t^T\lambda_t$ and adds $A_t^T\lambda_t$ to the derivative with respect to the shared parameter while $h_{t-1}$ is held fixed. Descending induction therefore gives the stated $\lambda_{t-1}$ recurrence and sums one parameter contribution for each of the $T$ transition uses. [F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The loss's direct dependence on $\theta$ contributes $(D_\theta\ell)^T$, and the dependence of $h_0(\theta)$ contributes $(Dh_0)^T\lambda_0$. Adding these to the $T$ transition contributions from step 2.2 gives the displayed formula. If $T=0$, there are no transition terms and the same chain rule reduces $J(\theta)=\ell(\theta,h_0(\theta))$ to the two remaining terms. This is exactly the algorithm's return value and gradient. [F2, F4, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix an input dimension $n\ge0$, finitely many operation nodes $1,\ldots,T$, and a designated output node $o$, either an input coordinate or an operation, whose value space is $\mathbb R$. Give input coordinate $i$ a label $\mathrm{in}_i$ distinct from all operation indices, and set $z_{\mathrm{in}_i}=x_i$ and $E_{\mathrm{in}_i}=\mathbb R$ with its standard Euclidean inner product. Operation node $j$ has an ordered list of parent slots $p_{j,1},\ldots,p_{j,r_j}$; each slot is either an input label $\mathrm{in}_i$ or an operation index $\ell<j$. Repeated parent slots are allowed and count separately. The graph is a finite straight-line program because every operation reads only earlier values and there are no data-dependent loops.

For each operation $j$, choose a dimension $d_j\ge0$, set $E_j=\mathbb R^{d_j}$ with its standard Euclidean inner product, take an open set $U_j\subseteq E_{p_{j,1}}\times\cdots\times E_{p_{j,r_j}}$ with the product inner product, and choose a primitive map $\phi_j:U_j\to E_j$. A smooth primitive is $C^1$: it is totally differentiable and its derivative matrix is continuous. For Hessian-vector products require the primitive to be $C^2$, meaning $C^1$ with a continuously differentiable derivative map. Derivatives are represented in these coordinates, and every transpose is the Euclidean transpose for the stated inner products; the gradient of a scalar output is the Euclidean gradient. The real-arithmetic primal recursion is $z_j=\phi_j(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})$ whenever the parent tuple lies in $U_j$. Its admissible input domain is the set of $x\in\mathbb R^n$ for which every operation in this recursion is defined. The graph's scalar output function $f$ is the value at $o$: it is $x_i$ when $o$ is input coordinate $i$, and $z_j$ when $o$ is operation node $j$.

The **primal tape** is the finite ordered record of input and node values, parent-slot indices, primitive identities, and (when applicable) selected branch labels. A deterministic replay starts from the identical checkpoint state and applies the identical primitive maps in the identical order, so it reproduces the same real-arithmetic values and local derivative inputs. Opaque solver calls are not primitive operations unless their complete deterministic map and derivative rule are explicitly supplied.

A piecewise-$C^1$ primitive is specified by finitely many open branch regions and a $C^1$ formula on each region; its primal boundary value, if any, is specified separately. If the current parent tuple lies strictly inside exactly one declared branch, the program uses that branch and its derivative. At a branch boundary or ambiguous branch selection, forward or reverse AD returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE; it does not silently choose a subgradient or generalized derivative. If no primal value is specified at a boundary, that input is outside the program's domain. All correctness theorems below apply on a fixed strict branch. The same convention applies to piecewise-$C^2$ primitives for Hessian-vector products.

## Statement

For a finite $C^1$ program with one scalar output $f$, on a fixed strict branch and at every admissible $x$, the reverse-mode algorithm returns $Df(x)^T1$, the gradient of $f$. More precisely, at any operation node $i$, if its value is temporarily treated as an independent variable and all later operations are recomputed from it, then the accumulated cotangent at $i$ is the derivative of the scalar output with respect to that independent node value.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The graph, its admissible input $x$, and a fixed strict branch.

[F1] [[def-finite-straight-line-computational-program]]: the output is obtained from finitely many primitive nodes in topological order, and repeated parent slots are distinct edges.

[F2] [[lem-finite-straight-line-program-defines-c1-map]]: every node map is $C^1$ on the fixed branch.

[F3] [[alg-reverse-mode-automatic-differentiation]]: reverse mode initializes operation and input cotangents to zero, seeds the scalar output node with cotangent $1$, and adds $D_k\phi_j^T\bar z_j$ to each parent slot in reverse topological order.

[F4] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the derivative of a composition is the ordered composition of its total derivatives.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** reverse induction on graph nodes.

1.1 For each input or operation node $i$, define a directed path from $i$ to the output by choosing one parent slot at each successive operation; when $i=o$, include the length-zero path. Associate to an edge from parent slot $k$ of node $j$ the linear map $D_k\phi_j$ at the stored primal arguments. Repeated slots give separate edges. [F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Fix a node $i$ and form the downstream map $F_i(u)$ by replacing its value with an independent $u$ while holding earlier node values fixed and then evaluating later operations in topological order. Repeated use of [F4] shows that the derivative contribution along a fixed path from $i$ to $o$ is the ordered product of its edge maps. At each operation, its derivative is linear in the concatenated parent direction, so contributions from distinct parent slots add. If $i=o$, the output is $u$ and the length-zero path contributes the identity; if there is no path from $i$ to $o$, $F_i$ is locally constant and the sum is zero. Thus $DF_i(z_i)$ is the sum of the path products over all paths from $i$ to $o$, and its cotangent is the transpose of that sum applied to $1$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The output-node path sum is the identity scalar $1$, matching the unit seed in [F3], whether the output is an input or an operation. For every other node, each path to $o$ begins with exactly one outgoing parent-slot edge $i\to j$, followed by a path from $j$ to $o$. Hence its path-sum recurrence is $\bar z_i=\sum_{j,k:p_{j,k}=i}D_k\phi_j^T\bar z_j$, with an additional identity seed only when $i=o$; this is exactly the initialization and accumulation in [F3]. Reverse induction gives $\bar z_i=DF_i(z_i)^T$ at operation nodes and, at inputs, $\bar x=Df(x)^T1$. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The algorithm returns precisely those input cotangents, proving the statement. [F3, step 3.1] ∎
