## Definition

Fix a finite dimension $d\ge1$ and a discrete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge0},P)$ as in [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]. A sequence $x_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an iterate process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_k$-measurable; a sequence $G_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an oracle process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_{k+1}$-measurable. These are coordinatewise instances of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]]. Assume the coordinates used in a conditional moment are square-integrable.

For deterministic stepsizes $\alpha_k>0$, the unconstrained Robbins–Monro/SGD update is
$$x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kG_k.$$
For a differentiable objective $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, the oracle is conditionally unbiased when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)$ coordinatewise almost surely; it has conditional bias $b_k$ when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)+b_k$. The conditional variance of a vector is the sum of the scalar conditional variances of its coordinates, using [[def-conditional-variance]]. By [[lem-conditional-variance-is-well-defined-and-has-the-second-moment-formula]], it satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=\|\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\|_2^2+\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)$$
almost surely. All conditional expectations are coordinatewise instances of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]], whose existence assumes the [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. No independence across iterations is part of this definition.

The conditional second-moment bound $\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le M_k^2$ and the conditional variance bound $\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)\le\sigma_k^2$ are distinct hypotheses; the latter combines with conditional unbiasedness through the displayed identity.

## Definition

On a filtered probability space [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]], a **real stochastic process** is a sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0}$ of real random variables [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] on the same space. It is **adapted** when $X_n^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F_n$ for every $n$ and every real Borel set $B$. It is **integrable** when $E|X_n|<\infty$ for every $n$, using [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].

An integrable adapted process satisfies both conditions at each fixed time. Integrability here does not mean $\sup_nE|X_n|<\infty$: the deterministic process $X_n=n$ has $E|X_n|=n<\infty$ at every time but unbounded supremum. Measurability and finiteness of each integral are separate requirements. No versions, limits or choices are selected.

## Definition

Assume AC. For real $X\in L^2(P)$ define $\operatorname{Var}(X\mid\mathcal G)=E[(X-E[X\mid\mathcal G])^2\mid\mathcal G]$ as an almost-sure class. Its integrability, nonnegativity, representative independence and second-moment formula are justified by the following lemma.

The conditional class is [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]], with [[def-axiom-of-choice]] inherited from existence. By [[cor-conditional-lp-contraction]], a version of the conditional mean is square integrable. The unbounded-factor rule [[thm-taking-out-what-is-known]] will apply to products whose integrability is verified in the well-definedness lemma, recorded under `justified_by`.

## Source notes

Durrett §4.1.2, printed pp.211–213, supplies the conditional $L^2$ machinery; the following local lemma establishes the variance formula.

## Statement

Assume AC. For real $X\in L^2(P)$, conditional variance is an integrable nonnegative class independent of representatives and satisfies $\operatorname{Var}(X\mid\mathcal G)=E[X^2\mid\mathcal G]-(E[X\mid\mathcal G])^2$ almost surely.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, real $X\in L^2(P)$, a sub-sigma-algebra G and the proposed conditional-variance definition.

[F1] Conditional variance is the conditional expectation of the squared residual. ([[def-conditional-variance]])

[F2] The conditional mean of X is square integrable. ([[cor-conditional-lp-contraction]])

[F3] Products of $L^2$ functions are integrable. ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]])

[F4] The known factor can be taken outside after product integrability is checked. ([[thm-taking-out-what-is-known]])

[F5] Conditional expectation is positive and linear. ([[thm-basic-algebra-and-order-properties-of-conditional-expectation]])

[F6] Almost-everywhere equal integrable functions have identical event integrals. ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]])

[F7] Conditional expectation fixes an integrable known variable. ([[lem-conditioning-a-known-variable-and-an-independent-variable]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Write $U=E[X\mid\mathcal G]$. It is in $L^2$ by [F2]. Since $(X-U)^2\le2X^2+2U^2$, the squared residual is integrable; it is nonnegative and measurable. Thus [F1] exists as an integrable nonnegative class by [F5]. If X or U is replaced by an almost-surely equal measurable representative, the square changes only on the union of those two measurable null sets. Its event integrals are unchanged by [F6], so its conditional class is unchanged. [F1, F2, F5, F6]

2.1 The product XU is integrable by [F3]; U is finite and G-measurable. Hence [F4] yields $E[XU\mid\mathcal G]=U E[X\mid\mathcal G]=U^2$. Also U squared is integrable and G-measurable, so [F7] gives $E[U^2\mid\mathcal G]=U^2$. Expanding the residual square and using [F5] gives $E[(X-U)^2\mid\mathcal G]=E[X^2\mid\mathcal G]-2U^2+U^2=E[X^2\mid\mathcal G]-U^2$. All three conditional inputs are integrable, so the subtraction involves finite classes only. [step 1.1, F3, F4, F5, F7] ∎

## Source notes

Durrett Theorems 4.1.9, 4.1.11, 4.1.14–4.1.15, printed pp.210–213. The local square expansion supplies the formula and checks every product before taking-out.

## Statement

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, real integrable X, and $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$; for the last clause a G-conditional version is H-measurable.

[F1] Conditional versions are measurable and integrable and have the defining event integrals. ([[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]])

[F2] Versions for the same input and sigma-algebra agree almost surely. ([[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Set $U=E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ and take a version $V=E[U\mid\mathcal H]$. For $A\in\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G$, $\int_A V=\int_A U=\int_A X$. Since $V$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable and integrable, [F2] identifies it with $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$. [F1, F2]

2.1 A version $W=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ is already $\mathcal G$-measurable and integrable. It has its own event integrals $\int_A W=\int_A W$ on every $A\in\mathcal G$, so it is a version of $E[W\mid\mathcal G]$; [F2] gives the second identity. Finally if $U$ itself is $\mathcal H$-measurable, its $\mathcal G$ event identities restrict to $\mathcal H$, so [F2] gives the additional assertion. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Source notes

Durrett Theorems 4.1.12–4.1.13, printed p.212; van der Vaart Lemma 1.9(v), printed p.4.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $L>0$, $\sigma\ge0$, and let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable with $L$-Lipschitz gradient and finite global infimum $f^*=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^d}f(x)\in\mathbb R$; the infimum need not be attained. Start at a deterministic $x_1$ and, on a discrete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge1},P)$, run stochastic gradient descent for an integer horizon $N\ge1$ with square-integrable oracle vectors $G_k$, adapted iterates $x_k$, and updates $x_{k+1}=x_k-\gamma_kG_k$. Suppose, almost surely for $k=1,\ldots,N$,
$$\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)\le\sigma^2,$$
where the conditional variance of a vector is the sum of the coordinate conditional variances, and let $0<\gamma_k<2/L$. Put $a_k=2\gamma_k-L\gamma_k^2$, $S_N=\sum_{k=1}^Na_k$, and $D_f:=\sqrt{2(f(x_1)-f^*)/L}\ge0$, so $D_f^2=2(f(x_1)-f^*)/L$. On an independent finite probability-space extension, choose $R\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $P(R=k)=a_k/S_N$ and output $x_R$. Then $S_N>0$ and
$$\frac1L\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_R)\|_2^2\le\frac{D_f^2+\sigma^2\sum_{k=1}^N\gamma_k^2}{\sum_{k=1}^N(2\gamma_k-L\gamma_k^2)}.$$

If $D_f>0$ and $\sigma>0$, the constant choice $\gamma_k=\min\{1/L,D_f/(\sigma\sqrt N)\}$ gives
$$\frac1L\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_R)\|_2^2\le\frac{2LD_f^2}{N}+\frac{2D_f\sigma}{\sqrt N}.$$
If $\sigma=0$, the choice $\gamma_k=1/L$ gives the bound $LD_f^2/N$. If $D_f=0<\sigma$, the choice $\gamma_k=1/(L\sqrt N)$ gives $\sigma^2/[L(2\sqrt N-1)]$. Thus the constant-step guarantee is $O(N^{-1}+N^{-1/2})$ for fixed $L,D_f,\sigma$, with the zero cases covered separately. No global-minimum or iterate-convergence conclusion is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the smooth objective, deterministic initial point, filtered SGD trajectory, square-integrable oracle, conditional unbiasedness and variance assumptions, and the stepsize range in the Statement.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC supplies the conditional-expectation classes used in the oracle assumptions and proof.

[A2] The local conditional-unbiasedness hypothesis is $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)$ almost surely.

[A3] The local conditional-variance hypothesis is $\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)\le\sigma^2$ almost surely.

[A4] The global lower-bound hypothesis is $f(x)\ge f^*$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$; no minimizer is required.

[F1] [[alg-stochastic-gradient-descent]]: the update is $x_{k+1}=x_k-\gamma_kG_k$.

[F2] [[def-stochastic-gradient-oracle-and-unconstrained-update]]: conditional oracle moments are coordinatewise, and the vector second moment is conditional squared mean plus conditional variance.

[F3] [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]] and [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]]: $x_k$ is $\mathcal F_k$-measurable and $G_k$ is $\mathcal F_{k+1}$-measurable.

[F4] [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]: vector iterates and oracle outputs are measurable maps into $\mathbb R^d$.

[F5] [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]: conditional expectations are almost-sure classes under AC.

[F6] [[def-conditional-variance]] and [[lem-conditional-variance-is-well-defined-and-has-the-second-moment-formula]]: the coordinate variance formula gives the vector conditional second-moment identity.

[F7] [[def-martingale-difference-sequence]]: each coordinate of $G_k-\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]$, with the filtration shifted by one index, is a martingale difference.

[F8] [[lem-sgd-trajectory-integrability]]: finite-horizon iterates, gradients, and objective values are integrable.

[F9] [[lem-l-smoothness-descent-inequality]]: $f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+(L/2)\|y-x\|_2^2$.

[F10] [[thm-taking-out-what-is-known]]: an integrable measurable factor may be taken outside conditional expectation when the products are integrable.

[F11] [[thm-basic-algebra-and-order-properties-of-conditional-expectation]]: conditional expectation is linear and order preserving and preserves ordinary expectation.

[F12] [[thm-tower-property-of-conditional-expectation]]: nested conditional expectations satisfy the tower identity.

[F13] [[lem-independent-finite-random-index-extension]]: a finite index with weights summing to one can be added independently, and $\mathbb E[H_R]=\sum_kP(R=k)\mathbb E[H_k]$ for integrable $H_k$.

[F14] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: norms and inner products use the Euclidean convention and satisfy Cauchy–Schwarz.

## Proof

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable with $L$-Lipschitz gradient for $L>0$, and suppose $f(x)\ge f_{\inf}$ for every $x$, where $f_{\inf}\in\mathbb R$ is a lower bound. Let $x_0$ be deterministic, $\Delta=f(x_0)-f_{\inf}$, and run the unconstrained update of [[def-stochastic-gradient-oracle-and-unconstrained-update]] with constant $0<\alpha\le1/L$. Suppose
$$\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)\le\sigma^2$$
almost surely for every $k$. After generating $x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1}$, independently choose $R$ uniformly from $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$ on the finite product extension of the trajectory space; equivalently, $\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_R)\|_2^2=N^{-1}\sum_{k<N}\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_k)\|_2^2$. Then
$$\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_R)\|_2^2\le\frac{2\Delta}{\alpha N}+L\alpha\sigma^2.$$
For fixed $\Delta,\sigma$, the stepsize $\alpha=\min\{1/L,\sqrt{2\Delta/(L\sigma^2N)}\}$ gives an $O(N^{-1/2})$ bound when $\Delta,\sigma>0$; zero cases have the stronger bounds specified in the proof. This is an optimization guarantee, not an inferential or central-limit theorem.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; $f,L,f_{\inf},x_0,\Delta,N$ and the stochastic update and conditional oracle assumptions in the Statement.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC supplies the conditional-expectation classes used in the proof.

[F1] [[def-stochastic-gradient-oracle-and-unconstrained-update]]: the update is $x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha G_k$, and conditional unbiasedness is interpreted coordinatewise almost surely.

[F2] [[lem-l-smoothness-descent-inequality]]: for an $L$-Lipschitz gradient, $f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+(L/2)\|y-x\|_2^2$.

[F3] [[def-conditional-variance]] and [[lem-conditional-variance-is-well-defined-and-has-the-second-moment-formula]]: for a square-integrable scalar coordinate, $\operatorname{Var}(X\mid\mathcal G)=\mathbb E[X^2\mid\mathcal G]-(\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G])^2$; summing this identity over the finitely many coordinates gives the vector second-moment identity.

[F4] [[thm-taking-out-what-is-known]]: finite measurable factors may be taken outside conditional expectation once products are integrable.

[F5] [[thm-basic-algebra-and-order-properties-of-conditional-expectation]]: conditional expectation is linear, preserves order, and preserves ordinary expectation.

[F6] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the Euclidean norm square is the sum of squared coordinates.

[F7] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$, and the Euclidean norm satisfies the triangle inequality.

[F8] [[thm-induction-principle]]: a property true at the first index and inherited by each successor holds at every natural index.

## Proof

1.1 The oracle definition [F1] requires each $G_k$ used in a conditional variance to be square-integrable. Since $x_0$ is deterministic and $\alpha$ is finite, the update and [F8] give square-integrable $x_k$ at every finite iteration by induction. The Lipschitz condition and triangle inequality in [F7] give $\|g_k\|_2\le\|\nabla f(0)\|_2+L\|x_k\|_2$. Applying [F2] at $0,x_k$, then using [F7] and $2ab\le a^2+b^2$, bounds $|f(x_k)|$ by $C(1+\|x_k\|_2^2)$ for a finite constant $C$; thus $f(x_k)$ is integrable. [F1, F2, F7, F8, given, induction, algebra]

2.1 Put $g_k=\nabla f(x_k)$. Apply [F2] with $y=x_k-\alpha G_k$ and condition on $\mathcal F_k$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Since $\alpha\le1/L$, $1-L\alpha/2\ge1/2$. Take ordinary expectations in step 2.1 and sum for $k=0,\ldots,N-1$. The terms $f(x_k)$ telescope and $\mathbb E f(x_N)\ge f_{\inf}$, so $\frac{\alpha}{2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\mathbb E\|g_k\|_2^2\le\Delta+\frac{NL\alpha^2\sigma^2}{2}.$ Dividing by $\alpha N/2$ gives $N^{-1}\sum_{k<N}\mathbb E\|g_k\|_2^2\le2\Delta/(\alpha N)+L\alpha\sigma^2$. $$\frac{\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\alpha_k\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_k)\|_2^2}{\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\alpha_k}\le \frac{2\Delta+2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k\beta_k^2+2L\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2\beta_k^2+L\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2\sigma_k^2}{\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k}.$$

## Definition

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and let $F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuously Fréchet differentiable: at every $w$, $DF(w)$ is a linear first-order approximation with normwise remainder tending to zero, and $w\mapsto DF(w)$ is continuous. Write its coordinate gradient as $\nabla F(w)=(\partial_jF(w))_{0\le j<d}$. Given an initial vector $w_{\mathrm{init}}\in\mathbb R^d$, a constant step size $\alpha>0$, a constant momentum parameter $\beta\ge0$, and an integer horizon $T\ge1$, initialize $w_0=w_1=w_{\mathrm{init}}$. For each integer $t=1,\ldots,T-1$, set

$$w_{t+1}:=w_t-\alpha\nabla F(w_t)+\beta(w_t-w_{t-1}).$$

Output $(w_0,w_1,\ldots,w_T)$. The gradient is evaluated at the current iterate $w_t$.
When $\beta=0$, every update is the fixed-step gradient-descent update with step size $\alpha$.

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$, let $0<c\le L$, and let $A\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ satisfy $A^{\mathsf T}=A$ and $x^{\mathsf T}Ax>0$ for every nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^d$. An eigenvalue of $A$ is a real number $\lambda$ such that $Av=\lambda v$ for some nonzero $v$; assume every eigenvalue lies in $[c,L]$. For a fixed center $w^\star\in\mathbb R^d$, define $F(w)=\tfrac12(w-w^\star)^{\mathsf T}A(w-w^\star)$. Then $w^\star$ is the unique minimizer of $F$. Put $\kappa=L/c$ and define

$$q:=\frac{\sqrt L-\sqrt c}{\sqrt L+\sqrt c}=\frac{\sqrt\kappa-1}{\sqrt\kappa+1}.$$

Here $\nabla F(w)=(\partial_jF(w))_{0\le j<d}$ is the vector of coordinate partial derivatives.

For any constant parameters $\alpha>0$ and $\beta\ge0$, finite horizon $T\ge1$, and initial vector $w_{\mathrm{init}}\in\mathbb R^d$, define the heavy-ball sequence by $w_0=w_1=w_{\mathrm{init}}$ and

$$w_{t+1}=w_t-\alpha\nabla F(w_t)+\beta(w_t-w_{t-1}),\qquad 1\le t<T.$$

For each scalar $\lambda\in[c,L]$, the associated scalar recurrence is $x_{t+1}=(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)x_t-\beta x_{t-1}$. Define its characteristic polynomial and root factor by

$$p_\lambda(r;\alpha,\beta):=r^2-(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)r+\beta,\qquad \rho_\lambda(\alpha,\beta):=\max\{|r|:p_\lambda(r;\alpha,\beta)=0\}.$$

This factor is the largest modulus of the two characteristic roots in $\mathbb C$ of the scalar recurrence for eigenvalue $\lambda$, not a one-step Euclidean norm contraction. The tuned parameters are

$$\alpha=\frac{4}{(\sqrt L+\sqrt c)^2},\qquad \beta=q^2.$$

For this choice, $\rho_\lambda(\alpha,\beta)=q$ for every $\lambda\in[c,L]$. If $c<L$, then $p_c(r;\alpha,\beta)=(r-q)^2$ and $p_L(r;\alpha,\beta)=(r+q)^2$; if $c=L$, the only modal polynomial is $r^2$ and its root factor is $0$.

For gradient descent with step $\gamma=2/(L+c)$, the modal multipliers are $1-\gamma\lambda$ and their largest absolute value over $[c,L]$ is

$$\rho_{\mathrm{GD}}=\frac{L-c}{L+c}=\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1}.$$

Thus $\rho_{\mathrm{GD}}>q$ when $c<L$, and both factors are $0$ when $c=L$. Moreover, among all constant heavy-ball parameters $\alpha'>0$ and $\beta'\ge0$, the supremum of their modal root factors over $\lambda\in[c,L]$ is at least $q$. The tuned parameters therefore minimize that interval worst-case root factor. When $c<L$, the repeated endpoint roots permit a linear polynomial prefactor multiplying $q^t$ or $(-q)^t$; the root factor does not assert a one-step norm contraction by $q$.

Since $A^{\mathsf T}=A$, [F4] makes $x\mapsto Ax$ self-adjoint; [F5] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis $u_1,\ldots,u_d$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_i\in[c,L]$. For the matrix $U$ with columns $u_i$, $U^{\mathsf T}U=I$ and $A=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)U^{\mathsf T}$. [given, F3, F4, F5, choose]

1.2 By [F7], write $u=\sqrt L$, $v=\sqrt c$, and $q=(u-v)/(u+v)$. Set $\alpha=4/(u+v)^2$, $\beta=q^2$, and $s_\lambda=1+q^2-\alpha\lambda$. Common denominators give $s_c=((u+v)^2+(u-v)^2-4v^2)/(u+v)^2=2q$ and $s_L=((u+v)^2+(u-v)^2-4u^2)/(u+v)^2=-2q$; since $s_\lambda$ is affine decreasing, $-2q\le s_\lambda\le2q$ on $[c,L]$. 1.3 For any fixed $\alpha'>0$ and $\beta'\ge0$, the statement defines $p_\lambda(r;\alpha',\beta')=r^2-(1+\beta'-\alpha'\lambda)r+\beta'$ and $\rho_\lambda$ for each $\lambda\in[c,L]$, whether or not $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$. This interval supremum is finite: with $M=1+\beta'+\alpha'L$, every root $z$ satisfies $|z|^2\le M|z|+\beta'$, hence $|z|\le\max\{1,M+\beta'\}$. [given, algebra]

2.1 By [F7], each $\lambda_i\ge c>0$ has a positive square root. Set $C=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{\lambda_1},\ldots,\sqrt{\lambda_d})U^{\mathsf T}$. Its factors are invertible, so $C$ is invertible; [F6] gives $C^\ast=C^{\mathsf T}$, and multiplication gives $C^\ast C=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)U^{\mathsf T}=A$. [given, F6, F7, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.2 For $c<L$, we have $q>0$ and step 1.2 gives $|s_\lambda|<2q$ for $c<\lambda<L$. The roots of $p_\lambda$ are $(s_\lambda\pm i\sqrt{4q^2-s_\lambda^2})/2$, whose squared modulus is $q^2$; at $c$ and $L$ the polynomials are $(r-q)^2$ and $(r+q)^2$. If $c=L$, then $q=0$, $\alpha=1/c$, $\beta=0$, and the only polynomial is $p_c(r)=r^2$. Thus every tuned modal root factor is $q$. [given, F7, step 1.2, algebra, cases]

2.3 Assume $c<L$ and fix arbitrary $\alpha'>0$, $\beta'\ge0$. Let $R=\sup_{\lambda\in[c,L]}\rho_\lambda(\alpha',\beta')$, finite by step 1.3. If $R\ge1$, then $R>q$ by step 1.2; if $R=0$, the endpoint polynomials force $\beta'=0$ and $\alpha'c=\alpha'L=1$, impossible since $c<L$, so in the remaining case $0<R<1$. The endpoint root products give $0\le\beta'\le R^2$. For real endpoint roots in $[-R,R]$, $p_c(R)=(R-r_1)(R-r_2)\ge0$ and $p_L(-R)=(-R-r_1)(-R-r_2)\ge0$; for conjugate roots these values are squared moduli. [given, step 1.2, step 1.3, assume-case, algebra]

3.1 The objective is $F(w)=\phi(w-w^\star)$ for $\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|Cx\|_2^2$. Applying [F8] to each increment $h$ gives $D F(w)[h]=\operatorname{Re}\langle C^\ast C(w-w^\star),h\rangle$, so [F9] yields $\nabla F(w)=C^\ast C(w-w^\star)=A(w-w^\star)$. Since $C$ is invertible, $F(w)=\tfrac12\|C(w-w^\star)\|_2^2\ge0$ with equality exactly at $w=w^\star$, proving unique minimization. [given, F8, F9, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 For $c<L$, at either endpoint the scalar recurrence has polynomial $(z-r)^2$ with $r=q$ or $r=-q$, so $r\ne0$. For arbitrary real $a,b$, substitution shows $x_t=(a+bt)r^t$ satisfies $x_{t+1}-2rx_t+r^2x_{t-1}=r^{t+1}((a+b(t+1))-2(a+bt)+(a+b(t-1)))=0$; choosing $a=x_0$ and $b=x_1/r-x_0$ matches any initial pair. Thus a repeated endpoint mode can contain $t r^t$, which explains why the root factor alone is not a one-step norm contraction. [given, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

3.3 In the case $0<R<1$ of [2.3], expanding its endpoint inequalities gives $\alpha'c\ge(1-R)(R-\beta')/R$ and $\alpha'L\le(1+R)(R+\beta')/R$. Since $\beta'\le R^2<R$, the first right-hand side is positive, so division yields $\kappa=L/c\le(1+R)(R+\beta')/((1-R)(R-\beta'))$. Also $(1+R)(R-\beta')-(1-R)(R+\beta')=2(R^2-\beta')\ge0$, hence $(R+\beta')/(R-\beta')\le(1+R)/(1-R)$ and $\kappa\le((1+R)/(1-R))^2$. By [F7], taking positive square roots and rearranging gives $R\ge(\sqrt\kappa-1)/(\sqrt\kappa+1)=q$; together with the $R\ge1$ case, every admissible pair has $R\ge q$. [given, F7, step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 Let $e_t=w_t-w^\star$ and $x_{i,t}=u_i^{\mathsf T}e_t$. By [F1] and step 3.1, $e_{t+1}=(1+\beta)e_t-\alpha A e_t-\beta e_{t-1}$ for $1\le t<T$. Since $Au_i=\lambda_i u_i$ and $A^{\mathsf T}=A$, projection onto $u_i$ gives $x_{i,t+1}=(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda_i)x_{i,t}-\beta x_{i,t-1}$, whose characteristic polynomial is $p_{\lambda_i}(r;\alpha,\beta)$. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 For gradient descent with $\gamma=2/(L+c)$, [F2] and step 3.1 give the scalar update $x_{i,t+1}=(1-\gamma\lambda_i)x_{i,t}$. The affine multiplier decreases from $(L-c)/(L+c)$ at $c$ to $-(L-c)/(L+c)$ at $L$, so its largest absolute value on $[c,L]$ is $\rho_{\mathrm{GD}}=(L-c)/(L+c)$. [given, F2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Put $s=\sqrt\kappa$. By step 4.2, $\rho_{\mathrm{GD}}=(\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1)=(s^2-1)/(s^2+1)$, while $q=(s-1)/(s+1)$ by its definition. If $s>1$, subtraction gives $\rho_{\mathrm{GD}}-q=2s(s-1)/((s^2+1)(s+1))>0$; if $s=1$, both factors are zero. This proves the claimed gradient-descent comparison. [given, F7, step 2.2, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 If $c=L$, step 2.2 gives tuned root factor $q=0$, which is minimal since root factors are nonnegative. If $c<L$, step 2.2 gives tuned interval factor $q$ and step 3.3 gives the lower bound $R\ge q$ for every constant admissible pair, so the tuned parameters are minimax; step 5.1 gives the strict comparison with gradient descent, while step 3.2 records the repeated-root qualification. [given, step 2.2, step 3.2, step 3.3, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. In orthonormal bases $\mathcal E=(e_j)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal F=(f_i)$ of $W$,

$$[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}=\overline{[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}}^{\mathsf T}.$$

Over $\mathbb R$ this is the transpose. The statement includes zero-sized bases.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A map $T:V\to W$ and orthonormal bases $\mathcal E=(e_j)$ and $\mathcal F=(f_i)$.

[L1] The adjoint satisfies $\langle Te_j,f_i\rangle=\langle e_j,T^*f_i\rangle$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]).

[L2] If $(e_i)_{i<r}$ is an orthonormal basis, then $v=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i$ for every vector $v$ ([[thm-bessel-inequality-and-finite-parseval-identity]]).

[L3] Matrix columns record the coordinates of images of basis vectors ([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]).

[L4] Transposition interchanges matrix rows and columns, and complex conjugation is an involution ([[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Write $A=[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}$ and $B=[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}$. Applying [L2] in $\mathcal F$ expands $Te_j=\sum_i\langle Te_j,f_i\rangle f_i$, and applying it in $\mathcal E$ expands $T^*f_i=\sum_j\langle T^*f_i,e_j\rangle e_j$. Since a coordinate column in a basis is unique, [L3] gives $A_{ij}=\langle Te_j,f_i\rangle$ and $B_{ji}=\langle T^*f_i,e_j\rangle$. [L2, L3]

2.1 By [L1] and conjugate symmetry, $B_{ji}=\overline{\langle e_j,T^*f_i\rangle}=\overline{\langle Te_j,f_i\rangle}=\overline{A_{ij}}$. Thus [L4] gives $B=\overline A^{\mathsf T}$. [step 1.1, L1, L4]

3.1 If either basis is empty, the same entrywise identity is vacuous and identifies the unique matrix of the required size. [step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Fix a matrix $C$ and consider the real-valued quadratic form

$$q(x):=\frac12\|Cx\|_2^2=\frac12 x^\ast C^\ast Cx.$$

Then

$$Dq(x)[h]=\operatorname{Re}\langle C^\ast Cx,h\rangle,$$

so the gradient is $C^\ast Cx$, and the Hessian is the constant Hermitian map
$h\mapsto C^\ast Ch$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A fixed matrix $C$, a vector $x$, and a perturbation direction $h$.

[L1] Matrix differentials satisfy the product and adjoint rules ([[prop-matrix-differentials-obey-sum-product-and-adjoint-rules]]).

[L2] Frobenius-linear functionals differentiate by inspection ([[prop-differentials-of-trace-and-frobenius-linear-functionals]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Expanding at $x+h$ gives $$q(x+h)=\frac12\|Cx+Ch\|_2^2 =\frac12\|Cx\|_2^2+\operatorname{Re}\langle Cx,Ch\rangle+\frac12\|Ch\|_2^2.$$ Hence $$Dq(x)[h]=\operatorname{Re}\langle C^\ast Cx,h\rangle,$$ so the gradient is $C^\ast Cx$. [L1, L2, algebra]

2.1 The derivative of the gradient map $x\mapsto C^\ast Cx$ is the constant linear map $h\mapsto C^\ast Ch$. Therefore the Hessian is $C^\ast C$. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be $F(x)=\tfrac12x^2$. Run heavy-ball momentum with $\alpha=\tfrac{27}{8}$, $\beta=\tfrac14$, and $w_0=w_1=1$. For every integer $t\ge0$, the resulting iterates are

$$w_t=-\frac35(-2)^t+\frac85\left(-\frac18\right)^t,$$

so the iterate sequence is unbounded and does not converge to a real limit.

## Example references

[[alg-heavy-ball-momentum]]

[[prop-gradient-of-a-quadratic-matrix-form]]

[[thm-reals-cauchy-complete|Completeness of the real numbers]]

[[thm-of-archimedean]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $F(x)=\tfrac12x^2$, heavy-ball parameters $\alpha=\tfrac{27}{8}$ and $\beta=\tfrac14$, and initial values $w_0=w_1=1$.

[F1] [[alg-heavy-ball-momentum]]: for fixed parameters, $w_{t+1}=w_t-\alpha\nabla F(w_t)+\beta(w_t-w_{t-1})$.

[F2] [[prop-gradient-of-a-quadratic-matrix-form]]: for $q(x)=\tfrac12\|Cx\|_2^2$, the gradient is $C^\ast Cx$.

[F3] [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]]: with its usual order and field structure, $\mathbb R$ is a complete ordered field.

[F4] [[thm-of-archimedean]]: in every complete ordered field, for every element $M$ there is a canonical natural number $n\ge1$ whose field embedding satisfies $M<n$.

## Verification

1.1 Taking $C=[1]$ in [F2] gives $\nabla F(x)=x$. Substituting the parameters and this gradient into [F1] yields $w_{t+1}=-\tfrac{17}{8}w_t-\tfrac14w_{t-1}$ for every $t\ge1$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The characteristic polynomial is $r^2+\tfrac{17}{8}r+\tfrac14=(r+2)(r+\tfrac18)$. Each geometric sequence $(-2)^t$ and $(-\tfrac18)^t$ therefore satisfies the recurrence in step 1.1. The stated linear combination has $w_0=1$ and $w_1=\tfrac65-\tfrac15=1$, so the recurrence and these initial values prove the displayed formula for all $t$ by induction. [given, step 1.1, algebra, induction]

3.1 For $t\ge1$, factor the expression as $w_t=(-2)^t\bigl(-\tfrac35+\tfrac85\,16^{-t}\bigr)$. Since $16^{-t}\le1/16$, the term in parentheses is at most $-\tfrac12$, hence $|w_t|\ge2^{t-1}$. Induction gives $2^{t-1}\ge t$ for $t\ge1$. For any starting index $N\ge1$ and any real $R>0$, put $B=\max\{N,R\}$; since $\mathbb R$ is a complete ordered field by [F3], [F4] supplies a natural number $t>B$, which we use under the usual embedding as an integer iteration index. Thus $t\ge N$ and $|w_t|\ge t>R$. Every tail is therefore unbounded. If the sequence converged to a real $\ell$, some tail would satisfy $|w_t-\ell|<1$ and hence $|w_t|<|\ell|+1$, a contradiction. [given, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra, induction] ∎

## Definition

Fix a dimension $d\ge1$, an initial vector $x_1\in\mathbb R^d$, a finite or infinite sequence of finite gradient vectors $g_t\in\mathbb R^d$, positive step sizes $\eta_t>0$, a decay parameter $\rho\in[0,1)$, and a denominator constant $\epsilon>0$. Use one-based coordinate notation $z_i:=z(i-1)$ for every vector $z\in\mathbb R^d$ and $1\le i\le d$. Set $r_0=0$. At each integer round $t\ge1$, update the second-moment estimate coordinatewise by

$$r_{t,i}=\rho r_{t-1,i}+(1-\rho)g_{t,i}^2\qquad(1\le i\le d),$$

and then set

$$x_{t+1,i}=x_{t,i}-\eta_t\frac{g_{t,i}}{\sqrt{r_{t,i}}+\epsilon}\qquad(1\le i\le d).$$

For a finite gradient sequence of length $T\ge0$, perform rounds $1\le t\le T$ and return the trajectory $(x_1,\ldots,x_{T+1})$; when $T=0$, return $(x_1)$. For an infinite gradient sequence, perform every round $t\ge1$, thereby defining and returning the iterate sequence $(x_t)_{t\ge1}$. The root, addition, and division in the update are coordinatewise. The procedure makes no convergence or regret claim.

## Definition references

[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: vectors in $\mathbb R^d$ have the stated real coordinates, and vector updates are interpreted coordinatewise.

[[lem-of-square-positive]]: every nonzero squared gradient coordinate is positive.

[[lem-of-zero-mult]]: a zero gradient coordinate has square zero.

[[thm-of-square-roots]]: each nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root.

[[def-ordered-field]]

[[lem-of-sign-rules]]: the decay coefficients and their complements are nonnegative, so the moment recurrence preserves nonnegativity.

[Bottou, Curtis, and Nocedal, RMSprop update](https://leon.bottou.org/publications/pdf/tr-optml-2016.pdf)

[Reddi, Kale, and Kumar, adaptive-method setup](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.09237)

## Remarks

This is the no-momentum RMSProp variant with a positive constant added outside the square root. It has no bias correction and defines only an update procedure.

## Definition

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge1$, an initial scalar $x_1\in[-1,1]$, a step parameter $\alpha>0$, moment parameters $\beta_1\in[0,1)$ and $\beta_2\in(0,1)$, a denominator parameter $\epsilon\ge0$, and a sequence of scalar gradients $g_1,\ldots,g_T$. Set $m_0=v_0=0$. At round $t$, update

$$m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)g_t,\qquad v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)g_t^2.$$

The input is admissible only when $v_t+\epsilon>0$ at every update. Set $\alpha_t=\alpha/\sqrt t$, compute $y_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_t m_t/\sqrt{v_t+\epsilon}$, and set $x_{t+1}=\max(-1,\min(1,y_{t+1}))$. Thus the iterate is projected onto $[-1,1]$ after the update. Return the trajectory $(x_1,\ldots,x_{T+1})$, whose final iterate is $x_{T+1}$. The denominator parameter is added inside the square root. No moment bias correction is applied.

[[def-interval]]: $[-1,1]$ is the closed scalar interval used for initialization and clipping.

[[thm-of-square-roots]]: every nonnegative real radicand has a unique nonnegative square root.

[[def-max-min]]

[[lem-finite-set-has-max]]: the displayed clipping operation is the maximum and minimum of finite real sets.

[[alg-adam-update]]: the published bias-corrected Adam procedure instead divides by $\sqrt{\widehat v_t}+\epsilon$; it is a distinct update convention.

[Reddi, Kale, and Kumar, Algorithm 1 and the inside-root epsilon variant](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.09237)

[Kingma and Ba, Adam Algorithm 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1412.6980)

## Remarks

This is the uncorrected scalar online variant used for the cited regret counterexamples. Its $\epsilon=0$ mode is defined only on gradient sequences with positive $v_t$ at every round; the counterexample sequences in the theorem meet that condition. The fixed-$\epsilon$ mode uses the source's addition inside the square root, not the published bias-corrected denominator convention.

## Definition

Fix a dimension $d\ge1$, a finite horizon $T\ge1$, a nonempty compact convex set $F\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, an initial point $x_1\in F$, positive step sizes $\alpha_t>0$, a fixed parameter $\beta_2\in(0,1)$, and parameters $\beta_{1,t}\in[0,1)$ for $1\le t\le T$. Set $m_0=v_0=\widehat v_0=0$ and update coordinatewise by

$$m_{t,i}=\beta_{1,t}m_{t-1,i}+(1-\beta_{1,t})g_{t,i},\qquad v_{t,i}=\beta_2v_{t-1,i}+(1-\beta_2)g_{t,i}^2,$$

$$\widehat v_{t,i}=\max\{\widehat v_{t-1,i},v_{t,i}\}.$$

If $\widehat v_{t,i}>0$, set $y_{t+1,i}=x_{t,i}-\alpha_t m_{t,i}/\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}$; if $\widehat v_{t,i}=0$, set $y_{t+1,i}=x_{t,i}$. Choose any minimizer

$$x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}\sum_{i=1}^d\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}(x_i-y_{t+1,i})^2.$$

Return the trajectory through $x_{T+1}$. The procedure uses the uncorrected first and second moments and the coordinatewise running maximum of the raw second moment. It contains no denominator stabilizer.

[[def-max-min]]

[[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]: a continuous real-valued function on the nonempty compact feasible set attains its minimum.

[[alg-amsgrad-update]]: the published procedure instead maxes bias-corrected second moments; it is not this raw-moment update.

## Statement

For every real $q\in[0,1)$, every $p\in\{1,2\}$, and every real $\delta>0$, there is an integer $N\ge1$ such that $n^p q^n<\delta$ for every integer $n\ge N$.

## Statement references

[[def-integer-power]]: $q^n$ is the natural integer power.

[[lem-geometric-sequence-null]]: if $0\le q<1$, then $q^n$ tends to zero.

[Reddi, Kale, and Kumar, Appendix B](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.09237)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $q\in[0,1)$, $p\in\{1,2\}$, and $\delta>0$.

[F1] [[lem-geometric-sequence-null]]: if $0\le s<1$, then for every positive tolerance there is an index after which $s^k$ is below that tolerance.

[F2] [[thm-of-archimedean]]: for every real $z$ there is an integer $N\ge1$ with $z<N$.

[F3] [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-integer-power]]: the powers and indices use natural-number recursion, with $q^{n+1}=q^nq$.

[F4] [[def-ordered-field]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]], and [[lem-of-inverse-positive]]: the real numbers are a totally ordered field, and positive denominators preserve inequalities when dividing.

## Proof

**Given:** $q,p,\delta$ as in the Statement.

1.1 If $q=0$, then $n^p q^n=0<\delta$ for every $n\ge1$, so take $N=1$. If $q>0$, set $s=(q+1)/2$, so $q<s<1$, and set $A=2^p-1\in\{1,3\}$. [given, F4, algebra, cases]

2.1 For every integer $n\ge1$, $(1+1/n)^p\le1+A/n$: for $p=1$ this is equality; for $p=2$, expand to $1+2/n+1/n^2$ and use $1/n^2\le1/n$. By [F2] choose $N_0\ge1$ so large that $q(1+A/N_0)\le s$. Then for every $n\ge N_0$, the ratio $((n+1)^p q^{n+1})/(n^p q^n)=q(1+1/n)^p\le s$. [given, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, choose, algebra]

3.1 Induction on $k\ge0$ using step 2.1 gives $(N_0+k)^p q^{N_0+k}\le N_0^p q^{N_0}s^k$. By [F1] choose $K$ with $N_0^p q^{N_0}s^K<\delta$. The ratio bound in step 2.1 is at most $s<1$, so the sequence $n^p q^n$ is nonincreasing for $n\ge N_0$; hence every $n\ge N_0+K$ satisfies $n^p q^n\le N_0^p q^{N_0}s^K<\delta$. This proves the Statement in the $q>0$ case, and step 1.1 proves the $q=0$ case. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, induction, choose, algebra] ∎

## Definition

An **ordered field** is a field $F$ ([[def-field]]) together with a subset
$P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*),
satisfying:

- **(O1) Trichotomy.** For each $x \in F$, exactly one of the following holds:
  $x \in P$, or $x = 0$, or $-x \in P$.
- **(O2) Closure.** If $x, y \in P$ then $x + y \in P$ and $x \cdot y \in P$.

We write $x > 0$ for $x \in P$ (read "$x$ is positive"), and define the order by

$$a < b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; b - a \in P, \qquad a \le b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; a < b \text{ or } a = b.$$

Thus $a > b$ means $b < a$, and $a \ge b$ means $b \le a$. An element $x$ with
$-x \in P$ (equivalently $x < 0$) is called **negative**.

## Remarks

- By trichotomy applied to $b - a$, for any $a, b$ exactly one of $a < b$,
  $a = b$, $a > b$ holds; this makes $\le$ a total order.
- (O2) says the positives are closed under addition and multiplication: sums and
  products of positives are positive.
- The rationals ([[thm-rat-ordered-field]]) and both constructions of the reals
  ([[thm-reals-ordered-field]], [[thm-reals-dedekind-ordered-field]]) are ordered
  fields, so every fact proved here from (O1)-(O2) holds in each of them.

## Definition

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $S \subseteq F$.

- $u \in F$ is an **upper bound** of $S$ if $s \le u$ for all $s \in S$; $S$ is
  **bounded above** if it has an upper bound.
- $u \in F$ is a **least upper bound** (or **supremum**, $\sup S$) of $S$ if $u$
  is an upper bound of $S$ and $u \le u'$ for every upper bound $u'$ of $S$.

$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty
$S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$.

## Remarks

- A least upper bound, if it exists, is unique (two least upper bounds are each
  $\le$ the other, so equal by antisymmetry of the order).
- Applying the property to $\{-s : s \in S\}$ yields the dual **greatest lower
  bound** (infimum) property, so the two are equivalent.
- The Dedekind-cut reals have this property by construction
  ([[thm-dedekind-complete]]); the Cauchy-sequence reals acquire it via
  [[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]. This definition is the target for the
  uniqueness theorem [[thm-uniqueness-complete-ordered-field]].

## Statement

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ have the **least-upper-bound property**:
every nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ that is bounded above has a least upper
bound $\sup S \in \mathbb{R}_C$. Hence, together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]],
$\mathbb{R}_C$ is a **complete ordered field** ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ bounded above by $U \in \mathbb{R}_C$.

[L1] Upper bound, least upper bound, and the least-upper-bound property ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

[L2] Every Cauchy sequence of reals converges to a real ([[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]]).

[L3] Convergence and the Cauchy condition for real sequences are quantified over positive rational $\varepsilon$ ([[def-real-limit]]).

[L4] $\mathbb{R}_C$ is Archimedean, so the reals $2^k$ are cofinal and $(b_0 - a_0)/2^k \to 0$ ([[lem-cauchy-reals-archimedean]]).

[L5] $\mathbb{R}_C$ is a totally ordered field: midpoints $(a + b)/2$, halving, and order arithmetic ([[thm-reals-ordered-field]], [[def-real-order]]).

[L6] The rationals embed densely; below any real lies a rational ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $s_0 \in S$ (possible as $S \ne \emptyset$); by [L6] choose a real $a_0 < s_0$, so $a_0$ is not an upper bound of $S$, and put $b_0 = U$, an upper bound of $S$. [given, L6, L5, L1]

2.1 Define $(a_k), (b_k)$ by bisection: given $a_k$ (not an upper bound) and $b_k$ (an upper bound), let $m = (a_k + b_k)/2$; if $m$ is an upper bound set $a_{k+1} = a_k, b_{k+1} = m$, otherwise set $a_{k+1} = m, b_{k+1} = b_k$. [step 1.1, L5]

3.1 An induction on $k$ shows each $b_k$ is an upper bound of $S$, each $a_k$ is not, $a_k \le a_{k+1} \le b_{k+1} \le b_k$, and $b_k - a_k = (b_0 - a_0)/2^k$. [step 2.1, L5, L1]

4.1 Given rational $\varepsilon > 0$, by [L4] choose $k$ with $(b_0 - a_0) < 2^k \hat\varepsilon$; then for all $j \ge k$, $b_j - a_j = (b_0 - a_0)/2^j \le (b_0 - a_0)/2^k < \hat\varepsilon$. [step 3.1, L4, L5]

5.1 For $j, l \ge k$ both $a_j, a_l, b_j, b_l$ lie in the nested interval $[a_k, b_k]$, so $|a_j - a_l| \le b_k - a_k < \hat\varepsilon$ and likewise $|b_j - b_l| < \hat\varepsilon$; hence $(a_k)$ and $(b_k)$ are Cauchy sequences of reals. [step 3.1, step 4.1, L3, L5]

6.1 By [L2], $(a_k)$ converges to a real $s$ and $(b_k)$ to a real $s'$. If $s < s'$, choose by [L6] a positive rational $\varepsilon$ with $3\hat\varepsilon < s'-s$. For all large $k$, convergence and step 4.1 give $|a_k-s| < \hat\varepsilon$, $|b_k-s'| < \hat\varepsilon$ and $b_k-a_k < \hat\varepsilon$, whence $s'-s \le |s'-b_k|+(b_k-a_k)+|a_k-s| < 3\hat\varepsilon$, a contradiction. If $s' < s$, choose $2\hat\varepsilon < s-s'$; for all large $k$, $a_k \le b_k$ and the two convergence bounds give $s-s' \le |s-a_k|+(a_k-b_k)+|b_k-s'| < 2\hat\varepsilon$, again a contradiction. Thus $s=s'$. For fixed $k$ and every $j \ge k$, step 3.1 gives $a_k \le a_j \le b_j \le b_k$. If $s<a_k$, choose $0<\hat\varepsilon<a_k-s$ and use $a_j\to s$; if $b_k<s$, choose $0<\hat\varepsilon<s-b_k$ and use $b_j\to s$. Each choice contradicts the displayed inequalities for all large $j$, so $a_k \le s \le b_k$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, L2, L3, L5, L6, algebra]

7.1 Every $t \in S$ satisfies $t \le b_k$ for all $k$, since each $b_k$ is an upper bound. If $s<t$, choose by [L6] a positive rational $\varepsilon$ with $\hat\varepsilon<t-s$. Since $b_k\to s$, eventually $|b_k-s|<\hat\varepsilon$, hence $b_k<s+\hat\varepsilon<t$, contradicting $t\le b_k$. Therefore $t\le s$, so $s$ is an upper bound of $S$. [step 3.1, step 6.1, L1, L3, L5, L6]

7.2 If $v$ is any upper bound of $S$, then for each $k$ some element of $S$ exceeds $a_k$, because $a_k$ is not an upper bound; hence $a_k<v$. If $v<s$, choose by [L6] a positive rational $\varepsilon$ with $\hat\varepsilon<s-v$. Since $a_k\to s$, eventually $|a_k-s|<\hat\varepsilon$, so $a_k>s-\hat\varepsilon>v$, a contradiction. Thus $s\le v$, and $s$ is the least upper bound. [step 3.1, step 6.1, L1, L3, L5, L6]

8.1 Hence $s = \sup S$ exists in $\mathbb{R}_C$; as $S$ was an arbitrary nonempty bounded-above set, $\mathbb{R}_C$ has the least-upper-bound property and is a complete ordered field. [step 7.1, step 7.2, L1] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$, let $x_0\in[-1,1]$, and let $k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$. Let real increments $\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_n$ satisfy $\delta_j\le0$ for $j\le k$ and $\delta_j\ge0$ for $j>k$. Define $c(y)=\max\{-1,\min\{1,y\}\}$ and $x_j=c(x_{j-1}+\delta_j)$. Then

$$x_n\ge\min\left\{1,x_0+\sum_{j=1}^n\delta_j\right\}.$$

## Statement references

[[def-max-min]]: maximum and minimum of finite real sets define the clipping map $c$.

[[def-interval]]: $[-1,1]$ is the closed interval with endpoints $-1$ and $1$.

[Reddi, Kale, and Kumar, Appendix B](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.09237)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $n,x_0,k,\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_n$ as in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-max-min]]: $\min\{a,b\}$ is the lesser element and $\max\{a,b\}$ is the greater element of a two-element real set.

[F2] [[def-ordered-field]] and [[lem-of-sign-rules]]: the real order is total, and adding the same real to both sides preserves order.

[F3] [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[thm-induction-principle]]: the finite sequence indices are natural numbers, and induction proves assertions across all of them.

[F4] [[def-finite-sum]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: the displayed partial sums are finite sums and obey the termwise addition laws.

## Proof

**Given:** The data and sign conditions in the Statement.

1.1 Put $s_j=x_0+\sum_{i=1}^j\delta_i$ and $s_0=x_0$. For $0\le j\le k$, induction gives $x_j\ge s_j$ and $x_j\le1$: the base is $x_0=s_0\in[-1,1]$; at a next nonpositive increment, $x_{j-1}+\delta_j\le1$, so clipping replaces it only by its maximum with $-1$, which is no smaller than $x_{j-1}+\delta_j\ge s_j$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, induction]

2.1 For $k\le j\le n$, induction gives $x_j\ge\min\{1,s_j\}$. The base follows from step 1.1 and $x_k\le1$. If $s_{j-1}\le1$, then $x_{j-1}\ge s_{j-1}$ and $\delta_j\ge0$, so $y:=x_{j-1}+\delta_j\ge s_j$. If $s_j<-1$, then $c(y)\ge-1>s_j$. If $-1\le s_j\le1$, both $1$ and $y$ are at least $s_j$, so $\min\{1,y\}\ge s_j$ and then $c(y)=\max\{-1,\min\{1,y\}\}\ge s_j$. If $s_j>1$, then $y>1$ and $c(y)=1$. In all cases $c(y)\ge\min\{1,s_j\}$. If instead $s_{j-1}>1$, the induction bound and $x_{j-1}\le1$ imply $x_{j-1}=1$; a nonnegative increment keeps the clipped value at $1$. Taking $j=n$ proves the Statement. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, induction, cases] ∎

## Definition

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathbb{R}$.

- $m$ is a **maximum** (or *greatest element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $s \le m$
  for every $s \in S$.
- $m$ is a **minimum** (or *least element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $m \le s$
  for every $s \in S$.

A set has at most one maximum: if $m_1$ and $m_2$ are both maxima then
$m_1 \in S$ gives $m_1 \le m_2$ and $m_2 \in S$ gives $m_2 \le m_1$, so
$m_1 = m_2$ by antisymmetry of the order, which is immediate from the trichotomy
axiom of an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
The same argument applies to minima, so we may write $\max S$ and $\min S$.

## Remarks

- A maximum is precisely an upper bound of $S$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]])
  that happens to lie in $S$; a minimum is a lower bound of $S$
  ([[def-bounded-set]]) that lies in $S$. In particular a set with a maximum is
  bounded above and a set with a minimum is bounded below.
- The empty set has neither a maximum nor a minimum, because the requirement
  $m \in S$ cannot be met.
- The membership requirement $m \in S$ is exactly what separates a maximum from a
  supremum, and it is the theme of this page. A supremum is a bound on the set
  and is not asked to belong to it; a maximum is an element of the set. The two
  agree exactly when the supremum happens to be attained ([[lem-max-is-sup]]),
  and they genuinely differ in general ([[fs-sup-belongs-to-set]]).
- Every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has both a maximum and a minimum
  ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]]), which is what licenses the notation
  $\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$. Infinite sets need not: the failure of attainment is
  an infinitary phenomenon.

## Statement

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ then $ab > 0$.
2. If $a > 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab < 0$.
3. If $a < 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab > 0$.
4. If $c > 0$ then $a < b \iff ac < bc$.
5. If $c < 0$ then $a < b \iff bc < ac$ (multiplication by a negative reverses order).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An ordered field $F$ with positive cone $P$, and elements $a, b, c \in F$.

[L1] For $x, y \in F$: $x < y \iff y - x \in P$; $x > 0 \iff x \in P$; $x < 0 \iff -x \in P$; and (trichotomy) for each $x$ exactly one of $x \in P$, $x = 0$, $-x \in P$ holds, so $0 \notin P$ and $x \in P \Rightarrow x \neq 0$ ([[def-ordered-field]]).

[L2] $P$ is closed under multiplication: if $u, v \in P$ then $uv \in P$ (axiom O2 of [[def-ordered-field]]).

[L3] In any field, $(-u)v = -(uv)$ and $(-u)(-v) = uv$ ([[lem-of-mult-neg]]).

[L4] In any field, $0 \cdot u = 0$ ([[lem-of-zero-mult]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Assume $a > 0$ and $b > 0$, i.e. $a \in P$ and $b \in P$; closure gives $ab \in P$, so $ab > 0$, proving claim 1. [assume-hyp, L1, L2]

1.2 Assume $a > 0$ and $b < 0$, i.e. $a \in P$ and $-b \in P$; closure gives $a(-b) \in P$. [assume-hyp, L1, L2]

1.3 Assume $a < 0$ and $b < 0$, i.e. $-a \in P$ and $-b \in P$; closure gives $(-a)(-b) \in P$. [assume-hyp, L1, L2]

1.4 Assume $c > 0$ and $a < b$, i.e. $c \in P$ and $b - a \in P$; closure gives $(b - a)c \in P$. [assume-hyp, L1, L2]

1.5 Assume $c < 0$ and $a < b$, i.e. $-c \in P$ and $b - a \in P$; closure gives $(b - a)(-c) \in P$. [assume-hyp, L1, L2]

2.1 Since $a(-b) = -(ab)$ by L3, step 1.2 gives $-(ab) \in P$, so $ab < 0$, proving claim 2. [step 1.2, L3, L1]

2.2 Since $(-a)(-b) = ab$ by L3, step 1.3 gives $ab \in P$, so $ab > 0$, proving claim 3. [step 1.3, L3, L1]

2.3 By distributivity $(b - a)c = bc - ac$, so step 1.4 gives $bc - ac \in P$, i.e. $ac < bc$: this is the forward direction of claim 4. [step 1.4, algebra, L1]

2.4 By L3 and distributivity $(b - a)(-c) = -((b - a)c) = -(bc - ac) = ac - bc$, so step 1.5 gives $ac - bc \in P$, i.e. $bc < ac$: this is the forward direction of claim 5. [step 1.5, L3, algebra, L1]

3.1 Conversely, assume $c > 0$ and $ac < bc$; by trichotomy exactly one of $a < b$, $a = b$, $b < a$ holds. If $a = b$ then $ac = bc$, contradicting $ac < bc$; if $b < a$ then the argument of step 2.3 applied to the pair $b < a$ gives $bc < ac$, so $bc - ac \in P$ (from $ac < bc$) while $ac - bc \in P$ (from $bc < ac$), putting the element $bc - ac$ and its negative $ac - bc$ both in $P$, which trichotomy forbids; hence $a < b$: this completes claim 4. [assume-hyp, step 2.3, L4, L1, algebra]

4.1 Conversely, assume $c < 0$ and $bc < ac$; by trichotomy exactly one of $a < b$, $a = b$, $b < a$ holds. If $a = b$ then $ac = bc$, contradicting $bc < ac$; if $b < a$ then the argument of step 2.4 applied to the pair $b < a$ gives $ac < bc$, so $ac - bc \in P$ (from $bc < ac$) while $bc - ac \in P$ (from $ac < bc$), putting the element $ac - bc$ and its negative $bc - ac$ both in $P$, which trichotomy forbids; hence $a < b$: this completes claim 5. [assume-hyp, step 2.4, L4, L1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every finite admissible run of the RMSProp, uncorrected Adam, or uncorrected AMSGrad procedures defined on this page, all moment coordinates are finite and all second-moment coordinates are nonnegative. Every denominator specified by the procedure is positive. For AMSGrad, a zero historical-maximum coordinate has zero current and previous first moments, and the raw second moment is positive whenever its historical maximum is positive; the zero-ratio convention is therefore consistent. Each weighted minimization over the compact feasible set attains a minimum.

## Statement references

[[alg-rmsprop]]: defines the exponential second-moment recurrence and positive stabilizer.

[[alg-adam]]: defines the uncorrected scalar moment recurrences, admissible denominators, and clipping update.

[[alg-amsgrad]]: defines the raw-moment recurrence, historical maximum, zero-coordinate convention, and compact-set minimization.

[Reddi, Kale, and Kumar, adaptive-moment procedures](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.09237)

[Bottou, Curtis, and Nocedal, RMSprop recurrence](https://leon.bottou.org/publications/pdf/tr-optml-2016.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Finite gradient inputs for the three procedures, their parameter ranges and initial zero moments, and the admissibility conditions in their Definitions.

[F1] [[alg-rmsprop]]: $r_0=0$ and $r_{t,i}=\rho r_{t-1,i}+(1-\rho)g_{t,i}^2$, with $0\le\rho<1$ and $\epsilon>0$.

[F2] [[alg-adam]]: $m_0=v_0=0$, $v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)g_t^2$, and each used radicand $v_t+\epsilon$ is positive.

[F3] [[alg-amsgrad]]: $m_0=v_0=\widehat v_0=0$, $\beta_2\in(0,1)$, $v_{t,i}=\beta_2v_{t-1,i}+(1-\beta_2)g_{t,i}^2$, and $\widehat v_{t,i}=\max\{\widehat v_{t-1,i},v_{t,i}\}$.

[F4] [[thm-induction-principle]]: a property true at the initial index and preserved at each finite successor holds at every finite round.

[F5] [[lem-of-square-positive]], [[lem-of-zero-mult]], and [[lem-of-sign-rules]]: coordinate squares are nonnegative, and nonnegative coefficients preserve nonnegativity under sums and products.

[F6] [[thm-of-square-roots]]: each nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root.

[F7] [[def-max-min]] and [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]: every two-element set of real numbers has a maximum.

[F8] [[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]: a compact subset of $\mathbb R^d$ is bounded, and a continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact subset attains its minimum.

[F9] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-of-square-monotone]], and [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: $|x_i-z_i|\le\|x-z\|_2$, the Euclidean norm satisfies the triangle inequality, and finite sums of nonnegative terms remain nonnegative.

## Proof

**Given:** The data and hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 For each procedure, induction over its finite horizon shows that every moment is a finite real and each second moment is nonnegative. The initial moments are zero. At a successor round, each recurrence is a finite sum of products of finite reals by [F1]–[F3] and [F9]; the coefficients $\rho,1-\rho,\beta_2,1-\beta_2$ are nonnegative, and each squared gradient is nonnegative by [F5], so the next second moment remains nonnegative. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F9, given, induction, algebra]

2.1 For RMSProp, [F6] supplies $\sqrt{r_{t,i}}\ge0$, so $\sqrt{r_{t,i}}+\epsilon>0$ by [F1]. For Adam, [F6] supplies $\sqrt{v_t+\epsilon}$ because $v_t\ge0$ and $\epsilon\ge0$; its positivity is the explicit admissibility condition in [F2]. Thus each stated quotient has a positive denominator. [F1, F2, F6, step 1.1, given, algebra]

2.2 In AMSGrad, both entries in each maximum are finite and nonnegative by [F3], [F5], and step 1.1. The maximum exists by [F7] and is nonnegative. If $\widehat v_{t,i}=0$, then $\widehat v_{t-1,i}=v_{t,i}=0$. Since $\beta_2>0$, $1-\beta_2>0$, and both summands defining $v_{t,i}$ are nonnegative, $v_{t-1,i}=0$ and $g_{t,i}=0$. Repeating this argument back to time zero gives every earlier $g_{s,i}=0$; the first-moment recurrence then gives $m_{t,i}=m_{t-1,i}=0$. Conversely, if $\widehat v_{t,i}>0$, some $v_{s,i}>0$ for $s\le t$, and then $v_{u+1,i}\ge\beta_2v_{u,i}>0$ for each $u\ge s$, so $v_{t,i}>0$. The zero-ratio convention in [F3] is therefore consistent with the recurrence. [F3, F5, F7, step 1.1, given, induction, algebra]

3.1 Fix a round and its finite vector $y$ and nonnegative weights $q_i=\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}$. Since $F$ is compact, [F8] bounds $\|x\|_2$ by some $B$ for $x\in F$. For $x,z\in F$, coordinatewise expansion and [F9] give $$\left|\sum_i q_i(x_i-y_i)^2-\sum_i q_i(z_i-y_i)^2\right|\le\|x-z\|_2\sum_i q_i(2B+2\|y\|_2).$$ Thus the objective is continuous on $F$. Since $F$ is nonempty and compact, [F8] gives a minimizer. The objective can be constant along zero-weight coordinates, so allowing any minimizer is necessary and sufficient. This proves the remaining well-definedness claim. [F3, F8, F9, step 2.2, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$. For
every $a \in F$ with $a \neq 0$ we have $a^2 > 0$, where $a^2 = a \cdot a$. In
particular, every nonzero square is positive.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An ordered field $F$ with positive cone $P$, and an element $a \in F$ with $a \neq 0$.

[L1] $x > 0 \iff x \in P$, and by trichotomy for $a \neq 0$ exactly one of $a \in P$, $-a \in P$ holds ([[def-ordered-field]]).

[L2] $P$ is closed under multiplication: if $u, v \in P$ then $uv \in P$ (axiom O2 of [[def-ordered-field]]).

[L3] In any field, $(-u)(-v) = uv$ ([[lem-of-mult-neg]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** cases.

1.1 Since $a \neq 0$, trichotomy leaves exactly two possibilities: $a \in P$ or $-a \in P$. [L1]

2.1 Case $a > 0$: then $a \in P$, so closure gives $a \cdot a \in P$, i.e. $a^2 > 0$. [assume-case pos, step 1.1, L2, L1]

2.2 Case $a < 0$: then $-a \in P$, so closure gives $(-a)(-a) \in P$; since $(-a)(-a) = a \cdot a = a^2$ by L3, we get $a^2 \in P$, i.e. $a^2 > 0$. [assume-case neg, step 1.1, L2, L3, L1]

3.1 The cases $a > 0$ and $a < 0$ exhaust all of $a \neq 0$ by trichotomy, and both yield $a^2 > 0$. [cases-exhaustive, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement

In any field $F$ ([[def-field]]), for every $a \in F$ we have $0 \cdot a = 0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$ and an element $a \in F$.

[L1] Field axioms ([[def-field]]): $0$ is the additive identity, so $0 + 0 = 0$ and $x + 0 = x$ for all $x$; multiplication distributes over addition, $(y + z) \cdot x = y \cdot x + z \cdot x$.

[L2] Field axioms ([[def-field]]): every element has an additive inverse, so addition admits cancellation: if $x + z = y + z$ then $x = y$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Since $0 + 0 = 0$, we have $0 \cdot a = (0 + 0) \cdot a$. [L1]

1.2 By distributivity, $(0 + 0) \cdot a = 0 \cdot a + 0 \cdot a$. [L1]

1.3 Since $0$ is the additive identity, $0 \cdot a = 0 \cdot a + 0$. [L1]

2.1 Combining the two expressions for $(0 + 0) \cdot a$ gives $0 \cdot a = 0 \cdot a + 0 \cdot a$. [step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 From steps 1.3 and 2.1, $0 \cdot a + 0 = 0 \cdot a + 0 \cdot a$. [step 1.3, step 2.1]

4.1 Cancelling $0 \cdot a$ from both sides yields $0 = 0 \cdot a$, that is $0 \cdot a = 0$. [step 3.1, L2] ∎

## Statement

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Real numbers $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$; for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ write $F_n := \{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$, so that $F_{n+1} = F_n \cup \{a_{n+1}\}$. A subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is nonempty and finite exactly when it equals $F_n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and some choice of $a_0, \dots, a_n$.

[A1] $P(n)$ denotes the statement: for all $a_0, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the set $F_n$ has a maximum and a minimum.

[L1] Maximum and minimum: $m = \max X$ means $m \in X$ and $x \le m$ for all $x \in X$; $m = \min X$ means $m \in X$ and $m \le x$ for all $x \in X$; each is unique when it exists ([[def-max-min]]).

[L2] Induction principle: if $P(0)$ holds and $P(n)$ implies $P(n+1)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $P(n)$ holds for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, where $n + 1$ denotes the successor $\sigma(n)$ ([[thm-induction-principle]], [[def-nat-addition]]).

[L3] The order on $\mathbb{R}$ is reflexive, total and transitive: $a \le a$; for all $a, b$ exactly one of $a < b$, $a = b$, $b < a$ holds, so at least one of $a \le b$ and $b \le a$ holds; and $a \le b$ with $b \le c$ gives $a \le c$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** induction.

1.1 Base case: $F_0 = \{a_0\}$, and $a_0 \in F_0$ with $a_0 \le a_0$ by reflexivity, so $a_0$ is both a maximum and a minimum of $F_0$; hence $P(0)$ holds. [base, A1, L1, L3]

1.2 Inductive hypothesis: fix $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and assume $P(n)$, that is, for all reals $a_0, \dots, a_n$ the set $F_n$ has a maximum and a minimum. [ih, A1]

2.1 Let $a_0, \dots, a_{n+1} \in \mathbb{R}$ be arbitrary; by the inductive hypothesis the set $F_n$ has a maximum $M$ and a minimum $m$, and $F_{n+1} = F_n \cup \{a_{n+1}\}$. [step 1.2, L1]

3.1 By totality at least one of $a_{n+1} \le M$ and $M \le a_{n+1}$ holds. If $a_{n+1} \le M$, then $M \in F_n \subseteq F_{n+1}$, every element of $F_n$ is $\le M$ because $M = \max F_n$, and $a_{n+1} \le M$ as well, so $M$ is a maximum of $F_{n+1}$. If $M \le a_{n+1}$, then $a_{n+1} \in F_{n+1}$, every $x \in F_n$ satisfies $x \le M \le a_{n+1}$ hence $x \le a_{n+1}$ by transitivity, and $a_{n+1} \le a_{n+1}$, so $a_{n+1}$ is a maximum of $F_{n+1}$. Either way $F_{n+1}$ has a maximum. [step 2.1, L1, L3]

3.2 Dually, at least one of $m \le a_{n+1}$ and $a_{n+1} \le m$ holds. If $m \le a_{n+1}$, then $m \in F_{n+1}$ and every element of $F_{n+1}$ is $\ge m$, so $m$ is a minimum of $F_{n+1}$. If $a_{n+1} \le m$, then $a_{n+1} \in F_{n+1}$ and every $x \in F_n$ satisfies $a_{n+1} \le m \le x$ hence $a_{n+1} \le x$ by transitivity, so $a_{n+1}$ is a minimum of $F_{n+1}$. Either way $F_{n+1}$ has a minimum. [step 2.1, L1, L3]

4.1 Since $a_0, \dots, a_{n+1}$ were arbitrary, $F_{n+1}$ has a maximum and a minimum for every such list, that is, $P(n)$ implies $P(n+1)$. [step 3.1, step 3.2, A1]

5.1 The base case and the inductive step give $P(n)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ by the induction principle; since a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is exactly a set of the form $F_n$, every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has both a maximum and a minimum. [step 1.1, step 4.1, given, L2, discharge-induction] ∎

## Remarks

- **Where the stipulation is discharged.** Finiteness itself is defined later, in [[def-countable]], as equinumerosity with a von Neumann natural; with that definition in hand [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that a subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is nonempty and finite exactly when it is listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$, which is the Given below. So nothing on this page rests on an assumption that is never paid for; it is paid for later, and the payment is recorded in `justified_by`.
- **Only the total order is used, never completeness.** The base case needs reflexivity, the inductive step needs totality and transitivity, and the induction itself runs over $\mathbb{N}$. The same induction works in any totally ordered field; what is recorded here is its specialisation to $\mathbb{R}$.
- Nonemptiness is essential: $\emptyset$ is finite and has no maximum ([[def-max-min]]). Finiteness is essential too: $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : 0 < x < 1\}$ is bounded and has no maximum ([[fs-sup-belongs-to-set]]).
- Combined with claim 1 of [[lem-max-is-sup]], this says every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a supremum, and that the supremum is attained, because it equals the maximum. The infimum half is *not* part of [[lem-max-is-sup]], which speaks only of maxima and suprema; it follows from the minimum proved here together with the reflection identity $\inf X = -\sup(-X)$ ([[lem-reflection]], [[thm-infimum-property]]).

## Statement

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Elements $a, b$ of an ordered field $F$.

[L1] For a positive factor $s > 0$ and any $t$: $t > 0 \iff st > 0$; this is [[lem-of-sign-rules]] (the rule $c > 0 \Rightarrow (x < y \iff xc < yc)$ taken at $x = 0$, $y = t$, $c = s$, using $0 \cdot s = 0$, [[lem-of-zero-mult]]).

[L2] Trichotomy: for $a, b$ exactly one of $a < b$, $a = b$, $a > b$ holds; and a sum of two nonnegatives with at least one positive is positive ([[def-ordered-field]]).

[L3] $|x| \ge 0$ and $|x|^2 = x^2$ for every $x$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The difference factors as $b^2 - a^2 = (b - a)(b + a)$. [algebra]

2.1 If $a, b \ge 0$ and $a < b$, then $b > 0$, so $b + a > 0$ by [L2], and $b - a > 0$; by [L1] with $s = b + a$ and $t = b - a$, $(b - a)(b + a) > 0$, i.e. $a^2 < b^2$. [L1, L2, step 1.1]

2.2 If $a, b \ge 0$ and $a^2 < b^2$, then $b^2 - a^2 > 0$, so $a, b$ are not both zero and $b + a > 0$ by [L2]; by [L1] with $s = b + a$, from $(b - a)(b + a) = b^2 - a^2 > 0$ we get $b - a > 0$, i.e. $a < b$. [L1, L2, step 1.1]

3.1 Hence for $a, b \ge 0$, $a < b \iff a^2 < b^2$. [step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 The $\le$ form follows by trichotomy: for $a, b \ge 0$, applying step 3.1 to the nonnegatives $b, a$ gives $a \le b \iff \lnot(b < a) \iff \lnot(b^2 < a^2) \iff a^2 \le b^2$. [step 3.1, L2]

5.1 For arbitrary $a, b$, [L3] gives $|a|, |b| \ge 0$ with $|a|^2 = a^2$ and $|b|^2 = b^2$; applying step 3.1 to $|a|, |b|$ yields $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a|^2 < |b|^2 \iff |a| < |b|$. [step 3.1, L3] ∎

## Statement

At an AMSGrad round, let $F\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, compact, and convex, let $x_t,x_{t+1}\in F$, let $\ell_t:F\to\mathbb R$ be convex, and let $g_t\in\partial\ell_t(x_t)$. Take $\alpha_t>0$ and $\beta_{1,t}\in[0,1)$. Write $q_{t,i}=\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}$, $Q_t=\operatorname{diag}(q_{t,1},\ldots,q_{t,d})$, and
$$\|z\|_{Q_t}^2:=\sum_iq_{t,i}z_i^2,\qquad E_t(z):=\sum_{i:q_{t,i}>0}\frac{z_i^2}{q_{t,i}},$$
with zero contribution from coordinates where $q_{t,i}=0$. For the AMSGrad update, every such zero coordinate has $m_{t,i}=m_{t-1,i}=0$. Then for every comparator $u\in F$,
$$\ell_t(x_t)-\ell_t(u)\le \frac{\|x_t-u\|_{Q_t}^2-\|x_{t+1}-u\|_{Q_t}^2}{2\alpha_t(1-\beta_{1,t})} +\frac{\alpha_t}{2(1-\beta_{1,t})}E_t(m_t) +\frac{\beta_{1,t}\alpha_t}{2(1-\beta_{1,t})}E_t(m_{t-1}) +\frac{\beta_{1,t}}{2\alpha_t(1-\beta_{1,t})}\|x_t-u\|_{Q_t}^2.$$

## Statement references

[[alg-amsgrad]]: defines the raw-moment recurrence, weighted minimization, and zero-coordinate convention.

[[lem-adaptive-moment-updates-well-defined]]: zero historical maximum implies zero current and previous first moments.

[[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]]: a subgradient gives the supporting inequality for the loss.

[[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: Cauchy–Schwarz and the Euclidean norm identities used in the weighted Young bound.

[Reddi, Kale, and Kumar, Appendix D](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.09237)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The AMSGrad state and update, a convex loss, a subgradient at $x_t$, a comparator $u\in F$, and $\alpha_t>0$, $\beta_{1,t}\in[0,1)$.

[F1] [[alg-amsgrad]]: $m_{t,i}=\beta_{1,t}m_{t-1,i}+(1-\beta_{1,t})g_{t,i}$, and $x_{t+1}$ minimizes the weighted squared distance from the specified $y_{t+1}$.

[F2] [[lem-adaptive-moment-updates-well-defined]]: $Q_t$ has finite nonnegative diagonal entries; if $q_{t,i}=0$, then $m_{t,i}=m_{t-1,i}=0$.

[F3] [[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]]: $\ell_t(x_t)-\ell_t(u)\le\langle g_t,x_t-u\rangle$.

[F4] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the inner product and squared weighted norms are finite coordinate sums.

[F5] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: $|\langle a,b\rangle|\le\|a\|_2\|b\|_2$; in particular the finite weighted-coordinate form follows by applying it to $a_i=m_{t-1,i}/\sqrt{q_{t,i}}$ and $b_i=\sqrt{q_{t,i}}(x_{t,i}-u_i)$ on positive-weight coordinates.

[F6] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]], [[thm-of-square-roots]], [[lem-of-square-positive]], [[lem-of-zero-mult]], [[def-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-sign-rules]], and [[lem-of-inverse-positive]]: segments between feasible points remain feasible; nonnegative coordinates have nonnegative roots; weighted squares are nonnegative; and division by a positive denominator preserves the displayed inequalities.

## Proof

**Given:** The state, update, convex loss, subgradient, comparator, and positive step size in the Statement.

1.1 Put $y_i=x_{t,i}-\alpha_t m_{t,i}/q_{t,i}$ when $q_{t,i}>0$ and $y_i=x_{t,i}$ otherwise. Let $p=x_{t+1}$, $D=\|u-p\|_{Q_t}^2\ge0$, and $c=\sum_i q_{t,i}(p_i-y_i)(u_i-p_i)$. Convexity of $F$ makes $p+s(u-p)\in F$ for $0<s\le1$. Minimality of $p$ gives $0\le2sc+s^2D$. If $c<0$, set $a=-c>0$ and $s=a/(D+a+1)$; then $0<s<1$ and $sD<a$, so $2sc+s^2D=s(-2a+sD)<-sa<0$, a contradiction. Thus $c\ge0$, and expansion of $\|u-y\|_{Q_t}^2$ yields $\|p-u\|_{Q_t}^2\le\|y-u\|_{Q_t}^2$. [F1, F2, F4, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 Expanding the right side from step 1.1 and using $m_{t,i}=0$ whenever $q_{t,i}=0$ gives $$\langle m_t,x_t-u\rangle\le\frac{\|x_t-u\|_{Q_t}^2-\|x_{t+1}-u\|_{Q_t}^2}{2\alpha_t}+\frac{\alpha_t}{2}E_t(m_t).$$ This follows coordinatewise from $y_i=x_{t,i}-\alpha_tm_{t,i}/q_{t,i}$ on positive weights; zero-weight coordinates contribute zero. [F1, F2, F4, F6, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Rearranging the first-moment recurrence in [F1] gives $$\langle g_t,x_t-u\rangle=\frac{\langle m_t,x_t-u\rangle-\beta_{1,t}\langle m_{t-1},x_t-u\rangle}{1-\beta_{1,t}}.$$ By [F2] zero-weight coordinates vanish; by [F5], weighted Cauchy–Schwarz on positive weights gives $|\langle m_{t-1},x_t-u\rangle|\le E_t(m_{t-1})^{1/2}\|x_t-u\|_{Q_t}$. For nonnegative $a,b$, $0\le(\sqrt{\alpha_t}a-b/\sqrt{\alpha_t})^2$ expands to $ab\le(\alpha_ta^2+b^2/\alpha_t)/2$, which bounds the negative cross term. Substituting step 2.1 and the subgradient inequality [F3] gives the stated four terms. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Run uncorrected AMSGrad for a finite horizon $T\ge1$ with $\alpha_t=\alpha/\sqrt t$, $\alpha>0$, $\beta_2\in(0,1)$, $0\le\beta_{1,t}\le\beta_1<\sqrt{\beta_2}$, and $\gamma=\beta_1/\sqrt{\beta_2}$. For each coordinate, interpret $m_{t,i}^2/\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}$ as zero when $\widehat v_{t,i}=0$. Then
$$\sum_{t=1}^T\alpha_t\sum_{i=1}^d\frac{m_{t,i}^2}{\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}} \le \frac{\alpha}{(1-\beta_1)(1-\gamma)\sqrt{1-\beta_2}} \sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{t=1}^T\frac{|g_{t,i}|}{\sqrt t}.$$

## Statement references

[[alg-amsgrad]]: gives the moment recurrences, historical maximum, and time-varying first-moment weights.

[[lem-adaptive-moment-updates-well-defined]]: all moment coordinates are finite and all second-moment coordinates are nonnegative; a zero second-moment coordinate has zero first moment.

[[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: finite-coordinate Cauchy–Schwarz.

[Reddi, Kale, and Kumar, Appendix D](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.09237)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite gradient vectors and AMSGrad recurrences in the Statement, with the stated parameter ranges.

[F1] [[alg-amsgrad]]: $m_{t,i}=\beta_{1,t}m_{t-1,i}+(1-\beta_{1,t})g_{t,i}$ and $v_{t,i}=\beta_2v_{t-1,i}+(1-\beta_2)g_{t,i}^2$.

[F2] [[lem-adaptive-moment-updates-well-defined]]: $0\le v_{t,i}\le\widehat v_{t,i}$; because $\beta_2>0$, $v_{t,i}=0$ exactly when $\widehat v_{t,i}=0$, and then all corresponding moment and gradient entries are zero.

[F3] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: for finite real lists, $(\sum_j a_jb_j)^2\le(\sum_j a_j^2)(\sum_j b_j^2)$.

[F4] [[def-integer-power]], [[def-natural-numbers]], [[def-finite-sum]], and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: $\beta^0=1$, $\beta^{n+1}=\beta^n\beta$, finite sums distribute over addition, and finite sums may be reindexed.

[F5] [[lem-of-square-monotone]] and [[thm-of-square-roots]]: if $0\le a\le b$, then $\sqrt a\le\sqrt b$.

[F6] [[def-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-sign-rules]], [[lem-of-inverse-positive]], and [[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]: positive coefficients preserve inequalities and positive denominators may be divided through.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Expanding the first-moment recurrence [F1] recursively gives $m_{t,i}=\sum_{j=1}^t a_{t,j}g_{j,i}$, where $a_{t,t}=1-\beta_{1,t}$ and $a_{t,j}=\beta_{1,t}a_{t-1,j}$ for $j<t$. Induction gives $0\le a_{t,j}\le\beta_1^{t-j}$: the terminal coefficient is at most $1$, and each earlier coefficient acquires one factor at most $\beta_1$. [F1, F6, given, induction, algebra]

2.1 By [F3] applied to $\sqrt{a_{t,j}}$ and $\sqrt{a_{t,j}}g_{j,i}$, $$m_{t,i}^2\le\left(\sum_{j=1}^ta_{t,j}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^ta_{t,j}g_{j,i}^2\right) \le\frac{1}{1-\beta_1}\sum_{j=1}^t\beta_1^{t-j}g_{j,i}^2,$$ because $\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\beta_1^k=(1-\beta_1^t)/(1-\beta_1)\le1/(1-\beta_1)$. The identity follows by multiplying the finite sum by $1-\beta_1$ and telescoping $\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}(\beta_1^k-\beta_1^{k+1})=1-\beta_1^t$ using [F4]; the denominator is positive by [F6]. [F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Iterating the second-moment recurrence [F1] gives $v_{t,i}=(1-\beta_2)\sum_{j=1}^t\beta_2^{t-j}g_{j,i}^2$. By [F2] and [F5], $\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}\ge\sqrt{v_{t,i}}$. If this value is zero, [F2] makes the energy term zero. Otherwise, for each nonzero $g_{j,i}$, $$\sqrt{v_{t,i}}\ge\sqrt{1-\beta_2}\,\sqrt{\beta_2^{t-j}}|g_{j,i}|.$$ The root recursion gives $\sqrt{\beta_2^n}=(\sqrt{\beta_2})^n$ for every integer $n\ge0$; induction proves this because both sides are nonnegative and have the same square. Also $\beta_1^n/(\sqrt{\beta_2})^n=(\beta_1/\sqrt{\beta_2})^n$ by the integer-power recursion, so $\beta_1^n/\sqrt{\beta_2^n}=\gamma^n$. Using step 2.1 termwise in the finite sum therefore gives $$\frac{m_{t,i}^2}{\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}} \le\frac{1}{(1-\beta_1)\sqrt{1-\beta_2}}\sum_{j=1}^t\gamma^{t-j}|g_{j,i}|.$$ Zero gradient terms contribute zero. [F1, F2, F5, F6, step 2.1, given, induction, algebra]

4.1 Multiply step 3.1 by $\alpha/\sqrt t$, sum over $t$ and coordinates, and reorder the finite sums. Since $1/\sqrt t\le1/\sqrt j$ for $t\ge j$ and $(1-\gamma)\sum_{k=0}^{T-j}\gamma^k=1-\gamma^{T-j+1}\le1$ by the same finite telescoping identity from step 2.1, $$\sum_{t=1}^T\alpha_t\sum_i\frac{m_{t,i}^2}{\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}} \le\frac{\alpha}{(1-\beta_1)\sqrt{1-\beta_2}} \sum_i\sum_{j=1}^T|g_{j,i}|\sum_{t=j}^T\frac{\gamma^{t-j}}{\sqrt t} \le\frac{\alpha}{(1-\beta_1)(1-\gamma)\sqrt{1-\beta_2}}\sum_i\sum_{j=1}^T\frac{|g_{j,i}|}{\sqrt j}.$$ This is the stated inequality. [F4, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎
