## Statement

Consider a finite rectified stack in a fully connected layered perceptron,
with widths $d_0,\ldots,d_L$, zero biases,
$Z_\ell=W_\ell X_{\ell-1}$, and $X_\ell=\rho(Z_\ell)$,
where $\rho(t)=\max(t,0)$. For an objective $J$ differentiable as a function
of the last activation, set $g_L=\nabla_{X_L}J(X_L)$ and define backward
signals by the zero-at-kink convention
$\gamma_{\ell,j}=\mathbf 1_{Z_{\ell,j}>0}$,
$h_\ell=\gamma_\ell\odot g_\ell$, and
$g_{\ell-1}=W_\ell^{\mathsf T}h_\ell$.
At realizations where all relevant preactivations are nonzero, these are
ordinary chain-rule gradients. At zeros they are specified backpropagation
signals; no ordinary derivative of ReLU at zero is asserted.

Without any independence assumptions, fix a layer $\ell$ and suppose every
$T_{ji}=W_{\ell,ji}\gamma_{\ell,j}g_{\ell,j}$ is square-integrable. Then
$$\mathbb E[g_{\ell-1,i}]=\sum_j\mathbb E[T_{ji}],\qquad \operatorname{Var}(g_{\ell-1,i})=\sum_j\operatorname{Var}(T_{ji})+2\sum_{j<k}\operatorname{Cov}(T_{ji},T_{ki}).$$
This is an exact atom-aware identity for the realized network signals. For any
specified bounded measurable random gate vector $q_\ell$ in place of
$\gamma_\ell$, define $T_{ji}=W_{\ell,ji}q_{\ell,j}g_{\ell,j}$. If every
redefined $T_{ji}$ is square-integrable, the same mean and covariance formulas
hold.

For the conditional recurrence, additionally assume at the layers in question
that the entries of $W_\ell$ are independent with a common symmetric centered
law of finite variance $\sigma_\ell^2$, that $Z_{\ell,j}$ is symmetric with
common zero probability $p_\ell$, and that the coordinates of $g_\ell$ have
common finite second moment $G_\ell$. Assume the gate vector $\gamma_\ell$
is independent of $g_\ell$ and $W_\ell$ is independent of $h_\ell$.
Write the fan-out as $\hat n_\ell=d_\ell$. Then
$$\mathbb E[g_{\ell-1,i}]=0,\qquad G_{\ell-1}=\operatorname{Var}(g_{\ell-1,i})=\frac{1-p_\ell}{2}\hat n_\ell\sigma_\ell^2G_\ell.$$
If these hypotheses hold for every $r\le\ell\le L$, then
$$G_{r-1}=G_L\prod_{\ell=r}^L\frac{1-p_\ell}{2}\hat n_\ell\sigma_\ell^2.$$
In particular, the source's atomless conditional case $p_\ell=0$ gives
$\operatorname{Var}(g_{\ell-1,i})=\frac12\hat n_\ell\sigma_\ell^2\mathbb E[g_{\ell,1}^2]$
and the corresponding product of half factors. If the downstream coordinate
is centered, $G_\ell$ is its variance. The conditional fan-out choice
$\sigma_\ell^2=2/\hat n_\ell$ makes each atomless product factor one.

These conditional identities do not establish that a nonzero actual-network
gradient satisfies their hypotheses. Indeed, if $\ell\ge2$,
$X_{\ell-1}$ is a ReLU output and $\sigma_\ell^2>0$, the assumption
$W_\ell\perp h_\ell$ already forces $h_\ell=0$ almost surely. If also
$p_\ell<1$ and gate independence holds, it forces $G_\ell=0$.
Thus the nonzero atomless backward preservation model with these full
independence assumptions is infeasible for such an actual ReLU layer; the
conditional implication and product remain valid, and the general covariance
identity above supplies the unconditional finite-network formula.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite stack, an objective differentiable as a function of $X_L$ with $g_L=\nabla_{X_L}J(X_L)$, and the backward-signal convention; square-integrable summands for the general identity; and, only for the conditional formulas, the stated symmetry, moments, and independence assumptions.

[F1] A fully connected layered perceptron evaluates each layer as a finite weighted sum followed by its specified activation. ([[def-feedforward-neural-network]])

[F2] At totally differentiable points, derivatives of a composition multiply in layer order. ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]])

[F3] A symmetric preactivation with zero probability $p$ has positive sign probability $(1-p)/2$. ([[lem-symmetric-rectifier-moments]])

[F4] Independent centered weights, independent of the input vector, give weighted-sum mean zero and variance equal to the sum of weight variances times input second moments. ([[lem-centered-independent-weighted-sum-variance]])

[F5] Products of independent integrable variables have factored expectations. ([[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]])

[F6] Variance and covariance are centered second moments. ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]])

[F7] Products of square-integrable variables are integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz. ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]])

[F8] A finite independent family has product joint law. ([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]])

[F9] Expectation is linear on integrable random variables, and respects their almost-sure order. ([[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]])

## Proof

1.1 At a realization with nonzero preactivations, the derivative of ReLU is the diagonal matrix with entries $\gamma_{\ell,j}$, and the affine derivative is $W_\ell$. The chain rule [F2] therefore gives the two backward identities in the Statement. The specified convention defines the same identities at zeros without using [F2] there. [given, F1, F2]

1.2 For fixed $i$, $g_{\ell-1,i}=\sum_jT_{ji}$. A finite sum of square-integrable variables is square-integrable: $(\sum_jT_{ji})^2\le d_\ell\sum_jT_{ji}^2$. By [F7] each pairwise product is integrable. Expanding the mean and centered square, then applying [F6] and expectation linearity [F9], gives exactly the asserted mean and covariance sums, without factoring any dependent variables. [given, F6, F7, F9, algebra]

1.3 Under the conditional assumptions, [F3] and gate independence give $\mathbb E[h_{\ell,j}^2]=\mathbb E[\gamma_{\ell,j}]\mathbb E[g_{\ell,j}^2]=(1-p_\ell)G_\ell/2$ by [F5]. For fixed $i$, the column of weights is centered, independent, and independent of $h_\ell$. Applying [F4] yields mean zero and variance $\sigma_\ell^2\sum_j\mathbb E[h_{\ell,j}^2]=((1-p_\ell)/2)d_\ell\sigma_\ell^2G_\ell$. This also equals the upstream second moment, proving the one-step formula. [given, F3, F4, F5]

2.1 Repeat step 1.3 for the finitely many layers $L,L-1,\ldots,r$. All generated upstream coordinates are centered and have the common second moment in step 1.3, so substitution gives the stated product, including a possibly uncentered terminal signal. Setting $p_\ell=0$ gives the original half-factor formulas and setting $\sigma_\ell^2=2/d_\ell$ makes those factors one. [step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 To prove the feasibility obstruction, let $q=\mathbb P(W_{\ell,11}<0)$. Symmetry and positive variance imply $q>0$: if $q=0$, symmetry gives $\mathbb P(W_{\ell,11}>0)=0$, forcing variance zero. By [F8], the event $E$ that all $d_\ell d_{\ell-1}$ matrix entries are strictly negative has probability $q^{d_\ell d_{\ell-1}}>0$. Since $X_{\ell-1}$ is coordinatewise nonnegative, all coordinates of $Z_\ell$ are nonpositive on $E$, so $\gamma_\ell=0$ and $h_\ell=0$ there, including when the input vector is zero. Independence of $W_\ell$ and $h_\ell$ now gives $0=\mathbb P(E\cap\{h_\ell\ne0\})=\mathbb P(E)\mathbb P(h_\ell\ne0)$, hence $h_\ell=0$ almost surely. If $p_\ell<1$, step 1.3's gate calculation gives $0=\mathbb E[h_{\ell,j}^2]=(1-p_\ell)G_\ell/2$, hence $G_\ell=0$. This proves the obstruction without declaring the valid conditional identities false. [given, F3, F5, F8, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

He et al. §2.2, Eqs. (14)–(16), multiply the atomless half factors under the
stated weight/incoming-gradient and gate/downstream-gradient independence
assumptions. Those are a conditional moment calculation, not a proof of their
realization by a nonzero finite ReLU gradient. Zero atoms also invalidate the
ordinary derivative at those realizations; choosing the zero-at-kink convention
addresses the algorithmic signal but does not establish the independence assumptions.

## Statement

Let $a\in\mathbb R$ and consider a finite rectified stack with zero biases,
widths $d_0,\ldots,d_L$, $Z_\ell=W_\ell X_{\ell-1}$, and
$X_\ell=\phi_a(Z_\ell)$, where $\phi_a(t)=t$ for $t>0$ and
$\phi_a(t)=at$ for $t\le0$. Put $n_\ell=d_{\ell-1}$ and
$\hat n_\ell=d_\ell$. Suppose each $W_\ell$ has independent entries
with a common symmetric centered law of finite variance $\sigma_\ell^2$ and
is independent of $X_{\ell-1}$. Suppose each layer input has coordinates with
a common finite second moment, and all preactivation coordinates are symmetric
about zero. Input coordinates may be dependent, and zero atoms are allowed.
Then, writing $V_\ell=\operatorname{Var}(Z_{\ell,1})$,
$$V_1=n_1\sigma_1^2\mathbb E[X_{0,1}^2],\qquad V_\ell=\frac{1+a^2}{2}n_\ell\sigma_\ell^2V_{\ell-1}\quad(2\le\ell\le L),\qquad V_L=V_1\prod_{\ell=2}^L\frac{1+a^2}{2}n_\ell\sigma_\ell^2.$$
Thus $\sigma_\ell^2=2/((1+a^2)n_\ell)$ preserves the forward
preactivation variance across the hidden layers.

For backward signals, take an objective $J$ differentiable as a function of
the last activation and set $g_L=\nabla_{X_L}J(X_L)$. Specify a finite kink
value $c_\ell$ and put
$\eta_{\ell,j}=\mathbf 1_{Z_{\ell,j}>0}+a\mathbf 1_{Z_{\ell,j}<0}+c_\ell\mathbf 1_{Z_{\ell,j}=0}$,
$h_\ell=\eta_\ell\odot g_\ell$, and
$g_{\ell-1}=W_\ell^{\mathsf T}h_\ell$.
They are ordinary chain-rule gradients when all relevant preactivations are
nonzero; when $a=1$ and $c_\ell=1$ the activation is linear and this also
holds at zeros. Otherwise a specified kink value is a backpropagation convention.
If the coordinates of $Z_\ell$ have common zero probability $p_\ell$,
the coordinates of $g_\ell$ have common finite second moment $G_\ell$,
$\eta_\ell$ is independent of $g_\ell$, and $W_\ell$ is independent of
$h_\ell$, then
$$G_{\ell-1}=\operatorname{Var}(g_{\ell-1,i})=\hat n_\ell\sigma_\ell^2\kappa_\ell G_\ell,\qquad \kappa_\ell=\frac{1+a^2}{2}(1-p_\ell)+c_\ell^2p_\ell.$$
The upstream coordinates have mean zero. If these conditional hypotheses hold
for every $r\le\ell\le L$, then
$$G_{r-1}=G_L\prod_{\ell=r}^L\hat n_\ell\sigma_\ell^2\kappa_\ell.$$
In the source's atomless case $p_\ell=0$, this retains the original backward
factor $(1+a^2)\hat n_\ell\sigma_\ell^2/2$ and the fan-out choice
$\sigma_\ell^2=2/((1+a^2)\hat n_\ell)$. For a noncentered terminal
signal $G_L$ is its second moment; for centered signals it is their variance.
The source's forward and atomless backward weight variances agree exactly when
$n_\ell=\hat n_\ell$. With atoms the conditional backward-preserving choice
is $1/(\hat n_\ell\kappa_\ell)$ when $\kappa_\ell>0$; if
$\kappa_\ell=0$ the upstream signal has zero variance for every finite
weight variance. These are conditional backward statements, and no independence
assumption or nonzero actual-gradient realization is inferred from initialization.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite stack and its forward moment assumptions, an objective differentiable as a function of $X_L$ with $g_L=\nabla_{X_L}J(X_L)$, the specified backward-signal convention, and the additional layerwise conditional hypotheses only for backward preservation.

[F1] The source initializer uses forward variance $2/((1+a^2)n_\ell)$ or backward variance $2/((1+a^2)\hat n_\ell)$. ([[alg-rectifier-variance-preserving-initialization]])

[F2] Symmetry gives PReLU second moment $(1+a^2)\mathbb E[Z^2]/2$, and the squared gate moment is $((1+a^2)/2)(1-p_0)+c^2p_0$. ([[lem-symmetric-rectifier-moments]])

[F3] Independent centered weights independent of an input vector give weighted-sum mean zero and variance $\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(W_i)\mathbb E[X_i^2]$. ([[lem-centered-independent-weighted-sum-variance]])

[F4] Totally differentiable compositions obey the total-derivative chain rule. ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]])

[F5] The ReLU forward recurrence allows zero atoms and has factor $n_\ell\sigma_\ell^2/2$ and the corresponding finite-depth product. ([[thm-relu-forward-variance-recurrence]])

[F6] Exact backward signals obey a covariance-sum identity; the ReLU half-factor product is conditional, and its full atomless independence assumptions force zero downstream second moment at a nondegenerate actual ReLU hidden layer. ([[thm-relu-backward-variance-recurrence]])

[F7] Expectations of products of independent integrable variables factor. ([[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]])

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F3] to a row of $W_\ell$. The preactivation is centered and has variance $n_\ell\sigma_\ell^2\mathbb E[X_{\ell-1,1}^2]$, which proves the raw-input relation. For $\ell\ge2$, [F2] and centered symmetry give $\mathbb E[X_{\ell-1,1}^2]=(1+a^2)V_{\ell-1}/2$, proving the forward recurrence without an atomlessness or coordinate-independence assumption. Successive substitution gives the finite product; the forward choice [F1] makes every hidden-layer factor one. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 At nonzero preactivations the derivative of PReLU is $1$ on the positive half-line and $a$ on the negative half-line, so [F4] gives the stated backward recursion for ordinary gradients there. At zeros the recursion is instead the specified convention, except in the linear case $a=1,c_\ell=1$, where it is the ordinary derivative everywhere. By [F2] and independence of the gate and $g_\ell$, [F7] gives $\mathbb E[h_{\ell,j}^2]=\kappa_\ell G_\ell$. [given, F2, F4, F7]

2.1 Apply [F3] to each column of $W_\ell$ and $h_\ell$, using the assumed matrix/signal independence. The upstream signal is centered and has variance $\sigma_\ell^2\sum_j\mathbb E[h_{\ell,j}^2]=\hat n_\ell\sigma_\ell^2\kappa_\ell G_\ell$. Iteration over the finite set of layers proves the backward product, just as for [F6]. If $p_\ell=0$ then $\kappa_\ell=(1+a^2)/2$ and the source's backward choice [F1] gives unit coefficient. For positive $\kappa_\ell$, solving the unit-coefficient equation gives $1/(\hat n_\ell\kappa_\ell)$; for zero $\kappa_\ell$ the coefficient vanishes for every finite weight variance. [given, F1, F3, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The positive source scales $2/((1+a^2)n_\ell)$ and $2/((1+a^2)\hat n_\ell)$ agree exactly when $n_\ell=\hat n_\ell$. At $a=0,c_\ell=0$, the forward and backward formulas specialize to [F5] and [F6], including the atom correction and feasibility caveat; at $a=1,c_\ell=1$, $\kappa_\ell=1$ for every zero probability, as required for the linear derivative. These substitutions also show why an arbitrary kink convention must not be silently identified with an ordinary derivative. [F1, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The atomless half-factor product is retained as the precise conditional
calculation in He et al. §2.2; the forward product is valid for actual finite
stacks satisfying the forward assumptions, with dependent coordinates and zero
atoms allowed. The backward independence hypotheses require separate verification
for an actual network. In particular, the ReLU specialization has the explicit
nonzero-feasibility obstruction proved in the backward theorem, even at one
hidden layer. No mean-field limit or empirical training claim supplies that gap.

## Example

Compare two one-unit preactivations. In the first, the input is $X=1$, the
bias is zero, and the weight $W$ equals $-1$ with probability $2/3$ and $2$
with probability $1/3$. In the second, the input $X$ is uniform on $[-2,2]$,
the independent weight $W$ equals $-1$ or $1$ with equal probabilities, and
the bias is $1$. In each case compute $\mathbb E[\operatorname{ReLU}(Z)^2]$
and compare it with $\frac12\operatorname{Var}(Z)$, where $Z=WX+b$. The first
case tests whether a zero-mean but nonsymmetric weight law suffices; the second
tests the effect of a nonzero bias despite symmetric weights and input.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two one-unit probability models specified in the Example.

[F1] If $Z$ is symmetric about zero and has no atom at zero, then $\mathbb E[\operatorname{ReLU}(Z)^2]=\frac12\mathbb E[Z^2]$. ([[lem-symmetric-rectifier-moments]])

[F2] Variance is the centered second moment, $\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\mathbb E[(Z-\mathbb E[Z])^2]$. ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]])

[F3] Expectations of nonnegative random variables are integrals against their probability laws. ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]])

## Verification


1.1 In the first case, $\mathbb E[W]=(-1)(2/3)+2(1/3)=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\operatorname{Var}(W)=\mathbb E[W^2]=2$. Since $\operatorname{ReLU}(Z)$ is $2$ with probability $1/3$ and zero otherwise, $\mathbb E[\operatorname{ReLU}(Z)^2]=4/3$, whereas $\frac12\operatorname{Var}(Z)=1$. [given, F2, algebra]

1.2 The first preactivation has $\mathbb P(Z>0)=1/3$ and $\mathbb P(Z<0)=2/3$, so its law is not symmetric despite its zero mean and absence of an atom at zero. The symmetric-preactivation hypothesis of [F1] fails; zero mean alone cannot replace it. [given, F1, algebra]

1.3 In the second case, conditioning on either value of $W$ shows that $WX$ is uniform on $[-2,2]$. Thus $Z=WX+1$ is uniform on $[-1,3]$, with mean $1$ and variance $(3-(-1))^2/12=4/3$; it has no atom at zero. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The density of $Z$ is $1/4$ on $[-1,3]$, so $\mathbb E[\operatorname{ReLU}(Z)^2]=\frac14\int_0^3 z^2\,dz=9/4$, while $\frac12\operatorname{Var}(Z)=2/3$. The nonzero bias has shifted the symmetric preactivation and invalidated the half-moment identity. [given, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

Let $Z_1,Z_2$ be independent and identically distributed symmetric real
random variables with no atom at zero, set $X_i=\operatorname{ReLU}(Z_i)$, and
form a second-layer zero-bias preactivation $T=W_1X_1+W_2X_2$ with arbitrary
real weights. Although each $Z_i$ is atomless, the event that both rectified
inputs vanish has probability $1/4$ and forces $T=0$.

For a complete finite-network signal calculation, also take a two-layer
width-one ReLU stack with $X_0=1$, mutually independent
$W_1,W_2\in\{-\sqrt2,\sqrt2\}$ with equal sign probabilities,
and an independent random sign $R\in\{-1,1\}$. Take objective
$J(X_2)=RX_2$, so $g_2=R$, and use zero-at-kink backpropagation.
Then $\operatorname{Var}(Z_1)=\operatorname{Var}(Z_2)=2$ but
$\mathbb P(Z_2=0)=1/2$ and $\operatorname{Var}(g_1)=1/2$.
The atomless half-factor coefficient would instead give $1$. This does not
refute the conditional theorem: its atomlessness and weight/gated-signal
independence hypotheses fail in this realized stack.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two-coordinate zero-event model and the independent finite random-sign scalar stack in the Example.

[F1] For $n$ IID symmetric atomless preactivations followed by ReLU, any next zero-bias weighted sum has an atom at zero of probability at least $2^{-n}$. ([[lem-iid-relu-layer-forces-zero-atom-next]])

[F2] Zero-at-kink backward signals satisfy $h_2=\mathbf 1_{Z_2>0}g_2$ and $g_1=W_2h_2$; the atomless half-factor formula requires additional hypotheses. ([[thm-relu-backward-variance-recurrence]])

## Verification

1.1 The example has $n=2$, so [F1] gives $\mathbb P(T=0)\ge2^{-2}=1/4$, independently of the values of $W_1,W_2$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 In the scalar stack, $Z_1$ is $\pm\sqrt2$ with equal probabilities. If $W_1<0$ then $X_1=0$ and $Z_2=0$; if $W_1>0$ then $Z_2$ is $2$ or $-2$ with equal probabilities. Thus the law of $Z_2$ gives probabilities $1/4,1/2,1/4$ to $-2,0,2$, respectively. Both preactivations have mean zero and variance $2$, and the second has zero probability $1/2$. [given, algebra]

2.1 Therefore the two first-layer preactivations can be atomless while the next preactivation is not atomless. Requiring the no-atom condition at every layer is incompatible with this finite IID ReLU stack. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F2], $g_1=\sqrt2 R$ exactly when both weights are positive, an event of probability $1/4$; it is zero otherwise. Independence and the centered sign $R$ give mean zero and variance $2(1/4)=1/2$. The atomless coefficient would be $(1/2)(1)(2)\mathbb E[R^2]=1$. Here $h_2=R$ on the same positive-weight event and zero otherwise: $\mathbb P(h_2\ne0\mid W_2<0)=0$, whereas $\mathbb P(h_2\ne0)=1/4$, so weight/gated-signal independence fails. The covariance identity and the specified kink convention remain valid; the atomless conditional recurrence is inapplicable. [given, F2, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $d\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz. For $x\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^d$, define the Clarke generalized directional derivative by

$$F^\circ(x;v):=\limsup_{z\to x,\,s\downarrow0,\,z,z+sv\in U}\frac{F(z+sv)-F(z)}{s}.$$

The **Clarke subdifferential** (also called the Clarke generalized gradient) is

$$\partial^\circ F(x):=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\langle \xi,v\rangle\le F^\circ(x;v)\text{ for every }v\in\mathbb R^d\}.$$

For locally Lipschitz $F$, this is a nonempty compact convex set and is equivalently the closed convex hull of all limits of ordinary gradients $\nabla F(x_k)$ along differentiability points $x_k\to x$. Its support function is $F^\circ(x;v)=\max_{\xi\in\partial^\circ F(x)}\langle\xi,v\rangle$. The pairing is Euclidean: $\langle a,b\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^d a_jb_j$.

The set-valued map $x\mapsto\partial^\circ F(x)$ is locally bounded and has closed graph: if $x_k\to x$, $\xi_k\in\partial^\circ F(x_k)$, and $\xi_k\to\xi$, then $\xi\in\partial^\circ F(x)$. Here locally bounded means that every point has a neighborhood on which all subgradients have bounded norm. For each fixed $v$, the function $x\mapsto F^\circ(x;v)$ is upper semicontinuous: if $a>F^\circ(x;v)$, some neighborhood $V$ of $x$ satisfies $F^\circ(y;v)<a$ for all $y\in V$.

A locally Lipschitz function $F$ **admits the chain rule along absolutely continuous arcs** if, for every arc $z:[0,T]\to U$ that is absolutely continuous on the compact interval $[0,T]$, for almost every $t\in[0,T]$ the derivative $(F\circ z)'(t)$ exists and equals $\langle\xi,\dot z(t)\rangle$ for every $\xi\in\partial^\circ F(z(t))$.

A **global Clarke gradient-flow trajectory** for $F$ is a curve $\theta:[0,\infty)\to U$ that is absolutely continuous on every compact time interval and satisfies $\dot\theta(t)\in-\partial^\circ F(\theta(t))$ for almost every $t\ge0$. The definition names a trajectory when it exists; it does not assert existence or continuation.

## Definition references

[Kaifeng Lyu and Jian Li, *Gradient Descent Maximizes the Margin of Homogeneous Neural Networks*, Appendix I.2–I.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.05890)

[Matus Telgarsky, *Deep Learning Theory* lecture notes, §9.1](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/)

## Definition

A finite binary sample is a list $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ with $n\ge1$ and $d\ge1$, features $x_i\in\mathbb R^d$, and labels $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$. The bias-free linear score with parameter $w\in\mathbb R^d$ is $x\mapsto\langle w,x\rangle$, and its signed margin on example $i$ is $m_i(w):=y_i\langle w,x_i\rangle$. The sample is **strictly linearly separable** if there exists $u\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\min_{1\le i\le n}m_i(u)>0$. Its **hard-margin feasible set** is $\mathcal F:=\{w\in\mathbb R^d:m_i(w)\ge1\text{ for all }i\}$, and its **hard-margin problem** is minimizing $\frac12\|w\|_2^2$ over $\mathcal F$. No intercept or bias term is present in this score or objective.

## Definition

A function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ has a **tight exponential tail** if there are positive constants $c,a,\mu_+,\mu_-,u_+,u_->0$ such that

$$f(u)\le c\bigl(1+e^{-\mu_+u}\bigr)e^{-au}\quad(u>u_+),$$

and

$$f(u)\ge c\bigl(1-e^{-\mu_-u}\bigr)e^{-au}\quad(u>u_-).$$

For a differentiable strictly decreasing loss $\ell$, the source applies this definition to $f=-\ell'$, the negative loss derivative.

## Statement

Let $n,d\ge1$, $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and $F(w)=\frac12\|Xw-y\|_2^2$. Define the full-batch fixed-step gradient iterates by $w_0=0$ and $w_{k+1}=w_k-\eta X^{\mathsf T}(Xw_k-y)$ for every integer $k\ge0$. Here $\lambda_{\max}(X^{\mathsf T}X)$ is the largest eigenvalue of the symmetric matrix $X^{\mathsf T}X$. If $X\ne0$ and $0<\eta\le1/\lambda_{\max}(X^{\mathsf T}X)$, then $w_k$ converges to the unique least-squares minimizer of smallest Euclidean norm. If $X=0$, then every $\eta>0$ gives the constant iterate $w_k=0$, which is the unique least-squares minimizer of smallest Euclidean norm.

## Statement references

[Trevor Hastie et al., *Surprises in High-Dimensional Ridgeless Least Squares Interpolation*, §2.2, Proposition 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.08560)

[Cornell CS 3780, *Linear Regression*, Lecture 12](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs3780/2026sp/slides/lec12.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite real matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, a vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, the quadratic objective $F(w)=\frac12\|Xw-y\|_2^2$, and the stated fixed-step iteration from $w_0=0$.

[F1] [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]: every self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F2] [[thm-least-squares-solutions-and-normal-equation]]: the least-squares minimizers of a finite-dimensional linear map are exactly the solutions of its normal equation, and any two minimizers differ by a vector in the map's kernel.

[F3] [[thm-a-plus-b-is-the-unique-minimum-norm-least-squares-solution]]: for every finite real matrix $A$ and right-hand side $b$, $A^+b$ is the unique least-squares minimizer of minimum Euclidean norm.

[F4] [[alg-gradient-descent]]: fixed-step Euclidean gradient descent uses the update $x_{k+1}=x_k-t_k\nabla f(x_k)$ when the iterate is not stationary.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** diagonalize the positive-semidefinite normal matrix and solve each scalar recurrence.

1.1 If $X=0$, then $F(w)=\frac12\|y\|_2^2$ for every $w$, and the displayed update leaves $w_0=0$ fixed. Since $\|w\|_2\ge0$ with equality only at $w=0$, this is the unique least-squares minimizer of minimum norm. [given, algebra]

1.2 Suppose $X\ne0$ and set $A=X^{\mathsf T}X$. The matrix $A$ is symmetric, and $\langle u,Au\rangle=\|Xu\|_2^2\ge0$, so its eigenvalues are nonnegative. By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $u_1,\ldots,u_d$ with $Au_j=\lambda_j u_j$ and $0\le\lambda_j\le\lambda_{\max}$. If $\lambda_j=0$, then $Xu_j=0$ and $\langle X^{\mathsf T}y,u_j\rangle=\langle y,Xu_j\rangle=0$; conversely, $Xz=0$ implies $Az=0$, so the zero-eigenvalue space is exactly $\ker X$. [F1, given, algebra, choose]

2.1 For any increment $h$, expansion of the square gives $F(w+h)=F(w)+\langle X^{\mathsf T}(Xw-y),h\rangle+\frac12\|Xh\|_2^2$; since the last term is $O(\|h\|_2^2)$, $\nabla F(w)=Aw-X^{\mathsf T}y$. Thus the iteration is $w_{k+1}=(I-\eta A)w_k+\eta X^{\mathsf T}y$, the fixed-step update in [F4]. Writing $c_{j,k}=\langle w_k,u_j\rangle$ and $b_j=\langle X^{\mathsf T}y,u_j\rangle$, for $\lambda_j>0$ induction on $k$ gives $c_{j,k}=\frac{1-(1-\eta\lambda_j)^k}{\lambda_j}b_j$; for $\lambda_j=0$, $c_{j,k}=0$ for all $k$. [F4, given, step 1.2, algebra, induction]

3.1 The step bound gives $0\le1-\eta\lambda_j<1$ for every positive eigenvalue, including the endpoint $\eta=1/\lambda_{\max}$ where the largest-eigenvalue factor is zero. Hence $c_{j,k}\to b_j/\lambda_j$ when $\lambda_j>0$, and the zero-eigenvalue coordinates remain zero. There are finitely many coordinates, so $w_k$ converges to a vector $w_\infty$ satisfying $Aw_\infty=X^{\mathsf T}y$ and $w_\infty\perp\ker X$. [given, F1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F2], the normal equation $Aw_\infty=X^{\mathsf T}y$ makes $w_\infty$ a least-squares minimizer, and every least-squares minimizer is $w_\infty+z$ for some $z\in\ker X$. The orthogonality in step 3.1 yields $\|w_\infty+z\|_2^2=\|w_\infty\|_2^2+\|z\|_2^2$, with equality to $\|w_\infty\|_2^2$ only for $z=0$. Thus $w_\infty$ is the unique minimum-norm least-squares minimizer, in agreement with [F3]. [F2, F3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and let $b\in\mathbb F^m$. Then $A^+b$ is
a least-squares solution of $Ax=b$, and among all least-squares solutions it
is the unique one of minimum Euclidean norm.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A scalar field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, a matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and a right-hand side $b\in\mathbb F^m$.

[L1] $AA^+$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{im}A$ ([[thm-aa-plus-and-a-plus-a-are-orthogonal-projections-onto-the-image-spaces]]).

[L2] $\operatorname{im}A^+=\operatorname{im}A^*$ ([[cor-moore-penrose-image-and-kernel-identities]]).

[L3] Least-squares minimisers are exactly the solutions of $A^*(Ax-b)=0$, and any two minimisers differ by an element of $\ker A$ ([[thm-least-squares-solutions-and-normal-equation]]).

[L4] $\ker A^*=(\operatorname{im}A)^\perp$ ([[thm-adjoint-kernel-and-range-orthogonality]]).

[L5] $\operatorname{im}A^*=(\ker A)^\perp$ ([[thm-adjoint-kernel-and-range-orthogonality]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], $AA^+b$ is the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto $\operatorname{im}A$. Therefore the residual $b-AA^+b$ lies in $(\operatorname{im}A)^\perp=\ker A^*$ by [L4], so $A^*(AA^+b-b)=0$ and [L3] shows that $A^+b$ is a least-squares minimiser. [L1, L3, L4]

1.2 By [L2] and [L5], $A^+b\in\operatorname{im}A^+=\operatorname{im}A^*=(\ker A)^\perp$. Thus $A^+b$ is orthogonal to every vector in $\ker A$. [L2, L5, algebra]

2.1 Let $x$ be any least-squares minimiser. By [L3], $x-A^+b\in\ker A$, so $x=A^+b+z$ for some $z\in\ker A$. Step 1.2 then gives $$ \|x\|_2^2=\|A^+b\|_2^2+\|z\|_2^2\ge \|A^+b\|_2^2. $$ [L3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Equality in step 2.1 holds only when $z=0$, so the least-squares minimiser of minimum Euclidean norm is unique and equals $A^+b$. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Step 1.1 proves the least-squares claim and steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove the minimum-norm claim. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

For a finite strictly linearly separable sample in $\mathbb R^d$, the hard-margin feasible set is nonempty and the problem of minimizing $\frac12\|w\|_2^2$ over that set attains a unique minimizer.

## Statement references

[[def-linear-separable-margin-and-hard-margin-svm|Strict separability and hard-margin problem]]

[Daniel Soudry et al., *The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Separable Data*, equation (4)](https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/volume19/18-188/18-188.pdf)

[Matus Telgarsky, *Deep Learning Theory* lecture notes, §10.1](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite sample as in [[def-linear-separable-margin-and-hard-margin-svm]], with a vector that strictly separates all of its examples.

[F1] [[def-linear-separable-margin-and-hard-margin-svm]]: the feasible constraints are the finitely many closed half-spaces $m_i(w)\ge1$, where each $m_i$ is a continuous linear functional.

[F2] [[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]: a nonempty closed and bounded subset of $\mathbb R^d$ is compact, and a continuous real-valued function on it attains its minimum.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct existence by compactness and uniqueness by strict convexity.

1.1 Strict separability gives $u$ with $m_i(u)>0$ for every $i$. Since the sample is finite, $a:=\min_i m_i(u)>0$. The scaled vector $u/a$ satisfies $m_i(u/a)=m_i(u)/a\ge1$, so the feasible set in [F1] is nonempty. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Put $R=\|u/a\|_2$ and $K=\mathcal F\cap\{w:\|w\|_2\le R\}$. The set $K$ is nonempty by step 1.1 and is closed and bounded by [F1], so [F2] makes it compact and gives a minimizer $w_*$ of $\frac12\|w\|_2^2$ on $K$. Every feasible vector outside the radius-$R$ ball has norm greater than $R$, while $u/a\in K$ has norm $R$; therefore no such vector improves on $w_*$. Hence $w_*$ is a global minimizer on $\mathcal F$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 If two distinct feasible minimizers $w,z$ existed, their midpoint would remain feasible because each $m_i$ is linear. But $\left\|\frac{w+z}{2}\right\|_2^2=\frac12\|w\|_2^2+\frac12\|z\|_2^2-\frac14\|w-z\|_2^2$ is strictly smaller than their common minimum value, a contradiction. Therefore the minimizer is unique. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For $\ell_{\exp}(u)=e^{-u}$ and $\ell_{\log}(u)=\log(1+e^{-u})$, the negative derivatives $-\ell_{\exp}'$ and $-\ell_{\log}'$ have tight exponential tails with $c=a=\mu_+=\mu_-=1$ and $u_+=u_-=1$ in the definition of a tight exponential tail.

## Statement references

[[def-tight-exponential-tail|Tight exponential-tail definition]]

[Daniel Soudry et al., *The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Separable Data*, Definition 2 and §2](https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/volume19/18-188/18-188.pdf)

[Matus Telgarsky, *Deep Learning Theory* lecture notes, §10.2](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The loss functions $\ell_{\exp}(u)=e^{-u}$ and $\ell_{\log}(u)=\log(1+e^{-u})$.

[F1] [[def-tight-exponential-tail]]: it suffices to bound $f(u)$ above by $(1+e^{-u})e^{-u}$ and below by $(1-e^{-u})e^{-u}$ for every $u>1$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** differentiate the two losses and compare their negative derivatives with the defining bounds.

1.1 The exponential loss has $-\ell_{\exp}'(u)=e^{-u}$. For $u>1$, $0<1-e^{-u}<1$, so $(1-e^{-u})e^{-u}\le e^{-u}\le(1+e^{-u})e^{-u}$, which is exactly the pair of bounds in [F1]. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The logistic loss has $-\ell_{\log}'(u)=e^{-u}/(1+e^{-u})$. For $r=e^{-u}\in(0,1)$, $1-r\le1/(1+r)\le1$ because $1-(1-r)(1+r)=r^2\ge0$ and $1\le1+r$. Multiplying by $r>0$ gives $(1-e^{-u})e^{-u}\le-\ell_{\log}'(u)\le e^{-u}\le(1+e^{-u})e^{-u}$ for $u>1$, as required by [F1]. [given, F1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $d,p\ge1$, let $X\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be an input set, and let $\Phi:\mathbb R^p\times X\to\mathbb R$ be the scalar output of a finite feedforward computation graph: the graph is finite and acyclic, its vertices are evaluated in a fixed topological order, and each non-input value is a scalar activation applied to a weighted sum of earlier values and a bias. For a finite sample $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ with $n\ge1$, $x_i\in X$, and $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, define the signed margin $q_i(\theta):=y_i\Phi(\theta;x_i)$, the minimum margin $q_{\min}(\theta):=\min_{1\le i\le n}q_i(\theta)$, and the exponential empirical risk $\mathcal L(\theta):=\sum_{i=1}^n e^{-q_i(\theta)}$. The score map is **positively homogeneous of degree $L>0$ in its parameters** if $\Phi(c\theta;x)=c^L\Phi(\theta;x)$ for every $c>0$, $\theta\in\mathbb R^p$, and $x\in X$; this then gives $q_i(c\theta)=c^Lq_i(\theta)$. For the gradient-flow results, assume each sample margin is locally Lipschitz, and let $\partial^\circ q_i(\theta)$ denote the closed convex hull of limits of ordinary gradients at differentiability points approaching $\theta$. Assume also that along every absolutely continuous arc $\theta(t)$, $\frac{d}{dt}q_i(\theta(t))=\langle h,\dot\theta(t)\rangle$ for every $h\in\partial^\circ q_i(\theta(t))$ at almost every $t$. For $\theta\ne0$, the normalized margin is $\bar\gamma(\theta):=q_{\min}(\theta)/\|\theta\|_2^L$. When $\mathcal L(\theta)<1$, define the smoothed normalized margin by $\widetilde\gamma(\theta):=\log(1/\mathcal L(\theta))/\|\theta\|_2^L$.

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.05890"
---

## Definition

Let $q_1,\ldots,q_N:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz functions, with $N,d\ge1$. Write $\partial^\circ q_i(\theta)$ for the closed convex hull of limits of ordinary gradients at differentiability points approaching $\theta$. The **margin-constrained problem** is to minimize $\frac12\|\theta\|_2^2$ subject to $q_i(\theta)\ge1$ for every $i$. A point $\theta$ is feasible when all these inequalities hold; an index $i$ is active at a feasible point when $q_i(\theta)=1$.

A feasible point $\theta$ is a **Clarke KKT point** if there are multipliers $\lambda_i\ge0$ and vectors $h_i\in\partial^\circ q_i(\theta)$ such that

$$\theta=\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i h_i,\qquad \lambda_i(q_i(\theta)-1)=0\quad(1\le i\le N).$$

A feasible point satisfies the **Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) in margin form** if there is a direction $v\in\mathbb R^d$ such that $\langle h_i,v\rangle>0$ for every active $i$ and every $h_i\in\partial^\circ q_i(\theta)$. If the same constraints are written $g_i(\theta):=1-q_i(\theta)\le0$, this condition is equivalently $\langle k_i,v\rangle<0$ for every active $i$ and $k_i\in\partial^\circ g_i(\theta)$, since $\partial^\circ g_i(\theta)=-\partial^\circ q_i(\theta)$.

A feasible point is an **$(\varepsilon,\delta)$-approximate Clarke KKT point** if there are $\lambda_i\ge0$ and $h_i\in\partial^\circ q_i(\theta)$ such that

$$\left\|\theta-\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i h_i\right\|_2\le\varepsilon,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i(q_i(\theta)-1)\le\delta,$$

where $\varepsilon,\delta>0$. The second inequality measures total complementary-slackness error; every summand is nonnegative at a feasible point.

## Definition references

[[def-clarke-subdifferential-and-gradient-flow|Clarke generalized gradient and Euclidean pairing]]

[[def-homogeneous-classifier-margin-and-exponential-risk|Training margins and homogeneity convention]]

[Kaifeng Lyu and Jian Li, *Gradient Descent Maximizes the Margin of Homogeneous Neural Networks*, Appendix C.1–C.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.05890)

## Remarks

The margin form fixes the sign convention for lower constraints $q_i\ge1$: a strict MFCQ direction increases every active margin. For upper constraints $g_i\le0$, the corresponding active directional derivatives are negative. This sign convention is used in all local KKT arguments on this page.

## Statement

Let $q:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz and positively homogeneous of degree $L>0$, meaning $q(c\theta)=c^Lq(\theta)$ for every $c>0$. For every $\theta\ne0$ and every $h\in\partial^\circ q(\theta)$, one has $\partial^\circ q(c\theta)=c^{L-1}\partial^\circ q(\theta)$ for $c>0$ and $\langle\theta,h\rangle=Lq(\theta)$.

## Statement references

[[def-clarke-subdifferential-and-gradient-flow|Clarke subdifferential convention]]

[Kaifeng Lyu and Jian Li, *Gradient Descent Maximizes the Margin of Homogeneous Neural Networks*, Theorem B.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.05890)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The locally Lipschitz map $q$, its positive homogeneity degree $L$, a nonzero parameter $\theta$, and the Clarke subdifferential convention.

[F1] [[def-clarke-subdifferential-and-gradient-flow]]: for locally Lipschitz maps, the Clarke subdifferential is the closed convex hull of limits of ordinary gradients along differentiability points.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** differentiate the homogeneity identity on the dense differentiability set, then pass to the Clarke closure.

1.1 If $q$ is differentiable at $x$, then $q$ is differentiable at $cx$ and the homogeneity identity gives $Dq(cx)[v]=c^{L-1}Dq(x)[v]$ for every direction $v$, by writing $q(cx+tv)=c^Lq(x+(t/c)v)$ and taking the difference-quotient limit as $t\to0$. [given, algebra]

1.2 At every differentiability point $x\ne0$, differentiating $q(cx)=c^Lq(x)$ with respect to $c$ at $c=1$ gives $\langle x,\nabla q(x)\rangle=Lq(x)$. [given, algebra]

2.1 Conversely, differentiability at $cx$ implies differentiability at $x$ by applying the same argument with scale $1/c$. Thus scaling by $c$ bijects the differentiability points and sends each gradient to $c^{L-1}$ times that gradient. Taking all gradient limits as $x\to\theta$, and then their closed convex hull as in [F1], proves $\partial^\circ q(c\theta)=c^{L-1}\partial^\circ q(\theta)$. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 For any gradient limit $h=\lim_k\nabla q(x_k)$ with differentiability points $x_k\to\theta$, continuity of $q$ gives $\langle\theta,h\rangle=Lq(\theta)$. This identity is preserved by convex combinations and limits, so [F1] yields it for every $h\in\partial^\circ q(\theta)$. [F1, step 1.2, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $N,d\ge1$ and let $q_1,\ldots,q_N:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be the locally Lipschitz sample-margin functions in a homogeneous-classifier model, and suppose each $q_i$ admits the Clarke chain rule along absolutely continuous arcs. Set $\mathcal L(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^N e^{-q_i(\theta)}$. Then

$$\partial^\circ\mathcal L(\theta)\subseteq\left\{-\sum_{i=1}^N e^{-q_i(\theta)}h_i:h_i\in\partial^\circ q_i(\theta)\right\}.$$

Along every absolutely continuous arc $\theta(t)$, for almost every $t$ and every choice $h_i(t)\in\partial^\circ q_i(\theta(t))$, the derivative is

$$\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal L(\theta(t))=-\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^N e^{-q_i(\theta(t))}h_i(t),\dot\theta(t)\right\rangle.$$

In particular, if the arc also satisfies the negative Clarke gradient-flow inclusion, its loss derivative is $-\|\dot\theta(t)\|_2^2$ almost everywhere.

## Statement references

[[def-clarke-subdifferential-and-gradient-flow|Clarke derivative and chain-rule convention]]

[[def-homogeneous-classifier-margin-and-exponential-risk|Finite homogeneous margin model]]

[Kaifeng Lyu and Jian Li, *Gradient Descent Maximizes the Margin of Homogeneous Neural Networks*, Appendix I.2–I.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.05890)

[Matus Telgarsky, *Deep Learning Theory* lecture notes, §§9.1 and 10.2](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite sample margins, their local Lipschitz and chain-rule hypotheses, and the empirical exponential risk.

[F1] [[def-clarke-subdifferential-and-gradient-flow]]: Clarke subdifferentials are closed convex hulls of limiting ordinary gradients and their support functions are the Clarke generalized directional derivatives.

[F2] [[def-homogeneous-classifier-margin-and-exponential-risk]]: the empirical exponential risk is the finite sum $\mathcal L=\sum_i e^{-q_i}$.

[F3] [[thm-strict-separation-of-a-point-from-a-closed-convex-set]]: a point outside a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space is strictly separated from that set by a linear functional.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** apply the smooth scalar chain rule to each margin and use support functions to prove the finite-sum subdifferential inclusion.

1.1 Put $f_i(\theta)=e^{-q_i(\theta)}$. At every differentiability point of $q_i$, ordinary differentiation gives $\nabla f_i=-e^{-q_i}\nabla q_i$. The exponential has nonzero derivative, so $f_i$ is differentiable exactly where $q_i$ is; passing to limits of gradients and then closed convex hulls as in [F1] gives $\partial^\circ f_i(\theta)=-e^{-q_i(\theta)}\partial^\circ q_i(\theta)$. Along an absolutely continuous arc, the assumed chain rule for $q_i$ and the one-variable chain rule give $(f_i\circ\theta)'=-e^{-q_i}\langle h_i,\dot\theta\rangle$ for every $h_i\in\partial^\circ q_i(\theta)$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 For any direction $v$, the limsup of the finite sum of difference quotients is at most the sum of their limsups, so $\mathcal L^\circ(\theta;v)\le\sum_i f_i^\circ(\theta;v)$. The right side is the support function of the nonempty compact convex set $C:=\sum_i\partial^\circ f_i(\theta)$ by [F1]. If some $g\in\partial^\circ\mathcal L(\theta)$ lay outside $C$, [F3] would give a direction $v$ with $\langle g,v\rangle>\sup_{c\in C}\langle c,v\rangle=\sum_i f_i^\circ(\theta;v)$, contradicting $\langle g,v\rangle\le\mathcal L^\circ(\theta;v)$. Thus $\partial^\circ\mathcal L(\theta)\subseteq C$. Using step 1.1 expands this inclusion to the displayed weighted-margin form. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Summing the ordinary arc derivatives from step 1.1 gives the displayed derivative formula. For a negative Clarke gradient-flow arc, step 2.1 supplies $h_i$ with $\dot\theta=\sum_i e^{-q_i}h_i$; substitution makes the derivative $-\langle\dot\theta,\dot\theta\rangle=-\|\dot\theta\|_2^2$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $x\notin C$. Then there are $a\ne0$ and $b\in\mathbb R$ such that $\langle a,z\rangle\le b<\langle a,x\rangle$ for every $z\in C$. ## Statement

Let $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^d$, with $n,d\ge1$, be strictly linearly separable, let $w^*$ be their unique Euclidean hard-margin vector, and let $\eta>0$. There are $1\le M\le d$, mutually orthogonal nonzero vectors $h_1,\ldots,h_M$ with $h_1=w^*$, fixed vectors $c,d_{k,m}$, and, for all sufficiently large integers $t$, a comparison sequence
$$G_t=\sum_{m=1}^M h_m\log^{\circ m}t+c+\sum_{1\le k<m\le M}\frac{d_{k,m}}{\prod_{j=k}^{m-1}\log^{\circ j}t},$$
whose margins $v_i^{\mathsf T}G_t$ all tend to $+\infty$. For each of $\mathcal L_{\exp}(w)=\sum_i e^{-v_i^{\mathsf T}w}$ and $\mathcal L_{\log}(w)=\sum_i\log(1+e^{-v_i^{\mathsf T}w})$, the defect
$$\delta_t=G_{t+1}-G_t+\eta\nabla\mathcal L(G_t)$$
is absolutely summable: $\sum_{t\ge T}\|\delta_t\|_2<\infty$ for some finite $T$. The hierarchy is obtained by recursively separating and projecting precisely the active constraints that have zero coefficient in every nonnegative dual representation; it imposes no generic-position assumption. If all first-stage active indices have a simultaneously positive dual representation, then $M=1$ and the correction sum is empty.

**Given:** The strictly separable finite vectors and the positive fixed number $\eta$ in the Statement.

Existence and uniqueness follow by restricting to a nonempty compact norm sublevel of the closed feasible set and strict convexity, exactly as for the original hard-margin problem. Let $J_m=\{i\in T_{m-1}:h_m^Ta_i=1\}$ and $D_m=T_{m-1}\setminus J_m$. There exist coefficients $\alpha_i\ge0$, $i\in J_m$, with $$h_m=\sum_{i\in J_m}\alpha_i a_i.$$ To prove this dual representation from a proved finite-dimensional supplier, apply [F4] to the matrix with columns $a_i$, $i\in J_m$, and right-hand side $h_m$. If no nonnegative representation existed, the alternative would give a vector $y$ with $a_i^{\mathsf T}y\ge0$ for active indices and $h_m^{\mathsf T}y<0$. Replace $y$ by its orthogonal projection into $H_{m-1}$, preserving these pairings. Then $h_m+\epsilon y$ preserves all active inequalities, preserves the finitely many inactive strict inequalities for sufficiently small positive $\epsilon$, and decreases squared norm because its derivative at zero is $2h_m^{\mathsf T}y<0$. This contradicts minimality, proving the representation. Define $S_m$ as the union of the positive-coordinate supports of all such nonnegative representations, and $T_m=J_m\setminus S_m$. Because there are finitely many indices, averaging one witness representation for each index in $S_m$ gives a single representation $$h_m=\sum_{i\in S_m}\alpha_i a_i,\qquad \alpha_i>0\quad(i\in S_m).$$ In particular $S_m\ne\varnothing$. Set $$E_m=\operatorname{span}\{a_i:i\in S_m\},\qquad H_m=H_{m-1}\cap E_m^\perp.$$ Let $Q_m$ be the orthogonal projector onto $E_m$, and let $R_m=R_{m-1}-Q_m$ be the orthogonal projector onto $H_m$. These are nested orthogonal projections by construction. Define $V_m=E_1\oplus\cdots\oplus E_m$ and its projector $P_m=I-R_m$. Thus $h_m\in E_m$, each $E_m\ne\{0\}$, and distinct $E_m$ are orthogonal. If $T_m\ne\varnothing$, its next projected data $b_i=R_mv_i$ are strictly separable in $H_m$. To prove this crucial assertion, suppose not. The origin then belongs to the convex hull of the $b_i$: otherwise the nearest point $b\ne0$ of that compact convex hull satisfies $b^Tb_i\ge\|b\|^2>0$ for every $i$, a strict separator. Thus there are $c_i\ge0$, not all zero, with $\sum_{i\in T_m}c_i b_i=0$. Consequently $\sum_{i\in T_m}c_i a_i$ lies in $E_m$ and can be written $\sum_{j\in S_m}d_j a_j$. For sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$, each $\alpha_j-\epsilon d_j$ remains positive, and $$h_m=\sum_{j\in S_m}(\alpha_j-\epsilon d_j)a_j+\sum_{i\in T_m}\epsilon c_i a_i.$$ This is an admissible nonnegative dual representation with a positive coefficient at an index of $T_m$, contradicting the definition of $S_m$. This proves strict separability, including that no next projected vector vanishes. Continue until $T_M=\varnothing$. If $i\in D_k$, then $v_i^Th_j=1$ for $j<k$, $v_i^Th_k>1$, and the later $v_i^Th_j$ are arbitrary finite constants. The $a_i$ span $E_m$, so $\max_i|a_i^Tc|\ge\delta_m\|c\|$ for some $\delta_m>0$, by compactness of the unit sphere. Therefore $\Phi_m(c)\to\infty$ when $\|c\|\to\infty$: one scalar summand tends uniformly to infinity and all the others have finite lower bounds. Thus $\Phi_m$ attains its minimum. Its Hessian satisfies $$z^T\nabla^2\Phi_m(c)z=\sum_{i\in S_m}\beta_i e^{-a_i^Tc}(a_i^Tz)^2>0\qquad(0\ne z\in E_m),$$ so the minimizer is unique. Its zero gradient is exactly the required equation. ## Statement

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}$ and $b\in\mathbb R^r$. Exactly one of the
following holds:

1. There is $x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $x\ge0$ and $Ax=b$.
2. There is $y\in\mathbb R^r$ with $A^Ty\ge0$ and $b^Ty<0$.

Inequalities between vectors are coordinatewise.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The matrix and vector in the Statement and the standard Euclidean
inner product.

[F1] The cone generated by any finite list of Euclidean vectors is closed
([[lem-finitely-generated-euclidean-cones-are-closed]]).

[F2] Every point has a unique nearest point in a nonempty closed convex
Euclidean set ([[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]]).

[F3] If $p$ is the nearest point to $b$ in a closed convex set $C$, then
$\langle b-p,c-p\rangle\le0$ for every $c\in C$
([[lem-projection-onto-a-closed-convex-set-has-the-variational-inequality]]).

## Proof

1.1 If $r=0$, then $\mathbb R^r=\{0\}$ and $b=0$. Alternative 1 holds with $x=0\in\mathbb R^n$, while alternative 2 is impossible because the only $y\in\mathbb R^0$ is $0$ and $b^Ty=0$. This handles the zero-dimensional ambient case. Now assume $r\ge1$. Let $C=\{\sum_{j=1}^n x_j A_j:x_j\ge0\}$, where $A_j$ are the columns of $A$. This is a nonempty convex cone and is closed by [F1]. If $b\in C$, its nonnegative coefficients give alternative 1. If $b\notin C$, let $p$ be its nearest point in $C$ by [F2] and put $z=b-p\ne0$. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Applying [F3] with $c=0$ and $c=2p$ gives both $\langle z,p\rangle\ge0$ and $\langle z,p\rangle\le0$, hence $\langle z,p\rangle=0$. Applying [F3] to arbitrary $c\in C$ then gives $\langle z,c\rangle\le0$. In particular $A_j^Tz\le0$ for every column, and $\langle z,b\rangle=\langle z,p+z\rangle=\|z\|_2^2>0$. Thus $y=-z$ satisfies $A^Ty\ge0$ and $b^Ty=-\|z\|_2^2<0$, which is alternative 2. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The alternatives cannot both hold: if $Ax=b$ with $x\ge0$ and $A^Ty\ge0$, then $b^Ty=x^TA^Ty\ge0$, contradicting $b^Ty<0$. Step 1.1 produces one alternative in every case, so exactly one holds. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ be a finite strictly linearly separable sample with $x_i\in\mathbb R^d$ and $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, use the bias-free score $w\mapsto\langle w,x_i\rangle$, and let $w^*$ be the unique minimizer of $\frac12\|w\|_2^2$ subject to $y_i\langle w,x_i\rangle\ge1$ for all $i$. Put $v_i:=y_ix_i$, let $X$ be the matrix with columns $v_i$, and write $\lambda_{\max}(XX^{\mathsf T})$ for its largest eigenvalue. Use either the logistic loss $\ell_{\log}(u)=\log(1+e^{-u})$ or the exponential loss $\ell_{\exp}(u)=e^{-u}$, empirical risk $\mathcal L(w)=\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\langle w,v_i\rangle)$, arbitrary finite initialization $w_0$, and full-batch fixed-step gradient descent $w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta\nabla\mathcal L(w_t)$. The source's tight-tail condition means that $f=-\ell'$ has constants $c,a,\mu_+,\mu_-,u_+,u_->0$ with $f(u)\le c(1+e^{-\mu_+u})e^{-au}$ for $u>u_+$ and $f(u)\ge c(1-e^{-\mu_-u})e^{-au}$ for $u>u_-$; both listed losses satisfy it with all six constants equal to $1$. For logistic loss take $0<\eta<8/\lambda_{\max}(XX^{\mathsf T})$. For exponential loss take a fixed positive step in the local-smoothness regime: assume a convex region containing every update segment on which $\nabla\mathcal L$ is $\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}$-Lipschitz, and require $0<\eta<2/\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}$.

Under these hypotheses, $\mathcal L(w_t)\to0$, $\|w_t\|_2\to\infty$, and $w_t/\|w_t\|_2\to w^*/\|w^*\|_2$. There are vectors $r_t$ with $w_t=w^*\log t+r_t$ and $\|r_t\|_2=O(\log\log t)$ as $t\to\infty$. Assuming Countable Choice for this almost-everywhere clause, for Lebesgue-almost every feature array among the strictly separable samples, the residual $r_t$ is bounded; in degenerate cases the expansion may include nonzero $\log\log t$ and further iterated-log terms. No population-risk or test-risk conclusion is asserted.

## Statement

For homogeneous sample margins $q_i$ of degree $L>0$, every feasible point of the problem $\min_\theta\frac12\|\theta\|_2^2$ subject to $q_i(\theta)\ge1$ satisfies MFCQ in the margin convention.

## Statement references

[[def-margin-kkt-and-mfcq|Margin-form MFCQ definition]]

[[def-homogeneous-classifier-margin-and-exponential-risk|Homogeneous sample-margin convention]]

[[lem-clarke-euler-identity-for-homogeneous-margins|Clarke Euler identity]]

[Kaifeng Lyu and Jian Li, *Gradient Descent Maximizes the Margin of Homogeneous Neural Networks*, Appendix C.2, Lemma C.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.05890)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The degree-$L$ homogeneous classifier margins and a feasible point $\theta$.

[F1] [[def-homogeneous-classifier-margin-and-exponential-risk]]: each sample margin satisfies $q_i(c\theta)=c^Lq_i(\theta)$ for every $c>0$, with $L>0$.

[F2] [[lem-clarke-euler-identity-for-homogeneous-margins]]: for $h_i\in\partial^\circ q_i(\theta)$, $\langle\theta,h_i\rangle=Lq_i(\theta)$ when $\theta\ne0$.

[F3] [[def-margin-kkt-and-mfcq]]: at a feasible point, MFCQ in margin form asks for one direction whose pairing with every Clarke subgradient of every active margin is strictly positive.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** use the parameter vector itself as the strict feasible direction.

1.1 By [F1], $q_i(0)=q_i(2\cdot0)=2^Lq_i(0)$. Since $2^L>1$, this forces $q_i(0)=0$ for every $i$. Thus a feasible point cannot be $\theta=0$, because feasibility requires every margin to be at least one. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Choose $v=\theta$. If no constraint is active, the universal condition in [F3] is vacuous. Otherwise, for each active index $i$, $q_i(\theta)=1$ and every $h_i\in\partial^\circ q_i(\theta)$ satisfies $\langle h_i,v\rangle=\langle\theta,h_i\rangle=Lq_i(\theta)=L>0$ by [F2]. Hence the same direction $v$ satisfies MFCQ for all active margins. [F2, F3, step 1.1, given, choose, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $N,p\ge1$ and let $q_1,\ldots,q_N:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz functions that are positively homogeneous of common degree $L>0$ and admit the Clarke chain rule along absolutely continuous arcs. Set $\mathcal L(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^N e^{-q_i(\theta)}$. Let $\theta:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^p$ be a global Clarke gradient-flow trajectory for $\mathcal L$, and suppose $\mathcal L(\theta(t_0))<1$ for some $t_0\ge0$. For $t\ge t_0$, the loss is nonincreasing, the smoothed normalized margin $\widetilde\gamma(\theta(t))=-\log\mathcal L(\theta(t))/\|\theta(t)\|_2^L$ is nondecreasing, $\mathcal L(\theta(t))\to0$, and $\|\theta(t)\|_2\to\infty$. Moreover, $0\le\bar\gamma(\theta(t))-\widetilde\gamma(\theta(t))\le(\log N)/\|\theta(t)\|_2^L$, so the normalized margin and smoothed normalized margin have the same finite positive limit.

## Statement references

[[def-clarke-subdifferential-and-gradient-flow|Global Clarke trajectory convention]]

[[def-homogeneous-classifier-margin-and-exponential-risk|Homogeneous classifier margins and normalized margins]]

[Kaifeng Lyu and Jian Li, *Gradient Descent Maximizes the Margin of Homogeneous Neural Networks*, Theorem 4.1 and Appendix A.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.05890)

[Matus Telgarsky, *Deep Learning Theory* lecture notes, §10.2](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite homogeneous margins, their local Lipschitz and Clarke chain-rule properties, the global Clarke flow, and a time $t_0$ with loss below one.

[F1] [[def-clarke-subdifferential-and-gradient-flow]]: a Clarke gradient-flow trajectory is locally absolutely continuous, and the subdifferential is nonempty compact convex with support function the Clarke generalized directional derivative.

[F2] [[def-homogeneous-classifier-margin-and-exponential-risk]]: $q_i(c\theta)=c^Lq_i(\theta)$ and $\mathcal L=\sum_i e^{-q_i}$.

[F3] [[lem-clarke-euler-identity-for-homogeneous-margins]]: every $h_i\in\partial^\circ q_i(\theta)$ satisfies $\langle\theta,h_i\rangle=Lq_i(\theta)$.

[F4] [[lem-clarke-sum-chain-rule-for-exponential-risk]]: along a Clarke flow, $\mathcal L'=-\|\dot\theta\|_2^2$ almost everywhere, and almost everywhere $\dot\theta=\sum_i e^{-q_i}h_i$ with $h_i\in\partial^\circ q_i(\theta)$.

[F5] [[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]: continuous real-valued functions attain finite extrema on closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** use Euler's identity to differentiate the radius and exponential risk, then compare the weighted average margin with the log inverse loss.

1.1 Put $\phi(t)=\mathcal L(\theta(t))$, $r(t)=\|\theta(t)\|_2$, and $z(t)=-\log\phi(t)$. By [F1], $\theta$ is locally absolutely continuous; local Lipschitz continuity of the margins makes these compositions locally absolutely continuous on each compact time interval where $r>0$. Since $\phi(t_0)<1$ and [F4] gives $\phi'=-\|\dot\theta\|_2^2\le0$ almost everywhere, $\phi(t)<1$ for all $t\ge t_0$. Thus every $q_i(\theta(t))>0$. Homogeneity gives $q_i(0)=0$, so $\theta(t)\ne0$ and $r(t)>0$. [F1, F2, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 At almost every $t\ge t_0$, set $a_i=e^{-q_i(\theta(t))}$, $p_i=a_i/\phi$, and $\mu=\sum_i p_iq_i(\theta(t))$. By [F4], choose $h_i\in\partial^\circ q_i(\theta(t))$ with $v:=\dot\theta=\sum_i a_ih_i$. Euler's identity [F3] yields $\langle\theta,v\rangle=L\phi\mu$, hence $(\log r)'=L\phi\mu/r^2>0$. Also $q_i=z-\log p_i$, so $\mu=z-\sum_i p_i\log p_i\ge z>0$ because $p_i>0$, $\sum_i p_i=1$, and $-\log p_i\ge0$. [F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The chain rule in [F4] gives $z'=\|v\|_2^2/\phi$. Differentiating $z/r^L$ and applying Cauchy–Schwarz, $\widetilde\gamma'=r^{-L}(\|v\|_2^2/\phi-L^2z\phi\mu/r^2)\ge L^2\phi\mu(\mu-z)/r^{L+2}\ge0$, because $\|v\|_2^2\ge\langle\theta,v\rangle^2/r^2=L^2\phi^2\mu^2/r^2$. Thus the smoothed margin is nondecreasing. [F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The function $u\mapsto q_{\min}(u):=\min_iq_i(u)$ is continuous on the unit sphere, so [F5] gives a finite maximum $C$. Homogeneity and $\phi\ge e^{-q_{\min}}$ imply $0<\widetilde\gamma(t_0)\le z/r^L\le\bar\gamma\le C$. Since $\widetilde\gamma$ is nondecreasing by step 3.1, it has a finite positive limit. Writing $A=\sum_i e^{-(q_i-q_{\min})}\in[1,N]$ gives $z=q_{\min}-\log A$ and $0\le\bar\gamma-z/r^L=\log A/r^L\le(\log N)/r^L$. [F2, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The nonincreasing loss has a limit $\phi_\infty\ge0$. If $\phi_\infty>0$, then $z\ge z(t_0)>0$ and $(r^2)'=2L\phi\mu\ge2L\phi_\infty z(t_0)>0$ almost everywhere by step 2.1, so $r\to\infty$ while $z$ remains bounded. This forces $z/r^L\to0$, contradicting the positive lower bound in step 4.1. Hence $\phi\to0$. If $r$ were bounded, the trajectory would lie in a compact ball on which every continuous $q_i$ is bounded above, forcing $\phi=\sum_i e^{-q_i}$ to stay bounded below by a positive number. Thus $r\to\infty$. The error bound in step 4.1 now tends to zero, so the normalized and smoothed margins converge to the same positive limit. [F2, F5, step 2.1, step 4.1, assume-contra, discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Statement

Let $N,d\ge1$ and let $q_1,\ldots,q_N:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz. Let $\theta_*$ be feasible for $q_i(\theta)\ge1$ and satisfy MFCQ in the margin convention. Suppose that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a feasible $\theta_\varepsilon$ with $\|\theta_\varepsilon-\theta_*\|_2\le\varepsilon$ and multipliers/subgradients witnessing that $\theta_\varepsilon$ is an $(\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$-approximate Clarke KKT point. Then $\theta_*$ is a Clarke KKT point.

## Statement references

[[def-clarke-subdifferential-and-gradient-flow|Clarke subdifferential and closed-graph convention]]

[[def-margin-kkt-and-mfcq|Approximate margin-KKT and MFCQ definitions]]

[Matus Telgarsky, *Deep Learning Theory* lecture notes, §9.1](https://mjt.cs.illinois.edu/dlt/)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Locally Lipschitz margins, a feasible point satisfying MFCQ, and for every tolerance a nearby feasible approximate KKT witness with stationarity and complementarity errors no larger than that tolerance.

[F1] [[def-clarke-subdifferential-and-gradient-flow]]: Clarke subdifferentials are compact, locally bounded, and have closed graph; for fixed $v$, their support function $q_i^\circ(\theta;v)$ is upper semicontinuous in $\theta$.

[F2] [[def-margin-kkt-and-mfcq]]: approximate KKT supplies nonnegative multipliers, subgradients, and the two error bounds; exact KKT is the corresponding zero-error stationarity and complementary-slackness condition.

[F3] [[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]: closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are compact.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** bound all approximate witnesses uniformly with the MFCQ direction, then apply the finite-intersection property to nested compact sets of witnesses.

1.1 Let $I=\{i:q_i(\theta_*)=1\}$. If $I=\varnothing$, every constraint has positive slack near $\theta_*$. Local boundedness in [F1] gives a common bound $M$ on all nearby subgradients. For any sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, the approximate witness in [F2] satisfies $\lambda_i\le\varepsilon/c_i$ for positive local slack bounds $c_i$, so its stationarity residual gives $\|\theta_*\|_2\le2\varepsilon+M\varepsilon\sum_i c_i^{-1}$. This holds for every small $\varepsilon$, hence $\theta_*=0$; setting all exact multipliers to zero gives KKT. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 Suppose $I\ne\varnothing$. By MFCQ choose $v$ and let $c>0$ be a common lower bound for $\langle h,v\rangle$ over active $i$ and $h\in\partial^\circ q_i(\theta_*)$; such a bound exists by compactness and finiteness. Then $q_i^\circ(\theta_*;-v)\le-c$ for each active $i$. Upper semicontinuity in [F1] gives a neighborhood where every active subgradient satisfies $\langle h,v\rangle\ge c/2$. Shrink it so each inactive constraint has slack at least $c_i>0$ and all subgradients are bounded by $M$. For any sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, the approximate witness has $\lambda_i\le\varepsilon/c_i$ for inactive $i$. Dotting its stationarity equation with $v$ therefore bounds the sum of active multipliers by $\frac{2}{c}((\|\theta_*\|_2+2\varepsilon)\|v\|_2+M\|v\|_2\varepsilon\sum_{i\notin I}c_i^{-1})$. Thus, for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, all multipliers and subgradients in every witness are uniformly bounded. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Choose an integer $m_0$ large enough that every approximate witness with $\varepsilon=1/m$ for $m\ge m_0$ lies in a fixed closed bounded box $B$ of the finite-dimensional space of parameters, multipliers, and subgradients, using step 1.2. For each $m\ge m_0$, let $K_m\subseteq B$ consist of feasible witnesses with $\|\theta-\theta_*\|_2\le1/m$, stationarity residual at most $1/m$, and aggregate complementarity residual at most $1/m$. The hypothesis makes every $K_m$ nonempty; continuity and the closed-graph property in [F1] make it closed. Hence each $K_m$ is compact by [F3], and $K_{m+1}\subseteq K_m$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 The nested family $(K_m)_{m\ge m_0}$ has the finite-intersection property, since every finite intersection equals its largest-index member. Compactness of $K_{m_0}$ therefore makes $\bigcap_{m\ge m_0}K_m$ nonempty. Any tuple in this intersection has $\theta=\theta_*$, zero stationarity residual, and zero complementarity residual, because each corresponding norm/error is at most $1/m$ for every $m$. It is consequently an exact Clarke KKT witness by [F2]. This argument selects one point from one nonempty intersection and uses no choice principle. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

4.1 Since $0\in\operatorname{conv}(S)$ and each Clarke subdifferential in $S$ is convex, group the finite convex combination by its constituent set. ## Statement

Let $N,p\ge1$ and let $q_1,\ldots,q_N:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz functions that are positively homogeneous of common degree $L>0$ and admit the Clarke chain rule along absolutely continuous arcs. Let $\theta$ be a global Clarke gradient-flow trajectory for $\mathcal L(\theta)=\sum_i e^{-q_i(\theta)}$, and suppose $\mathcal L(\theta(t_0))<1$. Put $u(t)=\theta(t)/\|\theta(t)\|_2$ after $t_0$. A limit point $u_*$ means that for every $T\ge t_0$ and $\rho>0$, some $t>T$ satisfies $\|u(t)-u_*\|_2<\rho$. Then $q_{\min}(u_*)>0$, and, writing $\theta_*=u_*/q_{\min}(u_*)^{1/L}$, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a feasible $\widehat\theta$ with $\|\widehat\theta-\theta_*\|_2\le\varepsilon$ that is an $(\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$-approximate Clarke KKT point for minimizing $\frac12\|\theta\|_2^2$ subject to $q_i(\theta)\ge1$.

## Statement references

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite positively homogeneous margins, their Clarke chain-rule property, a global flow, and a time when its exponential loss is below one.

[F1] [[def-clarke-subdifferential-and-gradient-flow]]: Clarke subdifferentials are locally bounded with closed graph, and a global flow is locally absolutely continuous and satisfies $\dot\theta\in-\partial^\circ\mathcal L(\theta)$ almost everywhere.

[F2] [[def-homogeneous-classifier-margin-and-exponential-risk]]: $q_i(c\theta)=c^Lq_i(\theta)$, $\mathcal L=\sum_i e^{-q_i}$, and the normalized margins are $q_{\min}(\theta)/\|\theta\|_2^L$ and $-\log\mathcal L(\theta)/\|\theta\|_2^L$.

[F3] [[def-margin-kkt-and-mfcq]]: an approximate KKT witness has nonnegative multipliers, margin subgradients, stationarity residual at most $\varepsilon$, and aggregate complementarity residual at most $\delta$.

[F4] [[lem-clarke-euler-identity-for-homogeneous-margins]]: $\partial^\circ q_i(c\theta)=c^{L-1}\partial^\circ q_i(\theta)$ and $\langle\theta,h_i\rangle=Lq_i(\theta)$.

[F5] [[lem-homogeneous-clarke-flow-margin-monotonicity]]: after $t_0$, the smoothed margin is nondecreasing, loss tends to zero, radius tends to infinity, and the smoothed and normalized margins converge to the same positive limit $\gamma_\infty$.

[F6] [[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]: the unit sphere in finite-dimensional Euclidean space is compact.

[F7] [[lem-clarke-sum-chain-rule-for-exponential-risk]]: almost everywhere along the flow, $v:=\dot\theta=\sum_i e^{-q_i}h_i$ for some $h_i\in\partial^\circ q_i(\theta)$.

Homogeneity gives $q_{\min}(u)=q_{\min}(\theta)/r^L=\bar\gamma(t)\ge\gamma_0$. [F2, F5, algebra]

2.1 Local boundedness in [F1] and compactness of the unit sphere [F6] give a common bound $B$ for $\|h\|_2$ over all $u$ on that sphere, all $i$, and $h\in\partial^\circ q_i(u)$. 3.1 At almost every $t\ge t_0$, choose the flow representation from [F7], put $v=\dot\theta$, and define $\beta=\langle\theta,v\rangle/(r\|v\|_2)$. Euler's identity [F4] gives $\langle\theta,v\rangle=L\phi\mu>0$, so $v\ne0$ and $0<\beta\le1$. Differentiating $\widetilde\gamma=z/r^L$ yields $\widetilde\gamma'=L(\mu/(\beta^2r^L)-z/r^L)(\log r)'\ge L\gamma_0(\beta^{-2}-1)(\log r)'$, since $\mu\ge z$ and $\mu/r^L\ge\bar\gamma\ge\gamma_0$. Also $\|u'\|_2\le\|v\|_2/r\le B\phi r^{L-2}\le[B/(L\gamma_0)](\log r)'$, because $(\log r)'=L\phi\mu/r^2$. 4.1 The normalized margin is $\bar\gamma(t)=q_{\min}(u(t))$ and converges to $\gamma_\infty>0$ by [F5]. 5.1 At this time $t$, choose $h_i$ from [F7], let $q_*=q_{\min}(\theta(t))$, and put $\widehat h_i=h_i/q_*^{(L-1)/L}\in\partial^\circ q_i(\widehat\theta)$ using [F4]. [[def-homogeneous-classifier-margin-and-exponential-risk|Parameter homogeneity and margin convention]]

[[def-margin-kkt-and-mfcq|Margin-form Clarke KKT conditions]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The degree-two homogeneous margin and the margin-form Clarke KKT definition.

[F1] [[def-homogeneous-classifier-margin-and-exponential-risk]]: a margin of degree $L$ satisfies $q(c\theta)=c^Lq(\theta)$.

[F2] [[def-margin-kkt-and-mfcq]]: a feasible point is Clarke KKT if nonnegative multipliers and Clarke subgradients satisfy stationarity and complementary slackness.

[F3] [[def-feedforward-neural-network]]: each non-input node evaluates an activation at a weighted sum of earlier node values and a bias.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** compute the gradient, the KKT multiplier, and the objective values at the two feasible points.

1.1 The stated two-node graph evaluates the hidden values $\theta_1^2$ and $\theta_2^2$ and combines them with its fixed output weights, so its score is $q(\theta)=\theta_1^2+4\theta_2^2$ and $q(c\theta)=c^2q(\theta)$ for every $c>0$. At $\theta_*=(1,0)$, $q(\theta_*)=1$ and $\nabla q(\theta_*)=(2,0)$, so $\nabla q(\theta_*)\in\partial^\circ q(\theta_*)$ and the multiplier $\lambda=\frac12$ gives $\theta_* =\lambda\nabla q(\theta_*)$. 2.1 The point $(0,\frac12)$ satisfies $q(0,\frac12)=1$ and is feasible. The objective at $\theta_*$ is $\frac12$, whereas at $(0,\frac12)$ it is $\frac12(\frac14)=\frac18<\frac12$. Therefore $\theta_*$ is not a global minimizer. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $Z$ have the standard normal law on $\mathbb R$. Suppose $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is analytic, nonpolynomial, satisfies $|\sigma(0)|\le B$ for some finite $B$, and is $L$-Lipschitz for a finite $L$. Then $0<\mathbb E[\sigma(Z)^2]<\infty$. Consequently the normalization constant

$$c_\sigma:=\bigl(\mathbb E[\sigma(Z)^2]\bigr)^{-1}$$

is a well-defined positive finite real number.

## Statement references

[Du et al., Condition 3.1 and equation (2)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/du19c.html)

[Feller, Gaussian distribution and finite second moment](https://archive.org/details/introductiontopr0000fell)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the activation $\sigma$, its constants $B,L$, and a standard normal random variable $Z$.

[A1] AC is assumed by the standard-normal-law and Gaussian-moment suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The standard normal law has second moment $1$. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] [[lem-gaussian-even-moment-bound-for-brownian-increments]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** bound the activation by an affine function of $|Z|$, then use continuity and nonpolynomiality for strict positivity.

1.1 Lipschitz continuity gives $|\sigma(z)|\le B+L|z|$, hence $\sigma(z)^2\le2B^2+2L^2z^2$. By [F1], $\mathbb E\sigma(Z)^2\le2B^2+2L^2<\infty$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

1.2 A nonpolynomial analytic function is not identically zero, so choose $z_0$ with $\sigma(z_0)\ne0$. Continuity gives an open interval around $z_0$ on which $|\sigma|\ge|\sigma(z_0)|/2$. The standard normal density is strictly positive on that interval, so its integral of $\sigma^2$ is positive. [A1, F1, given, choose]

2.1 The expectation is both finite and strictly positive by steps 1.1 and 1.2, so its reciprocal exists and is positive and finite. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $0\le s,t$ and a real random variable
$X_t-X_s$ has law $N(0,|t-s|)$, then, for every integer $m\ge1$,
$$E|X_t-X_s|^{2m}=c_m|t-s|^m,$$
where
$$c_m=E|Z|^{2m}=(2m-1)!!=1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)<\infty$$
for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. In particular, when $m\ge2$, this is the moment hypothesis
of the one-parameter Kolmogorov criterion with
$\alpha=2m$, $\beta=m-1$, and $C_T=c_m$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Times $s,t\ge0$, the stated increment law, and an integer $m\ge1$.

[F1] Under AC, $N(0,1)$ is the probability measure with density $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$, and $N(0,h)$ is its image under $x\mapsto\sqrt h\,x$, including $h=0$. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F2] A nonnegative expectation is the integral of the corresponding function against the random variable's law. [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]

[F3] Integration against the measure with density $\phi$ equals integration of the product with $\phi$ against Lebesgue measure. [[thm-integration-against-a-density]]

[F4] Increasing nonnegative measurable functions may be passed to the limit under the integral. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]

[F5] Compact-interval integration by parts includes its two endpoint terms. Under countable choice, a bounded Riemann-integrable function on a compact interval is Lebesgue integrable there with the same integral. [[thm-integration-by-parts]] [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]]

[F6] The power, product, and chain rules, together with $(e^x)'=e^x$, give $\phi'(x)=-x\phi(x)$. [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]] [[thm-chain-rule]] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]

[F7] The exponential is its nonnegative power series, so for $R>0$ and every integer $k\ge0$, $e^{R^2/2}\ge(R^2/2)^k/k!$. [[thm-exponential-definition-equivalence]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $Z$ be the coordinate map on the canonical $N(0,1)$ probability space. By [F1]--[F3], for each integer $r\ge0$, $$E|Z|^{2r}=\int_{\mathbb R}x^{2r}\phi(x)\,dx,$$ with either side initially allowed to be infinite. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 For an integer $R\ge1$ and $r\ge1$, [F5] on $[-R,R]$, applied to $u(x)=x^{2r-1}$ and $v(x)=\phi(x)$, is legitimate by [F6] and gives $$\int_{-R}^{R}x^{2r}\phi(x)\,dx=-2R^{2r-1}\phi(R)+(2r-1)\int_{-R}^{R}x^{2r-2}\phi(x)\,dx.$$ The sign and factor two come from the odd power at the two endpoints and the evenness of $\phi$. [F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 Taking $k=r+1$ in [F7] shows $$0\le R^{2r-1}\phi(R)\le\frac{2^{r+1}(r+1)!}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,R^3}\longrightarrow0.$$ The compact bridge in [F5] identifies every Riemann integral in step 1.2 with the corresponding Lebesgue integral. The truncated nonnegative integrands then increase to their whole-line counterparts, so [F4], step 1.1, and $\int\phi=1$ from [F1] yield recursively $$c_0=1,\qquad c_r=(2r-1)c_{r-1}.$$ Thus $c_m=(2m-1)!!$ and every $c_m$ is finite. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F4, F5, F7, algebra]

3.1 Put $h=|t-s|$. By [F1], the law $N(0,h)$ is that of $\sqrt h Z$; applying [F2] to the nonnegative function $x\mapsto|x|^{2m}$ and using step 2.1 gives $$E|X_t-X_s|^{2m}=E|\sqrt h Z|^{2m}=h^mc_m.$$ This includes $h=0$, when both sides vanish and the law is the Dirac mass at zero. [given, step 2.1, F1, F2, algebra]

4.1 If $m\ge2$, set $\alpha=2m$ and $\beta=m-1>0$. Then $m=1+\beta$, so step 3.1 reads $$E|X_t-X_s|^\alpha=c_m|t-s|^{1+\beta}.$$ The constant $C_T=c_m$ is finite and independent of $T$. AC is used through [F1], which supplies the normal-law probability measure, and through the countable-choice hypothesis of the compact bridge used in step 2.1; all truncations and the recurrence are canonical. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

Durrett, Section 7.1, printed p. 358, uses the finite even moments of a normal increment in the Brownian continuity argument. Steps 1.1--2.1 supply the full compact-truncation integration-by-parts calculation, including the boundary term and its limit.

## Statement

Let $r\in\mathbb R^n$, let $G$ be a real symmetric matrix with eigenvalues in $[\lambda,\Lambda]$ for some $0<\lambda\le\Lambda$, and suppose $0<\eta\Lambda\le1$. If an update has the form $r^+=(I-\eta G)r+R$ with $\|R\|_2\le\eta\lambda\|r\|_2/4$, then for the quadratic loss $L=\frac12\|r\|_2^2$ and $L^+=\frac12\|r^+\|_2^2$,

$$L^+\le(1-\eta\lambda/2)L.$$

## Statement references

[Du et al., empirical loss contraction, Theorems 5.1 and 6.1](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/du19c.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The residual vector, symmetric Gram matrix, eigenvalue bounds, step size, and remainder bound.

[F1] A real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis. [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]

[F2] The Euclidean norm satisfies the triangle inequality. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** bound the spectral norm of the linear contraction and then square the residual-norm bound.

1.1 By [F1], the eigenvalues $\mu_j$ of $G$ lie in $[\lambda,\Lambda]$, so those of $I-\eta G$ lie in $[1-\eta\Lambda,1-\eta\lambda]\subseteq[0,1-\eta\lambda]$. Expanding $r$ in an orthonormal eigenbasis gives $\|(I-\eta G)r\|_2^2=\sum_j(1-\eta\mu_j)^2r_j^2\le(1-\eta\lambda)^2\|r\|_2^2$. The norm triangle inequality [F2] with the remainder hypothesis then yields $\|r^+\|_2\le(1-3\eta\lambda/4)\|r\|_2$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Put $t=\eta\lambda\in(0,1]$. Then $(1-3t/4)^2\le1-t/2$, since $1-t/2-(1-3t/4)^2=t(1-9t/16)\ge7t/16>0$. Squaring the estimate in step 1.1 and multiplying by $1/2$ yields $L^+\le(1-\eta\lambda/2)L$. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎
