## Definition

Assume AC, DC and countable choice for the Gaussian probability-law constructions below. The displayed finite real network recurrences and empirical loss are deterministic definitions for fixed parameters. Fix positive integers $d,n,H,m$, training inputs $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\|x_i\|_2=1$, labels $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$, an analytic nonpolynomial activation $\sigma$ satisfying $|\sigma(0)|<\infty$ and finite Lipschitz constants for $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$, and the positive finite normalization $c_\sigma=(\mathbb E_{Z\sim N(0,1)}[\sigma(Z)^2])^{-1}$. A fully connected network of width $m$ and depth $H$ is the finite feedforward recurrence

$$x^{(0)}=x,\qquad x^{(h)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(1\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm fc}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

where $W^{(1)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}$, $W^{(h)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for $h\ge2$, $a\in\mathbb R^m$, and $\sigma$ acts coordinatewise. The residual network uses the same first layer and then

$$x^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(1)}x),\qquad x^{(h)}=x^{(h-1)}+\frac{c_{\rm res}}{H\sqrt m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(2\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm res}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

with $0<c_{\rm res}<1$. In either architecture, random initialization means all entries of all matrices $W^{(h)}$ and of $a$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables; all these entries are trained by full-batch gradient descent. The empirical quadratic loss is $L(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(f(x_i,\theta)-y_i)^2$.

For the fully connected architecture and the same fixed data, define the population matrices by

$$K_{ij}^{(0)}=\langle x_i,x_j\rangle.$$

For $1\le h<H$, let $(U_{ij}^{(h)},V_{ij}^{(h)})$ be a centered bivariate normal vector with covariance

$$A_{ij}^{(h)}=\begin{pmatrix}K_{ii}^{(h-1)}&K_{ij}^{(h-1)}\\K_{ji}^{(h-1)}&K_{jj}^{(h-1)}\end{pmatrix},$$

and put $K_{ij}^{(h)}=c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(U_{ij}^{(h)})\sigma(V_{ij}^{(h)})]$. For $h=H$, use the same bivariate-normal definition with $A_{ij}^{(H)}$ formed from $K^{(H-1)}$, and set

$$K_{ij}^{(H)}=c_\sigma K_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(U_{ij}^{(H)})\sigma'(V_{ij}^{(H)})].$$

When $H=1$, this last formula uses $K^{(0)}$ directly and there are no intermediate activation-covariance matrices. For the fully connected theorem, this terminal matrix is denoted $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$.

For the residual architecture with $H\ge2$, use a separate sequence $S^{(h)}$ and mean vector $b^{(h)}$. Set $S^{(0)}=K^{(0)}$. For $G^{(0)}\sim N_n(0,S^{(0)})$, put

$$S_{ij}^{(1)}=c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(0)})\sigma(G_j^{(0)})],\qquad b_i^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma}\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(0)})].$$

Write $\alpha=c_{\rm res}/H$. For $2\le h<H$, take a fresh centered Gaussian vector $G^{(h-1)}$ with covariance $S^{(h-1)}$, put $\mu_i^{(h-1)}=\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(h-1)})]$, and define

$$S_{ij}^{(h)}=S_{ij}^{(h-1)}+\alpha\bigl(b_i^{(h-1)}\mu_j^{(h-1)}+b_j^{(h-1)}\mu_i^{(h-1)}\bigr)+\alpha^2\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(h-1)})\sigma(G_j^{(h-1)})],\qquad b_i^{(h)}=b_i^{(h-1)}+\alpha\mu_i^{(h-1)}.$$

For $G\sim N_n(0,S^{(H-1)})$, define the residual terminal matrix by

$$K_{{\rm res},ij}^{(H)}=\frac{c_{\rm res}^2}{H^2}S_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(G_i)\sigma'(G_j)].$$

The fully connected and residual convergence statements use $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$ and $K_{\rm res}^{(H)}$, respectively. At $H=1$, the two architectures coincide; define $K_{\rm res}^{(1)}=K_{\rm fc}^{(1)}$. The residual recursion above is the scalar specialization of the source's general mean/second-moment recursion, equation (16); in particular it includes the mean cross terms. Its terminal Gaussian covariance is $S^{(H-1)}$, as determined by the finite-width last-layer Gram formula (14).

The residual recurrence has one identity contribution from $x^{(h-1)}$ and one nonlinear contribution at every layer $2\le h\le H$; the arrows below depict that convention for one generic layer and do not enter any proof.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth,node distance=1.3cm]
  \node (in) {$x^{(h-1)}$};
  \node[draw,rectangle,right=1.7cm of in] (act) {$\frac{c_{\rm res}}{H\sqrt m}\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})$};
  \node[draw,circle,right=2.0cm of act] (sum) {$+$};
  \node[right=1.2cm of sum] (out) {$x^{(h)}$};
  \draw[->] (in) -- (act);
```

## Statement

Assume AC, DC and countable choice. Under the hypotheses and notation defining the Du population Gram recursion, every fully connected matrix $K^{(h)}$, every residual feature second-moment matrix $S^{(h)}$, and both terminal matrices are finite, symmetric, and positive semidefinite. The fully connected matrices satisfy $K_{ii}^{(h)}=1$ for $0\le h<H$. For the residual sequence, $S^{(h)}-b^{(h)}(b^{(h)})^T$ is positive semidefinite for $1\le h<H$; its diagonal is not asserted to equal one.

## Statement references

[Du et al., Definition 5.1 and Appendix E](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/du19c.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite unit-norm data, activation, normalization, Gaussian covariance convention, and matrices from the definition.

[F1] The architecture and matrices are defined by the stated recurrences, with $c_\sigma>0$ and finite. [[def-du-overparameterized-network-architectures-and-gram-kernels]]

[F5] The normalizer satisfies $c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(Z)^2]=1$ for standard normal $Z$. [[lem-du-activation-normalizer-finite-positive]]

[F6] A property holding at zero and preserved by successor holds for every natural-number index. [[thm-induction-principle]]

[F2] A finite-dimensional positive semidefinite covariance matrix defines a possibly singular centered multivariate normal law, with the listed covariance and finite second moments. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F3] A real self-adjoint matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis. [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]

[F4] Countably many independent copies of a normal vector can be constructed, and expectations of products of integrable independent variables factor. [[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]] [[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]]

[A1] Assume AC as required by the multivariate normal-law supplier. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] Assume DC and countable choice as required by the independent-copy supplier. [[def-dependent-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]]

[F7] For two Borel probability laws on finite-dimensional real spaces, their product measure exists, has total mass one and satisfies the rectangle formula. Thus its two coordinate projections have the prescribed laws and are independent. [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]

[F8] If $X,Y$ have finite second moments, then $\mathbb E|XY|\le(\mathbb E X^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E Y^2)^{1/2}$. This ensures integrability of the Gaussian activation products in steps 2.1 and 4.1 and the terminal-coordinate products in steps 3.1 and 5.1. [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** induction on the layer index, using Gaussian feature vectors to express each quadratic form as an expectation of a square.

1.1 The input matrix $K^{(0)}$ is symmetric, and for $v\in\mathbb R^n$, $v^TK^{(0)}v=\|\sum_i v_ix_i\|_2^2\ge0$. Its diagonal entries are $\|x_i\|_2^2=1$, giving the base case. [base, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Assume the induction hypothesis that $K^{(h-1)}$ is finite, symmetric positive semidefinite, and has diagonal $1$, for some $1\le h<H$. By [F2]–[F3], take $G\sim N_n(0,K^{(h-1)})$; each pair $(G_i,G_j)$ has covariance $A_{ij}^{(h)}$. The growth bound $|\sigma(z)|\le|\sigma(0)|+L|z|$ and finite Gaussian second moments put each $\sigma(G_i)$ in $L^2$; [F8] then makes every product $\sigma(G_i)\sigma(G_j)$ integrable. Thus $K^{(h)}$ is finite and symmetric, and for every $v$, $v^TK^{(h)}v=c_\sigma\mathbb E[(\sum_i v_i\sigma(G_i))^2]\ge0$. Because $G_i\sim N(0,1)$, its diagonal is $c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(Z)^2]=1$ by [F5]. This establishes the induction step. [ih, A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For the fixed $H$, let $P(h)$ mean that $K^{(h)}$ is finite, symmetric positive semidefinite, and has diagonal $1$, for $0\le h<H$. Define $Q(k)$ to mean $P(j)$ for every $j\le\min(k,H-1)$. Step 1.1 gives $Q(0)$. If $Q(k)$ and $k+1<H$, step 2.1 applied with $h=k+1$ gives $P(k+1)$ and hence $Q(k+1)$; if $k+1\ge H$, $Q(k+1)$ adds no new index. By [F6], $Q(H-1)$ holds, so $K^{(H-1)}$ is finite, symmetric positive semidefinite, and has diagonal $1$; when $H=1$, this is exactly the base matrix $K^{(0)}$. By [F4], take independent $G,G'$ both distributed as $N_n(0,K^{(H-1)})$. The vector with coordinates $Y_i=\sqrt{c_\sigma}\,G'_i\sigma'(G_i)$ has finite second moments; $\sigma'$ is bounded because it is the derivative of a Lipschitz differentiable function. Factoring expectations of independent variables gives $\mathbb E[Y_iY_j]=c_\sigma K_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(G_i)\sigma'(G_j)]=K_{ij}^{(H)}$. Therefore $K^{(H)}$ is finite and symmetric, and $v^TK^{(H)}v=\mathbb E[(\sum_i v_iY_i)^2]\ge0$ for every $v$. This proves the fully connected terminal claim and discharges that induction. [A1, A2, F2, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra, discharge-induction]

3.2 For the residual base layer let $G_0\sim N_n(0,S^{(0)})$ and $V^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma}\,\sigma(G_0)$, with activation applied coordinatewise. Then $EV^{(1)}=b^{(1)}$ and $E[V^{(1)}(V^{(1)})^T]=S^{(1)}$ by [F1]. The growth bound used in step 2.1 proves finite second moments. For every $v$, $v^TS^{(1)}v=E[(v^TV^{(1)})^2]\ge0$, while $S^{(1)}-b^{(1)}(b^{(1)})^T$ is its covariance and has quadratic form $E[(v^T(V^{(1)}-EV^{(1)}))^2]\ge0$. Thus both matrices are symmetric positive semidefinite. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Suppose a finite-second-moment vector $V^{(h-1)}$ has mean $b^{(h-1)}$ and second-moment matrix $S^{(h-1)}$. Let $\mu$ be the Borel law of this generally non-Gaussian vector and let $\nu=N_n(0,S^{(h-1)})$, which exists by [F2]. Both are probability measures and hence sigma-finite. By [F7], on $(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n,\mu\times\nu)$ the coordinate projections $V$ and $G$ have laws $\mu$ and $\nu$ and are independent: for Borel sets $A,B$, the probability of $\{V\in A,G\in B\}$ is $\mu(A)\nu(B)$. Put $V^{(h)}=V+\alpha\sigma(G)$. Finite second moments follow from the growth bound and $(u+v)^2\le2u^2+2v^2$. Independence gives $EV^{(h)}=b^{(h-1)}+\alpha\mu^{(h-1)}$ and $E[V_i^{(h)}V_j^{(h)}]=S_{ij}^{(h-1)}+\alpha(b_i^{(h-1)}\mu_j^{(h-1)}+b_j^{(h-1)}\mu_i^{(h-1)})+\alpha^2E[\sigma(G_i)\sigma(G_j)]=S_{ij}^{(h)}$. For every $v$, $v^TS^{(h)}v=E[(v^TV^{(h)})^2]\ge0$, and $S^{(h)}-b^{(h)}(b^{(h)})^T$ is the covariance of $V^{(h)}$, so its quadratic form is also an expectation of a square. Thus both matrices are finite, symmetric positive semidefinite at this stage, which supplies the covariance hypothesis for the next stage. Iterating through the finitely many layers is justified by [F6]. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F4, F6, F7, F8, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

5.1 For $H\ge2$, take independent $G,G'\sim N_n(0,S^{(H-1)})$ and set $Y_i=(c_{\rm res}/H)G'_i\sigma'(G_i)$. The boundedness $|\sigma'|\le L$ gives finite second moments, and independence gives $E[Y_iY_j]=K_{{\rm res},ij}^{(H)}$. Consequently this terminal matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite. At $H=1$ it equals the already proved fully connected matrix by definition. This proves all residual assertions. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra, discharge-induction] ∎

## Statement

For any fixed finite real network obeying either architecture recurrence defined on the A page, let $u(\theta)=(f(x_i,\theta))_{i=1}^n\in\mathbb R^n$, let $y=(y_i)_{i=1}^n$, let $J(\theta)\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ have row $i$ equal to the gradient of $f(x_i,\theta)$ with respect to the vector of all trainable parameters, and set $G(\theta)=J(\theta)J(\theta)^T$. For the empirical quadratic loss $L(\theta)=\frac12\|u(\theta)-y\|_2^2$, one full-batch gradient-descent step with step size $\eta>0$ satisfies

$$u(\theta^+)=u(\theta)-\eta G(\theta)(u(\theta)-y)+R,$$

where $\theta^+=\theta-\eta J(\theta)^T(u(\theta)-y)$ and $R$ is the first-order Taylor remainder of the differentiable map $u$ at $\theta$ in direction $-\eta J(\theta)^T(u(\theta)-y)$. No size bound on $R$ is asserted here.

## Statement references

[Du et al., gradient-descent dynamics, §§4 and B.1](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/du19c.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** One finite network, its trainable parameter vector, a fixed data set and labels, and a step size $\eta>0$.

[F1] The network is a finite composition of linear maps and an analytic coordinatewise activation, so its output map is continuously differentiable in all trainable parameters. [[def-du-overparameterized-network-architectures-and-gram-kernels]]

[F2] Reverse accumulation through a finite $C^1$ parameterized recurrence gives the exact parameter gradient, including all parameter uses. [[thm-shared-parameter-backpropagation-gradient-formula]]

[F3] Fixed-step gradient descent updates the parameter by subtracting $\eta$ times the Euclidean gradient. [[alg-gradient-descent]]

[F4] Differentiability in finite-dimensional real parameter spaces means a linear first-order approximation with a remainder $o(\|h\|_2)$. [[def-real-frechet-derivative-on-real-and-complex-matrix-spaces]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** express the loss gradient by the output Jacobian and apply the defining first-order expansion of the output map.

1.1 Write $r=u(\theta)-y$. By the scalar chain rule applied to $\frac12\sum_i(u_i-y_i)^2$, the parameter gradient is $J(\theta)^Tr$. By [F3], $h:=\theta^+-\theta=-\eta J(\theta)^Tr$. [F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Since $u$ is differentiable, [F4] gives $u(\theta+h)=u(\theta)+J(\theta)h+R$, where $R:=u(\theta+h)-u(\theta)-J(\theta)h$ is the first-order remainder. Substitute $h=-\eta J(\theta)^Tr$ to get $J(\theta)h=-\eta J(\theta)J(\theta)^Tr=-\eta G(\theta)r$, which is the claimed identity. [F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $U$ be an open subset of a real matrix space $\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ or of
a complex matrix space $\mathbb C^{m\times n}$ viewed as a real vector space,
and let $F:U\to W$ take values in a finite-dimensional real normed vector
space $(W,\|\,\cdot\,\|_W)$.
We say that $F$ is **real Fr\'echet differentiable** at $A\in U$ if there is a real-linear map $L$ such that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ for which

$$\|F(A+H)-F(A)-L[H]\|_W\le\varepsilon\|H\|_F\qquad\text{whenever }A+H\in U\text{ and }\|H\|_F<\delta.$$

That map $L$ is the **real Fr\'echet derivative** of $F$ at $A$ and is denoted $DF(A)$. At $H=0$ the remainder is zero because $L[0]=0$. When the source matrix space has at least one entry, this is equivalently

$$\frac{\|F(A+H)-F(A)-L[H]\|_W}{\|H\|_F}\longrightarrow0\qquad(H\to0,\ H\ne0),$$

since a nonempty open neighborhood supplies nonzero increments arbitrarily close to zero. Thus the original positive-dimensional notion is unchanged. A source with zero entries is the zero vector space with its zero Frobenius norm ([[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]). Its only increment is $H=0$, and the unique real-linear map from it to $W$ is zero; the displayed normwise estimate holds identically. No punctured quotient limit at an isolated point is asserted.

## Statement

Assume AC, DC and countable choice. Fix hidden-layer feature vectors $\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_n\in\mathbb R^m$, form the matrix $\Phi\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}$ with rows $\phi_i^T$, and let the independent output-weight vector $a\sim N_m(0,I_m)$. Put $u=\Phi a$ and $G=\Phi\Phi^T$. Then for every $0<\delta<1$,

$$P\left\{\|u\|_2\le\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(G)}+\|\Phi\|_{\rm op}\sqrt{2\log(1/\delta)}\right\}\ge1-\delta,$$

where $\|\Phi\|_{\rm op}=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|\Phi v\|_2$. The probability is conditional on the fixed hidden-layer features and is over $a$ only.

## Statement references

[Du et al., random Gaussian output initialization and Appendix B](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/du19c/du19c-supp.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, DC, countable choice, fixed feature vectors, and an independent standard Gaussian output vector.

[A1] AC, DC and countable choice are assumed by the Gaussian concentration supplier. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[def-dependent-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] For a standard Gaussian vector $Z$ and an $L$-Lipschitz real function $g$, $P\{g(Z)\ge Eg(Z)+r\}\le e^{-r^2/(2L^2)}$ for $L>0,r>0$; for $L=0$ the upper-tail event is empty. [[thm-standard-gaussian-lipschitz-concentration]]

[F2] A standard multivariate normal vector has covariance identity, and a fixed linear functional has variance given by its covariance quadratic form. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F3] Cauchy–Schwarz bounds $\mathbb E|XY|$ by the product of the $L^2$ norms. [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]

[F4] The Euclidean norm satisfies the triangle inequality and hence the reverse triangle inequality. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** apply one-sided Gaussian concentration to the norm of a fixed linear image and bound its mean by its second moment.

1.1 [F4] gives $|\|\Phi a\|_2-\|\Phi b\|_2|\le\|\Phi(a-b)\|_2\le\|\Phi\|_{\rm op}\|a-b\|_2$, so $a\mapsto\|\Phi a\|_2$ is $\|\Phi\|_{\rm op}$-Lipschitz. Since $E[aa^T]=I_m$ by [F2], $E\|\Phi a\|_2^2=\operatorname{tr}(\Phi\Phi^T)=\operatorname{tr}(G)$; [F3] with $X=\|\Phi a\|_2$ and $Y=1$ yields $E\|\Phi a\|_2\le\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(G)}$. [F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 If $\|\Phi\|_{\rm op}=0$, then $u=0$ and the asserted event has probability one. Otherwise apply [F1] to $g(a)=\|\Phi a\|_2$ with $r=\|\Phi\|_{\rm op}\sqrt{2\log(1/\delta)}>0$. The upper-tail probability is at most $\exp(-\log(1/\delta))=\delta$, and the mean bound in step 1.1 gives the displayed threshold. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $u:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$, $L=\frac12\|u-y\|^2$, and $r_0=u(\theta_0)-y$. On the closed ball $B(\theta_0,R)$ suppose a block $J_*$ of the output Jacobian satisfies $J_*J_*^T\succeq(\lambda/2)I_n$ and $\|\nabla^2L\|\le S$, with $\lambda,S>0$. If $R>2\sqrt2\|r_0\|/\sqrt\lambda$ and $0<\eta\le1/S$, every fixed-step gradient-descent iterate stays in the ball,

$$L(\theta_k)\le(1-\eta\lambda/2)^kL(\theta_0),\qquad\sum_{k\ge0}\|\theta_{k+1}-\theta_k\|\le2\sqrt2\|r_0\|/\sqrt\lambda.$$

The assertion is trivial for $r_0=0$; otherwise the hypotheses imply $0<\eta\lambda/2\le1$.

## Statement references

[Du et al., output Gram descent mechanism](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/du19c/du19c-supp.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The output map, quadratic loss, ball, spectral and Hessian bounds, and step size.

[F1] Gradient descent uses $\theta^+=\theta-\eta\nabla L(\theta)$. [[alg-gradient-descent]]

[F2] For a scalar $C^2$ function on a segment, the first-order Taylor remainder is the integral of its second derivative against the linear remainder kernel. [[lem-taylor-integral-remainder]]

[F3] The Hessian norm is the induced operator norm on the finite-dimensional Euclidean parameter space. [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]

[F4] Euclidean Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|a^Tb|\le\|a\|_2\|b\|_2$ for all real vectors of the same finite dimension. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]

## Proof

1.1 Write $g=\nabla L=J^Tr$. Since $JJ^T\succeq J_*J_*^T$, $\|g\|^2=r^TJJ^Tr\ge(\lambda/2)\|r\|^2=\lambda L$ in the ball. For any step $\theta^+=\theta-hg$, $0<h\le\eta$, whose segment stays in the ball, put $\psi(s)=L(\theta-sg)$ for $0\le s\le h$. Then $\psi'(0)=-\|g\|^2$ and $\psi''(s)=g^TH_sg$, where $H_s=\nabla^2L(\theta-sg)$. By Euclidean Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] and the induced norm [F3], $|g^TH_sg|\le\|g\|\|H_sg\|\le\|g\|\|H_s\|\|g\|\le S\|g\|^2$; for $g=0$ the same bound is immediate. By [F2], $L^+=L-h\|g\|^2+\int_0^h(h-s)\psi''(s)\,ds\le L-h(1-Sh/2)\|g\|^2\le(1-h\lambda/2)L$. If $L>0$, nonnegativity of $L^+$ gives $h\lambda/2\le1$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 For such a segment with $L>0$, $\sqrt L-\sqrt{L^+}=(L-L^+)/(\sqrt L+\sqrt{L^+})\ge h\|g\|^2/(4\sqrt L)\ge(\sqrt\lambda/4)h\|g\|$. If $L=0$, $r=0$ and hence $g=0$, so the step is stationary. Telescoping any finite sequence of admissible full or truncated steps gives total parameter path length at most $4\sqrt{L_0}/\sqrt\lambda=2\sqrt2\|r_0\|/\sqrt\lambda$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Suppose there is a first proposed full step exiting the ball. Truncate that step at the first intersection with its boundary; this is a segment of length $h\|g\|$ with $h\le\eta$, wholly in the ball. Step 2.1 applies to all previous steps and this truncated step, giving total path length strictly less than $R$. Reaching the boundary from $\theta_0$ requires length at least $R$, a contradiction. Thus no exit occurs. Step 1.1 applied at every full step gives the loss rate, and taking the supremum of finite partial path lengths in step 2.1 gives the asserted series bound. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the segment between $c$ and $x$, and put
$$
P_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{f^{(j)}(c)}{j!}(x-c)^j.
$$
Then
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac1{n!}\int_c^x f^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n\,dt.
$$
If $M\ge0$ and $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ between $c$ and $x$, then
$$
|f(x)-P_n(x)|\le\frac{M|x-c|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}.
$$
The formula and bound include $x=c$ and oriented endpoints.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Derivatives defined by difference quotients, the oriented
Riemann integral of continuous functions, and the stated derivative bound.

[F1] [[def-continuity-and-derivative-on-real-interval]]: higher derivatives
are defined recursively; $C^{n+1}$ means they exist and are continuous.

[L1] [[lem-fundamental-theorem-and-integration-by-parts]]: for $C^1$ functions,
$\int f'=f(b)-f(a)$ and
$\int uv'=u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int u'v$.

[L2] [[lem-riemann-integral-linearity]]: integrals are homogeneous and
additive in the integrand.

[L3] [[lem-real-and-complex-modulus-rules]]: $|uv|=|u||v|$ and the triangle
inequality holds for real values.

[L4] [[lem-continuous-functions-riemann-integrable]]: the integral is
monotone in the integrand on a forward interval.

## Proof

1.1 For fixed $f,c,x$, define $I_m=\frac1{m!}\int_c^x f^{(m+1)}(t)(x-t)^m\,dt$ for $0\le m\le n$. For $m=0$, [L1] gives $I_0=f(x)-f(c)$. For $m\ge1$, apply integration by parts [L1] to $u(t)=f^{(m)}(t)$ and $v(t)=(x-t)^m/m!$. Since $v(x)=0$, $v(c)=(x-c)^m/m!$, and $v'(t)=-(x-t)^{m-1}/(m-1)!$, it gives $$ I_m=I_{m-1}-\frac{f^{(m)}(c)(x-c)^m}{m!}. $$ Induction from $I_0$ yields $I_n=f(x)-\sum_{j=0}^n f^{(j)}(c)(x-c)^j/j!=f(x)-P_n(x)$. The oriented integration-by-parts identity makes the same recurrence valid when $x<c$; if $x=c$, both sides are zero. [given, F1, L1, algebra, induction]

2.1 Let $d=|x-c|$ and $\psi(t)=f^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n/n!$. This is continuous. The triangle inequality in [L3], applied in both directions, gives $\bigl||\psi(s)|-|\psi(t)|\bigr|\le|\psi(s)-\psi(t)|$, so $|\psi|$ is continuous too and both functions are integrable. By [L2] and [L4], the integral is monotone in the integrand, so $$\left|\int_c^x\psi(t)\,dt\right| \le\int_{\min(c,x)}^{\max(c,x)}|\psi(t)|\,dt \le\frac{M}{n!}\int_{\min(c,x)}^{\max(c,x)}|x-t|^n\,dt.$$ The first inequality follows by integrating $-|\psi|\le\psi\le|\psi|$ on the forward interval and using $\int(-|\psi|)=-\int|\psi|$; orientation does not change the absolute value. The last power integral is $d^{n+1}/(n+1)$ by [L1], using its polynomial antiderivative on the segment to either side of $x$. Thus the bound is $Md^{n+1}/(n+1)!$. Combining this with step 1.1 proves the result. [given, L1, L2, L3, L4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

## Statement

Fix finite real parameters obeying either Du architecture recurrence, with all parameters equipped with the Euclidean norm (Frobenius norm on each matrix block). At a fixed initialization assume all hidden feature norms are at most $B_x$, all matrices $W^{(h)}(0)$ with $h\ge2$ have operator norm at most $B_w\sqrt m$, $\|a(0)\|_2\le B_a\sqrt m$, $\|a(0)\|_4\le B_4m^{1/4}$, and all backward feature derivatives $b_{i,h}(0)=\nabla_{x_i^{(h)}}f_i$ have coordinate maxima at most $B_bM$, where $M\ge1$. For fully connected networks allow $B_x,B_b\le A_0^H$ for a fixed $A_0\ge2$, while $B_w,B_a,B_4$ are fixed independent of $H$. There are $A\ge2,C\ge1$ depending only on $A_0$, these fixed bounds and the activation, with the following bounds; write $T=A^H$. In the residual case the constants depend also on fixed $c_{\rm res}$, and every $T$ below is replaced by a fixed $C$ independent of $H$. Uniformly on any parameter ball $\|\theta-\theta_0\|\le D$ with $D/\sqrt m\le c/T$ (fully connected) or $D/\sqrt m\le c$ (residual),

$$\max_{i,h}\|x_i^{(h)}(\theta)-x_i^{(h)}(\theta_0)\|\le TD/\sqrt m,\qquad \|J(\theta)\|_{\rm op}\le T\sqrt n,$$

$$\max_i\|\nabla^2 f_i(\theta)\|_{\rm op}\le \frac{TM(1+D)}{\sqrt m},\qquad \|J_H(\theta)J_H(\theta)^T-J_H(\theta_0)J_H(\theta_0)^T\|_{\rm op}\le\frac{TnD}{\sqrt m}.$$

In the residual last inequality the upper bound is $CnD/(H^2\sqrt m)$ for $H\ge2$. The residual first-layer and output-vector derivatives are bounded without a factor $1/H$. Consequently, if $r_0=u(\theta_0)-y$ and $L=\frac12\|u-y\|^2$, the loss Hessian on the ball satisfies

$$\|\nabla^2L\|_{\rm op}\le Tn+\frac{T\sqrt n\,(\|r_0\|+T\sqrt nD)M(1+D)}{\sqrt m}.$$

The constants in this last bound can again be fixed independent of $H$ for residual networks. For any segment from $\theta$ to $\theta+h$ contained in the ball, its output Taylor remainder satisfies

$$\|u(\theta+h)-u(\theta)-J(\theta)h\|\le \frac{T\sqrt n M(1+D)}{2\sqrt m}\|h\|^2,$$

with $T$ replaced by fixed $C$ in the residual case.

## Statement references

[Du et al., parameter perturbation and gradient arguments B.3–B.7 and C.3–C.7](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/du19c/du19c-supp.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The deterministic initialization bounds, the architecture, the parameter ball, and fixed activation constants $|\sigma(0)|\le B$, $|\sigma'|\le L$, $|\sigma''|\le\beta$.

[F1] The architectures and scalings are defined locally. [[def-du-overparameterized-network-architectures-and-gram-kernels]]

[F2] The chain rule gives the forward variations and backward feature derivatives of the finite network. [[thm-shared-parameter-backpropagation-gradient-formula]]

[F3] Euclidean Cauchy–Schwarz bounds vector inner products, coordinate products, and sums over parameter blocks in the estimates below. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]

[F4] Restricting a scalar $C^2$ output to a parameter line segment gives the first-order Taylor formula with integral remainder used in step 5.1. [[lem-taylor-integral-remainder]]

[F5] A $C^1$ vector-valued map whose derivative norm is bounded by $M$ on a segment is $M$-Lipschitz along that segment. [[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]]

[F6] Matrix operator norms are the induced norms on finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, and the parameter norm uses the Frobenius norm on matrix blocks. [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]

[F7] For $p=4$, $\|a\|_4=(\sum_r|a_r|^4)^{1/4}$. [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]

## Proof

1.1 Write $z_h=W_hx_{h-1}$ and $s_1=\sqrt{c_\sigma}$ in both architectures, $s_h=\sqrt{c_\sigma}$ for fully connected $h\ge2$, and $s_h=c_{\rm res}/H$ for residual $h\ge2$. A layer has feature Jacobian $P_h=(s_h/\sqrt m)\operatorname{diag}(\sigma'(z_h))W_h$ in the fully connected case, and $P_h=I+(s_h/\sqrt m)\operatorname{diag}(\sigma'(z_h))W_h$ in residual layers $h\ge2$. Within the stated ball, $\|W_h\|\le(B_w+D/\sqrt m)\sqrt m$. Products of consecutive $P_h$, $h\ge2$, therefore have norm at most $A^H$ in the fully connected case and $\prod_h(1+C/H)\le e^C$ in the residual case. All estimates below use only $h\ge2$ for matrix operator norms; the input is fixed. [F1, F2, given, algebra, F6]

2.1 Let $e_h=\|x_h(\theta)-x_h(\theta_0)\|$. Lipschitz continuity gives $e_1\le\sqrt{c_\sigma}LD/\sqrt m$. For fully connected layers, $e_h\le C e_{h-1}+CA_0^H D/\sqrt m$; for residual layers it gives $e_h\le(1+C/H)e_{h-1}+CD/(H\sqrt m)$, using the fixed upper feature bound in the residual case and the initial exponential envelope in the fully connected case. Summing the geometric recurrences gives $e_h\le TD/\sqrt m$ in the first case and $e_h\le CD/\sqrt m$ in the second. The imposed smallness of $D/\sqrt m$ keeps all feature norms in the required bounds and justifies the recurrences successively. Also $\|z_h(\theta)-z_h(\theta_0)\|\le TD$ or $CD$, since it is bounded by $\|W_h(\theta)\|e_{h-1}+D\|x_{h-1}(\theta_0)\|$ for $h\ge2$, and by $D$ for $h=1$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For a unit parameter direction $v$, let $\xi_h=D x_h[v]$. At the first layer $\|\xi_1\|\le C\|v_{W_1}\|/\sqrt m$. Subsequent layers obey $\xi_h=P_h\xi_{h-1}+(s_h/\sqrt m)\operatorname{diag}(\sigma'(z_h))v_{W_h}x_{h-1}$. The product bounds in step 1.1, the feature bounds in step 2.1, and Cauchy–Schwarz over layer blocks give $\max_h\|\xi_h\|\le T/\sqrt m$ or $C/\sqrt m$. For the residual case use $\sum_{h\ge2}s_h\|v_{W_h}\|\le c_{\rm res}(\sum_{h\ge2}\|v_{W_h}\|^2)^{1/2}/\sqrt H\le C$, retaining the separate first-layer term. Thus $\|D z_h[v]\|\le T$ or $C$, uniformly in $h$. Since $Df_i[v]=v_a^Tx_H+a^T\xi_H$ and $\|a\|\le C\sqrt m$, each output gradient has norm at most $T$ or $C$, proving $\|J\|\le T\sqrt n$ or $C\sqrt n$. This explicitly retains the output and first-layer terms with no $1/H$ bound. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra, F3]

3.2 Put $d_h=b_h(\theta)-b_h(\theta_0)$. The backward recurrence is $b_{h-1}=P_h^Tb_h$, with $d_H=a-a_0$. Decompose its difference as $P_h(\theta)^Td_h+(P_h(\theta)-P_h(\theta_0))^Tb_h(\theta_0)$. The latter is the sum of a weight-difference term bounded by $Ts_hD$ (respectively $Cs_hD$) and a gate-difference term bounded by $Cs_h B_bM\|z_h(\theta)-z_h(\theta_0)\|$, because $\|\operatorname{diag}(\sigma'(z_h)-\sigma'(z_{h,0}))b_{h,0}\|\le\beta B_bM\|z_h-z_{h,0}\|$. Summing the backward recurrence with the product bounds gives $\|d_h\|\le TM D$ or $CM D$. Hence $\|b_h(\theta)\|_\infty\le TM(1+D)$ or $CM(1+D)$. The crude $\ell_2$ bound $\|b_h(\theta)\|_2\le T\sqrt m$ or $C\sqrt m$ follows separately from step 1.1 and $\|a\|_2\le C\sqrt m$. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.3 For the last-hidden-layer Gram, put $X_i=x_i^{(H-1)}$, $Z_i=W_HX_i$ and $\gamma=c_\sigma$ or $c_{\rm res}^2/H^2$. Direct differentiation gives $G_{H,ij}=\gamma\langle X_i,X_j\rangle m^{-1}\sum_ra_r^2\sigma'(Z_{i,r})\sigma'(Z_{j,r})$. Subtract its initialized version in three parts: feature-inner-product change, derivative-gate change with $a_0^2$, and output-weight-square change. Step 2.1 bounds the first part by $T D/\sqrt m$ or $CD/\sqrt m$ before multiplying by $\gamma$. For the second part, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $m^{-1}\sum_ra_{0,r}^2|\Delta Z_{i,r}|\le m^{-1}\|a_0\|_4^2\|\Delta Z_i\|_2\le C\|\Delta Z_i\|_2/\sqrt m$; multiply by $\beta L$, and use step 2.1. For the third part, $m^{-1}\sum_r|a_r^2-a_{0,r}^2|\le m^{-1}\|a-a_0\|_2(\|a\|_2+\|a_0\|_2)\le CD/\sqrt m$. Feature norms and $|\sigma'|\le L$ bound all remaining factors. The entry error is consequently at most $TD/\sqrt m$ or $CD/(H^2\sqrt m)$. The operator norm is at most $n$ times this entry bound. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra, F3, F7]

4.1 For two unit parameter directions $v,w$, twice differentiating the output gives the mixed output-weight terms $v_a^TDx_H[w]+w_a^TDx_H[v]$, and the sum over layers of $\frac{s_h}{\sqrt m}b_h^T\left(\operatorname{diag}(\sigma''(z_h))(Dz_h[v]\odot Dz_h[w])+\operatorname{diag}(\sigma'(z_h))(v_{W_h}Dx_{h-1}[w]+w_{W_h}Dx_{h-1}[v])\right).$ This identity follows by differentiating every primitive twice and propagating each resulting second-order term through its downstream Jacobians; the linear skip has zero second derivative. The coordinate-product inequality $\|p\odot q\|_1\le\|p\|_2\|q\|_2$, steps 3.1–3.2, and $\sum_hs_h\le CH$ or $C$ bound the first part by $TM(1+D)/\sqrt m$ or $CM(1+D)/\sqrt m$. The terms involving $v_{W_h}Dx_{h-1}[w]$ use the $\ell_2$ backward bound and $\|Dx_{h-1}[w]\|\le T/\sqrt m$ or $C/\sqrt m$; summing with Cauchy–Schwarz over matrix blocks gives the same bound. The output-weight mixed terms are at most $T/\sqrt m$ or $C/\sqrt m$. This proves the output-Hessian bound, with polynomial factors in $H$ absorbed into $A^H$ only for the fully connected case. [F1, F2, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 The identity $\nabla^2L=J^TJ+\sum_i r_i\nabla^2f_i$ gives $\|\nabla^2L\|\le\|J\|^2+\sqrt n\|r\|\max_i\|\nabla^2f_i\|$. Integrating the Jacobian along the straight segment to initialization gives $\|r\|\le\|r_0\|+T\sqrt nD$ or $\|r_0\|+C\sqrt nD$. Substitution of steps 3.1 and 4.1 proves the claimed loss-Hessian bound, after enlarging $A,C$ to absorb squares of fixed exponential envelopes. For each coordinate the integral Taylor formula is $f_i(\theta+h)-f_i(\theta)-Df_i(\theta)h=\int_0^1(1-t)D^2f_i(\theta+th)[h,h]\,dt$. Step 4.1 bounds its absolute value by $TM(1+D)\|h\|^2/(2\sqrt m)$ or the corresponding residual constant. Summing coordinate squares gives the stated vector Taylor bound. [step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra, F3, F4, F5] ∎

## Statement

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural $m \ge 1$, reals $a < b$, and a function $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the hypotheses of the clause under discussion; points $s, t \in [a,b]$.

[L1] The vector-valued derivative and integral are componentwise: $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$, and $f$ is integrable exactly when every $f_i$ is, with $\bigl(\int_a^b f\bigr)_i = \int_a^b f_i$; equality of two elements of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is equality of all their coordinates ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]).

[L2] The second fundamental theorem: if $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ with $G' = g$ and $g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b g = G(b)-G(a)$ ([[thm-ftc-second-part]], [[def-derivative]]).

[L3] The mean value inequality on a subinterval ([[thm-mean-value-inequality]]): for $s<t$, $f$ continuous on $[s,t]$ and differentiable on $(s,t)$ with $\lVert f'\rVert_2 \le M$ there, $\lVert f(t)-f(s)\rVert_2 \le M(t-s)$.

[L4] Restricting the domain of a function preserves a limit and its value, the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition then quantifying over fewer points; in particular if $f$ is differentiable at $c$ as a function on $[a,b]$ and $c$ is a limit point of $[s,t] \subseteq [a,b]$, then the restriction of $f$ to $[s,t]$ is differentiable at $c$ with the same derivative ([[def-function-limit]], [[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]], [[def-limit-point-r]], [[def-interval]]).

[L5] Norms and the induced metric: $\lVert w\rVert_2 \ge 0$, $\lVert -w\rVert_2 = \lVert w\rVert_2$, and $d_2(u,w) = \lVert u-w\rVert_2$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]); $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ and $|t-s| = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]).

[L6] Lipschitz maps: $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $L \ge 0$ when $d_Y(f(x),f(x')) \le L\,d_X(x,x')$ for all $x,x'$ ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Under the hypotheses of clause 1, each component $f_i$ is differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ with derivative $f_i' = (f')_i$, and each $(f')_i$ is integrable on $[a,b]$. [L1]

1.2 Under the hypotheses of clause 2, if $s < t$ in $[a,b]$ then $f$ restricted to $[s,t]$ is continuous on $[s,t]$ and differentiable at every point of $(s,t)$ with the same derivative, since $(s,t) \subseteq (a,b)$ and every point of $(s,t)$ is a limit point of $[s,t]$. [L4]

2.1 Applying [L2] to $G := f_i$ and $g := (f')_i$ gives $\int_a^b (f')_i = f_i(b)-f_i(a)$ for every $i<m$. [step 1.1, L2]

2.2 Under the hypotheses of clause 2, for $s<t$ in $[a,b]$ the mean value inequality applies on $[s,t]$ and gives $\lVert f(t)-f(s)\rVert_2 \le M(t-s) = M|t-s|$. [step 1.2, L3, L5]

3.1 The $i$-th coordinate of $\int_a^b f'$ is $\int_a^b (f')_i$ and the $i$-th coordinate of $f(b)-f(a)$ is $f_i(b)-f_i(a)$; by step 2.1 these agree for every $i<m$, so the two vectors are equal, which is clause 1. [step 2.1, L1]

3.2 If $s = t$ then $\lVert f(t)-f(s)\rVert_2 = 0 = M|t-s|$; and if $t < s$ then step 2.2 applied with the roles exchanged gives $\lVert f(s)-f(t)\rVert_2 \le M|s-t|$, and $\lVert f(t)-f(s)\rVert_2 = \lVert -(f(s)-f(t))\rVert_2 = \lVert f(s)-f(t)\rVert_2$ while $|s-t| = |t-s|$. [step 2.2, L5]

4.1 Steps 2.2 and 3.2 cover all pairs $s,t \in [a,b]$, so $\lVert f(t)-f(s)\rVert_2 \le M|t-s|$ always; since $d_2(f(t),f(s)) = \lVert f(t)-f(s)\rVert_2$ and $d_{\mathbb{R}}(t,s) = |t-s|$, this is exactly the Lipschitz condition with constant $M \ge 0$, which is clause 2. [step 2.2, step 3.2, L5, L6] ∎

## Remarks

- **Two routes to the mean value inequality, and why the other one was taken.** When $f'$ happens to be integrable, clause 1 together with [[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]] gives $$\lVert f(b)-f(a)\rVert_2 = \Bigl\lVert\int_a^b f'\Bigr\rVert_2 \le \int_a^b \lVert f'\rVert_2 \le M(b-a),$$ the last step by monotonicity of the integral. That is a second proof of [[thm-mean-value-inequality]] **under an extra hypothesis**. The theorem is proved the other way, from the scalar mean value theorem, precisely because it then needs no integrability at all: it applies to every differentiable $f$. The point is not academic — the companion page's witness for the failure of the equality form is differentiable and is nowhere assumed integrable.

- **When is $f'$ integrable?** Continuity of $f'$ suffices, each component being then continuous and hence integrable, which is the classical form of clause 1 and is what [[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]] supplies for the scalar case. Clause 1 as stated is stronger: it asks only for integrability, exactly as [[thm-ftc-second-part]] does.

- **The scalar case of clause 2 is already published** as [[cor-bounded-derivative-implies-lipschitz]], for a function on an order-convex subset of $\mathbb{R}$. Clause 2 is its $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ analogue on a closed bounded interval, and it is proved from the vector mean value inequality rather than by applying the scalar statement coordinatewise, which would give the worse constant $\iota(m)\,M$.

- **Additivity is not needed above but is available**, so that clause 1 may be applied on any subinterval and the pieces reassembled ([[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], [[def-oriented-integral]]).

## Definition

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be the function space of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], with $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$.

### The $p$-norm, for a rational exponent $p \ge 1$

Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_p \;:=\; \Bigl(\sum_{k<n} |x_k|^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]), the sum is the finite
sum of [[def-finite-sum]], and both powers are the **rational** powers of
[[def-rational-power]].

**Every power written here is defined.** Each base $|x_k|$ is a nonnegative real
and $p > 0$, so $|x_k|^{p}$ is given by [[def-rational-power]] for $|x_k| > 0$
and by its supplementary clause $0^{p} = 0$ for $|x_k| = 0$; the sum of these
nonnegative terms is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), and
$1/p$ is a positive rational, so the outer power is defined for the same two
reasons. The value does not depend on which representative of $p$ or of $1/p$ is
used ([[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

**The exponent is rational in this definition.**
[[def-rational-power]] supplies the nonnegative-base powers used here, and
[[thm-minkowski-finite]] supplies the corresponding triangle inequality for
rational $p \ge 1$. This item makes no claim with $p$ ranging over a real
interval; its rational domain is unchanged.

### The maximum norm

For $n \ge 1$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;:=\; \max\{\, |x_k| \;:\; k < n \,\},$$

the maximum of a nonempty finite set of reals, which exists and is one of its
elements ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is required and propagates.** At $n = 0$ the set
$\{|x_k| : k<n\}$ is empty and has no maximum ([[def-max-min]]). This is the same
restriction the published [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries, for the same reason, and
**every statement on this page that mentions $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ inherits
it**. The $p$-norms for rational $p \ge 1$ carry no such restriction: at $n = 0$
each is the empty sum raised to a positive rational power, hence $0$.

### The three cases the rest of the page uses

- $\lVert x\rVert_1 = \sum_{k<n}|x_k|$, since $t^{1} = t$ for $t \ge 0$
  ([[lem-rational-power-laws]], and $0^{1} = 0$ by the supplementary clause).
- $\lVert x\rVert_2 = \bigl(\sum_{k<n}|x_k|^{2}\bigr)^{1/2} = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}x_k^{2}}$,
  which is exactly the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the
  exponent $2$ agrees with the integer power, so $|x_k|^{2} = x_k^{2}$
  ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), and $t^{1/2}$ is the unique nonnegative square root of
  $t$, which is $\sqrt{t}$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]).
  **The two notations denote the same function and no second Euclidean norm is
  introduced.**
- $\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ as above, for $n \ge 1$.

That each of these is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], and
that the metrics they induce are exactly the published $d_1$, $d_2$ and
$d_\infty$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], is
[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]; it is proved there
and is not assumed here.

## Remarks

- **Why $p \ge 1$.** The triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ is
  Minkowski's inequality, and [[thm-minkowski-finite]] is stated for rational
  $p \ge 1$. For $0 < p < 1$ the displayed expression is still defined but is not
  a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ for $n \ge 2$; nothing on this page asserts anything
  about that range, and the expression is never written with such an exponent.

- **Monotonicity in the base is what makes the comparisons below work.** For a
  fixed positive rational $r$ the map $a \mapsto a^{r}$ is strictly increasing on
  the positive reals ([[lem-rational-power-monotone]] clause 2), so an inequality
  between nonnegative sums passes through the outer power. That is the only
  property of rational powers used in the comparison chain of
  [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]].

- **The subscript $\infty$ is a name, not a number.** No arithmetic is performed
  with it, and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ is not $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ for any
  exponent; it is a separately defined function that happens to sit at the end of
  the family. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$ silently that
  [[def-interval]] records for the interval notation.

## Statement

Use either of the two architectures, its own terminal population kernel $K$, and independent Gaussian initialization. Assume AC, DC and countable choice and the activation and bounded-label hypotheses of the convergence theorems. Write $\lambda=\lambda_{\min}(K)>0$, $q=1+\log(16/\delta)$ and $M=\sqrt{1+\log(16mnH/\delta)}$. There are constants $A\ge2$ and $C\ge1$, depending only on the fixed activation bounds, its normalizer, the label bound, and, in the residual case, $c_{\rm res}$, with the following property. For the fully connected case put $T=A^H$; if

$$m\ge C\max\{T n^4/\lambda^4,T n/\delta,T n^2\log(16Hn/\delta)/\lambda^2\},$$

then with probability at least $1-\delta$, simultaneously:

$$\max_{i,h}\|x_i^{(h)}(0)\|\le T,\quad \max_{h\ge2}\|W^{(h)}(0)\|_{\rm op}\le C\sqrt m,\quad \|a(0)\|_2\le C\sqrt m,\quad \|a(0)\|_4\le C m^{1/4},$$

$$\max_{i,h}\|b_{i,h}(0)\|_\infty\le T M,\quad \lambda_{\min}(J_H(0)J_H(0)^T)\ge3\lambda/4,\quad \|u(0)-y\|^2\le Tnq.$$

Here $J_H$ is the Jacobian block of the last hidden-layer matrix, and $b_{i,h}$ is the derivative of the scalar output with respect to the hidden feature vector $x_i^{(h)}$, so $b_{i,H}=a$. In the residual case $H\ge2$, the same conclusions hold with $T$ replaced everywhere in the conclusions by $C$, provided

$$m\ge C\max\{n^4H^6/\lambda^4,n^2/(\lambda^2H^2),n/\delta,n^2\log(16Hn/\delta)/\lambda^2\}.$$

For residual depth one use the fully connected case. Constants may be enlarged, and $A$ may be increased, simultaneously in these conclusions.

## Statement references

[Du et al., initialization arguments B.1–B.2, C.1–C.2 and E.1–E.2](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/du19c/du19c-supp.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The architecture, its population recursion, the data, Gaussian initialization, width and confidence parameters in the Statement.

[F1] The architecture-specific population recurrences, including residual means, and their positive semidefiniteness are supplied locally. [[def-du-overparameterized-network-architectures-and-gram-kernels]] [[lem-du-population-gram-kernels-are-finite-symmetric-psd]]

[F2] Lipschitz functions of a standard Gaussian vector obey the stated one-sided concentration inequality; applying it to both signs gives a two-sided bound. [[thm-standard-gaussian-lipschitz-concentration]]

[F3] Gaussian vectors have the stated covariance and even moments $(2p-1)!!$. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]] [[lem-gaussian-even-moment-bound-for-brownian-increments]]

[F4] Conditional on hidden features, the Gaussian output norm is at most the square root of their total squared norm plus their operator norm times $\sqrt{2\log(1/\varepsilon)}$, with failure probability at most $\varepsilon$. [[lem-du-initial-output-gaussian-concentration]]

[F5] If $X,Y$ have finite second moments, then $\mathbb E|XY|\le(\mathbb E X^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E Y^2)^{1/2}$; expanding a square and applying this bound gives the $L^2$ triangle estimate used for residual feature variances. [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]

[F6] Euclidean Cauchy–Schwarz bounds inner products and the Euclidean norm satisfies the triangle inequality. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]

[F7] A nondegenerate bivariate normal vector has its Gaussian Lebesgue density. [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]

[F8] Differentiation may pass through an integral when parameter derivatives have a common integrable majorant. [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]

[F9] Integration by parts is valid on a compact interval when the derivatives are integrable. [[thm-integration-by-parts]]

[F10] Dominated convergence passes limits through integrals under a common integrable majorant. [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[F11] For nonnegative $Y$ and $a>0$, $P(Y\ge a)\le EY/a$. [[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]]

[F12] For square-integrable $Y$ and $a>0$, $P(|Y-EY|\ge a)\le\operatorname{Var}(Y)/a^2$. [[cor-chebyshev-inequality-for-random-variables]]

[F13] A real function continuous on a compact interval and differentiable in its interior has some derivative equal to its average rate of change; this turns the bounded $\rho$-derivatives in step 2.1 into Lipschitz bounds. [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]

[F14] Analyticity gives $\sigma''$, and the $\beta$-Lipschitz property of $\sigma'$ gives $|\sigma''|\le\beta$ wherever needed in step 2.1. [given]

[F16] A $1/4$-net of the Euclidean unit sphere in $\mathbb R^m$ exists with at most $9^m$ points. [[lem-epsilon-net-of-unit-sphere-has-cardinality-bound]]

[F17] Matrix operator norms are induced by the Euclidean vector norm. [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]

[F18] For $p=4$, $\|a\|_4=(\sum_r|a_r|^4)^{1/4}$. [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]

[F19] The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the matrix entry list, $\|\Phi\|_F^2=\sum_{i,r}\Phi_{ir}^2$; for any unit $v$, Euclidean Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|\Phi v\|_2^2=\sum_i(\sum_r\Phi_{ir}v_r)^2\le\sum_{i,r}\Phi_{ir}^2$, hence $\|\Phi\|_{\rm op}\le\|\Phi\|_F$. [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]

[F15] In the residual coupling, the feature vector and fresh Gaussian vector are independent, so $\operatorname{Cov}(V+\alpha\sigma(G))=\operatorname{Cov}(V)+\alpha^2\operatorname{Cov}(\sigma(G))\succeq\operatorname{Cov}(V)$. This is the construction in [[lem-du-population-gram-kernels-are-finite-symmetric-psd]] and yields the monotone variance lower bound in step 4.1.

## Proof

1.1 We give the scalar estimates used below explicitly. If $U,V$ are centered Gaussian variables with variances at most a fixed $Q$, then $|\sigma(z)|\le B+L|z|$ and [F3] imply $\|\sigma(U)\|_{2p}\le C\sqrt p$; [F5] then gives $\|\sigma(U)\sigma(V)\|_p\le Cp$ for integers $p\ge2$. The same last bound holds for $a^2\sigma'(U)\sigma'(V)$ when $a$ is an independent standard normal, because $|\sigma'|\le L$. After centering, each such variable $X$ satisfies $E|X|^p\le p! C^p$, enlarging $C$ using $p^p\le e^p p!$. Expanding its exponential series, for $|t|\le1/(2C)$ one has $Ee^{tX}\le1+\sum_{p\ge2}(C|t|)^p\le e^{2C^2t^2}$. For $m$ independent copies, apply [F11] to $\exp(t\sum_rX_r)$ with $t=s/(4C^2)$, and then to $\exp(-t\sum_rX_r)$, to obtain $P(|m^{-1}\sum_rX_r|>s)\le2e^{-cms^2}$ for $0<s\le c$. All constants are uniform over the covariances with these variance bounds. [F2, F3, F5, F11, given, algebra]

2.1 The Gaussian expectation maps needed in the population recurrences are Lipschitz functions of the three entries of their bivariate covariance on any region $v\le Q_{ii},Q_{jj}\le Q$, where $v>0$ is fixed. This applies to $E[g(U)g(V)]$ for $g=\sigma$ and $g=\sigma'$, and to the residual marginal map $s\mapsto E\sigma(\sqrt s Z)$. At fixed $\rho$, changing $s,t$ changes these expectations by at most $C(|\Delta s|+|\Delta t|)$: use the Lipschitz constants $L,\beta$, $s,t\ge v$, and [F5] to bound the resulting products. For fixed $s,t$ and $|\rho|<1$, the covariance matrix is positive definite, so [F7] supplies the density $\phi_{s,t,\rho}$. On any compact interval $|\rho|\le r<1$, its eigenvalues lie between $v(1-r)$ and $Q(1+r)$. Direct differentiation of the Gaussian density gives $\partial_\rho\phi_{s,t,\rho}=\sqrt{st}\,\partial_u\partial_v\phi_{s,t,\rho}$. Uniform eigenvalue bounds imply that $|g(u)g(v)\partial_\rho\phi_{s,t,\rho}(u,v)|$ is bounded by an integrable polynomial times $e^{-c(u^2+v^2)}$, uniformly on this interval; $g$ has at most linear growth and $g'$ is bounded. Thus [F8] justifies differentiating the expectation under the integral. On finite rectangles apply [F9] successively in $u$ and $v$; the boundary terms tend to zero as the rectangles expand because of Gaussian decay and the growth bound. The same integrable majorant and [F10] pass the rectangle limits, giving $\partial_\rho E[g(U)g(V)]=\sqrt{st}E[g'(U)g'(V)]$. Its absolute value is at most $QL^2$ for $g=\sigma$ and $Q\beta^2$ for $g=\sigma'$, since $|\sigma'|\le L$ and $|\sigma''|\le\beta$. At $\rho=\pm1$, the representation $U=\sqrt s Z$, $V=\sqrt t(\rho Z+\sqrt{1-\rho^2}Z')$ is dominated after multiplication by either pair of activations by $C(1+|Z|+|Z'|)^2$, which is integrable; [F10] gives continuity at both endpoints. Finally $\rho=Q_{ij}/\sqrt{st}$ is Lipschitz in the covariance entries when $s,t\ge v$. [F3, F5, F7, F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, algebra, F13]

3.1 Write $\widehat S_{ij}^{(h)}=\langle x_i^{(h)}(0),x_j^{(h)}(0)\rangle$ and, for residual layers, $\widehat b_i^{(h)}=m^{-1/2}\sum_r x_{i,r}^{(h)}(0)$. Conditional on previous layers, the preactivation pairs in distinct rows are independent centered Gaussians with covariance given by $\widehat S^{(h-1)}$. In the fully connected case, step 1.1 bounds each difference of $\widehat S_{ij}^{(h)}$ from its conditional mean by $Ct_0$, except with probability $\delta/(32Hn^2)$, where $t_0=\sqrt{\log(64Hn^2/\delta)/m}$. Its conditional mean is exactly the fully connected population expectation evaluated at $\widehat S^{(h-1)}$. Since the population diagonal is one, step 2.1 gives, while the error is at most a fixed small constant, $e_h\le C e_{h-1}+Ct_0$, where $e_h=\max_{ij}|\widehat S_{ij}^{(h)}-K_{ij}^{(h)}|$ and $e_0=0$. If $B>1$ is a fixed base for this recurrence, then $e_h\le B^Ht_0$ after enlarging its prefactor. Choose the statement constant $A\ge B^2$ and enlarge the width constant; its term $Tn^2\log(16Hn/\delta)/\lambda^2$, with $T=A^H$, then makes this error smaller than both the fixed stopping threshold and $c\lambda/n$. Conditional bounds and a union bound over $h,i,j$ therefore justify the estimates through layers $h<H$; the last hidden-feature norm is bounded by one further conditional application of the activation moment estimate, without identifying its covariance with the terminal derivative kernel. A first layer crossing the stopping threshold would contradict this recurrence. In particular all feature norms are bounded by a constant, hence by $T$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 In the residual case the population feature variances lie in a fixed compact interval $[v,Q]$ independent of $H$. Indeed the vector construction in [F1] gives $S^{(h)}-b^{(h)}(b^{(h)})^T\succeq S^{(1)}-b^{(1)}(b^{(1)})^T$, whose diagonal is $v=c_\sigma\operatorname{Var}(\sigma(Z))>0$. Positivity of $v$ follows from nonconstancy, continuity and the positive Gaussian density. Also $\sqrt{S_{ii}^{(h)}}\le\sqrt{S_{ii}^{(h-1)}}+\alpha(B+L\sqrt{S_{ii}^{(h-1)}})$ with $\alpha=c_{\rm res}/H$, so iteration gives a fixed upper bound. The nonlinear quadratic part has conditional fluctuation at most $C\alpha^2t_0$ by step 1.1. Each cross part is $\alpha m^{-1/2}\sum_r x_{i,r}^{(h-1)}\sigma(U_{j,r})$; its centered value has absolute size at most $C\alpha t_0$ by [F2], since its Lipschitz constant in the independent row Gaussians is at most $C\alpha\|x_i^{(h-1)}\|/\sqrt m$. The empirical mean has fluctuation at most $C\alpha t_0$ by [F2]. Step 2.1 now yields $e_h\le(1+C/H)e_{h-1}+Ct_0/H$, taking the maximum of the covariance and mean errors. The first layer has $e_1\le Ct_0$ by step 1.1 and [F2]. Hence $e_h\le Ct_0$ uniformly in $H$. The same stopping argument, now in $[v/2,2Q]$, and the width assumption justify the conditional estimates at every layer and give the feature bound through $h<H$. One further conditional step gives $\|x_i^{(H)}\|\le C$, using the same upper-norm recurrence, so $\max_{i,h}\|x_i^{(h)}\|\le C$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra, F15]

5.1 For either architecture, conditional on layers before the last, the last-hidden-layer Jacobian Gram entries are $s_H^2\widehat S_{ij}^{(H-1)}m^{-1}\sum_ra_r^2\sigma'(z_{i,r})\sigma'(z_{j,r})$, where $s_H^2=c_\sigma$ for the fully connected case and $s_H^2=c_{\rm res}^2/H^2$ for residual $H\ge2$. This follows by differentiating the last layer. The summands are independent across $r$. Steps 1.1–2.1, the feature bounds and errors just proved give entry error at most $B_2^Ht_0$ in the fully connected case, for a fixed base $B_2$ depending only on the fixed activation bounds, and at most $Ct_0/H^2$ in the residual case. Choose the statement constant $A$ also with $A\ge B_2^2$; the displayed logarithmic width term and a sufficiently large fixed multiplier then make both errors at most $\lambda/(4n)$. If an $n\times n$ matrix $E$ has entries bounded by $\varepsilon$, then for any $z$, $\|Ez\|_2\le\sqrt n\,\varepsilon\sum_j|z_j|\le n\varepsilon\|z\|_2$ by [F6], hence $\|E\|_{\rm op}\le n\varepsilon$. Thus $\|J_HJ_H^T-K\|_{\rm op}\le\lambda/4$. Both matrices are symmetric, and for every $z$, $z^TJ_HJ_H^Tz\ge z^TKz-|z^TEz|\ge(\lambda-\|E\|_{\rm op})\|z\|_2^2\ge3\lambda\|z\|_2^2/4$, where $E=J_HJ_H^T-K$. The Rayleigh-quotient characterization of the smallest eigenvalue now gives $\lambda_{\min}(J_HJ_H^T)\ge3\lambda/4$. [F1, F3, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

5.2 By [F16], choose a $1/4$-net $\mathcal N$ of the unit sphere with at most $9^m$ points. The Euclidean norm duality $\|z\|_2=\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}|x^Tz|$ follows from [F6], so $\|W\|_{\rm op}=\sup_{\|x\|=\|y\|=1}|x^TWy|$. For unit $x,y$, choose $v,w\in\mathcal N$ within $1/4$ of them. Then [F6] gives $|x^TWy-v^TWw|\le\|x-v\|_2\|W y\|_2+\|v\|_2\|W(y-w)\|_2\le\tfrac12\|W\|_{\rm op}$. Taking suprema yields $\|W\|_{\rm op}\le2\max_{v,w\in\mathcal N}|v^TWw|$. Each $v^TWw$ is standard normal, whose tail is at most $2e^{-t^2/2}$ by [F2]. Union bounds give $\|W^{(h)}\|\le C\sqrt m$ for all $h\ge2$ with failure at most $\delta/16$ when $m\ge C\log(16H/\delta)$, which follows from either displayed width because $\lambda\le c_\sigma L^2$ in the fully connected case and $\lambda\le C/H^2$ in the residual case. The latter bound follows by bounding the diagonal of its terminal kernel with step 4.1. Gaussian second and eighth moments and [F12] give $\|a\|_2\le C\sqrt m$ and $\|a\|_4\le Cm^{1/4}$ with failure at most $\delta/16$ when $m\ge C/\delta$, also implied by the widths. These arguments never bound $\|W^{(1)}\|$ on the whole input space, so no input-dimension condition is used. [F2, F3, F6, F12, F16, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra, F17, F18]

6.1 Conditional on hidden weights, $b_{i,h}(0)=P_{i,h}^Ta$, where $P_{i,h}$ is the product of downstream feature Jacobians. Their operator norms have fixed envelopes $B^H$ in the fully connected case and $B$ in the residual case, using $\prod_{l>h}(1+C/H)\le e^C$ for residual layers. Increase the conclusion constants so these envelopes are at most $T/2$ and $C/2$, respectively. Each coordinate is centered Gaussian of variance at most $(T/2)^2$ or $(C/2)^2$. Since $M^2=1+\log(16mnH/\delta)$, its two-sided tail is at most $2e^{-2M^2}\le\delta/(8mnH)$; a union bound over at most $mnH$ coordinates gives the asserted coordinate maxima with failure at most $\delta/8$. Finally [F4] and $\|\Phi\|_{\rm op}\le\|\Phi\|_F\le\sqrt n\max_i\|x_i^{(H)}\|$ give $\|u(0)\|\le C\sqrt{Tnq}$ or $C\sqrt{nq}$ with failure at most $\delta/16$. [F2, F3, F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 5.2, F19]

7.1 For the union bound, allocate at most $\delta/(32Hn^2)$ to each fully connected feature-covariance or terminal-feature-norm event in step 3.1; there are at most $2Hn^2$ such events. Allocate at most $\delta/(128Hn^2)$ to each residual covariance, cross-term, mean, or terminal-feature-norm event in step 4.1; there are at most $4Hn^2$ such events. Allocate at most $\delta/(64n^2)$ to each terminal-kernel entry event. The weight-matrix and readout norm events in step 5.2 each use $\delta/16$; backward coordinates use $\delta/8$ and the output norm uses $\delta/16$ in step 6.1. Even summing both architecture allocations, these budgets total at most $27\delta/64<\delta$. The thresholds are constant multiples of $t_0$ or $M$; increasing the fixed constants in the width and conclusions makes each displayed concentration bound meet its allocation without changing their forms. Adding the deterministic bounded-label contribution proves the simultaneous event. [F2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 5.2, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and $0<\epsilon<1$. There is a finite set $\mathcal N\subseteq S^{d-1}$ such that every $u\in S^{d-1}$ has some $v\in\mathcal N$ with $\|u-v\|_2\le\epsilon$, and
$$|\mathcal N|\le(1+2/\epsilon)^d.$$
Here $S^{d-1}=\{u\in\mathbb R^d:\|u\|_2=1\}$ by [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]. Such a set is called an $\epsilon$-net of the sphere.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $d\ge1$ and $0<\epsilon<1$.

[F1] The closed Euclidean ball and sphere are $\overline B_2(c,r)=\{x:\|x-c\|_2\le r\}$ and $S_2(c,r)=\{x:\|x-c\|_2=r\}$; the unit sphere is $S^{d-1}=S_2(0,1)$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]).

[F2] $d_2(x,y)=\|x-y\|_2$ is a metric, so it satisfies the triangle inequality ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

[F3] Closed Euclidean balls are Jordan measurable, with $V_1(r)=2r$ and the stated slicing recursion for $V_d(r)$ ([[thm-volume-recursion-for-closed-euclidean-balls]]).

[F4] An invertible linear map scales Jordan content by the absolute determinant; in particular $\operatorname{cont}(r\overline B_2(0,1))=r^d\operatorname{cont}(\overline B_2(0,1))$ for $r>0$ ([[thm-linear-images-scale-jordan-content-by-absolute-determinant]]).

[F5] Translation preserves Jordan content ([[thm-jordan-content-is-translation-invariant]]).

[F6] Jordan content is additive on finite disjoint families of bounded Jordan sets ([[cor-jordan-content-finite-additivity]]).

[F7] Jordan outer content is the infimum of volumes of finite rectangle covers, and the content of a Jordan set is its common inner/outer value ([[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]]).

[F8] The natural numbers are unbounded in $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]).

[F9] Every nonempty finite set of real numbers has a maximum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]]).

[F10] For rational $\alpha>0$, rational powers preserve order on positive bases, and $0^\alpha=0$ ([[lem-rational-power-monotone]], [[def-rational-power]]).

[F11] The Riemann integral is monotone and additive across a cut, and the integral of a constant $c$ on an interval $[a,b]$ is $c(b-a)$ ([[thm-multidimensional-integral-properties]], [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]]).

## Proof

1.1 Put $V_d=\operatorname{cont}(\overline B_2(0,1))$. This number is finite by [F3] and positive by induction on $d$: $V_1=2$, and for $d\ge2$ set $\alpha=(d-1)/2>0$. On $[-1/2,1/2]$, $1-t^2\ge3/4$, so [F10] gives $(1-t^2)^\alpha\ge(3/4)^\alpha>0$; on all of $[-1,1]$ this integrand is nonnegative. By [F11], splitting the integral at $-1/2$ and $1/2$ and comparing the middle part with the constant $(3/4)^\alpha$ shows $\int_{-1}^{1}(1-t^2)^\alpha\,dt\ge(3/4)^\alpha>0$. The volume recursion [F3] then gives $V_d>0$ from $V_{d-1}>0$. [given, F3, F10, F11, algebra]

1.2 Let $E=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\subseteq S^{d-1}$ have pairwise distances greater than $\epsilon$, and put $r=\epsilon/2$. The closed balls $\overline B_2(x_j,r)$ are pairwise disjoint: a point in two of them would, by the triangle inequality [F2], put the corresponding centers at distance at most $2r=\epsilon$, contrary to the separation. Each small ball lies in $\overline B_2(0,1+r)$, since $\|x_j\|_2=1$ and [F2] gives $\|y\|_2\le\|y-x_j\|_2+\|x_j\|_2\le r+1$. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 By scaling and translation invariance [F4, F5], every small ball in step 1.2 has content $r^dV_d$ and the large ball has content $(1+r)^dV_d$. ## Statement

Let the activation satisfy the Lipschitz and smoothness conditions $|\sigma(0)|\le C_\sigma$, $|\sigma(z)-\sigma(z')|\le L|z-z'|$, and $|\sigma'(z)-\sigma'(z')|\le\beta|z-z'|$ for finite constants, and also be analytic and nonpolynomial. Use the fully connected architecture and population matrix $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$ defined on this page, initialized with independent standard normal entries in all weight matrices and the output vector, and trained in all layers by full-batch gradient descent on $L(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(f(x_i,\theta)-y_i)^2$. Write $K^{(H)}=K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$ and put $\lambda_0=\lambda_{\min}(K^{(H)})$ and assume $\lambda_0>0$. For $0<\delta<1$, if the width and fixed step size satisfy

$$m=\Omega\!\left(2^{O(H)}\max\left\{\frac{n^4}{\lambda_0^4},\frac{n}{\delta},\frac{n^2\log(Hn/\delta)}{\lambda_0^2}\right\}\right),\qquad 0<\eta=O\!\left(\frac{\lambda_0}{n^2 2^{O(H)}}\right),$$

then with probability at least $1-\delta$ over initialization, every gradient-descent iterate $k\ge1$ satisfies

$$L(\theta^{(k)})\le\left(1-\frac{\eta\lambda_0}{2}\right)^kL(\theta^{(0)}).$$

The constants hidden in $O$ and $\Omega$ may depend on the fixed activation and label bounds but not on $n,H,m,\delta$; the step-size constant is small enough that $0<\eta\lambda_0/2<1$. In particular, $L(\theta^{(k)})\to0$ geometrically as $k\to\infty$.

[Du et al., Theorem 5.1 and §3.3](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/du19c.html)

[Du et al., Appendix B, Lemmas B.1–B.7 and proof of Theorem 5.1](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/du19c/du19c-supp.pdf)

**Given:** The data, architecture, activation, Gaussian initialization, positive terminal population eigenvalue $\lambda_0$, width, confidence and step-size hypotheses of the Statement.

[F1] The architecture-specific population kernel, including residual means and scaling, is defined locally and is positive semidefinite. [[def-du-overparameterized-network-architectures-and-gram-kernels]] [[lem-du-population-gram-kernels-are-finite-symmetric-psd]]

## Example

Assume AC, DC and countable choice, as in the population Gram lemma. Suppose two distinct training indices $i\ne j$ have the same input $x_i=x_j$. Then rows $i$ and $j$ of the population Gram matrix $K^{(H)}$ coincide, so $K^{(H)}$ has a nonzero null vector and its smallest eigenvalue is zero. Thus the strict-positivity hypothesis in the convergence theorems is substantive.

## Example references

[Du et al., Definition 5.1 and Appendix F.1](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/du19c.html)

[[def-du-overparameterized-network-architectures-and-gram-kernels|Population Gram recursion]]

[[lem-du-population-gram-kernels-are-finite-symmetric-psd|Positive semidefiniteness of the population Gram matrix]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The population Gram recursion, repeated input indices $i\ne j$, and the finite Gram-matrix lemma.

[F1] The initial Gram matrix is the input inner-product matrix. The fully connected entries depend on the corresponding bivariate covariance matrices; residual entries additionally depend on the corresponding means. [[def-du-overparameterized-network-architectures-and-gram-kernels]]

[F2] Every defined fully connected matrix $K^{(h)}$, every residual feature second-moment matrix $S^{(h)}$ (including $S^{(0)}=K^{(0)}$), and both terminal matrices are finite, symmetric and positive semidefinite. [[lem-du-population-gram-kernels-are-finite-symmetric-psd]]

[F3] A real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis. [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]

[F4] A property holding at zero and preserved by successor holds for every natural-number index. [[thm-induction-principle]]

[A1] AC, DC and countable choice are assumed for the population Gram supplier. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[def-dependent-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]]

## Verification

**Given:** $x_i=x_j$ for distinct indices $i,j$.

**Proof technique:** induction on the layer index.

1.1 The rows $i,j$ of $K^{(0)}$ coincide because $K_{i\ell}^{(0)}=\langle x_i,x_\ell\rangle=\langle x_j,x_\ell\rangle=K_{j\ell}^{(0)}$ for every $\ell$. This is the base case. [base, A1, F1, given, algebra]

1.2 Assume rows $i,j$ of $K^{(h-1)}$ coincide. By [F2], the matrix is symmetric, so the corresponding columns coincide as well. For each $\ell$, the covariance matrices $A_{i\ell}^{(h)}$ and $A_{j\ell}^{(h)}$ are equal. Thus the Gaussian activation expectations agree for $h<H$, and for $h=H$ both the derivative expectations and prefactors $K_{i\ell}^{(H-1)}$, $K_{j\ell}^{(H-1)}$ agree. Hence rows $i,j$ of the fully connected $K^{(h)}$ coincide. [ih, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 For the fixed $H$, let $P(h)$ assert that rows $i,j$ of $K^{(h)}$ coincide for $0\le h\le H$. Step 1.1 gives the base, and step 1.2 proves $P(h)$ from $P(h-1)$ for every $1\le h\le H$. By [F4], the fully connected terminal rows coincide. For $H=1$, the residual terminal matrix equals this fully connected terminal matrix by definition, so its rows also coincide. [A1, F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra, discharge-induction]

2.2 Now assume $H\ge2$. For $1\le h<H$, let $Q(h)$ assert both that rows $i,j$ of $S^{(h)}$ coincide and that $b_i^{(h)}=b_j^{(h)}$. The base $S^{(0)}=K^{(0)}$ has equal rows by step 1.1. At layer $1$, this equality and symmetry from [F2] make the pair covariance matrices for indices $(i,\ell)$ and $(j,\ell)$ identical for every $\ell$, and give $S_{ii}^{(0)}=S_{jj}^{(0)}$. Hence the Gaussian marginal means agree, so the defining formulas give $S_{i\ell}^{(1)}=S_{j\ell}^{(1)}$ for every $\ell$ and $b_i^{(1)}=b_j^{(1)}$; this proves $Q(1)$. For $2\le h<H$, assume $Q(h-1)$. Symmetry from [F2] and equal rows of $S^{(h-1)}$ give equal columns, so the covariance matrices for $(i,\ell)$ and $(j,\ell)$ coincide and $\mu_i^{(h-1)}=\mu_j^{(h-1)}$. In the mean recursion this gives $b_i^{(h)}=b_j^{(h)}$. In the second-moment recursion, the old-row terms agree, the terms $b_i^{(h-1)}\mu_\ell^{(h-1)}+b_\ell^{(h-1)}\mu_i^{(h-1)}$ agree with their $j$-row counterparts, and the Gaussian activation expectations agree; thus $S_{i\ell}^{(h)}=S_{j\ell}^{(h)}$ for every $\ell$. This proves $Q(h)$. Finite induction gives $Q(H-1)$. The terminal residual formula then has equal prefactors $S_{i\ell}^{(H-1)}=S_{j\ell}^{(H-1)}$ and equal derivative expectations because the corresponding pair covariance matrices coincide. Therefore the terminal residual rows coincide. [A1, F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra, discharge-induction]

3.1 For either terminal matrix, let $v=e_i-e_j\ne0$. Symmetry and equal rows imply $K^{(H)}v=0$. By [F2]–[F3], this matrix is positive semidefinite and has a nonzero null vector, so zero is an eigenvalue and the smallest eigenvalue is zero. This proves the residual branch and completes the example. [A1, F2, F3, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra, discharge-induction] ∎

## Example

Assume AC, DC and countable choice. Use depth $H=1$, the softplus activation $\sigma(t)=\log(1+e^t)$, width $m\ge1$, and orthonormal inputs $x_i=e_i$ in $\mathbb R^d$ for $1\le i\le n\le d$. Let $\mu=\mathbb E[\sigma(Z)]$ for standard normal $Z$, let $c_\sigma=(\mathbb E[\sigma(Z)^2])^{-1}$, put $\rho=c_\sigma\mu^2\in(0,1)$, and define the hidden-feature matrix by $\Phi_{ir}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(1)}_{r\cdot}x_i)$. If $u=(f(x_i,\theta^{(0)}))_{i=1}^n$ is the randomly initialized output vector and $e=n^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1)^T$, then

$$\mathbb E[e^T\Phi\Phi^Te]=1+(n-1)\rho,$$

where $\Phi$ is the hidden-feature matrix at initialization. Consequently, for every finite $C>0$, there is positive probability that $|e^Tu|>C\sqrt n$. A confidence-uniform bound $\|u\|_2\le C\sqrt n$ for all confidence levels is therefore unavailable in this example; this observation does not refute the finite-width convergence theorem, whose bounds depend on $\delta$.

## Example references

[Du et al., Gaussian output initialization and Appendix B, Lemmas B.4–B.5](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/du19c/du19c-supp.pdf)

[Toronto, Theory of Deep Learning, Lecture 6, slides 31–43, finite-width initialization context](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~rgrosse/courses/csc2541_2022/slides/lec06.pdf)

[[def-du-overparameterized-network-architectures-and-gram-kernels|Network initialization and hidden-feature definition]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The depth-one fully connected architecture, orthonormal inputs, softplus activation, independent Gaussian initialization, and the associated hidden-feature matrix.

[F1] At depth one, each hidden feature coordinate is $\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(1)}x_i)$ and each output weight is an independent standard normal. [[def-du-overparameterized-network-architectures-and-gram-kernels]]

[F2] The normalizer $c_\sigma$ is finite and positive for softplus, the standard normal law has an everywhere-positive density, and its second moment is $1$. [[lem-du-activation-normalizer-finite-positive]] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] [[lem-gaussian-even-moment-bound-for-brownian-increments]]

[F3] A standard Gaussian vector transformed by a fixed linear functional is normal with variance given by the corresponding quadratic form. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F4] Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the first absolute moment by the square root of the second moment. [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]

[F5] A finite-dimensional inner-product space is the direct sum of a subspace and its orthogonal complement. [[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]

[F6] Every finite-dimensional inner-product space has an orthonormal basis. [[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]]

[F7] Right multiplication of an iid standard Gaussian matrix by a fixed orthogonal matrix preserves its iid Gaussian law. [[lem-gaussian-matrix-orthogonal-unitary-invariance-and-block-independence]]

[A1] Assume AC as required by the normal-law suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] Assume countable choice as required by the iid Gaussian-matrix supplier. [[def-countable-choice]]

## Verification

**Given:** The setting in the Example, $Z\sim N(0,1)$, $s=\sigma(Z)$, and $\Phi_{ir}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(1)}_{r\cdot}x_i)$.

1.1 Softplus is positive and nonconstant. It is analytic, has derivative in $(0,1)$, and its second derivative is at most $1/4$, so it satisfies the activation regularity assumptions. By [F2] and [F4], $\mu$ is finite; because $\sigma(Z)\ge\log 2$ when $Z\ge0$ and the standard normal density is positive on $(0,1)$, $\mu>0$. Since softplus is nonconstant, choose $z_0$ with $\sigma(z_0)\ne\mu$; continuity and the positive Gaussian density give $\mathbb E[(s-\mu)^2]>0$. Expanding this finite square and using $\mathbb E s=\mu$ yields $\mathbb E[s^2]>\mu^2$. Therefore $0<\rho<1$. [A1, F2, F4, given, choose, algebra]

2.1 Let $U=\operatorname{span}\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$. By [F5], $\mathbb R^d=U\oplus U^\perp$, and [F6] supplies an orthonormal basis of $U^\perp$. Joining it to $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ gives the columns of an orthogonal matrix $Q$. By [F7], $W^{(1)}Q$ has the same iid Gaussian law as $W^{(1)}$, so all coordinates $W^{(1)}_{r\cdot}x_i$ are independent standard normals. Thus $\mathbb E[(\Phi\Phi^T)_{ii}]=c_\sigma\mathbb E[s^2]=1$, while for $i\ne j$, $\mathbb E[(\Phi\Phi^T)_{ij}]=c_\sigma\mu^2=\rho$. 3.1 Conditional on the hidden weights, $e^Tu=e^T\Phi a$ is a centered normal random variable with variance $S=e^T\Phi\Phi^Te\ge0$, by [F1] and [F3]. The nonnegative random variable $S$ has expectation $1+(n-1)\rho>\rho n/2$, so the event $S>\rho n/2$ has positive probability; otherwise its expectation would be at most $\rho n/2$. On this event, for any fixed $C>0$, the conditional probability of $|e^Tu|>C\sqrt n$ is at least $P\{|Z|>C\sqrt{2/\rho}\}>0$. Averaging over the hidden weights proves positive unconditional probability. ## Statement

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $G\in F^{a\times b}$ have the iid Gaussian law of
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]. If $U,V$
are compatible orthogonal matrices for $F=\mathbb R$ or unitary matrices for
$F=\mathbb C$, then $U^*GV$ has the same iid law as $G$. In particular, if
$W\in F^{n\times n}$ is orthogonal/unitary and $\Omega\in F^{n\times\ell}$
is iid Gaussian, then any two disjoint row blocks of $W^*\Omega$ are
independent standard Gaussian matrices.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice for the finite Gaussian law, and a finite iid Gaussian matrix and compatible orthogonal or unitary matrices.

[F1] [[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]: when $ab>0$, the joint density of $G$ is a constant times $e^{-\|G\|_F^2/2}$ over real coordinates in the real case and a constant times $e^{-\|G\|_F^2}$ in the normalized complex case; the entry coordinates are independent. When $a=0$ or $b=0$, the law is the point mass at the empty matrix.

[F2] Under Countable Choice, a real orthogonal coordinate map preserves Lebesgue measurable sets and their measure ([[cor-lebesgue-measure-is-invariant-under-orthogonal-linear-maps]]). The pullback therefore preserves nonnegative integrals: first this holds for indicators by the set identity, then for nonnegative simple functions by finite linearity, and finally for all nonnegative functions by their defining simple-function suprema.

[A1] Countable Choice supplies the finite-dimensional Lebesgue measure used by the Gaussian densities ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

1.1 If there are no entry coordinates, the matrix is deterministic and its law is unchanged. Otherwise regard the matrix as its finite list of real coordinates. Multiplying the independent scalar densities in [F1] gives joint density $C e^{-\|G\|_F^2/2}$ over $\mathbb R$ or $C'e^{-\|G\|_F^2}$ over $\mathbb C$. The maps $G\mapsto U^*GV$ are real-linear isometries for the Frobenius norm; their real Jacobian matrix $O$ satisfies $O^TO=I$, hence $|\det O|=1$. By [F2], this real orthogonal map preserves measure, also in the complex case viewed in $\mathbb R^{2ab}$. Its inverse preserves the Frobenius norm, so integrating over the preimage of any Borel set gives the same density integral over that set. Hence the transformed matrix has the same law. [given, F1, F2, A1, algebra]

2.1 In the nonempty-coordinate case, the density in [F1] factors over all transformed entries because its exponent is the sum of the entrywise squared moduli and its normalizing constant is the product of the scalar normalizers. Thus the entries remain independent and each retains its original scalar law. For an empty matrix the assertion about entries is vacuous. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

3.1 Apply the invariance with $U=W$ and $V=I$. For two nonempty disjoint row blocks, integrating out the other entries leaves the product of their block densities, which proves independence and the declared standard block laws. An empty block has the prescribed deterministic law and is independent of every other block, since each event for it has probability zero or one. [step 2.1, F1, algebra] ∎
