## Definition

For positive integers $n$ and $p$, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ and define its (uncentered, unit-variance-normalized) sample covariance matrix by
$$S(X):=\frac1nX^{\mathsf T}X\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}.$$
It is real symmetric and non-negative. If its eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, are $\lambda_1(S(X)),\ldots,\lambda_p(S(X))$, its empirical spectral distribution (ESD), normalized by the matrix dimension $p$, is
$$\mu_{S(X)}:=\frac1p\sum_{j=1}^p\delta_{\lambda_j(S(X))}.$$
The largest eigenvalue is $\lambda_{\max}(S(X)):=\max_j\lambda_j(S(X))$. When $S(X)$ has at least one positive eigenvalue, its smallest positive eigenvalue is $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S(X)):=\min\{\lambda_j(S(X)):\lambda_j(S(X))>0\}$. For a sequence $X_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_n}$, write $S_n=S(X_n)$ and $\mu_n=\mu_{S_n}$.

## Definition references

Bai and Silverstein, Chapter 3, §§3.1–3.3, printed pp. 39–58 ([complete book PDF](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

Junyi Liao, Chapter 2, §2.1, printed pp. 29–38 ([complete lecture notes](https://jurrivhleon.github.io/notes/rmt.pdf)).

## Definition

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$. For $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$, its Stieltjes transform, with the $(x-z)^{-1}$ convention, is
$$m_\mu(z):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{x-z}\,d\mu(x).$$
The integral is finite because $|x-z|^{-1}\le\eta^{-1}$ for every real $x$.

## Definition

For $\gamma>0$, set
$$a_\gamma=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2,\qquad b_\gamma=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2,\qquad r_+:=\max\{r,0\}\quad(r\in\mathbb R).$$
Define the Marchenko–Pastur set function on Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ by
$$\mu_\gamma(A):=\int_{A\cap(a_\gamma,b_\gamma)}\frac{\sqrt{(b_\gamma-x)(x-a_\gamma)}}{2\pi\gamma x}\,d\lambda(x)+\left(1-\frac1\gamma\right)_+\delta_0(A),$$
where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$. The formula defines a finite Borel measure; its total mass is established by the Marchenko–Pastur law below.

## Statement

Let $\xi=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_d)^{\mathsf T}$ have independent identically distributed real coordinates with $\mathbb E\xi_i=0$, $\mathbb E\xi_i^2=1$, and $\mu_4:=\mathbb E\xi_i^4<\infty$. Let $A$ be an independent random complex symmetric $d\times d$ matrix with $\mathbb E\|A\|_F^2<\infty$, where $\|A\|_F^2:=\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|^2$. Then
$$\mathbb E\left|\xi^{\mathsf T}A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A\right|^2\le C_{\mu_4}\,\mathbb E\|A\|_F^2,\qquad C_{\mu_4}:=\max\{\mu_4-1,2\}.$$

## Statement references

Bai and Silverstein, Chapter 3, §3.3, printed pp. 57–58 ([complete book PDF](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

Junyi Liao, Chapter 2, §2.1.3, printed pp. 35–37 ([complete lecture notes](https://jurrivhleon.github.io/notes/rmt.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The independent coordinates $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_d$ and independent random symmetric matrix $A$ in the Statement.

[F1] The coordinates of an IID family are mutually independent and have one common distribution ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]).

[F2] Independent random elements have the product joint law ([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]).

[F3] Fubini's theorem permits integration in either order for an integrable function on a sigma-finite product measure ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The moment hypotheses, independence, and the finite Frobenius-norm second moment in the Statement.

1.1 First fix a deterministic complex symmetric matrix $A$. Since $A_{ji}=A_{ij}$, $$\xi^{\mathsf T}A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A =\sum_i A_{ii}(\xi_i^2-1)+2\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}\xi_i\xi_j.$$ The diagonal summands have mean zero. Distinct diagonal summands are uncorrelated; a diagonal summand and an off-diagonal summand are uncorrelated because at least one independent centered coordinate occurs to the first power; and two off-diagonal summands are uncorrelated unless their unordered index pairs coincide. Therefore $$\mathbb E\left|\xi^{\mathsf T}A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A\right|^2 =(\mu_4-1)\sum_i|A_{ii}|^2+4\sum_{i<j}|A_{ij}|^2 \le C_{\mu_4}\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|^2.$$ Here $\mu_4\ge1$ follows from $\mathbb E\xi_i^2=1$ and Cauchy–Schwarz. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], the joint law of $(\xi,A)$ is the product of its marginal laws. The integrand is integrable: $|\xi^{\mathsf T}A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A|^2\le2\|A\|_F^2\|\xi\|_2^4+2d\|A\|_F^2$, and $\mathbb E\|\xi\|_2^4<\infty$ because $d$ is finite and $\mathbb E\xi_i^4<\infty$. Thus [F3] permits integration of the deterministic inequality in step 1.1 against the law of $A$, giving the asserted bound. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $B$ be a real symmetric non-negative $d\times d$ matrix, let $x\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$. Put $R=(B-zI)^{-1}$ and $R_x=(B+xx^{\mathsf T}-zI)^{-1}$. Then $1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx\ne0$,
$$R_x=R-\frac{Rxx^{\mathsf T}R}{1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx},$$
and
$$\left|\operatorname{tr}R_x-\operatorname{tr}R\right|\le\frac1\eta.$$

## Statement references

Bai and Silverstein, Chapter 3, §3.3, printed pp. 53–54 ([complete book PDF](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

Junyi Liao, Chapter 2, §2.1.3, printed pp. 35–36 ([complete lecture notes](https://jurrivhleon.github.io/notes/rmt.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The real symmetric matrix $B$, vector $x$, and non-real spectral parameter $z$ in the Statement.

[F1] A real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues ([[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]).

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], write $B=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)U^{\mathsf T}$ with $\lambda_j\ge0$. Thus $R$ exists, is normal, and $$x^{\mathsf T}Rx=\sum_j\frac{(U^{\mathsf T}x)_j^2}{\lambda_j-z},\qquad \operatorname{Im}(x^{\mathsf T}Rx)=\eta\sum_j\frac{(U^{\mathsf T}x)_j^2}{(\lambda_j-u)^2+\eta^2}.$$ If $x\ne0$, this imaginary part is strictly positive, so $1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx\ne0$; if $x=0$, the denominator is $1$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Direct multiplication verifies $$(B+xx^{\mathsf T}-zI)\left(R-\frac{Rxx^{\mathsf T}R}{1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx}\right)=I.$$ Since $B+xx^{\mathsf T}$ is also real symmetric and $z\notin\mathbb R$, its resolvent exists; hence the displayed expression is $R_x$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Taking traces in step 2.1 gives $$\operatorname{tr}(R_x-R)=-\frac{x^{\mathsf T}R^2x}{1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx}.$$ In the eigenbasis of [F1], $$|x^{\mathsf T}R^2x|\le\sum_j\frac{(U^{\mathsf T}x)_j^2}{(\lambda_j-u)^2+\eta^2} =\frac{\operatorname{Im}(x^{\mathsf T}Rx)}{\eta}.$$ Also $|1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx|\ge\operatorname{Im}(x^{\mathsf T}Rx)$ when $x\ne0$; for $x=0$ the trace difference is zero. Combining these inequalities proves the stated $1/\eta$ bound. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(Z_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite iid real array with $EZ_{11}=0$ and $EZ_{11}^2<\infty$. For every fixed $C<\infty$,
$$\frac1n\max_{1\le i\le\lfloor Cn\rfloor}\max_{1\le k\le n}\left|\sum_{j=1}^{k}Z_{ij}\right|\longrightarrow0\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
The maximum over an empty index set is zero. The same conclusion holds with row and column coordinates exchanged.

## Statement references

Bai and Silverstein, Chapters 3 and 5 ([complete book](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)); the argument below supplies its own counting and probability estimates.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The iid convention is [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]; [[cor-first-borel-cantelli-lemma-for-events]] applies to every summable sequence of event probabilities. The finite stopping and exponential estimates used below are proved in the argument.

## Proof

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the statement.

1.1 If $C\le0$ the claim is vacuous. Suppose $C>0$, set $v=EZ_{11}^2$ and fix $\varepsilon>0$. For a dyadic integer $m=2^\ell$ put $N=2m$, $I=\lceil2Cm\rceil$, $x=\varepsilon m$, $r=4$ and $y=x/r$. For one row write $Z_j=Z_{ij}$ and $W_j=Z_j\mathbf1_{\{Z_j\le y\}}$. These variables are independent with $EW_j=-E[Z_j\mathbf1_{\{Z_j>y\}}]\le0$ and $EW_j^2\le v$. For $t>0$ and $w\le y$, $e^{tw}\le1+tw+(e^{ty}-1-ty)w^2/y^2$: the function $(e^u-1-u)/u^2=\int_0^1(1-s)e^{su}\,ds$, extended continuously at zero, is increasing in $u$. Consequently $Ee^{tW_j}\le\exp\{v(e^{ty}-1-ty)/y^2\}$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Set $\psi=v(e^{ty}-1-ty)/y^2\ge0$. Independence shows that $M_k=\exp(t\sum_{j\le k}W_j-k\psi)$ has conditional expected next value at most $M_k$. If $\tau$ is the first $k\le N$ with $\sum_{j\le k}W_j\ge x$, stopping this finite sequence at $\tau$ or $N$ preserves the expectation bound $1$: condition each increment and observe that the indicator of not having stopped is determined by the preceding variables. On a crossing its stopped value is at least $e^{tx-N\psi}$. Nonnegativity therefore gives $P(\max_{k\le N}\sum_{j\le k}W_j\ge x)\le e^{-tx+N\psi}$. This proves the needed maximal bound directly. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $v=0$, every $Z_j=0$ almost surely and the conclusion follows. Otherwise choose $t>0$ by $e^{ty}=1+xy/(Nv)$. Then $N\psi\le x/y=r$, so the preceding probability is at most $e^r(Nv/(xy))^r\le K m^{-r}$, with $K$ depending only on $v,\varepsilon$. On the event that all $Z_j\le y$, the original and truncated partial sums agree; the complement has probability at most $NP(Z_{11}>y)$. Thus the positive original maximal tail is at most $NP(Z_{11}>y)+Km^{-r}$. Apply the same argument to $-Z_j$ for the negative tail and use a union bound over the $I$ rows. The result is $$P\left(\max_{i\le I,k\le N}\left|\sum_{j\le k}Z_{ij}\right|\ge\varepsilon m\right)\le K_Cm^2P(|Z_{11}|>\varepsilon m/4)+K'_Cm^{1-r}.$$ [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The right-hand side is summable over dyadic $m$: for every $a>0$, $\sum_\ell2^{2\ell}P(|Z_{11}|>a2^\ell)\le K_aE|Z_{11}|^2<\infty$, by summing the finite geometric progression $\sum_{\ell:\,a2^\ell<|Z_{11}|}2^{2\ell}$ under expectation. Also $\sum_\ell2^{(1-r)\ell}<\infty$. First Borel–Cantelli gives the displayed maximal estimate eventually on each dyadic block. Whenever $m\le n\le2m$, every $i\le Cn$ and $k\le n$ occurs in the corresponding block; division by $n\ge m$ bounds the desired ratio by $\varepsilon$ eventually. Intersecting over positive rational $\varepsilon$ proves convergence to zero. Exchanging the two coordinates preserves the iid law and gives the column version. [F1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Events $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ with $\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty$.

[L1] The infinitely-often event is the set limsup. ([[def-limsup-and-infinitely-often-event]])

[L2] If the sum of the measures is finite, then the measure of the set limsup is zero. ([[thm-first-borel-cantelli]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], the event $\{A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.}\}$ is exactly $\limsup_{n\to\infty}A_n$. [L1]

2.1 Applying [L2] to the probability measure $\mathbb P$ and the measurable sets $A_n$ gives $$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=\mathbb P\left(\limsup_{n\to\infty}A_n\right)=0.$$ [step 1.1, L2] ∎

## Statement

Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite real iid array with $E\xi_{11}=0$, $E\xi_{11}^2=1$ and $E|\xi_{11}|^2<\infty$. Let $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$, $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{i\le n,j\le p_n}$ and $G_n=X_nX_n^{\mathsf T}/n$. Suppose almost surely $\limsup_n\|X_n/\sqrt n\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$. For every fixed integer $k\ge1$, almost surely
$$\frac1n\operatorname{Tr}G_n^k\longrightarrow\mu_k(\gamma):=\sum_{s=1}^k\frac1k\binom{k}{s}\binom{k}{s-1}\gamma^s.$$
Positive eigenvalues exist eventually and, with $a=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2$ and $b=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2$, almost surely
$$\liminf_n\lambda_{\max}(G_n)\ge b,\qquad\limsup_n\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_n)\le a.$$
The edge conclusions follow from fixed polynomial trace witnesses and do not assume a weak empirical spectral limit.

## Statement references

Bai and Silverstein, Chapters 3 and 5 ([complete book](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)); the argument below supplies its own counting and probability estimates.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The integrable iid strong law is [[thm-kolmogorov-iid-l1-strong-law]]. The iid array convention is [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]].

[F2] The finite-dimensional spectral theorem and SVD are [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] and [[thm-singular-value-decomposition]].

[F3] Markov's inequality is [[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]] and the first Borel–Cantelli lemma is [[cor-first-borel-cantelli-lemma-for-events]].

## Proof

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the statement. Write $A_n=X_n/\sqrt n$ and $S_n=G_n$. For a bounded centered iid array $(\eta_{ij})$, write $Y_n=(\eta_{ij})_{i\le n,j\le p_n}$.

1.1 First replace $\xi$ by any bounded centered real iid entry $\eta$, of variance $v\ge0$. For a fixed integer $k\ge1$, set $$T_{n,k}=\frac1n\operatorname{Tr}\left(\frac{Y_nY_n^T}{n}\right)^k=\frac1{n^{k+1}}\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_k\le n}\sum_{j_1,\ldots,j_k\le p_n}\prod_{\ell=1}^k\eta_{i_\ell j_\ell}\eta_{i_{\ell+1}j_\ell},\qquad i_{k+1}=i_1.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Each summand is a length-$2k$ closed alternating walk on a bipartite graph: row labels and column labels are disjoint vertex types, and each distinct pair $(i,j)$ is an edge. Its graph is connected. An edge occurring once makes its expectation zero, by centering and independence. Every surviving walk therefore has at most $k$ distinct edges and at most $k+1$ vertices. There are finitely many equality patterns of the $2k$ vertex positions, with a bound depending only on $k$. A pattern with $r$ row and $s$ column vertices has exactly $(n)_r(p_n)_s$ injective labelings, and its summand expectations are uniformly bounded. Consequently, every pattern with $r+s\le k$ contributes $O(n^{-1})$ after normalization. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 1.1]

3.1 A pattern with $k+1$ vertices has exactly $k$ edges, its graph is a tree, and every edge is traversed exactly twice. The closed walk traverses each tree edge once in each direction. The order in which it first enters the children of each vertex makes this tree a rooted ordered tree, rooted at a row vertex. Conversely the contour walk of every such ordered tree supplies exactly one canonical equality pattern. This is a bijection: on a tree an edge cannot be left behind before its whole descendant excursion is completed, since that would force a third traversal. If the tree has $s$ odd-depth (column) vertices, its limiting labeling weight is $\gamma^s$, and its expectation is $v^k$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 2.1]

4.1 For completeness, the tree count can be extracted without any random-matrix theorem. Let $R(z)$ count ordered trees rooted at a row, with an edge contributing $z$ and each column vertex contributing $\gamma$. Let $C(z)$ count column-rooted trees with the same weights, including the root-column weight. The ordered list of subtrees gives, as formal power series, $$R=\frac1{1-zC},\qquad C=\frac\gamma{1-zR}.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 3.1]

5.1 Writing $H=R-1$, these equations give $C=\gamma+H$ and $$H=z(1+H)(\gamma+H).$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 4.1]

6.1 The formal coefficient identity for $H=z\Phi(H)$ is $$[z^k]H=\frac1k[u^{k-1}]\Phi(u)^k.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 5.1]

7.1 One direct verification uses formal residues: substitute $z=u/\Phi(u)$ into $\operatorname{Res}H(z)z^{-k-1}dz$. The resulting residue is $\operatorname{Res}(u^{-k}\Phi^k-u^{-k+1}\Phi^{k-1}\Phi')du$; the second coefficient is $(k-1)/k$ times the first, by differentiating $\Phi^k$. This proves the identity, including $k=1$. Applying it gives $$\mu_k(\gamma)=[z^k]H=\sum_{s=1}^k\frac1k\binom{k}{s}\binom{k}{s-1}\gamma^s.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 6.1]

8.1 Thus $$ET_{n,k}\longrightarrow v^k\mu_k(\gamma).$$ This explicitly counts all leading patterns, and the argument above bounds all nonleading patterns. It does not assume a spectral limit. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 7.1]

9.1 For a label assignment $w$, let $M_w$ be its walk monomial and $Z_w=M_w-EM_w$. Expand the fourth centered moment as a sum of $E(Z_{w_1}Z_{w_2}Z_{w_3}Z_{w_4})$, with normalization $n^{-4k-4}$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 8.1]

10.1 Join two of the four walks when their sets of matrix entries share an edge. A walk isolated in this graph is independent of the other three monomials, so its centered factor makes the expectation zero. Therefore every surviving configuration has at most two clusters of walks. Each cluster has a connected union graph because its walks are individually connected and consecutive walks in the cluster share an edge. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 9.1]

11.1 Moreover, no matrix-entry edge can occur just once in the total $8k$ factors. Indeed, if that edge occurs in $M_{w_t}$, then $EM_{w_t}=0$, so $Z_{w_t}=M_{w_t}$, and conditioning on all other entries makes the expectation zero. Thus a surviving configuration has at most $4k$ distinct edges. Its number of distinct vertices is at most the sum over its clusters of (edges plus one), hence at most $4k+2$. Sharing vertices between different edge-clusters only reduces this bound. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 10.1]

12.1 There are finitely many patterns at this fixed $k$. Bounded entries bound every centered product expectation by a constant depending only on $k$ and the entry bound. With $p_n=O(n)$, the count of labelings is $O(n^{4k+2})$. Therefore $$E|T_{n,k}-ET_{n,k}|^4=O(n^{-2}).$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 11.1]

13.1 Markov's inequality and the first Borel–Cantelli lemma show $T_{n,k}-ET_{n,k}\to0$ almost surely. Intersecting over all integer $k\ge1$ proves simultaneous fixed-degree trace convergence for bounded entries. Neither independence between different $n$ nor a monotone sequence $p_n$ was assumed. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 12.1]

14.1 **Rectangular strong law.** For every integrable iid nonnegative array $Z_{ij}$, $$\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i\le n,j\le p_n}Z_{ij}\longrightarrow\gamma EZ\quad\hbox{almost surely}.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 13.1]

15.1 To prove this, for each positive rational $t$ enumerate the cells of the nested rectangles $[m]\times[\lfloor tm\rfloor]$ in their successive increments. This is an enumeration of the whole quadrant, so the ordinary one-dimensional iid strong law applies at the rectangle cardinalities. It gives the limit $tEZ$ after division by $m^2$. Intersect these probability-one events over rational $t$. Bracket $p_n/n$ between rationals $t_-<\gamma<t_+$ and use nonnegativity, then let $t_\pm\to\gamma$. This proof accommodates arbitrary $p_n/n\to\gamma$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 14.1]

16.1 **Singular-value comparison.** For two real rectangular matrices $A,B$ of the same dimensions, pad their ordered singular-value lists with zeros to length $n$ when forming $AA^T,BB^T$. Then $$\sum_{i=1}^n(s_i(A)-s_i(B))^2\le\|A-B\|_F^2.$$ Here is an elementary proof of the underlying comparison. For symmetric matrices $U,V$ of dimension $d$ with ordered eigenvalues $\alpha,\beta$, orthogonal diagonalization expresses $\operatorname{Tr}(UV)$ as $\sum_{ij}\alpha_i\beta_jd_{ij}$, where $d_{ij}$ is the square of an orthogonal overlap and its row and column sums are one. For descending real sequences, this sum is at most $\sum_i\alpha_i\beta_i$: set $c_i=\sum_jd_{ij}\beta_j$; the sum of its first $r$ entries is at most the sum of the first $r$ entries of $\beta$, because the associated column weights lie in $[0,1]$ and sum to $r$. Summation by parts against descending $\alpha$, with equal total sums, proves the assertion. Expanding $\operatorname{Tr}(U-V)^2$ now bounds it below by $\sum_i(\alpha_i-\beta_i)^2$. Apply this result to the symmetric dilations $$\begin{pmatrix}0&A\\A^T&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \begin{pmatrix}0&B\\B^T&0\end{pmatrix}.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 15.1]

17.1 Their eigenvalues are the singular values, their negatives, and the required zeros. Both sides acquire a factor two, proving the comparison. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 16.1]

18.1 For $k\ge1$, the scalar factorization and Cauchy–Schwarz consequently give $$\left|\frac1n\sum_i s_i^{2k}-\frac1n\sum_i t_i^{2k}\right|\le2k\left(\frac{\|A-B\|_F^2}{n}\right)^{1/2}\left[\frac2n\sum_i(s_i^{4k-2}+t_i^{4k-2})\right]^{1/2}.$$ Indeed $|s^{2k}-t^{2k}|\le2k|s-t|(s^{2k-1}+t^{2k-1})$ for nonnegative $s,t$; squaring the last parenthesis is bounded by twice the sum of the squares. This inequality needs no operator-norm bound on $B$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 17.1]

19.1 For integer $K\ge1$, put $$m_K=E[\xi\mathbf1_{|\xi|\le K}],\qquad \eta^{(K)}=\xi\mathbf1_{|\xi|\le K}-m_K,\qquad v_K=E(\eta^{(K)})^2.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 18.1]

20.1 Then $0\le v_K\le1$ and $v_K\to1$. The residual $r_K=\xi-\eta^{(K)}$ has second moment $$\delta_K^2=Er_K^2=E[\xi^2\mathbf1_{|\xi|>K}]-m_K^2\longrightarrow0.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 19.1]

21.1 Let $B_n^{(K)}$ be the normalized matrix of these bounded centered entries, constructed from the same original array. On one probability-one event, phases 1–2 give for every integer $K$ and every integer $j\ge1$ $$\frac1n\operatorname{Tr}(B_n^{(K)}B_n^{(K)T})^j\longrightarrow v_K^j\mu_j(\gamma).$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 20.1]

22.1 The rectangular strong law, applied to $r_K^2$, also gives simultaneously in $K$ $$\frac1n\|A_n-B_n^{(K)}\|_F^2\longrightarrow\gamma\delta_K^2.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 21.1]

23.1 Intersect this event with the original coarse-norm event. For each outcome in the intersection there is a finite $C$ such that $\|A_n\|\le C$ eventually. Thus the $s_i^{4k-2}$ average in the comparison inequality is at most $C^{4k-2}$. The $t_i^{4k-2}$ average converges to $v_K^{2k-1}\mu_{2k-1}(\gamma)\le\mu_{2k-1}(\gamma)$. Consequently $$\limsup_n\left|\frac1n\operatorname{Tr}S_n^k-v_K^k\mu_k(\gamma)\right|\le2k\sqrt{\gamma}\,\delta_K\sqrt{2(C^{4k-2}+\mu_{2k-1}(\gamma))}.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 22.1]

24.1 Let $K\to\infty$. This proves, simultaneously for every fixed positive integer $k$, $$\frac1n\operatorname{Tr}S_n^k\longrightarrow\mu_k(\gamma)\quad\hbox{almost surely}.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 23.1]

25.1 In particular $n^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}S_n\to\gamma>0$, so eventually there is at least one positive eigenvalue. Every fixed polynomial with zero constant term has its normalized trace limit by linearity. There is no triangular truncation, hidden high-moment assumption, or appeal to an empirical-distribution limit. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 24.1]

26.1 Set $c=1+\gamma$, $d=2\sqrt\gamma$, so $a=c-d$, $b=c+d$, and define on $(a,b)$ $$w(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\sqrt{(b-x)(x-a)}.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 25.1]

27.1 We prove the exact positive-moment identity $$\mu_k(\gamma)=\int_a^b x^{k-1}w(x)\,dx\qquad(k\ge1).$$ This is only an identity for explicit numbers and integrals. No probability measure or spectral support theorem is asserted or used. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 26.1]

28.1 For real $z>0$ sufficiently small, substitute $x=c+d\cos\theta$. The generating function of the right-hand side is $$z\int_a^b\frac{w(x)}{1-zx}\,dx=\frac{zd^2}{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin^2\theta}{1-cz-dz\cos\theta}\,d\theta.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 27.1]

29.1 For $u>|v|$, substitution $t=\tan(\theta/2)$ directly gives $\int_0^\pi(u-v\cos\theta)^{-1}d\theta=\pi/\sqrt{u^2-v^2}$. Polynomial division in $\cos\theta$ then gives $$\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin^2\theta}{u-v\cos\theta}\,d\theta=\frac\pi{v^2}\left(u-\sqrt{u^2-v^2}\right),$$ with its continuous value when $v=0$. Hence the generating function above equals $$\frac{1-cz-\sqrt{(1-cz)^2-4\gamma z^2}}{2z}.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 28.1]

30.1 It is analytic near zero, vanishes there, and solves $H=z(1+H)(\gamma+H)$. The formal equation uniquely determines the coefficients recursively, so these coefficients equal the tree counts of phase 1. Expansion under the integral is justified by the uniformly convergent geometric series on $[a,b]$ for small $z$. This proves the identity, also when $a=0$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 29.1]

31.1 Consequently, for every polynomial $P$ with $P(0)=0$, $$\frac1n\operatorname{Tr}P(S_n)\longrightarrow\int_a^b\frac{P(x)}x w(x)\,dx.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 30.1]

32.1 At $a=0$, the quotient is the polynomial obtained by canceling the factor $x$, so there is no singularity to interpret. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 31.1]

33.1 Fix $L$ with $0<L<b$. For an integer $q\ge0$ use $P_q(x)=x^{q+1}(x-L)$. Its trace limit is $$I_q=\int_a^b x^q(x-L)w(x)\,dx.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 32.1]

34.1 Choose $\max(a,L)<t<u<b$. The positive contribution from $[t,u]$ is at least $t^q(t-L)\int_t^u w(x)dx$. The absolute negative contribution, supported in $[a,L]$ when that interval is nonempty, is at most $L^q L\int_a^b w(x)dx$. Since $t>L$ and $w>0$ on $(a,b)$, $I_q>0$ for some finite integer $q$ (and for all sufficiently large $q$). If $L\le a$, positivity follows directly. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 33.1]

35.1 If all eigenvalues of $S_n$ were at most $L$, every summand $P_q(\lambda)$ would be nonpositive, contradicting the eventually positive normalized trace. Thus $\lambda_{\max}(S_n)>L$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Intersecting over a countable sequence $L\uparrow b$ gives $\liminf\lambda_{\max}\ge b$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 34.1]

36.1 Fix $U>a$. If desired replace $U$ by a smaller number in $(a,b)$; proving the stronger bound for that smaller threshold proves the original bound. Thus assume $a<U<b$. Choose a fixed $B>b$ and use the polynomial $$Q_q(x)=x(U-x)(B-x)^{2q},\qquad q\ge0.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 35.1]

37.1 For every $x\ge0$, it vanishes at $0$, is nonpositive for $x\ge U$, and is positive for $0<x<U$ except at the irrelevant zero of the even factor. Its trace limit is $$J_q=\int_a^b(U-x)(B-x)^{2q}w(x)\,dx.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 36.1]

38.1 Choose $a<t<u<U$. The positive contribution on $[t,u]$ is at least $$(U-u)(B-u)^{2q}\int_t^u w(x)dx.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 37.1]

39.1 The absolute negative contribution on $[U,b]$ is at most $$(b-U)(B-U)^{2q}\int_a^b w(x)dx.$$ [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 38.1]

40.1 Because $B-u>B-U>0$ and the positive interval has positive integral, $J_q>0$ for some finite integer $q$. If $S_n$ had no positive eigenvalue below $U$, all its eigenvalues would be either $0$ or at least $U$, and therefore $\operatorname{Tr}Q_q(S_n)\le0$. The positive limiting trace excludes this for every sufficiently large $n$. Hence $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)<U$ eventually. Let $U\downarrow a$ through a countable sequence to obtain $\limsup\lambda_{\min}^{+}\le a$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 39.1]

41.1 For $\gamma=1$, $a=0$. The same argument chooses $0<t<u<U$ and proves an eventually positive eigenvalue below every prescribed $U>0$. The factor $x$ removes every exact zero eigenvalue, including arbitrary extra rank defects, so no rank theorem or lower-rank estimate is concealed in this case. Since eigenvalues are nonnegative, this also proves $\lambda_{\min}^{+}\to0$ in the square-aspect-ratio case. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 40.1] ∎

## Statement

For positive integers $n,p$ and a real matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$, set $S(X)=X^{\mathsf T}X/n$ and $\mu_{S(X)}=p^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^p\delta_{\lambda_j(S(X))}$, where the eigenvalues are counted with multiplicity. Then $\mu_{S(X)}$ is a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$, supported on $[0,\infty)$.

## Statement references

Bai and Silverstein, Chapter 3, §3.1, printed pp. 39–40 ([complete book PDF](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Positive integers $n,p$ and $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$.

[F1] [[def-sample-covariance-empirical-spectral-distribution]] defines $S(X)=X^{\mathsf T}X/n$ and $\mu_{S(X)}=p^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^p\delta_{\lambda_j(S(X))}$.

[F2] A real symmetric matrix has a real orthonormal eigenbasis ([[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]).

[F3] For every finite list of points of a measurable space, the equally weighted sum of their Dirac measures is a probability measure ([[lem-finite-empirical-measure-is-a-probability-law]]).

## Proof

1.1 The matrix $S(X)$ is symmetric because $(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{\mathsf T}=X^{\mathsf T}X$. For every $v\in\mathbb R^p$, $$v^{\mathsf T}S(X)v=\frac1n\|Xv\|_2^2\ge0.$$ By [F2], its eigenvalues are real; if $S(X)v=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$, the displayed quadratic-form identity gives $\lambda\|v\|_2^2\ge0$, hence $\lambda\ge0$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F3] to the finite list $\lambda_1(S(X)),\ldots,\lambda_p(S(X))$ in the Borel space $\mathbb R$. The resulting empirical measure is exactly [F1] and is a Borel probability measure. Step 1.1 shows it assigns no mass outside $[0,\infty)$. [F1, F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space, let $n\ge1$, and let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$. Define

$$P_n(A):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}(A),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$

Then $P_n$ is a probability measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$, an integer $n\ge1$, points $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$, and the displayed set function $P_n$.

[F1] [[def-dirac-measure]]: $\delta_x(A)=1$ when $x\in A$ and $0$ otherwise.

[F2] [[def-probability-measure]]: a probability measure is a countably additive measure of total mass one.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Each summand in $P_n(A)$ is nonnegative, $P_n(\varnothing)=0$, and $P_n(X)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n1=1$ by [F1]. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Let $(A_j)_{j\ge1}$ be pairwise disjoint. For each $j$, let $I_j:=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i\in A_j\}$. The sets $I_j$ are pairwise disjoint, and at most $n$ of them are nonempty, because each index $i$ belongs to at most one $I_j$. Their union is $\{i:x_i\in\bigcup_jA_j\}$. Hence the number of sample indices in $\bigcup_jA_j$ is $\sum_j\#I_j$, and dividing by $n$ gives $P_n(\bigcup_jA_j)=\sum_jP_n(A_j)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Steps 1.1–1.2 show that $P_n$ is a nonnegative countably additive set function with total mass one; by [F2] it is a probability measure. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For each positive integer $n$, let $Y_{n,1},\ldots,Y_{n,n}$ be independent random vectors in $\mathbb R^{d_n}$, let $B_n=\sum_{j=1}^{n}Y_{n,j}Y_{n,j}^{\mathsf T}$, and let $z=u+i\eta$ with fixed $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$. Define
$$M_n(z):=\frac1{d_n}\operatorname{tr}(B_n-zI)^{-1}.$$
If $d_n/n\to c$ for some $c\in(0,\infty)$, then $M_n(z)-\mathbb E[M_n(z)]\to0$ almost surely. More precisely, for every $t>0$,
$$\Pr\left\{|M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)|>t\right\} \le4\exp\left(-\frac{t^2d_n^2\eta^2}{4n}\right).$$

## Statement references

Bai and Silverstein, Chapter 3, §3.3, printed pp. 53–55 ([complete book PDF](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

Junyi Liao, Chapter 2, §2.1.3, printed pp. 35–38 ([complete lecture notes](https://jurrivhleon.github.io/notes/rmt.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the independent column vectors $Y_{n,j}$, and the fixed parameter $z$ with $\operatorname{Im}z=\eta>0$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice states every family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] For a real symmetric non-negative matrix, adding one rank-one matrix $yy^{\mathsf T}$ changes the unnormalized resolvent trace by at most $1/\eta$ ([[lem-rank-one-resolvent-update-and-trace-bound]]).

[F2] For independent random elements and a real measurable function whose change under replacement of coordinate $j$ is at most $c_j$, the two-sided McDiarmid bound is $2\exp(-2t^2/\sum_jc_j^2)$ ([[thm-mcdiarmid-bounded-differences]]).

[F3] If $\sum_n\Pr(E_n)<\infty$, then almost surely only finitely many $E_n$ occur ([[cor-first-borel-cantelli-lemma-for-events]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and notation of the Statement, including AC.

1.1 Fix all vectors except $Y_{n,j}$. Replacing that vector by another vector $Y'_{n,j}$ changes $B_n$ by removing $Y_{n,j}Y_{n,j}^{\mathsf T}$ and adding $Y'_{n,j}(Y'_{n,j})^{\mathsf T}$. Applying [F1] once to remove the first term and once to add the second shows that $\operatorname{tr}(B_n-zI)^{-1}$ changes by at most $2/\eta$. Hence each of the real and imaginary parts of $M_n(z)$ has coordinate oscillation at most $c_j=2/(d_n\eta)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F2] separately to $\operatorname{Re}M_n(z)$ and $\operatorname{Im}M_n(z)$. If a complex number has modulus greater than $t$, at least one of its real or imaginary parts has magnitude greater than $t/\sqrt2$. The union bound therefore gives $$\Pr\{|M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)|>t\} \le4\exp\left(-\frac{t^2d_n^2\eta^2}{4n}\right).$$ This is the stated estimate. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $d_n/n\to c>0$, for each fixed $t>0$ the exponent in step 2.1 is at most $-c_tn$ for all sufficiently large $n$, for some $c_t>0$. The probabilities are therefore summable. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Apply [F3] to the events in step 3.1 for each $t=1/k$, $k\ge1$, and intersect the resulting countable collection of probability-one events. On that event $M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)\to0$. [F3, step 3.1, choose] ∎

## Statement

For every $\gamma>0$, the set function $\mu_\gamma$ in the definition of the Marchenko–Pastur measure is a Borel probability measure supported on $[0,\infty)$. For every $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\eta:=\operatorname{Im}z>0$, its Stieltjes transform $m_\gamma(z)$ satisfies
$$1+z m_\gamma(z)=\frac{m_\gamma(z)}{1+\gamma m_\gamma(z)},\qquad \operatorname{Im}\bigl(1-\gamma-z-\gamma z m_\gamma(z)\bigr)\le-\eta.$$

## Statement references

Bai and Silverstein, Chapter 3, §3.3, printed pp. 52–58 ([complete book PDF](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

Junyi Liao, Theorem 2.1 and Lemmas 2.5–2.6, printed pp. 29–35 ([complete lecture notes](https://jurrivhleon.github.io/notes/rmt.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\gamma>0$, the endpoints $a=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2$, $b=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2$, and the formula defining $\mu_\gamma$.

[F1] The set function is the density $\sqrt{(b-x)(x-a)}/(2\pi\gamma x)$ on $(a,b)$ with an atom $(1-1/\gamma)_+$ at zero ([[def-marchenko-pastur-measure]]).

[F2] The identity theorem says holomorphic functions on a connected open set that agree on a set with an interior limit point agree throughout that set ([[thm-identity-theorem-holomorphic-functions]]).

[F3] Dominated convergence allows limits of integrands bounded by one integrable function to pass through the integral ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[F4] Integrating a nonnegative measurable function over measurable sets defines a measure ([[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The parameters and formula in the Statement.

1.1 Put $B=2\sqrt\gamma$, $A_0=1+\gamma$, and $x(\theta)=A_0+B\cos\theta$ for $0<\theta<\pi$. This substitution maps $(0,\pi)$ onto $(a,b)$ in reverse order, with $\sqrt{(b-x)(x-a)}=B\sin\theta$ and $|dx|=B\sin\theta\,d\theta$. Thus the continuous part of $\mu_\gamma$ becomes $(2/\pi)\sin^2\theta\,d\theta/x(\theta)$. For real $A>B$, the substitution $t=\tan(\theta/2)$ gives $$\int_0^\pi\frac{d\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}=2\int_0^\infty\frac{dt}{(A+B)+(A-B)t^2}=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{A^2-B^2}}.$$ Write $I_0(A)=\int_0^\pi(A+B\cos\theta)^{-1}d\theta=\pi/\sqrt{A^2-B^2}$. Since $\int_0^\pi\cos\theta\,d\theta=0$ and $\cos\theta/(A+B\cos\theta)=B^{-1}-A/[B(A+B\cos\theta)]$, $$I_1(A):=\int_0^\pi\frac{\cos\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}d\theta=\frac\pi B-\frac A B I_0(A),\quad I_2(A):=\int_0^\pi\frac{\cos^2\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}d\theta=-\frac A B I_1(A)=-\frac{A\pi}{B^2}+\frac{A^2}{B^2}I_0(A).$$ Therefore $$J(A):=\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin^2\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}\,d\theta=I_0(A)-I_2(A)=\frac{\pi(A-\sqrt{A^2-B^2})}{B^2}.$$ For $A=A_0>B$, the root is $|1-\gamma|$; if $\gamma=1$, direct cancellation $\sin^2\theta/(2+2\cos\theta)= (1-\cos\theta)/2$ gives the same value by continuity. Hence the continuous mass is $2J(A_0)/\pi=(A_0-|1-\gamma|)/(2\gamma)=\min(1,\gamma)/\gamma$. Adding $(1-1/\gamma)_+$ gives total mass one. Define $f_\gamma(x):=\sqrt{(b-x)(x-a)}/(2\pi\gamma x)$ for $a<x<b$ and $f_\gamma(x):=0$ otherwise. This is nonnegative and Borel measurable, and has finite integral by the calculation above. By [F4], $A\mapsto\int_A f_\gamma\,d\lambda$ is a finite Borel measure; the nonnegative multiple $(1-1/\gamma)_+\delta_0$ is a finite measure as well. Their sum is the displayed set function, so it is a Borel probability measure supported on $[0,\infty)$. [F1, F4, algebra, construct]

2.1 For $w=re^{i\theta}\in\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$, with $r>0$ and $-\pi<\theta<\pi$, define $q_0(w)=\sqrt r\,e^{i\theta/2}$. This is continuous, satisfies $q_0(w)^2=w$, and is holomorphic: for $h\to0$ with $w+h$ in the slit plane, $$\frac{q_0(w+h)-q_0(w)}h=\frac1{q_0(w+h)+q_0(w)}\longrightarrow\frac1{2q_0(w)}.$$ Set $\Omega=\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,B]$ and $q(A)=q_0(A-B)q_0(A+B)$ for $A\in\Omega$. Both factors are defined and holomorphic there, $q(A)^2=A^2-B^2$, and $q(A)>0$ for real $A>B$. The domain is connected: each $A-B=re^{i\theta}$ with $-\pi<\theta<\pi$ can be joined inside it to $B+1$ by continuously changing $r$ to $1$ and $\theta$ to $0$. The integral $J(A)$ is holomorphic on $\Omega$. Indeed, on any compact subset its denominator is bounded away from zero, and the difference quotient of its integrand tends pointwise to $-\sin^2\theta/(A+B\cos\theta)^2$ with a uniform integrable bound; [F3] justifies passing that limit through the integral. The identity theorem [F2] extends the formula from real $A>B$ (which has limit points inside $\Omega$) to all $A\in\Omega$. In particular it applies to $A_z=A_0-z$, whose imaginary part is negative. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $q=\sqrt{(1+\gamma-z)^2-4\gamma}$ on that branch. The substitution in step 1.1 and $1/[x(x-z)]=z^{-1}((x-z)^{-1}-x^{-1})$ give the transform of the continuous part as $[(A_z-q)-(A_0-|1-\gamma|)]/(2\gamma z)$. Adding the atom contributes $-(1-1/\gamma)_+/z$; simplifying in the cases $\gamma\le1$ and $\gamma>1$ gives $$m_\gamma(z)=\frac{1-\gamma-z-q}{2\gamma z}.$$ Since $q^2=(1-\gamma-z)^2-4\gamma z$, substitution verifies $\gamma z m_\gamma(z)^2+(z+\gamma-1)m_\gamma(z)+1=0$, which is the fixed-point equation in the Statement. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For $x\ge0$, $\operatorname{Im}(z/(x-z))=\eta x/|x-z|^2\ge0$. Integrating this identity against the probability measure from step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{Im}(z m_\gamma(z))\ge0$, so $\operatorname{Im}(1-\gamma-z-\gamma z m_\gamma(z))=-\eta-\gamma\operatorname{Im}(z m_\gamma(z))\le-\eta$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

If two holomorphic functions on a complex domain agree on a set with an accumulation point in the domain, then they agree everywhere on the domain.

Precisely, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a complex domain ([[def-complex-domain]]), let $f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose that some $a\in\Omega$ is an accumulation point of $\{z\in\Omega:f(z)=g(z)\}$. Then $f=g$ on $\Omega$. The requirement $a\in\Omega$ is essential.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A complex domain $\Omega$, holomorphic functions $f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb C$, an accumulation point $a\in\Omega$ of their agreement set, and the holomorphic difference $h:=f-g$ supplied by [[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]]. A nonempty subset of a connected space that is both open and closed is the whole space ([[def-connected-space]]).

[L1] For a holomorphic function $h$ on an open set $U$, the set of points having a neighbourhood on which $h$ vanishes is both open and closed in $U$ ([[lem-locally-zero-locus-clopen-holomorphic-function]]).

[L2] A holomorphic function has finite order $m$ at $a$ exactly when it factors near $a$ as $(z-a)^m q(z)$ with $q(a)\ne0$; its order is $+\infty$ exactly when it vanishes on a neighbourhood of $a$ ([[thm-zero-order-factorization-holomorphic-function]]).

[L3] If $f:U\to\mathbb C$ is complex differentiable at $a\in U$, then $f$ is continuous at $a$ ([[cor-complex-differentiability-implies-continuity]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The function $h$ vanishes at points arbitrarily close to $a$. If it had finite order there, [L2] would give $h(z)=(z-a)^m q(z)$ with $q(a)\ne0$, and [L3] would make $q$ nonzero on a smaller neighbourhood; then $h$ would have no zeros there other than possibly $a$, contrary to accumulation. Hence $h$ has infinite order at $a$, so [L2] makes it vanish on a neighbourhood of $a$. [given, L2, L3]

2.1 By [L1], the locally zero locus of $h$ is open and closed in $\Omega$; it is nonempty by step 1.1. Since $\Omega$ is connected, that locus is all of $\Omega$. [step 1.1, L1, given]

3.1 Therefore $h(z)=0$ for every $z\in\Omega$, which means $f(z)=g(z)$ throughout $\Omega$. [step 2.1] ∎

## Remarks

The accumulation point must belong to the domain. Accumulation only at a boundary point does not force identity, as the companion counterexample shows.

## Statement

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$, with Stieltjes transform $m_\mu(z)=\int (x-z)^{-1}\,d\mu(x)$ for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. For every $a<b$ and $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$\mu((a,b))+\tfrac12\mu(\{a\})+\tfrac12\mu(\{b\})=\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\frac1\pi\int_a^b\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(u+i\eta)\,du,\qquad \mu(\{x\})=\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\eta\,\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(x+i\eta).$$
If two Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R$ have the same Stieltjes transform on the upper half-plane, then they are equal.

## Statement references

Bai and Silverstein, Appendix B.2, printed pp. 514–523 ([complete book PDF](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

Junyi Liao, §1.3.1, printed pp. 17–18 ([complete lecture notes](https://jurrivhleon.github.io/notes/rmt.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A Borel probability measure $\mu$ and its Stieltjes transform under the $(x-z)^{-1}$ convention.

[F1] The transform is $m_\mu(z)=\int (x-z)^{-1}\,d\mu(x)$ for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$ ([[def-stieltjes-transform-of-a-real-probability-measure]]).

[F2] Fubini permits interchanging the integrals for an integrable function on the product measure space ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F3] Dominated convergence passes pointwise limits through an integral under an integrable bound ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[F4] A pi-system generating a sigma-algebra determines any containing lambda-system ([[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]).

[F5] Tonelli's theorem identifies the product integral of a nonnegative measurable function on a sigma-finite product with either iterated integral ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

## Proof

**Given:** $\mu$, and, for the uniqueness claim, two Borel probability measures $\mu,\nu$ with equal transforms.

1.1 For $\eta>0$, the imaginary part of the integrand in [F1] is $\eta/((x-u)^2+\eta^2)$. For each $x\in\mathbb R$, $$\int_a^b\frac{\eta}{(x-u)^2+\eta^2}\,du=\arctan\frac{b-x}{\eta}-\arctan\frac{a-x}{\eta}\le\pi.$$ Lebesgue measure restricted to $[a,b]$ and the probability measure $\mu$ are sigma-finite. Tonelli [F5] shows that the nonnegative product integrand has integral at most $\pi\mu(\mathbb R)=\pi$, so it belongs to $L^1$ on the product space. Fubini [F2] therefore gives $$\frac1\pi\int_a^b\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(u+i\eta)\,du=\int K_{\eta,a,b}(x)\,d\mu(x),\quad K_{\eta,a,b}(x)=\frac1\pi\left(\arctan\frac{b-x}{\eta}-\arctan\frac{a-x}{\eta}\right).$$ The kernel lies in $[0,1]$ and tends pointwise to $1$ on $(a,b)$, $1/2$ at either endpoint, and $0$ elsewhere. [F3] gives the interval formula in the Statement, including endpoint atoms. [F1, F2, F3, F5, given, algebra]

1.2 For any $x\in\mathbb R$, $$\eta\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(x+i\eta)=\int\frac{\eta^2}{(t-x)^2+\eta^2}\,d\mu(t).$$ The integrand is bounded by $1$ and tends to $\mathbf1_{\{x\}}(t)$ as $\eta\downarrow0$. Dominated convergence [F3] proves the atom formula. [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 If $m_\mu=m_\nu$, step 1.2 gives equality of their point masses at every $x$. Step 1.1 then gives $\mu((a,b))=\nu((a,b))$ for every $a<b$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The family $\mathcal P=\{\varnothing,\mathbb R\}\cup\{(a,b):a<b\}$ is a pi-system: the intersection of two open intervals is another open interval or empty. It generates the Borel sigma-algebra because open intervals form a basis. The class of Borel sets on which $\mu$ and $\nu$ agree is a lambda-system: it contains $\mathbb R$ because both measures are probabilities, is closed under complements by finite total mass, and is closed under disjoint countable unions by countable additivity. Step 2.1 and [F4] therefore give equality on every Borel set, so $\mu=\nu$. [F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A pi-system $\mathcal P$ on $X$, its generated lambda-system $\lambda_X(\mathcal P)$, and an arbitrary lambda-system $\mathcal D$ containing $\mathcal P$.

[L1] If $\mathcal P$ is a pi-system on $X$, then $\lambda_X(\mathcal P)$ is closed under binary intersections ([[lem-generated-lambda-system-closed-under-intersections]]).

[L2] A lambda-system on $X$ closed under binary intersections is a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[lem-lambda-system-with-finite-intersections-is-sigma]]).

[L3] The family $\lambda_X(\mathcal P)$ is the smallest lambda-system containing $\mathcal P$ ([[lem-generated-lambda-system-exists-and-is-minimal]]).

[L4] The family $\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$ is the smallest sigma-algebra containing $\mathcal P$ ([[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], [L2], and [L3], $\lambda_X(\mathcal P)$ is a sigma-algebra containing $\mathcal P$. Hence [L4] gives $\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\lambda_X(\mathcal P)$. [L1, L2, L3, L4]

1.2 The sigma-algebra $\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$ is a lambda-system: it contains $X$, is closed under relative differences because it is closed under complements and intersections, and is closed under increasing countable unions. Since it contains $\mathcal P$, [L3] gives $\lambda_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. [L3, L4, algebra]

2.1 Steps 1.1 and 1.2 prove equality. Minimality in [L3] also gives $\lambda_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$, so $\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L3] ∎

## Statement

Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite iid real array with $E\xi_{11}=0$, $E\xi_{11}^2=1$ and $E|\xi_{11}|^4<\infty$. Consider any deterministic rectangular sequence $R_n\times C_n$ with both $R_n/n$ and $C_n/n$ bounded above and bounded away from zero. Write $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{i\le R_n,j\le C_n}$ and $N_n=\max(R_n,C_n)$. There is a deterministic sequence $\delta_n\to0$, which may be chosen to decrease more slowly than any specified finite list of rates tending to zero and to satisfy $\delta_n\ge1/\log(n+2)$, such that, almost surely, $X_n$ equals its entrywise truncation at $\delta_n\sqrt{N_n}$ eventually. Set
$$\widehat\xi_{ij}^{(n)}=\xi_{ij}\mathbf1_{\{|\xi_{ij}|\le\delta_n\sqrt{N_n}\}},\quad\mu_n=E\widehat\xi_{11}^{(n)},\quad x_{ij}^{(n)}=\widehat\xi_{ij}^{(n)}-\mu_n.$$
Then $\sqrt{R_nC_n/N_n}|\mu_n|\to0$, $E|x_{11}^{(n)}|^2\le1$ tends to $1$, $|x_{ij}^{(n)}|\le2\delta_n\sqrt{N_n}$ eventually, and $E|x_{11}^{(n)}|^q\le K(2\delta_n\sqrt{N_n})^{q-3}$ for every integer $q\ge3$, with $K$ independent of $n,q$. Almost surely the following controls hold for the original entries and for the centered truncated entries:
$$\max_{i\le R_n}\left|N_n^{-1}\sum_{j\le C_n}|x_{ij}^{(n)}|^2-C_n/N_n\right|\to0,\qquad\max_{j\le C_n}\left|N_n^{-1}\sum_{i\le R_n}|x_{ij}^{(n)}|^2-R_n/N_n\right|\to0,$$
$$\max_{i\le R_n,j\le C_n}|x_{ij}^{(n)}|/\sqrt{N_n}\to0,\qquad N_n^{-2}\sum_{i\le R_n,j\le C_n}|x_{ij}^{(n)}|^4=O(1).$$
For every fixed $q>2$, the rectangular matrix with entry $N_n^{-q/2}|x_{ij}^{(n)}|^q$ has Frobenius norm tending to zero; the assertion also holds with a sign attached to each entry.

## Statement references

Bai and Silverstein, Chapters 3 and 5 ([complete book](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)); the argument below supplies its own counting and probability estimates.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] First Borel–Cantelli is [[cor-first-borel-cantelli-lemma-for-events]].

[F2] [[lem-uniform-row-partial-sums-of-nested-finite-variance-array]] applies because $E(\xi_{11}^2-1)^2<\infty$.

[F3] The integrable iid strong law is [[thm-kolmogorov-iid-l1-strong-law]], and dominated convergence is [[thm-dominated-convergence]].

## Proof

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the statement.

1.1 Fix a finite $D$ with $R_n,C_n\le Dn$ and $N_n\ge n/D$ eventually. For every $\varepsilon>0$, the union bound on a square of side $D2^{\ell+1}$ gives a constant times $2^{2\ell}P(|\xi_{11}|>\varepsilon2^{\ell/2})$ as a bound for the probability of any such large entry in that square. Its series over $\ell$ is finite: for every $t\ge0$ the geometric sum $\sum_{\ell:\,\varepsilon2^{\ell/2}<t}2^{2\ell}$ is at most a constant times $\varepsilon^{-4}t^4$, so expectation proves the assertion. F1 on dyadic blocks, followed by intersection over rational $\varepsilon>0$, proves $\max_{i\le R_n,j\le C_n}|\xi_{ij}|/\sqrt{N_n}\to0$ almost surely. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The dyadic probability series in step 1.1 converges separately for every threshold $\varepsilon=1/a$. Choose deterministic integers $L_a$ increasing so that its tail from $L_a$ onward is at most $2^{-a}$; impose also $L_a\ge a$, and every prescribed slow-rate constraint by increasing $L_a$ further. On the blocks $L_a\le\ell<L_{a+1}$ choose the truncation threshold as a suitable fixed multiple of $2^{\ell/2}/a$, large enough to cover the comparable dimensions and the adjacent dyadic interval. The sum of the resulting block probabilities is at most $\sum_a2^{-a}$. First Borel–Cantelli proves eventual equality to these truncations. A stepwise deterministic enlargement gives $\delta_n\to0$ as slowly as required, with $\delta_n\ge1/\log(n+2)$; enlarging a threshold preserves eventual equality. One may absorb every fixed dimensional comparison constant into $\delta_n$. Since $\delta_n\sqrt{N_n}\to\infty$, enlarge finitely many initial values further so that $\delta_n\sqrt{N_n}\ge\max(1,E|\xi_{11}|)$ for every $n$; this preserves all asymptotic and eventual-equality conclusions. [F1, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 Since $E\xi=0$, $|\mu_n|\le E[|\xi|\mathbf1_{|\xi|>\delta_n\sqrt{N_n}}]\le E|\xi|^4/(\delta_n^3N_n^{3/2})$. Therefore $\sqrt{R_nC_n/N_n}|\mu_n|\le K\delta_n^{-3}/N_n\to0$, by the selected slow rate. Dominated convergence gives $E|x_{11}^{(n)}|^2=E[\xi^2\mathbf1_{|\xi|\le\delta_n\sqrt{N_n}}]-\mu_n^2\to1$, and this variance is at most $1$. Moreover $|\mu_n|\le E|\xi|\le\delta_n\sqrt{N_n}$ for every $n$, so $|x_{ij}^{(n)}|\le L_n:=2\delta_n\sqrt{N_n}$ for every $n$. The third absolute moments are bounded by $4(E|\xi|^3+|\mu_n|^3)\le4(E|\xi|^3+(E|\xi|)^3)$, uniformly in $n$. Thus for $q\ge3$, $E|x|^q\le L_n^{q-3}E|x|^3\le KL_n^{q-3}$. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Apply F2 to the infinite centered finite-variance array $Z_{ij}=\xi_{ij}^2-1$. Using a fixed enlargement of the row bound and of the maximal partial-sum index covers every $R_n,C_n\le Dn$; division by $N_n\ge n/D$ proves the stated uniform row and column second-moment laws for the original entries. On the probability-one event of eventual truncation equality, $x_{ij}^{(n)}=\xi_{ij}-\mu_n$ throughout the rectangle. The difference of a normalized row squared sum from the original one is bounded by $2|\mu_n|\sqrt{(C_n/N_n)(N_n^{-1}\sum_j\xi_{ij}^2)}+(C_n/N_n)\mu_n^2$, by Cauchy–Schwarz; its maximum tends to zero because the original row laws bound these sums and $\mu_n\to0$. The column calculation is identical. This proves both centered-truncation diagonal laws explicitly. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Enumerate the cells of the infinite quadrant by successive square shells $\max(i,j)=k$, in fixed lexicographic order on each finite shell. The resulting sequence of $|\xi_{ij}|^4$ is iid and integrable; F3 at the square cardinalities $k^2$ gives $k^{-2}\sum_{i,j\le k}|\xi_{ij}|^4\to E|\xi|^4$. Enclosing each rectangle in a square of side $\lceil Dn\rceil$ gives $N_n^{-2}\sum_{i\le R_n,j\le C_n}|\xi_{ij}|^4=O(1)$. The maximum-entry conclusion for the centered entries follows from step 1.1 and $|\mu_n|/\sqrt{N_n}\to0$. Also $|\xi-\mu_n|^4\le8(|\xi|^4+|\mu_n|^4)$, so eventual equality to the truncations and $R_nC_n/N_n^2=O(1)$ give the fourth-power bound for the centered entries. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra, step 4.1]

6.1 For every fixed $q>2$, the square of the Frobenius norm of the indicated power matrix is bounded by $(\max|x_{ij}^{(n)}|/\sqrt{N_n})^{2q-4}N_n^{-2}\sum|x_{ij}^{(n)}|^4$, which tends to zero by step 5.1. Multiplying its entries by signs does not change the Frobenius norm. The original-entry assertion follows from the same calculation. All conclusions hold on the intersection of the countably many probability-one events already specified. [step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For each positive integer $n$, let $p_n$ be a positive integer with $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$, and let $X_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_n}$ have mutually independent entries with one common law, mean zero, variance one, and finite fourth moment. Set $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$ and let $\mu_n$ be its empirical spectral distribution normalized by $p_n$. Then $\mu_n$ converges weakly almost surely to the probability measure with density
$$\rho_\gamma(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\sqrt{(b_\gamma-x)(x-a_\gamma)}}{2\pi\gamma x},&a_\gamma<x<b_\gamma,\\0,&x\notin(a_\gamma,b_\gamma),\end{cases}\qquad a_\gamma=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2,\quad b_\gamma=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2,$$
and an atom of mass $(1-1/\gamma)_+$ at zero.

## Statement references

Bai and Silverstein, Chapter 3, §3.3, printed pp. 52–58 ([complete book PDF](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

Junyi Liao, Theorem 2.1 and §2.1.3, printed pp. 29–38 ([complete lecture notes](https://jurrivhleon.github.io/notes/rmt.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses and notation of the Statement, including the Axiom of Choice.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice states that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$ and $\mu_n=p_n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{p_n}\delta_{\lambda_j(S_n)}$; its eigenvalues are real and nonnegative ([[def-sample-covariance-empirical-spectral-distribution]], [[lem-sample-covariance-empirical-law-is-a-probability-measure]]).

[F2] For a probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$, $m_\mu(z)=\int(x-z)^{-1}\,d\mu(x)$ for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$ ([[def-stieltjes-transform-of-a-real-probability-measure]]).

[F3] For iid real coordinates of mean zero, variance one and fourth moment $\mu_4$, an independent complex symmetric matrix $A$ satisfies $\mathbb E|\xi^{\mathsf T}A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A|^2\le\max\{\mu_4-1,2\}\mathbb E\|A\|_F^2$ ([[lem-fourth-moment-quadratic-form-resolvent-bound]]).

[F4] If $B$ is real symmetric nonnegative, then $R=(B-zI)^{-1}$ and $R_x=(B+xx^{\mathsf T}-zI)^{-1}$ satisfy $R_x=R-Rxx^{\mathsf T}R/(1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx)$, and $|\operatorname{tr}R_x-\operatorname{tr}R|\le1/\eta$ for $z=u+i\eta$, $\eta>0$ ([[lem-rank-one-resolvent-update-and-trace-bound]]).

[F5] For $n$ independent rank-one summands in dimension $d_n$ with $d_n/n\to c>0$, the normalized resolvent trace concentrates almost surely about its expectation, with the stated exponential tail ([[lem-adapted-resolvent-trace-concentration]]).

[F6] The transform $m_\gamma$ of the Marchenko–Pastur probability law satisfies $1+zm=m/(1+\gamma m)$ and $\operatorname{Im}(1-\gamma-z-\gamma zm)\le-\operatorname{Im}z$ ([[lem-marchenko-pastur-formula-defines-a-finite-measure]]).

[F7] Stieltjes transforms determine Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R$ ([[lem-stieltjes-transform-inversion-and-uniqueness-on-the-real-line]]).

[F8] A tight sequence of Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R$ has a weakly convergent subsequence; the used extraction theorem assumes AC ([[cor-tightness-extracts-a-weakly-convergent-subsequence]]).

[F9] Chebyshev's inequality bounds a deviation probability by variance divided by squared deviation ([[thm-chebyshev-inequality]]).

[F10] If event probabilities have finite sum, almost surely only finitely many of those events occur ([[cor-first-borel-cantelli-lemma-for-events]]).

[F11] Weak convergence of probability measures is convergence of integrals against every bounded continuous function ([[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]).

[F12] The entries in each $X_n$ are mutually independent and identically distributed, so the rows are independent and each row has iid coordinates ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]).

[F13] Almost-sure convergence means convergence on an event of probability one ([[def-almost-sure-convergence-of-random-variables]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The independent-entry matrices, their common moment assumptions, $p_n/n\to\gamma$, and AC.

1.1 Fix $z=u+i\eta$ with $\eta>0$. Write the transpose of row $i$ of $X_n$ as $y_i\in\mathbb R^{p_n}$ and set $Q=(S_n-zI)^{-1}$, $m_n=p_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}Q=m_{\mu_n}(z)$ by [F1] and [F2]. For each $i$, let $S_i=S_n-y_iy_i^{\mathsf T}/n$, $Q_i=(S_i-zI)^{-1}$ and $\beta_i=n^{-1}y_i^{\mathsf T}Q_i y_i$. The matrices $S_n,S_i$ are nonnegative symmetric, so their resolvents exist; diagonalizing $S_i$ expresses $\beta_i$ as a sum of nonnegative weights times $(\lambda-z)^{-1}$ with $\lambda\ge0$. Thus $\operatorname{Im}\beta_i\ge0$ and $\operatorname{Im}(z\beta_i)\ge0$, since $\operatorname{Im}[z/(\lambda-z)]=\eta\lambda/|\lambda-z|^2\ge0$. Consequently $\operatorname{Im}[z(1+\beta_i)]\ge\eta$, so $|1+\beta_i|\ge\eta/|z|>0$. Applying [F4] with $x=y_i/\sqrt n$ gives $Q=Q_i-Q_i y_i y_i^{\mathsf T}Q_i/[n(1+\beta_i)]$, so $n^{-1}y_i^{\mathsf T}Qy_i=\beta_i/(1+\beta_i)$. Since $S_nQ=I+zQ$, taking normalized traces yields $$1+z m_n=\frac1{p_n}\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\beta_i}{1+\beta_i}.$$ [given, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 Put $\gamma_n=p_n/n$, $v_n=\gamma_n m_n=n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}Q$, and $\mu_4=\mathbb E\xi^4$ for the common entry law. Both $\beta_i$ and $v_n$ belong to the cone $\mathcal C_z=\{w:\operatorname{Im}w\ge0,\ \operatorname{Im}(zw)\ge0\}$: for $v_n$ use the same eigenvalue calculation on $Q$. For every $w\in\mathcal C_z$, $\operatorname{Im}[z(1+w)]\ge\eta$, so $|1+w|^{-1}\le|z|/\eta$. Conditional on $Q_i$, row $y_i$ is independent of it by [F12]. Applying [F3] conditionally and using $\|Q_i\|_F^2\le p_n/\eta^2$ gives $$\mathbb E\left|\beta_i-\frac1n\operatorname{tr}Q_i\right|\le\frac{\sqrt{C p_n}}{n\eta},\qquad C=\max\{\mu_4-1,2\}.$$ By [F4], $|\operatorname{tr}Q_i-\operatorname{tr}Q|\le1/\eta$, hence $\mathbb E|\beta_i-v_n|\le(\sqrt{Cp_n}+1)/(n\eta)$. For $f(w)=w/(1+w)$ and $w,v\in\mathcal C_z$, $|f(w)-f(v)|=|w-v|/(|1+w||1+v|)\le K_z|w-v|$, where $K_z=(|z|/\eta)^2$. Therefore [step 1.1] implies $$\mathbb E\left|1+zm_n-\frac{m_n}{1+\gamma_n m_n}\right|\le K_z\frac{\sqrt{Cp_n}+1}{p_n\eta}\longrightarrow0.$$ [F3, F4, F12, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F5] to the independent vectors $y_i/\sqrt n$, whose rank-one sum is $S_n$. For the fixed $z$, $m_n-a_n\to0$ almost surely, where $a_n=\mathbb E m_n$. Also $\mathbb E|m_n-a_n|\to0$: for every $\varepsilon>0$, $\mathbb E|m_n-a_n|\le\varepsilon+(2/\eta)\Pr(|m_n-a_n|>\varepsilon)$, and the tail bound in [F5] makes the second term tend to zero. Define $g_n(w)=1+zw-w/(1+\gamma_nw)$. The cone $\mathcal C_z$ is closed under nonnegative scaling and expectations, so it contains $m_n,a_n,\gamma_nm_n$ and $\gamma_na_n$. For $w,v\in\mathcal C_z$, the denominator estimate of step 2.1 applied to $\gamma_nw,\gamma_nv$ gives $|g_n(w)-g_n(v)|\le(|z|+K_z)|w-v|$. Taking expectations in the estimate of step 2.1 gives $g_n(a_n)\to0$. [F5, F13, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The sequence $(a_n)$ is bounded by $1/\eta$. Moreover $\operatorname{Im}(z m_n)=p_n^{-1}\sum_j\eta\lambda_j(S_n)/|\lambda_j(S_n)-z|^2\ge0$, so $\operatorname{Im}(1-\gamma_n-z-\gamma_n z a_n)\le-\eta$. The same closed-cone bound gives $|1+\gamma_na_n|\ge\eta/|z|$. Every convergent subsequence of $a_n$ therefore has a limit $a$, with $|1+\gamma a|\ge\eta/|z|$, satisfying $1+za=a/(1+\gamma a)$ and $\operatorname{Im}(1-\gamma-z-\gamma za)\le-\eta$. The two roots of the associated quadratic have corresponding values $D_j=1-\gamma-z-\gamma z a_j$ whose sum is $1-\gamma-z$, with imaginary part $-\eta$. Thus at most one root can have $\operatorname{Im}D_j\le-\eta$. By [F6], that root is $m_\gamma(z)$. All subsequential limits are consequently $m_\gamma(z)$, so $a_n\to m_\gamma(z)$ and step 3.1 gives $m_n(z)\to m_\gamma(z)$ almost surely. [F1, F6, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Perform steps 1.1–4.1 for each $z$ in the countable dense set $\{u+i\eta:u,\eta\in\mathbb Q,\eta>0\}$ and intersect their probability-one events. Also let $T_n=(np_n)^{-1}\sum_{i,j}X_{n,ij}^2$. Its mean is one and its variance is $(\mu_4-1)/(np_n)$. Since $p_n/n\to\gamma>0$, [F9] gives a summable bound $\Pr(|T_n-1|>\varepsilon)\le(\mu_4-1)/(\varepsilon^2np_n)$ for every $\varepsilon>0$; [F10] over positive rational $\varepsilon$ yields $T_n\to1$ almost surely. [F9, F10, F12, F13, step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 On this probability-one event, $\int x\,d\mu_n(x)=T_n$ and $\mu_n$ is supported on $[0,\infty)$ by [F1]. For every $R>0$, $\mu_n((R,\infty))\le T_n/R$, so the sequence is tight. By [A1] and [F8], every subsequence has a further weakly convergent subsequence with limit $\nu$. Along it, [F11] applied to $x\mapsto(x-z)^{-1}$ shows $m_\nu(z)=m_\gamma(z)$ on the dense set from step 5.1. The transforms are continuous because $|m_\nu(z)-m_\nu(w)|\le|z-w|/(\operatorname{Im}z\operatorname{Im}w)$ for $z,w\in\mathbb C^+$; equality therefore extends to all $z\in\mathbb C^+$. [F1, F8, F11, step 5.1, A1, algebra]

7.1 By [F7], every weak subsequential limit $\nu$ in step 6.1 equals $\mu_\gamma$. If $\mu_n$ did not converge weakly to $\mu_\gamma$, some bounded continuous test function and a subsequence would have integrals separated from its $\mu_\gamma$ integral by a fixed positive amount; tightness would give a further weakly convergent subsequence, contradicting its limit $\mu_\gamma$. Therefore $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu_\gamma$ almost surely. [F7, F8, F11, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every finite real random variable $X$ and every $t>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge t)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{t^2}.$$
Equivalently, if $\sigma_X>0$ and $c>0$, then $\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge c\sigma_X)\le1/c^2$. If $\sigma_X=0$, the first form remains valid for every $t>0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite real random variable $X$ and a real threshold $t>0$.

[L1] Variance is $\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2]$ and $\sigma_X^2=\operatorname{Var}(X)$ ([[def-variance-and-covariance]]).

[L2] Markov's inequality states $\mathbb P(Y\ge a)\le\mathbb E[Y]/a$ for nonnegative $Y$ and $a>0$ ([[thm-markov-inequality]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The variable $Y=(X-\mathbb E[X])^2$ is nonnegative, and for $t>0$ the events $\{Y\ge t^2\}$ and $\{|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge t\}$ are equal. [given, algebra]

2.1 Apply [L2] to $Y$ at the positive threshold $t^2$ and use [L1] to obtain the first inequality. [step 1.1, L1, L2]

3.1 If $\sigma_X>0$, substitute $t=c\sigma_X$ in step 2.1 and cancel $\sigma_X^2$ to obtain $1/c^2$. Conversely, given $t>0$, choose $c=t/\sigma_X>0$ in the standard-deviation form to recover step 2.1. If $\sigma_X=0$, step 2.1 gives probability at most zero for every $t>0$. [step 2.1, L1, choose, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $(X_n)$ and $X$ be real random variables on one probability space.  Write
$X_n\to X$ **almost surely** when
$$\mathbb P\bigl(\{\omega:X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)\text{ in }\mathbb R\}\bigr)=1.$$

## Statement

Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite real iid array with $E\xi_{11}=0$, $E\xi_{11}^2=1$ and $E|\xi_{11}|^4<\infty$, and let $p_h/h\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. Put $N_h=\max(h,p_h)$, $m_h=\min(h,p_h)$ and $y_h=m_h/N_h\to y:=\min(\gamma,\gamma^{-1})$. Take the centered slow truncations of the upper-left $h\times p_h$ blocks, orient each with $m_h$ rows and $N_h$ columns, and divide by $\sqrt{N_h}$, obtaining $Y_h$. For each fixed integer $\ell\ge1$, define $T_{h,\ell}$ by summing the products of the entries of $Y_h,Y_h^{\mathsf T},\ldots,Y_h,Y_h^{\mathsf T}$ along all paths of length $2\ell$, subject to every pair of vertices two positions apart being unequal. Its row and column endpoints are included in these exclusions. Then almost surely
$$\limsup_h\|T_{h,\ell}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le(2\ell+1)(\ell+1)y^{(\ell-1)/2}.$$
In particular, for the original untruncated $X_h=(\xi_{ij})_{i\le h,j\le p_h}$, almost surely $\limsup_h\|X_h/\sqrt h\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$.

## Statement references

Bai and Silverstein, Chapters 3 and 5 ([complete book](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)); the argument below supplies its own counting and probability estimates.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[lem-nested-iid-fourth-moment-truncation-and-diagonal-control]] supplies eventual truncation equality, the uniform third-moment bound, slow threshold, negligible mean matrix and diagonal laws.

[F2] Markov's inequality and first Borel–Cantelli are [[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]] and [[cor-first-borel-cantelli-lemma-for-events]].

[F3] [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] and [[thm-operator-norm-is-the-largest-singular-value]] identify the Hermitian norm and bound its even powers by their trace.

## Proof

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the statement.

1.1 Apply F1 to the original nested rectangular array and, as necessary, its transpose. Orient the centered truncated matrix with $p$ rows and $n$ columns, $p\le n$, and divide by $\sqrt n$. In this proof the original sequence index is $h$, $n=N_h=\max(h,p_h)$, $p=\min(h,p_h)$, and $y_n=p/n\to y\in(0,1]$. These dimensions are comparable to $h$; all probability series below are summed over $h$. Enlarge the slow truncation threshold by a fixed factor to bound the centered entries by $L_n=\delta_n\sqrt n$ with $\delta_n\ge1/\log(n+2)$, $\delta_n\to0$. F1 gives independent centered entries, variance at most one, and $E|x|^q\le CL_n^{q-3}$ for $q\ge3$. Define $Y=(x_{ij}/\sqrt n)$ and the restricted matrices $T_\ell$ as in the statement. The same arguments hold if the orientation changes infinitely often. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 Fix $\ell\ge1$. Set $N=4m\ell$, with integer $m$ chosen so that $m/\log n\to\infty$ and $\delta_n(m/\log n)^2\to0$; for example $m=\lceil\log n\,\delta_n^{-1/8}\rceil$. Since $\delta_n\ge1/\log n$, $N$ is polylogarithmic. Reversing each admissible path exchanges its endpoints and preserves its real weight, so $T_\ell$ is real symmetric. Thus its even-power trace bounds $\|T_\ell\|^{2m}$. Expand $E\operatorname{tr}T_\ell^{2m}$ into closed alternating walks of length $N$, split into $2m$ consecutive nonbacktracking blocks of length $2\ell$. Bound absolute expectations termwise. Any edge appearing exactly once vanishes by centering and independence. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Canonicalize row and column labels separately by order of first appearance. Innovations lead to a previously unvisited vertex and form a spanning tree of the visited vertices. Let $k$ be their number, so $k+1$ vertices are visited. Classify the second occurrence of each innovation edge as T3; all other noninnovation occurrences are T4. There are exactly $k$ T3 occurrences and $d=N-2k$ T4 occurrences. A T4 class is a distinct unoriented edge supporting at least one T4 occurrence; let $t$ be their number. Then $0\le t\le d$, and $t=0$ implies $d=0$. Every innovation edge appears at least twice. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, step 2.1]

4.1 **Moment bound.** An innovation edge of multiplicity two contributes at most one. An innovation edge of multiplicity $q\ge3$ contributes at most $CL_n^{q-3}$. A noninnovation edge of multiplicity $q\ge2$ contributes at most $CL_n^{q-1}$, a deliberately weaker bound valid for $L_n\ge1$. Consequently the product is bounded by $C^tL_n^{d-t}$. This follows by summing exponents: an innovation edge contributes $q-2-1_{q\ge3}$, while a noninnovation edge contributes $q-1$; the resulting total is $N-2k-t$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, step 3.1]

5.1 **Coding bound, including a replacement for Lemmas 5.5–5.6.** At each time keep the forest $F$ of innovation edges seen exactly once. At a T3 step the endpoint is selected among the neighbors of the current vertex in $F$. Call the step regular if there are at least two such neighbors; otherwise its endpoint is forced. Let $Q$ be the number of nonempty edge components of $F$ not containing the current vertex. An innovation leaves $Q$ unchanged. A regular T3 step increases $Q$ by one (deleting its edge leaves a nonempty component on the departure side); an irregular T3 leaves $Q$ unchanged. A T4 step leaves $F$ unchanged and changes $Q$ by at most one. Since $F$ starts and ends empty, there are at most $d$ regular T3 steps. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, step 4.1]

6.1 At any time the degree of the current vertex in $F$ is at most $2t+1$. To prove this, delete that vertex from the full innovation tree. Each incident open edge determines one branch. Except for the possible branch containing the initial vertex, the prefix walk crosses the cut of such a branch an even number of times. Its innovation-tree edge has been crossed exactly once, so some T4 class must cross this cut with odd multiplicity. A fixed T4 edge can join at most two branches at the deleted vertex. There are $t$ classes, proving the bound. This parity argument allows classes whose first T4 occurrence is in the future by harmless overcounting. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, step 5.1]

7.1 Given innovation and T3 positions, choose the $t$ T4 edge classes in at most $(k+1)^{2t}$ ways and assign all T4 positions to classes in at most $t^d$ ways. Innovation endpoints are forced by canonical order. At any T3 position there are at most $2t+1$ choices, and at most $d$ positions can be regular. A decision tree of depth at most $d$ with branching at most $2t+1$ has at most $(2t+1)^d$ leaves (pad shorter branches with forced dummy choices); no separate selection of regular positions is required. T4 endpoints are forced by current vertex and chosen class, or the code is invalid. Thus the remaining coding factor is at most $(k+1)^{2t}t^d(2t+1)^d\le(k+1)^{2t}3^d(t+1)^{2d}$. Interpret $0^0=1$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, step 6.1]

8.1 In block $b$, let $a_b$ count adjacent innovation/noninnovation pairs. Such a pair must have a NEW noninnovation edge: its departure vertex was just introduced, and immediate reversal is prohibited inside a block. It is therefore the first T4 occurrence of its class. Consequently $\sum a_b\le t$. Innovation runs have at most $a_b+1$ components; their alternating row/column innovations differ in number by at most one each. If $r,s$ count row and column innovations, then $k=r+s$ and $|r-s|\le t+2m$. Hence $r\ge(k-t-2m)/2$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, step 7.1]

9.1 For given $a_b$, innovation positions in block $b$ have at most $\binom{2\ell+1}{2a_b+1}$ patterns: a binary string with $a_b$ transitions $1\to0$ has this count, by specifying its alternating run endpoints, including a possible terminal run. Their product is at most $(2\ell+1)^{2t+2m}$. There are at most $(\ell+1)^{2m}$ choices of the $a_b$. Once innovation positions are fixed, T3 positions have at most $\binom{N-k}{k}$ choices. Labelings contribute at most $p^{r+1}n^s=n^{k+1}y_n^{r+1}\le n^{k+1}y_n^{(k-t-2m)/2}$, for $0<y_n\le1$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, step 8.1]

10.1 Combining all factors, with $A=(2\ell+1)(\ell+1)$, gives $$E\operatorname{tr}T_\ell^{2m}\le nA^{2m}y_n^{-m}\sum_{1\le k\le N/2}\binom{N-k}{k}y_n^{k/2}\delta_n^{N-2k}3^{N-2k}\sum_{t=0}^{N-2k}q_{n,k}^{t}(t+1)^{2(N-2k)},$$ where $q_{n,k}=C(2\ell+1)^2(k+1)^2/(\sqrt{ny_n}\delta_n)$. This derivation uses absolute values and requires no symmetry of the real entry law. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, step 9.1]

11.1 Uniformly in $k$, $q_{n,k}=n^{-1/2+o(1)}$. Set $a=-\log q_{n,k}$, so eventually $(\log n)/3\le a\le\log n$. For $d\ge1$, $$\sum_{t\ge0}e^{-at}(t+1)^{2d}\le2e^{a/2}\max\{1,(4d/(ae))^{2d}\}\le2n\,[C_1\max\{1,N/\log n\}^2]^d.$$ Indeed split the exponential into two halves, sum one geometric factor, and maximize $u^{2d}e^{-au/2}$ for $u=t+1\ge1$. For $d=0$ the finite inner sum is exactly one. Thus, after enlarging a fixed constant, let $\varepsilon_n=C_2\delta_n\max\{1,N/\log n\}^2\to0$; the trace is at most $$2n^2A^{2m}y_n^{-m}\sum_k\binom{N-k}{k}y_n^{k/2}\varepsilon_n^{N-2k}\le2n^2A^{2m}y_n^{-m}(y_n^{1/4}+\varepsilon_n)^N.$$ [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, step 10.1]

12.1 For the final inequality, $\binom{N-k}{k}\le\binom N{2k}$: map a $k$-subset of $\{1,\ldots,N-k\}$ to the $2k$-subset formed by the adjacent pairs $(b_i+i-1,b_i+i)$; these are disjoint and recover the original subset. The sum is consequently bounded by the binomial expansion with nonnegative coefficients. Since $N=4m\ell$, the last display equals $2n^2[A y_n^{(\ell-1)/2}]^{2m}(1+o(1))^N$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, step 11.1]

13.1 For $\eta>Ay^{(\ell-1)/2}$, Markov's inequality gives $P(\|T_\ell\|\ge\eta)\le2n^2e^{-cm}$ eventually, which is summable since $m/\log n\to\infty$. Borel–Cantelli and a countable sequence of $\eta$ prove the stated fixed-length norm bound. This completes all graph estimates locally. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, step 12.1]

14.1 In particular, $\limsup\|T_1\|\le6$. Since $YY^{\mathsf T}=T_1+D$ with $D=\operatorname{diag}(YY^{\mathsf T})$ and $\|D-I\|\to0$ by F1, $\limsup\|Y\|^2\le7$. Its norm is $\sqrt{p}\,|\mu_h|\to0$ by F1, since a constant $p\times n$ matrix of entry $a$ maps a vector to $a$ times its coordinate sum in every row and has norm $|a|\sqrt{pn}$. Thus the original normalized matrices have an eventual finite norm bound. Changing the normalization from $\sqrt{N_h}$ to $\sqrt h$ multiplies this norm by the bounded factor $\sqrt{N_h/h}$. This proves the independent coarse bound. [F1, step 1.1, F2, algebra, step 13.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces.

[L1] There is a singular value decomposition $Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$ with $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0$ ([[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $V=0$, then [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] gives $\lVert T\rVert=0$. Assume now that $V\ne0$, and choose an SVD from [L1] with orthonormal bases $(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$ of $V$ and $(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$ of $W$, where $n\ge1$. Write its positive singular values as $\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ and set $\sigma_j=0$ for $r<j\le n$. The SVD formula gives $Te_j=\sigma_jf_j$ only for $j\le r$, while $Te_j=0$ for $j>r$. In particular, when $r=0$, the formula is the empty sum, $T=0$, and the largest singular value on the nonzero domain is $\sigma_1=0$. [L1, algebra]

2.1 If $r>0$, write a unit vector as $v=\sum_{j=1}^n c_je_j$. Orthonormality of the input and output bases gives $$\lVert Tv\rVert^2=\sum_{j=1}^r \sigma_j^2|c_j|^2\le \sigma_1^2\sum_{j=1}^n |c_j|^2=\sigma_1^2.$$ Thus every unit vector satisfies $\lVert Tv\rVert\le\sigma_1$. If $r=0$, then $Tv=0$ for every $v$, and the same bound holds with $\sigma_1=0$. [L1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $n\ge1$, the unit right-singular vector $e_1$ exists. If $r>0$, then $f_1$ exists and $\lVert Te_1\rVert=\lVert\sigma_1f_1\rVert=\sigma_1$. If $r=0$, then $Te_1=0$ and $\lVert Te_1\rVert=0=\sigma_1$, without requiring any vector of $W$. Together with step 2.1, this proves that the maximum defining $\lVert T\rVert$ equals the largest singular value and is attained at $e_1$ whenever $V\ne0$, including $W=0$. [L1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite iid array of real random variables with mean zero, variance one and finite fourth moment. For each $n$, let $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{1\le i\le n,1\le j\le p_n}$ and suppose $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. For $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$ and $b_\gamma=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2$, the separate lower-edge estimate is
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\lambda_{\max}(S_n)\ge b_\gamma\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

## Statement references

Yin, Bai, and Krishnaiah, Theorem 3.1, printed p. 517 ([complete paper PDF](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/BF00353874.pdf)).

Baik and Silverstein, Theorem 1.1 for the identity population case, printed pp. 4–5 ([complete paper PDF](https://jack.math.ncsu.edu/spike.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions
