## Statement

Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite iid array of real random variables with mean zero, variance one and finite fourth moment. For each $n$, let $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{1\le i\le n,1\le j\le p_n}$ and suppose $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. For $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$, with $b_\gamma=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2$, the upper-edge bound is
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\lambda_{\max}(S_n)\le b_\gamma\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

## Statement references

Yin, Bai, and Krishnaiah, Theorem 3.1 and its high-moment proof in §4, printed pp. 517–520 ([complete paper PDF](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/BF00353874.pdf)).

Bai and Silverstein, Theorem 5.10, printed pp. 105–112 ([complete book PDF](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[lem-sample-covariance-spectrum-confinement]] gives a sharp norm confinement for the smaller Gram matrix after normalization by the larger rectangular dimension.

[F2] [[thm-singular-value-decomposition]] and [[thm-operator-norm-is-the-largest-singular-value]] identify the largest eigenvalue of either Gram matrix with the squared operator norm; these positive eigenvalues coincide.

## Proof

**Given:** The nested iid array, its upper-left rectangular blocks, and the hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Set $N_n=\max(n,p_n)$, $m_n=\min(n,p_n)$, $c_n=N_n/n\to c=\max(1,\gamma)$ and $y_n=m_n/N_n\to y=\min(\gamma,\gamma^{-1})$. Orient $X_n$ or its transpose as $Z_n$ with $m_n$ rows and $N_n$ columns. By F1, almost surely $\limsup\|Z_nZ_n^{\mathsf T}/N_n-(1+y)I\|\le2\sqrt y$. For each unit vector $v$, its quadratic form is at most $1+y$ plus this norm, so $\limsup\lambda_{\max}(Z_nZ_n^{\mathsf T}/N_n)\le(1+\sqrt y)^2$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 By F2, $\lambda_{\max}(S_n)=c_n\lambda_{\max}(Z_nZ_n^{\mathsf T}/N_n)$. The previous bound gives $\limsup\lambda_{\max}(S_n)\le c(1+\sqrt y)^2$. If $\gamma\le1$ this constant is $(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2$; if $\gamma\ge1$ it is $\gamma(1+\gamma^{-1/2})^2=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2$. The same identity holds at $\gamma=1$, even if the orientation changes infinitely often. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite iid array of real random variables with mean zero, variance one and finite fourth moment. For each $n$, let $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{1\le i\le n,1\le j\le p_n}$ and suppose $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. Let $s_{r_n}(X_n)$ be the smallest among the $r_n:=\min(n,p_n)$ singular values, counting zero values. Then, almost surely: if $\gamma<1$, $s_{r_n}(X_n)/\sqrt n\to1-\sqrt\gamma$, so $X_n$ has full column rank for all sufficiently large $n$; if $\gamma>1$, $s_{r_n}(X_n)/\sqrt n\to\sqrt\gamma-1$, so $X_n$ has full row rank for all sufficiently large $n$; and if $\gamma=1$, the smallest positive singular value is eventually defined and, divided by $\sqrt n$, tends to zero.

## Statement references

Bai and Yin, Theorem 1, official publication record; the complete paper was not retrieved ([publication record](https://doi.org/10.1214/aop/1176989118)).

Bai and Silverstein, Theorem 5.11, printed pp. 112–113 ([complete book PDF](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[lem-sample-covariance-spectrum-confinement]] supplies the nonbacktracking finite-fourth-moment confinement of the smaller Gram matrix.

[F2] [[lem-nonbacktracking-covariance-high-moment-bound]] supplies the independent coarse norm bound needed by [[lem-fixed-degree-covariance-trace-and-edge-witnesses]]. The latter proves $\limsup\lambda_{\min}^{+}(X_nX_n^{\mathsf T}/n)\le(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2$ and eventual existence of positive eigenvalues using fixed polynomial witnesses.

[F3] [[thm-singular-value-decomposition]] identifies the eigenvalues of the smaller Gram matrix with the squares of all $r_n=\min(n,p_n)$ singular values, including zeros; [[cor-rank-equals-number-of-nonzero-singular-values]] identifies full rectangular rank with positivity of all these values.

## Proof

**Given:** The nested iid array, its upper-left blocks, and the hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Write $N_n=\max(n,p_n)$, $r_n=\min(n,p_n)$, $c_n=N_n/n\to c=\max(1,\gamma)$ and $y_n=r_n/N_n\to y:=\min(\gamma,\gamma^{-1})$. Orient $X_n$ as $Z_n$ with $r_n$ rows. F1 and the quadratic-form lower bound give $\liminf\lambda_{\min}(Z_nZ_n^{\mathsf T}/N_n)\ge(1-\sqrt y)^2$ almost surely. By F3, $s_{r_n}(X_n)^2/n=c_n\lambda_{\min}(Z_nZ_n^{\mathsf T}/N_n)$, so its liminf is at least $c(1-\sqrt y)^2=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2$. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 If $\gamma\ne1$, this last constant is positive. Thus all $r_n$ singular values are positive eventually, and F3 gives eventual full column rank when $\gamma<1$ and full row rank when $\gamma>1$. The smallest positive eigenvalue of $X_nX_n^{\mathsf T}/n$ then equals $s_{r_n}(X_n)^2/n$. Its limsup is at most $(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2$ by F2; combined with step 1.1 this proves convergence of that squared singular value. Taking the nonnegative square root gives respectively $1-\sqrt\gamma$ and $\sqrt\gamma-1$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $\gamma=1$, F2 supplies positive eigenvalues eventually and a smallest positive eigenvalue with limsup at most zero. Nonnegativity makes its limit zero. F3 transfers this to the square of the smallest positive singular value divided by $n$, and the nonnegative square root tends to zero. No claim of eventual full rank at aspect one is needed. The argument for either endpoint uses confinement and independent trace witnesses, not MP weak convergence. [F2, F3, algebra, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. Then $\operatorname{rank} T$ equals the number of positive
singular values of $T$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces, and an SVD $$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$ with $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0=s_{r+1}=\cdots$.

[L1] Every linear map admits a singular value decomposition ([[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]).

[L2] Rank-nullity holds for linear maps with finite-dimensional domain ([[thm-rank-nullity]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], one has $Tv=0$ exactly when $\langle v,e_j\rangle=0$ for $1\le j\le r$, so $\ker T=\operatorname{span}(e_{r+1},\dots,e_n)$ and therefore $\operatorname{nullity}T=n-r$. [L1, algebra]

2.1 By [L2], $\operatorname{rank}T+\operatorname{nullity}T=n$. Combining this with step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{rank}T=r$, the number of positive singular values. [L2, step 1.1] ∎

For each $n$, let $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{1\le i\le n,1\le j\le p_n}$ and suppose $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. Set $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$ and let $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)$ denote its smallest positive eigenvalue whenever one exists. If $\gamma<1$, then almost surely $X_n$ has full column rank for all sufficiently large $n$, so $S_n$ has no zero eigenvalues eventually and $\lambda_{\min}(S_n)\to(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2$. If $\gamma>1$, then almost surely $X_n$ has full row rank for all sufficiently large $n$, so $S_n$ has exactly $p_n-n$ zero eigenvalues and $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)\to(\sqrt\gamma-1)^2$. If $\gamma=1$, then almost surely $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)\to0$.

## Statement references

Bai and Yin, Theorem 1, official publication record; the full paper was not retrievable ([publication record](https://doi.org/10.1214/aop/1176989118)).

Bai and Silverstein, Theorem 5.11, printed pp. 112–113 ([complete book PDF](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[thm-bai-yin-smallest-singular-value-limits]] supplies the lower singular-value limits, eventual full rectangular rank when $\gamma\ne1$, and the eventually defined closing positive edge when $\gamma=1$.

[F2] [[thm-singular-value-decomposition]] and [[cor-rank-equals-number-of-nonzero-singular-values]] identify positive covariance eigenvalues with squared positive singular values divided by $n$ and their number with the rank. The zero multiplicity is therefore $p_n-\operatorname{rank}X_n$ by [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]].

## Proof

**Given:** The nested iid array and hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 When $\gamma<1$, F1 gives full column rank eventually. Thus F2 gives no covariance zero eigenvalues eventually, and the least eigenvalue is $s_{p_n}(X_n)^2/n\to(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 When $\gamma>1$, F1 gives full row rank eventually. Then F2 gives exactly $p_n-n$ zero eigenvalues and identifies the smallest positive eigenvalue with $s_n(X_n)^2/n\to(\sqrt\gamma-1)^2$. [F1, F2, algebra, step 1.1]

3.1 When $\gamma=1$, F1 gives an eventually defined smallest positive singular value whose ratio to $\sqrt n$ tends to zero. F2 squares this ratio to obtain $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)\to0$. Intersecting the relevant probability-one supplier events proves every asserted almost-sure conclusion. [F1, F2, algebra, step 2.1] ∎

## Definition

For positive integers $d,N$, let $X\in\mathbb C^{d\times N}$ and let $T\in\mathbb C^{d\times d}$ be Hermitian positive semidefinite, meaning $T=T^*$ and $v^*Tv\ge0$ for every $v\in\mathbb C^d$. Let $T^{1/2}$ be its Hermitian positive semidefinite square root and set
$$A:=\frac1N T^{1/2}XX^*T^{1/2}.$$
For each distinct eigenvalue $\lambda$ of the Hermitian matrix $A$, let $P_\lambda$ be the orthogonal projection onto its eigenspace. The empirical spectral distribution of $A$, normalized by its dimension $d$, is
$$\mu_A:=\frac1d\sum_{\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(A)}\operatorname{rank}(P_\lambda)\,\delta_\lambda,$$
where $\delta_\lambda$ is the unit point mass at $\lambda$.
For a deterministic unit vector $x\in\mathbb C^d$, its directional spectral measure is
$$\mu_A^x:=\sum_{\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(A)}\|P_\lambda x\|_2^2\,\delta_\lambda.$$
For a Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$, set $\mathbf1_B(A):=\sum_{\lambda\in B\cap\operatorname{spec}(A)}P_\lambda$; then $\mu_A^x(B)=x^*\mathbf1_B(A)x$. Both measures are supported on the nonnegative real axis.

## Definition references

Bai, Miao, and Pan, §1, printed pp. 7–8 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

Bai and Silverstein, Chapter 3, §§3.1–3.3, printed pp. 39–58 ([full book PDF](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Positive integers $d,N$, the matrices and vector in the Definition, and the finite-dimensional spectral decomposition.

[F1] Every Hermitian matrix has real eigenvalues and mutually orthogonal eigenspace projections whose sum is the identity ([[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]).

[F2] For each real $\lambda$, $\delta_\lambda$ is the unit Borel point mass at $\lambda$ ([[def-dirac-measure]]).

[F3] Each point mass $\delta_\lambda$ is a Borel probability measure ([[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]).

## Verification

**Given:** The positive semidefinite matrix $T$, matrix $X$, and the definitions in the Definition.

1.1 By [F1], diagonalize $T=U\operatorname{diag}(t_1,\ldots,t_d)U^*$ with each $t_j\ge0$. Then $T^{1/2}:=U\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{t_1},\ldots,\sqrt{t_d})U^*$ is Hermitian positive semidefinite. With $B=N^{-1/2}T^{1/2}X$, the matrix $A=BB^*$ is Hermitian and $v^*Av=\|B^*v\|_2^2\ge0$ for every $v$; hence all its eigenvalues are nonnegative. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Each displayed set function is a finite nonnegative linear combination of the point masses defined in [F2], which are Borel probability measures by [F3]; its coefficients are nonnegative because $\operatorname{rank}(P_\lambda)/d\ge0$ and $\|P_\lambda x\|_2^2\ge0$. Thus both are finite Borel measures. By step 1.1 their finite supports lie in $[0,\infty)$. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

## Statement

For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on a nonempty set $X$ and a point $x_0\in X$.

[L3] A nonnegative extended series is the supremum of its finite partial sums, with the empty sum equal to $0$ ([[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]).

1.1 One has $\delta_{x_0}(\varnothing)=0$ and $\delta_{x_0}(X)=1$. [given, L1]

## Statement

For each positive integer $n$, let $N_n$ be a positive integer with $n/N_n\to c\in(0,\infty)$, and let $X_n\in\mathbb C^{n\times N_n}$ have independent identically distributed entries $\xi$ satisfying $\mathbb E\xi=0$ and $|\xi|\le K$ almost surely for a fixed $K<\infty$. Then there is a finite constant $C=C(K,c)$ such that, almost surely, $\|X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C\sqrt{N_n}$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

## Statement references

Bai and Silverstein, Chapter 3, full book PDF ([source](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The matrix sequence and bounded centered iid entry law of the Statement.

[F1] The entries in each matrix are mutually independent and have the common law specified in the Statement ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]).

[F2] If $\sum_n\mathbb P(E_n)<\infty$, then almost surely only finitely many $E_n$ occur ([[cor-first-borel-cantelli-lemma-for-events]]).

[F3] For an event $E$ and $a>0$, $\mathbb P(E)\le \mathbb E[Y]/a$ whenever $Y\ge a\mathbf1_E$ ([[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]]).

[F4] The operator norm is the maximum of $\|Av\|_2$ over unit vectors in the domain ([[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]).

## Proof

1.1 If $K=0$, every entry is zero almost surely and the conclusion is immediate. Assume $K>0$. Regard the complex unit sphere in $\mathbb C^d$ as the real unit sphere in $\mathbb R^{2d}$. For $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, a maximal $\varepsilon$-separated subset is an $\varepsilon$-net; the disjoint radius-$\varepsilon/2$ balls about its points lie in the radius-$(1+\varepsilon/2)$ ball, so volume comparison bounds its cardinality by $(1+2/\varepsilon)^{2d}$. If $\mathcal N_1,\mathcal N_2$ are such nets for the two unit spheres and $A$ is an $n\times N$ complex matrix, approximating unit vectors $u,v$ attaining $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=|u^*Av|$ gives $$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le (1-2\varepsilon)^{-1}\max_{u_0\in\mathcal N_1,\ v_0\in\mathcal N_2}|u_0^*Av_0|.$$ Indeed, the approximation error is at most $\|u-u_0\|\|A\|+\|v-v_0\|\|A\|\le2\varepsilon\|A\|$. [given, F4, algebra]

2.1 Fix deterministic unit vectors $u\in\mathbb C^n$ and $v\in\mathbb C^N$. Then $u^*X_nv=\sum_{i,j}\overline u_i v_j\xi_{ij}$ is a sum of independent centered complex variables. Each real or imaginary summand is bounded in absolute value by $K|u_i||v_j|$. If a centered real variable $Y$ is bounded by $b$, convexity of the exponential on $[-b,b]$ and $\mathbb EY=0$ give $\mathbb E e^{\lambda Y}\le\cosh(\lambda b)\le e^{\lambda^2b^2/2}$. Independence, exponential Markov inequality [F3], and optimization in $\lambda$ therefore give $$\mathbb P\{|u^*X_nv|>t\}\le4\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{4K^2}\right),$$ because $\sum_{i,j}K^2|u_i|^2|v_j|^2=K^2$. [given, F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Choose $\varepsilon=1/8$ in step 1.1. The product of the two net cardinalities is at most $17^{2(n+N_n)}$. Taking $t=L\sqrt{n+N_n}$ with $L$ large enough that $L^2/(4K^2)>2\log17+1$, the union bound and step 2.1 make the probability that the net maximum exceeds $t$ at most $4e^{-(n+N_n)}$. These probabilities are summable in $n$ because $N_n/n\to1/c>0$. By [F2], the net maximum is at most $L\sqrt{n+N_n}$ eventually almost surely. The net inequality in step 1.1 and boundedness of $n/N_n$ then yield $\|X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C\sqrt{N_n}$ eventually, with deterministic $C=C(K,c)$. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

The proof is the explicit finite-net and exponential-moment argument above; the sources record the standard norm-estimation context and are not imported as proof premises.

## Statement

$$\mathbb E\left|\xi^*A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A\right|^2\le C_{\mu_4,\tau}\,\mathbb E\|A\|_F^2,\qquad C_{\mu_4,\tau}:=\max\{\mu_4-1,1+|\tau|^2\}.$$

## Statement references

Bai, Miao, and Pan, Lemma 1 in §2, printed p. 12 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

Bai and Silverstein, Chapter 3, §3.3, printed pp. 57–58 ([full book PDF](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The independent vector and matrix, moment conditions, and Frobenius norm in the Statement.

[F1] IID means the coordinates are mutually independent and have one common law ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]).

[F2] The joint law of independent random elements is the product of their marginal laws ([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]).

[F3] Fubini's theorem permits integration in either order for an integrable function on a sigma-finite product space ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The moment hypotheses, independence, and finite Frobenius-norm second moment in the Statement.

1.1 First fix a deterministic complex matrix $A$. Centering the diagonal terms gives $$\xi^*A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A=\sum_iA_{ii}(|\xi_i|^2-1)+\sum_{i\ne j}\overline{\xi_i}A_{ij}\xi_j.$$ In the squared modulus, independence and $\mathbb E\xi_i=0$ make diagonal and off-diagonal parts uncorrelated; distinct diagonal terms are uncorrelated; and two off-diagonal terms have nonzero expectation only when their ordered index pairs agree or are reversed. Expanding those remaining terms yields $$\mathbb E|\xi^*A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A|^2=(\mu_4-1)\sum_i|A_{ii}|^2+\sum_{i\ne j}|A_{ij}|^2+|\tau|^2\sum_{i\ne j}A_{ij}\overline{A_{ji}}.$$ Here $\mu_4-1\ge0$ by Cauchy–Schwarz, and $|\tau|\le\mathbb E|\xi_1|^2=1$. Also $$\left|\sum_{i\ne j}A_{ij}\overline{A_{ji}}\right|\le\sum_{i\ne j}|A_{ij}||A_{ji}|\le\sum_{i\ne j}|A_{ij}|^2.$$ Thus the deterministic quadratic-form variance is at most $C_{\mu_4,\tau}\|A\|_F^2$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], $(\xi,A)$ has product joint law. The integrand is integrable because $$|\xi^*A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A|^2\le2\|A\|_F^2\|\xi\|_2^4+2d\|A\|_F^2,$$ and $\mathbb E\|\xi\|_2^4<\infty$ in finite dimension. Integrate the deterministic inequality from step 1.1 over the law of $A$; [F3] justifies the order of integration and gives the stated bound. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

Bai, Miao, and Pan, Lemma 1 in §2, printed p. 12 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

## Statement

Let $c>0$, let $H$ be a Borel probability measure on $[0,\infty)$, and fix $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. There is at most one $q\in\mathbb C$ satisfying $\operatorname{Im}q>0$, $u:=-(1-c)/z+cq$ with $\operatorname{Im}u>0$, and
$$q=\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{1}{t(1-c-czq)-z}\,dH(t).$$

## Statement references

Silverstein, Theorem 1.1 and equation (1.4), PDF pp. 2–3 ([full paper PDF](https://jack.math.ncsu.edu/strong.pdf)).

Bai, Miao, and Pan, equation (1.1), PDF pp. 3–4 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $c>0$, a Borel probability measure $H$ on $[0,\infty)$, $z\in\mathbb C^+$, and two candidate solutions $q_1,q_2$ satisfying the Statement.

[A1] The aspect ratio $c$ is positive.

[A2] $H$ is a countably additive Borel measure on $[0,\infty)$ with total mass one ([[def-probability-measure]]).

[A3] The spectral parameter is $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$.

[A4] Each candidate $q$ has positive imaginary part, $-(1-c)/z+cq$ has positive imaginary part, and $q$ satisfies the fixed-point equation in the Statement.

## Proof

1.1 For either candidate $q$, set $u=-(1-c)/z+cq\in\mathbb C^+$. Since $t\ge0$, $1+tu\ne0$ for every $t$, and the fixed-point equation becomes $q=-z^{-1}\int(1+tu)^{-1}\,dH(t)$. Substituting this into $u=-(1-c)/z+cq$ and using $(1+tu)^{-1}=1-tu/(1+tu)$ gives $$z=-\frac1u+c\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{t}{1+tu}\,dH(t).$$ All integrals are finite because $|t/(1+tu)|\le1/\operatorname{Im}u$. [given, A1, A2, A3, A4, algebra]

2.1 If $u_1\ne u_2$ are the transforms of two solutions, subtracting their equations in step 1.1 and dividing by $u_1-u_2$ yields $$\frac1{u_1u_2}=c\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{t^2}{(1+tu_1)(1+tu_2)}\,dH(t).$$ For either solution $u$, taking imaginary parts in step 1.1 gives $$\operatorname{Im}z=\operatorname{Im}u\left(\frac1{|u|^2}-c\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{t^2}{|1+tu|^2}\,dH(t)\right)>0,$$ so $c|u|^2\int t^2|1+tu|^{-2}\,dH(t)<1$. [A1, A2, A3, A4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Taking absolute values in the identity of step 2.1 and applying Cauchy–Schwarz gives $$1\le\left(c|u_1|^2\int\frac{t^2}{|1+tu_1|^2}\,dH(t)\right)^{1/2}\left(c|u_2|^2\int\frac{t^2}{|1+tu_2|^2}\,dH(t)\right)^{1/2}<1,$$ contradicting step 2.1. Hence $u_1=u_2$, and the relation $u=-(1-c)/z+cq$ with $c>0$ gives $q_1=q_2$. [A1, A2, A3, A4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

Silverstein, Theorem 1.1 and equation (1.4), PDF pp. 2–3 ([full paper PDF](https://jack.math.ncsu.edu/strong.pdf)).

## Statement

Let $B\in\mathbb C^{d\times d}$ be Hermitian positive semidefinite, let $x\in\mathbb C^d$, and let $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$. Set $R=(B-zI)^{-1}$ and $R_x=(B+xx^*-zI)^{-1}$. For the trace norm $\|M\|_1$, defined as the sum of the singular values of $M$, one has $1+x^*Rx\ne0$,
$$R_x=R-\frac{Rxx^*R}{1+x^*Rx},\qquad \|R_x-R\|_1\le\frac1\eta,\qquad |\operatorname{tr}R_x-\operatorname{tr}R|\le\frac1\eta.$$

## Statement references

Bai, Miao, and Pan, the rank-one identity in §2, printed pp. 12–13 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

Bai and Silverstein, Chapter 3, §3.3, printed pp. 53–54 ([full book PDF](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Hermitian positive semidefinite matrix $B$, vector $x$, and $z$ in the Statement.

[F1] A finite-dimensional Hermitian matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues ([[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]).

## Proof

**Given:** $B$, $x$, and $z=u+i\eta$ with $\eta>0$.

1.1 By [F1], write $B=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)U^*$ with $\lambda_j\ge0$. If $c=U^*x$, then $$q:=x^*Rx=\sum_j\frac{|c_j|^2}{\lambda_j-z},\qquad \operatorname{Im}q=\eta\sum_j\frac{|c_j|^2}{|\lambda_j-z|^2}=\eta\|Rx\|_2^2.$$ For $x\ne0$ this is positive, so $1+q\ne0$; for $x=0$ the denominator is one. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Direct multiplication, using step 1.1, gives $$ (B+xx^*-zI)\left(R-\frac{Rxx^*R}{1+x^*Rx}\right)=I.$$ The Hermitian matrix $B+xx^*$ has a resolvent at nonreal $z$, so the displayed inverse is $R_x$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The difference in step 2.1 is a rank-one matrix. Its trace norm equals the product of the two vector norms divided by $|1+q|$; normality of $R$ makes both vector norms $\|Rx\|_2$. Since $|1+q|\ge\operatorname{Im}q=\eta\|Rx\|_2^2$, step 1.1 gives $\|R_x-R\|_1\le1/\eta$. The inequality $|\operatorname{tr}M|\le\|M\|_1$ then gives the trace bound. The case $x=0$ has both differences zero. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

Bai, Miao, and Pan, §2, equations (2.1)–(2.2), printed pp. 12–13 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

## Statement

For each positive integer $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb C^{n\times N_n}$ have entries from one common iid law with mean zero, unit second absolute moment, and absolute value at most $K$, where $K$ is independent of $n$. Let $T_n\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be deterministic Hermitian positive semidefinite with $\|T_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M$, and let $x_n\in\mathbb C^n$ be deterministic with $\|x_n\|_2=1$. Assume $N_n/n\to\kappa\in(0,\infty)$. For fixed $z=u+i\eta$ with $\eta>0$, set
$$A_n:=\frac1{N_n}T_n^{1/2}X_nX_n^*T_n^{1/2},\qquad R_n(z):=(A_n-zI)^{-1}.$$
Then $x_n^*R_n(z)x_n-\mathbb E[x_n^*R_n(z)x_n]\to0$ almost surely. Moreover, for every $t>0$ there is a constant $C=C(K,M,z,\kappa)$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left\{|x_n^*R_n(z)x_n-\mathbb E[x_n^*R_n(z)x_n]|>t\right\}\le\frac{C}{t^4N_n^2}.$$

## Statement references

Bai, Miao, and Pan, §2, equations (2.1)–(2.3), printed pp. 12–13 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

Silverstein, Theorem 1.1 proof, PDF pp. 3–8 ([full paper PDF](https://jack.math.ncsu.edu/strong.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The bounded iid entries, deterministic PSD $T_n$, unit vectors $x_n$, and fixed $z\in\mathbb C^+$ in the Statement.

[F1] The entries are mutually independent with the stated common law ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]).

[F2] Independent columns have their product joint law ([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]).

[F3] Fubini permits the finite product-integral conditional averages used for the column filtration ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F4] The Hermitian rank-one resolvent update and nonzero denominator are given by [[lem-hermitian-rank-one-resolvent-update-and-trace-norm-bound]].

[F5] A summable sequence of probabilities has probability zero of occurring infinitely often ([[cor-first-borel-cantelli-lemma-for-events]]).

[F6] A finite-dimensional Hermitian PSD matrix has nonnegative real eigenvalues and a unitary eigenbasis ([[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]).

[F7] For a nonnegative random variable $Y$ and $a>0$, $\mathbb P(Y>a)\le\mathbb E[Y]/a$ ([[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]]).

[F8] The operator norm is the maximum of $\|Av\|_2$ over unit vectors in the domain ([[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and notation in the Statement.

1.1 We first prove a linear-form bound. If $\zeta_i$ are independent centered complex variables with $|\zeta_i|\le K$ and $a_i\in\mathbb C$, expansion of $\mathbb E|\sum_i a_i\zeta_i|^8$ has zero contribution whenever an index occurs exactly once. Each remaining equality pattern partitions the eight positions into blocks of sizes at least two. For a fixed pattern, the absolute sum is at most $K^8\prod_B\sum_i|a_i|^{|B|}\le K^8(\sum_i|a_i|^2)^4$, since $\sum_i|a_i|^r\le(\sum_i|a_i|^2)^{r/2}$ for $r\ge2$. There are finitely many such patterns, so $\mathbb E|\sum_i a_i\zeta_i|^8\le C_K(\sum_i|a_i|^2)^4$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Write $s_{n,j}=T_n^{1/2}X_{n,\cdot j}/\sqrt{N_n}$, $A_{n,j}=A_n-s_{n,j}s_{n,j}^*$, and $R_{n,j}=(A_{n,j}-zI)^{-1}$. By [F4], $$U_{n,j}:=x_n^*(R_n-R_{n,j})x_n=-\frac{(x_n^*R_{n,j}s_{n,j})(s_{n,j}^*R_{n,j}x_n)}{1+s_{n,j}^*R_{n,j}s_{n,j}}.$$ Diagonalizing $A_{n,j}$ as in [F6] gives $\operatorname{Im}(z(1+s_{n,j}^*R_{n,j}s_{n,j}))\ge\eta$, hence the denominator has modulus at least $\eta/|z|$. Conditional on all columns except $j$, each factor in the numerator is a linear form in the bounded independent entries of column $j$, with coefficient-vector norm at most $\sqrt M/(\eta\sqrt{N_n})$. Step 1.1 and Cauchy–Schwarz therefore give $\mathbb E|U_{n,j}|^4\le C N_n^{-4}$. [given, F2, F4, F6, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\mathcal F_{n,j}=\sigma(X_{n,\cdot1},\ldots,X_{n,\cdot j})$, and let $E_{n,j}$ be the finite-product average over the remaining columns. By [F2]–[F3], $$x_n^*R_nx_n-\mathbb E[x_n^*R_nx_n]=\sum_{j=1}^{N_n}(E_{n,j}-E_{n,j-1})x_n^*R_nx_n.$$ The leave-one-column resolvent $R_{n,j}$ depends on all columns except $j$, so its product-integral averages under $E_{n,j}$ and $E_{n,j-1}$ agree. Therefore the $j$th summand is $D_{n,j}:=(E_{n,j}-E_{n,j-1})U_{n,j}$. Integrating over column $j$ shows $E_{n,j-1}D_{n,j}=0$, so these are martingale differences. Conditional Jensen gives $\mathbb E|D_{n,j}|^4\le16\mathbb E|U_{n,j}|^4\le C N_n^{-4}$. [given, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Put $S_k=\sum_{j\le k}D_{n,j}$, $a_k=\mathbb E|S_k|^4$, $v_k:=E_{n,k-1}|D_{n,k}|^2$, and $w_k:=E_{n,k-1}|D_{n,k}|^4$. Expanding $|S_{k-1}+D_{n,k}|^4$, the term linear in $D_{n,k}$ vanishes after conditional integration; $|\operatorname{Re}(\overline S_{k-1}D_{n,k})|\le|S_{k-1}||D_{n,k}|$ and $4|S_{k-1}||D_{n,k}|^3\le2|S_{k-1}|^2|D_{n,k}|^2+2|D_{n,k}|^4$ give $$a_k\le a_{k-1}+8\mathbb E(|S_{k-1}|^2v_k)+3\mathbb E w_k.$$ By Cauchy–Schwarz and conditional Jensen, $\mathbb E(|S_{k-1}|^2v_k)\le\sqrt{a_{k-1}}\sqrt{\mathbb E v_k^2}\le\sqrt{a_{k-1}}\sqrt{\mathbb E w_k}\le C\sqrt{a_{k-1}}/N_n^2$, while $\mathbb E w_k\le C/N_n^4$. Induction gives $a_k\le C_0k^2/N_n^4$ for a fixed sufficiently large $C_0$ and $k\le N_n$, hence $\mathbb E|S_{N_n}|^4\le C_0/N_n^2$. [step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Apply [F7] to $Y=|S_{N_n}|^4$ and $a=t^4$ to obtain the stated $C/(t^4N_n^2)$ tail bound. Since $N_n/n\to\kappa>0$, the probabilities are summable in $n$; [F5] proves almost-sure convergence for this fixed $z$. [F5, F7, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

Bai, Miao, and Pan, §2, equations (2.1)–(2.3), printed pp. 12–13 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

## Statement

For each positive integer $n$, let $Y_{n,1},\ldots,Y_{n,N_n}$ be independent random vectors in $\mathbb C^n$, let $B_n=\sum_{j=1}^{N_n}Y_{n,j}Y_{n,j}^*$, and assume $N_n/n\to\kappa\in(0,\infty)$. Fix $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$, and define
$$M_n(z):=\frac1n\operatorname{tr}(B_n-zI)^{-1}.$$
Then for every $t>0$,
$$\mathbb P\{|M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)|>t\}\le4\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2n^2\eta^2}{4N_n}\right),$$
and $M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)\to0$ almost surely.

## Statement references

Bai, Miao, and Pan, §2, printed pp. 12–13 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

Bai and Silverstein, Chapter 3, §3.3, printed pp. 53–55 ([full book PDF](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Independent complex columns $Y_{n,j}$, the normalized resolvent trace, and $z=u+i\eta$ with $\eta>0$.

[F1] Adding one positive rank-one term changes the unnormalized Hermitian resolvent trace by at most $1/\eta$ ([[lem-hermitian-rank-one-resolvent-update-and-trace-norm-bound]]).

[F2] Independent random elements have product joint law ([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]).

[F3] Fubini's theorem permits integration in either order on the finite product spaces used to define the conditional averages ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F4] A summable sequence of event probabilities has probability zero of occurring infinitely often ([[cor-first-borel-cantelli-lemma-for-events]]).

[F5] For a nonnegative random variable $Y$ and $a>0$, $\mathbb P(Y>a)\le\mathbb E[Y]/a$ ([[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and notation of the Statement.

1.1 Replacing one column $Y_{n,j}$ by any other vector removes one positive rank-one term and adds another. Applying [F1] twice shows that $\operatorname{tr}(B_n-zI)^{-1}$ changes by at most $2/\eta$, so the real and imaginary parts of $M_n(z)$ each have coordinate oscillation at most $c_n:=2/(n\eta)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Let $f$ be either real part of $M_n(z)$ and use [F2]–[F3] to form its product-integral Doob averages $F_j$ over the first $j$ columns, integrating the remaining columns against their marginal laws. Boundedness $|\operatorname{tr}(B_n-zI)^{-1}|\le n/\eta$ makes these integrals finite. Then $D_j:=F_j-F_{j-1}$ has conditional mean zero and lies, conditionally on the first $j-1$ columns, in an interval of length at most $c_n$ by step 1.1. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 If a real random variable $D$ has mean zero and lies in an interval of width $c$, then $\log\mathbb E e^{\lambda D}$ has second derivative equal to a variance under an exponentially tilted law, at most $c^2/4$; the variance bound follows from $\mathbb E[(D-a)(b-D)]\ge0$ for interval endpoints $a\le D\le b$. Since the log moment and its first derivative vanish at $0$, integrating twice gives $\mathbb E e^{\lambda D}\le e^{\lambda^2c^2/8}$. Apply this conditional estimate to each $D_j$, iterate, and use [F5] with $\lambda=4t/(N_nc_n^2)$ to obtain each one-sided tail $\mathbb P\{f-\mathbb Ef\ge t\}\le e^{-2t^2/(N_nc_n^2)}$. The same bound applies to the lower tail and to the imaginary part. If a complex number has modulus greater than $t$, one of its real or imaginary parts has magnitude greater than $t/\sqrt2$, so the union bound and $c_n=2/(n\eta)$ give the displayed probability inequality. [F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Since $N_n/n\to\kappa\in(0,\infty)$, for every fixed $t>0$ the step 3.1 bound is at most $4e^{-a_t n}$ for all sufficiently large $n$ and some $a_t>0$. The probabilities are summable. Apply [F4] for $t=1/m$, $m\ge1$, and intersect the resulting countable probability-one events to conclude $M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)\to0$ almost surely. [given, F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

Bai, Miao, and Pan, §2, equations (2.1)–(2.3), printed pp. 12–13 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

## Statement

For every Hermitian positive semidefinite $A\in\mathbb C^{d\times d}$, its empirical spectral distribution $\mu_A$ is a Borel probability measure supported on $[0,\infty)$. For every deterministic unit vector $x\in\mathbb C^d$, its directional spectral measure $\mu_A^x$ is also a Borel probability measure supported on $[0,\infty)$.

## Statement references

Bai, Miao, and Pan, §1, printed pp. 7–8 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

Bai and Silverstein, Appendix B.2, printed pp. 514–523 ([full book PDF](https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60805/1/140.pdf)).

Directional and empirical spectral-measure definitions: [[def-sample-covariance-directional-spectral-measure|definition of the directional spectral measure]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A Hermitian positive semidefinite matrix $A\in\mathbb C^{d\times d}$ and, for the directional measure, a deterministic vector $x\in\mathbb C^d$ with $\|x\|_2=1$.

[F1] A finite-dimensional Hermitian matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis; its eigenvalues are real, and positive semidefiniteness makes them nonnegative ([[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]).

[F2] The empirical and directional measures are the finite Dirac sums stated in [[def-sample-covariance-directional-spectral-measure]].

[F3] A Borel probability measure is countably additive and has total mass one ([[def-probability-measure]]).

[F4] The Dirac measure $\delta_\lambda$ is the Borel unit point mass at $\lambda$ ([[def-dirac-measure]]).

## Proof

**Given:** $A$, $x$, and the definitions in the Statement.

1.1 By [F1], write $A=\sum_{j=1}^r\lambda_jP_j$ over its distinct eigenvalues, where the $P_j$ are mutually orthogonal projections, $\sum_jP_j=I$, and $\lambda_j\ge0$. Taking traces gives $\sum_j\operatorname{rank}(P_j)=d$. Thus the nonnegative weights $\operatorname{rank}(P_j)/d$ in [F2] sum to one; by [F3] and [F4], $\mu_A$ is a Borel probability measure supported on $[0,\infty)$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 For the unit vector $x$, the directional weights in [F2] are $\|P_jx\|_2^2\ge0$, and orthogonality gives $\sum_j\|P_jx\|_2^2=\|\sum_jP_jx\|_2^2=\|x\|_2^2=1$. By [F3] and [F4], the finite Dirac sum is a Borel probability measure; its support is contained in the nonnegative spectrum of $A$ by [F1]. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

Bai, Miao, and Pan, equation (1.8), printed p. 8 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

## Statement

For each positive integer $n$, let $N_n$ be a positive integer with $N_n/n\to\kappa\in(0,\infty)$, let $X_n\in\mathbb C^{n\times N_n}$ have entries from one common iid law with mean zero, second absolute moment one and $|X_{ij}|\le K$ almost surely for a fixed $K$, and let $T_n$ be deterministic Hermitian positive semidefinite (self-adjoint with $v^*T_nv\ge0$ for every $v$) with induced Euclidean operator norm $\|T_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M$. Define
$$A_n=N_n^{-1}T_n^{1/2}X_nX_n^*T_n^{1/2},\qquad \widetilde A_n=N_n^{-1}X_n^*T_nX_n,$$
$$R_n(z)=(A_n-zI_n)^{-1},\qquad \widetilde R_n(z)=(\widetilde A_n-zI_{N_n})^{-1},\qquad q_n(z)=\mathbb E\left[N_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\widetilde R_n(z)\right].$$
For every fixed $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$, the matrix $I_n+q_n(z)T_n$ is invertible and
$$\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}\left|x^*\left(\mathbb E R_n(z)+\frac1z(I_n+q_n(z)T_n)^{-1}\right)x\right|\longrightarrow0.$$

## Statement references

Bai, Miao, and Pan, complete Section 2 proof of Theorem 1, printed pp. 12–16 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

Silverstein, Theorem 1.1 proof, PDF pp. 3–8 ([full paper PDF](https://jack.math.ncsu.edu/strong.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The iid bounded entries, deterministic positive semidefinite $T_n$, aspect-ratio limit, and fixed $z\in\mathbb C^+$ in the Statement.

[F1] Independent centered complex coordinates with unit second absolute moment satisfy the stated second-moment quadratic-form bound, also conditionally when the coefficient matrix is independent ([[lem-complex-quadratic-form-fourth-moment-bound]]).

[F2] Adding one positive rank-one matrix has the Sherman–Morrison resolvent formula and trace-norm bound ([[lem-hermitian-rank-one-resolvent-update-and-trace-norm-bound]]).

[F3] For bounded iid entries, each deterministic unit-vector resolvent quadratic form differs from its expectation with fourth-tail bound $C/(t^4N_n^2)$ ([[lem-bounded-complex-resolvent-quadratic-form-concentration]]).

[F4] Hermitian positive semidefinite matrices have nonnegative eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis ([[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]).

[F5] The Stieltjes transform of a probability measure uses the $(t-z)^{-1}$ convention in the upper half-plane ([[def-stieltjes-transform-of-a-real-probability-measure]]).

[F6] The operator norm is the maximum of $\|Av\|_2$ over unit vectors in the domain ([[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]).

## Proof

1.1 Fix $n,z$, suppress the index $n$, write $N=N_n$, $s_j=T^{1/2}X_{\cdot j}/\sqrt N$, $R=(A-zI)^{-1}$, $R_j=(A-s_js_j^*-zI)^{-1}$, and $\beta_j=(1+s_j^*R_js_j)^{-1}$. The companion matrix $\widetilde A=N^{-1}X^*TX$ is positive semidefinite by [F4], so $q=N^{-1}\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde A-zI)^{-1}$ is the Stieltjes transform of an expected probability measure on $[0,\infty)$ by [F5] and has positive imaginary part. If $q=\int(\lambda-z)^{-1}\,dG(\lambda)$, then for every $t\ge0$, $$\operatorname{Im}\{z(1+tq)\}=\eta+t\int\frac{\lambda\eta}{|\lambda-z|^2}\,dG(\lambda)\ge\eta,$$ so $C:=(I+qT)^{-1}$ exists and $\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le |z|/\eta$. The same spectral calculation applied to $A-s_js_j^*$ gives $|\beta_j|\le |z|/\eta$. [given, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 Set $b_j=(1+N^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(TR_j))^{-1}$ and $\xi_j=s_j^*R_js_j-N^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(TR_j)$. The trace in $b_j$ is a Stieltjes transform with nonnegative weights: in an eigenbasis of $A-s_js_j^*$ its weights are $\langle v_k,Tv_k\rangle/N\ge0$. The inequality in step 1.1 therefore also gives $|b_j|\le |z|/\eta$. Conditional on all columns except $j$, [F1] and $\|T^{1/2}R_jT^{1/2}\|_F^2\le nM^2/\eta^2$ give $\mathbb E_j|\xi_j|^2\le C_1 n/N^2=O(N^{-1})$, where $\mathbb E_j$ integrates column $j$. For any deterministic unit $x$, set $$\alpha_j=x^*Cs_js_j^*R_jx-N^{-1}x^*CTR_jx.$$ This is a centered quadratic form in column $j$. Its coefficient matrix is $$N^{-1}(T^{1/2}R_jx)(x^*CT^{1/2}),$$ so it has rank at most one and Frobenius norm at most $M\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}/(N\eta)$. Thus [F1] gives $\mathbb E_j|\alpha_j|^2=O(N^{-2})$. Also $\mathbb E_j\alpha_j=0$ and $\beta_j-b_j=-\beta_jb_j\xi_j$. [given, F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For all sufficiently large $n$ we have $N=N_n\ge2$. Put $Y=[s_2\ \cdots\ s_N]$, $D=Y^*Y-zI_{N-1}$, and $C_-=YY^*-zI_n=A-s_1s_1^*-zI_n$. The matrix $\widetilde A-zI$ has block form $$\begin{pmatrix}s_1^*s_1-z&s_1^*Y\\Y^*s_1&D\end{pmatrix}.$$ For a block matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b^*\\b&D\end{pmatrix}$ with invertible $D$, solving its product with $(u,v)^T=(1,0)^T$ gives $v=-D^{-1}bu$ and $(a-b^*D^{-1}b)u=1$. Hence its inverse's upper-left entry is $(a-b^*D^{-1}b)^{-1}$. Here $(C_-)Y=YD$, so $(C_-)(I-YD^{-1}Y^*)=C_- -YY^*=-zI$ and $I-YD^{-1}Y^*=-zC_-^{-1}=-zR_1$. The Schur complement is therefore $s_1^*(I-YD^{-1}Y^*)s_1-z=-z(1+s_1^*R_1s_1)$, proving $(\widetilde R)_{11}=-\beta_1/z$. [given, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By exchangeability of the columns and step 2.2, $zq=-N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N\mathbb E\beta_j$. The identity $R^{-1}=\sum_j s_js_j^*-zI$ gives $\sum_j s_js_j^*R=I+zR$. The rank-one formula [F2] gives $s_js_j^*R=\beta_js_js_j^*R_j$. Substituting these identities and the formula for $zq$ yields $$\mathbb E R+\frac1zC=\frac1z\sum_{j=1}^N\mathbb E\left[\beta_j\left(Cs_js_j^*R_j-N^{-1}CT\,\mathbb E R\right)\right].$$ Testing against $x$ and adding then subtracting $N^{-1}x^*CTR_jx$ and $N^{-1}x^*CTRx$ decomposes the right side into three terms $\delta_1+\delta_2+\delta_3$. [given, F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 For the first term, $\delta_1=(N/z)\mathbb E(\beta_1\alpha_1)$. Since $b_1$ is independent of column 1 and $\mathbb E_1\alpha_1=0$, we have $\mathbb E(b_1\alpha_1)=0$. Therefore step 2.1, Cauchy–Schwarz, and the uniform bounds on $\beta_1,b_1$ imply $$|\delta_1|\le C_2N(\mathbb E|\xi_1|^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E|\alpha_1|^2)^{1/2}=O(N^{-1/2}).$$ [given, F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 For the second term, $R_1-R=\beta_1R_1s_1s_1^*R_1$. Conditional second moments of the two linear forms $x^*CTR_1s_1$ and $s_1^*R_1x$ are each $O(N^{-1})$, uniformly in the other columns. Cauchy–Schwarz and boundedness of $\beta_1$ yield $|\delta_2|=O(N^{-1})$. [given, F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.3 The third term is $\delta_3=z^{-1}\mathbb E[\beta_1x^*CT(R-\mathbb ER)x]$. Put $u=(CT)^*x$ and $v=x$; their norms are uniformly bounded by step 1.1. For $Q(w)=w^*(R-\mathbb ER)w$, direct expansion gives $$u^*(R-\mathbb ER)v=\frac14\{Q(u+v)-Q(u-v)-iQ(u+iv)+iQ(u-iv)\}.$$ After rescaling these vectors, [F3] and the union bound give a tail bounded by $C_3/(t^4N^2)$ for this bilinear form; zero vectors contribute zero. It is also bounded deterministically by $2\|u\|\|v\|/\eta$. Integrating the tail after splitting at $t=N^{-1/2}$ gives $\mathbb E|u^*(R-\mathbb ER)v|^2=O(N^{-1})$. Since $\beta_1$ is bounded, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\delta_3|=O(N^{-1/2})$. [given, F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The bounds in steps 4.1, 4.2, and 4.3 tend to zero uniformly over deterministic unit $x$. The tested resolvent identity in step 3.1 therefore proves the asserted supremum limit. [given, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 4.3, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

Bai, Miao, and Pan, equations (2.2)–(2.9), printed pp. 12–15 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)). The $N$-prefactor in their estimate (2.6) gives $O(N^{-1/2})$ after the displayed moment bounds; the proof above retains that corrected vanishing order. Their (2.8) term is bounded here by adapted resolvent concentration and polarization.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For each positive integer $n$, let $N_n$ be a positive integer with $N_n/n\to\kappa\in(0,\infty)$, let $X_n\in\mathbb C^{n\times N_n}$ have entries from one common iid law with mean zero, second absolute moment one and absolute value bounded by one fixed finite constant, and let $T_n$ be deterministic Hermitian positive semidefinite (self-adjoint with $v^*T_nv\ge0$ for every $v$) with uniformly bounded induced Euclidean operator norm. Suppose the empirical eigenvalue measures $H_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{\lambda_i(T_n)}$ converge weakly to a Borel probability measure $H$ on $[0,\infty)$. Put $c=\kappa^{-1}$ and $A_n=N_n^{-1}T_n^{1/2}X_nX_n^*T_n^{1/2}$, and let $F_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{\lambda_i(A_n)}$. Then there is a unique Borel probability measure $F_{c,H}$ on $[0,\infty)$ such that, almost surely, $F_n$ converges weakly to $F_{c,H}$. Its Stieltjes transform $m_{c,H}(z)=\int(t-z)^{-1}\,dF_{c,H}(t)$ is the unique $m\in\mathbb C$ satisfying $\operatorname{Im}m>0$, $u:=-(1-c)/z+cm$ with $\operatorname{Im}u>0$, and
$$m=\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{1}{t(1-c-czm)-z}\,dH(t)\qquad(\operatorname{Im}z>0).$$

## Statement references

Silverstein, Theorem 1.1 and its complete proof in Section 3 ([full paper PDF](https://jack.math.ncsu.edu/strong.pdf)).

Bai, Miao, and Pan, Section 2, including the sample-covariance resolvent conventions ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The assumptions, matrices, and empirical measures in the Statement, including AC.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice permits a choice function for every family of nonempty sets ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] The normalized eigenvalue measure of the complex Hermitian sample-covariance matrix $A_n$ is its empirical spectral distribution, defined as the rank-weighted finite spectral measure ([[def-sample-covariance-directional-spectral-measure]]).

[F2] Iid entries are mutually independent and share one common distribution ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]).

[F3] The Stieltjes transform convention is $m_\mu(z)=\int(t-z)^{-1}\,d\mu(t)$ for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$ ([[def-stieltjes-transform-of-a-real-probability-measure]]).

[F4] Markov's inequality bounds the mass of $\{t>R\}$ by the first moment divided by $R$ ([[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]]).

[F5] Tight families of Borel probabilities on a Polish space are relatively sequentially compact for weak convergence, under AC ([[thm-prokhorov-tightness-theorem-on-polish-spaces]]).

[F6] The bounded-entry resolvent has the deterministic equivalent $-(z(I+q_nT_n))^{-1}$, uniformly on deterministic unit-vector quadratic forms ([[lem-bounded-complex-resolvent-deterministic-equivalent]]).

[F7] The normalized resolvent trace concentrates almost surely about its expectation ([[lem-hermitian-resolvent-trace-concentration]]).

[F8] The deformed fixed-point equation has at most one solution satisfying the stated upper-half-plane conditions ([[lem-deformed-mp-fixed-point-solution-is-unique]]).

[F9] Equal Stieltjes transforms determine probability measures on the real line ([[lem-stieltjes-transform-inversion-and-uniqueness-on-the-real-line]]).

[F10] The normalized operator norm of bounded complex iid matrices is almost surely eventually bounded ([[lem-bounded-complex-iid-matrix-norm-bound]]).

[F11] The nonzero eigenvalues of $Y^*Y$ and $YY^*$ agree with multiplicity ([[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]).

[F12] A probability measure is a countably additive Borel measure of total mass one ([[def-probability-measure]]).

[F13] Integrals of nonnegative increasing measurable sequences converge to the integral of their pointwise limit ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]).

[F14] The ordered eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix vary continuously with the matrix in operator norm ([[lem-complex-hermitian-eigenvalues-lipschitz]]).

[F15] A Polish space is a separable topological space whose topology is induced by a complete metric ([[def-polish-space]]).

[F16] Weak convergence of Borel probabilities means convergence of integrals against all bounded continuous real-valued functions ([[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]).

[F17] The operator norm is the maximum of $\|Av\|_2$ over unit vectors in the domain ([[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]).

## Proof

1.1 Write $c_n=n/N_n$, let $\bar F_n(B)=\mathbb E F_n(B)$, and let $\bar G_n$ be defined similarly for $\widetilde A_n=N_n^{-1}X_n^*T_nX_n$. By [F14], each ordered eigenvalue is continuous in the matrix entries, so these setwise expectations are defined for Borel $B$. For disjoint Borel sets, countable additivity of the random ESDs followed by [F13] gives countable additivity of $\bar F_n$ and $\bar G_n$; their total masses are one. Independence and unit second moment give $\int t\,d\bar F_n(t)=n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}T_n$ and $\int t\,d\bar G_n(t)=N_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}T_n$. Both first moments are uniformly bounded because $c_n\to c>0$ and $\|T_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is uniformly bounded. By [F4], their tails above $R$ are at most the corresponding first moment divided by $R$, so both expected-measure sequences are tight on $[0,\infty)$. The half-line is Polish: it is a closed subset of the complete real line and $\mathbb Q\cap[0,\infty)$ is dense. By [A1] and [F5], every subsequence of $\bar F_n$ has a further weakly convergent subsequence. [given, A1, F1, F2, F4, F5, F12, F13, F14, F15, F17, algebra]

1.2 For each fixed $z\in\mathbb C^+$, [F7] gives $\int(t-z)^{-1}dF_n(t)-\int(t-z)^{-1}d\bar F_n(t)\to0$ almost surely. Intersect these probability-one events over the countable dense set $\{a+ib:a,b\in\mathbb Q,\ b>0\}$. [given, F7]

2.1 Fix $z\in\mathbb C^+$ and take any such subsequence with $\bar F_n\Rightarrow G$. Let $m_G(z)=\int(t-z)^{-1}dG(t)$ and $q_n(z)=\int(t-z)^{-1}d\bar G_n(t)$. By [F11], the two sample-covariance matrices have the same nonzero eigenvalues, so their transforms satisfy exactly $q_n=-(1-c_n)/z+c_n\int(t-z)^{-1}d\bar F_n(t)$. Hence $q_n\to u:=-(1-c)/z+cm_G(z)$. Moreover $\operatorname{Im}m_G(z)>0$. The first moments of $\bar G_n$ are bounded, so at least half of each $\bar G_n$ lies in some fixed interval $[0,L]$; consequently $\operatorname{Im}q_n(z)\ge\eta/(2(L+|z|)^2)$ and $\operatorname{Im}u>0$. [given, F3, F4, F11, F16, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F6] to an orthonormal eigenbasis of $T_n$. Its uniform quadratic-form error implies $$\int(t-z)^{-1}\,d\bar F_n(t)=-\frac1{z n}\operatorname{tr}(I+q_nT_n)^{-1}+o(1)=-\frac1z\int\frac{1}{1+q_nt}\,dH_n(t)+o(1).$$ Since $H_n\Rightarrow H$, all $H_n$ are supported in one compact interval, $q_n\to u$, and $\operatorname{Im}u>0$, the integrands converge uniformly on that interval to $-1/[z(1+ut)]$. Thus $m_G(z)=\int[-z(1+ut)]^{-1}dH(t)$. The relation for $u$ in step 2.1 gives $-z(1+ut)=t(1-c-czm_G(z))-z$, so $m_G$ satisfies the fixed-point equation in the Statement. The argument applies to every $z\in\mathbb C^+$ and every weak subsequential limit $G$. By [F8], all such limits have the same transform; [F9] makes them equal. At least one such limit exists by step 1.1, so call it $F_{c,H}$. Tightness then implies $\bar F_n\Rightarrow F_{c,H}$. [given, F3, F6, F8, F9, F16, F17, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 On the same event, [F10] gives $\|A_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L_1$ eventually for a finite deterministic $L_1$, so the random measures $F_n$ are eventually supported on $[0,L_1]$ and are tight. The half-line is Polish by the metric facts in step 1.1 and [F15]. By [A1] and [F5], every subsequence has a weakly convergent further subsequence. For each dense-set $z$, its transform equals that of $F_{c,H}$ by steps 3.1 and 1.2, since the real and imaginary parts of $(t-z)^{-1}$ are bounded continuous and [F16] applies to each. For any probability law $\mu$, its transform satisfies $|m_\mu(z)-m_\mu(w)|\le |z-w|/(\operatorname{Im}z\operatorname{Im}w)$, so equality on the dense set extends to all $\mathbb C^+$; [F9] identifies the subsequential limit as $F_{c,H}$. Every subsequence has the same further limit, and [F16] gives $F_n\Rightarrow F_{c,H}$ almost surely. [given, A1, F5, F9, F10, F15, F16, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

Silverstein, Theorem 1.1 and complete Section 3 proof ([full paper PDF](https://jack.math.ncsu.edu/strong.pdf)). The local proof makes the companion-transform relation and the uniqueness step explicit.

## Statement

Assume AC. A family $\mathcal A$ of Borel probabilities on a Polish space S is tight if and only if it is relatively sequentially compact for weak convergence.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[thm-hilbert-cube-universal-for-separable-metrizable-spaces]]: Every separable metrizable space is homeomorphic to a subspace of the Hilbert cube $[0,1]^{\mathbb N}$.

[F2] [[lem-standard-complete-metric-on-a-countable-product]]: Let $((X_n,d_n))_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be complete metric spaces with $d_n\le1$. On $\prod_nX_n$, the formula $D(x,y)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}2^{-(n+1)}d_n(x_n,y_n)$ defines a complete metric inducing the product topology. The empty product is the one-point space.

[F3] [[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]: **Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** (def-countable-choice). Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (def-metric-space) that is complete (def-complete-metric-space) and totally bounded (def-totally-bounded). Then $(X,d)$ is compact (def-metric-compactness).

**Where the axiom is spent, and why the weaker principle suffices.** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used exactly once, at step 3.1, to fix one finite $1/(n+1)$-net **together with a listing of it** for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ at once. The family of sets being chosen from is written down before any selection is made and does not depend on the earlier selections, which is precisely the situation countable choice covers and dependent choice (def-dependent-choice) is not needed for. Everything after step 3.1 is canonical: at each stage the construction takes the **least** admissible index in the listing already fixed.

As always on this page, the claim is an upper bound on the cost of the proof given here, not an assertion that $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is necessary for the theorem.

[F4] [[lem-probability-laws-on-a-compact-metric-space-have-weakly-convergent-subsequences]]: Assume AC. Every sequence of Borel probability laws on a compact metric K has a subsequence converging weakly to a Borel probability on K.

[F5] [[thm-portmanteau-theorem]]: For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

[F6] [[thm-continuity-from-below-for-measures]]: Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

[F7] [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]: Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

## Proof

**Given:** The objects, hypotheses and definitions in the statement. Its conclusions are to be established below.

1.1 The empty family satisfies both definitions vacuously. Otherwise fix a compatible complete metric on S. By F1 there is a homeomorphic embedding e into $H=[0,1]^{\mathbb N}$. H has complete metric $\rho(x,y)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}2^{-(j+1)}|x_j-y_j|$ by F2. It is totally bounded: choose an integer $N\ge1$ with tail $\sum_{j\ge N}2^{-(j+1)}<\eta/2$ and a finite mesh in coordinates $0,\ldots,N-1$ with weighted error below $\eta$/2, putting zero in later coordinates. AC restricted to countable nonempty families gives the countable choice required by F3, which makes H compact. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Assume tightness and take any sequence $\mu_n$ in the family. Push it forward by e. F4 gives a subsequence $\nu_{n_j}=e_*\mu_{n_j}\Rightarrow\nu$ on H. For every integer $m\ge1$, choose compact $K_m$ in S with all $\mu_n$($K_m$)>1-1/m. Their images are compact and closed in H, so F5 gives $\nu(e(K_m))\ge\limsup_j\nu_{n_j}(e(K_m))\ge1-1/m$. Hence the Borel set $E=\bigcup_{m\ge1}e(K_m)\subseteq e(S)$ has $\nu$ mass one. [F4, F5]

1.3 For Borel B in S, e(B) is Borel relative to e(S). Since E is ambient Borel and contained in e(S), $E\cap e(B)$ is Borel in H. Define $\mu(B)=\nu(E\cap e(B))$; disjoint unions are preserved and $\mu$(S)=$\nu$(E)=1. For closed F in S there is a closed Z in H with $Z\cap e(S)=e(F)$, by the relative topology. Then $\mu_{n_j}(F)=\nu_{n_j}(Z)$ and $\nu(Z)=\nu(Z\cap E)=\mu(F)$. The closed bound from F5 gives $\limsup_j\mu_{n_j}(F)\le\mu(F)$, hence weak convergence on S. This proves tightness implies relative sequential compactness without assuming e(S) is Borel. [F5]

1.4 For the reverse, let $U_i$ be any countable open cover of S. Fix $\varepsilon$>0. If no finite initial union works uniformly, AC selects $\mu_n$ in the family with $\mu_n(\bigcup_{i\le n}U_i)\le1-\varepsilon$. Relative sequential compactness gives a weakly convergent subsequence with probability limit $\mu$. For any fixed r, eventually $n_j$>=r, so for the fixed open set $G_r=\bigcup_{i\le r}U_i$ one has $\mu_{n_j}(G_r)\le1-\varepsilon$ eventually. The open bound in F5 yields $\mu(G_r)\le\liminf_j\mu_{n_j}(G_r)\le1-\varepsilon$. F6 as r tends to infinity would give $\mu$(S)<=1-$\varepsilon$, a contradiction. Thus a uniform finite initial union exists. [F5, F6]

2.1 Apply step 1.4 to the dense-center ball cover of radius $2^{-m}$ and loss $\varepsilon2^{-m-1}$ at each $m\ge1$. Let $C_m$ be the corresponding finite union of closed balls and $K=\bigcap_mC_m$. F7 bounds every $\mu$(S\K) by $\sum_m\varepsilon2^{-m-1}<\varepsilon$. K is closed in the complete S and is totally bounded: for any $\eta$ choose m with $2^{1-m}<\eta$ and select one point of K from each of the finitely many balls meeting it. These form an $\eta$-net. F3 makes K compact, proving tightness. [F3, F7, step 1.4] ∎

## Statement

For Hermitian $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, write their eigenvalues in
descending order with multiplicity as $\lambda_1(A)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n(A)$
and $\lambda_1(B)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n(B)$. Then, for every $j$,
$$|\lambda_j(A)-\lambda_j(B)|\le\|A-B\|_2.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Finite-dimensional Hermitian matrices $A,B$ and the operator $2$-norm.

[F1] A complex normal endomorphism has an orthonormal eigenbasis ([[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]).

[F2] For real self-adjoint matrices, Weyl's sum inequalities bound each ordered eigenvalue of a sum ([[thm-weyl-inequalities-for-self-adjoint-sums]]).

[F3] A real self-adjoint matrix has a real orthonormal eigenbasis ([[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]).

[F4] The operator $2$-norm is the supremum of $\|Ax\|_2$ over unit vectors and, for a real self-adjoint matrix, equals the largest absolute eigenvalue ([[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]], [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]).

## Proof


1.1 Write $A=R+iS$ with $R,S$ real. Hermitian symmetry gives $R^{\mathsf T}=R$ and $S^{\mathsf T}=-S$. Define $\mathcal R(A)=\begin{pmatrix}R&-S\\S&R\end{pmatrix}$ and $\Phi(x+iy)=(x,y)$. Direct multiplication gives $\Phi(Az)=\mathcal R(A)\Phi(z)$ and $\|\Phi(z)\|_2=\|z\|_2$; the transpose identities show $\mathcal R(A)$ is real symmetric. Applying the same construction to $A-B$ yields $\|\mathcal R(A)-\mathcal R(B)\|_2=\|A-B\|_2$ by the supremum definition in [F4]. [F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], $A=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1(A),\ldots,\lambda_n(A))U^*$ for a unitary $U$. Its realification is orthogonal, and the realification of the diagonal matrix has each $\lambda_j(A)$ twice on its diagonal. Therefore the descending eigenvalues of $\mathcal R(A)$ are $\lambda_1(A),\lambda_1(A),\ldots,\lambda_n(A),\lambda_n(A)$; the same holds for $B$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Put $M=\mathcal R(B)$, $N=\mathcal R(A-B)$, and $\delta=\|A-B\|_2$. By [F3] and step 1.1, every eigenvalue of the real symmetric $N$ lies in $[-\delta,\delta]$ using [F4]. Applying [F2] with the perturbation's largest eigenvalue for the upper bound and smallest eigenvalue for the lower bound gives $|\lambda_k(M+N)-\lambda_k(M)|\le\delta$ for every $k$. Taking $k=2j-1$ and using step 2.1 proves the claimed complex-Hermitian eigenvalue bound. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For each positive integer $n$, let $N_n$ be a positive integer with $N_n/n\to\kappa\in(0,\infty)$, let $X_n\in\mathbb C^{n\times N_n}$ have entries from one common iid law with mean zero, second absolute moment one and absolute value bounded by a fixed finite constant, and let $T_n$ be deterministic Hermitian positive semidefinite (self-adjoint with $v^*T_nv\ge0$ for every $v$) with uniformly bounded induced Euclidean operator norm and empirical eigenvalue measures $H_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{\lambda_i(T_n)}\Rightarrow H$. Let $x_n\in\mathbb C^n$ be deterministic unit vectors such that for every $w\in\mathbb C\setminus[0,\infty)$,
$$x_n^*(T_n-wI_n)^{-1}x_n\longrightarrow m_H(w):=\int_{[0,\infty)}(t-w)^{-1}\,dH(t).$$
For $A_n=N_n^{-1}T_n^{1/2}X_nX_n^*T_n^{1/2}$, define the directional spectral measure $\mu_n^{x_n}(B)=x_n^*\mathbf1_B(A_n)x_n$ for Borel $B\subseteq[0,\infty)$. Then almost surely $\mu_n^{x_n}\Rightarrow F_{c,H}$, where $c=\kappa^{-1}$ and $F_{c,H}$ is the probability measure characterized by
$$m_{c,H}(z)=\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{1}{t(1-c-czm_{c,H}(z))-z}\,dH(t),\qquad \operatorname{Im}z>0.$$

## Statement references

Bai, Miao, and Pan, Theorem 1 and complete Section 2 proof, printed pp. 8–16 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

Silverstein, Theorem 1.1 and complete Section 3 proof ([full paper PDF](https://jack.math.ncsu.edu/strong.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses, matrices, and directional measures in the Statement, including AC.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice permits a choice function for every family of nonempty sets ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] For Hermitian $A_n$ and unit $x_n$, the directional spectral measure is $\sum_{\lambda}\|P_\lambda x_n\|_2^2\delta_\lambda$ ([[def-sample-covariance-directional-spectral-measure]]).

[F2] This measure is a Borel probability because the spectral projections are orthogonal and sum to the identity ([[lem-hermitian-spectral-measure-is-probability]]).

[F3] The expected resolvent has deterministic equivalent $-(z(I+q_nT_n))^{-1}$, uniformly for deterministic unit-vector quadratic forms ([[lem-bounded-complex-resolvent-deterministic-equivalent]]).

[F4] The bounded-entry empirical spectral distribution converges almost surely to $F_{c,H}$ with the stated fixed-point transform ([[thm-general-population-sample-covariance-esd-limit-for-bounded-entries]]).

[F5] A bounded-entry directional resolvent quadratic form concentrates almost surely about its expectation ([[lem-bounded-complex-resolvent-quadratic-form-concentration]]).

[F6] Dominated convergence passes limits through integrals under a common integrable bound ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[F7] The normalized operator norm of bounded complex iid matrices is almost surely eventually bounded ([[lem-bounded-complex-iid-matrix-norm-bound]]).

[F8] Tight probability laws on a Polish space have weakly convergent subsequences under AC ([[thm-prokhorov-tightness-theorem-on-polish-spaces]]).

[F9] The Stieltjes transform uses $(t-z)^{-1}$ and determines a probability measure uniquely ([[def-stieltjes-transform-of-a-real-probability-measure]], [[lem-stieltjes-transform-inversion-and-uniqueness-on-the-real-line]]).

[F10] The nonzero eigenvalues of $Y^*Y$ and $YY^*$ agree with multiplicity ([[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]).

[F11] A Polish space is a separable topological space whose topology is induced by a complete metric ([[def-polish-space]]).

[F12] Weak convergence of Borel probabilities means convergence of integrals against every bounded continuous real-valued function ([[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]).

[F13] The operator norm is the maximum of $\|Av\|_2$ over unit vectors in the domain ([[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]).

## Proof

1.1 Fix $z\in\mathbb C^+$ and let $q_n(z)=\mathbb E[N_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(N_n^{-1}X_n^*T_nX_n-zI)^{-1}]$. By [F4], the empirical transforms of $A_n$ converge almost surely to $m_{c,H}(z)$; their absolute values are at most $1/\operatorname{Im}z$, so [F6] gives convergence of their expectations. By [F10], the nonzero eigenvalue equality for $A_n$ and $N_n^{-1}X_n^*T_nX_n$ gives $q_n=-(1-c_n)/z+c_n\mathbb E[n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(A_n-zI)^{-1}]$, with $c_n=n/N_n$. Hence $q_n(z)\to u(z):=-(1-c)/z+cm_{c,H}(z)$. [given, F4, F6, F9, F10, algebra]

2.1 For deterministic unit $x_n$, [F3] and [F5] yield $$x_n^*(A_n-zI)^{-1}x_n+\frac1z x_n^*(I+q_n(z)T_n)^{-1}x_n\longrightarrow0\quad\text{almost surely}.$$ The matrix inverses are uniformly bounded by $|z|/\operatorname{Im}z$ from the positive-measure resolvent estimate in the proof of [F3]. Since $T_n$ are uniformly bounded and $q_n\to u$, the resolvent identity gives $$\left\|(I+q_nT_n)^{-1}-(I+uT_n)^{-1}\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M(|z|/\operatorname{Im}z)^2|q_n-u|\longrightarrow0.$$ [given, F3, F5, F13, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $u\in\mathbb C^+$, $w=-1/u$ also lies in $\mathbb C^+$ and $(I+uT_n)^{-1}=u^{-1}(T_n-wI)^{-1}$. The population-resolvent hypothesis at this fixed $w$ therefore gives $x_n^*(I+uT_n)^{-1}x_n\to u^{-1}m_H(-1/u)$. By [F4], $m_{c,H}(z)=-z^{-1}\int(1+ut)^{-1}dH(t)=-[zu]^{-1}m_H(-1/u)$. Step 2.1 now proves $x_n^*(A_n-zI)^{-1}x_n\to m_{c,H}(z)$ almost surely for each fixed $z\in\mathbb C^+$. [given, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The resolvent in step 3.1 is the Stieltjes transform of $\mu_n^{x_n}$ by [F1]. Intersect the probability-one events over a countable dense subset of $\mathbb C^+$. By [F7], on this event the spectra of $A_n$ are eventually contained in one compact interval, so [F2] makes the directional measures a tight sequence of probabilities. The half-line is Polish: it is a closed subset of the complete real line with dense subset $\mathbb Q\cap[0,\infty)$, in the sense of [F11]. By [A1] and [F8], every subsequence has a weakly convergent further subsequence. Its transform agrees with $m_{c,H}$ on the dense set by step 3.1; continuity of Stieltjes transforms extends equality to all $\mathbb C^+$, and [F9] identifies that limit with $F_{c,H}$. Therefore every subsequence has the same further limit, which by the bounded-continuous-test definition [F12] proves $\mu_n^{x_n}\Rightarrow F_{c,H}$ almost surely. [given, A1, F1, F2, F7, F8, F9, F11, F12, F13, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite iid array of centered complex random variables with $\mathbb E|\xi_{11}|^2=\tau^2<\infty$ and $\mathbb E|\xi_{11}|^4<\infty$. For positive integers $n$, let $N_n$ be positive with $n/N_n\to c\in(0,\infty)$, and let $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{1\le i\le n,\,1\le j\le N_n}$. Then almost surely
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\|X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\sqrt{N_n}}\le(\sigma_R+\sigma_I)(1+\sqrt c),\qquad \sigma_R^2=\mathbb E(\operatorname{Re}\xi_{11})^2,\quad \sigma_I^2=\mathbb E(\operatorname{Im}\xi_{11})^2.$$
In particular, when $\tau^2=1$, the right side is at most $\sqrt2(1+\sqrt c)$.

## Statement references

Yin, Bai, and Krishnaiah, Theorem 3.1, as reconstructed in the current real finite-fourth-moment upper-edge supplier ([full paper PDF](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/BF00353874.pdf)).

Bai, Miao, and Pan, Section 2, printed pp. 12–16 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The common nested complex iid array and its centered finite-fourth-moment entry law.

[F1] Iid entries are independent and share one common distribution ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]).

[F2] For a real nested iid array with mean zero, variance one and finite fourth moment, $\limsup\lambda_{\max}(Z_n^{\mathsf T}Z_n/n)\le(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2$ almost surely when the number of columns divided by the number of rows tends to $\gamma>0$ ([[lem-largest-sample-covariance-eigenvalue-upper-bound]]).

[F3] The operator norm is the largest singular value, and the largest eigenvalue of $Z^*Z$ is its square ([[thm-operator-norm-is-the-largest-singular-value]], [[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]).

[F4] The operator norm is the maximum of $\|Av\|_2$ over unit vectors in the domain ([[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]).

## Proof

1.1 Write $\kappa_n=N_n/n\to1/c$, $\sigma_R^2=\mathbb E(\operatorname{Re}\xi_{11})^2$, and $\sigma_I^2=\mathbb E(\operatorname{Im}\xi_{11})^2$. Centering of $\xi_{11}$ makes both real coordinates centered, and $\sigma_R^2+\sigma_I^2=\tau^2$. If $\sigma_R>0$, the matrices $Z_n=\operatorname{Re}X_n/\sigma_R$ are upper-left blocks of one real iid array with mean zero, variance one and finite fourth moment. Applying [F2] with $\gamma=\kappa=1/c$ and then [F3] gives $$\limsup_n\frac{\|\operatorname{Re}X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\sqrt{N_n}}\le\sigma_R\frac{1+\sqrt\kappa}{\sqrt\kappa}=\sigma_R(1+\sqrt c)\quad\text{almost surely}.$$ If $\sigma_R=0$, the centered real part is zero almost surely, so the same bound holds. The identical argument for the imaginary part gives the bound with $\sigma_I$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The complex operator norm satisfies $\|X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|\operatorname{Re}X_n+i\operatorname{Im}X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|\operatorname{Re}X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\operatorname{Im}X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Intersecting the two probability-one events from step 1.1 proves the asserted limsup bound. Finally, $\sigma_R+\sigma_I\le\sqrt{2(\sigma_R^2+\sigma_I^2)}=\sqrt2\tau$ by Cauchy–Schwarz, giving the unit-variance consequence. [given, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

The real edge application uses the current local upper-edge proof for the same top-left nested blocks, finite-fourth-moment law, dimension ratio and normalization. The complex-to-real reduction and triangle bound are proved above.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite iid array of complex random variables with $\mathbb E\xi_{11}=0$, $\mathbb E|\xi_{11}|^2=1$, and $\mathbb E|\xi_{11}|^4<\infty$. For each positive integer $n$, let $N_n$ be positive with $n/N_n\to c\in(0,\infty)$ and let $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{1\le i\le n,\,1\le j\le N_n}$ be its upper-left block. Let $T_n$ be deterministic Hermitian positive semidefinite with uniformly bounded operator norm and empirical eigenvalue measures $H_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{\lambda_i(T_n)}\Rightarrow H$. Let $x_n\in\mathbb C^n$ be deterministic unit vectors such that, for every $w\in\mathbb C\setminus[0,\infty)$,
$$x_n^*(T_n-wI_n)^{-1}x_n\longrightarrow m_H(w):=\int_{[0,\infty)}(t-w)^{-1}\,dH(t).$$
Define $A_n=N_n^{-1}T_n^{1/2}X_nX_n^*T_n^{1/2}$ and $\mu_n^{x_n}(B)=x_n^*\mathbf1_B(A_n)x_n$ for Borel $B\subseteq[0,\infty)$. Then almost surely $\mu_n^{x_n}$ converges weakly to the probability measure $F_{c,H}$ whose Stieltjes transform is the unique $m\in\mathbb C$ satisfying $\operatorname{Im}m>0$, $u=-(1-c)/z+cm$ with $\operatorname{Im}u>0$, and
$$m=\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{1}{t(1-c-czm)-z}\,dH(t),\qquad \operatorname{Im}z>0.$$

## Statement references

Bai, Miao, and Pan, Theorem 1 and complete Section 2 proof, printed pp. 8–16 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

Silverstein, Theorem 1.1 and complete Section 3 proof ([full paper PDF](https://jack.math.ncsu.edu/strong.pdf)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The common nested iid array, finite-fourth-moment law, deterministic population matrices and directions, aspect ratio, and AC in the Statement.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice permits a choice function for every family of nonempty sets ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] For bounded complex iid entries with the stated population and direction hypotheses, the directional measures converge almost surely to $F_{c,H}$ ([[thm-directional-sample-covariance-resolvent-limit-for-bounded-entries]]).

[F2] A centered complex iid finite-fourth-moment array satisfies $\limsup\|X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}/\sqrt{N_n}\le\sqrt2(1+\sqrt c)$ almost surely ([[lem-complex-sample-covariance-norm-bound-from-real-edge]]).

[F3] A Hermitian directional spectral measure is a probability law ([[lem-hermitian-spectral-measure-is-probability]]).

[F4] Tight probability laws on a Polish space have weakly convergent subsequences under AC ([[thm-prokhorov-tightness-theorem-on-polish-spaces]]).

[F5] Equal Stieltjes transforms determine probability measures on the real line ([[lem-stieltjes-transform-inversion-and-uniqueness-on-the-real-line]]).

[F6] A Polish space is a separable topological space whose topology is induced by a complete metric ([[def-polish-space]]).

[F7] Iid entries are mutually independent and share one common law ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]).

[F8] The directional measure is $\sum_\lambda\|P_\lambda x_n\|_2^2\delta_\lambda$ for a deterministic unit vector ([[def-sample-covariance-directional-spectral-measure]]).

[F9] The Stieltjes transform convention is $m_\mu(z)=\int(t-z)^{-1}d\mu(t)$ on $\mathbb C^+$ ([[def-stieltjes-transform-of-a-real-probability-measure]]).

[F10] Weak convergence means convergence of integrals against all bounded continuous real-valued functions ([[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]).

[F11] The operator norm is the maximum of $\|Av\|_2$ over unit vectors in the domain ([[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]).

## Proof

1.1 Let $\xi$ have the common entry law. For integer $K$, set $\xi^{(K)}=\xi\mathbf1_{\{|\xi|\le K\}}-\mathbb E[\xi\mathbf1_{\{|\xi|\le K\}}]$, $\sigma_K^2=\mathbb E|\xi^{(K)}|^2$, and $\Delta^{(K)}=\xi-\xi^{(K)}$. Then $\sigma_K\to1$, and $\tau_K^2:=\mathbb E|\Delta^{(K)}|^2\to0$ because $\mathbb E\xi=0$ and $\mathbb E|\xi|^2<\infty$. For all sufficiently large $K$, $\sigma_K>0$; put $\zeta^{(K)}=\xi^{(K)}/\sigma_K$. These entries are centered, bounded, iid and have unit second absolute moment, while $\Delta^{(K)}$ is centered iid with finite fourth moment. At matrix level, $X_n=\sigma_K Z_n^{(K)}+D_n^{(K)}$, where $Z_n^{(K)}$ and $D_n^{(K)}$ are the common upper-left blocks formed from $\zeta^{(K)}$ and $\Delta^{(K)}$. [given, F1, F2, F7, algebra]

2.1 For each fixed sufficiently large integer $K$, [F2] applied to the original, standardized, and residual arrays gives almost surely $$\limsup_n\frac{\|X_n\|}{\sqrt{N_n}}\le C_c,\quad \limsup_n\frac{\|Z_n^{(K)}\|}{\sqrt{N_n}}\le C_c,\quad \limsup_n\frac{\|D_n^{(K)}\|}{\sqrt{N_n}}\le C_c\tau_K,$$ where $C_c=\sqrt2(1+\sqrt c)$. Intersect these events over the countable set of such $K$. Writing $A_n^{(K)}=N_n^{-1}T_n^{1/2}Z_n^{(K)}Z_n^{(K)*}T_n^{1/2}$, the identity $UU^*-VV^*=(U-V)U^*+V(U-V)^*$ yields $$\limsup_n\|A_n-\sigma_K^2A_n^{(K)}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M C_c^2(1+\sigma_K)\tau_K, \qquad \limsup_n\|\sigma_K^2A_n^{(K)}-A_n^{(K)}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M C_c^2|\sigma_K^2-1|,$$ where $M=\sup_n\|T_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. For positive semidefinite $B,C$ and $z\in\mathbb C^+$, the resolvent identity gives $\|(B-zI)^{-1}-(C-zI)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|B-C\|_{\mathrm{op}}/(\operatorname{Im}z)^2$. [given, F2, F11, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix $z\in\mathbb C^+$ and a deterministic unit direction sequence $x_n$. For each such $K$, [F1] applied to $Z_n^{(K)}$ gives $x_n^*(A_n^{(K)}-zI)^{-1}x_n\to m_{c,H}(z)$ almost surely, with the transform convention [F9]. By step 2.1, $$\limsup_n\left|x_n^*(A_n-zI)^{-1}x_n-m_{c,H}(z)\right|\le\frac{M C_c^2}{(\operatorname{Im}z)^2}\left((1+\sigma_K)\tau_K+|\sigma_K^2-1|\right)$$ on the probability-one event obtained by intersecting the events from step 2.1 with the almost-sure convergence event for this fixed truncation level. The right side tends to zero as $K\to\infty$, so the directional Stieltjes transforms converge almost surely at every fixed $z\in\mathbb C^+$. Intersecting over a countable dense set gives simultaneous convergence there. [given, F1, F9, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F2], $\|A_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M\|X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2/N_n$ is almost surely eventually bounded. Thus the directional laws are eventually supported on one compact interval; [F3] makes them probability measures and [F8] gives their exact spectral-measure meaning. They are therefore tight. The half-line is Polish: it is closed in the complete real line and has dense subset $\mathbb Q\cap[0,\infty)$, as required by [F6]. By [A1] and [F4], each subsequence has a weakly convergent further subsequence. Its transform equals $m_{c,H}$ on the dense set by step 3.1; continuity of Stieltjes transforms extends equality to $\mathbb C^+$, and [F5] identifies the subsequential limit as $F_{c,H}$. The bounded-continuous-test definition [F10] yields the stated weak convergence. Every subsequence has the same further limit, proving the asserted almost-sure limit. [given, A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F8, F10, F11, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

Bai, Miao, and Pan, Theorem 1 and Section 2, printed pp. 8–16 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)). The sampling convention is the upper-left block of one iid double array.
