## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite iid array of real random variables with mean zero, variance one and finite fourth moment. For each $n$, let $p_n$ be a positive integer with $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)\setminus\{1\}$ and let $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{1\le i\le n,\,1\le j\le p_n}$ be the upper-left block. Let $\beta_n\in\mathbb R^{p_n}$ be deterministic with $\|\beta_n\|_2=r>0$. Let $\varepsilon_n\in\mathbb R^n$ have independent centered components of variance $\sigma^2$, independent of $X_n$ (so its covariance is $\sigma^2I_n$), and let $z_{0,n}\in\mathbb R^{p_n}$ be independent of $(X_n,\varepsilon_n)$ with mean zero and covariance  $I_{p_n}$. Set $y_n=X_n\beta_n+\varepsilon_n$, $\widehat\beta_n=X_n^+y_n$, and $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$. Define the design-conditional prediction risk by $\mathcal R_n=\mathbb E_{\varepsilon_n,z_{0,n}}[(z_{0,n}^{\mathsf T}\widehat\beta_n-z_{0,n}^{\mathsf T}\beta_n)^2\mid X_n]$. If $\gamma<1$, then almost surely $\mathcal R_n\to\sigma^2\gamma/(1-\gamma)$. If $\gamma>1$, then almost surely $\mathcal R_n\to r^2(1-1/\gamma)+\sigma^2/(\gamma-1)$.

## Statement references

Hastie, Montanari, Rosset, and Tibshirani, Theorem 1 and Appendix C.2 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.08560)).

Bai, Miao, and Pan, Theorem 1 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The nested real iid design, deterministic signal, independent centered noise with covariance $\sigma^2I_n$, and AC in the Statement.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice permits a choice function for every family of nonempty sets ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[A2] The noise vector is independent of the design, centered, and has covariance $\sigma^2I_n$ as stated.

[A3] The test feature is independent of the design and noise, centered, and has covariance $I_{p_n}$ as stated.

[F1] The Moore–Penrose inverse $X^+$ is characterized by the four Penrose equations ([[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]]).

[F2] $X^+X$ and $XX^+$ are orthogonal projections with ranges $\operatorname{Ran}(X^+)$ and $\operatorname{Ran}(X)$, respectively ([[lem-moore-penrose-products-are-orthogonal-projectors]]).

[F3] Positive covariance eigenvalues are squared positive singular values divided by the sample size, and their number is the matrix rank ([[thm-singular-value-decomposition]], [[cor-rank-equals-number-of-nonzero-singular-values]]).

[F4] For the nested design, the smallest positive covariance eigenvalue has limit $(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2$ for $\gamma<1$ and $(\sqrt\gamma-1)^2$ for $\gamma>1$, with eventual full rectangular rank ([[thm-smallest-positive-eigenvalue-sample-covariance-edge]]).

[F5] The empirical spectral distribution of $S_n$ converges almost surely to the Marchenko–Pastur law with aspect ratio $\gamma$ ([[thm-marchenko-pastur-law-for-sample-covariance]]).

[F6] The directional spectral measure of $S_n$ in each deterministic unit direction converges almost surely to the isotropic specialization $F_{\gamma,\delta_1}$ ([[thm-directional-sample-covariance-resolvent-limit]]).

[F7] The Marchenko–Pastur probability law has an atom $(1-1/\gamma)_+$ at zero, positive support $[(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2,(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2]$, and transform satisfying $1+zm=m/(1+\gamma m)$ ([[def-marchenko-pastur-measure]], [[lem-marchenko-pastur-formula-defines-a-finite-measure]]).

[F8] Weak convergence gives convergence of integrals against every bounded continuous test function ([[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]).

[F9] The isotropic limit $F_{\gamma,\delta_1}$ equals the Marchenko–Pastur law: both Stieltjes transforms solve the same fixed-point equation, and the solution is unique ([[lem-deformed-mp-fixed-point-solution-is-unique]], [[lem-marchenko-pastur-formula-defines-a-finite-measure]]).

[F10] Dominated convergence passes limits through integrals under an integrable majorant ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[F11] Iid entries are independent and share one common law ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]).

## Proof

1.1 Put $P_{\ker X_n}=I_{p_n}-X_n^+X_n$. For any fixed $v\in\mathbb R^{p_n}$, $\mathbb E_{z_{0,n}}(z_{0,n}^{\mathsf T}v)^2=v^{\mathsf T}\mathbb E[z_{0,n}z_{0,n}^{\mathsf T}]v=\|v\|_2^2$, so the stated prediction risk equals $\mathbb E_{\varepsilon_n}[\|\widehat\beta_n-\beta_n\|_2^2\mid X_n]$. By [F2], $P_n:=X_n^+X_n$ is an orthogonal projection. The Penrose equation $X_nX_n^+X_n=X_n$ shows $\ker(P_n)=\ker(X_n)$: if $X_nv=0$, then $P_nv=0$, and if $P_nv=0$, then $X_nv=X_nX_n^+X_nv=X_nP_nv=0$. Hence $\operatorname{Ran}(P_n)=\ker(X_n)^\perp=\operatorname{Ran}(X_n^{\mathsf T})$ by the right-singular-vector basis in [F3], so $\widehat\beta_n-\beta_n=-P_{\ker X_n}\beta_n+X_n^+\varepsilon_n$. Conditional on $X_n$, the cross term has expectation zero because $\mathbb E[\varepsilon_n\mid X_n]=0$. Its noise contribution is $$\mathbb E_{\varepsilon_n}\|X_n^+\varepsilon_n\|_2^2=\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}(X_n^+(X_n^+)^{\mathsf T})=\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}((X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n)^+)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\operatorname{tr}(S_n^+),$$ where the middle equality follows by writing an SVD and the last uses $(aB)^+=a^{-1}B^+$ for $a>0$. With $x_n=\beta_n/r$, this proves the exact identity $$\mathcal R_n=r^2x_n^{\mathsf T}P_{\ker X_n}x_n+\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\operatorname{tr}(S_n^+).$$ [given, A2, A3, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Suppose $\gamma<1$ and set $a=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2>0$. By [F4], $X_n$ has full column rank eventually and every eigenvalue of $S_n$ is at least $a/2$ eventually. Thus the bias term in step 1.1 is zero and $p_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(S_n^+)=\int f(t)d\mu_n(t)$ for the bounded continuous function $f(t)=1/\max(t,a/2)$. By [F5] and [F8], this converges to $J_\gamma=\int t^{-1}d\mu_\gamma(t)$, since the Marchenko–Pastur support is bounded below by $a$. For $s>0$, define $m_\gamma(-s)=\int(t+s)^{-1}d\mu_\gamma(t)$. The integrands are bounded by $1/a$ and converge pointwise to $1/t$, so [F10] gives $m_\gamma(-s)\to J_\gamma$ as $s\downarrow0$. The fixed-point equation in [F7], initially stated for $z\in\mathbb C^+$, extends to $z=-s<0$ by dominated convergence in its defining integral; its denominator stays nonzero because $1+\gamma m_\gamma(-s)>0$. Taking $s\downarrow0$ yields $1+(\gamma-1)J_\gamma=0$, hence $J_\gamma=1/(1-\gamma)$. Since $p_n/n\to\gamma$, step 1.1 gives $\mathcal R_n\to\sigma^2\gamma/(1-\gamma)$. [given, A1, F4, F5, F7, F8, F10, F11, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $\gamma>1$ and set $a=(\sqrt\gamma-1)^2>0$. By [F4], $X_n$ has full row rank eventually, $S_n$ has exactly $p_n-n$ zero eigenvalues, and all positive eigenvalues are at least $a/2$ eventually. The continuous function $g(t)=\max(1-2t/a,0)$ equals one at zero and vanishes on the positive spectrum for all sufficiently large $n$. Hence $x_n^{\mathsf T}P_{\ker X_n}x_n=\int g(t)d\mu_n^{x_n}(t)\to\int g(t)dF_{\gamma,\delta_1}(t)=1-1/\gamma$ by [F6], [F7], and [F9]; [F9] identifies the limit with $\mu_\gamma$, on whose positive support $g=0$ and whose zero atom has mass $1-1/\gamma$. Define $h(0)=0$ and, for $t>0$, $h(t)=t^{-1}\min(1,\max(0,4t/a-1))$. This is bounded and continuous, equals zero at zero, and equals $1/t$ for $t\ge a/2$. Therefore $p_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(S_n^+)=\int h(t)d\mu_n(t)\to J_\gamma^+:=\int_{(0,\infty)}t^{-1}d\mu_\gamma(t)$ by [F5] and [F8]. [F7] gives $m_\gamma(-s)=(1-1/\gamma)/s+J_\gamma^++o(1)$ as $s\downarrow0$: subtract the zero atom and use [F10] by dominated convergence on the positive support, whose lower endpoint is $a>0$. To compute the constant term, write $\alpha=1-1/\gamma$ and substitute $m=\alpha/s+J_\gamma^++o(1)$ into $1+(\gamma-1-s)m-\gamma s m^2=0$, the fixed-point equation at $z=-s$ (again obtained by dominated convergence from [F7]). The coefficient of $s^{-1}$ vanishes because $\gamma\alpha=\gamma-1$; the constant term is $1-\alpha-(\gamma-1)J_\gamma^++o(1)$. It must vanish, so $J_\gamma^+=1/[\gamma(\gamma-1)]$. Using $p_n/n\to\gamma$ in step 1.1 proves $\mathcal R_n\to r^2(1-1/\gamma)+\sigma^2/(\gamma-1)$. [given, A1, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. A matrix $B\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is a
**Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse** of $A$ when

$$ABA=A,\qquad BAB=B,$$

and the two square products are self-adjoint:

$$ (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$

When such a matrix exists and is unique, it is denoted by $A^+$.

The four displayed relations are the **Penrose equations**. They are written in
the matrix product and adjoint conventions of
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] and
[[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]].

## Statement

Let $M\in\mathbb F^{p\times q}$ be any finite real or complex matrix, and let $M^\dagger$ be its unique Moore-Penrose inverse. Then $P=MM^\dagger$ and $Q=M^\dagger M$ are self-adjoint idempotents. The range of $P$ is $\operatorname{Ran}(M)$, and the range of $Q$ is $\operatorname{Ran}(M^\dagger)$. Thus both are orthogonal projections. If $M$ has full row rank, then $MM^\dagger=I_p$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite matrix $M\in\mathbb F^{p\times q}$ over $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

[F1] [[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]]: $M^\dagger$ satisfies $MM^\dagger M=M$, $M^\dagger M M^\dagger=M^\dagger$, and both $MM^\dagger$ and $M^\dagger M$ are self-adjoint.

[F2] [[thm-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse-exists-and-is-unique]]: every finite real or complex matrix has a unique matrix satisfying the four Moore-Penrose equations.
 
## Proof

1.1 By [F1], $P^*=P$ and $Q^*=Q$. Also $P^2=MM^\dagger MM^\dagger=M(M^\dagger M M^\dagger)=MM^\dagger=P$, and $Q^2=M^\dagger M M^\dagger M=(M^\dagger M M^\dagger)M=M^\dagger M=Q$. Hence both products are self-adjoint idempotents. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The range of $P$ is contained in $\operatorname{Ran}(M)$ because $P=MM^\dagger$, while $PM=M$ by [F1], so $\operatorname{Ran}(M)\subseteq\operatorname{Ran}(P)$. Thus $\operatorname{Ran}(P)=\operatorname{Ran}(M)$. The range of $Q$ is contained in $\operatorname{Ran}(M^\dagger)$, and $QM^\dagger=M^\dagger$ by [F1], so these ranges are equal. [F1, step 1.1]

3.1 A self-adjoint idempotent is the orthogonal projection onto its range: each vector $x$ decomposes as $Px+(I-P)x$, the first term lies in the range, the second lies in the kernel, and self-adjointness makes the range orthogonal to the kernel. The same argument applies to $Q$. If $M$ has full row rank, $\operatorname{Ran}(M)=\mathbb F^p$, so step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{Ran}(P)=\mathbb F^p$ and therefore $P=I_p$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Under the hypotheses of the sample-covariance resolvent deterministic-equivalent theorem, for each fixed $s>0$ the directional measures satisfy
$$\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{1}{t+s}\,d\mu_n^{x_n}(t)\longrightarrow\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{1}{t+s}\,dF_{c,H}(t)\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

## Statement references

Bai, Miao, and Pan, Theorem 1, printed pp. 8–9 ([full paper PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1720)).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses and directional measures in the Statement.

[F1] The directional measures converge almost surely weakly to $F_{c,H}$ ([[thm-directional-sample-covariance-resolvent-limit]]).

[F2] Weak convergence means convergence of integrals against every bounded continuous real-valued function ([[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]).

[F3] The directional spectral measure is $\sum_\lambda\|P_\lambda x_n\|_2^2\delta_\lambda$ for a deterministic unit vector ([[def-sample-covariance-directional-spectral-measure]]).

## Statement

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonnegative simple measurable function $s$.

[L1] The nonnegative integral is the supremum of the simple integrals of all simple minorants $0\le u\le s$ ([[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

[L2] The simple integral is monotone on nonnegative simple functions ([[prop-basic-properties-of-the-nonnegative-simple-integral]]).

[L3] The simple integral itself is well defined on every nonnegative simple function ([[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]], [[lem-well-definedness-of-the-simple-integral]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The function $s$ is one of its own admissible simple minorants, so [L1] gives $$\int s\,d\mu\ge\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$ [given, L1, L3]

1.2 If $u$ is any admissible simple minorant of $s$, then $u\le s$, so [L2] gives $$\int_{\mathrm{simple}} u\,d\mu\le\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$ Taking the supremum over all such $u$ in [L1] yields the reverse inequality. [L1, L2, L3]

2.1 The two inequalities from steps 1.1 and 1.2 give equality of the nonnegative and simple integrals on $s$. [step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Definition

For positive integers $n,p$, a real design matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$,
and a response vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, the **ridgeless minimum-norm
least-squares estimator** is

$$\widehat\beta:=X^+y.$$

Equivalently, it is the unique vector of smallest Euclidean norm among all
minimisers of $u\mapsto\|Xu-y\|_2^2$. The word *ridgeless* means that this
least-squares objective has no added positive quadratic penalty
$\lambda\|u\|_2^2$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Positive integers $n,p$, $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$, and
$y\in\mathbb R^n$.

[F1] The Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse $X^+$ is the unique matrix satisfying the
four Penrose equations ([[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]]).

[F2] For every finite real matrix $X$ and vector $y$, $X^+y$ is the unique
least-squares minimiser of minimum Euclidean norm
([[thm-a-plus-b-is-the-unique-minimum-norm-least-squares-solution]]).

## Verification

1.1 The existence-and-uniqueness theorem [F2] makes $X^+$ well-defined for this finite matrix; [F1] fixes the four equations that define it. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 By [F2], this vector is exactly the unique minimum-norm least-squares solution, which verifies the equivalent characterization. [given, F2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let
$\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^d[a_j,a_j+L]$ be a closed cube with
$L>0$, and let $U_1,U_2,\ldots$ be independent random vectors, each distributed
according to normalized Lebesgue measure on $\Omega$. For $n\ge1$, define the
Euclidean fill distance

$$h_n:=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\min_{1\le i\le n}\|x-U_i\|_2.$$

There are constants $C_d=2\sqrt d\,2^{1/d}$ and $n_d$ such that, for every
$n\ge n_d$,

$$\mathbb P\!\left\{h_n\le C_dL\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{1/d}\right\} \ge1-\frac1n.$$

## Statement references

[[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]

[[thm-finite-union-bound]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the cube $\Omega$, dimension $d$, and independent
uniform sample $U_1,U_2,\ldots$ as in the Statement.

[A1] Countable Choice means every countable family of nonempty sets has a
choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] Lebesgue outer measure agrees with volume on half-open boxes
([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]],
[[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]).

[F2] The probability of a finite union of events is at most the sum of their
probabilities ([[thm-finite-union-bound]]).

[F3] Independence means mutual independence of the whole family of random
elements ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]).

[F4] Under Countable Choice, Lebesgue measure is a complete measure extending
volume on half-open boxes, and every coordinate hyperplane is measurable
and null ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]],
[[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]]).

## Proof

1.1 For $n$ large enough that $t_n:=(n/(2\log n))^{1/d}\ge2$, put $m_n=\lfloor t_n\rfloor$ and partition each coordinate interval of $\Omega$ into $m_n$ equal half-open intervals, closing the last interval at its right endpoint. This gives $m_n^d$ disjoint cells covering $\Omega$. Each cell differs from a half-open box with the same coordinate bounds only on its boundary faces, which lie in finitely many coordinate hyperplanes. By [F4] those hyperplanes and every subset of their union are measurable and null, so each cell is measurable and has the same measure as that half-open box, namely $(L/m_n)^d$ by [F1]. The same argument for the boundary of $\Omega$ gives $\lambda_d(\Omega)=L^d$. Hence normalized Lebesgue measure assigns each cell probability $(L/m_n)^d/L^d=m_n^{-d}$. [given, A1, F1, F4, construct]

2.1 For a fixed cell, independence [F3] gives probability $(1-m_n^{-d})^n\le e^{-n/m_n^d}$ that it is empty. By [F2], the probability that some cell is empty is at most $m_n^d e^{-n/m_n^d}\le n e^{-2\log n}=1/n$, because $m_n^d\le n/(2\log n)$ and hence $n/m_n^d\ge2\log n$. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 On the complementary event every cell contains a sample point. Every $x\in\Omega$ belongs to one cell, whose Euclidean diameter is $L\sqrt d/m_n$; therefore $h_n\le L\sqrt d/m_n$. Since $t_n\ge2$ implies $m_n=\lfloor t_n\rfloor\ge t_n/2$, we obtain $$h_n\le2L\sqrt d\left(\frac{2\log n}{n}\right)^{1/d} =C_dL\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{1/d}.$$ The event has probability at least $1-1/n$ by step 2.1. ## Statement

Let $n \ge 1$. **Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then Lebesgue outer measure $\lambda_n^*$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]) is an outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-outer-measure]]): it vanishes at $\varnothing$, is monotone, and is
countably subadditive.

**The agreement clause is a theorem of ZF and needs no choice principle:**
$\lambda_n^*(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every elementary set $A$
([[def-elementary-set-in-rn]]), where $\mu_0$ is elementary volume. In
particular $\lambda_n^*(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
and $\lambda_n^*(\varnothing) = 0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $n \ge 1$, the Axiom of Countable Choice, the premeasure $\mu_0$ on the algebra $\mathcal{E}_n$, and its induced outer set function $\lambda_n^*$.

[L1] $\lambda_n^*$ is the outer set function induced by the premeasure $\mu_0$ on the algebra $\mathcal{E}_n$ of elementary sets ([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]).

[L2] Elementary volume $\mu_0$ is a sigma-finite premeasure on $\mathcal{E}_n$ ([[thm-box-volume-is-a-premeasure-on-the-elementary-algebra]]).

[F1] Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The outer set function induced by a premeasure is an outer measure ([[cor-premeasure-induced-set-function-is-an-outer-measure]]).

[F2] For every $A\in\mathcal A_0$, the outer measure induced by a premeasure satisfies $\mu^*(A)=\mu_0(A)$ ([[lem-induced-outer-measure-agrees-with-premeasure]]).

[F3] An **outer measure** on a set $X$ is a function $\mu^*:\mathcal P(X)\to[0,+\infty]$ that vanishes at the empty set, is monotone, and is countably subadditive ([[def-outer-measure]]).

[F4] The **Axiom of Countable Choice** says that for every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Elementary volume is a premeasure on the algebra $\mathcal{E}_n$ of subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$, and $\lambda_n^*$ is by definition the outer set function it induces, so both [F1] and [F2] apply to this pair. [L1, L2]

1.2 Under the Axiom of Countable Choice, an induced outer set function is an outer measure, which is the first assertion. [F1, F3, F4]

1.3 The identity $\lambda_n^*(A)=\mu_0(A)$ on the source algebra is [F2], whose statement carries no choice hypothesis, so the agreement clause holds in ZF alone; applied to a half-open box $B$, which is elementary, it gives $\lambda_n^*(B)=\mu_0(B)=\operatorname{vol}(B)$, and applied to $\varnothing$ it gives $\lambda_n^*(\varnothing)=0$. [F2, L2]

2.1 Steps 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 together are the Statement. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

## Statement

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. **Degenerate boxes.** If $a_i \le b_i$ are reals with $a_{i_0} = b_{i_0}$ for
   some $i_0 < n$, then every set $R$ between the open box
   $\{x : a_i < x_i < b_i\ (i<n)\}$ and the closed rectangle $[a,b]$ is Lebesgue
   measurable with $\lambda_n(R) = 0$.
2. **Coordinate hyperplanes.** For $i_0 < n$ and a real $c$, the set
   $$H_{i_0,c} \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : x_{i_0} = c \,\}$$
   is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(H_{i_0,c}) = 0$.

At $n = 1$ the hyperplane $H_{0,c}$ is the singleton $\{c\}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $n \ge 1$, the Axiom of Countable Choice, an index $i_0<n$ and a real $c$.

[L1] Every set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(R) = \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i)$, and it gives measure $0$ to all of them whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[L2] Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure on it ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

[L3] Assuming countable choice, every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]).

[F1] For a measure $\mu$ and measurable $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$, $\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k)$ ([[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]).

[F2] $[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\}$ ([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]).

[F3] A measurable set $N\in\mathcal A$ is **$\mu$-null** if $\mu(N)=0$ ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]); a sigma-algebra is closed under countable unions ([[def-sigma-algebra]]).

[F4] Every complete ordered field $F$ is Archimedean: for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]).

[F5] $B(a,b) := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i \le b_i \ \text{ for every } i < n \,\}$ ([[def-half-open-box]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Claim 1 is the degenerate case of the box theorem, whose value $\prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i)$ carries the factor $b_{i_0}-a_{i_0}=0$. [L1, F2, F5]

1.2 For a natural number $k$ put $P_k := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : x_{i_0}=c \text{ and } |x_i| \le k \text{ for every } i \ne i_0 \,\}$. This is always the closed rectangle with sides $[-k,k]$ for $i \ne i_0$ and the degenerate side $[c,c]$ in coordinate $i_0$. [F2]

2.1 Each $P_k$ is Lebesgue measurable of measure $0$ by claim 1. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L2, F3]

2.2 The union $\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}P_k$ is $H_{i_0,c}$, since a point of the hyperplane has finitely many coordinates and the Archimedean property supplies a natural $k$ above each $|x_i|$ and above $|c|$. [step 1.2, F4]

3.1 Therefore $H_{i_0,c}$ is a countable union of measurable sets, hence measurable, and countable subadditivity gives $\lambda_n(H_{i_0,c}) \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lambda_n(P_k) = 0$; at $n=1$ the set $H_{0,c}$ is $\{c\}$. [step 2.1, step 2.2, L2, L3, F1, F3] ∎

## Statement

Let $n,p\ge1$, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ and $\beta\in\mathbb R^p$
be deterministic, and let $\varepsilon\in\mathbb R^n$ and
$z_0\in\mathbb R^p$ be independent of one another and of $X$, with
$\mathbb E\varepsilon=0$, $\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon)=\sigma^2I_n$,
$\mathbb Ez_0=0$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(z_0)=I_p$. Set
$y=X\beta+\varepsilon$, $\widehat\beta=X^+y$,
$S=X^{\mathsf T}X/n$, and
$$\mathcal R(X):=\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,z_0} \left[(z_0^{\mathsf T}(\widehat\beta-\beta))^2\mid X\right].$$
Then
$$\mathcal R(X)=\|(I_p-X^+X)\beta\|_2^2+ \sigma^2\operatorname{tr}((X^{\mathsf T}X)^+) =\|(I_p-X^+X)\beta\|_2^2+ \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\operatorname{tr}(S^+).$$

## Statement references

[[def-ridgeless-minimum-norm-regression]]

[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]]

[[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $X,\beta,\varepsilon,z_0$ and their moment and independence
assumptions from the Statement.

[A1] The noise is independent of $X$, centered, and has covariance
$\sigma^2I_n$, so these are also its conditional first and second moments given
$X$.

[A2] The test vector is independent of $(X,\varepsilon)$, centered, and has
covariance $I_p$, so its conditional second moment given $(X,\varepsilon)$ is
$I_p$.

[F1] Every finite real matrix has a singular value decomposition
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]).

[F2] The Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse exists uniquely and satisfies the four
Penrose equations ([[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]],
[[thm-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse-exists-and-is-unique]]).

## Proof

1.1 Write a rank-$q$ singular value decomposition $X=U_qD_qV_q^{\mathsf T}$ with positive diagonal $D_q$. The four Penrose equations and uniqueness [F2] give $X^+=V_qD_q^{-1}U_q^{\mathsf T}$, $I_p-X^+X=I_p-V_qV_q^{\mathsf T}$, and $X^+(X^+)^{\mathsf T}=V_qD_q^{-2}V_q^{\mathsf T}=(X^{\mathsf T}X)^+$; the last equality follows by checking the four equations for $X^{\mathsf T}X=V_qD_q^2V_q^{\mathsf T}$. The same decomposition gives $S^+=n(X^{\mathsf T}X)^+$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For any fixed $v\in\mathbb R^p$, [A2] gives $\mathbb E[(z_0^{\mathsf T}v)^2\mid X,\varepsilon] =v^{\mathsf T}I_pv=\|v\|_2^2$. Taking $v=\widehat\beta-\beta$ and then expectation over $\varepsilon$ reduces $\mathcal R(X)$ to $\mathbb E_\varepsilon[\|\widehat\beta-\beta\|_2^2\mid X]$. [given, A2, algebra]

2.1 Put $Q=I_p-X^+X$. From the definition of $\widehat\beta$, $\widehat\beta-\beta=-Q\beta+X^+\varepsilon$. Expanding the squared norm, the cross term has conditional expectation zero by [A1], and the noise term is $$\mathbb E_\varepsilon[\|X^+\varepsilon\|_2^2\mid X] =\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}(X^+(X^+)^{\mathsf T}) =\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}((X^{\mathsf T}X)^+),$$ using step 1.1. Combining with step 1.2 and the scaling identity in step 1.1 proves the two displayed risk formulas. [given, A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or
$\mathbb C$, there exists a unique matrix $A^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$
satisfying the four Penrose equations of
[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ with $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

[L1] $A$ admits a singular value decomposition $A=U\Sigma V^*$ with $U$ and $V$ unitary and $\Sigma$ diagonal with the nonzero singular values on the diagonal ([[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]).

[L2] The Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse is defined by the four Penrose equations ([[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], after choosing singular values $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_r>0$ one may write $$ A=U \begin{bmatrix} \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_r) & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} V^*. $$ [L1, given]

2.1 Define $$ \Sigma^+:= \begin{bmatrix} \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^{-1},\dots,\sigma_r^{-1}) & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad B:=V\Sigma^+U^*. $$ Then $\Sigma\Sigma^+\Sigma=\Sigma$, $\Sigma^+\Sigma\Sigma^+=\Sigma^+$, and the two products $\Sigma\Sigma^+$ and $\Sigma^+\Sigma$ are diagonal with only $0$ and $1$ on the diagonal, hence are self-adjoint. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Multiplying the relations of step 2.1 by the unitary factors $U$ and $V$ shows $$ ABA=A,\qquad BAB=B,\qquad (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$ Thus $B$ is a Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse of $A$ in the sense of [L2]. [L2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $C$ be any other Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse of $A$, and put $D:=V^*CU$. Then the same unitary transport used in step 3.1 gives $$ \Sigma D\Sigma=\Sigma,\qquad D\Sigma D=D, $$ with $\Sigma D$ and $D\Sigma$ self-adjoint. [L2, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Write $$ \Sigma=\begin{bmatrix}S&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad D=\begin{bmatrix}X&Y\\Z&W\end{bmatrix}, $$ where $S=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_r)$. From $\Sigma D\Sigma=\Sigma$ one gets $SXS=S$, hence $X=S^{-1}$. Because $\Sigma D$ is self-adjoint, its upper-right block satisfies $SY=0$, so $Y=0$. Because $D\Sigma$ is self-adjoint, its lower-left block satisfies $ZS=0$, so $Z=0$. With these identities, the equation $D\Sigma D=D$ reduces to $$ \begin{bmatrix}X&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}X&0\\0&W\end{bmatrix}, $$ so $W=0$. Hence $D=\Sigma^+$ and therefore $C=V\Sigma^+U^*=B$. [step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Step 3.1 gives existence and step 5.1 gives uniqueness, so every finite real or complex matrix has a unique Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse. [step 3.1, step 5.1] ∎

## Statement

For each integer $d\ge1$ there are constants $A>1$ and $\kappa>0$ with the following property. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be any closed cube of positive side length $L$, including a rotated cube, and let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\subset\Omega$ be finite and nonempty. Define its Euclidean fill distance by
$$h_X=\sup_{z\in\Omega}\min_{1\le j\le m}\|z-x_j\|_2.$$
For every integer $n\ge1$ with $2nh_X/L\le\kappa$, every real polynomial $p$ of total degree at most $n$ satisfies
$$\sup_{z\in\Omega}|p(z)|\le A^n\max_{1\le j\le m}|p(x_j)|.$$
Moreover, for each $x\in\Omega$ there exist real coefficients $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m$, independent of $p$, such that simultaneously for all such polynomials
$$p(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_jp(x_j),\qquad \sum_{j=1}^m|\lambda_j|\le A^n.$$
No separation or Cartesian arrangement of the points is assumed. No choice principle is required.

## Statement references

[Rieger, Theorem 4.2.1](https://d-nb.info/994624026/34)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The dimension $d$, cube $\Omega$ of side length $L>0$, finite nonempty sample set $X$, and integer $n\ge1$ from the Statement. Total degree is the maximum sum of exponents of a monomial with nonzero coefficient.

[F1] Every closed bounded subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space is compact, with no choice principle needed ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[F2] A continuous image of a compact metric space is compact, without a choice principle ([[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]).

[F3] A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact metric space attains its maximum and minimum, without a choice principle ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

[F4] Euler's formula identifies $e^{it}=\cos t+i\sin t$, with $|e^{it}|=1$, and the derivatives of sine and cosine are cosine and minus sine ([[thm-eulers-formula]], [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]]).

## Proof

1.1 We first prove that for every real univariate polynomial $r$ of degree at most $N\ge1$, $$|r'(u)|\le\frac{100N}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\sup_{-1\le v\le1}|r(v)|\qquad(-1<u<1).$$ For $m\ge1$ define the finite trigonometric polynomial $$F_m(t)=\sum_{|k|<m}(1-|k|/m)e^{ikt}=\frac1m\left|\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}e^{ijt}\right|^2=\frac{\sin^2(mt/2)}{m\sin^2(t/2)}.$$ Here $i^2=-1$; the square identity follows by expanding the finite sum and counting pairs of indices with a prescribed difference, and the last identity follows from the finite geometric series, with continuous values at multiples of $2\pi$. For $|t|\le1/m$, differentiate the finite Fourier sum to obtain $|F'_m(t)|\le\sum_{|k|<m}|k|(1-|k|/m)\le m^2$. For $1/m\le|t|\le\pi$, differentiating the sine quotient gives $$|F'_m(t)|\le\frac{\pi^2}{t^2}+\frac{\pi^3}{m|t|^3},$$ because $|\sin(t/2)|\ge|t|/\pi$. This sine bound follows on $[0,\pi/2]$ by concavity of sine, whose second derivative is $-\sin\le0$, applied to the chord joining $(0,0)$ and $(\pi/2,1)$; symmetry gives the negative arguments. [given, F4, algebra]

1.2 Put $Q=[-1,1]^d$ and $Q_c=[-1/2,1/2]^d$. For a univariate polynomial of degree at most $n$, interpolate at $t_j=-1/2+j/n$ for $0\le j\le n$. The interpolation identity holds because its difference from the polynomial has degree at most $n$ and $n+1$ distinct roots; the root bound follows by successively factoring each distinct root. For $|t|\le1$ the absolute value of the $j$th Lagrange polynomial is at most $(3/2)^n n^n/(j!(n-j)!)$: numerator factors are at most $3/2$ and its denominator has absolute value $n^{-n}j!(n-j)!$. Summing these bounds gives $(3n)^n/n!\le(3e)^n$, where $$\log(n!)=\sum_{j=1}^n\log j\ge\int_1^n\log t\,dt=n\log n-n+1$$ proves $n!\ge(n/e)^n$. Applying this univariate estimate in each coordinate in turn, and taking suprema after each application, shows for every polynomial $p$ of total degree at most $n$ that $$\|p\|_Q\le R^n\|p\|_{Q_c},\qquad R=(3e)^d,$$ since its degree in each separate coordinate is at most $n$. Here and below $\|p\|_E=\sup_{z\in E}|p(z)|$. [given, algebra]

2.1 Integrating the bounds of step 1.1 over $[-\pi,\pi]$, with the near-zero interval contributing at most $2m$ and the other terms bounded by extending their elementary integrals to infinity, gives $$\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|F'_m(t)|\,dt\le\frac{2+2\pi^2+\pi^3}{2\pi}m\le20m.$$ For $m=1$ this also holds because $F_1=1$. Define $V_N=2F_{2N}-F_N$. Its Fourier coefficients for every $|k|\le N$ equal $1$: for $|k|<N$ they are $2(1-|k|/(2N))-(1-|k|/N)$, and for $|k|=N$ they are $2(1/2)$. For any trigonometric polynomial $T$ of degree at most $N$, integration of finite sums, using $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{ikt}\,dt=0$ for nonzero integer $k$ and $2\pi$ for $k=0$, therefore gives $$T(t)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}T(s)V_N(t-s)\,ds.$$ Differentiating this finite-sum identity and using periodicity and the integral bound yields $\|T'\|_\infty\le100N\|T\|_\infty$. Taking $T(t)=r(\cos t)$, a trigonometric polynomial of degree at most $N$ by expansion of powers of cosine, and using $T'(t)=-\sin(t)r'(\cos t)$ proves the inequality announced in step 1.1. All integrals here integrate continuous finite trigonometric sums or the displayed elementary bounds. [F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Define constants depending only on $d$ by $$a=(3/4)^d,\quad\delta=\min\{1/4,a/(8R)\},\quad G=600\sqrt d/\sqrt\delta,\quad\kappa=\min\{\delta/2,1/(2G)\},\quad A=2R/a.$$ Let $Y\subset Q$ be finite and nonempty with Euclidean fill distance $\eta$ and $n\eta\le\kappa$. The zero polynomial satisfies the desired inequality, so fix nonzero $p$ of degree at most $n$ and set $$q(u)=p(u)\prod_{i=1}^d(1-u_i^2)^n,\qquad S=\|q\|_Q,\qquad M=\max_{y\in Y}|p(y)|.$$ The coordinate degrees of $q$ are at most $3n$. On $Q_c$ its product weight is at least $a^n$, so $S\ge a^n\|p\|_{Q_c}>0$. The last inequality holds because a polynomial vanishing on a box with nonempty interior vanishes identically: fix all but one coordinate in the interior and apply the univariate root bound, then repeat in each coordinate. If some $|u_i|\ge1-\delta$, then $1-u_i^2\le2\delta$ while all other weight factors are at most $1$, and step 1.2 implies $$|q(u)|\le(2\delta)^n\|p\|_Q\le(2\delta R)^n\|p\|_{Q_c}\le(1/4)^nS<S.$$ The maximum of $|q|$ is attained on $Q$ by compactness and the extreme value theorem, so a maximizer $u_*$ lies in $[-1+\delta,1-\delta]^d$. [F1, F3, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 Take $y\in Y$ with $\|y-u_*\|_2\le\eta$; such a point exists because the minimum over the finite set is attained and is at most its supremum $\eta$. Since $\eta\le\kappa\le\delta/2$, the segment from $u_*$ to $y$ lies where every coordinate has absolute value at most $1-\delta/2$. Apply step 2.1 to each univariate coordinate slice of $q$, of degree at most $3n$ and norm at most $S$ on $[-1,1]$. At each point of this segment it gives $$|\partial_iq|\le\frac{300nS}{\sqrt{\delta-\delta^2/4}}\le\frac{600nS}{\sqrt\delta},\qquad\|\nabla q\|_2\le GnS.$$ Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus to the univariate polynomial $t\mapsto q(u_*+t(y-u_*))$: it follows directly here by integrating each power in this finite polynomial. [step 2.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, choose, algebra]

4.1 Fix $x\in Q$, enumerate $Y=\{y_1,\ldots,y_m\}$, and let $v(u)\in\mathbb R^D$ be the vector of all monomials in $u$ of total degree at most $n$, in any fixed order, where $D$ is their finite number. Let $K$ be the convex hull of $\{v(y_j),-v(y_j):1\le j\le m\}$. More explicitly it is the image of the closed bounded simplex of $2m$ nonnegative real coordinates summing to $1$, under the continuous map taking these coordinates to the corresponding weighted sum of these $2m$ vectors. Thus $K$ is nonempty and compact, and is convex because convex combinations of two sets of simplex weights remain simplex weights. Suppose $v(x)\notin A^nK$. The continuous squared distance from $v(x)$ attains a minimum at some $z\in A^nK$; put $b=v(x)-z\ne0$. For each $w\in A^nK$ the segment $z+t(w-z)$, $0\le t\le1$, lies in $A^nK$. Its squared distance to $v(x)$ equals $$\|b\|_2^2-2t\,b\mathbin\cdot(w-z)+t^2\|w-z\|_2^2.$$ Minimality at $t=0$ forces $b\mathbin\cdot(w-z)\le0$, since a strictly positive value would make this displayed expression smaller for sufficiently small positive $t$. [F1, F2, F3, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Therefore $b\mathbin\cdot z$ is the maximum of the linear functional $b\mathbin\cdot w$ on $A^nK$. A linear functional on this convex hull has maximum equal to the largest of its values on its finite generators: every convex weighted average is at most that largest value and that value is attained at a generator. Consequently $$b\mathbin\cdot v(x)=b\mathbin\cdot z+\|b\|_2^2>A^n\max_{1\le j\le m}|b\mathbin\cdot v(y_j)|.$$ This contradicts step 3.1 applied to the polynomial $u\mapsto b\mathbin\cdot v(u)$, because $x\in Q$. 6.1 Finally choose orthonormal coordinates along the edges of $\Omega$, with its center as origin, and multiply these coordinates by $2/L$. Composition in either direction preserves total polynomial degree because each coordinate is affine linear. The condition in the Statement is exactly $n\eta\le\kappa$. All selections made in the proof are finite or individual existential choices, so no choice axiom is used. [step 3.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every real $\theta$, $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real $\theta$.

[L1] [[def-complex-exponential]] defines $\exp z$ as the sum of the complex series with terms $z^n/n!$, where the factorial is embedded in the complex field.

[L2] [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]] states that for every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.

[L3] [[thm-direct-comparison-test]] states that if $0\le u_n\le v_n$ eventually and $\sum v_n$ converges, then $\sum u_n$ converges.

[L4] [[thm-absolute-convergence-of-complex-series]] states that every absolutely convergent complex series converges.

[L5] [[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]] states that a sequence in $\mathbb R^2$ converges exactly when each coordinate sequence converges.

[L6] [[lem-series-linearity]] states that convergent real series add and scale termwise, with the corresponding sums.

[L7] [[thm-grouping-of-series]] states that a convergent real series may be grouped into consecutive finite blocks without changing its sum.

[L8] [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]] defines sine and cosine by the real series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k\theta^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$ and $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k\theta^{2k}/(2k)!$.

[L9] [[def-complex-integer-powers]] defines natural complex powers by $z^0=1$ and $z^{n+1}=z^nz$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Put $a_n=(i\theta)^n/n!$, and define the parity masks by $e_n=a_n$ for even $n$ and $e_n=0$ for odd $n$, while $o_n=0$ for even $n$ and $o_n=a_n$ for odd $n$. By [L1] and [L2], $\sum a_n$ converges absolutely and has sum $\exp(i\theta)$. [L1, L2, construct]

1.2 Induction from $i^2=-1$ and the recursion in [L9] gives $i^{2k}=(-1)^k$ and $i^{2k+1}=i(-1)^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$. Hence $e_{2k}=(-1)^k\theta^{2k}/(2k)!$, $e_{2k+1}=0$, $o_{2k}=0$, and $o_{2k+1}=i(-1)^k\theta^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$. [L9, algebra]

2.1 Since $0\le|e_n|\le|a_n|$ and $0\le|o_n|\le|a_n|$, [L3] shows that both modulus series converge. Thus $\sum e_n$ and $\sum o_n$ are absolutely convergent and hence converge by [L4]. [L3, L4, step 1.1]

3.1 By [L5], the two coordinate series of $e$ and $o$ converge. Since $a_n=e_n+o_n$, applying [L6] in each coordinate gives $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e_n+\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}o_n$. [L5, L6, step 2.1]

3.2 Apply [L7] to each real coordinate series of $e$, with consecutive blocks $[2k,2k+2)$. By step 1.2 the real-coordinate blocks are $(-1)^k\theta^{2k}/(2k)!$ and the imaginary-coordinate blocks are $0$. Therefore [L8] identifies $\sum e_n=\cos\theta$. [L5, L7, L8, step 2.1, step 1.2]

3.3 Apply the same coordinatewise grouping to $o$. Its real-coordinate blocks are $0$ and its imaginary-coordinate blocks are $(-1)^k\theta^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$, so [L8] gives $\sum o_n=i\sin\theta$. [L5, L7, L8, step 2.1, step 1.2]

4.1 Substitute steps 3.2 and 3.3 into step 3.1 and use step 1.1: $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 3.3] ∎

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Reals $x,y$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Apply the addition law to $x+iy$ and Euler's formula. [given]

1.2 Multiplicativity of modulus, the Pythagorean identity, and positivity of $e^x$ give the modulus formula. [given]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a fixed closed cube with
positive side length, let $\sigma>0$, and set
$k_\sigma(x,z)=\exp(-\|x-z\|_2^2/(2\sigma^2))$ on $\Omega$. Let
$\mathcal H_\sigma$ be its real reproducing-kernel Hilbert space. For a finite
nonempty set $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\subset\Omega$, define its Euclidean fill
distance and Gaussian power function by
$$h_X:=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\min_{1\le j\le m}\|x-x_j\|_2,\qquad P_X(x):=\inf_{v\in\operatorname{span}\{k_\sigma(\cdot,x_j):1\le j\le m\}} \|k_\sigma(\cdot,x)-v\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}.$$
There are constants $C,c,h_0>0$, depending only on $d,\Omega,\sigma$, such
that every such $X$ with $0<h_X\le h_0$ satisfies
$$\sup_{x\in\Omega}P_X(x)\le C\exp\!\left(-c\frac{|\log h_X|}{h_X}\right).$$

## Statement references

[Rieger and Zwicknagl, Theorem 6.1 and proof](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s10444-008-9089-0.pdf)

[Belkin, Hsu, Ma, and Mandal, Appendix A, Theorem 1 and proof sketch](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1812.11118)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Gaussian kernel, cube $\Omega$, and real RKHS
$\mathcal H_\sigma$ from the Statement.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice says every countable sequence of nonempty
sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The Gaussian radial function is a real positive semidefinite kernel on
$\mathbb R^d$ ([[ex-gaussian-radial-kernel]]).

[F2] Under Countable Choice a real positive semidefinite kernel has a canonical
RKHS with the stated reproducing property
([[thm-canonical-rkhs-construction-and-reproducing-property]]).

[F3] The finite-dimensional span in the definition has a unique orthogonal
projection in a real inner-product space
([[lem-finite-dimensional-projection-in-a-real-inner-product-space]]).

[F4] There are $A>1$ and $\kappa>0$, depending only on $d$, such that on any closed cube of side length $L>0$, if a finite nonempty sample set has fill distance $h$ and $2nh/L\le\kappa$ for an integer $n\ge1$, then at each $x$ there are real coefficients $\lambda_j$ reproducing all polynomials of total degree at most $n$ with $\sum_j|\lambda_j|\le A^n$ ([[lem-dense-cube-polynomial-norming-and-reproduction]]).

## Proof

1.1 Let $z_c$ be the center of $\Omega$, let $L>0$ be its side length, and use orthonormal coordinates along its edges, writing $u(z)$ for the coordinates of $z-z_c$. These coordinates preserve distances and give $\|u(z)\|_2\le B=L\sqrt d/2$ for every $z\in\Omega$. Put $t=B^2/\sigma^2>0$. For a multi-index $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$, write $|\alpha|=\sum_i\alpha_i$, $\alpha!=\prod_i\alpha_i!$, and $u^\alpha=\prod_i u_i^{\alpha_i}$, and define $$\Phi_\alpha(z)=\exp(-\|u(z)\|_2^2/(2\sigma^2))\frac{u(z)^\alpha}{\sigma^{|\alpha|}\sqrt{\alpha!}}.$$ Multiplying the convergent exponential power series in the $d$ coordinates yields $$\sum_\alpha\Phi_\alpha(z)\Phi_\alpha(w)=e^{-(\|u(z)\|_2^2+\|u(w)\|_2^2)/(2\sigma^2)}e^{u(z)\cdot u(w)/\sigma^2}=k_\sigma(z,w).$$ The series is absolutely convergent, since replacing each coordinate product by its absolute value gives the finite value $e^{-(\|u(z)\|_2^2+\|u(w)\|_2^2)/(2\sigma^2)}\exp(\sum_i|u_i(z)u_i(w)|/\sigma^2)$. In particular the vector $\Phi(z)=(\Phi_\alpha(z))_\alpha$ is square summable with squared norm $k_\sigma(z,z)=1$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For any finite set of points $z_1,\ldots,z_q\in\Omega$ and real coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_q$, the reproducing property gives $$\left\|\sum_{j=1}^qa_jk_\sigma(\cdot,z_j)\right\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2=\sum_{j,l=1}^qa_ja_lk_\sigma(z_j,z_l)=\left\|\sum_{j=1}^qa_j\Phi(z_j)\right\|_{\ell^2}^2.$$ The second equality follows from step 1.1 by interchanging a finite sum with an absolutely convergent series. Thus this norm identity concerns finite kernel combinations and requires no description of the whole Gaussian RKHS or extension of its functions to $\mathbb R^d$. The RKHS used here is available under the stated Countable Choice hypothesis. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Fix $X$ as in the Statement, set $h=h_X$, and for now choose an integer $n\ge1$ such that $2nh/L\le\kappa$. Fix any $x\in\Omega$ and take coefficients $\lambda_j$ from [F4]. Define real coefficients $$b_j=\lambda_j\exp\left(\frac{\|u(x_j)\|_2^2-\|u(x)\|_2^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).$$ Then $\sum_j|b_j|\le e^{t/2}A^n$. For every $|\alpha|\le n$, the polynomial $z\mapsto u(z)^\alpha$ has total degree at most $n$, so reproduction implies $$\sum_jb_j\Phi_\alpha(x_j)=\frac{e^{-\|u(x)\|_2^2/(2\sigma^2)}}{\sigma^{|\alpha|}\sqrt{\alpha!}}\sum_j\lambda_ju(x_j)^\alpha=\Phi_\alpha(x).$$ Consequently all coordinates of $\Phi(x)-\sum_jb_j\Phi(x_j)$ with $|\alpha|\le n$ vanish. [F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.3 Write $\Phi_{>n}(z)$ for the coordinates with $|\alpha|>n$. Expanding $(\sum_i u_i(z)^2/\sigma^2)^r$ by multiplication shows that its monomial coefficient at multi-index $\alpha$ of size $r$ is $r!/\alpha!$: it counts the ordered $r$ choices of coordinates with the prescribed multiplicities. Hence $$\|\Phi_{>n}(z)\|_{\ell^2}^2=e^{-\|u(z)\|_2^2/\sigma^2}\sum_{r=n+1}^{\infty}\frac{(\|u(z)\|_2^2/\sigma^2)^r}{r!}\le\sum_{r=n+1}^{\infty}\frac{t^r}{r!}.$$ If $n+2\ge2t$, the ratio of any successive terms in the last tail is at most $1/2$, so summing the geometric majorant gives $$\sum_{r=n+1}^{\infty}\frac{t^r}{r!}\le\frac{2t^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\le2\left(\frac{et}{n+1}\right)^{n+1}.$$ For the final inequality, $\log(q!)=\sum_{j=1}^q\log j\ge\int_1^q\log s\,ds=q\log q-q+1$ for every integer $q\ge1$, and exponentiation yields $q!\ge(q/e)^q$. Thus the bound holds uniformly for every $z\in\Omega$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F3], the infimum defining $P_X(x)$ is attained by orthogonal projection onto the finite section span. The vector $\sum_j b_jk_\sigma(\cdot,x_j)$ is in that span, so its error norm is an upper bound for $P_X(x)$. Steps 2.1 and 2.2 show that its error norm is $\|\Phi_{>n}(x)-\sum_jb_j\Phi_{>n}(x_j)\|_{\ell^2}$. Apply the triangle inequality to these finitely many square-summable vectors and use steps 2.2 and 2.3 to obtain $$P_X(x)\le\sqrt2(1+e^{t/2}A^n)\left(\frac{et}{n+1}\right)^{(n+1)/2}.$$ The $\ell^2$ triangle inequality here can be obtained from the finite Euclidean triangle inequality on every initial finite collection of multi-indices and then passing to the supremum of their squared partial sums; thus no additional choice principle is involved. The bound is independent of $x$, and holds whenever $n\ge1$, $2nh/L\le\kappa$, and $n+2\ge2t$. [given, F3, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 Put $D=\kappa L/2>0$ and $n=\lfloor D/h\rfloor$. For all sufficiently small $h>0$ this integer satisfies $n\ge1$, $n+2\ge2t$, and $D/(2h)\le n\le D/h$; the lower bound follows from $\lfloor s\rfloor\ge s/2$ for $s\ge2$. Also $2nh/L\le\kappa$. Since $1+e^{t/2}A^n\le2e^{t/2}A^n$, the logarithm of the positive bound in step 3.1 is at most $$-\frac12(n+1)\log(n+1)+K(n+1),$$ where one may take $K=1+\frac32\log2+t/2+\log A+\frac12|\log(et)|>0$. Decrease $h_0>0$ until for all $0<h\le h_0$ the preceding integer conditions hold, $h<1$, $\log(n+1)\ge4K$, and $\log(n+1)\ge\frac12|\log h|$. Such an $h_0$ exists because $n\ge D/(2h)$ implies $\log(n+1)\ge|\log h|+\log(D/2)$, which tends to infinity and eventually exceeds $|\log h|/2$. [F4, step 3.1, choose, algebra]

5.1 For $0<h\le h_0$ the exponent in step 4.1 is at most $-(n+1)\log(n+1)/4$, and hence at most $-D|\log h|/(16h)$, by the two lower bounds for $n$ and $\log(n+1)$. Therefore step 3.1 gives, uniformly in $x\in\Omega$, $$P_X(x)\le\exp\left(-\frac D{16}\frac{|\log h|}{h}\right).$$ Taking the supremum over $x$ proves the Statement with $c=D/16$ and $C=1$, and also with any larger positive $C$. All constants depend only on $d$, $\Omega$, and $\sigma$. Countable Choice was used only through the canonical RKHS supplier in step 2.1; the reproduction and feature estimates add no further choice assumption. [step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

be a fixed closed cube with positive side length, let $\sigma>0$, and let

$x_1,x_2,\ldots$ be an iid sequence uniform on $\Omega$. For every

$$\sup_{x\in\Omega}|h(x)-h^*(x)|\le A\exp\!\left(-B\left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right)^{1/d}\right) (\|h^*\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}+\|h\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}).$$

[Belkin, Hsu, Ma, and Mandal, Appendix A, Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1812.11118)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the Gaussian RKHS $\mathcal H_\sigma$, target
$h^*$, and iid uniform sample from the Statement.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice says every countable sequence of nonempty
sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The Gaussian radial function is a real positive semidefinite kernel
([[ex-gaussian-radial-kernel]]).

[F2] Under Countable Choice, a real positive semidefinite kernel has a
canonical RKHS with the stated reproducing property
([[thm-canonical-rkhs-construction-and-reproducing-property]]).

[F3] A real RKHS has sections $k_x=k(\cdot,x)$ and satisfies
$\langle f,k_x\rangle=f(x)$ for every function $f$ in that space
([[def-positive-semidefinite-kernels-and-reproducing-kernel-hilbert-spaces]]).

[F4] The Gaussian power function has the stated bound
([[lem-gaussian-rbf-power-function-fill-distance-bound]]).

[F5] An iid uniform sample on a fixed product cube has Euclidean fill distance at most
$C_dL(\log n/n)^{1/d}$ with probability at least $1-1/n$
([[lem-iid-uniform-fill-distance-rate]]).

[F6] Every finite-dimensional subspace of a real inner-product space admits an
orthogonal projection ([[lem-finite-dimensional-projection-in-a-real-inner-product-space]]).

[F7] Under Countable Choice, an invertible linear map with matrix $Q$
sends Lebesgue measurable sets to measurable sets and multiplies their
measure by $|\det Q|>0$; translations preserve measurability and measure
([[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]],
[[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]).

## Proof

1.1 By [A1], [F1], and [F2], the Gaussian kernel has the real RKHS used in the Statement, with evaluation property [F3]. Let $X_n=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$ and $V_n=\operatorname{span}\{k_\sigma(\cdot,x_i):1\le i\le n\}$. For any interpolant $h$, put $g=h-h^*$. Then $g(x_i)=0$, so [F3] gives $\langle g,k_\sigma(\cdot,x_i)\rangle=0$ for each $i$ and hence $g\perp V_n$. By [F6] the projection $\Pi_{V_n}$ exists; therefore $$g(x)=\langle g,k_\sigma(\cdot,x)\rangle =\langle g,k_\sigma(\cdot,x)-\Pi_{V_n}k_\sigma(\cdot,x)\rangle.$$ The inner-product Cauchy--Schwarz inequality follows by expanding $\|u-tv\|^2\ge0$ and minimizing over real $t$ (with the zero-vector case immediate). Thus $|g(x)|\le\|g\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}P_{X_n}(x)$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, algebra]

2.1 The triangle inequality gives $\|g\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}\le\|h\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}+\|h^*\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}$. Taking the supremum in step 1.1 yields $$\sup_{x\in\Omega}|h(x)-h^*(x)|\le (\|h\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}+\|h^*\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}) \sup_{x\in\Omega}P_{X_n}(x).$$ [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Write $\Omega=v+Q[0,L]^d$ using its side length $L>0$ and an orthogonal matrix $Q$, and put $u_i=Q^{\mathsf T}(x_i-v)$. The affine map $F(u)=v+Qu$ bijects the product cube $C_0=[0,L]^d$ onto $\Omega$. For every Borel $E\subseteq C_0$, [F7] gives $\mathbb P(u_i\in E)=\lambda_d(F(E))/\lambda_d(\Omega)=|\det Q|\lambda_d(E)/(|\det Q|\lambda_d(C_0))=\lambda_d(E)/\lambda_d(C_0)$. The transformed samples remain independent: for finitely many Borel sets $E_i\subseteq C_0$, their joint event is $\bigcap_i\{x_i\in F(E_i)\}$, and independence of the $x_i$ makes its probability the product of the individual probabilities. These events are measurable since $F$ is a homeomorphism. Also $\|F(u)-F(w)\|_2=\|u-w\|_2$, so the fill distance of $\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}$ in $C_0$ equals $h_{X_n}$ in $\Omega$. By [F5], on an event of probability at least $1-1/n$, the fill distance $h_{X_n}$ is at most $\bar h_n=C_dL(\log n/n)^{1/d}$. For all sufficiently large $n$, $\bar h_n<\min(h_0,e^{-1})$; the function $u\mapsto|\log u|/u$ is decreasing on $(0,e^{-1}]$, so [F4] applies and gives $$\sup_xP_{X_n}(x)\le C\exp\!\left(-c\frac{|\log h_{X_n}|}{h_{X_n}}\right) \le C\exp\!\left(-\frac{c}{\bar h_n}\right) =C\exp\!\left(-\frac{c}{C_dL}\left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right)^{1/d}\right).$$ Using this bound in step 2.1 proves the displayed estimate with $A=C$ and $B=c/(C_dL)$, uniformly for every interpolant on that event. [given, A1, F4, F5, F7, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite iid
array of real random variables with mean zero, variance one, and finite fourth
moment. Let $p_n\ge1$ with $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)\setminus\{1\}$, and
let $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{1\le i\le n,\,1\le j\le p_n}$ be its upper-left block.
Let $\varepsilon_n$ have independent centered components of variance
$\sigma^2$, independent of $X_n$, and let $z_{0,n}$ be independent of
$(X_n,\varepsilon_n)$, centered, and have covariance $I_{p_n}$. Set
$S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$, $y_n=\varepsilon_n$,
$\widehat\beta_n=X_n^+y_n$, and
$$\mathcal R_n:=\mathbb E_{\varepsilon_n,z_{0,n}} \left[(z_{0,n}^{\mathsf T}\widehat\beta_n)^2\mid X_n\right].$$
Then almost surely
$$\mathcal R_n\longrightarrow \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{\sigma^2\gamma}{1-\gamma},&0<\gamma<1,\\[5pt] \displaystyle\frac{\sigma^2}{\gamma-1},&\gamma>1. \end{cases}$$

## Statement references

[[lem-ridgeless-risk-decomposition]]

[[cor-isotropic-minimum-norm-risk-closure-under-edge-gap]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The nested real iid design, positive aspect ratio $\gamma\ne1$,
independent centered noise with covariance $\sigma^2I_n$, centered test feature
with covariance $I_{p_n}$, and the Axiom of Choice from the Statement.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice permits a choice function for every family of
nonempty sets ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] For the nested real iid finite-fourth-moment design and every deterministic
signal sequence of fixed norm $r>0$, the design-conditional risk tends almost
surely to $\sigma^2\gamma/(1-\gamma)$ for $\gamma<1$ and to
$r^2(1-1/\gamma)+\sigma^2/(\gamma-1)$ for $\gamma>1$
([[cor-isotropic-minimum-norm-risk-closure-under-edge-gap]]).

[F2] The conditional risk for a deterministic signal is its squared projection
onto $\ker X_n$ plus the signal-independent noise term
([[lem-ridgeless-risk-decomposition]]).

[F3] Iid entries are independent and share one common distribution
([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]).

## Proof

1.1 For each $n$, let $e_{1,n}$ be the first standard basis vector in $\mathbb R^{p_n}$. For $a\in\{1,2\}$, let $\mathcal R_n^{(a)}$ denote the conditional risk with signal $\beta_n^{(a)}=a e_{1,n}$, and put $B_n=e_{1,n}^{\mathsf T}(I-X_n^+X_n)e_{1,n}$ and $V_n=(\sigma^2/n)\operatorname{tr}(S_n^+)$. [given, choose]

2.1 Applying [F2] to each auxiliary signal gives $\mathcal R_n^{(1)}=B_n+V_n$ and $\mathcal R_n^{(2)}=4B_n+V_n$. Applying [F1] with norms $1$ and $2$ gives almost-sure limits for both risks; the intersection of these two probability-one events still has probability one. The iid law is common in both applications by [F3]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The exact identities in step 2.1 give $V_n=(4\mathcal R_n^{(1)}-\mathcal R_n^{(2)})/3$. If $\gamma<1$, both risk limits in [F1] equal $\sigma^2\gamma/(1-\gamma)$, so $V_n$ tends to that quantity. If $\gamma>1$, their limits are respectively $1-1/\gamma+\sigma^2/(\gamma-1)$ and $4(1-1/\gamma)+\sigma^2/(\gamma-1)$; their indicated combination is $\sigma^2/(\gamma-1)$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For the zero signal in the Statement, [F2] identifies $\mathcal R_n$ with the same $V_n$. Step 3.1 therefore gives both asserted limits. [given, F2, step 3.1] ∎

$S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$,

$$B_n\longrightarrow0,\qquad V_n\longrightarrow\frac{\sigma^2\gamma}{1-\gamma},$$
and if $\gamma>1$,
$$B_n\longrightarrow r^2\left(1-\frac1\gamma\right),\qquad V_n\longrightarrow\frac{\sigma^2}{\gamma-1}.$$

## Example

For fixed signal norm $r\ge0$, noise standard deviation $\sigma\ge0$, and
aspect ratio $\gamma>0$, $\gamma\ne1$, the limiting risk has bias and variance
components
$$\begin{array}{c|cc} &\text{bias}&\text{variance}\\ 0<\gamma<1&0&\displaystyle\frac{\sigma^2\gamma}{1-\gamma}\\[5pt] \gamma>1&\displaystyle r^2\left(1-\frac1\gamma\right)& \displaystyle\frac{\sigma^2}{\gamma-1}. \end{array}$$
When $\sigma>0$, the underparameterized branch increases from limit $0$ as
$\gamma\downarrow0$ to $+\infty$ as $\gamma\uparrow1$. On the
overparameterized side its variance decreases to $0$, and its bias increases
to $r^2$. When $\sigma>0$, the total overparameterized risk is strictly
decreasing if $r\le\sigma$, and if $r>\sigma$ it has a unique minimum at
$\gamma_*=r/(r-\sigma)$. If $\sigma=0$, the underparameterized risk is $0$;
the overparameterized risk is $r^2(1-1/\gamma)$ and is strictly increasing
when $r>0$. The one-sided risk curves diverge at $\gamma=1$ only when
$\sigma>0$; no risk limit at $\gamma=1$ is asserted. For $\sigma>0$ the
global infimum over $\gamma\ne1$ is $0$, approached as $\gamma\downarrow0$
and not attained; if $r=0$, it is also approached as $\gamma\to\infty$. For
$\sigma=0$, the minimum $0$ is attained throughout $0<\gamma<1$.

## Example references

[[lem-isotropic-minimum-norm-risk-components]]

[[thm-isotropic-ridgeless-risk-across-interpolation-threshold]]

[Hastie, Montanari, Rosset, and Tibshirani, §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.08560)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $r\ge0$, $\sigma\ge0$, and $\gamma>0$ with $\gamma\ne1$.

[F1] The limiting bias and variance components are the two displayed branches
([[lem-isotropic-minimum-norm-risk-components]]).

## Verification

1.1 Summing the two components in [F1] gives the total risk $R(\gamma)=\sigma^2\gamma/(1-\gamma)$ for $0<\gamma<1$ and $R(\gamma)=r^2(1-1/\gamma)+\sigma^2/(\gamma-1)$ for $\gamma>1$. Differentiating the first expression gives $R'(\gamma)=\sigma^2/(1-\gamma)^2$, so it is strictly increasing for $\sigma>0$ and is identically zero for $\sigma=0$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 For $\gamma>1$, $$R'(\gamma)=\frac{r^2}{\gamma^2}-\frac{\sigma^2}{(\gamma-1)^2}.$$ If $\sigma>0$ and $r\le\sigma$, then $r/\gamma\le\sigma/\gamma<\sigma/(\gamma-1)$, so $R'<0$. If $r>\sigma>0$, the derivative vanishes exactly when $r(\gamma-1)=\sigma\gamma$, namely at $\gamma_*=r/(r-\sigma)>1$; it is negative before this point and positive after it, giving the unique minimum. If $\sigma=0$, the derivative is $r^2/\gamma^2$, which is positive for $r>0$ and zero for $r=0$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The limits at $\gamma\downarrow0$, $\gamma\uparrow1$, and $\gamma\to\infty$ follow directly from the formulas in [F1]. In particular, the singular terms at $\gamma=1$ vanish when $\sigma=0$ and diverge when $\sigma>0$. For $\sigma>0$ every finite-domain risk value is positive while the underparameterized branch tends to zero as $\gamma\downarrow0$, proving that its global infimum is $0$ and is not attained. When $\sigma=0$, the underparameterized branch equals $0$ identically. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $P,q\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^P$ be open, let $X$ be a set, and let $f:\Omega\times X\to\mathbb R^q$. Fix $\theta\in\Omega$ and suppose that for each $x\in X$ the map $\vartheta\mapsto f(\vartheta,x)$ is totally differentiable at $\theta$, meaning it has a linear first-order approximation with remainder $o(\|\vartheta-\theta\|_2)$. Write $D_\theta f(\theta,x)\in\mathbb R^{q\times P}$ for its derivative matrix in the standard Euclidean coordinates. The matrix-valued neural tangent kernel at $\theta$ is

$$K_\theta(x,x'):=D_\theta f(\theta,x)\,D_\theta f(\theta,x')^{T}\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}.$$

Equivalently, for $1\le a,b\le q$,
$$\bigl(K_\theta(x,x')\bigr)_{ab}=\sum_{p=1}^{P}\partial_{\theta_p}f_a(\theta,x)\,\partial_{\theta_p}f_b(\theta,x').$$
For a scalar-output model this is the scalar kernel $\sum_{p=1}^{P}\partial_{\theta_p}f(\theta,x)\partial_{\theta_p}f(\theta,x')$.

## Definition

Assume AC. Fix integers $L,n_0,\ldots,n_L\ge1$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and an activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. For each layer $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, let $W^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}\times n_\ell}$ and $b^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}}$. At initialization all entries of all matrices and bias vectors are mutually independent and each has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. These finite collections of entries have the corresponding finite-dimensional multivariate normal product law.

For an input $x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$, put $z^{(0)}(x)=x$ and, for $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, define the preactivation
$$u^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_\ell}}W^{(\ell)}z^{(\ell)}(x)+\beta b^{(\ell)}.$$
For $\ell+1<L$, set $z^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\sigma(u^{(\ell+1)}(x))$ coordinatewise; the output layer is linear and $f_\theta(x):=u^{(L)}(x)\in\mathbb R^{n_L}$. The parameter vector $\theta$ consists of every entry of the matrices and biases. The width $n_L$ is the fixed output dimension; the hidden widths are $n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1}$. A sequential hidden-width limit takes $n_1\to\infty$ first, then $n_2\to\infty$, and so on through $n_{L-1}\to\infty$.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\gamma$ be the standard Gaussian probability measure on $\mathbb R$ with density $\phi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$, let $H_m$ be the monic probabilists’ Hermite polynomial defined by $H_0=1$, $H_1(x)=x$, and $H_{m+1}(x)=xH_m(x)-mH_{m-1}(x)$, and put $h_m=H_m/\sqrt{m!}$. Then $(h_m)_{m\ge0}$ is a complete orthonormal basis of real $L^2(\gamma)$. Every $f\in L^2(\gamma)$ has the norm-convergent expansion $f=\sum_{m\ge0}a_mh_m$, where $a_m=\int f h_m\,d\gamma$, and $\sum_{m\ge0}a_m^2=\|f\|_{L^2(\gamma)}^2$. If $f$ is continuous and nonpolynomial, then $a_m\ne0$ for an unbounded set of indices $m$. Every globally Lipschitz real function belongs to $L^2(\gamma)$, so this conclusion applies to every globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation.

## Statement references

[Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler, Appendix A.4, Hermite expansion used in the sphere-positivity argument](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07572)

[MIT 18.102 Lecture 24, completeness of the Hermite-function basis (related treatment; the local proof below uses Gaussian Fourier uniqueness)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-102-introduction-to-functional-analysis-spring-2009/1826dc6d058501cc8fb679d7db07a785_MIT18_102s09_lec24.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the standard Gaussian measure $\gamma$; the monic probabilists’ Hermite polynomials $H_m$ and their normalized versions $h_m$.

[A1] AC is the axiom that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). It supplies countable choice for the Fourier uniqueness and $L^2$ completeness interfaces ([[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]]).

[F1] The standard Gaussian measure has Lebesgue density $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ ([[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]).

[F2] The $H_m$ are monic of degree $m$, orthogonal under $Z\sim N(0,1)$ with $\mathbb E[H_m(Z)H_n(Z)]=m!\,\delta_{mn}$, and span the polynomials degree by degree ([[def-monic-probabilists-hermite-polynomials]], [[lem-hermite-orthogonality-and-monomial-expansion]]).

[F3] Complex $L^2$ is complete under countable choice, and $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ is dense in Lebesgue $L^2(\mathbb R)$ ([[lem-complex-lp-completeness-density-and-inner-product]]).

[F4] With the convention $\widehat v(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R}v(x)e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\,dx$, the $L^1$ Fourier transform is well-defined and is unique: equal transforms of two $L^1$ functions imply equality almost everywhere ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]], [[cor-uniqueness-of-the-l-one-fourier-transform]]).

[F5] The complex exponential is its everywhere-convergent power series ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]).

[F6] For square-integrable real random variables, $\mathbb E|XY|\le(\mathbb E X^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E Y^2)^{1/2}$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]).

[F7] Pointwise convergence under one integrable majorant permits passage of integrals to the limit ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[F8] A standard normal variable has finite second moment ([[lem-standard-normal-fourth-moment]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $r\in L^2(\gamma)$ be orthogonal to every $h_m$. Each monomial $x^j$ is a finite linear combination of $H_0,\ldots,H_j$ by [F2], and each fixed polynomial is square-integrable under $\gamma$ because a polynomial times $e^{-x^2/2}$ has an integrable tail. Therefore $\int r(x)x^j\,d\gamma(x)=0$ for every $j\ge0$. [A1, F2, given]

1.2 Put $v(x)=r(x)\phi(x)$, so $v\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ by [F1] and [F6]. For every $a\ge0$, Cauchy–Schwarz and completion of the square give $\int |r(x)|e^{a|x|}\,d\gamma(x)\le\|r\|_2(\int e^{2a|x|}\,d\gamma)^{1/2}<\infty$, since each half-line integral is at most $e^{2a^2}$. [given, F1, F6]

2.1 Fix $\xi\in\mathbb R$. The partial sums $S_M(x)=\sum_{j=0}^M(-2\pi i\xi x)^j/j!$ converge pointwise to $e^{-2\pi i\xi x}$ and satisfy $|S_M(x)|\le e^{2\pi|\xi||x|}$ by [F5]. Applying [F7] with the integrable majorant from step 1.2 gives $\widehat v(\xi)=\lim_{M\to\infty}\int r(x)S_M(x)\,d\gamma(x)=0$, because every term is a scalar multiple of a zero moment from step 1.1. [F5, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 By [F4], $\widehat v=0$ implies $v=0$ Lebesgue-almost everywhere. Since $\phi(x)>0$ for all $x$, $r=0$ $\gamma$-almost everywhere. Thus the only $L^2(\gamma)$ function orthogonal to all the $h_m$ is zero. [A1, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 For arbitrary real $f\in L^2(\gamma)$, set $a_m=\int f h_m\,d\gamma$ and $S_M=\sum_{m=0}^M a_mh_m$. Orthogonality in [F2] gives $\|f-S_M\|_2^2=\|f\|_2^2-\sum_{m=0}^M a_m^2\ge0$ and, for $M>K$, $\|S_M-S_K\|_2^2=\sum_{K<m\le M}a_m^2$; hence the partial sums are Cauchy. View them in complex $L^2(\gamma)$; by [F3] and [A1] they converge there, and their limit is real because every $S_M$ is real. The residual $f-S$ is orthogonal to each $h_m$, hence zero by step 3.1. Therefore $f=S$ in $L^2(\gamma)$ and taking norms yields Parseval’s identity. [A1, F2, F3, step 3.1]

5.1 If only finitely many $a_m$ are nonzero, step 4.1 makes $f$ equal almost everywhere to a polynomial $p$. If $f$ is continuous and differs from $p$ at some point, it differs on a nonempty open interval, which has positive $\gamma$ measure by [F1]; hence $f=p$ everywhere, contrary to nonpolynomiality. Thus a continuous nonpolynomial $f$ has unbounded coefficient support. A globally Lipschitz $f$ obeys $|f(x)|\le |f(0)|+L|x|$; [F8] gives $\int |x|^2\,d\gamma<\infty$, so this growth bound implies $f\in L^2(\gamma)$. [F1, F8, step 4.1] ∎

## Definition

The **monic probabilists' Hermite polynomials** are the polynomials $H_m\in\mathbb R[x]$ defined by
$$H_0=1,\qquad H_1(x)=x,\qquad xH_m(x)=H_{m+1}(x)+m\,H_{m-1}(x)\quad(m\ge1).$$
The recurrence is solved for the higher polynomial, $H_{m+1}(x)=xH_m(x)-mH_{m-1}(x)$, so it determines $H_m$ uniquely by induction on $m$. Each $H_m$ is monic of degree $m$: $H_2=x^2-1$, $H_3=x^3-3x$ and $H_4=x^4-6x^2+3$; in general $H_m(x)=m!\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}\frac{(-1/2)^j x^{m-2j}}{j!\,(m-2j)!}$.

Under the AC assumption of the Gaussian-law supplier, these are the monic orthogonal polynomials for the standard normal law of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: they form an orthogonal system for the measure $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}dx$; orthogonality and the expansion of monomials in this system are proved separately on this page. The moments of that law are those of [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]], and the polynomial calculus used below is that of [[def-derivative]]. The defining property used in this batch is the recurrence; no choice principle is used.

## Statement

Assume AC, and let $Z\sim N(0,1)$ ([[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]). For the monic Hermite polynomials $H_m$ of [[def-monic-probabilists-hermite-polynomials]]:

(i) $\mathbb E[H_m(Z)]=0$ for every $m\ge1$, and $\mathbb E[H_m(Z)H_n(Z)]=m!\,\delta_{mn}$ for all $m,n\ge0$;

(ii) for every $m\ge0$, $x^m=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}c_{m,j}H_{m-2j}(x)$ with $c_{m,0}=1$ and
$$c_{m,j}=\frac{m!}{2^j\,j!\,(m-2j)!}=\binom{m}{2j}(2j-1)!!\in\mathbb Z\qquad(0\le j\le\lfloor m/2\rfloor);$$
equivalently, the monomials and the Hermite polynomials are related by a unitriangular change of basis in each finite degree;

(iii) consequently, for any $N\ge1$ and any $m_1,\dots,m_N\in\mathbb N$, the mixed monomial $\prod_{k=1}^Nx_k^{m_k}$ is a $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of products $\prod_kH_{m'_k}(x_k)$ with $m'_k\le m_k$ and $m'_k\equiv m_k\pmod2$, the coefficient of $\prod_kH_{m_k}$ being $1$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; a random variable $Z\sim N(0,1)$; the polynomials $H_m$ defined by $H_0=1$, $H_1(x)=x$ and $xH_m=H_{m+1}+mH_{m-1}$ ([[def-monic-probabilists-hermite-polynomials]]); $\varphi_Z(t)=\mathbb E[e^{itZ}]$ is the characteristic function of $Z$.

[F1] For $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and every real $t$, $\varphi_Z(t)=e^{-t^2/2}$ ([[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-normal-law]]).

[F2] If $\mathbb E|Y|^k<\infty$ then $\varphi_Y\in C^k(\mathbb R)$ with $\varphi_Y^{(j)}(t)=\mathbb E[(iY)^je^{itY}]$ for $0\le j\le k$; in particular $\varphi_Y^{(j)}(0)=i^j\mathbb E[Y^j]$ ([[lem-moments-give-derivatives-of-the-characteristic-function]]).

[F3] For $Z\sim N(0,1)$, $\mathbb E|Z|^{2m}=(2m-1)!!$ for every $m\ge1$ ([[lem-gaussian-even-moment-bound-for-brownian-increments]]); and $\mathbb E|XY|\le(\mathbb E X^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E Y^2)^{1/2}$ for square-integrable $X,Y$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]).

[F4] Derivative rules: if $g$ is differentiable then $t\mapsto g(-t)$ has derivative $-g'(-t)$, and $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$, $(\alpha f)'=\alpha f'$ ([[def-derivative]], [[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F5] Factorials: $m!$ is the product of $1,\dots,m$ with $0!=1$, and $\binom{m}{2j}=\frac{m!}{(2j)!(m-2j)!}$ ([[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]]).

[F6] Expectations of integrable variables are linear, monotone for real variables, and satisfy $|\mathbb E U|\le\mathbb E|U|$ ([[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Vanishing of odd moments: by [F1] the function $\varphi_Z(t)=e^{-t^2/2}$ is even, and by induction with [F4] each derivative $\varphi_Z^{(j)}$ has parity $(-1)^j$ (differentiating flips parity); hence $\varphi_Z^{(2k+1)}$ is odd and therefore $\varphi_Z^{(2k+1)}(0)=0$ for every $k\ge0$. All absolute moments of $Z$ are finite, since by [F3] $\mathbb E|Z|^{2m}=(2m-1)!!$ and [F3] gives $\mathbb E|Z|^{2m+1}\le(\mathbb E|Z|^{4m+2})^{1/2}<\infty$; so [F2] applies to every order and gives $\mathbb E[Z^{2k+1}]=i^{-(2k+1)}\varphi_Z^{(2k+1)}(0)=0$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 Derivative relation: $H_m'=mH_{m-1}$ for every $m\ge1$. This holds for $m=1$, since $H_1'=1=H_0$, and for $m=2$, since $H_2'=2x=2H_1$; for $m\ge2$, if it holds for all indices up to $m$, then differentiating $H_{m+1}=xH_m-mH_{m-1}$ with [F4] gives $H_{m+1}'=H_m+xH_m'-mH_{m-1}'=H_m+m\,xH_{m-1}-m(m-1)H_{m-2}$, and substituting $xH_{m-1}=H_m+(m-1)H_{m-2}$ yields $H_{m+1}'=(m+1)H_m$. [given, F4, algebra]

1.3 Monomial expansion: every $m\ge0$ admits the expansion $x^m=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}c_{m,j}H_{m-2j}$ with $c_{m,j}=\frac{m!}{2^jj!(m-2j)!}$. Indeed $x^0=H_0$ gives $m=0$; if the expansion holds for $m-1\ge0$, then multiplying by $x$ and using $xH_l=H_{l+1}+lH_{l-1}$ gives coefficient of $H_{m-2j}$ equal to $c_{m-1,j}+(m+1-2j)c_{m-1,j-1}$ (with $c_{r,l}:=0$ whenever $l<0$ or $2l>r$, and $xH_0=H_1$ supplying the boundary case), which equals $c_{m,j}$: for $j\ge1$ the common denominator $2^jj!(m-2j)!$ turns it into $\frac{(m-1)!(m-2j)+2j\,(m-1)!}{2^jj!(m-2j)!}=\frac{m!}{2^jj!(m-2j)!}$ (using [F5]), and for $j=0$ it gives $c_{m-1,0}=1=c_{m,0}$. By [F5], $c_{m,j}=\binom{m}{2j}(2j-1)!!$ is an integer and $c_{m,0}=1$. Moreover the monicity and degree $\deg H_l=l$ make the matrix of coefficients of $x^0,\dots,x^m$ in the basis $H_0,\dots,H_m$ unitriangular with diagonal entries $c_{m,0}=1$, so the expansion is the unique one and defines an invertible unitriangular change of basis in each finite degree. [given, F5, algebra]

2.1 Stein identity: for every real polynomial $p$, $\mathbb E[Zp(Z)]=\mathbb E[p'(Z)]$. Write $p(x)=\sum_{j=0}^da_jx^j$; then $\mathbb E[Zp(Z)]=\sum_{j=0}^da_j\mathbb E[Z^{j+1}]$ and $\mathbb E[p'(Z)]=\sum_{j=1}^dja_j\mathbb E[Z^{j-1}]$, both finite sums. The constant term contributes $a_0\mathbb E[Z]=0$ on the left and nothing on the right, and for every $j\ge1$ one has $\mathbb E[Z^{j+1}]=j\,\mathbb E[Z^{j-1}]$: when $j$ is even both sides vanish by step 1.1; when $j$ is odd, [F3] gives $\mathbb E[Z^{j+1}]=(j)!!$ and $j\mathbb E[Z^{j-1}]=j(j-2)!!=j!!$; here $(-1)!!:=1$ covers $j=1$, where both sides are $\mathbb E[Z^2]=1$. Hence the two sums are equal. [given, F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra, F6]

2.2 Multivariate expansion: let $N\ge1$ and $m_1,\dots,m_N\ge0$. Expanding each factor by step 1.3 and multiplying out, $\prod_kx_k^{m_k}=\sum_{j_1,\dots,j_N}\bigl(\prod_kc_{m_k,j_k}\bigr)\prod_kH_{m_k-2j_k}(x_k)$; each index $m'_k:=m_k-2j_k$ satisfies $m'_k\le m_k$ and $m'_k\equiv m_k\pmod2$, the coefficients are integers by step 1.3, and the single tuple $(j_1,\dots,j_N)=(0,\dots,0)$ contributes $\prod_kH_{m_k}$ with coefficient $1$. [given, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Zero means: $\mathbb E[H_0(Z)]=1$ and $\mathbb E[H_m(Z)]=0$ for every $m\ge1$, by induction on $m$: the case $m=1$ is $\mathbb E[Z]=0$ from step 1.1, and for $m\ge1$ the recurrence and step 2.1 give $\mathbb E[H_{m+1}(Z)]=\mathbb E[ZH_m(Z)]-m\mathbb E[H_{m-1}(Z)]=\mathbb E[H_m'(Z)]-m\mathbb E[H_{m-1}(Z)]=m\mathbb E[H_{m-1}(Z)]-m\mathbb E[H_{m-1}(Z)]=0$, where step 1.2 identifies $H_m'=mH_{m-1}$ and the induction hypothesis handles $\mathbb E[H_{m-1}]$. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra, F6]

4.1 Orthogonality: put $a(M,n):=\mathbb E[H_M(Z)H_n(Z)]$ for $M,n\ge0$. We show $a(M,n)=n!\,\delta_{Mn}$. First $a(0,n)=\mathbb E[H_n(Z)]=\delta_{0n}$ by step 3.1. For $M=1$ and $n\ge1$, step 2.1 gives $a(1,n)=\mathbb E[ZH_n]=\mathbb E[H_n\prime]=n a(0,n-1)$. For $M\ge2$ and $n\ge1$, the recurrence $H_M=xH_{M-1}-(M-1)H_{M-2}$, the Stein identity of step 2.1 applied to $p=H_{M-1}H_n$ and the derivative relation of step 1.2 give $a(M,n)=\mathbb E[ZH_{M-1}H_n]-(M-1)a(M-2,n)=\mathbb E[(H_{M-1}H_n)']-(M-1)a(M-2,n)=(M-1)a(M-2,n)+n\,a(M-1,n-1)-(M-1)a(M-2,n)=n\,a(M-1,n-1)$, while for $n=0$ and $M\ge1$ one has $a(M,0)=\mathbb E[H_M(Z)]=0$ by step 3.1. If $k\le M$ and $k\le n$, iteration gives $a(M,n)=n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)\,a(M-k,n-k)$; taking $k=n$ when $n\le M$ yields $a(M,n)=n!\,a(M-n,0)$, which is $0$ for $M>n$ and is $n!\,a(0,0)=n!$ for $M=n$ by step 3.1, while taking $k=M$ when $M<n$ yields $a(M,n)=n(n-1)\cdots(n-M+1)a(0,n-M)=0$ because $n-M\ge1$. Hence $a(M,n)=n!\,\delta_{Mn}$, which is claim (i) together with step 3.1. [given, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra, F6]

5.1 Conclusion: step 3.1 and step 4.1 prove (i); step 1.3 proves (ii) (including the unitriangularity clause); step 2.2 proves (iii). No step used anything beyond the published derivative, moment and characteristic-function facts listed above. [given, step 1.3, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

      url: "https://www.uomustansiriyah.edu.iq/media/lectures/9/9_2018_12_07!10_23_44_AM.pdf"
      locator: "\u00a710.3, 10.12\u201310.13; \u00a710.4, 10.20; \u00a710.2, p=2. Teschl (10.5), p.282, conjugates the first variable; this scaffold reverses that convention as required by MT-16c."
