## Statement

Assume countable choice. On every measure space, complex $L^p$ is complete for $1\le p\le\infty$, and every norm-convergent sequence has a subsequence of measurable representatives converging a.e. to its limit. For finite $p$, finite simple functions with finite-measure support are dense, and on $\mathbb R^n$ with Lebesgue measure, $n\ge1$, complex $C_c^\infty$ is dense. Complex $L^2$ has the first-variable-linear inner product $\int f\overline g$, its norm is $\|\cdot\|_2$, and Cauchy–Schwarz has the following equality criterion: if $g\ne0$, equality iff $f=cg$ a.e.; if $g=0$, equality for all $f$. The finite-tuple version uses a common scalar across components.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, an arbitrary measure space and exponents in the stated ranges; Euclidean Lebesgue measure for smooth density.

[F1] Complex Lp completeness and a.e. subsequences hold under countable choice ([[thm-complex-lp-completeness-and-almost-everywhere-subsequences]]).

[F2] Finite-simple density holds on arbitrary spaces and smooth density under countable choice on Euclidean spaces, both for finite p ([[thm-complex-finite-simple-and-smooth-compact-support-density-for-finite-p]]).

[F3] The $L^2$ form has the stated norm and equality criterion, also for finite tuples ([[thm-complex-l-two-inner-product-is-well-defined-and-cauchy-schwarz]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** Apply the separate completeness, density and pairing theorems with their exact hypotheses.

1.1 The measure space and exponent satisfy F1, and the assumed countable choice is exactly its additional hypothesis. It therefore supplies completeness for every $1\le p\le\infty$ and a.e.-convergent subsequences with the specified limit class. [F1, given]

1.2 For $p<\infty$, F2 applies to the same measure space and gives finite-simple approximants with finite-measure nonzero sets. In the Euclidean clause its Lebesgue and countable-choice hypotheses also hold, so it supplies smooth compactly supported approximants. [F2, given]

2.1 For $p=2$, F3 proves that the representative formula descends to an inner product and that its squared norm equals $\int|f|^2$. Thus its induced norm is the same $L^2$ norm used in step 1.1. F3 also supplies precisely the nonzero-second-argument scalar-multiple criterion and the zero-second-argument exception, and its finite-sum proof supplies the common-scalar tuple version. This collects the asserted interfaces without any additional analytic hypothesis. [F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

## Statement

For every $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, $n\ge1$, the integral defining $\widehat f(\xi)$ is absolutely convergent for every $\xi$ and unchanged by null-set modifications. Moreover $|\widehat f(\xi)|\le\|f\|_1$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integrable complex representative $f$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$, with the formula of [[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]].

[F1] The exponential satisfies $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$ for real $x,y$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]).

[F2] Integrable functions equal almost everywhere have equal integrals on every measurable set ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]).

[F3] The modulus of an integral is at most the integral of the modulus ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]).

## Proof

1.1 The exponential factor is continuous, hence measurable, and has modulus one. Thus the product is measurable and $\int|f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}|\,dx=\int|f|<\infty$. Its componentwise integral exists, and $|\widehat f(\xi)|\le\|f\|_1$. [F1, F3, given]

2.1 If $g=f$ outside a measurable null set $N$, the same modulus equality proves the product with $g$ integrable, and the two products agree outside $N$. Applying integral invariance on $\mathbb R^n$ gives identical values at this $\xi$. Since $\xi$ was arbitrary, this holds at every frequency; no union of frequency-dependent exceptional sets is taken. In particular a zero class has identically zero transform. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. If $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ and $\widehat f=\widehat g$, then $f=g$ almost everywhere. Equality of the transforms almost everywhere already suffices.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $n\ge1$, the stated inputs and [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] The transform is linear and continuous as a function of frequency ([[thm-fourier-transform-maps-l-one-to-bounded-uniformly-continuous-functions]]).

[F2] A function and its integrable transform obey inversion almost everywhere ([[thm-l-one-fourier-inversion]]).

## Proof

1.1 Set $h=f-g$. By linearity, $\widehat h=0$. If equality was given only almost everywhere, continuity still implies this everywhere: a nonzero value would remain bounded away from zero on an open ball, which contains a positive-volume box and cannot be null. Thus the transform of h is the zero integrable function. [F1, given]

2.1 F2 applies to h, since both h and its zero transform are integrable. It gives $h(x)=\int0\,d\xi=0$ almost everywhere, so $f=g$ as classes. Countable choice is inherited from inversion (and the Euclidean measure interface in the optional almost-everywhere hypothesis). [F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

## Statement

For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $z\in\mathbb C$.

[F1] A complex series converges absolutely when its real modulus series converges ([[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]).

[F2] Complex modulus is multiplicative, and natural factorials are positive and nonzero ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[def-complex-integer-powers]], [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).

[F3] For every real $x$, the real series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/n!$ converges absolutely ([[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]).

[F4] Absolute convergence of a complex series implies convergence ([[thm-absolute-convergence-of-complex-series]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Each factorial denominator is nonzero, and multiplicativity of modulus gives $|z^n/n!|=|z|^n/n!$. Thus its modulus series is the real exponential series at the nonnegative real $|z|$. [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F3] this modulus series converges; [F1] makes the complex series absolutely convergent, and [F4] gives convergence as well. [step 1.1, F1, F3, F4] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and let $G\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ for $\sigma\ge0$. Then $\mathbb E[G^2]=\sigma^2$ and $\mathbb E[G^4]=3\sigma^4$; in particular the fourth moment is finite. For independent centered normal coordinates $G_j\sim N(0,\sigma_j^2)$, every finite linear combination of the variables $G_j^2$ has finite second moment.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and a scalar centered normal variable with variance $\sigma^2\ge0$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: the standard normal law is defined under AC and has density $\phi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$.

[F1] [[thm-gaussian-integral]] and [[thm-substitution-for-improper-integrals]]: $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-x^2/2}\,dx=\sqrt{2\pi}$.

[F2] [[thm-integration-by-parts]]: on finite intervals, $\int u v'=uv|_{a}^{b}-\int u'v$ under its stated integrability hypotheses.

[F3] [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]]: a fixed polynomial times $e^{-x^2/2}$ tends to zero as $|x|\to\infty$ and is integrable after comparison with a weaker Gaussian tail.

[F4] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] gives $\exp'=\exp$; [[thm-chain-rule]] gives $(e^{u(x)})'=e^{u(x)}u'(x)$ for differentiable $u$ on an open interval. The product and scalar rules in [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]] give $(x^2)'=2x$, so $u(x)=-x^2/2$ has derivative $-x$.

[F5] [[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]]: for independent variables, integrable Borel functions of the individual variables have integrable product and factorized product expectation.

## Proof

1.1 Let $I_k:=\int_{\mathbb R}x^{2k}e^{-x^2/2}\,dx$ for $k=0,1,2$. These integrals are finite: outside a bounded interval, $|x|^{2k}e^{-x^2/4}$ is bounded by [F3], while $e^{-x^2/4}$ is integrable by [F1] after scaling. Thus integration by parts on $[-R,R]$ is valid, and its polynomial-exponential boundary terms vanish as $R\to\infty$ by [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, given]

2.1 Since $u(x)=-x^2/2$ is differentiable on $\mathbb R$ and the exponential is differentiable at every $u(x)$, the chain rule in [F4] gives $(e^{-x^2/2})'=-xe^{-x^2/2}$. All these functions and derivatives are continuous on $[-R,R]$, so the hypotheses of [F2] hold. Integration by parts gives $\int_{-R}^R x^2e^{-x^2/2}\,dx=[-xe^{-x^2/2}]_{-R}^R+\int_{-R}^R e^{-x^2/2}\,dx$ and $\int_{-R}^R x^4e^{-x^2/2}\,dx=[-x^3e^{-x^2/2}]_{-R}^R+3\int_{-R}^R x^2e^{-x^2/2}\,dx$. Letting $R\to\infty$, [F3] makes the boundary terms vanish and [F1] gives $I_1=I_0=\sqrt{2\pi}$ and $I_2=3I_1=3\sqrt{2\pi}$; integration against the standard-normal density gives $\mathbb E[G_0^2]=1$ and $\mathbb E[G_0^4]=3$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $\sigma>0$, the definition of $N(0,\sigma^2)$ is the law of $\sigma G_0$, so $\mathbb E[G^2]=\sigma^2\mathbb E[G_0^2]=\sigma^2$ and $\mathbb E[G^4]=\sigma^4\mathbb E[G_0^4]=3\sigma^4$. If $\sigma=0$, $G=0$ almost surely and both formulas hold. For distinct indices $i\ne j$, the squared coordinates are integrable by these second-moment formulas, so [F5] gives $\mathbb E[G_i^2G_j^2]=\sigma_i^2\sigma_j^2<\infty$. For $i=j$, the fourth-moment formula instead gives $\mathbb E[G_i^4]=3\sigma_i^4<\infty$. Thus every term in the square of a finite linear combination of the $G_j^2$ is integrable, proving that combination has finite second moment; the empty combination is zero. [A1, F5, step 2.1, given, cases, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $C_n$ be real symmetric positive-semidefinite $2\times2$ matrices converging entrywise to $C$, and suppose both diagonal entries of $C_n$ and of $C$ are positive. Let $(U_n,V_n)$ and $(U,V)$ have centered bivariate normal laws with covariance matrices $C_n$ and $C$, respectively; singular covariance matrices are allowed. For every globally Lipschitz $\tau:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb E[\tau(U_n)\tau(V_n)]\longrightarrow\mathbb E[\tau(U)\tau(V)].$$
For every bounded Borel function $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb E[g(U_n)g(V_n)]\longrightarrow\mathbb E[g(U)g(V)].$$
The second conclusion applies to any bounded measurable representative of an almost-everywhere derivative, including when the limiting pair is supported on a line.

## Statement references

[Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler, Appendix A.1 and A.4, Gaussian covariance and derivative expectations in the NTK recursion](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07572)

[[def-multivariate-normal-law|Finite Gaussian vectors are realized by a covariance square root times independent standard normals]]

[[lem-complex-lp-completeness-density-and-inner-product|Smooth compactly supported functions are dense in Lebesgue L²]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; positive limiting and approximating marginal variances; bivariate centered Gaussian vectors with the stated covariance matrices; either a globally Lipschitz feature $\tau$ or a bounded Borel feature $g$.

[A1] AC supplies the countable and dependent choice used in the finite Gaussian-law construction ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]]).

[F1] A finite centered multivariate normal vector with covariance $C$ can be represented as $C^{1/2}G$, where $G$ has independent standard-normal coordinates ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]]).

[F2] The standard normal coordinates have a positive density and finite second moments ([[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]).

[F3] Under countable choice, smooth compactly supported functions are dense in Lebesgue $L^2$ ([[lem-complex-lp-completeness-density-and-inner-product]]).

[F4] Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the absolute expectation of a product by the product of its marginal $L^2$ norms ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]).

[F5] Pointwise convergence under an integrable majorant passes through expectation ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Write $C_n=\begin{pmatrix}v_n&c_n\\c_n&w_n\end{pmatrix}$ and $d_n=\det C_n\ge0$. Since $v_n,w_n>0$, $\operatorname{tr}C_n+2\sqrt{d_n}>0$. The matrix $A_n=(C_n+\sqrt{d_n}I_2)/\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}C_n+2\sqrt{d_n}}$ is positive semidefinite. The identity $C_n^2-(\operatorname{tr}C_n)C_n+d_nI_2=0$ gives $A_n^2=C_n$ by expansion; the same formula defines $A$ for $C$, and entrywise convergence gives $A_n\to A$. [A1, F1, given, algebra, construct]

1.2 Fix a variance $s>\max(C_{11},C_{22})$. For all sufficiently large $n$, the marginal variances of $U_n,V_n$ lie in a compact subinterval of $(0,s)$, so their normal densities are bounded above by a common constant times the density of $N(0,s)$. The isometry $h\mapsto h\sqrt{\phi_s}$ from $L^2(N(0,s))$ into Lebesgue $L^2$ and [F3] provide bounded continuous functions $g_k$ with $\|g-g_k\|_{L^2(N(0,s))}\to0$. The density bound makes these approximation errors tend to zero uniformly for the marginals of all sufficiently large $n$ and for the two limiting marginals. [A1, F2, F3, given, construct]

2.1 Let $G=(G_1,G_2)$ have independent standard-normal coordinates and couple $(U_n,V_n)=A_nG$ and $(U,V)=AG$. By [F1] these have the required laws, and $A_n\to A$ gives $(U_n,V_n)\to(U,V)$ almost surely. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 By [F4], for each such $n$ the difference between $\mathbb E[g(U_n)g(V_n)]$ and $\mathbb E[g_k(U_n)g_k(V_n)]$ is bounded by $\|g-g_k\|_{L^2(U_n)}\|g\|_{L^2(V_n)}+\|g_k\|_{L^2(U_n)}\|g-g_k\|_{L^2(V_n)}$, which tends to zero uniformly in sufficiently large $n$ as $k\to\infty$ by step 1.2; the same bound applies to $(U,V)$. [F4, step 1.2]

3.1 If $\tau$ is globally Lipschitz, then it is continuous and has at most linear growth. The matrices $A_n$ are bounded, so $|\tau(U_n)\tau(V_n)|\le M(1+\|G\|_2^2)$ for one finite $M$ independent of all sufficiently large $n$; [F2] makes this majorant integrable. Almost-sure convergence in step 2.1 and [F5] prove the first expectation limit. [F2, F5, given, step 2.1]

4.1 For fixed $k$, $g_k$ is bounded and continuous, so step 2.1 and [F5] give $\mathbb E[g_k(U_n)g_k(V_n)]\to\mathbb E[g_k(U)g_k(V)]$. First take $n\to\infty$, then $k\to\infty$ in the error bounds of step 2.2. This proves the bounded-Borel expectation limit, including singular $C$. [F5, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $m\ge1$, let $C\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite, let $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ have the centered multivariate normal law with covariance $C$, let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be globally Lipschitz and nonconstant, and let $\beta>0$. Let $s$ be a bounded Borel representative of the almost-everywhere derivative of $\sigma$: it agrees with the ordinary derivative wherever that derivative exists, and its values on the remaining Lebesgue-null set are arbitrary. Define
$$S_{ij}:=\mathbb E[\sigma(Z_i)\sigma(Z_j)]+\beta^2,\qquad D_{ij}:=\mathbb E[s(Z_i)s(Z_j)]\quad(1\le i,j\le m).$$
Then $S$ is strictly positive definite and $D$ is positive semidefinite. Consequently, for every positive-semidefinite matrix $T\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$, the matrix $T\circ D+S$ is strictly positive definite, where $\circ$ denotes entrywise multiplication.

## Statement references

[Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler, Appendix A.4, recursive activation covariance and strictness](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07572)

[Gneiting, Theorem 1 and sphere conventions; the local proof below handles the two-point sphere directly](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.7077)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; a finite positive-definite covariance matrix $C$; its centered multivariate normal vector $Z$; a globally Lipschitz nonconstant activation $\sigma$; and $\beta>0$.

[A1] AC supplies countable and dependent choice, as needed by the Gaussian-law and absolute-continuity interfaces ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]]).

[F1] On every compact interval a Lipschitz function is absolutely continuous, and an absolutely continuous function has an integrable derivative almost everywhere whose integral recovers its increments ([[thm-c1-lipschitz-ac-bv-hierarchy]], [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]]).

[F2] A finite centered multivariate normal vector with covariance $C$ is realized as $C^{1/2}G$ for independent standard-normal coordinates $G_j$; each coordinate has the corresponding scalar normal law ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]], [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]).

[F3] A finite-dimensional real symmetric endomorphism has an orthonormal eigenbasis ([[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]).

[F4] Expectations of integrable variables are linear and satisfy Cauchy–Schwarz ([[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]], [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 On every compact interval, [F1] gives differentiability of $\sigma$ outside a null set. Taking a countable union over intervals $[-n,n]$ gives one Lebesgue-null exceptional set on $\mathbb R$. The continuous difference quotients $s_n(x)=n(\sigma(x+1/n)-\sigma(x))$ are bounded in modulus by the Lipschitz constant; their pointwise upper limit is a bounded Borel function and equals $\sigma'(x)$ wherever the derivative exists. Thus a representative $s$ as in the Statement exists. [A1, F1, given, construct]

1.2 Let $A=C^{1/2}$ and $G$ be the independent standard-normal vector in [F2]. Positive definiteness of $C$ makes $A$ invertible: if $Av=0$, then $v^TCv=v^TA^2v=\|Av\|_2^2=0$, so $v=0$. The product standard-normal density is positive on every nonempty open box; since $A^{-1}$ maps nonempty open sets to nonempty open sets, $Z=AG$ assigns positive probability to every nonempty open set in $\mathbb R^m$. [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], each $Z_i$ has a scalar normal law with variance $C_{ii}>0$, hence a density. Therefore changing $s$ on the exceptional null set changes none of the random variables $s(Z_i)$ almost surely. [F2, step 1.1]

2.2 Fix a nonzero vector $c\in\mathbb R^m$ and set $F(z)=\sum_{i=1}^m c_i\sigma(z_i)$. This function is continuous. If $\mathbb E[F(Z)^2]=0$, then for every integer $k\ge1$, $F(Z)^2\ge k^{-2}\mathbf 1_{\{|F(Z)|\ge1/k\}}$ forces $\mathbb P(|F(Z)|\ge1/k)=0$; the countable union gives $F(Z)=0$ almost surely. By the full-support conclusion of step 1.2, continuity forces $F(z)=0$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^m$. Choose $u,v$ with $\sigma(u)\ne\sigma(v)$. For each $j$, evaluate this identity at vectors whose coordinates other than $j$ are zero and whose $j$th coordinates are $u$ and $v$, then subtract; it gives $c_j(\sigma(u)-\sigma(v))=0$, so $c_j=0$. This contradicts $c\ne0$. Hence $\mathbb E[F(Z)^2]>0$ and $c^TSc=\mathbb E[F(Z)^2]+\beta^2(\sum_i c_i)^2>0$. [step 1.2, given, algebra, choose]

3.1 For any $c\in\mathbb R^m$, $c^TDc=\mathbb E[(\sum_i c_i s(Z_i))^2]\ge0$; the expectation is finite because $s$ is bounded. Thus $D$ is positive semidefinite. [F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Apply [F3] to $T$. Each eigenvalue $\lambda$ is nonnegative because for a unit eigenvector $q$, $\lambda=q^TTq\ge0$. If $q_1,\ldots,q_m$ is an orthonormal eigenbasis with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m$, the vectors $u_i=(\sqrt{\lambda_1}(q_1)_i,\ldots,\sqrt{\lambda_m}(q_m)_i)$ satisfy $T_{ij}=\langle u_i,u_j\rangle$. For $D$, the same finite-dimensional factorization applies because step 3.1 proves it is positive semidefinite, so there are vectors $v_i$ with $D_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle$. [F3, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Then $(T\circ D)_{ij}=\langle u_i\otimes v_i,u_j\otimes v_j\rangle$, so $T\circ D$ is positive semidefinite. Adding the strictly positive quadratic form of $S$ from step 2.2 shows $T\circ D+S$ is strictly positive definite. [step 2.2, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$.

1. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'$ extends
   continuously to $[a,b]$, then $f$ is Lipschitz.
2. Every Lipschitz $f$ is absolutely continuous.
3. Every absolutely continuous $f$ is continuous and has bounded variation.

Thus, with $C^1$ understood in the endpoint-extension sense of claim 1,
$C^1\subseteq\mathrm{Lipschitz}\subseteq AC\subseteq C\cap BV$ on a compact
interval.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A compact interval $[a,b]$ and a function $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$.

[L1] Absolute continuity is the finite disjoint-interval condition of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]].

[L2] Derivatives and continuity use [[def-derivative]] and [[def-continuity-real]].

[L3] A continuous real function on $[a,b]$ is bounded ([[cor-boundedness-theorem-r]]).

[L4] A continuous function with bounded derivative on an interval is Lipschitz ([[cor-bounded-derivative-implies-lipschitz]]).

[L5] The Lipschitz condition is $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L|x-y|$ for one $L\ge0$ ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]]).

[L6] Total variation is the supremum of partition sums ([[def-bounded-variation-and-total-variation]], [[def-partition-and-refinement]]).

[L7] Finite sums split and telescope ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

[L8] The canonical naturals are cofinal in $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Under claim 1, the continuous extension of $f'$ is bounded by some $M\ge0$ on $[a,b]$ by [L3]. The bounded-derivative theorem [L4] then makes $f$ Lipschitz with constant $M$. [L2, L3, L4]

1.2 If $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $L$, then for every finite disjoint family, $\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|\le L\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)$. For $L=0$ any positive $\delta$ works; for $L>0$ choose $\delta=\varepsilon/L$. This proves absolute continuity, including the empty family. [L1, L5, L7]

1.3 If $f$ is absolutely continuous, apply [L1] to the single interval with endpoints $x,y$ to obtain the usual $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity condition, so $f$ is continuous. [L1, L2]

1.4 For bounded variation, take $\delta>0$ from absolute continuity with $\varepsilon=1$. By [L8] choose a natural $N\ge1$ with $(b-a)/N<\delta$. Insert the points of the uniform $N$-partition into an arbitrary partition $P$. Inside each uniform block, the refined subintervals have disjoint interiors and total length at most $(b-a)/N<\delta$, so their endpoint oscillations sum to less than $1$. Summing over the $N$ blocks gives $V(f,P)\le N$, independent of $P$. Thus $f$ is BV. If $a=b$, its variation is $0$. [L1, L6, L7, L8]

2.1 Steps 1.1 through 1.4 prove all three inclusions and the asserted hierarchy. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, dependent choice, and a real function $F$ on the compact interval $[a,b]$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Assume (1). By [[thm-absolutely-continuous-functions-have-integrable-derivatives]], put $f=F'\in L^1$ a.e.; the first $L^1$ FTC [[thm-first-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-l-one]] says $I_f'=f$ a.e. [given]

2.1 The corollary [[cor-the-indefinite-integral-of-an-l-one-function-is-absolutely-continuous]] makes $I_f$ AC, so $H:=F-F(a)-I_f$ is AC and has derivative zero a.e. The zero-derivative theorem makes $H$ constant; $H(a)=0$, giving (2). [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Conversely, (2) says $F=F(a)+I_{F'}$, and the same corollary makes it AC. The singleton interval satisfies both clauses directly. [step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\gamma$ be standard Gaussian measure, let $h_m=H_m/\sqrt{m!}$ be the normalized probabilists’ Hermite basis, and let $f,g\in L^2(\gamma)$ have coefficients $a_m=\int f h_m\,d\gamma$ and $b_m=\int g h_m\,d\gamma$. For $\rho\in[-1,1]$, let $(X,Y)$ have the centered bivariate normal law with unit variances and correlation $\rho$. Then
$$\mathbb E[f(X)g(Y)]=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}a_mb_m\rho^m.$$
The series is absolutely convergent, including at $\rho=\pm1$. In particular, the Gaussian dual kernel of $f$ is $\sum_{m\ge0}a_m^2\rho^m$, and $\sum_{m\ge0}a_m^2=\|f\|_{L^2(\gamma)}^2$.

## Statement references

[Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler, Appendix A.4, Lemma 2, Hermite expansion of the dual activation kernel](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07572)

[[def-monic-probabilists-hermite-polynomials|Monic probabilists’ Hermite recurrence and explicit coefficients]]

[[lem-hermite-orthogonality-and-monomial-expansion|Gaussian Hermite orthogonality]]

[[lem-gaussian-ltwo-hermite-completeness|Completeness and Parseval in Gaussian L²]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; $f,g\in L^2(\gamma)$; their normalized Hermite coefficients; and a centered unit-variance Gaussian pair $(X,Y)$ of correlation $\rho\in[-1,1]$.

[A1] AC supplies the countable and dependent choice required by the Gaussian and Hermite suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]]).

[F1] The functions $h_m$ form a complete orthonormal basis of real $L^2(\gamma)$, so the Hermite expansions converge in norm and satisfy Parseval ([[lem-gaussian-ltwo-hermite-completeness]]).

[F2] The monic Hermite polynomials satisfy $H_0=1$, $H_1(x)=x$, $xH_m=H_{m+1}+mH_{m-1}$, and
$H_m(x)=m!\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}(-1/2)^j x^{m-2j}/(j!(m-2j)!)$ ([[def-monic-probabilists-hermite-polynomials]]).

[F3] The standard normal has density $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$, and finite Gaussian vectors may be realized from independent standard-normal coordinates ([[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]).

[F4] Expectations of products of integrable functions of independent coordinates factor ([[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]]).

[F5] Dominated convergence applies under a single integrable majorant ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[F6] The $L^2$ Cauchy–Schwarz inequality bounds product expectations ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]).

[F7] The real exponential is defined by its power series, has derivative equal to itself, and obeys $\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y)$ ([[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]).

[F8] The one-variable chain rule and product rule apply to the real generating function ([[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For real $s$ and $x$, set $G_x(s)=\exp(sx-s^2/2)$. By [F7]–[F8], $G_x'(s)=(x-s)G_x(s)$. Put $P_m(x)=G_x^{(m)}(0)$. Then $P_0=1$ and $P_1=x$; differentiating the identity $G_x'=(x-s)G_x$ $m$ times and setting $s=0$ gives $P_{m+1}=xP_m-mP_{m-1}$ for $m\ge1$. The Hermite recurrence in [F2] therefore gives $P_m=H_m$ for every $m$. [F2, F7, F8, algebra]

2.1 Realize the pair as $X=G_1$ and $Y=\rho G_1+\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,G_2$ for independent standard normals $G_1,G_2$. Completing the square gives $\mathbb E e^{aG_j}=e^{a^2/2}$ for each real $a$. By [F7] and [F4], $\mathbb E[G_s(X)G_t(Y)]=e^{\rho st}\,\mathbb E[e^{(s+\rho t)G_1-(s+\rho t)^2/2}]\,\mathbb E[e^{t\sqrt{1-\rho^2}G_2-t^2(1-\rho^2)/2}]=e^{\rho st}.$ The identity remains valid at $\rho=\pm1$. [A1, F3, F4, F7, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For any fixed finite $m,n$, differentiating the expectation identity in step 2.1 $m$ times in $s$ and $n$ times in $t$ at $(0,0)$ is justified as follows. On a bounded parameter rectangle, each derivative of the integrand is bounded by a constant times a polynomial in $|G_1|+|G_2|$ times $e^{R(|G_1|+|G_2|)}$ for some finite $R$; completing the square shows this is integrable. The mean-value theorem gives the same type of majorant for each difference quotient, so [F5] passes each of the finitely many derivatives through expectation. By step 1.1 the derivative on the left is $\mathbb E[H_m(X)H_n(Y)]$; differentiating $e^{\rho st}$ on the right gives $m!\rho^m$ if $m=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Hence $\mathbb E[H_m(X)H_n(Y)]=m!\delta_{mn}\rho^m$. [F3, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For finite partial sums $f_M=\sum_{m=0}^M a_mh_m$ and $g_M=\sum_{m=0}^M b_mh_m$, step 3.1 and orthonormality give $\mathbb E[f_M(X)g_M(Y)]=\sum_{m=0}^M a_mb_m\rho^m$. [F1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 By [F1], $f_M\to f$ and $g_M\to g$ in $L^2(\gamma)$. Since both marginals of $(X,Y)$ are $\gamma$, [F6] bounds the product-expectation error by $\|f_M-f\|_2\|g_M\|_2+\|f\|_2\|g_M-g\|_2$, which tends to zero. Also $\sum_m|a_mb_m\rho^m|\le(\sum_m a_m^2)^{1/2}(\sum_m b_m^2)^{1/2}$ by [F1] and Cauchy–Schwarz for sequences. Taking $M\to\infty$ proves the stated identity and endpoint absolute convergence; the case $f=g$ gives the dual-kernel formula. [F1, F6, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Sets $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, functions $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with $g[A] \subseteq B$ and $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$ at which $g$ is differentiable, and the point $b := g(c) \in B$, a limit point of $B$ at which $f$ is differentiable ([[def-derivative]], [[def-limit-point-r]]).

[L1] Carathéodory's characterisation ([[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]]), used in both directions: for $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, a point $p \in D$ that is a limit point of $D$ and $h : D \to \mathbb{R}$, the function $h$ is differentiable at $p$ if and only if there is $\eta : D \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $p$, with $h(y) - h(p) = \eta(y)(y - p)$ for every $y \in D$, and then $\eta(p) = h'(p)$.

[L2] Algebra of continuous functions ([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], claim 1): a product of two functions continuous at a point of their common domain is continuous there.

[L3] Composition of continuous functions ([[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]): if $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ has $g[A] \subseteq B$ and is continuous at $c \in A$, and if $\eta : B \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $g(c)$, then $\eta \circ g$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

[L4] A function differentiable at a point is continuous there ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], applied to $g$ on $A$ at $c$, fix $\psi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $g(x) - g(c) = \psi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$ and $\psi(c) = g'(c)$. [L1, choose]

1.2 By [L1], applied to $f$ on $B$ at $b$, fix $\varphi : B \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $b$, with $f(y) - f(b) = \varphi(y)(y - b)$ for every $y \in B$ and $\varphi(b) = f'(b)$. [L1, choose]

2.1 **The factorisation.** Let $x \in A$. Then $g(x) \in B$, so taking $y := g(x)$ in step 1.2 gives $f(g(x)) - f(b) = \varphi(g(x))\bigl(g(x) - b\bigr)$, and $g(x) - b = g(x) - g(c) = \psi(x)(x-c)$ by step 1.1. Since $(f \circ g)(c) = f(g(c)) = f(b)$, this reads $(f \circ g)(x) - (f \circ g)(c) = \chi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, where $\chi : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is the pointwise product $\chi := (\varphi \circ g)\,\psi$. [step 1.1, step 1.2]

2.2 **The outer factor is continuous at $c$.** By [L4] the function $g$ is continuous at $c$; by step 1.2 the function $\varphi$ is continuous at $b = g(c)$; and $g[A] \subseteq B$. So $\varphi \circ g$ is continuous at $c$ by [L3]. [step 1.2, L3, L4]

3.1 **The factor is continuous at $c$, with the right value.** $\chi$ is the product of $\varphi \circ g$, continuous at $c$ by step 2.2, with $\psi$, continuous at $c$ by step 1.1, so $\chi$ is continuous at $c$ by [L2]; and $\chi(c) = \varphi(g(c))\,\psi(c) = \varphi(b)\,\psi(c) = f'(b)\,g'(c)$. [step 1.1, step 2.2, L2]

4.1 By step 2.1 the function $\chi : A \to \mathbb{R}$ factors the increment of $f \circ g$ at $c$, and by step 3.1 it is continuous at $c$. So [L1], applied to $f \circ g$ on $A$ at the limit point $c$, gives that $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ with $(f \circ g)'(c) = \chi(c) = f'(g(c))\,g'(c)$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L1] ∎

## Remarks

- **Where the classical proof goes wrong, precisely.** It divides by $g(x) - g(c)$, which may vanish at points arbitrarily close to $c$ even when $g$ is differentiable at $c$ with $g'(c) = 0$; the usual repair defines an auxiliary function equal to the outer quotient off the bad set and to $f'(b)$ on it, and then proves that auxiliary function continuous. That auxiliary function is $\varphi \circ g$, and [[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]] is the observation that it exists before any repair is attempted.

- **What is composed is continuity, not differentiability.** The only theorem about composites used above is [[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]], and it needs no side hypothesis, unlike the corresponding statement for limits. That is the whole reason the proof has no cases.

- **The formula is about the point $g(c)$, not about $g$ near $c$.** Both derivatives on the right are taken at single points, and the theorem says nothing about $f$ on the image of any neighbourhood of $c$. In particular no hypothesis is placed on $g[A]$ beyond its lying in $B$.

## Statement

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space. Let $A:V\to V$ be self-adjoint and positive definite, meaning $\langle v,Av\rangle>0$ for every $v\ne0$. Let $C:V\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable, convex, and have a locally Lipschitz gradient, where $DC(z)[v]=\langle\nabla C(z),v\rangle$ and locally Lipschitz means Lipschitz on every compact subset of $V$. Assume $C$ attains its global minimum at $z_*\in V$. For every initial state $z_0\in V$, the solution of

$$\dot z(t)=-A\nabla C(z(t)),\qquad z(0)=z_0,$$

exists uniquely for all $t\ge0$ and converges to a global minimizer of $C$ as $t\to\infty$. In particular, for a finite data set of size $N\ge1$, a symmetric positive-definite Gram matrix $K$ gives this conclusion for the kernel-flow equation with $A=K/N$.

## Statement references

[Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler, §3, finite-data kernel gradient flow](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07572)

[[def-positive-semidefinite-kernels-and-reproducing-kernel-hilbert-spaces|A real kernel is positive semidefinite when every finite Gram quadratic form is nonnegative]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite-dimensional real inner product space $V$, the self-adjoint positive-definite map $A$, the continuously differentiable convex cost $C$ with locally Lipschitz gradient, a minimizer $z_*$, and initial value $z_0$.

[F1] A self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real inner product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis ([[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]).

[F2] A positive-semidefinite kernel has symmetric positive-semidefinite finite Gram matrices ([[def-positive-semidefinite-kernels-and-reproducing-kernel-hilbert-spaces]]).

[F3] A continuous vector field locally Lipschitz in the state has a unique local solution through each initial state ([[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]).

[F4] A closed bounded subset of Euclidean $\mathbb{R}^n$ is compact for every $n\ge1$ ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[F5] The derivative of a finite-dimensional composition is the composition of total derivatives ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** use the inverse-kernel metric to bound the orbit, then use convexity and integrability of the cost gap to identify its limit points.

1.1 By [F1], $A$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis; self-adjointness and positive definiteness make each eigenvalue positive. Thus $A^{-1}$ exists, is self-adjoint and positive definite, and $\|v\|_{A^{-1}}^2:=\langle v,A^{-1}v\rangle$ is a norm squared. Since $\nabla C$ is locally Lipschitz, the vector field $-A\nabla C$ is locally Lipschitz and [F3] gives a unique local solution. [F1, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 For $0<s\le1$, convexity gives $C(z+s(z_*-z))\le(1-s)C(z)+sC(z_*)$. Subtract $C(z)$, divide by $s$, and let $s\downarrow0$; differentiability and the definition of $\nabla C$ give $\langle\nabla C(z),z_*-z\rangle\le C(z_*)-C(z)$. Along any solution, expanding the squared inverse-metric norm to first order then gives $\frac{d}{dt}\|z-z_*\|_{A^{-1}}^2=-2\langle z-z_*,\nabla C(z)\rangle\le-2(C(z)-C(z_*))\le0.$ Hence the solution remains in the closed $A^{-1}$-metric ball centered at $z_*$ through $z_0$. In orthonormal coordinates its radius bounds the Euclidean norm because the smallest eigenvalue of $A^{-1}$ is positive, and continuity of that norm makes the ball closed. If $\dim V\ge1$, [F4] makes it compact; if $\dim V=0$, it is a subset of the singleton $V=\{0\}$ and is compact. [F1, F4, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The vector field is bounded and Lipschitz on a compact neighborhood of this ball. Picard–Lindelöf therefore supplies a uniform positive local existence time at every point of the ball. If the maximal forward solution had a finite endpoint, boundedness of the vector field would make $z(t)$ Cauchy as $t$ approached that endpoint; its limit lies in the ball, and the uniform local solution there extends the original solution, a contradiction. Thus the solution exists uniquely for all $t\ge0$. [F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Integrating the inequality in step 2.1 over $[0,T]$ gives $\int_0^T(C(z(t))-C(z_*))\,dt\le\frac12\|z_0-z_*\|_{A^{-1}}^2$. By [F5] and the flow equation, $\frac{d}{dt}C(z(t))=-\langle\nabla C(z(t)),A\nabla C(z(t))\rangle\le0$. The gap is therefore nonnegative, nonincreasing and integrable; it tends to zero. [F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The trajectory lies in a compact set, so it has a convergent subsequence $z(t_j)\to\bar z$ with $t_j\to\infty$. Continuity of $C$ and step 4.1 give $C(\bar z)=C(z_*)$, so $\bar z$ is a global minimizer. Apply step 2.1 with $\bar z$ in place of $z_*$: the distance $\|z(t)-\bar z\|_{A^{-1}}$ is nonincreasing and has a subsequence tending to zero, hence tends to zero. Thus the full trajectory converges to $\bar z$. [F4, step 2.1, step 4.1]

6.1 For a finite data set, [F2] makes $K$ symmetric positive semidefinite; if it is positive definite, then $A=K/N$ is self-adjoint positive definite because $N\ge1$. The preceding argument applies. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The IVP in the Statement and a compact cylinder about $(t_0,x_0)$ on which $F$ is bounded by $M$ and state-Lipschitz with constant $L$.

[L1] A contraction of a nonempty complete metric space has exactly one fixed point ([[thm-banach-fixed-point]]).

[L2] A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation ([[prop-first-order-ivp-is-equivalent-to-a-volterra-integral-equation]]).

[L3] Continuous $\mathbb R^n$-valued curves on a nonempty compact interval are complete in the supremum metric ([[lem-vector-valued-continuous-curve-space-is-complete]]).

[L4] Under $hM\le r$, the Picard operator preserves the closed curve ball ([[lem-picard-operator-preserves-a-closed-curve-ball]]).

[L5] Under $Lh<1$, the Picard operator is a contraction ([[lem-picard-operator-is-a-short-time-contraction]]).

[L6] Every interval in the real line is connected ([[cor-connected-subsets-of-the-line]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Choose $r>0$ and then $h>0$ so the cylinder lies in $D$, $hM\le r$, and $Lh<1$; the closed curve ball is nonempty and complete by [L3], is invariant by [L4], and its Picard operator is a contraction by [L5], so [L1] gives exactly one fixed point. [given, L1, L3, L4, L5]

2.1 By [L2] the fixed point is a solution. Any other solution cannot leave the state ball before time $h$, by the same first-exit estimate as [L4], so it is the same fixed point there. For two solutions on a larger common interval, their agreement set is nonempty and closed, and local repetition of this argument makes it open; the common interval is connected by [L6], so they agree throughout it. [step 1.1, L2, L4, L6] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Fix an integer $n_0\ge1$, a number $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz function $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ that is not a polynomial. Let $S^{n_0-1}=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}:\|x\|_2=1\}$, put $q=n_0^{-1}+\beta^2$, and define $\mu(z)=\sigma(\sqrt q\,z)$. Let $a_m=\int \mu(z)h_m(z)\,d\gamma(z)$ be its coefficients in the normalized probabilists’ Hermite basis $h_m=H_m/\sqrt{m!}$ of standard Gaussian measure $\gamma$. For $x,y\in S^{n_0-1}$, let $(U_{x,y},V_{x,y})$ be a centered Gaussian pair with variances $q$ and covariance $\beta^2+x\cdot y/n_0$, and set $k(x,y)=\mathbb E[\sigma(U_{x,y})\sigma(V_{x,y})]+\beta^2$. Then $k$ is strictly positive definite on $S^{n_0-1}$: for every finite list of pairwise distinct points $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$, $\sum_{i,j=1}^N c_i c_j k(x_i,x_j)>0$. The conclusion includes $n_0=1$, for which the sphere consists of the two points $-1$ and $1$.

## Statement references

[Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler, Appendix A.4, activation covariance expansion and positive definiteness](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07572)

[Gneiting, Theorem 1 and sphere conventions; the proof here treats every dimension directly](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.7077)

[[lem-gaussian-hermite-covariance-expansion|Correlated Gaussian Hermite covariance identity and endpoint convergence]]

[[lem-gaussian-ltwo-hermite-completeness|Completeness and Parseval for Gaussian L² Hermite expansions]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; $n_0\ge1$; $\beta>0$; a globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation; and a finite set of distinct unit vectors.

[A1] AC supplies the countable and dependent choice required by the Gaussian and Hermite suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]]).

[F1] The normalized probabilists’ Hermite polynomials are a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(\gamma)$, Parseval gives $\sum_m a_m^2=\|\mu\|_2^2$, and every globally Lipschitz real function belongs to $L^2(\gamma)$ ([[lem-gaussian-ltwo-hermite-completeness]]).

[F2] For a centered unit-variance Gaussian pair of correlation $r\in[-1,1]$, the expectation of two $L^2(\gamma)$ functions with Hermite coefficients $(a_m)$ and $(b_m)$ is $\sum_m a_mb_mr^m$, absolutely convergent at both endpoints ([[lem-gaussian-hermite-covariance-expansion]]).

[F3] Tonelli’s theorem permits interchange of sums of nonnegative terms ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F4] The inner product on $\mathbb R^{n_0}$ is the Euclidean dot product; tensor powers use the induced coordinate inner product ([[def-inner-product-space]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** expand the Gaussian feature covariance, show every power coefficient is positive, then separate finitely many points by a polynomial.

1.1 The marginal variance is $q$, and the standardized correlation is $r(x,y)=\frac{\beta^2+(x\cdot y)/n_0}{q}=\alpha(x\cdot y)+\delta,\qquad \alpha=\frac1{1+n_0\beta^2}>0,\quad \delta=\frac{n_0\beta^2}{1+n_0\beta^2}>0,\quad \alpha+\delta=1.$ The correlation lies in $[-1,1]$ because $|x\cdot y|\le1$ and the displayed covariance is a valid two-dimensional Gram covariance of the input and bias features. Applying [F2] to $\mu$ gives $k(x,y)=\beta^2+\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}a_r^2(\alpha x\cdot y+\delta)^r.$ The series is absolutely convergent since $|r(x,y)|\le1$ and $\sum_r a_r^2<\infty$. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Expanding each nonnegative power by the binomial theorem and using [F3], define $d_m=\mathbf1_{\{m=0\}}\beta^2+\alpha^m\sum_{r=m}^{\infty}a_r^2\binom rm\delta^{r-m}\quad(m\ge0).$ Then $k(x,y)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}d_m(x\cdot y)^m$. Moreover, [F3] and $\alpha+\delta=1$ give $\sum_m d_m=\beta^2+\sum_r a_r^2<\infty$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The rescaled function $\mu(z)=\sigma(\sqrt q z)$ is continuous and nonpolynomial: if it were a polynomial, then $\sigma(u)=\mu(u/\sqrt q)$ would be a polynomial because $q>0$. It is globally Lipschitz, so [F1] supplies its $L^2(\gamma)$ membership and Parseval. The function $\mu$ has infinitely many nonzero Hermite coefficients: otherwise [F1] would make it equal almost everywhere to a polynomial, and continuity would make that equality hold everywhere, contradicting nonpolynomiality. Thus for each $m$ there is an $r\ge m$ with $a_r\ne0$, and the corresponding term in [F3]’s sum is strictly positive because $\alpha,\delta>0$. Hence $d_m>0$ for every $m$, including $m=0$ because $\beta>0$. [F1, F3, step 2.1, given]

3.2 For any $c\in\mathbb R^N$, the quadratic form is $\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jk(x_i,x_j)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}d_m\left\|\sum_{i=1}^N c_i x_i^{\otimes m}\right\|_2^2\ge0.$ Indeed, $\langle x_i^{\otimes m},x_j^{\otimes m}\rangle=(x_i\cdot x_j)^m$ by the induced tensor inner product, and the convergent series may be evaluated termwise because $|x_i\cdot x_j|\le1$ and $\sum_m d_m<\infty$. [F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If this quadratic form were zero, positivity of every $d_m$ would force $\sum_i c_i x_i^{\otimes m}=0$ for every $m\ge0$. Consequently $\sum_i c_i p(x_i)=0$ for every polynomial $p$ on $\mathbb R^{n_0}$: each monomial of degree $m$ is a coordinate linear functional on $x^{\otimes m}$, and constants correspond to $m=0$. For each index $j$, take $p_j(x)=\prod_{i\ne j}\|x-x_i\|_2^2$, with the empty product equal to $1$. Then $p_j(x_i)=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $p_j(x_j)>0$, so $c_j=0$. This holds for every $j$, contradicting $c\ne0$. Thus the quadratic form in step 3.2 is strictly positive. [F4, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $F$ be either $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with conjugation equal to the identity on $\mathbb R$ and with complex conjugation as in [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. An **inner product** on an $F$-vector space $V$ is a function $\langle\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\rangle:V\times V\to F$ such that for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in F$:

1. $\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle$;
2. $\langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle}$;
3. $\langle v,v\rangle$ is real and nonnegative, and $\langle v,v\rangle=0$ if and only if $v=0$.

The first two clauses imply conjugate-linearity in the second argument: $\langle u,av+bw\rangle=\overline a\langle u,v\rangle+\overline b\langle u,w\rangle$. This is the linear-first convention of [[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]]. A vector space equipped with an inner product is an **inner product space**.

## Statement

Assume AC. Fix a finite data set $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$ with $N,n_0\ge1$, a depth $L\ge2$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and a horizon $T\ge0$. Let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be globally Lipschitz, twice continuously differentiable, and have bounded second derivative. Use the network parameterization and independent standard-normal initialization in the width-normalized network definition, with scalar output $n_L=1$. For each hidden-width tuple $(n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1})$, suppose a differentiable parameter path exists on $[0,T]$ and satisfies

$$\dot\theta_p(t)=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_{\theta_p}f_{\theta(t)}(x_i)\,d_i(t),$$

where $d:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^N$ is measurable and integrable. Write $K_t=(K_{\theta(t)}(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^N$ for the finite-data scalar neural tangent kernel. Suppose $\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_N\,dt$ is stochastically bounded in the prescribed sequential hidden-width limit, where $\|v\|_N=(N^{-1}\sum_i|v_i|^2)^{1/2}$ and stochastic boundedness means that for every $\varepsilon>0$ some $M<\infty$ satisfies the iterated-limit upper bound $\mathbb P(\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_Ndt>M)<\varepsilon$. Then, as $n_1\to\infty$ first and then $n_2,\ldots,n_{L-1}\to\infty$, for every $\varepsilon>0$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|K_t-K_0\|_{\mathrm{op}}>\varepsilon\right)\longrightarrow0.$$

## Statement references

[Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler, Theorem 2 and Appendix A.2–A.3, fixed-time NTK stability](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07572)

[[def-neural-tangent-kernel|The scalar NTK is the parameter-Jacobian Gram kernel]]

[[def-width-normalized-fully-connected-network|The hidden layers use fan-in normalization and independent Gaussian initialization]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the finite data set and fixed depth; the stated activation and positive bias scale; the source-normalized network with iid standard-normal parameters; an existing path on $[0,T]$; and a training direction with stochastically bounded integrated empirical norm.

[A1] AC is inherited from the network and Gaussian probability-law interfaces ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]]).

[F1] For a finite $C^1$ parameterized network, reverse accumulation sums every shared-parameter use and gives the total parameter gradient ([[thm-shared-parameter-backpropagation-gradient-formula]]).

[F2] The NTK is the Gram matrix of the parameter derivatives ([[def-neural-tangent-kernel]]).

[F3] In the model definition, weights and biases are independent standard normals, the forward map uses $W^{(\ell)}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$ and $\beta b^{(\ell)}$, and hidden activations are coordinatewise $\sigma$ ([[def-width-normalized-fully-connected-network]]).

[F4] Averages of iid square-integrable variables converge in probability to their means ([[cor-iid-finite-variance-weak-law]]); a centered normal has finite fourth moment ([[lem-standard-normal-fourth-moment]]).

[F5] The probability and norm conventions used in the conclusion are convergence in probability and the finite-dimensional operator norm ([[def-convergence-in-probability]]).

[F6] Cauchy–Schwarz and expectation linearity apply to the finite data averages ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]], [[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]).

[F7] A differentiable real function with uniformly bounded derivative is Lipschitz by the mean value theorem ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

[F8] A continuous real function differentiable except on a countable set, with Lebesgue-integrable derivative, is absolutely continuous and recovers its increments by integrating that derivative; apply coordinatewise to finite-dimensional parameter paths ([[thm-countably-exceptional-differentiability-and-integrable-derivative-imply-absolute-continuity]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** express the finite network derivatives by backpropagation, control normalized parameter and feature changes by an aggregate differential inequality, then apply the finite-data Jacobian recursion.

1.1 Regard the network as a finite composition of $C^1$ maps on its Euclidean parameter space; [F1] gives the shared-parameter gradients. Let $J_f(\theta(t))$ be the Jacobian of $(f_\theta(x_i))_{i=1}^N$. It is continuous in $\theta$ because $\sigma$ is $C^2$, and it is bounded on the compact image of the continuous path $\theta([0,T])$. The flow equation and $d\in L^1([0,T];\mathbb R^N)$ therefore imply $\dot\theta\in L^1([0,T])$. By [F8], applied to each of the finitely many parameter coordinates, $\theta$ is absolutely continuous and its increments equal the integrals of its derivative. Define the terminal array by $D^L_{1i}(t)=d_i(t)$, and obtain each hidden backpropagated array $D^{\ell+1}(t)\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}\times N}$ by weighting the derivative of each data-point output with $d_i(t)$. If $Z^\ell(t)\in\mathbb R^{n_\ell\times N}$ is the activation array, the weight and bias equations are $\dot W^{(\ell)}=-D^{\ell+1}(Z^\ell)^T/(N\sqrt{n_\ell})$ and $\dot b^{(\ell)}=-\beta D^{\ell+1}\mathbf1/N$, while hidden backpropagation is $D^\ell=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma\prime(U^\ell))(W^{(\ell)})^TD^{\ell+1}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$. Here division by $N$ acts on the data sum. [A1, F1, F3, F8, given, algebra]

2.1 For an array $R\in\mathbb R^{m\times N}$ write $\|R\|_{F,N}=\|R\|_F/\sqrt N$. Let $c=\sup|\sigma'|$ and $M_2=\sup|\sigma''|$, both finite by the hypotheses (taking a difference-quotient limit in the global Lipschitz inequality gives $c\le\operatorname{Lip}(\sigma)$), and set $w_\ell(t)=\|W^{(\ell)}(t)\|_{op}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$ and $a_\ell(t)=\|Z^\ell(t)\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$ for $1\le\ell<L$. Let $K^\ell$ be the tangent-kernel block for the preactivation array $U^\ell$, acting on direction arrays by $(\mathcal K^\ell D)_{ai}=N^{-1}\sum_{b,j}K^\ell_{(i,a),(j,b)}D_{bj}$, and put $B_\ell=\|\mathcal K^\ell\|_{op}$ using $\|\cdot\|_{F,N}$. The initial block and layerwise chain rule give $B_1\le\|X\|_F^2/(n_0N)+\beta^2$ and $B_{\ell+1}\le c^2w_\ell^2B_\ell+a_\ell^2+\beta^2$ for $1\le\ell<L$: the current-layer weight-and-bias Gram has operator norm at most $a_\ell^2+\beta^2$, while the preceding Jacobian is composed with $W^{(\ell)}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$ and diagonal activation derivatives of norm at most $c$. The backpropagation identity in step 1.1 also gives $\|D^\ell(t)\|_{F,N}\le c^{L-\ell}(\prod_{k=\ell}^{L-1}w_k(t))\|d(t)\|_N$. Recursively, each $B_\ell$ is bounded by a polynomial in the finitely many $a_k,w_k,c,\beta$, and each backpropagation norm is bounded by such a polynomial times $\|d(t)\|_N$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Cauchy–Schwarz in the data index and step 1.1 give, for $1\le\ell<L$, $\|\dot W^{(\ell)}\|_{op}/\sqrt{n_\ell}\le a_\ell\|D^{\ell+1}\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$. For hidden layers the chain rule gives $\dot U^\ell=-\mathcal K^\ell D^\ell$, so $\|\dot U^\ell\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}\le B_\ell\|D^\ell\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$; for $\ell=1$ this is the first-layer parameter Gram. The hidden-bias equation gives $\beta\|\dot b^{(\ell-1)}\|_2/\sqrt{n_\ell}\le\beta^2\|D^\ell\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$, and the first-layer matrix gives $\|\dot W^{(0)}\|_F/\sqrt{n_1}\le C\|D^1\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_1}$ with $C=\|X\|_F/\sqrt{n_0N}$. The output bias is excluded because its derivative contributes only the constant feature $\beta$ and changes no later feature or parameter derivative. By [F7], $|\sigma'(u)-\sigma\prime(v)|\le M_2|u-v|$; global Lipschitz continuity gives $\|\dot Z^\ell\|_{F,N}\le c\|\dot U^\ell\|_{F,N}$. Whenever $a_\ell(t),w_\ell(t)\le R$ for every hidden layer, the recurrence in step 2.1 gives $B_\ell\le P_\ell(R)$, where $P_1(R)=\|X\|_F^2/(n_0N)+\beta^2$ and $P_{\ell+1}(R)=c^2R^2P_\ell(R)+R^2+\beta^2$; backpropagation gives $\|D^\ell\|_{F,N}\le(cR)^{L-\ell}\|d\|_N$. Substituting these bounds in the displayed rates shows that each normalized activation, preactivation, hidden-bias, and weight change rate is at most a polynomial in $R$ times $\|d(t)\|_N/\sqrt{n_{\min}}$, with $n_{\min}=\min_{1\le k<L}n_k$. [F1, F3, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 For $1\le\ell<L$ define $\widetilde a_\ell=\|Z^\ell(t)-Z^\ell(0)\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$, $\widetilde u_\ell=\|U^\ell(t)-U^\ell(0)\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$, and $\widetilde w_\ell=\|W^{(\ell)}(t)-W^{(\ell)}(0)\|_{op}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$; for $0\le\ell<L-1$ put $\widetilde b_\ell=\beta\|b^{(\ell)}(t)-b^{(\ell)}(0)\|_2/\sqrt{n_{\ell+1}}$, and put $\widetilde w_0=\|W^{(0)}(t)-W^{(0)}(0)\|_F/\sqrt{n_1}$. Define $A(t)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L-1}(a_\ell(0)+w_\ell(0)+\widetilde a_\ell+\widetilde u_\ell+\widetilde w_\ell+\widetilde b_{\ell-1})+\widetilde w_0$. Each term of $A$ is absolutely continuous by [F8] and the norm/Lipschitz inequalities; the preceding estimates and the polynomial bounds in step 3.1 give, with $n_{\min}=\min_{1\le\ell<L}n_\ell$, $|\dot A(t)|\le Q(A(t))\|d(t)\|_N/\sqrt{n_{\min}}$ for a polynomial $Q$ with nonnegative coefficients depending only on $L,N,c,M_2,\beta$ and the fixed inputs. [F3, F4, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 Fix probability tolerance $\varepsilon>0$. Stochastic boundedness of $A(0)$ and of $\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_Ndt$ lets us restrict, except on a set of probability at most $2\varepsilon$, to $A(0)\le R$ and this integral at most $M$ for finite $R,M$. 6.1 For each layer, the exact tangent-kernel block recursion is $K^{\ell+1}_{(i,c),(j,d)}=\delta_{cd}(n_\ell^{-1}\sum_a Z^\ell_{ai}Z^\ell_{aj}+\beta^2)+n_\ell^{-1}\sum_{a,b}W^{(\ell)}_{ca}W^{(\ell)}_{db}\sigma'(U^\ell_{ai})\sigma'(U^\ell_{bj})K^\ell_{(i,a),(j,b)}$. It follows by applying the chain rule to each coordinate and splitting parameter derivatives into the current layer and earlier shared parameters, as in [F1]. The first term varies uniformly by the activation and hidden-bias estimates in step 5.1. For the second term, for each output index $c$ and data index $i$ use the vector $v_{c,i}(t)\in\mathbb R^{n_\ell}$ with entries $W^{(\ell)}_{ca}(t)\sigma'(U^\ell_{ai}(t))$. Their normalized Euclidean norms stay bounded. Their changes tend to zero in normalized Euclidean norm: the weight-change part is bounded by $c\|\Delta W_c\|_2/\sqrt{n_\ell}$, while Cauchy–Schwarz for the initial-weight part gives $n_\ell^{-1}\sum_a|W^{(\ell)}_{ca}(0)|^2|\Delta\sigma'_{ai}|^2\le(n_\ell^{-1}\sum_a|W^{(\ell)}_{ca}(0)|^4)^{1/2}(n_\ell^{-1}\sum_a|\Delta\sigma'_{ai}|^4)^{1/2}$. The output layer has fixed scalar dimension, so this is exactly $\sup_{t\le T}\|K_t-K_0\|_{op}\to0$ in probability. [F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, step 2.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be IID square-integrable real random variables, with $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)$. For $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|^2=\sigma^2/n,$$
and $S_n/n\to\mu$ in $L^2$ and in probability. Also $\mathbb P(|S_n/n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon>0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in def-independent-random-elements. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

[F2] [[thm-chebyshev-weak-law-for-uncorrelated-arrays]]: For each $n\ge1$, let $X_{n,1},\ldots,X_{n,r_n}$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space, pairwise uncorrelated within the row, where $r_n\ge0$ is finite. Set $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^{r_n}X_{n,k}$ and let $b_n>0$ be deterministic. If $v_n:=b_n^{-2}\sum_{k=1}^{r_n}\operatorname{Var}(X_{n,k})\longrightarrow0,$ then $(S_n-\mathbb ES_n)/b_n\to0$ in $L^2$ and in probability. More precisely, its second moment is $v_n$, and its probability of absolute value at least $\varepsilon>0$ is at most $v_n/\varepsilon^2$. No independence between rows is required.

[F3] For $n\ge1$, if $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ are independent real random variables and $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ are Borel measurable with each $g_i(X_i)$ integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable and $\mathbb E[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$ in $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses of the statement.

1.1 IID gives common mean and variance. For distinct indices, factorization of the integrable variables gives $\mathbb E(X_iX_j)=\mu^2$, hence zero covariance. Thus the first $n$ variables form an uncorrelated row. [F1, F3, given]

2.1 Apply the row result with $r_n=n$ and $b_n=n$. Its variance sum is $n\sigma^2$, so it gives the displayed identity, both convergences, and the probability bound. This calculation holds for $n=1$ and for $\sigma^2=0$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$ on one probability space, write
$X_n\to X$ **in probability** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

## Statement

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. If $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, differentiable except at countably
many points, and $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, then $F$ is absolutely continuous and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt$$
for every $x\in[a,b]$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, dependent choice, and a continuous $F$ with the stated countable exceptional set and integrable derivative.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $Z$ be the countable exceptional set. It is null by [[lem-countable-sets-are-null]]. If $A\subseteq[a,b]$ is null, [[lem-luzin-property-n-gives-an-integral-growth-estimate]] applied to $A\setminus Z$ gives $\lambda^*(F(A\setminus Z))=0$, while $F(A\cap Z)$ is countable and hence null. Thus $F$ has property $(N)$. [given]

2.1 For $u<v$, continuity gives the interval between $F(u)$ and $F(v)$ as a subset of $F([u,v])$. The latter image is contained in $F([u,v]\setminus Z)\cup F([u,v]\cap Z)$, whose second part is countable and whose first part has outer measure at most $\int_u^v|F'|$ by the growth lemma. Hence $|F(v)-F(u)|\le\int_u^v|F'|$. Summing over any partition bounds its variation by $\int_a^b|F'|<\infty$, so $F$ has bounded variation. [step 1.1]

3.1 Since $F$ is continuous by hypothesis, step 1.1 gives property $(N)$ and step 2.1 gives bounded variation. The reverse direction of [[thm-banach-zarecki-characterisation-of-absolute-continuity]] therefore makes $F$ AC, and [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] gives the displayed reconstruction formula at every endpoint. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Fix a finite list $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$ with $N,n_0\ge1$, a depth $L\ge2$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. Let $s$ be any bounded Borel representative of the almost-everywhere derivative of $\sigma$, meaning that it agrees with the ordinary derivative outside a Lebesgue-null set; such a representative exists and is bounded by the Lipschitz constant. For every tuple of positive integer hidden widths $(n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1})$, use the width-normalized network with independent standard-normal initialization and scalar linear output.

Put

$$\Sigma^1_{ij}=\frac{x_i\cdot x_j}{n_0}+\beta^2.$$

For $r=2,\ldots,L$, let $(U_i,U_j)$ have the centered Gaussian law with variances $\Sigma^{r-1}_{ii},\Sigma^{r-1}_{jj}$ and covariance $\Sigma^{r-1}_{ij}$, and define

$$\Sigma^r_{ij}=\mathbb E[\sigma(U_i)\sigma(U_j)]+\beta^2,\qquad \dot\Sigma^r_{ij}=\mathbb E[s(U_i)s(U_j)].$$

These Gaussian laws may be singular; their marginal variances are at least $\beta^2$, and their laws and expectations depend only on the displayed covariance. Define $\Theta^1_{ij}=\Sigma^1_{ij}$ and, for $r=2,\ldots,L$,

$$\Theta^r_{ij}=\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}\dot\Sigma^r_{ij}+\Sigma^r_{ij},\qquad K_\infty=(\Theta^L_{ij})_{i,j=1}^N.$$

At initialization, the finite-data neural tangent Gram matrix $K_0$ converges in probability to $K_\infty$ under the sequential hidden-width limit $n_1\to\infty$ first, then $n_2\to\infty$, and so on through $n_{L-1}$.

For the training conclusion, fix a horizon $T\ge0$. In addition, assume that $\sigma$ is twice continuously differentiable with bounded second derivative, that $d:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^N$ is measurable and integrable, and that for each width tuple a differentiable parameter path $\theta(t)$ exists on $[0,T]$ and satisfies

$$\dot\theta_p(t)=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_{\theta_p}f_{\theta(t)}(x_i)d_i(t).$$

Write $f_t(x)=f_{\theta(t)}(x)$ and $K_t(i,j)=K_{\theta(t)}(x_i,x_j)$, where $K_\theta$ is the finite-network neural tangent kernel. Define $\|v\|_N=(N^{-1}\sum_i|v_i|^2)^{1/2}$. Suppose $\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_Ndt$ is stochastically bounded in the prescribed sequential limit, meaning that for every $\varepsilon>0$ some $M<\infty$ makes the iterated-limit upper bound on $\mathbb P(\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_Ndt>M)$ less than $\varepsilon$. Then

$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability},$$

where $\|\cdot\|_{op}$ is the Euclidean operator norm. Along the path,

$$\dot f_t(x_i)=-\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N K_t(i,j)d_j(t),$$

and

$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\left\|f_t-f_0+\frac1N\int_0^tK_\infty d(s)\,ds\right\|_N\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability}.$$

Thus the finite-time output equation has the deterministic limiting kernel as its generator in the precise integrated-error sense displayed above.
## Statement references

[Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler, Theorems 1–2, sequential infinite-width NTK and training limits](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07572)

[[def-width-normalized-fully-connected-network]]: Hidden layers use $1/\sqrt{n_\ell}$ scaling and independent Gaussian initialization

[[lem-bivariate-gaussian-feature-expectations-continuous|Gaussian feature expectations are continuous, including singular covariance limits]]

[[lem-fixed-time-lazy-training-stability|The finite-data NTK stays close to its initialization on fixed time intervals]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; finite data; $L\ge2$; $\beta>0$; a globally Lipschitz activation; the source-normalized network and independent Gaussian parameters; and, for training, the additional $C^2$ bound, an existing path, and an integrated-direction bound.

[A1] AC supplies the finite Gaussian probability laws and the countable/dependent choice needed by the sequential construction ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]]).

[F1] The network definition fixes the layer dimensions, fan-in scaling, bias scale, scalar linear output, and independent standard-normal initialization ([[def-width-normalized-fully-connected-network]]).

[F2] A finite Gaussian law, including a singular one, is uniquely determined by its mean and covariance; the layer's independent Gaussian weights and biases have product laws ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]], [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multivariate-normal-law]], [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], [[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]]).

[F3] Empirical averages of iid square-integrable variables converge in probability to their means, and standard normals have finite fourth moment ([[cor-iid-finite-variance-weak-law]], [[lem-standard-normal-fourth-moment]]).

[F4] Bivariate Gaussian expectations of Lipschitz features and bounded Borel features vary continuously with covariance, including singular limits ([[lem-bivariate-gaussian-feature-expectations-continuous]]).

[F5] The pointwise total-derivative chain rule applies to the finite network at differentiability points ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[F6] Under the additional $C^2$ bounded-second-derivative, path-existence, and integrated-direction hypotheses, the finite-data NTK remains uniformly close to its initialization ([[lem-fixed-time-lazy-training-stability]]).

[F7] The probability limit uses the event-probability convention in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

[F8] A globally Lipschitz real function is absolutely continuous on every compact interval ([[thm-c1-lipschitz-ac-bv-hierarchy]]).

[F9] Under countable choice, every absolutely continuous real function on a compact interval is differentiable almost everywhere ([[thm-absolutely-continuous-functions-have-integrable-derivatives]]).
## Proof

**Proof technique:** establish almost-sure differentiability at initialization, induct on layer covariances and Jacobian blocks, then apply the separate fixed-time drift estimate.

1.1 By [F8], $\sigma$ is absolutely continuous on every compact interval; applying [F9] on $[-m,m]$ for each positive integer $m$ shows that it is differentiable outside a Lebesgue-null set. The forward difference quotients $s_0(x)=\limsup_{k\to\infty}k(\sigma(x+1/k)-\sigma(x))$ define a bounded Borel function and equal $\sigma\prime(x)$ wherever the derivative exists. Since the given representative $s$ also equals $\sigma\prime$ almost everywhere, there is a Lebesgue-null set $E$ outside which $\sigma$ is differentiable and $s=s_0=\sigma\prime$. For any fixed finite width tuple, condition on the preceding layers: every coordinate of every data-point preactivation is normal with variance $\|z^\ell(x_i)\|_2^2/n_\ell+\beta^2\ge\beta^2$. Thus each avoids $E$ almost surely, and a finite union shows all preactivations at initialization avoid $E$ almost surely. The finite network is therefore parameter-differentiable at initialization for every data point, and [F5] applies with derivative values $s(U)$. The first-layer covariance is $\Sigma^1$; its diagonal is positive, and its Jacobian Gram block is exactly $K^1_{(i,a),(j,b)}=\delta_{ab}\Sigma^1_{ij}$ because different neurons use disjoint parameters. 2.1 Let $C_n$ be the conditional empirical covariance of the layer-$(r-1)$ preactivation vectors across the $n_{r-1}$ neurons. By induction $C_n\to\Sigma^{r-1}$ in probability; conditional on the preceding layer, these vectors are iid centered Gaussian with covariance $C_n$ and diagonal entries at least $\beta^2$. Choose $R>1+\max_i\Sigma^{r-1}_{ii}$, so $\mathbb P(\max_i(C_n)_{ii}>R)\to0$. Write $L_\sigma$ for a global Lipschitz constant. If $Y_a=\sigma(U^{r-1}_a(x_i))\sigma(U^{r-1}_a(x_j))$, the Lipschitz bound $|\sigma(u)|\le|\sigma(0)|+L_\sigma|u|$, Gaussian fourth moments, and Cauchy--Schwarz give $\mathbb E[Y_a^2\mid C_n]\le M_R$ whenever all diagonal entries of $C_n$ are at most $R$, for a finite constant $M_R$. The conditional variance bound in [F3] therefore gives $\mathbb P(|n_{r-1}^{-1}\sum_aY_a-\mathbb E[Y_a\mid C_n]|>\eta)\le\mathbb P(\max_i(C_n)_{ii}>R)+M_R/(n_{r-1}\eta^2)\to0$. The conditional mean is a bivariate Gaussian feature expectation and converges by [F4] to $\mathbb E[\sigma(U_i)\sigma(U_j)]$. For $V_a=s(U^{r-1}_a(x_i))s(U^{r-1}_a(x_j))$, the same conditional variance estimate holds with $M_R=\|s\|_\infty^4$, and [F4] makes its conditional mean converge to $\dot\Sigma^r_{ij}$. Adding the bias Gram gives $\Sigma^r$. Each empirical feature Gram plus that bias Gram is positive semidefinite with diagonal at least $\beta^2$; the cone of positive-semidefinite matrices is closed, so its deterministic limit $\Sigma^r$ is positive semidefinite and defines the next Gaussian pairs. This proves the covariance and derivative recursions at every layer. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, given]

2.2 For a finite network, [F5] gives the exact tangent-kernel block recursion $K^{r}_{(i,c),(j,d)}=\delta_{cd}(n_{r-1}^{-1}\sum_a Z^{r-1}_{ai}Z^{r-1}_{aj}+\beta^2)+n_{r-1}^{-1}\sum_{a,b}W^{(r-1)}_{ca}W^{(r-1)}_{db}s(U^{r-1}_{ai})s(U^{r-1}_{bj})K^{r-1}_{(i,a),(j,b)}$. The first term is the current-layer weight-and-bias Gram, and the second is the contribution of all earlier shared parameters. At the first layer this block is the one in step 1.1. [F1, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 At this sequential stage the previous widths have already been taken to their limits while $n_{r-1}$ and $n_r$ are fixed, so the inductive block has limit $K^{r-1}_{(i,a),(j,b)}=\delta_{ab}\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}$ for the finitely many $a,b$. Substituting this block in the Jacobian term of step 2.2 leaves $\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}n_{r-1}^{-1}\sum_a W^{(r-1)}_{ca}W^{(r-1)}_{da}q_a$, where $q_a=s(U^{r-1}_a(x_i))s(U^{r-1}_a(x_j))$ and $|q_a|\le\|s\|_\infty^2$. The current weights are independent standard normals, independent of the preceding $U$ values. Conditional on those values, for $c=d$ the mean is $\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}n_{r-1}^{-1}\sum_aq_a$ and the variance is at most $2(\Theta^{r-1}_{ij})^2\|s\|_\infty^4/n_{r-1}$, using $\operatorname{Var}(W^2)=2$; for $c\ne d$ the mean is zero and the variance is at most $(\Theta^{r-1}_{ij})^2\|s\|_\infty^4/n_{r-1}$, using independence of the two rows. The empirical average of $q_a$ converges to $\dot\Sigma^r_{ij}$ by step 2.1, so the Jacobian term converges to $\delta_{cd}\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}\dot\Sigma^r_{ij}$. The covariance term converges to $\delta_{cd}\Sigma^r_{ij}$ by steps 2.1–2.2. Hence the limiting block is $\delta_{cd}(\Sigma^r_{ij}+\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}\dot\Sigma^r_{ij})=\delta_{cd}\Theta^r_{ij}$. Since the final layer has one output, its scalar block is $K_\infty$. [F2, F3, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Under the additional $C^2$ training hypotheses, [F6] and the initialization convergence from step 3.1 give $\sup_{t\le T}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}\le\sup_{t\le T}\|K_t-K_0\|_{op}+\|K_0-K_\infty\|_{op}\to0$ in probability. The parameter-flow equation and [F5] give $\dot f_t(x_i)=-N^{-1}\sum_jK_t(i,j)d_j(t)$. Integrating and subtracting the equation with $K_\infty$ yields $\sup_{t\le T}\|f_t-f_0+N^{-1}\int_0^tK_\infty d(s)\,ds\|_N\le N^{-1}\sup_{t\le T}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}\int_0^T\|d(s)\|_Nds$. For any $M>0$ and $\delta>0$, the product exceeds $\delta$ only if $\int_0^T\|d(s)\|_Nds>M$ or $\sup_{t\le T}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}>\delta N/M$; first use stochastic boundedness to choose $M$, then use kernel convergence. Thus the right side tends to zero in probability. [F5, F6, F7, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
