## Statement

Assume AC. Fix $n_0\ge1$, $L\ge2$, $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ that is not a polynomial. For $x,y$ on the unit sphere $S^{n_0-1}=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}:\|x\|_2=1\}$, define $\Sigma^1(x,y)=x\cdot y/n_0+\beta^2$. Recursively, for $r=2,\ldots,L$, let $(U,V)$ be a centered Gaussian pair whose covariance entries are $\Sigma^{r-1}(x,x),\Sigma^{r-1}(y,y),\Sigma^{r-1}(x,y)$, and set

$$\Sigma^r(x,y)=\mathbb E[\sigma(U)\sigma(V)]+\beta^2,\qquad D^r(x,y)=\mathbb E[s(U)s(V)],$$

where $s$ is any bounded Borel representative of the almost-everywhere derivative of $\sigma$. Set $\Theta^1=\Sigma^1$ and $\Theta^r(x,y)=\Theta^{r-1}(x,y)D^r(x,y)+\Sigma^r(x,y)$. Then for every finite list of pairwise distinct points $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in S^{n_0-1}$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$,

$$\sum_{i,j=1}^N c_ic_j\Theta^L(x_i,x_j)>0.$$

Thus the scalar limiting neural tangent kernel is strictly positive definite on every finite set of distinct sphere points, for every $n_0\ge1$ and $L\ge2$. In dimension $n_0=1$ this includes both antipodal points of $S^0=\{-1,1\}$.

## Statement references

[Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler, Proposition 2 and Appendix A.4, limiting NTK positivity](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07572)

[Gneiting, Theorem 1 and sphere conventions; this proof handles $S^0$ and every dimension directly](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.7077)

[[lem-biased-hermite-kernel-is-strictly-positive-definite|Positive bias gives an all-positive power series that separates every finite sphere subset]]

[[lem-gaussian-activation-covariance-strictness-and-ntk-recursion|A nonconstant Lipschitz activation preserves strict covariance positivity at nondegenerate Gaussian inputs]]

[[thm-sequential-infinite-width-ntk-limit|The limiting scalar NTK is given by the stated covariance and tangent recursions]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; $n_0\ge1$; $L\ge2$; $\beta>0$; a globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation; and finitely many pairwise distinct unit vectors.

[A1] AC supplies the Gaussian and Hermite probability constructions ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]]).

[F1] Every finite positive-semidefinite covariance matrix defines a centered Gaussian vector, singular cases included, and its covariance uniquely determines its law ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]], [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multivariate-normal-law]]).

[F2] A Lipschitz real function is absolutely continuous on compact intervals ([[thm-c1-lipschitz-ac-bv-hierarchy]]).

[F3] The Gaussian-L² Hermite basis is complete, and its covariance expansion plus the positive-bias coefficient argument give strict activation covariance on the sphere, including $n_0=1$ ([[lem-gaussian-ltwo-hermite-completeness]], [[lem-gaussian-hermite-covariance-expansion]], [[lem-biased-hermite-kernel-is-strictly-positive-definite]]).

[F4] For a finite nondegenerate Gaussian covariance matrix, a globally Lipschitz nonconstant activation has strictly positive activation covariance; its bounded Borel derivative representative yields a positive-semidefinite derivative Gram, and the Schur product of two positive-semidefinite matrices is positive semidefinite ([[lem-gaussian-activation-covariance-strictness-and-ntk-recursion]]).

[F5] The source-normalized infinite-width theorem gives $\Theta^1_{ij}=\Sigma^1_{ij}$ and $\Theta^r_{ij}=\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}\dot\Sigma^r_{ij}+\Sigma^r_{ij}$ entrywise, where $\dot\Sigma^r_{ij}$ is the Gaussian expectation of the two hidden-layer derivatives ([[def-neural-tangent-kernel]], [[def-width-normalized-fully-connected-network]], [[thm-sequential-infinite-width-ntk-limit]]).

[F6] Under countable choice, an absolutely continuous real function on a compact interval is differentiable almost everywhere ([[thm-absolutely-continuous-functions-have-integrable-derivatives]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** use the biased Hermite supplier for the potentially singular first covariance, then propagate strictness through positive-definite Gaussian covariances and the tangent recursion.

1.1 Fix pairwise distinct $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ on the sphere. The matrix $\Sigma^1$ is a Gram matrix because $\Sigma^1_{ij}=\langle(x_i/\sqrt{n_0},\beta),(x_j/\sqrt{n_0},\beta)\rangle$; it may be singular. Its diagonal is $q=n_0^{-1}+\beta^2>0$. By [F2] and [F6], on each compact interval $\sigma$ is absolutely continuous and differentiable almost everywhere; a countable union gives a null exceptional set, and the pointwise upper limit of bounded continuous difference quotients defines a bounded Borel representative $s_0$ equal to $\sigma\prime$ wherever it exists. The given representative $s$ agrees with $s_0$ outside a null set; include this set and the nondifferentiability set in one null set $E$. The multivariate Gaussian with covariance $\Sigma^1$ exists by [F1], and every coordinate has a positive-variance normal density and hence avoids $E$ almost surely, so the choice of representative does not change any expectation. [A1, F1, F2, F6, given, construct]

2.1 The covariance $\Sigma^2$ is strictly positive definite by [F3], applied to this finite set, with the same $n_0,\beta,\sigma$. The derivative matrix $D^2$ is positive semidefinite directly: for every $c\in\mathbb R^N$, $c^TD^2c=\mathbb E[(\sum_i c_i s(U_i))^2]\ge0$ for a common Gaussian vector $U$ of covariance $\Sigma^1$. Also, writing $u_i=(x_i/\sqrt{n_0},\beta)$, finite expansion gives $c^T(\Sigma^1\circ D^2)c=\mathbb E\left\|\sum_i c_i s(U_i)u_i\right\|_2^2\ge0,$ so $\Sigma^1\circ D^2$ is positive semidefinite. Hence $\Theta^2=\Sigma^2+\Sigma^1\circ D^2$ is strictly positive definite. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $r\ge3$ and suppose $\Sigma^{r-1}$ is strictly positive definite. Its Gaussian vector therefore satisfies the nondegenerate-covariance hypothesis of [F4]; the activation is nonconstant because a nonpolynomial function cannot be constant. Thus $\Sigma^r$ is strictly positive definite and $D^r$ is positive semidefinite. If $\Theta^{r-1}$ is positive semidefinite, [F4] makes $\Theta^{r-1}\circ D^r$ positive semidefinite; adding $\Sigma^r$ makes $\Theta^r$ strictly positive definite. [F4, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 Step 2.1 initializes the induction with both $\Sigma^2$ and $\Theta^2$ strictly positive definite. Repeated step 3.1 proves $\Theta^L$ strictly positive definite for each $L\ge2$. By [F5], this recursively defined kernel is the limiting NTK of the stated network on the chosen finite data set. Since the list was arbitrary, the claimed strict positive definiteness holds for every finite set of distinct sphere points, including the two points of $S^0$. [F5, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and use the source-normalized network with scalar output, a finite data set $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ with $N\ge1$, and limiting neural tangent Gram matrix $K_\infty$ from the sequential infinite-width theorem. For a target vector $y\in\mathbb R^N$, consider the finite-data least-squares loss $\mathcal L(f)=\frac1{2N}\sum_{i=1}^N(f_i-y_i)^2$ and its limiting kernel-gradient-flow equation

$$\dot f(t)=-\frac1N K_\infty(f(t)-y),\qquad f(0)=f_0.$$

Let $K_\infty=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N)Q^T$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $\lambda_i\ge0$. Then for every $t\ge0$,

$$\bigl(Q^T(f(t)-y)\bigr)_i=e^{-t\lambda_i/N}\,\bigl(Q^T(f_0-y)\bigr)_i\quad(1\le i\le N).$$

Zero-eigenvalue residual components remain constant. If the inputs are pairwise distinct points on $S^{n_0-1}$, with $n_0\ge1$, $L\ge2$, $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation, then $K_\infty$ is positive definite and $f(t)\to y$ as $t\to\infty$.

## Statement references

[Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler, §5, least-squares NTK dynamics and eigenmode decay](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07572)

[[thm-sequential-infinite-width-ntk-limit|The limiting finite-data kernel is the deterministic recursive NTK]]

[[prop-ntk-positive-definite-on-the-sphere|The limiting NTK is strictly positive definite on distinct unit-sphere inputs]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the source-normalized scalar-output network; a finite data set of size $N\ge1$ and its labels; the limiting kernel $K_\infty$; and an initial prediction vector $f_0$.

[F1] The finite-width tangent kernel is a Jacobian Gram matrix, hence every finite-data Gram matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite ([[def-neural-tangent-kernel]]).

[F2] Under the AC and source-normalized network hypotheses, the sequential theorem supplies the deterministic limiting Gram matrix as the probability limit of finite-width Gram matrices ([[thm-sequential-infinite-width-ntk-limit]]).

[F3] A self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real inner product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis ([[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]).

[F4] The exponential has derivative equal to itself ([[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]).

[F5] For distinct unit-sphere inputs under the listed assumptions, the recursive limiting NTK Gram matrix is positive definite ([[prop-ntk-positive-definite-on-the-sphere]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** diagonalize the symmetric Gram matrix and solve each scalar residual equation.

1.1 For any finite-width parameters $\theta$ and coefficients $c_i$, [F1] gives $c^TK_\theta c=\left\|\sum_{i=1}^Nc_i\nabla_\theta f_\theta(x_i)\right\|_2^2\ge0.$ Thus every $K_\theta$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Taking the finite-dimensional probability limit in [F2] preserves symmetry and each quadratic inequality, so $K_\infty$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F3] to $K_\infty$. In the orthogonal coordinates $r(t)=Q^T(f(t)-y)$, the flow equation becomes $\dot r_i(t)=-(\lambda_i/N)r_i(t)$. Differentiating $e^{t\lambda_i/N}r_i(t)$ using [F4] gives derivative zero, so it equals its initial value. Therefore $r_i(t)=e^{-t\lambda_i/N}r_i(0)$ for every $i$, including $\lambda_i=0$. [F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Under the sphere hypotheses, [F5] makes every eigenvalue strictly positive. Hence $e^{-t\lambda_i/N}\to0$ for every $i$, so each coordinate of $Q^T(f(t)-y)$ tends to zero. Since $Q$ is orthogonal, $f(t)-y\to0$ in Euclidean norm, proving convergence to the target vector. [F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Consider the scalar one-hidden-unit model $f_{a,w}(1)=aw^2$ with parameters $(a,w)\in\mathbb R^2$ and cost $C(a,w)=\tfrac12 f_{a,w}(1)^2$. At $(a,w)=(1,1)$, gradient flow for this cost has $\dot a=-1$ and $\dot w=-2$. Its two parameter features are $\partial_a f=w^2$ and $\partial_w f=2aw$, and its neural tangent kernel at the single input is $K(a,w)=w^4+4a^2w^2$. Along the local gradient-flow solution from $(1,1)$, both features change immediately and $\frac{d}{dt}K(a(t),w(t))|_{t=0}=-32$, so this finite-width model does not have a fixed NTK.

## Example references

[Chizat, Oyallon, and Bach, §§1.1 and 2.1, tangent operator of a differentiable parameterized model](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1812.07956)

[[def-neural-tangent-kernel|The scalar NTK is the sum of parameter-feature products]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The model $f_{a,w}(1)=aw^2$, the cost $C=\tfrac12f^2$, and initial parameters $(a,w)=(1,1)$.

[F1] The scalar neural tangent kernel is the sum of squares of the parameter derivatives ([[def-neural-tangent-kernel]]).

[F2] A polynomial vector field has a unique local solution through each initial point ([[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]).

## Verification
**Proof technique:** direct differentiation.

1.1 Differentiating $f=aw^2$ gives $\partial_af=w^2$ and $\partial_wf=2aw$. By [F1], $K(a,w)=(w^2)^2+(2aw)^2=w^4+4a^2w^2.$ At $(1,1)$, $f=1$, $\partial_aC=fw^2=1$, and $\partial_wC=2faw=2$, so the negative-gradient vector field has the stated initial velocity. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The vector field $(\dot a,\dot w)=(-aw^4,-2a^2w^3)$ is polynomial, hence locally Lipschitz; [F2] gives a differentiable local solution through $(1,1)$. Along it, $\frac{d}{dt}K=4w^3\dot w+8aw^2\dot a+8a^2w\dot w,$ which equals $-8-8-16=-32$ at $t=0$. Also $\frac{d}{dt}(w^2)|_{0}=2w\dot w=-4$ and $\frac{d}{dt}(2aw)|_{0}=2(\dot a w+a\dot w)=-6$, so both parameter features vary. A differentiable scalar function with nonzero derivative at zero is not constant on any right neighborhood of zero. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume AC. Fix $N,n_0\ge1$, a data set $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$, a depth $L\ge2$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and the scalar-output source-normalized network with independent standard-normal initialization. Let $\sigma(u)=\tanh u=(e^{2u}-1)/(e^{2u}+1)$. For each finite hidden-width tuple, let the parameter path on $[0,1]$ satisfy

$$\dot\theta_p(t)=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_{\theta_p}f_{\theta(t)}(x_i),\qquad 0\le t\le1,$$

so the empirical training direction is $d_i(t)=1$ for every datum and time. The finite-width path exists on every finite interval, and its integrated empirical direction norm on $[0,1]$ equals $1$. Consequently, as the hidden widths tend to infinity sequentially, the finite-data neural tangent kernel remains uniformly close in probability on $[0,1]$ to the deterministic recursive limiting kernel $K_\infty$ for this network and data set.

## Example references

[Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler, Theorem 2 and Appendix A.2–A.3, fixed-time lazy training](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07572)

[[thm-sequential-infinite-width-ntk-limit|Sequential initialization limit and finite-time stability under bounded integrated direction]]

[[def-width-normalized-fully-connected-network|The source-normalized finite network and Gaussian initialization]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\sigma(u)=\tanh u$, a fixed finite data set and finite depth, the positive bias scale, the source-normalized scalar-output network, and the constant training direction.

[F1] The exponential is positive, satisfies the addition formula, and has derivative equal to itself; sums, products, quotients with nonzero denominator, and compositions obey the derivative rules ([[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]], [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]]).

[F2] The mean value theorem bounds increments of a differentiable function by a uniform derivative bound ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

[F3] A locally Lipschitz finite-dimensional vector field has a unique local solution ([[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]).

[F4] The parameter-gradient formulas follow from reverse accumulation over shared parameters ([[thm-shared-parameter-backpropagation-gradient-formula]]); the finite-data NTK stays uniformly close in probability to its deterministic limit on any fixed interval under the hypotheses in the stability lemma and sequential-width theorem ([[lem-fixed-time-lazy-training-stability]], [[thm-sequential-infinite-width-ntk-limit]], [[def-neural-tangent-kernel]], [[def-width-normalized-fully-connected-network]]).

## Verification
**Proof technique:** verify the activation and direction hypotheses, then apply the sequential-width theorem.

1.1 Put $a=e^{2u}>0$. Then $|a-1|<a+1$, so $|\sigma(u)|<1$. The derivative rules in [F1] give $\sigma'(u)=4e^{2u}/(e^{2u}+1)^2=1-\sigma(u)^2$ and $\sigma''(u)=-2\sigma(u)\sigma'(u)$. Thus $|\sigma'|\le1$ and $|\sigma''|\le2$. By [F2], $|\sigma(u)-\sigma(v)|\le|u-v|$, so $\sigma$ is globally Lipschitz. Since $\sigma'(u)>0$, it is nonconstant; a polynomial of degree $m\ge1$ with leading coefficient $a_m\ne0$ satisfies $p(u)/u^m\to a_m$ as $u\to+\infty$, so its absolute value is unbounded. The bounded nonconstant $\sigma$ is therefore nonpolynomial. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 For each finite network, the parameter vector field for the constant direction is smooth and locally Lipschitz, so a local solution exists by [F3]. The output-layer weights and bias have bounded speed because all hidden activations are bounded by $1$, so they remain bounded on every compact time interval. Suppose the parameters in layers $k+1,\ldots,L-1$ are bounded on such an interval. Backpropagating through those layers multiplies the direction by their finite weight matrices and factors $\sigma'$ of modulus at most $1$, so each coordinate of the backpropagated direction at layer $k+1$ is bounded. The gradient formulas in [F4], together with $|\sigma|\le1$, then bound every derivative in layer $k$; integration bounds its weights and biases. Descending induction bounds all parameters on every compact interval. If the maximal local solution had a finite endpoint, the smooth vector field would be bounded on a compact ball containing the trajectory, so the trajectory would be Lipschitz in time and have a limit as the endpoint is approached. Applying [F3] at that limit extends the solution, a contradiction. Hence the path exists on $[0,1]$. For this direction, $\|d(t)\|_N=1$ at every time, so its integral is $1$. [F3, F4, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Step 1.1 supplies the globally Lipschitz $C^2$ activation and bounded second derivative, and step 2.1 supplies a finite-width solution and the required direction bound. Applying [F4] with $T=1$ gives $\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}\to0$ in probability under the stated sequential hidden-width limit. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Example

Assume AC. Fix $N,n_0\ge1$, a depth $L\ge2$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. Use the source-normalized network with scalar output and independent standard-normal initialization, and let $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ be pairwise distinct points of $S^{n_0-1}=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}:\|x\|_2=1\}$. Let $K_\infty$ be the limiting neural tangent Gram matrix on these inputs given by the sequential infinite-width theorem. Choose a unit eigenvector $v\in\mathbb R^N$ of $K_\infty$ with eigenvalue $\lambda>0$. For labels $y\in\mathbb R^N$ and $a\ne0$, initialize the limiting empirical least-squares kernel flow by $f_0=y+av$ and solve

$$\dot f(t)=-\frac1N K_\infty(f(t)-y).$$

Then $f(t)=y+a e^{-t\lambda/N}v$. The error stays entirely in this one kernel mode, and its Euclidean norm decays by the factor $e^{-t\lambda/N}$.

## Example references

[Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler, §5, least-squares kernel eigenmodes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07572)

[[prop-ntk-positive-definite-on-the-sphere|Distinct sphere inputs give strictly positive Gram eigenvalues]]

[[thm-sequential-infinite-width-ntk-limit|The deterministic limiting Gram matrix from the sequential width limit]]

[[thm-least-squares-ntk-mode-decay]]: Each residual eigenmode evolves by $e^{-t\lambda/N}$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the source-normalized scalar-output model; $N,n_0\ge1$, $L\ge2$, $\beta>0$, a globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation; pairwise distinct unit-sphere inputs; a unit eigenvector $v$ of their sequential limiting Gram matrix with eigenvalue $\lambda>0$; target vector $y$; and initial prediction $f_0=y+a v$ with $a\ne0$.

[F1] Distinct sphere inputs under the proposition's assumptions have a positive-definite limiting NTK Gram matrix ([[prop-ntk-positive-definite-on-the-sphere]]).

[F2] Least-squares kernel flow multiplies an eigenmode residual by $e^{-t\lambda/N}$ ([[thm-least-squares-ntk-mode-decay]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** substitute the single-mode initial residual into the exact eigenmode formula.

1.1 The initial residual is $f_0-y=a v$. Since $v$ is a unit eigenvector with eigenvalue $\lambda>0$, [F2] gives $f(t)-y=a e^{-t\lambda/N}v$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Taking norms and using $\|v\|_2=1$ yields $\|f(t)-y\|_2=|a|e^{-t\lambda/N}$, which tends to zero because $\lambda/N>0$. This is the single positive mode asserted in the Example. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $X$ be a set, let $k:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ be a symmetric positive-semidefinite kernel, fix $x\in X$, and use two observations at that same input. Their Gram matrix is $K=\kappa\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, where $\kappa=k(x,x)\ge0$. For labels $y=(1,-1)^T$ and initial prediction $f_0=(0,0)^T$, consider the two-point empirical least-squares kernel flow

$$\dot f(t)=-\frac12K(f(t)-y),\qquad f(0)=f_0.$$

The vector $v_-=(1,-1)^T/\sqrt2$ is a zero-eigenvalue mode of $K$, and the residual component in this mode remains unchanged, so the flow cannot reach $y$. The unquotiented Gram matrix has rank at most one. In particular, assume AC, fix $n_0\ge1$, $L\ge2$, $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, and use the width-normalized fully connected network with fan-in scaling $1/\sqrt{n_\ell}$, bias scale $\beta$, scalar output, and independent standard-normal initialization. For any $x\in S^{n_0-1}$, its sequential hidden-width limit kernel $K_\infty$ has $K_\infty(x,x)>0$ by the sphere-positivity proposition, but the Gram matrix for two observations at $x$ is still singular. This does not conflict with that proposition, which asserts strict positivity only for finite lists of pairwise distinct sphere points.

## Example references

[Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler, §5, finite-data kernel flow and zero modes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07572)

[[def-neural-tangent-kernel|Repeated inputs give repeated rows and columns in a scalar kernel Gram matrix]]

[[thm-least-squares-ntk-mode-decay|Zero-eigenvalue residual modes stay constant]]

[[prop-ntk-positive-definite-on-the-sphere|The sequential limiting NTK is strictly positive definite on distinct sphere inputs]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A set $X$, a symmetric positive-semidefinite scalar kernel $k:X\times X\to\mathbb R$, and two identical input observations at $x\in X$, so $\kappa=k(x,x)\ge0$; labels $(1,-1)^T$; initial prediction $(0,0)^T$; and, for the sphere comparison, AC, $n_0\ge1$, $L\ge2$, $\beta>0$, a globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation, the stated width-normalized scalar-output network, and $x\in S^{n_0-1}$.

[F1] A kernel Gram matrix on an input list has entries given by evaluating the kernel at each ordered input pair; in particular, repeating the input makes all four entries equal to $k(x,x)$.

## Verification
**Proof technique:** compute the two-by-two Gram eigenvectors and inspect the inconsistent target component.

1.1 Repeating the input makes every matrix entry equal to $\kappa$, so $K=\kappa\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Multiplication gives $Kv_-=0$ for $v_-=(1,-1)^T/\sqrt2$. Thus $K$ has rank at most one and the target $y=(1,-1)^T=\sqrt2v_-$ lies entirely in its nullspace. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Set $r_-(t)=v_-^T(f(t)-y)$. The flow equation, symmetry of $K$, and $Kv_-=0$ give $\dot r_-(t)=-\frac12v_-^TK(f(t)-y)=-\frac12(Kv_-)^T(f(t)-y)=0$. Since $r_-(0)=-\sqrt2$, this residual component stays nonzero for every $t\ge0$, so $f(t)\ne y$ at every finite time and the flow cannot converge to $y$. This is consistent with the sphere proposition because its strictness conclusion requires pairwise distinct inputs. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

[F2] For the source-normalized limiting NTK flow, least-squares residual components in zero-eigenvalue modes remain constant ([[thm-least-squares-ntk-mode-decay]]); the more general two-point claim here is checked directly above.

## Definition

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

## Definition

Fix $T>0$. A curve $\mu:[0,T]\to\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ is absolutely continuous of order two, written $\mu\in AC^2([0,T];\mathcal P_2)$, if it is continuous in $W_2$ and there is a nonnegative Lebesgue-measurable $g$ with $\int_0^T g(t)^2dt<\infty$ such that $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)\le\int_s^t g(r)dr$ for every $0\le s\le t\le T$. At an interior time $t$ where the limit exists, the metric derivative is $|\dot\mu_t|=\lim_{h\to0}W_2(\mu_{t+h},\mu_t)/|h|$; no endpoint derivative is required.

## Statement

Let $T>0$ and let $t\mapsto\mu_t$ be a narrowly continuous curve of Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$, where narrow continuity means convergence against every bounded continuous real test function. For a product-Borel set $E\subseteq[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$, write $E_t=\{x:(t,x)\in E\}$ and define $M(E)=\int_0^T\mu_t(E_t)dt$. Then $t\mapsto\mu_t$ is a probability kernel, $M$ is a finite Borel measure of total mass $T$, and for every nonnegative product-Borel $f$, $\int f\,dM=\int_0^T\int f(t,x)d\mu_t(x)dt$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $T>0$ and a narrowly continuous curve $(\mu_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ of Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$.

[F1] A Borel probability law on a Polish space is a countably additive measure on its Borel sigma-algebra with total mass one. [[def-borel-probability-law-on-a-polish-space]]

[F2] Narrow convergence of Borel probabilities implies the open-set lower bound $\mu(G)\le\liminf_n\mu_n(G)$ for every open $G$. [[thm-portmanteau-theorem]]

[F3] A lambda-system containing a pi-system contains the sigma-algebra it generates. [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]

[F4] A probability kernel has a probability measure in every section and measurable evaluations in its source variable. [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]

[F5] The Borel sigma-algebra on a product of second-countable spaces equals the product sigma-algebra, which is generated by measurable rectangles. [[lem-borel-product-of-second-countable-spaces]] [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]

[F6] Sections of product-measurable sets are measurable. [[thm-sections-of-product-measurable-sets-are-measurable]]

[F7] For a probability kernel $K$ and a nonnegative product-measurable function $f$, $s\mapsto\int f(s,t)K(s,dt)$ is measurable. [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]

[F8] Increasing limits pass through nonnegative Lebesgue integrals. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]

[F9] Every nonnegative measurable function has an increasing simple approximation; nonnegative simple integrals are finite sums of their level-set measures; increasing limits of measurable functions are measurable. [[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]] [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]] [[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]

[F10] A measure is zero on the empty set and countably additive on disjoint measurable unions. [[def-measure]]


## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $G\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and let $t_n\to t$. Narrow continuity gives $\mu_{t_n}\Rightarrow\mu_t$, so [F2] gives $\mu_t(G)\le\liminf_n\mu_{t_n}(G)$. Thus $t\mapsto\mu_t(G)$ is lower semicontinuous and hence Borel measurable. [given, F2]

1.2 Let $\mathcal D$ be the Borel sets $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ for which $t\mapsto\mu_t(A)$ is measurable. It contains the whole space because each section is a probability. If $A\in\mathcal D$, then $\mu_t(A^c)=1-\mu_t(A)$, so $A^c\in\mathcal D$. For pairwise disjoint $A_j\in\mathcal D$, countable additivity gives $\mu_t(\bigcup_jA_j)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{j=0}^N\mu_t(A_j)$, a measurable increasing limit. Hence $\mathcal D$ is a lambda-system. The open sets form a pi-system generating the Borel sigma-algebra and belong to $\mathcal D$ by step 1.1, so [F3] and [F9] give $\mathcal D=\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$. Together with [F4], this proves that $t\mapsto\mu_t$ is a probability kernel. [given, F1, F3, F4, F9, step 1.1]

2.1 By [F5], a product-Borel set $E$ is measurable for $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$. Its sections $E_t$ are Borel by [F6]. Since $t\mapsto\mu_t$ is a probability kernel by step 1.2, [F7] applied to $\mathbf1_E$ shows that $t\mapsto\mu_t(E_t)$ is measurable. Thus $M(E)=\int_0^T\mu_t(E_t)dt$ is defined; $M(\varnothing)=0$ and $M([0,T]\times\mathbb R^d)=\int_0^T1dt=T$. [F5, F6, F7, step 1.2]

3.1 If $E_j$ are disjoint product-Borel sets, their sections are disjoint and $\mu_t((\bigcup_jE_j)_t)=\sum_j\mu_t((E_j)_t)$. Integrating the increasing partial sums and using [F8] gives $M(\bigcup_jE_j)=\sum_jM(E_j)$; with step 1.2 this makes $M$ a finite Borel measure. For an indicator, the iterated-integral formula is the definition of $M$; finite nonnegative simple combinations give it for simple functions. For arbitrary nonnegative product-Borel $f$, use [F9] to choose $s_n\uparrow f$ and apply [F8] to both $M$ and the time-section integrals. This proves $\int f\,dM=\int_0^T\int f(t,x)d\mu_t(x)dt$. [F1, F8, F9, F10, step 2.1] ∎

## Definition

Let S be Polish in the sense of [[def-polish-space]]. A **Borel probability law on S** is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(S)$ with total mass one. Here $\mathcal B(S)$ is [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] and probability measure means [[def-probability-measure]]. A compatible complete metric may be fixed for a construction; it is not additional data in the law. The empty space admits no such law, since its measure must be both zero and one.

## Statement

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[lem-distance-to-set-is-lipschitz]]: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (def-metric-space), let $A \subseteq X$ be nonempty and let $x, y \in X$. Then

$$|d(x,A) - d(y,A)| \le d(x,y),$$

with $d(\cdot,A)$ the distance to a nonempty set (def-metric-bounded-diameter). Thus the real-valued function $u \mapsto d(u,A)$ changes by at most $d(u,v)$ between $u$ and $v$: it is **$1$-Lipschitz**.

[F2] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then $f\in L^1(\mu)$, $$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$ and hence $$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

## Proof

**Given:** The objects, hypotheses and definitions in the statement. Its conclusions are to be established below.

1.1 (i) implies (ii) because a uniformly continuous function is continuous. Suppose (ii), and let F be nonempty and closed. By F1, $f_m(x)=\max(0,1-md(x,F))$ is bounded and uniformly continuous. Moreover $f_m\downarrow\mathbf1_F$. Thus $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\int f_m\,d\mu$ for every m. F2 with majorant one gives (iii) as m tends to infinity. For F empty the inequality is zero<=zero. [F1, F2]

1.2 For G open, apply (iii) to its closed complement and use $\mu_n(G)=1-\mu_n(S\setminus G)$ to obtain (iv). Conversely the same complement calculation obtains (iii) from (iv). If A is a Borel continuity set, $A^\circ\subseteq A\subseteq\overline A$ and $\mu(A^\circ)=\mu(A)=\mu(\overline A)$. The open lower bound and closed upper bound therefore squeeze $\mu_n(A)$ to $\mu(A)$, proving (v). [given, algebra]

1.3 Assume (v), and fix a bounded continuous real f and $\eta$>0. The disjoint level sets with $\mu(f=t)\ge1/r$ number at most r for each positive integer r. Their union over r contains all positive-mass levels and is countable (each finite subset of the real line can be listed in increasing order). Choose finitely many increasing levels $t_0<\cdots<t_m$ outside this countable set, with $t_0<-\|f\|_\infty$, $t_m>\|f\|_\infty$ and mesh below $\eta$. Such levels exist in every open interval, since an interval is uncountable. [given, algebra]

2.1 For $A_j=\{t_{j-1}\le f<t_j\}$, continuity of f gives $\partial A_j\subseteq\{f=t_{j-1}\}\cup\{f=t_j\}$, so (v) applies. The simple function $s=\sum_jt_{j-1}\mathbf1_{A_j}$ satisfies $|f-s|\le\eta$ everywhere. Therefore $|\int f\,d\mu_n-\int f\,d\mu|\le2\eta+|\sum_jt_{j-1}(\mu_n(A_j)-\mu(A_j))|$. The finite sum tends to zero, by step 1.3 and (v). Letting $\eta$ tend to zero proves (i), closing all equivalences. [step 1.3] ∎

## Statement

Let $X,Y$ be second-countable topological spaces and give $X\times Y$ the
product topology. Then
$$\mathcal B(X\times Y)=\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Second-countable topological spaces $X,Y$ with their product
topology and the product sigma-algebra.

[F1] A second-countable space has an at most countable basis, and every open
set is a union of basis elements. ([[def-second-countable-space]])

[F2] Finite products of at most countable sets are at most countable.
([[thm-product-of-countable]])

[F3] The product topology is generated by coordinate projections; in the
binary product its basic open sets are open rectangles.
([[def-product-topology]])

[F4] The Borel sigma-algebra is generated by the open sets.
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]])

[F5] The product sigma-algebra is generated by measurable rectangles.
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]])

## Proof

**Given:** Second-countable spaces $X,Y$.

1.1 Choose at most countable bases $\mathcal U$ for $X$ and $\mathcal V$ for $Y$ using [F1]. Their product $\mathcal U\times\mathcal V$ is at most countable by [F2], and its members $U\times V$ form a basis for $X\times Y$ by [F3]. Each such rectangle lies in $\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y)$; every open subset of $X\times Y$ is a union of a subfamily of this countable basis, hence a countable union of those rectangles. By [F4], this proves $\mathcal B(X\times Y)\subseteq\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y)$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4]

2.1 The coordinate projections $\pi_X:X\times Y\to X$ and $\pi_Y:X\times Y\to Y$ are continuous by the definition of the product topology [F3]. For Borel $A\subseteq X$ and $C\subseteq Y$, $A\times C=\pi_X^{-1}(A)\cap\pi_Y^{-1}(C)$ is Borel in $X\times Y$. Thus every generator rectangle of the product sigma-algebra [F5] belongs to $\mathcal B(X\times Y)$, giving the reverse inclusion. [given, F3, F4, F5, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. If
$E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, then $E_x \in \mathcal B$ for every
$x \in X$ and $E^y \in \mathcal A$ for every $y \in Y$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Measurable spaces $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$, and a set $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$.

[L1] The product sigma-algebra $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ is generated by the measurable rectangles. ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]])

[L2] The generated sigma-algebra is the smallest sigma-algebra containing the generating family. ([[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]])

[A1] For fixed $x \in X$, $$(A \times B)_x = \begin{cases} B,& x \in A,\\ \varnothing,& x \notin A,\end{cases}$$ and for fixed $y \in Y$, $$(A \times B)^y = \begin{cases} A,& y \in B,\\ \varnothing,& y \notin B.\end{cases}$$

[A2] For fixed $x$, $$((X \times Y) \setminus E)_x = Y \setminus E_x,\qquad \left(\bigcup_{n \ge 1} E_n\right)_x = \bigcup_{n \ge 1} (E_n)_x,$$ and the analogous formulas hold for vertical sections.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $x \in X$ and let $\mathcal M_x$ be the family of sets $F \subseteq X \times Y$ such that $F_x \in \mathcal B$. By [A1], every measurable rectangle belongs to $\mathcal M_x$. By [A2], $\mathcal M_x$ is a sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$. Since [L1] says $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ is generated by the measurable rectangles, [L2] gives $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B \subseteq \mathcal M_x$. Therefore $E_x \in \mathcal B$. [A1, A2, L1, L2]

2.1 Fix $y \in Y$ and let $\mathcal N_y$ be the family of sets $F \subseteq X \times Y$ such that $F^y \in \mathcal A$. The same argument shows that $\mathcal N_y$ is a sigma-algebra containing all measurable rectangles, hence all of $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$. Therefore $E^y \in \mathcal A$. Since $x$ and $y$ were arbitrary, every horizontal and vertical section of $E$ is measurable. [step 1.1, L1, L2, A1, A2] ∎

## Definition

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

## Definition

Fix $T>0$ and an integer $d\ge1$. Let $t\mapsto\mu_t$ be a narrowly continuous curve in $\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ (so $t\mapsto\int f\,d\mu_t$ is continuous for every bounded continuous $f$), let $M$ be its space-time measure $M(dt,dx)=dt\,\mu_t(dx)$, and let $v:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be Borel. Its squared action is $A(\mu,v)=\int|v(t,x)|^2dM(t,x)$. If $A(\mu,v)<\infty$, say that $v$ solves the continuity equation for $\mu$ when
$$\int_0^T\!\int_{\mathbb R^d}(\partial_t\varphi(t,x)+\nabla_x\varphi(t,x)\cdot v(t,x))\,d\mu_t(x)\,dt=0$$
for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty((0,T)\times\mathbb R^d)$. This is the distributional meaning of $\partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\cdot(v_t\mu_t)=0$; the continuous representative fixes the endpoint laws.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d_1,d_2,d_3\ge1$, let $\alpha$ be a Borel probability on $\mathbb R^{d_1}\times\mathbb R^{d_2}$ and $\beta$ a Borel probability on $\mathbb R^{d_2}\times\mathbb R^{d_3}$, and suppose the second marginal of $\alpha$ and first marginal of $\beta$ are the same probability $\rho$ on $\mathbb R^{d_2}$. There is a Borel probability $\gamma$ on $\mathbb R^{d_1}\times\mathbb R^{d_2}\times\mathbb R^{d_3}$ whose $(x,y)$ marginal is $\alpha$ and whose $(y,z)$ marginal is $\beta$.

[[def-measure]]

[Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré, *Gradient Flows*, Chapter 8](https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~sayan/ambrosio.pdf)

## Diagram

In the diagram, $X=\mathbb R^{d_1}$, $Y=\mathbb R^{d_2}$, and $Z=\mathbb R^{d_3}$. It records the required projections from the joint law $\gamma$ onto the adjacent coordinate pairs. The arrows are pushforwards of $\gamma$; the proof below constructs the middle measure explicitly and does not infer existence from the picture.

\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth]
  \node (alpha) at (0,0) {$\alpha$ on $X\times Y$};
  \node (gamma) at (3.5,0) {$\gamma$ on $X\times Y\times Z$};
  \node (beta) at (7,0) {$\beta$ on $Y\times Z$};
  \draw[->] (gamma) -- node[above] {$(x,y)_\#$} (alpha);
  \draw[->] (gamma) -- node[above] {$(y,z)_\#$} (beta);
\end{tikzpicture}

The two outer laws have the same middle marginal $\rho$ on $Y$; the arrows specify that projecting the constructed triple law onto either adjacent pair recovers the corresponding outer law.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the Axiom of Choice, the two probability measures, and their common middle marginal $\rho$.

[F1] Euclidean spaces with their Borel sigma-algebras are standard Borel; finite products have the product Borel sigma-algebra. [[def-standard-borel-space]] [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]] [[lem-borel-product-of-second-countable-spaces]]

[F2] Under AC, a probability on a product of standard Borel spaces with second marginal $\rho$ disintegrates as $K_y(dx)\rho(dy)$ for a probability kernel $K$, with the specified joint law recovered by integrating the kernel. [[thm-disintegration-of-a-joint-law-on-standard-borel-spaces]]

[F3] Products of two probability measures exist, have mass one, and assign a rectangle the product of its factor masses. [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]

[F4] The sets measurable for the product sigma-algebra are generated by measurable rectangles, and a pi-system contained in a lambda-system generates a sigma-algebra contained in that lambda-system. [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]] [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]

[F5] Kernel evaluations on measurable sets are measurable; nonnegative measurable functions can be integrated against a kernel measurably, and sections of product-measurable sets are measurable. [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]] [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]] [[thm-sections-of-product-measurable-sets-are-measurable]]

[F6] Monotone convergence passes increasing nonnegative integrands through integrals; probability measures are countably additive. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] [[def-measure]]

[F7] If $P$ is a Borel probability law on a Polish space and $S$ is Borel into a Polish space, define $S_\#P(H)=P(S^{-1}(H))$; preimages show this is a Borel probability law and that coordinate marginals compose with coordinate projections. [[def-borel-probability-law-on-a-polish-space]] [[def-measure]]

## Proof
1.1 Apply [F2] to $\alpha$ with its second coordinate y as conditioning variable, obtaining a probability kernel $K_y(dx)$ with $\alpha(A\times B)=\int_BK_y(A)d\rho(y)$. The supplier conditions on the second marginal, so for $\beta$ first define the coordinate swap $S(y,z)=(z,y)$ and $\widehat\beta=S_\#\beta$ on $\mathbb R^{d_3}\times\mathbb R^{d_2}$. By [F7], this is a Borel probability whose second marginal is the common law $\rho$. Apply [F2] to $\widehat\beta$ to obtain a probability kernel $L_y(dz)$ with $\widehat\beta(C\times B)=\int_BL_y(C)d\rho(y)$, equivalently $\beta(B\times C)=\int_BL_y(C)d\rho(y)$. Thus for every Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_1}$, $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_2}$, and $C\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_3}$ both joint laws are disintegrated over the same conditioning law. [given, F1, F2, F7]

2.1 For each $y$, let $Q_y=K_y\otimes L_y$, the product probability on $\mathbb R^{d_1}\times\mathbb R^{d_3}$. For a rectangle $A\times C$, $Q_y(A\times C)=K_y(A)L_y(C)$ is measurable in $y$. The sets $D$ for which $y\mapsto Q_y(D)$ is measurable form a lambda-system: the whole space has value one, complements have value $1-Q_y(D)$, and disjoint unions have value the increasing limit of finite sums. Rectangles form a pi-system generating the product Borel sigma-algebra by [F1] and [F4]. Thus [F4] proves measurability for every Borel $D$. The same lambda-system argument applied to rectangles $B\times A\times C$ in the variables $(y,x,z)$ shows that $y\mapsto Q_y(E_y)$ is measurable for each Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_2}\times\mathbb R^{d_1}\times\mathbb R^{d_3}$, where $E_y=\{(x,z):(y,x,z)\in E\}$. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 Define $\widetilde\gamma(E)=\int Q_y(E_y)\,d\rho(y)$ on the product Borel sigma-algebra in the coordinate order $(y,x,z)$. It is nonnegative and has total mass one. For disjoint $E_j$, their sections are disjoint, so countable additivity of $Q_y$ followed by monotone convergence [F6] gives $\widetilde\gamma(\bigcup_jE_j)=\sum_j\widetilde\gamma(E_j)$. Hence $\widetilde\gamma$ is a Borel probability. [F3, F5, F6, step 2.1]

4.1 For Borel rectangles $B\times A\times\mathbb R^{d_3}$ and $B\times\mathbb R^{d_1}\times C$, the definition and the two identities in step 1.1 give respectively $\widetilde\gamma(B\times A\times\mathbb R^{d_3})=\int_BK_y(A)L_y(\mathbb R^{d_3})\,d\rho(y)=\alpha(A\times B)$ and $\widetilde\gamma(B\times\mathbb R^{d_1}\times C)=\int_BL_y(C)K_y(\mathbb R^{d_1})\,d\rho(y)=\beta(B\times C)$. Rectangles determine finite Borel measures by [F4], so these identities identify the two pair marginals in coordinate order $(y,x,z)$. Define the Borel coordinate permutation $P(y,x,z)=(x,y,z)$ and set $\gamma=P_\#\widetilde\gamma$, meaning $\gamma(H)=\widetilde\gamma(P^{-1}(H))$ for each Borel $H$; by [F7] this is a Borel probability. The coordinate projections satisfy $\operatorname{pr}_{x,y}\circ P(y,x,z)=(x,y)$ and $\operatorname{pr}_{y,z}\circ P(y,x,z)=(y,z)$, hence their pushforwards are exactly $\alpha$ and $\beta$. [F1, F2, F4, F7, step 1.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; for the attainment claim, $\mu,\nu\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$; for the lower-semicontinuity claim, $\mu_n,\nu_n,\mu,\nu\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ with narrowly convergent sequences $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ and $\nu_n\Rightarrow\nu$.

[F1] A product of two Borel probabilities is a Borel probability with the specified marginals; $\mathbb R^{2d}$ is Polish. [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]] [[def-polish-space]]

[F2] A narrowly convergent sequence of Borel probabilities on a Polish space is tight. A tight sequence on a Polish space has a weakly convergent subsequence under AC. [[cor-weakly-convergent-sequences-are-tight]] [[def-tight-family-of-probability-measures]] [[thm-prokhorov-tightness-theorem-on-polish-spaces]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]]

[F3] Coordinate projections are continuous, so weak convergence of joint laws implies weak convergence of their coordinate marginals; a probability law is determined by its values on measurable rectangles. [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]] [[cor-weak-limits-are-unique]]

[F4] For a nonnegative measurable function, integrals of an increasing sequence converge to the integral of its pointwise limit. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]

[F5] The product coupling has finite quadratic cost because $|x-y|^2\le2|x|^2+2|y|^2$ and both marginals have finite second moment. The corresponding iterated integrals are justified by Tonelli. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

## Proof
1.1 The product probability $\mu\otimes\nu$ is a coupling by [F1]. The inequality in [F5] gives its cost at most $2\int|x|^2d\mu+2\int|y|^2d\nu<\infty$. Thus the coupling set is nonempty and its cost infimum $c$ is finite and nonnegative. [given, F1, F5]

2.1 By AC choose couplings $\pi_n$ with $\int|x-y|^2d\pi_n\le c+1/n$. Their marginals are the fixed probabilities $\mu,\nu$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, tightness of each marginal supplies compact sets $K_1,K_2$ with $\mu(K_1^c)<\varepsilon/2$ and $\nu(K_2^c)<\varepsilon/2$. Then $\pi_n((K_1\times K_2)^c)\le\mu(K_1^c)+\nu(K_2^c)<\varepsilon$ for every $n$. Hence $(\pi_n)$ is tight on the Polish space $\mathbb R^{2d}$; [F2] gives a subsequence $\pi_{n_j}\Rightarrow\pi$. By [F3] its marginals are $\mu,\nu$. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 For $N\ge1$, the function $c_N(x,y)=\min\{|x-y|^2,N\}$ is bounded and continuous. Weak convergence therefore gives $\int c_Nd\pi=\lim_j\int c_Nd\pi_{n_j}\le\liminf_j\int|x-y|^2d\pi_{n_j}\le c$. Letting $N\uparrow\infty$ and using [F4] yields $\int|x-y|^2d\pi\le c$. Since $\pi$ is a coupling and $c$ is the infimum, equality holds; the infimum is attained. [F1, F3, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 Put $L=\liminf_nW_2(\mu_n,\nu_n)^2$. If $L=+\infty$, the asserted inequality is immediate. Otherwise choose a subsequence, still indexed $n_j$, along which the costs converge to $L$, and choose by AC couplings $\sigma_j$ with costs at most $W_2(\mu_{n_j},\nu_{n_j})^2+1/j$. The marginal sequences are tight by [F2]; choosing compact sets for each coordinate and applying the same union bound as in step 2.1 proves $(\sigma_j)$ is tight on $\mathbb R^{2d}$. A further subsequence converges weakly to a probability $\sigma$, whose marginals are $\mu,\nu$ by [F3]. For every $N$, bounded continuity of $c_N$ gives $\int c_Nd\sigma\le L$. Monotone convergence [F4] then gives $\int|x-y|^2d\sigma\le L$. The definition of $W_2$ and the coupling property imply $W_2(\mu,\nu)^2\le L$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. If $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ on a Polish space, then $\{\mu,\mu_1,\mu_2,\ldots\}$ is tight.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[thm-prokhorov-tightness-theorem-on-polish-spaces]]: Assume AC. A family $\mathcal A$ of Borel probabilities on a Polish space S is tight if and only if it is relatively sequentially compact for weak convergence.

## Proof

**Given:** The objects, hypotheses and definitions in the statement. Its conclusions are to be established below.

1.1 Consider any sequence of laws from the displayed family. If some law occurs infinitely often, it has a constant subsequence. Otherwise each law occurs only finitely often. Assign every law unequal to $\mu$ its least index in the original sequence. Removing finitely many selected terms for each bounded set of such indices leaves a subsequence whose assigned indices increase to infinity; its weak limit is $\mu$ by the given convergence. [given, algebra]

2.1 Thus every sequence in the family has a weakly convergent subsequence with a probability limit on S. The reverse implication of F1, with the stated AC and Polish hypotheses, yields tightness. [F1] ∎

## Definition

A family $\mathcal A$ of Borel probabilities on a metric space S is **tight** if, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a compact $K\subseteq S$ such that $\mu(S\setminus K)<\varepsilon$ for every $\mu\in\mathcal A$. One K must work for the whole family. Compactness is [[def-metric-compactness]]. The empty family is tight, witnessed by the empty compact set.

## Statement

Bounded continuous real tests determine Borel probability measures on any metric space. In particular, weak limits are unique.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[thm-portmanteau-theorem]]: For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

[F2] [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]: Let $\mathcal P$ be a $\pi$-system on $X$. Then $\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then $\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

## Proof

**Given:** The objects, hypotheses and definitions in the statement. Its conclusions are to be established below.

1.1 If $\mu$ and $\nu$ have equal integrals of every bounded continuous test, the constant sequence $\mu$ converges weakly to $\nu$. F1 gives $\mu(F)\le\nu(F)$ for every closed F. Reverse the roles to get equality. [F1]

2.1 The class of Borel sets on which the two probabilities agree contains S, is closed under complements and disjoint countable unions, and contains the closed sets by step 1.1. Closed sets form a $\pi$-system generating the Borel $\sigma$-algebra; F2 therefore gives equality on all Borel sets. If a sequence has two weak limits, uniqueness of each numerical integral limit gives the hypothesis of step 1.1, so those limits agree. [F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every integer $d\ge1$, the function $W_2$ defined on $\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ is a metric: for all $\mu,\nu,\lambda\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ it is finite and nonnegative, $W_2(\mu,\nu)=0$ exactly when $\mu=\nu$, $W_2(\mu,\nu)=W_2(\nu,\mu)$, and $W_2(\mu,\lambda)\le W_2(\mu,\nu)+W_2(\nu,\lambda)$.

[[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]

[Chizat and Bach, Appendix A.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and $\mu,\nu,\lambda\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$.

[F1] The quadratic coupling infimum is finite and attained by a coupling. [[def-wasserstein-two-space-and-couplings]] [[prop-existence-and-lower-semicontinuity-of-optimal-couplings]]

[F2] Given couplings of $\mu$ with $\nu$ and $\nu$ with $\lambda$, under AC there is a joint law of $(X,Y,Z)$ with those two pair marginals. [[lem-wasserstein-gluing]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F3] The scalar $L^2$ Minkowski inequality holds, including finite sums; applied to the nonnegative functions $|x-y|$ and $|y-z|$, it combines with the pointwise Euclidean triangle inequality. [[thm-minkowski-integral-inequality]]

[F4] If $P$ is a Borel probability law on a Polish space and $F$ is Borel into a Polish space, define $F_\#P(B)=P(F^{-1}(B))$; preimages make this a Borel probability law, coordinate marginals compose with coordinate maps, and $\int h\,d(F_\#P)=\int h(F)\,dP$ for nonnegative Borel h by change of variables for expectation. [[def-borel-probability-law-on-a-polish-space]] [[def-measure]] [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]

## Proof
1.1 The product coupling has finite cost by [F1], so $W_2$ is finite and nonnegative. The diagonal map $\Delta(x)=(x,x)$ is Borel, and its pushforward $\Delta_\#\mu$ is a Borel probability by [F4]. Its two coordinate marginals are $(\operatorname{pr}_i\circ\Delta)_\#\mu=\mu$, and its cost is $\int|\Delta(x)_1-\Delta(x)_2|^2d\mu(x)=0$ by [F4], hence $W_2(\mu,\mu)=0$. The coordinate swap $S(x,y)=(y,x)$ is Borel; for every coupling $\pi$ of $\mu,\nu$, [F4] shows $S_\#\pi$ is a probability with first marginal $\nu$ and second marginal $\mu$, while its cost is $\int|S(x,y)_1-S(x,y)_2|^2d\pi=\int|x-y|^2d\pi$ by [F4]. Since $S$ is its own inverse, this correspondence is onto and preserves costs, proving equality of the two infima. [given, F1, F4]

2.1 If $W_2(\mu,\nu)=0$, choose an optimal coupling $\pi$ using [F1]. Its integral of $|x-y|^2$ is zero. For each positive integer $k$, the set $\{|x-y|\ge1/k\}$ has $\pi$-measure zero, since its contribution to the integral is at least $k^{-2}$ times its measure. Their union is the complement of the diagonal, so $\pi$ is concentrated on the diagonal. For every Borel set $A$, both coordinate indicators agree $\pi$-almost everywhere, giving $\mu(A)=\pi(A\times\mathbb R^d)=\pi(\mathbb R^d\times A)=\nu(A)$. Conversely, if $\mu=\nu$, step 1.1 gives distance zero. [given, F1, step 1.1]

3.1 Choose optimal couplings $\pi_{12}$ of $(\mu,\nu)$ and $\pi_{23}$ of $(\nu,\lambda)$ using [F1]. Glue them by [F2] to obtain a Borel probability $\gamma$ on $\mathbb R^{3d}$. The Borel projection $Q(x,y,z)=(x,z)$ has pushforward $Q_\#\gamma$ a Borel probability by [F4]; its coordinate marginals are $\mu$ and $\lambda$, so it is a coupling. By [F4] its cost is $\int|u-v|^2d(Q_\#\gamma)(u,v)=\int|x-z|^2d\gamma(x,y,z)$. Pointwise, $|x-z|\le|x-y|+|y-z|$; applying [F3] on $(\mathbb R^{3d},\gamma)$ gives $W_2(\mu,\lambda)\le\left(\int|x-z|^2d\gamma\right)^{1/2}\le W_2(\mu,\nu)+W_2(\nu,\lambda).$ This proves the triangle inequality and all metric axioms. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and a $W_2$-Cauchy sequence $(\mu_n)_{n\ge1}$ in $\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$.

[F1] Any two consecutive laws have an optimal coupling, and two couplings with a common marginal can be glued under AC. [[prop-existence-and-lower-semicontinuity-of-optimal-couplings]] [[lem-wasserstein-gluing]]

[F2] Borel probabilities on Polish spaces are tight; Prokhorov's theorem extracts a weakly convergent subsequence from a tight sequence under AC. [[cor-weakly-convergent-sequences-are-tight]] [[def-tight-family-of-probability-measures]] [[thm-prokhorov-tightness-theorem-on-polish-spaces]] [[def-polish-space]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]] [[def-dependent-choice]]

[F3] Scalar Minkowski's inequality holds in $L^2$; for Euclidean-valued $U,V$, the pointwise triangle inequality gives $|U+V|\le|U|+|V|$, so scalar Minkowski applied to $|U|,|V|$ gives $\|U+V\|_2\le\|U\|_2+\|V\|_2$. Cauchy--Schwarz bounds first moments by second moments on a probability space, and Fatou's lemma holds for nonnegative measurable functions. [[thm-minkowski-integral-inequality]] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]] [[thm-fatou-lemma]]

[F4] Integrals of increasing nonnegative functions converge to the integral of their pointwise limit; pushforward integration satisfies $\int f\,d(T_\#\eta)=\int f(T(\omega))d\eta(\omega)$ for nonnegative measurable $f$. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]

[F5] A complete totally bounded metric space is compact under Countable Choice; AC supplies Countable Choice. [[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]]

[F6] Weak convergence is convergence against bounded continuous tests; continuous coordinate projections preserve it by composition of tests, and a probability law has a unique weak limit. [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]] [[cor-weak-limits-are-unique]]

[F7] If $P$ is a Borel probability law on a Polish space and $F$ is Borel into a Polish space, define $F_\#P(B)=P(F^{-1}(B))$; preimages show this is a Borel probability law and that coordinate marginals compose with the corresponding coordinate maps. [[def-borel-probability-law-on-a-polish-space]] [[def-measure]]

## Proof
1.1 For each k, the Cauchy property gives a threshold N_k such that $W_2(\mu_n,\mu_m)<2^{-k}$ whenever $n,m\ge N_k$. Set $n_1=N_1$ and recursively $n_{k+1}=\max\{N_{k+1},n_k+1\}$. Then $n_k<n_{k+1}$ and $W_2(\mu_{n_k},\mu_{n_{k+1}})\le2^{-k}$. By AC choose an optimal coupling $\pi_k$ of these consecutive laws for each k using [F1]. [given, F1, construct]

1.2 Put $S=(\mathbb R^d)^{\mathbb N}$, the set of all sequences of Euclidean vectors, and equip $S$ with $D(x,y)=\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j}\min(1,|x_j-y_j|)$. This metric induces the product topology: each coordinate projection is continuous from the bound on its summand, and a product neighborhood restricting finitely many coordinates contains a sufficiently small D-ball. A D-Cauchy sequence is Cauchy in each coordinate, so coordinate completeness gives a limit in S; bounding the first finitely many coordinate terms and then the geometric tail proves convergence in D. Sequences of rational vectors which are zero after finitely many coordinates form a countable dense subset, since the tail is arbitrarily small and each of finitely many coordinates can be approximated by rationals. Thus S is complete and separable, hence Polish by definition. [def. Polish space]

2.1 Set $Q_1=\pi_1$, the probability on the first two coordinates. For $N\ge2$, assume $Q_{N-1}$ is a probability on coordinates $1,\ldots,N$ with adjacent pair marginals $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_{N-1}$ and last marginal $\mu_{n_N}$. Regard it as a law on $\mathbb R^{d(N-1)}\times\mathbb R^d$, and regard $\pi_N$ as a law on $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d$; they have the common second/first marginal $\mu_{n_N}$. The gluing statement [F1] gives $Q_N$ on coordinates $1,\ldots,N+1$ preserving all earlier adjacent marginals and adding $\pi_N$. Let $I_N:(\mathbb R^d)^{N+1}\to S$ send $(x_1,\ldots,x_{N+1})$ to $(x_1,\ldots,x_{N+1},0,0,\ldots)$; this map is continuous for the product topology. Define $\eta_N=(I_N)_\#Q_N$, that is, $\eta_N(B)=Q_N(I_N^{-1}(B))$ for Borel $B\subset S$. By [F7] it is a Borel probability, and its first $N+1$ coordinates have law $Q_N$ while every later coordinate equals zero. [F1, F7, step 1.1]

2.2 The $j$th marginal of any $\eta_N$ is either $\mu_{n_j}$ (when $N+1\ge j$) or $\delta_0$. Each fixed probability $\mu_{n_j}$ is tight by [F2]; AC chooses a compact $K_j\subset\mathbb R^d$ containing zero with $\mu_{n_j}(K_j^c)<\varepsilon2^{-j-1}$. Countable subadditivity gives $\eta_N((\prod_jK_j)^c)\le\sum_{j\ge1}\varepsilon2^{-j-1}<\varepsilon$ for every $N$. The product $K=\prod_jK_j$ is compact in $S$: it is closed and complete, and it is totally bounded because for any radius one first makes the metric tail small and then takes finite nets in the finitely many compact coordinates; [F5] applies. Hence $(\eta_N)$ is tight. By [F2] and Prokhorov, a subsequence converges weakly to a probability $\eta$ on $S$. [F2, F5, step 1.2]

3.1 For fixed $k$, all sufficiently late $\eta_N$ have their $(k,k+1)$ coordinate marginal equal to $\pi_k$. The coordinate projection $S\to\mathbb R^{2d}$ is continuous, so the projected laws of $\eta_N$ converge weakly to the corresponding marginal of $\eta$; because they are eventually exactly $\pi_k$, uniqueness of weak limits [F6] shows that this marginal is $\pi_k$. Let $X_k(x)=x_k$ be the coordinate maps on $(S,\eta)$. By [F4] and the pair marginal identity, $\int_S|X_{k+1}-X_k|^2d\eta=\int|x-y|^2d\pi_k=W_2(\mu_{n_k},\mu_{n_{k+1}})^2\le4^{-k}.$ Therefore $\int|X_{k+1}-X_k|d\eta\le2^{-k}$ by Cauchy–Schwarz. Monotone convergence [F4] shows $\int\sum_k|X_{k+1}-X_k|d\eta\le\sum_k2^{-k}<\infty$, so this sum is finite almost everywhere. The convergence set is Borel; its pointwise limit there, extended by zero on the complement, is a Borel map $X_\infty:S\to\mathbb R^d$. [F2, F3, F4, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 2.2]

4.1 Minkowski [F3] gives, for $m>n$, $\|X_m-X_n\|_{L^2(\eta)}\le\sum_{k=n}^{m-1}\|X_{k+1}-X_k\|_2\le\sum_{k=n}^{m-1}2^{-k}$. Fatou's lemma [F3] as $m\to\infty$ yields $\|X_\infty-X_n\|_2\le\sum_{k=n}^{\infty}2^{-k}$. Since $X_1$ has law $\mu_{n_1}\in\mathcal P_2$, the same inequality at $n=1$ and Minkowski imply $\int|X_\infty|^2d\eta<\infty$. Let $\mu_\infty=(X_\infty)_\#\eta$, a Borel probability by [F7]. The map $x\mapsto(X_n(x),X_\infty(x))$ is Borel, so its pushforward is a Borel probability by [F7]; its marginals are the laws of $X_n$ and $X_\infty$, namely $\mu_{n_n}$ and $\mu_\infty$. Thus $\mu_\infty\in\mathcal P_2$, and this joint law is a coupling, so $W_2(\mu_{n_n},\mu_\infty)\le\|X_n-X_\infty\|_2\le\sum_{k=n}^{\infty}2^{-k}\longrightarrow0.$ The original Cauchy sequence converges to the same limit: for any $\epsilon>0$, choose n large enough that the displayed tail bound is below $\epsilon/2$ and $n_n$ exceeds the Cauchy threshold for $\epsilon/2$; then $W_2(\mu_m,\mu_{n_n})<\epsilon/2$ for all sufficiently large m and apply the triangle inequality [F1]. [F1, F3, F4, F7, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] The pairing is linear in the first argument, conjugate-linear in the second, conjugate symmetric and positive definite, and the induced length satisfies $\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$ with $\|v\|\ge0$ and $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]).

[A2] The induced length is the unique nonnegative square root of the diagonal pairing, and positive definiteness makes the radicand a nonnegative real ([[def-inner-product-norm]]).

[A3] Every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root: there is exactly one $s\ge0$ with $s^n=a$ for each $n\ge1$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]).

[A4] For complex scalars $z\overline z=|z|^2$, $|z|\ge0$, and $|z|=0$ exactly for $z=0$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

[A5] For real scalars $|x|\ge0$, $|x|=0$ exactly for $x=0$, and $|xy|=|x|\,|y|$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]).

[A6] For nonnegative reals, $a\le b$ if and only if $a^2\le b^2$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]]).

[A7] A finite list is linearly dependent when some choice of scalars, not all zero, makes the corresponding combination vanish; for the two-element list $(x,y)$ this means that $ax+by=0$ for scalars $a,b$ not both zero ([[def-linear-independence]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** Vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space $V$. In the real case read conjugation as the identity and $|\cdot|$ as the absolute value of $\mathbb R$, so that [A4] is replaced by [A5].

1.1 If $y=0$, then $\langle x,y\rangle=\langle x,0\cdot y\rangle=0\cdot\langle x,y\rangle=0$ by conjugate-linearity in the second argument, and $\|y\|=0$; hence $|\langle x,y\rangle|=0=\|x\|\,\|y\|$, while $x,y$ are dependent with witness scalars $(a,b)=(0,1)$ because $0\cdot x+1\cdot 0=0$ and $b\ne0$. [A1, A2, A7]

1.2 Suppose now $y\ne0$ and set $c=\langle x,y\rangle/\langle y,y\rangle$, a well-defined scalar because $\langle y,y\rangle=\|y\|^2>0$; expanding with linearity in the first argument, conjugate-linearity in the second and conjugate symmetry gives $0\le\|x-cy\|^2=\|x\|^2-c\,\overline{\langle x,y\rangle}-\overline c\,\langle x,y\rangle+|c|^2\|y\|^2=\|x\|^2-|\langle x,y\rangle|^2/\|y\|^2$. [A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, algebra]

2.1 Multiplying step 1.2 by the positive number $\|y\|^2$ gives $|\langle x,y\rangle|^2\le\|x\|^2\|y\|^2$, and since $|\langle x,y\rangle|$, $\|x\|$ and $\|y\|$ are nonnegative, monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives gives the inequality $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$. [A2, A6, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 If $x,y$ are dependent, then either $y=0$, which is step 1.1, or $x=cy$ for some scalar $c$ with $y\ne0$; in the second case $\langle x,y\rangle=c\|y\|^2$ and $\|cy\|^2=\langle cy,cy\rangle=|c|^2\|y\|^2$ with both norms nonnegative, so $\|x\|=|c|\,\|y\|$ by uniqueness of nonnegative square roots, and $|\langle x,y\rangle|=|c|\,\|y\|^2=\|x\|\,\|y\|$. [A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A6, A7, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Conversely suppose $|\langle x,y\rangle|=\|x\|\,\|y\|$ and $y\ne0$; then $\|y\|^2>0$ and step 1.2 gives $\|x-cy\|^2=\|x\|^2-\|x\|^2=0$, so $x-cy=0$ by positive definiteness, that is $x=cy$ and the pair is dependent by [A7]; together with steps 1.1 and 2.2 this proves the inequality and both directions of the equality statement. [A1, A7, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(X,d)$
be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) that is complete
([[def-complete-metric-space]]) and totally bounded ([[def-totally-bounded]]).
Then $(X,d)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]).

**Where the axiom is spent, and why the weaker principle suffices.**
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used exactly once, at step 3.1, to fix one finite
$1/(n+1)$-net **together with a listing of it** for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ at
once. The family of sets being chosen from is written down before any selection
is made and does not depend on the earlier selections, which is precisely the
situation countable choice covers and dependent choice
([[def-dependent-choice]]) is not needed for. Everything after step 3.1 is
canonical: at each stage the construction takes the **least** admissible index in
the listing already fixed.

As always on this page, the claim is an upper bound on the cost of the proof
given here, not an assertion that $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is necessary for the
theorem.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A complete, totally bounded metric space $(X,d)$, an open cover of it, and the Axiom of Countable Choice.

[L1] $(X,d)$ is compact when every family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$ with union $X$ has a finite subfamily with union $X$; $U$ open means every point of $U$ has a ball around it inside $U$ ([[def-metric-compactness]], [[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metric-ball]]).

[L2] $(X,d)$ is totally bounded: for every real $\delta > 0$ there is a finite $F \subseteq X$ with $X = \bigcup_{y \in F} B(y,\delta)$, and a nonempty finite set can be listed ([[def-totally-bounded]], [[def-metric-compactness]]).

[L3] Countable choice: for a family $(E_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets there is a function $n \mapsto e_n$ with $e_n \in E_n$ for every $n$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[L4] Recursion: for a set $A$, an element $a \in A$ and a function $f : A \to A$ there is a unique $g : \mathbb{N} \to A$ with $g(0) = a$ and $g(n+1) = f(g(n))$; a stage-dependent rule is handled on $A = \mathbb{N} \times Z$, the first coordinate of $g(n)$ then being $n$ ([[thm-recursion]], [[def-finite-sum]]).

[L5] Every nonempty subset of $\mathbb{N}$ has a least element, and the order of $\mathbb{N}$ is linear ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]], [[thm-nat-linear-order]]).

[L6] A function with domain a natural number all of whose values are nonempty sets has a choice function, in ZF ([[lem-finite-choice]]).

[L7] $(X,d)$ is complete: every Cauchy sequence converges in $X$; $(c_n)$ is Cauchy when for every rational $\eta > 0$ there is $K$ with $d(c_n,c_m) < \eta$ for $n,m \ge K$; and $c_n \to p$ when for every rational $\eta > 0$ there is $K$ with $d(c_n,p) < \eta$ for $n \ge K$ ([[def-complete-metric-space]], [[def-cauchy-in-metric]], [[def-metric-convergence]], [[def-sequence]]).

[L8] For every real $\eta > 0$ there is a natural $N \ge 1$ with $1/N < \eta$, and $1/N$ is a positive rational; reciprocals of positives are positive and reverse the order ([[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]], [[thm-of-archimedean]], [[lem-of-inverse-positive]]).

[L9] A metric is symmetric and satisfies the triangle inequality ([[def-metric-space]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** contradiction.

1.1 Suppose $(X,d)$ is complete and totally bounded and that some family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$ with union $X$ has no finite subfamily with union $X$; call a subset $S \subseteq X$ **finitely covered** when some finite subfamily of $\mathcal{U}$ has union containing $S$, so that $X$ itself is not finitely covered. [L1, assume-contra]

2.1 $X \ne \emptyset$, since the empty subfamily of $\mathcal{U}$ has union $\emptyset$ and would finitely cover an empty $X$; consequently, for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the set $E_n$ of pairs $(m,f)$ with $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and $f : \sigma(m) \to X$ such that $\{f(0), \dots, f(m)\}$ is a finite $1/(n+1)$-net for $X$ is nonempty. [L2, L8, step 1.1]

3.1 Countable choice applied to $(E_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ fixes, once and for all, a function $n \mapsto (m_n, f_n)$ with $(m_n,f_n) \in E_n$; this is the single appeal to a choice principle in this proof, and the family $(E_n)$ was written down at step 2.1 before any of it was made. [L3, step 2.1]

4.1 If $S \subseteq X$ is not finitely covered and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $S \cap B(f_n(i), 1/(n+1))$ fails to be finitely covered for at least one $i \le m_n$: otherwise finite choice applied to $i \mapsto \{\text{finite subfamilies of } \mathcal{U} \text{ covering } S \cap B(f_n(i), 1/(n+1))\}$ produces one such subfamily for each $i \le m_n$, and the concatenation of those finitely many finite lists is a finite subfamily of $\mathcal{U}$ whose union contains $S = \bigcup_{i \le m_n} \big(S \cap B(f_n(i), 1/(n+1))\big)$. [L2, L6, step 3.1]

5.1 Let $i(n,S)$ be the least $i \le m_n$ with $S \cap B(f_n(i), 1/(n+1))$ not finitely covered when such an $i$ exists, and $0$ otherwise; recursion on $\mathbb{N} \times \mathcal{P}(X)$ with starting value $(0, X)$ and rule $F(n,S) := \big(n+1,\ S \cap B(f_n(i(n,S)), 1/(n+1))\big)$ then produces $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathcal{P}(X)$ whose first coordinate at $n$ is $n$; write $A_n$ for its second coordinate and $c_n := f_n(i(n,A_n))$. [L4, L5, step 4.1]

6.1 By induction, no $A_n$ is finitely covered: $A_0 = X$ is not, by step 1.1, and if $A_n$ is not then step 4.1 supplies an admissible $i$, so $i(n,A_n)$ is one and $A_{n+1} = A_n \cap B(c_n, 1/(n+1))$ is not finitely covered either. In particular every $A_n$ is nonempty, since the empty set is finitely covered by the empty subfamily; moreover $A_{n+1} \subseteq A_n$ and $A_{n+1} \subseteq B(c_n, 1/(n+1))$. [step 4.1, step 5.1]

7.1 The sequence $(c_n)$ is Cauchy: for $m \ge n$ one has $A_{m+1} \subseteq A_{n+1} \subseteq B(c_n, 1/(n+1))$ and $A_{m+1} \subseteq B(c_m, 1/(m+1))$, and taking $z \in A_{m+1}$ gives $d(c_n,c_m) \le d(c_n,z) + d(z,c_m) < 1/(n+1) + 1/(m+1) \le 2/(n+1)$; so given a rational $\eta > 0$, a natural $N \ge 1$ with $1/N < \eta/2$ makes $d(c_n,c_m) < \eta$ for all $n,m \ge N$. [L8, L9, step 6.1]

8.1 By completeness $c_n \to p$ for some $p \in X$; since $\mathcal{U}$ has union $X$ there is $U \in \mathcal{U}$ with $p \in U$, and openness of $U$ gives a real $r > 0$ with $B(p,r) \subseteq U$. [L1, L7, step 7.1]

9.1 Take a natural $N \ge 1$ with $1/N < r/2$, then $K \in \mathbb{N}$ with $d(c_n,p) < 1/N$ for all $n \ge K$, and let $n$ be whichever of $N$ and $K$ is the greater; then $1/(n+1) < 1/N < r/2$ and $d(c_n,p) < r/2$, so every $y \in A_{n+1} \subseteq B(c_n,1/(n+1))$ satisfies $d(y,p) \le d(y,c_n) + d(c_n,p) < r$, that is $A_{n+1} \subseteq B(p,r) \subseteq U$. [L5, L7, L8, L9, step 8.1]

10.1 So the one-member subfamily $\{U\}$ of $\mathcal{U}$ has union containing $A_{n+1}$, making $A_{n+1}$ finitely covered and contradicting step 6.1; the assumption of step 1.1 therefore fails, every family of open sets with union $X$ has a finite subfamily with union $X$, and $(X,d)$ is compact. [L1, step 6.1, step 9.1, discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Remarks

**Why the nets have to be chosen with their listings.** Total boundedness asserts that a finite $1/(n+1)$-net exists for each $n$; it names none, and a bare net is a set, which carries no order in which its points may be scanned. The construction needs both: a net for each $n$, so that the sets $A_n$ shrink, and a listing of it, so that "the least admissible index" is meaningful. That is why the chosen object at step 3.1 is the pair $(m_n, f_n)$ and not the net alone.

**Non-dependent, and that is the whole point.** The sets $E_n$ of step 2.1 depend on $n$ and on $(X,d)$, and on nothing that the construction produces. Had the net at stage $n+1$ been required to depend on $A_n$ — for instance a net *of the set* $A_n$ rather than of $X$ — the selection would have been dependent and countable choice would not have licensed it; the cost would then have been the dependent choice of [[def-dependent-choice]], as in [[thm-sequentially-compact-implies-totally-bounded]]. Keeping the nets fixed in advance and intersecting with balls of $X$ is what holds the price down.

**Both hypotheses are needed.** A totally bounded space that is not complete need not be compact ([[fs-totally-bounded-implies-compact]], [[cex-totally-bounded-not-compact]]), and a complete space that is not totally bounded need not be compact either, $\mathbb{R}$ with its usual metric being complete and having no finite $1$-net.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For $d\ge1$ and $\mu_n,\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$, $W_2(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$ if and only if $\mu_n$ converges narrowly to $\mu$ and
$$\lim_{R\to\infty}\sup_{n\ge1}\int_{\{|x|>R\}}|x|^2d\mu_n(x)=0.$$
Tightness by itself is insufficient: for $e_1=(1,0,\ldots,0)$ and $\mu_n=(1-n^{-2})\delta_0+n^{-2}\delta_{ne_1}$, the sequence is tight and converges narrowly to $\delta_0$, but $W_2(\mu_n,\delta_0)=1$ for every $n$.

## Statement references

[[def-wasserstein-two-space-and-couplings]]

[[thm-wasserstein-two-is-a-metric]]

[[prop-existence-and-lower-semicontinuity-of-optimal-couplings]]

[[thm-portmanteau-theorem]]

[[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]

[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]

[[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]

[[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[Santambrogio, *Optimal Transport for Applied Mathematicians*, Chapter 5](https://math.univ-lyon1.fr/~santambrogio/OTAM-cvgmt.pdf)

[Chizat and Bach, Appendix A.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $d\ge1$, and probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ with finite second moments.

[F1] Under AC, each pair has an optimal coupling, and $W_2$ is the metric defined by the infimum of the quadratic coupling cost. [[def-wasserstein-two-space-and-couplings]] [[prop-existence-and-lower-semicontinuity-of-optimal-couplings]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F2] Narrow convergence means convergence of integrals of every bounded continuous function; the portmanteau theorem gives convergence on every Borel set whose boundary has limit measure zero. [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]] [[thm-portmanteau-theorem]]

[F3] Finite Borel measures have product measures; for probability residuals, the product has those residuals as marginals. [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]

## Proof
1.1 Suppose $W_2(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$. For each $n$ choose an optimal coupling $\pi_n$ and regard its coordinates as $X_n,Y$ with laws $\mu_n,\mu$. The cost gives $\int|X_n-Y|^2d\pi_n\to0$. For bounded continuous $\varphi$, choose a ball $B(0,K)$ with $\mu(B(0,K)^c)$ small. On the event $|Y|\le K$ and $|X_n-Y|\le\delta<1$, both points lie in the compact ball $\overline B(0,K+1)$, where $\varphi$ is uniformly continuous. The complement has probability at most $\mu(B(0,K)^c)+\delta^{-2}\int|X_n-Y|^2d\pi_n$. First choose $K$, then $δ$, and then $n$; the boundedness of $\varphi$ shows $\int\varphi d\mu_n-\int\varphi d\mu\to0$. Thus $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. [given, F1, F2]

1.2 Conversely suppose narrow convergence and the stated uniform tail condition. Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $R$ so that the second-moment tails outside $Q=[-R,R]^d$ of all $\mu_n$ and of $\mu$ are less than $\varepsilon$; the tail of $\mu$ vanishes because $\mu\in\mathcal P_2$. Enlarge R slightly if necessary so its coordinate faces have zero $\mu$-mass. Partition each coordinate interval $[-R,R]$ by finitely many levels that are not atoms of the corresponding one-dimensional marginal of $\mu$, with mesh small enough that each resulting rectangular cell has diameter at most $\varepsilon$. Such levels exist because each probability has at most countably many atoms. Together with $Q^c$, these cells form a finite Borel partition $(C_i)_{i=0}^N$ whose boundaries have $\mu$-measure zero. By [F2], $a_{n,i}:=\mu_n(C_i)\to a_i:=\mu(C_i)$ for each $i$. [given, F2]

2.1 Write $Z_n=X_n-Y$ and $a_n=\int|Z_n|^2d\pi_n\to0$. For $R>K$, on $\{|X_n|>R\}$ either $|Y|>K$ or $|Z_n|>R-K$. Since $|X_n|^2\le2|Y|^2+2|Z_n|^2$, for every $n$, $\int_{|X_n|>R}|X_n|^2d\pi_n\le 2\int_{|Y|>K}|Y|^2d\pi_n+2K^2\frac{a_n}{(R-K)^2}+2a_n.$ Given a target $\eta>0$, first choose K so the first term is below $\eta/4$; then choose N so $a_n<\eta/8$ for $n\ge N$; then choose R>K so the middle term is below $\eta/8$ for all $n\ge N$. The last term is below $\eta/4$. Finally enlarge R so the finitely many tails for $n<N$ are below $\eta$. This proves the required uniform tail limit. [given, F1, step 1.1]

2.2 For each bounded cell $C_i\subset Q$, match mass $r_{n,i}=\min(a_{n,i},a_i)$. If $r_{n,i}>0$, take $r_{n,i}$ times the product of the probability measures $\mu_n|_{C_i}/a_{n,i}$ and $\mu|_{C_i}/a_i$; if $r_{n,i}=0$, use the zero measure. This gives a coupling piece supported on $C_i\times C_i$ with cost at most $\varepsilon^2r_{n,i}$. Subtract its two marginals from $\mu_n$ and $\mu$. The residual measures have equal mass. If that mass is positive, their normalized product, multiplied by that mass, couples them; if it is zero there is no residual piece. The sum is a coupling $\pi_n$ of $\mu_n,\mu$. Its matched cost is at most $\varepsilon^2$. For the residual coupling, $|x-y|^2\le2|x|^2+2|y|^2$. Its residual second moments are bounded by the two tails outside $Q$ plus $dR^2\sum_{i=1}^N|a_{n,i}-a_i|$ on each side: inside a bounded cell, unmatched mass is exactly the positive part of the difference of its two cell masses. Therefore $W_2(\mu_n,\mu)^2\le\int|x-y|^2d\pi_n\le\varepsilon^2+4\varepsilon+4dR^2\sum_{i=1}^N|a_{n,i}-a_i|.$ For this fixed finite partition the sum tends to zero, so $\limsup_nW_2(\mu_n,\mu)^2\le\varepsilon^2+4\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves $W_2(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$. [F2, F3, step 1.2]

3.1 For the witness, the mass outside a ball of radius $R$ is at most $n^{-2}$ for indices $n>R$ and is zero for indices $n\le R$; hence the family is tight.
