## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $T>0$ and $\mu\in AC^2([0,T];\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d))$, then the metric derivative
$$|\dot\mu_t|=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{W_2(\mu_{t+h},\mu_t)}{|h|}$$
exists for almost every $t\in(0,T)$, is measurable and belongs to $L^2(0,T)$. For all $0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)\le\int_s^t|\dot\mu_r|dr.$$
It is the least nonnegative square-integrable upper control: if $g\in L^2(0,T)$ and $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)\le\int_s^t g(r)dr$ for all $s\le t$, then $|\dot\mu_t|\le g(t)$ almost everywhere.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then $F$ is differentiable for almost every $x\in(a,b)$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)$$
at every such point.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, reals $a<b$, and a function $f\in L^1([a,b])$.

[L1] The $L^1$ norm is the integral of the absolute value. ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]])

[L2] Differentiation along families shrinking nicely recovers the point value at almost every point. ([[thm-differentiation-along-families-shrinking-nicely]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Extend $f$ by $0$ outside $[a,b]$, obtaining a function $g$ on [L1, given, construct, algebra] $\mathbb{R}$. Because $g$ is bounded by $|f|$ on $[a,b]$ and vanishes elsewhere, $$\int_{\mathbb{R}}|g(t)|\,dt=\int_a^b|f(t)|\,dt<\infty,$$ so $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R})$. For $x\in(a,b)$ and every $r>0$, define $$E_r^+(x):=[x,x+r),\qquad E_r^-(x):=(x-r,x].$$ Each family shrinks nicely to $x$ with constant $\alpha=\tfrac12$, because $E_r^\pm(x)\subseteq B(x,r)$ and $\lambda(E_r^\pm(x))=r=\tfrac12\lambda(B(x,r))$. [L1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Apply [L2] to the set $A:=(a,b)$ and the family $E_r^+(x)$ from step [L2, step 1.1, algebra] 1.1. This gives a full-measure subset $A_+\subseteq(a,b)$ such that $$\lim_{r\to0^+}\frac1r\int_x^{x+r}g(t)\,dt=g(x)\qquad(x\in A_+).$$ Applying [L2] again to the family $E_r^-(x)$ gives another full-measure subset $A_-\subseteq(a,b)$ such that $$\lim_{r\to0^+}\frac1r\int_{x-r}^{x}g(t)\,dt=g(x)\qquad(x\in A_-).$$ Hence both one-sided limits hold for every $x\in A_+\cap A_-$, which still has full measure in $(a,b)$. At such an $x$, if $h>0$ is small then $$\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h} =\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}f(t)\,dt =\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}g(t)\,dt,$$ while for $h<0$, $$\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h} =\frac1{|h|}\int_{x+h}^{x}g(t)\,dt.$$ Both one-sided limits therefore equal $g(x)=f(x)$. [L2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Hence $F'(x)=f(x)$ for almost every $x\in(a,b)$. [step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T>0$, $d\ge1$, and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$, with space-time law $M(dt,dx)=dt\,\mu_t(dx)$. Put $a(t)=\int|v_t(y)|^2d\mu_t(y)$ and $N=\{t:a(t)=+\infty\}$. Then $a$ is measurable, $N$ is Borel and Lebesgue-null, and the Borel representative $\bar v(t,x)=0$ for $t\in N$ and $\bar v(t,x)=v(t,x)$ for $t\notin N$ agrees with $v$ $M$-almost everywhere. For $\varepsilon>0$, let $\rho_\varepsilon$ be the strictly positive centered Gaussian probability density with covariance $\varepsilon I_d$, and define
$$p_t^\varepsilon(x)=\int\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)d\mu_t(y),\quad j_t^\varepsilon(x)=\int\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)\bar v_t(y)d\mu_t(y),\quad v_t^\varepsilon(x)=j_t^\varepsilon(x)/p_t^\varepsilon(x).$$
Then $p_t^\varepsilon$ is a strictly positive smooth probability density for each $t$, $t\mapsto\mu_t^\varepsilon$ is narrowly continuous, $v_t^\varepsilon$ is Borel and locally Lipschitz in $x$ with local magnitude and Lipschitz bounds integrable in time, and $(\mu_t*\rho_\varepsilon,v_t^\varepsilon)$ solves the continuity equation. For almost every $t$,
$$\int|v_t^\varepsilon(x)|^2p_t^\varepsilon(x)dx\le\int|v_t(y)|^2d\mu_t(y).$$

1.1 The Gaussian second moment is finite: in one dimension $x^2e^{-x^2/(2\varepsilon)}$ is bounded on $[-1,1]$ and, outside it, is bounded by a constant times $e^{-x^2/(4\varepsilon)}$, which is integrable; product integration gives $\int|z|^2\rho_\varepsilon(z)dz=d\varepsilon$. For bounded continuous f, $y\mapsto\int f(y+z)\rho_\varepsilon(z)dz$ is bounded and continuous by dominated convergence, so narrow continuity of $\mu_t$ gives narrow continuity of $\mu_t^\varepsilon$. By [F1], $a\in L^1(0,T)$ and $N$ is a Borel null set. Use $\bar v$ from the statement; because $\bar v=v$ $M$-almost everywhere, the distributional equation and action are unchanged. 2.1 Fix a compact spatial set K. 2.2 For every t, the probability measure $p_t^\varepsilon(x)^{-1}\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)d\mu_t(y)$ averages $\bar v_t$ to $v_t^\varepsilon(x)$. Cauchy--Schwarz for this probability gives $\frac{|j_t^\varepsilon(x)|^2}{p_t^\varepsilon(x)}\le\int\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)|\bar v_t(y)|^2d\mu_t(y).$ Integrate in x and use Tonelli and $\int\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)dx=1$ to obtain $\int|v_t^\varepsilon|^2p_t^\varepsilon dx\le\int|\bar v_t|^2d\mu_t$ for every t; since $\bar v=v$ $M$-almost everywhere, this is the asserted a.e. action inequality. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Since $\bar v=v$ $M$-almost everywhere, the distributional continuity-equation identity also holds with $\bar v$. ## Statement

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$, and a real random variable
$X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$,
$$E[X]=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a standard normal random variable $Z$, and $X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ for $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$.

[A1] AC is required by the standard normal probability-law definition and the Gaussian even-moment supplier. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] [[lem-gaussian-even-moment-bound-for-brownian-increments]]

[F1] $N(0,1)$ is the law with density $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$, and $N(m,\sigma^2)$ is the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ under $N(0,1)$. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]

[F2] For a standard normal $Z$, $E[Z^2]=1$. [[lem-gaussian-even-moment-bound-for-brownian-increments]]

[F3] Cauchy–Schwarz gives $E|Z|\le (E[Z^2])^{1/2}$, so the standard normal is integrable. [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]

[F4] A nonnegative measurable function of a random element has expectation equal to its integral against the law, allowing infinity; the same identity holds for a signed function once its composite is integrable. [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]

[F5] Expectation is linear, and variance is $E[(X-E[X])^2]$ for square-integrable $X$. [[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]] [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]

[F6] A pointwise-convergent sequence dominated by one integrable function has convergent integrals. [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 By [F2], $E[Z^2]=1$. Since $Z$ has a probability law by [F1], $E[1^2]=1$, and Cauchy–Schwarz [F3] gives $E|Z|\le1$; hence $Z$ is integrable. For each integer $n\ge1$, $x\phi(x)$ is odd because $\phi$ is even; [F7] with $u=-x$ therefore gives $E[Z\mathbf 1_{\{|Z|\le n\}}]=\int_{-n}^{n}x\phi(x)\,dx=0$ by [F4]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F7, algebra]

2.1 As the integer $n\to\infty$, $Z\mathbf 1_{\{|Z|\le n\}}\to Z$ pointwise and $|Z\mathbf 1_{\{|Z|\le n\}}|\le|Z|$, which is integrable by step 1.1. Dominated convergence [F6] gives $E[Z]=0$. [step 1.1, F3, F6]

3.1 Put $W=m+\sigma Z$. Since $W^2\le2m^2+2\sigma^2Z^2$, [F2] gives $E[W^2]<\infty$. The nonnegative clause of [F4] and the common law in [F1] give $E[X^2]=E[W^2]<\infty$; Cauchy–Schwarz [F3] with the constant $1$ then makes both $X$ and $W$ integrable. By [F1] and [F4], $E[X]=E[m+\sigma Z]$. Linearity [F5] and step 2.1 give $E[X]=m+\sigma E[Z]=m$. Applying the same change of variables to $(X-m)^2$ gives $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-m)^2]=\sigma^2E[Z^2]=\sigma^2$ by [F2] and [F5]. When $\sigma=0$, the affine map is constant and the same equalities give variance zero. [step 2.1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra] ∎

The moment calculation is supplied locally from the library's proved Gaussian even-moment result and the normal-law push-forward definition. The cited sources document the scale-as-standard-deviation convention used in the detection-limit model.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and give $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ the uniform topology. Define
$$\mathcal E(\gamma)=\begin{cases}\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)|^2dt,&\gamma\text{ is absolutely continuous with }\dot\gamma\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^d),\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
Then $\mathcal E$ is lower semicontinuous. More precisely,
$$\mathcal E(\gamma)=\sup_{0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T}\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\frac{|\gamma(t_{i+1})-\gamma(t_i)|^2}{t_{i+1}-t_i},$$
where the supremum is over all finite partitions of $[0,T]$.

## Statement references

[[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[[def-countable-choice]]

[[def-dependent-choice]]

[[thm-c-c-is-dense-in-l-p-for-radon-measures]]

[[def-radon-measure-on-an-lch-space]]

[[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]]

[[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]

[[thm-first-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-l-one]]

[[thm-minkowski-integral-inequality]]

[Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré, *Gradient Flows*, Chapter 8, §8.2](https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~sayan/ambrosio.pdf)

[Santambrogio, *Optimal Transport for Applied Mathematicians*, Chapter 5, §5.3](https://math.univ-lyon1.fr/~santambrogio/OTAM-cvgmt.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $T>0$, and a continuous path $\gamma:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$.

[F1] Under DC, continuous compactly supported functions are dense in $L^2(0,T)$ for Lebesgue measure; uniform continuity approximates each continuous function uniformly by interval-step functions. [[thm-c-c-is-dense-in-l-p-for-radon-measures]] [[def-radon-measure-on-an-lch-space]] [[def-dependent-choice]]

[F2] The real Hilbert space $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^d)$ is complete and bounded linear functionals on it have unique Riesz representatives under Countable Choice. [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]] [[def-countable-choice]]

[F3] AC supplies Countable and Dependent Choice for [F1]–[F2] and the scalar Lebesgue FTC. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]] [[def-dependent-choice]] [[thm-first-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-l-one]]

[F4] Cauchy--Schwarz holds for finite sums. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]

## Proof
1.1 For a partition $P=(t_i)_{i=0}^N$, write $Q_P(\gamma)=\sum_i|\gamma(t_{i+1})-\gamma(t_i)|^2/(t_{i+1}-t_i)$ and set $C=\sup_PQ_P(\gamma)$. If $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous with square-integrable derivative, Cauchy--Schwarz [F4] on each interval gives $Q_P(\gamma)\le\int_0^T|\dot\gamma|^2dt$. [given, F4, algebra]

2.1 Suppose $C<\infty$. On interval-step functions $f(t)=c_i$ for $t_i<t<t_{i+1}$ define $\Lambda(f)=\sum_i c_i\cdot(\gamma(t_{i+1})-\gamma(t_i))$. Refinement leaves this value unchanged, so the functional is well-defined. Cauchy--Schwarz for the finite sums gives $|\Lambda(f)|\le\left(\sum_i|c_i|^2\Delta t_i\right)^{1/2}Q_P(\gamma)^{1/2}\le\sqrt C\|f\|_{L^2}.$ By [F1], interval-step functions are dense in $L^2$, so $\Lambda$ extends uniquely to a bounded linear functional on the real Hilbert space $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^d)$. [F1, given, step 1.1]

3.1 By [F2]–[F3], Riesz represents $\Lambda$ by some $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^d)$. Taking the step function equal to a fixed vector c on $(s,t)$ and zero elsewhere gives $c\cdot(\gamma(t)-\gamma(s))=\int_s^t c\cdot u(r)dr$ for every $c$ and every interval. Hence $\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)=\int_s^t u(r)dr$. The scalar FTC [F3] coordinatewise shows that $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous and $\dot\gamma=u$ almost everywhere. Thus $\mathcal E(\gamma)<\infty$. [F2, F3, step 2.1]

4.1 For this absolutely continuous path, the functional $\Lambda$ is integration against $\dot\gamma$ on interval-step functions. Since those functions are dense, its norm is $\|\dot\gamma\|_{L^2}$; for each fixed partition the squared norm of the restriction of $\Lambda$ to step functions constant on its intervals is exactly $Q_P(\gamma)$. Taking the supremum over partitions therefore gives $C=\|\dot\gamma\|_{L^2}^2=\mathcal E(\gamma)$. Conversely, steps 2.1–3.1 prove that finite C forces finite energy, so if $\mathcal E(\gamma)=+\infty$ then C is also infinite. Each $Q_P$ is continuous in the uniform topology because it uses finitely many point evaluations; their supremum is lower semicontinuous. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]). If $\mu$ is a Radon measure on an LCH space $X$ and $1\le p<\infty$, then $C_c(X)$ is dense in $L^p(\mu)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** DC, $\mu$ is Radon and $1\le p<\infty$.

[L1] Finite-measure-support simple functions are dense in $L^p$. ([[thm-simple-functions-with-finite-measure-support-are-dense-in-l-p-for-finite-p]])

[L2] Under the stated DC premise, LCH cutoffs exist between compact and open sets ([[lem-lch-urysohn-cutoff-for-a-compact-set-inside-an-open-set]]). Proof 2.1 is the exact use of DC.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 It suffices by [L1] to approximate $\mathbf1_E$ when $\mu(E)<\infty$. [L1, choose] Given $\eta>0$, outer regularity gives open $U\supseteq E$ with $\mu(U\setminus E)<\eta^p/2$, and inner regularity of $U$ gives compact $K\subseteq U$ with $\mu(U\setminus K)<\eta^p/2$. [L1]

2.1 Choose $f\in C_c(X)$ with $\mathbf1_K\le f\le\mathbf1_U$ by [L2]. [step 1.1, L2] Then $$|f-\mathbf1_E|\le\mathbf1_{U\setminus K}+\mathbf1_{U\setminus E}.$$ Since both indicators take only the values zero and one and their union is $U\setminus(K\cap E)$, while $0\le f,\mathbf1_E\le1$, the error is bounded by the indicator of that union. Hence $$\|f-\mathbf1_E\|_p^p\le\mu(U\setminus K)+\mu(U\setminus E)<\eta^p.$$ Thus $\|f-\mathbf1_E\|_p<\eta$. [step 1.1, L2]

3.1 Approximate the finitely many indicator terms of a simple function separately and sum the resulting $C_c$ functions. Then use [L1] and the triangle inequality. [step 2.1, L1] ∎

## Definition

For this page, a Borel measure $\mu$ on a locally compact Hausdorff space is
**Radon** when $\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact $K$, and, for every Borel
$E$ and every open $U$,
$$\mu(E)=\inf_{E\subseteq V\text{ open}}\mu(V),\qquad \mu(U)=\sup_{K\subseteq U\text{ compact}}\mu(K).$$
Cohn calls this convention regular. It does not assert compact inner
approximation for arbitrary Borel $E$.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For every integer $d\ge1$ there is a nonnegative function $\rho_d:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with continuous partial derivatives of every order, support exactly $[-1,1]^d$, strictly positive on $(-1,1)^d$, and Lebesgue integral $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_d(x)\,dx=1$. Here the support is the closure of the set where the function is nonzero.

## Statement references

[[def-countable-choice]]

[J. K. Hunter, MIT 18.102, Chapter 4, §9 Convolution, Lemma 58](https://math.mit.edu/~rbm/18-102-Sp16/Chapter4.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and an integer $d\ge1$.

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed in the product-Lebesgue identification used in [F4]. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] For every integer $N\ge0$, $u^N e^{-u}\to0$ as $u\to+\infty$; therefore a polynomial in $u$ times $e^{-u}$ tends to zero. [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]]

[F2] The exponential is smooth and positive, and the chain and product rules differentiate its affine composites and finite products. [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]] [[thm-chain-rule]] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]

[F3] Under Countable Choice, the Lebesgue measure of a box is its side-length product; a continuous function on a compact interval is bounded, and the nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous. [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]] [[thm-extreme-value-r]] [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] [[def-countable-choice]]

[F4] Under Countable Choice, Euclidean Lebesgue measure on a finite product is the product of the coordinate Lebesgue measures, and Tonelli factors nonnegative product integrals. [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] [[def-countable-choice]]

## Proof
1.1 Define $\phi(t)=e^{-1/t}$ for $t>0$ and $\phi(t)=0$ for $t\le0$. For each $k\ge0$, repeated chain and product rules give $\phi^{(k)}(t)=P_k(1/t)e^{-1/t}$ on $t>0$ for a polynomial $P_k$: it holds with $P_0=1$, and if $u=1/t$ then differentiation replaces $P_k(u)$ by the polynomial $u^2(P_k(u)-P_k'(u))$. By [F1], this derivative tends to $0$ as $t\downarrow0$. Its difference quotient at $0$ is $uP_k(u)e^{-u}$ with $u=1/t$, which also tends to $0$ by [F1]; from the left it is zero. Induction therefore gives every derivative at $0$ equal to $0$ and continuous there, so $\phi$ is smooth on $\mathbb R$. [F1, F2, given, induction]

2.1 Set $\Phi(t)=\phi(t+1)\phi(1-t)$. By [F2], $\Phi$ is smooth. It vanishes for $t\notin[-1,1]$ and is positive for $-1<t<1$, so its support is $[-1,1]$. Let $I=\int_{\mathbb R}\Phi(t)\,dt$. The extreme-value bound [F3] makes $\Phi$ bounded on $[-1,1]$, so $I<\infty$. Since $\Phi(0)=e^{-2}>0$, continuity gives $\delta\in(0,1)$ with $\Phi(t)\ge e^{-2}/2$ on $[-\delta,\delta]$; [F3] gives $I\ge\delta e^{-2}>0$. Hence $\psi=\Phi/I$ is smooth, supported on $[-1,1]$, positive on $(-1,1)$, and has integral one. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Define $\rho_d(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\prod_{j=1}^d\psi(x_j)$. Repeated coordinatewise chain and product rules give every partial derivative as $\prod_{j=1}^d\psi^{(\alpha_j)}(x_j)$ for its multi-index $\alpha$, so all partial derivatives are continuous. The function is nonnegative, vanishes outside $[-1,1]^d$, and is positive at every point of $(-1,1)^d$; therefore its support is exactly that closed cube. [F2, given, step 2.1]

4.1 For $d=1$, $\int\rho_1=1$ by step 2.1. By step 3.1, $\rho_d$ is a nonnegative Borel function supported in the compact cube. For $d\ge2$, split $\mathbb R^d=\mathbb R^{d-1}\times\mathbb R$. By [F4] and Tonelli, $\int\rho_d\,dx=(\int\rho_{d-1}\,dx)(\int\psi\,dt)$; the second factor is $1$ by step 2.1. Induction on $d$ proves $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_d\,dx=1$. [A1, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, induction] ∎

## Statement

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $m\in\mathbb N$ and $a>0$.

[L1] Every term of the exponential series is nonnegative at a nonnegative argument ([[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]).

[L2] The exponential reciprocal identity is [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and limits at infinity are [[def-limits-at-infinity]].

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $x>0$, retain term $m+1$ of the series at $ax$: $\exp(ax)\ge (ax)^{m+1}/\iota((m+1)!)$.   [L1, given]

2.1 Hence $0\le x^m/\exp(ax)\le \iota((m+1)!)/(a^{m+1}x)$.  [step 1.1, L2, algebra]

3.1 The upper bound tends to $0$, so the quotient tends to $0$.  [step 2.1, L2] ∎

## Statement

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be **nonempty** and compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $\sup f[K]$ and $\inf f[K]$ exist and are
**attained**: there are $p, q \in K$ with

$$f(q) \;=\; \inf f[K] \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; \sup f[K] \;=\; f(p) \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, the set $f[K]$ has a maximum and a minimum
([[def-max-min]]), namely $\max f[K] = f(p)$ and $\min f[K] = f(q)$.

**Nonemptiness of $K$ is a hypothesis, not an oversight.** For $K = \varnothing$
the set $f[K]$ is empty, and neither a supremum nor a maximum of the empty set
exists in this library ([[def-complete-ordered-field]] supplies suprema of
nonempty sets bounded above only).

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], proved from the cover machinery of metric
spaces; the proof below is $\mathbb{R}$-native, running through Heine-Borel for
$\mathbb{R}$ and the order-completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, and it uses no cover
argument beyond the one already spent in
[[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-set-r]]. That the two statements are the
same statement in two vocabularies is proved in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], later on this page.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, a function $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ continuous on $A$, and a nonempty compact set $K \subseteq A$; write $S := f[K]$.

[L1] $S = f[K]$ is compact ([[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-set-r]]), and it is nonempty because $K$ is.

[L2] $S$ is bounded: there is a real $M \ge 0$ with $|z| \le M$ for every $z \in S$, so $-M$ is a lower bound and $M$ an upper bound of $S$ ([[cor-boundedness-theorem-r]], [[def-bounded-set]]).

[L3] A compact subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is closed ([[thm-heine-borel-characterisation-r]], [[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]).

[L4] Least upper bounds: a nonempty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ bounded above has a supremum ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]); a nonempty subset bounded below has an infimum ([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]).

[L5] Epsilon characterisations: for nonempty $S$ bounded above and $u = \sup S$, every real $\varepsilon > 0$ admits $s \in S$ with $u - \varepsilon < s$; dually for $\ell = \inf S$ there is $s \in S$ with $s < \ell + \varepsilon$ ([[lem-sup-epsilon]], [[lem-inf-epsilon]]).

[L6] Closure: $\overline{S}$ is the set of points every neighbourhood of which meets $S$, and $S$ is closed exactly when $S = \overline{S}$ ([[thm-closure-characterisations-r]], [[def-neighbourhood-r]]).

[L7] A maximum of a set is an element of it that bounds it above, and a minimum is an element that bounds it below ([[def-max-min]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1] the set $S = f[K]$ is nonempty and compact, and by [L2] it is bounded; by [L3] it is closed. [L1, L2, L3]

2.1 By [L4] the supremum $u := \sup S$ and the infimum $\ell := \inf S$ exist. [step 1.1, L4]

3.1 **$u$ is adherent to $S$.** Let a real $\varepsilon > 0$ be given. By [L5] there is $s \in S$ with $u - \varepsilon < s$, and $s \le u < u + \varepsilon$ since $u$ bounds $S$ above; hence $|s - u| < \varepsilon$, that is $s \in N_{\varepsilon}(u) \cap S$. So every neighbourhood of $u$ meets $S$. [step 2.1, L5, L6]

3.2 **$\ell$ is adherent to $S$.** Symmetrically, [L5] gives $s \in S$ with $s < \ell + \varepsilon$, and $\ell \le s$ since $\ell$ bounds $S$ below; hence $s \in N_{\varepsilon}(\ell) \cap S$ for every real $\varepsilon > 0$. [step 2.1, L5, L6]

4.1 By [L6] the two steps above say $u \in \overline{S}$ and $\ell \in \overline{S}$; and $S$ is closed by step 1.1, so $\overline{S} = S$ and therefore $u \in S$ and $\ell \in S$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, L6]

5.1 Since $u \in S = f[K]$ there is $p \in K$ with $f(p) = u$, and since $\ell \in S$ there is $q \in K$ with $f(q) = \ell$. [step 4.1, choose]

6.1 For every $x \in K$ the value $f(x)$ lies in $S$, so $\ell \le f(x) \le u$, that is $f(q) \le f(x) \le f(p)$. Hence $u = \sup f[K] = f(p)$ is a maximum of $f[K]$ and $\ell = \inf f[K] = f(q)$ is a minimum of it, both attained at points of $K$. [step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, L7] ∎

## Remarks

- **The two ingredients, kept apart.** Compactness of $K$ enters only through the compactness of the image; order-completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ enters only in the existence of $\sup S$ and $\inf S$. The bridge between them is closedness of $S$: a closed set contains the adherent points of itself, and the supremum of a nonempty bounded set is always adherent to it, by [[lem-sup-epsilon]]. Neither ingredient can be dropped: over $\mathbb{Q}$ the supremum need not exist, and on a noncompact domain the supremum exists and is not attained ([[cex-evt-fails-on-the-open-interval-and-on-the-half-line]]).

- **Attainment is exactly what the epsilon characterisation cannot give on its own.** [[lem-sup-epsilon]] produces points of $S$ arbitrarily close to $\sup S$ for any nonempty bounded $S$; nothing there says one of them equals $\sup S$. What closedness adds is that the limiting value is not lost.

- **The converse.** If every continuous real function on a set $E$ attains a greatest value, then $E$ is compact. That is the content of [[thm-compactness-is-necessary-for-evt-and-uniform-continuity]], which exhibits, for every noncompact $E$, a bounded continuous function on $E$ with no greatest value.

## Statement

Assume Dependent Choice. Let $M$ be a finite Radon Borel measure on $\mathbb R^n$, where $n\ge1$. Then $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ is dense in $L^2(M)$.

## Statement references

[[def-dependent-choice]]

[[def-countable-choice]]

[[lem-dependent-choice-implies-countable-choice]]

[[def-radon-measure-on-an-lch-space]]

[[thm-c-c-is-dense-in-l-p-for-radon-measures]]

[[lem-smooth-unit-mass-compact-bump-on-euclidean-space]]

[[def-mollifier-family-generated-by-a-unit-mass-smooth-bump]]

[[thm-convolution-with-a-mollifier-is-smooth-and-differentiates-under-the-integral-sign]]

[Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré, *Gradient Flows*, Chapter 8, §8.2](https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~sayan/ambrosio.pdf)

[Santambrogio, *Optimal Transport for Applied Mathematicians*, Chapter 5, §5.3](https://math.univ-lyon1.fr/~santambrogio/OTAM-cvgmt.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** DC, a finite Radon measure $M$ on $\mathbb R^n$, and $f\in L^2(M)$.

[F1] Under DC, $C_c(\mathbb R^n)$ is dense in $L^2(M)$ for a Radon measure. [[def-dependent-choice]] [[def-radon-measure-on-an-lch-space]] [[thm-c-c-is-dense-in-l-p-for-radon-measures]]

[F2] DC implies Countable Choice, as required by the mollifier smoothness supplier. [[def-dependent-choice]] [[lem-dependent-choice-implies-countable-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]]

[F3] There exists a smooth compactly supported function of unit Lebesgue integral; its rescalings form a mollifier family, and convolution of a continuous compactly supported function with a mollifier is smooth. [[lem-smooth-unit-mass-compact-bump-on-euclidean-space]] [[def-mollifier-family-generated-by-a-unit-mass-smooth-bump]] [[thm-convolution-with-a-mollifier-is-smooth-and-differentiates-under-the-integral-sign]]

## Proof
1.1 By [F1], given $\epsilon>0$ choose $g\in C_c(\mathbb R^n)$ with $\|f-g\|_{L^2(M)}<\epsilon/2$. Extend g by zero on $\mathbb R^n$; it is bounded and uniformly continuous. Let $\rho_\delta$ be the mollifier generated by [F3]. Since $\rho$ has compact support, for some $R<\infty$ its support is contained in $B_R(0)$, and $\sup_x|(g*\rho_\delta)(x)-g(x)|\le\sup_{|z|\le R\delta,x}|g(x-z)-g(x)|\longrightarrow0$ by uniform continuity. [given, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 The function $g*\rho_\delta$ is smooth by [F2], and its support lies in the sum of the compact supports of g and $\rho_\delta$, hence is compact. Since M is finite, $\|g*\rho_\delta-g\|_{L^2(M)}\le M(\mathbb R^n)^{1/2}\|g*\rho_\delta-g\|_\infty.$ Choose $\delta$ small enough that this is below $\epsilon/2$ (if $M$ is zero, every $L^2(M)$ class is zero and the conclusion is immediate). The triangle inequality gives $\|f-g*\rho_\delta\|_{L^2(M)}<\epsilon$, proving density. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

In ZF, the Axiom of Dependent Choice implies the Axiom of Countable Choice:
every at most countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-choice-function]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]).

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] $\mathrm{DC}$: for every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R\subseteq X\times X$ entire on $X$ and every $a\in X$ there is a function $x:\mathbb N\to X$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n\mathbin R x_{n+1}$ for every $n$ ([[def-dependent-choice]], [[def-natural-numbers]], [[def-function]]).

[A2] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: for every family $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb N$ and $f(n)\in E_n$ for all $n$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). A choice function on the set $\mathcal E:=\{E_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ instead has domain $\mathcal E$ and selects an element of each of its members ([[def-choice-function]]).

[A3] For sets $A$ and $B$ the collection of functions $A\to B$ is a set ([[lem-the-set-of-functions-between-two-sets-is-a-set]], [[def-power-set]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]], [[def-ordered-pair]]); unions and intersections of indexed families are available ([[def-indexed-union-and-intersection]]), induction on $\mathbb N$ is available ([[thm-induction-principle]], [[def-natural-numbers]]), and every nonempty subset of $\mathbb N$ has a least element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]); a natural number is the set of its predecessors, so $\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}n=\mathbb N$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** $\mathrm{DC}$ and a family $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets.

1.1 Let $H$ be the set of all functions $s$ with $\operatorname{dom}s\in\mathbb N$ and $s(j)\in E_j$ for every $j<\operatorname{dom}s$: this is a set by [A3] applied inside $\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n$, and the empty function lies in $H$, so $H\ne\varnothing$. [A3]

2.1 Define $R\subseteq H\times H$ by $s\mathbin R t$ if and only if $\operatorname{dom}t=\operatorname{dom}s+1$ and $t(j)=s(j)$ for every $j<\operatorname{dom}s$. Then $R$ is entire on $H$: given $s\in H$, the set $E_{\operatorname{dom}s}$ is nonempty, and for any $x\in E_{\operatorname{dom}s}$ the function $t:=s\cup\{(\operatorname{dom}s,x)\}$ lies in $H$ with $s\mathbin R t$. [step 1.1, A1]

3.1 By [A1] applied to $H$, $R$ and the empty function there is a sequence $(s_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $H$ with $s_0=\varnothing$ and $s_n\mathbin R s_{n+1}$ for every $n$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, A1]

4.1 For every $n$ one has $\operatorname{dom}s_n=n$, by induction on $n$ from [A3]: $\operatorname{dom}s_0=\operatorname{dom}\varnothing=0$, and $\operatorname{dom}s_{n+1}=\operatorname{dom}s_n+1=n+1$. [step 3.1, A3]

4.2 The union $f:=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}s_n$ is a function: if $(j,y)$ and $(j,y')$ lie in $f$, they lie in $s_m$ and $s_{m'}$ for some $m,m'$, and with $m\le m'$ the relation gives $s_m\subseteq s_{m'}$, so $y=y'$. [step 3.1, A3]

5.1 Its domain is $\mathbb N$: $\operatorname{dom}f=\bigcup_n\operatorname{dom}s_n=\bigcup_nn=\mathbb N$ by [step 4.1] and [A3]. [step 4.1, A3]

5.2 For every $n\in\mathbb N$ one has $f(n)=s_{n+1}(n)\in E_n$: the point $n$ lies in $\operatorname{dom}s_{n+1}$ by [step 4.1] and $s_{n+1}\in H$ with $\operatorname{dom}s_{n+1}=n+1>n$. [step 4.1]

6.1 Put $\mathcal E:=\{E_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$. For each $E\in\mathcal E$, the set $\{n:E_n=E\}$ is a nonempty subset of $\mathbb N$, so let $n(E)$ be its least element and define $c(E):=f(n(E))$. Then $c$ has domain $\mathcal E$ and $c(E)\in E_{n(E)}=E$, so $c$ is a choice function on the set of members even when the indexed family has repetitions. [step 5.2, A2, A3]

7.1 Hence $f$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and $f(n)\in E_n$ for every $n$, which is exactly the indexed conclusion of [A2], while $c$ is the corresponding choice function on the set of member sets. Since the family was arbitrary, $\mathrm{DC}$ implies $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. [step 4.2, step 5.1, step 5.2, step 6.1, A2] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T>0$, let $d\ge1$, and let $b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be Borel. Suppose that for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ there are nonnegative $m_K,L_K\in L^1(0,T)$ such that for almost every $t$, $|b(t,x)|\le m_K(t)$ and $|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|\le L_K(t)|x-y|$ for all $x,y\in K$. For each $(s,x_0)$ there is a unique maximal absolutely continuous solution $X(\cdot;s,x_0)$ of $\dot X=b(t,X)$ with $X(s)=x_0$, where maximal means that it has no solution extension to a strictly larger interval in $[0,T]$; any maximal endpoint lying in $(0,T)$ can occur only if the trajectory leaves every compact subset of $\mathbb R^d$. If, in addition, $b(t,\cdot)$ is continuously differentiable for almost every $t$ and $D_xb$ has integrable local bounds, then the set of initial points whose trajectories exist between any fixed pair of times is open, its time map is one-to-one onto an open image with both map and inverse continuously differentiable, and the path map into the uniform path space is continuous on the set of trajectories existing through the full interval. On compact flow tubes the dependence on the starting time is locally absolutely continuous and satisfies $\partial_sX(t;s,x)=-D_xX(t;s,x)b(s,x)$ for almost every s, simultaneously for x in the tube. The spatial derivative $V_t=D_{x_0}X(t;s,x_0)$ satisfies $\dot V_t=D_xb(t,X_t)V_t$, $V_s=I_d$, almost everywhere.

## Statement references

[[def-countable-choice]]

[[thm-banach-fixed-point]]

[[lem-vector-valued-continuous-curve-space-is-complete]]

[[thm-first-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-l-one]]

[[thm-ftc-second-part]]

[[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]

[[thm-lebesgue-differentiation-theorem-for-locally-integrable-functions-on-r-n]]

[Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré, *Gradient Flows*, Chapter 8](https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~sayan/ambrosio.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the Borel field $b$, its locally integrable magnitude bounds $m_K$, its locally integrable Lipschitz bounds $L_K$, and, for the flow-regularity clause, its almost-everywhere continuous spatial derivative with locally integrable bounds.

[F1] Continuous vector-valued curves on a compact interval form a complete space in the supremum norm; a contraction on a nonempty complete metric space has a unique fixed point. [[lem-vector-valued-continuous-curve-space-is-complete]] [[thm-banach-fixed-point]]

[F2] If $f$ is integrable, its indefinite integral is absolutely continuous and has derivative $f$ almost everywhere under Countable Choice. [[thm-first-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-l-one]] [[def-countable-choice]]

[F3] The one-variable FTC integrates the derivative of the C1 state map along a line segment. [[thm-ftc-second-part]]

[F4] Dominated convergence applies to the matrix-valued coefficients bounded by an integrable local derivative bound. [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[F5] The derivative of a composition of differentiable maps is the composition of their derivatives. [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]

[F6] Every locally integrable real function has its value as the limit of local averages almost everywhere; this applies simultaneously to a countable family under Countable Choice. [[thm-lebesgue-differentiation-theorem-for-locally-integrable-functions-on-r-n]] [[def-countable-choice]]

## Proof
1.1 Fix an initial pair $(s,x_0)$ and a closed ball $K=\overline B(x_0,r)$. On a sufficiently short one-sided interval $J$ adjoining $s$, absolute continuity of the integrals of $m_K,L_K$ gives $\int_Jm_K\le r$ and $\int_JL_K<1$. On continuous curves taking values in $K$, define $\Phi(X)(t)=x_0+\int_s^t b(q,X(q))dq,$ with the oriented integral when J lies to the left of s. The integrand is measurable because $q\mapsto(q,X(q))$ is continuous and b is Borel; it is integrable because $|b(q,X(q))|\le m_K(q)$ almost everywhere. The map preserves the closed sup-norm ball of radius r about the constant curve $x_0$, and $\|\Phi(X)-\Phi(Y)\|_\infty\le(\int_JL_K)\|X-Y\|_\infty$. By [F1] it has a unique fixed point. The integral FTC [F2] makes this curve absolutely continuous and a solution almost everywhere. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 If two solutions have the same value at one time and remain in a compact K on a common compact interval, partition that interval into finitely many subintervals on which $\int L_K<1$. On each subinterval beginning at a time where the solutions agree, their integral equations bound their sup-norm difference by $(\int L_K)$ times itself, so the difference is zero. Induction over the partition proves uniqueness throughout the common interval. Their union therefore defines a unique maximal solution. If a maximal endpoint $\tau$ lies in $(0,T)$ and the path stays in a compact K as $t\to\tau$, then $|\dot X(t)|\le m_K(t)$ makes $X(t)$ Cauchy at $\tau$. Its limit is finite, and step 1.1 restarted at that limit extends the solution, contradicting maximality. Hence an interior maximal endpoint forces the path to leave every compact set. [given, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Assume the spatial derivative hypothesis. On a short interval and compact ball as in step 1.1, solutions from nearby initial points remain in a common compact ball. The contraction estimate gives $\|X(\cdot;s,x_0+h)-X(\cdot;s,x_0)\|_\infty\le C|h|$. Write $\Delta_h(t)=X(t;s,x_0+h)-X(t;s,x_0)$. The state-variable fundamental theorem of calculus [F3] gives $\Delta_h(t)=h+\int_s^t A_h(q)\Delta_h(q)dq,\quad A_h(q)=\int_0^1D_xb(q,X(q;s,x_0)+\theta\Delta_h(q))d\theta.$ Put $A(q)=D_xb(q,X(q;s,x_0))$ at the almost-everywhere times where the spatial differential exists, with value zero on its exceptional time set. The matrix equation $V(t)=I_d+\int_s^tA(q)V(q)dq$ has a unique continuous solution by the contraction argument of step 1.1, since $\int_JL_K<1$. Subtracting its product with h from the equation for $\Delta_h$ gives $\Delta_h(t)-V(t)h=\int_s^t A_h(q)(\Delta_h(q)-V(q)h)dq+\int_s^t(A_h(q)-A(q))V(q)h\,dq.$ Taking sup norms and absorbing the first term bounds the left side by $C|h|\int_J\|A_h-A\|dq=o(|h|)$. Thus $D_{x_0}X=V$; dominated convergence in the same integral equation proves continuity of V in $x_0$. The integral FTC [F2] yields $\dot V=A(t)V$ almost everywhere. Repeating on a finite cover by overlapping short intervals gives $C^1$ dependence throughout each common flow domain and continuous dependence in the uniform path norm on trajectories existing through the full interval. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Uniqueness makes the time map from s to t injective. Continuous dependence makes its domain open; solving backward from time t shows its image is open and its inverse is the backward flow, which is $C^1$ by step 3.1. The chain rule [F5] says the derivative of the inverse times V is the identity. Thus the time map is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism between its open domain and image. [F5, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 Fix a compact flow tube and a compact set K of states it visits. For a fixed target time t, choose a compact time interval J containing t and the varying start times, with all trajectories in the flow identity remaining in K. For trajectories with the same starting time, the integral equation gives $|X(r;s,y)-X(r;s,z)|\le|y-z|+\int_JL_K(q)|X(q;s,y)-X(q;s,z)|dq$; iterating this inequality yields the spatial Lipschitz bound $|X(t;s,y)-X(t;s,z)|\le e^{\int_JL_K}|y-z|$. For $s,s+h\in J$, the flow identity and the integral equation along the short backward segment give $X(t;s+h,x)=X(t;s,X(s;s+h,x))$ and $|X(s;s+h,x)-x|\le\int_{[s,s+h]}m_K(q)dq$, where the integral is over the unoriented interval. Hence $|X(t;s+h,x)-X(t;s,x)|\le e^{\int_JL_K}\int_{[s,s+h]}m_K(q)dq$. Summing over any disjoint adjacent intervals shows that $s\mapsto X(t;s,x)$ is locally absolutely continuous, uniformly for x in the tube. To identify its derivative, choose a countable dense subset Q of K. By [F6], outside one null set the functions $m_K,L_K$ and $s\mapsto b(s,q)$ for all $q\in Q$ have their values as limits of local averages; also the spatial Lipschitz bound holds at such s. Approximation by q and the common Lipschitz bound show that the averages of $b(r,x)$ over intervals shrinking to s converge to $b(s,x)$ uniformly for $x\in K$. For the solution started at x at time $s+h$, the magnitude bound gives $|X(r;s+h,x)-x|\le\int_{[s,s+h]}m_K=O(|h|)$ uniformly between s and s+h at these Lebesgue points. Replacing $b(r,x)$ by $b(r,X(r;s+h,x))$ in the average contributes at most $|h|^{-1}O(|h|)\int_{[s,s+h]}L_K(r)dr=O(|h|)$. The integral equation therefore gives $[X(s;s+h,x)-x]/h\to-b(s,x)$ uniformly on K. The flow identity $X(t;s+h,x)=X(t;s,X(s;s+h,x))$ and the spatial derivative from step 3.1 yield $\partial_sX(t;s,x)=-D_xX(t;s,x)b(s,x)$ almost everywhere on the tube. The right side has the integrable local bound $e^{\int_JL_K}m_K(s)$, consistent with and also giving the local absolute continuity. [F2, F6, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $J$ be a nonempty compact interval and $n\ge1$. Continuous $\mathbb R^n$-valued curves on $J$ are complete in the supremum metric

$$d_\infty(x,y):=\sup_{t\in J}\|x(t)-y(t)\|_2.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A $d_\infty$-Cauchy sequence $(x_m)$ in $C(J,\mathbb R^n)$.

[L1] For a nonempty compact metric space $K$, $C(K,\mathbb R)$ is complete in the supremum metric ([[thm-c-k-complete-in-the-sup-metric]]).

[L2] Any two norms on $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$, are equivalent ([[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Each coordinate sequence is supremum-Cauchy, so [L1] gives a continuous coordinate limit; assembling the finitely many coordinate limits defines a continuous curve $x:J\to\mathbb R^n$. [given, L1]

2.1 The maximum-coordinate errors tend uniformly to zero, and [L2] bounds the Euclidean norm by a constant multiple of the maximum norm; hence $d_\infty(x_m,x)\to0$, including when $J$ is a one-point interval. [step 1.1, L2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty complete metric space $(X,d)$, a contraction $f : X \to X$ with constant $q$ satisfying $0 \le q < 1$, a starting point $x_0 \in X$, and a real $\varepsilon > 0$. Write $C := d(x_1,x_0)/(1-q)$.

[A1] Contraction: $d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$, with $0 \le q < 1$ ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]).

[A2] $(X,d)$ is complete and nonempty ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).

[L1] Recursion: for $x_0 \in X$ and $f : X \to X$ there is a unique $n \mapsto x_n$ with $x_0$ as given and $x_{n+1} = f(x_n)$ ([[thm-recursion]]).

[L2] Induction on $\mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-induction-principle]]).

[L3] Integer powers and their laws: $q^{0} = 1$, $q^{n+1} = q^{n}q$, $q^{m+n} = q^{m}q^{n}$, and $q^{n} \ge 0$ for $q \ge 0$ ([[def-integer-power]], [[lem-power-laws]]).

[L4] Factorisation: $1 - q^{N} = (1-q)\sum_{k<N} q^{k}$ for $N \ge 1$, so $\sum_{k<N} q^{k} = (1-q^{N})/(1-q) \le 1/(1-q)$ when $0 \le q < 1$ ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]], [[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-of-inverse-positive]]).

[L5] Laws of finite sums: splitting, index shift, scaling and monotonicity ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[def-finite-sum]]).

[L6] $q^{k} \to 0$ for $|q| < 1$, and a constant multiple of a null sequence is null ([[lem-geometric-sequence-null]], [[thm-algebra-of-limits]], [[def-real-limit]]).

[L7] Triangle inequality (M3), symmetry (M2) and separation (M1) of a metric, and nonnegativity ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]).

[L8] A contraction is continuous, hence sequentially continuous ([[thm-metric-regularity-hierarchy]], [[thm-metric-continuity-characterisations]]).

[L9] Limits in a metric space are unique, and convergence may be tested with real $\varepsilon > 0$ ([[lem-metric-limits-unique]], [[def-metric-convergence]], [[def-cauchy-in-metric]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]).

[L10] $1 - q > 0$, so $1/(1-q) > 0$ and $C \ge 0$ ([[lem-of-inverse-positive]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** constructive.

1.1 $X$ is nonempty, so a starting point $x_0 \in X$ exists, and [L1] produces the sequence of iterates $(x_n)$ with $x_{n+1} = f(x_n)$ for every $n$. [A2, L1, construct]

1.2 If $f(y) = y$ and $f(z) = z$ then $d(y,z) = d(f(y),f(z)) \le q\,d(y,z)$, so $(1-q)\,d(y,z) \le 0$; since $1-q > 0$ this forces $d(y,z) \le 0$, and $d(y,z) \ge 0$ gives $d(y,z) = 0$ and $y = z$. [A1, L7, L10]

2.1 For every $n$, $d(x_{n+1},x_n) \le q^{\,n} d(x_1,x_0)$, by induction on $n$: at $n = 0$ this reads $d(x_1,x_0) \le 1 \cdot d(x_1,x_0)$; and if it holds at $n$ then $d(x_{n+2},x_{n+1}) = d(f(x_{n+1}),f(x_n)) \le q\,d(x_{n+1},x_n) \le q \cdot q^{\,n} d(x_1,x_0) = q^{\,n+1} d(x_1,x_0)$. [step 1.1, A1, L2, L3]

2.2 For all $n \le m$, $d(x_m,x_n) \le \sum_{k=n}^{m-1} d(x_{k+1},x_k)$, by induction on $m$ from the triangle inequality: at $m = n$ both sides are $0$, since an empty sum is $0$; and $d(x_{m+1},x_n) \le d(x_m,x_n) + d(x_{m+1},x_m)$. [step 1.1, L2, L5, L7]

3.1 Combining, for $n \le m$: $d(x_m,x_n) \le \sum_{k=n}^{m-1} q^{\,k} d(x_1,x_0) = d(x_1,x_0)\, q^{\,n} \sum_{j < m-n} q^{\,j} \le d(x_1,x_0)\, q^{\,n} \frac{1}{1-q} = q^{\,n} C$, using the index shift $q^{\,n+j} = q^{\,n}q^{\,j}$ and monotonicity of finite sums. This is claim 3. [step 2.1, step 2.2, L3, L4, L5, L10]

4.1 The sequence $(q^{\,n} C)$ of reals is null by [L6], so there is $N$ with $q^{\,n} C < \varepsilon$ for every $n \ge N$, the terms being nonnegative. Hence for all $m,n \ge N$ we get $d(x_m,x_n) \le q^{\min\{m,n\}} C < \varepsilon$ by step 3.1 and symmetry of $d$, so $(x_n)$ is Cauchy. [step 3.1, L6, L7, L9, L10]

5.1 By [A2] the sequence converges: $x_n \to x^{*}$ for some $x^{*} \in X$. [step 4.1, A2]

6.1 $f$ is continuous, so $f(x_n) \to f(x^{*})$, that is $x_{n+1} \to f(x^{*})$; and $x_{n+1} \to x^{*}$ as well, since given a real $\eta > 0$ an index $K$ with $d(x_k,x^{*}) < \eta$ for $k \ge K$ also serves for the shifted indices $n+1 \ge K$ when $n \ge K$. [step 5.1, L8, L9]

7.1 By uniqueness of limits $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$, so $x^{*}$ is a fixed point and the iterates from $x_0$ converge to it. [step 5.1, step 6.1, L9]

8.1 So a fixed point exists by step 7.1 and there is at most one by step 1.2, which is claim 1; the iterates from an arbitrary $x_0$ converge to a fixed point by step 7.1, hence to the unique one, which is claim 2; and claim 3 is step 3.1. [step 3.1, step 7.1, step 1.2, discharge-construct] ∎

## Remarks

- **Every hypothesis is used, and each has a witness for its necessity.** Completeness: $x \mapsto x/2$ on $(0,1]$ is a contraction with constant $1/2$ and no fixed point ([[cex-contraction-on-an-incomplete-space]]). Nonemptiness: the empty metric space is complete and the empty map is a contraction with no fixed point, which is why the statement says nonempty. A constant $q$ strictly below $1$: the condition $d(f(u),f(v)) < d(u,v)$ for $u \ne v$ is strictly weaker and does not suffice ([[fs-strict-contraction-has-a-fixed-point]], [[cex-strict-contraction-without-a-fixed-point]]).
- **The proof is constructive in a usable sense.** It does not merely assert a fixed point: it names the sequence that converges to it, from any starting point whatever, and step 3.1 bounds the distance to the limit in terms of the first step alone. That is what makes the theorem an algorithm rather than an existence statement, and [[cor-banach-error-estimates]] is the statement of the two bounds a computation actually uses.
- **Where the geometric series enters.** Only through [L4], which is the factorisation $1 - q^{N} = (1-q)\sum_{k<N} q^{k}$ read backwards ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]). No theory of infinite series is used or needed: every sum in the proof is finite, and the passage to the limit is made once, at step 4.1, through the null sequence $(q^n)$.
- **Uniqueness is cheaper than existence** and uses neither completeness nor recursion: step 1.2 is three lines from the contraction inequality alone. It is what makes claim 2 unambiguous, since it forces the limits obtained from different starting points to coincide.

## Statement

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Reals $a < b$, a function $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$, $f := G'$ integrable on $[a,b]$, and a partition $P = (n,t)$ of $[a,b]$.

[L1] For a partition $P = (n,t)$ of $[a,b]$: $t_0 = a$, $t_n = b$, $t_i < t_{i+1}$ for $i < n$, $\Delta_i = t_{i+1}-t_i > 0$, and $I_i = [t_i,t_{i+1}] \subseteq [a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]], [[def-interval]]).

[L2] $L(f,P) = \sum_{i<n}m_i\Delta_i$ and $U(f,P) = \sum_{i<n}M_i\Delta_i$ with $m_i = \inf f[I_i]$ and $M_i = \sup f[I_i]$, so $m_i \le f(\xi) \le M_i$ for every $\xi \in I_i$ ([[def-darboux-sums]], [[def-bounded-set]]).

[L3] $\underline{\int_a^b} f = \sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\overline{\int_a^b} f = \inf_P U(f,P)$, and $f$ integrable means the two agree, their common value being $\int_a^b f$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

[L4] Mean value theorem: if $u$ is continuous on $[p,q]$ with $p<q$ and differentiable at every point of $(p,q)$, there is $\xi \in (p,q)$ with $u(q)-u(p) = u'(\xi)(q-p)$ ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

[L5] A function differentiable at a point is continuous there, and the restriction of a differentiable function to a subinterval is differentiable with the same derivative at every point of that subinterval which is a limit point of it ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], [[def-derivative]], [[def-continuity-real]]).

[L6] Finite sums: telescoping $\sum_{i<n}(c_{i+1}-c_i) = c_n - c_0$, and monotonicity in the terms ([[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]], clauses 4 and 5).

[L7] Ordered-field arithmetic: multiplying an inequality by a positive real preserves it, the order is total and transitive, and a number that is an upper bound of a set and also a lower bound of another set lies between their supremum and infimum ([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $P = (n,t)$ be an arbitrary partition of $[a,b]$ and let $i < n$. The restriction of $G$ to $I_i = [t_i,t_{i+1}]$ is continuous on $I_i$ and differentiable at every point of $(t_i,t_{i+1})$, with the same derivative $f$ there, by [L5] and [L1]. [given, L1, L5]

2.1 By [L4] applied on $I_i$ there is $\xi_i \in (t_i,t_{i+1})$ with $G(t_{i+1}) - G(t_i) = f(\xi_i)\,\Delta_i$; since $\xi_i \in I_i$ and $\Delta_i > 0$, [L2] gives $m_i\Delta_i \le G(t_{i+1})-G(t_i) \le M_i\Delta_i$. [step 1.1, L1, L2, L4, L7]

3.1 Step 2.1 holds for every $i < n$, so monotonicity of finite sums applies to the three families and gives $\sum_{i<n}m_i\Delta_i \le \sum_{i<n}\bigl(G(t_{i+1})-G(t_i)\bigr) \le \sum_{i<n}M_i\Delta_i$. [step 2.1, L6]

4.1 The middle sum telescopes to $G(t_n) - G(t_0) = G(b) - G(a)$ by [L6] and [L1], so $L(f,P) \le G(b)-G(a) \le U(f,P)$ by [L2]. [step 3.1, L1, L2, L6]

5.1 Step 4.1 holds for **every** partition $P$, so $G(b)-G(a)$ is an upper bound of the set of lower sums and a lower bound of the set of upper sums; hence $\underline{\int_a^b} f \le G(b)-G(a) \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ by [L3] and [L7]. [step 4.1, L3, L7]

6.1 Since $f$ is integrable the two integrals coincide with $\int_a^b f$, so $\int_a^b f = G(b)-G(a)$. [step 5.1, L3] ∎

## Remarks

- **No choice principle is spent, and no sequence of tags is ever formed.** The usual proof selects one $\xi_i$ per subinterval and assembles the Riemann sum $\sum_i f(\xi_i)\Delta_i$, which is a choice from finitely many nonempty sets. The proof above never forms that family: step 2.1 proves, for an arbitrary fixed $i$, the *inequality* $m_i\Delta_i \le G(t_{i+1})-G(t_i) \le M_i\Delta_i$, which is a universally quantified statement about $i$ and needs no selection, and step 3.1 then sums the inequality. The telescoping identity supplies the middle term without any tags at all.

- **The hypothesis is differentiability at every point of the closed interval.** It is not enough to be differentiable on $(a,b)$ and continuous on $[a,b]$ in the argument as written, because step 2.1 uses the derivative only on open subintervals but the definition $f = G'$ has to name a function on all of $[a,b]$ for $\int_a^b f$ to mean anything. Changing $f$ at the two endpoints changes neither its integrability nor its integral ([[lem-changing-a-function-at-finitely-many-points]]), so the reader who prefers the weaker hypothesis loses nothing.

- **This is the half of the fundamental theorem that computes.** The other half, [[thm-ftc-first-part]], produces a primitive; this one evaluates an integral once a primitive is known, and it is the tool the companion page reaches for whenever a primitive is available. Where no primitive is at hand the companion page computes instead by splitting at a jump and using the integral of a constant; no claim is made here about how many of its computations take which route.

- **Forward references, orientation only.** The two witnesses showing neither hypothesis is removable are [[cex-a-function-with-a-primitive-that-is-not-integrable]] and [[cex-an-integrable-function-with-no-primitive]] on the companion page; nothing above depends on either.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then
$$\lim_{r\to0^+}A_rf(x)=f(x)$$
for Lebesgue-almost every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice and a function $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

[L1] Continuous compactly supported functions are recovered by small ball averages at every point. ([[lem-continuous-compactly-supported-functions-differentiate-by-ball-averages]])

[L2] For $1\le p<\infty$, $C_c(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is dense in $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$. ([[thm-c-c-rn-is-dense-in-l-p-of-rn]])

[L3] Chebyshev-Markov controls superlevel sets by the integral. ([[thm-chebyshev-markov-inequality-for-the-integral]])

[L4] The centered maximal operator is weak type $(1,1)$. ([[thm-hardy-littlewood-maximal-inequality-for-balls]])

[L5] Under Countable Choice, $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure on the Lebesgue sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^n$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]). For measurable sets, finite and countable unions have measure at most the corresponding sum, and inclusion implies monotonicity ([[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], [[prop-measure-monotonicity]]). In particular a countable union of measurable $\lambda_n$-zero sets has measure zero.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For each integer $m\ge1$ and each integer $j\ge1$, apply [L2] to the [L2, given, choose, construct] $L^1$ function $f\mathbf{1}_{B(0,m+1)}$ and choose $g_{m,j}\in C_c(\mathbb{R}^n)$ such that $$\int_{B(0,m+1)}|f-g_{m,j}|\,d\lambda<\frac{2^{-2j}}{5^n}.$$ Set $$h_{m,j}:=(f-g_{m,j})\mathbf{1}_{B(0,m+1)}.$$ [L2, given, choose, construct]

2.1 Let [L3, L4, L5, step 1.1, algebra] $$E_{m,j}:=\left\{x\in B(0,m):Mh_{m,j}(x)>2^{-j}\right\} \cup\left\{x\in B(0,m):|h_{m,j}(x)|>2^{-j}\right\}.$$ Both sets are Lebesgue measurable: the maximal superlevel set is open by the ball-average continuity argument in [L4], and $h_{m,j}$ is measurable. Finite subadditivity [L5], [L4] and [L3] give $$\lambda(E_{m,j}) \le \frac{5^n}{2^{-j}}\|h_{m,j}\|_1 +\frac{1}{2^{-j}}\|h_{m,j}\|_1 <2^{-j}+5^{-n}2^{-j}\le2^{1-j}.$$ [L3, L4, L5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For fixed $m$, put [step 2.1, algebra] $$N_m:=\bigcap_{N=1}^\infty\bigcup_{j\ge N}E_{m,j}.$$ The sets $E_{m,j}$, their countable unions, and $N_m$ are measurable by [L5]. By countable subadditivity [L5] and step 2.1 $$\lambda\!\left(\bigcup_{j\ge N}E_{m,j}\right) \le\sum_{j\ge N}\lambda(E_{m,j}) \le\sum_{j\ge N}2^{1-j}=2^{2-N}.$$ For every $N$, inclusion and monotonicity [L5] give $0\le\lambda(N_m)\le2^{2-N}$. Given $\epsilon>0$, choose $N$ with $2^{2-N}<\epsilon$; thus $\lambda(N_m)=0$. This uses small positive tail measures, without asserting that any $E_{m,j}$ is null. [L5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $x\in B(0,m)\setminus N_m$. Then there is $N_x$ such that [L1, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] $x\notin E_{m,j}$ for every $j\ge N_x$. Fix such a $j$ and take $0<r<1$. Since $x\in B(0,m)$, one has $B(x,r)\subseteq B(0,m+1)$, so $$A_r f(x)-f(x) =\big(A_rg_{m,j}(x)-g_{m,j}(x)\big)+A_rh_{m,j}(x)-h_{m,j}(x).$$ Therefore $$|A_r f(x)-f(x)| \le |A_rg_{m,j}(x)-g_{m,j}(x)|+Mh_{m,j}(x)+|h_{m,j}(x)| \le |A_rg_{m,j}(x)-g_{m,j}(x)|+2^{1-j}.$$ Now [L1] gives $A_rg_{m,j}(x)\to g_{m,j}(x)$, so $$\limsup_{r\to0^+}|A_r f(x)-f(x)|\le 2^{1-j}$$ for every $j\ge N_x$. Letting $j\to\infty$ yields $A_r f(x)\to f(x)$. [L1, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The bad set for radius differentiation is contained in [step 3.1, step 4.1, L5] $\bigcup_{m\ge1}N_m$, which is null by [L5]. Thus the convergence holds for almost every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, L5] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(\mu_t^\varepsilon,v_t^\varepsilon)$ be the Gaussian-regularized solution from the preceding lemma on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$, and write $\mu_t^\varepsilon=p_t^\varepsilon(x)dx$. There is a unique maximal local flow $X_t^\varepsilon(x)$ solving $\dot X_t^\varepsilon(x)=v_t^\varepsilon(X_t^\varepsilon(x))$, $X_0^\varepsilon(x)=x$. For $\mu_0^\varepsilon$-almost every x the path exists on all of $[0,T]$, the map from x to its path is Borel on this full-measure domain, and for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\mu_t^\varepsilon=(X_t^\varepsilon)_\#\mu_0^\varepsilon.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the positive smooth densities $p_t^\varepsilon$, the locally time-integrably Lipschitz vector field $v_t^\varepsilon$, its distributional continuity equation, and finite action.

[F1] The Gaussian-regularized pair has positive spatially smooth density, solves the continuity equation, and has finite action. [[lem-gaussian-regularization-of-continuity-equation]]

[F2] A Borel field with integrable local magnitude and Lipschitz bounds has a unique maximal local flow; its time maps are diffeomorphisms between their open domains and images, and an interior maximal endpoint requires escape from every compact set. [[lem-carath-ode-flow-with-integrable-local-bounds]]

[F3] A finite Borel probability on a Polish space is inner regular; on a Euclidean open set, compactly supported continuous functions are uniformly approximated by smooth compactly supported functions by convolving their zero extensions with a unit-mass bump of sufficiently small support. [[thm-borel-probability-measures-on-polish-spaces-are-inner-regular]] [[lem-smooth-unit-mass-compact-bump-on-euclidean-space]] [[def-mollifier-family-generated-by-a-unit-mass-smooth-bump]] [[thm-convolution-with-a-mollifier-is-smooth-and-differentiates-under-the-integral-sign]]

[F4] Tonelli and Fubini apply to the nonnegative action and integrable first-derivative terms; Holder bounds first moments by the square root of finite second action. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]

[F5] AC supplies Countable Choice, so every Borel probability on a Polish space is inner regular; a nonzero finite Borel measure inherits this by normalization. An open $E\subsetneq\mathbb R^d$ is Polish: $d_E(x,y)=|x-y|+|\operatorname{dist}(x,E^c)^{-1}-\operatorname{dist}(y,E^c)^{-1}|$ is a complete compatible metric, since a $d_E$-Cauchy sequence has a Euclidean limit and bounded reciprocal distance prevents that limit from lying on $E^c$; the case $E=\mathbb R^d$ uses its Euclidean metric. [F6] Dominated convergence applies to sequences bounded by an integrable function on either finite measure. [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[F7] Monotone convergence passes increasing nonnegative truncations through the measures and time integral. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]

## Proof
1.1 Apply [F2] to $v^\varepsilon$ and denote by $D_t$ the open set of initial points whose trajectories exist from time 0 through t, and by $E_t=X_t^\varepsilon(D_t)$ its open image. Fix $t\in(0,T]$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(E_t)$. For $0\le r\le t$ and $x\in D_{r,t}$, the set of states whose trajectories exist from r to t, define $\psi(r,x)=f(X^\varepsilon(t;r,x))$; extend it by zero outside $D_{r,t}$. Since $\operatorname{supp}f$ is compactly contained in $E_t$, its backward images form a compact subset of the flow domain. Thus $\psi$ has compact spatial support uniformly in r, is continuously differentiable in x, and is absolutely continuous in r locally. The start-time derivative from [F2] and the flow identity give $\partial_r\psi=\nabla f(X(t;r,x))\cdot[-D_xX(t;r,x)v_r^\varepsilon(x)]=-v_r^\varepsilon(x)\cdot\nabla_x\psi$ almost everywhere. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 For this fixed t define the restricted finite pushforward $\nu_t$ on $E_t$ by $\nu_t(B)=\mu_0^\varepsilon(\{x\in D_t:X_t^\varepsilon(x)\in B\})$ for Borel $B\subseteq E_t$. The set is Borel because $X_t^\varepsilon$ is continuous on the open domain $D_t$; preimages preserve disjoint unions, so $\nu_t$ is a finite Borel measure of mass $\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_t)$. The weak continuity-equation identity extends from smooth compact tests to compactly supported tests that are $C^1$ in x and absolutely continuous in r with locally integrable time derivative: multiply by a time cutoff, convolve in time and space on a fixed compact neighborhood, and pass to the limit. The terms converge because $p^\varepsilon$ is locally bounded, $p^\varepsilon v^\varepsilon$ is locally integrable in time and space by finite action, and the test and its spatial gradient converge uniformly while its time derivative converges in $L^1$. Apply this extension to $\eta(r)\psi(r,x)$ from step 1.1 for every smooth compactly supported time cutoff $\eta$. The transport equation leaves $\int\eta'(r)F(r)dr=0$, so $F(r)=\int\psi(r,x)d\mu_r^\varepsilon(x)$ is constant on $(0,t)$. Continuity of the flow and of $\mu_r^\varepsilon$ extends the identity to r=0,t, giving $\int f(y)d\mu_t^\varepsilon(y)=\int f(X_t^\varepsilon(x))d\mu_0^\varepsilon(x)$ for every $f\in C_c^\infty(E_t)$. Uniform mollification extends equality to every $f\in C_c(E_t)$; both measures are finite, so uniform limits pass through their integrals. For a compact $K\subset E_t$, choose n sufficiently large that the closed $1/n$-neighborhood of K is compactly contained in $E_t$ and set $f_n(x)=\max\{0,1-n\operatorname{dist}(x,K)\}$. Then $f_n\in C_c(E_t)$ and $f_n\downarrow\mathbf1_K$, so [F6] gives $\nu_t(K)=\mu_t^\varepsilon(K)$. By [F5], both finite Borel measures on the Polish space $E_t$ are inner regular; their agreement on compact sets therefore proves $\nu_t=\mu_t^\varepsilon|_{E_t}$. [F1, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1]

3.1 For every $r\in(0,T]$, step 2.1 gives equality of the restricted finite measures on $E_r$. Applying it to $y\mapsto\min\{N,|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2\}$ and letting $N\uparrow\infty$ by [F7] yields $\int_{D_r}|v_r^\varepsilon(X_r^\varepsilon(x))|^2d\mu_0^\varepsilon(x)=\int_{E_r}|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2d\mu_r^\varepsilon(y)\le\int|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2d\mu_r^\varepsilon(y)$. Let $\mathscr D=\{(r,x):x\in D_r\}$. This domain is relatively open in $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$ and $(r,x)\mapsto X_r^\varepsilon(x)$ is continuous on it: cover any compact trajectory segment through $(r,x)$ by finitely many local flow neighborhoods from [F2] and patch their continuous dependence on the initial point; time continuity follows from the integral equation. Thus the integrand is Borel; extend it by zero off $\mathscr D$. Tonelli [F4] then gives $\int\!\int_0^{\min\{T,\tau(x)\}}|v_r^\varepsilon(X_r^\varepsilon(x))|^2dr\,d\mu_0^\varepsilon(x)\le\int_0^T\!\int|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2d\mu_r^\varepsilon(y)dr<\infty.$ Thus for $\mu_0^\varepsilon$-almost every x the path has finite squared speed integral up to its maximal endpoint. Holder then makes its total path length finite. Such a path is Cauchy at any finite endpoint; it cannot escape every compact set, contradicting [F2] if an endpoint lies in $(0,T)$. At T it has a finite limit and extends continuously to T. Thus $\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_T)=1$. [F1, F2, F4, F7, step 2.1] 

4.1 For each t, step 2.1 identifies $\mu_t^\varepsilon|_{E_t}$ with $\nu_t=(X_t^\varepsilon)_\#(\mu_0^\varepsilon|_{D_t})$, where this restricted pushforward is the finite measure defined in step 2.1. Since $D_T\subseteq D_t$ and $\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_T)=1$ by step 3.1, $\nu_t(E_t)=\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_t)=1$. Hence $\mu_t^\varepsilon(E_t)=1$, and the equality of restricted measures extends to all Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^d$. Because $D_t$ is open and $X_t^\varepsilon$ is continuous there, extend $X_t^\varepsilon$ to all of $\mathbb R^d$ by setting it to zero off $D_t$; this is Borel and its pushforward is $\nu_t$ since $\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_t)=1$. Thus $\mu_t^\varepsilon=(X_t^\varepsilon)_\#\mu_0^\varepsilon$. This proves the claim for every t, with the unique flow given by [F2]. [F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A complete separable metric presentation $(P,d)$, a Borel probability $\mu$, and $\varepsilon>0$.

[F1] A Polish space has a complete compatible metric and a countable dense set. ([[def-polish-space]])

[F2] Measures are continuous from below and countably subadditive. ([[thm-continuity-from-below-for-measures]], [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]])

[F3] A closed totally bounded subset of a complete metric space is compact. ([[thm-complete-subspace-iff-closed]], [[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]])

[F4] A lambda-system containing a pi-system contains the sigma-algebra it generates. ([[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]])

## Proof

1.1 The empty $P$ is immediate, so suppose $P\ne\varnothing$ and enumerate a countable dense set as $(x_m)$. For each $r\ge1$, continuity from below chooses a finite union $U_r$ of $2^{-r-2}$-balls centered at the $x_m$ with $\mu(P\setminus U_r)<\varepsilon2^{-r-2}$. Countable choice makes these choices simultaneously. [F1, F2]

2.1 The set $K_0=\bigcap_r\overline{U_r}$ is closed. Countable subadditivity gives $\mu(P\setminus K_0)<\varepsilon/2$. For every scale, one of the finite closed-ball covers from step 1.1 covers $K_0$; choosing one point of $K_0$ from each nonempty member of that finite cover and doubling the radius gives a finite net with centres in $K_0$. Hence $K_0$ is totally bounded and [F3] makes it compact. [F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Every open $G$ contains a compact $K\subseteq G$ losing less than $\varepsilon$: for $G=P$ use $K_0$; otherwise intersect $K_0$ with the increasing closed sets $\{x:d(x,P\setminus G)\ge1/n\}$. Their union is $K_0\cap G$, so [F2] gives one with the required loss. [F2, step 2.1]

4.1 Let $\mathcal R$ be the Borel sets which, for every $\delta>0$, have compact $K\subseteq A\subseteq G$ with $G$ open and $\mu(G\setminus K)<\delta$. Step 3.1 puts every open set in $\mathcal R$. The tight compact set from step 2.1 shows that complements remain in $\mathcal R$: from $K\subseteq A\subseteq G$, use $K_0\setminus G\subseteq P\setminus A\subseteq P\setminus K$ and bound the loss by $\mu(P\setminus K_0)+\mu(G\setminus K)$. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 For pairwise disjoint $A_j\in\mathcal R$, continuity from below makes the measure of the tail of $\bigcup_jA_j$ arbitrarily small. A finite union of compact inner approximants handles that tail, while the union of the open outer approximants has loss bounded by the summable errors. Thus $\mathcal R$ is a lambda-system. Open sets are a pi-system generating the Borel sigma-algebra, so [F4] gives $\mathcal B(P)\subseteq\mathcal R$. The compact inner approximant for $A$ proves the statement. [F2, F4, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$. There is a Borel probability law $\eta$ on $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ such that $(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t$ for every $t$, and for $\eta$-almost every path $\gamma$, $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous, $\gamma(0)$ has law $\mu_0$, and $\dot\gamma(t)=v_t(\gamma(t))$ for almost every $t$. Its expected path action equals the Eulerian action:
$$\int\!\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)|^2dt\,d\eta(\gamma)=\int_0^T\!\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)dt.$$

## Proof
1.1 Set $\varepsilon_n=1/n$. For each n, let $D_n$ be the Borel full-$\mu_0^{\varepsilon_n}$-measure set of initial points whose regularized flow paths exist on all of $[0,T]$. The map $F_n:D_n\to C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$, $F_n(x)(t)=X_t^{\varepsilon_n}(x)$, is Borel by [F1]. Extend it by the zero path off $D_n$ and define $\eta_n=(F_n)_\#\mu_0^{\varepsilon_n}$; this is the law of a Borel random element and is a Borel probability. For every t, composition with evaluation gives $(e_t)_\#\eta_n=(X_t^{\varepsilon_n})_\#\mu_0^{\varepsilon_n}=\mu_t^{\varepsilon_n}$ by [F1]. The flow equation, the same marginal identity, and Tonelli give $\int\mathcal E(\gamma)d\eta_n(\gamma)=\int_0^T\!\int|v_t^{\varepsilon_n}(x)|^2d\mu_t^{\varepsilon_n}(x)dt\le A,$ where $A=\int_0^T\!\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)dt<\infty$. For every fixed t, $\mu_t^{\varepsilon_n}\Rightarrow\mu_t$: for bounded continuous f, first restrict y to a compact set carrying all but arbitrarily small $\mu_t$-mass using [F8], then use uniform continuity of f on a one-neighborhood of that compact and concentration of the Gaussian kernels at zero. [F1, F6, F8, F10]

1.2 The path space C with the uniform metric is Polish: it is complete by the continuous-curve completeness fact, and rational polygonal paths are countable and dense. By [F2], the sequence of initial laws is tight. Given $\delta>0$, choose compact K with $\mu_0^{\varepsilon_n}(K^c)<\delta/2$ for all n, and choose R so $A/R<\delta/2$. The set $K_R=\{\gamma:\gamma(0)\in K,\ \mathcal E(\gamma)\le R\}$ is closed by [F3] and compact by Arzela–Ascoli: its paths obey $|\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)|\le\sqrt{R|t-s|}$ and $\sup_t|\gamma(t)|\le\sup_{x\in K}|x|+\sqrt{RT}$. Markov's inequality, which follows from $\mathbf1_{\{\mathcal E>R\}}\le\mathcal E/R$, gives $\eta_n(K_R)\ge1-\delta$. Thus $(\eta_n)$ is tight; [F2] gives a weakly convergent subsequence, still denoted $\eta_n$, with Borel probability limit $\eta$. [F2, F3, F7]

2.1 For each t, evaluation $e_t:C\to\mathbb R^d$ is continuous, so weak convergence and the marginal convergence $\mu_t^{\varepsilon_n}\Rightarrow\mu_t$ imply $(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t$. By [F3], $\mathcal E$ is nonnegative and lower semicontinuous. For each integer k define $g_k(\gamma)=\min\{k,\inf_{\zeta\in C}[\mathcal E(\zeta)+k\|\gamma-\zeta\|_\infty]\}$. The triangle inequality makes $g_k$ k-Lipschitz, $0\le g_k\le\mathcal E$, and $g_k$ increases with k. If $a<\mathcal E(\gamma)$, lower semicontinuity gives a neighborhood of $\gamma$ where $\mathcal E>a$; outside that neighborhood the term $k\|\gamma-\zeta\|_\infty$ exceeds a for all sufficiently large k. Thus $g_k(\gamma)\uparrow\mathcal E(\gamma)$. By [F9], weak convergence gives $\int g_kd\eta=\lim_n\int g_kd\eta_n\le\liminf_n\int\mathcal E d\eta_n$ for every k. Monotone convergence [F9] yields $\int\mathcal E d\eta\le\liminf_n\int\mathcal E d\eta_n\le A$. In particular $\eta$-almost every path is absolutely continuous with square-integrable derivative. [F2, F3, F9, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 Give $[0,T]\times C$ the probability measure $\lambda=(dt/T)\otimes\eta$ and define the Borel random element $Z(t,\gamma)=(t,\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))$, setting the last coordinate to zero wherever the derivative limit is undefined. Measurability follows by expressing the derivative as the limit of measurable difference quotients; it agrees with the path derivative for $\lambda$-almost every pair. The law $\Pi$ of Z has $(t,x)$ marginal $M/T$ by the time-marginal identity in step 2.1. Disintegrate with the velocity as the conditioned coordinate, and put $b(t,x)=\int u\,K_{t,x}(du)$ where defined, zero otherwise. It is Borel by [F4]. Conditional Jensen and step 2.1 give $\int|b|^2dM\le T\int|u|^2d\Pi=\int\!\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)|^2dt\,d\eta(\gamma)\le A.$ The factor T cancels because $\Pi$ uses normalized time. [F4, F6, F7, step 2.1]

3.2 Fix a smooth compactly supported vector field $\xi(t,x)$. For a finite partition $P=(t_i)$ of mesh h, set $S_P(\gamma)=\sum_i\xi(t_i,\gamma(t_i))\cdot(\gamma(t_{i+1})-\gamma(t_i)).$ For every $AC^2$ path, bounded derivatives of $\xi$ imply $\left|\int_0^T\xi(t,\gamma(t))\cdot\dot\gamma(t)dt-S_P(\gamma)\right|\le C_\xi\left(h\sqrt T\,\mathcal E(\gamma)^{1/2}+h\mathcal E(\gamma)\right).$ Indeed on each interval $|\xi(t,\gamma_t)-\xi(t_i,\gamma_{t_i})|\le C_\xi(h+|\gamma_t-\gamma_{t_i}|)$, while Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}|\dot\gamma|\le\sqrt{hE_i}$ and $|\gamma_t-\gamma_{t_i}|\le\sqrt{hE_i}$; summing yields the bound. Its expectation is uniform over $\eta_n$ and $\eta$ by the action bound. For fixed P with N intervals, $S_P$ is continuous and $|S_P|^2\le N\|\xi\|_\infty^2\sum_i|\gamma(t_{i+1})-\gamma(t_i)|^2$. Pathwise Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\int|\gamma(t_{i+1})-\gamma(t_i)|^2d\eta_n\le(t_{i+1}-t_i)A$, so these sums have uniformly bounded second moments under $\eta_n$ and $\eta$. Thus $S_P$ is uniformly integrable, and weak convergence plus bounded truncations gives $\int S_Pd\eta_n\to\int S_Pd\eta$. Letting h tend to zero proves convergence of the expected path integrals. [F6, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Under $\eta_n$, the path derivative is $v_t^{\varepsilon_n}(\gamma(t))$; hence its expected $\xi$-pairing is $\int\xi(t,x)\cdot v_t^{\varepsilon_n}(x)d\mu_t^{\varepsilon_n}(x)dt$. By the convolution definitions, $\int\xi\cdot v^{\varepsilon_n}dM^{\varepsilon_n}=\int_0^T\!\int v_t(y)\cdot(\xi_t*\rho_{\varepsilon_n})(y)d\mu_t(y)dt\longrightarrow\int\xi\cdot v\,dM,$ since $\xi_t*\rho_{\varepsilon_n}\to\xi_t$ uniformly and $v\in L^1(M)$ by finite action and Holder. Combining with step 3.2 and the conditional-mean definition of b gives $\int\xi\cdot b\,dM=\int\xi\cdot v\,dM$. Smooth-test density [F5] implies $b=v$ M-almost everywhere. [F1, F5, F6, F7, step 3.1, step 3.2]

5.1 The time marginals of $\eta$ are $\mu_t$, so $\int|v(t,\gamma(t))|^2dt\,d\eta=A$. By step 3.1 the conditional mean of $\dot\gamma$ given $(t,\gamma(t))$ is b, which equals v by step 4.1. Therefore $\int\!\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)-v_t(\gamma(t))|^2dt\,d\eta=\int\mathcal E\,d\eta+A-2\int v\cdot b\,dM=\int\mathcal E\,d\eta-A\le0.$ The left side is nonnegative, so it is zero. Thus $\dot\gamma=v_t(\gamma(t))$ for $dt\,d\eta$-almost every pair, and the expected path action equals A. Together with the time marginals this is the claimed superposition law. [F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Then
$\mathbb P_X$ is a probability measure on $(S,\Sigma)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A random element $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$.

[L1] The law is defined by $\mathbb P_X(B)=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B))$ ([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]).

[L2] A random element is measurable, so measurable target sets have measurable preimages ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]).

[L3] A probability measure is a measure with total mass $1$ ([[def-probability-measure]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L2], every $B\in\Sigma$ has $X^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F$, so [L1] is well defined. Also $X^{-1}(\varnothing)=\varnothing$ and $X^{-1}(S)=\Omega$, so $$\mathbb P_X(\varnothing)=0,\qquad \mathbb P_X(S)=\mathbb P(\Omega)=1.$$ [L1, L2, L3]

1.2 If $(B_n)$ is a pairwise disjoint sequence in $\Sigma$, then the preimages $X^{-1}(B_n)$ are pairwise disjoint and $$X^{-1}\left(\bigcup_n B_n\right)=\bigcup_n X^{-1}(B_n).$$ Therefore $$\mathbb P_X\left(\bigcup_n B_n\right)=\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_n X^{-1}(B_n)\right)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(X^{-1}(B_n))=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P_X(B_n).$$ [L1, L2, L3]

2.1 Steps 1.1 and 1.2 show that $\mathbb P_X$ is a measure of total mass $1$, hence a probability measure by [L3]. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L3] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$. Then $t\mapsto\mu_t$ belongs to $AC^2([0,T];\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d))$ and, for almost every $t$,
$$|\dot\mu_t|\le\left(\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)\right)^{1/2}.$$
