## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and the narrowly continuous finite-action solution $(\mu_t,v_t)$.

[F1] There is a probability law $\eta$ on $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ whose time marginals are $\mu_t$, whose almost every path is absolutely continuous with $\dot\gamma(t)=v_t(\gamma(t))$ almost everywhere, and whose expected path action equals the Eulerian action. [[thm-superposition-for-finite-action-continuity-equations]]

[F2] Minkowski's integral inequality bounds the $L^2$ norm of a time integral by the time integral of the $L^2$ norms. [[thm-minkowski-integral-inequality]]

[F3] The metric derivative theorem identifies the least $L^2$ upper control of a Wasserstein curve with its metric derivative. [[thm-metric-derivative-of-ac2-wasserstein-curves]]

[F4] If $\eta$ is a Borel probability law on a Polish space and $F$ is Borel into a Polish space, define $F_\#\eta(B)=\eta(F^{-1}(B))$; countable additivity and total mass one follow from preimages and the measure axioms, coordinate marginals compose with coordinate maps, and $\int h\,d(F_\#\eta)=\int h(F)\,d\eta$ for nonnegative Borel h by change of variables for expectation. [[def-borel-probability-law-on-a-polish-space]] [[def-measure]] [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]

## Proof
1.1 For $0\le s<t\le T$, the evaluation map $E_{s,t}:C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)\to\mathbb R^{2d}$, $E_{s,t}(\gamma)=(\gamma(s),\gamma(t))$, is continuous. Define $\pi_{s,t}(B)=\eta(E_{s,t}^{-1}(B))$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{2d}$; by [F4] this is a Borel probability. Its coordinate marginals are $(e_s)_\#\eta=\mu_s$ and $(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t$, so $\pi_{s,t}$ is a coupling. Its quadratic cost satisfies $\int|x-y|^2d\pi_{s,t}(x,y)=\int|\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)|^2d\eta(\gamma)$ by [F4]. For $\eta$-almost every path, absolute continuity gives $|\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)|\le\int_s^t|\dot\gamma(r)|dr$. Minkowski [F2], applied with the path probability space and Lebesgue measure on $[s,t]$, yields $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)\le\left(\int\left(\int_s^t|\dot\gamma(r)|dr\right)^2d\eta\right)^{1/2}\le\int_s^t\left(\int|\dot\gamma(r)|^2d\eta\right)^{1/2}dr.$ The marginal identity and the pathwise velocity identity in [F1] identify the inner integral for almost every r as $\int|v_r(x)|^2d\mu_r(x)$. Put $g(r)=(\int|v_r|^2d\mu_r)^{1/2}$. Finite action gives $g\in L^2(0,T)$, and the displayed bound for every interval implies W2-continuity and the defining $AC^2$ upper-control inequality. [given, F1, F2, F4]

2.1 By [F3], the metric derivative exists almost everywhere and is no larger than any nonnegative $L^2$ upper control. Applying it to $g$ from step 1.1 gives $|\dot\mu_t|\le g(t)$ almost everywhere, as claimed. [F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and $\mu\in AC^2([0,T];\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d))$. There is a Borel vector field $v$ of finite action that solves the continuity equation and satisfies
$$\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)=|\dot\mu_t|^2$$
for almost every $t$. Every other Borel finite-action solution $w$ of the same continuity equation obeys the pointwise Pythagorean identity
$$\int|w_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)=|\dot\mu_t|^2+\int|w_t(x)-v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)$$
for almost every $t$. Consequently $v$ is the unique minimum-action velocity up to $dt\,\mu_t(dx)$-null sets and
$$\int_0^T|\dot\mu_t|^2dt=\min_w\int_0^T\!\int|w_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)dt,$$
where the minimum ranges over Borel finite-action fields solving the same continuity equation.

[F1] The real space $H=L^2(M;\mathbb R^d)$ with inner product $\langle u,w\rangle=\int u\cdot w\,dM$ is a Hilbert space; the Hilbert-space Riesz representation theorem holds under Countable Choice, which follows from AC. [F2] For every pair $\mu_t,\mu_{t+h}$ an optimal coupling exists; its quadratic cost is $W_2(\mu_t,\mu_{t+h})^2$. [[prop-existence-and-lower-semicontinuity-of-optimal-couplings]]

[F3] An absolutely continuous scalar function equals its initial value plus the integral of its derivative; its derivative is integrable almost everywhere. [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] [[thm-first-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-l-one]] [[def-countable-choice]] [[def-dependent-choice]]

[F8] Dominated convergence passes integrable test limits through the space-time integrals. [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[F4] Holder's inequality gives $\int_I s(t)\|\nabla\varphi_t\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}dt\le\|s\|_{L^2(I)}\|\nabla\varphi\|_{L^2(M|_I)}$. [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]

[F5] Cauchy--Schwarz holds for the coupling and real Hilbert-space inner products. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]

## Proof
1.1 We first prove the scalar transport estimate $\left|\int_0^T\!\int\partial_t\varphi(t,x)d\mu_t(x)dt\right|\le\int_0^T s(t)\|\nabla_x\varphi(t,\cdot)\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}dt\qquad\text{(1)}$ for $\varphi\in C_c^\infty((0,T)\times\mathbb R^d)$. Put $F(t)=\int\varphi(t,x)d\mu_t(x)$. If $r<t$, the time increment of $\varphi$ is bounded by $\|\partial_t\varphi\|_\infty(t-r)$, and its spatial increment under an optimal coupling is bounded by $\|\nabla\varphi\|_\infty W_2(\mu_r,\mu_t)$. The $AC^2$ control therefore makes F absolutely continuous. At an interior time t where the metric derivative exists, use an optimal coupling $\pi_h$ of $\mu_t,\mu_{t+h}$. Taylor's formula with bounded Hessian gives $\varphi(t,y)-\varphi(t,x)=\nabla_x\varphi(t,x)\cdot(y-x)+R_t(x,y),\quad |R_t(x,y)|\le C|y-x|^2.$ Cauchy--Schwarz and [F2] yield $\left|\int(\varphi(t,y)-\varphi(t,x))d\pi_h\right|\le\|\nabla\varphi(t,\cdot)\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}W_2(\mu_t,\mu_{t+h})+C W_2(\mu_t,\mu_{t+h})^2.$ After division by $|h|$, the remainder tends to zero and the first term tends to $s(t)\|\nabla\varphi_t\|_2$. The separate time increment converges to $\int\partial_t\varphi(t,x)d\mu_t(x)$ by narrow continuity and uniform convergence of the smooth time difference quotients. Hence $|F'(t)-\int\partial_t\varphi_t d\mu_t|\le s(t)\|\nabla\varphi_t\|_2$ almost everywhere. Since F vanishes near 0 and T, the absolutely-continuous FTC [F3] gives $\int_0^TF' =0$; integrating the pointwise derivative inequality proves (1). Holder [F4] will be used for the right side. [F2, F3, F4, F5, given]

2.1 Let $\mathcal G$ be the closure in H of $\{\nabla_x\varphi:\varphi\in C_c^\infty((0,T)\times\mathbb R^d)\}$. Define $\ell(\nabla\varphi)=-\int\partial_t\varphi\,dM$. Estimate (1) and [F4] show $|\ell(g)|\le\|s\|_{L^2(0,T)}\|g\|_H$. Thus if two tests have the same gradient in H their $\ell$ values agree; this defines a bounded linear functional on the gradient subspace and extends uniquely to $\mathcal G$. By [F1] and Riesz there is a unique $v\in\mathcal G$ with $\ell(g)=\langle g,v\rangle_H$ for all $g\in\mathcal G$, and $\|v\|_H\le\|s\|_2$. Choose a Borel representative of this $L^2(M)$ class. For every test $\varphi$, $\int(\partial_t\varphi+\nabla_x\varphi\cdot v)dM=0,$ so v solves the continuity equation and has finite action. [F1, F4, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 Fix an interval I with rational endpoints in $(0,T)$ and let $\mathcal G_I$ be the closure in $L^2(M|_{I\times\mathbb R^d})$ of gradients of tests compactly supported in the interior of I. The restriction $v\mathbf1_I$ belongs to $\mathcal G_I$: approximate v by global test gradients, multiply each by smooth time cutoffs converging to $\mathbf1_I$, and use [F8] dominated convergence; the time marginal is Lebesgue, so the endpoints are null. For tests supported in I, $v\mathbf1_I$ represents the restricted functional $\ell_I$. By (1), its norm is at most $\|s\|_{L^2(I)}$. Consequently $\int_I\|v_t\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}^2dt\le\int_I s(t)^2dt$ for every rational interval I. Apply [F3] to the indefinite integral of $q(t)=\|v_t\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}^2-s(t)^2$: the interval inequalities make its values nonincreasing first on rational endpoints and then, by continuity of the indefinite integral, on all endpoints; its derivative is therefore nonpositive almost everywhere. Thus $\|v_t\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}\le s(t)$ a.e. Applying [F6] to the solution v gives the reverse inequality. Hence equality holds almost everywhere. [F1, F3, F4, F6, F7, F8, step 2.1]

4.1 Let w be any other Borel finite-action solution and put h=w-v. Subtracting the two weak equations gives $\langle h,\nabla\varphi\rangle_H=0$ for every test. Therefore on each rational interval I, h is orthogonal to $\mathcal G_I$; step 3.1 has $v\mathbf1_I\in\mathcal G_I$, so $\int_I\int h_t\cdot v_t d\mu_tdt=0$. The scalar integrand is in $L^1(0,T)$ by Cauchy--Schwarz. Its indefinite integral has zero increments on all rational intervals and is therefore constant; [F3] makes the integrand zero almost everywhere. Thus $\langle h_t,v_t\rangle_{L^2(\mu_t)}=0$ a.e., and the Hilbert-space identity gives $\|w_t\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}^2=\|v_t+h_t\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}^2=\|v_t\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}^2+\|h_t\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}^2=s(t)^2+\|w_t-v_t\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}^2.$ Integrating proves the minimum value and uniqueness up to $M$-null sets. ## Definition

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

## Example

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R^d$. The curve $\mu_t=\delta_{a+tb}$ belongs to $AC^2([0,T];\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d))$, has constant metric speed $|b|$, and the Borel field $v_t(x)=b$ solves the continuity equation. Its action is $T|b|^2$, equal to the minimum action among fields solving that equation for this curve.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $T>0$, and $a,b\in\mathbb R^d$.

[F1] A coupling of two Dirac laws is forced to put all mass at the sole pair of support points, so the quadratic Wasserstein distance is $W_2(\delta_x,\delta_y)=|x-y|$. [[def-wasserstein-two-space-and-couplings]] [[def-dirac-measure]]

[F2] For a continuously differentiable scalar function, the total-derivative chain rule and fundamental theorem identify the integral of its derivative with its endpoint difference. [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] [[thm-ftc-second-part]]

[F3] The minimum-velocity theorem says the least action of any admissible velocity for an $AC^2$ curve is the integral of its squared metric speed. [[thm-ac2-curve-admits-minimal-velocity]]

## Proof
1.1 For $s,t\in[0,T]$, any coupling of $\delta_{a+sb}$ and $\delta_{a+tb}$ is concentrated at $((a+sb),(a+tb))$, hence [F1] gives $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)=|t-s||b|$. For every bounded continuous f, $f(a+tb)$ is continuous, so the curve is narrowly continuous. Thus it is $AC^2$ with constant metric derivative $|b|$ (the endpoint difference quotient is exactly $|b|$ at every interior time). [given, F1]

2.1 For $\varphi\in C_c^\infty((0,T)\times\mathbb R^d)$, the chain rule gives $\frac d{dt}\varphi(t,a+tb)=\partial_t\varphi(t,a+tb)+\nabla_x\varphi(t,a+tb)\cdot b.$ The left side integrates to zero over $[0,T]$ because the test vanishes near both time endpoints; this is exactly the weak continuity-equation identity for $\mu_t=\delta_{a+tb}$ and $v_t=b$. Its action is $\int_0^T|b|^2dt=T|b|^2$. By [F3] and step 1.1, this equals $\int_0^T|\dot\mu_t|^2dt$, the minimum action. [F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Example

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m_0,m_1\in\mathbb R^d$, and $\sigma_0,\sigma_1>0$. Let $\xi$ have density $(2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{-|z|^2/2}$ on $\mathbb R^d$, put $m_t=(1-t)m_0+tm_1$ and $\sigma_t=(1-t)\sigma_0+t\sigma_1$, and set $\mu_t=\operatorname{Law}(m_t+\sigma_t\xi)$ for $0\le t\le1$. Then $\mu_t$ is a constant-speed $W_2$ geodesic, meaning $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)=|t-s|W_2(\mu_0,\mu_1)$ for all $s,t\in[0,1]$, from the laws of $m_0+\sigma_0\xi$ to the law of $m_1+\sigma_1\xi$, with
$$W_2(\mu_0,\mu_1)^2=|m_1-m_0|^2+d(\sigma_1-\sigma_0)^2.$$
The Borel field
$$v_t(x)=m_1-m_0+\frac{\sigma_1-\sigma_0}{\sigma_t}(x-m_t)$$
solves the continuity equation and has action equal to this squared distance, hence is minimum-action. The strict positivity of $\sigma_0$ and $\sigma_1$ ensures $\sigma_t>0$ throughout; degenerate covariances are excluded.

[A1] AC implies Countable Choice. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The displayed density factors into standard normal coordinate densities; [A1] and Tonelli give each coordinate law $N(0,1)$. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

[F2] Each coordinate has mean zero and variance one by the normal moment theorem; finite sums give $E\xi=0$ and $E|\xi|^2=d$. Under any coupling of the scaled laws, the centered marginals therefore have second moments $d\sigma^2$ and $d\tau^2$. [[lem-normal-location-scale-mean-and-variance]] [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] [[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]] [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]

[F3] Holder bounds the centered cross moment by $\bigl(E|U|^2E|V|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$. [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]

[F4] The minimum-velocity theorem identifies the least action of an $AC^2$ curve with the integral of its squared metric speed. [[thm-ac2-curve-admits-minimal-velocity]]

[F5] Dominated convergence passes bounded continuous test functions through the Gaussian law as its affine parameters vary continuously. [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[F6] The total-derivative chain rule differentiates a smooth test along the affine path, and the FTC integrates that derivative. [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] [[thm-ftc-second-part]]

## Proof
1.1 Write $\mu_{m,\sigma}=\operatorname{Law}(m+\sigma\xi)$. Let $X,Y$ be any coupling of $\mu_{m,\sigma}$ and $\mu_{n,\tau}$, and set $U=X-m$, $V=Y-n$. Since $EU=EV=0$, expansion gives $E|X-Y|^2=|m-n|^2+E|U|^2+E|V|^2-2E(U\cdot V).$ By [F1] and [F2], this is at least $|m-n|^2+d(\sigma^2+\tau^2-2\sigma\tau)=|m-n|^2+d(\sigma-\tau)^2$. Conversely, couple the two laws by $X=m+\sigma\xi$, $Y=n+\tau\xi$ using the same standard Gaussian vector. The moments in [F1] give $E|X-Y|^2=|m-n|^2+d(\sigma-\tau)^2$. Taking the infimum proves $W_2(\mu_{m,\sigma},\mu_{n,\tau})^2=|m-n|^2+d(\sigma-\tau)^2.$ [A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Apply step 1.1 to $(m_s,\sigma_s)$ and $(m_t,\sigma_t)$. Their differences are $(t-s)(m_1-m_0)$ and $(t-s)(\sigma_1-\sigma_0)$, so $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)=|t-s|\sqrt{|m_1-m_0|^2+d(\sigma_1-\sigma_0)^2}.$ This proves the constant-speed geodesic claim and identifies its speed. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For each $z$, define $\gamma_z(t)=m_t+\sigma_tz$. Direct differentiation gives $\dot\gamma_z=m_1-m_0+(\sigma_1-\sigma_0)z=v_t(\gamma_z(t))$. Integrate over $t$ and the Gaussian law. The FTC [F6] and the test vanishing near both time endpoints make the time integral zero; its derivative is integrable since $v_t(\gamma_\xi(t))$ is affine in $\xi$ with finite first moment by [F2, F3]. The resulting identity is the weak continuity equation for $\mu_t$. Also $\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)=E|m_1-m_0+(\sigma_1-\sigma_0)\xi|^2=|m_1-m_0|^2+d(\sigma_1-\sigma_0)^2,$ using the zero coordinate means and unit variances in [F2]. Its time integral is the squared-distance value from step 1.1, so [F4] makes this velocity minimum-action. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the closure of a nonempty convex open set. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be differentiable, with differential Lipschitz on bounded sets in the uniform sense that for every bounded $B\subseteq\mathcal H$ there is a finite $L_B$ such that
$$\|dR_z-dR_{z'}\|_{\mathcal H^*}\le L_B\|z-z'\|_{\mathcal H}\qquad(z,z'\in B),$$
and bounded on every sublevel set of $R$. In particular, on each closed convex hull of a bounded feature image $\Phi(Q_r)$, both a finite Lipschitz constant $L_r$ and a finite norm bound $N_r$ for $dR$ are available. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.
For every $r>0$, require a nonempty closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, nested increasingly in $r$, such that
$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$
such that $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and there are fixed constants $C_1,C_2>0$ with
$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$
Here $\partial V(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ is the supporting set on $\Omega$, and in the growth bound $\|\partial V(u)\|$ means its minimum element norm, equivalently the bound requires a supporting vector of norm at most $C_1+C_2r$ at every $u\in Q_r$. No bound is imposed on the domain normal cone. The source Assumptions 2.1 use the stronger maximal bound for the ambient potential subgradients before adding the domain indicator; that original bound implies the bounded-selection condition used here. Taking a supremum over the relative-domain supporting set would instead include unbounded normal vectors at proper-domain boundaries and would incorrectly exclude the constrained branch. All original source hypotheses and conclusions are retained by this sufficient, weaker growth convention. For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$F(\mu)=R\!\left(\int_\Omega\Phi(u)\,d\mu(u)\right)+\int_\Omega V(u)\,d\mu(u)$$
when $\mu$ is concentrated on $\Omega$, the Bochner integral exists, and the scalar integral is finite; set $F(\mu)=+\infty$ otherwise. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite $F(\mu)$, write $m_\mu=\int_\Omega\Phi\,d\mu$ and define its first-variation potential on $\Omega$ by
$$F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u).$$
No convexity of $R$ is required by this definition.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(S,\Sigma,\sigma)$ be any probability space and let $d\ge1$. Set $K=L^2(\sigma;\mathbb R^d)$ be the space of measurable vector fields modulo equality $\sigma$-almost everywhere with finite squared norm. With
$$\langle X,Y\rangle_K=\int_SX(s)\cdot Y(s)\,d\sigma(s),\qquad \|X\|_K^2=\int_S|X(s)|^2\,d\sigma(s),$$
$K$ is a real Hilbert space. If $\Sigma$ is countably generated, then $K$ is separable. In particular this applies to every Borel probability on $S\subseteq\mathbb R^k$ with its relative Borel sigma-algebra, for any $k\ge1$ independent of the output dimension $d$, and to every finite label space. No separability claim is made for an arbitrary probability sigma-algebra.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the probability space $(S,\Sigma,\sigma)$, and $d\ge1$.

[F1] Scalar $L^2(\sigma)$ is the quotient of square-integrable measurable functions by equality almost everywhere, and its norm is complete by the Riesz–Fischer theorem. [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]]

[F2] Finite-measure simple functions are dense in scalar $L^2$. [[thm-simple-functions-with-finite-measure-support-are-dense-in-l-p-for-finite-p]]

[F3] AC implies Countable Choice. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]]

[F4] Finite-measure sets in a sigma-finite countably generated space can be approximated in symmetric-difference measure by a countable generating algebra. [[lem-countable-generators-yield-countable-set-algebras]] [[lem-finite-measure-sets-are-approximable-by-a-countable-generating-algebra]]

[F5] Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle X,Y\rangle|\le\|X\|_2\|Y\|_2$ for the displayed componentwise pairing. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]

## Proof


**Given:** AC and $(S,\Sigma,\sigma)$ as in the Statement.

1.1 First assume that $\Sigma$ is countably generated. By [F3] and [F4], its countable generating family generates a countable algebra $\mathcal A_0$ such that each $E\in\Sigma$ and each $\varepsilon>0$ admit $A\in\mathcal A_0$ with $\sigma(E\triangle A)<\varepsilon$. Relative Borel spaces $S\subseteq\mathbb R^k$ have countable generators obtained by intersecting $S$ with rational open boxes; every relative open set is a union of members of this countable base. Finite sigma-algebras are countably generated as well. These observations do not identify the label dimension $k$ with the output dimension $d$. [given, F3, F4]

2.1 The functions $\sum_{j=1}^m q_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$, with $q_j\in\mathbb Q$ and $A_j\in\mathcal A_0$, form a countable subset of scalar $L^2(\sigma)$. It is dense: by [F2], approximate any $f$ by a finite-measure simple function $\sum_j c_j\mathbf1_{E_j}$; approximate each $E_j$ in measure using [F4], then approximate each coefficient by a rational. The error satisfies $\|c\mathbf1_E-q\mathbf1_A\|_2\le |c-q|\sqrt{\sigma(E)}+|q|\sqrt{\sigma(E\triangle A)}$, so the finitely many choices make the total error arbitrarily small. [F2, F4, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 The vector space $K$ is the finite product of $d$ copies of scalar $L^2(\sigma)$; its displayed pairing is the sum of the coordinate pairings. [F5] gives a positive-definite inner product, and coordinatewise completeness from [F1] makes the finite product complete. This completeness argument applies to every probability space, without a countable-generation hypothesis. When $\Sigma$ is countably generated, the finite product of the countable dense scalar sets from step 2.1 is countable and dense in $K$, proving the asserted separability. [F1, F5, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1 \le p < \infty$. Then
every element of $L^p(\mu)$ can be approximated in $L^p$ by simple functions
whose supports have finite measure.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measure space, an exponent $1 \le p < \infty$, and $f \in L^p(\mu)$.

[L1] Every measurable function admits dominated simple approximations ([[cor-measurable-functions-admit-dominated-simple-approximations]]).

[L2] Dominated convergence applies in $L^1$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[L3] Elements of $L^p(\mu)$ are almost-everywhere classes, so one may choose a measurable representative when making pointwise constructions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Choose a measurable representative $u$ of $f$ by [L3]. For each [L1, L3, given, choose, construct] $m \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}$, [L1] gives a simple function $s_m$ with $|s_m| \le |u|$ and $s_m(x) \to u(x)$ for every $x$. Define $$ t_m := s_m\,\mathbf{1}_{\{|u| \ge 1/m\}}. $$ Then each $t_m$ is simple and $\operatorname{supp}(t_m) \subseteq \{|u| \ge 1/m\}$. [L1, L3, given, choose, construct]

2.1 Since $|u|^p$ is integrable, [step 1.1, algebra] $$ \mu(\{|u| \ge 1/m\}) \le m^p \int |u|^p\,d\mu < \infty, $$ so every $t_m$ has finite-measure support. Also $t_m(x) \to u(x)$ for every $x$: if $u(x)=0$ then eventually both sides are $0$, and if $u(x)\neq0$ then $\mathbf{1}_{\{|u(x)| \ge 1/m\}}=1$ for all large $m$. Finally $$ |u-t_m|^p \le (2|u|)^p, $$ whose right-hand side is integrable. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Applying [L2] to $|u-t_m|^p$ gives [L2, step 2.1] $$ \|f-t_m\|_p^p = \int |u-t_m|^p\,d\mu \longrightarrow 0. $$ So the simple functions with finite-measure support are dense in $L^p(\mu)$. [L2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\mathcal G$ be a countable family of subsets of a set $X$. Then there is a
countable algebra of subsets of $X$ that contains $\mathcal G$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, a set $X$, and a countable family $\mathcal G \subseteq \mathcal P(X)$.

[L1] Generated sigma-algebras are built from families of sets, and algebras are closed under complements and finite unions ([[def-generated-sigma-algebra]], [[def-algebra-of-subsets]]).

[L2] Countable sets are closed under finite products and countable unions ([[def-countable]], [[thm-product-of-countable]], [[thm-countable-union-of-countable]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** constructive.

1.1 If $\mathcal G=\varnothing$, then $\{\varnothing,X\}$ is a finite algebra [L1, given, algebra] of subsets of $X$ containing $\mathcal G$, so the conclusion holds. Assume now that $\mathcal G\ne\varnothing$. [L1, given, algebra]

1.2 Enumerate $\mathcal G = \{G_1,G_2,\dots\}$. For each $m \ge 1$, let [L1, given, choose, construct] $\mathcal A_m$ be the family of all unions of atoms of the finite partition generated by $G_1,\dots,G_m$; equivalently, the members of $\mathcal A_m$ are all finite Boolean combinations of those $m$ sets. Each $\mathcal A_m$ is a finite algebra on $X$ containing $G_1,\dots,G_m$. [L1, given, choose, construct]

2.1 Put [step 1.2, L1, choose, algebra] $$ \mathcal A := \bigcup_{m \ge 1} \mathcal A_m. $$ Then $\mathcal A$ contains every $G_j$. If $A,B \in \mathcal A$, choose $m$ with $A,B \in \mathcal A_m$; because $\mathcal A_m$ is an algebra, also $X \setminus A$ and $A \cup B$ lie in $\mathcal A_m \subseteq \mathcal A$. Thus $\mathcal A$ is an algebra of subsets of $X$. [step 1.2, L1, choose, algebra]

3.1 Each $\mathcal A_m$ is finite, so in particular countable, and [L2] makes [L2, step 2.1] their countable union $\mathcal A$ countable. Therefore $\mathcal A$ is a countable algebra containing $\mathcal G$. [L2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space whose sigma-algebra is
countably generated. Then there is a countable algebra
$\mathcal A_0 \subseteq \mathcal A$ such that for every $E \in \mathcal A$ with
$\mu(E) < \infty$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $A \in \mathcal A_0$
with

$$ \mu(E \triangle A) < \varepsilon. $$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, a sigma-finite measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ with $\mathcal A$ countably generated.

[L1] A countable generator yields a countable algebra ([[lem-countable-generators-yield-countable-set-algebras]]).

[L2] Sigma-finite measures admit an increasing exhaustion $X_1 \subseteq X_2 \subseteq \cdots$ by measurable finite-measure sets ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]).

[L3] If two families contain one another inside generated sigma-algebras, then they generate the same sigma-algebra ([[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-comparison-criterion]], [[def-generated-sigma-algebra]]).

[L4] Continuity from below and the symmetric-difference measure calculus are available ([[thm-continuity-from-below-for-measures]], [[prop-measure-of-a-set-difference]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $\mathcal G$ be a countable generator of $\mathcal A$, and choose a [L1, L2, L3, given, choose] sigma-finite exhaustion $(X_m)$ by [L2]. Apply [L1] to the countable family $\mathcal G \cup \{X_m : m \ge 1\}$ to obtain a countable algebra $\mathcal A_0 \subseteq \mathcal A$. Because $\mathcal G \subseteq \mathcal A_0 \subseteq \mathcal A$, [L3] gives $\sigma(\mathcal A_0)=\mathcal A$. [L1, L2, L3, given, choose]

1.2 Fix $m$ and let $\mathcal M_m$ be the family of measurable subsets [L4, algebra] $B \subseteq X_m$ for which every $\varepsilon > 0$ admits $A \in \mathcal A_0$ with $A \subseteq X_m$ and $\mu(B \triangle A) < \varepsilon$. Because $X_m \in \mathcal A_0$, the family $\mathcal M_m$ contains $\mathcal A_0 \cap X_m$. On the finite-measure space $X_m$, the class $\mathcal M_m$ is a sigma-algebra: complements are handled inside $X_m$, and increasing unions are handled by approximating one large stage and using continuity from below. Therefore $\mathcal M_m$ is a sigma-algebra containing the trace of $\mathcal A_0$, so it contains every measurable subset of $X_m$. [L4, algebra]

2.1 Now let $E \in \mathcal A$ with $\mu(E) < \infty$ and let $\varepsilon > 0$. [L4, choose, algebra] By [L4], choose $m$ so large that $\mu(E \setminus X_m) < \varepsilon/2$. Since $E \cap X_m$ is a measurable subset of $X_m$, the construction above yields $A \in \mathcal A_0$ with $A \subseteq X_m$ and $\mu((E \cap X_m) \triangle A) < \varepsilon/2$. Then $$ \mu(E \triangle A) \le \mu(E \setminus X_m) + \mu((E \cap X_m) \triangle A) < \varepsilon. $$ So finite-measure sets are approximable by members of the countable algebra $\mathcal A_0$. [L4, choose, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space and $T>0$, and equip $(0,T)$ with its Borel sigma-algebra and Lebesgue measure. Let $Z=L^2((0,T);H)$ consist of strongly measurable $H$-valued functions modulo equality almost everywhere with $\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_H^2\,dt<\infty$. Then
$$\langle u,v\rangle_Z=\int_0^T\langle u(t),v(t)\rangle_H\,dt$$
is a well-defined real inner product and its induced norm is complete. If $D\subset H$ is any countable dense set, the finite-valued step functions with values in $D$ and finitely many rational interval endpoints are dense in $Z$; in particular $Z$ is separable.

## Statement references

[[def-bochner-integrable-function]]

[[def-strongly-measurable-banach-valued-function]]

[[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]

[[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]

[[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré, Chapter 4](https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~sayan/ambrosio.pdf)

[Chizat and Bach, Assumptions 2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $H$, and $T>0$ as in the Statement.

[F1] Bochner strong measurability is almost-everywhere pointwise norm approximation by measurable simple functions; the norm-integrability criterion characterizes Bochner integrability. [[def-strongly-measurable-banach-valued-function]] [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]

[F2] Minkowski holds for scalar $L^2$, and monotone and dominated convergence hold for nonnegative measurable functions. [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[F3] The inner product on $H$ is positive definite and $H$ is complete. [[def-hilbert-space]] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]

[F4] Countable Choice is available under AC. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]]

[F5] Finite-measure subsets of a sigma-finite countably generated measure space are approximable in measure by a countable generating algebra. [[lem-countable-generators-yield-countable-set-algebras]] [[lem-finite-measure-sets-are-approximable-by-a-countable-generating-algebra]]

[F6] Finite-valued simple functions are dense in scalar $L^2$. [[thm-simple-functions-with-finite-measure-support-are-dense-in-l-p-for-finite-p]]

## Proof


**Given:** AC, $H$, and $T$ as in the Statement.

1.1 Pointwise Cauchy–Schwarz and scalar Cauchy–Schwarz show that the displayed pairing is integrable and bounded by $\|u\|_Z\|v\|_Z$. It is bilinear and symmetric; if $\int\|u\|_H^2=0$, then $\|u(t)\|_H=0$ almost everywhere, so the equivalence class is zero. Thus it is a real inner product. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Let $(u_n)$ be Cauchy in $Z$. By [F4], choose a subsequence $(u_{n_k})$ with $\|u_{n_{k+1}}-u_{n_k}\|_Z\le2^{-k}$. Use [F4] to choose strongly measurable representatives and modify them to zero on their exceptional null sets. Put $g_m(t)=\sum_{k=1}^m\|u_{n_{k+1}}(t)-u_{n_k}(t)\|_H$. Minkowski gives $\|g_m\|_2\le\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}=1$; monotone convergence then gives $g=\sum_k\|u_{n_{k+1}}-u_{n_k}\|_H\in L^2$. Hence $g<\infty$ almost everywhere, and completeness of $H$ gives a pointwise limit $u(t)$ there; put $u=0$ on the null set. [F2, F3, F4, given]

2.1 The limit $u$ is strongly measurable: the chosen representatives are strongly measurable and converge pointwise off a measurable null set, so their simple approximations give a strongly measurable limit. The tail estimate $\|u-u_{n_m}\|_H\le\sum_{k\ge m}\|u_{n_{k+1}}-u_{n_k}\|_H$ and [F2] show $\|u-u_{n_m}\|_Z\le\sum_{k\ge m}2^{-k}\to0$. Thus $u\in Z$ and the subsequence converges in norm. Since the original sequence is Cauchy, the full sequence converges to the same class; $Z$ is complete. [F1, F2, step 1.2]

3.1 Choose a countable dense set $D\subset H$. From strong measurability choose finite-valued simple functions $s_n$ converging pointwise almost everywhere to a representative $u$. Replace $s_n$ by $t_n=s_n\mathbf1_{\{\|s_n\|_H\le2\|u\|_H\}}$; then $t_n\to u$ pointwise and $\|u-t_n\|_H^2\le9\|u\|_H^2$, so dominated convergence makes finite-valued simple functions dense in $Z$. Their level sets have finite measure because $(0,T)$ has finite measure. The rational interval algebra is countable and generates the Borel sigma-algebra; [F5] approximates each level set in symmetric-difference measure. Replace each of the finitely many values by a nearby element of $D$ and each level set by a finite union of rational intervals. The squared error from changing a level set $E$ to $A$ is its coefficient norm squared times $\operatorname{Leb}(E\triangle A)$, and the value error tends to zero by density of $D$. These step functions form a countable dense family, so $Z$ is separable. [F1, F2, F5, F6, given, construct] ∎

## Definition

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

## Remarks

- The zero function is strongly measurable, witnessed by the constant zero
  simple sequence.
- A single measurable simple function is strongly measurable, witnessed by the
  constant sequence $s_n=s$ and $N=\varnothing$.

## Statement

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

## Facts & Assumptions

[L1] Bochner integrability means $L^1$ approximation by integrable simple functions and defines the integral as the norm limit of their integrals ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]]).

[L2] Nonnegative integrals are monotone and positively homogeneous ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) and additive ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

[L3] Pointwise limits and countable suprema of measurable scalar functions are measurable ([[thm-sequential-suprema-infima-limsup-liminf-and-pointwise-limits-are-measurable]]).

[L4] Scalar dominated convergence gives convergence in $L^1$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]); its nonnegative foundation is monotone convergence ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** A strongly measurable $f$ and the conventions in the Statement.

1.1 Prove necessity of scalar norm integrability. [given, L1, L2] Suppose first that $f$ is Bochner integrable and choose $(s_n)$ as in [L1]. For some $n$, $\int\|f-s_n\|<\infty$, while integrability of the simple function gives $\int\|s_n\|<\infty$. Since $\|f\|\leq\|f-s_n\|+\|s_n\|$, [L2] gives $\int\|f\|<\infty$. [given, L1, L2]

1.2 Prove approximation independence. [given, L1] If $(s_n)$ and $(t_n)$ are any two defining approximations, the simple norm inequality gives $\|\int s_n-\int t_n\|\leq\int\|s_n-t_n\|$, which is at most $\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-t_n\|$. Both terms tend to zero, so the two norm limits coincide. [given, L1]

1.3 Construct dominated simple approximants for sufficiency. [given, L3, construct] Conversely assume $\int\|f\|<\infty$. On the exceptional measurable null set of a strong approximation, replace both $f$ and every approximant by zero (and call the representative again $f$). Thus measurable simple functions $u_n$ converge pointwise to $f$; [L3] makes $\|f\|$ measurable. Define $s_n=u_n\mathbf1_{\{\|u_n\|\leq2\|f\|\}}$. Then $s_n$ is simple and measurable, $\|s_n\|\leq2\|f\|$, and $s_n\to f$ pointwise: when $f(\omega)\neq0$, the inequality defining the retained part holds eventually, while at a zero of $f$ either retained values tend to zero or the replacement is zero. [given, L3, construct]

2.1 Verify that the constructed simple functions are integrable. [L2, step 1.3] Each $s_n$ is integrable. Indeed, if a nonzero value $x$ occurs, its level set is contained in $\{2\|f\|\geq\|x\|\}$, whose measure is at most $2\int\|f\|/\|x\|<\infty$ by [L2]. [L2, step 1.3]

3.1 Obtain convergence in $L^1$. [L1, L4, step 1.3, step 2.1] The pointwise convergence in step 1.3 and $\|f-s_n\|\leq3\|f\|$ allow [L4] to be applied. Hence $\int\|f-s_n\|\to0$. Together with step 2.1 this is exactly the approximation required in [L1]. [L1, L4, step 1.3, step 2.1]

4.1 Step 1.1 proves necessity, step 3.1 proves sufficiency, and step 1.2 proves that the resulting integral is approximation-independent. The zero function, the empty measure space, and a single simple function are included by taking the constant zero or constant simple approximation. [L1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measure space and functions $f,g$ in the spaces named in the relevant clause of the Statement.

[L1] Holder's inequality for integrals is available ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]).

[L2] Membership in $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and $L^\infty(\mu)$ is defined in [[def-calligraphic-l-p-on-a-measure-space]] and [[def-l-infinity-on-a-measure-space]].

[L3] If $h\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then $|h|\le\|h\|_\infty$ almost everywhere ([[prop-essential-supremum-is-attained-as-the-least-essential-bound]]).

[L4] The nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[L5] The nonnegative integral is additive ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

[L6] Holder's inequality for finite sums gives, for nonnegative reals $a,b$, $$a+b\le 2^{1/q}(a^p+b^p)^{1/p}$$ when $q=p/(p-1)$ ([[thm-holder-finite-real-exponents]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** For $1 < p < infinity$, first use the two-term finite Holder inequality to show $|f + g|^p$ is integrable, then apply the standard Holder step to $|f + g| |f + g|^{p - 1}$. The cases $p = 1$ and $p = \infty$ are handled directly from subadditivity of absolute value and the essential-supremum bound.

1.1 If $p=1$, then $|f+g|\le|f|+|g|$ pointwise, so [L4, L5, given] $$\|f+g\|_1=\int|f+g|\,d\mu\le\int|f|\,d\mu+\int|g|\,d\mu=\|f\|_1+\|g\|_1.$$ [L4, L5, given]

1.2 Assume $1<p<\infty$ and let $q:=p/(p-1)$. Then [L1, L2, L4, L5, L6, given, algebra] $$\int |f+g|^p\,d\mu\le 2^{p-1}\left(\int |f|^p\,d\mu+\int |g|^p\,d\mu\right)<\infty.$$ Indeed, [L6] applied pointwise to the two-term families $(|f(x)|,|g(x)|)$ and $(1,1)$ gives $$|f(x)|+|g(x)|\le 2^{1/q}\bigl(|f(x)|^p+|g(x)|^p\bigr)^{1/p},$$ so $$|f+g|^p\le(|f|+|g|)^p\le 2^{p-1}(|f|^p+|g|^p)$$ pointwise. Thus $f+g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$. Put $C:=\|f+g\|_p$. If $C=0$, the claim is immediate. Otherwise $$|f+g|^p=|f+g|\,|f+g|^{p-1}\le |f|\,|f+g|^{p-1}+|g|\,|f+g|^{p-1}.$$ Because $(p-1)q=p$, the function $|f+g|^{p-1}$ lies in $\mathcal L^q(\mu)$ and has $q$-norm $C^{p-1}$. Integrating and applying [L1] with conjugate exponents $p$ and $q$ to each term yields $$C^p\le\|f\|_p\left(\int |f+g|^{(p-1)q}\,d\mu\right)^{1/q}+\|g\|_p\left(\int |f+g|^{(p-1)q}\,d\mu\right)^{1/q}.$$ Since $(p-1)q=p$, this becomes $$C^p\le(\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p)C^{p-1}.$$ If $C>0$, divide by $C^{p-1}$ to obtain the claim. [L1, L2, L4, L5, L6, given, algebra]

1.3 For $p=\infty$, let $M:=\|f\|_\infty$ and $N:=\|g\|_\infty$. Then [L2, L3, given] $$|f+g|\le |f|+|g|\le M+N.$$ Indeed, outside the union of the two null exceptional sets supplied by [L3], one has $|f|\le M$ and $|g|\le N$. Therefore $\|f+g\|_\infty\le M+N$. [L2, L3, given]

2.1 Steps 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3 prove the $p=1$, $1<p<\infty$, and $p=\infty$ cases. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, $T>0$, and $x:[0,T]\to H$ be continuous. For a finite partition $P=(t_i)_{i=0}^N$ with $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$, set
$$Q_P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\frac{\|x(t_{i+1})-x(t_i)\|_H^2}{t_{i+1}-t_i},\qquad C(x)=\sup_P Q_P(x).$$
If $C(x)<\infty$, then there is a strongly measurable $u\in L^2((0,T);H)$ such that $x(t)=x(0)+\int_0^t u(s)\,ds$ for every $t$, $x$ is norm-differentiable almost everywhere with derivative $u$, and
$$\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_H^2\,dt=C(x).$$

## Statement references

[[lem-bochner-time-l2-is-separable-hilbert]]

[[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]

[Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré, Chapter 4](https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~sayan/ambrosio.pdf)

[Chizat and Bach, Appendix B.2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $H,T,x$, and the finite partition bound $C(x)$.

[F1] The interval space $Z=L^2((0,T);H)$ with its Bochner inner product is a separable Hilbert space, and interval step functions with values in a countable dense subset of $H$ are dense in $Z$. [[lem-bochner-time-l2-is-separable-hilbert]]

[F2] A bounded real linear functional on a real Hilbert space has a unique Riesz representative, with equal norm. [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]

[F3] Strongly measurable Bochner-integrable functions admit integrable simple approximations, and Bochner integrability is equivalent to integrability of the norm. [[def-bochner-integrable-function]] [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]

[F4] Bochner integrals commute with bounded linear functionals, and Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the scalar pairings. [[thm-bounded-linear-maps-commute-with-bochner-integration]] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]

[F5] AC implies Countable and Dependent Choice, as needed for countable approximations and null-set unions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]] [[def-dependent-choice]]

[F6] Scalar locally integrable functions equal the limits of their centered interval averages almost everywhere. [[thm-lebesgue-differentiation-theorem-for-locally-integrable-functions-on-r-n]]

[F7] Markov's inequality and countable subadditivity show that sets with summable measures have a null limsup. [[thm-chebyshev-markov-inequality-for-the-integral]] [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]

## Proof


**Given:** AC, a continuous path $x$, and $C=C(x)<\infty$.

1.1 Let $S$ be the vector space of all finite $H$-valued interval step functions. It contains the dense family in [F1], hence is dense in $Z$. If $f(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}c_i\mathbf1_{(t_i,t_{i+1})}(t)$ on a partition $P$, define $\Lambda(f)=\sum_i\langle c_i,x(t_{i+1})-x(t_i)\rangle_H$. Refining $P$ leaves this sum unchanged, so $\Lambda$ is well-defined and linear on $S$. Finite-sum Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\Lambda(f)|\le\|f\|_Z Q_P(x)^{1/2}\le\sqrt C\,\|f\|_Z$. By [F1], $\Lambda$ extends uniquely to a bounded linear functional on $Z$, and [F2] represents it by $u\in Z$. [F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 Fix $0\le s<t\le T$ and $c\in H$. The function $c\mathbf1_{(s,t)}$ belongs to $S$, so its defining value is $\Lambda(c\mathbf1_{(s,t)})=\langle c,x(t)-x(s)\rangle_H$. By the Riesz representation in step 1.1 and commutation of bounded linear functionals with Bochner integrals, this equals $\int_s^t\langle c,u(r)\rangle_Hdr$. The identity holds for every $c\in H$; take $c$ equal to the difference of $x(t)-x(s)$ and $\int_s^tu(r)dr$ to see that its squared norm is zero. Thus $x(t)-x(s)=\int_s^t u(r)dr$ in $H$. [F2, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 By [F3], choose simple $H$-valued functions $s_n$ with $\int_0^T\|u-s_n\|_Hdt<2^{-3n}$ and put $g_n(t)=\|u(t)-s_n(t)\|_H$. Markov's inequality gives $\operatorname{Leb}\{g_n>2^{-n}\}\le2^{-2n}$; [F7] shows that outside a null set $g_n(t)\le2^{-n}$ eventually. Remove also the countable union of differentiation exceptional sets for all scalar functions $g_n$ and the finitely many indicators defining each $s_n$, using [F5] and [F6]. At each remaining interior $t$, the average of $g_n$ over either one-sided interval with endpoint $t$ has limsup at most $2g_n(t)$, since that interval lies in the centered interval of twice its length. The average of $\|s_n(q)-s_n(t)\|_H$ tends to zero: $s_n$ has finitely many values and each level-set indicator has density $1$ or $0$ at $t$. Therefore $\displaystyle \limsup_{h\to0}\left\|\frac1h\int_t^{t+h}u(q)dq-u(t)\right\|_H\le3g_n(t)$ for every $n$, and letting $n\to\infty$ proves the limit is zero. Step 2.1 identifies this average with $(x(t+h)-x(t))/h$, proving norm differentiability of $x$ with derivative $u$ almost everywhere. [F3, F5, F6, F7, step 2.1]

4.1 The norm of $\Lambda$ is exactly $\sqrt C$. The upper bound is step 1.1. For any partition $P$ with $Q_P(x)>0$, take the step function $f$ with $c_i=(x(t_{i+1})-x(t_i))/(t_{i+1}-t_i)$ on each interval. It belongs to $S$ and satisfies $\Lambda(f)=\|f\|_Z^2=Q_P(x)$, so $\|\Lambda\|_Z\ge|\Lambda(f)|/\|f\|_Z=\sqrt{Q_P(x)}$. If $Q_P(x)=0$, this lower bound is automatic. Taking the supremum over partitions gives $\|\Lambda\|_Z^2=C$. By [F2], $\|u\|_Z=\|\Lambda\|_Z$, proving the displayed energy identity. [F2, step 1.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

## Remarks

The zero function and every integrable simple function are Bochner integrable,
witnessed by constant approximating sequences. No choice principle is used in
this definition or in the Cauchy estimate.

## Statement

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

[L1] A bounded linear operator satisfies $\|Tx\|\leq C\|x\|$ for some finite $C$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]).

[L2] A Bochner integral is the norm limit of integrals of an $L^1$-approximating simple sequence ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]]).

[L3] The Banach-valued simple integral is linear and representation-independent ([[lem-banach-valued-simple-integral-is-well-defined]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** $T,f,E$ as in the Statement.

1.1 Restrict a defining approximation to the measurable set. Choose integrable simple $s_n$ with $\int\|f-s_n\|\to0$. Then $\mathbf1_ETs_n$ is an integrable $Y$-valued simple function: every nonzero level is a finite union of level sets of $\mathbf1_Es_n$. [given, L2, choose]

2.1 Prove Bochner integrability after applying $T$. By [L1], $\int\|\mathbf1_ETf-\mathbf1_ETs_n\|\leq C\int_E\|f-s_n\|\to0$. Thus [L2] makes $\mathbf1_ETf$ Bochner integrable. [L1, L2, step 1.1]

3.1 Commute $T$ with the defining limit. [L1, L2, L3, step 1.1, step 2.1] For each simple $s_n$, finite linearity in [L3] gives $T(\int_Es_n)=\int_ETs_n$. Boundedness makes $T$ norm-continuous, so taking limits in this equality and using [L2] proves the displayed identity. If $T=0$, $f=0$, or $E=\varnothing$, both sides are explicitly zero. [L1, L2, L3, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonnegative measurable function $f$ and a real number $t>0$.

[L1] The nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

## Definition

Assume AC. Fix an arbitrary probability label space $(S,\Sigma,\sigma)$ and $r>0$. Let $K=L^2(\sigma;\mathbb R^d)$ with its usual real Hilbert inner product, and let
$$C_r=\{X\in K:X(s)\in Q_r\text{ for }\sigma\text{-almost every }s\}.$$
Define the indicator $\iota_{C_r}$ to be $0$ on $C_r$ and $+\infty$ outside it, and define the localized lifted energy on $K$ by
$$E_r(X)=R\!\left(\int_S\Phi(X(s))\,d\sigma(s)\right)+\int_SV(X(s))\,d\sigma(s)+\iota_{C_r}(X).$$
The first integral is a Bochner integral. The space $K$ is Hilbert for every probability label space and is separable when $\Sigma$ is countably generated. The latter condition holds for finite labels and for Euclidean Borel labels of any dimension, including joint and triple transport-plan labels. For the flow from a law $\mu_0$ the particular choice is $(S,\sigma)=(\Omega,\mu_0)$ and $X_0(s)=s$. Values of representatives on $\sigma$-null sets do not affect $C_r$ or $E_r$.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space and let $E:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, lower semicontinuous, bounded below, and $\lambda$-convex, meaning
$$E((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)E(x)+tE(y)-\frac{\lambda}{2}t(1-t)\|x-y\|_H^2\quad(0\le t\le1).$$
For $x\in\operatorname{dom}E$, define
$$\partial_\lambda E(x)=\{\xi\in H:E(y)\ge E(x)+\langle\xi,y-x\rangle_H+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|y-x\|_H^2\text{ for every }y\in H\}.$$
For every $x_0\in\operatorname{dom}E$, there is a unique curve $x:[0,\infty)\to H$ which is absolutely continuous with square-integrable derivative on every bounded interval, satisfies $x(0)=x_0$ and $-\dot x(t)\in\partial_\lambda E(x(t))$ for almost every $t$, and obeys
$$E(x(t))-E(x(s))=-\int_s^t\|\dot x(r)\|_H^2\,dr\quad(0\le s\le t<\infty).$$
For almost every $t$, $-\dot x(t)$ is the unique minimum-norm element of $\partial_\lambda E(x(t))$. For two such curves $x,\widetilde x$ with initial values $x_0,\widetilde x_0$,
$$\|x(t)-\widetilde x(t)\|_H\le e^{-\lambda t}\|x_0-\widetilde x_0\|_H.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a separable real Hilbert space $H$, a proper lower-semicontinuous bounded-below $\lambda$-convex energy $E$, and $x_0$ with $E(x_0)<\infty$.

[F1] The Bochner space $Z=L^2((0,T);H)$ is a separable Hilbert space. [[lem-bochner-time-l2-is-separable-hilbert]]

[F2] If a continuous Hilbert-valued path has finite partition energy, it is an AC² path with a Bochner derivative and its squared derivative integral equals that partition energy. [[lem-hilbert-valued-path-energy-characterization]]

[F3] A bounded linear functional on a Hilbert space has a unique Riesz representative. [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]

[F4] AC supplies Countable and Dependent Choice. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]] [[def-dependent-choice]]

[F5] Cauchy–Schwarz holds for the Hilbert inner product. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]

[F6] Fatou's lemma passes lower bounds through pointwise limits of nonnegative measurable functions. [[thm-fatou-lemma]]

[F7] Every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence by the nested-interval property. [[thm-nested-interval-property]]

[F8] Scalar locally integrable functions are recovered almost everywhere by centered interval averages. [[thm-lebesgue-differentiation-theorem-for-locally-integrable-functions-on-r-n]]

[F9] The indefinite integral of an integrable real function is absolutely continuous. [[cor-the-indefinite-integral-of-an-l-one-function-is-absolutely-continuous]]

[F10] The indefinite integral of an integrable real function has that function as its derivative almost everywhere. [[thm-first-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-l-one]]





**Given:** AC, $H,E,\lambda$, and $x_0$ as in the Statement.

## Proof

1.1 For $0<\tau$ with $1+\lambda\tau>0$ and $z\in H$, set $\Psi_{\tau,z}(y)=E(y)+\|y-z\|_H^2/(2\tau)$. It is lower semicontinuous and $(\lambda+1/\tau)$-strongly convex, with positive strong-convexity coefficient. It is bounded below and coercive because $E$ is bounded below. Choose a minimizing sequence $(y_n)$ using [F4]. The midpoint inequality $\displaystyle \Psi_{\tau,z}\!\left(\frac{y_n+y_m}{2}\right)\le\frac{\Psi_{\tau,z}(y_n)+\Psi_{\tau,z}(y_m)}{2}-\frac{1+\lambda\tau}{8\tau}\|y_n-y_m\|_H^2$ and the lower bound by the infimum show that $(y_n)$ is Cauchy. Completeness of $H$ and lower semicontinuity give a minimizer, and strong convexity makes it unique. Call it $J_\tau z$. For $0<h<1$, set $y_h=(1-h)J_\tau z+hy$. Minimality at $y_h$, the $\lambda$-convex inequality, and expansion of the quadratic term give $\displaystyle 0\le h(E(y)-E(J_\tau z))-\frac{\lambda}{2}h(1-h)\|y-J_\tau z\|_H^2-\frac h\tau\langle z-J_\tau z,y-J_\tau z\rangle_H+\frac{h^2}{2\tau}\|y-J_\tau z\|_H^2.$ Divide by $h$ and let $h\downarrow0$ to obtain $\displaystyle E(y)\ge E(J_\tau z)+\left\langle\frac{z-J_\tau z}{\tau},y-J_\tau z\right\rangle_H+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|y-J_\tau z\|_H^2,$ so $(z-J_\tau z)/\tau\in\partial_\lambda E(J_\tau z)$. [given, F4, construct]

2.1 Starting at $x_0$, iterate $x_n=J_\tau x_{n-1}$. Comparison with the admissible point $x_{n-1}$ gives $\displaystyle E(x_n)+\frac{\|x_n-x_{n-1}\|_H^2}{2\tau}\le E(x_{n-1}).$ Thus $E(x_n)$ decreases and, for $m=\inf_HE$, $\sum_n\tau\|(x_{n-1}-x_n)/\tau\|_H^2\le2(E(x_0)-m)$. [given, step 1.1]

3.1 Let $x_\tau$ be the linear interpolation between the iterates and $\bar x_\tau(t)=x_n$ on $(t_{n-1},t_n]$; then $\dot x_\tau=-\xi_\tau$ and $\xi_\tau(t)\in\partial_\lambda E(\bar x_\tau(t))$. The action bound in step 2.1 gives $\|\xi_\tau\|_{L^2(0,T;H)}^2\le2(E(x_0)-m)$ and $\|x_\tau-\bar x_\tau\|_{L^\infty(0,T;H)}\le\sqrt{\tau}\|\xi_\tau\|_{L^2(0,T;H)}$. For two uniform meshes $\tau,\sigma$, put $\delta_\tau=x_\tau-\bar x_\tau$ and $q(t)=\|x_\tau(t)-x_\sigma(t)\|_H^2$. The subgradient monotonicity obtained by adding the defining inequalities for $\partial_\lambda E$ gives $\displaystyle \frac12q'(t)\le-\lambda\|\bar x_\tau(t)-\bar x_\sigma(t)\|_H^2+(\|\xi_\tau(t)\|_H+\|\xi_\sigma(t)\|_H)(\|\delta_\tau(t)\|_H+\|\delta_\sigma(t)\|_H).$ Using $\|\delta_\tau(t)\|_H\le\tau\|\xi_\tau(t)\|_H$ on each step and Cauchy–Schwarz in time, the interpolation-error terms obey $\displaystyle \int_0^T(\|\xi_\tau\|+\|\xi_\sigma\|)(\|\delta_\tau\|+\|\delta_\sigma\|)dt\le 2(\tau+\sigma)(\|\xi_\tau\|_{L^2}^2+\|\xi_\sigma\|_{L^2}^2),\quad\int_0^T\|\delta_\tau-\delta_\sigma\|^2dt\le2\tau^2\|\xi_\tau\|_{L^2}^2+2\sigma^2\|\xi_\sigma\|_{L^2}^2.$ When $\lambda\ge0$ its term in the differential inequality is nonpositive; when $\lambda<0$, $\|\bar x_\tau-\bar x_\sigma\|^2\le2q+2\|\delta_\tau-\delta_\sigma\|^2$ bounds it by $2|\lambda|q+2|\lambda|\|\delta_\tau-\delta_\sigma\|^2$. Since the action norms are uniformly bounded by step 2.1, for $0<\tau,\sigma\le1$ the differential inequality has the form $q'(t)\le4|\lambda|q(t)+r(t)$, $q(0)=0$, with $\int_0^T r(t)dt\le C(\tau+\sigma)$ and $C$ depending only on $T,\lambda,E(x_0)-m$. Multiplying by $e^{-4|\lambda|t}$ and integrating yields $\sup_{t\le T}q(t)\le C_T(\tau+\sigma)$, so the interpolants converge uniformly on every bounded time interval. [F1, F5, step 2.1]

4.1 Let $x$ be the uniform limit. Every finite partition $P$ satisfies $\sum_{[a,b]\in P}\|x(b)-x(a)\|_H^2/(b-a)\le\liminf_{\tau\downarrow0}\int_0^T\|\dot x_\tau\|_H^2\le2(E(x_0)-m)$, by Cauchy–Schwarz on each mesh interval and uniform convergence. [F2] gives $x\in AC^2$ and a derivative. The step functions $\xi_\tau$ are bounded in the separable Hilbert space [F1]; apply [F7] successively to their inner products with a countable dense family and take a diagonal subsequence. The limits define a bounded linear functional on the dense span, hence on the whole space, and [F3] represents its extension by $\xi\in L^2(0,T;H)$. Thus $\xi_\tau\rightharpoonup\xi$. Since $x_\tau(t)-x_0=-\int_0^t\xi_\tau(r)dr$ and the Bochner integral on $(0,t)$ is a bounded linear map, weak convergence and uniform convergence imply $\dot x=-\xi$. Also $\bar x_\tau\to x$ uniformly. [F1, F2, F3, F7, step 3.1]

5.1 For each fixed $y$ with $E(y)<\infty$, integrate the discrete inequality from step 1.1 over any measurable $A\subset(0,T)$. Weak convergence of $\xi_\tau$ and uniform convergence of $\bar x_\tau$ pass the linear term to its limit; lower semicontinuity of $E$ and Fatou's lemma [F6], applied to $E(\bar x_\tau)-m\ge0$, pass the energy term. Thus the subgradient inequality holds for almost every $t$, first for a countable dense subset of the graph (choose one graph point from each nonempty member of a countable base of $H\times\mathbb R$, using [F4]) $\{(y,E(y)):E(y)<\infty\}$ and then for every such $y$ by continuity in the graph variables. Hence $\xi(t)\in\partial_\lambda E(x(t))$ almost everywhere. [given, F6, step 1.1, step 4.1]

5.2 Work on $[0,T]$, choosing the construction on $[0,T+1]$ to allow small time translations. Put $u=\dot x=-\xi$ and $e(t)=E(x(t))$. The discrete bound $E(\bar x_\tau(t))\le E(x_0)$, uniform convergence and lower semicontinuity give $m\le e(t)\le E(x_0)$ for every $t$, where $m=\inf_HE$. As a lower-semicontinuous function of time, $e$ is measurable and bounded. Extend $u$ and $\xi$ by zero outside $(0,T+1)$. Time translations are continuous in $L^2(\mathbb R;H)$: this is immediate for interval step functions because the measure of the symmetric difference of an interval with its translate tends to zero, and holds for every $L^2$ function by the density in [F1] and the isometry of translations. For $0<a<b<T$ and sufficiently small $h>0$, put $q_h(r)=(x(r+h)-x(r-h))/(2h)=(2h)^{-1}\int_{-h}^h u(r+s)ds$ for $a<r<b$. Cauchy–Schwarz in the averaging variable and translation continuity give $q_h\to u$ in $L^2(a,b;H)$ and $\sup_h\|q_h\|_{L^2(a,b;H)}<\infty$. Indeed, $\int_a^b\|q_h-u\|_H^2dr\le(2h)^{-1}\int_{-h}^h\int_a^b\|u(r+s)-u(r)\|_H^2drds\to0$. [F1, F5, step 2.1, step 4.1]

6.1 For each sufficiently small fixed $h$, the subgradient inequalities at $x(r-h)$ and $x(r+h)$ hold for almost every $r\in(a,b)$ and imply $\langle\xi(r-h),q_h(r)\rangle_H+\lambda h\|q_h(r)\|_H^2\le(e(r+h)-e(r-h))/(2h)\le\langle\xi(r+h),q_h(r)\rangle_H-\lambda h\|q_h(r)\|_H^2$. Both pairings converge in $L^1(a,b)$ to $g(r)=\langle\xi(r),u(r)\rangle_H$, since translations of $\xi$ and $q_h$ converge in $L^2$ and Cauchy–Schwarz bounds their products. The quadratic remainder has $L^1$ norm at most $|\lambda|h\|q_h\|_{L^2(a,b;H)}^2\to0$. The sandwich therefore implies convergence of the entire centered energy quotient to $g$ in $L^1(a,b)$: if $L_h\le d_h\le U_h$, then $|d_h-g|\le|L_h-g|+|U_h-g|$ almost everywhere. [F5, step 5.1, step 5.2]

7.1 For every $0<a<b<T$ the exact integral identity is $\int_a^b(e(r+h)-e(r-h))/(2h)dr=(2h)^{-1}(\int_{b-h}^{b+h}e(r)dr-\int_{a-h}^{a+h}e(r)dr)$. By [F8] there is a full-measure set $B\subset(0,T)$ on which centered averages recover $e$. For any $a,b\in B$ with $a<b$, Step 6.1 and this exact identity give $e(b)-e(a)=\int_a^b g(r)dr$. Fix $a_*\in B$ and define $\widetilde e(t)=e(a_*)+\int_{a_*}^t g(r)dr$ on $[0,T]$. Here $g\in L^1(0,T)$ by Cauchy–Schwarz. Thus [F9] makes $\widetilde e$ absolutely continuous and [F10] gives $\widetilde e'=g$ almost everywhere, while the preceding equality implies $e=\widetilde e$ on $B$. This proves an absolutely continuous representative by an integral identity, without inferring it from an almost-everywhere derivative. [F5, F8, F9, F10, step 6.1]

8.1 Lower semicontinuity of $e$ and continuity of $\widetilde e$ give $e(t)\le\widetilde e(t)$ for every $t\in[0,T]$ by approaching $t$ through $B$. Fix $t\in(0,T]$. For sufficiently large $n$, put $I_n=(t-2^{-n},t-2^{-n-1})\subset(0,T)$ and choose $s_n\in I_n\cap B$ where the subgradient inclusion holds and $\|\xi(s_n)\|_H^2\le2|I_n|^{-1}\int_{I_n}\|\xi(r)\|_H^2dr$. Such points exist since the excluded set is null and the upper threshold exceeds the mean, with the zero-integral case treated by choosing a point where $\xi=0$. Since $(t-s_n)/|I_n|\le2$, one has $(t-s_n)\|\xi(s_n)\|_H^2\le4\int_{I_n}\|\xi\|_H^2\to0$. Consequently $|\langle\xi(s_n),x(t)-x(s_n)\rangle_H|\le((t-s_n)\|\xi(s_n)\|_H^2)^{1/2}(\int_{s_n}^t\|u\|_H^2)^{1/2}\to0$. The subgradient inequality at $s_n$ gives $e(t)\ge e(s_n)+\langle\xi(s_n),x(t)-x(s_n)\rangle_H+(\lambda/2)\|x(t)-x(s_n)\|_H^2$; using $e(s_n)=\widetilde e(s_n)$ and continuity of $x,\widetilde e$ yields $e(t)\ge\widetilde e(t)$. At $t=0$, the bound $e(r)\le E(x_0)$ for all $r$ and equality on $B$ give $\widetilde e(0)\le E(x_0)=e(0)$, proving equality there too. Thus $e=\widetilde e$ on $[0,T]$ and, for every $0\le s\le t\le T$, $E(x(t))-E(x(s))=\int_s^t\langle\xi(r),u(r)\rangle_Hdr=-\int_s^t\|\dot x(r)\|_H^2dr$. Since $T$ is arbitrary this holds for all finite endpoints. [F4, F5, step 5.1, step 5.2, step 7.1]


9.1 At almost every $t$, let $\zeta\in\partial_\lambda E(x(t))$. Applying its defining inequality to $x(t+h)$ for positive and negative $h$, then using differentiability of $x$ and $e$, gives $\langle\zeta,\dot x(t)\rangle_H=-\|\dot x(t)\|_H^2$. Since $\xi=-\dot x\in\partial_\lambda E(x(t))$, this says $\langle\zeta-\xi,\xi\rangle_H=0$ and hence $\|\zeta\|_H^2=\|\xi\|_H^2+\|\zeta-\xi\|_H^2$. Thus $\xi$ is the unique minimum-norm subgradient almost everywhere. [step 8.1, step 5.1]

10.1 For two solutions, $\lambda$-semiconvexity implies $\langle\xi-\tilde\xi,x-\tilde x\rangle_H\ge\lambda\|x-\tilde x\|_H^2$. Therefore $\frac12\frac d{dt}\|x-\tilde x\|_H^2=-\langle\xi-\tilde\xi,x-\tilde x\rangle_H\le-\lambda\|x-\tilde x\|_H^2$ almost everywhere. Grönwall proves the stated estimate and uniqueness. [step 5.1, step 9.1] ∎

## Statement

For each $k \in \mathbb{N}$ let $I_k = [a_k, b_k]$ be a closed bounded interval
with $a_k \le b_k$ ([[def-interval]]), and suppose the family is **nested**:

$$I_{k+1} \subseteq I_k \qquad (k \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $\ell_k = b_k - a_k \ge 0$ for the length of $I_k$. Then:

1. $\displaystyle\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k$ is **nonempty**. More precisely,
   with $a = \sup\{a_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ and
   $b = \inf\{b_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$, both of which exist, one has $a \le b$
   and $$\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k = [a, b].$$
2. $\displaystyle\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k$ is a **single point** if and only
   if $\ell_k \to 0$ ([[def-real-limit]]).

Every hypothesis is load bearing. Dropping closedness makes the intersection
empty; dropping boundedness does the same; and dropping nonemptiness of the
individual intervals is vacuously fatal.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Closed bounded intervals $I_k = [a_k, b_k]$ with $a_k \le b_k$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and $I_{k+1} \subseteq I_k$ for every $k$; the sequences $(a_k)$ and $(b_k)$ of reals ([[def-sequence]]); their ranges $A = \{a_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ and $B = \{b_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$, both nonempty; and $\ell_k = b_k - a_k$.

[L1] Closed bounded intervals: $[a,b] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : a \le x \le b\}$; it is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, it is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$, it has two distinct elements $a$ and $b$ when $a < b$, and its length is $b - a$ ([[def-interval]]).

[L2] Least-upper-bound property and uniqueness: a nonempty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ bounded above has a unique supremum; the supremum is an upper bound and is $\le$ every upper bound ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

[L3] Greatest-lower-bound property and uniqueness: a nonempty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ bounded below has a unique infimum; the infimum is a lower bound and is $\ge$ every lower bound ([[thm-infimum-property]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

[L4] Monotone sequences, and the fact that consecutive comparisons suffice: $x_k \le x_{k+1}$ for all $k$ makes $(x_k)$ nondecreasing, and $x_{k+1} \le x_k$ for all $k$ makes it nonincreasing ([[def-monotone-sequence]]).

[L5] Monotone convergence: a nondecreasing sequence whose range is bounded above converges to the supremum of its range, and a nonincreasing sequence whose range is bounded below converges to the infimum ([[thm-monotone-convergence]]).

[L6] Algebra of limits: if $u_k \to u$ and $v_k \to v$ then $u_k - v_k \to u - v$ ([[thm-algebra-of-limits]]).

[L7] A sequence of reals has at most one limit ([[lem-limit-unique]]).

[L8] Bounded above and bounded below, for a subset of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-bounded-set]]).

[L9] The order on $\mathbb{N}$ is total and transitive, so any two indices $k, l$ admit an index $m$ with $k \le m$ and $l \le m$, namely the larger of the two ([[def-nat-order]], [[thm-nat-linear-order]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Nestedness read on the endpoints: since $a_{k+1} \le b_{k+1}$, both $a_{k+1}$ and $b_{k+1}$ lie in $I_{k+1} \subseteq I_k$, so $a_k \le a_{k+1}$ and $b_{k+1} \le b_k$ for every $k$. [given, L1]

2.1 Hence $(a_k)$ is nondecreasing and $(b_k)$ is nonincreasing. [step 1.1, L4]

3.1 For all indices $k$ and $l$: choosing $m$ with $k \le m$ and $l \le m$ gives $a_k \le a_m \le b_m \le b_l$, so $a_k \le b_l$. [step 2.1, given, L9]

4.1 Every $b_l$ is therefore an upper bound of $A$ and every $a_k$ a lower bound of $B$; both sets are nonempty, so $a := \sup A$ and $b := \inf B$ exist and are unique. [step 3.1, L2, L3, L8]

5.1 $a \le b$: each $b_l$ is an upper bound of $A$, so $a \le b_l$ for every $l$ by leastness of the supremum; thus $a$ is a lower bound of $B$, and $a \le b$ by greatestness of the infimum. [step 4.1, L2, L3]

5.2 By monotone convergence, $a_k \to a$ and $b_k \to b$. [step 2.1, step 4.1, L5]

5.3 The intersection is exactly $[a,b]$: a real $x$ lies in every $I_k$ exactly when $a_k \le x \le b_k$ for every $k$, that is exactly when $x$ is an upper bound of $A$ and a lower bound of $B$, and by leastness of $a$ and greatestness of $b$ that holds exactly when $a \le x \le b$. [step 4.1, L1, L2, L3]

6.1 $\ell_k = b_k - a_k \to b - a$ by the algebra of limits. [step 5.2, L6]

6.2 Since $a \le b$, the interval $[a,b]$ is nonempty, so the intersection is nonempty; together with step 5.3 this is claim 1. [step 5.1, step 5.3, L1]

7.1 If $\ell_k \to 0$ then $b - a = 0$ by uniqueness of limits, so $a = b$ and the intersection is $[a,a] = \{a\}$, a single point. [step 5.3, step 6.1, L1, L7]

7.2 Conversely, if the intersection is a single point then $a = b$: it equals $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, and $a < b$ would give the two distinct elements $a$ and $b$. Hence $b - a = 0$ and $\ell_k \to 0$ by step 6.1. [step 5.1, step 5.3, step 6.1, L1]

8.1 Claim 1 is step 6.2 and claim 2 is the pair of implications in steps 7.1 and 7.2, so a nested sequence of nonempty closed bounded intervals has nonempty intersection, equal to $[a,b]$, and that intersection is a single point exactly when the lengths tend to $0$. [step 6.2, step 7.1, step 7.2] ∎

## Remarks

- **No Archimedean input is needed.** The lengths are handled entirely by the algebra of limits and the uniqueness of limits: $\ell_k$ always converges, to $b - a$, and the two directions of claim 2 are then the two directions of "$b - a = 0$". A proof that instead argues "if $b - a > 0$ then some $\ell_k$ is smaller" does need the Archimedean property ([[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]]), and it is avoidable, so it is avoided.

- **Nestedness gives more than it is usually stated to give.** The intersection is not merely nonempty; it is the closed interval $[a,b]$, and $a$ and $b$ are the limits of the endpoint sequences. The single-point case is exactly the case in which those two limits agree, and that is what makes the nested interval property usable as a *construction* of a real number, as in [[ex-nested-intervals-single-point]].

- **This is one of the standard equivalents of completeness.** Nested intervals together with the Archimedean property imply the least-upper-bound property, so the implication proved here is not reversible for free: it is half of an equivalence whose other half needs the Archimedean hypothesis separately. [[rem-completeness-routes]] records where this library stands on those routes.

- **The witnesses for the two deleted hypotheses** are [[cex-nested-open-intervals-empty]], which keeps boundedness and drops closedness, and [[cex-nested-unbounded-closed-empty]], which keeps closedness and drops boundedness. Neither is used above; each shows that the corresponding hypothesis cannot be removed.

## Statement

For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $f\in L^1[a,b]$ and its indefinite integral $I_f$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Given $\varepsilon>0$, apply [[thm-absolute-continuity-of-the-integral]] to $|f|$ and obtain $\delta>0$. [given, choose]

2.1 For disjoint intervals $[u_j,v_j]$ of total length below $\delta$, their union $E$ has measure below $\delta$, and $\sum_j|I_f(v_j)-I_f(u_j)|\le\int_E|f|<\varepsilon$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 This is the defining finite-family condition for absolute continuity; the empty family and $a=b$ give zero sums. [step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Fix an arbitrary probability label space $(S,\Sigma,\sigma)$, let $K=L^2(\sigma;\mathbb R^d)$, and let $C_r=\{X:X(s)\in Q_r\text{ for }\sigma\text{-almost every }s\}$. Write $A_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|d\Phi\|$, $B_r=\operatorname{Lip}_{Q_r}(d\Phi)$, $M_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|\partial V\|$, and let $L_r$ and $N_r$ be, respectively, a Lipschitz constant and a norm bound for $dR$ on the closed convex hull of $\Phi(Q_r)$. For all $X,Y\in C_r$, the smooth part $G_r(X)=R(\int\Phi(X)d\sigma)$ has the first-order expansion on $C_r$ with gradient $\nabla G_r(X)(s)=d\Phi_{X(s)}^*\nabla R(\int\Phi(X)d\sigma)$, and this gradient is Lipschitz with constant $L_rA_r^2+N_rB_r$. No separability of the label space is required for these estimates. Consequently $E_r(X)=G_r(X)+\int V(X)d\sigma+\iota_{C_r}(X)$ is $(\lambda_V-L_rA_r^2-N_rB_r)$-semiconvex on $K$.

**Given:** AC, $\sigma,Q_r,\Phi,R,V$ and the constants in the Statement.

[F2] The differential of $R$ has a unique Hilbert gradient with the same norm. [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]

[F3] The feature map is differentiable, $d\Phi$ is bounded and Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and $dR$ is Lipschitz on bounded sets; on the relevant bounded convex hull its norm has some finite bound. [[def-feature-measure-energy]]

[F6] On every segment in $Q_r$, semiconvexity of $V$ means $V(u)-(\lambda_V/2)|u|^2$ is convex. [[def-feature-measure-energy]]

**Given:** AC and the data above.

2.1 Write $m(Y)-m(X)=Dm(X)[Y-X]+O(\|Y-X\|_K^2)$ as in step 1.1. Fréchet differentiability of $R$ at $m(X)$ gives $R(m(Y))=R(m(X))+dR_{m(X)}[m(Y)-m(X)]+o(\|m(Y)-m(X)\|_{\mathcal H})$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

Adding the two inequalities and restricting to the convex set $C_r$ proves the claimed semiconvexity of $E_r$. [F3, F6, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and the hypotheses of the feature-measure energy definition. Fix any probability label space $(S,\Sigma,\sigma)$ and use the localized lift $E_r$ on $K=L^2(\sigma;\mathbb R^d)$. Separability of $K$ is not assumed or needed for the subdifferential formula and minimum-section conclusion. For a semiconvex functional $J:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ with coefficient $\alpha$, define
$$\partial_\alpha J(X)=\{\eta\in K:J(Y)\ge J(X)+\langle\eta,Y-X\rangle_K+\tfrac{\alpha}{2}\|Y-X\|_K^2\text{ for all }Y\in K\}.$$
The set $C_r$ is closed and convex, and $E_r$ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and lower bounded. Write $A_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|d\Phi\|$, $B_r=\operatorname{Lip}_{Q_r}(d\Phi)$, $M_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|\partial V\|$ in the bounded-selection convention, and let $L_r,N_r$ bound the Lipschitz constant and norm of $dR$ on the closed convex hull of $\Phi(Q_r)$. Let $C_r^{\rm sm}=L_rA_r^2+N_rB_r$ and $\lambda_E=\lambda_V-C_r^{\rm sm}$. For $X\in C_r$, its Hilbert subdifferential with coefficient $\lambda_E$ is exactly
$$\partial_{\lambda_E} E_r(X)=\left\{s\mapsto d\Phi_{X(s)}^*\nabla R\!\left(\int\Phi(X)d\sigma\right)+\zeta(s):\ \zeta\in K,\ \zeta(s)\in\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_{Q_r})(X(s))\text{ for }\sigma\text{-almost every }s\right\}.$$
The pointwise minimum-norm selection $u\mapsto\operatorname{argmin}\{|z|:z\in\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_{Q_r})(u)\}$ is Borel on $Q_r$ and has norm at most $M_r$; hence its composition with any $X\in C_r$ is a measurable member of $K$. More generally, for $a\in\mathcal H$ put $b_a(u)=d\Phi_u^*a$ and $S(a,u)=\operatorname{argmin}\{|z|:z\in b_a(u)+\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_{Q_r})(u)\}$. This full shifted minimum is jointly Borel in $(a,u)$, has $|S(a,u)|\le A_r\|a\|+M_r$, and the minimum-norm element of $\partial_{\lambda_E}E_r(X)$ is exactly $s\mapsto S(\nabla R(\int\Phi(X)d\sigma),X(s))$. It is generally different from the smooth gradient plus the minimum of the potential subdifferential alone.

**Given:** AC, $r,\sigma$ and $X\in C_r$.

1.1 The set $C_r$ is convex because $Q_r$ is convex. To show it is closed, take $X_n\in C_r$ with $X_n\to X$ in $K$. Tonelli [F6] implies $\sum_k|X_{n_k}(s)-X(s)|^2<\infty$ for almost every $s$, so $X_{n_k}(s)\to X(s)$ there; closedness of $Q_r$ gives $X\in C_r$. For lower semicontinuity of $E_r$, consider a sequence with finite energy liminf and pass to a subsequence of finite energies, so every term lies in $C_r$ and its limit lies there by the closure just proved. For any $u\in Q_r$, a vector $\zeta\in\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ supplied by [F2] gives $V(y)\ge V(u)+\zeta\cdot(y-u)+\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|y-u|^2$ for $y\in\Omega$, proving lower semicontinuity of $V$ at $u$. Fatou [F4] makes the potential integral lower semicontinuous along this sequence, and the smooth term is continuous by [F1]. A constant $Q_r$-valued function has finite energy because $Q_r$ is nonempty and $\Phi,V$ are bounded on it, while $R,V\ge0$ make $E_r$ bounded below. 1.2 Let $f=V+\iota_{Q_r}$. Since every point of $Q_r$ has a subgradient by [F2], the supporting inequality implies that $f$ is lower semicontinuous at every point of $Q_r$. For $\varepsilon>0$ small enough that $1+\varepsilon\lambda_V>0$, minimize $f(y)+|x-y|^2/(2\varepsilon)$. This is strongly convex and coercive, so it has a unique minimizer $J_\varepsilon x$. Its optimality inequality says $z_\varepsilon(x)=(x-J_\varepsilon x)/\varepsilon\in\partial_{\lambda_V}f(J_\varepsilon x)$; this follows by testing minimality at $(1-h)J_\varepsilon x+hy$, using semiconvexity of $f$, dividing by $h$, and letting $h\downarrow0$. Comparing the two optimality inequalities at $x$ and $x'$ and adding gives $\|J_\varepsilon x-J_\varepsilon x'\|\le(1+\varepsilon\lambda_V)^{-1}\|x-x'\|$, so $z_\varepsilon$ is continuous. For fixed $x\in Q_r$, comparison with $y=x$ shows $J_\varepsilon x\to x$. Passing to a limit in the defining subgradient inequalities shows the graph of $\partial g$ is closed; every convergent subsequence therefore limits to an element of $\partial_{\lambda_V}f(x)$. 2.1 The selected section has norm at most $M_r$ by [F2], so composition with a strongly measurable $X$ is measurable and square integrable; call it $\zeta_X\in K$. 3.1 Conversely, let $\eta\in\partial_{\lambda_E}E_r(X)$. Put $C=L_rA_r^2+N_rB_r$ and $\lambda_E=\lambda_V-C$. Then $E_r-\frac{\lambda_E}{2}\|\cdot\|_K^2$ is the sum of the convex integral $X\mapsto\int g(X)d\sigma$ and the differentiable convex function $G_r(X)+\frac C2\|X\|_K^2$. The convex sum rule here follows directly from one-sided directional derivatives: if $q$ is convex and $h$ is differentiable convex, a supporting vector $w$ of $q+h$ satisfies $q'(X;H)\ge\langle w-\nabla h(X),H\rangle$ for every feasible direction $H$; convex secant slopes dominate $q'(X;H)$, so $w-\nabla h(X)$ supports $q$. Apply this with $w=\eta-\lambda_EX$ to conclude that $\eta-\nabla G_r(X)-\lambda_VX$ supports the convex integral. The relative interior is nonempty by [F5]; on it, continuity [F5] extends the inequality from the dense subset. For a boundary point $y$, choose $y_0$ in the relative interior and let $B(y_0,\rho)$ be a relative ball contained in $Q_r$. For $y_n=(1-1/n)y+(1/n)y_0$, convexity gives a relative ball of radius $\rho/n$ around $y_n$ contained in $Q_r$, so $y_n$ is in the relative interior. Convexity gives $g(y_n)\le(1-1/n)g(y)+(1/n)g(y_0)$, and lower semicontinuity gives $g(y)\le\liminf_n g(y_n)$; hence $g(y_n)\to g(y)$ and the supporting inequality passes to $y$. Undoing the quadratic shift proves $\eta-\nabla G_r(X)$ is a $K$-section of $\partial_{\lambda_V}f(X(s))$, proving the reverse inclusion. [F1, F3, F5, step 2.1]

4.1 For the shifted selection, apply step 1.2 to $f_a(u)=\langle a,\Phi(u)\rangle+V(u)+\iota_{Q_r}(u)$, whose semiconvexity coefficient is $\alpha_a=\lambda_V-B_r\|a\|$. The pointwise projection inequality $|S(a,u)|\le|z|$ for every $z$ in the shifted set integrates over labels. The exact subdifferential formula from step 3.1 therefore proves that this measurable section is the unique minimum-norm Hilbert subgradient. [F1, F2, step 1.2, step 3.1] ∎
