## Definition

Assume AC. Let $\mu_0,\mu_1\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$. A generalized $W_2$ geodesic from $\mu_0$ to $\mu_1$ with base $\nu\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ is a probability measure $\pi$ on triples $(z,x,y)$ whose $(z,x)$ marginal is an optimal coupling of $\nu$ and $\mu_0$ and whose $(z,y)$ marginal is an optimal coupling of $\nu$ and $\mu_1$; its interpolating curve is $\mu_t=((1-t)x+ty)_\#\pi$. A functional $F$ is $\lambda$-convex along generalized geodesics if for every such $\pi$ its values satisfy $F(\mu_t)\le(1-t)F(\mu_0)+tF(\mu_1)-\frac{\lambda}{2}t(1-t)\int|x-y|^2d\pi$. A vector field $g_\mu\in L^2(\mu;\mathbb R^d)$ is a strong Wasserstein subgradient of $F$ at $\mu$ if for every $\eta\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ and every coupling $\gamma$ of $\mu$ and $\eta$, $F(\eta)\ge F(\mu)+\int g_\mu(x)\cdot(y-x)d\gamma+o\!\left((\int|y-x|^2d\gamma)^{1/2}\right)$ as the coupling action tends to zero, with a remainder uniform over all such couplings. The definition imposes no global displacement-convexity claim.

## Definition

Assume AC and the feature-measure energy hypotheses. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite energy, define $F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u)$ on $\Omega$, and extend this potential by $+\infty$ off $\Omega$. Its constrained subdifferential at $u$ is the local Fréchet subdifferential of $F'(\mu)+\iota_\Omega$ defined in the feature-measure-energy convention. A Wasserstein gradient flow from $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ is a curve $t\mapsto\mu_t$ in $AC^2_{\mathrm{loc}}([0,\infty);(\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d),W_2))$, with $\mu_{t=0}=\mu_0$, for which there is a Borel velocity $v_t(u)$ satisfying the finite-action continuity equation and $v_t(u)$ equals the negative minimum-norm element of $\partial(F'(\mu_t)+\iota_\Omega)(u)$ for $dt\,d\mu_t(u)$-almost every $(t,u)$. This definition does not assert that the energy is displacement convex.

## Statement

Assume AC and the feature-measure energy hypotheses. Fix $r>0$ and a nonempty closed convex constraint $D\subseteq\Omega$. For every continuous moment path $m:[0,T]\to\mathcal H$, the nonautonomous inclusion
$$\dot X(t)\in-\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_D)(X(t))-d\Phi_{X(t)}^*\nabla R(m(t))$$
has a unique forward solution from each $X(0)\in D\cap Q_r$; its characteristic map is jointly continuous in $(t,X(0))$ and locally Lipschitz in the initial point on each $Q_r$. Let $\mu_t$ and $\nu_t$ be two finite-action solutions on $[0,T]$ of the continuity equation with laws concentrated on $D\cap Q_r$ and velocities
$$v_t^\alpha(x)=-\operatorname{argmin}\{|q|:q\in d\Phi_x^*\nabla R(m_{\alpha_t})+\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_D)(x)\},\qquad\alpha\in\{\mu,\nu\},$$
where $m_\alpha=\int\Phi\,d\alpha$. The full shifted minimum selection is Borel; it need not be continuous in position. Each finite-action PDE solution with a continuous prescribed feature moment is the pushforward by its unique characteristic map. For starts in $D\cap Q_r$, these characteristics remain in a larger $Q_R$ uniformly on compact time intervals, and their velocity is the negative full shifted minimum almost everywhere. The same construction applies directly to any continuous forcing $a(t)\in\mathcal H$ in place of $\nabla R(m(t))$. Then for all $t\in[0,T]$,
$$W_2(\mu_t,\nu_t)\le e^{(C_r-\lambda_V)t}W_2(\mu_0,\nu_0),\qquad C_r=L_rA_r^2+N_rB_r.$$
Here $A_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|d\Phi\|$, $B_r=\operatorname{Lip}_{Q_r}(d\Phi)$, $M_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|\partial V\|$ in the bounded-selection convention, and $L_r,N_r$ are respectively a Lipschitz constant and a norm bound for $dR$ on the closed convex hull of $\Phi(Q_r)$. In particular, the localized measure-valued flow is unique for each initial law. The estimate does not assume that $v_t$ is continuous in position.

## Statement references

[[def-wasserstein-gradient-flow-for-feature-energy]]

[[lem-localized-lift-subdifferential]]

[[thm-superposition-for-finite-action-continuity-equations]]

[Chizat and Bach, Proposition 2.5 and Appendix B.2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

[Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré, Theorem 8.3.1](https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~sayan/ambrosio.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the regularity data, and two localized continuity-equation solutions.

[F1] Each finite-action solution has a path law concentrated on absolutely continuous trajectories satisfying its velocity equation almost everywhere. [[thm-superposition-for-finite-action-continuity-equations]]

[F2] The path laws can be disintegrated conditional on their initial points and joined using any coupling of their initial marginals. [[thm-disintegration-of-a-joint-law-on-standard-borel-spaces]] [[def-standard-borel-space]] [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]] [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]] [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]

[F3] The pointwise constrained subdifferential of $V+\iota_D$ is $\lambda_V$-monotone; the smooth feature gradient has the bounds $N_rB_r$ in position and $A_rL_r$ in feature moment. [[def-feature-measure-energy]]

[F4] AC supplies the superposition and disintegration constructions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F5] Closed bounded subsets of Euclidean space are compact. [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]

[F6] A uniformly equicontinuous family of maps from a compact metric space into a proper metric space with pointwise bounded images has a uniformly converging subsequence under AC. [[cor-arzela-ascoli-subsequence-theorem-for-proper-metric-targets]]

[F7] Lipschitz paths are absolutely continuous, have derivatives almost everywhere, and obey the scalar absolutely continuous fundamental theorem of calculus. Apply this coordinatewise for Euclidean paths. [[thm-lipschitz-characterisation-within-absolutely-continuous-functions]] [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]]




**Given:** AC, the data, and two solutions as in the Statement.

## Proof

1.1 Choose an optimal coupling $\gamma_0$ of $\mu_0,\nu_0$. By [F1], take path laws $\Pi_\mu,\Pi_\nu$ for the two solutions. Disintegrate each law conditional on its time-zero position, then combine the two kernels with $\gamma_0$ using [F2]. This gives a joint law of paths $(X,Y)$ with marginals $\Pi_\mu,\Pi_\nu$ and initial pair law $\gamma_0$. Set $D(t)=\mathbb E|X_t-Y_t|^2$. The path equations and the scalar chain rule show $D$ is absolutely continuous and $\displaystyle \frac12D'(t)=\mathbb E\langle X_t-Y_t,v_t^\mu(X_t)-v_t^\nu(Y_t)\rangle$ for almost every $t$. The product is integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz because both path actions and second moments are finite. [F1, F2, F4, construct]

1.2 We construct characteristics for any continuous $a:[0,T]\to\mathcal H$, with $M=\max_t\|a(t)\|$, $g(t,x)=d\Phi_x^*a(t)$, $f=V+\iota_D$ and $\lambda=\lambda_V$. The sets $Q_s$ cover $\Omega$: for $q\in Q_1$ the neighborhood condition puts $x\in\Omega$ in $Q_{1+|x-q|}$, increasing the radius slightly when necessary. Thus every bounded subset of $\Omega$ lies in a $Q_s$. Bounded supporting potential subgradients at $x,y\in Q_s$ give $|V(y)-V(x)|\le(C_1+C_2s)|y-x|+|\lambda||y-x|^2/2$. Subdivide the segment into $n$ equal pieces and let $n\to\infty$ to see that $V$ is $(C_1+C_2s)$-Lipschitz on $Q_s$. Therefore $f$ is proper, lower semicontinuous and $\lambda$-semiconvex, and its subdifferential is nonempty everywhere on $D$. Its supporting inequalities give $\langle\xi-\eta,x-y\rangle\ge\lambda|x-y|^2$. For $1+h\lambda>0$, the function $f(y)+|y-z|^2/(2h)$ is coercive and strongly convex: use a supporting inequality at a fixed point of $D$ for the quadratic lower bound. Finite-dimensional compactness gives its unique minimizer $J_hz$, and testing minimality along segments gives $(z-J_hz)/h\in\partial_\lambda f(J_hz)$. Adding two such inequalities gives $|J_hz-J_hw|\le|z-w|/(1+h\lambda)$. [F3, F4, F5, construct]


2.1 Write each full shifted selection as $d\Phi_x^*\nabla R(m_{\mu_t})+\xi_\mu(x)$ and $d\Phi_y^*\nabla R(m_{\nu_t})+\xi_\nu(y)$, with the two potential sections in $\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_D)$; they need not coincide as functions of position. Adding their supporting inequalities gives $\langle\xi_\mu(x)-\xi_\nu(y),x-y\rangle\ge\lambda_V|x-y|^2$. For the smooth terms, add and subtract $d\Phi_y^*\nabla R(m_{\mu_t})$: their difference has norm at most $N_rB_r|x-y|+A_rL_r|m_{\mu_t}-m_{\nu_t}|$. Along the joint law, $|m_{\mu_t}-m_{\nu_t}|\le A_r\mathbb E|X_t-Y_t|\le A_rD(t)^{1/2}$. Hence [F3] gives $\displaystyle \frac12D'(t)\le(C_r-\lambda_V)D(t).$ Multiplying by $e^{-2(C_r-\lambda_V)t}$ and differentiating proves $D(t)\le e^{2(C_r-\lambda_V)t}D(0)$. The time-$t$ path pair couples $\mu_t,\nu_t$, so $W_2^2(\mu_t,\nu_t)\le D(t)$; taking square roots and using optimality of $\gamma_0$ proves the stated estimate. If the initial laws agree, its right side is zero, proving uniqueness. [F1, F3, step 1.1]

2.2 For $h=T/n$, $h|\lambda|\le1/2$, define $x_0=u\in D\cap Q_r$, $x_k=J_h(x_{k-1}-hg(t_k,x_{k-1}))$, $v_k=(x_k-x_{k-1})/h$, and $\xi_k=-v_k-g(t_k,x_{k-1})\in\partial_\lambda f(x_k)$. Put $S_k=\sum_{j\le k}h|v_j|$. The neighborhood condition gives $x_k\in Q_{r+S_k}$. Compare $\xi_k$ with a supporting potential vector $\eta_{k-1}$ at $x_{k-1}$ of norm at most $C_1+C_2(r+S_{k-1})$. Monotonicity yields $(1+h\lambda)|v_k|^2\le-\langle g(t_k,x_{k-1})+\eta_{k-1},v_k\rangle$, so $|v_k|\le A+BS_{k-1}$, where $A=2(M+1)(C_1+C_2r)$ and $B=2(M+1)C_2$. Hence $S_k\le(1+hB)S_{k-1}+hA$ and $S_k\le S_*=(A/B)(e^{BT}-1)$, with $S_*=AT$ when $B=0$. All iterates and affine interpolants $X_h$ lie in $D\cap Q_R$, where $R=r+S_*+1$, and have speed at most $K=A+BS_*$. For each fixed $u$, their images lie in the compact ball $\overline B(u,KT)$ and they are uniformly Lipschitz. Arzelà–Ascoli gives a subsequence converging uniformly to a $K$-Lipschitz $D\cap Q_R$-valued path $X$. Both constant interpolants converge uniformly to $X$, $V(x_k)$ converges uniformly to $V(X)$ by step 1.2, and $g_h(t)=g(t_k,x_{k-1})$ converges uniformly to $g(t,X(t))$ by continuity of $a$ and the Lipschitz bound on $d\Phi$ on $Q_R$. [F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 Write $x_h^+(t)=x_k$ on $(t_{k-1},t_k]$. The discrete supporting inequality is $\langle X_h',x_h^+-z\rangle+V(x_h^+)+\langle g_h,x_h^+-z\rangle+(\lambda/2)|x_h^+-z|^2\le V(z)$ for every $z\in D$. Replace $x_h^+$ by $X_h$ only in the derivative pairing; its error is at most $K^2h$. Integrating over any $[b,c]\subset[0,T]$ makes that pairing the exact endpoint difference $(|X_h(c)-z|^2-|X_h(b)-z|^2)/2$. All other terms converge uniformly by step 2.2, yielding $(|X(c)-z|^2-|X(b)-z|^2)/2+\int_b^c[V(X)+\langle g(t,X),X-z\rangle+(\lambda/2)|X-z|^2]dt\le(c-b)V(z)$. Choose countably many dense $z\in D$ and differentiate this interval inequality where the scalar absolutely continuous functions and coordinates of $X$ are differentiable. Outside their common null set the inequality says $-X'-g(t,X)\in\partial_\lambda f(X)$, first for these tests and then for every $z\in D$ by continuity of $V$ on bounded sets. This proves the inclusion without any continuity or convergence assertion for the nonsmooth minimum field. [F5, F7, step 1.2, step 2.2]

4.1 Two solutions $X,Y$ to the same forcing have bounded images in a common $Q_s$. Monotonicity gives $(|X-Y|^2/2)'\le(MB_s-\lambda)|X-Y|^2$, so multiplication by the scalar integrating factor proves uniqueness. Therefore all converging Euler subsequences have the same limit and compactness gives uniform convergence of the entire family. For all starts in $D\cap Q_r$, step 2.2 gives the same radius $R$ and time-Lipschitz constant $K$; the same distance estimate gives $|X(t,u)-X(t,w)|\le e^{(MB_R-\lambda)t}|u-w|$. For different forcings $a,b$ and paths in $Q_s$, monotonicity gives $(|X-Y|^2/2)'\le c|X-Y|^2+A_s\|a-b\||X-Y|$, $c=(\max\|a\|)B_s-\lambda$. 4.2 Since $V\circ X$ is Lipschitz, at a time where it and $X$ are differentiable and the inclusion holds, test any $\eta\in\partial_\lambda f(X(t))$ against $X(t+h)$ for both signs of $h$. Division by $h$ and passage to zero give $(V\circ X)'=\langle\eta,X'\rangle$ for every such $\eta$ simultaneously. For $\xi=-X'-g(t,X)$ this gives $\langle\eta-\xi,X'\rangle=0$, so $|g+\eta|^2=|-X'|^2+|\eta-\xi|^2$. Thus $-X'$ is the full shifted minimum. Its Borel measurability for fixed forcing follows directly from $q_\varepsilon(t,x)=(x-J_\varepsilon(x-\varepsilon g(t,x)))/\varepsilon$: these are continuous, and monotonicity gives $(1+\varepsilon\lambda)|q_\varepsilon|^2\le\langle g(t,x)+\eta,q_\varepsilon\rangle$ for every $\eta\in\partial_\lambda f(x)$. Therefore $q_\varepsilon$ is bounded and its prox point tends to $x$. Continuity of $V$ passes the supporting inequalities to every cluster point $q$, placing it in the shifted subdifferential; the displayed inequality becomes its minimum-norm projection inequality. All cluster points equal the unique minimum, so the entire sequence converges. The pointwise limit of the continuous $q_\varepsilon$ is Borel. [F3, F7, step 1.2, step 3.1]

5.1 For any finite-action PDE solution with this velocity and fixed continuous forcing, [F1] represents it by absolutely continuous paths. Their positions lie in closed $D$ at every rational time and hence every time. Each path solves the inclusion, so uniqueness from step 4.1 identifies it with $X(\cdot,u)$, where $u$ is its initial point. Thus $\mu_t=X(t,\cdot)_\#\mu_0$, with the same radius bound from step 2.2 whenever $\mu_0$ is concentrated on $Q_r$. This argument uses neither a backward inverse nor continuity of the minimum field. With $a(t)=\nabla R(m(t))$ it proves the characteristic assertion in the Statement; steps 1.1–2.1 prove the self-consistent law stability assertion. [F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 4.1, step 4.2] ∎

## Statement

**Assume the Axiom of Choice.** Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space, let $Y$ be a proper metric space, and let $(f_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be an equicontinuous sequence in $C(X,Y)$. If $\{f_k(x):k\in\mathbb N\}$ is bounded for every $x\in X$, then some subsequence converges uniformly to a member of $C(X,Y)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Choice, a nonempty compact metric space $X$, a proper metric space $Y$, and a pointwise bounded equicontinuous sequence $(f_k)$.

[L1] Equicontinuity and compact coordinate closures make the uniform closure compact ([[cor-ascoli-arzela-for-compact-metric-domains]]).

[L2] Under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, every compact metric space is sequentially compact ([[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For each $x\in X$, the coordinate set $\{f_k(x):k\in\mathbb N\}$ is bounded. Its closure is closed and remains bounded, and therefore is compact by properness. [given]

2.1 By equicontinuity, step 1.1, and [L1], the uniform closure $H$ of $\{f_k:k\in\mathbb N\}$ is compact. [L1, step 1.1]

3.1 Choice implies the two weaker choice principles in [L2], so the compact metric space $H$ is sequentially compact. Hence $(f_k)$ has a subsequence converging in the uniform metric to some $f\in H\subseteq C(X,Y)$. [L2, step 2.1, choose]

4.1 Convergence in the uniform metric is uniform convergence, which gives the claimed subsequence and continuous limit. [step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(\mu_t,v_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $\mathbb R^d$, and fix $\nu\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$. For almost every $t\in(0,T)$, the scalar map $t\mapsto\frac12W_2^2(\mu_t,\nu)$ is differentiable and, for every optimal coupling $\gamma_t$ of $\mu_t$ and $\nu$,
$$\frac d{dt}\frac12W_2^2(\mu_t,\nu)\le\int_{\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d}(x-y)\cdot v_t(x)\,d\gamma_t(x,y).$$

## Statement references

[[def-wasserstein-two-space-and-couplings]]

[[thm-superposition-for-finite-action-continuity-equations]]

[[prop-existence-and-lower-semicontinuity-of-optimal-couplings]]

[Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré, Theorem 8.4.7](https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~sayan/ambrosio.pdf)

[Chizat and Bach, Appendix B.2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a finite-action continuity-equation solution, and $\nu\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$.

[F1] A finite-action continuity-equation solution has a path law on absolutely continuous curves whose time marginals are $\mu_t$ and whose path derivative is $v_t$ almost everywhere. [[thm-superposition-for-finite-action-continuity-equations]]

[F2] Optimal couplings exist for probability measures in $\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$. [[prop-existence-and-lower-semicontinuity-of-optimal-couplings]]

[F3] Standard Borel disintegration constructs a joint law of a path and a fixed endpoint from a coupling of their time-$t$ marginals. [[thm-disintegration-of-a-joint-law-on-standard-borel-spaces]] [[def-standard-borel-space]] [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]

[F4] A finite-action path law induces a continuous Hilbert-valued time curve with square-integrable derivative; its derivative is recovered almost everywhere by the path-energy characterization. [[lem-hilbert-valued-path-energy-characterization]]

[F5] The path-space $L^2$ is separable because the path space is Polish and its Borel sigma-algebra has a countable generator whose finite-measure sets are approximable by a countable algebra; simple functions are dense. [[lem-countable-generators-yield-countable-set-algebras]] [[lem-finite-measure-sets-are-approximable-by-a-countable-generating-algebra]] [[thm-simple-functions-with-finite-measure-support-are-dense-in-l-p-for-finite-p]]

[F6] AC supplies the optimal-plan, superposition and disintegration selections. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof


**Given:** AC, $T$, $(\mu_t,v_t)$, and $\nu$.

1.1 By [F1] and the AC construction [F6], choose a probability $\Pi$ on $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ with time marginals $\mu_t$ and path derivative $\dot\gamma(t)=v_t(\gamma(t))$ almost everywhere. Its expected action is finite. For $s<t$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|Z_t-Z_s\|_{L^2(\Pi)}^2\le(t-s)\int\!\int_s^t|\dot\gamma(q)|^2dq\,d\Pi$, so $Z_t(\gamma)=\gamma(t)$ is a continuous path in $H=L^2(\Pi;\mathbb R^d)$. For each partition $P=(t_i)$, the same estimate and summation give $\displaystyle \sum_i\frac{\|e_{t_{i+1}}-e_{t_i}\|_{L^2(\Pi)}^2}{t_{i+1}-t_i}\le\int\!\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)|^2dt\,d\Pi(\gamma)<\infty.$ The path space is Polish, so [F5] makes $H=L^2(\Pi;\mathbb R^d)$ separable. The pathwise fundamental theorem and Fubini show $Z_t=Z_0+\int_0^t(\gamma\mapsto v_q(\gamma(q)))dq$ in $H$; this Bochner integral exists by the finite action. Apply [F4] to the continuous Hilbert-valued path $Z_t$: its norm derivative is the displayed Bochner integrand almost everywhere, so $\dot Z_t(\gamma)=v_t(\gamma(t))$ in $L^2(\Pi)$ almost everywhere. [F1, F4, F5, construct]

2.1 The coupling $(Z_s,Z_t)_\#\Pi$ gives $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)\le\|Z_s-Z_t\|_H\le\int_s^t\|\dot Z_q\|_H dq$. Hence $t\mapsto W_2(\mu_t,\nu)$ is absolutely continuous; it is bounded on $[0,T]$, so its square is also absolutely continuous and differentiable almost everywhere. Choose a time where this scalar derivative and $Z_t$'s Hilbert derivative exist and the identities in step 1.1 hold. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 For any optimal coupling $\gamma_t$ supplied by [F2], disintegrate $\Pi$ conditionally on $Z_t=x$ using [F3] and combine that kernel with $\gamma_t(dx,dy)$. The resulting joint law of $(\gamma,y)$ has path marginal $\Pi$, endpoint marginal $\nu$, and $(Z_t,y)$ marginal $\gamma_t$. Thus $(Z_{t+h},y)$ is a coupling of $\mu_{t+h},\nu$, so optimality of $\gamma_t$ gives $\displaystyle \frac12W_2^2(\mu_{t+h},\nu)-\frac12W_2^2(\mu_t,\nu)\le\frac12\mathbb E\bigl[|Z_{t+h}-y|^2-|Z_t-y|^2\bigr].$ Divide by $h>0$ and let $h\downarrow0$. Differentiability of $Z$ in $L^2$ gives $\|Z_{t+h}-Z_t\|_H=O(h)$, so the quadratic increment term divided by $h$ tends to zero; Cauchy–Schwarz passes the linear term to $\mathbb E\langle Z_t-y,\dot Z_t\rangle$, which equals $\int(x-y)\cdot v_t(x)d\gamma_t$ by the marginals and derivative identity. The left side converges to the derivative at $t$. The construction works for every optimal $\gamma_t$, proving the inequality. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and the feature-measure energy hypotheses. Fix $r>0$ and $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ concentrated on $Q_r$. Define $g_\mu(u)=S(\nabla R(\int\Phi\,d\mu),u)$, the minimum-norm element of $d\Phi_u^*\nabla R(\int\Phi\,d\mu)+\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_{Q_r})(u)$. For every $\eta\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ concentrated on $Q_r$ and every coupling $\gamma$ of $\mu$ and $\eta$,
$$F(\eta)\ge F(\mu)+\int g_\mu(x)\cdot(y-x)d\gamma(x,y)+\frac{\lambda_V-C_r}{2}\int|y-x|^2d\gamma(x,y),\qquad C_r=L_rA_r^2+N_rB_r.$$
In particular, $g_\mu$ is a strong Wasserstein subgradient of the localized functional $F_r$, defined as $F$ on laws concentrated on $Q_r$ and $+\infty$ otherwise, in the all-coupling sense, with zero remainder after the stated quadratic term. Here $A_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|d\Phi\|$, $B_r=\operatorname{Lip}_{Q_r}(d\Phi)$, and $L_r,N_r$ are respectively a Lipschitz constant and norm bound for $dR$ on the closed convex hull of $\Phi(Q_r)$; put $\lambda_r=\lambda_V-C_r$. It is the unique minimum-norm vector field among all all-coupling strong subgradients in $L^2(\mu;\mathbb R^d)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $r$, $\mu,\eta$, and a coupling $\gamma$ as in the Statement.

[F1] The localized lifted energy has semiconvexity coefficient $\lambda_V-C_r$. [[lem-lifted-energy-lipschitz-gradient]]

[F2] The localized lifted subdifferential equals the smooth feature gradient plus the pointwise constrained potential subdifferential, and its minimum section is measurable. [[lem-localized-lift-subdifferential]]

[F3] The first marginal of a coupling is $\mu$ and the second is $\eta$. [[def-wasserstein-two-space-and-couplings]]

[F4] AC supplies the minimum section and Bochner integrability used to identify the lifted inner product with the coupling integral. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]] [[thm-bochner-dominated-convergence]]

## Proof


**Given:** AC and the data above.

1.1 On $(\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d,\gamma)$, set $X(x,y)=x$ and $Y(x,y)=y$. This is a Euclidean Borel probability label space of dimension $2d$, with output dimension $d$; the arbitrary-label lift and subdifferential formula therefore apply. These are admissible lifts because both marginals are concentrated on $Q_r$. Their laws are $\mu$ and $\eta$ by [F3], so their lifted energies are $F(\mu)$ and $F(\eta)$. The pointwise minimum section and smooth gradient in [F2] give the lifted subgradient $s(x,y)=g_\mu(x)\in L^2(\gamma;\mathbb R^d)$. [F2, F3, F4, construct]

2.1 Apply the semiconvex subgradient inequality [F1] to the two lifts. The Hilbert inner product is $\int g_\mu(x)\cdot(y-x)d\gamma$ and the squared displacement norm is $\int|y-x|^2d\gamma$. Substitution gives exactly the asserted inequality for this coupling. Since $\gamma$ was arbitrary, it holds for every coupling and proves the strong-subgradient claim. [F1, step 1.1]

3.1 Conversely let $h\in L^2(\mu)$ satisfy the all-coupling strong-subgradient inequality. Lift on $(\mathbb R^d,\mu)$ with $X(x)=x$, and take the coupling $(X,(1-t)X+tY)_\#\mu$ for any admissible $Y$. Its displacement norm is $t\|Y-X\|_2$. Dividing the strong inequality by $t$ gives the lower bound $\langle h,Y-X\rangle$ for the directional derivative of $E_r$ at $X$ in direction $Y-X$. Semiconvexity of $E_r$ implies its secant slope is at least that directional derivative plus $\lambda_r\|Y-X\|_2^2/2$; consequently $h\in\partial_{\lambda_r}E_r(X)$. The pointwise formula [F2] gives $h(x)\in d\Phi_x^*\nabla R(m_\mu)+\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_{Q_r})(x)$ almost everywhere. The full shifted minimum has norm no larger pointwise, so $\|g_\mu\|_2\le\|h\|_2$. Equality forces equality pointwise by strict convexity and the projection inequality. This proves the claimed minimality and uniqueness. [F1, F2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $f_n:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable,
suppose $f_n(\omega)\to f(\omega)$ in norm for almost every $\omega$, and let
$g$ be a nonnegative integrable scalar function with
$\|f_n(\omega)\|\leq g(\omega)$ almost everywhere for every $n$. Then $f$ and
all $f_n$ are Bochner integrable,

$$\int\|f_n-f\|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$

and $\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu$ in norm.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] Countable Choice selects one member from every countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[L1] Finite norm integral characterizes Bochner integrability for a strongly measurable function ([[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]).

[L2] Strong measurability is a.e. pointwise norm approximation by finite-valued measurable simple functions ([[def-strongly-measurable-banach-valued-function]]).

[L3] Pointwise scalar limits and countable suprema preserve measurability ([[thm-sequential-suprema-infima-limsup-liminf-and-pointwise-limits-are-measurable]]).

[L4] Scalar dominated convergence yields $L^1$ convergence ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[L5] A Bochner integral is bounded in norm by the integral of the pointwise norm ([[lem-bochner-integral-norm-inequality]]).

[L6] Simple Banach-valued integrals are linear ([[lem-banach-valued-simple-integral-is-well-defined]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The sequence, limit, domination, and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ in the Statement.

1.1 Select simultaneous strong-measurability witnesses. [given, A1, L2, choose] Use [A1] exactly once to choose, for every $n$, a simple approximation sequence witnessing the strong measurability in [L2]. Unite their exceptional null sets with those from convergence and domination; countable additivity makes the union null. Modify all functions and approximants to be zero there. We now have pointwise convergence everywhere and a doubly indexed family of simple approximants. [given, A1, L2, choose]

2.1 Obtain a common countable range and measurable distances. [L3, step 1.1] Let $D$ be $\{0\}$ together with all values of all selected simple approximants. It is countable. For each $n$, the range of $f_n$ lies in $\overline D$, hence the pointwise limit $f$ also takes values in $\overline D$. For $y\in D$, the functions $\|f_n-y\|$ are measurable by applying [L3] to the simple approximants, and $\|f-y\|$ is measurable by applying [L3] once more to $f_n\to f$. [L3, step 1.1]

3.1 Build finite-valued approximants to the limit. [L2, step 2.1, construct] Enumerate $D$ with repetitions as $(y_j)$. For each $m$, assign $s_m(\omega)$ to be the least-indexed nearest point to $f(\omega)$ among $y_1,\ldots,y_m$. The finitely many tie-broken Voronoi cells are measurable by step 2.1, so $s_m$ is simple; density gives $s_m(\omega)\to f(\omega)$. Thus $f$ is strongly measurable. [L2, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Apply the scalar dominated-convergence theorem. [L1, L4, step 3.1] Passing to the pointwise limit in $\|f_n\|\leq g$ gives $\|f\|\leq g$. By [L1], $f$ and every $f_n$ are Bochner integrable. Moreover $\|f_n-f\|\leq2g$, so [L4] gives $\int\|f_n-f\|\to0$. [L1, L4, step 3.1]

5.1 Pass from $L^1$ convergence to integral convergence. [L1, L5, L6, step 4.1] Combining simple approximations to $f_n$ and $f$, [L6] and approximation independence from [L1] show that $\int(f_n-f)=\int f_n-\int f$. Apply [L5]: $\|\int f_n-\int f\|\leq\int\|f_n-f\|\to0$ by step 4.1. If the measure space is empty or $g=0$ a.e., every integral is zero; no separate endpoint convention is needed. [L1, L5, L6, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and the feature-measure energy hypotheses. Let $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ have finite energy and be concentrated on $Q_r$, and let $X:[0,\infty)\to K=L^2(\mu_0;\mathbb R^d)$ be the Hilbert gradient flow of the localized lift $E_r$ from $X(0,s)=s$. Define $\mu_t=(X(t,\cdot))_\#\mu_0$, $m_t=\int\Phi(X(t,s))d\mu_0(s)$, and
$$v_t(u)=-S(\nabla R(m_t),u),$$
where $S(a,u)$ is the minimum-norm element of the full shifted set $d\Phi_u^*a+\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_{Q_r})(u)$. Then $v$ is Borel, $\int_0^T\int|v_t|^2d\mu_tdt<\infty$ for each $T<\infty$, and $\partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\cdot(v_t\mu_t)=0$ in distributions on $(0,T)\times\mathbb R^d$. The curve $\mu_t$ is in $AC^2([0,T];\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d),W_2)$, and $v$ is the minimum-action velocity, satisfying $\int_0^T\int|v_t|^2d\mu_tdt=\int_0^T|\dot\mu_t|_{W_2}^2dt$.

## Statement references

[[def-localized-hilbert-lift]]

[[thm-semiconvex-hilbert-gradient-flow]]

[[lem-localized-lift-subdifferential]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the localized lift, the initial law, and its Hilbert gradient flow.

[F1] The Hilbert flow is locally absolutely continuous, has a Bochner derivative, and its derivative is the negative Hilbert subgradient almost everywhere. [[thm-semiconvex-hilbert-gradient-flow]]

[F2] The Hilbert subdifferential is the smooth feature gradient plus the measurable pointwise constrained potential subgradient. [[lem-localized-lift-subdifferential]]

[F3] Bochner paths have strongly measurable representatives and their integrals commute with bounded linear functionals. [[lem-hilbert-valued-path-energy-characterization]] [[thm-bounded-linear-maps-commute-with-bochner-integration]]

[F4] A curve satisfying the finite-action continuity equation is $W_2$-absolutely continuous with squared metric speed bounded by its action. [[thm-continuity-equation-implies-ac2]]

[F5] AC is the inherited axiom in the flow and transport suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F6] An AC² Wasserstein curve has a minimum-action field in the spatial gradient closure, and every difference of two admissible fields annihilates those gradients. [[thm-ac2-curve-admits-minimal-velocity]]

[F7] Scalar domination passes limits through finite-measure integrals. [[thm-dominated-convergence]]




**Given:** AC and the data above.

## Proof

1.1 Since $m_t$ is the image of $X_t$ under Bochner integration, [F3] and the Lipschitz bound on $\Phi$ show $t\mapsto m_t$ is continuous. The full shifted selection $S(a,u)$ is jointly Borel by [F2], and $a(t)=\nabla R(m_t)$ is continuous, so $v$ is Borel. By [F1] and [F2], a representative of the Hilbert derivative satisfies $\dot X(t,s)=v_t(X(t,s))$ for almost every $(t,s)$. Its squared integral is $\int_0^T\int|v_t(u)|^2d\mu_t(u)dt=\int_0^T\|\dot X(t)\|_K^2dt<\infty$. [F1, F2, F3, F5]

2.1 For $\varphi\in C_c^\infty((0,T)\times\mathbb R^d)$, the scalar chain rule along the almost-everywhere absolutely continuous label paths gives $\displaystyle \frac d{dt}\varphi(t,X(t,s))=\partial_t\varphi(t,X(t,s))+\nabla_x\varphi(t,X(t,s))\cdot v_t(X(t,s))$ for almost every $(t,s)$. The right side is integrable: the test derivatives are bounded, $\mu_t$ is a probability, and [F1] gives finite $L^1$ velocity action on $[0,T]$. Integrating in $s$ and $t$, Fubini and the vanishing of $\varphi$ near $t=0,T$ give the weak continuity-equation identity for $\mu_t$. [F1, step 1.1]

2.2 The coupling $(X(s),X(t))_\#\mu_0$ gives $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)^2\le\|X(s)-X(t)\|_K^2$. Cauchy–Schwarz in time and [F1] imply $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)\le\int_s^t\|\dot X(q)\|_K\,dq$ for $s<t$. Thus $\mu\in AC^2$ on $[0,T]$. Alternatively [F4] applies to the continuity equation and the action bound from step 1.1. [F1, F4, step 1.1]


2.3 Fix a time $t$ and put $f_t(u)=\langle\nabla R(m_t),\Phi(u)\rangle+V(u)+\iota_{Q_r}(u)$. On $Q_r$ this function is bounded, lower semicontinuous and semiconvex, with a nonempty subdifferential and minimum section $g_t=-v_t$ bounded uniformly on compact time intervals by [F2]. For small $\varepsilon>0$ let $J_\varepsilon x$ minimize $f_t(y)+|x-y|^2/(2\varepsilon)$ and let $f_{t,\varepsilon}$ be the minimum value. The resolvent proof in [F2] gives $J_\varepsilon$ Lipschitz. Comparing the envelope at $x+h$ using $J_\varepsilon x$, and at $x$ using $J_\varepsilon(x+h)$, bounds the difference from $\langle(x-J_\varepsilon x)/\varepsilon,h\rangle$ by $O(|h|^2)$ locally. Thus $f_{t,\varepsilon}$ is $C^1$ and its gradient is $(x-J_\varepsilon x)/\varepsilon$. The monotonicity estimate from [F2] gives $|\nabla f_{t,\varepsilon}(x)|\le |g_t(x)|/(1+\varepsilon\alpha_t)$ on $Q_r$, with $\alpha_t$ a semiconvexity coefficient; the same proof gives pointwise convergence to $g_t(x)$. Dominated convergence yields convergence in $L^2(\mu_t)$. Each gradient belongs to the closure of gradients of compactly supported smooth functions: multiply the $C^1$ envelope by smooth cutoffs equal to one on $B_N$, with derivative $O(1/N)$, and then mollify. On $Q_r$ the envelope stays between the fixed lower bound and upper bound of $f_t$, so the cutoff derivative term tends to zero in $L^2(\mu_t)$; the other tail tends to zero by the bound just proved. Mollification converges uniformly in $C^1$ on each compact set. Therefore $g_t$ belongs to the spatial gradient closure in $L^2(\mu_t)$. [F2, F7, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Let $w$ be the minimum-action field for $\mu$ supplied by the AC² minimal-velocity theorem. Subtracting its continuity equation from that of $v$ and using time tensor tests shows $\int(v_t-w_t)\cdot\nabla\psi\,d\mu_t=0$ for almost every $t$, simultaneously for a countable set of compactly supported smooth $\psi$ dense in $C^1$ on each compact ball. Such a set is obtained by rational polynomial approximations and fixed smooth cutoffs; extend the equality to every compactly supported smooth test by uniform gradient approximation. By step 2.3, $v_t$ belongs to their $L^2(\mu_t)$ gradient closure. Hence $\langle v_t-w_t,v_t\rangle=0$. The minimal-velocity theorem also gives $w_t$ in this closure and $v_t-w_t$ orthogonal to it (equivalently its Pythagorean identity), so $\|v_t-w_t\|_2^2=0$. This is the required tangent-gradient orthogonality, including the constraint: for any absolutely continuous label path in $Q_r$, at any two-sided differentiability time and every $n\in N_{Q_r}(X_t)$, the inequalities $n\cdot(X_{t+h}-X_t)\le0$ for both signs of $h$ give $n\cdot\dot X_t=0$. Thus normal-cone terms contribute no velocity pairing; the constrained minimum cannot be replaced by an unconstrained selection. We have $v=w$ almost everywhere, so its squared action equals $\int_0^T|\dot\mu_t|_{W_2}^2dt$, as asserted. [F1, F2, F4, F6, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3] ∎

There is a unique curve $\mu:[0,\infty)\to\mathcal P_2(Q_r)$ in $AC^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ that starts at $\mu_0$, solves the continuity equation with velocity equal almost everywhere to the negative minimum-norm element of $\partial(F'(\mu_t)+\iota_{Q_r})$, and satisfies

$$\frac12\frac d{dt}W_2^2(\mu_t,\eta)+\frac{\lambda_r}{2}W_2^2(\mu_t,\eta)\le F(\eta)-F(\mu_t)$$
for each fixed $\eta\in\mathcal P_2(Q_r)$ and almost every $t>0$ (with the exceptional null set allowed to depend on $\eta$). Any two such localized flows obey $W_2(\mu_t,\nu_t)\le e^{-\lambda_r t}W_2(\mu_0,\nu_0)$.

**Given:** AC, $r$, $\mu_0$, and the model regularity hypotheses.

[F1] The localized lift is a proper lower-bounded semiconvex energy on a separable Hilbert space; its gradient flow exists uniquely for all time and satisfies the Hilbert energy identity. [[thm-semiconvex-hilbert-gradient-flow]] [[lem-lifted-energy-lipschitz-gradient]]

[F2] The Hilbert flow pushes forward to a finite-action continuity-equation solution and an $AC^2$ Wasserstein curve with the displayed minimum pointwise velocity. [[lem-localized-lift-generates-continuity-equation]]

[F3] The model energy has the all-coupling strong subgradient inequality with coefficient $\lambda_r$. [[lem-feature-energy-strong-wasserstein-subgradient]]

[F4] Along a finite-action continuity equation, squared distance to a fixed measure has derivative bounded above by the velocity-pairing with any optimal coupling. [[lem-w2-distance-derivative-under-a-continuity-equation]]

[F5] Any two localized continuity-equation solutions with these velocities satisfy the stated W2 stability estimate. [[lem-characteristics-unique-and-stable]]

[F6] AC is the inherited axiom in [F1]–[F5]. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

**Given:** AC, $r$, $\mu_0$ and the hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Form the label Hilbert space $K=L^2(\mu_0;\mathbb R^d)$ and the initial vector $X_0(s)=s$. This Euclidean Borel label space is countably generated, so its $d$-vector $L^2$ space is separable under the generalized label-space interface. It has finite $E_r$ because $F(\mu_0)<\infty$. [F1] yields the unique Hilbert gradient flow $X_t$ for all $t\ge0$. Define $\mu_t=(X_t)_\#\mu_0$. 2.1 The Hilbert energy identity in [F1] is $E_r(X_t)-E_r(X_s)=-\int_s^t\|\dot X_q\|_K^2dq$. By [F2], $\dot X_q(s)=v_q(X_q(s))$ almost everywhere and $E_r(X_q)=F(\mu_q)$. 2.2 Fix $\eta\in\mathcal P_2(Q_r)$ and a time where [F4] applies. Choose an optimal coupling $\gamma_t$ of $\mu_t,\eta$. The derivative estimate [F4] gives $\displaystyle \frac12\frac d{dt}W_2^2(\mu_t,\eta)\le\int(x-y)\cdot v_t(x)d\gamma_t=-\int g_{\mu_t}(x)\cdot(x-y)d\gamma_t.$ By [F3], $F(\eta)\ge F(\mu_t)+\int g_{\mu_t}(x)\cdot(y-x)d\gamma_t+\frac{\lambda_r}{2}W_2^2(\mu_t,\eta)$. 3.1 If $\mu$ and $\nu$ are two such solutions, [F5] gives their stability estimate; equal initial data imply $W_2(\mu_t,\nu_t)=0$ for every $t$, hence equality of the measures and uniqueness. The construction in step 1.1 proves existence. [F5, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and the feature-measure energy hypotheses. Let $r_0>0$ and let $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ have finite energy and be concentrated on $Q_{r_0}$. Set $M_0=\sup\{\|\nabla R(z)\|:R(z)\le F(\mu_0)\}$, $a=(1+M_0)C_1$, and $b=(1+M_0)C_2$. For $T<\infty$, define
$$r(T)=\begin{cases}(r_0+aT),&b=0,\\(r_0+a/b)e^{bT}-a/b,&b>0.\end{cases}$$
For every $R>r(T)$, the localized flow with indicator $\iota_{Q_R}$ remains in $Q_{r(T)}$ for $0\le t\le T$ and therefore solves the continuity equation with the constraint $\Omega$ alone on this interval. Localized flows with different cutoffs larger than $r(T)$ agree on $[0,T]$. In particular no trajectory starting in $Q_{r_0}$ can escape every cutoff in finite time.

## Statement references

[[def-feature-measure-energy]]

[[thm-localized-wasserstein-flow]]

[[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[Chizat and Bach, Proposition 2.5 and Appendix B.2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

[Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré, Chapter 4](https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~sayan/ambrosio.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the model assumptions, initial law and cutoff family.

[F1] Along a localized flow the energy decreases, and $R(m_{\mu_t})\le F(\mu_0)$ because $V\ge0$. [[thm-localized-wasserstein-flow]] [[def-feature-measure-energy]]

[F2] The constrained minimum-norm field is no larger than the admissible field obtained by adding zero from the cutoff normal cone; on $Q_s$ its norm is at most $(1+M_0)(C_1+C_2s)$. [[def-feature-measure-energy]] [[thm-localized-wasserstein-flow]]

[F3] If a point of $\Omega$ is within distance $s$ of $Q_r$, then it lies in $Q_{r+s}$. [[def-feature-measure-energy]]

[F4] AC supplies the locally absolutely continuous label paths representing the localized flow. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[thm-localized-wasserstein-flow]]

[F5] Solutions using the same $\Omega$-constrained velocity are unique by their W2 stability estimate. [[lem-characteristics-unique-and-stable]]

## Proof


**Given:** AC, $T$, and $\mu_0$ as in the Statement.

1.1 By [F1], $m_{\mu_t}$ stays in the $R$-sublevel set used to define $M_0$. The unconstrained part of the negative velocity has norm at most $M_0(C_1+C_2R)+(C_1+C_2R)=(a+bR)$. Since $0$ belongs to the normal cone of $Q_R$ at each point of $Q_R$, adding the cutoff constraint and taking the minimum norm cannot increase this bound by [F2]. Thus every localized label path has speed at most $a+bR$ before leaving $Q_R$. [F1, F2, F4]

2.1 Fix $R>r(T)$ and a label path starting at $u_0\in Q_{r_0}$. Let $s_R(t)=\int_0^t|\dot X_q|dq$. By [F3], its displacement from $u_0$ gives $\operatorname{dist}(X_t,Q_{r_0})\le s_R(t)$ and hence $X_t\in Q_{r_0+s_R(t)}$. At almost every time apply [F2] at its current radius (the bounded potential supporting vector at the current point remains admissible after restriction to $Q_R$), obtaining $s_R'(t)\le a+b(r_0+s_R(t))$ almost everywhere. If $b>0$, multiply by $e^{-bt}$ and integrate to get $r_0+s_R(t)\le(r_0+a/b)e^{bt}-a/b$; if $b=0$, integration gives $r_0+s_R(t)\le r_0+at$. Thus $r_0+s_R(t)\le r(t)$. This estimate holds for the entire localized path; in particular $r(T)<R$ places it in the relative $\Omega$-interior of $Q_R$ on this interval. The bound holds for almost every label, so the measure flow stays in $Q_{r(T)}$. [F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 For $x\in Q_{r(T)}$, the relative-neighborhood condition places an $\Omega$-neighborhood of $x$ inside $Q_R$ because $R>r(T)$. Thus the cutoff and $\Omega$ constraints have the same local normal cone along these paths, so each localized flow solves the equation with the common $\Omega$-constrained field. If two cutoffs exceed $r(T)$, [F5] gives equality for the common initial law. Taking $T$ arbitrary and increasing the cutoff constructs a compatible global flow, so finite-time escape from all cutoffs is impossible. [F3, F5, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and the full feature-measure energy hypotheses. Let $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ have finite energy and be concentrated on $Q_{r_0}$. There is a unique global curve $\mu:[0,\infty)\to\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ in $AC^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with $\mu_{t=0}=\mu_0$ that solves the continuity equation with the negative minimum-norm subgradient velocity of the extended potential $F'(\mu_t)+\iota_\Omega$. For every finite $T$, the curve is concentrated on some $Q_{r(T)}$ and satisfies
$$F(\mu_t)-F(\mu_s)=-\int_s^t\int|v_q(u)|^2d\mu_q(u)dq\qquad(0\le s\le t\le T).$$
For any $\mu_0,\nu_0$ concentrated on the same $Q_{r_0}$, their flows obey $\sup_{0\le t\le T}W_2(\mu_t,\nu_t)\le e^{K_TT}W_2(\mu_0,\nu_0)$ for a finite constant $K_T$ depending only on $T$, $r_0$, and a common upper bound for the initial energies. Consequently, W2-convergent initial laws in a common $Q_{r_0}$ have flows converging uniformly in W2 on every compact time interval.

## Statement references

[[def-feature-measure-energy]]

[[def-wasserstein-gradient-flow-for-feature-energy]]

[[lem-feature-flow-escape-bound]]

[[thm-localized-wasserstein-flow]]

[Chizat and Bach, Proposition 2.5 and Theorem 2.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

[Ambrosio, Gigli, and Giuseppe Savaré, Chapter 11](https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~sayan/ambrosio.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the model hypotheses, $\mu_0,\nu_0$, and a finite time horizon $T$.

[F1] Every localized flow exists uniquely, satisfies the continuity equation and energy identity, and has the localized stability estimate. [[thm-localized-wasserstein-flow]]

[F2] A finite-time radius can be chosen uniformly for initial laws in a fixed $Q_{r_0}$ with uniformly bounded initial energy; the cutoff equation agrees with the equation constrained only by $\Omega$. [[lem-feature-flow-escape-bound]]

[F3] AC supplies the local flows and their compatible path representatives. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F4] Continuous prescribed forcing has unique global constrained characteristics, uniform cutoff bounds for starts in a common $Q_r$, and finite-action PDE solutions are their pushforwards; the self-consistent localized laws obey W2 uniqueness. [[lem-characteristics-unique-and-stable]]

## Proof


**Given:** AC, $T$, and initial laws as in the Statement.

1.1 Let $E_*\ge\max(F(\mu_0),F(\nu_0))$ be a common energy bound. The escape estimate [F2] supplies a radius $R_T$ that works for both localized flows throughout $[0,T]$. By [F1], each localized flow exists on that interval and remains in a smaller $Q_{r(T)}\subset Q_{R_T}$, so the added cutoff normal cone is inactive and each curve solves the equation constrained by $\Omega$. If $S>T$, the curves constructed with a larger radius agree on $[0,T]$ by localized uniqueness [F1]; hence the finite-horizon curves patch to a well-defined global curve. [F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 The energy identity on $[0,T]$ is inherited from [F1]. Applying the localized stability estimate on the common radius $R_T$ gives $W_2(\mu_t,\nu_t)\le e^{K_Tt}W_2(\mu_0,\nu_0)$ for $0\le t\le T$; taking the supremum gives the displayed bound. Its right side tends to zero when the initial W2 distance does, proving compact-time uniform convergence. Since $T$ was arbitrary, existence, uniqueness, energy dissipation, and stability hold globally in time. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 We check uniqueness against every curve in the stated definition, without presuming its energy decreases or its support stays in a cutoff. Choose $q\in Q_1$. The neighborhood premise and derivative growth give $\|d\Phi_x\|\le C(1+|x|)$ on $\Omega$, after increasing $C$ to absorb $q$. Segment integration yields $\|\Phi(x)-\Phi(y)\|\le C(1+|x|+|y|)|x-y|$. Consequently every $\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ law has a Bochner feature moment, and coupling Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|m_\alpha-m_\beta\|\le C(1+(\int|x|^2d\alpha)^{1/2}+(\int|y|^2d\beta)^{1/2})W_2(\alpha,\beta)$. The same growth argument for bounded potential supporting vectors shows $V$ has at most quadratic growth. For a competing $AC^2$ solution, second moments are uniformly bounded on $[0,T]$ by the triangle inequality with $\delta_q$, so its moment and forcing $\nabla R(m_t)$ are continuous. The global fixed-forcing construction and superposition representation in [F4] therefore apply with $D=\Omega$. Starting in $Q_{r_0}$, this competitor is concentrated throughout $[0,T]$ on a single $Q_S$, using the uniform radius estimate of [F4] for its bounded forcing. Increase $S$ slightly so the added cutoff constraint is locally inactive relative to $\Omega$. Both the competitor and the constructed flow then solve the same localized model equation on a common larger cutoff, so the law uniqueness estimate in [F4] makes them equal. No energy bound on a previously unconfined competitor was assumed. This completes global uniqueness in the full stated class. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and the full feature-measure energy hypotheses. Let $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ be concentrated on a common $Q_{r_0}$, and let $\mu_{m,0}=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m\delta_{x_i^{(m)}(0)}$ be empirical laws with every particle in $Q_{r_0}$ and $W_2(\mu_{m,0},\mu_0)\to0$. Define $F_m(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=F(m^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i})$. Here $\partial F_m(x)$ is the Euclidean Fréchet subdifferential: $p\in\partial F_m(x)$ when $F_m(y)\ge F_m(x)+p\cdot(y-x)+o(\|y-x\|)$ as $y\to x$ in $\Omega^m$, with the remainder divided by $\|y-x\|$ tending to zero. A classical particle subgradient flow is a locally absolutely continuous vector $x^{(m)}(t)\in\Omega^m$ satisfying $\dot x^{(m)}(t)\in-m\partial F_m(x^{(m)}(t))$ almost everywhere, under the inner product $m^{-1}\sum_i x_i\cdot y_i$. Let $x_i^{(m)}(t)$ be such flows and put $\mu_{m,t}=m^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i^{(m)}(t)}$. If $\mu_t$ is the unique global measure-valued flow from $\mu_0$, then for every $T<\infty$ there is a finite constant $K_T$ independent of $m$ such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}W_2(\mu_{m,t},\mu_t)\le e^{K_TT}W_2(\mu_{m,0},\mu_0)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is a deterministic continuity estimate in the initial W2 error; it asserts no statistical rate for random initial particles and no conclusion for stochastic gradient descent.

[[thm-global-wasserstein-flow-existence-uniqueness-and-stability]]

[[thm-localized-wasserstein-flow]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $\mu_0$, the empirical initial laws, and their particle flows.

[F1] On an atomic probability label space with mass $1/m$ per label, the Hilbert inner product is $m^{-1}\sum_i x_i\cdot y_i$ and the lifted energy is exactly $F_m$. [[def-localized-hilbert-lift]] [[def-feature-measure-energy]] [[lem-label-l2-space-is-separable-hilbert]]

[F2] The localized flow equation on this atomic label space is the particle subgradient equation with the stated normalization. [[thm-localized-wasserstein-flow]]

[F3] W2-convergent initial laws in the common $Q_{r_0}$ have convergent initial energies: the bounded gradients make $\Phi,V$ Lipschitz on $Q_{r_0}$, coupling Cauchy–Schwarz gives convergence of their integrals, and continuity of $R$ gives convergence of $F$. Their initial energies are thus uniformly bounded, so the escape lemma supplies one cutoff radius for both flows on $[0,T]$. [[def-feature-measure-energy]] [[lem-feature-flow-escape-bound]]

[F4] Localized flows with the same model velocity satisfy the stability estimate $W_2(\mu_t,\nu_t)\le e^{K_Tt}W_2(\mu_0,\nu_0)$. [[lem-characteristics-unique-and-stable]]

[F5] AC supplies the flow and optimal coupling constructions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[prop-existence-and-lower-semicontinuity-of-optimal-couplings]]

## Proof


**Given:** AC and the hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Put the finite labels on the probability space $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ with mass $1/m$. The finite label sigma-algebra is countably generated, so the generalized label lemma gives a separable Hilbert space. Then $K=L^2(\{1,\ldots,m\};\mathbb R^d)$ has inner product $m^{-1}\sum_i x_i\cdot y_i$, and its lifted energy is $F(m^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i})=F_m$ by [F1]. A Euclidean subgradient $p$ represents the functional derivative in the weighted metric by $mp$, since $m^{-1}\sum_i(mp_i)\cdot h_i=\sum_i p_i\cdot h_i$. This gives the normalization of the two inclusions; the local supporting-set argument below proves their local subdifferential identification and the converse for every particle path. [F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Fix $m$, a finite interval $[0,T]$, and any classical particle path from the Statement. Its coordinate image is compact. Fix $q\in Q_1$ and first choose $r>1+\max_{i,t}|x_i^{(m)}(t)-q|$. The cutoff enlargement condition then puts the image in $Q_r^m$. Choose $R>r$; the same condition gives a relative $\Omega^m$-neighborhood of the image inside $Q_R^m$. Set $A_R=\sup_{Q_R}\|d\Phi\|$, $B_R=\operatorname{Lip}_{Q_R}(d\Phi)$, and choose the finite Lipschitz and norm bounds $L_R,N_R$ for $dR$ on the closed convex hull of $\Phi(Q_R)$. On the atomic label space write $G_R(X)=R(\int\Phi(X)d\sigma)$. Its gradient in the weighted Hilbert metric is $s\mapsto d\Phi_{X(s)}^*\nabla R(\int\Phi(X)d\sigma)$. Also $\|\int\Phi(X)d\sigma-\int\Phi(Y)d\sigma\|\le A_R\|X-Y\|_K$. Adding and subtracting $d\Phi_{X(s)}^*\nabla R(\int\Phi(Y)d\sigma)$ therefore gives the Lipschitz bound $$\|\nabla G_R(X)-\nabla G_R(Y)\|_K\le (L_RA_R^2+N_RB_R)\|X-Y\|_K.$$ Writing $C_R=L_RA_R^2+N_RB_R$, the smooth term is therefore $(-C_R)$-semiconvex in the weighted Hilbert metric, while the averaged potential is $\lambda_V$-semiconvex there. Since $\|X-Y\|_K^2=m^{-1}\sum_i|x_i-y_i|^2$, the corresponding Euclidean product coefficient for $F_m$ is $(\lambda_V-C_R)/m$. Because $Q_R^m$ and $\Omega^m$ agree locally along the path, the local Fréchet subdifferential in the Statement is the supporting subdifferential on $Q_R^m$ with this coefficient. Under the weighted Hilbert norm, $p\in\partial F_m(x)$ corresponds exactly to $mp\in\partial_{\lambda_V-C_R}E_R(x)$. [F1, F2, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 On a bounded neighborhood of the compact path image, the smooth feature gradient is bounded, and the two supporting inequalities for $V$ together with its bounded supporting selections give a local Lipschitz bound for the potential. Hence $F_m$ is locally Lipschitz there, so $e(t)=F_m(x^{(m)}(t))$ is absolutely continuous. At almost every time when $e$ and $x^{(m)}$ are differentiable and the inclusion holds, apply the semiconvex supporting inequality at $x^{(m)}(t)$ to $x^{(m)}(t+h)$ for positive and negative $h$. Dividing by $h$ and letting $h\to0$ gives $$e'(t)=\sum_i p_i(t)\cdot\dot x_i^{(m)}(t)=-m\sum_i|p_i(t)|^2=-\|\dot x^{(m)}(t)\|_K^2.$$ Since $F_m\ge0$, integration shows that the path has square-integrable derivative on $[0,T]$. Step 2.1 therefore identifies it as a solution of the localized Hilbert gradient-flow inclusion, and uniqueness of that flow identifies it with the atomic localized flow. The escape estimate [F3] consequently applies to every particle path in the Statement. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 By [F3], for each fixed $T$ the particle flows, now identified with localized flows, and the measure flow remain inside a common larger cutoff $Q_R$ and solve the same localized equation. Apply [F4] on that cutoff to get $W_2(\mu_{m,t},\mu_t)\le e^{K_Tt}W_2(\mu_{m,0},\mu_0)$ for $0\le t\le T$. Since $e^{K_Tt}\le e^{K_TT}$ when $K_T\ge0$ (replace it by $\max(K_T,0)$ otherwise), taking the supremum and using the assumed initial convergence proves the result. Assume AC. In $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, let $\sigma$ be normalized arc-length probability on the unit circle $S^1=\{x:|x|=1\}$ and let $\delta_0$ be the point mass at the origin. For radii $r_a=1/2$ and $r_b=2$, the support of $\sigma$ is contained in the ball $B(0,r_b)$ and separates the two spheres $r_aS^1$ and $r_bS^1$: every continuous path from one sphere to the other meets $S^1$. In contrast, the support of $\delta_0$ is contained in $B(0,r_b)$ but does not separate those spheres. These are only checks of the topological initialization condition; neither example asserts that any flow converges or that its limit is globally minimizing.

**Given:** The measures and radii in the Example.

2.1 Let $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb R^2$ be continuous with $|\gamma(0)|=1/2$ and $|\gamma(1)|=2$. The scalar map $t\mapsto|\gamma(t)|$ is continuous because $||x|-|y||\le|x-y|$. By [F2], it equals $1$ for some $t$, so $\gamma(t)\in S^1$ and the support separates the two spheres. [F2, step 1.1]

## Definition

Let $\mu$ be a finite positive Borel measure on $\mathbb C$ ([[def-radon-measure-on-an-lch-space]]).
Call an open set $V\subseteq\mathbb C$ **$\mu$-null** when $\mu(V)=0$. The
**support** of $\mu$ is the complement of the union of all open $\mu$-null sets,

$$\operatorname{supp}\mu:=\mathbb C\setminus\bigcup\{V\subseteq\mathbb C:V\text{ open and }\mu(V)=0\},$$

which is a closed subset of $\mathbb C$ ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).
Equivalently, $x\in\operatorname{supp}\mu$ if and only if $\mu(V)>0$ for every
open set $V\ni x$. A measure is **carried by** a Borel set $A$ when
$\mu(\mathbb C\setminus A)=0$, the terminology of
[[def-measure-concentrated-on-a-measurable-set]]. We say $\mu$ has **compact
support** when it is carried by some compact subset of $\mathbb C$.

## Remark

**The support is the smallest closed carrier, and the argument is choice-free.**
Let $\mathcal U$ be the union of all open $\mu$-null sets. The rational open
squares $B$ of $\mathbb R^2\cong\mathbb C$ form a countable basis
([[thm-rational-points-and-boxes-in-rn]]). Let $\mathcal N$ be the countable
family of those basis squares with $\mu(B)=0$. If $x\in\mathcal U$, then $x$ lies
in some open $\mu$-null $V$, and the basis property supplies a square
$B\in\mathcal N$ with $x\in B\subseteq V$; conversely every $B\in\mathcal N$ is
contained in $\mathcal U$. Hence $\mathcal U$ is the countable union of the
$\mu$-null sets $\mathcal N$ and is itself $\mu$-null by countable additivity
([[def-measure]]). Therefore $\mu(\mathbb C\setminus\operatorname{supp}\mu)=0$:
the support carries $\mu$. If $F$ is a closed set with
$\mu(\mathbb C\setminus F)=0$, then $\mathbb C\setminus F$ is an open $\mu$-null
set, so it is one of the sets in the defining union and
$\operatorname{supp}\mu\subseteq F$; the support is thus the smallest closed set
carrying $\mu$. In particular $\mu\neq0$ if and only if
$\operatorname{supp}\mu\neq\varnothing$, and if $\mu$ is carried by a compact
$K$, then $\operatorname{supp}\mu\subseteq K$ is compact.

## Statement

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Reals $a \le b$, a function $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ continuous on $[a,b]$, and a real $y$ with $f(a) \le y \le f(b)$ or $f(b) \le y \le f(a)$.

[L1] Scalar multiples of continuous functions are continuous, so $(-1)f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]]).

[L2] Recursion: for a set $X$, an element $x_0 \in X$ and a function $F : X \to X$ there is a unique $g : \mathbb{N} \to X$ with $g(0) = x_0$ and $g(k+1) = F(g(k))$ for every $k$ ([[thm-recursion]]).

[L3] Nested intervals: if $I_k = [a_k,b_k]$ with $a_k \le b_k$ and $I_{k+1} \subseteq I_k$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, then $\bigcap_{k} I_k$ is nonempty, and it is a single point exactly when the lengths $b_k - a_k$ tend to $0$ ([[thm-nested-interval-property]], [[def-interval]], [[def-real-limit]]).

[L4] Null geometric sequences: $|r| < 1$ implies $r^{k} \to 0$; and a constant multiple of a null sequence is null, while a constant sequence converges to that constant ([[lem-geometric-sequence-null]], [[thm-algebra-of-limits]], [[def-integer-power]], [[def-sequence]]).

[L5] Powers: $(2^{-1})^{k} = (2^{k})^{-1}$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[lem-power-laws]], [[def-integer-power]]).

[L6] Sequential criterion, the choice-free direction: if $f$ is continuous at $c$ and $x_k \in [a,b]$ with $x_k \to c$, then $f(x_k) \to f(c)$ ([[thm-sequential-criterion-for-continuity]], [[def-continuity-real]]).

[L7] Limits preserve non-strict inequalities ([[lem-limit-preserves-order]]).

[L8] Order and field arithmetic in $\mathbb{R}$: trichotomy and totality, so exactly one of $f(m) \ge y$ and $f(m) < y$ holds; halving and the ordered-field identities ([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]); and $|t| \le s$ whenever $-s \le t \le s$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** constructive.

1.1 **Reduction.** It is enough to prove the theorem under the hypothesis $f(a) \le y \le f(b)$. Indeed, in the remaining case $f(b) \le y \le f(a)$, put $h := (-1)f$ and $z := -y$; then $h$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ by [L1] and $h(a) = -f(a) \le -y = z \le -f(b) = h(b)$, so a point $c \in [a,b]$ with $h(c) = z$ is a point with $f(c) = y$. [L1, L8, suffices: assume f(a) le y le f(b)]

1.2 **The bisection map.** Assume $f(a) \le y \le f(b)$ and put $$X \;:=\; \bigl\{\, (u,v) \in \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \ : \ a \le u \le v \le b,\ f(u) \le y \le f(v) \,\bigr\},$$ so $(a,b) \in X$. For $(u,v) \in X$ write $m := (u+v)/2$, which satisfies $a \le u \le m \le v \le b$ and so lies in $[a,b]$, and define $$F(u,v) \;:=\; \begin{cases} (u,\ m) & \text{if } f(m) \ge y,\\ (m,\ v) & \text{if } f(m) < y. \end{cases}$$ By trichotomy exactly one clause applies, so $F$ is a function on $X$; and $F(u,v) \in X$ in both clauses, since in the first $f(u) \le y \le f(m)$ and in the second $f(m) \le y \le f(v)$. **The left half is tested first and the right half is taken only when the left is excluded, so nothing is selected.** [L8, construct]

2.1 **The nested sequence.** By [L2] applied to $X$, the element $(a,b)$ and the map $F$, there is a unique $g : \mathbb{N} \to X$ with $g(0) = (a,b)$ and $g(k+1) = F(g(k))$. Write $g(k) = (a_k,b_k)$ and $I_k := [a_k,b_k]$. Then for every $k$: $a \le a_k \le b_k \le b$ and $f(a_k) \le y \le f(b_k)$, because $g(k) \in X$; and $I_{k+1} \subseteq I_k$, since in either clause of the definition of $F$ the new endpoints lie in $[a_k,b_k]$ and the new interval is $[a_k,m_k]$ or $[m_k,b_k]$ with $m_k = (a_k+b_k)/2$. [step 1.2, L2, L8]

3.1 **The lengths.** In both clauses the new length is $m_k - a_k = (b_k - a_k)/2$ or $b_k - m_k = (b_k - a_k)/2$, so $b_{k+1} - a_{k+1} = (b_k - a_k)/2$; with $b_0 - a_0 = b - a$ an induction on $k$ gives $b_k - a_k = (b-a)\,(2^{-1})^{k}$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, that is $(b-a)/2^{k}$ by [L5]. Since $|2^{-1}| < 1$, [L4] gives $(2^{-1})^{k} \to 0$ and hence $b_k - a_k \to 0$. [step 2.1, L4, L5, L8]

4.1 **The point.** By [L3] applied to the nested family $(I_k)$, whose lengths tend to $0$ by step 3.1, the intersection $\bigcap_k I_k$ is a single point; call it $c$. Then $c \in I_0 = [a,b]$ and $a_k \le c \le b_k$ for every $k$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L3, construct]

5.1 **The endpoints converge to $c$.** Let a rational $\varepsilon > 0$ be given. By step 3.1 there is $K$ with $b_k - a_k < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$. For such $k$, from $a_k \le c \le b_k$ we get $-(b_k - a_k) \le a_k - c \le 0$ and $0 \le b_k - c \le b_k - a_k$, so $|a_k - c| \le b_k - a_k < \varepsilon$ and $|b_k - c| \le b_k - a_k < \varepsilon$ by [L8]. Hence $a_k \to c$ and $b_k \to c$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, L8]

6.1 **Passing to the limit.** The point $c$ lies in $[a,b]$, so $f$ is continuous at $c$, and [L6] applied to the two sequences of step 5.1 gives $f(a_k) \to f(c)$ and $f(b_k) \to f(c)$. [step 4.1, step 5.1, L6]

7.1 By step 2.1, $f(a_k) \le y$ for every $k$; the constant sequence with value $y$ converges to $y$ by [L4], so [L7] gives $f(c) \le y$. Likewise $y \le f(b_k)$ for every $k$ gives $y \le f(c)$. Hence $f(c) = y$. [step 2.1, step 6.1, L4, L7, L8]

8.1 A point $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$ has therefore been constructed, under the reduction of step 1.1 and hence in both cases of the hypothesis. [step 1.1, step 4.1, step 7.1, discharge-construct: c is the unique point of the nested intersection] ∎

## Remarks

- **Why the left half is tested first.** The bisection has to choose one of two halves at every stage, and if the rule were "choose a half in which the sign change persists" the construction would be a dependent choice, not a recursion. Testing $f(m) \ge y$ and taking the left half in that case makes the successor a function of its predecessor, so [[thm-recursion]] applies verbatim. The same device is used in [[thm-perfect-set-uncountable-r]] and in the bisection proof of Heine-Borel.

- **What the theorem does *not* say.** It does not say that $c$ is unique, and it does not say that the set of solutions is an interval; $f$ may take the value $y$ on a complicated set. It also does not say that a function with the intermediate value property is continuous — that converse is false, and the witness for it needs machinery that is not available at this point in the reading order.

- **Only the choice-free direction of the sequential criterion is used.** Step 6.1 turns a convergent sequence into a convergent image sequence, which is the implication proved in ZF ([[thm-sequential-criterion-for-continuity]]); the converse, which spends countable choice, is never invoked here.

## Example

Assume AC. Let $\Omega=\mathbb R$, $\mathcal H=\mathbb R$, $R(z)=z^2$, $\Phi(x)=\sin x$, and $V(x)=0$, so $F(\mu)=(\int\sin x\,d\mu(x))^2$ for every finite nonnegative Borel measure. This energy is convex under linear mixtures of measures, but it is not displacement convex along $W_2$ geodesics: along the geodesic from $\delta_0$ to $\delta_\pi$, its endpoint values are zero and its midpoint value is one.

**Given:** The feature-energy data in the Example.

[F2] The unique coupling of two Dirac probability measures is concentrated on their support-point pair, so their $W_2$ geodesic is the linear interpolation of those points. [[def-generalized-wasserstein-geodesic-and-strong-subgradient]]

## Proof


**Given:** $F$, $\mu_0,\mu_1$, and AC as in the Example.

1.1 For $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $0\le t\le1$, expansion gives $(1-t)a^2+tb^2-((1-t)a+tb)^2=t(1-t)(a-b)^2\ge0$. Thus the real square obeys the convexity inequality, including $t=0,1$ and $a=b$, by core algebra alone. [given, algebra]

2.1 For finite nonnegative measures $\mu_0,\mu_1$, write $a=\int\sin x\,d\mu_0$ and $b=\int\sin x\,d\mu_1$. Linearity of integration gives $F((1-t)\mu_0+t\mu_1)=((1-t)a+tb)^2\le(1-t)a^2+tb^2=(1-t)F(\mu_0)+tF(\mu_1)$ by step 1.1. Thus $F$ is mixture-convex. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $\mu_0=\delta_0$ and $\mu_1=\delta_\pi$, [F2] gives the geodesic $\mu_t=\delta_{\pi t}$. Then $F(\mu_0)=F(\mu_1)=0$, whereas $F(\mu_{1/2})=\sin^2(\pi/2)=1$. ## Example

Assume AC. In dimension $d\ge1$, take $\mathcal H=\{0\}$, $R=0$, $\Phi=0$, $\Omega=\mathbb R^d$, $V(x)=|x|^2/2$, and $Q_r=\overline B(0,r)$ for every $r>0$. This cutoff family has the required relative-neighborhood property, and $\sup_{Q_r}\|\partial V\|=r\le1+r$, so $C_1=C_2=1$ works. Thus $F(\mu)=\frac12\int|x|^2d\mu(x)$. For any $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$, the unique Wasserstein gradient flow is $\mu_t=(e^{-t}\operatorname{id})_\#\mu_0$. The corresponding $m$-particle gradient flow satisfies $x_i(t)=e^{-t}x_i(0)$ under the inner product $m^{-1}\sum_i x_i\cdot y_i$. For every empirical probability $\mu_{m,0}$ and every $t\ge0$,
$$W_2(\mu_{m,t},\mu_t)=e^{-t}W_2(\mu_{m,0},\mu_0),$$
so any initial convergence in $W_2$ persists uniformly on every compact time interval.

[Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré, Chapter 11](https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~sayan/ambrosio.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $d\ge1$, $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$, and an empirical initial probability $\mu_{m,0}$.

[F1] Expanding the defining inequality for $\partial_0V$ gives $V(y)-V(x)-x\cdot(y-x)=|y-x|^2/2\ge0$, and the first-order directional limit forces every subgradient to equal $x$. Thus the minimum-norm subgradient is $x$. [[def-feature-measure-energy]]

[F2] The quadratic Wasserstein distance is the infimum of the squared displacement cost over couplings. [[def-wasserstein-two-space-and-couplings]]

[F3] AC is assumed in the flow and transport results. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F4] Finite-action continuity-equation solutions are represented by absolutely continuous characteristic paths. [[thm-superposition-for-finite-action-continuity-equations]]

## Proof


**Given:** The data in the Example.

1.1 The characteristic equation $\dot x=-x$ with $x(0)=x_0$ has the solution $x(t)=e^{-t}x_0$, as direct differentiation verifies. Pushing $\mu_0$ forward by this map gives a continuity-equation solution with velocity $v_t(x)=-x$. Its action on $[0,T]$ is finite because $\int|x|^2d\mu_t=e^{-2t}\int|x|^2d\mu_0$. For compactly supported initial laws it is the flow identified by the global uniqueness theorem. For arbitrary $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2$, the same conclusion follows directly: every finite-action PDE solution with the prescribed smooth velocity $-x$ is represented by its unique characteristics via superposition, so it equals this pushforward, even when $\mu_0$ lies in no finite cutoff. [F1, F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 The metric $m^{-1}\sum_i x_i\cdot y_i$ gives the particle gradient of $m^{-1}\sum_i|x_i|^2/2$ equal to $(x_1,\dots,x_m)$, so the same scalar ODE gives $x_i(t)=e^{-t}x_i(0)$. Consequently $\mu_{m,t}=(e^{-t}\operatorname{id})_\#\mu_{m,0}$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 For $a>0$, pushing both marginals of any coupling forward by $x\mapsto ax$ multiplies its quadratic cost by $a^2$; applying the inverse scaling gives the reverse inequality for the infimum. Thus $W_2(a_\#\alpha,a_\#\beta)=aW_2(\alpha,\beta)$. Apply this with $a=e^{-t}$, $\alpha=\mu_{m,0}$, and $\beta=\mu_0$ to obtain the displayed identity. Since $e^{-t}\le1$, its supremum for $0\le t\le T$ is at most the initial W2 error, proving compact-time uniform convergence. [F2, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $M\ge0$, $\eta>0$, $L\ge0$, $\epsilon>0$, and let $w:[t_0,t_0+2M/\eta]\to[-M,0]$ and $\theta:[t_0,t_0+2M/\eta]\to\mathbb R^q$ be absolutely continuous until the first time $w$ reaches zero. Assume $w(t_0)\in[-M,0]$, $\theta(t_0)=\theta_0$, and, almost everywhere before the crossing,

$$w'(t)\ge\eta/2,\qquad q'(t)\le |w(t)|(\epsilon+Lq(t)),\qquad q(t)=|\theta(t)-\theta_0|.$$

Then $w$ reaches zero at some $\tau\le t_0+2M/\eta$. At the first such time,

$$q(\tau)\le \begin{cases}\dfrac{\epsilon}{L}\bigl(e^{LM^2/\eta}-1\bigr),&L>0,\\[4pt]\dfrac{\epsilon M^2}{\eta},&L=0.\end{cases}$$

Thus the crossing remains in $|\theta-\theta_0|<r_0$ whenever the displayed bound is less than $r_0$. The crossing-time bound depends on the initial negative-weight magnitude $M$.

## Statement references

[Chizat and Bach, Lemma C.18 and its proof, Appendix C.4.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The differential inequalities and initial data in the Statement.

[A1] The functions $w$ and $\theta$ are absolutely continuous on each interval before the first zero of $w$.

## Proof

**Given:** $M,\eta,L,\epsilon,w,\theta$ as in the Statement.

1.1 Suppose first that $M>0$ and $w$ has not reached zero by $t_0+2M/\eta$. Integrating $w'\ge\eta/2$ gives $w(t_0+2M/\eta)\ge w(t_0)+M\ge0$, contradicting the assumed strict negativity before the first crossing. Hence the first crossing time $\tau$ exists and satisfies the stated bound. If $M=0$, then $w(t_0)=0$ and $\tau=t_0$. [given, A1, algebra]

2.1 On $[t_0,\tau]$, $w$ is strictly increasing with $w'\ge\eta/2$, so it is an admissible absolutely continuous time change. Its inverse satisfies $dt/dw\le2/\eta$. If $L>0$, set $p=\epsilon+Lq$. The inequality for $q$ gives $dp/dw\le(2L/\eta)|w|p$, and integration from $w(t_0)$ to $0$ yields $p(\tau)\le\epsilon e^{LM^2/\eta}$. Rearranging gives $q(\tau)\le\epsilon(e^{LM^2/\eta}-1)/L$. If $L=0$, direct integration gives $q(\tau)\le(2\epsilon/\eta)\int_{w(t_0)}^0|s|ds=\epsilon w(t_0)^2/\eta\le\epsilon M^2/\eta$. The same bounds hold with zero right-hand side when $M=0$. [A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Source note

Chizat and Bach's printed proof claims a common crossing time $T<2/\eta$ for every $w_0\in[-M,0]$. Integrating $w'\ge\eta/2$ gives the correct worst-case bound $2M/\eta$. The estimate above proves hitting at an actual time $\tau$ and the corresponding $\theta$-displacement bound; it does not assert $w(T)=0$ at one fixed time for all initial weights.

## Statement

Let $X\subseteq\mathbb R^k$ and $Y\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be closed Euclidean subspaces. Let $\mu$ be a finite nonnegative Borel measure on $X$, define $\operatorname{spt}\mu=\{x:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}$, and let $f:X\to Y$ be continuous. Define the pushforward by $f_\#\mu(A)=\mu(f^{-1}(A))$ for Borel $A$. Then

$$\operatorname{spt}(f_\#\mu)=\overline{f(\operatorname{spt}\mu)}.$$

## Statement references

[Chizat and Bach, Lemma C.8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

[Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré, Chapter 8](https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~sayan/ambrosio.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mu$ and $f$ as in the Statement.

## Proof

1.1 If $y=f(x)$ for $x\in\operatorname{spt}\mu$ and $V$ is any open neighborhood of $y$, continuity makes $f^{-1}(V)$ an open neighborhood of $x$. Hence $f_\#\mu(V)=\mu(f^{-1}(V))>0$, so $y\in\operatorname{spt}(f_\#\mu)$. Taking the closure relative to $Y$, since support is closed, $\overline{f(\operatorname{spt}\mu)}\subseteq\operatorname{spt}(f_\#\mu)$. [given, construct]

2.1 The complement of $\operatorname{spt}\mu$ has $\mu$-measure zero: every point in it lies in a zero-measure open neighborhood, and the countable relative Euclidean basis gives a countable cover by zero-measure basis sets. If $y\notin\overline{f(\operatorname{spt}\mu)}$, choose an open neighborhood $V$ disjoint from that closure. Then $f^{-1}(V)\subseteq X\setminus\operatorname{spt}\mu$, so $f_\#\mu(V)=0$ and $y\notin\operatorname{spt}(f_\#\mu)$. Thus $\operatorname{spt}(f_\#\mu)\subseteq\overline{f(\operatorname{spt}\mu)}$. [given, step 1.1, choose] ∎

## Definition

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable space and let $\mu$ be a finite nonnegative measure on $(\mathbb R\times\Theta,\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal T)$ such that $\int|w|d\mu(w,\theta)<\infty$. Set $w_+=\max(w,0)$ and $w_-=\max(-w,0)$, and define finite nonnegative measures on $\Theta$ by

$$\alpha_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w_+d\mu,\qquad\beta_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w_-d\mu\quad(B\in\mathcal T).$$

The partially one-homogeneous signed projection is

$$h^1(\mu)=\alpha_\mu-\beta_\mu,\qquad h^1(\mu)(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w\,d\mu(w,\theta).$$

It is a finite signed measure. For every bounded measurable $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$, define its integral against this signed projection by

$\int_\Theta\varphi\,dh^1(\mu):=\int_\Theta\varphi d\alpha_\mu-\int_\Theta\varphi d\beta_\mu=\int_{\mathbb R\times\Theta}w\varphi(\theta)d\mu(w,\theta).$

Put $\lambda_\mu=\alpha_\mu+\beta_\mu$, so $\lambda_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}|w|d\mu$. Its total variation satisfies $|h^1(\mu)|(B)\le\lambda_\mu(B)$ for every $B\in\mathcal T$. Therefore $\int\widetilde Vd|h^1(\mu)|\le\int |w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu$ for every bounded nonnegative measurable $\widetilde V$.

If $\mathcal H$ is a separable real Hilbert space and $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ is bounded and strongly measurable, then for every $z\in\mathcal H$ the feature moment satisfies $\langle z,\int w\varphi(\theta)d\mu\rangle=\int\langle z,\varphi(\theta)\rangle dh^1(\mu)$, with the scalar integral defined above. The raw measures $\alpha_\mu$ and $\beta_\mu$ record positive and negative parameter weights before cancellation and need not be mutually singular; for example, if $\mu$ assigns mass one to each of $(1,\theta_0)$ and $(-1,\theta_0)$ and zero elsewhere, then $\alpha_\mu=\beta_\mu$ both assign mass one to $\theta_0$ while $h^1(\mu)=0$. Thus the signed projection does not by itself determine a penalty of the form $\int|w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, $\mu$, and the integrability assumption in the Definition.

[F1] For a nonnegative measurable $f$, the set function $B\mapsto\int_{\mathbb R\times B}f(w,\theta)d\mu$ is a measure. [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]

[F2] The nonnegative integral is monotone, so $0\le w_+,w_-\le|w|$ implies each of these measures has total mass at most $\int|w|d\mu$. [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]

[F3] A signed measure is a countably additive set function taking at most one infinite value; in particular a finite difference of finite measures is a finite signed measure. [[def-signed-measure]]

[F4] Total variation is the supremum of sums over countable measurable partitions. [[def-total-variation-of-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]

[F5] The Lebesgue integral is linear on integrable functions. [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]

[F6] A strongly measurable Banach-valued function is Bochner integrable exactly when its norm has finite integral. [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]

[F7] Bounded linear maps commute with Bochner integration. [[thm-bounded-linear-maps-commute-with-bochner-integration]]

## Proof

**Given:** The measurable space and measure in the Definition.

1.1 The coordinate $w$ is measurable, so $w_+$ and $w_-$ are nonnegative measurable functions. By [F1], $\alpha_\mu$ and $\beta_\mu$ are measures, and [F2] gives $\alpha_\mu(\Theta),\beta_\mu(\Theta)\le\int|w|d\mu<\infty$. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 For each measurable $B$, $w=w_+-w_-$ and both integrals are finite, so $\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w d\mu=\alpha_\mu(B)-\beta_\mu(B)$. Countable additivity of both finite measures makes their difference countably additive with finite real values, hence a finite signed measure by [F3]. For every $B\in\mathcal T$ and every countable measurable partition $(B_j)$ of $B$, $\sum_j|h^1(\mu)(B_j)|\le\sum_j(\alpha_\mu(B_j)+\beta_\mu(B_j))=\alpha_\mu(B)+\beta_\mu(B)$; taking the supremum in [F4] proves the stated pointwise total-variation bound. The weighted penalty inequality follows by monotonicity of the nonnegative integral, first for simple nonnegative weights and then by increasing simple approximation. For a finite-valued simple $\varphi$, linearity [F5] and the definitions of $\alpha_\mu,\beta_\mu$ give $\int\varphi d\alpha_\mu-\int\varphi d\beta_\mu=\int w\varphi d\mu$. For general bounded measurable $\varphi$, choose $M$ with $|\varphi|\le M$ and partition $[-M,M]$ into finitely many intervals of length at most $1/n$; assigning one endpoint on each measurable inverse image gives a finite-valued simple $\varphi_n$ with $\|\varphi_n-\varphi\|_\infty\le1/n$. The errors in the two $\alpha_\mu,\beta_\mu$ integrals are at most $(\alpha_\mu(\Theta)+\beta_\mu(\Theta))/n$, and the error in the $w\varphi$ integral is at most $\int|w|d\mu/n$. Letting $n\to\infty$ proves the identity. [F3, F4, F5, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ be bounded and strongly measurable. Simple approximants to $\varphi$ and to the measurable scalar coordinate $w$ show that $w\varphi(\theta)$ is strongly measurable; moreover $\|w\varphi(\theta)\|\le|w|\|\varphi\|_\infty$, so [F6] makes it Bochner integrable. For each $z\in\mathcal H$, [F7] moves the bounded functional $x\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle$ inside that Bochner integral, and step 2.1 identifies the resulting scalar integral with the pairing in the Definition. Equality of all inner products proves the displayed feature-moment factorization. [F2, F6, F7, given, step 2.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space. A **signed measure** on
$(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function
$$\nu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow \overline{\mathbb R}$$
such that:

1. $\nu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. $\nu$ takes at most one infinite sign: either $\nu(E)\neq-\infty$ for every
   $E\in\mathcal A$, or $\nu(E)\neq+\infty$ for every $E\in\mathcal A$;
3. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in
   $\mathcal A$,
   the series on the right is defined in the extended reals and
   $$\nu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \nu(E_n)$$
   ([[def-extended-reals]]).

The second and third clauses are load-bearing, not stylistic: together they
rule out the undefined form $(+\infty)+(-\infty)$ and require the disjoint
series to exist before countable additivity is asserted.

The next proposition proves the extra fact that if
$\nu(\bigcup_n E_n)$ is finite, then the real series $\sum_n \nu(E_n)$
converges absolutely in the sense of
[[def-absolute-and-conditional-convergence]].
