## Definition

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. For
$E\in\mathcal A$, define its **total variation on $E$** by
$$|\nu|(E):=\sup\left\{\sum_{n=0}^\infty |\nu(E_n)|:\ (E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\text{ is a countable measurable partition of }E\right\},$$
where, for a signed measure, the term $|\nu(E_n)|$ means the ordinary absolute
value when $\nu(E_n)\in\mathbb R$ and means $+\infty$ when
$\nu(E_n)\in\{+\infty,-\infty\}$; for a complex measure it is the usual complex
modulus. A countable measurable partition of $E$ means:

1. each $E_n$ lies in $\mathcal A$;
2. the sets $E_n$ are pairwise disjoint;
3. $E=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n$.

The sum on the right is a nonnegative extended series, so it is always defined
in $[0,+\infty] \subseteq \overline{\mathbb R}$.

For signed measures, a later proposition shows that finite partitions already
suffice. For complex measures, that finite-partition shortcut is not built into
the definition here.

## Definition

Let $d\ge2$, let $\mathbb S^{d-1}=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^d:|\theta|=1\}$, and let $\mu$ be a finite nonnegative Borel measure on $\mathbb R^d$ with $\int|u|^2d\mu(u)<\infty$. Define $\rho(u)=u/|u|$ for $u\ne0$. The **two-homogeneous projection** of $\mu$ is the set function on Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb S^{d-1}$

$$h^2(\mu)(A)=\int_{\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}}\mathbf1_A(\rho(u))|u|^2d\mu(u).$$

It is a finite nonnegative Borel measure: the integrand defines the weighted measure $|u|^2\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}$, and preimages under the continuous map $\rho$ preserve disjoint unions; its total mass is at most $\int|u|^2d\mu$. Mass at $u=0$ contributes zero. If $\Phi$ or $V$ is positively two-homogeneous, this projection records its radial integral on the sphere; the exact identities are stated separately.

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and let $f:\overline U\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuous. For $y\notin f(\partial U)$, put $K=f^{-1}(\{y\})\cap U$ and define $D(f,U,y)$ by

$$f_*[U]_K=D(f,U,y)[\mathbb R^d]_{\{y\}}\quad\text{in }H_d(\mathbb R^d,\mathbb R^d\setminus\{y\};\mathbb Z),$$

where $[U]_K$ is the unique relative orientation class restricting to the standard local generator on $K$, and $[\mathbb R^d]_{\{y\}}$ is the positive local generator. This integer is well-defined. It is nonzero only if $f^{-1}(y)\cap U\ne\varnothing$, and $D(\operatorname{id},U,y)=1$ whenever $y\in U$. If $U_1,U_2\subset U$ are disjoint bounded open sets, $y\notin f(\partial U_i)$ for $i=1,2$, and every point of $f^{-1}(y)\cap U$ lies in $U_1\cup U_2$, then

$$D(f,U,y)=D(f,U_1,y)+D(f,U_2,y).$$

If $H:[0,1]\times\overline U\to\mathbb R^d$ and $y:[0,1]\to\mathbb R^d$ are continuous and $y(t)\notin H_t(\partial U)$ for every $t$, then $D(H_0,U,y(0))=D(H_1,U,y(1))$.

## Statement references

[[lem-compatible-local-orientation-classes-exist-over-compact-subsets]]

[Chizat and Bach, Appendix C.3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

[Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, §2.2](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATch2.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The oriented open domains, maps, targets, and relative-homology construction in the Statement.

[F1] Every compact subset $K$ of a boundaryless $d$-manifold has a unique relative orientation class in $H_d(M,M\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$ restricting to the chosen local generator at every point; these classes commute with restriction to smaller compact supports. [[lem-compatible-local-orientation-classes-exist-over-compact-subsets]]

[F2] A continuous map of pairs induces a homomorphism on relative singular homology, and induced maps respect composition. [[prop-relative-homology-is-functorial-for-maps-of-pairs]]

[F3] Relative homology is the homology of the quotient singular-chain complex; excision identifies relative groups after removing a closed set lying in the interior of the relative subspace. [[def-relative-singular-homology]] [[thm-excision-for-singular-homology]]

[F4] At an interior point of $\mathbb R^d$, the local relative homology group $H_d(\mathbb R^d,\mathbb R^d\setminus\{y\};\mathbb Z)$ is free of rank one. [[thm-local-homology-detects-interior-points-boundary-points-and-dimension]]

## Proof

**Given:** The objects in the Statement and the relative-homology degree definition.

1.1 If $f^{-1}(y)\cap U=\varnothing$, then $K=\varnothing$ and $H_d(U,U\setminus K)=H_d(U,U)=0$, so $D(f,U,y)=0$. For the identity and $y\in U$, $K=\{y\}$ and the induced map sends the chosen local orientation generator to itself, so $D(\operatorname{id},U,y)=1$. [F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Under the additivity hypotheses, $K$ is the disjoint union of $K_i=K\cap U_i$. The closed set $Z=U\setminus(U_1\cup U_2)$ has closure in $U$ disjoint from $K$: the compact set $K$ lies in the open set $U_1\cup U_2$. Excision [F3] identifies $H_d(U,U\setminus K)$ with $H_d(U_1\cup U_2,(U_1\cup U_2)\setminus K)$. Since $U_1,U_2$ are disjoint open sets, every singular simplex in their union lies in exactly one of them, so this relative group and its chains split as the direct sum of the two relative groups. The unique orientation class [F1] therefore corresponds to $[U_1]_{K_1}+[U_2]_{K_2}$. The restrictions of $f$ commute with the inclusions of these pairs, so functoriality [F2] maps this sum to the sum of the two target classes. Their integer coefficients consequently satisfy $D(f,U,y)=D(f,U_1,y)+D(f,U_2,y)$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 For moving-target invariance set $g_t(x)=H_t(x)-y(t)$; translation identifies the target generator with the standard generator at $0$. The zero set $S=\{(t,x):g_t(x)=0\}$ is a closed subset of compact $[0,1]\times\overline U$ and is disjoint from $[0,1]\times\partial U$. Thus its projection $K_*\subset U$ is compact. Every $g_t$ defines a map of the fixed pair $(U,U\setminus K_*)$ into $(\mathbb R^d,\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\})$. The singular prism operator for the homotopy satisfies $\partial P+P\partial=(g_1)_\#-(g_0)_\#$; each prism over a simplex in $U\setminus K_*$ avoids $0$, so the chain homotopy descends to relative chains. Hence $(g_0)_*=(g_1)_*$ on $H_d(U,U\setminus K_*)$. Restriction compatibility in [F1] sends $[U]_{K_*}$ to $[U]_{K_t}$ for the actual time-$t$ zero set, so these two induced integers are exactly $D(H_0,U,y(0))$ and $D(H_1,U,y(1))$. They are equal, proving moving-target invariance. [F1, F2, F3, construct, step 2.1]

4.1 The target group is $\mathbb Z$ by [F4]; the source class is unique by [F1]; and the induced map exists by [F2]. Thus the integer in the Statement is well-defined. Steps 1.1–3.1 establish all asserted properties. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Degree construction diagram

For a compact preimage $K$, the definition applies the map of relative homology groups induced by $f$; the diagram records that map and its local orientation generators. The proof above establishes the properties independently of the diagram.

```tikzcd
H_d(U,U\setminus K;\mathbb Z) \arrow[r,"f_*"] \arrow[d,"\text{orientation class}"'] & H_d(\mathbb R^d,\mathbb R^d\setminus\{y\};\mathbb Z) \arrow[d,"\cong"] \\
\mathbb Z \arrow[r,"\times D(f,U,y)"'] & \mathbb Z
```

## Statement

Let $M$ be a boundaryless $n$-manifold, $R$ a commutative unital ring, and $K\subseteq M$ compact. Then $H_i(M,M\setminus K;R)=0$ for $i>n$, and restriction from $H_n(M,M\setminus K;R)$ to all local stalks at points of $K$ is injective. Every continuous section $s$ of the local $R$-homology system on $M$ is realized by a unique class $s_K$ in this relative group.

In particular an $R$-orientation determines a unique $[M]_K$ restricting to its generator at each point of $K$. These classes commute with restriction for compact-set inclusions and split over the finitely many components meeting $K$. No AC is needed.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[def-r-orientation-of-a-topological-manifold]] constructs the local $R$-system with ball restriction trivializations; orientations are its generator sections.

[F2] [[def-relative-singular-homology]] describes a relative class by a finite chain whose boundary lies in the omitted subspace.

[F3] [[thm-excision-for-singular-homology]] identifies support-relative groups with their coordinate-neighborhood versions.

[F4] [[lem-relative-homology-mayer-vietoris-for-closed-supports]] supplies the exact sequence with diagonal restriction and difference on overlaps.

[F5] [[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair-in-singular-homology]] and [[cor-homotopic-maps-induce-the-same-map-on-singular-homology]] compute relative homology through the explicit radial contractions below.

[F6] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] gives compactness and boundedness of closed Euclidean balls, compact sets and simplices. [[thm-compact-subset-of-a-hausdorff-space-is-closed]] gives closedness of their compact images in $M$.

[F7] [[thm-path-connected-implies-connected]] makes convex coordinate balls connected.

[F8] [[def-connected-component-and-quasicomponent]] makes the component through a point its largest connected subset.

[F9] [[thm-local-homology-detects-interior-points-boundary-points-and-dimension]] gives the point-local groups in every degree.

## Proof

**Given:** $M,n,R,K$ and, for the existence assertion, a supplied continuous section $s$ on $M$. Write $H_i(M\Vert A)=H_i(M,M\setminus A;R)$. For a compact support $A$, let $P(A)$ consist of the three assertions: vanishing in degrees above $n$, injectivity of restriction in degree $n$ to all its point stalks, and realization of every supplied section.

1.1 Suppose $P(A)$, $P(B)$ and $P(A\cap B)$ hold. In [F4]'s exact sequence, $H_{n+1}(M\Vert A\cap B)=0$ makes the diagonal map from $H_n(M\Vert A\cup B)$ injective. If a class restricts to zero at all points of $A\cup B$, its two images vanish by pointwise injectivity for $A,B$, so it is zero. The classes $s_A,s_B$ have equal restrictions to $A\cap B$, because their point values there coincide and restriction on that intersection is injective. Thus $(s_A,s_B)$ lies in the kernel of the difference map and lifts to $s_{A\cup B}$; its point restrictions are the required ones. For $i>n$, the terms $H_{i+1}(M\Vert A\cap B)$ and $H_i(M\Vert A)\oplus H_i(M\Vert B)$ are zero, so exactness also gives $H_i(M\Vert A\cup B)=0$. This proves $P(A\cup B)$. [F4, given]

1.2 Let $A$ be a nonempty compact convex subset in a coordinate neighborhood identified with all of $\mathbb R^n$, first with $n\ge1$, and fix $x\in A$. Choose $L>\sup_{a\in A}\lVert a-x\rVert$, which is finite by compactness. The radial homotopy about $x$ taking radius $\lVert y-x\rVert$ linearly to $L$ retracts both $\mathbb R^n\setminus A$ and $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{x\}$ to $S_L(x)$. To check the first assertion, if the initial radius is at most $L$, all movement is outward: if an outward multiple of $y-x$ met $A$, convexity with $x\in A$ would force $y\in A$, a contradiction. If the initial radius exceeds $L$, every intermediate radius is at least $L$ and is outside $A$. The same positive-radius formula works for the punctured space. The inclusion of complements therefore induces homology isomorphisms. The natural pair sequences [F5], together with the point-local calculation [F9], give isomorphisms $H_i(M\Vert A)\to H_i(M\Vert\{x\})$ for every $i$, by excision [F3]. They prove vanishing above $n$ and pointwise injectivity. [F1, F3, F5, F6, F9, given]

2.1 To realize a section over such an $A$, take a closed coordinate ball $D$ with $A\subset\operatorname{int}D$. Its ball trivialization from [F1] identifies $s$ over the connected open ball $\operatorname{int}D$ with a continuous function into a discrete module. Such a function is constant: any nonempty fiber and its nonempty complement would be a separation into open sets. The ball is connected by [F7]. The constant coordinate is a class in $H_n(M\Vert D)$, whose restriction to $A$ realizes $s$. For $n=0$, a nonempty compact convex coordinate support is a singleton and the ball comparison is the identity on $R$. The empty support has zero relative complex and satisfies all three assertions. Hence $P(A)$ holds for every compact convex coordinate support. A coordinate ball may always be identified with all of $\mathbb R^n$: in centered radius-$r$ coordinates, $y\mapsto y/(r-\lVert y\rVert)$ has continuous inverse $z\mapsto rz/(1+\lVert z\rVert)$. [F1, F2, F7, step 1.2]

3.1 Property $P$ holds for every finite union of compact convex subsets in one coordinate $\mathbb R^n$. Induct on their number. To adjoin the last set, its intersection with the preceding union is a union of fewer compact convex sets, since each pairwise intersection is compact and convex, possibly empty. Apply the induction hypothesis to that intersection and preceding union, then step 1.1. This proves the induction without assuming intersections are balls. [step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Let $A$ now be any compact subset of one such coordinate $\mathbb R^n$, and let $\alpha\in H_i(M\Vert A)$, $i\ge n$. By excision and [F2], represent it by a finite chain $z$ in the coordinate space with $\partial z$ supported outside $A$. Let $C$ be the union of the images of the finitely many simplex maps occurring with nonzero coefficient in $\partial z$. It is compact: a simplex is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F6], its continuous image is compact by pulling back covers, and finitely many compact images have compact union by taking finitely many finite subcovers. Thus $C$ is closed and disjoint from $A$. Take all closed balls centered at points of $A$ and small enough to miss $C$. Their interiors cover $A$; compactness gives finitely many with union $D$ containing $A$. Every chosen center belongs to $A$. Now $z$ represents $\alpha_D\in H_i(M\Vert D)$ restricting to $\alpha$. If $i>n$, step 3.1 gives $\alpha_D=0$, hence $\alpha=0$. [F2, F3, F6, step 3.1]

5.1 If $i=n$ and $\alpha$ vanishes at every point of $A$, the image of $\alpha_D$ in the group supported on each ball of step 4.1 has zero restriction at its center in $A$. The convex-support isomorphism of step 1.2 makes that ball-supported class zero. Hence $\alpha_D$ vanishes at every point of each ball, and therefore at every point of $D$. Pointwise injectivity from step 3.1 gives $\alpha_D=0$, and so $\alpha=0$. This proves injectivity for arbitrary compact coordinate supports. Existence for these supports is the same restriction from a large ball as in step 2.1: compactness puts $A$ inside that ball and the section has constant coordinate on its interior. Thus $P(A)$ holds for every compact coordinate support. When $A$ is empty, no balls are needed and the relative group is already zero. [F1, F2, F6, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1]

6.1 For a general compact $K\subset M$, consider all chart balls whose closures lie inside a larger chart ball. Their interiors cover $K$. These closures are compact by [F6] and continuous-image compactness, and are closed in $M$. Choose a finite subcover and put $K_j=K\cap\overline B_j$. These are compact, their union is $K$, and each lies in a chart homeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$. Induct on the number of pieces. The intersection of the last piece with the preceding union is the union of fewer compact chart pieces $K_j\cap K_m$. Property $P$ for a single piece is step 5.1; the same induction and step 1.1 therefore prove $P(K)$. Only finite covers and finite selections have been used. [F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 5.1]

7.1 Apply realization to the orientation section from [F1] to define $[M]_K$. Its uniqueness is the pointwise injectivity just proved. If $K\subset L$ are compact, the restriction of $[M]_L$ to $K$ has the same point values, hence equals $[M]_K$. Components of $M$ are open: each point has a connected coordinate-ball neighborhood by [F7], and that neighborhood lies in its component by [F8]. Thus their cover of $K$ has a finite subcover; disjointness shows these are all the components meeting $K$. Each such component is also closed, since its complement is a union of the other open components. Thus its intersection with $K$ is compact. Repeatedly applying [F4] to these disjoint supports, whose intersections have zero relative groups, gives the direct-sum decomposition and sends $[M]_K$ to the individual orientation classes. For $R=0$ all groups and sections are zero, and for empty $K$ the result is the unique zero class. All component arguments used only this local connectedness, and no AC or nondegenerate-simplex convention was used. [F1, F4, F7, F8, step 6.1] ∎

## Statement

A continuous map of pairs $f:(X,A)\to(Y,B)$, meaning $f(A)\subseteq B$,
induces $f_*:H_n(X,A;G)\to H_n(Y,B;G)$ for every $n$. Identity maps and
composites induce identity maps and composites.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A continuous $f:X\to Y$ with $f(A)\subseteq B$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The induced singular-chain map sends $C_n(A;G)$ into $C_n(B;G)$, hence $[c]\mapsto[f_\#c]$ defines a quotient-chain map. [given, construct]

2.1 It commutes with the quotient boundaries, so it maps cycles to cycles and boundaries to boundaries and hence descends to homology. The chain-level identity and composition laws persist after quotienting. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

The **relative singular homology group** of $(X,A)$ in degree $n$ is
$$H_n(X,A;G):=H_n(C_\bullet(X,A;G))=\ker\bar\partial_n/\operatorname{im}\bar\partial_{n+1}.$$
Equivalently, a relative cycle is an ordinary finite chain $c$ with
$\partial c\in C_{n-1}(A;G)$, modulo adding a chain in $A$ and an ordinary
boundary.

## Statement

If $Z\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, then
inclusion $(X-Z,A-Z)\to(X,A)$ induces isomorphisms
$H_n(X-Z,A-Z;G)\cong H_n(X,A;G)$ for every $n$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Use the cover $\{X\setminus\overline Z,\operatorname{int}A\}$: its cover-small quotient complex for $(X,A)$ consists, modulo small chains in $A$, of precisely the small chains avoiding $Z$. [given, construct]

2.1 The two inclusions from their small complexes to the corresponding full relative complexes are chain homotopy equivalences. The quotient identification in step 1.1 therefore induces the stated isomorphism. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $M$ be an $n$-manifold with boundary and $x\in M$. For any commutative unital coefficient ring $R$,
$$H_k(M,M\setminus\{x\};R)\cong\begin{cases}R,&x\in\operatorname{int}M\text{ and }k=n,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$
The boundary subset is independent of charts, and a nonempty manifold's dimension is intrinsic. Homeomorphisms preserve boundary and, for nonempty manifolds, dimension. A manifold is boundaryless exactly when it is locally Euclidean of its specified dimension. Dimension is not intrinsic for the empty space, and the zero coefficient ring cannot detect boundary or dimension; use integral coefficients for these conclusions. No AC is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[def-topological-manifold-with-and-without-boundary]] supplies half-space charts, the existential boundary subset, and the zero-dimensional convention.

[F2] [[thm-excision-for-singular-homology]] permits removal of $Z$ when its closure lies in the interior of the subspace of the pair.

[F3] [[cor-homology-of-spheres]] computes reduced sphere homology, including $S^0$.

[F4] [[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair-in-singular-homology]] supplies the pair sequence.

[F5] [[cor-homotopic-maps-induce-the-same-map-on-singular-homology]] identifies homology under explicit contractions and deformation retractions.

[F6] [[prop-relative-homology-is-functorial-for-maps-of-pairs]] sends homeomorphisms of pairs to isomorphisms.

## Proof

**Given:** $M,n,x,R$ as stated; homology groups in negative degrees are zero.

1.1 In any chart containing $x$, restrict to an open ball about its image if that image is above the hyperplane, or to the intersection of an open ball with the half-space if it is on the hyperplane. Translate the center to $0$ (only parallel to the hyperplane in the latter case). Write $U$ for the resulting neighborhood of $x$. Since $M$ is Hausdorff, $M\setminus\{x\}$ is open: separate each other point from $x$ by open sets and take their union. The closed set $Z=M\setminus U$ omits $x$, so $\overline Z=Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}(M\setminus\{x\})$. Thus [F2] and [F6] identify the local pair homology with that of $(B,B\setminus\{0\})$ or $(B_+,B_+\setminus\{0\})$, where the ball has radius $r>0$. [F1, F2, F6, given]

1.2 A point has exactly one singular generator in every degree. Its boundary is multiplication by $\sum_{i=0}^k(-1)^i$, namely identity for positive even $k$ and zero for odd $k$, with zero degree-zero boundary. Hence its homology is $R$ in degree zero and zero above. A nonempty contractible space has the same homology by [F5], with the degree-zero isomorphism induced by its map to a point. For a contractible $Y$ and nonempty $A\subseteq Y$, [F4] therefore identifies $H_k(Y,A;R)$ with $\widetilde H_{k-1}(A;R)$ for $k\ge1$ and gives $H_0(Y,A;R)=0$. At $k=1$ this is the kernel of the surjective augmentation $H_0(A;R)\to R$, and at higher degrees it follows from the two zero adjacent groups. Surjectivity uses any one point of the given nonempty $A$. [F4, F5, given]

2.1 At an interior chart point with $n\ge1$, $B$ contracts to $0$. For $\rho=r/2$, the homotopy $$h(y,t)=\left(1-t+\frac{t\rho}{\lVert y\rVert}\right)y$$ retracts $B\setminus\{0\}$ onto its radius-$\rho$ sphere: the norm is $(1-t)\lVert y\rVert+t\rho$, strictly between $0$ and $r$, and the sphere is fixed. Scaling identifies it with $S^{n-1}$. By [F3], [F5] and step 1.2, the pair group is $R$ exactly in degree $n$. This includes $n=1$, where the punctured interval has two components and the augmentation kernel is $\{(a,-a):a\in R\}$. When $n=0$, the chart pair is $(\{0\},\varnothing)$; its relative chain complex is the point complex calculated in step 1.2, giving the same conclusion. [F3, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2]

2.2 At a boundary chart point necessarily $n\ge1$. Choose $a=(0,\ldots,0,r/2)$. Both $B_+$ and $B_+\setminus\{0\}$ contract to $a$ by $(y,t)\mapsto(1-t)y+ta$. The ball and half-space are convex; for $t>0$ the last coordinate is positive, so the punctured homotopy never meets $0$, and at $t=0$ the input already avoids $0$. Their inclusion induces an isomorphism on $H_0$ and on every higher group, as seen by their maps to a point. The exact sequence [F4] gives zero relative groups in every degree. [F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 Now take $R=\mathbb Z$. The nonzero group in step 2.1 and the all-zero groups in step 2.2 are intrinsic to the pair $(M,M\setminus\{x\})$. Thus no point can be a boundary point in one chart and an interior point in another, even if different dimension labels are considered. This proves chart independence of [F1]'s boundary set and the formula in the statement. If a nonempty space has manifold dimension labels $n$ and $m$, some point is interior in an $n$-chart: every nonempty open subset of a positive-dimensional half-space meets its strict interior; for dimension zero every point is interior. The same point is interior for the other manifold structure by the zero/nonzero distinction. Its unique nonzero local degree is both $n$ and $m$, hence $n=m$. A homeomorphism identifies the local pairs by [F6], so preserves these data. [F1, F6, step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 If the boundary is empty, [F1]'s restriction to small balls gives Euclidean neighborhoods. Conversely, if $M$ is locally Euclidean of dimension $n$, the interior calculation of step 2.1 at every point gives a nonzero integral local group and precludes a boundary chart by step 2.2. This proves both directions of the stated equivalence. For empty $M$ the pointwise assertion and boundary equivalence are vacuous, but every dimension label is allowed. Zero coefficients make all local groups zero, without affecting the integral argument for intrinsic properties. The contractions explicitly include their endpoints, and the point calculation uses unnormalized chains; no omitted degenerate-generator convention or choice principle is involved. [F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the feature-energy hypotheses on a closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, and let $\mu_n,\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ be concentrated on $Q_r$, with finite feature energy and $W_2(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$. Then $F(\mu_n)\to F(\mu)$.

## Statement references

[[def-feature-measure-energy]]

[[def-wasserstein-two-space-and-couplings]]

[Chizat and Bach, Lemma A.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

[Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré, Chapter 8](https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~sayan/ambrosio.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The measures and cutoff in the Statement.

[F1] On $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz and at every point $x$ there is a supporting vector $\xi_x\in\partial_{\lambda_V}V(x)$ with $|\xi_x|\le C_1+C_2r$; the definition requires this bounded selection rather than a bound on the full relative-domain subdifferential. [[def-feature-measure-energy]]

[F2] $W_2(\mu_n,\mu)^2$ is the infimum of $\int|x-y|^2d\pi$ over all Borel couplings $\pi$ of $\mu_n,\mu$. [[def-wasserstein-two-space-and-couplings]]

[F3] Bounded linear maps commute with Bochner integration, so integrating a function against either marginal agrees with integrating its coordinate pullback against the coupling. [[thm-bounded-linear-maps-commute-with-bochner-integration]]

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the Statement.

1.1 For $x,y\in Q_r$, the segment between them lies in $Q_r$. The bound on $d\Phi$ and the fundamental theorem of calculus on this segment give $\|\Phi(x)-\Phi(y)\|\le L_\Phi|x-y|$. For $V$, divide the segment into $N$ equal pieces. The two $\lambda_V$-support inequalities at consecutive endpoints and the uniform bound $M_V$ on subgradients yield $|V(x_{j+1})-V(x_j)|\le M_V|x-y|/N+|\lambda_V||x-y|^2/(2N^2)$. Summing and letting $N\to\infty$ gives $|V(x)-V(y)|\le M_V|x-y|$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For any coupling $\pi\in\Gamma(\mu_n,\mu)$, [F3] and [F1] give $\|\int\Phi d\mu_n-\int\Phi d\mu\|\le L_\Phi\int|x-y|d\pi\le L_\Phi(\int|x-y|^2d\pi)^{1/2}$. The same coupling gives $|\int Vd\mu_n-\int Vd\mu|\le M_V(\int|x-y|^2d\pi)^{1/2}$. Taking the infimum over couplings and using [F2] makes both differences tend to zero. Continuity of $R$ then gives $F(\mu_n)\to F(\mu)$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $\Omega$ be the feature domain, and let $F(\mu)=R(\int_\Omega\Phi\,d\mu)+\int_\Omega V\,d\mu$ be finite on a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$, with $R$ differentiable and convex. Define $G_\mu(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u)$, where $m_\mu=\int_\Omega\Phi\,d\mu$. Then $\mu$ minimizes $F$ over all finite nonnegative Borel measures if and only if $G_\mu(u)\ge0$ for every $u\in\Omega$ and $G_\mu(u)=0$ for $\mu$-almost every $u$.

## Statement references

[[def-feature-measure-energy]]

[[thm-bounded-linear-maps-commute-with-bochner-integration]]

[[def-dirac-measure]]

[Chizat and Bach, Proposition 3.1 and Appendix C.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

[Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré, Chapter 10](https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~sayan/ambrosio.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The feature-measure energy, a finite nonnegative measure $\mu$, and a differentiable convex risk $R$. For the necessity direction assume $\mu$ is a minimizer; for sufficiency assume $G_\mu\ge0$ everywhere and $G_\mu=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere.

[F1] For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, set $F(\mu)=R(\int_\Omega\Phi(u)\,d\mu(u))+\int_\Omega V(u)\,d\mu(u)$ when $\mu$ is concentrated on $\Omega$, the Bochner integral exists, and the scalar integral is finite; set $F(\mu)=+\infty$ otherwise. [[def-feature-measure-energy]]

[F2] A bounded linear map commutes with Bochner integration on every measurable set: $T(\int_E f\,d\mu)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu$. [[thm-bounded-linear-maps-commute-with-bochner-integration]]

## Proof

**Given:** $\mu,R,\Phi,V$ as in the Statement.

1.1 Fix $u\in\Omega$. For $t\ge0$, the measure $\mu+t\delta_u$ from [F3] is nonnegative and $F(\mu+t\delta_u)$ is finite for sufficiently small $t$. Its right derivative at $t=0$ is $dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u)=G_\mu(u)$. If $\mu$ minimizes $F$, this derivative is nonnegative. Since $u$ was arbitrary, $G_\mu\ge0$ everywhere. [given, F1, F3, choose]

1.2 For $t$ in a neighborhood of $0$ with $1+t>0$, the measure $(1+t)\mu$ is admissible. Differentiating $F((1+t)\mu)$ at $0$ gives $dR_{m_\mu}[m_\mu]+\int V\,d\mu=\int G_\mu\,d\mu$ by [F2]. 2.1 For any finite-energy nonnegative $\nu$, convexity of $R$ gives $R(m_\nu)\ge R(m_\mu)+dR_{m_\mu}[m_\nu-m_\mu]$. By [F2], after adding the $V$ terms this is $F(\nu)-F(\mu)\ge\int G_\mu d\nu-\int G_\mu d\mu\ge0$. Infinite-energy competitors cannot lower $F$, so $\mu$ is a global minimizer. [given, F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be closed and convex, let $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ and $\widetilde V:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded Lipschitz maps, and set $\Phi(w,\theta)=w\varphi(\theta)$ and $V(w,\theta)=|w|\widetilde V(\theta)$. [Chizat and Bach, Lemma A.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The model and W2-convergent laws in the Statement.

[A1] AC supplies a sequence of couplings whose quadratic costs approach the W2 infimum. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] W2 is the infimum of quadratic coupling costs, so couplings can be chosen with RMS displacement tending to zero. [[def-wasserstein-two-space-and-couplings]]

[F2] Bounded linear maps commute with Bochner integration, so feature integrals against either marginal are integrals of their coordinate pullbacks against a coupling. [[thm-bounded-linear-maps-commute-with-bochner-integration]]

2.1 The same estimate with scalar $\widetilde V$ in place of $\varphi$ gives $\int Vd\mu_n\to\int Vd\mu$. ## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\Theta$ be either all of $\mathbb R^q$ or the compact closure of a nonempty bounded convex Euclidean domain and let $\phi:\Theta\to H$ and $W:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded $C^{1,1}$ maps, with $H$ separable Hilbert. Put $\Phi(w,\theta)=w\phi(\theta)$, $V(w,\theta)=|w|W(\theta)$, and assume the feature-energy hypotheses and the prescribed differentiable risk $R\ge0$. Let $\mu_t$ be any flow in the feature-energy Wasserstein definition. Write $m_t=\int w\phi(\theta)d\mu_t$, $f_t=\nabla R(m_t)$, $P_t=\int|w|W(\theta)d\mu_t$, $S(t)=\int w^2d\mu_t$ and $A(t)=\int|v_t|^2d\mu_t$. On every finite interval these quantities have continuous or absolutely continuous representatives as appropriate, and
$$F(\mu_t)-F(\mu_s)=-\int_s^t A(q)dq,\qquad S(t)-S(s)=-2\int_s^t(\langle f_q,m_q\rangle+P_q)dq.$$
These identities hold at every finite pair of endpoints. In particular $F(\mu_t)\le E_0:=F(\mu_0)<\infty$ and $\int_0^\infty A(t)dt\le E_0$. If $\sup_{t\ge0}\|m_t\|\le M$, then, with $D=\sup_{R(z)\le E_0}\|\nabla R(z)\|$,
$$0\le S(t)\le S(0)+2(DM+E_0)t.$$
No bounded-support assumption on the initial weights is required.

**Given:** AC and the hypotheses in the Statement.

[F1] A finite-action continuity-equation solution has a law of absolutely continuous characteristic paths with its time marginals and velocity. [[thm-superposition-for-finite-action-continuity-equations]]

[F2] The prescribed velocity is the negative minimum of the full constrained local subdifferential. [[def-wasserstein-gradient-flow-for-feature-energy]] [[def-feature-measure-energy]]

## Proof

**Given:** The data and assumptions in the Statement.

This follows from compactness for bounded $\Theta$; on the full Euclidean domain, boundedness and Lipschitz differential imply $\|D\phi(\theta)e\|\le2\|\phi\|_\infty+\operatorname{Lip}(D\phi)/2$ for unit $e$, by Taylor's inequality on a unit segment. The scalar bound is identical. On a finite horizon, W2 continuity bounds the second moments of $\mu_t$. Coupling Cauchy–Schwarz and $\|w\phi(\theta)-w'\phi(\theta')\|\le\|\phi\|_\infty|w-w'|+\|D\phi\|_\infty|w'|\,|\theta-\theta'|$ show norm continuity of $m_t$; hence $f_t$ is bounded and continuous there. [F2, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F1]. Along almost every path, the derivative of $w\phi(\theta)$ is $w'\phi(\theta)+wD\phi_\theta\theta'$, with norm at most $C(1+|w|)|v|$. Its path/time integral is finite by the uniform second-moment bound and Cauchy–Schwarz. The same bound controls the derivative of $|w|W(\theta)$. For a real AC path, its derivative is zero almost everywhere on its zero set: at a differentiability point with nonzero derivative that zero is isolated, and isolated zeroes form a countable set. Thus the formula $(|w|)'=\operatorname{sign}(w)w'$ with sign zero set to zero holds almost everywhere. Integrating the pathwise FTC and using Fubini gives AC representatives of $m_t,P_t$ with the integrated derivatives. Their time derivatives are bounded by $C(1+\sqrt{S(t)})\sqrt{A(t)}$, hence are in $L^2$ on finite intervals; [F3] identifies the norm derivative of $m_t$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Compose the AC moment with $R$: its differential is bounded on the compact image of the continuous moment path on the finite interval, so the composition is AC, and the ordinary Fréchet difference quotient gives derivative $\langle f_t,m_t'\rangle$ almost everywhere. Pair the inclusion [F2] with the characteristic velocity. At $w\ne0$ the potential derivatives are $\partial_w P_t=\langle f_t,\phi\rangle+\operatorname{sign}(w)W$ and $\nabla_\theta P_t=wD\phi^*f_t+|w|\nabla W$. Any domain normal $n$ satisfies $n\cdot\theta'=0$ at two-sided differentiability times: test its normal inequality against $\theta(t+h)$ for both signs of $h$. At $w=0$ the angular velocity is zero, and step 2.1 gives $w'=0$ almost everywhere on that zero set. The cusp and normal contributions therefore have zero pairing. If moments are uniformly bounded by $M$, the risk-sublevel bound gives $\|f_t\|\le D$, and $0\le P_t\le E_0$. ## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $q\ge1$, let $c\ge0$, and let $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ be bounded and continuously differentiable with bounded Lipschitz differential. For $s\in\{-1,1\}$ and $f\in\mathcal H$ put
$$H_{s,f}(\theta)=s\langle f,\varphi(\theta)\rangle+c.$$
Assume one of the following alternatives. In the bounded alternative, $\Theta$ is the closure of a bounded nonempty open convex subset of $\mathbb R^q$ with $C^1$ boundary, and $\partial_nH_{s,f}=0$ on its boundary for every $f$. In the unbounded alternative, $\Theta=\mathbb R^q$ and, for every $f$, $H_{s,f}(r\cdot)$ has a limit $H_{s,f}^\infty$ uniformly in $C^1(\mathbb S^{q-1})$ as $r\to\infty$.

Fix $s,f_0$ and $a_0<0$. Suppose $H:=H_{s,f_0}$ has dense regular values in its range and, in the unbounded alternative, the same holds for $H^\infty:=H_{s,f_0}^\infty$. Values whose level sets are empty count as regular. There exist numbers $a,b$ and $\epsilon>0$ with
$$a_0<a<b<0$$
such that the following two assertions hold on every finite interval $[t_0,t_1]$. Let $f:[t_0,t_1]\to\mathcal H$ be Borel with $\|f(t)-f_0\|\le\epsilon$ for every $t$, and let $\rho:[t_0,t_1]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuous. Every absolutely continuous path $\theta:[t_0,t_1]\to\Theta$ satisfying
$$\dot\theta(t)=-\rho(t)\nabla H_{s,f(t)}(\theta(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t$$
and $H(\theta(t_0))\le a$ satisfies $H(\theta(t))<b$ for all $t$. Every absolutely continuous path satisfying the equation with the opposite sign and $H(\theta(t_1))\le a$ satisfies $H(\theta(t))<b$ throughout the same interval. The constants do not depend on the interval, on $\rho$, or on the order in which the forcing values occur. In particular they apply after reversing time and reversing the forcing path. By decreasing $\epsilon$ if necessary, one also has $H_{s,f(t)}(\theta)\le b/2<0$ whenever $H(\theta)<b$.

[[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[[thm-uniform-boundedness-principle]]

[[cor-arzela-ascoli-subsequence-theorem-for-proper-metric-targets]]

[Chizat and Bach, Proposition C.4 and Appendix C.4.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the Hilbert space, feature, sign, forcing center, negative level, and one of the two domain alternatives in the Statement.

[F1] Pointwise bounded families of bounded linear maps on a Banach space have uniformly bounded operator norms under DC, which AC supplies. [[thm-uniform-boundedness-principle]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F2] Equicontinuous sequences of paths from a compact interval into a compact Euclidean set have uniformly convergent subsequences under AC. [[cor-arzela-ascoli-subsequence-theorem-for-proper-metric-targets]] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]

[F3] Scalar absolutely continuous functions obey the integral fundamental theorem of calculus; smooth compositions with absolutely continuous Euclidean paths obey the chain rule. Apply the latter coordinatewise where needed. [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]

**Given:** The data in the Statement; write $H_f=H_{s,f}$ and $H=H_{f_0}$.

Let $I=[u,v]$, let $C\subseteq I$ be closed, let $h:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let $Q:I\to\mathbb R$ be absolutely continuous with $h=Q$ on $C$. Suppose that $Q'\le-\kappa$ a.e. on $C$, for some $\kappa>0$, and that $h(t)+\kappa t$ is nonincreasing on every component interval of $I\setminus C$, including its endpoints by continuity. Put $U=h+\kappa t$ and $Z=Q+\kappa t$. If $x<y$ both belong to $C$, the complementary open intervals $(\alpha_j,\beta_j)$ of $C$ inside $(x,y)$ have endpoints in $C$. Absolute continuity of $Z$ and countable additivity of its integrable derivative give $Z(y)-Z(x)=\int_{C\cap[x,y]}Z'(t)\,dt+\sum_j\int_{\alpha_j}^{\beta_j}Z'(t)\,dt$. The series is absolutely convergent because the intervals are disjoint and $Z'\in L^1$. Each gap integral equals $Z(\beta_j)-Z(\alpha_j)=U(\beta_j)-U(\alpha_j)\le0$, and the integral over $C$ is nonpositive. Thus $U(y)\le U(x)$. For arbitrary $x<y$, if $[x,y]$ misses $C$ they lie in one gap. Otherwise let $x_*=\min(C\cap[x,y])$ and $y_*=\max(C\cap[x,y])$; monotonicity on the two possible end gaps and the preceding inequality yield $U(y)\le U(y_*)\le U(x_*)\le U(x)$. Hence $h(y)-h(x)\le-\kappa(y-x)$ on all of $I$. This explicitly excludes positive singular variation on the closed contact set; no absolute continuity of $h$ has been assumed or concluded. 2.1 The bounded alternative admits a direct trap. Choose a regular value $a\in(a_0,0)$ of $H$, and choose $b\in(a,0)$. Otherwise compactness of $\Theta$, the Neumann condition, and regularity give $\beta>0$ with $|\nabla H|\ge\beta$ on a thin neighborhood of $\{H=a\}$. An outward first crossing of $a$ is therefore impossible: any crossing would contain a subinterval with values in the collar increasing from a lower to a higher value, contrary to the integrated derivative inequality. A start with $H\le a$ consequently remains there. The argument also applies at the intersection with $\partial\Theta$, since the gradients are tangent there by Neumann and the path is constrained to $\Theta$. This proves the first assertion in the bounded alternative. [F3, given, construct, step 1.1]

3.1 For the rest of the proof take $\Theta=\mathbb R^q$. Write $r=|\theta|$ and $\omega=\theta/r$ when $r>0$. If its derivative had magnitude at least $\delta>0$ at arbitrarily large radii, its Lipschitz bound would keep the same sign with magnitude at least $\delta/2$ on a radial interval of a fixed positive length, forcing a fixed nonzero change of $H_f$ there; this contradicts uniform convergence. When that Lipschitz bound is zero, convergence makes the derivative identically zero. Thus the pushed-forward field extends continuously to $M$ with boundary components $(0,-\nabla_{\mathbb S}H_f^\infty)$. Denote this continuous Euclidean field on $M$ by $F_f$, and denote by $\widehat H$ the continuous extension of $H\circ\Psi^{-1}$ with boundary value $H^\infty$. [given, construct, step 2.1]

On the outer region the radial component difference is at most $\|d\varphi\|_\infty\|f-f_0\|$. Hence [F1] gives $\sup_{r\ge2}\|T_r\|<\infty$. This proves the required sphere bound uniformly in $r$ and, by passing to the pointwise limits, also on the boundary. 5.1 Choose $a\in(a_0,0)$ regular both for $H$ and for $H^\infty$. If $\widehat H$ has no values in a neighborhood of $a$, its continuous paths cannot cross that neighborhood, and the desired trap follows immediately. Otherwise choose $d>0$ and $\kappa>0$, with $a_0<a-2d<a+2d<0$, so that the following estimates hold on the band $\mathcal B=\{a-2d\le\widehat H\le a+2d\}$. The remaining region is compact; regularity of $a$ for $H$ and a smaller band give a positive lower bound there. If the boundary portion of the band is empty, only the compact interior argument is needed. [step 3.1, given, construct, step 4.1]

6.1 Every absolutely continuous solution $\gamma:[u,v]\to M$ of $\gamma'=F_0(\gamma)$ whose image lies in $\mathcal B$ obeys $\widehat H(\gamma(v))-\widehat H(\gamma(u))\le-\kappa(v-u)$, even if it touches the compactification boundary on a complicated closed time set. Choose a $C^1$ function $Q_0$ on $M$ equal to $H^\infty$ on the boundary: on a collar use its radial extension multiplied by a smooth cutoff that vanishes before the collar's inner edge, and extend by zero. This is $C^1$ because $H^\infty$ is $C^1$. The function $Q=Q_0\circ\gamma$ is absolutely continuous. At a.e. $t\in C$ its derivative equals the boundary directional derivative in step 5.1, since the radial component of $F_0$ is zero there; hence $Q'\le-\kappa$ a.e. on $C$. Apply the scalar gluing argument of step 1.1 to obtain the asserted estimate. In particular this argument does not infer absolute continuity from continuity of $\widehat H$, and does not presume uniqueness for the extended ODE at the boundary. [F3, step 1.1, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 Fix $\tau_*>0$ so small that every path in $M$ with speed at most $B:=1+\|F_0\|_\infty$ changes the value of $\widehat H$ by strictly less than $d$ on an interval of length at most $\tau_*$. There exists $e>0$, with $e\le1$, such that every absolutely continuous curve $\gamma:[0,\tau_*]\to M$ staying in $\mathcal B$ and satisfying $|\gamma'-F_0(\gamma)|\le e$ a.e. obeys $\widehat H(\gamma(\tau_*))-\widehat H(\gamma(0))\le-\kappa\tau_*/2$. Continuity of $F_0$ and the integral equations show that its limit solves $\gamma'=F_0(\gamma)$; the limit stays in the closed band. Step 6.1 gives an endpoint drop at least $\kappa\tau_*$, while uniform convergence and continuity of $\widehat H$ give a drop at most $\kappa\tau_*/2$. This contradiction proves the claim. [F2, step 6.1, construct]

## Statement

Let $W:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded and $C^1$, and suppose $V(w,\theta)=|w|W(\theta)$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex on $\mathbb R\times\Theta$ for one finite coefficient $\lambda$. Suppose either $\Theta=\mathbb R^q$, or $\Theta$ is the closure of a nonempty bounded connected open convex set with $C^1$ boundary and $dW(n)=0$ on that boundary. Then $W\equiv c$ for some $c\ge0$. In the full partial-model hypotheses, the Neumann assumption for $G_f=\langle f,\varphi\rangle+W$ at $f=0$ supplies the latter condition. Consequently, writing $H_+=\langle f,\varphi\rangle+c$ and $H_-=-\langle f,\varphi\rangle+c$, one has $H_-=2c-H_+$ and $\nabla H_-=-\nabla H_+$.

## Statement references

[[def-feature-measure-energy]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and the hypotheses in the Statement.

[F1] Global semiconvexity means that adding a fixed quadratic makes the potential convex on its convex domain. [[def-feature-measure-energy]]

## Proof

**Given:** The data and assumptions in the Statement.

1.1 Fix $s>0$ and two points $\theta_0,\theta_1\in\Theta$. Restrict the semiconvex inequality [F1] to the slice $w=s$ and divide it by $s$. Its quadratic error is bounded by $|\lambda|t(1-t)|\theta_1-\theta_0|^2/(2s)$. Letting $s\to\infty$ gives the convexity inequality for $W$, for every $0\le t\le1$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 If $\Theta=\mathbb R^q$, restrict $W$ to any line. A nonzero secant slope of a convex function forces its values to grow without bound in one of the two directions: for $a<b<c$, convexity makes the secant slope on $[b,c]$ at least that on $[a,b]$, and the reversed assertion treats a negative slope. Boundedness therefore makes every secant slope zero. Any two points lie on a line, so $W$ is constant. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 In the bounded case $W$ attains its maximum at a point $x$ of the compact closure. At an interior maximum $dW_x=0$. At a boundary maximum its tangential differential is zero, because local $C^1$ boundary charts give two-sided differentiable curves in every tangent direction, while the Neumann hypothesis gives zero normal differential. These tangent and normal directions span the ambient space, so again $dW_x=0$. For any $y\in\Theta$, the one-variable convex function $t\mapsto W(x+t(y-x))$ has right derivative $dW_x(y-x)=0$; its secant slope is at least this derivative. Hence $W(y)\ge W(x)$, and maximality gives equality. The final reflected formulas follow by direct differentiation. [step 1.1, given, algebra, step 2.1] ∎

## Source note

This is a consequence of the full inherited global-semiconvexity assumptions, not an added hypothesis restricting the approved claim. Chizat–Bach Assumptions 3.4 alone do not imply the global semiconvexity in their Assumptions 2.1: on $\Theta=[-1,1]$, take $\varphi=0$, $R=0$, and $W(\theta)=2+\cos(\pi\theta)$. These satisfy bounded $C^{1,1}$, positivity, Neumann and dense-regular-value conditions, but $\partial^2_{\theta\theta}V(s,0)=-s\pi^2$ for $s>0$, ruling out any global lower Hessian bound. This diagnoses that source implication; the locally proved result retains the actual full library hypotheses.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a nonempty closed subset of $\mathbb R^k$ and let $\sigma_n,\nu$ be finite signed Borel measures on $X$, with $\int f d\sigma_n\to\int f d\nu$ for every bounded continuous real function $f$ on $X$. Then their total variations have uniformly bounded masses and are uniformly tight. For every bounded norm-continuous map $\phi:X\to H$ into a separable real Hilbert space,
$$\left\|\int\phi d\sigma_n-\int\phi d\nu\right\|_H\longrightarrow0.$$
Also $\|\sigma_n-\nu\|_{BL}\to0$, where the bounded-Lipschitz norm uses $\|f\|_\infty+\operatorname{Lip}(f)\le1$. For every nonnegative $\psi\in C_c(X)$ and bounded nonnegative continuous $W$ on $X$,
$$\int\psi d\nu^+\le\liminf_n\int\psi d\sigma_n^+,\qquad \int Wd|\nu|\le\liminf_n\int Wd|\sigma_n|.$$
Signed Bochner integrals mean the difference of the two Jordan-part integrals. The same conclusions about moments and BL convergence hold as $t\to\infty$ for a narrowly convergent continuous-time family, by the sequential criterion. Here narrow convergence explicitly means convergence against every function in $C_b(X)$, not merely compactly supported tests.

## Statement references

[[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[[def-dependent-choice]]

[[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[[thm-jordan-decomposition-for-signed-measures]]

[[prop-jordan-parts-and-total-variation-formulas-for-signed-measures]]

[[cor-second-countable-lch-locally-finite-borel-measures-are-regular]]

[[thm-uniform-boundedness-principle]]

[[def-bochner-integrable-function]]

[[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and the hypotheses in the Statement.

[F1] Finite signed measures have Jordan/Hahn decompositions under AC, and variation is the sum of the Jordan parts and the supremum of partition sums. [[thm-jordan-decomposition-for-signed-measures]] [[prop-jordan-parts-and-total-variation-formulas-for-signed-measures]]

[F2] Finite Borel measures on the second-countable locally compact space $X$ are regular. [[cor-second-countable-lch-locally-finite-borel-measures-are-regular]]

[F3] A pointwise bounded family of continuous linear maps on a Banach space has uniformly bounded operator norms under DC, supplied by AC. [[thm-uniform-boundedness-principle]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[def-dependent-choice]] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[F4] Bounded strongly measurable functions on a finite measure space are Bochner integrable. [[def-bochner-integrable-function]] [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]

## Proof

**Given:** The data and assumptions in the Statement.

1.1 The supremum-norm space $C_b(X)$ is Banach: a uniformly Cauchy sequence converges pointwise, hence uniformly, and a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous. A signed measure $\sigma$ defines a bounded functional $T_\sigma f=\int f d\sigma$ of norm $|\sigma|(X)$. The upper bound is the variation inequality. For the reverse bound, use [F1] and [F2] to choose disjoint compact subsets of the two Hahn pieces with omitted variation arbitrarily small. The distance formula separating these compacts gives a bounded continuous function equal to $1$ and $-1$ there, with magnitude at most one, whose integral approaches $|\sigma|(X)$. Since $T_{\sigma_n}f$ converges for every $f$, [F3] gives $\sup_n|\sigma_n|(X)<\infty$. [F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 Put $y_n=\sigma_n-\nu$ and suppose their variations are not uniformly tight. Some $\epsilon>0$ then remains outside every compact ball for an arbitrarily late index: each fixed finite set of indices is tight by [F2]. Recursively choose $n_j$ increasing, radii $R_j\to\infty$, and $q_j\in C_c(X)$ with disjoint supports in $\{R_{j-1}<|x|<R_j\}$, $|q_j|\le1$, and $\int q_jdy_{n_j}\ge\epsilon/2$. At stage $j$, choose an index threshold so late that $|\int\sum_{i<j}q_i dy_n|<\epsilon/8$ thereafter, using narrow convergence. Enlarge the exclusion ball to make every earlier-index variation tail smaller than $\epsilon$, and select a later index with tail at least $\epsilon$. Regularity of its positive and negative Hahn pieces and distance cutoffs with compact support in that exterior produce $q_j$ with the required integral. Finally choose $R_j$ larger than its support and with $|y_{n_j}|(X\setminus B_{R_j})<\epsilon/8$. Increasing radii by one leaves gaps between the annuli. The locally finite sum $q=\sum_jq_j$ lies in $C_b(X)$ with $|q|\le1$. Its pairing with $y_{n_j}$ is at least $\epsilon/2-\epsilon/8-\epsilon/8=\epsilon/4$: the earlier terms are small by construction and the entire later sum is bounded by the chosen tail. This contradicts narrow convergence to zero. Thus the variations are uniformly tight. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Given $\delta>0$, choose compact $K$ with $\sup_n|\sigma_n|(X\setminus K)+|\nu|(X\setminus K)<\delta$. On $K$ a finite sum $\phi_\epsilon=\sum_{i=1}^N h_i\psi_i$, with $\psi_i\in C_c(X)$, approximates $\phi$ uniformly within $\epsilon$, and can be chosen with $\|\phi_\epsilon\|_\infty\le\|\phi\|_\infty$. To construct it, cover $K$ by finitely many relative balls on which $\phi$ varies by less than $\epsilon$, use distance cutoffs, normalize their sum near $K$, and multiply by a compact cutoff equal to one on $K$; choose $h_i$ as feature values at the centers. Its integral converges in norm by scalar narrow convergence of the finitely many $\psi_i$. The remaining norm error is at most $\epsilon(|\sigma_n|(X)+|\nu|(X))+2\|\phi\|_\infty(|\sigma_n|(X\setminus K)+|\nu|(X\setminus K))$. Let $\epsilon,\delta\downarrow0$ to prove the Bochner-moment conclusion; [F4] gives existence of all integrals. [F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The restrictions to $K$ of the bounded-Lipschitz unit ball have finite uniform $\epsilon$-nets. Explicitly take a finite $\epsilon$-net of points of $K$, round each function's values there to a rational grid in $[-1,1]$, and use its Lipschitz bound to control the error between those points. Only finitely many rounded value patterns occur; retain one actual function for each occurring pattern. Narrow convergence controls their finitely many pairings, while step 1.1 bounds the uniform approximation error on $K$ and step 2.1 bounds all tail errors. Letting the mesh and tail bound decrease proves BL convergence. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, step 3.1]

5.1 For $0\le q\le\psi$ with $q\in C_c(X)$, $\int\psi d\sigma_n^+\ge\int qd\sigma_n\to\int qd\nu$. The supremum of the last quantity over such $q$ equals $\int\psi d\nu^+$: use the Hahn pieces, compact regular approximation, and distance cutoffs to approximate their sign restriction. Similarly, for $q\in C_c(X)$ with $|q|\le W$, $\int Wd|\sigma_n|\ge\int qd\sigma_n\to\int qd\nu$, and the supremum is $\int Wd|\nu|$. For the lower bound in this supremum, multiply $W$ by a compact cutoff and a continuous function of magnitude at most one that is $1$ and $-1$ on compact subsets of the two Hahn pieces; omitted weighted variation tends to zero by [F2]. These prove the two lower-semicontinuity claims without assuming convergence of Jordan parts. Any failure of a continuous-time moment or BL limit yields a sequence $t_n\to\infty$ contradicting the result just proved. [F1, F2, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Source note

This is a local signed-convergence lemma for the Euclidean interface used in Chizat–Bach Appendix A.1/C.2.2. It is not an imported signed Prokhorov theorem. BL convergence alone on an unbounded domain is not being asserted sufficient for signed narrow convergence without further hypotheses.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\nu$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Then there exist positive
measures $\nu^+,\nu^-:(X,\mathcal A)\to[0,+\infty]$, at least one finite on $X$, such that
$$\nu=\nu^+-\nu^-,$$
and $\nu^+\perp \nu^-$.

These measures are unique: if $\nu=\mu-\eta$ with positive measures
$\mu\perp\eta$, then $\mu=\nu^+$ and $\eta=\nu^-$.

The following conditional assertion is choice-free: if a Hahn partition
$X=P\sqcup N$ is supplied, the formulas $\nu^+(E)=\nu(E\cap P)$ and
$\nu^-(E)=-\nu(E\cap N)$ construct these unique measures. Comparing
two supplied mutually singular positive decompositions also requires no AC.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A signed measure $\nu$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-signed-measure]]). Assume AC for the general existence assertion ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]); for the conditional assertion a Hahn partition is supplied.

[L1] Under AC, Hahn decomposition gives measurable sets $P,N$ with $P\sqcup N=X$, $P$ positive, and $N$ negative, unique up to null sets. ([[thm-hahn-decomposition-for-signed-measures]])

[L2] Mutual singularity means that the two set functions vanish on measurable subsets of complementary measurable pieces. ([[def-mutually-singular-measures]])

[L3] A measure is a nonnegative countably additive set function on a sigma-algebra. ([[def-measure]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For the general existence assertion, obtain a Hahn partition from [L1]; this invokes AC through the Hahn theorem's optimizing choices and its positive-subset lemma. For the conditional assertion start with the supplied partition instead. Define $\nu^+(E)=\nu(E\cap P)$ and $\nu^-(E)=-\nu(E\cap N)$. The signs follow from [[def-positive-negative-and-null-sets-for-a-signed-measure]], and countable additivity and the empty-set value follow from those of $\nu$, so these are positive measures by [L3]. [given, L1, L3]

2.1 At least one of $\nu^+(X)=\nu(P)$ and $\nu^-(X)=-\nu(N)$ is finite, since otherwise $\nu$ would take both infinite signs. By positivity the same side is finite on every measurable $E$. Thus the difference is always defined, and finite additivity gives $\nu(E)=\nu^+(E)-\nu^-(E)$. The defining formulas give $\nu^+(N)=\nu^-(P)=0$, hence mutual singularity by [L2]. [step 1.1, L2, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $\nu=\mu-\eta$ with positive mutually singular measures, with the displayed difference defined on every measurable set. Take one witnessing partition $P',N'$ from [L2]. On subsets of $P'$ one has $\nu=\mu\ge0$, and on subsets of $N'$ one has $\nu=-\eta\le0$. Thus this is another Hahn partition. A measurable subset of $P\setminus P'$ lies in positive $P$ and negative $N'$, so has value zero; the same holds on $P'\setminus P$. Splitting between these differences shows they are null sets. This comparison uses only the supplied partitions, not Hahn existence or further AC. [step 2.1, L2, algebra]

4.1 For every measurable $E$, $\mu(E)=\mu(E\cap P')=\nu(E\cap P')=\nu(E\cap P)=\nu^+(E)$: the first equality uses vanishing on $N'$, and the middle change of sets discards only the null differences from step 3.1. Similarly $\eta(E)=-\nu(E\cap N)=\nu^-(E)$. There is no subtraction of two infinite quantities. Hence the parts are unique; steps 1.1–4.1 also prove the choice-free conditional assertion because AC was used only to obtain the initial arbitrary Hahn partition. [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every Borel measure finite on compact sets on a second-countable LCH space is regular.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), $X$ is second-countable and LCH, and $\mu$ is finite on compact sets.

[L1] An LCH space has a base of open sets with compact closure. ([[lem-a-locally-compact-hausdorff-space-has-a-base-of-open-sets-with-compact-closure]])

[L2] Under Countable Choice, if every open set is sigma-compact, compact-finite Borel measures are regular ([[thm-locally-finite-borel-measures-are-regular-when-open-sets-are-sigma-compact]]). The stated choice assumption is spent only in this theorem.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $(B_n)$ be a given countable base and let $U$ be open. Take all indices $n$ for which $\overline{B_n}$ is compact and contained in $U$; this is a specified subfamily of the given base and needs no selection. For each $x\in U$, [L1] gives an open $W$ with $x\in W\subseteq\overline W\subseteq U$ and $\overline W$ compact. Choose one $B_n$ with $x\in B_n\subseteq W$; its closure is a closed subset of the compact $\overline W$, hence compact and contained in $U$. Thus the selected subfamily covers $U$, and $U$ is the union of the corresponding countably many compact closures. [L1, given, construct]

2.1 Thus every open set is sigma-compact. Apply [L2] under the stated Countable Choice premise to obtain regularity of $\mu$. [step 1.1, L2, given] ∎

## Definition

Let $d\ge1$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and let $f:\overline U\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuous. For $y\notin f(\partial U)$ the set $K=f^{-1}(\{y\})\cap U$ is compact in $U$: its closure preimage is closed in the compact set $\overline U$ and avoids $\partial U$. Give $U$ its standard orientation. Let $[U]_K\in H_d(U,U\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$ be the unique relative orientation class restricting to the standard local orientation generator at each $x\in K$; for $K=\varnothing$ use the zero class. Let $[\mathbb R^d]_{\{y\}}$ be the positive generator of $H_d(\mathbb R^d,\mathbb R^d\setminus\{y\};\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. The bounded-domain degree is the integer $\deg(f,U,y)$ determined by

$$f_*[U]_K=\deg(f,U,y)[\mathbb R^d]_{\{y\}},$$

where $f$ is regarded as a map of pairs $(U,U\setminus K)\to(\mathbb R^d,\mathbb R^d\setminus\{y\})$. The following local lemma proves that this definition is well-defined and has the required normalization, additivity, and moving-target homotopy properties.

## Definition

Assume AC for the flow clause below. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\rho_X)$ be an input probability space, let $\mathcal H=L^2(\rho_X)$, let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be measurable, and put $\Theta=\mathbb R^{p+1}$ for hidden affine parameters $\theta=(w,b)$. Assume $\phi_\theta(x)=\sigma(w\cdot x+b)$ belongs to $\mathcal H$ for each $\theta$. On $\Omega=\mathbb R\times\Theta$, define the feature map $\Phi(a,w,b)=a\phi_{(w,b)}\in\mathcal H$. For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\Omega$ for which the Bochner integral exists, its particle-measure predictor is

$$f_\mu=\int_\Omega \Phi(u)\,d\mu(u)\in\mathcal H.$$

The corresponding objective is $F(\mu)=R(f_\mu)+\int_\Omega V\,d\mu$, whenever the scalar integral is finite, with $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ a risk functional and $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ a regularizer. For the empirical particle law defined on measurable $A\subseteq\Omega$ by $\mu_m(A)=m^{-1}\#\{j:(m a_j,w_j,b_j)\in A\}$, one has $f_{\mu_m}(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\sigma(w_j\cdot x+b_j)$, so a finite one-hidden-layer network is a particle-measure predictor (with an optional constant output bias added separately). A feature-energy Wasserstein gradient flow means an $AC^2_{\rm loc}$ curve of probability measures satisfying the finite-action continuity equation with Borel velocity equal almost everywhere to the negative minimum-norm element of the constrained subdifferential of the first-variation potential. This is the earlier model-flow definition; no existence or uniqueness follows from this definition. The flow use below requires all of the feature-energy regularity hypotheses. In particular, the classical ReLU feature map is not asserted here to meet those hypotheses merely because it is positively homogeneous.

## Definition

Assume AC. Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable space, let $\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be convex and differentiable, let $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ be bounded and strongly measurable, and let $\widetilde V:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded and measurable. For each finite signed measure $\nu$ on $\Theta$ with $|\nu|(\Theta)<\infty$, write $\nu=\nu^+-\nu^-$ for its Jordan decomposition into mutually singular finite nonnegative measures, so $|\nu|=\nu^++\nu^-$. Define $m_\nu:=\int\varphi d\nu:=\int\varphi d\nu^+-\int\varphi d\nu^-$. Both Bochner integrals exist because $\varphi$ is bounded and strongly measurable and $\nu^+,\nu^-$ are finite. Scalar integrals against $\nu$ use the corresponding signed-measure integral. Assume $\Phi(w,\theta)=w\varphi(\theta)$ and $V(w,\theta)=|w|\widetilde V(\theta)$. Define

$J(\nu)=R\!\left(\int_\Theta\varphi\,d\nu\right)+\int_\Theta\widetilde V\,d|\nu|.$

For every finite nonnegative measure $\mu$ on $(\mathbb R\times\Theta,\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal T)$ with $\int|w|d\mu<\infty$ and $h^1(\mu)=\nu$, its feature moment and penalty are $m_\nu$ and $\int|w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu$, respectively, and its feature energy is

$F(\mu)=R\left(\int w\varphi(\theta)d\mu\right)+\int|w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu.$

Then $F(\mu)\ge J(\nu)$. Equality is attained by the finite nonnegative measure $\mu_\nu$ defined on measurable $A\subseteq\mathbb R\times\Theta$ by

$\mu_\nu(A)=\nu^+(\{\theta:(1,\theta)\in A\})+\nu^-(\{\theta:(-1,\theta)\in A\}).$

Thus $J(\nu)=\inf\{F(\mu):\mu\ge0,\ \int|w|d\mu<\infty,\ h^1(\mu)=\nu\}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the model, a finite signed measure $\nu$, and the signed projection in the Definition.

[A1] AC supplies the Jordan decomposition of each finite signed measure. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[thm-jordan-decomposition-for-signed-measures]]

[F1] $h^1(\mu)=\alpha_\mu-\beta_\mu$, with $\alpha_\mu(\Theta)+\beta_\mu(\Theta)=\int|w|d\mu$; for every bounded measurable scalar $\psi$, its pairing is $\int\psi dh^1(\mu)=\int w\psi(\theta)d\mu$, and $h^1(\mu)$ has finite total variation. [[def-partial-one-homogeneous-measure-projection]]

[F2] A bounded linear map commutes with Bochner integration, so feature moments are determined by all scalar evaluations. [[thm-bounded-linear-maps-commute-with-bochner-integration]]

[F5] Signed integrals are defined by approximation with simple functions; bounded strongly measurable functions are integrable against finite signed measures. [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]

[F3] Total variation is the supremum of the sums over countable measurable partitions. [[def-total-variation-of-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]

[F4] The nonnegative integral is monotone. [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]

[F7] For the Jordan decomposition, total variation satisfies $|\nu|=\nu^++\nu^-$. [[prop-jordan-parts-and-total-variation-formulas-for-signed-measures]]

[F6] Strongly measurable Banach-valued functions with integrable norm have Bochner integrals defined by simple-function approximation. [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]

## Proof

**Given:** AC, $\mu$, and $\nu=h^1(\mu)$ as in the Definition.

1.1 Let $\alpha,\beta$ be the raw measures in [F1]. For every countable measurable partition $(B_j)$ of a measurable set $B$, $\sum_j|\nu(B_j)|=\sum_j|\alpha(B_j)-\beta(B_j)|\le\alpha(B)+\beta(B)$. Taking the supremum in [F3] gives $|\nu|(B)\le(\alpha+\beta)(B)$. For a nonnegative simple $\widetilde V$, the definitions of $\alpha,\beta$ give $\int\widetilde Vd(\alpha+\beta)=\int|w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu$. If $M$ bounds $\widetilde V$, partition $[0,M]$ into finitely many intervals of length at most $1/n$ and assign an endpoint on each measurable inverse image. This gives nonnegative simple $V_n$ with $\|V_n-\widetilde V\|_\infty\le1/n$. The error on the left is at most $(\alpha(\Theta)+\beta(\Theta))/n$, and the error on the right is at most $\int|w|d\mu/n$; these bounds agree because $\alpha(\Theta)+\beta(\Theta)=\int|w|d\mu$. Taking $n\to\infty$ proves the identity for $\widetilde V$. Monotonicity [F4] and the measure domination, with $|\nu|$ a measure by [F7], give $\int\widetilde Vd|\nu|\le\int\widetilde Vd(\alpha+\beta)=\int|w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu$. [A1, F1, F3, F4, F7, given, algebra]

2.1 For every $z\in\mathcal H$, set $\psi_z(\theta)=\langle z,\varphi(\theta)\rangle$. For a finite-valued simple $\psi_z$, equality $h^1(\mu)=\nu$ and the signed simple-integral definition give $\int\psi_zdh^1(\mu)=\int\psi_zd\nu$. The measure $\lambda=\alpha_\mu+\beta_\mu+\nu^++\nu^-$ is finite by [F1] and [F7]. The bounded strongly measurable feature is Bochner integrable with respect to $\lambda$ by [F6], so simple approximants in $L^1(\lambda)$ extend the scalar integral equality to $\psi_z$; the signed-integral definition [F5] gives the same approximation for $\int\psi_zd\nu$. The raw pairing [F1] now gives $\int w\psi_z(\theta)d\mu=\int\psi_zd\nu$. By [F2], these are respectively $\langle z,\int w\varphi d\mu\rangle$ and $\langle z,\int\varphi d\nu\rangle$, so equality for every $z$ proves equality of feature moments. Adding the risk term to step 1.1 proves $F(\mu)\ge J(\nu)$. The section maps $\theta\mapsto(1,\theta)$ and $\theta\mapsto(-1,\theta)$ are measurable: preimages of measurable rectangles are either empty or measurable subsets of $\Theta$. Their preimages preserve disjoint unions, so the displayed formula defines a finite nonnegative measure, of mass $\nu^+(\Theta)+\nu^-(\Theta)=|\nu|(\Theta)$. The definition of $h^1$ gives $h^1(\mu_\nu)=\nu^+-\nu^- =\nu$ by [A1]. Direct integration on the two sections gives $\int|w|\widetilde Vd\mu_\nu=\int\widetilde Vd\nu^++\int\widetilde Vd\nu^-=\int\widetilde Vd|\nu|$ and $\int w\varphi d\mu_\nu=\int\varphi d\nu^+-\int\varphi d\nu^-=m_\nu$. Hence $F(\mu_\nu)=J(\nu)$. This proves the infimum identity and its attainment. [A1, F1, F2, F5, F6, F7, step 1.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Because
$|\nu|$ is a measure ([[thm-total-variation-is-a-measure]]), define
$$L^1(\nu):=L^1(|\nu|)$$
using the published meaning of $L^1$ from [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]].

If $f\in L^1(\nu)$, choose complex simple functions $s_n$ as in
[[thm-l-one-functions-admit-dominated-complex-simple-approximations]] with
$\int |f-s_n|\,d|\nu|\to0$. The simple-integral bound
[[prop-simple-integrals-are-bounded-by-total-variation]] makes
$(\int s_n\,d\nu)$ a Cauchy sequence in $\mathbb C$, and its limit is
independent of the chosen approximating sequence. Define
$$\int f\,d\nu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int s_n\,d\nu.$$

For a measurable set $E\in\mathcal A$, define
$$\int_E f\,d\nu:=\int f\mathbf 1_E\,d\nu.$$

## Definition

Let $d\ge2$, let $\rho_X$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^{d-1}$ with finite second moment, and define $s(t)=t|t|$ and $\sigma(t)=\max(t,0)$. For $\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_d)\in\mathbb R^d$, define the signed-square ReLU feature in $L^2(\rho_X)$ by

$$\Phi(\theta)(x)=\sigma\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}s(\theta_j)x_j+s(\theta_d)\right).$$

The two-copy parameterization uses this feature on one copy of $\mathbb R^d$ and its negative on the other copy; nonnegative measures on the disjoint union represent signed linear combinations of these features. The scalar signed-square map is continuously differentiable with derivative $s'(t)=2|t|$. This definition asserts differentiability of the resulting $L^2$ feature map only when its data law has the additional regularity needed for that conclusion; it does not assert that its differential is locally Lipschitz.

## Statement

Assume AC, the full feature-energy hypotheses on $\Omega=\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge2$, and positive two-homogeneity of $\Phi$ and $V$. Let $\mu_t$ be the resulting Wasserstein gradient flow on $[0,T]$. If $K=\operatorname{spt}\mu_0$ is compact, is contained in $B(0,r_b)$, and separates $r_a\mathbb S^{d-1}$ from $r_b\mathbb S^{d-1}$ for $0<r_a<r_b$, then for every $t\in[0,T]$ the support $\operatorname{spt}\mu_t$ separates $r'_a\mathbb S^{d-1}$ from $r'_b\mathbb S^{d-1}$ for some $0<r'_a<r'_b$ depending on the flow and $T$. Here separation means that every continuous path with endpoints on the two spheres intersects the stated support.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The flow, its characteristic map, and the initial support in the Statement.

[F1] On finite time intervals the energy flow exists and the energy decreases, so $R(m_{\mu_t})$ stays in the initial sublevel because $V\ge0$. [[thm-global-wasserstein-flow-existence-uniqueness-and-stability]]

[F2] For a continuous moment path the characteristic inclusion has a unique forward solution and a continuous characteristic map; the same supplier states W2 stability for finite-action continuity-equation solutions. [[lem-characteristics-unique-and-stable]]

[F3] A finite-action continuity-equation solution has a path law concentrated on AC trajectories solving its velocity equation. [[thm-superposition-for-finite-action-continuity-equations]]

[F4] For a continuous map, the support of the pushforward of a finite measure is the closure of the image of its support. [[lem-pushforward-support-is-closure-of-image]]

[F5] The relative-homology degree is normalized, additive, nonzero only when there is a preimage, and invariant under homotopies whose moving target avoids the boundary image. [[lem-bounded-domain-degree-properties]]

[A1] AC supplies the Wasserstein flow, superposition representation, and minimum-norm characteristic constructions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

**Given:** AC, the two-homogeneous feature-energy flow, and $K$ as in the Statement.

1.1 Since $R(m_{\mu_t})\le F(\mu_0)$, $\|dR_{m_{\mu_t}}\|$ is bounded on $[0,T]$ by [F1]. Differentiating $\Phi(ru)=r^2\Phi(u)$ gives $d\Phi_{ru}=r\,d\Phi_u$. If $\zeta\in\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$, substitute $y=rz$ into its defining inequality and use $V(rz)=r^2V(z)$; division by $r^2$ shows $r\zeta\in\partial_{\lambda_V}V(ru)$, and applying the same argument with $1/r$ proves equality of the scaled subdifferentials. The feature-energy bounds on the unit sphere therefore imply $|v_t(u)|\le C|u|$ uniformly on $[0,T]$. Along a characteristic, $r(t)=|X_t(u_0)|$ obeys $|r'(t)|\le Cr(t)$ whenever $r(t)>0$. Grönwall gives $e^{-Ct}|u_0|\le|X_t(u_0)|\le e^{Ct}|u_0|$; the lower bound prevents a nonzero trajectory from reaching zero, while two-homogeneity fixes the zero trajectory. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], the flow law has a path-space representation concentrated on AC trajectories solving its velocity equation, with initial law $\mu_0$. Each such path solves the nonautonomous characteristic inclusion for the moment path $m_{\mu_t}$; uniqueness in [F2] makes it $t\mapsto X_t(x)$ from its initial point $x$. Therefore $\mu_t=(X_t)_\#\mu_0$. The compact set $K$ has compact image $X_t(K)$; [F4] gives $\operatorname{spt}\mu_t=\overline{X_t(K)}=X_t(K)$. Continuity on $[0,T]\times K$ makes $M_K=\sup_{s\le T,u\in K}|X_s(u)|$ finite. [A1, F2, F3, F4, given, step 1.1]

3.1 Let $C_\infty$ be the unbounded component of $\mathbb R^d\setminus K$. It is unique because the complement of a sufficiently large ball is connected. It is an open connected subset of Euclidean space, hence path connected: small open balls show that each path component is open, and its complement, being a union of the other path components, is open as well. No point of $C_\infty$ lies in $B(0,r_a)$: a path in $C_\infty$ from such a point to a point outside $B(0,r_b)$ would contain a subpath from $r_a\mathbb S^{d-1}$ to $r_b\mathbb S^{d-1}$ lying in $C_\infty$ and avoiding $K$, contrary to the initial separation. Choose $\alpha>\max(r_b,M_K)$ and then $\beta>e^{CT}\alpha$. Set $A=B(0,\beta)\cap C_\infty$. Its boundary lies in $K\cup\beta\mathbb S^{d-1}$, and $A\cap B(0,r_a)=\partial A\cap B(0,r_a)=\varnothing$. [A1, given, choose, step 2.1]

4.1 For $y\in\alpha\mathbb S^{d-1}$, $y\in A$ and $X_s(\partial A)$ avoids $y$ for all $s\le T$: $X_s(K)\subset B(0,M_K)\subset B(0,\alpha)$, while the radial lower bound sends $\beta\mathbb S^{d-1}$ outside $B(0,\alpha)$. Homotopy invariance [F5] gives $D(X_t,A,y)=D(\operatorname{id},A,y)=1$. Choose $0<\eta<e^{-CT}r_a$. For every $y\in B(0,\eta)$ and $x\in\partial A$, $|X_s(x)|\ge e^{-Cs}|x|\ge e^{-CT}r_a>\eta$, so the target avoids $X_s(\partial A)$. Since $B(0,r_a)\cap A=\varnothing$, the identity degree there is zero; hence $D(X_t,A,y)=0$. [A1, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1]

5.1 Consider any path from $\eta\mathbb S^{d-1}$ to $\alpha\mathbb S^{d-1}$ and stop it the first time it reaches $\alpha\mathbb S^{d-1}$. Before that time it stays in $\overline{B(0,\alpha)}$, which is disjoint from $X_t(\beta\mathbb S^{d-1})$. If the stopped path avoided $X_t(K)$, then $\partial A\subset K\cup\beta\mathbb S^{d-1}$ would imply that it avoided $X_t(\partial A)$. The degree along that moving target path would be constant by [F5], contradicting its endpoint values $0$ and $1$ from step 4.1. Thus every such path meets $X_t(K)=\operatorname{spt}\mu_t$, proving separation. [A1, F5, step 2.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge2$, let $\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, and let $\Phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathcal H$ and $V:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and positively two-homogeneous. For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\lambda$ on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite second moment, define the feature-measure energy
$$F(\lambda):=R\!\left(\int_{\mathbb R^d}\Phi(u)d\lambda(u)\right)+\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(u)d\lambda(u).$$
The integrals are finite because the continuous two-homogeneous maps grow at most quadratically. For every such $\mu$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\Phi(u)d\mu(u)=\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}\Phi(\theta)dh^2(\mu)(\theta),\qquad\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(u)d\mu(u)=\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}V(\theta)dh^2(\mu)(\theta).$$

If $(\mu_n)$ is a sequence of such measures and $h^2(\mu_n)$ converges weakly as finite measures on the compact sphere to a finite nonnegative measure $\nu$, then the feature integrals converge in Hilbert norm, the regularizer integrals converge, and $F(\mu_n)\to R(\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}\Phi d\nu)+\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}Vd\nu$. The continuity of $R$ is the risk premise used for this energy conclusion; it holds in particular under the feature-energy hypotheses.

For the partially one-homogeneous model, let $\Theta$ be a closed Euclidean subset, let $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ be bounded and norm-continuous into a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\widetilde V:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded and measurable. Put $\Phi(w,\theta)=w\varphi(\theta)$ and $V(w,\theta)=|w|\widetilde V(\theta)$. For every finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R\times\Theta$ with $\int|w|d\mu<\infty$ and every $z\in\mathcal H$, the exact feature identity is
$$\left\langle z,\int w\varphi(\theta)d\mu\right\rangle=\int\langle z,\varphi(\theta)\rangle dh^1(\mu),$$
using the scalar pairing defined in the partial projection, and the penalty inequality is $\int|w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu\ge\int\widetilde Vdh^1(\mu)$. Define the lifted energy in this model by $F(\mu)=R(\int w\varphi(\theta)d\mu)+\int|w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu$. If finite signed projections $h^1(\mu_n)$ converge narrowly to $\nu$, meaning convergence against every bounded continuous real test on $\Theta$, then their feature moments converge weakly in $\mathcal H$ when $\varphi$ is bounded and continuous. If AC holds, then for closed Euclidean $\Theta$ and bounded norm-continuous $\varphi$ into a separable Hilbert space, they converge in Hilbert norm. Signed projection convergence alone does not imply penalty or full energy convergence for arbitrary lifts.
