## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two projection definitions and the hypotheses in the Statement.

[F1] $h^2(\mu)(A)=\int_{u\ne0}\mathbf1_A(u/|u|)|u|^2d\mu(u)$ is a finite measure on $\mathbb S^{d-1}$. [[def-two-homogeneous-measure-projection]]

[F2] For every bounded measurable scalar $\psi$, the projection pairing is $\int\psi dh^1(\mu)=\int w\psi(\theta)d\mu$, and $h^1(\mu)$ is a finite signed measure. [[def-partial-one-homogeneous-measure-projection]]

[F3] A bounded linear map commutes with Bochner integration, so equality of all scalar evaluations by elements of $\mathcal H^*$ determines equality of the Hilbert-valued integrals. [[thm-bounded-linear-maps-commute-with-bochner-integration]]

[F4] Under AC, signed narrow convergence on a closed Euclidean subset controls bounded norm-continuous Bochner moments in norm. [[lem-signed-narrow-convergence-controls-bochner-moments]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

**Given:** The measures and feature maps in the Statement.

1.1 On $\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}$, write $u=|u|\rho(u)$. Positive two-homogeneity gives $\Phi(u)=|u|^2\Phi(\rho(u))$ and $V(u)=|u|^2V(\rho(u))$; at $u=0$ both vanish. Integrating these identities and applying the definition of $h^2$ proves both displayed projection identities. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For weak convergence on the compact sphere, the masses $h^2(\mu_n)(\mathbb S^{d-1})$ are bounded. The continuous map $\Phi|_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}$ has compact image in $\mathcal H$. Given $\epsilon>0$, choose finitely many vectors $g_j=\Phi(\theta_j)$ whose open $\epsilon$-balls cover that image and put $U_j=\{\theta:\|\Phi(\theta)-g_j\|<\epsilon\}$. Define $r_j(\theta)=\operatorname{dist}(\theta,\mathbb S^{d-1}\setminus U_j)$ when the complement is nonempty, and $r_j\equiv1$ when $U_j=\mathbb S^{d-1}$. The continuous functions $\psi_j=r_j/(\sum_i r_i)$ are well-defined because the finite open sets cover the sphere, and $\psi_j(\theta)>0$ only when $\theta\in U_j$. Therefore $\|Phi(\theta)-\sum_j\psi_j(\theta)g_j\|<\epsilon$ uniformly. Weak convergence gives convergence of each scalar coefficient $\int\psi_jdh^2(\mu_n)$, hence strong convergence of the approximating vector integrals. The uniform approximation error is at most $\epsilon$ times the uniformly bounded masses, so $\int\Phi dh^2(\mu_n)\to\int\Phi d\nu$ in norm. Since $V|_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}$ is continuous, weak convergence also gives $\int Vdh^2(\mu_n)\to\int Vd\nu$. Continuity of $R$ proves the energy limit. [F1, given, choose, step 1.1]

3.1 In the partially one-homogeneous case, fix $z\in\mathcal H$ and apply [F2] to the bounded scalar function $\psi(\theta)=\langle z,\varphi(\theta)\rangle$. This gives the displayed feature identity for every $z$, hence equality of the Hilbert-valued feature moments because inner products determine vectors. For the penalty, $|w|-w=2w_-\ge0$, and [F2] applied to $\widetilde V$ gives $\int |w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu-\int\widetilde Vdh^1(\mu)=2\int w_-\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu\ge0.$ If $h^1(\mu_n)$ converges against bounded continuous scalar tests, testing against $\langle z,\varphi(\cdot)\rangle$ for each $z\in\mathcal H$ proves weak convergence of the feature moments. Under the additional AC, closed-Euclidean, separable-Hilbert assumptions in the Statement, [F4] improves this to norm convergence. Let $\mu_1$ assign mass one to $(1,\theta)$ and let $\mu_2$ assign mass two to $(1,\theta)$ and mass one to $(-1,\theta)$. Then both have $h^1$ equal to the measure assigning mass one to $\theta$, while their $|w|$ penalties for $\widetilde V\equiv1$ are $1$ and $3$, respectively. Thus $h^1$ convergence alone cannot imply penalty or energy convergence. [F2, F3, F4, given, algebra, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\mu_n,\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$, with $W_2(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$. Then $h^2(\mu_n)$ converges weakly as finite measures on $\mathbb S^{d-1}$ to $h^2(\mu)$. More generally, if $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ is closed and $\mu_n,\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R\times\Theta)$ converge in W2, with first coordinate $w\in\mathbb R$, then $h^1(\mu_n)$ converges weakly as finite signed measures against every bounded continuous test on $\Theta$ to $h^1(\mu)$.

[[def-two-homogeneous-measure-projection]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The quadratic transportation convergence and the projection definitions in the Statement.

[A1] AC supplies the couplings with cost tending to the W2 infimum used in the truncation proof. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] $W_2(\mu_n,\mu)^2$ is the infimum of $\int|x-y|^2d\pi$ over couplings; AC permits a coupling with cost at most $W_2^2+1/n^2$. [[def-wasserstein-two-space-and-couplings]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F2] For continuous $f$ on the sphere, $\int f\,dh^2(\alpha)=\int_{u\ne0}|u|^2f(u/|u|)d\alpha(u)$. For bounded continuous $\psi$ on $\Theta$, $\int\psi\,dh^1(\alpha)=\int w\psi(\theta)d\alpha$. [[def-two-homogeneous-measure-projection]] [[def-partial-one-homogeneous-measure-projection]]

[F3] The family $\mu_n$ has uniformly bounded second moments, and the chosen couplings $\pi_n$ have quadratic displacement tending to zero, by the W2 convergence and coupling-cost choice in [F1].

## Proof

**Given:** AC, the measures, and [F1]–[F3].

1.1 Let $(X_n,Y_n)$ have joint law $\pi_n$ and write $D_n=X_n-Y_n$. AC supplies the sequence of couplings in [A1]. Then $\mathbb E|D_n|^2\to0$, and $\sup_n\mathbb E|X_n|^2<\infty$ by $|X_n|^2\le2|Y_n|^2+2|D_n|^2$. For bounded continuous $\psi$, the function $H(w,\theta)=w\psi(\theta)$ is continuous on the closed Euclidean subspace $\mathbb R\times\Theta$ and has at most linear growth. Multiplying $H$ by a continuous radial cutoff of compact support in that closed subspace gives a uniformly continuous function, so convergence in probability of $D_n$ gives convergence of its expectations. The truncation error is uniformly small because $\mathbb E[|X_n|1_{|X_n|>R}]\le R^{-1}\mathbb E|X_n|^2$ and the same bound holds for $Y_n$. Hence $\mathbb EH(X_n)-\mathbb EH(Y_n)\to0$. By [F2], this is weak convergence of $h^1(\mu_n)$ against every such $\psi$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Fix continuous $f$ on $\mathbb S^{d-1}$ and set $\Psi_f(0)=0$, $\Psi_f(u)=|u|^2f(u/|u|)$ for $u\ne0$. This function is continuous and $|\Psi_f(u)|\le\|f\|_\infty|u|^2$. The quadratic moments are asymptotically uniformly integrable: if $|X_n|>R$, then either $|Y_n|>R/2$ or $|D_n|>R/2$. Using [A1], $|X_n|^2\le2|Y_n|^2+2|D_n|^2$, and splitting the term $|Y_n|^2\mathbf1_{|D_n|>R/2}$ at $|Y_n|=R/2$ gives $$\mathbb E[|X_n|^2\mathbf1_{|X_n|>R}]\le4\mathbb E|D_n|^2+4\mathbb E[|Y_n|^2\mathbf1_{|Y_n|>R/2}].$$ The right side tends uniformly to zero in the limit $n\to\infty$ followed by $R\to\infty$; the same estimate applies to $Y_n=Y$. A compactly supported continuous truncation of $\Psi_f$ has convergent integrals because it is uniformly continuous and $D_n\to0$ in probability. The asymptotic tail bound makes the truncation error tend to zero. Hence $\int\Psi_fd\mu_n\to\int\Psi_fd\mu$, which is weak convergence of $h^2(\mu_n)$ by [F2]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume that for every fixed $t$, $W_2(\mu_{m,t},\mu_t)\to0$ as $m\to\infty$, with both laws concentrated on a common cutoff for that finite time. Then both iterated limits exist and

$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\lim_{m\to\infty}F(\mu_{m,t})=\lim_{m\to\infty}\lim_{t\to\infty}F(\mu_{m,t})=F^*.$$

This is qualitative and gives no rate uniform in $m$ or $t$.

## Statement

Assume AC, a separable real Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, and the feature-energy hypotheses: $R$ is convex and differentiable with locally Lipschitz differential bounded on sublevels, $\Phi$ is Fr\acute{e}chet differentiable, $V$ is semiconvex, and the nested cutoff sets and derivative-growth bounds in the feature-energy definition hold. Let $d\ge2$, $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^{d-1}$, $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ be bounded and continuously differentiable with Lipschitz differential, and $\widetilde V:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded and continuously differentiable with Lipschitz differential; set $\Phi(w,\theta)=w\varphi(\theta)$ and $V(w,\theta)=|w|\widetilde V(\theta)$. For every $f\in\mathcal H$, require dense regular values for $G_f(\theta)=\langle f,\varphi(\theta)\rangle+\widetilde V(\theta)$. Retain either (i) $\Theta$ is the closure of a nonempty bounded connected open convex set with $C^1$ boundary and $dG_f(\theta)[n_\theta]=0$ on $\partial\Theta$ for every $f\in\mathcal H$, or (ii) $\Theta=\mathbb R^{d-1}$ and for every $f\in\mathcal H$, $G_f(r\cdot)$ converges uniformly in $C^1(\mathbb S^{d-2})$ to a limit with dense regular values as $r\to\infty$. Let $\nu$ be a finite signed projection with nonoptimal relaxed objective $J(\nu)$, set $m_\nu=\int\varphi d\nu$ by the signed Bochner-integral convention in the relaxed-objective definition, and define $G_+(\theta)=dR_{m_\nu}[\varphi(\theta)]+\widetilde V(\theta)$ and $G_-(\theta)=-dR_{m_\nu}[\varphi(\theta)]+\widetilde V(\theta)$. Assume at least one of $G_+,G_-$ is negative somewhere, as is necessary for a nonempty negative cone. Let $I\subseteq\{+,-\}$ be the nonempty set of signs with a negative value, choose a negative regular level $-\eta_s$ for each $s\in I$, and put $K_s=\{G_s\le-\eta_s\}$ for $s\in I$ and $K_s=\varnothing$ otherwise. For a finite signed measure $\sigma$ on $\Theta$, define

$$\|\sigma\|_{BL(\Theta)}:=\sup\left\{\left|\int f d\sigma\right|:f:\Theta\to\mathbb R,\ \|f\|_\infty+\operatorname{Lip}(f)\le1\right\},$$

where $\|f\|_\infty:=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|f(\theta)|$ and $\operatorname{Lip}(f):=\sup_{\theta\ne\theta'}|f(\theta)-f(\theta')|/|\theta-\theta'|$ for Euclidean distance, taking $0$ when there are no distinct points. Set $A=(\mathbb R_{>0}\times K_+)\cup(\mathbb R_{<0}\times K_-)$. There is $\epsilon>0$ such that if $\|h^1(\mu_{t_0})-\nu\|_{BL(\Theta)}<\epsilon$ and $\mu_{t_0}(A)>0$ for a Wasserstein gradient flow $\mu_t$, then for some $t_1>t_0$,

$$\|h^1(\mu_{t_1})-\nu\|_{BL(\Theta)}\ge\epsilon.$$

The statement retains both sign branches and both source boundary alternatives.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and the full hypotheses in the Statement.

[F1] The full globally semiconvex partial-model hypotheses imply $\widetilde V\equiv c\ge0$; in particular $G_-=2c-G_+$ and their angular gradients are opposite. The bounded branch uses the Neumann premise for $f=0$. [[lem-partial-homogeneous-penalty-is-constant-under-global-hypotheses]]

[F2] A negative inner sublevel of either sign function has a larger negative outer trap, robust under all sufficiently close time-dependent forcing, in both the bounded and compactified unbounded branches. [[lem-partial-homogeneous-negative-level-trapping]]

[F3] Every flow in the definition has finite total squared action and a superposition by its characteristic paths, without a bounded-initial-weight assumption. [[lem-partial-feature-flow-moment-and-energy-identities]] [[thm-superposition-for-finite-action-continuity-equations]]

[F4] Feature moments factor through the signed projection, not its individual raw or Jordan components. [[def-partial-one-homogeneous-measure-projection]] [[def-partial-homogeneous-relaxed-objective]]

## Proof

**Given:** The flow and signed projection in the Statement.

1.1 Boundedness and Lipschitz differential of $\varphi$ give a finite $C_\varphi=\|\varphi\|_\infty+\|D\varphi\|_\infty$ on either domain alternative. For any finite signed $\sigma$, test its BL norm with $\langle z,\varphi\rangle/C_\varphi$ for unit $z$ to obtain $\|\int\varphi d\sigma\|\le C_\varphi\|\sigma\|_{BL}$ (if $C_\varphi=0$ the assertion is immediate). Local Lipschitz continuity of $\nabla R$ near $m_\nu$ then bounds $\|f_t-f_\nu\|$ by $C\|h^1(\mu_t)-\nu\|_{BL}$ whenever this BL distance is small. This is a norm bound on the Hilbert forcing, on bounded and unbounded $\Theta$ alike. [F4, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F1] write $\widetilde V=c$. Apply [F2] to each nonempty $K_s$ using its level $-\eta_s$ as the inner threshold; if necessary choose a regular outer level strictly between that threshold and zero, also regular for the sphere limit in the unbounded case. The common forcing radius $\rho>0$ and constant $b>0$ can be chosen for the at most two branches. Whenever $\|f_t-f_\nu\|<\rho$, every favorable characteristic starting with $z=s w>0$ and $\theta\in K_s$ stays in the corresponding outer negative trap, satisfies $z'=-G_{s,t}(\theta)\ge b$, and retains its sign. Indeed its angular equation is $\theta'=-z\nabla G_{s,t}$, and time change by the positive factor $z/k(\theta)$ gives precisely the normalized curve in [F2]. On each finite interval all quantities are finite and $z\ge z(t_0)>0$, so this time change is legitimate; if its total normalized time is finite, the same trap follows on every finite physical interval. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Choose $\epsilon>0$ so that step 1.1 sends BL distance less than $\epsilon$ into the forcing ball in step 2.1. Suppose, to the contrary, that after $t_0$ this distance always remains less than $\epsilon$. By hypothesis the set of superposed paths starting in the union of the favorable cones has probability $P=\mu_{t_0}(A)>0$. Step 2.1 gives $|w'(t)|\ge b$ along every such path for almost every later time. Thus $A(t)\ge Pb^2$ for almost every $t>t_0$. Integrating on the infinite time interval contradicts the finite total action in [F3]. Hence there is a finite $t_1>t_0$ with distance at least $\epsilon$, as claimed. This action lower bound is positive before any signed projection is taken, so no opposite-sign mass can cancel it. [F2, F3, step 2.1] ∎

## Source note

The source's common-time version of Lemma C.18 is unnecessary. The proof uses positive action from retained favorable trajectories, not a claim that their signed projected mass dominates the opposite sign. The full hypotheses and both source boundary alternatives are retained.

Suppose the finite signed measures $h^1(\mu_t)$ converge weakly on $\Theta$ to a finite signed measure $\nu$, where weak convergence means convergence against every function in $C_b(\Theta)$. Define $m_\nu:=\int\varphi d\nu$ by the signed Bochner-integral convention for the relaxed objective. Put $a_\nu(\theta)=dR_{m_\nu}[\varphi(\theta)]$, $G_+(\theta)=a_\nu(\theta)+\widetilde V(\theta)$, and $G_-(\theta)=-a_\nu(\theta)+\widetilde V(\theta)$. Then $G_+=0$ for $\nu^+$-almost every point and $G_-=0$ for $\nu^-$-almost every point, where $\nu=\nu^+-\nu^-$ is the Jordan decomposition. This is the sign-correct formulation of stationarity for the reduced functional $J(\nu)=R(\int\varphi\,d\nu)+\int\widetilde V\,d|\nu|$.

The functions have a common finite magnitude bound $B\ge1$. The moments are uniformly bounded for all $t\ge0$: convergence bounds the tail, and finite-horizon continuity from [F2] bounds the remaining compact interval. Thus [F2] gives $S(t)\le S(0)+Ct$ and $\int_0^\infty A(t)dt<\infty$, where $A(t)=\int|v_t|^2d\mu_t$. [F1, F2, given]

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be convex and differentiable, let $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ be bounded and strongly measurable, and let $\widetilde V:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded and measurable. For a finite signed measure $\nu=\nu^+-\nu^-$, put $m_\nu=\int\varphi\,d\nu$, $G_+(\theta)=dR_{m_\nu}[\varphi(\theta)]+\widetilde V(\theta)$, and $G_-(\theta)=-dR_{m_\nu}[\varphi(\theta)]+\widetilde V(\theta)$. If $G_+,G_-\ge0$ everywhere, $G_+=0$ $\nu^+$-almost everywhere, and $G_-=0$ $\nu^-$-almost everywhere, then $\nu$ globally minimizes $J(\lambda)=R(\int\varphi\,d\lambda)+\int\widetilde V\,d|\lambda|$ over all finite signed measures $\lambda$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the signed measures, convex risk, feature, penalty, and signwise conditions in the Statement.

[A1] AC supplies the Jordan decompositions of the finite signed measures $\lambda$ and $\nu$. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[thm-jordan-decomposition-for-signed-measures]]

[F1] $|\lambda|=\lambda^++\lambda^-$ is the total-variation measure of a finite signed measure, and $\lambda=\lambda^+-\lambda^-$. [[def-partial-homogeneous-relaxed-objective]]

[F2] Bounded linear maps commute with Bochner integration, so $dR_{m_\nu}[\int\varphi\,d(\lambda-\nu)]=\int dR_{m_\nu}[\varphi]d(\lambda-\nu)$. [[thm-bounded-linear-maps-commute-with-bochner-integration]]

## Proof

## Statement

Assume AC, the feature-energy hypotheses, and positive two-homogeneity of $\Phi$ and $V$ on $\Omega=\mathbb R^d$. Let $\mu_t$ be a Wasserstein gradient flow with finite initial energy. Suppose the finite measures $h^2(\mu_t)$ converge weakly on $\mathbb S^{d-1}$ to a finite nonnegative measure $\nu$. Define $G_\nu(\theta)=dR_{m_\nu}[\Phi(\theta)]+V(\theta)$, where $m_\nu=\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}\Phi\,d\nu$. Then $G_\nu=0$ for $\nu$-almost every $\theta$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the model and flow in the Statement, and weak convergence of their spherical projections.

[A1] AC is inherited by the flow existence, path and minimum-norm velocity constructions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The flow velocity is a Borel version of the negative minimum-norm subgradient selection almost everywhere; the characteristic construction supplies its canonical pointwise Borel version. [[def-wasserstein-gradient-flow-for-feature-energy]] [[lem-characteristics-unique-and-stable]]

[F2] On every finite time interval the energy identity holds, $F(\mu_t)$ is nonincreasing, and $F\ge0$. [[thm-global-wasserstein-flow-existence-uniqueness-and-stability]]

[F3] For positive two-homogeneous $\Phi,V$, their integrals factor through $h^2$; weak convergence of $h^2$ on the compact sphere gives norm convergence of the feature moments. [[lem-mean-field-projection-identities]]

[F4] The full flow potential $P_t(u)=dR_{m_{\mu_t}}[\Phi(u)]+V(u)$ is two-homogeneous and semiconvex, so its supporting sets and their minimum-norm selections scale by $s$ under $u\mapsto su$ for $s>0$. [[def-feature-measure-energy]] [[def-wasserstein-gradient-flow-for-feature-energy]]

[F5] A W2-continuous path of laws has weakly continuous two-homogeneous projections. [[lem-w2-convergence-implies-homogeneous-projection-convergence]]

## Proof

**Given:** The assumptions and suppliers in [F1]–[F5].

1.1 Fix $t$ and $u\ne0$. Write $P_t(u)=dR_{m_{\mu_t}}[\Phi(u)]+V(u)$. If $\xi\in\partial P_t(u)$, the local subdifferential definition applied along $(1+s)u$ gives $$\liminf_{s\to0}\frac{P_t((1+s)u)-P_t(u)-s\langle\xi,u\rangle}{|s|\,|u|}\ge0.$$ Since $P_t((1+s)u)=(1+s)^2P_t(u)$, the one-sided limits for $s\downarrow0$ and $s\uparrow0$ are respectively $2P_t(u)-\langle\xi,u\rangle$ and its negative. Both must be nonnegative, so $\langle\xi,u\rangle=2P_t(u)$. By [F1], $v_t(u)$ is the negative of one such vector, giving $\langle v_t(u),u\rangle=-2P_t(u)$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For $s>0$, substitute $z=sy$ in the local subdifferential definition of $\partial P_t(su)$. Two-homogeneity gives $P_t(z)-P_t(su)-s\xi\cdot(z-su)=s^2(P_t(y)-P_t(u)-\xi\cdot(y-u))$, while $|z-su|=s|y-u|$. Thus $\xi\in\partial P_t(u)$ iff $s\xi\in\partial P_t(su)$; the reverse implication follows by scaling by $1/s$. Hence the minimum-norm selection scales by $s$, and $v_t(s\theta)=s v_t(\theta)$ wherever the canonical pointwise selection is defined. [A1, F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F3] to the weakly convergent projections. Then $m_{\mu_t}\to m_\nu$ in Hilbert norm. The differentials $dR_{m_{\mu_t}}$ converge in operator norm to $dR_{m_\nu}$ by local Lipschitz continuity; since $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on the sphere, $G_t(\theta):=P_t(\theta)$ converges uniformly to $G_\nu(\theta)$. 4.1 By [F5] and the uniform convergence in step 3.1, $a(t)$ is measurable. By [F3] and [F4], positive one-homogeneity of the velocity gives $\int|v_t(u)|^2d\mu_t(u)=\int|v_t(\theta)|^2dh^2(\mu_t)(\theta)$. Step 1.1 on the unit sphere gives $2G_t(\theta)=-\langle v_t(\theta),\theta\rangle$, so $4a(t)\le\int|v_t(\theta)|^2dh^2(\mu_t)(\theta)$. ## Statement

Assume AC and the full partially homogeneous hypotheses of the stationarity lemma: a separable real Hilbert space $\mathcal H$; the feature-energy hypotheses with convex differentiable $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ whose differential is locally Lipschitz on bounded subsets and bounded on sublevels; $d\ge2$; bounded continuously differentiable maps $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ and $\widetilde V:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$ with Lipschitz differentials; $\Phi(w,\theta)=w\varphi(\theta)$ and the semiconvex potential $V(w,\theta)=|w|\widetilde V(\theta)$; and the nested cutoff and derivative-growth conditions of the feature-energy definition. For every $f\in\mathcal H$, require dense regular values for $G_f(\theta)=\langle f,\varphi(\theta)\rangle+\widetilde V(\theta)$. Retain either (i) $\Theta$ is the closure of a nonempty bounded connected open convex set with $C^1$ boundary and $dG_f(\theta)[n_\theta]=0$ on $\partial\Theta$ for every $f\in\mathcal H$, or (ii) $\Theta=\mathbb R^{d-1}$ and, for every $f\in\mathcal H$, $G_f(r\cdot)$ converges uniformly in $C^1(\mathbb S^{d-2})$ as $r\to\infty$ to a function with dense regular values.

Let $\mu_t$ be a Wasserstein gradient flow in $\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R\times\Theta)$ with finite initial energy. Suppose the finite signed projections $\sigma_t=h^1(\mu_t)$ converge narrowly to a finite signed measure $\nu$, meaning convergence of integrals against every bounded continuous real test function on $\Theta$. Put $m_\nu=\int\varphi\,d\nu$, with the intrinsic signed Bochner-integral convention, and $J(\nu)=R(m_\nu)+\int\widetilde V\,d|\nu|$. Then
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\int|w|\widetilde V(\theta)\,d\mu_t(w,\theta)=\int\widetilde V\,d|\nu|,\qquad \lim_{t\to\infty}F(\mu_t)=J(\nu).$$
No separation condition on the initial support is required.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the full partial hypotheses, the flow $\mu_t$, and narrow signed-projection convergence in the Statement.

[F1] The intrinsic signed projection factors the feature moment: $m_t:=\int w\varphi(\theta)d\mu_t=\int\varphi\,d\sigma_t$. The relaxed-objective inequality gives $P_t:=\int|w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu_t\ge\int\widetilde V\,d|\sigma_t|$. [[def-partial-one-homogeneous-measure-projection]] [[def-partial-homogeneous-relaxed-objective]]

[F2] Narrow convergence of finite signed measures on a closed Euclidean domain gives norm convergence of their integrals against bounded norm-continuous Hilbert-valued maps. For bounded nonnegative continuous $W$, it also gives $\int Wd|\nu|\le\liminf_{t\to\infty}\int Wd|\sigma_t|$. [[lem-signed-narrow-convergence-controls-bochner-moments]]

[F3] The energy is nonnegative and nonincreasing. With $f_t=\nabla R(m_t)$ and $S(t)=\int w^2d\mu_t\ge0$, the exact identity $S(t)-S(s)=-2\int_s^t(\langle f_q,m_q\rangle+P_q)dq$ holds for every finite $0\le s\le t$. [[lem-partial-feature-flow-moment-and-energy-identities]]

[F4] Writing $a_\nu(\theta)=\langle\nabla R(m_\nu),\varphi(\theta)\rangle$, signwise stationarity gives $a_\nu+\widetilde V=0$ $\nu^+$-almost everywhere and $-a_\nu+\widetilde V=0$ $\nu^-$-almost everywhere. [[lem-partial-homogeneous-projection-limit-is-stationary]]

[A1] The existing AC assumption supplies the choice hypotheses inherited from these suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the Statement and [F1]–[F4].

1.1 By [F1] and [F2], $m_t\to m_\nu$ in Hilbert norm. Continuity of $R$ and local Lipschitz continuity of its differential imply $R(m_t)\to R(m_\nu)$ and $f_t\to f_\nu:=\nabla R(m_\nu)$ in norm, hence $\langle f_t,m_t\rangle\to\langle f_\nu,m_\nu\rangle$. By [F3], $F(\mu_t)$ decreases to a finite limit $E_\infty\ge0$. Since $F(\mu_t)=R(m_t)+P_t$, it follows that $P_t\to P_\infty:=E_\infty-R(m_\nu)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given]

2.1 Put $P_\nu=\int\widetilde V\,d|\nu|$. The static inequality [F1] and weighted-variation lower semicontinuity [F2], applied to the bounded nonnegative continuous function $\widetilde V$, give $P_\infty\ge\liminf_{t\to\infty}\int\widetilde V\,d|\sigma_t|\ge P_\nu$. This does not require convergence of the separate raw sign measures or their Jordan parts. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Integrate the two stationarity equalities [F4] against the respective finite Jordan parts. The intrinsic signed Bochner integral and $|\nu|=\nu^++\nu^-$ give $\langle f_\nu,m_\nu\rangle=\int a_\nu d\nu^+-\int a_\nu d\nu^-=-\int\widetilde Vd\nu^+-\int\widetilde Vd\nu^-=-P_\nu$. All integrands are bounded, so these integrals are finite. [F1, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 If $P_\infty>P_\nu$, let $\epsilon=(P_\infty-P_\nu)/2>0$. Steps 1.1 and 3.1 imply that there is a finite $T$ such that $\langle f_q,m_q\rangle+P_q\ge\epsilon$ for every $q\ge T$. The all-endpoint moment identity [F3] then gives $S(t)\le S(T)-2\epsilon(t-T)$ for every finite $t\ge T$. Choosing $t>T+S(T)/(2\epsilon)$ contradicts $S(t)\ge0$. Hence $P_\infty\le P_\nu$, which together with step 2.1 yields $P_\infty=P_\nu$. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 Therefore $P_t\to P_\nu$, and step 1.1 gives $F(\mu_t)\to R(m_\nu)+P_\nu=J(\nu)$. These are the two asserted limits. [F1, step 1.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Source note

Appendix C.4.2 motivates the projected-limit energy claim. The convergence of the lifted penalty is proved here from signwise stationarity, signed norm-moment convergence and the exact weight-moment identity; continuity of the penalty as a function of the signed projection is not assumed.

## Statement

Assume AC and the full two-homogeneous hypotheses on $\Omega=\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge2$: convex differentiable risk with the prescribed derivative bounds, positive two-homogeneity of $\Phi,V$, the dense-regular-value condition, and the feature-energy assumptions. Let $\mu_t$ be a Wasserstein gradient flow whose initial support is compact, lies in $B(0,r_b)$, and separates $r_a\mathbb S^{d-1}$ from $r_b\mathbb S^{d-1}$ for $0<r_a<r_b$. If $h^2(\mu_t)$ converges weakly as finite measures on $\mathbb S^{d-1}$ to $\nu$, then the measure $\nu$ viewed on $\mathbb R^d$ is a global minimizer of $F$ over finite nonnegative Borel measures, and $F(\mu_t)\to F(\nu)=\inf_{\lambda\ge0}F(\lambda)$.

## Statement references

[[def-feature-measure-energy]]

[[def-wasserstein-gradient-flow-for-feature-energy]]

[[def-two-homogeneous-measure-projection]]

[[lem-mean-field-first-variation-and-measure-optimality]]

[[lem-two-homogeneous-projection-limit-is-stationary]]

[[lem-two-homogeneous-escape-from-nonoptimal-projection]]

[[lem-flow-preserves-spherical-separation]]

[Chizat and Bach, Theorem 3.3 and Theorem C.16](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

[Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré, Theorem 11.2.1](https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~sayan/ambrosio.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the two-homogeneous flow, its separated initial support, and weak convergence of its projections.

[A1] AC is inherited by the flow, characteristic, degree and minimum-norm constructions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A weak two-homogeneous projection limit is stationary: $G_\nu=0$ $\nu$-almost everywhere. [[lem-two-homogeneous-projection-limit-is-stationary]]

[F2] If $\nu$ is not a minimizer, convexity and first-variation optimality give a direction where $G_\nu<0$; the regular-value hypothesis supplies the compact negative sublevel needed for escape. [[lem-mean-field-first-variation-and-measure-optimality]] [[lem-two-homogeneous-escape-from-nonoptimal-projection]]

[F3] Spherical separation is preserved for every finite time, and the support is the image of the initial support under the characteristic map. [[lem-flow-preserves-spherical-separation]]

[F4] In the nonoptimal case, positive mass in the negative cone forces the projection to exit every sufficiently small bounded-Lipschitz neighborhood of $\nu$. [[lem-two-homogeneous-escape-from-nonoptimal-projection]]

[F5] Weak convergence of $h^2(\mu_t)$ gives convergence of the feature moment in Hilbert norm and convergence of the regularizer integral. [[lem-mean-field-projection-identities]]

[F6] Under AC, an equicontinuous family of continuous functions from a compact metric space to a compact interval has compact closure in the uniform topology. [[cor-ascoli-arzela-for-compact-metric-domains]]

## Proof

**Given:** AC, the flow and convergence in the Statement, and [F1]–[F5].

1.1 Suppose for contradiction that $\nu$ is not a global minimizer. By [F1] and [F2], $G_\nu$ vanishes $\nu$-almost everywhere but is negative at some sphere point. Choose a negative regular sublevel $K$ with that point in its interior, as in [F2]. [A1, F1, F2, given, assume-contra]

2.1 Weak convergence on the compact sphere implies convergence of total masses by testing the constant function. The bounded-Lipschitz unit ball is equicontinuous and uniformly bounded; Arzelà–Ascoli [F6] gives a finite uniform $\delta$-net for it. Weak convergence controls each member of that finite net, and the convergent masses bound the error from replacing any test by its net representative. Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ proves bounded-Lipschitz convergence. Thus there is $t_0$ after which $\|h^2(\mu_t)-\nu\|_{BL}<\epsilon$, where $\epsilon$ is the escape radius from [F4]. By [F3], the support at $t_0$ separates some spheres $\rho_a\mathbb S^{d-1}$ and $\rho_b\mathbb S^{d-1}$ with $0<\rho_a<\rho_b$. For a point $\theta_0\in\operatorname{int}K$, the radial path $r\mapsto r\theta_0$ between these spheres must meet $\operatorname{spt}\mu_{t_0}$. That support point has positive radius and direction in $\operatorname{int}K$; every sufficiently small open neighborhood of it has positive $\mu_{t_0}$ mass, so the negative cone in [F4] has positive mass. [A1, F3, F4, F6, given, step 1.1]

3.1 Applying [F4] at time $t_0$ gives $t_1>t_0$ with $\|h^2(\mu_{t_1})-\nu\|_{BL}\ge\epsilon$, contradicting the choice of $t_0$. Thus $\nu$ is a global minimizer. [A1, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 By [F5], $F(\mu_t)\to F(\nu)$. Since $\nu$ is a minimizer over all finite nonnegative measures, $F(\nu)=\inf_{\lambda\ge0}F(\lambda)$. This proves both conclusions. [A1, F5, step 3.1, discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Statement

**Assume the Axiom of Choice.** Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space, let $Y$ be a metric space, and let $\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,Y)$. The closure of $\mathcal F$ in the uniform topology is compact if and only if $\mathcal F$ is metric-equicontinuous and pointwise relatively compact.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Choice, a nonempty compact metric space $X$, a metric space $Y$, and $\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,Y)$.

[L1] For a compact Hausdorff domain, compactness of the compact-open closure is equivalent to equicontinuity and pointwise relative compactness ([[cor-ascoli-arzela-for-compact-hausdorff-domains]]).

[L2] On a nonempty compact metric domain, the published compact-open topology equals the uniform topology ([[prop-compact-open-is-uniform-on-a-compact-metric-domain]]).

[L3] Topological-domain and metric equicontinuity agree on a metric domain ([[prop-topological-domain-equicontinuity-agrees-with-metric-equicontinuity]]).

[L4] The general and published compact-open topologies agree on a metric domain ([[prop-general-compact-open-topology-agrees-with-the-metric-definition]]).

[L5] Metric compactness agrees with compactness in the metric topology ([[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]]).

[L6] Every metric space is Hausdorff ([[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L5] and [L6], $X$ with its metric topology is compact Hausdorff, so [L1] applies to $\mathcal F$. [L1, L5, L6]

1.2 By [L4] and [L2], the general compact-open topology used in [L1] is the uniform topology; hence the two closures and their compactness are identical. [L2, L4]

2.1 By [L3], the equicontinuity condition in [L1] is exactly metric equicontinuity. Pointwise relative compactness is unchanged, so [L1] becomes the claimed equivalence in both directions. [L1, L3, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC, the full two-homogeneous hypotheses and separated compact initialization in the preceding global-minimizer theorem. If the Wasserstein gradient flow $\mu_t$ converges in $W_2$ to $\mu_\infty\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$, then $\mu_\infty$ is a global minimizer of $F$ over finite nonnegative measures.

## Statement references

[[thm-two-homogeneous-projected-limit-is-global-minimizer]]

[[lem-w2-convergence-implies-homogeneous-projection-convergence]]

[[def-two-homogeneous-measure-projection]]

[[lem-mean-field-projection-identities]]

[Chizat and Bach, Theorem 3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the assumptions in the Statement, and $W_2(\mu_t,\mu_\infty)\to0$.

[A1] AC is inherited from the flow and coupling construction. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] W2 convergence implies weak convergence of the two-homogeneous projections. [[lem-w2-convergence-implies-homogeneous-projection-convergence]]

[F2] The projected-limit theorem makes its weak limit a global minimizer and states that $F(\mu_t)$ converges to the energy of that limit. [[thm-two-homogeneous-projected-limit-is-global-minimizer]]

[F3] For a positive two-homogeneous feature and regularizer, $F(\lambda)=R(\int\Phi dh^2(\lambda))+\int Vdh^2(\lambda)$ whenever $\lambda$ has finite second moment. [[lem-mean-field-projection-identities]]

**Given:** AC and the data in the Statement.

1.1 Apply [F1] to obtain weak convergence $h^2(\mu_t)\rightharpoonup h^2(\mu_\infty)$. [A1, F1, given]

2.1 The projected-limit theorem [F2] applies to this weak limit. If it denotes the limit by $\nu$, then for every continuous test on the compact sphere both $\nu$ and $\rho:=h^2(\mu_\infty)$ give the limit of the same integrals $\int fdh^2(\mu_t)$. Testing $f\equiv1$ shows that both have the same total mass $M$. If $M=0$, both finite nonnegative measures are zero. If $M>0$, then $\nu/M$ and $\rho/M$ are Borel probability measures with equal integrals against every bounded continuous test, so uniqueness of weak probability limits gives $\nu=\rho$. Viewed as a measure on $\mathbb R^d$, this limit globally minimizes $F$ over all finite nonnegative Borel measures, exactly as asserted by the theorem. [[cor-weak-limits-are-unique]] [A1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 By [F3], the feature and regularizer integrals of $\mu_\infty$ equal those of its two-homogeneous projection, so $F(\mu_\infty)=F(h^2(\mu_\infty))$. By step 2.1, this equals the global minimum of $F$ over finite nonnegative Borel measures on $\mathbb R^d$, and therefore $\mu_\infty$ is itself a global minimizer. [F2, F3, step 2.1] ∎

## Example

Let $\mathcal H=\mathbb R^2$, $y=(1,0)$, $R(z)=\tfrac12\|z-y\|^2$, $\Theta=[0,2\pi]$, $\varphi(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$, and $V=0$. The one-particle measure assigning unit mass to $(a,\theta)$ represents $a\varphi(\theta)$ and can attain zero risk at $(a,\theta)=(1,0)$. If the feature is fixed at $\theta=\pi/2$ and only $a$ varies, the minimum risk is $1/2$. This finite-dimensional feature-energy example shows a representational distinction only; it makes no convergence claim about either training dynamics.

## Example references

[[def-feature-measure-energy]]

[Chizat and Bach, Sections 1.1 and 2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)

[Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré, Chapters 8 and 11](https://www2.stat.duke.edu/~sayan/ambrosio.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite-dimensional model and risk in the Example.

[F1] A one-particle measure at $(a,\theta)$ has feature moment $a\varphi(\theta)$ and objective $R(a\varphi(\theta))$. [[def-feature-measure-energy]]

## Verification

**Given:** $R$, $y$, $\varphi$, and [F1] as in the Example.

1.1 At $(a,\theta)=(1,0)$, $\varphi(0)=(1,0)=y$, so [F1] gives risk $R(y)=0$. Since $R$ is a squared norm divided by two, no objective value is negative; hence the moving model has minimum risk zero. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 With the feature fixed at $\pi/2$, $\varphi(\pi/2)=(0,1)$ and $\|a\varphi(\pi/2)-y\|^2=a^2+1$. Therefore $R(a\varphi(\pi/2))=(a^2+1)/2\ge1/2$, with equality at $a=0$. This gives the claimed fixed-feature minimum. [F1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

**Refuted claim:** the differential of the signed-square ReLU feature map is locally Lipschitz near the parameter $(1,1)$.

For input law with density $p(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ on $\mathbb R$, define $\Phi(w,b)(x)=\max\{w|w|x+b|b|,0\}$ as an element of $L^2(p(x)dx)$. This feature map is Fréchet differentiable near $(1,1)$, but its differential is not locally Lipschitz there.

## Statement references

[[def-signed-square-relu-feature-map]]

[Chizat and Bach, Proposition 4.3 and Lemma D.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)


[[def-signed-square-relu-feature-map]]

[Chizat and Bach, Appendix D.4.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09545)
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The signed-square feature and Gaussian density in the Statement.

[F1] The Gaussian density is continuous, positive on every real interval, and has finite second moment, so the feature belongs to $L^2$ and the kink hyperplane has measure zero. [[def-signed-square-relu-feature-map]]

[F2] For $w,b>0$, the preactivation is $r_{w,b}(x)=w^2x+b^2$ and its unique zero is $c(w,b)=-b^2/w^2$. [[def-signed-square-relu-feature-map]]

## Counterexample

**Given:** $\Phi$, $p$, and [F1]–[F2] in the Statement.

1.1 On a small neighborhood of $(1,1)$ with $w,b>0$, the root $c(w,b)$ is a smooth function of parameters. For an increment $h=(h_1,h_2)$, $$r_{(w,b)+h}(x)-r_{w,b}(x)=2wh_1x+2bh_2+h_1^2x+h_2^2.$$ The candidate differential is $D\Phi_{(w,b)}h=\mathbf1_{x>c(w,b)}(2wh_1x+2bh_2)$. Outside the interval between $c(w,b)$ and $c((w,b)+h)$, the two preactivations have the same sign; there the ReLU remainder is either zero or $h_1^2x+h_2^2$, whose $L^2(pdx)$ norm is $O(|h|^2)$ by the finite second moment in [F1]. The interval between the two roots has length $O(|h|)$ and lies in a fixed bounded neighborhood of $-1$; on it the pointwise remainder is $O(|h|)$, so its $L^2(pdx)$ norm is $O(|h|^{3/2})$. Thus the full remainder is $o(|h|)$, proving Fréchet differentiability and the displayed differential. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 At $(1,1)$ the derivative in direction $e_w=(1,0)$ is $2x\mathbf1_{x>-1}$. At $(1,1+\delta)$ it is $2x\mathbf1_{x>-(1+\delta)^2}$. For $0<\delta\le1/4$, their squared $L^2$ distance is $$4\int_{-(1+\delta)^2}^{-1}x^2p(x)\,dx\ge8p(2)\delta,$$ because the interval lies in $[-2,-1]$, where $x^2\ge1$ and $p(x)\ge p(2)$, and has length $2\delta+\delta^2\ge2\delta$. The operator norm difference of the two differentials is at least their difference on the unit vector $e_w$. Dividing by the parameter distance $\delta$ gives a quotient at least $\sqrt{8p(2)}/\sqrt\delta$, which diverges as $\delta\downarrow0$. Therefore the differential is not locally Lipschitz at $(1,1)$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Source note

Chizat and Bach's Lemma D.5 establishes differentiability under a finite-second-moment density assumption. The proposition's application does not establish local Lipschitzness of this differential, which is a separate feature-energy hypothesis.

## Definition

Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U$ be a nonempty subset of the real matrix space $\mathbb R^{n\times m}$, and let $\epsilon>0$. A **proper $\epsilon$-cover** of $U$ in Frobenius norm is a finite subset $V\subseteq U$ such that every $X\in U$ has some $Y\in V$ with $\lVert X-Y\rVert_F\le\epsilon$. The **proper Frobenius covering number** $N_F(U,\epsilon)$ is the least cardinality of such a cover when one exists, and is $+\infty$ otherwise. The cover is proper because its centers belong to $U$.

[Bartlett, Foster, and Telgarsky, §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.08498): defines the covering number using finite centers in the covered set.

## Definition

Let $L\ge1$ and let $d_0,\ldots,d_L\ge1$ be layer widths, with $K:=d_L\ge2$ output classes. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,L\}$, fix a matrix $M_i\in\mathbb R^{d_i\times d_{i-1}}$ and a vector activation $\sigma_i:\mathbb R^{d_i}\to\mathbb R^{d_i}$ satisfying $\sigma_i(0)=0$ and
$$\lVert\sigma_i(u)-\sigma_i(v)\rVert_2\le\rho_i\lVert u-v\rVert_2\qquad(u,v\in\mathbb R^{d_i})$$
for a fixed $\rho_i>0$. A network has matrices $A_i\in\mathbb R^{d_i\times d_{i-1}}$, no biases, and is evaluated by $h_0(x)=x$ and $h_i(x)=\sigma_i(A_i h_{i-1}(x))$, with score vector $F_A(x)=h_L(x)$. For a real matrix $B$, define $\lVert B\rVert_{2,1}:=\sum_j\lVert B_{\cdot j}\rVert_2$, the sum of the Euclidean norms of its columns. Write $\lVert A\rVert_\sigma$ for the induced Euclidean operator norm $\max_{\lVert u\rVert_2=1}\lVert Au\rVert_2$ and put $W:=\max_{0\le i\le L}d_i$.

For a network whose layer matrices all have nonzero operator norm, its **spectral network complexity relative to $(M_i)$** is
$$R_A:=\left(\prod_{i=1}^L\rho_i\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^L\left(\frac{\lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}}{\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma}\right)^{2/3}\right)^{3/2}.$$
If some $A_i=0$, the network is instead handled as the constant-zero score map: the recurrence gives $h_i=0$ and all later hidden vectors are zero. The displayed complexity is not defined in that zero-layer case.

The block diagram is schematic for $L\ge3$ and depicts the stated recurrence. Each node is the entire vector at one layer; the arrow labelled $A_i$ is the zero-bias linear map, followed by the vector activation shown in the next node. The omitted middle layers are represented by the ellipsis, and the widths are those in the definition. For $L=1$ or $L=2$, omit the ellipsis and use the corresponding initial segment of the recurrence. The diagram is illustrative and is not used in any proof.

  \node[draw,rounded corners] (h1) at (3.1,0) {$h_1=\sigma_1(A_1h_0)$};
  \node (dots) at (4.9,0) {$\cdots$};

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ be a fixed sample, and let $\mathcal G$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions into $[0,1]$. Write $\mathcal G|S$ for the set of column vectors $(g(z_1),\ldots,g(z_n))^\top$ as $g$ ranges over $\mathcal G$. For $0<\alpha\le\sqrt n$,
$$\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)\le\frac{4\alpha}{\sqrt n}+\frac{12}{n}\int_\alpha^{\sqrt n}\sqrt{\log N_F(\mathcal G|S,\epsilon)}\,d\epsilon,$$
where $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S$ is the one-sided empirical Rademacher complexity with $1/n$ normalization and $N_F$ is the proper Frobenius covering number of the sample-vector set, identified with $n\times1$ matrices. The set $\mathcal G|S$ is totally bounded because it lies in $[0,1]^n$.

## Statement references

[[def-rademacher-complexity]]: fixes the one-sided empirical sign average and its $1/n$ normalization.

[[def-sample-covering-number]]: defines $N_F$ using finite centers belonging to the covered set.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $n\ge1$, a fixed sample $S$, a nonempty $[0,1]$-valued function class, and the corresponding finite sign space.

[F1] The one-sided empirical complexity is $\mathbb E_\varepsilon\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_i g(z_i)$, where the signs are independent and uniform on $\{-1,+1\}$. [[def-rademacher-complexity]]

[F2] $N_F(U,\epsilon)$ is the least number of centers in a finite proper Frobenius $\epsilon$-cover of $U$. [[def-sample-covering-number]]

[F3] $\cosh x>0$, $\cosh$ is even, $\cosh' x=\sinh x$, $\tanh' x=\operatorname{sech}^2x$, and $\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1$. [[def-hyperbolic-functions]] [[thm-hyperbolic-identities-and-derivatives]]

[F4] For a bounded real random variable $Y$ and convex exponential, $\exp(\lambda\mathbb E Y)\le\mathbb E\exp(\lambda Y)$. [[thm-jensen-inequality-for-expectation]]

[F5] $\log$ is the increasing inverse of $\exp$ on positive reals, with $\log(xy)=\log x+\log y$ and $\log 1=0$. [[def-natural-logarithm]] [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]

[F6] If a real function is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, the mean value theorem gives $f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a)$ for some $c\in(a,b)$. [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]

[F7] The exponential, chain, and product rules give derivatives of $e^{-x^2/2}\cosh x$; the hyperbolic derivatives and identities in [F3] apply. [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] [[thm-chain-rule]] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]

[F8] For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space, $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert$. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]]

## Proof
1.1 For $x>0$, put $r(x)=x-\tanh x$. By [F3], $r(0)=0$ and $r'(x)=1-\operatorname{sech}^2x=\tanh^2x\ge0$. The mean value theorem [F6] therefore gives $r(x)\ge0$; at $x=0$ this is equality. Put $q(x)=e^{-x^2/2}\cosh x$. The derivative rules in [F3] and [F7] give $q'(x)=e^{-x^2/2}\cosh x\,(\tanh x-x)\le0$. Applying [F6] on $[0,x]$ for $x>0$ yields $q(x)\le q(0)=1$, and equality holds at $x=0$. Since $q$ is even, $\cosh x\le e^{x^2/2}$ for every real $x$. [F3, F6, F7, algebra]

1.2 Choose $g_0\in\mathcal G$ and subtract its sample vector $v_0$ from every vector in $\mathcal G|S$. The empirical Rademacher average is unchanged because $\mathbb E_\varepsilon\sum_i\varepsilon_i g_0(z_i)=0$, and translation preserves all Frobenius covering numbers. Write $U:=(\mathcal G|S)-v_0$; it contains $0$, and each vector has norm at most $\sqrt n$. For any $\epsilon>0$, partition $[-1,1]^n$ into finitely many boxes of side at most $\epsilon/\sqrt n$; from each box meeting $U$ take one member of that intersection. The resulting finite set is a proper $\epsilon$-cover, since two points in one box differ in Euclidean norm by at most $\epsilon$. Set $\epsilon_j=\sqrt n\,2^{-(j-1)}$. The singleton $V_1=\{0\}$ is a proper $\epsilon_1$-cover of $U$, so $|V_1|=N_F(U,\epsilon_1)=1$. For each finite truncation $N\ge2$ and each $2\le j\le N$, choose a proper $\epsilon_j$-cover $V_j$ of $U$ with the least possible cardinality, so $|V_j|=N_F(U,\epsilon_j)$; such a least cardinality exists because a finite cover exists and cover cardinalities are positive integers. Enumerate each finite cover and map every sample vector to the first center within $\epsilon_j$. [F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 Let $V$ be a nonempty finite set of vectors in $\mathbb R^n$ and let $R=\max_{v\in V}\lVert v\rVert_2$. For $T_v=\sum_i\varepsilon_i v_i$, independence of the signs and step 1.1 give $\mathbb E e^{\lambda T_v}=\prod_i\cosh(\lambda v_i)\le e^{\lambda^2R^2/2}$. If $R=0$ or $|V|=1$, $\mathbb E\max_{v\in V}T_v=0$. Otherwise, for $\lambda>0$, [F4] and $e^{\lambda\max_v T_v}\le\sum_{v\in V}e^{\lambda T_v}$ imply $\mathbb E\max_vT_v\le\log|V|/\lambda+\lambda R^2/2$. Choosing $\lambda=\sqrt{2\log|V|}/R$ gives $\mathbb E\max_vT_v\le R\sqrt{2\log|V|}$. [F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For any translated sample vector $v$, telescope $v=(v-v_N[v])+\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}(v_j[v]-v_{j+1}[v])$, since $v_1[v]=0$. The absolute residual sign sum is at most $\lVert(\varepsilon_i)_i\rVert_2\lVert v-v_N[v]\rVert_2\le\sqrt n\epsilon_N$ by [F8]. For each $j<N$, the set $V_j-V_{j+1}$ has at most $N_F(\mathcal G|S,\epsilon_{j+1})^2$ elements, because covering numbers are nonincreasing with radius, and every difference has norm at most $\epsilon_j+\epsilon_{j+1}=3\epsilon_{j+1}$. Step 2.1 bounds its expected maximum sign sum by $6\epsilon_{j+1}\sqrt{\log N_F(\mathcal G|S,\epsilon_{j+1})}$. Summing these bounds and dividing by $n$ gives $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)\le\epsilon_N/\sqrt n+(6/n)\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\epsilon_{j+1}\sqrt{\log N_F(\mathcal G|S,\epsilon_{j+1})}$. [F1, F2, F8, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra]

4.1 The function $f(\epsilon)=\sqrt{\log N_F(\mathcal G|S,\epsilon)}$ is nonincreasing in $\epsilon$. Since $\epsilon_{j+2}=\epsilon_{j+1}/2$, each summand obeys $\epsilon_{j+1}f(\epsilon_{j+1})\le2\int_{\epsilon_{j+2}}^{\epsilon_{j+1}}f(\epsilon)\,d\epsilon$. Therefore step 3.1 gives $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)\le\epsilon_N/\sqrt n+(12/n)\int_{\epsilon_{N+1}}^{\sqrt n}f(\epsilon)\,d\epsilon$. [F2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If $\sqrt n/4\le\alpha\le\sqrt n$, each signed average is at most $1$, so $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)\le1\le4\alpha/\sqrt n$. If $0<\alpha<\sqrt n/4$, choose the largest $N\ge1$ with $\epsilon_{N+1}>\alpha$; such an $N$ exists because $\epsilon_2=\sqrt n/2>\alpha$ and $\epsilon_j\to0$. Maximality gives $\epsilon_{N+2}\le\alpha$, hence $\epsilon_N=4\epsilon_{N+2}\le4\alpha$, and $\int_{\epsilon_{N+1}}^{\sqrt n}f\le\int_\alpha^{\sqrt n}f$. Substitution into step 4.1 proves the stated inequality for every $0<\alpha<\sqrt n/4$. Together, the two cases prove it for every $0<\alpha\le\sqrt n$. [F1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

## Statement

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Real numbers $x,y$.

[L1] $\exp(u+v)=\exp u\exp v$, $\exp(-u)=1/\exp u$, and $\exp u>0$ ([[thm-exponential-addition-formula]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]).

[L2] $\exp'=\exp$, and the chain, product, quotient, and algebra rules differentiate the displayed formulas ([[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[L3] If $a<b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, then some $c\in(a,b)$ satisfies $f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a)$ ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

[L4] $\exp x\to\infty$ as $x\to\infty$ and $\exp x\to0$ as $x\to-\infty$ ([[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]]).

[L5] A continuous real function takes every value between two values on a closed interval ([[thm-intermediate-value]]).

[L6] For every real $x$, $\sinh x=(\exp x-\exp(-x))/2$ and $\cosh x=(\exp x+\exp(-x))/2$; $\tanh x=\sinh x/\cosh x$ and $\operatorname{sech}x=1/\cosh x$; and, when $x\ne0$, $\coth x=\cosh x/\sinh x$ and $\operatorname{csch}x=1/\sinh x$. Moreover $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$, and $\sinh x\ne0$ when $x\ne0$ ([[def-hyperbolic-functions]]).

[L7] Differentiability implies continuity ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Substitute the exponential definitions of [L6] and use [L1]; collecting terms gives both addition formulas, parity, and $\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1$. [L1, L6, algebra]

2.1 Differentiating the exponential definitions of [L6] gives $(\sinh x)'=\cosh x$ and $(\cosh x)'=\sinh x$; on the domains supplied by [L6], differentiating the quotients and using step 1.1 gives the four displayed reciprocal-function derivatives. [step 1.1, L2, L6, algebra]

2.2 The exponential formulas give $\sinh x\to\infty$, $\cosh x\to\infty$, and $\tanh x\to1$ as $x\to\infty$; oddness gives the corresponding limits $-\infty$ and $-1$ at $-\infty$. [step 1.1, L1, L4, algebra]

3.1 By [L6], $\cosh x>0$ and $\sinh x$ is nonzero away from $0$; the defining formula gives $\sinh0=0$. Thus $\sinh'=\cosh>0$ everywhere. For $a<b$, step 2.1 and [L7] give the hypotheses of [L3] for $\sinh$ on $[a,b]$, so for some $c\in(a,b)$, $\sinh b-\sinh a=\cosh c\,(b-a)>0$. Hence $\sinh$ is strictly increasing. [step 2.1, L3, L6, L7, algebra]

4.1 The oddness and strict increase of $\sinh$ make $\sinh x>0$ for $x>0$. Thus for $0\le a<b$, step 2.1 and [L7] let [L3] give $\cosh b-\cosh a=\sinh c\,(b-a)>0$ for some $c\in(a,b)$, so $\cosh$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$. Also $\operatorname{sech}x>0$, so for $a<b$ the same argument gives $\tanh b-\tanh a=\operatorname{sech}^2c\,(b-a)>0$ for some $c\in(a,b)$; hence $\tanh$ is strictly increasing. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, L1, L3, L6, L7]

5.1 The functions are continuous by step 2.1 and [L7]. Their monotonicity, the values $\cosh0=1$, and the endpoint limits of step 2.2 let the intermediate value theorem give exactly the three stated ranges. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 2.2, L5, L7] ∎

      url: "https://www.cs.nyu.edu/~mohri/mls/lecture_4.pdf"

## Definition

Let $K\ge2$, let $D$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d\times\{1,\ldots,K\}$, and let $F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^K$ be a continuous score map. At $(x,y)$ its **multiclass margin** is
$$m_F(x,y):=F(x)_y-\max_{j\ne y}F(x)_j.$$
The predicted label is the smallest index maximizing $F(x)_j$. Its population zero-one error is
$$L_0(F):=D\bigl(\{(x,y):\operatorname*{argmax}_{1\le j\le K}F(x)_j\ne y\}\bigr).$$
For $\gamma>0$, the **ramp loss** is
$$\ell_\gamma(r):=\begin{cases}0,&r< -\gamma,\\1+r/\gamma,&-\gamma\le r\le0,\\1,&r>0.\end{cases}$$
The population ramp risk is $R_\gamma(F):=\int\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x,y))\,D(d(x,y))$. For a sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))$ of length $n\ge1$, the empirical ramp risk and empirical margin loss are
$$\widehat R_{\gamma,S}(F):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x_i,y_i)),\qquad\widehat L_{\gamma,S}(F):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{m_F(x_i,y_i)\le\gamma\}.$$
The score coordinates are continuous, and finite maxima, comparisons, and the piecewise-linear ramp preserve Borel measurability. Thus the classification event and ramp loss in the displayed integrals are Borel sets or functions, so the risks are well-defined for $D$.

## Definition references

[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]: Borel subsets are members of the sigma-algebra generated by open sets.

[[def-probability-measure]]: a probability measure is a measure of total mass one.

[[def-supervised-learning-problem]]: fixes measurable instance and label spaces, a joint law, predictors, and measurable losses.

[[def-population-and-empirical-risk]]: defines population risk as an extended nonnegative integral and empirical risk as a finite sample average.

[Bartlett, Foster, and Telgarsky, §3.1 and Appendix A.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.08498): gives the multiclass margin operator and the ramp convention.

[Mohri, Lecture 4, pp. 28–31](https://www.cs.nyu.edu/~mohri/mls/lecture_4.pdf): treats confidence margin, empirical margin loss, and margin-based risk bounds for binary scores.

## Statement

Let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ with $n,d,m\ge1$, and let $a,s\ge0$. Suppose
$$C:=\{A\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}:\lVert A-M\rVert_{2,1}\le a,\ \lVert A\rVert_\sigma\le s\}$$
is nonempty. Put $U:=\{XA:A\in C\}$. For every $\epsilon>0$,
$$\log N_F(U,\epsilon)\le5\,\frac{a^2\lVert X\rVert_F^2}{\epsilon^2}\log(2dm).$$
If $a\lVert X\rVert_F=0$ or $\epsilon\ge2a\lVert X\rVert_F$, then $N_F(U,\epsilon)=1$. Here $\lVert A-M\rVert_{2,1}$ is the column-sum norm of the transpose-difference, as fixed in the spectral-network-complexity definition, and $N_F$ is the proper Frobenius covering number.

## Statement references

[[def-spectral-network-complexity]]: defines the column-sum mixed norm and the induced Euclidean operator norm.

[[def-sample-covering-number]]: defines the proper cover whose centers must lie in $U$.

[[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]: defines the Euclidean matrix-entry norm used to measure cover error.

[Bartlett, Foster, and Telgarsky, Lemma 3.2 and Appendix A.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.08498): gives the Maurey sparsification route to this matrix-product cover.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Matrices $X,M$, dimensions and constants as in the Statement, and the nonempty feasible set $C$.

[F1] $\lVert Z\rVert_F^2$ is the sum of the squared absolute values of all entries of $Z$. [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]

[F2] $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert$ in a real or complex inner-product space. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]]

[F3] The Euclidean inner-product norm is homogeneous and satisfies the triangle inequality. [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]

[F4] $N_F(U,\epsilon)$ is the least size of a finite proper Frobenius cover of $U$. [[def-sample-covering-number]]

[F5] Closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional real Euclidean space are compact. [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]

[F6] $\log$ is strictly increasing on positive reals and satisfies $\log(xy)=\log x+\log y$. [[def-natural-logarithm]] [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]

[F7] The mixed norm is the sum of the Euclidean column norms, and $\lVert A\rVert_\sigma$ is the induced Euclidean operator norm. [[def-spectral-network-complexity]]

## Proof
1.1 For any $B\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}$, write its columns as $b_j$ and the columns of $X$ as $x_r$. By [F2], $\lVert Xb_j\rVert_2^2=\sum_i|\sum_rX_{ir}(b_j)_r|^2\le\lVert X\rVert_F^2\lVert b_j\rVert_2^2$. Summing over $j$ gives $\lVert XB\rVert_F\le\lVert X\rVert_F(\sum_j\lVert b_j\rVert_2^2)^{1/2}\le\lVert X\rVert_F\sum_j\lVert b_j\rVert_2=\lVert X\rVert_F\lVert B\rVert_{2,1}$; the middle inequality follows by squaring, since all column norms are nonnegative. Thus $\lVert A-A'\rVert_{2,1}\le2a$ for $A,A'\in C$, and the diameter of $U$ is at most $2a\lVert X\rVert_F$. If $a\lVert X\rVert_F=0$, $U$ is a singleton; if $\epsilon\ge2a\lVert X\rVert_F$, any one point of nonempty $U$ covers it. [F1, F2, F7, given, algebra]

1.2 Assume $a\lVert X\rVert_F>0$ and $0<\epsilon<2a\lVert X\rVert_F$. For each nonzero column $x_r$, each output coordinate $j$, and each sign $\eta\in\{-1,+1\}$, form the rank-one atom $V_{rj\eta}=\eta(x_r/\lVert x_r\rVert_2)e_j^\top$, where $e_j$ is the $j$th standard basis vector in $\mathbb R^m$. There are at most $2dm$ atoms and each has Frobenius norm $1$. For $B=A-M$, the expansion $XB=\sum_{r,j}(B)_{rj}x_re_j^\top$ has coefficient mass $\beta:=\sum_{r,j}|B_{rj}|\lVert x_r\rVert_2\le\lVert B\rVert_{2,1}\lVert X\rVert_F\le a\lVert X\rVert_F=:c$, by [F2] column by column. Hence $XB/c$ lies in the convex hull of these signed atoms: if $\beta<c$, fill the remaining weight with $0$, which is the midpoint of an atom and its negative. If $\beta=0$, the product is $0$. [F1, F2, F7, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For an integer $k\ge1$, sample $k$ atoms independently from the finite convex representation of $XB/c$ constructed in step 1.2. If $V_1,\ldots,V_k$ are these atoms and $\mathbb E V_1=XB/c$, expansion of the squared Frobenius norm and independence give $\mathbb E\lVert c k^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^kV_t-XB\rVert_F^2=(c^2/k)(\mathbb E\lVert V_1\rVert_F^2-\lVert\mathbb EV_1\rVert_F^2)\le c^2/k$. Therefore some ordered $k$-tuple gives a center within $c/\sqrt k$, and all such centers number at most $(2dm)^k$. Taking $k=\lceil c^2/\epsilon^2\rceil$ yields an external $\epsilon$-cover of the translated relaxed product set $XM+\{XB:\lVert B\rVert_{2,1}\le a\}$. [F1, step 1.2, given, algebra, construct]

3.1 The mixed-norm constraint set is convex: for $A,A'\in C$ and $0\le t\le1$, the column triangle inequality [F3] gives $\lVert t(A-M)+(1-t)(A'-M)\rVert_{2,1}\le ta+(1-t)a=a$. The operator-norm constraint is convex because for each unit vector $v$, $\lVert(tA+(1-t)A')v\rVert_2\le t\lVert Av\rVert_2+(1-t)\lVert A'v\rVert_2\le s$, and taking the supremum over $v$ preserves the bound. The mixed norm is continuous as a finite sum of continuous column norms. From [F7] and the Euclidean triangle inequality, $|\lVert A\rVert_\sigma-\lVert A'\rVert_\sigma|\le\lVert A-A'\rVert_\sigma\le\lVert A-A'\rVert_F$, where the last inequality follows from the rowwise Cauchy estimate in step 1.1; hence the operator norm is continuous and $C$ is closed. Also $\lVert A-M\rVert_F\le\lVert A-M\rVert_{2,1}\le a$, so $C$ is bounded. By [F5], $C$ is compact; its linear image $U$ is compact and convex. Project each external center $z$ from step 2.1 to a nearest point $p$ of $U$, which exists by compactness. For any $u\in U$, convexity gives $p+t(u-p)\in U$ for $0\le t\le1$. Put $\langle P,Q\rangle_F:=\sum_{i,j}P_{ij}Q_{ij}$. Minimality implies $0\le\lVert z-p-t(u-p)\rVert_F^2-\lVert z-p\rVert_F^2=-2t\langle z-p,u-p\rangle_F+t^2\lVert u-p\rVert_F^2$ for $t>0$; division by $t$ and passage to $t\downarrow0$ give $\langle z-p,u-p\rangle_F\le0$. Expanding $\lVert z-u\rVert_F^2$ then gives $\lVert p-u\rVert_F^2\le\lVert z-u\rVert_F^2$. Thus projection does not increase distance to any point of $U$, and the cover becomes proper without increasing its size. [F1, F3, F5, F7, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra, construct]

4.1 Put $q=a^2\lVert X\rVert_F^2/\epsilon^2>1/4$. Then $k=\lceil q\rceil\le q+1\le5q$, so step 2.1 and [F6] imply $\log N_F(U,\epsilon)\le k\log(2dm)\le5q\log(2dm)$. Together with step 1.1 this proves both cases of the Statement. [F4, F6, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space and a scalar $\lambda$.

[L1] The induced norm is a nonnegative square root, and positive definiteness detects the zero vector ([[def-inner-product-norm]]).

[L2] The induced norm is homogeneous ([[lem-inner-product-pairing-is-nondegenerate-and-norm-is-homogeneous]]).

[L3] Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]]).

[L4] If $z=a+bi$, then $\operatorname{Re}z=a$ and $|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Nonnegativity and definiteness follow directly from [L1], and homogeneity is [L2]. [L1, L2]

1.2 Expanding and using conjugate symmetry gives $\lVert u+v\rVert^2=\lVert u\rVert^2+2\operatorname{Re}\langle u,v\rangle+\lVert v\rVert^2$. From [L4], $|z|^2=(\operatorname{Re}z)^2+(\operatorname{Im}z)^2$, so $\operatorname{Re}z\le|z|$; now [L3] makes the expansion at most $(\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert)^2$. [L3, L4, algebra]

2.1 Both quantities in step 1.2 are nonnegative. If the left were larger, their squared order would also be larger, a contradiction. Hence the triangle inequality holds. [step 1.2, L1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the axiom of choice.

Fix a finite network architecture with $L\ge1$, widths $d_0,\ldots,d_L\ge1$, output size $K=d_L\ge2$, and activations as in the spectral-network-complexity definition. Let $s_i>0$, $b_i\ge0$, and reference matrices $M_i$ be such that the class
$$\mathcal F:=\{F_A:\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\le s_i,\ \lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}\le b_i\text{ for every }i\}$$
is nonempty. Let $D$ be any Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^{d_0}\times\{1,\ldots,K\}$, let $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))$ be an independent identically distributed sample from $D$ with $n\ge1$, and fix $\gamma>0$ and $0<\delta<1$. Define the ramp-loss class
$$\mathcal L_\gamma:=\{(x,y)\mapsto\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x,y)):F\in\mathcal F\}.$$
With probability at least $1-\delta$ over $S$, every $F\in\mathcal F$ satisfies
$$L_0(F)\le\widehat L_{\gamma,S}(F)+2\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)+3\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2n}},$$
where $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S$ is the one-sided empirical Rademacher complexity with $1/n$ normalization.

## Statement references

[[def-multiclass-margin-ramp-loss]]: defines multiclass margin, ramp risk, zero-one risk, and empirical margin loss.

[[def-spectral-network-complexity]]: fixes the network family and the layer constraints used to form $\mathcal F$.

[[def-rademacher-complexity]]: fixes the one-sided empirical Rademacher convention and normalization.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compactly constrained network class, Borel probability measure, iid sample, fixed margin level, confidence parameter, and ramp-loss class in the Statement.

[F1] Scores are formed by finite matrix layers and zero-origin Lipschitz activations; the margin is a finite maximum of score-coordinate differences, and the ramp loss takes values in $[0,1]$. [[def-spectral-network-complexity]] [[def-multiclass-margin-ramp-loss]]

[F2] Closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional real Euclidean space are compact. [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]

[F3] For bounded pointwise-convergent measurable functions, dominated convergence passes the limit through the probability integral. [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[F4] Independent random elements have the product joint law, and change of variables transfers integrable product-law functions to expectations; these facts justify the independent ghost sample, pairwise swaps, and expectation identities. [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]] [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]] [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]

[F5] The axiom of choice permits choosing one point from every nonempty member of a countable family of sets. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F6] If changing one independent coordinate changes a bounded measurable statistic by at most $1/n$, McDiarmid's inequality bounds each of its upper and lower tails by $\exp(-2nt^2)$; the lower-tail bound follows by applying the upper-tail bound to the negative statistic. [[thm-mcdiarmid-bounded-differences]]

[F7] The empirical Rademacher complexity is the expectation over independent uniform signs of the supremum of the normalized signed sample averages. [[def-rademacher-complexity]]

[F8] The logarithm is increasing and $\log(xy)=\log x+\log y$. [[def-natural-logarithm]] [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]

[F9] The rationals are dense in the reals: every nonempty open real interval contains a rational. [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]]

## Proof
1.1 Let $\Theta$ be the set of all feasible tuples $(A_1,\ldots,A_L)$. The mixed-norm constraints are closed because each is a finite sum of continuous Euclidean column norms. For each layer, $\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\le s_i$ is the intersection, over all unit vectors $v$, of the closed conditions $\lVert A_iv\rVert_2\le s_i$, by the induced-operator-norm definition. Each column $A_ie_j$ then has norm at most $s_i$, so all matrix entries are bounded. Hence $\Theta$ is closed and bounded in finite-dimensional Euclidean space and is compact by [F2]. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 For fixed $x$, induction over the layers shows that the score vector depends continuously on the matrix tuple: matrix multiplication is jointly continuous and each Lipschitz activation is continuous. Finite maxima, coordinate differences, and the ramp preserve continuity, so for fixed $(x,y)$ the loss $A\mapsto\ell_\gamma(-m_{F_A}(x,y))$ is continuous. If $A^{(r)}\to A$, these losses converge pointwise in $(x,y)$ and are bounded by one, so [F3] shows that $A\mapsto R_\gamma(F_A)$ is continuous. Each empirical loss and each finite signed sum of losses is also continuous in $A$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, given]

3.1 Identify the parameter tuples with $\mathbb R^p$, where $p:=\sum_{i=1}^L d_i d_{i-1}$. The balls $B(q,r)$ with $q\in\mathbb Q^p$ and $r\in\mathbb Q_{>0}$ form a countable family: each rational is a quotient of an integer by a positive integer, the integers have the enumeration $0,1,-1,2,-2,\ldots$, and finite tuples of natural numbers are enumerated by iterating the diagonal pairing $\pi(a,b):=(a+b)(a+b+1)/2+b$. They form a base because for any open $O\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $x\in O$, choose $\eta>0$ with $B(x,\eta)\subseteq O$, then use [F9] in each coordinate interval $(x_j-\eta/(4\sqrt p),x_j+\eta/(4\sqrt p))$ to choose $q\in\mathbb Q^p$ with $\lVert q-x\rVert_2<\eta/4$. Use [F9] again to choose a rational $r$ with $\lVert q-x\rVert_2<r<\eta-\lVert q-x\rVert_2$ (a nonempty interval with positive upper endpoint); then $x\in B(q,r)\subseteq B(x,\eta)\subseteq O$. Intersecting these balls with $\Theta$ gives a countable base for its subspace topology. Using [F5], choose one point of $\Theta$ from each nonempty basic intersection; the selected countable subset is dense in $\Theta$. By step 2.1, each supremum over $\Theta$ defining the uniform deviation or a signed empirical supremum equals the supremum over this countable dense subset. The losses are Borel in $(x,y)$ because the scores are continuous in $x$, the margin is a finite maximum of continuous coordinates, and the label set is finite. These countable suprema are therefore measurable. [F1, F5, F9, step 1.1, step 2.1, given]

4.1 Write $Z(S):=\sup_{F\in\mathcal F}(R_\gamma(F)-\widehat R_{\gamma,S}(F))$. Let $S'$ be an independent ghost sample from $D$. By the integral identities in [F4] and the inequality $\sup_F\mathbb E_{S'}U_F\le\mathbb E_{S'}\sup_F U_F$, $\mathbb E Z(S)\le\mathbb E_{S,S'}\sup_{F\in\mathcal F}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(\ell_F(x_i',y_i')-\ell_F(x_i,y_i)\bigr),$ where $\ell_F(x,y)=\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x,y))$. Swapping each iid pair $(z_i,z_i')$ leaves its law unchanged; introducing independent uniform signs $\varepsilon_i$ therefore leaves this expectation unchanged when each difference is multiplied by $\varepsilon_i$. The supremum of a sum is at most the sum of the suprema, and symmetry of the signs gives $\mathbb E Z(S)\le2\mathbb E_S\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)$. [F4, F7, step 3.1, given, algebra]

5.1 Replacing one sample coordinate changes $Z(S)$ by at most $1/n$, since every loss lies in $[0,1]$; it also changes $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)$ by at most $1/n$, by [F7] and the same range bound. Apply the upper-tail bound [F6] to $Z$ and to $-\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)$, each with failure probability $\delta/2$ and $t=\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2n)}$. Outside a set of probability at most $\delta$, both $Z(S)\le\mathbb EZ(S)+t$ and $\mathbb E\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)\le\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)+t$. Combining with step 4.1 gives $Z(S)\le\mathbb EZ(S)+t\le2\mathbb E\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)+t\le2\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)+3t$. [F6, F7, F8, step 4.1, given, algebra]

6.1 If the predicted label differs from $y$, some competing score is at least the true-label score, so $m_F(x,y)\le0$ and $\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x,y))=1$. Hence the zero-one loss is pointwise at most the ramp loss. Also $\ell_\gamma(-m)\le\mathbf1\{m\le\gamma\}$ for every real $m$, so empirical ramp risk is at most empirical margin loss. Apply the definition of $Z(S)$ and step 5.1 to conclude the stated bound for every $F\in\mathcal F$ simultaneously. [F1, step 5.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Fix an architecture and activations as in the spectral-network-complexity definition, with widths $d_0,\ldots,d_L$ and $W:=\max_i d_i$. Let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d_0}$ be any sample matrix, let $M_i\in\mathbb R^{d_i\times d_{i-1}}$, and fix $s_i>0$ and $b_i\ge0$. Suppose each feasible layer set
$$C_i:=\{A_i:\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\le s_i,\ \lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}\le b_i\}$$
is nonempty. Let $\mathcal H_X$ be the set of $n\times d_L$ score matrices whose $r$th row is $F_A(x_r)^\top$, for $A_i\in C_i$ and the $r$th row $x_r^\top$ of $X$. Then for every $\epsilon>0$,
$$\log N_F(\mathcal H_X,\epsilon)\le5\,\frac{\lVert X\rVert_F^2}{\epsilon^2}\log(2W^2)\left(\prod_{i=1}^L(\rho_i s_i)^2\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^L(b_i/s_i)^{2/3}\right)^3.$$
The logarithm is natural, an empty product equals $1$, and $N_F$ uses proper centers in the covered score-matrix set.

## Statement references

[[def-spectral-network-complexity]]: fixes the network recurrence, zero-origin Lipschitz activations, spectral norm, and mixed column-sum norm.

[[def-sample-covering-number]]: defines proper covers and their Frobenius radius.

[[lem-spectral-network-matrix-cover]]: supplies the proper product cover for a fixed input matrix and one constrained layer.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The architecture, activations, matrices, positive spectral bounds, nonnegative reference-distance bounds, nonempty layer sets, and sample matrix in the Statement.

[F1] Each activation fixes zero and is $\rho_i$-Lipschitz in Euclidean norm; each layer matrix has induced Euclidean norm at most $s_i$, and its transpose-difference from the reference has column-sum norm at most $b_i$. [[def-spectral-network-complexity]]

[F2] For a fixed input matrix $Z$, the one-layer image under a nonempty feasible matrix set has a proper Frobenius cover satisfying the stated matrix-product entropy estimate. [[lem-spectral-network-matrix-cover]]

[F3] The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of all matrix entries, so rowwise application of a $\rho_i$-Lipschitz map changes Frobenius distances by at most the factor $\rho_i$. [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]] [[def-spectral-network-complexity]]

[F4] A proper cover has centers in the covered set, and its covering number is the least size of such a finite cover. [[def-sample-covering-number]]

[F5] The natural logarithm is increasing and satisfies $\log(xy)=\log x+\log y$. [[def-natural-logarithm]] [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]

[F6] If $A=\sum_{j=1}^r\sigma_j u_jv_j^\top$ is a singular-value decomposition with $r>0$, then $A^\top=\sum_{j=1}^r\sigma_jv_ju_j^\top$ has the same positive singular values; the largest-singular-value theorem therefore gives equal operator norms. If $r=0$, both matrices are zero and their operator norms are zero by the same theorem. [[thm-singular-value-decomposition]] [[thm-operator-norm-is-the-largest-singular-value]]

## Proof
1.1 Write $Z_i(A)$ for the matrix of rowwise layer-$i$ activations, with $Z_0(A)=X$. Induction gives $\lVert Z_{i-1}(A)\rVert_F\le\lVert X\rVert_F\prod_{j<i}\rho_js_j$: rowwise zero-origin Lipschitzness gives $\lVert Z_i\rVert_F\le\rho_i\lVert Z_{i-1}A_i^\top\rVert_F$, and [F6] identifies $\lVert A_i^\top\rVert_\sigma=\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\le s_i$, so the induced norm gives $\lVert Z_{i-1}A_i^\top\rVert_F\le s_i\lVert Z_{i-1}\rVert_F$, row by row. [F1, F3, F6, given, induction, algebra]

1.2 If every $b_i=0$, each feasible layer set is the singleton $\{M_i\}$, so $\mathcal H_X$ is a singleton and the right side is zero. Otherwise set $r_i=b_i/s_i$, $T:=\sum_{i:r_i>0}r_i^{2/3}$, and $\alpha_i:=r_i^{2/3}/T$ for positive $r_i$, with $\alpha_i=0$ when $r_i=0$. These weights are nonnegative and sum to one over the varying layers. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Build finite proper covers of the attainable layer outputs successively. At layer $i$, suppose the previous attainable activation matrices have a proper $\eta$-cover with centers $V$ that are themselves attainable prefix outputs. For each such $V$, [F6] gives $\lVert A_i^\top\rVert_\sigma=\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma$, so apply [F2] to $\{VA_i^\top:A_i\in C_i\}$ with input $V$, reference $M_i^\top$, radius $e_i/\rho_i$, and $e_i:=\alpha_i\epsilon/\prod_{j>i}\rho_js_j$ when $b_i>0$. Map each product-cover center through the rowwise activation $\sigma_i$. Every resulting center is attainable by joining the prefix that realizes $V$ to its feasible layer matrix. For any actual prefix $Z$ within $\eta$ of $V$ and any $A_i\in C_i$, the activation output differs from $\sigma_i(VA_i^\top)$ by at most $\rho_i s_i\eta$; the layer cover adds at most $e_i$. Thus the next-stage cover radius is at most $\rho_i s_i\eta+e_i$. When $b_i=0$, use the single matrix $M_i$ and set $e_i=0$. [F1, F2, F4, F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, construct]

3.1 Starting with the exact cover $\{X\}$, the recurrence in step 2.1 gives final radius at most $\sum_i e_i\prod_{j>i}\rho_js_j=\epsilon\sum_{i:r_i>0}\alpha_i=\epsilon$. The cover is proper by construction. At each varying layer, [F2] and the bound from step 1.1 show that its cover-number logarithm is at most $5\frac{\lVert X\rVert_F^2\prod_{j<i}(\rho_js_j)^2}{(e_i/\rho_i)^2}\log(2d_{i-1}d_i).$ For each prior cover center $V$, the next cover has at most this uniform cardinality bound, so taking the union over the prior centers multiplies cardinalities by at most that factor. Since $d_{i-1},d_i\le W$, the logarithm of the final product cover is at most the sum of the displayed layer bounds. [F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 Substitute $e_i=\alpha_i\epsilon/\prod_{j>i}\rho_js_j$ into step 3.1. Each varying-layer term becomes $5\frac{\lVert X\rVert_F^2}{\epsilon^2}\log(2W^2)\left(\prod_{j=1}^L(\rho_js_j)^2\right)\frac{r_i^2}{\alpha_i^2}.$ By the choice in step 1.2, $\sum_{i:r_i>0}r_i^2/\alpha_i^2=T^3=(\sum_i(b_i/s_i)^{2/3})^3$. The all-zero case was handled in step 1.2, so the displayed bound follows in every case. [F5, step 1.2, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎
