## Statement

Assume the axiom of choice.

Fix a finite network architecture with $L\ge1$, widths $d_0,\ldots,d_L\ge1$, output size $K=d_L\ge2$, activations, and reference matrices as in the spectral-network-complexity definition. Let $s_i>0$, $b_i\ge0$, and let $\mathcal F$ be the nonempty class with layer constraints $\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\le s_i$ and $\lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}\le b_i$. Let $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))$ be an iid sample from any Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^{d_0}\times\{1,\ldots,K\}$, let $X$ be its input matrix with rows $x_i^\top$, and fix $n\ge1$, $\gamma>0$, and $0<\delta<1$. Set $W:=\max_{0\le i\le L}d_i$. With probability at least $1-\delta$, every $F_A\in\mathcal F$ satisfies
$$L_0(F_A)\le\widehat L_{\gamma,S}(F_A)+\frac8n+\frac{36\sqrt{20}\,\lVert X\rVert_F\sqrt{\log(2W^2)}\log n}{\gamma n}\left(\prod_{i=1}^L\rho_i s_i\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^L(b_i/s_i)^{2/3}\right)^{3/2}+3\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2n}}.$$
All logarithms are natural. The matrix norm on $X$ is the Frobenius norm, and the empirical margin loss uses the threshold convention $m_{F_A}(x_i,y_i)\le\gamma$.

## Statement references

[[def-multiclass-margin-ramp-loss]]: defines population error, ramp loss, and empirical margin loss.

[[def-spectral-network-complexity]]: fixes the architecture and mixed-norm/spectral-norm conventions.

[[lem-spectral-network-output-covering-entropy]]: bounds the proper Frobenius entropy of the sample score matrices.

[[lem-empirical-rademacher-covering-integral]]: bounds empirical Rademacher complexity by a truncated covering integral.

[[lem-multiclass-margin-rademacher-generalization]]: converts empirical loss-class complexity to a uniform margin-risk bound.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The nonempty bounded layer class, iid sample, sample matrix, fixed positive margin, and confidence level in the Statement.

[F1] For fixed sample inputs, the score matrices form the class covered in the output-entropy lemma, whose logarithmic covering bound has coefficient $5\lVert X\rVert_F^2\log(2W^2)\prod_i(\rho_i s_i)^2(\sum_i(b_i/s_i)^{2/3})^3$. [[lem-spectral-network-output-covering-entropy]]

[F2] At a fixed example the margin is the true-label score minus the maximum competing score, and the ramp is the stated piecewise-linear function with breakpoints $-\gamma$ and $0$. [[def-multiclass-margin-ramp-loss]]

[F3] For any nonempty $[0,1]$-valued loss class on the fixed sample and $0<\alpha\le\sqrt n$, its one-sided empirical Rademacher complexity is bounded by the truncated proper-covering integral. [[lem-empirical-rademacher-covering-integral]]

[F4] Under the axiom of choice, with probability at least $1-\delta$, the zero-one risk is bounded by the empirical margin loss, twice the loss-class empirical Rademacher complexity, and the stated confidence term. [[lem-multiclass-margin-rademacher-generalization]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F5] The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of all matrix entries. [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]

[F6] The natural logarithm is increasing and obeys its product law. [[def-natural-logarithm]] [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]


## Proof
1.1 Fix a realized sample and let $\mathcal U_X$ be its set of score matrices. For score matrices $P,Q$ and example $(x_i,y_i)$, the true-label coordinate changes by at most $\lVert P_{i\cdot}-Q_{i\cdot}\rVert_2$, and the maximum competing coordinate changes by at most the same amount, so [F2] gives margin change at most twice this row norm. On each linear piece of the ramp the absolute slope is either $0$ or $1/\gamma$; the pieces meet continuously at $-\gamma$ and $0$, so summing the changes over the at most three pieces between any two inputs proves $|\ell_\gamma(a)-\ell_\gamma(b)|\le|a-b|/\gamma$. Thus the corresponding loss-vector distance is at most $(2/\gamma)\lVert P-Q\rVert_F$. Mapping the centers of a proper $\gamma\epsilon/2$-cover of $\mathcal U_X$ to their loss vectors therefore gives a proper $\epsilon$-cover of the empirical loss-vector class. [F2, F5, given, algebra, construct]

2.1 Apply [F1] at radius $\gamma\epsilon/2$ and use step 1.1. For every $\epsilon>0$, $\log N_F(\mathcal L_\gamma|S,\epsilon)\le\frac{20\lVert X\rVert_F^2\log(2W^2)}{\gamma^2\epsilon^2}\left(\prod_i(\rho_i s_i)^2\right)\left(\sum_i(b_i/s_i)^{2/3}\right)^3=:\frac{K_\gamma}{\epsilon^2}.$ Here $\mathcal L_\gamma|S$ is the set of vectors of ramp-loss values on the fixed sample. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Use the truncated-integral bound [F3] with $\alpha=1/n$, which satisfies $0<1/n\le\sqrt n$. From step 2.1, $\sqrt{\log N_F(\mathcal L_\gamma|S,\epsilon)}\le\sqrt{K_\gamma}/\epsilon$. Since $\int_{1/n}^{\sqrt n}d\epsilon/\epsilon=\log(n\sqrt n)=\tfrac32\log n$, it follows that $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)\le\frac4{n\sqrt n}+\frac{18\sqrt{K_\gamma}\log n}{n}.$ When $n=1$ the integral is zero and the same expression holds. [F3, F6, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 Apply [F4] and substitute step 3.1. The term twice $4/(n\sqrt n)$ is at most $8/n$ because $n\ge1$. Also $\sqrt{K_\gamma}=\sqrt{20}\,\lVert X\rVert_F\sqrt{\log(2W^2)}\,\gamma^{-1}(\prod_i\rho_i s_i)(\sum_i(b_i/s_i)^{2/3})^{3/2}$. This yields exactly the stated inequality. [F4, F5, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the axiom of choice. Fix a network architecture with $L\ge1$, widths $d_0,\ldots,d_L\ge1$, $K=d_L\ge2$, zero-bias recurrence and zero-origin $\rho_i$-Lipschitz activations as in the spectral-network-complexity definition. Fix reference matrices $M_i\in\mathbb R^{d_i\times d_{i-1}}$. Let $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))$ be an iid sample of size $n\ge1$ from any Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^{d_0}\times\{1,\ldots,K\}$, and let $X$ be the matrix with rows $x_r^\top$. Fix $0<\delta<1$ and set $W:=\max_{0\le i\le L}d_i$. With probability at least $1-\delta$, simultaneously for every network with nonzero layer matrices and every margin $\gamma>0$,
$$L_0(F_A)\le\widehat L_{\gamma,S}(F_A)+\frac8n+\frac{72\sqrt{20}\,(1+\lVert X\rVert_F)\sqrt{\log(2W^2)}\log n}{\gamma n}\left(\prod_{i=1}^L\rho_i\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^L\left[\left(\frac1L+\lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}\right)\prod_{r\ne i}\left(\frac1L+\lVert A_r\rVert_\sigma\right)\right]^{2/3}\right)^{3/2}+3\sqrt{\frac{Q(A,X,\gamma,n,\delta)}{2n}},$$
where all logarithms are natural, an empty product equals $1$, and
$$\begin{aligned}Q(A,X,\gamma,n,\delta):={}&\log(6/\delta)+\log(2+n\gamma)+\log(2+n/\gamma)+2\log(2+\lVert X\rVert_F)\\&+2\sum_{i=1}^L\log\!\left(2+L\lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}\right)+2\sum_{i=1}^L\log\!\left(2+L\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\right). \end{aligned}$$

## Statement references

[[def-spectral-network-complexity]]: fixes the network recurrence, reference matrices, zero-origin activations, and layer norm conventions.

[[def-multiclass-margin-ramp-loss]]: defines population zero-one error and empirical margin loss.

[[lem-bounded-spectral-class-margin-generalization]]: supplies the fixed-margin bound for a class with fixed positive norm caps and reference-distance caps.

[[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]: defines the iid sampling assumption.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The network architecture, fixed reference matrices, iid sample, confidence parameter, and axiom-of-choice assumption in the Statement.

[F1] For fixed positive caps $s_i$ and nonnegative caps $b_i$, every nonempty constrained network class has the fixed-margin bound with leading factor $36\sqrt{20}$ and confidence term $3\sqrt{\log(2/\eta)/(2n)}$. [[lem-bounded-spectral-class-margin-generalization]]

[F2] The architecture uses zero-origin Lipschitz activations, and the sample matrix Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of all its entries. [[def-spectral-network-complexity]] [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]

[F3] The empirical margin loss is nondecreasing as a function of its positive threshold: if $0<\gamma_1\le\gamma_2$, then $\widehat L_{\gamma_1,S}(F)\le\widehat L_{\gamma_2,S}(F)$. [[def-multiclass-margin-ramp-loss]]

[F4] The product of finitely many at most countable sets is at most countable, and probability is countably subadditive. [[thm-product-of-countable]] [[lem-probability-measure-basic-identities]]

[F5] The natural logarithm is increasing and satisfies its product law. [[def-natural-logarithm]] [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]

[F6] The sample coordinates are independent and have the same distribution, as required by the fixed-margin result. [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]

[F7] The fixed-margin result assumes the axiom of choice through its McDiarmid supplier. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof
1.1 For each integer $j\in\mathbb Z$, put $\gamma_j:=2^j/n$ and $v_j:=2^{-|j|}/3$. Then $\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}v_j=(1+2\sum_{m\ge1}2^{-m})/3=1$, since $\sum_{m=1}^N2^{-m}=1-2^{-N}\to1$. Every $\gamma>0$ belongs to exactly one interval $[\gamma_j,2\gamma_j)$. For each positive integer $m$, put $w_m:=1/(m(m+1))=1/m-1/(m+1)$; the finite partial sum is $\sum_{m=1}^Nw_m=1-1/(N+1)$, so $\sum_{m\ge1}w_m=1$. [given, algebra]

2.1 The integers are countable by the enumeration $0,1,-1,2,-2,\ldots$; the other factors are positive integers, so repeated use of [F4] shows that the tuples indexed by $j\in\mathbb Z$, a positive integer $q$, and positive integers $k_i,l_i$ for $1\le i\le L$ form a countable set. For such a tuple set $\eta_{j,q,k,l}:=\delta v_j w_q\prod_iw_{k_i}w_{l_i}$. Let $J_N=\{-N,\ldots,N\}$ and $M_N=\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Finite distributivity gives the sum over $J_N\times M_N^{1+2L}$ as $\delta(\sum_{j\in J_N}v_j)(\sum_{q\in M_N}w_q)\prod_i(\sum_{k_i\in M_N}w_{k_i})(\sum_{l_i\in M_N}w_{l_i})$, which tends to $\delta$ by step 1.1. These finite boxes increase to the countable index set and contain every finite subset for large enough $N$; since all terms are nonnegative, their partial sums establish $\sum_{j,q,k,l}\eta_{j,q,k,l}=\delta$. For each tuple consider the layer class with caps $s_i=l_i/L$ and $b_i=k_i/L$; if it is empty its event is vacuous. Otherwise [F1] gives a fixed-margin result at $\gamma_j$ and confidence $\eta_{j,q,k,l}$, with its displayed sample-norm term evaluated at the realized $X$. [F1, F4, F6, F7, step 1.1, given, construct]

3.1 Apply countable subadditivity [F4] to the failure events from step 2.1. Their union has probability at most $\sum_{j,q,k,l}\eta_{j,q,k,l}=\delta$. Thus outside that union, all fixed-margin inequalities for every tuple hold simultaneously. [F4, step 2.1, given]

4.1 Fix any realized sample, any network with nonzero layer matrices, and any $\gamma>0$. Choose its unique $j$ from step 1.1 with $\gamma_j\le\gamma<2\gamma_j$, and set $q=\lfloor\lVert X\rVert_F\rfloor+1,\qquad k_i=\lfloor L\lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}\rfloor+1,\qquad l_i=\lfloor L\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\rfloor+1.$ These positive integers satisfy $\lVert X\rVert_F<q$, $\lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}<k_i/L$, and $0<\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma<l_i/L$. The network belongs to the corresponding constrained class. Also $\widehat L_{\gamma_j,S}(F_A)\le\widehat L_{\gamma,S}(F_A)$ by [F3], and $1/(\gamma_j n)<2/(\gamma n)$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, given, construct]

5.1 In the leading term of [F1], the cap expression satisfies $\left(\prod_i s_i\right)\left(\sum_i(b_i/s_i)^{2/3}\right)^{3/2}=\left(\sum_i\left(b_i\prod_{r\ne i}s_r\right)^{2/3}\right)^{3/2}.$ For the tuple selected in step 4.1, $q\le1+\lVert X\rVert_F$, $k_i/L\le\lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}+1/L$, and $l_i/L\le\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma+1/L$. Monotonicity of the sums and products therefore bounds [F1]'s leading term by the leading term in the Statement, using $1/(\gamma_jn)<2/(\gamma n)$. [F1, F2, step 4.1, given, algebra]

5.2 The confidence logarithm for this tuple equals $\log(2/\eta_{j,q,k,l})=\log(6/\delta)+|j|\log2+\log(q(q+1))+\sum_i\bigl(\log(k_i(k_i+1))+\log(l_i(l_i+1))\bigr).$ Put $t=n\gamma$. If $j\ge0$, then $2^j\le t$ and $|j|\log2\le\log(2+t)$. If $j<0$, then $t<2^{j+1}\le1$, so $\log(2+t)\ge\log2$ and $\log(2+1/t)\ge\log(1/t)$; their sum is at least $\log(2/t)>|j|\log2$. For each positive integer bin chosen as $m=\lfloor u\rfloor+1$, one has $m\le u+1$ and $m+1\le u+2$, hence $\log(m(m+1))\le2\log(u+2)$. ## Statement

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** At most countable sets $A$ and $B$, and the product $A \times B = \{\, (a,b) : a \in A,\ b \in B \,\}$.

[L1] Finite, countably infinite and at most countable; $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\varnothing$ is finite ([[def-countable]], [[def-natural-numbers]]).

[L2] A nonempty set is at most countable if and only if some surjection $\mathbb{N} \to$ it exists ([[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]]).

[L3] There is a bijection $\beta : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-n-cross-n-countable]], [[def-equinumerous]]).

[L4] A composition of surjections is a surjection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $A = \varnothing$ or $B = \varnothing$ then $A \times B = \varnothing$, which is finite and hence at most countable. [given, L1]

1.2 Assume instead $A \ne \varnothing$ and $B \ne \varnothing$; then [L2] provides surjections $f : \mathbb{N} \to A$ and $g : \mathbb{N} \to B$. [given, L2]

1.3 Fix the bijection $\beta : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ of [L3], in particular a surjection. [L3]

2.1 Define $t : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to A \times B$ by $t(m,n) = (f(m), g(n))$. It is surjective: any $(a,b) \in A \times B$ has $a = f(m)$ and $b = g(n)$ for some $m, n$, so $(a,b) = t(m,n)$. [step 1.2]

3.1 Hence $t \circ \beta : \mathbb{N} \to A \times B$ is a surjection by [L4], and $A \times B$ is nonempty, so it is at most countable by [L2]. [step 1.3, step 2.1, L2, L4]

4.1 Both cases give the conclusion: $A \times B$ is at most countable whenever $A$ and $B$ are. [step 1.1, step 3.1, L1] ∎

## Remarks

- Iterating gives the same conclusion for $A_1 \times A_2 \times \dots \times A_k$ for each fixed $k$: $(A_1 \times A_2) \times A_3$ is a product of two at most countable sets, and so on, so $k - 1$ applications of the theorem settle the case $k$. Stating this uniformly in $k$, as a single theorem quantified over $k$, needs finite sequences of sets and a recursive definition of the $k$-fold product, which this library does not yet have; the iterated form above is the honest statement of what is proved.

- The infinite product is a different matter and is **not** covered: $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ is a product of countably many two-element sets and is uncountable, by the same diagonal argument as [[thm-cantor-powerset]]. Countability is not preserved by infinite products of any kind.

- Together with [[lem-subset-of-countable]] this gives the countability of every set that can be coded by finitely many naturals, which is how [[thm-rationals-countable]] is proved.

## Example

Assume the axiom of choice. Take one layer with input width $1$, output width $2$, identity activation with Lipschitz constant $\rho_1=1$, reference matrix $M_1=0$, and layer matrix $A_1=(1,-1)^\top$. Let the input distribution be the point mass at $(x,y)=(1,1)$, so a sample of size $n=1$ always has $X=(1)$ and label $1$. At margin level $\gamma=1$ and confidence $\delta=1/10$, the score vector is $(1,-1)$, its margin is $2$, its empirical margin loss and population error are both zero, and the spectral network complexity is $R_A=2$. The simultaneous theorem's right-hand side is $8+3\sqrt{Q/2}$, where
$$Q=\log60+2\log3+2\log3+2\log4+2\log(2+\sqrt2)\approx13.72,$$
so the bound evaluates to approximately $15.86$. The example records the exact margin and complexity and shows the small-sample bound is valid but loose.

## Example references

[[def-spectral-network-complexity]]: defines the spectral complexity formula and induced operator norm.

[[def-multiclass-margin-ramp-loss]]: defines multiclass margin, empirical margin loss, and population error.

[[thm-spectral-margin-bound-for-multiclass-networks]]: supplies the simultaneous probability bound and its confidence expression.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The one-layer network, point-mass distribution, sample size, margin level, and confidence parameter in the Example.

[F1] The spectral norm is the induced Euclidean operator norm, the transpose-difference mixed norm sums its column Euclidean norms, and $R_A$ is their prescribed spectral-complexity expression. [[def-spectral-network-complexity]]

[F2] The margin is true-label score minus the largest competing score; empirical margin loss counts examples with margin at most the threshold, and population error is zero-one classification error. [[def-multiclass-margin-ramp-loss]]

[F3] Under the stated iid and choice assumptions, the simultaneous theorem has an additive $8/n$ term, a leading term proportional to $\log n$, and confidence term $3\sqrt{Q/(2n)}$. [[thm-spectral-margin-bound-for-multiclass-networks]]

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The only column of $A_1$ has Euclidean norm $\sqrt2$, so its induced operator norm is $\sqrt2$. The transpose $A_1^\top=(1,-1)$ has two scalar columns of absolute values $1$ and $1$, so $\lVert A_1^\top-M_1^\top\rVert_{2,1}=2$. Also $\lVert X\rVert_F=1$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Applying the network map to $x=1$ gives scores $(1,-1)$; [F2] therefore gives margin $1-(-1)=2$, empirical margin loss $\mathbf1\{2\le1\}=0$, and zero population error under the point-mass law. [F2, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Substitution into the spectral-complexity definition yields $R_A=\sqrt2\left((2/\sqrt2)^{2/3}\right)^{3/2}=2.$ For $n=1$ the leading term in [F3] vanishes because $\log1=0$, and $8/n=8$. Substituting $\delta=1/10$, $\gamma=1$, $\lVert X\rVert_F=1$, $L=1$, $\lVert A_1^\top-M_1^\top\rVert_{2,1}=2$, and $\lVert A_1\rVert_\sigma=\sqrt2$ into the theorem's $Q$ gives the displayed expression. The inequality is $0\le8+3\sqrt{Q/2}\approx15.86$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume the axiom of choice and take confidence level $\delta=1/2$. Let the input always be $x=1$ and let the label distribution assign probability $0.6$ to class $1$ and $0.4$ to class $2$. Use one identity-activation layer with $A_1=(1,0)^\top$ and reference $M_1=0$. For a sample of size $n=1$, at margin threshold $\gamma=1/2$ the event that the sampled label is class $1$ has probability $0.6$, has empirical margin loss zero, while the network's population zero-one error is $0.4$. The simultaneous theorem still permits this event because its $8/n$ term alone is $8$; the example shows that one zero empirical margin-loss observation does not itself determine population error.

## Example references

[[def-multiclass-margin-ramp-loss]]: defines the population zero-one error and empirical margin loss.

[[def-population-and-empirical-risk]]: defines population expectation and empirical averages.

[[thm-spectral-margin-bound-for-multiclass-networks]]: supplies the finite-sample bound including the additive $8/n$ term.

**Given:** The two-point label distribution, deterministic input, one-layer network, sample size, and margin threshold in the Example.

[F1] The network uses the zero-bias recurrence with an identity activation, and the operator norm is induced by the Euclidean norm. [[def-spectral-network-complexity]]

[F2] The margin is true score minus the maximum competing score; empirical margin loss counts margins at most $\gamma$ and population zero-one error is the probability of a wrong predicted label. [[def-multiclass-margin-ramp-loss]]

[F3] The theorem's upper bound includes the additive $8/n$ correction. [[thm-spectral-margin-bound-for-multiclass-networks]]

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The scores at $x=1$ are $(1,0)$. For label $1$ the margin is $1-0=1$; for label $2$ it is $0-1=-1$. Thus the network predicts class $1$ on both possible labeled outcomes. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 By the label probabilities in the Example and [F2], the population zero-one error is $0.4$. If the sample label is class $1$, which occurs with probability $0.6$, its only margin is $1>1/2$, so its empirical margin loss is $0$. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 For $n=1$, [F3] contributes $8/n=8$ to the theorem's right-hand side, already exceeding the population error $0.4$; all other displayed terms are nonnegative. Therefore the stated sample event is consistent with the theorem and demonstrates why empirical margin loss alone is not a population-error guarantee. [F3, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma_X)$ be a nonempty measurable instance space, let $\mathcal Y=\{1,\ldots,K\}$ have its discrete sigma-algebra with $K\ge2$, and equip $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$ and its finite powers with their product sigma-algebras. Let $P$ be a probability law on $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$. For an integer $m\ge1$, write a sample as $S=((X_1,Y_1),\ldots,(X_m,Y_m))$. A score map $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_K):\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$ is **coordinatewise measurable** when each $u_k:(\mathcal X,\Sigma_X)\to(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is measurable. Define its classifier by the least-index tie rule

$$h_u(x):=\min\{k\in\mathcal Y:u_k(x)=\max_{j\in\mathcal Y}u_j(x)\}$$

and its margin on label $y$ by

$$M_u(x,y):=u_y(x)-\max_{j\in\mathcal Y,\ j\ne y}u_j(x).$$

For each $k\in\mathcal Y$,
$$\{x:h_u(x)=k\}=\bigcap_{j<k}\{x:u_k(x)>u_j(x)\}\cap\bigcap_{j>k}\{x:u_k(x)\ge u_j(x)\},$$
and each comparison set is measurable; an intersection over no indices means $\mathcal X$. Since $\mathcal Y$ is finite, $M_u$ is measurable on $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$ as well. The population zero-one risk is
$$R_P(h_u):=P\{(x,y):h_u(x)\ne y\}.$$
For a sample $S$ of length $m$ and $\gamma\ge0$, the empirical margin loss is
$$\widehat L_\gamma(u;S):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1\{M_u(X_i,Y_i)\le\gamma\}.$$
The event defining $R_P(h_u)$ is measurable by measurability of $h_u$.

Fix integers $q\ge0$ and $r\ge1$. A fixed-helper finite parameter codebook consists of a helper string $s$ fixed independently of the sample, finite nonempty sets $D_1,\ldots,D_q$ with $|D_j|\le r$, a nonempty code set $\mathcal A\subseteq\prod_{j=1}^qD_j$, and one coordinatewise measurable decoder score map $g_{s,a}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$ for each $a\in\mathcal A$. For $q=0$, the empty product is the singleton containing the empty tuple. The codebook and all its decoders are fixed independently of the sample, so $|\mathcal A|\le r^q$.

Let $F:(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y)^m\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$ be measurable for the product sigma-algebra on its domain and the Borel sigma-algebra on $\mathbb R^K$. Let $\alpha:(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y)^m\to\mathcal A$ be measurable, where $\mathcal A$ has its discrete sigma-algebra, and write $f_S(x):=F(S,x)$. For $\epsilon>0$, the sample-dependent trained score map $f_S$ is $\epsilon$-compressible by this codebook on a sample $S$ if
$$\max_{k\in\mathcal Y}|f_S(X_i)_k-g_{s,\alpha(S)}(X_i)_k|\le\epsilon\qquad(1\le i\le m).$$
The code $\alpha(S)$ may depend on $S$; the helper string, codebook, and decoders remain fixed independently of the sample.

## Definition references

[[def-measurable-space]]: a measurable space consists of a set equipped with a sigma-algebra.

[[def-supervised-learning-problem]]: supplies measurable instance and label spaces, a joint probability law, measurable predictors, and a measurable loss.

[[def-population-and-empirical-risk]]: population risk is the nonnegative integral of the loss, and empirical risk is its finite sample average.

[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]: measurability is the preimage condition.

[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: finite product sigma-algebras are generated recursively by measurable rectangles.

[[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]: finite maxima and arithmetic combinations of measurable real-valued functions are measurable.

[Arora et al., §2, Definitions 1–2](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/arora18b/arora18b.pdf): score closeness on training inputs with a finite code family and a helper fixed before sampling.

[Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, Chapter 4 §4.2](https://www.inf.u-szeged.hu/~turan/ML-Konyv.pdf): finite measurable hypothesis classes and empirical/population zero-one risk conventions.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The measurable space $(\mathcal X,\Sigma_X)$, the finite discrete label space $\mathcal Y$, the product sigma-algebras, the law $P$, and a coordinatewise measurable score map $u$.

[F1] Finite maxima and arithmetic combinations of measurable real-valued functions are measurable. [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]

[F2] A map is measurable when preimages of measurable sets are measurable. [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]

[F3] The product sigma-algebra is generated by measurable rectangles, and finite products use the recursively formed product sigma-algebra. [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]

## Verification

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Definition.

1.1 For each $k$, the displayed fiber formula expresses $h_u^{-1}(\{k\})$ as a finite intersection. Each comparison set is the preimage of $(0,\infty)$ or $[0,\infty)$ under the measurable difference $u_k-u_j$, which is measurable by [F1] and [F2]. Hence every singleton fiber is measurable, and because $\mathcal Y$ is finite and discrete, $h_u$ is measurable. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 For each $y\in\mathcal Y$, the function $x\mapsto M_u(x,y)$ is measurable by finite maximization and subtraction in [F1]. For every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$, its inverse image under $M_u$ is the finite union over $y$ of $\{x:M_u(x,y)\in B\}\times\{y\}$, which belongs to the product sigma-algebra by [F3]. The error event is the finite union $\bigcup_{k\in\mathcal Y}h_u^{-1}(\{k\})\times(\mathcal Y\setminus\{k\})$, so it is measurable too. Thus the risk is defined as the probability of a measurable event. [given, F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

The following corrected finite-description form of Arora, Ge, Neyshabur, and Zhang's compression bound applies to a measurable sample-dependent score classifier. Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma_X)$ be a nonempty measurable space, let $\mathcal Y=\{1,\ldots,K\}$ have the discrete sigma-algebra with $K\ge2$, put $\Sigma_Z=\Sigma_X\otimes2^{\mathcal Y}$ on $Z=\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, and let $P$ be a probability law on $(Z,\Sigma_Z)$. Let $m\ge1$ and draw $S=((X_1,Y_1),\ldots,(X_m,Y_m))$ independently and identically distributed (IID) with law $P$, with sample space $Z^m$ carrying $\Sigma_Z^{\otimes m}$. Fix integers $q\ge0$, $r\ge1$, a helper string $s$ independent of $S$, finite nonempty parameter sets $D_1,\ldots,D_q$ with $|D_j|\le r$, a nonempty code set $\mathcal A\subseteq\prod_{j=1}^qD_j$ (with the empty product a singleton when $q=0$), a distortion tolerance $\epsilon>0$, and a confidence level $0<\delta<1$. For any score map $u$ with measurable coordinates, write $h_u(x)$ for the classifier that chooses the least index attaining the largest coordinate of $u(x)$. For each $a\in\mathcal A$, let $g_{s,a}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$ have measurable coordinates and put $h_{s,a}:=h_{g_{s,a}}$. Equip $\mathbb R^K$ with its Borel sigma-algebra. Let $F:Z^m\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$ be measurable for $\Sigma_Z^{\otimes m}\otimes\Sigma_X$, write $f_S(x)=F(S,x)$, and let $\alpha:Z^m\to\mathcal A$ be measurable for the discrete sigma-algebra on $\mathcal A$. Suppose that, for $P^m$-almost every $S$,
$$\max_{k\in\mathcal Y}|f_S(X_i)_k-g_{s,\alpha(S)}(X_i)_k|\le\epsilon\qquad(1\le i\le m)$$
With natural logarithms, define
$$R_P(h):=P\{(x,y):h(x)\ne y\},\qquad \widehat R_S(h):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1\{h(X_i)\ne Y_i\},$$
$$M_{f_S}(x,y):=f_S(x)_y-\max_{j\ne y}f_S(x)_j,\qquad \widehat L_\gamma(f_S;S):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1\{M_{f_S}(X_i,Y_i)\le\gamma\},\qquad \gamma\ge0.$$
Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over $S$,
$$R_P\bigl(h_{s,\alpha(S)}\bigr)\le\widehat L_{2\epsilon}(f_S;S)+\sqrt{\frac{q\log r+\log(1/\delta)}{2m}}.$$
In particular, the coordinatewise distortion $\epsilon$ only guarantees preservation of an observed label when its original score margin is strictly greater than $2\epsilon$. The conclusion bounds the selected compressed classifier $h_{s,\alpha(S)}$; it does not bound the original classifier $h_{f_S}$ unless a separate all-domain loss-preservation argument is supplied. The theorem assumes a suitable fixed-helper compressor and makes no claim that a network compression construction exists or that layer-stability or cushion hypotheses hold.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The measurable spaces and law $P$, an IID sample of size $m\ge1$, a fixed helper string and finite nonempty codebook with at most $r$ values in each of $q$ parameter positions, measurable training and compression maps, distortion $\epsilon>0$ on $P^m$-almost every sample, and $0<\delta<1$.

[F1] For a finite family of events $E_1,\ldots,E_n$, $P(\bigcup_{j=1}^nE_j)\le\sum_{j=1}^nP(E_j)$. [[lem-probability-measure-basic-identities]]

[F2] The helper string, codebook, and decoders are fixed independently of $S$, with at most $r^q$ codes. [[def-margin-preserving-compression]]

[F3] The measurable code selector may depend on $S$ and the coordinatewise distortion condition applies at every observed input on each successful sample. [[def-margin-preserving-compression]]

[F4] The natural logarithm is increasing and satisfies $\log(xy)=\log x+\log y$, $\log(x/y)=\log x-\log y$, and $\log 1=0$ for positive $x,y$. [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]

[F5] $\exp(\log x)=x$ for $x>0$. [[def-natural-logarithm]]

[F6] $\exp(-x)=1/\exp(x)>0$ for every real $x$. [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]

[F7] IID observations are mutually independent and share the same law. [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]

[F8] The sample space and finite products carry sigma-algebras generated by measurable rectangles. [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]

[F9] Measurability is defined by measurable preimages; compositions are measurable by successive preimages. [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]

[F10] Finite sums, scalar multiples, absolute values, and finite maxima of measurable real-valued functions are measurable. [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]

[F11] If $U$ is measurable and $0\le U\le1$ almost surely, then $\mathbb E\exp(\lambda(U-\mathbb EU))\le\exp(\lambda^2/8)$ for every real $\lambda$. [[lem-bounded-variable-hoeffding-mgf]]

[F12] Measurable coordinatewise functions of independent random elements remain independent. [[lem-measurable-functions-preserve-independence]]

[F13] For independent real random variables and nonnegative Borel functions $g_i$, the expectation of their finite product factors into the product of expectations. [[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]]

## Proof
1.1 For each sample coordinate $i$, the projections $S\mapsto(X_i,Y_i)$ and $S\mapsto X_i$ are measurable by [F8]. The map $T_i:S\mapsto(S,X_i)$ is measurable because the preimage of a measurable rectangle $B\times C$ is $B\cap\{S:X_i\in C\}$ and such rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra [F8]; composition with $F$ is measurable by [F9], so $S\mapsto f_S(X_i)$ is measurable. For each fixed $a$, $S\mapsto g_{s,a}(X_i)$ is measurable by [F9]. The selector $\alpha$ takes values in the finite set $\mathcal A$ by [F2], so the preimage of a Borel set under $S\mapsto g_{s,\alpha(S)}(X_i)$ is a finite union of intersections of measurable selector fibers and fixed-code preimages. By [F10], each coordinatewise distortion comparison is measurable, and the finite intersection over coordinates and sample positions makes the compression-success event measurable. The zero-one loss $\ell_a(x,y)=\mathbf1\{h_{s,a}(x)\ne y\}$ is measurable by the verified measurability properties in [F3]; composing it with the sample projections and taking a finite average shows that each $\widehat R_S(h_{s,a})$ is measurable. Since $\mathcal A$ is finite and $\alpha$ measurable, both selected risk maps $S\mapsto R_P(h_{s,\alpha(S)})$ and $S\mapsto\widehat R_S(h_{s,\alpha(S)})$ are measurable. The margins $M_{f_S}(X_i,Y_i)$ are measurable by [F10], hence so is their finite threshold average $\widehat L_{2\epsilon}(f_S;S)$. Thus every event in the Statement and proof is measurable. [given, F2, F3, F8, F9, F10, algebra]

1.2 On a sample satisfying the compression condition, if $M_{f_S}(X_i,Y_i)>2\epsilon$, then for each $j\ne Y_i$ the coordinatewise distortion bound [F3] gives $g_{s,\alpha(S)}(X_i)_{Y_i}-g_{s,\alpha(S)}(X_i)_j\ge f_S(X_i)_{Y_i}-f_S(X_i)_j-2\epsilon\ge M_{f_S}(X_i,Y_i)-2\epsilon>0$. Thus the decoded classifier predicts $Y_i$ at that observation. Each decoded training-error indicator is therefore at most $\mathbf1\{M_{f_S}(X_i,Y_i)\le2\epsilon\}$, and averaging gives $\widehat R_S(h_{s,\alpha(S)})\le\widehat L_{2\epsilon}(f_S;S)$. [given, F3, F10, algebra]

2.1 Fix $a\in\mathcal A$, write $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$ and $U_i=\ell_a(Z_i)$, and put $\mu=R_P(h_{s,a})=\int\ell_a\,dP$ by [F23]. Each $Z_i$ has law $P$ by [F7] and [F17], so [F18] gives $\mathbb E U_i=\mu$. The $U_i$ are independent by [F12], since $\ell_a$ is measurable by step 1.1. The function $x\mapsto\lambda(x-\mu)$ is continuous by [F20], and [F16] and [F21] make $g_\lambda(x):=\exp(\lambda(x-\mu))$ continuous. Its preimage of every open set is open; preimages preserve complements and countable unions, so [F22] makes preimages of all Borel sets Borel by [F9]. Thus $g_\lambda$ is a nonnegative Borel function. [given, F7, F9, F10, F12, F16, F17, F18, F19, F20, F21, F22, F23, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By finite-product factorization [F13], exponential addition [F15], and the bounded-variable MGF estimate [F11], $\mathbb E\exp\!\left(\lambda\sum_{i=1}^m(U_i-\mu)\right)=\prod_{i=1}^m\mathbb E\exp(\lambda(U_i-\mu))\le\exp(m\lambda^2/8)$ for every real $\lambda$. This finite MGF argument uses no choice principle by [A1]. [given, A1, F11, F13, F15, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For $t>0$, put $\lambda=-4t$. On $\{\sum_i(U_i-\mu)\le-mt\}$, strict increase of the exponential [F16] gives $\exp(\lambda\sum_i(U_i-\mu))\ge\exp(4mt^2)>0$ by [F6]. Markov's inequality [F14] and step 3.1 therefore give $P^m\{R_P(h_{s,a})-\widehat R_S(h_{s,a})\ge t\}\le\exp(m\lambda^2/8)/\exp(4mt^2)=\exp(-2mt^2)$. [given, F6, F14, F16, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Set $\tau=\sqrt{\log(r^q/\delta)/(2m)}$. Since $r^q\ge1$ and $0<\delta<1$, [F4] gives $\tau>0$. Applying step 4.1 to each fixed code at $t=\tau$ and using [F5]–[F6] gives failure probability at most $\exp(-2m\tau^2)=\exp(-\log(r^q/\delta))=\delta/r^q$. The union bound [F1] over at most $r^q$ codes by [F2] yields, with probability at least $1-\delta$, one event on which every $a\in\mathcal A$ satisfies $R_P(h_{s,a})\le\widehat R_S(h_{s,a})+\tau$. For $q=0$, $\log(r^q)=\log1=0$; for $q\ge1$, repeated use of the product law [F4] gives $\log(r^q)=q\log r$. The quotient law gives $\log(r^q/\delta)=q\log r+\log(1/\delta)$, so $\tau$ is the displayed complexity term. [given, F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The event from step 5.1 holds simultaneously for every fixed code, so it also holds for the sample-dependent choice $\alpha(S)$. The compression condition fails only on a $P^m$-null set. Intersecting the step 5.1 event with its full-measure success set and applying step 1.2 gives the stated risk inequality with probability at least $1-\delta$. [given, step 5.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, functions $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, a real $\alpha$, a point $c \in A$ at which $f$ and $g$ are continuous, and, for claim 4, the hypothesis $g(c) \ne 0$ together with $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$.

[L1] Continuity at $c$: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ such that every $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

[L2] A point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$, and never both; at an isolated point of its domain every function is continuous; at a limit point $c$ of $A$, continuity of $f$ at $c$ is exactly the statement that the limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and equals $f(c)$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-limit-point-r]], [[def-neighbourhood-r]], [[def-function-limit]]).

[L3] Algebra of function limits at a limit point $c$ of $A$: if the limits of $f$ and $g$ at $c$ exist with values $L$ and $M$, then the limits of $f+g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ at $c$ exist with values $L+M$, $\alpha L$ and $LM$; and if $M \ne 0$ then $c$ is a limit point of $A_0$, and the limit of $(f/g)|_{A_0}$ at $c$ exists and equals $L/M$ ([[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]]).

[L4] Sign preservation: if the limit of $g$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ exists and is nonzero, then $c$ is a limit point of $A_0 = \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$ ([[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]]).

[L5] Reverse triangle inequality: $\bigl||u| - |v|\bigr| \le |u - v|$ ([[cor-of-reverse-triangle]]); and $|u| \ge 0$, $|u| = 0$ exactly when $u = 0$, $|uv| = |u||v|$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]).

[L6] Maximum and minimum of a two-element set of reals exist ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]), and for all reals $u, v$ one has $\max\{u,v\} = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(u + v + |u-v|\bigr)$ and $\min\{u,v\} = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(u + v - |u-v|\bigr)$.

[L7] Ordered-field arithmetic in $\mathbb{R}$: trichotomy and totality of the order, the field identities, and $0 < 1$ so that $2 \ne 0$ and $t/2$ is defined ([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-field]]).

[L8] Integer powers: $a^{0} = 1$ and $a^{n+1} = a^{n} \cdot a$ ([[def-integer-power]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **Justification of the identity in [L6].** Let $u, v \in \mathbb{R}$. By totality either $u \ge v$ or $v \ge u$. If $u \ge v$ then $u - v \ge 0$, so $|u-v| = u-v$ and $\tfrac{1}{2}(u+v+|u-v|) = \tfrac{1}{2}(2u) = u = \max\{u,v\}$, while $\tfrac{1}{2}(u+v-|u-v|) = v = \min\{u,v\}$. If $v \ge u$ the same computation with the roles exchanged applies, since $|u-v| = v-u$ there. [L5, L6, L7]

1.2 **The isolated case.** Suppose $c$ is an isolated point of $A$, say $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ with $\eta > 0$ real. Then every function on $A$ is continuous at $c$ by [L2], which gives claims 1, 2 and 3 at once. For claim 4, assume $g(c) \ne 0$; then $c \in A_0$, and $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A_0 \subseteq N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ with $c$ in the left-hand side, so $c$ is an isolated point of $A_0$ and every function on $A_0$, in particular $(f/g)|_{A_0}$, is continuous at $c$. [L2]

1.3 **Claim 2, at any point of $A$.** Let a real $\varepsilon > 0$ be given and let $\delta > 0$ be as in [L1] for $f$ and this $\varepsilon$. For $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ the reverse triangle inequality gives $\bigl||f(x)| - |f(c)|\bigr| \le |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$. So $|f|$ is continuous at $c$, and no case distinction was needed. [L1, L5]

1.4 **Claim 5, constants and the identity.** If $f$ is constant then $|f(x) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$ for every $x \in A$ and every real $\varepsilon > 0$, so any $\delta > 0$ serves. For the identity, given a real $\varepsilon > 0$ take $\delta := \varepsilon$: every $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ has $|\mathrm{id}(x) - \mathrm{id}(c)| = |x - c| < \varepsilon$. Both are continuous at every point of $A$. [L1, L5, L7]

1.5 **The limit-point case, claim 1.** Suppose $c$ is a limit point of $A$. By [L2] the limits of $f$ and of $g$ at $c$ exist and equal $f(c)$ and $g(c)$. By [L3] the limits of $f+g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ at $c$ exist and equal $f(c)+g(c)$, $\alpha f(c)$ and $f(c)g(c)$, which are exactly the values of those three functions at $c$; by [L2] again, each of them is continuous at $c$. [L2, L3]

1.6 **The limit-point case, claim 4.** Suppose $c$ is a limit point of $A$ and $g(c) \ne 0$. Then $c \in A_0$, and by [L4] the point $c$ is a limit point of $A_0$. By [L3] the limit of $(f/g)|_{A_0}$ at $c$ exists and equals $f(c)/g(c)$, which is the value of $(f/g)|_{A_0}$ at $c$; by [L2] applied on the domain $A_0$, that function is continuous at $c$. [L2, L3, L4]

2.1 **Claims 1 and 4 in general.** By [L2] the point $c$ is either isolated in $A$ or a limit point of $A$; step 1.2 settles the first case and steps 1.5 and 1.6 the second. So claims 1 and 4 hold as stated. [step 1.2, step 1.5, step 1.6, L2]

3.1 **Claim 3.** By claim 1 the function $f - g = f + (-1)g$ is continuous at $c$, by step 1.3 so is $|f-g|$, and by claim 1 again so are $f + g + |f-g|$ and its scalar multiple by $1/2$. By step 1.1 that scalar multiple is the function $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$, so the maximum is continuous at $c$; the same argument with $-|f-g|$ gives the minimum. [step 1.1, step 1.3, step 2.1, L6, L7]

3.2 **Claim 5, powers and polynomials.** The map $x \mapsto x^{0}$ is the constant $1$ and $x \mapsto x^{1}$ is the identity, both continuous on $A$ by step 1.4; and if $x \mapsto x^{n}$ is continuous on $A$ then so is $x \mapsto x^{n+1} = x^{n} \cdot x$, being a product of two functions continuous on $A$ by step 2.1. By induction on $n$, $x \mapsto x^{n}$ is continuous on $A$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A polynomial function $a_0 + a_1x + \dots + a_nx^{n}$ is obtained from these by finitely many scalar multiplications and additions, each of which preserves continuity by step 2.1. [step 1.4, step 2.1, L8]

4.1 Claims 1 to 5 are proved, all of them at an arbitrary point $c$ of $A$ and therefore, applied at every point, on the whole of $A$; and no sequence and no choice principle was used. [step 1.3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

## Remarks

- **Why the two-case shape, and why it is not an inconvenience.** Continuity is defined at every point of the domain, including isolated points, where no limit exists ([[def-continuity-real]]). The algebra of limits therefore cannot be applied blindly; but at an isolated point every function is continuous, so the case is settled before it is opened. Claims 2 and 5 are proved directly from $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ and need no case distinction at all.

- **Absolute value, maximum and minimum are not in [[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]]**, and the reason is that they are not needed there. They are needed here: the extreme value theorem and the one-dimensional fixed point theorem both build auxiliary functions out of maxima, minima and differences, and [[thm-compactness-is-necessary-for-evt-and-uniform-continuity]] builds its witnesses out of $|x - x_0|$ and quotients.

- **The converse of claim 2 is false**: $|f|$ may be continuous while $f$ is continuous nowhere. The function equal to $1$ on $\mathbb{Q}$ and to $-1$ elsewhere has constant absolute value; that it is nowhere continuous follows from the argument of [[cex-dirichlet-is-nowhere-continuous]] applied verbatim, since that argument uses only that the two values are distinct.

## Statement

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g(A) \subseteq B$, and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$. If $g$ is continuous
at $c$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(c) \in B$, then $f \circ g$ is continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $g$ is continuous on $A$ and $f$ is continuous on $B$, then
$f \circ g$ is continuous on $A$.

**No side hypothesis is needed, and that is the whole point.** The composition
theorem for limits, [[thm-composition-of-function-limits]], must assume one of
two extra conditions: either $L \in B$ with $f(L) = M$, or $g \ne L$ on a
punctured neighbourhood of $c$; with both dropped the statement is false, which
is [[fs-naive-composition-of-limits]]. The first of those conditions is exactly
*continuity of $f$ at $L$* written out, so under the hypotheses above it holds
automatically and nothing has to be assumed. The mechanism is visible in the
proof: [[def-continuity-real]] quantifies over $|y - b| < \rho$ rather than over
$0 < |y - b| < \rho$, so the value $y = b$ that the limit version cannot control
is precisely the one the continuity hypothesis does control.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Sets $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, functions $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with $g(A) \subseteq B$ and $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, a point $c \in A$ at which $g$ is continuous, and the hypothesis that $f$ is continuous at $b := g(c) \in B$.

[L1] Continuity of $g$ at $c$: for every real $\rho > 0$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ such that every $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|g(x) - g(c)| < \rho$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

[L2] Continuity of $f$ at $b$: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $\rho > 0$ such that every $y \in B$ with $|y - b| < \rho$ satisfies $|f(y) - f(b)| < \varepsilon$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

[L3] Neighbourhoods and the unpunctured quantifier: the condition in [L2] is imposed at every $y \in B$ with $|y - b| < \rho$, the value $y = b$ included ([[def-neighbourhood-r]], [[def-continuity-real]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Write $b := g(c)$; by hypothesis $b \in B$, since $g(A) \subseteq B$ and $c \in A$. Also $(f \circ g)(c) = f(b)$. [given]

1.2 Let a real $\varepsilon > 0$ be given. By [L2] fix a real $\rho > 0$ such that every $y \in B$ with $|y - b| < \rho$ satisfies $|f(y) - f(b)| < \varepsilon$. [L2, choose]

2.1 By [L1], applied with this $\rho$, fix a real $\delta > 0$ such that every $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|g(x) - b| < \rho$. [step 1.2, L1, choose]

3.1 Let $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$. Then $g(x) \in B$ and $|g(x) - b| < \rho$ by step 2.1, so $y := g(x)$ is admissible in step 1.2 and gives $\bigl|f(g(x)) - f(b)\bigr| < \varepsilon$, that is $\bigl|(f \circ g)(x) - (f \circ g)(c)\bigr| < \varepsilon$. Note that the case $g(x) = b$ is included, by [L3]. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, L3]

4.1 The real $\varepsilon > 0$ was arbitrary and a $\delta > 0$ was produced for it, so $f \circ g$ is continuous at $c$; applying this at every point of $A$ gives continuity of $f \circ g$ on $A$ whenever $g$ is continuous on $A$ and $f$ on $B$. [step 3.1, L1, L2] ∎

## Remarks

- **The contrast with limits, in one sentence.** [[thm-composition-of-function-limits]] cannot control $f$ at the single value $L$, because [[def-function-limit]] never evaluates $f$ there; continuity of $f$ at that value is exactly the missing information, and it is hypothesis (i) of that theorem. So the present theorem is not a strengthening obtained by cleverness: it is the composition theorem under the hypothesis that makes the obstruction vanish.

- **What is not claimed.** Continuity of $f \circ g$ at $c$ does not follow from continuity of $g$ at $c$ alone together with $f$ merely having a limit at $b$; nor does it follow from continuity of $f$ at $b$ together with $g$ merely having a limit at $c$, since then $g(c)$ need not be $b$ at all. Both hypotheses above are hypotheses about the same two points, $c$ and $g(c)$.

## Statement

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $A\in\mathcal F$.
Then the indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ and an event $A$.

[L1] Expectation of a nonnegative random variable is its integral with respect to $\mathbb P$ ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

[L2] The complement identity gives $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$ ([[lem-probability-measure-basic-identities]]).

[L3] On nonnegative simple functions, the nonnegative integral is the simple integral $\sum_j c_j\mu(E_j)$ ([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]], [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The function $\mathbf 1_A$ is the simple function $$\mathbf 1_A=1\cdot\chi_A+0\cdot\chi_{A^c}.$$ Therefore [L1] and [L3] give $$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=1\cdot\mathbb P(A)+0\cdot\mathbb P(A^c).$$ [L1, L3]

2.1 Using [L2] only to note that $A^c$ is the complementary event in the same probability space, step 1.1 simplifies to $\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A)$. [step 1.1, L2] ∎

## Example

Let $\mathcal X=\{0,1\}$ and $\mathcal Y=\{1,2\}$, both with the discrete sigma-algebra, and let $P\{(0,1)\}=P\{(1,2)\}=1/2$. Define $\rho(t)=\max\{0,t\}$ and the two-class score maps
$$f(x)=(10\rho(1-x),\rho(x)),\qquad g(x)=(10,0),\qquad x\in\mathcal X.$$
Both maps can be realized by one-hidden-layer feedforward networks with ReLU hidden activation and identity output activation. Take the training score map to be constant, $F(S,x)=f(x)$ for every length-one sample, and take a constant selector into a fixed one-code codebook with $q=1$ and $r=1$, whose decoder is $g$. For the one-point training sample $S=((0,1))$, the scores agree exactly, so $g$ is a $1/10$-score compression of $f$ on $S$. Their least-index argmax classifiers agree at the observed input $0$ and differ at the unobserved input $1$. Their population zero-one risks are $R_P(h_f)=0$ and $R_P(h_g)=1/2$. This is only a single-sample witness: the fixed code does not meet the theorem's almost-sure compression hypothesis for this $P$, because it fails on the other possible one-point sample $((1,2))$.

## Example references

[[def-feedforward-neural-network]]: a finite acyclic computation graph evaluates hidden activations in topological order and uses identity output activations in a layered MLP.

[[def-margin-preserving-compression]]: a fixed helper and codebook can be paired with a sample-dependent code whose decoded scores are close on the observed inputs.

[[thm-finite-description-compression-bound]]: its high-probability conclusion bounds the selected compressed classifier under an almost-sure compression hypothesis.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two-point measurable classification problem, the law $P$, the one-point sample $S=((0,1))$, the constant training map $F(S,x)=f(x)$, the scores $f,g$, and the fixed one-code family described in the Example.

[F1] A feedforward computation graph is a finite directed acyclic graph evaluated in a topological order; a layered MLP has hidden activations and identity output activations. [[def-feedforward-neural-network]]

[F2] A finite score codebook is fixed independently of the sample, while its measurable selector may depend on the sample; compression on $S$ requires coordinatewise score error at most the stated tolerance on each observed input. [[def-margin-preserving-compression]]

[F3] Under the theorem's almost-sure compression hypothesis, the conclusion bounds the decoded classifier $h_{s,\alpha(S)}$, and makes no claim for the original classifier without separate all-domain loss preservation. [[thm-finite-description-compression-bound]]

## Verification

**Given:** The finite instance space $\mathcal X=\{0,1\}$, labels $\mathcal Y=\{1,2\}$, equal-mass law $P$, and score maps from the Example.

1.1 Let the two hidden ReLU units for $f$ be $u_1(x)=\rho(x)$ and $u_2(x)=\rho(1-x)$, with output coordinates $(10u_2,u_1)$. Let $g$ use one hidden unit $u_1(x)=\rho(x)$, output weights zero, and output biases $(10,0)$. These are finite one-hidden-layer graphs with hidden activation $\rho$ and identity output activation, as in [F1]. Direct evaluation gives $f(0)=g(0)=(10,0)$ and $f(1)=(0,1)$, $g(1)=(10,0)$. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 The least-index argmax rule predicts class $1$ for both maps at $x=0$; at $x=1$, $f$ predicts class $2$ and $g$ predicts class $1$. Under $P$, $f$ is correct on both support points, while $g$ errs exactly at $(1,2)$, so $R_P(h_f)=0$ and $R_P(h_g)=1/2$. Also $P^1\{S=((0,1))\}=1/2$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\mathcal A=\{a_0\}$ with one parameter slot whose only possible value is $a_0$, fix the helper string, decode $a_0$ to $g$, and let the compressor choose $a_0$ on every sample. On $S=((0,1))$, the maximum coordinate error is $0\le1/10$, so this sample is compressed and the predictions agree on the observed point. On $S'=((1,2))$, the maximum coordinate error is $10>1/10$, so this fixed compressor fails the almost-sure premise of the theorem under $P$. Therefore this example establishes only that single-sample agreement can coexist with different off-sample predictions and population risks; it does not contradict or invoke the theorem's high-probability conclusion. ## Statement

Let $(\mathsf Z,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ be a probability measure on it, and let $m\ge1$. If $Z_1,\ldots,Z_m,Z_*$ are IID random elements with law $P$, define $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ and, for $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, let $S^{(i)}$ be $S$ with coordinate $i$ replaced by $Z_*$. Then the random vectors $(S,Z_*)$ and $(S^{(i)},Z_i)$ have the same distribution on the finite product measurable space $(\mathsf Z^{m+1},\Sigma^{\otimes(m+1)})$.

## Statement references

Hardt, Recht, and Singer, §2.2, proof of Theorem 2.2: [full arXiv paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.01240).

Matni, Lecture 16, §3.1, proof of Theorem 2: [full lecture notes](https://nikolaimatni.github.io/courses/ese680-fall2019/scribe-notes/lecture16.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A common measurable target, a probability law $P$, and the IID random elements in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]: IID means mutual independence together with equality of all coordinate laws.

[F2] [[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]: for any finite selection of coordinate events, their intersection has probability equal to the product of their probabilities.

[F3] [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: finite product sigma-algebras are generated recursively by coordinate measurable rectangles.

[F4] [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]: a finite product measure is uniquely determined by its values on coordinate rectangles; this follows by iterating the stated two-factor uniqueness theorem.

## Proof

1.1 Fix $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and a measurable rectangle $B_1\times\cdots\times B_{m+1}$. By [F1] and [F2], its probability under $(S,Z_*)$ is $\prod_{j=1}^{m+1}P(B_j)$. The vector $(S^{(i)},Z_i)$ swaps coordinates $i$ and $m+1$, so the same rectangle has probability $\prod_{j=1}^{m+1}P(B_j)$ under that vector as well. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 Each vector is measurable: the preimage of a coordinate rectangle is a finite intersection of measurable coordinate events, and [F3] says these rectangles generate $\Sigma^{\otimes(m+1)}$. Thus both vector laws are probability measures on that product sigma-algebra. They agree on its generating coordinate rectangles by step 1.1; iterating [F4] along the recursive finite product in [F3] identifies both with the same product measure. Hence their distributions agree. [F3, F4, step 1.1, given] ∎

## Definition

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

A family $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ is
**independent** when it is independent as a family of event classes in the
sense of [[def-independent-families-of-event-classes]].

A family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of events is **independent** when the singleton event
classes $\bigl(\{A_i\}\bigr)_{i\in I}$ are independent. Equivalently, for every
finite choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_{i_k}\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_{i_k}).$$

For two events this reduces to the familiar identity
$\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)$.

## Definition

Fix a supervised prediction problem with observation space $\mathsf Z=\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, measurable predictor class $\mathcal F$, and nonnegative measurable loss $\ell$. Write $L_f(x,y)=\ell(f(x),y)$ for $f\in\mathcal F$. Fix a sample size $n\ge1$. A randomized learning rule at this sample size consists of internal randomness $U_n$ with law $Q_n$, independent of the sample, and an output $A_n(S,U_n)\in\mathcal F$ for every ordered sample $S\in\mathsf Z^n$. Assume the expected test losses below are finite. For $\varepsilon\ge0$, the rule has **uniform replacement stability at level $\varepsilon$** if, for every pair $S,S'\in\mathsf Z^n$ differing in at most one coordinate, and every test observation $z\in\mathsf Z$,

$$\left|\mathbb E_{U_n}L_{A_n(S,U_n)}(z)-\mathbb E_{U_n}L_{A_n(S',U_n)}(z)\right|\le\varepsilon.$$

The absolute value is outside expectation over the internal randomness. No permutation-invariance condition is imposed on the learning rule.

## Definition references

Hardt, Recht, and Singer, Definition 2.1: [full arXiv paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.01240).

Matni, Lecture 16, Definition 1: [full lecture notes](https://nikolaimatni.github.io/courses/ese680-fall2019/scribe-notes/lecture16.pdf).

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$ and consider a supervised prediction problem with measurable observation space $\mathsf Z=\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, probability law $P$, measurable predictor class $\mathcal F$, and nonnegative measurable loss $\ell$. For $f\in\mathcal F$ and $z=(x,y)$, write $L_f(z)=\ell(f(x),y)$, $R_P(f)=\int L_f(z)\,P(dz)$, and, for $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$, $\widehat R_S(f)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nL_f(Z_i)$. Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID with law $P$, and let $U_n$ be internal randomness independent of the sample. Suppose the randomized learning rule $A_n(S,U_n)$ takes values in $\mathcal F$, the joint loss map $(S,U_n,z)\mapsto L_{A_n(S,U_n)}(z)$ is measurable, and all displayed risks are integrable. If $A_n$ has uniform replacement stability at level $\varepsilon$, then

$$\left|\mathbb E_{S,U_n}\left[R_P(A_n(S,U_n))-\widehat R_S(A_n(S,U_n))\right]\right|\le\varepsilon.$$

The expectation is over both the IID sample and the algorithm's internal randomness. No permutation-invariance assumption on $A_n$ is required.

## Statement references

Hardt, Recht, and Singer, Theorem 2.2 and proof: [full arXiv paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.01240).

Matni, Lecture 16, Theorem 2 and proof: [full lecture notes](https://nikolaimatni.github.io/courses/ese680-fall2019/scribe-notes/lecture16.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The supervised prediction problem, IID sample, independent algorithmic randomness, measurable and integrable loss maps, and uniform replacement stability in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-supervised-learning-problem]]: the joint observation law is a probability measure and the loss is nonnegative and measurable.

[F2] [[def-population-and-empirical-risk]]: population risk is the nonnegative integral of test loss and empirical risk is its finite sample average.

[F3] [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]: the observations are mutually independent and have common law $P$.

[F4] [[lem-iid-sample-plus-ghost-point-are-exchangeable]]: if $Z_*$ is an independent observation with law $P$, then $(S,Z_*)$ and $(S^{(i)},Z_i)$ have the same law for each $i$, where $S^{(i)}$ replaces coordinate $i$ by $Z_*$.

[F5] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: for the integrable joint loss map, its product integral equals either iterated integral, including integration over the independent algorithm seed and test observation.

[F6] [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]: the integral of a finite sum of integrable functions is the sum of their integrals.

[F7] [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]: the absolute value of an integral is at most the integral of the absolute value.

[F8] [[def-uniform-stability]]: for every fixed adjacent pair of ordered samples and test observation, the difference of their expected losses over $U_n$ has absolute value at most $\varepsilon$.

[A1] The joint loss map is measurable and integrable, as required in the Statement, so Fubini and every displayed expectation are defined.

## Proof

1.1 Extend the sample by an independent ghost observation $Z_*\sim P$. By [F1], [F2], and [F5], $\mathbb E_{S,U_n}R_P(A_n(S,U_n))=\mathbb E_{S,U_n,Z_*}L_{A_n(S,U_n)}(Z_*)$. For each $i$, [F4] and independence of $U_n$ imply $\mathbb E_{S,U_n,Z_*}L_{A_n(S,U_n)}(Z_*)=\mathbb E_{S,U_n,Z_*}L_{A_n(S^{(i)},U_n)}(Z_i)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, given, construct]

## Statement

Let $n,T,d\ge1$, let $\beta>0$ and $L\ge0$, and let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be measurable spaces. Let $P$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, let $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$ be a measurable loss, and let $f_w:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ be a measurable predictor for every $w\in\mathbb R^d$. For $z=(x,y)$ set $g(w,z)=\ell(f_w(x),y)$ and assume this map and $(w,z)\mapsto\nabla_wg(w,z)$ are jointly measurable. For every observation $z$, assume $w\mapsto g(w,z)$ is totally differentiable and convex, its Euclidean gradient is $\beta$-Lipschitz, and its values are $L$-Lipschitz in the sense that $|g(w,z)-g(v,z)|\le L\|w-v\|_2$ for all $w,v\in\mathbb R^d$. Let $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ be IID with law $P$, and abbreviate $R_P(f_w)=\int g(w,z)\,P(dz)$ and $\widehat R_S(f_w)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^ng(w,Z_i)$. Let $I_1,\ldots,I_T$ be random indices in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, independent of $S$ and satisfying $\mathbb P(I_t=i)=1/n$ for every $1\le t\le T$ and $1\le i\le n$; dependence between indices at different times is allowed. From a fixed $w_0\in\mathbb R^d$, set

$$w_t=w_{t-1}-\alpha_t\nabla_wg(w_{t-1},Z_{I_t}),\qquad 1\le t\le T,$$

where the deterministic steps satisfy $0\le\alpha_t\le2/\beta$. Assume the displayed sample-dependent loss and risk maps are measurable and integrable. Then this randomized procedure has uniform replacement stability at level

$$\varepsilon_{\mathrm{stab}}=\frac{2L^2}{n}\sum_{t=1}^T\alpha_t,$$

and its expected population-minus-empirical risk gap satisfies

$$\left|\mathbb E_{S,I}\left[R_P(f_{w_T})-\widehat R_S(f_{w_T})\right]\right|\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{stab}}.$$

The result concerns the specified uniform-marginal sample-selection updates, including independent sampling with replacement and uniform random-permutation passes. It does not assert generalization for every stochastic-gradient oracle.

## Statement references

Hardt, Recht, and Singer, arXiv-version Theorem 3.8 and proof (conference Theorem 3.7): [full arXiv paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.01240).

Matni, Lecture 16, Lemma 2 and Theorem 3 with proof: [full lecture notes](https://nikolaimatni.github.io/courses/ese680-fall2019/scribe-notes/lecture16.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The IID supervised sample, independent uniform-marginal indices, fixed initialization, loss hypotheses, and integrability conditions in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]: convexity is the segment inequality on a convex Euclidean domain.

[F2] [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]] and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]: total differentiability means a linear first-order approximation with normwise $o(\|h\|_2)$ remainder, and the scalar gradient is the vector of its partial derivatives.

[F3] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: $\langle u,v\rangle$ is the Euclidean inner product and $\|u\|_2=\sqrt{\langle u,u\rangle}$.

[F4] [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]: for a totally differentiable scalar field, $D_vg(w,z)=\langle\nabla_wg(w,z),v\rangle$.

[F5] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: the Euclidean norm satisfies the triangle inequality and every normalized nonzero vector has norm $1$.

[F6] [[lem-convex-gradient-step-nonexpansive]]: for a differentiable convex loss with $\beta$-Lipschitz gradient, the update $w\mapsto w-\alpha\nabla\ell(w,z)$ is nonexpansive when $0\le\alpha\le2/\beta$.

[F7] [[def-uniform-stability]]: stability compares expected test losses for every fixed neighboring ordered sample pair and every fixed test observation.

[F8] [[thm-uniform-stability-implies-expected-generalization]]: uniform replacement stability at level $\varepsilon$ implies an absolute expected generalization gap at most $\varepsilon$ when the sample, algorithm, and risk maps satisfy its measurability and integrability hypotheses.

[F9] [[def-supervised-learning-problem]] and [[def-population-and-empirical-risk]]: the test loss, population risk, and empirical risk use the stated measurable loss and law $P$.

[F10] [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]: the observations are mutually independent and have the common law $P$.

[A1] The random index vector is independent of the sample and each coordinate is uniform; no independence between different indices is assumed.

[A2] The population-risk and empirical-risk random variables are measurable and integrable, as required in the Statement.

## Proof

1.1 Fix $w,z$ and suppose $\nabla_wg(w,z)\ne0$. Put $v=\nabla_wg(w,z)/\|\nabla_wg(w,z)\|_2$, which is a unit vector by [F3] and [F5]. The directional derivative of $t\mapsto g(w+tv,z)$ at $0$ is $\langle\nabla_wg(w,z),v\rangle=\|\nabla_wg(w,z)\|_2$ by [F2] and [F4]. The $L$-Lipschitz inequality in the Statement bounds every difference quotient by $L$, so passage to the derivative gives $\|\nabla_wg(w,z)\|_2\le L$; the same bound is immediate when the gradient is zero. [F2, F3, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 Fix neighboring samples $S,S'$ differing at coordinate $j$ and couple their runs using the same index vector. Put $\delta_t=\|w_t(S)-w_t(S')\|_2$, so $\delta_0=0$. If $I_t\ne j$, both runs apply the same convex-loss gradient step and [F6] gives $\delta_t\le\delta_{t-1}$. If $I_t=j$, the triangle inequality from [F5] and step 1.1 give $\delta_t\le\delta_{t-1}+2\alpha_tL$. Thus, pathwise, $\delta_t\le\delta_{t-1}+2\alpha_tL\mathbf1_{\{I_t=j\}}$. [A1, F1, F5, F6, step 1.1, given, construct]

3.1 Taking expectation in the pathwise inequality and using only $\mathbb P(I_t=j)=1/n$ yields $\mathbb E\delta_t\le\mathbb E\delta_{t-1}+2\alpha_tL/n$. Summing from $t=1$ to $T$ gives $\mathbb E\delta_T\le(2L/n)\sum_{t=1}^T\alpha_t$. [A1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For every test observation $z$, the value-Lipschitz hypothesis gives $\mathbb E_I|g(w_T(S),z)-g(w_T(S'),z)|\le L\mathbb E\delta_T\le(2L^2/n)\sum_t\alpha_t$. Hence the absolute difference of the two expected losses is at most this value, proving the stated uniform stability. [F7, step 3.1, given, algebra]

5.1 The sample is IID by [F10], the index vector is independent of it by [A1], and the risk maps $R_P(f_{w_T})$ and $\widehat R_S(f_{w_T})$ are measurable and integrable by [A2]; they use the loss and risk conventions of [F9]. Apply [F8] with the stability level from step 4.1 to obtain the expected generalization bound. [A1, A2, F8, F9, F10, step 4.1, given] ∎

## Statement

If a scalar-valued $f:U\to\mathbb R$ is totally differentiable at $a$, then $D_vf(a)=\langle\nabla f(a),v\rangle$ for every $v$. Among unit vectors $v$, this is at most $\|\nabla f(a)\|_2$; if the gradient is nonzero, equality holds exactly in the direction $\nabla f(a)/\|\nabla f(a)\|_2$. If the gradient is zero, every unit direction has directional derivative zero.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A scalar-valued totally differentiable $f$ at $a$ and a direction $v$.

[L1] A total derivative computes every directional derivative, and its matrix is the Jacobian ([[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

[L2] **Cauchy--Schwarz:** $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** cases.

1.1 By [L1], $D_vf(a)$ is the Jacobian row applied to $v$, namely $\sum_j\partial_jf(a)v_j=\langle\nabla f(a),v\rangle$. [L1, L2]

2.1 If $\nabla f(a)\ne0$ and $\|v\|_2=1$, [L2] gives $D_vf(a)\le\|\nabla f(a)\|_2$, with equality at $v=\nabla f(a)/\|\nabla f(a)\|_2$. [assume-case nonzero, step 1.1, L2, algebra]

3.1 If $\nabla f(a)=0$, step 1.1 makes every directional derivative zero; together with step 2.1 this proves the stated alternatives. [assume-case zero, step 1.1, step 2.1, cases-exhaustive] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge2$, $T,d\ge1$, and let $\beta,c>0$ and $L\ge0$. Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be measurable spaces, let $P$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, let $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$ be a measurable loss, and let $f_w:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ be a measurable predictor for every $w\in\mathbb R^d$. For every $z$, assume $g(\cdot,z)$ is totally differentiable, takes values in $[0,1]$, is $L$-Lipschitz in values, and has a $\beta$-Lipschitz Euclidean gradient; these mean, respectively,

$$|g(w,z)-g(v,z)|\le L\|w-v\|_2,\qquad \|\nabla_wg(w,z)-\nabla_wg(v,z)\|_2\le\beta\|w-v\|_2$$

for all $v,w\in\mathbb R^d$. No convexity is assumed. Let $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ be IID with law $P$, and abbreviate $R_P(f_w)=\int g(w,z)\,P(dz)$ and $\widehat R_S(f_w)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^ng(w,Z_i)$. Let $I_1,\ldots,I_T$ be random indices in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, independent of $S$ and satisfying $\mathbb P(I_t=i)=1/n$ for every $1\le t\le T$ and $1\le i\le n$; dependence between indices at different times is allowed. From a fixed $w_0\in\mathbb R^d$, define

$$w_t=w_{t-1}-\alpha_t\nabla_wg(w_{t-1},Z_{I_t}),\qquad 1\le t\le T,$$

where $0\le\alpha_T\le\cdots\le\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_t\le c/t$. Assume the resulting random variables $R_P(f_{w_T})$ and $\widehat R_S(f_{w_T})$ are measurable; they are integrable because $0\le g\le1$. Then the randomized procedure has uniform replacement stability and absolute expected population-minus-empirical risk gap at most

$$\left(1+\frac1{\beta c}\right)\frac{(2cL^2)^{1/(\beta c+1)}}{n-1}\,T^{\beta c/(\beta c+1)}.$$

If $L=0$, the right side is interpreted as $0$. The conclusion concerns only this expected gap for the stated random sample-selection procedure; it does not assert generalization for every stochastic-gradient oracle.

## Statement references

Hardt, Recht, and Singer, arXiv-version Theorem 3.12 and complete proof (conference Theorem 3.8): [full arXiv paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.01240).

Matni, Lecture 16, §4: [full lecture notes](https://nikolaimatni.github.io/courses/ese680-fall2019/scribe-notes/lecture16.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The supervised IID sample, independent uniform-marginal indices, fixed initialization, loss range/Lipschitz/smoothness assumptions, nonincreasing steps, and integrable risk maps in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]] and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]: total differentiability means a linear first-order approximation with normwise $o(\|h\|_2)$ remainder, and the scalar gradient is the vector of its partial derivatives.

[F2] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: $\langle u,v\rangle$ is the Euclidean inner product and $\|u\|_2=\sqrt{\langle u,u\rangle}$.

[F3] [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]: for a totally differentiable scalar field, $D_vg(w,z)=\langle\nabla_wg(w,z),v\rangle$.

[F4] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: the Euclidean norm satisfies the triangle inequality and every normalized nonzero vector has norm $1$.

## Statement

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Reals $a < c < b$ and a bounded $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$; and, for claim 3, reals $\alpha < \beta$, an integrable $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to \mathbb{R}$ and points $u,v,w \in [\alpha,\beta]$. Let a real $\varepsilon > 0$ be given.

[L1] Riemann's criterion on any closed bounded interval with distinct endpoints ([[thm-riemann-criterion]]).

[L2] A function integrable on $[p,q]$ is integrable on every $[p',q'] \subseteq [p,q]$ with $p' < q'$ ([[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]]).

[L3] For a partition $R = (n,t)$ and bounded $h$: $L(h,R) = \sum_{i<n}m_i\Delta_i$, $U(h,R) = \sum_{i<n}M_i\Delta_i$, and $L(h,R) \le \underline{\int} h \le \overline{\int} h \le U(h,R)$, the integral being the common value of the two when they agree ([[def-darboux-sums]], [[def-darboux-integral]]).

[L4] A partition of $[p,q]$ is a pair $(n,t)$ with $n \ge 1$, $t_0 = p$, $t_i < t_{i+1}$ for $i < n$ and $t_k = q$ for $k \ge n$; its subintervals are $[t_i,t_{i+1}]$ for $i<n$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]], [[def-interval]]).

[L5] Finite sums split at an intermediate index, with $\sum_{k=p}^{q-1}x_k = \sum_{j<q-p}x_{p+j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]], clause 3).

[L6] With oriented limits, $\int_v^u h = -\int_u^v h$ and $\int_u^u h = 0$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]).

[L7] Ordered-field arithmetic: adding a constant preserves an inequality, the order is total and transitive, and a real of absolute value below every positive real is $0$ ([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **Claim 1, forward.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then, since $a < c$ and $c < b$, [L2] gives integrability on $[a,c]$ and on $[c,b]$. [L2]

1.2 **The splice.** Let $P_1 = (n_1,t^1)$ be a partition of $[a,c]$ and $P_2 = (n_2,t^2)$ one of $[c,b]$. Define $P := (n_1+n_2,\ t)$ by $t_i := t^1_i$ for $i \le n_1$, $t_{n_1+j} := t^2_j$ for $j \le n_2$, and $t_k := b$ for $k \ge n_1+n_2$. The two prescriptions agree at $i = n_1$, where $t^1_{n_1} = c = t^2_0$; and $t_0 = a$, $t_{n_1+n_2} = t^2_{n_2} = b$, with $t_i < t_{i+1}$ for every $i < n_1+n_2$. So $P$ is a partition of $[a,b]$. [L4, construct]

1.3 **Claim 1, converse.** Suppose $f$ is integrable on $[a,c]$ and on $[c,b]$, and use [L1] on each to fix $P_1$ with $U(f,P_1)-L(f,P_1) < \varepsilon\cdot 2^{-1}$ and $P_2$ with $U(f,P_2)-L(f,P_2) < \varepsilon\cdot 2^{-1}$. [L1, choose]

2.1 The first $n_1$ subintervals of $P$ are those of $P_1$ and the last $n_2$ are those of $P_2$, with the matching lengths, so by [L3] and the splitting law [L5], $L(f,P) = L(f,P_1) + L(f,P_2)$ and $U(f,P) = U(f,P_1) + U(f,P_2)$. [step 1.2, L3, L4, L5]

3.1 For the splice $P$ of those two, step 2.1 gives $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$; as $\varepsilon > 0$ was arbitrary and $f$ is bounded, [L1] makes $f$ integrable on $[a,b]$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 1.3, L1, L7]

4.1 **Claim 2.** With $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P$ as above, [L3] puts $\int_a^b f$ between $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P)$, that is between $L(f,P_1)+L(f,P_2)$ and $U(f,P_1)+U(f,P_2)$ by step 2.1; and [L3] applied on $[a,c]$ and on $[c,b]$ puts $\int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$ between the same two numbers. [step 2.1, step 1.3, step 3.1, L3]

5.1 Those two numbers differ by less than $\varepsilon$ by step 1.3, so $\bigl|\int_a^b f - \int_a^c f - \int_c^b f\bigr| < \varepsilon$; as $\varepsilon > 0$ was arbitrary the difference is $0$, which is claim 2. [step 1.3, step 4.1, L7]

6.1 **Claim 3, first the sorted case.** Let $x \le y$ in $[\alpha,\beta]$. Then $\int_\alpha^y f = \int_\alpha^x f + \int_x^y f$. Indeed if $\alpha < x < y$ this is claim 2 applied on $[\alpha,y]$, where $f$ is integrable by [L2]; if $x = \alpha$ the middle term is $0$ by [L6] and the identity is trivial; and if $x = y$ the last term is $0$ by [L6] and the identity is again trivial. [step 5.1, L2, L6]

7.1 Put $F(x) := \int_\alpha^x f$ for $x \in [\alpha,\beta]$, which is defined by [L2] and [L6]. Then $\int_x^y f = F(y) - F(x)$ for **all** $x,y \in [\alpha,\beta]$: for $x < y$ this is step 6.1 rearranged; for $x = y$ both sides are $0$ by [L6]; and for $x > y$ the case already proved gives $\int_y^x f = F(x)-F(y)$, and [L6] negates both sides. [step 6.1, L2, L6, construct]

8.1 **Claim 3.** For arbitrary $u,v,w \in [\alpha,\beta]$, step 7.1 gives $\int_u^v f + \int_v^w f = \bigl(F(v)-F(u)\bigr) + \bigl(F(w)-F(v)\bigr) = F(w)-F(u) = \int_u^w f$. [step 7.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- **The oriented form is not proved by listing six orderings.** Step 7.1 shows that the oriented integral between two points is a *difference of values of one function of one variable*, after which claim 3 is the cancellation $(F(v)-F(u))+(F(w)-F(v)) = F(w)-F(u)$, valid however the three points are arranged and however many of them coincide. The case analysis is confined to the two lines of step 7.1, and no appeal to symmetry is made anywhere.

- **The function $F$ of step 7.1 is the integral function**, and it is given its own item, [[def-the-integral-function]], because the rest of the page is about it. Nothing there re-proves step 7.1; it cites this theorem.

- **Boundedness on the whole of $[a,b]$ is a hypothesis of claim 1 in both directions.** Boundedness on $[a,c]$ and on $[c,b]$ separately does give boundedness on the union, so the converse could be stated with the hypothesis split; it is stated globally because [[def-darboux-sums]] needs it globally to make $U(f,P)$ meaningful for a partition of $[a,b]$.
