## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The training law assigns weight $1/2$ to each of $X^{(0)}$ and $X^{(1)}$; independently choose the visible set uniformly from $\{\{1\},\{2\}\}$. The target is $T_{\rm norm}$, the encoder is the constant map $E(x,V)=z_*$, and the decoder returns $(-1,1)$ at both positions for every encoded sequence.

[F1] [[def-reconstruction-autoencoder]]: for a patch with positive standard deviation, $T_{\rm norm}(u)=(u-\bar u\mathbf 1)/s(u)$, and the masked-patch loss averages squared errors over positions in $[M]\setminus V$.

[F2] [[alg-masked-autoencoder-pretraining]]: the visible set is uniform among all size-$k$ subsets; the encoder sees only visible patches, while the decoder predicts every patch after mask tokens are inserted at missing positions.

[F3] [[def-expectation-on-a-finite-probability-space]]: expectation on a finite probability space is the weighted sum of the values over its outcomes.

[F4] [[def-feedforward-neural-network]]: each non-input vertex has a real bias, weights on its incoming edges, and an activation; in a layered MLP the output vertices use the identity activation.

## Definition

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

## Definition

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A_X,\mu_X)$ and $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal A_Z,\mu_Z)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces; that is, each has a countable measurable cover by sets of finite measure. Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_\theta}$ and $\Phi\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_\phi}$ be parameter sets of finite dimension. A latent-variable model with parameter $\theta\in\Theta$ consists of a measurable prior density $r_\theta(z)\ge0$ on $\mathcal Z$ and a decoder density $d_\theta(x\mid z)\ge0$ on $\mathcal X$ for each $z$, with
$$\int_{\mathcal Z} r_\theta(z)\,d\mu_Z(z)=1,\qquad \int_{\mathcal X} d_\theta(x\mid z)\,d\mu_X(x)=1.$$
The decoder is jointly measurable in $(x,z)$, and the joint model density is
$$p_\theta(x,z)=\gamma_\theta(z;x):=r_\theta(z)d_\theta(x\mid z)$$
relative to $\mu_X\otimes\mu_Z$. The decoder is also called the generative model: after drawing $z$ from the prior, it assigns a conditional density to the observation $x$.

For a fixed observation $x$, the evidence density and posterior density are
$$Z_\theta(x):=p_\theta(x):=\int_{\mathcal Z}\gamma_\theta(z;x)\,d\mu_Z(z),\qquad \pi_\theta(z\mid x):=\frac{\gamma_\theta(z;x)}{Z_\theta(x)}.$$
Use this posterior only when $0<Z_\theta(x)<\infty$. A variational encoder is a jointly measurable family of functions $q_\phi(z\mid x)\ge0$ on $\mathcal Z$, parameterized by $\phi\in\Phi$ and normalized by
$$\int_{\mathcal Z}q_\phi(z\mid x)\,d\mu_Z(z)=1$$
for every $(\phi,x)$; the same parameter $\phi$ is used for each observation. For an admissible triple $(\theta,\phi,x)$ require $0<Z_\theta(x)<\infty$ and
$$q_\phi(z\mid x)=0\quad\mu_Z\text{-almost everywhere on }\{z:\pi_\theta(z\mid x)=0\},\qquad \int_{\mathcal Z}q_\phi(z\mid x)\bigl(|\log\gamma_\theta(z;x)|+|\log q_\phi(z\mid x)|\bigr)\,d\mu_Z(z)<\infty.$$
Terms multiplied by $q_\phi=0$ are defined to be zero. The evidence lower bound is
$$\operatorname{ELBO}_{\theta,\phi}(x):=\int_{\mathcal Z}q_\phi(z\mid x)\bigl(\log\gamma_\theta(z;x)-\log q_\phi(z\mid x)\bigr)\,d\mu_Z(z).$$

A pathwise representation of the encoder at $x$ is a probability space $(\mathcal E,\mathcal F,\rho)$ whose law $\rho$ is independent of $\theta$ and $\phi$, together with a measurable map $g_\phi(\epsilon,x)$ such that the law of $g_\phi(\epsilon,x)$ for $\epsilon\sim\rho$ is the measure with density $q_\phi(\cdot\mid x)$ relative to $\mu_Z$. This representation defines how to generate encoder samples; it does not by itself assert that differentiation may pass through an expectation.

## Statement

Fix an observation $x$ in a VAE with latent reference measure $\mu_Z$. Let $\gamma_\theta(\cdot;x)$ be its nonnegative measurable joint-density slice, let $Z_\theta(x)=\int\gamma_\theta(z;x)\,d\mu_Z(z)\in(0,\infty)$, and let $\pi_\theta(z\mid x)=\gamma_\theta(z;x)/Z_\theta(x)$. Let $q_\phi(\cdot\mid x)$ be a measurable probability density satisfying $q_\phi=0$ $\mu_Z$-almost everywhere on $\{\pi_\theta=0\}$ and
$$\int q_\phi(z\mid x)\bigl(|\log\gamma_\theta(z;x)|+|\log q_\phi(z\mid x)|\bigr)\,d\mu_Z(z)<\infty.$$
Then the choice-free density-ratio identity is
$$\log Z_\theta(x)=\operatorname{ELBO}_{\theta,\phi}(x)+\int q_\phi(z\mid x)\log\!\left(\frac{q_\phi(z\mid x)}{\pi_\theta(z\mid x)}\right)\,d\mu_Z(z),$$
where the ratio integrand is zero when $q_\phi=0$. Under the Axiom of Choice, the final integral is the library reverse-KL divergence $D_{\rm KL}(q_\phi\mu_Z\|\pi_\theta\mu_Z)$ and is nonnegative; hence $\operatorname{ELBO}_{\theta,\phi}(x)\le\log Z_\theta(x)$.

## Statement references

[[def-variational-autoencoder|The VAE density, evidence, posterior, and ELBO definitions]].

[[thm-elbo-kl-decomposition|The generic choice-free density-ratio identity and AC-dependent KL branch]].

[[def-axiom-of-choice|The Axiom of Choice]].

[Blei, Kucukelbir, and McAuliffe, Variational Inference: A Review for Statisticians](https://www.cs.columbia.edu/~blei/papers/BleiKucukelbirMcAuliffe2016.pdf).

[Zheng, Hu, and Deng, 10-708 Lecture 13: Variational Inference II](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~epxing/Class/10708-15/notes/10708_scribe_lecture13.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A fixed observation $x$, the VAE joint-density slice, its positive finite evidence, an admissible encoder density, and AC for the library KL branch.

[F1] [[def-variational-autoencoder]]: at each admissible fixed $x$, $\gamma_\theta(\cdot;x)$ is nonnegative measurable, $0<Z_\theta(x)=\int\gamma_\theta\,d\mu_Z<\infty$, $\pi_\theta=\gamma_\theta/Z_\theta$, and $q_\phi$ is a probability density with the stated support and absolute log-integrability conditions.

[F2] [[thm-elbo-kl-decomposition]]: for a sigma-finite reference measure and such $\gamma,Z,\pi,q$, the density-ratio identity $\log Z=\operatorname{ELBO}(q)+\int q\log(q/\pi)\,d\mu$ holds without choice; under AC the integral is $D_{\rm KL}(q\mu\|\pi\mu)\ge0$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function; AC is invoked only for the library KL identification and nonnegativity in [F2].

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], $(\mu_Z,\gamma_\theta(\cdot;x),Z_\theta(x),\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x),q_\phi(\cdot\mid x))$ satisfies the sigma-finiteness, positive finite normalizer, support, and absolute log-integrability hypotheses of the generic decomposition. Its ELBO integral is exactly $\operatorname{ELBO}_{\theta,\phi}(x)$ by definition. [given, F1]

2.1 Apply [F2] to these objects. Its choice-free branch gives the displayed density-ratio identity. Under [A1], its second branch identifies the ratio integral as the nonnegative reverse-KL divergence, and rearranging yields the stated lower bound. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mu,\gamma,Z,\pi,q$ satisfy [[def-variational-family-and-elbo]], and put $Q=q\,\mu$ and $\Pi=\pi\,\mu$. The choice-free density-ratio identity
$$\log Z=\operatorname{ELBO}(q)+\int q\log(q/\pi)\,d\mu$$
holds, with the ratio integrand set to zero where $q=0$. Under AC, the final integral is the library reverse divergence $D(Q\|\Pi)$ and is nonnegative. Consequently
$$\operatorname{ELBO}(q)\le\log Z.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measure space $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$, measurable $\gamma\ge0$ with $0<Z=\int\gamma\,d\mu<\infty$, $\pi=\gamma/Z$, an admissible density $q$, and AC for the library KL clause.

[F1] [[def-variational-family-and-elbo]]: for densities, $q\ll_\mu\pi$ means $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{\pi=0\}$.

[F2] [[def-variational-family-and-elbo]]: admissibility requires $\int q(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|)d\mu<\infty$.

[F3] [[def-variational-family-and-elbo]]: $\operatorname{ELBO}(q)=\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)d\mu$.

[F4] [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]]: a nonnegative measurable function has integral zero exactly when it vanishes almost everywhere.

[F5] [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]: for probability measures $P\ll R$, under AC the directional divergence is $D(P\|R)=\int\log(dP/dR)dP$; its first argument is the measure absolutely continuous with respect to the second.

[F6] [[thm-kullback-leibler-is-nonnegative]]: under the published directional convention and AC, $D(P\|R)\ge0$ for probability measures $P,R$.

[F7] [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]: integrating a nonnegative measurable density over measurable sets defines a measure.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC states that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. It is invoked here only through [F5] and [F6].

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Define $Q(A)=\int_A q\,d\mu$ and $\Pi(A)=\int_A\pi\,d\mu$. These are probability measures by [F1] and [F7]. If $\Pi(A)=0$, [F4] applied to $\pi\mathbf1_A$ gives $\pi=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$. Then [F1] gives $q=0$ almost everywhere on $A$, so $Q(A)=0$ and $Q\ll\Pi$. Define $r=q/\pi$ on $\{\pi>0\}$ and $r=0$ on $\{\pi=0\}$. For every measurable $A$, $\int_A r\,d\Pi=\int_{A\cap\{\pi>0\}}q\,d\mu=Q(A)$, so $r=dQ/d\Pi$. [F1, F4, F7, construct, algebra]

2.1 On $\{q>0\}$, $\pi=\gamma/Z>0$ and $\log r=\log q-\log\gamma+\log Z$. The assumed absolute integrability and $\int q\,d\mu=1$ make all terms integrable. Hence $\int\log r\,dQ=\int q\log(q/\pi)\,d\mu=\log Z-\operatorname{ELBO}(q)$. This algebraic identity uses the explicit density ratio and no choice axiom. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [A1] and [F5], the integral $\int\log r\,dQ$ is $D(Q\|\Pi)$ under the library convention. Rearranging step 2.1 gives $\log Z=\operatorname{ELBO}(q)+D(Q\|\Pi)$. [A1, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The measures $Q$ and $\Pi$ are probabilities, so [F6] gives $D(Q\|\Pi)\ge0$. Step 3.1 then yields $\operatorname{ELBO}(q)\le\log Z$. [F6, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$ be a fixed nonempty finite data set, let $\Lambda$ be an open subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean parameter space for $\eta=(\theta,\phi)$, and fix $\eta_0=(\theta_0,\phi_0)\in\Lambda$. For each $i$, assume the VAE at $(\eta,x_i)$ is admissible and has a pathwise representation $g_\phi(\epsilon,x_i)$ under one parameter-independent probability law $\rho$. Assume there is one $\rho$-null set, common to every $i$ and $\eta\in\Lambda$, outside which $0<q_\phi(g_\phi(\epsilon,x_i)\mid x_i)<\infty$ and $0<\gamma_\theta(g_\phi(\epsilon,x_i);x_i)<\infty$; define the payoff below to be zero on that null set. Define
$$H_i(\eta,\epsilon):=\log\gamma_\theta(g_\phi(\epsilon,x_i);x_i)-\log q_\phi(g_\phi(\epsilon,x_i)\mid x_i),$$
with terms on a common $\rho$-null set defined to be zero. Assume each $H_i$ is jointly measurable and integrable for every $\eta\in\Lambda$. Outside one $\rho$-null set, each $H_i(\cdot,\epsilon)$ is continuously differentiable on $\Lambda$ with continuous gradient, and $\nabla_\eta H_i(\eta,\cdot)$ is measurable for every $\eta$. For every compact neighborhood $K\subset\Lambda$ of $\eta_0$, assume one nonnegative $M_{i,K}\in L^1(\rho)$ satisfies $\|\nabla_\eta H_i(\eta,\epsilon)\|_2\le M_{i,K}(\epsilon)$ for every $\eta\in K$ outside one common null set, and assume $\mathbb E_\rho\|\nabla_\eta H_i(\eta_0,\epsilon)\|_2^2<\infty$.

Let $I$ be uniform on $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ and independent of $\epsilon\sim\rho$. Then the finite-average objective
$$\overline{\mathcal L}(\eta):=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\operatorname{ELBO}_{\theta,\phi}(x_i)$$
is differentiable at $\eta_0$, and its one-example pathwise gradient estimate
$$G(\eta_0,I,\epsilon):=\nabla_\eta H_I(\eta_0,\epsilon)$$
satisfies $\mathbb E[G(\eta_0,I,\epsilon)]=\nabla_\eta\overline{\mathcal L}(\eta_0)$ and has finite coordinate variances. A parameter-independent Gaussian base law alone does not imply the differentiability, envelope, or second-moment hypotheses.

## Statement references

[[def-variational-autoencoder|The VAE ELBO and fixed-law encoder representation]].

[[thm-pathwise-simulation-gradient-is-unbiased-under-envelope|The published pathwise simulation-gradient theorem with a common integrable derivative envelope]].

[[thm-dominated-convergence|Dominated convergence used in the difference-quotient proof]].

[Kingma and Welling, Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes, arXiv v1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.6114v1).

[Blei, Kucukelbir, and McAuliffe, Variational Inference: A Review for Statisticians](https://www.cs.columbia.edu/~blei/papers/BleiKucukelbirMcAuliffe2016.pdf).

[Zheng, Hu, and Deng, 10-708 Lecture 13: Variational Inference II](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~epxing/Class/10708-15/notes/10708_scribe_lecture13.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite nonempty data set, the admissible VAE densities and fixed-law pathwise representations at each data point, the stated local sample-path regularity and common integrable derivative envelopes, and square-integrable pathwise gradients at $\eta_0$.

[F1] [[def-variational-autoencoder]]: the ELBO is the $q_\phi(\cdot\mid x)$-expectation of $\log\gamma_\theta(z;x)-\log q_\phi(z\mid x)$, and the law of $g_\phi(\epsilon,x)$ under $\rho$ has density $q_\phi(\cdot\mid x)$ relative to $\mu_Z$.

[F2] [[def-simulation-gradient-objective-and-payoff-oracle]]: a simulation payoff is jointly measurable and integrable at every parameter, and its objective is its expectation under the fixed probability law.

[F3] [[def-pathwise-simulation-gradient-estimator]]: for a fixed random input, the pathwise estimator is the pointwise derivative of the simulated payoff; this definition alone does not imply unbiasedness.

[F4] [[thm-pathwise-simulation-gradient-is-unbiased-under-envelope]]: for an integrable simulation payoff with almost-sure C1 sample paths, continuous measurable gradients, one common integrable gradient envelope on a neighborhood, and a square-integrable gradient at the base parameter, the objective is differentiable there and its gradient is the expectation of the pathwise gradient; each coordinate then has finite variance.

[F5] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the derivative of a differentiable composition is the composition of its derivatives, so the encoder gradient differentiates through the fixed-noise map.

[F6] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: almost-everywhere convergence under one integrable majorant permits passage of the limit through the integral.

## Proof

1.1 Fix $i$. By [F3], $G_i(\eta,\epsilon):=\nabla_\eta H_i(\eta,\epsilon)$ is the fixed-noise pathwise estimator. The pushforward condition in [F1] gives $\mathbb E_\rho H_i(\eta,\epsilon)=\operatorname{ELBO}_{\theta,\phi}(x_i)$ for every $\eta$. The absolute log-integrability in the VAE definition makes $H_i$ integrable; its joint measurability and integrability therefore meet the payoff conditions in [F2]. By [F5], its pointwise derivative is obtained through $g_\phi$ while the same $\epsilon$ is held fixed. [given, F1, F2, F3, F5]

2.1 Since $\Lambda$ is open, choose a closed ball $K$ centered at $\eta_0$ with $K\subset\Lambda$ and nonempty interior. The common envelope assumed on $K$ is an integrable majorant on an open neighborhood of $\eta_0$; the C1, continuity, measurability and square-integrability hypotheses are exactly those of [F4]. The full proof of [F4] applies the chain rule along parameter segments and then [F6] to the first-order difference quotients under this majorant. It gives $\nabla_\eta\operatorname{ELBO}_{\theta,\phi}(x_i)\vert_{\eta_0}=\mathbb E_\rho\nabla_\eta H_i(\eta_0,\epsilon)$ and finite coordinate variances. [given, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1]

3.1 The finite sum defining $\overline{\mathcal L}$ is differentiable at $\eta_0$ with gradient the average of these $N$ gradients. Independence and uniformity of $I$ give $\mathbb E[G]=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb E_\rho\nabla_\eta H_i(\eta_0,\epsilon)$, which is that average gradient. The finite mixture of the stated square-integrable gradients has finite second moment in each coordinate and therefore finite coordinate variance. [given, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix a finite dimension $d\ge1$, an open set $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, and a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. A simulation payoff is a jointly measurable map $H:\Theta\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $H(\theta,\cdot)$ is integrable for each $\theta\in\Theta$. Its objective is
$J(\theta):=\mathbb E[H(\theta,\cdot)].$
A payoff-oracle call at $\theta$ returns an integrable real random variable $Y(\theta)$ with $\mathbb E[Y(\theta)]=J(\theta)$. Two calls may use the same random input or different random inputs; their joint law is part of the chosen coupling. A single oracle call is one function evaluation, regardless of the cost of its internal simulation.

## Definition

Use [[def-simulation-gradient-objective-and-payoff-oracle]] and write $J(\theta)=\mathbb E[H(\theta,Z)]$ using one fixed random input $Z$ whose law does not depend on $\theta$. If, for almost every input, the map $\theta\mapsto H(\theta,Z)$ is differentiable, its pathwise (or reparameterized) gradient estimator is
$G_{\mathrm{pw}}(\theta,Z):=D_\theta H(\theta,Z).$
When $H(\theta,Z)=h(T(\theta,Z),\theta)$, with differentiable $T$ and $h$, the chain rule gives
$G_{\mathrm{pw}}=D_xh(T(\theta,Z),\theta)D_\theta T(\theta,Z)+\partial_\theta h(T(\theta,Z),\theta).$
The estimator differentiates the simulated outcome while holding the same random input fixed. This definition alone does not assert that its expectation equals $\nabla J(\theta)$.

## Statement

Gradients are Euclidean column vectors, and vector expectations are taken coordinatewise.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $H:\Theta\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be the simulation payoff from [[def-simulation-gradient-objective-and-payoff-oracle]], and fix $\theta_0\in\Theta$. Suppose there is an open ball $U$ about $\theta_0$ such that for almost every $\omega$, $H(\cdot,\omega)$ is continuously differentiable on $U$ and $\nabla_\theta H(\cdot,\omega)$ is continuous there, and $\nabla_\theta H(\theta,\cdot)$ is measurable for every $\theta\in U$. Assume $\|\nabla_\theta H(\theta,\omega)\|_2\le M(\omega)$ for all $\theta\in U$ outside one measurable null set, where $M$ is nonnegative and integrable, and assume $\mathbb E\|\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\cdot)\|_2^2<\infty$. Then $J(\theta)=\mathbb E H(\theta,\cdot)$ is Fréchet differentiable at $\theta_0$ and
$\nabla J(\theta_0)=\mathbb E[\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\cdot)].$
Thus the pathwise estimator from [[def-pathwise-simulation-gradient-estimator]] is unbiased at $\theta_0$ and has finite coordinate variances.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The payoff and objective, $\theta_0$, the neighborhood and pathwise differentiability, the common integrable derivative envelope, and the square-integrable pathwise gradient in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-pathwise-simulation-gradient-estimator]]: when the same random input is held fixed, the pathwise estimator is $D_\theta H(\theta,Z)$; the definition by itself does not assert unbiasedness.

[F2] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: for a differentiable composition, $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$. Gradients are column vectors represented using the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], so $D_\theta H(\theta,\omega)[h]=\langle\nabla_\theta H(\theta,\omega),h\rangle$.

[F3] [[thm-ftc-second-part]] and [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: if $q'$ is continuous on a compact interval, it is integrable there and $\int_a^b q'(t)\,dt=q(b)-q(a)$.

[F4] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: almost-everywhere convergence under one integrable majorant permits passage of the limit through the integral.

[F5] [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] and [[lem-variance-and-covariance-identities-for-random-variables]]: for square-integrable $X$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-(\mathbb E X)^2\le\mathbb E[X^2]$.

[F6] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$.

[F7] [[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]: expectation is linear for integrable variables and satisfies $|\mathbb E X|\le\mathbb E|X|$.

[F8] [[def-simulation-gradient-objective-and-payoff-oracle]]: the objective is $J(\theta)=\mathbb E[H(\theta,\cdot)]$.

## Proof

1.1 Fix nonzero $h\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\theta_0+h\in U$. For almost every $\omega$, set $q_\omega(t)=H(\theta_0+th,\omega)$ on $[0,1]$. By [F2], $q_\omega'(t)=\langle\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0+th,\omega),h\rangle$, which is continuous and hence integrable by [F3]. The FTC [F3] gives $H(\theta_0+h,\omega)-H(\theta_0,\omega)-\langle\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\omega),h\rangle=\int_0^1\langle\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0+th,\omega)-\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\omega),h\rangle\,dt.$ [given, F2, F3]

1.2 For each such $h$, the random variable $M_h(\omega):=\sup_{r\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]}\|\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0+rh,\omega)-\nabla_\theta H(\theta_0,\omega)\|_2$ is measurable: continuity in $t$ makes this countable supremum equal the supremum over $[0,1]$. It satisfies $0\le M_h\le2M$ almost surely. As $h\to0$, continuity of the sample gradient at $\theta_0$ gives $M_h\to0$ almost surely. [given, F1]

2.1 By [F8], $J(\theta)=\mathbb E[H(\theta,\cdot)]$. Taking expectations in step 1.1, linearity in [F7] moves the finite inner product through expectation, and [F6] bounds it by $M_h\|h\|_2$. The modulus bound in [F7] therefore bounds the absolute first-order remainder divided by $\|h\|_2$ by $\mathbb E M_h$. ## Definition

Inputs are a fixed nonempty finite data set $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$; a VAE model and admissible encoder from the preceding definition; a parameter-independent base law $\rho$ and pathwise map $g_\phi$ for every $x_i$; an initial parameter $\eta_0=(\theta_0,\phi_0)$; a finite positive integer $T$; and positive learning rates $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{T-1}$. Require the hypotheses of the dominated pathwise-gradient theorem at every parameter value reached by the procedure, and require each update below to remain in its open admissible parameter domain. Let $\mathcal N$ be the union of the theorem's common null set for finite positive log values and its null set on which the sample-path $C^1$ condition may fail; thus $\mathcal N$ is a common $\rho$-null set for all data indices and parameter values.

Set $\eta_0=(\theta_0,\phi_0)$. For each $t=0,\ldots,T-1$:

1. Draw $I_t$ uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ and draw $\epsilon_t$ from $\rho$, independently of $I_t$ and of earlier random draws.
2. If $\epsilon_t\in\mathcal N$, set $h_t=0$. Otherwise set $z_t=g_{\phi_t}(\epsilon_t,x_{I_t})$ and evaluate
   $$h_t=\log\gamma_{\theta_t}(z_t;x_{I_t})-\log q_{\phi_t}(z_t\mid x_{I_t}).$$
3. If $\epsilon_t\in\mathcal N$, set $G_t=0$. Otherwise, holding $\epsilon_t$ and $I_t$ fixed, compute the Euclidean gradient
   $$G_t=\nabla_{(\theta,\phi)}\bigl[\log\gamma_\theta(g_\phi(\epsilon_t,x_{I_t});x_{I_t})-\log q_\phi(g_\phi(\epsilon_t,x_{I_t})\mid x_{I_t})\bigr]\big|_{(\theta,\phi)=\eta_t}.$$
4. Update $\eta_{t+1}=\eta_t+\alpha_tG_t$.

Return $(\eta_0,\ldots,\eta_T)$ and $(h_t,G_t)_{0\le t<T}$. This finite procedure specifies stochastic ascent on the finite-average ELBO; it makes no claim that the iterates converge or reach a global maximum.

## Definition references

[[def-variational-autoencoder|The VAE model, ELBO, and fixed-law encoder sampler]].

[[thm-reparameterization-gradient-under-dominated-differentiation|The conditions under which these pathwise updates estimate the finite-average ELBO gradient]].

## Remarks

Under the stated derivative-envelope and second-moment hypotheses, the expected update direction before multiplication by $\alpha_t$ is the gradient of the finite-average ELBO and has finite coordinate variances. The Axiom of Choice identifies this ELBO as a lower bound on log evidence under the corollary's hypotheses.

If the prior and encoder are Gaussian and the expectation of their log-density difference is available analytically, that term can be evaluated exactly instead of sampled. This removes Monte Carlo variation from that term only; the decoder log-likelihood may still be sampled, and no universal variance or training guarantee follows.

## Remarks references

[[thm-reparameterization-gradient-under-dominated-differentiation|The finite-average pathwise-gradient theorem]].

[[cor-vae-elbo-kl-decomposition|The AC-dependent ELBO/KL identity]].

## Example

Assume AC and use Lebesgue measure for the latent densities. In the first model, a scalar latent variable $Z$ has prior $N(0,4)$, and conditional on $Z=z$ the observation is $X=(Y_1,Y_2)$ with $Y_1,Y_2$ IID $N(z,1)$. At the observed value $x=(2,4)$, the evidence is finite and positive and the posterior is $N(8/3,4/9)$. Restrict the encoder family to $q_m(z\mid x)=N(m,4/9)$ for $m\in[-1,1]$ and choose $m=0$. This encoder is admissible and its reverse-KL gap, with $D_{\rm KL}(q\|\pi):=\int q(z)\log(q(z)/\pi(z))\,dz$, is $D_{\rm KL}(q_0(\cdot\mid x)\|\pi(\cdot\mid x))=8>0$, so its ELBO is exactly $8$ below the log evidence.

In a second model, let $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and let the decoder density be $p(x\mid z)=N(x;0,1)$, independent of $z$. At observed value $x=0$, the posterior equals the prior. Choosing the encoder $q(z\mid 0)=N(0,1)$ gives zero reverse-KL gap and ELBO equal to the log evidence. This is one posterior-collapse configuration in which the decoder ignores the latent variable; it does not assert that VAE training always collapses.

**Given:** AC; the two stated latent-variable models and observations; the restricted encoder family in the first model; and the definitions of evidence, posterior, admissibility and ELBO.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function; AC is used by the Gaussian density suppliers and the library KL branch.

[F1] [[def-variational-autoencoder]]: for positive finite evidence, $\pi=\gamma/Z$; an encoder is admissible when it is a probability density supported where $\pi$ is positive with the stated absolute log-integrability; its ELBO is the integral of $\log\gamma-\log q$ under $q$.

[F2] [[thm-normal-normal-conjugate-update]]: with prior $N(\mu_0,\tau_0^2)$, positive known variance $\sigma^2$, and $n\ge1$ IID observations from $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, the evidence is finite and positive and the posterior has variance $(\tau_0^{-2}+n\sigma^{-2})^{-1}$ and mean equal to that variance times $\mu_0/\tau_0^2+n\bar y/\sigma^2$.

[F4] [[lem-normal-location-scale-mean-and-variance]]: a variable with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ has mean $m$ and finite variance $\sigma^2$.

[F5] [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]: for probability measures with densities $q$ and $\pi$ relative to one reference measure and $q\,\mu\ll\pi\,\mu$, the reverse divergence is $\int q\log(q/\pi)\,d\mu$.

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Example and Facts & Assumptions.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\mu\sim N(\mu_0,\tau_0^2)$ with $\tau_0^2>0$, and, conditional
on $\mu$, let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ be IID $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with known
$\sigma^2>0$ and $n\ge1$. The sampling data use the Borel sigma-algebra on
$\mathbb R^n$ with $n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. For every
$y_{1:n}\in\mathbb R^n$, define
$$V_n=(\tau_0^{-2}+n\sigma^{-2})^{-1},\qquad \mu_n=V_n\left(\frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2} +\frac{n\bar y}{\sigma^2}\right),\qquad \bar y=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^ny_i.$$
The evidence is finite and positive, and the posterior is $N(\mu_n,V_n)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $\mu_0\in\mathbb R$, $\tau_0^2,\sigma^2>0$, $n\ge1$, and observed real data $y_1,\ldots,y_n$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed by the Gaussian density normalization supplier. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[A2] The Axiom of Choice implies Countable Choice. [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]].

[F1] For $m\in\mathbb R$ and scale $s>0$, $N(m,s^2)$ has density $(2\pi s^2)^{-1/2}\exp(-(x-m)^2/(2s^2))$. [[lem-normal-location-scale-density]].

[F2] This normal density integrates to one under AC. [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]].

[F3] A proper prior probability and parameter-measurable sampling probability kernel constitute a Bayesian model. [[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]].

[F4] Evidence is the prior integral of the joint likelihood section; the normalized quotient is introduced only on finite positive evidence. [[def-posterior-evidence-normalizer-and-fiberwise-update]].

[F5] The likelihood-weighted prior can be normalized to a probability exactly when evidence is finite and positive. [[prop-fiberwise-posterior-propriety-iff-finite-positive-evidence]].

[F6] The dominated Bayes formula identifies the normalized density quotient as a posterior kernel. [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]].

[F7] A probability kernel has probability-measure sections and measurable event evaluations. [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]].

[F8] Arithmetic operations preserve measurability, and the exponential is continuous and has Borel preimages of Borel sets. [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] [[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]].

[F9] A nonnegative measurable density defines a measure; Tonelli factors its nonnegative integral on sigma-finite product spaces. [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]].

[F10] Under Countable Choice, $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite and agrees on Borel sets with the product of $n$ one-dimensional Lebesgue measures. [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]] [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]].

[F11] Independent random elements have their product law, and probability measures agreeing on a generating pi-system with a finite exhaustion agree everywhere. [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]] [[thm-measure-uniqueness-on-a-sigma-finite-pi-system]].

[F12] Product-coordinate maps are measurable on Euclidean Borel products, and integration of a nonnegative product-measurable function against a constant uniformly sigma-finite measure kernel is measurable in its parameter. [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]] [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]] [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]].

[F13] Every positive variance has a positive square root. [[thm-of-square-roots]].

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement and observed data $y_{1:n}$.

1.1 Let $\ell(\mu,y_{1:n})=\prod_{i=1}^n(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\exp(-(y_i-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2))$. The coordinate maps on the parameter-data product are measurable by [F12], so [F8] makes $\ell$ product-measurable. For each fixed $\mu$, [F10] and Tonelli [F9] show that $\ell(\mu,\cdot)$ integrates to one. On every product rectangle, the density measure $\ell(\mu,\cdot)\,d\lambda_n$ has the product of the $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ marginal probabilities by [F9] and [F10]; conditional independence gives the same rectangle values, so [F11] identifies it with the conditional sample law. Define $K(\mu,D)=\int_D\ell(\mu,y)\,d\lambda_n(y)$ for Borel $D$. By [F9] each section is a probability measure. The constant $\lambda_n$ kernel has the finite exhaustion $(-j,j]^n$ by [F10]; since $\ell(\mu,y)\mathbf1_D(y)$ is product-measurable, [F12] makes $\mu\mapsto K(\mu,D)$ measurable. Thus [F7] makes $K$ a probability kernel, and with the proper normal prior it gives the Bayesian model in [F3]. Now put $P=\tau_0^{-2}+n\sigma^{-2}>0$, $q=\mu_0\tau_0^{-2}+\sigma^{-2}\sum_i y_i$, and $r=\mu_0^2\tau_0^{-2}+\sigma^{-2}\sum_i y_i^2$. By [F1] at positive scales $\sqrt{\tau_0^2}$ and $\sqrt{\sigma^2}$, whose existence is [F13], the product of the prior and sample densities is $C\exp\{-\tfrac12(P\mu^2-2q\mu+r)\},\qquad C=(2\pi\tau_0^2)^{-1/2}(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}>0.$ [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, F13, given, algebra]

## Statement

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the standard-normal probability law and its specified density, and $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma>0$.

[F1] $N(m,\sigma^2)$ is the pushforward of $N(0,1)$ by $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$, and $N(0,1)$ has density $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]]

[F2] AC implies Countable Choice. [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F3] Under Countable Choice, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism transforms nonnegative Lebesgue integrals by its absolute Jacobian. [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]

[A1] AC holds; it is used in [F1] and implies the Countable Choice hypothesis of [F3]. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** apply the one-dimensional change-of-variables formula to the affine normal-law map.

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 By [A1] and [F2], Countable Choice holds, so the change-of-variables theorem [F3] applies. For $\sigma>0$, the map $T(x)=m+\sigma x$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R$ with derivative $\sigma$. [A1, F2, F3, given]

2.1 For any Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$, apply [F3] to the nonnegative Borel function $y\mapsto\mathbf1_B(y)\phi((y-m)/\sigma)/\sigma$. The change of variables gives $\int_B\frac1\sigma\phi((y-m)/\sigma)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R}\mathbf1_B(m+\sigma x)\phi(x)\,dx=N(m,\sigma^2)(B)$, where the last equality is the pushforward identity in [F1]. Therefore the displayed function is a density on every Borel set, proving the statement. [F1, F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $\Theta$ be a parameter set,
and for each $\theta\in\Theta$ let $E_\theta:X\to\mathbb R$ be a measurable
energy function. Its **partition function relative to $\mu$** is
$$Z_\theta:=\int_X e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x).$$
The admissible parameter set is
$$\Theta_\mu:=\{\theta\in\Theta:0<Z_\theta<\infty\}.$$
For $\theta\in\Theta_\mu$, the **energy-based probability measure** is the
measure with density $e^{-E_\theta}/Z_\theta$ relative to $\mu$:
$$P_\theta(A):=\frac{1}{Z_\theta}\int_A e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$
The restriction $0<Z_\theta<\infty$ is part of the definition; parameters
outside $\Theta_\mu$ do not define a normalized model by this formula.

## Definition references

[[def-measure-space]] defines the triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ used here.

[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]] defines measurability of $E_\theta$.

[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] defines the integral used for $Z_\theta$.

[[def-measure-with-density]] defines the measure with density $e^{-E_\theta}$ relative to $\mu$.

[[def-probability-measure]] defines a probability measure as a measure of total mass one.

[[lem-energy-based-density-is-a-probability-measure]] establishes the normalization's well-definedness.

## Statement

For every measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, measurable real energy $E_\theta$,
and parameter $\theta$ with $0<Z_\theta:=\int_X e^{-E_\theta}\,d\mu<\infty$,
the normalized measure
$$P_\theta(A):=Z_\theta^{-1}\int_A e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal A,$$
is a probability measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

## Statement references

[[def-energy-based-density-and-partition-function]] supplies the notation $Z_\theta$ and $P_\theta$.

[[def-measure-with-density]] identifies the nonnegative density integral as a measure.

[[def-probability-measure]] defines a probability measure by total mass one.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, a measurable real energy $E_\theta$, and $0<Z_\theta<\infty$.

[F1] [[def-energy-based-density-and-partition-function]]: $P_\theta(A)=Z_\theta^{-1}\int_A e^{-E_\theta}\,d\mu$ and admissibility requires $0<Z_\theta<\infty$.

[F2] [[def-measure-with-density]]: if $f\ge0$ is measurable, then $A\mapsto\int_A f\,d\mu$ is a measure.

[F3] [[def-probability-measure]]: a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$ with total mass one is a probability measure.

[F4] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]: the real exponential is the power-series sum $\exp(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}t^n/\iota(n!)$, with infinite radius of convergence.

[F5] [[cor-power-series-sums-are-continuous]]: a power-series sum is continuous at every point strictly inside its radius of convergence.

[F6] [[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]: a continuous real map has Borel preimages of Borel sets.

[F7] [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]: a measurable map composed with a Borel measurable outer map is measurable.

[F8] [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]: $\exp(t)>0$ for every real $t$.

## Proof

1.1 Define $\phi(t):=\exp(-t)$. By [F4], $\phi(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}(-1)^nt^n/\iota(n!)$ is a power-series sum with infinite radius, so [F5] makes $\phi$ continuous on $\mathbb R$. Thus [F6] makes it Borel measurable, and [F7] with the measurable energy from [F1] makes $x\mapsto\exp(-E_\theta(x))$ measurable. Its values are positive by [F8], hence nonnegative. Put $M_\theta(A):=\int_A e^{-E_\theta}\,d\mu$. Now [F2] makes $M_\theta$ a measure and $M_\theta(X)=Z_\theta$. Thus $P_\theta(\varnothing)=Z_\theta^{-1}M_\theta(\varnothing)=0$. For any pairwise disjoint sequence $(A_n)_{n\ge0}$, [F2] and finite-sum homogeneity give $P_\theta(\bigcup_{n\ge0}A_n)=Z_\theta^{-1}\sum_{n\ge0}M_\theta(A_n)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{n=0}^N Z_\theta^{-1}M_\theta(A_n)=\sum_{n\ge0}P_\theta(A_n)$. Therefore $P_\theta$ is a measure. [given, F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

2.1 Its total mass is $P_\theta(X)=Z_\theta^{-1}M_\theta(X)=1$, so [F3] makes $P_\theta$ a probability measure. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every real $x$, the series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ converges absolutely. Its power-series radius is therefore $+\infty$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real $x$.

[L1] Archimedes supplies a natural larger than any prescribed real ([[thm-of-archimedean]]).

[L2] A tail bounded termwise by a convergent geometric series converges ([[thm-direct-comparison-test]], [[thm-geometric-series]]), and absolute convergence implies convergence ([[lem-absolute-convergence-implies-convergence]]).

[L3] Factorials satisfy $(n+1)!=n!(n+1)$ and are nonzero naturals; every positive natural has a positive, hence nonzero, canonical real image ([[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], [[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $x=0$, the series is $1+0+0+\cdots$ and converges absolutely. Hence assume $x\ne0$. Choose $N\ge1$ with $\iota(N)>2|x|$. For $n\ge N$, the absolute terms $a_n=|x|^n/\iota(n!)$ are positive and satisfy $a_{n+1}/a_n=|x|/\iota(n+1)<1/2$.  [L1, L3, choose]

2.1 Thus $a_{N+j}\le a_N2^{-j}$ by induction, and the tail is dominated by a convergent geometric series.  [step 1.1, L2]

3.1 The zero case from step 1.1 and, when $x\ne0$, adding the finite initial segment to the convergent tail prove absolute convergence for arbitrary $x$. Hence every nonnegative radius works and the radius is $+\infty$.  [step 1.1, step 2.1, L2] ∎

## Statement

If $f(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_n(x-c)^n$ for $|x-c|<R$, then $f$ is continuous at every $x_0$ satisfying $|x_0-c|<R$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A power-series sum $f$ and a point $x_0$ strictly inside its radius.

[L1] The series converges uniformly on each closed interval strictly inside its radius ([[thm-power-series-uniform-on-compact-subintervals]]).

[L2] Every polynomial partial sum is continuous, since constants, the identity, powers, scalar multiples and finite sums are continuous ([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]).

[L3] A uniform limit of continuous real-valued functions is continuous ([[thm-uniform-limit-continuous-real-functions]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Choose $\delta>0$ so small that $[x_0-\delta,x_0+\delta]$ lies strictly inside $|x-c|<R$. [given, choose]

1.2 The polynomial partial sums are continuous on this interval by [L2] and converge uniformly there to $f$ by [L1]. [L1, L2]

2.1 By [L3], $f$ is continuous on that interval, and in particular at $x_0$. [step 1.2, L3] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice used by the library's Lebesgue-measure and
weak-derivative representative interfaces. Let $d\ge1$, let $\lambda_d$ be Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^d$,
and let $p:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ be a continuously differentiable
probability density, so $\int p\,d\lambda_d=1$. Write
$$P_p(A):=\int_A p\,d\lambda_d,\qquad A\in\mathcal L(\mathbb R^d),$$
which is a probability measure, and let $\mathbb E_p[f]:=\int f\,dP_p$ for integrable $f$.
Define the data score by $s_p(x):=\nabla\log p(x)$ when $p(x)>0$ and set
$s_p(x):=0$ when $p(x)=0$. For an energy model relative to $\lambda_d$ with
$0<Z_\theta=\int e^{-E_\theta}\,d\lambda_d<\infty$, assume
$E_\theta\in C^1(\mathbb R^d)$ and define its model score field by
$\psi_\theta:=-\nabla E_\theta$. Assume each component of $\psi_\theta$ is
locally integrable and has locally integrable weak first derivatives: for
each $i,j$, a locally integrable representative $g_{ij}$ satisfies
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi_{\theta,i}\,\partial_j\varphi\,d\lambda_d=-\int_{\mathbb R^d}g_{ij}\varphi\,d\lambda_d\qquad(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)).$$
Here $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ denotes the smooth compactly supported test
functions.
The weak derivatives are unique up to Lebesgue-null sets, and define
$\operatorname{div}\psi_\theta:=\sum_{i=1}^d g_{ii}$; the integrals below do
not depend on the chosen representatives. The $C^1$ convention is that the
first derivative exists everywhere and is continuous.
For each admissible $\theta$, assume
$$\mathbb E_p\|s_p\|^2<\infty,\qquad \mathbb E_p\|\psi_\theta\|^2<\infty,\qquad \mathbb E_p|\operatorname{div}\psi_\theta|<\infty.$$
Then the score-matching objective
$$J(\theta):=\frac12\mathbb E_p\|\psi_\theta-s_p\|^2$$
satisfies
$$J(\theta)=\mathbb E_p\left[\frac12\|\psi_\theta\|^2+\operatorname{div}\psi_\theta\right]+C_p,\qquad C_p:=\frac12\mathbb E_p\|s_p\|^2,$$
where $C_p$ is independent of $\theta$. No pointwise boundary limit at infinity
is assumed.

## Statement references

[Aapo Hyvärinen, Theorem 1 and Appendix A of the full JMLR paper](https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/volume6/hyvarinen05a/hyvarinen05a.pdf) states the score-matching identity under a pointwise boundary condition.

[Kevin P. Murphy, Chapter 24, Sections 24.1–24.3.4](https://github.com/probml/pml2-book/releases/download/2025-dec-10/book2.pdf) defines energy models, the model score and score matching.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement, including Countable Choice for the library Lebesgue measure interface and the three stated finite $p$-integrability conditions.

[A1] $p$ is a nonnegative $C^1$ probability density; for each admissible parameter, $E_\theta\in C^1$, its score field is locally integrable with locally integrable weak first derivatives, and the score and divergence have the stated finite $p$-moments.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]]: every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function; it is used only through [F3].

[F1] [[def-energy-based-density-and-partition-function]]: for $0<Z_\theta<\infty$, the model density is $e^{-E_\theta}/Z_\theta$, and $Z_\theta$ is independent of $x$.

[F2] [[def-measure-with-density]]: for a nonnegative measurable density $f$, $f\,d\mu$ is the measure $A\mapsto\int_A f\,d\mu$.

[F3] [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]: under Countable Choice, $\lambda_d$ is a complete measure on the Lebesgue sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^d$.

[F4] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: almost-everywhere convergence under one integrable majorant implies convergence of the corresponding integrals.

[F5] [[def-probability-measure]]: a measure of total mass one is a probability measure.

[F6] [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: a map on an open Euclidean set is $C^1$ when it is differentiable everywhere and its derivative entries are continuous.

[F7] [[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]: $g_{ij}$ is a weak derivative exactly when its signed test-function identity holds for every smooth compactly supported test function.

[F8] [[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]]: under Countable Choice, any two locally integrable representatives satisfying the same weak-derivative identity agree almost everywhere.

## Proof

1.1 The energy model has density $e^{-E_\theta}/Z_\theta$ by [F1]. By [F2], $P_p(A)=\int_Ap\,d\lambda_d$ is a measure; since $P_p(\mathbb R^d)=1$, [F5] makes it a probability measure. The $C^1$ score field is locally integrable by [F6], and [F8] makes the divergence independent of its weak-derivative representatives. Set $\rho(t)=0$ for $t\le0$ and $\rho(t)=e^{-1/t}$ for $t>0$, and define $\eta(r)=\rho(2-r)/(\rho(2-r)+\rho(r-1))$ for $r\ge0$. Then $\eta$ is smooth, equals $1$ on $[0,1]$, equals $0$ on $[2,\infty)$, and has values in $[0,1]$; $\chi(x)=\eta(\|x\|)$ is smooth because it is constant near the origin. The cutoff $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ equals $1$ on $B_R$, vanishes off $B_{2R}$, and satisfies $\|\nabla\chi_R\|_\infty\le C/R$, where $C=\|\nabla\chi\|_\infty$. Apply [F7] to each diagonal pair $(\psi_{\theta,i},g_{ii})$ with test function $p\chi_R$ and sum over $i$; expanding $\nabla(p\chi_R)$ gives $\int\chi_R\psi_\theta\cdot\nabla p\,d\lambda_d+\int p\psi_\theta\cdot\nabla\chi_R\,d\lambda_d=-\int p\chi_R\operatorname{div}\psi_\theta\,d\lambda_d$. The identity extends from smooth tests to this $C^1$ compactly supported test: set $b(x)=e^{-1/(1-\|x\|^2)}$ for $\|x\|<1$ and $b(x)=0$ otherwise, and normalize $\rho_0=b/(\int b\,d\lambda_d)$; the denominator is positive and finite, so $\rho_0$ is a smooth compactly supported unit-mass mollifier. For $\varphi=p\chi_R$, put $\varphi_\varepsilon=\varphi*\rho_{0,\varepsilon}$. Uniform continuity of $\varphi$ and $\nabla\varphi$ gives $\|\varphi_\varepsilon-\varphi\|_\infty+\|\nabla\varphi_\varepsilon-\nabla\varphi\|_\infty\to0$, with all supports in one compact set for $\varepsilon\le1$. Local integrability of $\psi_\theta$ and $g_{ii}$ therefore lets both sides converge to the displayed identity; the product rule gives its terms. [given, A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, F8, construct]

2.1 On $\{p>0\}$, $\nabla p=p s_p$; at a point with $p=0$, nonnegativity and differentiability make it a local minimum, so $\nabla p=0$ there too. Thus $\nabla p=p s_p$ everywhere. Componentwise $|\psi_\theta\cdot s_p|\le\sum_i|\psi_{\theta,i}s_{p,i}|$ and $2|ab|\le a^2+b^2$ imply $\int|\psi_\theta\cdot\nabla p|\,d\lambda_d\le\frac12\mathbb E_p(\|\psi_\theta\|^2+\|s_p\|^2)<\infty$ and $\int p|\operatorname{div}\psi_\theta|\,d\lambda_d<\infty$. Also $\|\psi_\theta\|\le(1+\|\psi_\theta\|^2)/2$, so the cutoff term from step 1.1 is bounded in absolute value by $\frac{C}{2R}(1+\mathbb E_p\|\psi_\theta\|^2)\to0$. [given, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $R=n$ for integers $n\to\infty$. Then $\chi_n\to1$ pointwise and $|\chi_n|\le1$. The first integrand in step 1.1 is dominated by $|\psi_\theta\cdot\nabla p|$ and the third by $p|\operatorname{div}\psi_\theta|$, both integrable by step 2.1. Applying [F4] to both terms and using the vanishing cutoff term from step 2.1 gives $\int\psi_\theta\cdot\nabla p\,d\lambda_d=-\int p\operatorname{div}\psi_\theta\,d\lambda_d$. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Expanding the square gives $J(\theta)=\frac12\mathbb E_p\|\psi_\theta\|^2+\frac12\mathbb E_p\|s_p\|^2-\int p\psi_\theta\cdot s_p\,d\lambda_d$. Since $\nabla p=p s_p$ by step 2.1, step 3.1 turns the last term into $+\mathbb E_p[\operatorname{div}\psi_\theta]$; the remaining data-score term is $C_p$, independent of $\theta$. [given, A1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The cutoff and integration-by-parts argument is choice-free once the Lebesgue measure and weak-derivative classes are available. Countable Choice is used for those two interfaces; no full Axiom of Choice is used. The cutoff estimate supplies the multivariate limit directly and does not rely on pointwise vanishing of $p\psi_\theta$ at infinity.

## Definition

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

## Definition

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, and $u,v,w\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. If both
$v$ and $w$ are weak $\alpha$-derivatives of $u$, then
$$v=w\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Omega.$$
Thus a weak derivative, when it exists, is unique as an almost-everywhere
class. No connectedness assumption is needed.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion holds because there is only the zero
class and no nonzero tests.

## Sources

- Juha Kinnunen, *Sobolev Spaces*, Chapter 1 §1.1, printed pp. 3–4,
  Definition 1.2 and the uniqueness proof immediately following Remarks 1.3.
  The proof subtracts the two weak identities and tests their difference to
  conclude equality almost everywhere. The library proof uses its published
  regular-distribution injection as the precise uniqueness interface.
- John K. Hunter, *Notes on Partial Differential Equations*, §3.1,
  Definitions 3.1–3.2, printed pp. 47–48, for the weak derivative convention.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, and $u,v,w\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ such that $v$ and $w$ both satisfy the weak derivative identity.

[F1] A weak $\alpha$-derivative satisfies the signed test identity for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]).

[F2] Under Countable Choice, the map from a locally integrable almost-everywhere class to its regular distribution is injective ([[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For every test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, the two weak derivative identities have the same left side. Subtracting them gives $$(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega (v-w)\varphi\,dx=0.$$ Since $(-1)^{|\alpha|}$ is nonzero, this says $\int_\Omega(v-w)\varphi\,dx=0$ for every test. [F1, given]

2.1 The difference $v-w$ is locally integrable, and its regular distribution therefore pairs with each test by this integral. Step 1.1 says that this regular distribution is zero. By [F2] and the stated Countable Choice hypothesis, its representing almost-everywhere class is zero; hence $v=w$ almost everywhere on all of $\Omega$. This argument applies to the whole open set, whether or not it is connected. [F2, step 1.1, given] ∎

## Definition

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $r$ be a positive
integer and $\theta\in\mathbb R^r$,
and let $E_\theta:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable in $x$ and continuously
differentiable in $\theta$. Define the energy model $P_\theta$ relative to $\mu$
only when
$$0<Z_\theta:=\int_\mathcal X e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x)<\infty,$$
with density $e^{-E_\theta}/Z_\theta$. Let $Q_0$ be a data probability
measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and let $K_\theta$ be a probability kernel
from $\mathcal X$ to itself which leaves $P_\theta$ invariant, meaning
$$\int_\mathcal X K_\theta(x,A)\,P_\theta(dx)=P_\theta(A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal A).$$
Let $\{*\}$ carry its full sigma-algebra, let $G_{0,\theta}(*,A):=Q_0(A)$,
and recursively compose the probability kernel $G_{j,\theta}$ from $\{*\}$ to
$\mathcal X$ with $K_\theta$ to obtain $G_{j+1,\theta}$. Define
$Q_{j,\theta}(A):=G_{j,\theta}(*,A)$; thus $Q_{0,\theta}=Q_0$ and
$$Q_{j+1,\theta}(A)=\int_\mathcal X K_\theta(x,A)\,Q_{j,\theta}(dx),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$
Finite probability-kernel composition makes each $Q_{j,\theta}$ a probability
measure. For an integer $k\ge1$, $Q_{k,\theta}$ is the $k$-step reconstruction law.

If $Q_0$ and $Q_{k,\theta}$ have specified nonnegative measurable densities
$r_{0,\theta}$ and $r_{k,\theta}$ relative to $P_\theta$, meaning
$Q_{j,\theta}(A)=\int_A r_{j,\theta}\,dP_\theta$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
for $j\in\{0,k\}$, and
$$\int|r_{j,\theta}\log r_{j,\theta}|\,dP_\theta<\infty\qquad(j\in\{0,k\}),$$
define their finite contrastive-divergence objective by
$$\operatorname{CD}_k(\theta):=\int r_{0,\theta}\log r_{0,\theta}\,dP_\theta-\int r_{k,\theta}\log r_{k,\theta}\,dP_\theta,$$
where $0\log0:=0$ and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. On a finite state
space where $P_\theta$ has positive mass at every state, write
$p_\theta(x):=P_\theta(\{x\})$ and $q_{j,\theta}(x):=Q_{j,\theta}(\{x\})$.
Then $r_{j,\theta}(x)=q_{j,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x)$ and the objective equals
$$\sum_{x:q_{0,\theta}(x)>0}q_{0,\theta}(x)\log\frac{q_{0,\theta}(x)}{p_\theta(x)}-\sum_{x:q_{k,\theta}(x)>0}q_{k,\theta}(x)\log\frac{q_{k,\theta}(x)}{p_\theta(x)},$$
since each finite-space integral is the sum of the integrand times the point
mass and $p_\theta r_{j,\theta}=q_{j,\theta}$.

For a positive integer $m$, the procedure takes independent data draws
$x^1,\ldots,x^m$ with common law $Q_0$, a transition sampler for $K_\theta$,
and a learning rate $\eta>0$; the
reconstruction chains are drawn independently conditional on their starts. Its
output is the updated parameter from the **stop-gradient CD-$k$ update**:

1. For each $i$, set $x^{i,0}=x^i$ and draw $x^{i,j+1}$ from
   $K_\theta(x^{i,j},\cdot)$ for $j=0,\ldots,k-1$.
2. Form
   $$\widehat g_k=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x^i)-\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x^{i,k})\right).$$
3. Update $\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\widehat g_k$.

When $\nabla_\theta E_\theta$ is integrable under $Q_0$ and $Q_{k,\theta}$,
the associated **population CD-$k$ direction** is
$$g_k(\theta):=\int\nabla_\theta E_\theta\,dQ_0-\int\nabla_\theta E_\theta\,dQ_{k,\theta}.$$
The procedure makes no claim that the chain has mixed in $k$ steps. The
parameter derivative of $Q_{k,\theta}$ is not stopped in the scalar objective's
definition; the update above deliberately omits that derivative.

## Statement

Let $r$ be a positive integer, let $\mathcal X$ be finite and nonempty, and
let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ be open. For each $x,y\in\mathcal X$, assume
the coordinate partial derivatives of $E_\theta(x)$ and $K_\theta(x,y)$ exist
and are continuous on $\Theta$. Let $K_\theta$ be strictly positive and
row-stochastic, so $K_\theta(x,y)>0$ and $\sum_yK_\theta(x,y)=1$. Use counting
measure as the reference measure, set
$$Z_\theta:=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}e^{-E_\theta(x)},\qquad p_\theta(x):=e^{-E_\theta(x)}/Z_\theta,$$
let $q_0$ be a fixed probability vector on $\mathcal X$, assume $p_\theta$ is
invariant for $K_\theta$, and fix an integer $k\ge1$. Define
$K_\theta^0=I$, $K_\theta^{s+1}=K_\theta^sK_\theta$, and
$q_{k,\theta}=q_0K_\theta^k$, where vectors are row vectors, and
$$\mathcal L(\theta):=-\sum_xq_0(x)\log p_\theta(x),\qquad \operatorname{CD}_k(\theta):=D_{\rm KL}(q_0\|p_\theta)-D_{\rm KL}(q_{k,\theta}\|p_\theta),$$
where for finite probability mass functions $a,b$ with $b(x)>0$,
$$D_{\rm KL}(a\|b):=\sum_{x:a(x)>0}a(x)\log\frac{a(x)}{b(x)}$$
with $\log$ the natural logarithm and zero-mass terms contributing zero. For each parameter coordinate $j$,
$$\partial_j\mathcal L(\theta)=\sum_xq_0(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\sum_xp_\theta(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x),$$
while
$$\partial_j\operatorname{CD}_k(\theta)=\sum_xq_0(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\sum_xq_{k,\theta}(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\sum_x\partial_jq_{k,\theta}(x)\log\frac{q_{k,\theta}(x)}{p_\theta(x)}.$$
The reconstruction-law derivative is
$$\partial_jq_{k,\theta}=\sum_{s=0}^{k-1}q_0K_\theta^s(\partial_jK_\theta)K_\theta^{k-1-s}.$$
Thus the population direction used by stop-gradient CD-$k$ is the first two
terms of the displayed $\partial_j\operatorname{CD}_k$ formula and omits the
explicit derivative through the $k$ transition kernels. It also replaces the
model expectation in the exact negative log-likelihood gradient by the finite
reconstruction law; no equality between these gradients is asserted.

For the finite-state path calculation, let $\Omega:=\mathcal X^{k+1}$ with its
full sigma-algebra, let $X_s$ be the $s$th coordinate map, and define
$$\mathbb P_\theta(A):=\sum_{(x_0,\ldots,x_k)\in A}q_0(x_0)\prod_{s=0}^{k-1}K_\theta(x_s,x_{s+1}),\qquad A\subseteq\Omega.$$
This is a probability measure. For every real $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$, set
$$g_f(x):=\begin{cases}\sum_yK_\theta^k(x,y)f(y),&q_0(x)>0,\\0,&q_0(x)=0.\end{cases}$$
Then $g_f(X_0)$ is a version of
$\mathbb E_{\mathbb P_\theta}[f(X_k)\mid\sigma(X_0)]$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite nonempty state space, open parameter domain, finite energy model, fixed data probability vector, positive differentiable stochastic matrix with invariant model law, and integer $k\ge1$.

[A1] For each state or state pair, the energy and transition entries have continuous coordinate partial derivatives on the open set $\Theta$; every entry of $K_\theta$ is positive and each row sums to one.

[F1] [[def-energy-based-density-and-partition-function]]: $p_\theta(x)=e^{-E_\theta(x)}/Z_\theta$ for an admissibly normalized energy model.

[F2] [[alg-contrastive-divergence-k]]: the reconstruction law obeys $Q_{j+1,\theta}(A)=\int K_\theta(x,A)\,Q_{j,\theta}(dx)$; on a finite state space this is row-vector multiplication by $K_\theta$.

[F3] [[alg-contrastive-divergence-k]]: the population stop-gradient direction is $\mathbb E_{q_0}\nabla_\theta E_\theta-\mathbb E_{q_{k,\theta}}\nabla_\theta E_\theta$.

[F4] [[def-finite-probability-vector]]: a finite probability vector has nonnegative coordinates summing to one.

[F5] [[def-derivative]]: the derivative at a real coordinate point is defined by the limit of its difference quotient.

[F6] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: finite sums, scalar multiples, products, and quotients (where the denominator is nonzero) obey the stated derivative rules.

[F7] [[thm-chain-rule]]: the derivative of a composition of differentiable real functions is the product of the outer derivative at the image and the inner derivative.

[F8] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: $\exp'(u)=\exp(u)$ for every real $u$.

[F9] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: for $u>0$, $\log'(u)=1/u$ for the natural logarithm.

[F10] [[def-measure]]: a measure vanishes on the empty set and is countably additive on pairwise disjoint sequences.

[F11] [[def-probability-measure]]: a measure with total mass one is a probability measure.

[F12] [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: a conditional-expectation version is integrable, measurable with respect to the conditioning sigma-algebra, and has the same integral as the conditioned variable on every event in that sigma-algebra.

[F13] [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]: $\exp(u)>0$ for every real $u$.

## Proof

1.1 Fix a coordinate $j$ and vary only $\theta_j$ in a small interval inside the open set $\Theta$. Since $\mathcal X$ is finite and each energy is real, [F13] makes every $e^{-E_\theta(x)}$ positive; hence [F1] gives $0<Z_\theta<\infty$. The formula for $p_\theta$ then gives positive coordinates summing to one, so it is a probability vector by [F4]. By [F6], [F7] and [F8], differentiating the finite sum gives $\partial_jZ_\theta=-\sum_xe^{-E_\theta(x)}\partial_jE_\theta(x)$. The same chain and quotient rules give $\partial_jp_\theta(x)/p_\theta(x)=-\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\partial_jZ_\theta/Z_\theta=-\partial_jE_\theta(x)+\sum_yp_\theta(y)\partial_jE_\theta(y)$; [F9] identifies the left side with $\partial_j\log p_\theta(x)$. Because $q_0$ is fixed and sums to one by [F4], differentiating $\mathcal L=-\sum_xq_0(x)\log p_\theta(x)$ and summing this identity yields the displayed likelihood-gradient formula. [given, A1, F1, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F13, algebra]

If $\partial_j(q_0K_\theta^k)=\sum_{s=0}^{k-1}q_0K_\theta^s(\partial_jK_\theta)K_\theta^{k-1-s}$, then entrywise application of [F6] to $q_0K_\theta^kK_\theta$ yields $\sum_{s=0}^{k-1}q_0K_\theta^s(\partial_jK_\theta)K_\theta^{k-s}+q_0K_\theta^k(\partial_jK_\theta)$, which is the same formula with $k+1$ by appending the $s=k$ term. Thus the stated product derivative holds for every $k$. Differentiating $\sum_xq_{k,\theta}(x)=1$ by [F6] gives $\sum_x\partial_jq_{k,\theta}(x)=0$. Strict positivity of $K_\theta$ and nonzero mass of $q_0$ imply $q_{k,\theta}(x)>0$ for every $x$, so the following logarithms are finite. [given, A1, F2, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 By the quotient rule [F6], $\partial_j(q_{k,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x))=\partial_jq_{k,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x)-q_{k,\theta}(x)\partial_jp_\theta(x)/p_\theta(x)^2$; the chain and logarithm derivative rules [F7, F9] then give $\partial_j\log(q_{k,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x))=\partial_jq_{k,\theta}(x)/q_{k,\theta}(x)-\partial_j\log p_\theta(x)$. 3.1 Since $q_0$ is fixed, the terms $q_0(x)\log q_0(x)$ in $D_{\rm KL}(q_0\|p_\theta)$ have zero derivative; applying the same product and logarithm rules [F6, F9] and using the log-density formula from step 1.1 and $\sum_xq_0(x)=1$ gives $\partial_jD_{\rm KL}(q_0\|p_\theta)=\sum_xq_0(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\sum_xp_\theta(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)$. Subtracting step 2.1 cancels the model expectations and yields the stated $\partial_j\operatorname{CD}_k$ formula. By [F3], the algorithm uses only its first two terms; the remaining sum is the derivative through $K_\theta^k$. Comparing with step 1.1 also shows that the algorithm replaces the exact likelihood negative phase $p_\theta$ by $q_{k,\theta}$. [given, F3, F4, F5, F6, F9, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Put $w(x_0,\ldots,x_k):=q_0(x_0)\prod_{s=0}^{k-1}K_\theta(x_s,x_{s+1})$. These weights are nonnegative. Summing successively over $x_k,\ldots,x_1$ and using the row sums of $K_\theta$ reduces $\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)$ to $\sum_{x_0}q_0(x_0)=1$. The set function $\mathbb P_\theta(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega)$ vanishes on the empty set and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence of subsets of finite $\Omega$ has only finitely many nonempty terms. Thus [F10] makes it a measure, and [F11] makes it a probability measure. [A1, F4, F10, F11, algebra, construct]

If the entries of $K_\theta^s$ sum the products along all length-$s$ paths, then $K_\theta^{s+1}(x,y)=\sum_zK_\theta^s(x,z)K_\theta(z,y)$ appends the final transition, so its entries sum the length-$(s+1)$ path weights; also $\sum_yK_\theta^{s+1}(x,y)=\sum_zK_\theta^s(x,z)\sum_yK_\theta(z,y)=1$. Thus $\mathbb P_\theta(X_0=x,X_k=y)=q_0(x)K_\theta^k(x,y)$. The function $g_f$ is finite-valued; for each Borel $C\subseteq\mathbb R$, $\{g_f(X_0)\in C\}=X_0^{-1}(\{x:g_f(x)\in C\})$, so $g_f(X_0)$ is $\sigma(X_0)$-measurable. 5.1 Every event in $\sigma(X_0)$ has the form $\{X_0\in B\}$ for some $B\subseteq\mathcal X$, since these preimages form a sigma-algebra and generate $\sigma(X_0)$. For every such event, step 4.2 gives $$\int \mathbf1_{\{X_0\in B\}}f(X_k)\,d\mathbb P_\theta=\sum_{x\in B}q_0(x)\sum_yK_\theta^k(x,y)f(y)=\int \mathbf1_{\{X_0\in B\}}g_f(X_0)\,d\mathbb P_\theta,$$ where terms with $q_0(x)=0$ vanish. The integrability and measurability from step 4.2 and this event-integral identity satisfy [F12], so $g_f(X_0)$ is the asserted conditional-expectation version. [F12, step 4.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set. A **probability vector** on
$\mathcal X$ is a family $P=(p_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$ of real numbers such that
$p_x\ge 0$ for every $x$ and $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x=1$. Its support is
$\operatorname{supp}P:=\{x\in\mathcal X:p_x>0\}$. Coordinates outside the
support are retained as zeros; they are not deleted from the alphabet.

For another probability vector $Q=(q_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$, the notation
$P\ll Q$ means $\operatorname{supp}P\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Q$. All
finite sums over $\mathcal X$ use the displayed alphabet and ordinary finite
real arithmetic, extended to $+\infty$ only where a later definition says so.

## Example

Let $\mathcal X=\{0,1\}$, $\theta\in\mathbb R$, and
$E_\theta(0)=0$, $E_\theta(1)=\theta$. Then
$$Z_\theta=1+e^{-\theta},\qquad p_\theta(1)=\frac{e^{-\theta}}{1+e^{-\theta}},\qquad p_\theta(0)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\theta}}.$$
Take $q_0=\delta_0$ and the transition kernel
$$K_\theta(x,y)=\frac12\mathbf1_{\{y=x\}}+\frac12p_\theta(y).$$
This kernel is strictly positive and leaves $p_\theta$ invariant. For $k=1$

$p_0(1)=1/2$. The population stop-gradient CD-1 direction for the negative
log-likelihood is $-1/4$, whereas the exact negative log-likelihood gradient is

$$\left.\frac{d}{d\theta}\operatorname{CD}_1(\theta)\right|_{\theta=0}=-\frac14-\frac18\log 3.$$
Thus the stop-gradient direction also omits a nonzero derivative of the
reconstruction law. This finite witness asserts no general sign or consistency

At $\theta=0$, the transition matrix and its state diagram are
$$K_0=\begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4\\1/4&3/4\end{pmatrix}.$$

## Definition

Let $X$ be a set, let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ (a family containing $\emptyset$ and $X$, closed under complements and countable unions), and let $\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty]$ be a countably additive measure with $\mu(\emptyset)=0$. Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$, meaning countably additive measures with $P(X)=Q(X)=1$. A function from $X$ to a Borel space is measurable when the inverse image of each Borel set belongs to $\mathcal A$. Assume that $P$ and $Q$ have finite-valued, nonnegative, measurable densities $p$ and $q$ with respect to the same measure $\mu$, meaning that $P(E)=\int_E p\,d\mu$ and $Q(E)=\int_E q\,d\mu$ for every $E\in\mathcal A$. In particular, $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$.

For a measurable discriminator $D:X\to[0,1]$, put $a(t)=-\ln t$ for $0<t\le1$ and $a(0)=+\infty$, and put $b(t)=-\ln(1-t)$ for $0\le t<1$ and $b(1)=+\infty$. In the products below, define $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$; a positive finite factor times $+\infty$ is $+\infty$. Define the log payoff and the unrestricted discriminator value by
$$
V(D;P,Q):=-\int p(x)a(D(x))\,d\mu(x)-\int q(x)b(D(x))\,d\mu(x),\qquad C(P,Q):=\sup_{D:X\to[0,1]\,\mathrm{measurable}}V(D;P,Q).
$$
Each integral is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral, defined as the supremum of the integrals of nonnegative simple minorants, so $V(D;P,Q)\in[-\infty,0]$. The supremum ranges over all measurable functions into $[0,1]$, including boundary values; it is not restricted to a finite-parameter discriminator family.

## Definition

In the common-density setting, put $m=(p+q)/2$. Additivity and nonnegative homogeneity of the integral give $\int m\,d\mu=1$. Define $r=p/m$ and $s=q/m$ where $m>0$, and define $r=s=0$ where $m=0$; then $0\le r,s\le2$ and $r+s=2$ wherever $m>0$. Let $\phi(0)=0$ and $\phi(t)=t\ln t$ for $t>0$. The density-defined Jensen–Shannon divergence is
$$
\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q):=\frac12\int m\phi(r)\,d\mu+\frac12\int m\phi(s)\,d\mu.
$$
The integrals are finite, and this formula is the average of the two density-relative-entropy terms from $p$ and $q$ to the mixture density $m$.

## Statement

For two probability measures $P,Q$ with finite-valued nonnegative densities $p,q$ relative to a common measure $\mu$, put $m=(p+q)/2$, $r=p/m$ and $s=q/m$ where $m>0$, and $r=s=0$ where $m=0$. Set $\phi(0)=0$ and $\phi(t)=t\ln t$ for $t>0$. The functions $m\phi(r)$ and $m\phi(s)$ are integrable, and the density-defined Jensen–Shannon divergence $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)=\tfrac12\int m\phi(r)\,d\mu+\tfrac12\int m\phi(s)\,d\mu$ is a finite nonnegative real number. It is zero if and only if $P=Q$, equivalently if and only if $p=q$ $\mu$-almost everywhere.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, probability measures $P,Q$, and finite-valued nonnegative measurable densities $p,q$ relative to $\mu$.

[F1] [[def-gan-minimax-objective]]: $P(E)=\int_Ep\,d\mu$ and $Q(E)=\int_Eq\,d\mu$ for every measurable $E$, and $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$.

[F2] [[def-gan-jensen-shannon-divergence]]: $m=(p+q)/2$; on $m>0$, $r=p/m$, $s=q/m$ satisfy $0\le r,s\le2$ and $r+s=2$; on $m=0$ set $r=s=0$. With $\phi(0)=0$ and $\phi(t)=t\ln t$ for $t>0$, $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)=\tfrac12\int m\phi(r)\,d\mu+\tfrac12\int m\phi(s)\,d\mu$.

[F3] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: for $t>0$, $\ln t=\int_1^t du/u$.

[F4] [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\ln$ is strictly increasing and $\ln1=0$.

[F5] [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]]: a nonnegative measurable function has integral zero exactly when it vanishes $\mu$-almost everywhere.

[F6] [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]: the Lebesgue integral is linear on integrable functions.

[F7] [[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]: the nonnegative Lebesgue integral is additive on nonnegative measurable functions.

[F8] [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]: the nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous for positive scalars.

[F9] [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]: sums and finite scalar multiples of real measurable functions are measurable.

[F10] [[thm-coordinatewise-measurability-into-r-n]]: a map into $\mathbb R^n$ is measurable when its coordinate functions are measurable.

[F11] [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]: composing a measurable map with a Borel map preserves measurability.

[F12] [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]: arithmetic operations, including pointwise products, preserve measurability when defined.

## Proof

1.1 Define $\psi(0)=1$ and $\psi(t)=t\ln t-t+1$ for $t>0$. If $0<t<1$, then $\ln t=-\int_t^1du/u>-(1-t)/t=1-1/t$, since $1/u<1/t$ for $t<u\le1$. If $t>1$, then $\ln t=\int_1^tdu/u>(t-1)/t=1-1/t$, since $1/u>1/t$ for $1\le u<t$. Thus $\psi(t)>0$ for $t\ne1$ and $\psi(1)=0$. Also $-1\le\phi(t)\le0$ for $0<t\le1$, by the first inequality and $\ln t\le0$; and $0\le\phi(t)\le t(t-1)\le2$ for $1\le t\le2$, since $\ln t=\int_1^tdu/u\le t-1$. At $t=0$, $\phi(0)=0$ and $\psi(0)=1$. Hence $\psi\ge0$ with equality exactly at $1$, $|\phi(t)|\le2$, and $\psi(t)\le5$ on $[0,2]$. [given, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], [F7] and [F8], $\int m\,d\mu=\tfrac12\int(p+q)\,d\mu=1$. By [F2], $0\le r,s\le2$. Coordinatewise measurability [F10], Borel composition [F11], and arithmetic/product closure [F9, F12] make $m\phi(r)$, $m\phi(s)$, and $\tfrac12m(\psi(r)+\psi(s))$ measurable. Step 1.1 gives $|m\phi(r)|,|m\phi(s)|\le2m$ and $0\le\tfrac12m(\psi(r)+\psi(s))\le5m$, so they are integrable. On $m>0$, $r+s=2$ and $\phi(t)=\psi(t)+t-1$, so $\phi(r)+\phi(s)=\psi(r)+\psi(s)\ge0$; when $m=0$ both products by $m$ vanish. Linearity in [F6] gives $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)=\int \tfrac12m(\psi(r)+\psi(s))\,d\mu\ge0$. [F1, F2, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)=0$, the nonnegative measurable function $h:=\tfrac12m(\psi(r)+\psi(s))$ has integral zero by step 2.1. By [F5], $h=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. On $m>0$, both $\psi(r)$ and $\psi(s)$ are nonnegative, so they must each be zero almost everywhere there; step 1.1 gives $r=s=1$ there, hence $p=q$. On $m=0$, nonnegativity and $m=(p+q)/2$ give $p=q=0$. Therefore $p=q$ $\mu$-almost everywhere, and [F1] implies $P(E)=Q(E)$ for every measurable $E$. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Conversely, suppose $P=Q$. If $\{p>q\}$ had positive measure, it would be the countable union over positive integers $n,k$ of $E_{n,k}:=\{p-q\ge1/n\}\cap\{p+q\ge1/k\}$, so some $E_{n,k}$ would have positive measure. On that set, $\mu(E_{n,k})/k\le\int_{E_{n,k}}(p+q)\,d\mu\le\int(p+q)\,d\mu=2\int m\,d\mu=2$ by [F1], [F7], [F8] and step 2.1, so its measure is finite. By [F1] and [F6], $0=P(E_{n,k})-Q(E_{n,k})=\int_{E_{n,k}}(p-q)\,d\mu\ge\mu(E_{n,k})/n>0$, a contradiction. The same argument with $p,q$ exchanged rules out $\{q>p\}$, hence $p=q$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. Then $r=s=1$ almost everywhere on $m>0$, so [F2] gives $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)=0$. [F1, F2, F6, F7, F8, F9, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Steps 3.1 and 3.2 prove that $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)$ is zero exactly when $P=Q$; step 2.1 proves it is finite and nonnegative. These are all claims in the Statement. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space, and let
$f = (f_1,\dots,f_n) : X \to \mathbb{R}^n$. Then $f$ is measurable if and only
if each coordinate function $f_j : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is measurable.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A natural number $n\ge1$, a measurable space $(X,\mathcal{A})$, and a function $f=(f_1,\dots,f_n):X \to \mathbb{R}^n$.

[L1] Rational open boxes generate the Borel sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$. ([[thm-rational-box-generators-of-the-borel-sigma-algebra-on-rn]])

[L2] A generating family on the codomain suffices to test measurability. ([[thm-generating-family-criterion-for-measurable-functions]])

[L3] Real-valued measurability is equivalent to threshold measurability. ([[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Suppose $f$ is measurable. Fix $j$ and a real $a$. Then $$\{x : f_j(x) > a\} = f^{-1}\!\big(\mathbb{R}^{j-1} \times (a,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}^{n-j}\big).$$ The displayed strip is open, hence Borel in $\mathbb{R}^n$, so the preimage is measurable. By [L3], each coordinate $f_j$ is measurable. [L3, given]

1.2 Conversely, suppose every coordinate $f_j$ is measurable. Let $B = \prod_{j=1}^n (a_j,b_j)$ be a rational open box. Then $$f^{-1}(B) = \bigcap_{j=1}^n \{x : a_j < f_j(x) < b_j\},$$ and each factor on the right is measurable by [L3]. Therefore $f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A}$ for every rational open box $B$. [L1, L3, algebra]

2.1 By [L1] and [L2], step 1.2 implies that $f$ is measurable. Together with [step 1.1, step 1.2, L1, L2] step 1.1, this proves the equivalence. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L1, L2]. [L1, L2, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎
