## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $P,Q$ be probability measures with finite-valued nonnegative measurable densities $p,q$ relative to $\mu$, normalized by $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$. For every measurable discriminator $D:X\to[0,1]$, define
$$
V(D;P,Q)=\int p\ln D\,d\mu+\int q\ln(1-D)\,d\mu,
$$
extending $\ln0=-\infty$ and making each zero-density term $0\cdot(-\infty)$ equal to $0$. Let $C(P,Q)$ be the supremum of $V(D;P,Q)$ over all such $D$. Put $m=(p+q)/2$, $r=p/m$ and $s=q/m$ where $m>0$, set $r=s=0$ where $m=0$, define $\phi(0)=0$ and $\phi(t)=t\ln t$ for $t>0$, and set $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)=\tfrac12\int m\phi(r)\,d\mu+\tfrac12\int m\phi(s)\,d\mu$. Then the measurable discriminator
$$
D^*(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{p(x)}{p(x)+q(x)},&p(x)+q(x)>0,\\[4pt]\dfrac12,&p(x)+q(x)=0\end{cases}
$$
maximizes $V$, and $C(P,Q)=-\ln4+2\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)$. Consequently $C(P,Q)\ge-\ln4$, with equality if and only if $P=Q$. Over the unrestricted class of probability densities, equality of the generator law with the data law is the unique global distribution optimum. This identity does not assert convergence of finite neural alternating optimization.

## Statement references

[[def-gan-minimax-objective|GAN minimax objective and density domain]]

[[def-gan-jensen-shannon-divergence|Density-defined Jensen–Shannon divergence]]

[[lem-gan-jensen-shannon-divergence-nonnegative-and-equality|Jensen–Shannon nonnegativity and equality]]

[Goodfellow et al., §4.1, Proposition 1, Theorem 1, equations (2)–(6), complete 9-page paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.2661)

[Li, §1.2, equations (9)–(11), complete 6-page lecture note](https://yingzhenli.net/home/pdf/imperial_dlcourse2022_gan_notes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, probability measures $P,Q$ with finite-valued nonnegative measurable densities $p,q$, and a measurable discriminator $D:X\to[0,1]$.

[F1] [[def-gan-minimax-objective]]: $V(D;P,Q)=-\int p(-\ln D)\,d\mu-\int q(-\ln(1-D))\,d\mu$, where $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$, and $C(P,Q)$ is the supremum over every measurable $D:X\to[0,1]$.

[F2] [[def-gan-jensen-shannon-divergence]]: with $m=(p+q)/2$, $r=p/m$, $s=q/m$ on $m>0$ and $r=s=0$ otherwise, $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)=\tfrac12\int m\phi(r)\,d\mu+\tfrac12\int m\phi(s)\,d\mu$.

[F3] [[lem-gan-jensen-shannon-divergence-nonnegative-and-equality]]: the two integrands $m\phi(r)$ and $m\phi(s)$ are integrable, and $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)$ is finite and nonnegative, with equality exactly when $P=Q$.

[F4] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: $\ln$ is differentiable on $(0,\infty)$ with derivative $1/t$.

[F5] [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\ln$ is strictly increasing, $\ln1=0$, and $\ln(xy)=\ln x+\ln y$ for $x,y>0$.

[F6] [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]: the nonnegative integral is monotone.

[F7] [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]: the Lebesgue integral is linear on integrable functions.

[F8] [[thm-coordinatewise-measurability-into-r-n]]: a map into $\mathbb R^2$ is measurable if its two coordinates are measurable.

[F9] [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]: composing a measurable map with a Borel map preserves measurability.

[F10] [[thm-chain-rule]]: if $g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $f$ is differentiable at $g(c)$, then $(f\circ g)'(c)=f'(g(c))g'(c)$.

[F11] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: sums and scalar multiples of differentiable functions are differentiable, with the sum and scalar-multiple derivative formulas.

[F12] [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]: a function differentiable at every point of an open interval is continuous at every point of that interval.

[F13] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: a function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable on its interior has a point where its derivative equals the average rate of change across the interval.

## Proof

1.1 Define $F:[0,\infty)^2\to[0,1]$ by $F(a,b)=a/(a+b)$ when $a+b>0$ and $F(0,0)=1/2$. It is continuous on the Borel set $\{a+b>0\}$ and constant on its singleton complement, hence Borel. By [F8], $x\mapsto(p(x),q(x))$ is measurable, and [F9] makes $D^*=F(p,q)$ measurable. [F8, F9, construct]

1.2 Fix $x$ and write $a=p(x)$ and $b=q(x)$. If $a,b>0$, the function $f(y)=a\ln y+b\ln(1-y)$ on $0<y<1$ is differentiable with $f'(y)=a/y-b/(1-y)=(a-(a+b)y)/(y(1-y))$: the derivative of $1-y$ is $-1$ by its difference quotient, [F4] differentiates $\ln$, [F10] applies the chain rule, and [F11] gives the sum and scalar rules. The denominator is positive; the numerator is positive for $y<y^*:=a/(a+b)$ and negative for $y>y^*$. By [F12], $f$ is continuous on every closed subinterval of $(0,1)$. For any $y\in(0,y^*)$, [F13] on $[y,y^*]$ gives $c\in(y,y^*)$ with $f(y^*)-f(y)=f'(c)(y^*-y)>0$. For any $y\in(y^*,1)$, [F13] on $[y^*,y]$ gives $c\in(y^*,y)$ with $f(y)-f(y^*)=f'(c)(y-y^*)<0$. At $y=0,1$ the payoff is $-\infty$. If $a=0<b$, then $f(y)=b\ln(1-y)\le0=f(0)$, with equality at $y=0$. If $b=0<a$, then $f(y)=a\ln y\le0=f(1)$, with equality at $y=1$. If $a=b=0$, every $y$ gives value $0$. In all four cases, $D^*(x)$ maximizes the pointwise payoff. [given, F4, F5, F10, F11, F12, F13, algebra]

2.1 For any measurable $D$, step 1.2 gives the pointwise loss inequality $p(-\ln D)+q(-\ln(1-D))\ge p(-\ln D^*)+q(-\ln(1-D^*))$, with zero-density endpoint terms interpreted as in [F1]. Monotonicity [F6] of the nonnegative integral therefore gives $V(D;P,Q)\le V(D^*;P,Q)$. Since $D^*$ is measurable by step 1.1, the supremum is attained and $C(P,Q)=V(D^*;P,Q)$. [F1, F6, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 On $m>0$, one has $p=mr$, $q=ms$, $D^*=r/2$ and $1-D^*=s/2$. Using $0\ln0=0$ when $r=0$ or $s=0$, the pointwise optimized payoff is $m\phi(r)+m\phi(s)-m(r+s)\ln2=m\phi(r)+m\phi(s)-2m\ln2$. On $m=0$, both densities and all displayed products are zero, so the same identity holds. The first two terms are integrable by [F3]; [F1] and [F7] give $\int m\,d\mu=1$. Hence [F7], [F2] and $\ln4=2\ln2$ give $C(P,Q)=2\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)-\ln4$. [F1, F2, F3, F7, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F3], $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)\ge0$, and it vanishes exactly when $P=Q$. Step 3.1 therefore gives $C(P,Q)\ge-\ln4$ with equality exactly at $P=Q$. The unrestricted density class contains the data law itself, so this value is attained there and no other generator law attains it. The argument establishes only the distribution-space optimum stated here. [F3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, a function $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$ at which $f$ is differentiable ([[def-derivative]], [[def-limit-point-r]]).

[L1] Carathéodory's characterisation ([[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]]): since $f$ is differentiable at the limit point $c$ of $A$, there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.

[L2] Algebra of continuous functions ([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]): sums, scalar multiples and products of functions continuous at a point of the common domain are continuous there (claim 1); and every constant function on $A$ and the identity $x \mapsto x$ on $A$ are continuous at every point of $A$ (claim 5).

[L3] Continuity of $f$ at $c$ is the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition of [[def-continuity-real]], and continuity on a set is continuity at each of its points.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix a function $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$. [L1, choose]

1.2 The identity $x \mapsto x$ on $A$ and every constant function on $A$ are continuous at $c$; hence so is $x \mapsto x - c$, which is the sum of the identity and the constant function with value $-c$. [L2]

2.1 The pointwise product $x \mapsto \varphi(x)(x - c)$ is continuous at $c$, being the product of two functions on $A$ continuous at $c$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L2]

3.1 For every $x \in A$ one has $f(x) = f(c) + \varphi(x)(x - c)$, so $f$ is the sum of the constant function with value $f(c)$ and the product of step 2.1. [step 1.1, L1]

4.1 A sum of two functions continuous at $c$ is continuous at $c$, so $f$ is continuous at $c$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L2, L3]

5.1 The point $c$ was an arbitrary point of $A$, a limit point of $A$, at which $f$ is differentiable; applying step 4.1 at every point of a set $S \subseteq A$ on which $f$ is differentiable gives continuity of $f$ at every point of $S$. [step 3.1, L3] ∎

## Remarks

- **Where the work actually is.** None of it is here. Carathéodory's characterisation already replaces the quotient by a product, and a product is visibly small when one factor is bounded near $c$ and the other tends to $0$; the algebra of continuous functions packages exactly that. A direct proof from the quotient would multiply and divide by $x - c$ and would have to say why that is legal, which is the same observation in a less convenient place.

- **The converse fails.** $x \mapsto |x|$ is continuous at $0$ and not differentiable there, which is [[cex-absolute-value-is-not-differentiable-at-zero]] on the companion page. So continuity is strictly weaker, and the gap is not exotic: it opens at a single corner.

- **What is *not* claimed.** Nothing here says that a function differentiable on a set has a continuous derivative, and nothing here says that $f'$ is defined anywhere except where it was assumed to be. Both are separate questions, and neither is settled on this page.

## Example

Let $X=\{a,b\}$ with counting measure $\mu(E)=|E|$. Let $P_{\rm data}$ put mass $1$ at $a$ and $P_G$ put mass $1$ at $b$, so their densities are $p(a)=1$, $p(b)=0$, $q(a)=0$, and $q(b)=1$. The ideal discriminator is $D^*(a)=1$ and $D^*(b)=0$, the density-defined Jensen–Shannon divergence is $\ln2$, and the optimized minimax value is $C(P_{\rm data},P_G)=0$. Thus disjoint supports give a saturated ideal discriminator; this calculation makes no claim about finite-network gradient behavior.

[[thm-optimal-discriminator-and-js-divergence|Optimal discriminator and Jensen–Shannon identity]]

**Given:** The two-point laws and counting measure in the Example.

1.1 Their densities are $p(a)=1,p(b)=0,q(a)=0,q(b)=1$. Thus $m(a)=m(b)=1/2$, $(r(a),s(a))=(2,0)$ and $(r(b),s(b))=(0,2)$. [given, F2, construct]

3.1 By [F1] and step 2.2, $C(P_{\rm data},P_G)=-\ln4+2\ln2=0$. The discriminator takes only the saturated endpoint values on the two supports, as claimed. [F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $\theta,\varphi\in\mathbb R$ be a generator and discriminator parameter, and let the generator minimize and the discriminator maximize the shared payoff $L(\theta,\varphi)=\theta\varphi$. Starting from any $(\theta_0,\varphi_0)\ne(0,0)$, use one exact unit-step generator gradient descent update followed by one exact unit-step discriminator gradient ascent update, with the discriminator update evaluated at the new generator parameter:
$$
\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n-\partial_\theta L(\theta_n,\varphi_n),\qquad \varphi_{n+1}=\varphi_n+\partial_\varphi L(\theta_{n+1},\varphi_n).
$$
The resulting parameter sequence repeats after six steps and does not converge. This scalar bilinear game is a finite-parameter adversarial-game illustration, not the GAN cross-entropy objective or a neural GAN; it shows why a distribution-space optimum alone is not a finite-parameter training-convergence theorem.

## Example references

[[thm-optimal-discriminator-and-js-divergence|Unrestricted distribution-space optimum and its scope]]

[Goodfellow et al., §4.2, final paragraph on finite MLP parameterization, complete 9-page paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.2661)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\theta_n,\varphi_n\in\mathbb R$, payoff $L(\theta,\varphi)=\theta\varphi$, generator descent first, discriminator ascent second at the updated $\theta$, unit step size, and a nonzero initial pair.

[F1] [[thm-optimal-discriminator-and-js-divergence]]: the proved GAN optimum is for the unrestricted distribution-space objective, and it asserts no convergence for finite neural alternating optimization.

## Verification

**Given:** The scalar payoff and exact alternating update rule in the Example, with $(\theta_0,\varphi_0)\ne(0,0)$.

1.1 For $h\ne0$, $\bigl(L(\theta+h,\varphi)-L(\theta,\varphi)\bigr)/h=\bigl((\theta+h)\varphi-\theta\varphi\bigr)/h=\varphi$, so $\partial_\theta L=\varphi$. Likewise $\bigl(L(\theta,\varphi+h)-L(\theta,\varphi)\bigr)/h=\theta$, so $\partial_\varphi L=\theta$. [given, algebra]

2.1 Substitution into the update gives $\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n-\varphi_n$ and $\varphi_{n+1}=\varphi_n+\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n$. Thus $x_{n+1}=Mx_n$ for $x_n=(\theta_n,\varphi_n)^\mathsf T$ and $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Matrix multiplication gives $M^2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $M^3=-I$. Hence $x_{n+3}=-x_n$ and $x_{n+6}=x_n$ for every $n$. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Since $x_0\ne0$, the subsequence $(x_{6k})_{k\ge0}$ is constantly $x_0$ and $(x_{6k+3})_{k\ge0}$ is constantly $-x_0\ne x_0$. group $(V,+,0_V)$, applied to the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. No second notion
of finite sum is introduced here.

### Independence of a list

A finite list $v : n \to V$ is **linearly independent** when, for every list of
scalars $\lambda : n \to F$,

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i = 0_V \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \lambda_i = 0_F \text{ for every } i < n,$$

and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some $\lambda : n \to F$ has
$\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V$ while $\lambda_j \ne 0_F$ for at least one
$j < n$. Such a $\lambda$ is called a **witness** to the dependence of $v$.

### Independence of a subset

A subset $S \subseteq V$ is **linearly independent** when **every injective**
finite list $v : n \to S$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) is linearly
independent, and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some injective
finite list into $S$ is linearly dependent.

**The injectivity clause is not decoration.** A linear combination in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]] is indexed by an arbitrary list $v : n \to S$,
which is **not** required to be injective. If the definition above quantified
over all such lists, then for any $w \in S$ the list $v : 2 \to S$ with
$v_0 = v_1 = w$ and the scalars $\lambda_0 = 1_F$, $\lambda_1 = -1_F$ would give

$$\sum_{i<2}\lambda_i v_i = (0_V + 1_F w) + (-1_F)w = w + (-w) = 0_V$$

with $\lambda_0 = 1_F \ne 0_F$ ([[def-field]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so **every** nonempty subset of
$V$ would be dependent and the notion would be empty. Quantifying over injective
lists is what makes the subset notion the intended one. It costs nothing for
lists: [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] shows that the vanishing condition
above already forces a list to be injective, so no injectivity hypothesis has to
be carried alongside independence of a list.

### The boundary cases are genuine cases

$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so both of the following are
instances of the definitions and neither is a convention.

- **The empty list is independent.** For $n = 0$ the only list of scalars is the
  empty one, and the condition "$\lambda_i = 0_F$ for every $i < 0$" holds
  vacuously.
- **$\varnothing \subseteq V$ is independent.** The only function $v : n \to
  \varnothing$ is the empty one, with $n = 0$, and it is independent by the
  previous point.
- **$\{0_V\}$ is dependent.** The list $v : 1 \to \{0_V\}$ with $v_0 = 0_V$ is
  injective, and taking $\lambda_0 = 1_F$ gives

  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), while $1_F \ne 0_F$ in a field
  ([[def-field]]). So $\{0_V\}$, and hence every subset of $V$ containing $0_V$,
  is linearly dependent.

          "quote": "Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

satisfies

## Definition

Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ be a finite nonempty set with this fixed ordering, and let $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^m$ and $q=(q_j)_{j=1}^m$ be probability vectors on $X$: their coordinates are nonnegative real numbers and $\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=\sum_{j=1}^m q_j=1$. A **coupling** of $p$ and $q$ is a real matrix $\pi=(\pi_{ij})_{i,j=1}^m$ satisfying
$$
\pi_{ij}\ge 0,\qquad \sum_{j=1}^m\pi_{ij}=p_i\quad(1\le i\le m),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\pi_{ij}=q_j\quad(1\le j\le m).
$$
Write $\Gamma(p,q)$ for the set of all such matrices. The first index records the source point and the second index records the destination point.

## Statement

Let $r,N\ge1$ be integers and let $g_1,\ldots,g_N\in\mathbb R^r$. Define
$$
C=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i g_i:\lambda_i\ge0\text{ for every }i\right\}.
$$
Then $C$ is closed in the Euclidean topology, and for all $x,y\in C$ and all real $\alpha,\beta\ge0$, one has $\alpha x+\beta y\in C$.

## Statement references

[Wouter Kager, A Short Simple Proof of Closedness of Convex Cones and Farkas' Lemma, Lemma and complete proof, pp. 1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.11678v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integers $r,N\ge1$, a list $g_1,\ldots,g_N\in\mathbb R^r$, and the set $C$ in the Statement.

[F1] On $\mathbb R^r$, coordinates are indexed by $k<r$, and $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<r} x_k y_k$ and $\|x\|_2^2=\langle x,x\rangle$; in particular $\langle x,x\rangle=0$ implies $x=0$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F2] A finite list is linearly independent exactly when every linear combination equal to zero has all coefficients zero ([[def-linear-independence]]).

[F3] For a square matrix over a field, having trivial kernel is equivalent to being invertible ([[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]]).

[F4] Every nonempty finite set of real numbers has an attained minimum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

[F5] On $\mathbb R^r$, $d_2(x,y)=\sqrt{\sum_{k<r}(x_k-y_k)^2}$ is a metric and $\|x-y\|_2=d_2(x,y)$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F6] A set is closed exactly when its complement is open, and a set is open when every point has a positive-radius metric ball contained in it ([[def-metric-topology]]).

[F7] Every nonzero real has positive square, $0^2=0$, and for $c\ge0$, $\sqrt c\ge0$ with $(\sqrt c)^2=c$; finite sums of nonnegative reals dominate each term, termwise inequalities may be summed, finite sums scale by a common scalar, and a zero sum of nonnegative terms forces every term to be zero ([[lem-of-square-positive]], [[def-integer-power]], [[lem-of-zero-mult]], [[thm-of-square-roots]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

[F8] Absolute values are nonnegative, vanish exactly at zero, satisfy $|ab|=|a||b|$ and $|a+b|\le |a|+|b|$, and obey $|a|^2=a^2$; squaring is monotone on nonnegative reals, and multiplication by a nonnegative real preserves nonstrict inequalities ([[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]], [[lem-of-triangle-inequality]], [[lem-of-square-monotone]], [[lem-of-sign-rules]], [[lem-of-zero-mult]]).

[F9] A metric is nonnegative ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]).

[F10] If a property holds at $0$ and passes from $n$ to $n+1$, it holds for every natural $n$ ([[thm-induction-principle]]).

## Proof

1.1 Take a representation $x=\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i g_i$ with every $\lambda_i\ge0$ and let $S=\{i:\lambda_i>0\}$. If the sublist indexed by $S$ is dependent, [F2] gives coefficients $c_i$, not all zero, with $\sum_{i\in S}c_i g_i=0$. Reverse all signs if needed so $J=\{i\in S:c_i>0\}$ is nonempty, and set $t=\min_{i\in J}\lambda_i/c_i>0$ using [F4]. Define $\lambda'_i=\lambda_i-tc_i$ for $i\in S$ and $\lambda'_i=0$ for $i\notin S$. For $i\in S$ with $c_i>0$, the minimum choice makes $\lambda'_i\ge0$ and makes at least one such coefficient zero; when $c_i\le0$, $\lambda'_i\ge\lambda_i>0$. Thus every $\lambda'_i\ge0$, the positive support strictly shrinks, and $\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda'_i g_i=x$. Repeating this finite support reduction at most $N$ times gives a representation of $x$ whose positive support is linearly independent. [given, F2, F4, choose, construct]

1.2 Fix a nonempty independent sublist indexed by $S=\{i_1,\ldots,i_s\}$, let $A:\mathbb R^s\to\mathbb R^r$ have these columns, and let $G=A^{\mathsf T}A$. If $Gz=0$, then $0=z^{\mathsf T}Gz=\|Az\|_2^2$, so [F1] gives $Az=0$ and [F2] gives $z=0$. Thus $G$ is invertible by [F3]. Put $B=G^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}$ and $P=AB$, so $BA=I$. The cone $C_S$ generated by this sublist is exactly $\{x\in\mathbb R^r:Px=x,\ (Bx)_k\ge0\text{ for }k<s\}$: if $x=Az$ with $z\ge0$, then $Bx=z$ and $Px=x$; conversely those displayed conditions give $x=P x=A(Bx)$ with nonnegative coefficients. Each coordinate of $Bx$ and $Px-x$ is a finite linear form $\ell(x)=\sum_{j<r}c_jx_j$. ## Statement

For $A\in M_n(F)$, the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ is invertible;
2. $x\mapsto Ax$ is a linear isomorphism;
3. $N(A)=\{0\}$;
4. $\operatorname{rank}(A)=n$;
5. $A$ has a pivot in every row and every column;
6. the RREF of $A$ is $I_n$;
7. for every $b\in F^n$, the equation $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A square matrix $A\in M_n(F)$.

[L1] RREF detects consistency and parametrises solutions by its nonpivot variables ([[thm-rref-consistency-and-free-variable-parametrisation]]).

[L2] Rank–nullity for matrices gives $\operatorname{rank}A+\dim N(A)=n$ ([[cor-matrix-rank-nullity]]).

[L3] Matrix rank equals the rank of $x\mapsto Ax$ ([[cor-matrix-rank-equals-the-rank-of-its-linear-map]]).

[L4] Matrix rank equals the number of pivots in any echelon form ([[thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank]]).

[L5] Matrix invertibility means existence of a two-sided matrix inverse ([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]).

[L6] A square matrix is invertible exactly when its multiplication map is a linear isomorphism ([[thm-invertible-matrices-correspond-to-linear-isomorphisms]]).

[L7] A linear map is injective exactly when its kernel is trivial ([[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]]).

[L8] A linear isomorphism is a linear map with a two-sided linear inverse ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L6], matrix invertibility is equivalent to the multiplication map being an isomorphism. An isomorphism has a two-sided inverse by [L8], hence is injective, and [L7] then gives $N(A)=\{0\}$. [L5, L6, L7, L8]

2.1 By [L2], trivial nullspace is equivalent to rank $n$, and [L4] makes this equivalent to having $n$ pivots. A square matrix has $n$ pivots exactly when every row and column contains one. [step 1.1, L2, L3, L4]

3.1 An $n\times n$ RREF with a pivot in every row and column is $I_n$. By [L1], RREF $I_n$ is equivalent to the assertion that every right-hand side produces a consistent system with no free variable, hence exactly one solution. [step 2.1, L1]

4.1 Under condition 7, define $S(b)$ to be the unique solution of $Ax=b$. Then $L_A(S(b))=b$, and uniqueness for the right-hand side $Ax$ gives $S(L_A(x))=x$. Moreover, linearity of $L_A$ from [L3] gives $L_A(S(\lambda y+z))=\lambda y+z=L_A(\lambda S(y)+S(z))$; applying the inverse function $S$ proves that $S$ is linear. Thus $L_A$ has a two-sided linear inverse and is a linear isomorphism by [L8], so [L6] returns condition 1. Together with steps 1.1–3.1, this closes the implication cycle and proves all seven conditions equivalent. For $n=0$, the unique empty matrix is $I_0$, its map on the zero space is bijective, and every condition holds. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, L3, L6, L8, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An ordered field $F$ and elements $x, y \in F$.

[L1] For every $u \in F$, $-|u| \le u \le |u|$, and $|u|$ equals $u$ or $-u$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]).

[L2] Order compatible with addition: if $a \le b$ and $c \le d$, then $a + c \le b + d$. [[lem-of-add-order]] states the STRICT forms and only those ($a < b \Rightarrow a + c < b + c$, and $a < b$ with $c < d$ giving $a + c < b + d$); the nonstrict form used here is those two together with the cases $a = b$ and $c = d$, settled by trichotomy, the order being total ([[def-ordered-field]]). Explicitly: if $a < b$ and $c < d$ the second strict form applies; if $a < b$ and $c = d$ the first gives $a + c < b + c = b + d$; if $a = b$ and $c < d$ the first gives $a + c < a + d = b + d$; and if $a = b$ and $c = d$ the two sides are equal.

[L3] Field and order arithmetic: $-(a + b) = -a + (-b)$, and $a \le b \iff -b \le -a$ ([[def-ordered-field]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], $-|x| \le x \le |x|$ and $-|y| \le y \le |y|$. [L1]

2.1 Adding the two chains of [step 1.1] with [L2] and using $-(|x| + |y|) = -|x| + (-|y|)$ from [L3] gives $-(|x| + |y|) \le x + y \le |x| + |y|$. [step 1.1, L2, L3]

3.1 By [L1] the value $|x + y|$ equals $x + y$ or $-(x + y)$; both $x + y \le |x| + |y|$ and $-(x + y) \le |x| + |y|$ hold by [step 2.1] and [L3] (the latter from $-(|x| + |y|) \le x + y$), so $|x + y| \le |x| + |y|$. [step 2.1, L1, L3] ∎

## Statement

Let $X$ be a set and let $p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy the reflexivity
axiom (M1') $p(x,x) = 0$ and the symmetry axiom (M2) $p(x,y) = p(y,x)$ of
[[def-metric-space]]. Then:

1. If $p$ satisfies the triangle inequality (M3), then $p(x,y) \ge 0$ for all
   $x, y \in X$.
2. If $p$ satisfies the strong triangle inequality (M3'), then
   $p(x,y) \ge 0$ for all $x, y \in X$.

In particular every metric, every pseudometric and every ultrametric
([[def-metric-space]]) takes only nonnegative values. Nonnegativity is therefore
a theorem about the axiom list this library uses, not a fourth axiom, and no
statement on this page needs to assume it separately.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A set $X$, points $x, y \in X$, and a function $p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M1') $p(a,a) = 0$ for every $a \in X$ and (M2) $p(a,b) = p(b,a)$ for all $a, b \in X$ ([[def-metric-space]]).

[A1] (M3) The triangle inequality $p(a,c) \le p(a,b) + p(b,c)$ holds for all $a, b, c \in X$ ([[def-metric-space]]).

[A2] (M3') The strong triangle inequality $p(a,c) \le \max\{p(a,b), p(b,c)\}$ holds for all $a, b, c \in X$ ([[def-metric-space]]).

[L1] Trichotomy of the order of $\mathbb{R}$: for reals $a, b$ exactly one of $a < b$, $a = b$, $b < a$ holds, so $a \ge 0$ fails exactly when $a < 0$ ([[def-real-order]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]).

[L2] Adding two strict inequalities: if $a < b$ and $c < d$ then $a + c < b + d$ ([[lem-of-add-order]]).

[L3] A two-element subset $\{a,b\}$ of $\mathbb{R}$ has a maximum, and that maximum is $a$ or $b$; if $a = b$ it is $a$ ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Instantiate [A1] at $a = x$, $b = y$, $c = x$: $p(x,x) \le p(x,y) + p(y,x)$. [A1]

1.2 Instantiate [A2] at $a = x$, $b = y$, $c = x$: $p(x,x) \le \max\{p(x,y), p(y,x)\}$. [A2]

1.3 Suppose, towards ruling it out, that $p(x,y) < 0$. [assume-hyp]

2.1 By (M1') the left side of step 1.1 is $0$ and by (M2) the right side is $p(x,y) + p(x,y)$, so $0 \le p(x,y) + p(x,y)$. [step 1.1, given]

2.2 By (M2) the two entries of the maximum in step 1.2 are the same real number, so that maximum equals $p(x,y)$ by [L3], and (M1') turns step 1.2 into $0 \le p(x,y)$, which is claim 2. [step 1.2, given, L3]

2.3 Adding the supposed inequality of step 1.3 to itself gives $p(x,y) + p(x,y) < 0 + 0 = 0$. [step 1.3, L2]

3.1 Steps 2.1 and 2.3 assert $0 \le p(x,y) + p(x,y)$ and $p(x,y) + p(x,y) < 0$, which trichotomy forbids; so the supposition of step 1.3 is untenable and $p(x,y) \ge 0$, which is claim 1. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, L1] ∎

## Remarks

- **What each claim uses.** Claim 1 is the familiar two-line argument $0 = p(x,x) \le p(x,y) + p(y,x) = 2p(x,y)$ followed by the observation that a negative real added to itself stays negative. Claim 2 does not need that second half at all: the strong triangle inequality delivers $0 \le p(x,y)$ in one step, because the maximum of a real number with itself is that number.
- **Symmetry is used in both claims and cannot be dropped.** Without (M2) the instantiation of step 1.1 only gives $0 \le p(x,y) + p(y,x)$, which leaves the possibility that one of the two values is negative and the other larger and positive. Dropping (M2) instead of weakening (M1) gives the notion usually called a quasimetric, which this library does not treat; for it the argument above is unavailable, so nonnegativity is not redundant there and is imposed as part of the definition ([[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]]).

## Definition

Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ be a nonempty finite set and let $d:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $d(x,y)=0$ if and only if $x=y$, $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$, and $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. Let $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^m$ and $q=(q_i)_{i=1}^m$ be probability vectors, so their coordinates are nonnegative and each vector sums to $1$. A coupling is an $m\times m$ matrix $\pi$ with $\pi_{ij}\ge0$, row sums $\sum_j\pi_{ij}=p_i$, and column sums $\sum_i\pi_{ij}=q_j$; write $\Gamma(p,q)$ for the set of all such matrices. Writing $d_{ij}=d(x_i,x_j)$, define the finite-metric 1-Wasserstein transport cost by
$$
W_1(p,q):=\min_{\pi\in\Gamma(p,q)}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^m d_{ij}\pi_{ij}.
$$

## Statement

Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ be a nonempty finite metric space, and let $p,q$ be probability vectors on $X$. The coupling set $\Gamma(p,q)$ is nonempty and compact in $\mathbb R^{m^2}$, so the finite-metric transport cost $W_1(p,q)$ attains its minimum. The normalized 1-Lipschitz potential set
$$
\mathcal L_1(X,d)=\{f\in\mathbb R^m:f_1=0,\ |f_i-f_j|\le d(x_i,x_j)\text{ for all }i,j\}
$$
is also nonempty and compact, so the linear functional $f\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^m(p_i-q_i)f_i$ attains a maximum on it.

## Statement references

[Peyré and Cuturi, Computational Optimal Transport, §§2.1–2.3 and 3.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1803.00567)

[Santambrogio, Introduction to Optimal Transport Theory, §§1.1–1.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1009.3856)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty finite set $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ with metric $d$, and probability vectors $p,q$ on $X$.

[F1] A probability vector has nonnegative coordinates with total sum one ([[def-finite-probability-vector]]).

[F2] A coupling is a nonnegative matrix whose row sums are $p_i$ and column sums are $q_j$ ([[def-finite-metric-coupling]]).

[F3] A metric has real values, vanishes exactly on equal points, is symmetric, and satisfies the triangle inequality ([[def-metric-space]]).

[F4] Every metric is nonnegative, although nonnegativity is not listed as a separate metric axiom ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]).

[F5] On $\mathbb R^n$ for $n\ge1$, $d_2(x,y)=\sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^2}$ is a metric ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Closedness and openness refer to its metric topology; a set is closed when its complement is open, and open sets contain a ball around each of their points ([[def-metric-topology]]).

[F6] A subset of $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$, is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[F7] Every lower semicontinuous real function on a nonempty compact Euclidean set attains a minimum, and every upper semicontinuous one attains a maximum ([[thm-euclidean-semicontinuous-extreme-value-theorem]]).

[F8] The real line has metric $d_{\mathbb R}(a,b)=|a-b|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), and continuity at $x$ means that for each $\varepsilon>0$ some $\delta>0$ makes $d_X(x,y)<\delta$ imply $d_Y(f(x),f(y))<\varepsilon$ ([[def-metric-continuity]]).

[F9] A continuous real function on a Euclidean subset is both lower and upper semicontinuous ([[def-semicontinuity-on-euclidean-subsets]]).

[F10] The finite-metric transport cost is $W_1(p,q)=\min_{\pi\in\Gamma(p,q)}\sum_{i,j}d(x_i,x_j)\pi_{ij}$ ([[def-finite-metric-wasserstein-one]]).

[F11] Every nonzero real has positive square and $0^2=0$; finite sums of nonnegative terms dominate each term, termwise inequalities may be summed, and finite sums scale by a common scalar; for nonnegative reals, comparison of squares is equivalent to comparison of the reals; square roots are nonnegative and square to their radicands; absolute values are nonnegative and satisfy $|a|=0\iff a=0$, $|ab|=|a||b|$, $|a+b|\le|a|+|b|$, and $|a|^2=a^2$; multiplication by a nonnegative real preserves nonstrict inequalities ([[lem-of-square-positive]], [[def-integer-power]], [[lem-of-zero-mult]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-of-square-monotone]], [[thm-of-square-roots]], [[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]], [[lem-of-triangle-inequality]], [[lem-of-sign-rules]]).

[F12] A property holding at $0$ and passing from $n$ to $n+1$ holds for every natural $n$ ([[thm-induction-principle]]).

## Proof

1.1 Define $\pi_{ij}=p_iq_j$. These entries are nonnegative by [F1], and their row sums are $p_i\sum_jq_j=p_i$ while their column sums are $q_j\sum_ip_i=q_j$. Thus $\pi\in\Gamma(p,q)$ and the coupling set is nonempty. [given, F1, F2, construct]

1.2 Flatten a matrix into $\mathbb R^{m^2}$ in row-major order, assigning entry $\pi_{ij}$ to library coordinate $k=(i-1)m+(j-1)<m^2$; likewise potential coordinate $f_i$ corresponds to library coordinate $i-1<m$. In any dimension $n\ge1$, for $u\in\mathbb R^n$ and $k<n$, [F11] gives $u_k^2\le\sum_{j<n}u_j^2$; by [F5,F11], $|u_k|^2=u_k^2\le d_2(u,0)^2$, and both $|u_k|$ and $d_2(u,0)$ are nonnegative, so [F11] gives $|u_k|\le d_2(u,0)$. By induction on $n$, every finite list satisfies $|\sum_{k<n}a_k|\le\sum_{k<n}|a_k|$: the empty case is equality and the successor step follows from $|a+b|\le|a|+|b|$ in [F11]. Thus for every finite linear form $L(z)=\sum_{k<n}c_kz_k$, this bound, $|ab|=|a||b|$, the coordinate estimate, multiplication by nonnegative coefficients, finite-sum monotonicity and scaling in [F11] give $|L(z)-L(w)|\le(\sum_{k<n}|c_k|)d_2(z,w)$. The same estimate holds for every affine form $H(z)=L(z)+b$, since the constant cancels in $H(z)-H(w)$. The set $\Gamma(p,q)$ is defined by finitely many affine equalities and weak inequalities. ## Statement

Let $n\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and compact. Every lower semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded below and attains a minimum. Dually, every upper semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded above and attains a maximum.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty compact Euclidean set $K$ and a lower semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$, with infima as in [[def-infimum]].

[L1] Lower semicontinuity is equivalent to relative openness of every strict superlevel set and to relative closedness of every weak sublevel set ([[thm-euclidean-semicontinuity-level-set-characterisations]]).

[L2] In a compact space, every family of closed sets with the finite intersection property has nonempty intersection ([[thm-compact-iff-finite-intersection-property]]).

[L3] Every nonempty real set bounded below has a greatest lower bound in $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-infimum-property]]).

[L4] If $m$ is the infimum of a nonempty real set, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ the set has an element $s<m+\varepsilon$ ([[lem-inf-epsilon]]).

[L5] For every real $x$ there is a natural number $n\ge1$ with $x<n$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]).

[L6] For every real $\varepsilon>0$ there is a natural number $n\ge1$ with $1/n<\varepsilon$ ([[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]]).

[L7] A metric space is compact when every open cover has a finite subcover ([[def-metric-compactness]]).

[L8] Every nonempty finite set of real numbers has a maximum and a minimum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For positive naturals $N$, the relatively open sets $U_N=\{x\in K:f(x)>-N\}$ cover $K$: apply [L5] to $-f(x)$. By [L7], finitely many $U_N$ cover, and [L8] gives a largest index $M$ among them. Since the sets are nested, $U_M=K$, so $f>-M$ on $K$ and $f[K]$ is bounded below. [L1, L5, L7, L8, given, algebra]

2.1 By [L3], $m=\inf f[K]$ exists. For every positive natural $N$, the set $F_N=K\cap\{f\le m+1/N\}$ is closed by [L1] and nonempty by [L4]. The family is nested, so every finite subfamily has nonempty intersection. [step 1.1, L1, L3, L4, algebra]

3.1 By [L2], choose $x_*\in\bigcap_NF_N$. If $f(x_*)>m$, [L6] gives $N\ge1$ with $1/N<f(x_*)-m$, contradicting $x_*\in F_N$. Thus $f(x_*)=m$. Applying the same argument to $-f$ proves that an upper semicontinuous function attains its maximum. [step 2.1, L2, L6, choose, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $n\ge1$, let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, let $f:A\to\mathbb R$, and let $a\in A$. Using the Euclidean metric and its balls ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-metric-ball]]), $f$ is upper semicontinuous at $a$ when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)<f(a)+\varepsilon$ for every $x\in A\cap B_2(a,\delta)$.

The function is **lower semicontinuous at $a$** when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that

$$f(a)-\varepsilon<f(x)\qquad(x\in A\cap B_2(a,\delta)).$$

It is upper or lower semicontinuous on $A$ when the corresponding condition holds at every point of $A$. These are relative notions on $A$; when $A$ is empty, each on-set condition is vacuous. A continuous function ([[def-metric-continuity]]) satisfies both conditions.

## Statement

Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ be a nonempty finite set, let $d:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $d(x,y)=0$ if and only if $x=y$, $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$, and $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$, and let $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^m$, $q=(q_i)_{i=1}^m$ have nonnegative coordinates with each vector summing to $1$. Let $\Gamma(p,q)$ consist of matrices $\pi_{ij}\ge0$ with row sums $p_i$ and column sums $q_j$, and let
$$
W_1(p,q)=\min_{\pi\in\Gamma(p,q)}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^m d(x_i,x_j)\pi_{ij}.
$$
Then
$$
W_1(p,q)=\max_{\substack{f\in\mathbb R^m,\ f_1=0\\ |f_i-f_j|\le d(x_i,x_j)\ \text{for all }i,j}}\sum_{i=1}^m(p_i-q_i)f_i.
$$
Both extrema are attained. Moreover, for every minimizing coupling $\pi$ and every maximizing vector $f$, $\pi_{ij}>0$ implies $f_i-f_j=d(x_i,x_j)$.

## Statement references

[Peyré and Cuturi, Computational Optimal Transport, §§2.1–2.3, 3.1, 3.3 and 6.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1803.00567)

[Santambrogio, Introduction to Optimal Transport Theory, §§1.1–1.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1009.3856)

[Arjovsky, Chintala and Bottou, Wasserstein GAN, §§2–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1701.07875)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite metric space, probability vectors, and coupling set in the Statement.

[F1] A metric is real-valued and satisfies separation, symmetry and the triangle inequality ([[def-metric-space]]).

[F2] Metric values are nonnegative, although this is derived from the metric axioms rather than assumed ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]).

[F3] The vectors $p,q$ have nonnegative coordinates and total mass one ([[def-finite-probability-vector]]).

[F4] $\Gamma(p,q)$ consists of nonnegative matrices with row sums $p_i$ and column sums $q_j$ ([[def-finite-metric-coupling]]).

[F5] $W_1(p,q)$ is the minimum coupling cost $\min_{\pi\in\Gamma(p,q)}\sum_{i,j}d(x_i,x_j)\pi_{ij}$ ([[def-finite-metric-wasserstein-one]]).

[F6] The coupling set is nonempty compact and its cost minimum is attained; the normalized 1-Lipschitz potential set is nonempty compact and its linear objective maximum is attained ([[lem-finite-metric-transport-optima-attained]]).

[F7] The nonnegative span of finitely many Euclidean vectors is closed and closed under nonnegative linear combinations ([[lem-finitely-generated-cone-is-closed]]).

[F8] If $C$ is a nonempty closed convex subset of $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$, and $y\notin C$, there are a nonzero vector $h$ and a real $\beta$ such that $\langle h,z\rangle\le\beta<\langle h,y\rangle$ for all $z\in C$ ([[thm-strict-separation-of-a-point-from-a-closed-convex-set]]).

[F9] A nonempty finite list of real numbers has an attained minimum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

[F10] On the library's $\mathbb R^n$, coordinates are indexed by $k<n$ and the Euclidean pairing is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F11] A subset of Euclidean space is convex when it contains $(1-t)x+ty$ for every pair of its points and every $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The finite metric space, probability vectors, and coupling set in the Statement.

1.1 For any $\pi\in\Gamma(p,q)$ and any $f\in\mathbb R^m$ with $f_1=0$ and $|f_i-f_j|\le d(x_i,x_j)$, the marginal equations give $\sum_i(p_i-q_i)f_i=\sum_{i,j}\pi_{ij}(f_i-f_j)\le\sum_{i,j}\pi_{ij}d(x_i,x_j)$. The inequality uses $\pi_{ij}\ge0$ and $f_i-f_j\le|f_i-f_j|\le d(x_i,x_j)$. Thus every feasible dual value is at most every feasible primal cost. [given, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 Write $d_{ij}=d(x_i,x_j)$, and for $i=1,\ldots,m$ let $e_i\in\mathbb R^m$ have value $1$ at library coordinate $k=i-1$ and $0$ at every other coordinate. For alphabet-indexed tuples $u=(u_i)_{i=1}^m$ and $v=(v_j)_{j=1}^m$, identify $(u,v,t)$ with the vector in $\mathbb R^{2m+1}$ whose coordinate $k<m$ is $u_{k+1}$, whose coordinate $m+k$ is $v_{k+1}$, and whose coordinate $2m$ is $t$. Let $K$ be the nonnegative span of $(e_i,e_j,d_{ij})$ for all $i,j$, together with $(0,0,1)$. By [F7], $K$ is closed and closed under nonnegative linear combinations. For $x,y\in K$ and $s\in[0,1]$, [F7] gives $sx+(1-s)y\in K$, so [F11] makes $K$ convex; the zero representation gives $0\in K$. Put $c_*=W_1(p,q)$, which is finite and attained by [F6]. For every $\varepsilon>0$, the vector $y_\varepsilon=(p,q,c_*-\varepsilon)$ under this identification is outside $K$: if it had a representation with coefficients $\lambda_{ij}\ge0$ and $t\ge0$, its first two coordinate blocks would make $\lambda\in\Gamma(p,q)$ and its last coordinate would give $c_*-\varepsilon=\sum_{i,j}d_{ij}\lambda_{ij}+t\ge c_*$, contradicting minimality. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F11]

2.1 Apply [F8] to $K$ and $y_\varepsilon$. It gives a vector $h$ and threshold $\beta$ with $\langle h,z\rangle\le\beta<\langle h,y_\varepsilon\rangle$ for all $z\in K$. Since $0\in K$, $\beta\ge0$. By [F7], $s z\in K$ for every $z\in K$ and $s\ge0$. If $\langle h,z\rangle>0$ for some $z\in K$, then $s\langle h,z\rangle\le\beta$ would fail for large $s$. Hence $\langle h,z\rangle\le0$ for every $z\in K$, while $\langle h,y_\varepsilon\rangle>0$. [F7, F8, F10, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Decompose $h=(a,b,g)$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ and $g\in\mathbb R$. By [F10], pairing with $(0,0,1)\in K$ gives $g\le0$. If $g=0$, pairing with every $(e_i,e_j,d_{ij})$ gives $a_i+b_j\le0$. Multiplying by $p_iq_j\ge0$ and summing yields $\sum_i p_i a_i+\sum_jq_jb_j=\sum_{i,j}p_iq_j(a_i+b_j)\le0$. When $g=0$ this left-hand side is $\langle h,y_\varepsilon\rangle$, contrary to step 2.1. Therefore $g<0$. [step 2.1, F3, F10, algebra]

4.1 Define $u_i=a_i/(-g)$ and $v_j=b_j/(-g)$. The generator inequalities and $g<0$ give $u_i+v_j\le d_{ij}$ for all $i,j$. Dividing the strict point inequality by $-g>0$ gives $\sum_i p_i u_i+\sum_jq_jv_j>c_*-\varepsilon$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Set $f_i=\min_{1\le j\le m}(d_{ij}-v_j)$, whose minimum is attained by [F9]. From $u_i+v_j\le d_{ij}$ we have $u_i\le f_i$. For any $i,k,j$, the triangle inequality gives $d_{ij}-v_j\le d_{ik}+d_{kj}-v_j$; taking finite minima yields $f_i\le d_{ik}+f_k$, and symmetry gives $|f_i-f_k|\le d_{ik}$. Also $f_j\le d_{jj}-v_j=-v_j$, so $-f_j\ge v_j$. Since $p,q$ are nonnegative, $\sum_i(p_i-q_i)f_i\ge\sum_i p_i u_i+\sum_jq_jv_j>c_*-\varepsilon$. Replacing $f_i$ by $f_i-f_1$ preserves all Lipschitz inequalities and the objective because $\sum_i p_i=\sum_iq_i=1$; the resulting vector is normalized with first coordinate zero. [step 4.1, F1, F3, F9, algebra]

6.1 Let $D$ be the attained maximum in [F6]. Step 5.1 shows $D>c_*-\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $D\ge c_*$; otherwise $\varepsilon=(c_*-D)/2$ contradicts that inequality. Step 1.1 gives $D\le c_*$. Hence $D=c_*=W_1(p,q)$, and both extrema are attained by [F6]. [step 1.1, step 5.1, F5, F6, algebra]

7.1 Let $\pi$ be any minimizing coupling and $f$ any maximizing normalized potential. By the marginal equations and optimal-value equality, $0=c_*-\sum_i(p_i-q_i)f_i=\sum_{i,j}\pi_{ij}\bigl(d_{ij}-(f_i-f_j)\bigr)$. Each summand is nonnegative by feasibility. If $\pi_{ij}>0$, its factor $d_{ij}-(f_i-f_j)$ must therefore be zero, proving $f_i-f_j=d_{ij}$. [step 1.1, step 6.1, F4, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $X=\{x_1,x_2\}$ have metric distance $d(x_1,x_2)=\delta>0$. For $a,b\in[0,1]$, let $p=(a,1-a)$ and $q=(b,1-b)$. Then $W_1(p,q)=\delta|a-b|$. If $a\ge b$, one attaining coupling is
$$
\pi=\begin{pmatrix}b&a-b\\0&1-a\end{pmatrix}
$$
and one attaining normalized potential is $f=(0,-\delta)$. If $b>a$, one attaining coupling and potential are
$$
\pi=\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\b-a&1-b\end{pmatrix},\qquad f=(0,\delta).
$$

## Example references

[Peyré and Cuturi, Computational Optimal Transport, §6.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1803.00567)

[Santambrogio, Introduction to Optimal Transport Theory, §1.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1009.3856)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two-point metric space, probability vectors, and parameter bounds in the Example.

[F1] A coupling is a nonnegative matrix with the stated row and column sums, and $W_1$ is its minimum transport cost ([[def-finite-metric-coupling]], [[def-finite-metric-wasserstein-one]]).

[F2] The minimum coupling cost equals the maximum over normalized vectors satisfying $|f_i-f_j|\le d(x_i,x_j)$; both extrema are attained ([[thm-finite-metric-transport-duality]]).

## Verification

1.1 If $a\ge b$, all entries of the displayed matrix are nonnegative, its row sums are $b+(a-b)=a$ and $1-a$, and its column sums are $b$ and $(a-b)+(1-a)=1-b$. Its cost is $\delta(a-b)$. If $b>a$, the second displayed matrix has nonnegative entries, row sums $a$ and $(b-a)+(1-b)=1-a$, column sums $a+(b-a)=b$ and $1-b$, and cost $\delta(b-a)$. Thus in either case it is a feasible coupling of cost $\delta|a-b|$. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

1.2 If $a\ge b$, the vector $(0,-\delta)$ is normalized and satisfies the Lipschitz constraint with equality; its objective is $(b-a)(-\delta)=\delta(a-b)$. If $b>a$, the vector $(0,\delta)$ is normalized and feasible, and its objective is $(b-a)\delta=\delta(b-a)$. Thus the displayed potential has value $\delta|a-b|$ in either case. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], the optimal primal and dual values coincide. The feasible plan in step 1.1 gives an optimal primal value at most $\delta|a-b|$, while the feasible potential in step 1.2 gives an optimal dual value at least that number. Equality of the optima forces both displayed values to be optimal and gives $W_1(p,q)=\delta|a-b|$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F2, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $n\ge1$ and let $X=\{0,1,\ldots,n\}$ with metric $d(i,j)=|i-j|$. Let $p=(p_i)_{i=0}^n$ and $q=(q_i)_{i=0}^n$ be probability vectors. Put $R_k=\sum_{i=0}^k(p_i-q_i)$ for $0\le k<n$. Define $\operatorname{sgn}(t)=1$ for $t>0$, $\operatorname{sgn}(t)=-1$ for $t<0$, and $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$. Then
$$
W_1(p,q)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|R_k|.
$$
An attaining normalized potential is given recursively by $f_0=0$ and $f_{k+1}=f_k-\operatorname{sgn}(R_k)$ for $0\le k<n$.

## Example references

## Definition

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space. Write $\mathcal B(X)$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the open sets of its metric topology. A Borel probability measure on $X$ is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(X)$ with total mass one. For Borel probability measures $\mu,\nu$ on $X$, let $\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)$ be the set of Borel probability measures $\gamma$ on $X\times X$, with its product topology and Borel sigma-algebra, such that for every $A\in\mathcal B(X)$,
$$\gamma(A\times X)=\mu(A),\qquad \gamma(X\times A)=\nu(A).$$
Define
$$W_1^X(\mu,\nu):=\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)}\int_{X\times X}d(x,y)\,d\gamma(x,y)\in[0,+\infty],$$
where the infimum is taken in the extended real line and $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$. The integrand is nonnegative and Borel: the triangle inequality and symmetry give
$$|d(x,y)-d(x',y')|\le d(x,x')+d(y,y'),$$
so $(x,y)\mapsto d(x,y)$ is continuous for the product topology; nonnegativity follows from the metric axioms.

## Statement

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $\varepsilon>0$. Then there are an integer $m\ge1$, distinct points $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in X$, a Borel partition $C_1,\ldots,C_m$ of $X$, and a Borel map $Q:X\to F:=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ such that $Q(x)=x_i$ for $x\in C_i$ and $d(x,Q(x))<\varepsilon$ for every $x\in X$. The partition assigns each point to a nearest point of $F$, and ties are assigned to the least index.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty compact metric space $(X,d)$ and $\varepsilon>0$.

[F1] Every open cover of a compact metric space has a finite subcover. [[def-metric-compactness]]

[F2] A metric is symmetric and satisfies the triangle inequality; its values are nonnegative. [[def-metric-space]] [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]

[F3] Every nonempty finite list of real numbers has an attained minimum. [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]

[F4] The Borel sigma-algebra contains every open and closed set and is closed under finite unions and intersections. [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For any $x\in X$, the ball $B(x,\varepsilon)$ is open: if $y\in B(x,\varepsilon)$, set $\delta=\varepsilon-d(x,y)>0$; whenever $d(y,z)<\delta$, [F2] gives $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)<\varepsilon$, so $B(y,\delta)\subseteq B(x,\varepsilon)$. Also $x\in B(x,\varepsilon)$, so $\{B(x,\varepsilon):x\in X\}$ is an open cover. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 By [F1], finitely many members of that cover still cover $X$. Each selected member is a ball with at least one center; since the list is finite, finite induction selects a center for every selected member without any choice axiom. Removing repeated centers and preserving their first-occurrence order leaves a finite nonempty distinct list $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ whose $\varepsilon$-balls cover $X$. [step 1.1, F1, construct]

3.1 For $i<j$, the function $h_{ij}(x)=d(x,x_i)-d(x,x_j)$ satisfies $|h_{ij}(x)-h_{ij}(y)|\le2d(x,y)$ by applying the triangle inequality in both directions to each distance. If $h_{ij}(x)<0$, then the ball of radius $-h_{ij}(x)/4$ around $x$ lies in $\{h_{ij}<0\}$; if $h_{ij}(x)>0$, then the ball of radius $h_{ij}(x)/4$ around $x$ lies in $\{h_{ij}>0\}$. Hence $\{h_{ij}<0\}$ is open and $\{h_{ij}\le0\}$ is closed. [step 2.1, F2, algebra]

4.1 Define $C_i:=\bigcap_{j<i}\{x:d(x,x_i)<d(x,x_j)\}\cap\bigcap_{j>i}\{x:d(x,x_i)\le d(x,x_j)\}$. These are Borel sets by [F4] and step 3.1. For each $x$, [F3] gives a least index minimizing the finite list $d(x,x_1),\ldots,d(x,x_m)$, so $x$ belongs to the corresponding $C_i$. If $i<j$, membership in $C_i$ gives $d(x,x_i)\le d(x,x_j)$ while membership in $C_j$ gives $d(x,x_j)<d(x,x_i)$; therefore the cells are disjoint and form a partition. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F3, F4]

5.1 Define $Q(x)=x_i$ on $C_i$. For every subset $A\subseteq F$, $Q^{-1}(A)=\bigcup_{i:x_i\in A}C_i$ is a finite union of Borel sets, so $Q$ is Borel. The net points from step 2.1 have $\varepsilon$-balls covering $X$; hence a nearest center is at distance less than $\varepsilon$ from every point. Thus $d(x,Q(x))<\varepsilon$ for all $x$. [step 2.1, step 4.1, F4] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, let $F=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\subseteq X$ be finite and nonempty with distinct ordered points, and let $f_1,\ldots,f_m\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $|f_i-f_j|\le d(x_i,x_j)$ for every $i,j$. Define
$$\widetilde f(x):=\min_{1\le i\le m}\bigl(f_i+d(x,x_i)\bigr)\qquad(x\in X).$$
Then $\widetilde f$ is 1-Lipschitz on $X$ and $\widetilde f(x_i)=f_i$ for every $i$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The metric space, finite set, and real values in the Statement.

[F1] A metric is symmetric and satisfies the triangle inequality. [[def-metric-space]]

[F2] Every nonempty finite set of reals has an attained minimum. [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For each $k$, every term in the defining minimum at $x_k$ satisfies $f_i+d(x_k,x_i)\ge f_k$, because $f_k-f_i\le d(x_k,x_i)$ by [F1] and the hypothesis. The term $i=k$ equals $f_k$, so $\widetilde f(x_k)=f_k$. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 For any $x,y\in X$ and every $i$, [F1] gives $d(x,x_i)\le d(x,y)+d(y,x_i)$. Thus $f_i+d(x,x_i)\le d(x,y)+f_i+d(y,x_i)$ for every $i$; taking finite minima yields $\widetilde f(x)\le d(x,y)+\widetilde f(y)$. Interchanging $x,y$ and using symmetry gives $\widetilde f(y)\le d(x,y)+\widetilde f(x)$, hence $|\widetilde f(x)-\widetilde f(y)|\le d(x,y)$. [given, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $(X,d)$ is a compact metric space, then its metric topology has an at-most-countable basis; equivalently, $X$ is second-countable.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice and a compact metric space $(X,d)$.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice selects one member from each member of a countable family of nonempty sets. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] Under the Axiom of Countable Choice, every compact metric space has an at-most-countable dense subset. [[lem-compact-metric-space-has-a-countable-dense-subset]]

[F2] A product of two at-most-countable sets is at most countable. [[thm-product-of-countable]]

[F3] For every $r>0$ there is an integer $n\ge1$ with $1/n<r$. [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]]

[F4] A metric-open set contains a positive-radius ball around each of its points, and $B(a,r)=\{x:d(x,a)<r\}$. [[def-metric-topology]] [[def-metric-ball]]

[F5] A topological space is second-countable when it has an at-most-countable basis. [[def-second-countable-space]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1], choose an at-most-countable dense set $D\subseteq X$. If $X=\varnothing$, the empty family is a countable basis. Otherwise set $\mathcal U:=\{B(a,1/n):a\in D,\ n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge1\}$. By [F2], the index set $D\times\{n\in\mathbb N:n\ge1\}$ and therefore $\mathcal U$ are at most countable. [A1, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 To check that $\mathcal U$ is a basis, let $O$ be open and $x\in O$. By [F4], choose $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq O$. Apply [F3] to $r/2$ to choose $n\ge1$ with $2/n<r$. Density of $D$ gives $a\in D$ with $d(x,a)<1/n$. Then $x\in B(a,1/n)$, and every $y\in B(a,1/n)$ satisfies $d(x,y)\le d(x,a)+d(a,y)<2/n<r$. Hence $x\in B(a,1/n)\subseteq O$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 By [F5], the at-most-countable basis $\mathcal U$ makes $X$ second-countable. [step 2.1, F5] ∎

## Statement

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(X,d)$
be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]], [[def-metric-space]]).
Then there is an at most countable set $D \subseteq X$ ([[def-countable]]) that
is dense in $X$, that is $\overline{D} = X$
([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

**Where the axiom is spent.** Once at step 2.1, to fix a finite $1/(n+1)$-net for
every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ at the same time; the family of sets chosen from is
written down before any selection and does not depend on the earlier ones. The
appeal to [[thm-countable-union-of-countable]] at step 4.1 carries the same
hypothesis $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and no more, so nothing further is spent there.
As always on this page the claim is an upper bound on the cost of this proof, not
an assertion that $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is necessary.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A compact metric space $(X,d)$ and the Axiom of Countable Choice.

[L1] A compact metric space is totally bounded: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a finite $F \subseteq X$ with $X = \bigcup_{y \in F} B(y,\varepsilon)$ ([[thm-compact-implies-complete-and-totally-bounded]], [[def-totally-bounded]], [[def-metric-ball]]).

[L2] Countable choice: for a family $(E_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets there is a function $n \mapsto e_n$ with $e_n \in E_n$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[L3] Finite sets are at most countable, and, assuming countable choice, a union $\bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n$ of at most countable sets is at most countable ([[def-countable]], [[thm-countable-union-of-countable]], [[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]]).

[L4] $x \in \overline{D}$ exactly when $B(x,r) \cap D \ne \emptyset$ for every real $r > 0$, and $D$ is dense when $\overline{D} = X$ ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]], [[thm-metric-closure-characterisation]]).

[L5] For every real $r > 0$ there is a natural $N \ge 1$ with $1/N < r$, and $0 < 1/(n+1) \le 1/N$ whenever $n + 1 \ge N$ ([[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]], [[thm-of-archimedean]], [[lem-of-inverse-positive]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$ let $E_n$ be the set of finite $1/(n+1)$-nets for $(X,d)$; each $E_n$ is nonempty because $(X,d)$ is compact and hence totally bounded. [L1]

2.1 Countable choice applied to $(E_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ fixes a function $n \mapsto F_n$ with $F_n \in E_n$ for every $n$, that is a finite $1/(n+1)$-net $F_n \subseteq X$ for each $n$; this is the only appeal to a choice principle here. [L2, step 1.1]

3.1 Put $D := \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} F_n \subseteq X$. [step 2.1]

4.1 Each $F_n$ is finite and therefore at most countable, so $D$ is at most countable by the countable union theorem, whose hypothesis is the same $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ already assumed. [L3, step 3.1]

4.2 $D$ is dense: given $x \in X$ and a real $r > 0$, take a natural $N \ge 1$ with $1/N < r$ and put $n := N$, so that $1/(n+1) < 1/N < r$; since $F_n$ is a $1/(n+1)$-net there is $y \in F_n$ with $d(x,y) < 1/(n+1) < r$, and that $y$ lies in $B(x,r) \cap D$. [L1, L4, L5, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 So every ball around every point of $X$ meets $D$, that is $\overline{D} = X$, and $D$ is an at most countable dense subset of $X$. [L4, step 4.1, step 4.2] ∎

## Remarks

**The word for this property is not used here.** A space with an at most countable dense subset has a standard name, and that name is not introduced at this point in the reading order; the statement therefore says what it means outright. Nothing below or elsewhere on this page depends on the terminology.

**Why a choice principle appears at all.** Total boundedness asserts that a finite $1/(n+1)$-net exists for each $n$; it names none, and there is no rule in this library that singles one out uniformly in $n$. Fixing one for every $n$ at once is precisely $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and it is spent in exactly the same way, and for exactly the same reason, as in [[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]].

**The empty space is covered by the statement.** If $X = \emptyset$ then every $F_n$ is empty, $D$ is empty, and $\overline{D} = \emptyset = X$; the empty set is finite and hence at most countable.

## Definition

A topological space $X$ is **second countable** when its topology has a basis $\mathcal B$ that is at most countable ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]], [[def-countable]]). Thus every open set is a union of members of one at most countable family $\mathcal B$.

## Remarks

The basis is global. This differs from first countability, where the countable family is allowed to depend on the point.

## Statement

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space that is compact or second-countable. Let $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ be distinct points, let $C_1,\ldots,C_m$ be a Borel partition of $X$, and let $\varepsilon>0$ satisfy $d(x,x_i)<\varepsilon$ for every $x\in C_i$. Let $\mu,\nu$ be Borel probability measures on $X$, set $p_i=\mu(C_i)$ and $q_j=\nu(C_j)$, and let $\pi=(\pi_{ij})$ be a finite coupling of the probability vectors $p,q$. Then there is a Borel probability measure $\gamma$ on $X\times X$ with marginals $\mu,\nu$ such that
$$\int_{X\times X}d(x,y)\,d\gamma(x,y)\le\sum_{i,j=1}^m\pi_{ij}d(x_i,x_j)+2\varepsilon.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The space, partition, measures, and finite coupling in the Statement.

[F1] For second-countable spaces with product topology, the Borel sigma-algebra on $X\times X$ equals $\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(X)$. [[lem-borel-product-of-second-countable-spaces]]

[F2] For sigma-finite factors the product measure exists on the product sigma-algebra and has the product rectangle values. For Borel probabilities on compact metric spaces, the section construction gives a probability on the full product-topology Borel sigma-algebra with the same rectangle values, without second countability. [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]] [[lem-borel-section-product-on-compact-metric-spaces]] [[def-metric-compactness]]

[F3] A finite coupling has nonnegative entries and the prescribed row and column sums. [[def-finite-metric-coupling]]

[F4] A probability vector has nonnegative coordinates summing to one. [[def-finite-probability-vector]]

[F5] The nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous, and is additive on nonnegative measurable functions. [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] [[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]

[F6] A metric is symmetric and satisfies the triangle inequality. [[def-metric-space]]

[F7] The metric cost is continuous on the product: the triangle inequality gives $|d(x,y)-d(x',y')|\le d(x,x')+d(y,y')$, and a continuous real-valued function is Borel. [[def-metric-space]] [[def-metric-topology]] [[def-product-topology]] [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]

[F8] A nonnegative function constant on each member of a finite measurable partition is simple, and its nonnegative integral is the finite sum of its values times the corresponding cell measures. [[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]] [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]] [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $p_i=0$, [F3] and nonnegativity imply $\pi_{ij}=0$ for every $j$; similarly, if $q_j=0$, then $\pi_{ij}=0$ for every $i$. For $p_i>0$ define $\mu_i(A)=\mu(A\cap C_i)/p_i$ for Borel $A\subseteq X$, and for $q_j>0$ define $\nu_j(A)=\nu(A\cap C_j)/q_j$. Countable additivity of $\mu,\nu$ is preserved by restriction to $C_i,C_j$ and multiplication by $1/p_i,1/q_j$; each restricted measure has total mass one after normalization. Hence these are Borel probability measures concentrated on $C_i,C_j$. [F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 Each conditional probability measure in step 1.1 is sigma-finite because $X$ has mass one. If $X$ is compact, the Borel section-product construction in [F2] applied to the probabilities $\mu_i,\nu_j$ on the full compact space $X$ gives a Borel product probability for each active pair; the cells themselves need not be compact. If $X$ is second-countable, [F1] and the ordinary product construction in [F2] give the same conclusion. Denote the chosen construction in either case by $\mu_i\times\nu_j$. Define $\gamma:=\sum_{i,j:p_i,q_j>0}\pi_{ij}(\mu_i\times\nu_j)$. Since zero rows and columns contribute zero by step 1.1, its total mass is $\sum_{i,j}\pi_{ij}=\sum_i p_i=1$. Thus $\gamma$ is a Borel probability measure. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 For Borel $A\subseteq X$, the rectangle formula [F2] and row sums give $\gamma(A\times X)=\sum_{i:p_i>0}\sum_{j:q_j>0}\pi_{ij}\mu_i(A)=\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\mu_i(A)=\sum_i\mu(A\cap C_i)=\mu(A)$. The same calculation using column sums gives $\gamma(X\times A)=\nu(A)$, so $\gamma$ has the required marginals. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The cost $d(x,y)$ is nonnegative Borel by [F7]. For each active pair with $p_i,q_j>0$, [F2] gives $(\mu_i\times\nu_j)(C_i\times C_j)=1$. For every other active pair $(k,\ell)\ne(i,j)$, disjointness of the partition forces $\mu_k(C_i)=0$ or $\nu_\ell(C_j)=0$, so [F2] gives its product measure zero on $C_i\times C_j$. Consequently the finite measure sum of step 2.1 gives $\gamma(C_i\times C_j)=\pi_{ij}$. On zero rows or columns both sides are zero by step 1.1. On each active block, [F6] gives $d(x,y)\le d(x,x_i)+d(x_i,x_j)+d(x_j,y)<d(x_i,x_j)+2\varepsilon$. The finite Borel step function $s(x,y):=\sum_{i,j}(d(x_i,x_j)+2\varepsilon)\mathbf1_{C_i\times C_j}(x,y)$ majorizes $d(x,y)$ on all blocks, including zero-mass ones. Monotonicity [F5], the block masses just computed and the simple-integral formula [F8] give $\int d\,d\gamma\le\int s\,d\gamma=\sum_{i,j}(d(x_i,x_j)+2\varepsilon)\pi_{ij}=\sum_{i,j}\pi_{ij}d(x_i,x_j)+2\varepsilon$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, F5, F6, F7, F8, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $X,Y$ be nonempty compact metric spaces, let $\mu,\nu$ be countably additive Borel probability measures on $X,Y$, and give $X\times Y$ its product topology. For every Borel set $E\subseteq X\times Y$, its section $E_x:=\{y\in Y:(x,y)\in E\}$ is Borel in $Y$, and $x\mapsto\nu(E_x)$ is Borel measurable. The formula
$$\lambda(E):=\int_X\nu(E_x)\,d\mu(x)$$
defines a Borel probability measure on $X\times Y$ satisfying
$$\lambda(A\times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B)$$
for every Borel $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$. In particular its coordinate marginals are $\mu,\nu$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact metric spaces, probabilities, and product topology in the Statement.

[F1] Distance to a nonempty set is 1-Lipschitz. A closed subset of a compact metric space is compact. [[lem-distance-to-set-is-lipschitz]] [[lem-closed-subset-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]

[F2] If an open set in $Y\times X$ contains $K\times\{x\}$ for compact $K\subseteq Y$, the tube lemma gives an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ with $K\times V$ contained in that set. It uses an indexed family of all admissible pairs of neighborhoods and one finite subcover, without choice. [[lem-tube-lemma-for-a-compact-metric-factor]]

[F3] Measures are continuous from below on increasing measurable sequences. [[thm-continuity-from-below-for-measures]]

[F4] A lambda-system containing a pi-system contains its generated sigma-algebra. [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]

[F5] Nonnegative integrals are monotone, homogeneous and finitely additive, agree with the simple integral, and preserve increasing pointwise limits. [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] [[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]

[F6] A Borel sigma-algebra is generated by the open sets. Continuous maps pull Borel sets back to Borel sets, and the product topology has open rectangles as a basis. [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] [[def-product-topology]] [[def-metric-topology]]

[F7] Finite sums and real scalar multiples of real Borel measurable functions are Borel measurable, as are increasing pointwise limits of nonnegative Borel functions. [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]

[F8] A measure takes nonnegative values and is countably additive on disjoint measurable sets. [[def-measure]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For an open set $G\subseteq Y$ with $G\ne Y$, put $K_n:=\{y:d(y,Y\setminus G)\ge1/n\}$ for integers $n\ge1$. By [F1] these sets are closed and compact. They increase, lie in $G$, and exhaust $G$: if $y\in G$, some ball $B(y,r)$ lies in $G$, so $d(y,Y\setminus G)\ge r>0$ and $y\in K_n$ for some $n$. If $G=Y$, use $K_n=Y$. Thus [F3] gives $\nu(G)=\sup_n\nu(K_n)$ for a specified compact exhaustion of each open $G$, including $G=\varnothing$. [given, F1, F3, F6, construct]

2.1 Let $U\subseteq X\times Y$ be open. The map $y\mapsto(x,y)$ is continuous for fixed $x$, so each $U_x$ is open. Put $h_U(x)=\nu(U_x)$. If $h_U(x)>a$ for $a\ge0$, step 1.1 provides one compact $K\subseteq U_x$ with $\nu(K)>a$. The coordinate interchange $S:Y\times X\to X\times Y$, $S(y,z)=(z,y)$, is a homeomorphism: it and its inverse take basic open rectangles to basic open rectangles by [F6]. Thus $S^{-1}(U)$ is open and contains $K\times\{x\}$. Apply [F2] in $Y\times X$ to obtain an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ with $K\times V\subseteq S^{-1}(U)$, or equivalently $V\times K\subseteq U$. For every $z\in V$, $K\subseteq U_z$ and $h_U(z)=\nu(U_z)$. The set $K$ is one of the closed sets in the exhaustion from step 1.1, and $U_z$ is open, so $K$ and $U_z\setminus K$ are Borel by [F6]. Their disjoint union is $U_z$; apply countable additivity to the disjoint sequence $K,U_z\setminus K,\varnothing,\ldots$ [F8]. Nonnegativity of $\nu$ [F8] then gives $h_U(z)=\nu(K)+\nu(U_z\setminus K)\ge\nu(K)>a$. Consequently $\{h_U>a\}$ is open for every real $a$ (for $a<0$ it is all of $X$). Hence $h_U$ is lower semicontinuous and Borel: the inverse images of real rays $(a,+\infty)$ are open, and these rays generate the real Borel sigma-algebra, as their rational subfamily generates all open intervals by countable unions and complements. [step 1.1, F2, F6, F8, choose]

3.1 Every Borel $E\subseteq X\times Y$ has Borel sections because the continuous map $y\mapsto(x,y)$ has inverse image $E_x$. Let $\mathcal D$ be the family of Borel $E$ for which $h_E(x):=\nu(E_x)$ is Borel. It contains $X\times Y$, with $h=1$. If $E\in\mathcal D$, then $h_{E^c}=1-h_E$ is Borel by [F7]. For disjoint $E_n\in\mathcal D$, countable additivity of $\nu$ gives $h_{\bigcup_n E_n}=\sum_nh_{E_n}$, an increasing limit of Borel partial sums and therefore Borel by [F7]. Thus $\mathcal D$ is a lambda-system. All open sets belong to it by step 2.1; the open sets form a pi-system generating $\mathcal B(X\times Y)$. By [F4], $\mathcal D=\mathcal B(X\times Y)$. [step 2.1, F4, F6, F7, construct]

4.1 Define $\lambda(E)=\int h_E\,d\mu$, which is meaningful and lies in $[0,1]$ by step 3.1 and [F5]. It has $\lambda(\varnothing)=0$ and $\lambda(X\times Y)=1$. For disjoint Borel $E_n$, step 3.1 gives $h_{\bigcup_nE_n}=\lim_N\sum_{n=1}^Nh_{E_n}$ increasingly. Finite additivity and monotone convergence [F5] yield $\lambda(\bigcup_nE_n)=\lim_N\sum_{n=1}^N\lambda(E_n)=\sum_n\lambda(E_n)$. Hence $\lambda$ is a countably additive Borel probability. [step 3.1, F5, construct]

5.1 For Borel $A\subseteq X,B\subseteq Y$, the rectangle $A\times B$ is Borel as the intersection of the two coordinate inverse images. Its section measure is $h_{A\times B}(x)=\mathbf1_A(x)\nu(B)$. The simple-integral formula [F5] gives $\lambda(A\times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B)$. Taking $B=Y$ or $A=X$ proves the marginal identities. [step 4.1, F5, F6] ∎

## Remarks

This construction works on the full Borel sigma-algebra of the product topology. It neither asserts nor uses equality with the sigma-algebra generated by Borel rectangles. It requires no simultaneous selection of finite nets. The integral convergence is over specified sequences, and the compact exhaustion in step 1.1 is given by a formula. A general optimal-coupling attainment theorem is not part of this lemma.

## Definition

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable function
$s:X\to[0,+\infty)\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]) is a
**nonnegative simple measurable function** when it has finite range.

Equivalently, there are pairwise disjoint measurable sets
$E_1,\dots,E_m\in\mathcal A$ and coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_m\in[0,+\infty)$
such that
$$s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}.$$
Any such display is a **simple representation** of $s$.

## Statement

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space whose metric topology has an at-most-countable basis. Let $\mu,\nu$ be countably additive Borel probability measures on $X$, and fix $x_0\in X$. Let $\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)$ be the Borel probability measures $\gamma$ on the product-topology space $X\times X$ satisfying $\gamma(A\times X)=\mu(A)$ and $\gamma(X\times A)=\nu(A)$ for every Borel set $A\subseteq X$, and define $W_1^X(\mu,\nu)=\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)}\int_{X\times X}d(x,y)\,d\gamma(x,y)$. Then $\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)$ is nonempty and
$$W_1^X(\mu,\nu)=\sup\left\{\int_X f\,d\mu-\int_X f\,d\nu:\ f:X\to\mathbb R,\ f(x_0)=0,\ |f(x)-f(y)|\le d(x,y)\text{ for all }x,y\in X\right\}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The space, measures, base point, and coupling-cost convention in the Statement.

[F1] For every $\varepsilon>0$, a compact metric space admits a finite ordered net, a Borel partition into nearest-center cells, and a Borel quantization map whose displacement is less than $\varepsilon$. [[lem-compact-metric-space-has-finite-borel-net-quantization]]

[F2] If a finite coupling has rows and columns given by the masses of such Borel cells, it lifts to a Borel coupling of $\mu,\nu$ with cost at most the finite cost plus $2\varepsilon$. [[lem-finite-metric-plan-lifts-to-a-borel-coupling]]

[F3] A finite 1-Lipschitz potential extends to the whole metric space by $\widetilde f(x)=\min_i(f_i+d(x,x_i))$, preserving its values and 1-Lipschitz bound. [[lem-mcshane-extension-from-a-finite-subset]]

[F4] On a finite nonempty metric space, the minimum coupling cost equals the maximum over normalized 1-Lipschitz potentials, and both extrema are attained. [[thm-finite-metric-transport-duality]]

[F5] The finite transport cost is the minimum of $\sum_{i,j}d(x_i,x_j)\pi_{ij}$ over nonnegative matrices with the prescribed probability-vector marginals. [[def-finite-metric-wasserstein-one]] [[def-finite-metric-coupling]] [[def-finite-probability-vector]]

[F6] The compact-space cost $W_1^X$ is the infimum of the Borel coupling costs in the Statement. [[def-compact-metric-wasserstein-one]]

[F7] Every nonempty finite set of reals has an attained maximum. [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]

[F8] A metric is symmetric, satisfies the triangle inequality, and is nonnegative. [[def-metric-space]] [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]

[F9] The nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous. [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]

[F10] The nonnegative integral is defined as the supremum of simple minorants, and it agrees with the simple integral; a nonnegative simple function integrates as the sum of its values times the measures of its disjoint level sets. [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] [[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]] [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]] [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]

[F11] The nonnegative integral is additive over finite sums of nonnegative measurable functions. [[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]

[F12] Real integrability and the signed integral are defined using positive and negative parts, and the signed integral is linear on integrable functions. [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]] [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]

[F13] A 1-Lipschitz function between metric spaces is continuous; continuous real-valued functions are Borel measurable, and product coordinate projections are continuous. [[def-metric-topology]] [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] [[def-product-topology]]
