## Example

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and let $p_U$ be a Lebesgue probability density on $\mathbb R^2$. Define the unit-scale affine coupling $T:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ by
$$T(u,v)=(u,u+v).$$
It is a global $C^1$ diffeomorphism with inverse $T^{-1}(x,y)=(x,y-x)$. Its Jacobian matrix is lower triangular,
$$DT(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det DT(u,v)=1.$$
The transformed model has density $p_X(x,y)=p_U(x,y-x)$. The first coordinate is unchanged and the second is shifted by the first.

## Example references

[Papamakarios et al., §3.1.1, PDF pp. 13–14](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.02762v1)

[Sheldon, COMPSCI 688 Lecture 23, Real-NVP, PDF pp. 5–6](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~sheldon/teaching/cs688/lec/lec23-annotated.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and a Lebesgue probability density $p_U$ on $\mathbb R^2$.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, asserts that every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] A $C^1$ map is totally differentiable at every point with continuous derivative matrix; a global $C^1$ diffeomorphism has a $C^1$ inverse, and a flow transports its base measure by $\mu_X(B)=\mu_U(T^{-1}(B))$. [[def-normalizing-flow]]

[F2] Under Countable Choice, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism transforms density $p_U$ by $p_U\circ T^{-1}\,|\det D(T^{-1})|$. [[thm-change-of-variables-density-for-diffeomorphic-flow]]

[F3] The Jacobian matrix records the total derivative in standard coordinates, and the Jacobian determinant is its determinant. [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-jacobian-determinant-of-a-c-one-map]]

[F4] The determinant of a lower triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries. [[thm-determinant-of-a-triangular-matrix]]

## Verification

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the Example.

1.1 Define $\widehat T(x,y)=(x,y-x)$. Direct substitution gives $\widehat T(T(u,v))=(u,v)$ and $T(\widehat T(x,y))=(x,y)$. Both maps are linear, so their first-order remainders vanish and their derivative matrices are constant; by [F1] they are $C^1$. Thus they are inverse bijections and $T$ is a global $C^1$ diffeomorphism. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

1.2 The linear map $T(u,v)=(u,u+v)$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, which is its Jacobian matrix by [F3]. It is lower triangular, so [F4] gives determinant $1\cdot1=1$. Its inverse has Jacobian matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}$, also lower triangular with determinant $1$. [given, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F2] to the base density $p_U$ and the inverse from step 1.1. Step 1.2 gives $|\det D(T^{-1})(x,y)|=1$, so the transformed density version is $p_X(x,y)=p_U(x,y-x)$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $\nu$ be the probability measure on $[0,1]$ with density $1$ relative to one-dimensional Lebesgue measure, let $i:[0,1]\to\mathbb R^2$ be $i(t)=(t,0)$, and define a measure on Borel sets $B\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ by
$$\mu(B)=\nu(i^{-1}(B)).$$
This probability measure is concentrated on the line segment $M=[0,1]\times\{0\}$ and satisfies $\mu(M)=1$. It is not the output of any normalizing flow $T:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ whose base measure has a Lebesgue density.

## Example references

[Papamakarios et al., §5.4–5.5, PDF pp. 34–36](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.02762v1)

[Sheldon, COMPSCI 688 Lecture 23, PDF pp. 2–4](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~sheldon/teaching/cs688/lec/lec23-annotated.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the interval probability measure $\nu$, the continuous embedding $i(t)=(t,0)$, and its image measure $\mu$.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, asserts that every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] A nonnegative measurable density $f$ defines a measure by $A\mapsto\int_A f\,d\lambda$. [[def-measure-with-density]]

[F2] A flow from a Lebesgue density through a global $C^1$ diffeomorphism has density $p_U\circ T^{-1}|\det D(T^{-1})|$. [[thm-change-of-variables-density-for-diffeomorphic-flow]]

[F3] A continuous map has Borel preimages of Borel sets. [[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]

[F4] Every closed box $[a,b]$ in $\mathbb R^n$ is Borel and Lebesgue measurable; its measure is $\prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i)$, so $[0,1]$ has one-dimensional Lebesgue measure $1$. [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]

[F5] A rectangle with a degenerate side is Lebesgue null under Countable Choice. [[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]]

[F6] A nonnegative measurable density integrates to zero over a measurable null set. [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]

[F7] A normalizing flow is a finite composition of global $C^1$ diffeomorphisms between open equal-dimensional Euclidean domains; its output measure is obtained by taking preimages under the flow. [[def-normalizing-flow]]

## Verification

**Given:** Countable Choice, the image measure $\mu$ of $\nu$ under $i$, and an arbitrary normalizing flow $T:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ with Lebesgue base density.

1.1 The function $i$ is continuous, so [F3] makes $i^{-1}(B)$ Borel for every Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^2$. For pairwise disjoint Borel sets $B_n$, their preimages are pairwise disjoint and $i^{-1}(\bigcup_nB_n)=\bigcup_ni^{-1}(B_n)$; countable additivity of $\nu$ therefore makes $\mu$ a measure. By [F1] and [F4], $\nu([0,1])=\int_{[0,1]}1\,d\lambda_1=\lambda_1([0,1])=1$, whence $\mu(\mathbb R^2)=1$ and $\mu(M)=\nu([0,1])=1$. [given, A1, F1, F3, F4]

1.2 The set $M=[0,1]\times\{0\}=[0,1]\times[0,0]$ is a closed box, hence Borel by [F4]. Its second side is degenerate, so [F5] gives $\lambda_2(M)=0$. [given, A1, F4, F5]

1.3 By [F7] and [F2], the flow output has a nonnegative Lebesgue density $q$ on $\mathbb R^2$. Applying [F1] and [F6] to the null set $M$ gives $\mu_X(M)=\int_Mq\,d\lambda_2=0$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F6, F7]

2.1 The target measure satisfies $\mu(M)=1$ by step 1.1, whereas every such flow output satisfies $\mu_X(M)=0$ by step 1.3. Therefore $\mu_X\ne\mu$, so no full-dimensional flow in the stated class represents this target law exactly. [given, step 1.1, step 1.3] ∎

## Definition

Let $d,q\ge1$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, and let $v:I\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta\to\mathbb R^d$. For a parameter $\theta\in\Theta$, write $v_\theta(t,z):=v(t,z,\theta)$. A **parameterized neural ordinary differential equation**, or **neural ODE**, on $I$ is the initial-value problem

$$\dot z(t)=v_\theta(t,z(t)),\qquad z(s)=z_s,$$

where $s\in I$ and $z_s\in\mathbb R^d$. A trajectory on an interval $J\subseteq I$ containing $s$ is a differentiable function $z:J\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfying both displayed conditions. Here $v_\theta$ is the state-velocity field. The term names this parameterized vector-field model and imposes no particular neural-network architecture. This definition alone asserts neither solution existence beyond its stated interval nor numerical accuracy.

## Statement

Let $T>0$, let $d,q\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $[0,T]$, and let $v:I\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly $C^\infty$. For every compact $K\subseteq\Theta$, suppose there are constants $L_K,M_K\ge0$ such that, for all $t\in[0,T]$, $\theta\in K$, and $z,w\in\mathbb R^d$,

$$\|v(t,z,\theta)-v(t,w,\theta)\|_2\le L_K\|z-w\|_2,\qquad \|v(t,0,\theta)\|_2\le M_K.$$

Then for each $\theta\in\Theta$, $s,t\in[0,T]$, and $z_s\in\mathbb R^d$, the neural ODE has a unique solution on all of $[0,T]$. Write $\Phi^\theta_{t,s}(z_s)$ for its value at time $t$. For each fixed $s,t$, the map $(z_s,\theta)\mapsto\Phi^\theta_{t,s}(z_s)$ is locally $C^\infty$. For each fixed $\theta$, $\Phi^\theta_{t,s}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism with inverse $\Phi^\theta_{s,t}$. Its state Jacobian $J_{t,s}:=D_{z_s}\Phi^\theta_{t,s}(z_s)$ satisfies

$$\frac{d}{dt}J_{t,s}=D_zv(t,\Phi^\theta_{t,s}(z_s),\theta)J_{t,s},\qquad J_{s,s}=I_d.$$

Time derivatives at $0$ and $T$ are one-sided.

## Statement references

[Teschl, *Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems*, Chapter 2, §§2.2–2.5](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~gerald/ftp/book-ode/ode.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite interval, open parameter domain, jointly smooth field, and compact-parameter-neighborhood Lipschitz and origin bounds in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-neural-ode]]: for fixed $\theta$, a trajectory solves $\dot z(t)=v_\theta(t,z(t))$ with its stated initial value.

[F2] [[thm-mean-value-inequality-for-total-derivatives]]: on a convex open state set, a uniform bound on the derivative operator norm implies the same Lipschitz bound for the map.

[F3] [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]: a continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact metric space is bounded.

[F4] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: a closed bounded subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space is compact.

[F5] [[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: a continuous field locally Lipschitz in the state has a unique local solution, and solutions through the same data agree on common intervals.

[F6] [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]: a Picard–Lindelöf IVP has a unique maximal solution on an open interval, and every other solution through the data is its restriction.

[F7] [[thm-gronwall-integral-inequality]]: from $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds$, nonnegative continuous $u,b$, and nondecreasing nonnegative $a$, one obtains $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$; the theorem also states the time-reflected form.

[F8] [[lem-ode-extension-from-a-compact-interior-region]]: if graph points of a solution approach a finite endpoint inside one compact subset of the open ODE domain, the solution extends past that endpoint; the statement also gives the reflected left-endpoint version.

[F9] [[thm-smooth-dependence-of-ode-solutions-on-parameters]]: a jointly smooth field has a common local solution interval and a solution map smooth in initial state and parameters near any base data.

[F10] [[thm-fundamental-theorem-for-nonautonomous-smooth-odes]]: for a smooth nonautonomous field, the local solution map is smooth in initial time and initial state near each base point.

[F11] [[thm-c1-dependence-of-solutions-on-initial-data]]: on a common compact local interval, the solution map is $C^1$ in initial state and its derivative solves the variational equation.

[F12] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$ for totally differentiable Euclidean maps.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** $T,d,q,\Theta,I,v$, and the constants $L_K,M_K$ from the Statement.

1.1 Fix $(t_0,z_0,\theta_0)\in I\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta$. Choose a closed time interval and a closed state ball about $(t_0,z_0)$ whose product lies in the open domain; it is compact by [F4]. The continuous function $(t,z)\mapsto\|D_zv(t,z,\theta_0)\|$ is bounded there by [F3]. For each fixed nearby $t$, [F2] on the open state ball gives a state-Lipschitz bound, while smoothness gives continuity of the field. Thus the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses hold locally at every point of the ODE domain. [F2, F3, F4, given, construct]

2.1 For each fixed $\theta$ and initial data, [F5] gives the unique local solution and [F6] gives its unique maximal solution on an open interval. Fix now a nonempty compact $K\subseteq\Theta$ and a bounded ball $B$ of initial states. For every $\theta\in K$, the assumptions imply $\|v(t,z,\theta)\|_2\le M_K+L_K\|z\|_2$ on $[0,T]$. For a trajectory starting at $s$ in $B$, its integral equation gives $u(\tau):=\|z(s+\tau)\|_2\le \sup_{x\in B}\|x\|_2+M_K\tau+L_K\int_0^\tau u(\sigma)\,d\sigma$ whenever $s+\tau\in[0,T]$. Apply [F7] with the nondecreasing function $a(\tau)=\sup_{x\in B}\|x\|_2+M_K\tau$; time reversal gives the same bound backward. Thus every such maximal trajectory while it lies in $[0,T]$ has norm at most $R:=(\sup_{x\in B}\|x\|_2+M_KT)e^{L_KT}$. If a right endpoint $\beta$ of its maximal interval belonged to $(s,T]$, the explicitly defined sequence $t_j=\beta-(\beta-s)/(j+1)$ would increase to $\beta$, and each graph point $(t_j,z(t_j))$ would lie in the compact cylinder $[0,T]\times\overline B_R\subset I\times\mathbb R^d$. By [F8] the solution would extend past $\beta$, contradicting maximality. The explicit sequence $t_j=\alpha+(s-\alpha)/(j+1)$ gives the same contradiction at any left endpoint $\alpha\in[0,s)$. Therefore every maximal solution contains all of $[0,T]$, and uniqueness follows from [F6]. The sequences are specified by their endpoint and use no choice axiom. [F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, given, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

3.1 Fix a base initial state, parameter, and times $s,t$; choose compact neighborhoods $B$ and $K$ of the state and parameter. Step 2.1 places the trajectories for these data in one closed bounded state ball, so $[0,T]\times\overline B_R\times K$ is compact by [F4]. At every point of this cylinder, [F9] and [F10] applied to the smooth augmented field $(z,\theta)'=(v(t,z,\theta),0)$ give an open neighborhood of initial time, state, and parameter, and a positive time radius on which the local transition map is smooth. A finite subcover exists by [F4], and the minimum of its finitely many time radii is positive. Partition the interval from $s$ to $t$ into finitely many segments shorter than this minimum. Each base trajectory node belongs to a selected chart; continuity lets us shrink the initial state and parameter neighborhoods successively so each perturbed node remains in the next chart. The full transition is therefore a finite composition of smooth local maps on a neighborhood of the base data. Since the base data were arbitrary, $(z_s,\theta)\mapsto\Phi^\theta_{t,s}(z_s)$ is locally $C^\infty$ for every fixed $s,t$. [F4, F9, F10, given, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 By uniqueness from step 2.1, solving from $s$ to $t$ and then from $t$ back to $s$ returns the original initial value; hence $\Phi^\theta_{s,t}\circ\Phi^\theta_{t,s}$ and $\Phi^\theta_{t,s}\circ\Phi^\theta_{s,t}$ are both identity maps. Both maps are smooth by step 3.1, so each $\Phi^\theta_{t,s}$ is a global $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism with the stated inverse. [step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 Fix $s,\theta,z_s$. At every interior time $r\in(0,T)$, smoothness of the field and [F10] give a common local interval for nearby initial states at $z_r:=\Phi^\theta_{r,s}(z_s)$. The hypotheses of [F11] hold there, so $A(t):=D_y\Phi^\theta_{t,r}(z_r)$ satisfies $A'(r)=D_zv(r,z_r,\theta)$ and $A(r)=I_d$. Uniqueness gives $\Phi^\theta_{t,s}=\Phi^\theta_{t,r}\circ\Phi^\theta_{r,s}$ near $t=r$; differentiating this identity in $z_s$ using [F12] yields $J_{t,s}=A(t)J_{r,s}$. Differentiating at $t=r$ therefore gives $\frac{d}{dt}J_{t,s}=D_zv(r,\Phi^\theta_{r,s}(z_s),\theta)J_{r,s}$. Since $r$ was arbitrary this holds on $(0,T)$; the local transitions at $0,T$ give the corresponding one-sided derivatives. At $t=s$, the transition is the identity and so $J_{s,s}=I_d$. [F1, F10, F11, F12, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated convex open domain, total differentiability, and uniform derivative bound.

[L1] A convex subset contains every line segment between two of its points ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]).

[L2] The chain rule for total derivatives is $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[L3] The vector mean-value inequality gives $\lVert f(b)-f(a)\rVert_2\le M(b-a)$ when the derivative norm is bounded by $M$ ([[thm-mean-value-inequality]]).

[L4] Total differentiability implies continuity at the point of total differentiability ([[thm-total-differentiability-gives-a-local-linear-bound-and-continuity]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $n=0$, both function values are the unique zero vector, so the left-hand side is $0$ and the right-hand side is nonnegative. If $x=y$ the conclusion is also immediate. For the remaining case $n\ge1$ and $x\ne y$, the source dimension is necessarily positive; put $\gamma(t)=x+t(y-x)$ for $0\le t\le1$; [L1] keeps $\gamma([0,1])$ in $U$. [L1, L2, L3]

2.1 The chain rule gives $(f\circ\gamma)'(t)=Df(\gamma(t))(y-x)$ for $0<t<1$, whose norm is at most $M\|y-x\|_2$ by hypothesis. [step 1.1, L2, algebra]

3.1 By [L4] the curve $f\circ\gamma$ is continuous at the endpoints, so [L3] applied on $[0,1]$ yields $\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L3, L4] ∎

## Statement

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An IVP satisfying the hypotheses of Picard-Lindelof.

[L1] A unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time ([[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]).

[L2] Locally unique solutions through the same data agree on every overlap ([[lem-locally-unique-ode-solutions-agree-and-glue-on-overlaps]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Take the union $I$ of the domains of all solutions through the initial point; [L1] makes the family nonempty, and the union of intervals containing $t_0$ is an interval. For $t\in I$, choose one such solution $x:J\to\mathbb R^n$ with $t\in J$. By [L1] at $(t,x(t))$, there is a local solution $y$ on an open interval $V$ about $t$. By [L2], $x$ and $y$ agree on $J\cap V$, so their union is a solution on $J\cup V$ through the original initial point. Hence $V\subseteq I$, proving that $I$ is open. [given, L1, L2]

2.1 By [L2], all values assigned at a time in $I$ agree, so their pointwise union is a well-defined solution; every other solution is its restriction, which proves maximality, and the same property forces uniqueness of the maximal solution. [step 1.1, L2] ∎

## Statement

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The continuous functions and integral inequality in the Statement.

[L1] The exponential is differentiable and $(\exp)'=\exp$ ([[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]).

[L2] For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]).

[L3] The chain rule gives $(f\circ g)'(c)=f'(g(c))g'(c)$ under its differentiability hypotheses ([[thm-chain-rule]]).

[L4] The product rule gives $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[L5] An integrable derivative satisfies $\int_a^b G'=G(b)-G(a)$ ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]).

[L6] If integrable $p\le q$ on an interval, then $\int p\le\int q$ ([[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]).

[L7] If $g$ is continuous on a nondegenerate compact interval, then its integral function is differentiable there with derivative $g$, including domain-relative endpoint derivatives ([[thm-ftc-first-part]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $T=t_0$, every displayed integral is zero and the conclusion is immediate. Assume $t_0<T$, and put $v(t)=\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds$ and $B(t)=\int_{t_0}^t b(s)\,ds$; [L7] gives $v'=bu$ and $B'=b$, after which [L3], [L4], and [L1] give $(e^{-B}v)'=e^{-B}b(u-v)\le e^{-B}ba$. [given, L1, L3, L4, L7]

2.1 Apply [L6] and [L5] to integrate the inequality, use $v(t_0)=0$, and divide by the positive factor from [L2]; this gives the displayed formula. If $a$ is nondecreasing, $a(s)\le a(t)$ and direct integration of the exponential derivative gives the stated simplification. ## Statement

Let $x:(\alpha,\beta)\to\mathbb R^n$ solve a Picard-Lindelof ODE and suppose $\beta<\infty$. If there are $t_j\uparrow\beta$ for which $(t_j,x(t_j))$ lies in one compact subset $K$ of the open ODE domain, then $x$ extends to a solution beyond $\beta$. A solution whose graph has a sequence approaching a compact interior endpoint state extends past that endpoint. The reflected statement holds at a finite left endpoint.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The solution, finite endpoint, compact set, and sequence in the Statement.

[L1] A bounded sequence in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$, has a convergent subsequence ([[cor-bolzano-weierstrass-in-rn]]).

[L2] For an integrable vector-valued function on $[a,b]$ with $a\le b$, $\left\|\int_a^b f\right\|_2\le\int_a^b\|f\|_2$ ([[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]]).

[L3] Picard-Lindelöf gives a unique local solution through each point of the open ODE domain ([[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]).

[L4] Locally unique solutions agreeing at a common endpoint glue to a solution on the union interval ([[lem-locally-unique-ode-solutions-agree-and-glue-on-overlaps]]).

[L5] A subset of Euclidean space is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Compactness makes the sequence of graph points $(t_j,x(t_j))$ bounded, so [L1] in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ gives a subsequence converging to $(\beta,p)$; [L5] makes $K$ closed, hence $(\beta,p)\in K$ and lies in the interior of the ODE domain. [given, L1, L5]

2.1 Choose a compact cylinder about $(\beta,p)$ inside the ODE domain and let $M$ bound the field there; for large $j$, $x(t_j)$ lies within half its state radius and $M(\beta-t_j)$ is smaller than the remaining half, so a first-exit argument using [L2] keeps the whole tail in that cylinder and gives $x(t)\to p$; [L3] starts a solution at $(\beta,p)$ and [L4] glues it to $x$ past $\beta$, with $M=0$ immediate. [step 1.1, L2, L3, L4] ∎

## Statement

Let $F(t,x,\lambda)$ be jointly $C^\infty$ in $(t,x,\lambda)$ on an open time-state-parameter
domain. Near any base data $(t_0,x_0,\lambda_0)$ there are a compact time
interval $I$ and a neighbourhood $W$ of $(x_0,\lambda_0)$ such that, for every
$(y,\lambda)\in W$, the solution of

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t),\lambda),\qquad x(t_0)=y,$$

is defined on $I$, and the resulting solution map is smooth in the pair
$(y,\lambda)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An open domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m$, a jointly smooth field $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and $(t_0,x_0,\lambda_0)\in D$. Put $d=n+m$, $z=(x,\lambda)$, $z_0=(x_0,\lambda_0)$ and $G(t,z)=(F(t,x,\lambda),0)\in\mathbb R^d$.

[L1] For a smooth system on an established common compact local interval, its solutions depend smoothly on the initial state ([[thm-smooth-dependence-of-solutions-on-initial-data]]). We use this only for a jointly smooth field, so all derivatives entering its variational proof are jointly continuous.

[F1] A bounded total derivative on a convex open set gives a Lipschitz bound; closed bounded Euclidean cylinders are compact, and continuous norms on them are bounded ([[thm-mean-value-inequality-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

[F2] Picard–Lindelof gives existence and uniqueness on a cylinder with field bound $M$, state-Lipschitz bound $L$, $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$; nearby initial states share one such time interval and compact graph cylinder ([[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]], [[cor-uniform-picard-lindelof-for-nearby-initial-values]]).

[F3] A classical solution is equivalent to its Volterra integral equation ([[prop-first-order-ivp-is-equivalent-to-a-volterra-integral-equation]]).

[F4] On a common compact interval the initial-state derivative exists, is continuous in that state, and solves the variational equation; the proof's difference-quotient and derivative-continuity estimates are uniform in time ([[thm-c1-dependence-of-solutions-on-initial-data]]). With jointly continuous state derivatives, those estimates and the variational equation also give joint continuity in time and initial state.

[F5] A linear matrix ODE with continuous coefficients has a unique solution on its given compact interval ([[lem-linear-matrix-odes-have-unique-global-solutions-on-a-given-interval]]). An affine linear equation is included by adjoining a constant component $1$; finite-dimensional multilinear-map spaces are represented by their coordinate arrays.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The field $G$ is jointly smooth on the open time-state domain $D$. Its last $m$ equations are $\lambda'=0$, so the parameter is constant along each augmented solution. Thus projection to the first $n$ coordinates identifies augmented solutions through $(y,\lambda)$ with solutions of the displayed original IVP, in both directions. [given, construct, F3]

2.1 Choose $a,r>0$ so $[t_0-a,t_0+a]\times\overline B(z_0,2r)\subseteq D$. By [F1], $G$ and $D_zG$ have bounds $M\ge1$ and $L\ge1$ on this cylinder, and the mean-value inequality on each open state ball gives the same state-Lipschitz bound $L$. Choose $H>0$ with $H<a$, $HM<r$ and $HL<1$. For every initial state $z\in B(z_0,r)$, the radius-$r$ cylinder centred at $z$ lies in the larger cylinder. Hence [F2] gives a unique augmented solution $Z(t,z)$ on $J=[t_0-H,t_0+H]$, all of whose graphs lie in that one compact cylinder. This establishes the common interval needed below. [F1, F2, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 Now [L1] applies to the jointly smooth field $G$ on the common interval $J$ of step 2.1, and gives smooth dependence of $Z(t,z)$ on $z$ near $z_0$. We record why this dependence has the joint regularity needed for time derivatives. At first order, [F4] gives $X_1=D_zZ$ and $X_1'=D_zG(t,Z)X_1$, $X_1(t_0)=I_d$. The coefficient is jointly continuous; the uniform-in-time estimates in [F4], combined with continuity of the solution of this linear equation in time, make $X_1$ jointly continuous. The solution $Z$ itself is jointly continuous by the same initial-data estimates and its continuity in time. [L1, F4, F5, step 2.1]

4.1 The higher-order argument does not require a new existence assumption. For $r\ge1$, use the finite-dimensional jet variables $X_0,\ldots,X_r$, where $X_j$ is a $j$-linear map and $X_0\in\mathbb R^d$. Repeated chain rules in [F3] give $X_0'=G(t,X_0)$ and $X_j'=D_zG(t,X_0)X_j+P_j(t,X_0,\ldots,X_{j-1})$ for $j\ge1$, with $P_1=0$. Here $P_j$ is the finite sum over partitions of the $j$ differentiation directions into at least two nonempty blocks, applying the corresponding higher derivative of $G$ to the lower jets indexed by those blocks. Initial values are $X_0(t_0)=z$, $X_1(t_0)=I_d$ and $X_j(t_0)=0$ for $j\ge2$. This jet field is jointly smooth. For nearby full jet initial values, $X_0$ exists on $J$ by step 2.1; successively each higher component is affine linear with bounded continuous coefficients and forcing on $J$, so [F5] gives its evolution there. The same linear integral estimates bound each component uniformly for nearby initial values, giving a common compact jet cylinder for each finite order. Thus [F4] legitimately applies to this enlarged system on $J$. Starting with its first-order variational equation, differentiation of the Volterra identities and uniqueness in [F5] identify the prescribed jet with $(Z,D_zZ,\ldots,D_z^rZ)$. Its highest component is $C^1$ in the initial state, so these identities upgrade $C^r$ to $C^{r+1}$; this uses the highest component, not merely the first one. Induction, with the uniform estimates of [F4], gives joint continuity of all state derivatives. [F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The equation $\partial_tZ=G(t,Z)$ now supplies all mixed derivatives: differentiating it in state variables gives the chain-rule expressions in the jointly continuous state jets, and their displayed jet equations permit subsequent time differentiation. Induction on the time order, using joint smoothness of $G$, proves joint smoothness on the open time interval $(t_0-H,t_0+H)$ and the initial-state neighbourhood. Put $I=[t_0-H/2,t_0+H/2]$; the solution map on $I$ therefore extends smoothly to an open time neighbourhood. Projection as in step 1.1 gives the claimed common local solutions and smooth dependence on $(y,\lambda)$, including the endpoints of $I$. All solutions and all jet evolutions are uniquely determined by their IVPs; the Picard sequences use prescribed iteration and the argument makes no family selection or additional Choice assumption. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open and let
$F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth. For every base point $(t_0,x_0)\in D$ there are
$h>0$ and an open neighbourhood $W$ of $(t_0,x_0)$ such that each initial pair
$(s,y)\in W$ has a unique solution on $[s-h,s+h]$, and the resulting local
solution map is smooth in the initial time and initial state.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth nonautonomous field $F(t,x)$ and a base point $(t_0,x_0)\in D$.

[L1] Autonomous smooth ODEs have unique local smooth flows ([[thm-fundamental-theorem-for-autonomous-smooth-odes]]).

[L2] Smooth parameter-dependent ODEs have solutions depending smoothly on the parameters ([[thm-smooth-dependence-of-ode-solutions-on-parameters]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 On the open state domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$, define the augmented autonomous field $V(s,x)=(1,F(s,x))$, so its equations are $s'(r)=1$ and $x'(r)=F(s(r),x(r))$. This field is smooth on $D$. Apply [L1] with open state domain $U=D$ at $(t_0,x_0)$: there are $h>0$ and an open neighbourhood $W\subseteq D$ of $(t_0,x_0)$ such that every initial pair in $W$ has a unique augmented solution on the common elapsed-time interval $[-h,h]$, taking values in $D$. [given, L1, construct]

2.1 The first equation forces $s(t)=s_0+t$ when $s(0)=s_0$, so the second equation becomes exactly the original nonautonomous system with initial time $s_0$. Reading the initial value $(s_0,x_0)$ as a parameter, [L2] makes the resulting solution map smooth in $(s_0,x_0)$. This is precisely the claimed local theorem for nonautonomous smooth ODEs. [L2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $F:D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and
$C^1$ in the state variable. Fix data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$ and a compact time
interval $I=[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ on which the corresponding solutions through nearby
initial states all exist. Then the solution map

$$\Phi:I\times U_0\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad \Phi(t,y)=x(t;y),$$

is $C^1$ in the initial-state variable $y$ on some neighbourhood $U_0$ of
$x_0$. For each $y\in U_0$, the derivative matrix
$D_y\Phi(t,y)$ is the solution of the variational equation along $t\mapsto x(t;y)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field $F$, the compact interval $I$, and the common local family $\Phi(t,y)=x(t;y)$ of solutions through nearby initial states.

[F1] The variational equation along a solution is $A'(t)=D_xF(t,x(t))A(t)$ with initial condition $A(t_0)=I_n$ ([[def-variational-equation-along-an-ode-solution]]).

[F2] Solutions satisfy the corresponding Volterra integral equation ([[prop-first-order-ivp-is-equivalent-to-a-volterra-integral-equation]]).

[L1] Nearby initial data and parameters give uniformly close solutions on one common compact time interval ([[thm-continuous-dependence-of-odes-on-initial-data-and-parameters]]).

[L2] Linear matrix ODEs on a compact interval have unique solutions ([[lem-linear-matrix-odes-have-unique-global-solutions-on-a-given-interval]]).

[L3] The norm of a vector-valued integral is at most the integral of the norm ([[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]]).

[L4] Gronwall's integral inequality controls difference equations of Volterra type ([[thm-gronwall-integral-inequality]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], after shrinking $U_0$ if needed, every solution graph $(t,\Phi(t,y))$ with $y\in U_0$ lies in one compact cylinder $K\subseteq D$. Fix $y\in U_0$, and let $A_y:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be the unique solution of the variational equation below. [F1, L1, L2]

$$A_y'(t)=D_xF(t,\Phi(t,y))A_y(t),\qquad A_y(t_0)=I_n,$$

whose existence on $I$ is given by [L2]. Because $D_xF$ is continuous on the compact set $K$, it is bounded and uniformly continuous there.

2.1 Fix $y\in U_0$ and an increment $u\in\mathbb R^n$ with $y+u\in U_0$. By [F2], the difference $z_u(t):=\Phi(t,y+u)-\Phi(t,y)$ satisfies the Volterra equation below, and the state-variable mean-value formula gives the matrix field $B_u$. [F2, L1, step 1.1, algebra]

$$z_u(t)=u+\int_{t_0}^{t}\bigl(F(s,\Phi(s,y+u))-F(s,\Phi(s,y))\bigr)\,ds.$$

For each $s\in I$, the one-variable mean-value formula in the state variable gives

$$F(s,\Phi(s,y+u))-F(s,\Phi(s,y))=B_u(s)\,z_u(s),$$

where

$$B_u(s):=\int_0^1 D_xF\bigl(s,\Phi(s,y)+\theta z_u(s)\bigr)\,d\theta.$$

By [L1], $z_u\to0$ uniformly on $I$ as $u\to0$, so the uniform continuity of $D_xF$ on $K$ gives

$$\varepsilon(u):=\sup_{s\in I}\|B_u(s)-D_xF(s,\Phi(s,y))\|\longrightarrow 0.$$

3.1 Put $\rho_u(t):=z_u(t)-A_y(t)u$. Subtracting the Volterra equations for $z_u$ and $A_yu$ gives the identity below. [L3, L4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

$$\rho_u(t)=\int_{t_0}^{t}B_u(s)\rho_u(s)\,ds+\int_{t_0}^{t}\bigl(B_u(s)-D_xF(s,\Phi(s,y))\bigr)A_y(s)u\,ds.$$

Let $M:=\sup_K\|D_xF\|$ and $C_y:=\sup_{s\in I}\|A_y(s)\|$. Then $\|B_u(s)\|\le M$, and [L3] gives, for $t\ge t_0$,

$$\|\rho_u(t)\|_2\le M\int_{t_0}^{t}\|\rho_u(s)\|_2\,ds + C_y\varepsilon(u)\|u\|(t-t_0).$$

Applying [L4] on $[t_0,t]$ and its time-reflected form on $[t,t_0]$ yields a constant $C'_y$ independent of $u$ such that $\sup_{t\in I}\|\rho_u(t)\|_2\le C'_y\varepsilon(u)\|u\|$. Since $\varepsilon(u)\to0$, this proves

$$\sup_{t\in I}\frac{\|\Phi(t,y+u)-\Phi(t,y)-A_y(t)u\|_2}{\|u\|}\longrightarrow 0.$$

Therefore $A_y(t)=D_y\Phi(t,y)$ for every $t\in I$.

4.1 For $y,y'\in U_0$, write $E(t):=A_{y'}(t)-A_y(t)$ and $C_y(t):=D_xF(t,\Phi(t,y))$. Then the continuity estimate below, together with the same Gronwall argument as in step 3.1, proves continuity of the derivative matrix. [L1, L3, L4, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

$$E(t)=\int_{t_0}^{t}C_{y'}(s)E(s)\,ds+\int_{t_0}^{t}\bigl(C_{y'}(s)-C_y(s)\bigr)A_y(s)\,ds.$$

By [L1], $\Phi(\,\cdot\,,y')\to\Phi(\,\cdot\,,y)$ uniformly on $I$ as $y'\to y$, so the uniform continuity of $D_xF$ on $K$ gives $\sup_{s\in I}\|C_{y'}(s)-C_y(s)\|\to0$. Applying [L3] and [L4] exactly as in step 3.1 shows $\sup_{t\in I}\|E(t)\|_2\to0$. Hence $y\mapsto D_y\Phi(t,y)=A_y(t)$ is continuous for each $t$, and the derivative matrix is exactly the variational-equation solution.

5.1 Steps 3.1 and 4.1 prove that $\Phi$ is $C^1$ in the initial-state variable and that its derivative matrix is the solution of the variational equation. [step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T>0$, let $d,q\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $[0,T]$, and let $v:I\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly $C^\infty$. For every compact $K\subseteq\Theta$, assume there are constants $L_K,M_K\ge0$ such that, for all $t\in[0,T]$, $\eta\in K$, and $z,w\in\mathbb R^d$,

$$\|v(t,z,\eta)-v(t,w,\eta)\|_2\le L_K\|z-w\|_2,\qquad \|v(t,0,\eta)\|_2\le M_K.$$

Fix $\theta\in\Theta$ and let $\Phi_t:=\Phi^\theta_{t,0}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be its flow. Let $p_0:\mathbb R^d\to(0,\infty)$ be a continuous probability density with respect to Lebesgue measure, define $\mu_0(E):=\int_Ep_0(z)\,dz$ for Borel $E$, and define the pushforward measure $\mu_t(E):=\mu_0(\Phi_t^{-1}(E))$. For $y\in\mathbb R^d$, set

$$p_t(y):=\frac{p_0(\Phi_t^{-1}(y))}{|\det D\Phi_t(\Phi_t^{-1}(y))|}.$$

Then $p_t$ is a density of $\mu_t$. For every $z_0\in\mathbb R^d$, write $z_t:=\Phi_t(z_0)$ and $J_t:=D\Phi_t(z_0)$; the determinant of $J_t$ is positive and

$$p_t(\Phi_t(z_0))=\frac{p_0(z_0)}{\det J_t}>0,\qquad \frac{d}{dt}\log p_t(z_t)=-\operatorname{tr}(D_zv(t,z_t,\theta))=-\sum_{i=1}^d\partial_{z_i}v_i(t,z_t,\theta),$$

The derivative identity holds for $0<t<T$ and has one-sided meanings at $0$ and $T$.

## Statement references

[Chen et al., §4 and Appendix A](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07366)

[Papamakarios et al., §4.1](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume22/19-1028/19-1028.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the neural ODE hypotheses in the Statement, a fixed $\theta\in\Theta$, and the positive continuous initial probability density $p_0$.

[F1] [[def-neural-ode]]: for fixed $\theta$, the state satisfies $\dot z=v_\theta(t,z)$ on its interval.

[F2] [[thm-neural-ode-global-smooth-flow]]: under the stated smoothness, compact-neighborhood global Lipschitz, and origin-bound hypotheses, $\Phi^\theta_{t,s}$ exists on $[0,T]$ and each time slice is a smooth diffeomorphism, with identity flow at $t=s$.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $U_0\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, $T>0$, and let $f$ be jointly $C^1$ on an open time-state domain. Suppose the ODE $x'(t)=f(t,x(t))$ has a common flow
$$\Phi:[0,T]\times U_0\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad x(t)=\Phi_t(x_0),$$
whose time slices $\Phi_t:U_0\to U_t$ are $C^1$ diffeomorphisms onto open sets $U_t$, with $\Phi_0=\operatorname{id}_{U_0}$. Let $p_0:U_0\to(0,\infty)$ be a continuous probability density with respect to Lebesgue measure, let $\mu_t$ be the pushforward of $p_0(x)\,dx$ under $\Phi_t$, and define
$$p_t(y):=\begin{cases}\dfrac{p_0(\Phi_t^{-1}(y))}{|\det D\Phi_t(\Phi_t^{-1}(y))|},&y\in U_t,\\0,&y\notin U_t.\end{cases}$$
Then $p_t$ is a density of $\mu_t$ on $\mathbb R^d$, the flow Jacobian has positive determinant, and
$$p_t(\Phi_t(x_0))=\frac{p_0(x_0)}{\det D\Phi_t(x_0)}>0,$$
and, for $0<t<T$,
$$\frac{d}{dt}\log p_t(x(t))=-\operatorname{div}_x f(t,x(t)),\qquad \operatorname{div}_x f:=\operatorname{tr}D_xf=\sum_{i=1}^d\partial_{x_i}f_i.$$
The derivative at $0$ or $T$ is understood one-sided.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Countable Choice axiom, the stated common C¹ flow of diffeomorphisms, and the positive continuous initial probability density.

[A1] Countable Choice is the assertion that every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]); it is used only through the change-of-variables supplier [F3].

[F1] A solution of a first-order system satisfies $x(t_0)=x_0$ and $x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$ on its interval ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]).

[F2] A measure with density $p_0$ relative to Lebesgue measure is defined by $\mu_0(E)=\int_Ep_0\,d\lambda_d$ ([[def-measure-with-density]]).

[F3] For a C¹ diffeomorphism $S:U\to V$ between open subsets of $\mathbb R^d$, Countable Choice and the nonnegative change-of-variables theorem give $\int_Vg(y)\,d\lambda_d(y)=\int_Ug(S(x))|\det DS(x)|\,d\lambda_d(x)$ for every nonnegative Lebesgue-measurable $g$ ([[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]).

[F4] If a vector field is continuous and C¹ in the state variable and the solutions through nearby initial states exist on a common compact interval $I=[s-a,s+a]$ for some $a>0$, then the solution map is C¹ in the initial state and its derivative $V_t$ solves $V'(t)=D_xf(t,x(t))V_t$ with $V_s=I_d$; endpoint derivatives are one-sided ([[thm-c1-dependence-of-solutions-on-initial-data]], [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]).

[F5] The derivative of a composite of totally differentiable maps is given by the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[F6] A continuous real function on a closed interval takes every value between its endpoint values ([[thm-intermediate-value]]).

[F7] For $z>0$, $\log z$ is defined as the inverse of the real exponential and $\log'(z)=1/z$ ([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]).

[F8] The determinant of a square matrix is the finite Leibniz sum over permutations ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

[F9] A real square matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is nonzero ([[thm-real-square-matrix-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]).

[F10] The determinant is a polynomial in its matrix entries, and polynomial functions are continuous ([[cor-determinant-is-a-polynomial-in-the-matrix-entries]], [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]).

[F11] The Leibniz determinant is column-multilinear and alternating ([[thm-leibniz-determinant-is-alternating-multilinear-and-normalized]]).

[F12] Sums and products of differentiable real functions obey the binary sum and product rules; repeated application over finitely many factors follows by induction ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

## Proof

1.1 For fixed $t$, the inverse-flow chain rule [F5] gives $D\Phi_t^{-1}(\Phi_t(x_0))D\Phi_t(x_0)=I$, so $D\Phi_t(x_0)$ is invertible and [F9] gives $\det D\Phi_t(x_0)\ne0$. Thus the formula for $p_t$ is continuous and positive on $U_t$ and zero outside, hence Borel measurable on $\mathbb R^d$. For any Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, apply [F3] to $g=\mathbf 1_{E\cap U_t}p_t|_{U_t}$. Change of variables gives $\int_Ep_t(y)\,dy=\int_{E\cap U_t}p_t(y)\,dy=\int_{\Phi_t^{-1}(E\cap U_t)}p_0(x)\,dx=\mu_0(\Phi_t^{-1}(E))=\mu_t(E)$ because $\Phi_t(U_0)=U_t$. Thus $p_t$ is a density of $\mu_t$ on all of $\mathbb R^d$. [A1, F2, F3, F5, F9, given]

2.1 Put $s:=T/2$. For $z\in U_s$ define $\Psi_t(z):=\Phi_t(\Phi_s^{-1}(z))$ for $0\le t\le T$. Each $\Psi_t(z)$ is a solution of the same ODE on the common interval $[0,T]=[s-s,s+s]$, and $\Psi_s(z)=z$. Apply [F4] to this family at the initial state $x(s)=\Phi_s(x_0)$ and initial time $s$: its derivative $V_t:=D_z\Psi_t(x(s))$ satisfies $V_t'=A_tV_t$, where $A_t:=D_xf(t,\Phi_t(x_0))$, and $V_s=I_d$, with one-sided derivatives at $0,T$. Since $\Phi_t=\Psi_t\circ\Phi_s$, the chain rule [F5] gives $J_t:=D\Phi_t(x_0)=V_tJ_s$, so $J_t'=A_tJ_t$ on $[0,T]$ and $J_0=I_d$, again with one-sided endpoint derivatives. Thus $J_t$ is continuous. Separately, the inverse-flow chain rule [F5] and [F9] give $\det J_t\ne0$ for each $t$; [F10] and continuity of $J_t$ give continuity of $t\mapsto\det J_t$. If this determinant were negative at any $t>0$, [F6] on $[0,t]$ with target $0$ would give a zero, contradicting nonsingularity; since $\det J_0=1$ by [F11], it is positive throughout. The density formula in step 1.1 therefore becomes $p_t(\Phi_t(x_0))=p_0(x_0)/\det J_t$. [F1, F4, F5, F6, F9, F10, F11, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix an interior time, write $A:=D_xf(t,\Phi_t(x_0))$ and $C:=J_t^{-1}J_t'$, and denote the columns of $J_t$ by $v_1,\ldots,v_d$. By the Leibniz formula [F8], differentiating each $d$-factor monomial with repeated binary product rules (induction on the number of factors) and distributing the finite sum gives $(\det J_t)'=\sum_{\sigma\in S_d}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sum_{j=1}^d(v_j')_{\sigma(j)}\prod_{i\ne j}(v_i)_{\sigma(i)}=\sum_{j=1}^d\det[v_1,\ldots,v_{j-1},v_j',v_{j+1},\ldots,v_d]$. Since $J_t'=J_tC$, if $C_j$ is column $j$ of $C$ then $v_j'=\sum_{k=1}^d C_{kj}v_k$. Multilinearity [F11] expands the $j$th determinant into $\sum_k C_{kj}\det[v_1,\ldots,v_{j-1},v_k,v_{j+1},\ldots,v_d]$; for $k\ne j$ the repeated columns make the determinant zero by alternation [F11], while $k=j$ gives $C_{jj}\det J_t$. Hence $(\det J_t)'=\det J_t\operatorname{tr}(C)$ and [F7] gives $(\log\det J_t)'=\operatorname{tr}(C)$. Since $C=J_t^{-1}AJ_t$, $\operatorname{tr}(C)=\sum_{i,j,k}(J_t^{-1})_{ij}A_{jk}(J_t)_{ki}=\sum_{j,k}A_{jk}(J_tJ_t^{-1})_{kj}=\sum_jA_{jj}=\operatorname{tr}(A)$. The density formula in step 2.1 has constant numerator $p_0(x_0)$, so [F7] and the chain rule [F5] give $(\log p_t(\Phi_t(x_0)))'=-(\det J_t)'/\det J_t=-\operatorname{tr}(D_xf(t,\Phi_t(x_0)))$. This proves the identity for $0<t<T$. [F4, F5, F7, F8, F11, F12, step 2.1, algebra, induction]

4.1 At the endpoints, step 2.1 gives the variational equation for $J_t$ on $[0,T]$, and [F1] makes its endpoint equations one-sided: $J'_{0+}=A_0J_0$ and $J'_{T-}=A_TJ_T$, where $A_r:=D_xf(r,\Phi_r(x_0))$. To differentiate the determinant there, use its finite Leibniz polynomial [F8]: as $t\downarrow0$, each matrix entry has expansion $J_{ij}(t)=J_{ij}(0)+t(J'_{0+})_{ij}+o(t)$, and as $t\uparrow T$ it has expansion $J_{ij}(t)=J_{ij}(T)+(t-T)(J'_{T-})_{ij}+o(|t-T|)$. Expanding each finite product in that polynomial, the terms linear in the increment are exactly the binary product-rule terms and all terms with at least two increments are little-oh of the increment. Thus the same finite expansion as in step 3.1 gives $(\det J)'_{0+}=\det J_0\operatorname{tr}(J_0^{-1}A_0J_0)=\det J_0\operatorname{tr}(A_0)$ and $(\det J)'_{T-}=\det J_T\operatorname{tr}(J_T^{-1}A_TJ_T)=\det J_T\operatorname{tr}(A_T)$. The determinants are positive by step 2.1, so one-sided differentiation of their logarithms [F7] gives $(\log\det J)'_{0+}=\operatorname{tr}(A_0)$ and $(\log\det J)'_{T-}=\operatorname{tr}(A_T)$. Using the density identity in step 2.1, $\log p_t(\Phi_t(x_0))=\log p_0(x_0)-\log\det J_t$, therefore its right derivative at $0$ and left derivative at $T$ are respectively $-\operatorname{tr}(A_0)$ and $-\operatorname{tr}(A_T)$. These are exactly the stated endpoint identities. [F1, F4, F7, F8, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $T>0$, let $d,q\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, and let $v:I\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly $C^\infty$ on an open time interval $I$ containing $[0,T]$. For each compact $K\subseteq\Theta$, suppose there are constants $L_K,M_K\ge0$ such that for all $t\in[0,T]$, $\theta\in K$, and $z,w\in\mathbb R^d$,

$$\|v(t,z,\theta)-v(t,w,\theta)\|_2\le L_K\|z-w\|_2,\qquad \|v(t,0,\theta)\|_2\le M_K.$$

Let $\Omega\subseteq\Theta$ be open with compact closure contained in $\Theta$, let $U_0\subseteq\Theta$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$, and let $u_0:U_0\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^1$. Write $u_\theta$ for the exact solution of $\dot u_\theta(t)=v(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)$, $u_\theta(0)=u_0(\theta)$, and let $\mathcal T:=\{(t,u_\theta(t),\theta):t\in[0,T],\theta\in\overline\Omega\}$ be its common compact trajectory tube. Let

$$\mathcal T_T:=\{(u_\theta(T),\theta):\theta\in\overline\Omega\}$$

be the terminal state-parameter slice. Let $U_\phi\subseteq\mathbb R^d\times\Theta$ and $U_\ell\subseteq I\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta$ be open sets containing $\mathcal T_T$ and $\mathcal T$, respectively, and let $\phi:U_\phi\to\mathbb R$ and $\ell:U_\ell\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Assume their first derivatives, measured in Euclidean operator norms, are bounded and uniformly continuous on $\mathcal T_T$ and $\mathcal T$, respectively. Define

$$\mathcal J(\theta)=\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)+\int_0^T\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)\,dt.$$

For each $\theta\in\Omega$, the exact continuous adjoint sensitivity procedure is:

1. Solve the state initial-value problem forward on $[0,T]$.
2. Solve the terminal adjoint problem backward,
   $$-p'(t)=D_u v(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^T p(t)+D_u\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^T,\qquad p(T)=D_u\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T.$$
3. Return the vector
   $$G(\theta)=D_\theta\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T+D_\theta u_0(\theta)^Tp(0)+\int_0^T\left(D_\theta\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^T+D_\theta v(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^Tp(t)\right)dt.$$

Here $D_u$ and $D_\theta$ denote Jacobian matrices in the displayed variables, $p(t)\in\mathbb R^d$, and $G(\theta)\in\mathbb R^q$. All state and adjoint equations and the integral are exact continuous mathematical objects. Replacing them by numerical solver outputs defines a finite computation and is outside this algorithm's accuracy guarantees.

## Example

On $[0,1]$, consider the two-rate linear neural ODE $u_1'(t)=-u_1(t)$, $u_2'(t)=\theta u_2(t)$ with $u(0)=(1,1)$ and objective $\mathcal J(\theta)=u_2(1;\theta)$, for $\theta$ in a neighborhood of $-100$. At $\theta=-100$, the decay rates are $1$ and $100$. The exact continuous-flow gradient is $\mathcal J'(-100)=\exp(-100)$. For the fixed-step Euler solver with $N\in\mathbb N$ and $N\ge1$ equal steps, its step count $N$ is the resolution setting; the finite computational graph has output $\mathcal J_N(\theta)=(1+\theta/N)^N$ and exact discrete adjoint gradient $\mathcal J_N'(-100)=(1-100/N)^{N-1}$. Thus changing the solver resolution from $N=50$ to $N=100$ changes the finite gradient from $-1$ to $0$. These values are exact for this finite calculation and assert no general solver-error or continuous-versus-discrete gradient bound.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $T=1$, $u(0)=(1,1)$, $v_\theta(t,u)=(-u_1,\theta u_2)$, terminal loss $u_2(1)$, and the $N$-step forward Euler graph for $N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$.

[F1] [[def-neural-ode]]: a neural ODE is the initial-value problem $\dot u=v_\theta(t,u)$ with specified initial state.

[F2] [[thm-neural-ode-global-smooth-flow]]: the stated smooth uniformly globally Lipschitz field has a unique smooth flow on the full finite interval.

[F3] [[alg-adjoint-sensitivity-method]]: the continuous procedure solves the terminal adjoint equation and returns its initial, terminal, running, and vector-field parameter contributions.

[F4] [[thm-continuous-ode-adjoint-gradient-formula]]: under common-tube and C1 objective hypotheses, the continuous adjoint expression is the exact derivative of the continuous objective.

[F5] [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]]: C1 initial and step maps together with a C1 terminal/running objective define one finite real-arithmetic graph and its reduced objective.

[F6] [[thm-discrete-adjoint-gradient-recursion]]: the backward recursion returns the exact gradient of that finite C1 graph.

[F7] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]: $e=\exp(1)$ and $\exp$ is the real exponential function.

[F8] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: $\exp$ is smooth and $(\exp)'=\exp$.

[F9] [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]: $\exp(x)>0$ for every real $x$.

[F10] [[lem-derivative-algebra-and-chain-rules]]: the sum, product, chain, and positive-integer power rules apply to the differentiable functions used below.

[F11] [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]: $\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y)$ for real $x,y$.

[A1] Take $I=\Theta=U_0=\mathbb R$ and $\Omega=(-101,-99)$, and set $u_0(\eta)=(1,1)$. The field $v(t,u,\eta)=(-u_1,\eta u_2)$ is jointly $C^\infty$. For every nonempty compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R$, $L_K=\max\{1,\sup_{\eta\in K}|\eta|\}$ and $M_K=0$ give the required state-Lipschitz and origin bounds; the empty compact case is vacuous. By [F7, F8], the exact solution $u_\eta(t)=(\exp(-t),\exp(\eta t))$ is continuous on the compact set $[0,1]\times\overline\Omega$, so its trajectory tube is compact. For the continuous adjoint, take $\phi(u,\eta)=u_2$ on the open set $U_\phi=\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R$ and $\ell(t,u,\eta)=0$ on the open set $U_\ell=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R$. These objectives are $C^1$, and their first derivatives are constant, hence bounded and uniformly continuous on the terminal slice and common trajectory tube. Thus the continuous and finite adjoint supplier hypotheses hold.

## Verification

      url: "https://www.its.caltech.edu/~niles/refs/giles00.pdf"

## Statement

Assume $T>0$. Let $u_\theta$ solve the parameter-dependent ODE of [[lem-parameter-ode-flow-tangent-on-common-tube]] on $[0,T]$. Let
$$J(\theta)=\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)+\int_0^T\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)\,dt,$$
where $\phi$ and $\ell$ are $C^1$ on a neighborhood of the trajectory tube and their first derivatives are bounded and uniformly continuous there. Let $S=D_\theta u_\theta$ be the tangent from that lemma. Let $p$ solve the terminal adjoint problem
$$-p'(t)=D_u f(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^Tp(t)+D_u\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^T,\qquad p(T)=D_u\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T.$$
Then
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T+D_\theta u_0(\theta)^Tp(0)+\int_0^T\bigl(D_\theta\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T+D_\theta f(t,u_\theta,\theta)^Tp(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$
This formula separates initial, terminal, running-cost and vector-field parameter terms. It applies only while the common-tube and differentiability hypotheses hold.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $T>0$, the common-tube ODE, $C^1$ initial map, objective, and bounded uniformly continuous first derivatives in the Statement.

[F1] [[lem-parameter-ode-flow-tangent-on-common-tube]]: the parameter flow is $C^1$ and $S'=D_uf\,S+D_\theta f$, $S(0)=D_\theta u_0$.

[F2] [[lem-ode-adjoint-pairing-integration-by-parts]]: if $S'=AS+B$ and $p'=-A^Tp-g$, then $p(T)^TS(T)-p(0)^TS(0)=\int_0^T(-g^TS+p^TB)\,dt$.

[F3] [[lem-linear-matrix-odes-have-unique-global-solutions-on-a-given-interval]]: a continuous coefficient linear matrix IVP has a unique solution on the full compact interval.

[F4] The total-derivative chain rule differentiates a composition of $C^1$ Euclidean maps ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[A1] All objective derivatives and ODE derivative coefficients are continuous and bounded on the common compact tube, and their first derivatives have the uniform continuity needed to differentiate the integral objective.

## Proof

1.1 Fix $\theta$ and write $A(t)=D_uf(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)$ and $g(t)=D_u\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^T$. The coefficient matrix $\mathcal C(t)=\begin{pmatrix}-A(t)^T&-g(t)\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ is continuous. Apply [F3] with initial time $T$ to the homogeneous matrix equation $Z'=\mathcal C(t)Z$, choosing an initial matrix whose first column is $(D_u\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T,1)^T$ and whose other columns are zero. Its first column is $(p(t),1)^T$ and solves the terminal adjoint equation. Any other solution embeds as a column of such a matrix solution, so uniqueness in [F3] gives uniqueness of $p$. [F3, given, construct]

1.2 By [F1] and the chain rule [F4], the terminal derivative is $D_\theta\phi^T+S(T)^TD_u\phi^T$. For the running term, a parameter increment $h$ gives $\Delta u(t)=S(t)h+o(\|h\|)$ uniformly in $t$ by [F1]. Uniform continuity of the objective derivatives on the common compact tube gives a uniform first-order remainder $o(\|h\|)$ along the segment from $(u_\theta(t),\theta)$ to $(u_{\theta+h}(t),\theta+h)$; the common integrable majorant permits integration of this remainder. Applying [F4] pointwise and integrating therefore gives the running derivative $\int_0^T(D_\theta\ell^T+S^TD_u\ell^T)\,dt$. Consequently $\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi^T+S(T)^TD_u\phi^T+\int_0^T(D_\theta\ell^T+S^TD_u\ell^T)\,dt$. [F1, F4, A1, given]

1.3 In [F2], set $A=D_uf$, $B=D_\theta f$, and $g=D_u\ell^T$. The adjoint equation in the Statement and tangent equation in [F1] satisfy its hypotheses. Transposing that row pairing identity and using $p(T)=D_u\phi^T$ gives $$S(T)^TD_u\phi^T-D_\theta u_0^Tp(0)=\int_0^T(-S^TD_u\ell^T+D_\theta f^Tp)\,dt.$$ [F1, F2, given]

2.1 Substitute step 1.3 into step 1.2; the terms involving $S^TD_u\ell^T$ cancel, leaving the asserted continuous adjoint gradient formula. [step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $N\ge1$, and for $0\le n\le N$ let $U_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_n}$ be open. A finite parameterized state-step graph consists of a $C^1$ initial map $x_0:\Theta\to U_0$ and $C^1$ step maps $\Psi_n:U_n\times\Theta\to U_{n+1}$ for $0\le n<N$, such that the recursion $x_{n+1}(\theta)=\Psi_n(x_n(\theta),\theta)$ is defined for every $\theta$ in the chosen parameter neighborhood. A $C^1$ running objective consists of maps $\ell_n:U_n\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ and a terminal objective $\phi:U_N\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$, all $C^1$. Its reduced objective is
$$J(\theta)=\phi(x_N(\theta),\theta)+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\ell_n(x_n(\theta),\theta).$$
The maps and objective define one finite real-arithmetic graph. A gradient of this graph is the derivative of this finite composition; it is not the derivative of an exact implicit solution unless the step map itself is that solution map.

## Statement

Use the setting of [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]]. Write $A_n=D_x\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, $B_n=D_\theta\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, and let $S_n=D_\theta x_n$. Then
$$S_0=D x_0(\theta),\qquad S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n.$$
Define $p_N=D_x\phi(x_N,\theta)^T$ and, backward for $n=N-1,\ldots,0$,
$$p_n=D_x\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+A_n^Tp_{n+1}.$$
The exact gradient of the finite objective is
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(x_N,\theta)^T+S_0^Tp_0+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\bigl(D_\theta\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}\bigr).$$
The recursion is the reverse derivative of the finite graph in exact real arithmetic; it makes no convergence claim about an iteration used to choose $\theta$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The open finite state-step graph, its $C^1$ maps, objective, trajectory and parameter in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]]: $x_{n+1}=\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$ and $J=\phi(x_N,\theta)+\sum_{n<N}\ell_n(x_n,\theta)$ with all displayed maps $C^1$.

[F2] [[alg-reverse-mode-automatic-differentiation]]: reverse mode accumulates each primitive pullback $D_k\phi_j^T\bar z_j$ at every parent slot in reverse topological order.

[F3] [[thm-reverse-mode-computes-gradient]]: reverse mode returns the exact gradient of the finite $C^1$ real-arithmetic graph.

[F4] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the derivative of a composition is the composition of its derivatives.

## Proof

1.1 By the chain rule [F4] applied to $x_{n+1}(\theta)=\Psi_n(x_n(\theta),\theta)$, $S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n$; differentiating the initial map gives $S_0=Dx_0(\theta)$. These are the forward tangent equations for this finite composition. [F1, F4]

1.2 Apply the reverse accumulation rule [F2] to the finite graph of states and objective summands in [F1]. The terminal contribution seeds $p_N=D_x\phi^T$; at each state node $x_n$, its local running-cost edge contributes $D_x\ell_n^T$, while its state-transition edge contributes $A_n^Tp_{n+1}$. Thus the accumulated state cotangent is exactly $p_n$ as defined in the Statement, and the direct parameter edges contribute $D_\theta\phi^T$ and $D_\theta\ell_n^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}$. By [F3], reverse mode returns the exact derivative of this finite C1 graph. [F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Differentiate the objective in [F1] using the forward sensitivities in step 1.1. The chain rule gives $$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi^T+S_N^TD_x\phi^T+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}(D_\theta\ell_n^T+S_n^TD_x\ell_n^T).$$ This is the direct tangent expression, with all derivatives evaluated along the trajectory. [F1, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 The adjoint equation gives $p_n^TS_n=D_x\ell_nS_n+p_{n+1}^TA_nS_n$. Since $S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n$, rearranging yields $$D_x\ell_nS_n=p_n^TS_n-p_{n+1}^TS_{n+1}+p_{n+1}^TB_n.$$ Summing over $n$ telescopes; $p_N=D_x\phi^T$ cancels the terminal tangent term in step 2.1 and leaves $S_0^Tp_0+\sum_n B_n^Tp_{n+1}$. Adding the direct parameter derivatives from step 2.1 gives the displayed adjoint formula. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume AC. Let $d,T\ge1$ be finite integers, let $I_d$ be the $d\times d$ identity matrix, and let $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_T\in(0,1)$. Set $\alpha_t=1-\beta_t$, $\bar\alpha_0=1$, and $\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s=1}^t\alpha_s$. Write $\lambda_d$ for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^d$ and define, for $v>0$,
$$\phi_{d,v}(y;m)=(2\pi v)^{-d/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|y-m\|_2^2}{2v}\right),\qquad y,m\in\mathbb R^d.$$
The notation $\|z\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^d z_i^2$ is the squared Euclidean norm. The displayed function is the Lebesgue density of $N_d(m,vI_d)$.

For each fixed $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, the forward chain has path density on $(\mathbb R^d)^T$
$$q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)=\prod_{t=1}^T \phi_{d,\beta_t}(x_t;\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1}).$$
Thus its transition from $x_{t-1}$ to $x_t$ is Gaussian with mean $\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1}$ and covariance $\beta_t I_d$. Each factor is a normalized density, and finite successive integration of the nonnegative product gives a probability density.

For a generic adjacent pair, the two model directions are shown below. The arrows indicate the direction in which each conditional density generates its target state; they assert no equality or inverse relation between the kernels.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth]
  \node (previous) at (0,0) {$x_{t-1}$};
  \node (current) at (4,0) {$x_t$};
  \draw[->] (previous) to[bend left=24] node[midway,above] {$q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})$} (current);
  \draw[->] (current) to[bend left=24] node[midway,below] {$p_{\theta,t}(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$} (previous);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

A learned reverse Gaussian model consists of finite-valued Borel maps $\mu_{\theta,t}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and fixed variances $\sigma_t^2\in(0,\infty)$, for $1\le t\le T$. It is the joint density
$$p_\theta(x_{0:T})=\phi_{d,1}(x_T;0)\prod_{t=1}^T\phi_{d,\sigma_t^2}(x_{t-1};\mu_{\theta,t}(x_t)).$$
Its prior is $p(x_T)=N_d(0,I_d)$, and its marginal density at $x_0$ is
$$p_\theta(x_0)=\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^T}p_\theta(x_{0:T})\,d\lambda_d(x_1)\cdots d\lambda_d(x_T),$$
whenever this integral is finite. The joint reverse density is normalized by successive integration of its Gaussian transition factors followed by the prior density.

For $t=1$, the forward-chain conditional $q(x_0\mid x_1,x_0)$ assigns probability one to every Borel set containing $x_0$ and zero to every Borel set not containing $x_0$; it is not a Lebesgue density. The separate learned reverse likelihood $p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)$ is the Gaussian density above with variance $\sigma_1^2>0$.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m,n\in\mathbb R^d$, and $v,w>0$. If $Q=N_d(m,vI_d)$ and $P=N_d(n,wI_d)$, then
$$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)=\frac d2\left(\frac vw-1+\log\frac wv\right)+\frac{\|m-n\|_2^2}{2w},$$
where the KL divergence is directional, its first argument is absolutely continuous with respect to its second, and $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

## Statement references

Gaussian density formula: [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]].

Directional KL convention: [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]].

Natural logarithm: [[def-natural-logarithm]].

Gaussian reverse-KL terms in diffusion objectives: [Ho, Jain, and Abbeel, §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.11239).

Gaussian reverse-process loss: [Prince, Chapter 18, “The reverse process and the tractable conditional”](https://csci4052u.science.ontariotechu.ca/generative_models/chapter_18_diffusion_models/notes.html).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $Q=N_d(m,vI_d)$ and $P=N_d(n,wI_d)$ with $d\ge1$ and $v,w>0$.

[A1] AC is assumed by the Gaussian-density supplier and the library KL definition. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] A positive-definite multivariate normal law has its displayed Lebesgue density. [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]].

[F2] A multivariate normal law has its specified mean and covariance. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]].

[F3] For probability measures $Q\ll P$, the library divergence is the expectation under $Q$ of the log Radon–Nikodym density ratio. [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]].

[F4] Expectation of an integrable random variable is its integral with respect to its probability law. [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** expand the Gaussian log-density ratio and integrate its quadratic terms.

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 By [F1], both Lebesgue densities are strictly positive, so $Q\ll P$. Expanding their Gaussian density formulas gives the log-density ratio $\log\frac{dQ}{dP}(x)=\frac d2\log\frac wv-\frac{\|x-m\|_2^2}{2v}+\frac{\|x-n\|_2^2}{2w}$. All terms are integrable under $Q$ because its covariance is finite. [A1, F1, F3, given]

2.1 Under $Q$, [F2] gives $\mathbb E_Q\|X-m\|_2^2=dv$, and expansion of $X-n=(X-m)+(m-n)$ gives $\mathbb E_Q\|X-n\|_2^2=dv+\|m-n\|_2^2$ because $\mathbb E_Q(X-m)=0$. Integrating the ratio in step 1.1 and applying the AC-dependent convention [F3] and expectation definition [F4] yields $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)=\frac d2\log\frac wv-\frac d2+\frac{dv+\|m-n\|_2^2}{2w}$, which is the stated formula. [A1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and the finite Gaussian forward chain with dimension $d\ge1$, horizon $T\ge1$, and schedule $0<\beta_t<1$ from the preceding definition. For each $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$ and $1\le t\le T$,
$$q(x_t\mid x_0)=N_d\!\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0,(1-\bar\alpha_t)I_d\right).$$
For every $2\le t\le T$, the conditional law given both endpoints is
$$q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)=N_d\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_t,\ \tilde\beta_t I_d\right),\qquad \tilde\beta_t=\frac{\beta_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}>0.$$
The formula for $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$ is only asserted for $t\ge2$; at $t=1$ the conditioning on $x_0$ makes $q(x_0\mid x_1,x_0)$ a point mass, not a Lebesgue density. The Gaussian conditional above does not assert that the unconditional reverse law $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$ is Gaussian.

## Statement references

Closed Gaussian forward marginal, posterior mean, and posterior variance: [Ho, Jain, and Abbeel, Eqs. (4), (6), and (7)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.11239).

Forward Gaussian composition and conditioned posterior: [Prince, Chapter 18, “The diffusion kernel” and “The tractable conditional”](https://csci4052u.science.ontariotechu.ca/generative_models/chapter_18_diffusion_models/notes.html).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a fixed $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, finite $d,T\ge1$, and $0<\beta_t<1$ for every $t$.

[A1] AC is assumed by the Gaussian-stack construction and the multivariate-normal conditional-law theorem. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] The forward path density factors into normalized transition densities $\phi_{d,\beta_s}(x_s;\sqrt{\alpha_s}x_{s-1})$, with $\alpha_s=1-\beta_s$ and $\bar\alpha_s=\prod_{r=1}^s\alpha_r$. [[def-forward-gaussian-diffusion-chain]].

[F2] A multivariate normal law is characterized by its scalar projection laws and has the stated mean and covariance. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]].

[F3] A finite stack of mutually independent Gaussian vectors is jointly multivariate normal, even when a covariance is singular. [[lem-finite-independent-gaussian-vectors-form-joint-multivariate-normal]].

[F4] If $(X,Y)$ is jointly Gaussian with positive-semidefinite block covariance and the observed block covariance $B$ is positive definite, then its conditional law has mean $a+CB^{-1}(y-b)$ and covariance $A-CB^{-1}C^T$. [[thm-multivariate-normal-conditional-law]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** standardize each transition to an independent Gaussian innovation, compute its finite affine sum, and apply the positive-definite-observation conditional-law formula to adjacent states.

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Under the forward path law with fixed $x_0$, for each $s$ put $\xi_s=(X_s-\sqrt{\alpha_s}X_{s-1})/\sqrt{\beta_s}$. Changing variables $x_s=\sqrt{\alpha_s}x_{s-1}+\sqrt{\beta_s}z$ in the last transition density in [F1] gives the conditional density $\phi_{d,1}(z;0)$, independent of the past. Thus for Borel past events $A$ and Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $\mathbb P(X_{1:s-1}\in A,\xi_s\in B)=\mathbb P(X_{1:s-1}\in A)N_d(0,I_d)(B)$. Each $\xi_s$ is standard Gaussian and independent of the previous path; since earlier innovations are measurable functions of that path, $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_t$ are mutually independent for every $t$. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Iterating $X_t=\sqrt{\alpha_t}X_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\xi_t$ gives $X_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sum_{s=1}^t\sqrt{\beta_s\prod_{r=s+1}^t\alpha_r}\,\xi_s$. By step 1.1 and [F3], the finite innovation stack is jointly Gaussian. Thus each scalar projection of $X_t$ is normal with mean $u\cdot\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0$ and, by independence, variance $u^T\left(\sum_{s=1}^t\beta_s\prod_{r=s+1}^t\alpha_r I_d\right)u$; [F2] identifies its law as multivariate normal with that mean and covariance. Since $\beta_s\prod_{r=s+1}^t\alpha_r=\prod_{r=s+1}^t\alpha_r-\prod_{r=s}^t\alpha_r$, the covariance sum telescopes to $(1-\bar\alpha_t)I_d$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix $t\ge2$. By step 2.1, $X_{t-1}$ is Gaussian, and by step 1.1, $\xi_t$ is independent of the past and standard Gaussian. The finite-stack result [F3] makes $(X_{t-1},\xi_t)$ jointly Gaussian. For any $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$, the projection of $(X_{t-1},X_t)$ is $(u+\sqrt{\alpha_t}v)\cdot X_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}v\cdot\xi_t$, a scalar projection of that Gaussian stack; hence [F2] makes the pair jointly Gaussian. Its means are $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0$ and $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0$, and its covariance blocks are $A=(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})I_d$, $C=\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})I_d$, and $B=(1-\bar\alpha_t)I_d$. The full block covariance is positive semidefinite because each of its quadratic forms is the variance of a scalar projection of $(X_{t-1},X_t)$. Since $0<\alpha_s<1$, we have $0<\bar\alpha_t<1$, so $B$ is positive definite. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Applying [F4] with these blocks gives conditional covariance $A-CB^{-1}C^T=\left((1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})-\frac{\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})^2}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\right)I_d=\frac{\beta_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}I_d$ and conditional mean $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0+\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}(x_t-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0)=\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_t$. For $t\ge2$, $\bar\alpha_{t-1}<1$ and $\beta_t>0$, so $\tilde\beta_t>0$. This is the asserted conditional law; no density for the degenerate $t=1$ conditional was used. [A1, F1, F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y\in\mathbb R^m$, with $d,m\ge1$, be
jointly multivariate normal with mean $(a,b)$ and positive-semidefinite block
covariance
$$\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\C^T&B\end{pmatrix},$$
where $B$ is positive definite. Then
$$S=A-CB^{-1}C^T$$
is positive semidefinite, and for every $y\in\mathbb R^m$ the probability law
$$K(y,\cdot)=N_d\!\left(a+CB^{-1}(y-b),S\right)$$
is defined. The map $K$ is a probability kernel and is a conditional law of
$X$ given $Y$: for all Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and
$F\subseteq\mathbb R^m$,
$$\mathbb P(X\in E,Y\in F)=\int_F K(y,E)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy).$$
The covariance $A$ and the conditional covariance $S$ may be singular.
Positive definiteness of $B$ is required; no pseudoinverse formula for
singular $B$ is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and a jointly Gaussian pair with the mean and block covariance
in the Statement.

[A1] AC is assumed by the multivariate-normal realization and zero-cross-covariance independence suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] A multivariate-normal law may have positive-semidefinite covariance and is characterized by having the stated scalar-normal linear projections; its mean and covariance are the stated $m$ and $\Sigma$. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]].

[F2] Jointly Gaussian blocks with zero cross-covariance are independent, including when either covariance block is singular. [[lem-joint-gaussian-blocks-with-zero-cross-covariance-are-independent]].

[F3] A law is the pushforward probability measure of its random element. [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]].

[F4] Integrating a nonnegative product-measurable function against a finite kernel gives a measurable function of the kernel parameter. [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]].

[F5] Independent random elements have their product joint law. [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]].

[F6] Tonelli evaluates nonnegative integrals on sigma-finite product spaces. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]].

[F7] Kernel evaluations are measurable and each probability-kernel section is a probability measure. [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]].

## Proof

**Given:** AC and the jointly Gaussian pair $(X,Y)$.

1.1 Since $B$ is positive definite, it is invertible and symmetric. For any $u\in\mathbb R^d$, put $v=-B^{-1}C^Tu$. Positive semidefiniteness of $\Sigma$ gives $0\le \begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}^T \Sigma\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix} =u^T(A-CB^{-1}C^T)u=u^TSu.$ Thus $S$ is positive semidefinite. This calculation uses no inverse of $A$. [given, algebra]

2.1 Put $D=CB^{-1}$ and $R=X-a-D(Y-b)$. Every linear projection of $(R,Y)$ is an affine scalar projection of the jointly Gaussian pair $(X,Y)$, hence is normal by the projection characterization in [F1]; therefore $(R,Y)$ is jointly Gaussian. Its mean is $(0,b)$, and block covariance calculation gives $\operatorname{Cov}(R,Y)=C-DB=0,\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(R)=A-DC^T-CD^T+DBD^T=S.$ The block-independence result [F2] therefore makes $R$ independent of $Y$, even if $S$ is singular. [A1, F1, F2, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\rho$ be the law of $R$, and define $K(y,E)=\int_{\mathbb R^d} \mathbf1_E\!\left(a+D(y-b)+r\right)\rho(dr).$ For each fixed $y$, this is the pushforward of the probability $\rho$ under the continuous affine map $r\mapsto a+D(y-b)+r$, so it is a probability measure by [F3]. The map $(y,r)\mapsto a+D(y-b)+r$ is continuous, hence the integrand is product-measurable for Borel $E$. The finite-kernel measurability theorem [F4] makes $y\mapsto K(y,E)$ Borel; therefore $K$ is a probability kernel by [F7]. Since $R\sim N_d(0,S)$ by [F1], its pushforward is $N_d(a+D(y-b),S)$ for every $y$. [A1, F1, F3, F4, F7, step 2.1]

4.1 By [F2] and [F5], the joint law of $(R,Y)$ is $\rho\otimes\mathbb P_Y$. The identity $X=a+D(Y-b)+R$ and Tonelli [F6] then give, for Borel $E,F$, $\mathbb P(X\in E,Y\in F) =\int_F\int_{\mathbb R^d}\mathbf1_E(a+D(y-b)+r)\rho(dr)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy) =\int_F K(y,E)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy).$ This is the defining conditional-law identity. It holds for every Borel observation set $F$, so the same kernel is a conditional law of $X$ given $Y$. The proof requires $B^{-1}$ only; singularity of $A$ or $S$ causes no change. [A1, F2, F5, F6, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
