## Statement

Assume AC. Fix a finite Gaussian forward chain and reverse model as defined above, with finite-valued Borel reverse means and fixed variances $\sigma_t^2\in(0,\infty)$. For the noise-prediction parameterization, let $\epsilon_\theta:\mathbb R^d\times\{1,\ldots,T\}\to\mathbb R^d$ be Borel and set
$$\mu_{\theta,t}(x_t)=\frac1{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left(x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\right),\qquad 1\le t\le T.$$
For each fixed observed $x_0$, require $0<p_\theta(x_0)<\infty$, define the proper posterior density
$$\pi_\theta(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)=\frac{p_\theta(x_{0:T})}{p_\theta(x_0)},$$
and let $Q_{x_0}$ and $\Pi_{\theta,x_0}$ be the path probability measures with Lebesgue densities $q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)$ and $\pi_\theta(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)$. Require $Q_{x_0}\ll\Pi_{\theta,x_0}$ and
$$\mathbb E_{q(\cdot\mid x_0)}\!\left[|\log q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)|+|\log p_\theta(x_{0:T})|\right]<\infty.$$
Here $\mathbb E_q[f]$ means the integral of $f$ against the path law with density $q(\cdot\mid x_0)$. Define
$$\operatorname{ELBO}_\theta(x_0)=\mathbb E_q\!\left[\log p_\theta(x_{0:T})-\log q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)\right].$$
Then
$$\log p_\theta(x_0)=\operatorname{ELBO}_\theta(x_0)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{x_0}\|\Pi_{\theta,x_0}),\qquad D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{x_0}\|\Pi_{\theta,x_0})\ge0.$$
The negative ELBO has the exact decomposition
$$-\operatorname{ELBO}_\theta(x_0)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q(x_T\mid x_0)\middle\|N_d(0,I_d)\right)+\mathbb E_{q(x_1\mid x_0)}[-\log p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)]+\sum_{t=2}^T\mathbb E_{q(x_t\mid x_0)}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\middle\|p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\right)\right].$$
In particular, for $t\ge2$, write
$$\tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0)=\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_t,\quad w_t=\frac{\beta_t^2}{2\sigma_t^2\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_t)},\quad C_t=\frac d2\left(\frac{\tilde\beta_t}{\sigma_t^2}-1+\log\frac{\sigma_t^2}{\tilde\beta_t}\right).$$
If $x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$ with $\epsilon\sim N_d(0,I_d)$, then the corresponding per-step KL term is
$$\mathbb E_\epsilon\!\left[w_t\left\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\right\|_2^2+C_t\right].$$
At $t=1$, the reconstruction term is the separate learned likelihood $p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)$ with variance $\sigma_1^2>0$; no Lebesgue density for $q(x_0\mid x_1,x_0)$ is used. For finite $T$, the terminal-prior KL is retained; no equality $q(x_T\mid x_0)=N_d(0,I_d)$ is assumed. The common unweighted objective
$$L_{\mathrm{simple}}(\theta;x_0)=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbb E_\epsilon\!\left[\left\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta\!\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon,t\right)\right\|_2^2\right]$$
drops the schedule weights and replaces the separate endpoint terms with noise-prediction losses, so it is not in general the exact maximum-likelihood objective.

## Statement references

Finite-chain ELBO decomposition and exact Gaussian posterior: [Ho, Jain, and Abbeel, §§2–3 and Appendix A, Eqs. (5)–(7), (17)–(22)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.11239).

Weighted noise prediction and the unweighted simple objective: [Ho, Jain, and Abbeel, §3.2 and §3.4, Eqs. (8)–(14)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.11239).

Independent full-chapter derivation: [Prince, Chapter 18, “The diffusion ELBO” and “Simplifying it”](https://csci4052u.science.ontariotechu.ca/generative_models/chapter_18_diffusion_models/notes.html).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a finite forward chain and reverse Gaussian model with positive finite variances, a fixed $x_0$, a Borel noise predictor, and finite absolute $q$-expectations of the log path densities in the Statement.

[A1] AC is assumed by the Gaussian conditional-law supplier and the library KL/ELBO interface. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] The forward and reverse path densities factor into normalized Gaussian transitions; their variances are finite and strictly positive. [[def-forward-gaussian-diffusion-chain]].

[F2] The forward marginal and, for $t\ge2$, the exact Gaussian law of $x_{t-1}$ conditioned on $x_t,x_0$ are as stated. [[thm-gaussian-forward-and-posterior-kernels]].

[F3] The variational-family interface requires $0<Z<\infty$ before it normalizes $\pi=\gamma/Z$. [[def-variational-family-and-elbo]].

[F9] An admissible density has the required support and finite $q$-integrability of $|\log\gamma|+|\log q|$. [[def-variational-family-and-elbo]].

[F4] Under those conditions, the log-evidence equals the ELBO plus reverse KL under AC, and the KL is nonnegative. [[thm-elbo-kl-decomposition]].

[F5] For positive isotropic Gaussian variances, the reverse KL is the sum of the variance term and squared-mean term in the proved formula. [[lem-isotropic-gaussian-kl-formula]].

[F6] Expectation of an integrable function is its integral with respect to the stated probability law. [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].

[F7] A probability law is the pushforward probability measure of its random element. [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]].

[F8] The library KL is directional: its first argument must be absolutely continuous with respect to its second. [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]].

[F10] A multivariate normal law has its specified mean and covariance, so a standard $d$-dimensional normal residual has second moment $d$. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** verify the path-space ELBO hypotheses, telescope the forward-density ratios, and evaluate the remaining Gaussian divergences.

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 The reverse path density is strictly positive and finite at every finite path because every Gaussian variance is positive and each mean is finite. Its path marginal on $x_{1:T}$ is a probability density by successive integration of its reverse kernels and prior. For fixed $x_0$, the decoder density satisfies $p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)\le(2\pi\sigma_1^2)^{-d/2}$, so integrating against that path marginal gives $p_\theta(x_0)<\infty$. It is strictly positive: on the positive-measure box $[-1,1]^{dT}$, the sets $\{p_\theta(x_{0:T})\ge1/n\}$ for positive integers $n$ cover the box because the density is positive everywhere. If all these sets had measure zero, their countable union would have measure zero, contradicting the positive measure of the box; one set therefore has positive measure, and the integral is positive. Thus $\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x_0)$ is a proper positive density. [F1, F7, given, construct]

1.2 The forward path density is a probability density and is positive everywhere. Its log is the finite sum $\log q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)=\sum_{t=1}^T\left[-\frac d2\log(2\pi\beta_t)-\frac{\|x_t-\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}\|_2^2}{2\beta_t}\right]$. Under $q$, each normalized residual $(x_t-\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1})/\sqrt{\beta_t}$ has law $N_d(0,I_d)$ and finite second moment $d$ by [F10], so $\mathbb E_q|\log q|<\infty$. Since the reverse density is also positive everywhere, $\pi_\theta>0$ everywhere and the support condition $Q_{x_0}\ll\Pi_{\theta,x_0}$ holds. [F1, F6, F7, F10, given]

2.1 Let $\gamma(x_{1:T})=p_\theta(x_{0:T})$ on path space with base measure $\lambda_{dT}$. Step 1.1 gives $Z=\int\gamma\,d\lambda_{dT}=p_\theta(x_0)\in(0,\infty)$ and the normalized target $\pi=\gamma/Z$; step 1.2 gives the support condition, and the Statement's integrability hypothesis together with step 1.2 gives $\mathbb E_q(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|)<\infty$. The direction is $Q_{x_0}\ll\Pi_{\theta,x_0}$, as required by [F8]. Therefore [F3], [F6], and [F9] apply, and [F4] gives the exact log-evidence identity and nonnegative reverse KL. [A1, F3, F4, F6, F8, F9, step 1.1, step 1.2]

2.2 For $t\ge2$, the Markov property and positive Gaussian densities give $q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})=q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)q(x_t\mid x_0)/q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)$. Substitute this into $p_\theta(x_{0:T})/q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)$. The ratios $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)/q(x_t\mid x_0)$ telescope, leaving $p_\theta(x_{0:T})/q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)=[p(x_T)/q(x_T\mid x_0)]p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)\prod_{t=2}^T p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)/q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$. Taking the $q$-expectation of the logarithm yields the stated endpoint-plus-step decomposition, with the t=1 term $-\mathbb E_{q(x_1\mid x_0)}\log p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)$. [F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 For $t\ge2$, substitute $x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon$ into the posterior mean in [F2]. Using $\bar\alpha_t=\alpha_t\bar\alpha_{t-1}$ and $\beta_t=1-\alpha_t$ gives $\tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0)=\frac1{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left(x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\epsilon\right)$. The reverse mean is the same expression with $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$ in place of $\epsilon$, so $\|\tilde\mu_t-\mu_{\theta,t}\|_2^2=\frac{\beta_t^2}{\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_t)}\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\|_2^2$. Both posterior and reverse variances are positive for $t\ge2$, so [F5] applies with $v=\tilde\beta_t$ and $w=\sigma_t^2$; it gives exactly the coefficient $w_t$ and constant $C_t$ in the Statement. [F2, F5, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The terminal term remains $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(x_T\mid x_0)\|N_d(0,I_d))$ in step 2.2 because finite $T$ and $0<\beta_t<1$ give $\bar\alpha_T>0$; the $t=1$ term remains the separate positive-variance decoder log-likelihood. For an explicit counterexample, take $d=1$, $T=2$, $\beta_1=\tfrac14$, $\beta_2=\tfrac12$, $\sigma_1^2=(2\pi)^{-1}$, and $\sigma_2^2=\tilde\beta_2=\tfrac15$. Then $\bar\alpha_1=\tfrac34$, $\bar\alpha_2=\tfrac38$, $w_2=\frac{(1/2)^2}{2(1/5)(1/2)(5/8)}=2$, and $C_2=\frac12(1-1+\log1)=0$. For a fixed datum $x_0$, set $\epsilon_\theta(x_1,1)=(x_1-\sqrt{3/4}\,x_0)/\sqrt{1/4}$ and $\epsilon_\theta(x_2,2)=(x_2-\sqrt{3/8}\,x_0)/\sqrt{5/8}+c$, with any $c\in\mathbb R$. These are finite Borel maps, and their Gaussian log densities have finite $q$-expectations because they are quadratic functions of finite-dimensional Gaussian variables. The first map makes $\mu_{\theta,1}(x_1)=x_0$, so the decoder density at its mean is $(2\pi\sigma_1^2)^{-1/2}=1$; integrating it against the normalized reverse path density gives $p_\theta(x_0)=1$ for every $c$. Under the forward chain, the $t=1$ noise error is zero and the $t=2$ error is $c$, so $L_{\mathrm{simple}}=c^2/2$, while the exact weighted $t=2$ ELBO contribution is $2c^2$ and its prior term is independent of $c$. Taking $c\ne0$ gives $L_{\mathrm{simple}}>0$ but exact negative log-likelihood $-\log p_\theta(x_0)=0$. Thus the unweighted loss is a surrogate, not in general the maximum-likelihood objective. [F1, F2, F5, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. Let $\gamma:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable and suppose
$$Z:=\int_\Omega\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
Define the normalized target density $\pi:=\gamma/Z$. Then $\int\pi\,d\mu=1$. For a measurable probability density $q\ge0$ (that is, $\int_\Omega q\,d\mu=1$), write $q\ll_\mu\pi$ to mean $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{\pi=0\}$. This is a support condition on the two densities. It ensures that the induced probability measures $Q:=q\,\mu$ and $\Pi:=\pi\,\mu$ have $Q\ll\Pi$.

The normalization follows from positive-scalar homogeneity of the nonnegative integral:
$$\int\pi\,d\mu=Z^{-1}\int\gamma\,d\mu=1.$$
The induced density set functions are measures by [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]. Their total masses are one: $Q(\Omega)=1$ by the probability-density hypothesis on $q$, and $\Pi(\Omega)=1$ by the preceding calculation. To verify the absolute-continuity claim, let $A\in\mathcal A$ satisfy $\Pi(A)=0$. Then $\int_A\pi\,d\mu=0$, so the zero-integral criterion gives $\pi=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$. The support condition then gives $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$, and hence $Q(A)=0$. The homogeneity and zero-integral criteria used here are [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] and [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]].

Call $q$ **admissible** when $q\ll_\mu\pi$ and
$$\int_\Omega q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty.$$
Use the extended logarithm $\log0=-\infty$, agreeing with [[def-natural-logarithm]] on positive inputs. Since $\int\gamma\,d\mu<\infty$ and $\int q\,d\mu=1$, both functions are finite $\mu$-almost everywhere: for either $f=\gamma$ or $f=q$, $\mu\{f=\infty\}\le n^{-1}\int f\,d\mu$ for every $n\ge1$. Interpret the weighted logarithmic terms on this measurable conull set and set them equal to zero on its measurable null complement, so the resulting functions remain measurable. In particular, set $q|\log\gamma|$, $q|\log q|$, $q\log\gamma$, and $q\log q$ equal to zero on $\{q=0\}$. On the set where $q>0$, admissibility implies $\gamma>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. Define the finite real number
$$\operatorname{ELBO}(q):=\int_\Omega q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu.$$
A **variational family** is a nonempty set of admissible densities. A maximizing member need not exist.

For a finite integer $m\ge1$, let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^m\Omega_j$, let each $(\Omega_j,\mathcal A_j,\mu_j)$ be sigma-finite, and let $\mu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\mu_j$. A **mean-field density** is a product $q(z)=\prod_{j=1}^m q_j(z_j)$ of probability densities $q_j$; it belongs to the admissible mean-field family only when the product satisfies the support and integrability conditions above. Tonelli gives $\int q\,d\mu=1$. The product form alone does not guarantee support or finite ELBO.

In a dominated Bayesian model, a posterior interpretation is available only with the model hypotheses and on fibers with finite positive evidence, as in [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] and [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. In particular, [[def-likelihood-density]] supplies separate likelihood versions but does not assert joint measurability in parameter and data. Supply the single jointly measurable density $\gamma$ explicitly before using Tonelli or a posterior-kernel formula. No quotient is formed at zero or infinite normalizer.

## Definition

Fix a finite data set $D=(x_0^{(1)},\ldots,x_0^{(N)})\subset\mathbb R^d$ with $N\ge1$, a finite Gaussian schedule of horizon $T\ge1$, fixed positive reverse variances, a Borel noise predictor $\epsilon_\theta$, and a mode from $\{\texttt{weighted-elbo},\texttt{simple}\}$. This procedure returns one stochastic loss estimate; it does not prescribe a parameter optimizer or claim optimizer convergence.

1. Choose $I$ uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, choose $J$ uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,T\}$ independently of $I$, and draw $\epsilon\sim N_d(0,I_d)$ independently.

2. Set
$$x_J=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_J}\,x_0^{(I)}+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_J}\,\epsilon.$$

3. If the mode is $\texttt{simple}$, return
$$\left\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_J,J)\right\|_2^2.$$

4. If the mode is $\texttt{weighted-elbo}$, first compute the exact terminal-prior term
$$K_T(x_0^{(I)})=\frac12\left[\bar\alpha_T\|x_0^{(I)}\|_2^2+d\left(-\bar\alpha_T-\log(1-\bar\alpha_T)\right)\right].$$
If $J=1$, return
$$K_T(x_0^{(I)})-T\log p_\theta(x_0^{(I)}\mid x_J).$$
If $J\ge2$, return
$$K_T(x_0^{(I)})+T\left[C_J+w_J\left\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_J,J)\right\|_2^2\right],$$
where $w_J$ and $C_J$ are the exact per-step coefficient and variance constant in the DDPM objective theorem.

Each branch returns one sampled objective contribution. The $J=1$ weighted branch uses the positive-variance learned reconstruction likelihood; it never evaluates a density for the degenerate forward conditional $q(x_0\mid x_1,x_0)$. This algorithm specifies the sampling procedure only; it makes no optimizer-convergence claim.

Terminal KL and weighted per-step terms: [[thm-ddpm-elbo-decomposition]].

Gaussian KL formula used for the terminal term: [[lem-isotropic-gaussian-kl-formula]].

Stochastic epsilon-prediction objective and simple-loss convention: [Ho, Jain, and Abbeel, Algorithm 1 and Eqs. (12)–(14)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.11239).

Independent textbook treatment: [Prince, Chapter 18, “The diffusion ELBO” and “Simplifying it”](https://csci4052u.science.ontariotechu.ca/generative_models/chapter_18_diffusion_models/notes.html).

## Definition

Let $T>0$, let $p_t$ be a strictly positive probability density on $\mathbb R^d$ for each $t\in[0,T]$, and let $q(s,x;t,y)$ be a jointly Borel, strictly positive transition density for $0\le s<t\le T$. Assume the marginal identity $p_t(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}p_s(x)q(s,x;t,y)\,dx$ and the Chapman–Kolmogorov identity $q(s,x;t,y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz$ whenever $s<r<t$. For $0\le u<v\le T$ define
$$K_{u,v}(y,A)=\frac{\int_A p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)\,dx}{p_{T-u}(y)}\qquad(A\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ Borel}),$$
and set $K_{u,u}(y,\cdot)=\delta_y$. This is the Bayes-reversed transition probability kernel from reverse time $u$ to reverse time $v$; its source state $y$ is the forward-time state at $T-u$ and its output $x$ is the state at $T-v$.

## Definition references

[Anderson, Sections 3–4](https://eva.fcien.udelar.edu.uy/pluginfile.php/166428/mod_resource/content/1/1982_andersonREVERSE-TIME%20DIFFUSION%20EQUATION%20MODELS.pdf): uses forward transition and marginal densities to describe finite-interval reversal under additional smoothness and uniqueness assumptions.

[Tang and Zhao, Section 2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.07487): states the score-based reverse-drift formula and marks its derivation as heuristic.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the positive Borel densities and marginal and Chapman–Kolmogorov identities in the definition, the measure-kernel convention, and Tonelli's theorem for nonnegative measurable functions.

[F1] A probability kernel assigns a probability measure to each source state and has a measurable evaluation function for each Borel target set. [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]

[F2] The integral of a nonnegative jointly Borel function over one variable is measurable in the remaining variable, and iterated nonnegative integrals may be interchanged. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

## Verification
1.1 For fixed $u<v$ and Borel $A$, the integrand $1_A(x)p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)$ is nonnegative and jointly Borel in $(y,x)$. Tonelli's parameter-integral clause [F2] makes its integral Borel in $y$; division by the positive Borel function $p_{T-u}(y)$ preserves measurability. For each fixed $y$ the numerator defines a measure in $A$ by countable additivity of the Lebesgue integral. [F2, F1]

2.1 Taking $A=\mathbb R^d$ in the formula gives $K_{u,v}(y,\mathbb R^d)=p_{T-u}(y)/p_{T-u}(y)=1$ by the marginal identity, so each $K_{u,v}(y,\cdot)$ is a probability measure. The identity kernel at $u=v$ is also a probability kernel. [F1, step 1.1]

3.1 If $u<v<w$, Tonelli and the two density ratios give $\displaystyle \int K_{v,w}(x,A)K_{u,v}(y,dx)=\frac{\int_A p_{T-w}(z)\int q(T-w,z;T-v,x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)\,dx\,dz}{p_{T-u}(y)}.$ The inner integral is $q(T-w,z;T-u,y)$ by forward Chapman–Kolmogorov, so the expression is $K_{u,w}(y,A)$. If two adjacent times coincide, composition with the identity kernel gives the same equality. [F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a real continuous local martingale on $[0,T]$ with $M_0=0$, where a local martingale means that some increasing stopping times tending to $T$ make the stopped processes martingales. Then there is a unique continuous increasing process $[M]$ with $[M]_0=0$ such that the step-endpoint and partial-increment sums of squared increments along every deterministic partition sequence whose mesh tends to zero converge uniformly in probability to $[M]$. Moreover $M_t^2-[M]_t$ is a continuous local martingale. For a continuous $d$-dimensional local martingale $M$ started at zero, polarization defines continuous covariations $[M^i,M^j]$ with $M^iM^j-[M^i,M^j]$ local martingales. More generally, if $X=M+A$ and $Z=N+C$ with continuous local martingales $M,N$ and continuous finite-variation processes $A,C$, then left-step sums define the localized integrals against $M,N$ and
$$X_tZ_t-X_0Z_0=\int_0^t X_s\,dZ_s+\int_0^t Z_s\,dX_s+[M,N]_t,$$
where finite-variation integrals are pathwise Lebesgue–Stieltjes integrals and local-martingale integrals are the limits of the displayed left-step sums. A continuous finite-variation local martingale is constant.

## Statement references

[van der Vaart, Theorem 5.64 and Section 5.8, printed pp. 80–82](https://diamhomes.ewi.tudelft.nl/~avandervaart/books/stochint.pdf): defines semimartingale covariation by integration by parts and proves convergence of squared-increment sums; the localized bounded-martingale proof below supplies the needed argument in the present library's convention.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a continuous local martingale $M$ with $M_0=0$, and a finite time horizon $T$.

[A1] AC is required by the supplied local-martingale and Doob interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]] [[thm-doob-lp-maximal-inequality]]

[F1] Martingale increments on disjoint consecutive intervals are orthogonal in $L^2$: their cross expectation is zero, and $E(M_T-M_0)^2$ is the sum of their second moments. [[lem-martingale-differences-are-orthogonal-in-l2]]

[F2] For an $L^2$ martingale, Doob's inequality bounds the expected squared path supremum by four times the terminal second moment; $L^2$ is complete, and dominated and monotone convergence apply in the limits below. [[thm-doob-lp-maximal-inequality]] [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] [[thm-dominated-convergence]] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]

[F3] A continuous process has uniformly vanishing oscillation on a compact time interval as the interval lengths tend to zero. [[def-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]]

[F4] The $L^2$ Cauchy–Schwarz inequality bounds $E(R^2Q)$ by $(ER^4)^{1/2}(EQ^2)^{1/2}$. [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]

## Proof
**Given:** the hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 For each integer $n\ge1$, let $\tau_n=\inf\{t\le T:|M_t|\ge n\}\wedge T$ and set $M^{(n)}=M^{\tau_n}$. The stopping-time definition and continuity make $\tau_n$ a stopping time and $|M^{(n)}|\le n$. A bounded local martingale is a true martingale: stop it along its localizing sequence, use the martingale event-integral identities, and pass to the limit by dominated convergence because the stopped variables are bounded by $n$. Every continuous path is bounded on $[0,T]$, so $\tau_n=T$ eventually on each path. It suffices to construct the claimed limit for each bounded martingale $M^{(n)}$ and show the constructions agree on overlaps. [A1, F2]

1.2 Fix one such bounded martingale $M$, with $|M_t|\le n$, and a deterministic partition $\pi=(t_0,\ldots,t_N)$ of $[0,T]$. Put $H^\pi_s=M_{t_k}$ for $t_k<s\le t_{k+1}$ and $\displaystyle I^\pi_t=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}M_{t_k}\bigl(M_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-M_{t\wedge t_k}\bigr),\qquad Q^\pi_t=\sum_{t_{k+1}\le t}(M_{t_{k+1}}-M_{t_k})^2+(M_t-M_{t_k})^2$ when $t_k\le t<t_{k+1}$, with the last partial term omitted at $t=T$. The process $I^\pi$ is a continuous martingale because it is a finite sum of bounded, left-measurable multiples of martingale increments. Orthogonality [F1] gives $E|I^\pi_T|^2=\sum_kE[M_{t_k}^2(\Delta_kM)^2]\le n^2 E(M_T-M_0)^2\le n^4$. Directly expanding each square yields the exact identity $M_t^2-M_0^2=2I^\pi_t+Q^\pi_t$. Hence $\|Q^\pi_T\|_2\le3n^2$, uniformly over all partitions. [F1]

2.1 For two partitions $\pi,\rho$, take their common refinement $\eta$. Refinement does not change a step sum with a fixed coefficient on each coarse interval, so $\displaystyle E|I^\pi_T-I^\rho_T|^2=E\sum_{[s,t]\in\eta}(H^\pi_s-H^\rho_s)^2(M_t-M_s)^2\le E\left[R_{\pi,\rho}^2Q^\eta_T\right],$ where $R_{\pi,\rho}=\sup_s|H^\pi_s-H^\rho_s|$. Uniform continuity [F3] gives $R_{\pi,\rho}\to0$ almost surely as both meshes tend to zero, and $R_{\pi,\rho}\le2n$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] and dominated convergence [F2] therefore make the last expectation tend to zero, using the uniform $L^2$ bound on $Q^\eta_T$ from step 1.2. Thus the terminal sums $I^\pi_T$ are Cauchy in $L^2$; completeness [F2] gives their $L^2$ limit, and Doob's inequality [F2] gives the same Cauchy property for $\sup_{t\le T}|I^\pi_t-I^\rho_t|$; for the continuous-time supremum, apply the discrete inequality on increasing finite rational grids and pass to their union by monotone convergence [F2]. Choose a subsequence whose successive expected squared sup errors are at most $2^{-4k}$. Markov's inequality and the union bound imply that this subsequence converges uniformly almost surely to a continuous process $I$; the full family converges uniformly in probability to $I$. Fatou's lemma applied to the uniformly Cauchy subsequence gives $L^2$ convergence of the path suprema, so the event-integral martingale identities pass to the $L^1$ limit. [F3, F4, F2, step 1.2]

3.1 The exact identity in step 1.2 shows that the partial-increment sums $Q^\pi$ converge uniformly in probability to $Q_t=M_t^2-M_0^2-2I_t$. A subsequence converges uniformly almost surely, so $Q$ is continuous. The step-endpoint sum differs from $Q^\pi$ by at most the maximal squared oscillation of $M$ over a partition interval; [F3] makes this tend to zero almost surely. Step-endpoint sums are nondecreasing. A uniformly convergent almost-sure subsequence of those sums therefore shows that $Q$ is increasing. Thus both covariation conventions converge to $Q$ along every vanishing-mesh sequence. Since $2I=M^2-M_0^2-Q$ is a martingale, $M^2-Q$ is a martingale; uniqueness of the partition-limit object follows from uniqueness of limits in probability. [step 1.2, F3, F2, step 2.1]

4.1 Apply the scalar result to $M^{(n)}$ for each $n$. On any event where $\tau_n=T$, the stopped and original paths agree on the whole horizon, so their squared-increment sums agree; these events increase to probability one. Therefore the stopped limits agree on overlaps and define the continuous increasing $[M]$ for the original local martingale, with $M^2-[M]$ a local martingale. For vector $M$, apply the scalar result to $M^i+M^j$ and $M^i-M^j$ and set $\displaystyle [M^i,M^j]=\tfrac14\bigl([M^i+M^j]-[M^i-M^j]\bigr).$ The identity $4xy=(x+y)^2-(x-y)^2$ makes this the limit of cross-increment sums. Taking the same linear combination of the two square-compensated local martingales gives $M^iM^j-[M^i,M^j]$ local martingale. [step 3.1]

4.2 Let $H$ be a bounded continuous adapted process and $N$ a bounded continuous martingale with $N_0=0$. For each partition $\pi$ set $\displaystyle J^\pi_t=\sum_k H_{t_k}\bigl(N_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-N_{t\wedge t_k}\bigr).$ On a common refinement $\eta$, martingale orthogonality [F1] gives $\displaystyle E|J^\pi_T-J^\rho_T|^2\le E\left[\sup_s|H^\pi_s-H^\rho_s|^2 Q^\eta_T(N)\right].$ The first factor tends to zero in $L^2$ by boundedness, continuity of $H$, and dominated convergence [F2]; the second has uniformly bounded $L^2$ norm by steps 1.2–2.1 applied to $N$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] makes the terminal sums Cauchy in $L^2$, whose limit exists by completeness [F2]. Doob's inequality [F2], applied on increasing finite rational grids and then passed to their union by monotone convergence [F2], makes the process sums Cauchy in $L^2$ of the path supremum. A subsequence with summable squared-sup errors converges uniformly almost surely to a continuous limit; Fatou gives $L^2$ convergence of the full process sums to it, so the event-integral martingale identities pass to the $L^1$ limit. This defines $\int H\,dN$ as the left-step limit. Localization extends the construction to continuous local martingales and locally bounded continuous adapted integrands. [F1, F2, step 1.2, step 3.1, F4]

5.1 Let $X=M+A$ and $Z=N+C$ as in the statement. Stop so that the local martingales and total variations of $A,C$ are bounded. On every partition the exact identity $\displaystyle X_tZ_t-X_0Z_0=\sum_kX_{t_k}\Delta_k Z+\sum_kZ_{t_k}\Delta_k X+\sum_k\Delta_kX\Delta_kZ$ holds at the terminal time. The first two sums split into the integrals against $M,N$ from step 4.2 and the ordinary Lebesgue–Stieltjes integrals against $A,C$. In the last sum, each cross term containing a finite-variation increment tends to zero, for example $|\sum\Delta_kM\Delta_kC|\le\max_k|\Delta_kM|\operatorname{Var}(C)\to0$ by continuity; the remaining $\sum\Delta_kM\Delta_kN$ converges to $[M,N]$ by steps 3.1–2.2. Passing to the limit proves the displayed product formula on the stopped interval, and localization proves it on $[0,T]$. [step 4.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, F3]

6.1 If $V$ is a continuous finite-variation local martingale, stop so that its total variation is bounded. Its stopped process is bounded after subtracting $V_0$, hence is a true square-integrable martingale. For any deterministic partition, orthogonality [F1] gives $E(V_T-V_0)^2=E\sum_k(\Delta_kV)^2$. Pathwise, $\sum_k(\Delta_kV)^2\le\max_k|\Delta_kV|\operatorname{Var}(V)$, which tends to zero by continuity [F3]; dominated convergence [F2] makes its expectation tend to zero. Thus $V_T=V_0$ almost surely. Applying this at rational terminal times and using continuity proves each stopped process is constant; removing the localizing stops proves the assertion. [F1, F3, F2] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ in the sense of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes in
this definition are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$; the filtration is
neither assumed complete nor right-continuous. The Axiom of Choice is declared
because the conditional-expectation classes used in clause 3 are supplied by
the Radon--Nikodym interface of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]],
which assumes it; the countable-choice obligations inherited from that
interface are declared as dependencies of this item.

1. **Adapted.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is **adapted** to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when $X_t$
   is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $t\ge0$. This is exactly the notion
   of [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

2. **Stopped process.** For a stopping time $\tau$ for $(\mathcal F_t)$
   [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] the **stopped process** is
   $$X^{\tau}_t(\omega):=X_{t\wedge\tau(\omega)}(\omega),\qquad t\ge0,$$
   with the convention $t\wedge\infty:=t$, so no value $X_\infty$ is ever
   required and $X^\tau_0=X_0$ identically. This formula defines a pathwise
   family; adaptedness of $X$ alone does not assert measurability or
   adaptedness of its stopped values. If in addition $\tau\le c$ for a
   deterministic constant $c$, then $X^\tau_t=X_{t\wedge\tau}$, and only the
   values of $X$ on $[0,c]$ enter. Stopping at a stopping time is not the same
   as replacing a process by a modification; it is a pathwise operation.

3. **Martingale.** $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **martingale** (an all-pairs
   continuous-time martingale) relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted,
   $E|M_t|<\infty$ for every $t\ge0$, and for all $0\le s\le t$
   $$E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$
   The equality is an equality of the almost-everywhere classes of
   [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; equivalently, every version
   of the conditional expectation on the left equals $M_s$ off one null set.
   At $s=t$ the identity reduces to the known-variable case. The word
   "continuous-time" refers to the index set only and does not assert path
   continuity.

4. **Local martingale.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **local martingale** relative
   to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted, $E|X_0|<\infty$, and there exist stopping times
   $(\tau_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $\tau_0\le\tau_1\le\cdots$ and
   $\tau_n\uparrow\infty$ almost surely such that for every $n\ge0$ the stopped process
   $$X^{\tau_n}-X_0=(X_{t\wedge\tau_n}-X_0)_{t\ge0}$$
   is a martingale in the sense of clause 3. The sequence $(\tau_n)$ is called
   a **localizing sequence**. Equivalently, every $X^{\tau_n}$ is a
   martingale: adaptedness makes the integrable variable $X_0$ measurable with
   respect to every $\mathcal F_t$, so the constant process with value $X_0$
   is a martingale and may be added to, or subtracted from, each stopped
   process. The centering merely makes every localized process start at $0$;
   apart from the required integrability of $X_0$, no claim is made that $X$
   is integrable at a positive deterministic time, and no claim is made that
   $X$ has continuous paths.

5. **Path and integrability attributes.** A process has **continuous paths**
   when $t\mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every $\omega$
   in an event of probability one; the usual almost-sure path conventions of
   [[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]] apply. A
   martingale $M$ is **square-integrable** when $EM_t^2<\infty$ for every
   $t\ge0$, and **$L^2$-bounded** when $\sup_{t\ge0}EM_t^2<\infty$. These are
   properties of the single process under consideration, not of its versions:
   a modification of a martingale need not be adapted, so every later statement
   names the adapted versions it uses.

The following remarks specify what follows directly from this vocabulary.

1. **A martingale is a local martingale.** If $M$ is a martingale, the constant
   sequence $\tau_n:=n$, $n\ge0$, localizes it: the stopped process $M^{n}-M_0$ is again
   a martingale by the martingale identity applied at the deterministic times
   $s\wedge n\le t\wedge n$. The converse fails; a local martingale need not be
   a martingale, and no such implication is used in this development.
2. **Localization after a separately justified stopping operation.** Suppose
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X$, $\sigma$ is a stopping time, $X^\sigma$ is
   adapted, and each $(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$ is a martingale. Then
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X^\sigma$. Indeed it still increases to infinity,
   $(X^\sigma)_0=X_0$, and the pathwise identity
   $$(X^\sigma)^{\tau_n}-(X^\sigma)_0=X^{\sigma\wedge\tau_n}-X_0=(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$$
   verifies exactly clause 4. The stopped-piece martingale assertion and
   adaptedness are hypotheses here, not consequences of the unrestricted
   all-pairs definition. They must be established in each application.
   The sequence $(\sigma\wedge\tau_n)$ is not a substitute for $(\tau_n)$:
   its almost-sure limit is $\sigma$, which need not be infinity.

No path continuity, no right continuity of the filtration, and no completeness
of the underlying probability space is imposed by this definition. Choice
enters only through the conditional-expectation interface named above,
whose countable-choice obligations are declared as dependencies of this item.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $N\in\mathbb N_0$, $p>1$, and $q=p/(p-1)$. If $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a nonnegative submartingale and $X_N\in L^p$, then
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}X_k\right\|_p\le q\|X_N\|_p.$$
In particular, for a martingale $M$ with $M_N\in L^p$,
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}|M_k|\right\|_p\le q\|M_N\|_p.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses, objects, and conventions in the Statement.

[F1] [[thm-doob-l1-maximal-inequality]] gives the refined level inequality with $X_N$ restricted to the crossing event.

[F2] [[thm-layer-cake-formula-for-l-p-powers]] converts truncated $p$th moments to tail integrals.

[F3] [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]] bounds the mixed terminal/maximal moment.

[F4] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] removes truncation.

[F5] [[cor-absolute-value-and-powers-of-a-martingale-are-submartingales]] applies the result to $|M|$.

[F6] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited from F1 and F5 through conditional expectation.

## Proof

1.1 Put $X_N^*=\max_{k\le N}X_k$ and fix $r>0$. Layer cake and F1 give $$\begin{aligned} \mathbb E(X_N^*\wedge r)^p &=\int_0^r p\lambda^{p-1}\mathbb P(X_N^*\ge\lambda)\,d\lambda\\ &\le\int_0^r p\lambda^{p-2}\mathbb E[X_N1_{\{X_N^*\ge\lambda\}}]\,d\lambda\\ &=q\,\mathbb E\!\left[X_N(X_N^*\wedge r)^{p-1}\right]. \end{aligned}$$ The last identity follows by integrating $p\lambda^{p-2}$ up to $X_N^*\wedge r$. [F1, F2]

2.1 Hölder bounds the last expression by $$q\|X_N\|_p\|X_N^*\wedge r\|_p^{p-1}.$$ If the truncated norm is nonzero, divide by its $(p-1)$st power; if it is zero, the desired inequality is immediate. Thus $\|X_N^*\wedge r\|_p\le q\|X_N\|_p$. [F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Let $r\uparrow\infty$. F4 yields $\|X_N^*\|_p\le q\|X_N\|_p$, including the case where a priori the maximal moment might be infinite. [F4, step 2.1]

4.1 If $M$ is a martingale, $|M_k|$ is a nonnegative submartingale by F5 and its terminal value is $|M_N|$. Applying step 3.1 proves the second display. AC is exactly the inherited dependence in F6. [F5, F6] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a filtration, and let $(D_k)_{k\ge1}$ be real square-integrable martingale differences relative to it. For $1\le i<j$, $E[D_iD_j]=0$, so their real $L^2$ inner product is zero. For every $n\ge0$, $E[(\sum_{k=1}^nD_k)^2]=\sum_{k=1}^nE[D_k^2]$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses and conventions in the statement.

[F1] Square-integrable variables have an integrable product by Cauchy–Schwarz. [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]].

[F2] Under AC for conditional-expectation existence, a finite measurable factor may be taken out when its product with the integrable input is integrable. [[thm-taking-out-what-is-known]].

[F3] Under AC for existence, conditional expectation is linear, order preserving and expectation preserving. [[thm-basic-algebra-and-order-properties-of-conditional-expectation]].

[F4] Finite linear combinations remain integrable and their integrals are linear. [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]].

[F5] We assume AC: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F6] A filtration is increasing: $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}$. [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]].

[F7] Each difference is measurable at its time and has zero conditional mean given its preceding time. [[def-martingale-difference-sequence]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 To justify finite integral linearity independently of the affected published proof, augment every finite disjoint simple display by its zero-coefficient complement. Pairwise intersections of two augmented displays partition the whole space and carry equal coefficients wherever nonempty, so finite additivity and $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ prove representation independence. Common refinements give simple monotonicity and additivity; scalar zero is handled directly and positive scalars termwise. Supremum over simple minorants, followed by increasing simple approximation and the standard sets $\{f_j\ge cs\}$ for $0<c<1$, gives monotone convergence and nonnegative additivity. Positive/negative and real/imaginary decompositions therefore give finite $L^1$ linearity. This repairs the exact foundation used by [F4] and by the cited conditional-expectation identities. For $i<j$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $E|D_iD_j|\le(E D_i^2)^{1/2}(E D_j^2)^{1/2}<\infty$. Iterating [F6] gives $\mathcal F_i\subseteq\mathcal F_{j-1}$, so [F7] makes $D_i$ measurable for the latter sigma-algebra. Both $D_j$ and $D_iD_j$ are integrable, so the unbounded-factor clause applies: $E[D_iD_j\mid\mathcal F_{j-1}]=D_iE[D_j\mid\mathcal F_{j-1}]=0$. Expectation preservation gives $E[D_iD_j]=0$. The AC assumption [F5] meets the existence hypotheses of [F2, F3, F7]. All conditional identities are identities of almost-sure classes; this argument selects no sequence of representatives. [given, F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, construct]

2.1 For a fixed positive $n$, expand the finite square as $\sum_{k=1}^nD_k^2+2\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}D_iD_j$. Every term is integrable by the assumptions and step 1.1. Finite integral linearity makes its expectation $\sum_{k=1}^nE D_k^2$, because every off-diagonal term vanishes. For $n=0$ both sides are zero by the empty-sum convention, and for $n=1$ there are no off-diagonal terms. [given, F4, step 1.1] ∎

## Definition

Fix processes $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ and $Y=(Y_t)_{t\ge0}$ of real random
variables on one probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$: for every
$\omega$ in a measurable event of probability one the paths $t\mapsto X_t$
and $t\mapsto Y_t$ are continuous on $[0,\infty)$
[[def-continuity-real]]. Fix $T>0$ and a deterministic partition sequence
$(\pi_n)$ of $[0,T]$ with mesh tending to $0$
[[def-quadratic-variation-along-a-partition-sequence]]. For each $n$ write
$\pi_n=(m_n,s^{(n)})$ and form the two families of **cross-increment partial
sums**
$$S^{\mathrm{step}}_n(t):=\sum_{\substack{1\le k\le m_n\\s^{(n)}_k\le t}}\bigl(X_{s^{(n)}_k}-X_{s^{(n)}_{k-1}}\bigr)\bigl(Y_{s^{(n)}_k}-Y_{s^{(n)}_{k-1}}\bigr),$$
$$S^{\mathrm{part}}_n(t):=S^{\mathrm{step}}_n(t)+\bigl(X_t-X_{s^{(n)}_{k(t)}}\bigr)\bigl(Y_t-Y_{s^{(n)}_{k(t)}}\bigr)\quad(k(t)<m_n),$$
with $S^{\mathrm{part}}_n(T):=S^{\mathrm{step}}_n(T)$ and $k(t)$ the largest
index in $\{0,\ldots,m_n\}$ with $s^{(n)}_{k(t)}\le t$; these are the cross sums corresponding to the
two conventions of
[[def-quadratic-variation-along-a-partition-sequence]] specialized to the pair
$(X,Y)$, and both are $0$ at $t=0$.

All suprema in probability statements below use measurable versions. For
any finite collection of the processes involved, including a candidate limit,
intersect their measurable probability-one continuity events and set all of
them to zero off that intersection. These representatives have everywhere
continuous paths and retain measurable fixed-time values. The partial-sum
paths are continuous; the step-sum paths are right-continuous on $[0,T)$
with the specified value at $T$. Their uniform distances from a continuous
candidate therefore equal suprema over $(\mathbb Q\cap[0,T])\cup\{T\}$,
which are finite measurable random variables. Another such normalization
agrees on a measurable probability-one event and gives the same probability
limits. Here indistinguishability means agreement at every time on a
measurable probability-one event. No completeness or adaptedness is needed
for this convention.

1. **Existence and value of the covariation.** We say that the **quadratic
   covariation $[X,Y]$ exists on $[0,T]$** when there is a real process
   $t\mapsto[X,Y]_t$ of real random variables with almost-sure continuous
   paths on $[0,T]$ such that for *every* deterministic partition
   sequence $(\pi_n)$ of $[0,T]$ with mesh tending to $0$ both families
   converge to it uniformly in probability on $[0,T]$:
   $$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\bigl|S^{\mathrm{step}}_n(t)-[X,Y]_t\bigr|\longrightarrow0, \qquad \sup_{0\le t\le T}\bigl|S^{\mathrm{part}}_n(t)-[X,Y]_t\bigr|\longrightarrow0,$$
   the convergence being convergence in probability
   [[def-convergence-in-probability]]. The two displayed requirements are part
   of one condition: the same process $[X,Y]$ must arise for every admissible
   sequence and for both conventions. When the condition holds we call
   $[X,Y]_t$ the **quadratic covariation of $X$ and $Y$ at time $t$**, and we
   write $[X]:=[X,X]$ and call it the **quadratic variation of $X$**. For two candidate limits $U,V$, fix a deterministic dyadic partition
   sequence. The triangle inequality bounds $\sup_t|U_t-V_t|$ by the sum
   of their uniform errors against its partial sums. For each
   $\varepsilon>0$ the probability that this supremum exceeds
   $\varepsilon$ is at most the sum of the two error probabilities at
   $\varepsilon/2$, and hence is zero. Taking $\varepsilon=1/j$,
   $j\ge1$, proves uniqueness on one measurable probability-one event; the definition is applied
   separately on each finite horizon, and when the covariations on all
   horizons are compatible we write the resulting process on $[0,\infty)$
   again as $[X,Y]$.

2. **Symmetry and polarization.** Exchanging the two factors does not change
   the definition, so $[X,Y]=[Y,X]$ whenever either side exists. The
   identities
   $$[X+Y]=[X]+2[X,Y]+[Y],\qquad [X-Y]=[X]-2[X,Y]+[Y]$$
   hold on the domain where all covariations appearing in them exist: the
   cross-increment sums are bilinear in the pair, so the displayed identities
   are exact at the level of partial sums for every partition, and probability
   limits pass through finite algebraic identities. In particular
   $[X,Y]=\tfrac12\bigl([X+Y]-[X]-[Y]\bigr)$ and
   $4[X,Y]=[X+Y]-[X-Y]$ on that domain.

3. **Bilinearity and insensitivity to constants.** If the covariations
   $[X_1,Y]$, $[X_2,Y]$ and $[X_1+X_2,Y]$ exist on $[0,T]$, then
   $[X_1+X_2,Y]=[X_1,Y]+[X_2,Y]$ there, and $[cX,Y]=c[X,Y]$ for real $c$;
   moreover $[X+c,Y]=[X,Y]$ for every real constant $c$, because the
   increments of a constant process are zero. These are again exact
   identities of partial sums plus uniqueness of limits.

4. **Zero covariation with a continuous finite-variation process.** Let
   $A=(A_t)$ be continuous on a full-measure event and suppose, for every
   $\omega$ in that event, that $t\mapsto A_t(\omega)$ has bounded variation
   on every finite interval in the sense of
   [[def-bounded-variation-and-total-variation]]. Then for
   each $T$ and each admissible partition sequence, the cross sums of $A$
   against any continuous process $Y$ satisfy
   $$\Bigl|\sum_k\bigl(A_{s_k}-A_{s_{k-1}}\bigr)\bigl(Y_{s_k}-Y_{s_{k-1}}\bigr)\Bigr| \le\Bigl(\max_k\sup_{u,v\in[s_{k-1},s_k]}|Y_u-Y_v|\Bigr)\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(A),$$
   because every sum of absolute $A$-increments is bounded by the path's total
   variation on $[0,T]$; the
   maximum tends to $0$ along vanishing meshes by uniform continuity of the
   continuous path $Y$ on the compact interval $[0,T]$. Hence $[A,Y]$ exists
   and equals the zero process for every such $A$ and every continuous $Y$,
   and in particular $[A,A']=0$ for two such processes. In the notation of the
   page this says that **continuous finite-variation parts contribute nothing
   to quadratic covariation**.

5. **Scope and choice.** The inputs and candidate limits have measurable
   fixed-time values and almost-sure continuous paths. The normalization above
   makes the uniform errors real random variables, as required by
   [[def-convergence-in-probability]]. No filtration or adaptedness is used.
   The algebra in clauses 2--3 passes to limits by the uniform triangle
   inequality and the union bound. In clause 4 the same estimate holds for
   every partial sum, including its terminal partial increment, because its
   intervals are disjoint; it thus proves uniform convergence to zero on the
   common continuity event. For each epsilon, the measurable events that some
   error after index n exceeds epsilon decrease to a null event; continuity
   from above of probability gives convergence in probability. Uniform
   continuity is justified by the choice-free finite-cover argument in
   [[def-quadratic-variation-along-a-partition-sequence]]. The partitions are
   given and normalization uses a finite intersection of supplied full-measure
   events, so no choice axiom is used. Existence for Brownian Ito processes is
   a separate theorem, not a presupposition of this definition.

## Statement

Let $m,r\ge1$, and let $A\in\mathbb R^m$ and $B,C\in\mathbb R^r$ have a joint Lebesgue density. Suppose this joint density factors as
$$p_{A,B,C}(a,b,c)=p_A(a)f(b-c)p_C(c)$$
almost everywhere, where $p_A$, $f$, and $p_C$ are probability densities on $\mathbb R^m$, $\mathbb R^r$, and $\mathbb R^r$, respectively. Then $D=B-C$ is independent of $A$, has density $f$, and the joint density of $(A,D)$ is $p_A(a)f(d)$.

## Statement references

[Anderson, Lemma 4, printed pp. 320–321](https://eva.fcien.udelar.edu.uy/pluginfile.php/166428/mod_resource/content/1/1982_andersonREVERSE-TIME%20DIFFUSION%20EQUATION%20MODELS.pdf): states the subtraction factorization used to prove independence of a reverse-noise increment.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the joint-density factorization in the statement, translation invariance of Lebesgue measure, and Tonelli's theorem.

[F1] Translation by a fixed vector preserves Lebesgue measure, hence the change of variables $b=d+c$ has Jacobian one. [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]

[F2] The nonnegative density can be integrated in successive variables, and the resulting section integrals are measurable. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

## Proof
1.1 Change variables $d=b-c$ in the joint density. For nonnegative Borel test functions, translation invariance [F1] gives $\displaystyle p_{A,D,C}(a,d,c)=p_{A,B,C}(a,d+c,c)=p_A(a)f(d)p_C(c),$ with no Jacobian factor. [F1]

2.1 Integrating this joint density over $c$ and using $\int p_C(c)dc=1$, Tonelli [F2] yields $p_{A,D}(a,d)=p_A(a)f(d)$. Its marginals are $p_A$ and $f$, so the product identity proves independence and identifies the density of $D$. [F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(M_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a continuous adapted $d$-dimensional local martingale with $M_0=0$. Let $(\sigma_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a continuous adapted process of invertible $d\times d$ matrices such that $\|\sigma_t^{-1}\|\le C$ for a deterministic finite constant $C$, and suppose every entry of $\sigma$ is locally square-integrable in time almost surely. Write $[M^i,M^j]$ for the continuous bracket characterized by the local-martingale property of $M^iM^j-[M^i,M^j]$, and assume
$$[M^i,M^j]_t=\int_0^t(\sigma_s\sigma_s^{\mathsf T})_{ij}\,ds\qquad(1\le i,j\le d).$$
Then the stochastic integral $B_t=\int_0^t\sigma_s^{-1}\,dM_s$, constructed as the localized $L^2$ limit of left-step sums, has a continuous version with $[B^i,B^j]_t=\delta_{ij}t$. Consequently $B$ is a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to the given filtration.

## Statement references

[Vector Lévy characterization](https://diamhomes.ewi.tudelft.nl/~avandervaart/books/stochint.pdf): identifies a continuous local martingale with identity bracket as Brownian motion; the local proof below supplies the inverse-matrix integral construction.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the filtered probability space and processes in the statement, the Axiom of Choice, the elementary definition of stochastic integration by predictable step sums, the $L^2$ martingale maximal inequality, and completeness of $L^2$.

[A1] The vector Lévy characterization requires AC; a continuous adapted local martingale starting at zero with covariations $[B^i,B^j]_t=\delta_{ij}t$ is standard vector Brownian motion, including independence of each increment from the earlier sigma-algebra. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[cor-vector-levy-characterization]]

[F1] An adapted continuous process is predictable, so the continuous matrix process $H_t=\sigma_t^{-1}$ and its bounded left-step approximations are admissible predictable integrands. [[lem-adapted-continuous-processes-are-progressively-measurable]] [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]

[F2] For a square-integrable martingale, Doob's $L^2$ inequality bounds the expected squared path supremum by four times the terminal second moment; $L^2$ is complete and the continuous-time supremum follows by applying the discrete inequality on finite rational grids and taking their increasing union. [[thm-doob-lp-maximal-inequality]] [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]]

[F3] Conditional expectation is an $L^1$ contraction, so martingale identities pass to $L^1$ limits. [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]

[F4] A continuous local martingale has continuous covariations, and each product minus its covariation is a local martingale. For bounded continuous adapted integrands, left-step sums define the stochastic integral and its bracket is the corresponding integral against the martingale bracket. [[lem-continuous-local-martingale-quadratic-variation]]

[F5] Under AC a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion exists on an auxiliary probability space, and the product of the original and auxiliary probability spaces carries the product probability measure with independent coordinate factors. [[cor-existence-and-scaling-of-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]

[F6] A standard Brownian motion, viewed as a Brownian Itô process with zero drift and identity dispersion, has covariations $[\bar B^i,\bar B^j]_t=\delta_{ij}t$. [[thm-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]]

## Proof
**Given:** AC, $M$, and $\sigma$ as in the statement. Put $H=\sigma^{-1}$ and localize at stopping times $\tau_n$ for which $M^{\tau_n}$ is square-integrable and $E\operatorname{tr}[M]_{T\wedge\tau_n}<\infty$; such a sequence exists by the local-martingale and local-square-integrability hypotheses. On $[0,T\wedge\tau_n]$, use deterministic partitions with mesh tending to zero and the left-step processes $H^{(m)}_s=H_{t_k}$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$, stopped at $\tau_n$.

1.1 Each $H^{(m)}$ is bounded and predictable by [F1]. For a bounded predictable step matrix $G$, define $I^G_t=\sum_kG_{t_k}(M_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-M_{t\wedge t_k})$, with the final interval stopped at $\tau_n$. Expanding the finite sum, using the martingale increment identities and product-compensator identity [F4], gives $\displaystyle E|I^G_T|^2=E\int_0^{T\wedge\tau_n}\operatorname{tr}(G_s\,d[M]_s\,G_s^{\mathsf T}).$ For two such integrands the same identity applies to their difference; Doob's inequality [F2] therefore bounds $E\sup_{t\le T}|I^{H^{(m)}}_t-I^{H^{(k)}}_t|^2$ by four times the displayed energy of $H^{(m)}-H^{(k)}$. The latter tends to zero: continuity gives uniform pathwise convergence of the left-step matrices to $H$, while $\|H^{(m)}-H^{(k)}\|\le2C$ and the stopped bracket has integrable trace, so dominated convergence applies. The Cauchy bound for the path suprema gives a uniform-in-probability limit. Choose a subsequence whose successive expected squared sup errors are at most $2^{-4k}$; Markov's inequality and the union bound show that it converges uniformly almost surely, giving a continuous adapted version $B^{(n)}$ on the stopped interval. [F1, F4, F2, F3]

2.1 For a bounded step integrand, quadratic sums on each step interval are the corresponding fixed linear combinations of the sums for $M$; the covariation limit [F4] therefore gives $[I^G]=\int G\,d[M]\,G^{\mathsf T}$. The product-compensator identity [F4] says each pair of coordinates of $I^G$ has product minus this bracket a martingale. The $L^2$ convergence in step 1.1 gives $L^1$ convergence of products by Cauchy–Schwarz, and the integrals of brackets converge in $L^1$ by dominated convergence. Hence the limit has bracket $\displaystyle [B^{(n)}]_t=\int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}H_s\,d[M]_s\,H_s^{\mathsf T}.$ The stopped constructions agree on overlapping stopped intervals because their defining sums agree there; letting $n\to\infty$ defines the continuous local martingale $B=\int H\,dM$ on $[0,T]$ with this bracket. [F4, step 1.1, F2, F3]

3.1 Substituting $H=\sigma^{-1}$ and the bracket from the statement gives $\displaystyle [B]_t=\int_0^t\sigma_s^{-1}\sigma_s\sigma_s^{\mathsf T}(\sigma_s^{-1})^{\mathsf T}\,ds=tI_d.$ Thus $B_0=0$, $B$ is continuous and adapted, and its coordinate brackets are $[B^i,B^j]_t=\delta_{ij}t$ on the finite interval $[0,T]$. [step 2.1]

4.1 The result [A1] is stated for a process and clock on $[0,\infty)$, so extend the finite-horizon process. First, each coordinate $B^i$ is a true square-integrable martingale on $[0,T]$: for the stopping times $\rho_n=\inf\{t\le T:|B^i_t|\ge n\}\wedge T$, the partition-increment definition gives $[B^{i,\rho_n}]_t=[B^i]_{t\wedge\rho_n}=t\wedge\rho_n$. Thus the stopped coordinate and its square minus $t\wedge\rho_n$ are bounded local martingales by [F4], hence martingales. Therefore $E|B^i_{t\wedge\rho_n}|^2=E(t\wedge\rho_n)\le T$. Continuity makes $\rho_n=T$ eventually almost surely; the stopped variables converge almost surely to $B^i_t$ and are uniformly integrable by their uniform $L^2$ bound. Passing the stopped martingale identities to the $L^1$ limit proves the claim. [F4, step 3.1]

4.2 Take an auxiliary standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion $\bar B$ independent of the original space on the product probability space [F5]. Let $\bar{\mathcal F}_s$ be its usual augmented natural filtration. Set $\widehat{\mathcal F}_t=\mathcal F_t\otimes\{\varnothing,\bar\Omega\}$ for $0\le t\le T$ and $\widehat{\mathcal F}_t=\mathcal F_T\otimes\bar{\mathcal F}_{t-T}$ for $t>T$. Define $\widehat B_t=B_t$ for $t\le T$ and $\widehat B_t=B_T+\bar B_{t-T}$ for $t>T$. The finite-horizon martingale property from step 4.1, independence in the product space, and the martingale property of $\bar B$ show by conditioning separately on intervals before, after, and across $T$ that $\widehat B$ is a continuous martingale adapted to $(\widehat{\mathcal F}_t)_{t\ge0}$. [F5, step 4.1]

4.3 For $t\le T$ the covariations of $\widehat B$ are those of $B$. For $t>T$, split any deterministic vanishing-mesh partition at $T$. The portions before and after $T$ converge to $[B]_T=TI_d$ and $[\bar B]_{t-T}=(t-T)I_d$ by step 3.1 and [F6]. The only cell crossing $T$ contributes cross-products of a pre-$T$ increment and a post-$T$ Brownian increment; their absolute values tend to zero by continuity of both paths. The same estimate holds for the partial-increment sums, uniformly in time. Thus $[\widehat B^i,\widehat B^j]_t=\delta_{ij}t$ for every $t\ge0$. The infinite-horizon hypotheses of [A1] now hold, so $\widehat B$ is standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to the extended filtration. Restricting its increment identities to $0\le s<t\le T$ gives that $B$ is standard Brownian motion relative to the original filtration, as required. [A1, F6, step 3.1, step 4.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ and let
$M=(M^1,\dots,M^d)$ be an adapted $\mathbb R^d$-valued process with continuous
paths such that every coordinate $M^i$ is a real continuous local martingale
relative to $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ in the sense of
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]. Suppose $M_0=0$ almost surely and
whose quadratic covariations in the sense of
[[def-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]] satisfy
$[M^i,M^j]_t=\delta_{ij}t$ for all $i,j$ and all $t\ge0$. Then $M$ is a
standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]],
and for all $0\le s<t$ the vector increment $M_t-M_s$ is independent of
$\mathcal F_s$ with law $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a filtered probability space with continuous-time filtration, an adapted $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous process $M$ whose coordinates are real continuous local martingales, with $M_0=0$ almost surely and $[M^i,M^j]_t=\delta_{ij}t$, a vector $\lambda\in\mathbb R^d$, and times $0\le s<t$.

[F1] **Martingale linearity.** Finite linear combinations of true integrable adapted martingales are martingales, by finite linearity of their event-integral identities. A true martingale is local using the deterministic localizers $\tau_k=k$. The coordinates are proved to be true martingales in step 1.1 before this observation is used. [[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]] [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]

[F2] **Bilinearity of covariation.** For continuous processes whose pairwise covariations exist the covariation is bilinear: $[X_1+X_2,Y]=[X_1,Y]+[X_2,Y]$ and $[cX,Y]=c[X,Y]$, because cross-increment sums are exactly bilinear and probability limits are unique. [[def-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]]

[F3] **Scalar characteristic exponential.** For a real continuous local martingale $N$ with $N_0=0$ almost surely and $[N]_t=t$, the characteristic-exponential lemma gives $E[e^{i\theta(N_t-N_s)}\mid\mathcal F_s]=e^{-\theta^2(t-s)/2}$. Here and throughout this proof $E[U+iV\mid\mathcal F_s]$ means $E[U\mid\mathcal F_s]+iE[V\mid\mathcal F_s]$, for real integrable $U,V$; equalities mean the two real almost-sure class identities. This is exactly the componentwise convention of the supplier. [[lem-characteristic-exponential-for-a-continuous-local-martingale-with-clock-t]] [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]

[F4] **Multivariate Fourier uniqueness and Gaussian laws.** Finite Borel measures on $\mathbb R^n$ with equal Fourier transforms are equal. The laws $N_1(0,t-s)$ and $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$ have finite second moments and mean zero. The latter law exists, can be realized as the product of independent $N(0,t-s)$ coordinates, and its Fourier transform at $\lambda$ is $e^{-(t-s)|\lambda|^2/2}$. [[cor-uniqueness-of-finite-borel-measures-from-their-fourier-transforms]] [[def-multivariate-normal-law]] [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multivariate-normal-law]] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]

[F5] **Conditional expectations and towers.** Conditional expectations are unique almost-sure classes; for $A\in\mathcal F_s$ one has $E[1_AX\mid\mathcal F_s]=1_AE[X\mid\mathcal F_s]$ and $E[1_AE[X\mid\mathcal F_s]]=E[1_AX]$; the tower property passes conditional laws from one time to an earlier time. [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]] [[thm-tower-property-of-conditional-expectation]]

[F6] **AC bookkeeping.** Choice is declared for conditional expectations, the characteristic-exponential supplier, Gaussian construction and Fourier uniqueness. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 First establish true coordinate martingales, without intersecting localizers. Apply [F3] to each $M^i$, since $[M^i]_t=t$. For $A\in\mathcal F_s$, let $\mu^i_A(C)=P(A\cap\{M^i_t-M^i_s\in C\})$. This finite positive Borel measure has transform $P(A)e^{-\theta^2(t-s)/2}$ by componentwise conditional event testing. Finite-measure Fourier uniqueness [F4] in dimension one identifies it with $P(A)N_1(0,t-s)$, including when $P(A)=0$, without normalization. With $A=\Omega$, this proves integrability and zero mean of each increment. At $s=0$, $M^i_0=0$ almost surely gives integrability of $M^i_t$; $M^i_0$ is itself integrable. Integrating the identity function against $\mu^i_A=P(A)N_1(0,t-s)$ gives $E[1_A(M^i_t-M^i_s)]=0$. The pushforward integral identity here follows first for indicators from the definition of $\mu^i_A$, then for simple functions and nonnegative increasing limits, and finally for integrable signed functions. Thus every coordinate is a true all-pairs martingale by its defining event tests. [F1, F3, F4, F5]

2.1 Fix $\lambda\in\mathbb R^d$ and put $X^\lambda_t=\sum_i\lambda_iM^i_t$. It is an integrable adapted martingale by step 1.1 and [F1], hence a local martingale, and has continuous paths on the finite intersection of the coordinate continuity events. It starts at zero almost surely. For every deterministic partition its square sums are exactly $\sum_{i,j}\lambda_i\lambda_j$ times the respective cross sums. Their uniform error is bounded by the sum of the finitely many absolute coefficients times the corresponding uniform errors. The union bound therefore proves existence, not merely a formal use of bilinearity, of $[X^\lambda]_t=|\lambda|^2t$ along every permitted sequence. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 For $\lambda\ne0$, $N^\lambda=X^\lambda/|\lambda|$ satisfies the hypotheses of [F3]. Apply its componentwise identity at frequency $\theta=|\lambda|$. This gives $E[e^{i\lambda\cdot(M_t-M_s)}\mid\mathcal F_s]=e^{-(t-s)|\lambda|^2/2}$. For $\lambda=0$ both sides are $1$. No common exceptional set for all frequencies is needed: each fixed frequency identity gives a numerical equality of event integrals. [F2, F3, F5, step 2.1]

4.1 Conditional law of the vector increment: for each $A\in\mathcal F_s$ define the finite Borel measure $Q_A(\Gamma):=E[1_A1_{\{M_t-M_s\in\Gamma\}}]$ on $\mathbb R^d$; its Fourier transform is $\int e^{i\lambda\cdot x}Q_A(dx)=E[1_Ae^{i\lambda\cdot(M_t-M_s)}]=P(A)e^{-(t-s)|\lambda|^2/2}$ by step 3.1 and [F5], which is $P(A)$ times the Fourier transform of $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$ by [F4]. By multivariate Fourier uniqueness [F4], $Q_A=P(A)N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$ for every $A\in\mathcal F_s$; in particular, with $A=\Omega$, the increment has law $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$, and with general $A$ the identity is exactly the independence of the increment from $\mathcal F_s$. [F4, F5, step 3.1]

5.1 Finite lists of increments: for $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$ the increments $M_{t_j}-M_{t_{j-1}}$ are independent with laws $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$. Induction on $n$: the case $n=1$ is step 4.1; given the claim for $n$ increments, the increment at $t_{n+1}$ has conditional law $N_d(0,(t_{n+1}-t_n)I_d)$ given $\mathcal F_{t_n}$ and is independent of $\mathcal F_{t_n}$ by step 4.1 applied with $s=t_n$, hence independent of the sigma-algebra generated by the earlier increments, and [F5] multiplies the joint law. [F5, step 4.1]

6.1 Conclusion and boundary cases: $M$ is adapted, continuous, starts at $0$ almost surely, and its finite-dimensional increment laws are those of a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion by step 5.1; this is precisely the defining increment condition, so $M$ is a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion with the stated filtration property. For $d=1$ the same Fourier event-test argument gives the scalar characterization; for $\lambda=0$ the linear combination is the zero process and the identity is trivial; the coordinate increments at $s=t$ are zero with law $N(0,0)$; the hypothesis $\delta_{ij}t$ excludes degenerate covariance matrices, and no independence of the coordinates is assumed in the proof — the Brownian definition derives it from the verified vector increment laws; and AC has the uses declared in [F6]. [F3, F4, F6, step 5.1] ∎



## Source notes

Van der Vaart states the multivariate Lévy characterization as Exercise 6.5, derived from the scalar theorem. The proof above uses the Cramér--Wold style reduction through linear functionals and multivariate Fourier uniqueness, which is the standard route when the exercise is not proved in the source. To avoid an unproved stopping assertion when combining coordinate localizers, the proof first derives true coordinate martingales from their unit clocks and then uses ordinary finite linearity.

## Statement

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$, and let $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a real process
that satisfies $X_t:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $t\ge0$, and has
continuous paths, in the strong sense that $s\mapsto X_s(\omega)$ is continuous
on $[0,\infty)$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$. Then $X$ is progressively
measurable and predictable relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ in the sense of
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]], including at time
zero under the generator convention $\{0\}\times A$, $A\in\mathcal F_0$. No
choice principle is used. Here a filtration means an increasing family of
sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$. The fixed-time measurability hypothesis
is the adaptedness terminology of clause 1 of
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]; only that clause is
used, not its conditional-expectation or martingale interface and its Choice
assumption.

If instead the paths are continuous only on an event $A\in\mathcal F$ with
$P(A)=1$, the conclusion holds for the modification that is set equal to $0$
off $A$ provided $A\in\mathcal F_0$; without such a measurability assumption on
the continuity event no predictability claim is made, because predictability
is a property of the given joint map.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** a probability space with a filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$, a real adapted process $X$ with continuous paths everywhere, a horizon $T>0$, and for $n\ge1$ the dyadic grid $t_k=kT/2^n$, $0\le k\le 2^n$.

[F1] $X$ is adapted: $X_u$ is $\mathcal F_u$-measurable for every $u\ge0$; in particular $X_u$ is $\mathcal F_T$-measurable for $u\le T$. [[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]

[F2] Each rectangle $C\times A$, where $C\in\mathcal B([0,T])$ and $A\in\mathcal F_u$ for some $u\le T$, belongs to $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F_T$, since $\mathcal F_u\subseteq\mathcal F_T$. Finite unions of these rectangles also belong to that sigma-algebra. [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]

[F3] A pointwise limit of measurable functions into $\mathbb R$ is measurable; the same theorem applied coordinatewise gives measurability of limits of jointly measurable maps. [[thm-sequential-suprema-infima-limsup-liminf-and-pointwise-limits-are-measurable]]

[F4] The generators of the predictable sigma-algebra are the sets $(s,u]\times A$ with $A\in\mathcal F_s$ and the time-zero sets $\{0\}\times A$ with $A\in\mathcal F_0$. The set $[0,T]\times\Omega$ is predictable, being the union of the generator $(0,T]\times\Omega$ and the time-zero generator $\{0\}\times\Omega$. [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $n\ge1$ and define, for $(s,\omega)\in[0,T]\times\Omega$, $$H^n_s(\omega):=\sum_{k=0}^{2^n-1}X_{t_k}(\omega)\,1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}(s)+X_0(\omega)\,1_{\{0\}}(s).$$ For a Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ the preimage is $\{H^n\in B\}=\bigl(\{0\}\times\{X_0\in B\}\bigr)\cup\bigcup_{k=0}^{2^n-1}\bigl((t_k,t_{k+1}]\times\{X_{t_k}\in B\}\bigr)$, a finite union of measurable rectangles of $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F_T$, since $X_{t_k}$ is $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable and $\mathcal F_{t_k}\subseteq\mathcal F_T$. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 Each $H^n$ is measurable for $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F_T$, and for every $(s,\omega)$ the identity $H^n_s(\omega)\to X_s(\omega)$ holds: at $s=0$ both sides equal $X_0(\omega)$, and for $s\in(0,T]$ the left endpoints $t_k$ of the dyadic intervals containing $s$ tend to $s$, so path continuity gives $X_{t_k}(\omega)\to X_s(\omega)$. [step 1.1, given]

2.2 Each $H^n$ is predictable: the preimage formula of step 1.1 exhibits each Borel inverse image as a finite union of generators of the predictable sigma-algebra, since $X_{t_k}$ is $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable and each interval $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ is a generator interval, while the time-zero term is $\{0\}\times\{X_0\in B\}$ with $\{X_0\in B\}\in\mathcal F_0$. [F1, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 By [F3] the pointwise limit $X$ restricted to $[0,T]\times\Omega$ is $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F_T$-measurable; $T>0$ was arbitrary, so $X$ is progressively measurable. [F3, step 2.1]

3.2 For each fixed $T$ the restriction of $X$ to $[0,T]\times\Omega$ is a pointwise limit of the predictable processes $H^n$ restricted to $[0,T]$, hence is predictable on that horizon by [F3]; and the horizon-$T$ pieces assemble to a globally predictable process because $[0,T]\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ and a set is predictable as soon as all its intersections with the countably many sets $[0,m]\times\Omega$, $m\ge1$, are. [F3, F4, step 2.2]

4.1 Collecting steps 3.1 and 3.2, an adapted process with everywhere continuous paths is progressively measurable and predictable. The time-zero case is included: $H^n_0=X_0$ at every stage and the generator $\{0\}\times A$, $A\in\mathcal F_0$, was used in step 2.2. For the final statement about $A\in\mathcal F_0$, the map $Y_t=X_t1_A$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable (its Borel inverse images are $(A\cap\{X_t\in B\})\cup(A^c\text{ if }0\in B)$), has continuous paths everywhere, and agrees with $X$ on $A$. Apply the conclusion to $Y$. No grid point, approximant or limit in the argument is chosen: the dyadic grids and the left endpoints are fixed functions of $n$, and pointwise limits are unique. [step 3.1, step 3.2, given] ∎

## Source notes

The approximation is the standard dyadic-step argument of van der Vaart, Section 5.1; continuous adapted processes generate the predictable sigma-algebra, and the left-continuous staircase approximants are predictable by construction. The time-zero section uses exactly the generators $\{0\}\times A$, $A\in\mathcal F_0$. The proof explicitly supplies the fixed-time measurable maps and does not invoke any conditional-expectation existence theorem.

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.
