## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be finite.

1. A standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion exists: one may take $d$
   independent copies of the constructed one-dimensional Brownian path and
   assemble them coordinatewise.
2. If $B$ is any standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion and $c>0$, then
   $$Y_t=c^{-1/2}B_{ct},\qquad t\ge0,$$
   is again standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion. Moreover, the random
   elements $B$ and $Y$ have the same law on $(\mathbb R^d)^{[0,\infty)}$
   equipped with its cylinder sigma-algebra.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a finite integer $d\ge1$, and, for the scaling assertion, a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion $B$ and a real $c>0$.

[F1] Under AC, standard one-dimensional Brownian motion exists, and its zero-repaired path random element has Wiener law on $C([0,\infty),\mathbb R)$; under Wiener measure the coordinate process has all Brownian finite-dimensional laws. The Borel sigma-algebra of this path space is generated by its evaluations. [[thm-existence-of-continuous-brownian-motion]] [[def-wiener-measure-on-continuous-path-space]] [[lem-borel-sigma-algebra-of-continuous-path-space-is-generated-by-coordinates]]

[F2] Under countable choice and dependent choice, every probability law is the common law of a countable independent family of random elements. AC supplies both required choice principles. [[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]] [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]]

[F3] A vector process is standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion exactly when its coordinate processes, regarded as cylinder-space random elements, are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]

[F4] For $c>0$, the scaled process $t\mapsto c^{-1/2}X_{ct}$ is standard one-dimensional Brownian motion whenever $X$ is. Measurable coordinatewise maps preserve independence. [[thm-brownian-scaling]] [[lem-measurable-functions-preserve-independence]]

[F5] Finite-coordinate cylinders generate the arbitrary product cylinder sigma-algebra and form a pi-system. A measurable random element has a probability law, and two finite measures agreeing on a generating pi-system and on the whole space are equal. [[def-coordinate-maps-and-cylinder-sigma-algebra]] [[lem-finite-coordinate-cylinders-form-a-pi-system]] [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] [[lem-finite-measure-uniqueness-on-a-pi-system]]

[F6] AC is the only ambient choice assumption. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** constructive.

1.1 Let $\mathsf W$ be Wiener measure on $C=C([0,\infty),\mathbb R)$ from [F1]. By [F2], on some probability space there is a countable independent family $(X_\alpha)_{\alpha\ge1}$ of $C$-valued random elements, each with law $\mathsf W$. Retain its first $d$ members. [F1, F2, construct]

1.2 For the scaling assertion, put $I=[0,\infty)$ and define $T_c:\mathbb R^I\to\mathbb R^I$ by $(T_cf)(t)=c^{-1/2}f(ct)$. This map is cylinder-measurable: the inverse image of a finite-coordinate cylinder supported on $F$ is a finite-coordinate cylinder supported on $cF$, with its base pulled back by coordinatewise scalar multiplication. [F5, construct]

2.1 Define $\widehat B_t^\alpha=\pi_t(X_\alpha)$ and $\widehat B_t=(\widehat B_t^1,\ldots,\widehat B_t^d)$ for $1\le\alpha\le d$ and $t\ge0$. Every $X_\alpha(\omega)$ is a continuous path. Its finite evaluation laws are Brownian by [F1], so $\widehat B^\alpha$ is standard one-dimensional Brownian motion, with the whole sample space as a continuity event and with its initial and increment laws supplied by $\mathsf W$. The inclusion $J:C\to\mathbb R^{[0,\infty)}$, $J(f)=(f(t))_t$, is measurable because every target cylinder pulls back through finitely many Borel evaluation maps by [F1] and [F5]. Therefore the process random elements $J\circ X_\alpha$ are independent by [F4]. [step 1.1, F1, F4, F5, construct]

2.2 Return now to the arbitrary standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion $B$ in the scaling hypothesis. By [F3], its coordinate-process random elements $\Phi_\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_t$ are independent and each coordinate is standard one-dimensional Brownian motion. Since $(Y_t^\alpha)_t=T_c\Phi_\alpha$, [F4] and step 1.2 show that the coordinate processes of $Y$ remain independent, while scalar Brownian scaling makes every one of them standard Brownian motion. [given, F3, F4, step 1.2]

3.1 Applying the coordinate equivalence [F3] to step 2.1 makes the assembled process $\widehat B$ a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion. This proves existence and realizes it from independent copies of the constructed scalar path law. [step 2.1, F3]

3.2 The reverse direction of [F3] applied to step 2.2 shows that $Y_t=c^{-1/2}B_{ct}$ is standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion. The same common coordinate argument includes continuity at $t=0$; it is not inferred from finite-dimensional laws. [F3, step 2.2]

4.1 Any two standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motions have the same finite-dimensional laws. Indeed, on a sorted finite time grid their vector increments are mutually independent with the same respective laws $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$ by [F3]. Their joint increment laws therefore agree on measurable rectangles and hence on the finite product sigma-algebra by [F5]; the cumulative-sum map gives equality of the evaluation-vector laws. An arbitrary finite, unordered, or repeated time list is a coordinate projection of the sorted distinct-time vector, and an empty list has the unit law. Applying this to $B$ and $Y$ uses step 3.2. [F3, F5, step 3.2]

5.1 The path maps $\Theta_B,\Theta_Y:\Omega\to(\mathbb R^d)^I$ are measurable because every finite-coordinate cylinder has a measurable preimage. Their laws are probabilities by [F5]. Step 4.1 makes those laws agree on all finite-coordinate cylinders, a generating pi-system, and their total masses are both one. Finite-measure uniqueness in [F5] therefore gives $\mathcal L(\Theta_B)=\mathcal L(\Theta_Y)$ on the full cylinder sigma-algebra. [F5, step 4.1]

6.1 The construction in steps 1.1--3.1 and the scaling and law conclusions in steps 1.2--5.1 establish both claims. When $d=1$, the construction and scaling reduce to the scalar results. The empty coordinate case $d=0$ is excluded; empty time lists and repeated times were handled in step 4.1. At $c=1$, $T_c$ is the identity, while $c=0$ is excluded because $c^{-1/2}$ is undefined and would not preserve Brownian covariance. AC is used through [F1] and [F3] for Brownian and Gaussian laws and through [F2] for the countable product; the finite truncation to $d$, fixed scaling map, and cylinder-law comparison use no further choice. Thus the required process exists and the displayed scaling has the same $d$-dimensional law. [F1, F2, F3, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 5.1, discharge-construct: step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Source notes

Durrett, printed p. 359, constructs multidimensional Brownian motion from independent scalar coordinates. Sousi, printed pp. 52--53, gives the same construction and states Brownian scaling. The proof above additionally records the whole-process cylinder-law equality and the exact path-space use of the independent-copy theorem.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a
standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion and let $X=(X^1,\dots,X^d)$ be an
$\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process driven by $B$,
$$dX^i_t=b^i_t\,dt+\sum_{k=1}^m\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its
progressive representative, usual-filtration, almost-sure coefficient-integrability and
vector-increment independence hypotheses. Indistinguishability and
measurable suprema use the full-event normalization convention of
[[def-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]].
All coefficient path integrals below use zero outside the common measurable
probability-one event on which every drift is locally absolutely integrable
and every diffusion entry is locally square-integrable. Such an event is
obtained by intersecting the finitely many coefficient conditions at integer
horizons; its complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions.
On this event, Cauchy–Schwarz makes every product
$\sigma^{ik}\sigma^{jk}$ locally integrable. The normalized covariance
integrals therefore have finite continuous paths and measurable time sections.

1. **Existence and value.** For every pair $i,j$ the quadratic covariation
   $[X^i,X^j]$ exists on every finite horizon in the sense of
   [[def-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]], and for every
   $t\ge0$
   $$[X^i,X^j]_t=\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s\,ds =\int_0^t(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s\,ds$$
   up to indistinguishability, where $(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}\sigma^{jk}$.
   In particular the real continuous Brownian Ito process
   $X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s$ has
   $[X]_t=\int_0^t\sigma_s^2\,ds$.

2. **Finite-variation parts contribute nothing.** If $A$ is a continuous
   process whose paths are absolutely continuous,
   $A_t=\int_0^ta_s\,ds$, and $Y$ is any continuous process, then the
   covariation of $A$ with $Y$ exists and is the zero process. Consequently in
   the decomposition $X^i=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_k\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s$
   the drift part contributes zero cross sums against every continuous
   process, including against the driving Brownian coordinates.
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, (H), an $m$-dimensional standard Brownian motion $B$, an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process $X$ with drift $b=(b^i)$ and dispersion matrix $\sigma=(\sigma^{ik})$, a finite horizon $T>0$, and an arbitrary deterministic partition sequence $(\pi_n)$ of $[0,T]$ with mesh $\delta_n\to0$.
 
[F1] **Class decomposition.** $X^i_t=X^i_0+A^i_t+M^i_t$ with the pathwise Lebesgue integral $A^i_t=\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds$ and the localized Ito integrals $M^{ik}:=\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s$, $M^i:=\sum_kM^{ik}$; every $M^{ik}$ is a continuous adapted process, unique up to indistinguishability, and $A^i$ is continuous and pathwise absolutely continuous. [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]] [[thm-localized-ito-integral]] [[def-continuity-real]]
 
[F2] **Definition of covariation.** $[U,V]$ exists on $[0,T]$ when the step-convention and partial-increment cross sums of a continuous pair $(U,V)$ converge, uniformly in probability on $[0,T]$, to one process for every deterministic vanishing-mesh partition sequence, and the object is unique when it exists; cross sums are bilinear in the pair, so exact partial-sum identities pass to limits, finite-variation parts contribute zero, and constants are invisible. [[def-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]] [[def-convergence-in-probability]]
 
[F3] **Scalar quadratic variation.** For a locally square-integrable predictable $H$, the step-convention sums of the local martingale $\int H\,dB$ satisfy $\sup_{t\le T}\bigl|\sum_{j:\,s_{j+1}\le t}\bigl(\int_{(s_j,s_{j+1}]}H\,dB\bigr)^2-\int_0^tH^2\,ds\bigr|\to0$ in probability, and the partial-increment convention has the same limit. [[thm-quadratic-variation-of-an-ito-integral]] [[def-quadratic-variation-along-a-partition-sequence]]
 
[F4] **Localized-integral interfaces.** For a locally square-integrable predictable $G$: the partial integral over $(u,v]$ is $\int 1_{(u,v]}G\,dB$; for finite energy, $E(\int_{(u,v]}G\,dB)^2=E\int_u^vG^2\,ds$ (isometry, applied to the restriction), and the integral vanishes on integrands that vanish $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-a.e.; the stopping identity identifies $(G\cdot B)_{t\wedge\sigma}$ with the integral of $G1_{(0,\sigma]}$; on the event $\{\tau_N\ge T\}$ the localized integral agrees with its stopped finite-energy piece; and continuous versions are indistinguishable. [[thm-localized-ito-integral]] [[thm-stopping-an-ito-integral]] [[thm-ito-isometry-and-linearity-in-predictable-l2]] [[thm-ito-integral-process-has-a-continuous-martingale-version]] [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]]
 
[F5] **Density of elementary integrands.** Every predictable $G$ with finite energy is a limit in $L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$ of bounded elementary predictable integrands; a bounded elementary integrand is of the form $\sum_a\xi_a1_{(t_a,t_{a+1}]}$ with $\xi_a$ bounded and $\mathcal F_{t_a}$-measurable, and its integral is the corresponding finite combination of Brownian increments. [[thm-density-of-elementary-predictable-processes-in-predictable-l2]] [[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]] [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]]
 
[F6] **Moments of ordinary Brownian sums.** For $0\le u<v$ and distinct coordinates $k\ne l$, conditional on $\mathcal F_u$ the two increments $B^k_v-B^k_u$ and $B^l_v-B^l_u$ are independent with laws $N(0,v-u)$; hence $E\bigl[(B^k_v-B^k_u)(B^l_v-B^l_u)\bigm|\mathcal F_u\bigr]=0$ and $E\bigl[(B^k_v-B^k_u)^2(B^l_v-B^l_u)^2\bigm|\mathcal F_u\bigr]=(v-u)^2$. [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] [[def-brownian-motion]] [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]
 
[F7] **Discrete martingale-difference bounds.** For square-integrable martingale differences $D_1,\dots,D_J$ with respect to a filtration: $E\bigl(\sum_{j\le J}D_j\bigr)^2=\sum_{j\le J}ED_j^2$; the process $\bigl(\max_{j\le J}|{\sum_{i\le j}D_i}|\bigr)$ is controlled by Doob's $L^2$ inequality $E\max_{j\le J}\bigl|\sum_{i\le j}D_i\bigr|^2\le4E\bigl(\sum_{i\le J}D_i\bigr)^2$; and $P(Z>\varepsilon)\le EZ^2/\varepsilon^2$ for nonnegative $Z$, directly from $\varepsilon^2 1_{\{Z>\varepsilon\}}\le Z^2$. [[lem-martingale-differences-are-orthogonal-in-l2]] [[thm-martingales-and-martingale-differences-correspond]] [[cor-absolute-value-and-powers-of-a-martingale-are-submartingales]] [[thm-doob-lp-maximal-inequality]] [[cor-chebyshev-inequality-for-random-variables]] [[thm-tower-property-of-conditional-expectation]]
 
[F8] **Cauchy--Schwarz, for sums and for expectations.** $|\sum_ja_jb_j|\le(\sum_ja_j^2)^{1/2}(\sum_jb_j^2)^{1/2}$ for reals, and $E|UV|\le(EU^2)^{1/2}(EV^2)^{1/2}$; for $f,g\in L^2(\mu)$ the $L^2$ Cauchy--Schwarz inequality $\int|fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2$ holds. [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]] [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]
 
[F9] **Uniform continuity and the finite-variation estimate.** A continuous real function on the compact interval $[0,T]$ is uniformly continuous, so the maximal oscillation over the intervals of a vanishing-mesh partition tends to $0$; and for a pathwise absolutely continuous $A$ with $A_t=\int_0^ta_s\,ds$ one has $\sum_j|A_{s_{j+1}}-A_{s_j}|\le\int_0^T|a_s|\,ds<\infty$ for the given path. [[thm-heine-cantor-r]] [[def-continuity-real]]
 
[F10] **AC bookkeeping.** Choice is declared for the ambient conditional-expectation and $L^2$ interfaces and the density theorem; AC supplies the countably chosen elementary approximations and versions; the energy localization times are canonical. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]
 
 
 
 

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Finite-variation estimate: let $A_t=\int_0^ta_s\,ds$ be pathwise absolutely continuous and $Y$ continuous. For a partition of $[0,T]$, [F9] gives $\sum_j|A_{s_{j+1}}-A_{s_j}|\le\int_0^T|a_s|\,ds$ and $\max_j|Y_{s_{j+1}}-Y_{s_j}|\le\max_j\sup_{u,v\in I_j}|Y_u-Y_v|\to0$ along vanishing meshes, so $\bigl|\sum_j(A_{s_{j+1}}-A_{s_j})(Y_{s_{j+1}}-Y_{s_j})\bigr|\le\bigl(\max_j\sup_{u,v\in I_j}|Y_u-Y_v|\bigr)\int_0^T|a_s|\,ds\to0$ almost surely; the partial-increment convention obeys the same bound, so the cross sums of $(A,Y)$ converge to $0$ for every admissible sequence and $[A,Y]=0$. [F2, F9, given]

1.2 Bilinearity: for continuous $X_1,X_2,Y$ whose displayed covariations exist, the partial sums satisfy $\sum_j\Delta(X_1+X_2)_j\Delta Y_j=\sum_j\Delta X_{1,j}\Delta Y_j+\sum_j\Delta X_{2,j}\Delta Y_j$ exactly, and $[cX_1,Y]=c[X_1,Y]$ likewise; passing to the common probability limit gives $[X_1+X_2,Y]=[X_1,Y]+[X_2,Y]$ and $[cX_1,Y]=c[X_1,Y]$. By induction the same holds for finite sums, and by symmetry also in the second slot. [F2, given]

1.3 Same coordinate, general integrands: let $H,K$ be locally square-integrable predictable and $M_H=\int H\,dB$, $M_K=\int K\,dB$. For every interval $I=(u,v]$ of a partition, linearity of the integral gives $\int_I(H+K)\,dB=\int_IH\,dB+\int_IK\,dB$, hence the exact identity $\Delta M_H\Delta M_K=\tfrac12\bigl[(\Delta M_H+\Delta M_K)^2-(\Delta M_H)^2-(\Delta M_K)^2\bigr]$ with $\Delta M_H+\Delta M_K=\int_I(H+K)\,dB$. Summing over the partition and applying the scalar quadratic-variation limit [F3] to the three locally square-integrable integrands $H+K,H,K$ yields convergence in probability, uniformly in $t$, of the cross sums to $\tfrac12\bigl[\int_0^t(H+K)^2ds-\int_0^tH^2ds-\int_0^tK^2ds\bigr]=\int_0^tHK\,ds$, for the step convention; the partial-increment convention has the same limit by [F3]. Hence $\bigl[\int H\,dB,\int K\,dB\bigr]_t=\int_0^tHK\,ds$ for locally square-integrable predictable $H,K$. [F3, F4, given]

1.4 Distinct coordinates, bounded elementary integrands: take $k\ne l$, and a common elementary coefficient partition for $H,K$ with $L$ blocks and an a.s. deterministic coefficient bound $C$. Refine $\pi_n$ by that fixed partition, obtaining $0=r_0<\cdots<r_J=T$ with mesh at most $\delta_n$. On $(r_j,r_{j+1}]$ the coefficients $\alpha_j,\beta_j$ are $\mathcal F_{r_j}$-measurable and bounded by $C$. The refined cross sum has increments $D_j=\alpha_j\beta_j(B^k_{r_{j+1}}-B^k_{r_j})(B^l_{r_{j+1}}-B^l_{r_j})$, $0\le j<J$. By [F6], their conditional means given $\mathcal F_{r_j}$ vanish and $ED_j^2\le C^4(r_{j+1}-r_j)^2$. Thus $S_q=\sum_{0\le j<q}D_j$, $0\le q\le J$, is a square-integrable martingale with $S_0=0$. Orthogonality and discrete Doob, extending it constantly after $J$ if necessary, give $E\max_{q\le J}|S_q|^2\le4C^4\delta_n T$. Therefore the refined step cross sums tend uniformly to zero in probability. The coefficients may depend on both Brownian coordinates; only the vector increment's independence of the past is used. [F4, F5, F6, F7]

1.5 For any continuous pair of integral paths $U,V$, the partial-increment cross sum differs from the step cross sum by $(U_t-U_{s_{j(t)}})(V_t-V_{s_{j(t)}})$ on its final interval. Its supremum is bounded by $\omega_U(\delta_n)\omega_V(\delta_n)\to0$ on their common continuity event. The measurable-supremum convention of [F2] makes this an almost-sure error bound and therefore an error tending to zero in probability. [F2, F9]

2.1 Refinement discrepancy: for sufficiently large $n$, a $\pi_n$ interval crosses at most one fixed coefficient boundary. Let $\omega_k(\delta)$ and $\omega_l(\delta)$ be the path moduli of the two Brownian coordinates on $[0,T]$. On a crossing interval, each original integral increment has absolute value at most $2C$ times its Brownian modulus, so the original cross product is bounded by $4C^2\omega_k(\delta_n)\omega_l(\delta_n)$. The two refined cross products together are bounded by $2C^2\omega_k(\delta_n)\omega_l(\delta_n)$. This also covers an intermediate time when only one refined increment has been completed. Hence the absolute difference between the original and refined step cross sums is uniformly bounded by $6LC^2\omega_k(\delta_n)\omega_l(\delta_n)$, which tends to zero almost surely by [F9]. This estimate uses interval oscillations, not the absolute full-interval increments, which could cancel. [F5, F9, step 1.4]

3.1 By steps 1.4 and 2.1 and the triangle/union bound, the original step cross sums for bounded elementary $H,K$ in distinct coordinates tend uniformly to zero in probability. Step 1.5 proves the same for partial-increment sums. Thus the two integral processes have zero covariation for every deterministic vanishing-mesh partition sequence. [F2, step 1.4, step 2.1, step 1.5]

4.1 Finite-energy approximation: write $C_n(H,K)(t)$ for the step cross sum of the two integral processes. Choose bounded elementary $H',K'$ with respective $L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$ errors at most $\eta>0$, using [F5] and [F10]. Bilinearity gives $C_n(H,K)-C_n(H',K')=C_n(H-H',K)+C_n(H',K-K')$. For either term, finite-sum Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the supremum over completed partial sums by the product of the two terminal quadratic sums' square roots. Taking expectation and using [F4], [F8] bounds the expected supremum of the difference by $\eta\|K\|_2+(\|H\|_2+\eta)\eta$, uniformly in $n$. This also covers $K=0$ and needs no bound of the form $\|K'\|_2^2\le2\|K\|_2^2$. The nonnegative indicator inequality bounds the approximation probability by this expectation divided by its error threshold. At fixed $\eta$ the elementary error vanishes by step 3.1; then let $\eta\downarrow0$. Step 1.5 handles partial increments. Thus distinct-coordinate covariation vanishes for finite-energy predictable integrands. [F4, F5, F8, F10, step 1.5, step 3.1]

5.1 Localization: let $\tau_N^H,\tau_N^K$ be the respective canonical energy stopping times, $N\ge1$, and put $\rho_N=\tau_N^H\wedge\tau_N^K$. These are nondecreasing stopping times tending to infinity almost surely, and the expected energies of both $H1_{(0,\rho_N]}$ and $K1_{(0,\rho_N]}$ are at most $N$. By [F4], on $\{\rho_N\ge T\}$ and a common probability-one agreement event the two original integrals equal their finite-energy stopped integrals on $[0,T]$. For any error threshold $\varepsilon$, the original cross-sum error probability is at most $P(\rho_N<T)$ plus the stopped cross-sum error probability. The latter tends to zero by step 4.1 for fixed $N$; the former tends to zero as $N\to\infty$. No bound on the cross sum on the exceptional event is needed. This proves zero covariation for locally square-integrable integrands in distinct coordinates, for both conventions. Positive indices are reindexed by $N=j+1$ when required. [F2, F4, step 4.1]

6.1 General matrix: $M^i=\sum_kM^{ik}$ and $M^j=\sum_lM^{jl}$ are finite sums; by the bilinearity of step 1.2 applied repeatedly, and the existence of each pairwise covariation from steps 1.3 and 5.1, $\bigl[M^i,M^j\bigr]=\sum_{k,l}\bigl[M^{ik},M^{jl}\bigr]=\sum_k\int_0^{\cdot}\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s\,ds + \sum_{k\ne l}0$, where the second sum is zero by step 5.1 applied to the locally square-integrable integrands $\sigma^{ik}$ and $\sigma^{jl}$; hence $[M^i,M^j]_t=\int_0^t(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s\,ds$. Every step was proved for an arbitrary deterministic vanishing-mesh sequence and for both conventions, so the existence clause of [F2] is met. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 5.1]

7.1 Drift parts contribute zero: the drift processes $A^i_t=\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds$ are pathwise absolutely continuous, so step 1.1 with $[F1]$ gives $[A^i,A^j]=0$ and $[A^i,Y]=0$ for every continuous $Y$, in particular for $Y=M^j$ and for $Y=B^k$. Therefore, using bilinearity [step 1.2] and $X^i=X^i_0+A^i+M^i$, $[X^i,X^j]=[A^i,A^j]+[A^i,M^j]+[M^i,A^j]+[M^i,M^j]=[M^i,M^j]=\int_0^{\cdot}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s\,ds$. This proves clause 2 of the statement for all continuous $Y$, since the estimate of step 1.1 applies to an arbitrary continuous second factor. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 6.1]

8.1 Boundary and consistency cases: for $d=1$ and $m=1$ the formula reads $[X]_t=\int_0^t\sigma_s^2ds$, and taking $H=K=1$ in step 1.3 recovers the Brownian identity $[B,B]_t=t$; if $\sigma\equiv0$, only the drift remains and its covariation is zero; if $b\equiv0$, only the drift term vanishes and the stochastic covariation generally remains nonzero (Brownian motion is the simplest example); at $t=0$ both sides vanish, since empty cross sums and empty integrals are $0$; and for a degenerate $d$-dimensional process with singular dispersion matrix the formula still holds matrix-wise, with no independence of the coordinates assumed. AC enters only through [F10], which supplies the approximations and versions; the energy stopping times are canonical. [F2, F10, step 1.3, step 6.1, step 7.1] ∎

## Source notes

Van der Vaart, Theorem 5.64, identifies covariation by partition limits; Lemma 5.77 gives the stochastic-integral covariation rule for a locally bounded predictable integrand. The arbitrary-partition, arbitrary locally square-integrable Brownian case here is proved directly by the conditional vector-increment estimate, explicit refinement error, finite-energy approximation and common localization. No independence of the general stochastic integrals is assumed.

## Statement

Let $X_t$ have continuous paths on $[0,T]$ and be Markov on $\mathbb R^d$, meaning its conditional future law given the past depends only on its current state; nonexplosive means it remains in $\mathbb R^d$ throughout this finite interval. Let it have forward generator
$$L_t\phi=b_t\cdot\nabla\phi+\tfrac12a_t:D^2\phi,$$
where $a_t=\sigma_t\sigma_t^{\mathsf T}$ is symmetric and $L_t^*r=-\partial_i(b_{t,i}r)+\tfrac12\partial_i\partial_j(a_{t,ij}r)$. Assume positive $C^{1,2}$ marginal densities $p_t$ and positive transition densities $q(s,x;t,y)$ satisfy the marginal identity and Chapman–Kolmogorov identity, and that $\partial_t p_t=L_t^*p_t$ and $\partial_tq(s,x;t,y)=L_t^{*,y}q(s,x;t,y)$ hold classically. Assume for every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ that the transition-density integrals can be differentiated in time, the resulting derivatives are integrable, and integration by parts in the state variable has no boundary term. Define $K_{u,v}$ by the Bayes-reversed kernel formula for $0\le u\le v\le T$. Then the reversed process $Y_u=X_{T-u}$ is Markov with transitions $K_{u,v}$, and for every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ and $0\le u<T$ its generator is
$$\widetilde L_u\phi(y)=\frac{L_{T-u}^*(p_{T-u}\phi)(y)-\phi(y)L_{T-u}^*p_{T-u}(y)}{p_{T-u}(y)}.$$
It solves the corresponding local martingale problem. Expanding the adjoint product rule gives
$$\widetilde L_u\phi=\widetilde b_u\cdot\nabla\phi+\tfrac12a_{T-u}:D^2\phi,\qquad \widetilde b_u=-b_{T-u}+\nabla\!\cdot a_{T-u}+a_{T-u}\nabla\log p_{T-u},$$
with $(\nabla\!\cdot a)_i=\sum_j\partial_j a_{ij}$.

## Statement references

[Anderson, Section 5, printed pp. 322–324](https://eva.fcien.edu.uy/pluginfile.php/166428/mod_resource/content/1/1982_andersonREVERSE-TIME%20DIFFUSION%20EQUATION%20MODELS.pdf): gives the reverse Kolmogorov-equation approach as context; the full kernel and martingale argument is proved here.

[Tang and Zhao, Section 2.2, PDF pp. 3–5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.07487): states the reverse-drift formula and explicitly gives a heuristic derivation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the positive density, forward equation, regularity, differentiation, and no-boundary-term hypotheses in the statement; $L^*$ is the formal adjoint of $L$ under Lebesgue integration.

[F1] The Bayes-reversed kernels are probability kernels and compose in reverse order by the forward marginal and Chapman–Kolmogorov identities. [[def-reversed-transition-kernels-for-diffusions]]

[F2] The transition density transports a test function by $P_{s,t}\phi(x)=\int q(s,x;t,y)\phi(y)dy$, and its density adjoint transports $r$ by $P^*_{s,t}r(y)=\int r(x)q(s,x;t,y)dx$. The assumed classical forward equation gives $\partial_tP^*_{s,t}r=L_t^*P^*_{s,t}r$ for the integrable densities used below.

[F3] Dominated convergence permits passage from the small-time transition quotient to its time derivative; Fubini permits the finite-time transition-density integrals to be composed. [[thm-dominated-convergence]] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

[F4] For $A_{ij}=a_{ij}p$, symmetry of $a$ and the product rule give
$$L_t^*(p\phi)-\phi L_t^*p=p\left(-b_i+\frac1p\partial_j(pa_{ij})\right)\partial_i\phi+\tfrac12pa_{ij}\partial_{ij}\phi.$$
This is an algebraic expansion of the displayed formal adjoint.

## Proof
**Given:** the process and hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Bayes' formula gives the one-step reversed conditional law: for Borel $A$, the joint density of $(X_{T-v},X_{T-u})$ is $p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)$, while the later marginal is $p_{T-u}(y)$. Their ratio is exactly $K_{u,v}(y,A)$. The kernel is normalized and composes by [F1], so the finite-dimensional reversed laws have the Markov factorization with these kernels. [F1]

1.2 Put $t=T-u$. For $h>0$ with $u+h\le T$, the transition formula gives $\displaystyle K_{u,u+h}\phi(y)=\frac{P^*_{t-h,t}(p_{t-h}\phi)(y)}{p_t(y)}.$ Expanding the numerator over the time interval of length $h$ and using $\partial_t p_t=L_t^*p_t$ yields $\displaystyle P^*_{t-h,t}(p_{t-h}\phi)=p_t\phi+h\{L_t^*(p_t\phi)-\phi L_t^*p_t\}+o(h).$ The differentiability and domination assumptions make the remainder divided by $h$ tend to zero locally in $y$. Division by $p_t(y)>0$ proves the displayed formula for $\widetilde L_u$ as the small-time generator. [F2, F3]

2.1 The reverse Chapman–Kolmogorov identity from [F1] and the local expansion in step 1.2 imply $\displaystyle K_{u,v}\phi-\phi=\int_u^vK_{u,r}(\widetilde L_r\phi)\,dr.$ Indeed, telescope over a partition $u=r_0<\cdots<r_n=v$ using $K_{u,r_{j+1}}=K_{u,r_j}K_{r_j,r_{j+1}}$; the local generator expansion gives the Riemann sums, and the stated domination permits their limit. For $s<v$, the Markov property in step 1.1 therefore gives $\displaystyle E\!\left[\phi(Y_v)-\phi(Y_s)-\int_s^v\widetilde L_r\phi(Y_r)dr\mid\mathcal G_s\right]=K_{s,v}\phi(Y_s)-\phi(Y_s)-\int_s^vK_{s,r}\widetilde L_r\phi(Y_s)dr=0.$ Thus the compensated test process is a martingale, in particular a local martingale. [F1, step 1.2, step 1.1, F3]

3.1 Expanding the adjoint in step 1.2, the drift part contributes $-p b_i\partial_i\phi$. The second-order product rule contributes $\partial_j(pa_{ij})\partial_i\phi+\tfrac12pa_{ij}\partial_{ij}\phi$ after summing and using symmetry of $a$. Divide by $p$ and use $p^{-1}\partial_j(pa_{ij})=\partial_j a_{ij}+a_{ij}\partial_j\log p$ to obtain the stated reverse drift and diffusion matrix. [step 1.2, F4] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Fix $t_0<T$, integers $d,r\ge1$, and a filtered probability space carrying a standard $r$-dimensional Brownian motion $W$. Let
$$dX_t=b(X_t,t)\,dt+\sigma(X_t,t)\,dW_t,\qquad X_t\in\mathbb R^d,$$
Assume this SDE has a unique nonexplosive strong solution, $X_{t_0}$ is almost surely bounded and independent of the Brownian process, and $a=\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T}$. Assume the coefficients and densities are smooth enough for the displayed derivatives and Itô identities to hold. Assume the marginal density $p_t(x)$ is positive wherever used and is a unique smooth solution of
$$\partial_t p_t=L_t^*p_t,\qquad L_t^*r=-\sum_i\partial_i(b_i r)+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_j(a_{ij}r).$$
Define the $r$-vector process $\widetilde W$ by $\widetilde W_{t_0}=0$ and
$$d\widetilde W_t^k=dW_t^k+c_k(X_t,t)\,dt,\qquad c_k(x,t)=p_t(x)^{-1}\sum_i\partial_i\!\left(p_t(x)\sigma_{ik}(x,t)\right).$$
Assume the augmented process $(X,\widetilde W)$ has a unique smooth joint density solving its augmented forward Kolmogorov equation for $t>t_0$, and for every $t>s\ge t_0$ its conditional joint density given $\widetilde W_s$ is the unique smooth solution of the corresponding conditional augmented equation; all displayed derivatives and density integrals are valid. Then the following hold.

1. For $t>s\ge t_0$, $X_t$ is independent of $\widetilde W_t-\widetilde W_s$, and this increment has law $N_r(0,(t-s)I_r)$.
2. Put $U=T-t_0$, $Y_u=X_{T-u}$, and $B_u=\widetilde W_{T-u}-\widetilde W_T$ for $0\le u\le U$. With $\mathcal G_u=\sigma(Y_v,B_v:0\le v\le u)$, $B$ is a standard $r$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to $(\mathcal G_u)$.
3. In the backward Itô convention, $Y$ satisfies
$$dY_u=\left[-b(Y_u,T-u)+(\nabla\!\cdot a)(Y_u,T-u)+a(Y_u,T-u)\nabla\log p_{T-u}(Y_u)\right]du+\sigma(Y_u,T-u)\,dB_u,$$
where $(\nabla\!\cdot a)_i=\sum_j\partial_j a_{ij}$. The score is asserted only where $p_{T-u}>0$; no density or score regularity beyond the stated hypotheses is implied.

## Statement references

[Anderson, Sections 3–4, printed pp. 317–322](https://eva.fcien.udelar.edu.uy/pluginfile.php/166428/mod_resource/content/1/1982_andersonREVERSE-TIME%20DIFFUSION%20EQUATION%20MODELS.pdf): states the bounded-start theorem and gives the augmented-density proof route, including the reverse-noise increment calculation and backward-Itô correction.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the strong solution and density hypotheses in the statement, and the augmented process $Z_t=(X_t,\widetilde W_t)$ whose diffusion matrix is $\Gamma(x,t)=\binom{\sigma(x,t)}{I_r}$ and whose drift is $(b(x,t),c(x,t))$.

[A1] AC is required by the multidimensional Itô and quadratic-covariation suppliers used in the backward-integral conversion. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The forward SDE has an adapted continuous strong solution; future solution segments are determined by the present state and future Brownian increments, which are independent of the present filtration. [[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]

[F2] The forward marginal density satisfies the displayed adjoint equation, and the augmented density satisfies the forward equation for drift $(b,c)$ and covariance blocks $a$, $\sigma$, $\sigma^{\mathsf T}$, and $I_r$. This is the smooth unique-density hypothesis of the statement; the operator follows from the Itô formula for $Z$.

[F3] For a smooth density $R(x,w,t)$ of $Z$, the augmented forward operator is
$$-\partial_i(b_iR)-\partial_{w_k}(c_kR)+\tfrac12\partial_i\partial_j(a_{ij}R)+\partial_i\partial_{w_k}(\sigma_{ik}R)+\tfrac12\Delta_wR.$$
The cross derivative appears because $d[X_i,\widetilde W_k]_t=\sigma_{ik}(X_t,t)dt$. [[thm-multidimensional-ito-formula-for-brownian-driven-processes]] [[thm-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]]

[F4] For $h>0$, $\varphi_h(w)=(2\pi h)^{-r/2}\exp(-|w|^2/(2h))$ is a probability density satisfying $\partial_h\varphi_h=\tfrac12\Delta_w\varphi_h$ and converging weakly to a point mass at zero as $h\downarrow0$; these identities follow by differentiating the displayed expression and the Gaussian integral.

[F5] If a conditional density has the factorization $p_{A,B\mid C}(a,b\mid c)=p_A(a)f(b-c)$ with probability densities, then $A$ is independent of $B-C$ and the latter has density $f$. [[lem-density-translation-factorization]]

[F6] Left-endpoint and right-endpoint sums against a continuous integrand differ in the limit by its quadratic covariation with the continuous semimartingale integrator. For $H_{ik}(t)=\sigma_{ik}(X_t,t)$,
$$d[H_{ik},\widetilde W^k]_t=\sum_j\partial_j\sigma_{ik}(X_t,t)\sigma_{jk}(X_t,t)\,dt,$$
by Itô's formula and the Brownian-Itô covariation formula. [[thm-multidimensional-ito-formula-for-brownian-driven-processes]] [[thm-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]]


## Proof
**Given:** the hypotheses and notation in the Statement.

1.1 For $t>t_0$ set $R(x,w,t)=p_t(x)\varphi_{t-t_0}(w)$. In [F3], the $x$-drift and $x$-diffusion terms combine to $\varphi_{t-t_0}(w)L_t^*p_t(x)$. The cross term is $\displaystyle \partial_i\partial_{w_k}(\sigma_{ik}p_t\varphi)=\partial_{w_k}\!\left(\varphi\,\partial_i(p_t\sigma_{ik})\right)=\partial_{w_k}(c_kp_t\varphi),$ which cancels the $-\partial_{w_k}(c_kR)$ term by the definition of $c_k$. The remaining $w$-diffusion term is $p_t\partial_t\varphi$, and $\partial_t p_t=L_t^*p_t$; hence the augmented equation's right side is $\partial_tR$. The initial limit is the law of $X_{t_0}$ times $\delta_0(dw)$ by [F4]. Uniqueness therefore identifies $R$ with the actual joint density of $(X_t,\widetilde W_t)$. [F3, F4, A1, F2]

1.2 The definition of $\widetilde W$ gives the forward-Itô equation $\displaystyle dX_i=\left(b_i-\sum_k\sigma_{ik}c_k\right)dt+\sum_k\sigma_{ik}\,d^{\mathrm f}\widetilde W_k.$ For $H_{ik}=\sigma_{ik}(X_t,t)$, right-endpoint sums equal left-endpoint sums plus the cross-increment sums defining $[H_{ik},\widetilde W_k]$. Their limits differ by the bracket in [F6]; consequently $\displaystyle \int_s^t H_{ik}\,d^{\mathrm f}\widetilde W_k=\int_s^t H_{ik}\,d^{\mathrm b}\widetilde W_k-\int_s^t\sum_j\partial_j\sigma_{ik}(X_r,r)\sigma_{jk}(X_r,r)\,dr,$ where the superscripts denote left-endpoint forward and right-endpoint backward Itô sums. This fixes the sign of the conversion. [F6]

2.1 Fix $s\ge t_0$ and condition on $\widetilde W_s=w_s$. Step 1.1 shows that $X_s$ has density $p_s$ independently of $\widetilde W_s$, so the conditional initial density at time $s$ is $p_s(x)\delta_{w_s}(dw)$. The candidate $R_s(x,w,t)=p_t(x)\varphi_{t-s}(w-w_s)$ has that initial limit. The calculation in step 1.1, with $\varphi_{t-s}(w-w_s)$ in place of $\varphi_{t-t_0}(w)$, proves that it solves the conditional augmented equation. By the assumed uniqueness, this is the conditional joint density of $(X_t,\widetilde W_t)$ given $\widetilde W_s=w_s$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, F4]

2.2 The resulting backward drift in the original time variable is $\displaystyle \widehat b_i=b_i-\sum_k\sigma_{ik}c_k-\sum_{j,k}\partial_j\sigma_{ik}\sigma_{jk}=b_i-\frac1{p_t}\sum_j\partial_j(p_t a_{ij}).$ Indeed, substituting $c_k=p_t^{-1}\sum_j\partial_j(p_t\sigma_{jk})$ and applying the product rule expands the last numerator as $\sum_k\sigma_{ik}\partial_j(p_t\sigma_{jk})+p_t\sum_{j,k}(\partial_j\sigma_{ik})\sigma_{jk}$. [F6, step 1.2]

3.1 For $s>t_0$, multiplying the conditional density in step 2.1 by the density $\varphi_{s-t_0}(w_s)$ from step 1.1 gives the joint density of $(X_t,\widetilde W_t,\widetilde W_s)$. Apply [F5] with $A=X_t$, $B=\widetilde W_t$, $C=\widetilde W_s$, and $f=\varphi_{t-s}$. For $s=t_0$, the same conclusion follows directly from step 2.1 with the deterministic value $\widetilde W_{t_0}=0$. Thus $X_t$ and $\widetilde W_t-\widetilde W_s$ are independent and the increment has law $N_r(0,(t-s)I_r)$, proving claim 1. [step 2.1, step 1.1, F5]

4.1 For $0\le u<v\le U$, put $s=T-v$ and $t=T-u$. Then $B_v-B_u=-(\widetilde W_t-\widetilde W_s)$, so by claim 1 this increment has law $N_r(0,(v-u)I_r)$. It is measurable with respect to the forward filtration at time $t$. Future $X$ and $\widetilde W$ segments are measurable functions of $X_t$ and the future Brownian increments of $W$, by strong uniqueness and the definition of $\widetilde W$; those future Brownian increments are independent of the time-$t$ filtration by [F1]. Since $\widetilde W_t-\widetilde W_s$ is independent of $X_t$ by claim 1, it is independent of the pair consisting of $X_t$ and all future Brownian increments, and thus of the entire future segment $(X_r,\widetilde W_r-\widetilde W_t)_{r\ge t}$. The variables $Y_q$ and $B_q$ for $q\le u$ are measurable with respect to that segment. Therefore $B_v-B_u$ is independent of $\mathcal G_u$. The process $B$ is continuous, starts at zero, and has these centered Gaussian increments independent of its past; hence it is standard Brownian motion in $(\mathcal G_u)$. [F1, step 3.1]

5.1 Reparameterize by $u=T-t$ and set $B_u=\widetilde W_{T-u}-\widetilde W_T$. Right-endpoint sums in forward time satisfy $\int_{T-u}^T H_s\,d^{\mathrm b}\widetilde W_s=-\int_0^uH_{T-r}\,dB_r$: each reversed increment is the negative of the corresponding right-endpoint forward increment. Therefore $Y_u-Y_0=-\int_0^u\widehat b(Y_r,T-r)dr+\int_0^u\sigma(Y_r,T-r)dB_r$. The drift is $-\widehat b_i=-b_i+p_t^{-1}\partial_j(p_ta_{ij})=-b_i+\partial_j a_{ij}+\sum_j a_{ij}\partial_j\log p_t$. With $t=T-u$, this is exactly the displayed reverse SDE and completes claim 3. [F6, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, (H), an $m$-dimensional standard Brownian motion $B$, an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process $X$ with coefficients $b=(b^i)$ and $\sigma=(\sigma^{ik})$, a function $f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, a finite horizon $T>0$, and an arbitrary deterministic partition sequence $(\pi_n)$ of $[0,T]$ with mesh $\delta_n\to0$. The stopping time $\rho_c$ is defined as in [F7].
 
[F1] **Componentwise class structure and predictability.** $X^i=X^i_0+A^i+M^i$ with $A^i_t=\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds$ and $M^i=\sum_kM^{ik}$, $M^{ik}=\int\sigma^{ik}dB^k$; after the stated null-event normalization the vector process is adapted with everywhere continuous paths and hence predictable, and so is every continuous function of $(s,X_s)$; products with the coefficients are predictable, and the composition $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$ is predictable and locally square-integrable because $\partial_if(\cdot,X)$ is continuous hence locally bounded. [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]] [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] [[lem-adapted-continuous-processes-are-progressively-measurable]] [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]] [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]]
 
[F2] **Localized-integral interfaces.** For finite energy: isometry $E(\int_0^TG\,dB^k)^2=E\int_0^TG^2ds$, restriction to subintervals, the Doob maximal bound, convergence of elementary sums, and uniqueness of continuous versions; for locally square-integrable integrands the stopped pieces are the finite-energy integrals of the truncations; and a bounded $\mathcal F_u$-measurable multiplier $c$ pulls out of the integral over an interval inside $(u,\infty)$. [[thm-localized-ito-integral]] [[thm-stopping-an-ito-integral]] [[thm-ito-isometry-and-linearity-in-predictable-l2]] [[thm-doob-maximal-bound-for-the-ito-integral]] [[thm-ito-integral-process-has-a-continuous-martingale-version]] [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]] [[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]
 
[F3] **Covariation matrix of the class.** For all $i,j$ the covariation exists and $[X^i,X^j]_t=\int_0^t(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s\,ds$, with $S_n^{ij}(t):=\sum_{l:\,t_{l+1}\le t}\Delta_lX^i\Delta_lX^j\to[X^i,X^j]_t$ uniformly in probability along every deterministic vanishing-mesh sequence and in both conventions. [[thm-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]] [[def-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]] [[def-quadratic-variation-along-a-partition-sequence]]
 
[F4] **Multivariable Taylor with third-order remainder.** Let $f\in C^3$ on an open set containing the closed segment from $a=(t_0,x_0)$ to $a+h=(t_0+h_0,x_0+h')$, $h'\in\mathbb R^d$. Then $f(a+h)=f(a)+\partial_tf(a)h_0+\sum_i\partial_if(a)h_i+\tfrac12\bigl(\partial^2_{tt}f(a)h_0^2+2h_0\sum_i\partial_t\partial_if(a)h_i+\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_jf(a)h_ih_j\bigr)+R$ with $|R|\le C_dM_3(|h_0|+|h'|)^3$, where $M_3$ bounds all third partial derivatives on a convex neighbourhood of the segment and $C_d=(d+1)^{3/2}$. Indeed the third derivative along the segment is bounded by $M_3(|h_0|+\sum_i|h_i|)^3\le C_dM_3(|h_0|+|h'|)^3$; this is the one-variable formula with remainder bound applied to $u\mapsto f(a+uh)$ on $[0,1]$. [[cor-second-order-taylor-expansion-with-the-hessian]] [[cor-multivariable-taylor-formula-with-peano-remainder]] [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]] [[def-taylor-polynomial-and-remainder]] [[cor-taylor-remainder-bound]]
 
[F5] **Weighted pullback of the covariation matrix.** If $w$ is continuous adapted with $|w|\le K$, then for every $i,j$ the terminal weighted sums satisfy $\sum_lw(t_l)\Delta_lX^i\Delta_lX^j\to\int_0^Tw_s(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_sds$ in probability; the weighted version is proved in steps 1.4--2.1 by block telescoping against the cumulative sums of [F3] and a staircase approximation. [[thm-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]] [[thm-ito-isometry-and-linearity-in-predictable-l2]]
 
[F6] **Staircase comparison and Riemann sums.** If $D\in\mathcal F_0$, $G$ is continuous adapted and bounded by a deterministic $K$ on $D\times[0,T]$, $g^{(n)}$ is its left-endpoint staircase, and $\int_0^TH^2ds\le c$ on $D$, then the isometry and dominated convergence show that the integrals of $1_Dg^{(n)}H$ converge to that of $1_DGH$ in $L^2(P)$. Also, for continuous $Z$ and pathwise integrable $h$, $\sum_jZ_{t_j}\int_{t_j}^{t_{j+1}}h_s\,ds\to\int_0^TZ_sh_s\,ds$ along vanishing meshes. [[thm-ito-isometry-and-linearity-in-predictable-l2]] [[thm-heine-cantor-r]] [[def-continuity-real]]
 
[F7] **Localization.** For $c>0$ put $D_c:=\{|X_0|\le c\}\in\mathcal F_0$ and $\rho_c:=\inf\{t:\max(|X_t|,\sum_i\int_0^t|b^i|,\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik})^2)\ge c\}\wedge T$. For $t<T$, $\{\rho_c\le t\}$ is the event that the running supremum on $[0,t]$ of the continuous adapted maximum in this display is at least $c$. That supremum equals the supremum over rational times together with $t$, so it is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable. For $t\ge T$ the stopping event is all of $\Omega$. Thus $\rho_c$ is a stopping time, and $\bar X^{(c)}:=1_{D_c}X^{\rho_c}$ is a continuous Brownian Ito process with initial value and coefficients multiplied by $1_{D_c}$ and the coefficients stopped at $\rho_c$. It is globally bounded by $c$, its total drift variations and diffusion energies on $[0,T]$ are at most $c$, and on $D_c\cap\{\rho_c\ge T\}$ it and all its integrals coincide with those of $X$. These events increase to a probability-one event as $c\to\infty$. [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]] [[thm-localized-ito-integral]] [[thm-stopping-an-ito-integral]] [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] [[thm-heine-cantor-r]]
 
[F8] **Cutoff and mollification.** Extend $f$ across $t=0$ on a small negative-time collar by $$\widetilde f(t,x)= \begin{cases}f(t,x),&t\ge0,\\3f(-t,x)-2f(-2t,x),&t<0. \end{cases}$$ The coefficients make both the value and the time derivative agree at $t=0$ ($3-2=1$ and $-3+4=1$), while the same value identity gives agreement of all spatial derivatives through order two; hence $\widetilde f$ is $C^{1,2}$ on a neighbourhood of the localized cylinder. To obtain the needed smooth cutoff from the available continuous-cutoff interface, choose compact sets $K\subseteq\operatorname{int}K'\subseteq K'$ inside a bounded open set $O$ in that neighbourhood, take the continuous compactly supported cutoff $\eta$ that equals $1$ on $K'$, and convolve $\eta$ with a sufficiently small compactly supported unit-mass mollifier. The result $\chi$ is smooth, equals $1$ on $K$, and has support in $O$. Thus $g:=\chi\widetilde f$ is compactly supported and $C^{1,2}$, and its mollifications are smooth with $g_\varepsilon,\partial_tg_\varepsilon,\partial_ig_\varepsilon,\partial_i\partial_jg_\varepsilon$ converging uniformly to the corresponding functions on the inner cylinder. For this derivative assertion write $g_\varepsilon(y)=\int\rho(z)g(y-\varepsilon z)dz$. Difference quotients and the fundamental theorem in each variable move each available derivative $\partial_t,\partial_i,\partial_i\partial_j$ onto $g$, dominated by its continuous derivative bound on a fixed compact set times $|\rho|$. Uniform continuity bounds the error by that derivative's modulus at shifts of size $\varepsilon R$ times $\int|\rho|$, which tends to zero. No mixed time-space derivative of $f$ is assumed. [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]] [[def-mollifier-family-generated-by-a-unit-mass-smooth-bump]] [[thm-convolution-with-a-mollifier-is-smooth-and-differentiates-under-the-integral-sign]] [[lem-a-compact-set-inside-a-bounded-open-set-admits-an-explicit-compactly-supported-cutoff]] [[thm-c-c-infinity-rn-is-dense-in-l-p-of-rn]]
 
[F9] **Estimates.** Cauchy--Schwarz for sums and expectations; dominated convergence; Fatou; and bounded-by-$R_n$ with $ER_n\to0$ implies convergence in probability to $0$. [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]] [[thm-dominated-convergence]] [[thm-fatou-lemma]] [[def-convergence-in-probability]]
 
[F10] **AC bookkeeping.** Choice is declared for the ambient conditional-expectation, completeness and density interfaces; all stopping levels, partitions and mollification scales are canonical. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]
 
 
 
 

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.
 
1.1 Reduction to a bounded localized problem: fix $c$ and replace $X$ by $\bar X^{(c)}=1_{D_c}X^{\rho_c}$ as in [F7]. This process is globally bounded by $c$, its total drift variations and diffusion energies on $[0,T]$ are at most $c$, and on $D_c\cap\{\rho_c\ge T\}$ both sides of its formula agree with those for the original process. Its stochastic integrands have finite energy bounded by $c\sup|\partial_if|^2$, and all continuous functions of $(s,\bar X^{(c)}_s)$ are bounded. It suffices to prove the identity for this bounded process; rename it and its coefficients $X,b,\sigma$. [F1, F2, F7, given]
 
1.2 Setup of the $C^3$ case: assume $f\in C^3$ on a neighbourhood of the compact cylinder $[0,T]\times[-c,c]^d$ with finite bounds $M_0,M_1,M_2,M_3$ on partial derivatives of orders $0,1,2,3$; write $\Delta t_j=t_{j+1}-t_j$ and $\Delta X_j=X_{t_{j+1}}-X_{t_j}$. [F1, F4, given]
 
1.3 Remainder control: Taylor's formula [F4] gives for each $j$ an expansion of $f(t_{j+1},X_{t_{j+1}})-f(t_j,X_{t_j})$ with third-order remainder $R_j$, $|R_j|\le C_dM_3(|\Delta t_j|+|\Delta X_j|)^3\le4C_dM_3(|\Delta t_j|^3+|\Delta X_j|^3)$; summing, $\sum_j|\Delta t_j|^3\le\operatorname{mesh}(\pi_n)^2T\to0$ and $\sum_j|\Delta X_j|^3\le\max_j|\Delta X_j|\sum_j|\Delta X_j|^2=\max_j|\Delta X_j|\sum_iQ_n(X^i)(T)$, where $Q_n(X^i)(t):=S_n^{ii}(t)$, $\max_j|\Delta X_j|\to0$ almost surely by everywhere continuity, and each $Q_n(X^i)(T)\to[X^i]_T$ in probability by [F3]. The finite sum is bounded in probability; multiplying it by a quantity tending to zero almost surely gives convergence to zero in probability (split the probability at a fixed large bound for the sum). Thus $\sum_j|R_j|\to0$, and hence $\sum_jR_j\to0$ in probability. [F3, F4, F6]
 
1.4 Weighted pullback, elementary weights: let $w=\sum_a\lambda_a1_{(u_a,u_{a+1}]}$ be elementary with bounded $\mathcal F_{u_a}$-measurable coefficients and deterministic block points. With the cumulative cross sums $S_n(v)$ on the original partition, [F3] gives uniform-in-$v$ convergence in probability to $\int_0^v(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}ds$. The sum over original intervals lying wholly in one block is the difference of its endpoint cumulative sums up to at most two boundary intervals. Each boundary contribution is bounded by $\|\lambda_a\|_\infty\max_l|\Delta_lX^i||\Delta_lX^j|$ and tends to zero almost surely by continuity. The finite block sum therefore converges to $\int_0^Tw_s(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_sds$ in probability. [F3, F6, given]
 
1.5 First-order terms: $\sum_j\partial_tf(t_j,X_{t_j})\Delta t_j\to\int_0^T\partial_tf(s,X_s)ds$ and $\sum_j\sum_i\partial_if(t_j,X_{t_j})\Delta_jA^i\to\int_0^T\sum_i\partial_if(s,X_s)b^i_s\,ds$ almost surely by the Riemann estimate [F6]; and the martingale part equals $\sum_{i,k}\int_0^Tg^{(n)}_i\sigma^{ik}dB^k$ for the left-endpoint staircases $g^{(n)}_i$ of $s\mapsto\partial_if(s,X_s)$, which converges in $L^2(P)$ to $\sum_{i,k}\int_0^T\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s dB^k_s$ by [F6] with $D=\Omega$ and the isometry. [F2, F5, F6, given]
 
2.1 Weighted pullback, continuous weights: for continuous adapted $w$ with $|w|\le K$ and its left-endpoint staircase $w^{(m)}$ on the grid of mesh $2^{-m}T$, uniform continuity gives $\sup_s|w^{(m)}_s-w_s|\to0$ almost surely. Fix $m$ first and apply step 1.4 as $n\to\infty$. The sum error is bounded by $\sup_s|w^{(m)}_s-w_s|Q_n(X^i)^{1/2}Q_n(X^j)^{1/2}$, where $Q_n(X^i)$ denotes its terminal value. Put $R_m=\sup_s|w^{(m)}_s-w_s|$ and $Z_n=Q_n(X^i)^{1/2}Q_n(X^j)^{1/2}$. For $L>0$, $P(R_mZ_n>\varepsilon)\le P(R_m>\varepsilon/L)+P(Z_n>L)$. Tightness of the quadratic factors makes the second term uniformly small for large $L$ (or for all sufficiently large $n$), and then large $m$ makes the first small. The limiting integral error is at most $R_m\int_0^T\sum_k|\sigma^{ik}\sigma^{jk}|ds\le cR_m$ by the localized total-energy bound and $2|ab|\le a^2+b^2$; it tends to zero almost surely and in $L^1$, since $R_m\le2K$. Taking $n\to\infty$ and then $m\to\infty$ proves [F5]. [F3, F6, F9, step 1.4]
 
3.1 Second-order terms: by step 2.1 applied to $w=\partial_i\partial_jf(\cdot,X)$, $\sum_l\tfrac12\partial_i\partial_jf(t_l,X_{t_l})\Delta_lX^i\Delta_lX^j\to\tfrac12\int_0^T\partial_i\partial_jf(s,X_s)(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_sds$ in probability for each pair $i,j$, hence for the finite sum. These are the complete spatial Hessian terms; no separate drift expansion is added. The time--space terms are bounded in absolute value by $M_2T\sum_i\max_l|\Delta_lX^i|$ and the pure time term by $\tfrac12M_2T\operatorname{mesh}(\pi_n)$, so both tend to zero by continuity. [F3, F6, step 2.1]
 
4.1 Assemble the $C^3$ case: summing the exact expansions of step 1.3 over $j$, the left side telescopes to $f(T,X_T)-f(0,X_0)$ and the right side is controlled by steps 1.3, 1.5 and 3.1; passing to the limit along $\pi_n$ gives the identity at $T$ in probability, hence almost surely, and then at each fixed $t\in[0,T]$ by restricting and augmenting the partition sequence. Intersect the full events for rational times and the endpoint $T$; continuity of both sides extends the equality to all times on that single full event. [F2, F3, step 1.3, step 1.5, step 3.1]
 
5.1 Reduction to $C^{1,2}$ by cutoff and mollification: for $f\in C^{1,2}$ take the collar extension, smooth cutoff and mollifications from [F8]. On the inner cylinder $[0,T]\times[-c,c]^d$ the smoothed functions and their derivatives $\partial_t,\partial_i,\partial_i\partial_j$ converge uniformly to those of $f$. Apply step 4.1 and let the mollification scale tend to zero: the drift integral converges by dominated convergence with bound $K'(1+\sum_i|b^i|+\sum_{i,k}(\sigma^{ik})^2)$; for each $i,k$ the stochastic difference has squared $L^2$ norm at most the uniform squared derivative error times $E\int_0^T(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2ds$, which tends to zero; and the left side converges uniformly on the inner cylinder. [F2, F5, F7, F8, F9, step 4.1]
 
6.1 Removal of the localization and conclusion: the identity for $\bar X^{(c)}$ agrees with the desired identity on $D_c\cap\{\rho_c\ge T\}$, and these events increase to a probability-one event by [F7]: every integer $c$ larger than the path supremum, total drift variation and total energy has $D_c$ true and $\rho_c=T$. Take countably many integer $c$ and horizons $T$ to obtain one full event. Hence the identity holds almost surely at every deterministic time and, by continuity of both sides, up to indistinguishability; the integrands are predictable and locally square-integrable by [F1] and [F2]. [F1, F2, F7, step 5.1]
 
7.1 Boundary and consistency cases: for $d=1$ and $m=1$ the formula is the one-dimensional formula of [[thm-ito-formula-one-dimensional]]; for $f(t,x)=x^i$ it reduces to the defining display of $X^i$; for $f(t,x)=|x|^2$ it gives $|X_t|^2=|X_0|^2+2\sum_i\int_0^tX^i_s\,dX^i_s+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2ds$; if $\sigma\equiv0$ the covariation matrix vanishes and the formula is the chain rule along an absolutely continuous path; at $t=0$ both sides equal $f(0,X_0)$; if $d=0$ is excluded there is nothing degenerate to treat, and a singular dispersion matrix is allowed because only the products $(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}$ enter the quadratic term. Independence and unit covariance of the coordinates are exactly the standard vector-Brownian convention already encoded in [F3]. AC enters only through [F10], and all localization and mollification parameters are canonical. [F3, F10, step 6.1] ∎

## Source notes

Van der Vaart, Theorem 5.85, states the multidimensional formula for continuous semimartingales with the full covariation matrix. Its supplied proof on printed pp.90–91 uses polynomials in dimension one and leaves the multidimensional extension to the reader. It is not a complete source proof of the present space-time Taylor argument; that argument is supplied here. The proof above follows the localized Taylor route of the one-dimensional item componentwise, with the two new ingredients made explicit: the covariance matrix enters only through the already proved covariation theorem, and the weighted pullback of the matrix covariation is proved rather than cited.

## Definition

Assume AC. Fix $T>0$, a compactly supported Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, a continuously differentiable function $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ bounded above and away from zero, and $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2dr$. For $t>0$ put
$$p_t(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(y-z)\,\mu(dz),\qquad q(s,x;t,y)=\phi_{v(t)-v(s)}(y-x)\quad(0\le s<t\le T),$$
where $\phi_a$ is the centered Gaussian density with covariance $aI_d$. Put $p_0=\mu$ as a probability measure, not as a Lebesgue density. For $0\le u<v<T$ define
$$K_{u,v}(y,dx)=\frac{p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)}{p_{T-u}(y)}\,dx,$$
and for $0\le u<T$ at the singular data endpoint define
$$K_{u,T}(y,A)=\frac{\int_A q(0,x;T-u,y)\,\mu(dx)}{p_{T-u}(y)}\quad(A\text{ Borel}).$$
Set $K_{u,u}(y,\cdot)=\delta_y$. These are the Bayes-reversed kernels of the additive Gaussian smoothing process, including the posterior kernel at the original data time; no density for $\mu$ is required.

## Definition references

[[def-gaussian-smoothed-data-law-and-transition-density|Gaussian-smoothed law and transition density]]: supplies the explicit positive-time marginal density, Gaussian transition density, and forward marginal and Chapman–Kolmogorov identities.

[Anderson, Sections 3–4](https://eva.fcien.udelar.edu.uy/pluginfile.php/166428/mod_resource/content/1/1982_andersonREVERSE-TIME%20DIFFUSION%20EQUATION%20MODELS.pdf): context for Bayes reversal from forward transition densities.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $\mu$, $g$, $v$, $p_t$, and $q$ in the definition.

[A1] The Gaussian smoothing supplier assumes AC, compact support, $p_t>0$ for $t>0$, the displayed transition density, the forward marginal identity, and Chapman–Kolmogorov; it defines $p_0=\mu$ without asserting a density there. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[def-gaussian-smoothed-data-law-and-transition-density]]

[F1] A probability kernel assigns a probability measure to each source state and has a measurable evaluation function for each Borel target set. [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]

[F2] Nonnegative joint Borel densities can be integrated in either order; parameter integrals are measurable. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

## Verification
1.1 For $u<v<T$, the integrand $1_A(x)p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)$ is jointly Borel and nonnegative; Tonelli [F2] makes its integral measurable in $y$, and countable additivity in $A$ follows from countable additivity of the integral. For $v=T$, the integrand $1_A(x)q(0,x;T-u,y)$ is jointly Borel and nonnegative relative to the finite measure $\mu$, so the same parameter-integral argument applies. All denominators are positive because $T-u>0$. [F2, A1, F1]

2.1 If $v<T$, the forward marginal identity [A1] gives $\int p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)dx=p_{T-u}(y)$; if $v=T$, the same identity with initial measure $\mu$ gives $\int q(0,x;T-u,y)\mu(dx)=p_{T-u}(y)$. Thus both formulas have total mass one. The equal-time kernel is a probability measure by definition. [A1, F1, step 1.1]

3.1 For $u<v<w<T$, composing the density ratios cancels $p_{T-v}(x)$, and Tonelli followed by forward Chapman–Kolmogorov [A1] gives $K_{u,v}K_{v,w}=K_{u,w}$. If $w=T$, the same computation leaves $\mu(dz)$ times $\displaystyle \int q(0,z;T-v,x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)dx=q(0,z;T-u,y),$ so the endpoint formula gives $K_{u,v}K_{v,T}=K_{u,T}$. Cases with equal adjacent times use the identity kernel. [A1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a finite horizon $T>0$ and a filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$. Let $M$ be a continuous adapted $d$-dimensional local martingale with $M_0=0$. Let $\sigma$ be a predictable process of invertible $d\times d$ matrices, with $\|\sigma_t^{-1}\|\le C$ for a finite deterministic constant $C$ and $\int_0^T\|\sigma_t\|_F^2dt<\infty$ almost surely. Suppose
$$[M^i,M^j]_t=\int_0^t(\sigma_s\sigma_s^{\mathsf T})_{ij}ds.$$
Then predictable elementary sums, completed in the localized bracket-energy norm, define $B=\int\sigma^{-1}dM$. It has an adapted continuous version, is standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion in the given filtration, and
$$M_t=\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s$$
up to indistinguishability. The integral on the right is the localized predictable Brownian integral defined by elementary sums and their $L^2$ completion. This construction on the given finite horizon does not require completeness or right continuity of the filtration, and no continuity of $\sigma$ is assumed.

## Statement references

[van der Vaart, Lemma 5.77, printed pp. 85–86, and Theorem 7.15, printed pp. 147–148](https://diamhomes.ewi.tudelft.nl/~avandervaart/books/stochint.pdf): predictable stochastic-integral bracket calculus and scalar inverse-diffusion reconstruction. The matrix-valued finite-horizon construction and recovery identity are proved below.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the processes, filtration, finite horizon, bracket identity, invertibility, integrability and AC in the Statement. Write $a=\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T}$, $A_t=\int_0^t\operatorname{tr}(a_s)ds$, and $H=\sigma^{-1}$.

[A1] AC supplies the countably selected approximants and versions and is inherited by the vector Lévy characterization and the $L^2$ interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[cor-vector-levy-characterization]]

[F1] Predictable sets are generated by $(s,t]\times E$, $E\in\mathcal F_s$, and time-zero sets. Predictable maps are progressive, and $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable for every stopping time $\tau$. [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]

[F2] Continuous local martingales have covariations and the product-compensator identity; a continuous finite-variation local martingale is constant. [[lem-continuous-local-martingale-quadratic-variation]]

[F3] The pi-lambda theorem and simple approximation apply on every finite measure space. Dominated convergence gives convergence in $L^2$ under square-integrable domination. [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]] [[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[F4] $L^2$ is complete. Doob's $L^2$ inequality on increasing finite rational grids, followed by monotone convergence, gives the continuous-martingale bound $E\sup_{t\le T}|N_t|^2\le4E|N_T|^2$. Conditional-expectation event identities pass to $L^1$ limits. [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] [[thm-doob-lp-maximal-inequality]] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]

## Proof

**Given:** the hypotheses and notation above. All process equalities below are up to indistinguishability; continuous versions are identified by equality at rational times on a common full event.

1.1 First work in the completed right-continuous augmentation of the given filtration. This preserves every continuous local martingale used here. Indeed, each original stopped true martingale $Q$ is uniformly integrable on $[0,T]$, since $Q_s=E[Q_T\mid\mathcal F_s]$; the uniform integrability follows by truncating the fixed integrable terminal variable. If $s_k\downarrow s$, continuity and uniform integrability give $Q_{s_k}\to Q_s$ in $L^1$. For an event in the completed intersection of the $\mathcal F_{s_k}$, its martingale event identity with $Q_t$ therefore passes to $Q_s$; completion adds only null-event identities. This proves the martingale property in the augmented filtration, while original localizers remain stopping times there. Countably many continuous processes can now be normalized on their common null exceptional set in the initial sigma-algebra. Let $\tau_n$ be the first time $|M|$ or $A$ reaches $n$, capped at $T$. These are increasing stopping times equal to $T$ eventually on each path in the common full event of continuity and finite energy, with $M^{\tau_n}$ bounded and $A_{T\wedge\tau_n}\le n$; the latter processes are continuous, and their hitting times are stopping times by progressive measurability and the rational-time test for continuous paths. Bounded stopping preserves a true continuous martingale on this usual augmented space: approximate the stop by finite-valued dyadic ceilings; the finite-sum conditional-expectation identities hold, and the stopped evaluations are uniformly integrable since on each finite grid they are conditional expectations of the fixed terminal value. Continuity and uniform integrability pass the identities to the limit. Thus the original localizers, used only in this argument and not in the definition of $\tau_n$, show that $M^{\tau_n}$ is a bounded local martingale. Dominated convergence in their event-integral identities, including at the terminal time $T$, makes it a true square-integrable martingale. Work first with one such stopped martingale $N=M^{\tau_n}$, bracket density $c_s=1_{s\le\tau_n}a_s$, and the finite measure $\mu(E)=E\int_0^T1_E(s,\omega)\operatorname{tr}(c_s)ds$ restricted to the original predictable sigma-algebra. All elementary approximants below are predictable for that original filtration; the stopped integrator $N$ is used in the augmented space. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Bounded elementary predictable functions are dense in $L^2(\mu)$. To see this without replacing $\mu$ by $dt\otimes P$, let $V$ be their $L^2(\mu)$ closure. Each interval-generator indicator belongs to $V$, and time-zero indicators have zero $\mu$ norm. The constant class is represented by $1_{(0,T]}$. The sets whose indicators belong to $V$ form a lambda-system: complements follow by subtraction from this constant class; for disjoint unions, finite partial sums converge in $L^2(\mu)$ because the squared tail norm is the tail measure and $\mu$ is finite. Intersections of generators are generators or empty, so [F3] makes every predictable-set indicator belong to $V$. Simple approximation, truncation and dominated convergence then give all of $L^2(\mu)$. Apply this entrywise for matrices. [F1, F3, F4]

1.3 For a bounded elementary matrix $G=\sum_kG_k1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}$ with $G_k$ measurable at $t_k$, define $I_N(G)_t=\sum_kG_k(N_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-N_{t\wedge t_k})$. Conditional martingale-increment identities and [F2] give $$E|I_N(G)_T|^2=E\int_0^T\operatorname{tr}(G_sc_sG_s^{\mathsf T})ds,$$ and $I_N(G)^iI_N(G)^j-\int_0^{\cdot}(G_sc_sG_s^{\mathsf T})_{ij}ds$ is a martingale. The coordinate product-compensators of $N$ are true martingales: $N$ is bounded, and its bracket entries are bounded in absolute value by $A_{T\wedge\tau_n}\le n$, so the local martingales from [F2] are bounded and the preceding dominated-convergence argument applies. The displayed identities now follow on each block by multiplying those true martingale identities by bounded $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable coefficients, and then summing; cross-block increments have conditional mean zero. For elementary $G$, the integral is bounded by a deterministic multiple of the bound on $N$, and its compensator is bounded by a deterministic multiple of $n$, so these product-compensators are true martingales as well. For two elementary matrices apply the same isometry to their difference and [F4] to obtain the maximal bound with factor $4$. Since $c$ is positive semidefinite, its energy is bounded by $E\int\|G\|_F^2\operatorname{tr}(c)ds=\|G\|_{L^2(\mu)}^2$. [F2, F4]

2.1 Thus for every predictable $J\in L^2(\mu)$, elementary approximants from step 1.2 have integrals converging in $L^2$ of the path supremum to $I_N(J)$. A subsequence with summable expected sup errors converges uniformly almost surely to a continuous version. Define its value at each time by the pointwise limit of this subsequence when finite, and zero otherwise; this is adapted and progressive and has continuous paths on the common full convergence event, without modifying a process on a potentially noninitial null event. Martingale event identities pass to the $L^1$ limit. Products converge in $L^1$ by Cauchy–Schwarz; the compensators converge in expected total variation by the same inequality in the energy inner product, since $\|J-G_m\|_{c}\to0$ and $\|G_m\|_c$ is bounded. Hence $$[I_N(J)]_t=\int_0^tJ_sc_sJ_s^{\mathsf T}ds.$$ Indeed the right side is continuous finite variation and the product minus it is a martingale, so uniqueness follows from [F2]. Uniqueness also follows in the energy completion, and the construction extends to every predictable $J$ of finite $c$ energy by truncation: $J1_{\{\|J\|\le k\}}$ lies in $L^2(\mu)$ and converges in energy by dominated convergence. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.2, step 1.3]

3.1 Since $H$ is bounded and predictable, step 2.1 applies. Set $B^{(n)}=I_{M^{\tau_n}}(H)$. The constructions agree up to the smaller localizer. For elementary integrands the stopping identity is the defining increment identity, with the stopped integrator; extension follows by the maximal bound, since the energy restricted to a stopped interval is no greater than the full energy. This comparison also applies when the two approximation sequences differ, by uniqueness of the energy completion. Therefore the $B^{(n)}$ paste to an adapted continuous local martingale $B=\int H\,dM$, with $$[B]_t=\int_0^tH_sa_sH_s^{\mathsf T}ds=tI_d.$$ This first constructs $B$ in the augmented filtration; [A1] makes it Brownian there. It has an adapted version in the original filtration: choose an increasing subsequence of localizers, still denoted by $\tau_n$, with $P(\tau_n<T)\le2^{-n}$, and original elementary $G_n$ approximating $H$ in the corresponding stopped energy so well that $P(\sup_{t\le T}|I_{M^{\tau_n}}(G_n)_t-B^{\tau_n}_t|>2^{-n})\le2^{-n}$. Steps 1.2–2.1 provide these choices. The unstopped elementary sums $I_M(G_n)$ are adapted to the original filtration; on $\{\tau_n=T\}$ they equal the stopped sums. The union bound and summability therefore give uniform almost-sure convergence to $B$ on a common full event. Define the value at each time as their pointwise limit when finite and zero otherwise. This gives the desired original-adapted version, with the same continuous paths and bracket almost surely. Its Brownian increments in the augmented filtration are independent of every earlier event in the original subfiltration as well. Thus the original-adapted version is Brownian in the original filtration. The Lévy supplier's proof uses only the stated finite set of times in $[0,T]$, so it needs no extension past $T$. [A1, step 2.1]

4.1 We prove the recovery identity rather than assume an associativity rule. Fix $n$ and write $N=M^{\tau_n}$ and $Z=B^{\tau_n}=I_N(H)$. For bounded elementary $K$, its defining sum against $Z$ is $I_N(KH)$. On one block, this follows by approximating $H$ in step 2.1: multiplication by the bounded left-measurable block coefficient and restriction to that block commute with both elementary sums and their $L^2$ limits; sum over the finitely many blocks. The right integral exists because $KH$ is bounded predictable. For the stopped Brownian motion $Z$, the coordinate product-compensators are also true martingales. Brownian Doob bounds give $E\sup_{t\le T}|B_t|^2<\infty$, so stopping the Brownian coordinate and product martingales is justified by the same finite-valued approximation and $L^1$ domination. Therefore the elementary isometry and maximal bound of step 1.3 apply to $Z$ as well. Since $[Z]_t=(t\wedge\tau_n)I_d$, elementary integrals against $Z$ have energy $E\int_0^{T\wedge\tau_n}\|K_s\|_F^2ds$. Applying steps 1.2–2.1 with this finite measure defines their completion, namely the stopped predictable Brownian integral. Choose elementary $K_j$ converging to $\sigma$ for that energy; this is possible since $E\int_0^{T\wedge\tau_n}\|\sigma_s\|_F^2ds\le n$. For the right integrals the exact identity $$E\int_0^{T\wedge\tau_n}\operatorname{tr}\bigl((K_j-\sigma)H a H^{\mathsf T}(K_j-\sigma)^{\mathsf T}\bigr)ds=E\int_0^{T\wedge\tau_n}\|K_j-\sigma\|_F^2ds$$ shows convergence to $I_N(\sigma H)=I_N(I_d)=N$. The left sums converge to $\int\sigma\,dZ$ in the same maximal norm. Thus $\int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}\sigma_s\,dB_s=M_{t\wedge\tau_n}$. Letting $n$ increase proves the recovery identity on all of $[0,T]$, with the usual predictable Brownian integral defined by these localized elementary completions. [step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎
