## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a continuous nonexplosive Markov diffusion on $[0,T]$ in $\mathbb R^d$, where nonexplosive means its paths remain in $\mathbb R^d$ throughout the interval and Markov means conditional future laws given the past depend only on the current state. It satisfies
$$dX_t=b_t(X_t)dt+\sigma_t(X_t)dW_t,$$
where $W$ is standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion and $\sigma_t(x)$ is square and invertible with $\sup_{t,x}\|\sigma_t(x)^{-1}\|<\infty$. Put $a_t(x)=\sigma_t(x)\sigma_t(x)^{\mathsf T}$. A transition density means $P(X_t\in dy\mid X_s=x)=q(s,x;t,y)dy$. Assume $p_t$ and $q(s,x;t,y)$ are positive probability densities, with $p_t$ having one continuous time derivative and two continuous state derivatives, and satisfying
$$p_t(y)=\int p_s(x)q(s,x;t,y)dx,\qquad q(s,x;t,y)=\int q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)dz\quad(s<r<t).$$
For $L_t\phi=b_t\cdot\nabla\phi+\tfrac12a_t:D^2\phi$, define its formal adjoint by $L_t^*r=-\partial_i(b_{t,i}r)+\tfrac12\partial_i\partial_j(a_{t,ij}r)$ and assume $\partial_t p_t=L_t^*p_t$ and $\partial_tq(s,x;t,y)=L_t^{*,y}q(s,x;t,y)$ classically. Assume that for every compactly supported smooth test function the transition integrals and their time derivatives are absolutely integrable, differentiation under those integrals is valid, and integration by parts in space has no boundary term. For each initial law, assume the reverse martingale problem for the operator defined by the Bayes-density expression below has a unique nonexplosive continuous solution in law; here this means existence and uniqueness in law of a continuous process for which each compact-test compensated process is a local martingale.

For $0\le u<v\le T$ define
$$K_{u,v}(y,dx)=\frac{p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)}{p_{T-u}(y)}\,dx,$$
and let $Y_u=X_{T-u}$ with reversed filtration $\mathcal G_u=\sigma(Y_r:0\le r\le u)$. Then these are the transition kernels of $Y$, and for $0\le u<T$ its generator on $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ is
$$\widetilde L_u\phi=p_{T-u}^{-1}\{L_{T-u}^*(p_{T-u}\phi)-\phi L_{T-u}^*p_{T-u}\}.$$
Consequently $Y$ solves the reverse SDE
$$dY_u=\left[-b_{T-u}(Y_u)+(\nabla\!\cdot a_{T-u})(Y_u)+a_{T-u}(Y_u)\nabla\log p_{T-u}(Y_u)\right]du+\sigma_{T-u}(Y_u)dB_u,$$
where $(\nabla\!\cdot a)_i=\sum_j\partial_j a_{ij}$ and $B$ is a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion in the reversed filtration. This theorem starts from the assumed positive density regime; it does not infer densities from strong SDE well-posedness.

## Statement references

[Song et al., Sections 3.2 and Appendix A.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2011.13456): downstream application of the state-dependent reverse-drift formula, citing Anderson; it is not used as the proof of the general Bayes-kernel theorem.

[Tang and Zhao, Section 2.2, PDF pp. 3–5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.07487): gives the formula and a heuristic derivation; it does not prove the density or martingale-problem hypotheses.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the Markov diffusion, densities, regularity, integrability, ellipticity, and reverse martingale-problem hypotheses in the Statement.

[A1] AC is required by the vector Lévy characterization and the local continuous-martingale calculus used below. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Bayes' formula gives the displayed reverse kernels; the forward marginal and Chapman–Kolmogorov identities make them probability kernels satisfying reverse Chapman–Kolmogorov. [[def-reversed-transition-kernels-for-diffusions]]

[F2] The reverse-kernel generator and compact-test martingale identity are obtained from the forward density equation and justified differentiation under its transition integrals. [[lem-reversed-kernels-and-generator-identity]]

[F3] For symmetric $a$, the formal adjoint product rule is
$$p^{-1}\{L_t^*(p\phi)-\phi L_t^*p\}=\left(-b_i+p^{-1}\partial_j(pa_{ij})\right)\partial_i\phi+\tfrac12a_{ij}\partial_{ij}\phi.$$
Thus the first-order coefficient is $-b+\nabla\!\cdot a+a\nabla\log p$. [[lem-reversed-kernels-and-generator-identity]]

[F4] For a continuous semimartingale $Y=M+A$ with local-martingale part $M$ and continuous finite-variation part $A$, the localized product formula identifies the covariation from the coordinate-product martingale tests. A continuous finite-variation local martingale is constant. [[lem-continuous-local-martingale-quadratic-variation]]

[F5] For a predictable invertible matrix process $\sigma$ with bounded inverse and finite pathwise squared energy, bracket $\int\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T}dt$ yields a Brownian inverse-diffusion integral and the recovery identity $M=\int\sigma\,dB$, without continuity of $\sigma$. [[lem-predictable-elliptic-martingale-brownian-reconstruction]]

[F6] The predictable sigma-algebra contains deterministic Borel time functions and adapted left-step processes; limits and Borel compositions of predictable maps are predictable. [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]

## Proof
**Given:** all hypotheses and notation in the Statement; AC as required by [A1].

1.1 For $u<v$, the joint density of $(X_{T-v},X_{T-u})$ is $p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)$. Dividing by the strictly positive later marginal $p_{T-u}(y)$ gives the conditional law of $X_{T-v}$ given $X_{T-u}=y$, exactly $K_{u,v}(y,dx)$. Its normalization and reverse Chapman–Kolmogorov identity follow from [F1], so $Y$ is Markov with those transitions. [F1]

2.1 Apply [F2] to the Bayes kernels. It gives, for every compactly supported smooth $\phi$, the reverse generator $\displaystyle \widetilde L_u\phi(y)=p_{T-u}(y)^{-1}\{L_{T-u}^*(p_{T-u}\phi)(y)-\phi(y)L_{T-u}^*p_{T-u}(y)\}$ and the corresponding compensated local martingale. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Expanding the adjoint by [F3] yields diffusion coefficient $a_{T-u}$ and drift $\widetilde b_u=-b_{T-u}+p_{T-u}^{-1}\nabla\!\cdot(p_{T-u}a_{T-u})=-b_{T-u}+\nabla\!\cdot a_{T-u}+a_{T-u}\nabla\log p_{T-u}$. [F3, step 2.1]

3.2 Fix $R$ and stop when $|Y|$ first reaches $R$. Compactly supported cutoffs equal to $x_i$ and $x_ix_j$ on the ball of radius $R$ turn the compact-test martingale identities into coordinate and coordinate-product identities. Subtracting the finite-variation drift in each coordinate identity gives continuous local martingales $M^i$. The product formula in [F4] shows that $Y_iY_j-Y_i(0)Y_j(0)-\int_0^{\cdot}(\widetilde b_iY_j+\widetilde b_jY_i)dr-[M_i,M_j]$ is a local martingale. The coordinate-product test shows that the same expression with $\int_0^{\cdot}a_{ij}(T-r,Y_r)dr$ in place of $[M_i,M_j]$ is a local martingale. Their difference is a continuous finite-variation local martingale, hence constant by [F4]; it starts at zero. Thus $[M_i,M_j]_u=\int_0^u a_{ij}(T-r,Y_r)dr$. Letting $R\uparrow\infty$ is valid because the assumed solution is nonexplosive. [F4, step 2.1]

4.1 To handle the Borel coefficients allowed by the SDE data, choose the predictable representative $\widehat Y$ obtained as follows: take left-step approximations with coefficients $Y_{kT/2^n}$, set their time-zero value to $Y_0$, and take their pointwise limit where finite and $0$ otherwise. These maps are predictable by [F6] and agree with $Y$ at every time on its common continuity event. The pair $(r,\widehat Y_r)$ is predictable, so the joint Borel coefficient gives a predictable matrix $\Sigma_r=\sigma_{T-r}(\widehat Y_r)$; inversion is Borel on invertible matrices, and $\|\Sigma_r^{-1}\|$ is uniformly bounded. Step 3.2 gives $\int_0^T\|\Sigma_r\|_F^2dr=\operatorname{tr}[M]_T<\infty$ almost surely, as well as $[M]_u=\int_0^u\Sigma_r\Sigma_r^{\mathsf T}dr$. Thus [F5] constructs $B=\int\Sigma^{-1}dM$ Brownian in the original reversed filtration, and proves $M=\int\Sigma\,dB$. Since $\widehat Y=Y$ on a common full event, this is the displayed reverse SDE with its original Borel coefficient. The assumed well-posedness and nonexplosion of the reverse martingale problem identify its law uniquely and complete the theorem. [F5, F6, A1, step 3.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and the compactly supported Gaussian smoothing setup: $X_t=X_0+\int_0^t g(r)dW_r$, with $X_0\sim\mu$ compactly supported, scalar $g\in C^1([0,T])$ bounded above and away from zero, $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2dr$, $p_t(x)=\int\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\mu(dz)$ for $t>0$, and forward transition density $q(s,x;t,y)=\phi_{v(t)-v(s)}(y-x)$. Fix $0<\epsilon<T$, put $Y_u=X_{T-u}$ for $0\le u\le T-\epsilon$, and use the Bayes-reversed kernels from the preceding definition. For $s_t=\nabla\log p_t$, define
$$\widetilde L_u\varphi(y)=g(T-u)^2\left(s_{T-u}(y)\cdot\nabla\varphi(y)+\tfrac12\Delta\varphi(y)\right),\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d).$$
Then $Y$ is Markov with those reversed kernels, and for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty$ the process
$$\varphi(Y_v)-\varphi(Y_0)-\int_0^v\widetilde L_r\varphi(Y_r)\,dr,\qquad 0\le v\le T-\epsilon,$$
is a martingale in the natural reversed filtration. The assertion is restricted to forward times at least $\epsilon$; it makes no score or density claim at $t=0$.

## Statement references

[Tang and Zhao, Section 2.2, PDF pp. 3–5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.07487): gives the plus-score reverse-drift formula and identifies the derivation as heuristic; the local argument below supplies the generator and martingale proof.

[Anderson, Section 5, printed pp. 322–324](https://eva.fcien.udelar.edu.uy/pluginfile.php/166428/mod_resource/content/1/1982_andersonREVERSE-TIME%20DIFFUSION%20EQUATION%20MODELS.pdf): context for the reverse Kolmogorov calculation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $\mu$, $g$, $v$, $p_t$, $q$, and $\epsilon$ as in the statement.

[A1] AC is assumed by the Gaussian smoothing, density, and score suppliers; their actual positive-time density and heat-equation claims apply to compactly supported arbitrary Borel $\mu$ and do not assert a density at zero. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[def-gaussian-smoothed-data-law-and-transition-density]] [[thm-gaussian-smoothing-density-and-forward-equation]] [[thm-gaussian-mixture-score-and-global-lipschitz-bound]]

[F1] For $t>0$, $p_t$ is positive and smooth and satisfies $\partial_t p_t=\tfrac12g(t)^2\Delta p_t$; $q$ is the Gaussian transition density and obeys the forward marginal and Chapman–Kolmogorov identities. [[def-gaussian-smoothed-data-law-and-transition-density]] [[thm-gaussian-smoothing-density-and-forward-equation]]

[F2] The score obeys $s_t=\nabla\log p_t$ and is smooth on every interval $[\epsilon,T]$. [[thm-gaussian-mixture-score-and-global-lipschitz-bound]]

[F3] The reverse kernels are probability kernels satisfying reverse Chapman–Kolmogorov, including the endpoint posterior against $\mu$. [[def-bayes-reversed-gaussian-smoothing-kernels]]

[F4] Dominated convergence justifies the positive-time small-interval limit on compact test supports; Fubini justifies composing the transition integrals. [[thm-dominated-convergence]] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

## Proof
**Given:** the hypotheses and notation in the Statement.

1.1 The Gaussian forward process is Markov by independent increments of its deterministic Itô integral. Bayes' formula gives the reversed conditional law of $X_{T-v}$ given $X_{T-u}=y$ as $K_{u,v}(y,dx)$; the density supplier's marginal identity normalizes it, and [F3] gives reverse Chapman–Kolmogorov. Thus $Y$ is Markov with these kernels. [F3, A1, F1]

1.2 Put $t=T-u$ and $\delta v=v(t)-v(t-h)$ for $h>0$. For $u+h\le T-\epsilon$, the reverse transition formula gives $\displaystyle K_{u,u+h}\varphi(y)=\frac{1}{p_t(y)}\int \varphi(x)p_{t-h}(x)\phi_{\delta v}(y-x)\,dx.$ The heat-kernel expansion, justified on the compact support of $\varphi$ by [F1, F4], is $\displaystyle \int \varphi(x)p_{t-h}(x)\phi_{\delta v}(y-x)dx=p_t(y)\varphi(y)+\frac{\delta v}{2}\left(\Delta(p_t\varphi)(y)-\varphi(y)\Delta p_t(y)\right)+o(\delta v).$ Since $\delta v/h\to g(t)^2$, the product rule gives $\displaystyle \lim_{h\downarrow0}\frac{K_{u,u+h}\varphi(y)-\varphi(y)}h=g(t)^2\left(\nabla\log p_t(y)\cdot\nabla\varphi(y)+\tfrac12\Delta\varphi(y)\right)=\widetilde L_u\varphi(y).$ The remainder is locally uniform in $y$ and dominated on the compact test support because $t\ge\epsilon$. [F1, F4, F2]

2.1 Reverse Chapman–Kolmogorov [F3] and the local expansion in step 1.2 imply the finite-time identity $\displaystyle K_{u,v}\varphi-\varphi=\int_u^v K_{u,r}(\widetilde L_r\varphi)\,dr.$ To see this, telescope over partitions of $[u,v]$, use the local expansion on each subinterval, and pass from the Riemann sums by the local uniform remainder and dominated convergence [F4]. For $s<v$, the Markov property from step 1.1 now gives $\displaystyle E\!\left[\varphi(Y_v)-\varphi(Y_s)-\int_s^v\widetilde L_r\varphi(Y_r)dr\mid\mathcal G_s\right]=K_{s,v}\varphi(Y_s)-\varphi(Y_s)-\int_s^vK_{s,r}\widetilde L_r\varphi(Y_s)dr=0.$ The integrand is bounded on the truncated time interval because $\varphi$ is compactly supported and the coefficients are smooth there. Thus the compensated test process is a martingale, as claimed. [F3, step 1.2, F4, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Fix $d\ge1$, $T>0$, a Borel probability measure $\mu$ supported in $\overline B(0,R)$ for a finite $R$, and $g\in C^1([0,T])$ with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$. Let $W$ be standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion with increments independent of the past, let $X_0\sim\mu$ be independent of future Brownian increments, and set
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t g(r)dW_r,\qquad v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2dr,\qquad p_t(x)=\int\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\mu(dz)\quad(t>0).$$
For $0<\epsilon<T$, set $Y_u=X_{T-u}$ on $0\le u\le T-\epsilon$. Then there is a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion $B$ in the usual augmentation of the natural reversed filtration such that
$$dY_u=g(T-u)^2\nabla\log p_{T-u}(Y_u)\,du+g(T-u)\,dB_u,\qquad 0\le u<T-\epsilon.$$
The reverse drift is globally Lipschitz in the state on this truncated interval, with constant at most $g_{\max}^2(1/v(\epsilon)+R^2/v(\epsilon)^2)$ when $\operatorname{supp}\mu\subseteq\overline B(0,R)$, and has linear growth. The endpoint coupling satisfies
$$\mathbb E|Y_{T-\epsilon}-X_0|^2=dv(\epsilon),\qquad W_2(\operatorname{Law}(Y_{T-\epsilon}),\mu)\le\sqrt{dv(\epsilon)},$$
where $W_2$ is the infimum of root mean-square cost over probability couplings with finite second moments. Consequently $Y_{T-\epsilon}=X_\epsilon$ converges to $X_0$ in $L^2$ and its law converges weakly to $\mu$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. No score or density regularity at $t=0$ is asserted.

## Statement references

[Gaussian smoothing density and forward equation](../../items/thm-gaussian-smoothing-density-and-forward-equation.md): supplies the positive-time density and heat equation for arbitrary compactly supported Borel initial law.

[Gaussian mixture score and global Lipschitz bound](../../items/thm-gaussian-mixture-score-and-global-lipschitz-bound.md): supplies the score identity, state-Lipschitz constant, and linear-growth bound on $[\epsilon,T]$.

[Gaussian smoothing endpoint weak limit](../../items/thm-gaussian-smoothing-endpoint-weak-limit.md): supplies the exact $L^2$, weak, and $W_2$ endpoint coupling estimate without a score claim at zero.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and the compact-support, Brownian, and noise hypotheses in the Statement.

[A1] AC is required by the supplied density, score, SDE, local-martingale, and Brownian reconstruction interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] On every $[\epsilon,T]$, $p_t$ is positive and smooth and solves $\partial_t p_t=\tfrac12g(t)^2\Delta p_t$; the Gaussian reverse kernels have the Bayes normalization and composition identities. [[thm-gaussian-smoothing-density-and-forward-equation]] [[def-bayes-reversed-gaussian-smoothing-kernels]]

[F2] The reverse generator on compact tests is $\widetilde L_u\varphi=g(T-u)^2(\nabla\log p_{T-u}\cdot\nabla\varphi+\tfrac12\Delta\varphi)$, and the compensated test process is a martingale. [[lem-reversed-smoothing-generator-and-martingale]]

[F3] The score is globally Lipschitz and has linear growth uniformly on $[\epsilon,T]$, with derivative bound $1/v(\epsilon)+R^2/v(\epsilon)^2$. [[thm-gaussian-mixture-score-and-global-lipschitz-bound]]

[F4] For a continuous semimartingale, coordinate and coordinate-product martingale tests identify the bracket via the proved product formula; the resulting bracket $\int g(T-u)^2I_ddu$ can be inverted to construct Brownian motion. [[lem-continuous-local-martingale-quadratic-variation]] [[lem-elliptic-local-martingale-brownian-representation]]

[F5] With $X_0$ compactly supported, $X_\epsilon$ has finite second moment and the coupling $(X_\epsilon,X_0)$ gives $E|X_\epsilon-X_0|^2=dv(\epsilon)$ and $W_2(\operatorname{Law}(X_\epsilon),\mu)\le\sqrt{dv(\epsilon)}$, hence weak convergence. [[thm-gaussian-smoothing-endpoint-weak-limit]]

[F6] Under globally Lipschitz state coefficients and linear growth on a complete usual filtered Brownian space, the SDE has a unique strong solution; solutions driven by the same initial value and Brownian motion are pathwise unique. [[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] [[thm-global-strong-well-posedness-for-lipschitz-ito-sdes]]

## Proof

**Given:** the hypotheses in the Statement, AC, and any fixed $0<\epsilon<T$.

1.1 By [F1], the reversed Gaussian kernels are normalized and compose, and [F2] gives the reverse martingale problem for $Y_u=X_{T-u}$ on $0\le u\le T-\epsilon$. In particular the reverse generator has drift $\beta_u(x)=g(T-u)^2\nabla\log p_{T-u}(x)$ and diffusion matrix $a_u(x)=g(T-u)^2I_d$. [F1, F2]

2.1 Fix $R_1$ and stop when $|Y|$ reaches $R_1$. Compactly supported cutoffs equal to $x_i$ and $x_ix_j$ on that ball turn the identities in [F2] into coordinate and coordinate-product martingales. Subtracting the finite-variation drift gives continuous local martingales $M^i$. The product formula in [F4] makes $Y_iY_j-Y_i(0)Y_j(0)-\int(\beta_iY_j+\beta_jY_i)dr-[M_i,M_j]$ a local martingale. The coordinate-product identity makes the same expression with $\int g(T-r)^2\delta_{ij}dr$ in place of $[M_i,M_j]$ a local martingale. Their difference is a continuous finite-variation local martingale, hence constant by [F4]; it starts at zero. Thus $[M]_u=\int_0^u g(T-r)^2I_d dr$. Letting $R_1\uparrow\infty$ is valid because $Y$ has continuous paths on the compact time interval. [F2, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 The process $\sigma_r=g(T-r)I_d$ is invertible with bounded inverse. Apply the inverse-diffusion construction in [F4] to define $B_u=\int_0^u g(T-r)^{-1}dM_r$. Its bracket is $uI_d$, so vector Lévy characterization makes $B$ Brownian in the raw reversed filtration. Completion preserves independence because it adds only null events. For the right-continuous augmentation, if $A$ lies in every $\mathcal G_{u_n}$ for a sequence $u_n\downarrow u$, then $B_t-B_{u_n}$ is independent of $A$ for $t>u_n$; continuity lets its characteristic-function identity pass to $B_t-B_u$. Thus $B$ remains Brownian in the usual augmentation. The decomposition of $M$ gives the displayed reverse SDE. [F4, A1, step 2.1]

4.1 By [F3], $\beta_u$ is globally Lipschitz in $x$ uniformly on the truncated interval, with constant at most $g_{\max}^2(1/v(\epsilon)+R^2/v(\epsilon)^2)$; its linear-growth bound follows by multiplying the supplied score bound by $g_{\max}^2$. The diffusion coefficient $g(T-u)I_d$ is deterministic and bounded. The initial value $Y_0=X_T$ has finite second moment since $X_0$ is bounded and the Gaussian increment has finite second moment. Thus [F6] gives a unique strong solution for the same initial value and Brownian motion $B$ on the usual augmented reversed filtration. Pathwise uniqueness identifies this solution with the weak solution $Y$ from step 3.1. [F3, F6, step 3.1]

5.1 Since $Y_{T-\epsilon}=X_\epsilon$, the endpoint coupling statement [F5] gives the exact mean-square error and $W_2$ bound. Because $v(\epsilon)\le g_{\max}^2\epsilon\to0$, the coupling proves $L^2$ convergence to $X_0$; the same supplier gives weak convergence of the laws to $\mu$. No part of this step evaluates a score at zero. [F5, step 4.1] ∎

Assume AC. ## Statement references

[Anderson, Sections 3–5](https://eva.fcien.udelar.edu.uy/pluginfile.php/166428/mod_resource/content/1/1982_andersonREVERSE-TIME%20DIFFUSION%20EQUATION%20MODELS.pdf): gives the state-dependent divergence correction.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and a standard one-dimensional Brownian motion $W$ with $W_0=0$.

[A1] AC is required by the Itô, SDE, and reverse-time interfaces used here. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Itô's formula for a smooth function of a Brownian-driven process gives drift $\tfrac12h''(W_t)$ and diffusion coefficient $h'(W_t)$ for $h(W_t)$. [[thm-multidimensional-ito-formula-for-brownian-driven-processes]]

[F2] A $C^1$ diffeomorphism changes a density by dividing by the absolute derivative of the inverse map. [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]

[F3] For a continuous Markov diffusion with positive smooth marginal and transition densities satisfying the forward equations and the stated differentiation and boundary conditions, the Bayes-reversed kernels have generator $p^{-1}(L^*(p\phi)-\phi L^*p)$ on compactly supported smooth tests. In dimension one its drift is $-b+a'+a\partial_x\log p$. [[lem-reversed-kernels-and-generator-identity]]

[F4] Globally Lipschitz coefficients with linear growth yield a unique nonexplosive strong solution. [[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] [[thm-global-strong-well-posedness-for-lipschitz-ito-sdes]]

[F5] For $t>0$, $W_t$ has the positive normalized density $\phi_t(x)=(2\pi t)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/(2t)}$. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]]

## Counterexample
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Define $\displaystyle \psi(y)=\begin{cases}\exp\!\left(-\frac1{1-y^2}\right),&|y|<1,\\0,&|y|\ge1.\end{cases}$ Every derivative extends continuously by zero at $y=\pm1$ because $u^{-m}e^{-1/u}\to0$ as $u\downarrow0$ for every integer $m\ge0$; hence $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$. Its first and second derivatives are bounded, and $\psi''$ is not identically zero, since a compactly supported function with zero second derivative would be affine and therefore zero. Choose $\alpha>0$ with $\alpha\|\psi'\|_\infty<1/2$ and set $h(y)=y+\alpha\psi(y)$. Then $h'(y)=1+\alpha\psi'(y)>1/2$, $h$ equals the identity outside $[-1,1]$, and it is strictly increasing and onto; the inverse function theorem makes it a smooth diffeomorphism. [A1]

2.1 Set $X_t=h(W_t)$ and $z=h^{-1}(x)$. By Itô's formula [F1], $\displaystyle dX_t=b(X_t)dt+\sigma(X_t)dW_t,\qquad b(x)=\tfrac12h''(h^{-1}(x)),\quad \sigma(x)=h'(h^{-1}(x)).$ Because $h'$ is bounded below by $1/2$, and $h''$ and $h'''$ are bounded and vanish outside a compact set, both $b$ and $\sigma$ are globally Lipschitz and bounded. Thus this diffusion is nonexplosive and uniformly elliptic, with $a(x)=\sigma(x)^2$. [F1, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 For $t>0$, $W_t$ has density $\phi_t$ by [F5], and the change-of-variables formula [F2] gives $\displaystyle p_t(x)=\frac{\phi_t(h^{-1}(x))}{h'(h^{-1}(x))}.$ Likewise, for $0\le s<t$ its transition density is $\displaystyle q(s,x;t,y)=\frac{\phi_{t-s}(h^{-1}(y)-h^{-1}(x))}{h'(h^{-1}(y))}.$ These densities are positive and smooth. They satisfy the marginal and Chapman–Kolmogorov identities because they are the images under $h$ of Brownian marginal and transition laws. [F5, F2, step 2.1]

3.2 Write $z=h^{-1}(x)$. Differentiating $a(x)=h'(z)^2$ and using $dz/dx=1/h'(z)$ gives $\displaystyle a'(x)=2h'(z)h''(z)\frac1{h'(z)}=2h''(z).$ Since $h''=\alpha\psi''$ is nonzero at some $y_*$, $a'(h(y_*))\ne0$. [step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Fix $0<\epsilon<T$ and reindex the actual process on $[\epsilon,T]$ as $\bar X_s=X_{\epsilon+s}$ on $[0,T-\epsilon]$. Write $\bar p_s=p_{\epsilon+s}$ and $\bar q(r,x;s,y)=q(\epsilon+r,x;\epsilon+s,y)$. The explicit formulas in step 3.1 are positive and smooth on this shifted interval, satisfy the marginal and Chapman–Kolmogorov identities because they are images of Brownian transition laws under the diffeomorphism $h$, and solve the forward density equations for the coefficients in step 2.1 by direct differentiation and the chain rule. Since $h$ equals the identity outside a compact set, these densities and their differentiated integrands have Gaussian tails; differentiation under transition integrals is absolutely integrable and integration by parts has no boundary term. The process is continuous, nonexplosive and Markov. Introduce reverse time $u\in[0,T-\epsilon]$ and $Y_u=\bar X_{T-\epsilon-u}=X_{T-u}$. The local generator lemma applies to this actual reversed process and gives drift $\displaystyle \widetilde b_u(x)=-b(x)+a'(x)+a(x)\partial_x\log p_{T-u}(x).$ For $|x|\ge1$, $h^{-1}(x)=x$, $h'(x)=1$, $h''(x)=0$, and $p_t(x)=\phi_t(x)$, so this drift is $-x/(T-u)$. On $|x|\le1$ it is smooth with bounded state derivative uniformly for $u\in[0,T-\epsilon]$, because $p_t$ has a positive minimum there. Thus $\widetilde b$ is globally Lipschitz with linear growth on the truncated interval; the reverse diffusion coefficient $\sigma$ is bounded, globally Lipschitz, and bounded away from zero. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 At $x_*=h(y_*)$, the actual reverse generator from [F3] has drift differing from the score-only expression $-b+a\partial_x\log p_t$ by the nonzero amount $a'(x_*)$. Choose $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ equal to $x-x_*$ near $x_*$; then $\phi'(x_*)=1$ and $\phi''(x_*)=0$, so the two proposed generators have different values at $x_*$. By continuity, the drift difference remains nonzero on an open interval about $x_*$, and the reversed marginal density is positive there. Thus the score-only coefficient is not the actual reverse generator on a set of positive reversed probability. This refutes the claim. [F3, step 3.2, step 4.1] ∎

## Example

Assume AC. Let $X_0$ have a compactly supported $C^\infty$ probability density $\rho$ on $\mathbb R^d$, let $W$ be standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion independent of $X_0$, and set $X_t=X_0+W_t$ on $[0,T]$. For $t>0$ its density is
$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}(2\pi t)^{-d/2}e^{-|x-z|^2/(2t)}\rho(z)\,dz.$$
Assume that $p_t$ is the unique smooth forward-density solution on $[0,T]$ and, in addition, Anderson's unique smooth joint-density and conditional-density hypotheses for $(X_t,\widetilde W_t)$, where $\widetilde W_0=0$ and, for $t>0$, $d\widetilde W_t=dW_t+\nabla\log p_t(X_t)dt$. Then on reverse times $0\le u<T$, the reverse drift is $\nabla\log p_{T-u}(Y_u)$ with unit diffusion covariance. The value of $\nabla\log p_0$ is not used in the time integral; the statement makes no score assertion at the data endpoint $u=T$.

## Example references

[Gaussian-smoothed law and transition density](../../items/def-gaussian-smoothed-data-law-and-transition-density.md): supplies the positive-time Gaussian convolution formula.

[Anderson, Sections 3–4](https://eva.fcien.udelar.edu.uy/pluginfile.php/166428/mod_resource/content/1/1982_andersonREVERSE-TIME%20DIFFUSION%20EQUATION%20MODELS.pdf): states the bounded-start reversal theorem with the augmented-density uniqueness hypotheses retained here.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the initial law and Brownian motion in the Example, and Anderson's unique smooth joint and conditional density premises.

[A1] Anderson's theorem requires bounded initial state independent of the forward Brownian process, a unique smooth forward density, unique smooth augmented joint density, and unique smooth conditional augmented density; strong SDE well-posedness alone does not supply these density hypotheses. [[thm-anderson-reverse-time-diffusion]]

[F1] In the additive Gaussian setup with $g\equiv1$, the positive-time marginal density is the displayed convolution, is positive, and solves $\partial_t p_t=\tfrac12\Delta p_t$. [[def-gaussian-smoothed-data-law-and-transition-density]] [[thm-gaussian-smoothing-density-and-forward-equation]]

## Verification
1.1 The compact support of $\rho$ makes $X_0$ almost surely bounded, and its independence from $W$ is part of the Example. The SDE has $b=0$ and $\sigma=I_d$, so it is a globally Lipschitz strong SDE; the convolution and heat equation in [F1] give the stated positive-time marginal density. The separate augmented joint and conditional uniqueness requirements are explicitly assumed, exactly as listed in [A1]. [A1, F1, given]

2.1 Apply Anderson's theorem with $t_0=0$, $b=0$, $a=I_d$, $\nabla\!\cdot a=0$, and $p_t$ from [F1]. Its reverse drift is $-b+\nabla\!\cdot a+a\nabla\log p_t=\nabla\log p_t$, and the reverse diffusion covariance is $I_d$. Since $p_t$ is only used for $t>0$, this gives the stated equation for $u<T$ and asserts nothing about a score at $u=T$. [A1, F1, step 1.1] ∎

## Example

Assume AC. Let $\theta>0$, $\sigma>0$, $\mu\in\mathbb R$, and let $X_0\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2/(2\theta))$ be independent of a standard Brownian motion. Consider
$$dX_t=-\theta(X_t-\mu)dt+\sigma dW_t.$$
For every finite horizon, $X_t$ is stationary with density $N(\mu,\sigma^2/(2\theta))$. Its time reversal has the same transition kernels and satisfies the same Ornstein–Uhlenbeck SDE; equivalently, the general reverse-drift formula gives $-\theta(x-\mu)$.

## Example references

[[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws|Normal-law conventions]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $\theta>0$, $\sigma>0$, an independent initial $N(\mu,\sigma^2/(2\theta))$ state, and standard Brownian motion.

[A1] AC is assumed by the Itô, deterministic Gaussian-integral, and reverse Brownian interfaces used below. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Itô's formula for the product of a differentiable deterministic factor and a Brownian-driven process gives the integrating-factor representation. [[thm-multidimensional-ito-formula-for-brownian-driven-processes]]

[F2] A deterministic Itô integral over $(s,t]$ is centered Gaussian with variance its squared-integrand integral and is independent of the earlier filtration. [[lem-deterministic-ito-integral-has-gaussian-independent-increments]]

[F3] A sum of independent Gaussian variables is Gaussian with mean and variance obtained by adding their means and variances; the characteristic function of an independent sum is the product of characteristic functions. [[lem-characteristic-functions-under-affine-maps-and-independent-sums]] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]

[F4] The normal law $N(m,q)$ has density $(2\pi q)^{-1/2}\exp(-(x-m)^2/(2q))$ and the stated mean and variance. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]]

[F5] Bayes' formula gives the reversed transition kernel as the forward joint density divided by the later marginal density; step 2.1 evaluates this ratio explicitly for the stationary Gaussian OU law.

[F6] The globally Lipschitz forward OU coefficients give a unique nonexplosive strong solution. [[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] [[thm-global-strong-well-posedness-for-lipschitz-ito-sdes]]

[F7] The Borel sigma-algebra on continuous path space is generated by coordinate evaluations; finite-coordinate cylinders form a pi-system, and probability measures agreeing on a generating pi-system are equal. [[lem-borel-sigma-algebra-of-continuous-path-space-is-generated-by-coordinates]] [[lem-finite-coordinate-cylinders-form-a-pi-system]] [[thm-measure-uniqueness-on-a-sigma-finite-pi-system]]

## Verification
1.1 Applying [F1] to $e^{\theta t}(X_t-\mu)$ gives, for $t\ge s$, $\displaystyle X_t-\mu=e^{-\theta(t-s)}(X_s-\mu)+\sigma\int_s^t e^{-\theta(t-r)}dW_r.$ The last term is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and by [F2] is centered normal with variance $\displaystyle \sigma^2\int_s^t e^{-2\theta(t-r)}dr=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}\left(1-e^{-2\theta(t-s)}\right).$ With $q=\sigma^2/(2\theta)$ and $X_0-\mu\sim N(0,q)$, the mean of $X_t$ is $\mu$ and its variance is $e^{-2\theta t}q+q(1-e^{-2\theta t})=q$. Independence and Gaussian addition [F3, F4] therefore give the same marginal law at every $t$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given]

2.1 Fix $s<t$ and write $r=e^{-\theta(t-s)}$, $U=X_s-\mu$, and $V=X_t-\mu=rU+\eta$, where $U\sim N(0,q)$ and $\eta\sim N(0,q(1-r^2))$ is independent of $U$ by step 1.1. Their joint density is proportional to $\displaystyle \exp\!\left[-\frac12\left(\frac{u^2}{q}+\frac{(v-ru)^2}{q(1-r^2)}\right)\right],\qquad \frac{u^2}{q}+\frac{(v-ru)^2}{q(1-r^2)}=\frac{(u-rv)^2}{q(1-r^2)}+\frac{v^2}{q}.$ Thus $X_s\mid X_t=y$ has law $N(\mu+r(y-\mu),q(1-r^2))$, exactly the forward transition law over the same time gap. Bayes' formula shows that the reversed transition kernels equal the forward OU transition kernels. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F5] and step 2.1, the reversed process starts from the stationary law and has the same transition kernels as the forward OU process. Indeed, the forward joint density along an ordered time list is the stationary density times the product of the forward transition densities. The Bayes identity in step 2.1 gives detailed balance for each transition factor, so reversing this product gives the Markov factorization with the same kernels in reverse-time order. Thus all finite-dimensional distributions of $Y$ equal those of the forward OU process. Extend each path constantly after $T$; the extended paths are random elements of $C([0,\infty),\mathbb R)$ because each coordinate evaluation is measurable. By [F7], their Borel laws are equal. On a forward OU path define $\displaystyle \Gamma(X)_u=\frac{X_u-X_0+\theta\int_0^u(X_r-\mu)\,dr}{\sigma},\quad 0\le u\le T.$ The integral equation makes $\Gamma(X)=W$; because the natural filtration of $X$ is contained in the forward filtration, this driver is Brownian relative to that natural filtration. The map from a continuous path to $\Gamma(X)$ is continuous in the uniform norm on $[0,T]$, so equality of path laws transfers this Brownian property to $B_u:=\Gamma(Y)_u$. Rearranging its definition gives $dY_u=-\theta(Y_u-\mu)\,du+\sigma\,dB_u$ in the natural reversed filtration. Finally, the stationary score is $\partial_x\log p(x)=-(x-\mu)/q=-2\theta(x-\mu)/\sigma^2$. With $b(x)=-\theta(x-\mu)$ and $a(x)=\sigma^2$, the score-form drift equals $-b(x)+a(x)\partial_x\log p(x)=\theta(x-\mu)-2\theta(x-\mu)=-\theta(x-\mu)$, as stated. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Put $C=C([0,\infty),\mathbb R)$, give $C$ the uniform-on-compacts topology,
and write $\pi_t(f)=f(t)$. Then
$$\mathcal B(C)=\sigma(\pi_t:t\ge0)=\sigma(\pi_q:q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,\infty)).$$
Here each expression on the right denotes the smallest sigma-algebra on $C$
making every displayed coordinate map measurable. No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The path space $C$, its uoc metric $d$, and its coordinate maps as in the Statement. Write $\mathcal G$ for the sigma-algebra generated by all coordinates and $\mathcal G_{\mathbb Q}$ for that generated by the nonnegative rational coordinates.

[F1] The uoc metric is $$d(f,g)=\sum_{n\ge1}2^{-n}(1\wedge M_n(f,g)),\qquad M_n(f,g)=\max_{0\le t\le n}|f(t)-g(t)|,$$ and its topology is compact convergence. [[def-uniform-on-compacts-metric-on-continuous-path-space]]

[F2] A Borel sigma-algebra is generated by the open sets, and a family of sets has a unique smallest generated sigma-algebra. [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] [[def-generated-sigma-algebra]] [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]]

[F3] Countable suprema and pointwise limits of measurable real functions are measurable; finite sums, scalar multiples, positive parts, and absolute values preserve measurability. [[thm-sequential-suprema-infima-limsup-liminf-and-pointwise-limits-are-measurable]] [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]

[F4] The rationals are countable and dense in the reals. There is a fixed bijection between $\mathbb N^2$ and $\mathbb N$, recursion constructs nested finite codes, finite products of countable sets are countable, and a subset of a countable set is countable. [[thm-rationals-countable]] [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]] [[thm-n-cross-n-countable]] [[thm-recursion]] [[thm-product-of-countable]] [[lem-subset-of-countable]]

[F5] Closed bounded real intervals are compact, continuous real functions on them are uniformly continuous, and for every $\delta>0$ there is $m\ge1$ with $1/m<\delta$. [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]] [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]]

[F6] Every nonnegative real has an integer part, and $2^{-j}\to0$. The geometric-series formula controls every tail $\sum_{n>N}2^{-n}$. [[lem-integer-part]] [[lem-geometric-sequence-null]] [[thm-geometric-series]]

[F7] Metric balls form a base for the metric topology. [[def-metric-topology]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $t\ge0$ and choose an integer $n\ge1$ with $t\le n$. If $\varepsilon>0$, then $$d(f,g)<2^{-n}\min\{1,\varepsilon\}$$ implies $2^{-n}(1\wedge M_n(f,g))<2^{-n}\min\{1,\varepsilon\}$ and hence $|\pi_t(f)-\pi_t(g)|\le M_n(f,g)<\varepsilon$. Thus every $\pi_t$ is continuous, so it is Borel measurable. Minimality in [F2] gives $\mathcal G_{\mathbb Q}\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal B(C)$. [F1, F2]

1.2 Fix $t\ge0$ and put $q_j=2^{-j}\lfloor2^jt\rfloor$. Then $q_j\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,\infty)$ and $0\le t-q_j<2^{-j}$, so $q_j\to t$ by [F6]. For every $f\in C$, continuity gives $\pi_{q_j}(f)\to\pi_t(f)$. Every $\pi_{q_j}$ is $\mathcal G_{\mathbb Q}$-measurable by definition, so [F3] makes $\pi_t$ measurable. Hence $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal G_{\mathbb Q}$ by minimality, and therefore $\mathcal G=\mathcal G_{\mathbb Q}$. [F2, F3, F6]

1.3 Let $D$ be the family of paths which, for some integers $N,m\ge1$, are affine on each interval $[k/m,(k+1)/m]$ for $0\le k<mN$, take rational values at all grid points $k/m$, and are constant after $N$. This family is countable without choice. Indeed, fix bijections $e:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Q$ and $p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N^2$. Nested use of $p^{-1}$ codes every finite sequence of naturals by one natural (and repeated application of $p$ decodes it); composing entries with $e$ codes every finite rational sequence. A further finite nesting codes $(N,m)$ together with that sequence, giving a surjection from a subset of $\mathbb N$ onto $D$. Thus [F4] makes $D$ at most countable. [F4, construct]

1.4 The family $D$ is uoc dense. Given $f\in C$ and $\varepsilon>0$, use [F6] to choose $N$ with $\sum_{n>N}2^{-n}<\varepsilon/2$. By [F5], $f$ is uniformly continuous on $[0,N]$; choose $m$ so that the oscillation of $f$ over distances at most $1/m$ is less than $\varepsilon/4$. By rational density, choose rational $a_k$ with $|a_k-f(k/m)|<\varepsilon/4$ for the finitely many $0\le k\le mN$ (finite induction, not a choice principle), and let $g\in D$ interpolate these values and remain constant after $N$. On a grid interval, convex interpolation and the triangle inequality give $|g(t)-f(t)|<\varepsilon/2$. Consequently $$d(f,g)\le\sum_{n=1}^N2^{-n}M_n(f,g)+\sum_{n>N}2^{-n}<\varepsilon.$$ This also covers $t=0$ and $t=N$. [F1, F4, F5, F6, construct]

1.5 Fix $f\in C$. For $n\ge1$, continuity and rational density give $$M_n(g,f)=\sup_{q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,n]}|\pi_q(g)-f(q)|.$$ Enumerating that rational set, [F3] makes $M_n(\,·\,,f)$ $\mathcal G_{\mathbb Q}$-measurable. The finite partial sums of the metric formula are measurable by [F3] and converge pointwise to $d(\,·\,,f)$, so this distance is measurable. Hence every metric ball, with an arbitrary center, belongs to $\mathcal G_{\mathbb Q}$. [F1, F3, F4]

2.1 The balls $B(h,r)$ with $h\in D$ and positive rational $r$ form a countable base: countability follows from [F4], while density from step 1.4 and the triangle inequality put such a ball around every point inside any prescribed open ball. For an open $U$, let $\mathscr V_U$ be the subfamily of these basic balls which are contained in $U$. It is countable by [F4], every member belongs to $\mathcal G_{\mathbb Q}$ by step 1.5, and $U=\bigcup\mathscr V_U$. Thus every open set is in $\mathcal G_{\mathbb Q}$; [F2] yields $\mathcal B(C)\subseteq\mathcal G_{\mathbb Q}$. Combining this with steps 1.1 and 1.2 proves all stated equalities. The zero path shows $C$ and $D$ are nonempty; singleton and zero-time coordinates cause no exception, and no countable family of nonempty sets was selected. [F2, F4, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.4, step 1.5] ∎

## Source notes

Van der Vaart and Wellner use the standard fact that the Borel sigma-algebra on a separable continuous-function space is generated by evaluations. The proof above supplies the complete uoc and rational-coordinate argument, including an explicit choice-free countable basis.

## Statement

The finite-coordinate cylinders in $E=\prod_{i\in I}E_i$ form a pi-system.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Two finite-coordinate cylinders $\pi_F^{-1}(A)$ and $\pi_G^{-1}(B)$.

[F1] Their supports $F,G$ are finite, and their bases are measurable in the respective finite product sigma-algebras.

## Proof

1.1 Put $H=F\cup G$ and let $p_F,p_G$ be the coordinate projections from $\prod_{H}E_i$. Then $C:=p_F^{-1}(A)\cap p_G^{-1}(B)$ is measurable in $\bigotimes_H\mathcal E_i$. [F1]

2.1 Directly from restriction of coordinates, $\pi_F^{-1}(A)\cap\pi_G^{-1}(B)=\pi_H^{-1}(C)$, a finite-coordinate cylinder. The family is nonempty because it contains $E$, so it is a pi-system. [step 1.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a time interval, and let $P_t$ be a probability law on $\mathbb R^d$ for each $t\in I$. Suppose $P_t$ has a density $p_t$ with respect to Lebesgue measure, meaning $P_t(A)=\int_A p_t(x)\,dx$ for every Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. On the set of points $x$ where $0<p_t(x)<\infty$ and the map $x\mapsto p_t(x)$ is differentiable, the **marginal score** of $P_t$ is

$$s_t(x):=\nabla_x\log p_t(x).$$

The score is a spatial vector field; this definition asserts no value where the density is zero, infinite, or not differentiable.

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $P_t$ be Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ for $0\le t\le T$. Suppose each $P_t$ has a positive finite Lebesgue density $p_t$ with $\int_{\mathbb R^d}p_t(x)\,dx=1$. Let $b_t(x)\in\mathbb R^d$ and $\sigma_t(x)\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}$, where $m\ge1$, and put $a_t(x)=\sigma_t(x)\sigma_t(x)^{\mathsf T}$. Assume $a_t$ is symmetric, all displayed derivatives exist continuously, and time derivatives at the endpoints are one-sided. Suppose $p_t$ satisfies the forward Fokker–Planck equation

$$\partial_t p_t=-\sum_i\partial_i(b_{t,i}p_t)+\frac12\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_j(a_{t,ij}p_t).$$

Define $s_t(x)=\nabla_x\log p_t(x)$ and $(\nabla\!\cdot a_t)_i(x)=\sum_j\partial_j a_{t,ij}(x)$, and set $v_t(x)=b_t(x)-\tfrac12(\nabla\!\cdot a_t)(x)-\tfrac12a_t(x)s_t(x)$. Assume $v$ has a global $C^1$ flow of diffeomorphisms $\Phi_{t,s}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ for $0\le s,t\le T$, with $\Phi_{s,s}$ the identity, $\Phi_{t,r}\circ\Phi_{r,s}=\Phi_{t,s}$, $\partial_t\Phi_{t,s}(x)=v_t(\Phi_{t,s}(x))$, and $\partial_s\Phi_{t,s}(x)=-D_x\Phi_{t,s}(x)v_s(x)$, where $D_x$ denotes the Jacobian matrix in the state variable. For $Z_0$ with law $P_0$, let $Z_t=\Phi_{t,0}(Z_0)$. Then $Z_t$ has law $P_t$ for every $t\in[0,T]$. Thus the deterministic probability-flow ordinary differential equation (ODE) has the same one-time marginals as the probability-law solution of the displayed forward equation; no equality of path laws is asserted.

Write $C_c^1(\mathbb R^d)$ for continuously differentiable real-valued functions with compact support. Here a time-dependent family of probability laws $\mu_t$ weakly solves $\partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\!\cdot(v_t\mu_t)=0$ if, for every continuously differentiable $\varphi(t,x)$ with a common compact spatial support,

$$\int\varphi(t,x)\,\mu_t(dx)-\int\varphi(0,x)\,\mu_0(dx)=\int_0^t\int(\partial_r\varphi(r,x)+v_r(x)\cdot\nabla_x\varphi(r,x))\,\mu_r(dx)\,dr.$$

[Song et al., Section 4.3 and Appendix D.1, equations (35)–(38)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.13456)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The positive density family, Fokker–Planck equation, coefficient regularity, global flow, and initial law in the Statement.

[A1] All derivatives in the Statement exist continuously, and the flow is global, jointly $C^1$, and consists of diffeomorphisms satisfying both displayed flow derivative identities.

[F1] The marginal score is $s_t(x)=\nabla_x\log p_t(x)$ at every point where $p_t$ is positive, finite, and spatially differentiable. [[def-marginal-score-function]]

[F2] If $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ are measurable and $f_n\uparrow f$, then $\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu$. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]

[F3] A class containing a $\pi$-system that generates the Borel $\sigma$-algebra and is a $\lambda$-system contains that $\sigma$-algebra. [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]

[F4] The law of a random element is its probability pushforward; equality of laws means equality on every Borel set. [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and notation in the Statement.

1.1 For symmetric $a_t$, the product rule gives $\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_j(a_{t,ij}p_t)=\nabla\!\cdot((\nabla\!\cdot a_t)p_t+a_t\nabla p_t)$, since $\sum_j\partial_j(a_{t,ij}p_t)=(\nabla\!\cdot a_t)_ip_t+\sum_j a_{t,ij}\partial_jp_t$. By [F1], $\nabla p_t=p_ts_t$. Substitution into the Fokker–Planck equation therefore yields $\partial_t p_t+\nabla\!\cdot(v_tp_t)=0$. For a time-dependent test $\varphi$ with common compact spatial support, differentiate $\int\varphi(t,x)p_t(x)dx$, substitute this equation, and integrate by parts; this gives exactly the weak continuity identity stated above. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

1.2 For $Z_t=\Phi_{t,0}(Z_0)$ and any continuously differentiable time-dependent test $\varphi$ with common compact spatial support, the pathwise chain rule gives $\frac{d}{dt}\varphi(t,Z_t)=\partial_t\varphi(t,Z_t)+\nabla_x\varphi(t,Z_t)\cdot v_t(Z_t)$. The derivative is bounded on the compact support by continuity of $v$ and $\varphi$, so it is integrable; taking expectations and integrating in time proves that $Q_t:=\operatorname{Law}(Z_t)$ satisfies the same weak continuity equation and has $Q_0=P_0$. [A1, F4, given]

2.1 Fix $t\in[0,T]$ and $\psi\in C_c^1(\mathbb R^d)$, and set $\varphi(r,x)=\psi(\Phi_{t,r}(x))$ for $0\le r\le t$. The flow identities in [A1] imply $\partial_r\varphi+v_r\cdot\nabla_x\varphi=0$; the support stays compact because it is the image of $\operatorname{supp}\psi$ under the continuous maps $\Phi_{r,t}$ on the compact interval $[0,t]$. Applying the weak equation from steps 1.1 and 1.2 gives $\int\psi\,dP_t=\int\psi(\Phi_{t,0}(x))\,P_0(dx)=\int\psi\,dQ_t$. Thus $P_t$ and $Q_t$ agree on every $C_c^1$ test. [A1, F4, given, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 For a bounded rational open box $R=\prod_{i=1}^d(a_i,b_i)$, let $h(z)$ be $0$ for $z\le0$, $3z^2-2z^3$ for $0<z<1$, and $1$ for $z\ge1$. Its derivative is $6z(1-z)\ge0$ on $(0,1)$ and is $0$ at the joins, so $h$ is nondecreasing and $C^1$. Set $\theta_n(u)=h(nu)$ and $g_n(x)=\prod_i\theta_n(x_i-a_i)\theta_n(b_i-x_i)$. Then $g_n\in C_c^1$, $0\le g_n\le1$, and $g_n\uparrow\mathbf1_R$ pointwise. Step 2.1 and [F2] give $P_t(R)=Q_t(R)$. Bounded rational open boxes, together with $\varnothing$ and $\mathbb R^d$, form a $\pi$-system. They generate the Borel sets because every point of an open set lies in a bounded rational open box contained in that set. The class $\mathcal D=\{A\text{ Borel}:P_t(A)=Q_t(A)\}$ contains $\mathbb R^d$, is closed under complements by equality of the total masses, and is closed under disjoint countable unions by countable additivity; hence it is a $\lambda$-system. By [F3], [F4], and the definition of law, $P_t=Q_t$ on all Borel sets, proving equality of the one-time marginals. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $T>0$, $0<\epsilon<T$, an integer $d\ge1$, and an integer $N\ge1$. Let $X_t\in\mathbb R^d$ be a continuous nonexplosive Markov diffusion on $[\epsilon,T]$, where nonexplosive means its paths remain in $\mathbb R^d$ on the whole interval, and Markov means its conditional future law given the past depends only on its current state. Write $P_t(A)=P(X_t\in A)$ for its law on each Borel set $A$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, let $W$ be an adapted standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments are independent of the earlier filtration and have laws $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$. Let $b_t(x)\in\mathbb R^d$ and $\sigma_t(x)\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be Borel maps. The process is a continuous Brownian Itô process in the sense that, up to indistinguishability,

$$X_t=X_\epsilon+\int_\epsilon^t b_r(X_r)\,dr+\left(\sum_{j=1}^d\int_\epsilon^t\sigma_{ij}(r,X_r)\,dW_r^j\right)_{i=1}^d,$$

where the drift integrals are pathwise Lebesgue integrals and the coordinate stochastic integrals are localized Itô integrals; assume $\int_\epsilon^T|b_r(X_r)|\,dr<\infty$ and $\int_\epsilon^T\|\sigma_r(X_r)\|_F^2\,dr<\infty$ almost surely, with $\|M\|_F^2=\sum_{i,j}|M_{ij}|^2$. Assume also that $\sigma_t(x)$ is invertible with $\sup_{t,x}\|\sigma_t(x)^{-1}\|<\infty$. Put $a_t(x)=\sigma_t(x)\sigma_t(x)^{\mathsf T}$. A transition density $q(s,x;t,y)$ means that $P(X_t\in dy\mid X_s=x)=q(s,x;t,y)\,dy$.

Assume the marginal densities $p_t$ and transition densities $q(s,x;t,y)$ are positive, finite, and normalized with respect to Lebesgue measure; $p_t$ has one continuous time derivative and two continuous state derivatives. For $\epsilon\le s<t\le T$, assume

$$p_t(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}p_s(x)q(s,x;t,y)\,dx,\qquad q(s,x;t,y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz\quad(s<r<t).$$

For $L_t\phi=b_t\cdot\nabla\phi+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}a_{t,ij}\partial_i\partial_j\phi$, define $L_t^*r=-\sum_i\partial_i(b_{t,i}r)+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_j(a_{t,ij}r)$. Assume $\partial_t p_t=L_t^*p_t$ and $\partial_tq(s,x;t,y)=L_t^{*,y}q(s,x;t,y)$ classically. For every compactly supported smooth test, assume transition integrals and their time derivatives are absolutely integrable, differentiation under those integrals is valid, and integration by parts in space has no boundary term.

For $0\le u<T-\epsilon$, set $s=T-u$ and define the reverse score $s_s(x)=\nabla_x\log p_s(x)$. With $a=\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T}$ and $(\nabla\!\cdot a)_i=\sum_j\partial_j a_{ij}$, define the reverse drift supplied by the positive-density reversal interface:

$$\widetilde b_u(x)=-b_{T-u}(x)+(\nabla\!\cdot a_{T-u})(x)+a_{T-u}(x)s_{T-u}(x),\qquad \widetilde\sigma_u(x)=\sigma_{T-u}(x).$$

Write $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ for infinitely differentiable real functions with compact support. For $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, define $\widetilde L_u\phi=\widetilde b_u\cdot\nabla\phi+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}a_{T-u,ij}\partial_i\partial_j\phi$. Assume that for every reverse initial law the martingale problem for $\widetilde L_u$ has a unique nonexplosive continuous solution in law; this means that each compact-test compensated process $\phi(Y_u)-\phi(Y_0)-\int_0^u\widetilde L_r\phi(Y_r)\,dr$ is a local martingale and its law is unique. The current reversal supplier's proof uses AC through its Brownian-reconstruction lemma, so AC is an explicit algorithm assumption here.

Set $S=T-\epsilon$, $h=S/N$, $u_k=kh$, and $t_k=T-u_k$ for $0\le k\le N$. Given step sizes $\eta_k>0$, the **predictor-corrector score-sampling algorithm** takes an initial draw $Y_0\sim P_T$ and mutually independent vectors $G_k,\xi_k\sim N_d(0,I_d)$, independent of $Y_0$. For $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, perform the following two operations:

1. **Predictor.** Compute one Euler–Maruyama step for the reverse equation:
   $$\widehat Y_{k+1}=Y_k+h\widetilde b_{u_k}(Y_k)+\sqrt h\,\widetilde\sigma_{u_k}(Y_k)G_k.$$

2. **Corrector.** Let $U_{k+1}(x)=-\log p_{t_{k+1}}(x)$, so $e^{-U_{k+1}}$ is the normalized target density $p_{t_{k+1}}$. Apply one unadjusted Langevin update with step size $\eta_k$:
   $$Y_{k+1}=\widehat Y_{k+1}-\eta_k\nabla U_{k+1}(\widehat Y_{k+1})+\sqrt{2\eta_k}\,\xi_k=\widehat Y_{k+1}+\eta_k s_{t_{k+1}}(\widehat Y_{k+1})+\sqrt{2\eta_k}\,\xi_k.$$

Return $Y_N$, the finite-step state at forward time $\epsilon$. The procedure requires an exact marginal score on $[\epsilon,T]$ and starts from the actual terminal law $P_T$; it does not replace $P_T$ by $N_d(0,I_d)$ unless they are equal.

## Definition references

[[thm-markov-diffusion-reversal-by-bayes-kernels|The positive-density Bayes-kernel reversal theorem]] is applied with horizon $S=T-\epsilon$ to $\overline X_r=X_{\epsilon+r}$, $0\le r\le S$, on the shifted filtration $\overline{\mathcal F}_r=\mathcal F_{\epsilon+r}$ and with Brownian motion $\overline W_r=W_{\epsilon+r}-W_\epsilon$. Brownian increments remain independent of $\overline{\mathcal F}_r$ by the original increment hypothesis, and the shifted filtration retains the usual conditions. The shifted coefficients are $\overline b_r(x)=b_{\epsilon+r}(x)$ and $\overline\sigma_r(x)=\sigma_{\epsilon+r}(x)$; changing variables in the Lebesgue and elementary stochastic integrals, then passing to their localized limits, gives $d\overline X_r=\overline b_r(\overline X_r)dr+\overline\sigma_r(\overline X_r)d\overline W_r$. Its marginal densities are $\overline p_r=p_{\epsilon+r}$ and its transition densities are $\overline q(r,x;s,y)=q(\epsilon+r,x;\epsilon+s,y)$. Positivity, normalization, Markov identities, forward equations, uniform nonsingularity, integrability, and the assumed reverse martingale problem transfer by this deterministic time translation. Its reverse process is $\overline X_{S-u}=X_{T-u}$ with natural reversed filtration $\mathcal G_u=\sigma(X_{T-v}:0\le v\le u)$, and its Bayes kernels become
$$\overline K_{u,v}(y,dx)=\frac{p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)}{p_{T-u}(y)}dx,\qquad0\le u<v\le S.$$
The supplier therefore gives precisely the displayed reverse coefficients and a Brownian driver in this reversed filtration, retaining Borel time dependence of $\sigma$.

[[def-marginal-score-function|The marginal score definition]] sets $s_t(x)=\nabla_x\log p_t(x)$ where the density is positive and differentiable.

[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion|The finite-dimensional Brownian convention]]

and [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process|the Brownian Itô-process convention]] fix the increment, filtration, and localized integral assumptions used in the forward diffusion input.

[[alg-unadjusted-langevin-algorithm|The unadjusted Langevin algorithm]] supplies the one-step corrector used at each time level.

[Song et al., Section 4.2 and Appendix G, Algorithm 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.13456)

[Särkkä and Solin, Algorithm 8.1](https://users.aalto.fi/~asolin/sde-book/sde-book.pdf)

[Durmus and Moulines, Section 1, equation (2)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1507.05021v3)

[Raginsky, Section 7.2](https://maxim.ece.illinois.edu/teaching/spring23/SDE_book.pdf)

## Remarks

This definition supplies no sampler convergence rate, no solver error bound, and no exactness claim for the finite predictor or unadjusted Langevin corrector. The corrector need not preserve its target density at a fixed positive step size. Errors from estimated scores, choosing a positive cutoff, substituting a terminal law, discretizing the reverse equation, and numerical integration require separate bounds.

## Example

Assume AC. Fix $\gamma>0$, $\theta>0$, and $T>0$. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0},P)$ be a complete filtered probability space with a right-continuous filtration. Let $W$ be an adapted standard one-dimensional Brownian motion such that, for every $0\le s<t$, $W_t-W_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N(0,t-s)$. Let $X_0$ be a finite $\mathcal F_0$-measurable random variable with law $N(0,\theta)$, independent of the Brownian process. Define

$$X_t=e^{-\gamma t}X_0+\sqrt{2\gamma\theta}\int_0^t e^{-\gamma(t-r)}\,dW_r,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$

This process solves $dX_t=-\gamma X_t\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma\theta}\,dW_t$. Every marginal has density $p(x)=(2\pi\theta)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/(2\theta)}$ and score $s(x)=-x/\theta$. Its forward Fokker–Planck equation has zero right-hand side, and the probability-flow vector field $v(x)=-\gamma x-\tfrac12(2\gamma\theta)s(x)$ is identically zero. Thus the probability-flow ODE is stationary and the exact finite-time terminal law is $P_T=N(0,\theta)$.

## Example references

[Särkkä and Solin, Section 5.2, Theorem 5.4 and Example 5.7; Section 6.1](https://users.aalto.fi/~asolin/sde-book/sde-book.pdf)

[Raginsky, Section 2.3 and Chapter 2, Problem 8](https://maxim.ece.illinois.edu/teaching/spring23/SDE_book.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $W$, $X_0$, and $X_t$ as in the Example.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed by the Brownian, Itô, and normal-law interfaces used in the verification. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Under the stated filtration and increment conditions, the displayed process has a continuous Brownian Itô representation with pathwise integrable drift and a localized Itô integral. [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]

[F2] For a one-dimensional Brownian Itô process and $f\in C^{1,2}$, $df(t,X_t)=(\partial_t f+b\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_x f)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma_t\partial_x f(t,X_t)\,dW_t$. [[thm-ito-formula-one-dimensional]]

[F3] A deterministic square-integrable integrand $h$ has centered normal Itô integral with variance $\int_0^t h(r)^2dr$. [[cor-deterministic-ito-integrals-are-gaussian]]

[F4] The deterministic Itô integral is an $L^2$ limit of elementary sums of Brownian increments. These sums are measurable with respect to the Brownian process; $L^2$ convergence implies convergence in probability, which has an almost-surely convergent subsequence. Defining its limit on the measurable convergence event gives a Brownian-process-measurable version. Measurable functions of independent random elements remain independent, and replacing a random variable by an almost-surely equal version preserves its joint law with $X_0$. [[def-independent-random-elements]] [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] [[lem-measurable-functions-preserve-independence]] [[thm-almost-sure-subsequence-from-convergence-in-probability]]

[F5] Independent scalar normal variables have the product characteristic function, and their sum is normal with the sum of their variances. [[lem-characteristic-functions-under-affine-maps-and-independent-sums]]

[F6] $N(0,\theta)$ for $\theta>0$ has density $(2\pi\theta)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/(2\theta)}$. [[lem-normal-location-scale-density]]

[F7] At positive density points, the marginal score is $\partial_x\log p(x)$. [[def-marginal-score-function]]

[F8] If $p_t$ is a positive classical solution of the displayed forward equation and the probability-flow field has a global $C^1$ flow, then the ODE flow law has the same one-time marginals. [[thm-probability-flow-ode-marginals]]

## Verification

1.1 Put $M_t=\int_0^t e^{\gamma r}\,dW_r$, so $X_t=e^{-\gamma t}(X_0+\sqrt{2\gamma\theta}M_t)$. Apply [F2] to $f(t,x)=e^{-\gamma t}x$ and the continuous Itô process $X_0+\sqrt{2\gamma\theta}M_t$. Its drift is zero and its diffusion coefficient is $\sqrt{2\gamma\theta}e^{\gamma t}$; the product rule gives $dX_t=-\gamma X_t\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma\theta}\,dW_t$, as asserted. [A1, F1, F2, given]

1.2 For fixed $t$, [F3] gives $M_t\sim N(0,\int_0^t e^{2\gamma r}dr)$. Equivalently the stochastic term in the Example is centered normal with variance $2\gamma\theta\int_0^t e^{-2\gamma(t-r)}dr=\theta(1-e^{-2\gamma t})$. Its deterministic-integrand Itô approximants are measurable functions of Brownian increments, and [F4] gives a Brownian-process-measurable version of their limit; that version is independent of $X_0$, and almost-sure equality preserves the joint law. The first term is $N(0,\theta e^{-2\gamma t})$, and [F5] gives $X_t\sim N(0,\theta e^{-2\gamma t}+\theta(1-e^{-2\gamma t}))=N(0,\theta)$. By [F6], its density is the one displayed in the Example. [A1, F3, F4, F5, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 Differentiating the density in [F6] gives $\partial_xp=-(x/\theta)p$ and $\partial_{xx}p=(x^2/\theta^2-1/\theta)p$. With $b(x)=-\gamma x$ and $a=2\gamma\theta$, the Fokker–Planck right-hand side is $-\partial_x(bp)+\tfrac12\partial_{xx}(ap)=\gamma\partial_x(xp)+\gamma\theta\partial_{xx}p=0$ by substitution of these derivatives. Thus $p_t=p$ is a positive smooth solution of the forward equation and [F7] gives $s(x)=-x/\theta$. [F6, F7, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The diffusion covariance $a$ is constant, so $\partial_xa=0$. Substituting $b=-\gamma x$, $a=2\gamma\theta$, and $s=-x/\theta$ into the probability-flow velocity gives $v(x)=-\gamma x-\tfrac12(2\gamma\theta)(-x/\theta)=0$. Its global flow is $\Phi_{t,s}(x)=x$, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism for each $s,t$. The hypotheses of [F8] hold by step 2.1, so the deterministic flow preserves the law $N(0,\theta)$ at each time, including $T$. [F7, F8, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]: $B$ is a standard Brownian
motion on a filtered probability space, adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$,
with $B_t-B_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ of law $N(0,t-s)$ for $0\le s<t$.
For this localized-calculus definition the filtration satisfies the usual
conditions, as required by
[[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]].

1. **Real continuous Brownian Ito process.** A real progressively measurable process
   $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **continuous Brownian Ito process** when there are
   * a finite real $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $X_0$,
   * a real progressively measurable process $b=(b_s)_{s\ge0}$
     [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]] with
     $\int_0^t|b_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every finite $t\ge0$, and
   * a real predictable process $\sigma=(\sigma_s)_{s\ge0}$, locally
     square-integrable in the sense that $\int_0^t\sigma_s^2\,ds<\infty$
     almost surely for every finite $t$
     [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]],

   such that, up to equality at all times on a measurable probability-one event,
   $$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s,\qquad t\ge0,$$
   where the first integral is the pathwise Lebesgue integral of $s\mapsto
   b_s(\omega)$ and the second is the localized Ito integral
   $\sigma\cdot B$ of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. One writes
   $\displaystyle dX_t=b_t\,dt+\sigma_t\,dB_t$ for the display, and $b$ is
   called the **drift** and $\sigma$ the **diffusion coefficient** of this
   representation.

2. **Multidimensional Brownian-driven process.** Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge1$ be
   finite integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional
   Brownian motion [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] that is adapted to
   $(\mathcal F_t)$ and whose vector increment $B_t-B_s$ is independent of
   $\mathcal F_s$ for $0\le s<t$, let $X_0$ be a finite
   $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vector, let $b$ be an
   $\mathbb R^d$-valued progressively measurable process with
   $\int_0^t|b^i_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i$ and finite $t$, and let
   $\sigma=(\sigma^{ik})$ be an $\mathbb R^{d\times m}$-valued predictable
   process, each entry predictable
   [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]], with
   $\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i,k$ and finite $t$.
   Then
   $$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
   defines an $\mathbb R^d$-valued **continuous Brownian Ito process** driven by
   $B$, using the progressive integral versions of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. Other progressive representatives agreeing on one measurable full event at every time represent the same process. No claim is made that an arbitrary null-path modification remains adapted.

The following well-definedness clauses are part of the definition and are used
throughout.

3. **The drift integral is a genuine pathwise integral.** Progressive
   measurability gives measurable sections and makes the positive and negative
   integrals $\mathcal F_t$-measurable by the parameter-integral part of Tonelli
   [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], applied to Lebesgue measure on $[0,t]$ and the probability measure on $\mathcal F_t$.
   On the event where both extended integrals are finite, their difference is
   the drift integral; set it to zero otherwise. This is an adapted measurable
   convention, is finite everywhere, and on one probability-one event is
   absolutely continuous on every finite interval (take the countable
   intersection over integer horizons). It is progressive: the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto\int_0^tb_s(\omega)\,ds$, with the preceding finite-value
   convention, is measurable on every $[0,T]\times\Omega$ by parameter
   integration, and is adapted. Thus the definition uses the standard
   almost-sure drift and local-energy classes under the usual conditions.

4. **The stochastic integral exists, is unique and is continuous.** By
   [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]] and
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]] the localized integral $\sigma\cdot B$ is a
   well-defined adapted process with continuous paths, unique up to
   indistinguishability, and each of its finite-energy pieces is a
   square-integrable martingale. The displayed integral representative is progressive; $X$ is adapted by its required progressive measurability and has
   continuous paths, $X_t$ is finite almost surely for each $t$, and
   $M^i_t:=\sum_k\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s$ is a continuous local
   martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ in the sense of
   [[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]] for every $i$, with the common energy localizers described in clause 6.

5. **The coefficients are not part of the process.** A continuous Brownian Ito
   process may admit several representations $X=X_0+b\cdot\mathrm{Leb}
   +\sigma\cdot B$ with different pointwise representatives $(b,\sigma)$ (for example, altering a coefficient only at the single time zero), even for the same Brownian
   motion and filtration; this does not assert nonuniqueness of their equivalence classes modulo $\mathrm dt\otimes P$; conversely, two processes with the same displayed
   integral representation and the same $X_0$ are indistinguishable. Every
   statement on this page that mentions a decomposition uses only properties
   common to all representations of the given process. The separate
   quadratic-covariation definition that follows this item on its owning page
   is formulated from $X$ itself and not from $(b,\sigma)$; no
   quadratic-covariation definition is made inside this item.

6. **The class is closed under stopping and under linear combinations.**
   If $\tau$ is a stopping time, the literal stopped process $X^\tau$ is
   progressive. Indeed on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto(t\wedge\tau(\omega),\omega)$ is measurable into
   $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F_T$: the truncated time $\tau\wedge T$
   is $\mathcal F_T$-measurable, minimum is continuous, and rectangle inverse
   images give the assertion. Compose with the progressive restriction of $X$.
   Its drift is $b1_{[0,\tau]}$ and its diffusion is
   $\sigma1_{[0,\tau]}$; these retain almost-sure integrability and the required
   progressive/predictable measurability. The drift identity is pathwise.
   For the stochastic identity, apply the finite-energy stopping identity of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]], clause 4, on the canonical energy intervals
   of $\sigma$. The truncated integrand has finite energy on these same
   intervals. Comparing its canonical intervals with them at their pairwise
   minima by clause 4 identifies the localized integrals there. Countably
   many full-event agreements and exhaustion then give the identity at all
   times on one full event. Thus stopping closure uses localization, not a
   direct application of clause 4 to a possibly infinite-energy integrand.
   For finitely many coefficients, use the common continuous energy
   $E_t=\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2ds$ and times
   $\kappa_n=\inf\{t:E_t\ge n\}\wedge n$, $n\ge1$.
   The same continuous-energy test as in the local-integrability definition
   makes these stopping times increasing to infinity almost surely, and bounds
   every stopped coefficient's expected energy by $n$. The preceding
   pairwise-minimum comparison shows that every integral stopped there is its
   finite-energy integral. Finite sums of these square-integrable martingales
   are martingales: finite sums preserve adaptation and integrability, and summing the integral test over any $A\in\mathcal F_s$ proves the conditional-expectation identity; hence their sums
   are local martingales with this common sequence. For fixed real constants,
   finite linear combinations of processes driven by the same vector Brownian
   motion have the combined coefficients. Their integrability follows from
   the triangle inequality and $(\sum_{j=1}^r u_j)^2\le r\sum_j u_j^2$.

7. **No pathwise integral against Brownian motion is defined.** The display
   defines the stochastic integral only as the localized limit of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]; no integral $\int_0^tH_s(\omega)\,dB_s(\omega)$
   along the individual path is asserted, and the page's examples show that
   the pathwise Riemann--Stieltjes route is unavailable.

No choice beyond the declared AC of the ambient interfaces enters the
construction: the coefficients $b,\sigma$ and the process are given data, and
the canonically localized integral is constructed in
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. The Axiom of Choice is declared because the
conditional-expectation and $L^2$ interfaces used downstream assume it, and
the countable-choice obligations inherited from those interfaces are declared
as dependencies of this item.
