## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let
$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s$ be a real continuous Brownian
Ito process [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], under its usual-filtration
conditions, and let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R)$, meaning that $f$, its first time
derivative $\partial_tf$ and its first two space derivatives
$\partial_xf,\partial^2_{x}f$ exist and are continuous on
$[0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every
$t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+b\,\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,\partial_xf(s,X_s)\,dB_s,$$
For the displayed integrands use the following representative convention.
Intersect the measurable full events of continuity of $X$, validity of its
decomposition, and local integrability of its coefficients at integer horizons.
Its complement is an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable null event by the usual
conditions. Replace $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ by zero there. This preserves the
decomposition up to indistinguishability and all coefficient classes, and
makes $X$ continuous everywhere and its coefficient path integrals locally
finite everywhere. All integrands below refer to these representatives.
The stochastic integral is the localized Ito integral of the predictable
locally square-integrable process $\sigma_s\partial_xf(s,X_s)$
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]] and the Lebesgue integral is the pathwise
integral of the progressively measurable process
$s\mapsto(\partial_tf+b\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf)(s,X_s)$,
which is pathwise integrable and finite almost surely for every $t$. In differential notation,
$df(t,X_t)=(\partial_tf+b\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma_t\partial_xf(t,X_t)\,dB_t$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, (H), a real continuous Brownian Ito process $X=X_0+A+M$ with $A_t=\int_0^tb_s\,ds$ and $M=\int\sigma\,dB$, a function $f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R)$, a finite horizon $T>0$, and an arbitrary deterministic partition sequence $(\pi_n)$ of $[0,T]$ with mesh $\delta_n\to0$. The stopping time $\rho_c$ is defined as in [F7] below.
 
[F1] **Paths, measurability and local boundedness.** After the statement's $\mathcal F_0$-null-event normalization, $X$ is adapted with everywhere continuous paths, hence predictable, and on each finite time interval a continuous path is bounded. Every continuous function of $(s,X_s)$ is predictable; its product with the predictable coefficient $\sigma$ is predictable, while its product with the progressively measurable drift $b$ is progressively measurable. [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]] [[lem-adapted-continuous-processes-are-progressively-measurable]] [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]
 
[F2] **Localized-integral interfaces.** For a predictable $G$ with finite energy: $E(\int_0^TG\,dB)^2=E\int_0^TG^2ds$, the integral over a subinterval is the integral of the restriction, the stopping identity holds, the elementary sums converge to the integral, and the Doob maximal bound $E\sup_{t\le T}(\int_0^tG\,dB)^2\le4E\int_0^TG^2ds$ holds. A locally square-integrable predictable $G$ has a localized integral whose stopped pieces are the finite-energy integrals of $G1_{(0,\rho]}$; and if $c$ is bounded and $\mathcal F_u$-measurable then the localized integral of $cG$ over an interval inside $(u,\infty)$ equals $c$ times that of $G$, because the finite-energy case follows from the elementary case and the $L^2$ isometry and the general case by stopping and uniqueness. [[thm-localized-ito-integral]] [[thm-stopping-an-ito-integral]] [[thm-ito-isometry-and-linearity-in-predictable-l2]] [[thm-doob-maximal-bound-for-the-ito-integral]] [[thm-ito-integral-process-has-a-continuous-martingale-version]] [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]]
 
[F3] **Quadratic variation and covariation of the class.** $[X]_t=\int_0^t\sigma_s^2\,ds$ and, more generally, $\sum_j\Delta_jX\Delta_jY\to[X,Y]=\int\xi\eta\,ds$ uniformly in probability for class processes; in particular with $\Delta_jX=X_{t_{j+1}}-X_{t_j}$ the step-convention sums $Q_n^X(t)=\sum_{j:\,t_{j+1}\le t}(\Delta_jX)^2$ and $Q_n^M(t)=\sum_{j:\,t_{j+1}\le t}(\Delta_jM)^2$ each satisfy $\sup_{t\le T}|Q_n^X(t)-\int_0^t\sigma_s^2ds|\to0$ and $\sup_{t\le T}|Q_n^M(t)-\int_0^t\sigma_s^2ds|\to0$ in probability for every deterministic vanishing-mesh sequence and both conventions. [[thm-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]] [[def-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]] [[def-quadratic-variation-along-a-partition-sequence]]
 
[F4] **Taylor expansion with a third-order remainder.** Let $f\in C^3$ on an open set containing the closed segment from $a=(t_0,x_0)$ to $a+h=(t_0+h_1,x_0+h_2)$. Then $f(a+h)=f(a)+\partial_tf(a)h_1+\partial_xf(a)h_2+\tfrac12\bigl(\partial^2_{tt}f(a)h_1^2+2\partial_t\partial_xf(a)h_1h_2+\partial^2_{xx}f(a)h_2^2\bigr)+R$ with $|R|\le M_3|h|^3$, where $M_3$ bounds the third partial derivatives on a ball containing the segment: apply the one-variable Taylor formula with remainder bound to $u\mapsto f(a+uh)$ on $[0,1]$. [[cor-second-order-taylor-expansion-with-the-hessian]] [[cor-multivariable-taylor-formula-with-peano-remainder]] [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]] [[def-taylor-polynomial-and-remainder]] [[cor-taylor-remainder-bound]]
 
[F5] **Staircase comparison and the weighted pullback of quadratic variation.** (a) If $D\in\mathcal F_0$, $G$ is continuous adapted and bounded on $D\times[0,T]$, $G^{(n)}$ is its left-endpoint staircase on $\pi_n$, and $\int_0^TH^2ds\le c$ on $D$, then the integrals of $1_DG^{(n)}H$ converge to that of $1_DGH$ in $L^2(P)$. Indeed the isometry bounds the squared distance by $E[1_D\sup_s|G^{(n)}_s-G_s|^2\int_0^TH^2ds]$, which tends to zero by dominated convergence. (b) If $w$ is continuous adapted with $|w|\le K$ and $M=\int\sigma\,dB$ is a finite-energy integral, then $\sum_jw(t_j)\Delta_jM^2\to\int_0^Tw_s\sigma_s^2\,ds$ in probability; this terminal-time weighted pullback is proved in steps 1.4--2.1 below. [[thm-ito-isometry-and-linearity-in-predictable-l2]] [[thm-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]] [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]]
 
[F6] **Bounded Riemann integrals.** If $Z$ is continuous on $[0,T]$ and $h$ pathwise Lebesgue-integrable, then $\sum_jZ_{t_j}\int_{t_j}^{t_{j+1}}h_s\,ds\to\int_0^TZ_sh_s\,ds$ along vanishing meshes, the error being at most $\max_j\sup_{I_j}|Z-Z_{t_j}|\int_0^T|h|$. A continuous function on the compact set $[0,T]$ and a continuous function on a compact cylinder are uniformly continuous, so maximal oscillations on the mesh intervals vanish. [[thm-heine-cantor-r]] [[def-continuity-real]]
 
[F7] **Localization of the class and of the coefficients.** For $c>0$ put $D_c:=\{|X_0|\le c\}\in\mathcal F_0$ and $\rho_c:=\inf\{t:\max(|X_t|,\int_0^t|b|,\int_0^t\sigma^2)\ge c\}\wedge T$. Then $\rho_c$ is a stopping time: for $t<T$, the event $\{\rho_c\le t\}$ is the event that the running supremum of the continuous adapted process $\max(|X|,\int|b|,\int\sigma^2)$ on $[0,t]$ is at least $c$. This supremum is the supremum over rational times together with $t$, hence is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable; for $t\ge T$ the stopping event is the whole space. The process $\bar X^{(c)}:=1_{D_c}X^{\rho_c}$ is a continuous Brownian Ito process with initial value $1_{D_c}X_0$ and coefficients $1_{D_c}b1_{[0,\rho_c]}$, $1_{D_c}\sigma1_{[0,\rho_c]}$. It is bounded by $c$, its drift variation and diffusion energy on $[0,T]$ are at most $c$, and on $D_c\cap\{\rho_c\ge T\}$ it and all its integrals coincide with those of $X$. These events increase to a probability-one event as $c\to\infty$, because $X$ is continuous and $\int|b|,\int\sigma^2$ are finite and continuous in the upper limit almost surely. [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]] [[thm-localized-ito-integral]] [[thm-stopping-an-ito-integral]] [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] [[thm-heine-cantor-r]]
 
[F8] **Cutoff and mollification on a cylinder.** Reflection across $t=0$ by $g(t,x):=f(t,x)$ for $t\ge0$ and $g(t,x):=2f(0,x)-f(-t,x)$ for $t<0$ extends $f$ to a $C^{1,2}$ function on a negative-time collar and agrees with $f$ on the nonnegative half-space. Choose compact cylinders $K\subseteq\operatorname{int}K'$ inside a bounded open set on which $g$ is defined. The cutoff lemma gives a continuous compactly supported cutoff equal to $1$ on $K'$; convolution with a sufficiently small compactly supported mollifier gives $\chi\in C_c^\infty$ equal to $1$ on $K$ and supported in that open set. Then $g_\varepsilon:=(\chi g)*\rho_\varepsilon$ is smooth and compactly supported, and on the inner cylinder the functions $g_\varepsilon,\partial_tg_\varepsilon,\partial_xg_\varepsilon,\partial^2_{xx}g_\varepsilon$ converge uniformly to $f,\partial_tf,\partial_xf,\partial^2_{xx}f$. To justify the derivative convergence, write the convolution as $\int \rho(z)(\chi g)(y-\varepsilon z)dz$. Difference quotients and the fundamental theorem in each variable move each available derivative ($\partial_t$, $\partial_x$, $\partial_{xx}$) onto $\chi g$, dominated on the fixed compact support by the corresponding continuous derivative bound times $|\rho(z)|$. On the inner cylinder $\chi=1$ on a neighbourhood; uniform continuity of each derivative bounds its convolution error by its modulus on shifts of size at most $\varepsilon R$ times $\int|\rho|$, where $R$ bounds the mollifier support. This tends to zero. [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]] [[def-mollifier-family-generated-by-a-unit-mass-smooth-bump]] [[thm-convolution-with-a-mollifier-is-smooth-and-differentiates-under-the-integral-sign]] [[lem-a-compact-set-inside-a-bounded-open-set-admits-an-explicit-compactly-supported-cutoff]] [[thm-c-c-infinity-rn-is-dense-in-l-p-of-rn]]
 
[F9] **Convergence tools and estimates.** Cauchy--Schwarz for sums and expectations; dominated convergence for pathwise Lebesgue integrals; Fatou's lemma; and the fact that a sequence bounded by $R_n$ with $ER_n\to0$ converges to $0$ in probability. [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]] [[thm-dominated-convergence]] [[thm-fatou-lemma]] [[def-convergence-in-probability]]
 
[F10] **AC bookkeeping.** Choice is declared for the ambient conditional-expectation, completeness and density interfaces; all stopping levels, partitions and mollification scales used below are canonical functions of the given data. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]
 
 
 
 

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.
 
1.1 Reduction to a bounded localized problem: fix $c>0$ and replace $X$ by $\bar X^{(c)}=1_{D_c}X^{\rho_c}$ as in [F7]. This is globally bounded by $c$, its drift variation and diffusion energy on $[0,T]$ are at most $c$, and on $D_c\cap\{\rho_c\ge T\}$ both sides of the desired formula agree with those for the original process. Thus the stochastic integrand has finite energy bounded by $c\sup|\partial_xf|^2$, and every continuous function of $(s,\bar X^{(c)}_s)$ is bounded on $[0,T]$. It remains to prove the identity for this bounded process; localization is removed at the end. To simplify notation, call the bounded process and its coefficients again $X,b,\sigma$. [F1, F2, F7, given]
 
1.2 Setup of the $C^3$ case: assume first that $f\in C^3$ on a neighbourhood of the cylinder $[0,T]\times[-c,c]$ with finite bounds $M_0,M_1,M_2,M_3$ for its partial derivatives of orders $0,1,2,3$ there. Van der Vaart states Theorem 5.79 for a continuous local martingale and a continuous finite-variation process; its proof discussion refers the direct Taylor argument to Chung and Williams and presents a polynomial proof of the more general Theorem 5.85. ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$ and let
$h\in L^2[0,T]$ be deterministic, choose a Borel representative of its
Lebesgue-equivalence class, and set $h(s,\omega):=h(s)$. This process is
predictable with finite energy. Then the Ito integral
$\int_0^Th_s\,dB_s$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] is centered
normal with variance $\int_0^Th^2ds$: its law is $N(0,\int_0^Th^2ds)$ in the
convention of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], where $N(0,0)$ is the
Dirac law at $0$. More generally, for deterministic $h_1,\dots,h_d\in L^2[0,T]$
the vector of integrals is jointly Gaussian in the sense of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: its law is $N_d(0,\Sigma)$ with
$$\Sigma_{jk}=\int_0^Th_j(s)h_k(s)\,ds .$$
In particular the covariance of the pair is
$\operatorname{Cov}(\int h_jdB,\int h_kdB)=\int h_jh_k$, the integrals are
uncorrelated exactly when $\int h_jh_k=0$, and integrals of deterministic
integrands with disjoint supports are independent.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the standing hypothesis (H), a horizon $T>0$, deterministic $h,h_1,\dots,h_d\in L^2[0,T]$ represented by Borel functions, and real coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_d$.

[F1] A deterministic step function is an elementary predictable integrand with deterministic coefficients, and its Ito integral is the finite sum $\sum_ka^m_k(B_{t^m_{k+1}}-B_{t^m_k})$; the Brownian increments over disjoint intervals are independent with laws $N(0,\Delta_k)$ and mean $0$. [[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]] [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]] [[def-brownian-motion]]

[F2] A finite linear combination of independent centered normal variables is centered normal, and a $N(0,\sigma^2)$ variable has characteristic function $t\mapsto e^{-\sigma^2t^2/2}$, including $\sigma=0$; a Borel probability law on $\mathbb R$ is determined by its characteristic function. [[lem-characteristic-functions-under-affine-maps-and-independent-sums]] [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-normal-law]] [[thm-uniqueness-of-a-law-from-its-characteristic-function]]

[F3] Convergence in $L^2(P)$ implies convergence in probability, which implies weak convergence of the laws. Weak convergence tests bounded continuous real functions; applying it separately to $x\mapsto\cos(tx)$ and $x\mapsto\sin(tx)$ and then combining the two real limits gives convergence of the complex characteristic functions. [[def-convergence-in-probability]] [[thm-convergence-in-probability-implies-convergence-in-distribution]] [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]

[F4] The integration map on predictable $L^2$ is linear and isometric, and the integral of $h$ is the $L^2(P)$-limit of the elementary integrals of any admissible elementary approximation; the approximation $h^m$ is admissible because $|h^m-h|$ in $L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$ equals the deterministic $L^2[0,T]$ distance. [[thm-ito-isometry-and-linearity-in-predictable-l2]] [[lem-general-ito-integral-is-independent-of-the-approximating-sequence-and-ae-representative]] [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]]

[F5] If $h^m\to h$ in $L^2[0,T]$, the reverse triangle inequality in the stated normed space gives
$$\bigl|\lVert h^m\rVert_2-\lVert h\rVert_2\bigr| \le \lVert h^m-h\rVert_2\longrightarrow0.$$
Hence $\int_0^T(h^m)^2ds=\lVert h^m\rVert_2^2\to
\lVert h\rVert_2^2=\int_0^Th^2ds$.
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]

[F6] A Borel probability law on $\mathbb R^d$ is $N_d(0,\Sigma)$ exactly when every projection $u\cdot X$ has law $N(0,u^T\Sigma u)$; such a vector has mean $0$ and covariance $\Sigma$. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F7] Under AC, hence Countable Choice, finite linear combinations of box
indicators are dense in $L^2(\mathbb R)$. Extend $h$ by zero outside $[0,T]$
and approximate that extension by such a box-step function. Its restriction to
$[0,T]$ agrees almost everywhere with a function
$\sum_ka_k1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}$ after adjoining the finitely many box endpoints
and $0,T$ to one partition. Thus deterministic step functions of the required
elementary form are dense in $L^2[0,T]$. [[thm-box-step-functions-are-dense-in-l-p-of-rn]] [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For a deterministic step function $h^m$ as in [F1], the integral $\sum_ka^m_k(B_{t^m_{k+1}}-B_{t^m_k})$ is a finite sum of independent centered normal variables with variances $(a^m_k)^2\Delta^m_k$, so by [F2] its law is $N(0,\sigma_m^2)$ with $\sigma_m^2=\sum_k(a^m_k)^2\Delta^m_k=\int_0^T(h^m)^2ds$; in particular its characteristic function is $\varphi_m(t)=e^{-\sigma_m^2t^2/2}$, and its mean is $0$. [F1, F2]

2.1 For general deterministic $h\in L^2[0,T]$, choose by [F7] step functions $h^m\to h$ in $L^2[0,T]$; by [F4] the elementary integrals converge to $\int_0^Th\,dB$ in $L^2(P)$, hence in probability and weakly by [F3]. Apply the real-valued weak-convergence test separately to $\cos(tx)$ and $\sin(tx)$ and combine the limits to obtain pointwise convergence of characteristic functions: $\varphi(t)=\lim_m\varphi_m(t)=\lim_me^{-\sigma_m^2t^2/2}=e^{-\sigma^2t^2/2}$ with $\sigma^2=\int_0^Th^2ds$, using [F5] for the convergence of variances and continuity of the exponential. [F3, F4, F5, F7, step 1.1]

3.1 By [F2] the function $t\mapsto e^{-\sigma^2t^2/2}$ is the characteristic function of $N(0,\sigma^2)$ and determines a unique Borel law, so the law of $\int_0^Th\,dB$ is $N(0,\sigma^2)$; consequently it is centered with variance $\int_0^Th^2ds$, and the case $\sigma=0$ (that is, $h=0$ in $L^2$) gives the Dirac law at $0$. [F2, step 2.1]

4.1 For a finite family, linearity [F4] gives $\sum_jc_j\int_0^Th_jdB=\int_0^T(\sum_jc_jh_j)dB$ in $L^2(P)$, and step 3.1 applied to the deterministic integrand $\sum_jc_jh_j$ shows that this projection is $N(0,\int_0^T(\sum_jc_jh_j)^2ds)=N(0,c^T\Sigma c)$ with $\Sigma_{jk}=\int_0^Th_jh_kds$; by [F6] the vector of the $d$ integrals therefore has law $N_d(0,\Sigma)$, hence is jointly Gaussian with mean $0$ and covariance $\Sigma$. [F4, F6, step 3.1]

5.1 The covariance identity is the $jk$ entry of $\Sigma$; the zero-covariance case is uncorrelatedness, which for the jointly Gaussian pair means independence, and disjoint supports make every mixed integral $\int h_jh_k$ vanish, so the corresponding integrals are independent. Deterministic integrands are the only class treated here. AC supplies the inherited ambient interfaces and the Countable Choice hypothesis of the deterministic density theorem recorded in [F7]; no further approximation premise is assumed. [F6, F7, step 4.1, given] ∎

## Source notes

Lawler, Exercise 3.8, states that deterministic integrands produce Gaussian integrals with variance equal to the squared $L^2$ norm, and Section 3.2 built the step-function case from independent Gaussian increments. The corollary here identifies the limit law by characteristic functions rather than by citing a weak-convergence theorem for Gaussian parameter families, so that every supplier lies on an earlier page of this track; the multivariate clause is the defining projection property of the multivariate normal law.

## Statement

If $X_n\to X$ in probability, then some subsequence $X_{n_k}$ converges to
$X$ almost surely.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $X_n\to X$ in probability.

[L1] Convergence in probability makes each fixed-threshold error probability eventually arbitrarily small ([[def-convergence-in-probability]]).

[L2] A summable sequence of event probabilities gives only finitely many of those events almost surely ([[cor-first-borel-cantelli-lemma-for-events]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** constructive.

1.1 Recursively choose $n_k>n_{k-1}$ least subject to the following bound. [L1, construct] $\mathbb P(|X_{n_k}-X|>2^{-k})<2^{-k}$; [L1] makes every choice possible. Put $A_k=\{|X_{n_k}-X|>2^{-k}\}$. [L1, construct]

2.1 The bounds in step 1.1 are summable, so [L2] applies. [step 1.1, L2, discharge-construct] It says only finitely many $A_k$ occur almost surely. Hence $|X_{n_k}-X|\le2^{-k}$ eventually almost surely, so $X_{n_k}\to X$ almost surely. [step 1.1, L2, discharge-construct] ∎

## Example

Assume AC, let $T>0$, and let $W=(W_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a standard one-dimensional Brownian motion. Set $X_t=W_t$ and let $P_t$ be the law of $X_t$ for $0\le t\le T$. Thus $P_0(A)=1$ when a Borel set $A$ contains $0$ and $P_0(A)=0$ otherwise. For every $t>0$, $P_t$ has density

$$p_t(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}e^{-x^2/(2t)},\qquad s_t(x)=-\frac{x}{t}.$$

The law $P_0$ has no Lebesgue density, so its marginal score is undefined at $t=0$. For every cutoff $0<\epsilon<T$, the score is defined throughout $[\epsilon,T]$, and

$$\mathbb E|W_\epsilon|^2=\epsilon,\qquad W_\epsilon\longrightarrow0\ \text{almost surely as }\epsilon\downarrow0,\qquad P_\epsilon\Rightarrow P_0.$$

Here $P_\epsilon\Rightarrow P_0$ means that $\int f\,dP_\epsilon\to\int f\,dP_0$ for every bounded continuous $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. Consequently a score-based procedure requiring an exact marginal score can use this family only after choosing a positive cutoff; the limit at the singular data endpoint is a statement about the laws, not a score value at zero.

## Example references

[Särkkä and Solin, Section 5.2, Theorem 5.4 and proof](https://users.aalto.fi/~asolin/sde-book/sde-book.pdf)

[Raginsky, Section 2.3](https://maxim.ece.illinois.edu/teaching/spring23/SDE_book.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $T>0$, and a standard one-dimensional Brownian motion $W$.

[A1] AC is assumed in the Brownian, normal-law, and deterministic score-sampling interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Brownian motion starts at zero almost surely, has a common full-measure event of continuous paths, and $W_t\sim N(0,t)$. [[def-brownian-motion]]

[F2] For $t>0$, the law $N(0,t)$ has density $(2\pi t)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/(2t)}$. [[lem-normal-location-scale-density]] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]

[F3] At a positive finite differentiable density, the marginal score is the spatial derivative of its logarithm. [[def-marginal-score-function]]

[F4] The law of a random element is its probability pushforward. [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]

[F5] Almost-everywhere convergence under an integrable bound implies convergence of integrals. [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[F6] Weak convergence of Borel probability measures is convergence of integrals against every bounded continuous real-valued function. [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]

## Verification

1.1 By [A1], [F1], and [F2], for each $t>0$ the law of $W_t$ has the displayed Gaussian density. Differentiation gives $\partial_x\log p_t(x)=-x/t$, so [F3] gives the stated score. At $t=0$, [F1] and [F4] give $P_0(\{0\})=1$. Any measure with a Lebesgue density assigns mass $\int_{\{0\}}p(x)\,dx=0$ to this singleton, so $P_0$ has no Lebesgue density. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

1.2 By [F2], changing variables $x=\sqrt\epsilon z$ yields $\mathbb E|W_\epsilon|^2=\int_{\mathbb R}x^2\frac{e^{-x^2/(2\epsilon)}}{\sqrt{2\pi\epsilon}}\,dx=\epsilon\int_{\mathbb R}z^2\frac{e^{-z^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,dz=\epsilon$. 2.1 Fix any sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ with $\epsilon_n\to0$. On the common continuity event from [F1], $W_{\epsilon_n}\to W_0=0$, so for bounded continuous $f$, $f(W_{\epsilon_n})\to f(0)$ almost surely and $|f(W_{\epsilon_n})|\le\|f\|_\infty$. The positive-time score conclusion in step 1.1 and the absence of a score at zero prove the stated truncation consequence. [F1, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, given] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real process
$B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the increments
   $B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}}$ are mutually independent and have laws
   $N(0,t_j-t_{j-1})$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every
   $\omega\in A$.

By
[[lem-brownian-gaussian-covariance-is-equivalent-to-independent-stationary-normal-increments]],
the first two clauses are equivalent to saying that $B$ is a centered Gaussian
process with covariance $\min(s,t)$. Clause 3 is additional: it cannot be
recovered from finite-dimensional distributions alone.

No filtration is part of this definition. In particular, no completed or
right-continuous filtration and no Markov or martingale assertion is silently
imposed. Modifications and indistinguishability retain the distinct meanings in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. The cases
$n=0$, $t_1=0$, and zero-length increments are respectively vacuous or already
covered by $B_0=0$; the increment list itself is strictly increasing.

Choice is declared because the normal-law and Gaussian/increment-equivalence
interfaces construct and identify normal laws under AC. The continuity clause
selects no path and makes no additional use of choice.

## Source notes

Sousi, Section 6.1 (printed p. 51), gives these three defining clauses. The
common full-measure event formulation makes the pathwise quantifier explicit.

## Example

Assume AC. Fix $T>0$ and a continuous function $\beta:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0},P)$ be a complete filtered probability space with a right-continuous filtration, and let $W$ be an adapted standard one-dimensional Brownian motion such that, for every $0\le s<t$, $W_t-W_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N(0,t-s)$. Put $B(t)=\int_0^t\beta(r)\,dr$, $X_0=0$, and

$$X_t=e^{-B(t)/2}\int_0^t e^{B(r)/2}\sqrt{\beta(r)}\,dW_r,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$

This solves the variance-preserving (VP) stochastic differential equation $dX_t=-\tfrac12\beta(t)X_t\,dt+\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,dW_t$. For $t>0$, its law $P_t$ has density and score

$$p_t(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v_t}}e^{-x^2/(2v_t)},\qquad s_t(x)=-\frac{x}{v_t},\qquad v_t=1-e^{-B(t)}.$$

Since $\beta$ is positive and continuous, $0<B(T)<\infty$ and $0<v_T<1$, so $P_T=N(0,v_T)\ne N(0,1)$. The predictor-corrector procedure defined above initializes from the actual terminal law $P_T$; replacing that draw by $N(0,1)$ changes the initial law for this finite schedule. No convergence or solver-error claim follows from this comparison.

## Example references

[Song et al., Section 3.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.13456)

[Särkkä and Solin, Sections 5.2 and 6.1](https://users.aalto.fi/~asolin/sde-book/sde-book.pdf)

[Raginsky, Sections 2.3 and 7.1](https://maxim.ece.illinois.edu/teaching/spring23/SDE_book.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the filtered Brownian motion and schedule $\beta$ in the Example, and its explicit process $X$.

[A1] AC, the usual filtration conditions, and independent Brownian increments relative to the filtration are the hypotheses of the Brownian Itô and deterministic-integral interfaces used below. [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A process with pathwise integrable drift and a localized Brownian Itô integral is a continuous Brownian Itô process under the stated filtration conditions. [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]

[F2] For a one-dimensional Brownian Itô process and a $C^{1,2}$ function, Itô's formula adds the drift, diffusion, and half-variance second-derivative terms. [[thm-ito-formula-one-dimensional]]

[F3] A deterministic square-integrable Itô integrand has a centered normal integral with variance equal to the integral of its square. [[cor-deterministic-ito-integrals-are-gaussian]]

[F4] A scalar normal law is the affine image of the standard normal law, and for positive variance $v$ it has density $(2\pi v)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/(2v)}$. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] [[lem-normal-location-scale-density]]

[F5] At positive finite differentiable density points, the marginal score is the derivative of the log density. [[def-marginal-score-function]]

[F6] The law of a random element is its probability pushforward. [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]

[F7] The predictor-corrector procedure's initial draw has law $P_T$. [[alg-predictor-corrector-score-sampling]]

## Verification

1.1 Write $K_t=\int_0^t e^{B(r)/2}\sqrt{\beta(r)}\,dW_r$, whose deterministic integrand is square-integrable because $B$ and $\beta$ are continuous on $[0,T]$. Since $B'(t)=\beta(t)$, apply [F2] to $f(t,x)=e^{-B(t)/2}x$ and the continuous Itô process $K_t$. The product rule gives $dX_t=-\tfrac12\beta(t)X_t\,dt+\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,dW_t$ and $X_0=0$. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 By [F3], $K_t$ is centered normal with variance $\int_0^t e^{B(r)}\beta(r)\,dr$. Differentiating $e^{B(r)}$ gives $\frac{d}{dr}e^{B(r)}=e^{B(r)}\beta(r)$, so this variance is $e^{B(t)}-1$. Multiplication by $e^{-B(t)/2}$ therefore gives $X_t\sim N(0,e^{-B(t)}(e^{B(t)}-1))=N(0,v_t)$. For $t>0$, positivity of $\beta$ implies $v_t>0$; [F4] supplies its displayed density. [F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 Differentiating the density in step 1.2 gives $\partial_x\log p_t(x)=-x/v_t$, so [F5] yields the score for every $t>0$. At $t=0$, $X_0=0$ almost surely; its law assigns mass one to $\{0\}$ and therefore has no Lebesgue density, since every Lebesgue-density measure assigns zero mass to that singleton. [F4, F5, given, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Continuity of $\beta$ on the compact interval makes $B(T)$ finite, and strict positivity gives $B(T)>0$. Hence $v_T=1-e^{-B(T)}$ lies strictly between zero and one. For any $v>0$, the density in [F4] and the substitution $x=\sqrt v z$ give $\int_{\mathbb R}x^2\frac{e^{-x^2/(2v)}}{\sqrt{2\pi v}}\,dx=v\int_{\mathbb R}z^2\frac{e^{-z^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,dz=v$. Step 2.1 shows the exact positive-time score is available at $T$, and [F7] prescribes initialization from $P_T$; replacing it by $N(0,1)$ changes that initial law. ## Definition

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a sigma-finite measure $\lambda$ on the Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^d$, and a Borel probability measure $\pi$ on $\mathbb R^d$. Here sigma-finite means that there are Borel sets $E_n$ with $\mathbb R^d=\bigcup_{n\ge1}E_n$ and $\lambda(E_n)<\infty$ for each $n$. A **conditional probability-density path** with endpoint law $\pi$ is a function measurable for $\mathcal B([0,1])\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ on time, state, and endpoint variables
$$\rho:[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty]$$
such that, for every $t\in[0,1]$, $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\,\lambda(dx)=1$ for $\pi$-almost every endpoint $x_1$. Its **mixture function** is
$$p_t(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1).$$
For a vector field $u_t(x\mid x_1)=(u_t^1,\ldots,u_t^d)$ measurable for the same product sigma-algebra, call it a **conditional velocity field** for $\rho$ when $\rho_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ and each component of $\rho_t(\cdot\mid x_1)u_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ are continuously differentiable in $(t,x)$ on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$ for $\pi$-almost every $x_1$, and
$$\partial_t\rho_t(x\mid x_1)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}\!\left(\rho_t(x\mid x_1)u_t^j(x\mid x_1)\right)=0$$
there. The sum is the spatial divergence of the conditional probability flux. At any $(t,x)$ where $p_t(x)>0$ and the numerator is finite, the **marginal velocity field** is
$$u_t(x):=\frac{\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)u_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1)}{p_t(x)}.$$
This definition assigns no value to the quotient where $p_t(x)=0$.

[Holderrieth and Erives, §§3.1–3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.02070)

## Statement

Let $\lambda$, $\pi$, and $\rho$ satisfy the conditional probability-density path definition, and for each $t\in[0,1]$ set $p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1)$. Then $p_t$ is a nonnegative measurable function and $\int_{\mathbb R^d}p_t(x)\,\lambda(dx)=1$ for every $t$; hence it is a probability density with respect to $\lambda$.

## Statement references

[Lipman et al., §3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.02747)

[Holderrieth and Erives, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.02070)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A sigma-finite Borel measure $\lambda$, a Borel probability measure $\pi$, and a conditional density $\rho_t$ normalized for $\pi$-almost every endpoint.

[F1] [[def-probability-path-and-velocity-field]]: $\rho_t(x\mid x_1)$ is product-measurable, nonnegative, and has $\lambda$-integral $1$ for $\pi$-almost every $x_1$; $p_t(x)$ is its $\pi$-mixture.

[F2] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: for a nonnegative product-measurable function on two sigma-finite measure spaces, the section integrals are measurable and either iterated integral equals the product integral.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Fix $t\in[0,1]$. The measures $\lambda$ and $\pi$ are sigma-finite, and $(x,x_1)\mapsto\rho_t(x\mid x_1)$ is nonnegative and product-measurable by [F1]. Tonelli's theorem [F2] therefore makes $x\mapsto p_t(x)$ measurable and gives $$\int_{\mathbb R^d}p_t(x)\,\lambda(dx)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\left(\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\,\lambda(dx)\right)\pi(dx_1).$$ [given, F1, F2]

2.1 The inner integral in step 1.1 equals $1$ for $\pi$-almost every $x_1$ by [F1]. Since $\pi$ is a probability measure, the right-hand side is $\int 1\,d\pi=1$. The mixture is nonnegative by [F1], so $p_t$ is a probability density with respect to $\lambda$. [step 1.1, F1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

The normalization is proved locally by Tonelli; the source citations document the conditional-to-marginal mixture convention.

title: Conditional continuity equations pass to the marginal path
status: draft

    - title: "Peter Holderrieth and Ezra Erives, Introduction to Flow Matching and Diffusion Models, §3.2"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/html/2506.02070"

## Statement

Let $\lambda$, $\pi$, and $\rho$ be as in the conditional probability-path definition. Suppose that for $\pi$-almost every $x_1$, the conditional continuity equation holds for all $(t,x)\in(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$. Suppose also that for every compact $K\subset(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$ there is a nonnegative $G_K\in L^1(\pi)$ which, for $\pi$-almost every $x_1$, bounds on $K$ the absolute values of $\rho_t(x\mid x_1)$, $\partial_t\rho_t(x\mid x_1)$, each component of $\rho_t(x\mid x_1)u_t(x\mid x_1)$, and each derivative $\partial_{x_j}(\rho_tu_t^j)(x\mid x_1)$. If $p_t(x)>0$ on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$, define
$$J_t(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)u_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1), \qquad u_t(x):=\frac{J_t(x)}{p_t(x)}.$$
Then $\partial_t p_t$ and each indicated flux derivative $\partial_{x_j}J_t^j$ exist and are continuous locally in $(t,x)$, and the marginal continuity equation
$$\partial_t p_t(x)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}\!\left(p_t(x)u_t^j(x)\right)=0$$
holds on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$. The domination hypothesis is a sufficient Leibniz condition for the time and spatial derivatives to pass through the $x_1$ integral.

## Statement references

[Lipman et al., §3.1 and Appendix A](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.02747)

[Holderrieth and Erives, §3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.02070)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The conditional path and field, the conditional continuity equation, local C1 regularity, local integrable domination in the endpoint variable, and positivity of the mixture density as stated.

[F1] [[def-probability-path-and-velocity-field]]: $p_t(x)=\int\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1)$, and the conditional continuity equation is $\partial_t\rho_t+\sum_j\partial_{x_j}(\rho_tu_t^j)=0$.

[F2] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: if a real function is continuous on a closed interval and differentiable in its interior, some interior derivative equals its endpoint difference quotient.

[F3] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: pointwise convergence under one integrable majorant permits passage of a sequence of integrals to the limit.

[F4] [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]: the integral is linear for integrable scalar components.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Fix a compact neighborhood $K$ of an interior point $(t,x)$. For any sequence of nonzero increments $h_n\to0$ small enough that the time segment from $t$ to $t+h_n$ stays in $K$, the mean value theorem [F2] bounds the difference quotient of $\rho_{t+h_n}(x\mid x_1)-\rho_t(x\mid x_1)$ by $G_K(x_1)$. The quotient converges for $\pi$-almost every $x_1$ to $\partial_t\rho_t(x\mid x_1)$. Dominated convergence [F3] therefore gives $$\partial_t p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\partial_t\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1).$$ The same argument for each flux component on its spatial coordinate segment gives $$\partial_{x_j}J_t^j(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\partial_{x_j}\!\left(\rho_t(x\mid x_1)u_t^j(x\mid x_1)\right)\pi(dx_1).$$ The local continuity of these derivatives follows from their pointwise continuity in $(t,x)$ and the same integrable majorant. [given, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Integrate the conditional continuity equation over $\pi$. All terms are integrable by $G_K$, so linearity [F4] and the identities of step 1.1 yield $$\partial_t p_t(x)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}J_t^j(x) =\int_{\mathbb R^d}\left(\partial_t\rho_t(x\mid x_1)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}(\rho_tu_t^j)(x\mid x_1)\right)\pi(dx_1)=0.$$ By definition $J_t=p_tu_t$ wherever $p_t>0$, proving the marginal continuity equation. [given, F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

The source proofs explicitly require differentiation under the endpoint integral. This item states local integrable domination for every derivative it exchanges and derives those exchanges from the mean value theorem and dominated convergence.

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$, fix $x_1\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $t\mapsto\mu_t(x_1)\in\mathbb R^d$ and $t\mapsto\sigma_t(x_1)\in(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable on $[0,1]$, with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints. For $z\in\mathbb R^d$, define the affine map
$$\psi_t(z\mid x_1):=\sigma_t(x_1)z+\mu_t(x_1).$$
For each $t$, this map is a diffeomorphism with inverse $\psi_t^{-1}(x\mid x_1)=(x-\mu_t(x_1))/\sigma_t(x_1)$. The unique vector field satisfying
$$\frac{d}{dt}\psi_t(z\mid x_1)=u_t(\psi_t(z\mid x_1)\mid x_1)$$
for every $z\in\mathbb R^d$ is
$$u_t(x\mid x_1)=\frac{\dot\sigma_t(x_1)}{\sigma_t(x_1)}(x-\mu_t(x_1))+\dot\mu_t(x_1).$$

## Statement references

[Lipman et al., §4 Theorem 3 and Appendix A](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.02747)

[Holderrieth and Erives, §3.2 Example 10](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.02070)

[Fjelde, Mathieu, and Dutordoir, Gaussian conditional path derivation](https://mlg.eng.cam.ac.uk/blog/2024/01/20/flow-matching.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $d$, $x_1$, and the continuously differentiable functions $\mu_t(x_1)$ and $\sigma_t(x_1)>0$ in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: vectors in $\mathbb R^d$ have coordinatewise addition and scalar multiplication.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Fix $t\in[0,1]$. Since $\sigma_t(x_1)>0$, solving $x=\sigma_t(x_1)z+\mu_t(x_1)$ gives the unique inverse $z=(x-\mu_t(x_1))/\sigma_t(x_1)$. Both the map and inverse are continuously differentiable in $z$, so $\psi_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ is a diffeomorphism. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For fixed $z$, differentiation gives $\frac{d}{dt}\psi_t(z\mid x_1)=\dot\sigma_t(x_1)z+\dot\mu_t(x_1)$. Substitute the inverse expression from step 1.1 to obtain $$\frac{d}{dt}\psi_t(z\mid x_1)=\frac{\dot\sigma_t(x_1)}{\sigma_t(x_1)}\bigl(\psi_t(z\mid x_1)-\mu_t(x_1)\bigr)+\dot\mu_t(x_1).$$ Thus the displayed $u_t$ satisfies the flow equation. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If another field $\widetilde u_t$ satisfies the same equation for every $z$, then for any $x$ choose the explicit inverse value $z=\psi_t^{-1}(x\mid x_1)$. ## Statement

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite second moment, mean $\int x\,\mu(dx)=0$, and $m_2:=\int\|x\|_2^2\,\mu(dx)<\infty$. Fix $a\in\mathbb R^d$ and $s>0$, define $T(x):=a+sx$, and let $\nu$ be the law of $T(X)$ when $X$ has law $\mu$. For every Borel probability measure $\gamma$ on $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d$ whose coordinate marginals are $\mu$ and $\nu$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d}\|y-x\|_2^2\,\gamma(dx,dy)\ \ge\ \|a\|_2^2+(1-s)^2m_2.$$
The law of $(X,T(X))$ under $\mu$ attains equality. Thus $T$ is an optimal transport map for the squared Euclidean cost between $\mu$ and its translated dilation $\nu$.

## Statement references

[Lipman et al., §4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.02747)

[Peyré and Cuturi, §2.6 Remark 2.31](https://arxiv.org/html/1803.00567)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Borel probability measure $\mu$, its zero mean and finite second moment $m_2$, the affine map $T(x)=a+sx$, and a coupling $\gamma$ with the stated marginals.

[F1] [[def-probability-measure]]: $\mu$ and $\gamma$ are countably additive probability measures on their stated Borel spaces.

[F2] [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]: the law of a Borel map $T$ under $\mu$ assigns to each Borel set $B$ the value $\mu(T^{-1}(B))$.

[F3] [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]: integrating a nonnegative or integrable function against the law of a random element equals integrating its composition against the original probability measure.

[F4] [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]: the law of a measurable random element is a Borel probability measure.

[F5] [[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]: a continuous map between Euclidean spaces has Borel preimages of Borel sets.

[F6] [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]: the integral is linear for integrable scalar components.

[F7] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: $\|x\|_2^2=\langle x,x\rangle$ on $\mathbb R^d$, with the coordinatewise Euclidean inner product.

[F8] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: $|\langle x,z\rangle|\le\|x\|_2\|z\|_2$ for Euclidean vectors.

[F9] [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]: for square-integrable real random variables $U,V$, $\mathbb E|UV|\le(\mathbb E U^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E V^2)^{1/2}$.

[F10] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]: expectation on a probability space is integration against its probability measure.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 The affine maps $T(x)=a+sx$ and $x\mapsto(x,T(x))$ are continuous, so their Borel preimages are Borel by [F5]; their laws are probability measures by [F2, F4]. Let $(X,Y)$ have joint law $\gamma$. The first marginal gives $\mathbb E_\gamma X=0$ and $\mathbb E_\gamma\|X\|_2^2=m_2$. The second marginal is the law of $a+sX$ under $\mu$, so change of variables [F3] and linearity [F6] give $\mathbb E_\gamma(Y-a)=0$ and $\mathbb E_\gamma\|Y-a\|_2^2=s^2m_2$. These second moments make all displayed costs finite; Cauchy–Schwarz [F8, F9] makes the cross term integrable. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10]

2.1 Expand $Y-X=a+(Y-a)-X$. The expectation of the cross term with $a$ vanishes because $\mathbb E_\gamma(Y-a)=\mathbb E_\gamma X=0$, so $$\mathbb E_\gamma\|Y-X\|_2^2=\|a\|_2^2+(1+s^2)m_2-2\mathbb E_\gamma\langle X,Y-a\rangle.$$ By [F8], pointwise $|\langle X,Y-a\rangle|\le\|X\|_2\|Y-a\|_2$. Applying [F9] to the two scalar norms gives $\mathbb E_\gamma\langle X,Y-a\rangle\le\sqrt{m_2\,s^2m_2}=s m_2$. Substitution proves the lower bound. [step 1.1, F8, F9, algebra]

3.1 The law of $(X,T(X))$ for $X\sim\mu$ is a coupling with marginals $\mu$ and $\nu$ by [F2, F4, F5]. Under this coupling $Y-a=sX$, so $\mathbb E\langle X,Y-a\rangle=sm_2$. The expansion in step 2.1 therefore gives cost $\|a\|_2^2+(1-s)^2m_2$, attaining the lower bound. [step 2.1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F10, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $d,q\ge1$, let $\lambda$ be a sigma-finite measure on the Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^d$, let $\pi$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$, and let $(\rho,u^c)$ be a conditional probability-density path and conditional velocity field relative to $(\lambda,\pi)$. Set
$$p_t(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1),\qquad J_t(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)u^c_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1).$$
Assume $0<p_t(x)<\infty$ and $J_t(x)$ is finite on $[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d$, and define $u^m_t(x):=J_t(x)/p_t(x)$. Suppose the conditional continuity equation holds on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$, and for every compact $K\subset(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$ there is a nonnegative $G_K\in L^1(\pi)$ that bounds on $K$, for $\pi$-almost every $x_1$, the absolute values of $\rho_t(x\mid x_1)$, $\partial_t\rho_t(x\mid x_1)$, each component of $\rho_tu^c_t$, and each corresponding spatial flux derivative.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, and let $v:\,[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly measurable and continuously differentiable in $\theta$, with jointly measurable parameter derivative. Define
$$\mathcal L_C(\theta):=\int_0^1\!\int_{\mathbb R^d}\!\int_{\mathbb R^d} \rho_t(x\mid x_1)\|v(t,x;\theta)-u^c_t(x\mid x_1)\|_2^2\,\pi(dx_1)\lambda(dx)\,dt,$$
and
$$\mathcal L_M(\theta):=\int_0^1\!\int_{\mathbb R^d} p_t(x)\|v(t,x;\theta)-u^m_t(x)\|_2^2\,\lambda(dx)\,dt.$$
Assume $\mathcal L_C(\theta)$ and $\mathcal L_M(\theta)$ are finite for every $\theta\in\Theta$, and define
$$C:=\int_0^1\!\int_{\mathbb R^d}\!\int_{\mathbb R^d} \rho_t(x\mid x_1)\|u^c_t(x\mid x_1)-u^m_t(x)\|_2^2\,\pi(dx_1)\lambda(dx)\,dt,$$
and assume $C<\infty$. For every compact $H\subset\Theta$ and coordinate $j$, suppose there are nonnegative integrable majorants $G^C_{H,j}$ on $dt\,\lambda(dx)\,\pi(dx_1)$ and $G^M_{H,j}$ on $dt\,\lambda(dx)$ such that for every $\theta\in H$, outside fixed null sets,
$$2\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\left|\left\langle\partial_{\theta_j}v(t,x;\theta),v(t,x;\theta)-u^c_t(x\mid x_1)\right\rangle\right|\le G^C_{H,j}(t,x,x_1),$$
and
$$2p_t(x)\left|\left\langle\partial_{\theta_j}v(t,x;\theta),v(t,x;\theta)-u^m_t(x)\right\rangle\right|\le G^M_{H,j}(t,x).$$
Then both objectives are finite and continuously differentiable on $\Theta$, and $\mathcal L_C(\theta)=\mathcal L_M(\theta)+C$. In particular, $C$ is independent of $\theta$ and $\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_C(\theta)=\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_M(\theta)$. Under the stated local domination, $(p,u^m)$ also satisfies the marginal continuity equation on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$. Uniform boundedness of $u^c,u^m,v,D_\theta v$ on compact parameter neighborhoods is a sufficient special case of the integrability and derivative-majorant assumptions above.

## Statement references

[Lipman et al., §3.2 Theorem 2 and Appendix A proof](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.02747)

[Holderrieth and Erives, §3.3 Theorem 12 and complete direct proof](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.02070)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The sigma-finite Borel measure $\lambda$, endpoint probability measure $\pi$, conditional probability path $(\rho,u^c)$, finite positive marginal density and finite flux, local endpoint domination, open parameter domain $\Theta$, parameter-regular vector field $v$, finite loss and variance integrals, and the integrable derivative majorants in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-probability-path-and-velocity-field]]: $p_t=\int\rho_t(\cdot\mid x_1)\,d\pi$ and the conditional continuity equation is $\partial_t\rho_t+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho_tu^c_t)=0$.

[F2] [[lem-conditional-mixture-is-a-probability-path]]: integrating a conditional density normalized for $\pi$-almost every endpoint gives a measurable mixture density of $\lambda$-integral one at each time.

[F3] [[lem-conditional-to-marginal-continuity-equation]]: the stated local $L^1(\pi)$ bounds permit the conditional time and flux derivatives to pass through the endpoint integral and imply $\partial_tp+\operatorname{div}_x(pu^m)=0$.

[F4] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: $\|a\|_2^2=\langle a,a\rangle$ and the Euclidean inner product is bilinear.

[F5] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: an $L^1$ function on a product of sigma-finite measure spaces may be integrated in either order, with equality of the iterated integrals.

[F6] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: a differentiable real function on an interval has each difference quotient equal to a derivative at an intermediate point.

[F7] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: pointwise convergence under one integrable majorant permits passage of the limit through the integral.

[F8] [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]: the integral is linear on $L^1$.

[F9] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: $|\langle a,b\rangle|\le\|a\|_2\|b\|_2$ for Euclidean vectors.

[F10] [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]: square-integrable scalar functions $U,V$ on a probability space satisfy $\int|UV|\le(\int U^2)^{1/2}(\int V^2)^{1/2}$.

[F14] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: for a nonnegative product-measurable function on sigma-finite spaces, its section integrals are measurable and either iterated integral equals the product integral.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 By [F1] and the mixture normalization result [F2], each $p_t$ is a probability density with respect to $\lambda$. Positivity makes $u^m=J/p$ well-defined on the open time interval. The hypotheses on $G_K$ are exactly the local domination assumptions of [F3], so the conditional continuity equation passes to the marginal and $\partial_tp+\operatorname{div}_x(pu^m)=0$. [given, F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Let $Q$ be the measure on time, state, and endpoint variables with density $\rho_t(x\mid x_1)$ relative to $dt\,\lambda(dx)\,\pi(dx_1)$. Product measurability from [F1], conditional normalization, and Tonelli [F14] show that $Q$ has total mass one and that its time-state marginal has density $p_t(x)$ relative to $dt\,\lambda(dx)$. In particular, Tonelli gives $\mathcal L_M(\theta)=\int\|v-u^m\|_2^2\,dQ$, so the finite marginal loss makes $v-u^m$ square-integrable under $Q$. The same identity gives $C=\int\|u^c-u^m\|_2^2\,dQ$, so $u^c-u^m$ is square-integrable under $Q$. By Euclidean Cauchy–Schwarz [F9] and random-variable Cauchy–Schwarz [F10], their inner-product term is integrable. At every $t,x$ where the integrals are defined, the definition of $J_t$ and $u^m_t$ gives $$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\bigl(u^c_t(x\mid x_1)-u^m_t(x)\bigr)\,\pi(dx_1)=J_t(x)-p_t(x)u^m_t(x)=0.$$ Expanding $v-u^c=(v-u^m)+(u^m-u^c)$ by bilinearity [F4], integrating first over $x_1$, and using Fubini [F5] for the integrable cross term gives $$\mathcal L_C(\theta)=\mathcal L_M(\theta)+\int_0^1\!\int\!\int\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\|u^c_t(x\mid x_1)-u^m_t(x)\|_2^2\,\pi(dx_1)\lambda(dx)dt.$$ The last integral is independent of $\theta$ and is the finite constant $C$ defined in the Statement. [given, F1, F2, F4, F5, F8, F9, F10, F14, algebra]

1.3 Fix $\theta_0\in\Theta$ and choose a compact parameter ball $H\subset\Theta$ whose interior contains $\theta_0$. For each coordinate direction, the chain and product rules give $$\partial_{\theta_j}\|v(t,x;\theta)-w\|_2^2 =2\langle\partial_{\theta_j}v(t,x;\theta),v(t,x;\theta)-w\rangle,$$ where $w$ is either $u^c_t(x\mid x_1)$ or $u^m_t(x)$. The functions $G^C_{H,j}$ and $G^M_{H,j}$ dominate the weighted derivatives on $H$. For a sequence of nonzero increments tending to zero in coordinate $j$, the mean value theorem [F6] bounds the weighted difference quotients by the same majorants; the pointwise quotients converge to the displayed derivatives. Dominated convergence [F7] therefore differentiates both objectives under their integrals. Applying the same domination to convergent parameter sequences shows the derivative integrals are continuous in $\theta$, so both objectives are $C^1$. [given, F2, F4, F5, F6, F7]

2.1 Step 1.2 proves $\mathcal L_C(\theta)=\mathcal L_M(\theta)+C$ for every $\theta$, with one finite constant independent of $\theta$. Both sides are differentiable by step 1.3, so differentiating this identity gives $\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_C(\theta)=\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_M(\theta)$. [step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

Lipman et al. state Theorem 2 under positive marginal density and give the Appendix A argument using squared-norm expansion, the mixture density, the marginal conditional-average formula, and Fubini; they explicitly assume sufficient decay and bounded $u_t,v_t,\nabla_\theta v_t$. Holderrieth and Erives give the complete direct expansion in §3.3, Theorem 12, including the parameter-independent squared-error term. This item states exact integrability and dominated-derivative hypotheses, of which bounded fields on compact parameter neighborhoods are a sufficient case, and gives a local endpoint majorant for the marginal continuity equation. Thus no informal tail-decay phrase is needed: the proof uses absolute integrability and no integration by parts at spatial infinity. It makes no optimizer, training-convergence, or sample-quality claim.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, fix $x_1\in\mathbb R^d$, and choose $\sigma_{\min}>0$. Let $Z$ have the standard multivariate normal law $N_d(0,I_d)$. For $t\in[0,1]$, define
$$\mu_t(x_1):=t x_1,\qquad \sigma_t:=1-(1-\sigma_{\min})t,\qquad \psi_t(z\mid x_1):=\sigma_t z+\mu_t(x_1),$$
and let $P_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ be the law of $\psi_t(Z\mid x_1)$. Then $P_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ is the Gaussian probability path with mean $\mu_t(x_1)$ and covariance $\sigma_t^2I_d$, and its Lebesgue density is
$$\rho_t(x\mid x_1)=(2\pi\sigma_t^2)^{-d/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\|x-\mu_t(x_1)\|_2^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right).$$
A conditional velocity field for this path is
$$u_t(x\mid x_1)=\frac{\sigma_{\min}-1}{\sigma_t}(x-tx_1)+x_1.$$
For each endpoint $x_1$, these densities and fields form a conditional path in the probability-path definition; hence they can be mixed against any Borel endpoint law. At $t=0$ the law is $N_d(0,I_d)$, and at $t=1$ it is the law of $x_1+\sigma_{\min}Z$, a Gaussian with mean $x_1$ and covariance $\sigma_{\min}^2I_d$. The affine endpoint map $T(z)=x_1+\sigma_{\min}z$ is optimal for squared Euclidean cost between these two laws: every coupling has cost at least
$$\|x_1\|_2^2+d(1-\sigma_{\min})^2,$$
and the law of $(Z,T(Z))$ attains this value.

## Statement references

[Lipman et al., §4 Theorem 3, §4.1, and Appendix A](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.02747)

[Peyré and Cuturi, §2.6 Remark 2.31](https://arxiv.org/html/1803.00567)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $d\ge1$, $x_1\in\mathbb R^d$, $\sigma_{\min}>0$, and $Z\sim N_d(0,I_d)$.

[A1] AC supplies the axiom required by the standard and multivariate Gaussian-law definitions and the Gaussian density theorem. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] and [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: scalar normal laws are affine images of the standard normal; $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ has scalar projections $N(u^Tm,u^T\Sigma u)$, mean $m$, and covariance $\Sigma$.

[F2] [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]: if $\Sigma$ is positive definite, $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ has Lebesgue density $(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m))$.

[F3] [[lem-affine-conditional-path-velocity]]: for a differentiable affine flow $\psi_t(z)=\sigma_tz+\mu_t$ with $\sigma_t>0$, its unique Eulerian field is $\dot\mu_t+(\dot\sigma_t/\sigma_t)(x-\mu_t)$.

[F4] [[lem-affine-dilation-is-quadratic-cost-optimal]]: for any centered probability law with second moment $m_2$, the map $z\mapsto a+sz$, $s>0$, is optimal for squared Euclidean cost to its affine image and has cost $\|a\|_2^2+(1-s)^2m_2$.

[F5] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: $\|x\|_2^2=\langle x,x\rangle$ on $\mathbb R^d$.

[F6] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: sums, products, and quotients by nonzero functions obey the ordinary derivative rules.

[F7] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: derivatives of compositions of differentiable Euclidean maps obey the chain rule.

[F8] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: $(\exp)'=\exp$.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Since $\sigma_t=(1-t)+t\sigma_{\min}>0$, every affine map $\psi_t$ is invertible. For each $v\in\mathbb R^d$, the projection of $\psi_t(Z\mid x_1)$ is $v^T\mu_t(x_1)+\sigma_t v^TZ$. By [F1], this is normal with mean $v^T\mu_t(x_1)$ and variance $\sigma_t^2\|v\|_2^2$. Thus $P_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ is multivariate normal with mean $\mu_t(x_1)$ and covariance $\sigma_t^2I_d$, which is positive definite. [given, A1, F1, F5, algebra]

1.2 By [F2], the Lebesgue density of $P_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ is $$\rho_t(x\mid x_1)=(2\pi\sigma_t^2)^{-d/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\|x-\mu_t(x_1)\|_2^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right).$$ It integrates to one for every $x_1$ and is continuous in $(t,x,x_1)$ because $\sigma_t>0$. Therefore for any endpoint probability law $\pi$ it is product-measurable and satisfies the conditional-density requirement in [[def-probability-path-and-velocity-field]]. [given, F2]

2.1 We have $\dot\mu_t(x_1)=x_1$ and $\dot\sigma_t=\sigma_{\min}-1$. Applying [F3] gives $u_t(x\mid x_1)=x_1+\frac{\sigma_{\min}-1}{\sigma_t}(x-tx_1)$. The density formula in step 1.2 and this affine field are continuously differentiable in $(t,x)$ by the algebra, chain, and exponential derivative rules [F6, F7, F8]. Thus $\rho_t$ and each component of $\rho_tu_t$ meet the regularity clauses of the conditional probability-path definition. [given, step 1.2, F3, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

2.2 At $t=0$ the parameters are $\mu_0=0,\sigma_0=1$; at $t=1$ they are $\mu_1=x_1,\sigma_1=\sigma_{\min}$. Thus the endpoints are the standard Gaussian law and the law of $x_1+\sigma_{\min}Z$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Put $r=x-tx_1$ and write $\dot\sigma=\sigma_{\min}-1$. We have $\partial_t r=-x_1$ and $\partial_t(\sigma_t^{-d})=-d\dot\sigma\sigma_t^{-d-1}$ by the product and quotient rules [F6]. Applying the chain rule [F7] to $-\|r\|_2^2/(2\sigma_t^2)$ and then the exponential derivative [F8] gives $$\partial_t\rho_t=\rho_t\left(-d\frac{\dot\sigma}{\sigma_t} +\frac{\langle r,x_1\rangle}{\sigma_t^2} +\frac{\dot\sigma\|r\|_2^2}{\sigma_t^3}\right), \qquad \nabla_x\rho_t=-\rho_t\frac{r}{\sigma_t^2}.$$ The field in step 2.1 has $\operatorname{div}_x u_t=d\dot\sigma/\sigma_t$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, F5, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

4.1 The product rule gives $$\operatorname{div}_x(\rho_tu_t) =\langle\nabla_x\rho_t,u_t\rangle+\rho_t\operatorname{div}_xu_t =\rho_t\left(-\frac{\langle r,x_1\rangle}{\sigma_t^2} -\frac{\dot\sigma\|r\|_2^2}{\sigma_t^3} +d\frac{\dot\sigma}{\sigma_t}\right).$$ Adding this to $\partial_t\rho_t$ in step 3.1 cancels each term, so the conditional continuity equation holds. [step 3.1, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

5.1 The standard Gaussian vector has mean $0$ and covariance $I_d$ by [F1]. Summing its $d$ coordinate second moments gives $\int\|z\|_2^2\,N_d(0,I_d)(dz)=d$. The endpoint law is the affine image under $T(z)=x_1+\sigma_{\min}z$. ## Definition

Let $d,q,B\ge1$, $N\ge0$, and $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open. Let $\lambda$ be a sigma-finite Borel measure on $\mathbb R^d$, let $\pi$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$, and let $\rho:[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty]$ and $u^c:[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly measurable. Assume $\int\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\,\lambda(dx)=1$ for every $t$ and for $\pi$-almost every $x_1$, and that for $\pi$-almost every $x_1$, $\rho_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ and every component of $\rho_tu^c_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ are continuously differentiable in $(t,x)$ on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$ and satisfy $$\partial_t\rho_t(x\mid x_1)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}\bigl(\rho_t(x\mid x_1)(u^c_t)^j(x\mid x_1)\bigr)=0.$$ For every compact $K\subset(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$, suppose there is a nonnegative $G_K\in L^1(\pi)$ bounding on $K$, for $\pi$-almost every $x_1$, the absolute values of $\rho_t$, $\partial_t\rho_t$, each component of $\rho_tu^c_t$, and each corresponding spatial flux derivative.

Define $p_t(x):=\int\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1)$ and $J_t(x):=\int\rho_t(x\mid x_1)u^c_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1)$. Assume $0<p_t(x)<\infty$ and $J_t(x)$ is finite on $[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d$, and put $u^m_t(x):=J_t(x)/p_t(x)$. Let $v:[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly measurable and continuously differentiable in $\theta$, with jointly measurable parameter derivative. Define $$\mathcal L_C(\theta):=\int_0^1\!\int\!\int\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\|v(t,x;\theta)-u^c_t(x\mid x_1)\|_2^2\,\pi(dx_1)\lambda(dx)dt$$ and $$\mathcal L_M(\theta):=\int_0^1\!\int p_t(x)\|v(t,x;\theta)-u^m_t(x)\|_2^2\,\lambda(dx)dt.$$ Assume, almost surely, that $\mathcal L_C(\theta_k)$ and $\mathcal L_M(\theta_k)$ are finite for every $k=0,\ldots,N$, and that $$C:=\int_0^1\!\int\!\int\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\|u^c_t(x\mid x_1)-u^m_t(x)\|_2^2\,\pi(dx_1)\lambda(dx)dt$$ is finite. Write $D_\theta v$ for the matrix with entries $(D_\theta v)_{ij}=\partial_{\theta_j}v^i$. For every compact $H\subset\Theta$ and coordinate $j$, suppose nonnegative integrable majorants $G^C_{H,j}$ on $dt\,\lambda(dx)\,\pi(dx_1)$ and $G^M_{H,j}$ on $dt\,\lambda(dx)$ satisfy, for every $\theta\in H$ outside fixed null sets, $$2\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\left|\left\langle\partial_{\theta_j}v(t,x;\theta),v(t,x;\theta)-u^c_t(x\mid x_1)\right\rangle\right|\le G^C_{H,j}(t,x,x_1)$$ and $$2p_t(x)\left|\left\langle\partial_{\theta_j}v(t,x;\theta),v(t,x;\theta)-u^m_t(x)\right\rangle\right|\le G^M_{H,j}(t,x).$$ Let $Q(dt,dx_1,dx):=dt\,\pi(dx_1)\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\lambda(dx)$ be the probability law of a training triple, with $dt$ Lebesgue probability measure on $[0,1]$. Take $\theta_0$ as fixed and let $\mathcal F_0$ be the trivial history. At iteration $k$, let $\mathcal F_k$ be the history before the batch, so $\theta_k$ is $\mathcal F_k$-measurable; draw $B$ independent triples with law $Q$, independently of $\mathcal F_k$, and set $\mathcal F_{k+1}$ to be the sigma-algebra generated by $\mathcal F_k$ and that batch. For a triple $w=(t,x_1,x)$, define $$\zeta(\theta,w):=2\,D_\theta v(t,x;\theta)^T\left(v(t,x;\theta)-u^c_t(x\mid x_1)\right).$$ For each $k,b$, set $\zeta_{k,b}:=\zeta(\theta_k,(T_{k,b},X_{1,k,b},X_{k,b}))$ and require it to be integrable on the joint training probability space.

Given the fixed initial parameter $\theta_0\in\Theta$ and deterministic step sizes $\eta_0,\ldots,\eta_{N-1}\ge0$, for each $k=0,\ldots,N-1$ set
$$g_k:=\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^{B}\zeta_{k,b}, \qquad \theta_{k+1}:=\theta_k-\eta_k g_k.$$
Assume all iterates $\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_N$ remain in $\Theta$ almost surely. Training uses only conditional samples and does not solve the neural ODE during these updates. After training, condition on the history $\mathcal F_N$, draw $X_0$ from a supplied initial probability law $\mu_0$ independently of $\mathcal F_N$, and return $X_1=\Phi^{\theta_N}_{1,0}(X_0)$, where $\Phi^{\theta_N}_{t,s}$ solves $\dot z(t)=v(t,z(t);\theta_N)$ with $z(s)=X_0$. This last step is well-defined if the field extends to an open time interval containing $[0,1]$, is jointly $C^\infty$ in time, state, and parameter, and on every compact parameter set $H\subset\Theta$ has uniform constants $L_H,M_H\ge0$ satisfying
$$\|v(t,z;\theta)-v(t,w;\theta)\|_2\le L_H\|z-w\|_2, \qquad \|v(t,0;\theta)\|_2\le M_H$$
for $t\in[0,1]$, $\theta\in H$, and $z,w\in\mathbb R^d$. Conditional on $\mathcal F_N$, the output law assigns mass $\mu_0(\{x:\Phi^{\theta_N}_{1,0}(x)\in A\})$ to each Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. The procedure gives no convergence guarantee for the parameter updates or equality of this output law with a desired data law.

## Statement

Take all inputs, laws, histories, notation, hypotheses, and instructions of the conditional flow-matching training and exact-flow sampling procedure, including its full conditional-path regularity, marginal positivity, finite-loss, derivative-majorant, fresh-batch independence, random-iterate integrability, and parameter-domain assumptions. In particular, the number of training rounds satisfies $N\ge0$, the batch size satisfies $B\ge1$, each $\theta_k$ is measurable with respect to the pre-batch history $\mathcal F_k$, and the $B$ training triples at round $k$ have the supplied law $Q$ independently of that history. For every $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, both $g_k$ and $\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_M(\theta_k)$ are integrable, and

$$\mathbb E[g_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_M(\theta_k)\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

The arithmetic update is defined for every prescribed nonnegative step size; remaining in the open parameter domain is a hypothesis, not a consequence of unbiasedness. If the additional exact-flow sampling hypotheses in that procedure hold, namely a jointly smooth extension of the field to an open time interval containing $[0,1]$ and the uniform state-Lipschitz and origin bounds on every compact parameter set, then its terminal output $X_1=\Phi^{\theta_N}_{1,0}(X_0)$ is well-defined and measurable. For every Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ its conditional output law is

$$\mathbb P(X_1\in A\mid\mathcal F_N)=\mu_0\bigl(\{x:\Phi^{\theta_N}_{1,0}(x)\in A\}\bigr)\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

For $N=0$, there is no batch update, $\theta_N=\theta_0$, and the exact-flow conclusion still applies under the same sampling hypotheses. These statements supply neither convergence of the parameter updates nor equality of the output law with a desired data law, nor a numerical solver or an error or cost bound.

## Statement references

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The conditional probability path and velocity, endpoint sampler, parameterized vector field and its sampled gradients, initial parameter, batch size, step sizes, supplied initial law, and exact-flow regularity hypotheses in the Algorithm.

[F1] [[def-probability-path-and-velocity-field]]: a conditional density path is normalized for the endpoint law almost everywhere, and its conditional velocity is defined by the conditional continuity equation.

[F2] [[thm-conditional-flow-matching-gradient-identity]]: under finite loss, positive finite marginal density, local endpoint domination for the conditional continuity equation, and dominated parameter derivatives, the conditional and marginal squared-loss gradients agree.

[F3] [[def-neural-ode]]: for a fixed parameter, the neural ODE is the initial-value problem $\dot z(t)=v(t,z(t);\theta)$ with the stated initial condition.

[F4] [[thm-neural-ode-global-smooth-flow]]: a jointly smooth field on an open time interval containing $[0,1]$, with uniform state-Lipschitz and origin bounds on compact parameter sets, has a unique global flow on $[0,1]$, and its terminal map is jointly smooth in initial state and parameter.

[F5] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the squared Euclidean loss is $\|a-b\|_2^2=\langle a-b,a-b\rangle$.

[F6] [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]: the expectation of a finite sum of integrable random vectors is the sum of their expectations, componentwise.

[F7] [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]: the law of a measurable map $S$ under $\mu_0$ assigns a Borel set $A$ the measure $\mu_0(S^{-1}(A))$.

[F8] [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: for an integrable real random variable, a conditional-expectation version is measurable, integrable, and has the same integrals on every event in the conditioning sigma-algebra; vector statements apply coordinatewise.

[F9] [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]: independent random elements have the product of their marginal laws as their joint law.

[F10] [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]: the expectation of an integrable function of a random element equals its integral against the law of that element.

[F11] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: an integrable function on a sigma-finite product can be integrated in either order with equal results.

[F12] [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]: the absolute value of an integrable scalar function's integral is bounded by the integral of its absolute value.

[F13] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: a nonnegative product-measurable function has a measurable section-integral function and equal iterated and product integrals.

[F14] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: a real function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable in its interior has each difference quotient equal to an interior derivative.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Algorithm.

1.1 Fix $k$ and a history for which $\theta_k=\theta\in\Theta$ and both losses at $\theta$ are finite. Choose a compact parameter box $H\subset\Theta$ with $\theta$ in its interior. Changing coordinates one at a time, the mean value theorem [F14] and the derivative majorants in [F2] bound the differences between each loss integrand at $\theta'$ and at $\theta$ by the corresponding sums of $|\theta'_j-\theta_j|G^C_{H,j}$ and $|\theta'_j-\theta_j|G^M_{H,j}$. Integrating these bounds proves local finiteness of both losses throughout the interior of $H$, so [F2] applies there and gives $\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_C(\theta)=\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_M(\theta)$. The sample gradient is the parameter gradient of the conditional squared loss by [F5]; since its triple has law $Q$, the expectation change-of-variables formula [F10] identifies its $Q$-mean with $\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_C(\theta)$. Thus its $Q$-mean is $\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_M(\theta)$. [given, F1, F2, F5, F10, F14, algebra]

2.1 Each $\zeta_{k,b}$, and hence $g_k$, is integrable by the explicit batch-integrability assumption. For fixed $\theta$, put $m(\theta):=\int_Q\zeta(\theta,w)\,Q(dw)$. Joint measurability, Tonelli [F13], and the local derivative majorants make $m$ measurable and finite; at each visited parameter step 1.1 gives $m(\theta_k)=\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_M(\theta_k)$. Fubini [F11] and the integral triangle inequality [F12] show that each coordinate of $m(\theta_k)$ is integrable, with its absolute expectation bounded by that of the corresponding sample-gradient coordinate. For every $A\in\mathcal F_k$, independence and the product-law fact [F9], the change-of-variables formula [F10], and Fubini [F11] give $$\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A g_k]=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_A\int_{Q^{\otimes B}}\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^B\zeta(\theta_k,w_b)\,Q^{\otimes B}(d(w_1,\ldots,w_B))\right]=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_M(\theta_k)],$$ where step 1.1 identifies each fixed-parameter $Q$-mean and [F6] gives linearity. Thus [F8] makes $\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_M(\theta_k)$ a version of $\mathbb E[g_k\mid\mathcal F_k]$; the batch estimate is unbiased conditionally on its pre-batch history. The arithmetic update is defined for every nonnegative step size when $\theta_k\in\Theta$. [given, F6, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For the realized $\theta_N$ satisfying the exact-flow bounds, [F3] identifies the sampling equation as a neural ODE and [F4] gives its unique solution on the full interval and joint continuity of $(x,\theta)\mapsto\Phi^\theta_{1,0}(x)$. The terminal output is therefore measurable as a function of the independent initial draw and the training history. Conditional on $\mathcal F_N$, $\theta_N$ is fixed, so [F7] identifies the conditional output law by $\mu_0(\{x:\Phi^{\theta_N}_{1,0}(x)\in A\})$ for each Borel set $A$. This verifies that the exact-flow output is defined; it makes no claim that the learned field realizes the target path. [given, F3, F4, F7] ∎

The smooth-flow supplier establishes global well-definedness under the stated additional regularity and uniform bounds. ## Example

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $a\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma_{\min}>0$, let $Z\sim N(0,1)$, and set
$$\sigma_t=1-(1-\sigma_{\min})t,\qquad X_t=\sigma_t Z+ta\quad(0\le t\le1).$$
Then $X_t\sim N(ta,\sigma_t^2)$, with density
$$\rho_t(x\mid a)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma_t}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-ta)^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right),$$
and a conditional velocity field is
$$u_t(x\mid a)=a+\frac{\sigma_{\min}-1}{\sigma_t}(x-ta).$$
For every fixed $z\in\mathbb R$, the particle path $t\mapsto\sigma_tz+ta$ is a straight line from $z$ to $a+\sigma_{\min}z$. The endpoint map $T(z)=a+\sigma_{\min}z$ is quadratic-cost optimal from $N(0,1)$ to $N(a,\sigma_{\min}^2)$, and its squared transport cost is $a^2+(1-\sigma_{\min})^2$.

## Example references

[Lipman et al., §4.1 Example II](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.02747)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $a\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma_{\min}>0$, and a standard normal random variable $Z$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is the assertion that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]); it is required by the Gaussian-law and density suppliers used by [F1].

[F1] [[thm-gaussian-conditional-optimal-transport-map]]: under AC, for $d\ge1$, fixed $x_1$, and $\sigma_{\min}>0$, the affine conditional Gaussian path has mean $tx_1$, scale $1-(1-\sigma_{\min})t$, the stated Gaussian density and velocity, and a quadratic-cost optimal endpoint map with cost $\|x_1\|_2^2+d(1-\sigma_{\min})^2$.

## Verification

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Example.

1.1 Apply [F1] with $d=1$ and $x_1=a$. It gives the law and density of $X_t$, the field $u_t(x\mid a)$, and the optimality of $T(z)=a+\sigma_{\min}z$ with cost $a^2+(1-\sigma_{\min})^2$. [given, A1, F1]

2.1 For fixed $z$, differentiation gives $\frac{d}{dt}(\sigma_tz+ta)=(\sigma_{\min}-1)z+a$. Substituting $x=\sigma_tz+ta$ into the displayed field yields $$u_t(x\mid a)=a+\frac{\sigma_{\min}-1}{\sigma_t}\,\sigma_tz=a+(\sigma_{\min}-1)z,$$ which is that particle derivative. Since $\sigma_t>0$, its dependence on $t$ is affine and the endpoints are $z$ and $a+\sigma_{\min}z$. [given, F1, algebra] ∎

## Example

$$\sigma_t=1-(1-\sigma_{\min})t,\qquad X_t=\sigma_t Z+t x_1,\qquad Z\sim N(0,1).$$
For either endpoint and each fixed $Z=z$, the conditional particle trajectory is a straight line. The marginal density is
$$p_t(x)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma_t}\left[ \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-ta)^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right)+ \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x+ta)^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right) \right],$$
and its marginal velocity field, defined by averaging the conditional velocity against the endpoint density at fixed $(t,x)$, is
$$u^m_t(x)=\frac{\sigma_{\min}-1}{\sigma_t}x+ \frac{a}{\sigma_t}\tanh\!\left(\frac{atx}{\sigma_t^2}\right), \qquad \tanh(y):=\frac{\exp(y)-\exp(-y)}{\exp(y)+\exp(-y)}.$$
The denominator in the definition of $\tanh$ is positive for every real input. The density is strictly positive, and $\partial_tp_t(x)+\partial_x(p_t(x)u^m_t(x))=0$ on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R$. For every $t\in(0,1)$, $x\mapsto u^m_t(x)$ is nonlinear.

## Example references

[Lipman et al., §4.1 Example II and the qualification that a conditional OT path does not make the marginal field optimal](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.02747)

[Holderrieth and Erives, §§3.2–3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.02070)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $a>0$, $\sigma_{\min}>0$, the two-point endpoint law, and the Gaussian conditional path in the Example.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is the assertion that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]); it is required by the Gaussian-law and density suppliers used by [F1].

[F1] [[thm-gaussian-conditional-optimal-transport-map]]: under AC, for each fixed endpoint $x_1$ the mean-linear Gaussian path has the displayed density and affine conditional velocity, and its density and flux satisfy the conditional continuity equation.

[F2] [[def-probability-path-and-velocity-field]]: the marginal density is $p_t(x)=\int\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1)$ and its velocity, where $p_t(x)>0$ and the flux is finite, is $u^m_t(x)=\int\rho_tu^c_t\,d\pi/p_t(x)$.

[F3] [[lem-conditional-mixture-is-a-probability-path]]: the endpoint mixture of normalized conditional densities is a probability density at each time.

[F4] [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]: a continuous real-valued function on a compact metric space is bounded.

[F5] [[lem-conditional-to-marginal-continuity-equation]]: if the conditional PDE derivatives admit the stated local integrable endpoint majorant, then the marginal density and flux satisfy the continuity equation.

[F6] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]: the real exponential is positive, has $\exp(0)=1$, and is defined on every real input.

[F7] [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]: $\exp(r+s)=\exp(r)\exp(s)$ for all real $r,s$.

[F8] [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]: $r<s$ implies $\exp(r)<\exp(s)$.

[F9] [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]: $\exp(-r)=1/\exp(r)$ and $\exp(r)>0$ for every real $r$.

## Verification

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Example.

1.1 Apply [F1] to the two endpoints $x_1=a$ and $x_1=-a$. Their conditional densities are positive and continuous in $(t,x)$, as are their time derivatives, fluxes, and spatial flux derivatives; $\sigma_t>0$ throughout $[0,1]$. Hence for each compact $K\subset(0,1)\times\mathbb R$ the finitely many such functions are bounded on $K$ by [F4]. Taking a common bound as the constant function $G_K$ gives an element of $L^1(\pi)$ because $\pi$ has total mass one. Thus [F5] applies. The mixture density is normalized by [F3] and is strictly positive because it is a sum of two positive Gaussian densities. [given, A1, F1, F3, F4, F5]

1.2 Put $$A_+(t,x):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-ta)^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right),\qquad A_-(t,x):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x+ta)^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right).$$ The common Gaussian normalizing factor cancels in the endpoint-weighted mean, so [F2] gives $$m_t(x):=\frac{\int x_1\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1)}{p_t(x)} =a\frac{A_+(t,x)-A_-(t,x)}{A_+(t,x)+A_-(t,x)}.$$ Expanding the two squares gives $A_+/A_-=\exp(2atx/\sigma_t^2)$ by [F7] and [F9]. Multiplying numerator and denominator by $\exp(-atx/\sigma_t^2)$ therefore yields $m_t(x)=a\tanh(atx/\sigma_t^2)$. [given, F2, F6, F7, F9, algebra]

2.1 For endpoint $x_1\in\{-a,a\}$, [F1] gives $$u^c_t(x\mid x_1)=cx+(1-tc)x_1, \qquad c:=\frac{\sigma_{\min}-1}{\sigma_t}.$$ Taking the endpoint-weighted mean and using step 1.2 gives $u^m_t(x)=cx+(1-tc)m_t(x)$. Since $\sigma_t=1+t(\sigma_{\min}-1)$, we have $\sigma_t-t(\sigma_{\min}-1)=1$ and hence $1-tc=1/\sigma_t$. Substitution gives the marginal velocity formula in the Example. [step 1.2, F1, F2, algebra]

3.1 Fix $t\in(0,1)$ and put $\beta:=a/\sigma_t>0$ and $k:=at/\sigma_t^2>0$. The formula for $\tanh$ and [F9] give $\tanh(-y)=-\tanh(y)$, so $u^m_t$ is odd. For $y>0$, put $r:=\exp(2y)>1$ and $s:=(r-1)/(r+1)\in(0,1)$ by [F6, F8]. Rewriting $\tanh(y)$ and $\tanh(2y)$ using [F7, F9] gives $$\tanh(y)=s,\qquad \tanh(2y)=\frac{r^2-1}{r^2+1}=\frac{2s}{1+s^2}<2s.$$ Thus for every $x>0$, step 2.1 gives $$u^m_t(2x)-2u^m_t(x)=\beta\bigl(\tanh(2kx)-2\tanh(kx)\bigr)<0.$$ An odd affine function must be linear through the origin, and every such function has $u(2x)-2u(x)=0$. Hence $u^m_t$ is not affine and is nonlinear. [step 2.1, F6, F7, F8, F9, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

The cited sources give the straight conditional Gaussian paths and the conditional-to-marginal velocity formula. The explicit two-endpoint mixture calculation is local. Its conclusion concerns nonlinearity of the marginal velocity; it makes no claim that the marginal field is a globally optimal transport field.
