## Statement

Let $q\ge1$ be an integer. Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_q$ be mutually independent integrable real random variables on a common probability space, with means $m_j=\mathbb E[Z_j]$, and suppose each is 1-sub-Gaussian, meaning that $\mathbb E[\exp(\lambda(Z_j-m_j))]\le\exp(\lambda^2/2)$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$. Then for every $t\ge0$,
$$
\mathbb P\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^q(Z_j-m_j)\ge t\right)\le \exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2q}\right),\qquad \mathbb P\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^q(Z_j-m_j)\le -t\right)\le \exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2q}\right).
$$

## Statement references

[Tor Lattimore and Csaba Szepesvári, *Bandit Algorithms*](https://tor-lattimore.com/downloads/book/book.pdf): §5.3, Theorem 5.3 and Corollary 5.5, PDF pp. 86–87 / printed pp. 77–78; the independent-sum step is Exercise 5.7.

[Sébastien Bubeck and Nicolò Cesa-Bianchi, *Regret Analysis of Stochastic and Nonstochastic Multi-armed Bandit Problems*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1204.5721): Chapter 2 §2.2, Equation (2.2) and fixed-sample MGF tail derivation, PDF pp. 13–14 / printed pp. 10–11.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite family of mutually independent integrable real random variables $Z_1,\ldots,Z_q$, their means $m_j$, and the 1-sub-Gaussian MGF bounds in the statement.

[F1] For each $j$ and every real $\lambda$, $\mathbb E[\exp(\lambda(Z_j-m_j))]\le\exp(\lambda^2/2)$ ([[def-centered-subgaussian-reward]]).

[F2] Independence means the generated sigma-algebras are independent ([[def-independent-random-elements]]); therefore the joint law of the finite vector is the product of its marginal laws ([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]).

[F3] Tonelli permits iterated integration of nonnegative product-measurable functions over sigma-finite product spaces ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); positive scalar factors may be taken outside nonnegative integrals ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[F4] Expectation of a nonnegative random variable is its Lebesgue integral ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

[F5] For a nonnegative random variable $W$ and $a>0$, $\mathbb P(W\ge a)\le\mathbb E[W]/a$ ([[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]]).

[F6] The real exponential satisfies $\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y)$ ([[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]), is positive ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]), and is strictly increasing ([[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

## Proof

1.1 Put $S=\sum_{j=1}^q(Z_j-m_j)$. For $q=1$ the desired MGF bound is [F1]. For $q\ge2$ and $\lambda\ge0$, the product-law identity in [F2] and the exponential addition formula in [F6] give $\mathbb E[e^{\lambda S}]=\int_{\mathbb R^q}\prod_{j=1}^q e^{\lambda(z_j-m_j)}\,d\!\left(\bigotimes_{j=1}^q\mathbb P_{Z_j}\right)(z_1,\ldots,z_q)$. The integrand is nonnegative and measurable by [F6]. Repeated application of Tonelli in [F3], grouping the first $q-1$ factors and the last factor, factors this integral into the product of the $q$ one-dimensional integrals. [F2, F3, F4, F6]

2.1 Each factor is at most $e^{\lambda^2/2}$ by [F1], so $\mathbb E[e^{\lambda S}]\le e^{q\lambda^2/2}$. The same argument with $-\lambda$ gives $\mathbb E[e^{-\lambda S}]\le e^{q\lambda^2/2}$. [step 1.1, F1, F6, algebra]

3.1 If $t>0$ and $\lambda>0$, strict increase and positivity of the exponential in [F6] identify $\{S\ge t\}=\{e^{\lambda S}\ge e^{\lambda t}\}$. Markov's inequality [F5] and step 2.1 yield $\mathbb P(S\ge t)\le e^{q\lambda^2/2-\lambda t}$. Choosing $\lambda=t/q$ gives $\mathbb P(S\ge t)\le e^{-t^2/(2q)}$. [given, step 2.1, F5, F6, choose, algebra]

4.1 Applying the same argument to $-S$ gives $\mathbb P(S\le-t)\le e^{-t^2/(2q)}$. At $t=0$ both asserted bounds reduce to the probability bound $1\le1$. [given, step 2.1, F5, F6, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix positive integers $n$ and $k$, write $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, and let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space. A finite-horizon $k$-armed stochastic bandit in **reward-stack form** consists of probability measures $P_i$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ with finite first absolute moments, and an independent table of integrable real random variables $(X_{s,i})_{1\le s\le n,\ i\in[k]}$ such that the table entries are mutually independent and each $X_{s,i}$ has law $P_i$. Its mean for arm $i$ is $\mu_i=\int_{\mathbb R}x\,P_i(dx)=\mathbb E[X_{s,i}]$, which does not depend on $s$. The learner may also use a random element $U$ for private randomization, provided $\sigma(U)$ is independent of the sigma-algebra generated by the entire table; a deterministic learner uses a constant $U$.

A non-anticipating policy chooses a measurable arm $A_t\in[k]$ at each round $t\in[n]$ using only $U$ and the previously observed history $(A_1,Y_1,\ldots,A_{t-1},Y_{t-1})$. Write $\mathcal H_{t-1}=\sigma(U,A_1,Y_1,\ldots,A_{t-1},Y_{t-1})$ for that history sigma-algebra. Define the pull count $T_i(0)=0$ and
$$
T_i(t)=\sum_{r=1}^{t}\mathbf 1_{\{A_r=i\}},\qquad Y_t=X_{T_{A_t}(t),A_t}.
$$
Thus each time arm $i$ is selected the learner receives the next unused entry in arm $i$'s reward stack. Set
$$
\mu^*=\max_{i\in[k]}\mu_i,\qquad \Delta_i=\mu^*-\mu_i\ge0,
$$
define the pseudo-regret $\bar R_n=\sum_{t=1}^n(\mu^*-\mu_{A_t})$, and define the realized reward regret $R_n^{\rm rew}=n\mu^*-\sum_{t=1}^nY_t$ and expected reward regret $R_n=\mathbb E[R_n^{\rm rew}]$.

Each $Y_t$ is integrable because it selects one entry of the finite table, so $|Y_t|\le\sum_{s=1}^n\sum_{i=1}^k|X_{s,i}|$ and the right-hand side is integrable. Hence $R_n^{\rm rew}$ is integrable as well.

## Definition references

[[def-online-decision-protocol]]: the learner chooses before the current round's feedback and uses only earlier revealed history.

[[def-adversary-and-feedback-model]]: a stochastic finite-arm environment has a fixed probability law for each arm, finite first moments, and the stated conditional reward-law convention.

[[def-static-dynamic-and-strongly-adaptive-regret]]: pseudo-regret is the sum of mean gaps along the action sequence; realized reward regret subtracts the observed rewards; expected regret integrates realized regret.

[[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]: table entries and learner randomization are measurable random elements, with the table entries real-valued.

[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]: the law of a random element is the pushforward probability measure on its measurable target space.

[[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]: expectation of an integrable measurable function of a random element equals its integral against the law, in particular for the identity function on the real line.

[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]: expectation of an integrable real random variable is its Lebesgue integral.

[[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]: finite linear combinations of integrable random variables are integrable and expectation is linear.

[[def-independent-random-elements]]: the table entries are mutually independent as random elements, and learner randomization is independent of the table.

## Definition

Input integers $k,n,m\ge1$ with $mk\le n$, and access to an $n$-round $k$-armed stochastic bandit. The output is the sequence of selected arms $A_1,\ldots,A_n$ and the committed arm $J$.

1. For rounds $t=1,\ldots,mk$, choose arm $A_t=1+((t-1)\bmod k)$ and observe its reward $Y_t$. Thus each arm is explored exactly $m$ times.
2. For each $i\in[k]$, form its exploration mean
   $$
   \widehat\mu_i=\frac1m\sum_{r=1}^m Y_{(r-1)k+i}.
   $$
3. Let $J$ be the least index attaining $\max_{i\in[k]}\widehat\mu_i$.
4. For every remaining round $t=mk+1,\ldots,n$, choose $A_t=J$ and observe its reward.

[[def-stochastic-bandit-and-pseudo-regret]]: the horizon, finite arm set, reward observations, and non-anticipating round order used by the procedure.

## Definition

Input integers $k,n$ with $1\le k\le n$, a confidence parameter $\delta\in(0,1)$, and access to an $n$-round $k$-armed stochastic bandit. Output the selected arms $A_1,\ldots,A_n$.

1. Initialize by choosing each arm once: set $A_t=t$ for $t=1,\ldots,k$, and observe each reward.
2. For each round $t=k+1,\ldots,n$, let $T_i(t-1)=\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\mathbf 1_{\{A_s=i\}}$. If $T_i(t-1)>0$, set $U_i(t-1)=\widehat\mu_i(t-1)+\sqrt{2\log(1/\delta)/T_i(t-1)}$ and $\widehat\mu_i(t-1)=\bigl(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\mathbf 1_{\{A_s=i\}}Y_s\bigr)/T_i(t-1)$.
   Set $U_i(t-1)=+\infty$ if $T_i(t-1)=0$.
3. Choose the least index $i$ attaining $\max_{j\in[k]}U_j(t-1)$ as $A_t$, then observe $Y_t$.

[[def-stochastic-bandit-and-pseudo-regret]]: the finite arm set, horizon, pull counts, observed rewards, and round order.

[[def-natural-logarithm]]: $\log$ is the inverse of the real exponential on positive reals.

[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: the natural logarithm is increasing and satisfies the product and quotient laws.

[Tor Lattimore and Csaba Szepesvári, *Bandit Algorithms*](https://tor-lattimore.com/downloads/book/book.pdf): Chapter 7 §7.1, Algorithm 3, PDF p. 112 / printed p. 103.

## Statement

In the finite reward-stack model, fix a round $t\in[n]$, an arm $i\in[k]$, an event $B\in\mathcal H_{t-1}$ with $B\subseteq\{A_t=i\}$, and a Borel set $C\subseteq\mathbb R$. Then
$$
\mathbb P(B\cap\{Y_t\in C\})=\mathbb P(B)P_i(C),\qquad \mathbb E[Y_t\mathbf 1_B]=\mu_i\mathbb P(B).
$$
In particular, the reward stack satisfies the fixed conditional reward-law and conditional-mean interface for finite-arm stochastic environments.

## Statement references

[[def-stochastic-bandit-and-pseudo-regret]]: the table entries are mutually independent, a policy uses only the revealed history and independent learner randomness, and each pull reveals the next unused entry of the chosen arm's stack.

[[def-adversary-and-feedback-model]]: the fixed conditional arm-law and conditional-mean identities required by the sequential stochastic reward model.

[Tor Lattimore and Csaba Szepesvári, *Bandit Algorithms*](https://tor-lattimore.com/downloads/book/book.pdf): §4.6, PDF p. 74 / printed p. 65; Exercise 4.4.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite reward-stack model, a non-anticipating policy, a round $t\in[n]$, an arm $i\in[k]$, and an event $B\in\mathcal H_{t-1}$ contained in $\{A_t=i\}$.

[F1] The policy uses only $U$ and the previously revealed actions and rewards; on a fixed action history, the observed rewards are exactly the corresponding initial entries of the arm stacks ([[def-stochastic-bandit-and-pseudo-regret]]).

[F2] The learner randomization and all table entries form a finite independent family ([[def-independent-random-elements]]), whose joint law is the finite product of its marginal laws ([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]).

[F3] For each arm $i$, every table entry has law $P_i$ and finite first absolute moment, with mean $\mu_i$ ([[def-stochastic-bandit-and-pseudo-regret]]).

[F4] Measurable functions of independent random elements remain independent ([[lem-measurable-functions-preserve-independence]]).

[F5] Expectations of finite products of mutually independent integrable real random variables factor ([[thm-expectation-of-products-of-independent-random-variables]]), and $\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_E]=\mathbb P(E)$ ([[cor-expectation-of-an-indicator-is-probability]]).

[F6] Expectation is the Lebesgue integral and is linear on integrable real random variables ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]], [[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]).

## Proof

1.1 Partition $B$ by the finitely many past action strings $\alpha=(a_1,\ldots,a_{t-1})\in[k]^{t-1}$. Let $c_j(\alpha)$ be the number of times arm $j$ occurs in $\alpha$, and write $B_\alpha=B\cap\{(A_1,\ldots,A_{t-1})=\alpha\}$. By the recursive non-anticipating policy rule, each $B_\alpha$ is measurable with respect to $U$ and the table entries $X_{s,j}$ with $s\le c_j(\alpha)$: along that fixed action string, those and only those stack entries have been revealed. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 If $B_\alpha$ is nonempty then $A_t=i$ on it, and the next reward is $Y_t=X_{c_i(\alpha)+1,i}$. This table entry is distinct from every coordinate determining $B_\alpha$. By [F2] it is independent of the vector of those coordinates, so the event $B_\alpha$ is independent of $\{X_{c_i(\alpha)+1,i}\in C\}$ for every Borel $C$. Its law is $P_i$, hence $\mathbb P(B_\alpha\cap\{Y_t\in C\})=\mathbb P(B_\alpha)P_i(C)$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 The events $B_\alpha$ partition $B$. Summing the identity in step 2.1 over the finite set $[k]^{t-1}$ gives $\mathbb P(B\cap\{Y_t\in C\})=\mathbb P(B)P_i(C)$ for every Borel $C$. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For each $\alpha$, the indicator $\mathbf 1_{B_\alpha}$ is a measurable function of the exposed-coordinate vector. By [F2] and [F4], it is independent of $X_{c_i(\alpha)+1,i}$. Both are integrable by [F3], so [F5] and [F6] give $\mathbb E[Y_t\mathbf 1_{B_\alpha}]=\mu_i\mathbb P(B_\alpha)$. Summing over the finite action strings yields $\mathbb E[Y_t\mathbf 1_B]=\mu_i\mathbb P(B)$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be a finite mutually independent family of real random variables on a common probability space, with independence in the sense of [[def-independent-random-elements]].

1. If every $X_i$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i\in I}X_i$ is integrable and
   $$\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{i\in I}X_i\right]=\prod_{i\in I}\mathbb E[X_i]$$
   in $\mathbb R$.
2. If every $X_i$ is nonnegative, the same identity holds in $[0,+\infty]$. A zero factor on the right makes the product zero even if another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise the usual extended nonnegative product is used.

The original finite-probability-space case is included: for a finite family of finite-valued real random variables, mutual atom independence as in [[def-independence-of-finite-random-variables]] suffices, and all expectations are finite. For $I=\varnothing$, both sides equal $1$. The converse is not asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ satisfying the independence and moment hypotheses of the applicable case in the Statement.

[L1] Independence of random elements means independence of their inverse-image sigma-algebras. ([[def-independent-random-elements]])

[L2] For an independent nonempty finite family of real random variables and Borel functions $g_i$, the product expectations factor in the nonnegative extended case, with the explicit zero-factor convention, and in the integrable case; in the latter case the product is integrable. ([[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]])

[L3] For finite-valued random variables, mutual atom independence factors the joint probabilities of attained values for every subfamily. ([[def-independence-of-finite-random-variables]])

[L4] On a general probability space, $\mathbb P(\varnothing)=0$ follows from the set-difference identity with $A=B$, and $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$. For disjoint events this is two-set additivity, which gives finite disjoint additivity by induction. ([[lem-probability-measure-basic-identities]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 In the original finite-valued case, let $J\subseteq I$ and let $B_i\subseteq\mathbb R$ be Borel for $i\in J$. Write $A_i$ for the finite attained-value set of $X_i$. The event $\bigcap_{i\in J}\{X_i\in B_i\}$ is the disjoint union of the joint atoms indexed by $\prod_{i\in J}(A_i\cap B_i)$. By [L3] and [L4], its probability is $$\sum_{(x_i)\in\prod_{i\in J}(A_i\cap B_i)}\prod_{i\in J}\mathbb P(X_i=x_i)=\prod_{i\in J}\sum_{x_i\in A_i\cap B_i}\mathbb P(X_i=x_i)=\prod_{i\in J}\mathbb P(X_i\in B_i).$$ Factoring finite sums proves the middle equality, including empty factors. Thus the family is independent in the sense of [L1]. Each variable is bounded because its attained-value set is finite, hence integrable on a probability space. [L1, L3, L4, algebra]

2.1 Suppose $I\ne\varnothing$ and every $X_i$ is integrable. Enumerate the finite set $I$ by $0,\ldots,n-1$ and apply [L2] with $g_i(x)=x$, which is Borel. It gives product integrability and the asserted real factorization. Selecting one enumeration of one finite set uses no axiom of choice. Step 1.1 supplies the required independence and integrability in the original finite-valued case. [L2, step 1.1]

3.1 Suppose $I\ne\varnothing$ and every $X_i$ is nonnegative. Apply [L2] to the same enumeration with $g_i(x)=\max(x,0)$, a continuous nonnegative Borel function. Since $g_i(X_i)=X_i$, [L2] gives the asserted extended factorization with precisely its zero-factor convention. [L2, step 2.1]

4.1 For $I=\varnothing$, the random product is the constant $1$, whose expectation is $1$ on a probability space, and the product of expectations is the empty product $1$. Steps 2.1 and 3.1 and this identity prove all stated cases. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n,k$ be integers with $n\ge\max\{k,2\}$. In an $n$-round $k$-armed stochastic bandit, suppose every reward-stack entry is 1-sub-Gaussian. Run the upper-confidence-bound algorithm with $\delta=n^{-2}$. For every arm $i$ with gap $\Delta_i>0$, its number of pulls satisfies
$$
\mathbb E[T_i(n)]\le 3+\frac{16\log n}{\Delta_i^2},
$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm and the expectation is over the reward table and learner randomization.

## Statement references

[[def-centered-subgaussian-reward]]: each reward is mean-centred and satisfies the exact MGF bound for every real parameter.

[Tor Lattimore and Csaba Szepesvári, *Bandit Algorithms*](https://tor-lattimore.com/downloads/book/book.pdf): Theorem 7.1 proof, §7.1, PDF pp. 114–117 / printed pp. 105–108; fixed-prefix warning, PDF p. 112 / printed p. 103.

[Sébastien Bubeck and Nicolò Cesa-Bianchi, *Regret Analysis of Stochastic and Nonstochastic Multi-armed Bandit Problems*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1204.5721): Theorem 2.1 proof, Chapter 2 §2.2, PDF pp. 14–15 / printed pp. 11–12.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An $n$-round reward-stack model with $n\ge\max\{k,2\}$, all reward entries 1-sub-Gaussian, a suboptimal arm $i$ with $\Delta_i>0$, and the UCB algorithm run with $\delta=n^{-2}$.

[F1] Each arm has finite mean $\mu_i$, gap $\Delta_i=\mu^*-\mu_i$, and stack entries $X_{s,i}$ are independent with law $P_i$ ([[def-stochastic-bandit-and-pseudo-regret]]).

[A1] Every table entry is centered 1-sub-Gaussian in the exact MGF sense ([[def-centered-subgaussian-reward]]).

[F2] For every deterministic $s\in[n]$, the prefix mean $\widehat\mu_{i,s}=s^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^sX_{r,i}$ satisfies $\mathbb P(\widehat\mu_{i,s}-\mu_i\ge x),\mathbb P(\widehat\mu_{i,s}-\mu_i\le-x)\le e^{-sx^2/2}$ for $x\ge0$ ([[lem-independent-subgaussian-prefix-tail]]).

[F3] After initialization, the UCB index of arm $i$ with $s>0$ observations is its observed-prefix mean plus $\sqrt{2\log(1/\delta)/s}$; the least-index maximizer is selected ([[alg-upper-confidence-bound-bandit]]).

[F4] For $n\ge2$, $\log n>0$ and $\log(n^2)=2\log n$ ([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]).

## Proof

1.1 Fix a suboptimal arm $i$, let $i^*$ be the least index with $\mu_{i^*}=\mu^*$, write $L=\log n>0$, and put $u_i=\lceil16L/\Delta_i^2\rceil$. For each deterministic prefix length $s\in[n]$, set $r_s=\sqrt{4L/s}$; by [F4] this is the UCB bonus when $\delta=n^{-2}$. If $u_i\ge n$, then $T_i(n)\le n\le u_i\le16L/\Delta_i^2+1$, which is stronger than the claim. Hence assume $u_i<n$, so $r_{u_i}\le\Delta_i/2$. [given, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Define the good event $G_i=\left(\bigcap_{s=1}^n\{\widehat\mu_{i^*,s}+r_s\ge\mu^*\}\right)\cap\{\widehat\mu_{i,u_i}+r_{u_i}<\mu^*\}$. On $G_i$, arm $i$ cannot be selected at any round when it already has $u_i$ pulls: its index is then below $\mu^*$, whereas the good event makes the index of arm $i^*$ at least $\mu^*$ for every possible deterministic prefix length $s\in[n]$. Since each pull increases $T_i$ by one, $T_i(n)\le u_i$ on $G_i$. [given, F1, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 The complement of the first event in $G_i$ is contained in the union of the $n$ deterministic-prefix events $\{\widehat\mu_{i^*,s}-\mu^*<-r_s\}$. By [F2] under [A1] and the union bound, its probability is at most $\sum_{s=1}^n e^{-sr_s^2/2}=n e^{-2L}=1/n$. This union is over fixed $s$, not the random pull count $T_{i^*}(t)$. [given, A1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Since $r_{u_i}\le\Delta_i/2$, the other failure event in $G_i$ is contained in $\{\widehat\mu_{i,u_i}-\mu_i\ge\Delta_i/2\}$. By [F2] under [A1] its probability is at most $e^{-u_i\Delta_i^2/8}\le e^{-2L}=n^{-2}$. Therefore $\mathbb P(G_i^c)\le1/n+1/n^2$. [given, A1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Always $T_i(n)\le n$, while step 2.1 gives $T_i(n)\le u_i$ on $G_i$. Thus $\mathbb E[T_i(n)]\le u_i+n\mathbb P(G_i^c)\le16L/\Delta_i^2+1+1+1/n\le16\log n/\Delta_i^2+3$, where $n\ge2$ was used in the last inequality. This proves the claim. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $k,n,m$ be positive integers with $mk\le n$. In an $n$-round $k$-armed stochastic bandit, suppose all reward-stack entries are 1-sub-Gaussian. Run explore-then-commit with exploration count $m$. Its expected reward regret satisfies
$$
R_n\le m\sum_{i=1}^k\Delta_i+(n-mk)\sum_{i=1}^k\Delta_i\exp\!\left(-\frac{m\Delta_i^2}{4}\right).
$$
This is an expected-regret bound, not a high-probability guarantee.

## Statement references

[[def-stochastic-bandit-and-pseudo-regret]]: finite arm means, gaps, reward-stack model, and expected reward regret.

[[def-centered-subgaussian-reward]]: each reward entry is centered at its finite mean and has MGF bounded by $e^{\lambda^2/2}$ for every real $\lambda$.

[[alg-explore-then-commit]]: deterministic round-robin exploration followed by commitment to an empirical-mean maximizer.

[[lem-independent-subgaussian-prefix-tail]]: two-sided tails for deterministic prefixes of independent sub-Gaussian rewards.

[[lem-finite-arm-regret-decomposes-into-expected-action-counts]]: expected reward regret equals the sum of arm gaps times expected pull counts under the conditional-mean hypothesis.

[Tor Lattimore and Csaba Szepesvári, *Bandit Algorithms*](https://tor-lattimore.com/downloads/book/book.pdf): Theorem 6.1 and proof, Chapter 6 §6.1, PDF pp. 101–102 / printed pp. 92–93.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integers $k,n,m\ge1$ with $mk\le n$, the stochastic reward-stack model, 1-sub-Gaussian reward entries, and explore-then-commit with least-index tie-breaking.

[F1] For each arm, $\mu_i$ is finite, $\Delta_i=\mu^*-\mu_i\ge0$, and expected reward regret is $R_n=\mathbb E[n\mu^*-\sum_{t=1}^nY_t]$ ([[def-stochastic-bandit-and-pseudo-regret]]).

[A1] Every table entry satisfies the exact centered 1-sub-Gaussian MGF bound ([[def-centered-subgaussian-reward]]).

[F2] The observed reward at each pull has the arm's fixed conditional law and conditional mean, even under adaptive choices on the independent reward stacks ([[lem-bandit-reward-table-has-fixed-conditional-laws]]; [[def-adversary-and-feedback-model]]).

[F3] Under the eventwise conditional-mean identity, expected regret decomposes as $R_n=\sum_{i=1}^k\Delta_i\,\mathbb E[T_i(n)]$ ([[lem-finite-arm-regret-decomposes-into-expected-action-counts]]).

[F4] During exploration, the algorithm pulls each arm exactly $m$ times and then commits to a least-index empirical-mean maximizer ([[alg-explore-then-commit]]).

[F5] For any fixed arm pair and deterministic prefix length, the centered sum of independent reward-table entries has the two-sided sub-Gaussian tail bound ([[lem-independent-subgaussian-prefix-tail]]).

## Proof

1.1 By [F2], the conditional-mean hypothesis of [F3] holds, so $R_n=\sum_{i=1}^k\Delta_i\mathbb E[T_i(n)]$. Let $J$ be the committed arm. The first $mk$ rounds pull each arm exactly $m$ times, and every later round pulls $J$; hence $T_i(n)=m+(n-mk)\mathbf1_{\{J=i\}}$. Taking expectations gives $R_n=m\sum_{i=1}^k\Delta_i+(n-mk)\sum_{i=1}^k\Delta_i\mathbb P(J=i)$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Fix an optimal arm $i^*$ with $\mu_{i^*}=\mu^*$. If a suboptimal arm $i$ is committed, its exploration mean is at least that of $i^*$, so $\{J=i\}\subseteq\left\{m^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^m(X_{s,i}-\mu_i)-m^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^m(X_{s,i^*}-\mu^*)\ge\Delta_i\right\}$. The displayed sum has $2m$ mutually independent centered 1-sub-Gaussian terms: the $m$ terms from arm $i$ and the negatives of the $m$ terms from arm $i^*$. Negation preserves the MGF bound by applying [A1] at $-\lambda$. Apply [F5] to these deterministic reward-stack prefixes with threshold $m\Delta_i$ to obtain $\mathbb P(J=i)\le\exp(-m\Delta_i^2/4)$. For an optimal arm the theorem's summand has $\Delta_i=0$, so no event bound is needed. [given, A1, F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Substituting these bounds on $\mathbb P(J=i)$ for each suboptimal arm into step 1.1, and using $\Delta_i\ge0$ for every arm, gives $R_n\le m\sum_{i=1}^k\Delta_i+(n-mk)\sum_{i=1}^k\Delta_i\exp(-m\Delta_i^2/4)$. The term with $n-mk=0$ is zero when exploration uses the whole horizon. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

This is a local sharpening of the coefficient-16 expected-pull bound; the algorithm and confidence radius are unchanged.

## Statement references

[Lattimore and Szepesvári, *Bandit Algorithms*, Theorem 7.1](https://tor-lattimore.com/downloads/book/book.pdf): proves the coefficient-16 count estimate; the smaller coefficient is proved here.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite independent reward table, UCB rule, horizon and suboptimal arm in the Statement.

[F1] An arm has fixed mean $\mu_i$, gap $\Delta_i=\mu^*-\mu_i$, and its $s$ observations are the first $s$ entries of its independent stack. [[def-stochastic-bandit-and-pseudo-regret]]

[F2] All reward entries satisfy the centered 1-sub-Gaussian MGF condition. [[def-centered-subgaussian-reward]]

[F3] UCB first plays every arm once, then selects an index maximizer with index $\widehat\mu_{i,s}+\sqrt{2\log(1/\delta)/s}$ at count $s\ge1$. [[alg-upper-confidence-bound-bandit]]

[F4] For each fixed prefix of length $s$, both centered mean tails at threshold $x\ge0$ are at most $e^{-sx^2/2}$. [[lem-independent-subgaussian-prefix-tail]]

[F5] Finite unions have probability at most the sum of their probabilities, and event probabilities are at most one. [[lem-probability-measure-basic-identities]]

## Statement

Let $n,k$ be integers with $n\ge\max\{k,2\}$. In an $n$-round $k$-armed stochastic bandit, suppose all reward-stack entries are 1-sub-Gaussian. Run the upper-confidence-bound algorithm with $\delta=n^{-2}$. Its expected reward regret satisfies
$$
R_n\le 3\sum_{i=1}^k\Delta_i+\sum_{i:\Delta_i>0}\frac{16\log n}{\Delta_i},
$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm. This is an expected-regret bound, not a high-probability guarantee.

## Statement references

[[def-stochastic-bandit-and-pseudo-regret]]: the finite reward-stack model, gaps, and expected reward regret.

[[def-centered-subgaussian-reward]]: the exact mean-centred MGF condition for each reward entry.

[[alg-upper-confidence-bound-bandit]]: the UCB index and the finite-horizon schedule used by the theorem.

[[lem-ucb-suboptimal-arm-expected-pulls]]: the deterministic-prefix expected-pull bound for each suboptimal arm.

[[lem-finite-arm-regret-decomposes-into-expected-action-counts]]: expected regret is the gap-weighted sum of expected pull counts under the fixed conditional-mean law.

[Tor Lattimore and Csaba Szepesvári, *Bandit Algorithms*](https://tor-lattimore.com/downloads/book/book.pdf): Theorem 7.1 and proof, Chapter 7 §7.1, PDF pp. 114–117 / printed pp. 105–108.

[Sébastien Bubeck and Nicolò Cesa-Bianchi, *Regret Analysis of Stochastic and Nonstochastic Multi-armed Bandit Problems*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1204.5721): Theorem 2.1 and proof, Chapter 2 §2.2, PDF pp. 14–15 / printed pp. 11–12; its confidence schedule and constants differ.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integers $n,k$ with $n\ge\max\{k,2\}$, the finite reward-stack model with all entries 1-sub-Gaussian, and UCB run with $\delta=n^{-2}$.

[F1] The gaps are $\Delta_i=\mu^*-\mu_i\ge0$ and expected reward regret is $R_n=\mathbb E[n\mu^*-\sum_{t=1}^nY_t]$ ([[def-stochastic-bandit-and-pseudo-regret]]).

[A1] Each reward stack entry satisfies $\mathbb E[\exp(\lambda(X_{s,i}-\mu_i))]\le\exp(\lambda^2/2)$ for every real $\lambda$ ([[def-centered-subgaussian-reward]]).

[F2] The reward-stack model satisfies the fixed conditional-mean identity required by the regret-decomposition result ([[lem-bandit-reward-table-has-fixed-conditional-laws]]).

[F3] Under that identity, $R_n=\sum_{i=1}^k\Delta_i\mathbb E[T_i(n)]$ ([[lem-finite-arm-regret-decomposes-into-expected-action-counts]]).

[F4] For every $i$ with $\Delta_i>0$, $\mathbb E[T_i(n)]\le3+16\log(n)/\Delta_i^2$ ([[lem-ucb-suboptimal-arm-expected-pulls]]).

[F5] The algorithm uses the natural logarithm and $\log(n)>0$ for $n\ge2$ ([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]).

## Proof

1.1 By [F2], the conditional-mean hypothesis of [F3] holds for the observed rewards of the UCB policy. Therefore $R_n=\sum_{i=1}^k\Delta_i\mathbb E[T_i(n)]$. [given, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 If $\Delta_i=0$, its summand is zero. For every remaining arm, substitute [F4] into step 1.1 and distribute the nonnegative coefficient $\Delta_i$ to obtain $R_n\le\sum_{i:\Delta_i>0}(3\Delta_i+16\log n/\Delta_i)=3\sum_{i=1}^k\Delta_i+\sum_{i:\Delta_i>0}16\log n/\Delta_i$. This is the asserted expected-regret bound. [given, A1, F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The unchanged finite reward-stack bandit, horizon $n\ge\max\{k,2\}$, centered 1-sub-Gaussian entries, and UCB with $\delta=n^{-2}$ in the Statement.

[F10] A stochastic arm law is a probability measure on the real Borel space with finite first absolute moment, and its mean is the integral of the identity function ([[def-stochastic-bandit-and-pseudo-regret]]).

## Definition

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $c\in[0,+\infty]$. Define the scalar set function $c\mu$ by three disjoint branches:

$$ (c\mu)(E):=\begin{cases}0,&c=0,\\c\,\mu(E),&0<c<+\infty,\\0,&c=+\infty\text{ and }\mu(E)=0,\\+\infty,&c=+\infty\text{ and }\mu(E)>0.\end{cases}$$

Thus neither the zero branch nor the infinite branch forms the undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

For measures $(\mu_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ on the same measurable space and weights $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$, their **countable weighted sum** is the pointwise set function

$$\left(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}c_k\mu_k\right)(E):=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(c_k\mu_k)(E),$$

using [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]. Finite weighted sums are defined by the corresponding finite partial sum, with the empty weighted sum the zero set function. The fact that all these set functions are measures is [[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]].

## Statement

Let $(\mu_k)$ be measures on one measurable space and let $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$. Each scalar multiple $c_k\mu_k$, defined by the zero, finite-positive, and positive-infinity branches of [[def-nonnegative-weighted-sum-of-measures]], is a measure. Every finite or countable weighted sum $\sum_kc_k\mu_k$ is also a measure.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Measures $(\mu_k)$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ and coefficients $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$.

[L1] Scalar multiplication has separate $c=0$, $0<c<+\infty$, and $c=+\infty$ branches, and weighted sums are pointwise nonnegative extended sums ([[def-nonnegative-weighted-sum-of-measures]]).

[L2] For a nonnegative extended double sequence, the two iterated sums are equal ([[thm-tonelli-for-nonnegative-double-series]]).

[L3] A measure vanishes at the empty set and is countably additive on disjoint measurable sequences ([[def-measure]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $c=0$, the set function $c\mu$ is the zero measure. [given, L1, L3]

1.2 For $0<c<+\infty$, $(c\mu)(\varnothing)=0$; for disjoint $(E_j)$, multiplying the finite partial-sum identities by $c$ and taking their supremum gives $c\mu(\bigcup_jE_j)=\sum_jc\mu(E_j)$, whether the common value is finite or $+\infty$. [given, L1, L3, algebra]

1.3 For $c=+\infty$, a disjoint union has $\mu$-measure zero exactly when every member has $\mu$-measure zero: this follows directly from countable additivity and nonnegativity. Hence the infinite branch takes value $0$ on the union exactly when every term value is $0$, and otherwise both it and the series of term values are $+\infty$; this branch is a measure without forming $0\cdot(+\infty)$. [given, L1, L3]

2.1 Steps 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 prove that every scalar multiple $c_k\mu_k$ is a measure for all possible coefficients. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3]

3.1 Put $\nu(E)=\sum_k(c_k\mu_k)(E)$. Then $\nu(\varnothing)=0$. [given, L1, step 2.1]

3.2 If $(E_j)$ is disjoint, then step 2.1 and Tonelli give $\nu(\bigcup_jE_j)=\sum_k\sum_j(c_k\mu_k)(E_j)=\sum_j\sum_k(c_k\mu_k)(E_j)=\sum_j\nu(E_j)$. [step 2.1, L1, L2, L3]

4.1 Steps 3.1 and 3.2 prove that the countable weighted sum is a measure; the same proof for a finite index range, or zero coefficients thereafter, gives every finite weighted sum, including the empty zero measure. [step 3.1, step 3.2, L3] ∎

## Statement

Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals with $a_k \ge 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ be its partial sums and let
$S = \{\, s_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ be the range of $(s_n)$ ([[def-series]]).
Then:

1. $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing ([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and $s_n \ge 0$ for every
   $n$;
2. $\sum a_k$ converges **if and only if** $S$ is bounded above
   ([[def-bounded-set]]), and in that case
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;=\; \sup S ,$$
   so in particular $s_n \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k$ for every $n$;
3. if $S$ is not bounded above then $s_n \to +\infty$
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]) and $\sum a_k$ diverges.

This is the theorem that makes the nonnegative theory work: for terms of one
sign, convergence is a boundedness question and no candidate limit is ever
needed. Every comparison test on this page is an application of it.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A sequence $(a_k)$ of reals with $a_k \ge 0$ for every $k$, its partial sums $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$, and the range $S = \{s_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$ ([[def-series]], [[def-finite-sum]], [[def-sequence]]).

[L1] The recursion clause of the finite sum: $s_{n+1} = s_n + a_n$ ([[def-finite-sum]]).

[L2] Consecutive comparisons suffice for monotonicity: $(x_k)$ is nondecreasing if and only if $x_k \le x_{k+1}$ for every $k$; and a nondecreasing sequence is bounded below by its first term ([[def-monotone-sequence]]).

[L3] Monotonicity of finite sums: if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

[L4] A monotone sequence converges if and only if it is bounded, that is if and only if there is $M$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every $k$ ([[cor-monotone-converges-iff-bounded]], [[def-sequence]]).

[L5] A nondecreasing sequence bounded above converges to the supremum of its range, which exists by the least-upper-bound property ([[thm-monotone-convergence]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-bounded-set]]).

[L6] A nondecreasing sequence whose range is not bounded above diverges to $+\infty$ ([[lem-monotone-unbounded-diverges]], [[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For every $n$, $s_{n+1} - s_n = a_n \ge 0$, so $s_n \le s_{n+1}$ and $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing. [given, L1, L2]

1.2 For every $n$, $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, all terms being nonnegative. [given, L3]

2.1 Claim 1 is steps 1.1 and 1.2 together. [step 1.1, step 1.2]

2.2 Since $s_n \ge 0$ we have $|s_n| = s_n$, so $(s_n)$ is bounded in the sense of [L4] if and only if $S$ is bounded above. [step 1.2, L4]

3.1 By [L4] applied to the monotone sequence $(s_n)$, the series converges if and only if $(s_n)$ is bounded, hence if and only if $S$ is bounded above. [step 1.1, step 2.2, L4]

4.1 If $S$ is bounded above then $(s_n)$ converges to $\sup S$, so $\sum a_k$ converges with sum $\sup S$; and since $\sup S$ is an upper bound of $S$, $s_n \le \sup S$ for every $n$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, L5]

4.2 If $S$ is not bounded above then $s_n \to +\infty$, and by step 3.1 the series diverges. [step 1.1, step 3.1, L6]

5.1 The equivalence and the identification of the sum as the supremum together make claim 2, and the divergence statement is claim 3. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2] ∎

## Remarks

- **"Bounded" and "bounded above" coincide here, and only here.** The equivalence used in step 2.2 rests on $s_n \ge 0$, which rests on every term being nonnegative. For a series with terms of both signs the partial sums can be bounded above and still fail to converge, so nothing in this theorem survives the loss of the sign hypothesis. That failure is exhibited by [[cex-comparison-needs-nonnegativity]] on the companion page.

- **Claim 3 is a strictly stronger statement than "diverges".** Divergence alone permits oscillation ([[def-series]]); for nonnegative terms it cannot occur, and the partial sums necessarily run to $+\infty$. This is what licenses the phrase "the series diverges to $+\infty$" for nonnegative terms, and it is what the Abel-Dini theorem later on this page uses.

- **This criterion is the monotone convergence property, worn differently.** The proof above is monotone convergence for $\mathbb{R}$ applied to the nondecreasing sequence of partial sums, and nothing is lost going back the other way. Given a nondecreasing sequence $(x_n)$ of reals, put $y_n := x_n - x_0 \ge 0$ and let $a_0 := 0$, $a_{k+1} := y_{k+1} - y_k \ge 0$; then $s_{n+1} = y_n$ ([[def-series]]), the partial sums are bounded exactly when $(x_n)$ is bounded above, and claim 1 returns the convergence of $(y_n)$ and so of $(x_n)$. Testing boundedness of partial sums is therefore not a device special to series. Read in the vocabulary of [[def-completeness-properties]] it is the property (MCT), which in an arbitrary ordered field already forces the Archimedean property on its own ([[lem-mct-implies-archimedean]]) and with it the least-upper-bound property ([[lem-mct-implies-lub]]). The translation just given is carried out in $\mathbb{R}$, since [[def-series]] is stated for sequences of reals and this library defines no series over a general ordered field.

## Definition

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field ([[def-real-numbers]]) and
a **sequence of reals** is a function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-sequence]]), written $(a_k)$; recall that $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$.

**Partial sums.** Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals. Its **sequence of partial
sums** is

$$s_n \;:=\; \sum_{k < n} a_k \qquad (n \in \mathbb{N}),$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. In particular $s_0 = 0$, the empty sum, and
$s_{n+1} = s_n + a_n$ for every $n$, those being exactly the two recursion clauses
that define the finite sum. Note that $s_n$ is the sum of the $n$ terms
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$, so the index $n$ counts terms rather than naming the last
one.

**Convergence, the sum, divergence.** The **series** of $(a_k)$, written
$\sum a_k$, **converges** when the sequence $(s_n)$ of partial sums converges
([[def-real-limit]]), and then the **sum of the series** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;:=\; \lim_{n} s_n .$$

The series **diverges** when $(s_n)$ does not converge. A convergent sequence of
reals has exactly one limit ([[lem-limit-unique]]), so the displayed symbol names
a single real number and nothing further has to be checked for it to be
well defined.

**Series with a general starting index.** Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a$ be a
function on $\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : k \ge m \,\}$, which we call a **family from
$m$** and write $(a_k)_{k \ge m}$. The series

$$\sum_{k \ge m} a_k$$

is by definition the series of the sequence $b_j := a_{j + m}$,
$j \in \mathbb{N}$, which is a genuine sequence of reals; it converges exactly
when that series converges, and its sum is then written
$\sum_{k = m}^{\infty} a_k$. Its partial sums are

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k \;=\; \sum_{j < n-m} a_{m+j} \qquad (n \ge m),$$

in the notation of [[def-finite-sum]], the value at $n = m$ being the empty sum
$0$. A sequence on $\mathbb{N}$ is the case $m = 0$, and the two readings of
$\sum a_k$ agree there, since $b_j = a_j$.

**This clause is not a convenience.** Sequences in this library are functions on
$\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ ([[def-sequence]]), while many of the
classical series are built from expressions that are undefined at the index $0$:
$1/k$, $1/k^{p}$ and $|a_k|^{1/k}$ all require $k \ge 1$. Writing such a series as
$\sum_{k \ge 1} a_k$ names an honest object, whereas writing it as a sequence on
$\mathbb{N}$ would require a value at an index where the defining expression has
none. Every statement on this page says which starting index it uses.

**Tail series.** For $N \in \mathbb{N}$, the **$N$-th tail series** of
$\sum a_k$ is $\sum_{k \ge N} a_k$, that is the series of the $N$-th tail
$a^{(N)}$ of [[def-sequence]], whose terms are $a^{(N)}_j = a_{j+N}$. The
$0$-th tail series is the series itself.

## Remarks

- **"Diverges" here means "does not converge", and nothing more.** A divergent
  series may have partial sums that run away to $+\infty$, or to $-\infty$, or
  that oscillate without settling anywhere. The three behaviours are not
  distinguished by the word, and no statement on this page uses "diverges" to
  mean "the partial sums are unbounded" unless it says so.

- **The symbol $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k$ is defined only for a convergent
  series.** It denotes a real number, not a formal object, and it is illegitimate
  to write it down before convergence has been established. Where a proof needs
  to speak of the series without knowing whether it converges, it speaks of
  $(a_k)$ and of $(s_n)$.

- **Two indices, doing different work.** The index $k$ runs over the terms and is
  bound; the index $n$ runs over the partial sums and is the variable in which the
  limit is taken. Confusing them is the commonest slip in the subject, and it is
  the reason the definition above fixes $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ rather than
  $\sum_{k \le n} a_k$: with this choice the recursion $s_{n+1} = s_n + a_n$ is
  the one supplied by [[def-finite-sum]], with no shift anywhere.

## Definition

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

## Remarks

- **Why $0! = 1$ is not imported.** The empty-product convention of an arbitrary
  monoid is fixed in [[def-monoid-finite-product]], which comes later in the
  reading order, so citing it here would be a dependency pointing the wrong way.
  Taking $0! = 1$ as the base clause of the factorial's own recursion costs
  nothing and owes nothing, and clause (a) then records the agreement.

- **The library's other factorial.** [[lem-factorial-beats-geometric]], later in
  the reading order, works with a real-valued factorial defined as the product
  $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ in $\mathbb{R}$. Clause (b) says that this is exactly
  $\iota(n!)$, so the two agree and no second notion has been created. That
  pointer is orientation only.

- **Check every clause at $k = 0$ and at $k = n$.** The falling factorial is
  defined by two regimes, one for $k \le n$ and one beyond, and the recursion
  above covers both because the truncated difference is $0$ past the end. The
  two values that get used constantly are $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ and
  $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, and both are clause (d).

## Statement

For every real $z\le0$,
$$
\exp(z)\le1+z+\frac{z^2}{2}.
$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real number $z\le0$ and the real exponential function.

[F1] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]: $\exp(0)=1$.

[F2] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: the real exponential is $C^\infty$, with derivative $(\exp)'=\exp$.

[F3] [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]: $\exp$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

[F4] [[lem-mean-value-theorem-on-closed-interval]]: a function continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$ has $f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a)$ for some $c\in(a,b)$.

## Proof

1.1 If $z=0$, the claim is equality. For $z<0$, fix any $a<b\le0$ and set $g(t)=1+t-\exp(t)$. By [F2], $g'(t)=1-\exp(t)\ge0$ for $t\le0$, because [F3] and [F1] give $\exp(t)\le\exp(0)=1$. Applying [F4] to $g$ on $[a,b]$ shows $g(b)-g(a)=g'(c)(b-a)\ge0$, so $g$ is nondecreasing on $(-\infty,0]$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

2.1 Now $g(0)=0$, so step 1.1 gives $g(t)\le0$ for every $t\le0$. Set $f(t)=1+t+t^2/2-\exp(t)$; then $f'(t)=g(t)$. Applying [F4] on $[z,0]$ gives $f(0)-f(z)=g(c)(-z)\le0$. Since $f(0)=0$, $f(z)\ge0$, which is the required inequality. [given, F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $k,n\ge1$ be integers, let $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, and let
$$
\Delta_k=\left\{p\in[0,1]^k:\sum_{i=1}^k p_i=1\right\}.
$$
On a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, let $(\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^n$ be the discrete filtration generated by the complete histories through round $t$, with $\mathcal F_0$ trivial; a complete pre-action history records past reward vectors, actions, and observed rewards. A reward vector is either fixed in advance or a deterministic function of the complete pre-action history. Thus, at a finite horizon with finitely many arms, there are finitely many possible histories. Before action $A_t$ is drawn, the current reward vector $x_t=(x_{t,1},\ldots,x_{t,k})\in[0,1]^k$ and sampling distribution $P_t=(P_{t,1},\ldots,P_{t,k})\in\Delta_k$ are $\mathcal F_{t-1}$-measurable, and $P_{t,i}>0$ for every $i$. The finite-valued measurable action $A_t\in[k]$ has conditional law $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$. The learner observes only $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$ and sets
$$
Y_t=1-X_t,\qquad y_{t,i}=1-x_{t,i},\qquad \widehat Y_{t,i}=\frac{\mathbf 1\{A_t=i\}Y_t}{P_{t,i}},\qquad \widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}.
$$
The quantity $\widehat Y_{t,i}$ is the importance-weighted loss estimate for arm $i$, and $\widehat X_{t,i}$ is its corresponding reward estimate. A fixed reward sequence is the oblivious case; allowing $x_t$ to depend on the history available before $A_t$ is drawn gives the non-anticipating past-adaptive case. In either case the current reward vector is chosen before the current action. For finite horizons and finite action histories generated by such a fixed or deterministic history-dependent sequence, all these estimates are finite and integrable.

## Definition references

[[def-online-decision-protocol]]: the learner selects its round-$t$ action using prior history before round-$t$ feedback.

[[def-adversary-and-feedback-model]]: bandit feedback reveals only the played reward, and non-anticipating rewards are fixed before the current action.

[[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]: a measurable finite-valued action is a random element of $[k]$.

[[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]: the round-history sigma-algebras are increasing and record information available before each action.

[[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: conditional expectation is characterized by equality of integrals on every event in the conditioning sigma-algebra.

[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]: expectations of the finite integrable estimates are Lebesgue integrals on the probability space.

## Statement

In the bandit importance-weighted estimator definition, fix a round $t$ and arm $i$, and write $p=P_{t,i}>0$ and $y=y_{t,i}$. Then
$$
\mathbb E[\widehat Y_{t,i}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=y_{t,i},\qquad \mathbb E[\widehat Y_{t,i}^{2}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=\frac{y_{t,i}^2}{P_{t,i}}.
$$
With conditional variance defined by $\operatorname{Var}(Z\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=\mathbb E[(Z-\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}])^2\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]$, one also has
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat Y_{t,i}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=\frac{y_{t,i}^2(1-P_{t,i})}{P_{t,i}}.
$$

## Statement references

[[def-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator]]: the arm probabilities, observed loss, and importance-weighted loss estimate used here.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite arm set $[k]$, a pre-action history at round $t$, a reward vector $x_t\in[0,1]^k$, and a distribution $P_t\in\Delta_k$ with $P_{t,i}>0$.

[F1] [[def-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator]]: given the pre-action history, $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$, $Y_t=y_{t,A_t}$, and $\widehat Y_{t,i}=\mathbf1\{A_t=i\}Y_t/P_{t,i}$.

[F2] [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: a conditional-expectation version is measurable and integrable and has the same integral as the original variable on every event in the conditioning sigma-algebra.

[F3] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]: expectation of an integrable random variable is its finite Lebesgue integral.

[F4] [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]: $\mathcal F_{t-1}$ is the sigma-algebra of information available before the round-$t$ action.

## Proof

1.1 Fix a positive-probability atom $H$ of the finite pre-action history. On $H$, $y_{t,i}$ and $P_{t,i}$ are fixed. By [F1], $\mathbb P(H\cap\{A_t=i\})=P_{t,i}\mathbb P(H)$; the estimator is $y_{t,i}/P_{t,i}$ on that event and zero on the rest of $H$. Hence $\int_H\widehat Y_{t,i}\,d\mathbb P=y_{t,i}\mathbb P(H)$. The function with value $y_{t,i}$ on each history atom is measurable and integrable, and finite additivity gives the same integral identity on every event in $\mathcal F_{t-1}$. By [F2], it is a conditional-expectation version, proving $\mathbb E[\widehat Y_{t,i}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=y_{t,i}$. [F1, F2, F3, F4]

1.2 On the same atom $H$, $\widehat Y_{t,i}^{\,2}$ is $y_{t,i}^2/P_{t,i}^2$ on $H\cap\{A_t=i\}$ and zero otherwise. Thus $\int_H\widehat Y_{t,i}^{\,2}\,d\mathbb P=(y_{t,i}^2/P_{t,i}^2)P_{t,i}\mathbb P(H)=(y_{t,i}^2/P_{t,i})\mathbb P(H)$. Extending over the finite atoms and applying [F2] proves $\mathbb E[\widehat Y_{t,i}^{\,2}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=y_{t,i}^2/P_{t,i}$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 At a fixed history, the centered estimator has value $y_{t,i}(1-P_{t,i})/P_{t,i}$ with probability $P_{t,i}$ and value $-y_{t,i}$ with probability $1-P_{t,i}$, by step 1.1. Its conditional variance is therefore $P_{t,i}[y_{t,i}(1-P_{t,i})/P_{t,i}]^2+(1-P_{t,i})y_{t,i}^2=y_{t,i}^2(1-P_{t,i})/P_{t,i}$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $k>1$ and $n\ge1$ be integers, and let $\eta>0$. Use the finite-arm bandit protocol with rewards in $[0,1]$ and conditional sampling as specified in the bandit importance-weighted estimator definition. Initialize $\widehat S_{0,i}=0$ for each $i\in[k]$. For rounds $t=1,\ldots,n$, perform the following operations:

1. Set
   $$
   P_{t,i}=\frac{\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,i})}{\sum_{j=1}^k\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,j})},\qquad i\in[k].
   $$
2. Draw a measurable finite-valued action $A_t$ with conditional probabilities $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$, and observe only $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$.
3. Form the loss estimates $\widehat Y_{t,i}=\mathbf1\{A_t=i\}(1-X_t)/P_{t,i}$ and reward estimates $\widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}$ for every $i\in[k]$.
4. Update $\widehat S_{t,i}=\widehat S_{t-1,i}+\widehat X_{t,i}$ for every $i\in[k]$.

The output is $(P_t,A_t,X_t,\widehat X_t,\widehat Y_t)_{t=1}^n$ and $\widehat S_n$. These operations use exact real arithmetic. The procedure assumes a probability space carrying the stated measurable draws; it makes no probability-space construction claim. Normalizing the weights $\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,i})$ is the exponential-weights step used by Hedge.

[[alg-hedge]]: initialize equal weights, normalize exponentials, draw an action, and update after feedback.

[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]: the real exponential used in the unnormalized weights.

[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]: every exponential weight is positive.

[[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]: each sampled arm is a measurable finite-valued random element.

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$ and $k>1$ be integers. Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in[0,1]^k$ be a reward sequence fixed before the learner's random choices, and run Exp3 with learning rate
$$
\eta=\sqrt{\frac{2\log k}{nk}}.
$$
Here $\log$ is the natural logarithm. For the well-definedness, finite-horizon completion, and two weight identities below, one may instead take any learning rate $\eta>0$ and any reward sequence admitted by the algorithm: rewards in $[0,1]^k$ fixed in advance or deterministic functions of the complete pre-action history. These procedure properties do not require the tuned learning rate.
Assume the run is on a probability space carrying the measurable, finite-valued actions with the conditional probabilities specified by Exp3; no probability-space construction is asserted. Every normalizing denominator is finite and positive, all estimates and cumulative estimates are finite, and the procedure completes its $n$ rounds. For every $t\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ and $i\in[k]$,
$$
\widehat S_{t,i}=t-\sum_{s=1}^t\widehat Y_{s,i},
$$
where the sum is empty when $t=0$. Consequently, for every $t\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$,
$$
P_{t,i}=\frac{\exp(-\eta\sum_{s<t}\widehat Y_{s,i})}{\sum_{j=1}^k\exp(-\eta\sum_{s<t}\widehat Y_{s,j})},\qquad i\in[k].
$$
For the following regret guarantees, use the tuned learning rate displayed above. Write $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$ and define expected regret against the best fixed arm by
$$
R_n=\max_{i\in[k]}\sum_{t=1}^n x_{t,i}-\mathbb E\left[\sum_{t=1}^n X_t\right].
$$
Then
$$
R_n\le\sqrt{2nk\log k}.
$$

The same bound holds when each $x_t$ is a deterministic function of the complete history available before $A_t$ is drawn, provided $x_t\in[0,1]^k$. In that past-adaptive case define
$$
R_n^{\mathrm{past}}=\max_{i\in[k]}\mathbb E\left[\sum_{t=1}^n(x_{t,i}-X_t)\right],
$$
with the maximum outside the expectation; then $R_n^{\mathrm{past}}\le\sqrt{2nk\log k}$. This is an expected fixed-arm regret bound, not a high-probability bound, an expected in-hindsight maximum bound for random reward vectors, or a policy-regret bound for a reward rule that responds to the current action.

## Statement references

[[alg-exp3]]: the sampling distribution, loss estimate, reward estimate, and cumulative update.

[[def-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator]]: the bandit feedback and importance-weighted estimate conventions.

[[def-adversary-and-feedback-model]]: oblivious and non-anticipating timing, distinguished from current-action-reactive timing.

[[def-static-dynamic-and-strongly-adaptive-regret]]: fixed-comparator and expected-regret conventions.

[[def-natural-logarithm]]: the natural logarithm is the inverse of the exponential on positive reals.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite horizon $n\ge1$, $k>1$ arms, reward vectors in $[0,1]^k$, Exp3 with any $\eta>0$ for its procedure properties and with the displayed tuned rate for the regret guarantees, and its probability space of learner draws. In the optional past-adaptive case each reward vector is selected from the pre-action history.

[A1] [[def-adversary-and-feedback-model]]: an oblivious adversary fixes the entire reward sequence before learner randomization; a non-anticipating adversary selects the current vector from past history before the current action; a reactive adversary may select it after seeing that action.

[F1] [[alg-exp3]]: $P_{t,i}=\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,i})/\sum_j\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,j})$.

[F2] [[def-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator]]: $Y_t=1-X_t$, $y_{t,i}=1-x_{t,i}$, $\widehat Y_{t,i}=\mathbf1\{A_t=i\}Y_t/P_{t,i}$, and $\widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}$.

[F3] [[lem-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator-has-conditional-moments]]: $\mathbb E[\widehat Y_{t,i}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=y_{t,i}$ and $\mathbb E[\widehat Y_{t,i}^{2}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=y_{t,i}^2/P_{t,i}$.

[F4] [[lem-exp-negative-argument-second-order-upper-bound]]: $\exp(z)\le1+z+z^2/2$ for every real $z\le0$.

[F5] [[lem-exponential-dominates-one-plus-x]]: $1+u\le\exp(u)$ for every real $u$.

[F6] [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]: $\exp(u+v)=\exp(u)\exp(v)$ for all real $u,v$.

[F7] [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]: $\exp(u)>0$ and $\exp(-u)=1/\exp(u)$ for all real $u$.

[F8] [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]: the real exponential is strictly increasing.

[F9] [[def-natural-logarithm]]: for $q>0$, $\exp(\log q)=q$.

[F10] [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\log$ is strictly increasing.

[F11] [[def-online-decision-protocol]]: the learner chooses from prior history before current-round feedback.

[F12] [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]: $\mathcal F_{t-1}$ records the information available before the round-$t$ action.

[F13] [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: conditional expectation versions have the same integrals as the original variable over every event in the conditioning sigma-algebra.

[F14] [[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]: expectation is linear on integrable random variables and preserves almost-sure order.

[F15] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]: expectation of an integrable variable is its Lebesgue integral.

## Example

Take one round with two actions, rewards $(x_{1,1},x_{1,2})=(0,1)$, and sampling probabilities $(P_{1,1},P_{1,2})=(1/10,9/10)$. The first arm's loss is $1$, so its importance-weighted loss estimate is $10$ with probability $1/10$ and $0$ with probability $9/10$. Its mean is $1$, second moment is $10$, and variance is $9$. The corresponding reward estimate is $-9$ or $1$ with those respective probabilities, despite the true first-arm reward being $0$.

## Example references

[[def-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator]]: the loss estimate is the observed loss divided by the probability of selecting its arm.

[[lem-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator-has-conditional-moments]]: the conditional mean, second moment, and variance formulas.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** One round, two arms, fixed rewards $(0,1)$, and conditional arm probabilities $(1/10,9/10)$.

[F1] [[def-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator]]: $Y_1=1-X_1$ and $\widehat Y_{1,i}=\mathbf1\{A_1=i\}Y_1/P_{1,i}$, with $\widehat X_{1,i}=1-\widehat Y_{1,i}$.

[F2] [[lem-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator-has-conditional-moments]]: for loss $y_i$ and arm probability $p_i>0$, the conditional mean, second moment, and variance are $y_i$, $y_i^2/p_i$, and $y_i^2(1-p_i)/p_i$.

## Verification

1.1 The first-arm loss is $y_{1,1}=1$. On $A_1=1$, which has probability $1/10$, its estimate is $1/(1/10)=10$; on $A_1=2$, which has probability $9/10$, its estimate is zero. [given, F1]

1.2 By [F2] with $y=1$ and $p=1/10$, the mean is $1$, the second moment is $1/(1/10)=10$, and the variance is $1^2(1-1/10)/(1/10)=9$. [F2, algebra]

2.1 Since $\widehat X_{1,1}=1-\widehat Y_{1,1}$, its values are $-9$ and $1$ on the two events, respectively, so it can fall outside the true reward range $[0,1]$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Take one round with two arms, reward vector $(1,0)$, learning rate $\eta>0$, and uniform initial probabilities. Run full-information Hedge with $\epsilon=\eta$ on losses $(0,1)$; its next distribution is $(\exp(\eta)/(\exp(\eta)+1),1/(\exp(\eta)+1))$. After the first round, Exp3 has next distribution $(1/2,1/2)$ if it sampled arm 1 and $(\exp(\eta)/(\exp(\eta)+\exp(-\eta)),\exp(-\eta)/(\exp(\eta)+\exp(-\eta)))$ if it sampled arm 2. Both outcomes differ from the full-information distribution.

## Example references

[[alg-exp3]]: the estimated rewards and exponential probability update.

[[alg-hedge]]: full-information losses, equal initial weights, and the exponential loss update.

[[def-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator]]: the observed reward and loss-based estimator formulas.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** One round, two arms, reward vector $(1,0)$, Exp3 learning rate $\eta>0$, full-information Hedge learning rate $\epsilon=\eta$, uniform initial weights, and the two update rules.

[F1] [[alg-exp3]]: Exp3 samples proportionally to $\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,i})$ and updates $\widehat S_{t,i}=\widehat S_{t-1,i}+\widehat X_{t,i}$.

[F2] [[alg-hedge]]: Hedge initializes both weights at one, samples from their normalized values, then updates $W_{t+1,i}=W_{t,i}\exp(-\eta\ell_{t,i})$ after observing the entire loss vector.

[F3] [[def-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator]]: $\widehat Y_{t,i}=\mathbf1\{A_t=i\}(1-X_t)/P_{t,i}$ and $\widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}$.

[F4] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]: $\exp(0)=1$.

[F5] [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]: $\exp(z)>0$ and $\exp(-z)=1/\exp(z)$ for real $z$.

[F6] [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]: $\exp$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

## Verification

1.1 Since $\widehat S_{0,1}=\widehat S_{0,2}=0$, Exp3 starts with probabilities $(1/2,1/2)$. If $A_1=1$, then $Y_1=0$ and $\widehat X_{1,1}=\widehat X_{1,2}=1$, so the next Exp3 distribution is uniform. If $A_1=2$, then $Y_1=1$, $P_{1,2}=1/2$, and $(\widehat Y_{1,1},\widehat Y_{1,2})=(0,2)$; hence $\widehat X_1=(1,-1)$ and the next distribution is $(\exp(\eta)/(\exp(\eta)+\exp(-\eta)),\exp(-\eta)/(\exp(\eta)+\exp(-\eta)))$. [given, F1, F3]

1.2 Full-information Hedge uses $\epsilon=\eta$ and sees losses $(0,1)$, so its next weights are $(1,\exp(-\eta))$ and its normalized distribution is $(\exp(\eta)/(\exp(\eta)+1),1/(\exp(\eta)+1))$. [given, F2, F5, algebra]

2.1 By [F4] and [F6], $\exp(\eta)>1$, so Hedge's first probability exceeds $1/2$ and differs from Exp3's first probability after $A_1=1$. Also $\exp(2\eta)>\exp(\eta)$, so the odds ratio after $A_1=2$ is $\exp(2\eta)$ for Exp3 and $\exp(\eta)$ for Hedge; these distributions differ as well. [F4, F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix integers $n\ge1$, $k>1$, and $M>1$. Write $[r]=\{1,\ldots,r\}$ for a positive integer $r$, and let
$$
\Delta_k=\left\{p\in[0,1]^k:\sum_{i=1}^k p_i=1\right\},\qquad \mathcal E=\Delta_k^M.
$$
An oblivious contextual bandit instance consists of reward vectors $x_t\in[0,1]^k$ and advice matrices $E(t)\in\mathcal E$, for $t\in[n]$, all fixed before the learner's private randomization. The matrix $E(t)$ is revealed before the round-$t$ action; its row $E(t)_m=(E(t)_{m,1},\ldots,E(t)_{m,k})$ is expert $m$'s probability distribution over the $k$ actions. The expected reward of expert $m$ on round $t$ is $\langle E(t)_m,x_t\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^k E(t)_{m,i}x_{t,i}$.

At round $t$, the learner's pre-action history consists of its earlier actions and observed rewards. Given that history and the revealed advice, it selects a distribution $P_t\in\Delta_k$, draws a measurable finite-valued action $A_t\in[k]$ with conditional probabilities $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$, and observes only $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$. Here $\mathcal F_{t-1}$ is the sigma-algebra generated by the pre-action history. For every fixed expert sequence and reward sequence, the **expected regret against the best fixed expert** is
$$
R_n=\mathbb E\left[\max_{m\in[M]}\sum_{t=1}^n\langle E(t)_m,x_t\rangle-\sum_{t=1}^n X_t\right],
$$
where expectation is over the learner's action draws. The regret random variable is bounded, so this expectation is finite. This protocol makes no stochastic generalization claim and imposes no shared-structure condition on the experts; it does not cover advice or rewards selected in response to the learner's current action.

## Definition references

[[def-online-decision-protocol|Online decision timing]]: the learner chooses each action from its pre-action history before observing current-round feedback.

[[def-adversary-and-feedback-model|Oblivious adversary and bandit feedback]]: an oblivious sequence is fixed before learner randomization, and bandit feedback reveals only the played reward.

[[def-static-dynamic-and-strongly-adaptive-regret|Expected-regret convention]]: expected regret is the expectation of the specified measurable, integrable regret random variable.

[[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable|Measurable random actions]]: a finite action draw is a measurable random element of the discrete action set.

[[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space|Pre-action filtration]]: the sigma-algebras generated by successive histories form a filtration.

[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable|Expectation]]: the expectation of an integrable real random variable is its Lebesgue integral on the underlying probability space.

## Definition

Given integers $n\ge1$, $k>1$, $M>1$, a learning rate $\eta>0$, and an instance from the contextual bandit protocol with finite expert advice, initialize $Q_{1,m}=1/M$ for $m\in[M]$. For rounds $t=1,\ldots,n$, perform the following operations:

1. Receive the advice matrix $E(t)$, whose $m$th row is $E(t)_m\in\Delta_k$.

2. Form the action distribution
$$
P_{t,i}=\sum_{m=1}^M Q_{t,m}E(t)_{m,i},\qquad i\in[k].
$$

3. Draw a measurable action $A_t\in[k]$ with conditional probabilities $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$ and observe only $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$.

4. For each $i\in[k]$, form
$$
\widehat X_{t,i}=1-\frac{\mathbf 1\{A_t=i\}(1-X_t)}{P_{t,i}}.
$$
When $P_{t,i}=0$, the action $A_t=i$ is impossible; in this case the quotient term is defined to be zero on every possible outcome.

5. For each expert $m\in[M]$, form its estimated reward
$$
\widetilde X_{t,m}=\sum_{i=1}^kE(t)_{m,i}\widehat X_{t,i}
$$
and update the expert distribution by
$$
Q_{t+1,m}=\frac{Q_{t,m}\exp(\eta\widetilde X_{t,m})}{\sum_{r=1}^M Q_{t,r}\exp(\eta\widetilde X_{t,r})}.
$$

The output is $(Q_t,P_t,A_t,X_t,\widehat X_t,\widetilde X_t)_{t=1}^n$ and $Q_{n+1}$. All arithmetic is over exact real numbers, and the procedure assumes a probability space carrying the stated finite-valued measurable draws. This is the $\gamma=0$ Exp4 update; no regret guarantee for bounded-loss Hedge is part of the algorithm.

[[def-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator|Importance-weighted loss estimate]]: on coordinates with positive sampling probability, the quotient term is the standard estimate of loss $1-X_t$; the zero-probability convention is handled locally here.

[[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable|Measurable finite actions]]: each action draw is a measurable finite-valued random element.

[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e|Real exponential]]: the update uses the real exponential function.

## Statement

For the exact-real Exp4 procedure, take any integers $n\ge1$, $k>1$, $M>1$, any finite real learning rate $\eta>0$, and every oblivious reward/advice instance and supplied measurable draws in its input scope. At every round $t\in[n]$, the expert vector $Q_t$ is a probability vector with strictly positive entries, the action mixture $P_t$ belongs to $\Delta_k$, and $P_{t,i}=0$ implies $E(t)_{m,i}=0$ for every expert $m$. Every action and expert reward estimate is finite; the corresponding estimated losses $1-\widehat X_{t,i}$ and $1-\widetilde X_{t,m}$ are nonnegative. The normalizing denominator is finite and strictly positive, so $Q_{t+1}$ again has strictly positive entries summing to one. The procedure completes its $n$ prescribed rounds and returns all specified outputs.

The zero-quotient convention is retained exactly. These conclusions do not require positive sampling probability for every action, a uniform exploration mixture, a bound on the magnitude of an importance-weighted estimate, or a restriction on the learning rate beyond $\eta>0$.

## Statement references

[[alg-exp4]]

[[def-contextual-bandit-protocol]]

[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]

[Lattimore and Szepesvári, *Bandit Algorithms*, §18.3 Algorithm 11](https://tor-lattimore.com/downloads/book/book.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The full finite-horizon Exp4 inputs in the Statement, using exact real arithmetic and the probability space carrying the algorithm's prescribed finite-valued measurable action draws.

[F1] The input has $n\ge1$, $k>1$, $M>1$, fixed rewards $x_t\in[0,1]^k$, and advice rows with $E(t)_{m,i}\ge0$ and $\sum_i E(t)_{m,i}=1$. The observed reward is $X_t=x_{t,A_t}\in[0,1]$; action draws are measurable, and the pre-action history consists of earlier actions and observed rewards. [[def-contextual-bandit-protocol]]

[F2] The algorithm initializes $Q_{1,m}=1/M$, sets $P_{t,i}=\sum_mQ_{t,m}E(t)_{m,i}$, and uses $\widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat L_{t,i}$ with $\widehat L_{t,i}=\mathbf1\{A_t=i\}(1-X_t)/P_{t,i}$ when $P_{t,i}>0$, and $\widehat L_{t,i}=0$ when $P_{t,i}=0$. It sets $\widetilde X_{t,m}=\sum_iE(t)_{m,i}\widehat X_{t,i}$ and normalizes $Q_{t,m}\exp(\eta\widetilde X_{t,m})$ to obtain $Q_{t+1,m}$. [[alg-exp4]]

[F3] The real exponential is finite and strictly positive at every finite real argument. [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]

[F4] Inverses and products of positive real numbers are positive, and positive multiplication preserves inequalities. [[lem-of-inverse-positive]], [[lem-of-sign-rules]]

[F5] Induction propagates a base assertion preserved at each successor through the finite sequence of rounds. [[thm-induction-principle]]

## Proof

1.1 At the first round, $M>1$ makes $1/M$ a finite strictly positive real by [F4]. The $M$ entries sum to one, so $Q_1$ is a strictly positive probability vector. [given, F2, F4, base, algebra]

1.2 Assume $Q_t$ is a strictly positive probability vector at a round $t\le n$. Every $P_{t,i}$ is a finite nonnegative sum. Reordering its finite double sum gives $\sum_iP_{t,i}=\sum_mQ_{t,m}\sum_iE(t)_{m,i}=\sum_mQ_{t,m}=1$. Hence each $P_{t,i}\in[0,1]$ and $P_t\in\Delta_k$. If $P_{t,i}=0$, every term $Q_{t,m}E(t)_{m,i}$ in this nonnegative sum is zero, and strict positivity of $Q_{t,m}$ forces $E(t)_{m,i}=0$ for every $m$. Thus unsupported actions carry no expert advice. [F1, F2, F4, IH, algebra]

2.1 Fix the round's action. Since $0\le X_t\le1$, a supported coordinate has finite nonnegative $\widehat L_{t,i}$ by [F4], while an unsupported coordinate has the defined value zero. Thus every $\widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat L_{t,i}$ is finite, with no division by zero. The finite sum defining $\widetilde X_{t,m}$ is also finite. As each advice row sums to one, $\widetilde L_{t,m}:=1-\widetilde X_{t,m}=\sum_iE(t)_{m,i}\widehat L_{t,i}\ge0$. The reasoning uses the zero convention even on null outcomes, so no pointwise undefined quotient is hidden behind a probability-zero claim. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By step 2.1, $\eta\widetilde X_{t,m}$ is a finite real number for every expert. By [F3], every weight $w_m=Q_{t,m}\exp(\eta\widetilde X_{t,m})$ is finite and strictly positive. Since $M$ is finite and nonzero, $Z_t=\sum_mw_m$ is finite and strictly positive. Therefore every $Q_{t+1,m}=w_m/Z_t$ is finite and strictly positive by [F4], and their sum is one. This is the induction step. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, IH, algebra]

4.1 By [F5], all stated invariants and finite estimates hold through round $n$, including $Q_{n+1}$. For fixed inputs, $Q_t$ and $P_t$ are functions of the finite past action sequence, and all other round records are functions of that sequence and the current action. The finite measurable action-history partitions therefore make the states and records measurable with finite ranges; in particular $P_t$ is pre-action measurable. There is at least one supported arm at each round because $\sum_iP_{t,i}=1$, and the algorithm's probability space supplies its measurable draw; no sampler construction is being assumed beyond the input contract. Each round performs only finite sums and the prescribed finite evaluations and draw. After exactly $n$ rounds the loop ends and returns $(Q_t,P_t,A_t,X_t,\widehat X_t,\widetilde X_t)_{t=1}^n$ and $Q_{n+1}$. This proves well-definedness and finite-horizon completion without any extra exploration or learning-rate hypothesis. [given, F1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, discharge-induction] ∎

## Statement

In Exp4, at every round $t\in[n]$ and for every expert $m\in[M]$, the expert's estimated reward satisfies
$$
\mathbb E[\widetilde X_{t,m}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=\langle E(t)_m,x_t\rangle.
$$
The assertion includes rounds where some actions have zero sampling probability; no componentwise unbiasedness claim is made for an unsupported action.

## Statement references

[[alg-exp4|Exp4 estimates and zero-probability convention]]: the estimated action rewards and expert rewards are defined in the algorithm.

[[lem-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator-has-conditional-moments|Conditional importance-weighted loss mean]]: on an arm with positive sampling probability, the estimated loss has conditional mean equal to its true loss.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A fixed oblivious instance with $n\ge1$, $k>1$, $M>1$, the Exp4 algorithm, and a round $t$.

[F1] [[alg-exp4]]: $P_{t,i}=\sum_{r=1}^M Q_{t,r}E(t)_{r,i}$, every $Q_{t,r}>0$, $\widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}$, and the quotient in $\widehat Y_{t,i}$ is set to zero when $P_{t,i}=0$.

[F2] [[def-contextual-bandit-protocol]]: $x_t$ and $E(t)$ are fixed before the learner's action, each advice row is a probability vector, and $\mathcal F_{t-1}$ records the pre-action history.

[F3] [[def-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator]]: for $P_{t,i}>0$, $\widehat Y_{t,i}=\mathbf1\{A_t=i\}(1-X_t)/P_{t,i}$ is the loss estimate for true loss $1-x_{t,i}$.

[F4] [[lem-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator-has-conditional-moments]]: when $P_{t,i}>0$, $\mathbb E[\widehat Y_{t,i}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=1-x_{t,i}$.

[F5] [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: conditional expectation is characterized by its integrals on pre-action history events; with a finite action set, its value on each positive-probability history is the finite conditional sum over actions.

## Proof

1.1 Fix a positive-probability pre-action history. On it, $Q_t$ and $E(t)$ are fixed. If $P_{t,i}=0$, then $0=\sum_r Q_{t,r}E(t)_{r,i}$ is a sum of nonnegative terms and every $Q_{t,r}>0$; hence $E(t)_{r,i}=0$ for every expert $r$. Such a coordinate contributes nothing to any expert reward estimate. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 If $P_{t,i}>0$, [F3] and [F4] give $\mathbb E[\widehat Y_{t,i}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=1-x_{t,i}$. For fixed expert $m$, its row sums to one, so $\widetilde X_{t,m}=1-\sum_i E(t)_{m,i}\widehat Y_{t,i}$. Distributing the finite conditional sum over the finite action set and using step 1.1 for unsupported coordinates yields $\mathbb E[\widetilde X_{t,m}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=1-\sum_{i:P_{t,i}>0}E(t)_{m,i}(1-x_{t,i})=\sum_{i=1}^kE(t)_{m,i}x_{t,i}$. The last equality uses that each row sums to one and the omitted coefficients are zero by step 1.1. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
