## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and let $H\in M_d(\mathbb R)$,
the square-matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]],
be symmetric positive definite in the sense of
[[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]]. Let $\lambda_d$ denote
the Lebesgue measure of
[[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]. Interpret the
displayed integral as the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\exp\!\left(-\frac12 u^{\mathsf T}Hu\right)\,d\lambda_d(u) =\frac{(2\pi)^{d/2}}{\sqrt{\det H}}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, an integer $d\ge1$, and a real symmetric positive-definite matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb R)$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

[F1] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the standard inner product is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{j<d}x_jy_j$, with norm $\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$.

[F2] [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] defines self-adjointness by $T=T^*$, and [[prop-self-adjoint-and-normal-matrix-criteria-in-orthonormal-bases]] says a real symmetric matrix in an orthonormal basis represents a self-adjoint endomorphism.

[F3] [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]: a self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F4] [[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]] defines real positive definiteness by symmetry and $v^{\mathsf T}Hv>0$ for every nonzero $v$; [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]] supplies a factorization $H=LL^{\mathsf T}$ with $L$ lower triangular and positive diagonal.

[F5] [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]], [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]], [[thm-determinant-of-transpose]], and [[thm-determinant-of-a-triangular-matrix]]: the determinant is defined by the Leibniz formula, determinants multiply, are unchanged by transpose, and a triangular determinant is the product of its diagonal entries.

[F6] [[thm-of-square-roots]]: every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root.

[F7] [[thm-gaussian-integral]]: $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi$.

[F8] [[thm-substitution-for-improper-integrals]]: a monotone differentiable surjection between intervals carries a convergent improper integral to the corresponding transformed integral when the proper substitution hypotheses hold on compact truncations.

[F9] [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]] and [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]: under Countable Choice, $\lambda_k$ is a measure and every bounded box is measurable with its volume; the boxes $[-m,m]^k$ therefore give a countable finite-measure cover of $\mathbb R^k$.

[F10] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: for nonnegative product-measurable functions on sigma-finite measure spaces, the product and iterated integrals agree.

[F11] [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]: under Countable Choice, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism transforms a nonnegative Lebesgue integral by the absolute Jacobian determinant.

[F12] [[thm-real-square-matrix-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]: a real square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.

[F13] [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]: matrix products are the usual finite coordinate sums and $I$ is the identity matrix.

[F14] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]], [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]], [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], and [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]: the Euclidean norm is continuous for the Euclidean metric, so $z\mapsto e^{-\|z\|_2^2/2}$ is continuous on each $\mathbb R^k$, hence Borel and Lebesgue measurable under Countable Choice; on $\mathbb R^k\times\mathbb R$, the product $e^{-\|z\|_2^2/2}e^{-t^2/2}$ is measurable for the product sigma-algebra because the coordinate projections are measurable by the measurable-rectangle definition and products of measurable functions are measurable.

[F15] [[thm-euclidean-lebesgue-measure-is-the-completion-of-the-product-of-lebesgue-measures]]: under the canonical identification $\mathbb R^{k+1}=\mathbb R^k\times\mathbb R$, $\lambda_{k+1}$ is the completion of $\lambda_k\times\lambda_1$, so the measures agree on product-measurable sets.

[F16] [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]] and [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]: the integral of a nonnegative simple function is the sum of its coefficients times the measures of its level sets, and the nonnegative integral is the supremum over simple minorants.

[F17] [[thm-nonnegative-measurable-functions-admit-increasing-simple-approximations]] and [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]: an increasing simple approximation to a nonnegative product-measurable function has the same simple integrals under $\lambda_{k+1}$ and $\lambda_k\times\lambda_1$ by [F15]–[F16]; monotone convergence therefore makes its two nonnegative integrals equal.

[F18] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]] and [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]]: under Countable Choice, a continuous function on $[-m,m]$, $m\ge1$, is bounded and Riemann integrable, and its Riemann and Lebesgue integrals agree.

## Proof

1.1 By [F2], the symmetric matrix $H$ represents a self-adjoint endomorphism of $\mathbb R^d$. By [F3], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $q_1,\ldots,q_d$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$. Positive definiteness [F4] gives $\lambda_j\|q_j\|_2^2=q_j^{\mathsf T}Hq_j>0$, so each $\lambda_j>0$. Writing $Q$ for the matrix with these columns and $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)$, we have $H=Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf T}$ and $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I$ by orthonormality. By the Leibniz definition of determinant in [F5], $\det I=1$; multiplicativity and transpose invariance then give $(\det Q)^2=1$. Also $\det\Lambda=\prod_j\lambda_j>0$ by [F5], hence $\det H=(\det Q)^2\det\Lambda=\prod_j\lambda_j>0$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F13, algebra, choose]

1.2 The substitution $x=\sqrt2\,t$ in [F8], followed by [F7], gives the improper Riemann value $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-x^2/2}\,dx=\sqrt{2\pi}$. On each $[-m,m]$, $m\ge1$, the continuous integrand has equal Riemann and Lebesgue integrals by [F14] and [F18]. The nonnegative measurable functions $e^{-x^2/2}\mathbf1_{[-m,m]}(x)$ increase to $e^{-x^2/2}$ on $\mathbb R$, so monotone convergence [F17] identifies $G_1:=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-x^2/2}\,d\lambda_1(x)$ with the limit of these proper integrals, namely $\sqrt{2\pi}$. [A1, F7, F8, F14, F17, F18, algebra]

2.1 By [F4], choose a lower-triangular $L$ with positive diagonal such that $H=LL^{\mathsf T}$. Then [F5] gives $\det H=(\det L)^2$ and $\det L>0$, so [F6] identifies $\sqrt{\det H}=\det L$. Since $\det L>0$, [F12] also shows that $L$ is invertible. [step 1.1, F4, F5, F6, F12, F13, algebra, choose]

2.2 For $k\ge1$ put $G_k:=\int_{\mathbb R^k}e^{-\|z\|_2^2/2}\,d\lambda_k(z)$. For each $k$, the spaces $\mathbb R^k$ and $\mathbb R$ are sigma-finite by [F9], and [F14] makes the product integrand product-measurable. By [F15]–[F17], its integral under $\lambda_{k+1}$ equals its integral under $\lambda_k\times\lambda_1$; Tonelli [F10] then gives $G_{k+1}=G_kG_1$. Starting at [step 1.2], induction yields $G_d=(2\pi)^{d/2}$. [A1, step 1.2, F1, F9, F10, F14, F15, F16, F17, ih, discharge-induction]

3.1 The linear map $T(u)=L^{\mathsf T}u$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^d$ by step 2.1, with Jacobian determinant $\det(L^{\mathsf T})=\det L>0$ by [F5]. Since $u^{\mathsf T}Hu=\|L^{\mathsf T}u\|_2^2$, [F11] gives $G_d=\det L\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-u^{\mathsf T}Hu/2}\,d\lambda_d(u)$. [A1, F1, F4, F5, F11, F13, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

## Definition

**Inputs and admissibility.** Take the finite-dimensional linear contextual bandit model and a confidence level $\delta\in(0,1)$. At each round, the nonempty available action set is finite and ordered with its feature vectors, or the available feature set is compact with a supplied attained measurable predictable maximizer for the score below. In the finite case evaluate the score for each action's feature and resolve ties by the first action. All model assumptions, including $\lambda>0$, the feature and parameter bounds, pre-reward information, and the conditional noise bound, are in force.

**Outputs.** Before each reward is observed, output the selected feature $A_t$; after the reward $X_t$ is observed, record it. At the horizon return the online sequence $(A_t,X_t)_{t=1}^n$ and terminal state $(V_n,b_n,\widehat\theta_n)$.

Initialize $V_0=\lambda I_d$, $b_0=0$, $\widehat\theta_0=0$, $W_0=\lambda^{-1}I_d$, and $D_0=\lambda^d$. At each round $t=1,\ldots,n$, compute

$$\rho_t=\sqrt\lambda\,m_2+\sqrt{2\log(1/\delta)+\log(D_{t-1}/D_0)},\qquad \beta_t=\max\{1,\rho_t^2\},$$

Next select an available feature vector

$$A_t\in\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal A_t}\left\{\langle\widehat\theta_{t-1},a\rangle+\sqrt{\beta_t}\,\sqrt{a^{\mathsf T}W_{t-1}a}\right\}.$$

For a finite ordered action set, evaluate every action's score and take the first maximizing action's feature; for a compact feature set, call the supplied selector once. After observing reward $X_t$, update

$$V_t=V_{t-1}+A_tA_t^{\mathsf T},\qquad b_t=b_{t-1}+A_tX_t.$$

Then compute the updated matrix state $W_t,D_t$ from $V_t$ by the following exact row procedure. Form the augmented matrix $M=[V_t\mid I_d]$, set $s=1$ and $D=1$, and for $k=0,\ldots,d-1$ choose the least row index $i\ge k$ whose current left-block entry $M_{ik}$ is nonzero. If no such row exists, return failure. If $i\ne k$, swap rows $i$ and $k$ and replace $s$ by $-s$. Set $p_k=M_{kk}$, replace $D$ by $Dp_k$, divide row $k$ by $p_k$, and for every $j\ne k$ set $\operatorname{row}_j\leftarrow\operatorname{row}_j-M_{jk}\operatorname{row}_k$. After the loop set $W_t$ to the right block and $D_t=sD$, and set $\widehat\theta_t=W_tb_t$. The failure branch is included in the procedure but is unreachable under the model because every $V_t$ is positive definite. For a compact feature set the supplied selector must return an attained maximizing feature measurably from pre-reward information.

## Definition references

[[def-linear-contextual-bandit-model]]: the context/feature map, conditional reward model, filtration, norm bound, and sample-sum ridge notation.

[[lem-linucb-ridge-information-matrix]]: the matrices $V_t$ are positive definite, invertible, and have positive determinant.

[[lem-linucb-ridge-estimates-are-measurable]]: the ridge estimate, information matrix, and response sum are measurable from the available data.

[Tor Lattimore and Csaba Szepesvári, *Bandit Algorithms*, §19.2 and §20.1](https://tor-lattimore.com/downloads/book/book.pdf)

## Statement

Assume AC and Countable Choice and the finite-dimensional linear contextual bandit model. For $\delta\in(0,1)$ and $1\le t\le n$, set

$$\rho_t=\sqrt\lambda\,m_2+\sqrt{2\log(1/\delta)+\log\!\left(\frac{\det V_{t-1}}{\lambda^d}\right)},\qquad C_t=\left\{\theta\in\mathbb R^d:\|\theta-\widehat\theta_{t-1}\|_{V_{t-1}}^2\le\rho_t^2\right\}.$$

Then

$$\mathbb P\{\theta^*\in C_t\text{ for every }1\le t\le n\}\ge1-\delta.$$

## Statement references

[Tor Lattimore and Csaba Szepesvári, *Bandit Algorithms*, Theorems 20.4–20.5](https://tor-lattimore.com/downloads/book/book.pdf)

[Abbasi-Yadkori, Pál, and Szepesvári, Theorem 3 and Corollary 10](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.2670)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, Countable Choice, the model's deterministic $\theta^*$ with $\|\theta^*\|_2\le m_2$, predictable feature vectors, reward equation, and conditional MGF bound.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: conditional-expectation versions exist under the supplied AC branch; the optional-sampling interface assumes AC.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]]: the Gaussian-integral supplier assumes Countable Choice.

[F1] [[def-linear-contextual-bandit-model]]: $X_t=\langle\theta^*,A_t\rangle+\eta_t$, $b_t=\sum_{s\le t}A_sX_s$, $V_t=\lambda I+\sum_{s\le t}A_sA_s^{\mathsf T}$, and $\|\theta^*\|_2\le m_2$.

[F2] [[lem-linucb-ridge-information-matrix]]: each $V_t$ is symmetric positive definite, $\det(V_t)\ge\lambda^d>0$, and $x^{\mathsf T}V_t^{-1}x\le\lambda^{-1}\|x\|_2^2$.

[F3] [[lem-linucb-gaussian-mixture-supermartingale]]: $Z_s=\sqrt{\det(V_0)/\det(V_s)}\exp(\frac12S_s^{\mathsf T}V_s^{-1}S_s)$ is a nonnegative integrable supermartingale with $Z_0=1$.

[F4] [[thm-optional-sampling-for-bounded-stopping-times]]: for an integrable supermartingale and stopping times $\sigma\le\tau$ bounded by a deterministic integer, $\mathbb E[Z_\tau]\le\mathbb E[Z_\sigma]$.

[F5] [[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]]: if $Y\ge0$ and $a>0$, then $\mathbb P(Y\ge a)\le\mathbb E[Y]/a$.

[F6] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-inner-product-norm]], and [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]: a symmetric positive-definite bilinear form is a real inner product; its induced norm satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz and the triangle inequality.

[F7] [[thm-determinant-of-a-triangular-matrix]]: $\det(\lambda I_d)=\lambda^d$ for $\lambda>0$.

[F8] [[lem-linucb-ridge-estimates-are-measurable]]: $V_t$, $\det(V_t)$, $b_t$, and $\widehat\theta_t$ are measurable through time $t+1$, so the confidence-ellipsoid events and radii are measurable.

[F9] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\log$ is defined on positive reals, continuous, and strictly increasing there.

[F10] [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]: finite sums and products of real-valued measurable functions are measurable.

[F11] [[def-sigma-algebra]]: a sigma-algebra is closed under complements and countable unions, so finite intersections follow by De Morgan's law.

## Proof

1.1 Since $V_0=\lambda I_d$ is diagonal, [F7] gives $\det V_0=\lambda^d>0$. On $\mathcal H_s=\mathcal F_{s+1}$, define $\sigma$ as the first $s\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ with $Z_s\ge1/\delta$, and set $\sigma=n$ if there is no such $s$. For $k<n$, $\{\sigma\le k\}=\bigcup_{s=0}^k\{Z_s\ge1/\delta\}\in\mathcal H_k$, while $\{\sigma\le n\}=\Omega$. Hence $\sigma$ is a stopping time bounded by $n$. [F1, F3, F7, construct]

1.2 For each $0\le s<n$, the model reward equation gives $b_s=G_s\theta^*+S_s=(V_s-\lambda I_d)\theta^*+S_s$. Therefore $$\widehat\theta_s-\theta^*=V_s^{-1}S_s-\lambda V_s^{-1}\theta^*.$$ [F1, algebra]

1.3 For fixed $s$, define $\langle x,y\rangle_{V_s}=x^{\mathsf T}V_sy$. By [F2] this form is symmetric and positive definite, so [F6] gives its induced norm triangle inequality. Also $\|V_s^{-1}S_s\|_{V_s}^2=S_s^{\mathsf T}V_s^{-1}S_s$ and $$\|\lambda V_s^{-1}\theta^*\|_{V_s}^2=\lambda^2(\theta^*)^{\mathsf T}V_s^{-1}\theta^*\le\lambda\|\theta^*\|_2^2\le\lambda m_2^2.$$ [F1, F2, F6, algebra]

2.1 By [F4], $\mathbb E[Z_\sigma]\le\mathbb E[Z_0]=1$. On the event that some $Z_s$ crosses $1/\delta$ by time $n$, the definition of $\sigma$ gives $Z_\sigma\ge1/\delta$. Thus [F5] yields $\mathbb P\{\exists s\le n:Z_s\ge1/\delta\}\le\delta$. [step 1.1, A1, A2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

3.1 Outside the crossing event bounded in step 2.1, every $0\le s\le n$ has $Z_s<1/\delta$. Taking logarithms in [F3]'s formula and using $\det V_0=\lambda^d$ from step 1.1 gives $$S_s^{\mathsf T}V_s^{-1}S_s<2\log(1/\delta)+\log\!\left(\frac{\det V_s}{\lambda^d}\right).$$ All logarithm arguments are positive by [F2]. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, F3, F9, algebra]

4.1 Apply the triangle inequality from step 1.3 to step 1.2, then use step 3.1. For $t=s+1$ this yields $$\|\widehat\theta_{t-1}-\theta^*\|_{V_{t-1}}\le\sqrt{S_{t-1}^{\mathsf T}V_{t-1}^{-1}S_{t-1}}+\sqrt\lambda m_2\le\rho_t.$$ The radius $\rho_t$ is measurable: its determinant input is measurable by [F8], the logarithm is continuous by [F9], and $x\mapsto\sqrt{x}$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ since $|\sqrt{x}-\sqrt y|^2\le|x-y|$ there; the radicand is nonnegative by [F2] and $\delta\in(0,1)$. By [F8] and [F10], the quadratic form defining $C_t$ is measurable. The finite intersection of these events is measurable by [F11], so $\{\theta^*\in C_t\text{ for every }1\le t\le n\}$ is measurable. Its probability is at least $1-\delta$ by step 2.1. [step 3.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, F1, F2, F8, F9, F10, F11, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. If $M$ is a martingale and $\sigma\le\tau$ are stopping times bounded by a deterministic $N$, then
$$\mathbb E[M_\tau\mid\mathcal F_\sigma]=M_\sigma\quad\text{a.s.},$$
so $\mathbb EM_\tau=\mathbb EM_\sigma$. For a submartingale $X$ the conditional and expectation inequalities point upward; for a supermartingale they point downward.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses, objects, and conventions in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-sigma-algebra-at-a-stopping-time]] gives the events usable in conditional testing.

[F2] [[lem-stopped-random-variable-is-measurable-at-the-stopping-time]] gives the required measurability of stopped values.

[F3] [[thm-bounded-predictable-transforms-preserve-martingales]] gives zero expected martingale transforms. [[cor-nonnegative-predictable-transforms-preserve-submartingale-gains]] gives the upward sign for submartingales and nonnegative holdings; applying it to $-X$ gives the downward sign for supermartingales.

[F4] [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]] identifies a conditional expectation from all event integrals.

[F5] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] supplies conditional-expectation representatives.

## Proof

1.1 Put $H_k=1_{\{\sigma<k\le\tau\}}$ for $1\le k\le N$. Both $\{\sigma<k\}=\{\sigma\le k-1\}$ and $\{\tau\ge k\}$ lie in $\mathcal F_{k-1}$, so $H$ is nonnegative, bounded, and predictable. On the probability-one event $\{\sigma\le\tau\le N\}$, the finite pathwise telescope is $$X_\tau-X_\sigma=\sum_{k=1}^NH_k(X_k-X_{k-1}).$$ The integral identities below use this almost-sure equality; no equality is asserted on a null outcome with $\tau>N$. [F1]

2.1 Fix $A\in\mathcal F_\sigma$. On $\{\sigma\ge k\}$, $H_k=0$; hence $$1_AH_k=1_{A\cap\{\sigma\le k-1\}}H_k,$$ and the first factor on the right is $\mathcal F_{k-1}$-measurable by F1. Thus $1_AH$ is another bounded nonnegative predictable process. [F1, step 1.1]

3.1 Apply F3's one-step conditional calculation and sum: for a submartingale, $$\int_A(X_\tau-X_\sigma)\,dP\ge0;$$ for a martingale equality holds, and for a supermartingale the inequality reverses. Almost-sure boundedness identifies every stopped value almost surely with a finite sum of integrable variables, while F2 gives $\mathcal F_\sigma$-measurability of $X_\sigma$. F4 therefore identifies the stated conditional relation. Taking $A=\Omega$ gives the expectation relation. AC has exactly the role in F5. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Definition

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

## Definition

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

## Statement

Assume AC and Countable Choice, the finite-dimensional linear contextual bandit model, and LinUCB with $\beta_t=\max\{1,\rho_t^2\}$ as defined in the algorithm. Suppose also that for every round $t$,

$$\sup_{a,b\in\mathcal A_t}\langle\theta^*,a-b\rangle\le1.$$

Define the random pseudo-regret by

$$\widehat R_n:=\sum_{t=1}^n\left(\max_{a\in\mathcal A_t}\langle\theta^*,a\rangle-\langle\theta^*,A_t\rangle\right).$$

Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$,

$$\widehat R_n\le\sqrt{8n\beta_n\log\!\left(\frac{\det V_n}{\det V_0}\right)}\le\sqrt{8dn\beta_n\log\!\left(1+\frac{nL^2}{d\lambda}\right)}.$$

**Algorithm properties.** For every admissible model input, the algorithm also completes exactly $n$ rounds and outputs $(A_t,X_t)_{t=1}^n$ and $(V_n,b_n,\widehat\theta_n)$. Count exact real arithmetic operations, comparisons, square roots, and logarithms with unit cost, and exclude generation of contexts, features, and rewards. Let $F$ be the rounds with finite action sets and let $m_t$ be the number of available actions at round $t\in F$; let $K$ be the compact-feature rounds. The procedure makes exactly $|K|$ calls to the supplied maximizing selector and uses $O(nd^3+d^2\sum_{t\in F}m_t)$ operations apart from selector costs.

## Statement references

[Tor Lattimore and Csaba Szepesvári, *Bandit Algorithms*, §19.3, Theorem 19.2](https://tor-lattimore.com/downloads/book/book.pdf)

[Abbasi-Yadkori, Pál, and Szepesvári, §5.1, Theorem 13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.2670)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, Countable Choice, the bandit model and LinUCB algorithm, and the per-round optimal-mean range bound in the Statement.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: the confidence supplier uses AC for conditional-expectation classes and bounded optional sampling.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]]: the confidence supplier uses Countable Choice for its Gaussian integral.

[F1] [[def-linear-contextual-bandit-model]]: the model's fixed $\theta^*$, feature bounds $\|a\|_2\le L$, information matrices $V_t$, and sample-sum ridge estimates.

[F2] [[alg-linucb]]: $A_t$ maximizes $U_t(a)=\langle\widehat\theta_{t-1},a\rangle+\sqrt{\beta_t}\sqrt{a^{\mathsf T}W_{t-1}a}$ and $\beta_t=\max\{1,\rho_t^2\}$.

[F3] [[thm-self-normalized-linear-confidence-ellipsoid]]: with probability at least $1-\delta$, the true parameter is in the ellipsoid of radius $\rho_t$ about $\widehat\theta_{t-1}$ for every round in the horizon.

[F4] [[lem-linucb-elliptical-potential]]: if $u_t=\|A_t\|_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}^2$, then $\sum_t\min\{1,u_t\}\le2\log(\det V_n/\det V_0)$ and $\det V_t/\det V_{t-1}=1+u_t\ge1$.

[F5] [[lem-linucb-trace-determinant-bound]]: $\log(\det V_n/\det V_0)\le d\log(1+nL^2/(d\lambda))$.

[F6] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$ in every real inner-product space; Cauchy–Schwarz also applies to the Euclidean inner product on $\mathbb R^n$.

[F7] [[lem-linucb-ridge-information-matrix]]: each $V_t$ is symmetric positive definite, so $\langle x,y\rangle_{V_t}:=x^{\mathsf T}V_ty$ is a real inner product and $V_t^{-1}$ is positive definite.

[F8] [[alg-linucb]]: the procedure initializes $W_0,D_0$, executes the stated finite loop, uses row swaps, nonzero row scalings, and row additions on the augmented matrix to construct $W_t,D_t$, and returns the specified online and terminal outputs. [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]] gives $\det(I_d)=1$ and $\det(\lambda I_d)=\lambda^d$ by its Leibniz formula; [[thm-determinant-under-elementary-row-operations]] gives the determinant changes for the row operations.

## Proof

1.1 For each round, [F7] makes $V_t$ invertible and gives $\det V_t\ge\lambda^d>0$. In the row procedure for an invertible $V_t$, after $k$ pivots the transformed left matrix has an identity block in the first $k$ columns and an invertible remaining square block; if its next pivot column were zero in every row $i\ge k$, that remaining block and hence the full matrix would be singular. Therefore the failure branch never occurs. The right block tracks the same invertible row operations as the left block, so once the left block is $I_d$ the right block is $V_t^{-1}$. Tracking determinant changes with [F8], after all row operations $1=\det(V_t)s/(\prod_{k=0}^{d-1}p_k)$, so the stored value $s\prod_{k=0}^{d-1}p_k$ is exactly $\det(V_t)$. Thus $W_t=V_t^{-1}$ and $D_t=\det(V_t)$ at every update; initially these identities follow directly from $V_0=\lambda I_d$, $W_0=\lambda^{-1}I_d$, and $D_0=\lambda^d$. Therefore each confidence logarithm is finite and nonnegative, every score is finite, and the model or supplied selector makes an attained measurable choice. The model supplies each finite reward and the update matrices remain positive definite by [F7]. Induction over the fixed loop proves that all $n$ rounds complete and the stated outputs exist. [F1, F2, F7, F8, algebra]

1.2 At each elimination pivot, searching and swapping rows costs $O(d)$ operations; normalizing one row and eliminating its column from at most $d-1$ rows costs $O(d^2)$. The $d$ pivots therefore cost $O(d^3)$. Each matrix update and multiplication by $b_t$ costs $O(d^2)$; one finite-action score costs $O(d^2)$ and a maximization over $m_t$ actions costs $O(d^2m_t)$. Storing the returned feature and reward costs $O(d)$ per round. Summing over $n$ rounds gives $O(nd^3+d^2\sum_{t\in F}m_t)$ operations, and there is exactly one selector call for each $t\in K$. [step 1.1, F2, F8, algebra]

2.1 On the confidence event $E=\{\theta^*\in C_t\text{ for all }1\le t\le n\}$ from [F3], step 1.1 and the nonnegative radius formula give $\rho_t\ge0$. Since $\beta_t\ge\rho_t^2$, the algorithm's radius $\sqrt{\beta_t}$ also contains $\theta^*$. [A1, A2, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For any $a\in\mathcal A_t$, [F7] makes $\langle x,y\rangle_{V_{t-1}}=x^{\mathsf T}V_{t-1}y$ a real inner product. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $$\langle\theta^*,a\rangle=\langle\widehat\theta_{t-1},a\rangle+\langle\theta^*-\widehat\theta_{t-1},V_{t-1}^{-1}a\rangle_{V_{t-1}}\le\langle\widehat\theta_{t-1},a\rangle+\sqrt{\beta_t}\,\sqrt{a^{\mathsf T}V_{t-1}^{-1}a}.$$ By step 1.1, $W_{t-1}=V_{t-1}^{-1}$, so the final expression is $U_t(a)$. [F1, F2, F3, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By the model, the true-mean maximum on $\mathcal A_t$ is attained and its value is measurable. For every $a\in\mathcal A_t$, step 3.1 gives $\langle\theta^*,a\rangle\le U_t(a)$, and the algorithm's maximization gives $U_t(a)\le U_t(A_t)$. Taking the maximum over $a$ yields $$\max_{a\in\mathcal A_t}\langle\theta^*,a\rangle\le U_t(A_t).$$ [F1, F2, step 3.1]

5.1 Applying Cauchy–Schwarz to $A_t$ and the confidence error as in step 3.1 yields $$\langle\theta^*,A_t\rangle\ge\langle\widehat\theta_{t-1},A_t\rangle-\sqrt{\beta_t}\,\sqrt{A_t^{\mathsf T}V_{t-1}^{-1}A_t}=U_t(A_t)-2\sqrt{\beta_t}\,\sqrt{u_t},$$ where step 1.1 identifies $W_{t-1}=V_{t-1}^{-1}$. Define $r_t=\max_{a\in\mathcal A_t}\langle\theta^*,a\rangle-\langle\theta^*,A_t\rangle$. By step 4.1, this gap is nonnegative and at most $2\sqrt{\beta_t}\sqrt{u_t}$. [F1, F2, F3, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The range hypothesis gives $r_t\le1$. By [F4], $\det V_t/\det V_{t-1}=1+u_t\ge1$, so the algorithm's determinant-defined $\beta_t$ is nondecreasing and $\beta_t\le\beta_n$. If $u_t\le1$, step 5.1 gives $r_t\le2\sqrt{\beta_n}\sqrt{u_t}$; if $u_t\ge1$, the range bound gives $r_t\le1\le2\sqrt{\beta_n}$. Thus in both cases $r_t\le2\sqrt{\beta_n}\min\{1,\sqrt{u_t}\}$. [F2, F4, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Squaring step 6.1 gives $r_t^2\le4\beta_n\min\{1,u_t\}$. Euclidean Cauchy–Schwarz on $(r_1,\ldots,r_n)$ and $(1,\ldots,1)$ therefore yields $$\widehat R_n=\sum_{t=1}^nr_t\le\sqrt{n\sum_{t=1}^nr_t^2}\le2\sqrt{n\beta_n\sum_{t=1}^n\min\{1,u_t\}}.$$ [step 6.1, F6, algebra]

8.1 Apply the sum bound in [F4] to step 7.1 to obtain $\widehat R_n\le\sqrt{8n\beta_n\log(\det V_n/\det V_0)}$. Then [F5] gives the second displayed bound. These inequalities hold on $E$, whose probability is at least $1-\delta$ by [F3]. [F3, F4, F5, step 7.1] ∎

title: "For every square matrix, including singular ones, a row swap negates the determinant, scaling a row by any scalar scales it, and row addition leaves it unchanged"

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\in M_n(R)$ be a matrix over a commutative ring.

1. Interchanging two rows changes $\det(A)$ to $-\det(A)$.
2. Multiplying one row by any $c\in R$ changes it to $c\det(A)$.
3. Adding $c$ times one row to a distinct row leaves it equal to $\det(A)$.

No invertibility assumption is made on $A$ or on $c$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A square matrix $A$ over a commutative ring and a row transformation.

[L1] Determinant is alternating and multilinear in its rows ([[cor-determinant-is-alternating-multilinear-in-the-rows]]).

[L2] Ring row transformations include swaps, scaling by any scalar, and addition of a multiple of a distinct row ([[def-row-transformations-over-a-commutative-ring]]).

[L3] Determinant takes values in the same commutative ring ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Row multilinearity gives $\det(\ldots,cR_p,\ldots)=c\det(A)$ for every scalar $c$, including $c=0$ and zero divisors. [L1, L2, L3]

2.1 Row antisymmetry gives $\det(A')=-\det(A)$ when $A'$ is obtained by a row swap. [step 1.1, L1, L2]

3.1 Replacing $R_p$ by $R_p+cR_q$ expands the new determinant as $\det(A)+cD$, where $D$ has row $R_q$ in both positions $p$ and $q$; alternation gives $D=0$, so the determinant is unchanged. [step 2.1, L1, L2, algebra]

4.1 The derivations used only row multilinearity and alternation, not cancellation, matrix invertibility or scalar invertibility. Hence all three formulas include singular matrices and arbitrary scalars. [step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the hypotheses of the LinUCB high-probability regret theorem, with $d\ge1$, $\lambda>0$, $L\ge1$, $m_2\ge0$, and horizon $n\ge2$. Run LinUCB with $\delta=1/n$. Let $\widehat R_n$ be its random pseudo-regret and define expected pseudo-regret by $R_n:=\mathbb E[\widehat R_n]$. Put

$$q_n:=\log\!\left(1+\frac{nL^2}{d\lambda}\right),\qquad B_n:=\sqrt{8dn\beta_nq_n},$$

where $\beta_n$ is the algorithm's confidence schedule, and set

$$c:=1+\frac{\log(1+L/\lambda)}{\log2},\qquad C_1:=4+2c+\frac{1+2\lambda m_2^2}{\log2},\qquad C:=\sqrt{8C_1c}+\frac{1}{\sqrt2\log2}.$$

Here $B_n$ is generally random through $\beta_n$ and the design matrix. Then

$$R_n\le\mathbb E[B_n]+1\le C\,d\sqrt n\log(nL).$$

This is an expected pseudo-regret bound; it is distinct from a high-probability bound on realized reward regret.

## Statement references

[Tor Lattimore and Csaba Szepesvári, *Bandit Algorithms*, §19.3, Corollary 19.3](https://tor-lattimore.com/downloads/book/book.pdf)

[Abbasi-Yadkori, Pál, and Szepesvári, §5.1, Theorem 13 and its expected-regret caveat](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.2670)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, Countable Choice, LinUCB's confidence schedule, the model hypotheses, and the per-round linear-mean range bound from the high-probability regret theorem.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is inherited through the conditional-expectation, supermartingale, and bounded optional-sampling interfaces in the confidence proof.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is inherited through the Gaussian integral in the confidence proof.

[F1] [[thm-linucb-regret]]: with probability at least $1-\delta$, $\widehat R_n\le\sqrt{8dn\beta_n\log(1+nL^2/(d\lambda))}$ when the per-round mean range is at most $1$.

[F2] [[alg-linucb]]: $\beta_n=\max\{1,(\sqrt\lambda m_2+\sqrt{2\log(1/\delta)+\log(\det V_{n-1}/\lambda^d)})^2\}$.

[F3] [[lem-linucb-trace-determinant-bound]]: applying its determinant bound to the first $n-1\ge1$ feature vectors and using monotonicity of $\log$ gives $\log(\det V_{n-1}/\lambda^d)\le d\log(1+(n-1)L^2/(d\lambda))\le d\log(1+nL^2/(d\lambda))=dq_n$.

[F4] [[def-linear-contextual-bandit-model]] and [F1]: the pseudo-regret is measurable and each round gap lies in $[0,1]$ under the theorem's range assumption, so $0\le\widehat R_n\le n$.

[F5] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]], [[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]], and [[cor-expectation-of-an-indicator-is-probability]]: expectations are integrals, preserve order and finite sums, and $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_E]=\mathbb P(E)$.

[F6] [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\log$ is increasing and $\log(xy)=\log x+\log y$ for positive arguments.

[F7] [[lem-linucb-ridge-estimates-are-measurable]] and [[alg-linucb]]: $\det V_{n-1}$, $\beta_n$, and $B_n$ are measurable; the deterministic bound in the proof makes $B_n$ integrable.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1] with $\delta=1/n$, there is an event $E$ with $\mathbb P(E)\ge1-1/n$ on which $\widehat R_n\le B_n$. By [F4], $\widehat R_n\le n$ on every outcome. Therefore $\widehat R_n\le B_n\mathbf1_E+n\mathbf1_{E^c}$ pointwise. Taking expectations and using $B_n\ge0$ and [F5] gives $$R_n\le\mathbb E[B_n\mathbf1_E]+n\mathbb P(E^c)\le\mathbb E[B_n]+1.$$ [A1, A2, F1, F4, F5, algebra, F7]

1.2 With $\delta=1/n$, [F2] and [F3] give $$\beta_n\le1+\left(\sqrt\lambda m_2+\sqrt{2\log n+dq_n}\right)^2\le1+2\lambda m_2^2+4\log n+2dq_n.$$ The first inequality uses $\max\{1,x\}\le1+x$ for $x\ge0$; the second uses $(a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2$. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Since $nL\ge2$, $\log n\le\log(nL)$ and $$1+\frac{nL^2}{d\lambda}\le1+\frac{nL^2}{\lambda}\le nL\left(1+\frac{L}{\lambda}\right).$$ By [F6], $q_n\le\log(nL)+\log(1+L/\lambda)\le c\log(nL)$. Hence step 1.2 and $d\ge1$, $\log(nL)\ge\log2$ imply $$\beta_n\le C_1d\log(nL).$$ [F6, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Step 2.1 and the definition of $B_n$ yield $$B_n=\sqrt{8dn\beta_nq_n}\le\sqrt{8C_1c}\,d\sqrt n\log(nL)$$ pointwise, hence the same upper bound holds for $\mathbb E[B_n]$. Also $d\sqrt n\log(nL)\ge\sqrt2\log2$, so $1\le d\sqrt n\log(nL)/(\sqrt2\log2)$. Combining these inequalities with step 1.1 proves $R_n\le C d\sqrt n\log(nL)$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F6, algebra, F7] ∎

The coordinate Euclidean norm is $\|a\|_2=\sqrt{a_1^2+a_2^2}$. This candidate violates the model's feature bound, although the matrix update formula still gives $V_1=\operatorname{diag}(5,1)$.

[F2] [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]: matrix products and the identity use their usual coordinate formulas.

1.1 The feature has norm $\|a\|_2=\sqrt{2^2+0^2}=2>1=L$, so it violates the model's candidate-feature hypothesis. The zero parameter and zero noise do not repair that failed assumption. [given, F1, algebra]

## Example references

[[def-linear-contextual-bandit-model]]: the finite-dimensional feature and reward model.

[[alg-linucb]]: LinUCB's confidence score, tie-breaking, and sample-sum update.

## Example

Consider one round with dimension $d=1$, regularization $\lambda=1$, feature bound $L=2$, parameter bound $m_2=1$, and deterministic parameter $\theta^*=1$. Let the context be constant and let the two available actions have scalar features $0$ and $2$. Use zero reward noise. Both candidate features satisfy the model's bound, but their true means are $0$ and $2$, so the linear-mean range is $2$.

## Example references

[[def-linear-contextual-bandit-model]]: all candidate features must have norm at most $L$ and the conditional noise MGF must be bounded by $e^{q^2/2}$.

[[thm-linucb-regret]]: the regret guarantee additionally assumes the true-mean range within each available action set is at most $1$.

[Tor Lattimore and Csaba Szepesvári, *Bandit Algorithms*, §19.3, Theorem 19.2](https://tor-lattimore.com/downloads/book/book.pdf)

[Abbasi-Yadkori, Pál, and Szepesvári, Theorem 13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.2670)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The one-round finite-dimensional linear contextual bandit instance in the Example.

[F1] [[def-linear-contextual-bandit-model]]: each candidate feature has Euclidean norm at most $L$, rewards are $\langle\theta^*,A_t\rangle+\eta_t$, and the conditional noise MGF bound is $e^{q^2/2}$.

[F2] [[thm-linucb-regret]]: its stated guarantee requires $\sup_{a,b\in\mathcal A_t}\langle\theta^*,a-b\rangle\le1$.

## Verification

1.1 The candidate features are $0$ and $2$, so both have absolute value at most $L=2$. The parameter satisfies $|\theta^*|=1=m_2$, and zero noise has conditional MGF $\mathbb E[e^{q\eta_1}\mid\mathcal F_1]=1\le e^{q^2/2}$ for every real $q$. Thus the instance satisfies the model hypotheses. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The true means are $\theta^*\cdot0=0$ and $\theta^*\cdot2=2$. Consequently $\sup_{a,b\in\{0,2\}}\theta^*(a-b)=2>1$, so the additional range premise of [F2] fails. This example therefore lies outside that theorem's stated guarantee and does not refute its conclusion under its hypotheses. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

## Definition references

[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel|A probability kernel assigns a probability measure at every input and has measurable event sections]].

[[def-countable|A set is finite when it is bijective with some natural number]].

[[def-cartesian-product|A Cartesian product pairs each element of A with an element of B]].

[[def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set|A sum over a finite set is defined by any enumeration, with permutation invariance ensuring a unique value]].

[[def-max-min|A maximum is an element of the set that bounds every element above]].

[[lem-of-abs-value|Absolute value is multiplicative and satisfies the triangle inequality]].

[[lem-triangle-inequality-finite|The absolute value of a finite sum is at most the sum of the absolute values]].

[[lem-finite-sum-laws|Finite sums preserve termwise inequalities and commute with scaling]].

[Sutton and Barto, *Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction*](https://web.stanford.edu/class/psych209/Readings/SuttonBartoIPRLBook2ndEd.pdf).

[Kaelbling, Littman, and Cassandra, Brown Technical Report CS-96-08](https://cs.brown.edu/research/pubs/techreports/reports/96/cs96-08.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite state set $S$ and a finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ for each $s\in S$.

[F1] [[def-countable]]: a set is finite when it is bijective with some natural number; a bijection transports finiteness.

[F2] [[thm-sum-rule]]: a finite indexed family of pairwise-disjoint finite sets has finite union.

[F3] [[thm-the-characterising-property-of-ordered-pairs]]: $(a,b)=(c,d)$ exactly when $a=c$ and $b=d$, so the second coordinate is unique.

## Verification

1.1 For each $s\in S$, let $D_s=\{(s,a):a\in A(s)\}$. The map $a\mapsto(s,a)$ is a bijection from $A(s)$ onto $D_s$, with inverse the second-coordinate projection, so $D_s$ is finite by [F1]. If $s\ne t$, no ordered pair can have both first coordinate $s$ and first coordinate $t$; hence the family $(D_s)_{s\in S}$ is pairwise disjoint. [given, F1, F3, construct]

2.1 By the definition of $D$, $D=\bigcup_{s\in S}D_s$. Since $S$ is finite and the blocks in step 1.1 are finite and pairwise disjoint, [F2] implies that $D$ is finite. [step 1.1, F2] ∎

## Remarks

For nonempty $S$, each $A(s)$ is nonempty, so the normalization for an admissible pair forces $\mathcal R$ to be nonempty. For every admissible $(s,a)$, $P(s'\mid s,a)\ge0$ and

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1, $$

 so $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ is a probability distribution. Also, $|\rho|\le M$ and $p\ge0$ give 

$$ |r(s,a)|\le\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\le M\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=M. $$

Thus both derived marginals are well defined and the expected reward is bounded by the maximum absolute reward. The separate marginals are derived from the joint law; specifying unrelated reward and transition marginals would not preserve their possible dependence.

## Definition

Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
[[def-nat-order]], which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]], proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
([[def-equinumerous]]).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

## Remarks

- **Convention: in this library "countable" alone always means "at most
  countable"**, so a finite set is countable. This is the convention of Halmos
  and of Tao, and it is the one that makes the theorems on this page read
  cleanly: subsets, products and unions of countable sets are countable, with no
  finite/infinite case split in the statement. The competing convention, used by
  Rudin among others, reserves "countable" for "countably infinite" and says
  "at most countable" for the disjunction. Under that convention every statement
  below still holds after replacing "countable" with "at most countable", but
  several would become false as literally written. Where the distinction
  matters, the long forms "countably infinite" and "at most countable" are used
  in full, and "uncountable" always means "not at most countable", on which the
  two conventions agree.

- **The three classes are exhaustive by construction**: every set is finite,
  countably infinite, or uncountable, since "uncountable" is defined as the
  negation of the disjunction. That they are also mutually exclusive, that is,
  that no set is both finite and countably infinite, is a genuine theorem
  amounting to $\mathbb{N} \not\approx n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and it is
  proved immediately above as claim 4 of [[lem-pigeonhole]]. So a countably
  infinite set is never finite, and "$A$ is infinite", meaning not finite, is
  implied by $A \approx \mathbb{N}$. The same lemma pins down finiteness itself:
  by its claim 3 a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number, so
  the number of elements of a finite set is well defined, and by its claim 5 no
  finite set is equinumerous with a proper subset of itself.

- **What the exclusivity is and is not used for below.** Nothing on this page
  needs it in order to run: the infinitude of $\mathbb{Q}$, for instance, is
  obtained by exhibiting a bijection $\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ directly
  ([[thm-rationals-countable]]) rather than by ruling out finiteness. It is used
  when the continuum hypothesis is instantiated at $\mathbb{N}$
  ([[rem-continuum-hypothesis]]), where $\mathbb{N}$ must be infinite as a fact
  rather than as a convention.

- **$0$ and the empty set.** $0 = \varnothing$, and $A \approx 0$ holds exactly
  when $A = \varnothing$, so the empty set is finite. This matters in the proofs
  below, where the empty case is always separated out: a surjection
  $\mathbb{N} \to A$ cannot exist when $A = \varnothing$, which is why
  [[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]] assumes $A$ nonempty.

- **Countability is a property of a set alone**, not of a set with structure. In
  particular $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable while carrying a dense order, and
  $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable; neither statement says anything on its own about
  the order or the arithmetic those sets carry.

## Statement

1. **Two blocks.** If $A$ and $B$ are finite and **disjoint**, then $A \cup B$ is
   finite and $\lvert A \cup B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert + \lvert B\rvert$
   ([[def-finite-cardinality]]).
2. **A finite partition.** If $I$ is a finite set and $(A_i)_{i \in I}$ is a
   family of finite sets that are pairwise disjoint, then $\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i$
   is finite and
   $\big\lvert\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\big\rvert = \sum_{i \in I}\lvert A_i\rvert$,
   the sum being that of [[def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set]].
3. **Splitting a sum along a partition of its index set.** Let $S$ be finite, let
   $J$ be finite, and let $(S_j)_{j \in J}$ be pairwise disjoint subsets of $S$
   with $\bigcup_{j \in J} S_j = S$. Then for $a : S \to \mathbb{R}$ or
   $a : S \to \mathbb{N}$,
   $$\sum_{i \in S} a_i = \sum_{j \in J}\Big(\sum_{i \in S_j} a_i\Big), \qquad \prod_{i \in S} a_i = \prod_{j \in J}\Big(\prod_{i \in S_j} a_i\Big).$$
   In particular $\sum_{i \in S \cup T} a_i = \sum_{i \in S} a_i + \sum_{i \in T} a_i$
   for disjoint finite $S$ and $T$.

**Disjointness is a hypothesis and not a formality.** It is spent at exactly one
step, the injectivity of the splice map, and dropping it makes clause 1 false;
the companion page carries that false statement with its smallest witness.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Finite sets as in the statement, and the truncated difference and the two finite sums of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Throughout, $\ast$ denotes either $+$ or $\cdot$ on $\mathbb{R}$ or on $\mathbb{N}$, $e$ the corresponding identity, and $\bigstar_{k<n} c_k$ the associated iterated operation; the four cases are proved by one argument, as in [[lem-finite-sum-permutation-invariance]].

[L1] Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]).

[L2] Cardinality ([[def-finite-cardinality]]): $\lvert A\rvert$ is the unique natural with $A \approx \lvert A\rvert$; $\lvert n\rvert = n$; $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$; a bijection transports finiteness and cardinality.

[L3] Sums over a finite index set ([[def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set]]): $\sum_{i \in S} a_i = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)}$ for any bijection $\varphi : \lvert S\rvert \to S$, the value being independent of $\varphi$; $\sum_{i \in n} a_i = \sum_{k<n} a_k$; reindexing along a bijection $T \to S$ leaves the value unchanged; and $\sum_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = e$.

[L4] Recursion clauses: $\bigstar_{k<0} c_k = e$ and $\bigstar_{k<\sigma(n)} c_k = \big(\bigstar_{k<n} c_k\big) \ast c_n$ ([[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], [[def-finite-sum]]).

[L5] Splitting at an index: for $p \le N$ and $q = N - p$, $\bigstar_{k<N} c_k = \big(\bigstar_{k<p} c_k\big) \ast \big(\bigstar_{j<q} c_{p+j}\big)$ (clause 3 of [[lem-nat-finite-sum-laws-and-the-canonical-embedding]], clause 3 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

[L6] Order and addition in $\mathbb{N}$: $p \le k$ gives a unique $j$ with $p + j = k$; $p + j < p + q \iff j < q$; addition is commutative; $\sigma(m) = m + 1$ ([[def-nat-order]], [[lem-nat-add-cancellative]], [[lem-nat-order-add-compatible]], [[lem-nat-add-commutative]], [[def-nat-addition]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]).

[L7] Maps ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]], [[def-equinumerous]]): composites and inverses of bijections are bijections, and an injective surjection is a bijection.

[L8] A subset of a finite set is finite ([[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], clause 1).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** induction.

1.1 The splice map. Let $A$, $B$ be finite and disjoint, put $p := \lvert A\rvert$, $q := \lvert B\rvert$, and fix bijections $f : p \to A$ and $g : q \to B$. Define $h : p + q \to A \cup B$ by $h(k) = f(k)$ when $k < p$, and, when $p \le k$, by $h(k) = g(j)$ for the unique $j$ with $p + j = k$; that $j$ satisfies $j < q$ because $p + j = k < p + q$. The map $h$ is well defined by [L6], it is surjective because every element of $A \cup B$ is some $f(k)$ or some $g(j)$, and it is injective: two indices below $p$ are separated by the injectivity of $f$, two indices at least $p$ by the injectivity of $g$ together with the uniqueness of $j$, and an index below $p$ from one at least $p$ because $f(k) \in A$, $g(j) \in B$ and $A \cap B = \varnothing$. **The last of these three cases is the only use of disjointness in the whole proof.** [L6, L7, construct]

1.2 Base cases of the two inductions below, at $m = 0$. A family indexed by $0 = \varnothing$ has empty union, so $\big\lvert\bigcup_{k<0} B_k\big\rvert = \lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0 = \sum_{k<0}\lvert B_k\rvert$; and a partition of $S$ indexed by $0$ forces $S = \varnothing$, so both sides of clause 3 are $e$. [base, L2, L3, L4]

1.3 Inductive hypothesis for both inductions, at $m$: for pairwise disjoint finite $B_0, \dots, B_{m-1}$ the union $\bigcup_{k<m} B_k$ is finite with cardinality $\sum_{k<m}\lvert B_k\rvert$; and for a partition of a finite set $S$ into pairwise disjoint $S_0, \dots, S_{m-1}$ one has $\bigstar_{i \in S} a_i = \bigstar_{k<m}\big(\bigstar_{i \in S_k} a_i\big)$. [ih]

2.1 Clause 1. By step 1.1 the map $h$ is a bijection $p + q \to A \cup B$, so $A \cup B \approx p+q$; hence $A \cup B$ is finite and $\lvert A \cup B\rvert = \lvert p+q\rvert = p + q = \lvert A\rvert + \lvert B\rvert$. [step 1.1, L2, L7]

3.1 Clause 3 for two blocks. Let $S$, $T$ be finite and disjoint and $a$ defined on $S \cup T$. With $p = \lvert S\rvert$, $q = \lvert T\rvert$ and the bijections $f, g, h$ of step 1.1 for the pair $S$, $T$, step 2.1 gives $\lvert S \cup T\rvert = p+q$, so $h$ may be used as the enumeration in [L3]. Then $\bigstar_{i \in S \cup T} a_i = \bigstar_{k<p+q} a_{h(k)} = \big(\bigstar_{k<p} a_{h(k)}\big) \ast \big(\bigstar_{j<q} a_{h(p+j)}\big) = \big(\bigstar_{k<p} a_{f(k)}\big) \ast \big(\bigstar_{j<q} a_{g(j)}\big) = \big(\bigstar_{i \in S} a_i\big) \ast \big(\bigstar_{i \in T} a_i\big)$, using [L5] at the second equality. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L3, L5]

3.2 Inductive step for clause 2, in the case of an index set $\sigma(m)$. Let $B_0, \dots, B_{m}$ be pairwise disjoint and finite. Then $\bigcup_{k<\sigma(m)} B_k = \big(\bigcup_{k<m} B_k\big) \cup B_m$, and these two sets are disjoint because each $B_k$ with $k < m$ is disjoint from $B_m$. By the hypothesis of step 1.3 the first is finite with cardinality $\sum_{k<m}\lvert B_k\rvert$, so clause 1 makes the union finite with cardinality $\sum_{k<m}\lvert B_k\rvert + \lvert B_m\rvert = \sum_{k<\sigma(m)}\lvert B_k\rvert$ by [L4]. [step 1.3, step 2.1, L4]

4.1 Clause 2. By step 1.2, step 3.2 and induction, the statement holds for every family indexed by a natural number $m$. For a general finite index set $I$ take a bijection $\varphi : m \to I$ with $m = \lvert I\rvert$; then $\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcup_{k<m} A_{\varphi(k)}$ and $\sum_{i \in I}\lvert A_i\rvert = \sum_{k<m}\lvert A_{\varphi(k)}\rvert$ by the definition of the sum over a finite index set, so the two statements coincide. [step 1.2, step 3.2, L1, L3]

5.1 Inductive step for clause 3, index set $\sigma(m)$. Let $S$ be finite and partitioned into pairwise disjoint $S_0, \dots, S_m$, and put $S' := \bigcup_{k<m} S_k$, which is finite by [L8] and disjoint from $S_m$. The hypothesis of step 1.3 applies to the partition of $S'$ into $S_0, \dots, S_{m-1}$, and step 3.1 applies to the disjoint pair $S'$, $S_m$, giving $\bigstar_{i \in S} a_i = \big(\bigstar_{i \in S'} a_i\big) \ast \big(\bigstar_{i \in S_m} a_i\big) = \big(\bigstar_{k<m}\bigstar_{i \in S_k} a_i\big) \ast \big(\bigstar_{i \in S_m} a_i\big) = \bigstar_{k<\sigma(m)}\big(\bigstar_{i \in S_k} a_i\big)$ by [L4]. [step 1.3, step 3.1, step 4.1, L4, L8]

6.1 Clause 3. By step 1.2, step 5.1 and induction it holds for every index set that is a natural number, and the general finite $J$ follows by reindexing along a bijection $m \to J$ exactly as in step 4.1. The two-block form is step 3.1. [step 1.2, step 3.1, step 5.1, L1, L3]

7.1 Clause 1 is step 2.1, clause 2 is step 4.1 and clause 3 is step 6.1; since $\ast$ was an arbitrary one of the four operations, both the sum and the product forms of clause 3 are proved. [step 2.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, discharge-induction] ∎

## Remarks

- **Why the splice map is built once.** The same bijection $p + q \to A \cup B$ proves clause 1 and, used as an enumeration, proves the two-block case of clause 3. Building it twice, once for cardinalities and once for sums, would be two chances to get the index arithmetic wrong.

- **The subtraction in the splice is legitimate.** Writing $h(k) = g(k - p)$ for $k \ge p$ means: the unique $j$ with $p + j = k$, which exists by the definition of $\le$ and is unique by cancellation. No negative number is formed anywhere.

- **Clause 3 is what the multinomial theorem needs.** Its outer sum is indexed by the set of weak compositions of $n$ into $m$ parts, and the induction on $m$ partitions that index set by the value of the last part. Without clause 3 that step could not be taken.

## Statement

For all sets $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$: $(a,b) = (c,d)$ if and only if $a = c$ and
$b = d$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** sets $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$.

[L1] $(a,b) := \{\{a\},\{a,b\}\}$ ([[def-ordered-pair]]).

[L2] $\{x,y\}$ is the set whose elements are exactly $x$ and $y$, and $\{x\} := \{x,x\}$ ([[def-unordered-pair-and-singleton]]).

[L3] $\{a,b\} = \{c,d\} \ \leftrightarrow\ \bigl((a = c \wedge b = d) \vee (a = d \wedge b = c)\bigr)$ ([[lem-unordered-pair-equality]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** cases.

1.1 Right to left: if $a = c$ and $b = d$ then $\{a\} = \{c\}$ and $\{a,b\} = \{c,d\}$, so $\{\{a\},\{a,b\}\}$ and $\{\{c\},\{c,d\}\}$ are the same set, that is $(a,b) = (c,d)$. [L1, L2]

1.2 Left to right, setting up: assume $\{\{a\},\{a,b\}\} = \{\{c\},\{c,d\}\}$. Applying the equality criterion for unordered pairs to these two sets, either $\{a\} = \{c\}$ and $\{a,b\} = \{c,d\}$, or $\{a\} = \{c,d\}$ and $\{a,b\} = \{c\}$. [L1, L3]

2.1 In the first alternative, $\{a\} = \{c\}$ reads $\{a,a\} = \{c,c\}$ and gives $a = c$. Then $\{a,b\} = \{c,d\}$ gives $a = c$ and $b = d$, or $a = d$ and $b = c$; in the second of these $b = c = a = d$, so $b = d$ holds as well. Either way $a = c$ and $b = d$. [assume-case first, step 1.2, L2, L3]

2.2 In the second alternative, $\{a,b\} = \{c\}$ reads $\{a,b\} = \{c,c\}$ and gives $a = c$ and $b = c$, while $\{a\} = \{c,d\}$ reads $\{a,a\} = \{c,d\}$ and gives $a = c$ and $a = d$. Hence $a = c$ and $b = c = a = d$. [assume-case second, step 1.2, L2, L3]

3.1 The two alternatives supplied by step 1.2 are exhaustive, so the left-to-right implication holds. [step 2.1, step 2.2, cases-exhaustive]

4.1 Both implications hold, which is the statement. [step 1.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $M\ge0$, $0\le\gamma<1$, and let $(\rho_j)_{j\ge1}$ be any real sequence with $|\rho_j|\le M$. Then the series

$$ \sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\gamma^j\rho_{j+1} $$

converges absolutely. Every partial sum and the limit satisfy

$$ \left|\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\gamma^j\rho_{j+1}\right|\le\frac{M}{1-\gamma}, \qquad |G|\le\frac{M}{1-\gamma}. $$

For every integer $N\ge0$,

$$ \left|G-\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\gamma^j\rho_{j+1}\right|\le\frac{M\gamma^N}{1-\gamma}, $$

where the partial sum at $N=0$ is empty and $\gamma^0=1$, including when $\gamma=0$.

## Statement references

[Sutton and Barto, *Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction*](https://web.stanford.edu/class/psych209/Readings/SuttonBartoIPRLBook2ndEd.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $M\ge0$, $0\le\gamma<1$, and a real sequence $(\rho_j)_{j\ge1}$ with $|\rho_j|\le M$.

[F1] [[thm-geometric-series]]: for $0\le\gamma<1$, $\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\gamma^j=1/(1-\gamma)$, with the series beginning at $j=0$.

[F2] [[thm-direct-comparison-test]]: if $0\le a_j\le b_j$ and $\sum b_j$ converges, then $\sum a_j$ converges.

[F3] [[lem-series-linearity]] and [[lem-series-tail-invariance]]: a convergent geometric series can be scaled and shifted; its tail beginning at $N$ has sum $\gamma^N/(1-\gamma)$.

[F4] [[lem-of-abs-value]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: the absolute value of a finite sum is at most the sum of the absolute values, and finite sums preserve termwise upper bounds.

[F5] [[lem-geometric-sequence-null]]: $\gamma^N\to0$ for $0\le\gamma<1$.

[F6] [[lem-limit-preserves-order]]: if two real sequences converge and one is eventually at most the other, their limits satisfy the same non-strict inequality.

[F7] [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]]: for a convergent series of nonnegative terms, every finite partial sum is at most its sum. 

## Proof

1.1 For every $j\ge0$, $0\le\gamma^j|\rho_{j+1}|\le M\gamma^j$. By [F1] and the scaling part of [F3], the majorant series $\sum_{j\ge0}M\gamma^j$ converges (and when $M=0$ it is the zero series); [F2] gives convergence of $\sum_{j\ge0}\gamma^j|\rho_{j+1}|$. Thus the stated series converges absolutely by definition of absolute convergence. [given, F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Every finite partial sum satisfies $\left|\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\gamma^j\rho_{j+1}\right|\le M\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\gamma^j\le M\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\gamma^j=M/(1-\gamma)$. The second inequality is [F7] applied to the nonnegative geometric series in [F1]. At $N=0$ the sum is empty and the inequality holds as well. [given, F1, F4, F7, algebra]

2.1 For $K\ge N$, [F4] gives $\left|\sum_{j=N}^{K-1}\gamma^j\rho_{j+1}\right|\le M\sum_{j=N}^{K-1}\gamma^j\le M\sum_{j=N}^{\infty}\gamma^j=M\gamma^N/(1-\gamma)$, where [F7] applies to the shifted geometric series and [F3] evaluates its sum. The finite tail sums converge to $G-\sum_{j<N}\gamma^j\rho_{j+1}$ by step 1.1, and each lies between the negatives and positives of the displayed bound; [F6] passes both inequalities to the limit. Therefore the required tail estimate holds. [step 1.1, F3, F4, F6, F7]

3.1 Taking $N=0$ in step 2.1 gives $|G|\le M/(1-\gamma)$. The right side of the tail bound tends to zero by [F5], so the partial sums converge to $G$ with the stated uniform remainder control. [step 2.1, F5] ∎

## Statement

Let $(a_k)$ and $(b_k)$ be sequences of reals and suppose there is
$K \in \mathbb{N}$ with

$$0 \;\le\; a_k \;\le\; b_k \qquad \text{for all } k \ge K .$$

Then:

1. if $\sum b_k$ converges then $\sum a_k$ converges ([[def-series]]);
2. if $\sum a_k$ diverges then $\sum b_k$ diverges.

The same statement holds verbatim for series with a general starting index $m$,
applied to the shifted sequences of [[def-series]].

The hypothesis is on the terms from some index on, not on all of them: finitely
many terms of either sequence may violate it, or be negative, without affecting
the conclusion. What may not be dropped is nonnegativity of $(a_k)$ from that
index on.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Sequences $(a_k)$, $(b_k)$ of reals and $K \in \mathbb{N}$ with $0 \le a_k \le b_k$ for all $k \ge K$; the partial sums $\alpha_j = \sum_{i<j} a_{K+i}$ and $\beta_j = \sum_{i<j} b_{K+i}$ of the $K$-th tail series ([[def-series]], [[def-finite-sum]]).

[L1] Monotonicity of finite sums: if $x_i \le y_i$ for all $i < j$ then $\sum_{i<j} x_i \le \sum_{i<j} y_i$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

[L2] A series converges if and only if its $K$-th tail series converges ([[lem-series-tail-invariance]]).

[L3] For a series of nonnegative terms: it converges if and only if the range of its partial sums is bounded above, and in the convergent case every partial sum is at most the sum ([[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]], [[def-bounded-set]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For every $i \in \mathbb{N}$ the index $K + i$ is at least $K$, so $0 \le a_{K+i} \le b_{K+i}$; in particular both tail series have nonnegative terms. [given]

1.2 Assume $\sum b_k$ converges. Then its $K$-th tail series $\sum_{k \ge K} b_k$ converges. [given, L2]

2.1 By monotonicity of finite sums, $\alpha_j \le \beta_j$ for every $j \in \mathbb{N}$. [step 1.1, L1]

2.2 That tail series has nonnegative terms, so its partial sums satisfy $\beta_j \le B$ for every $j$, where $B$ is its sum. [step 1.2, step 1.1, L3]

3.1 Hence $\alpha_j \le \beta_j \le B$ for every $j$, so the range of $(\alpha_j)$ is bounded above by $B$. [step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 The tail series $\sum_{k \ge K} a_k$ has nonnegative terms and partial sums bounded above, so it converges. [step 3.1, step 1.1, L3]

5.1 Therefore $\sum a_k$ converges, which is claim 1. [step 4.1, L2]

6.1 Claim 2 is the contrapositive of claim 1: if $\sum a_k$ diverges then $\sum b_k$ cannot converge. [step 5.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **Both nonnegativity hypotheses are used, and in different places.** $a_k \ge 0$ is what lets convergence of $\sum_{k \ge K} a_k$ be read off from boundedness of its partial sums, and $b_k \ge a_k \ge 0$ is what makes the sum of $\sum_{k \ge K} b_k$ an upper bound for the partial sums $\beta_j$. Drop the sign hypothesis and the theorem is false, not merely unproved; the companion page exhibits a pair with $a_k \le b_k$ for every $k$, $\sum b_k$ convergent and $\sum a_k$ divergent.

- **The comparison is with a series, not with a limit.** No quotient $a_k/b_k$ appears and no $b_k$ is required to be nonzero, which is what distinguishes this test from the limit comparison test proved next.

## Statement

Let $(a_k)$ and $(b_k)$ be sequences of reals whose series converge
([[def-series]]), and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $\sum (a_k + b_k)$ converges, with
   $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k + \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} b_k$;
2. $\sum c\,a_k$ converges, with
   $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} c\,a_k = c \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k$.

Moreover, for $c \ne 0$ and an arbitrary sequence $(a_k)$, whose series is not
assumed to converge:

3. $\sum c\,a_k$ converges **if and only if** $\sum a_k$ converges. Equivalently,
   $\sum a_k$ diverges if and only if $\sum c\,a_k$ diverges.

Claim 3 is the form used whenever a comparison is made against a constant
multiple of a known series.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Sequences $(a_k)$, $(b_k)$ of reals and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, with partial sums $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $t_n = \sum_{k<n} b_k$ ([[def-series]], [[def-finite-sum]]).

[L1] Additivity and scaling of finite sums: $\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$ and $\sum_{k<n} c\,a_k = c \sum_{k<n} a_k$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

[L2] Algebra of limits: if $x_n \to x$ and $y_n \to y$ then $x_n + y_n \to x + y$ and $c\,x_n \to c\,x$ ([[thm-algebra-of-limits]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The partial sums of $\sum (a_k + b_k)$ are $\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = s_n + t_n$, and those of $\sum c\,a_k$ are $\sum_{k<n} c\,a_k = c\,s_n$. [given, L1]

1.2 Assume $\sum a_k$ and $\sum b_k$ converge, say $s_n \to S$ and $t_n \to T$. [given]

2.1 Then $s_n + t_n \to S + T$, so $\sum(a_k + b_k)$ converges with sum $S + T$, which is claim 1. [step 1.2, step 1.1, L2]

2.2 Likewise $c\,s_n \to c\,S$, so $\sum c\,a_k$ converges with sum $c\,S$, which is claim 2. [step 1.2, step 1.1, L2]

3.1 For claim 3, let $c \ne 0$ and let $(a_k)$ be arbitrary. If $\sum a_k$ converges then $\sum c\,a_k$ converges by claim 2. [step 2.2]

3.2 Conversely, if $\sum c\,a_k$ converges then applying claim 2 to the sequence $(c\,a_k)$ and the scalar $1/c$, which exists since $c \ne 0$, shows that $\sum (1/c)(c\,a_k) = \sum a_k$ converges. [step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The two implications are claim 3, and its contrapositive form is the statement about divergence. [step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

## Remarks

- **There is no product rule here, and there is no rule for $\sum a_k b_k$.** The proof works because a finite sum is additive and homogeneous, and neither property has an analogue for products. Multiplying series is a genuinely harder question, requiring absolute convergence, and it is not treated on this page.

- **Claim 3 needs $c \ne 0$ and nothing else.** In particular it does not need either series to converge, which is what makes it usable in the divergence direction: scaling a divergent series by a nonzero constant leaves it divergent.

## Statement

Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals with partial sums $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$, let
$N \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $t_j := \sum_{i<j} a_{N+i}$ be the partial sums of the
$N$-th tail series $\sum_{k \ge N} a_k$ ([[def-series]]). Then:

1. $t_j = s_{j+N} - s_N$ for every $j \in \mathbb{N}$;
2. $\sum a_k$ converges **if and only if** its $N$-th tail series converges, and
   in that case
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;=\; s_N \;+\; \sum_{k=N}^{\infty} a_k ;$$
3. hence the following are equivalent: $\sum a_k$ converges; every tail series of
   $\sum a_k$ converges; some tail series of $\sum a_k$ converges.

In words: convergence of a series is a property of its terms from any index on,
and changing finitely many terms changes the sum but not the fact of convergence.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A sequence $(a_k)$ of reals, a natural number $N$, the partial sums $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ and the partial sums $t_j = \sum_{i<j} a_{N+i}$ of the $N$-th tail series ([[def-series]], [[def-finite-sum]]).

[L1] Splitting of finite sums: if $m \le n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $\sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$ is by definition $\sum_{i<n-m} a_{m+i}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]).

[L2] Convergence depends only on the tail: a sequence $(x_n)$ converges to $x$ if and only if its $N$-th tail $(x_{j+N})_{j}$ converges to $x$ ([[lem-limit-of-tail]], [[def-sequence]]).

[L3] Algebra of limits: if $x_j \to x$ and $y_j \to y$ then $x_j + y_j \to x + y$ and $x_j - y_j \to x - y$ ([[thm-algebra-of-limits]]).

[L4] A constant sequence $y_j = c$ converges to $c$, immediately from the definition of a limit ([[def-real-limit]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $j \in \mathbb{N}$ and put $n := j + N$, so that $N \le n$ and $n - N = j$. [given]

1.2 The family $(s_{j+N})_{j \in \mathbb{N}}$ is the $N$-th tail of the sequence $(s_n)$ of partial sums. [given, L2]

2.1 Splitting the partial sum $s_n$ at $N$ gives $s_n = \sum_{k<N} a_k + \sum_{k=N}^{n-1} a_k = s_N + \sum_{i<j} a_{N+i} = s_N + t_j$. [step 1.1, L1]

2.2 Suppose $\sum a_k$ converges, say $s_n \to S$; then the $N$-th tail $(s_{j+N})_j$ converges to $S$. [given, step 1.2, L2]

3.1 Claim 1 follows: $t_j = s_{j+N} - s_N$ for every $j \in \mathbb{N}$. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The constant sequence with value $s_N$ converges to $s_N$, so $t_j = s_{j+N} - s_N \to S - s_N$, and the $N$-th tail series converges with sum $S - s_N$. [step 2.2, step 3.1, L3, L4]

4.2 Conversely, suppose the $N$-th tail series converges, say $t_j \to T$; then $s_{j+N} = s_N + t_j \to s_N + T$ by the same two rules. [step 3.1, L3, L4]

5.1 So the $N$-th tail of $(s_n)$ converges to $s_N + T$, hence $(s_n)$ itself converges to $s_N + T$ and $\sum a_k$ converges. [step 4.2, step 1.2, L2]

6.1 Claim 2 follows: the two convergences are equivalent, and when they hold the sums are related by $S = s_N + T$, which is the displayed identity. [step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Claim 3 follows as well: if $\sum a_k$ converges then by claim 2 every tail series converges; every tail series converging trivially gives some tail series converging, the family of tails being indexed by all of $\mathbb{N}$; and if some tail series, say the $N$-th, converges then by claim 2 again $\sum a_k$ converges. [step 6.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **Where the hypothesis-free character comes from.** Nothing here assumes the terms have a sign or that any series converges: claim 1 is an identity between finite sums, valid always, and claims 2 and 3 are read off from it by two standard limit rules. That is why the lemma may be used to move between a series and its tails inside proofs that have not yet decided the convergence question.

- **The sum does change.** Only the fact of convergence is tail invariant. The identity in claim 2 is the exact bookkeeping: discarding the first $N$ terms lowers the sum by $s_N$, and no more.

## Statement

Let $(x_k)$ and $(y_k)$ be sequences of reals ([[def-sequence]]) converging to
$x$ and $y$ respectively ([[def-real-limit]]). If $x_k \le y_k$ eventually, that
is for all $k$ from some index on, then

$$\lim_{k} x_k \;\le\; \lim_{k} y_k .$$

In particular, if $x_k \ge 0$ eventually then $\lim_k x_k \ge 0$, and if
$a \le x_k \le b$ eventually then $a \le \lim_k x_k \le b$.

The conclusion is **not** strict, and cannot be made strict; see the remarks
below and the false statement at the end of this page.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Sequences $(x_k)$, $(y_k)$ of reals with $(x_k)$ converging to $x$, $(y_k)$ converging to $y$, and an index $K_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ with $x_k \le y_k$ for every $k \ge K_0$ ([[def-sequence]], [[def-real-limit]]). Write $z_k := y_k - x_k$ and $z := y - x$.

[L1] Convergence, quantified over rational $\varepsilon > 0$ ([[def-real-limit]]).

[L2] Difference rule: $(z_k) = (y_k - x_k)$ converges to $y - x = z$ ([[thm-algebra-of-limits]]).

[L3] Small rationals: for every real $\eta > 0$ there is a rational $\varepsilon$ with $0 < \varepsilon < \eta$, by density ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]) or by the Archimedean property ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) applied to $1/\eta$ ([[lem-of-inverse-positive]]).

[L4] Absolute value: $|u| < c$ if and only if $-c < u < c$, for $c > 0$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]).

[L5] Order arithmetic in $\mathbb{R}$: adding a constant preserves $<$ and $\le$; $u \le v$ and $v < w$ give $u < w$; trichotomy, so exactly one of $z < 0$, $z = 0$, $z > 0$ holds and the negation of $z < 0$ is $z \ge 0$; $u \le v$ if and only if $v - u \ge 0$; and $u < u$ is impossible ([[lem-of-add-order]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]).

[L6] The order on $\mathbb{N}$ is total, so any two indices admit a common upper bound ([[thm-nat-linear-order]]).

[L7] For $c \in \mathbb{R}$ the constant sequence $(c)$ converges to $c$ ([[def-sequence]], [[def-real-limit]]).

[L8] A sequence of reals has at most one limit ([[lem-limit-unique]]), which is what licenses writing $\lim_k x_k$ and $\lim_k y_k$ for the limits named in the statement; without it those symbols would not denote.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** contradiction.

1.1 By [L2] the sequence $(z_k)$ converges to $z = y - x$, and by hypothesis $z_k = y_k - x_k \ge 0$ for every $k \ge K_0$. [given, L2, L5]

1.2 Suppose, for contradiction, that $z < 0$. [assume-contra]

2.1 Then $-z > 0$, so by [L3] we may choose a rational $\varepsilon$ with $0 < \varepsilon < -z$. [step 1.2, L3, L5, choose]

3.1 Applying convergence of $(z_k)$ to this $\varepsilon$ gives $K_1 \in \mathbb{N}$ with $|z_k - z| < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K_1$, hence $z_k - z < \varepsilon$ and so $z_k < z + \varepsilon$ for all such $k$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L1, L4, L5]

4.1 Fix an index $k$ with $k \ge K_0$ and $k \ge K_1$. Then $0 \le z_k < z + \varepsilon < z + (-z) = 0$, so $0 < 0$, which is impossible. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, L5, L6]

5.1 The assumption $z < 0$ is therefore untenable; by trichotomy $z \ge 0$, that is $y - x \ge 0$, that is $x \le y$; since $x$ and $y$ are the unique limits of $(x_k)$ and $(y_k)$ by [L8], that is exactly $\lim_k x_k \le \lim_k y_k$. Since $(x_k)$ and $(y_k)$ were an arbitrary pair satisfying the hypotheses, the conclusion applies to every such pair, and the two stated special cases are instances of it. Let $(w_k)$ be convergent. If $w_k \ge 0$ from some index on, apply the conclusion to the pair consisting of the constant sequence $0$, which converges to $0$ by [L7], and of $(w_k)$: it gives $0 \le \lim_k w_k$. If $a \le w_k \le b$ from some index on, apply it first to the constant sequence $a$ and $(w_k)$, then to $(w_k)$ and the constant sequence $b$: it gives $a \le \lim_k w_k$ and $\lim_k w_k \le b$. [step 4.1, L5, L7, L8, discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Remarks

- The two special cases are instances of the main claim, discharged in step 5.1 by taking one of the two sequences constant; that a constant sequence converges to its value ([[def-sequence]]) is the only extra ingredient they need.

- **The inequality does not become strict.** From $x_k < y_k$ for every $k$ one may conclude only $\lim x_k \le \lim y_k$; the witness $x_k = 0 < 1/(k+1) = y_k$ has equal limits ([[fs-limit-preserves-strict-inequality]]). Intuitively, the order relation $<$ is not preserved by passage to a limit because a strict gap may shrink to nothing, while $\le$ is preserved because it is closed under that shrinking.

- The proof routes through the single sequence $(z_k) = (y_k - x_k)$ and the difference rule of [[thm-algebra-of-limits]]. That is not an economy of writing only: it isolates the one thing being proved, namely that a sequence eventually $\ge 0$ cannot have a negative limit.

## Statement

For any finite set $S$, let $B(S)=\mathbb R^S$, the set of real-valued functions on $S$. Define

$$ d_\infty(U,V)=\begin{cases}0,&S=\emptyset,\\ \max_{s\in S}|U(s)-V(s)|,&S\ne\emptyset.\end{cases} $$

Then $d_\infty$ is a metric on $B(S)$ and $(B(S),d_\infty)$ is complete.

## Statement references

[Mozgovoy, *Lecture Notes on Metric Spaces and Functional Analysis*](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/~mozgovoy/data/notes_MS_2014.pdf).

[Sutton and Barto, *Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction*](https://web.stanford.edu/class/psych209/Readings/SuttonBartoIPRLBook2ndEd.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite set $S$ and the function space $B(S)=\mathbb R^S$.

[F1] [[def-countable]]: finiteness means there is a natural number $n$ and a bijection from $n=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ onto $S$; if $S$ is nonempty then $n\ge1$.

[F2] [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]: for $n\ge1$, $d_\infty(x,y)=\max_{k<n}|x_k-y_k|$ and $d_2(x,y)=(\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^2)^{1/2}$ are metrics on $\mathbb R^n$.

[F3] [[thm-cauchy-criterion-via-lub]]: every Cauchy sequence of reals converges to a real.

[F4] [[def-metric-space]] and [[def-complete-metric-space]]: a metric satisfies separation, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; completeness means every Cauchy sequence converges in the same metric space.

[F5] [[def-cauchy-in-metric]], [[def-metric-convergence]], and [[def-real-limit]]: metric Cauchy and convergence, as well as real Cauchy and convergence, are tested with rational $\varepsilon>0$.

[F6] [[lem-limit-unique]]: a convergent real sequence has a unique limit.

[F7] [[thm-well-ordering-principle]]: every nonempty set of natural numbers has a least element.

[F8] [[thm-induction-principle]] and [[thm-nat-linear-order]]: induction holds on $\mathbb N$, and its order is total.

## Proof

1.1 If $S=\emptyset$, then $B(S)$ has exactly one element, the empty function. Its only distance is $0$; nonnegativity, symmetry, separation, and the triangle inequality all hold on this singleton, and every sequence in it is constant and convergent. [given, F4]

1.2 Suppose $S\ne\emptyset$. By [F1], fix $n\ge1$ and a bijection $e:n\to S$. Pulling functions back along $e$ identifies $B(S)$ with $\mathbb R^n$ and carries $d_\infty$ exactly to the max metric of [F2]; hence it is a metric. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 Let $(U_m)$ be Cauchy in $d_\infty$ on $B(S)$. For each $j<n$, define the real sequence $x^{(j)}_m:=U_m(e(j))$. Given rational $\varepsilon>0$, the metric Cauchy condition supplies $K$ such that $d_\infty(U_m,U_\ell)<\varepsilon$ for all $m,\ell\ge K$. Since the pulled-back $d_\infty$ is the maximum of the coordinate differences, $|x^{(j)}_m-x^{(j)}_\ell|<\varepsilon$ for every $j<n$ and $m,\ell\ge K$. Thus each coordinate sequence is Cauchy in $\mathbb R$. [step 1.2, F2, F5]

2.2 By [F3], each coordinate sequence converges. Denote its unique limit by $y_j\in\mathbb R$, using [F6]. [step 2.1, F3, F6]

2.3 Define $U:S\to\mathbb R$ by $U(e(j)):=y_j$ for $j<n$. This is well defined because $e$ is a bijection, and it uses no choice because every $y_j$ is uniquely determined. [step 1.2, step 2.2, F1, F6]

3.1 Fix rational $\varepsilon>0$. For each $j<n$, convergence to $y_j$ gives a nonempty set of natural thresholds $K$ such that $|x^{(j)}_m-y_j|<\varepsilon$ for all $m\ge K$. Let $K_j$ be its least member, using [F7]. [step 2.2, F5, F7]

3.2 The finite nonempty list $K_0,\ldots,K_{n-1}$ has a maximum $K$: start with $K_0$ and, at each successor, retain the larger of the current maximum and the next threshold, which exists by the total order on $\mathbb N$; induction proves the resulting value dominates every entry. Thus $K\ge K_j$ for all $j<n$. [step 1.2, step 3.1, F8]

4.1 For every $m\ge K$, step 3.2 implies $|U_m(e(j))-U(e(j))|<\varepsilon$ for every $j<n$. Their finite maximum is one of these coordinate differences, so $d_\infty(U_m,U)<\varepsilon$. Since this holds for every rational $\varepsilon>0$, $(U_m)$ converges to $U$ in $d_\infty$. Every Cauchy sequence therefore converges in $B(S)$, and together with the metric property from steps 1.1–1.2 this proves completeness. [step 1.2, step 2.3, step 3.2, F2, F4, F5] ∎

## Remarks

- **The proof is a finite-coordinate Cauchy argument.** The maximum norm makes each coordinate sequence Cauchy; completeness of the real line supplies its limit; one maximum of finitely many thresholds then gives convergence in the maximum norm.
- **The same argument proves completeness for the $d_1$ metric on $\mathbb R^n$.** Each coordinate difference is at most $d_1$. Given rational $\varepsilon>0$, choose for every coordinate a threshold at tolerance $\varepsilon/(2n)$, which is again a positive rational; after taking their finite maximum, monotonicity of finite sums gives $d_1(x^{(m)},y)\le n\varepsilon/(2n)=\varepsilon/2<\varepsilon$. The $d_\infty$ case is proved above. No later result on this page uses the $d_1$ observation.
- **No choice is spent.** The limit point is assembled coordinatewise from unique limits, each threshold is the least one that works, and a common threshold is obtained by taking the maximum of finitely many indices. This matters because completeness proofs elsewhere on this page do spend $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and the contrast is worth keeping visible.
- **The real completeness input is localised.** The Cauchy criterion in $\mathbb R$ is the only completeness theorem used. Its proof obtains real completeness from the least-upper-bound property through Bolzano–Weierstrass; the finite-coordinate argument adds no other completeness assumption.

## Remarks references

[[lem-metrics-on-rn|The $d_1$ and $d_\infty$ metrics]].

[[lem-finite-sum-laws|Monotonicity and constant-summand laws for finite sums]].
