## Statement

Fix a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, an admissible heuristic with cap $V_{\max}$, and $0<\epsilon_1<1$. Put $D(s,a)=[U(s,a)-V^*(s)]_+$, $\kappa=\lceil SA V_{\max}/\epsilon_1\rceil$, $N=SA(1+\kappa)$, and $C_1=1+\gamma V_{\max}$. Run Delayed Q-learning with a positive integer $m$ satisfying
$$m\ge\left\lceil\frac{C_1^2}{2\epsilon_1^2}\ln\frac{8N}{\delta}\right\rceil\qquad(0<\delta<1).$$
For $V_t(s)=\max_aQ_t(s,a)$, define
$$K_t=\left\{(s,a):Q_t(s,a)-\left(r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)V_t(s')\right)\le3\epsilon_1\right\}.$$
With probability at least $1-\delta$, all estimates remain optimistic, $Q_t(s,a)\ge Q^*(s,a)$ for every $t,s,a$; every attempted update whose first sample is taken with its pair outside $K_t$ succeeds; the number of successful updates is at most
$$G=\sum_{s,a}\left(1+\frac{D(s,a)}{\epsilon_1}\right);$$
and the number of visits selecting a pair outside $K_t$ is at most $2mG$. The additive $1$ in each pair's update allowance is necessary, including when $U(s,a)=V^*(s)$.

## Statement references

[[alg-delayed-q-learning|The delayed batch target, success threshold, and global learning flags]].

[[def-admissible-mdp-heuristic|The admissible initial upper values and discounted-value cap]].

[[def-pac-mdp-known-state-action-mdp|The known-state/action model used to evaluate escape pairs]].

[[lem-pac-mdp-adaptive-sample-concentration|Conditional tails for bounded reward/next-state targets under adaptive visits]].

[[thm-pac-mdp-value-functions|The optimal action value and finite-state greedy maximizer]].

[Strehl, Li, and Littman, *Reinforcement Learning in Finite MDPs: PAC Analysis*](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume10/strehl09a/strehl09a.pdf).

[Strehl et al., *PAC Model-Free Reinforcement Learning*](https://hunch.net/~jl/projects/RL/Delayed_Q/icml06.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The MDP, admissible heuristic, Delayed Q-learning algorithm, and parameters in the Statement.

[F1] [[lem-pac-mdp-adaptive-sample-concentration]]: for a bounded predictable target $Y_i\in[0,C_1]$, its sample mean differs from its predictable mean by at least $x$ with probability at most $2e^{-2mx^2/C_1^2}$; pair visits can be coupled to independent potential outcomes.

[F2] [[alg-delayed-q-learning]]: a successful update replaces $Q(s,a)$ by a nonnegative batch mean plus $\epsilon_1$, decreases that entry by at least $\epsilon_1$, and Q-values never otherwise change.

[F3] [[def-admissible-mdp-heuristic]] and [[thm-pac-mdp-value-functions]]: initially $Q=U\ge Q^*$, $0\le Q^*,V^*\le V_{\max}$, and an optimal action attaining $V^*(s)$ exists at each state.

[F4] [[def-pac-mdp-known-state-action-mdp]]: the Bellman residual outside $K_t$ is strictly greater than $3\epsilon_1$; the known model agrees with the true MDP on $K_t$.

[F5] [[thm-finite-union-bound]]: a finite union of events has probability at most the sum of their probabilities.

## Proof

1.1 Each successful update decreases one entry by at least $\epsilon_1$, while every updated entry stays nonnegative and starts at most $V_{\max}$, by [F2]. Therefore the total number of updates is at most $SA V_{\max}/\epsilon_1\le\kappa$. An unsuccessful batch disables that pair until a later global update; the initial attempt and at most one new attempt per global update give at most $1+\kappa$ attempts per pair, hence at most $N$ batch starts overall. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 Condition on a batch-start history at time $k_1$ for pair $(s,a)$ and freeze $V_{k_1}$. The next $m$ potential joint outcomes give targets $X_i=R_i+\gamma V_{k_1}(S_i')\in[0,C_1]$ with common mean $r(s,a)+\gamma P V_{k_1}$. By [F1], except with probability $2e^{-2m\epsilon_1^2/C_1^2}$, their average is within $\epsilon_1$ of that mean. Also, the fixed targets $X_i^*=R_i+\gamma V^*(S_i')$ lie in $[0,C_1]$ and have mean $Q^*(s,a)$, so their average is within $\epsilon_1$ of $Q^*(s,a)$ except with the same probability. By [F5], a finite union over the at most $N$ batch starts and these two error events has failure at most $4N e^{-2m\epsilon_1^2/C_1^2}\le\delta/2$. [given, F1, F3, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 On the event from step 2.1, if a batch begins outside $K_{k_1}$, then $Q_{k_1}(s,a)-[r+\gamma P V_{k_1}]>3\epsilon_1$. During that batch all action values can only decrease, so $V_{k_i}\le V_{k_1}$ at every sample time $k_i$. Its actual target average is therefore at most the frozen-target average, which is at most $r+\gamma P V_{k_1}+\epsilon_1$. The old value minus this average is strictly greater than $2\epsilon_1$, so the attempted update succeeds. [given, F1, F2, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Initially $Q\ge Q^*$ by [F3]. Induct over successful updates. Before an update, all current values satisfy $V_{k_i}\ge V^*$ by the induction hypothesis, so each actual target $R_i+\gamma V_{k_i}(S_i')$ is at least $R_i+\gamma V^*(S_i')$. Step 2.1 bounds the latter sample mean below by $Q^*(s,a)-\epsilon_1$. Adding the update bonus $\epsilon_1$ leaves the new entry at least $Q^*(s,a)$; unchanged entries remain optimistic. This proves the all-time optimism claim. The event used above has probability at least $1-\delta/2\ge1-\delta$. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, induction]

4.1 Fix a pair $(s,a)$. If $U(s,a)<V^*(s)$, choose an optimal action $a^*$ at $s$. On the optimism event, $Q_t(s,a^*)\ge Q^*(s,a^*)=V^*(s)$ for every $t$, while the pair's value never increases and therefore stays at most $U(s,a)<V^*(s)$. It is never selected, so it cannot be updated. If $U(s,a)\ge V^*(s)$ and the pair is selected, its current value is the greedy maximum and hence at least $V^*(s)$ by optimism of $a^*$. If the pair has $n\ge1$ successful updates, the value immediately before its $n$th update is at most $U(s,a)-(n-1)\epsilon_1$ and at least $V^*(s)$. Indeed, each of the first $n-1$ updates decreases it by at least $\epsilon_1$, and if any post-update value were below $V^*(s)$, the pair could never be selected again. Thus $n\le1+[U(s,a)-V^*(s)]_+/\epsilon_1$. The same bound holds when $n=0$ and in the first case. Summing over pairs proves the stated bound $G$. [given, F2, F3, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 It remains to count visits outside $K_t$. First, a failed attempted update that disables the learning flag must leave the pair inside $K$: since $b>t^*$, no Q table entry changed after that batch began, so the residual was constant through the batch; if it had been outside at batch start, step 3.1 would have forced success. Consequently a visit outside $K_t$ cannot occur with the flag still disabled: before sampling, [F2] tests $b\le t^*$, and an outside residual after the failed batch requires a later global update, which re-enables the flag. Now fix an outside visit for a pair while its flag is true. The next attempted batch occurs within at most $m$ visits to that pair. If the batch began outside $K$, step 3.1 makes it successful. If it began inside $K$, the residual became outside by the escape visit after a global update; with the pair's own Q value unchanged, other Q values only decrease, so its Bellman backup can only decrease and its residual remains outside through the attempted batch. Because a global update occurred after that batch began, a failed attempt does not disable the flag. The next attempted batch occurs within at most another $m$ visits and starts outside $K$, so step 3.1 makes it successful. Thus every interval between successive successful updates of this pair, including the initial interval, contains at most $2m$ outside visits. To include a possible final unfinished interval, count only intervals containing an outside visit. If the pair has $n$ successful updates and such an interval remains after the last update, its Q-value at an outside selection is at least $V^*(s)$ by step 4.1, while its $n$ previous updates have decreased it by at least $n\epsilon_1$. Hence $n\epsilon_1\le D(s,a)$ and these $n+1$ intervals number at most $1+D(s,a)/\epsilon_1$. If there is no such final interval, the at most $n$ completed intervals have the same bound by step 4.1. An interval with fewer than the $2m$ visits needed for its next success is included in this count; an interval with $2m$ outside visits would force that success by the preceding argument. Summing over pairs therefore gives at most $2mG$. [given, F2, F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $M$ be a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, write $S=|S|$ and $A=\max_s|A(s)|$, and fix $0\le\epsilon<(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, $0<\delta<1$, and an admissible heuristic with normalized cap $V_{\max}$. At $\epsilon=0$, if $V^*(s)=0$ at every state then $N_0=0$; no finite zero-tolerance extension holds uniformly over this class: already at $\gamma=0$, every fixed finite legal sample threshold $m$ and value-iteration tolerance $\beta$ admits an admissible one-state example for R-MAX with $N_0=\infty$ with positive probability. This does not assert failure for every fixed heuristic or model. The parameter formulas below are evaluated only when $\epsilon>0$. Assume now $\epsilon>0$. If $\epsilon\ge V_{\max}$, then $N_\epsilon=0$. Otherwise put
$$\eta=\epsilon/4,\quad b=\frac{\eta(1-\gamma)}{64V_{\max}},\quad m=\left\lceil\frac{8(S+\ln(16SA/\delta))}{b^2}\right\rceil,\quad \beta=\frac{\eta(1-\gamma)}{16},$$
and run R-MAX with sample threshold $m$ and value-iteration tolerance $\beta$. Let $E_\eta=\{(s,a):U(s,a)\ge V^*(s)-\eta\}$ and $\zeta=(m+1)|E_\eta|$. Define $q=\eta/(4V_{\max})$, and define $H$ and $M$ by
$$H=\begin{cases}1,&\gamma=0,\\ \max\{1,\lceil\ln(1/[\eta(1-\gamma)])/(-\ln\gamma)\rceil\},&0<\gamma<1,\end{cases}\qquad M=\left\lceil\frac{2(\zeta+1)+2\ln(2/\delta)}q\right\rceil.$$
Then $\mathbb P(N_\epsilon\le HM)\ge1-\delta$. For the uninformative heuristic $U(s,a)=V_{\max}=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, the bound is $\widetilde O(S^2A/[\epsilon^3(1-\gamma)^6])$, where $\widetilde O$ suppresses logarithmic factors.

[Szepesvári, *Algorithms for Reinforcement Learning*](https://old.sztaki.hu/~szcsaba/papers/RLAlgsInMDPs-lecture.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The MDP, heuristic, parameters, R-MAX algorithm, and bad-step count in the Statement.

[F1] [[lem-r-max-empirical-model-accuracy]]: with the stated $m$ and $\beta$, the simultaneous optimism and model/policy accuracy conditions hold with probability at least $1-\delta/2$, and updates plus escapes total at most $(m+1)|E_\eta|$.

[F2] [[thm-pac-mdp-escape-event-reduction]]: if those conditions hold with failure probability at most $\rho$, then taking $B=W=V_{\max}$ and $Q_c=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$ gives $N_{4\eta}\le HM$ with failure probability at most $2\rho$ for the displayed $H,M$.

[F3] [[def-admissible-mdp-heuristic]]: $0\le V^*(s)\le V_{\max}$ and $U(s,a)\le V_{\max}$.

[F4] [[thm-zero-tolerance-pac-mdp-boundary]]: at zero tolerance the all-zero-optimal-value case has no bad steps; fixed finite legal R-MAX parameters admit an admissible one-state model with infinitely many zero-bad steps, with failure probability exceeding any prescribed confidence tolerance.

## Proof

1.1 If $\epsilon=0$, apply [F4] to obtain both stated endpoint branches. No finite sample-size or positive bonus is defined by substituting zero into the later formulas. For the remainder assume $\epsilon>0$. [given, F4, cases]

1.2 If $\epsilon\ge V_{\max}$, then $V^*(s)-\epsilon\le0$ for every state and every continuation value is nonnegative, so no time is counted. Assume now $\epsilon<V_{\max}$. The stated $\eta$ satisfies $0<\eta<V_{\max}/4$ and $\eta(1-\gamma)<1$. Apply [F1] with confidence parameter $\delta/2$; its sample threshold is exactly the displayed $m$. On its event, R-MAX has the hypotheses of [F2] with $\zeta=(m+1)|E_\eta|$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Take $\rho=\delta/2$ in [F2]. Since $4\eta=\epsilon$, the theorem gives $\mathbb P(N_\epsilon\le HM)\ge1-\delta$. [step 1.2, F2, algebra]

3.1 For the uninformative heuristic, $|E_\eta|\le SA$ and $V_{\max}=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$. The displayed $b$ gives $m=O((S+\ln(SA/\delta))V_{\max}^2/[\eta^2(1-\gamma)^2])$. Also $H=O((1-\gamma)^{-1}\ln(1/[\eta(1-\gamma)]))$, since $-\ln\gamma\ge1-\gamma$ for $0<\gamma<1$, and $M=O((V_{\max}/\eta)(\zeta+\ln(2/\delta)))$. Using $\zeta\le(m+1)SA$ and $\eta=\epsilon/4$ yields $\widetilde O(S^2A/[\epsilon^3(1-\gamma)^6])$. [given, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC, and use the history-conditioned bad-step count $N_\epsilon$ for bounded-reward finite discounted MDPs. The endpoint $\epsilon=0$ has the following properties.

1. Fix any single learning rule whose action kernels depend only on its observed history and common supplied inputs, not on the unknown MDP reward means. For every finite real $B\ge0$ and $0<\delta<1/2$, some one-state, two-action MDP with $\gamma=0$, Bernoulli rewards and the common admissible heuristic $U(a)=U(b)=V_{\max}=1$ satisfies $\mathbb P(N_0>B)>\delta$. Thus no finite bound depending only on state/action sizes, confidence and discount can hold uniformly at zero tolerance, even allowing randomized history-dependent learners.
2. For R-MAX, fix any integer $m\ge1$, $0<\beta<1$, and a tie order selecting $a$ first. For each $0<p<1$, take one state, $\gamma=0$, $U(a)=U(b)=V_{\max}=1$, reward $a\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$ and deterministic reward $b=p/2$. Then $\mathbb P(N_0=\infty)\ge(1-p)^m$. For every $0<\delta<1$, some $p$ makes this probability exceed $\delta$; no fixed finite legal sample threshold gives a uniform finite zero-tolerance bound.
3. For Delayed Q-learning, fix any integer $m\ge1$, $0<\epsilon_1<1$, and a tie order selecting $b$ first. In the one-state model with $\gamma=0$, $U(a)=U(b)=V_{\max}=1$ and deterministic rewards $a=1$, $b=1-\epsilon_1$, the algorithm chooses $b$ forever and $N_0=\infty$ with probability one.
4. If $V^*(s)=0$ at every state of any bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, then every behavior has $N_0=0$. The impossibility is a uniform assertion over unknown models, not a claim that zero-tolerance behavior must always fail.

All models in clauses1–3 have nonempty finite state/action sets, rewards in $[0,1]$, and an admissible normalized cap. No parameter formula that divides by $\epsilon$ is evaluated at zero.

## Statement references

[[def-pac-mdp-sample-complexity|History-conditioned bad-step counts, including zero tolerance]].

[[def-pac-mdp-bounded-reward-model|Finite MDPs and bounded joint transition/reward laws]].

[[def-admissible-mdp-heuristic|Admissibility and the normalized reward-scale cap]].

[[thm-pac-mdp-value-functions|Nonnegative continuation values and optimal values]].

[[alg-r-max|Finite first-batch empirical models and fixed tie order]].

[[alg-delayed-q-learning|The positive bonus, delayed batch update and learning flags]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the learning-rule information restriction, the finite bound and confidence in clause1, and the legal algorithm parameters and models in clauses2–4.

[F1] [[def-pac-mdp-sample-complexity]] and [[thm-pac-mdp-value-functions]]: when $\gamma=0$, continuation value is the mean immediate reward under the current action distribution; $N_0$ counts exactly the times this is strictly below the largest action mean. Every continuation value is nonnegative and at most $V^*$.

[F2] [[def-pac-mdp-bounded-reward-model]] and [[def-admissible-mdp-heuristic]]: one-state self-transitions with any reward law on $[0,1]$ are allowed; at $\gamma=0$, $U=V_{\max}=1$ is admissible for these models.

[F3] [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]: probabilities on a finite outcome space are sums of nonnegative weights with total one.

[F4] [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: finite sums preserve inequalities and distribute over finite products; in particular, summing normalized finite conditional weights recursively yields a normalized law on a finite history tree.

[F5] [[thm-of-archimedean]]: a natural number exceeds every prescribed finite real bound.

[F6] [[alg-r-max]]: before the first $m$ observations an action retains its heuristic; afterwards its model uses only those observations. At $\gamma=0$, every rebuild sets known action values to their empirical reward means after its first sweep.

[F7] [[alg-delayed-q-learning]]: the initial values are $U$; a completed batch changes its entry only if the old value minus its mean target is at least $2\epsilon_1$. A failed batch with start time greater than the last global update disables further learning of that pair until a new global update.

## Proof

1.1 For clause1, choose an integer $T>2B$ by [F5] and choose $0<d<\min\{1/2,(1-2\delta)/T\}$. Define two one-state models $M_+,M_-$ whose action means are respectively $(1/2+d,1/2)$ and $(1/2,1/2+d)$, with Bernoulli rewards, discount zero, and common heuristic $1$. Their unique optimal actions are respectively $a,b$, and [F2] verifies their model and heuristic conditions. [given, F2, F5, choose, construct, algebra]

1.2 For clause2 use the stated R-MAX model, and let $E$ be the event that its first $m$ rewards from $a$ are all zero. Its action means are $p,p/2$, so $a$ is uniquely optimal and [F2] verifies admissibility. [given, F2, construct]

1.3 For clause3 the action means are $1,1-\epsilon_1$, so $a$ is uniquely optimal, the gap is $\epsilon_1>0$, and [F2] verifies all model and heuristic conditions. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 Couple the two length-$T$ histories of step 1.1 recursively. At equal histories draw the same action with the learning rule’s common action probabilities. For that action let $r_+,r_-$ be its two means, and assign reward-pair probabilities $\min(r_+,r_-)$ to $(1,1)$, $1-\max(r_+,r_-)$ to $(0,0)$, $[r_+-r_-]_+$ to $(1,0)$, and $[r_--r_+]_+$ to $(0,1)$. These weights are nonnegative, sum to one, have the desired Bernoulli marginals, and disagree with probability $d$. After histories differ, use the product of the two prescribed action/reward laws. Finite recursive multiplication and summation as in [F3]–[F4] defines a finite coupling; induction over rounds verifies each marginal is the learning rule’s actual length-$T$ law. [step 1.1, F3, F4, construct, induction, algebra]

2.2 Until $a$ becomes known, R-MAX always selects $a$, since both unknown values are $1$ and its tie order favors $a$. On $E$, the first rebuild sets its value to zero while $b$ remains unknown at $1$. It therefore selects $b$ for $m$ observations, then the two frozen empirical means are $0,p/2$. All later rebuilds and actions retain those means, so $b$ is selected forever. By [F1], all those later times are zero-bad. The first $m$ draws from $a$ have their Bernoulli law conditionally at each visit, hence $\mathbb P(E)=(1-p)^m$ and $E\subseteq\{N_0=\infty\}$. [step 1.2, F1, F6, algebra, induction]

## Statement

Let $M$ be a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, write $S=|S|$ and $A=\max_s|A(s)|$, and fix $0\le\epsilon<(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, $0<\delta<1$, and an admissible heuristic with normalized cap $V_{\max}$. At $\epsilon=0$, if $V^*(s)=0$ at every state then $N_0=0$; no finite zero-tolerance extension holds uniformly over this class: already at $\gamma=0$, every fixed finite legal batch size $m$ and bonus $\epsilon_1$ admits an admissible one-state example for Delayed Q-learning with $N_0=\infty$ with positive probability. This does not assert failure for every fixed heuristic or model. The parameter formulas below are evaluated only when $\epsilon>0$. Assume now $\epsilon>0$. If $\epsilon\ge V_{\max}$, then $N_\epsilon=0$. Otherwise put
$$\eta=\epsilon/4,\quad \epsilon_1=\frac{\eta(1-\gamma)}3,\quad \kappa=\left\lceil\frac{SA V_{\max}}{\epsilon_1}\right\rceil,\quad N=SA(1+\kappa),\quad C_1=1+\gamma V_{\max},$$
and choose
$$m=\left\lceil\frac{C_1^2}{2\epsilon_1^2}\ln\frac{16N}{\delta}\right\rceil.$$
Run Delayed Q-learning with $m$ and $\epsilon_1$. Write $D(s,a)=[U(s,a)-V^*(s)]_+$, $G=\sum_{s,a}(1+D(s,a)/\epsilon_1)$, and $\zeta=\lceil(2m+1)G\rceil$. Define $q,H,M$ by
$$q=\frac{\eta}{4V_{\max}},\qquad H=\begin{cases}1,&\gamma=0,\\ \max\{1,\lceil\ln(1/[\eta(1-\gamma)])/(-\ln\gamma)\rceil\},&0<\gamma<1,\end{cases}\qquad M=\left\lceil\frac{2(\zeta+1)+2\ln(2/\delta)}q\right\rceil.$$
Then $\mathbb P(N_\epsilon\le HM)\ge1-\delta$. Equivalently, up to logarithmic factors, the bound is
$$\widetilde O\!\left(\frac{V_{\max}(1+\gamma V_{\max})^2\left[\sum_{s,a}D(s,a)+SA\epsilon(1-\gamma)\right]}{\epsilon^4(1-\gamma)^4}\right),$$
where $\widetilde O$ suppresses logarithmic factors. The additive term remains when all heuristic slacks vanish. For $V_{\max}=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$ this gives $\widetilde O(SA/[\epsilon^4(1-\gamma)^8])$.

## Statement references

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The MDP, admissible heuristic, Delayed Q-learning algorithm, and bad-step count in the Statement.

[F1] [[lem-delayed-q-learning-optimism-and-update-counts]]: with the displayed $m$, all estimates are optimistic, update/escape events total at most $(2m+1)G$, and the lemma event has failure probability at most its confidence parameter.

[F2] [[thm-pac-mdp-escape-event-reduction]]: taking $B=W=V_{\max}$ and $Q_c=V_{\max}$, optimism, policy accuracy at most $\eta$, and complexity at most $\zeta$ yield $N_{4\eta}\le HM$ with failure at most twice the confidence parameter.

[F3] [[def-admissible-mdp-heuristic]]: $V^*(s)\le V_{\max}$, so $N_\epsilon=0$ when $\epsilon\ge V_{\max}$.

[F4] [[def-pac-mdp-known-state-action-mdp]]: an action outside $K_t$ has known-model value exactly $Q_t(s,a)$, using its dedicated absorbing state.

[F5] [[thm-pac-mdp-value-functions]]: the policy value in a finite MDP solves its Bellman equation.

[F6] [[alg-delayed-q-learning]]: Q-values start at $U\in[0,V_{\max}]$ and each successful update replaces one value by a nonnegative quantity no larger than its old value.

[F7] [[thm-zero-tolerance-pac-mdp-boundary]]: at zero tolerance the all-zero-optimal-value case has no bad steps; fixed finite legal Delayed Q-learning parameters admit an admissible one-state model with infinitely many zero-bad steps, with failure probability exceeding any prescribed confidence tolerance.

## Proof

1.1 If $\epsilon=0$, apply [F7] to obtain both stated endpoint branches. No finite sample-size or positive bonus is defined by substituting zero into the later formulas. For the remainder assume $\epsilon>0$. [given, F7, cases]

1.2 If $\epsilon\ge V_{\max}$, then [F3] and nonnegativity of continuation values imply no bad step. Otherwise $\eta=\epsilon/4<V_{\max}/4$ and $\eta(1-\gamma)<1$. The displayed batch size is the lemma threshold [F1] with internal failure parameter $\delta/2$, so with probability at least $1-\delta/2$ all Q-values are optimistic and the update/escape count is at most $\zeta$. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

1.3 At each original state $s$, let $a=\pi_t(s)$. If $(s,a)\notin K_t$, the known-model value of that action is exactly $Q_t(s,a)=V_t(s)$ by [F4]. If $(s,a)\in K_t$, its Bellman backup at $V_t$ differs from $Q_t(s,a)$ above by at most $3\epsilon_1$, by the definition of $K_t$. Thus $V_t(s)\le T^{\pi_t}_{M_t}V_t(s)+3\epsilon_1$. Subtract the fixed-point equation in [F5] for $V^{\pi_t}_{M_t}$ and take the maximum positive difference over states; the stochastic transition rows give $\|V_t-V^{\pi_t}_{M_t}\|_{\infty,+}\le\gamma\|V_t-V^{\pi_t}_{M_t}\|_{\infty,+}+3\epsilon_1$, hence $V_t-V^{\pi_t}_{M_t}\le3\epsilon_1/(1-\gamma)=\eta$. [given, F1, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 The residual sets $K_t$ are history-measurable and change only after a Q update; they satisfy the stability condition of [F2]. By [F6], the Q table remains in $[0,V_{\max}]$. Step 1.2 supplies optimism and the count bound; step 1.3 supplies policy accuracy. Apply [F2] with $\rho=\delta/2$. Since $4\eta=\epsilon$, it gives $\mathbb P(N_\epsilon\le HM)\ge1-\delta$. [given, F1, F2, F6, step 1.2, step 1.3]

3.1 From the definitions, $G=[\sum_{s,a}D(s,a)+|D|\epsilon_1]/\epsilon_1\le[\sum_{s,a}D(s,a)+SA\epsilon_1]/\epsilon_1$, where $|D|=\sum_s|A(s)|\le SA$, $m=O((1+\gamma V_{\max})^2\epsilon_1^{-2}\ln(16N/\delta))$, and $M=O((V_{\max}/\eta)(mG+\ln(2/\delta)))$. Also $H=O((1-\gamma)^{-1}\ln(1/[\eta(1-\gamma)]))$: for $0<\gamma<1$, the function $x-1-\ln x$ has its minimum $0$ at $x=1$, so $-\ln\gamma\ge1-\gamma$. Substituting $\epsilon_1=\epsilon(1-\gamma)/12$ and $\eta=\epsilon/4$ into $H(V_{\max}/\eta)mG$ gives a constant multiple of $\frac{V_{\max}(1+\gamma V_{\max})^2[\sum_{s,a}D(s,a)+SA\epsilon(1-\gamma)]}{\epsilon^4(1-\gamma)^4}\ln\frac{16N}{\delta}\ln\frac{1}{\eta(1-\gamma)}$. The remaining $H(V_{\max}/\eta)\ln(2/\delta)$ term is bounded by the same expression up to logarithmic factors because $m\ge1$ and $G\ge|D|\ge1$. For the uninformative heuristic, $\sum D\le SA/(1-\gamma)$ and $1+\gamma V_{\max}=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$; substitution yields $\widetilde O(SA/[\epsilon^4(1-\gamma)^8])$. [given, F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

## Statement

Let $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ be a real sequence for which there is a finite constant $K$ with $|a_n|\le Kn$ for every $n\ge1$. Suppose there is a finite constant $C\ge0$ such that $|a_{m+n}-a_m-a_n|\le C$ for all positive integers $m,n$. Then $a_n/n$ has a finite limit as $n\to\infty$.

## Statement references

[Formal almost-additive result](https://isa-afp.org/browser_info/current/AFP/Ergodic_Theory/Fekete.html): Subsection “Almost additive sequences,” lemma `almost_additive_converges`.

[Textbook Fekete proof](https://www.cs.purdue.edu/homes/spa/courses/pg17/mybook.pdf): §5.1, Theorem 5.1.

[Independent real-analysis treatment](https://www.unige.ch/math/folks/velenik/smbook/Mathematical_Appendix.pdf): Appendix B.1.3, Lemma B.5.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The linear bound and the almost-additivity inequality in the Statement.

## Proof

1.1 Set $b_n=a_n+C$ and $c_n=a_n-C$. The upper half of the assumed inequality gives $a_{m+n}\le a_m+a_n+C$, hence $b_{m+n}\le b_m+b_n$. The lower half gives $a_{m+n}\ge a_m+a_n-C$, hence $c_{m+n}\ge c_m+c_n$. Also $|b_n|,|c_n|\le Kn+C$, so both sequences are bounded linearly. [given, algebra]

2.1 For a linearly bounded subadditive sequence $b$, fix $k\ge1$ and write $n=qk+r$ with $0\le r<k$. Iterating subadditivity, with $b_0=0$ for the remainder case, gives $b_n\le q b_k+b_r$. The finitely many possible remainder values have a finite maximum $B_k$, so $b_n/n\le q b_k/n+B_k/n$ and therefore $\limsup_n b_n/n\le b_k/k$. Since this holds for every $k$ and $\liminf_n b_n/n\ge\inf_k b_k/k$, the limit $b_n/n$ exists and is finite. Applying the same argument to $-c_n$ proves that $c_n/n$ has a finite limit. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $b_n/n-c_n/n=2C/n\to0$ and $c_n/n\le a_n/n\le b_n/n$, the two limits from step 2.1 coincide and force $a_n/n$ to that same finite limit. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $S$ be a finite nonempty state set and let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty action set for each $s\in S$, as in the finite-MDP convention. Put $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$ with its discrete sigma-algebra. Equip $S$ with its power-set sigma-algebra, $[0,1]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra, and $S\times[0,1]$ with the product sigma-algebra. A finite MDP with bounded real rewards specifies a probability kernel $Q$ from $D$ to $S\times[0,1]$; equivalently, each admissible $(s,a)$ has a probability measure $Q(\cdot\mid s,a)$ on that product measurable space. The reward-coordinate projection $(s',\rho)\mapsto\rho$ is measurable because the preimage of each Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$ is the product rectangle $S\times B$. Define the next-state law by $P(s'\mid s,a)=Q(\{s'\}\times[0,1]\mid s,a)$ and the mean reward by $r(s,a)=\int_{S\times[0,1]}\rho\,Q(ds',d\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$. At each time, conditional on the observed history and the selected action, the next-state/reward pair has this law. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path-space construction under policies.

[Borel sigma-algebra](../items/def-borel-sigma-algebra.md): specifies the Borel events on the reward interval.

[Product sigma-algebra](../items/def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras.md): specifies measurable events on $S\times[0,1]$.

[Probability measure](../items/def-probability-measure.md): $Q(\cdot\mid s,a)$ is a probability measure for each admissible pair.

[Probability kernel](../items/def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel.md): the family $Q$ has measurable event sections over the finite pair set $D$.

## Definition

Input finite nonempty state and action sets, upper reward estimates $\widetilde r(s,a)$, empirical transition laws $\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$, nonnegative transition radii $b_p(s,a)$, a tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, and fixed orders of the states and actions for tie-breaking. For a vector $v\in\mathbb R^S$, write $\operatorname{span}(v)=\max_s v(s)-\min_s v(s)$ and let $\Delta(S)$ be the probability simplex on $S$. Initialize $u_0(s)=0$. At iteration $i\ge1$, compute
$$u_i(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[\widetilde r(s,a)+\max_{q\in\Delta(S):\|q-\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)\|_1\le b_p(s,a)}q\cdot u_{i-1}\right].$$
For every state-action pair $(s,a)$, compute a maximizing transition vector as follows, using $v=u_{i-1}$. Put $q=\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$, $c=\min\{1,b_p(s,a)/2\}$, and order the states $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ by nondecreasing $v(x_j)$, using the fixed state order to break ties. Set $j=1$ and $\ell=m$. While $c>0$ and $j<\ell$, advance $j$ while $q(x_j)=0$, then decrease $\ell$ while $j<\ell$ and $q(x_\ell)=1$. If $j\ge\ell$, stop. If $v(x_j)\ge v(x_\ell)$, stop. Otherwise set $d=\min\{c,q(x_j),1-q(x_\ell)\}$, replace $q(x_j)$ by $q(x_j)-d$ and $q(x_\ell)$ by $q(x_\ell)+d$, and replace $c$ by $c-d$; repeat. Each positive transfer either uses all remaining mass or exhausts a source coordinate or fills a destination coordinate, so the loop takes at most $2m+1$ positive transfers. It moves at most $b_p(s,a)/2$ mass, hence the resulting vector is feasible. Any feasible vector redistributes at most this much mass from coordinates it decreases to coordinates it increases. Pairing the least-valued available source with the greatest-valued available destination first maximizes the linear gain; the procedure continues exactly while such a pair has positive gain and capacity. Thus the resulting $q_{i,s,a}$ maximizes $q\cdot u_{i-1}$ over the stated confidence set. The inner maximum exists because each nonempty feasible subset of $\Delta(S)$ is compact.

For each state, compute $B_i(s,a)=\widetilde r(s,a)+q_{i,s,a}\cdot u_{i-1}$ for every action, record the first action $a_i(s)$ in the fixed action order attaining $\max_{a\in A(s)}B_i(s,a)$, and set $q_i(\cdot\mid s)=q_{i,s,a_i(s)}$. If $\operatorname{span}(u_i-u_{i-1})<\varepsilon$, return the stationary deterministic policy $\pi_i(s)=a_i(s)$, its corresponding maximizing transition rows $q_i$, the vector $u_{i-1}$ used in that backup, and the iteration index. The finite sort-and-fill operations and fixed tie rules make the returned quantities measurable functions of the estimates. Otherwise continue. The algorithm is a partial procedure unless a separate termination result is established.

## Definition

For a finite MDP with bounded rewards, a policy assigns a probability distribution on $A(s)$ to each finite observed history ending in state $s$, with each action probability a measurable function of the history; deterministic policies are included. For states $x,y$, start at $S_0=x$ and define $\tau_y=\inf\{t\ge0:S_t=y\}$. The MDP is communicating if $\inf_\pi\mathbb E_x^\pi[\tau_y]<\infty$ for every ordered pair $(x,y)$. Its raw diameter is $D_0=\max_{x,y}\inf_\pi\mathbb E_x^\pi[\tau_y]$, and its normalized diameter is $D=\max\{1,D_0\}$. Thus a one-state MDP has $D_0=0$ and $D=1$.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path-space construction. Fix a finite-horizon interaction of length $T$ in a finite MDP with bounded rewards and any nonanticipating policy: each action distribution is a measurable function of the revealed history, and policy randomization is independent of unexposed MDP samples. ## Statement

For every finite nonempty state/action system, bounded real upper rewards, probability-vector empirical centers, strictly positive transition radii, and tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, extended value iteration terminates. More precisely, write $F$ for its optimistic Bellman operator, put $\eta=\min_{s,a}\min\{1,b_p(s,a)/2\}>0$, and set $u_0=0$, $u_i=F(u_{i-1})$. Then
$$\operatorname{span}(u_i-u_{i-1})\le(1-\eta)^{i-1}\operatorname{span}(u_1),\qquad i\ge1.$$
When $\eta=1$, the span is zero for $i\ge2$. In particular, the positive UCRL2 confidence radii give finite stopping with tolerance $1/\sqrt{t_k}$ in every episode of a finite communicating MDP, including episodes whose confidence set misses the true model.

## Proof

1.1 For a probability vector $p$ and $0<\alpha\le1$, the ball $Q=\{q\in\Delta(S):\|q-p\|_1\le2\alpha\}$ equals the set of $z+w$ with $0\le z\le p$, $\sum z=1-\alpha$, $w\ge0$, and $\sum w=\alpha$. Indeed, if $q\in Q$, the coordinatewise minimum $p\wedge q$ has mass $1-\|p-q\|_1/2\ge1-\alpha$; scaling that minimum down to mass $1-\alpha$ gives such $z\le q$, and $w=q-z$. (For $\alpha=1$, take $z=0$.) Conversely $p-z$ and $w$ are nonnegative of mass $\alpha$, so $\|z+w-p\|_1\le2\alpha$. Consequently the support function is $\alpha\max_j v(j)+H_p^\alpha(v)$, where $H_p^\alpha(v)=\max_{0\le z\le p,\,\sum z=1-\alpha}z\cdot v$. This equality includes radii at least $2$, for which $\alpha=1$ and the ball is the whole simplex. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Put $\alpha_{s,a}=\min\{1,b_p(s,a)/2\}$. If $\eta<1$, step 1.1 writes $F(v)=\eta\max_j v(j)\mathbf1+(1-\eta)G(v)$, where $$G(v)(s)=\max_a\frac{\widetilde r(s,a)+(\alpha_{s,a}-\eta)\max_j v(j)+H_{\widehat P_{s,a}}^{\alpha_{s,a}}(v)}{1-\eta}.$$ The map $G$ is monotone in every coordinate. Each expression inside its maximum increases by $c$ on replacing $v$ by $v+c\mathbf1$, because its coefficient mass is $(\alpha_{s,a}-\eta)+(1-\alpha_{s,a})=1-\eta$. Thus $G(v+c\mathbf1)=G(v)+c\mathbf1$. If $m=\min(v-w)$ and $M=\max(v-w)$, monotonicity applied to $w+m\mathbf1\le v\le w+M\mathbf1$ implies $m\mathbf1\le G(v)-G(w)\le M\mathbf1$. The common scalar term in the expression for $F$ disappears from span, giving $\operatorname{span}(F(v)-F(w))\le(1-\eta)\operatorname{span}(v-w)$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Apply step 2.1 repeatedly to $u_i=F(u_{i-1})$ and $u_{i-1}=F(u_{i-2})$. This proves the displayed geometric bound by induction. Its right side tends to zero, so the strict span test holds at some finite iteration for every positive tolerance. If $\eta=1$, every row ball is the whole simplex and $F(v)(s)=\max_a\widetilde r(s,a)+\max_jv(j)$; hence $F(v)-F(w)$ is constant across states and every increment after the first has zero span. ## Statement

Let a finite MDP have $S\ge1$ states and at most $A\ge1$ actions per state, and let $T\ge1$ be an integer and $\delta\in(0,1)$. With probability at least $1-\delta$, simultaneously for all such pairs and all $1\le n\le T$,
$$|\widehat r_n(s,a)-r(s,a)|\le\sqrt{\frac{7\log(4SAT/\delta)}{2n}},\qquad \|\widehat P_n(\cdot\mid s,a)-P(\cdot\mid s,a)\|_1\le\sqrt{\frac{14S\log(4AT/\delta)}{n}},$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

## Statement references

[Axiom of Choice](../items/def-axiom-of-choice.md): assumed for the path-law and martingale suppliers.

[UCRL2 confidence analysis](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume11/jaksch10a/jaksch10a.pdf): Appendix A and §4.1, PDF pp. 10–11 and 22–24.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite bounded-reward MDP, its fixed conditional law for each state-action pair, and the parameters in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-bounded-reward-finite-mdp]]: conditional on the pre-observation history and the selected pair, the reward and next state have the fixed law $Q(\cdot\mid s,a)$.

[F2] [[lem-ucrl2-adaptive-sample-tape-representation]]: adaptive visits reveal prefixes of fixed i.i.d. sample tapes without changing the interaction law.

[F3] [[thm-azuma-hoeffding-inequality]]: for a martingale with increments of deterministic widths $c_k$, each one-sided tail is at most $\exp(-2t^2/\sum_k c_k^2)$.

[F4] [[def-martingale-difference-sequence]]: centered independent tape coordinates form a martingale-difference sequence in their natural filtration.

[F5] [[thm-martingales-and-martingale-differences-correspond]]: partial sums of martingale differences are martingales relative to the same filtration.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is used by [F2]'s path-space construction, [F3]'s conditional expectations, and [F4]–[F5]'s martingale interfaces; the finite union bounds and subset enumeration use no additional choice.

## Proof

1.1 By [F2], each pair's observed samples are prefixes of a fixed i.i.d. tape with law $Q(\cdot\mid s,a)$. By [F1], its reward coordinate has mean $r(s,a)$ and its next-state coordinate has law $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$. Rewards and indicators of next-state subsets lie in $[0,1]$. The finite tape construction uses AC exactly as stated in [A1]. [given, F1, F2, A1]

2.1 By [F4] and [F5], the centered reward tape prefix has martingale partial sums with width-one increments; applying [F3] to that sum and to its negative gives the two-sided prefix tail $2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}$. For a fixed pair and $n$, set $\varepsilon_r=\sqrt{7\log(4SAT/\delta)/(2n)}$. Step 1.1 bounds the failure probability by $2(\delta/(4SAT))^7$. Union over at most $SA$ pairs and $T$ possible prefix lengths gives at most $2SAT(\delta/(4SAT))^7\le\delta/2$. [given, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For transition observations, fix a subset $B\subseteq S$. By step 1.1, the indicators $\mathbf1_{\{S'\in B\}}$ have mean $P(B\mid s,a)$ and range $[0,1]$. Their centered tape coordinates satisfy [F4]; by [F5] their partial sums are martingales, so [F3] gives $2e^{-2n u^2}$ for a deviation larger than $u$. For two probability vectors $p,q$ on a finite set, $\|p-q\|_1=2\max_{B\subseteq S}|p(B)-q(B)|$: the positive coordinates of $p-q$ sum to half its $\ell^1$ norm, and choosing exactly those coordinates attains the maximum. Therefore an $\ell^1$ deviation larger than $\varepsilon$ implies that some subset indicator deviates by more than $\varepsilon/2$. A union bound over the $2^S$ subsets gives $2^{S+1}e^{-n\varepsilon^2/2}$. [given, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Set $L=\log(4AT/\delta)$ and $\varepsilon_p=\sqrt{14S L/n}$. Step 2.2 gives per-pair, per-prefix failure probability at most $2^{S+1}e^{-7SL}$. Union over at most $SAT$ pairs and prefixes is at most $SAT2^{S+1}e^{-7SL}\le\delta/2$: after dividing by $\delta/2$, its logarithm is $\log S+L+S\log2-7SL\le(2S)L-7SL\le0$, using $S\le2^{S-1}$ and $L\ge\log2$. Combining the reward failure bound from step 2.1 with the transition bound just obtained proves the simultaneous claim. [given, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. If $M$ is a martingale, then $D_n=M_n-M_{n-1}$, $n\ge1$, is a martingale difference sequence. Conversely, given a martingale difference sequence $D$ and any integrable $\mathcal F_0$-measurable real $M_0$, the process $M_n=M_0+\sum_{k=1}^nD_k$ is a martingale. For fixed $M_0$ these constructions are inverse.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses and conventions in the statement.

[F1] Conditional expectation is linear, order preserving and expectation preserving. [[thm-basic-algebra-and-order-properties-of-conditional-expectation]].

[F2] An integrable variable measurable for the conditioning sigma-algebra conditions to itself. [[lem-conditioning-a-known-variable-and-an-independent-variable]].

[F3] Finite linear combinations remain integrable and their integrals are linear. [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]].

[F4] Finite real sums, differences and products are measurable. [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]].

[F5] AC supplies the inherited conditional-expectation existence and any stated choice of versions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F6] A martingale difference is integrable and has zero conditional mean given the preceding sigma-algebra. [[def-martingale-difference-sequence]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 First reconstruct the finite-integral interface used below. Augment every finite disjoint display of a nonnegative simple function by the complement of its displayed sets with coefficient $0$. Intersections of two augmented displays partition the whole space, and equality of the functions makes their coefficients agree on every nonempty cell. Finite additivity and $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ therefore prove representation independence. Common augmented refinements give monotonicity and additivity term by term; homogeneity is direct when the scalar is zero and termwise when it is positive. Taking suprema over simple minorants gives nonnegative monotonicity, and increasing simple approximations together with the sets $\{f_j\ge cs\}$, $0<c<1$, give monotone convergence. Applying this to sums of increasing simple approximants gives nonnegative additivity. Positive/negative and real/imaginary decompositions now give the finite real and complex $L^1$ linearity used in [F3]. With this replacement for the affected foundation, the event-integral construction and uniqueness proof of the cited conditional-expectation algebra apply. For a martingale $M$, both $M_n$ and $M_{n-1}$ are $\mathcal F_n$-measurable. Their difference $D_n$ is measurable and integrable, with $E|D_n|\le E|M_n|+E|M_{n-1}|<\infty$. By linearity and conditioning the known $M_{n-1}$, $E[D_n\mid\mathcal F_{n-1}]=M_{n-1}-M_{n-1}=0$. This meets the difference definition. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, construct]

1.2 Conversely every summand $D_k$ for $k\le n$ is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable, as is $M_0$. The finite sum is adapted and integrable by [F3]–[F4]. Its next increment is $D_{n+1}$, so $E[M_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=E[M_n+D_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=M_n+0=M_n$. Thus it is a martingale [[def-martingale-submartingale-and-supermartingale]]. AC is inherited from the conditional classes; if versions of a class sequence are to be chosen, AC permits those countably many selections. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6]

2.1 The finite identities $\sum_{k=1}^n(M_k-M_{k-1})=M_n-M_0$ and $(M_0+\sum_{k=1}^nD_k)-(M_0+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}D_k)=D_n$ prove inverse reconstruction. For $n=0$ the sum is empty and equals zero, so the initial value is exactly the prescribed $M_0$. For class representatives these finite equalities hold almost surely. [step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path-law and conditional-expectation constructions. For a finite communicating MDP with rewards in $[0,1]$, let $V_n(s)$ be the supremum of the expected sum of the first $n$ rewards over all history-dependent policies starting from state $s$. For every state $s$, the limit $\lim_{n\to\infty}V_n(s)/n$ exists, is independent of $s$, and belongs to $[0,1]$.

## Statement references

[UCRL2 average-reward framework](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume11/jaksch10a/jaksch10a.pdf): §2 and Theorem 2, PDF pp. 2–4.

[Average-reward MDP treatment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/martyput/MDP_book/master/07%20Chapter/Book___chapter07.pdf): Chapter 7.

[Axiom of Choice](../items/def-axiom-of-choice.md): assumed for the path-law and conditional-expectation constructions.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite communicating MDP as defined in [[def-bounded-reward-finite-mdp]] and [[def-communicating-mdp-and-diameter]], and the Axiom of Choice for the induced path laws.

[F1] [[def-bounded-reward-finite-mdp]]: every reward lies in $[0,1]$ and the conditional next-state/reward law is fixed for each state-action pair.

[F2] [[def-communicating-mdp-and-diameter]]: every pair of states can be connected with expected hitting time arbitrarily close to at most the finite raw diameter $D_0$.

[F3] [[lem-almost-additive-sequence-has-limit]]: a linearly bounded sequence with uniformly bounded additive defect has a normalized limit.

[F4] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is used for the path laws in [F1] and the conditional-expectation constructions in [F5] and [F6].

[F5] [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]: conditional expectations are unique almost-sure classes; the proof uses versions only through conditional inequalities.

[F6] [[thm-tower-property-of-conditional-expectation]]: conditioning a finite-horizon reward sum at time $m$ and then taking expectation recovers its unconditional expectation.

[F7] [[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]: expectations are linear on integrable finite sums and preserve inequalities.

[F8] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]: bounded rewards and their finite sums are integrable and have the stated expectations.

## Proof

1.1 Set $V_0(s)=0$ for every state. Backward induction over the finite horizon gives the Bellman recurrence
$$V_{n+1}(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[r(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V_n(s')\right].$$
For the induction step, suppose that from every state the $n$-step supremum is attained by a deterministic Markov policy and equals $V_n$. Any history-dependent $(n+1)$-step policy may randomize its first action and may condition later actions on the first reward as well as the next state. Conditional on a first action $a$ and one-step outcome $(s',\rho)$, its continuation has expected reward at most $V_n(s')$ by the induction hypothesis, which is independent of the earlier history and reward. Thus its total expected reward is at most $r(s,a)+\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)V_n(s')$, averaged over its first-action distribution, and this average is at most the displayed maximum. A maximizing action exists because $A(s)$ is finite; choosing it and then using an attaining $n$-step policy from each possible next state attains equality. The base case $V_0=0$ is attained by the empty policy. This proves both the recurrence and that history dependence cannot improve $V_n$; the joint reward/next-state law is handled by its mean reward and next-state marginal.

For any $0\le j\le n$, splitting an $n$-step policy into its first $n-j$ and last $j$ rewards gives $V_n(y)\le V_{n-j}(y)+j$: the first part is at most the optimal $(n-j)$-step value and the last part is at most $j$ because rewards lie in $[0,1]$. For any $x,y$ and $\varepsilon>0$, [F2] gives a policy from $x$ whose hitting time $\tau_y$ has expectation at most $D_0+\varepsilon$. Follow it until $y$ is hit, then use an optimal policy for the remaining $n-\tau_y$ steps if $\tau_y\le n$. On that event the total reward is at least $V_{n-\tau_y}(y)\ge V_n(y)-\tau_y$, since pre-hit rewards are nonnegative. On $\tau_y>n$, the total reward is nonnegative and $V_n(y)\le n<\tau_y$. Taking expectations and using [F8] gives $V_n(x)\ge V_n(y)-\mathbb E[\tau_y]\ge V_n(y)-D_0-\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and interchanging $x,y$ proves $\max_s V_n(s)-\min_s V_n(s)\le D_0$. [given, F1, F2, F4, F8, construct, algebra]

2.1 Put $a_n=\max_s V_n(s)$; the maximum exists because $S$ is finite, and $0\le a_n\le n$ by [F1,F8]. For any $(m+n)$-step policy from $s$, the expected first $m$ rewards are at most $V_m(s)$, while conditional on the complete history through state $S_m$ the remaining $n$-step rule is an admissible policy from $S_m$ and its conditional expected reward is at most $V_n(S_m)\le a_n$. By [F4,F5,F6,F7], the unconditional expected total is therefore at most $V_m(s)+a_n\le a_m+a_n$, so $a_{m+n}\le a_m+a_n$. Conversely, choose $s_*$ attaining $a_m$ and use an optimal $m$-step policy from it; after observing $S_m=z$, continue with an optimal $n$-step policy from $z$. By step 1.1, $V_n(z)\ge a_n-D_0$ for every $z$, so [F4,F6,F7] give total expected reward at least $a_m+a_n-D_0$. Hence $a_{m+n}\ge a_m+a_n-D_0$, and $|a_{m+n}-a_m-a_n|\le D_0$. [given, F1, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, step 1.1, algebra] 

3.1 Apply [F3] to $(a_n)$ with $C=D_0$ to obtain $a_n/n\to\rho^*$ for some finite $\rho^*$. Step 1.1 gives $a_n-D_0\le V_n(s)\le a_n$ for every $s$, so division by $n$ proves $V_n(s)/n\to\rho^*$ for every state. The bounds $0\le V_n(s)\le n$ imply $\rho^*\in[0,1]$. [given, F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Definition

The learner is given a finite nonempty state set $\mathcal S$, a finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ for each $s\in\mathcal S$, the observed initial state $s_1\in\mathcal S$, a horizon $T\ge1$, a confidence parameter $\delta\in(0,1)$, and fixed orders of the states and each state's actions. Let $S=|\mathcal S|$ and $A=\max_{s\in\mathcal S}|A(s)|$. Its unknown environment is a finite communicating MDP on $\mathcal S$ and these action sets with rewards in $[0,1]$; the transition kernel, reward laws, and their means are not inputs to the learner. At interaction $t$, the learner observes the current state $S_t$, chooses an admissible action, and then observes the realized reward $\rho_t$ and next state $S_{t+1}$.

Initialize $t=1$ and $S_1=s_1$. At the start $t_k$ of episode $k$, let $N_k(s,a)$ be the total number of visits to $(s,a)$ before $t_k$. If $N_k(s,a)>0$, let $\widehat r_k(s,a)$ be the mean of the rewards observed on those visits and $\widehat P_k(\cdot\mid s,a)$ their empirical next-state law. If $N_k(s,a)=0$, set $\widehat r_k(s,a)=0$ and set $\widehat P_k(\cdot\mid s,a)$ to the point mass at the first state in the fixed state order. Put $n_k(s,a)=\max\{1,N_k(s,a)\}$ and
$$b^r_k(s,a)=\sqrt{\frac{7\log(2SAt_k/\delta)}{2n_k(s,a)}},\qquad b^p_k(s,a)=\sqrt{\frac{14S\log(2At_k/\delta)}{n_k(s,a)}}.$$
Set $\widetilde r_k(s,a)=\min\{1,\widehat r_k(s,a)+b^r_k(s,a)\}$. Run extended value iteration with these estimates/radii and tolerance $1/\sqrt{t_k}$, obtaining a stationary deterministic policy $\pi_k$. Set every within-episode count $v_k(s,a)=0$ and execute the following loop. While $t\le T$, observe $S_t$, choose $a_t=\pi_k(S_t)$, observe $\rho_t$ and $S_{t+1}$, increment $v_k(S_t,a_t)$ and the all-history count for $(S_t,a_t)$, record this reward/transition observation, and retain the observed next state as the current state for the next interaction. Increment $t$ by one. End the episode immediately after an interaction when its pair's count reaches $v_k(s,a)=\max\{1,N_k(s,a)\}$, where $N_k$ remains the episode-start count; if $t\le T$, begin the next episode, otherwise terminate. All action and transition-vector ties use the fixed orders. The positive radii ensure finite inner termination by the separate termination lemma. In particular, always $v_k(s,a)\le\max\{1,N_k(s,a)\}$; when $N_k(s,a)>0$, a completed triggering episode doubles that pair's total count.

## Definition

## Proof

1.1 Fix $T\ge2$. At any integer time $t\ge1$, use [F4] to apply [F5] to every fixed pair and prefix length $1\le n<t$. Rewards give two-sided probability $2e^{-2nu^2}$; subset indicators give the same bound. For probability vectors $p,q$, $\|p-q\|_1=2\max_{B\subseteq S}|p(B)-q(B)|$, by summing positive coordinates of $p-q$. Union over $2^S$ subsets therefore bounds an $\ell^1$ error exceeding $u$ by $2^{S+1}e^{-nu^2/2}$. Substituting the algorithm's radii, and unioning over at most $SAt$ pairs and prefixes, bounds reward failure at time $t$ by $2SAt(\delta/(2SAt))^7\le\delta/(64t^6)$, and transition failure by $SAt2^{S+1}(\delta/(2At))^{7S}\le\delta/(32t^6)$. The latter follows from $S2^{1-6S}\le1/32$, whose value at $S=1$ is $1/32$ and whose successive ratio is $(S+1)/(64S)<1$. Unobserved-pair reward radii exceed $1$ and transition radii exceed $2$, so their defaults cannot fail. Since $\sum_{t\ge1}t^{-6}\le1+\int_1^\infty x^{-6}dx=6/5$, with probability at least $1-\delta/8$ every confidence set at every time contains the true transition/reward means. Denote this event by $E$. There is no conditioning on an adaptively selected count in this argument. [given, F1, F4, F5, A1, algebra]

2.1 In an episode whose confidence set contains the true model, let $F$ be its optimistic Bellman operator. Its iterates $U_n=F^n0$ are optimal $n$-step values for the extended transition choices and fixed upper rewards, by finite-horizon backward induction and attained maxima. Upper rewards are in $[0,1]$, and true transitions and rewards are dominated admissible choices. Thus $U_n\ge V_n$. Also $\operatorname{span}(U_n)\le D$: from $x$, follow a true-model policy hitting $y$ in expected time at most $D+\xi$, and then an optimal remaining-horizon extended policy. The inequality $U_n(y)\le U_{n-j}(y)+j$ follows by dropping the last $j$ rewards, each at most one. For hitting time $\tau$, this yields total expected reward at least $U_n(y)-\mathbb E\tau$, including $\tau>n$ because $U_n(y)\le n$ and rewards are nonnegative. Take $\xi\downarrow0$ and interchange $x,y$. A true history policy's state/action path law can be realized in the extended system by its conditional action probabilities given state/action history; finite histories have finite state/action alphabets, so this averaging preserves its state transitions and hitting-time law. [given, F1, F3, algebra, construct, step 1.1]

3.1 Let $h_k$ be the vector used in the terminating backup, and let $d_k=F(h_k)-h_k$, with extrema $m_k,M_k$. By [F2], $M_k-m_k<\varepsilon_k=1/\sqrt{t_k}$. Monotonicity and additive homogeneity give $F^nh_k\le h_k+nM_k\mathbf1$. Also $F$ is sup-norm nonexpansive, since $v\le w+c\mathbf1$ implies $Fv\le Fw+c\mathbf1$ and conversely. Therefore $U_n\le h_k+nM_k\mathbf1+\|h_k\|_\infty\mathbf1$. Combine with $U_n\ge V_n$ and [F3], divide by $n$, and pass to the limit to get $\rho^*\le M_k$. Consequently $d_k(s)\ge\rho^*-\varepsilon_k$. For the chosen action and row, $d_k(s)=\widetilde r_k(s,a)+q_k(\cdot\mid s,a)h_k-h_k(s)$. On a good episode, $\widetilde r_k-r\le2b^r_k$ and $\|q_k-P\|_1\le2b^p_k$; step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{span}(h_k)\le D$. Centering $h_k$ halfway between its extrema bounds its sup norm by $D/2$, so $(q_k-P)h_k\le Db^p_k$. Hence each step of that episode obeys $\rho^*-r(s,a)\le (Ph_k)(s,a)-h_k(s)+Db^p_k(s,a)+2b^r_k(s,a)+\varepsilon_k$. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Subtract $\min h_k$ from each episode vector. On good episodes it lies in $[0,D]$. For the probabilistic argument define $w_k$ to be that vector when the episode's confidence set contains the true means and zero otherwise. This is measurable at the episode start, since true means are fixed parameters; its coordinates always lie in $[0,D]$. The increments $X_t=(Pw_{k(t)})(S_t,A_t)-w_{k(t)}(S_{t+1})$ are conditionally centered with conditional range width at most $D$. The reward differences $Y_t=r(S_t,A_t)-\rho_t$ are conditionally centered with width at most $1$, even if reward and next state are correlated. Apply [F5] separately with failure probability $\delta/4$ to obtain $\sum_{t\le T}X_t\le D\sqrt{(T/2)\log(4/\delta)}$ and $\sum_{t\le T}Y_t\le\sqrt{(T/2)\log(4/\delta)}$. These events and $E$ jointly have probability at least $1-\delta$, by step 1.1 and a union bound. On their intersection every episode is good; the sum of $(Ph_k)(S_t,A_t)-h_k(S_t)$ equals $\sum X_t$ plus episode endpoint differences, each at most $D$. [given, F1, F5, A1, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Write $K=\sum_s|A(s)|\le SA$ and $Q_T=\sum_{k,s,a}v_k(s,a)/\sqrt{\max\{1,N_k(s,a)\}}$. For a fixed visited pair, the first observation contributes one. Thereafter, for $N\ge1$ and $0\le v\le N$, rationalization gives $v/\sqrt N=(\sqrt{N+v}-\sqrt N)(\sqrt{1+v/N}+1)\le(1+\sqrt2)(\sqrt{N+v}-\sqrt N)$. Telescoping, including the first observation, and then Cauchy--Schwarz yield $Q_T\le(1+\sqrt2)\sum_{s,a}\sqrt{N_T(s,a)}\le(1+\sqrt2)\sqrt{SAT}$. A completed episode can be charged to a triggering pair. A pair with final count $N$ receives at most $1+\log_2\max\{1,N\}$ charges, because after its initial observation every charge doubles its total. The last incomplete episode adds at most one. Thus concavity of $\log$ gives $m\le1+K+K\log_2(1+T/K)$. When $T\ge K$, this is at most $K(3+\log_2(T/K))\le4\sqrt{KT}\le4\sqrt{SAT}$. For the last inequality set $x=T/K\ge1$: $4\sqrt x-3-\log_2x$ is positive at $1$ and has derivative $(2\sqrt x-1/\log2)/x>0$, since $\log2>1/2$. [given, F1, algebra, step 4.1]

6.1 On the joint event of step 4.1, sum step 3.1 and use $\max\{1,N_k(s,a)\}\le t_k\le T$. With $L_r=\log(2SAT/\delta)$ and $L_p=\log(2AT/\delta)$ this gives the fully explicit bound $$\Delta_T\le\left[D\sqrt{14S L_p}+\sqrt{14L_r}+1\right]Q_T+Dm+(D+1)\sqrt{\frac T2\log(4/\delta)}.$$ The $1$ in the bracket bounds the planning error $\sum_k\ell_k/\sqrt{t_k}$ by $Q_T$. This argument bounds realized regret; it does not replace rewards by their expectation without the martingale term. [given, F1, F3, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Put $L=\log(T/\delta)$ and $B=DS\sqrt{ATL}$. If $T<SA$, then $\Delta_T\le T\le\sqrt{SAT}<34B$, since $D\ge1$ and $L\ge\log2>1/2$. Suppose $T\ge SA$ and $S\ge2$. Then $L_r\le3L$, $L_p\le2L$ (because $2A\le SA\le T$), and $\log(4/\delta)\le2L$. Divide step 6.1 by $B$ and apply step 5.1, $D\ge1$, and $A\ge1$ to bound the resulting coefficient by $$(1+\sqrt2)\left[\sqrt{28}+\sqrt{42/S}+\frac1{\sqrt{SL}}\right]+\frac4{\sqrt{SL}}+\frac2{S\sqrt A}<\frac52\left(\frac{16}3+\frac{14}3+1\right)+4+1=\frac{65}2<34.$$ Here $S\ge2$, $L>1/2$, $\sqrt{28}<16/3$, $\sqrt{21}<14/3$, and $1+\sqrt2<5/2$ justify each numerical bound. [given, F3, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 Suppose $S=1$. Then $D=1$ by [F3], every Bellman vector $h_k$ has a single coordinate, and both transition rows are the point mass at the only state. Dividing the displayed inequality by $B=\sqrt{ATL}$ and using step 5.1 yields $$\frac{\Delta_T}{B}\le(1+\sqrt2)\left(\sqrt{\frac{14L_r}{L}}+\frac1{\sqrt L}\right)+\sqrt{\frac{\log(4/\delta)}{2AL}}\le(1+\sqrt2)\left(\sqrt{42}+\frac1{\sqrt L}\right)+1<\frac52\left(\frac{13}2+\frac32\right)+1=21<34.$$ The last strict inequality uses $L\ge\log2>1/2$, $\sqrt2<3/2$, and $\sqrt{42}<13/2$. At $T=1$, $\Delta_1\le1$, whereas $34DS\sqrt{A\log(2/\delta)}>1$, proving the second assertion at the remaining boundary with probability one. [given, F1, F3, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

## Original planned statement

Assume a finite communicating MDP with $S\ge1$ states, at most $A\ge1$ actions per state, rewards in $[0,1]$, and normalized diameter $D$. For every integer horizon $T\ge1$ and confidence parameter $\delta\in(0,1)$, UCRL2 satisfies, with probability at least $1-\delta$,
$$\Delta_T\le 34DS\sqrt{AT\log(T/\delta)},$$
where $\Delta_T=T\rho^*-R_T$ is the pathwise regret and $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

## Refutation

9.1 Consider one state $s$, two actions ordered $a_1<a_2$, deterministic self-transitions, and deterministic rewards $0$ for $a_1$ and $1$ for $a_2$. This is communicating with $S=1$, $A=2$, and $D=1$ by [F3]. At $T=1$ no pair has been observed before planning; both reward estimates are $0$, both transition laws are the same point mass, and the confidence bonuses coincide. Every EVI backup therefore ties the actions, so [F1] selects $a_1$. The optimal average reward is $\rho^*=1$, while $R_1=0$, hence $\Delta_1=1$ by [F3]. [given, F1, F3, construct, step 8.1]

10.1 Set $\delta=e^{-1/100000}$. The proposed right side is $34\sqrt{2/100000}=34/\sqrt{50000}<1$, since $34^2=1156<50000$. Thus the event asserted in the Statement has probability $0$, whereas its required probability is $1-\delta>0$. This contradicts the claim for the permitted horizon $T=1$. [given, step 9.1, algebra] ∎


## Remarks

The primary paper states the coefficient $34$ for $T>1$. The original planned all-horizon formula is retained verbatim above as a refuted claim. The positive logarithm offset supplies a proved all-horizon bound with the same coefficient. The local argument uses the actual Borel reward kernel and permits dependence of one reward and its accompanying next state.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited by the probability and Pinsker suppliers. Here a learning algorithm is not given the unknown MDP's reward or transition laws and, at each time, uses a fixed measurable probability kernel from the observed finite history to the admissible actions, the same kernel in every environment; its action randomization is independent of unexposed MDP samples. For all integers $S,A\ge10$, all real $D\ge\max\{1,20\log_A S\}$, all integers $T\ge DSA$, every such learning algorithm, and every prescribed initial state label, there exists a finite communicating MDP with exactly $S$ states including that label, exactly $A$ actions in each state, rewards in $[0,1]$, and normalized diameter at most $D$, such that the algorithm's expected regret from that initial state satisfies
$$\mathbb E[T\rho^*-R_T]\ge0.015\sqrt{DSAT}.$$
The MDP may depend on the algorithm, parameters, and prescribed initial state. The original planned statement with reversed minimax quantifiers and no feasibility condition $D\ge1$ is false; it is retained and refuted below.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[def-average-reward-and-regret]]: expected regret is $T\rho^*-\mathbb E R_T$.

[F2] [[def-communicating-mdp-and-diameter]]: hitting time starts at zero, and normalized diameter is the maximum of one and the raw ordered-pair hitting diameter.

[F4] [[thm-total-variation-bounds-for-expectations]]: a function in $[0,T]$ has expectation difference at most $T$ times event-supremum total variation.

## Proof

1.1 We use the proved local Pinsker inequality and the total-variation bound for expectations. All remaining probability calculations are supplied here. Write $\operatorname{kl}(p,q)$ for Bernoulli relative entropy. For $0<p<p+e<1$, $$\operatorname{kl}(p,p+e)=\int_p^{p+e}\frac{x-p}{x(1-x)}\,dx\le\frac{e^2}{2p(1-p-e)}.$$ Indeed, differentiating $p\log(p/x)+(1-p)\log((1-p)/(1-x))$ gives the integrand, and $x(1-x)\ge p(1-p-e)$ on the integration interval. Suppose two environments differ only at a single state-action pair $j$, at which one Bernoulli observation parameter changes from $p$ to $p+e$. Let $P_0$ and $P_j$ be their complete histories through the $T$th transition/reward, and let $N_j$ count uses of pair $j$. Their likelihood ratio is the product of the changed Bernoulli likelihood ratios at those uses. The initial law and all conditional action kernels are identical and cancel, including for randomized algorithms. Taking logarithms, conditioning on each past history and selected action, and summing gives exactly $$\operatorname{KL}(P_0\Vert P_j)=\mathbb E_0[N_j]\operatorname{kl}(p,p+e).$$ There is no absolute-continuity issue because both Bernoulli parameters lie strictly between zero and one and every unchanged kernel has the same support. The displayed identity also follows directly by expanding the finite history probabilities; all rewards used below have finite support. Since $0\le N_j\le T$, Pinsker implies $$\mathbb E_jN_j\le\mathbb E_0N_j+T\sqrt{\operatorname{KL}(P_0\Vert P_j)/2}.$$ For a family of $K$ candidate pairs with $n_j=\mathbb E_0N_j$ and $\sum_j n_j\le mT$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $K^{-1}\sum_j\sqrt{n_j}\le\sqrt{mT/K}$. These arguments hold for every algorithm without a deterministic-policy reduction. [given, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct, algebra]

2.1 First suppose $D\ge16$. In this branch, set $$k=\lfloor S/2\rfloor,\qquad b=\lfloor A/3\rfloor,\qquad B=A-b-1,\qquad K=kB,\qquad p=\frac8{3D},\qquad e=\frac7{20}\sqrt{\frac{pK}{T}}.$$ There are $k$ paired bad/good states $(x_i,y_i)$. If $S$ is odd, include one additional bare routing state. Arrange the bad states and the optional bare state into a breadth-first rooted $b$-ary tree of height $h$. At each bad state, $B$ useful actions have reward zero and move to its good partner with probability $p$, otherwise staying put. The remaining $b+1$ actions route deterministically toward the parent or one of the $b$ child slots, with missing slots giving self-loops; their rewards are zero. At each good state all $A$ actions have reward one and move to the paired bad state with probability $p$, otherwise staying put. At the optional bare state use the same routing actions and duplicate them to obtain exactly $A$ actions, all with reward zero. This uses exactly $S$ states and exactly $A$ actions per state. For each of the $K$ useful pairs $j$, environment $M_j$ changes just that pair's probability of entering its good state from $p$ to $p+e$. The baseline $M_0$ has no change. Fix the initial state at the bad root. Every environment is communicating. [given, step 1.1, F2, construct, algebra]

3.1 For every integer $A\ge10$, $$B\ge\frac7{12}A,\qquad B\le\frac23 A,\qquad b\ge A^{2/5},\qquad 2b^2\ge A^{6/5}.$$ For the first inequality, $A\ge12$ gives $B\ge2A/3-1\ge7A/12$, and $A=10,11$ are immediate. The second follows from $\lfloor A/3\rfloor\ge(A-2)/3$. For the last inequality, check $A=10,11,12,13$ directly; for $A\ge14$, $b\ge A/4$ and $A^{4/5}\ge8$, so $2b^2\ge A^2/8\ge A^{6/5}$. This last inequality implies $b\ge A^{2/5}$ because $A^{1/5}\ge\sqrt2$. The number of tree vertices is $n=\lceil S/2\rceil$. If $h=2$, breadth-first filling implies $n\ge b+2$, so $S\ge2b+3\ge2A/3\ge A^{4/5}$ and hence $h\le(5/2)\log_A S$. If $h\ge3$, it implies $S\ge2b^{h-1}$, so $$S\ge(2b^2)b^{h-3}\ge A^{6/5}A^{(2/5)(h-3)}=A^{2h/5}.$$ Thus always $h\le\max\{1,(5/2)\log_A S\}\le D/8$. The final inequality uses $D\ge16$ and $D\ge20\log_A S$. To hit a target good state from any state, first leave an initial good state if necessary (mean at most $1/p$), follow the tree path (at most $2h$ steps), and repeatedly take a useful action at the target bad state (mean at most $1/p$). 4.1 In $M_j$ the optimal average reward is $$\rho^*=\frac{p+e}{2p+e}=\frac12+\frac{e}{4p+2e}.$$ To prove this, take the function $v$ equal to $1/(2p+e)$ at every good state and zero elsewhere. Summing this inequality in conditional expectation gives average reward at most $\rho^*$, because $v$ is bounded. Routing to the special bad state and then always using its special action realizes the two-state chain with transitions $p+e$ and $p$, whose invariant good-state mass is $(p+e)/(2p+e)$. 5.1 We have $k\ge5S/11$ (even $S$ is immediate, and odd $S\ge11$ gives $(S-1)/(2S)\ge5/11$), so $$30\le K,\qquad \frac{35}{132}SA\le K\le\frac13 SA.$$ Because $pT\ge(8/3)SA$, $$\frac ep\le\frac7{20\sqrt8}<\frac18,\qquad p\le\frac16,\qquad1-p-e\ge\frac{13}{16},\qquad\sum_j\mathbb E_0N_j\le\frac{51}{100}T.$$ For the last assertion $SA\ge100$ gives $1/(2pT)\le3/1600<1/100$. Combining the preceding inequalities yields $$\frac1K\sum_j\mathbb E_j[T\rho^*-R_T]\ge L\left(\frac{c}{4+2e/p}-\frac{cm}{2K}-\frac{c^2}{4}\sqrt{\frac{m}{1-p-e}}\right).$$ Since $4+2e/p\le17/4$ and $\sqrt{(51/100)/(13/16)}<4/5$, the coefficient is greater than $$\frac7{85}-\frac{119}{40000}-\frac{49}{2000}=0.054877941\ldots>\frac1{20}.$$ Therefore at least one $j$ satisfies $$\mathbb E_j[T\rho^*-R_T]>\frac1{20}\sqrt{\frac{3D}{8}KT}\ge\frac1{20}\sqrt{\frac{35}{352}}\sqrt{DSAT}>0.015\sqrt{DSAT}.$$ The last coefficient is approximately $0.0157664$; alternatively square both positive sides to check it exactly. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, F3, F4, F5, construct, algebra]

6.1 Now suppose $1\le D<16$, the remaining allowed diameter range. The parameter condition gives $A\ge S^{20/D}>S^{5/4}$, so $S/A<S^{-1/4}\le10^{-1/4}<3/5$. All rewards in the baseline are independent Bernoulli variables of mean $1/2$. For each of the $K$ self-loop pairs $j$, environment $M_j$ changes that pair's reward mean to $1/2+e$, where $$e=\frac15\sqrt{K/T}\le\frac15.$$ The last inequality follows from $K\le SA\le T$ because $D\ge1$. Rewards may be generated independently conditional on state-action history; transitions are the same deterministic transitions in all environments. Every environment has diameter one and exactly the required numbers of states and actions. Its optimal average reward is $1/2+e$: no reward mean exceeds this, and the learner can reach the special state in at most one step and then repeatedly use its special self-loop. Here the testing calculation gives $$\operatorname{KL}(P_0\Vert P_j)\le\frac{10}{3}e^2\mathbb E_0N_j,\qquad \frac1K\sum_j\mathbb E_jN_j\le\frac TK+Te\sqrt{\frac{5T}{3K}},$$ because $1/2-e\ge3/10$ and $\sum_j\mathbb E_0N_j\le T$. The expected regret in $M_j$ is exactly $e(T-\mathbb E_jN_j)$. Consequently $$\frac1K\sum_j\mathbb E_j[T\rho^*-R_T]\ge\sqrt{KT}\left[\frac15\left(1-\frac1K\right)-\frac1{25}\sqrt{\frac53}\right]>\frac7{50}\sqrt{KT}.$$ Indeed, $K\ge40$ and $\sqrt{5/3}<13/10$ make the bracket at least $39/200-13/250=143/1000>7/50$. Thus at least one $j$ has regret greater than $(7/50)\sqrt{(2/5)SAT}$. Since $D<16$ and $(7/50)\sqrt{2/5}>0.06=4(0.015)$, this is greater than $0.015\sqrt{DSAT}$. Label the bad root in the large-diameter construction by the prescribed initial state; in the small-diameter construction any prescribed initial state works. Thus both branches prove the stated quantifiers. [given, step 1.1, step 5.1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct, algebra] ∎

## Original planned statement

There is a universal constant $c=0.015$ such that for every $S,A\ge10$, every $D\ge20\log_A S$, and every integer $T\ge DSA$, some finite communicating MDP with $S$ states, exactly $A$ actions per state, rewards in $[0,1]$, and diameter at most $D$ forces every learning algorithm to have expected regret at least $c\sqrt{DSAT}$.

## Refutation

7.1 Take $S=10$, $A=10^{40}$, $D=1/2$, and any integer $T\ge DSA$. These parameters satisfy $S,A\ge10$ and $D=20\log_A S$. For any two distinct states $x,y$, the hitting time $\tau_y$ from $x$ is at least one on every path, so its expectation under every policy is at least one. Thus every ten-state communicating MDP has raw diameter at least one, and [F2] also makes its normalized diameter at least one. [given, F2, construct, algebra, step 6.1]

8.1 No MDP with the required state count has diameter at most $1/2$. Consequently the existential MDP in the original planned statement does not exist for the admissible parameters of step 7.1, regardless of the algorithm or the constant. This refutes the exact original statement. Its phrase “some MDP ... every learning algorithm” additionally reverses the minimax quantifiers: the proof above establishes an MDP chosen after the learning rule, not a single environment hard for all rules. [given, F2, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The lower bound is for expected regret. It asserts no high-probability lower-tail event. The coefficient $0.015$ is retained: the large-diameter calculation gives more than $\frac1{20}\sqrt{35/352}\sqrt{DSAT}>0.015\sqrt{DSAT}$, with the small-diameter calculation stronger still. The explicit feasibility restriction and minimax quantifiers repair a false original statement; they are not inferences from the primary proof's deficient constant-transfer line.

## Statement

Assume AC. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one measurable space, with
$$\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}:=\sup_{A}|P(A)-Q(A)|,$$
the event-supremum convention without a factor $1/2$,
$$\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}\le\sqrt{\frac12D(P\|Q)}.$$
If $P\not\ll Q$, the right side is $+\infty$ by the definition of KL
divergence.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and probability measures $P,Q$ on the same measurable space.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC supplies the Radon–Nikodym construction used by the KL divergence.

[F1] [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]] and [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]]: if $P\not\ll Q$, then $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$; if $P\ll Q$ with $r=dP/dQ$, then $P(B)=\int_Br\,dQ$ for every measurable $B$, so $\int r\,dQ=1$, and $D(P\|Q)=\int r\log r\,dQ$ with $0\log0=0$ and finite negative part.

[F2] [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]: $\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|\in[0,1]$; this convention has no factor $1/2$.

[F3] [[thm-jensens-integral-inequality]]: for a probability measure, an integrable real function $f$, and convex $\varphi$ with $\varphi\circ f$ integrable, $\varphi(\int f)\le\int\varphi(f)$.

[F4] [[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]], [[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]], [[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]], and [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: the identity $L=\log$ transfers $L'(x)=1/x$ to $\log'(x)=1/x$; products and compositions obey the derivative rules; and the mean value theorem applies on closed subintervals of $(0,1)$. Also $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$: for $s\ge1$, $0\le\log(s)/s\le2/\sqrt{s}$ using $\log s=\int_1^sdu/u$ and $1/u\le1/\sqrt u$.

## Proof

1.1 If $P\not\ll Q$ or $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$, the inequality is immediate. Otherwise let $r=dP/dQ$ and $\varphi(t)=t\log t$ for $t>0$, with $\varphi(0)=0$. By [F4] and the product rule, $\varphi''(t)=1/t>0$ for $t>0$. The mean value theorem in [F4] makes $\varphi'$ increasing and hence $\varphi$ convex on $(0,\infty)$. The limit in [F4] makes this extension continuous at zero, so $\varphi$ is convex on $[0,\infty)$. Since $D(P\|Q)$ is finite and its negative part is bounded by [F1], $\varphi(r)$ is $Q$-integrable. Jensen [F3] and $\int r\,dQ=1$ give $D(P\|Q)=\int\varphi(r)\,dQ\ge\varphi(1)=0$. [A1, F1, F3, F4, given]

2.1 Fix a measurable event $A$, and put $a=P(A)$, $b=Q(A)$. If $b\in\{0,1\}$, absolute continuity gives $a=b$, so step 1.1 yields $D(P\|Q)\ge k(a,b)=0$. If $0<b<1$, normalize $Q$ on $A$ and on $A^c$. Their averages of $r$ are $a/b$ and $(1-a)/(1-b)$. Applying [F3] on each normalized probability space and adding yields $D(P\|Q)\ge a\log\frac ab+(1-a)\log\frac{1-a}{1-b}=:k(a,b),$ with $0\log0=0$ by continuity. [A1, F1, F3, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For fixed $0<b<1$, define $g(a)=k(a,b)-2(a-b)^2$ on $[0,1]$. Differentiating by [F4] gives $g''(a)=\frac1{a(1-a)}-4=\frac{(2a-1)^2}{a(1-a)}\ge0$ on $(0,1)$. For $a,b\in(0,1)$ with $a>b$, the mean value theorem applied to $g'$ on $[b,a]$ shows $g'(a)\ge g'(b)=0$, and applied to $g$ on $[b,a]$ shows $g(a)\ge g(b)=0$. For $a,b\in(0,1)$ with $a<b$, the same two applications on $[a,b]$ show $g'(a)\le g'(b)=0$ and $g(a)\ge g(b)=0$. The limit in [F4] makes $g$ continuous at $a=0,1$, so the inequality extends to those endpoints. If $b=0$ or $b=1$, absolute continuity gives $a=b$ and equality. Thus $k(a,b)\ge2(a-b)^2$ in every case. [F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Combining steps 2.1 and 3.1 gives $D(P\|Q)\ge2|P(A)-Q(A)|^2$ for every measurable $A$. Since the square is increasing on $[0,1]$, its supremum is the square of the supremum; using [F2] yields $D(P\|Q)\ge2\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}^2$, which is the claimed inequality. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ and $Q$ be probability measures on it, and let $f:E\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $|f|\le M$ pointwise for some finite $M\ge0$. With the convention
$$\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}|P(A)-Q(A)|,$$
one has
$$\left|\int f\,dP-\int f\,dQ\right|\le 2M\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}.$$
For every measurable $g:E\to\mathbb R$ with $0\le g\le M$ pointwise, one also has
$$\left|\int g\,dP-\int g\,dQ\right|\le M\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}.$$
Both integral differences are zero when $M=0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, probability measures $P,Q$, and measurable real functions $f,g$ satisfying $|f|\le M<\infty$ and $0\le g\le M$.

[F1] A probability measure has total mass one. [[def-probability-measure]]

[F2] Total variation here is the event supremum $\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}|P(A)-Q(A)|$ and has no half-factor. [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]

[F3] On nonnegative simple functions, the nonnegative Lebesgue integral agrees with the simple integral. [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]

[F4] The simple integral is the sum of the coefficients times the measures of the level sets; in particular, an indicator integrates to the measure of its set. [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]]

[F5] The nonnegative integral is additive, monotone, and nonnegatively homogeneous. [[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]

[F6] A real measurable function is integrable when its absolute value has finite nonnegative integral; the integral is linear on integrable functions. [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]] [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]

[F7] For every $\eta>0$ there is an integer $n\ge1$ with $1/n<\eta$. [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 If $M=0$, then $f=0$ and $g=0$ pointwise, so both claims hold. To prove the nonnegative claim for an arbitrary finite bound $L>0$, let $w:E\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $0\le w\le L$, fix an integer $n\ge1$, put $\Delta=L/n$, and define $A_k=\{x:w(x)\ge k\Delta\}$ for $1\le k\le n$ and $s_n=\Delta\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbf1_{A_k}$. The sets are measurable, $s_n$ is nonnegative simple, and $0\le w-s_n\le\Delta$ pointwise. [given, construct]

2.1 By [F3]–[F5], $\int s_n\,dP=\Delta\sum_{k=1}^nP(A_k)$ and likewise for $Q$, so $|\int s_n\,dP-\int s_n\,dQ|\le n\Delta\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}=L\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}$. Also $0\le\int(w-s_n)\,dP\le\Delta$ and $0\le\int(w-s_n)\,dQ\le\Delta$, because $w-s_n\le\Delta$ and both measures have mass one. The triangle inequality therefore gives $|\int w\,dP-\int w\,dQ|\le L\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}+2L/n$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Given any $\eta>0$, choose $n$ by [F7] with $1/n<\eta/(2L)$. The estimate in step 2.1 then gives $|\int w\,dP-\int w\,dQ|<L\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}+\eta$. If the bound by $L\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}$ failed, choosing $\eta$ to be half the positive excess would contradict this inequality. Taking $w=g$ and $L=M$ proves the stated nonnegative case when $M>0$. [F7, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For the signed case with $M>0$, let $h=f+M$. Then $h$ is measurable and $0\le h\le2M$, so step 3.1 with $w=h$ and $L=2M$ gives $|\int h\,dP-\int h\,dQ|\le2M\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}$. Also $|f|\le M$, so [F1], [F3]–[F5] give $\int|f|\,dP\le M$ and $\int|f|\,dQ\le M$; hence $f$ is integrable under both measures by [F6]. The constant $M$ has integral $M$ under each probability measure, so linearity [F6] gives $\int f\,dP-\int f\,dQ=\int h\,dP-\int h\,dQ$. This proves the signed case. [F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $S=\{0,1\}$ and let each state have one action. Both states are absorbing. The reward is always $0$ in state $0$ and always $1$ in state $1$. The MDP is not communicating, and its long-run average reward is $0$ from initial state $0$ and $1$ from initial state $1$.

## Proof

1.1 Starting from either state, the chain remains there at every time. From state $0$ every cumulative reward is $0$, so its average is $0$; from state $1$ every cumulative reward over $T$ steps is $T$, so its average is $1$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 No policy can leave either absorbing state. In particular, starting from $0$ there is no policy that reaches $1$ with finite expected hitting time, so the communicating condition fails.
