## Statement

Assume the finite-horizon imitation-learning setting with deterministic expert $\pi^*$, positive integer horizon $T$, expert surrogate $\ell(s,\theta)\in[0,1]$, learner policies $\pi_\theta$, and nonempty convex parameter set $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ defined previously. Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and use $\|x-y\|_2=(\sum_{r=1}^d(x_r-y_r)^2)^{1/2}$. Suppose for every state $s$, $\ell(s,\cdot)$ is $G$-Lipschitz and $\mu$-strongly convex on $K$, with constants $G\ge0$ and $\mu>0$, where Lipschitz means $|\ell(s,x)-\ell(s,y)|\le G\|x-y\|_2$ and strong convexity means $\ell(s,(1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)\le(1-\lambda)\ell(s,x)+\lambda\ell(s,y)-\frac\mu2\lambda(1-\lambda)\|x-y\|_2^2$ for $x,y\in K$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$. Assume also that $\theta\mapsto\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$ is Borel measurable for every state-action pair.

Run finite-trajectory DAgger for positive integers $N,m$, with per-decision expert-use probabilities $\beta_i\in[0,1]$ satisfying $\beta_1\le1$ and $\beta_i\le(1-\alpha)^{i-1}$ for $2\le i\le N$, where $\alpha\in(0,1]$ is fixed. Let $\hat\pi_i=\pi_{\theta_i}$ and $\pi_i=\beta_i\pi^*+(1-\beta_i)\hat\pi_i$. In round $i$, let $S_{ijt}$, $1\le j\le m$, $0\le t<T$, be the states of trajectory $j$, and define $\bar\ell_{ij}(\theta)=T^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\ell(S_{ijt},\theta)$, $\hat L_i(\theta)=m^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^m\bar\ell_{ij}(\theta)$, and $\hat\epsilon_N=\min_{\theta\in K}N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\hat L_i(\theta)$. Assume this minimum and every cumulative empirical-loss minimum are attained, and DAgger uses exact Follow-the-Leader updates.

Assume the samples are observed in a filtered probability space with nested sigma-algebras $\mathcal F_{i,j}$, where $\mathcal F_{1,0}=\mathcal F_0$, $\mathcal F_{i,0}=\mathcal F_{i-1,m}$ for $i>1$, and $\mathcal F_{i,j-1}\subseteq\mathcal F_{i,j}$. Suppose $\theta_i$ is $\mathcal F_{i,0}$-measurable, each trajectory state $S_{ijt}$ is $\mathcal F_{i,j}$-measurable, and the conditional rollout law satisfies $\mathbb E[\bar\ell_{ij}(\theta_i)\mid\mathcal F_{i,j-1}]=L_i(\theta_i)$ almost surely, where $L_i(\theta)=\sum_s d_{\pi_i}(s)\ell(s,\theta)$ is the true round-$i$ loss under the mixed rollout policy. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the conditional-expectation and martingale results used below. Let $\delta\in(0,1)$, define $H_0=0$ and $H_n=\sum_{r=1}^n1/r$, let $q_T$ be the least nonnegative integer with $T\le2^{q_T}$, and let $k_\alpha$ be the least positive integer with $k_\alpha\alpha\ge1$. Then with probability at least $1-\delta$, some $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ satisfies

$$\sum_s d_{\hat\pi_i}(s)\ell(s,\theta_i)\le\hat\epsilon_N+\frac{1+\frac{4G^2}{\mu}H_{N-1}+k_\alpha(q_T+2)}{N}+\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(1/\delta)}{mN}}.$$

For each fixed $m\ge1$, $\alpha\in(0,1]$, $\mu>0$, and $G\ge0$, there are constants $C,C'>0$ depending only on these parameters such that if $\delta\in(0,1/2]$ and $N\ge C T^2\ln(1/\delta)$, the right side is at most $\hat\epsilon_N+C'/T$. This is a surrogate-loss guarantee with interactive expert labels; it does not assert a finite-sample task-cost bound.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite-horizon MDP, expert and surrogate definitions, bounded strongly convex Lipschitz loss, exact empirical DAgger updates, nested sample filtration, conditional rollout-mean identity, attained empirical minima, geometric expert-use schedule, confidence parameter, and Axiom of Choice in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-imitation-learning-and-expert-surrogate-loss]]: $d_\pi$ is the normalized average state occupancy and $L_i(\theta)=\sum_s d_{\pi_i}(s)\ell(s,\theta)$ is the true round loss.

[F2] [[alg-dagger]]: $\hat L_i(\theta)=\frac1{mT}\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\ell(S_{ijt},\theta)$ and $\theta_{i+1}$ minimizes $\sum_{r=1}^i\hat L_r$.

[F3] [[lem-dagger-strongly-convex-follow-the-leader-regret]]: for bounded, $G$-Lipschitz, $\mu$-strongly convex round losses with attained cumulative minima, empirical FTL regret is at most $1+(4G^2/\mu)H_{N-1}$.

[F4] [[lem-dagger-mixture-occupancy]]: for every $g:S\to[0,1]$, the absolute difference between its mixed-policy and learner-policy occupancy expectations is at most $\min(1,T\beta_i)$.

[F5] [[thm-azuma-hoeffding-inequality]]: under AC, martingale increments with predictable endpoints of width at most $c_k$ satisfy $\mathbb P(M_n-M_0\ge t)\le\exp(-2t^2/\sum_kc_k^2)$.

[F6] [[def-martingale-difference-sequence]]: a martingale difference is integrable, adapted, and has zero conditional mean given the preceding sigma-algebra.

[F7] [[thm-martingales-and-martingale-differences-correspond]]: an adapted integrable martingale-difference sequence sums, from any integrable initial value, to a martingale.

[F8] [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]: a filtered probability space has nested sigma-algebras $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}$.

[F9] [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]]: adaptedness means time-$n$ measurability with respect to $\mathcal F_n$, and integrability means finite $E|X_n|$ at each time.

[F10] [[def-martingale-submartingale-and-supermartingale]]: an integrable adapted process is a martingale when $E[M_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=M_n$ almost surely.

[F11] [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]: conditional expectations are unique almost-sure equivalence classes of measurable integrable versions.

[F12] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC states that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

[F13] [[thm-basic-algebra-and-order-properties-of-conditional-expectation]]: conditional expectation is linear on integrable random variables.

[F14] [[lem-conditioning-a-known-variable-and-an-independent-variable]]: if an integrable variable is measurable with respect to the conditioning sigma-algebra, its conditional expectation is itself almost surely.

[F15] [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]: finite sums and products of real-valued Borel-measurable functions are Borel measurable.

[F16] [[thm-induction-principle]]: a property of positive integer indices that holds at the first index and is preserved by successors holds for every positive integer index.

[A1] For every state, $\ell(s,\cdot)$ is valued in $[0,1]$, $G$-Lipschitz, and $\mu$-strongly convex on the nonempty convex set $K$.

[A2] All cumulative empirical-loss minima and the minimum defining $\hat\epsilon_N$ are attained; the algorithm uses exact FTL updates.

[A3] The per-sample conditional mean identity $\mathbb E[\bar\ell_{ij}(\theta_i)\mid\mathcal F_{i,j-1}]=L_i(\theta_i)$ holds almost surely, with $\theta_i$ measurable before round $i$ and trajectory states measurable when revealed.

[A4] $0\le\beta_1\le1$ and $0\le\beta_i\le(1-\alpha)^{i-1}$ for $i\ge2$, with fixed $0<\alpha\le1$.

[A5] For the rate corollary, $0<\delta\le1/2$, while the main probability bound only requires $0<\delta<1$.

## Proof

1.1 For any realized sample sequence, $\hat L_i$ is a finite average of functions $\ell(S_{ijt},\cdot)$, so [A1] makes it $[0,1]$-valued, $G$-Lipschitz, and $\mu$-strongly convex on $K$. By [F2] and [A2], the iterates are exact FTL iterates and the hindsight minimum is attained. Applying [F3] samplewise gives $\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\hat L_i(\theta_i)\le\hat\epsilon_N+\frac{1+\frac{4G^2}{\mu}H_{N-1}}N$. [A1, A2, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Flatten the pairs $(i,j)$ in round-major order. Put $\mathcal G_0=\mathcal F_{1,0}$ and, for $r=(i-1)m+j$ with $1\le i\le N$ and $1\le j\le m$, put $\mathcal G_r=\mathcal F_{i,j}$; for every $r>mN$, put $\mathcal G_r=\mathcal G_{mN}$. Within each round the sigma-algebras are nested, and at round boundaries $\mathcal F_{i,0}=\mathcal F_{i-1,m}$, so $(\mathcal G_r)_{r\ge0}$ is an infinite filtration. Define $D_{(i-1)m+j}=L_i(\theta_i)-\bar\ell_{ij}(\theta_i)$ for the sample indices and set $D_r=0$ for $r>mN$. For each fixed round $i$, the policy probabilities are Borel functions of $\theta$, the finite occupancy recursion uses only finite sums and products, and $\ell(s,\cdot)$ is continuous by its Lipschitz property. Thus [F15] makes $L_i(\theta)$ Borel, so $L_i(\theta_i)$ is measurable with respect to $\mathcal G_{(i-1)m}=\mathcal F_{i,0}$ and hence with respect to each $\mathcal G_{r-1}$ in round $i$. Since the state set is finite and each statewise loss is continuous, $(s,\theta)\mapsto\ell(s,\theta)$ is measurable; the revealed states and preceding measurable parameter therefore make each $\bar\ell_{ij}(\theta_i)$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal G_r$. By [A1] and the probability-occupancy property in [F1], both $L_i(\theta_i)$ and $\bar\ell_{ij}(\theta_i)$ lie in $[0,1]$, so each sample increment is integrable and in $[-1,1]$; the zero extension has the same properties. For $r=(i-1)m+j\le mN$, [A3], [F13], and [F14] give $\mathbb E[D_r\mid\mathcal G_{r-1}]=L_i(\theta_i)-L_i(\theta_i)=0$. For $r>mN$, [F14] gives $\mathbb E[0\mid\mathcal G_{r-1}]=0$. Thus $D$ is an infinite adapted martingale-difference sequence by [F6], using the filtration and process conventions [F8, F9, F11]. [A1, A3, F1, F6, F8, F9, F11, F13, F14, F15, construct]

1.3 Put $q=1-\alpha$ and $k=k_\alpha$. For every integer $n\ge1$, $(1+\alpha)^n\ge1+n\alpha$: equality holds for $n=1$, and if it holds for $n$, then multiplication by $1+\alpha>0$ gives $(1+\alpha)^{n+1}\ge(1+n\alpha)(1+\alpha)=1+(n+1)\alpha+n\alpha^2\ge1+(n+1)\alpha$. Thus [F16] gives $(1+\alpha)^k\ge1+k\alpha\ge2$. Also $q(1+\alpha)=1-\alpha^2\le1$, so $q\le(1+\alpha)^{-1}$ and $q^k\le1/2$. For block $j\ge0$, let $I_j=\{jk+1,\ldots,(j+1)k\}$. If $j=0$, [A4] gives $\beta_1\le1=q^0$ and $\beta_i\le q^{i-1}\le1$ for the other indices; if $j\ge1$, every $i\in I_j$ satisfies $\beta_i\le q^{i-1}\le q^{jk}$. Thus each block contributes at most $k\min(1,T2^{-j})$. Let $J=\lceil N/k\rceil-1$, so the blocks $j=0,\ldots,J$ cover all sample indices. Their terms with $j\le q_T$ contribute at most $q_T+1$ inside the sum over blocks. If $J\ge q_T+1$, the identity $2^{-j}=2^{-(j-1)}-2^{-j}$ telescopes to $\sum_{j=q_T+1}^{J}2^{-j}=2^{-q_T}-2^{-J}\le2^{-q_T}$; if $J<q_T+1$, this tail is empty. Hence the remaining block contribution is at most $T2^{-q_T}\le1$, and $\sum_{i=1}^N\min(1,T\beta_i)\le k_\alpha(q_T+2)$. [A4, F16, algebra, induction]

2.1 By [F7], $M_0=0$ and $M_r=\sum_{k=1}^rD_k$ form a martingale on the infinite filtration $(\mathcal G_r)$. Its restriction to $r=0,\ldots,mN$ is the finite martingale required by [F5]. Each of its first $mN$ increments has predictable endpoints $-1$ and $1$, of width $2$, so [F5] and the AC hypothesis [F12] give $\mathbb P(M_{mN}\ge t)\le\exp(-t^2/(2mN))$. Taking $t=\sqrt{2mN\ln(1/\delta)}$ makes this probability at most $\delta$. Since $M_{mN}=m\sum_{i=1}^N(L_i(\theta_i)-\hat L_i(\theta_i))$, outside that event $\frac1N\sum_iL_i(\theta_i)\le\frac1N\sum_i\hat L_i(\theta_i)+\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(1/\delta)}{mN}}$. [A3, F5, F7, F10, F12, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 On the event from step 2.1, combine its mixed-policy loss bound with step 1.1 to obtain $\frac1N\sum_iL_i(\theta_i)\le\hat\epsilon_N+\frac{1+\frac{4G^2}{\mu}H_{N-1}}N+\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(1/\delta)}{mN}}$. [A2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Apply both directions of the absolute occupancy estimate [F4] with $g(s)=\ell(s,\theta_i)$, giving $\sum_sd_{\hat\pi_i}(s)\ell(s,\theta_i)\le L_i(\theta_i)+\min(1,T\beta_i)$. Average over $i$ and use step 3.1 and step 1.3. At least one of the $N$ own-occupancy losses is no larger than their average, so on the event of step 2.1 some $i$ satisfies the displayed inequality in the Statement. Its probability is at least $1-\delta$. [A1, F1, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.3, algebra]

5.1 For the rate claim, set $L=\ln(1/\delta)\ge\ln2$ and choose a fixed $C\ge3/\ln2$, so $N_0=CT^2L\ge3>e$. With $c=4G^2/\mu$, for $N\ge2$ we have $H_{N-1}=1+\sum_{r=2}^{N-1}1/r\le1+\sum_{r=2}^{N-1}\int_{r-1}^r dx/x=1+\ln(N-1)\le1+\ln N$, with the sum empty when $N=2$. The derivative of $x\mapsto[1+c(1+\ln x)]/x$ is $(c-1-c\ln x)/x^2\le0$ for $x\ge e$, so for $N\ge N_0$ the FTL term is at most $[1+c(1+\ln N_0)]/N_0=O((1+\ln T)/T^2)$, since $L\ge\ln2$ and $(1+\ln L)/L$ is bounded on $[\ln2,\infty)$. Also $q_T\le1+\log_2T$, so the mixing term is $O((1+\ln T)/T^2)$, while the Azuma term is at most $\sqrt{2/(mC)}/T$. As $1+\ln T\le T$ for $T\ge1$, the two former terms are $O(1/T)$ as well. This proves the stated rate on the same event as step 4.1. [A5, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC for existence. For real $X\in L^1(P)$, if $X$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[X\mid\mathcal G]=X$. If $P(\{X\in B\}\cap A)=P(X\in B)P(A)$ for every real Borel $B$ and $A\in\mathcal G$, then $E[X\mid\mathcal G]=EX$ almost surely.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, real integrable X and sub-sigma-algebra G; separately either X is G-measurable or its Borel events satisfy the displayed independence identity.

[F1] Conditional classes are characterized by measurable integrable versions with all event identities. ([[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]])

[F2] The version class is unique. ([[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]])

[F3] Nonnegative Borel functions admit increasing Borel simple approximations. ([[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]])

[F4] Increasing nonnegative simple limits pass through integrals. ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]])

[F5] Finite linear combinations and differences of integrable functions pass through the integral. ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $X$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable it itself meets every condition for a version: integrability is assumed and every event equality is $\int_A X=\int_A X$. Hence uniqueness gives the first identity. [F1, F2]

1.2 Fix $A\in\mathcal G$ under the independence hypothesis. For $h=\mathbf1_B$, $E[h(X)\mathbf1_A]=E[h(X)]P(A)$ is exactly that hypothesis. For nonnegative Borel simple $h=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{B_j}$, multiplication by $c_j$ and addition give the same equality. For a nonnegative Borel $h$ with $E[h(X)]<\infty$, compose the increasing Borel simple approximations $h_m\uparrow h$ from [F3] with $X$. Then $E[h_m(X)]\uparrow E[h(X)]<\infty$ and $E[h_m(X)\mathbf1_A]\uparrow E[h(X)\mathbf1_A]$ by [F4]. Passing to the limit in the finite equalities $E[h_m(X)\mathbf1_A]=P(A)E[h_m(X)]$ gives $E[h(X)\mathbf1_A]=P(A)E[h(X)]$. Every expectation here is finite, so multiplication by $P(A)=0$ is also defined. [given, F3, F4, F5]

2.1 Apply step 1.2 to $h(t)=t^+$ and $h(t)=t^-$. Their expectations are finite because $X\in L^1$, so subtracting yields $\int_A X=EX\,P(A)$. The constant $EX$ is finite, $\mathcal G$-measurable and integrable, and its integral on $A$ is $EX\,P(A)$. Since $A$ was arbitrary, [F1]–[F2] identify it with $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$. [step 1.2, F1, F2, F5] ∎

## Source notes

Durrett Examples 4.1.3–4.1.4, printed pp.207–208; van der Vaart Examples 1.4–1.5, printed p.2. The rectangle hypothesis is extended by simple approximation explicitly, without importing a general factorization theorem.

## Example

Let the states be $g$ (good) and $b$ (bad), with initial state $S_0=g$. At $g$ the actions are $c$ and $e$; action $c$ stays at $g$ with task cost $0$, while action $e$ moves to $b$ with cost $1$. At $b$ the actions are $r$ and $e$; action $r$ moves to $g$ with cost $0$, while action $e$ stays at $b$ with cost $1$. The transition is deterministic for every state/action pair. The deterministic expert chooses $c$ at $g$ and $r$ at $b$. For a parameter $\epsilon$ with $0<\epsilon\le1/T$, the learner chooses $e$ at $g$ with probability $\epsilon$ and $c$ otherwise, and always chooses $e$ at $b$. Use the statewise 0–1 expert-action disagreement as surrogate loss.

The diagram labels each deterministic transition by action/task-cost; the text specifies the two stochastic action probabilities of the learner. The expert occupancy is concentrated at $g$, so the behavior-cloning disagreement loss on expert states is $\epsilon$. Under the learner, the expected total task cost is

$$\sum_{k=1}^{T}\bigl(1-(1-\epsilon)^k\bigr),$$

which lies between $\epsilon T^2/8$ and $\epsilon T^2$. Thus an $\epsilon$ disagreement rate on expert states can correspond to quadratic-in-$T$ learner cost when a mistake moves the learner to states absent from expert demonstrations.

## Example references

[Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell, *A Reduction of Imitation Learning and Structured Prediction to No-Regret Online Learning*](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v15/ross11a/ross11a.pdf): Theorem 2.1 and §2.1, PDF pp. 1–2.

[Bagnell, Boots, and Choudhury, *Modern Adaptive Control and Reinforcement Learning*, Chapter 6](https://macrl-book.github.io/assets/pdf/6_macrl.pdf): PDF pp. 3–4 / printed pp. 56–57.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two-state transition/task-cost model, expert, learner, horizon, and surrogate loss in the Example.

[F1] [[def-imitation-learning-and-expert-surrogate-loss]]: $d_\pi$ is the normalized average of the state distributions at times $0,\ldots,T-1$, and the surrogate is the probability of taking an action different from the deterministic expert.

[A1] $T\ge1$ and $0<\epsilon\le1/T$.

## Verification

1.1 Under the expert, the state remains $g$ at every decision time, so $d_{\pi^*}$ is the point mass at $g$. The learner's action-disagreement probability at $g$ is $\epsilon$, hence its behavior-cloning surrogate loss averaged under $d_{\pi^*}$ equals $\epsilon$. [F1, A1, given]

1.2 Put $q=1-\epsilon$. The probability that the learner is at $g$ at time $t$ is $q^t$: it is $1$ at $t=0$, and if it is $g$ at time $t$ it remains there at the next state with probability $q$, while if it is $b$ it remains $b$. Thus the probability at time $t+1$ is $q^tq=q^{t+1}$. At decision time $t$, expected cost is $q^t\epsilon+(1-q^t)=1-q^{t+1}$. Summing for $t=0,\ldots,T-1$ gives the displayed cost. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 For each integer $k\ge1$, $(1-\epsilon)^k\ge1-k\epsilon$: the case $k=1$ is equality, and if it holds at $k$, multiplication by $1-\epsilon\ge0$ gives $(1-\epsilon)^{k+1}\ge(1-k\epsilon)(1-\epsilon)=1-(k+1)\epsilon+k\epsilon^2\ge1-(k+1)\epsilon$. Therefore $1-q^k\le k\epsilon$. [A1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 If $T=1$, the displayed cost is $\epsilon$, which lies between $\epsilon T^2/8$ and $\epsilon T^2$. Now assume $T\ge2$, so $0<\epsilon\le1/2$. Then $(1-\epsilon)^{-1}\ge1+\epsilon$ because $(1-\epsilon)^{-1}-(1+\epsilon)=\epsilon^2/(1-\epsilon)\ge0$. Also $(1+\epsilon)^k\ge1+k\epsilon$ for all $k\ge1$: it is equality for $k=1$, and multiplication by $1+\epsilon>0$ gives $(1+\epsilon)^{k+1}\ge(1+k\epsilon)(1+\epsilon)=1+(k+1)\epsilon+k\epsilon^2\ge1+(k+1)\epsilon$. Hence $q^k\le1/(1+k\epsilon)$. For $k\le T$, [A1] gives $k\epsilon\le1$, so $1-q^k\ge k\epsilon/(1+k\epsilon)\ge k\epsilon/2$. Let $r=\lceil T/2\rceil$; there are at least $T/2$ integer indices from $r$ through $T$, each at least $T/2$, so $\sum_{k=1}^T k\ge T^2/4$. The expected cost is at least $\epsilon T^2/8$. [A1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Summing the upper estimate $1-q^k\le k\epsilon$ from step 2.1 gives cost at most $\epsilon\sum_{k=1}^T k\le\epsilon T^2$. Together with the lower estimate from step 2.2, this proves the claimed bounds. [A1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

## Example

Let $S=\{s\}$, $A(s)=\{a^*,b\}$, and let both actions return deterministically to $s$ at every decision. For every time, set task costs $c_t(s,a^*)=0$ and $c_t(s,b)=1$. Let the expert always choose $a^*$, let the learner class contain both the expert and a learner that always chooses $b$, and define a candidate loss score by $\ell(s,\theta)=0$ for every class policy. Then the learner's score is zero under every state distribution, while its total task cost over horizon $T\ge1$ is $T$ and the expert's task cost is zero. This score fails the required disagreement-domination condition $\ell(s,\theta)\ge\sum_{a\ne\pi^*(s)}\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$, so the example does not contradict the DAgger task-cost lemma; it shows why that premise is necessary.

The diagram labels each deterministic self-transition by action/task-cost. The two actions have the same next state but different task costs.

## Example references

[Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell, *A Reduction of Imitation Learning and Structured Prediction to No-Regret Online Learning*](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v15/ross11a/ross11a.pdf): Theorem 2.2, §2.2, PDF pp. 2–3.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The one-state MDP, expert, learner, task costs, surrogate, and horizon in the Example.

[F1] [[def-imitation-learning-and-expert-surrogate-loss]]: the expert-action disagreement probability is $\sum_{a\ne\pi^*(s)}\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$, and task cost is the finite-horizon expected sum of per-time costs.

[A1] $T$ is an integer with $T\ge1$.

## Verification

1.1 The state is always $s$ under both policies, so every occupancy is the point mass at $s$. By the defined surrogate, the learner's expected surrogate loss is $\ell(s,\theta)=0$. Its disagreement probability is $1$, so [F1]'s required domination premise fails. [F1, A1, given]

2.1 At each of the $T$ decisions the learner pays cost $1$, while the expert pays cost $0$. Therefore $J(\hat\pi)=T$ and $J(\pi^*)=0$. Any unconditional claim that zero surrogate loss alone forces $J(\hat\pi)\le J(\pi^*)$ would assert $T\le0$, contradicting $T\ge1$. [A1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $S$ be a finite nonempty set, let $d$ be a probability distribution on $S$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set with probability distributions $q_s$ and $p_s$. On the power-set sigma-algebra of $A(s)$, define

$$\operatorname{TV}_{A(s)}(q_s,p_s):=\frac12\sum_{a\in A(s)}|q_s(a)-p_s(a)|.$$

Use the directional Kullback–Leibler divergence with natural logarithms, defined by

$$D_{\rm KL}(q_s\|p_s):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{a:q_s(a)>0}q_s(a)\log\frac{q_s(a)}{p_s(a)},&q_s(a)>0\Rightarrow p_s(a)>0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}$$

and the convention $0\log0=0$. Put

$$K:=\sum_{s:d(s)>0}d(s)D_{\rm KL}(q_s\|p_s)\in[0,+\infty].$$

Then

$$\sum_{s\in S}d(s)\operatorname{TV}_{A(s)}(q_s,p_s)\le\sqrt{K/2},$$

where the right side is $+\infty$ when $K=+\infty$.

## Statement references

[Achiam et al., *Constrained Policy Optimization*, §5.1, equation (7)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/achiam17a/achiam17a.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, a finite nonempty state set, probability weights $d(s)$, and finite nonempty action sets with probability distributions $q_s,p_s$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function; AC is invoked only to apply the published Pinsker theorem [F3]. The finite sums and weighting arguments are choice-free.

[F1] [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]: directional KL is $+\infty$ when the first probability law is not absolutely continuous with respect to the second; under absolute continuity it uses the natural logarithm and the convention $0\log 0=0$.

[F2] [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]: event-supremum total variation is $\sup_B|q(B)-p(B)|$ and has no factor $1/2$; on a finite power-set space it must be identified with the displayed half-$\ell^1$ convention.

[F3] [[thm-pinsker]]: under AC, event-supremum total variation between probability laws is at most $\sqrt{D_{\rm KL}(q\|p)/2}$; the result is immediate if the KL divergence is infinite.

## Proof

1.1 Fix one state $s$. Write $\Delta_a=q_s(a)-p_s(a)$; since both distributions have mass one, $\sum_a\Delta_a=0$. The set $B=\{a:\Delta_a\ge0\}$ consists of the nonnegative differences. The positive and negative parts of $\Delta$ therefore have equal sum, each equal to $\frac12\sum_a|\Delta_a|$. For every subset $C\subseteq A(s)$, $|\sum_{a\in C}\Delta_a|$ is at most this common sum, and $C=B$ attains it. Thus the event-supremum total variation in [F2] equals $\operatorname{TV}_{A(s)}(q_s,p_s)$. [F2, algebra, construct]

2.1 Apply [F3] to the probability measures $q_s$ and $p_s$ on the finite power-set space, and use step 1.1. This gives $\operatorname{TV}_{A(s)}(q_s,p_s)\le\sqrt{D_{\rm KL}(q_s\|p_s)/2}$, including the infinite-divergence case. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1, given]

3.1 If $K=+\infty$, the asserted inequality holds because each total-variation term is at most one. Suppose $K<\infty$ and put $m=K/2$. When $m=0$, step 2.1 gives $D_{\rm KL}(q_s\|p_s)\ge2\operatorname{TV}_{A(s)}(q_s,p_s)^2\ge0$ for every state. Since their $d$-weighted sum is zero, every state with $d(s)>0$ has zero divergence, so step 2.1 also gives zero total variation there. When $m>0$, for every $x\ge0$ the square $(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt m)^2\ge0$ gives $\sqrt{x}\le(\sqrt m+x/\sqrt m)/2$. Apply this with $x=D_{\rm KL}(q_s\|p_s)/2$ for states with $d(s)>0$, multiply by $d(s)$, and sum. Since $\sum_sd(s)=1$ and $\sum_sd(s)x_s=m$, the result is $\sum_sd(s)\sqrt{x_s}\le\sqrt m$. Step 2.1 now yields the claimed bound. [step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎
## Remarks

The finite-action equality in step 1.1 uses the event-supremum convention, not the total-variation norm of a signed measure. AC enters only in the KL/Pinsker branch; the finite-sum and weighted square-root arguments are choice-free.

## Definition

Let $M=(S,\mathcal R,(A(s))_{s\in S},p)$ be a finite Markov decision process with nonempty state set $S$ and finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ at each state. Put $\mathcal X=\{(s,a,\rho,s'):s\in S,\ a\in A(s),\ \rho\in\mathcal R,\ s'\in S\}$. Let $\mu$ be a probability distribution on $S$, let $\gamma\in[0,1)$, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and for each $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $b_i\in\mathbb R$, $C_i\ge0$, and $c_i:\mathcal X\to[-C_i,C_i]$. A **finite discounted constrained Markov decision process (CMDP)** is the tuple consisting of $M$, $\mu$, $\gamma$, and the bounded transition-cost functions and thresholds $(c_i,b_i)_{i=1}^m$. Its immediate reward signal is $r(s,a,\rho,s')=\rho$.

For a stationary Markov policy $\pi$, define the state-mass sequence recursively by $\mu_0^\pi=\mu$ and

$$\mu_{t+1}^\pi(s'):=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a).$$

This recurrence defines nonnegative finite-time masses; the result that each $\mu_t^\pi$ is a probability distribution is established separately.

## Definition references

## Definition

Let a finite discounted CMDP and a stationary policy $\pi$ be given. The **column transition matrix** $K_\pi$ has entry

$$K_\pi(s',s):=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a),$$

so that its column indexed by $s$ gives the next-state distribution from current state $s$. With the state-mass column vectors $\mu_t^\pi$ from the CMDP definition, the **normalized discounted state occupancy** is

$$d^\pi(s):=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\mu_t^\pi(s).$$

This normalization is part of the definition; the occupancy is a probability distribution by the separate well-definedness result below.

## Definition

Let a finite discounted CMDP have initial distribution $\mu$, discount $\gamma\in[0,1)$, $m$ bounded transition signals $c_i$, thresholds $b_i$, and finite-time state masses $\mu_t^\pi$ under a stationary policy $\pi$, as defined in the CMDP model. For any bounded transition signal $g$ on $(s,a,\rho,s')$, define its **expected discounted sum** under $\pi$ by

$$J_g^\pi(\mu):=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\sum_{s'\in S}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a)g(s,a,\rho,s').$$

The expected discounted reward is $J^\pi:=J_r^\pi(\mu)$ for the immediate reward signal $r(s,a,\rho,s')=\rho$, and the $i$th expected discounted cost is $J_{c_i}^\pi(\mu)$. The policy $\pi$ is **feasible** for the discounted-cost constraints exactly when $J_{c_i}^\pi(\mu)\le b_i$ for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$. Feasibility constrains these expectations; it does not assert a per-trajectory bound.

[[lem-normalized-discounted-state-occupancy-is-probability|The finite-time masses are probability distributions, so each bounded finite-time transition-signal expectation is bounded and the displayed discounted series is well defined.]]

## Statement

Let a finite discounted CMDP, a stationary policy $\pi$, its finite-time state-mass vectors $\mu_t^\pi$, its normalized discounted occupancy $d^\pi$, and the expected discounted signal $J_g^\pi(\mu)$ be as defined above. Each $\mu_t^\pi$ is a probability distribution, $d^\pi$ is a probability distribution, and for every bounded transition signal $g$ with $|g|\le B$, the series defining $J_g^\pi(\mu)$ converges absolutely and satisfies $|J_g^\pi(\mu)|\le B/(1-\gamma)$.

## Statement references

[[def-constrained-markov-decision-process|The initial state distribution and recursive finite-time state masses.]]

[[def-normalized-discounted-state-occupancy|The normalized occupancy formula.]]

[[def-discounted-cost-constraint|The finite-sum formula for expected discounted transition signals.]]

[[lem-bounded-discounted-return-converges|Absolute convergence and the uniform geometric bound for every bounded signal sequence.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite CMDP with initial distribution $\mu$, discount $0\le\gamma<1$, a stationary policy $\pi$, and the recursive state masses and occupancy defined in the linked items.

[F1] [[def-constrained-markov-decision-process]]: $\mu_0^\pi=\mu$ and $\mu_{t+1}^\pi(s')=\sum_{s,a,\rho}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$.

[F2] [[def-finite-markov-decision-process]]: for each admissible $(s,a)$, the joint next-state/reward masses are nonnegative and $\sum_{s',\rho}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1$.

[F3] [[def-finite-markov-decision-process]]: a stationary Markov policy has $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ and $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$.

[F4] [[def-normalized-discounted-state-occupancy]]: $d^\pi(s)=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t\mu_t^\pi(s)$.

[F5] [[def-discounted-cost-constraint]]: $J_g^\pi(\mu)$ is the series of finite sums of the time-$t$ transition masses multiplied by $g(s,a,\rho,s')$ and $\gamma^t$.

[F6] [[thm-geometric-series]]: for $0\le\gamma<1$, $\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t=1/(1-\gamma)$.

[F7] [[lem-bounded-discounted-return-converges]]: every real sequence bounded in absolute value by $B$ has an absolutely convergent $\gamma$-discounted series whose absolute value is at most $B/(1-\gamma)$.

[F8] [[thm-induction-principle]]: a property holding at $0$ and preserved from each natural number to its successor holds for every natural number.

## Proof

1.1 The initial vector $\mu_0^\pi=\mu$ is nonnegative and sums to one. If $\mu_t^\pi$ is a probability distribution, then the recurrence and [F2]–[F3] give nonnegative next masses and $\sum_{s'}\mu_{t+1}^\pi(s')=\sum_s\sum_{a\in A(s)}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s',\rho}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=\sum_s\mu_t^\pi(s)=1$. By [F8], every $\mu_t^\pi$ is a probability distribution. [F1, F2, F3, F8, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F4] and step 1.1, $d^\pi(s)\ge0$ and $\sum_s d^\pi(s)=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\sum_s\mu_t^\pi(s)=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t=1$ by [F6]. Interchanging the finite state sum with the nonnegative series is valid because $S$ is finite. Thus $d^\pi$ is a probability distribution. [F4, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For each $t$, the finite transition weights $\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$ are nonnegative and sum to one by step 1.1 and [F2]–[F3]. Hence their weighted sum of $g$ has absolute value at most $B$. Apply [F7] to this bounded sequence of time-$t$ signal sums; the series in [F5] converges absolutely and its absolute value is at most $B/(1-\gamma)$. [F2, F3, F5, F7, step 1.1, given] ∎

## Definition

Let a finite discounted CMDP, a stationary policy $\pi$, and a bounded transition signal $g$ be given. For $s\in S$, let $\delta_s$ be the initial distribution assigning probability one to $s$. The **state value** is $V_g^\pi(s):=J_g^\pi(\delta_s)$. For $a\in A(s)$, define the **action value** and **advantage** by

$$Q_g^\pi(s,a):=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\sum_{s'\in S}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\bigl(g(s,a,\rho,s')+\gamma V_g^\pi(s')\bigr),\qquad A_g^\pi(s,a):=Q_g^\pi(s,a)-V_g^\pi(s).$$

Taking $g=r$ gives reward values and advantages; taking $g=c_i$ gives the value and advantage for the $i$th cost. These quantities are finite because the signal is bounded, $0\le\gamma<1$, and the transition law is normalized.

## Statement

Let a finite discounted CMDP and two stationary policies $\pi,\pi'$ be given, with normalized discounted occupancies $d^\pi,d^{\pi'}$. Define

$$\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi):=\frac12\sum_{a\in A(s)}|\pi'(a\mid s)-\pi(a\mid s)|$$

and $\|x\|_1:=\sum_{s\in S}|x(s)|$ for a state vector. Then

$$\|d^{\pi'}-d^\pi\|_1\le\frac{2\gamma}{1-\gamma}\sum_{s\in S}d^\pi(s)\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi).$$

## Statement references

[[def-constrained-markov-decision-process|A finite CMDP has finite states and actions, a normalized joint transition law, and stationary policies.]]

[[def-normalized-discounted-state-occupancy]]: The normalized occupancy is $(1-\gamma)$ times the discounted sum of state-mass vectors.

[[lem-normalized-discounted-state-occupancy-is-probability|Each state-mass vector and the resulting occupancy are probability distributions.]]

[Achiam et al., *Constrained Policy Optimization*, supplementary material, Appendix 10.1](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/achiam17a/achiam17a-supp.pdf).

[Altman, *Constrained Markov Decision Processes*, Chapter 3 §3.1](https://www-sop.inria.fr/members/Eitan.Altman/TEMP/h.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite CMDP, $0\le\gamma<1$, stationary policies $\pi,\pi'$, and their state-mass vectors and normalized discounted occupancies.

[F1] [[def-constrained-markov-decision-process]]: $S$ and each $A(s)$ are finite, $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$ is a normalized joint law, $P(s'\mid s,a):=\sum_\rho p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$ is a probability distribution, and $\pi(a\mid s)$ is a probability distribution over $A(s)$.

[F2] [[def-normalized-discounted-state-occupancy]]: $d^\sigma=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t\mu_t^\sigma$ and the column transition matrix is $K_\sigma(s',s)=\sum_{a,\rho}\sigma(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$.

[F3] [[lem-normalized-discounted-state-occupancy-is-probability]]: every $\mu_t^\sigma$ and $d^\sigma$ is a probability distribution.

[F4] [[thm-geometric-series]]: $\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t=1/(1-\gamma)$ for $0\le\gamma<1$.

[F5] [[lem-geometric-sequence-null]]: $\gamma^n\to0$ for $0\le\gamma<1$.

## Proof

1.1 For $\sigma\in\{\pi,\pi'\}$, every entry of $K_\sigma$ is nonnegative and each column sums to one by [F1]. Thus $K_\sigma^t$ is column-stochastic for every $t$, and its induced matrix $1$-norm $\|A\|_1:=\max_s\sum_{s'}|A(s',s)|$ is one. The matrix series $G_\sigma:=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^tK_\sigma^t$ converges in this norm by [F4]; its finite partial sums satisfy $(I-\gamma K_\sigma)\sum_{t=0}^{N}\gamma^tK_\sigma^t=I-\gamma^{N+1}K_\sigma^{N+1}$, whose remainder norm tends to zero by [F5]. The same identity with multiplication on the other side shows $G_\sigma=(I-\gamma K_\sigma)^{-1}$. [F1, F4, F5, given, algebra]

1.2 By [F1], for each coordinate $s'$ of $(K_{\pi'}-K_\pi)d^\pi$, the triangle inequality gives $\sum_{s'}|((K_{\pi'}-K_\pi)d^\pi)(s')|\le\sum_{s,a,s'}d^\pi(s)|\pi'(a\mid s)-\pi(a\mid s)|P(s'\mid s,a)=2\sum_s d^\pi(s)\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi)$, because $\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)=1$. [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 The recurrence in [F1] and the matrix definition in [F2] give $\mu_t^\sigma=K_\sigma^t\mu$, hence $d^\sigma=(1-\gamma)G_\sigma\mu$. The inverse identity $G_{\pi'}-G_\pi=G_{\pi'}[(I-\gamma K_\pi)-(I-\gamma K_{\pi'})]G_\pi$ therefore yields $d^{\pi'}-d^\pi=\gamma G_{\pi'}(K_{\pi'}-K_\pi)d^\pi$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $\|G_{\pi'}\|_1\le\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t=1/(1-\gamma)$ by [F4] and column-stochasticity, combine step 2.1 with step 1.2 to obtain the claimed $1$-norm bound. [F4, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let a finite discounted CMDP, a bounded transition signal $g$, a bounded function $f:S\to\mathbb R$, and stationary policies $\pi,\pi'$ be given. All sums below over $a,\rho,s'$ range over $A(s),\mathcal R,S$, respectively. For a policy $\sigma$ define

$$\delta_f^g(s,a,\rho,s'):=g(s,a,\rho,s')+\gamma f(s')-f(s),\qquad \bar\delta_{f}^{g,\sigma}(s):=\sum_{a,\rho,s'}\sigma(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\delta_f^g(s,a,\rho,s').$$

Put

$$L_{\pi,f}^g(\pi'):=\sum_s d^\pi(s)\bigl(\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s)-\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi}(s)\bigr).$$

Then the exact performance-difference identity is

$$J_g^{\pi'}(\mu)-J_g^\pi(\mu)=\frac{L_{\pi,f}^g(\pi')}{1-\gamma}+\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\sum_s\bigl(d^{\pi'}(s)-d^\pi(s)\bigr)\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s).$$

## Statement references

[[def-constrained-markov-decision-process|Finite CMDP data and finite-time state masses.]]

[[def-discounted-cost-constraint]]: The expected discounted transition-signal sum $J_g^\pi(\mu)$.

[[def-normalized-discounted-state-occupancy]]: The normalized discounted state occupancy $d^\pi$.

[[lem-normalized-discounted-state-occupancy-is-probability|Probability mass and boundedness facts used to justify the discounted series.]]

[Achiam et al., *Constrained Policy Optimization*, supplementary material, Appendix 10.1](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/achiam17a/achiam17a-supp.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite discounted CMDP, bounded $g$ and $f$, stationary policies $\pi,\pi'$, and $0\le\gamma<1$.

[F1] [[def-constrained-markov-decision-process]]: the finite-time state masses obey the one-step transition recurrence with joint masses $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$.

[F2] [[def-discounted-cost-constraint]]: $J_g^\sigma(\mu)$ is the discounted series of finite sums of $g$ against the time-$t$ transition masses.

[F3] [[def-normalized-discounted-state-occupancy]]: $d^\sigma(s)=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t\mu_t^\sigma(s)$.

[F4] [[lem-normalized-discounted-state-occupancy-is-probability]]: every $\mu_t^\sigma$ is a probability distribution, and every bounded transition-signal discounted series is absolutely convergent.

[F5] [[lem-geometric-sequence-null]]: $\gamma^n\to0$ for $0\le\gamma<1$.

## Proof

1.1 Fix a policy $\sigma$. For each $t$, let $e_t^\sigma$ be the finite transition-mass sum of $g$ at time $t$, and let $h_t^\sigma:=\sum_s\mu_t^\sigma(s)f(s)$. By [F1] and the definition of $\delta_f^g$, the finite sum of $\delta_f^g$ at time $t$ is $e_t^\sigma+\gamma h_{t+1}^\sigma-h_t^\sigma$. Summing after multiplication by $\gamma^t$ for $t=0,\ldots,N$ telescopes to $\sum_{t=0}^N\gamma^t e_t^\sigma-h_0^\sigma+\gamma^{N+1}h_{N+1}^\sigma$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The remainder satisfies $|\gamma^{N+1}h_{N+1}^\sigma|\le\gamma^{N+1}\|f\|_\infty\to0$ by [F4] and [F5]. Also $|\delta_f^g|\le\|g\|_\infty+(1+\gamma)\|f\|_\infty$, so [F4] makes its discounted series convergent. Passing to the limit in step 1.1 and using [F2]–[F3] gives $J_g^\sigma(\mu)=\sum_s\mu(s)f(s)+(1-\gamma)^{-1}\sum_s d^\sigma(s)\bar\delta_f^{g,\sigma}(s)$. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Apply the identity in step 2.1 to $\sigma=\pi'$ and $\sigma=\pi$ and subtract; the initial terms $\sum_s\mu(s)f(s)$ cancel. Add and subtract $\sum_s d^\pi(s)\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s)$. The first resulting term is $L_{\pi,f}^g(\pi')$ by its definition, and the second is $\sum_s(d^{\pi'}(s)-d^\pi(s))\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s)$. Dividing by $1-\gamma>0$ gives the claimed identity. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let a finite discounted CMDP, a bounded transition signal $g$, a bounded function $f:S\to\mathbb R$, and stationary policies $\pi,\pi'$ be given. For each state define

$$\bar\delta_f^{g,\sigma}(s):=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\sum_{s'\in S}\sigma(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\bigl(g(s,a,\rho,s')+\gamma f(s')-f(s)\bigr),\qquad \sigma\in\{\pi,\pi'\}.$$

Set $\epsilon_f^g(\pi'):=\max_{s\in S}|\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s)|$ and

$$L_{\pi,f}^g(\pi'):=\sum_{s\in S}d^\pi(s)\bigl(\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s)-\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi}(s)\bigr),\qquad D_{\pi,f}^{\pm,g}(\pi'):=\frac{L_{\pi,f}^g(\pi')}{1-\gamma}\pm\frac{2\gamma\epsilon_f^g(\pi')}{(1-\gamma)^2}\sum_{s\in S}d^\pi(s)\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi),$$

where $\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi):=\frac12\sum_{a\in A(s)}|\pi'(a\mid s)-\pi(a\mid s)|$. Then

$$D_{\pi,f}^{-,g}(\pi')\le J_g^{\pi'}(\mu)-J_g^\pi(\mu)\le D_{\pi,f}^{+,g}(\pi').$$

These total-variation bounds are choice-free. Under the additional Axiom of Choice, define

$$\overline D_{\rm KL}^{\pi}(\pi'\|\pi):=\sum_{s:d^\pi(s)>0}d^\pi(s)D_{\rm KL}\bigl(\pi'(\cdot\mid s)\|\pi(\cdot\mid s)\bigr),$$

using natural logarithms and $+\infty$ when the first action law is not absolutely continuous with respect to the second. The same inequalities hold after replacing $\sum_s d^\pi(s)\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi)$ by $\sqrt{\overline D_{\rm KL}^{\pi}(\pi'\|\pi)/2}$; when the average KL is infinite, these KL-form inequalities are interpreted as the trivial extended bounds $-\infty\le J_g^{\pi'}(\mu)-J_g^\pi(\mu)\le+\infty$. Taking $g=r$ gives the reward bound, and taking $g=c_i$ gives the corresponding bound for each discounted cost.

[[def-normalized-discounted-state-occupancy]]: The normalized occupancy $d^\pi$.

[Achiam et al., *Constrained Policy Optimization*, §5.1](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/achiam17a/achiam17a.pdf).

[Achiam et al., *Constrained Policy Optimization*, supplementary material, Appendix 10.1](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/achiam17a/achiam17a-supp.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite discounted CMDP, bounded transition signal $g$, bounded function $f$, stationary policies $\pi,\pi'$, and $0\le\gamma<1$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is used only in the KL branch, through the Pinsker theorem and the directional KL definition; the total-variation proof below is choice-free.

[F1] [[def-constrained-markov-decision-process]]: the state and action sets are finite and nonempty, the transition/reward mass is normalized, and $g$ is bounded.

[F2] [[def-discounted-cost-constraint]]: $J_g^\sigma(\mu)$ is the expected discounted transition-signal series.

[F3] [[def-normalized-discounted-state-occupancy]] and [[lem-normalized-discounted-state-occupancy-is-probability]]: $d^\sigma$ is the normalized discounted state occupancy and is a probability distribution.

[F4] [[lem-mdp-performance-difference-identity-with-arbitrary-baseline]]: $J_g^{\pi'}(\mu)-J_g^\pi(\mu)=L_{\pi,f}^g(\pi')/(1-\gamma)+(1-\gamma)^{-1}\sum_s(d^{\pi'}(s)-d^\pi(s))\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s)$.

[F5] [[lem-discounted-occupancy-change-bounded-by-average-tv]]: $\|d^{\pi'}-d^\pi\|_1\le2\gamma(1-\gamma)^{-1}\sum_s d^\pi(s)\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi)$.

[F6] [[lem-finite-action-average-tv-controlled-by-kl]]: under AC, the same weighted average of finite-action total variations is at most the square root of half the weighted directional KL.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1] and [F3], $S$ is finite, $d^\pi,d^{\pi'}$ are probability distributions, and each finite sum defining $\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s)$ is bounded by $\|g\|_\infty+(1+\gamma)\|f\|_\infty$; hence $\epsilon_f^g(\pi')$ is finite. By [F2], the returns are the defined bounded-signal discounted sums. The identity [F4] writes their difference as $L_{\pi,f}^g(\pi')/(1-\gamma)$ plus the remainder $(1-\gamma)^{-1}\sum_s(d^{\pi'}(s)-d^\pi(s))\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s)$. The triangle inequality gives $|\sum_s(d^{\pi'}-d^\pi)\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}|\le\sum_s|d^{\pi'}-d^\pi||\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}|\le\epsilon_f^g(\pi')\|d^{\pi'}-d^\pi\|_1$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 Substitute [F5] into the remainder bound in step 1.1. The resulting error is at most $2\gamma\epsilon_f^g(\pi')(1-\gamma)^{-2}\sum_s d^\pi(s)\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi)$, which gives the two total-variation inequalities. [F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Assume AC. If $\overline D_{\rm KL}^{\pi}(\pi'\|\pi)=+\infty$, the stated extended KL inequalities are immediate. Otherwise [F6] bounds the average total variation in step 2.1 by $\sqrt{\overline D_{\rm KL}^{\pi}(\pi'\|\pi)/2}$. Replacing the nonnegative error term by this upper bound gives the two KL-form inequalities. This step alone uses AC; steps 1.1–2.1 do not. [A1, F6, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the theoretical average-KL comparison, and let a finite discounted CMDP have cost signals $c_1,\ldots,c_m$ with thresholds $b_1,\ldots,b_m$. Let $\theta\mapsto\pi_\theta$ be a stationary policy family on an open subset of $\mathbb R^d$ with fixed common support, and assume its policy coordinates are twice continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of the current parameter $\theta_k$. Choose a trust radius $\delta>0$, a backtracking factor $\beta\in(0,1)$, and a finite backtracking budget $L\ge0$. At iteration $k$, the finite data batch consists of $N\ge1$ rows $(s_j,a_j,\omega_j,\widehat A_j^r,\widehat A_{1,j}^c,\ldots,\widehat A_{m,j}^c)$ from trajectories generated in the CMDP under the current policy $\pi_{\theta_k}$, where $\omega_j\ge0$, $\sum_j\omega_j=1$, and $\pi_{\theta_k}(a_j\mid s_j)>0$. The advantage estimates are real numbers held fixed during the update, and the batch also includes real baseline-cost estimates $\widehat J_{i,k}$. The weights and estimates may come from any fixed rollout or critic estimator; this procedure assumes no accuracy property for them. It specifies the exact finite-data trust-region subproblem and line search; implementations that approximate the subproblem solve are discussed separately.

For $\theta$ near $\theta_k$, define the finite sample surrogates

$$\widehat L_r(\theta):=\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\left(\frac{\pi_\theta(a_j\mid s_j)}{\pi_{\theta_k}(a_j\mid s_j)}-1\right)\widehat A_j^r,\qquad \widehat L_i^c(\theta):=\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\left(\frac{\pi_\theta(a_j\mid s_j)}{\pi_{\theta_k}(a_j\mid s_j)}-1\right)\widehat A_{i,j}^c.$$

and $\widehat K(\theta):=\sum_j\omega_jD_{\rm KL}(\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s_j)\|\pi_{\theta_k}(\cdot\mid s_j))$. Put $g=\nabla\widehat L_r(\theta_k)$, $u_i=(1-\gamma)^{-1}\nabla\widehat L_i^c(\theta_k)$, $H=\nabla^2\widehat K(\theta_k)$, and $q_i=\widehat J_{i,k}-b_i$. The update procedure is:

1. If $H$ is not symmetric positive definite, meaning $x^THx>0$ for every nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^d$, return `no-step`. Otherwise form the local quadratic program

   $$\max_{x\in\mathbb R^d} g^Tx\quad\text{subject to}\quad q_i+u_i^Tx\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \frac12x^THx\le\delta.$$

2. If this program is feasible, let $x^*$ be its lexicographically least global maximizer. The feasible set is a closed subset of the compact ellipsoid, so the maximizer set is nonempty and compact. Minimize the first coordinate on that set, restrict to its nonempty compact minimizers, and repeat for each coordinate; the resulting point is the lexicographically least maximizer. If the program is infeasible and $m=1$, compute $v=H^{-1}u_1$. If $u_1=0$, return `no-step`, since the linearized cost cannot be reduced. Otherwise $u_1^Tv>0$ by positive definiteness, and use the cost-recovery proposal $x^*=-\sqrt{2\delta/(u_1^Tv)}\,v$. If the program is infeasible and $m>1$, return `no-step`.

3. For $j=0,\ldots,L$, set $\theta_j=\theta_k+\beta^jx^*$. Accept the first $\theta_j$ in the policy family's parameter domain for which $\widehat K(\theta_j)\le\delta$ and every sample cost estimate $\widehat J_{i,k}+(1-\gamma)^{-1}\widehat L_i^c(\theta_j)$ is at most $b_i$. If no candidate passes this sample check, return `no-step`; otherwise output the accepted parameter as $\theta_{k+1}$.

For finite constants $D_i\ge0$, optional nonnegative bounded transition signals $\Delta_i:\mathcal X\to[0,D_i]$ may be included in the supplied cost-advantage and baseline estimates by estimating the shaped costs $c_i+\Delta_i$. The exact theorem concerns exact policies and expectations; the line search above checks only the supplied sample estimates.

## Statement

Under the inputs and assumptions of the sample-based constrained policy
optimization update, with finite parameter dimension $d$ and nonnegative
integer backtracking budget $L$, the update has a unique mathematical output,
either `no-step` or an accepted parameter. Its proposals satisfy these properties.

If its matrix $H$ is symmetric positive definite and its local quadratic
program is feasible, the program has a nonempty compact global-maximizer set
and a unique lexicographically least global maximizer. This is the proposal
selected by the update and satisfies every linearized cost constraint and
the quadratic trust-region constraint.

If the program is infeasible with one cost and $u_1\ne0$, the inverse used
by the update exists, $a=u_1^TH^{-1}u_1>0$, and its recovery proposal is
$$ x^*=-\sqrt{2\delta/a}\,H^{-1}u_1. $$
It is the unique minimizer of $u_1^Tx$ on $\{x:x^THx/2\le\delta\}$,
satisfies $(x^*)^THx^*/2=\delta$, and decreases the linearized cost by
$\sqrt{2\delta a}$. It need not make the infeasible cost constraint feasible.
The non-positive-definite, zero-recovery-gradient and multiple-cost infeasible
branches return `no-step` as specified.

Once the specified exact subproblem decisions and operations have been
performed, backtracking terminates after at most $L+1$ candidate tests.
It returns the first passing candidate, which belongs to the parameter
domain and satisfies the empirical KL and all empirical cost tests, or
returns `no-step` if none passes. These are well-definedness and finite-search
properties of the exact mathematical update. They do not bound the cost of
exact feasibility/optimization operations or certify the true expected costs,
exact population KL, policy improvement, or convergence of sampled iterates.

## Statement references

[[alg-constrained-policy-optimization]]

[Achiam et al., Constrained Policy Optimization, Sections 6.1–6.3](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/achiam17a/achiam17a.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The complete inputs and hypotheses of the algorithm, its real
sample coefficients $g,u_i,q_i,H$, radius $\delta>0$, factor $0<\beta<1$,
and finite integer budget $L\ge0$. The algorithm's Axiom of Choice hypothesis
for its theoretical KL comparison is retained; the finite-dimensional
proposal argument below makes no additional use of choice.

[F1] [[alg-constrained-policy-optimization]] specifies all proposal branches, the lexicographic tie rule and the ordered sample-test search.

[F2] [[lem-definite-quadratic-forms-have-a-uniform-sphere-bound]] gives $c>0$ with $z^THz\ge c$ on the unit sphere for a positive definite quadratic form in positive dimension.

[F3] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] makes a closed bounded Euclidean set compact, and [[lem-closed-subset-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]] preserves compactness under closed restriction.

[F4] [[thm-extreme-value-metric]] gives attained maxima and minima for a continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space.

[F5] [[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]] makes a square real matrix with trivial nullspace invertible.

[F6] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] give Euclidean Cauchy–Schwarz, the triangle inequality, coordinate bounds and bilinear norm identities.

## Proof

1.1 First consider $d\ge1$ and symmetric positive definite $H$. By homogeneity, [F2] gives $x^THx\ge c\|x\|_2^2$ for all $x$, with zero handled directly. Put $C=\sum_{a,b}|H_{ab}|$. Coordinate bounds in [F6] and the identity $x_ax_b-y_ay_b=(x_a-y_a)x_b+y_a(x_b-y_b)$ give $|x^THx-y^THy|\le C\|x-y\|_2(\|x\|_2+\|y\|_2)$, so the quadratic form is continuous. The ellipsoid $E=\{x:x^THx/2\le\delta\}$ is therefore closed and contained in the ball of radius $\sqrt{2\delta/c}$, hence compact by [F3]. Each linear functional $x\mapsto v^Tx$ is continuous because $|v^T(x-y)|\le\|v\|_2\|x-y\|_2$. Thus the feasible set $F=E\cap\bigcap_i\{x:q_i+u_i^Tx\le0\}$ is a closed subset of $E$, and is compact. [F2, F3, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 If $F$ is nonempty, [F4] gives an attained maximum $M$ of $g^Tx$ on $F$. Its maximizer set $K_0=\{x\in F:g^Tx=M\}$ is nonempty and compact by closedness and [F3]. Successively for coordinates $h=1,\ldots,d$, let $a_h$ be the minimum of coordinate $h$ on $K_{h-1}$ and set $K_h=\{x\in K_{h-1}:x_h=a_h\}$. Each minimum exists by [F4], and each restriction remains nonempty and compact by [F3]. After $d$ restrictions all coordinates are fixed, so $K_d$ is a singleton. For any other maximizer, the first coordinate where it differs from this singleton must be greater, by the construction of that coordinate's minimum. The singleton is therefore exactly the unique lexicographically least maximizer. As a member of $F$, it satisfies all stated constraints. [F1, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

2.2 If $Hz=0$, then $z^THz=0$ and positive definiteness forces $z=0$. Thus [F5] supplies $H^{-1}$. In the single-cost recovery branch write $u=u_1\ne0$, $v=H^{-1}u$. Then $v\ne0$, $Hv=u$ and $a=u^Tv=v^THv>0$. For every $x\in E$, nonnegativity of the quadratic form at $x-(u^Tx/a)v$ gives $0\le x^THx-(u^Tx)^2/a$, using symmetry. Consequently $u^Tx\ge-\sqrt{2\delta a}$. For $x^*=-\sqrt{2\delta/a}\,v$, direct substitution gives $(x^*)^THx^*=2\delta$ and $u^Tx^*=-\sqrt{2\delta a}$, attaining the bound. If another point attains it, equality in the preceding inequalities gives $(x-(u^Tx/a)v)^TH(x-(u^Tx/a)v)=0$, hence $x=(u^Tx/a)v=x^*$ by positive definiteness. The recovery proposal is therefore unique, and its linearized cost is $q_1-\sqrt{2\delta a}$. Since it is the minimum over $E$, infeasibility implies that this last value is strictly positive, rather than implying feasibility. [F1, F5, F6, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The remaining proposal branches are the explicit returns in [F1]: non-positive-definite $H$, infeasible single-cost problem with $u_1=0$, and infeasible problem with $m>1$ all return `no-step`. If $d=0$, the only parameter displacement is the zero vector, so a feasible program has that unique maximizer, and in the infeasible case all $u_i=0$ and one of the specified no-step branches applies. Thus zero dimension introduces no missing proposal case. Together with steps 2.1 and 2.2, every branch either gives one uniquely specified proposal or returns `no-step`. [F1, F6, step 2.1, step 2.2, given, cases]

4.1 For a proposal $x^*$, the candidates $\theta_k+\beta^jx^*$ for integer $j=0,\ldots,L$ form a prescribed ordered list of $L+1$ points. The parameter-domain check precedes evaluation of the policy tests, so no value outside the domain is required. On the domain, the finite common-support policy probabilities define the empirical KL and surrogates in [F1]. Either there is a least passing index in this finite list, or there is none; [F1] returns its candidate or `no-step`, respectively. Inspecting successive indices therefore terminates in at most $L+1$ candidate tests. The definition of passing supplies exactly the stated sample inequalities. All choices and returns are single-valued by steps 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1 and this least-index rule, establishing the asserted output and finite-search properties. No step in this argument compares the sample estimates to population expectations. [F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

The source's practical approximate CPO implementation motivates the quadratic
program and the recovery direction. This lemma proves properties of the
library's explicitly specified exact finite-data update, including its
local lexicographic tie rule and finite search budget. It does not attribute

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$ and let $q$ be a positive definite quadratic form on $\mathbb R^n$. Then some $c>0$ satisfies $q(u)\ge c$ whenever $\|u\|_2=1$. For a negative definite $q$, some $c>0$ satisfies $q(u)\le-c$ on the same sphere.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A definite quadratic form $q$ on $\mathbb R^n$ with $n\ge1$.

[L1] The Euclidean norm is continuous, and a continuous map has closed preimages of closed sets ([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]], [[thm-metric-continuity-characterisations]]).

[L2] Heine--Borel says that a closed bounded Euclidean subset is compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[L3] A continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space attains its extrema ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The unit sphere is nonempty because it contains $e_0$, closed by [L1], and bounded since it lies in the radius-two ball about zero. [L1, given, algebra]

2.1 It is compact by [L2]. [step 1.1, L2]

3.1 The finite coordinate formula for $q$ makes it continuous; [L3] therefore gives a point where $q$ attains its minimum and maximum on the sphere. [step 2.1, L3, algebra]

4.1 In the positive definite case the attained minimum is positive, and in the negative definite case the attained maximum is negative, by the definition of definiteness. [step 3.1, given]

5.1 Taking $c$ to be the positive minimum or the negative maximum gives the asserted uniform signed bounds. [step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

An expected discounted-cost constraint bounds an expectation; by itself it does not bound the probability of any pathwise violation or guarantee safe exploration. The performance theorem concerns exact policy returns. Its total-variation branch is choice-free, while its average-KL branch assumes the Axiom of Choice. The practical CPO update instead uses sample estimates, a linearized reward/cost objective, a second-order KL approximation, conjugate-gradient solves, and a backtracking line search against sample-estimated constraints. Optional nonnegative cost shaping changes the constrained signal but supplies no error bound for the sample estimates or numerical solves. Consequently, the ideal theorem does not by itself certify the sampled iterates' true costs or imply convergence of the implementation; this remark asserts no such guarantee.

## Example

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In a one-state CMDP with discount $\gamma=0$, let the only costs be $0$ for `safe` and $1$ for `risky`, with threshold $b=1/20$. The old policy chooses `risky` with probability $1/100$, and the proposed policy chooses it with probability $1/5$. If a one-row rollout sample from the old policy observes `safe` and supplies zero baseline-cost and advantage estimates, the empirical line-search cost is zero and passes the threshold; this sample occurs with probability $99/100$.

[F1] [[def-constrained-markov-decision-process]]: the discounted CMDP has finite transition laws and the stated bounded cost signal.

[F2] [[def-discounted-cost-constraint]]: with $\gamma=0$, expected discounted cost is the one-step expected cost.

[F3] [[def-discounted-value-and-advantage-functions]]: $V_c^\pi(s)=J_c^\pi(\delta_s)$ and $A_c^\pi(s,a)=Q_c^\pi(s,a)-V_c^\pi(s)$.

[F4] [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]: for finite action probabilities, $D_{\rm KL}(q\|p)=\sum_aq(a)\log(q(a)/p(a))$ when $q\ll p$, with natural logarithms.

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix a scale $c>0$. For $0\leq\lambda<1/c$, define
$$\psi_{E,c}(\lambda):=\frac{-\log(1-c\lambda)-c\lambda}{c^2}.$$
On a discrete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, a pair of real processes $(S_t,V_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0}$ is a **one-sided sub-exponential pair at scale $c$** when $S_0=V_0=0$, $V_t\geq0$, and both processes are $\mathcal F_t$-measurable at each time, and for every $\lambda\in[0,1/c)$ there is a real process $(L_t^\lambda)_{t\in\mathbb N_0}$ that is nonnegative, integrable, and $\mathcal F_t$-measurable at each time, satisfies $\mathbb E L_0^\lambda\leq1$ and $\mathbb E[L_t^\lambda\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]\leq L_{t-1}^\lambda$ almost surely for each $t\geq1$, and obeys
$$\exp\!\left(\lambda S_t-\psi_{E,c}(\lambda)V_t\right)\leq L_t^\lambda\quad\text{almost surely for every }t\geq0.$$

For $\alpha\in(0,1)$, a Borel-measurable function $u:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ is a **one-sided sub-exponential uniform boundary with crossing probability $\alpha$ and scale $c$** if, for every discrete filtered probability space and every one-sided sub-exponential pair at scale $c$,
$$P\!\left(\exists t\geq1:S_t\geq u(V_t)\right)\leq\alpha.$$

## Definition references

[[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]: the filtration consists of sigma-algebras $\mathcal F_t\subseteq\mathcal F_{t+1}$ on one probability space, with time starting at zero.

[[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]]: a real process is adapted when each value is measurable with respect to the corresponding $\mathcal F_t$; integrability is imposed at every fixed time.

[[def-nonnegative-test-supermartingale]]: the auxiliary process $L^\lambda$ is nonnegative, adapted, integrable, satisfies the conditional supermartingale inequalities, and has initial expectation at most one.

[[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is explicitly assumed for the conditional-expectation convention used by the supplied supermartingale definitions.

[A Howard et al., Definition 1 (sub-$\psi$ condition), Definition 2 (uniform boundary), and $\psi_{E,c}$, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1810.08240v9)

[A Tropp, Lecture 26, §§26.4.3–26.4.4](https://tropp.caltech.edu/notes/Tro24-Probability-Theory-LN.pdf)

## Definition

Inputs are real bounds $a\leq b$, a nominal error level $\delta\in(0,1)$, an observation stream $(X_t)_{t\geq1}$ with $X_t\in[a,b]$ almost surely and $X_t$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_t$, a forecast stream $(\widehat X_t)_{t\geq1}$ with $\widehat X_t\in[a,b]$ almost surely and $\widehat X_t$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_{t-1}$, and, when $c=b-a>0$, an evaluation procedure for a Borel one-sided sub-exponential uniform boundary $u_{\delta/2,c}$ with crossing probability $\delta/2$ and scale $c$. The output is one interval $C_t$ at each positive integer time $t$.

1. If $c=0$, return $C_t=[a,a]$ at each time.

2. If $c>0$, initialize $\bar X_0=0$ and $V_0=0$. After receiving forecast $\widehat X_t$ and then observation $X_t$, update
$$\bar X_t=\left(1-\frac1t\right)\bar X_{t-1}+\frac{X_t}{t},\qquad V_t=V_{t-1}+(X_t-\widehat X_t)^2.$$
Return
$$C_t=\left[\bar X_t-\frac{u_{\delta/2,c}(V_t)}{t},\;\bar X_t+\frac{u_{\delta/2,c}(V_t)}{t}\right].$$

The procedure uses observations only through time $t$. The accumulated quantity $V_t$ is the observed sum of squared forecast errors; it is not a predictable conditional-variance process.

[[def-subexponential-uniform-boundary]]: the supplied boundary has the stated scale and crossing-probability guarantee.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0},P)$ be a discrete filtered probability space, let $a\leq b$ be real numbers, and put $c=b-a$. Fix $\delta\in(0,1)$ and write $\alpha=\delta/2$. For $c>0$, let $u_{\alpha,c}$ be any Borel one-sided sub-exponential uniform boundary with crossing probability $\alpha$ at scale $c$. Choose any versions $m_t=E[X_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]$ and define
$$\bar X_t=\frac1t\sum_{i=1}^tX_i,\qquad \mu_t=\frac1t\sum_{i=1}^tm_i,\qquad V_t=\sum_{i=1}^t(X_i-\widehat X_i)^2.$$
Let $C_t$ be the interval returned at time $t$ by the empirical-Bernstein interval-update algorithm, using $u_{\alpha,c}$ when $c>0$. Then
$$P\!\left(\mu_t\in C_t\text{ for every }t\geq1\right)\geq1-\delta.$$
The probability statement is independent of the chosen conditional-expectation versions. No common conditional mean is assumed. If there is a fixed real $\mu$ such that $E[X_i\mid\mathcal F_{i-1}]=\mu$ almost surely for every $i$, then $\mu_t=\mu$ simultaneously almost surely and the same intervals cover this fixed mean.

For $c>0$, the finite-mixture formula also supplies a valid boundary: choose an integer $J\geq1$, numbers $0<\lambda_j<1/c$, and weights $w_j>0$ with $\sum_{j=1}^Jw_j=1$. For every $v\geq0$, the unique nonnegative solution $s=u_{\alpha,c}(v)$ of
$$\sum_{j=1}^Jw_j\exp\!\left(\lambda_js-\psi_{E,c}(\lambda_j)v\right)=\frac1\alpha$$
defines a Borel one-sided sub-exponential uniform boundary with crossing probability $\alpha$ at scale $c$.

## Statement references

[Howard et al., Theorem 4, §4.1, and Appendix A.8 (arXiv v9 PDF pp. 14, 35)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1810.08240v9)

[Tropp, Lecture 26, §§26.4.3–26.4.4 (PDF pp. 397–399; printed lecture pages 382–385)](https://tropp.caltech.edu/notes/Tro24-Probability-Theory-LN.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume AC. The objects, hypotheses, conventions, error levels, versions, boundary, and interval process in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]: $(\mathcal F_t)$ is an increasing filtration on one probability space, indexed from time zero.

[F2] [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]]: each $X_t$ is an adapted real random variable; the almost-sure boundedness makes it integrable at each time.

[F3] [[def-predictable-discrete-time-process]]: each forecast $\widehat X_t$ is $\mathcal F_{t-1}$-measurable.

[F4] [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: a conditional-expectation version is real, integrable, measurable with respect to the conditioning sigma-algebra, and has the defining event integrals.

[F5] [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]: conditional expectations are unique almost-sure classes of versions; the notation is independent of the chosen representative up to almost-sure equality.

[F6] [[thm-basic-algebra-and-order-properties-of-conditional-expectation]]: conditional expectation is linear, positive, order-preserving, and preserves constants.

[F7] [[thm-taking-out-what-is-known]]: for a bounded measurable factor $Z$, $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

[F8] [[thm-tower-property-of-conditional-expectation]]: if $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely.

[F9] [[def-martingale-submartingale-and-supermartingale]]: an integrable adapted process is a supermartingale when its one-step conditional expectations are at most its current values almost surely.

[F10] [[def-nonnegative-test-supermartingale]]: under a null law, a test supermartingale is adapted, integrable, nonnegative, supermartingale, and has initial expectation at most one.

[F11] [[thm-mixture-of-null-supermartingales]]: a product-measurable mixture of null test supermartingales is again a null test supermartingale.

[F12] [[thm-villes-inequality]]: if $M$ is a nonnegative test supermartingale, then $P(\sup_{t\geq0}M_t\geq1/\alpha)\leq\alpha$.

[F13] [[def-subexponential-uniform-boundary]]: a scale-$c$ one-sided sub-exponential boundary bounds the crossing probability of every pair in its stated process class.

[F14] The exponential is positive, continuous and strictly increasing, has $\exp(0)=1$, and tends to $0$ at $-\infty$ and to $+\infty$ at $+\infty$. [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]] [[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]] [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]

[F15] A continuous real function on a closed bounded interval takes every value between its endpoint values. [[thm-intermediate-value]]

[F16] Strictly between any two real numbers lies a rational. [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]

[F17] On $(0,\infty)$, $\log'(x)=1/x$ and $\log x=\int_1^x dt/t$, so $\log1=0$. Derivatives obey the sum, product and chain rules, differentiability implies continuity, and the mean value theorem compares endpoint differences with interior derivatives. [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]] [[lem-derivative-algebra-and-chain-rules]] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]

[F18] Affine functions are continuous, finite sums and scalar multiples preserve continuity, and compositions of continuous real functions are continuous. [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]] [[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]

[F19] The open right rays $(r,\infty)$, $r\in\mathbb R$, generate the real Borel sigma-algebra. [[thm-seven-generators-of-the-borel-sigma-algebra-on-r]]

[L1] [[def-time-varying-target-confidence-sequence]]: an adapted target process has a confidence sequence when its random intervals are measurable and cover the target at all integer times with the stated probability.

[L2] [[alg-empirical-bernstein-confidence-sequence]]: when $c>0$, the algorithm updates $\bar X_t$ and $V_t$ from the observed data and returns the closed interval centered at $\bar X_t$ with radius $u_{\alpha,c}(V_t)/t$; when $c=0$, it returns $[a,a]$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is assumed for conditional-expectation existence and for the cited supermartingale and Ville interfaces.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $c=0$, then $X_t=\widehat X_t=a$ almost surely for every $t$. By [F6], each $m_t=a$ almost surely, so $\mu_t=a$ simultaneously almost surely and the algorithm's singleton $C_t=[a,a]$ covers it. If $c>0$, boundedness gives $X_t\in L^1(P)$; choose the versions in the Statement using [A1]. Any two versions agree almost surely by [F5], and the countable union of their exceptional null sets is null, so the all-times coverage probability does not depend on those choices. [given, F4, F5, F6, A1, L2, choose, algebra]

1.2 For $x>-1$ define $r(x)=(x-\log(1+x))/x^2$ when $x\ne0$ and $r(0)=1/2$. Direct integration gives $r(x)=\int_0^1 t/(1+tx)\,dt$. The integrand decreases in $x$ for every $t>0$, so $r$ is decreasing on $(-1,\infty)$. If $c>0$, $0<\lambda<1/c$, and $|\xi|\leq c$, then $x=\lambda\xi\geq-\lambda c>-1$, whence $\lambda\xi-\log(1+\lambda\xi)=(\lambda\xi)^2r(\lambda\xi)\leq(\lambda\xi)^2r(-\lambda c)=\psi_{E,c}(\lambda)\xi^2$. Exponentiating yields $\exp(\lambda\xi-\psi_{E,c}(\lambda)\xi^2)\leq1+\lambda\xi$; the same holds at $\lambda=0$ by equality. [given, F13, algebra]

1.3 Fix any one-sided sub-exponential pair at scale $c>0$ and any finite mixture parameters from the Statement. For each $j$, its defining condition [F13] supplies a dominating nonnegative test supermartingale $L^{\lambda_j}$. For $x=c\lambda_j\in(0,1)$, define $h(t)=-\log(1-t)-t$ on $t<1$. By [F17], $h(0)=0$ and the chain and sum rules give $h'(t)=1/(1-t)-1=t/(1-t)$. The function is continuous on $[0,x]$ and differentiable on $(0,x)$ by [F17]. The mean value theorem [F17] gives $h(x)-h(0)=x h'(\theta)\geq0$ for some $0<\theta<x<1$. Since $c^2>0$, $\psi_{E,c}(\lambda_j)=h(x)/c^2\geq0$. For each fixed $v\geq0$, $g_v(s)=\sum_jw_j e^{\lambda_js-\psi_{E,c}(\lambda_j)v}$ is continuous by [F14] and [F18]. Every term is strictly increasing in $s$, since $w_j>0$ and $\lambda_j>0$, so [F14] makes the sum strictly increasing. As $s\to-\infty$, each affine exponent tends to $-\infty$, so [F14] makes every term tend to zero; the finite sum tends to zero. As $s\to\infty$, its first term tends to infinity by [F14] and every other term is positive, so the sum tends to infinity. Also $g_v(0)=\sum_jw_j e^{-\psi_{E,c}(\lambda_j)v}\leq\sum_jw_j=1<1/\alpha$. The two limits give finite $s_-<0<s_+$ with $g_v(s_-)<1/\alpha<g_v(s_+)$; the intermediate value theorem [F15] on $[s_-,s_+]$ gives a root between them, and strict increase makes it unique and positive. Write this root as $u_{\alpha,c}(v)$. For each real $r\leq0$, $\{v\geq0:u_{\alpha,c}(v)<r\}$ is empty. For $r>0$, strict increase and the root equation give $\{v\geq0:u_{\alpha,c}(v)<r\}=\bigcup_{\substack{q\in\mathbb Q\\0<q<r}}\{v\geq0:g_v(q)>1/\alpha\}$. Indeed, if $u_{\alpha,c}(v)<r$, [F16] supplies a rational $q$ strictly between the positive root and $r$; conversely, $g_v(q)>1/\alpha$ implies $q>u_{\alpha,c}(v)$. For fixed $q$, $g_v(q)=\sum_jw_j e^{\lambda_jq-\psi_{E,c}(\lambda_j)v}$ is continuous in $v$ by [F14] and [F18], so each set in the union is open relative to $[0,\infty)$ and the union is open. To apply [F19] directly, if $r\geq0$, strict increase gives $\{v\geq0:u_{\alpha,c}(v)>r\}=\{v\geq0:g_v(r)<1/\alpha\}$, which is also relatively open by [F14] and [F18]; if $r<0$, this inverse image is all of $[0,\infty)$. Thus the inverse images of every open right ray are Borel. The real sets whose inverse images are Borel form a sigma-algebra, so [F19] implies that $u_{\alpha,c}$ is Borel. There are finitely many indices $j$ and countably many integer times, so the almost-sure domination inequalities for all $L^{\lambda_j}$ hold simultaneously outside one null set. The finite mixture $L_t=\sum_jw_jL_t^{\lambda_j}$ is a test supermartingale by [F11]; finite support makes its product measurability immediate. If $S_t\geq u_{\alpha,c}(V_t)$, then $L_t\geq g_{V_t}(S_t)\geq1/\alpha$. Ville's inequality [F12] bounds this crossing event by $\alpha$, so the root is a boundary as in [F13]. [given, F10, F11, F12, F13, F14, F15, F16, F17, F18, F19, A1, algebra]

2.1 On the increasing filtration [F1], for $t\geq1$ put $Y_t=X_t-m_t$, $\eta_t=\widehat X_t-m_t$, and $\xi_t=Y_t-\eta_t=X_t-\widehat X_t$. By [F6], $a\leq m_t\leq b$ almost surely, so $|\eta_t|\leq c$; by [F8], $E[Y_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=0$. Also [F3] and [F4] make $\eta_t$ bounded and $\mathcal F_{t-1}$-measurable, and $|\xi_t|\leq c$. Apply step 1.2 to $\xi_t$ and multiply by $e^{\lambda\eta_t}$. Taking conditional expectations, using [F6] and the bounded-factor identity [F7], gives $E[e^{\lambda Y_t-\psi_{E,c}(\lambda)\xi_t^2}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]\leq e^{\lambda\eta_t}(1-\lambda\eta_t)\leq1$, since $1-z\leq e^{-z}$ for $z=\lambda\eta_t<1$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, F7, F8, A1, step 1.2]

3.1 For each $0\leq\lambda<1/c$, define $M_0^\lambda=1$ and $M_t^\lambda=\exp\!\left(\lambda\sum_{i=1}^tY_i-\psi_{E,c}(\lambda)V_t\right)$. This process is nonnegative and adapted. At each fixed $t$, its exponent is bounded because $|Y_i|\leq c$ and $0\leq V_t\leq c^2t$, so it is integrable. The one-step inequality in step 2.1, multiplied by the bounded $\mathcal F_{t-1}$-measurable $M_{t-1}^\lambda$, proves the supermartingale condition. Thus [F9], [F10], and [A1] make $M^\lambda$ a nonnegative test supermartingale with initial expectation one, so $L_t^\lambda=M_t^\lambda$ verifies the domination condition in [F13]. Replacing every $Y_i,\eta_i$ by $-Y_i,-\eta_i$ gives the same conclusion for the pair $(-S_t,V_t)$, where $S_t=\sum_{i=1}^tY_i$. [F2, F3, F9, F10, A1, F13, step 2.1]

4.1 For the supplied boundary, [F13] and step 3.1 show that the crossing probability is at most $\alpha$ for both $(S_t,V_t)$ and $(-S_t,V_t)$. Outside their union, $|S_t|<u_{\alpha,c}(V_t)$ for every $t$. Since $S_t=t(\bar X_t-\mu_t)$, this is exactly $\mu_t\in C_t$ for every interval returned by [L2], with probability at least $1-2\alpha=1-\delta$. By [F1] and [F4], each $m_i$ is $\mathcal F_{i-1}$-measurable, so $\mu_t$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable; $\bar X_t,V_t$ are also $\mathcal F_t$-measurable by [F2] and [F3], and composition with the Borel boundary makes the interval endpoints measurable. Thus [L1] applies. If all $m_i=\mu$ almost surely for one fixed $\mu$, their countable intersection has probability one and then $\mu_t=\mu$ for all $t$, proving the fixed-mean clause. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F13, L1, L2, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

On a discrete filtered probability space [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]], a real process $(H_n)_{n\ge1}$ is **predictable** if $H_n$ is $\mathcal F_{n-1}$-measurable for every $n\ge1$. Real means finite-valued, as in [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. There is no $H_0$ convention and predictability alone imposes neither integrability nor boundedness.

Since $\mathcal F_{n-1}\subseteq\mathcal F_n$, every Borel preimage of $H_n$ is also in $\mathcal F_n$. Thus predictability implies adaptedness at the positive times. This is a preimage inclusion, requiring no choice or conditional expectation.

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC) [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0})$ be a discrete filtration
on a measurable space, and let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws
on $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$. A real-valued process $E=(E_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0}$ is
a **nonnegative test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$** if, for every
$P\in\mathcal P_0$, it is adapted and integrable under $P$
[[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]
[[def-martingale-submartingale-and-supermartingale]], satisfies
$P(E_t\ge0)=1$ for every $t$, and has $\mathbb E_P E_0\le1$.

The same process must satisfy the supermartingale condition under every law
in the null family; that is what makes the definition uniform over a composite
null. The initial value may be random and need not be bounded by one
pointwise. Time starts at zero.

## Remarks

A nonnegative test supermartingale is a standard sufficient process for
anytime-valid testing. Some literature uses **e-process** for a broader
class, allowing a process dominated under each null law by a different test
martingale. This item defines the planned common test-supermartingale class;
it does not assert that every e-process is itself a supermartingale.
