## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(\Lambda,\mathcal A,\pi)$ be a probability space and let
$\mathcal P_0$ be a family of laws on a common discrete filtered measurable
space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0})$. For each
$\lambda\in\Lambda$, let $E^\lambda=(E_t^\lambda)_{t\ge0}$ be a nonnegative
test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$. Suppose that, for every $t$, the map
$(\lambda,\omega)\mapsto E_t^\lambda(\omega)$ is measurable with respect to
$\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal F_t$. Before mixing, take its pointwise
nonnegative version $E_t^{\lambda,+}(\omega)=\max\{E_t^\lambda(\omega),0\}$,
and define
$$\overline E_t(\omega)=\int_\Lambda E_t^{\lambda,+}(\omega)\,\pi(d\lambda),\qquad \widetilde E_t(\omega)=\begin{cases}\overline E_t(\omega),&\overline E_t(\omega)<\infty,\\0,&\overline E_t(\omega)=\infty.\end{cases}$$
Then $\widetilde E=(\widetilde E_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a nonnegative test
supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$. The modification on the infinite-integral
set makes a real-valued version common to all null laws.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume AC. Let $\pi$, $\mathcal P_0$, and the product-measurable
family of component test supermartingales satisfy the Statement. If
$\mathcal P_0$ is empty, its lawwise conclusion is vacuous; otherwise fix any
$P\in\mathcal P_0$ when checking the test-supermartingale conditions.

[F1] [[def-nonnegative-test-supermartingale]]: under each $P\in\mathcal P_0$, every component is nonnegative, adapted, integrable, a supermartingale, and has initial expectation at most one.

[F2] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: for a nonnegative product-measurable function, section integrals are measurable and the product integral equals either iterated integral.

[F3] [[thm-optional-sampling-for-bounded-stopping-times]]: under AC, bounded stopping of a supermartingale gives a downward expectation inequality; deterministic times are bounded stopping times.

[F4] [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]: under AC, the conditional-expectation class exists and is represented by conditional-expectation versions.

[F5] [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: a conditional-expectation version is measurable and has the same integral as the original variable on every event in the conditioning sigma-algebra.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC supplies conditional-expectation classes used in the supermartingale and optional-sampling clauses.

## Proof

1.1 Fix $P\in\mathcal P_0$ and $t\ge0$. For every $\lambda$, $P(E_t^\lambda\ge0)=1$, so $E_t^{\lambda,+}=E_t^\lambda$ $P$-almost surely and has the same expectation. Apply F3 at the deterministic times $0$ and $t$ to get $\mathbb E_P E_t^{\lambda,+}=\mathbb E_P E_t^\lambda\le\mathbb E_P E_0^\lambda=\mathbb E_P E_0^{\lambda,+}\le1$. The pointwise nonnegative map $(\lambda,\omega)\mapsto E_t^{\lambda,+}(\omega)$ is product-measurable; Tonelli F2 makes $\overline E_t$ $\mathcal F_t$-measurable and gives $\mathbb E_P\overline E_t=\int_\Lambda\mathbb E_P E_t^{\lambda,+}\,\pi(d\lambda)\le1$. Hence $N_t=\{\overline E_t=\infty\}\in\mathcal F_t$ is null under every $P\in\mathcal P_0$. The common modification $\widetilde E_t=\overline E_t$ off $N_t$ and $0$ on $N_t$ is finite, adapted, nonnegative and integrable under every null law, with $\mathbb E_P\widetilde E_0\le1$. [F1, F2, F3, A1]

2.1 Fix $P\in\mathcal P_0$, $t\ge1$, and $A\in\mathcal F_{t-1}$. Since $E_s^{\lambda,+}=E_s^\lambda$ $P$-almost surely for $s=t-1,t$, the component supermartingale condition and the event-integral identity F5 give $\int_A E_t^{\lambda,+}\,dP=\int_A E_t^\lambda\,dP\le\int_A E_{t-1}^\lambda\,dP=\int_A E_{t-1}^{\lambda,+}\,dP$ for every $\lambda$. Tonelli F2 integrates these inequalities over $\pi$; since $N_t$ and $N_{t-1}$ are $P$-null, replacing the mixtures by $\widetilde E_t$ and $\widetilde E_{t-1}$ does not change these integrals. Thus $\int_A\widetilde E_t\,dP\le\int_A\widetilde E_{t-1}\,dP$. [F1, F2, F4, F5, A1, step 1.1]

3.1 Let $U=\mathbb E_P[\widetilde E_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]$, which exists by F4 and AC A1. For every $A\in\mathcal F_{t-1}$, the event-integral identity F5 and step 2.1 give $\int_A(U-\widetilde E_{t-1})\,dP\le0$. Take $A=\{U>\widetilde E_{t-1}\}$. If $P(A)>0$, then for some integer $m\ge1$ the subset where $U-\widetilde E_{t-1}\ge1/m$ has positive measure, making that integral strictly positive, a contradiction. Therefore $U\le\widetilde E_{t-1}$ almost surely. As $P$ and $t$ were arbitrary, $\widetilde E$ is a test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$. [F4, F5, A1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws on a common
discrete filtered measurable space and let $E=(E_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a nonnegative
test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$
[[def-nonnegative-test-supermartingale]]. For every $P\in\mathcal P_0$ and
every $\alpha\in(0,1)$,
$$P\!\left(\sup_{t\ge0}E_t\ge\frac1\alpha\right)\le\alpha.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume AC. If $\mathcal P_0$ is empty the conclusion is vacuous;
otherwise fix $P\in\mathcal P_0$, $\alpha\in(0,1)$, and the nonnegative test
supermartingale $E$. All stopping times below use the discrete filtration and
time starts at zero.

[F1] [[def-nonnegative-test-supermartingale]]: under every null law $P$, $E$ is adapted, integrable, nonnegative almost surely at each time, a supermartingale, and $\mathbb E_P E_0\le1$.

[F2] [[def-discrete-stopping-time]]: a map into $\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ is a stopping time when $\{\tau\le n\}\in\mathcal F_n$ for each $n$, and it is bounded if some deterministic $N$ satisfies $\tau\le N$ almost surely.

[F3] [[thm-optional-sampling-for-bounded-stopping-times]]: under AC, for bounded stopping times and a supermartingale the expectation inequality points downward.

[F4] [[thm-continuity-from-below-for-measures]]: for an increasing sequence of measurable events, the measure of the union is the limit of their measures.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC supplies the conditional-expectation clauses used by the supermartingale definition and bounded optional-sampling theorem.

## Proof

1.1 Fix any $\gamma\in(0,1)$ and define $\tau_\gamma=\inf\{t\ge0:E_t\ge1/\gamma\}$, with $\inf\varnothing=\infty$. For every $n$, $\{\tau_\gamma\le n\}=\bigcup_{k=0}^n\{E_k\ge1/\gamma\}\in\mathcal F_n$, so $\tau_\gamma$ is a stopping time. Also $\{\tau_\gamma\wedge N\le n\}=\{\tau_\gamma\le n\}$ for $n<N$ and is the whole space for $n\ge N$, so each $\tau_\gamma\wedge N$ is a bounded stopping time. [given, F1, F2, choose]

2.1 The constant time $0$ is a stopping time bounded by $0$, and step 1.1 shows $\tau_\gamma\wedge N$ is a bounded stopping time. Bounded optional sampling therefore gives $\mathbb E_P E_{\tau_\gamma\wedge N}\le\mathbb E_P E_0\le1$. [F1, F2, F3, A1, step 1.1]

3.1 On $\{\tau_\gamma\le N\}$, $E_{\tau_\gamma\wedge N}\ge1/\gamma$; on its complement the stopped value is $E_N\ge0$ almost surely. Hence $\mathbb E_P E_{\tau_\gamma\wedge N}\ge\gamma^{-1}P(\tau_\gamma\le N)$, and step 2.1 yields $P(\tau_\gamma\le N)\le\gamma$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The events $\{\tau_\gamma\le N\}$ increase with $N$ and their union is $\{\tau_\gamma<\infty\}=\bigcup_{t\ge0}\{E_t\ge1/\gamma\}$. Continuity from below and step 3.1 therefore give $P(\exists t\ge0:E_t\ge1/\gamma)\le\gamma$. [F4, step 3.1]

5.1 Let $H=\{\sup_{t\ge0}E_t\ge1/\alpha\}$ and suppose $q=P(H)>\alpha$. Since $q\le1$, $\beta=(\alpha+q)/2$ lies in $(\alpha,1)$, so $1/\beta<1/\alpha$. ## Statement

Each of the following families generates $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$:

1. all open subsets of $\mathbb R$;
2. all closed subsets of $\mathbb R$;
3. all open intervals $(a,b)$ with $a<b$;
4. all rational open intervals $(p,q)$ with $p,q\in\mathbb Q$ and $p<q$;
5. all half-open intervals $(a,b]$ with $a<b$;
6. all open right rays $(a,\infty)$;
7. all rational open right rays $(q,\infty)$ with $q\in\mathbb Q$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The seven displayed families of subsets of $\mathbb R$.

[L1] The Borel sigma-algebra is generated by the open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

[L2] Every open subset of $\mathbb R$ is a countable union of rational open intervals ([[lem-open-subsets-of-r-are-countable-unions-of-rational-intervals]]).

[L3] Strictly between any two real numbers lies a rational number ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]).

[L4] If each of two families lies in the sigma-algebra generated by the other, then they generate the same sigma-algebra ([[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-comparison-criterion]]).

[L5] The rationals are countably infinite: $\mathbb Q\approx\mathbb N$ ([[thm-rationals-countable]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Open and closed sets generate the same sigma-algebra by complementation. Open intervals are open, while [L2] expresses every open set using rational open intervals; hence the open intervals and the rational open intervals each generate the sigma-algebra in [L1]. [L1, L2, L4, algebra]

2.1 For $a<b$, rational density [L3] gives $(a,b]=\bigcap\{(a,q):q\in\mathbb Q,\ q>b\}$ and $(a,b)=\bigcup\{(a,q]:q\in\mathbb Q,\ a<q<b\}$. It also gives $(a,\infty)=\bigcup\{(a,q]:q\in\mathbb Q,\ q>a\}$ and $(a,\infty)=\bigcup\{(q,\infty):q\in\mathbb Q,\ q>a\}$. Finally $(-\infty,b]=\mathbb R\setminus(b,\infty)$ and $(a,b)=(a,\infty)\cap\bigcup_{q<b,\ q\in\mathbb Q}(-\infty,q]$. By [L5] all displayed rational-indexed unions and intersections are countable, so these identities give both generator inclusions for the half-open, real-ray, and rational-ray families. [step 1.1, L3, L5, algebra]

3.1 Applying [L4] to the inclusions in steps 1.1 and 2.1 shows that every displayed family generates $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L4] ∎

## Example

Let $U_1,U_2,\ldots$ be independent random variables, each uniform on $[0,1]$, let $\mathcal F_t=\sigma(U_1,\ldots,U_t)$, and at every time $t\geq1$ test the same null by rejecting when $U_t\leq\alpha$, for a fixed $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Each single-time test has rejection probability $\alpha$, but for every integer $n\geq2$, the probability of at least one rejection by time $n$ is $1-(1-\alpha)^n>\alpha$. Marginal level $\alpha$ at each time therefore does not give the same $\alpha$ bound for the event of ever rejecting.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The probability space carries the independent $[0,1]$-uniform random variables in the Example.

[A1] The variables $U_1,U_2,\ldots$ are mutually independent and each satisfies $P(U_t\leq x)=x$ for $0\leq x\leq1$.

## Verification

1.1 For every $t\geq1$, [A1] gives $P(U_t\leq\alpha)=\alpha$, so the test at that fixed time has level $\alpha$. [given, A1]

1.2 Independence in [A1] gives $P(U_t>\alpha\text{ for all }1\leq t\leq n)=\prod_{t=1}^nP(U_t>\alpha)=(1-\alpha)^n$. Taking the complement, $P(\exists t\leq n:U_t\leq\alpha)=1-(1-\alpha)^n$. [given, A1, algebra]

2.1 For $n\geq2$, $1-(1-\alpha)^n=\alpha+(1-\alpha)(1-(1-\alpha)^{n-1})>\alpha$, since both factors in the added term are positive. Thus the pointwise error bounds do not supply the same bound for all tests through time $n$. [given, A1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume AC, fix $\delta\in(0,1)$, and choose a Borel one-sided sub-exponential uniform boundary $u_{\delta/2,1}$ with crossing probability $\delta/2$ at scale $1$. Use the predictable linear forecast $\widehat X_t=1/4+(1/2)X_{t-1}$. Then $\widehat X_t\in[0,1]$ and $E[X_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=1/4$ almost surely. On the path $(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4)=(1,0,0,1)$, which has probability $9/256$, the algorithm has $\bar X_4=1/2$, $V_4=7/4$, and returns
$$C_4=\left[\frac12-\frac{u_{\delta/2,1}(7/4)}4,\;\frac12+\frac{u_{\delta/2,1}(7/4)}4\right].$$
The forecast is predictable and differs from the conditional mean when $X_{t-1}=1$; the full interval sequence still covers its target sequence with probability at least $1-\delta$.

## Definition

Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, $k:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ a real positive-semidefinite kernel, and $\mathcal H$ a real reproducing-kernel Hilbert space with kernel $k$. Let $X=(x_i)_{i=1}^n$ be a nonempty finite ordered training list in $\mathcal X$, let $K=(k(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^n$, let $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $\lambda>0$. Set $\tau=n\lambda$ and define the mean-square empirical objective

$$J(f)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-f(x_i))^2+\lambda\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal H}^2. $$

For any finite real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix $G\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, define its regularized kernel prediction system by $a_G=(G+\tau I_n)^{-1}y$ and $u_G=Ga_G$, where $I_n$ is the $n\times n$ identity matrix. The original training system uses $G=K$. The same definition applies to any positive-semidefinite matrix approximation $\widetilde K$ of $K$, with $a_{\widetilde K}=(\widetilde K+\tau I_n)^{-1}y$ and $u_{\widetilde K}=\widetilde K a_{\widetilde K}$. In either case $u_G=y-\tau a_G$. The scalar $\tau=n\lambda$ fixes the normalization between mean-square loss and the unnormalized finite linear system.

## Definition references

[[def-positive-semidefinite-kernels-and-reproducing-kernel-hilbert-spaces|A real positive-semidefinite kernel has nonnegative finite Gram quadratic forms, and its RKHS reproduces the kernel sections.]]

## Remarks

The definitions allow $K$ to be singular or zero. More generally, for every finite real symmetric positive-semidefinite $G$ and $\tau>0$, each nonzero $x$ satisfies $x^T(G+\tau I_n)x=x^TGx+\tau\lVert x\rVert_2^2\ge\tau\lVert x\rVert_2^2>0$. Thus each shifted matrix in the definition is positive definite and invertible, including when $G=K$ or $G=\widetilde K$; no full-rank assumption is placed on the kernel Gram matrix or on a sketch.

## Statement

Let $M,N\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric matrices such that $x^TMx\ge0$ and $x^TNx\ge0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$, where $n\ge1$, and let $\tau>0$. Write $I_n$ for the identity matrix, $A=M+\tau I_n$, and $B=N+\tau I_n$. For vectors use $\lVert x\rVert_2=(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2}$, and for a matrix $T$ use the induced Euclidean norm $\lVert T\rVert_2=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_2=1}\lVert Tx\rVert_2$. Positive definite means $x^TAx>0$ for every nonzero $x$, and analogously for $B$. Then $A$ and $B$ are positive definite and invertible, $\lVert A^{-1}\rVert_2,\lVert B^{-1}\rVert_2\le1/\tau$, and

$$A^{-1}-B^{-1}=A^{-1}(N-M)B^{-1},\qquad \lVert A^{-1}-B^{-1}\rVert_2\le\frac{\lVert M-N\rVert_2}{\tau^2}. $$

## Statement references

[[thm-non-negative-operator-characterisations|A finite-dimensional real symmetric positive-semidefinite operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis with nonnegative eigenvalues.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices $M,N\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and $\tau>0$.

[F1] [[thm-non-negative-operator-characterisations]]: every finite-dimensional real symmetric positive-semidefinite operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis and nonnegative eigenvalues.

## Proof

1.1 Since $\tau>0$ and $M,N$ are positive semidefinite, every nonzero $x$ satisfies $x^TAx=x^TMx+\tau\lVert x\rVert_2^2\ge\tau\lVert x\rVert_2^2>0$ and $x^TBx=x^TNx+\tau\lVert x\rVert_2^2\ge\tau\lVert x\rVert_2^2>0$. Thus $A$ and $B$ are positive definite and invertible. By [F1], write $M=U\operatorname{diag}(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n)U^T$ with $U$ orthogonal and each $\mu_i\ge0$. Then $A=U\operatorname{diag}(\mu_i+\tau)U^T$ and $A^{-1}=U\operatorname{diag}((\mu_i+\tau)^{-1})U^T$; applying the same diagonalization argument to $N$ gives the corresponding formula for $B^{-1}$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Orthogonality of $U$ gives $\lVert A^{-1}x\rVert_2^2=\sum_i (U^Tx)_i^2(\mu_i+\tau)^{-2}\le\tau^{-2}\lVert x\rVert_2^2$ for every $x$. Taking the supremum over unit vectors gives $\lVert A^{-1}\rVert_2\le1/\tau$; the identical calculation for $N$ gives $\lVert B^{-1}\rVert_2\le1/\tau$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $B-A=N-M$, multiplying out yields $A^{-1}(B-A)B^{-1}=A^{-1}-B^{-1}$. For every unit vector $x$, the definition of the induced norm gives $\lVert A^{-1}(N-M)B^{-1}x\rVert_2\le\lVert A^{-1}\rVert_2\lVert N-M\rVert_2\lVert B^{-1}\rVert_2$. Taking the supremum and using step 2.1 proves the asserted resolvent bound. [given, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, let $k:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ be a real positive-semidefinite kernel, and let $\mathcal H$ be a real reproducing-kernel Hilbert space with kernel $k$. Take a finite ordered list $X=(x_i)_{i=1}^n$ with $n\ge1$, a response vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and $\lambda>0$. Put $K=(k(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^n$ and $\tau=n\lambda$. Define $a=(K+\tau I_n)^{-1}y$, $f_0=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i k(\cdot,x_i)$, and $u=Ka$. Then $f_0$ is the unique minimizer over $f\in\mathcal H$ of

$$J(f)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-f(x_i))^2+\lambda\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal H}^2,$$

and its training evaluation vector is $u=y-\tau a$.

## Statement references

[[def-positive-semidefinite-kernels-and-reproducing-kernel-hilbert-spaces]]: A real RKHS contains each kernel section and satisfies $\langle f,k(\cdot,x)\rangle_{\mathcal H}=f(x)$.

[[def-regularized-kernel-prediction-system]]: The coefficient and fitted vectors are defined by $a=(K+\tau I)^{-1}y$ and $u=Ka=y-\tau a$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The kernel, RKHS, training list, response vector, and regularization parameter in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-positive-semidefinite-kernels-and-reproducing-kernel-hilbert-spaces]]: each section $k(\cdot,x_i)$ belongs to $\mathcal H$ and $\langle f,k(\cdot,x_i)\rangle_{\mathcal H}=f(x_i)$; every finite Gram matrix of $k$ is symmetric positive semidefinite.

[F2] [[def-regularized-kernel-prediction-system]]: $\tau=n\lambda$, the objective is the mean-square loss plus $\lambda\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal H}^2$, and $a=(K+\tau I_n)^{-1}y$.

[F3] [[lem-regularized-gram-matrix-inverse-bound]]: for $K\succeq0$ and $\tau>0$, $K+\tau I_n$ is invertible.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], $K$ is a real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix. Let $a=(K+\tau I_n)^{-1}y$, which exists by [F2]–[F3], and set $f_0=\sum_i a_i k(\cdot,x_i)$. The reproducing identities give $f_0(x_j)=\sum_i a_i k(x_j,x_i)=(Ka)_j$, so if $r=y-(f_0(x_i))_{i=1}^n$, then $r=y-Ka=\tau a$ by $(K+\tau I_n)a=y$. [given, F1, F2, F3, construct, algebra]

2.1 Fix any $h\in\mathcal H$. The reproducing identities yield $\langle f_0,h\rangle_{\mathcal H}=\sum_i a_i h(x_i)=a^T(h(x_i))_{i=1}^n$. Expanding both squared norms in $J(f_0+h)-J(f_0)$ gives $\frac1n\lVert (h(x_i))_{i=1}^n\rVert_2^2-\frac2n r^T(h(x_i))_{i=1}^n+2\lambda a^T(h(x_i))_{i=1}^n+\lambda\lVert h\rVert_{\mathcal H}^2$. Substituting $r=\tau a=n\lambda a$ cancels the two cross terms, leaving $\frac1n\lVert(h(x_i))\rVert_2^2+\lambda\lVert h\rVert_{\mathcal H}^2\ge0$. [given, step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra]

3.1 Step 2.1 shows $J(f_0+h)\ge J(f_0)$ for every $h$, so $f_0$ is a minimizer. Equality forces $\lambda\lVert h\rVert_{\mathcal H}^2=0$, hence $h=0$ because $\lambda>0$; the minimizer is unique. The evaluation computation in step 1.1 gives its fitted vector $u=Ka=y-\tau a$. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $K,\widetilde K\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric matrices such that $x^TKx\ge0$ and $x^T\widetilde Kx\ge0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$, with $n\ge1$, let $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $\tau>0$. Write $I_n$ for the identity matrix. For $G\in\{K,\widetilde K\}$ define $a_G=(G+\tau I_n)^{-1}y$ and $u_G=Ga_G$. Define $\lVert x\rVert_2=(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2}$ for vectors and $\lVert M\rVert_2=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_2=1}\lVert Mx\rVert_2$ for matrices. If $\lVert K-\widetilde K\rVert_2\le\delta$ for some $\delta\ge0$, then

$$\lVert a_K-a_{\widetilde K}\rVert_2\le\frac{\delta\lVert y\rVert_2}{\tau^2},\qquad \lVert u_K-u_{\widetilde K}\rVert_2\le\frac{\delta\lVert y\rVert_2}{\tau}. $$

In particular, let $S\in\mathbb R^{n\times s}$ with $s\ge0$ and $\widetilde K=KS(S^TKS)^\dagger S^TK$, where $M^\dagger$ denotes the unique matrix satisfying the four Moore–Penrose equations. Choose $0\le r\le n$ and an orthogonal eigenbasis $K=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)U^T$ with $U^TU=I_n$ and $\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n\ge0$. Write $U=(U_1\ U_2)$ with the first $r$ eigenvectors in $U_1$, let $\Lambda_2=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{r+1},\ldots,\lambda_n)$ and $\Lambda_2^{1/2}=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{\lambda_{r+1}},\ldots,\sqrt{\lambda_n})$, and set $\Omega_1=U_1^TS$ and $\Omega_2=U_2^TS$. If $\Omega_1$ has full row rank, meaning $\operatorname{rank}(\Omega_1)=r$, with the empty-row convention when $r=0$, then the same bounds hold with $\delta=\lambda_{r+1}+\lVert\Lambda_2^{1/2}\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger\rVert_2^2$, using $\lambda_{n+1}=0$ and zero norm for empty blocks.

## Statement references

[[def-regularized-kernel-prediction-system]]: The systems use $a_G=(G+\tau I)^{-1}y$ and $u_G=Ga_G=y-\tau a_G$.

[[def-psd-nystrom-approximation]]: The Nyström approximation is $KS(S^TKS)^\dagger S^TK$.

[[thm-psd-nystrom-order-and-exactness|The Nyström approximation is positive semidefinite.]]

[[thm-nystrom-deterministic-spectral-residual-bound|Under the full-row-rank leading-sketch hypothesis, the displayed deterministic spectral residual bound holds.]]

[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse|The Moore–Penrose inverse is the unique matrix satisfying the four Penrose equations.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Positive-semidefinite matrices $K,\widetilde K$, vector $y$, scalar $\tau>0$, and the norm error $\lVert K-\widetilde K\rVert_2\le\delta$ in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-regularized-kernel-prediction-system]]: for a positive-semidefinite matrix $G$, $a_G=(G+\tau I_n)^{-1}y$ and $u_G=Ga_G=y-\tau a_G$.

[F2] [[lem-regularized-gram-matrix-inverse-bound]]: $G+\tau I_n$ is invertible, $\lVert(G+\tau I_n)^{-1}\rVert_2\le1/\tau$, and the two shifted inverses satisfy the resolvent identity.

[F3] [[def-psd-nystrom-approximation]]: for a positive-semidefinite $K$ and finite sketch $S$, $\widetilde K=KS(S^TKS)^\dagger S^TK$ is the Nyström matrix.

[F4] [[thm-psd-nystrom-order-and-exactness]]: every such $\widetilde K$ is positive semidefinite.

[F5] [[thm-nystrom-deterministic-spectral-residual-bound]]: if $\Omega_1$ has full row rank, then $\lVert K-\widetilde K\rVert_2\le\lambda_{r+1}+\lVert\Lambda_2^{1/2}\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger\rVert_2^2$ under the eigenbasis and block definitions in the Statement.

## Proof

1.1 Put $A=K+\tau I_n$ and $B=\widetilde K+\tau I_n$. By [F2], both inverses exist and have norm at most $1/\tau$. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 The resolvent identity gives $a_K-a_{\widetilde K}=(A^{-1}-B^{-1})y=A^{-1}(\widetilde K-K)B^{-1}y$. Taking norms and applying the bounds from step 1.1 and the assumed Gram error gives $\lVert a_K-a_{\widetilde K}\rVert_2\le\delta\lVert y\rVert_2/\tau^2$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], $u_K=y-\tau a_K$ and $u_{\widetilde K}=y-\tau a_{\widetilde K}$. Subtracting these equalities and using step 2.1 gives $\lVert u_K-u_{\widetilde K}\rVert_2=\tau\lVert a_K-a_{\widetilde K}\rVert_2\le\delta\lVert y\rVert_2/\tau$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 In the Nyström case, [F4] supplies positive semidefiniteness of $\widetilde K$, and [F5] supplies the stated value of $\delta$ whenever $\Omega_1$ has full row rank. Substituting that bound into steps 2.1 and 3.1 proves the conditional Nyström conclusion. [given, F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $n\ge1$, $s\ge0$, $A\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$ be Hermitian positive semidefinite, and $S\in\mathbb F^{n\times s}$. In the Loewner order, where $B\preceq C$ means $C-B$ is positive semidefinite, the Nyström approximation in [[def-psd-nystrom-approximation]] satisfies
$0\preceq\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}\preceq A$.
If the sketch captures the range in the sense that $\operatorname{Ran}(AS)=\operatorname{Ran}(A)$, then $\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}=A$. Here rank, when used in the proof, means dimension of the range.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite Hermitian positive-semidefinite matrix $A$ and a conformal sketch $S$.

[F1] [[lem-nystrom-square-root-projector-identity]]: $\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}=A^{1/2}P_{\operatorname{Ran}(A^{1/2}S)}A^{1/2}$.

[F2] [[thm-non-negative-operator-characterisations]]: a finite-dimensional positive-semidefinite operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis with nonnegative eigenvalues.

[F3] [[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]]: $A^{1/2}$ is Hermitian positive semidefinite and $(A^{1/2})^2=A$.
 
## Proof

1.1 Put $M=A^{1/2}$ and $P=P_{\operatorname{Ran}(MS)}$. By [F1], for every vector $x$, $x^*\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}x=\|PMx\|_2^2\ge0$ and $x^*(A-\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}})x=\|(I-P)Mx\|_2^2\ge0$. Both matrices are Hermitian, so these quadratic-form inequalities prove $0\preceq\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}\preceq A$. [F1, F3, algebra]

1.2 Assume $\operatorname{Ran}(AS)=\operatorname{Ran}(A)$. By [F2], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_i\ge0$. In that basis the diagonal matrix with entries $\sqrt{\lambda_i}$ is positive semidefinite and squares to $A$, so it equals $A^{1/2}$ by uniqueness [F3]. Thus $A$ and $A^{1/2}$ have the same range and the same rank. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Let $B=A^{1/2}S$. Then $\operatorname{Ran}(B)\subseteq\operatorname{Ran}(A^{1/2})$ and $AS=A^{1/2}B$. The assumption gives $\operatorname{rank}(AS)=\operatorname{rank}(A)$, while a linear map cannot increase the dimension of a subspace's image, so $\operatorname{rank}(AS)\le\operatorname{rank}(B)\le\operatorname{rank}(A^{1/2})=\operatorname{rank}(A)$ by step 1.2. The ranks are equal, and the range inclusion therefore yields $\operatorname{Ran}(B)=\operatorname{Ran}(A^{1/2})$. [given, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The projection in [F1] is consequently the identity on $\operatorname{Ran}(A^{1/2})$. Since $A^{1/2}x$ lies in that range for every $x$, [F1] gives $\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}x=A^{1/2}A^{1/2}x=Ax$ for every $x$. Thus $\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}=A$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $n\ge1$, $s\ge0$, and let $A\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$ be Hermitian positive semidefinite with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n\ge0$. Let $S\in\mathbb F^{n\times s}$, and choose an integer $0\le k\le n$ and an orthonormal eigenbasis $U=(U_1\ U_2)$ with the first $k$ eigenvectors in $U_1$. Set
$\Lambda_1=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k)$,
$\Lambda_2=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{k+1},\ldots,\lambda_n)$,
$\Omega_1=U_1^*S$, and $\Omega_2=U_2^*S$. Empty blocks have norm zero, $\lambda_{n+1}:=0$, and the $0\times s$ matrix has full row rank vacuously. If $\Omega_1$ has full row rank, then, deterministically,

$$\|A-\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}\|_2\le\lambda_{k+1}+\|\Lambda_2^{1/2}\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger\|_2^2.$$

Here $\|M\|_2=\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Mx\|_2$ is the induced Euclidean operator norm. No probability assumption on $S$ is made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite Hermitian positive-semidefinite $A$, a conformal sketch $S$, an eigenvalue split at $k$, and full row rank of $\Omega_1$.

[F1] [[lem-nystrom-square-root-projector-identity]]: $\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}=A^{1/2}P_{\operatorname{Ran}(A^{1/2}S)}A^{1/2}$.

[F2] [[thm-non-negative-operator-characterisations]]: $A$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with nonnegative eigenvalues.

[F3] [[lem-moore-penrose-products-are-orthogonal-projectors]]: if $\Omega_1$ has full row rank, then $\Omega_1\Omega_1^\dagger=I_k$.

[F4] [[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]: every finite-dimensional linear map has a singular value decomposition.

[F5] [[thm-operator-norm-is-the-largest-singular-value]]: the induced operator norm equals the largest singular value.

[F6] [[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]]: the positive-semidefinite square root is unique.
 
## Proof

1.1 Put $M=A^{1/2}$, $Y=MS$, and let $P=P_{\operatorname{Ran}(Y)}$. By [F1], $A-\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}=M(I-P)M=X^*X$ for $X=(I-P)M$, since $P$ is self-adjoint and idempotent. A singular value decomposition from [F4] writes $X=U_X\Sigma_XV_X^*$ and $X^*X=V_X\Sigma_X^2V_X^*$; [F5] therefore gives $\|A-\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}\|_2=\|X\|_2^2$. [F1, F4, F5, algebra]

1.2 By [F2], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $U$ of $A$. The diagonal matrix whose entries are the nonnegative square roots of its eigenvalues is a positive-semidefinite square root, hence it is $A^{1/2}$ by uniqueness [F6]. Thus in this basis, $M=U\operatorname{diag}(\Lambda_1^{1/2},\Lambda_2^{1/2})U^*$ and $U^*Y=\begin{bmatrix}\Lambda_1^{1/2}\Omega_1\\\Lambda_2^{1/2}\Omega_2\end{bmatrix}$. For any unit vector $x=U(x_1,x_2)$, set $c=\Omega_1^\dagger x_1$. Then [F3] gives $\Omega_1c=x_1$, and $Yc=U\begin{bmatrix}\Lambda_1^{1/2}x_1\\\Lambda_2^{1/2}\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger x_1\end{bmatrix}\in\operatorname{Ran}(Y)$. [F2, F3, F6, algebra]

2.1 Orthogonal projection gives the shortest distance to its range, so $\|(I-P)Mx\|_2\le\|Mx-Yc\|_2 =\|\Lambda_2^{1/2}(x_2-\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger x_1)\|_2$. Write $G=\Lambda_2^{1/2}\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger$ and $H=\Lambda_2^{1/2}$. For unit $(x_1,x_2)$, the last norm is at most $\|G\|_2\|x_1\|_2+\|H\|_2\|x_2\|_2 \le(\|G\|_2^2+\|H\|_2^2)^{1/2}$ by the scalar Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Taking the supremum over unit $x$ yields $\|X\|_2^2\le\|G\|_2^2+\|H\|_2^2$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Since $H$ is diagonal with nonnegative entries, [F2] and [F5] give $\|H\|_2^2=\lambda_{k+1}$, including the declared empty-tail convention. Combine this with step 1.1 and step 2.1 to obtain $\|A-\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}\|_2\le\lambda_{k+1}+\|\Lambda_2^{1/2}\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger\|_2^2$. [F2, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $K\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with $x^TKx\ge0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$ and $n\ge1$, let $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $\tau>0$. Write $I_n$ for the identity matrix. Define $a=(K+\tau I_n)^{-1}y$ and $u=Ka$. For any vector $b\in\mathbb R^n$, define the actual residual $r=y-(K+\tau I_n)b$. Define $\lVert x\rVert_2=(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2}$ and $\lVert M\rVert_2=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_2=1}\lVert Mx\rVert_2$; then

$$\lVert b-a\rVert_2\le\frac{\lVert r\rVert_2}{\tau},\qquad \lVert Kb-u\rVert_2\le\frac{\lVert K\rVert_2\lVert r\rVert_2}{\tau}. $$

## Statement references

[[def-regularized-kernel-prediction-system]]: The exact coefficient and fitted vectors solve $(K+\tau I)a=y$ and $u=Ka$.

[[lem-regularized-gram-matrix-inverse-bound]]: The shifted Gram inverse has induced norm at most $1/\tau$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The positive-semidefinite matrix $K$, vector $y$, scalar $\tau>0$, exact solution $a$, and arbitrary approximate coefficient vector $b$ in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-regularized-kernel-prediction-system]]: $(K+\tau I_n)a=y$ and $u=Ka$.

[F2] [[lem-regularized-gram-matrix-inverse-bound]]: $K+\tau I_n$ is invertible and $\lVert(K+\tau I_n)^{-1}\rVert_2\le1/\tau$.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], $r=y-(K+\tau I_n)b=(K+\tau I_n)(a-b)$. Invertibility in [F2] therefore gives $b-a=-(K+\tau I_n)^{-1}r$, so $\lVert b-a\rVert_2\le\lVert r\rVert_2/\tau$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Since $u=Ka$, the training fitted-vector error is $Kb-u=K(b-a)$. For every vector $x$, the definition of the induced norm gives $\lVert Kx\rVert_2\le\lVert K\rVert_2\lVert x\rVert_2$. Applying this to $b-a$ and using step 1.1 proves $\lVert Kb-u\rVert_2\le\lVert K\rVert_2\lVert r\rVert_2/\tau$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

All matrix-vector operations below use exact real arithmetic. The inputs are a finite real symmetric matrix $K\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ with $n\ge1$ and $x^TKx\ge0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$, a vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, a scalar $\tau>0$, a finite sketch $S\in\mathbb R^{n\times s}$ with $s\ge0$, a residual tolerance $\eta\ge0$, and a finite nonnegative integer iteration budget $T$. Write $I_n$ for the identity matrix and $\lVert x\rVert_2=(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2}$ for the Euclidean norm. The Moore–Penrose inverse $M^\dagger$ is the unique matrix satisfying $MM^\dagger M=M$, $M^\dagger MM^\dagger=M^\dagger$, $(MM^\dagger)^T=MM^\dagger$, and $(M^\dagger M)^T=M^\dagger M$.

1. Form the Nyström matrix $\widetilde K=KS(S^TKS)^\dagger S^TK$. The formula is defined even when $S^TKS$ is singular or $s=0$.

2. Set $B=\widetilde K+\tau I_n$. Initialize $b_0=0$, $\widetilde r_0=y-Bb_0=y$, and $p_0=\widetilde r_0$.

3. For $j=0,1,\ldots,T$, recompute the actual residuals $\widetilde r_j=y-Bb_j$ and $r_j=y-(K+\tau I_n)b_j$. If both norms are at most $\eta$, return status `certified`, coefficient vector $b_j$, fitted vector $\widetilde Kb_j$, and both residuals. If $\widetilde r_j=0$ but $\lVert r_j\rVert_2>\eta$, return status `uncertified` with the same outputs. If $j=T$ and neither return condition holds, return status `budget-exhausted` with the same outputs.

4. Otherwise compute $q_j=Bp_j$. If $p_j^Tq_j=0$, return status `uncertified` with the current outputs. If $p_j^Tq_j>0$, set $\alpha_j=(\widetilde r_j^T\widetilde r_j)/(p_j^Tq_j)$, $b_{j+1}=b_j+\alpha_jp_j$, and $\widetilde r_{j+1}=\widetilde r_j-\alpha_jq_j$. If $\widetilde r_{j+1}=0$, recompute $r_{j+1}$ and return `certified` when $\lVert r_{j+1}\rVert_2\le\eta$, and otherwise return `uncertified`, together with the resulting outputs. If $\widetilde r_{j+1}\ne0$, set $\beta_j=(\widetilde r_{j+1}^T\widetilde r_{j+1})/(\widetilde r_j^T\widetilde r_j)$ and $p_{j+1}=\widetilde r_{j+1}+\beta_jp_j$, then continue at the next iteration.

The output always includes the actual residuals for both the Nyström system and the original system. `certified` asserts that both residuals meet the requested tolerance; `uncertified` and `budget-exhausted` make no solve-accuracy claim. In particular, exhausting the budget does not certify a solve. If $K$ is a Gram matrix and $\tau=n\lambda$, the original-system residual is the one used in the residual prediction certificate.

## Definition references

[[def-psd-nystrom-approximation]]: For a PSD matrix $K$, the Nyström matrix is $KS(S^TKS)^\dagger S^TK$.

[[thm-psd-nystrom-order-and-exactness]]: Every such Nyström matrix is positive semidefinite and is bounded above by $K$.

[[lem-regularized-gram-matrix-inverse-bound]]: Adding $\tau I$ with $\tau>0$ makes the Nyström system positive definite.

## Scope

The Gram-perturbation and residual bounds are deterministic finite-training-vector statements. A statistical risk here would be expected loss under a data-generating probability law; these bounds contain no such law, expected loss, or generalization term, so they do not by themselves give a statistical risk guarantee.

For a test input $x_*$, the kernel prediction is $k_*^Ta_K$, where $k_*=(k(x_*,x_i))_{i=1}^n$. An approximation certificate for the training Gram matrix alone does not bound the test cross-kernel vector $k_*$; an out-of-sample error bound requires a separate cross-kernel certificate.

Under AC, suppose the finite real PSD kernel $k$ also has a real RKHS $\mathcal H$ with reproducing sections, use the zero mean $m=0$, and observe the canonical finite Gaussian process with independent noise covariance $\tau I_n$. In the GP/KRR theorem take noise standard deviation $\sigma=\sqrt{\tau}>0$. Writing $a_K(Y)=(K+\tau I_n)^{-1}Y$ and $u_K(Y)=Ka_K(Y)$ for the random observation vector $Y$, the conditional-mean identity is

$$\mathbb E[f_X\mid Y]=K(K+\tau I_n)^{-1}Y=u_K(Y)\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

The shifted observed covariance $K+\tau I_n$ is positive definite because $\tau>0$. This optional interpretation uses the GP/KRR supplier and is separate from the choice-free deterministic matrix bounds.

For a fixed finite matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ or $\mathbb C^{m\times n}$, the cited range-finder results assume iid standard real or normalized complex Gaussian sketches, integers $k,p\in\mathbb N$ with $k\ge2$ and $p\ge2$, sketch width $\ell=k+p\le\min(m,n)$, exact arithmetic, and Countable Choice for the finite Gaussian probability law. They bound expected spectral error in those regimes. The theorem statements provide no per-draw bound or tail estimate for an arbitrary sketch supplied to the Nyström algorithm; a leverage-score or other sampling guarantee would require its own hypotheses and proof. The algorithm itself is specified in exact real arithmetic and includes residual statuses; no finite-precision rounding-error claim is made.

## Definition

Let $p,d\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:\Theta\times W\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ and $g:W\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Here $C^1$ means continuously differentiable on the open domain, and $C^2$ means that the derivative map is itself continuously differentiable. Gradients are column vectors, vector norms are Euclidean, and the norm of a matrix or linear map is the induced Euclidean operator norm.

For $(\theta,w)\in\Theta\times W$, define the inner stationarity residual $F(\theta,w):=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^d$, its state Jacobian $H(\theta,w):=D_wF(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$, and its parameter Jacobian $B(\theta,w):=D_\theta F(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^{d\times p}$. Thus $H$ is the inner Hessian and $B$ is the mixed derivative of the inner gradient. A point $(\theta_0,w_0)$ is stationary when $F(\theta_0,w_0)=0$. If a $C^1$ map $w^*:P\to Q$, for open neighborhoods $P\subseteq\Theta$ of $\theta_0$ and $Q\subseteq W$ of $w_0$, satisfies $w^*(\theta_0)=w_0$ and $F(\theta,w^*(\theta))=0$ for all $\theta\in P$, it is a local stationary branch. The associated outer objective is $J(\theta):=g(w^*(\theta),\theta)$, and its column gradient $\nabla_\theta J$ is called the hypergradient of that branch. The definition of a local stationary branch imposes no global-minimality requirement.

For $\mu>0$, the phrase globally $\mu$-strongly convex in $w$ means that $f(\theta,\cdot)$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^d$ and, for every $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$, satisfies

$$f(\theta,v)\ge f(\theta,u)+\nabla_w f(\theta,u)^T(v-u)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|v-u\|_2^2.$$

## Definition

Input positive dimensions $p,d$, open sets $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $C^2$ and $C^1$ scalar functions $f:\Theta\times W\to\mathbb R$ and $g:W\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$, a point $(\theta,w)\in\Theta\times W$, and finite real-arithmetic computational graphs whose outputs equal $f$ and $g$ on open neighborhoods of the evaluated inputs. The graph primitives for $f$ are $C^2$ and those for $g$ are $C^1$. Here $C^1$ means total differentiability with continuous derivative, $C^2$ means the derivative map is $C^1$, and all graph evaluations must remain on one unique strict branch. Define $F=\nabla_w f$, $H=D_wF$, $B=D_\theta F$, $c=\partial_\theta g$ with $w$ held fixed, and $d=\nabla_w g$; all gradients are column vectors. Also input a tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a positive integer solve budget $N$, a number $\mu>0$, and a valid certificate that the evaluated inner Hessian is symmetric and satisfies $x^THx\ge\mu\|x\|_2^2$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$. Finally input a deterministic solver $S$ with the following contract: on a real symmetric positive-definite linear operator and a right-hand side, $S$ terminates within $N$ iterations and returns either a failure status or a vector $\widetilde v$ and a report saying whether its own stopping test passed. The algorithm does not trust that report as an accuracy certificate; it recomputes the residual. All derivative and solver operations in this definition use exact real arithmetic.

If any graph evaluation is outside its declared domain, return DOMAIN_ERROR. If any piecewise primitive is at a branch boundary or has no unique strict active branch, return NONDIFFERENTIABLE and no gradient. Otherwise, use reverse mode on $f$ and take the state block of its returned gradient as the inner residual $r_{\rm in}:=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)$. Use reverse mode on $g$ and take its parameter and state blocks as $c:=\partial_\theta g(w,\theta)$ and $d:=\nabla_w g(w,\theta)$. In these expressions $c$ is the derivative with $w$ held fixed, and $d$ and $c$ are column vectors.

For any $u\in\mathbb R^d$, apply forward-over-reverse Hessian-vector differentiation to $f$ at $(\theta,w)$ in direction $(0,u)\in\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^d$. Let $\pi_\theta$ and $\pi_w$ denote projection onto the parameter and state coordinates of the returned vector. Define $M_Hu:=\pi_w\bigl(D(\nabla f)(\theta,w)(0,u)\bigr)$ and $M_Bu:=\pi_\theta\bigl(D(\nabla f)(\theta,w)(0,u)\bigr)$. Hessian symmetry makes $M_Hu=Hu=H^Tu$ and $M_Bu=B^Tu$.

Call $S$ on $M_H$ and right-hand side $d$ with tolerance $\tau$ and budget $N$. If $S$ returns failure, return $(r_{\rm in},\text{SOLVER\_FAILURE})$ with no hypergradient. If it returns a vector $\widetilde v$, compute the actual linear residual $\rho:=d-M_H\widetilde v$ and the reported hypergradient estimate $\widehat h:=c-M_B\widetilde v$. Return $(\widehat h,r_{\rm in},\rho,\text{CONVERGED})$ exactly when the solver reports its stopping test passed and $\|\rho\|_2\le\tau$; otherwise return the same numerical values with status TOLERANCE_OR_BUDGET_NOT_MET. The procedure makes no floating-point accuracy claim.

## Remarks

The solver is a supplied finite procedure, so its termination contract is an input requirement. The algorithm verifies the residual even when the solver reports success. Its estimate is still returned with a non-success status when the solver produces a vector whose residual misses the requested tolerance.

Under this algorithm's derivative-map convention, $Df$ is a $C^1$ map. Apply the total-derivative theorem to the coordinate representation of $Df$: each coordinate partial of $Df$ is the corresponding entry of $D(Df)$ and varies continuously. The coordinates of $Df$ are the first partials of $f$, so this supplies the continuous second coordinate partials required by the coordinate-$C^2$ definition and the Hessian-symmetry corollary. That symmetry applies to the full Hessian of $f$, hence its state block is $H=H^T$ and its parameter block in the state direction is $B^T$, as used above.

## Statement

Let $p,d\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:\Theta\times W\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ and $g:W\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Here $C^1$ means total differentiability with continuous derivative, and $C^2$ means the derivative map is $C^1$. Define $F(\theta,w)=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)$, $H(\theta,w)=D_wF(\theta,w)$, and $B(\theta,w)=D_\theta F(\theta,w)$. Suppose $F(\theta_0,w_0)=0$ and $H(\theta_0,w_0)$ is invertible. Then there are open neighborhoods $P\subseteq\Theta$ and $Q\subseteq W$ of $\theta_0$ and $w_0$ and a unique $C^1$ local stationary branch $w^*:P\to Q$ through $(\theta_0,w_0)$, meaning $w^*(\theta_0)=w_0$ and $F(\theta,w^*(\theta))=0$ for every $\theta\in P$. After shrinking $P$ if necessary, $H(\theta,w^*(\theta))$ is invertible and

$$Dw^*(\theta)=-H(\theta,w^*(\theta))^{-1}B(\theta,w^*(\theta)).$$

Write $H^{-T}:=(H^{-1})^T$. For $J(\theta)=g(w^*(\theta),\theta)$, where $\partial_\theta g$ holds $w$ fixed and gradients are column vectors, the hypergradient is

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta)=\partial_\theta g(w^*(\theta),\theta)-B(\theta,w^*(\theta))^T H(\theta,w^*(\theta))^{-T}\nabla_w g(w^*(\theta),\theta).$$

The local branch need not be a global inner optimizer. In the separate global regime where, for every $\theta\in P$, $f(\theta,\cdot)$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^d$ and, for some $\mu>0$, satisfies $f(\theta,v)\ge f(\theta,u)+\nabla_w f(\theta,u)^T(v-u)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|v-u\|_2^2$ for every $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$, each stationary point is the unique global minimizer.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Open parameter and state domains, the $C^2$ inner objective, the $C^1$ outer objective, a stationary point $(\theta_0,w_0)$, and an invertible inner Hessian at that point.

[F1] [[def-smooth-bilevel-learning-problem]]: $F=\nabla_w f$ is the inner stationarity residual, $H=D_wF$, $B=D_\theta F$, and the local outer objective is $J(\theta)=g(w^*(\theta),\theta)$.

[F2] [[thm-euclidean-implicit-function-theorem]]: for a $C^1$ residual with zero value and invertible state-block derivative, there are neighborhoods with a unique $C^1$ solution branch.

[L1] [[thm-euclidean-implicit-function-theorem]]: after shrinking the neighborhoods, the state-block derivative stays invertible along the branch and its derivative is minus the inverse state Jacobian times the parameter Jacobian.

[F3] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the derivative of a composition of finite-dimensional totally differentiable maps is the composition of their derivatives.

## Proof

1.1 Put $F(\theta,w)=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)$. Since $f$ is $C^2$, this residual is $C^1$ on the open product domain; it vanishes at $(\theta_0,w_0)$ and its state derivative is the invertible matrix $H(\theta_0,w_0)$. Applying [F2] gives open neighborhoods and a unique $C^1$ local branch $w^*$ through that point. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 The derivative clause of [L1], evaluated along this branch after shrinking its parameter neighborhood, gives $Dw^*(\theta)=-H(\theta,w^*(\theta))^{-1}B(\theta,w^*(\theta))$. [step 1.1, F1, L1, algebra]

2.2 The map $\theta\mapsto (w^*(\theta),\theta)$ is $C^1$, so [F3] applied to $g$ and this map yields $\nabla_\theta J=\partial_\theta g+(Dw^*)^T\nabla_w g$. [step 1.1, F1, F3, algebra]

3.1 Substitute step 2.1 into step 2.2 and use $(H^{-1}B)^T=B^TH^{-T}$. This is the asserted column-gradient hypergradient formula. [step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 In the stated global regime, fix any $\theta\in P$ and any stationary point $u\in\mathbb R^d$, so $\nabla_w f(\theta,u)=0$. For every $v\ne u$, the strong-convexity inequality gives $f(\theta,v)\ge f(\theta,u)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|v-u\|_2^2>f(\theta,u)$. Thus this arbitrary stationary point is the unique global minimizer, proving the claim for every stationary point wherever the global regime holds. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n}$ be open, and let
$F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$.  Suppose $(a,b)\in U$, $F(a,b)=0$, and the
**partial derivative in the second block**

$$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The dimensions, $C^1$ map, base point, zero equation, and invertible second-block derivative in the statement.

[L1] A $C^1$ map with invertible derivative has a local $C^1$ inverse $G$, with $DG(z)=DH(G(z))^{-1}$ throughout its inverse neighbourhood ([[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]).

[L2] Total differentiability is a linear approximation with an $o(\lVert h\rVert_2)$ remainder, and total derivatives obey the algebra and chain rules ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[thm-algebra-of-total-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[L3] Euclidean linear maps have their finite matrix descriptions ([[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]), and invertibility means having a two-sided linear inverse ([[def-invertible-euclidean-linear-map]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** reduction.

1.1 Define $H:U\to\mathbb R^{m+n}$ by $H(x,y):=(x,F(x,y))$. From [L2], the remainder after the linear map $(u,v)\mapsto(u,DF(x,y)(u,v))$ is $(0,r(u,v))$, so $H$ is differentiable with $$DH(x,y)(u,v)=(u,D_xF(x,y)u+D_yF(x,y)v).$$ Its matrix entries are continuous because those of $DF$ are, so $H$ is $C^1$. If $B:=D_yF(a,b)^{-1}$, the displayed derivative at $(a,b)$ has the two-sided inverse $(r,s)\mapsto(r,B(s-D_xF(a,b)r))$. Thus $DH(a,b)$ is invertible. [L2, L3, given, algebra]

2.1 Apply [L1] to $H$.  It has a $C^1$ inverse $G$ between neighbourhoods of $(a,b)$ and $(a,0)$.  Because the first component of $H$ is $x$, the identity $H(G(x,z))=(x,z)$ forces $G(x,z)=(x,\psi(x,z))$.  Define $\varphi(x):=\psi(x,0)$ after shrinking to product neighbourhoods $P,Q$. [step 1.1, L1]

3.1 For $(x,y)\in P\times Q$, the local injectivity of $H$ gives $F(x,y)=0\iff H(x,y)=(x,0)\iff (x,y)=G(x,0) \iff y=\varphi(x)$. This proves existence and local uniqueness; $\varphi$ is $C^1$ as a component of $G$.  [step 2.1]

4.1 Differentiate $F(x,\varphi(x))=0$. By [L2], $D_xF(x,\varphi(x))+D_yF(x,\varphi(x))D\varphi(x)=0$. For $(x,\varphi(x))=G(x,0)$, the derivative formula in [L1] makes $DH(x,\varphi(x))$ invertible. The block formula of step 1.1 then makes $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ invertible: solving $DH(u,v)=(0,s)$ gives $u=0$ and $D_yFv=s$. Multiplication by its inverse yields the asserted formula. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, L1, L2, L3]

5.1 Steps 1.1--4.1 prove all local existence, uniqueness, regularity, and derivative claims.  [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

Assume $H(\theta_0,w_0)$ is invertible. Write $c(w):=\partial_\theta g(w,\theta_0)$ and $d(w):=\nabla_w g(w,\theta_0)$, and use the induced Euclidean operator norm for matrices. If the adjoint algorithm at $w_0$ returns a vector $\widetilde v$, define $\rho:=d(w_0)-H(\theta_0,w_0)^T\widetilde v$ and $\widehat h:=c(w_0)-B(\theta_0,w_0)^T\widetilde v$. Suppose the evaluated Hessian is symmetric and has a valid lower-bound certificate $x^TH(\theta_0,w_0)x\ge\mu\|x\|_2^2$ for every $x$, for some $\mu>0$. Then

$$\|\widehat h-\nabla_\theta J(\theta_0)\|_2\le\frac{\|B(\theta_0,w^*(\theta_0))\|\,\|\rho\|_2}{\mu}.$$

There is also a separate approximate-state bound under stronger hypotheses. Put $R(w,\theta):=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)$ and $A(w):=D_wR(w,\theta_0)=H(\theta_0,w)$. Suppose $R$ is $C^2$ on an open neighborhood of $(w_0,\theta_0)$. Let $\widetilde w$ lie in a $C^1$ local inverse chart: for $r:=R(\widetilde w,\theta_0)$, there is a local inverse $\Psi$ of $w\mapsto R(w,\theta_0)$ with $\Psi(0)=w_0$, defined on a convex open residual neighborhood containing $0$ and $r$, with $\widetilde w=\Psi(r)$ and $\|D\Psi(y)\|\le\kappa$ along the segment from $0$ to $r$. Suppose the segment from $w_0$ to $\widetilde w$ lies in a convex state neighborhood where $\|A(w)^{-1}\|\le M$, $\|B(\theta_0,w)\|\le B_0$, and $A(w),B(\theta_0,w)$ are Lipschitz with constants $L_A,L_B$. Suppose also that $c,d$ are Lipschitz there with constants $L_c,L_d$ and $\|d(w_0)\|_2\le D_*$. If the adjoint algorithm at $\widetilde w$ returns $\widetilde v$, set $\rho:=d(\widetilde w)-A(\widetilde w)^T\widetilde v$ and $\widehat h:=c(\widetilde w)-B(\theta_0,\widetilde w)^T\widetilde v$. Assume the certificate $A(\widetilde w)=A(\widetilde w)^T$ and $x^TA(\widetilde w)x\ge\mu\|x\|_2^2$ for all $x$, with the same $\mu>0$. Then

$$\|\widehat h-\nabla_\theta J(\theta_0)\|_2\le\kappa\bigl(L_c+D_*(M^2L_AB_0+ML_B)+MB_0L_d\bigr)\|r\|_2+\frac{B_0}{\mu}\|\rho\|_2.$$

The first term bounds the implicit formula evaluated at an approximate state; it does not identify that formula with the derivative of a stopped iteration. The second term bounds the separate linear-solve error.

## Statement

Let $R(z,\theta)$ be $C^2$ near an exact solution $R(z_*,\theta_0)=0$, with $A(z)=R_z(z,\theta_0)$ invertible and $B(z)=R_\theta(z,\theta_0)$. The implicit sensitivity at a state $z$ is $S(z)=-A(z)^{-1}B(z)$. Suppose the local inverse $\Psi$ of $z\mapsto R(z,\theta_0)$, supplied near $z_*$ by the implicit function theorem, is defined on a convex residual neighborhood containing $0$ and $r=R(\tilde z,\theta_0)$, with $\|D\Psi(y)\|\le\kappa$ along their segment. Suppose also that the segment from $z_*$ to $\tilde z=\Psi(r)$ lies in a convex neighborhood where $\|A(z)^{-1}\|\le M$, $\|B(z)\|\le B_0$, and $A,B$ are Lipschitz with constants $L_A,L_B$. Then
$$\|S(\tilde z)-S(z_*)\|\le\kappa\bigl(M^2L_AB_0+ML_B\bigr)\|r\|.$$
This bounds the implicit sensitivity formula evaluated at an approximate state. It is not by itself a bound for the derivative of a stopped iteration.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The exact root, local inverse chart, residual, inverse-norm and Lipschitz bounds in the statement.

[F1] [[thm-euclidean-implicit-function-theorem]]: if the state Jacobian of a $C^1$ residual is invertible at a zero, there is a local $C^1$ solution branch and its derivative formula; applying the theorem to $R(z,\theta_0)-r=0$ gives the local inverse $\Psi(r)$.

[F2] [[thm-mean-value-inequality-for-total-derivatives]]: on a convex open set, a uniform derivative bound $\|Df(z)v\|\le M\|v\|$ implies $\|f(y)-f(x)\|\le M\|y-x\|$.

[F3] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the derivative of a composition is the composition of the derivatives at the corresponding points.

[A1] The residual segment lies inside the inverse chart and the state segment lies inside the neighborhood where all stated bounds hold.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** first control state error by residual, then perturb the inverse-Jacobian formula.

For $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, apply [F2] to $\gamma$ on the convex open interval $(0,1)$ at $\varepsilon$ and $1-\varepsilon$ to obtain $\|\Psi((1-\varepsilon)r)-\Psi(\varepsilon r)\|\le\kappa(1-2\varepsilon)\|r\|$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and using continuity of $\Psi$ at $0$ and $r$ gives $\|\tilde z-z_*\|\le\kappa\|r\|$. [F1, F2, F3, A1, given]

1.2 Put $A=A(\tilde z)$, $A_*=A(z_*)$, $B=B(\tilde z)$, and $B_*=B(z_*)$. The identities $S(\tilde z)-S(z_*)=(A_*^{-1}-A^{-1})B+A_*^{-1}(B_*-B)$ and $A_*^{-1}-A^{-1}=A^{-1}(A-A_*)A_*^{-1}$ follow by expansion and multiplication. [given, algebra]

2.1 The inverse bounds, $B$ bound, and Lipschitz bounds give $\|A_*^{-1}-A^{-1}\|\le M^2L_A\|\tilde z-z_*\|$ and $\|B_*-B\|\le L_B\|\tilde z-z_*\|$. The triangle and product inequalities then yield $\|S(\tilde z)-S(z_*)\|\le(M^2L_AB_0+ML_B)\|\tilde z-z_*\|$. [A1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 Substitute step 1.1 into step 2.1 to obtain the asserted residual bound. If $r=0$, local uniqueness gives $\tilde z=z_*$ and the same inequality reads $0\le0$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Boundary

Let $p,m\ge0$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open with $\theta_0\in\Theta$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be an open convex neighborhood of $z_*$, and let $G:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^2$ on an open neighborhood $U$ of $D\times\{\theta_0\}$. Here $C^1$ means total differentiability with continuous derivative, $C^2$ means the derivative map is $C^1$, and vector and operator norms are Euclidean and induced Euclidean norms. Write $G_z:=D_zG$ and $G_\theta:=D_\theta G$ for the state and parameter derivatives. Suppose $z_*=G(z_*,\theta_0)$, $G(D,\theta_0)\subseteq D$, $0\le q<1$, $\|G_z(z,\theta_0)\|\le q$ on $D$, and $G_z,G_\theta$ are Lipschitz in $z$ with constants $L_z,L_\theta$. Let $z_0:\Theta\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$, with all finite iterates at $\theta_0$ lying in $D$, and define $z_{k+1}(\theta)=G(z_k(\theta),\theta)$. Let $\phi$ be the exact local fixed-point branch, $s_*:=D\phi(\theta_0)$, $e_K:=Dz_K(\theta_0)$, $\delta_0:=\|z_0(\theta_0)-z_*\|_2$, $d_0:=\|Dz_0(\theta_0)-s_*\|$, and $C:=L_z\|s_*\|+L_\theta$. For every integer $K\ge1$,

$$\|e_K-s_*\|\le q^K d_0+C K q^{K-1}\delta_0,$$

where $q^0=1$ when $q=0$ and $K=1$. For the fixed-point residual $r_K:=z_K(\theta_0)-G(z_K(\theta_0),\theta_0)$, the primal-state estimate is $(1-q)\|z_K(\theta_0)-z_*\|_2\le\|r_K\|_2$. This primal residual estimate alone does not imply that the derivative of the finite $K$-step graph equals the exact fixed-point sensitivity.

For a separate finite shared-parameter recurrence, let $p_0,q_0\ge1$, let $\Theta_0\subseteq\mathbb R^{p_0}$ and $H\subseteq\mathbb R^{q_0}$ be open, let $T\ge0$, let $h_0:\Theta_0\to H$ and $\Phi_t:\Theta_0\times H\to H$ for $1\le t\le T$ and $\ell:\Theta_0\times H\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ on open domains containing the trajectory at $\theta\in\Theta_0$, and suppose every piecewise primitive is evaluated in one unique strict open $C^1$ branch. Set $h_t=\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$ and $J_T(\theta)=\ell(\theta,h_T)$; derivative matrices use Euclidean coordinates and transposes are Euclidean. Backpropagation differentiates this finite scalar graph: with $A_t=D_\theta\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, $B_t=D_h\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, $\lambda_T=(D_h\ell(\theta,h_T))^T$, and $\lambda_{t-1}=B_t^T\lambda_t$, its derivative is

$$\nabla_\theta J_T(\theta)=(D_\theta\ell(\theta,h_T))^T+\sum_{t=1}^T A_t^T\lambda_t+(Dh_0(\theta))^T\lambda_0.$$

This is the derivative of the finite training computation. The exact implicit hypergradient is the derivative of a local stationary or fixed-point branch. In particular, a small training residual is not by itself an error bound for the derivative of a stopped iteration; contraction and sensitivity hypotheses such as those stated above are needed.

## Definition

Let $n,d,v$ be positive integers, let $Q,K\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ and $V\in\mathbb R^{n\times v}$, let $c\in\mathbb R$, and for each query row $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ let $A_i\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ be a nonempty set of allowed keys. Write $q_i$ for row $i$ of $Q$, $k_j$ for row $j$ of $K$, $v_j$ for row $j$ of $V$, and $s_{ij}=c\sum_{r=1}^{d}Q_{ir}K_{jr}$ for $j\in A_i$. For a nonempty finite set $S\subseteq A_i$, its attention summary is

$$
\Sigma_i(S)=(m_i(S),\ell_i(S),z_i(S)),\qquad m_i(S)=\max_{j\in S}s_{ij},\quad \ell_i(S)=\sum_{j\in S}e^{s_{ij}-m_i(S)},\quad z_i(S)=\sum_{j\in S}e^{s_{ij}-m_i(S)}v_j.
$$

The empty set has the separate state $\bot$ and has no maximum or numeric summary coordinates. For disjoint nonempty $S,T\subseteq A_i$, define their merge by

$$
m'=\max(m_i(S),m_i(T)),\qquad \ell'=e^{m_i(S)-m'}\ell_i(S)+e^{m_i(T)-m'}\ell_i(T),\qquad z'=e^{m_i(S)-m'}z_i(S)+e^{m_i(T)-m'}z_i(T).
$$

and set $\Sigma_i(S)\star\Sigma_i(T)=(m',\ell',z')$. This summary stores the maximum score, a positive shifted normalizer, and the correspondingly shifted weighted value sum; dividing its third coordinate by its second gives the attention output on $S$.

## Definition

**Inputs:** Positive integers $n,d,v$, finite real matrices $Q,K\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ and $V\in\mathbb R^{n\times v}$, a real scale $c$, a positive integer key-block size $b$, and fixed nonempty allowed-key sets $A_1,\ldots,A_n\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$. The algorithm reads membership in each $A_i$ on demand; any caller-owned representation of the mask is input storage. All operations below are in exact real arithmetic. Set $J_t=\{(t-1)b+1,\ldots,\min(tb,n)\}$ for $t=1,\ldots,\lceil n/b\rceil$.

**Forward procedure:**

1. For each query row $i$, set the current summary to $\bot$.
2. For $t=1,\ldots,\lceil n/b\rceil$, form $I=J_t\cap A_i$. If $I=\varnothing$, skip this block and leave the summary unchanged. Otherwise compute $\Sigma_i(I)$. If the current summary is $\bot$, copy $\Sigma_i(I)$; otherwise merge the current summary with $\Sigma_i(I)$ using $\star$.
3. After the final block, write $Y_i=z_i/\ell_i$ and retain the final $m_i$ and $\ell_i$ for a later reverse pass.
4. Return $Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times v}$ and the retained row statistics.

**Reverse procedure:** Given a forward run with the same $Q,K,V,c,A_1,\ldots,A_n$ and an upstream matrix $G\in\mathbb R^{n\times v}$, initialize $dQ,dK,dV$ to zero. For each query row $i$, compute $\delta_i=\sum_{a=1}^{v}G_{ia}Y_{ia}$. For every block $J_t$ and each $j\in J_t\cap A_i$, recompute $s_{ij}$ from $Q,K$ and set

$$
p_{ij}=\frac{e^{s_{ij}-m_i}}{\ell_i},\qquad \gamma_{ij}=p_{ij}\left(\sum_{a=1}^{v}G_{ia}V_{ja}-\delta_i\right).
$$

Then, for $r=1,\ldots,d$, add to the query and key gradient arrays, and for $a=1,\ldots,v$, add to the value gradient array:

$$
(dQ)_{ir}\mathrel{+}=c\gamma_{ij}K_{jr},\qquad (dK)_{jr}\mathrel{+}=c\gamma_{ij}Q_{ir},\qquad (dV)_{ja}\mathrel{+}=p_{ij}G_{ia}.
$$

Return $dQ,dK,dV$. Do not store a full score or probability matrix: the reverse procedure recomputes one block's scores from the same inputs and fixed allowed-key sets. The prescribed reverse procedure treats the forward maxima and normalizers as frozen scaling statistics; it does not differentiate a maximum operation. The base algorithm has no dropout. Any dropout extension must replay the same realized dropout mask in its reverse pass.

## Statement

Let $n,d,v$ be positive integers, $Q,K\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ and $V\in\mathbb R^{n\times v}$ be finite real matrices, $c\in\mathbb R$, $b$ a positive integer, and $A_i\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ a fixed nonempty set of allowed keys for every query row $i$. Write $Q_i$ for row $i$ of $Q$, and $K_j,V_j$ for row $j$ of $K,V$. Let $Y,m_i,\ell_i$ be the forward outputs and row statistics of the exact tiled softmax attention algorithm, and fix an upstream matrix $G\in\mathbb R^{n\times v}$. Then each row of $Y$ equals the dense masked attention row

$$
Y_i=\frac{\sum_{j\in A_i}e^{cQ_iK_j^{\mathsf T}}V_j}{\sum_{j\in A_i}e^{cQ_iK_j^{\mathsf T}}},
$$

and the algorithm's recomputed reverse procedure returns the Euclidean gradients of the scalar function $\Phi(Q,K,V)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{a=1}^{v}G_{ia}Y_{ia}$ with respect to $Q,K,V$, while holding $c$, the sets $A_i$, and $G$ fixed. Its reverse rule treats the stored maxima as fixed normalization shifts, so the conclusion also holds when scores tie at a row maximum. Every row is defined because $A_i$ is nonempty; no convention for an all-masked row is asserted.

## Statement references

[Dao et al., §3.1 and Appendix C: exactness of the online tiled attention recurrence](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.14135)

[Dao et al., Appendix B.2–B.4: reverse-mode derivatives and block recomputation](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.14135)

[Milakov and Gimelshein, §3: online normalizer recurrence and its induction proof](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.02867)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite real inputs, the fixed nonempty allowed-key sets, the positive block size, the forward and reverse procedures, and the upstream matrix $G$.

[F1] [[def-scaled-dot-product-attention]]: masked attention uses row softmax of the scaled query-key scores and is defined only when each row has an allowed key.

[F2] [[def-attention-block-summary]]: for nonempty $S$, the summary coordinates are $\max_{j\in S}s_{ij}$, $\sum_{j\in S}e^{s_{ij}-m_i(S)}$, and $\sum_{j\in S}e^{s_{ij}-m_i(S)}V_j$; the empty set is the separate symbol $\bot$.

[F3] [[alg-exact-tiled-softmax-attention]]: the forward pass skips empty allowed blocks, copies the first nonempty block summary, merges later summaries, and the reverse pass recomputes $p_{ij}$ and accumulates the stated $dQ,dK,dV$ entries.

[F4] [[def-finite-straight-line-computational-program]]: a finite topologically ordered real-arithmetic graph has differentiable primitive maps on open domains and repeated input uses are separate parent slots.

[F5] [[thm-reverse-mode-computes-gradient]]: for a finite $C^1$ program with one scalar output on a fixed strict branch, reverse mode returns the exact derivative of that output.

[F6] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: for totally differentiable finite-dimensional maps, the derivative of a composition is the ordered composition of the derivatives.

[F7] [[alg-backpropagation-through-shared-parameter-recurrence]]: the same parameter vector is supplied to every transition.

[F8] [[thm-shared-parameter-backpropagation-gradient-formula]]: the gradient formula includes a pullback term for each transition using the shared parameter.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** identify the exact summary invariant, then differentiate the equivalent dense masked attention map and group repeated input contributions.

1.1 Fix a query row $i$ and let $S$ be the union of the allowed keys in the blocks processed so far. Initially $S=\varnothing$ and the algorithm's state is $\bot$. An empty allowed block leaves both $S$ and the state unchanged. If $S=\varnothing$ and the next allowed block $I$ is nonempty, copying $\Sigma_i(I)$ gives the defining summary of $S\cup I$. If $S$ and $I$ are both nonempty, the merged maximum is $\max(m_i(S),m_i(I))=m_i(S\cup I)$, and $e^{m_i(S)-m_i(S\cup I)}\ell_i(S)=\sum_{j\in S}e^{s_{ij}-m_i(S\cup I)}$ while $e^{m_i(I)-m_i(S\cup I)}\ell_i(I)=\sum_{j\in I}e^{s_{ij}-m_i(S\cup I)}$. The same two identities with $V_j$ inside each sum give the merged $z$ coordinate. Disjoint blocks therefore preserve the summary invariant. [F2, F3, given, construct]

2.1 The key blocks partition $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, so after the last block $S=A_i\ne\varnothing$. The maximum $m_i$ is finite and at least one term in $\ell_i=\sum_{j\in A_i}e^{s_{ij}-m_i}$ equals $1$, hence $\ell_i>0$. Dividing $z_i$ by $\ell_i$ and multiplying numerator and denominator by $e^{m_i}$ gives the displayed dense masked attention row. This also proves every retained $m_i,\ell_i$ is defined. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 With the allowed sets fixed, every score is a polynomial in the entries of $Q,K$; finite exponentials, sums, and division by the strictly positive dense denominator make the dense row map smooth on all of $\mathbb R^{n(2d+v)}$. Its scalarization $\Phi$ is therefore a finite $C^1$ real-arithmetic graph. The reverse-mode theorem and chain rule apply to this dense graph; the maximum used only to scale the tiled forward computation is not a primitive of this graph. [F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, given]

4.1 For $j,k\in A_i$, write $p_{ij}=e^{s_{ij}}/\sum_{\ell\in A_i}e^{s_{i\ell}}$, as justified by step 2.1. Direct quotient differentiation gives $\frac{\partial p_{ik}}{\partial s_{ij}}=p_{ik}\bigl(\mathbf 1_{\{k=j\}}-p_{ij}\bigr)$. Thus for $\Phi_i=\sum_aG_{ia}Y_{ia}$ the score derivative is $\frac{\partial\Phi_i}{\partial s_{ij}}=\sum_{k\in A_i}(\sum_aG_{ia}V_{ka})\frac{\partial p_{ik}}{\partial s_{ij}}=p_{ij}(\sum_aG_{ia}V_{ja}-\sum_aG_{ia}Y_{ia})=\gamma_{ij}$. The direct value derivative is $\nabla_{V_j}\Phi_i=p_{ij}G_i$. [F5, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Since $s_{ij}=c\sum_rQ_{ir}K_{jr}$, its coordinate derivatives are $\partial s_{ij}/\partial Q_{ir}=cK_{jr}$ and $\partial s_{ij}/\partial K_{jr}=cQ_{ir}$. The chain rule therefore gives the row-$i$ contributions $c\sum_{j\in A_i}\gamma_{ij}K_j$ to $Q_i$, $c\gamma_{ij}Q_i$ to $K_j$, and $p_{ij}G_i$ to $V_j$. Entries of other query rows receive no contribution from this row. [F6, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Set $\Theta=\mathbb R^{2nd+nv}$, $H=\mathbb R$, $h_0(\theta)=0$, $F_i(\theta,h)=h+\sum_aG_{ia}Y_{ia}(\theta)$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$, and terminal loss $\lambda(\theta,h)=h$. Step 3.1 makes every $F_i$ continuously differentiable on the open domain $\Theta\times H$. By induction on $i$, the recurrence state after $i$ transitions is $h_i=\sum_{r=1}^{i}\sum_aG_{ra}Y_{ra}(\theta)$: the formula holds at $i=0$ because $h_0=0$, and adding the $i$th transition term proves it at $i$ from its value at $i-1$. Thus its scalar output is $h_n=\Phi(\theta)$. The same parameter $\theta=(Q,K,V)$ is supplied at every transition, and the shared-parameter gradient formula sums each transition's parameter pullback. It therefore adds each row's pullback at the common $K,V$ inputs, while the row-specific $Q_i$ pullbacks occupy their corresponding rows. There is no direct loss or initial-state parameter term because $\lambda$ is $h$ and $h_0$ is constant. Thus the algorithm's reverse updates give $\nabla_Q\Phi,\nabla_K\Phi,\nabla_V\Phi$. [F7, F8, step 3.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 At the forward values, the summary invariant in steps 1.1–2.1 gives $\ell_i=\sum_{j\in A_i}e^{s_{ij}-m_i}$. Therefore, for each $j\in A_i$,

$$
p_{ij}=\frac{e^{s_{ij}-m_i}}{\ell_i}=\frac{e^{s_{ij}}}{\sum_{\ell\in A_i}e^{s_{i\ell}}}.
$$

This is the dense softmax probability evaluated at the current scores. Steps 4.1–6.1 differentiate the smooth dense attention map and show that substituting these probabilities into the reverse updates gives its exact gradient at these inputs. The stored $m_i$ and $\ell_i$ are used as normalization shifts in those updates; no derivative of either statistic is needed. The argument applies whether or not the maximum score is tied. [F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

In the unit-cost real-arithmetic model where scalar arithmetic, exponential evaluation, comparisons, and one allowed-key membership query each cost $O(1)$, the forward and reverse procedures of the exact tiled softmax attention algorithm use $O(n^2(d+v))$ arithmetic operations. The forward procedure retains the $Q,K,V$ inputs, the $n\times v$ output, and two scalar statistics per query, requiring $O(n(d+v))$ stored input and output scalars, with at most $O(b+v)$ additional live scalars for one block's scores and weighted-value summary. The reverse procedure additionally takes $G$ and returns $dQ,dK,dV$; counting these as input and output arrays, it also uses $O(n(d+v))$ stored input and output scalars and at most $O(b+v)$ additional live scalars. Neither procedure materializes an $n\times n$ score or probability array. Storage for a caller-owned mask representation is input storage and is not part of the additional workspace; if it is a dense array, its own $O(n^2)$ entries must be counted separately. The exactness of the forward and reverse outputs is the assertion of the tiled-attention exactness theorem. No hardware I/O or floating-point operation count is asserted.

## Statement references

[Dao et al., §3.1 and Appendix C: forward arithmetic and extra-memory count](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.14135)

[Dao et al., Appendix B.2–B.4: recomputed reverse pass and its linear extra-memory claim](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.14135)

[[thm-tiled-attention-exactness|Exact forward output and reverse-mode derivatives]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The positive integers $n,d,v,b$, fixed allowed-key sets, and the two procedures of the exact tiled softmax attention algorithm.

[F1] [[alg-exact-tiled-softmax-attention]]: the forward procedure processes one query row and one key block at a time, while the reverse procedure recomputes each permitted score and accumulates gradients into output arrays.

[F2] [[def-attention-block-summary]]: a nonempty block summary stores one scalar maximum, one scalar normalizer, and one vector in $\mathbb R^v$; an empty block stores no numeric state.

[F3] [[thm-tiled-attention-exactness]]: the two procedures return the dense masked attention and its exact vector-Jacobian product.

[F4] [[alg-exact-tiled-softmax-attention]]: the reverse procedure recomputes each block's scores and does not store a full score or probability matrix.

[A1] The mask membership accessor is read-only, has $O(1)$ query cost, and any storage for its representation is caller-owned input storage rather than algorithmic scratch.

[A2] The operation count is scalar arithmetic, exponential evaluation, comparisons, and mask membership queries; all are unit cost in this model.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** count the live arrays, block workspace, and operations in the explicit loops.

1.1 The forward procedure retains $Q,K,V,Y$ and $(m_i,\ell_i)_{i=1}^n$. Their scalar counts are $nd+nd+nv+nv+2n=O(n(d+v))$ because $d,v\ge1$. At any query and key block it stores at most $b$ scores and the current and block weighted-value vectors of length $v$, plus a constant number of scalars. This is $O(b+v)$ extra live storage, and it discards the block workspace before moving to the next block. [F1, F2, A1, given, algebra]

1.2 The forward loops examine at most $n^2$ query-key pairs. For each pair, the score dot product uses $O(d)$ operations; its normalized exponential and weighted-value contribution use $O(1+v)$ operations. Block maxima, merges, and loop overhead add at most $O(n^2)$ operations since $b\ge1$. Thus forward arithmetic is $O(n^2(d+v))$. Only one block's scores and weighted-value summaries are live, so no $n\times n$ score or probability array is allocated. [F1, F2, A2, given, algebra]

1.3 The reverse procedure's retained arrays are $Q,K,V,Y,G,dQ,dK,dV$ and the $2n$ row statistics. Their scalar counts are all $O(n(d+v))$. For one row and one key it recomputes one score and one probability, forms scalar inner products, and updates entries in the already allocated gradient arrays; it needs only a constant number of additional scalars, which is within $O(b+v)$. It does not store the recomputed probabilities across pairs. [F4, A1, given, algebra]

2.1 Each query-key pair in the reverse pass costs $O(d+v)$ operations: one score, one inner product with $V_j$, and vector updates with lengths $d$ and $v$. There are at most $n^2$ pairs, and the finite loop overhead is at most $O(n^2)$, so reverse arithmetic is $O(n^2(d+v))$. Since scores and probabilities are recomputed one at a time, this pass also creates no $n\times n$ array. The separate exactness claim is supplied by [F3]. [F3, F4, A2, given, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The workspace theorem counts scalar storage and operations for the explicitly defined real-arithmetic procedure. It does not count reads and writes between GPU high-bandwidth memory and on-chip SRAM, and it gives no hardware speedup claim. The FlashAttention paper's $\Theta(n^2d^2/M)$ HBM-access result assumes its stated memory model, block schedule, and range $d\le M\le nd$; its endpoint input-size argument is not a lower bound for every fixed memory size. Neither claim follows from the scalar workspace theorem here.

The maximum shift makes every exact-real exponent argument $s_{ij}-m_i$ nonpositive, but this does not specify rounded arithmetic or rule out underflow of very small finite-precision terms. Different floating-point accumulation orders can return different bit patterns. The base procedure includes no dropout; if an extension uses dropout, its fixed realized mask must be reused in the reverse pass because a different mask changes the differentiated function.

## Definition

Let $d,k$ be positive integers, let $1\le r\le\min(d,k)$, let $c\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and fix a matrix $W_0\in\mathbb R^{d\times k}$. A rank-$r$ adapter for the linear layer $x\mapsto W_0x$ consists of trainable factor matrices $B\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}$ and $A\in\mathbb R^{r\times k}$ and the updated weight matrix

$$W=W_0+cBA.$$

Its output on $x\in\mathbb R^k$ is $Wx=W_0x+cB(Ax)\in\mathbb R^d$. The base matrix $W_0$ is frozen, meaning that an adaptation procedure does not update its entries; only entries of $A$ and $B$ are trainable in this definition. The update matrix is $W-W_0=cBA$, whose rank is the dimension of its image as a linear map from $\mathbb R^k$ to $\mathbb R^d$. No bias, dropout, random initialization, optimization rule, or convergence guarantee is part of this definition.

## Definition

Fix positive integers $d,k,n$, an integer $1\le r\le\min(d,k)$, a frozen matrix $W_0\in\mathbb R^{d\times k}$, a nonzero scale $c\in\mathbb R$, a finite ordered data list $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ with $x_i\in\mathbb R^k$, and, for each data entry, a loss program $\ell_i$ that returns a real scalar wherever its primitive calls are defined. Let $T\ge0$ be a finite integer, let $I_0,\ldots,I_{T-1}$ be fixed finite nonempty ordered lists of indices in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ (repeated indices are allowed), let $\eta_0,\ldots,\eta_{T-1}\ge0$ be finite step sizes, and supply an initial matrix $A_0\in\mathbb R^{r\times k}$. The procedure has no dropout or random initialization; any random initialization must be sampled externally and supplied as $A_0$. Set $B_0=0\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}$.

Represent each loss evaluation by a specified finite real-arithmetic program with a scalar output. Each primitive is continuously differentiable on a declared open domain or is piecewise continuously differentiable, with finitely many open branch regions, a continuously differentiable formula on each region, and a separately specified primal boundary value when one is defined. Here $C^1$ means totally differentiable with continuous derivative. Check admissibility at the current factors on each step; a strict branch used at one step need not be the branch used at another.

$$L_t(A,B)=\frac{1}{|I_t|}\sum_{i\in I_t}\ell_i\!\left((W_0+cBA)x_i\right)$$

Starting with $t=0$, perform the following finite loop while $t<T$:

1. Evaluate the displayed program at $(A_t,B_t)$, visiting its primitive calls in evaluation order. At the first call with no primal value, return `DOMAIN_ERROR` with the current factors and step index $t$. At the first defined piecewise primitive whose input lies on a branch boundary or has ambiguous branch selection, return `NONDIFFERENTIABLE` with the current factors and step index $t$. If every primitive call has a value and every piecewise primitive is on a unique strict branch, run reverse-mode automatic differentiation on this same scalar-output program at $(A_t,B_t)$, with the selected branch choices, with respect to the ordered list of all entries of $A_t$ followed by all entries of $B_t$, each matrix flattened row by row. If reverse mode returns either failure status, return it with the current factors and step index $t$. No factor update is made on a failure status.
2. If reverse mode returns gradients, reshape the first and second blocks into $G^A_t\in\mathbb R^{r\times k}$ and $G^B_t\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}$, respectively, and set

$$A_{t+1}=A_t-\eta_tG^A_t,\qquad B_{t+1}=B_t-\eta_tG^B_t.$$

   Increment $t$ by one.

After $T$ successful updates, return `SUCCESS`, the matrices $A_T,B_T$, and the merged weight $W_0+cB_TA_T$. At $T=0$ return the supplied $A_0$, zero $B_0$, and $W_0$ without evaluating a loss. This is a finite real-arithmetic procedure; it asserts no convergence, minimization, generalization, floating-point accuracy, speed, or memory guarantee.

id: thm-low-rank-adapter-factorization-ambiguity
kind: theorem
title: "Rank capacity and factorization ambiguity of a low-rank adapter"
status: draft
